shelves.title: Pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy (antiquitin deficiency)
shelves.question: Why do some infants' seizures stop only with vitamin B6 — and what does treatment change?
shelves.balance: A blocked step in lysine breakdown floods the body with a compound that chemically switches off active vitamin B6, so the brain starves for B6 while the diet is normal. Large-dose pyridoxine overrides the block and stops seizures no standard drug touches — but it does not undo the metabolites' other damage: most patients still have intellectual disability, which is why treatment now adds lysine restriction and starts before birth when the risk is known.

cards.headline: The cause, found in 2006: a broken lysine enzyme, and a metabolite that switches off vitamin B6.
cards.summary: Mutations in ALDH7A1, which encodes antiquitin, abolished the enzyme's activity as an α-aminoadipic semialdehyde / piperideine-6-carboxylate dehydrogenase; the accumulating P6C inactivates pyridoxal 5′-phosphate by forming a Knoevenagel condensation product. Measurement of urinary α-AASA confirms the diagnosis, and gene analysis provides a means of prenatal diagnosis.
cards.people: Children with pyridoxine-dependent seizures.
cards.result: Mutations in ALDH7A1, which encodes antiquitin, abolished the enzyme's activity as an α-aminoadipic semialdehyde / piperideine-6-carboxylate dehydrogenase; the accumulating P6C inactivates pyridoxal 5′-phosphate by forming a Knoevenagel condensation product. Measurement of urinary α-AASA confirms the diagnosis, and gene analysis provides a means of prenatal diagnosis.
cards.watchOut: A discovery paper: it establishes cause and a diagnostic test, not treatment outcomes. A rare disease — the numbers are families, not cohorts.

cards.headline: 243 children tested: the real disease is wider — and easier to miss — than the classic picture.
cards.summary: 222 of the 243 had neither ALDH7A1 mutations nor a reported response to pyridoxine. Confirmed antiquitin deficiency ranged from ventriculomegaly on fetal ultrasound and a multisystem neonatal disorder to seizure onset after the first year of life with autistic features. Three diagnostic traps: some response to standard antiepileptic drugs; a pyridoxine response that is not instant or obvious in multisystem infants; and structural brain abnormalities that coexist and look like a sufficient explanation for the epilepsy.
cards.type: Diagnostic case series with clinician questionnaires.
cards.people: 243 patients with seizure disorders investigated for PDE (269 urine samples); ALDH7A1 sequencing in 21 patients with elevated urinary α-AASA and 16 with a clinical PDE diagnosis.
cards.result: 222 of the 243 had neither ALDH7A1 mutations nor a reported response to pyridoxine. Confirmed antiquitin deficiency ranged from ventriculomegaly on fetal ultrasound and a multisystem neonatal disorder to seizure onset after the first year of life with autistic features. Three diagnostic traps: some response to standard antiepileptic drugs; a pyridoxine response that is not instant or obvious in multisystem infants; and structural brain abnormalities that coexist and look like a sufficient explanation for the epilepsy.
cards.watchOut: A referral series — the 222-of-243 split describes who gets sent for testing, not how common the disease is.

cards.headline: Stop the seizures with B6, treat for life — and expect development to lag anyway.
cards.summary: To interrupt seizures: 100 mg pyridoxine-HCl intravenously, or oral/enteral pyridoxine at 30 mg/kg/day . Long-term: 15–30 mg/kg/day in infants, up to 200 mg/day in neonates and 500 mg/day in adults; pyridoxal phosphate up to 30 mg/kg/day is the alternative form. Despite seizure control, most patients have intellectual disability. Folinic-acid-responsive seizures are genetically the same disease. Prenatal maternal pyridoxine supplementation possibly improves outcome; a lysine-restricted diet may reduce the accumulating metabolites, with long-term benefit not yet documented.
cards.people: Patients with antiquitin deficiency, the main cause of pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy.
cards.result: To interrupt seizures: 100 mg pyridoxine-HCl intravenously, or oral/enteral pyridoxine at 30 mg/kg/day . Long-term: 15–30 mg/kg/day in infants, up to 200 mg/day in neonates and 500 mg/day in adults; pyridoxal phosphate up to 30 mg/kg/day is the alternative form. Despite seizure control, most patients have intellectual disability. Folinic-acid-responsive seizures are genetically the same disease. Prenatal maternal pyridoxine supplementation possibly improves outcome; a lysine-restricted diet may reduce the accumulating metabolites, with long-term benefit not yet documented.
cards.watchOut: The first intravenous dose can cause respiratory arrest in responders — give it with respiratory support ready. Keep oral pyridoxine going until biochemical or genetic testing excludes the diagnosis, so a late or masked response is not missed. The differential includes PNPO deficiency, which responds to pyridoxal phosphate rather than pyridoxine.
cards.source: Stockler S et al. Mol Genet Metab. 2011;104(1–2):48–60. PMID 21704546.

shelves.title: After a stroke: preventing the second one
shelves.question: Once a first stroke or TIA has happened, which treatments actually prevent the second one — and what does each cost in bleeding?
shelves.mesh: Stroke · Secondary Prevention · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors · Aspirin · Clopidogrel · Hemorrhage · Double-Blind Method · Humans
shelves.balance: Six trials define life after a first stroke: an antiplatelet (clopidogrel at least matches aspirin — CAPRIE), a short burst of two antiplatelets when the event is minor and the clock is early (CHANCE and POINT — benefit front-loaded, bleeding the price of duration), a high-intensity statin even without coronary disease (SPARCL, with its small hemorrhagic excess shown), an LDL driven under 70 rather than merely treated (Treat Stroke to Target, HR 0.78), and blood-pressure lowering that prevents recurrence in normotensives too (PROGRESS). (Panel position: AHA/ASA stroke prevention guideline — attributed, for developer verification.)

cards.headline: Clopidogrel vs aspirin in 19,185 patients: a real win, and an honestly modest one.
cards.summary: CAPRIE 1996 — annual rate of ischemic stroke, myocardial infarction, or vascular death 5.32% vs 5.83% (relative-risk reduction 8.7% , P=0.043) — 19,185 patients with recent ischemic stroke, recent MI, or symptomatic peripheral arterial disease; clopidogrel 75 mg vs aspirin 325 mg; mean follow-up 1.91 years.
cards.people: 19,185 patients, more than 6,300 in each of the clinical subgroups, recruited over 3 years; clopidogrel 75 mg once daily vs aspirin 325 mg once daily; followed for 1 to 3 years, mean follow-up 1.91 years
cards.result: There were 1,960 first events in the outcome cluster. On intention-to-treat analysis, patients treated with clopidogrel had an annual 5.32% risk of ischemic stroke, myocardial infarction, or vascular death compared with 5.83% with aspirin — a statistically significant (P=0.043) relative-risk reduction of 8.7% (95% CI 0.3–16.5). The corresponding on-treatment analysis yielded a relative-risk reduction of 9.4%
cards.watchOut: The margin is modest and only just significant — and in the stroke subgroup on its own the difference was smaller and not significant; the trial was not powered for its subgroups. On safety there were no major differences: severe gastrointestinal haemorrhage 0.52% vs 0.72% and intracranial haemorrhage 0.33% vs 0.47% both favoured clopidogrel
cards.source: CAPRIE Steering Committee. A randomised, blinded, trial of clopidogrel versus aspirin in patients at risk of ischaemic events (CAPRIE). Lancet. 1996;348(9038):1329–1339. DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(96)09457-3. PMID 8918275.

cards.headline: Two antiplatelets from day one after a minor stroke: stroke 8.2% vs 11.7% — and no extra severe bleeding.
cards.summary: CHANCE 2013 — stroke at 90 days 8.2% vs 11.7% (HR 0.68 ); moderate or severe hemorrhage 0.3% in both arms — 5,170 patients in China with minor ischemic stroke or high-risk TIA, treated within 24 hours; aspirin ran with clopidogrel for the first 21 days only.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, N Engl J Med 2013
cards.people: 5,170 patients at 114 centers in China, randomised within 24 hours after the onset of minor ischemic stroke or high-risk TIA; clopidogrel at an initial dose of 300 mg, followed by 75 mg per day for 90 days, plus aspirin 75 mg per day for the first 21 days — vs placebo plus aspirin 75 mg per day for 90 days
cards.result: Stroke (ischemic or hemorrhagic) occurred in 8.2% of patients in the clopidogrel–aspirin group, as compared with 11.7% of those in the aspirin group — HR 0.68 (0.57–0.81) , P<0.001. The combined outcome of stroke, myocardial infarction, or death from cardiovascular causes occurred in 8.4% vs 11.9%
cards.watchOut: The bleeding ledger was flat: moderate or severe hemorrhage occurred in 7 patients (0.3%) in the clopidogrel–aspirin group and 8 (0.3%) in the aspirin group, and the rate of hemorrhagic stroke was 0.3% in each group. But the dual therapy was deliberately short — aspirin stopped at 21 days — and the population was Chinese, with an early recurrence rate higher than many Western cohorts; the international test is the next card
cards.source: Wang Y, Wang Y, Zhao X, et al; CHANCE Investigators. Clopidogrel with aspirin in acute minor stroke or transient ischemic attack. N Engl J Med. 2013;369(1):11–19. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1215340. PMID 23803136 · NCT00979589.

cards.headline: POINT asked CHANCE’s question for a full 90 days, worldwide: fewer ischemic events — and the bleeding bill arrived.
cards.summary: POINT 2018 — major ischemic events 5.0% vs 6.5% (HR 0.75 ); major hemorrhage 0.9% vs 0.4% (HR 2.32 ) — 4,881 patients with minor ischemic stroke or high-risk TIA at 269 sites in 10 countries.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, N Engl J Med 2018
cards.people: 4,881 patients at 269 sites in 10 countries with minor ischemic stroke or high-risk TIA; clopidogrel (600 mg loading dose, then 75 mg daily) plus aspirin (2,432 patients) vs aspirin plus placebo (2,449), for 90 days. The trial was halted after 84% of the anticipated enrolment, when the combination had shown both lower ischemic risk and higher bleeding
cards.result: Major ischemic events (ischemic stroke, myocardial infarction, or death from ischemic vascular causes) occurred in 121 of 2,432 patients (5.0%) receiving clopidogrel plus aspirin and 160 of 2,449 (6.5%) receiving aspirin plus placebo — HR 0.75 (0.59–0.95) , P=0.02 — with most events occurring during the first week after the initial event
cards.watchOut: Major hemorrhage occurred in 23 patients (0.9%) receiving clopidogrel plus aspirin and 10 (0.4%) receiving aspirin plus placebo — HR 2.32 (1.10–4.87) , P=0.02. Read against CHANCE, the lesson is duration: the ischemic benefit is front-loaded into the first days, while the bleeding accumulates for as long as both drugs run
cards.source: Johnston SC, Easton JD, Farrant M, et al; POINT Investigators. Clopidogrel and aspirin in acute ischemic stroke and high-risk TIA. N Engl J Med. 2018;379(3):215–225. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1800410. PMID 29766750 · NCT00991029.

cards.headline: Atorvastatin 80 mg after a stroke — no coronary disease required: stroke 11.2% vs 13.1%.
cards.summary: SPARCL 2006 — fatal or nonfatal stroke 11.2% vs 13.1% (adjusted HR 0.84 ); hemorrhagic stroke 2.3% vs 1.4% — 4,731 patients 1–6 months after stroke or TIA, LDL cholesterol 100–190 mg/dL, no known coronary heart disease; median follow-up 4.9 years.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, N Engl J Med 2006
cards.people: 4,731 patients who had had a stroke or TIA within the previous 1 to 6 months, with LDL cholesterol 100–190 mg/dL and no known coronary heart disease; atorvastatin 80 mg daily (2,365) vs placebo (2,366); median follow-up 4.9 years
cards.result: A fatal or nonfatal stroke occurred in 265 patients (11.2%) receiving atorvastatin vs 311 (13.1%) receiving placebo — a 5-year absolute reduction of 2.2 percentage points, adjusted HR 0.84 (0.71–0.99) , P=0.03. The average LDL cholesterol level during the trial was 73 mg/dL with atorvastatin vs 129 mg/dL with placebo, and major cardiovascular events fell by 20%
cards.watchOut: The harm is on the card: hemorrhagic stroke occurred in 55 patients (2.3%) in the atorvastatin group vs 33 (1.4%) in the placebo group (HR 1.68) — a small absolute excess set against the larger ischemic gain, in a population enrolled for ischemic events. There was no difference in deaths from all causes
cards.source: The Stroke Prevention by Aggressive Reduction in Cholesterol Levels (SPARCL) Investigators. High-dose atorvastatin after stroke or transient ischemic attack. N Engl J Med. 2006;355(6):549–559. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa061894. PMID 16899775 · NCT00147602.

cards.headline: Lowering blood pressure after a stroke cut recurrence 28% — in hypertensive and non-hypertensive patients alike.
cards.summary: PROGRESS 2001 — recurrent stroke 10% vs 14% (relative risk reduction 28% ); perindopril plus indapamide −43% — 6,105 patients with previous stroke or TIA; mean follow-up 3.9 years.
cards.people: 6,105 individuals from 172 centres in Asia, Australasia, and Europe with a history of stroke or transient ischaemic attack; active treatment (3,051) comprised a flexible regimen based on perindopril 4 mg daily, with the diuretic indapamide added at the discretion of treating physicians, vs placebo (3,054); mean follow-up 3.9 years
cards.result: Over follow-up, active treatment reduced blood pressure by 9/4 mm Hg. 307 (10%) individuals assigned active treatment suffered a stroke, compared with 420 (14%) assigned placebo — relative risk reduction 28% (17–38) , P<0.0001. Active treatment also reduced the risk of total major vascular events by 26%, with similar reductions in the risk of stroke in hypertensive and non-hypertensive subgroups
cards.watchOut: The benefit lived in the combination: perindopril plus indapamide reduced blood pressure by 12/5 mm Hg and stroke risk by 43% (30–54) , while single-drug therapy reduced blood pressure by 5/3 mm Hg and produced no discernible reduction in the risk of stroke. There was no mortality difference — the card claims recurrence, not survival
cards.source: PROGRESS Collaborative Group. Randomised trial of a perindopril-based blood-pressure-lowering regimen among 6,105 individuals with previous stroke or transient ischaemic attack. Lancet. 2001;358(9287):1033–1041. DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(01)06178-5. PMID 11589932.

cards.headline: SPARCL said treat; Treat Stroke to Target said how low: an LDL under 70 beat 90–110.
cards.summary: Treat Stroke to Target 2020 — major cardiovascular events 8.5% vs 10.9% (adjusted HR 0.78 ) — 2,860 patients in France and South Korea after ischemic stroke or TIA with atherosclerotic disease; achieved LDL 65 vs 96 mg/dL; median follow-up 3.5 years; stopped early for insufficient funding.
cards.type: Parallel-group randomised trial, N Engl J Med 2020
cards.people: 2,860 patients in France and South Korea with ischemic stroke in the previous 3 months or a TIA within the previous 15 days, all with evidence of cerebrovascular or coronary-artery atherosclerosis; 1,430 assigned to each LDL cholesterol target group; all patients received a statin, ezetimibe, or both; median follow-up 3.5 years
cards.result: The mean LDL cholesterol level at baseline was 135 mg/dL, and the mean achieved level was 65 mg/dL in the lower-target group and 96 mg/dL in the higher-target group. The composite primary end point (ischemic stroke, myocardial infarction, new symptoms leading to urgent coronary or carotid revascularization, or death from cardiovascular causes) occurred in 121 patients (8.5%) in the lower-target group and 156 (10.9%) in the higher-target group — adjusted HR 0.78 (0.61–0.98) , P=0.04
cards.watchOut: The trial was stopped for administrative reasons — insufficient funding — after 277 of an anticipated 385 end-point events had occurred, so the estimate rests on fewer events than planned. On the reassuring side, the incidence of intracranial hemorrhage and newly diagnosed diabetes did not differ significantly between the two groups
cards.source: Amarenco P, Kim JS, Labreuche J, et al. A comparison of two LDL cholesterol targets after ischemic stroke. N Engl J Med. 2020;382(1):9–19. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1910355. PMID 31738483 · NCT01252875.

shelves.title: Thrombectomy for large-core stroke: the 2022–23 trials
shelves.question: In acute ischemic stroke with a large infarct core — patients thrombectomy used to exclude — does taking the clot out beat medical care alone?
shelves.mesh: Brain Ischemia · Cerebral Hemorrhage · Cerebral Infarction · Endovascular Procedures · Fibrinolytic Agents · Humans · Infarction, Middle Cerebral Artery · Intracranial Hemorrhages · Ischemic Stroke · Recovery of Function · Stroke · Thrombectomy · Tissue Plasminogen Activator · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: For a decade, thrombectomy was for small cores. Three trials in 2022–23, all stopped early, say large-core patients also fare better with it — about two to three times the chance of independence or moderate function — paid for with more bleeding inside the head on imaging. No trial showed a mortality difference, and even in the best trial only 1 in 5 reached independence.

cards.headline: SELECT2 2023: thrombectomy for large-core stroke — functional independence 20% vs 7%, stopped early for efficacy.
cards.summary: Generalized odds ratio 1.51 (95% CI 1.20–1.89) for a shift toward better modified Rankin scores with thrombectomy. Functional independence 20% vs 7% (relative risk 2.97, 1.60–5.51 ). Mortality was similar in the two groups.
cards.type: Randomized trial, international (stopped early for efficacy)
cards.people: 352 patients with large ischemic strokes (178 thrombectomy, 174 medical care)
cards.result: Generalized odds ratio 1.51 (95% CI 1.20–1.89) for a shift toward better modified Rankin scores with thrombectomy. Functional independence 20% vs 7% (relative risk 2.97, 1.60–5.51 ). Mortality was similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: The price is procedural — arterial dissection in 10 patients, cerebral-vessel perforation in 7 — though symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage was 1 patient in the thrombectomy group vs 2 on medical care.
cards.source: Sarraj A et al., N Engl J Med 2023 (PMID 36762865 · NCT03876457)

cards.headline: ANGEL-ASPECT 2023: the same answer in China — better Rankin distribution, more bleeding on scans.
cards.summary: Generalized odds ratio 1.37 (95% CI 1.11–1.69; P=0.004) for a shift toward better 90-day modified Rankin scores with endovascular therapy. The trial was stopped early after the second interim analysis.
cards.type: Randomized trial, China (stopped early for efficacy)
cards.people: 456 patients with large cerebral infarction (231 endovascular therapy, 225 medical management); about 28% in both groups also received intravenous thrombolysis
cards.result: Generalized odds ratio 1.37 (95% CI 1.11–1.69; P=0.004) for a shift toward better 90-day modified Rankin scores with endovascular therapy. The trial was stopped early after the second interim analysis.
cards.watchOut: Any intracranial hemorrhage occurred in 49.1% of the endovascular group vs 17.3% on medical care, and symptomatic hemorrhage in 6.1% vs 2.7% — most bleeds were silent, but the symptomatic rate more than doubled.
cards.source: Huo X et al., N Engl J Med 2023 (PMID 36762852 · NCT04551664)

cards.headline: RESCUE-Japan LIMIT 2022: the first large-core signal — Rankin 0–3 in 31% vs 13%.
cards.summary: Modified Rankin scale score 0–3 at 90 days in 31.0% on endovascular therapy vs 12.7% on medical care (relative risk 2.43, 95% CI 1.35–4.37; P=0.002 ). Early major neurologic improvement (NIHSS ≥8 points at 48 hours) 31.0% vs 8.8% .
cards.people: 203 patients with large cerebral infarction (101 endovascular therapy, 102 medical care); about 27% in each group received alteplase
cards.result: Modified Rankin scale score 0–3 at 90 days in 31.0% on endovascular therapy vs 12.7% on medical care (relative risk 2.43, 95% CI 1.35–4.37; P=0.002 ). Early major neurologic improvement (NIHSS ≥8 points at 48 hours) 31.0% vs 8.8% .
cards.watchOut: The smallest of the three trials, and its success bar was Rankin 0–3 — moderate disability counts as success; the win is less disability, not recovery. Any intracranial hemorrhage 58.0% vs 31.4%.

shelves.title: Tenecteplase vs alteplase: one bolus against the infusion
shelves.question: For a patient who qualifies for IV thrombolysis, is one-bolus tenecteplase as good as the hour-long alteplase infusion?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Brain Ischemia · Canada · Female · Fibrinolytic Agents · Humans · Intracranial Hemorrhages · Ischemic Stroke · Male · Prospective Studies · Stroke · Tenecteplase · Tissue Plasminogen Activator · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Two large trials, two continents, one answer: tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg is non-inferior to alteplase on 90-day function, with the same bleeding rate — and it is a single push instead of an infusion, which is why stroke systems have switched. Neither trial showed superiority; one showed a numerically higher death rate that was not significant and is not hidden.

cards.headline: AcT 2022: tenecteplase non-inferior to alteplase — excellent outcome 36.9% vs 34.8% in 1,577 patients.
cards.summary: Modified Rankin 0–1 at 90–120 days in 36.9% (296/802) on tenecteplase vs 34.8% (266/765) on alteplase — risk difference 2.1% (95% CI −2.6 to 6.9) , meeting the prespecified non-inferiority margin. Symptomatic hemorrhage at 24 hours 3.4% vs 3.2%. Death by 90 days 15.3% vs 15.4%.
cards.type: Pragmatic, open-label, registry-linked randomized non-inferiority trial, Canada
cards.people: 1,600 patients randomized (816 tenecteplase, 784 alteplase); 1,577 in the intention-to-treat population; median age 74
cards.result: Modified Rankin 0–1 at 90–120 days in 36.9% (296/802) on tenecteplase vs 34.8% (266/765) on alteplase — risk difference 2.1% (95% CI −2.6 to 6.9) , meeting the prespecified non-inferiority margin. Symptomatic hemorrhage at 24 hours 3.4% vs 3.2%. Death by 90 days 15.3% vs 15.4%.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and pragmatic — treating teams knew the drug. The claim is ‘no worse, and far simpler,’ not ‘better.’
cards.source: Menon BK et al., Lancet 2022 (PMID 35779553 · NCT03889249)

cards.headline: TRACE-2 2023: non-inferior again in China — Rankin 0–1 in 62% vs 58%.
cards.summary: Modified Rankin 0–1 at 90 days in 62% (439/705) on tenecteplase vs 58% (405/696) on alteplase (relative risk 1.07, 95% CI 0.98–1.16 ) — non-inferior. Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage within 36 hours 2% vs 2%.
cards.type: Phase 3, open-label randomized non-inferiority trial, China
cards.people: 1,430 patients with ischemic stroke eligible for IV thrombolysis but not for endovascular thrombectomy (716 tenecteplase, 714 alteplase)
cards.result: Modified Rankin 0–1 at 90 days in 62% (439/705) on tenecteplase vs 58% (405/696) on alteplase (relative risk 1.07, 95% CI 0.98–1.16 ) — non-inferior. Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage within 36 hours 2% vs 2%.
cards.watchOut: Death at 90 days was numerically higher on tenecteplase — 7% (46 patients) vs 5% (35), relative risk 1.31 (0.86–2.01) — not significant, but it points the wrong way and is kept visible.

shelves.title: Heparin in acute ischemic stroke: the answer from 20,000 patients
shelves.question: Does anticoagulating an acute ischemic stroke help — the old reflex, tested at scale?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Aged · Anticoagulants · Aspirin · Brain Ischemia · Cerebral Hemorrhage · Cerebrovascular Disorders · Chondroitin Sulfates · Dermatan Sulfate · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glasgow Coma Scale · Heparin · Heparinoids · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Male · Middle Aged · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors · Recurrence · Survival Analysis · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Before clots were dissolved or pulled out, the reflex order was heparin. In 19,435 randomized patients it prevented roughly as many ischemic recurrences as the hemorrhages it caused, and six-month disability was identical to the decimal point. The intravenous heparinoid version failed the same way. What actually changed stroke care was reperfusion and plain aspirin — not anticoagulation.

cards.headline: IST 1997: in 19,435 acute strokes, heparin traded clots for bleeds in equal measure — dead or dependent at 6 months, 62.9% vs 62.9%.
cards.summary: Death at 14 days 9.0% (876) on heparin vs 9.3% (905) without — not significant. Recurrent ischemic stroke fell ( 2.9% vs 3.8% ) but hemorrhagic stroke rose by the same amount ( 1.2% vs 0.4% ); death or non-fatal recurrent stroke 11.7% vs 12.0% , not significant. Dead or dependent at 6 months: identical, 62.9% in both groups.
cards.type: Randomized factorial trial (open), 467 hospitals in 36 countries
cards.people: 19,435 patients within 48 hours of acute ischemic stroke; heparin 5,000 or 12,500 IU subcutaneously twice daily vs no heparin, crossed with aspirin 300 mg vs no aspirin
cards.result: Death at 14 days 9.0% (876) on heparin vs 9.3% (905) without — not significant. shelves.title: Intracranial stenting for symptomatic stenosis: two trials, both stopped early, both against the stent
shelves.question: In patients with a recent stroke or TIA from 70–99% intracranial arterial stenosis, does adding a stent to aggressive medical therapy prevent further strokes?
shelves.balance: No — twice, with two different stents. In SAMMPRIS (451 patients), 30-day stroke or death was 14.7% with the Wingspan stent vs 5.8% on aggressive medical therapy alone, and the gap persisted at one year (20.0% vs 12.2%); enrollment was stopped for the early harm. VISSIT (112 patients), testing a balloon-expandable stent, was halted early after SAMMPRIS reported and pointed the same way — one-year stroke or hard TIA 36.2% vs 15.1%. The strokes the stent was meant to prevent happened around the procedure instead. Aggressive medical therapy — antiplatelet treatment, blood-pressure and risk-factor control — is the treatment.

shelves.title: B vitamins and folic acid for stroke prevention: the population's folate status decides
shelves.question: Does lowering homocysteine with B vitamins or folic acid prevent stroke?
shelves.balance: Folic acid prevented first stroke in a large trial in a non-fortified, low-folate population. In folate-replete populations after stroke, B-vitamin lowering was null to borderline. The answer depends on the population's folate status. Developer’s verdict: POSSIBLE in low-folate, non-fortified settings · MAYBE (weak evidence) for general use.

shelves.title: Clozapine: the one drug that works when others fail, and the suicide-risk trial
shelves.question: In schizophrenia that has failed other antipsychotics, does clozapine work — and does it reduce suicidal behavior?
shelves.mesh: Schizophrenia · Clozapine · Antipsychotic Agents · Chlorpromazine · Suicide, Attempted · Suicide Prevention · Humans
shelves.balance: Clozapine remains the only drug ever shown to work in truly treatment-resistant schizophrenia — 30% responded vs 4% on a high-dose standard drug, in patients who had already failed at least three agents and then failed a prospective haloperidol trial. The suicide trial was open-label (patients and clinicians knew the drug; only the raters were masked), and its benefit was in suicidal behavior overall (HR 0.76); completed suicides were rare and did not differ (5 vs 3). Clozapine's costs are real — blood monitoring for agranulocytosis, metabolic effects, sedation — and are why it is reserved for this population. Developer’s verdict: LIKELY for response in treatment-resistant schizophrenia · MAYBE (weak evidence) for reducing suicidal behavior (one open-label trial, gray-zone ratio).

shelves.title: Ketamine and esketamine for treatment-resistant depression: fast, brief, and not the whole story
shelves.question: Do ketamine and its S-enantiomer esketamine lift treatment-resistant depression quickly?
shelves.mesh: Depressive Disorder, Treatment-Resistant · Depressive Disorder, Major · Ketamine · Antidepressive Agents · Humans
shelves.balance: A single ketamine infusion beat an active placebo (midazolam, chosen so patients could not easily tell which drug they got) within 24 hours — 64% vs 28% response — but the separation was gone by day 7. Esketamine nasal spray, added to a newly started oral antidepressant, beat the oral drug plus placebo spray by 4 MADRS points at 4 weeks in one trial — while two sister trials (a fixed-dose study and a study in patients 65 and older) missed their primary endpoints. This is a fast, short-horizon effect on symptom scores, with dissociation and blood-pressure rises to manage; neither shelf card shows durability beyond weeks. Developer’s verdict: POSSIBLE — rapid short-term symptom improvement; durability unproven and two of three esketamine phase-3 trials missed.

shelves.title: Fluoxetine for depression in children and adolescents: works, best with therapy, warning attached
shelves.question: Does fluoxetine help depressed children and teenagers?
shelves.mesh: Depressive Disorder · Depressive Disorder, Major · Fluoxetine · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy · Adolescent · Child · Humans
shelves.balance: Fluoxetine is the one antidepressant with two positive placebo-controlled trials in youth. The first, in 96 patients aged 7–17, found 56% improved on 20 mg vs 33% on placebo. The large NIMH trial found fluoxetine alone (60.6% response) beat placebo (34.8%), and fluoxetine plus cognitive-behavioral therapy did best of all (71.0%), while CBT alone (43.2%) did not separate from placebo. The safety shadow is printed on the shelf: 7 of 439 TADS patients (1.6%) attempted suicide during 12 weeks (none completed), suicidal thinking improved most in the combination arm, and fluoxetine carries the FDA's boxed warning for adolescents. Developer’s verdict: POSSIBLE — two positive placebo-controlled trials; combination with CBT was best in the big trial; the boxed warning stands.

shelves.title: Varenicline for quitting smoking: the best quit rates, and the big safety trial that cleared it
shelves.question: Does varenicline help smokers quit, and is it neuropsychiatrically safe?
shelves.mesh: Smoking Cessation · Varenicline · Bupropion · Nicotinic Agonists · Tobacco Use Cessation Devices · Humans
shelves.balance: Varenicline roughly doubled-to-tripled quit rates in the pivotal trials: 44.0% abstinent at weeks 9–12 vs 29.5% on bupropion and 17.7% on placebo, with the advantage persisting, smaller, at one year (21.9% vs 16.1% vs 8.4%). The safety question that hung over the drug — reports of depression, agitation, and suicidality — was put to an 8,144-person trial enrolling smokers with and without psychiatric disorders: moderate-to-severe neuropsychiatric events did not differ significantly between varenicline, bupropion, patch, and placebo in either cohort, and varenicline again produced the highest abstinence. On this trial's evidence the FDA removed varenicline's boxed warning in 2016. Developer’s verdict: LIKELY — the highest quit rates of the first-line drugs, and no significant neuropsychiatric excess in the largest safety trial.

cards.people: 1,025 smokers; varenicline 1 mg twice daily vs bupropion SR 150 mg twice daily vs placebo, 12 weeks of treatment

shelves.title: Naltrexone for alcohol dependence: fewer relapses to heavy drinking
shelves.question: Does oral naltrexone help people with alcohol dependence stay off heavy drinking?
shelves.mesh: Alcoholism · Naltrexone · Acamprosate · Alcohol Deterrents · Narcotic Antagonists · Humans
shelves.balance: The small founding trial was strikingly positive: recently detoxified men on naltrexone relapsed to heavy drinking at less than half the placebo rate (23% vs 54%), and when they did drink, half as many progressed to a full relapse (50% vs 95%). The large pragmatic COMBINE trial found a smaller, real benefit when naltrexone was paired with structured medical management — 80.6% vs 75.1% of days abstinent, and a hazard ratio of 0.72 for a heavy-drinking day — while acamprosate showed no benefit alone or in combination, and the naltrexone advantage had faded a year after treatment ended. Expect a modest effect that needs the follow-up structure around it. Developer’s verdict: POSSIBLE — a large effect in the small early trial, a modest one in the big pragmatic trial, gone a year after treatment stopped.

shelves.title: Extended-release naltrexone vs buprenorphine for opioid dependence: the hard part is starting
shelves.question: How does monthly injected naltrexone compare with daily buprenorphine-naloxone for opioid use disorder?
shelves.mesh: Opioid-Related Disorders · Naltrexone · Buprenorphine, Naloxone Drug Combination · Narcotic Antagonists · Opiate Substitution Treatment · Humans
shelves.balance: Both trials were open-label — patients knew whether they were getting a monthly injection or a daily film — and both tell the same story: once people are actually on the medication, the two work about the same; the difference is getting on. In the US trial, only 72% of patients assigned to the injection completed detox and received it, vs 94% started on buprenorphine, and that induction gap drove the overall relapse difference (65% vs 57%). Among those successfully inducted, relapse was 52% vs 56%. Fatal overdoses were few and similar (2 vs 3). The Norwegian trial found the injection noninferior on retention and opioid-negative tests over 12 weeks. Developer’s verdict: POSSIBLE — comparable outcomes once started; buprenorphine is far easier to start, and that difference dominates the intention-to-treat result.

shelves.title: After a first psychotic episode: staying on antipsychotics prevents relapse, but the 7-year recovery data point the other way
shelves.question: After remission of a first psychotic episode, is it better to stay on antipsychotic maintenance or to reduce and stop?
shelves.mesh: Psychotic Disorders · Schizophrenia · Antipsychotic Agents · Quetiapine Fumarate · Recurrence · Humans
shelves.balance: The two trials answer two different questions and both answers stand. In the double-blind Hong Kong trial, stopping (switching to placebo) after a year of treatment nearly doubled relapse in the next year — 79% vs 41%. In the Dutch strategy trial, guided dose reduction or discontinuation also caused more early relapses (43% vs 21% by 2 years) — but at 7 years the reduction/discontinuation group had twice the full recovery rate (40.4% vs 17.6%; OR 3.49), driven by functional remission: holding a job, managing daily life. Symptomatic remission at 7 years was the same. Relapse prevention and long-run functioning pull in opposite directions, and the shelf says so rather than resolving it. Developer’s verdict: POSSIBLE — maintenance clearly prevents relapse in the first year; the single long follow-up found better functional recovery after early reduction/discontinuation. Two outcomes, two directions.

shelves.title: Brexanolone for postpartum depression: a 60-hour infusion with a fast, large effect
shelves.question: Does a single 60-hour brexanolone infusion relieve postpartum depression?
shelves.mesh: Depression, Postpartum · Pregnanolone · Antidepressive Agents · GABA Agonists · Humans · Female
shelves.balance: All three placebo-controlled trials — one small phase-2 and two phase-3 studies run by the drug's sponsor — point the same way: depression scores fell much further on brexanolone within 60 hours, and the advantage held to day 30. Remission at the end of the infusion ran 51–70% on the effective doses vs 9–38% on placebo, depending on the trial and dose. The practical costs are printed on the shelf: the drug is given as a supervised 60-hour inpatient infusion, it carries a boxed warning for excessive sedation and sudden loss of consciousness, and breastfeeding is paused during treatment. Samples are small by the standards of this library, and there is no independent replication. Developer’s verdict: POSSIBLE — rapid, large, consistent symptom improvement across three trials from one development program; small samples, no independent replication, burdensome administration.

shelves.title: STAR*D: what actually happened when depression treatment was measured step by step
shelves.question: In real-world practice, how many patients remit on a first antidepressant — and what happens when the first one fails?
shelves.mesh: Depressive Disorder, Major · Citalopram · Bupropion · Sertraline · Venlafaxine Hydrochloride · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors · Humans
shelves.balance: STAR*D is the largest practical answer available: with careful measurement-based dosing, about 28% of patients remitted on citalopram alone (33% by self-report scale) and 47% responded. For those who did not remit, switching to any of three chemically different antidepressants remitted about one in five — 21.3%, 17.6%, and 24.8%, with no significant difference between them and no tolerability winner. Because there was no placebo and no blinding, some of these remissions are the natural course of the illness and expectation effects; the trial's value is the honest arithmetic of sequential treatment, not proof that any step beats doing nothing. Developer’s verdict: POSSIBLE — about a third remit at step 1 and about a quarter of the remainder remit after a switch; no switch drug beat another. Open-label throughout.

shelves.title: Suvorexant for insomnia: modest, consistent gains from blocking orexin
shelves.question: Does the orexin blocker suvorexant improve sleep onset and maintenance?
shelves.mesh: Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders · Orexin Receptor Antagonists · Azepines · Triazoles · Polysomnography · Humans
shelves.balance: Across two 3-month trials totaling 2,040 patients, the higher age-adjusted dose (40 mg under 65, 30 mg at 65+) beat placebo on nearly every subjective and polysomnography endpoint — about 30 more minutes of subjective total sleep time at month 3 — and the lower dose (20/15 mg) still won on the maintenance measures. A separate year-long trial found the advantage persisted (subjective total sleep time +38.7 vs +16.0 minutes at month 1) and that stopping abruptly after a year produced no rebound insomnia or withdrawal. Printed on the shelf: the trials excluded patients with other sleep disorders, including sleep apnea, and enrolled primary insomnia only; somnolence was the commonest adverse effect, and the doses tested were above the 20 mg maximum later approved in the US. Developer’s verdict: LIKELY for modest improvements in sleep onset and maintenance in primary insomnia — consistent across trials and a full year of use; effect sizes are minutes, not transformations.

shelves.title: How low after a stroke: LDL target under 70 vs around 100 mg/dL
shelves.question: After an ischemic stroke or TIA, should LDL cholesterol be driven under 70 mg/dL, or is a target around 100 mg/dL enough?
shelves.mesh: Stroke · Cholesterol, LDL · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors · Ezetimibe · Humans
shelves.balance: One target trial answers directly: Treat Stroke to Target randomized patients after ischemic stroke or TIA to LDL <70 vs 90–110 mg/dL and found fewer major cardiovascular events at the lower target (8.5% vs 10.9%; adjusted HR 0.78, a 22% relative reduction) — in a trial stopped early for administrative reasons. The background trial, SPARCL (atorvastatin 80 mg vs placebo after stroke), is carded on Shelf #95 and is not duplicated here. With a single, early-stopped target trial, the honest label is: Developer's verdict: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Treat Stroke to Target (Amarenco 2020): LDL <70 beat 90–110 after stroke — 8.5% vs 10.9%
cards.summary: Primary composite 8.5% vs 10.9% (adjusted HR 0.78); achieved LDL 65 vs 96 mg/dL — 2,860 patients; trial stopped early for administrative reasons.
cards.type: RCT, parallel-group (Treat Stroke to Target), N Engl J Med 2020
cards.people: 2,860 patients in France and South Korea with recent ischemic stroke or TIA and cerebrovascular or coronary atherosclerosis; statin, ezetimibe, or both titrated to LDL <70 mg/dL (1,430) vs a target range of 90–110 mg/dL (1,430); median follow-up 3.5 years; mean baseline LDL 135 mg/dL.
cards.result: Mean achieved LDL: 65 mg/dL in the lower-target group vs 96 mg/dL in the higher-target group. The primary composite (ischemic stroke, MI, urgent coronary or carotid revascularization, or cardiovascular death) occurred in 121 patients ( 8.5% ) vs 156 ( 10.9% ) — adjusted HR 0.78 (0.61–0.98), P=0.04, a 22% relative reduction. Intracranial hemorrhage and newly diagnosed diabetes did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: Re-card with a different question: Shelf #95 cards this trial inside the broad secondary-prevention question; here it stands alone as the target-intensity trial. It was stopped for administrative reasons after 277 of a planned 385 end-point events — the effect estimate is less secure than its P value suggests.

shelves.title: Varenicline safety and efficacy: the neuropsychiatric fear, tested in 8,144 smokers
shelves.question: Is varenicline — the most effective single quit-smoking medicine — safe for the brain, including in people with psychiatric disorders?
shelves.mesh: Varenicline · Bupropion · Nicotinic Agonists · Smoking Cessation · Mental Disorders · Tobacco Use Cessation Devices · Humans
shelves.balance: For a decade varenicline carried a boxed warning for neuropsychiatric harm, built on case reports. EAGLES — 8,144 smokers, half with psychiatric disorders, randomized against bupropion, nicotine patch, and placebo — found no excess of moderate-to-severe neuropsychiatric events on varenicline in either cohort (1.3% vs 2.4% on placebo in the non-psychiatric cohort), and the FDA removed the boxed warning on the strength of it. The efficacy half of the same trial — varenicline quits more smokers than patch, bupropion, or placebo — is carded at its home on Shelf #225. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: EAGLES: in 8,144 smokers, varenicline caused no excess of moderate-to-severe neuropsychiatric events — the trial that removed the boxed warning (re-card; home Shelf #225)
cards.summary: Moderate-to-severe neuropsychiatric adverse events in smokers without psychiatric disorders: 1.3% on varenicline vs 2.4% on placebo (risk difference −1.28 , 95% CI −2.40 to −0.15) — 8,144 randomized smokers, with and without psychiatric disorders.
cards.type: Double-blind, triple-dummy, randomized, placebo- and active-controlled trial (EAGLES), Lancet 2016. Re-card of the card homed on Shelf #225, asked here for the safety question; counted once, at its home shelf.
cards.people: 8,144 participants were randomly assigned at 140 centres in 16 countries: 4,116 to the psychiatric cohort and 4,028 to the non-psychiatric cohort (safety populations 4,074 and 3,984). (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: In the non-psychiatric cohort, moderate and severe neuropsychiatric adverse events were reported by 13 (1.3%) of 990 participants on varenicline, 22 (2.2%) of 989 on bupropion, 25 (2.5%) of 1,006 on nicotine patch, and 24 (2.4%) of 999 on placebo. The varenicline–placebo risk difference was −1.28 (95% CI −2.40 to −0.15) and the bupropion–placebo risk difference −0.08 (−1.37 to 1.21); neither drug showed an excess over patch either. Event rates were higher in the psychiatric cohort in every arm, again without an excess attributable to varenicline or bupropion. Varenicline was also the most effective quit aid in the trial (the efficacy cards live on Shelf #225).
cards.watchOut: EAGLES was industry-funded (Pfizer, with GSK) at the FDA’s request, and it is the evidence on which the FDA removed the boxed warning from varenicline in December 2016. It was powered for the composite neuropsychiatric endpoint, not for rare events such as suicide, which remain a clinical-vigilance question rather than a trial answer.
cards.source: Anthenelli RM et al. Neuropsychiatric safety and efficacy of varenicline, bupropion, and nicotine patch in smokers with and without psychiatric disorders (EAGLES): a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled clinical trial. Lancet. 2016;387:2507-20. PMID 27116918 · NCT01456936.

shelves.title: Multidomain lifestyle intervention for cognition (FINGER): one positive cognitive score — no trial has shown dementia prevention
shelves.question: In older people at risk, does a multidomain intervention — diet, exercise, cognitive training, and vascular-risk monitoring — preserve cognition, or prevent dementia?
shelves.mesh: Cognition Disorders · Dementia · Diet · Exercise Therapy · Vascular Diseases · Risk Assessment · Humans
shelves.balance: The split stamp is the shelf. For cognition: FINGER — the one large, well-run positive trial — improved its neuropsychological composite by 0.022 Z points per year over 2 years (P=0.030) in selected at-risk Finns, a small but real signal, graded POSSIBLE. For dementia prevention: no trial has shown it. PreDIVA, which actually measured dementia over 6 years in 3,526 people, found 7% vs 7% (HR 0.92); MAPT found no significant cognitive effect of the multidomain programme with or without omega-3. FINGER never measured dementia incidence at all. Printed plainly, as the shelf requires: a multidomain programme may modestly support cognition in at-risk older adults; that it prevents dementia is MAYBE (weak evidence) — an extrapolation the dementia-endpoint trials have so far failed to confirm. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: FINGER (Ngandu 2015): the one positive trial — cognition improved by 0.022 points a year on the NTB composite (P=0.030); dementia was never an endpoint
cards.summary: Change in the comprehensive Neuropsychological Test Battery (NTB) total Z score at 2 years: 0.20 in the multidomain group vs 0.16 in the control group — a between-group difference of 0.022 per year (95% CI 0.002–0.042; P=0.030) — 1,260 at-risk Finnish adults aged 60–77.
cards.people: 1,260 individuals aged 60–77 recruited from national surveys, with a CAIDE dementia risk score of at least 6 and cognition at or slightly below the age-expected mean; 631 assigned to the multidomain intervention and 629 to control (general health advice); 1,190 had at least one post-baseline assessment. (The abstract record does not print the sex mix.)
cards.result: Estimated mean NTB change at 2 years was 0.20 (SD 0.51) with the intervention and 0.16 (SD 0.51) with control; the between-group difference in change per year was 0.022 (95% CI 0.002–0.042; P=0.030). Dropout was 12% overall. Adverse events occurred in 46 participants (7%) in the intervention group vs 6 (1%) in the control group, most commonly musculoskeletal pain (5% vs 0%).
cards.watchOut: Read the endpoint before the headline: FINGER measured a cognitive test score over 2 years in a selected, motivated, at-risk population — it did not measure dementia, and a 0.022-per-year Z-score difference is a small effect whose clinical weight is debated. It is the only positive trial of the three on this shelf, which is why the cognition claim is stamped POSSIBLE and the dementia claim (Cards 2–3, the trials that actually measured dementia) is stamped separately, and lower.

cards.headline: PreDIVA (2016): the trial that measured dementia found none prevented — 7% vs 7% over 6 years (HR 0.92)
cards.summary: Cumulative dementia incidence at 6 years: 121 of 1,853 patients (7%) in the intervention group vs 112 of 1,601 (7%) in the control group (hazard ratio 0.92; 95% CI 0.71–1.19 — a relative measure, printed beside the identical absolute rates; P=0.54) — 3,526 patients in 116 Dutch general practices.
cards.people: 3,526 individuals aged 70–78 recruited through 116 general practices in the Netherlands (1,890 intervention, 1,636 control); median follow-up 6.7 years; primary-outcome data for 98%. (The abstract record does not print the sex mix.)
cards.result: Dementia developed in 7% in both groups (HR 0.92; 95% CI 0.71–1.19; P=0.54). Disability scores were identical (mean ALDS 85.7 in both groups; adjusted difference −0.02; P=0.93). Mortality was 16% in both groups (HR 0.98) and incident cardiovascular disease did not differ (19% vs 17%; HR 1.06).
cards.watchOut: The usual-care problem is printed in the paper: Dutch usual care was already good and baseline vascular risk modest, leaving little room for a nurse-led intervention to add — which cuts both ways, since it is also a fair description of much real-world practice. Either way, this is the largest dementia-endpoint test of the multidomain idea, and it is null on dementia, disability, mortality, and cardiovascular disease alike.

cards.headline: MAPT (Andrieu 2017): multidomain intervention, omega-3, both, or neither — no significant effect on cognitive decline over 3 years
cards.summary: Change in the cognitive composite Z score at 36 months, versus placebo: +0.093 for multidomain plus omega-3 (adjusted P=0.142), +0.079 for multidomain plus placebo (P=0.179), +0.011 for omega-3 alone (P=0.812) — none significant — 1,680 French and Monegasque adults aged 70 or older with memory complaints.
cards.type: Randomized, placebo-controlled, four-arm trial (MAPT), Lancet Neurology 2017
cards.people: 1,680 community-dwelling, non-demented participants aged 70 or older with a spontaneous memory complaint, an instrumental-activity limitation, or slow gait, at 13 memory centres in France and Monaco; modified intention-to-treat population 1,525. (The abstract record does not print the sex mix.)
cards.result: No intervention arm separated significantly from placebo on the primary cognitive composite over 3 years. Serious adverse events were similarly frequent across arms (32–36% of participants), and four treatment-related deaths were recorded — two in the multidomain-plus-placebo group and two in the placebo group — with no safety signal attributed to the interventions.
cards.watchOut: MAPT is the middle trial of the shelf: FINGER’s selected at-risk population and intensive programme on one side, PreDIVA’s unselected population and dementia endpoint on the other, and a null cognitive result here in a memory-complaint population. A post-hoc literature exists suggesting benefit in higher-risk MAPT subgroups; subgroup rescues of null trials are hypothesis-generating, and this library does not grade on them.

shelves.title: Anti-amyloid antibodies in Alzheimer’s disease: amyloid falls decisively; decline slows by less than patients can feel — and ARIA is the price
shelves.question: In early Alzheimer’s disease, do anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies (lecanemab, donanemab) produce patient-important benefit — and at what risk?
shelves.mesh: Alzheimer Disease · Amyloid beta-Peptides · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Cognition · Humans
shelves.balance: The two halves of this shelf must never be quoted separately. The biomarker half is strong: lecanemab cut brain amyloid by 59.1 centiloids against placebo, donanemab cleared plaque on a stop-when-clear schedule, and both slowed decline on the CDR-SB scale — biomarker and scale efficacy this shelf grades LIKELY. The patient-important half is weaker, and its numbers are printed with their yardstick: lecanemab’s CDR-SB difference was −0.45 and donanemab’s −0.67, against a minimal clinically important difference of about 1.0–1.6 points at this disease stage (Reference 3). The harms are neither rare nor theoretical: ARIA-E in 12.6% on lecanemab (about a third of ApoE ε4 homozygotes) and 24.0% on donanemab, ARIA-H in 17.3% and 31.4% respectively, and three treatment-related deaths in the donanemab trial. Net clinical benefit is therefore stamped POSSIBLE — real slowing, below the feel-able threshold, bought with brain-swelling and bleeding risk that demands MRI monitoring. The aducanumab arc (surrogate approval, discordant trials, withdrawal) is carded on Card 3 as the standing warning against upgrading this stamp on biomarker data alone. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: Clarity AD (van Dyck 2023): lecanemab slowed CDR-SB decline by 0.45 points — against a meaningful-difference yardstick of about 1.0–1.6 — with ARIA-E in 12.6%
cards.summary: Change in CDR-SB (0–18; higher is worse) at 18 months: +1.21 on lecanemab vs +1.66 on placebo (difference −0.45; 95% CI −0.67 to −0.23; P<0.001). Amyloid burden fell by 59.1 centiloids more than placebo. ARIA with oedema or effusions (ARIA-E): 12.6%; infusion reactions 26.4% — 1,795 patients with early Alzheimer’s disease.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, phase III trial (Clarity AD), New England Journal of Medicine 2023
cards.people: 1,795 participants aged 50–90 with early Alzheimer’s disease (mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia) and amyloid confirmed on PET or in cerebrospinal fluid; 898 lecanemab 10 mg/kg intravenously every 2 weeks, 897 placebo; baseline CDR-SB about 3.2 in both groups. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: The primary endpoint favoured lecanemab: CDR-SB difference −0.45 (95% CI −0.67 to −0.23; P<0.001), with concordant secondary endpoints (ADAS-cog14 difference −1.44; ADCOMS −0.050; ADCS-MCI-ADL +2.0). In the 698-participant PET substudy, amyloid burden fell 59.1 centiloids more on lecanemab — the biomarker effect this shelf grades LIKELY. Harms: infusion-related reactions in 26.4%, and ARIA-E in 12.6%; the paper reports ARIA-H (haemorrhage) in 17.3%, and ARIA-E in about a third (32.6%) of apolipoprotein E ε4 homozygotes.
cards.watchOut: Both numbers, as this shelf requires: −0.45 is a real, statistically secure slowing — and Card 3’s yardstick puts the smallest CDR-SB change patients and clinicians can detect at roughly 1.0–1.6 points in this disease stage. The trial ran 18 months; whether the gap widens, holds, or closes with longer treatment, and how ARIA risk plays out outside trial monitoring (including alongside anticoagulants and thrombolysis), are open. Funded by Eisai and Biogen.
cards.source: van Dyck CH et al. Lecanemab in Early Alzheimer’s Disease. N Engl J Med. 2023. PMID 36449413 · NCT03887455. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2212948

cards.headline: TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 (Sims 2023): donanemab — CDR-SB −0.67 in low/medium tau; ARIA-E 24.0%, and three treatment-related deaths
cards.summary: In the low/medium-tau population: iADRS difference +3.25 points (95% CI 1.88–4.62) and CDR-SB difference −0.67 (−0.95 to −0.40) at 76 weeks — about a 35% relative slowing of decline. ARIA-E occurred in 24.0% on donanemab (52 symptomatic) vs 2.1% on placebo; three deaths in the donanemab group (and one on placebo) were considered treatment-related — 1,736 patients.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase III trial (TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2), JAMA 2023
cards.people: 1,736 participants with early symptomatic Alzheimer’s disease (mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia) and PET amyloid plus tau pathology, at 277 centres in 8 countries (mean age 73.0 years; 57.4% women); 1,182 (68.1%) had low/medium tau and 552 high tau; 76% completed the trial.
cards.result: Primary outcome (iADRS, low/medium tau): least-squares mean change −6.02 on donanemab vs −9.27 on placebo (difference 3.25; P<0.001); in the combined population the difference was 2.92. CDR-SB differences were −0.67 (low/medium tau) and −0.70 (combined). Of 24 gated outcomes, 23 were statistically significant. Harms: ARIA-E in 205 participants (24.0%; 52 symptomatic) vs 18 (2.1%; none symptomatic) on placebo; ARIA-H in 31.4% as reported in the paper; infusion reactions 8.7% vs 0.5%. Three donanemab deaths and one placebo death were considered treatment-related.
cards.watchOut: The strongest slowing numbers in the class come with the class’s heaviest harm card: one patient in four developed ARIA-E, and the three treatment-attributed deaths are printed in this card’s title, where they belong. Donanemab’s stop-on-clearance design (switching to placebo once amyloid cleared) is a genuine practical difference from lecanemab’s open-ended dosing. And the yardstick still applies: −0.67 on CDR-SB sits below Card 3’s ~1.0–1.6 meaningful-difference range for this stage. Tau burden modified the effect — high-tau patients gained less — so the headline number belongs to the low/medium-tau majority, not to everyone with Alzheimer’s disease.

cards.summary: Anchor- and distribution-based estimates from the National Alzheimer’s Coordinating Center dataset: a 1–2 point increase in CDR-SB (with 1–3 points on the MMSE and 3–5 on the Functional Activities Questionnaire) marks a clinically meaningful decline; in the mild stages the antibody trials enrolled, the working range is about 1.0–1.6 points.
cards.type: Methods analysis of the National Alzheimer’s Coordinating Center Uniform Data Set (2005–2016), Alzheimer’s and Dementia (TRCI) 2019
cards.people: Not a trial population: a retrospective analysis of a large US Alzheimer’s research dataset, estimating minimal clinically important differences (MCIDs) by clinician-anchored and distribution-based methods, stratified by disease severity. No registry number applies.
cards.result: On average, a 1–3 point MMSE decrease, a 1–2 point CDR-SB increase, and a 3–5 point FAQ increase indicated meaningful decline, with MCID values generally rising as disease severity increased; effect sizes for patients with clinician-judged meaningful decline were consistently in the acceptable MCID range. Applied to this shelf: both antibody effects (lecanemab −0.45, donanemab −0.67 on CDR-SB) are smaller than the smallest change this analysis calls meaningful at these stages (about 1.0–1.6 of the 1–2 range).
cards.watchOut: Why this card exists: the aducanumab precedent. Aducanumab won accelerated FDA approval in 2021 on amyloid reduction — a surrogate — with two discordant phase III trials behind it; coverage was restricted, the confirmatory programme failed to rescue it, and the drug was withdrawn in 2024. That arc is why this shelf grades amyloid clearance LIKELY, scale-score slowing as measured, and net patient-important benefit only POSSIBLE: a biomarker can be moved decisively while the benefit a patient can feel remains, on the best yardstick available, below the detectable line. Slowing that compounds over years beyond the trials’ 18 months could still matter — that is a hope about trajectories, not a trial result, and agents should repeat it only in that framing.

shelves.title: Carotid stenting versus endarterectomy: level at ten years in CREST, age decides in symptomatic disease — and a 2026 trial re-asks the question against modern medicine
shelves.question: In carotid stenosis, how do stenting and endarterectomy compare — in early hazard, in long-term protection, by age and symptoms — and against modern medical therapy alone?
shelves.mesh: Carotid Stenosis · Endarterectomy, Carotid · Stents · Stroke · Myocardial Infarction · Humans
shelves.balance: The through-line of six trials and one pooled analysis: after the periprocedural window, stenting and endarterectomy protect about equally for at least a decade (CREST at 10 years: 11.8% vs 9.9%, not significant). They differ in how they charge for that protection — periprocedural stroke 4.1% vs 2.3% with stenting, myocardial infarction 1.1% vs 2.3% with surgery (CREST) — and in symptomatic patients the early gap was wider and uglier (EVA-3S 9.6% vs 3.9%, stopped early; ICSS 8.5% vs 5.2%). Age is the strongest modifier: stenting’s periprocedural risk climbs steeply with age while surgery’s stays flat, making endarterectomy clearly superior at 70 and beyond (pooled hazard ratio 2.09 at 70–74). In asymptomatic disease, ACST-2 found both procedures down to about 1% procedural disabling stroke or death with 5-year stroke around 5% either way. And the newest evidence re-asks the founding question: in CREST-2 (reported 2026, and dated as such on its card), adding stenting to intensive medical therapy lowered 4-year events (2.8% vs 6.0%; P=0.02) while adding endarterectomy did not, significantly (3.7% vs 5.3%; P=0.24). Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: CREST (Brott 2010): no overall difference (7.2% vs 6.8%) — but the periprocedural trade was stroke with stenting, heart attack with surgery
cards.summary: Estimated 4-year rates of the primary composite (periprocedural stroke, myocardial infarction, or death, plus later ipsilateral stroke): 7.2% with stenting vs 6.8% with endarterectomy (hazard ratio 1.11; 95% CI 0.81–1.51; P=0.51 — not significant). Periprocedurally: stroke 4.1% vs 2.3% (P=0.01) and myocardial infarction 1.1% vs 2.3% (P=0.03), death 0.7% vs 0.3% — 2,502 patients.
cards.type: Randomized trial (CREST), New England Journal of Medicine 2010
cards.people: 2,502 patients with symptomatic or asymptomatic carotid stenosis, randomized to stenting or endarterectomy; median follow-up 2.5 years. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: No significant difference in the primary endpoint (7.2% vs 6.8%; HR 1.11), and no differential effect by symptomatic status (P=0.84) or sex (P=0.34). The 4-year rate of stroke or death was higher with stenting (6.4% vs 4.7%; HR 1.50; P=0.03). After the periprocedural period, ipsilateral stroke rates were similarly low (2.0% vs 2.4%; P=0.85).
cards.watchOut: CREST’s composite weights a periprocedural myocardial infarction (often biomarker-defined) the same as a stroke — patients and surgeons do not, which is why the component rates are printed separately on this card. CREST also credentialled its interventionists rigorously; real-world periprocedural rates have often been worse. The age interaction inside CREST — outcomes crossing over around age 70 — is quantified on Card 5.
cards.source: Brott TG et al. Stenting versus endarterectomy for treatment of carotid-artery stenosis. N Engl J Med. 2010. PMID 20505173 · NCT00004732. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa0912321

cards.headline: CREST at 10 years (Brott 2016): still no significant difference — primary composite 11.8% vs 9.9%; post-procedural ipsilateral stroke 6.9% vs 5.6%
cards.summary: Over 10 years of follow-up: primary composite 11.8% (95% CI 9.1–14.8) with stenting vs 9.9% (7.9–12.2) with endarterectomy (hazard ratio 1.10; 95% CI 0.83–1.44 — not significant). Post-procedural ipsilateral stroke: 6.9% vs 5.6% (HR 0.99; 95% CI 0.64–1.52) — the same 2,502 CREST patients.
cards.type: Long-term follow-up of a randomized trial (CREST), New England Journal of Medicine 2016
cards.people: The 2,502 CREST patients, assessed every 6 months for up to 10 years at 117 centres. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Neither endpoint separated the procedures over a decade: not the primary composite (HR 1.10), not post-procedural ipsilateral stroke (HR 0.99), and not in the symptomatic and asymptomatic subgroups analysed separately.
cards.watchOut: Durability is the answer to the ’stents restenose’ objection — after the periprocedural window, both procedures protect about equally for at least a decade. What 10-year equality cannot do is erase the periprocedural asymmetry on Card 1, or answer the modern question — procedure plus today’s medical therapy vs today’s medical therapy alone — which waited for CREST-2 (Reference 7). Same registration as Card 1 (the trial’s long-term extension).

cards.headline: EVA-3S (Mas 2006): stopped early for harm — 30-day stroke or death 9.6% with stenting vs 3.9% with endarterectomy
cards.summary: 30-day incidence of any stroke or death: 9.6% after stenting (95% CI 6.4–14.0) vs 3.9% after endarterectomy (2.0–7.2) — a relative risk of 2.5 (relative; 95% CI 1.2–5.1). Disabling stroke or death: 3.4% vs 1.5%. The trial was stopped prematurely after 527 patients for safety and futility.
cards.type: Multicentre, randomized, noninferiority trial (EVA-3S), New England Journal of Medicine 2006
cards.people: 527 patients with symptomatic carotid stenosis of at least 60%, randomized to stenting or endarterectomy before the trial was halted. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: At 30 days, stroke or death occurred in 9.6% after stenting vs 3.9% after endarterectomy (RR 2.5); at 6 months, any stroke or death was 11.7% vs 6.1% (P=0.02). Major local complications were more frequent after stenting and systemic (mainly pulmonary) complications after endarterectomy, neither significantly; cranial-nerve injury was more common after endarterectomy.
cards.watchOut: Context the trial itself supplies: EVA-3S allowed interventionists with modest carotid-stenting experience, and its stenting arm’s early hazard is the worst in this shelf’s literature — later trials with tighter credentialling (CREST) narrowed, but did not close, the periprocedural stroke gap. Carded as the symptomatic-patient caution: in recently symptomatic stenosis, the early window is where endarterectomy earned its default status.
cards.source: Mas JL et al. Endarterectomy versus stenting in patients with symptomatic severe carotid stenosis. N Engl J Med. 2006. PMID 17050890 · NCT00190398. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa061752

cards.headline: ICSS (Ederle 2010): 120-day stroke, death, or procedural heart attack 8.5% with stenting vs 5.2% with endarterectomy — cranial nerve palsy 1 vs 45 the other way
cards.summary: Between randomization and 120 days: stroke, death, or procedural myocardial infarction in 8.5% of the stenting group vs 5.2% of the endarterectomy group (72 vs 44 events; hazard ratio 1.69; 95% CI 1.16–2.45; P=0.006). Disabling stroke or death: 4.0% vs 3.2% (HR 1.28, not significant) — 1,713 symptomatic patients.
cards.type: Multicentre, international, randomized trial, interim safety analysis (ICSS), Lancet 2010
cards.people: 1,713 patients with recently symptomatic carotid artery stenosis (855 stenting, 858 endarterectomy), with blinded outcome adjudication and independent follow-up. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Any stroke was more frequent with stenting (65 vs 35 events; HR 1.92, relative) and all-cause death higher (19 vs 7 events; HR 2.76, relative). Against that: cranial nerve palsy occurred once after stenting vs 45 times after endarterectomy, and haematomas of any severity were fewer with stenting (31 vs 50; P=0.0197). Three procedural myocardial infarctions in the stenting group were all fatal; four in the endarterectomy group were all non-fatal.
cards.watchOut: An interim safety analysis — the trial’s primary 3-year fatal-or-disabling-stroke outcome had not been analysed — and its authors’ conclusion was plain: endarterectomy should remain the treatment of choice for patients suitable for surgery, pending long-term follow-up. Together with EVA-3S it forms the symptomatic-evidence pair behind this shelf’s framing; CREST (References 1–2) is the counterweight from a mixed symptomatic/asymptomatic population with stricter operator standards.
cards.source: Ederle J et al. cards.headline: The age card (Howard 2016, pooled): stenting’s periprocedural risk climbs steeply with age while surgery’s stays flat — at 70–74 the hazard ratio is 2.09 against stenting
cards.summary: Pooled individual data from 4 symptomatic-patient trials (4,754 patients): for stenting, periprocedural stroke-or-death hazard rose with age (hazard ratio 2.16 at 65–69 vs under 60, and roughly 4.0 at 70 or older); for endarterectomy it did not (P=0.34). Stenting-vs-surgery periprocedural hazard ratio: 1.61 at 65–69 and 2.09 (95% CI 1.32–3.32) at 70–74.
cards.type: Meta-analysis of individual patient data from four randomized trials (Carotid Stenosis Trialists’ Collaboration), Lancet 2016
cards.people: 4,754 patients with symptomatic carotid stenosis randomized to stenting or endarterectomy across four trials; 433 events over a median follow-up of 2.7 years. (A pooled population — no combined mean age is printed, by design: age is the variable under study.)
cards.result: Age modified only the periprocedural period: after the procedure, stroke risk was not associated with age within either treatment group, and the procedures did not differ by age post-procedurally (P=0.84). The authors’ conclusion: endarterectomy was clearly superior to stenting in patients aged 70–74 and older, with the difference almost wholly attributable to rising periprocedural stroke risk on stenting.
cards.watchOut: This is the evidence behind the clinic rule of thumb that the procedures cross over around age 70: below it, CREST-era stenting is a reasonable alternative for suitable anatomy; above it, the burden of proof sits on stenting. A pooled analysis — no registry number applies. Symptomatic patients only; the asymptomatic comparison has its own cards (6–7).

cards.headline: ACST-2 (Halliday 2021): in asymptomatic severe stenosis, procedural disabling stroke or death was about 1% with either procedure — and 5-year stroke about 5% with either
cards.summary: 3,625 asymptomatic patients: procedural disabling stroke or death in about 1% in both groups (15 allocated to stenting, 18 to endarterectomy); non-disabling procedural stroke in 48 vs 29. Five-year Kaplan–Meier estimates: fatal or disabling stroke 2.5% in each group; any stroke 5.3% with stenting vs 4.5% with endarterectomy (rate ratio 1.16, relative; P=0.33 — not significant).
cards.people: 3,625 patients with severe unilateral or bilateral carotid stenosis and no recent stroke or transient ischaemic attack, in 130 centres (1,811 stenting, 1,814 endarterectomy), where doctor and patient agreed a procedure was warranted but were substantially uncertain which; mean follow-up 5 years, with good medical therapy in both groups. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Serious complications were similarly uncommon after both procedures, and the long-term effects on fatal or disabling stroke were comparable: 2.5% at 5 years in each group. Combining non-procedural stroke across all stenting-vs-endarterectomy trials, the rate ratio was similar in symptomatic and asymptomatic patients (overall rate ratio 1.11; 95% CI 0.91–1.32 — relative).
cards.watchOut: ACST-2’s entry rule is its fence: both doctor and patient had already decided a procedure should be done — so it cannot say whether either procedure beats medical therapy alone (that is CREST-2, Card 7). Its other lesson is about era: a 1% procedural disabling-stroke-or-death rate in both arms is roughly half what the symptomatic trials of the 2000s reported, reflecting modern operators, devices, and medical therapy. Registered with ISRCTN (ISRCTN21144362).
cards.source: Halliday A et al. Second asymptomatic carotid surgery trial (ACST-2): a randomised comparison of carotid artery stenting versus carotid endarterectomy. Lancet. 2021. PMID 34469763 · ISRCTN21144362. DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(21)01910-3

cards.headline: CREST-2 (Brott 2026 — reported 2026): adding stenting to intensive medical therapy lowered 4-year events (2.8% vs 6.0%, P=0.02); adding endarterectomy did not, significantly (3.7% vs 5.3%)
cards.summary: Two parallel trials in high-grade (70% or more) asymptomatic stenosis. Stenting trial (1,245 patients): 4-year primary-outcome incidence 2.8% (95% CI 1.5–4.3) with stenting plus intensive medical management vs 6.0% (3.8–8.3) with medical management alone (P=0.02 for the absolute difference). Endarterectomy trial (1,240 patients): 3.7% (2.1–5.5) vs 5.3% (3.3–7.4) (P=0.24 — not significant).
cards.type: Two parallel, observer-blinded randomized trials (CREST-2), New England Journal of Medicine 2026 — carded and dated as a 2026 report
cards.people: 2,485 patients with high-grade (≥70%) asymptomatic carotid stenosis across 155 centres in five countries (1,245 in the stenting trial, 1,240 in the endarterectomy trial), all receiving intensive medical management. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: The primary outcome was any stroke or death within 44 days, or ipsilateral ischaemic stroke thereafter to 4 years. In the first 44 days of the stenting trial, no strokes or deaths occurred on medical therapy alone, vs seven strokes and one death with stenting; in the endarterectomy trial, three strokes on medical therapy vs nine with endarterectomy. Despite that early procedural cost, the stenting comparison favoured adding the procedure at 4 years (2.8% vs 6.0%; P=0.02), while the endarterectomy comparison did not reach significance (3.7% vs 5.3%; P=0.24).
cards.watchOut: Dated by design: this is a 2026 report, the newest evidence on the shelf, and agents should weight its vintage — it has had no time to be replicated or absorbed into guidelines, and secondary publications from the programme (including cognitive-outcome papers) are appearing alongside it. It also reframes the older cards: ’intensive medical management’ in CREST-2 is a far stronger comparator than the background therapy of the 2000s trials, which is precisely why a procedural benefit had to be re-proven — and why, for endarterectomy, it narrowly was not.
cards.source: Brott TG et al. Medical Management and Revascularization for Asymptomatic Carotid Stenosis. N Engl J Med. 2026. PMID 41269206 · NCT02089217. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2508800

shelves.title: CGRP therapies for migraine prevention: roughly half of patients respond, versus a quarter on placebo — in trials that mostly ran twelve weeks
shelves.question: In episodic and chronic migraine, do CGRP-pathway therapies — the monoclonal antibodies and the oral gepants — prevent attacks better than placebo and better than older preventives, and what remains unknown?
shelves.mesh: Migraine Disorders · Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide Receptor Antagonists · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Topiramate · Humans
shelves.balance: Printed the way this shelf insists — as absolute responder percentages, drug vs placebo: STRIVE (erenumab) 43.3% at 70 mg and 50.0% at 140 mg vs 26.6%; HALO episodic (fremanezumab) 47.7% vs 27.9%, and in chronic migraine 40.8% vs 18.1%; EVOLVE-1 (galcanezumab) 62.3% vs 38.6%; ADVANCE (atogepant, oral) about 61% at 60 mg. In monthly-migraine-day terms the antibodies and the gepant alike buy roughly 1.3–1.9 days a month beyond placebo. The one head-to-head trial (HER-MES) favoured erenumab over topiramate on both response (55.4% vs 31.2%; odds ratio 2.76, relative) and tolerability (discontinuation for adverse events 10.6% vs 38.9%). Now the two standing cautions. First, time: the pivotal trials behind these numbers ran a median of about 12 weeks (STRIVE and EVOLVE-1 ran 6 months) — durability and rare harms beyond that window rest on extension studies, not blinded trials. Second, biology: CGRP is a potent vasodilator, and long-term cardiovascular safety of blocking it for years remains open; the trial-era harms were mostly injection-site reactions, constipation, and nausea, with erenumab additionally carrying constipation and hypertension warnings on its label. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: STRIVE (Goadsby 2017): erenumab — at least 50% fewer migraine days in 43.3% (70 mg) and 50.0% (140 mg) vs 26.6% on placebo
cards.summary: Monthly migraine days by months 4–6 fell by 3.2 (70 mg) and 3.7 (140 mg) vs 1.8 on placebo (P<0.001 for both). A reduction of 50% or more was achieved by 43.3% and 50.0% vs 26.6% (P<0.001) — 955 patients with episodic migraine, treated for 6 months.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (STRIVE), New England Journal of Medicine 2017
cards.people: 955 patients with episodic migraine (baseline average 8.3 migraine days a month), randomized to monthly subcutaneous erenumab 70 mg (317), erenumab 140 mg (319), or placebo (319) for 6 months. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Both doses beat placebo on the primary endpoint (change in monthly migraine days) and on acute-medication days (down 1.1 and 1.6 days vs 0.2) and physical-function scores. Rates of adverse events were similar between erenumab and placebo.
cards.watchOut: A 6-month trial — the longest placebo-controlled run on this shelf — and its authors’ own caution stands: long-term safety and durability require further study. Responder percentages are the honest currency here (roughly 17–23 extra responders per 100 treated); days-per-month differences beyond placebo were 1.4–1.9. Constipation and a later hypertension label warning attach to erenumab in practice (see the shelf balance); neither was a signal inside this trial’s window.
cards.source: Goadsby PJ et al. A Controlled Trial of Erenumab for Episodic Migraine. N Engl J Med. 2017. PMID 29171821 · NCT02456740. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1705848

cards.headline: HALO episodic (Dodick 2018): fremanezumab cut monthly migraine days by 1.5 (monthly dosing) beyond placebo; responders 47.7% vs 27.9%
cards.summary: Over 12 weeks, monthly migraine days fell by 4.0 days on monthly fremanezumab and 3.9 on a single quarterly-intended dose, vs 2.6 on placebo — differences of −1.5 and −1.3 days (P<0.001). The proportion with at least a 50% reduction, as reported in the paper, was 47.7% vs 27.9% — 875 patients with episodic migraine.
cards.people: 875 patients aged 18–70 with episodic migraine (mean age 41.8 years; 85% women), randomized to monthly fremanezumab 225 mg, a single 675 mg dose, or placebo; patients who had failed two preventive classes were excluded; 90.4% completed.
cards.result: Mean monthly migraine days fell from about 9 at baseline to 4.9 (monthly), 5.3 (single higher dose), and 6.5 (placebo) at 12 weeks — differences vs placebo of −1.5 days (95% CI −2.01 to −0.93) and −1.3 days (−1.79 to −0.72), both P<0.001. Discontinuations for adverse events were few; the commonest were injection-site reactions, with isolated cases of diarrhoea, anxiety, and depression (two patients each).
cards.watchOut: Twelve weeks. The responder percentages (47.7 vs 27.9) are this card’s headline because the shelf prints absolute responder rates for every trial — but note the trial excluded patients who had already failed two preventive classes, so its population is kinder than a refractory-migraine clinic. As with the whole shelf, durability and long-term safety were explicitly left for further research by the authors.
cards.source: Dodick DW et al. Effect of Fremanezumab Compared With Placebo for Prevention of Episodic Migraine: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2018. PMID 29800211 · NCT02629861. DOI 10.1001/jama.2018.4853
