cards.headline: HALO chronic (Silberstein 2017): fremanezumab in chronic migraine — at least 50% fewer headache days in 41% (monthly) vs 18% on placebo
cards.summary: Headache days per month fell by 4.6 (monthly) and 4.3 (quarterly) vs 2.5 on placebo (P<0.001 for both); a reduction of at least 50% was achieved by 41% (monthly; 40.8% as reported) and 38% (quarterly) vs 18% (18.1%) on placebo — 1,130 patients with chronic migraine, over 12 weeks.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase III trial (HALO-CM), New England Journal of Medicine 2017
cards.people: 1,130 patients with chronic migraine, randomized to fremanezumab quarterly (376), fremanezumab monthly (379), or placebo (375) for 12 weeks; baseline headache days about 13 a month in each group. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Both regimens beat placebo on the primary endpoint (least-squares mean reductions of 4.3 ± 0.3 and 4.6 ± 0.3 vs 2.5 ± 0.3 headache days a month; P<0.001) and on the 50%-responder endpoint (38% and 41% vs 18%; P<0.001). Abnormalities of hepatic function occurred in 5 patients in each fremanezumab group (1%) vs 3 on placebo (under 1%); injection-site reactions were common.
cards.watchOut: Chronic migraine is the heavier disease — and note the placebo arm also improved by 2.5 days a month, a reminder of how much of migraine-trial movement is regression and expectation, which is exactly why the shelf prints drug-minus-placebo responder gaps rather than within-arm improvements. Twelve weeks; the authors state plainly that long-term durability and safety require further study.

cards.headline: EVOLVE-1 (Stauffer 2018): galcanezumab — migraine days down 4.7 vs 2.8 on placebo; responders 62.3% vs 38.6%
cards.summary: Monthly migraine headache days over 6 months fell by 4.7 days (120 mg) and 4.6 (240 mg) vs 2.8 on placebo (both P<0.001); the proportion achieving at least a 50% reduction, as reported in the paper, was 62.3% on 120 mg vs 38.6% on placebo — 858 patients in the intention-to-treat population.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (EVOLVE-1), JAMA Neurology 2018
cards.people: 858 adults aged 18–65 (mean age 40.7 years; 83.7% women) with 4–14 migraine headache days a month, randomized 2:1:1 to placebo, galcanezumab 120 mg, or galcanezumab 240 mg monthly for 6 months; no other preventives allowed.
cards.result: Both doses met the primary objective (reductions of 4.7 and 4.6 days vs 2.8 on placebo; P<0.001), with all key secondary endpoints — including 50%, 75%, and 100% responder thresholds, acute-medication days, and quality-of-life scores — significant after multiplicity adjustment. There were no meaningful differences between the 120 mg and 240 mg doses. Completion was 81.9%, and discontinuation for adverse events was under 5% in every group.
cards.watchOut: EVOLVE-1’s responder gap (about 24 extra responders per 100) is the widest on this shelf — read it beside its high placebo response (38.6%), which reflects an episodic-migraine trial population with frequent attacks and close diary follow-up. Six months of treatment is longer than most cards here, but it is still not the timescale on which these drugs are actually taken, and the trial says nothing about cardiovascular outcomes (see shelf balance).

cards.headline: HER-MES (Reuter 2022): the head-to-head — erenumab beat topiramate on response (55.4% vs 31.2%; OR 2.76, relative) and on staying on treatment (discontinuation 10.6% vs 38.9%)
cards.summary: Over 24 weeks in 777 patients: discontinuation because of adverse events — the primary endpoint — in 10.6% on erenumab vs 38.9% on topiramate (odds ratio 0.19, relative). At least 50% fewer monthly migraine days in the last 3 months: 55.4% vs 31.2% (odds ratio 2.76, relative; 95% CI 2.06–3.71) — absolute percentages printed beside both ratios.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, double-dummy, active-controlled phase IV trial (HER-MES), Cephalalgia 2022
cards.people: 777 adults with at least 4 migraine days a month, naive to both study drugs, at 82 sites in Germany, randomized to erenumab (70 or 140 mg monthly) plus oral placebo, or topiramate (50–100 mg/day, individually titrated) plus injection placebo, for 24 weeks; 95.1% completed. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Erenumab won the tolerability primary endpoint by a wide margin (discontinuation for adverse events 10.6% vs 38.9%; OR 0.19; P<0.001) and the efficacy secondary endpoint (≥50% responders 55.4% vs 31.2%; OR 2.76; P<0.001). No new safety signals occurred.
cards.watchOut: The shelf’s only active-comparator card, and the comparison flatters the antibody twice over: topiramate’s cognitive and paraesthesia burden is the commonest reason patients abandon oral preventives, and a double-dummy design cannot hide which burden is whose for long. Even so, the tolerability gap is the most decision-relevant number on this shelf for a patient choosing between an injection and a daily tablet — and efficacy favoured the antibody on top of it. Industry-conducted (erenumab’s makers); single-country; 24 weeks.

cards.headline: ADVANCE (Ailani 2021): atogepant — the oral gepant; migraine days down 4.2 on 60 mg vs 2.5 on placebo, responders about 61%; constipation and nausea the common adverse events
cards.summary: Change in monthly migraine days over 12 weeks: −3.7 (10 mg), −3.9 (30 mg), −4.2 (60 mg) vs −2.5 on placebo (differences −1.2, −1.4, −1.7 days; all P<0.001). The proportion with at least a 50% reduction reached about 61% at the 60 mg dose, as reported in the paper — 873 patients in the efficacy analysis.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, phase III trial (ADVANCE), New England Journal of Medicine 2021
cards.people: 910 adults with 4–14 migraine days a month enrolled (873 in the efficacy analysis), randomized to atogepant 10, 30, or 60 mg daily or placebo for 12 weeks; baseline migraine days 7.5–7.9 a month. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: All three doses beat placebo on the primary endpoint and on headache days; most secondary endpoints favoured atogepant. The commonest adverse events were constipation (6.9–7.7% across doses) and nausea (4.4–6.1%). Serious adverse events included one case each of asthma and optic neuritis in the 10 mg group.
cards.watchOut: The gepant card matters because it removes the injection: an oral CGRP drug with antibody-class efficacy shifts the comparison toward tolerability and preference. Twelve weeks only — the authors state that longer and larger trials are needed for effect and safety — and rimegepant’s prevention evidence (every-other-day dosing) is thinner still and is not carded here. Nothing on this shelf yet answers what years of CGRP blockade do to cardiovascular physiology; see the balance.

shelves.title: First-line antiseizure medicines (SANAD II): lamotrigine holds focal epilepsy, valproate holds generalised — behind a teratogenicity fence
shelves.question: In newly diagnosed epilepsy, which antiseizure medicine should be started first — and where the winner is valproate, what does winning cost?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Anticonvulsants · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Epilepsies, Partial · Lamotrigine · Levetiracetam
shelves.balance: Start where SANAD II landed. In focal epilepsy, levetiracetam — the modern default — FAILED noninferiority against lamotrigine for time to 12-month remission (HR 1.18, against a limit of 1.329), per-protocol analyses favoured lamotrigine outright (HR 1.32 and 1.37), lamotrigine caused fewer adverse reactions (33% vs 44% on levetiracetam and 45% on zonisamide), and lamotrigine was cost-dominant. In generalised or unclassifiable epilepsy, levetiracetam failed noninferiority against valproate the same way (HR 1.19), and valproate cut treatment failure (HR 0.65, relative). Now the asterisk, printed on the shelf rather than footnoted: valproate in pregnancy carries roughly a 10% risk of major congenital malformations and lowers the exposed child's IQ by about 7–10 points, and regulators fence it away from women and girls of childbearing potential unless alternatives have failed and a pregnancy-prevention programme is in place. Both things are true at once: valproate is the most effective first drug for generalised epilepsy, and a large group of patients must not take it. SANAD I (2007) is the anchor — it pointed the same way a trial generation earlier. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: SANAD II focal (Marson 2021): levetiracetam FAILED noninferiority vs lamotrigine — HR 1.18 against a 1.329 limit
cards.summary: 990 patients with newly diagnosed focal epilepsy: time to 12-month remission on levetiracetam vs lamotrigine, HR 1.18 (97.5% CI 0.95–1.47) — noninferiority not met; per-protocol, lamotrigine was superior (HR 1.32). Adverse reactions 33% on lamotrigine vs 44% levetiracetam, 45% zonisamide.
cards.type: Randomized, open-label, controlled noninferiority trial (SANAD II), Lancet 2021
cards.people: 990 participants aged 5 years or older with newly diagnosed focal epilepsy, recruited across UK adult and paediatric neurology services and followed for a further 2 years: lamotrigine 330, levetiracetam 332, zonisamide 328. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Levetiracetam did not meet noninferiority for time to 12-month remission (HR 1.18; 97.5% CI 0.95–1.47; the noninferiority limit was 1.329); zonisamide did meet noninferiority in the intention-to-treat analysis (HR 1.03; 0.83–1.28). Per-protocol, 12-month remission was superior on lamotrigine versus both levetiracetam (HR 1.32; 1.05–1.66) and zonisamide (HR 1.37; 1.08–1.73). Adverse reactions: 33% lamotrigine, 44% levetiracetam, 45% zonisamide. Lamotrigine was superior in the cost-utility analysis (net health benefit 1.403 QALYs vs 1.222 levetiracetam and 1.232 zonisamide at £20,000 per QALY).
cards.watchOut: Open-label, as a first-line epilepsy trial almost has to be — patients and clinicians knew the drug. The headline is a failed noninferiority, not a proven large harm: the confidence interval for levetiracetam (0.95–1.47) crosses 1. But noninferiority was the claim levetiracetam needed, it missed intention-to-treat and lost outright per-protocol, and it cost more for more adverse reactions. The authors' conclusion is the shelf's: these findings do not support levetiracetam or zonisamide as first-line treatments for focal epilepsy.
cards.source: Marson A et al. cards.headline: SANAD II generalised (Marson 2021): levetiracetam failed noninferiority vs valproate (HR 1.19) — and valproate carries the teratogenicity asterisk
cards.summary: 520 patients with generalised or unclassifiable epilepsy: levetiracetam vs valproate HR 1.19 for time to 12-month remission — noninferiority not met; valproate also won on treatment failure (HR 0.65, relative). The efficacy winner is fenced off from women of childbearing potential: major malformations ~10%, IQ −7 to −10 in exposed children.
cards.type: Randomized, open-label, controlled noninferiority trial (SANAD II), Lancet 2021
cards.people: 520 participants aged 5 years or older (median age 13.9 years, range 5.0–94.4; 65% male) with newly diagnosed generalised (397) or unclassified (123) epilepsy, recruited at 69 UK centres: levetiracetam 260, valproate 260.
cards.result: Levetiracetam did not meet the criteria for noninferiority against valproate for time to 12-month remission (HR 1.19; the noninferiority limit was an HR of 1.314). Valproate was superior for time to treatment failure (HR 0.65, a relative effect). In the unclassified-epilepsy subgroup the direction favoured levetiracetam — the one corner where it led.
cards.watchOut: The teratogenicity asterisk, in full: valproate taken in pregnancy is associated with major congenital malformations in roughly 10% of exposed children and with IQ scores about 7–10 points lower, alongside other neurodevelopmental disorders. UK and EU regulators restrict valproate in women and girls of childbearing potential to cases where alternatives have failed, under a formal pregnancy-prevention programme. So this trial's winner is unavailable, by design, to a large share of the people who develop generalised epilepsy young — which is precisely why the less effective levetiracetam remains in widespread use. Efficacy and the fence coexist; neither cancels the other.
cards.source: Marson A et al. cards.headline: SANAD I focal (Marson 2007): lamotrigine beat carbamazepine on treatment failure — the anchor SANAD II confirmed
cards.summary: 1,721 patients: for time to treatment failure, lamotrigine was significantly better than carbamazepine (HR 0.78; 0.63–0.97), gabapentin (HR 0.65) and topiramate; per-protocol remission analyses suggested noninferiority to carbamazepine.
cards.type: Randomized, unblinded, controlled trial (SANAD, arm A), Lancet 2007
cards.people: 1,721 patients in UK hospital outpatient clinics for whom carbamazepine was deemed standard treatment, randomized to carbamazepine, gabapentin, lamotrigine, oxcarbazepine, or topiramate. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: For time to treatment failure, lamotrigine was clinically better than carbamazepine (HR 0.78; 95% CI 0.63–0.97), gabapentin (0.65; 0.52–0.80), and topiramate; per-protocol, the differences in 12-month remission at 2 and 4 years (0 and 5 percentage points) suggested lamotrigine's noninferiority to carbamazepine. Lamotrigine was therefore also a cost-effective alternative.
cards.watchOut: Unblinded, and its comparator set is dated — no levetiracetam arm, which is why SANAD II had to be run. Its role on this shelf is the anchor: the lamotrigine-first answer for focal epilepsy is now two trial generations deep.

cards.headline: SANAD I generalised (Marson 2007): valproate better tolerated than topiramate, more efficacious than lamotrigine
cards.summary: 716 patients: valproate beat lamotrigine on treatment failure overall (HR 0.76; 0.62–0.94) and in idiopathic generalised epilepsy (HR 0.68; 0.53–0.89); no significant difference vs topiramate, which was worse tolerated.
cards.type: Randomized, unblinded, controlled trial (SANAD, arm B), Lancet 2007
cards.people: 716 patients with generalised-onset seizures or seizures difficult to classify, randomized to valproate, lamotrigine, or topiramate (recruited 1999–2004, follow-up to 2006). (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Valproate was significantly better than lamotrigine for time to treatment failure overall (HR 0.76; 95% CI 0.62–0.94) and in the idiopathic generalised subgroup (0.68; 0.53–0.89). There was no significant difference between valproate and topiramate on efficacy, but valproate was better tolerated. The authors concluded valproate should remain the drug of first choice for many patients with generalised and unclassified epilepsies.

shelves.title: Levodopa first in Parkinson's disease: the old drug wins on quality of life — and starting it early changes nothing long-term
shelves.question: In early Parkinson's disease, should treatment start with levodopa or with a levodopa-sparing drug — and does levodopa's timing change the disease?
shelves.mesh: Antiparkinson Agents · Dopamine Agonists · Drug Therapy, Combination · Levodopa · Monoamine Oxidase Inhibitors · Parkinson Disease
shelves.balance: Levodopa-phobia — delaying the best drug for fear of spending it — is retired by this shelf. PD MED randomized 1,620 people to start on levodopa or to spare it (agonist or MAO-B inhibitor first): patient-rated mobility ran 1.8 points better on levodopa, sustained over 7 years, with no mortality penalty. Print the yardstick beside the effect, as this shelf insists: 1.8 points on the PDQ-39 mobility dimension is below the published minimal-important-difference estimates for that dimension (~3.2 points; the trial's own protocol used 6 points) — a real but modest edge, bought with the oldest, cheapest drug. LEAP then asked the timing question directly and answered it with a null: starting levodopa 40 weeks earlier changed nothing measurable at week 80, and five-year follow-up found no significant dyskinesia penalty for starting early (46/160 vs 62/161, P=0.06 — numerically favouring early, if anything). The agonists' price list is carded, not whispered: impulse-control disorders in 17.1% of agonist-treated patients vs 6.9% of those not taking one, in DOMINION's 3,090-patient cross-section. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: PD MED (Gray 2014): starting on levodopa beat sparing it — PDQ-39 mobility 1.8 points better, sustained over 7 years
cards.summary: 1,620 patients with early Parkinson's: mobility scores averaged 1.8 points (95% CI 0.5–3.0; P=0.005) better on levodopa than on levodopa-sparing therapy, with no increase or attrition of benefit over 7 years — and 1.8 points sits below the ~3.2-point minimal important difference estimated for that dimension.
cards.type: Pragmatic, open-label, randomized trial (PD MED), Lancet 2014
cards.people: 1,620 patients newly diagnosed with Parkinson's disease (recruited 2000–2009), randomized to levodopa (528), dopamine agonist (632), or MAO-B inhibitor (460); median follow-up 3 years, observation to 7 years. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: PDQ-39 mobility scores averaged 1.8 points better in patients assigned to levodopa than in those assigned to levodopa-sparing therapy (95% CI 0.5–3.0; P=0.005). MAO-B inhibitors beat dopamine agonists by 1.4 points (0.0–2.9; P=0.05). EQ-5D utility scores averaged 0.03 better with levodopa (P=0.0002). There was no mortality penalty for starting levodopa (dementia HR 0.81 and institutional admission HR 0.86 — relative effects, both non-significant).
cards.watchOut: The MCID caveat, printed fairly: the trial protocol defined 6 points as the minimally important difference on the PDQ-39 mobility dimension, and published estimates for that dimension run about 3.2 points — the 1.8-point average advantage clears neither. What carries the shelf is the pattern, not the single number: the edge persisted for 7 years, quality-of-life utility agreed, the sparing strategies never caught up, and levodopa is the cheapest drug in the comparison. Open-label by design — a pragmatic trial of drug classes, not molecules.
cards.source: Gray R et al. Lancet. 2014. PMID 24928805 · ISRCTN69812316. DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(14)60683-8

cards.headline: LEAP (Verschuur 2019): delayed-start null — levodopa showed no disease-modifying effect
cards.summary: 445 patients with early Parkinson's: change in UPDRS score at week 80 was −1.0 points on early-start levodopa vs −2.0 on delayed-start (difference 1.0; 95% CI −1.5 to 3.5; P=0.44). No significant difference — levodopa treats symptoms; this trial found no sign it changes the disease.
cards.type: Multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled, delayed-start randomized trial (LEAP), New England Journal of Medicine 2019
cards.people: 445 patients with early Parkinson's disease, randomized to levodopa/carbidopa 100/25 mg three times daily for 80 weeks (222) or placebo for 40 weeks followed by the same drug for 40 weeks (223). Baseline UPDRS 28.1 vs 29.3 points. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: The between-group difference in change in total UPDRS score from baseline to week 80 was 1.0 point (95% CI −1.5 to 3.5; P=0.44) — no significant difference, which implies levodopa had no disease-modifying effect in this design. Symptom progression between weeks 4 and 40 was slower on levodopa (the symptomatic effect), and early initiation was noninferior to delayed initiation in the second phase.
cards.watchOut: A delayed-start design is the cleanest test of disease modification available, and it returned a clean null — the delayed group caught up completely once treated, the signature of a purely symptomatic drug. The practical corollary matters as much: nothing was lost by the delay either, so timing can be governed by symptoms, not by fear in either direction. Card 3 follows the same patients to five years.

cards.headline: LEAP at five years (Frequin 2024): no dyskinesia penalty for starting levodopa early — 46/160 vs 62/161, P=0.06
cards.summary: Five-year follow-up of the LEAP cohort: dyskinesia occurred in 46 of 160 patients who started levodopa early vs 62 of 161 who started 40 weeks later (P=0.06) — the numerical direction favours early start, and the difference is not significant.
cards.type: Long-term follow-up of a randomized delayed-start trial (LEAP), Movement Disorders 2024
cards.people: The LEAP trial cohort (445 randomized) followed long-term; five-year dyskinesia data in 321 patients (160 early-start, 161 delayed-start). (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: The follow-up compared outcomes in patients first treated with a low dose of levodopa 40 weeks earlier versus 40 weeks later, over the subsequent 5 years. Dyskinesia: 46/160 early-start vs 62/161 delayed-start (P=0.06) — no significant excess in the early group on the outcome clinicians feared most.
cards.watchOut: The old fear was specific: early levodopa was supposed to buy later dyskinesia. Five years out, the early starters had numerically LESS dyskinesia — the opposite direction, and not significant, so the card claims no advantage, only the absence of the feared penalty. Follow-up of a trial cohort is no longer the full randomized comparison (attrition applies), which is why this card supports, and does not lead, the shelf.

cards.headline: The agonist price list: impulse-control disorders in 17.1% on agonists vs 6.9% without (DOMINION) — and CALM-PD's trade in full
cards.summary: DOMINION (3,090 patients): an impulse-control disorder was present in 17.1% of patients taking a dopamine agonist vs 6.9% of those not taking one. CALM-PD (301 patients): starting pramipexole delayed dyskinesia and wearing-off (28% vs 51% on levodopa) but controlled symptoms less well (UPDRS improvement 4.5 vs 9.2 points) with more somnolence (32.4% vs 17.3%).
cards.type: Cross-sectional study (DOMINION), Archives of Neurology 2010 · Randomized controlled trial (CALM-PD), JAMA 2000 — two exhibits on one card
cards.people: DOMINION: 3,090 patients with treated idiopathic Parkinson's disease receiving routine care at 46 movement-disorder centres in the United States and Canada, assessed with validated gambling, sexual-behaviour, buying, and binge-eating instruments, by raters blinded to medication status. CALM-PD: 301 patients with early Parkinson's disease at 22 US and Canadian sites, randomized to pramipexole (151) or carbidopa/levodopa. (The abstract records do not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: DOMINION: 13.6% of all patients had at least one impulse-control disorder (problem/pathological gambling 5.0%, compulsive sexual behaviour 3.5%, compulsive buying 5.7%, binge-eating disorder 4.3%; 3.9% had two or more). Dopamine agonist treatment was associated with 2- to 3.5-fold increased odds of an impulse-control disorder (relative), a class effect across all four disorders. CALM-PD: dopaminergic motor complications (wearing off, dyskinesias, on-off fluctuations) developed in 28% on initial pramipexole vs 51% on initial levodopa (HR 0.45, relative) — but levodopa improved total UPDRS nearly twice as much (9.2 vs 4.5 points; P<0.001), and somnolence was more common on pramipexole (32.4% vs 17.3%; P=0.003).
cards.watchOut: DOMINION is cross-sectional — it measures association at a moment, not incidence caused over time, and it is carded as such; the class-wide consistency and the size of the gap (17.1% vs 6.9%) are why it anchors the price list rather than a smaller study. CALM-PD is the honest other side: agonists genuinely delayed motor complications. The shelf's verdict is not that agonists are bad drugs — it is that sparing levodopa out of fear costs more, in control and in behaviour, than it saves.

shelves.title: Middle meningeal artery embolization for chronic subdural hematoma: fewer reoperations in two trials — but one primary endpoint missed, one trial null, and the pooled estimate is not significant
shelves.question: In chronic subdural hematoma, does embolizing the middle meningeal artery — added to surgery or usual care — prevent the hematoma coming back?
shelves.mesh: Embolization, Therapeutic · Hematoma, Subdural, Chronic · Meningeal Arteries · Recurrence · Reoperation · Stroke
shelves.balance: Three large randomized trials ran at once, and they do not agree cleanly — which is why this shelf is POSSIBLE, not more. EMBOLISE (surgical patients) cut reoperation from 11.3% to 4.1%. STEM (surgical or nonsurgical care) cut its treatment-failure composite from 36% to 16%. But MAGIC-MT, the largest trial, MISSED its primary endpoint (6.7% vs 9.9%, P=0.10) — printed on this shelf's face, not footnoted — and EMPROTECT, in high-risk post-surgical patients, missed too (14.8% vs 21.0%, P=0.13). Pool the three NEJM trials and the recurrence estimate is RR 0.50 with a confidence interval that crosses 1 (0.23–1.06, P=0.058): not significant overall, significant only in the nonsurgical subgroup, and with no effect on functional outcome (RR 1.01). The procedure's own harms are small but real — in EMBOLISE, 2.0% had a serious procedure-related event by 30 days, including disabling stroke in 2 patients. A promising adjunct whose best-supported use may be in patients managed without surgery; the developer ruled POSSIBLE on Nov 7, 2026. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: EMBOLISE (Davies 2024): embolization plus surgery cut reoperation to 4.1% vs 11.3%
cards.summary: 400 patients with symptomatic subacute or chronic subdural hematoma needing surgical evacuation: hematoma recurrence or progression leading to repeat surgery within 90 days in 4.1% vs 11.3% (relative risk 0.36, labeled relative; P=0.008) — an absolute difference of 7.2 points. The other side, on the same card: mortality at 90 days 5.1% vs 3.0% , and serious procedure-related adverse events in 2.0% by 30 days, including disabling stroke in 2 patients.
cards.type: Prospective, multicenter, randomized, adaptive-design trial (EMBOLISE), New England Journal of Medicine 2024
cards.people: 400 patients (197 embolization plus surgery, 203 surgery alone) with symptomatic subacute or chronic subdural hematoma and an indication for surgical evacuation; surgery had already occurred before randomization in 34.0%. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Hematoma recurrence or progression leading to repeat surgery occurred in 8 patients (4.1%) in the embolization group vs 23 (11.3%) with surgery alone (relative risk 0.36 [0.11–0.80], P=0.008 — a relative effect; the absolute difference is 7.2 percentage points). Functional deterioration at 90 days: 11.9% vs 9.8% (risk difference 2.1 points [−4.8 to 8.9], meeting the trial's noninferiority margin). Mortality at 90 days was 5.1% vs 3.0% — numerically higher with embolization, on small numbers.
cards.watchOut: The benefit is a reoperation endpoint, not a functional one — deterioration rates were similar. Harms ride on the same card: by 30 days, serious adverse events related to the embolization procedure had occurred in 4 patients (2.0%), including disabling stroke in 2; no additional events by 180 days. Industry-funded (Medtronic). The trial answers the surgical-adjunct question only — patients managed without surgery are STEM and MAGIC-MT territory (References 2–3).

cards.headline: STEM (Fiorella 2025): treatment failure 16% vs 36% — a composite driven by recurrence and reoperation
cards.summary: 310 patients with symptomatic chronic subdural hematoma, surgical or nonsurgical standard care: the primary composite — recurrent or residual hematoma >10 mm at 180 days, reoperation or surgical rescue, or major disabling stroke, MI, or neurologic death — occurred in 16% vs 36% (odds ratio 0.36; P=0.001), an absolute difference of 20 points. Deaths through 180 days ran the other way numerically: 8% vs 5% .
cards.type: Multicenter, randomized trial (STEM), New England Journal of Medicine 2025
cards.people: 310 patients enrolled (149 embolization, 161 control); 189 were to receive surgical standard treatment and 121 nonsurgical. Mean age 73 years; 70% men. The primary efficacy analysis included 249 patients (120 vs 129).
cards.result: A primary-outcome event occurred in 19 of 120 patients (16%) in the embolization group vs 47 of 129 (36%) in the control group (odds ratio 0.36 [0.20–0.66], P=0.001). The primary safety outcome — major disabling stroke or death within 30 days — was 3% in both groups (4 of 144 vs 5 of 166). Through 180 days, 12 patients (8%) in the embolization group and 9 (5%) in the control group had died; death from neurologic causes occurred in 1 (1%) vs 3 (2%).
cards.watchOut: Read the composite before the headline: most of its weight is radiographic recurrence/residual hematoma and reoperation, not death or disability — and all-cause deaths at 180 days were numerically more frequent with embolization (8% vs 5%), on small counts. Industry-funded (Balt USA). The trial mixed surgical and nonsurgical patients; the pooled analysis on Card 5 suggests the nonsurgical subgroup is where the effect concentrates.

cards.headline: MAGIC-MT (Liu 2024): the primary endpoint MISSED — 6.7% vs 9.9%, P=0.10
cards.summary: 722 patients in China with symptomatic nonacute subdural hematoma: symptomatic recurrence or progression within 90 days in 6.7% vs 9.9% (difference −3.3 points [−7.4 to 0.8]; P=0.10 — not significant ). Serious adverse events were lower with embolization: 6.7% vs 11.6% (P=0.02). The missed primary is this shelf's honesty anchor: the largest trial did not prove its main claim.
cards.type: Multicenter, open-label, randomized trial (MAGIC-MT), New England Journal of Medicine 2024
cards.people: 722 patients (360 embolization, 362 usual care) with symptomatic nonacute subdural hematoma with mass effect, at Chinese centers; burr-hole drainage was performed in 78.3%. Patients whose condition warranted craniotomy were excluded. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Symptomatic recurrence or progression within 90 days occurred in 24 patients (6.7%) in the embolization group and 36 (9.9%) in the usual-care group (between-group difference −3.3 percentage points [−7.4 to 0.8]; P=0.10) — the primary endpoint was not met. The incidence of serious adverse events was lower in the embolization group than in the usual-care group (6.7% vs 11.6%, P=0.02).
cards.watchOut: A missed primary endpoint in the largest trial is the single strongest reason this shelf is POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY, and it is printed here at full size. The confidence interval (−7.4 to +0.8 points) still includes a meaningful benefit — 'missed' is not 'disproven' — but a shelf that quotes EMBOLISE and STEM without this card would be advertising, not evidence. The lower serious-adverse-event rate is a genuine counterweight and is printed with it.

cards.headline: EMPROTECT (Shotar 2025): primary endpoint missed in high-risk post-surgical patients — 14.8% vs 21.0%, P=0.13
cards.summary: 342 patients in France who had surgery for a first or recurrent chronic subdural hematoma and were at high risk of recurrence: recurrence at 6 months in 14.8% vs 21.0% (odds ratio 0.64 [0.36–1.14]; P=0.13 — not significant ). Repeat surgery: 4.3% vs 8.3% (P=0.14). Procedure-related complications: minor 1.8%, major 0.6%.
cards.type: Multicenter, open-label, randomized clinical trial with blinded endpoint assessment (EMPROTECT), JAMA 2025
cards.people: 342 randomized patients (171 embolization, 171 standard care) at 12 French centers; median age 77 years (IQR 68–83); 274 (80.1%) men; 308 (90.1%) completed the trial.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — chronic subdural hematoma recurrence at 6 months, adjudicated blinded — was observed in 24 of 162 patients (14.8%) in the intervention group and 33 of 157 (21.0%) in the control group (after imputation: odds ratio 0.64 [0.36–1.14]; adjusted absolute difference −6 points [−14 to 2]; P=0.13). No secondary endpoint differed significantly. Repeat surgery for homolateral recurrence: 7 of 162 (4.3%) vs 13 of 157 (8.3%) (P=0.14).
cards.watchOut: The second missed primary on this shelf — and in the population (post-surgical, high recurrence risk) where the adjunct case looked strongest. The authors' own caution is the card's: the effect estimate's magnitude is consistent with the positive trials, so the finding argues for better patient selection, not for abandoning the procedure — but consistency of point estimates is not proof, and two of four large trials missing their primaries is the fact pattern behind the POSSIBLE stamp.

cards.headline: Pooled (Gillespie 2025): recurrence RR 0.50 — but the interval crosses 1 (0.23–1.06); benefit significant only without surgery
cards.summary: Meta-analysis of the three NEJM trials (EMBOLISE, STEM, MAGIC-MT; 1,432 patients): recurrence or progression RR 0.50 (0.23–1.06), P=0.058 — NOT significant overall (relative measure). In patients managed with surgery : RR 0.60 (0.19–1.88), not significant. In nonsurgical management: RR 0.36 (0.22–0.60), significant. Functional outcome: RR 1.01 — no effect.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 3 randomized trials (random-effects), Acta Neurochirurgica 2025
cards.people: 1,432 patients pooled from MAGIC-MT, EMBOLISE, and STEM. (EMPROTECT, Card 4, reported after this analysis's search and is not in the pool.)
cards.result: Overall, embolization reduced symptomatic progression or recurrence but not significantly (relative risk 0.50 [0.23–1.06], P=0.058). For the group undergoing surgery, embolization was not associated with reduced recurrence (RR 0.60 [0.19–1.88], P=0.194). For nonsurgical management, embolization reduced progression (RR 0.36 [0.22–0.60], P<0.001). Embolization did not influence functional outcome (RR 1.01 [0.97–1.04], P=0.790). All figures are relative effects, printed as the analysis reports them.
cards.watchOut: The wide overall interval (0.23–1.06) is heterogeneity speaking: three trials, three populations, three primary endpoints. A later four-trial pooling using a treatment-failure endpoint (Xi 2025, PMID 41065869) found RR 0.55 [0.41–0.74] — significant — which shows how much the answer moves with the endpoint chosen; this shelf prints the more conservative recurrence pooling as its headline and names the other here rather than silently picking the friendlier number.

shelves.title: Preventing delirium: multicomponent bundles work — the founding trial was matched, not randomized, and prevention is the whole game
shelves.question: In hospitalized older patients, can delirium be prevented — and does anything here treat it once it starts?
shelves.mesh: Clinical Protocols · Delirium · Hospitalization · Incidence · Logistic Models · Prospective Studies
shelves.balance: The design caveat comes first, in the shelf's first lines, because the founding trial is routinely misdescribed: Inouye 1999 was a controlled MATCHED study, not a randomized trial — 852 patients, delirium 9.9% on the intervention units vs 15.0% on usual care (matched OR 0.60). The randomized and meta-analytic evidence that followed points the same way: Hshieh's meta-analysis pooled OR 0.47 for incident delirium, and the Burton Cochrane review found multicomponent interventions reduced delirium incidence to 10.5% vs 18.4% (RR 0.57 — a 43% relative reduction, moderate-certainty evidence), with mortality and length-of-stay benefits unproven. Marcantonio's randomized geriatrics-consultation trial in hip fracture cut delirium from 50% to 32%. And the shelf's boundary is printed in its founding card: once delirium was established, severity and recurrence did not improve — these bundles prevent; they do not treat. Treatment is the next shelf's null. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: Inouye 1999 (HELP): delirium 9.9% vs 15.0% — a MATCHED study, not a randomized trial; and once delirium started, severity and recurrence were null
cards.summary: 852 patients aged 70 or older: delirium developed in 9.9% of the intervention group vs 15.0% of the usual-care group (matched OR 0.60; 95% CI 0.39–0.92); total delirium days 105 vs 161 (P=0.02), episodes 62 vs 90. Severity of delirium and recurrence rates did NOT differ — prevention worked; treatment of established delirium did not.
cards.type: Prospective matched controlled study — NOT randomized (Hospital Elder Life Program), New England Journal of Medicine 1999
cards.people: 852 patients aged 70 years or older admitted to the general-medicine service of a teaching hospital: one intervention unit and two usual-care units, enrolled by a prospective matching strategy — matched, not randomized. (The abstract record does not print the sex mix.)
cards.result: The intervention was a set of standardized protocols for six risk factors: cognitive impairment, sleep deprivation, immobility, visual impairment, hearing impairment, and dehydration; overall adherence was 87%. Delirium developed in 9.9% vs 15.0% (matched OR 0.60; 0.39–0.92). The total number of days with delirium (105 vs 161) and episodes (62 vs 90) were significantly lower. Sleep-medication use fell, and cognitive impairment improved among patients impaired at admission.
cards.watchOut: Cite this study correctly: it is the most influential delirium-prevention paper ever published and it was NOT randomized — unit-level allocation with prospective matching leaves room for confounding that the later randomized literature (References 3–4) had to close. Its second lesson is printed in its own results: among patients who developed delirium anyway, severity and recurrence were unchanged. The bundle is a fence, not a cure.
cards.source: Inouye SK et al. A multicomponent intervention to prevent delirium in hospitalized older patients. N Engl J Med. 1999. PMID 10053175. DOI 10.1056/NEJM199903043400901 (Pre-registration era — no registry number applies.)

cards.headline: Hshieh 2015: meta-analysis of multicomponent interventions — incident delirium pooled OR 0.47
cards.summary: 14 interventional studies: 11 demonstrated significant reductions in delirium incidence, pooled OR 0.47 (95% CI 0.38–0.58); in the randomized-or-matched subset the reduction was 44% (OR 0.56; 0.42–0.76, relative). Falls also fell (OR 0.38); length of stay and institutionalization only trended.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, JAMA Internal Medicine 2015
cards.people: Fourteen interventional studies of multicomponent nonpharmacological delirium-prevention interventions in hospitalized patients (literature from 1999 to Dec 2013); 11 studies contributed to the delirium-incidence meta-analysis. (A meta-analysis — no single age or sex mix applies.)
cards.result: Pooled across 11 studies, delirium incidence fell with an odds ratio of 0.47 (95% CI 0.38–0.58); restricted to randomized or matched trials, OR 0.56 (0.42–0.76). Falls decreased significantly (OR 0.38; 0.25–0.60). Length of stay (mean difference −0.16 days) and institutionalization (OR 0.95) trended toward benefit without reaching significance.
cards.watchOut: Odds ratios flatter prevention effects when events are common — read 0.47 as a strong relative signal, and take the absolute rates from the Cochrane card (10.5% vs 18.4%). Heterogeneity across bundles is real: 'multicomponent' names a family of interventions sharing ingredients (orientation, mobilization, sleep protection, hydration, vision and hearing aids), not one fixed protocol.

cards.headline: Burton 2021 (Cochrane): multicomponent prevention — delirium 10.5% vs 18.4% (RR 0.57, a 43% relative reduction); mortality unproven
cards.summary: 22 randomized trials, 5,718 patients outside ICU: multicomponent interventions probably reduce delirium incidence (10.5% vs 18.4%; RR 0.57; 95% CI 0.46–0.71; 14 studies, 3,693 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). Inpatient mortality: RR 1.17, not significant, low-certainty — prevention of delirium, not of death.
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomized controlled trials, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2021
cards.people: 5,718 hospitalised adults cared for outside intensive care or high-dependency units, in 22 randomized trials; 14 trials (3,693 participants) compared a multicomponent intervention with usual care. (The review does not print a single age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Multicomponent non-pharmacological interventions probably reduce the incidence of delirium compared with usual care (RR 0.57; 95% CI 0.46–0.71 — a 43% relative reduction — with absolute incidences of 10.5% vs 18.4%; moderate-certainty evidence, downgraded for risk of bias). There may be little or no effect on inpatient mortality (5.2% vs 4.5%; RR 1.17; 0.79–1.74; low-certainty evidence).
cards.watchOut: Every included trial carried performance-bias risk — bundles cannot be blinded — and the certainty is moderate, not high. The LIKELY on this shelf rests on convergence across designs (matched, randomized, meta-analytic), not on any single flawless trial. What the review does not show matters equally: no proven effect on mortality, and little on length of stay.

cards.headline: Marcantonio 2001: proactive geriatrics consultation in hip fracture — delirium 32% vs 50% in a randomized trial
cards.summary: 126 patients aged 65 or older admitted emergently for hip-fracture repair: delirium in 32% with proactive geriatrics consultation vs 50% with usual care; severe delirium 12% vs 29%.
cards.type: Randomized, controlled trial, Journal of the American Geriatrics Society 2001
cards.people: 126 consenting patients 65 years or older (mean age 79 ± 8 years; 79% women) admitted emergently for surgical repair of a hip fracture, randomized to proactive geriatrics consultation or usual care.
cards.result: A geriatrician's proactive consultation — structured recommendations on oxygen delivery, fluids, pain control, medication review, bowel and bladder care, nutrition, early mobilization, and environmental orientation, made before or within 24 hours of surgery and followed daily — reduced delirium from 50% to 32% and severe delirium from 29% to 12%.
cards.watchOut: One centre, 126 patients, 2001 — a small trial by modern standards, and the intervention was a person (a geriatrician with a checklist and daily follow-through), which is harder to scale than a poster. It earns its place as the randomized proof of concept in the highest-risk surgical population, agreeing with the ward-based bundle evidence — and it is the bridge to the hip-fracture shelf (#342).
cards.source: Marcantonio ER et al. Reducing delirium after hip fracture: a randomized trial. J Am Geriatr Soc. 2001. PMID 11380742. DOI 10.1046/j.1532-5415.2001.49108.x (Pre-registration era — no registry number applies.)

shelves.title: Gabapentinoids for chronic pain: real but modest in nerve pain, split by condition — null in sciatica, and prescribed far beyond the evidence
shelves.question: For which pains do pregabalin and gabapentin actually work, how many patients benefit per hundred treated — and what follows them off-label?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Analgesics · Chronic Disease · Diabetic Neuropathies · Dizziness · Neuralgia
shelves.balance: This shelf splits because the evidence splits. Postherpetic neuralgia is the strong suit: pregabalin produced at least 50% pain relief in 32% vs 13% on placebo at 300 mg (NNT 5.3) and an NNT of 3.9 at 600 mg (Derry, Cochrane 2019) — real, and still leaving most patients without substantial relief. Diabetic neuropathy is thinner: 31% vs 24% at 300 mg, for an NNT of about 20. Fibromyalgia sits between (NNT roughly 11–12; pregabalin's fibromyalgia detail is cross-pointed to Shelf #391). Gabapentin's own Cochrane numbers are of the same modest family (postherpetic neuralgia NNT 6.7; diabetic neuropathy 5.9). Then the null, printed: in sciatica — one of the commonest reasons these drugs are started — pregabalin did nothing in a properly blinded trial (PRECISE). The harm ledger is carded too: the FDA's December 2019 warning on respiratory depression, the UK's 2019 scheduling of both drugs as controlled drugs, and an estimated 83% of gabapentinoid use that is off-label. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: Derry 2019 (Cochrane): pregabalin — postherpetic neuralgia NNT 5.3 at 300 mg and 3.9 at 600 mg; diabetic neuropathy NNT about 20
cards.summary: Postherpetic neuralgia, at least 50% pain relief: 32% on pregabalin 300 mg vs 13% on placebo (NNT 5.3; 4 studies, 713 participants). Painful diabetic neuropathy at 300 mg: 31% vs 24% (NNT 22 — about 20; 11 studies, 2,931 participants). Somnolence and dizziness were consistently more common on pregabalin (at 600 mg: dizziness 22% vs 4.4%; somnolence 15% vs 4.5%).
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review (Derry et al.), Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2019
cards.people: Adults with neuropathic pain in randomized trials pooled by condition: postherpetic neuralgia, painful diabetic neuropathy, mixed or post-traumatic neuropathic pain, and fibromyalgia analysed in the companion review (Reference 2). Most trials ran 8–13 weeks. (A systematic review — no single age or sex mix applies.)
cards.result: Evidence showed efficacy for pregabalin in postherpetic neuralgia, painful diabetic neuropathy, and mixed or unclassified post-traumatic neuropathic pain; no efficacy in HIV neuropathy; and inadequate evidence in central neuropathic pain. At 300 mg, at least 30% pain relief in postherpetic neuralgia was 50% vs 25% (NNT 3.9). The reviewers' summary is the shelf's: some people will derive substantial benefit, more will have moderate benefit, but many will have no benefit or will discontinue treatment.
cards.watchOut: NNTs of 4–6 sound respectable until read as their mirror image: even in the best condition, most treated patients do not reach 50% relief attributable to the drug — and the trials run for weeks on medicines taken for years. Enriched-enrollment designs in parts of this literature flatter pooled estimates. The condition splits on this shelf (LIKELY for postherpetic neuralgia, POSSIBLE for diabetic neuropathy) come straight from these numbers.
cards.source: Derry S et al. Pregabalin for neuropathic pain in adults. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2019. PMID 30673120. DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD007076.pub3 (Systematic review — no registry number applies.)

cards.headline: Derry 2016 (Cochrane): pregabalin in fibromyalgia — substantial benefit in 22–24% vs about 14% (NNT roughly 11–12)
cards.summary: Eight studies: with pregabalin 300–600 mg daily, about 22–24% of fibromyalgia patients achieved substantial benefit (at least 50% pain intensity reduction) vs about 14% on placebo — roughly 9 extra responders per 100 treated, with NNTs between 7 and 14 across outcomes; moderate benefit (at least 30%) in 39–43% vs 28%.
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review (Derry et al.), Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2016
cards.people: Adults with fibromyalgia: five classic-design trials (3,283 participants) randomized to pregabalin 150, 300, 450, or 600 mg daily or placebo, assessed after 8–13 weeks of stable treatment, plus two enriched-enrollment randomized-withdrawal studies. (A systematic review — no single age or sex mix applies.)
cards.result: Pregabalin increased substantial benefit (450 mg: RR 1.8; 95% CI 1.4–2.1, relative; 1,874 participants, high-quality evidence) and moderate benefit (RR 1.5), with a similar magnitude of effect on global-impression outcomes. No studies included active comparators.
cards.watchOut: Fibromyalgia's pregabalin effect is real and small, in trials whose last-observation-carried-forward imputation the reviewers themselves flag as liable to overestimate benefit. Pregabalin's fibromyalgia detail is cross-pointed to Shelf #391; this card carries the headline numbers for the split verdict on this shelf.
cards.source: Derry S et al. Pregabalin for pain in fibromyalgia in adults. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2016. PMID 27684492 (Systematic review — no registry number applies; the PubMed record for this review carries no MeSH headings.)

cards.headline: Wiffen 2017 (Cochrane): gabapentin — postherpetic neuralgia substantial benefit 32% vs 17% (NNT 6.7); diabetic neuropathy 38% vs 21% (NNT 5.9)
cards.summary: Gabapentin at 1,200 mg daily or more: substantial benefit (at least 50% pain relief or global impression 'very much improved') in postherpetic neuralgia 32% vs 17% on placebo (NNT 6.7; 8 studies, 2,260 participants) and in painful diabetic neuropathy 38% vs 21% (NNT 5.9; 6 studies, 1,277 participants). Adverse-event withdrawals 11% vs 8.2% (NNH 30).
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review (Wiffen et al.), Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2017
cards.people: 5,914 participants across 37 studies of oral gabapentin or gabapentin enacarbil, predominantly in postherpetic neuralgia and painful diabetic neuropathy; study duration typically 4–12 weeks. (A systematic review — no single age or sex mix applies.)
cards.result: Moderate benefit (at least 30% relief or 'much/very much improved') in postherpetic neuralgia was 46% vs 25% (NNT 4.8). For all conditions combined, adverse-event withdrawals were more common with gabapentin than placebo (11% vs 8.2%; RR 1.4, relative; NNH 30), as were dizziness and somnolence.
cards.watchOut: Gabapentin's diabetic-neuropathy NNT (5.9) looks better than pregabalin's (about 20 at 300 mg) — but cross-review comparisons mix doses, eras, formulations (including enacarbil), and outcome definitions, and no adequate head-to-head trial exists; the shelf prints both without declaring a winner between the drugs. What the reviews agree on: benefit concentrates in a minority of patients, and dizziness and somnolence tax everyone treated.
cards.source: Wiffen PJ et al. Gabapentin for chronic neuropathic pain in adults. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2017. PMID 28597471. DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD007938.pub4 (Systematic review — no registry number applies.)

cards.headline: PRECISE (Mathieson 2017): pregabalin for sciatica — the null, printed; more adverse events on the drug
cards.summary: 209 patients with sciatica: leg-pain intensity at week 8 was 3.7 on pregabalin vs 3.1 on placebo (adjusted mean difference 0.5; 95% CI −0.2 to 1.2; P=0.19), and at week 52, 3.4 vs 3.0 (P=0.46) — no significant difference on the primary outcome or on ANY secondary outcome. Adverse events: 227 reported in the pregabalin group vs 124 on placebo.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (PRECISE), New England Journal of Medicine 2017
cards.people: 209 patients with sciatica — moderate-to-severe leg pain radiating below the knee with features suggesting nerve-root involvement — randomized to pregabalin 150 mg daily adjusted to a maximum of 600 mg (108) or matching placebo (101) for up to 8 weeks. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Treatment with pregabalin did not significantly reduce the intensity of leg pain associated with sciatica and did not significantly improve disability, back-pain intensity, or quality of life over 8 weeks or at 52 weeks. Dizziness was more common in the pregabalin group, and the total count of adverse events was nearly double (227 vs 124).
cards.watchOut: Sciatica is the everyday prescription — back-and-leg pain fills the clinics where gabapentinoids are started — and it is the indication with a properly blinded null. A drug can be genuinely effective for postherpetic neuralgia and useless for sciatica; indication discipline is this shelf's whole argument. This card is why the shelf's split verdict grades the sciatica/back strand as a LIKELY null.
cards.source: Mathieson S et al. Trial of pregabalin for acute and chronic sciatica (PRECISE). N Engl J Med. 2017. PMID 28328324 · ACTRN12613000530729. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1614292

cards.headline: The harm ledger: gabapentin with opioids — adjusted odds of opioid-related death 1.49 (Gomes 2017); the FDA's 2019 respiratory-depression warning
cards.summary: Ontario nested case-control study (1,256 opioid-related deaths, 4,619 controls): concomitant gabapentin use was associated with increased odds of opioid-related death (adjusted OR 1.49; 95% CI 1.18–1.88), with a dose gradient (high-dose aOR 1.58). On the same ledger: the FDA warned in December 2019 that gabapentinoids can cause serious breathing problems, especially combined with opioids or in lung disease; the UK made both drugs controlled drugs (Class C) in April 2019; and an estimated 83% of gabapentinoid use is off-label.
cards.type: Population-based nested case-control study (Gomes et al.), PLoS Medicine 2017 — OBSERVATIONAL; the FDA warning (Dec 2019) and UK scheduling (2019) are carded on the same card
cards.people: Opioid users in Ontario, Canada, 1997–2013: 1,256 cases who died of an opioid-related cause, matched with up to four controls each (4,619 after matching). Gabapentin exposure in the 120 days before the index date: 12.3% of cases vs 6.8% of controls.
cards.result: After multivariable adjustment, co-prescription of gabapentin with opioids was associated with significantly increased odds of opioid-related death (aOR 1.49; 1.18–1.88), with moderate-dose (aOR 1.56) and high-dose (aOR 1.58) gradients. The study's negative control behaved as expected: concomitant NSAID use showed no significant association with opioid-related death.
cards.watchOut: Labeled honestly: Gomes is observational, and an adjusted OR of 1.49 sits inside the 0.5–2.0 band where the developer holds associations are not solid proof on their own. The card's weight comes from the dose gradient, the plausible mechanism (additive respiratory depression), the clean negative control, and two regulators acting on the same concern — the FDA's December 2019 respiratory-depression warning for both gabapentin and pregabalin, and the UK's 2019 controlled-drug scheduling. The ~83% off-label estimate (from US prescribing analyses) frames the exposure: most of this risk is taken for indications the trials never tested.
cards.source: Gomes T et al. Gabapentin, opioids, and the risk of opioid-related death: a population-based nested case-control study. PLoS Med. 2017. PMID 28972983. DOI 10.1371/journal.pmed.1002396 · FDA Drug Safety Communication, Dec 19, 2019: FDA warns about serious breathing problems with seizure and nerve pain medicines gabapentin and pregabalin. (Observational study — no registry number applies.)

shelves.title: Multivitamins and cognition: a small, replicated test-score benefit inside COSMOS — against a 12-year null in PHS II, and no dementia endpoint anywhere
shelves.question: Does a daily multivitamin slow cognitive aging in older adults — and has any trial ever tested the outcome people actually fear, dementia?
shelves.mesh: Cognition · Cognitive Dysfunction · Dietary Supplements · Vitamins · Minerals · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: Hold-boundary finding, printed first because it governed how this shelf was built: Shelves #48–#60 — the developer's dietary-supplements set — are held for new cards until his supplements paper publishes. The gate checked those shelves and the dataset before building: neither COSMOS nor PHS II is carded anywhere in #48–#60 (the word 'multivitamin' appears there only inside Shelf #48's folic-acid trial tablet), so this shelf is the trials' first and only home, and NOTHING was added to the held shelves. The evidence itself splits by trial generation. Inside COSMOS, three non-overlapping cognitive substudies point the same small way: global cognition +0.07 SD (COSMOS-Mind), memory-first benefit (COSMOS-Web), and a pooled +0.07 SD (P=0.0009) the authors equate to about 2 years less cognitive aging. Against that stands PHS II: 5,947 men followed for 12 years, difference −0.01 SD — null. And the fence around everything: NO trial on this shelf has a dementia endpoint; every number here is a test-score difference of 0.07 SD, whose real-world meaning is unproven. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: COSMOS-Mind (Baker 2023): multivitamin improved global cognition by +0.07 SD over 3 years; cocoa extract did nothing
cards.summary: 2,262 older adults, 3-year 2×2 factorial trial (telephone cognitive battery): daily multivitamin-mineral vs placebo — global cognition +0.07 SD (95% CI 0.02 to 0.12; P=0.007), with benefits also on memory and executive function composites. The trial's primary endpoint, cocoa extract, was null ( +0.03 SD, P=0.28 ) — the multivitamin result was the prespecified secondary endpoint.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, 2×2 factorial clinical trial (COSMOS-Mind, ancillary to COSMOS), Alzheimer's & Dementia 2023
cards.people: 2,262 participants enrolled (mean age 73 years; 60% women; 89% non-Hispanic White); 92% completed baseline and at least one annual assessment. Registry: the parent COSMOS trial is NCT02422745; COSMOS-Mind is NCT03035201, as carried in the pooled COSMOS record (Reference 3).
cards.result: Cocoa extract had no effect on global cognition (mean z-score difference 0.03 [−0.02 to 0.08]; P=0.28). Daily multivitamin-mineral supplementation, relative to placebo, produced a statistically significant benefit on global cognition (mean z = 0.07 [0.02 to 0.12]; P=0.007); the effect was most pronounced in participants with a history of cardiovascular disease (0.14 vs 0.06 without history; nominal interaction P=0.01). Benefits were also observed for the memory and executive-function composites, and the cocoa-by-multivitamin interaction was not significant for any composite.
cards.watchOut: Hierarchy discipline: the multivitamin finding was this trial's prespecified SECONDARY endpoint — its primary (cocoa) failed — so the card prints that order rather than letting the positive result pose as the trial's main event. An effect of 0.07 SD is small by any yardstick, in a cohort 89% non-Hispanic White, measured by telephone testing. It is a signal worth the POSSIBLE stamp, replicated inside COSMOS (References 2–3) — and contradicted by the larger, longer PHS II (Reference 4).
cards.source: Baker LD et al. Effects of cocoa extract and a multivitamin on cognitive function: A randomized clinical trial. Alzheimers Dement. 2023;19:1308–1319. PMID 36102337 · NCT03035201. DOI 10.1002/alz.12767

cards.headline: COSMOS-Web (Yeung 2023): memory improved at year 1 and across 3 years; other domains null
cards.summary: 3,562 older adults, internet-based cognitive testing: daily multivitamin (Centrum Silver) vs placebo — the prespecified primary outcome, immediate recall (ModRey) at 1 year, was significantly better on multivitamin ( P=0.025 ), as was average recall across 3 years (P=0.011); the authors translate the effect as the equivalent of 3.1 years less age-related memory change. Secondary outcomes — novel object recognition, executive function — showed no significant effects .
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (COSMOS-Web, ancillary to COSMOS), American Journal of Clinical Nutrition 2023
cards.people: 3,562 older adults randomly assigned to daily multivitamin or placebo and evaluated annually for 3 years with an internet-based neuropsychological battery. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Compared with placebo, participants assigned to multivitamin had significantly better ModRey immediate recall at 1 year — the prespecified primary endpoint (t(5889)=2.25, P=0.025) — and across the 3 years of follow-up on average (t(5889)=2.54, P=0.011). Multivitamin supplementation had no significant effects on the secondary outcomes (novel object recognition; executive function). A cross-sectional age-association analysis estimated the intervention effect as equivalent to 3.1 years of age-related memory change.
cards.watchOut: One domain moved — memory, on one test family — and the rest did not; the card prints the null secondaries beside the positive primary. The '3.1 years' figure is a translation from a cross-sectional age gradient, not three years of dementia delayed; no dementia endpoint exists in COSMOS-Web or anywhere on this shelf. Web-based self-administered testing in volunteers is a selected population.
cards.source: Yeung LK et al. Multivitamin Supplementation Improves Memory in Older Adults: A Randomized Clinical Trial. Am J Clin Nutr. 2023;118:273–282. PMID 37244291 · NCT04582617. DOI 10.1016/j.ajcnut.2023.05.011

cards.headline: COSMOS pooled (Vyas 2024): across 5,203 participants in three substudies, global cognition +0.07 SD (P=0.0009)
cards.summary: Prespecified meta-analysis within COSMOS of three non-overlapping cognitive substudies (Clinic n=573, Mind n=2,158, Web n=2,472): multivitamin vs placebo — global cognition +0.07 SD (0.03 to 0.11; P=0.0009) and episodic memory +0.06 SD (P=0.0007); the authors equate the global effect to reducing cognitive aging by 2 years . In the in-person Clinic subcohort alone, global cognition was +0.06 SD with an interval touching zero (−0.003 to 0.13); episodic memory +0.12 SD was significant.
cards.type: In-person clinic subcohort trial analysis plus prespecified meta-analysis of 3 COSMOS cognitive substudies, American Journal of Clinical Nutrition 2024
cards.people: Meta-analysis across non-overlapping participants: COSMOS-Clinic (n=573, in-person testing), COSMOS-Mind (n=2,158), COSMOS-Web (n=2,472) — 5,203 participants drawn from the parent COSMOS trial of 21,442 US adults aged ≥60 years.
cards.result: In COSMOS-Clinic, daily multivitamin use was associated with a more favorable 2-year change in episodic memory (mean difference 0.12 SD [0.002 to 0.23]) but the global-cognition difference (0.06 SD [−0.003 to 0.13]) and executive function/attention (0.04 SD [−0.04 to 0.11]) were not significant. The meta-analysis of the three substudies showed benefit on global cognition (0.07 SD [0.03 to 0.11]; P=0.0009) and episodic memory (0.06 SD [0.03 to 0.10]; P=0.0007); the authors state the global-cognition magnitude is equivalent to reducing cognitive aging by 2 years.
cards.watchOut: This is a within-one-trial-programme pooling — three substudies of the same parent trial, same supplement, same sponsor ecosystem — so it sharpens COSMOS's own estimate rather than independently replicating it. The independent replication attempt already exists, is larger and longer, and is null: PHS II, next card. Both statements stay on the shelf together; the POSSIBLE stamp is exactly the distance between them.

cards.headline: PHS II (Grodstein 2013): 5,947 men, 12 years of daily multivitamin — cognition difference −0.01 SD, null
cards.summary: 5,947 male physicians aged ≥65, randomized to daily multivitamin or placebo with up to 4 cognitive assessments over 12 years : mean difference in cognitive change for the global composite −0.01 SD (−0.04 to 0.02) and for verbal memory −0.005 SD — no benefit at any assessment . The largest, longest multivitamin-cognition trial ever run is a null, and it is carded at the same size as the COSMOS positives.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Physicians' Health Study II cognitive substudy), Annals of Internal Medicine 2013
cards.people: 5,947 male physicians aged 65 years or older; cognitive substudy began 1998, with up to 4 repeated telephone cognitive assessments over 12 years of treatment (1997–2011).
cards.result: No difference was found in mean cognitive change over time between the multivitamin and placebo groups, or in mean cognition level at any of the 4 assessments. For the global composite score, the mean difference in cognitive change over follow-up was −0.01 SD units (−0.04 to 0.02); for the secondary verbal-memory endpoint, −0.005 SD (−0.04 to 0.03). The authors note the vitamin doses may have been too low, or the population too well-nourished, to benefit.
cards.watchOut: The counterweight card, and the reason the shelf is POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY. Differences worth naming honestly: PHS II tested an earlier multivitamin formulation in exceptionally well-nourished male physicians, and COSMOS tested Centrum Silver in a broader, older, mixed-sex population — 'different trial, different answer' is possible. But the burden of proof sits with the positive claim, and the only other large long trial found nothing. No dementia endpoint here either — 12 years, and dementia incidence was still not the measured outcome.

shelves.title: Hearing aids and cognitive decline: the trial's primary result was NULL — a prespecified higher-risk cohort analysis is the only positive signal
shelves.question: In older adults with hearing loss, does treating the hearing loss slow cognitive decline?
shelves.mesh: Hearing Loss · Hearing Aids · Cognition · Cognitive Dysfunction · Health Education · Atherosclerosis
shelves.balance: The null prints first, because the null is the trial's primary result: in ACHIEVE's full cohort of 977 older adults, hearing intervention vs health-education control changed 3-year cognition by 0.002 SD (P=0.96) — as close to zero as trials get. The positive finding lives one level down, in a prespecified analysis by recruitment cohort: participants who came from the long-running ARIC cardiovascular cohort — older, with more risk factors and lower baseline cognition — declined 48% slower on the intervention (relative figure; absolute difference 0.191 SD, P=0.027), while de novo community volunteers showed no benefit; the interaction was significant (P=0.010). That pattern — help for the higher-risk, nothing for the healthy volunteer — is biologically coherent and prespecified, which earns POSSIBLE for the higher-risk group; it is still one subgroup of one trial, which is why it earns no more. No dementia endpoint; no significant adverse events attributed to either intervention. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: ACHIEVE (Lin 2023): PRIMARY RESULT NULL — 3-year cognitive change differed by 0.002 SD (P=0.96)
cards.summary: 977 adults aged 70–84 with untreated hearing loss and no substantial cognitive impairment: hearing intervention (audiological counselling + hearing aids) vs health-education control — 3-year change in global cognition −0.200 vs −0.202 SD ; difference 0.002 SD (−0.077 to 0.081; P=0.96 ). The trial's primary analysis is a clean null, and it leads this shelf.
cards.type: Multicentre, parallel-group, randomised controlled trial (ACHIEVE), Lancet 2023
cards.people: 977 participants (490 hearing intervention, 487 control) at 4 US community sites; mean age 76.8 years; 523 (54%) women; 88% White. Recruited from two populations: 238 (24%) from the ARIC observational cohort and 739 (76%) de novo community volunteers.
cards.result: In the primary analysis combining the ARIC and de novo cohorts, 3-year cognitive change was not significantly different between groups (−0.200 SD [−0.256 to −0.144] hearing intervention vs −0.202 [−0.258 to −0.145] control; difference 0.002 [−0.077 to 0.081]; P=0.96). Other prespecified sensitivity analyses varying analytical parameters did not change the total-cohort result. No significant adverse events were attributed to either the hearing intervention or the health-education control.
cards.watchOut: Print this card's number whenever the shelf is quoted: 0.002. Any summary of ACHIEVE that leads with the subgroup (next card) without this null is misquoting the trial. Note the control was an active health-education programme, not nothing — a fair, even generous comparator — and the intervention was unmasked, as hearing aids cannot be blinded.

cards.headline: ACHIEVE, ARIC cohort: 48% slower decline (relative) — absolute difference 0.191 SD, P=0.027; interaction P=0.010 (same trial, prespecified cohort analysis)
cards.summary: Within ACHIEVE's prespecified analysis by recruitment population, the 238 ARIC participants — older, more cardiovascular risk factors, lower baseline cognition — showed a hearing-intervention benefit: 3-year cognitive decline 48% slower (relative figure) with an absolute between-group difference of 0.191 SD (P=0.027); de novo volunteers showed no benefit. The cohort-by-treatment interaction was significant ( P=0.010 ). Same trial as Card 1 — not a second trial, and not independent confirmation.
cards.type: Prespecified cohort (sensitivity) analysis within a randomised controlled trial (ACHIEVE), Lancet 2023. Same trial as Card 1 — counted as this shelf's second card, not as a separate trial
cards.people: The 238 ACHIEVE participants recruited from the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC) study — who were older, had more risk factors for cognitive decline, and had lower baseline cognitive scores than the 739 de novo volunteers.
cards.result: A prespecified sensitivity analysis showed a significant difference in the effect of the hearing intervention on 3-year cognitive change between the ARIC and de novo cohorts (interaction P=0.010). In the ARIC cohort the intervention was associated with meaningfully slower decline — the trial report gives the between-group difference as 0.191 SD (P=0.027), commonly summarised as a 48% relative slowing of decline; in the de novo cohort the effect was essentially absent. The investigators' interpretation, printed as theirs: a hearing intervention might reduce cognitive change over 3 years in populations at increased risk of cognitive decline, but not in populations at decreased risk.
cards.watchOut: Subgroup discipline applies in full: one trial, one prespecified-but-secondary split, 238 people. What raises it above the usual subgroup fishing is that the split was prespecified, the interaction test (not just the within-subgroup P value) is significant, and the direction matches the risk logic — more decline to prevent in ARIC. What keeps it at POSSIBLE is everything else: it needs its own trial in high-risk patients before it should drive policy, and hearing aids carry independent quality-of-life reasons to be fitted that do not depend on this cognitive claim at all.

shelves.title: Smoking cessation before surgery: intensive programmes cut complications — brief advice and late varenicline do not
shelves.question: Does helping smokers quit before surgery reduce postoperative complications — and how much intervention does it take?
shelves.mesh: Smoking Cessation · Preoperative Care · Postoperative Complications · Nicotine · Varenicline · Smoking
shelves.balance: The dose makes the effect. Intensive programmes — weekly counselling plus nicotine replacement, started 4–8 weeks before surgery — produced the shelf's large numbers: cessation RR 10.76 and complication RR 0.42 in relative terms (Cochrane), complications 18% vs 52% (Møller) and 21% vs 41% (Lindström). Brief interventions raised quitting modestly (RR 1.30, relative) and did not reduce complications (RR 0.92, NS). Varenicline started a week before surgery improved quitting over the following year and did not reduce complications (RR 0.94, NS). Stated on the shelf, as required: the intensive-intervention pool behind the headline relative effects is only ~210 patients in 2 trials — the direction is consistent across every cut; the sizes are upper bounds until a larger trial exists. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: Cochrane (Thomsen 2014): intensive intervention — cessation RR 10.76, any complication RR 0.42, wound RR 0.31 (all relative); brief intervention — cessation RR 1.30, complications RR 0.92 NS. The intensive pool is only ~210 patients
cards.summary: 13 trials, 2,010 participants. Intensive intervention (multisession counselling from ≥4 weeks before surgery, NRT offered): cessation at surgery RR 10.76 [4.55–25.46], relative ; any postoperative complication RR 0.42 [0.27–0.65], relative ; wound complications RR 0.31 [0.16–0.62], relative — each pooled from 2 trials, 210 participants , the small base stated here as the shelf requires. Brief intervention: cessation RR 1.30 [1.16–1.46], relative; complications RR 0.92 [0.72–1.19] — not significant . Long-term cessation held only for intensive intervention (RR 2.96, relative).
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of 13 randomized trials (CD002294, 2014 update)
cards.people: 2,010 participants across 13 trials of people who smoked before surgery; the intensive-intervention comparisons rest on 2 trials with 210 participants. The record does not state a pooled mean age or sex split.
cards.result: Ten trials evaluated behavioural support on cessation at the time of surgery; nicotine replacement was offered or recommended in eight. The effect was larger for intensive intervention (pooled RR 10.76 [4.55–25.46], 2 trials, 210 participants) than for brief interventions (RR 1.30 [1.16–1.46], 7 trials, 1,141 participants). For postoperative complications: intensive intervention reduced any complications (RR 0.42 [0.27–0.65]) and wound complications (RR 0.31 [0.16–0.62]), both from the same 2 trials and 210 participants; brief interventions showed no evidence of a reduction in any complication (RR 0.92 [0.72–1.19], 4 trials, 493 participants) or wound complications (RR 0.99). Only the intensive intervention retained a significant effect on long-term cessation (RR 2.96 [1.57–5.55]).
cards.watchOut: Big relative effects, small base — the shelf states both halves of that sentence. RR 10.76 for quitting and RR 0.42 for complications come from ~210 patients in 2 trials (Cards 2 and 3 are those trials), so the direction is consistent and the precision is not. The brief-intervention null on complications is the dose signal: a leaflet and a chat do not move surgical outcomes; a programme might.

cards.headline: Møller 2002: the intensive programme behind the Cochrane pool — complications 18% vs 52%
cards.summary: 120 smokers scheduled for hip or knee replacement, randomized 6–8 weeks before surgery to a smoking intervention (weekly counselling plus nicotine replacement, aiming at cessation or ≥50% reduction) or control; 108 analyzed. Overall complications 18% vs 52% (P=0.0003) — an absolute difference of 34 points. Wound-related complications 5% vs 31% (P=0.001); cardiovascular complications 0% vs 10% (P=0.08); secondary surgery 4% vs 15% (P=0.07). Median stay 11 vs 13 days.
cards.people: 120 patients randomized at three hospitals in Denmark (60 intervention, 60 control); 52 control and 56 intervention patients were analyzed after exclusions for postponed or cancelled operations. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: The overall complication rate was 18% in the smoking intervention group and 52% in controls (P=0.0003). The most significant effects were for wound-related complications (5% vs 31%, P=0.001), cardiovascular complications (0% vs 10%, P=0.08), and secondary surgery (4% vs 15%, P=0.07). The median length of stay was 11 days (range 7–55) in the intervention group and 13 days (8–65) in the control group. The main analysis was by intention to treat, with a masked outcome assessor.
cards.watchOut: A 34-point absolute difference from a behavioural intervention is an enormous effect — larger than most drugs ever produce — in 108 analyzed patients at three Danish hospitals. Treat the direction as trustworthy (it repeats in Card 3 and in the Cochrane pool) and the size as an upper bound: small single-country trials of programmes their own teams deliver tend to flatter the programme.
cards.source: Møller AM et al. Effect of preoperative smoking intervention on postoperative complications: a randomised clinical trial. Lancet. 2002;359:114–117. PMID 11809253. The record carries no DOI and no registry databank entry.

cards.headline: Lindström 2008: starting 4 weeks before surgery still worked — complications 21% vs 41%
cards.summary: 117 daily smokers undergoing hernia repair, laparoscopic cholecystectomy, or hip/knee prosthesis, randomized to cessation therapy (individual counselling plus nicotine substitution) starting 4 weeks before surgery and continuing 4 weeks after, vs standard care: any postoperative complication 21% vs 41% (P=0.03) — a 49% relative risk reduction; NNT 5 [3–40]. Among those who actually abstained, complications were 15% vs 35% in continuing smokers — a per-protocol cut, stated as such and not significant.
cards.people: 117 patients enrolled (of 238 assessed; 76 declined) at 4 university-affiliated hospitals in Stockholm, Sweden; daily smokers aged 18–79 undergoing primary hernia repair, laparoscopic cholecystectomy, or hip or knee prosthesis. The record does not state a sex split. Registry verified against the record: NCT00533000.
cards.result: An intention-to-treat analysis showed an overall complication rate of 41% in the control group and 21% in the intervention group (P=0.03) — a relative risk reduction of 49% and a number needed to treat of 5 [3–40]. A per-protocol analysis showed abstainers had fewer complications (15%) than those who continued to smoke or only reduced (35%), although this difference was not statistically significant. Outcome assessment was blinded; follow-up for the primary outcome was 30 days.
cards.watchOut: The practical card on this shelf: four weeks is enough runway — the intervention does not need Møller's 6–8 weeks to show an effect. The NNT of 5 comes with a wide interval (3–40) from 117 patients, and the flattering per-protocol comparison (abstainers vs continuing smokers) is exactly the comparison randomization exists to replace — it is stated labeled, and it was not significant.

cards.headline: Varenicline before surgery (Wong 2012): quitting rose (36.4% vs 25.2% at 12 months) — complications did NOT fall (RR 0.94, NS)
cards.summary: 286 elective-surgery patients, varenicline started 1 week before surgery (12 weeks total) vs placebo, both with counselling: 12-month abstinence 36.4% vs 25.2% — RR 1.45 [1.01–2.07], relative; P=0.04 . But on the outcome this shelf is about, the Cochrane pooling of this same trial found no effect on postoperative complications (RR 0.94 [0.52–1.72]) and no significant effect on quitting by the time of surgery (RR 1.49 [0.98–2.26]). Nausea was more common on varenicline (13.3% vs 3.7%); serious adverse events did not differ. Carded honestly: a drug that helps people quit after surgery is not thereby a drug that prevents surgical complications.
cards.type: Double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial (Wong 2012), Anesthesiology 2012; complications outcome as pooled in the Cochrane review, Card 1
cards.people: 286 patients undergoing elective noncardiac surgery, randomized to varenicline or placebo at multiple centers; both groups received in-hospital and telephone counselling for 12 months. The record does not state a mean age or sex split, and carries no registry databank entry.
cards.result: The 7-day point prevalence abstinence at 12 months was 36.4% for varenicline vs 25.2% for placebo (relative risk 1.45 [1.01–2.07]; P=0.04), with significant differences also at 3 months (43.7% vs 31.9%) and 6 months (35.8% vs 25.9%). The adverse-event profile was similar except nausea (13.3% vs 3.7%, P=0.004). In the Cochrane review's pooling, this trial showed no detected effect on postoperative complications (RR 0.94 [0.52–1.72]) and no significant increase in cessation at the time of surgery (RR 1.49 [0.98–2.26]).
cards.watchOut: Timing is the likely story: varenicline began one week before surgery — too late for much preoperative abstinence, which is the exposure the complications benefit tracks in Cards 2 and 3. For varenicline's general quit efficacy and safety, see Shelf #225 and Shelf #310; this card answers only the perioperative question, and its answer splits: quits yes (later), complications no.
