shelves.title: Shingles vaccine and dementia: two birthday cut-offs, two falls in dementia diagnoses — for the old vaccine
shelves.question: Does herpes zoster (shingles) vaccination prevent or delay dementia?
shelves.mesh: Australia · Dementia · Electronic Health Records · Herpes Zoster · Herpes Zoster Vaccine · Humans · Vaccination · Wales
shelves.balance: No randomised trial exists, but two countries accidentally ran the next best thing. In Wales, zoster-vaccine eligibility turned on an exact birthday; people a week younger were vaccinated at 47% and people a week older at 0.01%, and the vaccinated side accumulated 3.5 percentage points fewer dementia diagnoses over seven years — a 20% relative reduction [6.5–33.4]. In Australia, the same design on a different birthday line found the same direction (eligibility effect 1.8 percentage points [0.4–3.3]) with balanced comparison groups and quiet negative controls. POSSIBLE, capped by three fences: the designs are quasi-experimental, the outcomes are recorded diagnoses rather than adjudicated dementia, and the vaccine both experiments studied is the live-attenuated one most programmes have replaced with a recombinant vaccine whose dementia evidence is still ordinary observational data. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

cards.headline: The Wales natural experiment (Eyting 2025, Nature): a birthday cut-off split otherwise identical people — dementia diagnoses fell 3.5 percentage points (20% relative)
cards.summary: In Wales, eligibility for the live-attenuated zoster vaccine turned on an exact date of birth: people born before 2 September 1933 were never eligible; people born on or after it were. Vaccine uptake jumped from 0.01% among those one week too old to 47.2% among those one week younger — a regression-discontinuity comparison of people who differ by days of age and by little else. Receiving the vaccine reduced the probability of a new dementia diagnosis over seven years by 3.5 percentage points [95% CI 0.6–7.1], P=0.019 — a 20.0% relative reduction [6.5–33.4] . The effect was stronger among women than men, and the authors confirmed it in England and Wales combined using death certificates (deaths with dementia as the primary cause) rather than diagnoses.
cards.type: Quasi-experimental study — regression discontinuity on a date-of-birth eligibility rule, using electronic health records (Wales), Nature 2025. Not a randomised trial; no registry ID applies.
cards.people: Adults in Wales born just before or just after 2 September 1933, followed for new dementia diagnoses over seven years; the comparison groups are defined by week of birth around the eligibility threshold.
cards.result: Receiving the zoster vaccine reduced the probability of a new dementia diagnosis over a follow-up period of 7 years by 3.5 percentage points (95% confidence interval, 0.6 to 7.1; P=0.019), corresponding to a 20.0% (95% CI, 6.5 to 33.4) relative reduction. The protective effect was stronger among women than men. The findings were confirmed in a different population (England and Wales combined), with a different type of data (death certificates) and a related outcome (deaths with dementia as primary cause).
cards.watchOut: This is the strongest design short of randomisation — an eligibility rule acting as a coin flip — and it is still not randomisation: the estimate is a local effect at the threshold (people aged about 80), diagnoses in health records are not adjudicated dementia, and the vaccine studied is the live-attenuated vaccine (Zostavax), which most programmes have since replaced with the recombinant vaccine. Whether the effect belongs to suppressing the virus, to the vaccine platform, or to something else is unresolved — which is why this shelf is slow-lane and its stamp is capped.
cards.source: Eyting M et al. A natural experiment on the effect of herpes zoster vaccination on dementia. Nature. 2025;641(8062):438–446. PMID 40175543. DOI 10.1038/s41586-025-08800-x

cards.headline: The Australian replication (Pomirchy 2025, JAMA): a second date-of-birth experiment, a second fall in dementia diagnoses — with negative controls behaving
cards.summary: Australia’s programme (from November 2016) made the live-attenuated vaccine free at ages 70–79, so people whose 80th birthday fell just before the start never became eligible and those just after it did. In 101,219 patients from 65 general practices, eligibility jumped vaccination probability by 16.4 percentage points [13.2–19.5] across the threshold, and being eligible reduced the probability of a new dementia diagnosis over 7.4 years by 1.8 percentage points [0.4–3.3], P=.01 . The comparison groups were balanced on prior preventive care and prior diagnoses, and eligibility did not change uptake of other preventive services or diagnoses of other common chronic conditions — the negative controls a confounded analysis would be expected to fail.
cards.type: Quasi-experimental study — regression discontinuity on a date-of-birth eligibility rule, primary-care records (Australia), JAMA 2025. Not a randomised trial; no registry ID applies.
cards.people: 101,219 patients (52.7% women) in 65 Australian general practices; comparison by week of birth around the 2 November 1936 eligibility threshold created by the programme’s 1 November 2016 start.
cards.result: Eligibility for HZ vaccination decreased the probability of receiving a new dementia diagnosis during 7.4 years by 1.8 percentage points (95% CI, 0.4 to 3.3 percentage points; P=.01). Eligibility did not affect the probability of taking up other preventive health services (including other vaccinations) or of receiving a diagnosis of common chronic conditions other than dementia.
cards.watchOut: Two dilutions explain why the Australian number is smaller than the Welsh one: the eligibility jump in actual vaccination was smaller (16.4 vs 47.2 percentage points), and this is the effect of being made eligible, not of being vaccinated — the per-vaccinated effect is larger than either headline. The outcome is again a recorded diagnosis, not an adjudicated endpoint. Concordance across two countries, two health systems and two data types is the finding; neither study can say the recombinant vaccine now in use does the same.
cards.source: Pomirchy M et al. Herpes zoster vaccination and dementia occurrence. JAMA. 2025;333(23):2083–2092. PMID 40267506. DOI 10.1001/jama.2025.5013

cards.headline: Reading the two natural experiments together: the best non-randomised evidence in the vaccine literature — for a vaccine most clinics no longer stock
cards.summary: Two countries ran the same accident: a birthday line, near-identical people on either side, and dementia diagnoses falling on the eligible side in both — 20% relative over seven years in Wales , with the Australian eligibility effect pointing the same way and its negative controls quiet. That is about as persuasive as observational evidence is allowed to get, and it still is not a randomised trial: the outcomes are diagnoses in records, the mechanism is unknown, and the exposure is the live-attenuated vaccine. The recombinant vaccine (Shingrix) that replaced it has only ordinary claims-based association studies behind it so far — the design class that healthy-vaccinee bias eats alive — and no randomised trial of zoster vaccination for dementia prevention exists or is named on this shelf . If the question moves, it will move through recombinant-era natural experiments and cohorts built to resist that bias; until one reports, the shelf grades what the two experiments showed, for the vaccine they studied.
cards.type: Synthesis card — no new study. This card reads Cards 1 and 2 together and states why this shelf is slow-lane.
cards.people: The populations of Cards 1 and 2: adults around age 80 in Wales and Australia, compared across date-of-birth eligibility thresholds for the live-attenuated zoster vaccine.
cards.result: The evidence establishes a dementia-diagnosis reduction associated with live-attenuated zoster vaccination in two independent quasi-experiments with concordant direction and clean negative controls. It does not establish the effect for the recombinant vaccine, does not identify a mechanism, and does not measure adjudicated dementia or dementia mortality as a primary outcome.
cards.watchOut: Do not cite this shelf as ‘the shingles vaccine prevents dementia’ without its fences: the claim is about a specific vaccine, at a specific age, measured as diagnoses in records, by designs one step below randomisation. It is, even so, the shelf on this slate most likely to be re-graded by future evidence — in either direction.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cards 1–2 on this shelf (PMID 40175543; PMID 40267506).

shelves.title: Exercise for depression
shelves.question: Does exercise treat major depression, which modalities and intensities work best, and how strong is the evidence?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Major Depressive Disorder · Exercise Therapy · Antidepressive Agents · Yoga · Exercise · Psychotherapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Exercise shows moderate pooled reductions in depression — walking or jogging Hedges' g -0.62, yoga -0.55 and strength training -0.49 versus active controls in a 218-study network meta-analysis — but confidence in that network was low for walking or jogging and very low for other treatments, only one study met Cochrane low-risk-of-bias criteria, and in the Cochrane review the effect disappeared when only the six most rigorous trials were pooled (standardised mean difference -0.18, 95% CI -0.47 to 0.11). A real but uncertain benefit: POSSIBLE. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

cards.headline: Network meta-analysis of 218 studies: walking or jogging, yoga and strength training reduced depression most
cards.summary: The 2024 network meta-analysis (218 studies): walking or jogging (g −0.62 ), yoga (−0.55) and strength training (−0.49) showed the largest reductions in depression versus active controls, with moderate effects also for mixed aerobic exercise and tai chi — but CINeMA confidence was low to very low.
cards.type: Network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
cards.people: 14,170 participants in 218 unique studies with 495 arms, in people meeting clinical cut-offs for major depression; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Compared with active controls, moderate reductions in depression were found for walking or jogging (n=1210, Hedges' g -0.62, 95% credible interval -0.80 to -0.45), yoga (n=1047, g -0.55, -0.73 to -0.36), strength training (n=643, g -0.49, -0.69 to -0.29), mixed aerobic exercises (n=1286, g -0.43, -0.61 to -0.24) and tai chi or qigong (n=343, g -0.42, -0.65 to -0.21). Effects were proportional to the intensity prescribed, and strength training and yoga appeared the most acceptable modalities. However, only one study met the Cochrane criteria for low risk of bias, and confidence by CINeMA was low for walking or jogging and very low for other treatments.
cards.watchOut: Expectancy effects cannot be excluded — participants and staff were generally unblinded — and the authors' own confidence grading is low to very low despite the moderate pooled effect sizes.
cards.source: Noetel M et al. Effect of exercise for depression: systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. BMJ. 2024 Feb 14;384:e075847. PMID: 38355154. Systematic review registration: PROSPERO CRD42018118040, as stated in the record.

cards.headline: Cochrane review: moderate pooled effect, but not significant in the six most rigorous trials
cards.summary: Cochrane (35 trials, 1,356 participants): exercise versus no treatment or control gave a moderate pooled effect (SMD −0.62 [−0.81 to −0.42]) — but restricted to the six most rigorous trials (464 participants), the effect was −0.18 and not significant .
cards.people: 2,326 participants in 39 trials in adults (aged 18 and over) with depression; 37 trials provided data for meta-analyses. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: For the 35 trials (1,356 participants) comparing exercise with no treatment or a control intervention, the pooled standardised mean difference for depression at end of treatment was -0.62 (95% CI, -0.81 to -0.42), a moderate clinical effect, with moderate heterogeneity (I(2)=63%). When only the six trials (464 participants) with adequate allocation concealment, intention-to-treat analysis and blinded outcome assessment were included, the pooled standardised mean difference was not statistically significant (-0.18, 95% CI, -0.47 to 0.11). Pooled data from eight trials (377 participants) with long-term follow-up found a small effect in favour of exercise (standardised mean difference -0.33, 95% CI, -0.63 to -0.03).
cards.watchOut: Multiple sources of bias in many trials: randomisation was adequately concealed in only 14 studies, 15 used intention-to-treat analyses and 12 used blinded outcome assessors. This sensitivity result is the main reason the shelf is not stamped higher.
cards.source: Cooney GM et al. Exercise for depression. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2013 Sep 12;2013(9):CD004366. PMID: 24026850. Registry ID: none in the record's databank — Cochrane systematic review, not a single trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: exercise probably helps depression, but the rigorous-trial evidence is weak
cards.summary: Both syntheses land on the same headline and the same warning: a moderate average benefit whose size shrinks as trial quality rises. Exercise probably helps depression; how much is genuinely unsettled — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: 218 studies (14,170 participants) in the network meta-analysis and 39 trials (2,326 participants) in the Cochrane review, in adults with depression or major depressive disorder.
cards.result: Both syntheses pool to the same moderate headline effect (Hedges' g -0.62 for walking or jogging versus active controls; standardised mean difference -0.62 versus no treatment or control in Cochrane), yet both flag the same weakness: CINeMA confidence low to very low in the network analysis, and a non-significant -0.18 (95% CI, -0.47 to 0.11) when Cochrane pooled only its six most rigorous trials. This shelf is stamped POSSIBLE: exercise is a reasonable adjunct alongside psychotherapy and antidepressants, as the network meta-analysis concludes, but it is not proven as a stand-alone treatment by low-bias trials.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote the -0.62 pooled effect without the rigorous-subset result beside it; unblinded, expectancy-prone small trials dominate this literature.

shelves.title: Concussion: strict rest vs early activity
shelves.question: After concussion, does strict rest help recovery, or does early, graduated activity do better?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Athletic Injuries · Brain Concussion · Exercise · Exercise Therapy · Female · Humans · Male · Prospective Studies · Recovery of Function · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY — strict rest does not help and may harm: prescribed 5-day strict rest produced more symptoms and slower resolution than usual care (Thomas 2015). Early activity helps when it is prescribed and dosed: subsymptom-threshold aerobic exercise sped median recovery from 17 to 13 days (Leddy 2019) and replicated with a relative 48% lower risk of persistent symptoms (Leddy 2021). Generic 'resume activity at 72 hours' advice was null on intention-to-treat in the larger PedCARE trial, with benefit only in adherent participants — so the claim is for prescribed, targeted early activity, not simply telling patients to push through. Evidence is in adolescents/young people; adults are extrapolation. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

cards.headline: Thomas 2015: strict rest for 5 days gave more symptoms, not faster recovery
cards.summary: Thomas 2015: strict rest for 5 days after concussion produced more symptoms, not faster recovery — total symptom score 187.9 vs 131.9 over 10 days — with no neurocognitive or balance advantage. Rest is not neutral; prescribed strictly, it harms.
cards.people: 99 patients aged 11-22 years presenting to a paediatric emergency department within 24 hours of concussion (88 completed all procedures: 45 strict rest, 43 usual care); mean age and sex distribution not stated in the abstract
cards.result: No clinically significant difference in neurocognitive or balance outcomes. The strict-rest group reported more daily postconcussive symptoms (total symptom score over 10 days 187.9 vs 131.9; P<.03) and slower symptom resolution than usual care (1-2 days rest, then stepwise return). Strict-rest participants also attended less school on days 2-5 (3.8 vs 6.7 hours total; P<.05).
cards.watchOut: Usual care already included 1-2 days of rest — this trial refutes prolonged strict rest, not brief initial rest. Symptom outcomes are self-reported and the rest prescription itself may have focused attention on symptoms, as the authors note.
cards.source: Thomas DG et al. Pediatrics. 2015;135(2):213-223. PMID: 25560444. Registry: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01101724.

cards.headline: Leddy 2019: early subsymptom aerobic exercise sped recovery 17 to 13 days
cards.summary: Leddy 2019 (103 adolescents): early subsymptom aerobic exercise shortened median recovery to 13 days vs 17 with stretching (p=.009); delayed recovery was 4% vs 14% (not significant).
cards.people: 103 adolescent athletes aged 13-18 years seen within 10 days of sport-related concussion; aerobic exercise n=52 (24 female, 46%), stretching n=51 (24 female, 47%); seen a mean of about 4.9 days after injury
cards.result: Median recovery was 13 days (IQR 10-18.5) with aerobic exercise vs 17 days (IQR 13-23) with placebo-like stretching (P=.009) — an absolute difference of 4 days in medians. Delayed recovery (30+ days) occurred in 2 participants (4%) in the aerobic group vs 7 (14%) in the stretching group, a nonsignificant difference (P=.08).
cards.watchOut: Sport-related concussion in adolescents at specialist concussion centres, with treadmill testing to set the exercise threshold; not tested in adults, non-sport concussion, or without the threshold assessment. Anchor note: the task brief named 'Ledoux 2019 JAMA Pediatrics' for this card — the JAMA Pediatrics trial is Leddy 2019; Ledoux is the PedCARE investigator (reference 4).
cards.source: Leddy JJ et al. JAMA Pediatr. 2019;173(4):319-325. PMID: 30715132. Registry: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02710123.

cards.headline: Leddy 2021: replication — early targeted aerobic exercise cut persistent-symptom risk
cards.summary: Leddy 2021, the replication: aerobic exercise gave a relative 48% lower risk of persistent symptoms (hazard ratio 0.52 for stretching vs aerobic [0.28–0.97]) — a relative measure, printed as one.
cards.people: 118 adolescent athletes aged 13-18 years presenting within 10 days of sport-related concussion at three US sports-medicine concussion centres (61 aerobic exercise, 57 stretching); sex breakdown by arm not stated in the abstract
cards.result: On survival analysis, aerobic-exercise participants were more likely to recover within 4 weeks, with a relative 48% reduced risk of persistent post-concussive symptoms for aerobic vs stretching (hazard ratio for stretching vs aerobic exercise 0.52, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.97; P=.039) — a relative measure; the abstract reports no absolute persistent-symptom rates to pair with it. No adverse events were reported, and adherence was good.
cards.watchOut: Replication in the same population (adolescent athletes, specialist centres) as the 2019 trial, so generalisability — not internal validity — is the open question; exercise was individually heart-rate-targeted using monitored adherence.
cards.source: Leddy JJ et al. Lancet Child Adolesc Health. 2021;5(11):792-799. PMID: 34600629. Registry: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02959216.

cards.headline: PedCARE (Ledoux 2022): generic early resumption was null intention-to-treat, safe, and helped adherent children
cards.summary: PedCARE (Ledoux 2022): generic early activity resumption was null intention-to-treat (adjusted difference −1.3 [−3.6 to 1.1]) and safe; among adherent children, activity at 72 hours did reduce symptoms (−4.3 [−8.4 to −0.2]) — the dose only counts if taken.
cards.people: 456 children/youth aged 10 to under 18 years with acute concussion in three Canadian paediatric emergency departments; early-activity group n=227 (mean age 13.3 (SD 2.1) years, 44.5% women), rest-until-asymptomatic group n=229 (mean age 13.3 (SD 2.2) years, 43.7% women)
cards.result: No adverse events were identified in either group. Intention-to-treat symptoms at 2 weeks did not differ significantly (adjusted mean difference -1.3, 95% CI -3.6 to 1.1). Among adherent participants, starting physical activity at 72 hours reduced symptoms at 2 weeks vs rest (adjusted mean difference -4.3, 95% CI -8.4 to -0.2), but many participants were non-adherent to their assigned protocol.
cards.watchOut: The adherent-participant result is a per-protocol analysis and is hypothesis-supporting, not proof; the honest headline is safety plus a null ITT result for unstructured early resumption, which is why this shelf's positive claim is limited to prescribed, targeted aerobic exercise.
cards.source: Ledoux AA et al (PedCARE). Br J Sports Med. 2022;56(5):271-278. PMID: 34836880. Registry: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02893969.

cards.headline: Synthesis: brief rest, then prescribed early activity — not strict rest — LIKELY
cards.summary: Brief rest, then prescribed early activity — not strict rest: two positive RCTs and one null ITT with an adherence signal. LIKELY.
cards.people: Four RCTs, all in young people: 99 aged 11-22 (Thomas), 103 and 118 adolescent athletes aged 13-18 (Leddy 2019 and 2021), and 456 children/youth aged 10 to under 18 (PedCARE)
cards.result: Strict rest worsened total symptom burden (187.9 vs 131.9 over 10 days) with no neurocognitive or balance gain. Prescribed subsymptom aerobic exercise shortened median recovery by 4 days (13 vs 17) and, on replication, gave a relative 48% lower risk of persistent symptoms (HR 0.52, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.97). Unstructured early resumption was safe (no adverse events in PedCARE or Leddy 2021) but null intention-to-treat (-1.3, 95% CI -3.6 to 1.1). Stamp proposed: LIKELY.
cards.watchOut: Thin outside adolescents: no adult, military, or non-sport concussion RCT is carded, and no in-flight trial is named on this card because the 2024-2026 sweep returned chiefly secondary analyses of these same trials rather than a new adult trial — adult use remains extrapolation until such a trial reports.
cards.source: Synthesis of Thomas 2015 (PMID: 25560444), Leddy 2019 (PMID: 30715132), Leddy 2021 (PMID: 34600629) and Ledoux 2022 (PMID: 34836880); no additional source.

shelves.title: Cholinesterase inhibitors for Alzheimer's dementia
shelves.question: Do donepezil and its class improve cognition, function or time to institutional care in Alzheimer's dementia — and by how much?
shelves.mesh: Alzheimer Disease/diagnosis/drug therapy/economics · Cholinesterase Inhibitors/adverse effects/economics/therapeutic use · Cognition · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Disease Progression · Donepezil · Health Care Costs
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Donepezil produces small, consistent gains in cognition and function — 0.8 MMSE points and 1.0 activities-of-daily-living points in the long pragmatic AD2000 trial, and a -2.67-point ADAS-Cog difference in the Cochrane synthesis — but AD2000 found no delay to institutional care (42% vs 44% at 3 years) and no benefit on disability progression, behaviour, carer wellbeing or costs. The class effect is real but small, and it does not change the course to institutional care.

cards.headline: AD2000: donepezil gave small cognitive and functional gains but no delay to institutional care
cards.summary: AD2000: cognition averaged 0.8 MMSE points better [0.5 to 1.2] and function 1.0 ADL point better on donepezil — with no delay to institutional care , the outcome the trial was designed to test.
cards.people: 565 community-resident patients with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease entered the run-in; 486 were rerandomised to donepezil (5 or 10 mg/day) or placebo. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Over the first 2 years cognition averaged 0.8 MMSE points better (95% CI 0.5-1.2; p<0.0001) and functionality 1.0 Bristol activities-of-daily-living points better (0.5-1.6; p<0.0001) with donepezil. There was no significant benefit on institutionalisation (42% vs 44% at 3 years; p=0.4) or progression of disability (58% vs 59% at 3 years; p=0.4); the relative risk of entering institutional care was 0.97 (95% CI 0.72-1.30) — a ratio inside the 0.5-2.0 band and not evidence of an effect. No significant differences were seen in behavioural symptoms, carer psychopathology, costs, caregiver time, adverse events or deaths, or between 5 mg and 10 mg. The authors concluded donepezil was not cost effective, with benefits below minimally relevant thresholds.
cards.watchOut: The trial's own authors judged the small score gains below minimally relevant thresholds; score improvements must not be presented as delayed institutional care, for which the trial was null.
cards.source: Courtney C et al.; AD2000 Collaborative Group. Long-term donepezil treatment in 565 patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD2000): randomised double-blind trial. Lancet. 2004 Jun;363(9427):2105-15. PMID: 15220031. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Cochrane synthesis: donepezil 10 mg gave small benefits on cognition, function and global state at 26 weeks
cards.summary: Cochrane: donepezil 10 mg — ADAS-Cog difference −2.67 [−3.31 to −2.02], MMSE +1.05 at 24–26 weeks; small benefits, more withdrawals and adverse events.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (Cochrane)
cards.people: 30 studies involving 8,257 participants with mild, moderate or severe dementia due to Alzheimer's disease; in the main 24-26-week analysis the mean age was about 75 years. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: At 24-26 weeks, donepezil 10 mg/day versus placebo: ADAS-Cog mean difference -2.67 (95% CI -3.31 to -2.02; 1,130 participants, 5 studies), MMSE mean difference 1.05 (0.73 to 1.37; 1,757 participants, 7 studies), Severe Impairment Battery mean difference 5.92 (4.53 to 7.31; 1,348 participants, 5 studies), and activities of daily living (severe-disease scale) mean difference 1.03 (0.21 to 1.85; 733 participants, 3 studies). cards.headline: Synthesis: small symptomatic gains, no delay to institutional care
cards.summary: Small symptomatic gains, no disease-course effect — LIKELY, for the small-gain claim only.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: the AD2000 pragmatic trial (565 entered, 486 rerandomised) and the Cochrane synthesis (30 studies, 8,257 participants).
cards.result: Both sources agree the gains are small: 0.8 MMSE points in AD2000 and a -2.67 ADAS-Cog difference in the Cochrane main analysis, with more withdrawals and adverse events on donepezil, and AD2000 — the trial designed to test it — found institutionalisation at 42% vs 44% and disability progression at 58% vs 59%. This shelf is stamped LIKELY: a small symptomatic benefit is likely real, and a delay to institutional care is likely absent on this evidence.

shelves.title: Ocrelizumab for relapsing multiple sclerosis
shelves.question: Does ocrelizumab reduce relapses and disability progression versus interferon beta-1a in relapsing MS?
shelves.mesh: Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Antigens, CD20 · B-Lymphocytes/immunology · Brain/diagnostic imaging · Disease Progression · Immunologic Factors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Infusions, Intravenous/adverse effects
shelves.balance: LIKELY: In the twin OPERA trials ocrelizumab lowered the annualised relapse rate to 0.16 versus 0.29 on interferon beta-1a in both trials (a 46% and 47% relative reduction, with the absolute rates printed beside it), and pooled confirmed disability progression was lower in absolute terms (9.1% vs 13.6% at 12 weeks; 6.9% vs 10.5% at 24 weeks), although the hazard ratio of 0.60 sits inside the 0.5-2.0 band and is not solid evidence on its own. MRI lesion counts fell sharply. Infusion reactions were common (34.3%) and the trials were 96 weeks, so longer-term safety rests on follow-up beyond this shelf's anchor.

cards.headline: OPERA I and II: ocrelizumab halved relapse rates versus interferon beta-1a in two identical trials
cards.summary: OPERA I and II (identical twin trials): annualised relapse rate 0.16 vs 0.29 in both — a 46–47% relative reduction vs interferon beta-1a, absolute rates printed beside it.
cards.type: Two identical randomised controlled trials (phase 3, reported in one paper)
cards.people: 821 patients (trial 1) and 835 patients (trial 2) with relapsing multiple sclerosis, randomised to intravenous ocrelizumab 600 mg every 24 weeks or subcutaneous interferon beta-1a 44 μg three times weekly for 96 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Annualised relapse rate was 0.16 with ocrelizumab versus 0.29 with interferon beta-1a in trial 1 (46% relative lower rate; P<0.001) and 0.16 versus 0.29 in trial 2 (47% relative lower rate; P<0.001), with the absolute rates printed here beside the relative figures. In prespecified pooled analyses, disability progression confirmed at 12 weeks occurred in 9.1% versus 13.6% (hazard ratio 0.60; 95% CI 0.45 to 0.81; P<0.001) and at 24 weeks in 6.9% versus 10.5% (hazard ratio 0.60; 95% CI 0.43 to 0.84; P=0.003) — hazard ratios inside the 0.5-2.0 band, carried by the absolute differences and the concordant relapse and MRI results rather than by the ratio alone. Gadolinium-enhancing lesions per scan were 0.02 versus 0.29 (trial 1) and 0.02 versus 0.42 (trial 2). Infusion-related reactions occurred in 34.3% of ocrelizumab patients; serious infection in 1.3% versus 2.9%; neoplasms in 0.5% versus 0.2%.
cards.watchOut: Comparator is interferon beta-1a, not placebo or a newer high-efficacy therapy; 96 weeks cannot settle long-term risks such as malignancy, and the authors themselves called for larger, longer safety studies.
cards.source: Hauser SL et al.; OPERA I and OPERA II Clinical Investigators. Ocrelizumab versus Interferon Beta-1a in Relapsing Multiple Sclerosis. N Engl J Med. 2017 Jan;376(3):221-234. PMID: 28002679. Registry IDs (record's databank): ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01247324 and NCT01412333.

cards.headline: Synthesis: consistent twin-trial benefit on relapses, progression and MRI, against an older comparator
cards.summary: Consistent twin-trial benefit on relapses, confirmed progression (pooled 9.1% vs 13.6% at 12 weeks) and MRI lesions — against an older comparator; LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: OPERA I (821 patients) and OPERA II (835 patients), 96 weeks each.
cards.result: Two identical trials gave near-identical results — relapse rate 0.16 versus 0.29 in both, pooled 12-week confirmed progression 9.1% versus 13.6% and 24-week 6.9% versus 10.5%, and near-elimination of gadolinium-enhancing lesions. This shelf is stamped LIKELY: the direction and size are consistent across two large trials, while the disability hazard ratio (0.60) sits inside the 0.5-2.0 band and the comparator is interferon, so the stamp rests on the whole pattern, not the ratio alone.
cards.watchOut: Nothing on this shelf compares ocrelizumab with other modern disease-modifying therapies, and no mortality outcome is reported in the record.

shelves.title: OnabotulinumtoxinA for chronic migraine prevention
shelves.question: Does botulinum toxin A reduce headache days in chronic migraine?
shelves.mesh: Botulinum Toxins, Type A/therapeutic use · Intention to Treat Analysis · Migraine Disorders/therapy · Patient Compliance · Patient Selection · Severity of Illness Index
shelves.balance: LIKELY: In the pooled PREEMPT twin trials, onabotulinumtoxinA reduced headache days by -8.4 versus -6.6 on placebo at 24 weeks — a between-group difference of about 1.8 headache days, statistically robust across two identical large trials but modest in size against a large placebo response. Adverse events were more frequent on active treatment (62.4% vs 51.7%), mostly mild to moderate, with discontinuation for adverse events in 3.8% versus 1.2%.

cards.headline: PREEMPT pooled: headache days fell by 8.4 on onabotulinumtoxinA versus 6.6 on placebo
cards.summary: PREEMPT pooled: headache days fell −8.4 vs −6.6 at week 24 (P<.001) — a between-group difference of about 1.8 days .
cards.type: Pooled analysis of two identical randomised controlled trials (phase 3)
cards.people: 1,384 adults with chronic migraine randomised to onabotulinumtoxinA 155-195 U (n=688) or placebo (n=696), injected every 12 weeks, in the 24-week double-blind phases of PREEMPT 1 and 2. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Mean change from baseline in frequency of headache days at week 24 was -8.4 with onabotulinumtoxinA versus -6.6 with placebo (P<.001), a between-group difference of about 1.8 headache days, with significant differences favouring onabotulinumtoxinA at all time points and for all secondary efficacy variables except frequency of acute headache pain medication intakes. Adverse events occurred in 62.4% of onabotulinumtoxinA patients versus 51.7% of placebo patients, were mostly mild to moderate, and led to discontinuation in 3.8% versus 1.2%; no unexpected treatment-related adverse events were identified.
cards.watchOut: Both groups improved substantially, so most of the fall in headache days is not drug-specific; the drug-attributable gain is the roughly 1.8-day difference, in chronic migraine only — this record does not cover episodic migraine.
cards.source: Dodick DW et al.; PREEMPT Chronic Migraine Study Group. OnabotulinumtoxinA for treatment of chronic migraine: pooled results from the double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled phases of the PREEMPT clinical program. Headache. 2010 Jun;50(6):921-36. PMID: 20487038. Registry IDs (record's databank): ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00156910 and NCT00168428.

cards.summary: A real but modest reduction on a large placebo response, with a tolerability cost (adverse events 62.4% vs 51.7%) — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: 1,384 adults pooled from the two identical PREEMPT trials.
cards.result: Headache days fell -8.4 versus -6.6 at 24 weeks in a prespecified pooling of two identical trials, consistent across secondary headache measures, with a tolerability cost (adverse events 62.4% vs 51.7%). shelves.title: The newer orexin antagonists: daridorexant and lemborexant for insomnia
shelves.question: Do daridorexant and lemborexant improve sleep onset and maintenance versus placebo, and how do they compare with a Z-drug?
shelves.mesh: Imidazoles · Pyrrolidines/adverse effects · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders/drug therapy · Delayed-Action Preparations · Hypnotics and Sedatives/therapeutic use · Polysomnography · Pyridines/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two daridorexant phase 3 trials and two lemborexant phase 3 trials consistently improved objective sleep onset and maintenance versus placebo — daridorexant 50 mg cut wake-after-sleep-onset by a further 18.3 minutes at month 3, and lemborexant beat both placebo and zolpidem ER on second-half-of-night wakefulness in older adults. The 10 mg daridorexant dose did not separate on the polysomnography primaries, and daytime-functioning gains were clearest at daridorexant 50 mg. Adverse-event rates were close to placebo in the daridorexant trials.

cards.headline: Daridorexant 25 mg and 50 mg improved sleep onset and maintenance in two phase 3 trials; 10 mg did not
cards.summary: Daridorexant: month-3 wake-after-sleep-onset differences vs placebo of −18.3 min (50 mg) and −11.9 min (25 mg), onset latency −11.7 and −7.6 min; the 10 mg dose did not separate.
cards.type: Two randomised controlled trials (phase 3, reported in one paper)
cards.people: Study 1: 930 adults with insomnia disorder (daridorexant 50 mg n=310, 25 mg n=310, placebo n=310). Study 2: 924 adults (25 mg n=309, 10 mg n=307, placebo n=308). Treatment every evening for 3 months. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: In study 1 at month 3, least-squares mean differences versus placebo for wake time after sleep onset (WASO) and latency to persistent sleep (LPS) were -18.3 min (95% CI -23.9 to -12.7) and -11.7 min (-16.3 to -7.0) for 50 mg, and -11.9 min (-17.5 to -6.2) and -7.6 min (-12.3 to -2.9) for 25 mg, all significant; self-reported total sleep time improved by 19.8 min (50 mg) and 9.9 min (25 mg), and daytime sleepiness-domain scores improved significantly only at 50 mg. In study 2, 25 mg significantly reduced WASO (-10.3 min at month 3) but its LPS differences did not meet the study-wise significance threshold, and 10 mg showed no significant WASO or LPS difference versus placebo. Overall adverse-event incidence was comparable across groups (about 38% on daridorexant versus 33-34% on placebo); nasopharyngitis and headache were most common. One death (cardiac arrest) occurred in the study-1 daridorexant 25 mg group and was not deemed treatment-related.
cards.watchOut: Effects are minutes of polysomnography-measured sleep over 3 months, not clinical events; the dose response matters — 10 mg failed the primary endpoints and daytime benefit was confined to 50 mg.
cards.source: Mignot E et al. Safety and efficacy of daridorexant in patients with insomnia disorder: results from two multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trials. Lancet Neurol. 2022;21:125-139. PMID: 35065036. Registry IDs (record's databank): ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03545191 (study 1) and NCT03575104 (study 2).

cards.headline: SUNRISE 1: lemborexant beat placebo on onset and maintenance, and zolpidem on late-night wakefulness, in older adults
cards.summary: SUNRISE 1: lemborexant onset ratios 0.77/0.72 — inside the 0.5–2.0 band, printed beside the absolute results — and a late-night wakefulness advantage over zolpidem ER.
cards.people: 1,006 participants aged 55 years and older with insomnia disorder (median age 63 years, range 55-88; 869 [86.4%] women), randomised to placebo (n=208), zolpidem tartrate extended release 6.25 mg (n=263), lemborexant 5 mg (n=266) or lemborexant 10 mg (n=269) for 1 month.
cards.result: At nights 29-30, latency to persistent sleep treatment ratios versus placebo were 0.77 (95% CI 0.67-0.89; P<.001) for lemborexant 5 mg and 0.72 (0.63-0.83; P<.001) for 10 mg — ratios inside the 0.5-2.0 band, printed beside the absolute-scale results: sleep efficiency improved by 7.1% (5 mg) and 8.0% (10 mg) versus placebo, and wake-after-sleep onset fell by 24.0 and 25.4 minutes versus placebo. Wake-after-sleep onset in the second half of the night was significantly lower than with zolpidem, by 6.7 minutes (5 mg; P=.004) and 8.0 minutes (10 mg; P<.001). Six participants reported serious adverse events (4 zolpidem, 2 lemborexant 5 mg), none treatment-related; other adverse events were mostly mild or moderate.
cards.watchOut: One month of polysomnography outcomes in adults 55 and older who were predominantly women; the zolpidem comparison covers one secondary endpoint (late-night wakefulness), not overall superiority, and no next-day-driving or falls outcomes are reported in the record.
cards.source: Rosenberg R et al. cards.headline: SUNRISE 2: lemborexant's subjective sleep benefits persisted over a 6-month placebo-controlled period
cards.summary: SUNRISE 2: lemborexant's subjective sleep benefits persisted over 6 months of placebo-controlled treatment.
cards.people: 949 participants aged 18 years or older with insomnia disorder, randomised to placebo, lemborexant 5 mg or lemborexant 10 mg; the 6-month placebo-controlled period is reported in this record. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Decreases in patient-reported sleep onset latency and wake after sleep onset, and increases in subjective sleep efficiency, were significantly greater with both lemborexant doses than placebo at the end of month 6 and at most time points over the 6 months; significantly more lemborexant participants were sleep onset and sleep maintenance responders, and quality of sleep improved significantly versus placebo. The abstract reports these results as significance statements without minute figures, so none are printed here. The majority of treatment-emergent adverse events were mild or moderate, serious events were few, and there were no deaths.
cards.watchOut: Outcomes here are patient-reported (subjective) rather than polysomnographic, and the second 6 months of the study were active-treatment-only with no placebo comparison.

shelves.title: Lithium for relapse prevention and suicide in mood disorders
shelves.question: Does lithium prevent mood-episode relapse and suicide in bipolar and unipolar mood disorders?
shelves.mesh: Antimanic Agents/therapeutic use · Bipolar Disorder/complications/drug therapy · Lithium Compounds/therapeutic use · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Self-Injurious Behavior/complications/prevention & control · Suicide Prevention · Bipolar Disorder/drug therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED ONLY, pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, slow lane; suicide/mortality claim): the Cipriani meta-analysis of 48 randomised trials found fewer suicides on lithium versus placebo (odds ratio 0.13, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.66), printed here — as this shelf must — beside deaths from any cause in the same analysis (odds ratio 0.38, 0.15 to 0.95), with no clear benefit on deliberate self harm (0.60, 0.27 to 1.32). Suicide events in these trials were rare, so the confidence intervals are wide. cards.headline: Cipriani 2013: fewer suicides and fewer deaths from any cause on lithium versus placebo, from rare events
cards.summary: Cipriani 2013: suicides on lithium vs placebo, odds ratio 0.13 [0.03 to 0.66] — printed beside all-cause deaths (odds ratio 0.38 ), as a mortality claim requires; both rest on rare events.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
cards.people: 48 randomised controlled trials, 6,674 participants with unipolar or bipolar mood disorders, comparing lithium with placebo or active drugs in long-term treatment. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Lithium was more effective than placebo in reducing suicides (odds ratio 0.13, 95% confidence interval 0.03 to 0.66) and — printed beside the suicide figure, as any mortality claim on this shelf requires — deaths from any cause (odds ratio 0.38, 0.15 to 0.95). No clear benefit was observed for deliberate self harm versus placebo (0.60, 0.27 to 1.32; a ratio inside the 0.5-2.0 band). In unipolar depression, lithium was associated with reduced suicide (0.36, 0.13 to 0.98) and total deaths (0.13, 0.02 to 0.76) versus placebo. Against individual active comparators, a statistically significant difference was found only against carbamazepine, for deliberate self harm.
cards.watchOut: Suicide is a rare outcome in randomised trials, so these odds ratios rest on very few events with wide confidence intervals; the trials were designed for relapse and efficacy outcomes, not powered for suicide, and absolute event rates are not given in the record, so none are printed here.

shelves.title: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation for major depression
shelves.question: Does rTMS beat sham stimulation for acute major depression?
shelves.mesh: Audiometry · Major Depressive Disorder/psychology/therapy · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation/adverse effects/instrumentation · Major Depressive Disorder/physiopathology/therapy · Dominance, Cerebral/physiology · Evoked Potentials, Motor/physiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two multisite sham-controlled trials found active rTMS superior to sham — in the NIMH trial remission was 14.1% versus 5.1% — but absolute remission rates were low, the earlier trial's primary result depended on a post hoc correction for baseline imbalance, and response/remission definitions and timing differed between trials. The direction favours rTMS; the size of the benefit in ordinary practice is less certain than the direction.

cards.headline: O'Reardon 2007: active TMS beat sham on depression scores at weeks 4 and 6, in a post hoc-corrected primary analysis
cards.summary: O'Reardon 2007: active TMS beat sham at weeks 4 and 6 — in a post hoc-corrected primary analysis, flagged on the card.
cards.people: 301 medication-free patients with major depression who had not benefited from prior treatment, randomised to active TMS (n=155) or sham TMS (n=146), five sessions per week for 4-6 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Active TMS was significantly superior to sham on the Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale at week 4 — with a post hoc correction for inequality in symptom severity between groups at baseline — and on the 17- and 24-item Hamilton scales at weeks 4 and 6. Response rates were significantly higher with active TMS on all three scales at weeks 4 and 6, and remission rates were approximately twofold higher at week 6, significant on the MADRS and HAMD24 but not the HAMD17. The record's abstract does not print the absolute response or remission percentages, so none are given here. Dropout for adverse events was low (4.5%), with effects generally mild and limited to transient scalp discomfort or pain.
cards.watchOut: The headline week-4 primary result required a post hoc correction for baseline imbalance — a fragility the reader should keep attached to this card; this was a medication-free, treatment-resistant population, not first-episode depression.
cards.source: O'Reardon JP et al. Efficacy and safety of transcranial magnetic stimulation in the acute treatment of major depression: a multisite randomized controlled trial. Biol Psychiatry. 2007;62:1208-16. PMID: 17573044. Registry ID (record's databank): ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00104611.

cards.headline: George 2010 (NIMH): remission 14.1% on active rTMS versus 5.1% on sham, with rigorous sham masking
cards.summary: George 2010 (NIMH, rigorous sham): remission 14.1% vs 5.1% ; odds 4.2 times greater, with a wide interval printed beside the absolute rates.
cards.people: About 860 outpatients screened, yielding 199 antidepressant drug-free patients with unipolar nonpsychotic major depressive disorder; the intention-to-treat sample was 190. Daily weekday treatment for 3 weeks, continued blinded for up to 3 further weeks in improvers. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Remission rates were 14.1% with active rTMS versus 5.1% with sham (P=.02); the odds of attaining remission were 4.2 times greater with active rTMS (95% confidence interval 1.32-13.24) — a ratio outside the 0.5-2.0 band but with a wide interval, printed here beside the absolute rates (14.1% vs 5.1%, an absolute difference of about 9 percentage points). Patients, treaters and raters were effectively masked, minimal adverse effects did not differ by arm, and retention was 88% (90% sham, 86% active).
cards.watchOut: Even in the positive trial, about 86% of actively treated patients did not remit; the wide confidence interval on the odds ratio (1.32-13.24) means the true advantage could be much smaller than 4.2-fold.
cards.source: George MS et al. Daily left prefrontal transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy for major depressive disorder: a sham-controlled randomized trial. Arch Gen Psychiatry. 2010;67:507-16. PMID: 20439832. Registry ID (record's databank): ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00149838.

cards.headline: Synthesis: rTMS beats sham, with low absolute remission and one fragile primary analysis
cards.summary: rTMS beats sham, with low absolute remission and one fragile primary analysis — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: O'Reardon 2007 (301 patients) and George 2010 (199 enrolled, 190 in the intention-to-treat sample).
cards.result: Both multisite sham-controlled trials favoured active rTMS on symptom scores, response and remission; the cleaner trial (George 2010, with an active sham and effective masking) found remission in 14.1% versus 5.1%. This shelf is stamped POSSIBLE: the direction is supported by two trials, but absolute remission is low, one primary analysis needed a post hoc correction, and the remission odds ratio's interval is wide.
cards.watchOut: Do not present rTMS remission as common — on the best trial roughly one in seven remitted on active treatment — and do not extrapolate to psychotic, bipolar or medication-continuing populations, which these trials did not study.

shelves.title: Prazosin for PTSD nightmares
shelves.question: Does prazosin reduce nightmares and improve sleep in PTSD?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic alpha-Antagonists/therapeutic use · Blood Pressure/drug effects · Case-Control Studies · Combat Disorders/complications/drug therapy/psychology · Cross-Over Studies · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Dreams/drug effects
shelves.balance: Split — POSSIBLE in the small early trials / MAYBE (weak evidence) overall after the large null VA trial: the early single-centre evidence was positive (a 40-veteran parallel trial reported prazosin significantly superior on nightmares, sleep quality and global status, with large effect sizes but no numeric scores in its record), while the large multicentre VA Cooperative Study of 304 veterans found no difference from placebo on nightmare, sleep-quality or global-change scores at 10 or 26 weeks. The discordance is by trial size and setting, and this shelf keeps it two-handed: benefit is possible in the populations the small trials studied, and unproven — MAYBE (weak evidence) — as a general claim after the large null trial.

cards.headline: Early trials: prazosin significantly reduced trauma nightmares in a 40-veteran placebo-controlled trial
cards.summary: Early trials: a 40-veteran trial found significant nightmare reduction with large reported effect sizes — its record prints no numeric scores, and the card says so.
cards.people: 40 veterans (mean age 56 ± 9 years) with chronic PTSD, distressing trauma nightmares and sleep disturbance, randomised to evening prazosin (mean dose 13.3 ± 3 mg/day) or placebo for 8 weeks; the evaluable sample was 34. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: In the evaluable sample, prazosin was significantly superior to placebo for reducing trauma nightmares and improving sleep quality and global clinical status, with large effect sizes reported by the authors; prazosin also shifted dream characteristics from trauma-nightmare-like toward normal dreaming. The record's abstract reports these results qualitatively and prints no numeric outcome scores, so none are given here. Blood pressure changes from baseline to end of study did not differ significantly between prazosin and placebo. The authors note an earlier 10-veteran placebo-controlled crossover study from the same programme, also positive, described within this record.
cards.watchOut: A small, single-centre trial (34 evaluable) from the programme that developed the treatment; its record gives significance and 'large effect sizes' without the numbers needed to check the size of the benefit.
cards.source: Raskind MA et al. A parallel group placebo controlled study of prazosin for trauma nightmares and sleep disturbance in combat veterans with post-traumatic stress disorder. Biol Psychiatry. 2007;61:928-34. PMID: 17069768. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: VA Cooperative Study (PACT): prazosin did not beat placebo on nightmares, sleep quality or global change in 304 veterans
cards.summary: VA Cooperative Study (PACT, 304 veterans): between-group differences of 0.2, 0.1 and 0 points on its three primary outcomes — null .
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (multicentre, VA Cooperative Studies Program)
cards.people: 304 veterans with chronic PTSD and frequent nightmares, recruited at 13 VA medical centres, randomised to prazosin (n=152) or placebo (n=152) for 26 weeks; dose escalated to a daily maximum of 20 mg in men and 12 mg in women. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: At 10 weeks there were no significant differences between prazosin and placebo on any primary outcome: change in the CAPS recurrent-distressing-dreams item (between-group difference 0.2; 95% CI -0.3 to 0.8; P=0.38), change in Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index score (0.1; -0.9 to 1.1; P=0.80), or Clinical Global Impression of Change score (0; -0.3 to 0.3; P=0.96). There were no significant differences at 26 weeks or in other secondary outcomes. Supine systolic blood pressure fell by a mean 6.7 mm Hg more on prazosin, and new or worsening suicidal ideation occurred in 8% of the prazosin group versus 15% of the placebo group.
cards.watchOut: This is the largest and only multicentre trial on the shelf, and it is null on every primary outcome — it cannot be waved away as underpowered; equally, its population (chronic PTSD in VA care, on stable concurrent treatment) is not identical to the earlier trials' populations.

cards.headline: Synthesis: small early trials positive, the one large multicentre trial null — the discordance stands
cards.summary: Small early trials positive, the one large multicentre trial null — the discordance stands; split stamp as proposed.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: the early parallel trial (40 randomised, 34 evaluable) and the VA Cooperative Study (304 randomised).
cards.result: The evidence splits by size: a small single-centre trial reported significant benefit with large effect sizes (no numeric scores in its record), and the 304-veteran multicentre trial found between-group differences of 0.2, 0.1 and 0 points on its three primary outcomes, all non-significant, at both 10 and 26 weeks. This shelf is therefore split-stamped — POSSIBLE for benefit in settings like the early trials, MAYBE (weak evidence) for the general claim — and neither half may be quoted without the other.
cards.watchOut: Do not resolve this discordance by averaging: the large trial's null is the strongest single piece of evidence, and the small trials' positives are the least independently replicated. Any use of prazosin for nightmares is an extrapolation decision, not a settled evidence claim.

shelves.title: Acupuncture for chronic pain
shelves.question: Does acupuncture relieve chronic pain (back/neck, osteoarthritis, headache, shoulder) more than sham acupuncture and more than no treatment?
shelves.mesh: Acupuncture Therapy/methods · Chronic Pain/therapy · Pain Measurement · Acupuncture Therapy/methods/psychology/trends · Chronic Pain/diagnosis/psychology/therapy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic/methods
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: In individual-patient-data meta-analyses pooling roughly 18,000-21,000 patients, acupuncture beat both sham and no-acupuncture controls for each chronic pain condition, but the specific effect over sham was small — about 0.15-0.23 standard deviations in the 2012 analysis, and close to 0.2 standard deviations in the 2018 update — versus about 0.5 standard deviations against no treatment. Most of the benefit over doing nothing is therefore not needle-specific, though the sham difference was statistically robust and the effect largely persisted at 1 year (about a 15% decrease).

cards.headline: Vickers 2012 IPD meta-analysis: acupuncture beat sham by 0.15-0.23 SD and no treatment by about 0.5 SD
cards.summary: Vickers 2012 (individual-patient data): acupuncture beat sham by 0.15–0.23 SD and no treatment by about 0.5 SD .
cards.type: Individual-patient-data meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
cards.people: 29 of 31 eligible randomised trials, 17,922 patients analysed, across back and neck pain, osteoarthritis, chronic headache and shoulder pain; trials were included only if allocation concealment was unambiguously adequate. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Acupuncture was superior to both sham and no-acupuncture control for each pain condition (P<.001 for all comparisons). Against sham, patients receiving acupuncture had pain scores 0.23 (95% CI 0.13-0.33) SDs lower for back and neck pain, 0.16 (0.07-0.25) for osteoarthritis and 0.15 (0.07-0.24) for chronic headache; against no-acupuncture control the effect sizes were 0.55 (0.51-0.58), 0.57 (0.50-0.64) and 0.42 (0.37-0.46) SDs respectively. Results were robust to sensitivity analyses including publication-bias analyses. The authors concluded acupuncture is a reasonable referral option, that it is more than a placebo, and that the sham differences are relatively modest, suggesting factors beyond needling contribute importantly to the therapeutic effect.
cards.watchOut: The comparison that isolates the needle's specific effect is the sham comparison, and it is small (0.15-0.23 SD); the larger no-treatment comparison bundles in context, attention and natural history.
cards.source: Vickers AJ et al. Acupuncture for chronic pain: individual patient data meta-analysis. Arch Intern Med. 2012;172:1444-53. PMID: 22965186. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — meta-analysis, not a single trial.

cards.headline: Vickers 2018 update: the pattern held in 39 trials and 20,827 patients, with effects persisting at 1 year
cards.summary: Vickers 2018 update: the pattern held across 39 trials and 20,827 patients , with effects persisting at 1 year.
cards.type: Individual-patient-data meta-analysis (update) of randomised controlled trials
cards.people: 39 randomised trials, 20,827 patients, for nonspecific musculoskeletal pain, osteoarthritis, chronic headache or shoulder pain, with adequate allocation concealment required. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: An additional 13 trials were identified for this update. Acupuncture was superior to sham as well as to no-acupuncture control for each pain condition (all P<.001), with differences close to 0.5 SDs compared with no-acupuncture control and close to 0.2 SDs compared with sham. The effects of acupuncture persisted over time with only a small decrease, approximately 15%, in treatment effect at 1 year. Effect sizes were smaller in sham-controlled trials that used a penetrating needle for sham and in trials with a high-intensity control-arm intervention.
cards.watchOut: The update confirms, rather than enlarges, the specific effect: close to 0.2 SD over sham. Sham technique itself changes the measured effect, which is part of why the specific-effect estimate stays contested.
cards.source: Vickers AJ et al. Acupuncture for Chronic Pain: Update of an Individual Patient Data Meta-Analysis. J Pain. 2018;19:455-474. PMID: 29198932. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — meta-analysis, not a single trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: better than sham by a small margin, better than nothing by a moderate one
cards.summary: Better than sham by a small margin, better than nothing by a moderate one — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: the 2012 IPD meta-analysis (17,922 patients) and its 2018 update (20,827 patients).
cards.result: Two successive individual-patient-data meta-analyses, restricted to trials with adequate allocation concealment, give the same shape: about 0.15-0.23 SD (2012) and close to 0.2 SD (2018) over sham, and about 0.42-0.57 SD (2012) and close to 0.5 SD (2018) over no treatment, with roughly 85% of the effect retained at 1 year. This shelf is stamped POSSIBLE: a specific effect beyond sham is moderately supported and consistently estimated, and it is small.
cards.watchOut: Never quote the no-treatment effect size as the effect of acupuncture itself; and never quote the sham effect without its size — 'statistically superior to sham' and '0.2 SD' are the same finding stated two ways.

shelves.title: Topical NSAIDs for chronic musculoskeletal pain
shelves.question: Do topical NSAIDs relieve osteoarthritis and other chronic musculoskeletal pain, and with what harm trade versus oral NSAIDs?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Topical · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Chronic Pain/drug therapy · Diclofenac/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Ketoprofen/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Musculoskeletal Pain/drug therapy · Numbers Needed To Treat
shelves.balance: LIKELY: The Cochrane synthesis found topical diclofenac and topical ketoprofen beat their carrier in 6-12-week osteoarthritis trials — numbers needed to treat for clinical success of 9.8 and 6.9, with about 60% of participants achieving much reduced pain against a carrier response of around half — on moderate-quality evidence. The few trials against oral NSAIDs showed similar efficacy (low-quality evidence). Local skin reactions increased with diclofenac but not ketoprofen; systemic adverse-event reporting was poor, so the harm advantage over oral NSAIDs is plausible and consistent with the pharmacology but thinly documented in these trials. The evidence is almost entirely knee osteoarthritis.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2016: topical diclofenac and ketoprofen beat carrier for osteoarthritis pain, NNTs 9.8 and 6.9
cards.summary: Cochrane 2016: clinical success NNT 9.8 (topical diclofenac) and 6.9 (ketoprofen) vs carrier over 6–12 weeks; about 60% achieved much-reduced pain.
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised controlled trials (Cochrane)
cards.people: 39 studies, 10,631 participants with chronic musculoskeletal pain of moderate or severe intensity; 33 studies compared a topical NSAID with carrier, and all studies examined osteoarthritis. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: In studies lasting 6 to 12 weeks, topical diclofenac and topical ketoprofen were significantly more effective than carrier, with about 60% of participants achieving much reduced pain. The number needed to treat for clinical success (at least 50% pain reduction or equivalent) was 9.8 (95% CI 7.1 to 16) for topical diclofenac (6 trials, 2,343 participants) and 6.9 (5.4 to 9.3) for topical ketoprofen (4 trials, 2,573 participants), both moderate-quality evidence; there was too little information to analyse other topical NSAIDs. Clinical success with carrier alone occurred in around half of participants. Few trials compared a topical with an oral NSAID, but overall they showed similar efficacy (low-quality evidence). These efficacy results were almost completely derived from people with knee osteoarthritis.
cards.watchOut: The carrier (vehicle gel) itself produced success in about half of participants — response rates about twice those seen with oral placebo in indirect comparison — so the drug-attributable gain is the NNT gap, not the 60% headline.
cards.source: Derry S et al. Topical NSAIDs for chronic musculoskeletal pain in adults. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2016;4:CD007400. PMID: 27103611. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — systematic review, not a single trial.

cards.summary: Harms in the same record: more local skin reactions with diclofenac; systemic adverse events poorly reported , and the card says so.
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised controlled trials (Cochrane) — harms and comparisons
cards.people: Same evidence base as the efficacy card: 39 studies, 10,631 participants, all in osteoarthritis.
cards.result: There was an increase in local adverse events (mostly mild skin reactions) with topical diclofenac compared with carrier or oral NSAIDs, but no increase with topical ketoprofen (moderate-quality evidence). Reporting of systemic adverse events such as gastrointestinal upsets was poor; where reported there was no difference between topical NSAID and carrier (very low-quality evidence). Serious adverse events were infrequent and not different between topical NSAID and carrier (very low-quality evidence). A substantial amount of data from completed, unpublished studies was unavailable (up to 6,000 participants), much of it probably relating to formulations never marketed.
cards.watchOut: 'No difference in systemic events' here is very low-quality evidence built on poor reporting — it supports, but does not prove, the safety advantage over oral NSAIDs; and up to 6,000 participants' worth of unpublished data could not be included.

cards.summary: Good pain relief for a minority, chiefly in knee osteoarthritis, at mainly local cost — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: one Cochrane synthesis, 39 studies and 10,631 participants.
cards.result: Topical diclofenac (NNT 9.8) and ketoprofen (NNT 6.9) each beat carrier over 6-12 weeks on moderate-quality evidence, matched oral NSAIDs in the few head-to-head trials (low-quality evidence), and cost mainly local skin reactions, with systemic-event data too poorly reported to grade above very low quality. shelves.title: Lisdexamfetamine for binge-eating disorder
shelves.question: Does lisdexamfetamine reduce binge-eating days in adults with moderate-to-severe binge-eating disorder?
shelves.mesh: Binge-Eating Disorder/drug therapy · Dextroamphetamine/administration & dosage/adverse effects/pharmacology · Dopamine Uptake Inhibitors/administration & dosage/adverse effects/pharmacology · Lisdexamfetamine Dimesylate · Severity of Illness Index · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Lisdexamfetamine Dimesylate/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Three placebo-controlled trials from one programme agree: the dose-ranging trial found 50 mg and 70 mg (not 30 mg) reduced binge-eating days and raised 4-week cessation rates (42.2% and 50.0% versus 21.3% on placebo), and the two pivotal trials found treatment differences of -1.35 and -1.66 binge-eating days per week. The harm side is stimulant-typical: any treatment-emergent adverse event in 84.7% on drug versus 58.7% on placebo in the dose trial, dry mouth, insomnia and headache most common in the pivotal trials, with small mean rises in pulse and blood pressure and weight loss of about 4-5 kg versus about 0 kg on placebo in the dose trial.

cards.headline: Dose-ranging trial: 50 mg and 70 mg reduced binge days and doubled 4-week cessation; 30 mg did not separate
cards.summary: Dose-ranging trial: 50 mg and 70 mg separated from placebo (30 mg did not); 4-week cessation 42.2% and 50.0% vs 21.3%.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (phase 2, forced dose titration)
cards.people: 259 adults with moderate to severe binge-eating disorder in the safety analysis and 255 in the intention-to-treat analysis, randomised to lisdexamfetamine 30, 50 or 70 mg/day or placebo (1:1:1:1) for 11 weeks at 30 sites. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At week 11, nontransformed mean binge-eating days per week fell by 3.3 on placebo and by 3.5, 4.1 and 4.1 days on 30, 50 and 70 mg respectively; on the primary log-transformed analysis the 50 mg (P=.008) and 70 mg (P<.001) groups separated significantly from placebo while 30 mg did not (P=.88). Four-week binge-eating cessation was achieved by 21.3% on placebo versus 42.2% on 50 mg (P=.01) and 50.0% on 70 mg (P<.001). Any treatment-emergent adverse event occurred in 58.7% on placebo versus 84.7% on combined lisdexamfetamine; serious treatment-emergent events occurred in 1.5% of treated participants. Mean weight change was -0.1 kg on placebo versus -4.9 kg on both 50 mg and 70 mg (P<.001 for each dose versus placebo).
cards.watchOut: A single 11-week trial from the development programme; weight loss and stimulant adverse events are part of the effect profile, and the record reports heart-rate changes as consistent with the known safety profile without printing a full cardiovascular dataset.
cards.source: McElroy SL et al. Efficacy and safety of lisdexamfetamine for treatment of adults with moderate to severe binge-eating disorder: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA Psychiatry. 2015;72:235-46. PMID: 25587645. Registry ID (record's databank): ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01291173.

cards.headline: Two pivotal phase 3 trials: binge-eating days fell by 1.35 and 1.66 more per week than on placebo
cards.summary: Two pivotal trials: binge-eating days fell by 1.35 and 1.66 more per week than on placebo.
cards.type: Two randomised controlled trials (phase 3, reported in one paper)
cards.people: Adults meeting DSM-IV-TR criteria for binge-eating disorder: study 1, n=383; study 2, n=390; randomised 1:1 to placebo or lisdexamfetamine (50 or 70 mg/day, dose-optimised) to week 12. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Least-squares mean treatment differences for change from baseline in binge-eating days per week at weeks 11-12 significantly favoured lisdexamfetamine in both studies: study 1, -1.35 (95% CI -1.70 to -1.01); study 2, -1.66 (-2.04 to -1.28); both P<.001. Treatment-emergent adverse events reported by at least 10% of lisdexamfetamine participants were dry mouth, insomnia and headache. Serious treatment-emergent events occurred in 1.6% and 0.6% of lisdexamfetamine participants in studies 1 and 2, versus 1.1% of placebo participants in each study. Across studies, mean increases from baseline at week 12 with lisdexamfetamine ranged from 4.41 to 6.31 beats per minute for pulse, 0.2 to 1.45 mm Hg for systolic and 1.06 to 1.83 mm Hg for diastolic blood pressure.
cards.watchOut: Both pivotal trials come from the same sponsor programme as the dose-ranging trial, ran 12 weeks, and used binge-eating days — a symptomatic outcome — with no longer-term relapse, weight-trajectory or cardiovascular outcome data in the record.
cards.source: McElroy SL et al. Lisdexamfetamine Dimesylate for Adults with Moderate to Severe Binge Eating Disorder: Results of Two Pivotal Phase 3 Randomized Controlled Trials. cards.headline: Synthesis: consistent reduction in binge-eating days at 50-70 mg, with a stimulant harm profile
cards.summary: Consistent reduction in binge-eating days at 50–70 mg, with a stimulant harm profile — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: the dose-ranging trial (255 in the intention-to-treat analysis) and the two pivotal trials (383 and 390 participants).
cards.result: Across three trials the effective doses (50 and 70 mg) consistently reduced binge-eating days — by 1.35 and 1.66 days per week beyond placebo in the pivotal trials — and roughly doubled 4-week cessation in the dose trial (42.2% and 50.0% versus 21.3%), while 30 mg did not separate. Adverse events were substantially more common on drug (84.7% vs 58.7% for any event in the dose trial), with small pulse and blood-pressure rises. This shelf is stamped LIKELY for short-term reduction in binge-eating days in moderate-to-severe binge-eating disorder.
cards.watchOut: All three trials are short (11-12 weeks) and from one development programme; nothing on this shelf addresses maintenance of effect after stopping, misuse liability in this population, or outcomes beyond binge-eating days.

shelves.title: Prolonged antibiotics for persistent symptoms attributed to Lyme disease
shelves.question: Do longer courses of antibiotics help patients with persistent symptoms after Lyme disease?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Antimalarials/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Clarithromycin/administration & dosage · Doxycycline/administration & dosage · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Therapy, Combination · Hydroxychloroquine/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: LIKELY (for the null): Three randomised programmes converge. In PLEASE (281 patients), 12 weeks of doxycycline or clarithromycin-hydroxychloroquine after 2 weeks of open-label ceftriaxone gave SF-36 physical-component scores of 35.0 and 35.6 versus 34.8 on placebo (P=0.69). In the two Klempner trials (129 patients), 90 days of intravenous then oral antibiotics improved quality-of-life scores no more than placebo (among seropositive patients, improvement in 37% on antibiotics versus 40% on placebo). The one discordant note is Fallon's small trial (37 patients): 10 weeks of IV ceftriaxone gave a moderate cognitive improvement at week 12 that was not sustained to week 24, with adverse events in 26.1% on ceftriaxone versus 7.1% on placebo. The defensible claim is that longer antibiotic courses do not produce durable benefit for persistent symptoms attributed to Lyme disease, while carrying line and drug harms — not that patients' symptoms are unreal; baseline impairment in these trials was severe.

cards.headline: PLEASE: 12 extra weeks of oral antibiotics after ceftriaxone did not improve quality of life (SF-36 physical 35.0 / 35.6 versus 34.8, P=0.69)
cards.summary: PLEASE (281 patients): SF-36 physical scores 35.0 / 35.6 vs 34.8 on placebo (P=0.69) after 12 extra weeks of oral antibiotics.
cards.people: 281 patients with persistent symptoms attributed to Lyme disease underwent randomisation; 280 were analysed (86 doxycycline, 96 clarithromycin plus hydroxychloroquine, and 98 placebo), all after open-label intravenous ceftriaxone for 2 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At week 14, the SF-36 physical-component summary score (range 15 to 61) did not differ significantly among the groups: 35.0 (95% CI, 33.5 to 36.5) with doxycycline, 35.6 (95% CI, 34.2 to 37.1) with clarithromycin-hydroxychloroquine, and 34.8 (95% CI, 33.4 to 36.2) with placebo (P=0.69; difference for doxycycline versus placebo 0.2 [95% CI, -2.4 to 2.8]). Scores also did not differ at subsequent visits (P=0.35), though scores in all groups rose significantly from baseline. Adverse-event rates were similar; four serious adverse events thought drug-related occurred during the open-label ceftriaxone phase, and none during the randomised phase.
cards.watchOut: Every participant received 2 weeks of ceftriaxone before randomisation, so the trial tests longer versus shorter total therapy, not antibiotics versus none; the across-group improvement from baseline is exactly the pattern placebo and time produce, and cannot be credited to the randomised drugs.

cards.summary: Klempner 2001: 90 days of IV plus oral antibiotics no better than placebo in either serogroup; the trials were stopped early; improvement 37% vs 40%.
cards.people: 78 patients seropositive for IgG antibodies to Borrelia burgdorferi and 51 patients seronegative, all with well-documented, previously treated Lyme disease but persistent musculoskeletal pain, neurocognitive symptoms, or dysesthesia, often with fatigue. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Patients received intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily for 30 days followed by oral doxycycline 200 mg daily for 60 days, or matching placebos. After a planned interim analysis, the data and safety monitoring board recommended discontinuation because data from the first 107 patients made a significant difference in efficacy highly unlikely with the planned enrolment of 260. Among seropositive patients on antibiotics, the SF-36 physical- or mental-component score improved in 37%, was unchanged in 29%, and worsened in 34%; on placebo, improvement in 40%, no change in 26%, and worsening in 34% (P=0.96). Results were similar for seronegative patients. Baseline assessments documented severe impairment in health-related quality of life.
cards.watchOut: Stopped early for futility, so the trials are smaller than planned — but the point estimates themselves show no trend favouring antibiotics (37% versus 40% improved), which is why the null does not rest on power alone.

cards.headline: Fallon 2008: repeated IV ceftriaxone improved cognition at week 12, but the gain was gone by week 24
cards.summary: Fallon 2008: a week-12 cognitive gain on repeated IV ceftriaxone was gone by week 24 .
cards.people: 37 patients with well-documented Lyme disease, at least 3 weeks of prior IV antibiotics, current positive IgG Western blot, and objective memory impairment (23 ceftriaxone and 14 placebo), plus 20 healthy controls for practice effects; 3,368 patients were screened to enrol 37.
cards.result: Across six cognitive domains, a significant treatment-by-time interaction favoured the antibiotic-treated group at week 12; the improvement was generalised and moderate in magnitude, but was not sustained to week 24. On secondary outcomes, patients with more severe fatigue, pain, and impaired physical functioning who received antibiotics were improved at week 12, sustained to week 24 for pain and physical functioning. Adverse events from the study medication or the PICC line occurred in 6 of 23 (26.1%) patients given IV ceftriaxone and 1 of 14 (7.1%) given placebo, resolving without permanent injury.
cards.watchOut: The smallest and most selected of the three programmes (37 of 3,368 screened), with a transient primary-outcome benefit and a 26.1% adverse-event rate — it qualifies the null, it does not overturn the two larger null programmes.

cards.headline: Synthesis: prolonged antibiotics do not durably help persistent post-Lyme symptoms — LIKELY the null, with one transient small-trial exception
cards.summary: Prolonged antibiotics do not durably help persistent post-Lyme symptoms — LIKELY, for the null.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: 281 patients in PLEASE, 129 in the two Klempner trials, and 37 in Fallon — all randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, in patients with persistent symptoms after treated Lyme disease.
cards.result: The two larger programmes are flatly null on quality of life (PLEASE differences of 0.2 and 0.9 SF-36 points versus placebo; Klempner improvement in 37% on antibiotics versus 40% on placebo), and the smallest trial's cognitive benefit at week 12 had relapsed by week 24. LIKELY therefore stamps the null for durable benefit from longer courses. The trials simultaneously document severe baseline impairment — the symptoms are real; the prolonged-antibiotic remedy is what failed.
cards.watchOut: Do not cite Fallon's week-12 result without its week-24 relapse and its adverse-event rates, and do not extend this shelf to treatment of acute Lyme disease, which is a different question not carded here.
