shelves.title: Acute migraine treatment: the gepants
shelves.question: Do oral gepants (ubrogepant, rimegepant) relieve migraine pain at two hours versus placebo — the acute-treatment counterpart to the prevention shelf?
shelves.mesh: Analgesics/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Dizziness/chemically induced · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Migraine Disorders/drug therapy · Nausea/chemically induced · Pain/drug therapy · Pain Management
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two separate phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled single-attack trials — one per drug — both met their co-primary endpoints at 2 hours. Ubrogepant 50 mg gave pain freedom in 21.8% versus 14.3% on placebo (ACHIEVE II, 1,686 randomised) and rimegepant 75 mg gave 21% versus 11% (Croop 2019, 1,466 randomised), with most-bothersome-symptom freedom also ahead in both. The absolute gains are modest (about 7–10 percentage points for pain freedom), which the cards print beside the rates; the claim carded is a real, replicated acute benefit, not a large one.

cards.headline: ACHIEVE II 2019: ubrogepant 50 mg beat placebo on pain freedom at 2 hours — 21.8% vs 14.3%
cards.summary: ACHIEVE II 2019: ubrogepant 50 mg beat placebo on pain freedom at 2 hours — 21.8% vs 14.3% .
cards.type: Phase 3, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, single-attack trial
cards.people: 1,686 adults with migraine with or without aura (2–8 attacks per month) randomised at 99 US clinics to ubrogepant 50 mg (562), ubrogepant 25 mg (561) or placebo (563); 1,465 received study treatment (mean age 41.5 years; 90% female) and 1,355 were evaluable for efficacy.
cards.result: Pain freedom at 2 hours: 21.8% (101/464) on ubrogepant 50 mg, 20.7% (90/435) on 25 mg, and 14.3% (65/456) on placebo (absolute difference for 50 mg vs placebo 7.5%, 95% CI 2.6% to 12.5%; P=.01). Absence of the most bothersome symptom at 2 hours: 38.9% (50 mg), 34.1% (25 mg) and 27.4% (placebo) (absolute difference 11.5%, 5.4% to 17.5%; P=.01 for 50 mg; the 25 mg comparison was P=.07). The most common adverse events within 48 hours were nausea (2.0% on 50 mg vs 2.0% on placebo) and dizziness (1.4% vs 1.6%).
cards.watchOut: Single-attack, placebo-only comparison: no head-to-head against a triptan, and the absolute pain-freedom gain is about 7.5 percentage points — most treated attacks still do not end pain-free at 2 hours.
cards.source: Lipton RB et al. Effect of Ubrogepant vs Placebo on Pain and the Most Bothersome Associated Symptom in the Acute Treatment of Migraine: The ACHIEVE II Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2019;322(19):1887-1898. PMID: 31742631. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02867709, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Croop 2019: rimegepant 75 mg beat placebo on pain freedom at 2 hours — 21% vs 11%
cards.summary: Croop 2019: rimegepant 75 mg beat placebo on pain freedom at 2 hours — 21% vs 11% .
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre trial
cards.people: 1,466 adults aged 18 or older with at least a 1-year history of migraine, randomised at 69 US centres to rimegepant 75 mg orally disintegrating tablet (732) or placebo (734) for a single attack of moderate or severe pain; 1,351 were evaluated for efficacy (669 rimegepant, 682 placebo). The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: At 2 hours post-dose, freedom from pain was 21% on rimegepant versus 11% on placebo (risk difference 10, 95% CI 6 to 14; p<0.0001) and freedom from the most bothersome symptom was 35% versus 27% (risk difference 8, 3 to 13; p=0.0009) — absolute differences printed as the trial reported them. The most common adverse events were nausea (2% rimegepant vs <1% placebo) and urinary tract infection (1% vs <1%); no treated participant reported a serious adverse event.
cards.watchOut: Also a single-attack placebo comparison, of one formulation (orally disintegrating tablet): it does not compare rimegepant with triptans or with ubrogepant, and pain freedom at 2 hours was still only 21%.
cards.source: Croop R et al. Efficacy, safety, and tolerability of rimegepant orally disintegrating tablet for the acute treatment of migraine: a randomised, phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet. 2019;394(10200):737-745. PMID: 31311674. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03461757, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two drugs, two positive placebo trials — a real but modest acute benefit, LIKELY
cards.summary: Two drugs, two positive placebo trials — a real but modest acute benefit: LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: ACHIEVE II (1,686 randomised, ubrogepant) and Croop 2019 (1,466 randomised, rimegepant).
cards.result: Each gepant rests on its own pivotal trial, and the two trials agree in direction and size: pain freedom at 2 hours of 21.8% and 21% on active drug against 14.3% and 11% on placebo. That replication across two drugs of the same class is what carries the class claim to LIKELY; the absolute gains (7.5–10 percentage points) are printed on both cards so the benefit is not overstated. This shelf is acute treatment only: CGRP therapies for migraine PREVENTION live on Shelf #336 and are not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote either trial as evidence a gepant beats a triptan — neither trial had an active comparator.
cards.source: Synthesis of Lipton RB et al. JAMA. 2019;322(19):1887-1898. PMID: 31742631; Croop R et al. Lancet. 2019;394(10200):737-745. PMID: 31311674. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Cluster headache: galcanezumab prevention and high-flow oxygen
shelves.question: Does galcanezumab reduce weekly attack frequency in episodic cluster headache — and does high-flow oxygen abort attacks versus air?
shelves.mesh: Analgesics/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Cluster Headache/prevention & control · Drug Administration Schedule · Injections, Subcutaneous/adverse effects · Placebos/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: Split — POSSIBLE on both halves, each resting on a single trial. Galcanezumab 300 mg monthly reduced weekly episodic cluster attacks by 8.7 versus 5.2 on placebo across weeks 1–3 (difference 3.5 attacks per week, P=0.04) in a trial stopped early at 106 of a planned 162 patients (Goadsby 2019). High-flow oxygen rendered 78% of attacks pain-free at 15 minutes versus 20% on air in a 109-patient crossover trial (Cohen 2009) — a large effect, but a single trial, so the single-trial ceiling caps both halves at POSSIBLE. Both stamps are PROPOSED on single-trial evidence.

cards.headline: Goadsby 2019: galcanezumab cut weekly episodic cluster attacks by 3.5 more than placebo over weeks 1–3
cards.summary: Goadsby 2019: galcanezumab cut weekly episodic cluster attacks by 3.5 more than placebo over weeks 1–3 — a statistically fragile difference in an early-stopped trial.
cards.people: 106 patients with episodic cluster headache (at least one attack every other day, at least four total attacks, no more than eight per day at baseline; cluster periods lasting at least 6 weeks) randomised to galcanezumab 300 mg subcutaneously at baseline and 1 month (49) or placebo (57); recruitment was halted before the planned 162 because too few volunteers met eligibility. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Mean baseline attack frequency was 17.8 (SD 10.1) per week on galcanezumab and 17.3 (10.1) on placebo. The mean reduction in weekly attack frequency across weeks 1–3 was 8.7 attacks with galcanezumab versus 5.2 with placebo (difference 3.5 attacks per week, 95% CI 0.2 to 6.7; P=0.04). At week 3, 71% of the galcanezumab group versus 53% of the placebo group had a reduction of at least 50% in weekly attack frequency. Injection-site pain occurred in 8% of the galcanezumab group; there were no other substantial between-group differences in adverse events.
cards.watchOut: A single trial, stopped early for slow recruitment at two-thirds of its planned size, with a P value of 0.04 on the primary endpoint and a confidence interval reaching 0.2 attacks per week: supportive, not definitive — and episodic cluster only, not chronic.
cards.source: Goadsby PJ et al. Trial of Galcanezumab in Prevention of Episodic Cluster Headache. N Engl J Med. 2019;381(2):132-141. PMID: 31291515. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02397473, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Cohen 2009: high-flow oxygen made 78% of cluster attacks pain-free at 15 minutes, vs 20% on air
cards.summary: Cohen 2009: high-flow oxygen made 78% of cluster attacks pain-free at 15 minutes, vs 20% on air.
cards.people: 109 adults aged 18–70 years with cluster headache at a single London hospital, each treating 4 attacks alternately with high-flow oxygen or air; 57 patients with episodic and 19 with chronic cluster headache were available for the primary analysis (150 oxygen-treated and 148 air-treated attacks).
cards.result: For the primary endpoint — pain-free, or adequate relief, at 15 minutes — oxygen achieved 78% (95% CI 71% to 85%) of attacks versus 20% (14% to 26%) on air (P<.001), an absolute difference of about 58 percentage points. There were no important adverse events.
cards.watchOut: A single crossover trial from one centre, with attacks (not patients) as the unit of the headline analysis, and air as the comparator rather than subcutaneous sumatriptan, the licensed standard it would replace or accompany in practice.
cards.source: Cohen AS et al. High-flow oxygen for treatment of cluster headache: a randomized trial. JAMA. 2009;302(22):2451-2457. PMID: 19996400. Registry ID: ISRCTN94092997, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one trial each — prevention and abortion both POSSIBLE, neither yet replicated
cards.summary: One trial each — prevention and abortion both POSSIBLE, neither yet replicated.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Goadsby 2019 (106 patients, prevention) and Cohen 2009 (109 patients, acute abortion).
cards.result: The two halves of cluster care each have exactly one randomised trial behind them. Oxygen's effect is large (78% vs 20% pain-free at 15 minutes); galcanezumab's is smaller and statistically fragile (difference 3.5 attacks per week, 95% CI 0.2 to 6.7, in an early-stopped trial). Under this library's single-trial ceiling both are stamped POSSIBLE. The questions are different — preventing attacks over a cluster period versus aborting an attack already under way — and neither trial substitutes for the other.
cards.watchOut: Do not merge the two halves into a single 'cluster treatment works' claim: a patient can need both, and each claim stands or falls on its own single trial.

shelves.title: Myasthenia gravis: thymectomy and complement inhibition
shelves.question: Does thymectomy improve outcomes in non-thymomatous acetylcholine-receptor-positive generalised myasthenia (MGTX) — and does eculizumab help refractory disease (REGAIN)?
shelves.mesh: Combined Modality Therapy · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage · Hospitalization · Myasthenia Gravis/classification,drug therapy,surgery · Prednisone/administration & dosage · Severity of Illness Index · Thymectomy
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — thymectomy: in MGTX (126 patients), thymectomy plus prednisone beat prednisone alone over 3 years on both co-primary outcomes (time-weighted Quantitative Myasthenia Gravis score 6.15 vs 8.99; prednisone dose 44 mg vs 60 mg), a single randomised trial, so POSSIBLE. MAYBE (weak evidence) — eculizumab: REGAIN's pre-specified primary analysis MISSED (worst-rank MG-ADL difference −11.7, 95% CI −24.3 to 0.96; p=0.0698), and its authors state the secondary and sensitivity analyses were inconsistent with the primary result — a missed primary endpoint is weak evidence of benefit, printed as MAYBE (weak evidence), never as established efficacy.

cards.headline: MGTX 2016: thymectomy plus prednisone beat prednisone alone over 3 years — QMG score 6.15 vs 8.99 and less prednisone
cards.summary: MGTX 2016: thymectomy plus prednisone beat prednisone alone over 3 years — QMG score 6.15 vs 8.99 and less prednisone.
cards.type: Multicentre randomised trial with blinded outcome rating
cards.people: 126 patients aged 18–65 years with generalised non-thymomatous myasthenia gravis of less than 5 years' duration, Myasthenia Gravis Foundation of America class II–IV, and elevated acetylcholine-receptor antibody, randomised at 36 sites to extended transsternal thymectomy plus alternate-day prednisone or prednisone alone.
cards.result: Over 3 years, the time-weighted average Quantitative Myasthenia Gravis score (0–39, higher = more severe) was 6.15 with thymectomy versus 8.99 with prednisone alone (P<0.001), and the time-weighted average alternate-day prednisone dose was 44 mg versus 60 mg (P<0.001). Fewer thymectomy patients required azathioprine immunosuppression (17% vs 48%, P<0.001) or were hospitalised for exacerbations (9% vs 37%, P<0.001). Treatment-associated complications did not differ significantly between groups (P=0.73).
cards.watchOut: A single randomised trial of one surgical technique (extended transsternal) in patients under 65 with disease under 5 years: it does not cover older patients, ocular disease, or minimally invasive thymectomy approaches.
cards.source: Wolfe GI et al. Randomized Trial of Thymectomy in Myasthenia Gravis. N Engl J Med. 2016;375(6):511-522. PMID: 27509100. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00294658, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: REGAIN 2017: eculizumab MISSED its primary endpoint — worst-rank MG-ADL difference −11.7 (95% CI −24.3 to 0.96), p=0.0698
cards.summary: REGAIN 2017: eculizumab MISSED its primary endpoint — worst-rank MG-ADL difference −11.7 (95% CI −24.3 to 0.96), p=0.0698.
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre study
cards.people: 125 patients aged at least 18 years with anti-acetylcholine receptor antibody-positive refractory generalised myasthenia (MG-ADL score 6 or more, MGFA class II–IV, previously treated with at least two immunosuppressive therapies, or one plus chronic IVIG or plasma exchange) randomised at 76 sites in 17 countries to intravenous eculizumab (62) or placebo (63) for 26 weeks.
cards.result: The primary efficacy endpoint — change in MG-ADL total score by worst-rank ANCOVA — showed NO significant difference: least-squares mean rank 56.6 (SEM 4.5) on eculizumab versus 68.3 (4.5) on placebo (rank-based treatment difference −11.7, 95% CI −24.3 to 0.96; p=0.0698). No deaths or meningococcal infections occurred. Myasthenia exacerbations were reported by 6 (10%) eculizumab patients versus 15 (24%) on placebo, and rescue therapy was required by 6 (10%) versus 12 (19%) — secondary counts the authors set against a primary result they describe as inconsistent with the secondary and sensitivity analyses.
cards.watchOut: The headline is the missed primary endpoint: the worst-rank analysis the trial pre-specified did not separate eculizumab from placebo, and the authors themselves call that analytical approach an important limitation while stating further research is needed. Secondary signals do not convert a missed primary into proven efficacy.
cards.source: Howard JF Jr et al. Safety and efficacy of eculizumab in anti-acetylcholine receptor antibody-positive refractory generalised myasthenia gravis (REGAIN): a phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre study. Lancet Neurol. 2017;16(12):976-986. PMID: 29066163. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01997229, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: surgery has its trial; complement inhibition has a missed primary — split stamp
cards.summary: Surgery has its trial (POSSIBLE); complement inhibition has a missed primary (MAYBE (weak evidence)).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: MGTX (126 patients, thymectomy, 3 years) and REGAIN (125 patients, eculizumab, 26 weeks).
cards.result: Two different populations and two different verdicts. In early, non-thymomatous generalised disease, thymectomy improved both co-primary outcomes over 3 years in its one randomised trial (POSSIBLE). In refractory disease, eculizumab's one phase 3 trial missed its pre-specified primary analysis (p=0.0698, confidence interval crossing zero), which this library stamps MAYBE (weak evidence) — the secondary exacerbation and rescue counts (10% vs 24% and 10% vs 19%) are hypothesis-generating beside a null primary, not a substitute for it.
cards.watchOut: Never present REGAIN as a positive trial: any summary of this shelf that leads with exacerbation counts and omits the missed primary endpoint misstates the evidence.
cards.source: Synthesis of Wolfe GI et al. N Engl J Med. 2016;375(6):511-522. PMID: 27509100; Howard JF Jr et al. Lancet Neurol. 2017;16(12):976-986. PMID: 29066163. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Parkinson's disease with motor complications: deep brain stimulation
shelves.question: Does subthalamic DBS improve quality of life and motor function versus best medical therapy — in advanced disease, and earlier at first motor complications?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Antiparkinson Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Deep Brain Stimulation/adverse effects · Dyskinesias/etiology,therapy · Parkinson Disease/complications,drug therapy,therapy · Severity of Illness Index · Combined Modality Therapy
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials at two disease stages agree. In advanced disease (Deuschl 2006, 156 patients), subthalamic stimulation beat medication alone on quality of life and off-medication motor scores at 6 months. In earlier disease (EARLYSTIM, Schuepbach 2013, 251 patients, mean age 52), stimulation plus medical therapy improved the PDQ-39 by 7.8 points while medical therapy alone worsened by 0.2 (difference 8.0 points, P=0.002) over 2 years. The benefit carries a real surgical price — serious adverse events were more frequent with stimulation in both trials, including a fatal intracerebral haemorrhage in the 2006 trial — and the cards print that price beside the benefit.

cards.headline: Deuschl 2006: subthalamic stimulation beat medication alone on quality of life and off-medication motor scores at 6 months
cards.summary: Deuschl 2006: subthalamic stimulation beat medication alone on quality of life and off-medication motor scores at 6 months.
cards.people: 156 patients under 75 years of age with advanced Parkinson's disease and severe motor symptoms, enrolled as 78 pairs and randomised to subthalamic neurostimulation plus medication or medical management alone, followed for 6 months.
cards.result: Neurostimulation produced greater improvement than medication alone in the Parkinson's Disease Questionnaire (PDQ-39) score (50 of 78 pairs favouring stimulation, P=0.02) and in off-medication UPDRS part III motor severity (55 of 78 pairs, P<0.001), with mean improvements of 9.5 and 19.6 points respectively; PDQ-39 subscales for mobility, activities of daily living, emotional well-being, stigma and bodily discomfort improved by 24 to 38 percent. Serious adverse events were more common with neurostimulation than medication alone (13% vs 4%, P<0.04) and included a fatal intracerebral haemorrhage.
cards.watchOut: Six months only, in patients under 75 with severe motor complications, and unblinded (surgery cannot be blinded): the effect sizes are large, but so is the early surgical risk the same card reports.
cards.source: Deuschl G et al. A randomized trial of deep-brain stimulation for Parkinson's disease. N Engl J Med. 2006;355(9):896-908. PMID: 16943402. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00196911, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: EARLYSTIM 2013: stimulation at first motor complications improved quality of life by 8.0 points over medical therapy at 2 years
cards.summary: EARLYSTIM 2013: stimulation at first motor complications improved quality of life by 8.0 points over medical therapy at 2 years.
cards.people: 251 patients with Parkinson's disease and early motor complications (mean age 52 years; mean disease duration 7.5 years) randomised to subthalamic neurostimulation plus medical therapy or medical therapy alone, followed for 2 years.
cards.result: The PDQ-39 summary index improved by 7.8 points in the neurostimulation group and worsened by 0.2 points on medical therapy alone (between-group difference 8.0 points, P=0.002). Neurostimulation was also superior for motor disability, activities of daily living, levodopa-induced motor complications (all P<0.001) and time with good mobility and no dyskinesia (P=0.01). Serious adverse events occurred in 54.8% of the neurostimulation group versus 44.1% on medical therapy; serious events related to implantation or the device occurred in 17.7% of patients.
cards.watchOut: A younger, earlier population than the 2006 trial (mean age 52): the result supports earlier stimulation in selected patients, not stimulation at diagnosis, and more than half the surgical group had a serious adverse event of some kind over 2 years.
cards.source: Schuepbach WMM et al. Neurostimulation for Parkinson's disease with early motor complications. N Engl J Med. 2013;368(7):610-622. PMID: 23406026. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00354133, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two trials, two stages, same direction — LIKELY, with the surgical price on the card
cards.summary: Two trials, two stages, same direction — LIKELY, with the surgical price on the card.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Deuschl 2006 (156 patients, advanced disease) and EARLYSTIM 2013 (251 patients, early motor complications).
cards.result: Quality of life and motor function improved with subthalamic stimulation at both stages tested: PDQ-39 separation of 8.0 points at 2 years in early disease (EARLYSTIM) echoes the 2006 advanced-disease result. Two concordant randomised trials carry the benefit claim to LIKELY. shelves.title: Essential tremor: MR-guided focused ultrasound thalamotomy
shelves.question: Does unilateral focused-ultrasound thalamotomy reduce hand tremor versus sham in medication-refractory essential tremor?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Essential Tremor/therapy · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Postoperative Complications · Thalamus/surgery · Ultrasonic Therapy/adverse effects,methods · Ultrasonography, Interventional
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One sham-controlled randomised trial (Elias 2016, 76 patients) found hand tremor improved by 8.3 points more with focused ultrasound thalamotomy than with sham at 3 months (95% CI 5.9 to 10.7; P<0.001), and a 5-year follow-up of the same trial's cohort (Cosgrove 2023) shows the improvement largely held (combined hand tremor/motor scores still 40.4% better than baseline at 60 months). A follow-up cohort of the SAME trial is durability evidence, not a second trial — so under the single-trial ceiling the stamp is POSSIBLE. Gait disturbance (36%) and paraesthesias or numbness (38%), persisting at 12 months in 9% and 14%, are part of the claim.

cards.headline: Elias 2016: focused ultrasound thalamotomy beat sham by 8.3 points on hand tremor at 3 months
cards.summary: Elias 2016: focused ultrasound thalamotomy beat sham by 8.3 points on hand tremor at 3 months.
cards.type: Randomised, sham-controlled trial with blinded video rating
cards.people: 76 patients with moderate-to-severe essential tremor that had not responded to at least two trials of medical therapy, randomised 3:1 to unilateral MRI-guided focused ultrasound thalamotomy or a sham procedure; sham patients could cross over to active treatment after 3 months. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Hand-tremor scores (32-point scale, higher = more severe) improved from 18.1 points at baseline to 9.6 at 3 months with thalamotomy, versus 16.0 to 15.8 with sham (between-group difference in mean change 8.3 points, 95% CI 5.9 to 10.7; P<0.001), and the improvement was maintained at 12 months (change from baseline 7.2 points, 6.1 to 8.3). Disability and quality-of-life measures also improved versus sham (P<0.001 for both). Adverse events in the thalamotomy group included gait disturbance in 36% and paraesthesias or numbness in 38% of patients, persisting at 12 months in 9% and 14% respectively.
cards.watchOut: The only sham-controlled trial, with 76 patients and a 3:1 allocation: after month 3 the control group crossed over, so all longer-term data are uncontrolled — and the lesion is unilateral and irreversible, unlike adjustable stimulation.

shelves.title: Relapsing multiple sclerosis: fingolimod vs placebo and vs interferon
shelves.question: Does oral fingolimod reduce relapses and MRI activity versus placebo (FREEDOMS) and versus intramuscular interferon beta-1a (TRANSFORMS)?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Arrhythmias, Cardiac/chemically induced · Brain/pathology · Disability Evaluation · Disease Progression · Fingolimod Hydrochloride · Herpesviridae Infections/etiology,mortality
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two large double-blind trials agree. Against placebo (FREEDOMS, 1,272 patients, 24 months), fingolimod cut the annualised relapse rate to 0.18 (0.5 mg) and 0.16 (1.25 mg) versus 0.40. Against intramuscular interferon beta-1a (TRANSFORMS, 1,292 patients, 12 months), the rate was 0.16 (0.5 mg) versus 0.33. The disability-progression hazard ratios (0.70 and 0.68) sit inside this library's 0.5–2.0 caution band and were NOT significant against interferon, so the LIKELY stamp rests on relapse rates and MRI measures, not on a disability claim. Harms carded include bradycardia and AV block at initiation, macular oedema, and two fatal infections at the 1.25 mg dose in TRANSFORMS.

cards.headline: FREEDOMS 2010: fingolimod cut the annualised relapse rate to 0.18 (0.5 mg) vs 0.40 on placebo over 24 months
cards.summary: FREEDOMS 2010: fingolimod cut the annualised relapse rate to 0.18 (0.5 mg) vs 0.40 on placebo over 24 months.
cards.people: 1,272 patients aged 18–55 years with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (EDSS 0–5.5, one or more relapses in the previous year or two or more in the previous 2 years) randomised to oral fingolimod 0.5 mg, fingolimod 1.25 mg, or placebo daily for 24 months; 1,033 (81.2%) completed the study. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: The annualised relapse rate was 0.18 on fingolimod 0.5 mg and 0.16 on 1.25 mg versus 0.40 on placebo (P<0.001 for either dose). The risk of disability progression was lower on fingolimod (hazard ratio 0.70 for 0.5 mg and 0.68 for 1.25 mg, P=0.02 for both) — relative measures inside the 0.5–2.0 band this library does not treat as solid on their own; the cumulative probability of 3-month-confirmed progression was 17.7% (0.5 mg), 16.6% (1.25 mg) and 24.1% (placebo). Both doses were superior on all MRI measures (P<0.001). Adverse events related to fingolimod included bradycardia and atrioventricular conduction block at initiation, macular oedema, elevated liver-enzyme levels and mild hypertension.
cards.watchOut: The relapse result is the strong finding; the disability hazard ratios of 0.70/0.68 are modest relative effects, and the trial says nothing about safety beyond 24 months — the authors state the benefits must be weighed against possible long-term risks.
cards.source: Kappos L et al. A placebo-controlled trial of oral fingolimod in relapsing multiple sclerosis. N Engl J Med. 2010;362(5):387-401. PMID: 20089952. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00289978, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: TRANSFORMS 2010: fingolimod 0.5 mg beat interferon beta-1a on relapse rate — 0.16 vs 0.33 over 12 months
cards.summary: TRANSFORMS 2010: fingolimod 0.5 mg beat interferon beta-1a on relapse rate — 0.16 vs 0.33 over 12 months.
cards.people: 1,292 patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis and at least one recent relapse, randomised to oral fingolimod 1.25 mg, fingolimod 0.5 mg, or intramuscular interferon beta-1a 30 µg weekly for 12 months; 1,153 (89%) completed the study. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: The annualised relapse rate was 0.20 (95% CI 0.16 to 0.26) on fingolimod 1.25 mg and 0.16 (0.12 to 0.21) on 0.5 mg versus 0.33 (0.26 to 0.42) on interferon beta-1a (P<0.001 for both comparisons), and MRI findings supported the primary result. cards.watchOut: Twelve months only, and superiority was on relapses and MRI — not disability, where the groups did not differ; the fatal infections were at the higher, non-standard 1.25 mg dose but belong on the card.

shelves.title: Painful diabetic neuropathy and postherpetic neuralgia: duloxetine and high-dose capsaicin
shelves.question: Does duloxetine relieve painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy — and does the 8% capsaicin patch relieve postherpetic neuralgia versus a low-dose control patch?
shelves.mesh: Demography · Depression/drug therapy,etiology · Diabetic Neuropathies/blood,complications,drug therapy,urine · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Duloxetine Hydrochloride · Pain Measurement/drug effects,methods · Personality Inventory
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Each treatment rests on a single randomised trial here. Duloxetine 60 mg and 120 mg/day beat placebo on the 24-hour Average Pain Score in a 12-week trial of 457 patients with painful diabetic neuropathy (Goldstein 2005) — though the abstract reports the pain separation without responder percentages, which the card states plainly. One 60-minute application of the 8% capsaicin patch reduced postherpetic neuralgia pain by −29.6% versus −19.9% on a low-dose control patch over weeks 2–8 (Backonja 2008, 402 patients), a difference of −9.7 percentage points, with a responder odds ratio of 1.56 that sits inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band. Two single trials, two different pains: POSSIBLE for each, claimed separately.

cards.headline: Goldstein 2005: duloxetine 60 mg and 120 mg/day beat placebo on 24-hour average pain in diabetic neuropathy
cards.summary: Goldstein 2005: duloxetine 60 mg and 120 mg/day beat placebo on 24-hour average pain in diabetic neuropathy.
cards.people: 457 patients with pain due to diabetic peripheral polyneuropathy (type 1 or type 2 diabetes; diagnosis confirmed by a Michigan Neuropathy Screening Instrument score of at least 3) randomised to duloxetine 20 mg/day, 60 mg/day, 120 mg/day (60 mg twice daily), or placebo for 12 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Duloxetine 60 mg/day and 120 mg/day showed statistically significantly greater improvement than placebo on the weekly mean 24-hour Average Pain Score (11-point scale), beginning 1 week after randomisation and continuing through the 12-week trial, and separated from placebo on nearly all secondary and health-related outcome measures. Significantly more patients in all three active groups achieved a 50% reduction in the 24-hour Average Pain Score than on placebo — the abstract reports this responder result without printing the percentages, and this card does not invent them. Less than 20% of patients discontinued because of adverse events.
cards.watchOut: The record's abstract gives the direction and significance of the pain effect but no mean pain-score values and no responder percentages: the size of the average benefit cannot be quantified from this record, which is one reason the shelf is POSSIBLE rather than higher.

cards.headline: Backonja 2008: one application of the 8% capsaicin patch cut postherpetic pain by −29.6% vs −19.9% on control over weeks 2–8
cards.summary: Backonja 2008: one application of the 8% capsaicin patch cut postherpetic pain by −29.6% vs −19.9% on control over weeks 2–8.

shelves.title: Bell's palsy: prednisolone, with or without an antiviral
shelves.question: Does early prednisolone increase full recovery from Bell's palsy — and does adding valaciclovir help?
shelves.mesh: Acyclovir/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Antiviral Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Bell Palsy/drug therapy · Drug Therapy, Combination · Facial Nerve/physiology · Factor Analysis, Statistical · Glucocorticoids/adverse effects,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trial programmes agree on both halves of the question. Prednisolone started within 72 hours raised recovery to 83.0% versus 63.6% without it at 3 months and 94.4% versus 81.6% at 9 months (Sullivan 2007, factorial, 551 randomised), and the Scandinavian trial programme (829 patients) found higher complete recovery with prednisolone at every baseline severity at 12 months (Axelsson 2012). Acyclovir/valaciclovir added nothing in either programme — no benefit alone and no added benefit combined. Steroid benefit and antiviral null each rest on two randomised datasets: LIKELY for both.

cards.headline: Sullivan 2007: early prednisolone raised Bell's palsy recovery to 94.4% vs 81.6% at 9 months; acyclovir added nothing
cards.summary: Sullivan 2007: early prednisolone raised Bell's palsy recovery to 94.4% vs 81.6% at 9 months; acyclovir added nothing.
cards.people: 551 patients with Bell's palsy recruited within 72 hours of symptom onset, randomised to 10 days of prednisolone, acyclovir, both, or placebo; final outcomes were assessed for 496 patients.
cards.result: At 3 months, recovery of facial function was 83.0% in the prednisolone groups versus 63.6% without prednisolone (P<0.001), versus 71.2% in the acyclovir groups and 75.7% without acyclovir (adjusted P=0.50). At 9 months the proportions were 94.4% (prednisolone) versus 81.6% (no prednisolone) (P<0.001), and 85.4% (acyclovir) versus 90.8% (no acyclovir) (adjusted P=0.10); patients treated with both drugs recovered at 79.7% at 3 months and 92.7% at 9 months. There were no serious adverse events in any group.
cards.watchOut: Treatment began within 72 hours of onset — the result does not cover late presentation — and most patients recover substantially even untreated (81.6% by 9 months), so the steroid's absolute gain is about 13–19 percentage points, printed beside the rates.
cards.source: Sullivan FM et al. Early treatment with prednisolone or acyclovir in Bell's palsy. N Engl J Med. 2007;357(16):1598-1607. PMID: 17942873. Registry ID: ISRCTN71548196, from the record's databank fields.

cards.summary: Axelsson 2012: prednisolone raised complete recovery at 12 months at every severity — severe palsy 51% vs 31%; valaciclovir added nothing.
cards.type: Combined severity analysis of a prospective, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre trial (Scandinavian Bell's Palsy Study)
cards.people: 829 patients aged 18–75 years treated within 72 hours of onset at 16 centres in Sweden and 1 in Finland, randomised to prednisolone plus placebo (210), valaciclovir plus placebo (207), prednisolone plus valaciclovir (206), or double placebo (206), with 12 months of follow-up; complete recovery defined as a Sunnybrook score of 100.
cards.result: Complete recovery at 12 months was significantly higher with prednisolone than without at every baseline severity: severe palsy 51% versus 31% (P=0.02), moderate 68% versus 51% (P=0.004), and mild 83% versus 73% (P=0.02). Prednisolone also reduced synkinesis at 12 months in moderate and mild palsy (P=0.04 and P<0.0001) but not in severe palsy. Valaciclovir added no significant effect to prednisolone on recovery rate or synkinesis at 12 months.
cards.watchOut: A severity-stratified analysis of one trial programme rather than a second independent trial of the combination question: it corroborates Sullivan's factorial result in a different population and healthcare system, using a stricter complete-recovery definition (Sunnybrook 100).
cards.source: Axelsson S et al. Bell's palsy - the effect of prednisolone and/or valaciclovir versus placebo in relation to baseline severity in a randomised controlled trial. cards.headline: Synthesis: give the steroid early; the antiviral earns nothing — LIKELY on both halves
cards.summary: Give the steroid early; the antiviral earns nothing — LIKELY on both halves.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Sullivan 2007 (551 randomised, factorial) and the Scandinavian programme reported by Axelsson 2012 (829 randomised).
cards.result: Across 1,380 randomised patients in two programmes, early prednisolone consistently increased recovery (absolute gains of roughly 10–20 percentage points depending on severity and time point), and the antiviral arm was null in both — alone (71.2% vs 75.7% at 3 months for acyclovir in Sullivan) and added to prednisolone (Axelsson). The shelf's claim is therefore double: prednisolone works, LIKELY; adding an antiviral does not, LIKELY the null.
cards.watchOut: Both programmes treated within 72 hours; neither speaks to steroids started later, and neither tested valaciclovir at the doses or durations a clinician might improvise outside the trial protocols.

shelves.title: Fluoxetine for stroke recovery: FLAME's promise vs FOCUS/AFFINITY's nulls
shelves.question: Does fluoxetine started soon after stroke improve motor/functional recovery — the small positive FLAME trial against the large pragmatic FOCUS-family trials?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Fluoxetine/pharmacology,therapeutic use · Motor Skills/drug effects,physiology · Recovery of Function/drug effects,physiology · Stroke/drug therapy,physiopathology · Administration, Oral · Antidepressive Agents, Second-Generation/administration & dosage,adverse effects
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): The small, selected FLAME trial (118 patients with moderate-to-severe motor deficit) found fluoxetine improved Fugl-Meyer motor scores at 90 days (adjusted mean 34.0 vs 24.3 points, p=0.003). Two large pragmatic trials then tested the question at scale and both were null on functional outcome: FOCUS (3,127 patients; modified Rankin common odds ratio 0.951, 95% CI 0.839 to 1.079) and AFFINITY (1,280 patients; adjusted common odds ratio 0.94, 0.76 to 1.15), with more fractures — and in AFFINITY more falls and seizures — on fluoxetine. Over 4,400 patients in the large trials outweigh 118 in the small one: LIKELY that routine fluoxetine does not improve functional recovery after stroke. This is a functional-outcome shelf, not a mortality claim.

cards.headline: FLAME 2011: fluoxetine improved Fugl-Meyer motor scores at 90 days — adjusted mean 34.0 vs 24.3 points in 118 selected patients
cards.summary: FLAME 2011: fluoxetine improved Fugl-Meyer motor scores at 90 days — adjusted mean 34.0 vs 24.3 points in 118 selected patients.
cards.people: 118 patients aged 18–85 years at nine French stroke centres with ischaemic stroke and hemiplegia or hemiparesis (Fugl-Meyer motor scale score 55 or less) randomised to fluoxetine 20 mg daily (59) or placebo (59) for 3 months starting 5–10 days after stroke, all with physiotherapy; 113 were analysed.
cards.result: Fugl-Meyer motor scale improvement at day 90 was significantly greater on fluoxetine (adjusted mean 34.0 points, 95% CI 29.7 to 38.4) than placebo (24.3 points, 19.9 to 28.7; p=0.003). Adverse events were similar overall: hyponatraemia 4% in both groups, transient digestive disorders 25% versus 11%, hepatic enzyme disorders 9% versus 18%, and insomnia 33% versus 36%. Two patients died before day 90 and three withdrew.
cards.watchOut: Small (118 patients), single-country, and restricted to patients with moderate-to-severe motor deficit receiving physiotherapy, with a motor-scale endpoint rather than a functional outcome: exactly the profile of a promising early result that large pragmatic trials must confirm — and on this shelf, they did not.
cards.source: Chollet F et al. Fluoxetine for motor recovery after acute ischaemic stroke (FLAME): a randomised placebo-controlled trial. Lancet Neurol. 2011;10(2):123-130. PMID: 21216670. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00657163, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: FOCUS 2019: fluoxetine did NOT improve functional outcome in 3,127 patients — mRS common odds ratio 0.951; fractures increased
cards.summary: FOCUS 2019: fluoxetine did NOT improve functional outcome in 3,127 patients — mRS common odds ratio 0.951; fractures increased.
cards.type: Pragmatic, multicentre, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial
cards.people: 3,127 patients aged 18 or older with a clinical stroke diagnosis and focal neurological deficits, enrolled 2–15 days after onset at 103 UK hospitals, randomised to fluoxetine 20 mg daily (1,564) or placebo (1,563) for 6 months; modified Rankin Scale (mRS) data at 6 months were available for 1,553 patients in each group.
cards.result: The distribution of mRS categories at 6 months was similar between groups (common odds ratio adjusted for minimisation variables 0.951, 95% CI 0.839 to 1.079; p=0.439) — a relative measure sitting inside the 0.5–2.0 band and statistically null. Patients on fluoxetine developed new depression less often by 6 months (13.43% vs 17.21%; difference 3.78%, 95% CI 1.26 to 6.30; p=0.0033) but had more bone fractures (2.88% vs 1.47%; difference 1.41%, 0.38 to 2.43; p=0.0070). There were no significant differences in any other event at 6 or 12 months.
cards.watchOut: FOCUS enrolled a broad, unselected stroke population rather than FLAME's motor-deficit subgroup — that breadth is its strength for the routine-use question and its limitation for any claim about the narrow FLAME phenotype.
cards.source: FOCUS Trial Collaboration. Effects of fluoxetine on functional outcomes after acute stroke (FOCUS): a pragmatic, double-blind, randomised, controlled trial. Lancet. 2019;393(10168):265-274. PMID: 30528472. Registry ID: ISRCTN83290762, stated in the record's abstract; the MEDLINE record carries no databank SI field.

cards.headline: AFFINITY 2020: the second large trial was also null — adjusted common odds ratio 0.94 — with more falls, fractures and seizures
cards.summary: AFFINITY 2020: the second large trial was also null — adjusted common odds ratio 0.94 — with more falls, fractures and seizures.
cards.people: 1,280 adults (aged 18 or older) with acute stroke in the previous 2–15 days, imaging consistent with ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke, and a persisting deficit (mRS 1 or more), recruited at 43 stroke units in Australia (532), New Zealand (42) and Vietnam (706) and randomised to fluoxetine 20 mg daily (642) or placebo (638) for 6 months; mRS data at 6 months were available for 624 (97%) and 632 (99%).
cards.result: The distribution of mRS categories at 6 months was similar between groups (adjusted common odds ratio 0.94, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.15; p=0.53) — again a null relative measure inside the 0.5–2.0 band. Compared with placebo, fluoxetine patients had more falls (3% vs 1%; p=0.018), bone fractures (3% vs 1%; p=0.014) and epileptic seizures (2% vs <1%; p=0.038) at 6 months. Mean duration of trial treatment was 167 days (SD 48.1).
cards.watchOut: An ethnically diverse population including haemorrhagic stroke and a large Vietnamese cohort: the null is consistent with FOCUS rather than explained by population, and the harm pattern (falls, fractures, seizures) replicates the FOCUS fracture signal.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the large trials govern — routine fluoxetine for stroke recovery is LIKELY a null, with real harms
cards.summary: The large trials govern — routine fluoxetine for stroke recovery is LIKELY a null, with real harms.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: FLAME (118 patients), FOCUS (3,127 patients) and AFFINITY (1,280 patients).
cards.result: The discordance resolves by size and design: one small, selected, motor-endpoint trial was positive (34.0 vs 24.3 Fugl-Meyer points); two large pragmatic trials totalling 4,407 patients found functional-outcome odds ratios of 0.951 and 0.94, both null, and both found more fractures on fluoxetine. The FOCUS depression finding (13.43% vs 17.21% new depression) is a symptom outcome, not recovery of function, and does not rescue the shelf's question. Acute reperfusion and secondary-prevention stroke shelves are separate questions and are not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote FLAME without FOCUS and AFFINITY beside it; FLAME alone is the marketing version of this evidence, not the balance of it.

shelves.title: Drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy: surgery vs continued medication
shelves.question: In temporal lobe epilepsy uncontrolled by medication, does surgery free patients from disabling seizures versus continued drug therapy?
shelves.mesh: Anticonvulsants/therapeutic use · Disease-Free Survival · Employment/statistics & numerical data · Epilepsy, Temporal Lobe/drug therapy,surgery · Neurosurgery/methods · Postoperative Complications · Temporal Lobe/surgery
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Both randomised trials point the same way with large absolute effects. In Wiebe 2001 (80 patients), 58% of surgical patients versus 8% on continued medication were free of seizures impairing awareness at 1 year (P<0.001). In ERSET (Engel 2012), surgery soon after two drug failures left 11 of 15 patients seizure-free in year 2 versus 0 of 23 on continued medication (P<.001) — a striking result in a trial stopped at 38 of a planned 200 patients, which is why the effect is carded with its small numbers printed rather than as a percentage triumph. Surgical adverse effects (10% in Wiebe) and memory decline after resection (ERSET) are on the cards.

cards.headline: Wiebe 2001: surgery freed 58% from awareness-impairing seizures at 1 year, vs 8% on medication alone
cards.summary: Wiebe 2001: surgery freed 58% from awareness-impairing seizures at 1 year, vs 8% on medication alone.
cards.type: Randomised, controlled trial with blinded outcome assessment
cards.people: 80 patients with temporal-lobe epilepsy randomised to surgery (40) or treatment with antiepileptic drugs for one year (40); optimal medical therapy and primary outcomes were assessed by epileptologists unaware of treatment assignment. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: At one year, the cumulative proportion free of seizures impairing awareness of self and surroundings was 58% in the surgical group versus 8% in the medical group (P<0.001) — an absolute difference of 50 percentage points. Surgical patients also had fewer seizures impairing awareness and significantly better quality of life (P<0.001 for both). Four patients (10%) had adverse effects of surgery; one patient in the medical group died.
cards.watchOut: Eighty patients at a single programme's era of practice (2001), unblindable by design, in patients already selected as surgical candidates: the comparison is surgery versus more drugs in drug-resistant disease, not surgery for newly diagnosed epilepsy.
cards.source: Wiebe S et al. A randomized, controlled trial of surgery for temporal-lobe epilepsy. N Engl J Med. 2001;345(5):311-318. PMID: 11484687. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — a pre-registration-era trial (2001).

cards.headline: ERSET 2012: early surgery left 11 of 15 patients seizure-free in year 2, vs 0 of 23 on continued medication
cards.summary: ERSET 2012: early surgery left 11 of 15 patients seizure-free in year 2, vs 0 of 23 on continued medication.
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, controlled, parallel-group trial (stopped early)
cards.people: 38 participants (18 men and 20 women; aged 12 years or older) with mesial temporal lobe epilepsy and disabling seizures for no more than 2 consecutive years after adequate trials of 2 brand-name antiepileptic drugs, at 16 US epilepsy surgery centres, randomised to continued drug treatment (23) or standardised anteromesial temporal resection plus drugs (15); planned enrolment was 200 but the trial was halted prematurely for slow accrual.
cards.result: Freedom from disabling seizures during year 2 was achieved by 11 of 15 surgical patients versus 0 of 23 medical patients (odds ratio infinite, 95% CI 11.8 to infinity; P<.001). The intention-to-treat quality-of-life advantage for surgery was not statistically significant (QOLIE-89 treatment effect 8.5 points, 95% CI −1.0 to 18.1; P=.08). Memory decline on the Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test occurred in 4 participants (36%) after surgery. Adverse events included a transient neurological deficit from a postoperative stroke in one surgical participant and 3 cases of status epilepticus in the medical group; 7 medical-group participants crossed over to surgery before follow-up ended.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-eight patients against a planned 200: the direction is unambiguous (0 of 23 versus 11 of 15) but every secondary estimate is imprecise, crossovers blur the comparison, and the authors themselves direct that results be interpreted with appropriate caution.
cards.source: Engel J Jr et al. Early surgical therapy for drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy: a randomized trial. JAMA. 2012;307(9):922-930. PMID: 22396514. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00040326, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two trials, one direction, large absolute effects — LIKELY surgery wins in drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy
cards.summary: Two trials, one direction, large absolute effects — LIKELY surgery wins in drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Wiebe 2001 (80 patients, established drug resistance) and ERSET 2012 (38 patients, early after two drug failures).
cards.result: Seizure freedom of 58% versus 8% at 1 year (Wiebe) and 11 of 15 versus 0 of 23 in year 2 (ERSET) are effects far outside any plausible bias band for an unblindable surgical question, in two different eras of the referral pathway. That concordance carries the claim to LIKELY despite ERSET's small size — its result is printed as counts, not inflated into percentages. First-line drug CHOICE in new-onset epilepsy (SANAD II) lives on Shelf #337 and is not re-carded here: this shelf begins only after drugs have failed.
cards.watchOut: Both trials enrolled surgical candidates after specialist evaluation; neither supports surgery before an adequate trial of medication, and memory decline after dominant-side resection is a real cost the cards keep visible.

shelves.title: Antipsychotic comparative effectiveness in chronic schizophrenia (CATIE & CUtLASS)
shelves.question: Do second-generation antipsychotics outperform first-generation drugs on effectiveness, discontinuation, and quality of life in chronic schizophrenia?
shelves.mesh: Antipsychotic Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Benzodiazepines/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Chronic Disease · Dibenzothiazepines/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Lipids/blood · Olanzapine · Patient Compliance
shelves.balance: LIKELY (no class advantage): Two large publicly funded pragmatic trials agree that second-generation antipsychotics (SGAs) as a class do not outperform first-generation drugs (FGAs). In CATIE (1,493 patients), 74% discontinued their assigned drug before 18 months; olanzapine lasted longest, but the first-generation perphenazine performed similarly to quetiapine, risperidone and ziprasidone — while olanzapine caused more weight gain and metabolic change, and perphenazine more extrapyramidal discontinuation. In CUtLASS (227 patients), the hypothesis that SGAs improve quality of life over a year was excluded, with a trend favouring FGAs. The claim carded is the class-level null, not that individual drugs are interchangeable in every patient.

cards.headline: CATIE 2005: 74% stopped their assigned antipsychotic before 18 months; perphenazine matched most second-generation drugs
cards.summary: CATIE 2005: 74% stopped their assigned antipsychotic before 18 months; perphenazine matched most second-generation drugs.
cards.people: 1,493 patients with chronic schizophrenia at 57 US sites, randomised to olanzapine (7.5–30 mg/day), the first-generation drug perphenazine (8–32 mg/day), quetiapine (200–800 mg/day), risperidone (1.5–6.0 mg/day), or (after its FDA approval) ziprasidone (40–160 mg/day) for up to 18 months; 1,432 received at least one dose. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Overall, 74% of patients (1,061 of 1,432) discontinued their study medication before 18 months: 64% on olanzapine, 75% on perphenazine, 82% on quetiapine, 74% on risperidone and 79% on ziprasidone. Time to discontinuation for any cause was significantly longer on olanzapine than on quetiapine (P<0.001) or risperidone (P=0.002), but did not reach the authors' reported significance for perphenazine (P=0.021) or ziprasidone (P=0.028). Discontinuation for intolerable side effects differed between groups (P=0.04): olanzapine had more discontinuation for weight gain or metabolic effects, perphenazine more for extrapyramidal effects, and olanzapine was associated with greater weight gain and increases in measures of glucose and lipid metabolism.
cards.watchOut: CATIE's primary measure is time to discontinuation — an effectiveness composite of efficacy, tolerability and patient choice — not a symptom score; and patients with tardive dyskinesia were not assigned perphenazine, a design feature that matters when generalising the comparison.
cards.source: Lieberman JA et al. Effectiveness of antipsychotic drugs in patients with chronic schizophrenia. N Engl J Med. 2005;353(12):1209-1223. PMID: 16172203. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the record carries no databank SI field.

cards.headline: CUtLASS 2006: second-generation drugs did NOT improve quality of life over first-generation drugs across 1 year
cards.summary: CUtLASS 2006: second-generation drugs did NOT improve quality of life over first-generation drugs across 1 year.
cards.type: Pragmatic, multisite randomised controlled trial of drug classes, with blinded assessments
cards.people: 227 people aged 18–65 years with DSM-IV schizophrenia and related disorders, at 14 community psychiatric services in the English NHS, whose medication was under review for inadequate response or adverse effects, randomised to a prescription of first-generation or second-generation antipsychotics (other than clozapine), the individual drug chosen by the managing psychiatrist; assessments at 12, 26 and 56 weeks.
cards.result: The primary hypothesis — that second-generation drugs would significantly improve Quality of Life Scale scores over the year — was excluded. Participants in the first-generation arm showed a trend toward GREATER improvements in quality-of-life and symptom scores; participants reported no clear preference for either drug group, and costs of care were similar. The authors state that neither inadequate power nor patterns of drug discontinuation accounted for the result.
cards.watchOut: A class-level, pragmatic comparison in patients changing medication for clinical reasons: it does not test any single drug pair, excludes clozapine, and its quality-of-life endpoint answers a different question from the short-term symptom trials on which the second-generation reputation rested.
cards.source: Jones PB et al. Randomized controlled trial of the effect on Quality of Life of second- vs first-generation antipsychotic drugs in schizophrenia: Cost Utility of the Latest Antipsychotic Drugs in Schizophrenia Study (CUtLASS 1). shelves.title: After ECT works: continuation therapy to prevent relapse
shelves.question: In patients who respond to ECT for major depression, does continuation pharmacotherapy (nortriptyline ± lithium) or continuation ECT prevent relapse?
shelves.mesh: Antidepressive Agents/therapeutic use · Major Depressive Disorder/drug therapy,therapy · Drug Therapy, Combination · Electroconvulsive Therapy · Lithium Carbonate/therapeutic use · Nortriptyline/therapeutic use · Recurrence
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Without continuation treatment, relapse after successful ECT is near-universal — 84% within 24 weeks on placebo in Sackeim 2001. Nortriptyline plus lithium cut that to 39% (nortriptyline alone: 60%) in the same randomised trial. The CORE trial (Kellner 2006, 201 remitted patients) then found continuation ECT and the nortriptyline–lithium combination statistically indistinguishable (relapse 37.1% vs 31.6% over 6 months), both far below the historical placebo rate. Two randomised trials support the core claim — continuation treatment prevents most relapses and the two strategies are comparable — while both cards keep visible that even the best strategy still let roughly a third relapse.

cards.headline: Sackeim 2001: after ECT remission, relapse was 84% on placebo, 60% on nortriptyline, and 39% on nortriptyline plus lithium
cards.summary: Sackeim 2001: after ECT remission, relapse was 84% on placebo, 60% on nortriptyline, and 39% on nortriptyline plus lithium.
cards.people: 84 patients with unipolar major depression who had remitted after an open ECT course (of 290 recruited and 159 meeting remitter criteria) at two university hospitals and one private psychiatric hospital, randomised to 24 weeks of placebo (29), nortriptyline (target level 75–125 ng/mL) (27), or nortriptyline plus lithium (target 0.5–0.9 mEq/L) (28); the trial was stratified by medication resistance and psychotic depression in the index episode.
cards.result: Over 24 weeks, relapse rates were 84% (95% CI 70% to 99%) on placebo, 60% (41% to 79%) on nortriptyline alone, and 39% (19% to 59%) on the nortriptyline–lithium combination; the combination was superior to both placebo and nortriptyline alone in time to relapse. All but one relapse on the combination occurred within 5 weeks of ECT termination, whereas relapse continued throughout treatment in the other groups. Medication-resistant patients, women, and those with more severe symptoms after ECT relapsed faster.
cards.watchOut: Only 84 of 290 recruited patients reached randomisation — a selected remitter population — and even the winning combination relapsed 39% within 6 months; the trial compares three drug strategies, not continuation ECT.
cards.source: Sackeim HA et al. Continuation pharmacotherapy in the prevention of relapse following electroconvulsive therapy: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2001;285(10):1299-1307. PMID: 11255384. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — a pre-registration-era trial (recruitment 1993–1998).

cards.headline: Kellner 2006 (CORE): continuation ECT and nortriptyline–lithium were indistinguishable — relapse 37.1% vs 31.6% over 6 months
cards.summary: Kellner 2006 (CORE): continuation ECT and nortriptyline–lithium were indistinguishable — relapse 37.1% vs 31.6% over 6 months.
cards.people: 201 patients with DSM-IV unipolar depression who had remitted with a course of bilateral ECT at five academic medical centres, randomised to continuation ECT (10 treatments) or continuation pharmacotherapy with lithium plus nortriptyline for 6 months.
cards.result: Relapse occurred in 37.1% of the continuation-ECT group and 31.6% of the pharmacotherapy group; 46.1% and 46.3% respectively remained in remission at study end, and 16.8% and 22.1% dropped out. Kaplan–Meier and Cox analyses showed no statistically significant difference in time to relapse (mean time to relapse 9.1 [SD 7.0] weeks for continuation ECT vs 6.7 [4.6] weeks for pharmacotherapy; P=.13). Both groups' relapse proportions were significantly lower than a historical placebo control from a similarly designed study — the Sackeim 2001 placebo arm carded above.
cards.watchOut: Unmasked by necessity (ECT cannot be blinded), with the placebo comparison historical rather than randomised within this trial; and 'no significant difference' between two active strategies in 201 patients is comparability within the trial's precision, not proven exact equivalence.

cards.summary: Treat on after ECT, by drugs or by ECT — either beats stopping: LIKELY.

shelves.title: Obsessive-compulsive disorder: exposure therapy, SSRIs, and their combination
shelves.question: In OCD, does exposure-and-response-prevention beat or augment SSRIs — in adults, and in children (POTS)?
shelves.mesh: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy · Combined Modality Therapy · Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder/therapy · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Sertraline/therapeutic use · Chromatography, Gas · Clomipramine/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY: In children and adolescents (POTS, 112 patients), CBT, sertraline and their combination all beat placebo on symptom change, the combination beat either treatment alone, and remission was 53.6% combined, 39.3% CBT alone, 21.4% sertraline alone and 3.6% placebo. In adults still symptomatic on an SRI, adding exposure-and-response-prevention beat adding stress-management training (Simpson 2008, 108 patients). Two randomised trials at two ages agree that exposure-based CBT works, works added to an SRI, and that the combination is the strongest start in youth — LIKELY.

cards.headline: POTS 2004: in children with OCD, combined CBT + sertraline beat either alone; remission 53.6% vs 3.6% on placebo
cards.summary: POTS 2004: in children with OCD, combined CBT + sertraline beat either alone; remission 53.6% vs 3.6% on placebo.
cards.people: 112 outpatients aged 7–17 years with a primary DSM-IV diagnosis of OCD and a Children's Yale-Brown Obsessive-Compulsive Scale (CY-BOCS) score of 16 or higher, at 3 US academic centres, randomised to CBT alone, sertraline alone, combined CBT and sertraline, or pill placebo for 12 weeks; 97 (87%) completed treatment.
cards.result: All three active treatments beat placebo on CY-BOCS change (CBT P=.003, sertraline P=.007, combined P=.001 versus placebo), and combined treatment was superior to CBT alone (P=.008) and to sertraline alone (P=.006), which did not differ from each other. Clinical remission (CY-BOCS 10 or less) was 53.6% (95% CI 36% to 70%) for combined treatment, 39.3% (24% to 58%) for CBT alone, 21.4% (10% to 40%) for sertraline alone and 3.6% (0% to 19%) for placebo. Site differences emerged for CBT and sertraline but not for combined treatment.
cards.watchOut: A 12-week trial in treatment-seeking youth at academic centres: it answers initial treatment, not maintenance, and the CBT-alone versus sertraline-alone remission difference (39.3% vs 21.4%) was itself not significant (P=.24) even though both beat placebo on symptom change.
cards.source: Pediatric OCD Treatment Study (POTS) Team. Cognitive-behavior therapy, sertraline, and their combination for children and adolescents with obsessive-compulsive disorder: the Pediatric OCD Treatment Study (POTS) randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2004;292(16):1969-1976. PMID: 15507582. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the record carries no databank SI field.

cards.headline: Simpson 2008: adding exposure-and-response-prevention to an SRI beat adding stress-management training in adults with residual OCD
cards.summary: Simpson 2008: adding exposure-and-response-prevention to an SRI beat adding stress-management training in adults with residual OCD.
cards.people: 108 adult outpatients with primary OCD and a Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS) score of 16 or more despite a therapeutic SRI dose for at least 12 weeks, at two academic outpatient clinics, randomised to 17 twice-weekly sessions of exposure-and-response-prevention or stress-management training while continuing SRI pharmacotherapy, assessed at week 8.
cards.result: Exposure-and-response-prevention was superior to stress-management training in reducing OCD symptoms: at week 8, significantly more ERP patients achieved a decrease in symptom severity of at least 25% on the Y-BOCS and achieved minimal symptoms (Y-BOCS 12 or less) — the abstract reports these responder contrasts as significant without printing the percentages, and this card does not invent them. The authors note that 17 sessions were not sufficient to help most of these patients achieve minimal symptoms.
cards.watchOut: An augmentation trial in SRI partial responders with an active psychological control (stress management), not a placebo: it shows ERP adds something specific beyond structured therapy contact, but the absence of abstract-level percentages limits how large that something can be stated to be.

shelves.title: PTSD: trauma-focused psychotherapies head-to-head
shelves.question: Do prolonged exposure and cognitive processing therapy reduce PTSD symptoms versus present-centred or waitlist controls in veterans and assault survivors?
shelves.mesh: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy · Military Personnel/psychology · Stress Disorders, Post-Traumatic/therapy · United States · United States Department of Veterans Affairs · Veterans/psychology · Chronic Disease
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Both anchor trials are positive but modest or small. Prolonged exposure beat present-centred therapy in 284 women veterans and active-duty personnel (Schnurr 2007) — but by an effect size of 0.27, with loss of PTSD diagnosis in 41.0% versus 27.8% (odds ratio 1.80, inside this library's 0.5–2.0 caution band). Cognitive processing therapy beat a waitlist in just 60 veterans (Monson 2006), 40% of the treated intention-to-treat sample no longer meeting PTSD criteria after treatment. Positive randomised evidence at two sites with two therapies, but small effects against active control and a tiny waitlist trial: POSSIBLE, not LIKELY.

cards.headline: Schnurr 2007: prolonged exposure beat present-centred therapy in women veterans — diagnosis lost in 41.0% vs 27.8%, effect size 0.27
cards.summary: Schnurr 2007: prolonged exposure beat present-centred therapy in women veterans — diagnosis lost in 41.0% vs 27.8%, effect size 0.27.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial with blinded assessors
cards.people: 284 women with PTSD (277 veterans and 7 active-duty personnel) at 9 VA medical centres, 2 VA readjustment counselling centres and 1 military hospital, randomised to prolonged exposure (141) or present-centred therapy (143), each delivered as 10 weekly 90-minute sessions, with follow-up to 6 months.
cards.result: Prolonged exposure produced a greater reduction in PTSD symptom severity than present-centred therapy (effect size 0.27; P=.03). The prolonged-exposure group was more likely to no longer meet PTSD diagnostic criteria (41.0% vs 27.8%; odds ratio 1.80, 95% CI 1.10 to 2.96; P=.01) — a relative measure inside the 0.5–2.0 band this library does not treat as solid on its own — and to achieve total remission (15.2% vs 6.9%; odds ratio 2.43, 1.10 to 5.37; P=.01). Most between-group differences occurred immediately after treatment and were consistent over time in longitudinal analyses.
cards.watchOut: The comparator was a real supportive therapy, not a waitlist, which makes the test fair — and the margin honest but small: most women in both groups still met PTSD criteria after treatment, and total remission was 15.2% even on prolonged exposure.
cards.source: Schnurr PP et al. Cognitive behavioral therapy for posttraumatic stress disorder in women: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2007;297(8):820-830. PMID: 17327524. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00032617, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Monson 2006: cognitive processing therapy beat waitlist in 60 veterans — 40% no longer met PTSD criteria after treatment
cards.summary: Monson 2006: cognitive processing therapy beat waitlist in 60 veterans — 40% no longer met PTSD criteria after treatment.
cards.people: 60 veterans (54 men, 6 women) with chronic military-related PTSD, randomised to cognitive processing therapy or a waiting list; overall dropout was 16.6% (20% from CPT, 13% from the waiting list). The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Random regression analyses of the intention-to-treat sample showed significant improvements in PTSD and comorbid symptoms with CPT compared with the waiting list. Forty percent of the intention-to-treat CPT sample did not meet criteria for a PTSD diagnosis at posttreatment assessment, and 50% had a reliable change in PTSD symptoms. There was no relationship between PTSD disability status and outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Sixty patients against a waitlist — the weakest control condition in psychotherapy research, which inflates apparent effects — in chronic, treatment-seeking veterans: encouraging, as the authors say, but a small base for a general claim.

shelves.title: Anorexia nervosa: family-based treatment, and olanzapine for weight restoration
shelves.question: Does family-based treatment beat individual therapy for adolescent anorexia (Lock) — and does olanzapine aid weight restoration in adults (Attia)?
shelves.mesh: Anorexia Nervosa/psychology,therapy · Body Mass Index · Body Weight · Evidence-Based Medicine · Family Therapy · Personality Inventory · Psychotherapy
shelves.balance: Split — POSSIBLE on both halves, one trial each. Family-based treatment (FBT) and adolescent-focused individual therapy produced equal full remission at end of treatment in Lock 2010 (121 adolescents), but FBT was significantly superior at 6- and 12-month follow-up — a durability advantage in a single trial. Olanzapine produced a statistically significant but modest extra weight gain in adults (Attia 2019, 152 outpatients: BMI rising 0.259 versus 0.095 points per month) with NO significant benefit on obsessionality. Neither result supports a stronger stamp: FBT's advantage is follow-up-only in one trial, and olanzapine's is a small effect on weight alone, not on the illness's psychology.

cards.headline: Lock 2010: family-based treatment matched individual therapy at end of treatment, then beat it at 6 and 12 months
cards.summary: Lock 2010: family-based treatment matched individual therapy at end of treatment, then beat it at 6 and 12 months on full remission.
cards.people: 121 participants aged 12–18 years with a DSM-IV diagnosis of anorexia nervosa (excluding the amenorrhea requirement) at Stanford University and the University of Chicago, randomised to family-based treatment or adolescent-focused individual therapy — 24 outpatient hours over 12 months — and assessed at end of treatment and at 6 and 12 months after treatment; full remission defined as weight at least 95% of expected plus a global Eating Disorder Examination score within 1 SD of published means.
cards.result: There were NO differences in full remission between the treatments at end of treatment, but at both the 6- and 12-month follow-ups FBT was significantly superior to individual therapy on full remission — the abstract reports the remission contrasts as significant without printing the follow-up percentages, and this card does not invent them. FBT was significantly superior for partial remission at end of treatment (not at follow-up), for body mass index percentile at end of treatment (not at follow-up), and for change in Eating Disorder Examination score at end of treatment (not at follow-up).
cards.watchOut: The FBT advantage is a follow-up advantage on one outcome (full remission) in one 121-patient trial: at the moment treatment ended, the two therapies were indistinguishable on the primary measure.
cards.source: Lock J et al. Randomized clinical trial comparing family-based treatment with adolescent-focused individual therapy for adolescents with anorexia nervosa. Arch Gen Psychiatry. 2010;67(10):1025-1032. PMID: 20921118. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00149786, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Attia 2019: olanzapine added a modest extra weight gain in adult anorexia — BMI +0.259 vs +0.095 per month — and no psychological benefit
cards.summary: Attia 2019: olanzapine added a modest extra weight gain in adult anorexia — BMI +0.259 vs +0.095 per month — and no psychological benefit.
cards.people: 152 adult outpatients with anorexia nervosa (96% women; mean body mass index 16.7) at five North American sites, randomised to olanzapine (75) or placebo (77) with weekly visits for 16 weeks; primary outcomes were rate of change in body weight and in obsessionality (Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale).
cards.result: The increase in BMI over time was greater on olanzapine than placebo (0.259 [SD 0.051] versus 0.095 [SD 0.053] BMI points per month; significant treatment-by-time interaction) — an extra gain of roughly 0.16 BMI points per month. There was NO significant difference between groups in change in the YBOCS obsessions subscale (−0.325 versus −0.017 points per month) and no significant differences in the frequency of blood-test abnormalities assessing potential metabolic disturbances.
cards.watchOut: A weight-only, small-magnitude effect over 16 weeks in adults: the drug did not touch obsessionality, and a 16-week outpatient trial in a sample with mean BMI 16.7 does not address medical instability, longer-term weight maintenance, or adolescents.
cards.source: Attia E et al. Olanzapine Versus Placebo in Adult Outpatients With Anorexia Nervosa: A Randomized Clinical Trial. Am J Psychiatry. 2019;176(6):449-456. PMID: 30654643. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01170117, from the record's databank fields.

cards.summary: Different ages, different tools, each POSSIBLE on a single trial.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Lock 2010 (121 adolescents, psychotherapy) and Attia 2019 (152 adults, drug versus placebo).
cards.result: The shelf's two halves do not compete: FBT is the adolescent intervention with a follow-up remission advantage over individual therapy, and olanzapine is an adult adjunct with a modest weight effect (about 0.16 extra BMI points per month) and no demonstrated psychological benefit. Each rests on one trial, so each is POSSIBLE. Lisdexamfetamine for BINGE-eating disorder — the opposite pole of eating pathology — lives on Shelf #578 and is not re-carded here.

shelves.title: Bulimia nervosa: fluoxetine and cognitive behavioural therapy
shelves.question: Does fluoxetine 60 mg reduce binge–purge frequency versus placebo — and how does CBT compare with interpersonal psychotherapy?
shelves.mesh: Ambulatory Care · Body Mass Index · Bulimia/diagnosis,drug therapy,psychology · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Drug Administration Schedule · Fluoxetine/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Patient Dropouts
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two older randomised trials support their halves, neither with the precision this library would want for LIKELY. Fluoxetine 60 mg/day beat placebo on binge-eating and vomiting frequency in an 8-week trial of 387 women (1992) — but the record's abstract reports the superiority without printing the episode-frequency numbers, and the card says so. CBT beat interpersonal psychotherapy clearly at end of treatment (recovered 29% vs 6%; remitted 48% vs 28%) in Agras 2000 (220 patients) — but by 1-year follow-up the difference was no longer significant, because IPT caught up. A drug effect stated without abstract-level figures, and a therapy advantage that converges within a year: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Fluoxetine Bulimia Nervosa Collaborative Study Group 1992: fluoxetine 60 mg beat placebo on binge and vomiting frequency in 387 women
cards.summary: Fluoxetine Bulimia Nervosa Collaborative Study Group 1992: fluoxetine 60 mg beat placebo on binge and vomiting frequency in 387 women (the abstract does not quantify the effect).
cards.people: 387 women with bulimia nervosa treated as outpatients, randomised to fluoxetine 60 mg/day, fluoxetine 20 mg/day, or placebo for 8 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Fluoxetine 60 mg/day proved superior to placebo in decreasing the frequency of weekly binge-eating and vomiting episodes at endpoint; the 20 mg/day dose produced an effect between that of 60 mg and placebo. Depression, carbohydrate craving, and pathological eating attitudes and behaviours also improved significantly with fluoxetine, with the higher dose again showing the more robust effect. Insomnia, nausea, asthenia and tremor occurred significantly more often on fluoxetine, with no significant difference between groups in discontinuation because of adverse events. The abstract reports these contrasts without printing the episode-frequency values, and this card does not invent them.
cards.watchOut: An 8-week, industry-era trial whose abstract gives direction and significance but no numbers a reader can weigh: the dose-response pattern (60 > 20 > placebo) is the strongest internal evidence, and 8 weeks says nothing about durability.
cards.source: Fluoxetine Bulimia Nervosa Collaborative Study Group. Fluoxetine in the treatment of bulimia nervosa. A multicenter, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial. Arch Gen Psychiatry. 1992;49(2):139-147. PMID: 1550466. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — a pre-registration-era trial (1992).

cards.headline: Agras 2000: CBT beat IPT at end of treatment (recovered 29% vs 6%) — but the gap closed by 1 year
cards.summary: Agras 2000: CBT beat IPT at end of treatment (recovered 29% vs 6% ) — but the gap closed by 1 year.
cards.people: 220 patients meeting DSM-III-R criteria for bulimia nervosa, randomised to 19 sessions of cognitive-behavioural therapy or interpersonal psychotherapy over 20 weeks and evaluated for 1 year after treatment.
cards.result: At end of treatment CBT was significantly superior to IPT: recovered 29% versus 6%, remitted 48% versus 28%, and meeting community norms for eating attitudes and behaviours 41% versus 27%; among treatment completers, 45% on CBT versus 8% on IPT had recovered. At follow-up, however, there were NO significant differences between the treatments — 40% of CBT completers versus 27% of IPT completers had recovered. The authors conclude CBT acts significantly more rapidly and should be the preferred psychotherapy, with IPT catching up over time.
cards.watchOut: The headline is speed, not final state: an end-of-treatment comparison flatters the faster therapy, and the authors' own follow-up shows the untreated-by-CBT group converging — quote both time points or quote neither.
cards.source: Agras WS et al. A multicenter comparison of cognitive-behavioral therapy and interpersonal psychotherapy for bulimia nervosa. Arch Gen Psychiatry. 2000;57(5):459-466. PMID: 10807486. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the record carries no databank SI field.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a drug with unquantified abstract-level benefit, a therapy that wins on speed — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: A drug with an unquantified abstract-level benefit, a therapy that wins on speed — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: the 1992 fluoxetine trial (387 women) and Agras 2000 (220 patients).
cards.result: Fluoxetine 60 mg has a placebo-controlled win the abstract does not quantify; CBT has a quantified win over IPT that is large at 20 weeks (recovered 29% vs 6%) and non-significant at a year. Neither trial was ever followed by a larger modern replication on this shelf, so both claims sit at POSSIBLE — real randomised support, honestly limited.
cards.watchOut: Do not present CBT's end-of-treatment margin as a lasting superiority, and do not attach a percentage reduction to fluoxetine that the trial's record does not print.
