shelves.title: Continuing antidepressants after recovery: maintenance vs discontinuation
shelves.question: In patients well on antidepressants in primary care, does continuing treatment prevent relapse versus tapering to placebo (ANTLER) — and what does the older maintenance trial base show?
shelves.mesh: Antidepressive Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Anxiety Disorders/epidemiology · Citalopram/therapeutic use · Depressive Disorder/drug therapy,epidemiology · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Maintenance Chemotherapy · Primary Health Care
shelves.balance: LIKELY: The modern primary-care trial and the older trial base agree. In ANTLER (478 patients in UK general practices, well and considering stopping), relapse by 52 weeks was 39% on maintenance versus 56% on tapering to placebo (hazard ratio 2.06, 95% CI 1.56 to 2.70 — just beyond this library's 2.0 solid-evidence line, with a 17-percentage-point absolute difference beside it). The Geddes 2003 synthesis of 31 maintenance trials (4,410 participants) found the same pattern at larger scale: relapse 18% on continued antidepressants versus 41% on discontinuation. Two independent evidence layers, one absolute difference of about 17–23 percentage points in each: LIKELY that continuing prevents relapse in patients like those enrolled — people with recurrent depression or long treatment histories, not everyone who has ever taken an antidepressant.

cards.headline: ANTLER 2021: stopping antidepressants raised 52-week relapse to 56% vs 39% on maintenance — hazard ratio 2.06
cards.summary: ANTLER 2021: stopping antidepressants raised 52-week relapse to 56% vs 39% on maintenance — hazard ratio 2.06, relative.
cards.people: 478 adults treated in 150 UK general practices who had a history of at least two depressive episodes or had taken antidepressants for 2 years or longer, felt well enough to consider stopping, and were taking citalopram, fluoxetine, sertraline or mirtazapine; randomised to maintain current therapy (238) or taper to matching placebo (240). Average age 54 years; 73% women. Adherence to the trial assignment was 70% in the maintenance group and 52% in the discontinuation group.
cards.result: By 52 weeks, relapse had occurred in 92 of 238 maintenance patients (39%) versus 135 of 240 discontinuation patients (56%) (hazard ratio 2.06, 95% CI 1.56 to 2.70; P<0.001) — a relative measure just beyond the 2.0 line this library treats as solid, printed with its absolute rates (39% vs 56%) beside it. Secondary outcomes were generally in the same direction, and the discontinuation group had more symptoms of depression, anxiety and withdrawal than the maintenance group.
cards.watchOut: Participants were selected for high relapse risk (recurrent episodes or years of treatment) AND for feeling well enough to consider stopping: the 56% relapse rate does not predict what happens when a first-episode, low-risk patient stops, and imperfect adherence (52% in the discontinuation arm) blurs the contrast toward the null.
cards.source: Lewis G et al. Maintenance or Discontinuation of Antidepressants in Primary Care. N Engl J Med. 2021;385(14):1257-1267. PMID: 34587384. Registry ID: ISRCTN15969819, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Geddes 2003: across 31 maintenance trials, relapse was 18% on continued antidepressants vs 41% after discontinuation
cards.summary: Geddes 2003: across 31 maintenance trials, relapse was 18% on continued antidepressants vs 41% after discontinuation.
cards.type: Systematic review and pooled analysis of randomised trials
cards.people: 31 randomised trials totalling 4,410 participants with depressive disorders who had responded to acute antidepressant treatment and were randomised to continue the antidepressant or switch to placebo; most trials were of 12 months' duration. The abstract does not state a pooled mean age.
cards.result: Continuing antidepressant treatment reduced the odds of relapse by 70% (95% CI 62% to 78%; 2p<0.00001) compared with discontinuation — a relative odds measure; the absolute rates beside it were an average relapse rate of 41% on placebo versus 18% on active treatment. The effect seemed to persist for up to 36 months, although most trials lasted 12 months, and seemed largely independent of underlying relapse risk and of treatment durations before and within randomisation. More participants allocated antidepressants withdrew than on placebo (18% vs 15%; odds ratio 1.30, 95% CI 1.07 to 1.59).
cards.watchOut: A pooling of mostly 12-month, pre-2003 trials in patients who had already responded to the drug being continued — a design that enriches for drug-responsive, relapse-prone patients; evidence beyond 36 months requires confirmation, as the authors state.
cards.source: Geddes JR et al. Relapse prevention with antidepressant drug treatment in depressive disorders: a systematic review. Lancet. 2003;361(9358):653-661. PMID: 12606176. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a systematic review, not a single trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: maintenance prevents relapse in recurrent depression — LIKELY, in the population actually studied
cards.summary: Maintenance prevents relapse in recurrent depression — LIKELY, in the population actually studied.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: ANTLER (478 primary-care patients) and Geddes 2003 (31 trials, 4,410 participants).
cards.result: The absolute numbers tell one story twice: 39% versus 56% relapse over a year in modern primary care (ANTLER), and 18% versus 41% across the older maintenance trial base (Geddes). Continuing an antidepressant after recovery prevents roughly one relapse for every four to six high-risk patients treated for a year. The claim is population-bound — recurrent or long-treated depression — and this shelf does not extend it to first-episode patients. STAR*D acute sequencing lives on Shelf #230 and collaborative-care organisation on Shelf #533; neither is re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Never quote the Geddes '70% reduction' without its absolute rates (41% to 18%): it is a relative odds reduction, and this library's wording standard requires the absolute figures beside it.
cards.source: Synthesis of Lewis G et al. N Engl J Med. 2021;385(14):1257-1267. PMID: 34587384; Geddes JR et al. Lancet. 2003;361(9358):653-661. PMID: 12606176. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Bipolar depression: quetiapine and lurasidone
shelves.question: Do quetiapine and lurasidone treat acute bipolar depression versus placebo — the depressive pole that antimanic trials do not cover?
shelves.mesh: Antidepressive Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Bipolar Disorder/drug therapy · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Isoindoles/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Lurasidone Hydrochloride · Placebos · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY — quetiapine: a pooled analysis of FOUR randomised placebo-controlled trials in bipolar II depression (Young 2013; 776 patients across the dose arms reported) found MADRS improvement of −15.58 (300 mg) and −14.88 (600 mg) versus −11.61 on placebo (both p<0.001), with significantly higher response and remission at week 8. POSSIBLE — lurasidone: one large monotherapy trial in bipolar I depression (Loebel 2014, PREVAIL; 505 patients) found MADRS improvement of −15.4 at both dose ranges versus −10.7 on placebo (effect size 0.51) — a single pivotal trial, so POSSIBLE under the single-trial ceiling. Note the populations differ (bipolar II for the quetiapine pooling, bipolar I for lurasidone) and the cards keep them separate.

cards.headline: Young 2013: pooling four trials, quetiapine beat placebo on MADRS in bipolar II depression — −15.58 (300 mg) vs −11.61
cards.summary: Young 2013: pooling four trials, quetiapine beat placebo on MADRS in bipolar II depression — −15.58 (300 mg) vs −11.61.
cards.type: Pooled analysis of four randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials (BOLDER I and II; EMBOLDEN I and II)
cards.people: Patients with bipolar II disorder in a depressive episode, randomised across four 8-week trials to quetiapine 300 mg/day (n=283), quetiapine 600 mg/day (n=289) or placebo (n=204) as monotherapy. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Mean MADRS total score improvement from baseline to week 8 was −15.58 on quetiapine 300 mg and −14.88 on 600 mg versus −11.61 on placebo (p<0.001 for both); effect sizes were 0.44 (300 mg) and 0.47 (600 mg). Significantly higher proportions on quetiapine at both doses achieved response and remission at week 8 (p<0.01). Common adverse events included dry mouth, somnolence, sedation, dizziness and headache; rates of mania and hypomania were similar for quetiapine and placebo.
cards.watchOut: A sponsor-programme pooling restricted to bipolar II depression: the placebo arm itself improved by −11.61 MADRS points, so the drug's added effect is about 3–4 points, and the pooling does not cover bipolar I depression, where the lurasidone card below is the shelf's evidence.
cards.source: Young AH et al. Quetiapine monotherapy in bipolar II depression: combined data from four large, randomized studies. Int J Bipolar Disord. 2013;1:10. PMID: 25505677. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the record carries no databank SI field; the four trials are identified in the abstract by sponsor study codes (BOLDER I [5077US/0049], BOLDER II [D1447C00135], EMBOLDEN I [D1447C00001], EMBOLDEN II [D1447C00134]).

cards.headline: Loebel 2014 (PREVAIL): lurasidone monotherapy beat placebo on MADRS in bipolar I depression — −15.4 vs −10.7, effect size 0.51
cards.summary: Loebel 2014 (PREVAIL): lurasidone monotherapy beat placebo on MADRS in bipolar I depression — −15.4 vs −10.7, effect size 0.51.
cards.people: 505 patients with a major depressive episode associated with bipolar I disorder, randomised to lurasidone 20–60 mg/day (166), lurasidone 80–120 mg/day (169), or placebo (170) for 6 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Mean MADRS reduction at week 6 was −15.4 in both lurasidone dose groups (effect size 0.51 for each) versus −10.7 on placebo, a significant difference for both; CGI-BP depression severity scores likewise improved more on lurasidone (−1.8 and −1.7; effect sizes 0.61 and 0.50) versus −1.1 on placebo. Discontinuation for adverse events was similar across groups (6.6%, 5.9% and 6.5%); the most frequent lurasidone adverse events were nausea, headache, akathisia and somnolence, with minimal changes in weight, lipids and glycaemic measures.
cards.watchOut: A single 6-week trial in bipolar I depression: it supports acute monotherapy, not maintenance, not bipolar II, and not adjunctive use — and the placebo group improved by −10.7 MADRS points, so the added drug effect is about 4–5 points.
cards.source: Loebel A et al. Lurasidone monotherapy in the treatment of bipolar I depression: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study. Am J Psychiatry. 2014;171(2):160-168. PMID: 24170180. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00868699, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: both drugs beat placebo acutely — LIKELY for the four-trial drug, POSSIBLE for the single-trial drug
cards.summary: Both drugs beat placebo acutely — LIKELY for the four-trial drug, POSSIBLE for the single-trial drug.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Young 2013 (four pooled trials, 776 patients in bipolar II depression) and Loebel 2014 (505 patients in bipolar I depression).
cards.result: Quetiapine's claim rests on four concordant trials pooled (added MADRS benefit about 3–4 points over a large placebo response); lurasidone's rests on one well-sized trial (added benefit about 4–5 points, effect size 0.51). The stamps differ because the evidence bases differ in count, not because one drug is declared better — no head-to-head trial is carded here, and the populations (bipolar II vs bipolar I) do not even fully overlap. shelves.title: ADHD in adults: stimulant and non-stimulant medications
shelves.question: In adults with ADHD, do methylphenidate, amphetamines, and atomoxetine improve core symptoms versus placebo — and how do they compare?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic alpha-2 Receptor Agonists/therapeutic use · Attention Deficit Disorder with Hyperactivity/drug therapy · Bupropion/therapeutic use · Central Nervous System Stimulants/therapeutic use · Clonidine/therapeutic use · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Methylphenidate/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY (short-term): The Cortese 2018 network meta-analysis of 133 double-blind randomised trials (51 in adults; efficacy analysis in 8,131 adults) found amphetamines (SMD −0.79), methylphenidate (−0.49), bupropion (−0.46) and atomoxetine (−0.45) all superior to placebo on clinician-rated core symptoms in adults at about 12 weeks, while modafinil was not (0.16). Head-to-head differences favoured amphetamines. The same analysis found these drugs less well tolerated than placebo in adults (dropout-for-adverse-event odds ratios 2.33–3.26), and data were insufficient at 26 and 52 weeks — so the LIKELY stamp is explicitly a SHORT-TERM stamp, which the balance and the card both state.

cards.headline: Cortese 2018: across 133 RCTs, amphetamines, methylphenidate, bupropion and atomoxetine all beat placebo in adults — modafinil did not
cards.summary: Cortese 2018: across 133 RCTs, amphetamines, methylphenidate, bupropion and atomoxetine all beat placebo in adults — modafinil did not.
cards.type: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of double-blind randomised controlled trials
cards.people: 133 double-blind RCTs (81 in children and adolescents, 51 in adults, 1 in both); the adult efficacy analysis closest to 12 weeks covered 8,131 adults and the adult tolerability analysis 5,362 adults. Medications compared: amphetamines (including lisdexamfetamine), atomoxetine, bupropion, clonidine, guanfacine, methylphenidate and modafinil, against each other or placebo.
cards.result: In adults, on clinician-rated ADHD core symptoms closest to 12 weeks, standardised mean differences versus placebo were −0.79 (95% CI −0.99 to −0.58) for amphetamines, −0.49 (−0.64 to −0.35) for methylphenidate, −0.46 (−0.85 to −0.07) for bupropion and −0.45 (−0.58 to −0.32) for atomoxetine; modafinil was NOT better than placebo (0.16, −0.28 to 0.59). In head-to-head comparisons, efficacy differences favoured amphetamines over modafinil, atomoxetine and methylphenidate in adults (SMDs −0.94 to −0.29). Tolerability in adults was worse than placebo for amphetamines (odds ratio for dropout due to side effects 3.26, 95% CI 1.54 to 6.92), methylphenidate (2.39, 1.40 to 4.08) and atomoxetine (2.33, 1.28 to 4.25) — relative harm measures above the 2.0 line, printed beside the efficacy figures. Confidence in the estimates ranged from high or moderate for some comparisons to low or very low for most indirect comparisons, and data were insufficient for the 26- and 52-week timepoints.
cards.watchOut: A network synthesis, not a single trial: most adult comparisons are indirect and graded low or very low confidence, nearly all underlying trials are short (about 12 weeks), and the authors state that new research is urgently needed on long-term effects — the shelf's claim expires at the short term.
cards.source: Cortese S et al. Comparative efficacy and tolerability of medications for attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder in children, adolescents, and adults: a systematic review and network meta-analysis. Lancet Psychiatry. 2018;5(9):727-738. PMID: 30097390. Registry ID: PROSPERO CRD42014008976, stated in the record's abstract (registration of the review); the MEDLINE record carries no databank SI field.

cards.summary: Short-term adult efficacy is LIKELY; long-term benefit and best-drug certainty are not established.
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: Cortese 2018 (133 double-blind RCTs; 51 adult trials, 8,131 adults in the efficacy analysis).
cards.result: Four drug classes separate from placebo on adult core symptoms at about 12 weeks, with the largest point estimate for amphetamines (−0.79) and the authors' own bottom line supporting amphetamines as the preferred first choice in adults on combined efficacy and tolerability — against dropout-for-side-effect odds ratios above 2 for the same drugs. shelves.title: Borderline personality disorder: dialectical behaviour and mentalization-based therapy
shelves.question: Does dialectical behaviour therapy reduce parasuicidal behaviour versus treatment as usual (Linehan) — and does mentalization-based treatment beat structured clinical management (Bateman)?
shelves.mesh: Borderline Personality Disorder/psychology,therapy · Chronic Disease · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy · Hospitalization · Length of Stay · Psychotherapy · Self Mutilation/psychology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Linehan 1991 randomised chronically parasuicidal women with borderline personality disorder to a year of dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) or community treatment as usual and found fewer and less medically severe parasuicide episodes, better therapy retention and fewer inpatient days on DBT — in a single small early trial whose abstract does not even state its sample size. Bateman 2009 (134 patients) found 18 months of mentalization-based treatment (MBT) produced a steeper decline in crisis events, suicide attempts and hospitalisation than structured clinical management — though both structured treatments improved substantially. Structured specialist therapy helping, with MBT ahead of a strong active control, is real but thin randomised evidence: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Linehan 1991: a year of DBT cut parasuicide frequency and severity versus treatment as usual in chronically parasuicidal women
cards.summary: Linehan 1991: a year of DBT cut parasuicide frequency and severity vs treatment as usual in chronically parasuicidal women.
cards.people: Women who met criteria for borderline personality disorder and were chronically parasuicidal, randomised to dialectical behaviour therapy or treatment as usual in the community for 1 year, with assessments every 4 months. The abstract does not state the sample size or mean age.
cards.result: At most assessment points and across the entire year, patients receiving DBT had fewer incidences of parasuicide and less medically severe parasuicides, were more likely to stay in individual therapy, and had fewer inpatient psychiatric days than the treatment-as-usual group. There were NO between-group differences on depression, hopelessness, suicide ideation or reasons for living, although scores on all four measures decreased over the year in both groups.
cards.watchOut: The founding DBT trial: a single small study (its abstract does not report the sample size) in women selected for chronic parasuicidality, against unstructured community care — it establishes that DBT beat what patients otherwise got in 1991, not how it compares with other structured therapies, which is the question the second card takes up.
cards.source: Linehan MM et al. Cognitive-behavioral treatment of chronically parasuicidal borderline patients. Arch Gen Psychiatry. 1991;48(12):1060-1064. PMID: 1845222. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — a pre-registration-era trial (1991).

cards.headline: Bateman 2009: mentalization-based treatment beat structured clinical management on crisis events over 18 months — but both improved substantially
cards.summary: Bateman 2009: mentalization-based treatment beat structured clinical management on crisis events over 18 months — but both improved substantially.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial with blinded independent evaluators
cards.people: 134 patients consecutively referred to a specialist personality disorder treatment centre and meeting criteria for borderline personality disorder, randomised to 18 months of outpatient mentalization-based treatment or structured clinical management; 11 therapists of equal experience and training delivered both, with independent assessments every 6 months.
cards.result: Substantial improvements were observed in BOTH conditions across all outcome variables. Patients allocated to MBT showed a steeper decline in self-reported and clinically significant problems, including suicide attempts and hospitalisation, than those allocated to structured clinical management; the primary outcome was the composite of suicidal and severe self-injurious behaviour and hospitalisation, analysed with mixed-effects models — the abstract reports the direction of these contrasts without printing event rates, and this card does not invent them. The authors conclude that structured treatments improve outcomes in borderline personality disorder and that a focus on specific psychological processes brings additional benefits.
cards.watchOut: The comparator was itself a structured, active treatment delivered by equally experienced therapists — so the trial shows an incremental advantage for MBT's specific focus, not a therapy-versus-nothing effect; and the authors call for independent replication by other research groups.
cards.source: Bateman A et al. Randomized controlled trial of outpatient mentalization-based treatment versus structured clinical management for borderline personality disorder. Am J Psychiatry. 2009;166(12):1355-1364. PMID: 19833787. Registry ID: ISRCTN27660668, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: structured specialist therapy helps; the specific-therapy margins are single-trial — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Structured specialist therapy helps; the specific-therapy margins are single-trial — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Linehan 1991 (chronically parasuicidal women, DBT vs community care) and Bateman 2009 (134 patients, MBT vs structured clinical management).
cards.result: Read together, the pair traces the field's own learning curve: DBT beat unstructured usual care on behaviour (fewer, less severe parasuicides; fewer inpatient days) without separating on depression or hopelessness; a generation later, MBT beat an equally structured control by a margin the authors describe as a steeper decline rather than a categorical difference. Two single trials, two different therapies and controls: the shared, defensible claim — structured specialist psychotherapy improves outcomes in borderline personality disorder, with specific models adding something — is POSSIBLE.
cards.watchOut: Do not use Linehan 1991 to claim DBT beats other modern structured therapies (its control was 1991 community care), and do not use Bateman 2009 to claim MBT is the only effective model (its control improved substantially too).
cards.source: Synthesis of Linehan MM et al. Arch Gen Psychiatry. 1991;48(12):1060-1064. PMID: 1845222; Bateman A et al. Am J Psychiatry. 2009;166(12):1355-1364. PMID: 19833787. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Cryptococcal meningitis in HIV: single-dose liposomal amphotericin and the ACTA combinations
shelves.question: In HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis, is a single high dose of liposomal amphotericin (with flucytosine and fluconazole) as good as a week of amphotericin — and which oral partner regimen saves most lives (AMBITION-cm, ACTA)?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Africa South of the Sahara · AIDS-Related Opportunistic Infections/drug therapy,mortality · Amphotericin B/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Antifungal Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Therapy, Combination
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: mortality outcomes throughout): Two large African randomised trials settle the induction question. AMBITION-cm (844 randomised) found a single high dose of liposomal amphotericin B plus 14 days of flucytosine and fluconazole noninferior to the WHO-recommended week of amphotericin B deoxycholate for 10-week mortality (24.8% vs 28.7%), with fewer grade 3–4 adverse events (50.0% vs 62.3%). ACTA (721 patients) found 1 week of amphotericin and a fully oral fluconazole-plus-flucytosine regimen both noninferior to 2 weeks of amphotericin, flucytosine superior to fluconazole as the amphotericin partner (10-week mortality 31.1% vs 45.0%; hazard ratio 0.62 — a relative figure inside the 0.5–2.0 band, believed here as randomised data with absolute rates beside it), and the lowest mortality with 1 week of amphotericin plus flucytosine (24.2%). The stamp is LIKELY and proposed only, because every load-bearing figure is mortality.

cards.headline: AMBITION-cm 2022: single-dose liposomal amphotericin was noninferior for 10-week death — 24.8% vs 28.7% — with fewer severe adverse events
cards.summary: AMBITION-cm 2022: single-dose liposomal amphotericin was noninferior for 10-week death — 24.8% vs 28.7% — with fewer severe adverse events. (Tier C — mortality outcome; PROPOSED.)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised, controlled, noninferiority trial in five African countries
cards.people: 844 HIV-positive adults with cryptococcal meningitis randomised 1:1 to a single high dose of liposomal amphotericin B (10 mg/kg on day 1) plus 14 days of flucytosine and fluconazole, or the WHO-recommended control (7 days of amphotericin B deoxycholate plus flucytosine, then 7 days of fluconazole); 814 included in the intention-to-treat population. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Death from any cause at 10 weeks (the primary end point) occurred in 101 participants (24.8%; 95% CI 20.7 to 29.3) in the liposomal amphotericin group and 117 (28.7%; 24.4 to 33.4) in the control group (difference −3.9 percentage points; the upper boundary of the one-sided 95% CI was 1.2 percentage points, within the 10-point noninferiority margin; P<0.001 for noninferiority). Fungal clearance from cerebrospinal fluid was −0.40 vs −0.42 log10 colony-forming units per millilitre per day. Grade 3 or 4 adverse events occurred in 50.0% of the liposomal group vs 62.3% of controls.
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority at a wide 10-percentage-point margin in a disease killing a quarter of patients: 'as good as' here means within that margin, and the regimen still requires flucytosine access — the drug whose availability is the binding constraint in much of the endemic world.
cards.source: Jarvis JN et al. Single-Dose Liposomal Amphotericin B Treatment for Cryptococcal Meningitis. N Engl J Med. 2022;386(12):1109-1120. PMID: 35320642. Registry ID: ISRCTN72509687, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: ACTA 2018: one week of amphotericin, or oral fluconazole plus flucytosine, matched two weeks — and flucytosine was the partner that saved lives (10-week mortality 31.1% vs 45.0% with fluconazole)
cards.summary: ACTA 2018: one week of amphotericin, or oral fluconazole plus flucytosine, matched two weeks — and flucytosine was the partner that saved lives.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial with factorial partner-drug assignment
cards.people: 721 HIV-infected adults with cryptococcal meningitis in Africa, randomised to an oral regimen (fluconazole 1200 mg/day plus flucytosine for 2 weeks), 1 week of amphotericin B, or 2 weeks of amphotericin B; patients receiving amphotericin were also randomised to fluconazole or flucytosine as partner drug; all received fluconazole consolidation and were followed to 10 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Mortality at 2 weeks was 18.2% (41 of 225) in the oral-regimen group, 21.9% (49 of 224) with 1 week of amphotericin and 21.4% (49 of 229) with 2 weeks; at 10 weeks it was 35.1% (79 of 225), 36.2% (81 of 224) and 39.7% (91 of 229) respectively — both shorter strategies met the 10-percentage-point noninferiority margin against 2 weeks. As amphotericin's partner, flucytosine beat fluconazole: 71 deaths (31.1%) vs 101 (45.0%) at 10 weeks (hazard ratio 0.62, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.84; P=0.002 — a relative figure). One week of amphotericin plus flucytosine had the lowest 10-week mortality of any combination (24.2%; 95% CI 16.2 to 32.1). Severe anaemia and other side effects were more frequent with 2 weeks than with 1 week of amphotericin or the oral regimen.
cards.watchOut: The partner-drug comparison pools across the amphotericin-duration arms, and the 'best combination' figure (24.2%) is a subgroup of the factorial with a wide confidence interval — directionally consistent with AMBITION-cm's flucytosine-containing winner, but not a separately powered arm.
cards.source: Molloy SF et al. Antifungal Combinations for Treatment of Cryptococcal Meningitis in Africa. N Engl J Med. 2018;378(11):1004-1017. PMID: 29539274. Registry ID: ISRCTN45035509, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one dose (or one week), always with flucytosine — LIKELY, proposed (Tier C)
cards.summary: One dose (or one week), always with flucytosine — LIKELY, proposed (Tier C).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: AMBITION-cm (844 randomised, five African countries) and ACTA (721 patients).
cards.result: The two trials converge on the same practical regimen logic: long amphotericin courses are unnecessary — a single liposomal dose (10-week mortality 24.8% vs 28.7% for the week-long standard) or one week of deoxycholate does the work — and flucytosine is the partner drug that matters (ACTA mortality 31.1% vs 45.0% against fluconazole partnering; AMBITION-cm's winning arm contains it). Mortality in every arm of both trials remained 24–40%, which is the honest frame: these regimens are better and simpler, and the disease is still lethal. LIKELY, proposed pending the developer's personal verdict because the claims are mortality claims.
cards.watchOut: Both trials are African, resource-limited-setting trials in HIV-associated disease; they do not directly answer cryptococcal meningitis in transplant recipients or other hosts, where no shelf here claims evidence.
cards.source: Synthesis of Jarvis JN et al. N Engl J Med. 2022;386(12):1109-1120. PMID: 35320642; Molloy SF et al. N Engl J Med. 2018;378(11):1004-1017. PMID: 29539274. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Acromegaly: pasireotide versus octreotide, and pegvisomant
shelves.question: In medically untreated acromegaly, does pasireotide beat octreotide on biochemical control (the PAOLA head-to-head) — and where does the growth-hormone-receptor antagonist pegvisomant fit?
shelves.mesh: Acromegaly/drug therapy,etiology · Adenoma/complications,drug therapy · Antineoplastic Agents, Hormonal/therapeutic use · Growth Hormone-Secreting Pituitary Adenoma/complications,drug therapy · Octreotide/therapeutic use · Somatostatin/analogs & derivatives,therapeutic use · Therapeutic Equivalency
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY for pasireotide's superiority on biochemical control — two randomised trials, in treatment-naïve patients (control achieved by 31.3% vs 19.2% on octreotide LAR) and in patients inadequately controlled on first-generation analogues (PAOLA: 15% and 20% on pasireotide 40 mg and 60 mg vs 0% on continued octreotide/lanreotide) — bought with substantially more hyperglycaemia (57.3% vs 21.7% hyperglycaemia-related events in the naïve trial). POSSIBLE for pegvisomant: one small 12-week placebo-controlled trial (112 patients) with a steep dose response in IGF-1 normalisation (10% placebo; 54%, 81% and 89% at 10, 15 and 20 mg daily) — a single short trial caps its half at POSSIBLE. Pasireotide's other pituitary use, Cushing's disease, is Shelf #749 and is cross-referenced, not duplicated.

cards.headline: Colao 2014: in medically naïve acromegaly, pasireotide LAR beat octreotide LAR on biochemical control — 31.3% vs 19.2% — with far more hyperglycaemia
cards.summary: Colao 2014: in medically naïve acromegaly, pasireotide LAR beat octreotide LAR on biochemical control — 31.3% vs 19.2% — with far more hyperglycaemia.
cards.type: Prospective, randomised, double-blind head-to-head superiority trial
cards.people: 358 patients with medically naïve acromegaly (previous pituitary surgery without medical treatment, or de novo with a visible adenoma) at 84 sites in 27 countries, randomised to pasireotide LAR 40 mg every 28 days (176) or octreotide LAR 20 mg every 28 days (182) for 12 months, with titration permitted at months 3 and 7. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Biochemical control (growth hormone below 2.5 μg/L and normal IGF-1) at month 12 was achieved by 31.3% on pasireotide LAR versus 19.2% on octreotide LAR (P=0.007); normal IGF-1 alone was achieved by 38.6% versus 23.6% (P=0.002), while growth hormone below 2.5 μg/L was similar (48.3% vs 51.6%). Hyperglycemia-related adverse events were much more common with pasireotide (57.3% vs 21.7%). Among patients not achieving control, 31.0% on pasireotide and 22.2% on octreotide had not received the recommended dose increase.
cards.watchOut: Even the winning arm controlled only about a third of patients, and the price is metabolic: more than half the pasireotide group had a hyperglycaemia-related event. This is a relative-efficacy win, not a clean one.
cards.source: Colao A et al. Pasireotide versus octreotide in acromegaly: a head-to-head superiority study. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2014;99(3):791-9. PMID: 24423324. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the record carries no databank registration entry.

cards.headline: PAOLA 2014: in patients inadequately controlled on octreotide or lanreotide, pasireotide achieved control in 15–20% versus 0% on continued first-generation therapy
cards.summary: PAOLA 2014: in patients inadequately controlled on first-generation analogues, pasireotide achieved control in 15–20% vs 0% on continued therapy.
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised phase 3 trial (patients and investigators unmasked to drug assignment, masked to pasireotide dose)
cards.people: 198 patients with acromegaly inadequately controlled after at least 6 months on high-dose octreotide LAR or lanreotide, randomised to pasireotide LAR 40 mg (65), pasireotide LAR 60 mg (65) or continued octreotide/lanreotide as active control (68), every 28 days for 24 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 24 weeks, biochemical control (mean growth hormone below 2.5 μg/L and normalised IGF-1) was achieved by ten patients (15%) on pasireotide 40 mg and 13 (20%) on pasireotide 60 mg, versus no patients on active control (absolute differences 15.4%, 95% confidence interval 7.6 to 26.5, p=0.0006, and 20.0%, 11.1 to 31.8, p<0.0001). The most common adverse events were hyperglycaemia (33% on 40 mg, 31% on 60 mg, 14% on control), diabetes (21%, 26%, 8%) and diarrhoea (16%, 19%, 5%), mostly grade 1 or 2; serious adverse events were reported in six (10%), two (3%) and three (5%) patients respectively.
cards.watchOut: A 0% control rate reflects a deliberately refractory population (already failing the control drugs), so the absolute gains (15–20% controlled) are the honest headline alongside the comparison — four of five switched patients still did not reach control.
cards.source: Gadelha MR et al. Pasireotide versus continued treatment with octreotide or lanreotide in patients with inadequately controlled acromegaly (PAOLA): a randomised, phase 3 trial. cards.headline: Trainer 2000: pegvisomant normalised IGF-1 in 89% at 20 mg daily versus 10% on placebo — in 12 weeks
cards.summary: Trainer 2000: pegvisomant normalised IGF-1 in 89% at 20 mg daily vs 10% on placebo — in 12 weeks.
cards.people: 112 patients with acromegaly given subcutaneous pegvisomant (10 mg, 15 mg or 20 mg daily) or placebo for 12 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix, or the per-group numbers.
cards.result: Mean (±SD) serum IGF-1 fell from baseline by 4.0±16.8% on placebo, 26.7±27.9% on 10 mg, 50.1±26.7% on 15 mg and 62.5±21.3% on 20 mg of pegvisomant (P<0.001 for each dose versus placebo), and IGF-1 concentrations became normal in 10%, 54%, 81% and 89% of patients respectively (P<0.001 for each comparison with placebo). Among patients on 15 or 20 mg, ring size, soft-tissue swelling, excessive perspiration and fatigue all decreased significantly, and the total symptom-and-sign score improved in all pegvisomant groups (P≤0.05). shelves.title: Medical therapy for Cushing's disease: pasireotide and osilodrostat
shelves.question: In persistent/recurrent Cushing's disease, do pasireotide (phase II/III programme) and osilodrostat (LINC-3) normalize cortisol versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adrenocorticotropic Hormone/blood · Blood Glucose/analysis · Glucagon/blood · Hydrocortisone/urine · Insulin/blood · Oligopeptides/adverse effects,pharmacokinetics,therapeutic use · Pituitary ACTH Hypersecretion/drug therapy,metabolism
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two different mechanisms, each supported at phase 3 level but neither with a conventional placebo-controlled induction trial. Pasireotide's phase 3 trial (162 patients) randomised between two doses with no placebo arm: urinary free cortisol normalised at month 6 in 15% (600 μg twice daily) and 26% (900 μg) of patients, after a 15-day phase 2 proof-of-concept in which 76% reduced urinary cortisol and 17% normalised it — with hyperglycaemia-related adverse events in 118 of 162 phase 3 patients. Osilodrostat's LINC-3 used a randomised-withdrawal design: among responders randomised at week 26, 86% maintained a complete response on continued osilodrostat versus 29% switched to placebo at week 34 (odds ratio 13.7 — a relative measure well outside the 0.5–2.0 caution band, printed with its absolute rates), at the cost of hypocortisolism in 51% of all treated patients. Single-programme evidence for each drug caps the shelf at POSSIBLE. Pasireotide's acromegaly programme is Shelf #745, cross-referenced rather than duplicated.

cards.summary: Pasireotide phase 2 2009: 15 days of pasireotide lowered urinary free cortisol in 76% of patients and normalised it in 17% — single-arm proof of concept.
cards.people: 39 patients with de novo Cushing's disease who were candidates for pituitary surgery, or persistent/recurrent disease after surgery without prior pituitary irradiation, self-administering subcutaneous pasireotide 600 μg twice daily for 15 days at multiple centres; 29 patients formed the primary efficacy analysis. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: After 15 days, 22 of 29 patients (76%) in the primary efficacy analysis showed a reduction in urinary free cortisol levels, of whom five (17%) had normal urinary free cortisol (responders). Serum cortisol and plasma ACTH levels were also reduced. Steady-state pasireotide concentrations were achieved within 5 days, and responders appeared to have higher pasireotide exposure than nonresponders.
cards.watchOut: Fifteen days, no control group, 29 analysed patients: this card is the programme's proof of concept only — regression to the mean and spontaneous fluctuation cannot be excluded from a single-arm cortisol study, which is why the phase 3 card carries the shelf's weight.

cards.headline: Pasireotide phase 3 2012: urinary cortisol normalised in 15% (600 μg) and 26% (900 μg) at month 6 — a dose-comparison trial with no placebo arm, and hyperglycaemia in 118 of 162 patients
cards.summary: Pasireotide phase 3 2012: urinary cortisol normalised in 15% (600 µg) and 26% (900 µg) at month 6 — a dose-comparison trial with no placebo arm, and hyperglycaemia the price. (An unrelated DNA-testing review returned by a from-memory lookup was rejected and not carded — disclosed in the pack summary.)
cards.type: Double-blind, randomised phase 3 trial (two active doses; no placebo group)
cards.people: 162 adults with Cushing's disease and urinary free cortisol at least 1.5 times the upper limit of normal, randomised to subcutaneous pasireotide 600 μg twice daily (82) or 900 μg twice daily (80), with a 300 μg dose increase for inadequate response at month 3 and open-label treatment to month 12. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Twelve of 82 patients in the 600-μg group and 21 of 80 in the 900-μg group met the primary endpoint — urinary free cortisol at or below the upper limit of normal at month 6 without a dose increase. Median urinary free cortisol fell by approximately 50% by month 2 and remained stable in both groups; normal levels were achieved more often in patients whose baseline level did not exceed 5 times the upper limit of normal. Serum and salivary cortisol and plasma corticotropin fell, and clinical signs and symptoms diminished. Pasireotide was associated with hyperglycemia-related adverse events in 118 of 162 patients, and glucose-lowering medication was started in 74 of 162.
cards.watchOut: Without a placebo arm, the normalisation rates (15% and 26%) cannot be netted against spontaneous variation — the trial's internal evidence is the dose gradient and the ~50% median cortisol fall. And the metabolic cost is large: nearly three-quarters of patients had a hyperglycaemia-related event.

cards.headline: LINC-3 2020: on randomised withdrawal, osilodrostat maintained complete response in 86% versus 29% switched to placebo — relative odds 13.7
cards.summary: LINC-3 2020: on randomised withdrawal, osilodrostat maintained complete response in 86% vs 29% switched to placebo — relative odds 13.7.
cards.type: Phase 3 study with open-label dose optimisation followed by a double-blind, randomised withdrawal period
cards.people: 137 enrolled patients aged 18–75 years with persistent or recurrent Cushing's disease (mean 24-hour urinary free cortisol above 1.5 times the upper limit of normal), recruited at 66 sites in 19 countries; median age 40.0 years and 106 (77%) were female. Of these, 72 (53%) were eligible for the randomised withdrawal at week 26 (36 continued osilodrostat, 35 switched to placebo, one not randomised).
cards.result: At week 34, more patients maintained a complete response (mean 24-hour urinary free cortisol at or below the upper limit of normal, without up-titration) on osilodrostat than on placebo: 31 (86%) versus ten (29%) (odds ratio 13.7, 95% confidence interval 3.7 to 53.4; p<0.0001 — a relative measure, printed with its absolute rates). At week 24, before withdrawal, 72 (53%; 43.9 to 61.1) of all 137 patients had a complete response without up-titration after week 12. The most common adverse events were nausea (42%), headache (34%), fatigue (28%) and adrenal insufficiency (28%); hypocortisolism occurred in 70 (51%) patients and adrenal-hormone-precursor-related events in 58 (42%). One patient died after the core study phase, unrelated to study drug.
cards.watchOut: A withdrawal design proves the drug was holding cortisol down in people who had already responded and tolerated it — it does not estimate the response rate in an unselected new patient (that figure is the 53% complete response at week 24 in the open-label phase). Hypocortisolism in half of treated patients is the mechanism overshooting, and needs monitoring.
cards.source: Pivonello R et al. Efficacy and safety of osilodrostat in patients with Cushing's disease (LINC 3): a multicentre phase III study with a double-blind, randomised withdrawal phase. cards.headline: Synthesis: cortisol can be normalised medically — pasireotide in a minority at a metabolic price, osilodrostat with a strong withdrawal proof and a hypocortisolism price
cards.summary: Cortisol can be normalised medically — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: pasireotide phase 2 (29 analysed) and phase 3 (162 randomised), and LINC-3 (137 enrolled; 71 randomised in withdrawal).
cards.result: The two programmes answer the shelf's question with different proof shapes. Pasireotide: cortisol fell in most patients (76% reduced at 15 days in phase 2; median ~50% fall in phase 3) but normalised in a minority (17% phase 2; 15–26% by dose in phase 3), with hyperglycaemia-related events in 118 of 162 phase 3 patients. Osilodrostat: 53% of all enrolled patients reached complete response by week 24, and withdrawal randomised the responders to an 86% versus 29% maintenance split (relative odds 13.7) — strong evidence the drug holds cortisol down, in a population pre-selected for response. Cross-referenced, not duplicated: pasireotide for acromegaly is Shelf #745.
cards.watchOut: Neither programme compares against surgery, the definitive therapy for Cushing's disease, and neither was designed around mortality or the long-term complications of hypercortisolism; both drugs trade one hormone problem for a managed other (hyperglycaemia; hypocortisolism).
cards.source: Synthesis of Boscaro M et al. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2009;94(1):115-22. PMID: 18957506; Colao A et al. N Engl J Med. 2012;366(10):914-24. PMID: 22397653; Pivonello R et al. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2020;8(9):748-761. PMID: 32730798. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Starting buprenorphine in the emergency department (D'Onofrio)
shelves.question: Does ED-initiated buprenorphine with primary-care referral engage more patients in addiction treatment at 30 days than referral or brief intervention alone?
shelves.mesh: Buprenorphine/therapeutic use · Emergency Service, Hospital · HIV Infections/epidemiology · Health Services/statistics & numerical data · Hospitals, Teaching · Hospitals, Urban · Naloxone/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: In the single randomised trial (329 ED patients), ED-initiated buprenorphine with 10 weeks of primary-care follow-up engaged 78% of patients in addiction treatment at 30 days, vs 37% with referral alone and 45% with brief intervention — a large effect on a process outcome (treatment engagement), with no significant difference in opioid-negative urine tests (57.6% vs 53.8% and 42.9%). The trial's own authors state the findings require replication in other centres, and a single trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: D'Onofrio 2015: ED-initiated buprenorphine engaged 78% in treatment at 30 days vs 37% (referral) and 45% (brief intervention)
cards.summary: D'Onofrio 2015: ED-initiated buprenorphine engaged 78% in treatment at 30 days vs 37% (referral) and 45% (brief intervention).
cards.people: 329 opioid-dependent patients treated at one urban teaching hospital emergency department (2009–2013), randomised to referral (104), screening/brief intervention with facilitated referral (111), or ED-initiated buprenorphine/naloxone with referral to primary care for 10-week follow-up (114). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Engagement in addiction treatment on day 30 (primary outcome): 78% (89 of 114; 95% CI 70% to 85%) with buprenorphine vs 37% (38 of 102; 28% to 47%) with referral and 45% (50 of 111; 36% to 54%) with brief intervention (P<0.001). Self-reported illicit opioid use fell from 5.4 days per week to 0.9 days with buprenorphine vs 5.4 to 2.3 days (referral) and 5.6 to 2.4 days (brief intervention). Opioid-negative urine rates did NOT differ significantly (57.6% buprenorphine, 53.8% referral, 42.9% brief intervention; P=0.17), nor did HIV risk (P=0.66). Inpatient addiction-treatment use was lower with buprenorphine (11% vs 37% and 35%; P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: Single centre and single trial, with a process primary outcome: engagement is not abstinence, and the urine-test result was null. The authors themselves state the findings require replication in other centres before widespread adoption.
cards.source: D'Onofrio G et al. Emergency department-initiated buprenorphine/naloxone treatment for opioid dependence: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2015;313(16):1636-1644. PMID: 25919527. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00913770 (from the record's databank fields).

cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: D'Onofrio 2015 (329 ED patients with opioid dependence).

shelves.title: Injectable opioid agonist treatment: hydromorphone and diacetylmorphine (SALOME, NAOMI)
shelves.question: For people with severe opioid use disorder unresponsive to oral therapy, is injectable hydromorphone non-inferior to injectable diacetylmorphine (SALOME) — and does diacetylmorphine beat oral methadone (NAOMI)?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Cocaine-Related Disorders/epidemiology · Drug Overdose · Heroin/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Heroin Dependence/drug therapy,epidemiology · Hydromorphone/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Illicit Drugs
shelves.balance: LIKELY: In treatment-refractory, long-term injecting opioid use disorder, supervised injectable diacetylmorphine beat oral methadone on retention in treatment (87.8% vs 54.1%; relative rate ratio 1.62) and on reduction in illicit-drug use or illegal activity (67.0% vs 47.7%) in NAOMI, and injectable hydromorphone was non-inferior to diacetylmorphine on street-heroin use in the double-blind SALOME trial — at the cost of overdose and seizure harms concentrated in the diacetylmorphine arms, which is why both programmes are supervised-injection programmes, not prescriptions.

cards.headline: NAOMI 2009: injectable diacetylmorphine retained 87.8% in treatment vs 54.1% on oral methadone
cards.summary: NAOMI 2009: injectable diacetylmorphine retained 87.8% in treatment vs 54.1% on oral methadone.
cards.people: 226 long-term users of injectable heroin in Canada who had not benefited from at least two previous treatment attempts (including at least one methadone treatment), randomised to oral methadone (111) or injectable diacetylmorphine (115); primary outcomes assessed at 12 months in 95.2% of participants. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Retention in addiction treatment was 87.8% with diacetylmorphine vs 54.1% with methadone (relative rate ratio for retention 1.62, 95% CI 1.35 to 1.95; P<0.001). The reduction in rates of illicit-drug use or other illegal activity was 67.0% vs 47.7% (relative rate ratio 1.40, 1.11 to 1.77; P=0.004) — both rate ratios are relative measures, so the absolute percentages are printed beside them. The most common serious adverse events with diacetylmorphine injections were overdoses (in 10 patients) and seizures (in 6 patients).
cards.watchOut: Open-label, in patients who had already failed methadone at least once — the comparison is rescue therapy in a refractory population, not first-line treatment, and delivery requires settings where prompt medical intervention is available, as the authors state.
cards.source: Oviedo-Joekes E et al. Diacetylmorphine versus methadone for the treatment of opioid addiction. N Engl J Med. 2009;361(8):777-786. PMID: 19692689. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00175357 (from the record's databank fields).

cards.headline: SALOME 2016: injectable hydromorphone was non-inferior to diacetylmorphine, with fewer related serious adverse events (5 vs 24)
cards.summary: SALOME 2016: injectable hydromorphone was non-inferior to diacetylmorphine, with fewer related serious adverse events (5 vs 24).
cards.people: 202 long-term street opioid injectors in Vancouver, Canada, randomised to injectable hydromorphone (100) or diacetylmorphine (102), up to three times daily under supervision for 6 months; mean (SD) age 44.33 (9.63) years and 30.7% (62 of 202) women.
cards.result: Non-inferiority of hydromorphone was confirmed in the per-protocol analysis for days of street heroin use (mean difference −1.44 days; 90% CI −3.22 to 0.27; margin 4 days), although the margin was not excluded in the intention-to-treat analysis (−2.34; −4.14 to −0.52). Non-inferiority was confirmed for days of any street-acquired opioids in both analyses and for the proportion of urinalyses positive for street heroin markers. There were 29 serious adverse events considered related to the injection medication: 5 with hydromorphone vs 24 with diacetylmorphine (relative rate ratio 0.21, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.69); seizures and overdoses accounted for 25 of the 29.
cards.watchOut: The headline non-inferiority for street-heroin days rests on the per-protocol analysis — the intention-to-treat analysis did not exclude the margin — and both arms are supervised injectable treatments for a narrow, refractory population.

cards.headline: Synthesis: diacetylmorphine beats methadone in refractory users; hydromorphone is its non-inferior stand-in — LIKELY
cards.summary: Diacetylmorphine beats methadone in refractory users; hydromorphone is its non-inferior stand-in — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: NAOMI (226 patients, Canada) and SALOME (202 patients, Vancouver).
cards.result: NAOMI establishes the class against oral methadone in treatment-refractory injectors (retention 87.8% vs 54.1%); SALOME establishes hydromorphone as a non-inferior alternative where diacetylmorphine is unavailable or contraindicated, with fewer related serious adverse events (5 vs 24). Both trials are Canadian supervised-injection programmes; generalisability runs to similarly supervised settings only.

cards.summary: CAM2038 2018: weekly/monthly depot buprenorphine non-inferior to daily sublingual buprenorphine–naloxone.
cards.type: Outpatient, double-blind, double-dummy randomised non-inferiority trial
cards.people: 428 treatment-seeking adults with moderate-to-severe opioid use disorder at 35 US sites, randomised to weekly (phase 1) then monthly (phase 2) subcutaneous depot buprenorphine with daily sublingual placebo (213) or daily sublingual buprenorphine–naloxone with matched placebo injections (215); 263 men (61.4%) and 165 women (38.6%); mean (SD) age 38.4 (11.0) years.

shelves.title: Gabapentin for alcohol use disorder
shelves.question: Does gabapentin increase abstinence and reduce heavy drinking versus placebo — and does the enacarbil prodrug formulation replicate it?
shelves.mesh: Alcohol Abstinence · Alcoholism/drug therapy · Amines/therapeutic use · Central Nervous System Depressants/adverse effects · Cyclohexanecarboxylic Acids/therapeutic use · Ethanol/adverse effects · GABA Modulators/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — immediate-release gabapentin: two single-programme placebo-controlled trials are positive, with a dose-response in Mason 2014 (abstinence 17.0% at 1800 mg/day vs 4.1% on placebo; no heavy drinking 44.7% vs 22.5%) and, in Anton 2020, benefit concentrated in patients with more alcohol-withdrawal symptoms (no heavy drinking 27% vs 9% overall). POSSIBLE the null — the enacarbil prodrug: the one large multisite trial of gabapentin enacarbil XR 1200 mg/day (Falk 2019, 346 patients) found no benefit on any drinking outcome (no heavy drinking days 28.3% vs 21.5%, p=0.157), with lower gabapentin exposure than the positive immediate-release trials. Topic-file correction: the enacarbil trial is Falk 2019, not Anton 2020 — Anton 2020 tested immediate-release gabapentin itself.

cards.headline: Mason 2014: gabapentin dose-dependently raised abstinence (17.0% at 1800 mg vs 4.1% placebo) and no-heavy-drinking rates (44.7% vs 22.5%)
cards.summary: Mason 2014: gabapentin dose-dependently raised abstinence (17.0% at 1800 mg vs 4.1% placebo) and no-heavy-drinking rates (44.7% vs 22.5%).
cards.people: 150 men and women over 18 years with current alcohol dependence at a single-site outpatient clinical research facility, randomised to gabapentin 0 (placebo), 900 mg, or 1800 mg/day with manual-guided counselling. The abstract does not state mean age.

No heavy drinking: 22.5% (13.6% to 37.2%), 29.6% (19.1% to 42.8%) and 44.7% (31.4% to 58.8%) respectively (P=0.02; NNT 5 for 1800 mg). Mood, sleep and craving measures showed similar linear dose effects. There were no serious drug-related adverse events; 9 of 150 participants terminated for adverse events and 85 of 150 completed the study, without differences among groups.
cards.watchOut: Single site, 150 patients, 57% completion: a positive dose-ranging trial of this size is exactly the profile that later multisite trials often shrink — see the enacarbil card below for the formulation caveat.

cards.headline: Anton 2020: gabapentin beat placebo overall (no heavy drinking 27% vs 9%) — with the effect concentrated in high-withdrawal-symptom patients
cards.summary: Anton 2020: gabapentin beat placebo overall (no heavy drinking 27% vs 9%) — with the effect concentrated in high-withdrawal-symptom patients.
cards.people: 96 treatment-seeking individuals meeting DSM-5 criteria for alcohol use disorder who also met recent alcohol-withdrawal criteria, randomised after 3 abstinent days to gabapentin up to 1200 mg/day or placebo with nine medical-management visits; 90 were evaluable (44 gabapentin, 46 placebo); mean (SD) age 49.6 (10.1) years, 69 men (77%), 85 white (94%); participants averaged 83% baseline heavy-drinking days.
cards.result: No heavy drinking days: 12 of 44 (27%) on gabapentin vs 4 of 46 (9%) on placebo (difference 18.6%, 95% CI 3.1 to 34.1; P=0.02; NNT 5.4). cards.summary: Falk 2019: gabapentin enacarbil XR was null across every drinking outcome in a 346-patient multisite trial.

shelves.title: Yoga for chronic low back pain (Saper, Sherman)
shelves.question: Is a structured yoga programme non-inferior to physical therapy (Saper) or superior to education (Sherman) for chronic low back pain?
shelves.mesh: Chronic Pain/ethnology,therapy · Comparative Effectiveness Research · Low Back Pain/ethnology,therapy · Patient Compliance · Patient Education as Topic · Physical Therapy Modalities/adverse effects · Poverty
shelves.balance: LIKELY: A structured yoga programme was non-inferior to physical therapy for function and pain at 12 weeks in Saper 2017 (320 adults), and superior to a self-care book in Sherman 2011 (function mean difference −2.5 points at 12 weeks, maintained at 26 weeks) — but NOT superior to conventional stretching classes in Sherman, which bounds the claim: yoga works about as well as other structured exercise-based care, not better than all of it. Behavioural interventions are unblindable by nature; both trials are labelled as such.

cards.headline: Saper 2017: yoga was non-inferior to physical therapy for function and pain in chronic low back pain
cards.summary: Saper 2017: yoga was non-inferior to physical therapy for function and pain in chronic low back pain.
cards.type: 12-week, single-blind, three-group randomised non-inferiority trial with a 40-week maintenance phase (unblindable intervention)
cards.people: 320 predominantly low-income, racially diverse adults with nonspecific chronic low back pain at an academic safety-net hospital and seven affiliated community health centres, randomised to 12 weekly yoga classes, 15 physical-therapy visits, or an educational book and newsletters. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Yoga was non-inferior to physical therapy on both primary outcomes at 12 weeks: one-sided 95% lower confidence limits were 0.83 for back-related function (Roland Morris Disability Questionnaire; prespecified margin 1.5) and 0.97 for pain (11-point scale; margin 1.0). Yoga was not superior to education for either outcome. Yoga and physical-therapy participants were 21 and 22 percentage points less likely than education participants to use pain medication at 12 weeks, and improvements were maintained at 1 year. Adverse events were mostly mild, self-limited joint and back pain and did not differ between yoga and physical therapy.
cards.watchOut: Participants could not be blinded, and the physical-therapy group had disproportionate loss to follow-up — both stated by the authors; non-inferiority here means 'about as good as PT', not 'better than doing nothing structured'.
cards.source: Saper RB et al. Yoga, Physical Therapy, or Education for Chronic Low Back Pain: A Randomized Noninferiority Trial. Ann Intern Med. 2017;167(2):85-94. PMID: 28631003. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01343927 (from the record's databank fields).

shelves.title: Spinal manipulation for low back pain (UK BEAM and the chiropractic-care trials)
shelves.question: Does adding spinal manipulation to GP care (UK BEAM) or chiropractic care to usual medical care improve low-back-pain outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Back Pain/rehabilitation · Exercise Therapy/adverse effects,methods · Manipulation, Spinal/adverse effects,methods · Private Sector · Public Sector · Chiropractic/methods · Combined Modality Therapy/methods
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Adding manipulation-based care to usual care produced small-to-moderate improvements in two large pragmatic trials — UK BEAM (manipulation followed by exercise improved disability scores by 1.9 points more than GP best care at 3 months and 1.3 at 12 months; manipulation alone 1.6 and 1.0) and Goertz 2018 in US service members (pain −1.1 points and disability −2.2 points at 6 weeks with chiropractic care added). The effects are real but small on 24-point disability scales, the interventions are unblindable by nature, and satisfaction effects (Goertz +2.5 points) run larger than pain effects — hence POSSIBLE, not LIKELY.

cards.headline: UK BEAM 2004: manipulation plus exercise improved disability by 1.9 points over GP best care at 3 months, 1.3 at 12 months
cards.summary: UK BEAM 2004: manipulation plus exercise improved disability by 1.9 points over GP best care at 3 months, 1.3 at 12 months.
cards.type: Pragmatic randomised trial with factorial design (unblindable intervention)
cards.people: 1,334 patients consulting about low back pain at 181 general practices and 63 community settings across the United Kingdom, randomised to GP 'best care' alone or with exercise classes, spinal manipulation (NHS or private premises), or manipulation followed by exercise. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: All groups improved over time. Versus best care, additional improvement in Roland Morris disability questionnaire scores was: exercise +1.4 points at 3 months (95% CI 0.6 to 2.1) but not significant at 12 months; manipulation +1.6 (0.8 to 2.3) at 3 months and +1.0 (0.2 to 1.8) at 12 months; manipulation followed by exercise +1.9 (1.2 to 2.6) at 3 months and +1.3 (0.5 to 2.1) at 12 months. There was no difference between manipulation in NHS and private premises, and no serious adverse events occurred.
cards.watchOut: Pragmatic and unblinded, against a GP-care comparator, with gains of 1–2 points on a disability questionnaire — the trial's own characterisation is 'moderate benefit at three months, small benefit at 12 months' for the combined package.
cards.source: UK BEAM Trial Team. United Kingdom back pain exercise and manipulation (UK BEAM) randomised trial: effectiveness of physical treatments for back pain in primary care. BMJ. 2004;329(7479):1377. PMID: 15556955. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this trial predates routine trial registration.

cards.headline: Goertz 2018: adding chiropractic care to usual medical care improved pain (−1.1) and disability (−2.2) at 6 weeks in service members
cards.summary: Goertz 2018: adding chiropractic care to usual medical care improved pain (−1.1) and disability (−2.2) at 6 weeks in service members.
cards.type: Three-site pragmatic comparative-effectiveness clinical trial using adaptive allocation (unblindable intervention)
cards.people: 750 active-duty US service members aged 18–50 years with musculoskeletal low back pain at two large military medical centres and one smaller military hospital; mean (SD) age 30.9 (8.7) years, 175 (23.3%) female, 243 (32.4%) nonwhite; intervention period 6 weeks, with usual medical care (self-care, medications, physical therapy, pain clinic referral) with or without chiropractic care (spinal manipulative therapy plus adjunct procedures).
cards.result: At 6 weeks, adjusted mean differences favoured usual care plus chiropractic care over usual care alone: pain intensity −1.1 points (95% CI −1.4 to −0.7; 0–10 scale), disability −2.2 points (−3.1 to −1.2; Roland Morris 0–24), and satisfaction +2.5 points (2.1 to 2.8). Perceived improvement and self-reported pain-medication use also favoured the chiropractic group (odds ratio 0.73, 0.54 to 0.97, for medication use, as reported). Statistically significant site × time × group interactions were found in all models. No serious related adverse events were reported.
cards.watchOut: Young, active-duty military population over 6 weeks, unblinded, with significant site interactions — transportability to civilian chronic low back pain is limited, and the satisfaction gain (+2.5) was more than double the pain gain (−1.1).
cards.source: Goertz CM et al. Effect of Usual Medical Care Plus Chiropractic Care vs Usual Medical Care Alone on Pain and Disability Among US Service Members With Low Back Pain: A Comparative Effectiveness Clinical Trial. JAMA Netw Open. 2018;1(1):e180105. PMID: 30646047. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01692275 (from the record's databank fields).

cards.headline: Synthesis: small, consistent, short-horizon gains from adding manipulation-based care — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Small, consistent, short-horizon gains from adding manipulation-based care — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: UK BEAM (1,334 primary-care patients) and Goertz 2018 (750 service members).
cards.result: Both trials find the same order of effect for adding manipulation/chiropractic care to usual care: about 1 point on a 0–10 pain scale and 1–2 points on a 0–24 disability scale, largest early (3 months in BEAM; 6 weeks in Goertz) and attenuating thereafter (BEAM: 1.3 points at 12 months for the combined package). Neither trial blinded participants, and neither isolates manipulation from the exercise and attention bundled with it.
cards.watchOut: Do not present these as manipulation-specific effects: BEAM's biggest arm combined manipulation WITH exercise, and Goertz's chiropractic package included exercise and other manual therapies.

shelves.title: Muscle relaxants for acute low back pain: the null shelf
shelves.question: Do non-benzodiazepine muscle relaxants add anything to NSAIDs in acute low back pain — the pooled RCT answer (Cashin) and the ED head-to-heads (Friedman)?
shelves.mesh: Benzodiazepines/therapeutic use · Low Back Pain/diagnosis,drug therapy,etiology · Muscle Relaxants, Central/therapeutic use · Parasympatholytics/therapeutic use · Acetaminophen/therapeutic use · Acute Disease · Amitriptyline/analogs & derivatives,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): Adding a muscle relaxant to an NSAID does not produce a clinically important benefit in acute low back pain. The Cashin 2021 synthesis of 31 trials (6,505 participants) found very-low-certainty evidence of a small, not clinically important pain reduction (−7.7 points on a 0–100 scale at ≤2 weeks), no disability reduction, and a possible increase in adverse events (relative risk 1.6); the two Friedman ED trials then found cyclobenzaprine and diazepam each added nothing to naproxen on function at 1 week (between-group differences 0.3 and 0 points). A concordant null across a 31-trial synthesis and two direct trials carries LIKELY under the large-null rule.

cards.headline: Cashin 2021: across 31 trials, non-benzodiazepine antispasmodics gave a small, not clinically important pain reduction and may increase adverse events
cards.summary: Cashin 2021: across 31 trials, non-benzodiazepine antispasmodics gave a small, not clinically important pain reduction and may increase adverse events.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
cards.people: 49 trials included in the review, of which 31 trials sampling 6,505 participants were quantitatively analysed; adults (≥18 years) with non-specific low back pain, comparing muscle relaxants with placebo, usual care, waiting list, or no treatment; searches from inception to 23 February 2021. The abstract does not state a pooled mean age.
cards.result: For acute low back pain, very low certainty evidence showed non-benzodiazepine antispasmodics were associated with a reduction in pain intensity at ≤2 weeks vs control (mean difference −7.7 points on a 0–100 scale, 95% CI −12.1 to −3.3) but NOT a reduction in disability (−3.3, −7.3 to 0.7). Low and very low certainty evidence showed antispasmodics might increase the risk of an adverse event (relative risk 1.6, 1.2 to 2.0 — a relative measure) and might have little to no effect on acceptability (0.8, 0.6 to 1.1). The authors conclude considerable uncertainty exists and that large, high-quality placebo-controlled trials are urgently needed; most included trials were at high risk of bias. The adverse-event relative risk of 1.6 sits inside the library's 0.5–2.0 caution band on its own terms.
cards.watchOut: The small pooled pain difference comes with very low certainty — the synthesis is evidence of no clinically important effect plus genuine uncertainty, not proof of exact zero; other relaxant classes and chronic durations had few trials.
cards.source: Cashin AG et al. Efficacy, acceptability, and safety of muscle relaxants for adults with non-specific low back pain: systematic review and meta-analysis. BMJ. 2021;374:n1446. PMID: 34233900. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a systematic review; its PROSPERO registration (CRD42019126820) is stated in the record's abstract.

cards.headline: Friedman 2015: adding cyclobenzaprine (or oxycodone/acetaminophen) to naproxen improved function by 0.3 points more than naproxen alone — nothing
cards.summary: Friedman 2015: adding cyclobenzaprine (or oxycodone/acetaminophen) to naproxen improved function by 0.3 points more than naproxen alone — nothing.
cards.people: 323 ED patients with nontraumatic, nonradicular acute low back pain of ≤2 weeks' duration and Roland-Morris Disability Questionnaire (RMDQ) score >5 at one urban ED in the Bronx, New York, randomised to naproxen plus placebo (107), cyclobenzaprine 5 mg (108), or oxycodone/acetaminophen (108) for 10 days, with a standardised education session. Demographic characteristics were comparable among groups; the abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: All groups improved substantially on naproxen (mean RMDQ improvement at 1 week: 9.8 placebo, 10.1 cyclobenzaprine, 11.1 oxycodone/acetaminophen, from baseline medians of ~19–20). Between-group differences in mean RMDQ improvement: cyclobenzaprine vs placebo 0.3 points (98.3% CI −2.6 to 3.2; P=0.77); oxycodone/acetaminophen vs placebo 1.3 (−1.5 to 4.1; P=0.28). The authors conclude the findings do not support use of these additional medications in this setting.
cards.watchOut: One ED, one NSAID backbone, 1-week primary outcome: the trial rules out a meaningful add-on effect in ED-managed acute low back pain, not every relaxant in every setting.
cards.source: Friedman BW et al. Naproxen With Cyclobenzaprine, Oxycodone/Acetaminophen, or Placebo for Treating Acute Low Back Pain: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2015;314(15):1572-1580. PMID: 26501533. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01587274 (from the record's databank fields).

cards.headline: Friedman 2017: diazepam added to naproxen improved disability by exactly the same 11 points as placebo
cards.summary: Friedman 2017: diazepam added to naproxen improved disability by exactly the same 11 points as placebo.
cards.people: 114 ED patients with acute, nontraumatic, nonradicular low back pain of ≤2 weeks' duration and RMDQ score >5 in an urban health care system, randomised to a 1-week course of naproxen plus diazepam 5 mg or naproxen plus identical placebo; 112 (98%) provided 1-week outcome data; baseline characteristics did not differ substantially between groups. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Mean RMDQ improvement at 1 week was 11 points in both groups (naproxen+diazepam 11, 95% CI 9 to 13; naproxen+placebo 11, 8 to 13). At 1 week, 18 of 57 diazepam patients (32%) reported moderate or severe pain vs 12 of 55 placebo patients (22%); at 3 months, 6 of 50 (12%) vs 5 of 53 as reported. The trial was powered around a 5-point between-group RMDQ difference as the threshold for clinical significance; the observed difference was 0.
cards.watchOut: 114 patients and a benzodiazepine (not a non-benzodiazepine antispasmodic): it closes the 'benzodiazepines might differ' escape hatch for this setting rather than re-testing the Cashin class question.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a 31-trial synthesis and two direct ED trials agree — LIKELY the null for add-on relaxants
cards.summary: A 31-trial synthesis and two direct ED trials agree — LIKELY the null for add-on relaxants.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Cashin 2021 (31 trials, 6,505 participants), Friedman 2015 (323 ED patients) and Friedman 2017 (114 ED patients).
cards.result: Every layer of the evidence points the same way: pooled, muscle relaxants buy at most −7.7 points of pain on a 0–100 scale at very low certainty with no disability benefit and a possible adverse-event increase (relative risk 1.6); head-to-head against an NSAID alone, cyclobenzaprine adds 0.3 RMDQ points and diazepam adds 0. The shelf's claim is narrow — no clinically important ADD-ON benefit in acute low back pain — and on that claim the null is LIKELY.
cards.watchOut: Chronic low back pain and spasticity indications are different questions with thin trial bases (Cashin); do not export this null to them.

shelves.title: Ketamine infusions for chronic pain and complex regional pain
shelves.question: Do ketamine infusions produce durable relief in CRPS and other chronic pain states beyond the infusion window (the Schwartzman and Sigtermans RCTs)?
shelves.mesh: Analgesics/administration & dosage · Analysis of Variance · Complex Regional Pain Syndromes/drug therapy · Drug Administration Schedule · Injections, Intravenous/methods · Ketamine/administration & dosage · Outpatients
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two small randomised placebo-controlled trials of multi-day ketamine infusion in complex regional pain syndrome type 1 found significant pain relief during and shortly after infusion — in Sigtermans 2009, pain scores over 12 weeks were significantly lower with ketamine (lowest at week 1: 2.68 vs 5.45), but the difference had lost significance by week 12 (P=0.07) and there was NO functional improvement; Schwartzman 2009 likewise reported significant reductions in many pain parameters over 3 months of follow-up. Psychomimetic side effects were common (76% vs 18% in Sigtermans). Durability beyond the infusion window is the unproven half of the claim, which caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Schwartzman 2009: 10 days of outpatient ketamine infusion significantly reduced many CRPS pain parameters vs placebo
cards.summary: Schwartzman 2009: 10 days of outpatient ketamine infusion significantly reduced many CRPS pain parameters vs placebo — an abstract that reports significance without effect sizes.
cards.people: Patients with complex regional pain syndrome, randomised to intravenous ketamine or placebo infused 4 hours daily for 10 days (maximum ketamine rate 0.35 mg/kg/h, not exceeding 25 mg/h), with clonidine and midazolam (versed) given to both groups; evaluated for at least 2 weeks before treatment and for 3 months after. The abstract does not state the number randomised, mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Intravenous ketamine resulted in statistically significant (p<0.05) reductions in many pain parameters, while the placebo group showed no treatment effect in any parameter. The authors conclude the results warrant a larger randomised placebo-controlled trial using higher doses and longer follow-up. (The record's abstract reports significance qualitatively, without effect sizes — none are printed here, because a figure that is not in the fetched abstract does not go on a card.)
cards.watchOut: No sample size or effect sizes in the abstract, both groups received clonidine and midazolam alongside the infusion, and the authors themselves call for a larger trial: this is a signal-confirming pilot-grade RCT, not a dosing guide.
cards.source: Schwartzman RJ et al. Outpatient intravenous ketamine for the treatment of complex regional pain syndrome: a double-blind placebo controlled study. Pain. 2009;147(1-3):107-115. PMID: 19783371. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this trial predates routine registry reporting for this journal/era.

cards.headline: Sigtermans 2009: ketamine infusion relieved CRPS-1 pain for weeks, not durably — significance lost by week 12, no functional gain
cards.summary: Sigtermans 2009: ketamine infusion relieved CRPS-1 pain for weeks, not durably — significance lost by week 12, no functional gain.
cards.people: 60 patients with complex regional pain syndrome type 1 (48 women) with severe pain and median (range) disease duration 7.4 (0.1–31.9) years, randomised to a 4.2-day intravenous infusion of low-dose S(+)-ketamine (30) or placebo (30) with dose tailored to effect and side effects; final ketamine dose 22.2 ± 2.0 mg/h per 70 kg. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Pain scores (0–10 numerical rating) over the 12-week study period were significantly lower with ketamine than placebo (P<0.001); the lowest pain score was at the end of week 1 (ketamine 2.68 ± 0.51 vs placebo 5.45 ± 0.48), and by week 12 the difference had lost significance (P=0.07). Treatment did not cause functional improvement. Mild-to-moderate psychomimetic side effects during infusion were much more common with ketamine (76% vs 18%, P<0.001) and were acceptable to most patients.
cards.watchOut: Sixty patients, one centre's infusion protocol, and a benefit that decays to non-significance by 12 weeks with no functional improvement: relief during the weeks after infusion is shown; durable disease modification is not.
cards.source: Sigtermans MJ et al. Ketamine produces effective and long-term pain relief in patients with Complex Regional Pain Syndrome Type 1. Pain. 2009;145(3):304-311. PMID: 19604642. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this trial predates routine registry reporting for this journal/era.

cards.headline: Synthesis: short-window relief is real in two small trials; durability is not shown — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Short-window relief is real in two small trials; durability is not shown — POSSIBLE. (Ketamine for depression is carded on its own shelf and not repeated here.)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Schwartzman 2009 (CRPS, 10-day outpatient infusion; n not stated in the abstract) and Sigtermans 2009 (60 CRPS-1 patients, 4.2-day inpatient infusion).
cards.result: Both trials beat placebo on pain in the infusion's aftermath, and the better-reported trial shows the effect waning (week 1: 2.68 vs 5.45; week 12: P=0.07) with no functional improvement and a 76% psychomimetic side-effect rate.
