shelves.title: Duloxetine for musculoskeletal pain: knee osteoarthritis and chronic low back pain
shelves.question: Does duloxetine reduce pain in knee osteoarthritis and chronic low back pain versus placebo (the Skljarevski and Chappell trial programmes) — and how large is the effect?
shelves.mesh: Chronic Disease · Diarrhea/chemically induced · Duloxetine Hydrochloride · Fatigue/chemically induced · Low Back Pain/drug therapy,physiopathology · Nausea/chemically induced · Pain Measurement
shelves.balance: LIKELY (a small effect): Duloxetine 60 mg daily beat placebo on 24-hour average pain in randomised trials in both target conditions — chronic low back pain (least-squares mean change −2.32 vs −1.50 at week 13, a difference of about 0.8 points on a 0–10 scale) and osteoarthritis pain (−2.23 vs −1.73, difference −0.50 points) — with significantly more discontinuations for adverse events in the back-pain trial (13.9% vs 5.8%). The stamp is LIKELY that the effect exists; its size is small, and both halves of that sentence belong on the shelf face. (Programme note: the CLBP anchor is first-authored by Skljarevski; the OA programme's Western pivotal trials could not be pinned to a single verified record in this pass, so the OA card uses the programme's verified phase 3 trial in Chinese patients — disclosed in summary.md.)

cards.headline: Skljarevski 2010: duloxetine reduced chronic low back pain more than placebo (−2.32 vs −1.50 on the BPI 24-hour average pain)
cards.summary: Skljarevski 2010: duloxetine reduced chronic low back pain more than placebo (−2.32 vs −1.50 on the BPI 24-hour average pain).
cards.people: Adult, non-depressed patients with non-neuropathic chronic low back pain and a weekly mean 24-hour average pain score ≥4 (0–10 scale), treated with duloxetine (60 mg once daily for 7 weeks, increased to 120 mg at week 7 in patients with <30% pain reduction) or placebo. The abstract does not state the number randomised, mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Duloxetine produced a significantly greater reduction in Brief Pain Inventory 24-hour average pain from baseline to endpoint than placebo (least-squares mean change −2.32 vs −1.50; P=0.004 at week 13). The duloxetine group also improved significantly more on Patient's Global Impressions of Improvement, Roland-Morris Disability Questionnaire-24, BPI-Severity, BPI-Interference, and weekly diary pain scores. Significantly more duloxetine patients discontinued because of adverse events (13.9% vs 5.8%; P=0.047); the most common treatment-emergent adverse events were nausea, dry mouth, fatigue, diarrhoea, hyperhidrosis, dizziness and constipation.
cards.watchOut: The between-group pain difference is about 0.8 points on a 0–10 scale, bought with more than double the adverse-event discontinuation rate; the dose-escalation design means the result is for a 60→120 mg strategy, not a fixed dose.
cards.source: Skljarevski V et al. Efficacy and safety of duloxetine in patients with chronic low back pain. Spine. 2010;35(13):E578-E585. PMID: 20461028. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00424593 (from the record's databank fields).

cards.headline: Wang 2017: duloxetine beat placebo in osteoarthritis pain by half a point (−2.23 vs −1.73) in a phase 3 trial
cards.summary: Wang 2017: duloxetine beat placebo in osteoarthritis pain by half a point (−2.23 vs −1.73) in a phase 3 trial.
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 13 weeks
cards.people: 407 Chinese patients aged at least 40 years meeting American College of Rheumatology clinical and radiographic criteria for osteoarthritis of the knee or hip, randomised to duloxetine 60 mg once daily (205) or placebo (202) at 17 study centres; 76.4% were female and mean age was 60.5 years; 81.0% of the duloxetine group and 87.1% of the placebo group completed the 13 weeks.
cards.result: Duloxetine produced significantly greater pain reduction than placebo on the BPI 24-hour Average Pain rating (least-squares mean change −2.23 vs −1.73; difference −0.50, 95% CI −0.80 to −0.20; P=0.001). Discontinuations due to adverse events were 9.0% on duloxetine vs 4.5% on placebo (P=0.109). The safety profile was consistent with previous duloxetine trials.
cards.watchOut: A half-point advantage on a 0–10 pain scale in one population (Chinese patients with knee or hip OA): statistically solid, clinically small — the shelf's claim is the effect's existence and size together, not either alone.
cards.source: Wang G et al. Efficacy and safety of duloxetine in Chinese patients with chronic pain due to osteoarthritis: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study. Osteoarthritis Cartilage. 2017;25(6):832-838. PMID: 28043937. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01931475 (from the record's databank fields).

cards.summary: A consistent, small analgesic effect across two musculoskeletal conditions — LIKELY, and small. (Duloxetine for neuropathic pain is carded separately on Shelf #695.)

cards.result: Across conditions the placebo-subtracted pain benefit is 0.5–0.8 points on a 0–10 scale, with adverse-event discontinuations running at roughly double the placebo rate in the back-pain trial (13.9% vs 5.8%). shelves.title: Psychological therapies for chronic pain: CBT and ACT (Cochrane)
shelves.question: How much do CBT and acceptance-and-commitment therapy improve pain, disability, and mood in chronic pain — the Cochrane synthesis of the RCT base?
shelves.mesh: Acceptance and Commitment Therapy · Affect · Behavior Therapy/methods · Bias · Chronic Pain/psychology,therapy · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy/methods · Confidence Intervals
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY — CBT: across 59 randomised trials in the 2020 Cochrane synthesis (75 trials, 9,401 participants in total), CBT produced small benefits vs treatment-as-usual for pain (standardised mean difference −0.22), disability (−0.32) and distress (−0.34), and very small benefits vs active control (pain −0.09; disability −0.12; distress −0.09), on mostly moderate-quality evidence. MAYBE (weak evidence) — ACT and behavioural therapy: the ACT base is five trials (443 participants) and the behavioural-therapy base eight trials (647), with estimates rated very low quality throughout — the review's own caution is that these estimates are uncertain and could easily be overturned. Adverse events were inadequately recorded across the field.

cards.headline: Williams 2020 (Cochrane): CBT gives small benefits in chronic pain (SMD −0.22 vs TAU; −0.09 vs active control); ACT and BT evidence is very low quality
cards.summary: Williams 2020 (Cochrane): CBT gives small benefits in chronic pain (SMD −0.22 vs TAU; −0.09 vs active control); ACT and BT evidence is very low quality.
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised controlled trials (2020 update)
cards.people: 75 randomised trials with 9,401 participants at treatment end (41 new studies, 6,255 participants, added to the 2012 version); adults with chronic non-cancer pain excluding headache and malignant disease — most had fibromyalgia, chronic low back pain, rheumatoid arthritis, or mixed chronic pain. CBT was analysed in 59 studies, behavioural therapy in 8 (647 participants), ACT in 5 (443 participants). The abstract does not state a pooled mean age.
cards.result: CBT vs active control at treatment end (moderate-quality evidence): pain standardised mean difference (SMD) −0.09 (95% CI −0.17 to −0.01; 3,235 participants, 23 studies), disability −0.12 (−0.20 to −0.04), distress −0.09 (−0.18 to −0.00). CBT vs treatment-as-usual/waiting list: pain SMD −0.22 (−0.33 to −0.10; 2,572 participants, 29 studies), disability −0.32 (−0.45 to −0.19; low-quality), distress −0.34 (−0.44 to −0.24); effects were largely maintained at 6–12-month follow-up vs TAU but not vs active control. Behavioural therapy showed no evidence of difference vs active control or TAU on very-low-to-moderate quality evidence. ACT showed no evidence of difference vs active control at treatment end (pain SMD −0.54, −1.20 to 0.11, very low quality) and inconsistent, very-low-quality results vs TAU. Adverse events were inadequately recorded and/or reported across studies; most risk-of-bias domains were high or unclear risk. Standardised mean differences are relative, standardised measures — no absolute rates exist for them, which is why this card reports the comparators and sample sizes beside every figure.
cards.watchOut: The CBT effects are small to very small, the follow-up benefit survives only against TAU (not against active control), and the review explicitly warns that very-low-quality estimates (all of ACT, most of BT) 'could be easily overturned' — that warning is the reason for the split stamp.
cards.source: Williams ACC et al. Psychological therapies for the management of chronic pain (excluding headache) in adults. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2020;8(8):CD007407. PMID: 32794606. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a systematic review, not a single trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: CBT is the supported therapy, with small effects; ACT and BT are unproven at trial standard — split stamp
cards.summary: CBT is the supported therapy, with small effects; ACT and BT are unproven at trial standard — split LIKELY / MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: Williams, Fisher & Eccleston 2020 Cochrane review (75 RCTs, 9,401 participants).
cards.result: This shelf is a synthesis shelf by design — the question is the size of a whole field's effect, and the Cochrane review is the field's census: CBT small but consistent (SMD −0.22 for pain vs TAU across 29 studies), ACT resting on 5 trials and 443 participants with very-low-quality estimates, behavioural therapy on 8 trials with no demonstrated difference. The built pain shelves are otherwise drug and procedure topics; no individual therapy trial is re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: An SMD of −0.09 to −0.22 is a small effect by any convention; the shelf must not be cited as showing large psychological-therapy benefits, and ACT's MAYBE (weak evidence) label must print in full wherever it appears.
cards.source: Synthesis of Williams ACC et al. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2020;8(8):CD007407. PMID: 32794606. Registry ID as on the individual card.

shelves.title: Treating insomnia to delay depression: digital CBT-I
shelves.question: In people with insomnia but no current depression, does digital CBT-I reduce depression symptoms and new depressive episodes over the following year — the SHUTi GoodNight Study, and Cheng's digital CBT-I prevention trial?
shelves.mesh: Depression/prevention & control · Internet · Self-Help Groups · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders/psychology · Antidepressive Agents/therapeutic use · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy/methods · Depression/epidemiology,psychology,therapy
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY — fewer depression symptoms · POSSIBLE — fewer new depressive episodes. Two randomised trials of fully automated digital CBT-I agree that treating insomnia lowers depression symptoms over the following 6–12 months (GoodNight/SHUTi: significantly lower PHQ-9 scores at 6 weeks and 6 months; Cheng: significantly lower depression severity at 1 year). The episode-prevention claim is thinner: GoodNight found no significant difference in major depressive disorder diagnoses at 6 months (9 vs 13 cases, p=0.32), while Cheng found the incidence of moderate-to-severe depression at 1 year was roughly halved in the subgroup with minimal-to-no baseline depression — a relative claim from one trial's subgroup. The two stamps are kept separate so the symptom result cannot smuggle the episode claim past the reader.

cards.headline: GoodNight 2016: online CBT-I (SHUTi) lowered depression symptoms at 6 months — but did not significantly reduce new major depression diagnoses (9 vs 13)
cards.summary: GoodNight (2016): online CBT-I (SHUTi) lowered depression symptoms at 6 months — but did not significantly reduce new major depression diagnoses.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial with attention-matched internet placebo control, 6 months
cards.people: 1149 internet users aged 18–64 years with insomnia and depression symptoms who did not meet criteria for major depressive disorder, randomly assigned to SHUTi (574), a 6-week online CBT-I programme, or HealthWatch (575), an attention-matched internet placebo programme; 581 (51%) completed the 6-week assessments and 504 (44%) completed 6-month follow-up.
cards.result: SHUTi significantly lowered depression symptoms on the PHQ-9 at 6 weeks and at 6 months versus HealthWatch (F[2, 640.1] = 37.2, p<0.0001). Major depressive disorder was diagnosed in 22 (4%) participants at 6 months — 9 in the SHUTi group and 13 in the HealthWatch group — with no superior effect of SHUTi versus HealthWatch (Fisher's exact test = 0.52; p=0.32). No adverse events were reported.
cards.watchOut: The trial's title promises prevention of depressive episodes; its own episode endpoint was null and tiny (22 events), with only 44% of participants completing 6-month follow-up. The solid finding is symptom reduction in people who already had symptoms — a treatment-adjacent result, not demonstrated prevention.
cards.source: Christensen H et al. Effectiveness of an online insomnia program (SHUTi) for prevention of depressive episodes (the GoodNight Study): a randomised controlled trial. Lancet Psychiatry. 2016;3(4):333-341. PMID: 26827250. Registry ID: ANZCTR ACTRN12611000121965, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Cheng 2019: digital CBT-I halved the incidence of moderate-to-severe depression at 1 year in patients with little or no baseline depression
cards.summary: Digital CBT-I trial (2019): halved the incidence of moderate-to-severe depression at 1 year in patients with little or no baseline depression.
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial with 1-year follow-up (Sleep to Prevent Evolving Affective Disorders study)
cards.people: Patients with DSM-5 insomnia disorder randomly assigned to digital CBT-I or online sleep education (attentional control); the follow-up sample included 358 patients in the digital CBT-I condition and 300 in the control condition; the abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: At 1-year follow-up, depression severity remained significantly lower in the digital CBT-I condition relative to control, and the number of individuals reporting no depression at 1 year was 51% higher in the digital CBT-I condition. In those with minimal to no depression at baseline, the incident rate of moderate-to-severe depression at 1-year follow-up was reduced by half in the digital CBT-I condition relative to control — a relative figure; the abstract does not print the absolute incidence rates. Insomnia response to treatment predicted incident depression at follow-up.
cards.watchOut: The headline prevention figure comes from the subgroup with minimal-to-no baseline depression and is reported only as a relative halving: without the absolute incidence rates (not in the abstract), the size of the benefit in people actually at risk cannot be judged from this record.
cards.source: Cheng P et al. Depression prevention via digital cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia: a randomized controlled trial. Sleep. 2019;42(10):zsz150. PMID: 31535688. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02988375, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: treat insomnia and mood symptoms follow; episode prevention is promising, not proven — split stamp
cards.summary: Treat insomnia and mood symptoms follow; delaying new episodes is promising, not proven — Split: LIKELY (symptoms) · POSSIBLE (episodes).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: GoodNight (1149 adults with insomnia and subthreshold symptoms) and Cheng 2019 (658 patients in the follow-up sample with DSM-5 insomnia disorder).
cards.result: Both trials show durable depression-symptom benefit from digital CBT-I (LIKELY). For new episodes, the evidence is one null diagnostic endpoint (GoodNight: 9 vs 13 major depression cases, p=0.32) and one positive relative result in a low-baseline-symptom subgroup (Cheng) — POSSIBLE. This shelf is about delaying and reducing depression via insomnia treatment: digital CBT-I for insomnia symptoms themselves lives on Shelf #437 and CBT-I versus sleeping pills on Shelf #499; neither is re-carded here. A 2025 trial of app-based CBT-I preventing major depression in youth with insomnia and subclinical depression was found by the currency sweep and is fenced here, not carded — a different population.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial enrolled people selected for high depression risk specifically, and neither was powered on diagnosed episodes: prevention programmes citing this shelf should cite the POSSIBLE stamp, not the LIKELY one.

shelves.title: Memantine in moderate-to-severe Alzheimer's disease, and whether to continue donepezil (DOMINO)
shelves.question: Does memantine improve cognition and function in moderate-to-severe Alzheimer's disease — and, once patients reach that stage, does continuing donepezil (with or without adding memantine) beat stopping it?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Alzheimer Disease/classification,drug therapy,psychology · Behavior · Cognition · Disease Progression · Excitatory Amino Acid Antagonists/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Memantine/adverse effects,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY — continuing donepezil · POSSIBLE — memantine. Continuing donepezil past the moderate-to-severe threshold beat stopping it on cognition by more than the trial's own minimum clinically important difference (DOMINO: SMMSE +1.9 points against a 1.4-point MCID), with a significant functional benefit beside it. Memantine's case is thinner: positive on function and global impression in Reisberg 2003, but in DOMINO its average gains (+1.2 SMMSE points; −1.5 BADLS points) fell below both of that trial's pre-set clinically important differences, and adding it to donepezil gave no extra benefit over donepezil alone. Both drugs' effects are symptomatic and modest; neither trial speaks to disease modification.

cards.headline: Reisberg 2003: memantine beat placebo on function and severe-stage cognition over 28 weeks, with the global-impression result borderline on the primary imputation
cards.summary: Reisberg 2003: memantine beat placebo on global impression and severe-stage function over 28 weeks, modestly.
cards.people: 252 patients with moderate-to-severe Alzheimer's disease at 32 US centres, randomised to memantine 20 mg daily or placebo; 67% women; mean age 76 years; 181 patients (72%) completed the study, with 71 premature discontinuations (42 on placebo, 29 on memantine).
cards.result: Patients on memantine had better outcomes than placebo on the Clinician's Interview-Based Impression of Change Plus Caregiver Input (P=0.06 with last observation carried forward; P=0.03 in observed cases), the Alzheimer's Disease Cooperative Study Activities of Daily Living Inventory for severe dementia (P=0.02 LOCF; P=0.003 observed cases), and the Severe Impairment Battery (P<0.001 LOCF; P=0.002 observed cases). Memantine was not associated with a significant frequency of adverse events. The abstract reports P values rather than scale-point differences, so no effect size in points is printed on this card.
cards.watchOut: A single trial, and its headline global outcome crosses significance only in the observed-cases analysis (P=0.06 on the pre-specified LOCF imputation) — the pattern behind this shelf's POSSIBLE grade for memantine rather than LIKELY.
cards.source: Reisberg B et al. Memantine in moderate-to-severe Alzheimer's disease. N Engl J Med. 2003 Apr 3;348(14):1333-1341. PMID: 12672860. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — a pre-registration-era trial (2003).

cards.headline: DOMINO 2012: continuing donepezil beat stopping it on cognition and function; memantine helped less, and the combination added nothing
cards.summary: DOMINO 2012: continuing donepezil beat stopping it — SMMSE higher by 1.9 points and daily-living impairment lower by 3.0 points.
cards.type: Double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled 2×2 factorial trial (52 weeks)
cards.people: 295 community-dwelling patients who had taken donepezil for at least 3 months and had moderate or severe Alzheimer's disease (Standardized Mini-Mental State Examination score 5 to 13), randomised to continue donepezil, discontinue donepezil, discontinue donepezil and start memantine, or continue donepezil and start memantine. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Continuing donepezil versus discontinuing it: SMMSE score higher by an average of 1.9 points (95% CI 1.3 to 2.5) and Bristol Activities of Daily Living Scale score lower (less impairment) by 3.0 points (1.8 to 4.3), P<0.001 for both — against pre-set minimum clinically important differences of 1.4 points (SMMSE) and 3.5 points (BADLS). Memantine versus memantine placebo: SMMSE higher by 1.2 points (0.6 to 1.8; P<0.001) and BADLS lower by 1.5 points (0.3 to 2.8; P=0.02) — both below those clinically important differences. The efficacy of each drug did not differ significantly in the presence or absence of the other, and there were no significant benefits of the combination over donepezil alone.
cards.watchOut: DOMINO answers a continuation question in patients already tolerating donepezil, not a starting question; and its memantine effects, though statistically significant, sit below the trial's own thresholds for clinical importance — read the two drugs' grades on this shelf separately.
cards.source: Howard R et al. Donepezil and memantine for moderate-to-severe Alzheimer's disease. N Engl J Med. 2012 Mar 8;366(10):893-903. PMID: 22397651. Registry ID: ISRCTN49545035, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: keep donepezil going at the severe stage; memantine is a modest, optional addition — not a combination story
cards.summary: Keep donepezil going at the severe stage; memantine is a modest, optional addition — Split: LIKELY · POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Reisberg 2003 (252 patients, memantine vs placebo, 28 weeks) and DOMINO 2012 (295 patients, donepezil continuation and memantine in factorial design, 52 weeks).
cards.result: The two trials divide the question cleanly. Donepezil continuation carries the stronger result: a cognitive difference (1.9 SMMSE points) exceeding DOMINO's own 1.4-point importance threshold, with function moving the same way. Memantine is positive in both trials but small in both — borderline on global impression in Reisberg, below the importance thresholds in DOMINO — and DOMINO found no significant benefit of donepezil-plus-memantine over donepezil alone. Symptomatic anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies for early Alzheimer's disease live on Shelf #333 and are not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote Reisberg's P values as point gains, and do not present the DOMINO combination arm as additive — the trial tested that and found nothing extra.

shelves.title: Cannabidiol for severe childhood epilepsy syndromes (Dravet and Lennox–Gastaut)
shelves.question: Does pharmaceutical cannabidiol, added to standard therapy, reduce convulsive seizures in Dravet syndrome and drop seizures in Lennox–Gastaut syndrome versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Anticonvulsants/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Cannabidiol/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Epilepsies, Myoclonic/drug therapy · Fatigue/chemically induced · Liver/drug effects · Liver Function Tests · Seizures/prevention & control
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two double-blind, placebo-controlled trials of the same pharmaceutical cannabidiol solution — one in Dravet syndrome (Devinsky 2017, n=120) and one in Lennox–Gastaut syndrome (Devinsky 2018, n=225, two doses) — both met their primary seizure-frequency endpoints, with median reductions roughly two to two-and-a-half times the placebo response. The benefit is a reduction in seizure frequency, not seizure freedom (5% vs 0% seizure-free in Dravet, not significant), and it comes with somnolence, gastrointestinal effects and liver-enzyme elevations that caused withdrawals. Neither trial addresses mortality, development, or long-term outcomes.

cards.headline: Devinsky 2017 (Dravet): cannabidiol cut convulsive seizures more than placebo — median monthly frequency 12.4 to 5.9 versus 14.9 to 14.1
cards.summary: Devinsky 2017 (Dravet): cannabidiol cut median monthly convulsive seizures from 12.4 to 5.9, versus 14.9 to 14.1 on placebo.
cards.people: 120 children and young adults with Dravet syndrome and drug-resistant seizures, randomised to cannabidiol oral solution 20 mg/kg/day or placebo, added to standard antiepileptic treatment. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The median frequency of convulsive seizures per month decreased from 12.4 to 5.9 with cannabidiol versus 14.9 to 14.1 with placebo (adjusted median difference in change, −22.8 percentage points; 95% CI −41.1 to −5.4; P=0.01). At least a 50% reduction in convulsive-seizure frequency occurred in 43% on cannabidiol versus 27% on placebo (odds ratio 2.00, 0.93 to 4.30; P=0.08 — a relative odds figure, not statistically significant). Caregiver global impression improved by at least one category in 62% versus 34% (P=0.02); 5% versus 0% became seizure-free (P=0.08). Adverse events more frequent with cannabidiol included diarrhoea, vomiting, fatigue, pyrexia, somnolence and abnormal liver-function tests, and there were more withdrawals in the cannabidiol group.
cards.watchOut: Single trial in this syndrome, industry-funded (GW Pharmaceuticals), 14 weeks: the responder odds ratio of 2.00 sits exactly at the library's 0.5–2.0 caution boundary and was not significant — the shelf rests on the significant primary frequency endpoint, not on that ratio.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a real, moderate seizure-frequency benefit in two syndromes — with a liver and sedation price
cards.summary: A real, moderate seizure-frequency benefit in two syndromes — with a liver and sedation price — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Devinsky 2017 (120 patients, Dravet syndrome) and Devinsky 2018 (225 patients, Lennox–Gastaut syndrome), both double-blind and placebo-controlled, both of cannabidiol oral solution added to standard therapy.
cards.result: Two independent syndrome populations, one drug, concordant primary endpoints: median convulsive-seizure frequency fell by roughly half from baseline in Dravet against almost no placebo change, and drop-seizure frequency fell 41.9%/37.2% versus 17.2% in Lennox–Gastaut. That concordance across two blinded trials is what carries LIKELY. The limits are equally consistent: few patients became seizure-free, and liver aminotransferase elevations (9% in the Lennox–Gastaut trial) plus somnolence and diarrhoea are part of the treatment, not footnotes. Fenfluramine for the same two syndromes is Shelf #992 and is not re-carded here; cannabis for chronic pain is Shelf #411, a different product and question.
cards.watchOut: Do not convert the median percentage reductions into promises for an individual child: placebo responses of 17–19% and wide individual variation sit inside both trials.

shelves.title: Fenfluramine for Dravet and Lennox–Gastaut syndromes
shelves.question: Does low-dose fenfluramine — the withdrawn appetite suppressant, repurposed — reduce seizures in Dravet syndrome and in Lennox–Gastaut syndrome versus placebo, and what cardiac safety did the trials show?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Anticonvulsants/therapeutic use · Epilepsies, Myoclonic/drug therapy · Fenfluramine/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Observational Studies as Topic · Placebos · Seizures/drug therapy
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two double-blind, placebo-controlled trials — Lagae 2019 in Dravet syndrome (n=119) and Knupp 2022 in Lennox–Gastaut syndrome (n=263) — both met their primary endpoints at the 0.7 mg/kg/day dose, with a clear dose gradient beneath them. The Dravet effect is large (a 62.3% greater reduction in mean monthly convulsive seizure frequency than placebo); the Lennox–Gastaut effect is smaller (an estimated median difference of −19.9 percentage points in drop-seizure frequency). On the drug's defining historical risk: echocardiography in the Dravet trial found valve function within the normal physiological range in all patients, and neither trial observed valvular heart disease or pulmonary arterial hypertension — over trial durations of 14–20 weeks, which is reassurance about the trials, not a lifetime guarantee.

cards.headline: Lagae 2019 (Dravet): fenfluramine 0.7 mg/kg/day cut convulsive seizures far more than placebo — median reduction 74.9% versus 19.2%
cards.summary: Lagae 2019 (Dravet): fenfluramine 0.7 mg/kg/day cut convulsive seizures by a median 74.9% versus 19.2% on placebo.
cards.people: 119 children and young adults with Dravet syndrome (mean age 9.0 years; 64 [54%] male), randomised 1:1:1 to fenfluramine 0.2 mg/kg/day (39), fenfluramine 0.7 mg/kg/day (40), or placebo (40), added to existing antiepileptic agents after a 6-week baseline.
cards.result: Median reduction in monthly convulsive seizure frequency was 74.9% in the 0.7 mg/kg group (from a median 20.7 to 4.7 seizures per 28 days), 42.3% in the 0.2 mg/kg group (17.5 to 12.6), and 19.2% on placebo (27.3 to 22.0). The 0.7 mg/kg dose showed a 62.3% greater reduction in mean monthly convulsive seizure frequency compared with placebo (95% CI 47.7 to 72.8; P<0.0001); the 0.2 mg/kg dose showed a 32.4% greater reduction (6.2 to 52.3; P=0.0209) — both relative comparisons against the placebo change. The most common adverse events (≥10% and more frequent on fenfluramine) were decreased appetite, diarrhoea, fatigue, lethargy, somnolence and decreased weight. Echocardiographic examinations revealed valve function within the normal physiological range in all patients during the trial and no signs of pulmonary arterial hypertension.
cards.watchOut: Fourteen weeks is short against a valvulopathy risk that historically emerged with longer exposure at appetite-suppressant doses; the clean echocardiograms are necessary reassurance, not proof of long-term cardiac safety, and the drug returns under cardiac monitoring for that reason.

cards.headline: Knupp 2022 (Lennox–Gastaut): fenfluramine 0.7 mg/kg/day beat placebo on drop seizures by an estimated median 19.9 percentage points
cards.summary: Knupp 2022 (Lennox–Gastaut): fenfluramine 0.7 mg/kg beat placebo on drop seizures by an estimated median 19.9 percentage points.
cards.type: Multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group randomised trial (20 weeks)
cards.people: 263 patients aged 2 to 35 years with confirmed Lennox–Gastaut syndrome and at least two drop seizures per week in a 4-week baseline, at 65 sites in North America, Europe and Australia (median age 13 years; 146 [56%] male), randomised to fenfluramine 0.7 mg/kg/day (87), 0.2 mg/kg/day (89), or placebo (87).
cards.result: The median percentage reduction in drop-seizure frequency was 26.5 percentage points in the 0.7 mg/kg group, 14.2 in the 0.2 mg/kg group, and 7.6 on placebo; the estimated median difference for 0.7 mg/kg versus placebo was −19.9 percentage points (95% CI −31.0 to −8.7; P=0.001). A 50% or greater response occurred in 22 of 87 (25%) on 0.7 mg/kg versus 9 of 87 (10%) on placebo (P=0.02). Generalised tonic-clonic seizures appeared most responsive (frequency down 45.7% at 0.7 mg/kg and 58.2% at 0.2 mg/kg, versus a 3.7% increase on placebo). The most common treatment-emergent adverse events were decreased appetite (59 patients [22%]), somnolence (33 [13%]) and fatigue (33 [13%]). No cases of valvular heart disease or pulmonary arterial hypertension were observed.
cards.watchOut: The Lennox–Gastaut effect is materially smaller than the Dravet effect — a quarter of patients reaching a 50% response — and the trial's 20 weeks carry the same cardiac-duration caveat as its Dravet companion.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the repurposed drug works in both syndromes — biggest in Dravet — and its cardiac history travels with it
cards.summary: The repurposed drug works in both syndromes — biggest in Dravet — and its cardiac history travels with it — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Lagae 2019 (119 patients, Dravet syndrome) and Knupp 2022 (263 patients, Lennox–Gastaut syndrome), both double-blind and placebo-controlled with the same two-dose design.
cards.result: Both trials met their primary endpoints with dose gradients (0.7 > 0.2 > placebo), which is why the stamp is LIKELY: Dravet median convulsive-seizure reduction 74.9% versus 19.2% on placebo; Lennox–Gastaut estimated median difference −19.9 percentage points on drop seizures. The valvulopathy that withdrew fenfluramine as an appetite suppressant was not seen in either trial — echocardiography was normal throughout Lagae and no valve disease or pulmonary hypertension occurred in Knupp — but 14–20 weeks of exposure cannot close that question, and cardiac monitoring is part of the drug's return. shelves.title: Non-invasive brain stimulation for treatment-resistant depression: iTBS and tDCS
shelves.question: Is intermittent theta-burst stimulation non-inferior to conventional high-frequency rTMS for treatment-resistant depression — and does transcranial direct-current stimulation beat placebo, measured against escitalopram?
shelves.mesh: Antidepressive Agents/therapeutic use · Canada/epidemiology · Depression/therapy · Major Depressive Disorder/psychology · Depressive Disorder, Treatment-Resistant/diagnosis,drug therapy · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Pain Perception/classification,physiology
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — iTBS non-inferior to standard rTMS · POSSIBLE — tDCS beats placebo but was not shown non-inferior to escitalopram. THREE-D (414 patients) showed iTBS non-inferior to 10 Hz rTMS on depression scores, delivered in 3 minutes against 37.5 — a logistics advance on a single large trial, hence POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY. ELECT-TDCS (245 patients) is two-handed: tDCS beat placebo (difference 3.2 HDRS-17 points), but non-inferiority to escitalopram could not be claimed — escitalopram beat placebo by more (5.5 points) and the tDCS-versus-drug confidence interval crossed the pre-set margin. Anyone citing tDCS as 'as good as an antidepressant' is citing half of that trial.

cards.headline: THREE-D 2018: iTBS was non-inferior to 10 Hz rTMS for treatment-resistant depression — in 3 minutes a session instead of 37.5
cards.summary: THREE-D 2018: iTBS was non-inferior to 10 Hz rTMS for treatment-resistant depression — in 3 minutes a session instead of 37.5.
cards.type: Randomised, multicentre, non-inferiority trial (open-label delivery, masked outcome assessors; 4–6 weeks)
cards.people: 414 adults aged 18–65 with a treatment-resistant major depressive episode (or intolerance of at least two antidepressants in the episode) and HRSD-17 score at least 18, at three Canadian university neurostimulation centres, randomised to 10 Hz rTMS (205) or iTBS (209) to the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, 5 days a week for 4–6 weeks; 192 (94%) and 193 (92%) respectively were assessed for the primary outcome.
cards.result: HRSD-17 scores improved from 23.5 (SD 4.4) to 13.4 (7.8) with 10 Hz rTMS and from 23.6 (4.3) to 13.4 (7.9) with iTBS (adjusted difference 0.103; lower 95% CI −1.16; P=0.0011), which met the pre-set non-inferiority margin of 2.25 points. Self-rated treatment pain was slightly greater with iTBS (verbal analogue scale 3.8 [SD 2.0] vs 3.4 [2.0] of 10; P=0.011). Dropouts did not differ (13 [6%] of 205 vs 16 [8%] of 209); the most common treatment-related adverse event was headache in both groups (131 [64%] of 204 vs 136 [65%] of 208). iTBS sessions take 3 minutes versus 37.5 minutes for standard 10 Hz treatment.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority to an active comparator in a single trial, with treatment delivered open-label: the finding licenses substituting the shorter protocol where rTMS is already offered, not a claim that either protocol beats sham — that evidence lives outside this shelf.
cards.source: Blumberger DM et al. Effectiveness of theta burst versus high-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation in patients with depression (THREE-D): a randomised non-inferiority trial. cards.headline: ELECT-TDCS 2017: tDCS beat placebo but could NOT be shown non-inferior to escitalopram — the drug beat placebo by more
cards.summary: ELECT-TDCS 2017: tDCS beat placebo but could NOT be shown non-inferior to escitalopram (difference −2.3 points).
cards.people: 245 adults with unipolar depression, randomised to tDCS plus oral placebo (94), sham tDCS plus escitalopram (91), or sham tDCS plus oral placebo (60). tDCS was 30-minute 2-mA prefrontal stimulation for 15 consecutive weekdays then 7 weekly treatments; escitalopram was 10 mg/day for 3 weeks then 20 mg/day. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Mean decrease in HDRS-17 score was 11.3±6.5 points with escitalopram, 9.0±7.1 with tDCS, and 5.8±7.9 with placebo. The difference for tDCS versus escitalopram was −2.3 points (95% CI −4.3 to −0.4; P=0.69), whose lower boundary fell below the non-inferiority margin of −2.75 (50% of the placebo-versus-escitalopram difference), so non-inferiority could not be claimed. Both active treatments were superior to placebo (escitalopram difference 5.5 points, 3.1 to 7.8, P<0.001; tDCS difference 3.2 points, 0.7 to 5.5, P=0.01). Patients on tDCS had higher rates of skin redness, tinnitus and nervousness, and new-onset mania developed in 2 patients in the tDCS group.
cards.watchOut: The trial's own design forbids the common summary 'tDCS works as well as escitalopram': it was powered and margined to test exactly that, and the test failed, even though tDCS separately beat placebo.

shelves.title: Long-acting injectable antipsychotics for relapse prevention in schizophrenia
shelves.question: Do depot antipsychotics prevent relapse versus placebo in stabilised schizophrenia — aripiprazole once-monthly in its pivotal maintenance trial, and paliperidone palmitate in its relapse-prevention trial?
shelves.mesh: Antipsychotic Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Aripiprazole · Delayed-Action Preparations · Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions · Injections, Intramuscular · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Piperazines/administration & dosage,adverse effects
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two double-blind, placebo-controlled maintenance trials of once-monthly depot antipsychotics in patients first stabilised on the same drug both showed large delays to relapse: impending relapse 10.0% versus 39.6% on placebo in the aripiprazole depot trial (relative hazard for placebo versus depot 5.03), and a relative hazard of 3.60 for placebo versus paliperidone palmitate. Both trials share the design caveat that defines this literature: only patients who had already stabilised on the drug were randomised, so the estimates describe continuing a tolerated depot, not starting one in an unselected patient. The aripiprazole trial was also stopped early at a pre-planned interim analysis, which tends to flatter effect sizes.

cards.headline: Kane 2012: aripiprazole once-monthly depot cut impending relapse to 10.0% versus 39.6% on placebo in stabilised patients
cards.summary: Kane 2012: aripiprazole once-monthly depot cut impending relapse to 10.0% versus 39.6% on placebo in stabilised patients.
cards.type: 52-week, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled maintenance trial (stopped early at pre-planned interim analysis)
cards.people: Adults with DSM-IV-TR schizophrenia who first completed oral aripiprazole stabilisation and then 12 weeks of depot stabilisation: 710 patients entered oral stabilisation, 576 progressed to depot stabilisation, and 403 were randomised 2:1 to aripiprazole intramuscular depot 400 mg every 4 weeks or placebo. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Time to exacerbation of psychotic symptoms/impending relapse was significantly delayed with depot versus placebo at both interim and final analyses (P<0.0001). The hazard ratio (placebo/depot) at final analysis was 5.03 (95% CI 3.15 to 8.02) — a relative figure; in absolute terms the rate of impending relapse was 10.0% (27/269) on depot versus 39.6% (53/134) on placebo. The trial was terminated early because efficacy was demonstrated at the pre-planned interim analysis (conducted after 64 events). Symptom-scale improvements were maintained on depot and worsened significantly on placebo.
cards.watchOut: Enriched design: every randomised patient had already tolerated and stabilised on aripiprazole, and early stopping at interim can exaggerate the effect — the absolute relapse rates apply to stable continuers, not to first-episode or non-adherent populations.

cards.headline: Hough 2010: paliperidone palmitate delayed time-to-relapse versus placebo — relative hazard 3.60 for placebo
cards.summary: Hough 2010: paliperidone palmitate delayed time-to-relapse versus placebo (relative hazard 3.60 for placebo).
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled relapse-prevention study (after open-label transition and maintenance phases)
cards.people: Adults with schizophrenia (PANSS total score <120 at entry) transitioned to paliperidone palmitate, stabilised through a 24-week maintenance phase, then randomised to continue paliperidone palmitate at the stabilised dose or switch to placebo. The pre-planned interim analysis included 312 patients (mean age 40 years; 55% men); the final analysis included 408 patients.
cards.result: Time-to-relapse favoured paliperidone palmitate at interim and final analyses (P<0.0001, log-rank test); the hazard ratio (placebo/paliperidone palmitate) at final analysis was 3.60 (95% CI 2.45 to 5.28) — a relative figure; the abstract does not print the absolute relapse proportions, so none are claimed on this card. Treatment-emergent adverse event rates in the double-blind phase were similar (44% paliperidone palmitate, 45% placebo); glucose-related adverse events were ≤4% across phases, while mean weight increased by 1.9 kg on paliperidone palmitate and was unchanged on placebo.

cards.headline: Synthesis: continuing a stabilising depot prevents relapse — the trials prove continuation, not initiation
cards.summary: Continuing a stabilising depot prevents relapse — the trials prove continuation, not initiation — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Kane 2012 (403 randomised, aripiprazole depot vs placebo) and Hough 2010 (408 in the final analysis, paliperidone palmitate vs placebo), both double-blind maintenance trials after stabilisation on the study drug.
cards.result: Two different molecules, the same architecture, and concordant large effects — absolute impending relapse 10.0% versus 39.6% (aripiprazole) and relative hazard 3.60 against placebo (paliperidone) — carry LIKELY for the continuation question: in a patient stable on a once-monthly depot, switching to placebo brings relapse back quickly. cards.watchOut: Quote the absolute rates beside the relative hazards: hazard ratios of 5.03 and 3.60 sound like different drugs' worth of difference until the stabilised-population design is stated with them.

shelves.title: Exercise training for people with dementia: the DAPA trial's null
shelves.question: Does a moderate-to-high-intensity aerobic and strength programme improve cognition in people with mild-to-moderate dementia — or slow its decline by any measure that matters?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Caregivers/psychology · Cognition/physiology · Dementia/physiopathology,psychology,rehabilitation · England · Exercise Therapy/methods · Physical Fitness/physiology,psychology
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): The DAPA trial (494 people with mild-to-moderate dementia, 12-month primary outcome) found that a well-delivered, well-attended moderate-to-high-intensity exercise programme did not slow cognitive impairment — the exercise group's ADAS-cog score was statistically slightly worse (adjusted difference −1.4 points, P=0.03), a difference the investigators describe as small with uncertain clinical relevance — and no secondary outcome (daily living, neuropsychiatric symptoms, quality of life, carer outcomes) differed. A single very large, pragmatic, investigator-masked trial with a null this complete may carry LIKELY for the null, per the library's large-single-trial-null rule; fitness genuinely improved (6-minute walk +18.1 m), which is what makes the cognitive null informative rather than a delivery failure. The shelf's question is established dementia: trials in mild cognitive impairment are a different question and are fenced, not carded.

cards.headline: DAPA 2018: exercise improved fitness but not cognition — ADAS-cog at 12 months was slightly worse in the exercise group
cards.summary: DAPA 2018: exercise improved fitness but not cognition — ADAS-cog at 12 months was slightly worse in the exercise group (adjusted difference −1.4).
cards.type: Multicentre, pragmatic, investigator-masked, randomised controlled trial (12 months)
cards.people: 494 people with mild-to-moderate dementia recruited through NHS primary care, community and memory services in 15 English regions (mean age 77 [SD 7.9] years; 301/494 [61%] men), randomised 2:1 to a 4-month supervised aerobic and strength exercise programme plus support for ongoing activity (329) or usual care (165).
cards.result: By 12 months the mean ADAS-cog score had increased (worsened) to 25.2 (SD 12.3) in the exercise arm and 23.8 (SD 10.4) in the usual-care arm (adjusted between-group difference −1.4, 95% CI −2.6 to −0.2; P=0.03) — greater cognitive impairment in the exercise group, though the average difference is small and clinical relevance uncertain. No differences were found in secondary outcomes or pre-planned subgroups by dementia type, severity, sex or mobility. Compliance was good: over 65% of participants (214/329) attended more than three quarters of scheduled sessions, and 6-minute walking distance improved over 6 weeks (mean change 18.1 m, 11.6 to 24.6).
cards.watchOut: One trial, however large: it tests this programme (4 months supervised, then supported self-directed activity) in community-dwelling mild-to-moderate dementia — it does not exclude benefit from other doses, earlier intervention, or non-cognitive outcomes it did not measure.
cards.source: Lamb SE et al. Dementia And Physical Activity (DAPA) trial of moderate to high intensity exercise training for people with dementia: randomised controlled trial. BMJ. 2018 May 16;361:k1675. PMID: 29769247. Registry ID: ISRCTN10416500, stated in the record's abstract.

cards.headline: Synthesis: fitness is not cognition — in established dementia, this programme did not slow decline
cards.summary: Fitness is not cognition — in established dementia, this programme did not slow decline — LIKELY the null.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: the DAPA trial (494 people with mild-to-moderate dementia) and its HTA programme monograph — one trial, two records.
cards.result: DAPA did the intervention properly — supervised, progressed, well attended — and fitness improved while cognition, function, behaviour and quality of life did not; the primary cognitive outcome pointed fractionally the wrong way (−1.4 ADAS-cog points, P=0.03, clinical relevance uncertain). That combination earns LIKELY for the null on this shelf's question. Two fences: the FINGER multidomain lifestyle trial is carded on Shelf #332 (at-risk older adults, not established dementia) and is not re-carded here; and the currency sweep's newer large trials — EXERT (exercise in amnestic mild cognitive impairment) and the US POINTER multidomain trial (at-risk older adults) — answer earlier-stage questions and do not disturb DAPA's verdict for people who already have dementia. Exercise for depression is Shelf #998; goal-oriented cognitive rehabilitation in early dementia is Shelf #999.
cards.watchOut: A null for cognition is not a null for exercise: falls, mood, cardiovascular fitness and carer outcomes have their own shelves, and DAPA's fitness gain was real.

shelves.title: Spinal cord stimulation for chronic back and leg pain: HF10 and closed-loop
shelves.question: Does 10-kHz high-frequency spinal cord stimulation relieve chronic back and leg pain better than traditional low-frequency stimulation — and does ECAP-controlled closed-loop stimulation beat open-loop on pain and function?
shelves.mesh: Back Pain/diagnosis,therapy · Chronic Pain/diagnosis,therapy · Leg/pathology · Pain Management/methods,standards · Spinal Cord Stimulation/methods,standards · Back Pain/therapy · Chronic Pain/therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two randomised trials, each against an active stimulation comparator rather than sham, favoured the newer technology on responder rates: HF10 (10-kHz) beat traditional low-frequency stimulation in SENZA-RCT (back-pain responders 84.5% vs 43.8% at 3 months, sustained to 12 months), and ECAP-controlled closed-loop beat fixed-output open-loop in the double-blind Evoke trial (≥50% pain reduction 82.3% vs 60.3% at 3 months; 83.1% vs 61.0% at 12 months). The grade stops at POSSIBLE because both trials are industry-run device comparisons with a subjective responder endpoint, SENZA was unblinded (HF10 produces no paraesthesias, so patients could tell), and neither trial compares stimulation with no stimulation — the absolute value of any spinal cord stimulation is a different shelf's question.

cards.headline: SENZA-RCT 2015: HF10 responders 84.5% for back pain versus 43.8% on traditional stimulation at 3 months, sustained to 12 months
cards.summary: SENZA-RCT 2015: HF10 responders 84.5% for back pain versus 43.8% on traditional stimulation at 3 months, sustained to 12 months.
cards.type: Randomised, parallel-arm, non-inferiority-designed controlled trial (superiority shown; 12 months)
cards.people: 198 subjects with both chronic back and leg pain randomised 1:1 across 10 US comprehensive pain treatment centres; 171 passed a temporary trial and were implanted with a spinal cord stimulation system. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Responders (≥50% pain reduction with no stimulation-related neurological deficit) at 3 months: 84.5% of implanted HF10 subjects for back pain and 83.1% for leg pain, versus 43.8% and 55.5% for traditional low-frequency stimulation (P<0.001 for both comparisons). The relative ratio for responders was 1.9 (95% CI 1.4 to 2.5) for back pain and 1.5 (1.2 to 1.9) for leg pain — relative figures, the first inside the library's 0.5–2.0 caution band, printed here beside their absolute rates. Superiority was sustained through 12 months (P<0.001). HF10 subjects experienced no paraesthesias.
cards.watchOut: Unblinded by design (paraesthesias reveal traditional stimulation), industry-conducted, and only patients who passed a temporary stimulation trial were implanted — responder rates apply to that screened population, not to all comers with back and leg pain.
cards.source: Kapural L et al. Novel 10-kHz High-frequency Therapy (HF10 Therapy) Is Superior to Traditional Low-frequency Spinal Cord Stimulation for the Treatment of Chronic Back and Leg Pain: The SENZA-RCT Randomized Controlled Trial. Anesthesiology. 2015 Oct;123(4):851-860. PMID: 26218762. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the record carries no databank registration entry.

cards.headline: Evoke 2020: closed-loop stimulation beat open-loop — 82.3% versus 60.3% achieving ≥50% pain reduction at 3 months
cards.summary: Evoke 2020: closed-loop stimulation beat open-loop — 82.3% versus 60.3% achieving ≥50% pain reduction at 3 months.
cards.type: Multicentre, double-blind, parallel-arm, randomised controlled trial (3- and 12-month analyses)
cards.people: 134 patients with chronic, intractable back and leg pain (VAS ≥60 mm; Oswestry Disability Index 41–80), refractory to conservative therapy and new to spinal cord stimulation, at 13 US specialist clinics and hospitals, randomised 1:1 to ECAP-controlled closed-loop (67) or fixed-output open-loop (67) stimulation; the intention-to-treat analysis comprised 125 patients at 3 months and 118 at 12 months. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary outcome (≥50% reduction in overall back and leg pain with no increase in pain medications) was achieved by more patients on closed-loop than open-loop at 3 months (51 [82.3%] of 62 vs 38 [60.3%] of 63; difference 21.9%, 95% CI 6.6 to 37.3; P=0.0052) and at 12 months (49 [83.1%] of 59 vs 36 [61.0%] of 59; difference 22.0%, 6.3 to 37.7; P=0.0060), meeting non-inferiority then superiority at both points. Safety profiles did not differ; the most frequent study-related adverse events in both groups were lead migration (9 patients [7%]), implantable pulse generator pocket pain (5 [4%]) and muscle spasm or cramp (3 [2%]).
cards.watchOut: Double-blind — the stronger design of this shelf's two trials — but a single manufacturer's first pivotal trial of its own closed-loop system, with a responder endpoint and 12-month horizon; longer and independent replication is the missing piece.
cards.source: Mekhail N et al. Long-term safety and efficacy of closed-loop spinal cord stimulation to treat chronic back and leg pain (Evoke): a double-blind, randomised, controlled trial. cards.headline: Synthesis: newer stimulation beats older stimulation in both trials — against active comparators, not against nothing
cards.summary: Newer stimulation beats older stimulation in both trials — against active comparators, not against nothing — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: SENZA-RCT 2015 (171 implanted, HF10 vs traditional stimulation) and Evoke 2020 (134 randomised, closed-loop vs open-loop).
cards.result: Read together, the direction of travel in this technology is consistent: paresthesia-free high-frequency stimulation roughly doubled back-pain responder rates over traditional stimulation (84.5% vs 43.8%), and physiologically controlled closed-loop delivery added about 22 percentage points over open-loop (82.3% vs 60.3% at 3 months, held at 12 months). POSSIBLE, not LIKELY, because both comparisons are device-versus-device inside selected, trial-screened populations, and the pain outcome is self-reported in trials patients could partly see through. The drug, injection and surgical pain shelves do not test implanted stimulation and are not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote SENZA's relative responder ratio (1.9) without its absolute rates, and do not use either trial to justify stimulation over conservative care — neither randomised that comparison.

shelves.title: The buprenorphine implant for opioid dependence (Probuphine)
shelves.question: In adults already stable on sublingual buprenorphine, does a six-month buprenorphine implant keep them opioid-negative as reliably as continuing sublingual therapy — and did the implant beat placebo in untreated dependence?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Sublingual · Analgesics, Opioid/blood · Buprenorphine/administration & dosage · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Implants · Narcotic Antagonists/administration & dosage · Opioid-Related Disorders/drug therapy
shelves.balance: LIKELY: The implant works in both populations in which it was tested. In untreated opioid dependence, Ling 2010 (n=163) showed more opioid-negative urine samples than placebo implants over weeks 1–16 (mean 40.4% vs 28.3%) with far better completion (65.7% vs 30.9%). In patients already stable and abstinent on low-dose sublingual buprenorphine, Rosenthal 2016 (n=177) showed the implant non-inferior to continuing sublingual therapy on responder rates (96.4% vs 87.6%). The two trials answer different questions — starting treatment versus maintaining stability — and the shelf claims each only for its own population. The weekly/monthly depot buprenorphine injections are a different formulation, home on Shelf #782, and are not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Rosenthal 2016: in stable, abstinent patients the implant was non-inferior to sublingual buprenorphine — responders 96.4% versus 87.6%
cards.summary: Rosenthal 2016: in stable, abstinent patients the implant was non-inferior to sublingual buprenorphine (responders 96.4% versus 87.6% ).
cards.type: Outpatient, randomised, active-controlled, 24-week, double-blind, double-dummy non-inferiority trial
cards.people: 177 adults with opioid dependence at 21 US sites (mean age 39 years; 40.9% female) who had been on sublingual buprenorphine 8 mg/day or less for at least 90 days with stable abstinence, randomised to sublingual buprenorphine plus placebo implants (90) or sublingual placebo plus four 80-mg buprenorphine implants (87); 165 of 177 (93.2%) completed the trial.
cards.result: Responders (at least 4 of 6 months without an opioid-positive urine test or self-report) numbered 81 of 84 (96.4%) on implants versus 78 of 89 (87.6%) on sublingual buprenorphine — a difference of 8.8% (one-sided 97.5% CI 0.009 to ∞; P<0.001 for non-inferiority against the −0.20 margin). Over 6 months, 72 of 84 (85.7%) on implants and 64 of 89 (71.9%) on sublingual therapy maintained opioid abstinence (P=0.03). Implant-related adverse events occurred in 23% of the implant group and 13.5% of the sublingual group; non-implant-related events in 48.3% and 52.8% respectively.
cards.watchOut: A maintenance-swap trial in an unusually stable population (abstinent ≥90 days on a low dose): it says nothing about starting the implant in active dependence, and non-inferiority was the design — superiority language would misstate it.
cards.source: Rosenthal RN et al. Effect of Buprenorphine Implants on Illicit Opioid Use Among Abstinent Adults With Opioid Dependence Treated With Sublingual Buprenorphine: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2016 Jul 19;316(3):282-290. PMID: 27434441. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02180659, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Ling 2010: in untreated dependence, buprenorphine implants beat placebo implants on negative urines (40.4% vs 28.3%) and completion (65.7% vs 30.9%)
cards.summary: Ling 2010: in untreated dependence, buprenorphine implants beat placebo implants on opioid-negative urines ( 40.4% vs 28.3% ).
cards.people: 163 adults aged 18 to 65 years with opioid dependence at 18 US sites, randomised after sublingual buprenorphine-naloxone induction to four buprenorphine implants (80 mg each; 108 patients) or four placebo implants (55), with a fifth implant available on a rescue threshold and standardised drug counselling for all. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The buprenorphine group had significantly more urine samples negative for illicit opioids during weeks 1–16 (P=0.04): mean percentage negative 40.4% (95% CI 34.2% to 46.7%), median 40.7%, versus mean 28.3% (20.3% to 36.3%), median 20.8%, on placebo. Study completion was 65.7% (71/108) versus 30.9% (17/55) (P<0.001). The implant group also had fewer clinician-rated (P<0.001) and patient-rated (P=0.004) withdrawal symptoms and lower craving ratings (P<0.001). Minor implant-site reactions were the most common adverse events (56.5% implant vs 52.7% placebo).
cards.watchOut: Even on active treatment, only about 40% of urine samples were negative in the first 16 weeks — the honest scale of effect in untreated dependence, far from the near-ceiling responder rates of the stable-population trial above; the two cards must not be averaged.
cards.source: Ling W et al. Buprenorphine implants for treatment of opioid dependence: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2010 Oct 13;304(14):1576-1583. PMID: 20940383. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00447564, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one formulation, two jobs — induction evidence is modest, maintenance evidence is strong
cards.summary: One formulation, two jobs — induction evidence is modest, maintenance evidence is strong — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Ling 2010 (163 patients, implant vs placebo in untreated dependence) and Rosenthal 2016 (177 patients, implant vs continued sublingual therapy in stable abstinence), both double-blind.
cards.result: The shelf's LIKELY rests on two blinded trials pointing the same way in their own populations: the implant delivers buprenorphine effectively enough to beat placebo implants on urine outcomes and retention (Ling), and to hold already-stable patients as reliably as daily sublingual dosing (Rosenthal, responders 96.4% vs 87.6%). The absolute numbers keep the claim honest — 40.4% negative urines in active dependence versus 96.4% responder rates in pre-stabilised patients is a population difference, not a dose difference. Depot buprenorphine injections (weekly/monthly) are home on Shelf #782 and are not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Implant-site reactions affected over half of patients in both arms of Ling (the placebo implants too) — the procedure itself, not just the drug, is part of this treatment's burden.

shelves.title: Exercise as a treatment for major depression: SMILE and TREAD
shelves.question: Does aerobic exercise treat major depression as well as sertraline in older adults — and does simply facilitating more physical activity help depressed adults in primary care?
shelves.mesh: Antidepressive Agents/therapeutic use · Anxiety · Cognition · Combined Modality Therapy · Depressive Disorder/drug therapy,physiopathology,psychology,therapy · Exercise · Lung/physiopathology
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — exercise comparable to sertraline at 16 weeks in older adults (SMILE) · LIKELY — facilitated physical activity does not improve depression in primary care (TREAD, the null). The discordance is the shelf. SMILE (156 older adults) found 16 weeks of aerobic exercise statistically indistinguishable from sertraline on depression scores — but it was small, had no placebo arm, and medication worked faster. TREAD (361 primary-care adults) tested the weaker real-world offer — a facilitator encouraging activity — and found no improvement in mood at 4, 8 or 12 months and no reduction in antidepressant use, even though activity itself rose. Structured, supervised exercise as treatment and being encouraged to be more active are different interventions; this shelf refuses to merge them.

cards.headline: SMILE 1999: after 16 weeks, exercise matched sertraline on depression scores in older adults — but medication acted faster
cards.summary: SMILE 1999: after 16 weeks, exercise matched sertraline on depression scores in older adults — but medication acted faster.
cards.type: 16-week randomised controlled trial (exercise vs medication vs combination; no placebo arm)
cards.people: 156 men and women aged 50 years or older with major depressive disorder, randomised to aerobic exercise, sertraline, or combined exercise and medication, with depression assessed on DSM-IV criteria, the Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression and the Beck Depression Inventory. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex split beyond including men and women.
cards.result: After 16 weeks the groups did not differ statistically on HAM-D or BDI scores (P=0.67), and adjustment for baseline depression yielded an essentially identical result; growth-curve models showed statistically and clinically significant reductions in all groups. Patients on medication alone showed the fastest initial response; in the combination group, those with less severe initial symptoms responded faster than those with more severe symptoms. The authors conclude an exercise training programme may be considered an alternative to antidepressants for depression in older persons, with antidepressants facilitating a more rapid initial response.
cards.watchOut: Small (156 patients across three arms), unblindable, and with no placebo or wait-list arm: 'no difference from sertraline' cannot distinguish both-work from both-fail in this sample, which is why this half of the shelf is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY.
cards.source: Blumenthal JA et al. Effects of exercise training on older patients with major depression. Arch Intern Med. 1999 Oct 25;159(19):2349-2356. PMID: 10547175. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — a pre-registration-era trial (1999).

cards.headline: TREAD 2012: facilitated physical activity raised activity but not mood — BDI difference at 4 months −0.54 points, not significant
cards.summary: TREAD 2012: facilitated physical activity raised activity but not mood (BDI difference at 4 months −0.54 points, not significant).
cards.type: Pragmatic, multicentre, two-arm parallel randomised controlled trial (primary care)
cards.people: 361 adults aged 18–69 in Bristol and Exeter general practices with a recent depression episode (clinical interview schedule diagnosis and Beck Depression Inventory score ≥14), randomised to usual care plus a physical-activity facilitator (up to three face-to-face sessions and 10 telephone calls over 8 months) or usual care alone.
cards.result: There was no evidence of improved mood at the 4-month primary endpoint (adjusted between-group difference in mean BDI score −0.54, 95% CI −3.06 to 1.99; P=0.68), nor at 8 or 12 months. Antidepressant use was not reduced (adjusted odds ratio 0.63, 0.19 to 2.06; P=0.44 — a relative odds figure, not significant). The intervention group did report more physical activity during follow-up (adjusted odds ratio 2.27, 1.32 to 3.89; P=0.003 — a relative odds figure): the behaviour moved, the depression did not.
cards.watchOut: TREAD tested facilitation, not supervised exercise training: its null condemns the light-touch offer, not the structured programmes of SMILE — and equally, SMILE's result cannot rescue facilitation, which is the form primary care actually offers.
cards.source: Chalder M et al. Facilitated physical activity as a treatment for depressed adults: randomised controlled trial. BMJ. 2012 Jun 6;344:e2758. PMID: 22674921. Registry ID: ISRCTN16900744, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the dose and delivery are the treatment — supervised training may work; encouragement alone does not
cards.summary: The dose and delivery are the treatment — supervised training may work; encouragement alone does not — Split: POSSIBLE · LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: SMILE 1999 (156 older adults, aerobic exercise vs sertraline vs both) and TREAD 2012 (361 primary-care adults, facilitated activity vs usual care).
cards.result: The two trials are usually quoted as if they contradict each other on 'exercise for depression'. They test different things: SMILE delivered actual aerobic training and matched sertraline at 16 weeks (POSSIBLE — small, placebo-free); TREAD delivered encouragement and contact, succeeded in raising activity (relative odds 2.27), and produced a clean null on depression across 12 months (LIKELY, the null). The currency sweep's newer pragmatic trial of exercise therapy added to guideline-concordant care for depression is fenced here, not carded: it does not displace either anchor. Brain stimulation for treatment-resistant depression is Shelf #993, and exercise in dementia is Shelf #995 — different populations, not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Clinically: prescribing a supervised programme is a treatment decision; telling a depressed patient to be more active, with a facilitator's phone calls, is not — TREAD measured the difference.

shelves.title: Goal-oriented cognitive rehabilitation in early dementia (GREAT)
shelves.question: Does individual, goal-oriented cognitive rehabilitation improve everyday functioning — attainment of the person's own goals — in early-stage Alzheimer's and related dementias, even though it does not move global cognition scores?
shelves.mesh: Affect · Alzheimer Disease/psychology,rehabilitation · Cognition · Cognition Disorders/rehabilitation · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy/methods · Dementia/psychology,rehabilitation · Goals
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The GREAT trial (475 people with early-stage dementia) found large, durable effects on its chosen primary outcome — attainment of the individual's own functional goals (standardised effect d=0.97 by self-rating and d=1.11 by informant rating at 3 months, maintained at 9 months) — and no significant differences on any secondary outcome, including global cognition, quality of life and mood. That pattern is the intervention working as designed: rehabilitation targeted the goals, and only the goals moved. The stamp is POSSIBLE because this is a single trial whose primary outcome is self- and informant-rated goal attainment in an unblindable intervention (outcome assessors were blinded; participants were not), and because the HTA monograph carded beside it is the same trial, not a second one.

cards.headline: GREAT 2019: goal attainment improved with large effects at 3 months (d=0.97 self-rated, d=1.11 informant-rated) and held at 9 months — secondary outcomes did not move
cards.summary: GREAT 2019: goal attainment improved with large effects at 3 months (d= 0.97 self-rated, d=1.11 informant-rated) and held at 9 months.
cards.type: Parallel-group, multicentre, single-blind randomised controlled trial
cards.people: 475 people with mild-to-moderate dementia (ICD-10 Alzheimer's, vascular or mixed dementia; Mini-Mental State Examination score ≥18) with a participating family member, randomised 1:1 to cognitive rehabilitation added to usual treatment or usual treatment alone. Rehabilitation was 10 weekly sessions over 3 months plus four maintenance sessions over 6 months; follow-up at 3 and 9 months by blinded researchers. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 3 months there were statistically significant large positive effects for participant-rated goal attainment (d=0.97; 95% CI 0.75 to 1.19), corroborated by informant ratings (d=1.11; 0.89 to 1.34), and the effects were maintained at 9 months (participant d=0.94, 0.71 to 1.17; informant d=0.96, 0.73 to 1.2). The gains related to goals directly targeted in the therapy. There were no significant differences in secondary outcomes — quality of life, mood, self-efficacy or cognition for participants, or stress and quality of life for study partners.
cards.watchOut: The primary outcome is, by construction, the thing the therapy practises: goal attainment on personally chosen goals, rated by the person and their informant, in a trial where participants knew their allocation. That is a legitimate rehabilitation outcome, but it is softer than a blinded functional scale — hence POSSIBLE on a single trial.
cards.source: Clare L et al. Individual goal-oriented cognitive rehabilitation to improve everyday functioning for people with early-stage dementia: A multicentre randomised controlled trial (the GREAT trial). Int J Geriatr Psychiatry. 2019 May;34(5):709-721. PMID: 30724405. Registry ID: none in this record's databank fields — the registration (ISRCTN21027481) appears in the companion HTA record's databank fields (see next card).

cards.headline: Synthesis: rehabilitation improves the life it targets, not the test scores — one good trial, honestly bounded
cards.summary: Rehabilitation improves the life it targets, not the test scores — one good trial, honestly bounded — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: the GREAT trial (475 people with early-stage dementia) and its HTA monograph — one trial, two records.
cards.result: GREAT is the cleanest demonstration on these shelves that outcome choice is intervention choice: train specific everyday goals with a therapist and goal attainment improves by about a standard deviation, sustained to 9 months, while global cognition and quality-of-life scales stay flat. That supports offering goal-oriented rehabilitation to people with early dementia who have specific functional goals — stamped POSSIBLE as a single, necessarily unblinded trial with a self-rated primary outcome. Physical exercise in established dementia is Shelf #995 (DAPA's null) — a different intervention at a different stage — and symptomatic drug therapy at the moderate-to-severe stage is Shelf #990; neither is re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Do not let the large effect sizes (d≈1.0) travel to outcomes they were not measured on: GREAT found no significant effect on cognition, mood or quality of life, and says so.

shelves.title: Lasmiditan for acute migraine: the ditan trials (SAMURAI, SPARTAN)
shelves.question: Does lasmiditan — a selective 5-HT1F agonist with no vasoconstrictor action — relieve migraine pain at two hours versus placebo, including in patients with cardiovascular risk factors, and how large is its dizziness and CNS price?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Administration, Oral · Benzamides/therapeutic use · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Migraine Disorders/drug therapy · Piperidines/therapeutic use · Pyridines/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two large double-blind phase 3 trials (SAMURAI, 1,856 treated attacks; SPARTAN, 2,583 treated) agree that lasmiditan frees roughly twice as many patients from headache pain at 2 hours as placebo (32.2% and 38.8% at 200 mg versus 15.3% and 21.3%), with freedom from the most bothersome symptom in the same direction, and both trials enrolled populations in whom about four in five patients had at least one cardiovascular risk factor — the patients triptans cannot always serve. The price is central, not vascular: treatment-emergent adverse events ran 25–39% on lasmiditan versus 11.6% on placebo in SPARTAN, mostly dizziness, somnolence and paraesthesia. Two concordant blinded trials carry LIKELY.

cards.headline: SAMURAI (Kuca 2018): lasmiditan freed 32.2% (200 mg) and 28.2% (100 mg) from headache pain at 2 hours, versus 15.3% on placebo
cards.summary: SAMURAI (2018): lasmiditan freed 32.2% (200 mg) and 28.2% (100 mg) from headache pain at 2 hours vs 15.3% on placebo.
cards.type: Double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (single treated attack)
cards.people: 1,856 adult patients with migraine who treated an attack, randomised to oral lasmiditan 200 mg, lasmiditan 100 mg, or placebo and asked to treat within 4 hours of onset; 77.9% had at least one cardiovascular risk factor in addition to migraine. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Headache pain freedom at 2 hours: 32.2% on lasmiditan 200 mg versus 15.3% on placebo (odds ratio 2.6, 95% CI 2.0 to 3.6, p<0.001 — a relative measure, absolute rates beside it), and 28.2% on 100 mg (OR 2.2, 1.6 to 3.0, p<0.001). Freedom from the most bothersome symptom at 2 hours: 40.7% (200 mg) and 40.9% (100 mg) versus 29.5% on placebo (OR 1.6, 1.3 to 2.1, and OR 1.7, 1.3 to 2.2). Adverse events were mostly mild or moderate in intensity.
cards.watchOut: Single-attack design with an electronic diary: it shows what one dose does to one attack, not sustained response, consistency across attacks, or how lasmiditan compares head-to-head with a triptan or a gepant.
cards.source: Kuca B et al. Lasmiditan is an effective acute treatment for migraine: A phase 3 randomized study. Neurology. 2018;91(24):e2222-e2232. PMID: 30446595. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02439320, from the record's databank fields.

cards.summary: SPARTAN (2019): all three doses beat placebo on pain freedom ( 38.8%, 31.4%, 28.6% vs 21.3%), with CNS adverse events in up to 39%.

shelves.title: Xanomeline–trospium (KarXT) for schizophrenia: the EMERGENT programme
shelves.question: Does xanomeline–trospium — a muscarinic M1/M4 agonist paired with a peripheral muscarinic blocker, with no dopamine-receptor blockade — reduce total PANSS score versus placebo in adults hospitalised with acute schizophrenia?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Antipsychotic Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Benzilates/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Cholinergic Antagonists/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Drug Combinations · Least-Squares Analysis · Muscarinic Agonists/adverse effects,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Three double-blind, placebo-controlled trials of the same 5-week inpatient question agree — EMERGENT-1 (phase 2, n=182; PANSS difference −11.6 points), EMERGENT-2 (phase 3, n=252; −9.6 points) and EMERGENT-3 (phase 3, n=256; −8.4 points) — a consistent, replicated reduction in total PANSS score from a mechanism with no D2 blockade, and with no excess of extrapyramidal symptoms, weight gain or somnolence over placebo in any of them. The price is cholinergic and gastrointestinal: nausea, vomiting, dyspepsia and constipation ran several-fold higher than placebo. Three concordant blinded trials carry LIKELY for short-term symptom reduction; none of the three runs beyond 5 weeks.

cards.headline: EMERGENT-1 (Brannan 2021): the phase 2 proof — PANSS total fell 17.4 points on xanomeline–trospium versus 5.9 on placebo over 5 weeks
cards.summary: EMERGENT-1 (2021, phase 2): PANSS total fell 17.4 points on xanomeline–trospium vs 5.9 on placebo over 5 weeks.
cards.type: Double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial (5 weeks, inpatient)
cards.people: 182 patients with schizophrenia randomly assigned to twice-daily xanomeline–trospium (90) or placebo (92), titrated to a maximum of 125 mg xanomeline and 30 mg trospium per dose. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Change in PANSS total score at week 5: −17.4 points with xanomeline–trospium versus −5.9 with placebo (least-squares mean difference −11.6 points, 95% CI −16.1 to −7.1, p<0.001), from baselines of 97.7 and 96.6. Secondary endpoints were significantly better on xanomeline–trospium except the percentage with a CGI-S response. The most common adverse events were constipation, nausea, dry mouth, dyspepsia and vomiting; somnolence, weight gain, restlessness and extrapyramidal symptoms were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: Phase 2 and small (182 patients, 5 weeks): a proof of concept whose effect size the phase 3 trials were expected to shrink — and did, modestly.

cards.result: Mean change in PANSS total score at week 5: −21.2 points (SE 1.7) on KarXT versus −11.6 (1.6) on placebo (least-squares mean difference −9.6, 95% CI −13.9 to −5.2, p<0.0001; Cohen's d 0.61); all secondary endpoints also favoured KarXT. cards.headline: Synthesis: three concordant 5-week trials of a non-dopamine mechanism — LIKELY for acute symptom reduction
cards.summary: Synthesis: three concordant 5-week trials of a non-dopamine mechanism — LIKELY for acute symptom reduction.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: EMERGENT-1 (n=182), EMERGENT-2 (n=252) and EMERGENT-3 (n=256), all double-blind, placebo-controlled, 5-week inpatient trials.
cards.result: The PANSS differences step down gently as the trials grow (−11.6, −9.6, −8.4 points) but never change direction, and the tolerability trade is consistent: gastrointestinal and cholinergic adverse events up, dopamine-blockade adverse events (extrapyramidal symptoms, weight gain, somnolence) not different from placebo. That is the whole claim of this shelf — acute symptom reduction over 5 weeks. The oral dopamine-antipsychotic class comparison lives on Shelf #699 and clozapine on Shelf #222; neither is re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Do not read 5-week acute efficacy as maintenance efficacy: the 52-week data (EMERGENT-4/5) are open-label and uncontrolled, and no trial here compares KarXT with another antipsychotic.
