shelves.title: Pimavanserin: Parkinson's disease psychosis, and relapse prevention in dementia-related psychosis (HARMONY)
shelves.question: Does the selective 5-HT2A inverse agonist pimavanserin improve psychosis in Parkinson's disease without worsening motor function — and, in dementia-related psychosis, does continuing it after an open-label response delay relapse versus switching to placebo?
shelves.mesh: Analysis of Variance · Antiparkinson Agents/therapeutic use · Antipsychotic Agents/therapeutic use · Parkinson Disease/drug therapy,psychology · Piperidines/therapeutic use · Psychotic Disorders/drug therapy · Serotonin 5-HT2 Receptor Agonists/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Each half of this shelf rests on exactly one randomised trial, so each is capped at POSSIBLE. In Parkinson's disease psychosis, one 6-week phase 3 trial (199 randomised) improved SAPS-PD scores by −3.06 points more than placebo with no worsening of motor function reported. In dementia-related psychosis, HARMONY (392 entering open-label treatment; 217 responders randomised) found relapse in 13% continuing pimavanserin versus 28% switched to placebo (hazard ratio 0.35) — but the randomised population is the minority who already responded and tolerated the drug, and the trial was stopped early for efficacy, which inflates effect estimates. One trial per question, one of them an enriched withdrawal design: POSSIBLE on both halves.

cards.headline: Cummings 2014: pimavanserin improved Parkinson's psychosis scores by −3.06 SAPS-PD points versus placebo at 6 weeks, without worsening motor function
cards.summary: Cummings (2014): pimavanserin improved Parkinson's psychosis scores by −3.06 SAPS-PD points vs placebo at 6 weeks, without worsening motor function.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (6 weeks, after a 2-week non-pharmacological lead-in)
cards.people: 199 adults (aged 40 years or older) with Parkinson's disease psychosis randomly allocated to pimavanserin 40 mg per day or placebo; antipsychotic treatment was not permitted, antiparkinsonian medication and deep brain stimulation were allowed. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: In the primary analysis population (95 pimavanserin, 90 placebo), SAPS-PD score change was −5.79 on pimavanserin versus −2.73 on placebo (difference −3.06, 95% CI −4.91 to −1.20, p=0.001; Cohen's d 0.50). Ten patients on pimavanserin discontinued because of an adverse event (four due to psychotic disorder or hallucination within 10 days) versus two on placebo. The authors report pimavanserin was well tolerated with no significant safety concerns or worsening of motor function.
cards.watchOut: A single trial with a lead-in phase designed to suppress the placebo response: the −3.06-point difference is on a scale whose clinical meaning at the individual level is debated, and there is no second trial to confirm it.

cards.headline: HARMONY (Tariot 2021): among open-label responders, relapse occurred in 13% continuing pimavanserin versus 28% switched to placebo (hazard ratio 0.35)
cards.summary: HARMONY (2021): among open-label responders, relapse occurred in 13% continuing pimavanserin vs 28% switched to placebo (HR 0.35 relative).
cards.type: Phase 3, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled discontinuation (withdrawal) trial, stopped early for efficacy
cards.people: 392 patients with psychosis related to Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease dementia, dementia with Lewy bodies, frontotemporal dementia or vascular dementia entered 12 weeks of open-label pimavanserin; 217 (61.8%) had a sustained response and were randomised to continue pimavanserin (105) or switch to placebo (112) for up to 26 weeks; 41 were withdrawn for administrative reasons when the trial stopped. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Relapse of psychosis occurred in 12 of 95 patients (13%) in the pimavanserin group and 28 of 99 (28%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio 0.35, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.73, p=0.005 — a relative measure, absolute rates beside it). During the double-blind phase, adverse events occurred in 41.0% on pimavanserin and 36.6% on placebo; headache, constipation, urinary tract infection and asymptomatic QT prolongation occurred with pimavanserin.
cards.watchOut: An enriched design: the randomised comparison covers only the 61.8% who responded to and tolerated open-label pimavanserin, and early stopping for efficacy tends to exaggerate the hazard ratio. The result supports continuing the drug in responders; it says nothing about starting it in unselected dementia psychosis.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two single-trial answers, one of them enriched — POSSIBLE on both halves
cards.summary: Synthesis: two single-trial answers, one of them enriched — POSSIBLE on both halves.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Cummings 2014 (Parkinson's psychosis, n=199) and HARMONY (dementia-related psychosis withdrawal, 217 randomised of 392 entering).
cards.result: The shelf's two questions have different evidence shapes. Parkinson's psychosis: a conventional parallel trial, positive on its rating scale, unreplicated. Dementia-related psychosis: a withdrawal trial in proven responders, positive on relapse (13% vs 28%), stopped early. Neither design flaw is fatal, but with one trial apiece the single-trial ceiling holds both halves at POSSIBLE. The dopamine-blocking antipsychotic shelves test a different mechanism and are not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Do not generalise HARMONY to starting pimavanserin in all dementia psychosis: most of the randomised benefit estimate comes from a responder-enriched, early-stopped trial.

shelves.title: VMAT2 inhibitors for tardive dyskinesia: valbenazine (KINECT-3) and deutetrabenazine (AIM-TD)
shelves.question: Do vesicular monoamine transporter-2 inhibitors reduce involuntary movements in tardive dyskinesia versus placebo — valbenazine in KINECT-3 and deutetrabenazine in AIM-TD — the first drug class ever approved for this iatrogenic disorder?
shelves.mesh: Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale · Antipsychotic Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Drug Therapy, Combination · Mood Disorders/drug therapy · Psychotic Disorders/drug therapy · Schizophrenia/drug therapy
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two independent phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials of two different VMAT2 inhibitors point the same way on the same scale: valbenazine 80 mg improved AIMS dyskinesia score by −3.2 versus −0.1 on placebo at 6 weeks (KINECT-3), and deutetrabenazine 24 and 36 mg/day improved it by −3.2 and −3.3 versus −1.4 on placebo at 12 weeks (AIM-TD), with adverse-event rates close to placebo in both. Two concordant blinded trials of a class, on a clinician-rated movement scale, carry LIKELY — for short-term movement reduction, in patients whose underlying psychiatric treatment continues.

cards.headline: KINECT-3 (Hauser 2017): valbenazine 80 mg/day improved AIMS dyskinesia score by −3.2 versus −0.1 on placebo at 6 weeks
cards.summary: KINECT-3 (2017): valbenazine 80 mg/day improved AIMS dyskinesia score by −3.2 vs −0.1 on placebo at 6 weeks.
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (6 weeks)
cards.people: 225 participants (intent-to-treat) with schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder or a mood disorder and moderate or severe tardive dyskinesia, randomised to placebo, valbenazine 40 mg/day or valbenazine 80 mg/day; about 65% had schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder and 85.5% were receiving concomitant antipsychotics; 205 completed the study. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Least-squares mean change in AIMS dyskinesia score (items 1–7, blinded central video raters) at week 6: −3.2 in the 80 mg/day group versus −0.1 on placebo, a significant difference; the 40 mg/day group improved by −1.9 versus −0.1. The incidence of adverse events was consistent with previous studies, and psychiatric status remained stable.
cards.watchOut: Six weeks is short for a chronic, potentially permanent disorder, and the abstract reports no patient-centred outcome (function, stigma, quality of life) — the claim is movement-score reduction, nothing wider.
cards.source: Hauser RA et al. KINECT 3: A Phase 3 Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial of Valbenazine for Tardive Dyskinesia. Am J Psychiatry. 2017;174(5):476-484. PMID: 28320223. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02274558, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: AIM-TD (Anderson 2017): deutetrabenazine 24 and 36 mg/day improved AIMS score by −3.2 and −3.3 versus −1.4 on placebo at 12 weeks; the 12 mg dose did not separate
cards.summary: AIM-TD (2017): deutetrabenazine 24 and 36 mg/day improved AIMS by −3.2 and −3.3 vs −1.4 on placebo at 12 weeks.
cards.type: Double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (12 weeks, fixed doses)
cards.people: 298 patients aged 18–80 years with tardive dyskinesia (at least 3 months before screening) at 75 US and European centres, randomised to deutetrabenazine 12, 24 or 36 mg/day or placebo (about 74–75 per group); 222 comprised the modified intention-to-treat population. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Least-squares mean AIMS improvement at week 12: −3.3 points (36 mg/day) and −3.2 (24 mg/day) versus −1.4 on placebo (treatment differences −1.9, 95% CI −3.09 to −0.79, p=0.001, and −1.8, −3.00 to −0.63, p=0.003); the 12 mg/day dose (−2.1) did not differ significantly from placebo (difference −0.7, p=0.217). Adverse-event rates were similar across groups (44–51% deutetrabenazine, 47% placebo); serious adverse events occurred in 5%, 8% and 3% on the three doses versus 6% on placebo. Two patients (1%) in the deutetrabenazine groups died, neither death deemed related to the study drug.
cards.watchOut: The effective doses sit at the top of the tested range and the lowest dose failed — dose matters, and the 12-week horizon still leaves long-term benefit and harm open.

shelves.title: Suzetrigine, the NaV1.8 inhibitor, for acute pain
shelves.question: Does suzetrigine — a selective peripheral NaV1.8 sodium-channel blocker with no opioid activity — relieve moderate-to-severe acute pain after abdominoplasty and bunionectomy versus placebo, and how does it compare with hydrocodone–acetaminophen in the same trials?
shelves.mesh: Acute Pain/drug therapy · Acetaminophen/therapeutic use · Pain Measurement/drug effects,methods · Analgesics, Non-Narcotic/therapeutic use · Hydrocodone/therapeutic use · Postoperative Pain/drug therapy · Voltage-Gated Sodium Channel Blockers/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY: The programme is four randomised, double-blind trials in two surgical pain models: the phase 2 VX-548 trials (highest dose only separated from placebo) and the two phase 3 suzetrigine trials (1,118 abdominoplasty and 1,073 bunionectomy patients), in which suzetrigine beat placebo on the prespecified SPID48 endpoint in both models (least-squares mean differences 48.4 and 29.3). LIKELY attaches to the placebo comparison only: neither phase 3 trial achieved its key secondary endpoint of superiority over hydrocodone–acetaminophen, and the abstracts describe pain reduction as similar to the opioid combination — a new non-opioid that matches, not beats, a standard opioid combination over 48 hours.

cards.headline: Suzetrigine phase 3 pair (Bertoch 2025): SPID48 beat placebo after abdominoplasty (difference 48.4) and bunionectomy (29.3) — but superiority over hydrocodone–acetaminophen was not achieved in either trial
cards.summary: Suzetrigine phase 3 pair (2025): SPID48 beat placebo after abdominoplasty (difference 48.4 ) and bunionectomy ( 29.3 ) — superiority over hydrocodone-acetaminophen not shown.
cards.type: Two phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo- and active-controlled trials (48 hours)
cards.people: Adults with moderate-to-severe acute pain (verbal categorical rating scale, and 4 or greater on the numeric pain rating scale) after abdominoplasty (n=1,118) or bunionectomy (n=1,073), randomised to suzetrigine (100 mg, then 50 mg every 12 hours), hydrocodone bitartrate/acetaminophen (5/325 mg every 6 hours), or placebo for 48 hours. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: The primary endpoint (time-weighted sum of pain-intensity difference over 48 hours, SPID48, versus placebo) was achieved in both trials: least-squares mean difference 48.4 (95% CI 33.6 to 63.1, p<0.0001) after abdominoplasty and 29.3 (14.0 to 44.6, p=0.0002) after bunionectomy. Neither trial achieved the first key secondary endpoint of superiority over hydrocodone bitartrate/acetaminophen on SPID48. Time to a 2-point or greater reduction in pain score was faster on suzetrigine than placebo (119 vs 480 minutes after abdominoplasty; 240 vs 480 minutes after bunionectomy). Adverse events were mild to moderate.
cards.watchOut: The active-comparator result is a non-result by design hierarchy: 'not superior' in a trial not powered as a non-inferiority test against the opioid cannot be read as proven equivalence, and 48 hours after two specific operations is the whole evidence window.
cards.source: Bertoch T et al. Suzetrigine, a Nonopioid NaV 1.8 Inhibitor for Treatment of Moderate-to-severe Acute Pain: Two Phase 3 Randomized Clinical Trials. Anesthesiology. 2025;142(6):1085-1099. PMID: 40117446. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields.

cards.summary: VX-548 phase 2 (2023): only the highest dose reduced pain vs placebo (SPID48 differences 37.8 and 36.8); lower doses were similar to placebo.

shelves.title: Cenobamate as adjunctive therapy for uncontrolled focal seizures
shelves.question: Does adjunctive cenobamate reduce focal seizure frequency versus placebo in adults whose seizures persist on one to three antiseizure drugs — in its dose-response trial and its phase 2 fixed-dose trial?
shelves.mesh: Anticonvulsants/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Chemotherapy, Adjuvant/adverse effects,methods · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Drug Resistant Epilepsy/drug therapy · Epilepsies, Partial/drug therapy · Seizures/drug therapy · Anticonvulsants/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two double-blind, placebo-controlled trials agree on a dose-related effect: the dose-response trial (437 randomised) found median seizure-frequency reductions of −55.0% at 200 and 400 mg versus −24.0% on placebo, with maintenance responder rates of 56% and 64% versus 25%; the fixed-dose phase 2 trial (222 randomised) found a median reduction of 55.6% versus 21.5% and a responder rate of 50.4% versus 22.2% at 200 mg. Two concordant blinded trials carry LIKELY. The price rises with dose: treatment-emergent adverse events reached 90% at 400 mg, discontinuation for adverse events 20%, and one serious case of DRESS occurred at 200 mg in the dose-response trial — the slow-titration warning on the shelf face is part of the evidence, not an afterthought.

cards.headline: Krauss 2020: adjunctive cenobamate cut median seizure frequency by −55.0% at 200 and 400 mg versus −24.0% on placebo; maintenance responder rates 56% and 64% versus 25%
cards.summary: Krauss (2020): adjunctive cenobamate cut median seizure frequency by −55.0% at 200 and 400 mg vs −24.0% on placebo.
cards.type: Multicentre, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled dose-response trial (6-week titration, 12-week maintenance)
cards.people: 437 adults aged 18–70 years with focal seizures despite 1–3 antiepileptic drugs at 107 centres in 16 countries, randomised to cenobamate 100 mg (108), 200 mg (110) or 400 mg (111) once daily or placebo (108), after an 8-week baseline.
cards.result: Median percentage change in 28-day focal seizure frequency: −24.0% on placebo versus −35.5% (100 mg, p=0.0071), −55.0% (200 mg, p<0.0001) and −55.0% (400 mg, p<0.0001). Responder rates (50% or greater reduction) in the maintenance phase: 25% on placebo versus 40% (100 mg; odds ratio 1.97, 95% CI 1.08 to 3.56 — a relative measure), 56% (200 mg; OR 3.74, 2.06 to 6.80) and 64% (400 mg; OR 5.24, 2.84 to 9.67). Treatment-emergent adverse events: 70% placebo, 65% (100 mg), 76% (200 mg), 90% (400 mg); discontinuation for adverse events 5%, 10%, 14% and 20% respectively. One serious case of drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) occurred in the 200 mg group. No deaths were reported.
cards.watchOut: The abstract does not report the seizure-freedom rates the trial is often quoted for, so none are printed here. Eighteen weeks of blinded treatment in a lifelong disease, and the dose that works best is also the dose a fifth of patients stopped for adverse events.

shelves.title: Efgartigimod for generalised myasthenia gravis (ADAPT)
shelves.question: Does the FcRn antagonist efgartigimod — which lowers circulating IgG, including the pathogenic acetylcholine-receptor antibodies — produce a clinically meaningful improvement in generalised myasthenia gravis versus placebo (ADAPT)?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Antibodies, Monoclonal/therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/therapeutic use · Autoantibodies/immunology · Headache/drug therapy · Immunoglobulin Fc Fragments/therapeutic use · Longitudinal Studies
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: ADAPT is a single randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (167 patients), and a single pivotal trial caps at POSSIBLE. Within it, the effect is large: among acetylcholine-receptor antibody-positive patients, 68% on efgartigimod were MG-ADL responders in cycle 1 versus 30% on placebo (odds ratio 4.95), with adverse events no more frequent than placebo (77% vs 84%) and no deaths. The subcutaneous programme (ADAPT-SC) showed non-inferiority of the subcutaneous form to the intravenous form — a formulation result, not a second placebo-controlled efficacy trial — so it is fenced in the synthesis and does not lift the stamp.

cards.headline: ADAPT (Howard 2021): 68% of antibody-positive patients on efgartigimod were MG-ADL responders in cycle 1, versus 30% on placebo (odds ratio 4.95)
cards.summary: ADAPT (2021): 68% of antibody-positive patients on efgartigimod were MG-ADL responders in cycle 1 vs 30% on placebo.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (individualised cycles of four weekly infusions)
cards.people: 167 patients aged at least 18 years with generalised myasthenia gravis (MG-ADL score at least 5, on a stable dose of at least one myasthenia treatment) at 56 centres in 15 countries, randomised to efgartigimod 10 mg/kg (84) or placebo (83); 129 (77%) were acetylcholine-receptor antibody-positive. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — MG-ADL responders (2-point or greater improvement sustained for at least 4 weeks) among antibody-positive patients in cycle 1 — occurred in 44 of 65 (68%) on efgartigimod versus 19 of 64 (30%) on placebo (odds ratio 4.95, 95% CI 2.21 to 11.53, p<0.0001 — a relative measure, absolute rates beside it). Treatment-emergent adverse events: 65 of 84 (77%) on efgartigimod versus 70 of 83 (84%) on placebo, most frequently headache (29% vs 28%) and nasopharyngitis (12% vs 18%). Serious adverse events in four (5%) efgartigimod patients and seven (8%) on placebo; three patients in each group discontinued; there were no deaths.
cards.watchOut: One trial, with the primary analysis confined to the antibody-positive 77% and to the first treatment cycle; how benefit accumulates or fades over repeated cycles is extension-study territory, not randomised evidence.

shelves.title: Tofersen for SOD1 amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (VALOR)
shelves.question: In ALS caused by SOD1 mutations, does intrathecal tofersen — an antisense oligonucleotide against SOD1 — lower CSF SOD1 and plasma neurofilament light versus placebo (VALOR), and what does the long-term early- versus delayed-start comparison show, given the trial's primary clinical endpoint at 28 weeks was not met?
shelves.mesh: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis/blood,cerebrospinal fluid,drug therapy,genetics · Biomarkers/blood,cerebrospinal fluid · Injections, Spinal · Neurofilament Proteins/blood · Oligonucleotides, Antisense/administration & dosage,pharmacology,therapeutic use · Recovery of Function/drug effects · Superoxide Dismutase-1/cerebrospinal fluid,genetics
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE for the biomarker and early-start pattern; MAYBE (weak evidence) for proven clinical benefit. VALOR (108 patients) did exactly what the molecule promises on biomarkers — greater reductions in CSF SOD1 and plasma neurofilament light than placebo — and missed its primary clinical endpoint: in the faster-progression subgroup, ALSFRS-R change at week 28 was −6.98 on tofersen versus −8.14 on placebo (difference 1.2 points, 95% CI −3.2 to 5.5, p=0.97). The long-term integrated VALOR/open-label-extension report (up to 3.5 years or more of follow-up) found numerically less decline with early start than delayed start across function, respiratory, strength and quality-of-life measures — an early-versus-delayed comparison after everyone received the drug, not a randomised placebo comparison, and its survival statement rests on expected natural history, not on a randomised control. No randomised survival benefit is claimed on this shelf.

cards.headline: VALOR (Miller 2022): tofersen lowered CSF SOD1 and plasma neurofilament light, but the primary clinical endpoint was not met (ALSFRS-R difference 1.2 points, p=0.97)
cards.summary: VALOR (2022): tofersen lowered CSF SOD1 and plasma neurofilament light, but the primary clinical endpoint was not met.
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (eight doses over 24 weeks; primary endpoint at week 28) with an open-label extension
cards.people: 108 adults with SOD1 ALS randomly assigned 2:1 to intrathecal tofersen 100 mg (72) or placebo (36); the primary analysis subgroup predicted to have faster progression numbered 39 on tofersen and 21 on placebo; 95 participants (88%) entered the open-label extension. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Tofersen led to greater reductions in CSF SOD1 concentration and plasma neurofilament light than placebo. In the faster-progression subgroup, ALSFRS-R change to week 28 was −6.98 on tofersen versus −8.14 on placebo (difference 1.2 points, 95% CI −3.2 to 5.5, p=0.97); secondary clinical endpoints did not differ significantly. In the combined randomised-plus-extension analysis at 52 weeks, ALSFRS-R change was −6.0 in the early-start cohort versus −9.5 in the delayed-start cohort (difference 3.5 points, 95% CI 0.4 to 6.7). Lumbar-puncture-related adverse events were common; neurologic serious adverse events occurred in 7% of tofersen recipients.
cards.watchOut: The trial is the discordance itself: biomarkers moved, the prespecified clinical endpoint did not. The 52-week early-versus-delayed comparison is not placebo-controlled and its differences were, for most endpoints, not multiplicity-adjusted.

cards.headline: Long-term VALOR + extension (Miller 2026): over 148 weeks, early start showed numerically less decline than delayed start on function, respiratory, strength and quality-of-life measures
cards.summary: Long-term VALOR + extension (2026): over 148 weeks, early start showed numerically less decline than delayed start on function and respiration (non-randomised comparison).
cards.type: Integrated analysis of the randomised VALOR trial and its open-label extension (early-start versus placebo/delayed-start)
cards.people: 108 participants with SOD1 ALS and 42 unique SOD1 pathogenic variants at 32 sites in 10 countries; mean (SD) age 48.1 (12.6) years in the early-start group (n=72) and 51.2 (11.6) in the placebo/delayed-start group (n=36), with 60% and 53% men respectively; 95 of 108 (88%) entered the extension, 46 completed it, and follow-up from the start of VALOR could reach 3.5 years or more (192–276 weeks).
cards.result: Over 148 weeks, earlier initiation was associated with numerically less decline than later initiation in ALSFRS-R score (−9.9 vs −13.5 points), slow vital capacity (−13.8% vs −18.1%), handheld dynamometry megascore (−0.38 vs −0.43 points) and quality-of-life scores (ALS Assessment Questionnaire-5, 17.0 vs 22.5 points). The authors state tofersen prolonged survival relative to the expected natural history of SOD1-ALS — a comparison against expected natural history, not against a randomised control group. Most adverse events were consistent with ALS progression or procedural effects; all serious neurological adverse events were reversible and few led to discontinuation.
cards.watchOut: After week 28 everyone was on tofersen, so the long-term contrast is timing, not drug versus no drug; 'numerically less decline' is the abstract's own wording, and the survival sentence has no randomised comparator. This card is a second report of the VALOR programme, counted once as evidence.

shelves.title: Inebilizumab for neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (N-MOmentum)
shelves.question: Does the CD19 B-cell-depleting antibody inebilizumab reduce the risk of an NMOSD attack versus placebo in aquaporin-4-positive and -negative patients (N-MOmentum, stopped early for efficacy)?
shelves.mesh: Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/therapeutic use · Hospitalization · Neuromyelitis Optica/complications,drug therapy · Severity of Illness Index
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: N-MOmentum is a single randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (230 dosed), and a single pivotal trial caps at POSSIBLE — even though its effect is large: attacks occurred in 12% on inebilizumab versus 39% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.272). Two features hold the stamp down rather than the effect size: the randomised period was stopped before complete enrolment on the data-monitoring committee's recommendation because of clear efficacy, and early-stopped trials overestimate effects; and there is no second inebilizumab trial. The satralizumab SAkura programme — a different drug for the same disease — is fenced as class context in the synthesis, not counted as this shelf's second trial.

shelves.title: Basivertebral nerve ablation for vertebrogenic chronic low back pain (INTRACEPT)
shelves.question: In chronic low back pain with Modic type 1 or 2 changes, does intraosseous radiofrequency ablation of the basivertebral nerve (Intracept) improve pain and function versus a sham procedure (INTRACEPT randomised trial)?
shelves.mesh: Catheter Ablation/methods · Chronic Pain/physiopathology,surgery · Low Back Pain/physiopathology,surgery · Pain Measurement · Spine/innervation,physiopathology,surgery
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: INTRACEPT is a single sham-controlled randomised trial (225 randomised), and a single trial caps at POSSIBLE. At 3 months the treatment arm's Oswestry Disability Index fell 20.5 points versus 15.2 on sham (p=0.019, per-protocol), with responders (10-point or greater ODI improvement) at 75.6% versus 55.3% — a real but modest margin over a sham arm that itself improved substantially, in a per-protocol primary analysis. The 2-year report follows only the treated arm against its own baseline, because most sham patients crossed over: durability within the treated group, not randomised durability. One sham-controlled trial plus an uncontrolled extension: POSSIBLE.

cards.summary: INTRACEPT (2018): ODI fell 20.5 points after basivertebral nerve ablation vs 15.2 after sham at 3 months; responders 75.6% vs 55.4%.
cards.type: Prospective, randomised, double-blind, sham-controlled multicentre trial (FDA investigational device exemption)
cards.people: 225 patients with chronic low back pain and type 1 or type 2 Modic changes at the treated vertebral bodies, randomised to basivertebral nerve radiofrequency ablation (147) or sham (78); mean age 47 years (range 25–69) and mean baseline ODI 42. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: At 3 months, average ODI decreased 20.5 points in the treatment arm versus 15.2 points in the sham arm (p=0.019, per-protocol population). A responder analysis (ODI decrease of 10 points or more) showed 75.6% of the treatment arm versus 55.3% of the sham arm achieving a clinically meaningful improvement at 3 months. Follow-up continued to 12 months.
cards.watchOut: The primary analysis is per-protocol rather than intention-to-treat, and the sham arm's 15.2-point improvement shows how much of the treated response is contextual — the randomised margin over sham is 5.3 ODI points, not 20.5.

shelves.title: Scopolamine for seasickness: the naval trial, and the patch question
shelves.question: Does scopolamine prevent seasickness — oral scopolamine, alone or with ephedrine, in a naval trial at sea, and the transdermal patch travellers actually use?
shelves.mesh: Clinical Trials as Topic · Drug Therapy, Combination · Ephedrine/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Motion Sickness/drug therapy · Placebos · Scopolamine/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Motion Sickness/prevention & control
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two small, old randomised trials support scopolamine at sea. Laitinen 1981 (30 naval cadets, double-blind, placebo-controlled) confirmed the superiority of oral scopolamine 0.3 mg — alone or combined with ephedrine 25 mg — over placebo, with ephedrine adding no clear benefit. Price 1981 found transdermal scopolamine (applied 4 to 16 hours before motion) protective against motion sickness at sea versus placebo (P=0.0001), with oral dimenhydrinate also better than placebo (P=0.05) and minimal dry mouth, drowsiness and blurred vision on the patch. That is the whole randomised patch evidence this gate could pin in English: two trials from 1981 with small numbers, which caps the shelf at POSSIBLE exactly as the topic drafting anticipated. The German-language transdermal report (Becker 1984, PMID 6499689) was verified at drafting and is fenced as background, not carded.

cards.headline: Laitinen 1981: oral scopolamine beat placebo in 30 naval cadets at sea; adding ephedrine did not clearly help
cards.summary: Laitinen (1981): oral scopolamine beat placebo in 30 naval cadets at sea; adding ephedrine did not clearly help (the abstract reports no percentages, and none are printed).
cards.people: 30 naval cadets during a sea crossing, given capsules of scopolamine hydrobromide 0.3 mg, scopolamine 0.3 mg plus ephedrine hydrochloride 25 mg, or placebo, prophylactically three times daily. The abstract does not state mean age; the topic record describes the participants as young healthy male volunteers.
cards.result: The superiority of scopolamine and of scopolamine plus ephedrine over placebo was confirmed (the abstract reports no percentages, and none are printed here); ephedrine did not clearly increase scopolamine's effectiveness. One subject in the scopolamine group and one in the placebo group interrupted treatment. Seasickness symptoms and drug side-effects both decreased by the third day of the study.
cards.watchOut: Thirty cadets, one crossing, and an abstract without a single number: this card can carry direction (better than placebo) but no effect size, and day-3 improvement mixes drug effect with habituation to the sea.

cards.headline: Price 1981: the scopolamine patch protected against motion sickness at sea (P=0.0001 versus placebo)
cards.summary: Price (1981): the scopolamine patch protected against motion sickness at sea (P=0.0001 vs placebo).
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial of transdermal delivery (design as described in the record's abstract)
cards.people: Volunteers exposed to motion at sea; transdermal scopolamine was applied 4 to 16 hours before exposure, and comparators were oral dimenhydrinate (1.5 hours before motion and again 2.5 hours after it began) and placebo. cards.result: Against placebo, transdermal scopolamine provided protection against motion sickness at a significance level of P=0.0001, and oral dimenhydrinate at P=0.05. Dry mouth, drowsiness and blurred vision associated with transdermal scopolamine were minimal. The abstract reports no event rates, so none are printed here.
cards.watchOut: A 1981 delivery-system study whose abstract gives significance levels without denominators or rates: it establishes that the patch beat placebo in that study, and nothing about how large the benefit is, how it compares with modern antiemetics, or how it performs on multi-day voyages.

cards.headline: Synthesis: scopolamine works at sea in the forms tested — POSSIBLE, on 1981 evidence alone
cards.summary: Synthesis: scopolamine works at sea in the forms tested — POSSIBLE, on 1981 evidence alone.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Laitinen 1981 (30 naval cadets, oral) and Price 1981 (transdermal, numbers not stated in the abstract).
cards.result: The oral and transdermal forms each beat placebo in their own small sea trial, and the combination with ephedrine added nothing clear. Forty-plus years later the patch remains in use on exactly this evidence base: no newer randomised trial was found in the currency sweep, and neither carded abstract quantifies the benefit. A traveller choosing the patch is choosing a plausibly effective, minimally sedating option whose effect size this library cannot honestly state.
cards.watchOut: Anticholinergic cautions (glaucoma, urinary retention, confusion in older travellers) come from the drug class, not from these trials, whose young sea-going volunteers cannot speak for older cruise passengers.

shelves.title: Corticosteroids after significant head injury (CRASH)
shelves.question: In adults with clinically significant head injury, does intravenous methylprednisolone reduce death within 14 days versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Craniocerebral Trauma/drug therapy,mortality · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage · Methylprednisolone/administration & dosage · Double-Blind Method · Glasgow Coma Scale · Survival Rate · Humans · Adult · Middle Aged · Female · Male
shelves.balance: LIKELY (harm) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality harm): The one large randomised test (CRASH, 10,008 adults with head injury and Glasgow Coma Scale score of 14 or less) found corticosteroids INCREASED death: within 14 days, 21.1% died on methylprednisolone versus 17.9% on placebo (relative risk 1.18 relative, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.27; P=0.0001), and the 6-month report of the same trial (counted once) found death in 25.7% versus 22.3% (relative risk 1.15 relative, 1.07 to 1.24; P=0.0001), with no subgroup — by injury severity or time since injury — escaping the harm. Recruitment was stopped early by the data monitoring committee when the harm emerged. This is the library's clearest harm verdict in brain injury: steroids after head injury kill more people than they save, and no benefit claim of any kind survives this record.

cards.headline: CRASH 2004: methylprednisolone increased death within 14 days after head injury (21.1% vs 17.9%; relative risk 1.18)
cards.summary: CRASH 2004: methylprednisolone increased death within 14 days after head injury (21.1% vs 17.9%; relative risk 1.18)
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled trial (multicentre, international) — stopped early by the data monitoring committee
cards.people: 10,008 adults with head injury and a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 14 or less, randomised within 8 hours of injury to a 48-hour infusion of corticosteroid (methylprednisolone) or placebo; the abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Compared with placebo, the risk of death from all causes within 2 weeks was higher in the group allocated corticosteroids (1,052 [21.1%] vs 893 [17.9%] deaths; relative risk 1.18 relative, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.27; P=0.0001). The relative increase in deaths did not differ by injury severity (P=0.22) or time since injury (P=0.05). The trial had planned to recruit 20,000 patients; in May 2004 the data monitoring committee disclosed the unmasked results to the steering committee, which stopped recruitment.
cards.watchOut: The trial refuted the very hypothesis it was built to confirm — a 1997 systematic review had suggested steroids might reduce death by 1–2% — and the cause of the excess deaths remains unclear; what is not unclear is the direction and size of the effect in 10,008 patients.
cards.source: Roberts I et al. Effect of intravenous corticosteroids on death within 14 days in 10008 adults with clinically significant head injury (MRC CRASH trial): randomised placebo-controlled trial. Lancet. 2004. PMID: 15474134. Registry ID: ISRCTN ISRCTN74459797, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: CRASH 6-month report 2005: the mortality excess persisted (25.7% vs 22.3%), and death or severe disability was not reduced
cards.summary: CRASH 6-month report 2005: the mortality excess persisted (25.7% vs 22.3%), and death or severe disability was not reduced
cards.type: Six-month outcomes report of the same CRASH trial — counted once as evidence
cards.people: The same 10,008 adults randomised in CRASH; data at 6 months were obtained for 9,673 (96.7%) patients.
cards.result: The risk of death was higher in the corticosteroid group than in the placebo group (1,248 [25.7%] vs 1,075 [22.3%] deaths; relative risk 1.15 relative, 95% CI 1.07 to 1.24; P=0.0001), as was the risk of death or severe disability (1,828 [38.1%] vs 1,728 [36.3%]; relative risk 1.05 relative, 0.99 to 1.10; P=0.079). cards.watchOut: A follow-up report of the same trial, not a second trial: it extends the harm finding to 6 months and must never be pooled with the 14-day report as independent evidence.

cards.headline: Synthesis: corticosteroids after head injury increase death at 2 weeks and at 6 months — LIKELY (harm)
cards.summary: Synthesis: corticosteroids after head injury increase death at 2 weeks and at 6 months — LIKELY (harm)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: CRASH 14-day report 2004 and CRASH 6-month report 2005 — one trial, 10,008 adults with head injury.
cards.result: One very large trial, reported twice, gives one answer: a 48-hour methylprednisolone infusion after significant head injury raised all-cause mortality by about 3 percentage points at 2 weeks (21.1% vs 17.9%) and at 6 months (25.7% vs 22.3%), with no severity or timing subgroup showing benefit. The stamp is proposed pending the developer's personal verdict because the claim is mortality harm (Tier C).
cards.watchOut: Do not let the historical practice ('steroids were given for 30 years') soften this: CRASH is exactly the large, simple, randomised test the question needed, and it found harm.

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED: Disclosure first: the anchor pinned in the topic file for this shelf (PMID 40067302) is, on verification, a prospective multicentre COHORT study of children — not the randomised comparison the topic file described — so it is carded below labelled as observational, and the shelf's randomised anchor is the small adult trial pinned by title search instead. That trial (Jagannatha 2016, 38 adults with severe TBI and refractory intracranial hypertension) found hypertonic saline lowered ICP faster per bolus than equiosmolar mannitol (slope of ICP fall, P=0.0001) and avoided the progressive ICP rise seen with mannitol, but 6-month mortality (6 vs 10 deaths; P=0.41) and dichotomised Glasgow Outcome Scale scores (P=0.21) did not differ. The paediatric cohort (445 children) likewise found no adjusted difference in mortality (7.1% hypertonic saline vs 11.0% mannitol; P=.34) or functional outcomes. Faster ICP physiology, no demonstrated outcome advantage: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) on outcomes.

cards.headline: Jagannatha 2016: hypertonic saline lowered ICP faster per bolus than mannitol, but 6-month mortality and outcome scores did not differ (38 adults)
cards.summary: Jagannatha 2016: hypertonic saline lowered ICP faster per bolus than mannitol, but 6-month mortality and outcome scores did not differ (38 adults)
cards.type: Prospective randomised controlled trial (single centre, severe TBI) — the randomised anchor pinned at build after the topic file's anchor failed verification as a trial
cards.people: 38 patients with severe traumatic brain injury and refractory intracranial hypertension, treated for over 450 episodes with equiosmolar boluses of 20% mannitol (20 patients) or 3.0% hypertonic saline (18 patients), with ICP monitored for 6 days; the abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: ICP and cerebral perfusion pressure were comparable between the groups. The mannitol group had a progressive increase in ICP over the study period (P=0.01); a similar increase was not seen in the hypertonic saline group (P=0.1). The percentage of time ICP remained below 20 mmHg on day 6 was higher with hypertonic saline (63% versus 49%; P=0.3). The duration of inotrope requirement was less with hypertonic saline (P=0.06). The slope of fall in ICP in response to a bolus at a given baseline ICP was higher with hypertonic saline than mannitol (P=0.0001). In-hospital mortality tended to be lower with hypertonic saline (3 versus 10 deaths; P=0.07), while mortality at 6 months was not different (6 versus 10; P=0.41), and dichotomised Glasgow Outcome Scale scores at 6 months were comparable (P=0.21).
cards.watchOut: Thirty-eight patients: the in-hospital mortality gap (3 vs 10) is the kind of small-number signal that evaporates by 6 months in this very record — the trial's own conclusion is that the immediate physiological advantages did not translate into long-term benefit.
cards.source: Jagannatha AT et al. An equiosmolar study on early intracranial physiology and long term outcome in severe traumatic brain injury comparing mannitol and hypertonic saline. J Clin Neurosci. 2016. PMID: 26924183. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Chong 2025: in 445 children with TBI, hypertonic saline was not associated with better survival or function than mannitol — a prospective COHORT study, not a randomised trial
cards.summary: Chong 2025: in 445 children with TBI, hypertonic saline was not associated with better survival or function than mannitol — a prospective COHORT study, not a randomised trial
cards.type: Prospective, multicentre cohort study (28 paediatric ICUs, Asia, Latin America and Europe) — observational; the topic file's pinned anchor, carded here with its design stated on its face
cards.people: 445 children (aged under 18 years) with moderate to severe traumatic brain injury (Glasgow Coma Scale score 13 or less), median age 5.0 (IQR 2.0–11.0) years, 279 (62.7%) boys, 344 (77.3%) with severe TBI; 184 children (41.3%) received 3% hypertonic saline, 82 (18.4%) received 20% mannitol, 69 (15.5%) received both agents and 110 (24.7%) received neither.
cards.result: The mortality rate was 7.1% (13 of 184 patients) in the hypertonic saline group and 11.0% (9 of 82 patients) in the mannitol group (P=.34). After adjusting for age, sex, presence of child abuse, time between injury and hospital arrival, lowest GCS score in the first 24 hours, and presence of extradural hemorrhage — and in inverse-probability-weighted analyses — no between-group differences in mortality, hospital discharge Pediatric Cerebral Performance Category scores, or 3-month Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended Pediatric Version scores were observed. The authors state that future large multicentre randomized clinical trials are required to validate these findings.
cards.watchOut: Treatment was chosen by clinicians, not randomised: children given one agent, both, or neither differed at baseline in ways adjustment can only partly repair, so this card supports the randomised trial's null rather than standing as a test in its own right.
cards.source: Chong SL et al. Clinical Outcomes of Hypertonic Saline vs Mannitol Treatment Among Children With Traumatic Brain Injury. JAMA Network Open. 2025. PMID: 40067302. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: hypertonic saline moves ICP faster; neither the small adult RCT nor the paediatric cohort shows an outcome advantage — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Synthesis: hypertonic saline moves ICP faster; neither the small adult RCT nor the paediatric cohort shows an outcome advantage — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Jagannatha 2016 (38 adults with severe TBI, randomised) and Chong 2025 (445 children with moderate-to-severe TBI, observational cohort).
cards.result: The randomised evidence for choosing between the two osmotic agents is one 38-patient trial: hypertonic saline produced a steeper ICP fall per bolus and no late ICP creep, with identical 6-month mortality and outcome scores. The largest paediatric dataset is observational and points the same way (no adjusted survival or functional difference). Agent choice can reasonably rest on physiology, sodium and renal considerations, and local practice — not on a proven outcome difference, which no record here shows.
cards.watchOut: This shelf was rebuilt at build: the topic file's anchor turned out to be a cohort study wearing a trial's clothes. Treat any future citation of PMID 40067302 as randomised evidence as an error.

shelves.title: Seizure prophylaxis after traumatic brain injury: phenytoin and levetiracetam
shelves.question: In patients with severe head injury, does prophylactic phenytoin prevent early post-traumatic seizures, and how does levetiracetam compare?
shelves.mesh: Epilepsy, Post-Traumatic/prevention & control · Phenytoin/blood,therapeutic use · Levetiracetam · Anticonvulsants/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Seizures/etiology,prevention & control · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Adult · Female · Male
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED, for the first-week claim, with the levetiracetam comparison at POSSIBLE: The one large double-blind trial (Temkin 1990, 404 patients with serious head trauma) found phenytoin cut seizures in the first week from 14.2% on placebo to 3.6% (risk ratio 0.27 relative, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.62; P<0.001) — and did nothing thereafter: seizures between day 8 and one year were 21.5% versus 15.7%, and by two years 27.5% versus 21.1%. So prophylaxis prevents early seizures only, and does not prevent later epilepsy. The head-to-head levetiracetam trial (Szaflarski 2010, 52 patients, single-blind) found no difference in seizure occurrence (5 of 34 vs 3 of 18 during continuous EEG; P=1.0), with better adjusted long-term functional scores on levetiracetam in a very small sample — an alternative at POSSIBLE, not a proven equal.

cards.headline: Temkin 1990: phenytoin prevented seizures in the first week only (3.6% vs 14.2%); no benefit from day 8 to two years
cards.summary: Temkin 1990: phenytoin prevented seizures in the first week only (3.6% vs 14.2%); no benefit from day 8 to two years
cards.people: 404 eligible patients with serious head trauma, randomly assigned to phenytoin (208) or placebo (196) for one year in double-blind fashion, with an intravenous loading dose within 24 hours of injury and serum levels maintained in the high therapeutic range; follow-up continued for two years. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Between drug loading and day 7, 3.6 percent of the patients assigned to phenytoin had seizures, as compared with 14.2 percent of patients assigned to placebo (P<0.001; risk ratio 0.27 relative, 95 percent confidence interval, 0.12 to 0.62). Between day 8 and the end of year 1, 21.5 percent of the phenytoin group and 15.7 percent of the placebo group had seizures; at the end of year 2, the rates were 27.5 percent and 21.1 percent, respectively (P>0.2 for each comparison; risk ratio, 1.20 relative, 95 percent confidence interval, 0.71 to 2.02). The authors state the lack of a late effect could not be attributed to differential mortality, low phenytoin levels, or treatment of some early seizures in patients assigned to placebo.
cards.watchOut: The benefit is real but narrowly fenced: one week of seizure prevention, bought with a year of drug exposure in the trial's design. Nothing here supports continuing prophylaxis beyond the early period, and late post-traumatic epilepsy was not prevented.
cards.source: Temkin NR et al. A randomized, double-blind study of phenytoin for the prevention of post-traumatic seizures. N Engl J Med. 1990. PMID: 2115976. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields (pre-registration-era trial). cards.headline: Szaflarski 2010: levetiracetam and phenytoin did not differ in seizure occurrence (5/34 vs 3/18 on continuous EEG) in a 52-patient single-blind trial
cards.summary: Szaflarski 2010: levetiracetam and phenytoin did not differ in seizure occurrence (5/34 vs 3/18 on continuous EEG) in a 52-patient single-blind trial
cards.type: Prospective, randomised, single-blinded comparative trial (single centre)
cards.people: 52 patients with severe traumatic brain injury (89%) or subarachnoid haemorrhage, randomised 2:1 at a single centre to intravenous levetiracetam (34) or (fos)phenytoin (18), with continuous EEG monitoring for the initial 72 hours; the abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: There were no differences between groups in seizure occurrence during continuous EEG (levetiracetam 5 of 34 vs phenytoin 3 of 18; P=1.0) or at 6 months (1 of 20 vs 0 of 14; P=1.0), or in mortality (14 of 34 vs 4 of 18; P=0.227). When controlling for baseline severity, levetiracetam patients experienced better long-term outcomes: the Disability Rating Scale score was lower at 3 months (P=0.042) and the Glasgow Outcome Scale score was higher at 6 months (P=0.039). There were no differences in side effects (all P>0.15) except a lower frequency of worsened neurological status (P=0.024) and gastrointestinal problems (P=0.043) in levetiracetam-treated patients.
cards.watchOut: Fifty-two patients, single-blind, and a mixed population (11% subarachnoid haemorrhage): the functional-outcome differences come from adjusted analyses in a handful of patients, and the seizure comparison — 5 events versus 3 — can exclude almost nothing. It licenses levetiracetam as a plausible alternative, not as a proven equivalent.
cards.source: Szaflarski JP et al. Prospective, randomized, single-blinded comparative trial of intravenous levetiracetam versus phenytoin for seizure prophylaxis. Neurocrit Care. 2010. PMID: 19898966. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00618436, named in the record's abstract (not in its databank fields). cards.headline: Synthesis: prophylaxis works for week one only; levetiracetam is a plausible but unproven substitute — LIKELY (early) / POSSIBLE (levetiracetam)
cards.summary: Synthesis: prophylaxis works for week one only; levetiracetam is a plausible but unproven substitute — LIKELY (early) / POSSIBLE (levetiracetam)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Temkin 1990 (404 patients, phenytoin vs placebo, double-blind) and Szaflarski 2010 (52 patients, levetiracetam vs phenytoin, single-blind).
cards.result: The architecture of this literature is one strong trial and one small one. Temkin settles that phenytoin prevents early post-traumatic seizures (3.6% vs 14.2% in week one) and equally settles that it does not prevent late seizures. Szaflarski shows levetiracetam is used in the same role with no seizure signal against it, in a trial far too small to prove equivalence. The stamp is LIKELY for the first-week phenytoin claim and POSSIBLE for levetiracetam as its alternative.
cards.watchOut: Do not cite the levetiracetam trial for the claim that prophylaxis itself works — it has no placebo arm; that claim belongs to Temkin alone, and only for the first week.
cards.source: Synthesis of Temkin NR et al. N Engl J Med. 1990. PMID: 2115976; Szaflarski JP et al. Neurocrit Care. 2010. PMID: 19898966. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Erythropoietin in traumatic brain injury (EPO-TBI)
shelves.question: In patients with moderate-to-severe TBI, does epoetin alfa improve neurological outcome at 6 months or reduce mortality versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Brain Injuries/drug therapy,mortality · Erythropoietin/therapeutic use · Glasgow Outcome Scale · Double-Blind Method · Venous Thrombosis/epidemiology · Treatment Outcome · Humans · Adult · Middle Aged · Young Adult · Female · Male
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, neurological outcome with mortality co-reported): The one large double-blind trial (EPO-TBI, 606 patients with moderate-to-severe TBI in 29 centres across seven countries) found erythropoietin did not reduce severe neurological dysfunction at 6 months: an Extended Glasgow Outcome Scale level of 1–4 in 44% on erythropoietin versus 45% on placebo (relative risk 0.99 relative, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.18; P=0.90). Six-month mortality was 11% versus 16% (relative risk 0.68 relative, 0.44 to 1.03; P=0.07) — not significant, and the trial's own interpretation is that the effect on mortality remains uncertain; no mortality benefit is claimed on this shelf. Lower-limb deep venous thrombosis was not increased (16% vs 18%).

cards.headline: EPO-TBI 2015: erythropoietin did not improve 6-month neurological outcome (GOS-E 1–4 in 44% vs 45%); mortality 11% vs 16%, not significant
cards.summary: EPO-TBI 2015: erythropoietin did not improve 6-month neurological outcome (GOS-E 1–4 in 44% vs 45%); mortality 11% vs 16%, not significant
cards.people: 606 patients with moderate or severe traumatic brain injury, randomly assigned within 24 hours of injury at 29 university-affiliated centres in seven countries (Australia, New Zealand, France, Germany, Finland, Ireland, and Saudi Arabia) to erythropoietin 40,000 units subcutaneously (308) or placebo (298), once per week for a maximum of three doses; primary-outcome data were available for 596 patients. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Compared with placebo, erythropoietin did not reduce the proportion of patients with a GOS-E level of 1–4 — death, vegetative state, and severe disability — (134 [44%] of 302 patients in the erythropoietin group vs 132 [45%] of 294 in the placebo group; relative risk [RR] 0.99 relative [95% CI 0.83–1.18], p=0.90). Erythropoietin did not significantly affect 6-month mortality versus placebo (32 [11%] of 305 patients had died at 6 months in the erythropoietin group vs 46 [16%] of 297 in the placebo group; RR 0.68 relative [95% CI 0.44–1.03], p=0.07) or increase the occurrence of deep venous thrombosis of the lower limbs (48 [16%] of 305 vs 54 [18%] of 298; RR 0.87 relative [95% CI 0.61–1.24], p=0.44). The authors conclude the effect of erythropoietin on mortality remains uncertain.
cards.watchOut: The mortality point estimate (RR 0.68 relative) sits inside a confidence interval reaching 1.03: this trial neither proves a survival benefit nor excludes one, and the stamp covers the neurological-outcome null — the primary outcome — not a mortality claim in either direction.
cards.source: Nichol A et al. Erythropoietin in traumatic brain injury (EPO-TBI): a double-blind randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2015. PMID: 26452709. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00987454, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: one large blinded trial, no neurological benefit, mortality unresolved — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Synthesis: one large blinded trial, no neurological benefit, mortality unresolved — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: EPO-TBI 2015 (606 patients with moderate-to-severe TBI).
cards.result: EPO-TBI is the definitive test of erythropoietin as a neuroprotectant after TBI: 606 patients, double-blind, and a primary-outcome estimate centred exactly on no effect (RR 0.99 relative). The stamp is proposed pending the developer's personal verdict because mortality is co-reported with a non-significant trend (Tier C). Erythropoietin for transfusion avoidance in critical illness is a different question and is not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Animal neuroprotection data and subgroup mortality whispers do not outrank this trial; if a future trial tests the mortality signal directly, this shelf returns for re-review under the challenger-trial rule.

shelves.title: Progesterone for acute traumatic brain injury (ProTECT III and SYNAPSE)
shelves.question: In patients with moderate-to-severe acute TBI, does early intravenous progesterone improve functional outcome versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Brain Injuries/drug therapy · Progesterone/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Glasgow Outcome Scale · Double-Blind Method · Infusions, Intravenous · Treatment Failure · Humans · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Female · Male
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, functional outcome with mortality as a component/secondary outcome): Two large phase 3 double-blind trials, run in parallel and published side by side, are concordantly null. ProTECT III (882 patients randomised before stopping for futility) found no difference in favourable outcome at 6 months (relative benefit 0.95 relative, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.06; P=0.35), with more phlebitis/thrombophlebitis on progesterone (relative risk 3.03 relative, 1.96 to 4.66). SYNAPSE (1,195 patients with severe TBI) found favourable outcome in 50.4% on progesterone versus 50.5% on placebo (adjusted odds ratio 0.96 relative, 0.77 to 1.18), with mortality similar in the two groups. Two thousand randomised patients across two trials, both null: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: ProTECT III 2014: progesterone did not improve favourable outcome after TBI (relative benefit 0.95) — stopped for futility
cards.summary: ProTECT III 2014: progesterone did not improve favourable outcome after TBI (relative benefit 0.95) — stopped for futility
cards.type: Double-blind, multicentre, phase 3 randomised trial — stopped early for futility
cards.people: 882 of the planned 1,140 patients with severe, moderate-to-severe, or moderate acute TBI (Glasgow Coma Scale score 4 to 12) underwent randomization before the trial was stopped for futility; study treatment (intravenous progesterone or placebo) was initiated within 4 hours after injury and administered for a total of 96 hours. The median age was 35 years, 73.7% were men, 15.2% were black, and the mean Injury Severity Score was 24.4; the most frequent mechanism was a motor vehicle accident.
cards.result: There was no significant difference between the progesterone group and the placebo group in the proportion of patients with a favorable outcome — defined as an increase framed against a stratified dichotomy of the Extended Glasgow Outcome Scale at 6 months — (relative benefit of progesterone, 0.95 relative; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.85 to 1.06; P=0.35). Phlebitis or thrombophlebitis was more frequent in the progesterone group (relative risk 3.03 relative; CI, 1.96 to 4.66). There were no significant differences in the other prespecified safety outcomes. Mortality was a secondary outcome; the abstract prints no mortality figures.
cards.watchOut: A futility stop is not an underpowered shrug: the trial was halted because the accumulating data made the targeted 10-percentage-point benefit implausible, and the confidence interval excludes it.
cards.source: Wright DW et al. Very early administration of progesterone for acute traumatic brain injury. N Engl J Med. 2014. PMID: 25493974. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00822900, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: SYNAPSE 2014: progesterone did not improve 6-month Glasgow Outcome Scale scores in severe TBI (favourable outcome 50.4% vs 50.5%)
cards.summary: SYNAPSE 2014: progesterone did not improve 6-month Glasgow Outcome Scale scores in severe TBI (favourable outcome 50.4% vs 50.5%)
cards.people: 1,195 patients, 16 to 70 years of age, with severe TBI (Glasgow Coma Scale score of 8 or less and at least one reactive pupil), randomly assigned to progesterone or placebo; dosing began within 8 hours after injury and continued for 120 hours. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Proportional-odds analysis with covariate adjustment showed no treatment effect of progesterone as compared with placebo (odds ratio, 0.96 relative; confidence interval, 0.77 to 1.18). The proportion of patients with a favorable outcome on the Glasgow Outcome Scale (good recovery or moderate disability) was 50.4% with progesterone, as compared with 50.5% with placebo. Mortality was similar in the two groups. No relevant safety differences were noted between progesterone and placebo.
cards.watchOut: The two phase 2 single-centre trials that launched this programme were positive; the two phase 3 multicentre trials were not. SYNAPSE is the record's own lesson, printed in its conclusions, that robust preclinical and early-phase data do not guarantee phase 3 benefit.
cards.source: Skolnick BE et al. A clinical trial of progesterone for severe traumatic brain injury. N Engl J Med. 2014. PMID: 25493978. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01143064, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: two phase 3 trials, 2,077 patients, no benefit — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Synthesis: two phase 3 trials, 2,077 patients, no benefit — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: ProTECT III 2014 (882 randomised) and SYNAPSE 2014 (1,195 patients) — two independent phase 3 trials.
cards.result: Progesterone after acute TBI has had its definitive test twice: started within 4 hours (ProTECT III) or 8 hours (SYNAPSE), continued for 4–5 days, in moderate through severe injury — and neither trial moved 6-month functional outcome, with SYNAPSE's favourable-outcome rates identical to one decimal place (50.4% vs 50.5%). The stamp is proposed pending the developer's personal verdict because the outcome instruments embed mortality (Tier C).
cards.watchOut: This is the TBI neuroprotection pattern in full — animal promise, small positive trials, large null trials (the same arc as erythropoietin on Shelf #1263 and citicoline on Shelf #1267) — and the phase 2 papers should never be quoted without the phase 3 pair beside them.
cards.source: Synthesis of Wright DW et al. N Engl J Med. 2014. PMID: 25493974; Skolnick BE et al. N Engl J Med. 2014. PMID: 25493978. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Prophylactic hypothermia in severe traumatic brain injury (POLAR)
shelves.question: In patients with severe TBI, does early sustained prophylactic hypothermia (33–35 °C) improve neurological outcome at 6 months versus normothermia?
shelves.mesh: Brain Injuries, Traumatic/complications,mortality,physiopathology,therapy · Hypothermia, Induced/adverse effects · Intracranial Pressure · Hospital Mortality · Treatment Outcome · Humans · Adult · Female · Male
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, functional outcome with mortality embedded): For PROPHYLACTIC hypothermia — cooling before pressure rises — POLAR (511 patients with severe TBI) found favourable neurologic outcome at 6 months in 48.8% on early sustained hypothermia (33–35 °C) versus 49.1% on normothermia (relative risk 0.99 relative, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.19; P=.94). For THERAPEUTIC hypothermia — cooling to treat established intracranial hypertension — the neighbouring Eurotherm3235 trial (387 patients) found WORSE outcomes with hypothermia: favourable outcome 26% versus 37% (adjusted common odds ratio for a worse GOS-E distribution 1.53 relative, 1.02 to 2.30; P=0.04), and recruitment was suspended over safety concerns. Neither use is supported; the therapeutic use leans harmful.

cards.headline: POLAR 2018: early prophylactic hypothermia did not improve 6-month neurologic outcome in severe TBI (48.8% vs 49.1%)
cards.summary: POLAR 2018: early prophylactic hypothermia did not improve 6-month neurologic outcome in severe TBI (48.8% vs 49.1%)
cards.type: Multicentre randomised trial (6 countries), outcome assessed by blinded assessors
cards.people: 511 patients with severe traumatic brain injury recruited out-of-hospital and in emergency departments in 6 countries and randomised (266 to prophylactic hypothermia, 245 to normothermia); 500 provided ongoing consent (mean age 34.5 years [SD 13.4]; 402 men [80.2%]) and 466 completed the primary outcome evaluation. Prophylactic hypothermia targeted 33–35 °C for at least 72 hours and up to 7 days if intracranial pressures were elevated, followed by gradual rewarming; normothermia targeted 37 °C.
cards.result: Favorable outcomes (Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended score 5–8) at 6 months occurred in 117 patients (48.8%) in the hypothermia group and 111 (49.1%) in the normothermia group (risk difference, 0.4% [95% CI, −9.4% to 8.7%]; relative risk with hypothermia, 0.99 relative [95% CI, 0.82 to 1.19]; P=.94). Hypothermia was initiated rapidly after injury (median 1.8 hours) and rewarming occurred slowly (median 22.5 hours). In the hypothermia and normothermia groups, the rates of pneumonia were 55.0% vs 51.3%, respectively, and rates of increased intracranial bleeding were 18.1% vs 15.4%, respectively.
cards.watchOut: The intervention was delivered as designed — cooling started a median 1.8 hours after injury and held for at least 72 hours — so the null cannot be blamed on late or brief cooling.
cards.source: Cooper DJ et al. Effect of Early Sustained Prophylactic Hypothermia on Neurologic Outcomes Among Patients With Severe Traumatic Brain Injury: The POLAR Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2018. PMID: 30357266. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00987688, from the record's databank fields (the abstract also names ANZCTR ACTRN12609000764235). cards.headline: Eurotherm3235 2015: hypothermia used to TREAT raised intracranial pressure produced worse functional outcomes (favourable outcome 26% vs 37%)
cards.summary: Eurotherm3235 2015: hypothermia used to TREAT raised intracranial pressure produced worse functional outcomes (favourable outcome 26% vs 37%)
cards.type: Multicentre randomised trial — recruitment suspended for safety concerns; a NEIGHBOURING question (therapeutic, not prophylactic, cooling) carded beside POLAR
cards.people: 387 adults with an intracranial pressure of more than 20 mm Hg despite stage 1 treatments (mechanical ventilation and sedation management), enrolled at 47 centers in 18 countries and randomly assigned to standard care alone or hypothermia (32 to 35 °C) plus standard care; in both groups, stage 3 treatments (barbiturates and decompressive craniectomy) were used if all stage 2 treatments failed.
cards.result: Recruitment was suspended owing to safety concerns. Stage 3 treatments were required to control intracranial pressure in 54% of the patients in the control group and in 44% of the patients in the hypothermia group. The adjusted common odds ratio for the Extended Glasgow Outcome Scale score was 1.53 relative (95% confidence interval, 1.02 to 2.30; P=0.04) — with an odds ratio below 1.0 defined as favouring hypothermia, this indicates a worse outcome in the hypothermia group. A favorable outcome (GOS-E score 5 to 8) occurred in 26% of the patients in the hypothermia group and in 37% of the patients in the control group (P=0.03).
cards.watchOut: Hypothermia did control pressure more often (fewer stage 3 escalations) while making overall outcome worse — the cleanest demonstration in this literature that lowering ICP is a surrogate that can divorce from patient outcome.
cards.source: Andrews PJ et al. Hypothermia for Intracranial Hypertension after Traumatic Brain Injury. N Engl J Med. 2015. PMID: 26444221. Registry ID: ISRCTN ISRCTN34555414, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: prophylactic cooling does not help; therapeutic cooling for raised ICP made outcomes worse — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Synthesis: prophylactic cooling does not help; therapeutic cooling for raised ICP made outcomes worse — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: POLAR 2018 (511 patients, prophylactic hypothermia) and Eurotherm3235 2015 (387 patients, therapeutic hypothermia for intracranial hypertension).
cards.result: Read together, the pair closes the hypothermia question in TBI from both directions: cooling everyone early changes nothing (48.8% vs 49.1% favourable), and cooling to chase a pressure number leaves fewer patients with a favourable outcome (26% vs 37%). Fever avoidance and normothermia are not on trial here and are not impugned by this shelf. The stamp is proposed pending the developer's personal verdict because the outcome scales embed mortality (Tier C).
cards.watchOut: Eurotherm3235 answers a neighbouring question, not POLAR's: it is carded as the therapeutic-use evidence and must not be pooled with POLAR as a second prophylaxis trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cooper DJ et al. JAMA. 2018. PMID: 30357266; Andrews PJ et al. N Engl J Med. 2015. PMID: 26444221. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Amantadine for disorders of consciousness after traumatic brain injury
shelves.question: In patients with traumatic disorders of consciousness in rehabilitation, does amantadine accelerate functional recovery versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Amantadine/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Brain Injuries/complications,drug therapy · Coma, Post-Head Injury/drug therapy · Persistent Vegetative State/drug therapy,etiology · Disability Evaluation · Recovery of Function · Dopamine Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Humans · Adult · Female · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: The one randomised trial (Giacino 2012, 184 patients in a vegetative or minimally conscious state 4–16 weeks after TBI, in inpatient rehabilitation) found amantadine accelerated functional recovery DURING the 4-week treatment period — the Disability Rating Scale improved faster by 0.24 points per week (P=0.007) — but the advantage did not persist: during the 2-week washout, improvement in the amantadine group slowed significantly (slope difference 0.30 points per week; P=0.02), and overall improvement from baseline to week 6 was similar in the two groups. A real but treatment-bound acceleration on a recovery-rate surrogate, from a single trial: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Giacino 2012: amantadine accelerated functional recovery during 4 weeks of treatment (DRS slope difference 0.24 points/week), with the advantage lost after stopping
cards.summary: Giacino 2012: amantadine accelerated functional recovery during 4 weeks of treatment (DRS slope difference 0.24 points/week), with the advantage lost after stopping
cards.people: 184 patients who were in a vegetative or minimally conscious state 4 to 16 weeks after traumatic brain injury and were receiving inpatient rehabilitation, randomly assigned to amantadine or placebo for 4 weeks and followed for 2 weeks after treatment was discontinued; the abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: During the 4-week treatment period, recovery was significantly faster in the amantadine group than in the placebo group, as measured by the Disability Rating Scale score (difference in slope, 0.24 points per week; P=0.007). In a prespecified subgroup analysis, the treatment effect was similar for patients in a vegetative state and those in a minimally conscious state. The rate of improvement in the amantadine group slowed during the 2 weeks after treatment (weeks 5 and 6) and was significantly slower than the rate in the placebo group (difference in slope, 0.30 points per week; P=0.02). The overall improvement in DRS scores between baseline and week 6 (2 weeks after treatment was discontinued) was similar in the two groups. There were no significant differences in the incidence of serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: The headline is a rate, not a destination: patients on amantadine got better faster while taking it and then slowed, so by week 6 the groups had improved by similar amounts. Whether longer treatment sustains the faster pace is a question this trial does not answer.
cards.source: Giacino JT et al. Placebo-controlled trial of amantadine for severe traumatic brain injury. N Engl J Med. 2012. PMID: 22375973. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00970944, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Citicoline for traumatic brain injury (COBRIT)
shelves.question: In patients with complicated mild-to-severe TBI, does citicoline improve functional and cognitive status at 90 days versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Brain Injuries/complications,drug therapy · Cognition Disorders/complications,drug therapy · Cytidine Diphosphate Choline/therapeutic use · Nootropic Agents/therapeutic use · Glasgow Coma Scale · Double-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome · Humans · Adolescent · Adult · Middle Aged · Young Adult · Female · Male
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED: The one large double-blind phase 3 trial (COBRIT, 1,213 patients with complicated mild, moderate or severe TBI at 8 US level 1 trauma centres) found citicoline for 90 days did not improve functional or cognitive status: favourable improvement on the Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended was 35.4% on citicoline versus 35.6% on placebo, the global test across the 9-scale core battery gave an odds ratio of 0.98 relative (95% CI 0.83 to 1.15) at 90 days, neither severity subgroup showed a treatment effect, and at 180 days the groups still did not differ (global odds ratio 0.87 relative, 0.72 to 1.04). A large blinded null with tight intervals, on a drug approved for TBI in 59 countries: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: COBRIT 2012: citicoline did not improve functional or cognitive status at 90 days (global odds ratio 0.98) in 1,213 patients
cards.summary: COBRIT 2012: citicoline did not improve functional or cognitive status at 90 days (global odds ratio 0.98) in 1,213 patients
cards.people: 1,213 patients with traumatic brain injury classified as complicated mild, moderate, or severe, at 8 US level 1 trauma centers, randomised between July 2007 and February 2011 to a 90-day regimen of daily enteral or oral citicoline 2000 mg or placebo; the abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Rates of favorable improvement for the Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended were 35.4% in the citicoline group and 35.6% in the placebo group. For all other scales the rate of improvement ranged from 37.3% to 86.5% in the citicoline group and from 42.7% to 84.0% in the placebo group. The citicoline and placebo groups did not differ significantly at the 90-day evaluation (global odds ratio [OR], 0.98 relative [95% CI, 0.83-1.15]); there was no significant treatment effect in the 2 severity subgroups (global OR, 1.14 relative [95% CI, 0.88-1.49] and 0.89 relative [95% CI, 0.72-1.49] for moderate/severe and complicated mild TBI, respectively). At the 180-day evaluation, the groups did not differ significantly with respect to the primary outcome (global OR, 0.87 relative [95% CI, 0.72-1.04]).
cards.watchOut: The battery casts a wide net — nine functional and cognitive scales at two time points, plus severity subgroups — and every estimate sits on the null; multiplicity cannot rescue a benefit that appears nowhere. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Zafonte RD et al. Effect of citicoline on functional and cognitive status among patients with traumatic brain injury: Citicoline Brain Injury Treatment Trial (COBRIT). JAMA. 2012. PMID: 23168823. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00545662, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: a widely approved neuroprotectant failed its definitive blinded test — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Synthesis: a widely approved neuroprotectant failed its definitive blinded test — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: COBRIT 2012 (1,213 patients with complicated mild-to-severe TBI).
cards.result: COBRIT is the direct, adequately sized test of citicoline after TBI, and it is null on function, null on cognition, null at 90 days and null at 180 days. Regulatory approval in 59 countries predates this trial and does not outrank it. Citicoline joins the shelf-row of TBI neuroprotection nulls — progesterone (Shelf #1264), erythropoietin (Shelf #1263) — each settled by its own large trial, none re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Small earlier trials and non-blinded series in other countries are the usual counter-citation; they are exactly the evidence class COBRIT was designed to supersede.
cards.source: Synthesis of Zafonte RD et al. JAMA. 2012. PMID: 23168823. Registry ID as on the individual card.
