shelves.title: Cariprazine for acute schizophrenia
shelves.question: In adults with an acute exacerbation of schizophrenia, does cariprazine (1.5–6 mg/day) reduce total PANSS score versus placebo over 6 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adult · Antipsychotic Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects,pharmacology · Aripiprazole/administration & dosage,adverse effects,pharmacology · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Piperazines/administration & dosage,adverse effects,pharmacology · Schizophrenia/drug therapy
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two independent randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials in acute exacerbation of schizophrenia both found cariprazine superior to placebo on PANSS total score at 6 weeks. In the fixed-dose trial (Durgam 2015, 617 patients, with an aripiprazole active-control arm), the least-squares mean differences versus placebo were −6.0 points at 3 mg/day (95% CI −10.1 to −1.9; adjusted P=.0044) and −8.8 points at 6 mg/day (−12.9 to −4.7; P<.0001), with CGI-S differences of −0.4 and −0.5. In the international flexible-dose trial (Kane 2015, 446 patients in the safety population), the differences were −6.8 points at 3–6 mg/day (P=0.003) and −9.9 points at 6–9 mg/day (P<0.001). The consistent harms are akathisia, extrapyramidal symptoms and tremor (each ≥5% and twice the placebo rate in Kane), and insomnia; metabolic changes were small and prolactin fell in all groups in Kane. Effect sizes are in the usual antipsychotic range.

cards.headline: Durgam 2015: cariprazine 3 mg and 6 mg beat placebo on PANSS total score at 6 weeks (−6.0 and −8.8 points) in acute schizophrenia, alongside an aripiprazole control
cards.summary: Durgam 2015: cariprazine 3 mg and 6 mg beat placebo on PANSS total score at 6 weeks (−6.0 and −8.8 points) in acute schizophrenia, alongside an aripiprazole control
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo- and active-controlled trial (fixed dose)
cards.people: 617 patients meeting DSM-IV-TR criteria for schizophrenia with acute exacerbation, randomised to placebo (153), cariprazine 3 mg/day (155), cariprazine 6 mg/day (157), or aripiprazole 10 mg/day (152) for 6 weeks of double-blind treatment, in a multinational trial conducted April 2010 to December 2011. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Least-squares mean differences in PANSS total score change at week 6 significantly favoured cariprazine versus placebo: 3 mg/day −6.0 (95% CI −10.1 to −1.9; adjusted P=.0044) and 6 mg/day −8.8 (−12.9 to −4.7; adjusted P<.0001). CGI-S differences were −0.4 (−0.6 to −0.2; P=.0044) and −0.5 (−0.7 to −0.3; P<.0001). Aripiprazole also separated from placebo (PANSS −7.0 [−11.0 to −2.9]; P=.0008), confirming assay sensitivity. Common treatment-emergent adverse events (≥10%) were insomnia (all groups), akathisia (cariprazine 6 mg/day), and headache (placebo and cariprazine 6 mg/day).
cards.watchOut: Six weeks in acutely exacerbated inpatients is the standard antipsychotic registration design; it grades short-term symptom reduction, not relapse prevention or long-term safety. The aripiprazole arm validates the trial rather than ranking cariprazine against it (no head-to-head test was reported).
cards.source: Durgam S et al. Cariprazine in acute exacerbation of schizophrenia: a fixed-dose, phase 3, randomized, double-blind, placebo- and active-controlled trial. J Clin Psychiatry. 2015. PMID: 26717533. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01104766, from the record's databank fields. cards.summary: Kane 2015: cariprazine 3–6 mg and 6–9 mg beat placebo on PANSS (−6.8 and −9.9 points) in a second international phase 3 trial
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (flexible dose ranges)
cards.people: 446 patients with acute exacerbation of schizophrenia in the safety population, randomised to placebo (147), cariprazine 3–6 mg/day (151), or cariprazine 6–9 mg/day (148) for 6 weeks of double-blind treatment; 60.5% of patients completed the study. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At week 6, least-squares mean differences versus placebo favoured cariprazine on PANSS total score (3–6 mg/day: −6.8, P=0.003; 6–9 mg/day: −9.9, P<0.001) and on CGI-S (3–6 mg/day: −0.3, P=0.012; 6–9 mg/day: −0.5, P<0.001). Common treatment-emergent adverse events (≥5% and twice the placebo rate) in both cariprazine groups were akathisia, extrapyramidal disorder, and tremor, mostly mild to moderate. Mean changes in metabolic parameters were generally small and similar between groups, and prolactin levels decreased in all groups.
cards.watchOut: Only 60.5% completed the study, so the mixed-model estimates lean on missing-data assumptions; the record's MeSH includes 'Hyponatremia/chemically induced', reproduced as printed, though the abstract does not discuss it. Doses up to 9 mg/day exceed the 1.5–6 mg/day range in the topic question and in current labelling.

shelves.title: Adjunctive brexpiprazole for major depressive disorder
shelves.question: In adults with major depression responding inadequately to an antidepressant, does adjunctive brexpiprazole (2–3 mg/day) improve MADRS score versus adjunctive placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Antidepressive Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Antipsychotic Agents/therapeutic use · Major Depressive Disorder/drug therapy · Depressive Disorder, Treatment-Resistant/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination/adverse effects · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Quinolones/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Thiophenes/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: LIKELY — with the analysis population disclosed on the cards: both phase 3 trials' headline results come from the 'efficacy population per final protocol' (patients meeting amended criteria for inadequate response throughout an 8-week prospective antidepressant run-in), not the full randomised set. Within that population, adjunctive brexpiprazole 2 mg reduced MADRS by −8.36 versus −5.15 on placebo at 6 weeks (P=.0002; Thase 2015a), and in the twin trial brexpiprazole 3 mg reduced MADRS by −8.29 versus −6.33 (P=.0079) while 1 mg did NOT separate (−7.64 vs −6.33; P=.0737; Thase 2015b). So the supported doses are 2–3 mg/day; the 1 mg dose failed its primary test. Harms: akathisia (7.4% at 2 mg vs 1.0% placebo; 13.5% at 3 mg vs 2.3%) and weight gain (8.0% vs 3.1% at 2 mg). Absolute MADRS advantages are about 2–3 points over an already-treated baseline.

cards.headline: Thase 2015 (2 mg trial): adjunctive brexpiprazole 2 mg beat placebo on MADRS at 6 weeks (−8.36 vs −5.15; P=.0002) in antidepressant inadequate responders
cards.summary: Thase 2015 (2 mg trial): adjunctive brexpiprazole 2 mg beat placebo on MADRS at 6 weeks (−8.36 vs −5.15; P=.0002) in antidepressant inadequate responders
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled adjunctive trial (after an 8-week prospective antidepressant run-in)
cards.people: Adults with major depressive disorder (DSM-IV-TR) and historical inadequate response to 1–3 antidepressants, who remained inadequately responsive after an 8-week prospective open-label phase on a physician-determined antidepressant, then randomised to antidepressant + brexpiprazole 2 mg/day (175) or antidepressant + placebo (178) for 6 weeks (July 2011–May 2013). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: In the efficacy population per final protocol, brexpiprazole reduced mean MADRS total score versus placebo at week 6 (−8.36 vs −5.15; P=.0002), and improved the Sheehan Disability Scale mean score (−1.35 vs −0.89; P=.0349). The most common treatment-related adverse events were weight gain (brexpiprazole 8.0%; placebo 3.1%) and akathisia (7.4% vs 1.0%).
cards.watchOut: The headline analysis uses the amended 'per final protocol' efficacy population, and the design enriches for patients who failed a further 8 weeks of antidepressant — results apply to that inadequate-responder population, not to first-line depression. A 3.2-point MADRS advantage is modest against a −5.15 placebo-adjunct response.

cards.headline: Thase 2015 (1 mg/3 mg trial): brexpiprazole 3 mg beat placebo on MADRS (−8.29 vs −6.33; P=.0079); 1 mg did not (P=.0737)
cards.summary: Thase 2015 (1 mg/3 mg trial): brexpiprazole 3 mg beat placebo on MADRS (−8.29 vs −6.33; P=.0079); 1 mg did not (P=.0737)
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled adjunctive trial (dose-ranging)
cards.people: Adults with major depressive disorder and inadequate response to 1–3 prior antidepressants followed by 8 weeks of prospective open-label antidepressant treatment, randomised 1:1:1 to double-blind brexpiprazole 3 mg/day (213), brexpiprazole 1 mg/day (211), or placebo (203) as adjuncts for 6 weeks (June 2011–September 2013), in the efficacy population per final protocol. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Brexpiprazole 3 mg showed greater MADRS improvement than placebo at week 6 (−8.29 vs −6.33; P=.0079), whereas 1 mg did not (−7.64 vs −6.33; P=.0737). Both doses improved Sheehan Disability Scale scores versus placebo (LS mean differences −0.49 [P=.0158] and −0.48 [P=.0191]). The most frequent adverse events were akathisia (4.4% at 1 mg, 13.5% at 3 mg, 2.3% placebo), headache (9.3%, 6.1%, 7.7%), and weight increase (6.6%, 5.7%, 0.9%). AIMS and Barnes Akathisia Rating Scale changes were significantly greater with 3 mg versus placebo.
cards.watchOut: The same amended per-protocol population caveat as the twin trial, and the failed 1 mg arm matters for dosing claims: this shelf supports 2–3 mg/day, not 'brexpiprazole' at any dose. Akathisia at 3 mg (13.5%) is the dose-limiting harm in this record.

shelves.title: Vortioxetine for major depressive disorder
shelves.question: In adults with major depressive disorder, does vortioxetine (5–20 mg/day) improve MADRS score versus placebo over 8 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Major Depressive Disorder/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Piperazines/administration & dosage,adverse effects,pharmacology · Placebos · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors/administration & dosage,adverse effects,pharmacology · Sulfides/administration & dosage,adverse effects,pharmacology · Treatment Failure · Vortioxetine · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT — one negative trial, one positive only at the higher dose — with a correction to the topic file on the cards' faces: the topic file describes its pinned anchor (Mahableshwarkar 2015, PMID 26035186) as showing that 'vortioxetine improved depression scores versus placebo with a dose-related signal'. The record shows the opposite: that trial's own conclusion is that vortioxetine 10 mg and 15 mg 'did not differ significantly from placebo on MADRS total score after 8 weeks' (469 randomised). The second trial (Jacobsen 2015, 462 randomised) found vortioxetine 20 mg significantly reduced MADRS versus placebo (−14.41 vs −10.77 mean change; P=.002), while 10 mg missed significance (P=.058). So the honest record is: of the two carded trials, one is null at 10/15 mg and one is positive only at 20 mg. Nausea is the characteristic adverse event across the programme. The stamp is a split, not the topic file's unqualified positive.

cards.headline: Mahableshwarkar 2015: vortioxetine 10 mg and 15 mg did NOT differ significantly from placebo on MADRS at 8 weeks (negative trial, 469 patients)
cards.summary: Mahableshwarkar 2015: vortioxetine 10 mg and 15 mg did NOT differ significantly from placebo on MADRS at 8 weeks (negative trial, 469 patients)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (8 weeks) — NEGATIVE on its primary endpoint
cards.people: 469 adults aged 18–75 years with major depressive disorder (DSM-IV-TR) and a MADRS total score of at least 26, randomised 1:1:1 to vortioxetine 10 mg (157), vortioxetine 15 mg (152), or placebo (160) once daily for 8 weeks, in a US trial conducted August 2010 to May 2012.
cards.result: Differences from placebo in the primary endpoint (change in MADRS total score at week 8) were not statistically significant for vortioxetine 10 mg or vortioxetine 15 mg. Nausea, headache, dry mouth, constipation, diarrhoea, vomiting, dizziness and flatulence were reported in at least 5% of vortioxetine subjects. Discontinuation due to adverse events occurred in 7 subjects (4.4%) on placebo, 8 (5.2%) on vortioxetine 10 mg, and 12 (7.9%) on vortioxetine 15 mg. Sexual-function (ASEX) scores were similar across groups, and there were no clinically significant trends on suicidal ideation/behaviour (C-SSRS), laboratory values, ECG or vital signs. The authors conclude: 'In this study, vortioxetine did not differ significantly from placebo on MADRS total score after 8 weeks of treatment in MDD subjects.'
cards.watchOut: This is the card the topic file misdescribed: its one-line summary claimed a positive, dose-related result for a trial whose published conclusion is a null. The record governs. (The record's own MeSH includes 'Treatment Failure', consistent with the result.)

cards.headline: Jacobsen 2015: vortioxetine 20 mg beat placebo on MADRS at 8 weeks (−14.41 vs −10.77; P=.002); 10 mg did not (P=.058)
cards.summary: Jacobsen 2015: vortioxetine 20 mg beat placebo on MADRS at 8 weeks (−14.41 vs −10.77; P=.002); 10 mg did not (P=.058)
cards.people: 462 adults with recurrent major depressive disorder (DSM-IV-TR), randomised 1:1:1 to vortioxetine 10 mg (155), vortioxetine 20 mg (150), or placebo (157) once daily for 8 weeks, in a multicentre trial conducted July 2010 to January 2012.
cards.result: Mean (SE) reductions in MADRS total score at week 8 were −10.77 (±0.807) on placebo, −12.96 (±0.832) on vortioxetine 10 mg (P=.058 vs placebo — not significant), and −14.41 (±0.845) on vortioxetine 20 mg (P=.002 vs placebo). shelves.title: Lumateperone for schizophrenia
shelves.question: In adults hospitalised with an acute exacerbation of schizophrenia, does lumateperone 42 mg/day reduce PANSS score versus placebo at 4 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antipsychotic Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Heterocyclic Compounds, 4 or More Rings/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Humans · Male · Schizophrenia/drug therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (450 patients aged 18–60 with an acute exacerbation of schizophrenia, at 12 US sites) found lumateperone 42 mg/day (60 mg of the tosylate salt) superior to placebo at day 28 on PANSS total score (least-squares mean difference −4.2; 95% CI −7.8 to −0.6; P=.02; effect size −0.3) and on CGI-S (−0.3; P=.003), in the prespecified modified intention-to-treat population (n=435). The 28 mg dose did NOT meet the primary endpoint (PANSS difference −2.6; P=.16). Both doses were well tolerated, without clinically significant motor adverse effects or cardiometabolic/endocrine changes versus placebo in this 4-week trial. A single pivotal trial with a modest effect size earns POSSIBLE. Correction on the card's face: the topic file attributes the trial to 'Lieberman et al.'; the record's first author is Correll CU (JAMA Psychiatry 2020), and the abstract describes enrolled patients with acute exacerbation without stating they were hospitalised.

cards.headline: Correll 2020: lumateperone 42 mg beat placebo on PANSS at day 28 (−4.2 points; P=.02) in acute schizophrenia; the 28 mg dose missed (P=.16)
cards.summary: Correll 2020: lumateperone 42 mg beat placebo on PANSS at day 28 (−4.2 points; P=.02) in acute schizophrenia; the 28 mg dose missed (P=.16)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (4 weeks)
cards.people: 450 patients aged 18 to 60 years with schizophrenia experiencing an acute exacerbation of psychosis, enrolled at 12 US clinical sites (November 2014–July 2015) and randomised 1:1:1 (150 per arm) to lumateperone tosylate 60 mg (equivalent to 42 mg lumateperone), lumateperone tosylate 40 mg (28 mg), or placebo once daily for 4 weeks. Mean (SD) age was 42.4 (10.2) years; 346 (77.1%) were male; mean baseline PANSS total score was 89.8 (10.3) and mean CGI-S 4.8 (0.6).
cards.result: In the prespecified modified intention-to-treat efficacy analysis (n=435), lumateperone 42 mg met the primary and key secondary endpoints: PANSS total score difference versus placebo −4.2 (least-squares mean difference; 95% CI −7.8 to −0.6; P=.02; effect size −0.3) and CGI-S difference −0.3 (−0.5 to −0.1; P=.003; effect size −0.4). For 28 mg, the PANSS difference was −2.6 (−6.2 to 1.1; P=.16 — not significant), though its CGI-S difference reached significance (−0.2; P=.02). Both lumateperone doses were well tolerated without clinically significant treatment-emergent motor adverse effects or changes in cardiometabolic or endocrine factors versus placebo.
cards.watchOut: Four weeks is short even by antipsychotic-trial standards, the PANSS effect (−4.2 points, effect size −0.3) is at the small end for the class, and the lower dose failed the primary endpoint — the supported claim is narrow: 42 mg, acute treatment, one trial. The topic file's attribution to Lieberman et al. is corrected here (first author Correll); Dr. Kane is among the co-authors.
cards.source: Correll CU et al. Efficacy and Safety of Lumateperone for Treatment of Schizophrenia: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Psychiatry. 2020. PMID: 31913424. shelves.title: Zuranolone for major depressive disorder (non-postpartum)
shelves.question: In adults with major depressive disorder, does a 14-day course of zuranolone 50 mg/day reduce HAM-D score versus placebo by day 15?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Allosteric Regulation · Antidepressive Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Major Depressive Disorder/classification,drug therapy · Dizziness/chemically induced · Double-Blind Method · Female · GABA Modulators/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Humans · Least-Squares Analysis · Male · Middle Aged · Nausea/chemically induced · Pregnanes/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Pyrazoles/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Receptors, GABA-A/metabolism · Pregnanolone
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — with two scope corrections on the card's face. First, dose: the topic question asks about a 50 mg/day course, but the carded phase 2 trial used SAGE-217 (zuranolone) 30 mg/day for 14 days; the 50 mg dose belongs to the later phase 3 programme, which is not carded here. Second, size: the trial randomised only 89 patients. Within it, zuranolone produced a larger HAM-D reduction at day 15 than placebo (least-squares mean change −17.4 vs −10.3 points; difference −7.0; 95% CI −10.2 to −3.9; P<0.001), with secondary endpoints generally in the same direction, no serious adverse events, and headache, dizziness, nausea and somnolence as the commonest adverse events (more frequent on zuranolone). The authors themselves state that further trials are needed to determine durability and safety. The topic file notes the later phase 3 results in MDD were mixed; that programme is fenced here, not carded, and the postpartum question is homed on Shelf #836.

cards.headline: Gunduz-Bruce 2019: SAGE-217 (zuranolone) 30 mg for 14 days reduced HAM-D by 7.0 points more than placebo at day 15 — a phase 2 trial of 89 patients
cards.summary: Gunduz-Bruce 2019: SAGE-217 (zuranolone) 30 mg for 14 days reduced HAM-D by 7.0 points more than placebo at day 15 — a phase 2 trial of 89 patients
cards.type: Double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial (14 days of treatment)
cards.people: 89 patients with major depression, randomly assigned 1:1 to SAGE-217 30 mg once daily (45) or placebo (44) for 14 days, in a double-blind phase 2 trial. Mean baseline HAM-D score was 25.2 in the SAGE-217 group and 25.7 in the placebo group. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The least-squares mean (±SE) change in HAM-D score from baseline to day 15 was −17.4±1.3 points on SAGE-217 versus −10.3±1.3 points on placebo (least-squares mean difference −7.0 points; 95% CI −10.2 to −3.9; P<0.001). Differences in secondary endpoints (response, remission, CGI-I and further scales, assessed through day 42) were generally in the same direction. There were no serious adverse events. The most common adverse events in the SAGE-217 group were headache, dizziness, nausea, and somnolence, and adverse events were more common in the SAGE-217 group than in the placebo group.
cards.watchOut: Eighty-nine patients and a day-15 primary endpoint: the trial demonstrates rapid symptom change, not a durable antidepressant effect, and the −7.0 point difference is larger than typical antidepressant-placebo differences — a pattern small early trials often show and larger trials often shrink. The dose (30 mg) is not the 50 mg dose named in the topic question.

shelves.title: Dextromethorphan–bupropion (AXS-05) for major depressive disorder
shelves.question: In adults with major depressive disorder, does dextromethorphan–bupropion improve MADRS score versus placebo at 6 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Bupropion/therapeutic use · Major Depressive Disorder/diagnosis,drug therapy · Dextromethorphan/adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Quality of Life
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised, double-blind phase 3 trial (GEMINI, 327 patients with major depressive disorder) found dextromethorphan–bupropion (AXS-05, 45 mg–105 mg tablets, twice daily after a 3-day lead-in) superior to placebo on MADRS change at week 6 (least-squares mean −15.9 vs −12.0 points; difference −3.87; P=.002), with separation already at week 1 (P=.007) and week 2 (P<.001), remission in 39.5% versus 17.3% (difference 22.2 percentage points; P<.001) and response in 54.0% versus 34.0% (difference 20.0 points; P<.001). The most common adverse events were dizziness, nausea, headache, somnolence and dry mouth; the trial reports no psychotomimetic effects, weight gain, or increased sexual dysfunction. A single phase 3 trial earns POSSIBLE. One record-keeping flag: the abstract prints its confidence intervals in reversed order (e.g. '95% CI, −1.39 to −6.36' for the −3.87 difference, and a CGI-S difference of −0.48 with CI '−0.48 to −0.79'); the figures are quoted as printed and flagged on the card rather than silently repaired.

cards.headline: GEMINI (Iosifescu 2022): AXS-05 beat placebo on MADRS at week 6 (−15.9 vs −12.0 points), with remission 39.5% vs 17.3% — one phase 3 trial, 327 patients
cards.summary: GEMINI (Iosifescu 2022): AXS-05 beat placebo on MADRS at week 6 (−15.9 vs −12.0 points), with remission 39.5% vs 17.3% — one phase 3 trial, 327 patients
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (6 weeks)
cards.people: 327 patients with a DSM-5 diagnosis of major depressive disorder, randomised 1:1 to dextromethorphan–bupropion (163; 45 mg–105 mg tablet once daily for days 1–3, twice daily thereafter) or placebo (164) for 6 weeks (June–December 2019). Mean baseline MADRS total scores were 33.6 and 33.2 respectively. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The least-squares mean change in MADRS total score at week 6 was −15.9 points on dextromethorphan–bupropion versus −12.0 on placebo (least-squares mean difference −3.87; the record prints the 95% confidence interval as '−1.39 to −6.36' — reversed order as printed; P=.002). Improvement was superior at all time points including week 1 (P=.007) and week 2 (P<.001). Remission (MADRS ≤10) was achieved by 39.5% versus 17.3% (treatment difference 22.2 percentage points; 95% CI 11.7 to 32.7; P<.001) and clinical response (≥50% MADRS reduction) by 54.0% versus 34.0% (difference 20.0 points; 95% CI 8.4 to 31.6; P<.001). Most secondary endpoints significantly favoured treatment; the CGI-S difference at week 6 is printed as −0.48 with the interval again in reversed order ('−0.48 to −0.79'; P=.002). The most common adverse events were dizziness, nausea, headache, somnolence, and dry mouth; treatment was not associated with psychotomimetic effects, weight gain, or increased sexual dysfunction.
cards.watchOut: The abstract's confidence intervals for the two headline differences are printed in reversed order and one (CGI-S) has its point estimate sitting on the interval boundary — an internal awkwardness of the published abstract, flagged here as the gate rules require rather than repaired. The trial is the single pivotal for this indication, and its comparator is placebo, not bupropion alone: GEMINI cannot separate the dextromethorphan contribution from the combination's pharmacokinetic boosting (that question belongs to the component-comparison trial, not carded here).

shelves.title: Lamotrigine for maintenance treatment of bipolar I disorder
shelves.question: In adults with bipolar I disorder recently recovered from a mood episode, does lamotrigine maintenance prolong time to intervention for a new mood episode versus placebo (and how does it compare with lithium)?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antidepressive Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Antimanic Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Bipolar Disorder/diagnosis,drug therapy,psychology · Depressive Disorder/diagnosis,drug therapy,psychology · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Lamotrigine · Lithium Carbonate/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Long-Term Care · Male · Middle Aged · Personality Inventory · Treatment Outcome · Triazines/administration & dosage,adverse effects
shelves.balance: LIKELY — with the enrichment design disclosed on both cards: in each trial, patients were first stabilised on OPEN-LABEL lamotrigine (other drugs withdrawn) and only those who stabilised were randomised, a design that selects lamotrigine tolerators/responders and must temper any lamotrigine-versus-lithium reading. Two 18-month randomised, double-blind maintenance trials, one in recently depressed patients (Calabrese 2003) and one in recently manic/hypomanic patients (Bowden 2003), found both lamotrigine and lithium superior to placebo at prolonging time to intervention for any mood episode. The polarity split is consistent: lamotrigine was superior to placebo against DEPRESSIVE episodes (Calabrese: time to intervention for depression, p=.047; 57% intervention-free for depression at 1 year vs 45% placebo; median survival 200 days on lamotrigine vs 93 on placebo for any episode), while lithium's clearest strength was against MANIC episodes (Calabrese: p=.026; Bowden: p=.006). Headache was the commonest adverse event. Lamotrigine for epilepsy is Shelf #337 — a different question.

cards.headline: Calabrese 2003 (recently depressed): lamotrigine and lithium both prolonged time to intervention vs placebo over 18 months (median 200 and 170 vs 93 days); lamotrigine's strength was depression
cards.summary: Calabrese 2003 (recently depressed): lamotrigine and lithium both prolonged time to intervention vs placebo over 18 months (median 200 and 170 vs 93 days); lamotrigine's strength was depression
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled maintenance trial (18 months) after open-label lamotrigine stabilisation (enriched design)
cards.people: 966 currently or recently depressed bipolar I outpatients entered an 8–16-week open-label phase in which lamotrigine (titrated to 200 mg/day) was added and concomitant drugs withdrawn; the 463 who stabilised were randomised to lamotrigine (50, 200 or 400 mg/day; 221), lithium (0.8–1.1 mEq/L; 121), or placebo (121) monotherapy for up to 18 months (September 1997–August 2001). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Time to intervention (addition of pharmacotherapy) for any mood episode was statistically superior for both lamotrigine and lithium versus placebo (p=.029); median survival times were 200 days (lamotrigine), 170 days (lithium) and 93 days (placebo). Intervention for depression was nearly three times as frequent as for mania. Lamotrigine was superior to placebo at prolonging time to intervention for a depressive episode (p=.047); the proportions intervention-free for depression at 1 year were lamotrigine 57%, lithium 46%, placebo 45%. Lithium was superior to placebo against manic/hypomanic episodes (p=.026); intervention-free for mania at 1 year: lamotrigine 77%, lithium 86%, placebo 72%. Headache was the most frequent adverse event in all three groups.
cards.watchOut: Enrichment: fewer than half of the 966 entrants (463) reached randomisation, and all had already tolerated and stabilised on lamotrigine — the randomised population is pre-selected in lamotrigine's favour, which is why the lamotrigine-versus-placebo result is stronger evidence than any lamotrigine-versus-lithium comparison drawn from it. The lamotrigine arms pool three doses (50/200/400 mg).
cards.source: Calabrese JR et al. A placebo-controlled 18-month trial of lamotrigine and lithium maintenance treatment in recently depressed patients with bipolar I disorder. J Clin Psychiatry. 2003. PMID: 14628976. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Acamprosate for alcohol dependence
shelves.question: In adults with alcohol dependence who have completed detoxification, does acamprosate increase continuous abstinence over 6–12 months versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acamprosate · Adult · Alcoholism/drug therapy,epidemiology · Double-Blind Method · Ethanol/poisoning · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Recurrence · Taurine/administration & dosage,adverse effects,analogs & derivatives,therapeutic use · Temperance · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — positive in the European trials, null in the US COMBINE trial, and the shelf carries both. In the anchor European trial (Whitworth 1996, 455 patients, 360 days), acamprosate roughly doubled continuous abstinence at the end of treatment (18.3% vs 7.1%; p=0.007), with mean cumulative abstinence duration 138.8 vs 103.8 days (p=0.012) and a higher proportion without treatment failure throughout (p<0.001); at 27 months, 11.9% vs 4.9% remained continuously abstinent. In COMBINE (Anton 2006, 1,383 recently abstinent US volunteers, 16 weeks), by contrast, acamprosate showed NO significant effect on drinking versus placebo, either alone or combined with naltrexone and/or behavioural intervention — while naltrexone and the behavioural intervention did show effects. The transatlantic disagreement is unresolved by these records (differences in populations, abstinence requirements at entry, and concurrent care are the usual explanations offered, none proven); the stamp is a split, and quoting only the European result would misstate the library's evidence.

cards.headline: Whitworth 1996: acamprosate doubled continuous abstinence at 360 days (18.3% vs 7.1%; p=0.007) in 455 patients with alcohol dependence
cards.summary: Whitworth 1996: acamprosate doubled continuous abstinence at 360 days (18.3% vs 7.1%; p=0.007) in 455 patients with alcohol dependence
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (360 days, with follow-up to 27 months)
cards.people: 455 patients aged 18–65 years with chronic or episodic alcohol dependence in a multicentre European trial, randomly allocated to acamprosate (1,998 mg/day if bodyweight above 60 kg; 1,332 mg/day if 60 kg or below; 224 in the intention-to-treat analysis) or placebo (224) for 360 days; seven patients were excluded from the intention-to-treat analysis because they received no medication. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: The proportion without treatment failure (relapse or non-attendance) was higher on acamprosate throughout the treatment period (p<0.001, Mantel-Cox). At the end of treatment, 41 (18.3%) acamprosate-treated and 16 (7.1%) placebo-treated patients had been continuously abstinent (p=0.007). Mean cumulative abstinence duration was greater on acamprosate (138.8 [SD 137.5] vs 103.8 [119.0] days; p=0.012). Of those withdrawn, 104 (52 per group) relapsed, 69 were lost to follow-up, and 63 refused to continue. At 27-month follow-up (148 completers), 27 (11.9%) versus 11 (4.9%) remained continuously abstinent, with mean cumulative abstinence duration 230.8 (259.1) vs 183.0 (235.2) days. Apart from occasional diarrhoea, side-effects did not differ between groups.
cards.watchOut: Attrition was heavy (94 acamprosate and 85 placebo patients completed the treatment phase of 224 per arm), and 'treatment failure' counts non-attendance as failure — a conservative but attendance-sensitive endpoint. Continuous abstinence even on acamprosate was under one in five: the drug roughly doubled a low rate.

cards.people: 1,383 recently alcohol-abstinent volunteers (median age 44 years) with DSM-IV primary alcohol dependence, at 11 US academic sites (January 2001–January 2004), randomised across eight groups receiving medical management with 16 weeks of naltrexone (100 mg/day) and/or acamprosate (3 g/day) and/or placebos, with or without a combined behavioural intervention (CBI); a ninth group (157) received CBI only, without pills.
cards.result: During treatment, percent days abstinent was higher with naltrexone plus medical management (80.6), CBI plus medical management and placebos (79.2), and naltrexone plus CBI plus medical management (77.1) than with placebos and medical management only (75.1), with a significant naltrexone × behavioural-intervention interaction (P=.009); naltrexone also reduced the risk of a heavy drinking day (hazard ratio 0.72 relative, 97.5% CI 0.53 to 0.98; P=.02). shelves.title: Bupropion sustained-release for smoking cessation
shelves.question: In adult smokers, does bupropion SR (150–300 mg/day) increase prolonged abstinence at 12 months versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antidepressive Agents, Second-Generation/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Bupropion/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Delayed-Action Preparations · Depression · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Nicotine/adverse effects · Smoking Cessation/methods,statistics & numerical data · Substance Withdrawal Syndrome/drug therapy · Tobacco Use Disorder/drug therapy · Weight Gain/drug effects
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials agree that bupropion sustained-release roughly doubles one-year abstinence. In the dose-ranging trial (Hurt 1997, 615 smokers, 7 weeks of treatment), carbon-monoxide-confirmed cessation at end of treatment rose with dose (19.0% placebo, 28.8% at 100 mg, 38.6% at 150 mg, 44.2% at 300 mg; P<0.001), and at one year the rates were 12.4%, 19.6%, 22.9% and 23.1% — significant for the 150 mg (P=0.02) and 300 mg (P=0.01) doses but not 100 mg (P=0.09). In Jorenby 1999 (893 smokers), 12-month abstinence was 30.3% on bupropion versus 15.6% on placebo (P<0.001), 16.4% on nicotine patch alone (not meaningfully above placebo), and 35.5% on bupropion plus patch (higher than bupropion alone but not significantly). Bupropion also blunted post-cessation weight gain in both trials. Insomnia and headache were the commonest adverse events; discontinuation for adverse events was 11.9% on bupropion versus 3.8% on placebo in Jorenby. Varenicline is homed on Shelves #225/#310 — a different drug — and bupropion within AXS-05 for depression is Shelf #1435.

cards.headline: Hurt 1997: bupropion SR showed a dose response for quitting, with 1-year abstinence 23.1% at 300 mg vs 12.4% on placebo (615 smokers)
cards.summary: Hurt 1997: bupropion SR showed a dose response for quitting, with 1-year abstinence 23.1% at 300 mg vs 12.4% on placebo (615 smokers)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled dose-ranging trial (7 weeks treatment, 52 weeks follow-up)
cards.people: 615 smokers randomly assigned to placebo or bupropion SR at 100, 150 or 300 mg/day for 7 weeks, with brief counselling at baseline, weekly during treatment, and at 8, 12, 26 and 52 weeks; the target quit date was one week after treatment began. Smokers with current depression were excluded, but not those with a history of major depression. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At the end of 7 weeks, carbon-monoxide-confirmed cessation rates were 19.0% (placebo), 28.8% (100 mg), 38.6% (150 mg) and 44.2% (300 mg) (P<0.001). At one year the rates were 12.4%, 19.6%, 22.9% and 23.1% respectively; the 150 mg (P=0.02) and 300 mg (P=0.01) groups, but not the 100 mg group (P=0.09), were significantly better than placebo. Among continuously abstinent subjects, mean weight gain was inversely associated with dose (2.9 kg placebo; 2.3 kg at 100/150 mg; 1.5 kg at 300 mg; P=0.02). No effects on depression scores (Beck Depression Inventory) were observed. Thirty-seven subjects stopped treatment prematurely because of adverse events, with similar frequency across groups.
cards.watchOut: Absolute one-year quit rates remain modest (about one in four at the best dose), and the trials excluded smokers with current depression — the population in whom bupropion's dual role is most often discussed is not the population tested here.
cards.source: Hurt RD et al. A comparison of sustained-release bupropion and placebo for smoking cessation. N Engl J Med. 1997. PMID: 9337378. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.summary: Jorenby 1999: bupropion beat placebo at 12 months (30.3% vs 15.6%); bupropion plus patch reached 35.5%, patch alone 16.4%
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (four arms, 9 weeks treatment, 12 months follow-up)
cards.people: 893 smokers randomised to sustained-release bupropion (244), nicotine patch (244), bupropion plus nicotine patch (245), or placebo (160), double-blind and placebo-controlled; treatment was 9 weeks of bupropion (150 mg/day for 3 days, then 150 mg twice daily) or placebo, plus 8 weeks of nicotine patch (21 mg/day weeks 2–7, 14 mg week 8, 7 mg week 9) or placebo; the target quit day was usually day 8. Smokers with clinical depression were excluded. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Abstinence rates at 12 months were 15.6% (placebo), 16.4% (nicotine patch), 30.3% (bupropion; P<0.001 vs placebo) and 35.5% (bupropion plus patch; P<0.001); abstinence was higher with combination therapy than with bupropion alone, but the difference was not statistically significant. By week 7, weight gain averaged 2.1 kg (placebo), 1.6 kg (patch), 1.7 kg (bupropion) and 1.1 kg (combination). A total of 311 subjects (34.8%) discontinued one or both medications; 79 stopped because of adverse events (placebo 3.8%, patch 6.6%, bupropion 11.9%, combination 11.4%). The most common adverse events were insomnia and headache.
cards.watchOut: The patch's own 12-month rate (16.4%) barely exceeded placebo (15.6%) in this trial — a result that should not be generalised to all nicotine-replacement evidence, which has its own shelves; within this record it is simply what the four-arm comparison showed. Discontinuation for adverse events was three times the placebo rate on bupropion-containing arms.

shelves.title: Behavioural activation for depression
shelves.question: In adults with major depression, is behavioural activation delivered by junior psychological workers non-inferior to full cognitive behavioural therapy for depressive symptoms at 12 months?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Antidepressive Agents/therapeutic use · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy/economics,methods · Comorbidity · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Depression/diagnosis,economics,psychology,therapy · Major Depressive Disorder/diagnosis,economics,psychology,therapy · Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders · Direct Service Costs · Directive Counseling/economics · Educational Status · England · Female · Humans · Linear Models · Male · Middle Aged · Quality of Life · Quality-Adjusted Life Years · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One large randomised non-inferiority trial (COBRA, 440 adults with major depressive disorder recruited from primary care and psychological therapy services in England) found behavioural activation delivered by junior mental health workers non-inferior to cognitive behavioural therapy delivered by psychological therapists on PHQ-9 at 12 months: in the modified intention-to-treat population both groups averaged 8.4 points (mean difference 0.1; 95% CI −1.3 to 1.5; p=0.89) against a non-inferiority margin of 1.9 points, and the per-protocol analysis agreed (difference 0.0; −1.5 to 1.6). The trial's cost analysis favoured behavioural activation (the authors' conclusion is that it can be delivered with less intensive and costly training 'with no lesser effect than CBT'), though the abstract as fetched does not print a specific cost figure, so none is printed on the card. Treatment was open-label (outcome assessors masked), and 21% of the behavioural-activation group versus 14% of the CBT group were not assessable for the primary outcome in the modified ITT population. A single — albeit large and well-designed — non-inferiority trial earns POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: COBRA (Richards 2016): behavioural activation by junior workers was non-inferior to CBT on PHQ-9 at 12 months (both 8.4 points; difference 0.1, 95% CI −1.3 to 1.5)
cards.summary: COBRA (Richards 2016): behavioural activation by junior workers was non-inferior to CBT on PHQ-9 at 12 months (both 8.4 points; difference 0.1, 95% CI −1.3 to 1.5)
cards.type: Randomised, controlled, non-inferiority trial (open-label treatment, masked outcome assessors)
cards.people: 440 adults aged 18 years or older meeting DSM-IV criteria for major depressive disorder, recruited from primary care and psychological therapy services in Devon, Durham and Leeds (UK) between September 2012 and April 2014, randomly assigned 1:1 to behavioural activation from junior mental health workers (221) or CBT from psychological therapists (219). Exclusions included current psychological therapy, alcohol/drug dependence, acute suicidality or a suicide attempt in the previous 2 months, cognitive impairment, bipolar disorder and psychosis. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Behavioural activation was non-inferior to CBT (non-inferiority margin 1.9 PHQ-9 points). Modified intention-to-treat: CBT 8.4 PHQ-9 points (SD 7.5) versus BA 8.4 (7.0); mean difference 0.1 points (95% CI −1.3 to 1.5; p=0.89); 175 (79%) of the BA group and 189 (86%) of the CBT group were assessable. Per protocol (at least eight sessions): CBT 7.9 (7.3) versus BA 7.8 (6.5); mean difference 0.0 (−1.5 to 1.6; p=0.99); 135 (61%) and 151 (69%) assessable respectively. Two (1%) non-trial-related deaths occurred (one multidrug toxicity in the BA group, one cancer in the CBT group), and 15 depression-related but not treatment-related serious adverse events occurred in three (2%) BA participants and eight (4%) CBT participants. The authors conclude BA is a simpler treatment that junior workers can deliver with less intensive and costly training, with no lesser effect than CBT.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority within a 1.9-point PHQ-9 margin is a bounded claim: BA could be up to ~1.5 points worse and still meet it, though the point estimate was 0.1. Differential assessability (79% vs 86% in the modified ITT) is a modest attrition concern. The workforce conclusion (junior workers suffice) is the trial's real payload and applies to its UK service context; the abstract prints no exact cost saving, so the card does not invent one.

shelves.title: Riluzole for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
shelves.question: In adults with ALS, does riluzole 100 mg/day prolong tracheostomy-free survival versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis/drug therapy,mortality,physiopathology · Double-Blind Method · Excitatory Amino Acid Antagonists · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Prognosis · Proportional Hazards Models · Prospective Studies · Riluzole · Survival Analysis · Thiazoles/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, survival is the primary claim): Two double-blind placebo-controlled trials agree. In Bensimon 1994 (155 outpatients), 12-month survival was 74% on riluzole 100 mg/day versus 58% on placebo (P=0.014), with the advantage concentrated in bulbar-onset disease (73% vs 35%) and a smaller but still significant advantage at the end of the placebo-controlled period (49% vs 37%; P=0.046); muscle-strength deterioration was slower (P=0.028). In the confirmatory dose-ranging trial (Lacomblez 1996, 959 outpatients, 50/100/200 mg/day for up to 18 months), tracheostomy-free survival rose dose-dependently (50.4% placebo; 55.3%, 56.8% and 57.8% across doses) with a significant dose-related decrease in the risk of death or tracheostomy (P=0.04) and, after adjustment for prognostic factors, a 35% relative decrease in the risk of death at the 100-mg dose (P=0.002). The benefit is a survival extension measured in proportions alive, not a functional cure: the dose-ranging trial found no significant treatment effect on functional measures.

cards.headline: Bensimon 1994: riluzole improved 12-month survival (74% vs 58%) in ALS, driven by bulbar-onset disease
cards.summary: Bensimon 1994: riluzole improved 12-month survival (74% vs 58%) in ALS, driven by bulbar-onset disease
cards.type: Prospective, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, stratified by site of onset (bulbar vs limb)
cards.people: 155 outpatients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis randomised to riluzole 100 mg/day or placebo; analyses at 12 months and at the end of the placebo-controlled period (median follow-up 573 days). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: After 12 months, 57 of 77 patients (74%) in the riluzole group were still alive versus 45 of 78 (58%) on placebo (P=0.014). In bulbar-onset disease, one-year survival was 73% (11 of 15) versus 35% (6 of 17) (P=0.014); in limb-onset disease it was 74% versus 64% (P=0.17). At the end of the placebo-controlled period the advantage had narrowed (49% [38 of 77] vs 37% [29 of 78]) but remained significant overall (P=0.046) and in bulbar-onset disease (53% [8 of 15] vs 18% [3 of 17]; P=0.013). Deterioration of muscle strength was significantly slower with riluzole (P=0.028). Adverse reactions included asthenia, spasticity and mild aminotransferase elevations; 27 riluzole patients versus 17 placebo patients withdrew.
cards.watchOut: A 155-patient trial whose headline rests heavily on the small bulbar-onset subgroup (15 vs 17 patients); the overall-population result is the primary reading and it attenuates over time.

cards.result: Tracheostomy-free survival rates were 50.4% (placebo), 55.3% (50 mg; P=0.23 Wilcoxon, P=0.25 log-rank), 56.8% (100 mg; P=0.05 Wilcoxon, P=0.076 log-rank) and 57.8% (200 mg; P=0.061 Wilcoxon, P=0.075 log-rank). shelves.title: Edaravone for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
shelves.question: In adults with early ALS within 2 years of onset and preserved respiratory function, does intravenous edaravone slow decline in ALSFRS-R score over 24 weeks versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis/diagnosis,drug therapy · Antipyrine/administration & dosage,adverse effects,analogs & derivatives,pharmacology · Double-Blind Method · Edaravone · Female · Free Radical Scavengers/administration & dosage,adverse effects,pharmacology · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Severity of Illness Index · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The evidence splits by population. The broad confirmatory phase 3 trial (Abe 2014, 206 patients) was NEGATIVE: ALSFRS-R change over 24 weeks was −5.70 on edaravone versus −6.35 on placebo (difference 0.65; P=0.411) and the authors concluded efficacy was not demonstrated. The later trial in the narrowly selected population identified by post-hoc analysis of that failure (Abe/Writing Group 2017, 137 patients randomised: definite or probable ALS, duration ≤2 years, every ALSFRS-R item ≥2, FVC ≥80%, with a 1–4 point decline during a 12-week run-in) found a smaller decline on edaravone (−5.01 vs −7.50 points; least-squares mean difference 2.49 points, 95% CI 0.99 to 3.98; P=0.0013). A benefit demonstrated only inside a post-hoc-defined subset, after the unselected trial missed, caps at POSSIBLE and applies only to patients who match the narrow criteria.

shelves.title: Siponimod for secondary progressive multiple sclerosis
shelves.question: In adults with secondary progressive MS, does siponimod 2 mg/day reduce the risk of 3-month confirmed disability progression versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Azetidines/therapeutic use · Benzyl Compounds/therapeutic use · Cohort Studies · Disease Progression · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Multiple Sclerosis, Chronic Progressive/drug therapy,pathology · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One large event-driven phase 3 trial (EXPAND, 1,651 randomised) found siponimod reduced the risk of 3-month confirmed disability progression versus placebo (26% [288 of 1,096] vs 32% [173 of 545]; hazard ratio 0.79 relative, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.95; a 21% relative risk reduction; P=0.013). A single trial, however large, caps at POSSIBLE on this library's scale. The price list is the S1P class's own: lymphopenia, raised liver transaminases, bradycardia/bradyarrhythmia at initiation, macular oedema, hypertension, varicella zoster reactivation and convulsions all occurred more frequently with siponimod; serious adverse events were reported in 18% versus 15%.

cards.headline: EXPAND 2018: siponimod cut 3-month confirmed disability progression (HR 0.79 relative) in SPMS
cards.summary: EXPAND 2018: siponimod cut 3-month confirmed disability progression (HR 0.79 relative) in SPMS
cards.type: Event-driven and exposure-driven, double-blind, phase 3 trial at 292 clinics and MS centres in 31 countries
cards.people: 1,651 patients (age 18–60 years) with SPMS and EDSS 3.0–6.5 randomised 2:1 to once-daily oral siponimod 2 mg (1,105) or placebo (546) for up to 3 years or until a prespecified number of progression events; 1,645 in the analyses. Mean time since first MS symptoms was 16.8 years (SD 8.3) and since conversion to SPMS 3.8 years (SD 3.5); 64% had not relapsed in the previous 2 years and 56% needed walking assistance. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: 288 (26%) of 1,096 patients receiving siponimod and 173 (32%) of 545 receiving placebo had 3-month confirmed disability progression (hazard ratio 0.79 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.65 to 0.95; relative risk reduction 21%; P=0.013). Adverse events occurred in 89% (975 of 1,099) on siponimod versus 82% (445 of 546) on placebo; serious adverse events in 18% (197) versus 15% (83). Lymphopenia, increased liver transaminase concentration, bradycardia and bradyarrhythmia at treatment initiation, macular oedema, hypertension, varicella zoster reactivation, and convulsions occurred more frequently with siponimod; initial dose titration mitigated cardiac first-dose effects.
cards.watchOut: A hazard ratio of 0.79 sits inside the range this library treats cautiously for observational data; here it is a randomised primary endpoint, but from a single trial, in a population where most patients were no longer relapsing — the absolute difference is about 6 percentage points over the trial's course.
cards.source: Kappos L et al. Siponimod versus placebo in secondary progressive multiple sclerosis (EXPAND): a double-blind, randomised, phase 3 study. Lancet (London, England). 2018. PMID: 29576505. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01665144, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Ofatumumab for relapsing multiple sclerosis
shelves.question: In adults with relapsing MS, does monthly subcutaneous ofatumumab reduce the annualised relapse rate versus oral teriflunomide?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/adverse effects,therapeutic use · B-Lymphocytes · Brain/pathology · Crotonates/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Disease Progression · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Hydroxybutyrates · Injections, Subcutaneous/adverse effects · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Male · Multiple Sclerosis, Relapsing-Remitting/drug therapy,pathology · Nitriles · T-Lymphocytes · Toluidines/adverse effects,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two parallel double-blind, double-dummy phase 3 trials (ASCLEPIOS I and II, 1,882 patients combined) found ofatumumab roughly halved the annualised relapse rate versus teriflunomide: 0.11 versus 0.22 in trial 1 (difference −0.11, 95% CI −0.16 to −0.06; P<0.001) and 0.10 versus 0.25 in trial 2 (difference −0.15, −0.20 to −0.09; P<0.001) — relative reductions of about 50% and 60%. In the pooled trials, disability worsening confirmed at 3 months occurred in 10.9% versus 15.0% (hazard ratio 0.66 relative; P=0.002) and at 6 months in 8.1% versus 12.0% (HR 0.68 relative; P=0.01), with disability improvement confirmed at 6 months in 11.0% versus 8.1% (HR favouring ofatumumab). Two concordant blinded trials against an active comparator earn LIKELY.

cards.headline: ASCLEPIOS I & II 2020: ofatumumab halved annualised relapse rates versus teriflunomide in both twin trials (0.11 vs 0.22; 0.10 vs 0.25)
cards.summary: ASCLEPIOS I & II 2020: ofatumumab halved annualised relapse rates versus teriflunomide in both twin trials (0.11 vs 0.22; 0.10 vs 0.25)
cards.type: Two double-blind, double-dummy, phase 3 trials (reported together)
cards.people: 1,882 patients with relapsing multiple sclerosis randomised to subcutaneous ofatumumab 20 mg every 4 weeks (after loading doses at days 1, 7 and 14; 946 patients) or oral teriflunomide 14 mg daily (936), for up to 30 months; median follow-up 1.6 years. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The annualised relapse rates in the ofatumumab and teriflunomide groups were 0.11 and 0.22 respectively in trial 1 (difference −0.11, 95% CI −0.16 to −0.06; P<0.001) and 0.10 and 0.25 in trial 2 (difference −0.15, −0.20 to −0.09; P<0.001). In the pooled trials, the percentage of patients with disability worsening confirmed at 3 months was 10.9% with ofatumumab and 15.0% with teriflunomide (hazard ratio 0.66 — a relative measure; P=0.002); at 6 months, 8.1% and 12.0% (HR 0.68 relative; P=0.01); and the percentage with disability improvement confirmed at 6 months was 11.0% and 8.1% (hazard ratio favouring ofatumumab, as reported). Secondary endpoints also included MRI lesion counts, serum neurofilament light chain and brain volume change.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is teriflunomide, a modest-efficacy oral agent — these trials rank ofatumumab above teriflunomide, not above the other high-efficacy antibodies; the fetched abstract text ends before the adverse-event summary, so no comparative harm rates are printed here.
cards.source: Hauser SL et al. Ofatumumab versus Teriflunomide in Multiple Sclerosis. The New England journal of medicine. 2020. PMID: 32757523. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02792218, NCT02792231, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Safinamide for Parkinson's disease with motor fluctuations
shelves.question: In adults with Parkinson's disease and motor fluctuations on levodopa, does safinamide 50–100 mg/day increase daily ON time without troublesome dyskinesia versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Aged · Alanine/analogs & derivatives,therapeutic use · Antiparkinson Agents/therapeutic use · Benzylamines/therapeutic use · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Levodopa/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Motor Activity/drug effects,radiation effects · Parkinson Disease/drug therapy,physiopathology · Severity of Illness Index
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trials agree. In Study 016 (Borgohain 2014, 669 patients), mean increases in total ON time with no or non-troublesome dyskinesia at 24 weeks were 1.36 hours (100 mg) and 1.37 hours (50 mg) versus 0.97 hours on placebo, with least-squares differences significantly favouring both doses, alongside significant improvements in OFF time, UPDRS Part III and CGI-C. In SETTLE (Schapira 2017, 549 patients), the mean change in daily ON time without troublesome dyskinesia was +1.42 hours on safinamide versus +0.57 hours on placebo (least-squares mean difference 0.96 hours, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.37; P<0.001). The consistent price is dyskinesia (14.6% vs 5.5% in SETTLE). Two concordant blinded trials earn LIKELY for a symptomatic gain of roughly half an hour to an hour of good ON time over placebo.

cards.headline: Study 016 (Borgohain 2014): safinamide 50 mg and 100 mg increased good ON time by ~1.4 hours vs 0.97 on placebo
cards.summary: Study 016 (Borgohain 2014): safinamide 50 mg and 100 mg increased good ON time by ~1.4 hours vs 0.97 on placebo
cards.type: Phase III, multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group trial (24 weeks)
cards.people: 669 patients with Parkinson's disease and motor fluctuations on levodopa randomised to oral safinamide 100 mg/day (224), 50 mg/day (223) or placebo (222); primary endpoint total ON time with no or non-troublesome dyskinesia from Hauser patient diaries. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At week 24, mean (SD) increases in total ON time with no or non-troublesome dyskinesia were 1.36 (2.625) hours for safinamide 100 mg/day, 1.37 (2.745) hours for 50 mg/day, and 0.97 (2.375) hours for placebo; least-squares mean differences in both safinamide groups were significantly higher versus placebo (the abstract does not print the numerical differences). Improvements in OFF time, UPDRS Part III and CGI-C were significantly greater in both safinamide groups versus placebo. There were no significant between-group differences in incidences of treatment-emergent adverse events or of events leading to discontinuation.
cards.watchOut: Diary-based ON time is a patient-reported symptomatic measure with wide variability (SDs around 2.5 hours dwarf the ~0.4-hour raw separation); the trial's own least-squares analysis, not the raw means, carries the significance.

shelves.title: Rivastigmine for dementia associated with Parkinson's disease
shelves.question: In adults with mild-to-moderate dementia associated with Parkinson's disease, does rivastigmine improve cognition and global function versus placebo over 24 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Cholinesterase Inhibitors/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Dementia/drug therapy,etiology · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Nausea/chemically induced · Parkinson Disease/complications · Phenylcarbamates/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Rivastigmine · Tremor/chemically induced · Vomiting/chemically induced
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One large pivotal trial (EXPRESS, Emre 2004, 541 patients) found modest benefits over 24 weeks: rivastigmine patients improved by a mean of 2.1 points on the 70-point ADAS-cog (from a baseline of 23.8) while placebo patients worsened by 0.7 points (from 24.3) (P<0.001) — a between-group separation of roughly 2.8 points — and mean ADCS-CGIC scores at 24 weeks were 3.8 versus 4.3 (P=0.007), with clinically meaningful worsening in 13.0% versus 23.1%. The gastrointestinal and tremor price was substantial (nausea 29.0% vs 11.2%; vomiting 16.6% vs 1.7%; tremor 10.2% vs 3.9%). A single trial with moderate effects caps at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: EXPRESS (Emre 2004): rivastigmine gave modest cognitive and global benefits in Parkinson's dementia, with high nausea and vomiting rates
cards.summary: EXPRESS (Emre 2004): rivastigmine gave modest cognitive and global benefits in Parkinson's dementia, with high nausea and vomiting rates
cards.people: 541 patients in whom mild-to-moderate dementia developed at least 2 years after a clinical diagnosis of Parkinson's disease, randomised to placebo or rivastigmine 3–12 mg/day; 410 completed the study. Primary efficacy variables were the ADAS-cog cognitive subscale and the ADCS-CGIC global impression. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Rivastigmine-treated patients had a mean improvement of 2.1 points in the 70-point ADAS-cog score, from a baseline of 23.8, compared with a 0.7-point worsening in the placebo group, from a baseline of 24.3 (P<0.001). Clinically meaningful improvements on the ADCS-CGIC were observed in 19.8% of the rivastigmine group and 14.5% of the placebo group, and clinically meaningful worsening in 13.0% and 23.1% respectively (mean score at 24 weeks 3.8 vs 4.3; P=0.007). All secondary efficacy variables also favoured rivastigmine. The most frequent adverse events were nausea (29.0% rivastigmine vs 11.2% placebo; P<0.001), vomiting (16.6% vs 1.7%; P<0.001) and tremor (10.2% vs 3.9%; P=0.01). The authors describe the improvements as moderate and similar to those reported in trials of rivastigmine for Alzheimer's disease.
cards.watchOut: Only 410 of 541 patients completed the study; in a dementia trial with this much gastrointestinal intolerance, functional unblinding (patients and raters guessing allocation from nausea and tremor) is a real risk to the subjective global-impression endpoint.
cards.source: Emre M et al. Rivastigmine for dementia associated with Parkinson's disease. The New England journal of medicine. 2004. PMID: 15590953. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Deutetrabenazine for chorea in Huntington's disease
shelves.question: In adults with chorea associated with Huntington's disease, does deutetrabenazine reduce the Unified Huntington's Disease Rating Scale total maximal chorea score versus placebo over 12 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic Uptake Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Chorea/drug therapy · Cytochrome P-450 CYP2D6/metabolism · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Huntington Disease/drug therapy · Maintenance Chemotherapy/methods · Male · Middle Aged · Tetrabenazine/analogs & derivatives,therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One pivotal double-blind trial (First-HD, Frank 2016, 90 patients) found deutetrabenazine improved the total maximal chorea score from 12.1 to 7.7, versus 13.2 to 11.3 on placebo — a mean between-group difference of −2.5 units (95% CI −3.7 to −1.3; P<0.001) on a 0–28 scale — with treatment success on the Patient Global Impression of Change in 51% versus 20% (P=0.002) and on the Clinical Global Impression of Change in 42% versus 13%. cards.headline: First-HD 2016: deutetrabenazine reduced total maximal chorea by 2.5 units more than placebo over 12 weeks
cards.summary: First-HD 2016: deutetrabenazine reduced total maximal chorea by 2.5 units more than placebo over 12 weeks
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial at 34 Huntington Study Group sites (8-week titration, 4-week maintenance, 1-week washout)
cards.people: 90 ambulatory adults with manifest Huntington disease and a baseline total maximal chorea score of 8 or higher (range 0–28; lower is less chorea), randomised to deutetrabenazine (45) or placebo (45) between August 2013 and August 2014; mean age 53.7 years; 40 women (44.4%).
cards.result: In the deutetrabenazine group, mean total maximal chorea scores improved from 12.1 (95% CI 11.2 to 12.9) to 7.7 (6.5 to 8.9), whereas in the placebo group scores improved from 13.2 (12.2 to 14.3) to 11.3 (10.0 to 12.5); the mean between-group difference was −2.5 units (95% CI −3.7 to −1.3; P<0.001). Treatment success on the Patient Global Impression of Change occurred in 23 patients (51%) on deutetrabenazine versus 9 (20%) on placebo (P=0.002), and on the Clinical Global Impression of Change in 19 (42%) versus 6 (13%). The trial was designed to detect a 2.7-unit treatment difference.
cards.watchOut: Twelve weeks of treatment in 90 patients: the observed effect (−2.5) is slightly smaller than the difference the trial was powered to detect (2.7), and nothing here speaks to longer-term chorea control, falls, or swallowing and mood outcomes.
cards.source: Frank S et al. Effect of Deutetrabenazine on Chorea Among Patients With Huntington Disease: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2016. PMID: 27380342. shelves.title: Atogepant for preventive treatment of migraine
shelves.question: In adults with episodic migraine, does daily oral atogepant reduce mean monthly migraine days versus placebo over 12 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide Receptor Antagonists/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Constipation/chemically induced · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Male · Middle Aged · Migraine Disorders/prevention & control · Nausea/chemically induced · Piperidines/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Pyridines/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Pyrroles/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Spiro Compounds/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Young Adult
shelves.balance: LIKELY: The episodic-migraine anchor trial (ADVANCE, Ailani 2021; 873 patients in the efficacy analysis) found all three atogepant doses beat placebo on the change in mean monthly migraine days across 12 weeks: −3.7 (10 mg), −3.9 (30 mg) and −4.2 days (60 mg) versus −2.5 days on placebo (mean differences −1.2, −1.4 and −1.7 days; all P<0.001). The programme's chronic-migraine trial (PROGRESS, 755 in the modified intention-to-treat population) pointed the same way in that harder population (−7.5 and −6.9 versus −5.1 days; differences −2.4 and −1.8; adjusted P<0.0001 and P=0.0009) and is carded as programme support, not as episodic-migraine evidence. The commonest adverse events were constipation (roughly 7–11%) and nausea (roughly 4–10%). Two blinded phase 3 trials of the same drug and endpoint earn LIKELY.

cards.headline: ADVANCE 2021: atogepant cut monthly migraine days by 1.2–1.7 days more than placebo in episodic migraine
cards.summary: ADVANCE 2021: atogepant cut monthly migraine days by 1.2–1.7 days more than placebo in episodic migraine
cards.type: Phase 3, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial (12 weeks)
cards.people: Adults with 4 to 14 migraine days per month randomised 1:1:1:1 to once-daily oral atogepant 10 mg (214 in the efficacy analysis), 30 mg (223), 60 mg (222) or placebo (214); 910 enrolled and 873 in the efficacy analysis; mean baseline migraine days per month ranged from 7.5 to 7.9 across groups. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Changes from baseline in mean monthly migraine days across the 12 weeks were −3.7 days with 10-mg atogepant, −3.9 with 30 mg, −4.2 with 60 mg and −2.5 with placebo. Mean differences from placebo were −1.2 days (95% CI −1.8 to −0.6) at 10 mg, −1.4 (−1.9 to −0.8) at 30 mg and −1.7 (−2.3 to −1.2) at 60 mg (P<0.001 for all comparisons). Secondary endpoints favoured atogepant except the AIM-D Performance of Daily Activities and Physical Impairment scores at the 10-mg dose. The most common adverse events were constipation (6.9 to 7.7% across atogepant doses) and nausea (4.4 to 6.1%); serious adverse events included one case each of asthma and optic neuritis in the 10-mg group.
cards.watchOut: The placebo group itself lost 2.5 migraine days per month, so the drug-attributable gain is the 1.2–1.7-day difference; episodic migraine only — the chronic-migraine result sits on the next card and must not be quoted for this population.

shelves.title: Intravenous immunoglobulin versus plasma exchange for Guillain–Barré syndrome
shelves.question: In adults with Guillain–Barré syndrome unable to walk unaided, is intravenous immunoglobulin at least as effective as plasma exchange for recovery of walking and disability at 4 weeks and beyond?
shelves.mesh: Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Immunoglobulins/administration & dosage · Injections, Intravenous · Middle Aged · Motor Activity · Plasma Exchange · Polyradiculoneuropathy/physiopathology,therapy · Random Allocation
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials agree that IVIg is at least as effective as plasma exchange. In the Dutch trial (van der Meché 1992, 150 patients), improvement by at least one motor grade at 4 weeks occurred in 53% on IVIg versus 34% on plasma exchange (difference 19 percentage points, 95% CI 3 to 34; P=0.024), the median time to improvement by one grade was 27 versus 41 days (P=0.05), and the IVIg group had significantly fewer complications and less need for artificial ventilation. In the international Plasma Exchange/Sandoglobulin trial (1997, 379 assessed), mean improvement on the disability scale at 4 weeks was 0.8 grades on IVIg versus 0.9 on plasma exchange and 1.1 on the combination — no significant differences, with the IVIg-versus-exchange difference small enough to exclude a 0.5-grade difference at the 95% confidence level, and no differences in time to unaided walking or ventilation discontinuation up to 48 weeks. One trial leans IVIg-superior, the larger one says equivalent: the honest joint reading is at-least-as-effective, with no gain from combining both.

cards.headline: Dutch GBS Trial 1992: IVIg improved one grade or more in 53% vs 34% on plasma exchange at 4 weeks
cards.summary: Dutch GBS Trial 1992: IVIg improved one grade or more in 53% vs 34% on plasma exchange at 4 weeks
cards.type: Multicentre randomised trial (open treatment, predefined outcome)
cards.people: 150 patients with Guillain–Barré syndrome for less than two weeks who were unable to walk independently, randomly assigned to five plasma exchanges (each 200–250 mL/kg) or five doses of intravenous immune globulin (0.4 g/kg per day). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: After 150 patients had been treated, strength had improved by one grade or more in 34% of those treated with plasma exchange versus 53% of those treated with immune globulin (difference 19 percentage points, 95% CI 3 to 34; P=0.024). The median time to improvement by one grade was 41 days with plasma exchange and 27 days with immune globulin (P=0.05). The immune globulin group had significantly fewer complications and less need for artificial ventilation. The authors' conclusion — IVIg is at least as effective as plasma exchange and may be superior — is printed as their reading of a single 150-patient trial and is tempered by the larger trial on the next card.
cards.watchOut: Treatment could not be blinded (exchange versus infusion), and the superiority margin comes from one modest-sized trial; the complication and ventilation advantages, while significant, are secondary outcomes.

shelves.title: Stellate ganglion block for PTSD
shelves.question: In adults with PTSD, do two stellate ganglion block injections improve CAPS/PCL-5 symptom scores versus sham injections at 8 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Anesthetics, Local · Animals · Autonomic Nerve Block · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Injections · Male · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Ropivacaine · Stellate Ganglion · Stress Disorders, Post-Traumatic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One multisite blinded sham-procedure randomised trial (Rae Olmsted 2020, 113 active-duty service members with PTSD symptoms) found paired right-sided stellate ganglion blocks at weeks 0 and 2 reduced CAPS-5 total symptom severity by −12.6 points at 8 weeks versus −6.1 points with sham (adjusted changes; P=.01) — a modest between-group difference of about 6.5 points on an 80-point scale. A single trial in a selected military population with mild-to-moderate baseline severity and 8 weeks of follow-up earns POSSIBLE. The Hanling et al. 2016 trial named in the topic draft was not pinned to a verified record at build and is fenced without figures.

cards.headline: Rae Olmsted 2020: two stellate ganglion blocks beat sham on CAPS-5 at 8 weeks (−12.6 vs −6.1 points; P=.01) in 113 service members
cards.summary: Rae Olmsted 2020: two stellate ganglion blocks beat sham on CAPS-5 at 8 weeks (−12.6 vs −6.1 points; P=.01) in 113 service members
cards.type: Multisite, blinded, sham-procedure, randomized clinical trial (2:1 ratio; 3 US Army Interdisciplinary Pain Management Centers)
cards.people: 113 eligible active-duty service members (100 male, 13 female; mean [SD] age 37.3 [6.7] years) on stable psychotropic medication with a PTSD Checklist-Civilian Version score of at least 32 at screening, randomised to stellate ganglion block (74) or sham (39); 108 (95.6%) completed the study. Baseline mean CAPS-5 scores were 37.6 (11.2) (SGB) and 39.8 (14.4) (sham) on a 0–80 scale; 91 (80.0%) met CAPS-5 PTSD criteria. Prior SGB, selected psychiatric or substance use disorders, moderate/severe traumatic brain injury and recent suicidal ideation were exclusions.
cards.result: In an intent-to-treat analysis, the adjusted mean CAPS-5 total symptom severity change from baseline to 8 weeks was −12.6 points (95% CI −15.5 to −9.7) with SGB versus −6.1 points (−9.8 to −2.3) with sham (P=.01). The trial's planned responder framing was an improvement of 10 or more points on mean CAPS-5; the abstract reports mean changes rather than responder proportions, so none are carded. The authors note the mild-moderate baseline severity and short follow-up limit generalisability and frame SGB as meriting further trials as a PTSD treatment adjunct.
cards.watchOut: The sham group itself improved by 6.1 points — half the active group's gain is shared with a sham procedure — and the population (active-duty, mostly male, subthreshold cases included) is narrower than civilian PTSD practice. Eight weeks is the whole of the controlled record.
cards.source: Rae Olmsted KL et al. Effect of Stellate Ganglion Block Treatment on Posttraumatic Stress Disorder Symptoms: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA psychiatry. 2020. PMID: 31693083. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03077919, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: L-methylfolate as adjunctive therapy for SSRI-resistant depression
shelves.question: In adults with major depression responding inadequately to an SSRI, does adjunctive L-methylfolate 15 mg/day improve response and remission versus adjunctive placebo?
shelves.mesh: Chemotherapy, Adjuvant · Major Depressive Disorder · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors · Tetrahydrofolates · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — split by trial, as the programme was designed: Papakostas 2012 reports TWO sequential parallel comparison design trials in one paper. The first (148 outpatients with SSRI-resistant major depression; L-methylfolate 7.5 mg/day rising to 15 mg/day) found NO significant difference between treatment groups. The second (75 patients; L-methylfolate 15 mg/day throughout) found significantly greater efficacy than continued SSRI plus placebo on both primary outcome measures (response rate and change in depression symptom score) and two secondary severity measures, with a number needed to treat for response of approximately 6 and adverse-event rates no different from placebo. One positive small trial at the 15 mg dose after one null trial earns POSSIBLE for the 15 mg strategy — and the shelf carries the null first trial on its face, not underneath it.

cards.headline: Papakostas 2012: the 7.5 mg lead-in trial was null; the 15 mg trial was positive (NNT for response ≈6) — two trials, one paper
cards.summary: Papakostas 2012: the 7.5 mg lead-in trial was null; the 15 mg trial was positive (NNT for response ≈6) — two trials, one paper
cards.type: Two multicenter sequential parallel comparison design randomized, double-blind trials (60 days each, in two 30-day periods; SSRI doses held constant)
cards.people: Trial 1: 148 outpatients with SSRI-resistant major depressive disorder, randomised 2:3:3 to L-methylfolate for 60 days (7.5 mg/day for 30 days, then 15 mg/day for 30 days), placebo for 30 days then L-methylfolate 7.5 mg/day for 30 days, or placebo for 60 days. Trial 2: 75 patients with an identical design except L-methylfolate was 15 mg/day during both 30-day periods. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix for either trial.
cards.result: In the first trial, no significant difference was observed in outcomes between the treatment groups. In the second trial, adjunctive L-methylfolate at 15 mg/day showed significantly greater efficacy compared with continued SSRI plus placebo on both primary outcome measures (response rate and degree of change in depression symptom score) and two secondary outcome measures of symptom severity; the number needed to treat for response was approximately 6 in favour of adjunctive L-methylfolate 15 mg/day. The abstract prints no response percentages, so none are carded. L-methylfolate was well tolerated, with rates of adverse events no different from placebo. The authors conclude adjunctive L-methylfolate 15 mg/day may be an effective, safe and relatively well tolerated strategy for partial or non-responders to SSRIs.
cards.watchOut: The positive result is the SECOND, smaller trial (75 patients) after the first (148 patients) failed — a dose-escalation redesign tested in fewer people. Sequential parallel comparison designs enrich for placebo non-response in ways that complicate generalisation to ordinary clinic augmentation.
cards.source: Papakostas GI et al. L-methylfolate as adjunctive therapy for SSRI-resistant major depression: results of two randomized, double-blind, parallel-sequential trials. The American journal of psychiatry. 2012. PMID: 23212058. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00321152 and NCT00955955, from the record's databank fields.
