shelves.title: N-acetylcysteine as adjunctive treatment for schizophrenia
shelves.question: In adults with chronic schizophrenia on stable antipsychotics, does adjunctive N-acetylcysteine (1 g twice daily) improve negative symptoms and overall psychopathology versus placebo over 24 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Acetylcysteine · Adult · Analysis of Variance · Double-Blind Method · Female · Free Radical Scavengers · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Movement Disorders · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Schizophrenia
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One multicenter double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Berk 2008, 140 people with chronic schizophrenia on maintenance antipsychotics; 84 completed treatment) found adjunctive N-acetylcysteine 1 g twice daily improved PANSS total (mean difference −5.97, 95% CI −10.44 to −1.51; P=.009), PANSS negative (−1.83, −3.33 to −0.32; P=.018) and PANSS general scores, both Clinical Global Impression scales, and akathisia, over 24 weeks — with NO significant change on the PANSS positive subscale. The authors describe moderate effect sizes. Later augmentation trials named in the topic draft were not pinned to verified records at build and are fenced; on the pinned record alone — one trial, 40% non-completion — the stamp is POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Berk 2008: adjunctive NAC improved PANSS total (−5.97) and negative symptoms versus placebo over 24 weeks, with no effect on positive symptoms
cards.summary: Berk 2008: adjunctive NAC improved PANSS total (−5.97) and negative symptoms versus placebo over 24 weeks, with no effect on positive symptoms
cards.type: Randomized, multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (24 weeks, plus a 4-week discontinuation phase)
cards.people: 140 people with chronic schizophrenia on maintenance antipsychotic medication, randomized to oral N-acetylcysteine 1 g twice daily or placebo as add-on treatment; 84 completed treatment. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Intent-to-treat analysis showed NAC improved more than placebo on PANSS total (−5.97 [95% CI −10.44 to −1.51]; P=.009), PANSS negative (mean difference −1.83 [−3.33 to −0.32]; P=.018) and PANSS general (−2.79 [−5.38 to −0.20]; P=.035), CGI-Severity (−0.26 [−0.44 to −0.08]; P=.004) and CGI-Improvement (−0.22 [−0.41 to −0.03]; P=.025). No significant change on the PANSS positive subscale was seen. NAC was also associated with an improvement in akathisia (P=.022). The authors report endpoint effect sizes consistent with moderate benefits and frame NAC as a potential safe, moderately effective augmentation strategy.
cards.watchOut: Only 84 of 140 randomised patients completed treatment, and the benefit is concentrated in negative and general symptoms — the positive-symptom null matters for how this shelf may be quoted. Changes after the 4-week discontinuation phase are part of the design but no figures are printed for them in the abstract. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Berk M et al. N-acetyl cysteine as a glutathione precursor for schizophrenia--a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial. Biological psychiatry. 2008. PMID: 18436195. shelves.title: Repetitive TMS to augment psychotherapy for PTSD
shelves.question: In combat veterans with PTSD receiving cognitive processing therapy, does adjunctive high-frequency rTMS to the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex improve CAPS scores versus sham stimulation?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Cognition · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy · Combat Disorders · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Psychotherapy, Group · Stress Disorders, Post-Traumatic · Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation · Treatment Outcome · United States · Veterans · Young Adult
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): The pinned trial contradicts the topic draft on two facts, and the record governs both. First, the stimulation was LOW frequency — 1 Hz continuously for 30 minutes (1,800 pulses) over the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex — not the 'high-frequency' stimulation the question names. Second, the trial did NOT report a null: Kozel 2018 (103 combat veterans randomised to active or sham rTMS immediately before weekly cognitive processing therapy) reports significantly greater symptom reductions with active rTMS on CAPS and PCL across treatment and 6-month follow-up — but every significance claim rests on ONE-TAILED tests (P≤0.023 and P≤0.017, one-tailed), only 60% of participants completed treatment and 57% completed the 6-month assessment. One-tailed significance, heavy attrition, and a single trial: MAYBE (weak evidence), with the authors' positive claim and its statistical footing both printed on the card.

cards.headline: Kozel 2018: 1 Hz (not high-frequency) rTMS before CPT beat sham on CAPS and PCL — on one-tailed tests, with 40% not completing treatment
cards.summary: Kozel 2018: 1 Hz (not high-frequency) rTMS before CPT beat sham on CAPS and PCL — on one-tailed tests, with 40% not completing treatment
cards.type: Randomized sham-controlled trial (parallel design; rTMS immediately prior to weekly cognitive processing therapy for 12–15 sessions)
cards.people: 103 veterans aged 18–60 years with current combat-related PTSD symptoms (of 515 screened), randomized to active rTMS (n=54) or sham rTMS (n=49), each immediately before weekly CPT; the coil was positioned over the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex at 110% of motor threshold, 1 Hz continuously for 30 minutes, 1,800 pulses per treatment. Sixty-two participants (60%) completed treatment and 59 (57%) completed the 6-month assessment. Participants were predominantly male and limited to one era of conflicts, as the abstract states.
cards.result: The rTMS+CPT group showed greater symptom reductions from baseline on both CAPS and PCL across CPT sessions and follow-up assessments than sham+CPT (t[df ≥325] ≤−2.01, P≤0.023, ONE-TAILED, for CAPS; t[df ≥303] ≤−2.14, P≤0.017, ONE-TAILED, for PCL). Blinded raters assessed participants at baseline, after the 5th and 9th treatments, and at 1, 3 and 6 months post-treatment. The abstract prints no CAPS point differences or effect sizes, so none are carded. The authors conclude the addition of rTMS to CPT produced significantly greater PTSD symptom reduction early in treatment, sustained to six months.
cards.watchOut: Three cautions compound: the reported significance uses one-tailed P values (the corresponding two-tailed values would be roughly double — borderline by conventional standards); attrition was high (40% did not complete treatment); and the topic draft both mislabelled the frequency (1 Hz is low-frequency stimulation) and reversed the trial's conclusion. rTMS for depression is homed on Shelves #574/#993 and is not re-carded here.
cards.source: Kozel FA et al. Repetitive TMS to augment cognitive processing therapy in combat veterans of recent conflicts with PTSD: A randomized clinical trial. Journal of affective disorders. 2018. PMID: 29351885. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Viloxazine extended-release for ADHD
shelves.question: In children and adolescents with ADHD, does once-daily viloxazine ER reduce ADHD Rating Scale total score versus placebo over 6–8 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Attention Deficit Disorder with Hyperactivity · Child · Delayed-Action Preparations · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Male · Treatment Outcome · Viloxazine
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Nasser 2020, 477 children aged 6–11 years with ADHD; 460 in the intent-to-treat population) found viloxazine ER (SPN-812) 100 mg and 200 mg once daily significantly reduced ADHD-RS-5 total score versus placebo from week 1 through end of study at 6 weeks (P=0.0004 and P<0.0001 at end of study), with significant improvements on CGI-I, Conners 3-PS composite and functional impairment scores, treatment-related adverse events of somnolence, decreased appetite and headache in at least 5%, and discontinuation for adverse events under 5%. The pinned trial covers children 6–11 only: the adolescent and adult trials named in the topic draft were not pinned to verified records at build and are fenced without figures, so the shelf's verified population is narrower than its question. One trial: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Nasser 2020: viloxazine ER 100 mg and 200 mg significantly reduced ADHD-RS-5 scores versus placebo over 6 weeks in children aged 6–11
cards.summary: Nasser 2020: viloxazine ER 100 mg and 200 mg significantly reduced ADHD-RS-5 scores versus placebo over 6 weeks in children aged 6–11
cards.type: Phase III, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled 6-week trial
cards.people: 477 male and female children aged 6–11 years with a confirmed DSM-5 ADHD diagnosis, ADHD-Rating Scale-5 score of at least 28 and Clinical Global Impression-Severity score of at least 4, free of ADHD medication for at least 1 week, randomized to once-daily SPN-812 (viloxazine extended-release) 100 mg, 200 mg, or placebo (intent-to-treat population n=460); the majority were male (63%) and either White (51.3%) or African American (43.7%).
cards.result: Statistically significant improvements in ADHD-RS-5 total score were observed in both the 100 mg and 200 mg groups versus placebo at week 1 (P=0.0004 and P=0.0244) and maintained through end of study (P=0.0004 and P<0.0001). Significant improvements at end of study were also seen on CGI-I (P=0.0020 and P<0.0001), Conners 3-PS Composite T-score (P=0.0003 and P=0.0002) and WFIRS-P total average score (P=0.0019 and P=0.0002). The abstract prints P values rather than point-score changes, so no ADHD-RS-5 magnitudes are carded. Treatment-related adverse events reported in at least 5% included somnolence, decreased appetite and headache; the discontinuation rate due to adverse events was under 5%.
cards.watchOut: Six weeks, one trial, children aged 6–11 only — the adolescent half of the shelf question, and adult ADHD (homed on Shelf #707), are not evidence on this shelf. Effect sizes in score points are not printed in the abstract and must not be imported from secondary sources.

shelves.title: Psilocybin-assisted therapy for alcohol use disorder
shelves.question: In adults with alcohol use disorder, does psilocybin-assisted psychotherapy (two psilocybin sessions) reduce the percentage of heavy drinking days versus an active-placebo (diphenhydramine) assisted therapy over 32 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Alcohol Drinking · Alcoholism · Diphenhydramine · Double-Blind Method · Female · Hallucinogens · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Psilocybin · Psychotherapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One double-blind randomised trial (Bogenschutz 2022, 95 adults with alcohol dependence, 93 dosed and analysed) found two psilocybin sessions embedded in 12 weeks of manualised psychotherapy reduced the percentage of heavy drinking days over the 32-week double-blind period to 9.7% versus 23.6% with diphenhydramine active placebo (mean difference 13.9 percentage points, 95% CI 3.0 to 24.7; P=.01), with lower mean daily alcohol consumption and no serious adverse events among psilocybin recipients. A single trial of 95 participants, in a design where functional unblinding is likely (a psychedelic versus a sedating antihistamine), earns POSSIBLE. Psilocybin for treatment-resistant depression and MDMA for PTSD are homed on Shelf #409 and are not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Bogenschutz 2022: psilocybin-assisted therapy cut heavy drinking days to 9.7% versus 23.6% with diphenhydramine over 32 weeks
cards.summary: Bogenschutz 2022: psilocybin-assisted therapy cut heavy drinking days to 9.7% versus 23.6% with diphenhydramine over 32 weeks
cards.type: Double-blind randomized clinical trial (2 academic centers, United States; 12 weeks of manualized psychotherapy with medication sessions at weeks 4 and 8)
cards.people: 95 adults aged 25 to 65 years (mean [SD] age 46 [12] years; 42 [44.2%] female) with a DSM-IV diagnosis of alcohol dependence and at least 4 heavy drinking days in the 30 days before screening, randomized to psilocybin (49) or diphenhydramine (46); 93 received at least one dose and entered the primary analysis. Major psychiatric and drug use disorders, hallucinogen use and current AUD treatment were exclusions; the sample was predominantly non-Hispanic White (78.9%).
cards.result: Percentage of heavy drinking days during the 32-week double-blind period following the first dose was 9.7% in the psilocybin group versus 23.6% in the diphenhydramine group (mean difference 13.9 percentage points; 95% CI 3.0 to 24.7; F1,86=6.43; P=.01). Mean daily alcohol consumption (standard drinks per day) was also lower in the psilocybin group (no figures printed). Study medication was psilocybin 25 mg/70 kg versus diphenhydramine 50 mg at the first session, and psilocybin 25–40 mg/70 kg versus diphenhydramine 50–100 mg at the second; psychotherapy included motivational enhancement therapy and cognitive behavioral therapy. There were no serious adverse events among participants who received psilocybin.
cards.watchOut: Functional unblinding is the standing caveat for psychedelic trials: participants receiving high-dose psilocybin versus diphenhydramine can usually infer their allocation, and expectancy can move a self-reported drinking outcome (timeline followback). The effect is an effect of psilocybin PLUS 12 weeks of psychotherapy against active placebo PLUS the same therapy — not of the drug alone.
cards.source: Bogenschutz MP et al. Percentage of Heavy Drinking Days Following Psilocybin-Assisted Psychotherapy vs Placebo in the Treatment of Adult Patients With Alcohol Use Disorder: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA psychiatry. 2022. PMID: 36001306. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02061293, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Repeated intravenous ketamine for chronic PTSD
shelves.question: In adults with chronic PTSD, do repeated intravenous ketamine infusions reduce CAPS-5 severity versus midazolam control at 2 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Antidepressive Agents · Chronic Disease · Depression · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Ketamine · Male · Middle Aged · Receptors, N-Methyl-D-Aspartate · Stress Disorders, Post-Traumatic · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One small randomised controlled trial (Feder 2021, 30 adults with chronic PTSD) found six intravenous ketamine infusions (0.5 mg/kg) over 2 weeks improved CAPS-5 total scores significantly more than midazolam (0.045 mg/kg) active control: at week 2 the mean CAPS-5 score was 11.88 points lower with ketamine (d=1.13, 95% CI 0.36 to 1.91), with 67% responders versus 20% on midazolam, and parallel improvement in depression scores; among ketamine responders the median time to loss of response was 27.5 days. Thirty patients and a response that fades within about a month cap the stamp at POSSIBLE. The group's 2014 single-infusion crossover trial named in the topic draft was not pinned to a verified record at build and is fenced without figures. Ketamine for treatment-resistant depression is homed on Shelves #223/#407.

cards.headline: Feder 2021: six ketamine infusions beat midazolam on CAPS-5 at 2 weeks (11.88 points lower; 67% vs 20% responders) — in 30 patients
cards.summary: Feder 2021: six ketamine infusions beat midazolam on CAPS-5 at 2 weeks (11.88 points lower; 67% vs 20% responders) — in 30 patients
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (six infusions over 2 consecutive weeks; psychoactive placebo control)
cards.people: 30 individuals with chronic PTSD, randomly assigned 1:1 to six infusions of ketamine (0.5 mg/kg) or midazolam (0.045 mg/kg) over 2 weeks, with clinician-rated and self-report assessments 24 hours after the first infusion and at weekly visits. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The ketamine group showed significantly greater improvement in CAPS-5 and in Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale total scores than the midazolam group from baseline to week 2. At week 2, the mean CAPS-5 total score was 11.88 points (SE=3.96) lower in the ketamine group than the midazolam group (d=1.13, 95% CI 0.36 to 1.91). Sixty-seven percent of ketamine participants were treatment responders, compared with 20% on midazolam. Among ketamine responders, the median time to loss of response was 27.5 days following the 2-week course. Ketamine infusions were well tolerated overall, without serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Fifteen patients per arm: the responder percentages are 10 versus 3 people, and the confidence interval on the effect size (0.36 to 1.91) is very wide. The benefit's median durability — under a month after the course ends — is part of the result, not a footnote.
cards.source: Feder A et al. A Randomized Controlled Trial of Repeated Ketamine Administration for Chronic Posttraumatic Stress Disorder. The American journal of psychiatry. 2021. PMID: 33397139. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02397889, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Imagery rehearsal therapy for trauma-related nightmares
shelves.question: In adults with PTSD and chronic nightmares, does imagery rehearsal therapy reduce nightmare frequency and improve sleep quality versus a waitlist control over 10 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Chronic Disease · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy · Dreams · Female · Humans · Imagery, Psychotherapy · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Sex Offenses · Sickness Impact Profile · Sleep Wake Disorders · Stress Disorders, Post-Traumatic · Survivors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised controlled trial (Krakow 2001, 168 women with chronic nightmares after sexual assault, 95% with moderate-to-severe PTSD) found three sessions of imagery rehearsal therapy significantly reduced nights per week with nightmares, number of nightmares per week, and improved sleep quality (PSQI) and PTSD symptoms (PSS and CAPS) versus waitlist control, sustained between 3- and 6-month follow-up, with intent-to-treat analyses confirming moderate effect sizes (mean Cohen d=0.60 for treatment versus 0.14 for controls). Note the timing: the record's follow-up is at 3 and 6 MONTHS, not the '10 weeks' in the shelf question — disclosed on the card. One trial in a specific population (female sexual-assault survivors) earns POSSIBLE. Prazosin for PTSD nightmares is homed on Shelf #575 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Krakow 2001: imagery rehearsal therapy reduced nightmares and improved sleep and PTSD symptoms versus waitlist, sustained to 6 months
cards.summary: Krakow 2001: imagery rehearsal therapy reduced nightmares and improved sleep and PTSD symptoms versus waitlist, sustained to 6 months
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (conducted 1995–1999, New Mexico; 3 treatment sessions; follow-up at 3 and 6 months)
cards.people: 168 women with chronic nightmares; 95% had moderate-to-severe PTSD, 97% had experienced rape or other sexual assault, 77% reported life-threatening sexual assault and 58% repeated sexual abuse in childhood or adolescence. Participants were randomized to imagery rehearsal therapy (n=88) or waitlist control (n=80); controls continued any ongoing treatment. A total of 114 participants completed follow-up at 3 and/or 6 months. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Comparing baseline to follow-up, treatment significantly reduced nights per week with nightmares (Cohen d=1.24; P<.001), number of nightmares per week (d=0.85; P<.001), and improved sleep on the PSQI (d=0.67; P<.001) and PTSD symptoms on the PSS (d=1.00; P<.001) and CAPS (d=1.53; P<.001); controls showed small, nonsignificant improvements (mean d=0.21). Improvements in the treatment group were present at 3 months and sustained without further intervention between 3 and 6 months. Intent-to-treat analysis (n=168) confirmed significant differences for nightmares, sleep and PTSD (all P<.02), with moderate effect sizes for treatment (mean d=0.60) versus small for controls (mean d=0.14). PTSD symptoms decreased by at least one level of clinical severity in 65% of the treatment group, versus worsening or no change in 69% of controls (P<.001).
cards.watchOut: A waitlist control cannot blind or match attention, outcomes are largely self-reported, and only 114 of 168 completed follow-up (the intent-to-treat analysis mitigates but does not erase this). The population — women after sexual assault — is specific; generalisation to combat or mixed-trauma nightmares is extrapolation.
cards.source: Krakow B et al. Imagery rehearsal therapy for chronic nightmares in sexual assault survivors with posttraumatic stress disorder: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2001. PMID: 11476655. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Pregabalin for generalised anxiety disorder
shelves.question: In adults with generalised anxiety disorder, does pregabalin (150–600 mg/day) reduce Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale scores versus placebo (and how does it compare with lorazepam) over 4–6 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anticonvulsants · Anxiety Disorders · Dizziness · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Male · Placebos · Pregabalin · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Sleep · Treatment Outcome · gamma-Aminobutyric Acid
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Pande 2003, 276 patients with DSM-IV generalised anxiety disorder) found pregabalin 150 mg/day (HAM-A change −9.2) and 600 mg/day (−10.3) both significantly beat placebo (−6.8) over 4 weeks, with lorazepam 6 mg/day at −12.0 in the same trial — pregabalin effective, and somewhat below the benzodiazepine comparator on the raw change — separating from placebo as early as week 1, with somnolence and dizziness the most frequent adverse events and no withdrawal syndrome on taper. The further fixed-dose trials named in the topic draft were not pinned to verified records at build and are fenced without figures; on the pinned record (one 4-week trial) the stamp is POSSIBLE. Pregabalin's pain and restless-legs questions are homed on Shelves #345/#929.

cards.headline: Pande 2003: pregabalin 150 mg and 600 mg beat placebo on HAM-A over 4 weeks (−9.2 and −10.3 vs −6.8); lorazepam reached −12.0
cards.summary: Pande 2003: pregabalin 150 mg and 600 mg beat placebo on HAM-A over 4 weeks (−9.2 and −10.3 vs −6.8); lorazepam reached −12.0
cards.type: Double-blind placebo-controlled trial (1-week placebo lead-in, 4 weeks of treatment, 1-week dose taper)
cards.people: 276 patients with DSM-IV generalized anxiety disorder randomly assigned to pregabalin 150 mg/day (69), pregabalin 600 mg/day (70), lorazepam 6 mg/day (68) or placebo (69) and receiving at least one dose; completion was 90% on pregabalin 150 mg, 71% on pregabalin 600 mg, 59% on lorazepam and 73% on placebo. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Mean baseline-to-endpoint decreases in total Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale score were −9.2 (pregabalin 150 mg/day), −10.3 (pregabalin 600 mg/day) and −12.0 (lorazepam), all significantly greater than placebo (−6.8). Pregabalin significantly reduced the HAM-A score versus placebo as early as the week 1 observation. The most frequent adverse events for pregabalin and lorazepam were somnolence and dizziness. There were no serious adverse events reported by patients given pregabalin, and no withdrawal syndrome was associated with pregabalin treatment over the 1-week taper.
cards.watchOut: Four weeks is the whole controlled horizon, and the trial's own numbers put pregabalin's raw HAM-A reduction below lorazepam's — 'comparable to lorazepam' readings go beyond this record. The 59% completion rate in the lorazepam arm also warns against over-reading the comparator contrast.
cards.source: Pande AC et al. Pregabalin in generalized anxiety disorder: a placebo-controlled trial. The American journal of psychiatry. 2003. PMID: 12611835. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. shelves.question: In adults with social anxiety disorder, do manualised cognitive-behavioural therapy and psychodynamic therapy each beat a waitlist control on remission, and how do their long-term outcomes compare?

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The pinned record is the SOPHO-NET programme's 24-month follow-up report (Leichsenring 2014): of the patients treated with CBT (N=209) or psychodynamic therapy (N=207) in the parent multicentre randomised trial, response rates were approximately 70% in BOTH conditions by 2 years and remission rates nearly 40% in both, with rates stable or increasing over follow-up and no significant differences between the therapies after 6 months; short-term intention-to-treat analyses in the parent trial had shown some small significant differences favouring CBT. cards.type: Long-term (6, 12 and 24 months) follow-up report of a multicentre randomized clinical trial programme
cards.people: Outpatients with social anxiety disorder who had been treated with cognitive-behavioral therapy (N=209) or psychodynamic therapy (N=207) in the previous SOPHO-NET trial, assessed 6, 12 and 24 months after the end of therapy. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: For both CBT and psychodynamic therapy, response rates were approximately 70% by the 2-year follow-up and remission rates were nearly 40% for both treatment conditions. Rates of response and remission were stable or tended to increase for both treatments over the 24-month follow-up, and no significant differences were found between the treatment conditions after 6 months. The authors note that in the short term, intention-to-treat analyses in the parent trial yielded some statistically significant but small differences in favour of CBT on several outcome measures, with no differences in outcome in the long term. The parent trial's waitlist-control comparison is referenced as previously reported; this follow-up record prints no waitlist figures, and none are carded.
cards.watchOut: This card is a follow-up report, not the parent trial report: it can carry the long-term CBT-versus-psychodynamic comparison (a dead heat) but cannot itself verify the therapies against waitlist. Attrition over 24 months is not quantified in the abstract.

shelves.title: Andexanet alfa for factor Xa inhibitor–associated intracerebral haemorrhage (ANNEXA-I)
shelves.question: In patients with intracerebral haemorrhage within 15 hours of taking a factor Xa inhibitor, does andexanet alfa, compared with usual care (predominantly prothrombin complex concentrate), improve haemostatic efficacy without excess thrombotic harm?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Factor Xa Inhibitors · Aged · Male · Female · Cerebral Hemorrhage · Middle Aged · Recombinant Proteins · Factor Xa · Hematoma · Aged, 80 and over · Atrial Fibrillation · Acute Disease
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: thrombotic events including ischaemic stroke are a headline safety outcome, and 30-day death is reported). ANNEXA-I is the only randomised trial of andexanet in intracerebral haemorrhage: haemostatic efficacy was better with andexanet (67.0% vs 53.1%; adjusted difference 13.4 percentage points; P=0.003), but thrombotic events were more frequent (10.3% vs 5.6%; P=0.048), including ischaemic stroke (6.5% vs 1.5%), and there were no appreciable differences in modified Rankin scale scores or death within 30 days. The primary endpoint is itself a composite surrogate (haematoma expansion, NIHSS change, and rescue-therapy use), efficacy was assessed in an interim-analysis population, and the trial's functional outcome was neutral. A real benefit on bleeding control, a real thrombotic cost, no functional gain: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: ANNEXA-I 2024: haemostatic efficacy 67.0% vs 53.1% (P=0.003), but thrombotic events 10.3% vs 5.6% and ischaemic stroke 6.5% vs 1.5%; no difference in 30-day death
cards.summary: ANNEXA-I 2024: haemostatic efficacy 67.0% vs 53.1% (P=0.003), but thrombotic events 10.3% vs 5.6% and ischaemic stroke 6.5% vs 1.5%; no difference in 30-day death
cards.people: 530 patients who had taken a factor Xa inhibitor within 15 hours before an acute intracerebral haemorrhage, randomised to andexanet (n=263) or usual care (n=267); atrial fibrillation was the most common indication for the anticoagulant, and 85.5% of the usual-care group received prothrombin complex concentrate. Efficacy was assessed in an interim analysis of 452 patients; safety in all 530. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Haemostatic efficacy (haematoma expansion ≤35% at 12 hours, NIHSS increase <7 points at 12 hours, and no rescue therapy between 3 and 12 hours) was achieved in 150 of 224 patients (67.0%) on andexanet versus 121 of 228 (53.1%) on usual care (adjusted difference 13.4 percentage points; 95% CI 4.6 to 22.2; P=0.003). Anti-factor Xa activity fell by a median 94.5% versus 26.9% at the 1–2-hour nadir (P<0.001). Thrombotic events occurred in 27 of 263 (10.3%) versus 15 of 267 (5.6%) (difference 4.6 points; 95% CI 0.1 to 9.2; P=0.048); ischaemic stroke occurred in 17 (6.5%) versus 4 (1.5%). There were no appreciable differences in modified Rankin scale scores or death within 30 days (the abstract prints no death rates).
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint bundles a radiographic measure, a short-horizon NIHSS threshold, and rescue-therapy use — better 'haemostatic efficacy' did not translate into better function or survival in this trial. Efficacy is reported from an interim analysis population (452 of 530 randomised), and the thrombotic excess — roughly 1 extra ischaemic stroke per 20 patients treated — is the price printed on the same card.
cards.source: Connolly SJ et al. Andexanet for Factor Xa Inhibitor-Associated Acute Intracerebral Hemorrhage. The New England journal of medicine. 2024. PMID: 38749032. shelves.title: Early intensive blood-pressure lowering in acute intracerebral haemorrhage (INTERACT2; ATACH-2; INTERACT3)
shelves.question: In patients with acute spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage within six hours, does intensive systolic BP lowering (target <140 mm Hg within one hour), compared with guideline-recommended lowering (<180 mm Hg), reduce death and major disability at 90 days?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Aged · Antihypertensive Agents · Blood Pressure · Cerebral Hemorrhage · Disability Evaluation · Female · Humans · Hypertension · Male · Middle Aged · Single-Blind Method · Time Factors
shelves.balance: SPLIT — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: death and disability are the primary outcomes). The answer depends on how low and in what package. INTERACT2 (2,839 patients, target <140 within 1 hour vs <180) narrowly missed its primary outcome — death or major disability 52.0% vs 55.6% (OR 0.87; P=0.06) — while its prespecified ordinal analysis favoured intensive lowering (OR 0.87 for greater disability; P=0.04), with identical mortality (11.9% vs 12.0%). ATACH-2 (1,000 patients, nicardipine to 110–139 vs 140–179 mm Hg, stopped for futility) was cleanly null on death or disability (38.7% vs 37.7%; RR 1.04) with more renal adverse events on intensive treatment (9.0% vs 4.0%; P=0.002). INTERACT3 (7,036 patients) showed that a care bundle built around early intensive lowering to <140 improved functional outcome (common OR 0.86; P=0.015) — but the bundle also protocolised glucose, temperature, and anticoagulation reversal, so its result cannot be credited to blood pressure alone. Gentle early lowering toward <140: POSSIBLE. Pushing to 110–139: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: INTERACT2 2013: primary outcome narrowly missed (52.0% vs 55.6%; OR 0.87, P=0.06) but ordinal shift favoured intensive lowering; mortality identical
cards.summary: INTERACT2 2013: primary outcome narrowly missed (52.0% vs 55.6%; OR 0.87, P=0.06) but ordinal shift favoured intensive lowering; mortality identical
cards.people: 2,839 patients with spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage within the previous 6 hours and elevated systolic blood pressure, randomised to intensive lowering (target <140 mm Hg within 1 hour) or guideline-recommended treatment (target <180 mm Hg) with agents of the physician's choice; the primary outcome was determined in 2,794. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Death or major disability (modified Rankin scale 3–6) at 90 days occurred in 719 of 1,382 (52.0%) on intensive treatment versus 785 of 1,412 (55.6%) on guideline treatment (odds ratio 0.87; 95% CI 0.75 to 1.01; P=0.06). The prespecified ordinal analysis showed significantly lower Rankin scores with intensive treatment (OR for greater disability 0.87; 95% CI 0.77 to 1.00; P=0.04). Mortality was 11.9% versus 12.0%, and nonfatal serious adverse events 23.3% versus 23.6%.
cards.watchOut: This trial is quoted both ways in the literature — 'positive on the shift analysis' and 'negative on its primary endpoint' — and both are true; the card leads with the primary endpoint, as the gate requires. The achieved separation between groups was smaller than the targets suggest, which cuts both ways: it may dilute a real effect, and it means 'intensive' here was gentler than the label.

cards.headline: ATACH-2 2016: nicardipine to 110–139 mm Hg did not reduce death or disability (38.7% vs 37.7%) and doubled renal adverse events; stopped for futility
cards.summary: ATACH-2 2016: nicardipine to 110–139 mm Hg did not reduce death or disability (38.7% vs 37.7%) and doubled renal adverse events; stopped for futility
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, stopped early for futility
cards.people: 1,000 patients with intracerebral haemorrhage (volume <60 cm³) and a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 5 or more, randomised within 4.5 hours to intravenous nicardipine targeting systolic 110–139 mm Hg (n=500) or 140–179 mm Hg (n=500). Mean systolic pressure at baseline was 200.6 mm Hg; mean age was 61.9 years and 56.2% of patients were Asian; the abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: Death or disability (modified Rankin scale 4–6) at 3 months occurred in 38.7% (186 of 481) on intensive treatment versus 37.7% (181 of 480) on standard treatment (relative risk 1.04; 95% CI 0.85 to 1.27). Enrolment was stopped for futility at a prespecified interim analysis. Treatment-related serious adverse events within 72 hours were 1.6% versus 1.2%, but renal adverse events within 7 days were significantly more frequent with intensive treatment (9.0% vs 4.0%; P=0.002).
cards.watchOut: ATACH-2 tested a lower target with a single protocolised drug, started fast — its null result is the strongest evidence against very intensive lowering, and it should not be blended with INTERACT2's gentler comparison. Its population (smaller haematomas, GCS ≥5, predominantly Asian and North American centres) bounds generalisation to large or deep-coma haemorrhages.

cards.headline: INTERACT3 2023: a care bundle built on early intensive lowering improved functional outcome (common OR 0.86) — but the bundle was more than blood pressure
cards.summary: INTERACT3 2023: a care bundle built on early intensive lowering improved functional outcome (common OR 0.86) — but the bundle was more than blood pressure
cards.people: 7,036 patients with acute spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage presenting within 6 hours, enrolled at 121 hospitals in nine low- and middle-income countries and one high-income country (Chile); 3,221 were assigned to the care bundle and 3,815 to usual care in the modified intention-to-treat population. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The care bundle — early intensive systolic lowering (target <140 mm Hg), strict glucose control, antipyrexia (target ≤37.5 °C), and rapid reversal of warfarin-related anticoagulation (target INR <1.5), each within 1 hour where abnormal — reduced the likelihood of a poor functional outcome at 6 months (common odds ratio 0.86; 95% CI 0.76 to 0.97; P=0.015 on the ordinal modified Rankin scale). Serious adverse events were fewer with the bundle (16.0% vs 20.1%; P=0.0098).
cards.watchOut: A bundle trial cannot attribute its benefit to blood-pressure lowering: glucose, fever, and anticoagulation-reversal protocols changed at the same time, in hospitals selected for lacking consistent protocols beforehand. INTERACT3 supports protocolised early care in such settings; it is not a third vote on the pharmacological question INTERACT2 and ATACH-2 asked.
cards.source: Ma L et al. shelves.title: Tranexamic acid for hyperacute primary intracerebral haemorrhage (TICH-2; STOP-AUST)
shelves.question: In patients with acute primary intracerebral haemorrhage within eight hours, does tranexamic acid, compared with placebo, reduce death and dependence at 90 days?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antifibrinolytic Agents · Cerebral Hemorrhage · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Stroke · Tranexamic Acid · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: mortality is a reported outcome). TICH-2 (2,325 patients, tranexamic acid within 8 hours) found no difference in functional status at day 90 (adjusted OR 0.88; 95% CI 0.76–1.03; P=0.11) and no difference in 90-day case fatality (22% vs 21%), despite fewer deaths by day 7 (9% vs 11%; adjusted OR 0.73; P=0.04) and fewer serious adverse events. The smaller spot-sign-guided STOP-AUST trial (100 patients) likewise found no reduction in haematoma growth (44% vs 52%; OR 0.72; P=0.41). One caveat on the topic draft: it credits TICH-2 with 'less haematoma expansion', but the TICH-2 record's abstract prints no expansion figures, so none are carded. A large definitive trial plus a concordant mechanistic trial, both null on their primaries: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for functional benefit, with an early-mortality signal that did not persist to 90 days.

cards.headline: TICH-2 2018: no improvement in 90-day functional status (adjusted OR 0.88, P=0.11); fewer day-7 deaths but 90-day fatality unchanged (22% vs 21%)
cards.summary: TICH-2 2018: no improvement in 90-day functional status (adjusted OR 0.88, P=0.11); fewer day-7 deaths but 90-day fatality unchanged (22% vs 21%)
cards.people: 2,325 adults with intracerebral haemorrhage at 124 sites in 12 countries, randomised within 8 hours of symptom onset to tranexamic acid (1 g bolus then 1 g over 8 hours; n=1,161) or matching placebo (n=1,164); the primary outcome was assessed in 2,307 (99%). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Functional status at day 90 (ordinal modified Rankin scale) did not differ between groups (adjusted odds ratio 0.88; 95% CI 0.76 to 1.03; P=0.11). Deaths by day 7 were fewer on tranexamic acid (101 [9%] vs 123 [11%]; adjusted OR 0.73; 95% CI 0.53 to 0.99; P=0.04), but case fatality at 90 days was the same (250 [22%] vs 249 [21%]; adjusted hazard ratio 0.92; 95% CI 0.77 to 1.10; P=0.37). Serious adverse events were fewer with tranexamic acid at days 2, 7, and 90.
cards.watchOut: The day-7 mortality difference is a secondary timepoint that had vanished by day 90 — quoting it without the 90-day figure misstates the trial. The abstract reports no haematoma-expansion numbers, so the common summary 'TXA reduces expansion but not outcome' is not supported by this record; expansion is addressed by the STOP-AUST card below.

cards.people: 100 patients with acute intracerebral haemorrhage and a CT-angiography spot sign at 13 centres in Australia, Finland, and Taiwan, randomised within 4.5 hours to tranexamic acid (1 g then 1 g over 8 hours; n=50) or placebo (n=50). Median age was 71 years (IQR 57–79) and median haematoma volume 14.6 mL; the abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: Haematoma growth (>33% relative or >6 mL absolute at 24 hours) occurred in 22 of 50 (44%) on tranexamic acid versus 26 of 50 (52%) on placebo (odds ratio 0.72; 95% CI 0.32 to 1.59; P=0.41). shelves.title: Early minimally invasive evacuation of supratentorial intracerebral haemorrhage (ENRICH; MISTIE III)
shelves.question: In patients with acute supratentorial intracerebral haemorrhage of 30–80 mL treated within 24 hours, does early minimally invasive trans-sulcal parafascicular evacuation, compared with guideline-based medical management, improve utility-weighted functional outcome at 180 days?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Basal Ganglia Hemorrhage · Bayes Theorem · Cerebral Hemorrhage · Minimally Invasive Surgical Procedures · Treatment Outcome · Neuroendoscopy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: mortality is a headline result). ENRICH (300 patients) is the first positive surgical ICH trial: utility-weighted modified Rankin score at 180 days was 0.458 with minimally invasive parafascicular evacuation versus 0.374 with medical management (difference 0.084; posterior probability of superiority 0.981 against a prespecified 0.975 threshold), and 30-day mortality was lower with surgery (9.3% vs 18.0%). But the benefit was concentrated in lobar haemorrhages (difference 0.127) with none in anterior basal-ganglia haemorrhages (−0.013) — a stratum the trial itself stopped enrolling for futility under its adaptation rule — and the analysis is Bayesian with an adaptive design. MISTIE III (506 patients), testing a different technique (catheter aspiration plus alteplase) at a later window, was neutral on good functional outcome at 365 days (45% vs 41%; P=0.33). One positive, device-specific, subgroup-dependent trial against a neutral predecessor: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: ENRICH 2024: utility-weighted outcome better with early minimally invasive evacuation (0.458 vs 0.374), benefit confined to lobar haemorrhages; 30-day death 9.3% vs 18.0%
cards.summary: ENRICH 2024: utility-weighted outcome better with early minimally invasive evacuation (0.458 vs 0.374), benefit confined to lobar haemorrhages; 30-day death 9.3% vs 18.0%
cards.people: 300 patients with a lobar (69.3%) or anterior basal-ganglia (30.7%) haemorrhage of 30–80 mL, randomised within 24 hours of last known well to minimally invasive trans-sulcal parafascicular evacuation plus guideline-based medical care or medical care alone. After 175 patients, a prespecified adaptation rule stopped enrolment of basal-ganglia haemorrhages. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The mean utility-weighted modified Rankin score at 180 days was 0.458 in the surgery group and 0.374 in the control group (difference 0.084; 95% Bayesian credible interval 0.005 to 0.163; posterior probability of superiority 0.981, against the prespecified threshold of 0.975). The difference was 0.127 (credible interval 0.035 to 0.219) for lobar haemorrhages and −0.013 (−0.147 to 0.116) for anterior basal-ganglia haemorrhages. Death by 30 days occurred in 9.3% of the surgery group and 18.0% of controls. Five surgery patients (3.3%) had postoperative rebleeding with neurological deterioration.
cards.watchOut: The headline result is an average over a population the trial redefined mid-course: after adaptation, only lobar haemorrhages were enrolled, and the basal-ganglia estimate is a null from a stopped stratum. The device-and-approach specificity (a proprietary parafascicular system, early surgery, selected volumes) means ENRICH does not vindicate 'evacuation' in general — as the MISTIE III card shows.

cards.headline: MISTIE III 2019: catheter evacuation with alteplase did not improve good functional outcome at 1 year (45% vs 41%; P=0.33)
cards.summary: MISTIE III 2019: catheter evacuation with alteplase did not improve good functional outcome at 1 year (45% vs 41%; P=0.33)
cards.people: 506 patients with spontaneous supratentorial intracerebral haemorrhage of 30 mL or more at 78 hospitals, randomised to image-guided minimally invasive catheter evacuation plus alteplase (1.0 mg every 8 hours for up to nine doses; n=255) or standard medical care (n=251); 499 were in the modified intention-to-treat analysis. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Good functional outcome (modified Rankin score 0–3 at 365 days) was achieved by an estimated 45% of the MISTIE group and 41% of the standard-care group (adjusted risk difference 4%; 95% CI −4 to 12; P=0.33). Deaths at 30 days were 24 (9%) with MISTIE versus 37 (15%) with standard care (P=0.07), and at 7 days 2 (1%) versus 10 (4%) (P=0.02). Symptomatic bleeding (2% vs 1%) and brain infection (1% vs 0%) were similar.
cards.watchOut: MISTIE's technique (stereotactic catheter plus thrombolysis, clot reduction over days) is not ENRICH's technique (early trans-sulcal removal), so its null result does not directly refute ENRICH — but it does refute any generic claim that 'minimally invasive evacuation works'. Its 30-day mortality gap (9% vs 15%) without a functional benefit is the same shape as ENRICH's, one size smaller and non-significant.

cards.summary: Synthesis: early parafascicular evacuation probably helps lobar ICH; the broader evacuation claim failed its previous test — POSSIBLE

shelves.title: Early decompressive craniectomy for malignant middle-cerebral-artery infarction (pooled DECIMAL/DESTINY/HAMLET; DESTINY II)
shelves.question: In patients aged 60 or younger with malignant MCA infarction treated within 48 hours, does decompressive craniectomy, compared with conservative care, reduce mortality and change the distribution of disability?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aphasia · Decompression, Surgical · Female · Humans · Infarction, Middle Cerebral Artery · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Male · Middle Aged · Neurosurgical Procedures · Patient Selection · Prospective Studies · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Stroke · Tomography, X-Ray Computed · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: this is a mortality claim, the clearest in the stroke library). The pooled individual-patient analysis of DECIMAL, DESTINY, and HAMLET (93 patients aged 18–60, treated within 48 hours, pooled prospectively while the trials were still recruiting) found survival of 78% with decompressive surgery versus 29% with conservative care — mortality 22% versus 71%, an absolute reduction of about 50 points (NNT 2) — with more survivors at modified Rankin ≤4 (75% vs 24%) and ≤3 (43% vs 21%). DESTINY II then extended the question to patients over 60 (112 patients): survival without severe disability was 38% versus 18% (OR 2.91), mortality 33% versus 70% — but no survivor in either group achieved a Rankin score of 0–2, and most survivors needed assistance with most bodily needs. The mortality effect is large, consistent, and replicated across the age boundary; what surgery buys is survival, much of it with substantial disability: LIKELY.

cards.headline: Pooled DECIMAL/DESTINY/HAMLET 2007: decompressive surgery cut 1-year mortality from 71% to 22% (NNT 2) in patients ≤60
cards.summary: Pooled DECIMAL/DESTINY/HAMLET 2007: decompressive surgery cut 1-year mortality from 71% to 22% (NNT 2) in patients ≤60
cards.type: Prospectively planned pooled individual-patient analysis of three randomised trials
cards.people: 93 patients aged 18–60 years with space-occupying middle-cerebral-artery infarction, included in one of the three European trials (DECIMAL, DESTINY, HAMLET) and treated within 48 hours of stroke onset; the pooled protocol and outcomes were defined while the trials were still recruiting, without knowledge of individual trial results. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: At 1 year, more surgical patients had a modified Rankin score ≤4 (75% vs 24%; pooled absolute risk reduction 51%; 95% CI 34 to 69), a score ≤3 (43% vs 21%; absolute reduction 23%; 95% CI 5 to 41), and had survived (78% vs 29%; absolute reduction 50%; 95% CI 33 to 67) — numbers needed to treat of 2 for survival with Rankin ≤4, 4 for survival with Rankin ≤3, and 2 for survival irrespective of function. The effect was highly consistent across the three trials.
cards.watchOut: This card is a pooled analysis — the canonical citation for three small trials that were each stopped early — and is labelled as such; the constituent trials are not separately carded. The ethical weight of the result sits in the distribution it creates: surgery converts death into survival, a substantial share of it at Rankin 4 (unable to walk or attend to bodily needs unaided).

cards.headline: DESTINY II 2014: in patients over 60, hemicraniectomy improved survival without severe disability (38% vs 18%) and cut mortality (33% vs 70%) — but no survivor was disability-free
cards.summary: DESTINY II 2014: in patients over 60, hemicraniectomy improved survival without severe disability (38% vs 18%) and cut mortality (33% vs 70%) — but no survivor was disability-free
cards.people: 112 patients aged 61 years or older (median 70; range 61–82) with malignant middle-cerebral-artery infarction, randomised within 48 hours to hemicraniectomy or conservative intensive care. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: Survival without severe disability (modified Rankin score 0–4) at 6 months was 38% with hemicraniectomy versus 18% with conservative treatment (odds ratio 2.91; 95% CI 1.06 to 7.49; P=0.04), driven by lower mortality (33% vs 70%). No patient in either group achieved a score of 0–2; scores of 3 were seen in 7% versus 3%, scores of 4 in 32% versus 15%, and scores of 5 in 28% versus 13%. Infections were more frequent with surgery; herniation more frequent in controls.
cards.watchOut: In the over-60 population the trade is starkest: surgery roughly halves mortality, and essentially every additional survivor lives with moderate-to-severe disability. The trial answers the survival question definitively and the values question not at all — consent conversations, not the data, carry that part.

shelves.title: Endovascular thrombectomy for acute basilar-artery occlusion (ATTENTION; BAOCHE; BEST; BASICS)
shelves.question: In patients with acute basilar-artery occlusion, does endovascular thrombectomy plus best medical care, compared with best medical care alone, improve functional outcome at 90 days?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Administration, Intravenous · Arterial Occlusive Diseases · Basilar Artery · Brain Ischemia · Endovascular Procedures · Fibrinolytic Agents · Intracranial Hemorrhages · Prospective Studies · Quality of Life · Stroke · Thrombectomy · Thrombolytic Therapy · Treatment Outcome · Recovery of Function
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: mortality and stroke outcomes). Four randomised trials in two generations. The first generation was neutral: BEST (131 patients, stopped early for crossover and poor recruitment) found no intention-to-treat difference in Rankin 0–3 at 90 days (42% vs 32%; adjusted OR 1.74, non-significant), and BASICS (300 patients, ~79% receiving intravenous thrombolysis) found 44.2% vs 37.7% (RR 1.18; 95% CI 0.92–1.50). The second generation, both from China, was clearly positive: ATTENTION (340 patients, within 12 hours) found Rankin 0–3 in 46% vs 23% (adjusted rate ratio 2.06) with mortality 37% vs 55%, and BAOCHE (217 patients, 6–24 hours, stopped early for superiority) found 46% vs 24% (adjusted rate ratio 1.81) with mortality 31% vs 42%. Symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage ran higher with thrombectomy throughout (5–6% vs 0–1% in the positive trials). Two large, concordant, positive trials on top of two explicable neutral ones: LIKELY — with the generalisability caveat that both positive trials are single-country (China) with lower background thrombolysis rates than BASICS.

cards.headline: ATTENTION 2022: thrombectomy within 12 hours doubled good functional status (46% vs 23%) and cut mortality (37% vs 55%) in basilar occlusion
cards.summary: ATTENTION 2022: thrombectomy within 12 hours doubled good functional status (46% vs 23%) and cut mortality (37% vs 55%) in basilar occlusion
cards.people: 340 patients with basilar-artery occlusion at 36 centres in China, randomised 2:1 within 12 hours of the estimated occlusion time to endovascular thrombectomy (n=226) or best medical care (n=114); intravenous thrombolysis was used in 31% of the thrombectomy group and 34% of controls. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Good functional status (modified Rankin score 0–3) at 90 days occurred in 104 patients (46%) with thrombectomy versus 26 (23%) with medical care (adjusted rate ratio 2.06; 95% CI 1.46 to 2.91; P<0.001). Mortality at 90 days was 37% versus 55% (adjusted risk ratio 0.66; 95% CI 0.52 to 0.82). Symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage occurred in 12 patients (5%) with thrombectomy and none with medical care; procedural complications occurred in 14% of the thrombectomy group, including one death from arterial perforation.
cards.watchOut: A single-country trial whose control-arm outcomes (23% good status, 55% mortality) describe a severe, largely non-thrombolysed population; centres whose basilar patients routinely receive intravenous thrombolysis (as in BASICS) should expect a smaller absolute margin. The 5% symptomatic haemorrhage rate is part of the same result, not a footnote.

cards.headline: BAOCHE 2022: thrombectomy at 6–24 hours improved good functional status (46% vs 24%); trial stopped early for superiority
cards.summary: BAOCHE 2022: thrombectomy at 6–24 hours improved good functional status (46% vs 24%); trial stopped early for superiority
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, stopped early at interim analysis
cards.people: 217 patients with basilar-artery stroke presenting 6–24 hours after symptom onset in China, randomised to medical therapy plus thrombectomy (n=110) or medical therapy alone (n=107); randomisation occurred at a median of 663 minutes after onset. Thrombolysis was used in 14% of the thrombectomy group and 21% of controls. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: A modified Rankin score of 0–3 at 90 days occurred in 51 patients (46%) with thrombectomy versus 26 (24%) with medical therapy (adjusted rate ratio 1.81; 95% CI 1.26 to 2.60; P<0.001). Enrolment was halted at a prespecified interim analysis because of thrombectomy's superiority. Mortality at 90 days was 31% versus 42% (adjusted risk ratio 0.75; 95% CI 0.54 to 1.04). Symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage occurred in 6 of 102 (6%) versus 1 of 88 (1%), and procedural complications in 11% of thrombectomy patients.

cards.people: 131 patients with vertebrobasilar occlusion presenting within 8 hours at 28 centres in China, randomised to endovascular therapy plus standard medical therapy (n=66) or standard medical therapy alone (n=65), before the trial was terminated early because of a high crossover rate and poor recruitment. cards.result: On intention-to-treat analysis there was no evidence of a difference in Rankin score 0–3 at 90 days (28 of 66 [42%] vs 21 of 65 [32%]; adjusted odds ratio 1.74; 95% CI 0.81 to 3.74). Prespecified per-protocol (44% vs 25%; adjusted OR 2.90) and as-treated (47% vs 24%; adjusted OR 3.02) analyses favoured intervention. cards.headline: BASICS 2021: with ~79% thrombolysed in both arms, thrombectomy did not significantly improve favourable outcome (44.2% vs 37.7%; RR 1.18)
cards.summary: BASICS 2021: with ~79% thrombolysed in both arms, thrombectomy did not significantly improve favourable outcome (44.2% vs 37.7%; RR 1.18)
cards.people: 300 patients with stroke from basilar-artery occlusion, randomised within 6 hours to endovascular therapy (n=154) or standard medical care (n=146) in an international trial; intravenous thrombolysis was used in 78.6% and 79.5% of the two groups, and endovascular treatment began at a median of 4.4 hours. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: A favourable functional outcome (Rankin score 0–3 at 90 days) occurred in 68 of 154 patients (44.2%) with endovascular therapy versus 55 of 146 (37.7%) with medical care (risk ratio 1.18; 95% CI 0.92 to 1.50). Symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage occurred in 4.5% versus 0.7% (risk ratio 6.9; 95% CI 0.9 to 53.0); mortality at 90 days was 38.3% versus 43.2% (risk ratio 0.87; 95% CI 0.68 to 1.12). The authors note the confidence interval does not exclude a substantial benefit.
cards.watchOut: BASICS is not a refutation of ATTENTION and BAOCHE so much as a measurement in a different substrate — high thrombolysis rates, earlier treatment, a less severely affected control group (37.7% good outcome versus 23–24% in the Chinese trials). The four trials together say thrombectomy helps, with the margin depending on what medical care alone achieves locally.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two positive trials over two neutral first attempts — thrombectomy for basilar occlusion is LIKELY beneficial, margin varies with background care
cards.summary: Synthesis: two positive trials over two neutral first attempts — thrombectomy for basilar occlusion is LIKELY beneficial, margin varies with background care
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: BEST 2020 (131 patients), BASICS 2021 (300 patients), ATTENTION 2022 (340 patients), BAOCHE 2022 (217 patients).
cards.result: The pattern across 988 randomised patients is coherent: where control-arm outcomes are poor and thrombolysis infrequent (ATTENTION, BAOCHE), thrombectomy roughly doubles good functional status and reduces mortality; where medical care already achieves good outcomes (BASICS), the added margin is smaller and non-significant. Symptomatic haemorrhage of 4.5–6% with thrombectomy is the consistent cost.
cards.watchOut: Tier C note for the developer: mortality is printed beside functional outcome on every card, as the gate requires. Both positive trials are from one country and one was stopped early with a mid-trial outcome change (disclosed on its card); the stamp is LIKELY, not a Level A certainty label, for exactly those reasons.

shelves.title: MRI-guided intravenous thrombolysis for stroke of unknown onset (WAKE-UP; EXTEND)
shelves.question: In patients with ischaemic stroke of unknown time of onset and an MRI diffusion–FLAIR mismatch, does alteplase, compared with placebo, improve functional outcome at 90 days?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Administration, Intravenous · Aged · Brain Ischemia · Diffusion Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Female · Fibrinolytic Agents · Humans · Intracranial Hemorrhages · Magnetic Resonance Imaging, Interventional · Male · Middle Aged · Stroke · Thrombectomy · Thrombolytic Therapy · Time-to-Treatment · Tissue Plasminogen Activator · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: death and haemorrhage are reported outcomes). WAKE-UP (503 patients, stopped early when funding ended, at 503 of a planned 800) found a favourable outcome (Rankin 0–1 at 90 days) in 53.3% on alteplase versus 41.8% on placebo (adjusted OR 1.61; P=0.02), with numerically more deaths (4.1% vs 1.2%; OR 3.38; P=0.07) and symptomatic haemorrhage (2.0% vs 0.4%). EXTEND (225 patients, also terminated early) asked an adjacent question — perfusion-imaging selection at 4.5–9 hours or on awakening — and also found more Rankin 0–1 outcomes with alteplase (35.4% vs 29.5%; adjusted RR 1.44; P=0.04) with more symptomatic haemorrhage (6.2% vs 0.9%), though its ordinal analysis was not significant. Two positive but prematurely stopped trials using different imaging selection, with a consistent haemorrhage cost and a worrying, non-significant mortality imbalance in WAKE-UP: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: WAKE-UP 2018: MRI-guided alteplase improved excellent outcome (53.3% vs 41.8%; adjusted OR 1.61) in unknown-onset stroke; deaths numerically higher (4.1% vs 1.2%)
cards.summary: WAKE-UP 2018: MRI-guided alteplase improved excellent outcome (53.3% vs 41.8%; adjusted OR 1.61) in unknown-onset stroke; deaths numerically higher (4.1% vs 1.2%)
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled trial, stopped early (funding cessation)
cards.people: 503 patients with stroke of unknown time of onset whose MRI showed a diffusion-weighted lesion without FLAIR hyperintensity (indicating onset within roughly 4.5 hours), randomised to intravenous alteplase (n=254) or placebo (n=249); patients for whom thrombectomy was planned were excluded. The trial stopped after 503 of an anticipated 800 patients when funding ended. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: A favourable outcome (Rankin score 0–1) at 90 days occurred in 131 of 246 patients (53.3%) on alteplase versus 102 of 244 (41.8%) on placebo (adjusted odds ratio 1.61; 95% CI 1.09 to 2.36; P=0.02); the ordinal analysis also favoured alteplase (adjusted common OR 1.62; P=0.003). There were 10 deaths (4.1%) on alteplase and 3 (1.2%) on placebo (odds ratio 3.38; 95% CI 0.92 to 12.52; P=0.07). Symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage was 2.0% versus 0.4% (odds ratio 4.95; 95% CI 0.57 to 42.87; P=0.15).
cards.watchOut: The mortality imbalance (10 vs 3 deaths) is not statistically significant and the trial was stopped for funding rather than data reasons — but it is printed here in full because a benefit claim for thrombolysis in a milder-stroke population must carry it. Early stopping also means the sample is smaller than planned, and the population excludes thrombectomy candidates, so the result applies to the MRI-selected, non-thrombectomy pathway.

cards.headline: EXTEND 2019: perfusion-selected alteplase at 4.5–9 hours increased excellent outcome (35.4% vs 29.5%; adjusted RR 1.44) with more symptomatic haemorrhage (6.2% vs 0.9%)
cards.summary: EXTEND 2019: perfusion-selected alteplase at 4.5–9 hours increased excellent outcome (35.4% vs 29.5%; adjusted RR 1.44) with more symptomatic haemorrhage (6.2% vs 0.9%)
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial, terminated early
cards.people: 225 patients with ischaemic stroke and hypoperfused but salvageable tissue on automated perfusion imaging, randomised to intravenous alteplase (n=113) or placebo (n=112) between 4.5 and 9.0 hours after onset, or on awakening within 9 hours of the midpoint of sleep. The trial was terminated after 225 of a planned 310 patients because of loss of equipoise after another trial's positive results. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary outcome (Rankin score 0–1 at 90 days) occurred in 40 patients (35.4%) on alteplase versus 33 (29.5%) on placebo (adjusted risk ratio 1.44; 95% CI 1.01 to 2.06; P=0.04). Symptomatic intracerebral haemorrhage occurred in 7 patients (6.2%) versus 1 (0.9%) (adjusted risk ratio 7.22; 95% CI 0.97 to 53.5; P=0.05). The secondary ordinal analysis of Rankin scores did not show a significant between-group difference in functional improvement.
cards.watchOut: EXTEND answers a neighbouring question, not WAKE-UP's: perfusion selection in known-window and wake-up patients, not diffusion–FLAIR mismatch in unknown-onset patients. Its dichotomous primary was positive while its ordinal analysis was not — the same fragility pattern as WAKE-UP's non-significant mortality imbalance, in the opposite direction. Both trials stopped early; neither is definitive alone.

cards.headline: Synthesis: imaging selection extends thrombolysis beyond the clock in two stopped-early trials — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: imaging selection extends thrombolysis beyond the clock in two stopped-early trials — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: WAKE-UP 2018 (503 patients, diffusion–FLAIR mismatch, unknown onset) and EXTEND 2019 (225 patients, perfusion imaging, 4.5–9 hours or wake-up).
cards.result: Both trials support the same principle — treat the tissue, not the clock — with absolute gains in excellent outcome of about 11.5 and 5.9 percentage points, against symptomatic haemorrhage rates of 2.0% and 6.2%. The selection methods differ, so the shelf endorses imaging-guided selection in principle rather than one protocol.
cards.watchOut: Tier C note for the developer: WAKE-UP's death counts (10 vs 3) are printed on its card beside the benefit, as the gate requires; EXTEND's abstract does not print mortality counts, and none are supplied. Two early-stopped trials with discordant secondary analyses keep this shelf at POSSIBLE.

shelves.title: Intensive blood-pressure lowering after successful thrombectomy (ENCHANTED2/MT; BP-TARGET; BEST-II)
shelves.question: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke and successful reperfusion after thrombectomy with sustained hypertension, does intensive systolic lowering (target <120 mm Hg), compared with standard management (140–180 mm Hg), improve functional outcome?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Adolescent · Adult · Brain Ischemia · Stroke · Blood Pressure · Treatment Outcome · China · Thrombectomy · Ischemic Stroke
shelves.balance: LIKELY (harm) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: functional outcome after stroke, with mortality reported). ENCHANTED2/MT (821 patients, target <120 vs 140–180 mm Hg after successful reperfusion) was stopped early because of persistent efficacy and safety concerns: intensive lowering worsened functional outcome (common OR 1.37 for a poorer Rankin distribution), increased early neurological deterioration (OR 1.53) and major disability (OR 2.07), with no difference in symptomatic haemorrhage or mortality. BP-TARGET (324 patients, target 100–129 vs 130–185) found no reduction in its primary outcome of radiographic intraparenchymal haemorrhage (42% vs 43%; adjusted OR 0.96). BEST-II (120 patients, a phase 2 futility trial of <140 and <160 targets vs ≤180) did not meet its futility boundaries but estimated only a 25% and 14% predicted probability that a future trial of the lower targets would succeed. The largest trial shows harm, the mechanistic trial shows no haemorrhage benefit, and the pilot shows low promise: intensive lowering after successful thrombectomy should be avoided — LIKELY (harm).

cards.headline: ENCHANTED2/MT 2022: intensive lowering to <120 mm Hg after reperfusion worsened outcome (common OR 1.37); trial stopped early for harm/futility concerns
cards.summary: ENCHANTED2/MT 2022: intensive lowering to <120 mm Hg after reperfusion worsened outcome (common OR 1.37); trial stopped early for harm/futility concerns
cards.type: Randomised, open-label, blinded-endpoint trial, stopped early
cards.people: 821 patients with persistently elevated systolic pressure (≥140 mm Hg for >10 minutes) after successful reperfusion by thrombectomy for large-vessel-occlusion stroke, at 44 hospitals in China, randomised to a systolic target of <120 mm Hg (n=407) or 140–180 mm Hg (n=409), achieved within 1 hour and sustained for 72 hours; primary-outcome data were available for 404 and 406 patients. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The likelihood of a poor functional outcome at 90 days (ordinal modified Rankin scale) was greater with intensive treatment (common odds ratio 1.37; 95% CI 1.07 to 1.76). Early neurological deterioration was more frequent (common OR 1.53; 95% CI 1.18 to 1.97) and major disability at 90 days more common (OR 2.07; 95% CI 1.47 to 2.93). There were no significant differences in symptomatic intracerebral haemorrhage, serious adverse events, or mortality between groups (the abstract prints no mortality rates). The trial was stopped after review of outcome data because of persistent efficacy and safety concerns.
cards.watchOut: This is the harm-defining trial for post-reperfusion blood pressure: the intervention did exactly what it was designed to do (lower pressure quickly and sustain it) and patients did worse. It enrolled patients with sustained hypertension after reperfusion in one country; it does not address blood-pressure management after unsuccessful reperfusion or in non-thrombectomy stroke.

cards.headline: BP-TARGET 2021: intensive target (100–129 mm Hg) did not reduce radiographic intraparenchymal haemorrhage (42% vs 43%; adjusted OR 0.96)
cards.summary: BP-TARGET 2021: intensive target (100–129 mm Hg) did not reduce radiographic intraparenchymal haemorrhage (42% vs 43%; adjusted OR 0.96)
cards.people: 324 adults with acute ischaemic stroke from large-vessel occlusion successfully treated with endovascular therapy at four French centres, randomised to a systolic target of 100–129 mm Hg (n=162) or standard care at 130–185 mm Hg (n=162) for 24 hours; mean achieved systolic pressure in the first 24 hours was 128 vs 138 mm Hg. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary outcome — radiographic intraparenchymal haemorrhage on CT at 24–36 hours — occurred in 65 of 154 patients (42%) in the intensive group and 68 of 157 (43%) in the standard group (adjusted odds ratio 0.96; 95% CI 0.60 to 1.51; P=0.84). Hypotensive events occurred in 12 of 158 (8%) versus 5 of 160 (3%). Mortality within the first week was 11 of 158 (7%) versus 7 of 160 (4%).
cards.watchOut: BP-TARGET's primary outcome is a radiographic finding, not a clinical outcome, and its achieved pressure separation was modest (128 vs 138 mm Hg) — it refutes a haemorrhage-prevention rationale for intensive lowering at these targets, but the functional-outcome verdict comes from ENCHANTED2/MT. Its one-week mortality counts (11 vs 7) are printed as the record gives them, without a claim.

cards.headline: BEST-II 2023: lower post-thrombectomy targets did not meet futility criteria, but predicted probability of a successful future trial was only 25% and 14%
cards.summary: BEST-II 2023: lower post-thrombectomy targets did not meet futility criteria, but predicted probability of a successful future trial was only 25% and 14%
cards.people: 120 patients with acute ischaemic stroke who had undergone successful endovascular therapy at three US centres, randomised to systolic targets of <140 mm Hg, <160 mm Hg, or ≤180 mm Hg for 24 hours; 113 (94.2%) completed the trial. Mean (SD) age was 69.6 (14.5) years and 69 (58%) were women.
cards.result: Mean utility-weighted Rankin scores at 90 days were 0.51 (<140 target), 0.47 (<160), and 0.58 (≤180); mean follow-up infarct volumes were 32.4, 50.7, and 46.4 mL respectively. Neither lower target met the prespecified harm-futility boundaries (futility P=0.99 for infarct volume; P=0.93 for utility-weighted Rankin), but the predicted probability of success of a future superiority trial was 25% for the <140 target and 14% for the <160 target — which the authors read as a low probability of benefit from lower targets.
cards.watchOut: A futility design cannot prove harm or benefit; BEST-II's contribution is probabilistic and its point estimates are noisy (the <160 group's infarct volume was the largest of the three). Its value on this shelf is that an independent US pilot, designed to keep lower targets alive if promising, instead estimated their prospects as poor.

cards.summary: Synthesis: after successful thrombectomy, intensive systolic lowering harms functional recovery and prevents nothing — LIKELY (harm)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: ENCHANTED2/MT 2022 (821 patients), BP-TARGET 2021 (324 patients), BEST-II 2023 (120 patients).
cards.result: The three trials triangulate: a large trial stopped early for worse functional outcomes on intensive lowering; a mechanistic trial showing no haemorrhage reduction to justify it; a pilot estimating a future trial of lower targets would probably fail. The practical rule the record supports: after successful reperfusion, do not drive systolic pressure below 120, and be wary of aggressive lowering generally.
cards.watchOut: Tier C note for the developer: mortality is addressed on each card as the record presents it (no significant difference in ENCHANTED2/MT, rates not printed; 11 vs 7 one-week deaths in BP-TARGET). The harm claimed here is functional — worse disability and early deterioration — not mortality, and the cards do not overstate it.

shelves.title: Intensive versus standard insulin therapy for hyperglycaemia in acute ischaemic stroke (SHINE; GIST-UK)
shelves.question: In hyperglycaemic patients with acute ischaemic stroke, does intensive intravenous insulin targeting glucose 80–130 mg/dL, compared with standard subcutaneous insulin targeting 80–179 mg/dL, improve 90-day functional outcome?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Brain Ischemia · Female · Fibrinolytic Agents · Humans · Hyperglycemia · Hypoglycemia · Hypoglycemic Agents · Infusions, Intravenous · Injections, Subcutaneous · Insulin · Male · Middle Aged · Stroke · Tissue Plasminogen Activator · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: functional outcome after stroke; mortality was GIST-UK's primary endpoint). SHINE (1,151 patients, stopped for futility) achieved clean glucose separation (mean 118 vs 179 mg/dL during treatment) and found no difference in favourable 90-day outcome (20.5% vs 21.6%; adjusted relative risk 0.97; P=0.55), with severe hypoglycaemia occurring only in the intensive group (2.6% vs 0%). GIST-UK (933 patients, stopped early for slow enrolment against a planned 2,355) tested glucose-potassium-insulin infusion against saline and found no reduction in its primary outcome of 90-day death (odds ratio 1.14; 95% CI 0.86–1.51). Two null trials of two different intensive-glucose strategies, one definitive in size and separation: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: SHINE 2019: intensive glucose control (achieved 118 vs 179 mg/dL) did not improve favourable outcome (20.5% vs 21.6%); severe hypoglycaemia 2.6% vs 0%; stopped for futility
cards.summary: SHINE 2019: intensive glucose control (achieved 118 vs 179 mg/dL) did not improve favourable outcome (20.5% vs 21.6%); severe hypoglycaemia 2.6% vs 0%; stopped for futility
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial, stopped for futility
cards.people: 1,151 adults with hyperglycaemia and acute ischaemic stroke enrolled within 12 hours at 63 US sites, randomised to continuous intravenous insulin targeting 80–130 mg/dL (n=581) or subcutaneous sliding-scale insulin targeting 80–179 mg/dL (n=570) for up to 72 hours; 1,118 (97%) completed the trial. Mean age was 66 years (SD 13.1), 529 (46%) were women, and 920 (80%) had diabetes.
cards.result: A favourable 90-day outcome (Rankin score adjusted for baseline severity) occurred in 119 of 581 patients (20.5%) on intensive treatment versus 123 of 570 (21.6%) on standard treatment (adjusted relative risk 0.97; 95% CI 0.87 to 1.08; P=0.55). Enrolment was stopped for futility at a prespecified interim analysis. Treatment was stopped early for hypoglycaemia or other adverse events in 11.2% versus 3.2%, and severe hypoglycaemia occurred only in the intensive group (15 of 581 [2.6%]; risk difference 2.58%; 95% CI 1.29 to 3.87).
cards.watchOut: SHINE is the clean version of this null: the glucose targets were actually achieved and separated by ~60 mg/dL, so 'the intervention wasn't delivered' is not available as an excuse. Its favourable-outcome definition is severity-adjusted, which is why the headline rates (about 21% in both arms) look low for a stroke trial.

cards.headline: GIST-UK 2007: glucose-potassium-insulin infusion did not reduce 90-day death (OR 1.14, CI 0.86–1.51); trial stopped at 933 of 2,355 planned patients
cards.summary: GIST-UK 2007: glucose-potassium-insulin infusion did not reduce 90-day death (OR 1.14, CI 0.86–1.51); trial stopped at 933 of 2,355 planned patients
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, stopped early for slow enrolment
cards.people: 933 patients presenting within 24 hours of stroke onset with admission plasma glucose of 6.0–17.0 mmol/L (≈108–306 mg/dL), randomised to variable-dose glucose-potassium-insulin infusion for 24 hours (targeting capillary glucose 4–7 mmol/L (≈72–126 mg/dL)) or saline control with no glucose intervention. The trial had been powered for 2,355 patients to detect a 6-point mortality difference. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: There was no significant reduction in the primary outcome of death at 90 days (odds ratio 1.14; 95% CI 0.86 to 1.51; P=0.37), and no significant differences in secondary outcomes. Mean plasma glucose was modestly lower with GKI (mean difference 0.57 mmol/L (≈10 mg/dL); P<0.001) and mean systolic blood pressure was also lower (difference 9.0 mm Hg; P<0.0001). The authors state the study was underpowered and alternative results cannot be excluded.
cards.watchOut: GIST-UK differs from SHINE in both intervention (a fixed GKI infusion versus titrated insulin) and comparator (no treatment versus standard insulin), and its glucose separation was small — its null is weak evidence alone. It also lowered blood pressure by 9 mm Hg as an off-target effect, muddying attribution. The shelf's LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) rests on SHINE; GIST-UK is concordant support, and its mortality-primary design is why the shelf is Tier C.

cards.headline: Synthesis: tight glucose control after ischaemic stroke does not improve outcome and causes hypoglycaemia — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Synthesis: tight glucose control after ischaemic stroke does not improve outcome and causes hypoglycaemia — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: SHINE 2019 (1,151 patients) and GIST-UK 2007 (933 patients).
cards.result: Across two strategies and two eras, normalising glucose after acute ischaemic stroke bought nothing measurable in function or survival, and in SHINE it bought a 2.6% severe-hypoglycaemia rate. Standard, gentler insulin regimens remain the evidence-consistent default.
cards.watchOut: Tier C note for the developer: GIST-UK's primary outcome was 90-day death (OR 1.14, printed on its card); SHINE's abstract does not print a mortality comparison, and none is supplied. The null claimed here is about benefit, and the hypoglycaemia harm in SHINE is part of the same record.
