shelves.title: Head positioning in acute stroke (HeadPoST)
shelves.question: In patients with acute stroke, does lying flat (0°) for the first 24 hours, compared with sitting up at ≥30°, improve disability outcomes at 90 days?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Cross-Over Studies · Disability Evaluation · Female · Head · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Positioning · Posture · Stroke
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: disability and mortality outcomes after stroke). HeadPoST is a single but definitive trial: 11,093 patients with acute stroke (85% ischaemic) in a pragmatic cluster-randomised crossover design across nine countries, comparing lying flat with sitting up at ≥30° for the first 24 hours. There was no shift in 90-day disability (unadjusted odds ratio 1.01; 95% CI 0.92 to 1.10; P=0.84), mortality was identical (7.3% vs 7.4%), and there were no differences in serious adverse events including pneumonia. A very large, precise null from one well-executed trial: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — head position in the first day can be chosen for comfort and nursing care, not outcome.

cards.headline: HeadPoST 2017: lying flat vs sitting up for 24 hours made no difference to 90-day disability (OR 1.01) or mortality (7.3% vs 7.4%) in 11,093 patients
cards.summary: HeadPoST 2017: lying flat vs sitting up for 24 hours made no difference to 90-day disability (OR 1.01) or mortality (7.3% vs 7.4%) in 11,093 patients
cards.people: 11,093 patients with acute stroke (85% ischaemic) admitted to hospitals in nine countries, cared for lying flat (0°) or sitting up (head elevated ≥30°) according to their hospital's randomised assignment, with the position started soon after admission (median 14 hours from symptom onset) and maintained for 24 hours. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: There was no significant shift in the distribution of 90-day disability (modified Rankin scale) between the lying-flat and sitting-up groups (unadjusted odds ratio 1.01; 95% confidence interval 0.92 to 1.10; P=0.84). Mortality within 90 days was 7.3% lying flat and 7.4% sitting up (P=0.83). There were no significant differences in serious adverse events, including pneumonia. Patients in the lying-flat group were less likely to maintain the position for the full 24 hours (87% vs 95%; P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: Cluster randomisation by hospital and a median 14-hour delay to positioning mean HeadPoST tests a ward policy applied in the first day, not a hyperacute physiological intervention in the first hour — a very-early-positioning claim would need a different trial. Within what it tested, though, the confidence interval is narrow enough to exclude any worthwhile effect.
cards.source: Anderson CS et al. Cluster-Randomized, Crossover Trial of Head Positioning in Acute Stroke. The New England journal of medicine. 2017. PMID: 28636854. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02162017, from the record's databank fields. cards.result: HeadPoST is larger than the rest of this slate's trials combined and its null is correspondingly firm: neither the cerebral-perfusion rationale for lying flat nor the aspiration rationale for sitting up produced a measurable outcome difference, including no difference in pneumonia.

shelves.title: Nerinetide for acute ischaemic stroke treated with thrombectomy (ESCAPE-NA1; ESCAPE-NEXT)
shelves.question: In patients with large-vessel occlusion stroke undergoing endovascular thrombectomy, does the neuroprotectant nerinetide, compared with placebo, improve functional outcome at 90 days?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Brain Ischemia · Disks Large Homolog 4 Protein · Double-Blind Method · Endovascular Procedures · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neuroprotective Agents · Peptides · Stroke · Thrombectomy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: functional outcome after stroke, with mortality a secondary outcome in both trials). ESCAPE-NA1 (1,105 thrombectomy patients) found no overall benefit (Rankin 0–2 at 90 days: 61.4% vs 59.2%; adjusted risk ratio 1.04; P=0.35), with a prespecified interaction suggesting benefit only in patients not receiving alteplase — plausibly because alteplase-generated plasmin cleaves the peptide. The topic draft asked for ESCAPE-NEXT's status to be checked at build: it has now reported (Lancet 2025), and in exactly the population the interaction nominated — thrombectomy without prior thrombolysis, 850 patients — nerinetide again showed no benefit (Rankin 0–2: 45% vs 46%; odds ratio 0.97; P=0.82). A subgroup hypothesis that was tested head-on and failed to confirm is stronger evidence of the null than the original trial alone: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: ESCAPE-NA1 2020: nerinetide did not improve good outcome after thrombectomy (61.4% vs 59.2%; P=0.35); an alteplase interaction generated the follow-up hypothesis
cards.summary: ESCAPE-NA1 2020: nerinetide did not improve good outcome after thrombectomy (61.4% vs 59.2%; P=0.35); an alteplase interaction generated the follow-up hypothesis
cards.people: 1,105 patients with acute ischaemic stroke from large-vessel occlusion within a 12-hour window, undergoing endovascular thrombectomy at 48 hospitals in eight countries, randomised to a single intravenous dose of nerinetide 2.6 mg/kg (n=549) or saline placebo (n=556); all patients received alteplase in usual care when indicated. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: A favourable functional outcome (modified Rankin score 0–2 at 90 days) was achieved by 337 of 549 patients (61.4%) on nerinetide and 329 of 556 (59.2%) on placebo (adjusted risk ratio 1.04; 95% CI 0.96 to 1.14; P=0.35). Secondary outcomes were similar between groups, and serious adverse events occurred equally. The trial observed evidence of treatment-effect modification: the treatment effect was inhibited in patients receiving alteplase.
cards.watchOut: The alteplase interaction — the finding that launched a confirmatory trial — was an effect-modification observation inside an overall null trial, the classic setup for a subgroup mirage. It is carded here as the record presents it, and the next card shows what happened when it was tested directly. Mortality was a secondary outcome; the abstract prints no mortality rates, and none are supplied.
cards.source: Hill MD et al. Efficacy and safety of nerinetide for the treatment of acute ischaemic stroke (ESCAPE-NA1): a multicentre, double-blind, randomised controlled trial. cards.headline: ESCAPE-NEXT 2025: in thrombectomy patients without thrombolysis — the subgroup ESCAPE-NA1 nominated — nerinetide was again null (45% vs 46%; P=0.82)
cards.summary: ESCAPE-NEXT 2025: in thrombectomy patients without thrombolysis — the subgroup ESCAPE-NA1 nominated — nerinetide was again null (45% vs 46%; P=0.82)
cards.people: 850 patients with acute ischaemic stroke from anterior-circulation large-vessel occlusion within 12 hours, undergoing endovascular thrombectomy without treatment with a plasminogen activator, at 77 centres in nine countries, randomised to nerinetide 2.6 mg/kg (n=454) or saline placebo (n=396). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: A favourable functional outcome (modified Rankin score 0–2 at 90 days) was achieved by 206 participants (45%) on nerinetide and 181 (46%) on placebo (odds ratio 0.97; 95% CI 0.72 to 1.30; P=0.82). Serious adverse events occurred equally between groups. The authors conclude nerinetide did not improve outcomes but was not associated with excess adverse events, and that further study would need to identify the ideal timing and sub-population.
cards.watchOut: Freshness check, as the topic draft required: this is the trial built on ESCAPE-NA1's interaction, published in 2025, and it is a clean null in the enriched population. A later year-1 follow-up report of the same trial exists (Journal of the American Heart Association 2026, PMID 42333641); it is a follow-up report of these same patients — the trial is counted once, and the follow-up is fenced here by name without separate figures.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the neuroprotection hypothesis was tested twice, including once in its own favoured subgroup, and failed both times — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Synthesis: the neuroprotection hypothesis was tested twice, including once in its own favoured subgroup, and failed both times — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)

cards.result: Nerinetide is the rare neuroprotectant whose escape route was actually walked: a biologically coherent interaction (plasmin cleaves the peptide) was prespecified, a dedicated trial enrolled only the favoured population, and the result was a point estimate of 0.97. The programme's honest conclusion is that nerinetide, as dosed and timed in these trials, does not improve outcome after thrombectomy.

shelves.title: Anticoagulation versus aspirin for embolic stroke of undetermined source (NAVIGATE ESUS; RE-SPECT ESUS)
shelves.question: In patients with recent embolic stroke of undetermined source, does rivaroxaban 15 mg daily, compared with aspirin, prevent recurrent stroke without excess major bleeding?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aspirin · Brain Ischemia · Factor Xa Inhibitors · Female · Hemorrhage · Humans · Intracranial Embolism · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors · Rivaroxaban · Secondary Prevention · Stroke
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: recurrent stroke is the primary outcome). Two large trials tested empirical anticoagulation for ESUS against aspirin, with two different drugs, and both failed. NAVIGATE ESUS (7,213 patients, rivaroxaban 15 mg) was terminated early: recurrent stroke or systemic embolism occurred at 5.1% per year on rivaroxaban versus 4.8% on aspirin (HR 1.07; P=0.52), while major bleeding was higher on rivaroxaban (1.8% vs 0.7% per year; HR 2.72; P<0.001). RE-SPECT ESUS (5,390 patients, dabigatran) completed: recurrent stroke 4.1% versus 4.8% per year (HR 0.85; 95% CI 0.69 to 1.03; P=0.10), with major bleeding not significantly different (1.7% vs 1.4% per year) but more clinically relevant non-major bleeding on dabigatran. Empirical anticoagulation for unselected ESUS is closed by 12,603 randomised patients: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference), with bleeding harm demonstrated for rivaroxaban.

cards.headline: NAVIGATE ESUS 2018: rivaroxaban was not superior to aspirin (5.1% vs 4.8% per year) and caused more major bleeding (1.8% vs 0.7% per year); stopped early
cards.summary: NAVIGATE ESUS 2018: rivaroxaban was not superior to aspirin (5.1% vs 4.8% per year) and caused more major bleeding (1.8% vs 0.7% per year); stopped early
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind phase 3 trial, terminated early
cards.people: 7,213 patients with recent ischaemic stroke presumed embolic but without arterial stenosis, lacune, or an identified cardioembolic source, at 459 sites, randomised to rivaroxaban 15 mg daily (n=3,609) or aspirin 100 mg daily (n=3,604); patients had been followed a median of 11 months when the trial was terminated early for lack of benefit on stroke risk and for bleeding with rivaroxaban. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary efficacy outcome (first recurrence of ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke or systemic embolism) occurred in 172 patients on rivaroxaban (annualised rate 5.1%) and 160 on aspirin (4.8%) (hazard ratio 1.07; 95% CI 0.87 to 1.33; P=0.52). Recurrent ischaemic stroke rates were identical (4.7% per year in both groups). Major bleeding occurred in 62 patients on rivaroxaban (1.8% per year) versus 23 on aspirin (0.7% per year) (hazard ratio 2.72 relative; 95% CI 1.68 to 4.39; P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: The 15 mg rivaroxaban dose (reduced from the atrial-fibrillation dose) is sometimes blamed for the null; the companion trial's full-dose dabigatran result, on the next card, is the answer to that objection. Early termination for futility plus harm is itself informative — the data monitoring process saw no path to benefit.

cards.headline: RE-SPECT ESUS 2019: dabigatran was not superior to aspirin for recurrent stroke (4.1% vs 4.8% per year; HR 0.85, P=0.10)
cards.summary: RE-SPECT ESUS 2019: dabigatran was not superior to aspirin for recurrent stroke (4.1% vs 4.8% per year; HR 0.85, P=0.10)
cards.people: 5,390 patients with embolic stroke of undetermined source at 564 sites, randomised to dabigatran (150 mg or 110 mg twice daily by age/renal criteria; n=2,695) or aspirin 100 mg daily (n=2,695), with a median follow-up of 19 months. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Recurrent strokes occurred in 177 patients (6.6%; 4.1% per year) on dabigatran and 207 (7.7%; 4.8% per year) on aspirin (hazard ratio 0.85 relative; 95% CI 0.69 to 1.03; P=0.10). Ischaemic strokes occurred at 4.0% versus 4.7% per year (HR 0.84). Major bleeding occurred at 1.7% per year on dabigatran versus 1.4% on aspirin (HR 1.19; 95% CI 0.85 to 1.66), while clinically relevant non-major bleeding was more frequent on dabigatran (1.6% vs 0.9% per year).
cards.watchOut: The point estimate (HR 0.85) leans toward dabigatran without reaching significance — the honest reading is 'not shown superior', in a trial large enough that any true effect is modest at best. Dabigatran's cleaner bleeding profile than rivaroxaban's in these trials should not be read as a head-to-head comparison; the drugs were never randomised against each other here.

cards.result: The ESUS hypothesis — that most cryptogenic embolic strokes are covert cardioembolism best treated with anticoagulation — was tested at full scale with two different anticoagulants and not confirmed. Aspirin remains the default for unselected ESUS; the trials redirect the field toward finding the actual mechanism (prolonged rhythm monitoring, atrial cardiopathy markers) rather than treating the category.

shelves.title: Antiplatelet versus anticoagulant therapy for cervical artery dissection (CADISS; TREAT-CAD)
shelves.question: In patients with acute extracranial carotid or vertebral artery dissection, does anticoagulation, compared with antiplatelet therapy, prevent ipsilateral stroke or death in the first three months?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anticoagulants · Aspirin · Carotid Artery, Internal, Dissection · Clopidogrel · Dipyridamole · Female · Hemorrhage · Heparin · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Mortality · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors · Recurrence · Secondary Prevention · Stroke · Treatment Outcome · Vertebral Artery Dissection · Warfarin · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the endpoint is stroke or death). Genuine equipoise survives both trials, and the shelf should say so plainly. CADISS final results (250 patients, antiplatelet vs heparin-then-warfarin): recurrent stroke at 1 year was low overall — 6 of 250 (2.4%) on intention-to-treat — with no significant difference between groups for any outcome. (The topic draft's 'ipsilateral stroke ≈2% vs 1%' comes from the earlier 3-month CADISS report; the pinned final-results record does not print per-arm event counts in its abstract, and none are carded.) TREAT-CAD (194 patients, aspirin 300 mg vs vitamin K antagonist) failed to show aspirin non-inferior on its per-protocol composite of clinical and MRI outcomes (23% vs 15%; absolute difference 8%, 95% CI −4 to 21; non-inferiority P=0.55), with all seven ischaemic strokes in the aspirin group and no deaths. One trial says 'no detectable difference at very low event rates'; the other says 'aspirin not proven non-inferior, with a stroke imbalance against it'. Neither licenses certainty: POSSIBLE, unresolved.

cards.headline: CADISS final results 2019: recurrent stroke was rare (2.4% at 1 year overall) and did not differ between antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy
cards.summary: CADISS final results 2019: recurrent stroke was rare (2.4% at 1 year overall) and did not differ between antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy
cards.type: Randomised, open-label trial with blinded endpoint review
cards.people: 250 patients with extracranial carotid (118) or vertebral (132) artery dissection with symptom onset within 7 days, at 46 centres in the UK and Australia, randomised to antiplatelet therapy (n=126) or anticoagulation with heparin followed by warfarin (n=124) for 3 months. Mean (SD) age was 49 (12) years; the abstract does not state the sex mix. One-year follow-up was complete for all participants.
cards.result: The recurrent stroke rate at 1 year was 6 of 250 (2.4%) on intention-to-treat analysis and 5 of 197 (2.5%) in the per-protocol analysis of imaging-confirmed dissections. There were no significant differences between treatment groups for any outcome, and no difference in residual narrowing or occlusion at 3 months among the 181 patients with confirmed dissection and complete imaging (P=0.97). The abstract does not print per-arm event counts for the primary endpoint (ipsilateral stroke and death).
cards.watchOut: A correction carried on this card: secondary sources often quote CADISS as '2% vs 1%' for ipsilateral stroke — those figures come from the trial's earlier 3-month report, not from this final-results record, whose abstract reports the pooled 1-year rate only. With six events in total, CADISS could not have distinguished the strategies even if one were twice as good; its real finding is that recurrence on either treatment is uncommon.

cards.headline: TREAT-CAD 2021: aspirin was NOT shown non-inferior to vitamin K antagonists (composite 23% vs 15%); all 7 ischaemic strokes were on aspirin
cards.summary: TREAT-CAD 2021: aspirin was NOT shown non-inferior to vitamin K antagonists (composite 23% vs 15%); all 7 ischaemic strokes were on aspirin
cards.people: 194 patients with symptomatic, MRI-verified cervical artery dissection within 2 weeks, at ten stroke centres in Switzerland, Germany, and Denmark, randomised to aspirin 300 mg daily (n=100) or a vitamin K antagonist (n=94) for 90 days; the per-protocol population was 173 (91 aspirin, 82 antagonist). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — a composite of clinical outcomes (stroke, major haemorrhage, death) and MRI outcomes (new ischaemic or haemorrhagic lesions), assessed in the per-protocol population — occurred in 21 of 91 patients (23%) on aspirin versus 12 of 82 (15%) on vitamin K antagonists (absolute difference 8%; 95% CI −4 to 21; non-inferiority P=0.55), so non-inferiority of aspirin was not shown against the 12% margin. Seven patients (8%) in the aspirin group and none in the antagonist group had ischaemic strokes; one antagonist patient had a major extracranial haemorrhage; there were no deaths.
cards.watchOut: Two cautions in opposite directions: the composite is dominated by silent MRI lesions (14 vs 11 patients), which inflates both arms' event rates beyond clinical events; and the clinical stroke split (7 vs 0) is the kind of small-number imbalance that can arise by chance yet cannot be waved away. The trial was analysed per-protocol for its primary endpoint, as non-inferiority designs require — and it still did not cross.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two small trials, one uninformative null and one failed non-inferiority — the dissection question stays open: POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: two small trials, one uninformative null and one failed non-inferiority — the dissection question stays open: POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: CADISS final results 2019 (250 patients) and TREAT-CAD 2021 (194 patients).
cards.result: Total randomised evidence: 444 patients and a handful of clinical events. CADISS establishes that recurrence is low on either strategy; TREAT-CAD establishes that aspirin has not earned a non-inferiority claim and carries the only stroke imbalance in the literature. Clinicians choosing anticoagulation for high-risk features (intraluminal thrombus, recurrent events) or antiplatelets for simplicity are both within the evidence.
cards.watchOut: Tier C note for the developer: the endpoint is stroke or death; TREAT-CAD recorded no deaths, and CADISS's abstract does not split its few events by arm — both facts are stated on the cards rather than filled in. This is one of the slate's genuinely unresolved shelves, and the stamp says so.

shelves.title: Early versus delayed DOAC initiation after AF-related ischaemic stroke (ELAN; TIMING; OPTIMAS)
shelves.question: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke and atrial fibrillation, does early initiation of a direct oral anticoagulant (within 48 hours for minor/moderate stroke, day 6–7 for major stroke), compared with later guideline-based initiation, reduce recurrent ischaemic events without increasing symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Anticoagulants · Atrial Fibrillation · Embolism · Hemorrhage · Intracranial Hemorrhages · Ischemic Stroke · Stroke · Treatment Outcome · Time Factors · Factor Xa Inhibitors · Recurrence
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: recurrent stroke and intracranial haemorrhage are the primary outcomes). Three randomised trials now triangulate the timing question. ELAN (2,013 patients, severity-stratified early vs later start) estimated the 30-day composite of recurrent ischaemic stroke, systemic embolism, major extracranial bleeding, symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage, or vascular death at 2.9% early versus 4.1% later (risk difference −1.18 points; 95% CI −2.84 to 0.47), with symptomatic haemorrhage at 0.2% in both groups — an estimation design, not a superiority proof. TIMING (888 patients) found early initiation (≤4 days) non-inferior to delayed (5–10 days) on its 90-day composite (6.89% vs 8.68%), with no symptomatic haemorrhage in either arm. OPTIMAS (3,621 patients analysed, the largest) found early initiation (≤4 days) non-inferior to delayed (7–14 days) on its 90-day composite — 3.3% in both groups — with symptomatic haemorrhage at 0.6% versus 0.7%. Early initiation is safe and non-inferior across 6,522 randomised patients, with point estimates consistently favouring earlier treatment: LIKELY.

cards.headline: ELAN 2023: early DOAC start estimated 30-day composite at 2.9% vs 4.1% later; recurrent stroke 1.4% vs 2.5%; symptomatic ICH 0.2% in both groups
cards.summary: ELAN 2023: early DOAC start estimated 30-day composite at 2.9% vs 4.1% later; recurrent stroke 1.4% vs 2.5%; symptomatic ICH 0.2% in both groups
cards.type: Randomised, open-label trial with blinded assessment (estimation design)
cards.people: 2,013 patients with acute ischaemic stroke and atrial fibrillation at 103 sites in 15 countries (37% minor, 40% moderate, 23% major stroke), randomised to early anticoagulation (within 48 hours for minor/moderate stroke, day 6–7 for major stroke; n=1,006) or later anticoagulation (day 3–4, 6–7, or 12–14 by severity; n=1,007). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: A primary-outcome event (recurrent ischaemic stroke, systemic embolism, major extracranial bleeding, symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage, or vascular death within 30 days) occurred in 29 participants (2.9%) in the early group and 41 (4.1%) in the later group (risk difference −1.18 percentage points; 95% CI −2.84 to 0.47). Recurrent ischaemic stroke occurred in 14 (1.4%) versus 25 (2.5%) by 30 days (odds ratio 0.57; 95% CI 0.29 to 1.07) and 18 (1.9%) versus 30 (3.1%) by 90 days. Symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage occurred in 2 participants (0.2%) in both groups by 30 days.
cards.watchOut: ELAN was designed to estimate, not to prove: its confidence interval runs from 2.84 points better to 0.47 points worse, so it cannot by itself declare early treatment superior or non-inferior. Its contribution is a severity-stratified schedule and event rates that the two non-inferiority trials then confirmed at larger scale.

cards.headline: TIMING 2022: early NOAC initiation (≤4 days) was non-inferior to delayed (5–10 days); no symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage in either arm
cards.summary: TIMING 2022: early NOAC initiation (≤4 days) was non-inferior to delayed (5–10 days); no symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage in either arm
cards.people: 888 patients with acute ischaemic stroke and atrial fibrillation at 34 Swedish stroke units, randomised within 72 hours to early (≤4 days; n=450) or delayed (5–10 days; n=438) initiation of a non-vitamin K oral anticoagulant of the investigator's choice. Mean age was 78.3 years (SD 9.9) and 46.2% were women; no patient was lost to 90-day follow-up.
cards.result: The primary outcome (recurrent ischaemic stroke, symptomatic intracerebral haemorrhage, or all-cause mortality at 90 days) occurred in 31 patients (6.89%) with early initiation and 38 (8.68%) with delayed initiation (absolute risk difference −1.79%; 95% CI −5.31 to 1.74; P for non-inferiority = 0.004 against a 3% margin). Ischaemic stroke rates were 3.11% versus 4.57% and all-cause mortality 4.67% versus 5.71%. No patient in either group had a symptomatic intracerebral haemorrhage.
cards.watchOut: TIMING's 'delayed' arm started at 5–10 days — earlier than the traditional 1-3-6-12-day rule's later tiers for severe stroke — so the trial compares early with moderately early, in a registry-based Swedish population. The absence of any symptomatic haemorrhage in 888 patients is reassuring but bounds only relatively common harm.

cards.headline: OPTIMAS 2024: in 3,621 patients, early DOAC initiation (≤4 days) was non-inferior to delayed (7–14 days) — primary outcome 3.3% in both groups
cards.summary: OPTIMAS 2024: in 3,621 patients, early DOAC initiation (≤4 days) was non-inferior to delayed (7–14 days) — primary outcome 3.3% in both groups
cards.people: 3,648 patients with atrial fibrillation and acute ischaemic stroke at 100 UK hospitals, randomised to early (≤4 days) or delayed (7–14 days) initiation of any direct oral anticoagulant; 3,621 were in the modified intention-to-treat analysis (1,814 early, 1,807 delayed; 1,981 men and 1,640 women). The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: The primary outcome (recurrent ischaemic stroke, symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage, unclassifiable stroke, or systemic embolism at 90 days) occurred in 59 of 1,814 participants (3.3%) in the early group and 59 of 1,807 (3.3%) in the delayed group (adjusted risk difference 0.000; 95% CI −0.011 to 0.012), meeting the 2-percentage-point non-inferiority margin (P for non-inferiority = 0.0003); superiority was not identified (P=0.96). Symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage occurred in 11 (0.6%) early versus 12 (0.7%) delayed participants.
cards.watchOut: OPTIMAS enrolled patients whose physician was uncertain about optimal timing — an equipoise population that may under-represent the largest, haemorrhage-prone infarcts, where clinicians were not uncertain and did not enrol. Within the population studied, though, this is the largest and most precise of the three trials, and its result anchors the shelf.

cards.headline: Synthesis: early DOAC initiation after AF-related stroke is safe and non-inferior in three trials totalling 6,522 patients — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: early DOAC initiation after AF-related stroke is safe and non-inferior in three trials totalling 6,522 patients — LIKELY
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: TIMING 2022 (888 patients), ELAN 2023 (2,013 patients), OPTIMAS 2024 (3,621 patients analysed).
cards.result: Three designs — registry-based non-inferiority, severity-stratified estimation, and a large pragmatic non-inferiority trial — converge: starting a DOAC within about 4 days (or on ELAN's severity-stratified schedule) does not increase symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage (≤0.7% everywhere) and does not lose ischaemic protection; point estimates for recurrent stroke favour earlier starts in ELAN and TIMING.
cards.watchOut: Tier C note for the developer: recurrent stroke, haemorrhage, and (in TIMING) mortality are printed with absolute rates on each card. 'Non-inferior' is the proven claim; superiority of early initiation is suggested by two point estimates and proven by none, and the cards do not upgrade it.

shelves.title: Colchicine for secondary prevention after non-cardioembolic ischaemic stroke or high-risk TIA (CONVINCE)
shelves.question: In patients with non-cardioembolic ischaemic stroke or high-risk TIA, does long-term colchicine 0.5 mg daily added to standard care, compared with standard care alone, reduce major adverse cardiovascular events?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Colchicine · Hospitalization · Ischemic Attack, Transient · Ischemic Stroke · Myocardial Infarction · Recurrence · Secondary Prevention · Stroke · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the primary outcome is a cardiovascular-event composite). CONVINCE (3,144 patients in the intention-to-treat analysis) found its primary composite — first fatal or non-fatal recurrent ischaemic stroke, myocardial infarction, cardiac arrest, or hospitalisation for unstable angina — in 9.8% on colchicine versus 11.7% on usual care (hazard ratio 0.84 relative; 95% CI 0.68 to 1.05; P=0.12, against a prespecified significance threshold of 0.048). The trial finished early, before its planned 367 outcomes accrued, because of COVID-era budget constraints. One correction to the topic draft: it places CONVINCE in The Lancet Neurology; the record's journal is The Lancet (vol 404, pp 125–133), and the card follows the record. A single, under-accrued, open-label trial with a point estimate favouring treatment and an interval crossing 1: the ITT null stands at POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — benefit is neither shown nor excluded. The coronary colchicine trials are a different population and are not imported here.

shelves.title: Prehospital glyceryl trinitrate in ultra-acute presumed stroke (RIGHT-2)
shelves.question: In patients with presumed stroke within four hours, treated by paramedics before hospital arrival, does a transdermal glyceryl trinitrate patch, compared with sham, improve functional outcome at 90 days?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Cutaneous · Aged · Emergency Medical Services · Female · Humans · Hypertension · Male · Middle Aged · Nitroglycerin · Prospective Studies · Single-Blind Method · Stroke · Treatment Outcome · Vasodilator Agents
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: functional outcome and death after stroke). RIGHT-2 (1,149 patients randomised by paramedics at a median of 71 minutes from onset) found no difference in 90-day modified Rankin scores in patients with confirmed stroke or TIA (adjusted common odds ratio 1.25 for a poorer outcome; 95% CI 0.97 to 1.60; P=0.083) or in the full intention-to-treat cohort (OR 1.04; P=0.69), despite lowering systolic pressure by 5.8 mm Hg. The point estimate in the confirmed-stroke cohort leans toward harm, not benefit. One disclosure: the topic draft reports a harm signal in the intracerebral-haemorrhage subgroup (worse outcomes, more early deaths); the record's abstract does not print subgroup results, so no subgroup figures are carded and the claim is neither confirmed nor denied here. A single large, well-conducted, sham-controlled trial with a null-to-harm-leaning result: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for prehospital GTN as tested.

cards.people: 1,149 adults with presumed stroke within 4 hours of onset (face-arm-speech-time score 2–3, systolic pressure ≥120 mm Hg) treated by 516 paramedics from eight UK ambulance services, randomised to transdermal glyceryl trinitrate 5 mg daily for 4 days (n=568) or a sham dressing (n=581); median time to randomisation was 71 minutes. shelves.title: Remote ischaemic conditioning for acute ischaemic stroke (RICAMIS; RESIST)
shelves.question: In patients with acute moderate ischaemic stroke ineligible for reperfusion therapy, does twice-daily remote ischaemic conditioning for 10–14 days, compared with usual care alone, improve excellent functional outcome at 90 days?
shelves.mesh: Aged · China · Female · Humans · Ischemic Postconditioning · Ischemic Stroke · Male · Middle Aged · Nervous System Diseases · Recovery of Function · Treatment Outcome · Upper Extremity
shelves.balance: SPLIT — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: functional outcome after stroke). Two large trials of the same intervention family disagree. RICAMIS (1,893 patients with acute moderate ischaemic stroke in China, open-label with blinded endpoint assessment) found excellent outcome (Rankin 0–1 at 90 days) in 67.4% with twice-daily bilateral arm conditioning for 10–14 days versus 62.0% with usual care (risk difference 5.4%; odds ratio 1.27; P=0.02). RESIST (1,500 patients in Denmark, sham-controlled, conditioning started prehospital) found no improvement in 90-day Rankin distribution in its target stroke population (odds ratio 0.95; 95% CI 0.75 to 1.20; P=0.67) — with the sham group's median Rankin score (1) numerically better than the conditioning group's (2). The designs differ (in-hospital confirmed moderate stroke, open-label, versus prehospital all-comers including haemorrhage, TIA, and mimics, sham-controlled), which may explain the divergence without resolving it. One correction to the topic draft: it describes RICAMIS's population as 'ineligible for reperfusion therapy'; the RICAMIS record's abstract describes acute moderate ischaemic stroke randomised within 48 hours and does not state reperfusion ineligibility, so the card follows the record. Genuine two-trial tension: SPLIT.

cards.headline: RICAMIS 2022: remote ischaemic conditioning increased excellent outcome (67.4% vs 62.0%; OR 1.27, P=0.02) in moderate ischaemic stroke
cards.summary: RICAMIS 2022: remote ischaemic conditioning increased excellent outcome (67.4% vs 62.0%; OR 1.27, P=0.02) in moderate ischaemic stroke
cards.people: 1,893 patients with acute moderate ischaemic stroke at 55 hospitals in China, randomised within 48 hours to remote ischaemic conditioning (five cycles of 5-minute cuff inflation to 200 mm Hg and 5-minute deflation, both upper limbs, for 10–14 days; n=922) plus guideline-based treatment, or guideline-based treatment alone (n=971); 1,776 (93.8%) completed the trial. Mean (SD) age was 65 (10.3) years and 606 patients (34.1%) were women.
cards.result: Excellent functional outcome (modified Rankin score 0–1) at 90 days occurred in 582 patients (67.4%) in the conditioning group and 566 (62.0%) in the control group (risk difference 5.4%; 95% CI 1.0 to 9.9; odds ratio 1.27; 95% CI 1.05 to 1.54; P=0.02). Adverse events occurred in 6.8% (59 of 863) versus 5.6% (51 of 913). The authors state the findings require replication in another trial before concluding efficacy.
cards.watchOut: Open-label treatment with a usual-care control invites performance and co-intervention bias that blinded endpoint assessment only partly removes; the trial is single-country; and the authors' own conclusion asks for replication — which the next card supplies, with the opposite result. The record's abstract does not describe the population as reperfusion-ineligible (the topic draft's description), and the card does not adopt that description.

cards.headline: RESIST 2023: sham-controlled prehospital conditioning did not improve 90-day outcome (OR 0.95, P=0.67)
cards.summary: RESIST 2023: sham-controlled prehospital conditioning did not improve 90-day outcome (OR 0.95, P=0.67)
cards.people: 1,500 patients with prehospital stroke symptoms of less than 4 hours at four Danish stroke centres, randomised to remote ischaemic conditioning (cuff ≤200 mm Hg; n=749) or sham (cuff 20 mm Hg; n=751), started in the ambulance, repeated in hospital, then twice daily for 7 days in a subset; 1,433 (96%) completed the trial. Median age was 71 years and 591 (41%) were women. Of randomised patients, 10% had TIA and 27% a stroke mimic; the target population with a final stroke diagnosis numbered 902 (82% ischaemic, 18% intracerebral haemorrhage).
cards.result: In the target population, the median modified Rankin score at 90 days was 2 (IQR 1–3) with conditioning and 1 (IQR 1–3) with sham; conditioning was not significantly associated with improved functional outcome (odds ratio 0.95; 95% CI 0.75 to 1.20; P=0.67). Serious adverse events in all randomised patients were similar (23.7% vs 24.3% with one or more events). Upper-extremity pain or skin petechiae occurred in 7.2% with conditioning versus 1.5% with sham.
cards.watchOut: RESIST is not RICAMIS with a sham: it treated earlier (prehospital), briefer (7 days in a subset), and in an all-comer population where over a third had no stroke at all — dilution that biases toward the null. But it is the only sham-controlled trial here, and its point estimate sits on the sham side. Both directions of caution belong on the shelf.

shelves.title: Bypass surgery for haemorrhagic moyamoya disease (Japan Adult Moyamoya Trial)
shelves.question: In adults with haemorrhagic moyamoya disease, does extracranial–intracranial bypass surgery plus medical care, compared with medical care alone, reduce rebleeding, death, and disability?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cerebral Hemorrhage · Cerebral Revascularization · Female · Humans · Japan · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Moyamoya Disease · Postoperative Complications · Proportional Hazards Models · Prospective Studies · Secondary Prevention · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the composite includes death and disability; also flagged here as a TWO-TRIAL-GATE EXCEPTION CANDIDATE — this is the only randomised trial in moyamoya disease, and none other exists to pair with it). The Japan Adult Moyamoya Trial (80 patients, 5 years of follow-up) found its primary composite of all adverse events in 6 of 42 surgical patients (14.3%) versus 13 of 38 non-surgical patients (34.2%) (annual rates 3.2% vs 8.2%/year; P=0.048 by Kaplan–Meier analysis), and rebleeding in 5 (11.9%) versus 12 (31.6%) (2.7% vs 7.6%/year; P=0.042) — while the Cox hazard ratios' confidence intervals both cross 1 (0.391 [0.148–1.029] for the composite; 0.355 [0.125–1.009] for rebleeding), and the authors themselves call the difference 'statistically marginal'. A correction to the topic draft: its '5-year rebleed risk roughly 12% vs 42%' is not what the record prints — the record gives crude proportions of 11.9% vs 31.6% and the annual rates above; the card follows the record. One small single-country trial in a rare disease, with a real but fragile signal: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: JAM Trial 2014: bypass surgery reduced adverse events (14.3% vs 34.2%) and rebleeding (11.9% vs 31.6%) over 5 years — with hazard-ratio intervals crossing 1

cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (the only RCT in moyamoya disease)
cards.people: 80 adults with moyamoya disease who had had an intracranial haemorrhage within the preceding year, at 22 institutes in Japan, randomised to bilateral extracranial–intracranial direct bypass plus conservative care (n=42) or conservative care alone (n=38), and observed for 5 years. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary endpoint (all adverse events) occurred in 6 patients (14.3%) in the surgical group and 13 (34.2%) in the non-surgical group; Kaplan–Meier analysis gave annual rates of 3.2%/year versus 8.2%/year (P=0.048), with a Cox hazard ratio of 0.391 relative (95% CI 0.148 to 1.029). Rebleeding attacks occurred in 5 patients (11.9%) versus 12 (31.6%) (2.7%/year vs 7.6%/year; P=0.042), with a hazard ratio of 0.355 relative (95% CI 0.125 to 1.009). The authors describe the Kaplan–Meier differences as 'statistically marginal' while suggesting a preventive effect of direct bypass against rebleeding.
cards.watchOut: Hold the two analyses apart: the log-rank/Kaplan–Meier comparisons reach P<0.05 while both Cox confidence intervals include 1.0 — with 80 patients and 17 rebleeding events, the result is genuinely fragile, and the authors' own word is 'marginal'. The topic draft's 'roughly 12% vs 42%' five-year rebleed figures do not appear in the record's abstract (which prints 11.9% vs 31.6% crude and 2.7% vs 7.6% per year); the record's figures are the carded ones.

shelves.title: Stenting versus medical therapy for symptomatic vertebral artery stenosis (VIST; VAST)
shelves.question: In patients with recently symptomatic vertebral artery stenosis of at least 50%, does vertebral artery stenting plus best medical therapy, compared with best medical therapy alone, prevent subsequent stroke?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Prospective Studies · Recurrence · Stents · Stroke · United Kingdom · Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the primary outcome is fatal or non-fatal stroke). Both trials stopped short of answering the question. VIST (179 patients analysed, reported as a full Health Technology Assessment monograph rather than a journal paper) found its primary endpoint — fatal or non-fatal stroke in any territory — in 5 patients in the stent group versus 12 in the medical group (hazard ratio 0.40; 95% CI 0.14 to 1.13; P=0.08), was underpowered after failing its recruitment target, and could stent only 61 of the 91 patients assigned to stenting because stenosis was not confirmed in many; extracranial stenting caused no perioperative complications, while two strokes occurred during intracranial stenting. VAST (115 patients, phase 2, stopped early for regulatory and funding reasons) found a 30-day composite of vascular death, myocardial infarction, or stroke in 5% with stenting versus 2% with medical treatment, and territory stroke over a median 3 years in 12% versus 7%. A favourable point estimate from an underpowered trial against a periprocedural-harm signal from a small one: the question is unresolved — POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: VIST 2019 (HTA monograph): primary endpoint 5 vs 12 events favouring stenting (HR 0.40, P=0.08), in an underpowered trial that stented only 61 of 91 assigned patients
cards.summary: VIST 2019 (HTA monograph): primary endpoint 5 vs 12 events favouring stenting (HR 0.40, P=0.08), in an underpowered trial that stented only 61 of 91 assigned patients
cards.type: Randomised, open-label, blinded-endpoint trial (full report published as an HTA monograph)
cards.people: 182 patients with symptomatic vertebral artery stenosis of at least 50% at 14 UK hospitals, randomised to vertebral angioplasty/stenting plus best medical treatment (n=91) or best medical treatment alone (n=88); three patients who contributed no follow-up data were excluded, leaving 179 analysed, with median follow-up of 3.5 years. Of 61 patients actually stented, 48 (78.7%) had extracranial and 13 (21.3%) intracranial stenosis. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary endpoint (fatal or non-fatal stroke in any arterial territory) occurred in five patients (including one fatal stroke) in the stent group and 12 (including two fatal strokes) in the medical group (hazard ratio 0.40 relative; 95% confidence interval 0.14 to 1.13; P=0.08), an absolute risk reduction of 25 strokes per 1000 person-years. No perioperative complications occurred with extracranial stenting; two strokes occurred during intracranial stenting. The authors state the trial was underpowered because it failed to reach target recruitment, and that non-confirmation of stenosis in the stented group was a second major limitation.
cards.watchOut: Two structural caveats define this trial: a third of the stent-assigned patients were never stented (stenosis not confirmed on the table), so intention-to-treat dilutes whatever stenting does; and 17 total primary events cannot support a firm conclusion at HR 0.40 or any other value. The report's format — a full HTA monograph (Health Technology Assessment 2019; Vol 23, No 41), not a journal article — is disclosed here as the draft flagged; the record is a complete trial report, not a summary.

cards.headline: VAST 2015: phase 2 trial stopped early — 30-day vascular events 5% with stenting vs 2% with medical therapy; territory stroke over 3 years 12% vs 7%
cards.summary: VAST 2015: phase 2 trial stopped early — 30-day vascular events 5% with stenting vs 2% with medical therapy; territory stroke over 3 years 12% vs 7%
cards.type: Randomised, open-label phase 2 trial, stopped early
cards.people: 115 patients with a recent vertebrobasilar transient ischaemic attack or minor stroke and intracranial or extracranial vertebral artery stenosis of at least 50%, at seven Dutch hospitals, randomised to stenting plus best medical treatment (n=57) or best medical treatment alone (n=58), before the trial was stopped because new regulatory requirements (prespecified stent types, external monitoring) had no funding. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary outcome (vascular death, myocardial infarction, or any stroke within 30 days) occurred in 3 patients (5%; 95% CI 0 to 11) in the stenting group and 1 patient (2%; 95% CI 0 to 5) in the medical group. During a median follow-up of 3 years, stroke in the territory of the symptomatic vertebral artery occurred in 7 patients (12%) with stenting and 4 (7%) with medical treatment, and the full composite in 19% versus 17%. The authors conclude stenting carries a major periprocedural vascular complication in about one in 20 patients, and that the low recurrence rate on medical treatment alone questions the need for a phase 3 trial.
cards.watchOut: VAST and VIST pull in opposite directions on the same small evidence base: VAST's signal is early procedural harm with no later gain in 115 patients; VIST's is a later benefit signal with no extracranial procedural cost in 179. Anatomical mix differs (VAST included intracranial stenoses, where VIST's only procedural strokes also occurred) — the most defensible joint reading is that extracranial vertebral stenting looks safe but unproven, and intracranial stenting looks hazardous.

shelves.title: Clazosentan to prevent vasospasm-related morbidity after aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage (CONSCIOUS programme)
shelves.question: In patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage secured by clipping or coiling, does the endothelin-receptor antagonist clazosentan, compared with placebo, reduce vasospasm-related morbidity and mortality?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Dioxanes · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glasgow Outcome Scale · Humans · Infarction · Ischemia · Middle Aged · Placebos · Pyridines · Pyrimidines · Subarachnoid Hemorrhage · Sulfonamides · Tetrazoles · Treatment Outcome · Vasospasm, Intracranial
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the phase 3 primary composites include all-cause mortality). This shelf is the library's cleanest surrogate-versus-outcome arc. CONSCIOUS-1 (413 patients, phase 2 dose-finding) did exactly what the pharmacology promised: moderate or severe angiographic vasospasm fell dose-dependently from 66% on placebo to 23% at clazosentan 15 mg/h (65% relative reduction; P<0.0001), with no significant effect on its morbidity/mortality endpoints. The phase 3 trials then failed to convert the surrogate: CONSCIOUS-2 (clipping; 1,157 randomised) found the primary composite in 21% on clazosentan 5 mg/h versus 25% on placebo (relative risk reduction 17%; 95% CI −4 to 33; P=0.10), with poor functional outcome numerically worse on clazosentan (29% vs 25%) and mortality 6% in both groups. CONSCIOUS-3 (coiling) was halted after CONSCIOUS-2 at 577 of 1,500 planned patients: its 15 mg/h arm did significantly reduce the primary composite (15% vs 27%; OR 0.47; P=0.007) — a correction to the topic draft's blanket statement that both phase 3 trials 'failed their composites' — but neither dose improved functional outcome (poor outcome 24% placebo, 25% at 5 mg/h, 28% at 15 mg/h), and mortality was 6%, 4%, and 6%. A drug that abolishes the angiographic lesion without improving how patients do, across two phase 3 trials: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for clinical benefit. The later Japanese REACT programme is fenced in the synthesis, not carded.

cards.headline: CONSCIOUS-1 2008: clazosentan cut moderate/severe angiographic vasospasm from 66% to 23% at the highest dose (65% relative reduction) — a phase 2 surrogate result
cards.summary: CONSCIOUS-1 2008: clazosentan cut moderate/severe angiographic vasospasm from 66% to 23% at the highest dose (65% relative reduction) — a phase 2 surrogate result
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 dose-finding trial
cards.people: 413 patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage, randomised to placebo or intravenous clazosentan at 1, 5, or 15 mg/h, begun within 56 hours and continued for up to 14 days; the primary endpoint was moderate or severe angiographic vasospasm on centrally read angiography at days 7–11. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Moderate or severe vasospasm was reduced dose-dependently, from 66% in the placebo group to 23% in the 15 mg/h group (relative risk reduction 65%; 95% CI 47 to 78; P<0.0001). No significant effects were seen on the locally assessed morbidity/mortality endpoint (all-cause mortality, new cerebral infarct, delayed ischaemic deficit from vasospasm, or rescue therapy); a post hoc centrally assessed version of that endpoint showed a non-significant trend (37%, 28%, and 29% across the dose groups versus 39% on placebo). Clazosentan increased pulmonary complications, hypotension, and anaemia.
cards.watchOut: Everything on this card is the 'before' picture: a dramatic effect on the angiogram, none demonstrated on patients. The post hoc central re-adjudication that produced the favourable trend is the kind of analysis that should generate a phase 3 question — which it did — not an answer. The trial predates routine registration databank fields; no registry ID is in the record, and none is supplied.

cards.headline: CONSCIOUS-2 2011: in clipped patients, clazosentan 5 mg/h did not significantly reduce the morbidity/mortality composite (21% vs 25%; P=0.10); mortality 6% in both groups
cards.summary: CONSCIOUS-2 2011: in clipped patients, clazosentan 5 mg/h did not significantly reduce the morbidity/mortality composite (21% vs 25%; P=0.10); mortality 6% in both groups
cards.people: Patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage secured by surgical clipping at 102 sites in 27 countries, randomised to clazosentan 5 mg/h (n=768) or placebo (n=389) for up to 14 days; the all-treated dataset comprised 764 and 383 patients. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary composite endpoint at week 6 (all-cause mortality, vasospasm-related new cerebral infarcts, delayed ischaemic neurological deficit from vasospasm, and rescue therapy) occurred in 161 of 764 patients (21%) on clazosentan and 97 of 383 (25%) on placebo (relative risk reduction 17%; 95% CI −4 to 33; P=0.10). Poor functional outcome (extended Glasgow Outcome Scale ≤4 at week 12) occurred in 29% on clazosentan versus 25% on placebo. Mortality at week 12 was 6% in both groups. Lung complications, anaemia, and hypotension were more common with clazosentan.
cards.watchOut: Note what the point estimates do: the vasospasm composite leans slightly toward the drug while functional outcome leans slightly against it — the signature of a surrogate disconnect, not of a near-miss. The tested dose (5 mg/h) was below CONSCIOUS-1's most effective dose, a design choice the CONSCIOUS-3 card takes up.

cards.people: Patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage secured by endovascular coiling, randomised to clazosentan 5 mg/h (n=194), 15 mg/h (n=188), or placebo (n=189); the trial was halted prematurely after CONSCIOUS-2 reported, having enrolled 577 of a planned 1,500 patients (571 treated). cards.result: The primary composite endpoint (all-cause mortality; vasospasm-related new infarcts or delayed ischaemic deficits; rescue therapy) at 6 weeks occurred in 50 of 189 patients (27%) on placebo, 47 of 194 (24%) on clazosentan 5 mg/h (odds ratio 0.79; 95% CI 0.48 to 1.29; P=0.34), and 28 of 188 (15%) on clazosentan 15 mg/h (odds ratio 0.47; 95% CI 0.28 to 0.82; P=0.007). cards.watchOut: Precision matters here, and the card corrects the topic draft: CONSCIOUS-3 did not simply 'fail' — its high-dose arm significantly reduced a vasospasm-weighted composite in a trial stopped at 38% of planned enrolment, while the patient-centred outcome (functional status) was null-to-worse at the same dose. A composite that can be won while patients do no better is measuring the surrogate, not the disease. Early stopping further inflates the composite estimate.

shelves.title: Ultra-early tranexamic acid after aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage (ULTRA)
shelves.question: In patients with CT-confirmed aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage, does ultra-early short-course tranexamic acid started in the emergency department, compared with standard care, improve functional outcome at six months?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antifibrinolytic Agents · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Netherlands · Prospective Studies · Subarachnoid Hemorrhage · Time Factors · Tranexamic Acid · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: functional outcome after subarachnoid haemorrhage). ULTRA (955 patients) tested the strongest version of the antifibrinolytic idea: tranexamic acid started immediately on CT diagnosis — 1 g bolus then 1 g every 8 hours until aneurysm treatment or 24 hours. Good clinical outcome (modified Rankin 0–3) at 6 months occurred in 60% on tranexamic acid versus 64% on usual care (adjusted odds ratio 0.86; 95% CI 0.66 to 1.12), and rebleeding before aneurysm treatment, though numerically lower (10% vs 14%; odds ratio 0.71; 95% CI 0.48 to 1.04), was not significantly reduced either. A single large, well-conducted trial whose point estimates lean against the intervention on outcome: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for ultra-early tranexamic acid as tested.

cards.headline: ULTRA 2021: ultra-early tranexamic acid did not improve 6-month outcome (good outcome 60% vs 64%; adjusted OR 0.86) and did not significantly reduce rebleeding (10% vs 14%)
cards.summary: ULTRA 2021: ultra-early tranexamic acid did not improve 6-month outcome (good outcome 60% vs 64%; adjusted OR 0.86) and did not significantly reduce rebleeding (10% vs 14%)
cards.type: Randomised, open-label trial with masked outcome assessment
cards.people: 955 adults with spontaneous CT-proven subarachnoid haemorrhage (presumed aneurysmal) at eight treatment centres and 16 referring hospitals in the Netherlands, randomised to tranexamic acid started immediately after diagnosis (1 g bolus, then 1 g every 8 hours, stopped before aneurysm treatment or at 24 hours; n=480) plus usual care, or usual care alone (n=475). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Good clinical outcome (modified Rankin score 0–3) at 6 months occurred in 287 of 475 patients (60%) in the tranexamic acid group and 300 of 470 (64%) in the control group (treatment-centre adjusted odds ratio 0.86; 95% CI 0.66 to 1.12). Rebleeding after randomisation and before aneurysm treatment occurred in 49 patients (10%) on tranexamic acid and 66 (14%) on control (odds ratio 0.71; 95% CI 0.48 to 1.04). Other serious adverse events were comparable between groups.
cards.watchOut: ULTRA's design pre-empts the usual excuses: treatment was genuinely ultra-early and genuinely short, stopped before aneurysm securement — and the rebleeding reduction it aimed for did not reach significance while the outcome estimate leaned the other way. The trial does not address prolonged antifibrinolytic courses (the historical regimens that reduced rebleeding at the cost of ischaemia) — it retires the modern, short version of the idea.

shelves.title: Platelet transfusion after antiplatelet-associated intracerebral haemorrhage (PATCH)
shelves.question: In patients with spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage who were taking antiplatelet therapy, does platelet transfusion improve functional outcome versus standard care alone?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Cerebral Hemorrhage/chemically induced/mortality/therapy · Europe · Female · Humans · Length of Stay · Male · Middle Aged · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors/adverse effects · Platelet Transfusion · Stroke/chemically induced/mortality/therapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — a single randomised trial found platelet transfusion made things worse: the odds of death or dependence at 3 months were about doubled. The trial was open-label (with masked outcome assessment) and enrolled 190 patients over nearly seven years, so the estimate is imprecise, but the direction is consistent across the primary analysis, serious adverse events and in-hospital deaths, and the authors recommend against the practice. PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C): the primary outcome embeds death. PROPOSED as a two-trial-gate exception candidate: this is the only randomised trial of the question; the shelf should be withdrawn or re-scoped if the developer rejects the exception.

cards.headline: PATCH: platelet transfusion shifted patients towards death or dependence at 3 months (adjusted common OR 2.05)
cards.summary: PATCH: platelet transfusion shifted patients towards death or dependence at 3 months (adjusted common OR 2.05)
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, open-label, masked-endpoint phase 3 trial (60 hospitals in the Netherlands, UK and France; transfusion within 90 minutes of diagnostic imaging)
cards.people: 190 adults with supratentorial intracerebral haemorrhage presenting within 6 hours of symptom onset, who had used antiplatelet therapy for at least 7 days beforehand and had a Glasgow Coma Scale score of at least 8; 97 were assigned to platelet transfusion plus standard care and 93 to standard care alone. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: The primary outcome — a shift towards death or dependence on the modified Rankin Scale at 3 months — favoured standard care: adjusted common odds ratio 2.05 (95% CI 1.18 to 3.56; p=0.0114) for the transfusion group. Serious adverse events during the hospital stay occurred in 40 (42%) of the transfusion group versus 28 (29%) of the standard-care group, and 23 (24%) versus 16 (17%) died during the hospital stay.
cards.watchOut: Open-label treatment (outcome assessors were masked). Enrolment took from 2009 to 2015 to reach 190 patients, and the trial pooled patients on different antiplatelet regimens; the confidence interval is wide, but every reported measure points the same way, towards harm. The registry ID is stated in the record's abstract text, not its databank fields.
cards.source: Baharoglu MI et al. Platelet transfusion versus standard care after acute stroke due to spontaneous cerebral haemorrhage associated with antiplatelet therapy (PATCH): a randomised, open-label, phase 3 trial. Lancet (London, England). 2016. PMID: 27178479. Registry ID: Netherlands Trial Register NTR1303, as stated in the record's abstract text (not in its databank fields). cards.headline: Synthesis: the only randomised test says platelet transfusion harms this population — POSSIBLE (harm)
cards.summary: Synthesis: the only randomised test says platelet transfusion harms this population — POSSIBLE (harm)
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: PATCH (Baharoglu 2016), 190 patients with antiplatelet-associated intracerebral haemorrhage.
cards.result: The biological hope — that transfused platelets would limit haematoma growth in patients whose own platelets were drug-inhibited — was not borne out: transfusion was associated with roughly double the odds of death or dependence, more serious adverse events and more in-hospital deaths. On this record, platelet transfusion for antiplatelet-associated intracerebral haemorrhage should not be given.
cards.watchOut: A single, modest-sized, open-label trial carries this shelf; a confirmatory trial would strengthen or overturn it, and the shelf should be re-swept if one appears. The result applies to patients on antiplatelet therapy before the bleed, not to thrombocytopenic or anticoagulant-associated haemorrhage.

shelves.title: Screening for cognitive impairment in primary care — patient and family outcomes (Fowler; IU CHOICE)
shelves.question: In primary care patients aged 65 and over, does systematic screening for cognitive impairment (versus no screening) improve health-related quality of life, depression, or anxiety for patients or their care partners?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Female · Aged · Male · Dementia · Family · Quality of Life · Mass Screening · Aged, 80 and over · Caregivers · Primary Health Care
shelves.balance: Two randomised trials, a quarter-century of screening enthusiasm apart, give the same answer: none. IU CHOICE (4,005 patients aged 65+ in Indiana safety-net and university clinics) found no effect of cognitive screening on health-related quality of life at 12 months (effect size 0.009, 95% CI −0.063 to 0.080) and depression and anxiety differences inside prespecified equivalency margins. Fowler 2026 (29 clinics, 1,808 patient–family dyads) extended the question to families and to a screening-plus-collaborative-care arm: only 5.1% of screened patients tested positive, over a third of positives offered diagnostic work-up in the intensive arm declined it, and at 24 months family members' physical and mental quality-of-life scores did not differ between arms (differences −0.21 and 0.58, both intervals crossing zero), nor did depression, anxiety, or caregiver outcomes. Screening finds cases; it does not, by itself or with collaborative care attached, make patients or families measurably better or worse off. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: Fowler 2026: cognitive screening (with or without collaborative dementia care) did not improve family members' quality of life at 24 months
cards.summary: Fowler 2026: cognitive screening (with or without collaborative dementia care) did not improve family members' quality of life at 24 months
cards.people: 1,808 patient–family member dyads: patients aged 65 or older without a dementia diagnosis attending 29 primary care clinics in three US health systems, randomised by clinic-facing arm allocation to cognitive screening plus collaborative dementia care management, screening with primary-care follow-up only, or no screening (usual care). Family members' health-related quality of life (SF-36 physical and mental component scores) was the primary outcome at 24 months; secondary outcomes included family depression and anxiety (PHQ-9, GAD-7) and caregiver burden, preparedness, and self-efficacy.
cards.result: Screening yield was low: 62 patients (5.1%) screened positive and, in the screening-plus-collaborative-care arm, 35.7% of those offered diagnostic assessment declined it. At 24 months, family members in the screening-plus-collaborative-care arm did not differ from no-screening on SF-36 physical component scores (difference −0.21 points, 95% CI −1.26 to 0.85) or mental component scores (difference 0.58, CI −0.18 to 1.33), and there were no between-group differences in family depression or anxiety or in any caregiver outcome at 24 months. Findings were consistent across racial and ethnic subgroups.
cards.watchOut: The trial tests a screening programme, not dementia treatment: with only 5.1% screening positive and a third declining work-up, very few dyads received the collaborative care that might plausibly help, so the null is as much about the funnel as about the care. Usual-care contamination (clinicians diagnosing impairment outside the programme) also narrows the contrast. The null is nonetheless what a health system buying this programme would obtain.
cards.source: Fowler NR et al. Screening for Cognitive Impairment in Primary Care and Outcomes for Family Members: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Intern Med. 2026. PMID: 42008257. Registry ID: NCT03300180, from the record. MeSH: Humans · Female · Aged · Male · Dementia · Family · Quality of Life · Mass Screening · Aged, 80 and over · Caregivers · Primary Health Care

cards.headline: IU CHOICE 2020: cognitive screening did not change patients' quality of life at 12 months (effect size 0.009, CI −0.063 to 0.080); depression and anxiety were equivalent
cards.summary: IU CHOICE 2020: cognitive screening did not change patients' quality of life at 12 months (effect size 0.009, CI −0.063 to 0.080); depression and anxiety were equivalent
cards.people: 4,005 primary care patients aged 65 or older without a documented dementia or severe mental illness diagnosis, attending clinics in two Indiana health systems (a safety-net and a university system), randomised to cognitive screening or no screening. Outcomes were measured at 1, 6, and 12 months: health-related quality of life (SF-36) as the primary outcome, and depressive and anxiety symptoms (PHQ-9, GAD-7) as secondary outcomes, tested for equivalence against prespecified margins (0.30 SD for quality of life; 2.0 and 1.8 points respectively).
cards.result: There was no difference in health-related quality of life between screening and no-screening groups at 12 months (effect size 0.009, 95% CI −0.063 to 0.080; P=.81). Differences in depressive symptoms (1.013 at 12 months, 97.5% CI −0.270 to 2.296) and anxiety symptoms (0.468, CI −0.483 to 1.419; P=.28) fell within the prespecified equivalency margins — screening neither helped nor measurably harmed psychological outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Equivalence here is against generous margins (2 points on the PHQ-9), so small harms or benefits inside those bounds remain possible; but combined with Fowler's 24-month family data the picture is consistent. Note that IU CHOICE's 2014 protocol paper (PMID: 24903469) is a different record from these results — the card cites the 2020 results paper actually fetched and verified. No registry ID is shown in the results record.
cards.source: Fowler NR et al. Effect of Cognitive Screening on Health-Related Quality of Life and Depression and Anxiety Symptoms in Older Adults (IU CHOICE). J Am Geriatr Soc. 2020. PMID: 31792940. Registry ID: none shown in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: cognitive screening in primary care — for patients (IU CHOICE) and for families (Fowler 2026) — changed no measured quality-of-life, mood, or caregiver outcome
cards.summary: Synthesis: cognitive screening in primary care — for patients (IU CHOICE) and for families (Fowler 2026) — changed no measured quality-of-life, mood, or caregiver outcome
cards.people: 5,813 older adults (plus 1,808 family members) across Fowler 2026 (n=1,808 dyads) and IU CHOICE (n=4,005).
cards.result: Quality of life: effect size 0.009 (CI −0.063 to 0.080) at 12 months; family SF-36 differences −0.21 (CI −1.26 to 0.85) and 0.58 (CI −0.18 to 1.33) at 24 months. Depression and anxiety equivalent. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: Neither trial measured whether screening improves downstream disease-specific management, safety (driving, finances), or advance planning — outcomes where benefit is hypothesised but, on this evidence, unproven. A positive screen still obliges a careful diagnostic conversation with the individual patient; the null is about population screening programmes, not about evaluating someone who presents with cognitive concern.

shelves.title: Postnatal depression screening with psychological therapy (PoNDER; Morrell)
shelves.question: In postnatal women, does health-visitor screening for depression with referral to psychological therapy (listening visits or CBT) reduce depression at 6 months versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Cluster Analysis · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy · Community Health Nursing · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Depression, Postpartum · Family Practice · Female · Humans · Pregnancy · Professional Role · Surveys and Questionnaires · United Kingdom
shelves.balance: One large cluster-randomised trial from UK primary care. PoNDER trained health visitors to identify postnatal depression (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale at 6–8 weeks and again at 8 months) and to deliver psychological support — nondirective listening visits (counselling) or cognitive-behavioural therapy — in home visits, versus usual primary care. Among women identified as at risk at 6 weeks (EPDS ≥12), 33.9% in intervention clusters still scored EPDS ≥12 at 6 months versus 45.6% in control clusters (P=0.036), and mean EPDS scores were lower (9.2 vs 11.3; adjusted P=0.001); across all women the figures were 11.7% versus 16.4% (P=0.003). Listening visits and CBT did not differ from each other (P=0.74). The absolute benefit is meaningful (about 12 points in the at-risk group) and the intervention was cost-effective at NICE thresholds in the trial's analysis — but the trial's own authors warn the estimate is imprecise and 'the true effect may be small'; a single cluster trial with a wide interval keeps this at POSSIBLE. Benefit persisted to 12 months and faded by 18.

cards.headline: PoNDER 2009: health-visitor screening plus psychological support cut depression at 6 months in at-risk mothers (EPDS ≥12: 33.9% vs 45.6%); listening visits and CBT performed equally
cards.summary: PoNDER 2009: health-visitor screening plus psychological support cut depression at 6 months in at-risk mothers (EPDS ≥12: 33.9% vs 45.6%); listening visits and CBT performed equally
cards.people: 101 clusters of general practices in the Trent region of England; 7,649 eligible women, of whom 4,084 consented to follow-up. Health visitors in intervention clusters were trained to identify depressive symptoms (EPDS administered at 6–8 weeks and 8 months postnatally) and to provide psychological support in home visits — women were allocated within clusters to listening visits (counselling) or cognitive-behavioural therapy; control clusters provided usual postnatal care. The prespecified primary analysis covered women at risk of depression (EPDS ≥12 at 6 weeks); outcomes were measured at 6, 12, and 18 months.
cards.result: Among at-risk women, the proportion with EPDS ≥12 at 6 months was 33.9% in intervention clusters (93 of 271 with outcome data) versus 45.6% in control clusters (67 of 147) (P=0.036) — an absolute difference of about 12 percentage points. Mean EPDS scores were 9.2 versus 11.3 (adjusted P=0.001). Among all women (not just at-risk), EPDS ≥12 at 6 months was 11.7% versus 16.4% (P=0.003). There was no difference between the counselling and CBT arms (P=0.74). The benefit remained evident at 12 months but was no longer evident at 18 months. The trial's economic analysis found the strategy cost-effective at the NICE threshold, and its authors note the treatment-effect estimate has a wide confidence interval, so the true effect may be small.
cards.watchOut: Outcome data were available for only part of the at-risk sample (271 intervention, 147 control women), so attrition could bias the estimate in either direction; the cluster design and single-region delivery (Trent, England) limit generalisation. The intervention bundles screening with treatment — the trial cannot say the EPDS screen itself, without the trained-visitor therapy behind it, does anything, which is the same screening-programme lesson as Shelves #1961 and #1965 read in reverse: here the pathway behind the screen was staffed. No registry ID is shown in the HTA record.
cards.source: Morrell CJ et al. Clinical effectiveness of health visitor training in psychologically informed approaches for depression in postnatal women: pragmatic cluster randomised trial in primary care (PoNDER). Health Technol Assess. 2009. PMID: 19555590. Registry ID: none shown in the record. shelves.title: Brief intervention for drug use in primary care (ASPIRE)
shelves.question: In primary-care patients who screen positive for illicit drug use, does a brief intervention (with or without a booster) reduce drug use versus screening with information only?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Health Services · Hospitals, Urban · Humans · Male · Mass Screening · Middle Aged · Motivational Interviewing · Primary Health Care · Self Report · Substance-Related Disorders · Treatment Outcome · Unsafe Sex
shelves.balance: ASPIRE randomised 528 primary-care patients who screened positive for drug use (main drug marijuana in 63%, cocaine in 19%, opioids in 17%) to a 10–15 minute brief negotiated interview, a 30–45 minute motivational-interviewing intervention with a booster, or no brief intervention (all groups received a written list of treatment and mutual-help resources). At six months, days of use of the main drug were 12 in the control group, 11 with the brief negotiated interview (incidence rate ratio 0.97, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.22) and 12 with motivational interviewing (incidence rate ratio 1.05, 0.84 to 1.32; P=.81 for both comparisons) — and there were no significant effects on any secondary outcome, hair testing included, or in any severity subgroup. A large, complete (98% follow-up), unambiguous null for the alcohol-derived brief-intervention model applied to drug use. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: ASPIRE: neither brief intervention cut drug use — days of use 12 (control) vs 11 and 12 (interventions) at six months
cards.summary: ASPIRE: neither brief intervention cut drug use — days of use 12 (control) vs 11 and 12 (interventions) at six months
cards.people: 528 adult primary-care patients at an urban hospital-based internal medicine practice in Boston, identified by screening (ASSIST substance-specific scores ≥4) between 2009 and 2012; 63% reported marijuana as their main drug, 19% cocaine and 17% opioids. The interventions were a brief negotiated interview (10–15 minutes, by health educators) and MOTIV, a motivational-interviewing adaptation (30–45 minutes by master's-level counsellors, plus a 20–30 minute booster); the comparison group received no brief intervention. All participants received a written list of substance use disorder treatment and mutual-help resources. The primary outcome was days of use of the self-identified main drug in the past 30 days at six months; 98% completed follow-up.
cards.result: Mean adjusted days of main-drug use at six months were 12 for no brief intervention versus 11 for the brief negotiated interview (incidence rate ratio 0.97, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.22) and 12 for MOTIV (incidence rate ratio 1.05, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.32; P=.81 for both comparisons against no brief intervention). There were no significant effects of either intervention on any other outcome — including hair testing, ASSIST severity scores, drug-use consequences and health care utilisation — or in analyses stratified by main drug or severity. The authors concluded the results do not support widespread implementation of screening and brief intervention for drug use in primary care.
cards.watchOut: The control group was not 'nothing' — screening plus a written resource list is itself a minimal intervention, so the trial tests the added value of counselling, which was nil. Results concern drug use identified by screening in primary care; they do not speak to brief intervention for alcohol, the separate question on which the model was built.
cards.source: Saitz R et al. Screening and brief intervention for drug use in primary care: the ASPIRE randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2014. PMID: 25096690. Registry ID: NCT00876941, from the record. shelves.title: Nabiximols (cannabis extract) for cannabis dependence (Lintzeris)
shelves.question: In people seeking treatment for cannabis dependence, does nabiximols oromucosal spray reduce cannabis use versus placebo over 12 weeks?
shelves.balance: Two Australian randomised trials of the cannabinoid agonist nabiximols (THC:cannabidiol oromucosal spray) support a during-treatment benefit. In the outpatient dependence trial (Lintzeris 2019; 128 treatment-seeking adults who had not responded to prior treatment), nabiximols recipients reported using cannabis on 35.0 days over 12 weeks versus 53.1 days on placebo — an estimated difference of 18.6 days (95% CI 3.5 to 33.7; P=.02) — with comparable retention and tolerability. In the inpatient withdrawal trial (Allsop 2014; 51 patients), a six-day nabiximols course significantly reduced withdrawal severity (P=.01) and more than tripled treatment retention (hazard ratio 3.66, 95% CI 1.18 to 11.37) — but after medication stopped, post-withdrawal cannabis use fell equally in both groups (P=.75). The pattern is consistent: an agonist that works while taken, with no demonstrated carry-over after it stops. PROPOSED LIKELY for reducing use during treatment.

cards.headline: Lintzeris 2019: nabiximols — cannabis used on 35.0 days versus 53.1 days on placebo over 12 weeks (difference 18.6 days, P=.02)
cards.summary: Lintzeris 2019: nabiximols — cannabis used on 35.0 days versus 53.1 days on placebo over 12 weeks (difference 18.6 days, P=.02)
cards.people: 128 adults (mean age 35.0 years) with ICD-10 cannabis dependence seeking treatment at four specialist outpatient services in New South Wales, Australia, who had not responded to prior treatment attempts and had used cannabis on a mean of 25.7 of the past 28 days. Participants received 12 weeks of weekly clinical review and structured counselling plus flexible-dose nabiximols (up to 32 sprays daily; mean achieved 17.6 sprays, about 47.5 mg THC and 44.0 mg cannabidiol) or matched placebo (mean 18.5 sprays daily). The primary outcome was self-reported days of illicit cannabis use across the 12 weeks.
cards.result: The placebo group reported significantly more days using cannabis during the 12 weeks (mean 53.1 days, SD 33.0) than the nabiximols group (mean 35.0 days, SD 32.4): estimated difference 18.6 days (95% CI 3.5 to 33.7 days; P=.02). Treatment retention was comparable (49.2% nabiximols versus 44.8% placebo completed), health status improved comparably in both groups, other substance use did not change substantially, and the medication was well tolerated with few adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Use was self-reported (no urinary confirmation of the primary outcome), retention was under 50% in both arms, and participants were previous treatment non-responders — a harder-to-treat group than first presentations. The PubMed record for this trial carries no MeSH headings; that gap is in the record, not an omission here. Study medications were provided free by GW Pharmaceuticals, as named in the publication's full text.
