cards.summary: Allsop 2014: six days of nabiximols eased inpatient cannabis withdrawal and tripled retention — but use after discharge fell equally on placebo
cards.people: 51 cannabis-dependent treatment seekers at two inpatient sites in New South Wales, Australia, randomised to a six-day regimen of nabiximols (Sativex; maximum 86.4 mg THC and 80 mg cannabidiol daily) or placebo during a nine-day admission with standardised psychosocial interventions, followed for 28 days. Outcomes were withdrawal and craving severity (Cannabis Withdrawal Scale), retention in withdrawal treatment, adverse events, and post-withdrawal cannabis use.
cards.result: Nabiximols significantly reduced overall withdrawal severity versus placebo (P=.01), including irritability, depression and cravings, with more limited benefit on sleep disturbance, anxiety, appetite loss, physical symptoms and restlessness. Nabiximols patients stayed in treatment longer (unadjusted hazard ratio 3.66, 95% CI 1.18 to 11.37; P=.02; number needed to treat 2.84 for successful retention), could not reliably tell which treatment they had received, and reported no greater intoxication. At follow-up, however, both groups had reduced cannabis use with no advantage for nabiximols (P=.75), and adverse events did not differ between groups.
cards.watchOut: This trial answers the withdrawal question, not the 12-week dependence question — it is carded as the second trial because it tests the same drug in the same population, but its own lasting-use result is null. Fifty-one patients and a six-day course make it a supporting, not load-bearing, card.
cards.source: Allsop DJ et al. Nabiximols as an agonist replacement therapy during cannabis withdrawal: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA Psychiatry. 2014. PMID: 24430917. Registry ID: ACTRN12611000398909, from the record. shelves.title: N-acetylcysteine for cannabis dependence (Gray)
shelves.question: In adolescents with cannabis dependence, does N-acetylcysteine increase abstinence versus placebo when both groups receive contingency management and cessation counselling?
shelves.mesh: Acetylcysteine · Adolescent · Cannabinoids · Counseling · Double-Blind Method · Excitatory Amino Acid Antagonists · Female · Humans · Male · Marijuana Abuse · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: The same investigative group ran the same trial design — N-acetylcysteine 1200 mg twice daily plus contingency management and counselling — in two age groups and got opposite answers, and this shelf keeps them separate rather than pooling them away. In 116 cannabis-dependent adolescents (ages 15–21), N-acetylcysteine more than doubled the odds of negative urine cannabinoid tests during eight weeks of treatment (odds ratio 2.4, 95% CI 1.1 to 5.2). In 302 adults (ages 18–50) over twelve weeks, the odds ratio was 1.00 (95% CI 0.63 to 1.59; p=0.984), with 22.3% versus 22.4% of urine tests negative. PROPOSED SPLIT: POSSIBLE benefit in adolescents (a single small trial), LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) in adults (a larger, precise null).

cards.headline: Gray 2012 (adolescents): N-acetylcysteine doubled the odds of negative urine tests (odds ratio 2.4, 95% CI 1.1 to 5.2)
cards.summary: Gray 2012 (adolescents): N-acetylcysteine doubled the odds of negative urine tests (odds ratio 2.4, 95% CI 1.1 to 5.2)
cards.people: 116 treatment-seeking cannabis-dependent adolescents (ages 15–21 years) randomised to N-acetylcysteine 1200 mg twice daily or placebo for eight weeks; all participants also received a contingency management intervention and brief (under 10 minutes) weekly cessation counselling. The primary efficacy measure was the odds of negative weekly urine cannabinoid test results during treatment, analysed intention-to-treat; tolerability was measured by adverse event frequency.
cards.result: Participants receiving N-acetylcysteine had more than twice the odds of negative urine cannabinoid tests during treatment compared with placebo (odds ratio 2.4, 95% CI 1.1 to 5.2). Exploratory secondary abstinence outcomes favoured N-acetylcysteine but were not statistically significant. N-acetylcysteine was well tolerated with minimal adverse events. The authors noted this was the first randomised pharmacotherapy trial for cannabis dependence in any age group to yield a positive primary cessation outcome on intention-to-treat analysis.
cards.watchOut: A single small trial (116 participants) with a surrogate biochemical endpoint over eight weeks; the confidence interval runs from a trivial 1.1 to a large 5.2, and the supportive secondary outcomes were not significant. The record shows no registry ID. The adult replication below is the reason this shelf is split rather than positive. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.headline: Gray 2017 (adults): the same drug, dose and design — odds ratio 1.00 (95% CI 0.63 to 1.59); no benefit
cards.summary: Gray 2017 (adults): the same drug, dose and design — odds ratio 1.00 (95% CI 0.63 to 1.59); no benefit
cards.people: 302 treatment-seeking adults (ages 18–50) with cannabis use disorder at six US National Drug Abuse Treatment Clinical Trials Network sites, randomised to N-acetylcysteine 1200 mg twice daily (n=153) or placebo (n=149) for twelve weeks; all received contingency management and medical management. The primary outcome was the odds of negative urine cannabinoid tests during treatment.
cards.result: There was no statistically significant difference in cannabis abstinence between N-acetylcysteine and placebo (odds ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.59; p=0.984): 22.3% of urine tests were negative on N-acetylcysteine versus 22.4% on placebo. Medication non-adherence was common, but exploratory analyses within medication-adherent subgroups also showed no differential benefit. The authors contrasted this with the prior adolescent finding and suggested developmental and other differences might explain the discrepancy.
cards.watchOut: This card is why the adolescent result cannot be generalised: the adult trial is larger, longer and precisely null, including among adherent participants. Whether adolescence itself is the modifier, or the adolescent trial was a small-sample positive, is unresolved — the shelf records both rather than choosing. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

shelves.title: As-needed nalmefene for alcohol dependence (ESENSE)
shelves.question: In adults with alcohol dependence at high drinking risk, does as-needed nalmefene reduce heavy drinking days and total consumption versus placebo over six months?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Alcohol Drinking · Alcoholism · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Naltrexone · Narcotic Antagonists · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: The ESENSE programme tested a different treatment model: nalmefene 18 mg taken only on days the patient felt at risk of drinking, aiming at reduced drinking rather than abstinence, with all patients receiving a motivational adherence intervention. In ESENSE 2 (718 patients), nalmefene beat placebo on heavy drinking days (−1.7 days/month, 95% CI −3.1 to −0.4; p=0.012) at six months, while total alcohol consumption fell by a non-significant −5.0 g/day (p=0.088). In the pooled subgroup of patients from ESENSE 1 and ESENSE 2 who remained at high drinking risk after initial assessment (667 patients), both co-primary outcomes were clearly positive: −3.2 heavy drinking days (95% CI −4.8 to −1.6; P<0.0001) and −14.3 g/day total consumption (−20.8 to −7.8; P<0.0001). Adverse events were more frequent on nalmefene, with similar dropout rates. Two concordant trials with the clearest effect in persistent high-risk drinkers: PROPOSED LIKELY for a modest reduction in heavy drinking.

cards.headline: ESENSE 2: as-needed nalmefene cut heavy drinking days by 1.7 per month versus placebo (p=0.012); total consumption difference not significant
cards.summary: ESENSE 2: as-needed nalmefene cut heavy drinking days by 1.7 per month versus placebo (p=0.012); total consumption difference not significant
cards.people: 718 adults with alcohol dependence, at least 6 heavy drinking days and at least WHO medium drinking-risk-level consumption in the four weeks before screening, randomised to 24 weeks of as-needed nalmefene 18 mg/day (n=358) or placebo (n=360). Co-primary outcomes were change from baseline to month six in heavy drinking days and in total alcohol consumption.
cards.result: Nalmefene was significantly superior to placebo on heavy drinking days (group difference −1.7 days/month, 95% CI −3.1 to −0.4; p=0.012) and better but not significant on total alcohol consumption (group difference −5.0 g/day in the last month, 95% CI −10.6 to 0.7; p=0.088). Patients who had not reduced their drinking before randomisation benefited more. Clinical Global Impression improvements and liver enzyme reductions were greater with nalmefene; adverse events were more common with nalmefene, though adverse events leading to dropout were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: One of two co-primary outcomes missed significance in this trial, and the absolute effect — under two fewer heavy drinking days a month — is modest. Outcomes are self-reported drinking (timeline follow-back), and the trials were industry-conducted; the pooled analysis below is what firms up the consumption outcome, in a subgroup.
cards.source: Gual A et al. A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, efficacy study of nalmefene, as-needed use, in patients with alcohol dependence. Eur Neuropsychopharmacol. 2013. PMID: 23562264. Registry ID: ESENSE 2 is NCT00812461, per the pooled ESENSE analysis record carded below; the ESENSE 2 record itself lists no registry ID. cards.headline: ESENSE 1+2 pooled high-risk subgroup: −3.2 heavy drinking days and −14.3 g/day versus placebo (both P<0.0001)
cards.summary: ESENSE 1+2 pooled high-risk subgroup: −3.2 heavy drinking days and −14.3 g/day versus placebo (both P<0.0001)
cards.type: Pooled subgroup analysis of two randomized trials
cards.people: 667 patients pooled from ESENSE 1 and ESENSE 2 who had at least a high drinking risk level (men >60 g/day; women >40 g/day) at both screening and randomisation — that is, who had not already reduced their drinking after initial assessment (placebo n=332; nalmefene n=335). All received as-needed nalmefene 18 mg or placebo plus the BRENDA motivational and adherence intervention over six months; outcomes were heavy drinking days and total alcohol consumption at month six by timeline follow-back.
cards.result: Nalmefene was superior to placebo on both co-primary outcomes in this subgroup: heavy drinking days treatment difference −3.2 days (95% CI −4.8 to −1.6; P<0.0001) and total alcohol consumption −14.3 g/day (95% CI −20.8 to −7.8; P<0.0001), with greater improvements in clinical status and liver parameters on nalmefene. Adverse events, and adverse events leading to dropout, were more common with nalmefene than placebo.
cards.watchOut: A subgroup defined by early non-response — the right target population for the drug, but selected post-randomisation in part (non-reduction after assessment), so its larger effect sizes should not be quoted as the whole-population result. This analysis represents ESENSE 1 within this shelf; ESENSE 1's own primary report is not separately carded.

shelves.title: Topiramate for alcohol dependence (Johnson)
shelves.question: In adults with alcohol dependence, does topiramate reduce heavy drinking versus placebo over 14 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Alcoholism · Behavior Therapy · Double-Blind Method · Excitatory Amino Acid Antagonists · Female · Fructose · GABA Modulators · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Compliance · Topiramate
shelves.balance: Two double-blind randomised trials from the same programme, four years apart, agree. The 2007 JAMA trial (371 adults with alcohol dependence, topiramate titrated to up to 300 mg/day over 14 weeks with weekly compliance enhancement) found topiramate reduced the percentage of heavy drinking days versus placebo — by 8.44 percentage points (95% CI 3.07 to 13.80; P=.002) in the conservative analysis treating all dropouts as relapsed, and by 16.19 points in the prespecified mixed-model analysis — with all other drinking outcomes also favouring topiramate (P<.001). The group's earlier Lancet trial (150 patients, 12 weeks) had found the same pattern: 27.6% fewer heavy drinking days and 26.2% more abstinent days (both p=0.0003), corroborated by gamma-glutamyl transferase. The cost is tolerability: paraesthesia in 50.8% versus 10.6%, taste perversion, anorexia and concentration difficulty all clearly more common on topiramate. PROPOSED LIKELY.

cards.headline: Johnson 2007 (JAMA): topiramate cut heavy drinking days by 8.4–16.2 percentage points versus placebo over 14 weeks
cards.summary: Johnson 2007 (JAMA): topiramate cut heavy drinking days by 8.4–16.2 percentage points versus placebo over 14 weeks
cards.people: 371 men and women aged 18 to 65 years with alcohol dependence at 17 US sites, randomised to topiramate up to 300 mg/day (n=183) or placebo (n=188) for 14 weeks, with a weekly compliance enhancement intervention in both arms. The primary efficacy variable was self-reported percentage of heavy drinking days; secondary outcomes included percentage of days abstinent, drinks per drinking day, and plasma gamma-glutamyl transferase.
cards.result: Treating all dropouts as relapse to baseline, topiramate reduced the percentage of heavy drinking days from baseline to week 14 by a mean difference of 8.44% (95% CI 3.07% to 13.80%; P=.002) versus placebo; the prespecified mixed-model analysis showed a larger difference of 16.19% (95% CI 10.79% to 21.60%; P<.001), and all other drinking outcomes favoured topiramate (P<.001 for all comparisons). Adverse events more common with topiramate than placebo included paraesthesia (50.8% vs 10.6%), taste perversion (23.0% vs 4.8%), anorexia (19.7% vs 6.9%) and difficulty with concentration (14.8% vs 3.2%).
cards.watchOut: The effect size depends on the analysis: the headline shrinks by half when dropouts are counted as relapses, which is the more honest number for a drug with this side-effect burden. Drinking outcomes are self-reported, though the earlier trial's enzyme corroboration supports them. Topiramate for alcohol dependence is off-label use in most jurisdictions — an evidence statement, not a regulatory one.
cards.source: Johnson BA et al. Topiramate for treating alcohol dependence: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2007. PMID: 17925516. Registry ID: NCT00210925, from the record. cards.headline: Johnson 2003 (Lancet): the earlier trial — 27.6% fewer heavy drinking days and 26.2% more abstinent days on topiramate
cards.summary: Johnson 2003 (Lancet): the earlier trial — 27.6% fewer heavy drinking days and 26.2% more abstinent days on topiramate
cards.people: 150 individuals with alcohol dependence randomised to oral topiramate (escalating dose 25–300 mg/day, n=75) or placebo (n=75) for 12 weeks, as an adjunct to weekly standardised medication compliance management. Primary efficacy variables were self-reported drinking measures and plasma gamma-glutamyl transferase, an objective index of alcohol consumption; craving was the secondary variable.
cards.result: At study end, topiramate patients had 2.88 fewer drinks per day (95% CI −4.50 to −1.27; p=0.0006), 3.10 fewer drinks per drinking day (p=0.0009), 27.6% fewer heavy drinking days (p=0.0003) and 26.2% more days abstinent (p=0.0003) than placebo patients, with a significantly lower log plasma gamma-glutamyl transferase ratio (p=0.0046). Topiramate-induced differences in craving were also significantly greater than with placebo and were highly correlated with the drinking changes.
cards.watchOut: A 150-patient single-programme trial; its percentage effects look larger than the later trial's because they are expressed as relative differences in drinking measures rather than the JAMA trial's percentage-point differences — the two are concordant in direction, not directly comparable in size. The record shows no registry ID (a 2003 trial, before routine registration).

shelves.title: Supervised injectable heroin versus optimised oral methadone (RIOTT)
shelves.question: In people with chronic heroin addiction who have not responded to optimised oral methadone, does supervised injectable heroin (or injectable methadone) reduce regular street-heroin use versus continuing optimised oral methadone?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · England · Female · Heroin · Heroin Dependence · Humans · Illicit Drugs · Injections · Male · Methadone · Middle Aged · Narcotics · Prescription Drugs · Young Adult
shelves.balance: RIOTT randomised 127 chronic heroin users in England who had been on conventional oral treatment for at least six months yet still injected street heroin on at least half of days, to supervised injectable heroin, supervised injectable methadone, or continued optimised oral methadone, for 26 weeks in supervised injecting clinics. On the primary outcome — at least half of weekly urine specimens negative for street heroin during weeks 14–26 — injectable heroin produced 72% responders versus 27% on oral methadone (odds ratio 7.42, 95% CI 2.69 to 20.46; p<0.0001; number needed to treat about 2.2), with the difference evident within six weeks. Injectable methadone sat between (39%) and was not significantly different from oral methadone (odds ratio 1.74, 0.66 to 4.60). A single, necessarily open-label trial with an objective urine endpoint and a very large effect in a narrowly defined, treatment-refractory population: PROPOSED POSSIBLE, held below LIKELY by the single-trial, single-country-programme base. (The neighbouring Canadian SALOME question is homed on Shelf #781 and is not duplicated here.)

cards.headline: RIOTT: supervised injectable heroin — 72% responders versus 27% on optimised oral methadone (odds ratio 7.42, p<0.0001)
cards.summary: RIOTT: supervised injectable heroin — 72% responders versus 27% on optimised oral methadone (odds ratio 7.42, p<0.0001)
cards.people: 127 chronic heroin addicts in England who had received conventional oral treatment for at least six months but continued to inject street heroin regularly (on ≥50% of days in the preceding three months), randomised by minimisation to supervised injectable methadone (n=42), supervised injectable heroin (n=43), or optimised oral methadone (n=42), treated for 26 weeks in three supervised injecting clinics. The primary outcome was 50% or more of weekly urinalysis specimens negative for street heroin during weeks 14–26, analysed intention-to-treat.
cards.result: Patients on injectable heroin were significantly more likely to achieve the primary outcome (72%, n=31) than those on oral methadone (27%, n=11): odds ratio 7.42 (95% CI 2.69 to 20.46; p<0.0001), with a number needed to treat of 2.17 (95% CI 1.60 to 3.97); adjusted figures were 66% versus 19% (odds ratio 8.17, 2.88 to 23.16). Injectable methadone (39%, n=16) was not significantly different from oral methadone (odds ratio 1.74, 95% CI 0.66 to 4.60; p=0.264) but was significantly worse than injectable heroin (odds ratio 4.26, 1.63 to 11.14; p=0.003), a comparison the study was not powered for. Retention at 26 weeks was 88% on injectable heroin, 81% on injectable methadone and 69% on oral methadone, and differences were evident within the first six weeks.
cards.watchOut: Open-label by necessity — patients and clinicians knew who was injecting pharmaceutical heroin — though the endpoint is laboratory urinalysis rather than self-report. The population is highly selected (persistent injectors despite optimised oral treatment), the setting is a supervised-clinic programme that few systems offer, and 127 patients in one country's programme is the entire randomised base for the UK model; harms and serious adverse events are not detailed in the record carded here.
cards.source: Strang J et al. Supervised injectable heroin or injectable methadone versus optimised oral methadone as treatment for chronic heroin addicts in England after persistent failure in orthodox treatment (RIOTT): a randomised trial. Lancet. 2010. PMID: 20511018. Registry ID: ISRCTN01338071, from the record. shelves.title: Cognitive and exposure therapies for problem gambling
shelves.question: In adults with problem gambling, do cognitive therapy or exposure therapy reduce gambling severity versus waitlist, and how do the two compare?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy · Female · Gambling · Humans · Implosive Therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: The anchor trial behind this shelf does not contain the waitlist comparison the question asks about: Smith and colleagues randomised 87 problem gamblers to cognitive therapy (44) or exposure therapy (43) with no untreated control arm, so the trial can compare the two therapies but cannot by itself show either beats nothing. Within that limit, gambling severity (Victorian Gambling Screen) improved in both groups, and the therapies were statistically indistinguishable — mean difference −0.18 points at 12 weeks (95% CI −4.48 to 4.11) and 1.47 points at six months (−4.46 to 7.39) — intervals too wide to declare equivalence either. Only 59% completed treatment, which is itself a finding about this field. The supporting CBT programmes of Petry and Ladouceur are literature context, not a second carded trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — both therapies improved symptoms in the only head-to-head randomised test, with efficacy against no treatment untested on this shelf.

cards.headline: Smith 2015: cognitive versus exposure therapy — both improved gambling symptoms; no difference between them, and no waitlist arm
cards.summary: Smith 2015: cognitive versus exposure therapy — both improved gambling symptoms; no difference between them, and no waitlist arm
cards.people: 87 adult problem gamblers at a South Australian gambling therapy service who started intervention, randomised to problem-gambling-specific cognitive therapy (n=44) or exposure (behavioural) therapy (n=43). The primary outcome was the participant-rated Victorian Gambling Screen at baseline, treatment end, and 1-, 3- and 6-month follow-up. Fifty-one participants (59%) completed the intervention (30 cognitive therapy, 21 exposure therapy).
cards.result: Both groups experienced comparable reductions (improvement) in Victorian Gambling Screen scores, with a mean between-group difference of −0.18 (95% CI −4.48 to 4.11) at 12 weeks and 1.47 (95% CI −4.46 to 7.39) at six-month follow-up. The authors concluded that cognitive and exposure therapies are both viable and effective treatments for problem gambling, and called for large-scale trials comparing them individually and combined, with better retention.
cards.watchOut: There is no waitlist or placebo arm in this record — the topic draft's 'versus waitlist' comparison does not exist in the trial, so improvement over time cannot be separated from regression to the mean, expectancy, or natural recovery on this card. The confidence intervals are wide enough to include a meaningful advantage for either therapy, so 'no difference found' is not 'proven equal'. Dropout of 41% overall, asymmetric between arms, further softens the result. The record shows no registry ID.
cards.source: Smith DP et al. Cognitive versus exposure therapy for problem gambling: Randomised controlled trial. Behav Res Ther. 2015. PMID: 25917008. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Mirtazapine for methamphetamine use disorder (Colfax)
shelves.question: In people who use methamphetamine, does mirtazapine reduce methamphetamine use versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic alpha-Antagonists · Adult · Amphetamine-Related Disorders · Central Nervous System Stimulants · Directive Counseling · Double-Blind Method · Drug Monitoring · Homosexuality, Male · Humans · Male · Medication Adherence · Methamphetamine · Mianserin · Middle Aged · Mirtazapine · Risk Factors · Sexual Behavior · Sexual Partners · Treatment Outcome · Urine Specimen Collection
shelves.balance: Two double-blind placebo-controlled trials from the same San Francisco programme, a decade apart and in overlapping populations, both found mirtazapine 30 mg daily reduced methamphetamine-positive urine tests when added to counselling. Colfax 2011 (60 methamphetamine-dependent, sexually active men who have sex with men, 12 weeks): relative risk of a positive urine test 0.57 (95% CI 0.35 to 0.93; P=.02), with positivity falling from 73% to 44% on mirtazapine versus 67% to 63% on placebo, and parallel reductions in sexual risk behaviour. Coffin 2020 (120 cisgender men and transgender women who have sex with men, 24 weeks of treatment plus 12 weeks follow-up): risk ratio 0.67 (0.51 to 0.87) at week 12, 0.75 (0.56 to 1.00) at week 24 and 0.73 (0.57 to 0.96) at week 36, despite medication adherence under 40%. One caution: both trials come from a single programme and a specific population. PROPOSED LIKELY.

cards.headline: Colfax 2011: mirtazapine cut methamphetamine-positive urines (relative risk 0.57, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.93) in 60 men who have sex with men
cards.summary: Colfax 2011: mirtazapine cut methamphetamine-positive urines (relative risk 0.57, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.93) in 60 men who have sex with men
cards.people: 60 actively using, methamphetamine-dependent, sexually active men who have sex with men in San Francisco, randomised to daily oral mirtazapine 30 mg or placebo for 12 weeks; both arms received weekly 30-minute substance use counselling and weekly urine collection. The primary outcome was reduction in methamphetamine-positive urine test results; 93% completed the final visit and 85% of follow-up visits were completed.
cards.result: In the primary intention-to-treat analysis, the mirtazapine group had fewer methamphetamine-positive urine tests than placebo (relative risk 0.57, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.93; P=.02): positivity fell from 73% (22/30) to 44% (12/27) on mirtazapine versus 67% (20/30) to 63% (17/27) on placebo, a number needed to treat of 3.1 for a negative weekly urine test. Most sexual risk behaviours decreased significantly more on mirtazapine (for example, episodes of unprotected anal sex with serodiscordant partners, P=.003). There were no serious adverse events related to study drug and no significant difference in adverse events by arm; adherence was 48.5% by medication event monitoring and 74.7% by self-report.
cards.watchOut: Sixty participants, one city, one specific population (sexually active MSM), and adherence measured electronically was under half — the effect emerged despite, not because of, perfect dosing. A phase 2 result; the replication card below is what raises the stamp.
cards.source: Colfax GN et al. Mirtazapine to reduce methamphetamine use: a randomized controlled trial. Arch Gen Psychiatry. 2011. PMID: 22065532. Registry ID: NCT00497081, from the record. cards.headline: Coffin 2020: the replication held — positive urines lower at 12, 24 and 36 weeks (risk ratios 0.67, 0.75, 0.73)
cards.summary: Coffin 2020: the replication held — positive urines lower at 12, 24 and 36 weeks (risk ratios 0.67, 0.75, 0.73)
cards.people: 120 community-recruited adults in San Francisco (115 cisgender men and 5 transgender women) who had sex with men, had methamphetamine use disorder and were actively using, randomised to mirtazapine 30 mg daily or matched placebo for 24 weeks with background counselling, plus 12 weeks of follow-up. Primary outcomes were positive urine test results for methamphetamine over 12, 24 and 36 weeks; mean visit completion was 66%.
cards.result: By week 12, methamphetamine-positive urine results had declined significantly more on mirtazapine than placebo (risk ratio 0.67, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.87), with reductions persisting at 24 weeks (risk ratio 0.75, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.00) and at 36 weeks, after treatment ended (0.73, 0.57 to 0.96). At week 24 the mirtazapine group also reported fewer sexual partners and fewer episodes of condomless anal sex with serodiscordant partners, plus net reductions in depressive symptoms and insomnia severity. Medication adherence by electronic dispenser was low (38.5% mirtazapine versus 39.5% placebo over weeks 2–12) and did not differ by arm; there were no serious adverse events associated with the study drug.
cards.watchOut: The week-24 confidence interval touches 1.00, and adherence was poor in both arms — intention-to-treat effects are therefore diluted estimates of the pharmacological effect, in both directions of interpretation. The population remained men and transgender women who have sex with men; efficacy in women who do not, or in people who inject, is not established by these trials.
cards.source: Coffin PO et al. Effects of Mirtazapine for Methamphetamine Use Disorder Among Cisgender Men and Transgender Women Who Have Sex With Men: A Placebo-Controlled Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Psychiatry. 2020. PMID: 31825466. Registry ID: NCT01888835, from the record. shelves.title: Bupropion plus naltrexone for methamphetamine use disorder (ADAPT-2)
shelves.question: In adults with moderate or severe methamphetamine use disorder, does the combination of extended-release bupropion and injectable naltrexone increase treatment response versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Amphetamine-Related Disorders · Bupropion · Delayed-Action Preparations · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Injections · Male · Medication Adherence · Methamphetamine · Middle Aged · Naltrexone · Narcotic Antagonists · Young Adult
shelves.balance: ADAPT-2 was a multisite, double-blind trial using a two-stage sequential parallel comparison design (403 participants in stage 1, 225 re-randomised in stage 2) of extended-release injectable naltrexone 380 mg every three weeks plus oral extended-release bupropion 450 mg/day. Response — at least three of four urine samples methamphetamine-negative at the end of a stage — was higher on the combination in both stages (16.5% versus 3.4%; 11.4% versus 1.8%), giving a weighted average response of 13.6% versus 2.5% on placebo, a treatment effect of 11.1 percentage points (P<0.001). Statistically robust, but the absolute terms matter: even on active treatment, about six of seven participants did not meet the response definition over 12 weeks. One trial, a demanding two-drug regimen, serious adverse events in 3.6% of the combination group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: ADAPT-2: response 13.6% on bupropion–naltrexone versus 2.5% on placebo (treatment effect 11.1 percentage points, P<0.001)
cards.summary: ADAPT-2: response 13.6% on bupropion–naltrexone versus 2.5% on placebo (treatment effect 11.1 percentage points, P<0.001)
cards.type: Randomized trial (double-blind, placebo-controlled, two-stage sequential parallel comparison)
cards.people: Adults with moderate or severe methamphetamine use disorder at multiple US sites. In stage 1, 403 participants were randomised (in a 0.26:0.74 ratio favouring placebo, per the design) to extended-release injectable naltrexone (380 mg every three weeks) plus oral extended-release bupropion (450 mg/day) or matching placebos for six weeks; placebo non-responders (225 participants) were re-randomised in stage 2 for a further six weeks. Urine samples were collected twice weekly; response was defined as at least three methamphetamine-negative samples out of four at the end of a stage, and the primary result is the weighted average across stages.
cards.result: In stage 1, 18 of 109 participants (16.5%) on naltrexone–bupropion responded versus 10 of 294 (3.4%) on placebo; in stage 2, 13 of 114 (11.4%) versus 2 of 111 (1.8%). The weighted average response was 13.6% with naltrexone–bupropion and 2.5% with placebo — an overall treatment effect of 11.1 percentage points (Wald z-test statistic 4.53; P<0.001). Adverse events on the combination included gastrointestinal disorders, tremor, malaise, hyperhidrosis and anorexia; serious adverse events occurred in 8 of 223 participants (3.6%) who received the combination during the trial.
cards.watchOut: The relative benefit is large but the absolute response is low — 13.6% met a short-term urine-based response definition, and the trial says nothing about sustained abstinence, retention beyond 12 weeks, or function. The sequential parallel comparison design's weighted estimate is less intuitive than a simple parallel-group difference and depends on the design's assumptions; a conventional replication does not exist on this card.
cards.source: Trivedi MH et al. Bupropion and Naltrexone in Methamphetamine Use Disorder. N Engl J Med. 2021. PMID: 33497547. Registry ID: NCT03078075, from the record. shelves.title: Buprenorphine–naloxone: brief taper versus extended maintenance in prescription opioid dependence (POATS)
shelves.question: In people dependent on prescription opioids, does extended buprenorphine–naloxone maintenance outperform a brief taper — and does adjunctive drug counselling add benefit?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Buprenorphine · Combined Modality Therapy · Counseling · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Interview, Psychological · Male · Naloxone · Narcotic Antagonists · Opiate Substitution Treatment · Opioid-Related Disorders · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: One large two-phase randomised trial (POATS, 653 outpatients dependent on prescription opioids, 10 US sites). Brief treatment failed almost everyone: after a 2-week stabilisation and 2-week taper, only 6.6% had a successful outcome. Patients who did not succeed entered extended treatment, and while taking buprenorphine–naloxone for 12 weeks 49.2% had successful outcomes — but 8 weeks after that taper ended, success had fallen back to 8.6%. The drug works while it is taken; stopping it, even after 12 weeks, returns most patients to opioid use. Adjunctive opioid-dependence counselling added nothing to standard medical management in either phase. PROPOSED LIKELY — a single trial, but large, multisite, and internally decisive: the contrast between on-treatment and post-taper outcomes is the finding, and it is stark. No mortality claim is made.

cards.headline: POATS phase 1: a brief buprenorphine–naloxone taper succeeded in only 6.6% of prescription-opioid-dependent patients
cards.summary: POATS phase 1: a brief buprenorphine–naloxone taper succeeded in only 6.6% of prescription-opioid-dependent patients
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (phase 1 of a 2-phase adaptive design)
cards.people: 653 treatment-seeking outpatients dependent on prescription opioids at 10 US sites. Phase 1 was brief treatment: 2 weeks of buprenorphine–naloxone stabilisation, a 2-week taper, and 8 weeks of post-medication follow-up. In both phases patients were randomised to standard medical management (SMM) alone or SMM plus opioid-dependence counselling; all received buprenorphine–naloxone. A successful outcome was a predefined composite of minimal or no opioid use on urine-confirmed self-report.
cards.result: Only 43 of 653 patients (6.6%) achieved a successful outcome in phase 1, with no difference between SMM and SMM plus counselling. In secondary analyses, chronic pain did not affect opioid-use outcomes; a history of ever using heroin was associated with lower success in phase 2 while on treatment.
cards.watchOut: Phase 1 was deliberately brief — the trial was designed to test whether short treatment could work in this population, and it could not. The 6.6% figure should not be quoted as the success rate of buprenorphine treatment generally; it is the success rate of a 4-week exposure followed by taper and follow-up.
cards.source: Weiss RD et al. Adjunctive counseling during brief and extended buprenorphine-naloxone treatment for prescription opioid dependence: a 2-phase randomized controlled trial. cards.people: The 360 patients whose phase 1 outcome was unsuccessful entered phase 2: 12 weeks of extended buprenorphine–naloxone treatment, a 4-week taper, and 8 weeks of post-medication follow-up, again randomised to SMM with or without added counselling.
cards.result: At week 12 of extended treatment, 49.2% (177 of 360) had successful outcomes, with no difference between counselling conditions. shelves.title: Agitation in Alzheimer's disease: citalopram reduced agitation (CitAD) but escitalopram failed its trial (S-CitAD)
shelves.question: In people with Alzheimer's disease and clinically significant agitation, does a citalopram-class SSRI reduce agitation compared with placebo, and at what cost in QT prolongation and cognition?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Alzheimer Disease · Arrhythmias, Cardiac · Caregivers · Citalopram · Cognition · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Psychomotor Agitation · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors · Severity of Illness Index · Stress, Psychological · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: This is the dementia slate's cleanest class-balance shelf: the same question asked twice, with two near-identical drugs, and answered two different ways. In CitAD (186 outpatients with probable Alzheimer's disease and clinically significant agitation, all receiving a psychosocial intervention), citalopram titrated to 30 mg/day beat placebo on both primary outcomes at 9 weeks — the agitation subscale difference was -0.93 points (95% CI -1.80 to -0.06), and 40% of citalopram patients versus 26% on placebo had moderate or marked global improvement. The costs were measured, not theoretical: MMSE scores fell an extra 1.05 points and the QT interval lengthened by 18.1 ms. The replication attempt then failed: in S-CitAD (173 patients who had not responded to a psychosocial intervention), escitalopram up to 15 mg/day did not significantly improve agitation at 12 weeks, and drug-related QT prolongation appeared again. So the class claim does not survive its own replication — what survives is a drug- and dose-specific signal for citalopram 30 mg, bought with cognitive and cardiac effects in exactly the population least able to afford either. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit for citalopram; escitalopram ineffective): citalopram probably reduces agitation modestly; escitalopram should not be substituted on a class assumption.

cards.headline: CitAD 2014: citalopram improved agitation on both primary outcomes at 9 weeks (global improvement 40% vs 26%), with MMSE -1.05 points and QT +18.1 ms
cards.summary: CitAD 2014: citalopram improved agitation on both primary outcomes at 9 weeks (global improvement 40% vs 26%), with MMSE -1.05 points and QT +18.1 ms
cards.people: 186 outpatients with probable Alzheimer's disease and clinically significant agitation at 8 US and Canadian academic centres; all received a psychosocial intervention and were randomised to citalopram (n=94) or placebo (n=92) for 9 weeks, citalopram titrated from 10 mg/day toward 30 mg/day over 3 weeks on response and tolerability.
cards.result: Citalopram beat placebo on both primary outcomes: NBRS-A treatment difference -0.93 (95% CI -1.80 to -0.06; P=.04), and moderate or marked improvement on the mADCS-CGIC in 40% vs 26% (odds ratio 2.13; 95% CI 1.23 to 3.69; P=.01) — a 14-percentage-point absolute gain. The CMAI, total NPI, and caregiver distress scores also favoured citalopram; the NPI agitation subscale, ADLs, and rescue lorazepam use did not. Harms: cognition worsened (-1.05 MMSE points; 95% CI -1.97 to -0.13; P=.03) and the QT interval prolonged (18.1 ms; 95% CI 6.1 to 30.1; P=.01).
cards.watchOut: The benefit was shown at 30 mg/day — above the dose regulators later capped in older adults because of QT prolongation — and the trial itself concludes the cognitive and cardiac effects may limit practical application at that dose. The NPI agitation subscale, arguably the most face-valid agitation measure, did not significantly improve.
cards.source: Porsteinsson AP et al.. Effect of citalopram on agitation in Alzheimer disease: the CitAD randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2014. PMID: 24549548. Registry ID: NCT00898807. cards.headline: S-CitAD 2025: escitalopram did not significantly improve agitation at 12 weeks; drug-related QT prolongation seen
cards.summary: S-CitAD 2025: escitalopram did not significantly improve agitation at 12 weeks; drug-related QT prolongation seen
cards.people: 173 adults with Alzheimer's dementia and significant agitation who had not responded to a psychosocial intervention, at 27 community-based centres; randomised to escitalopram (n=84; up to 15 mg/day) or placebo (n=89) for 12 weeks while the psychosocial intervention continued. The trial randomised fewer than its 392-patient target.
cards.result: Escitalopram was not effective: the proportion of participants with clinically significant improvement in agitation at 12 weeks did not differ significantly from placebo (the treatment made no difference), and drug-related QT interval prolongation was observed. The authors conclude that clinicians should be cautious in recommending escitalopram as an alternative to citalopram for this condition.
cards.watchOut: Under-enrolment (173 of a planned 392) limits precision, so this is a failed demonstration rather than proof of zero effect; but the burden of proof sits with the drug, and the QT signal replicated even when efficacy did not.

shelves.title: Agitation in Alzheimer's dementia: brexpiprazole 2 mg reduced agitation modestly across a four-trial programme
shelves.question: In people with Alzheimer's dementia and agitation, does brexpiprazole reduce agitation (CMAI total score) compared with placebo over 12 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aggression · Alzheimer Disease · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Quinolones · Thiophenes · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Brexpiprazole is the one antipsychotic with a regulatory approval for agitation in Alzheimer's dementia, and its programme is consistent in direction but modest in size. The confirmatory trial (345 patients) found a least-squares mean CMAI advantage of -5.32 points over placebo at 12 weeks for the pooled 2-3 mg doses (95% CI -8.77 to -1.87; P=.003; Cohen d 0.35). The two earlier trials were less tidy: in the first (433 randomised), only the 2 mg fixed dose separated from placebo (-3.77; P=.040) while 1 mg did nothing; in the second (270 randomised), flexible 0.5-2 mg dosing missed its primary endpoint (-2.34; P=.15), with benefit appearing only in a post-hoc maximum-dose subgroup. A Japanese phase 2/3 trial then confirmed both 1 mg (-3.7) and 2 mg (-7.2) over 10 weeks. Read together: a real but small effect at about 2 mg/day. The counterweight is class, not data from these trials: brexpiprazole is an atypical antipsychotic, and the class carries a boxed warning for increased mortality in older adults with dementia-related psychosis, which any prescribing decision has to weigh against a five-point CMAI gain. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: brexpiprazole probably reduces agitation modestly at 2 mg/day; the effect size, not the p-value, is the story.

cards.headline: Brexpiprazole 2023 (confirmatory trial): CMAI improved -22.6 vs -17.3 on placebo at 12 weeks (difference -5.32; P=.003; effect size 0.35)
cards.summary: Brexpiprazole 2023 (confirmatory trial): CMAI improved -22.6 vs -17.3 on placebo at 12 weeks (difference -5.32; P=.003; effect size 0.35)
cards.people: 345 patients with agitation in Alzheimer's dementia (care facility or community settings) at 123 European and US sites; randomised 2:1 to brexpiprazole (fixed 2 mg/day or 3 mg/day) or placebo for 12 weeks; stable Alzheimer's disease medications permitted.
cards.result: Change in CMAI total score from baseline to week 12: -22.6 on brexpiprazole (baseline 80.6) vs -17.3 on placebo (baseline 79.2); least-squares mean difference -5.32 (95% CI -8.77 to -1.87; P=.003; Cohen d 0.35). No treatment-emergent adverse event reached 5% incidence with an incidence greater than placebo; discontinuation because of adverse events was 5.3% on brexpiprazole vs 4.3% on placebo.
cards.watchOut: The primary analysis pools the 2 mg and 3 mg doses; the record does not show that 3 mg adds anything over 2 mg, and the pooled effect (d 0.35) is small against a CMAI range of 29-203.

cards.headline: Brexpiprazole 2020 (two earlier trials): 2 mg fixed dose positive (-3.77; P=.040); the flexible-dose trial missed its primary endpoint (P=.15)
cards.summary: Brexpiprazole 2020 (two earlier trials): 2 mg fixed dose positive (-3.77; P=.040); the flexible-dose trial missed its primary endpoint (P=.15)
cards.type: Two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials (fixed-dose and flexible-dose)
cards.people: Two 12-week randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials in agitation in Alzheimer's dementia: Study 1, 433 randomised (fixed dose: brexpiprazole 2 mg/day, 1 mg/day, or placebo); Study 2, 270 randomised (flexible-dose brexpiprazole 0.5-2 mg/day or placebo).
cards.result: Study 1: brexpiprazole 2 mg/day beat placebo on CMAI change (adjusted mean difference -3.77; 95% confidence limits -7.38 to -0.17; P=.040); 1 mg/day did not (0.23; P=.90). Study 2: flexible dosing did not reach statistical superiority (-2.34; 95% confidence limits -5.49 to 0.82; P=.15); a post-hoc analysis of patients titrated to the 2 mg/day maximum did separate (-5.06; P=.012). Adverse events at 5% or more included headache, insomnia, dizziness, somnolence, and urinary tract infection, mostly mild or moderate.
cards.watchOut: One of the programme's two original trials was negative on its primary analysis; the positive post-hoc subgroup is supportive, not confirmatory. The efficacy signal clusters at the 2 mg dose.

shelves.title: Agitation in Alzheimer's disease: dextromethorphan-quinidine reduced agitation in a single phase 2 trial
shelves.question: In people with Alzheimer's disease and agitation, does dextromethorphan-quinidine reduce agitation (CMAI / NPI agitation) compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Aggression · Alzheimer Disease · Dextromethorphan · Double-Blind Method · Drug Combinations · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Placebos · Psychomotor Agitation · Quinidine · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Dextromethorphan-quinidine — the combination marketed for pseudobulbar affect — was tested for Alzheimer agitation in a single phase 2 trial using a sequential parallel comparison design, an enrichment design built to extract signal from small samples. Across its two consecutive 5-week stages the combination beat placebo on the NPI Agitation/Aggression domain (combined analysis P<.001); in stage 1, scores fell from 7.1 to 3.8 on drug versus 7.0 to 5.3 on placebo (least-squares mean difference -1.5; 95% CI -2.3 to -0.7; P<.001). Falls were more common on drug (8.6% vs 3.9%), as were serious adverse events (7.9% vs 4.7%); there was no signal for sedation, cognitive worsening, or clinically significant QTc prolongation over 10 weeks. The design caveat matters: stage 2 re-randomised only placebo non-responders, so the combined estimate is not a plain parallel-group estimate, and no confirmatory trial of this combination for this indication could be pinned at build time — the related dextromethorphan-bupropion programme is a different product and is not carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: a promising, unreplicated result — enough to justify the confirmatory trial, not enough to treat the benefit as established.

cards.headline: Dextromethorphan-quinidine 2015: NPI Agitation/Aggression fell 7.1 to 3.8 vs 7.0 to 5.3 on placebo in stage 1 (difference -1.5; P<.001); falls 8.6% vs 3.9%
cards.summary: Dextromethorphan-quinidine 2015: NPI Agitation/Aggression fell 7.1 to 3.8 vs 7.0 to 5.3 on placebo in stage 1 (difference -1.5; P<.001); falls 8.6% vs 3.9%
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial with sequential parallel comparison design
cards.people: 220 patients with probable Alzheimer disease and clinically significant agitation (MMSE 8-28) at 42 US sites; stable antidepressant, antipsychotic, hypnotic, and antidementia medications allowed. Stage 1: randomised 3:4 to dextromethorphan-quinidine 20/10 mg (n=93) or placebo (n=127) for 5 weeks. Stage 2: drug patients continued; placebo patients were stratified by response and re-randomised 1:1. 194 patients (88.2%) completed the study.
cards.result: The combined stage 1 + stage 2 analysis showed significantly reduced NPI Agitation/Aggression scores for dextromethorphan-quinidine vs placebo (P<.001). Stage 1 between-group difference: -1.5 (95% CI -2.3 to -0.7; P<.001). Stage 2 difference: -1.6 (95% CI -2.9 to -0.3; P=.02). Adverse events: falls 8.6% vs 3.9%, diarrhoea 5.9% vs 3.1%, urinary tract infection 5.3% vs 3.9%; serious adverse events 7.9% vs 4.7%. No association with cognitive impairment, sedation, or clinically significant QTc prolongation.
cards.watchOut: The sequential parallel comparison design re-randomises placebo non-responders in stage 2, enriching the sample for a drug signal; effect estimates from this design do not read like ordinary parallel-group trials, and the fall excess (8.6% vs 3.9%) is the harm to watch in a frail population.

shelves.title: Agitation in dementia: mirtazapine did not reduce agitation (SYMBAD) — and more patients died on it
shelves.question: In people with dementia and agitation, does mirtazapine reduce agitation compared with placebo — and is it safe in this population?
shelves.mesh: Aged, 80 and over · Anti-Anxiety Agents · Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale · Caregivers · Dementia · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Mirtazapine · Psychomotor Agitation · Quality of Life · United Kingdom
shelves.balance: SYMBAD asked whether mirtazapine — widely prescribed for agitation in dementia precisely because it is perceived as the safer alternative to antipsychotics — actually works. In 204 people with probable or possible Alzheimer's disease and agitation unresponsive to non-drug treatment (CMAI score 45 or more) at 26 UK centres, mirtazapine titrated to 45 mg made no difference to agitation at 12 weeks: adjusted mean difference -1.74 CMAI points (95% CI -7.17 to 3.69; P=.53). Adverse events were as common on mirtazapine as on placebo (66% vs 64%). The balance line, though, is mortality: by week 16, 7 patients in the mirtazapine group had died versus 1 in the control group — a post-hoc difference of marginal statistical significance (P=.065) in a trial not powered for mortality. That is a possible harm signal, not a demonstrated one; but a drug with no shown benefit does not need a proven harm to fail its risk-benefit test, and the trial's own conclusion is that the data do not support mirtazapine for agitation in dementia. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (no difference; possible harm): mirtazapine probably does not reduce agitation in dementia, and SYMBAD's mortality imbalance is a standing reason for caution. Tier C: the shelf carries a mortality imbalance in its balance.

cards.headline: SYMBAD 2021: CMAI at 12 weeks no different on mirtazapine vs placebo (difference -1.74; P=.53); deaths by week 16 were 7 vs 1
cards.summary: SYMBAD 2021: CMAI at 12 weeks no different on mirtazapine vs placebo (difference -1.74; P=.53); deaths by week 16 were 7 vs 1
cards.people: 204 participants with probable or possible Alzheimer's disease, agitation unresponsive to non-drug treatment, and CMAI score of 45 or more, at 26 UK centres; randomised 1:1 to mirtazapine (titrated to 45 mg) or placebo; primary outcome was reduction in CMAI score at 12 weeks.
cards.result: Mean CMAI scores at 12 weeks were not significantly different between mirtazapine and placebo (adjusted mean difference -1.74; 95% CI -7.17 to 3.69; P=.53) — the treatment made no difference to agitation. Adverse events occurred in 67 of 102 mirtazapine participants (66%) and 65 of 102 controls (64%). More deaths occurred in the mirtazapine group by week 16 (7 vs 1), with post-hoc analysis suggesting marginal statistical significance (P=.065).
cards.watchOut: The mortality comparison is post-hoc and the trial was not powered for it; quote the 7 vs 1 with its P=.065 attached, as a signal — never as a proven increase in deaths. The efficacy confidence interval also cannot exclude a small benefit, which is why the stamp is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY.
cards.source: Banerjee S et al.. Study of mirtazapine for agitated behaviours in dementia (SYMBAD): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet. 2021. PMID: 34688369. shelves.title: Depression in dementia: neither sertraline nor mirtazapine beat placebo (HTA-SADD)
shelves.question: In people with dementia and depression, do sertraline or mirtazapine improve depressive symptoms compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Alzheimer Disease · Antidepressive Agents · Dementia · Depressive Disorder · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Mental Disorders · Mianserin · Mirtazapine · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Sertraline
shelves.balance: HTA-SADD is the definitive pragmatic test of the two antidepressants most commonly prescribed for depression in dementia. In 326 people with probable or possible Alzheimer's disease and depression (Cornell Scale score 8 or more), neither sertraline (target 150 mg/day) nor mirtazapine (45 mg/day) reduced depression scores versus placebo at 13 weeks — mean differences of 1.17 (95% CI -0.23 to 2.58; P=.10) and 0.01 (95% CI -1.37 to 1.38; P=.99) respectively — and the null persisted unchanged to 39 weeks. What the drugs did add was adverse reactions: 43% of sertraline and 41% of mirtazapine participants versus 26% on placebo, with more severe serious adverse events on drug. Deaths were equal — 5 patients in every group by week 39 — so this is not a mortality shelf; it is a clean efficacy null with a tolerability cost, in the exact population and care setting where these drugs are prescribed first-line. The authors' conclusion, that the present practice of using these antidepressants first-line for depression in Alzheimer's disease should be reconsidered, is the one the data support. PROPOSED LIKELY (no difference): sertraline and mirtazapine do not improve depression in dementia beyond placebo with usual care.

cards.headline: HTA-SADD 2011: Cornell depression scores at 13 weeks no different for sertraline (difference 1.17; P=.10) or mirtazapine (0.01; P=.99) vs placebo; adverse reactions 43% and 41% vs 26%
cards.summary: HTA-SADD 2011: Cornell depression scores at 13 weeks no different for sertraline (difference 1.17; P=.10) or mirtazapine (0.01; P=.99) vs placebo; adverse reactions 43% and 41% vs 26%
cards.people: 326 participants from old-age psychiatry services in nine centres in England, with probable or possible Alzheimer's disease, depression lasting at least 4 weeks, and a Cornell Scale for Depression in Dementia score of 8 or more; randomised 1:1:1 to sertraline (target 150 mg/day; n=107), mirtazapine (45 mg/day; n=108), or placebo (n=111), all with standard care; outcomes assessed to 39 weeks.
cards.result: Decreases in depression scores at 13 weeks did not differ between placebo and sertraline (mean difference 1.17; 95% CI -0.23 to 2.58; P=.10) or mirtazapine (0.01; 95% CI -1.37 to 1.38; P=.99) — the treatment made no difference — and the findings persisted to 39 weeks. Fewer controls had adverse reactions (26%) than sertraline (43%; P=.010) or mirtazapine (41%; P=.031) participants, and severe serious adverse events were fewer on placebo (P=.003). Five patients in every group died by week 39.
cards.watchOut: Participants were recruited from specialist old-age psychiatry services and all received standard care, so the null is a statement about adding these drugs to good usual care, not about untreated depression. Mirtazapine for agitation — a different question — is Shelf #2342 (SYMBAD), where the same drug also failed.

shelves.title: Dementia: 7-week cognitive stimulation therapy improved cognition (Spector 2003); weekly maintenance did not improve cognition further (Orrell 2014)
shelves.question: In people with mild-to-moderate dementia, does group cognitive stimulation therapy improve cognition and quality of life compared with usual care — and do maintenance sessions sustain any gain?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Cholinesterase Inhibitors · Cognition · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy · Communication · Dementia · Evidence-Based Medicine · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Quality of Life · Sex Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Cognitive stimulation therapy is the dementia shelf where the induction works and the top-up does not — on cognition, at least. In Spector's single-blind multicentre trial, 201 people with dementia randomised to twice-weekly group CST for 7 weeks improved significantly more than usual-care controls on the MMSE (P=.044), on ADAS-Cog (P=.014), and on quality of life (P=.028); the number needed to treat for an improvement of 4 or more ADAS-Cog points was 6 — a showing the authors noted compares favourably with trials of drugs for dementia. A decade later, Orrell's maintenance trial first gave all 236 participants that same 7-week programme, then randomised them to weekly maintenance CST for 24 weeks or usual care: the primary cognition outcome did not significantly improve, although self-rated quality of life at 6 months (P=.03), proxy-rated quality of life and activities of daily living at 3 months, and — in the subgroup taking cholinesterase inhibitors — MMSE scores did. PROPOSED SPLIT: POSSIBLE (benefit) for the standard 7-week CST course on cognition and quality of life; POSSIBLE (no difference) for weekly maintenance on cognition, with the quality-of-life gains the maintenance trial did show carried on the face.

cards.headline: CST 2003 (Spector): twice-weekly group CST for 7 weeks improved MMSE (P=.044), ADAS-Cog (P=.014), and quality of life (P=.028); number needed to treat 6
cards.summary: CST 2003 (Spector): twice-weekly group CST for 7 weeks improved MMSE (P=.044), ADAS-Cog (P=.014), and quality of life (P=.028); number needed to treat 6
cards.people: 201 older people with dementia in a single-blind multicentre randomised trial; 115 randomised within centres to the CST intervention group and 86 to the control (usual care) group. CST was an evidence-based group programme of themed sessions, twice weekly for 7 weeks.
cards.result: At follow-up the intervention group had significantly improved relative to controls on the Mini-Mental State Examination (P=0.044), the Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale–Cognition (P=0.014), and Quality of Life–Alzheimer's Disease scales (P=0.028), by intention-to-treat analysis of covariance. Using a criterion of 4 or more points of improvement on ADAS-Cog, the number needed to treat was 6.
cards.watchOut: The record reports p-values and the number needed to treat but no effect sizes or confidence intervals, and outcome assessment was single-blind; the stamp grades accordingly. This 2003 trial predates trial registration and its record carries no registry identifier.

cards.headline: Maintenance CST 2014 (Orrell): weekly maintenance after standard CST did not significantly improve the primary cognition outcome; quality of life improved
cards.summary: Maintenance CST 2014 (Orrell): weekly maintenance after standard CST did not significantly improve the primary cognition outcome; quality of life improved
cards.type: Single-blind, multicentre, pragmatic randomised controlled trial
cards.people: 236 people with dementia from 9 care homes and 9 community services; all received the standard 7-week, 14-session CST programme before randomisation, then weekly maintenance CST groups for 24 weeks or usual care. Primary outcomes were cognition and quality of life at 6 months.
cards.result: At the 6-month primary end-point there was a significant benefit for self-rated quality of life (QoL-AD; P=0.03) but no significant improvement in the primary cognition outcome (the treatment made no difference to cognition overall). At 3 months, proxy-rated quality of life (QoL-AD P=0.01; DEMQOL P=0.03) and activities of daily living (P=0.04) improved; the subgroup taking acetylcholinesterase inhibitors showed cognitive (MMSE) benefits at 3 and 6 months (P=0.03).
cards.watchOut: The cognition-positive finding is a subgroup (participants on cholinesterase inhibitors), not the primary analysis; quality-of-life end-points were positive at several time-points and should not be inflated into a cognition claim.
cards.source: Orrell M et al.. Maintenance cognitive stimulation therapy for dementia: single-blind, multicentre, pragmatic randomised controlled trial. Br J Psychiatry. 2014. PMID: 24676963. shelves.title: Alzheimer's disease: vitamin E slowed functional decline but memantine did not (TEAM-AD)
shelves.question: In people with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease already on a cholinesterase inhibitor, do high-dose vitamin E, memantine, or their combination slow functional decline compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Alzheimer Disease · Antioxidants · Caregivers · Cholinesterase Inhibitors · Disease Progression · Dopamine Agents · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Male · Memantine · Middle Aged · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome · Vitamin E
shelves.balance: TEAM-AD, the VA cooperative study, randomised 613 patients with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease — all already taking a cholinesterase inhibitor — to vitamin E (alpha tocopherol) 2000 IU/day, memantine 20 mg/day, both, or placebo, and followed them for a mean of 2.27 years. Vitamin E slowed functional decline: ADCS-ADL scores fell 3.15 units less than on placebo (95% CI 0.92 to 5.39; adjusted P=.03), which the investigators translate as a delay in clinical progression of about 19% per year relative to placebo, roughly 6.2 months over the follow-up period, with the least increase in caregiver time. Memantine did not significantly slow decline (1.98 units less; 95% CI -0.24 to 4.20; adjusted P=.40) — the treatment made no difference — and neither did the combination, so adding memantine appeared to erase the vitamin E advantage, though the trial cannot say why. Serious adverse events classed as infections or infestations were more frequent in the memantine (31 events) and combination (44 events) groups than on placebo (13 events). The population was drawn from Veterans Affairs medical centres and was predominantly male, which bounds generalisation. PROPOSED SPLIT: POSSIBLE (benefit) for high-dose vitamin E on functional decline; LIKELY (no difference) for memantine in cholinesterase-inhibitor-treated mild-to-moderate disease.

cards.headline: TEAM-AD 2014: vitamin E slowed ADCS-ADL decline by 3.15 units vs placebo (adjusted P=.03); memantine (1.98 units; P=.40) and the combination did not
cards.summary: TEAM-AD 2014: vitamin E slowed ADCS-ADL decline by 3.15 units vs placebo (adjusted P=.03); memantine (1.98 units; P=.40) and the combination did not
cards.type: Double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group randomised trial (TEAM-AD VA Cooperative Study)
cards.people: 613 patients with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease taking an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, at 14 Veterans Affairs medical centres; randomised to alpha tocopherol 2000 IU/day (n=152), memantine 20 mg/day (n=155), the combination (n=154), or placebo (n=152), with a mean follow-up of 2.27 years. The primary outcome was the ADCS-ADL Inventory score (range 0-78); 561 participants contributed follow-up data.
cards.result: ADCS-ADL decline was 3.15 units less in the alpha tocopherol group than placebo (95% CI 0.92 to 5.39; adjusted P=.03) — a delay in clinical progression of 19% per year relative to placebo, or about 6.2 months over the follow-up. The memantine group declined 1.98 units less than placebo (95% CI -0.24 to 4.20; adjusted P=.40), not significant; the combination also showed no significant benefit. Caregiver time increased least in the alpha tocopherol group. Serious adverse events of infections or infestations were more frequent with memantine (31 events in 23 participants) and the combination (44 events in 31) than placebo (13 events in 11).
cards.watchOut: A single trial in a predominantly male veteran population; earlier vitamin E evidence in more severe Alzheimer's disease and in MCI (Shelf #2346, where vitamin E was null for progression) answers different questions. The combination arm's null result beside vitamin E alone is unexplained and should not be over-read as proven antagonism.

shelves.title: Amnestic mild cognitive impairment: donepezil and vitamin E did not delay progression to Alzheimer's disease over 3 years (Petersen 2005)
shelves.question: In amnestic mild cognitive impairment, do donepezil or vitamin E delay progression to Alzheimer's disease over three years compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Alzheimer Disease · Apolipoprotein E4 · Apolipoproteins E · Cholinesterase Inhibitors · Cognition Disorders · Disease Progression · Donepezil · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Indans · Nootropic Agents · Piperidines · Proportional Hazards Models · Treatment Failure · Vitamin E
shelves.balance: The Alzheimer's Disease Cooperative Study trial randomised 769 people with amnestic mild cognitive impairment to donepezil 10 mg/day, vitamin E 2000 IU/day, or placebo for three years, with progression to possible or probable Alzheimer's disease as the primary outcome (overall progression rate about 16% per year; 212 progressions). At three years, neither drug delayed progression: hazard ratio 0.80 for donepezil (95% CI 0.57 to 1.13; P=.42) and 1.02 for vitamin E (95% CI 0.74 to 1.41; P=.91) — the treatment made no difference to the primary outcome. Two honest qualifications belong on the face: prespecified 6-month-interval analyses showed donepezil lowered the likelihood of progression during the first 12 months (P=.04), supported by secondary outcomes, and among carriers of one or more APOE epsilon4 alleles the donepezil benefit was evident throughout the three years — subgroup findings that generated hypotheses no dedicated trial has since confirmed. Vitamin E showed no benefit at any point, in any subgroup. The other cholinesterase-inhibitor programmes in MCI (rivastigmine, galantamine) were likewise null for progression, so this shelf is the class answer for MCI — distinct from cholinesterase inhibitors' symptomatic use in established dementia. PROPOSED LIKELY (no difference): for the question asked — delaying progression over three years — neither donepezil nor vitamin E works.

cards.headline: Petersen 2005: progression to Alzheimer's disease at 3 years — donepezil HR 0.80 (P=.42), vitamin E HR 1.02 (P=.91); both null
cards.summary: Petersen 2005: progression to Alzheimer's disease at 3 years — donepezil HR 0.80 (P=.42), vitamin E HR 1.02 (P=.91); both null
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Alzheimer's Disease Cooperative Study)
cards.people: 769 subjects with the amnestic subtype of mild cognitive impairment in a double-blind trial; randomised to vitamin E 2000 IU daily, donepezil 10 mg daily, or placebo for three years. The primary outcome was clinically possible or probable Alzheimer's disease; 212 subjects progressed (about 16% per year).
cards.result: There were no significant differences in the probability of progression to Alzheimer's disease for vitamin E (hazard ratio 1.02; 95% CI 0.74 to 1.41; P=0.91) or donepezil (hazard ratio 0.80; 95% CI 0.57 to 1.13; P=0.42) versus placebo over three years. Prespecified interval analyses showed donepezil reduced the likelihood of progression during the first 12 months (P=0.04), and among APOE epsilon4 carriers the donepezil benefit was evident throughout the three-year follow-up; vitamin E showed no benefit at any point in any subgroup.
cards.watchOut: The 12-month and APOE epsilon4 findings are time-window and subgroup analyses around a null primary endpoint; they are hypothesis-generating, not a basis for prescribing donepezil in MCI. The record carries no registry identifier.

shelves.title: Apathy in Alzheimer's disease: methylphenidate reduced apathy scores over 6 months (ADMET 2)
shelves.question: In people with Alzheimer's disease and apathy, does methylphenidate reduce apathy compared with placebo over six months?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Alzheimer Disease · Apathy · Central Nervous System Stimulants · Female · Humans · Male · Methylphenidate
shelves.balance: ADMET 2 randomised 200 people with Alzheimer's disease, mild-to-moderate cognitive impairment, and frequent or severe apathy to methylphenidate 10 mg twice daily or placebo for 6 months, with two coprimary outcomes. The symptom outcome was met: NPI apathy scores fell 1.25 points more on methylphenidate than placebo (95% CI -2.03 to -0.47; P=.002), the largest separation arriving in the first 100 days, and the hazard ratio for reaching no apathy symptoms was 2.16 (95% CI 1.19 to 3.91; P=.01). The global-impression coprimary outcome was not significant (odds ratio 1.90 for an improved rating; 95% CI 0.95 to 3.84; P=.07). Cognition and quality of life did not differ significantly between groups; 17 serious adverse events occurred, none judged related to the study drug, and the overall safety profiles were similar. So: a real but modest score benefit from the one adequately sized trial, on a symptom scale whose global counterpart just missed significance — the earlier, smaller ADMET pilot programme points the same way but is not carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: methylphenidate probably reduces measured apathy in Alzheimer's disease; whether patients or caregivers feel a difference of this size is less certain.

The odds ratio for an improved global-impression rating was 1.90 (95% CI 0.95 to 3.84; P=.07), not significant. Cognitive measures and quality of life did not differ significantly. cards.watchOut: One of two coprimary outcomes was not met, and the effect (about 1.25 points on the NPI apathy subscale) is modest; a stimulant in an elderly dementia population also deserves longer safety follow-up than 6 months before the stamp could rise.

shelves.title: Amnestic mild cognitive impairment: aerobic exercise did not beat stretching-and-balance exercise on cognition (EXERT)
shelves.question: In sedentary older adults with amnestic MCI, does 18 months of moderate-to-high-intensity aerobic exercise preserve cognition compared with low-intensity stretching, balance and range-of-motion exercise?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Alzheimer Disease · Biomarkers · Cognition · Cognitive Dysfunction · Exercise · Exercise Therapy · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neuropsychological Tests · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: EXERT, the phase 3 trial of exercise in sedentary older adults with amnestic mild cognitive impairment, randomised 296 participants to moderate-to-high-intensity aerobic training or to low-intensity stretching, balance, and range-of-motion exercise — an active control, not a sedentary one — with the first 12 months supervised and adherence high (81% of aerobic sessions and 87% of stretching sessions attended). The primary cognitive outcome (a global composite built on ADAS-Cog-Exec) did not differ between intensities (p=0.3) — the treatment made no difference between the two exercise prescriptions. The arresting finding is what did not happen in either arm: cognition did not decline over 12 months, and mean hippocampal volume loss was low at 0.51% for both groups. That stability is exactly what this design cannot explain: with no non-exercise control group, it may reflect the stretching programme itself, the supervision and social contact both arms received, practice effects, or volunteer selection. The record carries no registry identifier. Exercise in established dementia is a different question, answered elsewhere in the library. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (no difference): aerobic intensity confers no shown cognitive advantage over low-intensity structured exercise in amnestic MCI; whether exercise itself preserves cognition is a question EXERT's design cannot answer.

cards.headline: EXERT 2025: cognitive trajectory at 12 months no different between aerobic training and stretching/balance control (p=0.3); neither group declined
cards.summary: EXERT 2025: cognitive trajectory at 12 months no different between aerobic training and stretching/balance control (p=0.3); neither group declined
cards.type: Phase 3, multicentre, randomised controlled trial with active (low-intensity exercise) control (EXERT)
cards.people: 296 sedentary older adults with amnestic mild cognitive impairment in a phase 3 multicentre randomised trial; randomised to moderate-high intensity aerobic training or low-intensity stretching/balance/range-of-motion exercise for 18 months (12 months supervised), with assessments every 6 months and a global cognitive composite (ADAS-Cog-Exec) as the primary outcome.
cards.result: Intervention effects on cognition did not differ between aerobic training and the stretching control (regression coefficient -0.078, SE 0.074; p=0.3). There was no 12-month cognitive decline in either group, and mean 12-month hippocampal volume loss for both groups was 0.51%. Supervised-session adherence was 81% (aerobic) and 87% (stretching).
cards.watchOut: There is no sedentary or usual-care arm, so the trial cannot support a claim that exercise itself preserves cognition — only that intensity did not matter between two structured programmes. The record carries no registry identifier, and a companion paper comparing EXERT participants with an external observational cohort is not a randomised comparison and is not carded.

shelves.title: Focal seizures: adjunctive perampanel reduced seizure frequency across three phase 3 trials (Studies 304, 305, 306)
shelves.question: In adults with refractory focal (partial-onset) seizures, does adjunctive perampanel increase responder rates and reduce seizure frequency compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Anticonvulsants · Child · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Epilepsies, Partial · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Nitriles · Pyridones · Seizures · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Perampanel's pivotal programme is three double-blind placebo-controlled trials in patients aged 12 and over with refractory partial-onset seizures on 1-3 antiseizure medicines, and the direction is consistent. Study 306 (706 patients) showed a dose-ordered median seizure-frequency change: -23.3% on 4 mg and -30.8% on 8 mg versus -10.7% on placebo (P=.0026 and P<.0001), with 50% responder rates of 28.5% and 34.9% versus 17.9% — absolute gains of about 11 and 17 points. Study 305 (386 patients) found responder rates of 33.3% (8 mg) and 33.9% (12 mg) versus 14.7% on placebo, both significant. Study 304 (388 patients) was positive on its median-frequency endpoint (-26.3% and -34.5% vs -21.0%) but its responder endpoint did not reach significance — the honest weak joint in the programme, carried on this shelf's face. The minimum effective dose is 4 mg/day (Study 306); dizziness is the dose-related price, with somnolence, irritability, headache, falls, and ataxia behind it. Absolute gains are moderate — roughly one additional responder per six to nine patients treated at effective doses. PROPOSED LIKELY: adjunctive perampanel at 4-12 mg/day reduces focal seizure frequency.

cards.headline: Study 304: median seizure-frequency change -26.3% (8 mg) and -34.5% (12 mg) vs -21.0% on placebo (significant); responder rates 37.6% and 36.1% vs 26.4% (not significant)

cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase III trial (Study 304)
cards.people: 388 patients aged 12 and over with drug-resistant partial-onset seizures despite 1-3 antiseizure medicines; randomised 1:1:1 to once-daily perampanel 8 mg, 12 mg, or placebo, with a 6-week titration and 13-week maintenance phase. Primary endpoint: percent change in seizure frequency; the 50% responder rate was the EU-registration primary endpoint.
cards.result: Median percent change in seizure frequency: -21.0% (placebo), -26.3% (8 mg; P=0.0261 vs placebo), -34.5% (12 mg; P=0.0158). Fifty percent responder rates during maintenance were 26.4%, 37.6%, and 36.1% respectively — not statistically significant for 8 mg (P=0.0760) or 12 mg (P=0.0914). Discontinuation was 17.5% overall, 10.3% for adverse events; the most frequent were dizziness, somnolence, irritability, headache, fall, and ataxia.
cards.watchOut: This trial's responder-rate endpoint — the figure clinicians most often quote — did not reach significance; the shelf's LIKELY stamp rests on the frequency endpoints here plus the two companion trials, not on Study 304 alone.

cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase III trial (Study 305)
cards.people: 386 patients aged 12 and over with uncontrolled partial-onset seizures despite at least two prior antiseizure medicines and currently receiving 1-3; randomised equally to once-daily perampanel 8 mg, 12 mg, or placebo over a 19-week double-blind phase (6-week titration, 13-week maintenance).
cards.result: Fifty percent responder rates: 14.7% (placebo), 33.3% (8 mg; P=0.002), 33.9% (12 mg; P<0.001) — absolute gains of about 19 points. Median percent change in seizure frequency per 28 days: -9.7%, -30.5% (P<0.001), -17.6% (P=0.011). Results for complex partial plus secondarily generalised seizures were consistent. The most frequent adverse events (10% or more in any group) were dizziness, somnolence, fatigue, and headache, with an apparent dose effect for all but headache.
cards.watchOut: The 12 mg dose did not outperform 8 mg on median frequency change (-17.6% vs -30.5%) — more perampanel is not more effect, while adverse events climb with dose.
