shelves.title: Focal seizures: adjunctive brivaracetam — significant only at 50 mg in one trial and at 100 mg in another that missed its primary testing strategy
shelves.question: In adults with uncontrolled focal seizures, does adjunctive brivaracetam reduce seizure frequency compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Anticonvulsants · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Epilepsies, Partial · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pyrrolidinones · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: A correction first, on the face: the drafting sketch for this shelf described the anchor trial as showing significant effects at 50 mg and 100 mg. The fetched records say otherwise, and this pack follows the records. In Biton 2014 (N01253; 400 patients; fixed doses of 5, 20, or 50 mg/day given without titration), only 50 mg/day beat placebo on the primary endpoint — a 12.8% reduction in partial-onset seizure frequency over placebo (P=.025) — with a 50% responder rate of 32.7% versus 16.7% (P=.008); the 5 mg and 20 mg doses did not separate at all (reductions over placebo of -0.9% and 4.1%). In Ryvlin 2014 (N01252; 399 patients; doses 20, 50, or 100 mg/day), the trial formally missed its primary endpoint, because its sequential testing strategy required significance at 50 mg first and 50 mg was not significant (6.5%; P=.261); the 100 mg dose was significant (11.7% over placebo; P=.037; responders 36.0% vs 20.0%; P=.023). So the programme supports a real but small effect at the top of the tested dose range, with the two trials disagreeing about which dose that is. Somnolence, dizziness, and fatigue were the common adverse events, mostly mild to moderate. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: brivaracetam probably reduces focal seizure frequency modestly at 50-100 mg/day; effects at 20 mg/day and below were not shown.

cards.headline: Biton 2014 (N01253): only 50 mg/day beat placebo — 12.8% frequency reduction over placebo (P=.025), responders 32.7% vs 16.7%; 5 mg and 20 mg null
cards.summary: Biton 2014 (N01253): only 50 mg/day beat placebo — 12.8% frequency reduction over placebo (P=.025), responders 32.7% vs 16.7%; 5 mg and 20 mg null
cards.type: Phase III randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, fixed-dose trial (N01253)
cards.people: 400 adults aged 16-70 with uncontrolled partial-onset seizures despite 1-2 antiseizure medicines and at least 8 seizures in the 8-week baseline; randomised 1:1:1:1 to twice-daily placebo or brivaracetam 5, 20, or 50 mg/day without titration for 12 weeks (396 in the intention-to-treat population). Primary endpoint: percent reduction over placebo in baseline-adjusted partial-onset seizure frequency per week.
cards.result: Percent reduction over placebo: -0.9% for 5 mg/day (P=0.885), 4.1% for 20 mg/day (P=0.492), and 12.8% for 50 mg/day (P=0.025). At 50 mg/day the 50% responder rate was 32.7% vs 16.7% on placebo (P=0.008) and median percent reduction from baseline was 30.5% vs 17.8% (P=0.003). Most treatment-emergent adverse events were mild to moderate; somnolence, dizziness, and fatigue were among those reported more often than on placebo.
cards.watchOut: Two of the three doses tested showed no effect whatsoever; any summary claiming a class-flat benefit across 5-100 mg misreads this trial. (The record itself labels this study N01253 — the companion Ryvlin trial below is N01252.)

cards.headline: Ryvlin 2014 (N01252): primary endpoint missed under sequential testing (50 mg P=.261); 100 mg/day significant — 11.7% over placebo (P=.037), responders 36.0% vs 20.0%
cards.summary: Ryvlin 2014 (N01252): primary endpoint missed under sequential testing (50 mg P=.261); 100 mg/day significant — 11.7% over placebo (P=.037), responders 36.0% vs 20.0%
cards.type: Phase III randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (N01252)
cards.people: 399 patients aged 16-70 with uncontrolled focal seizures (with or without secondary generalisation) despite 1-2 concomitant antiseizure medicines (levetiracetam use capped at 20%); randomised 1:1:1:1 to brivaracetam 20, 50, or 100 mg/day or placebo without up-titration for 12 weeks. The primary endpoint was percent reduction over placebo in baseline-adjusted focal seizure frequency per week, tested sequentially (50 mg, then 100 mg, then 20 mg).
cards.result: The study did not meet its primary efficacy endpoint under the predefined sequential strategy: reductions over placebo were 6.8% (20 mg; P=0.239), 6.5% (50 mg; P=0.261), and 11.7% (100 mg; P=0.037). Responder rates were 27.3%, 27.3%, and 36.0% (100 mg P=0.023) vs 20.0% on placebo. Complete seizure freedom was rare (at most 4 of 100 in any arm). Treatment-emergent adverse events were somewhat more frequent on brivaracetam (56.6-63.0%) than placebo (53.0%); headache, somnolence, dizziness, and fatigue were most frequent.
cards.watchOut: Because the sequential gate failed at 50 mg, the 100 mg result — though nominally significant — is formally a secondary finding in a trial that missed its primary endpoint; the stamp reflects that fragility.

shelves.title: Focal seizures: adjunctive lacosamide 400 mg/day increased responder rates in two randomised trials
shelves.question: In adults with partial-onset seizures uncontrolled on 1-3 antiseizure medicines, does adjunctive lacosamide reduce seizure frequency compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acetamides · Administration, Oral · Anticonvulsants · Ataxia · Dizziness · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Therapy, Combination · Epilepsies, Partial · Humans · Lacosamide · Nausea · Placebos · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Two double-blind placebo-controlled trials anchor lacosamide, and they agree. In Ben-Menachem 2007 (418 patients on 1-2 antiseizure medicines), median seizure-frequency reduction rose with dose — 10% on placebo, 26% on 200 mg/day, 39% on 400 mg/day, and 40% on 600 mg/day — with the reductions over placebo significant at 400 mg (P=.0023) and 600 mg (P=.0084); 50% responder rates were 22%, 33%, 41%, and 38% respectively, and the 200 mg dose did not separate. Chung 2010 (405 patients, mostly on 2-3 medicines) confirmed the pattern against a higher placebo response: median reductions of 37.3% (400 mg; P=.008) and 37.8% (600 mg; P=.006) versus 20.8% on placebo, with responder rates of 38.3% and 41.2% versus 18.3% (P<.001) — absolute responder gains of about 20 points at 400 mg/day. The dose lesson is the same in both trials: 400 mg/day captures the benefit, while 600 mg/day adds dose-related dizziness, nausea, diplopia, ataxia, and nystagmus without adding efficacy. Neither record carries a registry identifier. PROPOSED LIKELY: adjunctive lacosamide at 400 mg/day reduces focal seizure frequency and roughly doubles the odds of a 50% response over placebo.

Intention-to-treat analysis.

Fifty percent responder rates: 22%, 33%, 41% (P=0.0038), and 38% (P=0.0141). Dose-related adverse events included dizziness, nausea, fatigue, ataxia, abnormal vision, diplopia, and nystagmus. Lacosamide did not affect plasma concentrations of concomitant antiseizure medicines.
cards.watchOut: Attrition was substantial (418 randomised, 312 completed) and the 200 mg dose's failure bounds the claim: the benefit is a 400 mg/day story.

shelves.title: Infantile spasms: adding vigabatrin to hormonal therapy stopped spasms more often — without better development at 18 months (ICISS)
shelves.question: In infants with infantile spasms, does combining vigabatrin with hormonal treatment (prednisolone or tetracosactide) stop spasms more reliably than hormonal treatment alone?
shelves.mesh: Anticonvulsants · Cosyntropin · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Therapy, Combination · Electroencephalography · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Hormones · Humans · Infant · Male · Prednisolone · Spasms, Infantile · Treatment Outcome · Vigabatrin
shelves.balance: ICISS randomised 377 infants with infantile spasms and a hypsarrhythmic (or similar) EEG at 102 hospitals to hormonal therapy (prednisolone or tetracosactide) plus vigabatrin, or hormonal therapy alone — open-label treatment with masked electro-clinical outcome assessment. The combination won the primary outcome clearly: no witnessed spasms on and between days 14 and 42 in 72% of the combination group versus 57% on hormonal therapy alone (difference 15.0%; 95% CI 5.1 to 24.9; P=.002), with serious adverse reactions necessitating hospitalisation in 17 versus 16 infants and no deaths attributable to treatment. The planned 18-month follow-up is the necessary cold water: development (Vineland composite scores 73.9 vs 72.7; P=.55) and the presence of epilepsy at 18 months (30.0% vs 29.2%) did not differ between arms — the treatment made no difference to the outcomes families ultimately care most about. What did predict better development was achieving early spasm cessation by any route (Vineland 79.1 vs 63.2) and shorter lead-time to treatment. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit — spasm cessation): combination therapy probably stops spasms more reliably; a developmental dividend from the combination itself was not shown.

cards.headline: ICISS 2017: spasm cessation on days 14-42 in 72% on hormonal therapy plus vigabatrin vs 57% on hormonal therapy alone (difference 15.0%; P=.002)
cards.summary: ICISS 2017: spasm cessation on days 14-42 in 72% on hormonal therapy plus vigabatrin vs 57% on hormonal therapy alone (difference 15.0%; P=.002)
cards.type: Multicentre, open-label randomised trial with masked outcome assessment (ICISS)
cards.people: 377 infants with a clinical diagnosis of infantile spasms and hypsarrhythmic (or similar) EEG within 7 days, enrolled at 102 hospitals (UK, Germany, Australia, New Zealand, Switzerland); randomised 1:1 to hormonal therapy with vigabatrin (n=186) or hormonal therapy alone (n=191). Hormonal therapy was prednisolone 10 mg four times daily or intramuscular tetracosactide depot 0.5 mg on alternate days; vigabatrin dose was 100 mg/kg per day. Parents and clinicians were unmasked; outcome assessors were masked.
cards.result: No spasms were witnessed between days 14 and 42 in 133 of 186 infants (72%) on combination therapy compared with 108 of 191 (57%) on hormonal therapy alone (difference 15.0%; 95% CI 5.1 to 24.9; P=.002), by intention-to-treat analysis of parent-recorded seizure diaries. Serious adverse reactions necessitating hospitalisation occurred in 17 infants on combination therapy and 16 on hormonal therapy alone (infection most common); there were no deaths attributable to treatment.
cards.watchOut: Treatment was open-label and the primary outcome rests on parent-recorded diaries, which tempers certainty despite masked electro-clinical assessment; vigabatrin's known retinal toxicity concern is a longer-horizon issue this trial's 6-week primary window cannot address.

cards.headline: ICISS 18-month follow-up: development (Vineland 73.9 vs 72.7; P=.55) and epilepsy (30.0% vs 29.2%) no different between arms
cards.summary: ICISS 18-month follow-up: development (Vineland 73.9 vs 72.7; P=.55) and epilepsy (30.0% vs 29.2%) no different between arms
cards.type: Planned 18-month follow-up of a multicentre open-label randomised trial (ICISS)
cards.people: 362 of the 377 ICISS infants (181 per arm) assessed at 18 months of age for development (Vineland Adaptive Behaviour Scales composite) and epilepsy outcomes, with assessors masked to treatment allocation.
cards.result: Mean Vineland scores did not differ significantly between the combination and hormonal-alone groups (73.9 vs 72.7; P=.55), nor did the presence of epilepsy at 18 months (30.0% vs 29.2%; P=.90) or of spasms (15.0% vs 15.7%). Initial spasm cessation between days 14 and 42 was associated with higher 18-month Vineland scores (79.1 vs 63.2; difference 15.9; 95% CI 12.4 to 19.5; P<.001) and a higher likelihood of no seizures at 18 months; longer lead-time to treatment was associated with worse development and epilepsy outcomes.
cards.watchOut: The link between early cessation and better development is an association across both arms, not a randomised effect of the combination — the randomised comparison for development is null, and quoting the association as a combination benefit would over-read the design.

shelves.title: Drug-resistant childhood epilepsy: the ketogenic diet beat no dietary change in children (Neal 2008) but not a further antiseizure medicine in infants (KIWE)
shelves.question: In children with drug-resistant epilepsy, does a ketogenic diet reduce seizure frequency compared with no dietary change (and, in infants, compared with a further antiseizure medicine)?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Age Factors · Brain · Child · Child, Preschool · Data Interpretation, Statistical · Epilepsy · Female · Food, Formulated · Humans · Ketones · Lipid Metabolism · Male · Patient Compliance · Surveys and Questionnaires · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Two randomised trials ask two different versions of this question and answer them differently. Neal 2008 randomised 145 children aged 2-16 with drug-resistant epilepsy (daily seizures, at least two medicines failed) to start the ketogenic diet immediately or after a 3-month delay with no other treatment change: at 3 months, mean seizure count stood at 62.0% of baseline in the diet group versus 136.9% in controls (a 75% relative difference; 95% CI 42.4 to 107.4; P<.0001), and more than 50% seizure reduction occurred in 38% versus 6% — a 32-percentage-point absolute gap — in an unblinded trial where only 103 of 145 children contributed data. KIWE (2023) asked the harder, more clinical question in 136 infants: the classic ketogenic diet versus simply trying a further antiseizure medicine. At weeks 6-8, median seizures per day were 5 on the diet versus 3 on medicine (incidence rate ratio 1.33; 95% CI 0.84 to 2.11) — no difference shown; serious adverse events were similar (51% vs 45%), and three deaths in the diet arm were judged unrelated to treatment by the investigators and the safety committee. KIWE stopped early for slow recruitment and end of funding. PROPOSED SPLIT: in children, the diet probably beats changing nothing; in infants, it has not beaten the simpler option of another medicine.

cards.headline: Neal 2008: at 3 months, mean seizures 62.0% of baseline on the ketogenic diet vs 136.9% in delayed-start controls; over 50% reduction in 38% vs 6%
cards.summary: Neal 2008: at 3 months, mean seizures 62.0% of baseline on the ketogenic diet vs 136.9% in delayed-start controls; over 50% reduction in 38% vs 6%
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial with delayed-start (wait-list) control, unblinded
cards.people: 145 children aged 2-16 years with at least daily seizures (or more than 7 per week) who had failed at least two antiseizure medicines and had never been on the ketogenic diet, at two hospital centres and a residential epilepsy centre; randomised to the ketogenic diet immediately (n=73) or after a 3-month delay with no other treatment change (n=72). Neither families nor investigators were blinded; data from 103 children were analysed.
cards.result: After 3 months, the mean percentage of baseline seizures was significantly lower in the diet group than controls (62.0% vs 136.9%; 75% decrease; 95% CI 42.4 to 107.4; P<.0001). Twenty-eight children (38%) in the diet group had a greater than 50% seizure reduction compared with four (6%) controls (P<.0001); five children (7%) on the diet had a greater than 90% reduction versus none. The most frequent side effects at 3 months were constipation, vomiting, lack of energy, and hunger.
cards.watchOut: Attrition was heavy (103 of 145 analysed; 16 never received their intervention, 10 withdrew, 6 of them for intolerance) and the control was no change rather than an active alternative — this trial shows the diet beats waiting, which is a lower bar than beating another treatment.
cards.source: Neal EG et al.. The ketogenic diet for the treatment of childhood epilepsy: a randomised controlled trial. Lancet Neurol. 2008. PMID: 18456557. Registry ID: NCT00564915. cards.headline: KIWE 2023: median daily seizures at weeks 6-8 were 5 on the ketogenic diet vs 3 on a further antiseizure medicine (IRR 1.33; 95% CI 0.84 to 2.11) — no difference
cards.summary: KIWE 2023: median daily seizures at weeks 6-8 were 5 on the ketogenic diet vs 3 on a further antiseizure medicine (IRR 1.33; 95% CI 0.84 to 2.11) — no difference
cards.type: Phase 4, multicentre, open-label randomised clinical trial (KIWE)
cards.people: 136 infants aged 1-24 months with drug-resistant epilepsy (at least 4 seizures per week despite at least two antiseizure medicines) at 19 UK hospitals; randomised to a classic ketogenic diet (n=78) or a further antiseizure medication (n=58) for 8 weeks; 61 and 47 infants respectively contributed primary-outcome data (modified intention-to-treat). Treatment allocation was masked from research nurses but not from families. The trial terminated early because of slow recruitment and end of funding.
cards.result: The median number of seizures per day during weeks 6-8 was similar between groups (5 [IQR 1-16] on the diet vs 3 [IQR 2-11] on medicine; incidence rate ratio 1.33; 95% CI 0.84 to 2.11) — the treatment made no difference shown. At least one serious adverse event occurred in 40 of 78 diet infants (51%) and 26 of 58 medicine infants (45%); the most common were seizures in both groups. Three infants died, all assigned to the ketogenic diet; the deaths were judged unrelated to treatment by local principal investigators and confirmed by the data safety monitoring committee.
cards.watchOut: Early termination left the trial underpowered, so this is an absence of demonstrated difference rather than proof of equivalence; the point estimate numerically favours the medicine arm, and the three diet-arm deaths — though judged unrelated — belong on the face of any summary.

shelves.title: Drug-resistant focal epilepsy: vagus nerve stimulation beat low-stimulation control modestly in two randomised trials (E03, E05)
shelves.question: In people with medically intractable partial-onset seizures, does vagus nerve stimulation reduce seizure frequency compared with low-stimulation control?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Anticonvulsants · Double-Blind Method · Electric Stimulation Therapy · Epilepsies, Partial · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pain Measurement · Patient Participation · Patient Satisfaction · Prospective Studies · Prostheses and Implants · Vagus Nerve
shelves.balance: Vagus nerve stimulation was established the hard way: both pivotal trials implanted the device in everyone and randomised high (presumed therapeutic) versus low (presumed subtherapeutic) stimulation — an active control that shrinks the visible separation and caps the certainty any shelf can claim. E05 (196 patients) found an average seizure-frequency reduction of 28% on high stimulation versus 15% on low (P=.04). E03 (114 patients) found mean reductions of 24.5% versus 6.1% (P=.01), with 50% or greater reductions in 31% versus 13% (P=.02). The absolute separation is therefore about 13-18 percentage points of seizure frequency over 3 months — real, but modest, and measured against a control stimulation that may not be wholly inert. Voice alteration and dyspnoea (E05) and transient hoarseness during stimulation trains (E03) were the characteristic adverse effects; one E03 patient with no previous cardiac history had a myocardial infarction during the third month of stimulation — recorded here because the record reports it, without an attribution claim. Both trials predate trial-registration norms and neither record carries a registry identifier. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: VNS probably reduces focal seizure frequency modestly beyond low-level stimulation, in patients who have failed medicines and are not optimal surgical candidates.

cards.headline: E05 1998 (Handforth): average seizure reduction 28% on high stimulation vs 15% on low stimulation (P=.04)
cards.summary: E05 1998 (Handforth): average seizure reduction 28% on high stimulation vs 15% on low stimulation (P=.04)
cards.people: 196 patients with at least 6 partial-onset seizures per 30 days (complex partial or secondarily generalised), on unaltered antiseizure medicines; all were implanted with left vagus nerve stimulating leads and a programmable generator, then randomised after a 2-week ramp-up to high stimulation (n=94, ages 13-54) or low stimulation (n=102, ages 15-60) and assessed over 3 months in a multicentre double-blind active-control design.
cards.result: Patients receiving high stimulation had an average 28% reduction in total seizure frequency compared with a 15% reduction in the low-stimulation group (P=0.04); global evaluation scores also favoured high stimulation, as rated by a blinded interviewer and by patients. High stimulation was associated with more voice alteration and dyspnoea. No changes in gastric, cardiac, or pulmonary function indicators occurred.
cards.watchOut: The control is low stimulation, not no stimulation — if low stimulation has any effect of its own, the 13-point separation understates the effect versus nothing; if expectation effects differ between arms, it may overstate it. Either way the design caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.
cards.source: Handforth A et al.. Vagus nerve stimulation therapy for partial-onset seizures: a randomized active-control trial. Neurology. 1998. PMID: 9674777. shelves.title: Refractory focal epilepsy: anterior thalamic deep brain stimulation reduced seizures in the blinded phase (SANTE)
shelves.question: In adults with refractory focal epilepsy, does bilateral deep brain stimulation of the anterior nucleus of the thalamus reduce seizure frequency compared with sham stimulation?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anterior Thalamic Nuclei · Deep Brain Stimulation · Depression · Double-Blind Method · Electric Stimulation Therapy · Epilepsies, Partial · Epilepsy · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Functional Laterality · Humans · Longitudinal Studies · Male · Memory Disorders · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SANTE randomised 110 adults with medically refractory partial seizures (median baseline 19.5 seizures per month) to bilateral stimulation of the anterior nuclei of the thalamus or to no stimulation for a 3-month blinded phase, after which everyone received stimulation. In the last month of the blinded phase the stimulated group had a 29% greater reduction in seizures than the control group on the model-based estimate (P=.002); the unadjusted median declines were 40.4% versus 14.5%. Complex partial and 'most severe' seizures were significantly reduced. In the open phase that followed, benefit persisted — a 56% median reduction in seizure frequency and a 54% responder rate at 2 years, with 14 patients seizure-free for at least 6 months — but uncontrolled follow-up cannot separate device effect from time, expectation, and medication changes. Harms were modest but real: five deaths occurred, none attributed to implantation or stimulation; no participant had symptomatic haemorrhage or brain infection; two had acute transient stimulation-associated seizures; and stimulated participants were more likely to report depression or memory problems as adverse events even though formal cognition and mood testing showed no group differences. The record carries no registry identifier. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: anterior thalamic DBS probably reduces refractory focal seizures; the blinded separation is one trial deep.

cards.headline: SANTE 2010: 29% greater seizure reduction than control in the last blinded month (P=.002); median declines 40.4% vs 14.5%; 56% median reduction at 2 years (open phase)
cards.summary: SANTE 2010: 29% greater seizure reduction than control in the last blinded month (P=.002); median declines 40.4% vs 14.5%; 56% median reduction at 2 years (open phase)
cards.people: 110 adults with medically refractory partial seizures, including secondarily generalised seizures (baseline monthly median seizure frequency 19.5), at multiple centres; implanted with bilateral anterior thalamic electrodes and randomised to stimulation or no stimulation for a 3-month blinded phase, followed by unblinded stimulation for all.
cards.result: In the last month of the blinded phase, the stimulated group had a 29% greater reduction in seizures compared with the control group (generalised estimating equations model; P=0.002); unadjusted median declines were 40.4% (stimulated) and 14.5% (control). By 2 years there was a 56% median percent reduction in seizure frequency; 54% of patients had a seizure reduction of at least 50%, and 14 patients were seizure-free for at least 6 months. Five deaths occurred, none from implantation or stimulation; there was no symptomatic haemorrhage or brain infection; two participants had acute, transient stimulation-associated seizures. Cognition and mood testing showed no group differences, but depression and memory problems were more often reported as adverse events in the stimulated group.
cards.watchOut: The 2-year figures are open-label and uncontrolled; the blinded 3-month separation is the trial's evidentiary core. Subjective depression and memory complaints diverged from formal testing — both are reported here because the record reports both.

shelves.title: Dravet syndrome: stiripentol cut convulsive seizures sharply in a small syndrome-dedicated trial (STICLO)
shelves.question: In children with Dravet syndrome (severe myoclonic epilepsy in infancy) whose seizures persist on valproate and clobazam, does adjunctive stiripentol reduce convulsive seizures compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Anxiety Agents · Anticonvulsants · Benzodiazepines · Child, Preschool · Clobazam · Dioxolanes · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Epilepsies, Myoclonic · Female · Humans · Infant · Male · Syndrome · Valproic Acid
shelves.balance: STICLO is the oldest leg of the Dravet tripod — cannabidiol and fenfluramine for Dravet syndrome live elsewhere in this library — and it remains the most dramatic. Forty-one children with severe myoclonic epilepsy in infancy whose seizures persisted on valproate plus clobazam were randomised to add stiripentol or placebo for a 2-month double-blind period. Responders (more than 50% reduction in clonic or tonic-clonic seizure frequency) were 71% on stiripentol (15 of 21 — nine of them free of clonic or tonic-clonic seizures) versus 5% on placebo (1 of 20, none seizure-free); the 95% confidence interval for the difference runs from 42.2 to 85.7 percentage points, and mean seizure frequency changed by -69% on stiripentol versus +7% on placebo (P<.0001). Moderate side effects (drowsiness, loss of appetite) occurred in 21 children on stiripentol versus 8 on placebo, and mostly disappeared when the dose of the companion medicines was reduced — stiripentol inhibits the metabolism of clobazam and valproate, which is part of how the combination works and part of its management burden. The sample is tiny and the blinded period short; the effect, as far as it goes, is not small. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: stiripentol probably produces large short-term reductions in Dravet convulsive seizures when added to valproate and clobazam; a single 41-child trial caps the stamp despite the effect size.

cards.headline: STICLO 2000: responders 71% on stiripentol (15/21; 9 seizure-free) vs 5% on placebo (1/20); seizure frequency -69% vs +7% (P<.0001)

cards.people: 41 children with severe myoclonic epilepsy in infancy (Dravet syndrome) in a randomised, placebo-controlled, add-on trial; after a 1-month baseline, stiripentol (n=21) or placebo (n=20) was added to valproate and clobazam for a 2-month double-blind period, followed by open stiripentol. Responders were defined as more than 50% reduction in clonic (or tonic-clonic) seizure frequency during the second double-blind month versus baseline.
cards.result: Fifteen of 21 patients (71%) were responders on stiripentol (95% CI 52.1 to 90.7), including nine free of clonic or tonic-clonic seizures, versus 1 of 20 (5%) on placebo (95% CI 0 to 14.6); the 95% CI of the difference was 42.2 to 85.7 points. Percentage change from baseline was -69% on stiripentol versus +7% on placebo (P<.0001). Twenty-one patients on stiripentol had moderate side effects (drowsiness, loss of appetite) versus 8 on placebo; side effects disappeared when the dose of co-medication was decreased in 12 of the 21 cases.
cards.watchOut: Forty-one children and a 2-month blinded period: the confidence interval for the responder difference is wide even though it excludes small effects, and durability beyond 2 months rests on the open phase, which is uncontrolled.

shelves.question: In people with tuberous sclerosis complex and treatment-resistant focal seizures, does adjunctive everolimus increase seizure response compared with placebo?

shelves.balance: EXIST-3 randomised 366 patients aged 2-65 with tuberous sclerosis complex and treatment-resistant focal-onset seizures (at least 16 seizures in the 8-week baseline) to placebo or everolimus titrated to a low (3-7 ng/mL) or high (9-15 ng/mL) trough exposure, added to 1-3 antiseizure medicines across 99 centres. Response — at least a 50% reduction in seizure frequency during the maintenance period — was 15.1% on placebo, 28.2% on low exposure (P=.0077), and 40.0% on high exposure (P<.0001): absolute gains of about 13 and 25 percentage points. Median percentage reductions in seizure frequency were 14.9%, 29.3% (P=.0028), and 39.6% (P<.0001), the same dose-ordered pattern. That gradient across two independently randomised exposure arms strengthens the causal reading of what is still a single trial. The price was graded too: grade 3 or 4 adverse events in 11% on placebo, 18% on low exposure, and 24% on high exposure, and serious adverse events in 3% versus 14% in both everolimus arms — an imbalance in serious events that belongs on the face of any benefit claim. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: adjunctive everolimus probably reduces TSC-associated focal seizures, with high exposure more effective and less well tolerated; one trial, however large and internally consistent, is one trial.

cards.headline: EXIST-3 2016: response rates 15.1% on placebo, 28.2% on low-exposure everolimus (P=.0077), 40.0% on high-exposure (P<.0001); serious adverse events 3% vs 14% and 14%
cards.summary: EXIST-3 2016: response rates 15.1% on placebo, 28.2% on low-exposure everolimus (P=.0077), 40.0% on high-exposure (P<.0001); serious adverse events 3% vs 14% and 14%
cards.people: 366 patients aged 2-65 years with tuberous sclerosis complex and treatment-resistant focal-onset seizures (16 or more in an 8-week baseline) receiving 1-3 concomitant antiseizure medicines, at 99 centres in 25 countries; randomised 1:1:1 to placebo (n=119), low-exposure everolimus (trough 3-7 ng/mL; n=117), or high-exposure everolimus (trough 9-15 ng/mL; n=130), with 6-week titration and 12-week maintenance; patients, investigators, and sponsor team masked.
cards.result: Response rate (at least 50% reduction in seizure frequency): 15.1% on placebo versus 28.2% on low-exposure everolimus (P=0.0077) and 40.0% on high-exposure (P<0.0001). Median percentage reduction in seizure frequency: 14.9% vs 29.3% (P=0.0028) and 39.6% (P<0.0001). Grade 3 or 4 adverse events occurred in 11% (placebo), 18% (low), and 24% (high); serious adverse events were reported in 3% on placebo versus 14% in each everolimus group; adverse events led to discontinuation in 2%, 5%, and 3% respectively.
cards.watchOut: The serious-adverse-event imbalance (14% vs 3%) is substantial for a chronic add-on therapy in a population that includes young children; the benefit claim and the harm figures must be quoted together.
cards.source: French JA et al.. shelves.title: Medically intractable focal epilepsy: responsive neurostimulation reduced seizures versus sham in the blinded period (RNS pivotal trial)
shelves.question: In adults with medically intractable focal seizures from 1-2 foci, does responsive cortical neurostimulation reduce seizure frequency compared with sham stimulation?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Anticonvulsants · Cerebral Cortex · Cognition Disorders · Disability Evaluation · Double-Blind Method · Electric Stimulation Therapy · Epilepsies, Partial · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Mood Disorders · Neuropsychological Tests · Quality of Life · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: The RNS pivotal trial implanted 191 adults with medically intractable partial seizures arising from 1 or 2 predetermined foci with a responsive neurostimulator, then randomised them 1:1 to stimulation delivered in response to detected abnormal electrocorticographic activity or to no stimulation for a 12-week blinded period. Seizures fell 37.9% in the treatment group versus 17.3% in the sham group (P=.012) — an absolute separation of about 21 percentage points against an implanted, device-carrying control, which is the honest comparison for an implanted therapy. There was no difference between groups in adverse events during the blinded period. In the 84-week open-label period that followed, the reduction was sustained in the treatment group and emerged in the sham group once stimulation began; overall quality of life improved significantly (P<.02), with no deterioration in mood or neuropsychological function. The open-label accrual cannot be separated from expectation and time, so the blinded 12 weeks carry the claim. The record carries no registry identifier. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: responsive neurostimulation probably reduces disabling focal seizures in the narrow population trialled — adults who have failed at least two antiseizure medicines, with 3 or more seizures per month and 1-2 localisable foci.

cards.headline: RNS pivotal trial 2011: seizures fell 37.9% on responsive stimulation vs 17.3% on sham over the 12-week blinded period (P=.012)
cards.summary: RNS pivotal trial 2011: seizures fell 37.9% on responsive stimulation vs 17.3% on sham over the 12-week blinded period (P=.012)
cards.type: Multicentre, double-blind, randomised controlled (sham-controlled) trial (RNS System pivotal trial)
cards.people: 191 adults with medically intractable partial epilepsy, implanted with a responsive neurostimulator connected to depth or subdural leads at 1 or 2 predetermined seizure foci; one month after implantation, randomised 1:1 to stimulation in response to detections (n=97) or no stimulation (sham; n=94) for a 12-week blinded period, followed by an 84-week open-label period in which all received stimulation.
cards.result: Seizures were significantly reduced in the treatment group (-37.9%) compared with the sham group (-17.3%) during the blinded period (P=0.012), with no difference between groups in adverse events. During the open-label period the reduction was sustained in the treatment group and seizures were significantly reduced in the former sham group once stimulation began. Overall quality of life improved significantly (P<0.02), with no deterioration in mood or neuropsychological function.
cards.watchOut: Twelve blinded weeks is short for an implanted lifelong therapy, and the sham arm's 17.3% reduction shows how much improvement an implant plus attention can produce on its own; long-term responder figures from the open phase are uncontrolled.
cards.source: Morrell MJ et al.. Responsive cortical stimulation for the treatment of medically intractable partial epilepsy. Neurology. 2011. PMID: 21917777. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis: dimethyl fumarate roughly halved relapse rates versus placebo in two phase 3 trials, with disability progression reduced in DEFINE (DEFINE; CONFIRM)
shelves.question: In relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, does oral dimethyl fumarate reduce relapses and disability progression compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Brain/pathology · Dimethyl Fumarate · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fumarates/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Infections/etiology · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Multiple Sclerosis, Relapsing-Remitting/drug therapy,pathology
shelves.balance: Two phase 3 placebo-controlled trials of oral dimethyl fumarate (BG-12) in relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis agree. In DEFINE, the proportion of patients relapsing by 2 years was 27% on twice-daily BG-12 and 26% on thrice-daily dosing versus 46% on placebo, and the annualized relapse rate was 0.17 and 0.19 versus 0.36 — relative reductions of 53% and 48%. Confirmed disability progression was 16% and 18% versus 27% on placebo (relative reductions 38% and 34%). CONFIRM repeated the relapse result against placebo (annualized relapse rate 0.22 and 0.20 versus 0.40; relative reductions 44% and 51%), with a glatiramer acetate reference arm at 0.29, but its disability-progression reductions (21% and 24%) were not significant — the trial was not designed to compare BG-12 with glatiramer, and any head-to-head reading is post hoc. The consistent harms are flushing and gastrointestinal events, with falls in lymphocyte counts. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): two large randomised trials show an approximate halving of relapse activity; the disability claim rests on DEFINE alone.

cards.headline: DEFINE 2012: relapses by 2 years in 27% (twice-daily) and 26% (thrice-daily) on BG-12 vs 46% on placebo; disability progression 16-18% vs 27%
cards.summary: DEFINE 2012: relapses by 2 years in 27% (twice-daily) and 26% (thrice-daily) on BG-12 vs 46% on placebo; disability progression 16-18% vs 27%
cards.people: Patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis randomised to oral BG-12 240 mg twice daily, BG-12 240 mg three times daily, or placebo for 2 years. The primary end point was the proportion of patients who had a relapse by 2 years; other end points were the annualized relapse rate, time to confirmed progression of disability, and MRI findings.
cards.result: The estimated proportion relapsing was 27% (twice daily) and 26% (thrice daily) versus 46% on placebo (P<0.001 for both). Annualized relapse rate was 0.17 and 0.19 versus 0.36, relative reductions of 53% and 48% (P<0.001). Confirmed disability progression occurred in 16% and 18% versus 27%, relative risk reductions of 38% (P=0.005) and 34% (P=0.01). BG-12 also reduced gadolinium-enhancing and new/enlarging T2 lesions (P<0.001). Adverse events included flushing, gastrointestinal events (diarrhoea, nausea, upper abdominal pain), decreased lymphocyte counts and raised liver aminotransferases.
cards.watchOut: The thrice-daily dose added nothing over twice daily; DEFINE is the only one of the two trials where the disability-progression endpoint reached significance.
cards.source: Gold R et al.. Placebo-controlled phase 3 study of oral BG-12 for relapsing multiple sclerosis. N Engl J Med. 2012. PMID: 22992073. Registry ID: NCT00420212 (named in the record's abstract). cards.headline: CONFIRM 2012: annualized relapse rate 0.22 (twice-daily) and 0.20 (thrice-daily) on BG-12 vs 0.40 on placebo; glatiramer reference arm 0.29; disability reductions not significant
cards.summary: CONFIRM 2012: annualized relapse rate 0.22 (twice-daily) and 0.20 (thrice-daily) on BG-12 vs 0.40 on placebo; glatiramer reference arm 0.29; disability reductions not significant
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind (placebo arms), placebo-controlled phase 3 trial with open-label active reference arm (CONFIRM)
cards.people: Patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis randomised to BG-12 240 mg twice or three times daily, placebo, or open-label glatiramer acetate as a reference comparator, for 2 years. The primary end point was the annualized relapse rate; the study was not designed to test superiority or noninferiority of BG-12 against glatiramer acetate.
cards.result: Annualized relapse rate was 0.22 (twice daily), 0.20 (thrice daily) and 0.29 (glatiramer) versus 0.40 on placebo — relative reductions of 44% (P<0.001), 51% (P<0.001) and 29% (P=0.01). Reductions in disability progression versus placebo (21%, 24% and 7%) were not significant. All active treatments reduced new/enlarging T2 lesions. Flushing and gastrointestinal events were more frequent with BG-12, injection-related events with glatiramer; no malignant neoplasms or opportunistic infections were reported with BG-12, and lymphocyte counts decreased.
cards.watchOut: Comparisons of BG-12 against glatiramer acetate are post hoc and nominal only; the trial answers the placebo question, not a head-to-head question.

cards.summary: Synthesis: two trials, relapse rates roughly halved; disability benefit shown once — LIKELY
cards.people: Two randomised phase 3 trials (DEFINE and CONFIRM) of dimethyl fumarate 240 mg twice or three times daily versus placebo over 2 years in relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, CONFIRM adding an open-label glatiramer reference arm.

shelves.title: Relapsing multiple sclerosis: natalizumab cut relapses by about two-thirds and progression risk by 42% relative versus placebo — with progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy appearing in the add-on trial (AFFIRM; SENTINEL)
shelves.question: In relapsing multiple sclerosis, does natalizumab reduce relapses and sustained disability progression compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Antibodies, Monoclonal/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Brain/pathology · Cell Adhesion Molecules/antagonists & inhibitors · Disease Progression · Drug Hypersensitivity/etiology · Fatigue/chemically induced · Female · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Integrin alpha4 · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Male · Middle Aged · Multiple Sclerosis, Relapsing-Remitting/drug therapy,pathology · Natalizumab · Proportional Hazards Models · Secondary Prevention
shelves.balance: Natalizumab is among the most effective relapse-suppressing treatments tested in relapsing multiple sclerosis, and its two phase 3 trials define both halves of the answer. In AFFIRM, natalizumab monotherapy reduced the risk of sustained disability progression by 42% relative over 2 years (hazard ratio 0.58; cumulative probability 17% versus 29% on placebo) and the clinical relapse rate at 1 year by 68% relative. In SENTINEL, adding natalizumab to interferon beta-1a in patients still relapsing on interferon cut the annualized relapse rate to 0.34 versus 0.75 and reduced the relative risk of sustained progression by 24% (hazard ratio 0.76; cumulative probability 23% versus 29%). The counterweight is in SENTINEL itself: two cases of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, one fatal, occurred in natalizumab-treated patients — the opportunistic brain infection that has governed this drug's use and monitoring ever since. Hypersensitivity reactions occurred in 4% in AFFIRM, serious in 1%. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): large, consistent randomised effects on relapses and progression, with a rare but potentially fatal harm that post-dates the monotherapy trial and must travel with the claim.

cards.headline: AFFIRM 2006: natalizumab cut sustained disability progression risk by 42% relative (17% vs 29% cumulative) and 1-year relapse rate by 68% relative vs placebo
cards.summary: AFFIRM 2006: natalizumab cut sustained disability progression risk by 42% relative (17% vs 29% cumulative) and 1-year relapse rate by 68% relative vs placebo
cards.people: 942 patients with relapsing multiple sclerosis randomised to natalizumab 300 mg (n=627) or placebo (n=315) by intravenous infusion every 4 weeks for over 2 years. Primary end points were the rate of clinical relapse at 1 year and the rate of sustained progression of disability (EDSS) at 2 years.
cards.result: Natalizumab reduced the risk of sustained progression by 42% relative (hazard ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.77; P<0.001); cumulative probability of progression was 17% versus 29%. The clinical relapse rate at 1 year fell by 68% relative (P<0.001), new or enlarging T2 lesions by 83% relative (mean 1.9 vs 11.0), and gadolinium-enhancing lesions by 92% at 1 and 2 years. Fatigue (27% vs 21%) and allergic reaction (9% vs 4%) were more frequent; hypersensitivity reactions of any kind occurred in 25 patients (4%), serious in 8 (1%).
cards.watchOut: AFFIRM closed before the progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy signal emerged in the companion trial; its safety readout cannot be quoted without SENTINEL's.
cards.source: Polman CH et al.. A randomized, placebo-controlled trial of natalizumab for relapsing multiple sclerosis. N Engl J Med. 2006. PMID: 16510744. cards.headline: SENTINEL 2006: natalizumab added to interferon beta-1a cut relapses (0.34 vs 0.75 per year) and progression risk by 24% relative — and produced two cases of PML, one fatal
cards.summary: SENTINEL 2006: natalizumab added to interferon beta-1a cut relapses (0.34 vs 0.75 per year) and progression risk by 24% relative — and produced two cases of PML, one fatal
cards.people: 1,171 patients who had relapsed during the previous year despite interferon beta-1a therapy, randomised to continue interferon beta-1a plus natalizumab 300 mg (n=589) or placebo (n=582) intravenously every 4 weeks for up to 116 weeks. Primary end points were the clinical relapse rate at 1 year and the cumulative probability of disability progression sustained for 12 weeks at 2 years.
cards.result: Combination therapy reduced the relative risk of sustained progression by 24% (hazard ratio 0.76, 95% CI 0.61 to 0.96; P=0.02); cumulative probability of progression at 2 years was 23% versus 29%. The annualized relapse rate over 2 years was 0.34 versus 0.75 (P<0.001), and new or enlarging T2 lesions 0.9 versus 5.4 (P<0.001). Two cases of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, one of them fatal, were diagnosed in natalizumab-treated patients.
cards.watchOut: The PML cases occurred on combination therapy; subsequent practice — JC-virus antibody risk stratification and monotherapy use — post-dates both trials and is not itself trialled evidence.
cards.source: Rudick RA et al.. Natalizumab plus interferon beta-1a for relapsing multiple sclerosis. N Engl J Med. 2006. PMID: 16510745. Registry ID: NCT00030966 (named in the record's abstract). shelves.title: Relapsing multiple sclerosis: teriflunomide cut relapse rates by about a third relative in two phase 3 trials, with disability benefit only at the 14 mg dose (TEMSO; TOWER)
shelves.question: In relapsing multiple sclerosis, does oral teriflunomide reduce relapses compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Alanine Transaminase/blood · Brain/pathology · Crotonates/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Dihydroorotate Dehydrogenase · Disability Evaluation · Disease Progression · Enzyme Inhibitors/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Fatigue/drug therapy · Female · Humans · Hydroxybutyrates · Male · Middle Aged · Multiple Sclerosis, Relapsing-Remitting/drug therapy,pathology · Nitriles · Oxidoreductases Acting on CH-CH Group Donors/antagonists & inhibitors · Secondary Prevention · Toluidines/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Oral teriflunomide gives a modest, consistent reduction in relapse activity in relapsing multiple sclerosis — about a third — in two phase 3 placebo-controlled trials. In TEMSO, the annualized relapse rate was 0.37 on either 7 mg or 14 mg versus 0.54 on placebo (relative reductions 31.2% and 31.5%), and confirmed disability progression was 20.2% on 14 mg versus 27.3% on placebo (P=0.03), with the 7 mg dose not significant on progression (21.7%, P=0.08). TOWER confirmed the relapse effect (0.32 on 14 mg and 0.39 on 7 mg versus 0.50 on placebo) and again found the progression benefit only at 14 mg (hazard ratio 0.68; the 7 mg hazard ratio was 0.95). The price is hepatic and cosmetic: alanine aminotransferase at or above the upper limit of normal in 54-57% on teriflunomide versus 35.9% on placebo in TEMSO (levels at least 3 times the limit were similar, about 6-7% in all groups), plus diarrhoea, nausea and hair thinning. TOWER recorded four deaths, none judged related to study drug, including one suicide in the 14 mg group. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): the effect is real but smaller than the fumarate and monoclonal shelves beside it, and the licensed 14 mg dose is the one with progression evidence.

cards.headline: TEMSO 2011: teriflunomide cut the annualized relapse rate from 0.54 to 0.37 (about 31% relative) at both doses; progression benefit only at 14 mg
cards.summary: TEMSO 2011: teriflunomide cut the annualized relapse rate from 0.54 to 0.37 (about 31% relative) at both doses; progression benefit only at 14 mg
cards.people: 1,088 patients aged 18-55 with multiple sclerosis, EDSS 0-5.5, and at least one relapse in the previous year or two in the previous 2 years, randomised 1:1:1 to placebo, teriflunomide 7 mg, or teriflunomide 14 mg once daily for 108 weeks. The primary end point was the annualized relapse rate; the key secondary end point was disability progression confirmed for at least 12 weeks.
cards.result: Annualized relapse rate was 0.54 on placebo versus 0.37 at either teriflunomide dose (relative risk reductions 31.2% and 31.5%, P<0.001). Confirmed disability progression: 27.3% on placebo, 21.7% on 7 mg (P=0.08) and 20.2% on 14 mg (P=0.03). Both doses beat placebo on MRI endpoints. Diarrhoea, nausea and hair thinning were more common on teriflunomide. ALT at least 1 times the upper limit of normal occurred in 54.0% (7 mg) and 57.3% (14 mg) versus 35.9% on placebo; ALT at least 3 times the limit was similar across groups (6.3%, 6.7%, 6.7%). Serious infections: 1.6%, 2.5% and 2.2%. No deaths occurred.
cards.watchOut: The 7 mg dose's progression result missed significance; only 14 mg carries both relapse and progression evidence.

cards.headline: TOWER 2014: relapse rate 0.32 (14 mg) and 0.39 (7 mg) vs 0.50 on placebo; disability hazard ratio 0.68 at 14 mg, 0.95 at 7 mg
cards.summary: TOWER 2014: relapse rate 0.32 (14 mg) and 0.39 (7 mg) vs 0.50 on placebo; disability hazard ratio 0.68 at 14 mg, 0.95 at 7 mg
cards.people: 1,169 adults with relapsing multiple sclerosis, EDSS 5.5 or less, randomised 1:1:1 to placebo, teriflunomide 7 mg or teriflunomide 14 mg once daily; treatment duration was variable, ending 48 weeks after the last patient was enrolled. Primary endpoint was the annualized relapse rate; the key secondary endpoint was time to sustained accumulation of disability (at least 1 EDSS point sustained 12 weeks).
cards.result: Annualized relapse rate: 0.50 on placebo (95% CI 0.43-0.58) versus 0.32 on 14 mg (P=0.0001) and 0.39 on 7 mg (P=0.0183). Teriflunomide 14 mg reduced the risk of sustained disability accumulation (hazard ratio 0.68, 95% CI 0.47-1.00; P=0.0442); 7 mg did not (hazard ratio 0.95; P=0.7620). Common adverse events were ALT increases (8% placebo, 11% 7 mg, 14% 14 mg), hair thinning (4%, 10%, 13%) and headache. Serious adverse events were similar across groups (about 12-13%). Four deaths occurred — none considered related to study drug (respiratory infection on placebo; traffic accident on 7 mg; suicide and Gram-negative septicaemia with disseminated intravascular coagulation on 14 mg).
cards.watchOut: The disability confidence interval at 14 mg reaches 1.00, and variable treatment duration makes TOWER a confirmation of the relapse effect more than an independent progression proof.

shelves.title: Relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis: alemtuzumab halved relapse rates versus interferon beta-1a in two phase 3 trials, with disability benefit only in previously treated patients — and delayed autoimmunity in up to a fifth (CARE-MS I & II)
shelves.question: In relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, does alemtuzumab reduce relapses and disability progression compared with subcutaneous interferon beta-1a?
shelves.mesh: Adjuvants, Immunologic/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Administration, Cutaneous · Adolescent · Adult · Alemtuzumab · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Female · Glatiramer Acetate · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Infusions, Intravenous · Male · Middle Aged · Multiple Sclerosis, Relapsing-Remitting/drug therapy · Peptides/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Recurrence · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Against an active comparator — high-dose subcutaneous interferon beta-1a — alemtuzumab roughly halved relapse rates in both of its phase 3 trials. In CARE-MS II (patients who had relapsed on prior therapy), the relapse rate ratio was 0.51 (a 49.4% relative improvement; 35% of alemtuzumab patients relapsed versus 51% on interferon) and sustained accumulation of disability was 13% versus 20% (hazard ratio 0.58, a 42% relative improvement). In CARE-MS I (treatment-naïve patients), the relapse rate ratio was 0.45 (54.9% relative improvement; relapse-free at 2 years 78% versus 59%), but the disability endpoint was not met (8% versus 11%; hazard ratio 0.70, P=0.22). The harm profile is the other half of this shelf and is unlike any neighbour: infusion reactions in about 90%, infections in 67-77%, and delayed secondary autoimmunity — thyroid disorders in 16-18% by 2 years and immune thrombocytopenia in about 1% in both trials, with two cases of thyroid papillary carcinoma in CARE-MS I. These harms, not the relapse numbers, are why the drug sits behind monitoring programmes. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): two randomised active-comparator trials agree on relapses; the disability claim holds only in the previously treated population.

cards.headline: CARE-MS II 2012: alemtuzumab vs interferon beta-1a after prior-therapy relapse — relapse rate ratio 0.51, sustained disability 13% vs 20%
cards.summary: CARE-MS II 2012: alemtuzumab vs interferon beta-1a after prior-therapy relapse — relapse rate ratio 0.51, sustained disability 13% vs 20%
cards.type: Randomised, rater-masked, active-comparator phase 3 trial (CARE-MS II)
cards.people: Adults aged 18-55 with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis and at least one relapse on interferon beta or glatiramer acetate, randomised (1:2:2 allocation including a discontinued 24 mg arm) to subcutaneous interferon beta-1a 44 micrograms three times weekly, or intravenous alemtuzumab 12 mg/day for 5 days at baseline and 3 days at 12 months, over 2 years. Rater-masked. Coprimary endpoints were relapse rate and time to 6-month sustained accumulation of disability; 202 interferon and 426 alemtuzumab 12 mg patients entered the primary analyses.
cards.result: Relapses occurred in 104 (51%) interferon patients versus 147 (35%) on alemtuzumab (rate ratio 0.51, 95% CI 0.39-0.65; P<0.0001 — a 49.4% relative improvement); 65% versus 47% were relapse-free at 2 years. Sustained accumulation of disability: 54 (13%) versus 40 (20%) (hazard ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.38-0.87; P=0.008 — a 42% relative improvement). On alemtuzumab 12 mg: infusion-associated reactions in 393/435 (90%), infections in 334 (77%) versus 134 (66%) on interferon (mostly mild-moderate, none fatal), thyroid disorders in 69 (16%), and immune thrombocytopenia in 3 (1%).
cards.watchOut: Patients and treating clinicians were unmasked (only raters were blinded), so relapse ascertainment carries some open-label risk; the 24 mg arm was dropped mid-trial for recruitment reasons.
cards.source: Coles AJ et al.. Alemtuzumab for patients with relapsing multiple sclerosis after disease-modifying therapy: a randomised controlled phase 3 trial. Lancet. 2012. PMID: 23122650. Registry ID: NCT00548405 (named in the record's abstract). cards.headline: CARE-MS I 2012: first-line alemtuzumab vs interferon — relapse rate ratio 0.45, but the disability endpoint missed (8% vs 11%, P=0.22)
cards.summary: CARE-MS I 2012: first-line alemtuzumab vs interferon — relapse rate ratio 0.45, but the disability endpoint missed (8% vs 11%, P=0.22)
cards.type: Randomised, rater-masked, active-comparator phase 3 trial (CARE-MS I)
cards.people: Previously untreated adults aged 18-50 with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, randomised 2:1 to intravenous alemtuzumab 12 mg/day (5 days at baseline, 3 days at 12 months) or subcutaneous interferon beta-1a 44 micrograms three times weekly, over 2 years. Rater-masked. Coprimary endpoints were relapse rate and time to 6-month sustained accumulation of disability; 376 alemtuzumab and 187 interferon patients entered the primary analyses.

cards.headline: Synthesis: relapses halved against interferon in both trials; disability benefit only after prior therapy; autoimmunity is the price — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: relapses halved against interferon in both trials; disability benefit only after prior therapy; autoimmunity is the price — LIKELY
cards.people: Two randomised, rater-masked phase 3 trials of two annual courses of alemtuzumab versus subcutaneous interferon beta-1a 44 micrograms over 2 years: CARE-MS I (treatment-naïve, n=563 analysed) and CARE-MS II (relapsed on prior therapy, n=628 analysed).
cards.result: Relapse rate ratios 0.45 and 0.51 (relative improvements 54.9% and 49.4%); relapse-free at 2 years 78% vs 59% and 65% vs 47%. Sustained disability accumulation reduced in CARE-MS II (13% vs 20%, HR 0.58) but not CARE-MS I (8% vs 11%, HR 0.70, NS). Harms: thyroid autoimmunity 16-18%, immune thrombocytopenia about 1%, infections 67-77%, infusion reactions about 90%. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Autoimmune events accrue for years after dosing; the 2-year trial windows understate the lifetime monitoring burden that defines this drug in practice.
cards.source: Synthesis of Coles AJ et al. Lancet. 2012 (PMID: 23122650) and Cohen JA et al. Lancet. 2012 (PMID: 23122652).

shelves.title: Relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis: short-course cladribine cut relapse rates by over half versus placebo in its single pivotal trial, with dose-dependent lymphopenia (CLARITY)
shelves.question: In relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, do short courses of oral cladribine reduce relapses compared with placebo over two years?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Analysis of Variance · Brain/pathology · Cladribine/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Disability Evaluation · Disease Progression · Double-Blind Method · Female · Herpes Zoster/etiology · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Intention to Treat Analysis · Lymphopenia/chemically induced · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Male · Middle Aged · Multiple Sclerosis, Relapsing-Remitting/drug therapy,pathology · Young Adult
shelves.balance: CLARITY is the single pivotal placebo-controlled trial of short-course oral cladribine in relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, and its effects were large: the annualized relapse rate at 96 weeks was 0.14 on the 3.5 mg/kg cumulative dose and 0.15 on 5.25 mg/kg versus 0.33 on placebo (relative reductions of about 58% and 55%), relapse-free rates were 79.7% and 78.9% versus 60.9%, and the risk of 3-month sustained disability progression fell by about a third (hazard ratios 0.67 and 0.69). The treatment is given as a few short courses totalling 8-20 days per year, which makes the harm ledger specific: lymphocytopenia in 21.6% (3.5 mg/kg) and 31.5% (5.25 mg/kg) versus 1.8% on placebo, and herpes zoster in 8 and 12 patients versus none. The higher dose bought no extra efficacy, so the lower cumulative dose is the one the evidence favours. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — flagged for the developer's personal verdict as a single-trial shelf: one trial, however large and clean, carries the whole claim, and questions the trial cannot answer (long-horizon malignancy and infection risk after immune reconstitution) sit outside its 96 weeks.

cards.headline: CLARITY 2010: cladribine cut the annualized relapse rate to 0.14-0.15 vs 0.33 on placebo and progression risk by about a third; lymphocytopenia in up to 31.5%
cards.summary: CLARITY 2010: cladribine cut the annualized relapse rate to 0.14-0.15 vs 0.33 on placebo and progression risk by about a third; lymphocytopenia in up to 31.5%
cards.people: 1,326 patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis randomised approximately 1:1:1 to cladribine tablets at a cumulative dose of 3.5 mg/kg or 5.25 mg/kg, or matching placebo, given as short courses over 96 weeks (2 or 4 courses in the first 48 weeks, then 2 courses from week 48 — 8 to 20 treatment days per year). The primary end point was the relapse rate at 96 weeks.
cards.result: Annualized relapse rate: 0.14 (3.5 mg/kg) and 0.15 (5.25 mg/kg) versus 0.33 on placebo (P<0.001 for both) — relative reductions of about 58% and 55%. Relapse-free: 79.7% and 78.9% versus 60.9% (P<0.001). Risk of 3-month sustained disability progression: hazard ratio 0.67 (95% CI 0.48-0.93; P=0.02) and 0.69 (95% CI 0.49-0.96; P=0.03). MRI lesion counts were significantly reduced (P<0.001 for all comparisons). Adverse events more frequent on cladribine: lymphocytopenia 21.6% and 31.5% versus 1.8%, and herpes zoster in 8 and 12 patients versus none on placebo.
cards.watchOut: The extension study re-randomised dose duration rather than drug versus placebo, so there is no second placebo-controlled efficacy trial; the malignancy question that delayed this drug's approval in some jurisdictions is not addressed within 96 weeks.
cards.source: Giovannoni G et al.. A placebo-controlled trial of oral cladribine for relapsing multiple sclerosis. N Engl J Med. 2010. PMID: 20089960. Registry ID: NCT00213135 (named in the record's abstract). shelves.title: Vitamin D in multiple sclerosis: high-dose cholecalciferol reduced disease activity in clinically isolated syndrome (D-Lay MS), but made no difference added to interferon in established relapsing-remitting disease (SOLAR; CHOLINE)
shelves.question: In clinically isolated syndrome or early relapsing MS, does high-dose vitamin D reduce disease activity (relapses and MRI lesions) compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Humans · Male · Cholecalciferol/administration & dosage,adverse effects,blood · Double-Blind Method · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Multiple Sclerosis/blood,diagnosis,etiology,therapy · Vitamin D Deficiency/blood,complications,diet therapy · Vitamins/administration & dosage,adverse effects,blood · Administration, Oral · Placebos/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Pulse Therapy, Drug/adverse effects · Follow-Up Studies · Methylprednisolone/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Combined Modality Therapy/adverse effects,methods · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Vitamin D in multiple sclerosis splits cleanly by setting. As monotherapy at the very start of the disease, it worked: in D-Lay MS, untreated patients with clinically isolated syndrome and low vitamin D randomised to cholecalciferol 100,000 IU every 2 weeks had less disease activity over 24 months than on placebo (60.3% versus 74.1%; hazard ratio 0.66), with all MRI secondary outcomes favouring vitamin D — though relapse itself, the clinical component, was not significantly reduced (17.9% versus 21.8%; hazard ratio 0.69, P=0.16). As an add-on to interferon beta-1a in established relapsing-remitting disease, it did not: SOLAR missed its primary endpoint (no-evidence-of-disease-activity in 36.3% versus 35.3%; odds ratio 0.93, P=0.80 — the treatment made no difference), with only exploratory MRI lesion outcomes favouring vitamin D, and CHOLINE likewise missed its primary annualized-relapse-rate endpoint, its favourable results confined to the completer subset. Severe adverse events in D-Lay MS were 17 versus 13, none attributed to cholecalciferol. PROPOSED SPLIT: POSSIBLE (benefit) for high-dose vitamin D monotherapy in clinically isolated syndrome, on a single trial whose significant endpoint is MRI-driven; POSSIBLE (no difference) for vitamin D added to interferon in established relapsing-remitting MS, on two trials that both missed their primary endpoints. Flagged for the developer's personal verdict (SPLIT stamp).

cards.headline: D-Lay MS 2025: high-dose vitamin D in CIS cut disease activity (60.3% vs 74.1%; HR 0.66) — but relapse alone was not significantly reduced
cards.summary: D-Lay MS 2025: high-dose vitamin D in CIS cut disease activity (60.3% vs 74.1%; HR 0.66) — but relapse alone was not significantly reduced
cards.people: 316 untreated patients aged 18-55 with clinically isolated syndrome typical of MS within 90 days, serum vitamin D below 100 nmol/L, and MRI meeting dissemination-in-space criteria or at least 2 lesions with oligoclonal bands, randomised 1:1 at 36 French centres to oral cholecalciferol 100,000 IU (n=163) or placebo (n=153) every 2 weeks for 24 months. The primary outcome was disease activity: relapse and/or MRI activity (new and/or contrast-enhancing lesions).
cards.result: Disease activity occurred in 94 patients (60.3%) on vitamin D versus 109 (74.1%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.66, 95% CI 0.50-0.87; P=0.004); median time to disease activity 432 versus 224 days. All three reported MRI secondary outcomes favoured vitamin D: MRI activity (57.1% vs 65.3%; HR 0.71), new lesions (46.2% vs 59.2%; HR 0.61), contrast-enhancing lesions (18.6% vs 34.0%; HR 0.47). All 10 clinical secondary outcomes were non-significant, including relapse: 17.9% versus 21.8% (HR 0.69, 95% CI 0.42-1.16; P=0.16). Severe adverse events: 17 versus 13 patients, none related to cholecalciferol.
cards.watchOut: The significant primary endpoint is a composite dominated by MRI events; the patient-facing component (relapse) did not reach significance, and the population had low vitamin D by design.
cards.source: Thouvenot E et al.. High-Dose Vitamin D in Clinically Isolated Syndrome Typical of Multiple Sclerosis: The D-Lay MS Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2025. PMID: 40063041. Registry ID: NCT01817166 (named in the record's abstract). cards.headline: SOLAR 2019: vitamin D3 added to interferon beta-1a made no difference to NEDA-3 at 48 weeks (36.3% vs 35.3%; P=0.80)
cards.summary: SOLAR 2019: vitamin D3 added to interferon beta-1a made no difference to NEDA-3 at 48 weeks (36.3% vs 35.3%; P=0.80)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 add-on trial (SOLAR)
cards.people: 229 patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis on subcutaneous interferon beta-1a 44 micrograms three times weekly and serum 25(OH)D below 150 nmol/L, randomised 1:1 to add oral vitamin D3 14,007 IU/day (n=113) or placebo (n=116) for 48 weeks. The (revised) primary outcome was the proportion with no evidence of disease activity (NEDA-3) at week 48.
cards.result: NEDA-3 at 48 weeks: 36.3% on vitamin D3 versus 35.3% on placebo (odds ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.53-1.63; P=0.80) — the treatment made no difference on the primary outcome. Exploratory MRI outcomes favoured vitamin D3: combined unique active lesions incidence rate ratio 0.68 (95% CI 0.52-0.89; P=0.0045) and total T2 lesion volume change (P=0.035). The record classifies this as Class II evidence that supplementation did not promote NEDA-3.
cards.watchOut: The primary outcome was revised during the trial, and the positive MRI findings are exploratory; a 48-week window is short for an add-on question.
cards.source: Hupperts R et al.. Randomized trial of daily high-dose vitamin D3 in patients with RRMS receiving subcutaneous interferon beta-1a. Neurology. 2019. PMID: 31594857. Registry ID: NCT01285401 (named in the record's abstract). cards.headline: CHOLINE 2019: cholecalciferol added to interferon missed its primary relapse-rate endpoint; completer analyses favoured vitamin D
cards.summary: CHOLINE 2019: cholecalciferol added to interferon missed its primary relapse-rate endpoint; completer analyses favoured vitamin D
cards.people: 181 patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, low serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D (below 75 nmol/L), on interferon beta-1a 44 micrograms subcutaneously three times weekly, randomised 1:1 to cholecalciferol 100,000 IU or placebo every other week for 96 weeks. The primary outcome was the change in annualized relapse rate at 96 weeks.
cards.result: The primary end point was not met — cholecalciferol did not significantly affect the annualized relapse rate in the full population (the record's own evidence classification states this plainly). Among the 90 patients who completed 2-year follow-up (45 per arm), all efficacy parameters favoured cholecalciferol: relapse rate reduction (P=0.012), fewer new hypointense T1 lesions (P=0.025), lower T1 lesion volume (P=0.031), and less EDSS progression (P=0.026). Adverse events were balanced between groups.
cards.watchOut: Half the randomised patients did not complete follow-up, so the favourable completer analysis is exactly the analysis most exposed to attrition bias; the intention-to-treat answer is the null.
cards.source: Camu W et al.. Cholecalciferol in relapsing-remitting MS: A randomized clinical trial (CHOLINE). Neurol Neuroimmunol Neuroinflamm. 2019. PMID: 31454777. Registry ID: NCT01198132 (named in the record's abstract). randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (choline) 181 patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, low serum 25-hydroxyvitamin d (below 75 nmol/l), on interferon beta-1a 44 micrograms subcutaneously three times weekly, randomised 1:1 to cholecalciferol 100,000 iu or placebo every other week for 96 weeks. the primary outcome was the change in annualized relapse rate at 96 weeks. the primary end point was not met — cholecalciferol did not significantly affect the annualized relapse rate in the full population (the record's own evidence classification states this plainly). among the 90 patients who completed 2-year follow-up (45 per arm), all efficacy parameters favoured cholecalciferol: relapse rate reduction (p=0.012), fewer new hypointense t1 lesions (p=0.025), lower t1 lesion volume (p=0.031), and less edss progression (p=0.026). adverse events were balanced between groups. half the randomised patients did not complete follow-up, so the favourable completer analysis is exactly the analysis most exposed to attrition bias; the intention-to-treat answer is the null. camu w et al.. cholecalciferol in relapsing-remitting ms: a randomized clinical trial (choline). neurol neuroimmunol neuroinflamm. 2019. pmid: 31454777. registry id: nct01198132 (named in the record's abstract). mesh: adult · cholecalciferol/deficiency,therapeutic use · double-blind method · female · follow-up studies · humans · immunosuppressive agents/therapeutic use · interferon beta-1a/therapeutic use · male · middle aged · multiple sclerosis, relapsing-remitting/blood,diagnostic imaging,drug therapy · vitamin d deficiency/blood,diagnostic imaging,drug therapy

shelves.title: Relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis failing therapy: stem cell transplantation nearly abolished confirmed disability progression versus switching drugs in a single randomised trial (3 vs 34 progressors; MIST)
shelves.question: In relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis with breakthrough activity on disease-modifying therapy, does non-myeloablative autologous HSCT prevent disability progression compared with switching to another disease-modifying therapy?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Antilymphocyte Serum/therapeutic use · Combined Modality Therapy · Cyclophosphamide/therapeutic use · Disease Progression · Female · Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation/adverse effects · Humans · Immunologic Factors/therapeutic use · Immunosuppressive Agents/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Multiple Sclerosis, Relapsing-Remitting/drug therapy,therapy · Young Adult
shelves.balance: MIST produced the largest treatment separation ever recorded in a multiple sclerosis trial, and it did so on the hard endpoint. In 110 patients with relapsing-remitting MS who had relapsed at least twice in the prior year despite disease-modifying therapy, non-myeloablative autologous haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (cyclophosphamide plus antithymocyte globulin conditioning) was compared with switching to a different or higher-efficacy disease-modifying therapy. Disease progression — an EDSS rise of at least 1.0 point sustained on two evaluations 6 months apart after year 1 — occurred in 3 transplanted patients versus 34 on continued therapy (hazard ratio 0.07, 95% CI 0.02-0.24). Mean EDSS improved in the transplant group during the first year (3.38 to 2.36) while worsening on therapy (3.31 to 3.98), a between-group difference of -1.7 points. There were no deaths and no non-haematopoietic grade 4 toxicities in the transplant group. The caveats are structural, and they are on the face: a single trial of 110 patients, open-label treatment (EDSS was assessed blinded), median follow-up of 2 years, and a highly selected, young, actively relapsing population at four expert centres. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — flagged for the developer's personal verdict as an OUTSTANDING-SINGLE: a landmark single randomised trial on a hard disease-progression endpoint, per the Nov 8, 2026 rule.

cards.headline: MIST 2019: progression in 3 patients after stem cell transplant vs 34 on continued disease-modifying therapy (HR 0.07); EDSS improved 3.38 to 2.36 vs worsened 3.31 to 3.98
cards.summary: MIST 2019: progression in 3 patients after stem cell transplant vs 34 on continued disease-modifying therapy (HR 0.07); EDSS improved 3.38 to 2.36 vs worsened 3.31 to 3.98
cards.type: Randomised, open-label clinical trial with blinded EDSS assessment (MIST)
cards.people: 110 patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, at least 2 relapses while receiving disease-modifying therapy in the prior year, and EDSS 2.0-6.0, randomised at 4 centres (US, Europe, South America) to nonmyeloablative autologous HSCT with cyclophosphamide 200 mg/kg and antithymocyte globulin 6 mg/kg (n=55) or to a disease-modifying therapy of higher efficacy or a different class than the prior year (n=55). Open-label treatment; the primary end point was disease progression (EDSS increase of at least 1.0 point after at least 1 year, confirmed 6 months apart). Median follow-up 2 years (mean 2.8).
cards.result: Disease progression occurred in 3 patients in the HSCT group and 34 in the therapy group; median time to progression was not calculable for HSCT and 24 months for therapy (hazard ratio 0.07, 95% CI 0.02-0.24; P<0.001). During the first year, mean EDSS decreased (improved) from 3.38 to 2.36 with HSCT and increased (worsened) from 3.31 to 3.98 on therapy (between-group mean difference -1.7, 95% CI -2.03 to -1.29; P<0.001). There were no deaths, and no HSCT patient developed a nonhaematopoietic grade 4 toxicity.
cards.watchOut: A single trial, and a small one for a procedure of this intensity: 110 highly selected patients, median follow-up 2 years. Fertility, late malignancy and very-late autoimmune effects of conditioning sit outside the record's window. (Note: the slate draft quoted denominators of 52 and 51; the record reports the events against the 55-per-arm randomised population, and the record governs.)

shelves.title: Multiple sclerosis walking impairment: dalfampridine produced timed-walk responders in 35-43% versus 8-9% on placebo across two phase 3 trials, with responders walking about 25% faster
shelves.question: In people with multiple sclerosis and walking impairment, does extended-release dalfampridine (fampridine) increase walking speed compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: 4-Aminopyridine/blood,therapeutic use · Adult · Aged · Disability Evaluation · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Movement Disorders/drug therapy,etiology · Multiple Sclerosis/blood,complications,drug therapy · Potassium Channel Blockers/blood,therapeutic use · Walking/physiology · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Extended-release dalfampridine (fampridine) is a responder drug: in two phase 3 placebo-controlled trials it made a consistent minority of people with multiple sclerosis walk measurably faster, and did nothing detectable for the rest. In the 2010 confirmatory trial, timed-walk responders — patients with consistent improvement on the Timed 25-Foot Walk — were 42.9% on dalfampridine 10 mg twice daily versus 9.3% on placebo over 9 weeks; the earlier 2009 phase 3 trial found the near-identical separation of 35% versus 8% over 14 weeks. Responders' walking speed improved by about 25% in both trials (24.7% and 25.2%), and the effect was maintained across the dosing interval. There is no claim here about relapses, progression or disability accumulation — the drug treats a symptom, in the subset who respond, and the responder definition was built into both trials' primary endpoints. Seizure risk at higher-than-licensed doses is the class warning from the wider record; within these trials the records report no new safety findings. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): two consistent randomised trials on a pre-specified responder endpoint, for walking speed only.

cards.headline: Dalfampridine phase 3 (2010): timed-walk responders 42.9% vs 9.3% on placebo; responders walked 24.7% faster
cards.summary: Dalfampridine phase 3 (2010): timed-walk responders 42.9% vs 9.3% on placebo; responders walked 24.7% faster
cards.people: Patients with definite multiple sclerosis of any course type at 39 centres, randomised to dalfampridine extended-release 10 mg twice daily (n=120) or placebo (n=119) for 9 weeks. The primary outcome was the proportion of timed-walk responders — consistent improvement on the Timed 25-Foot Walk; the modified intention-to-treat population was 119 dalfampridine and 118 placebo patients.
cards.result: Timed-walk responders: 51/119 (42.9%) on dalfampridine versus 11/118 (9.3%) on placebo (P<0.0001) — an absolute difference of about 34 percentage points. Among dalfampridine responders, mean walking-speed improvement over the 8-week efficacy period was 24.7% from baseline (95% CI 21.0-28.4%), and 25.7% at the last on-treatment visit 8-12 hours postdose, showing the effect persisted between doses. There were no new safety findings.
cards.watchOut: The responder endpoint identifies the benefiting subset after the fact of randomisation — most patients (57%) did not meet it, and the trial offers no way to predict responders in advance.
cards.source: Goodman AD et al.. A phase 3 trial of extended release oral dalfampridine in multiple sclerosis. Ann Neurol. 2010. PMID: 20976768. Registry ID: none in the record.
