cards.headline: Fampridine phase 3 (2009): timed-walk responders 35% vs 8% on placebo; responders' speed improved 25.2%
cards.summary: Fampridine phase 3 (2009): timed-walk responders 35% vs 8% on placebo; responders' speed improved 25.2%
cards.people: 301 patients with any type of multiple sclerosis and ambulatory deficits, randomised to sustained-release fampridine 10 mg twice daily (n=229) or placebo (n=72) for 14 weeks; the modified intention-to-treat population was 296. The primary outcome was the proportion of timed-walk responders (consistent improvement on the Timed 25-Foot Walk), with the 12-item Multiple Sclerosis Walking Scale used to validate the response criterion.
cards.result: Timed-walk responders: 78/224 (35%) on fampridine versus 6/72 (8%) on placebo (P<0.0001) — an absolute difference of about 27 percentage points. Walking speed in fampridine responders improved 25.2% (95% CI 21.5-28.8%), maintained throughout treatment, versus 4.7% in placebo responders; responders also improved more on the 12-item walking scale than non-responders (-6.84 vs +0.05 points; P=0.0002). Safety data were consistent with previous studies.
cards.watchOut: The randomisation was unbalanced (229 vs 72 by design), and fampridine/dalfampridine is the same molecule under two names — these are two trials of one drug, not two drugs agreeing.
cards.source: Goodman AD et al.. Sustained-release oral fampridine in multiple sclerosis: a randomised, double-blind, controlled trial. Lancet. 2009. PMID: 19249634. shelves.title: Aquaporin-4-positive NMOSD: eculizumab cut adjudicated relapses to 3% versus 43% on placebo in a single trial stopped early for effect — disability unchanged within the trial, one death on treatment (PREVENT)
shelves.question: In aquaporin-4-IgG-positive neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, does eculizumab prevent relapses compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Aquaporin 4/immunology · Autoantibodies/blood · Complement C5/antagonists & inhibitors · Complement Inactivating Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Disability Evaluation · Disease Progression · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Headache/chemically induced · Humans · Immunoglobulin G/blood · Immunosuppressive Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Male · Neuromyelitis Optica/drug therapy,immunology · Quality of Life · Respiratory Tract Infections/etiology · Secondary Prevention
shelves.balance: PREVENT nearly abolished relapses in aquaporin-4-IgG-positive neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder — a disease where each relapse can take sight or the ability to walk, and recovery is poor. In 143 adults (pre-treatment annualized relapse rate about 2.0; 76% continuing background immunosuppression), adjudicated relapses occurred in 3 of 96 patients on eculizumab versus 20 of 47 (43%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.06, 95% CI 0.02-0.20), and the adjudicated annualized relapse rate was 0.02 versus 0.35 (rate ratio 0.04). The trial was stopped after 23 of the 24 prespecified relapses because the timing of the final event could not be estimated. Two qualifications belong on the face: disability scores did not differ significantly between groups over the trial's course (EDSS change -0.18 versus +0.12; least-squares mean difference -0.29, 95% CI -0.59 to 0.01) — the benefit is relapse prevention, not measured disability gain — and there was one death from pulmonary empyema in the eculizumab group, alongside more upper respiratory infections and headaches. Terminal complement blockade also carries the meningococcal risk that governs vaccination practice around this drug class. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — flagged for the developer's personal verdict as an OUTSTANDING-SINGLE (landmark single randomised blinded trial; relapse is the disease's major-complication endpoint) and because the balance carries a death in the treatment arm.

cards.headline: PREVENT 2019: adjudicated relapses in 3/96 on eculizumab vs 20/47 (43%) on placebo (HR 0.06); one death from pulmonary empyema on eculizumab
cards.summary: PREVENT 2019: adjudicated relapses in 3/96 on eculizumab vs 20/47 (43%) on placebo (HR 0.06); one death from pulmonary empyema on eculizumab
cards.people: 143 adults with aquaporin-4-IgG-positive NMOSD randomised 2:1 to intravenous eculizumab (900 mg weekly for 4 doses, then 1,200 mg every 2 weeks) or matched placebo; stable-dose immunosuppressive therapy could continue (76% did). Mean annualized relapse rate in the 24 months before enrolment was 1.99. The primary end point was the first adjudicated relapse; the trial was stopped after 23 of 24 prespecified adjudicated relapses.
cards.result: Adjudicated relapses: 3 of 96 (3%) on eculizumab versus 20 of 47 (43%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.06, 95% CI 0.02-0.20; P<0.001) — an absolute difference of about 40 percentage points. Adjudicated annualized relapse rate 0.02 versus 0.35 (rate ratio 0.04, 95% CI 0.01-0.15). EDSS change did not differ significantly (-0.18 vs +0.12; difference -0.29, 95% CI -0.59 to 0.01). Upper respiratory tract infections and headaches were more common on eculizumab; one eculizumab patient died of pulmonary empyema.
cards.watchOut: Early stopping on the sponsor-facing side of an overwhelming effect can inflate the estimate, and three-quarters of patients were on background immunosuppression, so the pure monotherapy effect is less precisely known than the headline.

shelves.title: CIDP: intravenous immunoglobulin improved disability in 54% versus 21% on placebo (ICE), and weekly subcutaneous immunoglobulin prevented relapse in maintenance — 33-39% versus 63% relapsing or withdrawn (PATH)
shelves.question: In chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy, does immunoglobulin — intravenous for induction, subcutaneous for maintenance — improve disability and prevent relapse compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Caprylates · Chromatography · Cross-Over Studies · Disability Evaluation · Double-Blind Method · Endpoint Determination · Female · Humans · Immunoglobulins, Intravenous/isolation & purification,therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Polyradiculoneuropathy, Chronic Inflammatory Demyelinating/therapy · Recurrence · Research Design · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Immunoglobulin works at both ends of CIDP care, and each route has its own randomised proof. For induction, ICE randomised 117 patients to intravenous immunoglobulin (a 10% caprylate-chromatography purified preparation, given every 3 weeks) or placebo: 54% improved by at least 1 INCAT disability point and sustained the improvement to week 24, versus 21% on placebo — an absolute difference of 33.5 percentage points — with grip strength also improved and, in the blinded extension, a longer time to relapse for those who stayed on immunoglobulin (P=0.011). For maintenance, PATH took 172 patients already known to respond to intravenous immunoglobulin and randomised them to weekly subcutaneous immunoglobulin at 0.2 or 0.4 g/kg or placebo for 24 weeks: relapse or withdrawal occurred in 63% on placebo versus 39% (low dose) and 33% (high dose) — absolute risk reductions of 25 and 30 percentage points, with no significant difference between the two subcutaneous doses. Serious adverse events were uncommon in both trials (in ICE, 0.8% of immunoglobulin infusions versus 1.9% of placebo infusions). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): two randomised trials answer the induction and maintenance questions separately and consistently.

cards.headline: ICE 2008: IVIg improved disability in 54% vs 21% on placebo, sustained to week 24 (difference 33.5 points)
cards.summary: ICE 2008: IVIg improved disability in 54% vs 21% on placebo, sustained to week 24 (difference 33.5 points)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial with response-conditional crossover (ICE)
cards.people: 117 patients with CIDP meeting INCAT neurophysiological criteria, in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, response-conditional crossover trial: immunoglobulin intravenous (10% caprylate-chromatography purified) or placebo every 3 weeks for up to 24 weeks, with non-responders crossing over; responders could enter a blinded 24-week extension. The primary outcome was the percentage maintaining an improvement of at least 1 point in adjusted INCAT disability score through week 24.
cards.result: In the first period, 32/59 (54%) on immunoglobulin versus 12/58 (21%) on placebo improved and maintained it to week 24 (treatment difference 33.5%, 95% CI 15.4-51.7; P=0.0002). Grip strength improved in the dominant hand (difference 10.9 kPa; P=0.0008) and non-dominant hand (8.6 kPa; P=0.005); crossover results were similar. In the extension, patients continuing immunoglobulin had a longer time to relapse than those switched to placebo (P=0.011). Serious adverse events occurred in 0.8% of immunoglobulin infusions versus 1.9% of placebo infusions; the commonest immunoglobulin events were headache, pyrexia and hypertension.
cards.watchOut: The trial tested one specific purified preparation; it is carded as the immunoglobulin class question because no head-to-head preparation trial exists, but strict equivalence of all products is assumed, not shown.
cards.source: Hughes RA et al.. Intravenous immune globulin (10% caprylate-chromatography purified) for the treatment of chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (ICE study): a randomised placebo-controlled trial. Lancet Neurol. 2008. PMID: 18178525. Registry ID: NCT00220740 (named in the record's abstract). cards.headline: PATH 2018: subcutaneous immunoglobulin maintenance — relapse or withdrawal 33-39% vs 63% on placebo over 24 weeks
cards.summary: PATH 2018: subcutaneous immunoglobulin maintenance — relapse or withdrawal 33-39% vs 63% on placebo over 24 weeks
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 withdrawal-maintenance trial (PATH)
cards.people: 172 adults with definite or probable CIDP who had responded to intravenous immunoglobulin, at 69 centres, randomised 1:1:1 to weekly subcutaneous immunoglobulin (a 20% solution) at 0.2 g/kg or 0.4 g/kg, or placebo (2% human albumin), for 24 weeks. The primary outcome was the proportion with a CIDP relapse or withdrawn for any other reason during treatment.
cards.result: Relapse or withdrawal: 36/57 (63%) on placebo versus 22/57 (39%) on low-dose and 19/58 (33%) on high-dose subcutaneous immunoglobulin (P=0.0007) — absolute risk reductions of 25 percentage points (95% CI 6-41) and 30 points (12-46); high versus low dose did not differ (6 points; P=0.32). Causally related adverse events occurred in 27% overall (18% placebo, 30% low dose, 34% high dose). Eleven serious adverse events occurred in 6 patients (3%); only one — an acute allergic skin reaction on low-dose — was judged causally related.
cards.watchOut: PATH enrolled only known intravenous-immunoglobulin responders, so it answers maintenance in responders — it cannot support starting subcutaneous treatment in unselected or immunoglobulin-naïve patients.
cards.source: van Schaik IN et al.. Subcutaneous immunoglobulin for maintenance treatment in chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (PATH): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial. Lancet Neurol. 2018. PMID: 29122523. Registry ID: NCT01545076 (named in the record's abstract). cards.summary: Synthesis: induction and maintenance each proven against placebo — LIKELY

shelves.title: Parkinson's motor fluctuations: opicapone 50 mg once daily cut OFF time by about an hour a day versus placebo in two phase 3 trials — lower doses failed (BIPARK I & II)
shelves.question: In Parkinson's disease with end-of-dose motor fluctuations on levodopa, does once-daily opicapone reduce daily OFF time compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antiparkinson Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects,pharmacology · Catechol O-Methyltransferase Inhibitors/administration & dosage,pharmacology · Catechols/administration & dosage,pharmacology · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Dyskinesia, Drug-Induced/etiology,prevention & control · Europe · Female · Humans · Levodopa/administration & dosage,adverse effects,pharmacology · Male · Middle Aged · Nitriles/administration & dosage,pharmacology · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Oxadiazoles/administration & dosage,pharmacology · Parkinson Disease/drug therapy
shelves.balance: Once-daily opicapone 50 mg, added to levodopa, buys about an hour of OFF time a day — and two phase 3 trials put the number in the same place. In BIPARK I, the change in absolute OFF time was -116.8 minutes on opicapone 50 mg versus -56.0 minutes on placebo (difference -60.8 minutes; P=0.0015), and opicapone was non-inferior to entacapone given with every levodopa dose (-96.3 minutes); the 5 mg and 25 mg doses were not significantly different from placebo. BIPARK II repeated the design without the entacapone arm: OFF time fell by 118.8 minutes on 50 mg versus 64.5 minutes on placebo (adjusted difference -54.3 minutes; P=0.008), again with 25 mg not significant (-37.2 minutes; P=0.11), and the reduction persisted through a 1-year open-label phase. The excess harm is the expected dopaminergic one — dyskinesia was the commonest adverse event on opicapone in BIPARK I (18 of 115 patients at 50 mg versus 5 of 121 on placebo). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): consistent, dose-specific effects in two randomised trials — for the 50 mg dose only.

cards.headline: BIPARK I 2016: opicapone 50 mg cut OFF time by 116.8 min vs 56.0 min on placebo (difference -60.8 min) and was non-inferior to entacapone
cards.summary: BIPARK I 2016: opicapone 50 mg cut OFF time by 116.8 min vs 56.0 min on placebo (difference -60.8 min) and was non-inferior to entacapone
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo- and active-controlled trial (BIPARK I)
cards.people: 600 patients with Parkinson's disease and end-of-dose motor fluctuations on levodopa at 106 European centres, randomised to opicapone 5 mg, 25 mg or 50 mg once daily, placebo, or entacapone 200 mg with every levodopa intake, for 14-15 weeks. The primary endpoint was the change in absolute time in the off state from patient diaries; 590 patients formed the full analysis set.
cards.result: Change in OFF time: -116.8 minutes on opicapone 50 mg versus -56.0 minutes on placebo (mean difference -60.8 minutes, 95% CI -97.2 to -24.4; P=0.0015) and -96.3 minutes on entacapone; opicapone 50 mg was non-inferior to entacapone (difference -26.2 minutes; P=0.0051 for non-inferiority). Opicapone 5 mg (P=0.056) and 25 mg (P=0.080) were not significantly different from placebo. Dyskinesia was the most frequent adverse event (18 patients on opicapone 50 mg, 17 on 5 mg, 10 on entacapone, 9 on 25 mg, 5 on placebo), followed by insomnia and constipation; serious adverse events were few and similar across groups.
cards.watchOut: Only the 50 mg dose cleared significance; the near-miss P values at 5 mg and 25 mg are dose-finding information, not near-proof of benefit.
cards.source: Ferreira JJ et al.. Opicapone as an adjunct to levodopa in patients with Parkinson's disease and end-of-dose motor fluctuations: a randomised, double-blind, controlled trial. Lancet Neurol. 2016. PMID: 26725544. Registry ID: NCT01568073; EudraCT 2010-021860-13 (both named in the record's abstract). cards.headline: BIPARK II 2017: opicapone 50 mg cut OFF time by 118.8 min vs 64.5 min on placebo (difference -54.3 min; P=0.008); 25 mg not significant
cards.summary: BIPARK II 2017: opicapone 50 mg cut OFF time by 118.8 min vs 64.5 min on placebo (difference -54.3 min; P=0.008); 25 mg not significant
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (BIPARK II)
cards.people: 427 patients with Parkinson's disease and end-of-dose motor fluctuations (mean awake OFF time at least 1.5 hours, excluding morning akinesia) on levodopa, randomised to opicapone 25 mg/day (n=129), opicapone 50 mg/day (n=154) or placebo (n=144) in a 14-15-week double-blind phase, followed by a 1-year open-label phase on opicapone. The primary outcome was the change from baseline in absolute OFF time from patient diaries.
cards.result: Least-squares mean OFF-time change: -64.5 minutes on placebo, -101.7 minutes on 25 mg (adjusted difference -37.2 minutes, 95% CI -80.8 to 6.4; P=0.11 — not significant) and -118.8 minutes on 50 mg (adjusted difference -54.3 minutes, 95% CI -96.2 to -12.4; P=0.008). The OFF-time reduction was sustained through the open-label phase (-126.3 minutes at 1 year). The most common adverse events on opicapone were dyskinesia, constipation and dry mouth; 11.9% discontinued during the double-blind phase.
cards.watchOut: Diary-measured OFF time is a symptomatic endpoint; neither BIPARK trial addresses progression, falls or quality of life as primary outcomes.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two trials, one effective dose, about an hour a day — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: two trials, one effective dose, about an hour a day — LIKELY
cards.people: Two randomised double-blind trials of once-daily opicapone added to levodopa in Parkinson's disease with end-of-dose fluctuations (BIPARK I, n=600, with entacapone comparator; BIPARK II, n=427).
cards.result: OFF-time difference versus placebo at 50 mg: -60.8 minutes (BIPARK I) and -54.3 minutes (BIPARK II); 25 mg not significant in BIPARK II and 5/25 mg not significant in BIPARK I. Non-inferior to entacapone in BIPARK I. Principal excess harm: dyskinesia. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for the 50 mg dose.

shelves.title: Parkinson's OFF episodes: istradefylline cut OFF time by roughly 0.7-1 hour a day versus placebo across three randomised trials — a real but small diary-measured effect
shelves.question: In Parkinson's disease treated with levodopa, does the adenosine A2A antagonist istradefylline reduce OFF time compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adenosine A2 Receptor Antagonists · Aged · Antiparkinson Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Catechol O-Methyltransferase Inhibitors · Chronic Disease · Dopamine Agonists/administration & dosage · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Dyskinesia, Drug-Induced/etiology · Enzyme Inhibitors/administration & dosage · Female · Humans · Levodopa/administration & dosage · Male · Nausea/chemically induced · Parkinson Disease/drug therapy · Purines/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Safety · Selegiline/administration & dosage · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Istradefylline, the adenosine A2A antagonist, reduces OFF time by a modest amount — somewhere under an hour to about an hour a day — and the record behind it is uneven in design even where it agrees in direction. The first randomised trial (2003, n=83) was explicitly exploratory, with no prespecified primary outcome among 19 analysed variables: OFF time fell by 1.2 hours on istradefylline while rising 0.5 hours on placebo (P=0.004), and ON time with dyskinesia increased even though dyskinesia severity did not. A 231-patient phase 3 trial in 2008 found a placebo-corrected OFF-time reduction of 0.7 hours at 20 mg/day (P=0.03), with no significant change in ON time with troublesome dyskinesia. A 373-patient Japanese trial in 2013 found OFF-time reductions of about 1 hour at both 20 mg and 40 mg versus 0.23 hours on placebo (P=0.003 for both), with dyskinesia the commonest adverse event (about 12-13% versus 4%). None of the trials shows an effect on UPDRS motor scores or global impression beyond the diary endpoints. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): three randomised trials point the same way, but the effect is small, diary-measured, and the founding trial was exploratory — enough for moderate confidence, not more.

cards.headline: Istradefylline 2003: OFF time fell 1.2 hours vs a 0.5-hour rise on placebo in a small exploratory trial with no prespecified primary outcome
cards.summary: Istradefylline 2003: OFF time fell 1.2 hours vs a 0.5-hour rise on placebo in a small exploratory trial with no prespecified primary outcome
cards.people: 83 patients with levodopa-treated Parkinson's disease with both motor fluctuations and peak-dose dyskinesias, randomised to placebo (n=29), istradefylline up to 20 mg/day (n=26) or up to 40 mg/day (n=28) for 12 weeks. The study was exploratory: there was no prespecified primary outcome measure, and 19 outcome variables were analysed. (The slate draft named Bara-Jimenez as first author; the record's first author is Hauser — the record governs.)
cards.result: By home diary, the proportion of awake time OFF fell by 7.1% on istradefylline versus a 2.2% increase on placebo (P=0.008); OFF time decreased by 1.2 hours versus an increase of 0.5 hours (P=0.004). Dyskinesia severity was unchanged, but ON time with dyskinesia increased (percent P=0.002; hours P=0.001). UPDRS scores and Clinical Global Impression did not differ. Withdrawals: 24% on placebo, 20% on istradefylline. Nausea was the most common adverse event.
cards.watchOut: With 19 outcomes and no prespecified primary, the significant diary results carry a multiple-comparison discount the later trials only partly repay.
cards.source: Hauser RA et al.. Randomized trial of the adenosine A(2A) receptor antagonist istradefylline in advanced PD. Neurology. 2003. PMID: 12913187. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Istradefylline phase 3 (2008): placebo-corrected OFF-time reduction of 0.7 hours at 20 mg/day (P=0.03)
cards.summary: Istradefylline phase 3 (2008): placebo-corrected OFF-time reduction of 0.7 hours at 20 mg/day (P=0.03)
cards.people: 231 subjects with Parkinson's disease on stable levodopa regimens (90% also on other antiparkinsonian medication) with at least 3 hours of average daily OFF time, randomised to istradefylline 20 mg once daily (n=116) or placebo (n=115) for 12 weeks in a multicentre double-blind phase 3 study.
cards.result: Istradefylline produced significant placebo-corrected reductions in daily OFF time: 4.6% of awake time (P=0.03) and 0.7 hours (P=0.03). Changes in ON time with troublesome dyskinesia did not differ significantly between groups. Withdrawals for adverse events: 5.2% on istradefylline, 6.1% on placebo. Dyskinesia, lightheadedness, tremor, constipation and weight decrease were reported more often on istradefylline.
cards.watchOut: A 0.7-hour diary difference is at the edge of what patients can feel; the trial's own framing is statistical, and ON-time quality (troublesome dyskinesia) did not improve.
cards.source: Hauser RA et al.. Study of istradefylline in patients with Parkinson's disease on levodopa with motor fluctuations. Mov Disord. 2008. PMID: 18831530. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.summary: Istradefylline Japanese trial 2013: OFF time fell about 1 hour at 20 mg and 40 mg vs 0.23 hours on placebo (P=0.003)
cards.people: 373 Japanese patients with Parkinson's disease and motor complications on levodopa, randomised to placebo (n=126), istradefylline 20 mg/day (n=123) or 40 mg/day (n=124) for 12 weeks. The primary efficacy variable was the change in daily OFF time.

shelves.title: Parkinson's motor fluctuations: apomorphine infusion cut OFF time by 2.47 hours a day versus 0.58 on saline in the first double-blind trial of the therapy (TOLEDO)
shelves.question: In Parkinson's disease with motor fluctuations uncontrolled by oral therapy, does continuous subcutaneous apomorphine infusion reduce OFF time compared with saline infusion?
shelves.mesh: Age Factors · Aged · Analysis of Variance · Antiparkinson Agents/administration & dosage · Apomorphine/administration & dosage · Double-Blind Method · Female · Gait Disorders, Neurologic/complications,drug therapy · Humans · Infusions, Subcutaneous · Longitudinal Studies · Male · Middle Aged · Parkinson Disease/complications,drug therapy · Severity of Illness Index · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Apomorphine infusion was used for decades on open-label evidence; TOLEDO is its first double-blind trial, and it confirms the clinical impression at meaningful size. In 106 patients with Parkinson's disease for more than 3 years and motor fluctuations uncontrolled despite optimised oral or transdermal therapy, waking-hours subcutaneous infusion of apomorphine (mean final dose 4.68 mg/h) reduced daily OFF time by 2.47 hours over 12 weeks, versus 0.58 hours on saline placebo infusion — a difference of -1.89 hours per day (95% CI -3.16 to -0.62; P=0.0025). The infusion was well tolerated with no unexpected safety signals in the trial, though 6 apomorphine patients withdrew because of treatment-related adverse events. What the trial does not give is duration or comparison: 12 blinded weeks, no head-to-head against deep brain stimulation or intestinal levodopa gel, and an open-label extension that cannot separate drug effect from expectation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — flagged for the developer's personal verdict as a single-trial shelf: one well-conducted randomised trial, a large symptomatic effect, and nothing behind it if the estimate is optimistic.

cards.headline: TOLEDO 2018: apomorphine infusion cut OFF time by 2.47 h/day vs 0.58 h/day on saline infusion (difference -1.89 h; P=0.0025)
cards.summary: TOLEDO 2018: apomorphine infusion cut OFF time by 2.47 h/day vs 0.58 h/day on saline infusion (difference -1.89 h; P=0.0025)
cards.people: 107 patients with Parkinson's disease diagnosed more than 3 years earlier and motor fluctuations not adequately controlled by medical treatment, at 23 European hospitals, randomised 1:1 to apomorphine 3-8 mg/h or placebo saline by subcutaneous infusion during waking hours (about 16 h/day) for 12 weeks, with dose and oral medication adjustable over the first 4 weeks. The primary endpoint was the absolute change in daily OFF time from patient diaries in the full analysis set (n=106).
cards.result: OFF time changed by -2.47 hours per day (SD 3.70) on apomorphine (mean final dose 4.68 mg/h) versus -0.58 hours per day (SD 2.80) on placebo — a difference of -1.89 hours per day (95% CI -3.16 to -0.62; P=0.0025). Apomorphine was well tolerated without unexpected safety signals; 6 apomorphine patients withdrew because of treatment-related adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Saline infusion is a strong placebo ritual and diaries are subjective; the -0.58 h placebo response shows part of the context effect the -1.89 h difference already nets out — but 12 weeks cannot speak to skin nodules, neuropsychiatric effects or durability over years.
cards.source: Katzenschlager R et al.. Apomorphine subcutaneous infusion in patients with Parkinson's disease with persistent motor fluctuations (TOLEDO): a multicentre, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial. shelves.title: Levodopa-induced dyskinesia: extended-release amantadine reduced dyskinesia scores and OFF time in two randomised trials — with hallucinations in up to a quarter of patients (EASE LID; EASE LID 3)
shelves.question: In Parkinson's disease with levodopa-induced dyskinesia, does extended-release amantadine reduce dyskinesia and OFF time compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Amantadine/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Antiparkinson Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Drug Delivery Systems · Dyskinesia, Drug-Induced/drug therapy,etiology · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Levodopa/adverse effects · Male · Middle Aged · North America · Parkinson Disease/drug therapy · Retrospective Studies · Severity of Illness Index · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Extended-release amantadine (274 mg at bedtime) is the first drug shown in randomised trials to reduce levodopa-induced dyskinesia — and it trims OFF time at the same time, which no antidyskinetic before it had done. In EASE LID, the Unified Dyskinesia Rating Scale total score fell by 15.9 points on amantadine ER versus 8.0 on placebo at week 12 (difference -7.9; P<0.001), and OFF time fell 0.6 hours while rising 0.3 hours on placebo (difference -0.9 hours; P=0.02). EASE LID 3, a smaller trial of identical design, found the same pattern larger: dyskinesia score change -20.7 versus -6.3 (difference -14.4; P<0.0001) and an OFF-time difference of -1.1 hours (P=0.0199). The harm side is substantial and consistent: in EASE LID, visual hallucinations in 23.8% versus 1.7%, peripheral oedema 23.8% versus 0, dizziness 22.2% versus 0, and adverse-event discontinuation in 20.6% versus 6.9%; EASE LID 3 discontinuations were 19% versus 8%. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): two concordant randomised trials on both endpoints, with a tolerability price that belongs in the same sentence.

cards.headline: EASE LID 2017: amantadine ER cut dyskinesia scores by 7.9 points more than placebo and OFF time by 0.9 hours — hallucinations in 23.8% vs 1.7%
cards.summary: EASE LID 2017: amantadine ER cut dyskinesia scores by 7.9 points more than placebo and OFF time by 0.9 hours — hallucinations in 23.8% vs 1.7%
cards.people: Patients with Parkinson's disease on levodopa with at least 1 hour of troublesome dyskinesia daily of at least mild functional impact, at 44 North American sites, randomised to extended-release amantadine 274 mg at bedtime or placebo for up to 25 weeks; 126 randomised, 121 in the modified intention-to-treat population. The primary endpoint was the change in Unified Dyskinesia Rating Scale total score at week 12; OFF time was a key secondary endpoint. (The slate draft named Hauser as first author; the record's first author is Pahwa — the record governs.)
cards.result: UDysRS change at week 12: -15.9 points on amantadine ER versus -8.0 on placebo (treatment difference -7.9, 95% CI -12.5 to -3.3; P<0.001). OFF time: -0.6 hours versus +0.3 hours (difference -0.9 hours, 95% CI -1.6 to -0.2; P=0.02). Adverse events on amantadine ER versus placebo: visual hallucinations 23.8% vs 1.7%, peripheral oedema 23.8% vs 0%, dizziness 22.2% vs 0%. Discontinuation for adverse events: 20.6% vs 6.9%.
cards.watchOut: One in five patients stopped the drug for adverse events; the efficacy averages are computed over a population that tolerates it better than the average clinic patient may.
cards.source: Pahwa R et al.. ADS-5102 (Amantadine) Extended-Release Capsules for Levodopa-Induced Dyskinesia in Parkinson Disease (EASE LID Study): A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Neurol. 2017. cards.headline: EASE LID 3 2017: dyskinesia score difference -14.4 points and OFF-time difference -1.1 hours, replicating EASE LID
cards.summary: EASE LID 3 2017: dyskinesia score difference -14.4 points and OFF-time difference -1.1 hours, replicating EASE LID
cards.people: Patients with Parkinson's disease with at least 1 hour of troublesome dyskinesia of at least mild functional impact, randomised to extended-release amantadine 274 mg at bedtime or placebo for 13 weeks. The primary efficacy analysis was the change in Unified Dyskinesia Rating Scale total score at week 12 in the modified intention-to-treat population (37 amantadine, 38 placebo); OFF time was a key secondary measure.
cards.result: UDysRS change: -20.7 points on amantadine ER versus -6.3 on placebo (treatment difference -14.4, 95% CI -20.4 to -8.3; P<0.0001). OFF time: -0.5 hours versus +0.6 hours (difference -1.1 hours, 95% CI -2.0 to -0.2; P=0.0199). Common adverse events versus placebo: dry mouth 13.5% vs 2.6%, nausea 13.5% vs 2.6%, decreased appetite 10.8% vs 0%, insomnia 10.8% vs 0%, orthostatic hypotension 10.8% vs 0%, visual hallucinations 8.1% vs 5.3%. Discontinuation for adverse events: 19% vs 8%.
cards.watchOut: Small trial (75 in the efficacy population), so its larger point estimate should be read as replication of direction, not a more precise size; a pooled analysis of the two trials (UDysRS difference -10.1 points) exists in the record set but is not carded separately (one-home rule).

shelves.title: Parkinson's disease modification: rasagiline's delayed-start signature appeared at 1 mg in ADAGIO and at both doses in TEMPO but failed outright at 2 mg in ADAGIO — the claim remains unproven
shelves.question: In early Parkinson's disease, does starting rasagiline immediately rather than 9 months later leave patients ahead — the delayed-start test of disease modification?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Indans/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Male · Middle Aged · Monoamine Oxidase Inhibitors/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Neuroprotective Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Parkinson Disease/classification,drug therapy · Research Design · Severity of Illness Index
shelves.balance: This shelf grades one claim only: that starting rasagiline early changes the disease's course, as tested by the delayed-start design. The design's logic is that if early starters remain ahead after everyone is on the drug, the head start cannot be a mere symptomatic effect. TEMPO (404 patients) found exactly that pattern over 12 months: patients on rasagiline 2 mg/day for the full year had a 2.29-unit smaller increase in total UPDRS than patients switched from placebo to rasagiline 2 mg at 6 months (P=0.01), with the 1 mg group also ahead (-1.82 units; P=0.05). ADAGIO (1,176 patients, 72 weeks) then split by dose: early-start 1 mg met all three prespecified hierarchical endpoints (baseline-to-week-72 change 2.82 versus 4.52 points; P=0.02), but early-start 2 mg failed the same endpoint outright (3.47 versus 3.11 points; P=0.60 — the delayed group nominally ahead). A disease-modifying drug should not lose its signature when the dose doubles, and regulators declined the claim; the ADAGIO authors themselves wrote that the results 'must be interpreted with caution'. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) for the disease-modification claim: the design produced its predicted pattern in three of four dose-arms across two trials and failed in the fourth, which is precisely the shape of an unproven claim. Rasagiline's symptomatic benefit is a separate question and is not graded here. Flagged for the developer's personal verdict: this is a claim-interpretation shelf where reasonable readers split.

cards.headline: TEMPO delayed-start 2004: a year of rasagiline beat a 6-month delay by 2.29 UPDRS units at 2 mg and 1.82 units at 1 mg
cards.summary: TEMPO delayed-start 2004: a year of rasagiline beat a 6-month delay by 2.29 UPDRS units at 2 mg and 1.82 units at 1 mg
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, delayed-start trial (TEMPO delayed-start analysis)
cards.people: 404 subjects with early Parkinson's disease not requiring dopaminergic therapy at 32 US and Canadian sites, randomised in a double-blind delayed-start design to rasagiline 1 mg/day or 2 mg/day for 1 year, or placebo for 6 months followed by rasagiline 2 mg/day for 6 months. The main outcome was the change in total UPDRS score from baseline to 12 months; 371 subjects entered the 1-year efficacy analysis.
cards.result: Subjects treated with rasagiline 2 mg/day for 1 year had a 2.29-unit smaller increase in mean adjusted total UPDRS score than subjects treated with placebo for 6 months then rasagiline 2 mg/day (P=0.01). The mean adjusted difference between the delayed-start group and those receiving rasagiline 1 mg/day for 1 year was -1.82 units (P=0.05). The authors concluded that 12 months of rasagiline at either dose produced less functional decline than a 6-month delay.
cards.watchOut: TEMPO's delayed arm all received 2 mg in phase 2 regardless of phase-1 assignment possibilities, and the 12-month horizon is short for a modification claim; the differences (about 2 UPDRS units) are small against a 176-point scale.
cards.source: Parkinson Study Group. A controlled, randomized, delayed-start study of rasagiline in early Parkinson disease. Arch Neurol. 2004. PMID: 15096406. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: ADAGIO 2009: early-start rasagiline 1 mg met all three delayed-start endpoints — 2 mg failed the key one (P=0.60)
cards.summary: ADAGIO 2009: early-start rasagiline 1 mg met all three delayed-start endpoints — 2 mg failed the key one (P=0.60)
cards.people: 1,176 subjects with untreated Parkinson's disease randomised to early-start rasagiline 1 mg or 2 mg daily for 72 weeks, or placebo for 36 weeks followed by the same rasagiline dose for 36 weeks (delayed-start). A positive result required all three hierarchical UPDRS endpoints: superiority to placebo in rate of change weeks 12-36; superiority to delayed-start in baseline-to-week-72 change; and noninferiority of slope weeks 48-72.
cards.result: At 1 mg/day, early-start met all endpoints: rate of worsening weeks 12-36 was 0.09 vs 0.14 points/week (P=0.01); baseline-to-week-72 change 2.82 vs 4.52 points (P=0.02); week 48-72 slopes identical (0.085/week; noninferiority P<0.001). At 2 mg/day the second endpoint failed: baseline-to-week-72 change was 3.47 points early-start versus 3.11 delayed-start (P=0.60). The authors concluded the 1 mg results were consistent with a possible disease-modifying effect, the 2 mg results were not, and that the divergence means the study 'must be interpreted with caution'.
cards.watchOut: The 2 mg failure is not a detail: a genuine disease-modifying effect should strengthen or persist with dose, and its disappearance is the strongest internal evidence against the claim. UPDRS is also symptom-sensitive, so residual symptomatic effects can masquerade as modification in this design.
cards.source: Olanow CW et al.. A double-blind, delayed-start trial of rasagiline in Parkinson's disease. N Engl J Med. 2009. PMID: 19776408. Registry ID: NCT00256204 (named in the record's abstract). cards.summary: Synthesis: the delayed-start signature appeared in three of four dose-arms and vanished in the fourth — MAYBE (weak evidence) for disease modification
cards.people: Two randomised double-blind delayed-start trials of rasagiline in early Parkinson's disease: TEMPO (n=404; 6-month delay, 12-month readout) and ADAGIO (n=1,176; 36-week delay, 72-week readout, three hierarchical endpoints).

cards.watchOut: This shelf must never be quoted as showing rasagiline 'slows Parkinson's': it shows a design-dependent pattern that failed its own prespecified test at one of two doses in the definitive trial.

shelves.title: Parkinson's disease: exenatide's 3.5-point phase 2 motor advantage vanished in the 194-patient phase 3 trial — no evidence of disease modification (Exenatide-PD3)
shelves.question: In Parkinson's disease, does once-weekly exenatide slow motor progression compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Exenatide · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neurologic Examination/drug effects · Parkinson Disease/drug therapy · Peptides/administration & dosage · Treatment Outcome · Venoms/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: Exenatide in Parkinson's disease is the clearest small-positive, large-null sequence in this slate, and the two trials are carded in that order on purpose. The 2017 single-centre phase 2 trial (62 patients) found that after 48 weeks of weekly exenatide and a 12-week washout, off-medication motor scores had improved 1.0 points on exenatide while worsening 2.1 points on placebo — an adjusted difference of -3.5 points (P=0.0318) that persisted beyond exposure and launched the disease-modification hypothesis. The 2025 phase 3 Exenatide-PD3 trial (194 patients, six UK centres, 96 weeks) tested the same regimen against the same off-medication motor endpoint and found nothing: scores worsened by 5.7 points on exenatide and 4.5 points on placebo (adjusted coefficient 0.92, 95% CI -1.56 to 3.39; P=0.47 — the treatment made no difference), and the authors concluded there is no evidence to support exenatide as a disease-modifying treatment. Serious adverse events were similar (9% versus 11% in phase 3; 6 versus 2 in phase 2, none judged treatment-related). PROPOSED SPLIT: POSSIBLE (benefit) on the phase 2 record alone, superseded by POSSIBLE (no difference) on the phase 3 record — the shelf's operative answer is the phase 3 null. Flagged for the developer's personal verdict (SPLIT stamp).

cards.headline: Exenatide phase 2 (2017): off-medication motor scores 3.5 points better than placebo after washout (P=0.0318) in 62 patients
cards.summary: Exenatide phase 2 (2017): off-medication motor scores 3.5 points better than placebo after washout (P=0.0318) in 62 patients
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial (single centre)
cards.people: 62 patients with moderate Parkinson's disease (on dopaminergic treatment with wearing-off, Hoehn and Yahr stage 2.5 or less on treatment) at a single centre, randomised 1:1 to subcutaneous exenatide 2 mg or placebo once weekly for 48 weeks plus a 12-week washout. The primary outcome was the adjusted difference in off-medication MDS-UPDRS part 3 motor score at 60 weeks; 31 exenatide and 29 placebo patients were analysed.
cards.result: At 60 weeks, off-medication part 3 scores had improved by 1.0 points on exenatide and worsened by 2.1 points on placebo — an adjusted mean difference of -3.5 points (95% CI -6.7 to -0.3; P=0.0318). Injection-site reactions and gastrointestinal symptoms were common in both groups. Six serious adverse events occurred on exenatide and two on placebo, none judged related to the study interventions.
cards.watchOut: Sixty-two patients at one centre, with a 3.5-point difference whose confidence interval nearly reaches zero; the authors themselves could not distinguish disease modification from a long-lasting symptomatic effect.
cards.source: Athauda D et al.. Exenatide once weekly versus placebo in Parkinson's disease: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet. 2017. PMID: 28781108. Registry ID: NCT01971242 (named in the record's abstract). cards.headline: Exenatide-PD3 (2025): no benefit on the primary outcome at 96 weeks in 194 patients (adjusted coefficient 0.92; P=0.47)
cards.summary: Exenatide-PD3 (2025): no benefit on the primary outcome at 96 weeks in 194 patients (adjusted coefficient 0.92; P=0.47)
cards.people: 194 participants aged 25-80 with Parkinson's disease (Hoehn and Yahr stage 2.5 or less on treatment, on dopaminergic treatment) at six UK research hospitals, randomised 1:1 to extended-release exenatide 2 mg subcutaneously once weekly or visually identical placebo for 96 weeks. The primary outcome was the MDS-UPDRS part III score off dopaminergic medication at 96 weeks, analysed intention-to-treat.
cards.result: At 96 weeks, off-medication part III scores had worsened by a mean of 5.7 points (SD 11.2) on exenatide and 4.5 points (SD 11.4) on placebo (adjusted coefficient 0.92, 95% CI -1.56 to 3.39; P=0.47) — the treatment made no difference. At least one serious adverse event occurred in 9 (9%) exenatide and 11 (11%) placebo participants. The authors concluded the findings provide no evidence to support exenatide as a disease-modifying treatment for Parkinson's disease.
cards.watchOut: A null this size does not exclude a small effect (the interval runs from -1.56 to +3.39 points), but it excludes the effect the phase 2 trial appeared to show, which is the claim this shelf was built to test.
cards.source: Vijiaratnam N et al.. shelves.title: Huntington's chorea: tetrabenazine cut chorea by 5.0 units versus 1.5 on placebo in its single trial — with a suicide and suicidal ideation among its serious adverse events (TETRA-HD)
shelves.question: In Huntington's disease, does tetrabenazine reduce chorea compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Accidental Falls · Anti-Dyskinesia Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Breast Neoplasms/chemically induced · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Huntington Disease/drug therapy · Psychomotor Agitation/etiology · Suicide · Tetrabenazine/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: TETRA-HD is the single randomised trial of tetrabenazine for Huntington's chorea, and both its benefit and its danger are in the same record. In 84 ambulatory patients titrated over 7 weeks to a maximum of 100 mg/day, the UHDRS chorea score fell by 5.0 units on tetrabenazine versus 1.5 units on placebo over 12 weeks (adjusted mean effect -3.5 units, 95% CI -5.2 to -1.9; P<0.0001), with a significant benefit on clinical global improvement as well. Against that: five withdrawals in the tetrabenazine group versus one on placebo, and five serious adverse events in four tetrabenazine subjects — a drowning suicide, a complicated fall, restlessness with suicidal ideation, and a breast cancer — versus none on placebo. The suicide and suicidal ideation in a drug that depletes monoamines, in a disease with elevated baseline suicide risk, are why this drug carries its depression and suicidality warnings; they are printed here, in the balance, not buried. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — flagged for the developer's personal verdict as a single-trial shelf whose balance carries a treatment-group suicide.

cards.result: Chorea severity fell by 5.0 units on tetrabenazine versus 1.5 units on placebo (adjusted mean effect size -3.5 units, 95% CI -5.2 to -1.9; P<0.0001), with significant benefit on clinical global improvement ratings. shelves.title: Huntington's chorea: valbenazine cut maximal chorea scores by 4.6 points versus 1.4 on placebo in a single phase 3 trial, with somnolence the commonest adverse event (KINECT-HD)
shelves.question: In Huntington's disease, does valbenazine reduce chorea compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Male · Adult · Humans · Female · Huntington Disease/complications,drug therapy · Chorea/drug therapy,chemically induced · Tetrabenazine/adverse effects,analogs & derivatives · Antipsychotic Agents/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome · Valine/analogs & derivatives
shelves.balance: KINECT-HD is the single phase 3 trial of valbenazine — a selective VMAT2 inhibitor taken once daily — for Huntington's chorea. In 125 analysed adults with genetically confirmed disease and a Total Maximal Chorea score of at least 8, the least-squares mean change in chorea score from baseline to the week 10-12 maintenance period was -4.6 on valbenazine (up to 80 mg/day) versus -1.4 on placebo (difference -3.2, 95% CI -4.4 to -2.0; P<0.0001). Tolerability over the 12 weeks was comparatively clean: the commonest adverse event was somnolence (16% versus 3%), serious treatment-emergent events were single cases in each arm (angioedema from a shellfish allergy on valbenazine; colon cancer and psychosis on placebo), and — in explicit contrast to the older VMAT2 shelf beside this one — no suicidal behaviour or worsening of suicidal ideation was reported on valbenazine. Twelve weeks in one trial cannot exclude the class's depression risk over years, and the record says so in its own interpretation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — flagged for the developer's personal verdict as a single-trial shelf.

cards.headline: KINECT-HD 2023: valbenazine cut maximal chorea by 4.6 points vs 1.4 on placebo (difference -3.2; P<0.0001); somnolence 16% vs 3%
cards.summary: KINECT-HD 2023: valbenazine cut maximal chorea by 4.6 points vs 1.4 on placebo (difference -3.2; P<0.0001); somnolence 16% vs 3%
cards.people: 128 adults with genetically confirmed Huntington's disease and chorea (UHDRS Total Maximal Chorea score at least 8) at 46 Huntington Study Group sites in the USA and Canada, randomised 1:1 to valbenazine (up to 80 mg/day as tolerated) or placebo for 12 weeks. The primary endpoint was the least-squares mean change in Total Maximal Chorea score from the screening/baseline average to the week 10-12 maintenance average in the full-analysis set (n=125).
cards.result: Total Maximal Chorea change: -4.6 on valbenazine versus -1.4 on placebo (least-squares mean difference -3.2, 95% CI -4.4 to -2.0; P<0.0001). The most common treatment-emergent adverse event was somnolence (10/64, 16%, versus 2/63, 3%). Serious treatment-emergent adverse events: one on valbenazine (angioedema from an allergic reaction to shellfish) and two on placebo (colon cancer, psychosis). No clinically important changes in vital signs, ECGs or laboratory tests, and no suicidal behaviour or worsening of suicidal ideation on valbenazine.
cards.watchOut: Twelve weeks is short against a decades-long disease, and doses were titrated to tolerance (up to 80 mg), so the trial grades the titration strategy; the open-label extension is uncontrolled.
cards.source: Furr Stimming E et al.. shelves.title: Primary dystonia: pallidal deep brain stimulation beat sham in two small trials — movement scores improved 15.8 versus 1.4 points in generalized/segmental dystonia, severity 5.1 versus 1.3 in cervical dystonia
shelves.question: In medically refractory primary dystonia, does pallidal deep brain stimulation improve movement scores compared with sham stimulation?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Deep Brain Stimulation/adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Dystonic Disorders/classification,physiopathology,therapy · Female · Globus Pallidus · Humans · Male · Severity of Illness Index
shelves.balance: Pallidal deep brain stimulation for medically refractory primary dystonia rests on two small sham-controlled trials — every patient implanted, half switched on — and both are positive at 3 months. In Kupsch's trial of generalized or segmental dystonia (40 patients), the Burke-Fahn-Marsden movement score improved by 15.8 points on active stimulation versus 1.4 points on sham (P<0.001); when the sham group crossed to active treatment, it gained a similar benefit, and the whole cohort's improvement was sustained at 6 months. In Volkmann's cervical dystonia trial (62 patients), the TWSTRS severity score fell 5.1 points on active stimulation versus 1.3 points on sham (between-group difference 3.8 points; P=0.0024). The harms are the surgery's, and both trials report them plainly: in Kupsch, 22 adverse events in 19 patients including 4 stimulator-site infections and a lead dislodgment, with dysarthria the most frequent event; in Volkmann, adverse events in about a third of each group, the serious ones typically related to the implant procedure or device. The blinded phases are only 3 months long, the samples are 40 and 62, and treating physicians were unmasked in Volkmann (outcome videos were scored by masked experts). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): two concordant sham-controlled trials with large score differences, graded moderate rather than strong because of size and the short blinded window.

cards.headline: Kupsch 2006: pallidal stimulation improved dystonia movement scores by 15.8 points vs 1.4 on sham at 3 months (P<0.001)
cards.summary: Kupsch 2006: pallidal stimulation improved dystonia movement scores by 15.8 points vs 1.4 on sham at 3 months (P<0.001)
cards.type: Randomised, sham-controlled trial with blinded video assessment (implanted in all patients)
cards.people: 40 patients with primary segmental or generalized dystonia, all implanted with a deep-brain stimulation device, randomised to active neurostimulation or sham stimulation for 3 months. The primary end point was the change in the movement subscore of the Burke-Fahn-Marsden Dystonia Rating Scale (0-120), assessed from videotapes by two investigators unaware of treatment status; all patients then received open-label stimulation for a further 6-month assessment.
cards.result: Movement score change at 3 months: -15.8 points (SD 14.1) on neurostimulation versus -1.4 points (SD 3.8) on sham (P<0.001). During the open-label extension the improvement was sustained in the original stimulation group and the sham group gained a similar benefit after switching on; at 6 months of active treatment the combined cohort showed substantial improvement in movement symptoms (except speech and swallowing), disability and quality of life versus baseline. Twenty-two adverse events occurred in 19 patients, including 4 infections at the stimulator site and 1 lead dislodgment; dysarthria was the most frequent adverse event.
cards.watchOut: Forty patients and a 3-month blinded phase; the open-label convergence after switch-on is consistent with a real effect but is also exactly what expectation and time would predict, so the 3 blinded months carry the claim.
cards.source: Kupsch A et al.. Pallidal deep-brain stimulation in primary generalized or segmental dystonia. N Engl J Med. 2006. PMID: 17093249. cards.headline: Volkmann 2014: cervical dystonia severity fell 5.1 points on active stimulation vs 1.3 on sham (difference 3.8; P=0.0024)
cards.summary: Volkmann 2014: cervical dystonia severity fell 5.1 points on active stimulation vs 1.3 on sham (difference 3.8; P=0.0024)
cards.type: Randomised, sham-controlled trial with masked patients and masked video raters (Volkmann 2014)
cards.people: 62 patients aged 18-75 with cervical dystonia of at least 3 years' duration and TWSTRS severity at least 15, inadequately responding to botulinum toxin or oral drugs, at centres in Germany, Norway and Austria; all were implanted and randomised 1:1 to active pallidal neurostimulation or sham (0 V) for 3 months, after which the sham group was activated. Patients were masked; treating physicians were not. The primary endpoint was the change in TWSTRS severity score at 3 months, scored from standardised videos by two masked experts; 60 patients had 3-month outcome data.
cards.result: TWSTRS severity reduction at 3 months: -5.1 points (SD 5.1) on neurostimulation versus -1.3 points (SD 2.4) on sham (mean between-group difference 3.8 points, 95% CI 1.8-5.8; P=0.0024), intention-to-treat. Adverse events: 21 events (5 serious) in 11/32 neurostimulation patients versus 20 events (11 serious) in 9/30 sham patients; serious events were typically related to the implant procedure or device, and 11 of 16 resolved without sequelae. The commonest non-serious events were dysarthria (4 vs 3), involuntary movements (5 vs 1) and depression (1 vs 2).
cards.watchOut: Everyone bore the surgical risk, including the sham group — so the trial grades stimulation, not the decision to operate; the authors themselves called for longer follow-up before routine recommendation.

randomised, sham-controlled trial with masked patients and masked video raters (volkmann 2014) 62 patients aged 18-75 with cervical dystonia of at least 3 years' duration and twstrs severity at least 15, inadequately responding to botulinum toxin or oral drugs, at centres in germany, norway and austria; all were implanted and randomised 1:1 to active pallidal neurostimulation or sham (0 v) for 3 months, after which the sham group was activated. patients were masked; treating physicians were not. the primary endpoint was the change in twstrs severity score at 3 months, scored from standardised videos by two masked experts; 60 patients had 3-month outcome data. twstrs severity reduction at 3 months: -5.1 points (sd 5.1) on neurostimulation versus -1.3 points (sd 2.4) on sham (mean between-group difference 3.8 points, 95% ci 1.8-5.8; p=0.0024), intention-to-treat. adverse events: 21 events (5 serious) in 11/32 neurostimulation patients versus 20 events (11 serious) in 9/30 sham patients; serious events were typically related to the implant procedure or device, and 11 of 16 resolved without sequelae. the commonest non-serious events were dysarthria (4 vs 3), involuntary movements (5 vs 1) and depression (1 vs 2). everyone bore the surgical risk, including the sham group — so the trial grades stimulation, not the decision to operate; the authors themselves called for longer follow-up before routine recommendation. volkmann j et al.. pallidal neurostimulation in patients with medication-refractory cervical dystonia: a randomised, sham-controlled trial. lancet neurol. 2014. pmid: 25127231. registry id: nct00148889 (named in the record's abstract). mesh: aged · austria · deep brain stimulation/instrumentation,methods · disability evaluation · follow-up studies · germany · globus pallidus/physiology,surgery · humans · male · middle aged · norway · placebos · severity of illness index · single-blind method · torticollis/therapy · treatment outcome

shelves.title: Tourette's disorder in youth: aripiprazole reduced tic scores versus placebo in two randomised trials — adults have no randomised record in this build
shelves.question: In children, adolescents and adults with Tourette's disorder, does aripiprazole reduce tic severity (YGTSS) compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Antipsychotic Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Aripiprazole · Child · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Neurologic Examination/drug effects · Piperazines/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Quinolones/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Tourette Syndrome/diagnosis,drug therapy
shelves.balance: Aripiprazole reduces tics in children and adolescents with Tourette's disorder in two randomised trials, and that population limit belongs in the first sentence: no adult trial is carded here, because the randomised record is paediatric. In Yoo's 10-week trial (61 patients aged 6-18), the Yale Global Tic Severity Scale total tic score fell 15.0 points on aripiprazole versus 9.6 on placebo (P=0.0196), with global-improvement response in 66% versus 45%. In Sallee's 8-week phase 3 trial (133 patients aged 7-17), least-squares mean differences versus placebo were -6.3 points at low dose and -9.9 points at high dose (both significant), with 69% and 74% rated much or very much improved versus 38% on placebo. The metabolic ledger in Yoo is the caution: body weight, body mass index and waist circumference all increased significantly on aripiprazole (prolactin fell); in Sallee the commonest adverse events were sedation (up to 18.2%), somnolence (up to 15.6%) and fatigue, with no serious adverse events or deaths. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for children and adolescents over 8-10 weeks; the adult half of the drafted question has no randomised record in this build and is not graded.

cards.headline: Yoo 2013: aripiprazole cut total tic scores by 15.0 vs 9.6 points on placebo in 61 children and adolescents (P=0.0196)
cards.summary: Yoo 2013: aripiprazole cut total tic scores by 15.0 vs 9.6 points on placebo in 61 children and adolescents (P=0.0196)
cards.people: 61 children and adolescents aged 6-18 with DSM-IV Tourette's disorder and a Yale Global Tic Severity Scale total tic score of at least 22, randomised 1:1 to aripiprazole or placebo for 10 weeks at multiple centres (2008-2010). The primary outcome was the mean change in YGTSS total tic score (last observation carried forward); 89% completed the study.
cards.result: Total tic score change: -15.0 points (SD 8.4) on aripiprazole versus -9.6 (SD 8.8) on placebo (P=0.0196). Tourette's Syndrome Clinical Global Impression-Improvement response: 66% versus 45%; the severity-of-illness change also differed significantly (P=0.0321). No early discontinuations were due to adverse events, and treatment-emergent adverse event incidence did not differ significantly (P=0.7550). Aripiprazole significantly decreased serum prolactin (P<0.0001) but significantly increased body weight (P=0.0055), body mass index (P=0.0142) and waist circumference (P=0.0270).
cards.watchOut: Small (n=61) and 10 weeks long; the weight and waist gains over just 10 weeks are the finding that matters most for a drug a child may take for years.
cards.source: Yoo HK et al.. A multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of aripiprazole in children and adolescents with Tourette's disorder. J Clin Psychiatry. 2013. PMID: 24021518. Registry ID: NCT00706589 (named in the record's abstract). cards.headline: Sallee 2017: phase 3 — tic-score differences of -6.3 (low dose) and -9.9 (high dose) points versus placebo in 133 youth
cards.summary: Sallee 2017: phase 3 — tic-score differences of -6.3 (low dose) and -9.9 (high dose) points versus placebo in 133 youth
cards.people: 133 patients aged 7-17 with Tourette's disorder at 76 sites in the US, Canada, Hungary and Italy, randomised 1:1:1 to weight-banded low-dose aripiprazole (5 or 10 mg/day), high-dose aripiprazole (10 or 20 mg/day) or placebo for 8 weeks. The primary endpoint was the change in Yale Global Tic Severity Scale Total Tic Score at week 8 in the intention-to-treat population.
cards.result: Least-squares mean treatment differences versus placebo in YGTSS Total Tic Score: -6.3 points (95% CI -10.2 to -2.3) at low dose and -9.9 points (95% CI -13.8 to -5.9) at high dose, both statistically significant. Clinical Global Impression improvement (much or very much improved): 69% (low dose) and 74% (high dose) versus 38% on placebo. The most common adverse events were sedation (18.2% low dose, 8.9% high dose, 2.3% placebo), somnolence (11.4%, 15.6%, 2.3%) and fatigue (6.8%, 15.6%, 0%). No serious adverse events or deaths occurred.
cards.watchOut: Eight weeks; the high-dose advantage over low dose (about 3.6 points) was bought with more somnolence and fatigue, and neither trial follows children through the growth and metabolic horizon that matters.

shelves.title: Acute migraine in the emergency department: a single dose of dexamethasone probably reduces headache recurrence (pooled relative risk 0.74, NNT 9) — though the largest trial was null
shelves.question: In patients treated in the emergency department for acute migraine, does a dose of dexamethasone reduce headache recurrence within 24–72 hours compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anti-Inflammatory Agents/administration & dosage · Dexamethasone/administration & dosage · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Injections, Intravenous · Male · Migraine Disorders/prevention & control · Pain Measurement · Placebos · Recurrence
shelves.balance: A single dose of parenteral dexamethasone added to standard emergency department migraine treatment probably reduces headache recurrence within 72 hours — but the trial record is small and mixed, and the pooled estimate does the heavy lifting. The largest single trial (Rowe 2008, 126 patients analysed) missed: relapse at 48-72 hours was 22% on dexamethasone versus 32% on placebo (odds ratio 0.6, 95% CI 0.3-1.3). An earlier, smaller trial (Innes 1999, 98 patients) was clearly positive for severe recurrence (18% versus 45%; odds ratio 0.28). The 2008 BMJ meta-analysis of all seven randomised trials found recurrence reduced by 26% relative (relative risk 0.74, 95% CI 0.60-0.90; number needed to treat 9), with no effect on pain relief for the index headache itself and no excess of side effects. Correction made on the face of this pack: the drafting slate named this shelf's anchor as 'Singh, Headache 2008' at PMID 18047499 — that record is in fact the Rowe 2008 trial, and the Singh 2008 paper (PMID 18976336) is a meta-analysis, not a trial. The shelf is built on the records as fetched. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a modest relative reduction in recurrence, resting on a pooled analysis of small trials whose largest member was null.

cards.headline: Rowe 2008: IV dexamethasone 15 mg did not significantly cut migraine relapse — 22% vs 32% at 48-72 hours (OR 0.6, CI crosses 1)
cards.summary: Rowe 2008: IV dexamethasone 15 mg did not significantly cut migraine relapse — 22% vs 32% at 48-72 hours (OR 0.6, CI crosses 1)
cards.people: Adults presenting with acute migraine to 4 emergency departments, randomised double-blind to intravenous dexamethasone 15 mg (n=64) or placebo (n=62) in addition to standard intravenous abortive therapy; 126 patients analysed. Relapse was a return visit or a headache precluding normal activity, assessed at 48-72 hours and 7 days.
cards.result: At 48-72 hours, relapses occurred in 14/64 (22%) on dexamethasone versus 20/62 (32%) on placebo (odds ratio 0.6, 95% CI 0.3-1.3 — not significant). By day 7: 18/64 (28%) versus 25/62 (40%) (odds ratio 0.6, 95% CI 0.3-1.3). Relapse was more common when pain was incompletely relieved at discharge (odds ratio 2.2). Median pain fell from 8/10 at presentation to 2/10 at discharge in both groups.
cards.watchOut: The biggest trial of the question is the null one; the confidence interval still allows a useful benefit, but this record alone would not carry the shelf.
cards.source: Rowe BH et al.. Randomized controlled trial of intravenous dexamethasone to prevent relapse in acute migraine headache. Headache. 2008. PMID: 18047499. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Innes 1999: dexamethasone 24 mg cut severe recurrent headache from 45% to 18% (OR 0.28; P=.005)
cards.summary: Innes 1999: dexamethasone 24 mg cut severe recurrent headache from 45% to 18% (OR 0.28; P=.005)
cards.people: 98 adults (of 100 randomised) aged 19-65 with migraine severe enough to require parenteral therapy at 2 community hospital emergency departments; after abortive therapy, blinded nurses gave dexamethasone 24 mg intravenously or placebo. The primary outcome was severe recurrent headache (provoking a physician visit or interfering with daily activity) at 48-72 hours.
cards.result: Severe recurrent headache occurred in 9/49 (18%) on dexamethasone versus 22/49 (45%) on placebo (odds ratio 0.28, 95% CI 0.11-0.69; P=.005). Any recurrence occurred in 65 of 98 patients overall. Dexamethasone patients were shifted toward milder recurrence categories (12 in the mildest class versus 4 on placebo).
cards.watchOut: Small, older, and the most positive trial of the set — exactly the profile that inflates pooled estimates; the placebo group was also more often female at baseline.

cards.headline: Colman 2008 (BMJ meta-analysis of 7 RCTs): recurrence relative risk 0.74 (0.60-0.90), NNT 9; no effect on the index headache
cards.summary: Colman 2008 (BMJ meta-analysis of 7 RCTs): recurrence relative risk 0.74 (0.60-0.90), NNT 9; no effect on the index headache
cards.people: Meta-analysis of seven randomised controlled trials in which single-dose parenteral dexamethasone was added to standard abortive therapy and compared with placebo for acute migraine in adults, with recurrence assessed within 72 hours.
cards.result: Dexamethasone reduced headache recurrence versus placebo (relative risk 0.74, 95% CI 0.60-0.90) — a 26% relative reduction, number needed to treat 9. Acute pain reduction for the index headache did not differ (weighted mean difference 0.37, 95% CI -0.20 to 0.94). Side-effect profiles were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: A pooled estimate over small, heterogeneous trials — two of its members are the cards above, and they disagree; the meta-analysis is carded as the summary of that disagreement, not as an eighth trial.
cards.source: Colman I et al.. Parenteral dexamethasone for acute severe migraine headache: meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials for preventing recurrence. BMJ. 2008. PMID: 18541610. cards.headline: Synthesis: small mixed trials, a positive pooled estimate — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: small mixed trials, a positive pooled estimate — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Two emergency department randomised trials (Innes 1999, n=98; Rowe 2008, n=126) and the BMJ meta-analysis of all seven trials (Colman 2008).
cards.result: Severe recurrence 18% vs 45% (Innes); all relapse 22% vs 32%, not significant (Rowe); pooled recurrence relative risk 0.74 (Colman), NNT 9. No benefit on the index headache. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The claim is recurrence prevention only; dexamethasone does not treat the presenting attack, and relapse tracks incomplete pain relief at discharge more than steroid assignment in the largest trial.

shelves.balance: Six days of frovatriptan across the perimenstrual window clearly reduces menstrual migraine in two randomised trials, with a dose gradient. In the 546-woman crossover trial (Silberstein 2004), a menstrual migraine occurred in 67% of placebo periods versus 52% on frovatriptan 2.5 mg once daily and 41% on twice daily (both P<0.0001; twice daily beat once daily, P<0.001). In women whose menstrual migraine had already proved difficult to treat (Brandes 2009, 410 women), headache-free perimenstrual periods averaged 0.92 of 3 on twice-daily frovatriptan and 0.69 on once daily versus 0.42 on placebo (P<0.001 and P<0.02). Severity fell too, and adverse events resembled placebo in both trials. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): two consistent randomised trials, a within-trial dose response, and absolute incidence reductions of 15-26 percentage points per treated cycle.

cards.headline: Silberstein 2004: menstrual migraine in 41% of twice-daily frovatriptan periods vs 67% on placebo (52% once daily)
cards.summary: Silberstein 2004: menstrual migraine in 41% of twice-daily frovatriptan periods vs 67% on placebo (52% once daily)
cards.people: 546 women (mean age 37.6 years) with menstrually associated migraine in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled three-way crossover trial; each woman treated three perimenstrual periods with placebo, frovatriptan 2.5 mg once daily, and frovatriptan 2.5 mg twice daily, each for 6 days starting 2 days before the anticipated attack. The primary endpoint was the incidence of menstrual migraine during the 6-day window.
cards.result: Incidence of menstrual migraine: 67% on placebo, 52% on once-daily frovatriptan, 41% on twice-daily frovatriptan (both regimens superior to placebo, P<0.0001; twice daily superior to once daily, P<0.001). Severity, duration, and rescue-medication use were all reduced in a dose-dependent manner. Adverse events were similar to placebo.
cards.watchOut: A crossover in a cyclical condition is efficient but period effects and expectancy carry across cycles; the result applies to women with predictable cycles who can time a 6-day course.
cards.source: Silberstein SD et al.. A randomized trial of frovatriptan for the intermittent prevention of menstrual migraine. Neurology. 2004. PMID: 15277618. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Brandes 2009: in difficult-to-treat menstrual migraine, headache-free periods averaged 0.92 (twice daily) vs 0.42 on placebo
cards.summary: Brandes 2009: in difficult-to-treat menstrual migraine, headache-free periods averaged 0.92 (twice daily) vs 0.42 on placebo
cards.people: 410 women with documented inadequate response to triptans for acute treatment of menstrual migraine, randomised in a parallel-group double-blind trial to frovatriptan 2.5 mg once or twice daily or placebo for three perimenstrual periods (6-day courses starting 2 days before the anticipated attack); 85% completed all three periods.
cards.result: Mean number of headache-free perimenstrual periods (of 3): 0.92 on twice-daily frovatriptan, 0.69 on once daily, 0.42 on placebo (P<0.001 twice daily and P<0.02 once daily versus placebo). When migraine occurred, severity was reduced on both regimens (P<0.001). Both regimens were well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: The population had already failed acute triptan treatment — a selected, harder-to-treat group, which makes the consistency with the 2004 trial more, not less, reassuring; the record's MeSH includes an indexing artefact ('History, 16th Century'), copied verbatim per library rule.

shelves.title: Medication-overuse headache: withdrawal plus a preventive from the start probably beats either alone at curing the overuse — though headache days fell equally on all three strategies (Carlsen 2020)
shelves.question: In medication-overuse headache, which strategy works best — abrupt withdrawal plus preventive medication, preventive medication alone, or withdrawal alone?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Analgesics/adverse effects · Angiotensin II Type 1 Receptor Blockers/administration & dosage · Denmark · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Headache Disorders, Secondary/chemically induced,drug therapy,prevention & control · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Migraine Disorders/drug therapy · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Tension-Type Headache/drug therapy
shelves.balance: One open-label randomised trial has compared the three strategies clinicians actually argue about in medication-overuse headache, and its answer needs care: on the primary outcome — reduction in headache days per month at 6 months — the three strategies did NOT differ significantly (reductions of 12.3 days for withdrawal plus preventive from the start, 9.9 for preventive alone, and 8.5 for withdrawal alone; P=.20 — the treatments made no difference on that endpoint). The combined strategy won on the secondary outcomes that arguably matter more: 74.2% reverted to episodic headache versus 60.0% (preventive alone) and 41.7% (withdrawal alone) (P=.03), and 96.8% were cured of medication overuse versus 74.3% and 88.9% (P=.03). The drafting slate described the combined strategy as producing 'the largest reduction in headache days' — numerically true, but that comparison was not significant, and the pack grades the shelf on the secondary endpoints with the primary null stated first. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for withdrawal plus preventive from the start — flagged for the developer's personal verdict as a single-trial shelf whose primary endpoint was null.

cards.headline: Carlsen 2020: headache days fell 12.3 vs 9.9 vs 8.5 per month across the three strategies (P=.20, no difference) — but reversion to episodic headache was 74% vs 60% vs 42%
cards.summary: Carlsen 2020: headache days fell 12.3 vs 9.9 vs 8.5 per month across the three strategies (P=.20, no difference) — but reversion to episodic headache was 74% vs 60% vs 42%
cards.type: Open-label randomised clinical trial, three arms (Carlsen 2020)
cards.people: 120 adults with medication-overuse headache (migraine and/or tension-type headache) at the Danish Headache Center, randomised open-label 1:1:1 to (1) withdrawal plus preventive treatment from the start, (2) preventive treatment without withdrawal, or (3) withdrawal alone with optional preventive after 2 months; 102 completed 6-month follow-up. The primary outcome was change in headache days per month.
cards.result: Headache days per month fell by 12.3 (withdrawal plus preventive), 9.9 (preventive alone), and 8.5 (withdrawal alone) — no significant difference (P=.20). Migraine days, acute-medication use, and pain intensity also did not differ. Reversion to episodic headache: 23/31 (74.2%) versus 21/35 (60.0%) versus 15/36 (41.7%) (P=.03). Cure of medication overuse: 30/31 (96.8%) versus 26/35 (74.3%) versus 32/36 (88.9%) (P=.03) — a relative chance of cure 1.3 (95% CI 1.1-1.6) for the combined strategy versus preventive alone.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, single-centre, 120 patients — and the headline strategy comparison rests on secondary endpoints after a null primary; expectancy effects in an unblinded withdrawal trial are real.
cards.source: Carlsen LN et al.. Comparison of 3 Treatment Strategies for Medication Overuse Headache: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Neurol. 2020. PMID: 32453406. Registry ID: NCT02993289. shelves.title: Trigeminal neuralgia: botulinum toxin type A injections probably reduce pain — responders 68-86% versus 15-32% on placebo in two small trials, with no advantage for the higher dose
shelves.question: In trigeminal neuralgia inadequately controlled or intolerant of standard drugs, do botulinum toxin type A injections reduce pain intensity and attack frequency compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Botulinum Toxins, Type A/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neuromuscular Agents/therapeutic use · Pain Measurement · Treatment Outcome · Trigeminal Neuralgia/drug therapy
shelves.balance: Two small randomised double-blind trials from the same research group agree that intradermal/submucosal botulinum toxin type A injections reduce trigeminal neuralgia pain for at least 8-12 weeks. In Wu 2012 (42 patients, 75 U versus saline), responders (at least 50% reduction in mean pain score at week 12) were 68.2% versus 15.0%, with pain intensity separating from week 2 and attack frequency from week 1. In Zhang 2014 (84 patients), response at week 8 was 70.4% on 25 U and 86.2% on 75 U versus 32.1% on placebo — with no significant difference between the two doses, so the lower dose carries the same evidence with less exposure. Adverse events were few and mild to moderate in both trials. The limits are structural: 126 patients in total, one centre and one group, 8-12 week horizons, and no comparison against carbamazepine or surgery. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): consistent, sizeable responder separations in two small trials — moderate confidence, not more.

cards.headline: Wu 2012: botulinum toxin A 75 U — responders 68.2% vs 15.0% on saline at week 12
cards.summary: Wu 2012: botulinum toxin A 75 U — responders 68.2% vs 15.0% on saline at week 12
cards.people: 42 patients with trigeminal neuralgia randomised double-blind to intradermal and/or submucosal botulinum toxin type A 75 U (n=22) or saline (n=20) injected where the pain was experienced; 40 completed. Responders were patients with at least a 50% reduction in mean pain score at week 12.
cards.result: Botulinum toxin significantly reduced pain intensity from week 2 and pain attack frequency from week 1, maintained through week 12. Responders: 68.18% on botulinum toxin versus 15.00% on placebo. More treated patients reported improvement on the Patient Global Impression of Change. Few treatment-related adverse events; the treatment was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: Forty-two patients from one centre; facial weakness or asymmetry from injections near facial muscles is the harm to watch in practice, and 12 weeks says nothing about repeat-injection durability.
cards.source: Wu CJ et al.. Botulinum toxin type A for the treatment of trigeminal neuralgia: results from a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Cephalalgia. 2012. PMID: 22492424. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Zhang 2014: response 70.4% (25 U) and 86.2% (75 U) vs 32.1% on placebo — the two doses did not differ
cards.summary: Zhang 2014: response 70.4% (25 U) and 86.2% (75 U) vs 32.1% on placebo — the two doses did not differ
cards.people: 84 patients with classical trigeminal neuralgia randomised double-blind to placebo (n=28), botulinum toxin type A 25 U (n=27), or 75 U (n=29) by local multi-point intradermal/submucosal injection, followed weekly for 8 weeks.
cards.result: Visual analogue pain scores fell significantly on both doses versus placebo from week 1 through week 8, with no significant difference between 25 U and 75 U. Response rates at week 8: 70.4% (25 U) and 86.2% (75 U) versus 32.1% (placebo). 'Much' or 'very much' improved on global impression: 66.7% and 75.9% versus 32.1%. All adverse reactions were mild or moderate.
cards.watchOut: Same investigative group as Wu 2012 — the two trials corroborate each other but are not fully independent replication; the flat dose response argues for the 25 U dose if the treatment is used.
cards.source: Zhang H et al..
