shelves.title: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension: acetazolamide added to diet probably improves visual fields modestly — a 0.71 dB advantage in the single trial, with clearer gains in papilloedema and quality of life (IIHTT)
shelves.question: In idiopathic intracranial hypertension with mild visual loss, does acetazolamide plus a weight-reduction diet improve visual field function compared with diet alone?
shelves.mesh: Acetazolamide/therapeutic use · Adult · Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Combined Modality Therapy · Diet, Sodium-Restricted · Female · Humans · Male · Pseudotumor Cerebri/complications,diet therapy,drug therapy · Quality of Life · Treatment Outcome · Vision Disorders/drug therapy,etiology · Weight Loss
shelves.balance: The Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension Treatment Trial is the only randomised trial of acetazolamide in this disease, and its headline effect is modest and borderline: on top of the same low-sodium weight-reduction diet, acetazolamide (titrated to a maximum tolerated dose up to 4 g/day) improved perimetric mean deviation by 1.43 dB at 6 months versus 0.71 dB on placebo — a treatment difference of 0.71 dB whose 95% confidence interval runs from 0 to 1.43 (P=.050). The supporting outcomes were stronger: papilloedema grade improved by an extra 0.70 (P<.001) and vision-related quality of life by 6.35 points (P=.003). One confound travels with the result: the acetazolamide group also lost more weight (-7.50 kg versus -3.45 kg; difference -4.05 kg), and weight loss itself treats this disease, so the trial cannot fully separate the drug's effect from the extra weight loss it caused (largely through taste and appetite effects). The authors themselves left 'the clinical importance of this improvement' undetermined. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — flagged for the developer's personal verdict as a single-trial shelf with a borderline primary endpoint.

cards.headline: IIHTT 2014: visual field improved 0.71 dB more on acetazolamide than placebo (P=.050); papilloedema and vision-related quality of life clearly better
cards.summary: IIHTT 2014: visual field improved 0.71 dB more on acetazolamide than placebo (P=.050); papilloedema and vision-related quality of life clearly better
cards.people: 165 participants with idiopathic intracranial hypertension and mild visual loss (perimetric mean deviation -2 to -7 dB; mean age 29, all but 4 women) at 38 North American sites, randomised double-masked to a low-sodium weight-reduction diet plus acetazolamide titrated to the maximum tolerated dose up to 4 g/day (n=86) or matching placebo (n=79) for 6 months. The primary outcome was change in perimetric mean deviation in the most affected eye.
cards.result: Perimetric mean deviation improved by 1.43 dB on acetazolamide versus 0.71 dB on placebo (difference 0.71 dB, 95% CI 0 to 1.43; P=.050). Papilloedema grade treatment effect -0.70 (95% CI -0.99 to -0.41; P<.001); vision-related quality of life (VFQ-25) treatment effect 6.35 points (P=.003). Weight fell by 7.50 kg on acetazolamide versus 3.45 kg on placebo (difference -4.05 kg; P<.001).
cards.watchOut: A primary endpoint at P=.050 with a confidence interval touching zero, in mild visual loss only — the trial says nothing about fulminant or severe IIH, where surgery is the question; and the drug group's extra 4 kg of weight loss is entangled with the drug effect.
cards.source: Wall M et al.. Effect of acetazolamide on visual function in patients with idiopathic intracranial hypertension and mild visual loss: the idiopathic intracranial hypertension treatment trial. JAMA. 2014. PMID: 24756514. Registry ID: NCT01003639. shelves.title: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension in women with obesity: bariatric surgery lowered intracranial pressure far more than community weight management over two years in a single small trial (IIH:WT)
shelves.question: In women with idiopathic intracranial hypertension and obesity, does bariatric surgery lower intracranial pressure more than a community weight-management intervention?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Bariatric Surgery/trends · Body Mass Index · Female · Humans · Intracranial Pressure/physiology · Pseudotumor Cerebri/diagnosis,epidemiology,therapy · Treatment Outcome · Weight Loss/physiology · Weight Reduction Programs/trends · Young Adult
shelves.balance: In women with active idiopathic intracranial hypertension and a body mass index of at least 35, bariatric surgery lowered intracranial pressure substantially more than a community weight-management programme, and the gap widened over two years: adjusted differences of -6.0 cm of cerebrospinal fluid at 12 months (P=.001) and -8.2 cm at 24 months (P<.001), driven by much larger weight loss (-21.4 kg at 12 months, -26.6 kg at 24 months). Quality of life also improved more after surgery. The trial is small and specific: 66 women randomised, 54 in the primary analysis; the comparator was a named community programme (Weight Watchers), not usual care; and surgery's risks, though not the trial's focus, are permanent in a way a diet programme's are not. Visual outcomes were secondary and the trial was not powered for blindness prevention. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — flagged for the developer's personal verdict as a single-trial shelf in women only.

cards.headline: IIH:WT 2021: intracranial pressure fell 6.0 cm CSF more after bariatric surgery than community weight management at 12 months, 8.2 cm more at 24 months
cards.summary: IIH:WT 2021: intracranial pressure fell 6.0 cm CSF more after bariatric surgery than community weight management at 12 months, 8.2 cm more at 24 months
cards.people: 66 women with active idiopathic intracranial hypertension and body mass index at least 35 at 5 UK NHS hospitals, randomised to bariatric surgery (n=33) or a community weight management intervention (Weight Watchers; n=33); 64 remained at 12 months and 54 were in the primary analysis. The primary outcome was change in lumbar puncture opening pressure at 12 months.
cards.result: Intracranial pressure was lower in the surgery arm by an adjusted mean of 6.0 cm CSF at 12 months (95% CI -9.5 to -2.4; P=.001) and 8.2 cm at 24 months (95% CI -12.2 to -4.2; P<.001); per-protocol differences were larger (-7.2 and -8.7 cm). Weight was lower by 21.4 kg at 12 months and 26.6 kg at 24 months. Quality of life (SF-36) improved more after surgery at both time points (P=.04 and P=.006).
cards.watchOut: Women only, BMI at least 35, and a physiological primary endpoint; the trial cannot tell us whether surgery prevents visual loss better than dieting, and surgical harms sit outside its 66 patients.
cards.source: Mollan SP et al.. Effectiveness of Bariatric Surgery vs Community Weight Management Intervention for the Treatment of Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Neurol. 2021. PMID: 33900360. Registry ID: NCT02124486. shelves.title: Cluster headache: non-invasive vagus nerve stimulation probably aborts episodic attacks (34-48% vs 6-11% on sham) but made no difference in chronic cluster headache in either ACT trial
shelves.question: In cluster headache, does non-invasive cervical vagus nerve stimulation abort attacks compared with sham stimulation?
shelves.mesh: Cluster Headache/therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pain Measurement · Treatment Outcome · United States · Vagus Nerve Stimulation/instrumentation,methods
shelves.balance: Non-invasive cervical vagus nerve stimulation for acute cluster headache splits cleanly by subtype, and the split was seen twice. In ACT1 (133 patients in the intent-to-treat population), the primary endpoint — pain relief at 15 minutes for the first attack — was NOT met overall (26.7% on active stimulation versus 15.1% on sham; P=.1); in the prespecified episodic cluster subgroup it was clearly positive (34.2% versus 10.6%; P=.008), while chronic cluster went the other way numerically (13.6% versus 23.1%). ACT2 (92 patients) repeated the pattern: overall 14% versus 12% pain-free at 15 minutes (no difference), but in episodic cluster 48% versus 6% (P<0.01), and in chronic cluster 5% versus 13%. Two trials whose overall primaries were null and whose episodic subgroups agree are evidence for the episodic claim and against the chronic one — this shelf is stamped accordingly. PROPOSED SPLIT: POSSIBLE (benefit) for acute treatment of episodic cluster headache; POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for chronic cluster headache. Flagged for the developer's personal verdict (SPLIT stamp).

cards.headline: ACT1 2016: primary endpoint missed overall (26.7% vs 15.1%, P=.1) — episodic cluster responded 34.2% vs 10.6% (P=.008), chronic did not
cards.summary: ACT1 2016: primary endpoint missed overall (26.7% vs 15.1%, P=.1) — episodic cluster responded 34.2% vs 10.6% (P=.008), chronic did not
cards.people: 150 enrolled patients with cluster headache randomised 1:1 to non-invasive vagus nerve stimulation or sham for up to 1 month double-blind; the intent-to-treat population was 133 (60 active: 38 episodic, 22 chronic; 73 sham: 47 episodic, 26 chronic). The primary endpoint was pain relief (pain intensity 0 or 1) at 15 minutes for the first treated attack, without rescue medication through 60 minutes.
cards.result: Response: 26.7% on active stimulation versus 15.1% on sham overall (P=.1 — not significant). Episodic cluster: 34.2% versus 10.6% (P=.008), with sustained response also significantly higher (P=.008). Chronic cluster: 13.6% versus 23.1% (P=.48). Adverse device effects were reported by 35/150 subjects (11 active, 24 sham); no serious device effects occurred.
cards.watchOut: The episodic result is a prespecified subgroup of a trial whose primary endpoint failed — the strongest reason it is graded POSSIBLE, not LIKELY, even with ACT2 pointing the same way.
cards.source: Silberstein SD et al.. Non-Invasive Vagus Nerve Stimulation for the ACute Treatment of Cluster Headache: Findings From the Randomized, Double-Blind, Sham-Controlled ACT1 Study. Headache. 2016. PMID: 27593728. Registry ID: NCT01792817. cards.headline: ACT2 2018: overall pain-free rates 14% vs 12% (no difference); episodic cluster 48% vs 6% (P<0.01); chronic 5% vs 13%
cards.summary: ACT2 2018: overall pain-free rates 14% vs 12% (no difference); episodic cluster 48% vs 6% (P<0.01); chronic 5% vs 13%
cards.people: 92 patients with episodic or chronic cluster headache in the full analysis set (48 active stimulation: 14 episodic, 34 chronic; 44 sham: 13 episodic, 31 chronic), treating attacks over a 2-week double-blind period after a 1-week run-in. The primary endpoint was the proportion of all treated attacks pain-free within 15 minutes without rescue treatment.
cards.result: Total cohort: 14% of attacks pain-free on active stimulation versus 12% on sham — not significantly different. Episodic cluster: 48% versus 6% (P<0.01). Chronic cluster: 5% versus 13% — no difference, numerically favouring sham. The authors concluded the treatment is superior to sham in episodic but not chronic cluster headache.
cards.watchOut: The episodic subgroup here is only 27 patients (14 active, 13 sham) — a large percentage difference on a small base; the chronic subgroup, the trial's majority, showed nothing.
cards.source: Goadsby PJ et al.. Non-invasive vagus nerve stimulation for the acute treatment of episodic and chronic cluster headache: A randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled ACT2 study. shelves.title: Migraine with aura: single-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation during the aura probably increases pain freedom at 2 hours (39% vs 22% on sham) — one trial (Lipton 2010)
shelves.question: In migraine with aura, does single-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation applied during the aura increase pain freedom at 2 hours compared with sham?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Migraine with Aura/therapy · Pain Management · Time Factors · Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation/adverse effects,methods · Treatment Outcome · United States · Visual Perception · Young Adult
shelves.balance: A single sham-controlled trial supports single-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation, applied during the aura, as an acute treatment for migraine with aura: pain-free at 2 hours in 39% on active stimulation versus 22% on sham (therapeutic gain 17 percentage points, 95% CI 3-31; P=.0179), with sustained pain freedom at 24 and 48 hours also favouring the device and no device-related serious adverse events. The caveats are the usual single-trial ones, plus attrition built into the design: of 267 enrolled, only 164 treated an attack and entered the outcome analysis, and the population was narrowly defined (aura preceding at least 30% of attacks, headache following more than 90% of auras). Later studies of the device were open-label and are not carded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — flagged for the developer's personal verdict as a single-trial shelf.

cards.headline: Lipton 2010: pain-free at 2 hours in 39% on single-pulse TMS vs 22% on sham (gain 17 points; P=.0179)
cards.summary: Lipton 2010: pain-free at 2 hours in 39% on single-pulse TMS vs 22% on sham (gain 17 points; P=.0179)
cards.people: Adults aged 18-68 with migraine with aura (visual aura before at least 30% of attacks) at 18 US centres; 267 enrolled in phase one, 201 randomised in phase two to a portable single-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation device or sham, treating up to three attacks over 3 months starting during aura. 164 patients treated at least one attack and form the modified intention-to-treat set (82 per arm). The primary outcome was pain-free response 2 hours after the first attack.
cards.result: Pain-free at 2 hours: 32/82 (39%) on active stimulation versus 18/82 (22%) on sham (therapeutic gain 17%, 95% CI 3-31%; P=.0179). Sustained pain-free rates at 24 and 48 hours significantly favoured active stimulation. Non-inferiority was shown for nausea, photophobia, and phonophobia at 2 hours. No device-related serious adverse events; adverse events were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: Only 164 of 267 enrolled patients treated an attack and contributed outcomes — a two-phase enrichment design; and the claim is for migraine with aura treated during the aura, not for migraine generally.
cards.source: Lipton RB et al.. Single-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation for acute treatment of migraine with aura: a randomised, double-blind, parallel-group, sham-controlled trial. Lancet Neurol. 2010. PMID: 20206581. Registry ID: NCT00449540. shelves.title: Acute migraine: remote electrical neuromodulation of the upper arm probably relieves pain (relief 66.7% vs 38.8% on sham) — a single large trial (Yarnitsky 2019)
shelves.question: In acute migraine, does smartphone-controlled remote electrical neuromodulation of the upper arm relieve pain at 2 hours compared with sham stimulation?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Migraine Disorders/therapy · Pain Management/methods · Transcutaneous Electric Nerve Stimulation/instrumentation,methods · Treatment Outcome · Wireless Technology/instrumentation
shelves.balance: Remote electrical neuromodulation — a smartphone-controlled device stimulating the upper arm to trigger conditioned pain modulation — beat sham clearly in its single large sham-controlled trial (Yarnitsky 2019, 252 randomised): pain relief at 2 hours in 66.7% versus 38.8% (therapeutic gain 27.9 points; P<.0001) and pain freedom in 37.4% versus 18.4% (P=.003), sustained at 48 hours, with device-related adverse events in 4.8% versus 2.4%. Correction made on the face of this pack: the drafting slate claimed a second consistent sham-controlled trial in adolescents/adults. No such record could be resolved this run — the only other randomised REN record found is a 19-patient paediatric emergency-department feasibility pilot (PMID 39290050), which was not powered for efficacy and is not carded. The shelf therefore rests on one trial, however clean, and is stamped and flagged accordingly. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — flagged for the developer's personal verdict as a single-trial shelf.

cards.headline: Yarnitsky 2019: pain relief at 2 hours in 66.7% on remote electrical neuromodulation vs 38.8% on sham; pain-free 37.4% vs 18.4%
cards.summary: Yarnitsky 2019: pain relief at 2 hours in 66.7% on remote electrical neuromodulation vs 38.8% on sham; pain-free 37.4% vs 18.4%
cards.people: 252 adults with migraine (2-8 attacks per month) at 7 US and 5 Israeli sites, randomised 1:1 to active or sham stimulation from a smartphone-controlled wireless device applied to the upper arm for 30-45 minutes within 1 hour of attack onset (perceptible but non-painful intensity). The primary endpoint was pain relief at 2 hours (efficacy sets: 99 active, 103 sham).
cards.result: Pain relief at 2 hours: 66.7% (66/99) on active stimulation versus 38.8% (40/103) on sham (therapeutic gain 27.9 points, 95% CI 15.6-40.2; P<.0001). Pain-free: 37.4% versus 18.4% (P=.003). Most-bothersome-symptom relief: 46.3% versus 22.2% (P=.0008). Superiority was sustained at 48 hours. Device-related adverse events: 4.8% (6/126) versus 2.4% (3/126) (P=.499).
cards.watchOut: The sham device mimicked the sensation; whether blinding held is not directly reported, and conditioned-pain-modulation devices are unusually exposed to expectation effects — one reason a second trial matters and its absence caps this stamp.
cards.source: Yarnitsky D et al.. Remote Electrical Neuromodulation (REN) Relieves Acute Migraine: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled, Multicenter Trial. Headache. 2019. PMID: 31074005. Registry ID: NCT03361423. shelves.title: Migraine prevention: daily supraorbital trigeminal stimulation probably reduces migraine days — responders 38.1% vs 12.1% on sham in the single small PREMICE trial
shelves.question: In episodic migraine, does daily supraorbital external trigeminal nerve stimulation reduce monthly migraine days compared with sham stimulation?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Migraine Disorders/prevention & control · Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: The PREMICE trial randomised 67 patients with episodic migraine to daily 20-minute supraorbital external trigeminal nerve stimulation with the tested device (named in the record as the Cefaly device) or sham for 3 months. Migraine days fell significantly in the active group (6.94 to 4.88 per month; P=.023) and not on sham (6.54 to 6.22), and the 50% responder rate was 38.1% versus 12.1% (P=.023) — a therapeutic gain of 26 points. Migraine attacks, headache days, and acute drug intake also fell on active treatment only. No adverse events occurred in either group. The record itself classifies the evidence as Class III, the trial is small and 3 months long, and the sham's credibility (verum stimulation is perceptible) is the standing question for this device class. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — flagged for the developer's personal verdict as a single small trial.

cards.headline: PREMICE 2013: 50% responders 38.1% on supraorbital stimulation vs 12.1% on sham; migraine days 6.94 → 4.88 vs 6.54 → 6.22
cards.summary: PREMICE 2013: 50% responders 38.1% on supraorbital stimulation vs 12.1% on sham; migraine days 6.94 → 4.88 vs 6.54 → 6.22
cards.people: 67 patients with at least 2 migraine attacks per month at 5 Belgian tertiary headache clinics, randomised 1:1 after a 1-month run-in to daily 20-minute supraorbital transcutaneous stimulation (verum) or sham for 3 months; intention-to-treat analysis. Primary outcomes were change in monthly migraine days and the 50% responder rate.
cards.result: Monthly migraine days fell from 6.94 to 4.88 on verum (P=.023) and from 6.54 to 6.22 on sham (P=.608). The 50% responder rate was 38.1% on verum versus 12.1% on sham (P=.023). Monthly migraine attacks (P=.044), headache days (P=.041), and acute antimigraine drug intake (P=.007) also fell significantly on verum only. No adverse events in either group.
cards.watchOut: Sixty-seven patients, 3 months, and a perceptible active stimulus against sham — blinding integrity is the weak point of every trial of this device type, and the record grades its own evidence Class III.
cards.source: Schoenen J et al.. Migraine prevention with a supraorbital transcutaneous stimulator: a randomized controlled trial. Neurology. 2013. PMID: 23390177. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Ruptured aneurysm: coiling cut death or dependence at 1 year (23.5% vs 30.9%) in ISAT's both-treatments-suitable population — BRAT's all-comers found no overall difference and far more retreatment after coiling
shelves.question: In subarachnoid haemorrhage from a ruptured intracranial aneurysm suitable for either treatment, does endovascular coiling reduce death or dependency compared with neurosurgical clipping?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Adult · Aged · Aneurysm, Ruptured/mortality,surgery,therapy · Embolization, Therapeutic/adverse effects · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Intracranial Aneurysm/mortality,surgery,therapy · Middle Aged · Neurosurgical Procedures/adverse effects · Quality of Life · Recurrence · Subarachnoid Hemorrhage/surgery,therapy · Survival Rate · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: For a ruptured aneurysm suitable for either treatment, the two randomised trials point in related but not identical directions, and the difference is the population. ISAT (2,143 patients, mostly good-grade with anterior-circulation aneurysms that both teams accepted as suitable for either approach) found death or dependence at 1 year in 23.5% after coiling versus 30.9% after clipping — an absolute reduction of 7.4 percentage points (P=.0001) — with the survival advantage significant out to 7 years, less epilepsy after coiling, but a higher late rebleeding risk. BRAT (500 enrolled at a single centre, all-comers) found no significant overall difference in poor outcome at 6 years (P=.24) — a trial heavily diluted by crossover, since 38% of patients assigned to coiling were actually clipped, against 1.9% the other way; coiled aneurysms were completely obliterated far less often (48% versus 96%) and retreated more often (16.4% versus 4.6%), yet posterior-circulation aneurysms favoured coiling in BRAT too, and no recurrent haemorrhage occurred in coiled patients followed to 6 years. BRAT is carded from its 6-year results paper; the 3-year record (PMID 23991842) carries no abstract data in PubMed, so no figures are taken from it. PROPOSED SPLIT: POSSIBLE (benefit) for coiling in ISAT-type patients — good-grade, aneurysm judged suitable for either treatment; POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for functional outcome across BRAT's all-comer population, with coiling's durability costs (obliteration, retreatment) stated on the face. Tier C: the primary outcome is death or dependency. Flagged for the developer's personal verdict.

cards.headline: ISAT 2005: dead or dependent at 1 year in 23.5% after coiling vs 30.9% after clipping (absolute reduction 7.4 points; P=.0001)
cards.summary: ISAT 2005: dead or dependent at 1 year in 23.5% after coiling vs 30.9% after clipping (absolute reduction 7.4 points; P=.0001)
cards.people: 2,143 patients with ruptured intracranial aneurysms at 42 centres (mainly UK and Europe) whose aneurysms were suitable for either treatment, randomised to endovascular coiling (n=1,073) or neurosurgical clipping (n=1,070); 1-year outcomes are reported for 1,063 and 1,055 patients respectively. The primary outcome was death or dependence (modified Rankin scale 3-6) at 1 year.
cards.result: Dead or dependent at 1 year: 250/1,063 (23.5%) after coiling versus 326/1,055 (30.9%) after clipping — absolute risk reduction 7.4% (95% CI 3.6-11.2; P=.0001). The early survival advantage was maintained and significant up to 7 years (log rank P=.03). Epilepsy risk was substantially lower after coiling; late rebleeding risk was higher after coiling, though low in absolute terms.
cards.watchOut: ISAT randomised only the minority of screened patients whose aneurysms suited both treatments — disproportionately good-grade and anterior circulation; its answer does not automatically transfer to poor-grade or posterior-circulation presentations.
cards.source: Molyneux AJ et al.. International subarachnoid aneurysm trial (ISAT) of neurosurgical clipping versus endovascular coiling in 2143 patients with ruptured intracranial aneurysms: a randomised comparison of effects on survival, dependency, seizures, rebleeding, subgroups, and aneurysm occlusion. Lancet. 2005. PMID: 16139655. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: BRAT 6-year results: no overall difference in poor outcome (P=.24) — with 38% crossover from coiling to clipping, obliteration 48% vs 96%, retreatment 16.4% vs 4.6%
cards.summary: BRAT 6-year results: no overall difference in poor outcome (P=.24) — with 38% crossover from coiling to clipping, obliteration 48% vs 96%, retreatment 16.4% vs 4.6%
cards.people: 500 patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage enrolled at a single centre; 471 randomised (238 to clipping, 233 to coiling) and 408 treated patients form the reported cohort. Crossover was at the treating physician's discretion: 75/199 (38%) assigned to coiling were crossed to clipping, versus 4/209 (1.9%) the other way. The primary outcome was poor outcome (modified Rankin scale above 2) by assigned treatment; 336 patients were examined at 6 years.
cards.result: No significant difference between treatments in poor outcome at 6 years (P=.24), as at 3 years. Complete aneurysm obliteration at 6 years: 96% (111/116) after clipping versus 48% (23/48) after coiling (P<.0001). Retreatment: 4.6% (13/280) clipping versus 16.4% (21/128) coiling (P<.0001). No difference for anterior-circulation aneurysms; posterior-circulation aneurysms favoured coiling, and no recurrent haemorrhage was known in coiled patients over 6 years. The authors note the trial was underpowered for small differences.
cards.watchOut: With 38% one-way crossover, BRAT's intention-to-treat comparison is heavily diluted toward no difference — its null is weaker evidence against coiling than ISAT's positive is for it, and the two trials enrolled quite different case mixes.
cards.source: Spetzler RF et al.. The Barrow Ruptured Aneurysm Trial: 6-year results. J Neurosurg. 2015. PMID: 26115467. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage: oral nimodipine reduced cerebral infarction (22% vs 33%) and poor outcome (20% vs 33%) in the British trial, with the earlier Allen trial in support
shelves.question: After aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage, does oral nimodipine reduce cerebral infarction and poor outcome compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Aged · Blood Pressure/drug effects · Cerebral Infarction/mortality,prevention & control · Clinical Trials as Topic · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Multicenter Studies as Topic · Nimodipine/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Prognosis · Random Allocation · Recurrence · Subarachnoid Hemorrhage/drug therapy,mortality · Time Factors
shelves.balance: Oral nimodipine is one of the few drug treatments in aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage backed by two positive placebo-controlled trials from the pre-registration era — the reason it became and remains standard care. The British aneurysm nimodipine trial (Pickard 1989, 554 patients) gave nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours for 21 days: cerebral infarction occurred in 22% versus 33% on placebo (a 34% relative reduction), and poor outcome (death or severe disability) in 20% versus 33% — 55/278 versus 91/278 — a 40% relative reduction, an absolute difference of about 13 percentage points. The earlier American trial (Allen 1983, 125 neurologically normal patients after haemorrhage) used intravenous then oral nimodipine against a narrower endpoint: a severe persistent deficit or death from arterial spasm in 1/56 on nimodipine versus 8/60 on placebo (P=.03). Both trials predate modern trial registration and modern SAH care (most patients today also have their aneurysm secured early), so the absolute gains belong to their era; the direction has never been reversed by a later trial. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit). Tier C: the British trial's poor-outcome endpoint embeds death.

cards.headline: Pickard 1989: cerebral infarction 22% vs 33% and poor outcome 20% vs 33% on oral nimodipine vs placebo
cards.summary: Pickard 1989: cerebral infarction 22% vs 33% and poor outcome 20% vs 33% on oral nimodipine vs placebo
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (British aneurysm nimodipine trial)
cards.people: 554 patients admitted within 96 hours of subarachnoid haemorrhage to 4 UK regional neurosurgical units, randomised double-blind to nimodipine 60 mg orally every 4 hours for 21 days (n=278) or placebo (n=276), followed for 3 months with intention-to-treat analysis. Endpoints were cerebral infarction and poor outcome (death or severe disability).
cards.result: Cerebral infarction: 61/278 (22%) on nimodipine versus 92/276 (33%) on placebo — a 34% relative reduction (95% CI 13-50%). Poor outcome: 55/278 (20%) versus 91/278 (33%) as printed in the record — a 40% relative reduction (95% CI 20-55%), about 13 percentage points absolute. The treatment was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: Conducted 1985-87, before early aneurysm securing and modern neurocritical care; the record's placebo denominator for poor outcome is printed as 278 although 276 were randomised — the percentages are quoted as the record gives them.
cards.source: Pickard JD et al.. Effect of oral nimodipine on cerebral infarction and outcome after subarachnoid haemorrhage: British aneurysm nimodipine trial. BMJ. 1989. PMID: 2496789. cards.headline: Allen 1983: severe deficit or death from vasospasm in 1/56 on nimodipine vs 8/60 on placebo (P=.03)
cards.summary: Allen 1983: severe deficit or death from vasospasm in 1/56 on nimodipine vs 8/60 on placebo (P=.03)
cards.people: 125 neurologically normal patients with subarachnoid haemorrhage from intracranial aneurysms, enrolled within 96 hours at multiple institutions in a prospective double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial of nimodipine (intravenous then oral, per the era's protocol) for 21 days; the endpoint was a deficit from cerebral arterial spasm that persisted and was severe, or caused death, by the end of treatment (116 patients in the reported comparison).
cards.result: Severe persistent deficit or death from spasm: 1/56 on nimodipine versus 8/60 on placebo (P=.03, Fisher's exact test). Among patients with deficits, greater subarachnoid blood burden predicted worse outcome on placebo but not on nimodipine. No side effects from nimodipine were reported.
cards.watchOut: Small, restricted to patients neurologically normal after the bleed, and graded on a spasm-specific endpoint — it corroborates the British trial's direction; it cannot carry an outcome claim on its own. (Anchor re-resolved this run: the correct record is PMID 6338383.)

shelves.title: Chronic subdural haematoma: dexamethasone made functional outcomes worse (favourable outcome 83.9% vs 90.3% on placebo) and caused more adverse events in the 748-patient Dex-CSDH trial
shelves.question: In symptomatic chronic subdural haematoma, does a tapering course of dexamethasone improve functional outcome compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Aged · Combined Modality Therapy · Dexamethasone/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Persons with Disabilities · Female · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Hematoma, Subdural, Chronic/complications,drug therapy,mortality,surgery · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Male · Middle Aged · Reoperation/statistics & numerical data · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Dexamethasone for symptomatic chronic subdural haematoma was widely used on the theory that it would calm the haematoma's inflammatory membranes; the one large randomised trial showed the opposite. Dex-CSDH randomised 748 adults (mean age 74; 94% underwent surgical evacuation during the admission) to a 2-week tapering course of oral dexamethasone or placebo alongside standard care. At 6 months, a favourable outcome (modified Rankin scale 0-3) occurred in 83.9% on dexamethasone versus 90.3% on placebo — an absolute reduction of 6.4 percentage points in favour of placebo (P=.01) — and more adverse events occurred on dexamethasone (the trial's full funder report records serious adverse events in 16.0% versus 6.4%). The one endpoint favouring the drug was repeat surgery for recurrence: 1.7% versus 7.1%. Correction made on the face of this pack: the drafting slate described the 2024 Health Technology Assessment report (PMID 38512045) as 'a second UK placebo-controlled trial' — it is the same Dex-CSDH trial's monograph report (same 748 patients, same ISRCTN80782810), not a second trial, and it is not carded as one. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm) on the primary functional outcome — flagged for the developer's personal verdict as a single (large, definitive) trial, Tier C because the Rankin scale embeds death.

cards.headline: Dex-CSDH 2020: favourable outcome at 6 months in 83.9% on dexamethasone vs 90.3% on placebo (difference -6.4 points; P=.01); repeat surgery 1.7% vs 7.1%
cards.summary: Dex-CSDH 2020: favourable outcome at 6 months in 83.9% on dexamethasone vs 90.3% on placebo (difference -6.4 points; P=.01); repeat surgery 1.7% vs 7.1%
cards.people: 748 adults with symptomatic chronic subdural haematoma at UK centres (mean age 74; 94% surgically evacuated during the index admission; 60% in both groups had a modified Rankin score of 1-3 at admission), randomised 1:1 to a 2-week tapering course of oral dexamethasone starting at 8 mg twice daily (n=375) or placebo (n=373), with surgery decided by the treating clinician. The primary outcome was favourable outcome (modified Rankin scale 0-3) at 6 months; 680 patients had primary-outcome data.
cards.result: Favourable outcome: 286/341 (83.9%) on dexamethasone versus 306/339 (90.3%) on placebo (difference -6.4 percentage points, 95% CI -11.4 to -1.4; P=.01). Repeat surgery for recurrence: 6/349 (1.7%) versus 25/350 (7.1%). More adverse events occurred in the dexamethasone group (the trial's funder monograph reports serious adverse events in 60/375 [16.0%] versus 24/373 [6.4%]).
cards.watchOut: Ninety-four per cent had surgery, so the trial answers 'dexamethasone alongside usual (mostly surgical) care'; the role of steroids in the minority managed without surgery is not defined by it. The favourable repeat-surgery result is a real counter-signal and is stated, not suppressed.
cards.source: Hutchinson PJ et al.. Trial of Dexamethasone for Chronic Subdural Hematoma. N Engl J Med. 2020. PMID: 33326713. Registry ID: ISRCTN80782810. shelves.title: Critically ill adults: continuous EEG found far more seizures than routine EEG but made no difference to 6-month mortality (49% vs 48%) in the CERTA trial
shelves.question: In critically ill adults with altered consciousness and no recent seizure, does continuous EEG reduce 6-month mortality compared with routine (repeated spot) EEG?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Consciousness/physiology · Critical Illness/therapy · Electroencephalography/methods · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Seizures/diagnosis,physiopathology,therapy
shelves.balance: Continuous EEG in critically ill adults with altered consciousness does what it is supposed to do diagnostically — and, in the only randomised trial, none of it changed who lived. CERTA randomised 364 patients (Glasgow Coma Scale 11 or less or equivalent, no recent seizure) to 30-48 hours of continuous EEG or two 20-minute routine EEGs. Six-month mortality — the primary outcome — was 89/182 versus 88/182 (adjusted relative risk 1.02, 95% CI 0.83-1.26; P=.85 — the treatment made no difference). Continuous monitoring detected more interictal features (adjusted RR 1.26) and far more seizures (adjusted RR 3.37), and antiseizure therapy was changed more often (RR 1.84) — a clean demonstration that better detection plus more treatment changes did not translate into survival in this population. No subgroup showed an effect. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — flagged for the developer's personal verdict: a single trial with a mortality primary endpoint, Tier C.

cards.headline: CERTA 2020: 6-month mortality 89/182 on continuous EEG vs 88/182 on routine EEG (adjusted RR 1.02; P=.85) — despite triple the seizure detection
cards.summary: CERTA 2020: 6-month mortality 89/182 on continuous EEG vs 88/182 on routine EEG (adjusted RR 1.02; P=.85) — despite triple the seizure detection
cards.people: 364 critically ill adults with impaired consciousness (Glasgow Coma Scale score 11 or less, or Full Outline of Responsiveness score 12 or less) and no recent seizures or status epilepticus, at 4 Swiss tertiary hospitals, randomised 1:1 to continuous EEG for 30-48 hours or two routine 20-minute EEGs; cerebral and non-cerebral causes of coma were both included. The primary outcome was mortality at 6 months.
cards.result: Mortality at 6 months: 89/182 (49%) on continuous EEG versus 88/182 (48%) on routine EEG (adjusted relative risk 1.02, 95% CI 0.83-1.26; P=.85). Continuous EEG increased detection of interictal features (adjusted RR 1.26; P=.004) and seizures (adjusted RR 3.37; P=.001) and adaptations of antiseizure therapy (RR 1.84; P=.01). No subgroup (age, disability, comorbidity, depth of coma, diagnosis) showed significant effect modification.
cards.watchOut: A 364-patient trial cannot exclude a modest mortality effect in either direction (the interval runs 0.83-1.26); what it excludes is the large benefit that detection statistics alone might have suggested.
cards.source: Rossetti AO et al.. Continuous vs Routine Electroencephalogram in Critically Ill Adults With Altered Consciousness and No Recent Seizure: A Multicenter Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Neurol. 2020. PMID: 32716479. Registry ID: NCT03129438. shelves.title: Intraventricular haemorrhage: alteplase through the drain made no difference to good functional outcome (48% vs 45%) but cut mortality (18% vs 29%) — while doubling survival with severe disability (CLEAR III)
shelves.question: In intracerebral haemorrhage with intraventricular extension obstructing the third or fourth ventricle, does intraventricular alteplase through an external ventricular drain improve functional outcome compared with saline irrigation?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Cerebral Intraventricular Hemorrhage/diagnostic imaging,therapy · Drainage/methods · Female · Fibrinolytic Agents/therapeutic use · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Proportional Hazards Models · Severity of Illness Index · Sodium Chloride/therapeutic use · Stroke/diagnostic imaging,therapy · Therapeutic Irrigation/methods · Tissue Plasminogen Activator/therapeutic use · Tomography, X-Ray Computed · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: CLEAR III is the library's clearest mortality-disability trade-off, and both sides of it belong in the first paragraph. In 500 patients with intracerebral haemorrhage under 30 mL and intraventricular blood obstructing the third or fourth ventricle, irrigating the external ventricular drain with alteplase (1 mg up to every 8 hours, up to 12 doses) versus saline did NOT improve the primary outcome: good functional outcome (modified Rankin scale 0-3) at 180 days in 48% versus 45% (risk ratio 1.06, 95% CI 0.88-1.28; P=.554). But mortality at 180 days was significantly lower with alteplase (18% versus 29%; hazard ratio 0.60; P=.006) — and the proportion surviving with severe disability (Rankin 5) was higher (17% versus 9%; risk ratio 1.99). Ventriculitis (7% versus 12%) and overall serious adverse events (46% versus 60%) were less frequent with alteplase, and symptomatic bleeding did not differ (2% versus 2%). Whether trading deaths for severely disabled survivors is a benefit is a values question the trial cannot answer; this shelf reports the exchange rate and stamps the two endpoints separately. PROPOSED SPLIT: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for functional outcome; POSSIBLE (benefit) for mortality, with the severe-disability increase printed beside it. Tier C. Flagged for the developer's personal verdict.

cards.headline: CLEAR III 2017: good outcome 48% vs 45% (no difference) — but mortality 18% vs 29% (HR 0.60) and Rankin-5 survival 17% vs 9% on alteplase
cards.summary: CLEAR III 2017: good outcome 48% vs 45% (no difference) — but mortality 18% vs 29% (HR 0.60) and Rankin-5 survival 17% vs 9% on alteplase
cards.people: 500 patients with stable non-traumatic intracerebral haemorrhage under 30 mL, intraventricular haemorrhage obstructing the 3rd or 4th ventricle, and a routinely placed external ventricular drain, randomised double-blind across multiple regions to up to 12 doses of alteplase 1 mg or 0.9% saline every 8 hours through the drain (249 versus 251). The primary outcome was good functional outcome (modified Rankin scale 0-3) at 180 days by blinded central adjudication; 491 patients had follow-up data.
cards.result: Good outcome: 48% on alteplase versus 45% on saline (risk ratio 1.06, 95% CI 0.88-1.28; P=.554); adjusted difference 3.5% (P=.420). Mortality at 180 days: 46 (18%) versus 73 (29%) (hazard ratio 0.60, 95% CI 0.41-0.86; P=.006). Rankin 5 (severe disability): 42 (17%) versus 21 (9%) (risk ratio 1.99, 95% CI 1.22-3.26; P=.007). Ventriculitis 7% versus 12% (P=.048); serious adverse events 46% versus 60% (P=.002); symptomatic bleeding 2% versus 2% (P=.771).
cards.watchOut: The mortality and disability results are two views of one shift in the outcome distribution — quoting the 11-point mortality reduction without the doubling of Rankin-5 survival misrepresents the trial; the record's mortality percentages (18% vs 29%) are quoted as printed.
cards.source: Hanley DF et al.. Thrombolytic removal of intraventricular haemorrhage in treatment of severe stroke: results of the randomised, multicentre, multiregion, placebo-controlled CLEAR III trial. Lancet. 2017. shelves.title: Acute vascular brain injury: device-based fever prevention halved fever burden but made no difference to functional recovery in the futility-stopped INTREPID trial
shelves.question: In critically ill patients with acute vascular brain injury (ischaemic stroke, ICH or SAH), does proactive device-based fever prevention improve functional outcome compared with standard fever treatment?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Fever/diagnosis,etiology,prevention & control · Intensive Care Units · Recovery of Function · Critical Illness/mortality,therapy · Hemorrhagic Stroke/complications,mortality,physiopathology,therapy · Ischemic Stroke/complications,mortality,physiopathology,therapy · Critical Care/methods · Adolescent · Young Adult · Adult · Aged, 80 and over
shelves.balance: INTREPID tested whether preventing fever, rather than treating it when it appears, improves recovery after acute vascular brain injury — and answered the mechanism question yes and the outcome question no. In 686 enrolled critically ill patients with ischaemic stroke, intracerebral haemorrhage, or subarachnoid haemorrhage, an automated surface device targeting 37.0 °C for up to 14 days roughly halved daily fever burden versus standard tiered fever treatment (0.37 versus 0.73 °C-hour; P<.001). Three-month functional recovery did not differ (median modified Rankin score 4.0 in both groups; odds ratio for a favourable shift 1.09, 95% CI 0.81-1.46; P=.54 — the treatment made no difference), and major adverse events were at least as frequent with prevention (82.2% versus 75.9%). Enrolment was stopped at a planned interim analysis for futility after 686 of 1,176 planned patients, so the null is a futility-stopped null: it excludes the effect the trial was powered for, not every conceivable small benefit. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — flagged for the developer's personal verdict: a single trial, stopped early, with an outcome scale that embeds death. Tier C.

cards.headline: INTREPID 2024: fever burden halved (0.37 vs 0.73 °C-hour) but 3-month functional outcome identical (OR 1.09; P=.54); stopped for futility
cards.summary: INTREPID 2024: fever burden halved (0.37 vs 0.73 °C-hour) but 3-month functional outcome identical (OR 1.09; P=.54); stopped for futility
cards.type: Open-label randomised clinical trial with blinded outcome assessment (INTREPID)
cards.people: 686 critically ill patients with acute vascular brain injury (ischaemic stroke, intracerebral haemorrhage, or subarachnoid haemorrhage) at 43 intensive care units in 7 countries, randomised open-label (blinded outcome assessment) to device-based fever prevention targeting 37.0 °C (n=339) or standard tiered fever treatment at 38 °C or above (n=338); the primary analysis population was 677. Enrolment stopped after a planned interim analysis showed futility for the functional endpoint.
cards.result: Daily mean fever burden: 0.37 °C-hour on prevention versus 0.73 on standard care (difference -0.35, 95% CI -0.51 to -0.20; P<.001). Functional recovery at 3 months did not differ (median modified Rankin score 4.0 versus 4.0; odds ratio for favourable shift 1.09, 95% CI 0.81-1.46; P=.54). Major adverse events: 82.2% versus 75.9%, including death, pneumonia, sepsis, and malignant cerebral oedema; infections 33.8% versus 34.5%.
cards.watchOut: Stopped at 686 of 1,176 planned patients for futility — the confidence interval (0.81-1.46) still admits modest benefit or harm; and the three stroke subtypes were pooled, with fever-burden reductions largest in the haemorrhage groups.

shelves.title: Severe traumatic brain injury: ICP-monitor-guided care made no difference to outcome or 6-month mortality versus imaging-and-examination-guided care in the BEST TRIP trial
shelves.question: In severe traumatic brain injury, does management guided by an intracranial-pressure monitor improve outcome compared with management guided by imaging and clinical examination?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Brain/diagnostic imaging,physiopathology · Brain Injuries/complications,mortality,physiopathology · Female · Humans · Intracranial Hypertension/diagnosis,etiology · Intracranial Pressure · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Length of Stay · Male · Monitoring, Physiologic/instrumentation,methods · Neurologic Examination · Survival Rate · Tomography, X-Ray Computed · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: BEST TRIP is the only randomised trial of intracranial-pressure monitoring itself, and it found that care built around the monitor was not superior to care built around imaging and clinical examination. In 324 patients aged 13 or older with severe traumatic brain injury in Bolivia and Ecuador, the composite primary outcome (survival, consciousness, functional and neuropsychological status across 21 measures) scored at the 56th percentile with pressure-guided care versus the 53rd with imaging/clinical care (P=.49 — the treatment made no difference). Six-month mortality was 39% versus 41% (P=.60). One finding cuts against any reading of the imaging-based protocol as 'doing less': brain-specific treatments (hyperosmolar fluids, hyperventilation) were used on MORE days in the imaging/clinical group (4.8 versus 3.4 days; P=.002) — the trial compared two active management protocols, not monitoring versus neglect, and it was conducted in a pre-hospital and ICU system quite different from North American or European trauma care. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — flagged for the developer's personal verdict: a single trial, single-region, with a composite embedding mortality. Tier C.

cards.headline: BEST TRIP 2012: composite outcome percentile 56 with ICP-guided care vs 53 with imaging/clinical care (P=.49); 6-month mortality 39% vs 41%
cards.summary: BEST TRIP 2012: composite outcome percentile 56 with ICP-guided care vs 53 with imaging/clinical care (P=.49); 6-month mortality 39% vs 41%
cards.people: 324 patients aged 13 years or older with severe traumatic brain injury treated in intensive care units in Bolivia and Ecuador, randomised to guidelines-based management driven by monitored intraparenchymal intracranial pressure (target 20 mm Hg or less) or by imaging and clinical examination. The primary outcome was a composite percentile across 21 measures of survival time, impaired consciousness, functional status at 3 and 6 months, and neuropsychological status at 6 months, assessed by examiners unaware of assignment.
cards.result: Primary composite: 56 in the pressure-monitoring group versus 53 in the imaging-clinical group (P=.49). Six-month mortality: 39% versus 41% (P=.60). Median ICU stay 12 versus 9 days (P=.25). Days of brain-specific treatment were higher in the imaging-clinical group (4.8 versus 3.4; P=.002). Serious adverse events were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: A two-country Latin American setting with different pre-hospital care and resources limits transfer to other trauma systems — the standing criticism of this trial — and the composite percentile outcome is less legible than its mortality component, which is also null.
cards.source: Chesnut RM et al.. A trial of intracranial-pressure monitoring in traumatic brain injury. N Engl J Med. 2012. PMID: 23234472. Registry ID: NCT01068522. shelves.title: Aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage: early prophylactic lumbar drainage probably improves outcome — unfavourable outcome 32.6% vs 44.8% in the single EARLYDRAIN trial
shelves.question: After aneurysm treatment for subarachnoid haemorrhage, does early prophylactic lumbar CSF drainage improve outcome compared with standard care?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Female · Middle Aged · Male · Subarachnoid Hemorrhage/complications,surgery · Drainage/adverse effects,methods · Cerebral Infarction/complications · Brain Ischemia/complications · Aneurysm/complications · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: EARLYDRAIN randomised 287 patients after aneurysm treatment for subarachnoid haemorrhage (all clinical grades; clipping or coiling within 48 hours) to an early prophylactic lumbar drain (5 mL/hour, started within 72 hours) plus standard care, or standard care alone, at 19 centres in Germany, Switzerland, and Canada. Unfavourable outcome (modified Rankin scale 3-6) at 6 months occurred in 32.6% with drainage versus 44.8% without — a risk ratio of 0.73 (95% CI 0.52-0.98) and an absolute difference of 12 percentage points (P=.04) — and secondary infarctions at discharge were fewer (28.5% versus 39.9%; risk ratio 0.71). The result is promising and fragile in the usual single-trial ways: open-label treatment (though outcome assessors were masked), a primary P value of .04, and a recruitment history spanning 2011-2016 with 20 invalid randomisations excluded before the intention-to-treat set. It also tests prophylactic drainage added to standard care — not drainage as rescue therapy for established delayed cerebral ischaemia. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — flagged for the developer's personal verdict as a single-trial shelf, Tier C because the outcome scale embeds death.

cards.headline: EARLYDRAIN 2023: unfavourable outcome at 6 months in 32.6% with early lumbar drainage vs 44.8% without (RR 0.73; P=.04)
cards.summary: EARLYDRAIN 2023: unfavourable outcome at 6 months in 32.6% with early lumbar drainage vs 44.8% without (RR 0.73; P=.04)
cards.type: Pragmatic, open-label randomised clinical trial with blinded endpoint evaluation (EARLYDRAIN)
cards.people: 287 analysable adults with acute aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage of all clinical grades at 19 centres in Germany, Switzerland, and Canada; aneurysm treated by clipping or coiling within 48 hours. 144 were randomised to an additional lumbar drain (5 mL/hour, started within 72 hours of the haemorrhage, median day 2) and 143 to standard care only. The trial was open-label with blinded endpoint evaluation; the primary outcome was unfavourable outcome (modified Rankin scale 3-6) at 6 months, assessed by masked assessors.
cards.result: Unfavourable outcome: 47/144 (32.6%) with lumbar drainage versus 64/143 (44.8%) with standard care (risk ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.52-0.98; absolute risk difference -0.12, 95% CI -0.23 to -0.01; P=.04). Secondary infarctions at discharge: 41 (28.5%) versus 57 (39.9%) (risk ratio 0.71, 95% CI 0.49-0.99; P=.04).
cards.watchOut: One trial, an open-label intervention, and a primary result at P=.04 — a handful of outcomes reclassified would erase significance; 307 patients were randomised and 287 analysed after invalid randomisations (mainly consent) were removed.

shelves.title: Aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage: intravenous magnesium made no difference to outcome in two phase 3 trials (MASH-2; IMASH) — the question is closed
shelves.question: After aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage, does intravenous magnesium sulphate improve functional outcome compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Female · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Magnesium Sulfate/administration & dosage · Male · Middle Aged · Neuroprotective Agents/administration & dosage · Pilot Projects · Subarachnoid Hemorrhage/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Intravenous magnesium after aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage is a closed question: two phase 3 placebo-controlled trials, run independently on different continents, both found nothing. MASH-2 (1,204 patients in Europe and South America; magnesium sulphate 64 mmol/day) found poor outcome at 3 months in 26.2% on magnesium versus 25.3% on placebo (risk ratio 1.03, 95% CI 0.85-1.25), and its updated meta-analysis of seven randomised trials (2,047 patients) gave a pooled risk ratio of 0.96 (0.86-1.08). IMASH (327 patients in Hong Kong and China; infusion titrated to double the serum level) found favourable outcome at 6 months in 64% versus 63% (odds ratio 1.0, 95% CI 0.7-1.6), with no subgroup — grade, age, hypertension, haematoma, aneurysm site or size, treatment mode — showing benefit. The pilot-era promise did not survive either definitive trial. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference). Tier C: poor outcome embeds death. Contrast nimodipine (Shelf #2390): same disease, same era of enthusiasm — opposite verdict, because its trials were positive.

cards.headline: MASH-2 2012: poor outcome in 26.2% on magnesium vs 25.3% on placebo (RR 1.03); updated meta-analysis RR 0.96
cards.summary: MASH-2 2012: poor outcome in 26.2% on magnesium vs 25.3% on placebo (RR 1.03); updated meta-analysis RR 0.96
cards.people: 1,204 patients aged 18 or older with aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage admitted within 4 days, at 8 centres in Europe and South America, randomised double-blind to intravenous magnesium sulphate 64 mmol/day (n=606) or placebo (n=597 analysed). The primary outcome was poor outcome (modified Rankin scale 4-5, or death) at 3 months, analysed by intention to treat.
cards.result: Poor outcome: 158 patients (26.2%) on magnesium versus 151 (25.3%) on placebo (risk ratio 1.03, 95% CI 0.85-1.25). The trial's updated meta-analysis of seven randomised trials (2,047 patients) found magnesium not superior to placebo (risk ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.86-1.08). The authors concluded routine administration cannot be recommended.
cards.watchOut: A fixed-dose regimen; the 'wrong dose or timing' objection was separately answered by IMASH's titrated regimen — also null — which is why this shelf reads the question as closed.

shelves.title: Depression after one failed antidepressant: augmenting with aripiprazole probably beats switching — remission 28.9% vs 22.3% in the single large VAST-D trial of veterans
shelves.question: In major depression unresponsive to one adequate antidepressant course, is it better to switch to bupropion, augment with bupropion, or augment with aripiprazole?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antidepressive Agents/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Antipsychotic Agents/therapeutic use · Aripiprazole/therapeutic use · Bupropion/administration & dosage · Major Depressive Disorder/drug therapy · Drug Resistance · Drug Substitution · Drug Synergism · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Remission Induction · United States · Veterans
shelves.balance: VAST-D is the single large trial of the second-step choice in major depression that has not responded to one adequate antidepressant course, and its answer is a modest ranking, not a breakthrough. In 1,522 patients (85.2% men; US veterans) randomised to switch to bupropion, augment with bupropion, or augment with aripiprazole, 12-week remission was 22.3% (switch), 26.9% (augment-bupropion), and 28.9% (augment-aripiprazole). Only the aripiprazole-augmentation versus switch comparison was significant (relative risk 1.30, 95% CI 1.05-1.60; P=.02) — an absolute gain of 6.6 percentage points — and response rates also favoured aripiprazole augmentation (74.3% versus 62.4% and 65.6%). Relapse did not differ. The costs were asymmetric, as expected: anxiety was more frequent in both bupropion groups (24.3% and 22.5% versus 16.6%), while somnolence, akathisia, and weight gain were more frequent on aripiprazole. The authors themselves call the effect modest and ask for cost-effectiveness analysis before net utility can be judged. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for aripiprazole augmentation over switching — flagged for the developer's personal verdict as a single-trial shelf in a predominantly male veteran population.

cards.headline: VAST-D 2017: remission 28.9% augmenting with aripiprazole vs 22.3% switching to bupropion (RR 1.30; P=.02); augmenting with bupropion 26.9%, not significant
cards.summary: VAST-D 2017: remission 28.9% augmenting with aripiprazole vs 22.3% switching to bupropion (RR 1.30; P=.02); augmenting with bupropion 26.9%, not significant
cards.people: 1,522 patients with nonpsychotic major depressive disorder unresponsive to at least one adequate antidepressant course, at 35 US Veterans Health Administration centres (mean age 54.4 years; 85.2% men), randomised 1:1:1 to switch to bupropion (n=511), augment with bupropion (n=506), or augment with aripiprazole (n=505) for a 12-week acute phase (with continuation to 36 weeks); 74.7% completed the acute phase. The primary outcome was remission (QIDS-C16 score 5 or less at two consecutive visits).
cards.result: Remission at 12 weeks: 22.3% (switch), 26.9% (augment-bupropion), 28.9% (augment-aripiprazole). Aripiprazole augmentation exceeded switching (relative risk 1.30, 95% CI 1.05-1.60; P=.02); other remission comparisons were not significant. Response: 74.3% (aripiprazole) versus 62.4% (switch) and 65.6% (augment-bupropion), both significant. Relapse did not differ. Anxiety was more frequent in the bupropion groups (24.3% switch, 22.5% augment-bupropion, versus 16.6%); somnolence, akathisia, and weight gain were more frequent with aripiprazole.
cards.watchOut: A predominantly male veteran population with one prior failed course; the winning margin is 6.6 percentage points of remission bought with an antipsychotic's adverse-effect profile, and there is no placebo arm — all three strategies are active, commonly used care.

shelves.title: Major depression: pharmacogenomic guidance steered prescribing away from drug–gene interactions and produced a small, nonpersistent remission gain in the single large PRIME Care trial
shelves.question: In major depressive disorder starting or switching antidepressant treatment, does providing pharmacogenomic drug–gene interaction results to clinicians improve remission compared with usual care?
shelves.mesh: Antidepressive Agents/metabolism, pharmacology, therapeutic use · Clinical Decision-Making · Major Depressive Disorder/drug therapy, genetics · Drug Interactions/genetics · Female · Humans · Inappropriate Prescribing/prevention & control · Male · Middle Aged · Pharmacogenetics · Pharmacogenomic Testing · Remission Induction · Treatment Outcome · United States · United States Department of Veterans Affairs
shelves.balance: PRIME Care is the largest randomised trial of pharmacogenomic-guided antidepressant prescribing, and its two answers point in different strengths of direction. Giving clinicians commercial drug–gene interaction results at the point of prescribing changed what they prescribed, decisively: within 30 days, an estimated 59.3% of guided patients received an antidepressant with no predicted drug–gene interaction versus 25.7% under usual care (odds ratio 4.32 for no versus moderate/substantial interaction). The clinical dividend was small and not durable at the final time point: remission across the 24 weeks favoured guided care (odds ratio 1.28; risk difference 2.8 percentage points, 95% CI 0.6 to 5.1), but remission at week 24 itself did not differ significantly (estimated risk difference 1.5 points, 95% CI -2.4 to 5.3; P=.45), with 130 versus 126 patients in remission. The population was 75% male US veterans starting or switching a single antidepressant. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): testing reliably steers prescribing away from predicted interactions, and probably buys a small, early remission advantage — an absolute effect of about 3 points at its best estimate, in a single trial. Flagged for the developer's personal verdict as a single-trial shelf. (The pre-emptive panel-testing question lives at Shelf #472; this shelf is testing at the point of an antidepressant start or switch.)

cards.headline: PRIME Care 2022: pharmacogenomic guidance shifted prescribing away from drug–gene interactions (59.3% vs 25.7% interaction-free) and raised remission modestly over 24 weeks (OR 1.28; +2.8 points) — but not at week 24 itself (P=.45)
cards.summary: PRIME Care 2022: pharmacogenomic guidance shifted prescribing away from drug–gene interactions (59.3% vs 25.7% interaction-free) and raised remission modestly over 24 weeks (OR 1.28; +2.8 points) — but not at week 24 itself (P=.45)
cards.type: Pragmatic, multicentre, randomised clinical trial (PRIME Care)
cards.people: 1,944 patients with major depressive disorder (mean age 48; 25% women) initiating or switching treatment with a single antidepressant, and their 676 clinicians, at 22 US Department of Veterans Affairs medical centres; randomised to care guided by a commercial pharmacogenomic test's drug–gene interaction results (n=966) or usual care with results released after 24 weeks (n=978). Co-primary outcomes were prescriptions with a predicted drug–gene interaction within 30 days and remission (PHQ-9 of 5 or less) across 24 weeks, rated blind.
cards.result: Estimated risks of receiving an antidepressant with none, moderate, and substantial drug–gene interactions were 59.3%, 30.0%, and 10.7% in the guided group versus 25.7%, 54.6%, and 19.7% in usual care (odds ratio 4.32, 95% CI 3.47 to 5.39, for no versus moderate/substantial interaction; P<.001). Remission over 24 weeks was higher with guided care (odds ratio 1.28, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.57; P=.02; risk difference 2.8%, 95% CI 0.6% to 5.1%), but at week 24 remission did not differ significantly (130 vs 126 patients in remission; estimated risk difference 1.5%, 95% CI -2.4% to 5.3%; P=.45). 79% completed the 24-week assessment.
cards.watchOut: A process outcome (prescribing) is proven; the patient outcome is a 2.8-point average remission difference whose own final-time-point estimate is null — quote both, and note the veteran, mostly male population and the single commercial test used.
cards.source: Oslin DW et al.. Effect of Pharmacogenomic Testing for Drug-Gene Interactions on Medication Selection and Remission of Symptoms in Major Depressive Disorder: The PRIME Care Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2022. PMID: 35819423. Registry ID: NCT03170362. shelves.title: Recurrent depression: mindfulness-based cognitive therapy with taper support performed comparably to maintenance antidepressants over two years in PREVENT — no superiority, a real alternative
shelves.question: In people with recurrent depression in remission on maintenance antidepressants, is mindfulness-based cognitive therapy with tapering support as effective as continuing maintenance antidepressants for preventing relapse over two years?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Antidepressive Agents/administration & dosage, therapeutic use · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy/methods · Combined Modality Therapy · Major Depressive Disorder/drug therapy, prevention & control · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Mindfulness/methods · Quality of Life · Recurrence · Single-Blind Method · Socioeconomic Factors · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: For people with recurrent depression who want an alternative to staying on antidepressants, PREVENT is the definitive head-to-head: 424 patients with three or more previous episodes, all on maintenance antidepressants, were randomised to mindfulness-based cognitive therapy with support to taper or stop the drug (MBCT-TS) or to continue maintenance antidepressants for 24 months. Time to relapse or recurrence did not differ (hazard ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.18; P=.43) — the trial was designed to test superiority and found none, so the honest reading is comparability, not proven equivalence, though both groups had enduring positive outcomes on relapse, residual symptoms, and quality of life. The wider evidence leans the same way with more optimism: the individual-patient-data meta-analysis of 9 trials (1,258 patients) found MBCT reduced relapse risk versus non-MBCT controls over 60 weeks (hazard ratio 0.69) and versus active treatments (hazard ratio 0.79), with larger effects in patients with more residual symptoms. Serious adverse events in PREVENT were balanced (five in each group, including two deaths in each, none attributable). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference — MBCT with taper support performed comparably to maintenance antidepressants in the one head-to-head trial): an alternative for patients who prefer it, not a superior one.

cards.headline: PREVENT 2015: relapse hazard on MBCT with taper support vs maintenance antidepressants 0.89 (95% CI 0.67-1.18; P=.43) over 24 months — no superiority, comparable outcomes
cards.summary: PREVENT 2015: relapse hazard on MBCT with taper support vs maintenance antidepressants 0.89 (95% CI 0.67-1.18; P=.43) over 24 months — no superiority, comparable outcomes
cards.people: 424 adults with three or more previous major depressive episodes, on a therapeutic dose of maintenance antidepressants, recruited from 95 UK general practices; randomised single-blind (assessors masked) to mindfulness-based cognitive therapy with tapering support (n=212) or maintenance antidepressants (n=212) for 24 months. The primary outcome was time to relapse or recurrence of depression.
cards.result: Time to relapse or recurrence did not differ between MBCT with taper support and maintenance antidepressants over 24 months (hazard ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.18; P=.43). Five adverse events, including two deaths, were reported in each group; none was attributable to the interventions or the trial. Both treatments were associated with enduring positive outcomes in relapse or recurrence, residual depressive symptoms, and quality of life.
cards.watchOut: A superiority trial that found none is not a formal non-inferiority proof — the confidence interval still admits up to 18% relative more relapses on MBCT; patients randomised were those already stable on maintenance medication.
cards.source: Kuyken W et al.. Effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of mindfulness-based cognitive therapy compared with maintenance antidepressant treatment in the prevention of depressive relapse or recurrence (PREVENT): a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2015. PMID: 25907157. Registry ID: ISRCTN26666654. cards.headline: Individual-patient-data meta-analysis 2016: MBCT cut relapse risk vs non-MBCT controls (HR 0.69) and vs active treatments (HR 0.79) over 60 weeks
cards.summary: Individual-patient-data meta-analysis 2016: MBCT cut relapse risk vs non-MBCT controls (HR 0.69) and vs active treatments (HR 0.79) over 60 weeks
cards.type: Individual patient data meta-analysis of randomised trials
cards.people: Individual patient data from 9 randomised trials, 1,258 patients with recurrent depression (mean age 47.1; 75% women); one further eligible study could not supply data. Relapse was assessed over a 60-week follow-up.
cards.result: Patients receiving MBCT had a reduced risk of depressive relapse within 60 weeks compared with those who did not receive MBCT (hazard ratio 0.69, 95% CI 0.58 to 0.82) and compared with active treatments (hazard ratio 0.79, 95% CI 0.64 to 0.97). Sociodemographic and psychiatric variables did not significantly modify the effect; greater residual depressive symptoms before treatment were associated with a larger MBCT effect.
cards.watchOut: The pooled comparators are mostly usual care or placebo-like controls, not maintenance antidepressants — the meta-analysis supports MBCT works, while PREVENT alone answers the 'instead of my antidepressant' question.
cards.source: Kuyken W et al.. Efficacy of Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy in Prevention of Depressive Relapse: An Individual Patient Data Meta-analysis From Randomized Trials. shelves.title: Major depression after an inadequate antidepressant response: adjunctive aripiprazole improved scores and remission in two concordant pivotal trials — with akathisia in about a quarter
shelves.question: In major depression with inadequate response to an antidepressant, does adjunctive aripiprazole increase response and remission compared with adjunctive placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antidepressive Agents/therapeutic use · Antipsychotic Agents/adverse effects, therapeutic use · Aripiprazole · Major Depressive Disorder/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Piperazines/adverse effects, therapeutic use · Quinolones/adverse effects, therapeutic use · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Adding aripiprazole to an antidepressant that has already failed is supported by the twin pivotal trials that founded atypical-antipsychotic augmentation. Both used the same enrichment design — a prospective antidepressant course, then randomisation of inadequate responders to adjunctive aripiprazole or placebo for 6 weeks. Berman 2007 (362 randomised): depression scores fell 8.8 points on aripiprazole versus 5.8 on placebo (P<.001). Marcus 2008 (381 randomised): the same separation (8.5 versus 5.7 points; P=.001), with remission in 25.4% versus 15.2% (P=.016) and response in 32.4% versus 17.4% (P<.001) — absolute gains of about 10 and 15 percentage points. The price is consistent and characteristic: akathisia in roughly a quarter of aripiprazole patients (23.1% and 25.9% versus about 4% on placebo) and restlessness in about 14%, though discontinuations for adverse events stayed low (2-4%). The trials were 6 weeks long and industry-run; durability and the metabolic ledger of longer use sit outside them. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): two concordant randomised trials with the same design and the same result — the strategy VAST-D later ranked against switching (Shelf #2398).

cards.headline: Berman 2007: adjunctive aripiprazole beat placebo on depression scores (-8.8 vs -5.8 MADRS points; P<.001); akathisia 23.1% vs 4.5%
cards.summary: Berman 2007: adjunctive aripiprazole beat placebo on depression scores (-8.8 vs -5.8 MADRS points; P<.001); akathisia 23.1% vs 4.5%
cards.people: Adults with major depressive disorder and an inadequate response to a prospective 8-week antidepressant course (fluoxetine, paroxetine controlled-release, sertraline, venlafaxine extended-release, or escitalopram class agents), randomised double-blind to adjunctive aripiprazole (2-20 mg/day; n=184) or adjunctive placebo (n=178) for 6 weeks. The primary endpoint was change in Montgomery–Åsberg Depression Rating Scale total score.
cards.result: Mean MADRS change was significantly greater with adjunctive aripiprazole (-8.8) than adjunctive placebo (-5.8; P<.001), from a baseline mean of 26.0. Adverse events in at least 10%: akathisia (23.1% on aripiprazole vs 4.5% on placebo), headache (6.0% vs 10.8%), and restlessness (14.3% vs 3.4%). Discontinuation for adverse events was 2.2% versus 1.7%; one aripiprazole patient discontinued for akathisia.
cards.watchOut: Enrichment by prospective non-response defines the population — these are proven inadequate responders, not first-line patients; 6 weeks says nothing about maintenance benefit or long-term metabolic cost.

shelves.title: Treatment-resistant depression in primary care: adding mirtazapine to an SSRI or SNRI made no clinically important difference in the 480-patient MIR trial
shelves.question: In treatment-resistant depression in primary care, does adding mirtazapine to an SSRI or SNRI improve depressive symptoms compared with adding placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Antidepressive Agents/therapeutic use · Depressive Disorder, Treatment-Resistant/drug therapy · Drug Therapy, Combination · England · Female · General Practice · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Mirtazapine/therapeutic use · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Serotonin and Noradrenaline Reuptake Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Adding mirtazapine to an SSRI or SNRI is one of the commonest combination moves in primary-care depression — and the one large trial of it found no clinically important benefit. MIR randomised 480 primary-care patients whose depression had not responded adequately to at least 6 weeks of an SSRI or SNRI to add mirtazapine or placebo for 12 weeks, with follow-up to a year. Depression scores at 12 weeks were lower on mirtazapine, but the adjusted difference (-1.83 BDI-II points, 95% CI -3.92 to 0.27; P=.09) included the null and sat below the threshold of clinical importance the trial was designed around; adverse effects were more common on mirtazapine and more often stopped the drug. A single trial, however large and well-placed, leaves the confidence interval admitting a small benefit — which is why the stamp is POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): the routine combination, directly tested in the population that receives it, did not deliver a clinically important effect. Flagged for the developer's personal verdict as a single-trial shelf.

cards.headline: MIR 2018: BDI-II difference -1.83 points favouring added mirtazapine (95% CI -3.92 to 0.27; P=.09) — no clinically important benefit; more adverse effects
cards.summary: MIR 2018: BDI-II difference -1.83 points favouring added mirtazapine (95% CI -3.92 to 0.27; P=.09) — no clinically important benefit; more adverse effects
cards.people: 480 primary-care patients in England with treatment-resistant depression (inadequate response to at least 6 weeks of an SSRI or SNRI at an adequate dose), randomised to mirtazapine or placebo in addition to their usual SSRI or SNRI, stratified by centre and minimised by baseline score, sex, and current psychological therapy; 431 (89.8%) contributed the primary 12-week outcome, with follow-up at 24 and 52 weeks. The primary outcome was Beck Depression Inventory II score at 12 weeks.
cards.result: BDI-II scores at 12 weeks were 18.0 (SD 12.3) on mirtazapine versus 19.7 (SD 12.4) on placebo; the adjusted difference was -1.83 points (95% CI -3.92 to 0.27; P=.09) — the interval includes no effect. Adverse effects were more common in the mirtazapine group and were associated with participants stopping the trial drug. The authors concluded the study did not find evidence of a clinically important benefit for adding mirtazapine to an SSRI or SNRI in treatment-resistant primary-care depression.
cards.watchOut: The interval admits up to about a 4-point BDI-II benefit, so 'no clinically important benefit' is the trial's verdict, not proof of zero effect; mirtazapine for agitation in dementia (SYMBAD, Shelf #2342) is a different question.

shelves.title: Bipolar I depression: cariprazine 1.5 mg/day improved depression scores in two phase 3 trials — the 3.0 mg dose failed in both
shelves.question: In bipolar I depression, does cariprazine improve depressive symptoms (MADRS) compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antipsychotic Agents/administration & dosage, adverse effects · Bipolar Disorder/diagnosis, drug therapy, psychology · Depression/diagnosis, drug therapy · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Monitoring · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Piperazines/administration & dosage, adverse effects · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Cariprazine for bipolar I depression has a consistent programme answer, and it is dose-specific: 1.5 mg/day works, 3.0 mg/day does not clearly. In Durgam 2016 (571 patients in the intent-to-treat population), the 1.5 mg dose beat placebo on depression scores by 4.0 points (significant after multiplicity adjustment), the 3.0 mg dose's 2.5-point advantage was not significant after adjustment, and 0.75 mg was indistinguishable from placebo. The second phase 3 trial (493 patients) repeated the pattern almost exactly: 1.5 mg significant on both the primary depression score (difference -2.5; adjusted P=.0417) and global severity, 3.0 mg not significant. Akathisia and insomnia were the commonest adverse events in the first trial; in the second, akathisia, restlessness, nausea, and fatigue — with mean weight gains of half a kilogram or less and small metabolic changes in both. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for cariprazine 1.5 mg/day: two concordant phase 3 trials, the same dose winning twice and the higher dose failing twice — a shelf whose dose ceiling is part of the answer.

cards.headline: Durgam 2016: cariprazine 1.5 mg/day beat placebo by 4.0 MADRS points (significant after adjustment); 3.0 mg (-2.5) not significant after adjustment; 0.75 mg null
cards.summary: Durgam 2016: cariprazine 1.5 mg/day beat placebo by 4.0 MADRS points (significant after adjustment); 3.0 mg (-2.5) not significant after adjustment; 0.75 mg null
cards.people: 571 patients with bipolar I depression in the intent-to-treat population, randomised double-blind to placebo (n=141) or cariprazine 0.75 mg/day (n=140), 1.5 mg/day (n=145), or 3.0 mg/day (n=145) for an 8-week trial with the primary endpoint at week 6. The primary outcome was change in Montgomery–Åsberg Depression Rating Scale total score.
cards.result: Cariprazine 1.5 mg/day showed significantly greater MADRS improvement than placebo (least squares mean difference -4.0, 95% CI -6.3 to -1.6; significant after adjustment for multiple comparisons). The 3.0 mg/day difference (-2.5, 95% CI -4.9 to -0.1) was not significant when adjusted for multiple comparisons, and 0.75 mg/day was similar to placebo. Global severity showed the same pattern. The most common adverse events (at least 10%) on cariprazine were akathisia and insomnia; weight gain was slightly higher than on placebo.
cards.watchOut: Flat-to-inverted dose response: more drug did not mean more benefit, in either trial — the shelf must not be read as supporting the 3.0 mg dose.
