cards.people: 493 adults with bipolar I disorder in a current depressive episode, randomised double-blind to placebo (n=167), cariprazine 1.5 mg/day (n=168), or cariprazine 3.0 mg/day (n=158) for 6 weeks. The primary outcome was change in Montgomery–Åsberg Depression Rating Scale total score.

shelves.title: Bipolar depression: lumateperone 42 mg improved depression scores as monotherapy and added to lithium or valproate in two randomised trials, with minimal extrapyramidal or metabolic signal
shelves.question: In major depressive episodes of bipolar I or II disorder, does lumateperone improve depressive symptoms compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Antipsychotic Agents/therapeutic use · Bipolar Disorder/complications, drug therapy · Major Depressive Disorder/drug therapy, etiology · Double-Blind Method · Female · Heterocyclic Compounds, 4 or More Rings/adverse effects, therapeutic use · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Lumateperone 42 mg improves bipolar depression in two settings, with an unusually quiet side-effect profile for its class. As monotherapy (Calabrese 2021, 377 patients with bipolar I or II depression), it beat placebo on depression scores by 4.6 points at day 43 (effect size -0.56), with superiority in both bipolar I and bipolar II subgroups; somnolence and nausea were the only adverse events meaningfully above placebo, extrapyramidal events were at placebo rates, and weight and metabolic measures barely moved. Added to lithium or valproate in inadequate responders (Suppes 2023, 529 patients), the 42 mg dose again separated (difference -2.4 points; P=.02) while the 28 mg dose did not reach significance on the primary endpoint (P=.10). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for lumateperone 42 mg: two positive randomised trials — monotherapy and adjunctive — with the lower adjunctive dose failing, which sharpens rather than blurs the dose answer.

cards.headline: Calabrese 2021: lumateperone 42 mg monotherapy beat placebo by 4.6 MADRS points at day 43 (effect size -0.56), in bipolar I and II alike
cards.summary: Calabrese 2021: lumateperone 42 mg monotherapy beat placebo by 4.6 MADRS points at day 43 (effect size -0.56), in bipolar I and II alike
cards.people: 377 patients with a major depressive episode associated with bipolar I or bipolar II disorder, randomised double-blind to lumateperone 42 mg/day (n=188) or placebo (n=189) once each evening for 6 weeks. The primary endpoint was change in Montgomery–Åsberg Depression Rating Scale score at day 43.
cards.result: Lumateperone produced significantly greater MADRS improvement than placebo (least squares mean difference -4.6 points; effect size -0.56) and greater improvement on global bipolar severity (difference -0.9; effect size -0.46), with significant superiority in both the bipolar I and bipolar II subgroups. Somnolence and nausea were the only treatment-emergent adverse events at a clinically meaningful excess over placebo; extrapyramidal symptom events were low and similar to placebo, and changes in weight, vital signs, and metabolic or endocrine measures were minimal.
cards.watchOut: Six weeks, one monotherapy trial; the bipolar II claim rests on a subgroup of it — consistent and prespecified in direction, but a subgroup nonetheless.

cards.people: 529 patients with bipolar I or II disorder in a major depressive episode with inadequate response to lithium or valproate, randomised double-blind to adjunctive lumateperone 28 mg (n=176), lumateperone 42 mg (n=177), or placebo (n=176) for 6 weeks. shelves.title: Depression after acute coronary syndrome: escitalopram cut major adverse cardiac events over eight years (40.9% vs 53.6%) in the single EsDEPACS trial — with mortality itself unchanged
shelves.question: In patients with depression after acute coronary syndrome, does 24 weeks of escitalopram reduce long-term major adverse cardiac events compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acute Coronary Syndrome/mortality, psychology, therapy · Adult · Aged · Antidepressive Agents, Second-Generation/therapeutic use · Citalopram/therapeutic use · Depression/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Incidence · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction/epidemiology · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention · Proportional Hazards Models · Risk
shelves.balance: EsDEPACS is the first antidepressant trial to separate on hard cardiac outcomes, and it did so in a single Korean centre. Three hundred patients with depression after a recent acute coronary syndrome were randomised to 24 weeks of escitalopram or placebo and followed for a median of 8.1 years. Major adverse cardiac events — the composite of all-cause death, myocardial infarction, and percutaneous coronary intervention — occurred in 40.9% on escitalopram versus 53.6% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.69, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.96; P=.03): an absolute difference of 12.7 percentage points over eight years. The components must be read with the composite: myocardial infarction was significantly reduced (8.7% versus 15.2%; hazard ratio 0.54; P=.04), intervention trended the same way (P=.07), but all-cause mortality (20.8% versus 24.5%; hazard ratio 0.82; P=.43) and cardiac death (P=.48) did not differ significantly — the mortality claim is not established by this trial, and this shelf does not make it. Earlier post-MI antidepressant trials (SADHART, ENRICHD — Shelves #2289 and #2288) showed safety and symptom effects, not event reduction. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — flagged for the developer's personal verdict as an OUTSTANDING-SINGLE under the Nov 8, 2026 rule (landmark single randomised blinded trial, hard MACE endpoint), Tier C because the balance carries a cardiovascular-event claim whose mortality component is null.

cards.headline: EsDEPACS 2018: MACE in 40.9% on escitalopram vs 53.6% on placebo over a median 8.1 years (HR 0.69; P=.03) — MI reduced (HR 0.54), mortality not (HR 0.82; P=.43)
cards.summary: EsDEPACS 2018: MACE in 40.9% on escitalopram vs 53.6% on placebo over a median 8.1 years (HR 0.69; P=.03) — MI reduced (HR 0.54), mortality not (HR 0.82; P=.43)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial with long-term follow-up (EsDEPACS)
cards.people: 300 patients with depression and recent acute coronary syndrome at one South Korean university hospital, randomised double-blind to escitalopram in flexible doses of 5-20 mg/day (n=149) or matched placebo (n=151) for 24 weeks; all 300 completed follow-up to a median of 8.1 years (interquartile range 7.5-9.0). The primary outcome was major adverse cardiac events: all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction, and percutaneous coronary intervention.
cards.result: MACE occurred in 61 patients (40.9%) on escitalopram and 81 (53.6%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.69, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.96; P=.03). Components: all-cause mortality 20.8% versus 24.5% (hazard ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.51 to 1.33; P=.43); cardiac death 10.7% versus 13.2% (hazard ratio 0.79; P=.48); myocardial infarction 8.7% versus 15.2% (hazard ratio 0.54, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.96; P=.04); percutaneous coronary intervention 12.8% versus 19.9% (hazard ratio 0.58; P=.07).
cards.watchOut: Single centre, single country, 300 patients; a 24-week drug exposure is being credited with an 8-year event separation, and the composite is carried by infarction and intervention, not by survival — generalizability is the authors' own stated caveat.
cards.source: Kim JM et al.. Effect of Escitalopram vs Placebo Treatment for Depression on Long-term Cardiac Outcomes in Patients With Acute Coronary Syndrome: The EsDEPACS Randomized Clinical Trial. shelves.title: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder: sertraline works on continuous dosing (62% vs 34% much improved), and symptom-onset dosing is probably effective — its trial's primary scale just missed
shelves.question: In premenstrual dysphoric disorder, does sertraline — continuous or symptom-onset dosing — improve symptoms compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: 1-Naphthylamine/analogs & derivatives, therapeutic use · Adult · Analysis of Variance · Depression · Double-Blind Method · Efficiency · Female · Humans · Irritable Mood · Luteal Phase · Premenstrual Syndrome/drug therapy, physiopathology · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Sertraline · Severity of Illness Index · Social Adjustment
shelves.balance: Sertraline treats premenstrual dysphoric disorder, and the dosing can probably be shortened to the symptomatic window — though the trial of that shorter strategy was mixed on its own primary scale. Continuous flexible-dose sertraline (Yonkers 1997, 243 randomised) beat placebo clearly: daily symptom scores fell from 64 to 44 versus 62 to 54 (P<.001), depression-scale scores fell 44% versus 29% (P<.002), and 62% versus 34% were rated much or very much improved (P<.001), with parallel gains in functioning. The 2015 symptom-onset trial (252 women, dosing from symptom onset to the first days of menses over 6 cycles) missed its primary outcome narrowly — the Premenstrual Tension Scale difference was 1.88 points (95% CI 0.01 to 3.75; P=.06) — while its secondary measures favoured sertraline (depressive-symptom difference 5.14 points, P=.02; response 67.0% versus 52.4%, P=.02) and abrupt monthly cessation produced no discontinuation symptoms. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): the drug's efficacy is established by the continuous-dosing trial; symptom-onset dosing is supported on secondary outcomes with a missed primary, and the pack grades it as probably effective rather than proven.

shelves.title: Treatment-resistant depression: inhaled nitrous oxide improved depression scores within hours in two very small crossover trials — 44 patients in total
shelves.question: In treatment-resistant major depression, does inhaled nitrous oxide produce rapid antidepressant effects compared with placebo gas?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antidepressive Agents/therapeutic use · Cross-Over Studies · Depression/drug therapy · Major Depressive Disorder/drug therapy · Depressive Disorder, Treatment-Resistant/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Nitrous Oxide/adverse effects, therapeutic use · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Inhaled nitrous oxide produces rapid antidepressant effects in treatment-resistant depression — in two crossover trials so small that the whole evidence base is 44 patients. The proof-of-concept trial (Nagele 2015, 20 patients) found a single 1-hour inhalation of 50% nitrous oxide improved depression scores versus placebo gas at 2 hours (difference -4.8 points) and 24 hours (-5.5 points; P<.001), with response in 20% versus 5% and remission in 15% versus 0% — differences whose confidence intervals are very wide. The phase 2 trial (24 patients, three-way crossover) found nitrous oxide superior to placebo overall (P=.01), no difference between 25% and 50% concentrations (P=.58), effects that were individually non-significant at 2 and 24 hours but significant by week 2 (-5.19 points at 25%, P=.02; -7.00 at 50%, P=.001), and adverse events that declined substantially with the lower dose (P<.001). Three patients stopped nitrous oxide in the first trial; no serious adverse events occurred in either. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real rapid signal, replicated in design if not in size — hours-to-two-weeks endpoints in two dozen-patient crossovers cap the stamp.

cards.headline: Nagele 2015: 50% nitrous oxide beat placebo gas by 4.8 HDRS points at 2 hours and 5.5 at 24 hours (P<.001); response 20% vs 5%
cards.summary: Nagele 2015: 50% nitrous oxide beat placebo gas by 4.8 HDRS points at 2 hours and 5.5 at 24 hours (P<.001); response 20% vs 5%
cards.type: Blinded, placebo-controlled crossover trial (proof of concept)
cards.people: 20 patients with treatment-resistant major depression in a blinded, placebo-controlled crossover trial; each received a 1-hour inhalation of 50% nitrous oxide/50% oxygen and of 50% nitrogen/50% oxygen (placebo) in random order. The primary endpoint was change on the 21-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale 24 hours after treatment.
cards.result: Depressive symptoms improved significantly after nitrous oxide versus placebo at 2 hours (mean HDRS-21 difference -4.8 points, 95% CI -1.8 to -7.8; P=.002) and at 24 hours (-5.5 points, 95% CI -2.5 to -8.5; P<.001). Response (at least 50% reduction) occurred in 4 patients (20%) after nitrous oxide versus 1 (5%) after placebo (odds ratio 4.0, 95% CI 0.45 to 35.79); remission in 3 (15%) versus none. Treatment was discontinued in 3 patients on nitrous oxide and briefly interrupted in 2; no serious adverse events occurred, and all adverse events were brief and mild to moderate.
cards.watchOut: Twenty patients, a 24-hour primary endpoint, and response/remission intervals so wide they include almost anything — this is a signal-detection trial, and three of twenty patients could not complete the nitrous oxide inhalation.
cards.source: Nagele P et al.. Nitrous Oxide for Treatment-Resistant Major Depression: A Proof-of-Concept Trial. Biol Psychiatry. 2015. PMID: 25577164. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: PTSD: EMDR and fluoxetine both beat placebo over 8 weeks, but EMDR's gains persisted at 6 months while the stopped drug's did not — one trial, benefit concentrated in adult-onset trauma
shelves.question: In posttraumatic stress disorder, is eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR) as effective as an established antidepressant, and do its gains persist after treatment ends?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Combined Modality Therapy · Depression/drug therapy · Desensitization, Psychologic · Double-Blind Method · Eye Movements · Female · Fluoxetine/therapeutic use · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Stress Disorders, Post-Traumatic/drug therapy, therapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: This shelf answers the head-to-head and durability question, and the one randomised trial of it found a split verdict by trauma timing. Van der Kolk 2007 randomised 88 adults with PTSD to 8 weeks of EMDR, fluoxetine, or pill placebo, with blinded ratings after treatment and at 6-month follow-up. Both active treatments beat placebo acutely in the trial's reporting; the separation came after treatment stopped: the EMDR group maintained its gains at 6 months while the fluoxetine group's gains largely eroded after discontinuation — and the benefit accrued primarily to adult-onset trauma survivors, among whom 75.0% of the EMDR group achieved asymptomatic end-state functioning at follow-up versus none in the fluoxetine group (child-onset: 33.3% on EMDR, and for most childhood-onset patients neither treatment produced complete remission). The record's abstract reports the follow-up contrast in detail but gives no acute-phase effect sizes, and none are claimed here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for EMDR's durability advantage — flagged for the developer's personal verdict: a single 88-patient trial carries the head-to-head claim, and trauma-focused therapy as a class (prolonged exposure, cognitive processing therapy) lives at Shelf #702.

cards.headline: van der Kolk 2007: at 6 months after 8 weeks of treatment, EMDR gains held while fluoxetine gains eroded — asymptomatic end-state in 75.0% of adult-onset EMDR patients vs 0% on fluoxetine
cards.summary: van der Kolk 2007: at 6 months after 8 weeks of treatment, EMDR gains held while fluoxetine gains eroded — asymptomatic end-state in 75.0% of adult-onset EMDR patients vs 0% on fluoxetine
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial with blinded raters and 6-month follow-up (van der Kolk 2007)
cards.people: 88 adults with DSM-IV posttraumatic stress disorder randomised to eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR), fluoxetine, or pill placebo for 8 weeks (2000-2003), assessed by blind raters post-treatment and at 6-month follow-up. The primary outcome was the Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale; the secondary outcome was the Beck Depression Inventory-II.
cards.result: The psychotherapy intervention was more successful than pharmacotherapy in achieving sustained reductions in PTSD and depression symptoms, with the benefit accruing primarily for adult-onset trauma survivors. At 6-month follow-up, 75.0% of adult-onset versus 33.3% of child-onset trauma subjects receiving EMDR achieved asymptomatic end-state functioning, compared with none in the fluoxetine group. For most childhood-onset trauma patients, neither treatment produced complete symptom remission. The authors concluded brief EMDR produced substantial and sustained reduction of PTSD and depression in most victims of adult-onset trauma, with SSRIs a reliable first-line intervention for moderate relief in childhood-onset trauma.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports no acute-phase effect sizes, so this card grades the durability contrast only; the adult-onset/child-onset split is a subgroup of an 88-patient trial, and the fluoxetine arm's 'relapse' partly reflects discontinuation of an effective drug — the comparison is EMDR's legacy versus a stopped medication.

shelves.balance: A single high dose of hydrocortisone within hours of trauma was one of prevention psychiatry's most attractive ideas — and the larger, later trial did not confirm it. The 2011 pilot (Zohar; 25 patients with acute stress symptoms given intravenous hydrocortisone 100-140 mg or placebo within 6 hours of trauma) reported favourable changes in the trajectory of acute stress and later PTSD symptoms, a qualitative result the record states without event rates. The definitive emergency-department trial (118 patients, same strategy, 13-month follow-up) found no difference between hydrocortisone and placebo in PTSD prevalence or symptom severity — the treatment made no difference — with one subgroup signal: a significant interaction with time of trauma, and lower PTSD prevalence at 13 months in patients treated at night, when endogenous cortisol is low. Both records carry the same registry identifier (NCT00855270), indicating one research programme. PROPOSED SPLIT: POSSIBLE (benefit) on the pilot record alone, superseded by POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) in the larger trial — the shelf's operative answer is the null, with the nocturnal subgroup left as a research lead, not a claim. Flagged for the developer's personal verdict (SPLIT stamp).

cards.people: 25 patients with acute stress symptoms in a prospective, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot study; a single intravenous bolus of high-dose hydrocortisone (100-140 mg) or placebo was given within 6 hours of a traumatic event. (A parallel animal study in the same report examined dendritic and molecular correlates and is not carded.)
cards.result: Early single high-dose hydrocortisone attenuated core symptoms of acute stress and of subsequent PTSD and was associated with significant favourable changes in the trajectory after trauma, expressed as a reduced risk of developing PTSD. The record reports no PTSD event rates or effect sizes for the clinical pilot.
cards.watchOut: A 25-patient pilot whose record states its conclusion without numbers cannot carry a prevention claim; the same registry identifier appears on the 2023 trial's record — one programme, two reports, very different sizes.

cards.headline: Emergency-department trial 2023: hydrocortisone within 6 hours did NOT reduce PTSD at 13 months (prevalence and severity no different) — a night-time subgroup interaction only
cards.summary: Emergency-department trial 2023: hydrocortisone within 6 hours did NOT reduce PTSD at 13 months (prevalence and severity no different) — a night-time subgroup interaction only
cards.people: 118 consented patients with acute stress symptoms in a prospective, double-blind, randomised, controlled trial; a single intravenous bolus of hydrocortisone or placebo was administered within 6 hours of the traumatic event in the emergency department, with blood sampling before dosing and follow-up to 13 months.
cards.result: At 13 months, the hydrocortisone group did not differ from the placebo group in PTSD prevalence or symptom severity. A significant interaction between time of trauma (night, when cortisol levels are low) and treatment was found: lower PTSD prevalence at 13 months in the hydrocortisone night group. The authors concluded hydrocortisone within 6 hours was not effective in preventing PTSD compared with placebo, with nocturnal administration suggested as a research direction.
cards.watchOut: The night-time finding is a subgroup interaction in a null trial — hypothesis-generating only; and the shared registry number with the pilot means these are not two independent programmes replicating each other.
cards.source: Carmi L et al.. Hydrocortisone in the emergency department: a prospective, double-blind, randomized, controlled posttraumatic stress disorder study. CNS Spectr. 2023. PMID: 35678177. Registry ID: NCT00855270 (the same identifier carried by the 2011 pilot's record). shelves.title: Chronic PTSD: SSRIs improve core symptoms — sertraline responders 53% vs 32%, paroxetine effective at both doses in a 551-patient trial
shelves.question: In chronic posttraumatic stress disorder, do SSRIs improve core PTSD symptoms compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Analysis of Variance · Antidepressive Agents/adverse effects, therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Quality of Life · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors/adverse effects, therapeutic use · Sertraline/adverse effects, therapeutic use · Single-Blind Method · Stress Disorders, Post-Traumatic/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SSRIs were the first drug class proven for chronic PTSD, and the two pivotal trials here agree on a modest, real effect. Brady 2000 (187 outpatients, mean illness duration 12 years) found sertraline superior to placebo on three of four primary measures over 12 weeks — symptom scores fell 33.0 versus 23.2 points (P=.02) — with a responder rate of 53% versus 32% (P=.008); the intrusion/re-experiencing cluster, notably, did not separate (P=.14), while avoidance/numbing and arousal did. The paroxetine fixed-dose trial (551 patients) found both 20 mg and 40 mg significantly better than placebo on the primary symptom measure, on all three symptom clusters, and on social and occupational impairment and comorbid depression, in men and women and across trauma types; its record reports significance without effect sizes, and none are invented here. Insomnia was sertraline's only clearly excess adverse effect (16.0% versus 4.3%). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): two concordant pivotal trials — symptom relief of moderate size, not remission for most, and the drug half of a field where trauma-focused therapy (Shelf #702) carries the larger effects.

cards.headline: Brady 2000: sertraline responders 53% vs 32% on placebo (P=.008); symptom scores -33.0 vs -23.2 (P=.02); re-experiencing cluster did not separate
cards.summary: Brady 2000: sertraline responders 53% vs 32% on placebo (P=.008); symptom scores -33.0 vs -23.2 (P=.02); re-experiencing cluster did not separate
cards.people: 187 outpatients with PTSD of moderate-to-marked severity (mean age 40; mean illness duration 12 years; 73% women) at 14 US centres, randomised double-blind after a 2-week placebo lead-in to flexible-dose sertraline 50-200 mg/day (n=94) or placebo (n=93) for 12 weeks. Primary measures included the Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale (CAPS-2), Impact of Event Scale, and global impression scales.
cards.result: Sertraline improved significantly more than placebo on CAPS-2 total score (change -33.0 vs -23.2; P=.02), global severity (-1.2 vs -0.8; P=.01), and global improvement (2.5 vs 3.0; P=.02); the Impact of Event Scale showed a trend (-16.2 vs -12.1; P=.07). Responders (at least 30% CAPS-2 reduction plus much/very much improved): 53% versus 32% (P=.008). Avoidance/numbing (P=.02) and arousal (P=.03) clusters separated; re-experiencing/intrusion did not (P=.14). Insomnia was the only adverse effect significantly more frequent on sertraline (16.0% vs 4.3%; P=.01).
cards.watchOut: A 21-point responder advantage still leaves nearly half of treated patients non-responders, and the signature intrusion symptoms were the cluster that did not significantly improve.
cards.source: Brady K et al.. Efficacy and safety of sertraline treatment of posttraumatic stress disorder: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2000. PMID: 10770145. Registry ID: none — pre-registration-era trial. cards.headline: Paroxetine fixed-dose trial 2001: both 20 mg and 40 mg beat placebo on symptoms, all three clusters, functioning, and comorbid depression (551 patients)
cards.summary: Paroxetine fixed-dose trial 2001: both 20 mg and 40 mg beat placebo on symptoms, all three clusters, functioning, and comorbid depression (551 patients)
cards.people: 551 outpatients with chronic PTSD (Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale score of at least 50), randomised double-blind to placebo (n=186), paroxetine 20 mg/day (n=183), or paroxetine 40 mg/day (n=182) for 12 weeks. Efficacy was assessed by change in CAPS-2 total score and global-improvement response.
cards.result: Both paroxetine dose groups demonstrated significantly greater improvement than placebo on the primary outcome measures in the intent-to-treat analysis, and statistically significant improvement on all three PTSD symptom clusters (re-experiencing, avoidance/numbing, hyperarousal), social and occupational impairment, and comorbid depression. Effects held for men and women and did not vary by trauma type, time since trauma, or baseline severity. Both doses were well tolerated. The record reports significance without effect sizes.
cards.watchOut: No effect sizes in the record — the sertraline trial's numbers are the shelf's quantitative anchor, and the two drugs should not be assigned each other's effect sizes.
cards.source: Marshall RD et al.. Efficacy and safety of paroxetine treatment for chronic PTSD: a fixed-dose, placebo-controlled study. Am J Psychiatry. 2001. PMID: 11729013. shelves.title: Panic disorder: CBT and imipramine each beat placebo, the combination's advantage appeared only in maintenance — and after stopping, CBT's benefit endured while the drug's faded
shelves.question: In panic disorder, how do cognitive-behavioural therapy, imipramine, and their combination compare acutely, in maintenance, and after treatment is stopped?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Analysis of Variance · Antidepressive Agents, Tricyclic/therapeutic use · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy · Combined Modality Therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Imipramine/therapeutic use · Male · Panic Disorder/diagnosis, drug therapy, therapy · Severity of Illness Index
shelves.balance: The landmark four-clinic trial (Barlow 2000, 312 patients) answers three questions at once, and the answer changes with time. Acutely (3 months), cognitive-behavioural therapy and imipramine each beat placebo on the Panic Disorder Severity Scale (response 48.7% and 45.8% versus 21.7%), and the combination (60.3%) was not significantly better than either alone. In the 6-month maintenance phase the combination did pull ahead (response 57.1%, significantly above either monotherapy), and among responders imipramine's responses were of higher quality. After all treatment stopped, the picture inverted: at 6-month post-discontinuation follow-up, response was highest for CBT plus placebo (41.0%) and CBT alone (31.9%), lower for the combination (26.3%), and lowest for imipramine alone (19.7%) — the drug's gains depended on staying on it, while CBT's persisted. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large trial carries all three comparisons, flagged for the developer's personal verdict as a single-trial shelf.

cards.headline: Barlow 2000: acutely, CBT (48.7%) and imipramine (45.8%) each beat placebo (21.7%); the combination (60.3%) was not significantly better than either alone
cards.summary: Barlow 2000: acutely, CBT (48.7%) and imipramine (45.8%) each beat placebo (21.7%); the combination (60.3%) was not significantly better than either alone
cards.people: 312 patients with panic disorder at four US anxiety research clinics, randomised double-blind to imipramine alone (up to 300 mg/day, n=83), CBT alone (n=77), placebo alone (n=24), CBT plus imipramine (n=65), or CBT plus placebo (n=63). Treatment was weekly for 3 months (acute phase), then monthly for 6 months (maintenance, responders), then 6 months of post-discontinuation follow-up. Response was defined on the Panic Disorder Severity Scale (PDSS) and Clinical Global Impression (CGI).
cards.result: Acute phase: both imipramine and CBT were significantly superior to placebo on the PDSS (response 45.8%, 48.7%, and 21.7%; P=.05 and P=.03) but not significantly different on the CGI (48.2%, 53.9%, 37.5%); the combination's acute response (60.3% PDSS, 64.1% CGI) was not significantly different from the other groups. Maintenance: imipramine and CBT remained superior to placebo (PDSS response 37.8%, 39.5%, 13.0%; P=.02 for both), and combined therapy's maintenance response (57.1% PDSS) was significantly better than CBT alone (P=.04) and imipramine alone (P=.03), though not better than CBT plus placebo; among responders, imipramine produced a response of higher quality. After discontinuation (intent-to-treat CGI response): CBT plus placebo 41.0%, CBT alone 31.9%, combination 26.3%, imipramine alone 19.7%, placebo 13% — CBT appeared durable in follow-up.
cards.watchOut: The placebo-only arm was small (n=24), the combination's acute edge was not significant, and its maintenance edge vanished once treatment stopped — timing, not just efficacy, is this trial's message.
cards.source: Barlow DH et al.. Cognitive-behavioral therapy, imipramine, or their combination for panic disorder: A randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2000. PMID: 10815116. cards.summary: Synthesis: one trial — both monotherapies work, the combination's edge is maintenance-only, CBT's benefit is the one that survives stopping — POSSIBLE, single-trial flag
cards.people: One randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Barlow 2000, n=312) of CBT, imipramine, their combination, and placebo controls in panic disorder, with maintenance and post-discontinuation phases.
cards.result: Acute PDSS response: CBT 48.7%, imipramine 45.8%, combination 60.3% (not significantly above monotherapies), placebo 21.7%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), flagged for the developer's personal verdict (single trial).

shelves.title: Body dysmorphic disorder: fluoxetine beat placebo (response 53% vs 18%), and continuing escitalopram after response halved 6-month relapse (18% vs 40%)
shelves.question: In body dysmorphic disorder, do serotonin reuptake inhibitors improve symptoms compared with placebo, and does continuing them after response prevent relapse?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fluoxetine/therapeutic use · Humans · Male · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Somatoform Disorders/diagnosis, drug therapy, psychology · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Body dysmorphic disorder has a thin pharmacotherapy record, but its two placebo-controlled trials point the same way. Phillips 2002 — the first placebo-controlled study in the disorder — randomised 67 patients to 12 weeks of fluoxetine or placebo: response in 53% on fluoxetine versus 18% on placebo (P=.003), with benefit from week 8; notably, patients with the delusional variant responded as often as non-delusional patients, and no delusional patient responded to placebo. The relapse-prevention trial answered the next question: after 14 weeks of open-label escitalopram (67.0% responded), the 58 responders randomised to continue escitalopram or switch to placebo for 6 months relapsed at 18% versus 40%, with time to relapse significantly longer on continued drug (hazard ratio 2.72, 95% CI 1.01 to 8.57 — an interval wide enough to include a small effect), and a third of continued patients improved further. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): concordant acute and continuation evidence, but from two small specialist-centre trials totalling 125 randomised patients.

cards.headline: Phillips 2002: fluoxetine response 53% vs 18% on placebo (P=.003) — including in the delusional variant, where no placebo patient responded
cards.summary: Phillips 2002: fluoxetine response 53% vs 18% on placebo (P=.003) — including in the delusional variant, where no placebo patient responded
cards.people: 67 adults with DSM-IV body dysmorphic disorder or its delusional variant (of 74 enrolled), randomised double-blind after a 1-week placebo lead-in to fluoxetine or placebo for 12 weeks. The primary outcome was the Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale Modified for Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD-YBOCS).
cards.result: Fluoxetine was significantly more effective than placebo on the BDD-YBOCS from week 8 through week 12 (P<.001). Response occurred in 18 of 34 patients (53%) on fluoxetine versus 6 of 33 (18%) on placebo (P=.003). Delusional patients responded as often as non-delusional patients, and no delusional patient responded to placebo. Response was independent of disorder duration and severity and of comorbid major depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder, or personality disorder. Fluoxetine was generally well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: Sixty-seven patients at a specialist centre; the record predates modern registration, and the BDD-YBOCS effect is reported as a significance test rather than a point difference.
cards.source: Phillips KA et al.. A randomized placebo-controlled trial of fluoxetine in body dysmorphic disorder. Arch Gen Psychiatry. 2002. PMID: 11926939. cards.headline: Escitalopram relapse prevention 2016: continuing the drug after response halved relapse (18% vs 40%) and delayed time to relapse (HR 2.72, 95% CI 1.01-8.57)
cards.summary: Escitalopram relapse prevention 2016: continuing the drug after response halved relapse (18% vs 40%) and delayed time to relapse (HR 2.72, 95% CI 1.01-8.57)
cards.people: 100 adults with DSM-IV body dysmorphic disorder treated open-label with escitalopram for 14 weeks (phase 1); the 58 responders were then randomised double-blind to continue escitalopram or switch to placebo for 6 months (phase 2).
cards.result: Phase 1: 67.0% of treated subjects responded to escitalopram, with significant improvement in severity, insight, depression, functioning, and quality of life. Phase 2: time to relapse was significantly longer with escitalopram than placebo (hazard ratio 2.72, 95% CI 1.01 to 8.57); relapse proportions were 18% on escitalopram versus 40% on placebo. Body dysmorphic severity decreased further during continuation, with 35.7% of continued subjects showing further improvement.
cards.watchOut: A continuation trial in initial responders cannot speak to acute efficacy, and the hazard ratio's interval (1.01-8.57) barely excludes no effect — the 18% versus 40% relapse proportions are the steadier read.
cards.source: Phillips KA et al.. Pharmacotherapy Relapse Prevention in Body Dysmorphic Disorder: A Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial. Am J Psychiatry. 2016. PMID: 27056606. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Trichotillomania: N-acetylcysteine helped adults (56% vs 16% much improved) but made no difference in children — a clean age split across two trials
shelves.question: In trichotillomania (hair-pulling disorder), does N-acetylcysteine reduce hair pulling compared with placebo — in adults, and in children?
shelves.mesh: Acetylcysteine/adverse effects, therapeutic use · Adolescent · Adult · Double-Blind Method · Excitatory Amino Acid Agents/adverse effects, therapeutic use · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Personality Inventory/statistics & numerical data · Psychometrics · Trichotillomania/diagnosis, drug therapy, psychology · Young Adult
shelves.balance: A SPLIT shelf, split by age. In adults, Grant 2009 (50 patients, 12 weeks of N-acetylcysteine 1200-2400 mg/day versus placebo) found significantly greater reductions on both hair-pulling scales (P<.001 and P=.001), with 56% much or very much improved versus 16% on placebo (P=.003), improvement first appearing after 9 weeks, and no adverse events in the N-acetylcysteine group. In children and adolescents, the identically designed trial (Bloch 2013, 39 patients aged 8-17) found no difference between N-acetylcysteine and placebo on any primary or secondary measure — responders 25% versus 21% — with both groups improving over time regardless of assignment. The paediatric authors state the contrast plainly: adult efficacy cannot be assumed in children, and behavioural therapy (which has evidence in both age groups) should precede pharmacotherapy in children. PROPOSED SPLIT: POSSIBLE (benefit) in adults / POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) in children — flagged for the developer's personal verdict (SPLIT stamp; two small trials, opposite results).

cards.headline: Grant 2009 (adults): 56% much or very much improved on N-acetylcysteine vs 16% on placebo (P=.003); both pulling scales significant; no adverse events on NAC
cards.summary: Grant 2009 (adults): 56% much or very much improved on N-acetylcysteine vs 16% on placebo (P=.003); both pulling scales significant; no adverse events on NAC
cards.people: 50 adults with trichotillomania (45 women, 5 men; mean age 34.3 years) in a 12-week, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial at an ambulatory care centre; N-acetylcysteine 1200-2400 mg/day or placebo. Outcomes included the Massachusetts General Hospital Hair Pulling Scale and the Psychiatric Institute Trichotillomania Scale.
cards.result: N-acetylcysteine produced significantly greater reductions in hair-pulling symptoms on the Massachusetts General Hospital Hair Pulling Scale (P<.001) and the Psychiatric Institute Trichotillomania Scale (P=.001). Fifty-six percent of patients were much or very much improved on N-acetylcysteine versus 16% on placebo (P=.003), with significant improvement first noted after 9 weeks. No adverse events occurred in the N-acetylcysteine group, and it was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: Fifty patients, one centre, and a 9-week lag before separation — the adult result is striking but unreplicated. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Grant JE et al.. N-acetylcysteine, a glutamate modulator, in the treatment of trichotillomania: a double-blind, placebo-controlled study. Arch Gen Psychiatry. 2009. PMID: 19581567. cards.summary: Bloch 2013 (children/adolescents): NO difference on any measure — responders 25% on NAC vs 21% on placebo; both groups improved with time
cards.people: 39 children and adolescents aged 8 to 17 years with trichotillomania in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled add-on study of N-acetylcysteine versus matching placebo for 12 weeks. The primary outcome was change on the Massachusetts General Hospital-Hairpulling Scale.
cards.result: No significant difference between N-acetylcysteine and placebo was found on any primary or secondary outcome measure. On several measures, subjects improved significantly with time regardless of treatment assignment. Responders: 25% on N-acetylcysteine versus 21% on placebo. The authors concluded there was no benefit of N-acetylcysteine in children with trichotillomania, in contrast to the adult trial, and recommended referral to behavioural therapy before pharmacological treatment in children.
cards.watchOut: The paediatric trial was an add-on design and smaller (n=39), but its null was complete — no measure, no trend claimed — so it reads as a true age split rather than an underpowered near-miss. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

shelves.title: Generalised anxiety disorder: duloxetine beat placebo by 3.1 anxiety-scale points across three trials — with 14% stopping for adverse events
shelves.question: In generalised anxiety disorder, does duloxetine improve anxiety symptoms and functioning compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antidepressive Agents/therapeutic use · Anxiety Disorders/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Duloxetine Hydrochloride · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Multicenter Studies as Topic · Placebos · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Severity of Illness Index · Statistics as Topic/methods · Thiophenes/adverse effects, therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Duloxetine's generalised anxiety record is a standard regulatory package: three placebo-controlled trials, a consistent moderate effect on anxiety scores, and a tolerability cost paid mainly in nausea and early discontinuation. The pooled analysis of the three trials (1,163 patients) found anxiety scores fell 11.1 points on duloxetine versus 8.0 on placebo (P≤.001) — a 3.1-point advantage on the Hamilton Anxiety Scale — with global functioning improving 46% versus 25% (P≤.001). In the active-controlled trial (487 patients), duloxetine 60-120 mg and venlafaxine extended-release each beat placebo (P=.007 and P<.001), with no claim of difference between the two drugs; discontinuation for adverse events was 14.2% on duloxetine and 11.0% on venlafaxine versus 1.9% on placebo, and nausea was the commonest adverse event in the pooled data. The pooled trials ran 9-10 weeks and excluded comorbid psychiatric conditions. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): three concordant trials — a real but modest average effect, bought with a one-in-seven early dropout rate for adverse events.

cards.headline: Pooled analysis of three trials: anxiety scores -11.1 on duloxetine vs -8.0 on placebo (P≤.001); functioning improved 46% vs 25%
cards.summary: Pooled analysis of three trials: anxiety scores -11.1 on duloxetine vs -8.0 on placebo (P≤.001); functioning improved 46% vs 25%
cards.type: Pooled analysis of three randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials (Allgulander 2007)
cards.people: Individual-patient pooled data from three double-blind, placebo-controlled trials of duloxetine in generalised anxiety disorder (two 10-week flexible-dose 60-120 mg/day trials and one 9-week fixed-dose 60 or 120 mg/day trial): 668 patients on duloxetine and 495 on placebo. Mean age 42.4 years; 65% women. Outcomes were the Hamilton Anxiety Scale (HAMA) and the Sheehan Disability Scale.
cards.result: Duloxetine-treated patients improved significantly more on HAMA total score (mean change -11.1 points) than placebo-treated patients (-8.0 points; P≤.001). Sheehan Disability Scale global functioning improved 46% on duloxetine versus 25% on placebo (P≤.001). Nausea was the most common of twelve treatment-emergent adverse events occurring more often on duloxetine. The pooled studies were short-term and excluded patients with comorbid psychiatric conditions.
cards.watchOut: A pooled analysis is a summary of the same trials that support the label, not independent replication; the 3.1-point score advantage is an average over a selected, comorbidity-free trial population.
cards.source: Allgulander C et al.. Pharmacotherapy of generalized anxiety disorder: results of duloxetine treatment from a pooled analysis of three clinical studies. Curr Med Res Opin. 2007. cards.headline: Hartford 2007: duloxetine and venlafaxine XR each beat placebo (P=.007, P<.001); adverse-event discontinuation 14.2% and 11.0% vs 1.9%
cards.summary: Hartford 2007: duloxetine and venlafaxine XR each beat placebo (P=.007, P<.001); adverse-event discontinuation 14.2% and 11.0% vs 1.9%
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo- and active-controlled trial (Hartford 2007)
cards.people: 487 adults with DSM-IV generalised anxiety disorder in a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, flexible-dose trial of duloxetine 60-120 mg/day (n=162), venlafaxine extended-release 75-225 mg/day (n=164), or placebo (n=161) for 10 weeks. The primary outcome was change in Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale total score.
cards.result: Both duloxetine (P=.007) and venlafaxine XR (P<.001) improved Hamilton Anxiety scores significantly more than placebo. Overall discontinuation rates did not differ among groups, but discontinuation for adverse events was significantly higher on duloxetine (14.2%, P<.001) and venlafaxine XR (11.0%, P=.001) than placebo (1.9%). shelves.title: Generalised anxiety disorder: hydroxyzine beat placebo in two older trials (-12.2 vs -9.6 anxiety points at 12 weeks) and matched bromazepam — sedation is the price
shelves.question: In generalised anxiety disorder, does hydroxyzine reduce anxiety symptoms compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Ambulatory Care · Anti-Anxiety Agents/adverse effects, therapeutic use · Anxiety Disorders/diagnosis, drug therapy, psychology · Double-Blind Method · Family Practice · Female · Follow-Up Studies · France · Histamine H1 Antagonists/adverse effects, therapeutic use · Humans · Hydroxyzine/adverse effects, therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Care Team · Personality Inventory · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Hydroxyzine is the shelf's curiosity: a sedating antihistamine with two positive placebo-controlled trials in generalised anxiety disorder, both from the 1990s-2000s French literature. The larger (Llorca 2002, 334 randomised outpatients, 12 weeks) found anxiety scores fell 12.16 points on hydroxyzine 50 mg/day versus 9.64 on placebo (P=.019), with responder (P=.003) and remission (P=.028) advantages, maintained efficacy, and no statistically significant difference from the bromazepam 6 mg/day active comparator; drowsiness was actually more frequent with bromazepam. The earlier 4-week trial (Ferreri 1994, 133 patients) found significant superiority from week 1, persisting a week after abrupt discontinuation without rebound — at the price of more side effects overall (52% versus 35%), led by transient sleepiness (28% versus 14%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real, modest anxiolytic effect in two trials of their era — no comparison with modern first-line agents exists, and current labelling cautions (not addressed in these records) should be checked before use.

cards.headline: Llorca 2002: hydroxyzine beat placebo over 12 weeks (HAM-A -12.16 vs -9.64, P=.019) and matched bromazepam; responders and remitters also favoured hydroxyzine
cards.summary: Llorca 2002: hydroxyzine beat placebo over 12 weeks (HAM-A -12.16 vs -9.64, P=.019) and matched bromazepam; responders and remitters also favoured hydroxyzine
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo- and active-controlled trial (Llorca 2002)
cards.people: 334 of 369 selected adult outpatients with DSM-IV generalised anxiety disorder (Hamilton Anxiety score of at least 20) in a multicentre, randomised, double-blind French trial: hydroxyzine 50 mg/day, bromazepam 6 mg/day, or placebo, after a 2-week placebo run-in and with a 4-week placebo run-out. The primary outcome was change in Hamilton Rating Scale for Anxiety (HAM-A) at 12 weeks.
cards.result: Intent-to-treat HAM-A change was -12.16 (SD 7.74) on hydroxyzine versus -9.64 (SD 7.74) on placebo (P=.019). Responder percentage (P=.003), remission rate (P=.028), global severity (P=.001), maintenance of efficacy (P=.022), and day-84 Hospital Anxiety and Depression scores (P=.008) also favoured hydroxyzine. There was no statistically significant difference between hydroxyzine and bromazepam. Except for drowsiness, which was more frequent with bromazepam, safety was comparable across the three groups.
cards.watchOut: 'No significant difference from bromazepam' is an absence of demonstrated difference in a trial not designed as a noninferiority study — not proof of equivalence to a benzodiazepine.

cards.headline: Ferreri 1994: superiority from week 1 over 4 weeks, persisting a week after abrupt stop without rebound; side effects 52% vs 35%, sleepiness 28% vs 14%
cards.summary: Ferreri 1994: superiority from week 1 over 4 weeks, persisting a week after abrupt stop without rebound; side effects 52% vs 35%, sleepiness 28% vs 14%
cards.people: 133 patients with generalised anxiety disorder (DSM-III-R, with a 6-month duration criterion) in a multicentre randomised double-blind trial of hydroxyzine 50 mg/day versus placebo for 4 weeks, with an evaluation one week after abrupt discontinuation of active treatment.
cards.result: The decrease in anxiety scores was significant for hydroxyzine versus placebo by the end of the first week on all rating criteria, remained superior through the 4-week study, and persisted at the evaluation one week after abrupt discontinuation, without rebound anxiety or withdrawal symptoms. Side effects were reported by 52% on hydroxyzine versus 35% on placebo; the commonest were sleepiness (28% vs 14%), dry mouth (14% vs 5%), weight gain (12% vs 10%), loss of concentration (9% vs 8%), and insomnia (9% vs 6%), with sleepiness appearing in the first week and progressively disappearing.
cards.watchOut: A 4-week trial from 1994 with a sedation-driven side-effect profile; the 'no rebound' observation covers a single week after stopping.
cards.source: Ferreri M et al.. [Value of hydroxyzine in generalized anxiety disorder: controlled double-blind study versus placebo]. Encephale. 1994. PMID: 7875114. cards.people: Two randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials of hydroxyzine 50 mg/day in generalised anxiety disorder: Llorca 2002 (n=334 randomised, 12 weeks, with bromazepam comparator) and Ferreri 1994 (n=133, 4 weeks).

shelves.title: PTSD: five-session written exposure therapy was noninferior to prolonged exposure and to cognitive processing therapy — and patients actually finished it (dropout 12.5% vs 35.6%)
shelves.question: In posttraumatic stress disorder, is brief written exposure therapy (five sessions) as effective as prolonged exposure or cognitive processing therapy, with better completion?
shelves.mesh: Male · Humans · Adult · Middle Aged · Female · Stress Disorders, Post-Traumatic/diagnosis · Implosive Therapy · Veterans/psychology · Treatment Outcome · Writing
shelves.balance: Written exposure therapy (WET) — five sessions built around 30 minutes of in-session writing about the trauma, with no homework — has now been tested head-to-head against the two flagship trauma-focused therapies in randomised noninferiority trials, and met noninferiority in both. Against prolonged exposure in 178 veterans (Sloan 2023), symptom change on the CAPS-5 was noninferior at every assessment (noninferiority margin 10 points), and dropout was a third of the longer therapy's: 12.5% versus 35.6%. Against cognitive processing therapy in 169 active-duty service members, WET was likewise noninferior (largest between-group difference 3.96 points, upper confidence bound below the 10-point margin at all timepoints), with session completion 76.5% versus 54.8% for the 12-session therapy. Two cautions temper the stamp: a 10-point CAPS-5 margin is generous, and 'noninferior for symptom change' says nothing about which patients need the fuller treatments. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the efficiency claim — comparable outcomes in five sessions with far less attrition — is the shelf's real finding, and attrition is a hard behavioural outcome, not a rating-scale artefact.

cards.headline: Sloan 2023 (veterans): WET noninferior to prolonged exposure on CAPS-5 at every timepoint — with dropout 12.5% vs 35.6%
cards.summary: Sloan 2023 (veterans): WET noninferior to prolonged exposure on CAPS-5 at every timepoint — with dropout 12.5% vs 35.6%
cards.people: 178 veterans with PTSD at three US Veterans Affairs medical centres in a randomised noninferiority trial (2019-2022): written exposure therapy (n=88; five to seven 45-60 minute sessions including 30 minutes of in-session written imaginal exposure) versus prolonged exposure (n=90; eight to fifteen 90-minute sessions with in vivo homework). The primary outcome was change in Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale for DSM-5 (CAPS-5) score to the 20-week assessment; noninferiority was a between-group difference under 10 points.
cards.result: Changes in PTSD symptom severity with written exposure therapy were noninferior to prolonged exposure at all assessments (10, 20, and 30 weeks); the largest between-treatment difference, at 10 weeks, favoured written exposure therapy. Participants were significantly less likely to drop out of written exposure therapy than prolonged exposure (11 of 88 [12.5%] vs 32 of 90 [35.6%]; Cramér V 0.27). The authors concluded written exposure therapy may transcend previously observed barriers to PTSD treatment for patients and clinicians.
cards.watchOut: The 10-point CAPS-5 noninferiority margin is wide — 'noninferior' here means 'not worse by 10 points or more'; the dropout advantage, by contrast, is a directly observed outcome with no margin involved.

cards.headline: Sloan 2022 (service members): WET noninferior to cognitive processing therapy (largest difference 3.96 points); completion 76.5% vs 54.8%
cards.summary: Sloan 2022 (service members): WET noninferior to cognitive processing therapy (largest difference 3.96 points); completion 76.5% vs 54.8%
cards.people: 169 active-duty military service members with PTSD at Texas military bases in a randomised noninferiority trial (2016-2020): written exposure therapy (85 participants; 5 weekly sessions, no between-session assignments) versus cognitive processing therapy (84 participants; 12 twice-weekly sessions). The primary outcome was CAPS-5 symptom severity at 10, 20, and 30 weeks; the noninferiority margin was 10 points (upper bound of the 1-sided 95% CI).
cards.result: Written exposure therapy was noninferior to cognitive processing therapy: the largest difference in outcome change between conditions was 3.96 points, and the 1-sided 95% CI upper limit stayed below 10 points at every timepoint (4.59 at week 30 to 6.81 at week 10). Between-condition effect sizes were small (0.06 to 0.22). Completion of all sessions was 76.5% (65 of 85) with written exposure therapy versus 54.8% (47 of 84) with cognitive processing therapy.
cards.watchOut: Both trials come from the therapy's developers and from military/veteran systems; whether the efficiency holds in civilian primary-care PTSD populations is untested in this record.

shelves.title: PTSD: propranolol before memory-reactivation sessions added an 11.5-point CAPS advantage over reactivation alone — one 60-patient trial of reconsolidation blockade
shelves.question: In chronic posttraumatic stress disorder, does propranolol given before trauma-memory reactivation sessions reduce PTSD symptoms more than placebo with the same reactivation?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Implosive Therapy/methods · Male · Memory, Episodic · Middle Aged · Premedication · Propranolol/adverse effects, therapeutic use · Stress Disorders, Post-Traumatic/drug therapy, psychology
shelves.balance: Reconsolidation blockade is psychiatry's most theory-driven PTSD treatment: reactivate the trauma memory while beta-blockade blunts its re-storage, and the memory should lose emotional force. Brunet 2018 tested it properly — 60 adults with long-standing PTSD, propranolol or placebo 90 minutes before a brief weekly memory-reactivation session for 6 weeks, double-blind — and the drug added a real increment over reactivation alone: an adjusted post-treatment CAPS advantage of 11.50 points and a patient-rated advantage growing to 14.58 points by week 6. But read the within-group effect sizes before celebrating: reactivation with placebo alone produced a CAPS effect size of 1.25 — the ritual itself did much of the work — and there is no long-term follow-up in this record, so durability, the theory's core promise, is untested here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), flagged for the developer's personal verdict: a single 60-patient trial of a novel mechanism, however elegant.

cards.headline: Brunet 2018: propranolol before weekly memory reactivation beat placebo-plus-reactivation by 11.50 CAPS points after 6 weeks (patient-rated difference 14.58)
cards.summary: Brunet 2018: propranolol before weekly memory reactivation beat placebo-plus-reactivation by 11.50 CAPS points after 6 weeks (patient-rated difference 14.58)
cards.people: 60 adults with long-standing PTSD in a 6-week, double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised trial; propranolol or placebo was administered 90 minutes before a brief trauma-memory reactivation session, once weekly for 6 consecutive weeks. Outcomes were the Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale (CAPS) and the patient-rated PTSD Checklist-Specific (PCL-S), analysed intention-to-treat.
cards.result: The estimated group difference in posttreatment CAPS score, adjusted for pretreatment values, was a statistically significant 11.50 points in favour of propranolol. On the PCL-S, the time-by-group interaction averaged a 2.43-point greater decrease per week, a total significant difference of 14.58 points above placebo. Within-group pre-to-posttreatment effect sizes were large in both arms (CAPS Cohen's d 1.76 propranolol, 1.25 placebo; PCL-S d 2.74 and 0.55). Per-protocol analyses were similar. The authors called pre-reactivation propranolol a novel and efficacious treatment and stated that replication with long-term follow-up in various trauma populations is required.

shelves.title: Severe mental illness: Individual Placement and Support beat usual vocational rehabilitation on all vocational outcomes in the six-centre European trial — fidelity to the model was what made it work
shelves.question: In severe mental illness, does Individual Placement and Support (IPS) supported employment improve vocational outcomes compared with usual vocational rehabilitation?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Employment · Employment, Supported · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Interpersonal Relations · Male · Mental Disorders/psychology, rehabilitation · Middle Aged · Outcome and Process Assessment, Health Care/methods · Prognosis · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Rehabilitation Centers · Rehabilitation, Vocational/methods · Schizophrenia/rehabilitation
shelves.balance: Individual Placement and Support (IPS) — rapid placement into ordinary competitive jobs with integrated clinical support, rather than train-then-place rehabilitation — is the best-evidenced vocational intervention in severe mental illness, and the European EQOLISE trial is its international anchor. The record carded on this shelf is the trial's predictors report, which states the trial's verdict directly: across six European centres, IPS was more effective than usual vocational rehabilitation for all vocational outcomes. The same report identifies who benefits and what makes it work: previous work history, fewer unmet social needs, better relationships with vocational workers, remission, and swifter service uptake predicted employment and longer work; and the only service characteristic associated with greater IPS effectiveness was closeness to the original IPS model — fidelity. One honesty note, printed here on the shelf's face: the employment rates themselves (the figures most often quoted from EQOLISE) sit in the trial's main outcome report, a separate publication not carded on this shelf, so this shelf claims the direction and the predictors, not rates it cannot show. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the direction is stated by the trial's own indexed report and concordant with the wider IPS literature, but the shelf's citable record carries no effect sizes.

cards.headline: EQOLISE predictors report: IPS 'more effective for all vocational outcomes' than usual vocational rehabilitation across six European centres; fidelity to the model predicted effectiveness
cards.summary: EQOLISE predictors report: IPS 'more effective for all vocational outcomes' than usual vocational rehabilitation across six European centres; fidelity to the model predicted effectiveness
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial — predictors report (Catty 2008, EQOLISE)
cards.people: Participants with severe mental illness in an international six-centre randomised controlled trial (the EQOLISE trial) comparing Individual Placement and Support (IPS) with usual vocational rehabilitation, as reported in this secondary analysis of predictors of employment outcomes. Patient characteristics and early process variables were tested as predictors; service characteristics were explored as predictors of IPS effectiveness.
cards.result: The trial found IPS more effective for all vocational outcomes. Patients with a previous work history, fewer met social needs, and better relationships with their vocational workers were more likely to obtain employment and to work longer; remission and swifter service uptake were associated with working more. Having an IPS service closer to the original IPS model was the only service characteristic associated with greater effectiveness. The authors concluded that maintaining high IPS fidelity and targeting relational skills would improve employment outcomes in vocational interventions generally.
cards.watchOut: This record is the trial's predictors paper: it states the direction of the main result ('more effective for all vocational outcomes') but reports no employment rates or effect sizes. The main outcome report is a separate publication and is not carded here — rates quoted from it elsewhere should not be attributed to this shelf.

shelves.title: Early-phase schizophrenia: long-acting injectables delayed first hospitalisation in the US PRELAPSE trial (hazard ratio 0.56) — but Europe's EULAST trial found no advantage over oral treatment at keeping patients on medication
shelves.question: In early-phase schizophrenia, do long-acting injectable antipsychotics delay first hospitalisation compared with usual-care oral treatment?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antipsychotic Agents/administration & dosage, pharmacology · Aripiprazole/administration & dosage, pharmacology · Delayed-Action Preparations · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Injections · Male · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Schizophrenia/drug therapy · Time Factors · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Two large randomised trials in early-phase schizophrenia point in different directions, and they asked slightly different questions. PRELAPSE (489 patients; 39 US clinics cluster-randomised to encourage long-acting injectable aripiprazole once-monthly versus clinician's-choice usual care) found first hospitalisation significantly delayed: 22% versus 36% hospitalised over two years, hazard ratio 0.56 (95% CI 0.34–0.92), number needed to treat 7. EULAST (511 patients individually randomised in Europe and Israel to long-acting injectable versus oral paliperidone or aripiprazole, open-label) found no difference in its primary endpoint, time to all-cause discontinuation (hazard ratio 1.16, 95% CI 0.94–1.43). The designs differ in ways that matter: PRELAPSE tested a clinic-level policy of encouraging one injectable against unrestricted usual care (which could itself include injectables), while EULAST tested the formulations head-to-head and counted discontinuation for any reason, not hospitalisation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real hospitalisation signal from one trial, unconfirmed — and partly undercut on a neighbouring endpoint — by the other.

cards.headline: Kane 2020 (PRELAPSE): encouraging long-acting aripiprazole delayed first hospitalisation — 22% vs 36% hospitalised, hazard ratio 0.56, NNT 7
cards.summary: Kane 2020 (PRELAPSE): encouraging long-acting aripiprazole delayed first hospitalisation — 22% vs 36% hospitalised, hazard ratio 0.56, NNT 7
cards.people: 489 participants aged 18–35 with schizophrenia confirmed by structured interview and under 5 years of lifetime antipsychotic use, in the PRELAPSE cluster-randomised trial: 39 US mental health centres randomised to encourage long-acting aripiprazole once-monthly (19 clinics; 234 enrolled) or to clinician's-choice usual care (20 clinics; 255 enrolled), followed for 2 years. The primary outcome was time to first psychiatric hospitalisation, adjudicated by a committee masked to assignment.
cards.result: 52 of 234 (22%) in the injectable-encouragement clinics versus 91 of 255 (36%) under usual care had at least one hospitalisation. Mean survival time to first hospitalisation was 613.7 days versus 530.6 days; hazard ratio 0.56 (95% CI 0.34–0.92; P = .02) favouring the injectable strategy. The number needed to treat to prevent one additional hospitalisation was 7.
cards.watchOut: This was an encouragement design: clinics, not patients, were randomised, usual-care clinicians could still prescribe injectables, and only one molecule (aripiprazole once-monthly) was encouraged — the result supports a policy of offering the injectable early more than it proves formulation superiority.

cards.headline: Winter-van Rossum 2023 (EULAST): no difference between injectable and oral antipsychotics in time to all-cause discontinuation (hazard ratio 1.16, p = 0.18)
cards.summary: Winter-van Rossum 2023 (EULAST): no difference between injectable and oral antipsychotics in time to all-cause discontinuation (hazard ratio 1.16, p = 0.18)
cards.type: Randomised open-label clinical trial (Winter-van Rossum 2023, EULAST)
cards.people: 511 participants with DSM-IV schizophrenia whose first psychotic episode was 6 months to 7 years before screening, individually randomised at 50 sites in 15 European countries and Israel to long-acting injectable paliperidone, long-acting injectable aripiprazole, or the oral formulation of the same drug (combined injectable n = 264; combined oral n = 247), followed for up to 19 months. The primary endpoint was discontinuation of treatment for any reason.
cards.result: Discontinuation did not differ between the combined groups: 64% of the injectable group and 71% of the oral group met all-cause discontinuation criteria (hazard ratio 1.16, 95% CI 0.94–1.43; p = 0.18). During the study, 121 psychiatric hospitalisations occurred in 103 patients; the abstract reports no between-group hospitalisation comparison. The authors concluded there is no reason to prescribe long-acting injectables instead of oral antipsychotics if the goal is to prevent discontinuation.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and its endpoint was staying on treatment for any reason — a different question from PRELAPSE's hospitalisation endpoint. A null on discontinuation does not directly refute a hospitalisation benefit, but it removes the simplest proposed mechanism (that injectables keep people on medication longer) in this population.
cards.source: Winter-van Rossum I et al.. shelves.title: Multiple sclerosis fatigue: amantadine, modafinil and methylphenidate all failed to beat placebo in one head-to-head crossover trial — and caused more side effects
shelves.question: In multiple sclerosis-related fatigue, do amantadine, modafinil or methylphenidate reduce fatigue compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Amantadine/administration & dosage, adverse effects, pharmacology · Central Nervous System Stimulants/administration & dosage, adverse effects, pharmacology · Cross-Over Studies · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions · Fatigue/drug therapy, etiology · Female · Humans · Male · Methylphenidate/administration & dosage, adverse effects, pharmacology · Middle Aged · Modafinil/administration & dosage, adverse effects, pharmacology · Multiple Sclerosis/complications · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Severity of Illness Index
shelves.balance: TRIUMPHANT-MS is the one properly powered test of the three drugs most prescribed for multiple sclerosis fatigue. In a four-period crossover trial, 141 patients each took amantadine, modafinil, methylphenidate and placebo in turn; fatigue scores (Modified Fatigue Impact Scale) improved by roughly 11–13 points on every arm including placebo, and no drug beat placebo (overall medication effect p = 0.20). Adverse events were commoner on each drug (39–40% of participants) than on placebo (31%), and the three serious adverse events occurred on active treatment. Older, smaller trials of amantadine and modafinil were mixed and underpowered; none outweighs this trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: Nourbakhsh 2021 (TRIUMPHANT-MS): none of amantadine, modafinil or methylphenidate beat placebo on MS fatigue (overall p = 0.20); adverse events were more frequent on the drugs
cards.summary: Nourbakhsh 2021 (TRIUMPHANT-MS): none of amantadine, modafinil or methylphenidate beat placebo on MS fatigue (overall p = 0.20); adverse events were more frequent on the drugs
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial (Nourbakhsh 2021, TRIUMPHANT-MS)
cards.people: 141 patients with multiple sclerosis who reported fatigue (Modified Fatigue Impact Scale score above 33) at two US academic centres, randomised double-blind in a four-sequence, four-period crossover to receive amantadine (up to 100 mg twice daily), modafinil (up to 100 mg twice daily), methylphenidate (up to 10 mg twice daily) and placebo, each for up to 6 weeks with 2-week washouts; primary outcome the MFIS at the highest tolerated dose in week 5 of each period; 136 participants contributed to the primary analysis.
cards.result: Estimated mean MFIS total scores were 51.3 at baseline and 40.6 on placebo, 41.3 on amantadine, 39.0 on modafinil and 38.6 on methylphenidate (p = 0.20 for the overall medication effect) — none of the drugs was superior to placebo. Adverse events were reported by 31% of participants on placebo versus 39% on amantadine, 40% on modafinil and 40% on methylphenidate; three serious adverse events occurred on active treatment (pulmonary embolism and myocarditis on amantadine; a multiple sclerosis exacerbation requiring hospital admission on modafinil). The authors concluded the results do not support indiscriminate use of these medications for fatigue in multiple sclerosis.
cards.watchOut: A crossover trial in patients selected for high fatigue is exactly where regression to the mean and context effects are largest — fatigue improved about 11 points on placebo. The trial cannot exclude benefit in individual responders, but at group level the three standard drugs performed no better than placebo while causing more adverse events.

shelves.title: Parkinson's disease with poor early-morning control: overnight rotigotine patch improved early-morning motor scores and nocturnal sleep scores versus placebo (RECOVER) — one trial
shelves.question: In Parkinson's disease with unsatisfactory early-morning motor control, does overnight rotigotine patch improve early-morning function and sleep compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Dopamine Agonists/therapeutic use · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Motor Activity/drug effects · Parkinson Disease/complications · Severity of Illness Index · Sleep Wake Disorders/drug therapy, etiology · Tetrahydronaphthalenes/therapeutic use · Thiophenes/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: RECOVER is the single randomised trial built for this question. In 287 patients with unsatisfactory early-morning motor control, rotigotine (2–16 mg/24 h transdermal patch) beat placebo on both coprimary endpoints at the end of maintenance: early-morning motor examination (UPDRS Part III) improved by 7.0 points versus 3.9 (treatment difference −3.55, 95% CI −5.37 to −1.73; P = 0.0002), and nocturnal sleep disturbance (PDSS-2) improved by 5.9 points versus 1.9 (difference −4.26, 95% CI −6.08 to −2.45; P < 0.0001). Nausea (21% vs 9%), application-site reactions (15% vs 4%) and dizziness (10% vs 6%) were the commonest costs. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one trial, moderate gains on rating scales over roughly three months. Flagged Tier C as a single-trial benefit shelf.

cards.headline: Trenkwalder 2011 (RECOVER): rotigotine improved early-morning UPDRS III by −3.55 points and PDSS-2 sleep scores by −4.26 points versus placebo
cards.summary: Trenkwalder 2011 (RECOVER): rotigotine improved early-morning UPDRS III by −3.55 points and PDSS-2 sleep scores by −4.26 points versus placebo
cards.people: 287 subjects with Parkinson's disease and unsatisfactory early-morning motor symptom control, randomised double-blind 2:1 to rotigotine patch (2–16 mg/24 h; n = 190) or placebo (n = 97), titrated to optimal dose over 1–8 weeks with 4 weeks of dose maintenance; coprimary endpoints early-morning UPDRS Part III motor score (measured before any medication) and the modified Parkinson's Disease Sleep Scale (PDSS-2), analysed as change from baseline to end of maintenance.
cards.result: At end of maintenance, UPDRS Part III had fallen by 7.0 points on rotigotine (baseline 29.6) versus 3.9 on placebo (baseline 32.0) — treatment difference −3.55 (95% CI −5.37 to −1.73; P = 0.0002) — and PDSS-2 total score had fallen by 5.9 points (baseline 19.3) versus 1.9 (baseline 20.5) — difference −4.26 (95% CI −6.08 to −2.45; P < 0.0001). The most frequently reported adverse events were nausea (rotigotine 21%, placebo 9%), application-site reactions (15% vs 4%) and dizziness (10% vs 6%).
cards.watchOut: Short trial (titration plus 4 weeks at the maintenance dose) with last-observation-carried-forward analysis, in patients selected for early-morning problems; it does not address longer-term outcomes, dyskinesia, or comparison with adjusting the timing of oral levodopa.
cards.source: Trenkwalder C et al.. Rotigotine effects on early morning motor function and sleep in Parkinson's disease: a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled study (RECOVER). shelves.title: Major depression: wake therapy plus bright light and sleep stabilisation (added to duloxetine) produced faster, higher remission than daily exercise — and the lead held at 29 weeks
shelves.question: In major depression, does a chronotherapeutic intervention — wake therapy combined with bright light and sleep-phase stabilisation — speed and sustain antidepressant response compared with an exercise control?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Antidepressive Agents/administration & dosage · Combined Modality Therapy · Denmark · Major Depressive Disorder/drug therapy, therapy · Duloxetine Hydrochloride · Exercise · Female · Humans · Logistic Models · Male · Middle Aged · Phototherapy · Prospective Studies · Seasons · Single-Blind Method · Sleep Phase Chronotherapy · Thiophenes/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: One Danish trial programme: 75 patients, all started on duloxetine, randomised to a chronotherapeutic package (three wake-therapy nights in one week, then daily morning bright light and sleep-time stabilisation) versus daily exercise. The chronotherapy group responded within two weeks (response 41.4% vs 12.8%; odds ratio 4.8) and stayed ahead at week 9 (response 71.4% vs 47.3%, odds ratio 2.8; remission 45.6% vs 23.1%). In the 20-week follow-up report, remission at week 29 was 61.9% versus 37.9% (odds ratio 2.6; P = 0.01), with lower endpoint depression scores (7.5 vs 10.1). The caveats are structural: a single-centre programme, 75 patients, an active exercise comparator that itself helped, and assessor-blinded (not double-blind) delivery of a conspicuous intervention. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit). Flagged Tier C as a single-programme benefit shelf.

cards.headline: Martiny 2012: chronotherapy beat exercise on speed and depth of response — week 2 response 41.4% vs 12.8%; week 9 remission 45.6% vs 23.1%
cards.summary: Martiny 2012: chronotherapy beat exercise on speed and depth of response — week 2 response 41.4% vs 12.8%; week 9 remission 45.6% vs 23.1%
cards.people: 75 adults with DSM-IV major depressive disorder who completed a 1-week run-in starting duloxetine, randomised to a 9-week chronotherapeutic intervention (n = 37) — three wake therapies in the intervention week combined with daily morning bright light therapy and sleep-time stabilisation, then 7 weeks of continued light and stabilisation — or to daily exercise (n = 38); primary outcome the 17-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale, scored by assessors blinded to allocation.
cards.result: Immediately after the intervention phase (week 2), response was 41.4% with chronotherapy versus 12.8% with exercise (odds ratio 4.8, 95% CI 1.7–13.4; P = .003) and remission 23.9% versus 5.4% (odds ratio 5.5, 95% CI 1.7–17.8; P = .004). At week 9, response was 71.4% versus 47.3% (odds ratio 2.8, 95% CI 1.1–7.3; P = .04) and remission 45.6% versus 23.1% (odds ratio 2.8; P = .04). All treatment elements were well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: Both groups received duloxetine, and the comparator (daily exercise) is itself an active antidepressant intervention — the trial estimates the added value of the chronotherapy package over exercise, not over no treatment. Wake therapy is conspicuous; only the outcome assessors were blinded.
cards.source: Martiny K et al.. A 9-week randomized trial comparing a chronotherapeutic intervention (wake and light therapy) to exercise in major depressive disorder patients treated with duloxetine. J Clin Psychiatry. 2012. cards.headline: Martiny 2015 (follow-up of the same cohort): remission at week 29 was 61.9% with chronotherapy versus 37.9% with exercise (odds ratio 2.6; P = 0.01)
cards.summary: Martiny 2015 (follow-up of the same cohort): remission at week 29 was 61.9% with chronotherapy versus 37.9% with exercise (odds ratio 2.6; P = 0.01)
cards.people: The same 75-patient randomised cohort followed for a further 20 weeks (29 weeks in total), with medication free to be altered during the follow-up phase; remission rate was the primary outcome, assessed every 4 weeks.
cards.result: Remission at week 29 was 61.9% in the wake-therapy group versus 37.9% in the exercise group (odds ratio 2.6, 95% CI 1.3–5.6; P = 0.01), and endpoint Hamilton scores were lower with chronotherapy (7.5 vs 10.1; difference 2.7 points, 95% CI 0.5–4.8; P = 0.02). The authors describe this as the first study to show adjunctive short-term wake therapy with long-term bright light therapy attaining and maintaining remission.
cards.watchOut: This is a follow-up report of the same 75 patients, not an independent second trial — the shelf rests on one randomised cohort, and medication changes during follow-up were uncontrolled.
