shelves.title: Migraine prevention from the supplement shelf: riboflavin, magnesium and butterbur each beat placebo in one small trial — butterbur carries a liver warning
shelves.question: In people with migraine, do the supplement preventives patients buy for themselves — high-dose riboflavin, oral magnesium, or butterbur root extract — reduce attack frequency compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Migraine Disorders/physiopathology, prevention & control · Placebos · Riboflavin/therapeutic use · Severity of Illness Index · Time Factors
shelves.balance: Before (and alongside) prescription preventives, three supplements have each passed one proper placebo-controlled test for migraine prevention. Riboflavin 400 mg/day (55 patients): 59% achieved at least a halving of attacks versus 15% on placebo (p=0.002). Magnesium 600 mg/day (81 patients): attack frequency fell 41.6% versus 15.8% in weeks 9–12 (p<0.05), at the cost of diarrhoea in about one in five. Butterbur root extract 75 mg twice daily (245 patients): attack frequency fell 48% versus 26% on placebo over 4 months, with 68% versus 49% reaching a ≥50% reduction. Each result rests on a single small trial from the 1990s–2000s with no modern replication — and butterbur is the special case: the trials used a specific pyrrolizidine-alkaloid-free extract, because raw butterbur contains liver-toxic alkaloids; unprocessed products are not what was tested and are not safe to substitute. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), with the butterbur caution on the shelf's face.

cards.headline: Riboflavin 400 mg/day: 59% of patients halved their attacks vs 15% on placebo (p=0.002; NNT 2.3)
cards.summary: Riboflavin 400 mg/day: 59% of patients halved their attacks vs 15% on placebo (p=0.002; NNT 2.3)
cards.people: 55 patients with migraine in a 3-month randomised trial of riboflavin 400 mg daily versus placebo; outcomes attack frequency and headache days, analysed intention-to-treat.
cards.result: Riboflavin was superior to placebo on attack frequency (p=0.005) and headache days (p=0.012). Responders (≥50% improvement): 59% on riboflavin vs 15% on placebo (p=0.002); number needed to treat 2.3. Three minor adverse events occurred (diarrhoea and polyuria on riboflavin; abdominal cramps on placebo), none serious.
cards.watchOut: A single small 1998 trial; the effect has never been retested at this scale, and riboflavin at this dose is a pharmacological dose of a vitamin, not a dietary top-up. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.summary: Magnesium 600 mg/day: attack frequency fell 41.6% vs 15.8% on placebo in weeks 9–12; diarrhoea in 18.6%
cards.people: 81 patients aged 18–65 with migraine (mean 3.6 attacks/month) in a multicentre prospective double-blind trial of oral magnesium (trimagnesium dicitrate) 600 mg/day versus placebo for 12 weeks after a 4-week baseline.

cards.headline: Butterbur extract 75 mg twice daily: attack frequency fell 48% vs 26% on placebo over 4 months; the 50 mg dose was not significant
cards.summary: Butterbur extract 75 mg twice daily: attack frequency fell 48% vs 26% on placebo over 4 months; the 50 mg dose was not significant
cards.people: 245 patients aged 18–65 with 2–6 migraine attacks per month, randomised to a standardised Petasites hybridus root extract 75 mg twice daily, 50 mg twice daily, or placebo for 4 months; main outcome percentage change in monthly attack frequency.
cards.result: Attack frequency fell 48% on 75 mg (p=0.0012 vs placebo), 36% on 50 mg (p=0.127 — not significant) and 26% on placebo. Responders (≥50% reduction): 68% on 75 mg vs 49% on placebo (p<0.05). Possibly related adverse events were mainly mild gastrointestinal symptoms, predominantly burping.
cards.watchOut: Safety is the shelf's standing warning: the trial used a standardised extract processed to remove pyrrolizidine alkaloids, which are hepatotoxic; butterbur products that are not certified PA-free are a different and hazardous proposition, and regulators in several countries have acted against butterbur products over liver injury. Product tested: Petadolex (Weber & Weber, Germany), a proprietary butterbur root extract standardised to at least 15% petasins with no detectable pyrrolizidine alkaloids — not interchangeable with unprocessed butterbur products. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Lipton RB et al.. Petasites hybridus root (butterbur) is an effective preventive treatment for migraine. Neurology. 2004. PMID: 15623680. shelves.title: Fampridine for walking in MS: a consistent responder subgroup — about 35–43% walk meaningfully faster, versus 8–9% on placebo
shelves.question: In people with multiple sclerosis and walking impairment, does fampridine (dalfampridine, 4-aminopyridine) 10 mg twice daily improve walking speed compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: 4-Aminopyridine/administration & dosage, adverse effects, therapeutic use · Administration, Oral · Aged · Delayed-Action Preparations · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Multiple Sclerosis/drug therapy · Potassium Channel Blockers/administration & dosage, adverse effects, therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Walking
shelves.balance: Fampridine is the one symptomatic MS drug aimed squarely at walking, and its two phase 3 trials tell an unusually consistent story — with a catch built into the design. Both trials defined response as consistent improvement on the timed 25-foot walk across visits. In MS-F203 (301 patients, 14 weeks), 35% on fampridine were responders versus 8% on placebo (p<0.0001); in MS-F204 (239 patients, 9 weeks), 42.9% versus 9.3% (p<0.0001). Responders walked about 25% faster, an effect maintained between doses, and reported less ambulatory disability on the MS Walking Scale. The catch: the majority do not respond, and the drug does nothing measurable for them — this is a try-it-and-stop-if-no-response medicine, and both trials were short. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): two concordant large trials with a validated, clinically meaningful responder definition — strong evidence, short of a Level A stamp on this library's scale.

cards.headline: MS-F203: timed-walk responders 35% on fampridine vs 8% on placebo (p<0.0001); responders walked 25.2% faster
cards.summary: MS-F203: timed-walk responders 35% on fampridine vs 8% on placebo (p<0.0001); responders walked 25.2% faster
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (Goodman 2009, MS-F203)
cards.people: 301 patients with any type of multiple sclerosis and ambulatory deficits, randomised to sustained-release fampridine 10 mg twice daily (n=229) or placebo (n=72) for 14 weeks; primary outcome the proportion of timed-walk responders (consistent improvement on the timed 25-foot walk).
cards.result: Timed-walk responders: 78/224 (35%) on fampridine vs 6/72 (8%) on placebo (p<0.0001). Among responders, walking speed improved 25.2% (95% CI 21.5–28.8) on fampridine vs 4.7% (1.0–8.4) in the small placebo responder group, maintained throughout treatment. Responders improved more on the 12-item MS Walking Scale than non-responders (−6.84 vs +0.05 points; p=0.0002). Safety was consistent with previous studies.
cards.watchOut: The responder analysis is the trial's prespecified primary outcome, not a post-hoc subgroup — but it still means the average patient should expect no benefit: roughly two in three do not respond, and response can only be found by trying the drug.
cards.source: Goodman AD et al.. Sustained-release oral fampridine in multiple sclerosis: a randomised, double-blind, controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2009. PMID: 19249634. cards.headline: MS-F204: responders 42.9% vs 9.3% (p<0.0001); effect maintained 8–12 hours after a dose
cards.summary: MS-F204: responders 42.9% vs 9.3% (p<0.0001); effect maintained 8–12 hours after a dose
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (Goodman 2010, MS-F204)
cards.people: 239 patients with definite MS of any course type at 39 centres, randomised to extended-release dalfampridine 10 mg twice daily (n=120) or placebo (n=119) for 9 weeks; primary outcome the percentage of timed-walk responders.
cards.result: Timed-walk responders: 51/119 (42.9%) on dalfampridine vs 11/118 (9.3%) on placebo (p<0.0001). Responders' walking speed improved on average 24.7% (95% CI 21.0–28.4) during the efficacy period and 25.7% at the last on-treatment visit 8–12 hours post-dose, showing the effect persists between doses. No new safety findings.
cards.watchOut: Nine weeks is short for a chronic therapy; the trials establish symptomatic benefit in responders, not any effect on relapses, progression, or disability accumulation.

shelves.title: High-dose biotin in progressive MS: the small first trial was positive, the 642-patient replication was null — 'cannot be recommended'
shelves.question: In people with progressive multiple sclerosis, does high-dose biotin (MD1003, 100 mg three times daily) reverse or slow disability compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Biotin/administration & dosage, adverse effects, pharmacology · Disease Progression · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Multiple Sclerosis, Chronic Progressive/drug therapy · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Vitamin B Complex/administration & dosage, adverse effects, pharmacology
shelves.balance: High-dose pharmaceutical biotin (MD1003) was proposed to support neuronal and oligodendrocyte energetics in progressive MS, a field with almost no options — which is why its rise and fall is worth a shelf. The first randomised trial (MS-SPI; 154 patients) reported disability reversal in 12.6% on biotin versus 0% on placebo (p=0.005) over 12 months. The replication, SPI2 (642 patients across 13 countries, designed to confirm), found improvement in 12% versus 9% (odds ratio 1.35, 95% CI 0.81–2.26 — not significant), and its authors concluded MD1003 'cannot be recommended' — adding a practical harm that has nothing to do with MS: high-dose biotin distorts laboratory tests that use biotinylated antibodies (the subject of Shelf #58, cross-pointed, not duplicated here). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): the large, well-run replication outweighs the small positive first trial.

cards.headline: MS-SPI: disability reversal in 12.6% on MD1003 vs 0% on placebo over 12 months (p=0.005; n=154)
cards.summary: MS-SPI: disability reversal in 12.6% on MD1003 vs 0% on placebo over 12 months (p=0.005; n=154)
cards.people: 154 patients with progressive MS, baseline EDSS 4.5–7 and documented worsening in the previous 2 years, randomised to MD1003 (biotin 100 mg three times daily) or placebo for 12 months, followed by 12 months of MD1003 for all; primary endpoint disability reversal at month 9 confirmed at month 12 (EDSS fall ≥1 point, or ≥20% faster timed 25-foot walk).
cards.result: 13 patients (12.6%) on MD1003 achieved the primary endpoint versus none on placebo (p=0.005). MD1003 also reduced EDSS progression and improved clinical impression of change; efficacy appeared maintained over follow-up and the safety profile was similar to placebo.
cards.watchOut: A zero-event placebo arm in 154 patients is a fragile base for a positive claim — a handful of placebo responders would have erased the significance. This is the textbook setup for a replication failure, and the replication duly failed. Product tested: MD1003, MedDay Pharmaceuticals' high-dose pharmaceutical-grade biotin — not an over-the-counter biotin supplement.
cards.source: Tourbah A et al.. MD1003 (high-dose biotin) for the treatment of progressive multiple sclerosis: A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study. Multiple sclerosis (Houndmills, Basingstoke, England). 2016. PMID: 27589059. Registry ID: none recorded in the PubMed record. cards.headline: SPI2: improvement 12% on MD1003 vs 9% on placebo (OR 1.35, 0.81–2.26) in 642 patients — null; authors: 'cannot be recommended'
cards.summary: SPI2: improvement 12% on MD1003 vs 9% on placebo (OR 1.35, 0.81–2.26) in 642 patients — null; authors: 'cannot be recommended'
cards.people: 642 patients aged 18–65 with primary or secondary progressive MS (EDSS 3.5–6.5, documented progression, no relapses for 2 years) at 90 clinics in 13 countries, randomised to MD1003 100 mg three times daily (n=326) or placebo (n=316); primary endpoint confirmed improvement in EDSS or timed 25-foot walk at month 12, confirmed at month 15.
cards.result: Primary outcome: 39/326 (12%) on MD1003 vs 29/316 (9%) on placebo improved (OR 1.35, 95% CI 0.81–2.26 — not significant). Treatment-emergent adverse events were balanced (84% vs 85%), as were serious events (26% vs 26%); one death occurred in the MD1003 group. Despite mitigation strategies, MD1003 caused inaccurate results in laboratory tests using biotinylated antibodies.
cards.watchOut: The trial allowed concomitant disease-modifying therapies and enrolled a broader population than MS-SPI; neither difference plausibly explains away a null this size in the very population the first trial claimed to help. Product tested: MD1003, MedDay Pharmaceuticals' high-dose pharmaceutical-grade biotin.

shelves.title: Souvenaid (Fortasyn Connect) in prodromal Alzheimer's: the 24-month primary outcome was null; a 36-month analysis on a much-reduced set turned positive
shelves.question: In people with prodromal Alzheimer's disease, does a daily multinutrient drink (Fortasyn Connect, marketed as Souvenaid) slow cognitive decline compared with a control drink?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Alzheimer Disease/diet therapy · Docosahexaenoic Acids/administration & dosage, pharmacology · Double-Blind Method · Eicosapentaenoic Acid/administration & dosage, pharmacology · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Phospholipids/administration & dosage, pharmacology · Prodromal Symptoms
shelves.balance: Souvenaid is a medical-food drink (the Fortasyn Connect multinutrient combination: omega-3s, uridine, choline, phospholipids, B vitamins and antioxidants — named because only this formulation has been trialled) sold for early Alzheimer's disease. The LipiDiDiet trial randomised 311 people with prodromal Alzheimer's to the active drink or an isocaloric control for 24 months: the primary neuropsychological composite did not differ (treatment difference 0.098, 95% CI −0.041 to 0.237; p=0.166), partly because the control group declined far less than expected. A 36-month continuation analysis reported significant slowing on the 5-item composite, dementia-rating and memory measures — but on a much-reduced dataset (162 of 311 completed; 81 had data eligible for the efficacy analysis after censoring at open-label product or Alzheimer's medication). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): a null primary endpoint followed by a positive long-term analysis in a minority of the original cohort is a hypothesis, not a demonstration.

cards.headline: LipiDiDiet 24 months: primary cognitive composite null (difference 0.098, −0.041 to 0.237; p=0.166) in 311 with prodromal Alzheimer's
cards.summary: LipiDiDiet 24 months: primary cognitive composite null (difference 0.098, −0.041 to 0.237; p=0.166) in 311 with prodromal Alzheimer's
cards.people: 311 people with prodromal Alzheimer's disease (International Working Group-1 criteria) at 11 sites in Finland, Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden, randomised to the Fortasyn Connect drink 125 mL daily (n=153) or an isocaloric control drink (n=158) for 24 months; primary endpoint change in a neuropsychological test battery composite.
cards.result: Mean NTB change: −0.028 (SD 0.453) on active vs −0.108 (0.528) on control; estimated treatment difference 0.098 (95% CI −0.041 to 0.237; p=0.166 — not significant). Control-group decline (−0.108) was far less than the prestudy estimate (−0.4), leaving the endpoint underpowered. Dropout was 21%; serious adverse events occurred in 22% vs 19%, none judged related to the intervention. Secondary endpoints (cognition/function measures and hippocampal atrophy) favoured the active drink.
cards.watchOut: The named product's one large trial missed its primary endpoint. Secondary-endpoint signals in an underpowered trial are hypothesis-generating — they justified the longer analysis carded beside this one, not a claim. Product tested: Souvenaid, the medical-food drink containing Nutricia's Fortasyn Connect multinutrient combination — named because only this formulation has been trialled.

cards.headline: 36-month analysis: significant slowing on the NTB 5-item composite (difference 0.212, 0.044–0.380; p=0.014) — in 81 participants with eligible data of 311 randomised
cards.summary: 36-month analysis: significant slowing on the NTB 5-item composite (difference 0.212, 0.044–0.380; p=0.014) — in 81 participants with eligible data of 311 randomised
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 36-month analysis (Soininen 2021, LipiDiDiet)
cards.people: The LipiDiDiet cohort followed to 36 months with a modified intention-to-treat analysis censoring data collected after starting open-label active product or Alzheimer's medication; 162 of 311 participants completed the 36-month study and 81 had 36-month data eligible for the efficacy analysis.
cards.result: Over 36 months the active group declined significantly less on the NTB 5-item composite (between-group difference 0.212, 95% CI 0.044–0.380; p=0.014), the Clinical Dementia Rating–Sum of Boxes (−45% relative difference in decline; p=0.014) and memory (−76%; p=0.008), with less brain atrophy; effect sizes were small to medium (Cohen's d 0.25–0.31).
cards.watchOut: Attrition is the whole story here: three-quarters of the randomised cohort contributes no eligible 36-month efficacy data, and censoring at medication start can itself differ by arm. A positive analysis on a surviving minority cannot repair a null primary endpoint at 24 months. Product tested: Souvenaid (Nutricia Fortasyn Connect).

shelves.title: Aripiprazole added to an antidepressant in treatment-resistant depression: remission roughly doubled in midlife adults, and rose from 29% to 44% over age 60 — at the price of akathisia
shelves.question: In adults — including older adults — with major depression that has not responded adequately to an antidepressant, does adding aripiprazole improve remission compared with adding placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Antidepressive Agents/therapeutic use · Antipsychotic Agents/adverse effects, therapeutic use · Aripiprazole · Major Depressive Disorder/drug therapy, psychology · Double-Blind Method · Drug Resistance · Endpoint Determination · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Piperazines/adverse effects, therapeutic use · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Quinolones/adverse effects, therapeutic use · Treatment Failure · Young Adult
shelves.balance: When a first antidepressant fails, adding low-dose aripiprazole is one of the best-tested augmentation strategies. In the confirmatory midlife trial (349 patients who had prospectively failed an 8-week antidepressant course), adding aripiprazole (2–20 mg/day) cut MADRS scores by −10.1 versus −6.4 on added placebo and doubled remission (36.8% vs 18.9%; p<0.001) over 6 weeks. The older-adult trial matters most for this library's readers: in 181 patients over 60 who had not remitted on venlafaxine, adding aripiprazole produced remission in 44% versus 29% (OR 2.0, 95% CI 1.1–3.7; NNT 6.6) over 12 weeks — but akathisia affected 26% (vs 12%) and drug-induced parkinsonism 17% (vs 2%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): real, replicated remission gains, with a movement-side-effect price that is highest in exactly the older patients the second trial studied.

cards.headline: Remission 36.8% on adjunctive aripiprazole vs 18.9% on adjunctive placebo at 6 weeks in prospectively confirmed non-responders
cards.summary: Remission 36.8% on adjunctive aripiprazole vs 18.9% on adjunctive placebo at 6 weeks in prospectively confirmed non-responders
cards.people: 1,147 patients with major depression and a history of inadequate antidepressant response entered an 8-week single-blind phase (open antidepressant plus adjunctive placebo); the 349 who still had not responded adequately were randomised to adjunctive aripiprazole 2–20 mg/day (n=177) or adjunctive placebo (n=172) for 6 weeks; primary outcome change in MADRS total score.
cards.result: MADRS change: −10.1 on aripiprazole vs −6.4 on placebo (p<0.001). Remission at week 14: 36.8% vs 18.9% (p<0.001). Completion was high (83% vs 87%); discontinuation for adverse events 6.2% vs 1.7%. The authors note this was the third consecutive positive trial of the programme, with no failed trial.
cards.watchOut: A 6-week horizon in an industry programme; remission gains of this size with an antipsychotic augment also import the class's metabolic and movement risks, which a short efficacy trial only partly captures.

cards.headline: Over 60: remission 44% with aripiprazole augmentation vs 29% (OR 2.0, 1.1–3.7; NNT 6.6); akathisia 26%, parkinsonism 17%
cards.summary: Over 60: remission 44% with aripiprazole augmentation vs 29% (OR 2.0, 1.1–3.7; NNT 6.6); akathisia 26%, parkinsonism 17%
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in older adults (Lenze 2015)
cards.people: 468 adults older than 60 with treatment-resistant major depression (MADRS ≥15) received venlafaxine extended-release first; the 181 who did not remit were randomised to add aripiprazole (target 10 mg, maximum 15 mg daily; n=91) or placebo (n=90) for 12 weeks; primary endpoint remission at both final visits.
cards.result: Remission: 40/91 (44%) on aripiprazole vs 26/90 (29%) on placebo (OR 2.0, 95% CI 1.1–3.7; p=0.03; NNT 6.6, 95% CI 3.5–81.8). Akathisia: 26% vs 12%. Parkinsonism: 17% vs 2%. No excess of treatment-emergent suicidal ideation (21% vs 29% among those assessed) or other measured safety variables.
cards.watchOut: The NNT's confidence interval runs to 81.8 — the benefit estimate is imprecise — and one in four older patients got akathisia. In this age group the trial supports a careful, monitored trial of augmentation, not a reflex one.

shelves.title: Agomelatine for major depression: the 50 mg dose beat placebo acutely (the 25 mg dose did not), and continuing it halved relapse — with liver-enzyme elevations to watch
shelves.question: In adults with major depressive disorder, does agomelatine treat acute depression and prevent relapse after response compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acetamides/adverse effects, pharmacology, therapeutic use · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Major Depressive Disorder/drug therapy, prevention & control · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Hypnotics and Sedatives/adverse effects, pharmacology, therapeutic use · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Melatonin/agonists · Middle Aged · Receptor, Melatonin, MT1/agonists · Receptor, Melatonin, MT2/agonists · Secondary Prevention · Serotonin 5-HT2 Receptor Antagonists · Substance Withdrawal Syndrome/epidemiology, prevention & control · Treatment Outcome · Naphthalenes
shelves.balance: Agomelatine — a melatonin-receptor agonist and 5-HT2C antagonist, marketed in Europe and elsewhere but not approved in the United States — has a two-part placebo-controlled record. Acutely, in 511 patients with moderate-to-severe depression, the 50 mg dose improved Hamilton scores significantly more than placebo at 8 weeks (treatment difference 2.5 points; p=0.004) while the 25 mg dose did not (p=0.505); sleep measures improved on 50 mg, and clinically notable transient transaminase elevations occurred in 4.5% of the 50 mg group. For continuation, patients who had responded to agomelatine were randomised to continue or switch to placebo: relapse over 6 months was 21.7% versus 46.6% (p=0.0001), with no discontinuation-syndrome pattern after abrupt switching. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real but dose-specific acute effect and a strong relapse-prevention result, bounded by the failed 25 mg dose and the liver monitoring the drug requires.

cards.headline: Acute trial: agomelatine 50 mg beat placebo on HAM-D (difference 2.5 points; p=0.004); 25 mg did not (p=0.505); transaminase elevations in 4.5% at 50 mg
cards.summary: Acute trial: agomelatine 50 mg beat placebo on HAM-D (difference 2.5 points; p=0.004); 25 mg did not (p=0.505); transaminase elevations in 4.5% at 50 mg
cards.people: 511 outpatients with moderate-to-severe major depressive disorder (mean baseline HAM-D17 27.0) randomised to agomelatine 25 mg, agomelatine 50 mg, or placebo once daily for 8 weeks; primary outcome change in HAM-D17 total score.
cards.result: At week 8, agomelatine 50 mg improved HAM-D17 significantly more than placebo (treatment difference 2.5; p=0.004); agomelatine 25 mg did not separate (p=0.505). Secondary outcomes (CGI-Improvement p=0.012, CGI-Severity p=0.003, anxiety–depression total p=0.014, getting to sleep p<0.001, sleep quality p=0.002) all favoured 50 mg. Both doses were generally well tolerated, but clinically notable transient aminotransferase elevations occurred in 4.5% of the 50 mg group.
cards.watchOut: One of the two doses failed its primary comparison in the programme's own trial — dose matters, and the effective dose is the one with the liver signal. (A case of rhabdomyolysis appears among the record's index terms; the abstract reports the transaminase finding as the notable laboratory signal.)

cards.headline: Relapse prevention: continuing agomelatine after response — relapse 21.7% vs 46.6% over 6 months after switch to placebo (p=0.0001)
cards.summary: Relapse prevention: continuing agomelatine after response — relapse 21.7% vs 46.6% over 6 months after switch to placebo (p=0.0001)
cards.people: Patients with major depressive disorder who responded to 8–10 weeks of open agomelatine 25–50 mg were randomised to continue agomelatine (n=165) or switch to placebo (n=174) for 24 weeks; main outcome time to relapse.
cards.result: Relapse incidence was significantly lower on continued agomelatine (p=0.0001): cumulative 6-month relapse 21.7% vs 46.6% on placebo — an absolute difference of about 25 percentage points. The result held in the severe-baseline subgroup. Tolerability resembled placebo, and no early-relapse or withdrawal pattern appeared after abrupt cessation.
cards.watchOut: An enriched design: only agomelatine responders entered, so the result shows continuation works for people the drug already helped — it is not evidence about starting agomelatine, and relapse-prevention trials of this shape flatter the drug by construction.
cards.source: Goodwin GM et al.. shelves.title: Omega-3 as a treatment for major depression: two small 8-week trials — an add-on benefit in 28 patients, EPA matching fluoxetine in 60 — not the prevention question
shelves.question: In adults with major depressive disorder, do omega-3 fatty acids (EPA/DHA) improve depressive symptoms as a treatment — added to usual care or compared with an antidepressant?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Major Depressive Disorder/drug therapy · Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders · Double-Blind Method · Fatty Acids, Omega-3/therapeutic use · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Placebos · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales/statistics & numerical data · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Fish oil for depression is asked about constantly, and this shelf answers the treatment question only — omega-3 for preventing depression is a separate shelf (#2024) and is not duplicated here. The treatment record pinned is two small, short trials. Su (28 patients with major depression) added omega-3 (6.6 g/day) to usual treatment for 8 weeks and found a significantly greater fall in Hamilton scores than added placebo (p<0.001). Jazayeri (60 outpatients) compared EPA 1,000 mg/day, fluoxetine 20 mg/day, and the combination for 8 weeks: response rates were 56%, 50% and 81% respectively, with EPA statistically comparable to fluoxetine and the combination superior to either alone from week 4. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): the direction is consistent, but 88 patients across two 8-week trials — one without a placebo-only arm — cannot carry more than that.

cards.headline: Add-on omega-3 (6.6 g/day) beat add-on placebo on Hamilton scores over 8 weeks in 28 patients with major depression (p<0.001)
cards.summary: Add-on omega-3 (6.6 g/day) beat add-on placebo on Hamilton scores over 8 weeks in 28 patients with major depression (p<0.001)
cards.people: 28 patients with major depressive disorder in an 8-week double-blind trial of omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids 6.6 g/day versus placebo, each added on top of the patients' usual treatment; outcome the 21-item Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression.
cards.result: The omega-3 group had a significantly greater decrease in Hamilton scores than the placebo group (p<0.001). The authors describe the findings as preliminary evidence that omega-3 could improve the short-term course of illness, and report it was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-eight patients and 8 weeks, with the abstract reporting a p-value but not the score difference — the size of the benefit cannot be judged from the record, only its direction. The publication does not name a commercial product for the omega-3 capsules used.
cards.source: Su KP et al.. Omega-3 fatty acids in major depressive disorder. A preliminary double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. European neuropsychopharmacology : the journal of the European College of Neuropsychopharmacology. 2003. PMID: 12888186. Registry ID: none recorded in the PubMed record. cards.headline: EPA 1,000 mg matched fluoxetine (response 56% vs 50%); the combination reached 81% — in 60 outpatients over 8 weeks
cards.summary: EPA 1,000 mg matched fluoxetine (response 56% vs 50%); the combination reached 81% — in 60 outpatients over 8 weeks
cards.people: 60 outpatients with major depressive disorder (Hamilton ≥15) randomised to EPA 1,000 mg/day, fluoxetine 20 mg/day, or both, for 8 weeks with a double-dummy design; primary outcome change in the 17-item Hamilton scale, analysed in the 48 patients who completed at least 4 weeks.
cards.result: Response (≥50% Hamilton reduction): 50% on fluoxetine, 56% on EPA, 81% on the combination. The combination was significantly better than either treatment alone from week 4; EPA and fluoxetine did not differ significantly from each other. Treatment, age of onset and baseline severity significantly affected week-8 scores.
cards.watchOut: No placebo arm: in major depression, 'as good as fluoxetine over 8 weeks in 60 patients' cannot exclude that both arms rode spontaneous improvement and trial effects — the same caution this library applies to every active-comparator-only design. Product tested: EPA supplied as plusEPA soft gels by Minami Nutrition (Edegem, Belgium), per the research group's report of this trial programme. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

shelves.title: The MIND diet didn't beat a control diet in its one randomised trial
shelves.question: In cognitively unimpaired older adults with a family history of dementia, does the MIND diet slow cognitive decline compared with a control diet when both groups receive the same mild caloric restriction?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Brain · Caloric Restriction · Cognition · Cognitive Dysfunction · Dementia · Diet, Mediterranean · Humans
shelves.balance: Among 604 cognitively unimpaired older adults with a family history of dementia, a body-mass index over 25 and a suboptimal diet, three years on the MIND diet did not slow cognitive decline any more than a control diet when both groups received the same mild caloric restriction, counselling and weight-loss support. Global cognition improved slightly in both groups (+0.205 versus +0.170 standardised units); the between-group difference was 0.035 (95% CI −0.022 to 0.092), P = 0.23, and MRI measures of brain structure changed similarly in the two groups. The observational studies that linked MIND-style eating to less dementia show an association, not trial proof — people who eat that way differ in many other ways — and this trial is the randomised test of the diet itself, fenced here as observational background rather than evidence of effect. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): one large, long randomised trial with a null primary outcome and null imaging outcomes.

cards.headline: Barnes 2023: global cognition +0.205 versus +0.170 SD units over 3 years — difference 0.035 (P = 0.23), no advantage for the MIND diet
cards.summary: Barnes 2023: global cognition +0.205 versus +0.170 SD units over 3 years — difference 0.035 (P = 0.23), no advantage for the MIND diet
cards.type: Two-site, randomised, controlled trial (Barnes 2023, MIND diet trial)
cards.people: 604 older adults without cognitive impairment but with a family history of dementia, a body-mass index greater than 25 and a suboptimal diet, at two sites, assigned 1:1 to the MIND diet (301) or a control diet (303) for 3 years; all participants received counselling on adherence to their assigned diet plus support to promote weight loss, with mild caloric restriction in both groups, and 93.4% completed the trial.
cards.result: From baseline to year 3, global cognition scores improved by 0.205 standardised units in the MIND-diet group and 0.170 in the control-diet group — a mean difference of 0.035 standardised units (95% CI −0.022 to 0.092), P = 0.23. Changes in white-matter hyperintensities, hippocampal volumes and total gray- and white-matter volumes on MRI were similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: The control was not 'usual eating' — it was a structured diet with the same mild caloric restriction and support — so the trial tests what the MIND diet adds on top of eating more carefully, not diet versus nothing. Cognition improved slightly in both arms, which counselling, test practice effects and weight loss could all contribute to, and the trial cannot separate those. Funded by the National Institute on Aging.
cards.source: Barnes LL et al.. Trial of the MIND Diet for Prevention of Cognitive Decline in Older Persons. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2023. PMID: 37466280. Registry ID: NCT02817074. cards.summary: Synthesis: the one randomised test of the MIND diet was null on cognition and on MRI — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)

cards.result: The global cognition difference was 0.035 standardised units (95% CI −0.022 to 0.092), P = 0.23, and MRI changes were similar — no significant advantage for the MIND diet. The diet's reputation rests on observational associations between dietary patterns and dementia, which are association, not trial proof, and which this randomised trial did not confirm. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: A null for the MIND diet as tested — cognitively unimpaired volunteers, three years, both groups dieting with support — does not rule out benefits of dietary patterns in other populations or over much longer horizons, and it does not test the Mediterranean or DASH diets as such.

shelves.title: Midodrine for orthostatic hypotension: standing pressure up 22 mmHg at the top dose and symptoms improved in two trials — with supine hypertension as the price
shelves.question: In patients with neurogenic orthostatic hypotension (autonomic failure), does midodrine improve standing blood pressure and orthostatic symptoms compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Adrenergic alpha-Agonists/adverse effects/*therapeutic use · Analysis of Variance · Dizziness · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Hypotension, Orthostatic/*drug therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Midodrine/adverse effects/*therapeutic use · Sympathomimetics/adverse effects/*therapeutic use · Systole · Vasoconstrictor Agents/adverse effects/*therapeutic use
shelves.balance: Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension — the blood pressure collapse on standing that comes with autonomic failure — has few drug options, and midodrine, a vasoconstrictor prodrug, is the standard one. Two double-blind trials from the 1990s support it. In the multicentre trial (171 patients), midodrine 10 mg three times daily improved standing systolic pressure at every visit (p<0.001), lightheadedness by the second week (p=0.001), and global symptom relief as rated by both patients (p=0.03) and investigators (p<0.001). In the dose-ranging trial (97 patients), the 10 mg dose raised standing systolic pressure by 22 mmHg (28%; p<0.001 versus placebo) and improved dizziness, weakness, syncope, energy and ability to stand. The costs are intrinsic to a pressor drug: tingling scalp, urinary urgency or retention, and supine hypertension — lying-down blood pressure must be watched. Standing pressure is a surrogate, but here the symptoms moved with it, which is more than most surrogate stories offer. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Low 1997: midodrine 10 mg three times daily improved standing pressure at every visit (p<0.001) and lightheadedness by week 2
cards.summary: Low 1997: midodrine 10 mg three times daily improved standing pressure at every visit (p<0.001) and lightheadedness by week 2
cards.people: 171 patients with neurogenic orthostatic hypotension in a 25-centre randomised placebo-controlled study: a 6-week design with single-blind run-in and washout around a double-blind phase (weeks 2–4) of midodrine 10 mg three times daily or placebo; 162 evaluable.
cards.result: Standing systolic pressure improved at all time points on midodrine (p<0.001 at visits 2–5), lightheadedness improved by the end of week 2 (p=0.001), and global symptom relief was rated better by patients (p=0.03) and investigators (p<0.001). Main adverse effects were pilomotor reactions (gooseflesh, scalp tingling), urinary retention, and supine hypertension.
cards.watchOut: Three weeks of double-blind treatment is short for a lifelong condition, and standing pressure remains a surrogate — though the symptom outcomes in this trial genuinely moved with it.
cards.source: Low PA et al.. Efficacy of midodrine vs placebo in neurogenic orthostatic hypotension. A randomized, double-blind multicenter study. Midodrine Study Group. JAMA. 1997. PMID: 9091692. cards.headline: Jankovic 1993: midodrine 10 mg raised standing systolic pressure 22 mmHg (28%) and improved syncope, dizziness and ability to stand
cards.summary: Jankovic 1993: midodrine 10 mg raised standing systolic pressure 22 mmHg (28%) and improved syncope, dizziness and ability to stand
cards.people: 97 patients (ages 22–86) with orthostatic hypotension due to autonomic failure, randomised double-blind to placebo or midodrine 2.5, 5 or 10 mg three times daily for 4 weeks after a placebo run-in week, with doses titrated weekly in the higher-dose groups.
cards.result: Midodrine 10 mg increased standing systolic pressure by 22 mmHg (28%; p<0.001 versus placebo) and significantly improved (p<0.05) dizziness/lightheadedness, weakness/fatigue, syncope, low energy, impaired ability to stand, and feelings of depression. Side effects were reported by 27% on midodrine versus 22% on placebo — scalp pruritus/tingling in 13.5%, supine hypertension in 8%, urinary urgency in 4%.
cards.watchOut: The benefit concentrated at the 10 mg dose; the 2.5 mg dose did little. Supine hypertension is the standing warning with any pressor in autonomic failure.
cards.source: Jankovic J et al.. Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension: a double-blind, placebo-controlled study with midodrine. The American Journal of Medicine. 1993. PMID: 7687093. shelves.title: Feverfew for migraine prevention: one trial marginally positive, one null overall — the honest verdict is maybe
shelves.question: In people with migraine, does feverfew (the standardised CO2 extract MIG-99) reduce migraine frequency compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Carbon Dioxide · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Migraine Disorders/*prevention & control · Phytotherapy/*adverse effects · Plant Extracts/adverse effects · Tanacetum parthenium/*adverse effects
shelves.balance: Feverfew is the classic herbal migraine preventive, and its modern evidence is two trials of one standardised CO2 extract, MIG-99 — which between them give a genuinely mixed answer. The larger trial (170 patients, 6.25 mg three times daily, 16 weeks) found attacks fell by 1.9 per month on MIG-99 versus 1.3 on placebo (p=0.0456), with a responder odds ratio of 3.4 (p=0.0049) and adverse events no commoner than placebo. The earlier dose-ranging trial (147 patients, three doses) found no significant difference on its primary endpoint in either the full or the confirmatory analysis — the dose-dependent signal appeared only in the pre-defined subgroup of patients with at least four attacks a month at baseline (n=49; p=0.001). A marginal positive and a primary-endpoint null is the profile of a weak-evidence stamp. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).

cards.headline: Diener 2005: MIG-99 cut attacks by 1.9/month versus 1.3 on placebo (p=0.0456); responder odds ratio 3.4
cards.summary: Diener 2005: MIG-99 cut attacks by 1.9/month versus 1.3 on placebo (p=0.0456); responder odds ratio 3.4
cards.people: 170 patients with migraine by International Headache Society criteria (89 on extract, 81 on placebo, intention-to-treat) randomised double-blind to the feverfew CO2-extract MIG-99 6.25 mg three times daily or placebo for 16 weeks after a 4-week baseline; primary endpoint migraine attacks per 28 days in treatment months 2–3 versus baseline.
cards.result: Migraine frequency fell by 1.9 attacks per month on MIG-99 versus 1.3 on placebo (p=0.0456); logistic regression of responder rates gave an odds ratio of 3.4 in favour of MIG-99 (p=0.0049). Adverse events possibly related to study medication occurred in 8.4% on MIG-99 versus 10.2% on placebo. The record names the tested product — the standardised CO2 extract MIG-99; it does not name a manufacturer.
cards.watchOut: Statistically positive but marginally so (p=0.0456), and the absolute advantage over placebo is about half an attack a month. Both of the shelf's trials test MIG-99 — other feverfew preparations are untested by these data.

shelves.title: SAMe (S-adenosylmethionine) added to an antidepressant that has not worked
shelves.question: For major depression that has not responded to a standard antidepressant, does adding SAMe (S-adenosylmethionine) help?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antidepressive Agents · Depressive Disorder · Major Depressive Disorder · Double-Blind Method · Drug Resistance · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — the evidence is split one-for-one: Papakostas 2010 (n = 73, SAMe target 1,600 mg/day) doubled response (36.1% vs 17.6%), while Sarris 2018 (n = 107, 800 mg/day) found nothing (response 54.3% vs 50.0%). The dose difference keeps a benefit plausible but unproven — POSSIBLE, no higher.

cards.headline: Adding SAMe doubled response rates in 73 antidepressant non-responders
cards.summary: Adding SAMe doubled response rates in 73 antidepressant non-responders
cards.people: 73 adults with major depressive disorder who had not responded to a serotonin reuptake inhibitor, kept on a stable dose; adjunctive oral SAMe (target 800 mg twice daily) or placebo for 6 weeks, double-blind
cards.result: Hamilton scale response: 36.1% with SAMe vs 17.6% with placebo; remission 25.8% vs 11.7% — numbers needed to treat of about 6 for response and 7 for remission. Discontinuation for adverse events was no higher on SAMe (5.1% vs 8.8%).
cards.watchOut: Small and short — a proof-of-concept trial the authors say warrants replication. The record names no SAMe brand or formulation.

cards.headline: A larger trial at half the dose found no benefit
cards.summary: A larger trial at half the dose found no benefit
cards.people: 107 outpatients with non-remittent major depressive disorder on antidepressants; adjunctive SAMe 800 mg/day or placebo for 8 weeks, double-blind
cards.result: Depression (MADRS) scores fell in both groups with no significant between-group difference (P = 0.51). Response at week 8: 54.3% on SAMe vs 50.0% on placebo; remission 43.5% vs 38.3% — all non-significant. No biomarker (genotype, homocysteine, folate, BDNF) identified responders. SAMe was implicated in one case of serotonin-syndrome-like symptoms.
cards.watchOut: The placebo response was very high (50%) despite rigorous screening, which can drown a real effect — and the dose was half of the positive trial's target dose, so this is not a direct replication. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.headline: What this means
cards.summary: What this means
cards.result: One small trial at 1,600 mg/day is clearly positive; one somewhat larger trial at 800 mg/day is flatly null. Whether the difference is dose, luck, or the high placebo response is unresolved. SAMe augmentation is a reasonable experiment for a non-responder — not an established treatment.
cards.watchOut: No third trial adjudicates the split. SAMe is sold as a dietary supplement in the US and is not FDA-regulated for purity or dose; the card names no brand because the trial records name none.

shelves.title: Intranasal oxytocin for social deficits in autism
shelves.question: Does intranasal oxytocin improve social functioning in people with autism spectrum disorder?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intranasal · Adult · Child Development Disorders, Pervasive · Cross-Over Studies · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Male · Oxytocin · Placebo Effect · Prefrontal Cortex · Social Behavior · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — early small studies (a single-dose experiment in 40 men; a biomarker-adjusted trial of 32 children) suggested benefit, but the 290-child, 24-week SOARS-B trial found a between-group difference of −0.2 points on its primary social outcome (95% CI −1.5 to 1.0; P = 0.61). The large, long, rigorous trial governs the stamp.

cards.headline: A single oxytocin dose shifted social judgements and prefrontal activity in 40 autistic men
cards.summary: A single oxytocin dose shifted social judgements and prefrontal activity in 40 autistic men
cards.people: 40 high-functioning adult men with autism spectrum disorder at the University of Tokyo; single-dose intranasal oxytocin 24 IU vs placebo, crossover, with brain imaging
cards.result: After oxytocin, participants based social judgements on nonverbal information more often (P = 0.03) and responded faster (P = 0.02), and activity in the medial prefrontal cortex — diminished in this task in autism — increased (P < 0.001), with neural effects predicting behavioural effects.
cards.watchOut: A single-dose laboratory experiment on a surrogate task, not a treatment trial — it cannot show that repeated oxytocin helps anyone socially.
cards.source: Watanabe T et al.. Mitigation of sociocommunicational deficits of autism through oxytocin-induced recovery of medial prefrontal activity: a randomized trial. JAMA Psychiatry. 2014. PMID: 24352377. Registry ID: UMIN000002241 and UMIN000004393. cards.summary: The definitive trial — 290 children over 24 weeks — found no difference at all (SOARS-B)
cards.people: 290 children and adolescents aged 3–17 with autism spectrum disorder; intranasal oxytocin (total target dose 48 IU daily) or placebo for 24 weeks, double-blind

shelves.title: GLP-1 drugs for alcohol use disorder: the largest trial cut heavy drinking days by 13.7 points more than placebo — smaller trials are mixed, and the biggest numbers are observational
shelves.question: In alcohol use disorder, do GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide, exenatide) reduce heavy drinking and craving?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · *Alcoholism/drug therapy/complications · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · *Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · *Obesity/complications/epidemiology/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome · *Semaglutide/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Comorbidity
shelves.balance: Probably — with the evidence still young and concentrated. The strongest card is a 26-week Danish randomised trial in treatment-seeking patients with alcohol use disorder and obesity (Klausen 2026): once-weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg reduced heavy drinking days by 41.1 percentage points from baseline against 26.4 points on placebo, an estimated treatment difference of −13.7 points (95% CI −22.0 to −5.4; P = 0.0015). Two small phase 2 trials point the same way on some outcomes and not others: low-dose semaglutide reduced laboratory alcohol self-administration and drinks per drinking day but not drinking days (Hendershot 2025, n = 48), and oral semaglutide missed its primary craving endpoint while reducing heavy drinking days (Schacht 2026, n = 50). The class's other full-size trial is a caution: weekly exenatide for 26 weeks did not significantly reduce heavy drinking days overall (Klausen 2022, n = 127), though it blunted brain alcohol-cue reactivity and helped the obese subgroup in exploratory analysis. The very large numbers — a 50–56% lower risk of alcohol use disorder incidence and recurrence with semaglutide in electronic health records (Wang 2024) — are relative measures from observational data and cannot separate the drug from the kind of patient who receives it. No trial has yet tested hard outcomes (hospitalisation, liver events, mortality), follow-up is at most 26 weeks, and adverse events are the familiar gastrointestinal ones. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one solid positive trial, two supportive small ones, one null — a real but unconfirmed effect. Tier C: early, small, mostly single-centre evidence for a new indication, taken to the developer personally.

cards.headline: Klausen 2026 (Lancet): weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg cut heavy drinking days by 13.7 percentage points more than placebo over 26 weeks in alcohol use disorder with obesity
cards.summary: Klausen 2026 (Lancet): weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg cut heavy drinking days by 13.7 percentage points more than placebo over 26 weeks in alcohol use disorder with obesity
cards.type: Single-centre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, 26 weeks (Klausen 2026)
cards.people: 108 treatment-seeking participants with moderate-to-severe alcohol use disorder and comorbid obesity (54 women, 54 assigned to each arm), randomised to once-weekly subcutaneous semaglutide titrated to 2.4 mg or saline placebo, both on top of standard cognitive behavioural therapy; 88 participants (81%) completed the intervention. The primary endpoint was reduction in the number of heavy drinking days at 26 weeks, analysed intention-to-treat with multiple imputation.
cards.result: Heavy drinking days fell by 41.1 percentage points from baseline on semaglutide (95% CI −48.7 to −33.5) versus 26.4 points on placebo (−34.1 to −18.6): an estimated treatment difference of −13.7 percentage points (95% CI −22.0 to −5.4; P = 0.0015). The abstract reports substantial effects on multiple secondary alcohol-related and somatic outcomes without enumerating them. Adverse events were transient, generally mild-to-moderate gastrointestinal effects, and occurred more often on semaglutide.
cards.watchOut: Single-centre, and every participant had comorbid obesity — the population in whom a weight-loss drug's drinking effect is most plausible and least separable from weight loss itself. The endpoint is drinking behaviour over 26 weeks, not alcohol-related harm; whether the effect survives stopping the drug, or appears in alcohol use disorder without obesity, is untested in this record.

cards.headline: Hendershot 2025: low-dose semaglutide reduced laboratory drinking and craving in 48 non-treatment-seeking adults — but not the number of drinking days
cards.summary: Hendershot 2025: low-dose semaglutide reduced laboratory drinking and craving in 48 non-treatment-seeking adults — but not the number of drinking days
cards.type: Phase 2 double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial, 9 weeks (Hendershot 2025)
cards.people: 48 non-treatment-seeking adults with alcohol use disorder at one US academic centre, randomised to once-weekly subcutaneous semaglutide (0.25 mg for 4 weeks, 0.5 mg for 4 weeks, 1.0 mg for 1 week) or placebo. The primary outcome was laboratory alcohol self-administration after treatment; drinking and craving were followed prospectively at weekly visits.
cards.result: Semaglutide reduced the amount consumed in the post-treatment laboratory session (grams of alcohol: β −0.48, 95% CI −0.85 to −0.11; P = .01; peak breath alcohol concentration: β −0.46; P = .03 — standardised effects the authors describe as medium to large). It did not change average drinks per calendar day or the number of drinking days, but did reduce drinks per drinking day (β −0.41; P = .04) and weekly craving (β −0.39; P = .01), and predicted greater reductions in heavy drinking over time (β 0.84, 95% CI 0.71 to 0.99; P = .04). In the subgroup who smoked, cigarettes per day also fell faster on semaglutide.
cards.watchOut: A laboratory self-administration endpoint in 48 people at doses below the usual obesity dose and for 9 weeks: it demonstrates the drug reaches the behaviour, not that it treats the disorder. The pattern — less per occasion, same number of occasions — is an intensity effect, and the trial was not powered for clinical outcomes.

cards.headline: Schacht 2026: oral semaglutide missed its primary craving endpoint but reduced heavy drinking days and drinks per drinking day in 50 treatment-seeking adults
cards.summary: Schacht 2026: oral semaglutide missed its primary craving endpoint but reduced heavy drinking days and drinks per drinking day in 50 treatment-seeking adults
cards.type: Phase 2 double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial, 8 weeks (Schacht 2026)
cards.people: 50 treatment-seeking adults with moderate-to-severe alcohol use disorder randomised to oral semaglutide (3 mg/day for 4 weeks, then 7 mg/day for 4 weeks) or placebo. The primary outcome was laboratory alcohol cue-elicited craving at week 6; heavy drinking days and drinks per day in the last 4 weeks were key pre-registered secondary outcomes.
cards.result: Oral semaglutide did not significantly reduce laboratory-assessed craving or drinks per day versus placebo — the primary endpoint was missed. It did significantly reduce heavy drinking days (b = −0.580, 95% CI −1.012 to −0.148) and drinks per drinking day (b = −1.177, 95% CI −2.307 to −0.047), as well as naturalistic craving, cannabis use days and alcohol-related consequences, and more participants on semaglutide dropped at least one WHO risk drinking level. The effect sizes are regression coefficients; the full text tabulates baseline drinking levels by arm but reports end-of-treatment levels only in a figure, so absolute on-treatment rates cannot be stated exactly. At baseline the groups were drinking heavily: a mean of 5.4 (placebo) versus 4.5 (semaglutide) heavy drinking days per week and 6.6 versus 6.3 drinks per calendar day (full-text Table 1).
cards.watchOut: When the primary endpoint misses and the secondaries hit, the honest summary is 'promising, unconfirmed': with 50 participants and 8 weeks, multiplicity across the many secondary outcomes is a real concern, and the doses used are the low end of the oral range.
cards.source: Schacht JP et al. Oral Semaglutide for Alcohol Use Disorder: A Randomized Clinical Trial. The American Journal of Psychiatry. 2026. PMID: 42522065. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Klausen 2022: weekly exenatide for 26 weeks did NOT significantly reduce heavy drinking days — brain cue reactivity fell, and only the obese subgroup drank less
cards.summary: Klausen 2022: weekly exenatide for 26 weeks did NOT significantly reduce heavy drinking days — brain cue reactivity fell, and only the obese subgroup drank less
cards.people: 127 treatment-seeking patients with alcohol use disorder randomised to once-weekly exenatide 2 mg subcutaneously or placebo for 26 weeks, both with standard cognitive behavioural therapy. The primary outcome was reduction in heavy drinking days; a subgroup underwent functional MRI and dopamine-transporter imaging.
cards.result: Exenatide did not significantly reduce the number of heavy drinking days compared with placebo — the trial's primary result is null. It did significantly attenuate functional-MRI alcohol cue reactivity in the ventral striatum and septal area, and dopamine transporter availability was lower on exenatide. In exploratory analyses, exenatide significantly reduced heavy drinking days and total alcohol intake in the subgroup with obesity (BMI over 30). Adverse events were mainly gastrointestinal. In the full text (Table 2), heavy drinking days fell by 26.8 percentage points on placebo and 19.6 points on exenatide (estimated difference 6.0 points, 95% CI −7.4 to 19.4; P = 0.37), from baselines of 17.3 and 16.7 heavy drinking days per month — both groups improved a lot on cognitive behavioural therapy, and the drug added nothing overall.
cards.watchOut: This is the cautionary card of the shelf: the same Danish group's earlier, larger trial with a different GLP-1 drug missed its primary endpoint, and its positive signals are a brain-imaging surrogate and an exploratory subgroup — the same subgroup (obesity) that the group's later semaglutide trial then enrolled by design. Class effect, drug effect and population effect are not yet separable. The exploratory BMI split cuts both ways: in the lean subgroup (BMI under 25; n = 52) exenatide significantly increased heavy drinking days by 27.5 percentage points (95% CI 4.7 to 50.2; P = 0.024) relative to placebo, so the obese-subgroup benefit sits inside a subgroup pattern that also contains a significant result in the harm direction (full text).

cards.headline: Wang 2024 (observational): in health records of 83,825 people with obesity, semaglutide was associated with 50–56% lower risk of alcohol use disorder diagnosis and recurrence
cards.summary: Wang 2024 (observational): in health records of 83,825 people with obesity, semaglutide was associated with 50–56% lower risk of alcohol use disorder diagnosis and recurrence
cards.type: Retrospective electronic-health-record cohort study (Wang 2024) — observational, not a trial
cards.people: Electronic health records of 83,825 patients with obesity and no prior alcohol use disorder diagnosis, prescribed semaglutide or other anti-obesity medications and followed for 12 months for a first alcohol use disorder diagnosis; recurrence was studied in a separate population of 4,254 patients with obesity and a prior alcohol use disorder diagnosis (full text); a second population of 598,803 patients with type 2 diabetes was analysed the same way. This is a retrospective cohort comparison, not a randomised trial.
cards.result: Semaglutide was associated with a 50–56% lower risk of both incidence and recurrence of alcohol use disorder over 12 months compared with other anti-obesity medications — relative measures, consistent across sex, age group, race and diabetes status in the obesity population, with similar findings in the diabetes population. The full text’s matched cohorts put absolute rates on the relative figures: over 12 months, incident AUD was diagnosed in 0.37% on semaglutide versus 0.73% on other anti-obesity medications (HR 0.50, 95% CI 0.39–0.63), while among patients with prior AUD, recurrence was 22.6% versus 43.0% (HR 0.44, 95% CI 0.38–0.52); in the diabetes population, incident AUD was 0.32% versus 0.52% (HR 0.56, 95% CI 0.43–0.74).
cards.watchOut: Confounding is the whole question here: people prescribed semaglutide differ from people prescribed older anti-obesity drugs in income, engagement, weight trajectory and clinician attention, and an alcohol diagnosis in a record is not the same as drinking measured in a trial. Read this card as the hypothesis the randomised trials are now testing — at a fraction of the effect size.
cards.source: Wang W et al. Associations of semaglutide with incidence and recurrence of alcohol use disorder in real-world population. Nature Communications. 2024. PMID: 38806481. cards.headline: Synthesis: one positive 26-week trial, two small trials positive on secondary drinking measures, one full-size trial null on its primary endpoint — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: one positive 26-week trial, two small trials positive on secondary drinking measures, one full-size trial null on its primary endpoint — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.people: Four randomised trials (108, 48, 50 and 127 participants; 9–26 weeks) of semaglutide or exenatide in alcohol use disorder, and one very large retrospective health-record study (83,825 patients with obesity; 598,803 with type 2 diabetes).
cards.result: The randomised evidence converges on intensity rather than frequency: heavy drinking days and drinks per drinking day fall (treatment difference −13.7 percentage points for heavy drinking days in the largest trial), while total drinking days and laboratory craving are inconsistent, and the exenatide trial's primary endpoint was null. The observational association (50–56% lower risk, relative) is far larger than anything the trials show and should be discounted accordingly. Nothing here addresses alcohol-related hospitalisation, liver disease or death, and no trial followed patients after the drug stopped. The shelf's neighbours: psilocybin-assisted therapy for alcohol use disorder is on shelf #1515; this shelf covers the GLP-1 drug class only.
cards.watchOut: Three of the four trials are single-centre and two come from the same Danish group (whose positive semaglutide trial enrolled exactly the obese subgroup their null exenatide trial had flagged); industry-independent replication in alcohol use disorder without obesity, and trials powered for clinical harm outcomes, are what would move this stamp.
cards.source: Synthesis of Klausen MK et al. The Lancet. 2026 (PMID: 42070571); Hendershot CS et al. JAMA Psychiatry. 2025 (PMID: 39937469); Schacht JP et al. shelves.title: Capsaicin for postherpetic neuralgia: the clinic-applied 8% patch beats its control patch by a modest margin; the old 0.075% creams were never shown to do much beyond placebo
shelves.question: In adults with postherpetic neuralgia, does capsaicin — the clinic-applied 8% patch or low-concentration creams — reduce pain versus control?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Topical · Aged · Analgesics/therapeutic use · Capsaicin/administration & dosage/adverse effects/*therapeutic use · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Endpoint Determination · Female · Humans · Male · Neuralgia, Postherpetic/*drug therapy · Pain Measurement · Socioeconomic Factors · Transdermal Patch · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: The two forms of capsaicin have very different evidence. For the clinic-applied 8% patch, the randomised trial carded here (Irving 2011, PMID: 21087403) found mean pain fell by 32.0% with the patch versus 24.4% with a low-dose control patch over weeks 2–8 (both figures are relative reductions from baseline), with at least 30% pain relief in 46% versus 34% of patients; the Cochrane pooling of high-concentration capsaicin in postherpetic neuralgia (Derry 2017, PMID: 28085183; four studies, 1,272 participants) found about 10% more patients much or very much improved than with control, a number needed to treat of 8.8. The patch's first large trial (Backonja 2008) is already carded on shelf #695 and is not re-carded here. For the home-applied 0.075% creams, the two small double-blind trials from 1989–1993 (Watson 1993, PMID: 8364943; Bernstein 1989, PMID: 2768576) reported statistically significant pain relief but published few responder numbers, and the Cochrane review of low-concentration capsaicin (Derry 2012, PMID: 22972149) concluded there were insufficient data to conclude it works, with a suggestion of no meaningful effect beyond placebo and local skin reactions at a number needed to harm of 2.5. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE for the clinic-applied 8% patch; MAYBE (weak evidence) for low-concentration creams. Tier C: taken to the developer personally, because within this shelf the patch's benefit rests on one carded trial plus a pooled analysis that includes the trial held on shelf #695.

cards.headline: Irving 2011: a single 60-minute application of the 8% capsaicin patch cut pain by 32.0% versus 24.4% on the control patch; 46% versus 34% achieved at least 30% relief
cards.summary: Irving 2011: a single 60-minute application of the 8% capsaicin patch cut pain by 32.0% versus 24.4% on the control patch; 46% versus 34% achieved at least 30% relief
cards.type: Randomised double-blind controlled trial of the 8% capsaicin patch, 418 patients with postherpetic neuralgia (Irving 2011)
cards.people: 418 patients with postherpetic neuralgia randomised to a single 60-minute application of the capsaicin 8% patch or an identical-appearing low-concentration (0.04%) capsaicin control patch — an active control used because the real patch's burning sensation would otherwise unblind the trial — with pain followed for 12 weeks.
cards.result: Mean pain intensity fell by 32.0% from baseline in the 8% patch group versus 24.4% in the control group during weeks 2–8 (p = 0.011); these are relative reductions from each group's own baseline, an absolute difference of about 8 percentage points of baseline pain. The proportion achieving at least a 30% pain reduction was 46% versus 34% (p = 0.02), and the benefit was maintained over the full 12 weeks. Adverse events were mainly application-site reactions, transient and mild to moderate.
cards.watchOut: The control patch is itself a (very weak) capsaicin treatment, so the trial measures the high-dose patch against a near-placebo that preserves blinding — the true advantage over no treatment is somewhat larger than shown, but so is the burning: most recipients feel significant application pain, and the patch must be applied in clinic with pre-treatment local anaesthetic. A single application helping for 12 weeks is the claim; repeat-application data are thinner.
cards.source: Irving GA et al. A multicenter, randomized, double-blind, controlled study of NGX-4010, a high-concentration capsaicin patch, for the treatment of postherpetic neuralgia. Pain Medicine. 2011. PMID: 21087403. Registry ID: NCT00300222, from the record. 46% versus 34% achieved at least 30% relief in adults with postherpetic neuralgia, does capsaicin — the clinic-applied 8% patch or low-concentration creams — reduce pain versus control? randomised double-blind controlled trial of the 8% capsaicin patch, 418 patients with postherpetic neuralgia (irving 2011) 418 patients with postherpetic neuralgia randomised to a single 60-minute application of the capsaicin 8% patch or an identical-appearing low-concentration (0.04%) capsaicin control patch — an active control used because the real patch's burning sensation would otherwise unblind the trial — with pain followed for 12 weeks. mean pain intensity fell by 32.0% from baseline in the 8% patch group versus 24.4% in the control group during weeks 2–8 (p = 0.011); these are relative reductions from each group's own baseline, an absolute difference of about 8 percentage points of baseline pain. the proportion achieving at least a 30% pain reduction was 46% versus 34% (p = 0.02), and the benefit was maintained over the full 12 weeks. adverse events were mainly application-site reactions, transient and mild to moderate. the control patch is itself a (very weak) capsaicin treatment, so the trial measures the high-dose patch against a near-placebo that preserves blinding — the true advantage over no treatment is somewhat larger than shown, but so is the burning: most recipients feel significant application pain, and the patch must be applied in clinic with pre-treatment local anaesthetic. a single application helping for 12 weeks is the claim; cards.headline: Derry 2017 (Cochrane, high-concentration capsaicin): about 10% more patients much or very much improved than control in postherpetic neuralgia — number needed to treat 8.8
cards.summary: Derry 2017 (Cochrane, high-concentration capsaicin): about 10% more patients much or very much improved than control in postherpetic neuralgia — number needed to treat 8.8
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials of high-concentration (8%) capsaicin (Cochrane, Derry 2017)
cards.people: Eight randomised double-blind studies with 2,488 participants across chronic neuropathic pain conditions; the postherpetic neuralgia analysis pools four studies with 1,272 participants, comparing a single application of the 8% capsaicin patch against a low-concentration capsaicin control patch, with outcomes at 8 and 12 weeks. The PHN pool includes the Backonja 2008 trial, which is carded on shelf #695 and not re-carded here.
cards.result: In postherpetic neuralgia, high-concentration capsaicin produced about 10% more patients reporting themselves much or very much improved than control, at both 8 and 12 weeks; the number needed to treat for one additional patient much or very much improved at 8 weeks was 8.8 (95% CI 5.3 to 26). Local skin reactions were common with the high-concentration patch, and serious adverse events did not differ between groups in the pooled data.
cards.watchOut: The effect is real but modest — roughly one extra good responder for every nine patients treated — and it is measured against an active low-dose control, not against the oral drugs (gabapentinoids, tricyclics) that are the usual first line; no head-to-head trial against them exists. Pooling mixes PHN with other neuropathic pains for some outcomes, so this shelf uses only the PHN-specific figures.
cards.source: Derry S et al. Topical capsaicin (high concentration) for chronic neuropathic pain in adults. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2017. PMID: 28085183. cards.headline: Watson 1993: 0.075% capsaicin cream significantly improved every pain measure over six weeks versus vehicle — in 143 patients, with no responder rates published in the abstract
cards.summary: Watson 1993: 0.075% capsaicin cream significantly improved every pain measure over six weeks versus vehicle — in 143 patients, with no responder rates published in the abstract
cards.type: Randomised double-blind vehicle-controlled trial of 0.075% capsaicin cream, 143 patients with postherpetic neuralgia (Watson 1993)
cards.people: 143 patients with postherpetic neuralgia (131 evaluable; 93 had had PHN for more than 12 months and 49 for 6–12 months) applying 0.075% capsaicin cream or its vehicle to the painful area for six weeks, followed by an open-label extension in 77 patients treated for up to two years.
cards.result: At six weeks the capsaicin group showed statistically significant improvement in all efficacy variables — pain severity, pain relief, sleep, mood and global evaluation — while the vehicle group showed essentially no change. In the open-label phase, benefit was maintained or amplified in 86% of patients; burning, stinging or erythema occurred in 9% during long-term treatment, and no serious adverse events were reported.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports significance, not size: no responder percentages are given for the blinded phase, so how much better than vehicle the cream actually was cannot be stated from this record. Capsaicin cream burns on application, which threatens blinding in every cream trial — patients can usually tell which tube they have — and the two-year figures come from an uncontrolled extension in the patients who chose to continue.
cards.source: Watson CP et al. A randomized vehicle-controlled trial of topical capsaicin in the treatment of postherpetic neuralgia. Clinical Therapeutics. 1993. PMID: 8364943. cards.headline: Bernstein 1989: significantly greater relief with 0.075% cream than vehicle in 32 elderly patients — almost 80% of the capsaicin group reported some relief
cards.summary: Bernstein 1989: significantly greater relief with 0.075% cream than vehicle in 32 elderly patients — almost 80% of the capsaicin group reported some relief
cards.type: Randomised double-blind vehicle-controlled trial of 0.075% capsaicin cream, 32 patients with postherpetic neuralgia (Bernstein 1989)
cards.people: 32 elderly patients with postherpetic neuralgia applying 0.075% capsaicin cream or vehicle cream for six weeks, assessed on physician and patient ratings of pain relief and on pain severity scores.
cards.result: The capsaicin group achieved significantly greater relief than the vehicle group on all outcome variables, including physician and patient global ratings and both pain scales; almost 80% of the capsaicin-treated patients experienced some pain relief. No serious adverse effects were observed.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-two patients, six weeks, 1989 methods: 'some relief' in 80% is a soft endpoint, the abstract gives no vehicle-group percentage to compare it with, and application-site burning makes true blinding doubtful. This is the founding trial of the cream literature — historically important, evidentially thin, and exactly the kind of record the later Cochrane review weighed and found insufficient.

cards.headline: Derry 2012 (Cochrane, low-concentration capsaicin): insufficient data to conclude the creams work — a suggestion of no meaningful effect beyond placebo; skin reactions number needed to harm 2.5
cards.summary: Derry 2012 (Cochrane, low-concentration capsaicin): insufficient data to conclude the creams work — a suggestion of no meaningful effect beyond placebo; skin reactions number needed to harm 2.5
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials of low-concentration topical capsaicin (Cochrane, Derry 2012)
cards.people: Six randomised double-blind studies with 389 participants with chronic neuropathic pain (including postherpetic neuralgia), all published before 1996, comparing low-concentration capsaicin creams (0.075% or less, applied several times daily for six to eight weeks) against placebo or vehicle cream.
cards.result: Only two of the six studies reported the proportion of patients with at least 50% pain relief, and the reviewers judged the data too few and too inconsistent to pool into a reliable estimate. Their conclusion: there are insufficient data to conclude that low-concentration capsaicin has any meaningful effect beyond placebo in chronic neuropathic pain, while local skin reactions were common, with a number needed to harm of 2.5 (95% CI 2.1 to 3.1).
cards.watchOut: This review is the reason the creams carry the weaker half of this shelf's split stamp: the two positive PHN cream trials carded above are inside this pool, and the reviewers still could not extract a dependable benefit from them. 'Insufficient data' is not proof of no effect — but after three decades without a better trial, the burden of proof has not been met.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one delivery system earned its stamp and the other did not — POSSIBLE for the 8% patch, MAYBE (weak evidence) for the creams
cards.summary: Synthesis: one delivery system earned its stamp and the other did not — POSSIBLE for the 8% patch, MAYBE (weak evidence) for the creams
cards.people: Five records in postherpetic neuralgia: one randomised trial of the 8% patch (418 patients) plus the Cochrane high-concentration review (four PHN studies, 1,272 participants — a pool that includes the Backonja 2008 trial already carded on shelf #695 and not re-carded here); two small double-blind trials of 0.075% cream (143 and 32 patients) plus the Cochrane low-concentration review (six studies, 389 participants).
cards.result: 8% patch: pain down 32.0% versus 24.4% on control (relative reductions), at least 30% relief in 46% versus 34%, and a pooled number needed to treat of 8.8 for being much or very much improved. 0.075% cream: two small positive trials without published responder rates, judged by Cochrane to provide insufficient data for any conclusion, with local skin reactions at a number needed to harm of 2.5. Neither form has been compared head-to-head with standard oral neuropathic-pain drugs; the lidocaine 5% patch alternative is covered on shelf #1457.
cards.watchOut: The patch's pooled estimate leans partly on a trial this shelf deliberately does not re-card (Backonja 2008, shelf #695) — read the two shelves together for the full patch record. Cream trials predate modern reporting standards, and their burning side effect makes their blinding suspect; a clinician choosing the cream today is choosing tradition and low cost over demonstrated effect.
