shelves.title: Cluster headache: sumatriptan aborts three attacks in four within 15 minutes — verapamil prevention rests on a single 30-patient trial
shelves.question: In cluster headache, does subcutaneous sumatriptan abort attacks, and does verapamil prevent them?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adult · Cluster Headache/drug therapy,physiopathology · Double-Blind Method · Drug Tolerance · Female · Humans · Indoles/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Injections, Subcutaneous · Male · Receptors, Serotonin/drug effects · Sulfonamides/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Sumatriptan · Vasoconstrictor Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the abortive half of this shelf is solidly evidenced and the preventive half is not. In the randomised crossover trial (Sumatriptan Cluster Headache Study Group 1991, PMID: 1647496), 6 mg of subcutaneous sumatriptan relieved 74% of attacks to no or mild pain within 15 minutes versus 26% on placebo, left 46% completely pain-free at 15 minutes versus 10%, and cut the need for rescue oxygen from 49% to 13%. The dose-comparison trial (Ekbom 1993, PMID: 8396833) confirms the size of the effect in 134 patients — relief at 15 minutes in 35% on placebo, 75% on 6 mg and 80% on 12 mg — and shows the higher dose buys nothing but adverse events, so 6 mg is the dose. Prevention is a different evidential world: the only placebo-controlled trial of verapamil, the standard preventive, randomised 30 patients for 14 days and reported a significant reduction in attack frequency and abortive-medication use (Leone 2000, PMID: 10746617) — but its abstract prints no effect sizes at all, so the shelf can say verapamil beat placebo in a small short trial and nothing more precise. Galcanezumab prevention and high-flow oxygen are homed at shelf #690, and vagus nerve stimulation at #2385. PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (benefit: subcutaneous sumatriptan aborts attacks) / POSSIBLE (benefit: verapamil prevention, on one 30-patient trial) (Tier C: the verapamil claim rests on a single small trial whose abstract reports no effect sizes).

cards.headline: Sumatriptan Cluster Headache Study Group 1991: relief within 15 minutes in 74% of attacks on sumatriptan versus 26% on placebo; 46% versus 10% completely pain-free
cards.summary: Sumatriptan Cluster Headache Study Group 1991: relief within 15 minutes in 74% of attacks on sumatriptan versus 26% on placebo; 46% versus 10% completely pain-free
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial (Sumatriptan Cluster Headache Study Group 1991)
cards.people: 49 patients with cluster headache in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial; each treated one attack with subcutaneous sumatriptan 6 mg and another with placebo, in random order. Results for both attacks were fully evaluable in 39 patients. A response was defined as complete or almost complete relief (no pain or mild pain) within 15 minutes of injection.
cards.result: Headache severity decreased within 15 minutes in 74% of sumatriptan-treated attacks versus 26% of placebo-treated attacks (P < 0.001) — an absolute difference of 48 percentage points. Patients were free of pain within 10 minutes in 36% versus 3%, and by 15 minutes in 46% versus 10% (both P < 0.001). Oxygen was required as additional treatment 15 minutes after injection in 13% of sumatriptan attacks versus 49% of placebo attacks. Functional disability and ipsilateral conjunctival injection also fell more with sumatriptan. The drug was well tolerated with no serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: A crossover in 49 patients, with both attacks evaluable in only 39 — small, but the effect is so large (roughly threefold relative relief, 48 points absolute) that imprecision is not the concern. The trial predates modern reporting: no confidence intervals are printed in the abstract, and tolerability over a whole cluster period of repeated daily injections is a separate question this single-attack design cannot answer.
cards.source: The Sumatriptan Cluster Headache Study Group. Treatment of acute cluster headache with sumatriptan. The New England journal of medicine. 1991. PMID: 1647496. cards.headline: Ekbom 1993: at 15 minutes, relief in 35% on placebo, 75% on sumatriptan 6 mg and 80% on 12 mg — the higher dose added adverse events, not efficacy
cards.summary: Ekbom 1993: at 15 minutes, relief in 35% on placebo, 75% on sumatriptan 6 mg and 80% on 12 mg — the higher dose added adverse events, not efficacy
cards.people: 134 inpatients with cluster headache in a multicentre, double-blind, randomised crossover dose-comparison study of subcutaneous sumatriptan 6 mg, sumatriptan 12 mg and placebo, with headache improvement to mild or no pain recorded at 5, 10 and 15 minutes.
cards.result: At 10 minutes, headache relief was reported by 25% (placebo), 49% (6 mg) and 63% (12 mg) of patients; at 15 minutes the figures were 35%, 75% and 80% respectively (P < 0.001 for all comparisons with placebo). The 12 mg dose was not significantly better than 6 mg and was associated with more adverse events; the authors recommend 6 mg for the acute treatment of cluster headache.
cards.watchOut: An inpatient population treated under observation — real-world attacks treated at home may differ, and the record is indexed with a "Cross-Sectional Studies" MeSH term although the abstract describes a randomised crossover trial; the design as described in the abstract is what this card reports. The flat dose-response above 6 mg is the clinically useful finding.
cards.source: Ekbom K et al. Subcutaneous sumatriptan in the acute treatment of cluster headache: a dose comparison study. Acta neurologica Scandinavica. 1993. PMID: 8396833. cards.headline: Leone 2000: verapamil 360 mg/day beat placebo over 14 days in 30 patients — the only placebo-controlled trial of the standard preventive, and its abstract reports no effect sizes
cards.summary: Leone 2000: verapamil 360 mg/day beat placebo over 14 days in 30 patients — the only placebo-controlled trial of the standard preventive, and its abstract reports no effect sizes
cards.people: 30 patients with episodic cluster headache in a double-blind, double-dummy trial: after a 5-day run-in, 15 received verapamil 120 mg three times daily and 15 received placebo three times daily for 14 days.
cards.result: The authors report a significant reduction in attack frequency and in abortive-agent consumption in the verapamil group compared with placebo, with mild side effects. No numerical results — no attack counts, rates, or effect estimates — are printed in the abstract, and this card therefore states the finding only as the authors report it: a statistically significant reduction of unstated size, over 14 days, in 30 patients.
cards.watchOut: This is the entire placebo-controlled evidence base for the most widely used cluster preventive: 30 patients, 14 days, no effect sizes in the abstract. Verapamil's place in practice rests on this trial plus long clinical experience and open series — the shelf reports the trial for exactly what it is and does not inflate it. Chronic cluster headache was not studied.
cards.source: Leone M et al. Verapamil in the prophylaxis of episodic cluster headache: a double-blind study versus placebo. Neurology. 2000. PMID: 10746617. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: abortive treatment is proven, prevention is customary — SPLIT (LIKELY sumatriptan / POSSIBLE verapamil)
cards.summary: Synthesis: abortive treatment is proven, prevention is customary — SPLIT (LIKELY sumatriptan / POSSIBLE verapamil)
cards.people: Two randomised crossover trials of subcutaneous sumatriptan (49 and 134 patients) and one 30-patient, 14-day placebo-controlled trial of verapamil.
cards.result: Sumatriptan 6 mg subcutaneously: relief within 15 minutes in 74–75% of attacks versus 26–35% on placebo; pain-free at 15 minutes in 46% versus 10%; 12 mg adds nothing but adverse events. Verapamil 360 mg/day: a significant reduction in attack frequency and abortive use over 14 days in the only placebo-controlled trial, with no effect size available from the record. A patient can be told the injection will probably end the attack in minutes; the preventive prescription rests on far thinner ice.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote this shelf for oxygen (homed at #690, where high-flow oxygen beat air in its own trial) or for galcanezumab or vagus stimulation (#690, #2385). The verapamil gap is the honest headline for prevention: no larger or longer placebo-controlled trial exists in the carded record.

shelves.title: Topiramate versus botulinum toxin in chronic migraine: two small pilot trials found no difference in efficacy — and far more adverse events on topiramate
shelves.question: In chronic migraine, does topiramate prevent attacks as well as botulinum toxin (onabotulinumtoxinA)?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Botulinum Toxins, Type A/administration & dosage · Chronic Disease · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fructose/administration & dosage,analogs & derivatives · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Migraine Disorders/drug therapy,pathology,prevention & control · Pilot Projects · Prospective Studies · Topiramate · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Two small double-blind pilot trials have randomised chronic-migraine patients directly between the two standard preventives, and neither found an efficacy difference. Mathew 2009 (PMID: 19912346, n = 60) reported improvement in 68–83% of patients in both groups, a ≥50% reduction in headache/migraine days at month 9 in 40.9% on onabotulinumtoxinA and 42.9% on topiramate, and no significant between-group differences except one secondary measure at month 9. Cady 2011 (PMID: 21070228, n = 59) likewise found statistically significant improvement within both groups but not between them. What did differ was tolerability: in Mathew, 24.1% of topiramate patients discontinued for treatment-related adverse events versus 7.7% on onabotulinumtoxinA, with 87 treatment-related adverse events in 25 topiramate patients versus 41 in 18 onabotulinumtoxinA patients. Neither trial was powered as an equivalence or non-inferiority study, so the honest reading is "no difference demonstrated in two small pilots", not "proven equal". Each drug against placebo is homed elsewhere: onabotulinumtoxinA at shelf #571 (PREEMPT) and topiramate at shelf #2677. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (no difference demonstrated between the two treatments — similar efficacy in two small pilot trials; topiramate caused more adverse events and discontinuations) (not Tier C: two concordant randomised trials, though both are pilots).

cards.headline: Mathew 2009: ≥50% responders at month 9 were 40.9% on onabotulinumtoxinA and 42.9% on topiramate — but 24.1% of the topiramate group quit for adverse events versus 7.7%
cards.summary: Mathew 2009: ≥50% responders at month 9 were 40.9% on onabotulinumtoxinA and 42.9% on topiramate — but 24.1% of the topiramate group quit for adverse events versus 7.7%
cards.people: 60 patients with chronic migraine at a single centre, randomised double-blind to onabotulinumtoxinA (maximum 200 units at baseline and month 3, fixed-site plus follow-the-pain) with oral placebo, or topiramate (titrated to 100 mg/day, optionally 200 mg/day) with placebo saline injections. 36 of 60 completed 9 months of active treatment (19/30 onabotulinumtoxinA, 17/30 topiramate).
cards.result: Between 68% and 83% of patients in both groups reported at least slight improvement on the Physician Global Assessment at months 1, 3, 6 and 9, with no significant between-group differences except marked improvement at month 9 (onabotulinumtoxinA 27.3% versus topiramate 60.9%, P = .0234). At month 9, 40.9% (onabotulinumtoxinA) and 42.9% (topiramate) reported a ≥50% reduction in headache/migraine days; headache/migraine days fell and MIDAS and HIT-6 scores improved in both groups. Tolerability diverged: 41 treatment-related adverse events in 18 onabotulinumtoxinA patients versus 87 in 25 topiramate patients; discontinuation for treatment-related adverse events in 7/29 (24.1%) on topiramate versus 2/26 (7.7%) on onabotulinumtoxinA.
cards.watchOut: A pilot: 60 randomised, only 36 completed, and the month-9 responder percentages are calculated on completers with differing denominators (29 and 26 in the adverse-event counts) — attrition this large can manufacture or erase differences. The single significant between-group result (marked improvement at month 9 favouring topiramate) sits among many comparisons and should not be quoted alone.
cards.source: Mathew NT et al. A double-blind comparison of onabotulinumtoxina (BOTOX) and topiramate (TOPAMAX) for the prophylactic treatment of chronic migraine: a pilot study. Headache. 2009. PMID: 19912346. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cady 2011: both treatments improved chronic migraine over 12 weeks; the differences were within groups, not between them
cards.summary: Cady 2011: both treatments improved chronic migraine over 12 weeks; the differences were within groups, not between them
cards.people: 59 subjects with chronic migraine at multiple centres, randomised double-blind to topiramate plus placebo injections (n = 30) or onabotulinumtoxinA injections plus placebo tablets (n = 29), with daily headache diaries over a 4-week baseline and 12-week active period; non-responders could enter a 12-week open-label onabotulinumtoxinA extension (20 volunteered).
cards.result: The primary endpoint, Physician Global Assessment responder rate, indicated improvement in both groups over 12 weeks. Results were statistically significant within groups but not between groups across secondary endpoints (headache days, migraine days, headache-free days, acute-medication days, severity, MIDAS, HIT-6). By week 26 (after the open-label extension) subjects had a significant within-group reduction in headache days per month versus baseline. The authors conclude the two treatments demonstrated similar efficacy as judged by global assessment and supported by secondary measures. The abstract reports no between-group effect estimates or confidence intervals.
cards.watchOut: Also a pilot, and the abstract gives almost no numbers — no responder rates, no day counts, no adverse-event breakdown — so this card corroborates the direction of Mathew 2009 (improvement in both, no between-group difference) without adding quantitative weight. The week-26 figure mixes in an open-label extension and is within-group only.
cards.source: Cady RK et al. A multi-center double-blind pilot comparison of onabotulinumtoxinA and topiramate for the prophylactic treatment of chronic migraine. Headache. 2011. PMID: 21070228. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: no demonstrated winner on efficacy in 119 randomised patients; topiramate is the harder drug to stay on — POSSIBLE (no difference demonstrated)
cards.summary: Synthesis: no demonstrated winner on efficacy in 119 randomised patients; topiramate is the harder drug to stay on — POSSIBLE (no difference demonstrated)
cards.people: Two double-blind pilot trials, 60 and 59 patients, one single-centre over 9 months and one multicentre over 12 weeks, both using double-dummy designs (injections plus tablets in both arms).
cards.result: Efficacy: improvement in both arms in both trials; ≥50% responder rates at month 9 of 40.9% versus 42.9% (Mathew); no significant between-group efficacy differences in either trial. Tolerability: treatment-related adverse events 87 versus 41 events and adverse-event discontinuations 24.1% versus 7.7%, against topiramate (Mathew). The choice between the two preventives, on this evidence, turns on tolerability, route and patient preference — not on any demonstrated efficacy gap.
cards.watchOut: Absence of a demonstrated difference in two pilots totalling 119 patients is not proof of equivalence — a modest real advantage for either drug remains compatible with these data. For each drug versus placebo, see shelf #571 (onabotulinumtoxinA, PREEMPT) and shelf #2677 (topiramate).
cards.source: Synthesis of Mathew NT et al. Headache. 2009 (PMID: 19912346); Cady RK et al. Headache. 2011 (PMID: 21070228).

shelves.title: Malformation risk in pregnancy differs fivefold between antiseizure medicines: valproate about 1 in 10, lamotrigine and levetiracetam about 2–3 in 100 — and the risk climbs with dose
shelves.question: In women taking antiseizure medicines in pregnancy, how do malformation risks compare between drugs?
shelves.mesh: Abnormalities, Drug-Induced/epidemiology · Adult · Anticonvulsants/therapeutic use · Carbamazepine/therapeutic use · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Epilepsy/drug therapy · Female · Humans · Lamotrigine/therapeutic use · Levetiracetam/therapeutic use · Logistic Models · Male · Oxcarbazepine/therapeutic use · Phenobarbital/therapeutic use · Phenytoin/therapeutic use · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Complications/drug therapy · Topiramate/therapeutic use · Valproic Acid/therapeutic use · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Two large prospective pregnancy registries, on different continents with different methods, give the same ordering at the extremes. In EURAP (Tomson 2018, PMID: 29680205), major congenital malformations followed 10.3% of valproate-exposed pregnancies, 6.5% phenobarbital, 6.4% phenytoin, 5.5% carbamazepine, 3.9% topiramate, 3.0% oxcarbazepine, 2.9% lamotrigine and 2.8% levetiracetam — and risk rose with dose at conception for carbamazepine, lamotrigine, phenobarbital and valproate. The North American registry (Hernández-Díaz 2012, PMID: 22551726) found 9.3% for valproate, 5.5% phenobarbital, 4.2% topiramate, 3.0% carbamazepine, 2.9% phenytoin, 2.4% levetiracetam and 2.0% lamotrigine, with risk ratios versus lamotrigine of 5.1 for valproate, 2.9 for phenobarbital and 2.2 for topiramate. The registries disagree in the middle of the table (carbamazepine 5.5% versus 3.0%; phenytoin 6.4% versus 2.9%, on small exposure numbers) but agree on what matters most for drug choice: valproate is in a class of its own, and lamotrigine and levetiracetam sit at the bottom, within the range reported for unexposed pregnancies. These are observational data — women are not randomised to drugs, and dose and indication confound — but the size, the dose-response and the cross-registry agreement make the ordering secure. Neurodevelopmental outcomes after exposure (the NEAD question) are a different question and are not covered by this shelf. PROPOSED LIKELY (malformation risk differs substantially between antiseizure medicines — valproate highest at about 1 in 10, lamotrigine and levetiracetam lowest at about 2–3 in 100 — and rises with dose) (Tier C: prospective observational registries; randomisation is impossible, so this evidence type is the ceiling for the question).

cards.headline: Tomson 2018 (EURAP): malformations in 10.3% of valproate pregnancies versus 2.9% on lamotrigine and 2.8% on levetiracetam — with dose-dependence for four drugs
cards.summary: Tomson 2018 (EURAP): malformations in 10.3% of valproate pregnancies versus 2.9% on lamotrigine and 2.8% on levetiracetam — with dose-dependence for four drugs
cards.people: Prospective cohort of the EURAP international registry (42 countries, pregnancies enrolled 1999–2016): 7,555 eligible pregnancies exposed to antiseizure-drug monotherapy at conception, 7,355 exposed to one of the eight most-used drugs, with follow-up to 1 year after birth.
cards.result: Prevalence of major congenital malformations: valproate 142/1,381 (10.3%), phenobarbital 19/294 (6.5%), phenytoin 8/125 (6.4%), carbamazepine 107/1,957 (5.5%), topiramate 6/152 (3.9%), oxcarbazepine 10/333 (3.0%), lamotrigine 74/2,514 (2.9%), levetiracetam 17/599 (2.8%). Risk increased with dose at conception for carbamazepine (p = 0.0140), lamotrigine (p = 0.0145), phenobarbital (p = 0.0390) and valproate (p < 0.0001). After adjustment, all carbamazepine and valproate doses and phenobarbital above 80 mg/day carried significantly higher risk than lamotrigine at ≤325 mg/day; valproate at ≤650 mg/day still exceeded levetiracetam (OR 2.43, 95% CI 1.30–4.55). The authors note the lamotrigine, levetiracetam and oxcarbazepine rates lie within the range reported for unexposed offspring.
cards.watchOut: Observational: drug choice is confounded by indication, dose and seizure type, and the registry adjusted rather than randomised. Phenytoin (125 exposures, 8 events) and topiramate (152 exposures, 6 events) estimates are fragile — the authors themselves urge caution there. Absolute risks also depend on the malformation-ascertainment window (1 year here), which is longer than in the North American registry.
cards.source: Tomson T et al. Comparative risk of major congenital malformations with eight different antiepileptic drugs: a prospective cohort study of the EURAP registry. The Lancet. Neurology. 2018. PMID: 29680205. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hernández-Díaz 2012 (North American registry): valproate 9.3% and a risk ratio of 5.1 versus lamotrigine (2.0%); topiramate 4.2%, with cleft lip in 1.4% of exposed infants
cards.summary: Hernández-Díaz 2012 (North American registry): valproate 9.3% and a risk ratio of 5.1 versus lamotrigine (2.0%); topiramate 4.2%, with cleft lip in 1.4% of exposed infants
cards.type: Prospective pregnancy-registry cohort study (Hernández-Díaz 2012, North American AED Pregnancy Registry)
cards.people: Pregnant women enrolled in the North American AED Pregnancy Registry 1997–2011; major malformations confirmed from medical records among infants exposed to a single antiseizure drug in the first trimester, compared across drugs and against an unexposed group.
cards.result: Risk of major malformations: valproate 9.3% (30/323), phenobarbital 5.5% (11/199), topiramate 4.2% (15/359), carbamazepine 3.0% (31/1,033), phenytoin 2.9% (12/416), levetiracetam 2.4% (11/450), lamotrigine 2.0% (31/1,562). Risk ratios versus lamotrigine: valproate 5.1 (95% CI 3.0–8.5), phenobarbital 2.9 (1.4–5.8), topiramate 2.2 (1.2–4.0). Valproate was associated with neural tube defects, hypospadias, cardiac defects and oral clefts; phenobarbital with cardiac defects and oral clefts; 5 topiramate-exposed infants (1.4%) had a cleft lip. Seizures occurred during pregnancy in 23% of women on valproate and 31% on lamotrigine.
cards.watchOut: Volunteer-enrolled registry with telephone-interview exposure data — self-selection and reporting biases are possible, and several drug groups are small (phenobarbital 199, valproate 323 exposures). Its carbamazepine (3.0%) and phenytoin (2.9%) rates sit well below EURAP's (5.5% and 6.4%): the middle of the table is method-sensitive, the ends are not.
cards.source: Hernández-Díaz S et al. Comparative safety of antiepileptic drugs during pregnancy. Neurology. 2012. PMID: 22551726. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the ends of the table are secure — valproate about 1 in 10, lamotrigine and levetiracetam about 2–3 in 100, dose matters — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: the ends of the table are secure — valproate about 1 in 10, lamotrigine and levetiracetam about 2–3 in 100, dose matters — LIKELY
cards.people: Two independent prospective registries: EURAP (7,355 analysed pregnancies, 42 countries, follow-up to 1 year) and the North American AED Pregnancy Registry (enrolments 1997–2011, outcomes confirmed from medical records).
cards.result: Valproate: 10.3% (EURAP) and 9.3% (North American) — roughly one malformation per ten exposed pregnancies in both. Lamotrigine: 2.9% and 2.0%; levetiracetam: 2.8% and 2.4%. Phenobarbital is consistently next-worst (6.5% and 5.5%); topiramate sits in between (3.9% and 4.2%) with a specific cleft-lip signal (1.4% in the North American data). EURAP adds the dose gradient: risk rises with dose for valproate, carbamazepine, lamotrigine and phenobarbital, so the lowest effective dose of a lower-risk drug is the combined lesson of both registries.
cards.watchOut: Malformations only: this shelf says nothing about neurodevelopmental outcomes after prenatal exposure, where valproate also fares worst in the NEAD cohort — a separate question, not carded here. Nor does it weigh seizure control in pregnancy: uncontrolled convulsions carry their own fetal risk, and the registries record that women on lamotrigine had more seizures in pregnancy (31%) than women on valproate (23%) in the North American data.
cards.source: Synthesis of Tomson T et al. The Lancet. Neurology. 2018 (PMID: 29680205); Hernández-Díaz S et al. Neurology. 2012 (PMID: 22551726).

shelves.title: Topiramate in chronic migraine: about 1.5–3 more headache-free days a month than placebo — a real but modest gain, with paraesthesia in up to half of patients
shelves.question: In adults with chronic migraine, does topiramate reduce monthly headache days?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Anticonvulsants/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Chronic Disease · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fructose/adverse effects,analogs & derivatives,therapeutic use · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Migraine Disorders/drug therapy · Topiramate · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials of topiramate 100 mg/day in chronic migraine agree on a real, modest effect. The larger (Silberstein 2007, PMID: 17300356; 306 patients in the efficacy population) reduced migraine/migrainous days by 6.4 per month versus 4.7 on placebo (P = .010) and migraine days by 5.6 versus 4.1 (P = .032) — a placebo-subtracted gain of roughly 1.5–1.7 days a month. The smaller European trial (Diener 2007, PMID: 17441971; 59 patients, 78% with acute-medication overuse at baseline) found a larger separation: migraine days fell 3.5 ± 6.3 on topiramate versus 0.2 ± 4.7 on placebo (P < 0.05). The price is tolerability: paraesthesia in 28.8% (Silberstein) and 53% (Diener) of topiramate patients, with adverse-event discontinuation of 10.9% versus 6.1% in the larger trial, and only about 55% of patients completing either arm there. Head-to-head against onabotulinumtoxinA is shelf #2675; onabotulinumtoxinA against placebo (PREEMPT) is shelf #571. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) (not Tier C: two concordant randomised trials, one of 306 patients).

cards.headline: Silberstein 2007: migraine/migrainous days fell 6.4 a month on topiramate versus 4.7 on placebo (P = .010); paraesthesia 28.8%; only ~55% completed
cards.summary: Silberstein 2007: migraine/migrainous days fell 6.4 a month on topiramate versus 4.7 on placebo (P = .010); paraesthesia 28.8%; only ~55% completed
cards.people: Randomised, placebo-controlled, parallel-group multicentre trial: 328 randomised, 306 in the intent-to-treat efficacy population (153 per arm), adults 18–65 with ≥15 headache days a month, at least half migrainous. Topiramate was titrated from 25 mg/day to 100 mg/day (mean final maintenance dose 86 mg/day) over 16 weeks of double-blind treatment; other preventives were not allowed.
cards.result: Topiramate reduced the mean monthly number of migraine/migrainous days by 6.4 versus 4.7 on placebo (P = .010) and migraine days by 5.6 versus 4.1 (P = .032) — absolute advantages of about 1.7 and 1.5 days a month. Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 82.5% on topiramate and 70.2% on placebo; the commonest on topiramate were paraesthesia (28.8%), upper respiratory infection (13.8%) and fatigue (11.9%). Discontinuation for adverse events: 10.9% versus 6.1%. Completion was 55.8% (topiramate) and 55.2% (placebo). There were no serious adverse events or deaths.
cards.watchOut: Nearly half of both arms failed to complete 16 weeks — the day-count gains are estimated under substantial attrition, and the placebo response itself (−4.7 days) is large, as chronic-migraine trials consistently show. The placebo-subtracted benefit (~1.5 days/month) is the number to quote, not the raw −6.4.
cards.source: Silberstein SD et al. Efficacy and safety of topiramate for the treatment of chronic migraine: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Headache. 2007. PMID: 17300356. cards.headline: Diener 2007: migraine days fell 3.5 on topiramate versus 0.2 on placebo — in a 59-patient trial where 78% had medication overuse and 53% got paraesthesia
cards.summary: Diener 2007: migraine days fell 3.5 on topiramate versus 0.2 on placebo — in a 59-patient trial where 78% had medication overuse and 53% got paraesthesia
cards.people: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in patients with chronic migraine (≥15 migraine days a month for ≥3 months; ≥12 migraine days in the 4-week baseline): 32 patients in the intent-to-treat population received topiramate (titrated to a target 100 mg/day, flexible 50–200 mg/day; mean modal dose 100 ± 17 mg/day) and 27 received placebo, for 16 weeks. Existing preventives other than antiepileptic drugs were continued; 78% met criteria for acute medication overuse at baseline.
cards.result: Mean monthly migraine days fell by 3.5 ± 6.3 on topiramate versus 0.2 ± 4.7 on placebo (P < 0.05). MIDAS disability scores improved significantly versus placebo (P = 0.042); MSQ and HIT-6 did not differ significantly. Treatment-emergent adverse events: 75% versus 37%; paraesthesia in 53% of topiramate patients versus 7% on placebo, with nausea, dizziness, dyspepsia, fatigue, anorexia and attention disturbance each in 6% versus 0–4%. Completion: 75% versus 52%.
cards.watchOut: Small (59 patients) with wide standard deviations (±6.3 days) — the point estimate of the separation is larger than in Silberstein 2007 but far less precise, and the population (mostly medication-overuse, other preventives continued) differs from the larger trial. The two trials agree on direction and on the paraesthesia burden, not on exact size.
cards.source: Diener HC et al. Topiramate reduces headache days in chronic migraine: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study. Cephalalgia. 2007. PMID: 17441971. cards.headline: Synthesis: a consistent, modest reduction in migraine days over placebo — LIKELY (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: a consistent, modest reduction in migraine days over placebo — LIKELY (benefit)
cards.people: Two randomised placebo-controlled trials of topiramate ~100 mg/day for 16 weeks in chronic migraine: 306 patients in the efficacy population of the larger trial, 59 in the smaller.
cards.result: Migraine or migrainous days: −6.4 versus −4.7 a month (Silberstein, P = .010); migraine days −3.5 versus −0.2 (Diener, P < 0.05). Placebo-subtracted gain: roughly 1.5–3.3 days a month across the two trials. Paraesthesia affected 29–53% of topiramate patients and adverse-event discontinuation ran about 11% versus 6% where reported. Topiramate works for chronic migraine — modestly, and at a tolerability price a substantial minority will not pay.
cards.watchOut: These are 16-week trials in patients with ≥15 headache days a month; they do not address episodic migraine (a separate, larger literature), longer-term persistence, or comparison with onabotulinumtoxinA — that head-to-head question is shelf #2675, and onabotulinumtoxinA versus placebo is shelf #571.
cards.source: Synthesis of Silberstein SD et al. Headache. 2007 (PMID: 17300356); Diener HC et al. Cephalalgia. 2007 (PMID: 17441971).

shelves.title: Childhood absence epilepsy: ethosuximide matches valproate on seizures and beats it on attention; lamotrigine is clearly the weakest of the three
shelves.question: In childhood absence epilepsy, which first drug — ethosuximide, valproate or lamotrigine — controls seizures with least attentional harm?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Analysis of Variance · Anticonvulsants/blood,therapeutic use · Attention Deficit and Disruptive Behavior Disorders/chemically induced · Child · Child, Preschool · Double-Blind Method · Epilepsy, Absence/drug therapy · Ethosuximide/adverse effects,blood,therapeutic use · Female · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Lamotrigine · Male · Seizures/chemically induced · Treatment Outcome · Triazines/adverse effects,blood,therapeutic use · Valproic Acid/adverse effects,blood,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: One large double-blind randomised trial has compared the three standard first drugs head-to-head in 453 children with newly diagnosed childhood absence epilepsy, and its two reports (16 weeks and 12 months, both carded here and flagged as the same trial) give a clean answer. Freedom from treatment failure at 16 weeks was 53% on ethosuximide and 58% on valproic acid — statistically indistinguishable (OR 1.26, 95% CI 0.80–1.98) — and both were far above lamotrigine at 29% (Glauser 2010, PMID: 20200383). At 12 months the pattern held: 45%, 44% and 21% (Glauser 2013, PMID: 23167925). The tiebreaker is attention: attentional dysfunction affected 49% of children on valproic acid versus 33% on ethosuximide at 16 weeks (OR 1.95, 95% CI 1.12–3.41), and the difference persisted at 12 months, when valproate also produced the largest share of adverse-event discontinuations. Ethosuximide is therefore the trial's own conclusion as optimal initial monotherapy: equal seizure control to valproate, less cognitive cost, and lamotrigine relegated by a two-to-threefold efficacy gap. PROPOSED LIKELY (ethosuximide is the optimal first drug) (Tier C: a single trial programme — both cards are reports of the one randomised trial, NCT00088452).

cards.headline: Glauser 2010: freedom from treatment failure at 16 weeks — ethosuximide 53%, valproate 58%, lamotrigine 29%; attentional dysfunction 49% on valproate versus 33% on ethosuximide
cards.summary: Glauser 2010: freedom from treatment failure at 16 weeks — ethosuximide 53%, valproate 58%, lamotrigine 29%; attentional dysfunction 49% on valproate versus 33% on ethosuximide
cards.people: 453 children with newly diagnosed childhood absence epilepsy in a double-blind, randomised, controlled trial (ethosuximide 156, lamotrigine 149, valproic acid 148). Doses were increased until the child was seizure-free, the maximal allowable or highest tolerable dose was reached, or a treatment-failure criterion was met. Primary outcome: freedom from treatment failure at 16 weeks; secondary outcome: attentional dysfunction.
cards.result: Freedom-from-failure rates for ethosuximide (53%) and valproic acid (58%) were similar (OR with valproic acid vs ethosuximide 1.26, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.98; P = 0.35) and both were higher than lamotrigine (29%; OR ethosuximide vs lamotrigine 2.66, 95% CI 1.65 to 4.28; OR valproic acid vs lamotrigine 3.34, 95% CI 2.06 to 5.42; P < 0.001 for both). Discontinuation because of adverse events did not differ significantly among the three drugs. Attentional dysfunction was more common with valproic acid than ethosuximide (49% vs 33%; OR 1.95, 95% CI 1.12 to 3.41; P = 0.03).
cards.watchOut: "Freedom from treatment failure" is a composite of seizure control, tolerability and global outcome — the right pragmatic endpoint for first-drug choice, but it means the seizure-freedom component alone is not separately quantified in the abstract. The attentional finding is a secondary outcome; it is nonetheless prespecified, large (16 percentage points), and it persisted at 12 months.
cards.source: Glauser TA et al. Ethosuximide, valproic acid, and lamotrigine in childhood absence epilepsy. The New England journal of medicine. 2010. PMID: 20200383. cards.headline: Glauser 2013 (12-month report of the same trial): ethosuximide 45%, valproate 44%, lamotrigine 21% still free from failure; valproate's attentional disadvantage persisted
cards.summary: Glauser 2013 (12-month report of the same trial): ethosuximide 45%, valproate 44%, lamotrigine 21% still free from failure; valproate's attentional disadvantage persisted
cards.type: 12-month follow-up report of the same randomised trial (Glauser 2013; same trial as Glauser 2010)
cards.people: The 12-month report of the same double-blind randomised trial (NCT00088452): 453 children enrolled and randomised, 446 in the efficacy cohort after 7 were deemed ineligible. Main outcome: freedom from failure 12 months after randomisation, including a video-EEG assessment; cognitive outcome: attentional dysfunction at the month-12 visit. THIS CARD IS A LATER REPORT OF THE SAME TRIAL AS THE GLAUSER 2010 CARD ABOVE, not an independent study.
cards.result: By 12 months only 37% of all enrolled children remained free from treatment failure on their first drug. Freedom-from-failure rates: ethosuximide 45%, valproic acid 44% (OR 0.94, 95% CI 0.58–1.52; P = 0.82), lamotrigine 21% (OR ethosuximide vs lamotrigine 3.08, 95% CI 1.81–5.33; valproic acid vs lamotrigine 2.88, 95% CI 1.68–5.02; P < 0.001 for both). Almost two-thirds of the 125 failures for lack of seizure control were in the lamotrigine group; the largest subgroup (42%) of the 115 adverse-event discontinuations was in the valproic acid group. The higher attentional-dysfunction rate on valproic acid persisted at 12 months (P < 0.01). The authors conclude ethosuximide is the optimal initial empirical monotherapy, and note this is the first randomised trial meeting ILAE class I evidence criteria for childhood absence epilepsy.
cards.watchOut: Same children, same randomisation — this report extends the horizon; it does not replicate the finding. The sobering number is the overall one: by 12 months, 63% of children had failed their first drug for seizures or adverse events, whichever of the three they started on.
cards.source: Glauser TA et al. Ethosuximide, valproic acid, and lamotrigine in childhood absence epilepsy: initial monotherapy outcomes at 12 months. Epilepsia. 2013. PMID: 23167925. Registry ID: NCT00088452 (ClinicalTrials.gov) — the same trial as the Glauser 2010 card. cards.headline: Synthesis: ethosuximide first — equal seizure control to valproate at 16 weeks and 12 months, less attentional harm, and lamotrigine a distant third — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: ethosuximide first — equal seizure control to valproate at 16 weeks and 12 months, less attentional harm, and lamotrigine a distant third — LIKELY
cards.people: One double-blind randomised trial of 453 children with newly diagnosed childhood absence epilepsy, reported at 16 weeks (2010) and 12 months (2013) — the only head-to-head randomised comparison of the three standard first drugs.
cards.result: Freedom from treatment failure: ethosuximide 53% → 45%, valproate 58% → 44%, lamotrigine 29% → 21% (16 weeks → 12 months). Ethosuximide versus valproate: no significant difference at either horizon (OR 1.26 and 0.94). Either versus lamotrigine: odds ratios of 2.7–3.3 in ethosuximide/valproate's favour. Attentional dysfunction: 49% on valproate versus 33% on ethosuximide at 16 weeks, persisting at 12 months, alongside the largest share of adverse-event discontinuations on valproate. On efficacy the first two drugs tie; on the brain of a school-age child they do not.
cards.watchOut: A single trial programme carries this shelf — there is no second randomised comparison to confirm it, and the trial's own class I designation is the authors' claim as reported. The comparison also predates wider use of newer agents in absence epilepsy; nothing here speaks to drugs outside the three randomised.
cards.source: Synthesis of Glauser TA et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2010 (PMID: 20200383); Glauser TA et al. Epilepsia. 2013 (PMID: 23167925) — two reports of one trial, NCT00088452.

shelves.title: Ocrelizumab in primary progressive MS: the first drug to beat placebo — confirmed progression in 32.9% versus 39.3% over at least two years
shelves.question: In adults with primary progressive multiple sclerosis, does ocrelizumab slow disability progression?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Antigens, CD20 · B-Lymphocytes/immunology · Brain/diagnostic imaging · Disease Progression · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous/adverse effects · Intention to Treat Analysis · Lymphocyte Count · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Male · Middle Aged · Multiple Sclerosis, Chronic Progressive/drug therapy,immunology · T-Lymphocytes · Young Adult
shelves.balance: ORATORIO (Montalban 2017, PMID: 28002688) is the single randomised trial behind ocrelizumab in primary progressive multiple sclerosis: 732 patients randomised 2:1 to intravenous ocrelizumab 600 mg or placebo every 24 weeks for at least 120 weeks. Confirmed disability progression at 12 weeks occurred in 32.9% on ocrelizumab versus 39.3% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.76, 95% CI 0.59–0.98; P = 0.03) — a relative reduction of about a quarter, and an absolute difference of 6.4 percentage points. The 24-week confirmed progression result was nearly identical (29.6% versus 35.7%; HR 0.75), timed 25-foot walk worsened less (38.9% versus 55.1% by week 120), T2 lesion volume fell on ocrelizumab and rose on placebo (−3.4% versus +7.4%), and brain-volume loss was slightly smaller (0.90% versus 1.09%). Against that: neoplasms occurred in 2.3% of ocrelizumab patients versus 0.8% on placebo, and infusion reactions, upper respiratory infections and oral herpes were commoner, with no significant difference in serious adverse events or serious infections. The effect is real but modest, it comes from one trial, and the neoplasm imbalance needs the long-term observation the authors themselves call for. Ocrelizumab in relapsing MS is a different question, homed at shelf #570. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) (Tier C: a single randomised trial, with a modest absolute effect and an unresolved neoplasm signal).

cards.headline: Montalban 2017 (ORATORIO): 12-week confirmed disability progression in 32.9% on ocrelizumab versus 39.3% on placebo (HR 0.76); neoplasms 2.3% versus 0.8%
cards.summary: Montalban 2017 (ORATORIO): 12-week confirmed disability progression in 32.9% on ocrelizumab versus 39.3% on placebo (HR 0.76); neoplasms 2.3% versus 0.8%
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (Montalban 2017, ORATORIO)
cards.people: 732 patients with primary progressive multiple sclerosis in a phase 3, double-blind trial, randomised 2:1 to intravenous ocrelizumab 600 mg or placebo every 24 weeks for at least 120 weeks and until a prespecified number of confirmed disability progression events had occurred. Primary endpoint: the percentage of patients with disability progression confirmed at 12 weeks, in a time-to-event analysis.
cards.result: 12-week confirmed disability progression: 32.9% with ocrelizumab versus 39.3% with placebo (hazard ratio 0.76, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.98; P = 0.03) — an absolute difference of 6.4 percentage points. 24-week confirmed progression: 29.6% versus 35.7% (HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.58 to 0.98; P = 0.04). By week 120, timed 25-foot walk performance had worsened by 38.9% versus 55.1% (P = 0.04); total T2-weighted MRI lesion volume changed by −3.4% versus +7.4% (P < 0.001); brain-volume loss was 0.90% versus 1.09% (P = 0.02). There was no significant difference in the Physical Component Summary score of the SF-36. Infusion-related reactions, upper respiratory tract infections and oral herpes infections were more frequent with ocrelizumab. Neoplasms occurred in 2.3% of ocrelizumab patients and 0.8% of placebo patients; rates of serious adverse events and serious infections did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: One trial, and the confidence interval for the primary endpoint reaches 0.98 — the result is statistically secure but not roomy, and a 6.4-percentage-point absolute reduction over two-plus years means most treated patients progress anyway. The neoplasm imbalance (2.3% versus 0.8%) is based on small numbers and is neither confirmed nor dismissed by this trial; the authors state that extended observation is required for long-term safety.
cards.source: Montalban X et al. Ocrelizumab versus Placebo in Primary Progressive Multiple Sclerosis. The New England journal of medicine. 2017. PMID: 28002688. Registry ID: NCT01194570 (ClinicalTrials.gov). cards.headline: Synthesis: a genuine first — a quarter relative slowing of confirmed progression, modest in absolute terms, from a single trial — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: a genuine first — a quarter relative slowing of confirmed progression, modest in absolute terms, from a single trial — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.people: One phase 3 randomised trial, 732 patients with primary progressive MS, treated for at least 120 weeks — the entire placebo-controlled evidence base for ocrelizumab in this disease form.
cards.result: Confirmed disability progression at 12 weeks: 32.9% versus 39.3% (HR 0.76, 0.59–0.98); at 24 weeks: 29.6% versus 35.7% (HR 0.75). Walking speed, MRI lesion volume and brain-volume loss all moved in the same direction. Harms: more infusion reactions and minor infections; neoplasms 2.3% versus 0.8%, unresolved. In a disease that previously had no proven therapy, a relative slowing of about a quarter is a real advance — and, in absolute terms, a small one for the individual patient deciding today.
cards.watchOut: Do not transfer this result to relapsing MS (shelf #570, where ocrelizumab was compared with interferon beta-1a, not placebo) or to other B-cell therapies, which have their own trial records. The shelf cannot answer how long benefit persists beyond the trial's event-driven follow-up, or whether the neoplasm signal grows with exposure.
cards.source: Synthesis of Montalban X et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2017 (PMID: 28002688).

shelves.title: Nabiximols for MS spasticity: two positive but borderline trials — the clearest signal is that about 40% of patients get a worthwhile response
shelves.question: In multiple sclerosis spasticity, does nabiximols (THC:CBD oromucosal spray) reduce spasticity versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Cannabidiol/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Cannabinoids/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Central Nervous System/drug effects,physiopathology · Double-Blind Method · Dronabinol/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Multiple Sclerosis/complications,drug therapy,physiopathology · Muscle Spasticity/drug therapy,etiology,physiopathology · Placebos · Plant Extracts/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials of the THC:CBD oromucosal spray nabiximols (Sativex) as add-on treatment for multiple sclerosis spasticity both reached statistical significance on their primary endpoints — narrowly. Collin 2007 (PMID: 17355549) randomised 189 patients for 6 weeks: the spasticity numerical rating scale improved significantly more on active treatment (P = 0.048, intention-to-treat), the objective Ashworth score did not reach significance, and 40% of treated patients achieved a >30% improvement (P = 0.014). Novotna 2011 (PMID: 21362108) used an enriched design: of 572 patients given single-blind nabiximols for 4 weeks, the 272 who improved by ≥20% were the pool from which 241 were randomised to continue nabiximols or switch to placebo for 12 weeks; the spasticity score difference favoured nabiximols (P = 0.0002) — but the abstract prints no effect size, and by design the randomised phase can only speak about patients who already responded and tolerated the drug. Neither abstract names a manufacturer; Novotna's record names the tested product as nabiximols (Sativex®). The fair summary is a real symptomatic benefit concentrated in a responder minority, demonstrated with borderline statistics in unenriched patients. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) (not Tier C: two concordant randomised trials, though one is enriched and neither abstract reports a mean effect size).

cards.headline: Collin 2007: spasticity score improved significantly more on cannabis-based medicine (P = 0.048); 40% of treated patients achieved >30% benefit; the Ashworth score did not reach significance
cards.summary: Collin 2007: spasticity score improved significantly more on cannabis-based medicine (P = 0.048); 40% of treated patients achieved >30% benefit; the Ashworth score did not reach significance
cards.people: 189 subjects with definite multiple sclerosis and spasticity, randomised double-blind to a standardised oromucosal whole-plant cannabis-based medicine containing delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) and cannabidiol (CBD) (n = 124) or placebo (n = 65) for 6 weeks. Primary endpoint: change in a daily subject-recorded Numerical Rating Scale of spasticity; secondary endpoints included the Ashworth score and a subjective spasm measure. Primary analysis population: 184 (intention-to-treat).
cards.result: The active preparation was significantly superior on the primary endpoint (P = 0.048). All secondary efficacy measures favoured active treatment but did not achieve statistical significance, including the clinician-rated Ashworth score. In the responder analysis, 40% of subjects on active treatment achieved >30% benefit (P = 0.014). Eight withdrawals were attributed to adverse events — six on active preparation and two on placebo. The abstract reports P values rather than the mean between-group difference in spasticity scores, so the size of the average effect cannot be stated from this record.
cards.watchOut: P = 0.048 is a borderline primary result, and the dissociation matters: patients felt less spastic while the objective Ashworth measure did not significantly move — a pattern compatible with a genuine symptomatic effect, with partial unblinding from psychoactive effects, or both. The 2:1 randomisation and the small placebo arm (65) limit precision.
cards.source: Collin C et al. Randomized controlled trial of cannabis-based medicine in spasticity caused by multiple sclerosis. European journal of neurology. 2007. PMID: 17355549. Registry ID: none in the record. The record describes the tested product as a standardised oromucosal whole-plant cannabis-based medicine (THC:CBD); it does not name a brand or manufacturer. cards.headline: Novotna 2011: in an enriched design, patients who had already responded to nabiximols kept their benefit on the drug and lost it on placebo (P = 0.0002) — a result that applies only to initial responders
cards.summary: Novotna 2011: in an enriched design, patients who had already responded to nabiximols kept their benefit on the drug and lost it on placebo (P = 0.0002) — a result that applies only to initial responders
cards.people: 572 subjects with multiple sclerosis spasticity not fully relieved by current antispasticity therapy received nabiximols (Sativex®) as add-on therapy, single-blind, for 4 weeks. The 272 who achieved ≥20% improvement in spasticity entered the randomised phase; 241 were randomised double-blind to nabiximols or placebo for 12 weeks. Primary endpoint: the between-treatment difference in mean spasticity Numeric Rating Scale during the randomised phase.
cards.result: The intention-to-treat analysis showed a highly significant difference in favour of nabiximols on the primary endpoint (P = 0.0002). Responder analysis, spasm frequency score, sleep disturbance scores and patient, carer and clinician global impressions of change were all significant in favour of nabiximols. The abstract reports no mean difference or confidence interval for the primary endpoint, so the size of the maintained benefit cannot be quantified from this record — only its statistical security within the enriched population.
cards.watchOut: The enriched design is the point and the limitation: fewer than half of starters (272/572) improved ≥20% in the run-in, and the randomised result describes only that responder subset — it cannot estimate the average effect in an unselected clinic population, and withdrawal of an effective-feeling drug can exaggerate the contrast with placebo. Read together with Collin 2007, not instead of it.
cards.source: Novotna A et al. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group, enriched-design study of nabiximols (Sativex), as add-on therapy, in subjects with refractory spasticity caused by multiple sclerosis. cards.summary: Synthesis: a symptomatic benefit real enough to detect twice, concentrated in responders — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.people: Two double-blind placebo-controlled trials of nabiximols in MS spasticity: one conventional parallel-group trial (189 patients, 6 weeks) and one enriched withdrawal-style trial (572 starters, 241 randomised responders, 12 weeks).
cards.result: Collin 2007: primary spasticity score P = 0.048 in favour of active treatment; >30% responders 40% on active treatment; Ashworth score not significant. Novotna 2011: maintained benefit in initial responders, P = 0.0002, with all secondary endpoints concordant. Neither abstract reports a mean effect size. The defensible claim is narrow: nabiximols relieves perceived spasticity for a substantial minority of patients — about 4 in 10 achieving >30% improvement in the unenriched trial — while average effects across all-comers are small and imprecisely reported.
cards.watchOut: This shelf is about nabiximols the defined THC:CBD product, not cannabis in general, and about spasticity symptoms — not disease modification, walking, or falls. Nabiximols for cannabis dependence is a different question (shelf #1981). Neither carded abstract quantifies dizziness, somnolence or other adverse-event rates, so the shelf makes no comparative tolerability claim.

shelves.title: Phenylbutyrate–taurursodiol in ALS: one small phase 2 trial showed slower decline and longer survival — the phase 3 trial did not confirm it, and the product was withdrawn
shelves.question: In adults with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, does sodium phenylbutyrate–taurursodiol slow functional decline or prolong survival?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis/drug therapy · Disease Progression · Double-Blind Method · Drug Combinations · Female · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Male · Middle Aged · Phenylbutyrates/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Severity of Illness Index · Taurochenodeoxycholic Acid/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: The randomised evidence for the fixed-dose coformulation of sodium phenylbutyrate and taurursodiol (developed by Amylyx Pharmaceuticals, named as the trial funder in the record) is a single phase 2 trial, CENTAUR (Paganoni 2020, PMID: 32877582): 137 patients with definite ALS within 18 months of symptom onset, randomised 2:1, declined on the ALSFRS-R at −1.24 points per month on the drug versus −1.66 on placebo over 24 weeks (difference 0.42 points per month, 95% CI 0.03–0.81; P = 0.03), with no significant differences in any secondary outcome and mainly gastrointestinal adverse events. A long-term analysis of the same trial (Paganoni 2021, PMID: 33063909 — a second report of CENTAUR, flagged as such on its card) found median survival of 25.0 months in those originally randomised to the drug versus 18.5 months on placebo (HR 0.56, 95% CI 0.34–0.92), in a design where most placebo patients crossed to the drug in the open-label extension. Regulatory context, not from a carded record: the sponsor subsequently ran the larger phase 3 PHOENIX trial, announced in 2024 that it had not met its endpoints, and withdrew the product from the market; no peer-reviewed PHOENIX results paper was found in PubMed when this shelf was built, so no PHOENIX figures are printed here. The shelf therefore preserves what the phase 2 record actually showed, and its non-confirmation, side by side. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit in one small phase 2 trial — not confirmed by the phase 3 trial, after which the product was withdrawn) (Tier C: a single small phase 2 programme; the survival analysis is an open-label-extension follow-up of the same patients).

cards.headline: Paganoni 2020 (CENTAUR): ALSFRS-R declined 0.42 points per month more slowly on phenylbutyrate–taurursodiol than placebo (P = 0.03); every secondary outcome was non-significant
cards.summary: Paganoni 2020 (CENTAUR): ALSFRS-R declined 0.42 points per month more slowly on phenylbutyrate–taurursodiol than placebo (P = 0.03); every secondary outcome was non-significant
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial (Paganoni 2020, CENTAUR)
cards.people: 137 participants with definite ALS and symptom onset within the previous 18 months, randomised 2:1 in a multicentre, double-blind trial to sodium phenylbutyrate–taurursodiol (3 g sodium phenylbutyrate + 1 g taurursodiol, once daily for 3 weeks then twice daily; n = 89) or placebo (n = 48) for 24 weeks. Primary outcome: rate of decline in ALSFRS-R total score (0–48, higher is better). The record names Amylyx Pharmaceuticals as funder; it does not print a brand name for the coformulation.
cards.result: In the modified intention-to-treat analysis, the mean rate of change in ALSFRS-R was −1.24 points per month on the active drug versus −1.66 on placebo (difference 0.42 points per month, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.81; P = 0.03) — about a 25% relative slowing of decline over 24 weeks. Secondary outcomes — rates of decline in isometric muscle strength, plasma phosphorylated neurofilament H levels and slow vital capacity, and time to death, tracheostomy, permanent ventilation or hospitalisation — did not differ significantly between groups. Adverse events with the active drug were mainly gastrointestinal. The authors state that longer and larger trials are necessary.
cards.watchOut: A phase 2 trial of 137 patients with a confidence interval whose lower bound (0.03) nearly touches zero, and a clean sweep of non-significant secondary outcomes — the profile of a promising signal, not an established treatment. The 2:1 randomisation leaves only 48 placebo patients, so every comparison is fragile to a few outcomes.

cards.headline: Paganoni 2021 (long-term survival analysis of the same CENTAUR trial): median survival 25.0 versus 18.5 months (HR 0.56) for original randomisation to the drug — with most placebo patients later crossing over
cards.summary: Paganoni 2021 (long-term survival analysis of the same CENTAUR trial): median survival 25.0 versus 18.5 months (HR 0.56) for original randomisation to the drug — with most placebo patients later crossing over
cards.type: Long-term survival analysis of the CENTAUR trial with open-label extension (Paganoni 2021; same trial as Paganoni 2020)
cards.people: All 137 participants originally randomised in CENTAUR, followed for all-cause mortality for up to 35 months after randomisation; participants completing the 24-week randomised phase could receive the drug in an open-label extension, and vital status was obtained for 135 of 137. THIS CARD IS A LATER ANALYSIS OF THE SAME TRIAL AS THE PAGANONI 2020 CARD ABOVE, not an independent study.
cards.result: Median overall survival was 25.0 months among participants originally randomised to sodium phenylbutyrate–taurursodiol versus 18.5 months among those originally randomised to placebo (hazard ratio 0.56, 95% CI 0.34–0.92; P = .023) — a 6.5-month longer median survival associated with starting the drug at baseline rather than later or never. Because most placebo-group participants received the drug in the open-label extension, the comparison is early-start versus delayed-start/no-start combined, not drug versus no drug throughout.
cards.watchOut: Survival was not the randomised phase's primary outcome, follow-up treatment was unblinded and self-selected (patients well enough to enter the extension differ from those who were not), and the analysis inherits all the fragility of the 137-patient parent trial. A hazard ratio of 0.56 from such a design is hypothesis-strengthening, not confirmatory — and the phase 3 trial that followed did not confirm the benefit (see synthesis).

cards.summary: Synthesis: a genuine phase 2 signal that phase 3 did not confirm — POSSIBLE (benefit in one small phase 2 trial; product withdrawn after non-confirmation)
cards.people: One phase 2 randomised trial (137 patients, 24 weeks) and its long-term survival follow-up, constituting the whole carded record; the subsequent phase 3 PHOENIX trial exists as sponsor announcement and regulatory action, not as a peer-reviewed results paper found in PubMed at build.
cards.result: Functional decline: 0.42 ALSFRS-R points per month slower on the drug (95% CI 0.03–0.81), with all secondary outcomes non-significant. Survival on extended follow-up: median 25.0 versus 18.5 months (HR 0.56, 0.34–0.92), in a crossover-contaminated comparison. Then the decisive fact: the larger confirmatory trial did not confirm benefit and the product was withdrawn from the market. This shelf's stamp grades the carded phase 2 record as it stands — POSSIBLE benefit, unreplicated — and the withdrawal is stated so the shelf is never quoted as a live treatment recommendation.
cards.watchOut: Do not cite the CENTAUR survival hazard ratio without its design: 137 patients, open-label extension, delayed-start contamination. And do not cite this shelf as evidence about any currently marketed ALS therapy — the product it describes is no longer sold. Riluzole, the long-standing ALS drug, is homed at shelf #1440.

shelves.title: Non-invasive ventilation in ALS: in patients without severe bulbar dysfunction it prolongs survival by months with quality of life maintained — the largest survival effect of any ALS intervention trialled
shelves.question: In amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, does non-invasive ventilation prolong survival and improve quality of life?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis/therapy · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Positive-Pressure Respiration · Quality of Life · Respiratory Insufficiency/etiology,therapy · Sleep Apnea Syndromes/etiology,therapy · Survival · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer turns on bulbar function. The single randomised trial (Bourke 2006, PMID: 16426990) enrolled 92 patients and randomised 41 of them when they developed orthopnoea with weak inspiratory muscles or symptomatic hypercapnia: non-invasive ventilation (NIV) versus standard care. In the subgroup with better bulbar function (n = 20), NIV conferred a median survival benefit of 205 days (P = 0.006) with quality of life maintained or improved for most of that period; in patients with poor bulbar function, NIV improved some sleep-related quality-of-life measures (P = 0.018) but conferred no survival benefit. The Cochrane synthesis (Radunovic 2017, PMID: 28982219) — carded here as the field's synthesis, with the explicit caveat that its conclusions rest on this same single 41-patient trial — quantifies the overall effect as median survival 219 versus 171 days (+48 days, 95% CI 12–91; P = 0.0062), and +205 days in the better-bulbar subgroup (216 versus 11 days). The review notes further placebo-controlled trials are no longer ethically feasible, so this one small trial is likely to remain the evidence ceiling. PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (benefit in patients without severe bulbar dysfunction) / POSSIBLE (sleep-symptom relief only in severe bulbar dysfunction) (Tier C: the entire randomised base is one 41-patient trial).

cards.headline: Bourke 2006: NIV gave a median survival benefit of 205 days in ALS patients with better bulbar function (P = 0.006), with quality of life maintained — and no survival benefit in poor bulbar function
cards.summary: Bourke 2006: NIV gave a median survival benefit of 205 days in ALS patients with better bulbar function (P = 0.006), with quality of life maintained — and no survival benefit in poor bulbar function
cards.people: 92 of 102 eligible patients with ALS participated and were assessed every 2 months; 41 were randomised — to non-invasive ventilation (n = 22) or standard care (n = 19) — when they developed orthopnoea with maximum inspiratory pressure below 60% predicted, or symptomatic hypercapnia. Primary outcomes were quality-of-life measures (SF-36 mental component summary and the sleep apnoea quality-of-life index symptoms domain), as time maintained above 75% of baseline and as mean improvement; survival was also assessed.
cards.result: NIV improved both quality-of-life measures and survival in all patients and in the subgroup with better bulbar function (n = 20), which showed improvement in several quality-of-life measures and a median survival benefit of 205 days (P = 0.006), with quality of life maintained for most of this period. In patients with poor bulbar function, NIV improved some quality-of-life indices including the sleep symptoms domain (P = 0.018) but conferred no survival benefit. The authors conclude that in ALS without severe bulbar dysfunction, the survival benefit from NIV is much greater than that from currently available neuroprotective therapy, while in severe bulbar impairment NIV improves sleep-related symptoms but is unlikely to confer a large survival advantage.
cards.watchOut: Only 41 of 92 enrolled patients reached a randomisation trigger, and the pivotal better-bulbar subgroup is 20 patients — the 205-day figure, though statistically secure within the trial (P = 0.006), rests on very small numbers and an unblinded intervention (NIV cannot be blinded), so the quality-of-life outcomes are vulnerable to expectation effects in a way the survival outcome is not. Randomisation at a clinical trigger also means the result applies to patients at that stage, not to starting NIV at diagnosis.

Neurology. 2006. PMID: 16426990. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Radunovic 2017 (Cochrane): moderate-quality evidence from this same single trial — median survival 219 versus 171 days overall; the review is a synthesis of Bourke 2006, not independent confirmation
cards.summary: Radunovic 2017 (Cochrane): moderate-quality evidence from this same single trial — median survival 219 versus 171 days overall; the review is a synthesis of Bourke 2006, not independent confirmation
cards.type: Systematic review (Radunovic 2017, Cochrane) — conclusions rest on the single Bourke 2006 trial
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review (second update) of randomised and quasi-randomised trials of non-invasive or tracheostomy-assisted ventilation in ALS. Two NIV trials involving 54 participants were identified; one (13 participants, early versus late NIV) had incomplete data the authors could not obtain, so the review's conclusions rest on the single 41-participant trial carded above (Bourke 2006). No tracheostomy-ventilation RCTs were found.
cards.result: The review reports moderate-quality evidence that median survival was significantly longer with NIV: 219 days versus 171 days on standard care — 48 days longer (estimated 95% CI 12 to 91 days; P = 0.0062) — accompanied by enhanced quality of life. In the subgroup with normal to moderately impaired bulbar function (20 participants), median survival was 205 days longer (216 versus 11 days; P = 0.0059) with better quality of life (low-quality evidence). In poor bulbar function (21 participants), NIV did not prolong survival or improve quality of life overall, though the sleep-apnoea quality-of-life symptoms domain improved by some measures. Neither trial reported intervention-related adverse-effect data. The reviewers note that more RCT evidence will be difficult to generate because withholding NIV from a control group is no longer ethically justifiable.
cards.watchOut: Carded for its pooled quantification and its quality grading (moderate for survival, low for the subgroup quality-of-life claims), not as a second source of evidence: it analyses the same 41 randomised patients as the Bourke card. Anyone quoting "two sources" for NIV in ALS from this shelf would be double-counting one trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: offer NIV when respiratory symptoms arrive — expect months of extra life with maintained quality of life if bulbar function is preserved; sleep relief, not survival, if it is not — SPLIT
cards.summary: Synthesis: offer NIV when respiratory symptoms arrive — expect months of extra life with maintained quality of life if bulbar function is preserved; sleep relief, not survival, if it is not — SPLIT
cards.people: One randomised trial (41 patients randomised at a respiratory trigger, within a 92-patient cohort) and the Cochrane synthesis built upon it — together the complete randomised evidence base for NIV in ALS.
cards.result: Overall median survival 219 versus 171 days (+48 days, 95% CI 12–91). Better bulbar function: +205 days median survival (216 versus 11 days) with quality of life maintained for most of the gained period. Poor bulbar function: no survival prolongation; sleep-related symptoms improved (P = 0.018 in the trial). No adverse-effect data were reported in either record. The size of the better-bulbar survival effect exceeds anything shown for ALS drug therapy, which is why a 41-patient trial has anchored practice for two decades.
cards.watchOut: The trial randomised patients when they developed orthopnoea or hypercapnia — it does not answer whether starting NIV earlier (or by spirometric thresholds alone) does better, and it says nothing about tracheostomy ventilation, for which no randomised trials exist. Bulbar status is the fork in this shelf: quote the survival figure only with its subgroup attached.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bourke SC et al. The Lancet. Neurology. 2006 (PMID: 16426990); Radunovic A et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2017 (PMID: 28982219) — the review synthesises the same trial, as flagged on its card.

shelves.title: A second IVIG course in poor-prognosis Guillain–Barré syndrome: no improvement in disability — and more serious adverse events, including thromboembolism
shelves.question: In Guillain–Barré syndrome predicted to recover poorly after one course of IVIG, does a second course improve outcome?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Double-Blind Method · Female · Guillain-Barre Syndrome/drug therapy · Humans · Immunoglobulins, Intravenous/administration & dosage · Male · Middle Aged · Netherlands · Prognosis · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Worldwide, about a quarter of severely affected Guillain–Barré patients are given a second course of intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) when the prognosis looks poor — a practice SID-GBS (Walgaard 2021, PMID: 33743237) tested directly and found wanting. Patients with a poor prognosis (modified Erasmus GBS Outcome Score ≥6) on their first standard IVIG course were randomised to a second 2 g/kg course or placebo: 93 patients in the modified intention-to-treat analysis (49 second-dose, 44 placebo). The adjusted common odds ratio for improvement on the GBS disability score at 4 weeks was 1.4 (95% CI 0.6–3.3; P = 0.45) — no demonstrated benefit, in a trial whose point estimate, if anything, is too imprecise to exclude a moderate effect in either direction. The harm side is not ambiguous in direction: serious adverse events in the first 30 days occurred in 35% of the second-dose group versus 16% on placebo, including thromboembolic events, and four patients in the intervention group died 13–24 weeks after randomisation. The authors' conclusion — a second IVIG course should not be considered for poor prognosis — is the shelf's conclusion. First-course IVIG versus plasma exchange is a different question, homed at shelf #1449. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference — and caused more serious adverse events) (Tier C: a single randomised trial).

cards.headline: Walgaard 2021 (SID-GBS): second IVIG course — adjusted common OR for disability improvement 1.4 (0.6–3.3, P = 0.45); serious adverse events 35% versus 16%
cards.summary: Walgaard 2021 (SID-GBS): second IVIG course — adjusted common OR for disability improvement 1.4 (0.6–3.3, P = 0.45); serious adverse events 35% versus 16%
cards.people: Patients aged ≥12 years with Guillain–Barré syndrome at 59 Dutch hospitals, enrolled on day 1 of a standard IVIG course (2 g/kg over 5 days). Of 327 patients included, 112 had a poor prognosis (modified Erasmus GBS Outcome Score ≥6); 93 were in the modified intention-to-treat analysis — 49 randomised to a second IVIG course (2 g/kg over 5 days, given 7–9 days after inclusion) and 44 to placebo. Primary outcome: GBS disability score 4 weeks after inclusion. Patients, outcome adjudicators, monitors and the steering committee were masked.
cards.result: The adjusted common odds ratio for improvement on the GBS disability score at 4 weeks was 1.4 (95% CI 0.6–3.3; P = 0.45) — no significant benefit from the second course. Patients given the second course had more serious adverse events than those given placebo (35% versus 16% in the first 30 days), including thromboembolic events. Four patients in the intervention group died, 13–24 weeks after randomisation. The authors conclude that the study provides no evidence that poor-prognosis patients benefit from a second IVIG course, that it entails a risk of serious adverse events, and that a second course should not be considered for treatment of Guillain–Barré syndrome because of a poor prognosis.
cards.watchOut: The confidence interval (0.6–3.3) is wide: 93 analysed patients cannot exclude a moderate benefit or moderate harm on the disability score, so "no difference demonstrated" is the precise claim — but with a point estimate near null, a doubled serious-adverse-event rate, and four deaths in the intervention arm, the burden of proof now sits on anyone proposing a second course. The trial selected patients by a prognostic score (mEGOS ≥6); it does not address second courses given for treatment-related fluctuation, a different clinical situation.
cards.source: Walgaard C et al. Second intravenous immunoglobulin dose in patients with Guillain-Barré syndrome with poor prognosis (SID-GBS): a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial. cards.headline: Synthesis: do not give a second IVIG course for poor prognosis — no benefit shown, real harm signal — LIKELY (no difference, with more serious adverse events)
cards.summary: Synthesis: do not give a second IVIG course for poor prognosis — no benefit shown, real harm signal — LIKELY (no difference, with more serious adverse events)
cards.people: One double-blind randomised trial, 93 poor-prognosis patients analysed of 112 identified among 327 enrolled, conducted across 59 hospitals in the Netherlands over 2010–2018.
cards.result: Disability improvement at 4 weeks: adjusted common OR 1.4 (0.6–3.3; P = 0.45). Serious adverse events within 30 days: 35% on the second course versus 16% on placebo, including thromboembolic events; four deaths occurred in the intervention group at 13–24 weeks. A widely used rescue practice fails its first randomised test on efficacy and shows the expected toxicity of a second large immunoglobulin load. The trial redirects the field, in its authors' words, toward trials of other immune modulators for severely affected patients.
cards.watchOut: Scope limits: poor-prognosis patients (mEGOS ≥6) after a first course — not all GBS patients, not treatment-related fluctuations after initial improvement, and not plasma exchange or other second-line immunotherapies, none of which this trial tested. First-course IVIG versus plasma exchange is shelf #1449.
cards.source: Synthesis of Walgaard C et al. The Lancet. Neurology. 2021 (PMID: 33743237).

shelves.title: CBT for schizophrenia: a real but small symptom effect that shrinks towards zero in blinded trials — and no proven edge over other talking therapies
shelves.question: In schizophrenia, does adding cognitive behavioural therapy to antipsychotics improve symptoms and functioning?
shelves.mesh: Bias · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy · Humans · Outcome Assessment, Health Care/statistics & numerical data · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Publication Bias/statistics & numerical data · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic/statistics & numerical data · Schizophrenia/therapy · Schizophrenic Psychology
shelves.balance: A small effect, honestly measured. The bias-conscious synthesis (Jauhar 2014, PMID: 24385461) pooled 34 randomised trials of CBT added to standard care (including antipsychotics): overall symptoms improved with an effect size of −0.33 (95% CI −0.47 to −0.19), positive symptoms −0.25 and negative symptoms −0.13. But masking mattered enormously: in trials where outcome assessors were blinded, the overall effect fell to −0.15 (95% CI −0.27 to −0.03) and the positive-symptom effect to −0.08, no longer significant — against −0.62 and −0.57 in unblinded trials. The Cochrane head-to-head review (Jones 2018, PMID: 30480760) then asked the sharper question — CBT versus OTHER psychosocial therapies, 36 trials, 3,542 participants — and found no clear advantage on relapse (RR 1.05), rehospitalisation (RR 0.96), mental state, social functioning or quality of life, on mostly low-quality evidence; the one consistent edge was satisfaction, measured as fewer people leaving the study early (RR 0.86). So the answer is: yes, CBT helps symptoms a little on top of medication; no, it has not been shown to beat cheaper, simpler supportive therapies; and functioning outcomes are essentially unproven rather than disproven. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — small average symptom benefit, bias-sensitive, not Tier C (multi-trial symptom shelf).

cards.headline: Jauhar 2014: across 34 trials CBT beat control on overall symptoms by an effect size of −0.33 — but in blinded trials the effect fell to −0.15, and for positive symptoms to a non-significant −0.08
cards.summary: Jauhar 2014: across 34 trials CBT beat control on overall symptoms by an effect size of −0.33 — but in blinded trials the effect fell to −0.15, and for positive symptoms to a non-significant −0.08
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs (Jauhar 2014)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials of cognitive-behavioural therapy for the symptoms of schizophrenia, providing end-of-treatment data on overall symptoms (34 studies), positive symptoms (33) and negative symptoms (34). Participants were people with schizophrenia receiving standard care, typically including antipsychotic medication, with CBT as an add-on.
cards.result: Pooled effect sizes favoured CBT: overall symptoms −0.33 (95% CI −0.47 to −0.19), positive symptoms −0.25 (−0.37 to −0.13), negative symptoms −0.13 (−0.25 to −0.01). Masking of outcome assessment significantly moderated the effect: for overall symptoms, blinded trials gave −0.15 (−0.27 to −0.03) versus −0.62 (−0.88 to −0.35) unblinded (P = 0.001); for positive symptoms, −0.08 (−0.18 to 0.03, non-significant) versus −0.57 (−0.76 to −0.39) (P < 0.001). Use of an active control intervention did not moderate effect size, and there was no consistent evidence of publication bias.
cards.watchOut: The headline −0.33 is the average across mostly unblinded trials; the blinded-trial estimate (−0.15 overall, −0.08 for positive symptoms) is the more defensible number, and it is small. This is a symptoms shelf: it says nothing about relapse, admission or functioning, which the Cochrane head-to-head review covers — with null results.
cards.source: Jauhar S et al. Cognitive-behavioural therapy for the symptoms of schizophrenia: systematic review and meta-analysis with examination of potential bias. Br J Psychiatry. 2014.
