cards.headline: Jones 2018 (Cochrane): CBT versus other psychosocial therapies in 36 trials and 3,542 people — no clear advantage on relapse, rehospitalisation, mental state, functioning or quality of life
cards.summary: Jones 2018 (Cochrane): CBT versus other psychosocial therapies in 36 trials and 3,542 people — no clear advantage on relapse, rehospitalisation, mental state, functioning or quality of life
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 36 RCTs (Jones 2018, Cochrane)
cards.people: 36 randomised trials (3,542 participants) comparing CBT plus standard care with another psychosocial therapy plus standard care — 14 trials against 'active' comparators and 14 against 'non-active' ones in the reviewers' classification. Outcomes included relapse, global state, mental state, adverse events, social functioning, quality of life and satisfaction.
cards.result: No difference in long-term relapse (RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.29; 375 participants, 5 studies) or long-term rehospitalisation (RR 0.96, 0.82 to 1.14; 943 participants, 8 studies); long-term mental state RR 0.82 (0.67 to 1.01). Social functioning and quality-of-life scores were similar between groups, on single small trials. The one clear difference favoured CBT on satisfaction, measured as leaving the study early (RR 0.86, 0.75 to 0.99; 2,392 participants, 26 studies). Evidence quality was mostly low or very low; the reviewers conclude there is no clear and convincing advantage for CBT over other, sometimes much less sophisticated and expensive, psychosocial therapies.
cards.watchOut: A null against other therapies is not a null against nothing: both reviews can be right — CBT helps a little versus waiting-list or treatment-as-usual controls, and so do befriending, supportive counselling and other structured therapies. Commissioners choosing the cheapest credible structured therapy are not contradicted by this evidence.
cards.source: Jones C et al. Cognitive behavioural therapy plus standard care versus standard care plus other psychosocial treatments for people with schizophrenia. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2018. PMID: 30480760. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a small, real symptom benefit on top of antipsychotics — halved or more when assessors are blinded — and no demonstrated superiority over other talking therapies
cards.summary: Synthesis: a small, real symptom benefit on top of antipsychotics — halved or more when assessors are blinded — and no demonstrated superiority over other talking therapies
cards.people: Two complementary syntheses: Jauhar 2014 (34 trials, CBT versus control conditions, with bias moderation) and Jones 2018 Cochrane (36 trials, 3,542 participants, CBT versus other psychosocial therapies head-to-head).
cards.result: Versus control: overall symptom effect −0.33, shrinking to −0.15 in blinded trials; positive symptoms −0.25 shrinking to a non-significant −0.08 blinded; negative symptoms −0.13. Versus other therapies: relapse RR 1.05, rehospitalisation RR 0.96, no functioning or quality-of-life advantage; satisfaction (study retention) RR 0.86 favouring CBT. The fair summary for a patient is: worth offering, expect modest symptom relief, do not expect it to keep you out of hospital, and a simpler therapy may do as much.
cards.watchOut: Neither review can rescue the functioning claim in the shelf question: functional outcomes were sparse, single-trial and null. Nor do these data address CBT for psychosis in first-episode services specifically — early-intervention packages, which include family work and supported employment alongside therapy, are a separate shelf (#2686).
cards.source: Synthesis of Jauhar S et al. Br J Psychiatry. 2014 (PMID: 24385461); Jones C et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2018 (PMID: 30480760).

shelves.title: Family intervention in schizophrenia: relapse roughly halved in the trial literature (RR 0.55, NNT 7) — one of the strongest psychosocial effects in psychiatry, with a quality caveat
shelves.question: In schizophrenia, do family interventions reduce relapse and readmission?
shelves.mesh: Expressed Emotion · Family Relations · Family Therapy · Humans · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Schizophrenia/therapy · Secondary Prevention · Social Support
shelves.balance: Yes — and the size of the effect is unusual for a psychosocial treatment. The Cochrane review (Pharoah 2010, PMID: 21154340) pooled 53 randomised trials of community family intervention versus standard care: relapse fell with a relative risk of 0.55 (95% CI 0.5 to 0.6) — a 45% relative reduction — with a number needed to treat of 7 (95% CI 6 to 8); hospital admission fell too (RR 0.78, NNT 8), and medication compliance improved (RR 0.60 for non-compliance outcomes as reported, NNT 6). The earlier independent meta-analysis (Pitschel-Walz 2001, PMID: 11215551), 25 studies, found the relapse rate reduced by about 20 percentage points as the authors report it, with effects particularly marked when intervention continued beyond 3 months. Both syntheses carry the same warning: many trials were small and poorly reported, blinding of assessors was uncommon, and effects may be overestimated. Even discounted for that, a halving of relapse replicated across two decades of trials is not plausibly all bias. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — large, consistent relative effect on the outcome that matters most to families; not Tier C.

cards.headline: Pharoah 2010 (Cochrane): 53 RCTs — family intervention cut relapse (RR 0.55, NNT 7), reduced hospital admission (RR 0.78) and improved medication compliance
cards.summary: Pharoah 2010 (Cochrane): 53 RCTs — family intervention cut relapse (RR 0.55, NNT 7), reduced hospital admission (RR 0.78) and improved medication compliance
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 53 RCTs (Pharoah 2010, Cochrane)
cards.people: 53 randomised or quasi-randomised trials of community-orientated family psychosocial intervention versus standard care for people with schizophrenia or schizophrenia-like conditions, identified through the Cochrane Schizophrenia Group Trials Register. Interventions were designed largely around reducing high expressed emotion (criticism, hostility, over-involvement) in families.
cards.result: Family intervention decreased the frequency of relapse (n = 2,981, 32 RCTs, RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.5 to 0.6, NNT 7, 95% CI 6 to 8) — a 45% relative reduction. It also reduced hospital admission (n = 481, 8 RCTs, RR 0.78, 0.6 to 1.0, NNT 8) and encouraged compliance with medication (n = 695, 10 RCTs, RR 0.60, 0.5 to 0.7, NNT 6), without obviously affecting dropout from care (RR 0.74, 0.5 to 1.0). It appeared to improve social impairment and levels of expressed emotion; no data suggested it either prevents or promotes suicide. The reviewers warn the treatment effects may be overestimated because of poor methodological quality in many trials.
cards.watchOut: The relapse estimate rests on 32 trials but the admission estimate on only 8 trials and 481 people, with a confidence interval touching 1.0. 'Family intervention' is a family of programmes — psychoeducation, crisis management, problem-solving — pooled together; the review cannot say which ingredient carries the effect, and delivery in trials was by motivated specialist teams.
cards.source: Pharoah F et al. Family intervention for schizophrenia. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2010. PMID: 21154340. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Pitschel-Walz 2001: an independent meta-analysis of 25 studies found relapse rates about 20 points lower when relatives were included in treatment — strongest when intervention lasted over 3 months
cards.summary: Pitschel-Walz 2001: an independent meta-analysis of 25 studies found relapse rates about 20 points lower when relatives were included in treatment — strongest when intervention lasted over 3 months
cards.people: 25 intervention studies of family programmes that educated relatives of people with schizophrenia and helped them cope with the illness; the main criterion was the patient's relapse rate, measured by significant worsening of symptoms or rehospitalisation in the first years after hospitalisation.
cards.result: The authors report that the relapse rate can be reduced by 20 percent (their wording; read as roughly 20 percentage points on the rates in these studies) if relatives are included in treatment. The effect was particularly marked when family interventions continued for longer than 3 months. Different comprehensive family interventions had similar results; the bifocal approach — psychosocial support to relatives and patients in addition to medical treatment — was clearly superior to medication-only standard treatment, and adding patient-focused intervention on top of family intervention did not yield significantly better results than either alone.
cards.watchOut: An older, pre-CONSORT literature: the '20 percent' figure is the authors' summary of heterogeneous studies with varying relapse definitions and follow-up lengths, and it should be quoted as their figure, not converted into a precise modern estimate. Its value is corroboration — a second team, a decade earlier, found the same direction and a duration-response pattern.
cards.source: Pitschel-Walz G et al. The effect of family interventions on relapse and rehospitalization in schizophrenia--a meta-analysis. Schizophrenia Bulletin. 2001. PMID: 11215551. Registry ID: none — pre-registration era. cards.headline: Synthesis: relapse roughly halved (RR 0.55, NNT 7), admissions down, compliance up — deliver it for months, not weeks, and expect the true effect to be somewhat smaller than the trials claim
cards.summary: Synthesis: relapse roughly halved (RR 0.55, NNT 7), admissions down, compliance up — deliver it for months, not weeks, and expect the true effect to be somewhat smaller than the trials claim
cards.people: Cochrane synthesis of 53 RCTs (Pharoah 2010) plus the independent 25-study meta-analysis (Pitschel-Walz 2001), together spanning the family-intervention literature from its origins to 2010.
cards.result: Relapse: RR 0.55 (0.5–0.6), NNT 7. Hospital admission: RR 0.78, NNT 8. Medication compliance: improved, NNT 6. Duration signal: interventions beyond 3 months performed best. Consistent caveat across both reviews: trial quality is mediocre and effects are probably overestimated — but the direction has never reversed in any major synthesis. For services, this is among the best-supported things a team can offer a family after a psychosis admission.
cards.watchOut: These trials recruited families willing and able to engage — often co-resident, motivated relatives. The evidence does not tell us the effect in families who refuse contact, nor whether brief psychoeducation leaflets or apps reproduce what months of structured sessions achieved. Suicide outcomes were absent, not reassuring.
cards.source: Synthesis of Pharoah F et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2010 (PMID: 21154340); Pitschel-Walz G et al. Schizophrenia Bulletin. 2001 (PMID: 11215551).

shelves.title: Early-intervention services in first-episode psychosis: better symptoms, fewer admissions and more work or study while the service lasts — gains that fade once it ends
shelves.question: In first-episode psychosis, do early-intervention services improve recovery versus standard care?
shelves.mesh: Early Medical Intervention/methods · Education/statistics & numerical data · Employment/statistics & numerical data · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Psychotic Disorders/psychology/therapy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Regression Analysis · Schizophrenia/therapy · Schizophrenic Psychology · Severity of Illness Index
shelves.balance: While the service is running, yes, across the board. The meta-analysis of the randomised trials (Correll 2018, PMID: 29800949; 10 trials, 2,176 patients) found early-intervention services superior to treatment as usual on all 13 analysable outcomes: treatment discontinuation RR 0.70, at least one psychiatric hospitalisation RR 0.74 (a 26% relative reduction), involvement in school or work RR 1.13, and total symptom severity SMD −0.32. The two flagship trials agree: RAISE/NAVIGATE (Kane 2016, PMID: 26481174; 404 participants, 34 US clinics) produced greater improvement in quality of life and psychopathology and more work/school involvement over 2 years, with the largest gains in those whose untreated psychosis had lasted under 74 weeks; OPUS (Bertelsen 2008, PMID: 18606949; 547 patients) improved symptoms at 2 years. The catch is durability: at OPUS's 5-year follow-up, three years after the intensive service ended, the symptom advantages had equalised — only fewer days in hospital (149 vs 193) and less supported housing (4% vs 10%) persisted. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — for outcomes during and shortly after the intervention; the honest rider is that nobody has shown the clinical gains survive discharge from the service. Not Tier C.

cards.headline: Correll 2018: across 10 RCTs and 2,176 patients, early-intervention services beat usual care on every analysable outcome — discontinuation RR 0.70, hospitalisation RR 0.74, symptoms SMD −0.32
cards.summary: Correll 2018: across 10 RCTs and 2,176 patients, early-intervention services beat usual care on every analysable outcome — discontinuation RR 0.70, hospitalisation RR 0.74, symptoms SMD −0.32
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 10 RCTs (Correll 2018)
cards.people: Systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression of randomised trials comparing early-intervention services (EIS) with treatment as usual in first-episode psychosis or early-phase schizophrenia-spectrum disorders; 10 trials, mean duration 16.2 months (range 9–24), 2,176 patients, mean age 27.5 years, 62.3% male.
cards.result: EIS was associated with better outcomes at end of treatment for all 13 meta-analysable outcomes, including: all-cause treatment discontinuation RR 0.70 (95% CI 0.61 to 0.80); at least one psychiatric hospitalisation RR 0.74 (0.61 to 0.90) — a 26% relative reduction; involvement in school or work RR 1.13 (1.03 to 1.24); total symptom severity SMD −0.32 (−0.47 to −0.17); positive symptoms SMD −0.22; negative symptoms SMD −0.28. Superiority was evident at 6, 9–12 and 18–24 months for most outcomes.
cards.watchOut: End-of-treatment effects: the trials mostly measured people while the intensive service was still wrapped around them, which is exactly when an assertive service should win. The meta-analysis cannot answer the policy question that matters most — what happens in the years after transfer back to standard care — for which OPUS's 5-year follow-up is the key evidence, and it is sobering.
cards.source: Correll CU et al. Comparison of Early Intervention Services vs Treatment as Usual for Early-Phase Psychosis: A Systematic Review, Meta-analysis, and Meta-regression. JAMA Psychiatry. 2018. PMID: 29800949. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Kane 2016 (RAISE): NAVIGATE comprehensive care in 34 US community clinics — greater quality-of-life and symptom improvement over 2 years, strongest when untreated psychosis had lasted under 74 weeks
cards.summary: Kane 2016 (RAISE): NAVIGATE comprehensive care in 34 US community clinics — greater quality-of-life and symptom improvement over 2 years, strongest when untreated psychosis had lasted under 74 weeks
cards.type: Cluster-randomised trial, 34 clinics (Kane 2016, RAISE Early Treatment Program)
cards.people: Cluster-randomised trial: 34 clinics in 21 US states assigned to NAVIGATE — a multidisciplinary team-based programme (medication management, family psychoeducation, resilience-focused therapy, supported employment/education) — or community care. 404 participants (mean age 23) with schizophrenia-spectrum first-episode psychosis and ≤6 months of antipsychotic treatment, followed ≥2 years; outcomes rated by masked central assessors. Primary outcome: Heinrichs-Carpenter Quality of Life Scale total score.
cards.result: The 223 NAVIGATE recipients stayed in treatment longer and experienced greater improvement in quality of life and psychopathology, and greater involvement in work and school, than the 181 community-care participants. Median duration of untreated psychosis was 74 weeks; participants below that median improved more on quality of life and psychopathology than those with longer untreated psychosis and those in community care. Hospitalisation rates were low and did not differ between groups.
cards.watchOut: A programme trial, not a drug trial: NAVIGATE bundles several components with their own evidence (family intervention, supported employment), so RAISE cannot attribute its gains to 'early intervention' as a single ingredient. The duration-of-untreated-psychosis interaction is a subgroup finding — hypothesis-strengthening, not proof that 74 weeks is a biological deadline.
cards.source: Kane JM et al. Comprehensive Versus Usual Community Care for First-Episode Psychosis: 2-Year Outcomes From the NIMH RAISE Early Treatment Program. Am J Psychiatry. 2016. PMID: 26481174. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01321177, from the record's databank listing. cards.headline: Bertelsen 2008 (OPUS 5-year follow-up): the 2-year symptom advantage had equalised by 5 years — but OPUS patients had spent 44 fewer days in hospital and fewer lived in supported housing
cards.summary: Bertelsen 2008 (OPUS 5-year follow-up): the 2-year symptom advantage had equalised by 5 years — but OPUS patients had spent 44 fewer days in hospital and fewer lived in supported housing
cards.people: OPUS randomised 547 patients with first-episode psychosis in Copenhagen and Aarhus to 2 years of intensive early intervention (assertive community treatment, family involvement, social-skills training) or standard community mental-health care; this report covers the 5-year follow-up (301 assessed at 5 years; intention-to-treat analysis, blinded assessment).
cards.result: At 2 years the intensive programme had improved psychotic (OR −0.32) and negative (OR −0.45) symptom dimensions; by 5 years those effects had equalised between groups. Two secondary differences persisted in favour of the intensive group across the 5 years: fewer days hospitalised (mean 149 vs 193 days; mean difference 44 days, 95% CI 0.15 to 88.12) and fewer patients living in supported housing (4% vs 10%; OR 2.3, 1.1 to 4.8).
cards.watchOut: Attrition matters: only 301 of 547 were assessed at 5 years, so the 'equalisation' could partly reflect who stayed in follow-up. And the trial tests a 2-year service followed by standard care — it does not test whether continuing intensive care beyond 2 years would preserve the gains, the obvious next question.
cards.source: Bertelsen M et al. Five-year follow-up of a randomized multicenter trial of intensive early intervention vs standard treatment for patients with a first episode of psychotic illness: the OPUS trial. Arch Gen Psychiatry. 2008. PMID: 18606949. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: fund the service for what it provably does — fewer admissions, better symptoms, more engagement while it runs — and do not promise families a permanent change of trajectory
cards.summary: Synthesis: fund the service for what it provably does — fewer admissions, better symptoms, more engagement while it runs — and do not promise families a permanent change of trajectory
cards.people: Ten RCTs meta-analysed (Correll 2018), the US implementation trial (RAISE, 404 participants), and the longest randomised follow-up (OPUS, 547 patients to 5 years).
cards.result: During treatment: discontinuation RR 0.70, hospitalisation RR 0.74, school/work involvement RR 1.13, symptom SMD −0.32. After the service ends (OPUS): symptom gains equalise by 5 years; hospital days (149 vs 193) and supported housing (4% vs 10%) still favour the early-intervention group. Shorter untreated psychosis predicts larger benefit (RAISE). The evidence supports early-intervention services as effective care, not as a cure delivered in a 2-year dose.
cards.watchOut: Comparators were 'standard care' in well-resourced Danish and US systems; the margin over weaker usual care elsewhere could be larger, and over already-good community teams smaller. Mortality and suicide were not outcomes these trials could settle — OPUS's suicide analysis is reported within the trial programme, not carded here.
cards.source: Synthesis of Correll CU et al. JAMA Psychiatry. 2018 (PMID: 29800949); Kane JM et al. Am J Psychiatry. 2016 (PMID: 26481174); Bertelsen M et al. Arch Gen Psychiatry. 2008 (PMID: 18606949).

shelves.title: Levodopa–carbidopa intestinal gel: off-time cut by about 4 hours a day, roughly 1.9 hours more than optimised oral therapy — at the price of a jejunal tube and its complications
shelves.question: In advanced Parkinson's disease with motor fluctuations despite oral therapy, does levodopa–carbidopa intestinal gel increase on-time without troublesome dyskinesia?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Carbidopa/administration & dosage/adverse effects/pharmacology · Double-Blind Method · Female · Gels/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Humans · Infusions, Parenteral/adverse effects/instrumentation/methods · Jejunum/drug effects/surgery · Levodopa/administration & dosage/adverse effects/pharmacology · Male · Middle Aged · Parkinson Disease/drug therapy · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: The one double-blind trial says yes, clearly. Olanow 2014 (PMID: 24361112) randomised 66 analysable patients with advanced Parkinson's and motor complications, all with a percutaneous gastrojejunostomy tube, to intestinal-gel levodopa–carbidopa plus oral placebo or oral immediate-release levodopa–carbidopa plus placebo gel: over 12 weeks off-time fell by 4.04 hours on gel versus 2.14 hours on oral therapy (difference −1.91 hours, 95% CI −3.05 to −0.76), and on-time without troublesome dyskinesia rose by 4.11 versus 2.24 hours (difference 1.86 hours). The large open-label programme (Fernandez 2013, PMID: 23287001; 192 patients) found almost the same diary numbers at 12 weeks (off-time −3.9 hours, good on-time +4.6 hours) — and showed the cost side plainly: 87.5% reported an adverse event, abdominal pain in 30.7%, device-insertion complications in 21.4%, serious events in 31.3%, and 12.5% discontinued. The trial records name the formulation and the sponsor (AbbVie, as funder in the record) but no brand name. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C — a single small double-blind trial, however clean, plus open-label support; the benefit is real but the intervention is a device-drug package whose harms are procedural. The apomorphine-infusion comparison (TOLEDO) is homed at #2371 and is cross-referenced, not re-carded.

cards.headline: Olanow 2014: in the only double-blind trial, intestinal gel cut off-time by 4.04 h/day versus 2.14 h on oral levodopa–carbidopa (difference −1.91 h) and added 1.86 h of good on-time
cards.summary: Olanow 2014: in the only double-blind trial, intestinal gel cut off-time by 4.04 h/day versus 2.14 h on oral levodopa–carbidopa (difference −1.91 h) and added 1.86 h of good on-time
cards.people: 12-week randomised, double-blind, double-dummy trial at 26 centres in Germany, New Zealand and the USA. Adults ≥30 years with advanced Parkinson's disease and motor complications had a percutaneous gastrojejunostomy tube placed, then were allocated to levodopa–carbidopa intestinal gel plus oral placebo (35 in the efficacy set) or immediate-release oral levodopa–carbidopa plus placebo gel (31). Primary endpoint: change in off-time; key secondary: on-time without troublesome dyskinesia.
cards.result: Off-time decreased by a mean of 4.04 h (SE 0.65) on intestinal gel versus 2.14 h (0.66) on oral therapy — difference −1.91 h (95% CI −3.05 to −0.76; P = 0.0015). On-time without troublesome dyskinesia increased by 4.11 h versus 2.24 h — difference 1.86 h (0.56 to 3.17; P = 0.0059). Adverse events occurred in 95% of the gel group (14% serious) and 100% of the oral group (21% serious) among those who had the tube procedure, mainly associated with the gastrojejunostomy tube itself. Funded by AbbVie, as stated in the record.

Small (66 patients), short (12 weeks), industry-funded, with last-observation-carried-forward imputation.

cards.headline: Fernandez 2013: in 192 patients treated open-label, off-time fell 3.9 h/day at 12 weeks — but 87.5% had an adverse event, 31.3% a serious one, and 12.5% stopped treatment
cards.summary: Fernandez 2013: in 192 patients treated open-label, off-time fell 3.9 h/day at 12 weeks — but 87.5% had an adverse event, 31.3% a serious one, and 12.5% stopped treatment
cards.people: Pre-planned interim analysis of a prospective open-label 54-week international study of levodopa–carbidopa intestinal gel in advanced Parkinson's disease with motor fluctuations despite optimised therapy; 192 patients with the gastrojejunostomy tube inserted at least 12 weeks before the data cut-off; mean Parkinson's duration 12.4 years; mean exposure 256.7 days.
cards.result: From a baseline off-time of 6.7 h/day, off-time fell by a mean of 3.9 (±3.2) h/day and on-time without troublesome dyskinesia rose by 4.6 (±3.5) h/day at week 12. Adverse events were reported by 168 patients (87.5%): most commonly abdominal pain (30.7%), complication of device insertion (21.4%) and procedural pain (17.7%). Serious adverse events occurred in 60 patients (31.3%); 24 (12.5%) discontinued, 14 (7.3%) because of adverse events; 4 (2.1%) died, none of the deaths judged related to the gel.
cards.watchOut: Open-label diary outcomes in patients who chose an invasive therapy are inflated by expectation and by survivorship — those who could not tolerate the tube leave the averages. Read this card for the harm and burden ledger (which blinding cannot manufacture) and the Olanow trial for the efficacy estimate.

cards.headline: Synthesis: about 2 extra hours of good on-time a day over oral therapy, bought with a permanent jejunal tube, frequent device problems and a 1-in-8 discontinuation rate
cards.summary: Synthesis: about 2 extra hours of good on-time a day over oral therapy, bought with a permanent jejunal tube, frequent device problems and a 1-in-8 discontinuation rate
cards.people: One double-blind double-dummy RCT (66 patients, 12 weeks) and one large open-label programme (192 patients, interim at ≥12 weeks).
cards.result: Off-time: −4.04 h/day on gel vs −2.14 h/day on oral therapy (net −1.91 h); good on-time net +1.86 h/day. Open-label replication of the diary gains (−3.9 h off-time) alongside the real-world costs: adverse events 87.5%, serious 31.3%, discontinuation 12.5%. For a patient whose fluctuations survive optimised oral therapy and apomorphine, this is a genuine option — chosen with the complication rates in view, not just the diary gains.
cards.watchOut: No randomised comparison exists against the other device-aided therapies — apomorphine infusion (#2371) or deep brain stimulation (#692) — so this shelf cannot rank them; selection between them in practice turns on cognition, surgical fitness and patient preference, none of which these trials randomised.
cards.source: Synthesis of Olanow CW et al. Lancet Neurol. 2014 (PMID: 24361112); Fernandez HH et al. Parkinsonism Relat Disord. 2013 (PMID: 23287001).

shelves.title: D-cycloserine augmentation of exposure therapy: a small benefit at the end of treatment in the individual-patient analysis (d ≈ 0.25) that fades by follow-up — and vanishes in the conventional meta-analysis
shelves.question: In anxiety disorders treated with exposure therapy, does D-cycloserine augmentation improve outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Antidepressive Agents/therapeutic use · Anxiety Disorders/drug therapy/therapy · Combined Modality Therapy · Cycloserine/pharmacology · Drug Synergism · Excitatory Amino Acid Agonists/pharmacology · Humans · Implosive Therapy/methods · N-Methylaspartate/agonists · Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder/drug therapy/therapy · Outcome Assessment, Health Care/statistics & numerical data · Stress Disorders, Post-Traumatic/drug therapy/therapy
shelves.balance: At most a small, short-lived nudge. The strongest analysis — individual participant data from 21 of 22 eligible double-blind trials, 1,047 participants (Mataix-Cols 2017, PMID: 28122091) — found D-cycloserine superior to placebo augmentation from pre-treatment to post-treatment (mean difference −3.62 points on a standardised 0–100 metric; d = −0.25), but not to mid-treatment, and the pre-to-follow-up contrast just missed significance (P = .05; d = −0.19). The conventional aggregate meta-analysis (McGuire 2017, PMID: 27314661; 20 RCTs, 957 participants) found smaller, non-significant effects overall (g = 0.15; response RR 1.08; remission RR 1.11), with a nominally significant effect only in the anxiety-disorders subgroup (g = 0.33) and not for OCD or PTSD separately. Antidepressant co-treatment did not moderate the effect, and no patient- or study-level moderator reliably identified responders. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — two syntheses agree the ceiling is 'small'; they disagree on whether the average clears zero, which is exactly what POSSIBLE is for. Not Tier C: multi-trial, symptom outcomes only.

cards.headline: Mataix-Cols 2017: individual data from 1,047 participants in 21 trials — D-cycloserine beat placebo augmentation at post-treatment (d = −0.25) but not at mid-treatment, and the follow-up effect just missed significance
cards.summary: Mataix-Cols 2017: individual data from 1,047 participants in 21 trials — D-cycloserine beat placebo augmentation at post-treatment (d = −0.25) but not at mid-treatment, and the follow-up effect just missed significance
cards.people: Systematic review and individual-participant-data meta-analysis of double-blind randomised trials of D-cycloserine versus placebo as augmentation of exposure-based CBT in specific phobia, social anxiety disorder, panic disorder with or without agoraphobia, OCD and PTSD. Raw data were obtained for 21 of 22 eligible trials (1,047 of 1,073 participants); outcomes were ranked onto a common 0–100 metric and modelled with a three-level multilevel model, controlling for antidepressant use.
cards.result: Participants receiving D-cycloserine improved more from pre-treatment to post-treatment (mean difference −3.62, 95% CI −6.43 to −0.81; P = .01; d = −0.25), but not from pre- to mid-treatment (−1.66; P = .32; d = −0.14), and the pre-treatment-to-follow-up difference was borderline (−2.98, −5.99 to 0.03; P = .05; d = −0.19). Additional analyses showed lower symptom severity on D-cycloserine at post-treatment and follow-up. Antidepressants did not moderate the effect, and none of the prespecified patient- or study-level moderators was associated with outcome.
cards.watchOut: An effect of d = 0.25 on a ranked symptom metric is small — roughly the difference between a good and an average course of exposure therapy — and the follow-up estimate's confidence interval includes zero. The extinction-learning rationale predicts benefit only when exposure sessions themselves succeed, a moderator the trials measured too crudely to confirm; the shelf should not be read as 'give DCS with any exposure programme'.
cards.source: Mataix-Cols D et al. D-Cycloserine Augmentation of Exposure-Based Cognitive Behavior Therapy for Anxiety, Obsessive-Compulsive, and Posttraumatic Stress Disorders: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Individual Participant Data. JAMA Psychiatry. 2017. PMID: 28122091. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: McGuire 2017: pooling published results from 20 RCTs (957 participants), the augmentation effect was small and non-significant overall (g = 0.15) — significant only within anxiety disorders (g = 0.33)
cards.summary: McGuire 2017: pooling published results from 20 RCTs (957 participants), the augmentation effect was small and non-significant overall (g = 0.15) — significant only within anxiety disorders (g = 0.33)
cards.people: Conventional aggregate-data meta-analysis of 20 randomised placebo-controlled trials (957 participants) of D-cycloserine-augmented exposure therapy for anxiety disorders, OCD and PTSD, searching PubMed, PsycINFO and Scopus to May 2015; effect sizes calculated for treatment efficacy, treatment response and diagnostic remission, with subgroup and meta-regression moderator analyses.
cards.result: Across all conditions, D-cycloserine showed a small, non-significant benefit over placebo augmentation for efficacy (g = 0.15), response (RR 1.08) and remission (RR 1.11). The effect was moderately significant for anxiety disorders specifically (g = 0.33; P = .03). At initial follow-up the pooled effects remained small and non-significant (g = 0.21; response RR 1.06; remission RR 1.12). Specific moderators (comorbidity, medication status, gender, publication year) emerged in some analyses.
cards.watchOut: Aggregate meta-analysis of published summary data is the weaker design here — it cannot harmonise outcome timing or adjust for antidepressant use as the IPD analysis did — so where the two disagree, the IPD estimate deserves more weight. The anxiety-only subgroup signal (g = 0.33) comes from multiple subgroup cuts and should be treated as exploratory.
cards.source: McGuire JF et al. A Meta-Analysis of D-Cycloserine in Exposure-Based Treatment: Moderators of Treatment Efficacy, Response, and Diagnostic Remission. J Clin Psychiatry. 2017. PMID: 27314661. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.summary: Synthesis: expect, at best, a small extra gain by the end of a course of exposure therapy — not a durable one, and not one anyone can yet target to the right patient
cards.people: Individual-participant-data meta-analysis (21 trials, 1,047 participants) and a conventional meta-analysis (20 trials, 957 participants) of the same trial literature.

shelves.title: Surgery for drug-resistant trigeminal neuralgia: microvascular decompression leaves 70% pain-free off medication at 10 years; Gamma Knife leaves about 45% — with far fewer serious complications and a 1-in-5 numbness rate
shelves.question: In trigeminal neuralgia failing carbamazepine, do surgical options (microvascular decompression, radiosurgery) give durable relief?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Child · Child, Preschool · Disease-Free Survival · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Hearing Disorders/etiology · Humans · Male · Microsurgery · Middle Aged · Nerve Compression Syndromes/surgery · Postoperative Complications · Proportional Hazards Models · Recurrence · Sex Factors · Treatment Outcome · Trigeminal Nerve/surgery · Trigeminal Neuralgia/surgery
shelves.balance: Durable relief is real for both operations — but no randomised trial has ever compared them, so every number here is a within-series rate, and the two flagship series differ in era, case mix and follow-up method. Microvascular decompression (Barker 1996, PMID: 8598865): 1,185 patients operated for medically intractable trigeminal neuralgia, median follow-up 6.2 years; at 10 years 70% were free of pain without medication and a further 4% had only occasional pain not needing long-term medication, with recurrences concentrated in the first 2 years and an annual recurrence rate under 1% after year 10 — at a cost of 2 operative deaths (0.2%), 1 brain-stem infarction (0.1%) and ipsilateral hearing loss in 1%. Gamma Knife radiosurgery (Régis 2016, PMID: 26339857): 497 patients with medically refractory classical trigeminal neuralgia, median follow-up 43.8 months; 91.75% became pain-free initially (median 10 days), but the actuarial probability of remaining pain-free without medication fell to 64.9% at 5 years and 45.3% at 10 years (67.8% maintained relief without further surgery at 10 years); facial hypesthesia reached an actuarial 21.1% at 7 years, though very bothersome numbness occurred in only 0.6%, and there were no operative deaths. The authors of the radiosurgery series themselves state that a randomised or case-matched comparison with decompression would be required to rank them. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C — observational series only, presented side by side without a fabricated head-to-head. Drug treatment, including botulinum toxin for refractory cases, is homed elsewhere (#2382).

cards.headline: Barker 1996: microvascular decompression in 1,185 patients — 70% pain-free without medication at 10 years, against 0.2% operative mortality and 1% ipsilateral hearing loss
cards.summary: Barker 1996: microvascular decompression in 1,185 patients — 70% pain-free without medication at 10 years, against 0.2% operative mortality and 1% ipsilateral hearing loss
cards.people: Prospective long-term cohort (annual questionnaires) of 1,185 patients undergoing microvascular decompression of the trigeminal nerve for medically intractable trigeminal neuralgia over a 20-year period at a single centre; 1,155 followed for ≥1 year; median follow-up 6.2 years. Outcomes: pain recurrence, reoperation, complications, and predictors of recurrence by proportional-hazards modelling.
cards.result: Thirty percent of patients had a recurrence of tic during follow-up and 11% underwent a second operation. Ten years after surgery, 70% (Kaplan–Meier) had excellent results — free of pain without medication — and an additional 4% had occasional pain not requiring long-term medication; after 10 years the annual recurrence rate was under 1%. Predictors of recurrence: female sex, symptoms for more than 8 years, venous compression of the root entry zone, and lack of immediate postoperative pain cessation. Major complications: 2 deaths shortly after operation (0.2%), 1 brain-stem infarction (0.1%), and ipsilateral hearing loss in 16 patients (1%).
cards.watchOut: A single pioneering centre's series across two decades: results reflect one team's selection and technique, and patients offered open posterior-fossa surgery are typically younger and fitter than those offered radiosurgery — the central reason the two series on this shelf cannot be subtracted from each other. Questionnaire follow-up also softens outcome ascertainment compared with examination.
cards.source: Barker FG 2nd et al. The long-term outcome of microvascular decompression for trigeminal neuralgia. N Engl J Med. 1996. PMID: 8598865. Registry ID: none — pre-registration era cohort study. 1,155 followed for ≥1 year; median follow-up 6.2 years. outcomes: pain recurrence, reoperation, complications, and predictors of recurrence by proportional-hazards modelling. thirty percent of patients had a recurrence of tic during follow-up and 11% underwent a second operation. ten years after surgery, 70% (kaplan–meier) had excellent results — free of pain without medication — and an additional 4% had occasional pain not requiring long-term medication; after 10 years the annual recurrence rate was under 1%. predictors of recurrence: female sex, symptoms for more than 8 years, venous compression of the root entry zone, and lack of immediate postoperative pain cessation. major complications: 2 deaths shortly after operation (0.2%), 1 brain-stem infarction (0.1%), and ipsilateral hearing loss in 16 patients (1%). a single pioneering centre's series across two decades: results reflect one team's selection and technique, and patients offered open posterior-fossa surgery are typically younger and fitter than those offered radiosurgery — the central reason the two series on this shelf cannot be subtracted from each other. questionnaire follow-up also softens outcome ascertainment compared with examination. barker fg 2nd et al. the long-term outcome of microvascular decompression for trigeminal neuralgia. n engl j med. 1996. pmid: 8598865. registry id: none — pre-registration era cohort study. mesh: adolescent · adult · aged · aged, 80 and over · child · child, preschool · disease-free survival · female · follow-up studies · hearing disorders/etiology · humans · male · microsurgery · middle aged · nerve compression syndromes/surgery · postoperative complications · proportional hazards models · recurrence · sex factors · treatment outcome · trigeminal nerve/surgery · trigeminal neuralgia/surgery

cards.headline: Régis 2016: Gamma Knife radiosurgery in 497 patients — 91.75% initially pain-free, but 45.3% still pain-free off medication at 10 years; numbness in about a fifth, severe in 0.6%
cards.summary: Régis 2016: Gamma Knife radiosurgery in 497 patients — 91.75% initially pain-free, but 45.3% still pain-free off medication at 10 years; numbness in about a fifth, severe in 0.6%
cards.type: Retrospective analysis of a prospective cohort, n = 497 (Régis 2016)
cards.people: Historical cohort of 497 patients with medically refractory classical trigeminal neuralgia, never previously treated with Gamma Knife surgery, treated 1992–2010 at one university hospital with a single 4-mm isocenter on the cisternal trigeminal nerve (median maximum dose 85 Gy) and followed for at least 1 year (median 43.8 months, range 12–174.4); median age 68.3 years. Data collected prospectively and evaluated retrospectively.
cards.result: 456 patients (91.75%) were initially pain-free, at a median of 10 days. Actuarial probabilities of remaining pain-free without medication were 71.8% at 3 years, 64.9% at 5, 59.7% at 7 and 45.3% at 10 years; 157 of those initially pain-free (34.4%) had at least one recurrence (median delay 24 months), while the actuarial rate of maintaining pain relief without further surgery was 67.8% at 10 years. The actuarial hypesthesia rate was 20.4% at 5 years and 21.1% at 7 years, stable thereafter; very bothersome facial hypesthesia was reported by only 3 patients (0.6%). The authors conclude the technique is safe and effective long-term, while stating that a randomised trial or case-matched study would be required to compare it with microvascular decompression.
cards.watchOut: An older cohort (median age 68.3) treated over 18 years with evolving Gamma Knife models and imaging — and 'pain-free without medication' is a stricter endpoint than the 'maintained relief' figure (67.8%) quoted beside it; readers must not mix the two. The comparison patients and surgeons actually want — matched MVD versus GKS — does not exist in this literature.
cards.source: Régis J et al. Long-term safety and efficacy of Gamma Knife surgery in classical trigeminal neuralgia: a 497-patient historical cohort study. J Neurosurg. 2016. PMID: 26339857. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: decompression offers the best durability (70% medication-free at 10 years) with small but real operative risk; radiosurgery offers a gentler procedure with slower decay of benefit and a 1-in-5 numbness rate
cards.summary: Synthesis: decompression offers the best durability (70% medication-free at 10 years) with small but real operative risk; radiosurgery offers a gentler procedure with slower decay of benefit and a 1-in-5 numbness rate
cards.people: Two large single-centre series: microvascular decompression, 1,185 patients, median follow-up 6.2 years (Barker 1996); Gamma Knife radiosurgery, 497 patients, median follow-up 43.8 months (Régis 2016). No randomised or matched comparison exists.
cards.result: Pain-free without medication at 10 years: 70% (MVD, Kaplan–Meier) versus 45.3% (GKS, actuarial). Serious harm: MVD — death 0.2%, brain-stem infarction 0.1%, hearing loss 1%; GKS — no procedural mortality reported, facial hypesthesia ≈21% by 7 years (very bothersome 0.6%), and about a third of initial responders recurred. Cross-series subtraction is not a treatment effect: it is a description of two literatures, in differently selected patients, and the shelf presents it as exactly that.
cards.watchOut: Percutaneous ablative procedures (radiofrequency, glycerol, balloon compression) are not carded here — their series are smaller and older, and this shelf answers the slate's question about the two operations with the largest long-term datasets. Patients with multiple sclerosis or secondary trigeminal neuralgia are outside both series' core populations.
cards.source: Synthesis of Barker FG 2nd et al. N Engl J Med. 1996 (PMID: 8598865); Régis J et al. J Neurosurg. 2016 (PMID: 26339857).

shelves.title: High-dose methylprednisolone after spinal cord injury: a benefit that exists only inside the 8-hour, post-hoc window of NASCIS II — bought, when the infusion runs to 48 hours, with more sepsis and pneumonia
shelves.question: In acute traumatic spinal cord injury, does high-dose methylprednisolone improve neurological recovery, and at what cost?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adolescent · Adult · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Injections, Intravenous · Male · Methylprednisolone/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Motor Activity · Multicenter Studies as Topic · Naloxone/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Sensation · Spinal Cord Injuries/drug therapy/physiopathology · Time Factors
shelves.balance: This is the most contested shelf in the batch, and the cards show why. NASCIS II (Bracken 1990, PMID: 2278545; 487 patients) was negative overall: the claimed benefit appears only in the subgroup treated within 8 hours of injury, where methylprednisolone (30 mg/kg bolus, then 5.4 mg/kg/h for 23 hours) improved 6-month motor change scores (16.0 vs 11.2; P = 0.03) and pinprick and touch sensation versus placebo; treatment after 8 hours, and naloxone at any time, did nothing. NASCIS III (Bracken 1997, PMID: 9168289; 499 patients, all given the bolus) had no placebo arm: extending the infusion to 48 hours helped only the subgroup started 3–8 hours after injury (motor recovery P = .01 at 6 months in that stratum) and that same group had more severe sepsis and severe pneumonia, with mortality unchanged (P = .97). The Cochrane synthesis (Bracken 2012, PMID: 22258943) concludes the within-8-hours regimen improves motor recovery — noting the result was replicated in a Japanese trial but not in the French one — and that complications and mortality were not significantly increased overall. Guideline bodies have famously split over whether a post-hoc subgroup of one trial should drive practice; this shelf takes no side beyond its stamp. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit, within-8-hours subgroup only) / POSSIBLE (harm, 48-hour extension), Tier C: subgroup-dependent, single-programme evidence with a live methodological controversy stated on its face.

cards.headline: Bracken 1990 (NASCIS II): overall a negative trial — the methylprednisolone benefit (motor change 16.0 vs 11.2) appears only in patients treated within 8 hours of injury
cards.summary: Bracken 1990 (NASCIS II): overall a negative trial — the methylprednisolone benefit (motor change 16.0 vs 11.2) appears only in patients treated within 8 hours of injury
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Bracken 1990, NASCIS II)
cards.people: Multicentre randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 487 patients with acute spinal-cord injury, 95% treated within 14 hours of injury: methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg bolus then 5.4 mg/kg/h for 23 hours (n = 162); naloxone 5.4 mg/kg bolus then 4.0 mg/kg/h for 23 hours (n = 154); or placebo bolus and infusion (n = 171). Motor and sensory function were assessed on admission and at 6 weeks and 6 months.
cards.result: At 6 months, patients treated with methylprednisolone within 8 hours of injury improved significantly more than placebo on motor function (neurologic change scores 16.0 vs 11.2; P = 0.03), pinprick sensation (11.4 vs 6.6; P = 0.02) and touch (8.9 vs 4.3; P = 0.03); the benefit appeared in both complete and incomplete lesions. Patients treated with methylprednisolone more than 8 hours after injury, and all patients treated with naloxone, did not differ from placebo. Mortality and major morbidity were similar in all three groups.
cards.watchOut: The 8-hour cut was not the trial's primary framing: the overall comparison was null, and the benefit rests on a time-stratified subgroup — the reason this remains contested three decades later. Change scores on a motor index are also not the same as walking again; the abstract reports no functional-independence outcome for the subgroup.
cards.source: Bracken MB et al. A randomized, controlled trial of methylprednisolone or naloxone in the treatment of acute spinal-cord injury. Results of the Second National Acute Spinal Cord Injury Study. N Engl J Med. 1990. PMID: 2278545. Registry ID: none — pre-registration era. cards.headline: Bracken 1997 (NASCIS III): no placebo arm — 48 hours of methylprednisolone beat 24 hours only in the 3-to-8-hour subgroup, and that group had more severe sepsis and severe pneumonia
cards.summary: Bracken 1997 (NASCIS III): no placebo arm — 48 hours of methylprednisolone beat 24 hours only in the 3-to-8-hour subgroup, and that group had more severe sepsis and severe pneumonia
cards.type: Randomised double-blind trial without placebo arm (Bracken 1997, NASCIS III)
cards.people: Double-blind randomised trial in 499 patients with acute spinal cord injury at 16 North American centres, all treated within 8 hours of injury and all given a 30 mg/kg methylprednisolone bolus before randomisation: methylprednisolone infusion for 24 hours (n = 166), for 48 hours (n = 167), or tirilazad mesylate for 48 hours (n = 166). Outcomes: motor-function change and Functional Independence Measure at 6 weeks and 6 months.
cards.result: Overall, the 48-hour group showed improved motor recovery at 6 weeks (P = .09) and 6 months (P = .07) versus the 24-hour group — not conventionally significant. Within the subgroup whose treatment began 3 to 8 hours after injury, the 48-hour effect was significant at 6 weeks (P = .04) and 6 months (P = .01), with more patients improving a full neurologic grade (P = .03); but that group also had more severe sepsis and severe pneumonia than the other groups, while other complications and mortality were similar (P = .97). Tirilazad's motor recovery matched 24-hour methylprednisolone. The authors recommend 24 hours of treatment if started within 3 hours, and 48 hours if started at 3–8 hours.
cards.watchOut: Because every patient received the steroid bolus, NASCIS III cannot test whether methylprednisolone beats nothing — it compares durations, on the assumption NASCIS II's subgroup was real. Its headline overall comparisons miss significance (P = .07–.09); the practice-changing claim again lives in a time subgroup, now with a harm signal attached to it.
cards.source: Bracken MB et al. Administration of methylprednisolone for 24 or 48 hours or tirilazad mesylate for 48 hours in the treatment of acute spinal cord injury. Results of the Third National Acute Spinal Cord Injury Randomized Controlled Trial. JAMA. 1997. PMID: 9168289. Registry ID: none — pre-registration era. cards.headline: Bracken 2012 (Cochrane): the within-8-hours regimen improves motor recovery — replicated in a Japanese trial, not in the French one — with no overall increase in complications or mortality
cards.summary: Bracken 2012 (Cochrane): the within-8-hours regimen improves motor recovery — replicated in a Japanese trial, not in the French one — with no overall increase in complications or mortality
cards.people: Cochrane review of all randomised trials of steroid treatment for human acute spinal cord injury (8 trials, 7 using methylprednisolone), including the NASCIS programme and Japanese and French trials, with additional data obtained from original authors to permit meta-analysis.
cards.result: Methylprednisolone sodium succinate improved neurologic outcome up to one year after injury when given within 8 hours of injury as a 30 mg/kg bolus over 15 minutes followed by 5.4 mg/kg/h for 23 hours; meta-analysis of the three relevant trials showed significant recovery in motor function, with the initial North American result replicated in the Japanese trial but not the French trial. Extending treatment to 48 hours produced additional improvement in motor and functional status, particularly when treatment could not start until 3–8 hours after injury. Overall there was no evidence of significantly increased complications or mortality from the 23- or 48-hour therapy. The reviewer — the NASCIS principal investigator — concludes this is the only pharmacologic therapy shown efficacious in a phase 3 trial within 8 hours, and calls for more randomised trials.
cards.watchOut: A one-author Cochrane review written by the principal investigator of the trials it vindicates — a conflict readers should know about when weighing its reassurance on harms against NASCIS III's own sepsis and pneumonia signal. The non-replication in the French trial is reported inside the review itself, to its credit, but is easy to miss.
cards.source: Bracken MB. Steroids for acute spinal cord injury. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2012. PMID: 22258943. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a small motor-score benefit confined to a post-hoc 8-hour window, a harm signal at 48 hours, and a controversy the evidence itself has never settled
cards.summary: Synthesis: a small motor-score benefit confined to a post-hoc 8-hour window, a harm signal at 48 hours, and a controversy the evidence itself has never settled
cards.people: NASCIS II (487 patients, placebo-controlled), NASCIS III (499 patients, duration comparison), and the Cochrane synthesis of 8 trials.
cards.result: Benefit: 6-month motor change 16.0 vs 11.2 points (within-8-hours subgroup, NASCIS II); one of two external replications positive. No benefit when started after 8 hours. Harm: more severe sepsis and severe pneumonia in the 48-hour, started-at-3–8-hours subgroup of NASCIS III; no overall mortality difference (P = .97). Everything on this shelf after the first sentence is subgroup analysis — clinicians who give the drug and clinicians who refuse it are both reading the same numbers, which is precisely why the stamp is SPLIT and Tier C.
cards.watchOut: Later guideline disagreement (some bodies recommend offering 24-hour treatment within 8 hours, others recommend against routine use) is context, not carded evidence, and is deliberately not quantified here. Nothing on this shelf addresses steroids started after 8 hours except NASCIS II's null, or steroid use in penetrating injury.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bracken MB et al. N Engl J Med. 1990 (PMID: 2278545); Bracken MB et al. JAMA. 1997 (PMID: 9168289); Bracken MB. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2012 (PMID: 22258943).

shelves.title: Aspirin + paracetamol + caffeine for acute migraine: pain-free at 2 hours in 19.6% versus 9.0% on placebo, and superior to each of its components alone in the head-to-head trial
shelves.question: In migraine, does the combination of aspirin, paracetamol and caffeine beat single analgesics for acute attacks?

shelves.balance: Yes — the combination beats placebo clearly and beats its own ingredients head-to-head. The placebo-controlled meta-analysis (Diener 2022, PMID: 34519136; 7 randomised trials, 3,306 participants) found pain freedom at 2 hours in 19.6% on the fixed combination versus 9.0% on placebo (rate ratio 2.2, 95% CI 1.4 to 3.3 — a relative measure; the absolute gain is about 11 percentage points) and pain relief at 2 hours in 54.3% versus 31.2% (RR 1.7), with adverse events more frequent on the combination (10.9% vs 7.8%; RR 1.7). The pivotal six-arm trial behind the 'beats single analgesics' claim (Diener 2005, PMID: 16162254; 1,743 patients treating migraine or tension-type headache attacks) found the triple combination — two tablets of aspirin 250 mg + paracetamol 200 mg + caffeine 50 mg, a formulation the abstract names as Thomapyrin — significantly superior on time to 50% pain relief to the same doses without caffeine (P = 0.0181), to aspirin alone (P = 0.0398), to paracetamol alone (P = 0.0016), to caffeine alone and to placebo (both P < 0.0001). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — consistent randomised evidence for an over-the-counter question; not Tier C. Triptan comparisons are a different shelf question and are not claimed here.

cards.headline: Diener 2022: across 7 placebo-controlled trials (3,306 participants), the combination left 19.6% pain-free at 2 hours versus 9.0% on placebo — with more adverse events (10.9% vs 7.8%)
cards.summary: Diener 2022: across 7 placebo-controlled trials (3,306 participants), the combination left 19.6% pain-free at 2 hours versus 9.0% on placebo — with more adverse events (10.9% vs 7.8%)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of randomised, blinded, placebo-controlled parallel-group trials of fixed-dose aspirin + paracetamol (acetaminophen) + caffeine (APC) for treating a migraine attack; 7 studies, 3,306 participants (2,147 APC, 1,159 placebo). Primary outcomes: pain-free at 2 hours and pain relief at 2 hours.
cards.result: Pain-free at 2 hours: 19.6% on APC versus 9.0% on placebo (rate ratio 2.2, 95% CI 1.4 to 3.3) — a relative doubling on an absolute gain of about 11 percentage points. Pain relief at 2 hours: 54.3% versus 31.2% (RR 1.7, 1.6 to 1.9). Adverse events were more frequent with APC than placebo (10.9% vs 7.8%; RR 1.7, 1.3 to 2.2). The authors conclude APC is superior to placebo for acute migraine attacks, with clinically relevant efficacy on both primary outcomes.
cards.watchOut: The pain-free rate ratio of 2.2 flatters a modest absolute result: four of five treated patients are not pain-free at 2 hours. Formulations across the seven trials were the standard fixed combination, but doses per brand and country vary — the shelf answers for the tested combination, not for any home-made mixture of the three drugs.
cards.source: Diener HC et al. Aspirin, paracetamol (acetaminophen) and caffeine for the treatment of acute migraine attacks: A systemic review and meta-analysis of randomized placebo-controlled trials. Eur J Neurol. 2022. PMID: 34519136. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Diener 2005: in a 1,743-patient six-arm trial, the triple combination beat the dual combination, aspirin alone, paracetamol alone, caffeine alone and placebo on time to 50% pain relief
cards.summary: Diener 2005: in a 1,743-patient six-arm trial, the triple combination beat the dual combination, aspirin alone, paracetamol alone, caffeine alone and placebo on time to 50% pain relief
cards.people: Multicentre randomised double-blind single-dose placebo-controlled parallel-group trial in 1,743 patients who habitually treated episodic tension-type headache or migraine attacks with non-prescription analgesics. Arms (two tablets each): the fixed combination of aspirin 250 mg + paracetamol 200 mg + caffeine 50 mg per tablet — named in the abstract as Thomapyrin; aspirin + paracetamol without caffeine; aspirin 500 mg; paracetamol 500 mg; caffeine 50 mg; and placebo. Primary endpoint: time to 50% pain relief (intention-to-treat).
cards.result: The fixed triple combination was statistically significantly superior to the combination without caffeine (P = 0.0181), aspirin alone (P = 0.0398), paracetamol alone (P = 0.0016), caffeine alone (P < 0.0001) and placebo (P < 0.0001) on the primary endpoint; all active treatments except caffeine alone also differed significantly from placebo (P < 0.0001). Superiority extended to secondary endpoints including time to pain intensity of 10 mm, weighted sum of pain-intensity differences, impairment of daily activities and global efficacy assessment. All treatments were well tolerated and the incidence of adverse events was low.
cards.watchOut: The trial pooled migraine and tension-type headache attacks in one analysis, so its P-values are for headache attacks in over-the-counter users, not migraine alone — the migraine-specific effect sizes come from the 2022 meta-analysis card. Several superiority margins are slender (P = 0.0398 against aspirin alone), and the study was of a named commercial formulation; equivalent generic fixed combinations deliver the same doses, but that equivalence is pharmacological reasoning, not something this trial tested brand by brand.
cards.source: Diener HC et al. The fixed combination of acetylsalicylic acid, paracetamol and caffeine is more effective than single substances and dual combination for the treatment of headache: a multicentre, randomized, double-blind, single-dose, placebo-controlled parallel group study. Cephalalgia. 2005. PMID: 16162254. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a genuine, modest over-the-counter win — about 1 in 5 pain-free at 2 hours versus 1 in 11 on placebo, and each ingredient earns its place in the combination
cards.summary: Synthesis: a genuine, modest over-the-counter win — about 1 in 5 pain-free at 2 hours versus 1 in 11 on placebo, and each ingredient earns its place in the combination
cards.people: Placebo-controlled meta-analysis (7 trials, 3,306 participants) plus the pivotal six-arm head-to-head trial (1,743 patients).
cards.result: Versus placebo: pain-free at 2 h 19.6% vs 9.0% (absolute gain ≈11 points); pain relief 54.3% vs 31.2%; adverse events 10.9% vs 7.8%. Versus components: the triple combination beat aspirin + paracetamol, aspirin alone, paracetamol alone and caffeine alone on time to 50% relief. For a patient whose attacks respond to simple analgesics, the fixed combination is a rational first step before triptans — with the usual aspirin and paracetamol cautions, and caffeine's own contribution to medication-overuse headache kept in mind.
cards.watchOut: No carded trial here compares the combination with a triptan, and none addresses frequent use: daily caffeine-containing analgesics are a recognised route into medication-overuse headache, which these single-dose trials cannot detect. Aspirin-containing products remain unsuitable for children and for patients with aspirin sensitivity or bleeding risk.
cards.source: Synthesis of Diener HC et al. Eur J Neurol. 2022 (PMID: 34519136); Diener HC et al. Cephalalgia. 2005 (PMID: 16162254).

shelves.title: Intratympanic gentamicin for refractory Ménière disease: the strongest vertigo control of the intratympanic options, bought with hearing — and the dosing schedule sets the price
shelves.question: In refractory Ménière disease, does intratympanic gentamicin control vertigo, and at what cost to hearing?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage, therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Ear, Middle · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Gentamicins/administration & dosage, therapeutic use · Humans · Male · Meniere Disease/complications · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Treatment Outcome · Vertigo/drug therapy, etiology
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the vertigo control is real, and so is the hearing bill; the schedule decides how big each is. The only double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Postema 2008, PMID: 18607963) found intratympanic gentamicin significantly reduced vertigo-complaint scores and aural fullness over one year in unilateral Ménière disease, at a mean hearing cost of about 8 dB in the treated ear (its abstract reports no sample size and no effect sizes — the shelf states the finding unquantified rather than inventing numbers). The pooled uncontrolled literature (Chia 2004, PMID: 15241234; 27 series) puts complete vertigo control between roughly two-thirds and four-fifths of patients depending on technique — titration dosing best at 81.7% complete and 96.3% complete-or-substantial control, low-dose worst at 66.7% complete — while overall hearing loss ranged from 13.1% with weekly dosing to 34.7% with multiple daily dosing, with no significant difference between techniques in profound hearing loss. The network meta-analysis of the randomised literature (Ahmadzai 2020, PMID: 32870918; 18 RCTs, 1,231 patients) ranked intratympanic gentamicin highest for complete vertigo control against placebo and worse than intratympanic steroid for hearing change, on an evidence base the reviewers rated mostly unclear or high risk of bias. So for the patient whose vertigo remains disabling despite conservative treatment, gentamicin is the most effective intratympanic option for stopping attacks — bought with a real, dose- and schedule-dependent risk to the hearing of an ear that may already be the patient's worse one. The head-to-head against intratympanic methylprednisolone (Patel 2016) is homed at shelf #633, where steroid matched gentamicin's vertigo control; this shelf answers the prior question — gentamicin against placebo and against its own dosing schedules. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit: vertigo control) / POSSIBLE (harm: hearing loss, schedule-dependent); Tier C (one small placebo-controlled trial whose abstract reports no numbers, resting on uncontrolled series for the rates).

cards.headline: Postema 2008: the only double-blind placebo-controlled trial — gentamicin significantly cut vertigo complaints and aural fullness, at a mean hearing cost of about 8 dB
cards.summary: Postema 2008: the only double-blind placebo-controlled trial — gentamicin significantly cut vertigo complaints and aural fullness, at a mean hearing cost of about 8 dB
cards.people: Patients with unilateral Ménière disease in a prospective, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial of intratympanic gentamicin; vertigo complaints, aural fullness and tinnitus were scored before, during and up to 1 year after treatment, with hearing monitored by pure-tone audiometry. The abstract does not report the sample size.
cards.result: Gentamicin treatment resulted in a significant reduction of the score for vertigo complaints and the score for perceived aural fullness versus placebo. A small increase in hearing loss (average 8 dB) was measured in the gentamicin group. No effect sizes, event counts or sample size are reported in the abstract — the finding is stated here exactly as quantified there: significant on symptoms, small on average hearing, unquantified beyond that.
cards.watchOut: This is the entire placebo-controlled base for a treatment in routine use, and its abstract withholds the numbers a reader needs — no n, no vertigo-score values, no hearing-loss rate. The 8 dB figure is a mean: it is compatible with most patients losing little and a minority losing much, which is exactly the distribution the uncontrolled series (next card) describe.
cards.source: Postema RJ et al. Intratympanic gentamicin therapy for control of vertigo in unilateral Menire's disease: a prospective, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial. Acta Oto-Laryngologica. 2008. PMID: 18607963. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Chia 2004: across 27 series, titration dosing controlled vertigo best (81.7% complete) — and hearing loss ran from 13.1% (weekly) to 34.7% (multiple daily dosing)
cards.summary: Chia 2004: across 27 series, titration dosing controlled vertigo best (81.7% complete) — and hearing loss ran from 13.1% (weekly) to 34.7% (multiple daily dosing)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of published intratympanic gentamicin series for Ménière disease, 1978–2002, grouped by delivery technique: multiple daily dosing (7 studies, n = 218), weekly dosing (2 studies, n = 84), low-dose (8 studies, n = 253), continuous microcatheter (4 studies, n = 156) and titration dosing (6 studies, n = 269). Vertigo control was classed complete, substantial or poor; hearing loss partial or profound.
cards.result: The titration method showed significantly better complete vertigo control (81.7%, P = 0.001) and effective (complete plus substantial) control (96.3%, P < 0.05) than other methods; the low-dose method showed significantly worse complete control (66.7%, P < 0.001) and a trend to worse effective control (86.8%, P = 0.05). For hearing: the weekly method trended toward less overall hearing loss (13.1%, P = 0.08) and the multiple-daily method showed significantly more overall hearing loss (34.7%, P < 0.01); no significant difference in profound hearing loss was found between methods. The degree of vestibular ablation did not correlate significantly with vertigo control or hearing outcome.
cards.watchOut: These are case series without comparators, pooled across two decades of changing technique and case mix — the percentages describe what treated cohorts experienced, not what gentamicin causes versus no treatment, and Ménière vertigo remits spontaneously in a substantial share of patients over the follow-up these series used. The schedule gradient (more doses, more hearing loss) is the most trustworthy signal in the card because it is consistent and mechanistically expected.
cards.source: Chia SH et al. Intratympanic gentamicin therapy for Ménière's disease: a meta-analysis. Otology & Neurotology. 2004. PMID: 15241234. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ahmadzai 2020: in the randomised network, gentamicin ranked first for complete vertigo control — and worse than intratympanic steroid for hearing
cards.summary: Ahmadzai 2020: in the randomised network, gentamicin ranked first for complete vertigo control — and worse than intratympanic steroid for hearing
cards.type: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of RCTs (Ahmadzai 2020)
cards.people: Systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis of randomised trials in Ménière disease: 18 unique RCTs, 1,231 patients, covering placebo, intratympanic gentamicin, oral high-dose betahistine, intratympanic steroid, and intratympanic steroid plus high-dose betahistine. Protocol registered with PROSPERO (CRD42019119129).
cards.result: The network meta-analysis of complete vertigo control suggested intratympanic gentamicin was associated with the highest probability of achieving better complete vertigo control compared with placebo, followed by intratympanic steroid plus high-dose betahistine. For hearing change, intratympanic gentamicin was worse than intratympanic steroid; the reviewers note gentamicin may perform well for vertigo control but be detrimental to hearing preservation at high cumulative dose and short injection intervals. Overall risk-of-bias appraisal suggested the evidence base was at unclear or high risk of bias.
cards.watchOut: A ranking, not a measurement: 'highest probability of complete vertigo control' rests on indirect comparisons across small trials the reviewers themselves rated unclear or high risk of bias, and the network cannot price the hearing harm in the same units as the vertigo benefit — that trade-off remains a clinical judgement, informed by the schedule data on the Chia card.
cards.source: Ahmadzai N et al. Pharmacologic and surgical therapies for patients with Meniere's disease: A systematic review and network meta-analysis. PLoS One. 2020. PMID: 32870918. Registry ID: PROSPERO CRD42019119129 (review protocol, as stated in the record). cards.headline: Synthesis: best vertigo control of the intratympanic options, paid for in hearing — the dosing schedule is the dose of both
cards.summary: Synthesis: best vertigo control of the intratympanic options, paid for in hearing — the dosing schedule is the dose of both
cards.people: One small double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Postema 2008, abstract unquantified), one meta-analysis of 27 uncontrolled series totalling about 980 patients (Chia 2004), and one network meta-analysis of 18 RCTs (1,231 patients; Ahmadzai 2020).
cards.result: Benefit: gentamicin significantly reduced vertigo complaints versus placebo in the one blinded trial; series report complete control in 66.7% (low-dose) to 81.7% (titration) and effective control up to 96.3%. Harm: mean hearing loss about 8 dB in the trial; overall hearing loss across series from 13.1% (weekly dosing) to 34.7% (multiple daily dosing), with profound loss not significantly different between schedules. The gentamicin-versus-steroid head-to-head (Patel 2016) is homed at shelf #633 and is not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Nothing here compares gentamicin with the natural history of Ménière disease over years, and nothing prices bilateral disease, where ablating vestibular function on one side carries a different risk. The shelf supports gentamicin as an effective, hearing-costly option for refractory unilateral vertigo — not as a first-line treatment, and not at the most aggressive schedules.
cards.source: Synthesis of Postema RJ et al. Acta Oto-Laryngologica. 2008 (PMID: 18607963); Chia SH et al. Otology & Neurotology. 2004 (PMID: 15241234); Ahmadzai N et al. PLoS One. 2020 (PMID: 32870918).

shelves.title: Statins after aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage: the small trials' vasospasm promise, answered by STASH — 803 patients, no improvement in outcome and no harm either
shelves.question: After aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage, does acute statin treatment improve long-term functional outcome?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Female · Homeostasis · Humans · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Intracranial Aneurysm/therapy · Ischemia · Ischemic Attack, Transient · Male · Middle Aged · Odds Ratio · Placebos · Pravastatin/therapeutic use · Regression Analysis · Subarachnoid Hemorrhage/therapy · Time Factors · Ultrasonography, Doppler, Transcranial · Vasospasm, Intracranial/therapy
shelves.balance: The small trials promised; the big trial answered no. Two early phase II trials reported striking relative reductions on vasospasm physiology: pravastatin 40 mg in 80 patients cut vasospasm incidence by 32% relative and vasospasm-related delayed ischaemic deficits by 83% relative (Tseng 2005, PMID: 16049199 — relative measures as reported; the abstract does not give the absolute event rates), and a 39-patient simvastatin 80 mg pilot found the drug safe and feasible with numerically less vasospasm and infarction (Chou 2008, PMID: 18658043). STASH then randomised 803 patients to simvastatin 40 mg or placebo for up to 21 days (PMID: 24837690): favourable outcome (modified Rankin 0–2) at 6 months in 271 of 391 on simvastatin versus 289 of 412 on placebo, adjusted common odds ratio 0.97 (95% CI 0.75 to 1.25), deaths 10% versus 9%, serious adverse events 18% in both groups — no benefit on long-term or short-term outcome, and no safety concern either. The pattern is the familiar one: a surrogate (vasospasm on Doppler and angiography) improved in small single-centre trials while the patient-centred outcome did not move in the adequately powered multicentre trial. Routine acute statin treatment after aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage is therefore not supported; this is a 'does not work for this purpose' answer, not a safety warning. The magnesium half of the slate question is homed at shelf #2397 (MASH-2) and nimodipine at #2390; neither is re-carded here. Tseng 2007 (PMID: 17413047) is a second report of the same 80-patient pravastatin trial (rescue therapy and 6-month outcome) and is not carded separately. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference); Tier C (the verdict rests on one definitive outcome trial against small positive pilots — a mortality/functional-outcome shelf).

cards.headline: Tseng 2005: pravastatin cut vasospasm by 32% relative and delayed ischaemic deficits by 83% relative in 80 patients — surrogate outcomes, no absolute rates in the abstract
cards.summary: Tseng 2005: pravastatin cut vasospasm by 32% relative and delayed ischaemic deficits by 83% relative in 80 patients — surrogate outcomes, no absolute rates in the abstract
cards.people: 80 patients (aged 18–84) with aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage, randomised within 72 hours of ictus to oral pravastatin 40 mg or placebo daily for up to 14 days. Primary endpoints were transcranial-Doppler vasospasm incidence, duration and severity and duration of impaired autoregulation; secondary endpoints were vasospasm-related delayed ischaemic deficits (DIDs) and disability at discharge.
cards.result: The incidences of vasospasm and severe vasospasm were reduced by 32% (P = 0.006) and 42% (P = 0.044) respectively in relative terms, the duration of severe vasospasm was shortened by 0.8 days (P = 0.068), and the duration of impaired autoregulation was shortened bilaterally (P ≤ 0.01). The incidence of vasospasm-related DIDs and mortality were decreased by 83% (P < 0.001) and 75% (P = 0.037) respectively in relative terms, as reported by the authors; the abstract does not report the absolute event rates behind these relative reductions. No treatment-related complication was observed.
cards.watchOut: Every headline number on this card is a relative reduction on a physiological or composite endpoint in 80 patients at one centre, with the absolute rates unreported in the abstract — an 83% relative reduction in DIDs could be a large absolute benefit or a handful of events, and the abstract does not let the reader tell. A 6-month follow-up report of this same trial (Tseng 2007, PMID: 17413047) exists and is not a second trial.
cards.source: Tseng MY et al. Effects of acute treatment with pravastatin on cerebral vasospasm, autoregulation, and delayed ischemic deficits after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage: a phase II randomized placebo-controlled trial. Stroke. 2005. PMID: 16049199. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Chou 2008: simvastatin 80 mg was safe and feasible in 39 patients — vasospasm 5/19 versus 8/20, infarcts 2/19 versus 5/20, deaths 0 versus 3
cards.summary: Chou 2008: simvastatin 80 mg was safe and feasible in 39 patients — vasospasm 5/19 versus 8/20, infarcts 2/19 versus 5/20, deaths 0 versus 3
cards.people: 39 statin-naïve patients with Fisher grade 3 aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage, double-blind randomised to simvastatin 80 mg/day (n = 19) or placebo (n = 20), stratified by Hunt and Hess grade. Primary endpoints were death and drug morbidity; vasospasm was angiographically confirmed.
cards.result: Mortality was 0 of 19 in the simvastatin group and 3 of 20 in the placebo group. Study drug was withdrawn in one subject in each group for reversible liver-enzyme or creatine-kinase elevation. Angiographically confirmed vasospasm occurred in 5 of 19 simvastatin-treated subjects versus 8 of 20 on placebo, and vasospasm-related ischaemic infarcts in 2 of 19 versus 5 of 20. The authors conclude simvastatin for prevention of delayed cerebral ischaemia is safe and feasible after subarachnoid haemorrhage and that a larger study was needed to test efficacy.
cards.watchOut: A pilot designed for safety and feasibility: with 39 patients, the favourable numerical differences (including 0 versus 3 deaths) are compatible with chance, and the authors say so by design. Its correct use is as the feasibility bridge to STASH — not as evidence of benefit.
cards.source: Chou SH et al. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot study of simvastatin in aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage. Stroke. 2008. PMID: 18658043.
