cards.headline: STASH 2014: 803 patients — simvastatin 40 mg did not improve 6-month outcome (favourable outcome 271/391 vs 289/412; common OR 0.97, 0.75–1.25), with no safety signal
cards.summary: STASH 2014: 803 patients — simvastatin 40 mg did not improve 6-month outcome (favourable outcome 271/391 vs 289/412; common OR 0.97, 0.75–1.25), with no safety signal
cards.type: Multicentre randomised double-blind phase 3 trial (STASH, Kirkpatrick 2014)
cards.people: 803 patients aged 18–65 with confirmed aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage presenting within 96 hours of ictus, randomised at 35 neurosurgical centres in nine countries to simvastatin 40 mg (n = 391) or placebo (n = 412) once daily for up to 21 days. Primary outcome: distribution of modified Rankin Scale score at 6 months, analysed by intention to treat; 782 patients (97%) had outcome data.
cards.result: Favourable outcome (mRS 0–2) was recorded in 271 patients in the simvastatin group versus 289 in the placebo group; the adjusted ordinal analysis gave a common odds ratio of 0.97 (95% CI 0.75 to 1.25; P = 0.803). At 6 months there were 37 deaths (10%) in the simvastatin group and 35 (9%) in the placebo group (log-rank P = 0.592). Serious adverse events were reported in 70 patients (18%) on simvastatin and 74 (18%) on placebo, with no suspected unexpected serious adverse reactions. The authors conclude patients with subarachnoid haemorrhage should not be treated routinely with simvastatin during the acute stage.
cards.watchOut: STASH tested simvastatin 40 mg started within 96 hours for up to 21 days in patients up to 65 — it does not address continuing a pre-existing statin prescription, other statins or doses, or patients over 65, and its confidence interval (0.75–1.25) excludes a large benefit but not a small one in either direction. Within those bounds it is the definitive trial the pilots called for, and it is null.
cards.source: Kirkpatrick PJ et al. Simvastatin in aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage (STASH): a multicentre randomised phase 3 trial. The Lancet Neurology. 2014. PMID: 24837690. Registry ID: ISRCTN75948817 (Current Controlled Trials, as listed in the record). cards.headline: Synthesis: the vasospasm signal was real in small trials and irrelevant at scale — acute statins after aneurysmal SAH do not improve outcome
cards.summary: Synthesis: the vasospasm signal was real in small trials and irrelevant at scale — acute statins after aneurysmal SAH do not improve outcome
cards.people: Two small randomised pilots (pravastatin, n = 80, Tseng 2005; simvastatin 80 mg, n = 39, Chou 2008) and one multicentre phase 3 trial (simvastatin 40 mg, n = 803, STASH 2014).
cards.result: Pilots: relative reductions of 32% in vasospasm and 83% in delayed ischaemic deficits (Tseng, absolutes unreported); vasospasm 5/19 versus 8/20 and infarcts 2/19 versus 5/20 (Chou). Phase 3: favourable 6-month outcome 271/391 versus 289/412 (common OR 0.97, 95% CI 0.75–1.25), deaths 10% versus 9%, serious adverse events 18% versus 18%. The magnesium question from the same slate topic is answered at shelf #2397 and nimodipine at #2390; neither is re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote the pilots' relative reductions without STASH beside them: this shelf exists because the small-trial numbers are still cited as if the phase 3 trial had not happened. Equally, STASH is a verdict on starting simvastatin acutely for neuroprotection — it says nothing about statins for their ordinary cardiovascular indications in these patients once the acute phase has passed.
cards.source: Synthesis of Tseng MY et al. Stroke. 2005 (PMID: 16049199); Chou SH et al. Stroke. 2008 (PMID: 18658043); Kirkpatrick PJ et al. The Lancet Neurology. 2014 (PMID: 24837690).

shelves.title: Capsaicin 8% patch for painful diabetic neuropathy: a modest, local pain reduction from a single clinic application — relief without systemic drug exposure
shelves.question: In painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy, does the capsaicin 8% patch relieve pain?
shelves.mesh: Blood Glucose/metabolism · Capsaicin/*administration & dosage · Diabetic Neuropathies/complications, *drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Pain Measurement · Sensory System Agents/*administration & dosage · Sleep Wake Disorders/drug therapy, etiology · Statistics, Nonparametric · Time Factors · Transdermal Patch
shelves.balance: One placebo-controlled trial carries the efficacy claim. In 369 patients with painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy, a single 30-minute application of the capsaicin 8% patch reduced average daily pain by 27.4% versus 20.9% on a placebo patch between weeks 2 and 8 (P = .025) (Simpson 2017, PMID: 27746370) — a modest absolute separation of about 6.5 percentage points on percentage pain reduction, with a faster median time to response (19 versus 72 days) and small improvements in sleep interference. The safety half of the question is better populated: in a 52-week open-label randomised study of 468 patients, repeated patch treatments (up to seven, at least eight weeks apart) plus standard care produced no deterioration in sensory perception or reflexes and no negative signal on neuropathy scales versus standard care alone, at the price of application-site pain in 28–29% (Vinik 2016, PMID: 27919222). The patch's appeal is what it does not do: no systemic exposure, no drug interactions, no sedation — in a population usually offered sedating systemic drugs. Its limits are equally plain: one efficacy trial, and a placebo problem (the active patch burns on application, the placebo patch much less, so blinding is fragile). The postherpetic-neuralgia evidence for the same patch is homed at shelf #2565, and the duloxetine comparison at #695; neither is re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) (Tier C: a single placebo-controlled efficacy trial).

cards.headline: Simpson 2017: one 30-minute capsaicin 8% application cut foot pain by 27.4% versus 20.9% on placebo patch over weeks 2–8 (P = .025)
cards.summary: Simpson 2017: one 30-minute capsaicin 8% application cut foot pain by 27.4% versus 20.9% on placebo patch over weeks 2–8 (P = .025)
cards.people: 369 adults with painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy randomised 1:1 to a single 30-minute treatment with capsaicin 8% patch (n = 186) or placebo patch (n = 183) applied to the painful areas of the feet, followed for 12 weeks. Primary endpoint: percentage reduction in average daily pain score from baseline to weeks 2–8.
cards.result: Pain fell by 27.4% on capsaicin versus 20.9% on placebo (P = .025), with separation visible from week 2. Median time to treatment response was 19 days versus 72 days. Sleep interference scores improved modestly more with capsaicin (weeks 2–8, P = .030; weeks 2–12, P = .020). Apart from application-site reactions, treatment-emergent adverse events were similar between groups, and there was no deterioration in sensory perception of sharp, cold, warm or vibration stimuli.
cards.watchOut: Blinding is fragile: the active patch burns on application and the placebo patch largely does not, so patients can guess their allocation — a known inflation risk for subjective pain endpoints. The placebo patch itself produced a 20.9% pain reduction, so the drug-attributable gain is the 6.5-point gap, not the headline 27.4%. The record names the treatment by formulation and dose (capsaicin 8% patch) only; no brand or manufacturer is named in it.
cards.source: Simpson DM et al.. Capsaicin 8% Patch in Painful Diabetic Peripheral Neuropathy: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Study. The Journal of Pain. 2017. PMID: 27746370. cards.headline: Vinik 2016: a year of repeated capsaicin 8% patch treatments caused no sensory or neurological deterioration versus standard care alone
cards.summary: Vinik 2016: a year of repeated capsaicin 8% patch treatments caused no sensory or neurological deterioration versus standard care alone
cards.people: 468 patients with painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy randomised in Europe to capsaicin 8% patch repeat treatment (30-minute applications, n = 156; 60-minute, n = 157; one to seven treatments at ≥8-week intervals) plus standard of care, or standard of care alone (n = 155), for 52 weeks. Primary objective was safety, assessed by the Norfolk Quality of Life–Diabetic Neuropathy score, the Utah Early Neuropathy Scale and standardised sensory testing.
cards.result: By end of study, Norfolk QOL-DN total score improved more with patch plus standard care (−27.6% for 30-minute and −32.8% for 60-minute applications) than with standard care alone (−6.7%), and UENS scores likewise moved favourably (−2.1 and −3.0 versus −1.2). No detrimental change appeared in any Norfolk or UENS subscale and no worsening in sharp, warm, cold or vibration perception. The commonest adverse events were application-site pain (28.2% and 29.3%), burning sensation (9.0% and 9.6%) and application-site erythema (7.7% and 8.9%).
cards.watchOut: Open-label and designed for safety, not efficacy: the quality-of-life differences are unblinded comparisons against standard care and cannot be read as proof of pain relief — that claim rests on the Simpson trial alone. Registration was retrospective (posted after the study began), as the record itself states.
cards.source: Vinik AI et al.. Capsaicin 8% patch repeat treatment plus standard of care (SOC) versus SOC alone in painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy: a randomised, 52-week, open-label, safety study. BMC Neurology. 2016. PMID: 27919222. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01478607. randomised open-label 52-week safety study (vinik 2016) 468 patients with painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy randomised in europe to capsaicin 8% patch repeat treatment (30-minute applications, n = 156; 60-minute, n = 157; one to seven treatments at ≥8-week intervals) plus standard of care, or standard of care alone (n = 155), for 52 weeks. primary objective was safety, assessed by the norfolk quality of life–diabetic neuropathy score, the utah early neuropathy scale and standardised sensory testing. by end of study, norfolk qol-dn total score improved more with patch plus standard care (−27.6% for 30-minute and −32.8% for 60-minute applications) than with standard care alone (−6.7%), and uens scores likewise moved favourably (−2.1 and −3.0 versus −1.2). no detrimental change appeared in any norfolk or uens subscale and no worsening in sharp, warm, cold or vibration perception. the commonest adverse events were application-site pain (28.2% and 29.3%), burning sensation (9.0% and 9.6%) and application-site erythema (7.7% and 8.9%). open-label and designed for safety, not efficacy: the quality-of-life differences are unblinded comparisons against standard care and cannot be read as proof of pain relief — that claim rests on the simpson trial alone. registration was retrospective (posted after the study began), as the record itself states. vinik ai et al.. capsaicin 8% patch repeat treatment plus standard of care (soc) versus soc alone in painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy: a randomised, 52-week, open-label, safety study. bmc neurology. 2016. pmid: 27919222. registry id: clinicaltrials.gov nct01478607. mesh: administration, cutaneous · adult · aged · capsaicin/administration & dosage, *adverse effects · diabetic neuropathies/complications, *drug therapy · female · humans · male · middle aged · neuralgia/*drug therapy, etiology · *outcome assessment, health care · sensory system agents/administration & dosage, *adverse effects · *standard of care

cards.headline: Synthesis: modest pain relief from one small trial, a reassuring year-long safety profile, and a treatment whose main cost is a painful half-hour in clinic
cards.summary: Synthesis: modest pain relief from one small trial, a reassuring year-long safety profile, and a treatment whose main cost is a painful half-hour in clinic
cards.people: One double-blind placebo-controlled efficacy trial (n = 369, 12 weeks) and one open-label randomised safety study (n = 468, 52 weeks), both in painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy of the feet.
cards.result: Efficacy: pain −27.4% versus −20.9% (weeks 2–8), response at a median 19 versus 72 days, small sleep gains. Safety over a year of repeat use: no sensory deterioration on formal testing; application-site pain in roughly 3 of 10 treatments. The balance is a local, non-systemic option with a small average effect — most attractive where systemic neuropathic-pain drugs are limited by sedation, interactions or renal function.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial compares the patch with duloxetine, pregabalin or amitriptyline, so this shelf cannot rank it against the systemic standards — those comparisons do not exist in the record. Effect durability beyond 12 weeks per application is inferred from the repeat-treatment schedule, not measured against placebo.
cards.source: Synthesis of Simpson DM et al. The Journal of Pain. 2017 (PMID: 27746370); Vinik AI et al. BMC Neurology. 2016 (PMID: 27919222).

shelves.title: Oral versus intravenous methylprednisolone for MS relapses: the large double-blind COPOUSEP trial found oral treatment non-inferior at 28 days (81% vs 80% improved), and the earlier small-trial synthesis agrees
shelves.question: In adults having a multiple sclerosis relapse, is oral high-dose methylprednisolone as effective as intravenous methylprednisolone?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adolescent · Adult · Double-Blind Method · Female · France · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage* · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Male · Methylprednisolone/administration & dosage* · Middle Aged · Multiple Sclerosis, Relapsing-Remitting/drug therapy* · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: LIKELY (no difference): One large double-blind non-inferiority trial and an earlier Cochrane synthesis of five small trials point the same way. In COPOUSEP (199 patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis treated within 15 days of a relapse), oral methylprednisolone 1,000 mg daily for 3 days was non-inferior to the same dose given intravenously: 81% of the oral group and 80% of the intravenous group had improved by day 28 without retreatment (absolute difference 0.5 percentage points, 90% CI −9.5 to 10.4, against a pre-set 15% non-inferiority margin) (Le Page E et al., PMID: 26135706). The Cochrane review (Burton JM et al., PMID: 23235634) pooled five older trials (215 patients) and likewise found no significant difference in disability recovery at four weeks (mean EDSS difference −0.22, P = 0.20) or in MRI activity — though only two of its five trials used modern methods, which is why COPOUSEP carries the weight. Adverse events in COPOUSEP were similar by route; insomnia was reported more often with oral treatment (77% vs 64%). A cost-utility analysis of the same COPOUSEP trial (Michel M et al., PMID: 34598781 — a secondary report of the carded trial, not carded separately) found oral treatment cost-effective, with larger savings if relapses are treated at home. The practical conclusion: the route is a logistics, comfort and cost decision, not an efficacy one. Tier C is set because the non-inferiority claim rests on one pivotal trial.

cards.headline: COPOUSEP 2015: oral methylprednisolone non-inferior to intravenous — 81% vs 80% improved by day 28 (difference 0.5 points, 90% CI −9.5 to 10.4)
cards.summary: COPOUSEP 2015: oral methylprednisolone non-inferior to intravenous — 81% vs 80% improved by day 28 (difference 0.5 points, 90% CI −9.5 to 10.4)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind non-inferiority trial (COPOUSEP, Le Page 2015)
cards.people: 199 patients aged 18–55 with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis and a relapse within the previous 15 days (mean time from relapse onset to treatment about 7 days), at 13 French MS centres; 100 were assigned oral and 99 intravenous methylprednisolone 1,000 mg once daily for 3 days, double-dummy (placebo capsules and saline infusions), with patients, physicians, nurses and assessors all masked. The per-protocol population was 82 oral and 90 intravenous.
cards.result: By day 28, 66 of 82 patients (81%) in the oral group and 72 of 90 (80%) in the intravenous group had improved by at least one point on the most affected Kurtzke Functional System Scale score without needing retreatment — an absolute difference of 0.5 percentage points (90% CI −9.5 to 10.4), inside the pre-set 15% non-inferiority margin. Adverse-event rates were similar overall; insomnia was more frequent with oral treatment (77 of 100 patients, 77%, vs 63 of 99, 64%).
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority against a generous 15% margin, in a per-protocol analysis: the data exclude a large inferiority of the oral route, not a small one. Patients were 18–55 with relapsing-remitting disease treated early; the trial does not address progressive MS or relapses severe enough to need plasma exchange.
cards.source: Le Page E et al. Oral versus intravenous high-dose methylprednisolone for treatment of relapses in patients with multiple sclerosis (COPOUSEP): a randomised, controlled, double-blind, non-inferiority trial. cards.headline: Burton 2012 (Cochrane): five small trials, 215 patients — no significant difference in relapse recovery or MRI activity between oral and intravenous steroids
cards.summary: Burton 2012 (Cochrane): five small trials, 215 patients — no significant difference in relapse recovery or MRI activity between oral and intravenous steroids
cards.people: Five randomised or quasi-randomised trials (215 patients over 16 with clinically definite multiple sclerosis and relapses within six weeks) comparing oral with intravenous steroids. Only one outcome — EDSS improvement at four weeks — was common to three trials, and two trials reported MRI outcomes.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in relapse recovery at week 4 (mean EDSS difference −0.22, P = 0.20; the abstract prints the confidence limits as 0.71 to 0.26, read conventionally as −0.71 to 0.26, spanning no effect) and no difference in MRI gadolinium-enhancement activity. The reviewers conclude that oral steroid therapy may be a practical and effective alternative to intravenous therapy for MS relapses.
cards.watchOut: Only two of the five trials used current, rigorous methods, and the pooled sample is smaller than COPOUSEP alone — this synthesis supports, but cannot carry, the equivalence claim. It also predates COPOUSEP, whose rigorous design it explicitly anticipated.
cards.source: Burton JM et al. Oral versus intravenous steroids for treatment of relapses in multiple sclerosis. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2012. PMID: 23235634. cards.summary: Synthesis: oral and intravenous high-dose methylprednisolone recover MS relapses equally — the choice is logistics, comfort and cost
cards.people: One large double-blind non-inferiority trial (199 randomised, 172 per-protocol) and one Cochrane synthesis of five earlier small trials (215 patients).
cards.result: Day-28 improvement 81% (oral) vs 80% (intravenous), difference 0.5 percentage points with the confidence interval excluding the 15% non-inferiority margin; the small-trial synthesis found no difference in four-week disability recovery or MRI activity. shelves.title: Ganaxolone for CDKL5 deficiency disorder: the first controlled trial in the syndrome cut major motor seizures by a median 30.7% versus 6.9% on placebo — real, modest, and so far only 17 weeks deep
shelves.question: In children and adults with CDKL5 deficiency disorder, does ganaxolone reduce convulsive seizure frequency versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Child · Child, Preschool · Double-Blind Method · Epileptic Syndromes*/drug therapy,enzymology · Humans · Infant · Pregnanolone*/analogs & derivatives · Prospective Studies · Protein Serine-Threonine Kinases/deficiency · Seizures/drug therapy,enzymology · Spasms, Infantile*/drug therapy,enzymology · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one phase 3 randomised trial (Marigold, Knight EMP et al., PMID: 35429480) in 101 children and young people aged 2–21 years with CDKL5 deficiency disorder and refractory major motor seizures found a median percentage change in 28-day major motor seizure frequency of −30.7% on ganaxolone versus −6.9% on placebo over 17 weeks (p=0.0036; Hodges–Lehmann median difference −27.1%, 95% CI −47.9 to −9.6). Tolerability was broadly similar between arms (treatment-emergent adverse events 86% vs 88%; serious adverse events 12% vs 10%), with somnolence, pyrexia and upper respiratory infections commoner on ganaxolone, and no deaths in the double-blind phase. A 2025 systematic review of antiseizure medications in CDKL5 encephalopathy (Kalinowska-Doman A et al., PMID: 40834685) independently describes ganaxolone's effect as a modest reduction of approximately 30% in seizure frequency, in a field where most evidence is small and uncontrolled. This is a single trial in a rare syndrome, with a surrogate frequency outcome over 17 weeks and no long-term controlled data yet. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): ganaxolone modestly reduces major motor seizure frequency in CDKL5 deficiency disorder over the short term; durability and developmental benefit are unproven.

cards.headline: Knight 2022 (Marigold): ganaxolone cut median 28-day major motor seizure frequency by −30.7% versus −6.9% on placebo over 17 weeks (p=0.0036)
cards.summary: Knight 2022 (Marigold): ganaxolone cut median 28-day major motor seizure frequency by −30.7% versus −6.9% on placebo over 17 weeks (p=0.0036)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (Marigold, Knight 2022)
cards.people: 101 patients aged 2–21 years (median age 6 years, IQR 3 to 10) with a pathogenic or probably pathogenic CDKL5 variant and at least 16 major motor seizures per 28 days in each 4-week period of an 8-week historical period, at 39 outpatient clinics in eight countries; randomised to enteral adjunctive ganaxolone (n=50; maximum 63 mg/kg per day if ≤28 kg or 1800 mg/day if >28 kg) or matching placebo (n=51) for 17 weeks after a 6-week prospective baseline. The primary endpoint was analysed in 100 patients.
cards.result: Median percentage change in 28-day major motor seizure frequency from baseline to the 17-week double-blind phase was −30.7% (IQR −49.5 to −1.9) in the ganaxolone group and −6.9% (−24.1 to 39.7) in the placebo group (p=0.0036, Wilcoxon rank-sum test); the Hodges–Lehmann estimate of the median difference was −27.1% (95% CI −47.9 to −9.6). Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 43 (86%) of 50 ganaxolone patients and 45 (88%) of 51 placebo patients; somnolence, pyrexia and upper respiratory tract infections occurred in at least 10% of the ganaxolone group and more frequently than with placebo. Serious adverse events occurred in six (12%) ganaxolone and five (10%) placebo patients; two (4%) ganaxolone and four (8%) placebo patients discontinued; there were no deaths in the double-blind phase.
cards.watchOut: A single trial of 101 patients in a rare syndrome, funded by the manufacturer (Marinus Pharmaceuticals), with a 17-week frequency outcome: it cannot show effects on development, behaviour, or long-term seizure trajectories, and the wide confidence interval on the median difference (−47.9 to −9.6) leaves the true size of benefit uncertain. The open-label extension was still ongoing at publication.
cards.source: Knight EMP et al. Safety and efficacy of ganaxolone in patients with CDKL5 deficiency disorder: results from the double-blind phase of a randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial. The Lancet. Neurology. 2022. PMID: 35429480. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03572933, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Kalinowska-Doman 2025 (systematic review): across CDKL5 antiseizure treatments, ganaxolone showed a modest ~30% seizure-frequency reduction; the wider evidence base is small and mostly uncontrolled
cards.summary: Kalinowska-Doman 2025 (systematic review): across CDKL5 antiseizure treatments, ganaxolone showed a modest ~30% seizure-frequency reduction; the wider evidence base is small and mostly uncontrolled
cards.people: Systematic review (PRISMA) of studies published January 2019 to October 2024 on antiseizure medication effectiveness in CDKL5 deficiency disorder, in which epilepsy appears in 90% of cases within the first 12 months of life and is highly drug-resistant; the reviewer also searched clinicaltrials.gov for trial results.
cards.result: The most well-studied medications were classic antiseizure medications, among which clobazam, lamotrigine, valproic acid and vigabatrin were considered the most effective; only about 30% of patients were identified as responders to sodium channel blockers. Ganaxolone demonstrated a modest reduction of approximately 30% in seizure frequency. Cannabidiol showed variable efficacy across patient populations, with the most pronounced benefits in reducing motor seizures, and the ketogenic diet demonstrated approximately a 50% reduction of seizures as an adjunctive therapy. The reviewers conclude that, because of the low number of patients studied worldwide, information on treatment options and outcomes is limited and larger prospective studies are needed.
cards.watchOut: A single-reviewer narrative systematic review without pooled effect estimates: its ~30% figure for ganaxolone restates the Marigold trial rather than adding independent controlled evidence, and most comparator treatments it summarises rest on uncontrolled reports. It is carded for context on how thin the whole CDKL5 treatment literature is, not as a second efficacy estimate.
cards.source: Kalinowska-Doman A et al. Antiseizure medications in CDKL5 encephalopathy- systematic review. Seizure. 2025. PMID: 40834685. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: one well-run trial, a real but modest frequency reduction, and nothing yet on the outcomes that matter most in this syndrome
cards.summary: Synthesis: one well-run trial, a real but modest frequency reduction, and nothing yet on the outcomes that matter most in this syndrome
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: the Marigold phase 3 trial (101 patients) and a 2025 systematic review of antiseizure medications in CDKL5 deficiency disorder.
cards.result: Seizure frequency: median −30.7% on ganaxolone versus −6.9% on placebo at 17 weeks (median difference −27.1%, 95% CI −47.9 to −9.6; p=0.0036). Safety over 17 weeks: adverse events 86% vs 88%, serious adverse events 12% vs 10%, no deaths. Development, behaviour, quality of life and long-term seizure control: no controlled data in either record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Tier C is set because the entire controlled evidence base is one 101-patient, 17-week, manufacturer-funded trial in a rare syndrome; a second controlled trial or mature open-label follow-up could move this stamp in either direction. Seizure-frequency reduction is not the same as developmental gain in CDKL5 deficiency disorder, and this shelf should not be quoted as showing one.

shelves.title: Rufinamide for Lennox–Gastaut syndrome: drop attacks fell by a median 42.5% versus a 1.4% rise on placebo in the pivotal trial, and the pooled studies agree
shelves.question: In patients with Lennox–Gastaut syndrome, does adjunctive rufinamide reduce drop seizures versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Anticonvulsants/administration & dosage*,adverse effects · Child · Child, Preschool · Epilepsy/drug therapy* · Epilepsy, Absence/drug therapy · Epilepsy, Generalized/drug therapy · Epilepsy, Tonic-Clonic/drug therapy · Female · Humans · Male · Syndrome · Treatment Outcome · Triazoles/administration & dosage*,adverse effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the pivotal trial (Glauser T et al., PMID: 18401024) randomised 138 patients aged 4–30 years with Lennox–Gastaut syndrome and found a median percentage reduction in total seizure frequency of 32.7% on adjunctive rufinamide versus 11.7% on placebo (p=0.0015), with tonic–atonic ('drop attack') seizures reduced by a median 42.5% on rufinamide versus a 1.4% increase on placebo (p<0.0001) and higher 50% responder rates for both total and tonic–atonic seizures. A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis specific to Lennox–Gastaut syndrome (Sharawat IK et al., PMID: 34273668) pooled five placebo-controlled studies (265 rufinamide, 203 placebo patients) and found an average percentage reduction in total seizure frequency per 28 days of 29.3% versus 8.3% (difference 20.9%, 95% CI 14.4% to 27.3% as printed in the record; p<0.00001), at the cost of more treatment-emergent adverse events (60.2% vs 50.7%; RR 1.24 relative, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.51). Somnolence (24.3% vs 12.5%) and vomiting (21.6% vs 6.3%) were the commonest harms in the pivotal trial. The evidence is one pivotal trial plus small pooled studies, all short-term, in a syndrome where complete seizure freedom is rare. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): rufinamide reduces total and drop-attack seizures in Lennox–Gastaut syndrome by a clinically useful margin, with mild-to-moderate tolerability costs.

cards.headline: Glauser 2008: rufinamide cut total seizures by a median 32.7% versus 11.7% on placebo, and drop attacks by 42.5% versus a 1.4% increase (p<0.0001)
cards.summary: Glauser 2008: rufinamide cut total seizures by a median 32.7% versus 11.7% on placebo, and drop attacks by 42.5% versus a 1.4% increase (p<0.0001)
cards.people: 138 patients aged 4–30 years with Lennox–Gastaut syndrome — multiple seizure types including tonic–atonic and atypical absence seizures, at least 90 seizures in the month before baseline, and a recent slow spike-and-wave EEG — randomised after a 28-day baseline to adjunctive rufinamide (n=74) or placebo (n=64) on top of their other antiepileptic drugs.
cards.result: The median percentage reduction in total seizure frequency was greater with rufinamide than placebo (32.7% vs 11.7%, p=0.0015). Tonic–atonic ('drop attack') seizure frequency differed strongly between groups (p<0.0001): a 42.5% median percentage reduction with rufinamide versus a 1.4% increase with placebo. The rufinamide group had greater improvement in seizure severity (p=0.0041) and a higher 50% responder rate than placebo for total seizures (p=0.0045) and for tonic–atonic seizures (p=0.002). Adverse events reported by at least 10% of rufinamide patients were somnolence (24.3% with rufinamide vs 12.5% with placebo) and vomiting (21.6% vs 6.3%).
cards.watchOut: One trial of 138 patients with short double-blind follow-up: responder and frequency outcomes are reported as p-values and medians without confidence intervals in the record, seizure freedom is not reported, and the population (ages 4–30, very high baseline seizure counts) is the severe end of Lennox–Gastaut syndrome. Injury from drop attacks — the outcome families fear most — was not itself an endpoint.

cards.headline: Sharawat 2021 (meta-analysis): across five placebo-controlled studies, rufinamide reduced total seizure frequency by 29.3% versus 8.3% on placebo (difference 20.9%), with more adverse events (60.2% vs 50.7%)
cards.summary: Sharawat 2021 (meta-analysis): across five placebo-controlled studies, rufinamide reduced total seizure frequency by 29.3% versus 8.3% on placebo (difference 20.9%), with more adverse events (60.2% vs 50.7%)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 5 placebo-controlled studies (Sharawat 2021)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of rufinamide in Lennox–Gastaut syndrome: ten studies including 557 patients in total; the placebo-controlled efficacy analysis pooled five studies enrolling 265 patients in the rufinamide group and 203 in the placebo group, with an additional analysis of uncontrolled studies of at least 20 patients.
cards.result: The average percentage reduction in total seizure frequency per 28 days during the double-blind phase was 29.3% in the rufinamide group compared with 8.3% in the placebo group (difference between the two groups 20.9%, 95% CI 14.4% to 27.3% as printed in the record in negative form; p<0.00001). Rufinamide was also more efficacious than placebo for individual seizure types — tonic-clonic, atypical absence, atonic, focal and myoclonic seizures (all p<0.00001). The number of patients with at least one treatment-emergent adverse event was significantly higher with rufinamide (60.2% vs 50.7%, p=0.02; RR 1.24 relative, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.51). The authors conclude rufinamide is efficacious as adjunctive therapy in Lennox–Gastaut syndrome with mild adverse reactions.
cards.watchOut: The pooled placebo-controlled base is still only 468 patients and is dominated by the single pivotal trial, so the meta-analysis largely restates Glauser 2008 with smaller studies around it; the record prints the between-group difference with negative signs (−14.4% to −27.3%), which this card renders as the magnitude of the advantage. Uncontrolled studies were used only for the supplementary efficacy estimate, not the placebo comparison.

shelves.title: Cannabidiol for tuberous sclerosis seizures: 48.6% fewer seizures at 25 mg/kg/day versus 26.5% on placebo — and 50 mg added diarrhoea and liver-enzyme rises, not benefit
shelves.question: In patients with tuberous sclerosis complex and drug-resistant seizures, does adjunctive cannabidiol reduce seizure frequency versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Anticonvulsants/administration & dosage*,adverse effects · Cannabidiol/administration & dosage*,adverse effects · Child · Child, Preschool · Diarrhea/chemically induced · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Infant · Internationality · Male · Middle Aged · Seizures/diagnosis*,drug therapy*,epidemiology · Sleepiness/drug effects · Treatment Outcome · Tuberous Sclerosis/diagnosis*,drug therapy*,epidemiology · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the GWPCARE6 trial (Thiele EA et al., PMID: 33346789) randomised 224 patients aged 1–65 years with tuberous sclerosis complex and medication-resistant epilepsy to cannabidiol 25 mg/kg/day, cannabidiol 50 mg/kg/day, or placebo for 16 weeks. Seizures fell by 48.6% (95% CI 40.4% to 55.8%) on the 25 mg dose and 47.5% (39.0% to 54.8%) on the 50 mg dose versus 26.5% (14.9% to 36.5%) on placebo — a percentage reduction from placebo of 30.1% (95% CI 13.9% to 43.3%; P<.001) and 28.5% (11.9% to 42.0%; nominal P=.002) respectively, i.e. the higher dose added nothing on efficacy. It did add harm: diarrhoea in 31% (25 mg) and 56% (50 mg) versus 25% on placebo, somnolence in 13% and 26% versus 9%, discontinuations for adverse events in 8, 10 and 2 patients respectively, and elevated liver transaminases in 28 cannabidiol patients (18.9%) versus none on placebo. A meta-analysis across the Dravet, Lennox–Gastaut and tuberous sclerosis randomised trials (Talwar A et al., PMID: 36206805) found the same pattern for tuberous sclerosis specifically (odds of a ≥50% seizure reduction OR 1.99 relative, 95% CI 1.06 to 3.76) alongside more adverse and serious adverse events overall. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): cannabidiol reduces tuberous sclerosis seizures versus placebo, the 25 mg/kg/day dose carries the better safety profile, and liver-enzyme and interaction monitoring are part of the treatment, not an afterthought.

cards.headline: Thiele 2021 (GWPCARE6): cannabidiol cut TSC seizures by 48.6% (25 mg/kg/day) and 47.5% (50 mg/kg/day) versus 26.5% on placebo — the higher dose added harm, not efficacy
cards.summary: Thiele 2021 (GWPCARE6): cannabidiol cut TSC seizures by 48.6% (25 mg/kg/day) and 47.5% (50 mg/kg/day) versus 26.5% on placebo — the higher dose added harm, not efficacy
cards.people: 224 patients (median age 11.4 years, range 1.1–56.8; 93 female, 41.5%) with a clinical diagnosis of tuberous sclerosis complex and medication-resistant epilepsy — at least 8 TSC-associated seizures during the 4-week baseline, at least 1 seizure in at least 3 of the 4 weeks, and taking at least 1 antiepileptic medication — at 46 sites in six countries; randomised to cannabidiol 25 mg/kg/day (n=75), cannabidiol 50 mg/kg/day (n=73), or matched placebo (n=76) for 16 weeks; 201 completed treatment.
cards.result: The percentage reduction from baseline in TSC-associated seizures (the primary endpoint type) was 48.6% (95% CI 40.4% to 55.8%) for cannabidiol 25 mg/kg/day, 47.5% (39.0% to 54.8%) for 50 mg/kg/day, and 26.5% (14.9% to 36.5%) for placebo; the percentage reduction from placebo was 30.1% (95% CI 13.9% to 43.3%; P<.001) for the 25 mg dose and 28.5% (11.9% to 42.0%; nominal P=.002) for the 50 mg dose. The most common adverse events were diarrhoea (placebo 19 [25%]; 25 mg 23 [31%]; 50 mg 41 [56%]) and somnolence (placebo 7 [9%]; 25 mg 10 [13%]; 50 mg 19 [26%]). Eight patients on 25 mg, 10 on 50 mg and 2 on placebo discontinued because of adverse events, and 28 patients taking cannabidiol (18.9%) had elevated liver transaminase levels versus none taking placebo.
cards.watchOut: Sixteen weeks in a lifelong condition, with a largely paediatric population (median age 11.4) despite the 1–65 eligibility; the 50 mg comparison carries only a nominal p-value, and the transaminase signal (18.9% vs 0%) means the result applies to cannabidiol given with liver monitoring, in patients already on other antiepileptic drugs whose levels cannabidiol can alter.
cards.source: Thiele EA et al. Add-on Cannabidiol Treatment for Drug-Resistant Seizures in Tuberous Sclerosis Complex: A Placebo-Controlled Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA neurology. 2021. cards.headline: Talwar 2023 (meta-analysis): across six RCTs in Dravet, Lennox–Gastaut and tuberous sclerosis, cannabidiol raised the odds of a ≥50% seizure reduction in TSC (OR 1.99 relative) — and raised adverse events too
cards.summary: Talwar 2023 (meta-analysis): across six RCTs in Dravet, Lennox–Gastaut and tuberous sclerosis, cannabidiol raised the odds of a ≥50% seizure reduction in TSC (OR 1.99 relative) — and raised adverse events too
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of six randomised controlled trials of highly purified oral cannabidiol (10 to 50 mg/kg/day, up to 16 weeks) in drug-resistant epilepsy due to Dravet syndrome, Lennox–Gastaut syndrome, or tuberous sclerosis complex; all included studies were assessed as low risk of bias; subgroup analyses were performed by syndrome and by concomitant clobazam.
cards.result: In the pooled analysis, cannabidiol was more efficacious than placebo for the ≥50% responder outcome (OR 2.45 relative, 95% CI 1.81 to 3.32; p<0.01). By syndrome, the odds of a ≥50% reduction in seizures with cannabidiol were: Dravet syndrome OR 2.26 (95% CI 1.38 to 3.70), Lennox–Gastaut syndrome OR 2.98 (1.83 to 4.85), and tuberous sclerosis complex OR 1.99 (1.06 to 3.76). Compared with placebo, cannabidiol was associated with increased adverse events (OR 1.81 relative, 95% CI 1.33 to 2.46) such as diarrhoea, somnolence and sedation, and with more serious adverse events (OR 2.86 relative, 95% CI 1.63 to 5.05). Dosage and clobazam co-therapy were significantly associated with both greater seizure control and more side effects.
cards.watchOut: The tuberous sclerosis subgroup rests essentially on the single GWPCARE6 trial, so the meta-analysis confirms rather than extends it; odds ratios are relative measures and overstate the absolute responder gain, and the pooled harm estimates mix doses (10–50 mg/kg/day) and syndromes. The clobazam interaction cuts both ways — more seizure control and more sedation.

cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: GWPCARE6 (224 patients with tuberous sclerosis complex) and a six-trial meta-analysis across the three cannabidiol epilepsy syndromes.
cards.result: Seizure reduction versus placebo: 30.1% relative percentage reduction at 25 mg/kg/day (P<.001) and 28.5% at 50 mg/kg/day (nominal P=.002) in GWPCARE6; TSC responder odds OR 1.99 relative (95% CI 1.06 to 3.76) in the meta-analysis. Harms: diarrhoea 31%/56% vs 25%, somnolence 13%/26% vs 9%, elevated transaminases 18.9% vs 0%, serious adverse events OR 2.86 relative across the pooled trials. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Tier C is set because the tuberous sclerosis evidence is one 16-week trial; long-term seizure, developmental and safety outcomes in TSC are not in these records. This shelf is distinct from the cannabidiol Dravet/Lennox–Gastaut shelf #991 — same drug, different syndrome and trial — and from the everolimus TSC seizure pack #2357, a different treatment entirely.
cards.source: Synthesis of Thiele EA et al. JAMA neurology. 2021 (PMID: 33346789); Talwar A et al. Experimental neurology. 2023 (PMID: 36206805).

shelves.title: Eslicarbazepine acetate as a focal-seizure adjunct: responders 34% at 800 mg and 43% at 1200 mg versus 20% on placebo — efficacy climbs with dose, and so do dropouts
shelves.question: In adults with refractory focal seizures, does adjunctive eslicarbazepine acetate reduce seizure frequency versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Adverse Drug Reaction Reporting Systems · Aged · Anticonvulsants/adverse effects,pharmacokinetics,therapeutic use* · Dibenzazepines/adverse effects,pharmacokinetics,therapeutic use* · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Synergism · Drug Therapy, Combination · Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions · Epilepsies, Partial/blood,drug therapy* · Female · Humans · Male · Metabolic Clearance Rate/physiology · Middle Aged · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — in the pivotal phase III trial (Elger C et al., PMID: 19243424), 402 adults with refractory partial-onset seizures on one to two antiepileptic drugs had responder rates of 20% on placebo versus 23% on eslicarbazepine acetate 400 mg, 34% on 800 mg and 43% on 1200 mg once daily, with median relative reductions in seizure frequency of 16%, 26%, 36% and 45% respectively (seizure frequency significantly lower than placebo at 1200 mg, p=0.0003, and 800 mg, p=0.0028). A 2022 meta-analysis of ten randomised trials (2,565 people; Fei Y et al., PMID: 35911890) found the same dose pattern: in adults, 400 mg/day did not improve response, 800 mg/day improved the response rate (OR 2.16 relative, 95% CI 1.65 to 2.83) without significantly increasing severe adverse events, and 1200 mg/day improved response (OR 2.49 relative) but significantly increased severe adverse events (OR 3.72 relative). In the pivotal trial, discontinuation for adverse events rose with dose — 3.9% on placebo, 4% at 400 mg, 8.2% at 800 mg and 19.6% at 1200 mg — with dizziness, headache and diplopia the commonest effects. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): adjunctive eslicarbazepine acetate at 800–1200 mg once daily reduces refractory focal seizures, with 800 mg the better-tolerated effective dose and the benefit in children not established by the pooled record.

cards.headline: Elger 2009: responder rates rose with dose — 20% placebo, 23% at 400 mg, 34% at 800 mg, 43% at 1200 mg — and median relative seizure reduction reached 45% at the top dose
cards.summary: Elger 2009: responder rates rose with dose — 20% placebo, 23% at 400 mg, 34% at 800 mg, 43% at 1200 mg — and median relative seizure reduction reached 45% at the top dose
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase III trial (Elger 2009)
cards.people: 402 adults with refractory partial-onset seizures (simple or complex, with or without secondary generalisation), with at least 4 partial-onset seizures per 4 weeks despite one to two antiepileptic drugs, in a multicentre parallel-group study: after an 8-week single-blind placebo baseline, patients were randomised to placebo (n=102) or once-daily eslicarbazepine acetate 400 mg (n=100), 800 mg (n=98) or 1200 mg (n=102), titrated in weekly 400 mg steps to a 12-week maintenance phase. The most frequent concomitant drugs were carbamazepine (56–62%), lamotrigine (25–27%) and valproic acid (22–28%).
cards.result: Seizure frequency per 4 weeks over the maintenance period (primary endpoint) was significantly lower than placebo in the 1200 mg group (p=0.0003) and the 800 mg group (p=0.0028) on ANCOVA of log-transformed seizure frequency. Responder rate was 20% (placebo), 23% (400 mg), 34% (800 mg) and 43% (1200 mg). Median relative reduction in seizure frequency was 16% (placebo), 26% (400 mg), 36% (800 mg) and 45% (1200 mg). Efficacy was similar with or without concomitant carbamazepine. Discontinuation rates caused by adverse events were 3.9% (placebo), 4% (400 mg), 8.2% (800 mg) and 19.6% (1200 mg); adverse events in more than 10% of any group were dizziness, headache and diplopia, and most adverse events were mild or moderate.
cards.watchOut: A 12-week maintenance phase in highly refractory adults (at least 4 seizures per 4 weeks on existing therapy): the absolute responder gain at 800 mg is 14 percentage points over a 20% placebo rate, seizure freedom is not reported in the record, and the 1200 mg dose's extra efficacy comes with a five-fold higher adverse-event discontinuation rate than placebo (19.6% vs 3.9%).
cards.source: Elger C et al. Efficacy and safety of eslicarbazepine acetate as adjunctive treatment in adults with refractory partial-onset seizures: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group phase III study. Epilepsia. 2009. PMID: 19243424. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Fei 2022 (meta-analysis of 10 RCTs, 2,565 people): 800 mg/day improved response (OR 2.16 relative) without significantly more severe adverse events; 1200 mg worked but severe adverse events rose (OR 3.72 relative); children unproven
cards.summary: Fei 2022 (meta-analysis of 10 RCTs, 2,565 people): 800 mg/day improved response (OR 2.16 relative) without significantly more severe adverse events; 1200 mg worked but severe adverse events rose (OR 3.72 relative); children unproven
cards.people: Meta-analysis of ten randomised controlled trials including 2,565 people with focal-onset epilepsy (adults and children), pooled with a random-effects model; efficacy outcomes were the response rate (≥50% reduction in seizure frequency) and the effective rate (≥75% reduction), and tolerability was assessed as severe adverse events leading to drug discontinuation.
cards.result: For adults, eslicarbazepine acetate 400 mg/day did not improve the response rate or the effective rate. At 800 mg/day, the response rate improved (OR 2.16 relative, 95% CI 1.65 to 2.83; p<0.001) and the effective rate improved (OR 2.16 relative, 95% CI 1.41 to 3.30; p<0.001) without significantly increased severe adverse events (OR 1.58 relative, 95% CI 0.90 to 2.78; p=0.11). At 1200 mg/day, the response rate (OR 2.49 relative; p<0.001) and effective rate (OR 3.09 relative; p=0.04) improved, but severe adverse events increased significantly (OR 3.72 relative; p<0.001). For children, eslicarbazepine acetate did not significantly improve the response rate (OR 1.76 relative; p=0.22) or the effective rate (OR 2.17 relative; p=0.13).
cards.watchOut: Odds ratios are relative measures and flatter the absolute gains (the pivotal trial's own responder rates — 34% vs 20% at 800 mg — are the honest scale); the record carries no MeSH list and reports no heterogeneity statistics in its abstract, and the paediatric null may reflect too few children rather than true inefficacy.
cards.source: Fei Y et al. Adjunctive Treatment With Eslicarbazepine Acetate for Adults and Children With Focal-Onset Epilepsy: A Meta-Analysis. Frontiers in neurology. 2022. PMID: 35911890. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Synthesis: a dose-dependent benefit with a dose-dependent price — 800 mg once daily is where the pooled record lands
cards.summary: Synthesis: a dose-dependent benefit with a dose-dependent price — 800 mg once daily is where the pooled record lands
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: the pivotal phase III trial (402 adults) and a ten-trial meta-analysis (2,565 adults and children).
cards.result: Responder rates in the pivotal trial: 20% placebo, 34% at 800 mg, 43% at 1200 mg; median relative seizure-frequency reduction 16%, 36% and 45% respectively. Pooled adult response: OR 2.16 relative at 800 mg and OR 2.49 relative at 1200 mg, with severe adverse events significantly increased only at 1200 mg (OR 3.72 relative). Children: no significant pooled benefit. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
cards.watchOut: All trials are short (weeks of maintenance) in refractory focal epilepsy; nothing here speaks to monotherapy, newly diagnosed epilepsy, or long-term retention, and cross-trial comparisons with other focal adjuncts (perampanel shelf #2349, cenobamate shelf #1115) are not licensed by these records — each drug's shelf stands on its own placebo comparison.

shelves.title: Zonisamide for refractory focal seizures: Cochrane's pool says one extra patient halves their seizures for every six treated — with one extra withdrawal for every fifteen
shelves.question: In adults with refractory focal seizures, does adjunctive zonisamide reduce seizure frequency versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Age Factors · Aged · Anticonvulsants/adverse effects,therapeutic use* · Child · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Epilepsies, Partial/drug therapy* · Epilepsy, Complex Partial/drug therapy · Female · Headache/chemically induced · Humans · Isoxazoles/adverse effects,therapeutic use* · Male · Middle Aged · Pharyngitis/chemically induced · Placebos · Sleep Wake Disorders/chemically induced · Treatment Outcome · Zonisamide
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — in the pivotal dose-ranging trial (Brodie MJ et al., PMID: 15660766), 351 patients with refractory partial seizures on one to three antiepileptic drugs had a 51.2% decrease in complex partial seizure frequency on zonisamide 500 mg/day versus 16.3% on placebo (p<0.0001), with complex partial responder rates of 52.3% versus 21.3% (p<0.001) and a significant dose-response for all seizures. A contemporary review of the four randomised trials (848 patients; Brodie MJ, PMID: 16316744) found the same pattern at doses of at least 300 mg/day. The updated Cochrane review (Brigo F et al., PMID: 32715463) pooled eight studies (1,636 participants) and found, on moderate-certainty evidence, that zonisamide 300–500 mg/day raised the chance of at least a 50% relative reduction in seizure frequency versus placebo (RR 1.90 relative, 95% CI 1.63 to 2.22; number needed to treat 6), while also raising treatment withdrawal (RR 1.59 relative, 95% CI 1.18 to 2.13; number needed to harm 15) and specific harms including ataxia (RR 3.85 relative), somnolence (RR 1.52 relative), agitation (RR 2.35 relative) and anorexia (RR 2.74 relative). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): adjunctive zonisamide at 300–500 mg/day is an effective option for refractory focal seizures, with roughly one extra responder for every six treated and one extra withdrawal for every fifteen.

cards.headline: Brodie 2005: zonisamide 500 mg/day cut complex partial seizure frequency by 51.2% versus 16.3% on placebo (p<0.0001), with responders 52.3% versus 21.3%
cards.summary: Brodie 2005: zonisamide 500 mg/day cut complex partial seizure frequency by 51.2% versus 16.3% on placebo (p<0.0001), with responders 52.3% versus 21.3%
cards.people: 351 patients with refractory partial (localisation-related) seizures receiving a stable regimen of one to three antiepileptic drugs, randomised (2:1:1:2) to placebo or zonisamide 100 mg, 300 mg or 500 mg/day after a 12-week baseline, with a 6-week titration phase followed by an 18-week fixed-dose assessment phase. Primary efficacy parameters were the change in complex partial seizure frequency and the proportion of complex partial responders (≥50% decrease) for 500 mg/day versus placebo.
cards.result: Compared with placebo, zonisamide 500 mg/day produced a significantly greater decrease in complex partial seizure frequency from baseline (51.2% vs 16.3%; p<0.0001) and a significantly higher proportion of complex partial responders (52.3% vs 21.3%; p<0.001). Both 500 mg/day and 300 mg/day were statistically superior to placebo in reducing the frequency of 'all seizures' and of simple partial plus complex partial seizures, and for all seizures a significant dose-response relation was observed (p<0.0001). The most common adverse events were somnolence, headache, dizziness and nausea during titration, and headache and pharyngitis during the fixed-dose phase.
cards.watchOut: The headline comparison is the highest dose only, over an 18-week fixed-dose phase; the 100 mg arm's results are not detailed in the record, and the trial predates modern reporting — no confidence intervals are given for the primary percentages, so the precision of the 51.2% versus 16.3% contrast cannot be judged from the record alone.
cards.source: Brodie MJ et al. Dose-dependent safety and efficacy of zonisamide: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study in patients with refractory partial seizures. Epilepsia. 2005. PMID: 15660766. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Brodie 2006 (review of four RCTs, 848 patients): doses of at least 300 mg/day were efficacious, with responder rates of 35–42% and 20–27% of patients reaching a ≥75% reduction
cards.summary: Brodie 2006 (review of four RCTs, 848 patients): doses of at least 300 mg/day were efficacious, with responder rates of 35–42% and 20–27% of patients reaching a ≥75% reduction
cards.type: Review of four randomised placebo-controlled trials (Brodie 2006)
cards.people: Review of four randomised, placebo-controlled trials (duration up to 6 months) in the United States and Europe including 848 patients in total with refractory partial seizures, covering zonisamide doses from 100 to 600 mg/day, plus pooled tolerability data from all four trials (and more than 2 million patient-years of worldwide use at the time of writing).
cards.result: Four randomised trials showed doses of zonisamide of at least 300 mg/day to be efficacious in refractory partial seizures in adults. In the pivotal European study, zonisamide 500 mg/day was significantly superior to placebo in reducing complex partial seizure frequency (−51% versus −16%), all partial seizures and all seizures, with dose-dependent benefit over the 100–500 mg/day range. Supporting trials confirmed significant increases in median seizure-frequency reduction (up to 41%) and responder rates (35–42%) versus placebo at 400–600 mg/day, enabling 20–27% of patients to attain a ≥75% reduction in seizure frequency. Pooled data showed adverse events generally of mild-to-moderate severity with few leading to discontinuation, and an incidence of serious adverse events comparable to placebo.
cards.watchOut: A narrative review by the pivotal trial's first author, not an independent meta-analysis — its pooled tolerability summary has no denominators in the record, and its efficacy ranges restate the same four trials carded elsewhere on this shelf. It is carded because the miner named it as an anchor; the independent quantitative synthesis is the Cochrane card below.
cards.source: Brodie MJ. Zonisamide as adjunctive therapy for refractory partial seizures. Epilepsy research. 2006. PMID: 16316744. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Brigo 2020 (Cochrane): zonisamide 300–500 mg/day nearly doubled the chance of halving seizures (RR 1.90 relative; NNT 6) on moderate-certainty evidence, with more withdrawals (NNH 15)
cards.summary: Brigo 2020 (Cochrane): zonisamide 300–500 mg/day nearly doubled the chance of halving seizures (RR 1.90 relative; NNT 6) on moderate-certainty evidence, with more withdrawals (NNH 15)
cards.people: Updated Cochrane review of randomised controlled trials of add-on zonisamide versus placebo or another antiepileptic drug in people with focal epilepsy uncontrolled by one or more concomitant antiepileptic drugs: eight studies, 1,636 participants, with GRADE certainty assessments and an intention-to-treat approach for the primary analyses. No new studies were found since the 2018 version; searches ran to September 2019.
cards.result: The overall risk ratio for at least a 50% relative reduction in seizure frequency for zonisamide 300 mg to 500 mg/day compared with placebo was 1.90 relative (95% CI 1.63 to 2.22; 7 trials, 1,371 participants; moderate-certainty evidence), and for any dose (100–500 mg/day) it was 1.86 relative (95% CI 1.60 to 2.17; 7 trials, 1,429 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). The number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome was 6 (95% CI 4.1 to 6.8). The risk ratio for treatment withdrawal was 1.59 relative (95% CI 1.18 to 2.13) at 300–500 mg/day and 1.44 relative (1.08 to 1.93) at any dose, with a number needed to treat for an additional harmful outcome of 15 (95% CI 9.3 to 36.7). Adverse effects more likely with zonisamide than placebo included ataxia (RR 3.85 relative, 99% CI 1.36 to 10.93; low-certainty), somnolence (RR 1.52 relative, 99% CI 1.00 to 2.31; moderate-certainty), agitation (RR 2.35 relative, 99% CI 1.05 to 5.27; low-certainty) and anorexia (RR 2.74 relative, 99% CI 1.64 to 4.60; low-certainty). Five of the eight studies were sponsored by the drug's manufacturers, and the maximum stable-dose phase evaluated was 18 weeks.
cards.watchOut: Moderate certainty, not high: most trials were industry-sponsored, two had high attrition-bias risk, the minimum effective and maximum tolerated doses could not be identified, and 18 weeks of stable dosing cannot confirm longer-term efficacy. The review's results cannot be extrapolated to monotherapy or to other seizure types — the claim is strictly add-on therapy in focal epilepsy.
cards.source: Brigo F et al. Zonisamide add-on therapy for focal epilepsy. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2020. PMID: 32715463. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: four trials and a Cochrane pool point the same way — a genuine, dose-dependent adjunct benefit with a real tolerability bill
cards.summary: Synthesis: four trials and a Cochrane pool point the same way — a genuine, dose-dependent adjunct benefit with a real tolerability bill
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: the pivotal dose-ranging trial (351 patients), a review of the four randomised trials (848 patients), and the Cochrane pool (8 studies, 1,636 participants).
cards.result: Efficacy: ≥50% relative responder advantage RR 1.90 relative (95% CI 1.63 to 2.22) at 300–500 mg/day, NNT 6; pivotal-trial frequency reduction 51.2% vs 16.3% at 500 mg. Harms: withdrawal RR 1.59 relative, NNH 15; ataxia, somnolence, agitation and anorexia all significantly commoner than on placebo. Duration of evidence: up to about 6 months. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The three cards are not three independent bodies of evidence — the review and the Cochrane pool both rest on the same small set of mostly industry-sponsored trials. The stamp is LIKELY because the pooled estimate is precise and dose-consistent, not because the trial base is large or long.
cards.source: Synthesis of Brodie MJ et al. Epilepsia. 2005 (PMID: 15660766); Brodie MJ. Epilepsy research. 2006 (PMID: 16316744); Brigo F et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2020 (PMID: 32715463).

shelves.title: Levetiracetam for juvenile myoclonic epilepsy: in the only randomised trial, 58.3% halved their myoclonic days versus 23.3% on placebo — a big effect resting on 120 patients
shelves.question: In patients with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, does adjunctive levetiracetam reduce myoclonic seizure days versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Anticonvulsants/therapeutic use* · Chi-Square Distribution · Child · Double-Blind Method · Epilepsies, Myoclonic/complications,drug therapy* · Epilepsy, Generalized/complications,drug therapy* · Evaluation Studies as Topic · Humans · Levetiracetam · Middle Aged · Piracetam/analogs & derivatives*,therapeutic use · Retrospective Studies · Severity of Illness Index
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the only randomised trial in this population (Noachtar S et al., PMID: 18285535) randomised 122 adolescents and adults with idiopathic generalised epilepsy with myoclonic seizures — 93.4% of them juvenile myoclonic epilepsy — who were still having myoclonic seizures on monotherapy, to adjunctive levetiracetam 3000 mg/day or placebo. A reduction of at least 50% in days per week with myoclonic seizures occurred in 58.3% on levetiracetam versus 23.3% on placebo (p<0.001; OR 4.77 relative, 95% CI 2.12 to 10.77), freedom from myoclonic seizures during the evaluation period in 25.0% versus 5.0% (p=0.004), and freedom from all seizure types in 21.7% versus 1.7% (p<0.001). The only adverse events more frequent with levetiracetam were somnolence and neck pain. The effect size is large and internally consistent, but it rests on a single trial of 120 evaluable patients with a 12-week evaluation period, in a condition treated for decades. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): adjunctive levetiracetam substantially reduces myoclonic seizure days in juvenile myoclonic epilepsy over the short term; long-term and comparative evidence is absent from the randomised record.

cards.headline: Noachtar 2008: 58.3% on adjunctive levetiracetam halved their myoclonic seizure days versus 23.3% on placebo (OR 4.77 relative), and 25.0% became free of myoclonic seizures versus 5.0%
cards.summary: Noachtar 2008: 58.3% on adjunctive levetiracetam halved their myoclonic seizure days versus 23.3% on placebo (OR 4.77 relative), and 25.0% became free of myoclonic seizures versus 5.0%
cards.people: 122 randomised patients (120 evaluable: levetiracetam n=60, placebo n=60), adolescents (≥12 years) and adults (≤65 years) with idiopathic generalised epilepsy who had myoclonic seizures on more than 8 days during a prospective 8-week baseline despite antiepileptic monotherapy; diagnoses were juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (93.4%) or juvenile absence epilepsy (6.6%). Treatment was adjunctive levetiracetam 3000 mg/day with a 4-week up-titration, a 12-week evaluation period, and a 6-week down-titration/conversion period.
cards.result: A reduction of at least 50% in the number of days per week with myoclonic seizures was seen in 58.3% of the levetiracetam group and 23.3% of the placebo group (p<0.001) during the treatment period; levetiracetam patients were more likely to respond (OR 4.77 relative, 95% CI 2.12 to 10.77; p<0.001). Freedom from myoclonic seizures during the evaluation period was higher with levetiracetam (25.0% vs 5.0%; p=0.004), as was freedom from all seizure types (21.7% vs 1.7%; p<0.001). The only adverse events more frequent with levetiracetam were somnolence and neck pain. The authors note this was the first published randomised controlled trial of adjunctive antiepileptic therapy in idiopathic generalised epilepsy with myoclonic seizures.
cards.watchOut: One trial, 120 evaluable patients, a fixed high dose (3000 mg/day) and a 12-week evaluation window in a lifelong epilepsy: the record cannot speak to lower doses, to tonic-clonic seizure outcomes separately, to pregnancy-age management questions that dominate juvenile myoclonic epilepsy care, or to durability. The 6.6% with juvenile absence epilepsy mean the result is a generalised-epilepsy-with-myoclonus result, applied here to the juvenile myoclonic majority.
cards.source: Noachtar S et al. Levetiracetam for the treatment of idiopathic generalized epilepsy with myoclonic seizures. Neurology. 2008. PMID: 18285535. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Stopping epilepsy medicine after remission: the MRC trial says 41% recur within 2 years of withdrawal versus 22% who continue — a real, front-loaded risk that does not appear to ruin long-term prognosis
shelves.question: In people with epilepsy in sustained remission, does withdrawing antiseizure medication increase seizure recurrence versus continuing treatment?
shelves.mesh: Actuarial Analysis · Adult · Anticonvulsants/administration & dosage* · Child · Drug Administration Schedule · Electroencephalography · Epilepsy/drug therapy*,physiopathology · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Patient Compliance · Prognosis · Recurrence · Remission Induction
shelves.balance: LIKELY (harm) — on the recurrence question the randomised record is unusually direct: the MRC Antiepileptic Drug Withdrawal Study (PMID: 1673736) randomised 1,013 patients who had been seizure-free for at least 2 years to continued treatment or slow withdrawal, and by 2 years after randomisation 78% of those who continued treatment remained seizure-free versus 59% of those who withdrew — i.e. recurrence in 22% versus 41% over the first 2 years — although thereafter the difference between the groups diminished. The study's prognostic index (PMID: 8518603) identifies who carries the risk: age 16 or older, taking more than one antiepileptic drug, seizures after starting treatment, a history of primary or secondarily generalised tonic-clonic seizures, a history of myoclonic seizures, and an abnormal EEG all increased recurrence risk, while longer seizure-free time reduced it. The long-term follow-up of patients who did recur (Chadwick D et al., PMID: 8917053) adds the balancing fact: by 3 years after a recurrence 95% had experienced a further 1-year remission and by 5 years 90% a further 2-year remission, with no evidence that having discontinued treatment before the recurrence worsened the outcome — withdrawal raises the short-term chance of a seizure without demonstrably worsening the long-term prognosis of the epilepsy. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm): withdrawing antiseizure medication after at least 2 years' remission roughly doubles 2-year recurrence (41% vs 22%), a harm that is front-loaded and individually predictable in part, but not shown to damage long-term remission prospects.

cards.headline: MRC 1991: by 2 years, 78% who continued treatment remained seizure-free versus 59% who withdrew — recurrence 22% versus 41% — though the gap narrowed thereafter
cards.summary: MRC 1991: by 2 years, 78% who continued treatment remained seizure-free versus 59% who withdrew — recurrence 22% versus 41% — though the gap narrowed thereafter
cards.type: Prospective multicentre randomised trial (MRC Antiepileptic Drug Withdrawal Study, 1991)
cards.people: 1,013 patients who had been free of seizures for at least 2 years, in a prospective multicentre randomised study of continued antiepileptic treatment versus slow withdrawal; comparison of randomised and eligible-but-non-randomised patients suggested the results should apply to a wider patient population.
cards.result: By 2 years after randomisation, 78% of patients in whom treatment was continued and 59% of those in whom it was withdrawn remained seizure free, but thereafter the differences between the two groups diminished. Non-compliance with continued treatment accounted for only a small proportion of the risk in the continuing group. The most important factors determining outcome were longer seizure-free periods (reducing the risk) and more than one antiepileptic drug and a history of tonic-clonic seizures (increasing the risk); other factors (e.g. a history of neonatal seizures, specific electroencephalographic features) seemed to have smaller effects, but even in this large study the confidence intervals for those observations were wide.
cards.watchOut: A 1991 trial of slow withdrawal in patients already in at least 2 years' remission — it does not cover withdrawal after shorter remissions, abrupt discontinuation, or modern drug mixes, and 'the difference diminished thereafter' means the 41% versus 22% contrast is a statement about the first 2 years, not a lifetime sentence. Group authorship means the record carries no individual first author.
cards.source: Medical Research Council Antiepileptic Drug Withdrawal Study Group. Randomised study of antiepileptic drug withdrawal in patients in remission. Lancet (London, England). 1991. PMID: 1673736. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: MRC prognostic index 1993: recurrence risk after remission is predictable in part — polytherapy, tonic-clonic or myoclonic history and an abnormal EEG raise it; longer remission lowers it
cards.summary: MRC prognostic index 1993: recurrence risk after remission is predictable in part — polytherapy, tonic-clonic or myoclonic history and an abnormal EEG raise it; longer remission lowers it
cards.type: Prognostic index from a randomised trial cohort (MRC, 1993)
cards.people: The 1,013 patients randomised in the Medical Research Council antiepileptic drug withdrawal study (minimum remission of 2 years), across centres in six European countries; a Cox proportional hazards model was built on part of the sample and tested by split-sample validation, which suggested the model was well calibrated.
cards.result: Factors that increased the risk of seizures recurring were: being 16 years or older; taking more than one antiepileptic drug; experiencing seizures after starting antiepileptic drug treatment; a history of primary or secondarily generalised tonic-clonic seizures; a history of myoclonic seizures; and having an abnormal electroencephalogram. The risk of seizures recurring decreased with increasing time without seizures. The model allowed estimation of the risk of recurrence in the next 1 and 2 years under continued treatment and under slow withdrawal, and the authors describe it as the best available aid at the time for counselling patients in remission who ask about stopping treatment, while noting it required validation in a broader population.
cards.watchOut: A prognostic model is not a treatment trial: it stratifies the risk quantified by the 1991 card but adds no new randomised contrast, its coefficients come from a 1980s–90s European cohort on older drugs, and split-sample (internal) validation is weaker than external validation — individual counselling should treat its estimates as approximate.
cards.source: Medical Research Council Antiepileptic Drug Withdrawal Study Group. Prognostic index for recurrence of seizures after remission of epilepsy. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 1993. PMID: 8518603. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Chadwick 1996: after a post-withdrawal recurrence, remission usually returns — 95% had a further 1-year remission by 3 years — and prior discontinuation did not worsen the outcome
cards.summary: Chadwick 1996: after a post-withdrawal recurrence, remission usually returns — 95% had a further 1-year remission by 3 years — and prior discontinuation did not worsen the outcome
cards.type: Long-term follow-up of a randomised trial cohort (Chadwick 1996)
cards.people: Continued follow-up of a cohort of 409 patients from the MRC Antiepileptic Drug Withdrawal Study who had a recurrence of seizures after randomisation, examining the risk of further seizures, the probability of further remission, and the prognostic factors involved.
cards.result: By 3 years after a seizure, 95% of patients had experienced a further 1-year remission of their epilepsy, and by 5 years 90% had experienced a further 2-year remission. The most important factors contributing to the risk of further seizures after a first post-randomisation seizure were the previous seizure-free interval, having partial seizures at recurrence, and having previously experienced seizures while receiving treatment. There was no evidence that the group who had discontinued or reduced treatment before their first post-randomisation seizure had a different outcome from those who continued treatment. The authors conclude there is no evidence that discontinuation of antiepileptic drugs modifies the long-term prognosis of a person's epilepsy, although it does increase the risk of seizures in the 1- to 2-year period after discontinuation.
cards.watchOut: This cohort is selected twice over — patients who entered a withdrawal trial and then recurred — so its reassuring remission figures describe people whose epilepsy had already shown it could remit, not everyone who stops medication. It also cannot capture the non-seizure costs of a recurrence (driving, employment, injury), which sit outside these records entirely.
cards.source: Chadwick D et al. Outcomes after seizure recurrence in people with well-controlled epilepsy and the factors that influence it. The MRC Antiepileptic Drug Withdrawal Group. Epilepsia. 1996. PMID: 8917053. Registry ID: none in the record. partial seizures at recurrence, and having previously experienced seizures while receiving treatment. there was no evidence that the group who had discontinued or reduced treatment before their first post-randomisation seizure had a different outcome from those who continued treatment. the authors conclude there is no evidence that discontinuation of antiepileptic drugs modifies the long-term prognosis of a person's epilepsy, although it does increase the risk of seizures in the 1- to 2-year period after discontinuation. this cohort is selected twice over — patients who entered a withdrawal trial and then recurred — so its reassuring remission figures describe people whose epilepsy had already shown it could remit, not everyone who stops medication. it also cannot capture the cards.headline: Synthesis: withdrawal buys a roughly doubled 2-year recurrence risk, front-loaded and partly predictable — but no demonstrated long-term prognostic damage
cards.summary: Synthesis: withdrawal buys a roughly doubled 2-year recurrence risk, front-loaded and partly predictable — but no demonstrated long-term prognostic damage
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: the MRC randomised withdrawal study (1,013 patients), its prognostic index (same cohort), and the long-term follow-up of the 409 patients who recurred.
cards.result: Recurrence by 2 years: 41% after slow withdrawal versus 22% on continued treatment (seizure-free 59% vs 78%), with the gap diminishing thereafter. Risk modifiers: polytherapy, tonic-clonic or myoclonic history, seizures after starting treatment, abnormal EEG and age ≥16 raise risk; longer remission lowers it. After a recurrence: 95% regain a 1-year remission by 3 years, and prior withdrawal did not worsen outcomes. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm).
cards.watchOut: Tier C is set not for weakness of the randomised contrast — 1,013 patients is large for this question — but for age and indirectness: 1990s drugs, slow-withdrawal protocols and a ≥2-year-remission population. The three cards are one study programme, not three studies, and the shelf must not be read as three independent confirmations.

shelves.title: First epilepsy medicine after 65: lamotrigine, gabapentin and carbamazepine controlled seizures equally in 593 older patients — but only 35.5% stayed on carbamazepine for a year, versus 55.8% on lamotrigine
shelves.question: In older adults with new-onset epilepsy, how do lamotrigine, gabapentin and carbamazepine compare on seizure control and tolerability?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aging/physiology* · Amines/administration & dosage,adverse effects*,blood · Anticonvulsants/administration & dosage,adverse effects*,blood · Carbamazepine/administration & dosage,adverse effects*,blood · Cerebral Infarction/complications · Cyclohexanecarboxylic Acids/administration & dosage,adverse effects*,blood · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Epilepsy/drug therapy*,epidemiology,etiology · Gabapentin · Hospitals, Veterans/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Lamotrigine · Patient Compliance/statistics & numerical data · Patient Selection · Treatment Outcome · Triazines/administration & dosage,adverse effects*,blood · United States · United States Department of Veterans Affairs/statistics & numerical data · gamma-Aminobutyric Acid/administration & dosage,adverse effects*,blood
shelves.balance: SPLIT — seizure control did not separate the three drugs, but tolerability did, decisively. In the VA Cooperative trial (Rowan AJ et al., PMID: 15955935), 593 elderly patients with newly diagnosed seizures (mean age 72 years, most commonly after cerebral infarction, taking an average of seven comedications) were randomised to gabapentin 1500 mg/day, lamotrigine 150 mg/day or carbamazepine 600 mg/day for 12 months, with retention in the trial as the primary outcome. Early terminations were 44.2% on lamotrigine, 51% on gabapentin and 64.5% on carbamazepine (p=0.0002), and terminations for adverse events were 12.1%, 21.6% and 31% respectively (p=0.001) — lamotrigine significantly better than carbamazepine (p<0.0001) and gabapentin (p=0.015) on adverse-event termination, and gabapentin significantly better than carbamazepine (p=0.008) on retention. There were no significant differences in seizure-free rate at 12 months. PROPOSED SPLIT: for an older adult starting treatment, the record supports choosing on tolerability — lamotrigine first, gabapentin second, carbamazepine last — while expecting similar seizure control from all three.

cards.headline: Rowan 2005 (VA Cooperative): seizure control was identical across lamotrigine, gabapentin and carbamazepine — but 12-month retention was 55.8%, 49% and 35.5%, driven by adverse events
cards.summary: Rowan 2005 (VA Cooperative): seizure control was identical across lamotrigine, gabapentin and carbamazepine — but 12-month retention was 55.8%, 49% and 35.5%, driven by adverse events
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, double-dummy trial (VA Cooperative Study, Rowan 2005)
cards.people: 593 elderly subjects with newly diagnosed seizures at 18 centres (mean age 72 years; the most common aetiology was cerebral infarction; patients had multiple medical conditions and took an average of seven comedications), randomised double-blind, double-dummy to gabapentin 1500 mg/day, lamotrigine 150 mg/day, or carbamazepine 600 mg/day; the primary outcome measure was retention in the trial for 12 months. Mean plasma levels at 6 weeks were gabapentin 8.67 ± 4.83 µg/mL, lamotrigine 2.87 ± 1.60 µg/mL and carbamazepine 6.79 ± 2.92 µg/mL, and remained stable throughout the trial.
cards.result: Early terminations: lamotrigine 44.2%, gabapentin 51%, carbamazepine 64.5% (p=0.0002); significant paired comparisons were lamotrigine versus carbamazepine (p<0.0001) and gabapentin versus carbamazepine (p=0.008). Terminations for adverse events: lamotrigine 12.1%, gabapentin 21.6%, carbamazepine 31% (p=0.001); significant paired comparisons were lamotrigine versus carbamazepine (p<0.0001) and lamotrigine versus gabapentin (p=0.015). There were no significant differences in seizure-free rate at 12 months. The authors conclude that the main limiting factor in patient retention was adverse drug reactions, that patients taking lamotrigine or gabapentin did better than those taking carbamazepine, and that lamotrigine and gabapentin should be considered as initial therapy for older patients with newly diagnosed seizures.
cards.watchOut: A VA population — predominantly older men with heavy comorbidity and polypharmacy — at fixed target doses (lamotrigine 150 mg/day is a modest dose; carbamazepine 600 mg/day in a 72-year-old is not), so the ranking is a ranking of these regimens in these patients, not of the molecules at any dose. Retention is a composite of efficacy, tolerability and everything else that makes an older patient stop a drug; the seizure-free rates themselves did not differ, and their exact values are not given in the record.
cards.source: Rowan AJ et al. New onset geriatric epilepsy: a randomized study of gabapentin, lamotrigine, and carbamazepine. Neurology. 2005. PMID: 15955935. Registry ID: none in the record.
