shelves.title: Asenapine for acute schizophrenia: better than placebo across its four-trial programme (−3.6 PANSS points, responder OR 1.9 relative) — effective, and honestly average for its class
shelves.question: In adults with acute schizophrenia, does asenapine improve symptoms versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adult · Antipsychotic Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use* · Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders · Dibenzocycloheptenes · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Heterocyclic Compounds, 4 or More Rings/therapeutic use* · Humans · Male · Patient Compliance/statistics & numerical data · Risperidone/therapeutic use* · Schizophrenia/diagnosis,drug therapy* · Severity of Illness Index
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the pivotal placebo- and risperidone-controlled trial (Potkin SG et al., PMID: 17960962), 174 patients with acute schizophrenia received sublingual asenapine 5 mg twice daily, placebo, or risperidone 3 mg twice daily for 6 weeks; asenapine beat placebo significantly on PANSS total score (p<.005), the negative subscale (p=.01), the general psychopathology subscale (p<.005), the positive subscale (p=.01) and CGI-S (p<.01), with overall adverse-event incidence comparable to placebo, whereas risperidone was associated with substantial weight gain and prolactin elevation. A meta-analysis pooling the four asenapine development-programme trials (Szegedi A et al., PMID: 23290326) confirmed superiority over placebo on PANSS total change (−3.6 points by LOCF, p=.002; −4.1 by MMRM, p=.001) with responder odds of OR 1.9 relative (p<.001), an effect comparable to the active controls in the same trials but somewhat lower than effect sizes reported in the literature for other second-generation antipsychotics. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): asenapine is an effective acute-schizophrenia treatment of modest average effect size — real, replicated across its development programme, and not a standout among its class.

cards.headline: Potkin 2007: asenapine beat placebo on PANSS total, negative, positive and general subscales and CGI-S over 6 weeks (all p≤.01), with placebo-level overall adverse events
cards.summary: Potkin 2007: asenapine beat placebo on PANSS total, negative, positive and general subscales and CGI-S over 6 weeks (all p≤.01), with placebo-level overall adverse events
cards.people: 174 patients with acute schizophrenia (DSM-IV criteria) in the intent-to-treat population (received at least one dose and at least one postbaseline assessment), in a 6-week trial conducted August 2001 to May 2002, randomised to sublingual asenapine 5 mg twice daily, placebo twice daily, or oral risperidone 3 mg twice daily; the primary outcome was improvement from baseline in PANSS total score, with CGI-S and PANSS subscales as secondary outcomes.
cards.result: At study end or last observation, mean improvements on PANSS total, negative subscale and general psychopathology subscale scores were all significantly greater with asenapine than with placebo (p<.005, p=.01 and p<.005 respectively). Compared with placebo, improvements on CGI-S and the PANSS positive subscale were significantly greater with both asenapine (p<.01 and p=.01) and risperidone (p<.005 and p<.05). Overall incidence rates of adverse events were comparable for asenapine and placebo, whereas risperidone was associated with substantial weight gain and prolactin elevation. The authors conclude asenapine was effective and well tolerated in acute schizophrenia and may provide a new option for control of negative symptoms. The record reports significance levels rather than the PANSS point changes themselves.
cards.watchOut: A small (174-patient), 6-week, single-dose trial from the development programme, and the record gives p-values without the actual PANSS point differences — the size of the benefit cannot be judged from this card alone, which is why the pooled card below carries the numbers. 'May provide an option for negative symptoms' rests on one subscale result in an acute-episode trial, not on a trial in predominant negative symptoms.
cards.source: Potkin SG et al. Efficacy and tolerability of asenapine in acute schizophrenia: a placebo- and risperidone-controlled trial. The Journal of clinical psychiatry. 2007. PMID: 17960962. cards.headline: Szegedi 2012 (meta-analysis of 4 trials): asenapine beat placebo by −3.6 PANSS points (LOCF) with responder OR 1.9 relative — comparable to active controls, somewhat below other second-generation agents' literature effects
cards.summary: Szegedi 2012 (meta-analysis of 4 trials): asenapine beat placebo by −3.6 PANSS points (LOCF) with responder OR 1.9 relative — comparable to active controls, somewhat below other second-generation agents' literature effects
cards.people: Meta-analyses pooling the four asenapine trials from the asenapine development programme for acute schizophrenia, examining mean change in PANSS total score and PANSS responder rates versus placebo and other antipsychotics, supplemented by a network meta-analysis combining the asenapine trials with two previously published meta-analyses of second-generation antipsychotics.
cards.result: Asenapine was superior to placebo on mean change in PANSS total score (last observation carried forward: −3.6, p=.002; mixed model for repeated measures: −4.1, p=.001), an effect comparable to active controls from the same trials (LOCF: −4.0, p=.002; MMRM: −4.8, p=.001). PANSS responder rates were significantly better with asenapine versus placebo (OR 1.9 relative; p<.001) and comparable to active controls (OR 1.7 relative; p=.002). Effect sizes for asenapine were somewhat lower than those reported in the literature for other second-generation antipsychotics, and the network meta-analysis found asenapine's efficacy comparable to that of other agents, with estimated differences ranging from 3.9 points (95% CI 0.3 to 7.4) greater than ziprasidone to 2.9 points (95% CI −0.1 to 5.9) less than olanzapine.
cards.watchOut: A sponsor-programme meta-analysis: all four pooled trials are the manufacturer's own development trials, and the cross-drug comparisons are indirect (network and literature-based), so 'somewhat lower than other agents' is a softer claim than the placebo contrast. A −3.6-point average PANSS advantage is statistically solid but clinically modest at the individual-patient level.

shelves.question: In adults with acute schizophrenia, does paliperidone extended-release improve symptoms versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antipsychotic Agents/administration & dosage* · Delayed-Action Preparations · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions · Dyskinesia, Drug-Induced/etiology · Female · Humans · Isoxazoles/administration & dosage* · Male · Middle Aged · Paliperidone Palmitate · Patient Dropouts · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Pyrimidines/administration & dosage* · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Schizophrenia/drug therapy* · Schizophrenic Psychology · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders/chemically induced · Tachycardia/chemically induced · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — in the pivotal 6-week trial (Kane J et al., PMID: 17092691), 628 patients with acute schizophrenia received paliperidone extended-release 6, 9 or 12 mg once daily or placebo (with an olanzapine arm for assay sensitivity); all three paliperidone doses significantly improved PANSS total score, all PANSS Marder factor scores (p<0.001) and personal and social functioning (p<0.001) versus placebo, with significantly more patients achieving at least a 30% relative reduction in PANSS total score (p<0.001), mean weight change under 1 kg, and movement-disorder adverse events similar to placebo at 6 mg but higher at 9 and 12 mg. An individual-participant-data meta-analysis (Hodkinson A et al., PMID: 34429113) pooling 13 paliperidone studies (3,821 participants) found a PANSS advantage of −6.01 points versus placebo (95% CI −8.7 to −3.32), with low heterogeneity (I²=4.3%) — while also showing that clinical study reports recorded nearly twice as many adverse events (relative difference 1.93) and almost eight times as many serious adverse events (relative difference 7.93) as the journal publications of the same trials. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): paliperidone extended-release is an effective acute-schizophrenia treatment with a consistent moderate effect; its published tolerability picture is rosier than the underlying study reports justify.

cards.headline: Kane 2007: all three paliperidone ER doses (6, 9, 12 mg) beat placebo on PANSS and functioning at 6 weeks (p<0.001), with weight change under 1 kg and dose-related movement effects
cards.summary: Kane 2007: all three paliperidone ER doses (6, 9, 12 mg) beat placebo on PANSS and functioning at 6 weeks (p<0.001), with weight change under 1 kg and dose-related movement effects
cards.people: 628 patients with acute schizophrenia in a 6-week, multicentre, double-blind, randomised, parallel-group study of once-daily paliperidone extended-release tablets at 6 mg, 9 mg and 12 mg versus placebo, with an olanzapine treatment arm included; paliperidone ER uses OROS technology and undergoes limited hepatic metabolism. Outcomes were PANSS score, PANSS Marder factor scores, personal and social functioning, and the proportion with at least a 30% relative reduction in PANSS total score.
cards.result: All doses of paliperidone ER demonstrated significant improvement in PANSS score, all PANSS Marder factor scores (p<0.001) and personal and social functioning versus placebo (p<0.001); the PANSS total score also improved significantly in the olanzapine arm. Significantly higher percentages of paliperidone ER patients demonstrated a ≥30% relative reduction in PANSS total score versus placebo (p<0.001). The incidence of movement-disorder-related adverse events and rating-scale measurements were similar to placebo for the 6 mg group and higher in the 9 mg and 12 mg groups. In the paliperidone ER groups there were no reports of glucose-related adverse events or clinically relevant changes in plasma lipid levels, and changes in mean body weight were under 1 kg. The record reports significance levels rather than the PANSS point changes themselves.
cards.watchOut: Six weeks in acute illness, with the record giving p-values rather than effect sizes for the primary outcome — the magnitude judgement on this shelf comes from the IPD meta-analysis card, not from this trial's abstract. 'No glucose-related adverse events' over 6 weeks in a trial population is not a metabolic clean bill of health for years of treatment.
cards.source: Kane J et al. Treatment of schizophrenia with paliperidone extended-release tablets: a 6-week placebo-controlled trial. Schizophrenia research. 2007. PMID: 17092691. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hodkinson 2021 (IPD meta-analysis): paliperidone beat placebo by −6.01 PANSS points across 13 studies (3,821 participants) — and study reports held nearly twice the adverse events the publications showed
cards.summary: Hodkinson 2021 (IPD meta-analysis): paliperidone beat placebo by −6.01 PANSS points across 13 studies (3,821 participants) — and study reports held nearly twice the adverse events the publications showed
cards.people: Individual-participant-data (IPD) and clinical-study-report meta-analysis of randomised placebo-controlled trials of risperidone, paliperidone or paliperidone palmitate in schizophrenia or bipolar disorder, searching MEDLINE, CENTRAL, EMBASE and PsycINFO to December 2020 and obtaining IPD and clinical study reports through the Yale University Open Data Access project; 35 studies were identified, with IPD available for 22 (63%). The paliperidone estimate rests on 13 studies and 3,821 participants.
cards.result: The one-stage IPD meta-analysis showed a significant reduction in PANSS score for paliperidone versus placebo (mean difference −6.01, 95% CI −8.7 to −3.32; I²=4.3%; 13 studies, 3,821 participants), alongside risperidone (−5.83, 95% CI −10.79 to −0.87; 4 studies, 1,131 participants) and paliperidone palmitate (−7.89, 95% CI −12.1 to −3.69; 5 studies, 2,209 participants). Clinical study reports reported nearly two times more adverse events (4,434 vs 2,296; relative difference 1.93, 95% CI 1.86 to 2.00) and almost eight times more serious adverse events (650 vs 82; relative difference 7.93, 95% CI 6.32 to 9.95) than the journal publications of the same trials.
cards.watchOut: The pooled paliperidone estimate mixes formulations and indications in its parent review (the −6.01 figure is the paliperidone subgroup as printed), IPD were available for only 63% of studies, and the harms-reporting contrast (publications versus study reports) is a finding about the literature's reliability that should temper confidence in every published tolerability claim for this drug class — including the Kane card above.
cards.source: Hodkinson A et al. Benefits and harms of Risperidone and Paliperidone for treatment of patients with schizophrenia or bipolar disorder: a meta-analysis involving individual participant data and clinical study reports. BMC medicine. 2021. PMID: 34429113. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a consistent −6-point PANSS advantage over placebo, with a tolerability record that needs the study-report correction applied
cards.summary: Synthesis: a consistent −6-point PANSS advantage over placebo, with a tolerability record that needs the study-report correction applied
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: the pivotal 6-week trial (628 patients) and an IPD meta-analysis (13 paliperidone studies, 3,821 participants).
cards.result: Efficacy: all doses significant versus placebo in the pivotal trial; pooled PANSS mean difference −6.01 points (95% CI −8.7 to −3.32), I²=4.3%. Functioning: significantly improved versus placebo in the pivotal trial. Tolerability as published: weight change <1 kg, movement effects dose-related; as documented in study reports: roughly double the adverse events and eightfold the serious adverse events of the publications. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
cards.watchOut: This shelf covers oral paliperidone extended-release for acute treatment only; the long-acting injectable (palmitate) maintenance question is shelved separately (#994) and is not re-carded here. Six-week acute efficacy does not by itself establish relapse prevention or long-term metabolic safety.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kane J et al. Schizophrenia research. 2007 (PMID: 17092691); Hodkinson A et al. BMC medicine. 2021 (PMID: 34429113).

shelves.title: Amisulpride for acute schizophrenia: 400–800 mg/day topped the dose-response curve and beat haloperidol on parkinsonism — but the anchor trials never included a true placebo
shelves.question: In adults with acute schizophrenia, does amisulpride improve symptoms versus placebo and versus haloperidol?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adult · Amisulpride · Antipsychotic Agents/administration & dosage*,adverse effects · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Haloperidol/administration & dosage*,adverse effects · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neurologic Examination/drug effects · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Schizophrenia/diagnosis,drug therapy* · Sulpiride/administration & dosage,adverse effects,analogs & derivatives* · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the anchor evidence is comparative rather than placebo-controlled, and this shelf says so plainly. In the dose-ranging trial (Puech A et al., PMID: 9696517), 319 patients with acute exacerbation of schizophrenia received fixed doses of amisulpride 400, 800 or 1200 mg/day, haloperidol 16 mg/day, or amisulpride 100 mg/day as a potentially subtherapeutic comparator for 4 weeks: efficacy on BPRS total score and the PANSS positive subscale followed a bell-shaped dose-response curve, with 400 and 800 mg/day the most effective treatments for positive symptoms, and parkinsonism did not increase significantly at 400–1200 mg/day versus the 100 mg group, whereas the increase was significant for haloperidol (p<0.05). A pooled analysis of three studies (612 patients; Peuskens J et al., PMID: 12126869) found amisulpride 400–800 mg/day improved the BPRS anxiety/depression subscore more than haloperidol 15–20 mg/day and risperidone 8 mg/day combined comparators (mean improvement 5.6 ± 6.1 versus 4.4 ± 5.5 and 3.7 ± 4.7; p=0.011), with a larger advantage in more severely depressed patients (p=0.001) visible from the second week. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): amisulpride at 400–800 mg/day treats acute positive symptoms at least as well as haloperidol with less parkinsonism, and helps depressive symptoms in acute episodes — but no true placebo arm exists in the anchor record, which caps the stamp.

cards.headline: Puech 1998: amisulpride 400 and 800 mg/day were the most effective doses for positive symptoms in a bell-shaped dose-response, with less parkinsonism than haloperidol 16 mg/day
cards.summary: Puech 1998: amisulpride 400 and 800 mg/day were the most effective doses for positive symptoms in a bell-shaped dose-response, with less parkinsonism than haloperidol 16 mg/day
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind dose-ranging trial versus haloperidol (Puech 1998)
cards.people: 319 patients with acute exacerbation of schizophrenia in a 4-week, double-blind, randomised dose-ranging study: fixed doses of amisulpride 400, 800 and 1200 mg/day and haloperidol 16 mg/day were compared with amisulpride 100 mg/day, used as a potentially subtherapeutic dose rather than a placebo. Efficacy was measured on BPRS total score and the PANSS positive subscale; parkinsonism was assessed on neurological examination.
cards.result: Efficacy data (BPRS total score and PANSS positive subscale) in the amisulpride groups generated a bell-shaped dose-response curve, with 400 mg/day and 800 mg/day being the most effective treatments for positive symptoms. Parkinsonism did not increase significantly between baseline and endpoint with amisulpride 400, 800 and 1200 mg/day compared with the amisulpride 100 mg/day group, whereas the difference was significant for haloperidol (p<0.05). The authors conclude that amisulpride 400 mg and 800 mg/day is highly effective in treating the positive symptoms of schizophrenia, with fewer extrapyramidal side-effects than haloperidol 16 mg/day. The record reports the dose-response pattern qualitatively, without per-dose score changes.
cards.watchOut: There is no placebo arm: the comparator is a low (100 mg) amisulpride dose assumed subtherapeutic, so the trial shows a dose-response and a haloperidol comparison, not a placebo-subtracted effect size — and 4 weeks is short even for acute treatment. Haloperidol at 16 mg/day is a high dose by modern standards, which flatters the extrapyramidal comparison.
cards.source: Puech A et al. Amisulpride, and atypical antipsychotic, in the treatment of acute episodes of schizophrenia: a dose-ranging study vs. haloperidol. The Amisulpride Study Group. Acta psychiatrica Scandinavica. 1998. PMID: 9696517. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Peuskens 2002 (pooled, 3 studies, 612 patients): amisulpride improved depressive symptoms in acute episodes more than haloperidol or risperidone (5.6 vs 4.4 and 3.7 points; p=0.011)
cards.summary: Peuskens 2002 (pooled, 3 studies, 612 patients): amisulpride improved depressive symptoms in acute episodes more than haloperidol or risperidone (5.6 vs 4.4 and 3.7 points; p=0.011)
cards.type: Pooled analysis of three randomised trials (Peuskens 2002)
cards.people: Pooled analysis of three studies (n=612) comparing amisulpride 400–800 mg/day (n=339) with haloperidol 15–20 mg/day (n=160) and risperidone 8 mg/day (n=113) in acute exacerbations of schizophrenia, assessing affective symptoms on the BPRS anxiety/depression subscore, including a subgroup with more severe depression at baseline (subscore ≥16).
cards.result: At endpoint, the mean improvement in the anxiety/depression subscore showed a significant (p=0.011) difference in favour of amisulpride (5.6 ± 6.1) compared with haloperidol (4.4 ± 5.5) and risperidone (3.7 ± 4.7). Amisulpride provided a significantly greater improvement than both haloperidol and risperidone in more severely depressed patients (BPRS anxiety/depression subscore ≥16 at baseline; p=0.001), and this advantage was seen from the 2nd week of treatment.
cards.watchOut: A secondary-outcome pooled analysis of depressive symptoms within acute-episode trials — not a trial in depressive schizophrenia — with high comparator doses (haloperidol 15–20 mg, risperidone 8 mg) and a subscore, not a depression scale, as the measure. It supports an affective-symptom advantage over those comparators; it does not add a placebo contrast for the primary schizophrenia question.
cards.source: Peuskens J et al. Amisulpride improves depressive symptoms in acute exacerbations of schizophrenia: comparison with haloperidol and risperidone. European neuropsychopharmacology : the journal of the European College of Neuropsychopharmacology. 2002. PMID: 12126869. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: dose-response plus active-comparator wins, but the missing placebo arm is the honest headline limitation
cards.summary: Synthesis: dose-response plus active-comparator wins, but the missing placebo arm is the honest headline limitation
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: a 319-patient dose-ranging trial versus haloperidol and a low-dose control, and a 612-patient pooled analysis versus haloperidol and risperidone. No separate systematic-review card is included: no amisulpride meta-analysis with a placebo contrast was verified for this shelf in-session.
cards.result: Positive symptoms: bell-shaped dose-response peaking at 400–800 mg/day (Puech). Parkinsonism: no significant increase at 400–1200 mg/day versus low-dose control; significant increase on haloperidol 16 mg/day. Depressive symptoms: improvement 5.6 points on amisulpride versus 4.4 (haloperidol) and 3.7 (risperidone), p=0.011. Placebo-subtracted efficacy: not estimable from the anchor records. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Clinicians reading this shelf should know amisulpride's wider reputation rests on literature beyond these two records; within the discipline of this library, only what is carded counts, and what is carded here is comparative evidence from the 1990s development programme at comparator doses higher than current practice.
cards.source: Synthesis of Puech A et al. Acta psychiatrica Scandinavica. 1998 (PMID: 9696517); Peuskens J et al. European neuropsychopharmacology : the journal of the European College of Neuropsychopharmacology. 2002 (PMID: 12126869).

shelves.question: In adults with bipolar I depression already taking lithium or valproate, does adjunctive lurasidone improve depression versus placebo?

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — this shelf asks the adjunctive question only: in PREVAIL 1 (Loebel A et al., PMID: 24170221), 348 patients with bipolar I depression who had had an insufficient response to mood-stabiliser monotherapy were randomised to 6 weeks of adjunctive lurasidone or placebo, each added to therapeutic levels of lithium or valproate. Lurasidone reduced the MADRS total score significantly more than placebo at week 6 (−17.1 versus −13.5; effect size 0.34), with parallel advantages on CGI-BP depression severity (−1.96 versus −1.51; effect size 0.36), anxiety symptoms, quality of life and functional impairment. Discontinuation for adverse events was actually lower on lurasidone than placebo (6.0% vs 7.9%); the commonest lurasidone adverse events were nausea, somnolence, tremor, akathisia and insomnia, and changes in weight, lipids and glycaemic measures were minimal over 6 weeks. The margin over placebo is modest — about 3.6 MADRS points on top of a large placebo-plus-mood-stabiliser response — and it rests on this single adjunctive trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): adding lurasidone to lithium or valproate improves bipolar I depression modestly over 6 weeks. The lurasidone monotherapy question is a different shelf's business (#706) and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Loebel 2014 (PREVAIL 1): adjunctive lurasidone beat placebo on MADRS by −17.1 versus −13.5 at 6 weeks (effect size 0.34) in patients already on lithium or valproate
cards.summary: Loebel 2014 (PREVAIL 1): adjunctive lurasidone beat placebo on MADRS by −17.1 versus −13.5 at 6 weeks (effect size 0.34) in patients already on lithium or valproate
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled adjunctive trial (PREVAIL 1, Loebel 2014)
cards.people: 348 patients with bipolar I depression who had had an insufficient response to monotherapy with mood-stabilising agents, randomised to 6 weeks of double-blind adjunctive lurasidone (N=183) or placebo (N=165), each added to therapeutic levels of either lithium or valproate. The primary endpoint was change from baseline to week 6 on the Montgomery–Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS); the key secondary endpoint was the depression severity score on the Clinical Global Impressions scale for bipolar illness (CGI-BP).
cards.result: Lurasidone significantly reduced mean MADRS total score at week 6 compared with placebo (−17.1 versus −13.5; effect size 0.34). Endpoint reduction in CGI-BP depression severity was also significantly greater with lurasidone (−1.96 versus −1.51; effect size 0.36), as were improvement in anxiety symptoms and patient-reported quality of life and functional impairment. Discontinuation rates due to adverse events were 6.0% (lurasidone) and 7.9% (placebo). The adverse events most frequently reported for lurasidone were nausea, somnolence, tremor, akathisia and insomnia, and minimal changes in weight, lipids and measures of glycaemic control were observed during treatment.
cards.watchOut: Six weeks, one trial, and a placebo group that improved by −13.5 MADRS points on lithium or valproate alone — the drug's incremental contribution is the 3.6-point gap, and response/remission rates are not given in the record. The population is bipolar I depression with prior insufficient mood-stabiliser response; bipolar II and monotherapy questions are outside this card.
cards.source: Loebel A et al. Lurasidone as adjunctive therapy with lithium or valproate for the treatment of bipolar I depression: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study. shelves.title: Cognitive remediation for schizophrenia: 40 studies and 2,104 participants show durable gains in cognition — and in daily functioning when rehabilitation comes with it
shelves.question: In people with schizophrenia, does cognitive remediation improve cognition and functioning versus control interventions?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Clinical Trials as Topic/methods,standards · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy*/methods,standards · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Sample Size · Schizophrenia/therapy* · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the anchor for this shelf is itself the field's reference meta-analysis (Wykes T et al., PMID: 21406461): 40 studies (109 reports) with 2,104 participants, at least 70% diagnosed with schizophrenia and all receiving standard care, comparing cognitive remediation against control interventions. The pooled effects on global cognition and functioning were durable at follow-up and were described by the authors as small-to-moderate; the effect on symptoms was small and disappeared at follow-up. No treatment element — remediation approach, duration, or computer use — was associated with cognitive outcome, methodological rigour did not moderate any effect (even the most rigorous studies showed similar small-to-moderate effects), and remediation worked better in clinically stable patients. Functioning effects were significantly stronger when cognitive remediation was delivered together with other psychiatric rehabilitation, and much larger when a strategic (transfer-focused) approach was combined with adjunctive rehabilitation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): cognitive remediation produces durable small-to-moderate gains in cognition and, especially when paired with rehabilitation, in everyday functioning — the record's own abstract reports no pooled point estimates, which is why this shelf grades the consistency and durability of the finding rather than a number it does not print.

cards.headline: Wykes 2011 (meta-analysis, 40 studies, 2,104 participants): cognitive remediation gave durable small-to-moderate gains in global cognition and functioning; symptom effects were small and faded
cards.summary: Wykes 2011 (meta-analysis, 40 studies, 2,104 participants): cognitive remediation gave durable small-to-moderate gains in global cognition and functioning; symptom effects were small and faded
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 40 studies (109 reports) identified by database searches to June 2009 plus direct contact with key researchers, in which at least 70% of participants had a diagnosis of schizophrenia, all received standard care, and there was a comparison group and an allocation procedure; data were available to calculate effect sizes on cognition and/or functioning for 2,104 participants. Methodological moderators were extracted with the Clinical Trials Assessment Measure and verified by study authors in 94% of cases; data extraction was by two independent reviewers with excellent reliability.
cards.result: The meta-analysis (2,104 participants) yielded durable effects on global cognition and functioning; the record describes the effects as small-to-moderate but prints no pooled effect-size values in its abstract. The symptom effect was small and disappeared at follow-up assessment. No treatment element (remediation approach, duration, computer use, etc.) was associated with cognitive outcome, and cognitive remediation was more effective when patients were clinically stable. Significantly stronger effects on functioning were found when cognitive remediation was provided together with other psychiatric rehabilitation, and a much larger effect was present when a strategic approach was adopted together with adjunctive rehabilitation. Despite variability in methodological rigour, rigour did not moderate any therapy effect, and even in the most rigorous studies there were similar small-to-moderate effects. The authors conclude that cognitive remediation benefits people with schizophrenia and, combined with psychiatric rehabilitation, generalises to functioning relative to rehabilitation alone, and that the benefits cannot be attributed to poor study methods.
cards.watchOut: The abstract — the record this library cards from — reports no numerical effect sizes, so any specific number quoted for this meta-analysis elsewhere (in either direction) is not verifiable from the record and is deliberately not printed here. The search closed in June 2009, control conditions ranged widely, and 'functioning' gains were conditional on pairing remediation with rehabilitation: remediation alone, on this record, is a cognition intervention with a functioning hope attached.
cards.source: Wykes T et al. A meta-analysis of cognitive remediation for schizophrenia: methodology and effect sizes. The American journal of psychiatry. 2011. PMID: 21406461. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: durable cognition gains, functioning gains when rehabilitation is added, no symptom claim — a rehabilitation adjunct, not a treatment for psychosis itself
cards.summary: Synthesis: durable cognition gains, functioning gains when rehabilitation is added, no symptom claim — a rehabilitation adjunct, not a treatment for psychosis itself
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: the Wykes 2011 meta-analysis (40 studies, 2,104 participants), which is both the miner's anchor and the systematic-review evidence for this question; no second review card is added, to avoid double-counting overlapping trial sets.
cards.result: Global cognition: durable small-to-moderate benefit versus control. Functioning: durable benefit, significantly stronger with adjunctive psychiatric rehabilitation and a strategic approach. Symptoms: small effect, gone at follow-up. Moderators: clinical stability helped; treatment format, duration and computer use did not matter; study rigour did not explain the effects. Numerical pooled effect sizes: not printed in the record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The stamp is POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY for one stated reason: the record establishes direction, durability and moderators across 40 studies, but without printed effect sizes the size of benefit a service can expect cannot be pinned from the carded evidence. Newer meta-analyses exist in the literature but were not carded here; this shelf should be refreshed against one before any stronger stamp is proposed.
cards.source: Synthesis of Wykes T et al. The American journal of psychiatry. 2011 (PMID: 21406461).

shelves.title: Vilazodone for major depression: one 8-week trial beat placebo on the MADRS by 2.5 points, with response 44% versus 30% — and diarrhoea in nearly a third
shelves.question: In adults with major depressive disorder, does vilazodone improve depression versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Antidepressive Agents, Second-Generation/adverse effects · Antidepressive Agents, Second-Generation/therapeutic use · Benzofurans/adverse effects · Benzofurans/therapeutic use · Major Depressive Disorder/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Indoles/adverse effects · Indoles/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Piperazines/adverse effects · Piperazines/therapeutic use · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors/adverse effects · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Vilazodone Hydrochloride · Young Adult
shelves.balance: One phase 3 trial (Khan A et al., PMID: 21527122) randomised 481 adults with major depressive disorder to vilazodone titrated to 40 mg/day or placebo for 8 weeks. Vilazodone improved the primary outcome — least-squares mean MADRS change −13.3 versus −10.8 on placebo (p=.009) — and the response rate was 44% versus 30% (p=.002), but remission did not separate significantly on either the MADRS (27.3% vs 20.3%, p=.066) or the HDRS-17 (24.2% vs 17.7%, p=.088). The benefit is therefore real but modest: a roughly 2.5-point extra MADRS fall and about one extra responder in seven, bought with diarrhoea in 31% versus 11%, nausea in 26% versus 6%, and discontinuation for adverse events in 5.1% versus 1.7%. Sexual function and weight were no different from placebo in this trial. This shelf rests on a single short trial with no active comparator, so how vilazodone compares with established antidepressants is not answered here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a genuine but modest short-term antidepressant effect, with tolerability — not efficacy — the main practical limit.

cards.headline: Khan 2011: vilazodone 40 mg beat placebo on MADRS change (−13.3 vs −10.8, p=.009) and response (44% vs 30%), but remission was not significantly different
cards.summary: Khan 2011: vilazodone 40 mg beat placebo on MADRS change (−13.3 vs −10.8, p=.009) and response (44% vs 30%), but remission was not significantly different
cards.people: 481 adults with DSM-IV-TR major depressive disorder in a phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled 8-week study (March 2008–February 2009); vilazodone was titrated to 40 mg once daily.
cards.result: Primary endpoint (MADRS change, intention-to-treat): least-squares mean −13.3 on vilazodone versus −10.8 on placebo (p=.009). MADRS response 44% versus 30% (p=.002). Remission was not significant: MADRS 27.3% versus 20.3% (p=.066); HDRS-17 24.2% versus 17.7% (p=.088). Vilazodone also separated on HDRS-17 (p=.026), HDRS-21 (p=.029), Hamilton Anxiety (p=.037), CGI-S (p=.004) and CGI-I (p=.004). Discontinuation for adverse events 5.1% versus 1.7%; diarrhoea 31% versus 11%, nausea 26% versus 6%, headache 13% versus 10%. Sexual-function (CSFQ) effects were small and similar to placebo, and weight effects did not differ from placebo.
cards.watchOut: A single 8-week, industry-era phase 3 trial with no active comparator and no maintenance data: it shows vilazodone beats placebo short-term, not that it matches or beats any established antidepressant, and the headline response gain coexists with a non-significant remission result — the outcome patients feel most.
cards.source: Khan A et al. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, 8-week study of vilazodone, a serotonergic agent for the treatment of major depressive disorder. The Journal of clinical psychiatry. 2011. PMID: 21527122. Registry ID: NCT00683592. shelves.title: Levomilnacipran ER for major depression: all three doses beat placebo on the MADRS, with a dose gradient from −3.2 to −4.9 points
shelves.question: In adults with major depressive disorder, does levomilnacipran extended-release improve depression versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cyclopropanes*/administration & dosage · Cyclopropanes*/adverse effects · Cyclopropanes*/chemistry · Delayed-Action Preparations/administration & dosage · Delayed-Action Preparations/adverse effects · Delayed-Action Preparations/chemistry · Major Depressive Disorder/diagnosis · Major Depressive Disorder/drug therapy · Major Depressive Disorder/psychology · Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Monitoring · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Milnacipran · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors/administration & dosage · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors/adverse effects · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors/chemistry · Stereoisomerism · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: One phase 3 trial (Asnis GM et al., PMID: 23561229) randomised 724 outpatients with major depressive disorder to placebo or fixed-dose levomilnacipran sustained release 40, 80 or 120 mg once daily for 8 weeks. Every dose beat placebo on the primary MADRS change, with a clear dose gradient in the least-squares mean difference: −3.23 (p=.0186), −3.99 (p=.0038) and −4.86 (p=.0005). The 80 mg and 120 mg doses also separated on disability (Sheehan Disability Scale), HDRS-17 and global impression measures; the 40 mg dose separated only on the primary scale. The common adverse events — headache, nausea, constipation, dry mouth, increased heart rate and hyperhidrosis — are the expected noradrenergic profile of a serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor, and the record reports the drug as generally well tolerated. The evidence is a single short fixed-dose trial: no active comparator, no maintenance phase, and no remission rates in the record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a consistent, dose-ordered short-term effect on depression scores, with comparative and long-term questions unanswered.

cards.headline: Asnis 2013: levomilnacipran ER beat placebo at every dose — MADRS differences −3.23 (40 mg), −3.99 (80 mg) and −4.86 (120 mg)
cards.summary: Asnis 2013: levomilnacipran ER beat placebo at every dose — MADRS differences −3.23 (40 mg), −3.99 (80 mg) and −4.86 (120 mg)
cards.people: 724 outpatients meeting DSM-IV-TR criteria for major depressive disorder with a current episode of at least 8 weeks, randomised after a 1-week placebo lead-in to placebo (n=179) or levomilnacipran sustained release 40 mg (n=181), 80 mg (n=181) or 120 mg (n=183) once daily for 8 weeks, followed by a 2-week down-taper.
cards.result: Primary endpoint (MADRS change): least-squares mean differences versus placebo of −3.23 (p=.0186) at 40 mg, −3.99 (p=.0038) at 80 mg and −4.86 (p=.0005) at 120 mg. The 80 mg and 120 mg doses also beat placebo on the Sheehan Disability Scale (−2.51 and −2.57, p<.05), HDRS-17 (−2.09 and −2.34, p<.05), CGI-S (−0.43, p<.01; −0.35, p<.05) and CGI-I (−0.34 and −0.32, p<.05). Most common treatment-emergent adverse events (≥10% in any group): headache, nausea, constipation, dry mouth, increased heart rate and hyperhidrosis.
cards.watchOut: One 8-week fixed-dose trial, no active comparator, and the record reports score changes rather than response or remission proportions — so the size of benefit a patient would notice, and any ranking against other SNRIs, cannot be read off this trial.
cards.source: Asnis GM et al. Efficacy and safety of levomilnacipran sustained release 40 mg, 80 mg, or 120 mg in major depressive disorder: a phase 3, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study. The Journal of clinical psychiatry. 2013. PMID: 23561229. Registry ID: NCT00969709. shelves.title: Transdermal selegiline for major depression: one small 6-week outpatient trial found greater improvement on every scale — but its record reports no effect sizes
shelves.question: In adults with major depressive disorder, does transdermal selegiline improve depression versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Cutaneous · Adult · Antidepressive Agents/administration & dosage · Antidepressive Agents/adverse effects · Major Depressive Disorder/diagnosis · Major Depressive Disorder/drug therapy · Major Depressive Disorder/psychology · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Monoamine Oxidase Inhibitors/administration & dosage · Monoamine Oxidase Inhibitors/adverse effects · Personality Inventory · Selegiline/administration & dosage · Selegiline/adverse effects · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: The randomised record carded here is one trial (Bodkin JA et al., PMID: 12411221): 177 adult outpatients with major depressive disorder received a transdermal selegiline patch (20 mg over a 20-cm² patch, once daily) or placebo for 6 weeks, on a tyramine-restricted diet. The record reports greater improvement with selegiline on all measures used — the 17- and 28-item Hamilton scales, the Montgomery–Åsberg scale and Clinical Global Impression severity and improvement — with separation on the Hamilton and Montgomery–Åsberg scores as early as week 1. Critically, the record reports no numeric effect sizes, response rates or remission rates, so the size of the benefit cannot be stated from the evidence in hand. Tolerability in the trial was close to placebo apart from application-site reactions, with no orthostatic hypotensive or hypertensive reactions observed. One small, short trial with qualitative reporting is the definition of a weak base. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): transdermal selegiline may improve major depression over 6 weeks, but the magnitude is unquantified in this record and replication at this dose and diet condition is not carded here.

cards.headline: Bodkin 2002: transdermal selegiline beat placebo on every depression scale used over 6 weeks — separation from week 1, but no effect sizes reported in the record
cards.summary: Bodkin 2002: transdermal selegiline beat placebo on every depression scale used over 6 weeks — separation from week 1, but no effect sizes reported in the record
cards.people: 177 adult outpatients with major depressive disorder, randomised after a 1-week placebo lead-in to transdermal selegiline 20 mg via a 20-cm² patch once daily (n=89) or placebo (n=88) for 6 weeks; all followed a tyramine-restricted diet during the trial and for 2 weeks after.
cards.result: Greater improvement at 6 weeks with selegiline than placebo on all measures: Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (17- and 28-item), Montgomery–Åsberg Depression Rating Scale, and CGI severity and improvement; a statistically significant drug–placebo difference on the Hamilton and Montgomery–Åsberg scores was seen as early as week 1. The record reports no numeric score differences, response rates or remission rates. Adverse-event profile did not differ from placebo except application-site reactions (more common with selegiline); no orthostatic hypotensive or hypertensive reactions were observed.
cards.watchOut: The absence of any number in the record is the central limitation: 'greater improvement on all measures' in 177 patients over 6 weeks cannot be converted into a benefit a clinician can weigh, and the tyramine-restricted diet used in the trial is part of the tested condition, not an incidental detail.
cards.source: Bodkin JA et al. Transdermal selegiline in major depression: a double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group study in outpatients. The American journal of psychiatry. 2002. PMID: 12411221. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: SWITCH: decompressive craniectomy for severe deep brain haemorrhage — unfavourable outcome 44% versus 58%, a difference that just missed significance in a trial stopped early for funding
shelves.question: In patients with severe deep supratentorial intracerebral haemorrhage, does decompressive craniectomy plus medical treatment improve survival and function versus medical treatment alone?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Middle Aged · Male · Decompressive Craniectomy*/methods · Female · Cerebral Hemorrhage*/surgery · Aged · Adult · Treatment Outcome · Combined Modality Therapy
shelves.balance: SWITCH (Beck J et al., PMID: 38761811) randomised 201 adults aged 18–75 with severe deep (basal ganglia or thalamus) intracerebral haemorrhage in 42 European stroke centres to decompressive craniectomy plus best medical treatment or best medical treatment alone; 197 gave delayed consent and the trial was stopped early for lack of funding. The primary outcome — modified Rankin Scale 5–6 (severe disability or death) at 180 days — occurred in 42 of 95 (44%) surgical patients versus 55 (58%) medical patients (adjusted risk ratio 0.77, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.01; adjusted risk difference −13%, 95% CI −26 to 0; p=0.057). The per-protocol analysis leaned the same way (47% vs 60%; aRR 0.76, 0.58 to 1.00). Severe adverse events were similar (41% vs 44%). The authors themselves call this weak evidence, and the record is explicit that survival in both groups is associated with severe disability and that the results do not apply to haemorrhages in other locations. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): the point estimate favours surgery by a clinically large margin, but an underpowered, early-stopped trial whose confidence interval touches no-effect cannot carry a stronger stamp.

cards.headline: SWITCH 2024: mRS 5–6 at 180 days in 44% with craniectomy versus 58% with medical care alone (aRR 0.77, 95% CI 0.59–1.01; p=0.057) — trial stopped early for lack of funding
cards.summary: SWITCH 2024: mRS 5–6 at 180 days in 44% with craniectomy versus 58% with medical care alone (aRR 0.77, 95% CI 0.59–1.01; p=0.057) — trial stopped early for lack of funding
cards.people: 201 adults (18–75 years) with severe intracerebral haemorrhage involving the basal ganglia or thalamus (median age 61; median haematoma volume 57 mL) randomised in 42 stroke centres in nine European countries; 197 gave delayed informed consent (96 surgery plus medical, 101 medical alone).
cards.result: Primary outcome (mRS 5–6 at 180 days, intention-to-treat): 42/95 (44%) with decompressive craniectomy plus best medical treatment versus 55 (58%) with best medical treatment alone — adjusted risk ratio 0.77 (95% CI 0.59 to 1.01), adjusted risk difference −13% (−26 to 0), p=0.057. Per-protocol: 36/77 (47%) versus 44/73 (60%), aRR 0.76 (0.58 to 1.00), aRD −15% (−28 to 0). Severe adverse events: 42/103 (41%) surgery versus 41/94 (44%) medical. The trial was stopped early due to lack of funding.
cards.watchOut: Early stopping left the trial underpowered for its own primary outcome, and the endpoint bundles death with survival in a severely disabled state (mRS 5) — a family weighing this operation is choosing between distributions of death and severe disability, not between death and recovery. Results apply only to deep (basal ganglia/thalamus) haemorrhage.
cards.source: Beck J et al. shelves.title: CHANCE-2: in CYP2C19 loss-of-function carriers after minor stroke or TIA, ticagrelor cut 90-day stroke to 6.0% versus 7.6% on clopidogrel — with more total bleeding but no more severe bleeding
shelves.question: In CYP2C19 loss-of-function carriers with minor stroke or high-risk TIA, does ticagrelor plus aspirin prevent recurrent stroke better than clopidogrel plus aspirin?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aspirin/therapeutic use · Clopidogrel/adverse effects · Clopidogrel/therapeutic use · Cytochrome P-450 CYP2C19/genetics · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Incidence · Ischemic Attack, Transient/drug therapy · Ischemic Attack, Transient/genetics · Ischemic Stroke/drug therapy · Ischemic Stroke/epidemiology · Ischemic Stroke/genetics · Ischemic Stroke/prevention & control · Loss of Function Mutation* · Male · Middle Aged · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Purinergic P2Y Receptor Antagonists/adverse effects · Purinergic P2Y Receptor Antagonists/therapeutic use · Secondary Prevention · Ticagrelor/adverse effects · Ticagrelor/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: CHANCE-2 (Wang Y et al., PMID: 34708996) randomised 6,412 Chinese patients with minor ischaemic stroke or TIA who carried CYP2C19 loss-of-function alleles, within 24 hours of onset, to ticagrelor (180 mg load, then 90 mg twice daily) or clopidogrel (300 mg load, then 75 mg daily) for 90 days, both with aspirin for the first 21 days. Stroke within 90 days occurred in 191 patients (6.0%) on ticagrelor versus 243 (7.6%) on clopidogrel — hazard ratio 0.77 (95% CI 0.64 to 0.94; p=0.008), a 23% relative risk reduction with absolute rates of 6.0% versus 7.6% printed beside it. Severe or moderate bleeding did not differ (0.3% in both groups), but any bleeding was more common on ticagrelor (5.3% vs 2.5%). The gain is real but modest in absolute terms — about 1.6 fewer strokes per 100 patients treated — and it is proven only in a genotype-selected, almost entirely Han Chinese population treated within 24 hours. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a genotype-guided switch that helps the subgroup in whom clopidogrel activation is impaired, not a general reason to prefer ticagrelor after stroke.

cards.headline: CHANCE-2 2021: stroke at 90 days 6.0% on ticagrelor versus 7.6% on clopidogrel (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.64–0.94) in CYP2C19 loss-of-function carriers
cards.summary: CHANCE-2 2021: stroke at 90 days 6.0% on ticagrelor versus 7.6% on clopidogrel (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.64–0.94) in CYP2C19 loss-of-function carriers
cards.people: 6,412 patients in China (median age 64.8 years, 33.8% women, 98.0% Han Chinese) with minor ischaemic stroke or TIA carrying CYP2C19 loss-of-function alleles, randomised within 24 hours of symptom onset; ticagrelor n=3,205, clopidogrel n=3,207; both groups received aspirin for 21 days.
cards.result: Primary efficacy (new stroke within 90 days): 191 (6.0%) ticagrelor versus 243 (7.6%) clopidogrel — hazard ratio 0.77 (95% CI 0.64 to 0.94; p=0.008), i.e. a 23% relative risk reduction alongside absolute rates of 6.0% and 7.6%. Primary safety (severe or moderate bleeding): 9 (0.3%) versus 11 (0.3%). Any bleeding: 170 (5.3%) versus 80 (2.5%). Secondary outcomes were generally in the same direction as the primary outcome.
cards.watchOut: The result is conditional on genotype testing, a 24-hour treatment window, and a population that was 98% Han Chinese, in whom CYP2C19 loss-of-function alleles are common. It does not show ticagrelor is better in non-carriers, in major stroke, or beyond 90 days.
cards.source: Wang Y et al. Ticagrelor versus Clopidogrel in CYP2C19 Loss-of-Function Carriers with Stroke or TIA. The New England journal of medicine. 2021. PMID: 34708996. Registry ID: NCT04078737. shelves.title: SPS3: adding clopidogrel to aspirin after lacunar stroke did not prevent recurrence — it doubled major haemorrhage and raised mortality; a lower blood-pressure target only trended to benefit
shelves.question: In patients with recent lacunar stroke, does adding clopidogrel to aspirin prevent recurrent stroke versus aspirin alone, and at what bleeding cost?
shelves.mesh: Aspirin/adverse effects · Aspirin/therapeutic use · Clopidogrel · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination/adverse effects · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Hemorrhage/chemically induced · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors/adverse effects · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Recurrence · Stroke/epidemiology · Stroke/prevention & control · Stroke, Lacunar/drug therapy · Ticlopidine/adverse effects · Ticlopidine/analogs & derivatives · Ticlopidine/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: SPS3 tested two questions in 3,020 patients with recent MRI-defined lacunar stroke. The antiplatelet comparison (PMID: 22931315) was double-blind: clopidogrel 75 mg plus aspirin 325 mg versus aspirin alone over a mean 3.4 years. Recurrent stroke was not significantly reduced (2.5% versus 2.7% per year; HR 0.92, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.16), nor was recurrent ischaemic stroke (HR 0.82, 0.63 to 1.09) or disabling/fatal stroke (HR 1.06). Major haemorrhage almost doubled (2.1% versus 1.1% per year; HR 1.97, 1.41 to 2.71; p<0.001) and all-cause mortality rose (113 versus 77 deaths; HR 1.52, 1.14 to 2.04; p=0.004), a difference not explained by fatal haemorrhage. The blood-pressure comparison (PMID: 23726159), in the same factorial cohort, achieved systolic pressures of 127 versus 138 mm Hg and found non-significant reductions in all stroke (HR 0.81, 0.64 to 1.03; p=0.08) with a significant reduction in intracerebral haemorrhage (HR 0.37, 0.15 to 0.95; p=0.03). PROPOSED LIKELY (harm): for the shelf's question the answer is unusually clear — long-term dual antiplatelet therapy after lacunar stroke buys bleeding and death, not protection; the gentler blood-pressure signal is hypothesis-supporting, not proven.

cards.headline: SPS3 antiplatelet trial 2012: recurrent stroke 2.5%/year on dual therapy versus 2.7%/year on aspirin alone (HR 0.92, NS) — while major haemorrhage doubled (HR 1.97) and mortality rose (HR 1.52)
cards.summary: SPS3 antiplatelet trial 2012: recurrent stroke 2.5%/year on dual therapy versus 2.7%/year on aspirin alone (HR 0.92, NS) — while major haemorrhage doubled (HR 1.97) and mortality rose (HR 1.52)
cards.people: 3,020 patients with recent symptomatic lacunar infarcts confirmed by MRI (mean age 63, 63% men), randomised double-blind to clopidogrel 75 mg daily or placebo, all receiving aspirin 325 mg daily; mean follow-up 3.4 years.
cards.result: Recurrent stroke: 125 events (2.5% per year) on dual therapy versus 138 (2.7% per year) on aspirin alone — HR 0.92 (95% CI 0.72 to 1.16). Recurrent ischaemic stroke HR 0.82 (0.63 to 1.09); disabling or fatal stroke HR 1.06 (0.69 to 1.64). Major haemorrhage: 105 (2.1% per year) versus 56 (1.1% per year) — HR 1.97 (1.41 to 2.71; p<0.001). All-cause mortality: 113 deaths on dual therapy versus 77 on aspirin alone — HR 1.52 (1.14 to 2.04; p=0.004), not accounted for by fatal haemorrhages (9 vs 4). Of classifiable recurrent ischaemic strokes, 71% were lacunar.
cards.watchOut: This is long-term dual therapy in lacunar (small-vessel) stroke specifically — it does not contradict short-course dual therapy after minor non-lacunar stroke or stenting, which are different questions on other shelves. The mortality excess, though unexplained by fatal bleeding, was a pre-specified safety signal in a large blinded trial and should not be waved away.
cards.source: SPS3 Investigators et al. Effects of clopidogrel added to aspirin in patients with recent lacunar stroke. The New England journal of medicine. 2012. PMID: 22931315. Registry ID: NCT00059306. cards.headline: SPS3 blood-pressure trial 2013: targeting systolic <130 versus 130–149 mm Hg gave a non-significant stroke reduction (HR 0.81, p=0.08) but significantly fewer intracerebral haemorrhages (HR 0.37)
cards.summary: SPS3 blood-pressure trial 2013: targeting systolic <130 versus 130–149 mm Hg gave a non-significant stroke reduction (HR 0.81, p=0.08) but significantly fewer intracerebral haemorrhages (HR 0.37)
cards.people: The same 3,020-patient SPS3 cohort (1,519 higher-target, 1,501 lower-target), randomised open-label in a 2×2 factorial design and followed a mean of 3.7 years; sites in North America, Latin America and Spain.
cards.result: Achieved systolic pressure at 1 year: 138 mm Hg (higher target) versus 127 mm Hg (lower target). All stroke: HR 0.81 (95% CI 0.64 to 1.03; p=0.08). Disabling or fatal stroke: HR 0.81 (0.53 to 1.23; p=0.32). Composite of myocardial infarction or vascular death: HR 0.84 (0.68 to 1.04; p=0.32). Intracerebral haemorrhage: HR 0.37 (0.15 to 0.95; p=0.03). Treatment-related serious adverse events were infrequent.
cards.watchOut: The blood-pressure arm was open-label and its primary result missed significance — it supports, but does not prove, a <130 mm Hg target after lacunar stroke. Do not let its favourable trend soften the antiplatelet arm's clear harm finding; they are separate randomisations.

cards.headline: Synthesis: in lacunar stroke, more antiplatelet was worse and lower pressure was probably better — one factorial trial, two opposite lessons
cards.summary: Synthesis: in lacunar stroke, more antiplatelet was worse and lower pressure was probably better — one factorial trial, two opposite lessons
cards.people: One factorial trial programme, 3,020 patients with recent lacunar stroke, followed 3.4–3.7 years.
cards.result: Dual antiplatelet versus aspirin alone: recurrent stroke HR 0.92 (NS), major haemorrhage HR 1.97, mortality HR 1.52. Lower versus higher systolic target: all stroke HR 0.81 (p=0.08), intracerebral haemorrhage HR 0.37 (p=0.03). PROPOSED LIKELY (harm) for adding clopidogrel long-term.

shelves.title: VNS-REHAB: implanted vagus nerve stimulation paired with rehab improved arm scores by 2.6 extra points, with 47% versus 24% achieving a meaningful response at 90 days
shelves.question: In patients with upper-limb weakness after ischaemic stroke, does vagus nerve stimulation paired with rehabilitation improve arm function versus rehabilitation with sham stimulation?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Case-Control Studies · Combined Modality Therapy/methods · Exercise Therapy/methods · Female · Humans · Implantable Neurostimulators/adverse effects · Ischemic Stroke/complications · Ischemic Stroke/rehabilitation · Male · Middle Aged · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Paresis/etiology · Recovery of Function/physiology · Stroke Rehabilitation/methods · Treatment Outcome · Upper Extremity/physiopathology · Vagus Nerve Stimulation/instrumentation · Vocal Cord Paralysis/epidemiology
shelves.balance: VNS-REHAB (Dawson J et al., PMID: 33894832) randomised 108 patients with moderate-to-severe arm weakness at least 9 months after ischaemic stroke, in 19 UK and US services, to rehabilitation paired with active implanted vagus nerve stimulation or with sham (0 mA) stimulation; everyone received the implant, and patients, therapists and assessors were masked. After 6 weeks of in-clinic therapy, Fugl-Meyer Upper Extremity scores rose 5.0 points (SD 4.4) with active stimulation versus 2.4 (3.8) with sham — a between-group difference of 2.6 points (95% CI 1.0 to 4.2; p=0.0014). At 90 days a clinically meaningful response was achieved by 23 of 53 (47%) versus 13 of 55 (24%) — a difference of 24 percentage points (95% CI 6 to 41; p=0.0098) alongside the absolute rates of 47% and 24%. One surgery-related serious adverse event (vocal cord paresis) occurred, in the control group. The effect is statistically solid but modest in size, from a single industry pivotal trial, in a chronic population with an implanted device and its surgical burden. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real incremental gain over intensive rehabilitation alone, to be weighed against implantation and cost.

cards.headline: VNS-REHAB 2021: FMA-UE gain 5.0 versus 2.4 points after in-clinic therapy (difference 2.6, 95% CI 1.0–4.2; p=0.0014); meaningful response at 90 days 47% versus 24%
cards.summary: VNS-REHAB 2021: FMA-UE gain 5.0 versus 2.4 points after in-clinic therapy (difference 2.6, 95% CI 1.0–4.2; p=0.0014); meaningful response at 90 days 47% versus 24%
cards.people: 108 patients with moderate-to-severe arm weakness at least 9 months after ischaemic stroke (baseline FMA-UE 20–50), randomised at 19 stroke rehabilitation services in the UK and USA to active VNS (n=53) or sham stimulation (n=55); all were implanted, and received 6 weeks of in-clinic therapy (18 sessions) plus a home exercise programme.
cards.result: Primary outcome (FMA-UE change the day after in-clinic therapy): +5.0 points (SD 4.4) active versus +2.4 (3.8) sham — between-group difference 2.6 (95% CI 1.0 to 4.2; p=0.0014). At 90 days, clinically meaningful FMA-UE response: 23/53 (47%) versus 13/55 (24%) — difference 24% (6 to 41; p=0.0098). 106 of 108 completed the study. One serious adverse event related to surgery (vocal cord paresis) occurred in the control group.
cards.watchOut: A single pivotal trial of 108 patients sponsored around a proprietary implanted device: the 2.6-point average advantage sits below many published thresholds for a clearly perceptible change, the responder analysis is more favourable than the mean difference, and there is no comparison with simply doing more rehabilitation.
cards.source: Dawson J et al. Vagus nerve stimulation paired with rehabilitation for upper limb motor function after ischaemic stroke (VNS-REHAB): a randomised, blinded, pivotal, device trial. Lancet (London, England). 2021. PMID: 33894832. Registry ID: NCT03131960. shelves.title: RATULS: robot-assisted arm training did not improve arm function (44% success versus 42% on usual care) in the largest trial — while pooled smaller trials in Cochrane show small gains
shelves.question: In patients with upper-limb impairment after stroke, does robot-assisted training improve arm function versus usual care or matched therapy?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Recovery of Function · Robotics/education · Stroke Rehabilitation/instrumentation · Treatment Outcome · United Kingdom · Upper Extremity/physiopathology
shelves.balance: The evidence genuinely splits by trial size. RATULS (Rodgers H et al., PMID: 31128926), a pragmatic UK trial of 770 stroke patients with moderate-to-severe upper-limb limitation, found Action Research Arm Test success at 3 months in 103 of 232 (44%) with robot-assisted training, 118 of 234 (50%) with an enhanced upper-limb therapy programme, and 85 of 203 (42%) with usual care — robot training did not improve function versus usual care (adjusted OR 1.17, 98.3% CI 0.70 to 1.96) or versus matched therapy (aOR 0.78, 0.48 to 1.27). The Cochrane review (Mehrholz J et al., PMID: 30175845), pooling 45 trials and 1,619 participants — mostly far smaller than RATULS — found electromechanical and robot-assisted training improved activities of daily living (SMD 0.31, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.52), arm function (SMD 0.32, 0.18 to 0.46) and arm strength (SMD 0.46, 0.16 to 0.77), on high-quality-rated evidence but with wide variation in dose, device and patients. PROPOSED SPLIT: small pooled trials say a small benefit exists; the one large pragmatic trial, testing the intervention as actually deliverable, says it does not beat usual care — routine adoption is not supported by RATULS, and any real effect is likely small and dose- or device-dependent.

cards.headline: RATULS 2019: ARAT success 44% robot versus 42% usual care (aOR 1.17, 98.3% CI 0.70–1.96) and 50% with enhanced therapy — no improvement from robot training in 770 patients
cards.summary: RATULS 2019: ARAT success 44% robot versus 42% usual care (aOR 1.17, 98.3% CI 0.70–1.96) and 50% with enhanced therapy — no improvement from robot training in 770 patients
cards.people: 770 stroke patients aged at least 18 with moderate or severe upper-limb functional limitation, 1 week to 5 years after first stroke, at four UK centres; randomised to robot-assisted training (n=257), enhanced upper limb therapy (n=259) or usual care (n=254), with training/therapy 45 minutes, three times weekly for 12 weeks.
cards.result: Primary outcome (ARAT-defined upper-limb success at 3 months): 103/232 (44%) robot, 118/234 (50%) enhanced therapy, 85/203 (42%) usual care. Versus usual care: robot aOR 1.17 (98.3% CI 0.70 to 1.96); enhanced therapy aOR 1.51 (0.90 to 2.51) — neither significant. Robot versus enhanced therapy: aOR 0.78 (0.48 to 1.27). Serious adverse events: 39/257 (15%) robot, 33/259 (13%) enhanced therapy, 20/254 (8%) usual care, none attributable to the intervention.
cards.watchOut: RATULS tested one robotic gym system at one deliverable dose in a broad, largely chronic population; its null does not exclude benefit from other devices, much higher doses, or very early treatment — but it is the only trial large enough to detect the modest effect the pooled literature claims.
cards.source: Rodgers H et al. Robot assisted training for the upper limb after stroke (RATULS): a multicentre randomised controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2019. PMID: 31128926. cards.headline: Cochrane 2018 (Mehrholz): across 45 small trials, robot/electromechanical arm training improved daily activities (SMD 0.31), arm function (SMD 0.32) and strength (SMD 0.46)
cards.summary: Cochrane 2018 (Mehrholz): across 45 small trials, robot/electromechanical arm training improved daily activities (SMD 0.31), arm function (SMD 0.32) and strength (SMD 0.46)
cards.people: 45 randomised trials, 1,619 participants after stroke, comparing electromechanical or robot-assisted arm training with other rehabilitation, placebo or no treatment; searches to January–February 2018.
cards.result: Activities of daily living: SMD 0.31 (95% CI 0.09 to 0.52; p=0.0005; 24 studies, 957 participants). Arm function: SMD 0.32 (0.18 to 0.46; p<0.0001; 41 studies, 1,452 participants). Arm muscle strength: SMD 0.46 (0.16 to 0.77; p=0.003; 23 studies, 826 participants). Dropout did not increase (risk difference 0.00, −0.02 to 0.02) and adverse events were rare. Reviewers rated the evidence high quality but cautioned about variation in training intensity, duration, device type, participant characteristics and measurements.
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials are mostly small and heterogeneous (I² up to 76%), and the review predates RATULS — adding a 770-patient null trial to pools totalling 1,619 would shrink these standardised effects materially. Small-study pools in rehabilitation are prone to optimism.

shelves.title: DARS: adding co-careldopa to stroke rehabilitation did not improve walking — 41% walked independently at 8 weeks versus 45% on placebo
shelves.question: In patients recovering from stroke, does adding co-careldopa (levodopa) to occupational and physical therapy improve walking and arm function versus therapy alone?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Brain Ischemia/complications · Brain Ischemia/therapy · Carbidopa/adverse effects · Carbidopa/therapeutic use · Dopamine Agents/adverse effects · Dopamine Agents/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Drug Combinations · Female · Humans · Intracranial Hemorrhages/complications · Intracranial Hemorrhages/therapy · Levodopa/adverse effects · Levodopa/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Mobility Limitation · Occupational Therapy/methods · Physical Therapy Modalities* · Prospective Studies · Stroke/drug therapy · Stroke Rehabilitation/methods · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: DARS (Ford GA et al., PMID: 31122493) randomised 593 patients, on average 18 days after ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke and unable to walk 10 metres, at 51 UK stroke rehabilitation services to 6 weeks of co-careldopa or matched placebo taken 45–60 minutes before routine occupational and physical therapy sessions. The primary outcome — walking independently (Rivermead Mobility Index ≥7) at 8 weeks — was reached by 125 of 308 (41%) on co-careldopa versus 127 of 285 (45%) on placebo (OR 0.78, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.15): no evidence of benefit, with the point estimate favouring placebo. Mortality at 12 months did not differ (7% vs 6%), serious adverse events were largely similar, and vomiting during therapy was more frequent on the drug (6.2% vs 3.2%). This is a large, double-blind, pragmatic trial that directly tests the dopaminergic-enhancement hypothesis at a deliverable dose and timing, and it fails it. PROPOSED LIKELY (no benefit): co-careldopa as given in DARS should not be added to routine stroke rehabilitation to improve walking; different doses, timings or subgroups remain speculation the authors raise but this trial does not support.

cards.headline: DARS 2019: independent walking at 8 weeks in 41% on co-careldopa versus 45% on placebo (OR 0.78, 95% CI 0.53–1.15) — no benefit from levodopa timed to therapy
cards.summary: DARS 2019: independent walking at 8 weeks in 41% on co-careldopa versus 45% on placebo (OR 0.78, 95% CI 0.53–1.15) — no benefit from levodopa timed to therapy
cards.people: 593 patients (mean age 68.5 years) with new or recurrent ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke 5–42 days earlier, unable to walk 10 m and scoring under 7 on the Rivermead Mobility Index, at 51 UK NHS stroke rehabilitation services; co-careldopa n=308, placebo n=285, drug taken before therapy sessions for 6 weeks (initial doses 62.5 mg, then 125 mg co-careldopa).
cards.result: Primary outcome (Rivermead Mobility Index ≥7 at 8 weeks): 125/308 (41%) co-careldopa versus 127/285 (45%) placebo — OR 0.78 (95% CI 0.53 to 1.15). Mortality at 12 months: 22 (7%) versus 17 (6%). Serious adverse events largely similar between groups. Vomiting during therapy sessions, the most frequent adverse event, occurred in 19 (6.2%) on co-careldopa versus 9 (3.2%) on placebo. Primary outcome data were available for all 593 patients.
cards.watchOut: DARS tests one dose schedule started a mean of 18 days post-stroke alongside routine (not intensive) therapy. Its null is strong for that regimen; claims for other doses, earlier starts or biomarker-selected subgroups are hypotheses generated by this failure, not findings.

shelves.title: Perampanel for generalised tonic-clonic seizures: 64% achieved at least a halving of seizures versus 40% on placebo, and 31% were seizure-free during maintenance versus 12%
shelves.question: In adults with idiopathic generalised epilepsy and primary generalised tonic-clonic seizures, does adjunctive perampanel reduce seizure frequency versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anticonvulsants/therapeutic use · Child · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination/methods · Epilepsy, Generalized/drug therapy · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Nitriles · Pyridones/therapeutic use · Seizures/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Study 332 (French JA et al., PMID: 26296511) randomised 164 patients aged 12 and over with drug-resistant primary generalised tonic-clonic (PGTC) seizures in idiopathic generalised epilepsy to adjunctive perampanel (titrated from 2 mg to 8 mg/day) or placebo over 4 weeks of titration and 13 weeks of maintenance. Perampanel produced a greater median percent reduction in PGTC seizure frequency per 28 days and a higher 50% responder rate — 64.2% versus 39.5% (p=0.0019). During maintenance, 30.9% of perampanel patients achieved PGTC seizure freedom versus 12.3% on placebo. The most frequent adverse events were dizziness (32.1%) and fatigue (14.8%). The trial is a single, short, industry-funded study of 164 patients, and its abstract as indexed reports the median-change figures in garbled form; the responder and seizure-freedom proportions are the cleanest numbers in the record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a large relative effect on a resistant population, held at POSSIBLE because one 17-week trial cannot speak to long-term control, behaviour effects, or comparison with other adjuncts. This shelf is the generalised-epilepsy question only; adjunctive perampanel in focal seizures is shelf #2349.

cards.headline: French 2015 (Study 332): 50% responder rate 64.2% on perampanel versus 39.5% on placebo (p=0.0019); seizure freedom during maintenance 30.9% versus 12.3%
cards.summary: French 2015 (Study 332): 50% responder rate 64.2% on perampanel versus 39.5% on placebo (p=0.0019); seizure freedom during maintenance 30.9% versus 12.3%
cards.people: 164 patients aged 12 years or older with drug-resistant primary generalised tonic-clonic seizures in idiopathic generalised epilepsy, randomised to adjunctive perampanel (up-titrated 2 to 8 mg/day over 4 weeks, then 13 weeks maintenance) or placebo; full analysis set 162 (81 per arm).
cards.result: Primary endpoint (median percent change in PGTC seizure frequency per 28 days, titration plus maintenance versus baseline): a significantly greater reduction with perampanel than placebo (p<0.0001). Key secondary (50% responder rate, maintenance versus baseline): 64.2% perampanel versus 39.5% placebo (p=0.0019). PGTC seizure freedom during maintenance: 30.9% versus 12.3%. Most frequent treatment-emergent adverse events on perampanel: dizziness 32.1%, fatigue 14.8%. The study provides Class I evidence per the authors.
cards.watchOut: One 17-week trial of 164 patients funded by the manufacturer. The indexed abstract's median-percent-change figures are typographically corrupted in the record, so this card leans on the responder and freedom proportions; long-term retention, psychiatric/behavioural effects (a class concern with perampanel), and pregnancy considerations are outside this record.
cards.source: French JA et al. Perampanel for tonic-clonic seizures in idiopathic generalized epilepsy A randomized trial. Neurology. 2015. PMID: 26296511. Registry ID: NCT01393743. shelves.title: MycarinG: rozanolixizumab lowered MG-ADL by about 3.4 points versus 0.8 on placebo at day 43 — headache in over a third was the price
shelves.question: In patients with generalised myasthenia gravis, does rozanolixizumab improve myasthenia activities-of-daily-living scores versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Infant, Newborn · Humans · Adolescent · Adult · Activities of Daily Living* · Myasthenia Gravis*/drug therapy · Receptors, Cholinergic · Autoantibodies · Double-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized
shelves.balance: MycarinG (Bril V et al., PMID: 37059507) randomised 200 adults with acetylcholine-receptor or MuSK autoantibody-positive generalised myasthenia gravis (MGFA class II–IVa, MG-ADL at least 3, quantitative MG score at least 11) at 81 centres to weekly subcutaneous infusions for 6 weeks of rozanolixizumab 7 mg/kg, 10 mg/kg, or placebo. By day 43 the MG-ADL score had fallen by a least-squares mean of −3.37 (7 mg/kg) and −3.40 (10 mg/kg) versus −0.78 on placebo — differences of −2.59 (95% CI −4.09 to −1.25) and −2.62 (−3.99 to −1.16), both p<0.0001, a clinically meaningful margin on this scale with no advantage for the higher dose. Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 81–83% on rozanolixizumab versus 67% on placebo, led by headache (45% and 38% versus 19%), diarrhoea and pyrexia; serious events were similar (8%, 10%, 9%) and there were no deaths. One 6-week phase 3 trial of an FcRn blocker: durability, retreatment cycles and infection risk over years are not in this record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a clear short-term functional gain in antibody-positive disease, including the MuSK subgroup other agents often miss.

cards.headline: MycarinG 2023: MG-ADL change at day 43 −3.37 (7 mg/kg) and −3.40 (10 mg/kg) versus −0.78 on placebo — differences of about −2.6 points, both p<0.0001
cards.summary: MycarinG 2023: MG-ADL change at day 43 −3.37 (7 mg/kg) and −3.40 (10 mg/kg) versus −0.78 on placebo — differences of about −2.6 points, both p<0.0001
cards.people: 200 adults with AChR- or MuSK-positive generalised myasthenia gravis (MGFA class II–IVa; MG-ADL ≥3 with non-ocular symptoms; QMG ≥11) at 81 centres in Asia, Europe and North America; randomised 1:1:1 to rozanolixizumab 7 mg/kg (n=66), 10 mg/kg (n=67) or placebo (n=67), weekly subcutaneous infusions for 6 weeks.
cards.result: Primary endpoint (MG-ADL change to day 43): least-squares mean −3.37 (SE 0.49) at 7 mg/kg and −3.40 (0.49) at 10 mg/kg versus −0.78 (0.49) on placebo; differences −2.59 (95% CI −4.09 to −1.25) and −2.62 (−3.99 to −1.16), both p<0.0001. TEAEs: 52/64 (81%), 57/69 (83%) and 45/67 (67%); most frequent were headache (45%, 38%, 19%), diarrhoea (25%, 16%, 13%) and pyrexia (13%, 20%, 1%). Serious TEAEs 8%, 10% and 9%; no deaths.
cards.watchOut: Six weeks is one treatment cycle: the trial does not show how long benefit lasts, how often cycles must repeat, or cumulative infection risk from sustained IgG lowering. The flat dose–response (7 mg/kg equals 10 mg/kg) argues against assuming more drug means more benefit.

shelves.title: RAISE: daily self-injected zilucoplan lowered MG-ADL by 4.4 points versus 2.3 on placebo at 12 weeks in AChR-positive myasthenia
shelves.question: In patients with generalised myasthenia gravis, does zilucoplan improve myasthenia activities-of-daily-living scores versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Activities of Daily Living · COVID-19* · Myasthenia Gravis*/drug therapy · Complement C5/therapeutic use · Immunologic Factors/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome · Peptides, Cyclic
shelves.balance: RAISE (Howard JF et al., PMID: 37059508) randomised 174 adults with acetylcholine-receptor-positive generalised myasthenia gravis (MGFA class II–IV, MG-ADL at least 6, quantitative MG score at least 12) at 75 sites to daily self-injected subcutaneous zilucoplan 0.3 mg/kg or matched placebo for 12 weeks. The primary outcome — MG-ADL change at week 12 — was −4.39 (95% CI −5.28 to −3.50) on zilucoplan versus −2.30 (−3.17 to −1.43) on placebo, a least-squares mean difference of −2.09 (−3.24 to −0.95; p=0.0004), a clinically meaningful margin. Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 77% versus 70%, most commonly injection-site bruising (16% vs 9%); serious events and serious infections were similar, and one death in each group (COVID-19 on zilucoplan, cerebral haemorrhage on placebo) was judged unrelated to study drug. As a complement C5 inhibitor, zilucoplan joins the mechanism tested for eculizumab on shelf #691, but in a self-administered daily peptide form and a broader AChR-positive population. One 12-week trial: long-term meningococcal and infection risk management and durability sit outside this record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
