shelves.title: HERCULES: tolebrutinib cut 6-month confirmed disability progression to 22.6% versus 30.7% on placebo in non-relapsing secondary progressive MS — with more liver-enzyme elevations
shelves.question: In patients with non-relapsing secondary progressive multiple sclerosis, does tolebrutinib slow disability progression versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Agammaglobulinaemia Tyrosine Kinase*/antagonists & inhibitors · Disability Evaluation · Disease Progression · Double-Blind Method · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Multiple Sclerosis, Chronic Progressive*/blood · Multiple Sclerosis, Chronic Progressive*/diagnosis · Multiple Sclerosis, Chronic Progressive*/drug therapy · Protein Kinase Inhibitors*/adverse effects · Protein Kinase Inhibitors*/therapeutic use · Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitors*/administration & dosage · Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitors*/adverse effects · Alanine Transaminase/blood · Liver/drug effects · Liver/enzymology · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: HERCULES (Fox RJ et al., PMID: 40202696) randomised 1,131 patients with non-relapsing secondary progressive multiple sclerosis — a population with no approved treatment — 2:1 to tolebrutinib 60 mg daily or placebo in an event-driven, double-blind trial with median follow-up of 133 weeks. Confirmed disability progression sustained at least 6 months occurred in 22.6% on tolebrutinib versus 30.7% on placebo (HR 0.69, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.88; p=0.003) — a 31% relative risk reduction with the absolute rates of 22.6% and 30.7% printed beside it, roughly 8 fewer progressors per 100 treated over the trial's follow-up. Serious adverse events were more common on tolebrutinib (15.0% vs 10.4%), and alanine aminotransferase rose above 3 times the upper limit of normal in 4.0% versus 1.6% — the liver signal that has shadowed this drug class. One large well-conducted trial in an untreated niche earns more than MAYBE, but a single trial with a hepatic warning and no approved status keeps it below LIKELY. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the first randomised evidence that progression independent of relapses can be slowed in this population, pending replication and liver-safety clarification.

cards.people: 1,131 participants with non-relapsing secondary progressive multiple sclerosis, randomised 2:1 to tolebrutinib 60 mg once daily (n=754) or matching placebo (n=377) in a phase 3, double-blind, event-driven trial; median follow-up 133 weeks.

The liver-enzyme signal (4.0% vs 1.6% with ALT >3× ULN, and more serious adverse events overall) means the risk conversation is as important as the efficacy one; regulatory status was not established by this record.

shelves.title: Rivastigmine in dementia with Lewy bodies: 63% improved by at least 30% on neuropsychiatric measures versus 30% on placebo over 20 weeks — benefits faded after stopping
shelves.question: In people with dementia with Lewy bodies, does rivastigmine improve cognition, apathy and hallucinations versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Carbamates/therapeutic use · Cholinesterase Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Lewy Body Disease/drug therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Phenylcarbamates* · Rivastigmine · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: The single randomised trial (McKeith I et al., PMID: 11145488) enrolled 120 patients with dementia with Lewy bodies in the UK, Spain and Italy, giving rivastigmine up to 12 mg daily or placebo for 20 weeks, followed by a 3-week washout. On treatment, rivastigmine patients were significantly less apathetic and anxious and had fewer delusions and hallucinations than controls; 37 patients (63%) on rivastigmine versus 18 (30%) on placebo showed at least 30% improvement from baseline on the neuropsychiatric assessment — both pre-defined primary efficacy measures differed significantly. Computerised and neuropsychological testing favoured rivastigmine, particularly on tasks with a substantial attentional component. After discontinuation the differences tended to disappear, marking this as a symptomatic, on-treatment effect. Nausea, vomiting and anorexia — the known cholinesterase-inhibitor effects — were more frequent on rivastigmine, though tolerability was judged acceptable in this multimorbid group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a coherent behavioural and attentional benefit in a condition with few options, from one small 20-week trial conducted before modern diagnostic criteria settled. Rivastigmine for Parkinson's disease dementia is a different population, shelved at #1446.

shelves.title: Nabilone for agitation in Alzheimer's dementia: one 39-person crossover trial shows less agitation — and sedation in 45% of treatment phases
shelves.question: In people with moderate-to-severe Alzheimer's dementia and agitation, does nabilone reduce agitation versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Aggression/drug effects · Alzheimer Disease/drug therapy · Antipsychotic Agents/therapeutic use · Cognition · Double-Blind Method · Dronabinol/analogs & derivatives, therapeutic use · Female · Homes for the Aged · Humans · Male · Nursing Homes · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: The entire randomised case for nabilone in Alzheimer's agitation rests on one small trial: Herrmann 2019 (PMID: 31182351), a 14-week double-blind crossover in 39 people with moderate-to-severe Alzheimer's disease, found agitation lower on nabilone than placebo (Cohen Mansfield Agitation Inventory treatment difference −4.0, 95% CI −6.5 to −1.5), with total neuropsychiatric symptoms and caregiver distress also favouring nabilone — but sedation was far commoner on nabilone (45% versus 16%), and in the 25 participants who completed the Severe Impairment Battery, cognition favoured placebo (−4.6 points). The wider cannabinoid literature points the same way on symptoms and the same way on weakness of evidence: Bahji 2020 (PMID: 31835954) pooled nine trials and 205 participants across all cannabinoids (only one trial used nabilone) and found improvement on agitation and neuropsychiatric measures, rated low quality overall. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): a real but preliminary signal from very few patients, bought with substantial sedation, in a population where sedating drugs carry their own harms.

cards.headline: Herrmann 2019: nabilone cut agitation scores versus placebo in 39 people with moderate-to-severe Alzheimer's (CMAI difference −4.0) — but sedation hit 45% versus 16%
cards.summary: Herrmann 2019: nabilone cut agitation scores versus placebo in 39 people with moderate-to-severe Alzheimer's (CMAI difference −4.0) — but sedation hit 45% versus 16%
cards.people: 39 patients with moderate-to-severe Alzheimer's disease (mean age 87, standardised Mini-Mental State Examination 6.5, baseline Cohen Mansfield Agitation Inventory 67.9; 77% male), recruited from a long-term care facility and geriatric psychiatry clinics, in a 14-week randomised double-blind crossover trial: nabilone (target 1–2 mg; mean achieved dose 1.6 mg) versus placebo, six weeks each with a one-week washout.
cards.result: Agitation, the primary outcome, favoured nabilone: Cohen Mansfield Agitation Inventory treatment difference −4.0 (95% CI −6.5 to −1.5, p=0.003). Secondary outcomes also favoured nabilone: Neuropsychiatric Inventory–Nursing Home total −4.6 (−7.5 to −1.6, p=0.004), caregiver distress −1.7 (p=0.041), and standardised MMSE +1.1 (0.1 to 2.0, p=0.026). Against that, in the 25 participants who completed the Severe Impairment Battery, the treatment difference favoured placebo (−4.6, −7.3 to −1.8, p=0.003). Clinician global improvement (47% on nabilone versus 23% on placebo) was not significant (p=0.09). Sedation occurred in 45% of nabilone phases versus 16% of placebo phases (p=0.02), though treatment-limiting sedation did not differ significantly (p=0.22). There were no crossover or treatment-order effects.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-nine participants in a crossover design is a fragile base for a prescribing decision: the confidence interval for the agitation effect is wide, the two cognition measures point in opposite directions (MMSE favouring nabilone, the Severe Impairment Battery favouring placebo), and nearly half of nabilone phases involved sedation — in people with severe dementia, sedation can mask as calm while worsening function and falls risk. Fourteen weeks says nothing about longer-term safety.
cards.source: Herrmann N et al. Randomized Placebo-Controlled Trial of Nabilone for Agitation in Alzheimer's Disease. The American Journal of Geriatric Psychiatry. 2019. PMID: 31182351. cards.headline: Bahji 2020 (systematic review and meta-analysis): across nine cannabinoid trials in dementia (205 people), agitation and neuropsychiatric scores improved — but only one trial used nabilone and overall quality was low
cards.summary: Bahji 2020 (systematic review and meta-analysis): across nine cannabinoid trials in dementia (205 people), agitation and neuropsychiatric scores improved — but only one trial used nabilone and overall quality was low
cards.people: Nine clinical trials (205 participants, 44% female, mean age 78, 85% with Alzheimer's disease) of cannabinoids for neuropsychiatric symptoms of dementia in North America and Europe: tetrahydrocannabinol in three trials, dronabinol in five, and nabilone in one.
cards.result: Cannabinoids were associated with significant improvements across neuropsychiatric instruments: Cohen Mansfield Agitation Inventory standardised mean difference −0.80 (95% CI −1.45 to −0.16), Neuropsychiatric Inventory −0.61 (−1.07 to −0.15), and nocturnal actigraphy −1.05 (−1.56 to −0.54). Trial completion was 93% (193 of 205) and no serious treatment-related adverse events were reported. Efficacy was associated with baseline dementia severity and dose. The overall study quality was rated as low, and the authors describe the evidence as preliminary.
cards.watchOut: This is a class-level pool dominated by dronabinol and tetrahydrocannabinol trials; it cannot be read as nine trials of nabilone. The nabilone-specific evidence remains the single 39-person crossover trial carded above, and pooling small, low-quality trials can manufacture precision the underlying studies do not have.
cards.source: Bahji A et al. Cannabinoids for the Neuropsychiatric Symptoms of Dementia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. The Canadian Journal of Psychiatry. 2020. PMID: 31835954. cards.headline: Synthesis: one small positive crossover trial plus a low-quality class-level meta-analysis — a signal worth a definitive trial, not yet a treatment
cards.summary: Synthesis: one small positive crossover trial plus a low-quality class-level meta-analysis — a signal worth a definitive trial, not yet a treatment
cards.people: Herrmann 2019 (39 participants, the only nabilone trial) set against Bahji 2020 (nine cannabinoid trials, 205 participants, one using nabilone).
cards.result: Agitation: CMAI −4.0 points (95% CI −6.5 to −1.5) for nabilone in the single trial; class-level standardised mean difference −0.80 for cannabinoids. Harms: sedation 45% versus 16% in the nabilone trial; one cognition battery favoured placebo. Certainty: low throughout. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Do not let the meta-analysis SMD be quoted as a nabilone effect size — it is mostly other cannabinoids. The honest summary for families is: nabilone reduced measured agitation in one very small, short trial, at the cost of sedation in nearly half of treatment phases, and nobody yet knows whether that trade is worth it over months. Tier C is set because the agent-specific evidence is a single 39-person crossover trial.

shelves.title: Olanzapine with samidorphan: weight gain cut from 6.6% to 4.2% of body weight at 24 weeks — blunted, not abolished, with antipsychotic effect preserved
shelves.question: In adults with schizophrenia, does combining samidorphan with olanzapine reduce olanzapine-associated weight gain compared with olanzapine alone, without losing antipsychotic efficacy?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Antipsychotic Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Drug Combinations · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Naltrexone/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · Narcotic Antagonists/therapeutic use · Olanzapine/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Schizophrenia/drug therapy · Weight Gain/drug effects · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the weight effect is replicated across a phase 2 and a phase 3 trial and points the same way in both. In ENLIGHTEN-2 (Correll CU et al., PMID: 32791894), 561 adults with schizophrenia gained a least-squares mean of 4.21% of body weight on olanzapine/samidorphan versus 6.59% on olanzapine alone at 24 weeks (difference −2.38%); 17.8% versus 29.8% gained at least 10% of body weight (odds ratio 0.50). The phase 2 study (Martin WF et al., PMID: 30845818) found the same pattern at 12 weeks — 2.6% versus 4.1% mean gain — with PANSS improvement equivalent across groups, and ENLIGHTEN-2 likewise found similar symptom improvement between arms. But mitigation is not abolition: patients on the combination still gained weight, still reported weight gain as an adverse event in 24.8% of cases, and fasting metabolic measures changed little and similarly in both groups within 24 weeks. Whether sparing roughly 2.4 percentage points of weight gain prevents diabetes or cardiovascular events over years is untested. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real, replicated reduction in olanzapine-associated weight gain with efficacy preserved — a partial answer to olanzapine's main liability, not a solution to it.

cards.headline: Correll 2020 (ENLIGHTEN-2): 4.21% versus 6.59% mean weight gain at 24 weeks; ≥10% gain in 17.8% versus 29.8% (odds ratio 0.50)
cards.summary: Correll 2020 (ENLIGHTEN-2): 4.21% versus 6.59% mean weight gain at 24 weeks; ≥10% gain in 17.8% versus 29.8% (odds ratio 0.50)
cards.people: 561 adults aged 18–55 with schizophrenia, randomised to the single-tablet olanzapine/samidorphan combination (n=280) or olanzapine alone (n=281) for 24 weeks; 538 had at least one post-baseline weight assessment. Primary endpoints were percent change in body weight and the proportion gaining ≥10% at week 24.
cards.result: Least-squares mean weight change was 4.21% (SE 0.68) on the combination versus 6.59% (SE 0.67) on olanzapine alone — a difference of −2.38% (SE 0.76), statistically significant. Weight gain of ≥10% occurred in 17.8% versus 29.8% (odds ratio 0.50; number needed to treat 7.29) and ≥7% in 27.5% versus 42.7% (odds ratio 0.50; NNT 6.29). Waist circumference increased less on the combination, schizophrenia symptom improvement was similar between groups, and metabolic changes were small and similar. Adverse events in ≥10%: weight gain 24.8% versus 36.2%, somnolence 21.2% versus 18.1%, dry mouth 12.8% versus 8.0%, increased appetite 10.9% versus 12.3%.
cards.watchOut: The combination blunts but does not prevent weight gain — the average patient still gained over 4% of body weight in 24 weeks, and the trial is far too short to show whether the spared weight translates into less diabetes or cardiovascular disease. The record carries no registry identifier, and the trial was designed and reported by the combination's developer.
cards.source: Correll CU et al. Effects of Olanzapine Combined With Samidorphan on Weight Gain in Schizophrenia: A 24-Week Phase 3 Study. The American Journal of Psychiatry. 2020. PMID: 32791894. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Martin 2019 (phase 2): 37% relative less weight gain with samidorphan added (2.6% versus 4.1% mean gain at 12 weeks), PANSS improvement equivalent
cards.summary: Martin 2019 (phase 2): 37% relative less weight gain with samidorphan added (2.6% versus 4.1% mean gain at 12 weeks), PANSS improvement equivalent
cards.people: 309 patients with schizophrenia at international centres, after a 1-week open-label olanzapine lead-in, randomised to olanzapine plus placebo (n=75) or olanzapine plus samidorphan 5 mg (n=80), 10 mg (n=86) or 20 mg (n=68) for 12 weeks.
cards.result: Antipsychotic efficacy on PANSS total score was equivalent across all groups. Mean percent weight change was 4.1% (2.9 kg) on olanzapine plus placebo versus 2.6% (1.9 kg) pooled across samidorphan doses — described by the authors as 37% relative less weight gain (the absolute gains are printed alongside: 4.1% versus 2.6%). By dose: 2.8% (2.1 kg) at 5 mg, 2.1% (1.5 kg) at 10 mg, 2.9% (2.2 kg) at 20 mg. Somnolence, sedation, dizziness and constipation occurred at ≥5% frequency and at least twice the placebo-combination rate; other safety measures were comparable.
cards.watchOut: A 12-week phase 2 study with a lead-in that enriched for patients who tolerated olanzapine; the pooled-dose headline mixes three doses with no clean dose–response (the middle dose performed best numerically). It supports the phase 3 result rather than standing alone.
cards.source: Martin WF et al. Mitigation of Olanzapine-Induced Weight Gain With Samidorphan, an Opioid Antagonist: A Randomized Double-Blind Phase 2 Study in Patients With Schizophrenia. cards.headline: Synthesis: two trials, one direction — roughly a third less weight gained, efficacy intact, metabolic destiny unknown
cards.summary: Synthesis: two trials, one direction — roughly a third less weight gained, efficacy intact, metabolic destiny unknown
cards.people: Two randomised double-blind trials of olanzapine plus samidorphan versus olanzapine alone in schizophrenia: a 309-patient phase 2 study over 12 weeks and the 561-patient ENLIGHTEN-2 phase 3 study over 24 weeks.
cards.result: Weight: 2.6% versus 4.1% mean gain at 12 weeks (phase 2); 4.21% versus 6.59% at 24 weeks (phase 3), with ≥10% gain in 17.8% versus 29.8% (odds ratio 0.50). Efficacy: PANSS improvement equivalent (phase 2) and symptom improvement similar (phase 3). Harms: somnolence, sedation, dizziness, constipation and dry mouth somewhat more frequent on the combination; no new safety signal. Long-term metabolic outcomes: unmeasured. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Both trials come from the developer's programme, run 12–24 weeks, and use weight — not diabetes, cardiovascular events, or adherence — as the outcome. A patient who would not take olanzapine at all because of weight may still not be rescued by a version that leaves a 4% average gain; the honest claim is mitigation. Tier C is not set: the finding rests on two randomised trials including a phase 3 study.
cards.source: Synthesis of Correll CU et al. The American Journal of Psychiatry. 2020 (PMID: 32791894); Martin WF et al. The American Journal of Psychiatry. 2019 (PMID: 30845818).

shelves.title: Omaveloxolone in Friedreich ataxia: mFARS improved by 2.4 points against placebo at 48 weeks in the single registrational trial — a real signal on a rating scale, in a disease with no other drug
shelves.question: In people with Friedreich ataxia, does omaveloxolone slow neurological decline compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Accidental Falls · Activities of Daily Living · Adolescent · Adult · Antioxidants/metabolism · Double-Blind Method · Exercise Test · Female · Friedreich Ataxia/drug therapy/metabolism/physiopathology · Humans · Male · Mitochondria/metabolism · NF-E2-Related Factor 2/metabolism · Oxidative Stress · Signal Transduction · Treatment Outcome · Triterpenes/therapeutic use · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one registrational randomised trial, positive on its primary endpoint, in a progressive disease with no approved treatment at the time. In MOXIe part 2 (Lynch DR et al., PMID: 33068037), patients on omaveloxolone 150 mg daily improved by −1.55 points on the modified Friedreich's Ataxia Rating Scale over 48 weeks while placebo patients worsened by +0.85 — a between-group difference of −2.40 points (p=0.014). The delayed-start analysis of the open-label extension (Lynch DR et al., PMID: 36444905) found that difference preserved after the placebo group switched to drug (−2.91 points at 72 extension weeks), which is the pattern a disease-slowing drug should show and a purely symptomatic one should not — though extension analyses are not randomised comparisons. Harms were modest: reversible aminotransferase rises without bilirubin elevation, and more headache, nausea and fatigue. What 2.4 mFARS points mean in years of walking or independence is not established by these data. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the only randomised evidence in Friedreich ataxia favours omaveloxolone, on a rating-scale endpoint, from a single trial programme. Tier C is set because the evidence is one trial and its open-label extension.

cards.headline: Lynch 2021 (MOXIe part 2): mFARS −1.55 on omaveloxolone versus +0.85 on placebo at 48 weeks — difference −2.40 points, p=0.014
cards.summary: Lynch 2021 (MOXIe part 2): mFARS −1.55 on omaveloxolone versus +0.85 on placebo at 48 weeks — difference −2.40 points, p=0.014
cards.people: 103 patients aged 16–40 with genetically confirmed Friedreich ataxia and baseline mFARS scores of 20–80, at 11 institutions in the US, Europe and Australia, randomised to omaveloxolone 150 mg/day (n=51) or placebo (n=52); the full analysis set held 40 and 42 patients.
cards.result: Change in mFARS at 48 weeks was −1.55 (±0.69) on omaveloxolone and +0.85 (±0.64) on placebo, a treatment difference of −2.40 (±0.96) points, p=0.014 — the trial's primary endpoint. Transient, reversible aminotransferase increases occurred without rises in total bilirubin or other signs of liver injury; headache, nausea and fatigue were more common on omaveloxolone.
cards.watchOut: Only 82 of 103 randomised patients contributed to the full analysis set, the endpoint is a clinician rating scale rather than a milestone such as loss of ambulation, and 48 weeks is short in a disease that progresses over decades. A 2.4-point difference is statistically real; its size in lived terms is the open question.

cards.headline: Lynch 2023 (delayed-start extension): the −2.17-point gap at the end of the blinded trial was preserved (−2.91) after 72 weeks of open-label treatment — the early-start group never caught down
cards.summary: Lynch 2023 (delayed-start extension): the −2.17-point gap at the end of the blinded trial was preserved (−2.91) after 72 weeks of open-label treatment — the early-start group never caught down
cards.type: Delayed-start analysis of an open-label extension (Lynch 2023)
cards.people: Patients who completed MOXIe part 1 or part 2 and entered the open-label extension on omaveloxolone, comparing those originally randomised to omaveloxolone with those originally randomised to placebo (delayed start), followed through up to 144 weeks.
cards.result: Non-inferiority testing showed the mFARS difference seen at the end of blinded part 2 (−2.17 ± 1.09 points) was preserved after 72 weeks in the extension (−2.91 ± 1.44 points): patients who started late did not catch up to those who started early. Patients originally on omaveloxolone showed no worsening in mFARS relative to their extension baseline through 144 weeks.
cards.watchOut: An extension analysis, not a randomised comparison: everyone knew they were on drug, there was no concurrent placebo group, and patients who remain in extensions are survivors of the original trial in every sense. It is consistent with disease modification; it cannot prove it. The record carries no registry identifier.
cards.source: Lynch DR et al. Efficacy of Omaveloxolone in Friedreich's Ataxia: Delayed-Start Analysis of the MOXIe Extension. Movement Disorders. 2023. PMID: 36444905. cards.headline: Synthesis: one positive trial plus a supportive extension — benefit on a rating scale, durability suggested, clinical milestones untested
cards.summary: Synthesis: one positive trial plus a supportive extension — benefit on a rating scale, durability suggested, clinical milestones untested
cards.people: One randomised placebo-controlled trial (103 randomised, 82 analysed, 48 weeks) and its open-label delayed-start extension analysis — the entire controlled record for omaveloxolone in Friedreich ataxia.
cards.result: Neurological function: mFARS difference −2.40 points versus placebo at 48 weeks (p=0.014), with the between-group gap preserved in delayed-start analysis at 72 extension weeks. Harms: reversible transaminase rises without bilirubin elevation; headache, nausea, fatigue more common. Hard outcomes (ambulation, falls, independence, survival): not demonstrated. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Do not let a rating-scale result be quoted as 'slows the disease' without the qualifiers: one trial, one sponsor programme, a surrogate-adjacent endpoint, and an extension without a control group. The delayed-start pattern is genuinely the right shape for disease modification, which is why this is POSSIBLE rather than MAYBE — but replication by an independent trial would change the grade more than any reanalysis. Tier C is set for the single-trial base.
cards.source: Synthesis of Lynch DR et al. Annals of Neurology. 2021 (PMID: 33068037); Lynch DR et al. Movement Disorders. 2023 (PMID: 36444905).

shelves.title: Mobile stroke units: 90-day outcomes better in both large prospective studies and the pooled analysis — excellent outcome odds up by about two-thirds, thrombolysis about half an hour sooner
shelves.question: In acute ischaemic stroke, does dispatching a mobile stroke unit — a CT-equipped ambulance that starts thrombolysis before hospital arrival — improve functional outcome at 90 days versus conventional ambulance care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Ambulances · Disability Evaluation · Emergency Medical Services · Ischemic Stroke · Mobile Health Units · Odds Ratio · Severity of Illness Index · Time-to-Treatment · Tissue Plasminogen Activator · Tomography, X-Ray Computed
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — consistent, sizeable, and entirely non-randomised at the level of the individual patient. In Berlin's B_PROUD study (Ebinger M et al., PMID: 33528537; 1,543 patients), dispatch of a mobile stroke unit (MSU) was associated with lower disability at 3 months (median modified Rankin Scale 1 versus 2; common odds ratio for worse outcome 0.71, 95% CI 0.58 to 0.86), with death in 7.1% versus 8.8% on the coprimary disability scale. In the US BEST-MSU study (Grotta JC et al., PMID: 34496173; 1,515 enrolled, 1,047 thrombolysis-eligible), patients on MSU weeks reached thrombolysis at a median 72 versus 108 minutes, 97.1% of eligible patients were treated versus 79.5%, excellent outcome (mRS 0–1) was 55.0% versus 44.4%, and 90-day mortality was 8.9% versus 11.9%. The 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis (Turc G et al., PMID: 35129584) pools the field in the same direction: excellent outcome adjusted odds ratio 1.64 (1.27 to 2.13; 5 studies, 3,228 patients), onset-to-thrombolysis shortened by a median 31 minutes, and no increase in mortality or symptomatic haemorrhage. No study randomised individual patients — B_PROUD allocated by MSU availability and BEST-MSU by alternating weeks — so system and selection effects cannot be fully excluded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): MSUs speed thrombolysis and are associated with better 90-day function, on prospective but non-randomised evidence.

cards.headline: B_PROUD (Ebinger 2021): median mRS 1 versus 2 at 3 months (common OR for worse outcome 0.71, 0.58–0.86); death 7.1% versus 8.8%
cards.summary: B_PROUD (Ebinger 2021): median mRS 1 versus 2 at 3 months (common OR for worse outcome 0.71, 0.58–0.86); death 7.1% versus 8.8%
cards.type: Prospective nonrandomised controlled intervention study (Ebinger 2021, B_PROUD)
cards.people: 1,543 patients with acute cerebral ischaemia in Berlin (mean age 74 years; 47% women) eligible for thrombolysis or thrombectomy, compared by initial dispatch: mobile stroke unit plus conventional ambulance (749) versus conventional ambulance alone (794), February 2017 to October 2019; 1,337 (87%) had 3-month mRS scores.
cards.result: Patients with an MSU dispatched had lower median mRS at month 3 (1; IQR 0–3) than patients without (2; IQR 0–3; common OR for worse mRS 0.71, 95% CI 0.58 to 0.86; P<.001). On the coprimary 3-tier disability scale, none-to-moderate disability was 80.3% versus 78.0%, severe disability 12.6% versus 13.3%, and death 7.1% versus 8.8% (common OR for worse outcome 0.73, 0.54 to 0.99; P=.04).
cards.watchOut: Allocation was by whether an MSU was available at dispatch, not by randomisation — the comparison is adjusted, and residual confounding (time of day, distance, case mix) is the standing alternative explanation for part of the effect.
cards.source: Ebinger M et al. Association Between Dispatch of Mobile Stroke Units and Functional Outcomes Among Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke in Berlin. JAMA. 2021. PMID: 33528537. cards.headline: BEST-MSU (Grotta 2021): thrombolysis at 72 versus 108 minutes; mRS 0–1 in 55.0% versus 44.4%; mortality 8.9% versus 11.9%
cards.summary: BEST-MSU (Grotta 2021): thrombolysis at 72 versus 108 minutes; mRS 0–1 in 55.0% versus 44.4%; mortality 8.9% versus 11.9%
cards.type: Prospective multicentre alternating-week controlled trial (Grotta 2021, BEST-MSU)
cards.people: 1,515 patients enrolled within 4.5 hours of acute stroke onset at US centres, of whom 1,047 were eligible for tissue plasminogen activator (617 managed by mobile stroke unit, 430 by standard emergency medical services) in alternating MSU and EMS weeks.
cards.result: Median onset-to-thrombolysis time was 72 minutes on MSU versus 108 minutes on EMS weeks, and 97.1% of eligible MSU patients received thrombolysis versus 79.5% on EMS weeks. The mean utility-weighted mRS at 90 days was 0.72 versus 0.66 (adjusted odds ratio for a score ≥0.91, 2.43; 95% CI 1.75 to 3.36; P<0.001), mRS 0–1 was achieved by 55.0% versus 44.4%, and 90-day mortality was 8.9% versus 11.9%.
cards.watchOut: Alternating-week allocation is a cluster design, not patient-level randomisation, and the primary analysis is restricted to thrombolysis-eligible patients — the group an MSU is most able to help. The mortality gap (8.9% versus 11.9%) is a secondary outcome in a non-blinded service comparison.
cards.source: Grotta JC et al. Prospective, Multicenter, Controlled Trial of Mobile Stroke Units. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2021. PMID: 34496173. Registry ID: NCT02190500. cards.headline: Turc 2022 meta-analysis: excellent outcome adjusted OR 1.64 (1.27–2.13); thrombolysis 31 minutes sooner; no mortality or haemorrhage penalty
cards.summary: Turc 2022 meta-analysis: excellent outcome adjusted OR 1.64 (1.27–2.13); thrombolysis 31 minutes sooner; no mortality or haemorrhage penalty
cards.people: Studies comparing mobile stroke unit deployment with usual care in suspected stroke (literature 1960–2021): excellent-outcome analysis 5 studies, 3,228 patients; onset-to-thrombolysis analysis 13 studies, 3,322 patients; thrombolysis-delivery analysis 7 studies, 4,790 patients.
cards.result: MSU use was associated with excellent outcome (mRS 0–1 at 90 days; adjusted OR 1.64, 95% CI 1.27 to 2.13; P<.001), reduced disability across the full mRS range (adjusted common OR 1.39, 1.14 to 1.70), good outcome mRS 0–2 (crude OR 1.25, 1.09 to 1.44), a median 31-minute reduction (95% CI 23 to 39) in onset-to-intravenous-thrombolysis time, more thrombolysis delivery (crude OR 1.83, 1.58 to 2.12), and more thrombolysis within 60 minutes (crude OR 7.71, 4.17 to 14.25). MSU use was not associated with increased 7-day or 90-day mortality or symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage.
cards.watchOut: The pooled studies are the same non-randomised service evaluations carded above, assessed with ROBINS-I — meta-analysis cannot wash out the allocation problem, and overlapping populations between reports had to be disentangled with unpublished data.
cards.source: Turc G et al. Comparison of Mobile Stroke Unit With Usual Care for Acute Ischemic Stroke Management: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. JAMA Neurology. 2022. PMID: 35129584. cards.headline: Synthesis: faster lysis and better function in every large dataset — bought with a service redesign, proven without patient-level randomisation
cards.summary: Synthesis: faster lysis and better function in every large dataset — bought with a service redesign, proven without patient-level randomisation
cards.people: Two large prospective controlled studies (Berlin, n=1,543; US, n=1,515) and a 2022 meta-analysis (excellent-outcome pool n=3,228).
cards.result: Excellent outcome: adjusted OR 1.64 (1.27–2.13) pooled; mRS 0–1 55.0% versus 44.4% in BEST-MSU. Disability shift: common OR 0.71 (0.58–0.86) for worse outcome in B_PROUD. Time: thrombolysis ~31–36 minutes sooner. Mortality: 8.9% versus 11.9% (BEST-MSU) and 7.1% versus 8.8% (B_PROUD), with no pooled mortality or haemorrhage penalty. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: the evidence is prospective but non-randomised, so the developer reviews it personally.
cards.watchOut: An MSU is a system intervention — staffing, dispatch geography, and hospital networks differ by city — so the effect sizes are best read as 'what organised MSU systems achieved in Berlin and US trial networks', not as a guaranteed local return.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ebinger M et al. JAMA. 2021 (PMID: 33528537); Grotta JC et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2021 (PMID: 34496173); Turc G et al. JAMA Neurology. 2022 (PMID: 35129584).

shelves.title: Straight to thrombectomy versus the drip first: the largest trial met its non-inferiority margin — the pooled analysis of all six trials did not
shelves.question: In large-vessel-occlusion stroke treated with thrombectomy, does going straight to thrombectomy match bridging intravenous thrombolysis first — or does skipping the drip lose recanalisation and outcome?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Stroke · Brain Ischemia · Intracranial Hemorrhages · Ischemic Stroke · Thrombolytic Therapy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer depends on which evidence you stand on, and the bigger evidence is the cautious one. The IRIS collaboration's individual-participant meta-analysis of all six randomised trials (Majoie CB et al., PMID: 37640037; 2,313 patients presenting directly to thrombectomy centres) found a 90-day outcome shift favouring bridging (median mRS 2 with thrombolysis plus thrombectomy versus 3 with thrombectomy alone; adjusted common odds ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.04 for thrombectomy alone) and did NOT establish non-inferiority against its prespecified 0.82 lower boundary; symptomatic haemorrhage and mortality did not differ significantly, though any intracranial haemorrhage was less frequent without the drip (odds ratio 0.82, 0.68 to 0.99). The largest single trial, DIRECT-MT (Yang P et al., PMID: 32374959; 656 patients in China), did meet its own wider non-inferiority margin (adjusted common OR 1.07, 0.81 to 1.40) — yet even there, successful reperfusion before thrombectomy was 2.4% without alteplase versus 7.0% with it, and overall successful reperfusion was 79.4% versus 84.5%; mortality was 17.7% versus 18.8%. So skipping the drip loses early reperfusion, has not been proven equal on outcome in the pooled data, and saves some non-symptomatic bleeding. PROPOSED SPLIT: non-inferiority shown in one large trial under its own margin, not established when all six trials are pooled.

cards.headline: IRIS 2023 (six trials, 2,313 patients): acOR 0.89 (0.76–1.04) for thrombectomy alone — non-inferiority not established; any ICH less without the drip (OR 0.82)
cards.summary: IRIS 2023 (six trials, 2,313 patients): acOR 0.89 (0.76–1.04) for thrombectomy alone — non-inferiority not established; any ICH less without the drip (OR 0.82)
cards.type: Individual participant data meta-analysis of six randomised trials (Majoie 2023, IRIS collaboration)
cards.people: 2,313 participants in six randomised trials of endovascular thrombectomy alone (1,153) versus intravenous thrombolysis plus thrombectomy (1,160), all presenting directly at thrombectomy-capable centres; primary outcome 90-day modified Rankin Scale; non-inferiority boundary 0.82 for the adjusted common odds ratio (analogous to a 5% absolute difference in functional independence).
cards.result: Median mRS at 90 days was 3 (IQR 1–5) with thrombectomy alone and 2 (IQR 1–4) with bridging. The adjusted common odds ratio for a shift toward improved outcome with thrombectomy alone was 0.89 (95% CI 0.76 to 1.04), which did not establish non-inferiority. Any intracranial haemorrhage occurred less frequently with thrombectomy alone (OR 0.82, 0.68 to 0.99); symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage and mortality did not differ significantly. Between-trial variability was small and related mainly to thrombolytic choice and dose and country.
cards.watchOut: Every patient in these trials presented directly to a thrombectomy centre — the pooled answer does not govern drip-and-ship transfers, where the drip is often the only reperfusion available during transport. Non-inferiority also failed narrowly: the point estimate (0.89) sits between the two trials' stories, not at clear inferiority.
cards.source: Majoie CB et al. Value of intravenous thrombolysis in endovascular treatment for large-vessel anterior circulation stroke: individual participant data meta-analysis of six randomised trials. The Lancet. 2023. PMID: 37640037. Registry ID: PROSPERO CRD42023411986. cards.headline: DIRECT-MT (Yang 2020): non-inferior on outcome within a 20% margin (acOR 1.07, 0.81–1.40) — but reperfusion before thrombectomy 2.4% versus 7.0%
cards.summary: DIRECT-MT (Yang 2020): non-inferior on outcome within a 20% margin (acOR 1.07, 0.81–1.40) — but reperfusion before thrombectomy 2.4% versus 7.0%
cards.people: 656 patients with anterior-circulation large-vessel occlusion at 41 academic tertiary centres in China, randomised to thrombectomy alone (327) or intravenous alteplase 0.9 mg/kg within 4.5 hours followed by thrombectomy (329).
cards.result: Thrombectomy alone was non-inferior for the 90-day mRS distribution (adjusted common odds ratio 1.07, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.40; P=0.04 for non-inferiority against a 0.8 lower boundary). Successful reperfusion before thrombectomy occurred in 2.4% on thrombectomy alone versus 7.0% on combination therapy, and overall successful reperfusion in 79.4% versus 84.5%. Mortality at 90 days was 17.7% versus 18.8%.
cards.watchOut: The trial's non-inferiority margin (lower boundary 0.8) tolerates up to a fifth worse odds of a better outcome — 'non-inferior' here is a wide tolerance, and the pooled IRIS analysis used a tighter boundary (0.82) on six times the patients and failed it. A single-country trial with high operator experience.
cards.source: Yang P et al. Endovascular Thrombectomy with or without Intravenous Alteplase in Acute Stroke. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2020. PMID: 32374959. Registry ID: NCT03469206. cards.headline: Synthesis: keep the drip where it costs no time — the pooled data never proved skipping it is equal, and early reperfusion is measurably lost
cards.summary: Synthesis: keep the drip where it costs no time — the pooled data never proved skipping it is equal, and early reperfusion is measurably lost
cards.people: Six randomised trials pooled at participant level (2,313 patients), with the largest constituent trial (656 patients) carded separately.
cards.result: Outcome shift for thrombectomy alone: acOR 0.89 (0.76–1.04) pooled — non-inferiority not established — versus acOR 1.07 (0.81–1.40) in DIRECT-MT under a wider margin. Early reperfusion: 2.4% versus 7.0% (DIRECT-MT). Any intracranial haemorrhage: OR 0.82 (0.68–0.99) favouring thrombectomy alone; symptomatic haemorrhage and mortality not significantly different. PROPOSED SPLIT, not Tier C: a participant-level meta-analysis of six randomised trials carries the shelf.
cards.watchOut: Both halves of the split are real: centres where the drip genuinely delays the angio suite face a different trade from the trial average, which is why the IRIS authors themselves call for individualised decisions rather than a blanket skip.
cards.source: Synthesis of Majoie CB et al. The Lancet. 2023 (PMID: 37640037); Yang P et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2020 (PMID: 32374959).

shelves.title: Late-window thrombectomy works: functional independence 49% versus 13% (DAWN) and 45% versus 17% (DEFUSE 3) in imaging-selected patients 6–24 hours after onset
shelves.question: In patients with large-vessel occlusion presenting 6–24 hours after onset selected by clinical–core or perfusion mismatch, does thrombectomy improve functional outcome versus medical care alone?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Bayes Theorem · Cerebral Infarction · Combined Modality Therapy · Disability Evaluation · Endovascular Procedures · Female · Fibrinolytic Agents · Humans · Intracranial Hemorrhages · Male · Middle Aged · Stroke · Thrombectomy · Time-to-Treatment
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two trials, stopped early for efficacy, with effects too large to be fragile. In DAWN (Nogueira RG et al., PMID: 29129157; 206 patients last known well 6–24 hours earlier with a clinical-deficit/infarct mismatch), functional independence at 90 days was 49% with thrombectomy versus 13% with standard care (adjusted difference 33 percentage points, 95% credible interval 24 to 44), and the utility-weighted disability score was 5.5 versus 3.4 (adjusted difference 2.0 points); symptomatic haemorrhage was 6% versus 3% (P=0.50) and mortality 19% versus 18%. In DEFUSE 3 (Albers GW et al., PMID: 29364767; 182 patients at 6–16 hours with perfusion mismatch), functional independence was 45% versus 17% (P<0.001), the outcome distribution shifted favourably (odds ratio 2.77, P<0.001), and mortality was 14% versus 26% (P=0.05), with symptomatic haemorrhage 7% versus 4% (P=0.75). Both trials selected patients by imaging or clinical mismatch — small infarct, large threatened territory — so the benefit belongs to that selected minority, not to all late presenters. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): in mismatch-selected large-vessel occlusion 6–24 hours from onset, thrombectomy roughly triples functional independence.

cards.headline: DAWN (Nogueira 2018): functional independence 49% versus 13% at 90 days; mortality 19% versus 18%; symptomatic haemorrhage 6% versus 3%
cards.summary: DAWN (Nogueira 2018): functional independence 49% versus 13% at 90 days; mortality 19% versus 18%; symptomatic haemorrhage 6% versus 3%
cards.people: 206 patients with intracranial internal-carotid or proximal middle-cerebral occlusion, last known well 6–24 hours earlier, with a mismatch between clinical deficit severity and infarct volume (criteria stratified by age under/over 80), randomised to thrombectomy plus standard care (107) or standard care alone (99); enrolment stopped at a prespecified interim analysis.
cards.result: The mean utility-weighted modified Rankin score at 90 days was 5.5 with thrombectomy versus 3.4 with standard care (adjusted difference 2.0 points, 95% credible interval 1.1 to 3.0; posterior probability of superiority >0.999). Functional independence (mRS 0–2) was 49% versus 13% (adjusted difference 33 percentage points, 24 to 44). Symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage did not differ significantly (6% versus 3%, P=0.50), nor did 90-day mortality (19% versus 18%, P=1.00).
cards.watchOut: The mismatch entry criteria are the result: DAWN screened for a small core with a disproportionately severe deficit, a minority of late presenters. Early stopping for efficacy can inflate effect sizes, though a 36-point absolute gap leaves room for shrinkage and still matters.
cards.source: Nogueira RG et al. Thrombectomy 6 to 24 Hours after Stroke with a Mismatch between Deficit and Infarct. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2018. PMID: 29129157. cards.headline: DEFUSE 3 (Albers 2018): functional independence 45% versus 17%; mortality 14% versus 26% (P=0.05); symptomatic haemorrhage 7% versus 4%
cards.summary: DEFUSE 3 (Albers 2018): functional independence 45% versus 17%; mortality 14% versus 26% (P=0.05); symptomatic haemorrhage 7% versus 4%
cards.type: Randomised open-label trial with blinded outcome assessment (Albers 2018, DEFUSE 3)
cards.people: 182 patients at 38 US centres, last known well 6–16 hours earlier, with proximal middle-cerebral or internal-carotid occlusion, initial infarct under 70 mL, and perfusion-imaging mismatch ratio of 1.8 or more, randomised to thrombectomy plus medical therapy (92) or medical therapy alone (90); terminated early for efficacy.
cards.result: Endovascular therapy was associated with a favourable shift in the 90-day mRS distribution (odds ratio 2.77, P<0.001) and more functional independence (mRS 0–2 in 45% versus 17%, P<0.001). Mortality at 90 days was 14% versus 26% (P=0.05). Symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage (7% versus 4%, P=0.75) and serious adverse events (43% versus 53%, P=0.18) did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: Open-label treatment with blinded outcome assessment, stopped early at 182 of a planned larger sample — the mortality difference sits exactly at P=0.05 and should be read as supportive, not standalone. Perfusion selection (infarct <70 mL, mismatch ≥1.8) again defines a chosen subgroup.
cards.source: Albers GW et al. Thrombectomy for Stroke at 6 to 16 Hours with Selection by Perfusion Imaging. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2018. PMID: 29364767. Registry ID: NCT02586415. cards.headline: Synthesis: two selection strategies, one conclusion — treat the mismatch, not the clock alone
cards.summary: Synthesis: two selection strategies, one conclusion — treat the mismatch, not the clock alone
cards.people: Two randomised trials totalling 388 patients with large-vessel occlusion 6–24 hours from last known well, selected by clinical–core mismatch (DAWN) or perfusion mismatch (DEFUSE 3).
cards.result: Functional independence at 90 days: 49% versus 13% (DAWN) and 45% versus 17% (DEFUSE 3). Mortality: 19% versus 18% (DAWN) and 14% versus 26% (DEFUSE 3). Symptomatic haemorrhage: 6% versus 3% and 7% versus 4%, neither significant. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit), Tier C: the shelf carries a mortality-benefit signal in DEFUSE 3, which the developer reviews personally.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial enrolled unselected late presenters or large-core patients; extrapolating these numbers beyond mismatch-selected patients would overstate the benefit, and both trials' early stopping argues for reading the pooled direction rather than either point estimate alone.
cards.source: Synthesis of Nogueira RG et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2018 (PMID: 29129157); Albers GW et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2018 (PMID: 29364767).

shelves.title: Tenecteplase at 4.5–24 hours (TIMELESS): median Rankin 3 in both groups — no benefit in perfusion-selected patients, most of whom had thrombectomy anyway
shelves.question: In perfusion-selected ischaemic stroke 4.5–24 hours from onset, does tenecteplase improve functional outcome versus placebo without excess symptomatic haemorrhage?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Brain Ischemia · Fibrinolytic Agents · Intracranial Hemorrhages · Perfusion · Perfusion Imaging · Stroke · Tenecteplase · Thrombectomy · Tissue Plasminogen Activator · Treatment Outcome · Double-Blind Method · Ischemic Stroke · Infarction, Middle Cerebral Artery · Carotid Artery Diseases · Brain · Time-to-Treatment
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a clean null in exactly the population chosen to favour the drug. In TIMELESS (Albers GW et al., PMID: 38329148), 458 patients with middle-cerebral or internal-carotid occlusion and perfusion-proven salvageable tissue were randomised to tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg or placebo at 4.5–24 hours (median about 12–13 hours from last known well); 77.3% then underwent thrombectomy. The median 90-day modified Rankin score was 3 in each group, and the adjusted common odds ratio for the outcome distribution was 1.13 (95% CI 0.82 to 1.57; P=0.45). Safety was as the question hoped — mortality 19.7% versus 18.2% and symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage 3.2% versus 2.3%, no significant excess — but with no efficacy signal to weigh it against. The plausible reading is that once thrombectomy is coming, a late drip adds nothing measurable; the trial cannot speak to late thrombolysis where thrombectomy is unavailable. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): tenecteplase at 4.5–24 hours did not improve 90-day function in perfusion-selected patients, without a significant haemorrhage penalty.

cards.headline: TIMELESS (Albers 2024): adjusted common OR 1.13 (0.82–1.57; P=0.45); mortality 19.7% versus 18.2%; symptomatic haemorrhage 3.2% versus 2.3%
cards.summary: TIMELESS (Albers 2024): adjusted common OR 1.13 (0.82–1.57; P=0.45); mortality 19.7% versus 18.2%; symptomatic haemorrhage 3.2% versus 2.3%
cards.people: 458 patients with ischaemic stroke from middle-cerebral or internal-carotid occlusion and salvageable tissue on perfusion imaging, randomised to tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg (228) or placebo (230) at 4.5–24 hours after last known well (median ~12 hours tenecteplase, ~13 hours placebo); 77.3% subsequently underwent thrombectomy.
cards.result: The median modified Rankin score at 90 days was 3 in each group; the adjusted common odds ratio for the score distribution was 1.13 (95% CI 0.82 to 1.57; P=0.45). In the safety population, 90-day mortality was 19.7% on tenecteplase and 18.2% on placebo, and symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage occurred in 3.2% and 2.3% respectively.
cards.watchOut: Three of four patients had thrombectomy, which itself reperfuses — the trial tests tenecteplase as an adjunct in thrombectomy-capable systems, not as standalone late reperfusion. The confidence interval (0.82–1.57) also cannot exclude a modest benefit or harm; the stamp is a null on the primary analysis, not proof of exact equivalence.

cards.summary: Synthesis: late tenecteplase joins the list of reperfusion ideas that imaging selection alone could not rescue
cards.people: One randomised double-blind trial, 458 perfusion-selected patients at 4.5–24 hours, most proceeding to thrombectomy.
cards.result: Primary outcome: adjusted common OR 1.13 (0.82–1.57), median mRS 3 versus 3. Mortality 19.7% versus 18.2%; symptomatic haemorrhage 3.2% versus 2.3%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference), Tier C: a single trial carries the shelf.

shelves.title: Alteplase for minor nondisabling stroke: no gain over antiplatelet care in either trial — PRISMS stopped at a third of its sample with a 3.2% bleed signal, ARAMIS found dual antiplatelets non-inferior
shelves.question: In minor ischaemic stroke (low NIHSS) within 4.5 hours, does alteplase improve excellent outcome versus aspirin-based care — or does bleeding erase any gain?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intravenous · Administration, Oral · Aged · Aspirin · Bayes Theorem · Brain Ischemia · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fibrinolytic Agents · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Nervous System Diseases · Severity of Illness Index · Stroke · Time-to-Treatment · Tissue Plasminogen Activator · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in minor nondisabling stroke, thrombolysis has never beaten tablets. PRISMS (Khatri P et al., PMID: 29998337) randomised 313 patients with NIHSS 0–5 and non-disabling deficits to alteplase or aspirin 325 mg within 3 hours, then stopped far short of its planned 948 patients: favourable outcome (mRS 0–1) at 90 days was 78.2% on alteplase versus 81.5% on aspirin (adjusted risk difference −1.1%, 95% CI −9.4% to 7.3%), while symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage occurred in 5 alteplase patients (3.2%) versus none on aspirin (risk difference 3.3%, 0.8% to 7.4%). ARAMIS (Chen HS et al., PMID: 37367978) then tested the stronger antiplatelet strategy in 760 patients within 4.5 hours: dual antiplatelet therapy was non-inferior to alteplase for excellent outcome (93.8% versus 91.4%; risk difference 2.3%, −1.5% to 6.2%; P for non-inferiority <.001), with symptomatic haemorrhage in 0.3% versus 0.9%. Most minor-stroke patients recover well anyway — the ceiling is high, the bleed is real, and no trial has found headroom for the drip. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): alteplase does not improve excellent outcome over aspirin-based care in minor nondisabling stroke, and carries a small haemorrhage excess.

cards.headline: PRISMS (Khatri 2018): favourable outcome 78.2% alteplase versus 81.5% aspirin (adjusted difference −1.1%, −9.4% to 7.3%); symptomatic haemorrhage 3.2% versus 0%
cards.summary: PRISMS (Khatri 2018): favourable outcome 78.2% alteplase versus 81.5% aspirin (adjusted difference −1.1%, −9.4% to 7.3%); symptomatic haemorrhage 3.2% versus 0%
cards.people: 313 patients (mean age 62 years; 46% women; median NIHSS 2) with acute ischaemic stroke, NIHSS 0–5, deficits judged not clearly disabling, treated within 3 hours at 53 US stroke networks, randomised to intravenous alteplase 0.9 mg/kg with oral placebo (156) or aspirin 325 mg with intravenous placebo (157); 281 (89.8%) completed the trial, which was designed for 948 patients and terminated very early.
cards.result: At 90 days, 122 patients (78.2%) on alteplase versus 128 (81.5%) on aspirin achieved a favourable outcome (mRS 0–1; adjusted risk difference −1.1%, 95% CI −9.4% to 7.3%). Five alteplase patients (3.2%) versus no aspirin patients had symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage within 36 hours (risk difference 3.3%, 0.8% to 7.4%). The authors concluded alteplase did not increase favourable outcome, while noting the very early termination precludes definitive conclusions.
cards.watchOut: A third of the planned sample: the confidence interval spans from 9 points worse to 7 points better, so PRISMS alone proves neither equivalence nor harm on function — its firm finding is the 3.2% symptomatic bleed rate against zero. Enrolment required deficits judged non-disabling, the subgroup with least to gain.
cards.source: Khatri P et al. Effect of Alteplase vs Aspirin on Functional Outcome for Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke and Minor Nondisabling Neurologic Deficits: The PRISMS Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2018. PMID: 29998337. Registry ID: NCT02072226. cards.headline: ARAMIS (Chen 2023): dual antiplatelets non-inferior to alteplase — excellent outcome 93.8% versus 91.4% (difference 2.3%, −1.5% to 6.2%); haemorrhage 0.3% versus 0.9%
cards.summary: ARAMIS (Chen 2023): dual antiplatelets non-inferior to alteplase — excellent outcome 93.8% versus 91.4% (difference 2.3%, −1.5% to 6.2%); haemorrhage 0.3% versus 0.9%
cards.type: Randomised open-label blinded-endpoint non-inferiority trial (Chen 2023, ARAMIS)
cards.people: 760 patients with minor nondisabling stroke (NIHSS ≤5 with ≤1 point on key single items; median NIHSS 2; median age 64 years; 31.0% women) at 38 hospitals in China, randomised within 4.5 hours to dual antiplatelet therapy (clopidogrel 300 mg load then 75 mg daily plus aspirin 100 mg daily for ~12 days, then guideline therapy to 90 days; 393) or intravenous alteplase 0.9 mg/kg then guideline antiplatelets (367); 719 (94.6%) completed the trial.
cards.result: Excellent functional outcome (mRS 0–1) at 90 days occurred in 93.8% (346/369) on dual antiplatelets versus 91.4% (320/350) on alteplase (risk difference 2.3%, 95% CI −1.5% to 6.2%); the lower limit of the one-sided 97.5% CI (−1.5%) exceeded the −4.5% non-inferiority margin (P for non-inferiority <.001). Symptomatic intracerebral haemorrhage occurred in 1 of 371 (0.3%) on dual therapy versus 3 of 351 (0.9%) on alteplase.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority to alteplase is only as meaningful as alteplase's own unproven benefit in this population — ARAMIS shows tablets match the drip, not that either beats natural history. Open-label treatment (blinded endpoints) in a single country, and excellent-outcome rates above 91% in both arms confirm how favourable this population's prognosis already is.
cards.source: Chen HS et al. Dual Antiplatelet Therapy vs Alteplase for Patients With Minor Nondisabling Acute Ischemic Stroke: The ARAMIS Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2023. PMID: 37367978. Registry ID: NCT03661411. cards.headline: Synthesis: two designs, one ceiling — minor nondisabling stroke recovers on tablets, and the drip's only consistent product is bleeding risk
cards.summary: Synthesis: two designs, one ceiling — minor nondisabling stroke recovers on tablets, and the drip's only consistent product is bleeding risk
cards.people: Two randomised trials totalling 1,073 patients with minor nondisabling stroke (NIHSS 0–5): PRISMS (alteplase versus aspirin, n=313, stopped early) and ARAMIS (dual antiplatelets versus alteplase, n=760).
cards.result: Excellent/favourable outcome: 78.2% versus 81.5% (PRISMS, alteplase versus aspirin) and 93.8% versus 91.4% (ARAMIS, dual therapy versus alteplase, non-inferior). Symptomatic haemorrhage: 3.2% versus 0% (PRISMS) and 0.3% versus 0.9% (ARAMIS). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference), Tier C: PRISMS' early termination and ARAMIS' non-inferiority design leave the null less than airtight, so the developer reviews it personally.
cards.watchOut: Both trials excluded disabling deficits within a low NIHSS — a patient whose 'minor' score hides a disabling hand or speech deficit is a different, untested question, and neither shelf nor trials should be read onto them.
cards.source: Synthesis of Khatri P et al. JAMA. 2018 (PMID: 29998337); Chen HS et al. JAMA. 2023 (PMID: 37367978).

shelves.title: Cilostazol dual therapy in high-risk stroke (CSPS.com): recurrence 3% versus 7% (HR 0.49) with no excess of severe bleeding — in one open-label Japanese trial stopped at half its target
shelves.question: In high-risk non-cardioembolic ischaemic stroke, does dual antiplatelet therapy with cilostazol plus aspirin or clopidogrel prevent recurrence better than single antiplatelet therapy without more major bleeding?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Aspirin · Brain Ischemia · Cilostazol · Clopidogrel · Constriction, Pathologic · Dual Anti-Platelet Therapy · Female · Humans · Japan · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Male · Middle Aged · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors · Risk Factors · Stroke · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a halving of recurrence, from a single open-label trial that stopped early. In CSPS.com (Toyoda K et al., PMID: 31122494), 1,884 Japanese patients with high-risk non-cardioembolic stroke (at least 50% stenosis of a major artery, or two or more vascular risk factors) were randomised to cilostazol 100 mg twice daily added to aspirin or clopidogrel, versus aspirin or clopidogrel alone, for up to 3.5 years. Recurrent ischaemic stroke occurred in 29 of 932 (3%; annualised 2.2%) on dual therapy versus 64 of 947 (7%; annualised 4.5%) on monotherapy (hazard ratio 0.49, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.76; P=0.0010) — a 51% relative reduction, printed beside the absolute rates. Severe or life-threatening bleeding was not increased (annualised 0.6% versus 0.9%; HR 0.66, 0.27 to 1.60; P=0.35), and any bleeding events were 4% in both groups. The cautions are structural: the trial was open-label, enrolled 1,884 of a planned 4,000 patients before stopping for slow recruitment, and studied only Japanese patients — a population in which cilostazol is licensed and commonly used. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): cilostazol-based dual therapy cut recurrence without a bleeding penalty in this single trial; confirmation outside Japan does not exist.

cards.headline: CSPS.com (Toyoda 2019): recurrence 3% versus 7% (HR 0.49, 0.31–0.76); severe or life-threatening bleeding 0.6% versus 0.9% annualised (HR 0.66, not significant)
cards.summary: CSPS.com (Toyoda 2019): recurrence 3% versus 7% (HR 0.49, 0.31–0.76); severe or life-threatening bleeding 0.6% versus 0.9% annualised (HR 0.66, not significant)
cards.people: 1,884 patients with high-risk non-cardioembolic ischaemic stroke confirmed on MRI at 292 hospitals in Japan — at least 50% stenosis of a major intracranial or extracranial artery or at least two vascular risk factors — randomised to cilostazol 100 mg twice daily plus aspirin (81–100 mg) or clopidogrel (50–75 mg) (932 analysed) or the same single agents alone (947 analysed), for 0.5 to 3.5 years (median follow-up 1.4 years); the trial stopped after enrolling 1,884 of an anticipated 4,000 patients because of slow recruitment.
cards.result: Ischaemic stroke recurred in 29 of 932 (3%; annualised rate 2.2%) on cilostazol dual therapy versus 64 of 947 (7%; annualised 4.5%) on monotherapy (hazard ratio 0.49, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.76; P=0.0010) — a 51% relative reduction alongside the absolute rates. Severe or life-threatening bleeding occurred at annualised rates of 0.6% versus 0.9% (HR 0.66, 0.27 to 1.60; P=0.35). Any adverse events (28% versus 24%), serious adverse events (10% versus 15%), and any bleeding events (4% versus 4%) were similar; gastrointestinal bleeding affected under 1% in both groups.
cards.watchOut: Open-label treatment with a soft-ish endpoint pathway, early stopping at 47% of target enrolment (early-stopped trials tend to overestimate effects), and a single-country population in which cilostazol pharmacogenetics and background care differ from Western practice. The bleeding confidence interval (0.27–1.60) cannot exclude a real increase.
cards.source: Toyoda K et al. Dual antiplatelet therapy using cilostazol for secondary prevention in patients with high-risk ischaemic stroke in Japan: a multicentre, open-label, randomised controlled trial. The Lancet Neurology. 2019. PMID: 31122494. Registry ID: NCT01995370. cards.headline: Synthesis: the strongest long-term dual-therapy signal in secondary stroke prevention — and still one trial, one country, half-recruited
cards.summary: Synthesis: the strongest long-term dual-therapy signal in secondary stroke prevention — and still one trial, one country, half-recruited
cards.people: One randomised open-label trial, 1,884 high-risk Japanese patients, median 1.4 years of follow-up.
cards.result: Recurrent ischaemic stroke: 3% versus 7% (HR 0.49, 0.31–0.76). Severe or life-threatening bleeding: annualised 0.6% versus 0.9% (HR 0.66, not significant). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: a single-trial benefit claim on a stroke outcome, which the developer reviews personally.
cards.watchOut: Unlike the short-course dual therapy of the minor-stroke trials, CSPS.com continued dual therapy for years — its bleeding neutrality over that horizon is the surprising half of the result and the half most in need of independent replication.
cards.source: Synthesis of Toyoda K et al. The Lancet Neurology. 2019 (PMID: 31122494).

shelves.title: ARCADIA: apixaban for cryptogenic stroke with atrial cardiopathy — recurrent stroke 4.4% per year on both drugs (HR 1.00); the trial stopped for futility
shelves.question: In cryptogenic stroke with atrial cardiopathy but no atrial fibrillation, does apixaban prevent recurrent stroke versus aspirin?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Female · Aged · Male · Atrial Fibrillation · Double-Blind Method · Canada · Stroke · Aspirin · Pyridones · Hemorrhage · Heart Diseases · Ischemic Stroke · Anticoagulants · Intracranial Hemorrhages · Pyrazoles
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — as clean a futility result as stroke prevention produces. ARCADIA (Kamel H et al., PMID: 38324415) randomised 1,015 patients with cryptogenic stroke and atrial cardiopathy (an abnormal P-wave measure, NT-proBNP over 250 pg/mL, or a left atrial diameter index of at least 3 cm/m²) but no atrial fibrillation, to apixaban 5 or 2.5 mg twice daily or aspirin 81 mg daily. After a mean 1.8 years the trial was stopped for futility at a planned interim analysis: recurrent stroke occurred in 40 patients in each group, an annualised rate of 4.4% in both (hazard ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.55). The safety ledger ran the other way from expectation — symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage occurred in 0 patients on apixaban versus 7 on aspirin (annualised 1.1%), and other major haemorrhage in 5 patients in each group (annualised 0.7% versus 0.8%; HR 1.02, 0.29 to 3.52). Atrial cardiopathy, as these three markers define it, marks risk but does not identify patients whose strokes are clot-driven in a way apixaban can prevent. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): apixaban did not reduce recurrent stroke versus aspirin in cryptogenic stroke with atrial cardiopathy and no fibrillation.

cards.headline: ARCADIA (Kamel 2024): 40 recurrent strokes in each arm (4.4% per year; HR 1.00, 0.64–1.55); symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage 0 on apixaban versus 7 on aspirin
cards.summary: ARCADIA (Kamel 2024): 40 recurrent strokes in each arm (4.4% per year; HR 1.00, 0.64–1.55); symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage 0 on apixaban versus 7 on aspirin
cards.people: 1,015 participants (mean age 68.0 years; 54.3% women) with cryptogenic stroke and atrial cardiopathy — P-wave terminal force over 5000 μV·ms in lead V1, NT-proBNP over 250 pg/mL, or left atrial diameter index at least 3 cm/m² — and no atrial fibrillation at randomisation, at 185 US and Canadian sites; apixaban 5 mg or 2.5 mg twice daily (507) versus aspirin 81 mg daily (508); mean follow-up 1.8 years; the trial was stopped for futility after a planned interim analysis with 1,015 of a target 1,100 enrolled.
cards.result: Recurrent stroke occurred in 40 patients on apixaban and 40 on aspirin (annualised rate 4.4% in both groups; hazard ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.55). Symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage occurred in 0 patients on apixaban and 7 on aspirin (annualised rate 1.1% on aspirin). Other major haemorrhage occurred in 5 patients in each group (annualised 0.7% versus 0.8%; HR 1.02, 0.29 to 3.52). All participants, including those later diagnosed with atrial fibrillation, were analysed as randomised.
cards.watchOut: A futility stop means the result is 'no benefit large enough to chase', with a confidence interval (0.64–1.55) that still admits a moderate effect either way. The zero-versus-seven haemorrhage split is a small-number secondary finding, not evidence that aspirin is the more dangerous drug at these doses.
cards.source: Kamel H et al. Apixaban to Prevent Recurrence After Cryptogenic Stroke in Patients With Atrial Cardiopathy: The ARCADIA Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2024. PMID: 38324415. Registry ID: NCT03192215. cards.summary: Synthesis: a biomarker-defined risk state that anticoagulation does not modify — treat the fibrillation if it appears, not the cardiopathy label

shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — the oldest, most replicated result in stroke care. The Cochrane network meta-analysis (Langhorne P et al., PMID: 32324916) pooled 29 randomised trials with 5,902 participants comparing organised inpatient stroke-unit care with an alternative service, and at a median one year found less poor outcome (odds ratio 0.77, 95% CI 0.69 to 0.87), less death (OR 0.76, 0.66 to 0.88), less death or institutional care (OR 0.76, 0.67 to 0.85), and less death or dependency (OR 0.75, 0.66 to 0.85) — all moderate-quality evidence, and robust when restricted to securely randomised trials with blinded outcome assessment. In absolute terms the review equates this to two extra survivors, six more patients living at home, and six more living independently for every 100 treated. The benefit was independent of age, sex, initial stroke severity, and stroke type, was clearest for units in a discrete stroke ward (network OR 0.74, 0.62 to 0.89 for poor outcome), and came with no systematic increase in length of stay. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): organised stroke-unit care reduces death and dependency versus general-ward care.

cards.headline: Langhorne 2020 (Cochrane): poor outcome OR 0.77 (0.69–0.87), death OR 0.76 (0.66–0.88), death or dependency OR 0.75 (0.66–0.85) at a median one year
cards.summary: Langhorne 2020 (Cochrane): poor outcome OR 0.77 (0.69–0.87), death OR 0.76 (0.66–0.88), death or dependency OR 0.75 (0.66–0.85) at a median one year
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review and network meta-analysis (Langhorne 2020)
cards.people: 29 randomised trials, 5,902 participants admitted to hospital after stroke: 20 trials (4,127 participants) comparing organised stroke-unit care with a general ward, 6 trials (982) comparing different forms of organised care, and 3 trials (793) with more than one comparison; organised care took the form of a dedicated stroke ward, a mobile stroke team, or a mixed rehabilitation ward.
cards.result: Compared with the alternative service, organised stroke-unit care improved outcomes at the end of scheduled follow-up (median one year): poor outcome OR 0.77 (95% CI 0.69 to 0.87), death OR 0.76 (0.66 to 0.88), death or institutional care OR 0.76 (0.67 to 0.85), and death or dependency OR 0.75 (0.66 to 0.85), all moderate-quality evidence. Expressed absolutely, this equates to two extra survivors, six more living at home, and six more living independently per 100 patients. Benefits persisted in securely randomised trials with blinded outcome assessment and were independent of age, sex, severity, and stroke type. By type, a dedicated stroke ward showed poor-outcome OR 0.78 (0.68 to 0.91) in direct comparison and 0.74 (0.62 to 0.89) in the network analysis; a mobile stroke team did not differ significantly (direct OR 0.80, 0.52 to 1.22, low-quality). Length of stay showed no systematic increase, though its analysis carried substantial heterogeneity (I²=85%).
cards.watchOut: The constituent trials span decades during which both stroke-unit and general-ward care evolved, so the pooled odds ratios describe organised care versus the conventional care of each trial's era, not versus a modern general ward. 'Stroke unit' is a bundle — staffing, protocols, early mobilisation, swallow and physiology management — and no trial can say which components carry the effect.
cards.source: Langhorne P et al. Organised inpatient (stroke unit) care for stroke: network meta-analysis. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2020. PMID: 32324916. shelves.title: VERSE: intensive speech therapy started within two weeks of stroke did not improve communication recovery — 50.3% versus 52.1% recovered at 12 weeks
shelves.question: In acute stroke, does intensive early speech therapy within the first weeks improve communication recovery versus usual-care therapy — the VERSE question?
shelves.mesh: Aphasia · Humans · Prospective Studies · Speech · Speech Therapy · Stroke · Stroke Rehabilitation · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — more therapy, started earlier, did not buy more recovery in the window the trial allowed. VERSE (Godecke E et al., PMID: 33019888) randomised 246 patients with aphasia after acute stroke at 17 hospitals in Australia and New Zealand to usual-care therapy, or to one of two intensive regimens (20 sessions of usual-care-plus or prescribed VERSE therapy) beginning within 14 days. At 12 weeks, communication recovery on the Western Aphasia Battery–Revised Aphasia Quotient was 50.3% (95% CI 45.7 to 54.8) in the combined high-intensity groups versus 52.1% (46.1 to 58.1) on usual care — a difference of −1.8 points (95% CI −8.7 to 5.0), with no difference in non-fatal or fatal adverse events (P=0.72). The null is about intensity and timing in the first 12 weeks, not about therapy itself: usual care in this trial was itself active therapy, and the dose question over longer horizons is a separate shelf. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): intensive aphasia therapy within 14 days did not improve 12-week communication recovery versus usual-care therapy.

cards.headline: VERSE (Godecke 2021): recovery 50.3% high-intensity versus 52.1% usual care (difference −1.8, −8.7 to 5.0); adverse events no different (P=0.72)
cards.summary: VERSE (Godecke 2021): recovery 50.3% high-intensity versus 52.1% usual care (difference −1.8, −8.7 to 5.0); adverse events no different (P=0.72)
cards.people: 246 patients with aphasia after acute stroke (of 13,654 screened, 3,477 had aphasia and 866 were eligible) at 17 acute hospitals in Australia and New Zealand, 2014–2018, randomised to usual care (81), usual care-plus (82; 20 extra sessions of non-prescribed therapy), or VERSE prescribed therapy (83; 20 sessions), all intensive therapy beginning within 14 days; the primary outcome was assessed in 217 participants (88%) at 12 weeks, 14 having died, 9 withdrawn, and 6 too unwell.
cards.result: Communication recovery on the Western Aphasia Battery–Revised Aphasia Quotient at 12 weeks was 50.3% (95% CI 45.7 to 54.8) in the combined high-intensity groups (147 assessed) and 52.1% (46.1 to 58.1) in usual care (70 assessed), a difference of −1.8 (95% CI −8.7 to 5.0). There was no difference between groups in non-fatal or fatal adverse events (P=0.72).
cards.watchOut: Only 7% of screened stroke patients reached randomisation, and 'usual care' here was real therapy delivered in trial hospitals — the comparison is intensive-plus-early against a good standard, not against nothing. Twelve weeks is early in aphasia recovery; the trial cannot exclude later separation, and its confidence interval admits up to a 5-point benefit or 8.7-point harm.
cards.source: Godecke E et al. A randomized control trial of intensive aphasia therapy after acute stroke: The Very Early Rehabilitation for SpEech (VERSE) study. International Journal of Stroke. 2021. PMID: 33019888. MeSH: Aphasia · Humans · Prospective Studies · Speech · Speech Therapy · Stroke · Stroke Rehabilitation · Treatment Outcome

shelves.title: How much speech therapy for aphasia? The RELEASE participant-level analysis: gains clustered above 20 hours total, at 2–4 or 9+ hours a week — under 20 hours, comprehension gains vanished
shelves.question: In post-stroke aphasia, how much does the dose, intensity and timing of speech–language therapy change language recovery — what does the individual-participant evidence say?
shelves.mesh: Aphasia · Humans · Language Therapy · Stroke · Stroke Rehabilitation
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for enough therapy, delivered often enough; the dose itself was never randomised, so this is a map, not a proof. The RELEASE collaboration (PMID: 34847708) pooled individual data from 959 participants in 25 trials and modelled how speech–language therapy (SLT) regimen relates to language gains. The greatest overall-language and comprehension gains were associated with a total dosage of more than 20 to 50 hours (overall language +18.37 points on the Western Aphasia Battery–Aphasia Quotient, 95% CI 10.58 to 26.16; comprehension +5.23, 1.51 to 8.95 on the Aachen Token Test), with the greatest clinical gains at 2–4 and at 9+ hours per week and at a frequency of 3–5+ days per week for overall language and functional communication. Below the floor there was nothing: evidence of comprehension gains was absent for SLT of 20 hours or less, under 3 hours per week, and 3 days per week or less. Mixed receptive–expressive therapy, functionally tailored, with prescribed home practice, was associated with the greatest overall gains. Because dose was observed, not assigned, motivated and less-impaired patients may simply accumulate more therapy — the analysis adjusted for age, sex, time since stroke, and baseline severity, but cannot fully remove that confounding. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): language recovery is greatest with frequent, functionally tailored therapy totalling well over 20 hours; very low doses show no measurable gain.

cards.headline: RELEASE 2022: 959 participants, 25 trials — >20–50 hours gave +18.37 WAB-AQ points (10.58–26.16); ≤20 hours, <3 h/week, or ≤3 days/week showed no comprehension gain
cards.summary: RELEASE 2022: 959 participants, 25 trials — >20–50 hours gave +18.37 WAB-AQ points (10.58–26.16); ≤20 hours, <3 h/week, or ≤3 days/week showed no comprehension gain
cards.people: 959 individual participants with post-stroke aphasia from 25 published, unpublished, and emerging trials (databases searched to September 2015), with patient-level data on stroke, language, therapy regimen, and trial risk of bias; outcomes standardised across overall language, auditory comprehension, naming, and functional communication, adjusted for age, sex, time post-stroke, and baseline aphasia severity.
cards.result: Greatest gains in overall language and comprehension were associated with >20 to 50 hours total SLT dosage (18.37 [95% CI 10.58 to 26.16] Western Aphasia Battery–Aphasia Quotient points; 5.23 [1.51 to 8.95] Aachen Aphasia Test–Token Test points). Greatest clinical gains in overall language, functional communication, and comprehension were associated with 2 to 4 and with 9+ SLT hours per week, and with frequency of 3–5+ days per week (overall language and functional communication) and 4–5 days per week (comprehension). Evidence of comprehension gains was absent for SLT ≤20 hours, <3 hours per week, and ≤3 days per week. Mixed receptive–expressive therapy, functionally tailored, with prescribed home practice was associated with the greatest overall gains; relative variance was under 30% and trial risk of bias was low to moderate.
cards.watchOut: Dose, intensity, and frequency were the regimens trials happened to deliver, not randomised assignments — these are adjusted associations within trial data, labelled exploratory by the authors themselves, and the counterintuitive double peak (2–4 and 9+ hours/week) warns against reading the curve as a prescription. The search closed in September 2015.
cards.source: RELEASE Collaborators. Dosage, Intensity, and Frequency of Language Therapy for Aphasia: A Systematic Review-Based, Individual Participant Data Network Meta-Analysis. Stroke. 2022. PMID: 34847708. Registry ID: PROSPERO CRD42018110947. MeSH: Aphasia · Humans · Language Therapy · Stroke · Stroke Rehabilitation

cards.headline: Synthesis: a floor and a shape, not a dose prescription — under ~20 hours nothing measurable, above it the gains the VERSE-era services rarely fund
cards.summary: Synthesis: a floor and a shape, not a dose prescription — under ~20 hours nothing measurable, above it the gains the VERSE-era services rarely fund
cards.people: One individual-participant-data network meta-analysis (959 participants, 25 trials) is the verified evidence base for the dose question.
cards.result: Overall language gain at >20–50 hours total dose: +18.37 WAB-AQ points (10.58–26.16). Comprehension gain at that dose: +5.23 Token Test points (1.51–8.95). Null zones: ≤20 hours total, <3 hours/week, ≤3 days/week (comprehension). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: the dose–response rests on non-randomised regimen comparisons, so the developer reviews it personally.
cards.watchOut: Read beside the VERSE shelf, the pair is coherent rather than contradictory: VERSE shows that front-loading intensity into the first 12 weeks adds nothing over good usual care, while RELEASE suggests cumulative dose over the whole recovery period is where gains live — different levers, different clocks.
cards.source: Synthesis of RELEASE Collaborators. Stroke. 2022 (PMID: 34847708).
