shelves.title: Modafinil for debilitating post-stroke fatigue (MIDAS): fatigue scores fell by 7.4 points and quality of life rose in a 36-patient crossover trial
shelves.question: In debilitating post-stroke fatigue, does modafinil improve fatigue severity versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Benzhydryl Compounds · Cross-Over Studies · Double-Blind Method · Fatigue · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Modafinil · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Quality of Life · Severity of Illness Index · Stroke · Wakefulness-Promoting Agents
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a real signal in a very small room. MIDAS (Bivard A et al., PMID: 28404841) was a single-centre phase 2 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial in stroke survivors at least 3 months out with severe fatigue (Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory score of at least 60): 232 survivors were screened and 36 randomised to modafinil 200 mg daily or placebo for 6 weeks, a 1-week washout, then the opposite treatment for 6 weeks. Patients on modafinil reported significantly less fatigue than on placebo (within-person difference −7.38 points on the 0–100 fatigue inventory, 95% CI −21.76 to −2.99 as printed in the record; P<0.001) and better stroke-specific quality of life (+11.81 points, 95% CI 2.31 to 21.31; P=0.0148), while cognition (Montreal Cognitive Assessment) and depression/anxiety/stress scores did not significantly improve (P>0.05). Post-stroke fatigue has few tested treatments, which makes the signal valuable — and a 36-patient single-centre crossover, with fatigue measured by self-report in a condition where expectation effects are plausible despite blinding, is exactly the design most prone to flattering a drug. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): modafinil reduced fatigue severity and improved quality of life in one small crossover trial; replication in a larger parallel-group trial is still owed.

cards.headline: MIDAS (Bivard 2017): fatigue −7.38 points versus placebo (P<0.001); quality of life +11.81 (P=0.0148); cognition and mood not significantly improved
cards.summary: MIDAS (Bivard 2017): fatigue −7.38 points versus placebo (P<0.001); quality of life +11.81 (P=0.0148); cognition and mood not significantly improved
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover phase 2 trial (Bivard 2017, MIDAS)
cards.people: 36 stroke survivors with non-resolving fatigue at least 3 months after stroke (Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory ≥60; 232 screened) at a single centre, randomised to modafinil 200 mg daily or placebo for 6 weeks, 1-week washout, then crossed to the other treatment for 6 weeks; outcomes were within-person, baseline-adjusted differences.
cards.result: Fatigue fell significantly on modafinil versus placebo (Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory difference −7.38; 95% CI −21.76 to −2.99 as printed in the record; P<0.001), and Stroke-Specific Quality of Life improved (+11.81; 95% CI 2.31 to 21.31; P=0.0148). Montreal Cognitive Assessment and Depression, Anxiety and Stress Scale scores were not significantly improved (P>0.05).
cards.watchOut: Thirty-six patients, one centre, six weeks per arm: the trial can detect a within-person symptom shift but says nothing about durability, safety in wider stroke populations, or benefit in milder fatigue (entry required a score of at least 60 of 100). The printed confidence interval for the fatigue difference is asymmetric around the point estimate in the record and is quoted exactly as published.
cards.source: Bivard A et al. MIDAS (Modafinil in Debilitating Fatigue After Stroke): A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled, Cross-Over Trial. Stroke. 2017. PMID: 28404841. cards.headline: Synthesis: the only randomised fatigue result in this population points the right way — and is one small trial deep
cards.summary: Synthesis: the only randomised fatigue result in this population points the right way — and is one small trial deep
cards.people: One single-centre crossover trial, 36 patients with severe post-stroke fatigue.

shelves.title: Fitness training after stroke: disability scores improved (SMD 0.52 for cardiorespiratory training) and walking and balance with them — deaths were too few to judge (19 in 3,017)
shelves.question: After stroke, does structured physical-fitness training — cardiorespiratory, resistance, or mixed — improve disability, walking and death versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Exercise Therapy · Humans · Middle Aged · Muscle Strength · Oxygen Consumption · Physical Fitness · Physical Functional Performance · Postural Balance · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Resistance Training · Stroke · Stroke Rehabilitation · Survivors · Walking · Walking Speed
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for function and fitness, with mortality honestly untested. The Cochrane review (Saunders DH et al., PMID: 32196635) pooled 75 randomised studies with 3,017 mostly ambulatory stroke survivors: cardiorespiratory training improved disability scores at the end of intervention (standardised mean difference 0.52, 95% CI 0.19 to 0.84; 8 studies, 462 participants; moderate-certainty evidence), mixed training improved them modestly (SMD 0.23, 0.03 to 0.42; low-certainty), and cardiorespiratory fitness itself rose (VO2 peak mean difference 3.40 mL/kg/min, 2.98 to 3.83), alongside benefits for walking speed and balance. Death was not influenced by any intervention — risk differences were all 0.00 — but with only 19 deaths among 3,017 participants at end of intervention and 19 among 1,469 at follow-up, the review is explicit that it cannot determine whether training reduces death or dependence. The constituent trials agree at the intensive end: in Globas C et al. (PMID: 21885867), 3 months of high-intensity aerobic treadmill training in chronic stroke improved VO2 peak by 6.4 mL/kg/min (P<.001) and 6-minute walk distance by 53 m (P<.001) versus conventional physiotherapy. No serious adverse events were attributed to training in the review. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): fitness training after stroke improves disability, fitness, and walking; an effect on death is unknown, not disproven.

cards.headline: Saunders 2020 (Cochrane): disability SMD 0.52 (0.19–0.84) cardiorespiratory, 0.23 (0.03–0.42) mixed; VO2 peak +3.40 mL/kg/min; death risk difference 0.00 throughout
cards.summary: Saunders 2020 (Cochrane): disability SMD 0.52 (0.19–0.84) cardiorespiratory, 0.23 (0.03–0.42) mixed; VO2 peak +3.40 mL/kg/min; death risk difference 0.00 throughout
cards.people: 75 randomised studies, 3,017 mostly ambulatory stroke survivors: cardiorespiratory training (32 studies, 1,631 participants), resistance training (20 studies, 779), and mixed training (23 studies, 1,207), versus usual care, no intervention, or a non-exercise intervention; searches to July 2018.
cards.result: Death was not influenced by any intervention (risk differences all 0.00; low-certainty evidence), with few deaths overall (19 of 3,017 at end of intervention; 19 of 1,469 at end of follow-up), and no study assessed death or dependence as a composite. Disability improved at end of intervention with cardiorespiratory training (SMD 0.52, 95% CI 0.19 to 0.84; 8 studies, 462 participants; P=0.002; moderate-certainty) and mixed training (SMD 0.23, 0.03 to 0.42; 9 studies, 604 participants; P=0.02; low-certainty); data were too few for resistance training on disability. VO2 peak rose after cardiorespiratory training (mean difference 3.40 mL/kg/min, 2.98 to 3.83; moderate-certainty), with further benefits for walking speed and balance, some mobility benefits persisting after training stopped. No serious adverse events were reported.
cards.watchOut: Mostly ambulatory survivors in mostly small trials with varied disability scales — the SMD is an average across instruments, not a promise on any one scale — and imbalanced exposure between groups was a common bias. The review's own successor reviews (noted on the record) now split this question further; the 2020 pooled answer stands as carded.
cards.source: Saunders DH et al. Physical fitness training for stroke patients. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2020. PMID: 32196635. cards.headline: Globas 2012: high-intensity treadmill training in chronic stroke — VO2 peak +6.4 mL/kg/min and 6-minute walk +53 m versus conventional physiotherapy (both P<.001)
cards.summary: Globas 2012: high-intensity treadmill training in chronic stroke — VO2 peak +6.4 mL/kg/min and 6-minute walk +53 m versus conventional physiotherapy (both P<.001)
cards.people: 38 ambulatory patients over 60 years old with residual hemiparetic gait, more than 6 months after stroke, randomised to 3 months (3 sessions weekly) of progressive high-intensity aerobic treadmill exercise or conventional-care physiotherapy; 36 completed (18 per group).
cards.result: Treadmill training but not conventional care improved VO2 peak (difference 6.4 mL/kg/min, P<.001) and 6-minute walk distance (53 m, P<.001); maximum walking speed (0.13 m/s, P=.01), balance (P<.05), and the mental subscore of the SF-12 (P<.01) also improved more with treadmill training. VO2 peak and 6-minute walk performance remained above baseline 1 year after training ended, though walk distance had fallen from its post-training peak (P<.01).
cards.watchOut: A 36-completer single trial in selected ambulatory chronic survivors able to tolerate high-intensity training — it illustrates the top of the dose range in the Cochrane pool, not the average patient, and its 1-year data show gains decay once training stops.
cards.source: Globas C et al. Chronic stroke survivors benefit from high-intensity aerobic treadmill exercise: a randomized control trial. Neurorehabilitation and Neural Repair. 2012. PMID: 21885867. shelves.title: Preventing post-stroke depression: escitalopram cut new depression to 8.5% versus 22.4% on placebo — problem-solving therapy helped in the main analysis but not the conservative one
shelves.question: In patients without depression after stroke, do escitalopram or problem-solving therapy prevent new post-stroke depression versus placebo or usual care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Citalopram · Depression · Depressive Disorder · Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Problem Solving · Psychotherapy · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors · Stroke · Stroke Rehabilitation
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the drug passed every analysis; the therapy passed only some. In the single prevention trial (Robinson RG et al., PMID: 18505948), 176 non-depressed patients within 3 months of stroke were randomised to escitalopram (59), placebo (58), or problem-solving therapy (59) for 12 months. New depression developed in 8.5% on escitalopram (3 major, 2 minor cases) and 11.9% on problem-solving therapy (5 major, 2 minor) versus 22.4% on placebo (11 major, 2 minor) — adjusted hazard ratios for placebo versus each treatment of 4.5 (95% CI 2.4 to 8.2) and 2.2 (1.4 to 3.5), both P<.001, with adverse events not significantly different between groups. Under the conservative intention-to-treat analysis — counting all 27 patients who never started treatment as depressed — escitalopram remained superior (23.1% versus 34.5%; adjusted HR 2.2, 1.2 to 3.9; P=.007) while problem-solving therapy did not (30.5% versus 34.5%; adjusted HR 1.1, 0.8 to 1.5; P=.51). A later re-examination of the same cohort over 8–10 years (Robinson RG et al., PMID: 28029510) found problem-solving therapy independently associated with longer time to death in an adjusted survival model — a model-based finding without absolute mortality rates in the record, from a post-hoc analysis. PROPOSED SPLIT: escitalopram prevents post-stroke depression in this trial under both analyses; problem-solving therapy's prevention effect is analysis-dependent, with a hypothesis-generating survival association.

cards.headline: Robinson 2008: depression in 8.5% on escitalopram and 11.9% on problem-solving therapy versus 22.4% on placebo — conservative analysis keeps only escitalopram (23.1% versus 34.5%)
cards.summary: Robinson 2008: depression in 8.5% on escitalopram and 11.9% on problem-solving therapy versus 22.4% on placebo — conservative analysis keeps only escitalopram (23.1% versus 34.5%)
cards.people: 176 non-depressed patients within 3 months of acute stroke at multiple sites (July 2003 to October 2007), randomised for 12 months to double-blind escitalopram (59), double-blind placebo (58), or non-blinded problem-solving therapy (59); the outcome was new major or minor post-stroke depression by structured interview and DSM-IV research criteria.
cards.result: Depression developed in 5 of 59 patients on escitalopram (8.5%; 3 major, 2 minor), 7 of 59 on problem-solving therapy (11.9%; 5 major, 2 minor), and 13 of 58 on placebo (22.4%; 11 major, 2 minor). Placebo patients were significantly more likely to develop depression than escitalopram patients (adjusted HR 4.5, 95% CI 2.4 to 8.2; P<.001) and problem-solving-therapy patients (adjusted HR 2.2, 1.4 to 3.5; P<.001), adjusted for mood-disorder history and robust to age, sex, site, and impairment severity. In the conservative intention-to-treat analysis (all 27 non-starters counted as depressed), escitalopram remained superior (23.1% versus 34.5%; adjusted HR 2.2, 1.2 to 3.9; P=.007) but problem-solving therapy did not (30.5% versus 34.5%; adjusted HR 1.1, 0.8 to 1.5; P=.51). Adverse events, including hospitalisations and nausea, did not differ significantly between groups.
cards.watchOut: One trial, 176 patients, and the therapy arm could not be blinded — expectation and contact-time effects sit inside the problem-solving result, which is also the arm whose significance evaporates under the conservative analysis. The escitalopram hazard ratios are expressed as placebo-versus-treatment in the record and are quoted that way here.

cards.headline: Robinson & Jorge 2017 (same cohort, 8–10 years): problem-solving therapy independently associated with longer time to death in an adjusted model — no absolute rates reported
cards.summary: Robinson & Jorge 2017 (same cohort, 8–10 years): problem-solving therapy independently associated with longer time to death in an adjusted model — no absolute rates reported
cards.type: Long-term follow-up re-examination of the randomised cohort (Robinson 2017)
cards.people: 122 of 129 eligible patients from the 2008 prevention trial were contacted 8–10 years later (7 lost to follow-up); families and survivors were interviewed for vital status, date, and cause of death; time to death was modelled (Weibull) adjusting for age, physical-illness severity, sex, stroke severity, and post-entry depression history.
cards.result: Problem-solving therapy significantly and independently increased the time to mortality in the adjusted model, whereas older age and major depression significantly and independently decreased it. The record reports no absolute mortality rates or hazard ratio for the treatment effect, so the size of the association cannot be stated from the record.
cards.watchOut: A post-hoc re-examination of a small trial cohort, with a model-based endpoint and no absolute numbers in the record — carded to complete the trial's story and flagged as hypothesis-generating; it does not upgrade the therapy's prevention result, which failed the conservative analysis on the depression endpoint itself.
cards.source: Robinson RG et al. Prevention of Poststroke Mortality Using Problem-Solving Therapy or Escitalopram. The American Journal of Geriatric Psychiatry. 2017. PMID: 28029510. shelves.title: SPRINT MIND: intensive blood-pressure control cut mild cognitive impairment (HR 0.81) but not dementia itself (HR 0.83, not significant) — the trial stopped early with too few dementia cases
shelves.question: In hypertensive adults, does intensive systolic control (target <120 mm Hg) reduce mild cognitive impairment and dementia versus standard control (<140 mm Hg)?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antihypertensive Agents · Blood Pressure · Cardiovascular Diseases · Cognitive Dysfunction · Dementia · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Hypertension · Male · Middle Aged · Proportional Hazards Models
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the earlier, softer endpoint moved; the disease endpoint did not reach significance. In SPRINT MIND (Williamson JD et al., PMID: 30688979), 9,361 hypertensive adults (mean age 67.9 years; 35.6% women; no diabetes or prior stroke) were randomised to a systolic target under 120 mm Hg (4,678) or under 140 mm Hg (4,683); over a median 5.11 years of follow-up, adjudicated probable dementia occurred in 149 versus 176 patients (7.2 versus 8.6 cases per 1,000 person-years; hazard ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.04 — not significant). Mild cognitive impairment was significantly reduced (14.6 versus 18.3 per 1,000 person-years; HR 0.81, 0.69 to 0.95), as was the composite of impairment or dementia (20.2 versus 24.1 per 1,000 person-years; HR 0.85, 0.74 to 0.97). The parent trial's early stop for cardiovascular benefit (median intervention 3.34 years) left fewer dementia cases than planned, and the authors state the dementia analysis may be underpowered. The brain-imaging substudy (Nasrallah IM et al., PMID: 31408137) leans the same way: white-matter lesion volume grew less on intensive treatment (increase 0.92 versus 1.45 cm³; between-group difference −0.54 cm³, −0.87 to −0.20), while total brain volume fell slightly more (−3.7 cm³ difference, −6.3 to −1.1) — small, opposing-direction anatomical signals. PROPOSED SPLIT: intensive control reduces mild cognitive impairment and slows white-matter lesion accrual, with dementia prevention suggested but not proven.

cards.headline: SPRINT MIND (Williamson 2019): dementia 149 versus 176 cases (HR 0.83, 0.67–1.04); MCI HR 0.81 (0.69–0.95); composite HR 0.85 (0.74–0.97)
cards.summary: SPRINT MIND (Williamson 2019): dementia 149 versus 176 cases (HR 0.83, 0.67–1.04); MCI HR 0.81 (0.69–0.95); composite HR 0.85 (0.74–0.97)
cards.people: 9,361 adults aged 50 or older with hypertension but no diabetes or stroke history, at 102 US and Puerto Rican sites, randomised to systolic targets <120 mm Hg (4,678) or <140 mm Hg (4,683); mean age 67.9 years, 3,332 women (35.6%); 8,563 (91.5%) completed at least one cognitive assessment; median intervention 3.34 years within median total follow-up of 5.11 years; the parent trial was stopped early for cardiovascular benefit.
cards.result: Adjudicated probable dementia occurred in 149 intensive-group versus 176 standard-group participants (7.2 versus 8.6 cases per 1,000 person-years; HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.04), not a significant reduction. Mild cognitive impairment was significantly reduced (14.6 versus 18.3 per 1,000 person-years; HR 0.81, 0.69 to 0.95), as was the composite of mild cognitive impairment or probable dementia (20.2 versus 24.1 per 1,000 person-years; HR 0.85, 0.74 to 0.97). The authors note early termination and fewer-than-expected dementia cases may have left the dementia endpoint underpowered.
cards.watchOut: The dementia confidence interval (0.67–1.04) is compatible with anything from a one-third relative reduction to none — the honest statement is 'unproven', not 'disproven'. Participants had no diabetes or prior stroke, so the result does not directly cover the highest-dementia-risk hypertensive groups.

randomised clinical trial (williamson 2019, sprint mind) 9,361 adults aged 50 or older with hypertension but no diabetes or stroke history, at 102 us and puerto rican sites, randomised to systolic targets <120 mm hg (4,678) or <140 mm hg (4,683); mean age 67.9 years, 3,332 women (35.6%); 8,563 (91.5%) completed at least one cognitive assessment; median intervention 3.34 years within median total follow-up of 5.11 years; the parent trial was stopped early for cardiovascular benefit. adjudicated probable dementia occurred in 149 intensive-group versus 176 standard-group participants (7.2 versus 8.6 cases per 1,000 person-years; hr 0.83, 95% ci 0.67 to 1.04), not a significant reduction. mild cognitive impairment was significantly reduced (14.6 versus 18.3 per 1,000 person-years; hr 0.81, 0.69 to 0.95), as was the composite of mild cognitive impairment or probable dementia (20.2 versus 24.1 per 1,000 person-years; hr 0.85, 0.74 to 0.97). the authors note early termination and fewer-than-expected dementia cases may have left the dementia endpoint underpowered. the dementia confidence interval (0.67–1.04) is compatible with anything from a one-third relative reduction to none — the honest statement is 'unproven', not 'disproven'. participants had no diabetes or prior stroke, so the result does not directly cover the highest-dementia-risk hypertensive groups. williamson jd et al. effect of intensive vs standard blood pressure control on probable dementia: a randomized clinical trial. jama. 2019. pmid: 30688979. registry id: nct01206062. mesh: aged · aged, 80 and over · antihypertensive agents · blood pressure · cardiovascular diseases · cognitive dysfunction · dementia · female · follow-up studies · humans · hypertension · male · middle aged · proportional hazards models

cards.headline: SPRINT MIND MRI substudy (Nasrallah 2019): white-matter lesions grew less on intensive treatment (−0.54 cm³ difference) while total brain volume fell slightly more (−3.7 cm³)
cards.summary: SPRINT MIND MRI substudy (Nasrallah 2019): white-matter lesions grew less on intensive treatment (−0.54 cm³ difference) while total brain volume fell slightly more (−3.7 cm³)
cards.people: 670 SPRINT participants with baseline brain MRI at 27 US sites (mean age 67.3 years; 40.4% women), of whom 449 (67.0%) completed follow-up MRI at a median 3.97 years; intensive group 355 at baseline, standard group 315.
cards.result: Mean white-matter lesion volume increased from 4.57 to 5.49 cm³ on intensive treatment (change 0.92 cm³, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.14) versus 4.40 to 5.85 cm³ on standard treatment (change 1.45 cm³, 1.21 to 1.70) — a between-group difference in change of −0.54 cm³ (−0.87 to −0.20). Mean total brain volume decreased by 30.6 cm³ on intensive treatment versus 26.9 cm³ on standard treatment (between-group difference −3.7 cm³, −6.3 to −1.1). The authors describe both differences as small.
cards.watchOut: A third of the substudy cohort lacked follow-up imaging, lesion volumes are a surrogate whose clinical exchange rate is debated, and the two anatomical signals point in opposite directions (fewer lesions, slightly more volume loss) — supportive context for the cognitive findings, not an independent verdict.
cards.source: Nasrallah IM et al. Association of Intensive vs Standard Blood Pressure Control With Cerebral White Matter Lesions. JAMA. 2019. PMID: 31408137. Registry ID: NCT01206062. shelves.title: ASPREE: daily aspirin did not prevent dementia, Alzheimer's disease, or cognitive decline in 19,114 healthy older adults (dementia HR 1.03)
shelves.question: In healthy older adults, does daily low-dose aspirin prevent dementia and cognitive decline versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal · Aspirin · Cognitive Dysfunction · Dementia · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Prospective Studies · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — the largest prevention experiment ever run on the question, and flat. In ASPREE's cognitive analysis (Ryan J et al., PMID: 32213642), 19,114 community-dwelling adults aged 70 or older (65 for US minorities), free of cardiovascular disease, disability, and diagnosed dementia, were randomised to aspirin 100 mg daily or placebo and followed a median 4.7 years, with 964 participants triggered into full dementia assessment and 575 adjudicated dementia cases (41% clinically probable Alzheimer's disease). There was no substantial difference in all-dementia risk (hazard ratio 1.03, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.17), probable Alzheimer's disease (HR 0.96, 0.74 to 1.24), or mild cognitive impairment (HR 1.12, 0.92 to 1.37), and cognitive change over time was similar in both groups. The record is graded Class II evidence that low-dose aspirin does not significantly reduce dementia, Alzheimer's disease, mild cognitive impairment, or cognitive decline in healthy older adults. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): aspirin started in healthy old age does not prevent dementia or cognitive decline.

cards.headline: ASPREE cognition (Ryan 2020): 575 dementia cases; HR 1.03 (0.91–1.17) for dementia, 0.96 for probable Alzheimer's, 1.12 for MCI — cognitive change identical
cards.summary: ASPREE cognition (Ryan 2020): 575 dementia cases; HR 1.03 (0.91–1.17) for dementia, 0.96 for probable Alzheimer's, 1.12 for MCI — cognitive change identical
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial analysis (Ryan 2020, ASPREE)
cards.people: 19,114 community-dwelling participants in the US and Australia aged at least 70 years (at least 65 for US minorities), free of cardiovascular disease, physical disability, and diagnosed dementia, randomised 1:1 to aspirin 100 mg daily or placebo; median follow-up 4.7 years; cognition assessed with the Modified Mini-Mental State Examination, Hopkins Verbal Learning Test–Revised, Symbol Digit Modalities Test, and Controlled Oral Word Association Test, with triggered dementia adjudication by DSM-IV criteria in 964 participants.
cards.result: There were 575 adjudicated dementia cases, 41% classified as clinically probable Alzheimer's disease. Risk did not differ substantially between aspirin and placebo for all dementia triggers (HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.17), probable Alzheimer's disease (HR 0.96, 0.74 to 1.24), or mild cognitive impairment (HR 1.12, 0.92 to 1.37), and cognitive change over time was similar in the two groups. The authors conclude there was no evidence aspirin reduced dementia, MCI, or cognitive decline (Class II evidence).
cards.watchOut: Aspirin was started at 70-plus in people without vascular disease — the trial cannot judge midlife aspirin or aspirin after vascular events, and 4.7 years may be short against dementia's long incubation. The point estimates sit on both sides of 1.00 across endpoints, which is what a true null looks like.
cards.source: Ryan J et al. Randomized placebo-controlled trial of the effects of aspirin on dementia and cognitive decline. Neurology. 2020. PMID: 32213642. Registry ID: NCT01038583. shelves.title: Statins do not prevent dementia: 31 dementia cases on statin versus 31 on placebo in 26,340 randomised patients (Cochrane) — and no cognitive test moved
shelves.question: Do statins prevent dementia or cognitive decline in people at risk — and does stopping a statin in established dementia change cognition or quality of life?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Alzheimer Disease · Anticholesteremic Agents · Cognition · Dementia · Humans · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors · Middle Aged · Pravastatin · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Simvastatin
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — the prevention half of this question has a large, consistent randomised answer. The Cochrane review (McGuinness B et al., PMID: 26727124) found two double-blind placebo-controlled trials totalling 26,340 participants aged 40 to 82 (11,610 aged 70 or older), all with vascular disease or vascular risk factors, treated with simvastatin or pravastatin for a mean 3.2 and 5 years, at low risk of bias. The one trial reporting dementia incidence (20,536 participants) found 31 cases in each group (odds ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.61 to 1.65). Both trials assessed cognition on five different tests with no differences between statin and placebo (high-quality evidence), and withdrawal for adverse events did not differ (OR 0.94, 0.83 to 1.05; discontinuation under 5%). The review's verdict is that there is good evidence statins given in late life to people at vascular risk do not prevent cognitive decline or dementia — the observational promise that prompted the question did not survive randomisation. The question's second half — whether stopping a statin in established dementia changes cognition or quality of life — has no verified randomised trial behind it in this build, and this shelf claims nothing for it. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): statins do not prevent dementia or cognitive decline in at-risk adults.

cards.headline: McGuinness 2016 (Cochrane): dementia 31 versus 31 cases (OR 1.00, 0.61–1.65); five cognitive tests all null; withdrawal OR 0.94 (0.83–1.05)
cards.summary: McGuinness 2016 (Cochrane): dementia 31 versus 31 cases (OR 1.00, 0.61–1.65); five cognitive tests all null; withdrawal OR 0.94 (0.83–1.05)
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (McGuinness 2016)
cards.people: Two double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trials, 26,340 participants aged 40 to 82 years (11,610 aged 70 or older), all with a history of, or risk factors for, vascular disease; simvastatin in one trial and pravastatin in the other; mean follow-up 3.2 years and 5 years; both trials at low risk of bias; searches to 11 November 2015.
cards.result: Only one study reported dementia incidence (20,536 participants): 31 cases in the statin group and 31 in the placebo group (OR 1.00, 95% CI 0.61 to 1.65; moderate-quality evidence, downgraded for imprecision). Both studies assessed cognitive function — at different times on different scales, so results were not pooled — and found no differences between statin and placebo on five different cognitive tests (high-quality evidence). Treatment discontinuation for non-fatal adverse events was under 5% in both studies, with no difference in withdrawal risk (OR 0.94, 0.83 to 1.05). The authors conclude there is good evidence that statins given in late life to people at risk of vascular disease do not prevent cognitive decline or dementia.
cards.watchOut: Only two trials ever measured the outcomes, and only one counted dementia — 62 cases in total — so small preventive effects cannot be excluded, though the cognitive-test evidence (high quality, five instruments) points the same way. Participants were at moderate-to-high vascular risk; prevention in low-risk or midlife populations is extrapolated, not tested.
cards.source: McGuinness B et al. Statins for the prevention of dementia. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2016. PMID: 26727124. cards.people: Two randomised placebo-controlled trials (26,340 participants) summarised by Cochrane; no verified randomised withdrawal trial in established dementia was found for this build.

shelves.title: Galantamine in mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's: cognition better by 3.3–3.9 ADAS-cog points at 16–24 mg/day in two large trials — a symptomatic gain, with global and daily-function benefits alongside
shelves.question: In mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease, does galantamine improve cognition, daily function and behaviour versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Aged · Alzheimer Disease · Behavioral Symptoms · Body Weight · Cholinesterase Inhibitors · Cognition · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Galantamine · Humans · Male · Neuropsychological Tests · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two concordant registration trials with the class's familiar small, real, symptomatic effect. In the USA-10 trial (Tariot PN et al., PMID: 10881251; 978 patients with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease), galantamine at 16 and 24 mg/day beat placebo on cognition at 5 months by 3.3 and 3.6 ADAS-cog points (both P<0.001), with significantly better clinician-rated global change (CIBIC-plus), activities of daily living, and behavioural symptoms; discontinuations for adverse events were 6–10% on galantamine versus 7% on placebo, and adverse events were predominantly mild gastrointestinal symptoms. In USA-1 (Raskind MA et al., PMID: 10881250; 636 patients), the pattern repeated at 6 months — treatment effects of 3.9 points (24 mg/day) and 3.8 points (32 mg/day) on ADAS-cog (both P<0.001), better CIBIC-plus outcomes (P<0.05), no modification by APOE genotype, and scores maintained near baseline at 12 months in patients continuing 24 mg/day. The Cochrane class review (Birks J, PMID: 16437532) puts the cholinesterase inhibitors' shared effect at about −2.7 ADAS-cog points (95% CI −3.0 to −2.3) across 13 trials, with about 29% leaving treatment for adverse events versus 18% on placebo. Nothing here slows the disease itself; the benefit is a few points of cognition and function for some months. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): galantamine 16–24 mg/day produces small, consistent symptomatic improvements in cognition, global state, daily function, and behaviour in mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease.

cards.headline: USA-10 (Tariot 2000): ADAS-cog differences of 3.3 points (16 mg) and 3.6 points (24 mg) versus placebo (both P<0.001); adverse-event discontinuations 6–10% versus 7%
cards.summary: USA-10 (Tariot 2000): ADAS-cog differences of 3.3 points (16 mg) and 3.6 points (24 mg) versus placebo (both P<0.001); adverse-event discontinuations 6–10% versus 7%
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled trial (Tariot 2000, Galantamine USA-10 Study Group)
cards.people: 978 patients with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease in a 5-month multicentre double-blind trial, randomised after a 4-week placebo run-in to placebo or galantamine escalated over up to 8 weeks to maintenance doses of 8, 16, or 24 mg/day; outcomes included ADAS-cog, CIBIC-plus, the AD Cooperative Study activities-of-daily-living inventory, and the Neuropsychiatric Inventory.
cards.result: At 5 months, galantamine–placebo differences on ADAS-cog were 3.3 points for 16 mg/day and 3.6 points for 24 mg/day (P<0.001 versus placebo for both). The 16 and 24 mg/day groups also had significantly better outcomes on CIBIC-plus, activities of daily living, and behavioural symptoms. Discontinuations for adverse events were low in all galantamine groups (6 to 10%) and comparable to placebo (7%); adverse events were notably gastrointestinal and mostly mild, which the authors attribute in part to the slow dose escalation.
cards.watchOut: A 5-month symptomatic trial: ADAS-cog differences of 3–4 points are the class's typical magnitude — statistically solid, clinically modest — and the 8 mg/day arm's results are not reported in the record's abstract, so the shelf's claim is confined to 16–24 mg/day. No disease-modification endpoint was tested.
cards.source: Tariot PN et al. A 5-month, randomized, placebo-controlled trial of galantamine in AD. The Galantamine USA-10 Study Group. Neurology. 2000. PMID: 10881251. randomised placebo-controlled trial (tariot 2000, galantamine usa-10 study group) 978 patients with mild-to-moderate alzheimer's disease in a 5-month multicentre double-blind trial, randomised after a 4-week placebo run-in to placebo or galantamine escalated over up to 8 weeks to maintenance doses of 8, 16, or 24 mg/day; outcomes included adas-cog, cibic-plus, the ad cooperative study activities-of-daily-living inventory, and the neuropsychiatric inventory. at 5 months, galantamine–placebo differences on adas-cog were 3.3 points for 16 mg/day and 3.6 points for 24 mg/day (p<0.001 versus placebo for both). the 16 and 24 mg/day groups also had significantly better outcomes on cibic-plus, activities of daily living, and behavioural symptoms. discontinuations for adverse events were low in all galantamine groups (6 to 10%) and comparable to placebo (7%); adverse events were notably gastrointestinal and mostly mild, which the authors attribute in part to the slow dose escalation. a 5-month symptomatic trial: adas-cog differences of 3–4 points are the class's typical magnitude — statistically solid, clinically modest — and the 8 mg/day arm's results are not reported in the record's abstract, so the shelf's claim is confined to 16–24 mg/day. no disease-modification endpoint was tested. tariot pn et al. a 5-month, randomized, placebo-controlled trial of galantamine in ad. the galantamine usa-10 study group. neurology. 2000. pmid: 10881251. mesh: activities of daily living · aged · alzheimer disease · behavioral symptoms · body weight · cholinesterase inhibitors · cognition · dose-response relationship, drug · double-blind method · female · galantamine · humans · male · neuropsychological tests · severity of illness index · treatment outcome

cards.headline: USA-1 (Raskind 2000): ADAS-cog effects of 3.9 points (24 mg) and 3.8 points (32 mg) at 6 months (both P<0.001); scores held near baseline at 12 months on continued treatment
cards.summary: USA-1 (Raskind 2000): ADAS-cog effects of 3.9 points (24 mg) and 3.8 points (32 mg) at 6 months (both P<0.001); scores held near baseline at 12 months on continued treatment
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled trial with open-label extension (Raskind 2000, Galantamine USA-1 Study Group)
cards.people: 636 patients with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease in a 6-month multicentre double-blind trial, randomised to placebo or galantamine escalated to 24 or 32 mg/day, with eligible patients then entering a 6-month open-label phase on 24 mg/day; primary measures were ADAS-cog/11 and CIBIC-plus, with the Disability Assessment for Dementia as a secondary measure.
cards.result: Galantamine significantly improved cognition versus placebo at 6 months, with treatment effects of 3.9 points at the lower dose and 3.8 points at the higher dose on ADAS-cog/11 (P<0.001 for both), and both doses produced better CIBIC-plus outcomes than placebo (P<0.05). Response was not affected by APOE genotype. At 12 months, mean ADAS-cog/11 and Disability Assessment scores had not significantly changed from baseline in patients who received 24 mg/day throughout. The most common adverse events were predominantly gastrointestinal and decreased during long-term treatment; there was no evidence of hepatotoxicity.
cards.watchOut: The 12-month 'maintenance' observation comes from an open-label extension without a placebo group — staying near baseline while untreated Alzheimer's declines is suggestive, not randomised proof of slowed decline. The 32 mg/day dose exceeds the later standard maintenance range and is not the dose this shelf recommends reading forward.
cards.source: Raskind MA et al. Galantamine in AD: A 6-month randomized, placebo-controlled trial with a 6-month extension. The Galantamine USA-1 Study Group. Neurology. 2000. PMID: 10881250. cards.headline: Birks 2006 (Cochrane, class context): cholinesterase inhibitors averaged −2.7 ADAS-cog points (95% CI −3.0 to −2.3) across 13 trials; 29% versus 18% left treatment for adverse events
cards.summary: Birks 2006 (Cochrane, class context): cholinesterase inhibitors averaged −2.7 ADAS-cog points (95% CI −3.0 to −2.3) across 13 trials; 29% versus 18% left treatment for adverse events
cards.people: 13 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials of donepezil, galantamine, or rivastigmine in mild, moderate, or severe dementia due to Alzheimer's disease, with treatment periods of 6 months and 1 year at recommended doses (Cochrane Dementia and Cognitive Improvement Group register searched June 2005).
cards.result: Treatment produced improvements in cognitive function averaging −2.7 points (95% CI −3.0 to −2.3) on the 70-point ADAS-cog scale, with blinded clinicians rating global state more positively in treated patients and benefits also seen on activities of daily living and behaviour; the review notes none of these treatment effects are large. More patients left cholinesterase-inhibitor groups for adverse events (approximately 29%) than placebo groups (18%), with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhoea significantly more frequent on treatment. Head-to-head studies showed no evidence of efficacy differences between the three drugs.
cards.watchOut: A class-level average across three drugs and severities — it calibrates galantamine's two trials rather than adding a third galantamine experiment, and its adverse-event dropout figures (29% versus 18%) are higher than the galantamine trials' own, reflecting the whole class and older titration practice.
cards.source: Birks J. Cholinesterase inhibitors for Alzheimer's disease. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2006. PMID: 16437532. cards.headline: Synthesis: two trials, one effect size, honestly small — galantamine earns the class's standard verdict, not a bigger one
cards.summary: Synthesis: two trials, one effect size, honestly small — galantamine earns the class's standard verdict, not a bigger one
cards.people: Two randomised placebo-controlled trials (978 and 636 patients with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease) plus the Cochrane class review (13 trials).
cards.result: ADAS-cog advantage versus placebo: 3.3–3.6 points at 5 months (16–24 mg/day) and 3.8–3.9 points at 6 months (24–32 mg/day), all P<0.001; global, functional, and behavioural endpoints significantly better in USA-10 and global outcomes better in USA-1. Class average: −2.7 points (95% CI −3.0 to −2.3). Adverse-event discontinuation: 6–10% versus 7% (USA-10). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), not Tier C: two concordant randomised trials carry the shelf.
cards.watchOut: Set beside the library's class shelf for cholinesterase inhibitors in Alzheimer's disease, this shelf is the galantamine-specific record; the two overlap in spirit but card different trials, and neither claims any effect on the disease's course or on institutionalisation.

shelves.title: Donepezil in vascular dementia: cognition improved by about 2 ADAS-cog points in two pooled trials (1,219 patients) — global benefit clearest at 5 mg, withdrawals doubled at 10 mg
shelves.question: In vascular dementia, does donepezil improve cognition and global function versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Cardiovascular System · Cholinesterase Inhibitors · Cognition · Dementia, Vascular · Diarrhea · Donepezil · Double-Blind Method · Female · Headache · Humans · Indans · Internationality · Male · Middle Aged · Nausea · Neuropsychological Tests · Nootropic Agents · Piperidines · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a small symptomatic gain in a condition with no approved treatment, from two identical industry trials. The combined analysis (Román GC et al., PMID: 16192723) pooled two 24-week randomised, double-blind trials totalling 1,219 patients with vascular dementia: both donepezil doses (5 and 10 mg/day) improved cognition versus placebo on ADAS-cog and MMSE (P<0.01), global function improved on CIBIC-plus at 5 mg/day (P<0.001 versus placebo; the 10 mg comparison was P=0.006) and on the Clinical Dementia Rating sum-of-boxes at 10 mg/day (P<0.01), and instrumental daily-living function improved at both doses (P<0.05). In the larger constituent trial reported separately (Black S et al., PMID: 12970516; 603 patients, mean age 73.9 years), week-24 ADAS-cog effect sizes were −1.90 points at 5 mg/day (P=0.001) and −2.33 at 10 mg/day (P<0.001), daily-living scores improved by −1.31 points at both doses (P=0.02), and withdrawals for adverse events were 11.1% on placebo, 11.1% on 5 mg, and 21.8% on 10 mg (P=0.005 versus placebo). The dose lesson cuts against escalation: the lower dose carried the cleanest global result with placebo-level tolerability. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): donepezil produces small improvements in cognition and some global and functional measures in vascular dementia, best supported at 5 mg/day.

cards.headline: Black 2003: ADAS-cog −1.90 (5 mg, P=0.001) and −2.33 (10 mg, P<0.001) at 24 weeks; daily-living benefit −1.31 at both doses; withdrawals 21.8% on 10 mg versus 11.1% on placebo
cards.summary: Black 2003: ADAS-cog −1.90 (5 mg, P=0.001) and −2.33 (10 mg, P<0.001) at 24 weeks; daily-living benefit −1.31 at both doses; withdrawals 21.8% on 10 mg versus 11.1% on placebo
cards.people: 603 patients (mean age 73.9 years; 55.2% men) with probable (70.5%) or possible (29.5%) vascular dementia by NINDS-AIREN criteria, randomised to 24 weeks of donepezil 5 mg/day (198), donepezil 10 mg/day after 28 days at 5 mg (206), or placebo (199); analyses were intention-to-treat.
cards.result: At week 24, both donepezil groups improved significantly on cognition versus placebo (ADAS-cog mean change effect size −1.90 for 5 mg/day, P=0.001; −2.33 for 10 mg/day, P<0.001). Global function improved significantly on CIBIC-plus only at 5 mg/day (P=0.014, observed cases) and on the Clinical Dementia Rating sum-of-boxes only at 10 mg/day (P=0.007). Activities of daily living improved at both doses (effect size −1.31; P=0.02 for each). Withdrawals for adverse events were 11.1% on placebo, 11.1% on 5 mg/day, and 21.8% on 10 mg/day (P=0.005 versus placebo).
cards.watchOut: Global-function significance flips between instruments and doses (CIBIC-plus at 5 mg, CDR sum-of-boxes at 10 mg) — a pattern consistent with small effects measured several ways rather than a robust global benefit, and the 10 mg dose doubled adverse-event withdrawals for an extra 0.4 ADAS-cog points.
cards.source: Black S et al. Efficacy and tolerability of donepezil in vascular dementia: positive results of a 24-week, multicenter, international, randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trial. Stroke. 2003. PMID: 12970516. cards.headline: Román 2005 combined analysis (two identical trials, 1,219 patients): cognition P<0.01 at both doses; CIBIC-plus P<0.001 at 5 mg; instrumental daily-living benefit at both doses
cards.summary: Román 2005 combined analysis (two identical trials, 1,219 patients): cognition P<0.01 at both doses; CIBIC-plus P<0.001 at 5 mg; instrumental daily-living benefit at both doses
cards.type: Combined analysis of two randomised trials (Román 2005)
cards.people: 1,219 patients with vascular dementia enrolled at 109 sites in the USA, Europe, Canada, and Australia in two identical 24-week randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled studies, randomised to donepezil 5 mg/day (406), 10 mg/day after brief titration (421), or placebo (392) — the pooled set includes the Black 2003 trial carded above and its identical twin.
cards.result: Both donepezil groups showed significant improvements in cognition versus placebo (ADAS-cog and MMSE, P<0.01). Global function benefits were significant on CIBIC-plus in the 5 mg/day group (P<0.001 versus placebo; 10 mg/day P=0.006) and on the CDR sum-of-boxes in the 10 mg/day group (P<0.01; 5 mg/day P=0.09). Functional benefits were seen on the ADFACS total score at 10 mg/day (P=0.02; 5 mg/day P=0.08) and on ADFACS instrumental activities of daily living at both doses (P<0.05). Donepezil was well tolerated, with low withdrawal rates due to adverse events.
cards.watchOut: A pooled re-presentation of two trials, one of which is carded separately above — the patient count must not be added to Black 2003's as if independent. The analysis is the sponsor programme's own summary, and several secondary endpoints sit between P=0.05 and P=0.09 depending on dose and instrument.
cards.source: Román GC et al. Donepezil in vascular dementia: combined analysis of two large-scale clinical trials. Dementia and Geriatric Cognitive Disorders. 2005. PMID: 16192723. shelves.title: Donepezil in Lewy-body dementia: the phase 2 trial was strongly positive (MMSE +3.8 at 5 mg) — the confirmatory phase 3 missed both co-primary endpoints, with MMSE benefit only at 10 mg
shelves.question: In dementia with Lewy bodies, does donepezil improve cognition and neuropsychiatric symptoms versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Cholinesterase Inhibitors · Cognition · Donepezil · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Indans · Lewy Body Disease · Male · Neuropsychological Tests · Nootropic Agents · Piperidines · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the small trial promised more than the confirmatory trial delivered. In the exploratory phase 2 trial (Mori E et al., PMID: 22829268; 140 Japanese patients), donepezil 5 and 10 mg/day beat placebo on the MMSE at 12 weeks (mean differences 3.8 points, 95% CI 2.3 to 5.3, and 2.4 points, 0.9 to 3.9; P<0.001 and P=0.001), on clinician-rated global change (P<0.001 at every dose including 3 mg), and on behavioural measures (P<0.001 at 5 and 10 mg), with caregiver burden reduced at 10 mg (P=0.004) and safety consistent with the known donepezil profile. The larger confirmatory phase 3 trial (Ikeda M et al., PMID: 25713599; 142 patients) then missed its predefined bar: superiority required significance on both co-primary endpoints (MMSE and the NPI-2 hallucinations/fluctuations score), and neither dose achieved it — MMSE improved significantly only at 10 mg (2.2 ± 0.4 versus 0.6 ± 0.5 points on placebo; P=0.016; the 5 mg change was not significant, P=0.232), NPI-2 differences from placebo were not significant at either dose, and parkinsonism was slightly more frequent at 10 mg though UPDRS motor scores barely changed. The cognition signal survived confirmation at the higher dose; the neuropsychiatric claim — half the original question — did not. PROPOSED SPLIT: donepezil improves cognition modestly in Lewy-body dementia (clearest at 10 mg), while a neuropsychiatric benefit was shown in phase 2 but not confirmed in phase 3.

cards.headline: Mori 2012 (phase 2): MMSE differences of 3.8 points (5 mg) and 2.4 points (10 mg) versus placebo; behaviour improved (P<0.001); caregiver burden down at 10 mg (P=0.004)
cards.summary: Mori 2012 (phase 2): MMSE differences of 3.8 points (5 mg) and 2.4 points (10 mg) versus placebo; behaviour improved (P<0.001); caregiver burden down at 10 mg (P=0.004)
cards.people: 140 patients with dementia with Lewy bodies at 48 specialty centres in Japan, randomised to placebo (35) or donepezil 3 mg (35), 5 mg (33), or 10 mg (37) daily for 12 weeks; cognition by MMSE and domain-specific tests, behaviour by the Neuropsychiatric Inventory, caregiver burden by the Zarit interview, global function by CIBIC-plus, and motor safety by UPDRS part III.
cards.result: Donepezil 5 and 10 mg/day were significantly superior to placebo on the MMSE (5 mg: mean difference 3.8, 95% CI 2.3 to 5.3, P<0.001; 10 mg: 2.4, 0.9 to 3.9, P=0.001) and on CIBIC-plus (P<0.001 for each; 3 mg was also superior on CIBIC-plus, P<0.001, but not on the MMSE, P=0.017 as reported against the trial's threshold). Significant improvements were found in behavioural measures (P<0.001) at 5 and 10 mg/day and in caregiver burden (P=0.004) at 10 mg/day. Safety was consistent with the known donepezil profile and similar among groups.

cards.headline: Ikeda 2015 (confirmatory phase 3): co-primary endpoints not achieved — MMSE significant only at 10 mg (P=0.016), NPI-2 not significant at either dose
cards.summary: Ikeda 2015 (confirmatory phase 3): co-primary endpoints not achieved — MMSE significant only at 10 mg (P=0.016), NPI-2 not significant at either dose
cards.people: 142 patients with probable dementia with Lewy bodies, randomised to placebo or donepezil 5 mg or 10 mg once daily for the 12-week double-blind phase; co-primary endpoints were change in MMSE and in the Neuropsychiatric Inventory NPI-2 (hallucinations and fluctuations), with superiority requiring simultaneous significance on both; safety included adverse events and UPDRS part III.
cards.result: The predefined superiority of donepezil over placebo was not confirmed in either active group. MMSE improved significantly versus placebo at 10 mg (2.2 ± 0.4 versus 0.6 ± 0.5 points, mean ± standard error; P=0.016) but not at 5 mg (1.4 ± 0.5; P=0.232). NPI-2 improved from baseline in the active groups, but differences from placebo were not significant. Most adverse events were mild or moderate; parkinsonism incidence was slightly higher at 10 mg, with minimal UPDRS change and no significant difference from placebo.
cards.watchOut: The record for this trial carries no MeSH terms (the card's source line says so). The authors suggest caregiver education in the trial may have compressed the neuropsychiatric contrast — plausible, but a post-hoc explanation; on the prespecified test, the neuropsychiatric claim failed.

cards.headline: Synthesis: believe the cognition, discount the behaviour — the phase 3 trial is the referee, and it split its verdict by endpoint
cards.summary: Synthesis: believe the cognition, discount the behaviour — the phase 3 trial is the referee, and it split its verdict by endpoint
cards.people: Two randomised placebo-controlled Japanese trials totalling 282 patients with dementia with Lewy bodies: exploratory phase 2 (n=140) and confirmatory phase 3 (n=142), each 12 weeks.
cards.result: MMSE versus placebo: +3.8 (5 mg) and +2.4 (10 mg) in phase 2; +2.2 at 10 mg (P=0.016) and non-significant at 5 mg in phase 3. Neuropsychiatric outcomes: significant in phase 2 (P<0.001); not significant in phase 3, whose co-primary endpoints were not achieved. Motor safety: no significant UPDRS worsening in either trial. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C: small single-country trials with a split confirmatory result, which the developer reviews personally.
cards.watchOut: Both trials are Japanese, 12 weeks long, and modest in size; Lewy-body dementia's fluctuating course makes short MMSE windows noisy in both directions — the shelf's split stamp is the accurate summary of a genuinely split record.

shelves.title: Music-based therapy in dementia: depressive symptoms slightly better and overall behavioural problems possibly better at the end of treatment — agitation, cognition and every long-term outcome unmoved
shelves.question: In people with dementia, do music-based therapeutic interventions reduce agitation, depression and behavioural symptoms versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Humans · Anxiety/therapy · Bias · Cognition · Dementia/therapy/psychology · Depression/therapy · Music Therapy/methods · Quality of Life · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the benefit is narrow and short-lived. The 2025 Cochrane review (30 randomised trials, 1,720 participants) found moderate-certainty evidence that music-based interventions probably improved depressive symptoms slightly at the end of treatment (standardised mean difference −0.23, 95% CI −0.42 to −0.04; 9 studies, 441 participants) and low-certainty evidence they may have improved overall behavioural problems (SMD −0.31, 95% CI −0.60 to −0.02; 10 studies, 385 participants) versus usual care. But the symptoms families ask about most did not move: agitation or aggression likely did not improve (SMD −0.05, 95% CI −0.27 to 0.17; 11 studies, 503 participants, moderate certainty), and neither did anxiety, social behaviour or cognition; at four or more weeks after treatment ended there was no evidence of benefit for any outcome. A second meta-analysis of 22 trials (1,780 patients) reached more optimistic conclusions on cognition, quality of life and neuropsychiatric symptoms, but its abstract reports vote counts of positive trials rather than pooled effect sizes, so the Cochrane GRADE-rated estimates govern the stamp. No serious adverse events were reported in the Cochrane set. PROPOSED SPLIT: a small, real, end-of-treatment gain in depressive symptoms (and possibly overall behavioural problems), with agitation, cognition and durability null.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2025: depression SMD −0.23 and overall behavioural problems SMD −0.31 at end of treatment — but agitation SMD −0.05 (null) and no long-term effect on anything
cards.summary: Cochrane 2025: depression SMD −0.23 and overall behavioural problems SMD −0.31 at end of treatment — but agitation SMD −0.05 (null) and no long-term effect on anything
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis (van der Steen 2025, update of the 2018 review)
cards.people: 30 randomised controlled trials with 1,720 participants with dementia of varying severity, conducted in 15 countries; most participants resided in institutions. Interventions were music-based therapeutic interventions of at least five sessions (individual in 7 studies, group in the rest; most mixing active and receptive musical elements), compared with usual care or with other activities, with outcomes at end of treatment and at four or more weeks afterwards.
cards.result: Versus usual care at end of treatment: depressive symptoms probably improved slightly (SMD −0.23, 95% CI −0.42 to −0.04; 9 studies, 441 participants; moderate-certainty evidence); overall behavioural problems may have improved (SMD −0.31, 95% CI −0.60 to −0.02; 10 studies, 385 participants; low certainty); agitation or aggression likely did not improve (SMD −0.05, 95% CI −0.27 to 0.17; 11 studies, 503 participants; moderate certainty). Emotional well-being (SMD 0.14, 95% CI −0.29 to 0.56), anxiety (SMD −0.15, 95% CI −0.39 to 0.09), social behaviour (SMD 0.22, 95% CI −0.14 to 0.57) and cognition (SMD 0.19, 95% CI −0.02 to 0.41) showed no improvement, and low/very-low-certainty evidence showed no long-term benefit (four or more weeks after treatment) for any outcome. Versus other activities, only social behaviour may have improved (SMD 0.52, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.96; 4 studies, 84 participants). Adverse effects were inconsistently recorded; no serious adverse events were reported.
cards.watchOut: The included studies were at high risk of performance bias (participants and staff cannot be blinded to music), and several pooled estimates rest on low or very low certainty evidence — the behavioural-problems gain in particular could shrink or vanish in better trials. Effects are standardised mean differences on symptom scales, not absolute symptom counts, so the clinical size of a −0.23 SMD is modest by construction.
cards.source: van der Steen JT et al. Music-based therapeutic interventions for people with dementia. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2025. PMID: 40049590. cards.headline: Lin 2023: across 22 trials, most individual trials favoured music therapy on cognition, quality of life and neuropsychiatric symptoms — but the abstract pools no effect sizes
cards.summary: Lin 2023: across 22 trials, most individual trials favoured music therapy on cognition, quality of life and neuropsychiatric symptoms — but the abstract pools no effect sizes
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Lin 2023)
cards.people: 22 trials from 21 studies with 1,780 patients with dementia, identified from PubMed, Embase and the Cochrane databases to April 2023, comparing music-based therapies with non-music therapies.
cards.result: In 15 trials, music-based therapies significantly improved cognition compared with non-music therapies; in 11 trials they significantly improved quality of life; and in six trials they significantly improved neuropsychiatric symptoms. The authors concluded music-based therapy is a safe and effective alternative approach for patients with dementia. The abstract reports these as counts of individually significant trials and prints no pooled standardised effect or confidence interval for any outcome.
cards.watchOut: Vote-counting significant trials is the weakest form of synthesis: it ignores trial size, effect magnitude and the trials that found nothing, and it conflicts with the Cochrane review's GRADE-rated cognition estimate (SMD 0.19, 95% CI −0.02 to 0.41 — not significant). This card is the optimistic counterweight, not the governing estimate.
cards.source: Lin TH et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: a small end-of-treatment mood gain is the defensible claim; agitation, cognition and durability are not supported
cards.summary: Synthesis: a small end-of-treatment mood gain is the defensible claim; agitation, cognition and durability are not supported
cards.people: Two syntheses of the randomised music-therapy literature in dementia: the 2025 Cochrane review (30 studies, 1,720 randomised participants, GRADE-rated) and a 2023 meta-analysis (22 trials, 1,780 patients, no pooled effects in its abstract).
cards.result: Depressive symptoms: SMD −0.23 (95% CI −0.42 to −0.04), moderate certainty. Overall behavioural problems: SMD −0.31 (95% CI −0.60 to −0.02), low certainty. Agitation/aggression: SMD −0.05 (95% CI −0.27 to 0.17), moderate certainty — null. Cognition: SMD 0.19 (95% CI −0.02 to 0.41) — null in the GRADE-rated analysis despite the second review's positive vote count. Long term (≥4 weeks after treatment): no benefit for any outcome. PROPOSED SPLIT, with the small short-term mood/behaviour gain and the agitation/cognition/durability nulls both on the face of the shelf.
cards.watchOut: Unblindable interventions with subjective outcomes are exactly where small pooled SMDs most often overstate real benefit; the stamp therefore credits only the moderate-certainty depression estimate at full weight and marks everything else by its certainty grade. Tier C is not set: the shelf rests on a current Cochrane meta-analysis, not a single trial or observational data.
cards.source: Synthesis of van der Steen JT et al. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2025 (PMID: 40049590); Lin TH et al. Psychiatry Research. 2023 (PMID: 37783097).

shelves.title: Solanezumab in preclinical Alzheimer's disease (A4): no slowing of cognitive decline over 240 weeks — amyloid accumulated more slowly, cognition did not follow
shelves.question: In amyloid-positive preclinical Alzheimer's disease, does solanezumab slow cognitive decline versus placebo — the prevention-stage anti-amyloid test?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Alzheimer Disease/diagnostic imaging/drug therapy/psychology · Amyloid beta-Peptides · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/adverse effects/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Brain/diagnostic imaging/drug effects · Positron-Emission Tomography · Aged, 80 and over
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the prevention-stage test of anti-amyloid therapy, solanezumab did not slow cognitive decline. In the A4 trial, 1,169 cognitively normal older adults with elevated brain amyloid were randomised to solanezumab (up to 1,600 mg intravenously every 4 weeks) or placebo for 240 weeks: the mean change in Preclinical Alzheimer Cognitive Composite score was −1.43 on solanezumab versus −1.13 on placebo (difference −0.30, 95% CI −0.82 to 0.22; P=0.26) — numerically favouring placebo. Brain amyloid did accumulate more slowly on solanezumab (mean increase 11.6 versus 19.3 centiloids on PET), so the drug engaged amyloid biology without converting it into cognition. Amyloid-related imaging abnormalities with oedema occurred in less than 1% in each group; ARIA with microhaemorrhage or haemosiderosis occurred in 29.2% on solanezumab versus 32.8% on placebo. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): four and a half years of monomeric-amyloid targeting in preclinical Alzheimer's disease produced no cognitive benefit in its single large phase 3 trial.

cards.headline: A4 (Sperling 2023): PACC change −1.43 on solanezumab versus −1.13 on placebo over 240 weeks (difference −0.30, P=0.26) — amyloid rose more slowly, cognition did not
cards.summary: A4 (Sperling 2023): PACC change −1.43 on solanezumab versus −1.13 on placebo over 240 weeks (difference −0.30, P=0.26) — amyloid rose more slowly, cognition did not
cards.people: 1,169 persons aged 65 to 85 years with preclinical Alzheimer's disease: global Clinical Dementia Rating score 0, Mini-Mental State Examination score 25 or more, and elevated brain amyloid on 18F-florbetapir PET; mean age 72 years, approximately 60% women, 75% with a family history of dementia. Randomised 1:1 to solanezumab up to 1,600 mg intravenously every 4 weeks (578) or placebo (591) for 240 weeks.
cards.result: The primary end point, change in Preclinical Alzheimer Cognitive Composite (PACC) score at 240 weeks, was −1.43 in the solanezumab group and −1.13 in the placebo group (difference −0.30; 95% CI −0.82 to 0.22; P=0.26) — no slowing of cognitive decline, with the point estimate favouring placebo. Amyloid levels on brain PET increased by a mean of 11.6 centiloids on solanezumab versus 19.3 centiloids on placebo. ARIA with oedema occurred in less than 1% of participants in each group; ARIA with microhaemorrhage or haemosiderosis in 29.2% on solanezumab versus 32.8% on placebo.
cards.watchOut: A single trial of one antibody that binds soluble monomeric amyloid: the null convicts solanezumab in preclinical disease, not every anti-amyloid strategy — plaque-clearing antibodies are a different pharmacology and are carded on their own shelves. The 240-week horizon is long for a trial but short against a decades-long disease, and the PACC is a composite sensitive to practice effects; neither caveat rescues a point estimate that favoured placebo.
cards.source: Sperling RA et al. Trial of Solanezumab in Preclinical Alzheimer's Disease. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2023. PMID: 37458272. Registry ID: NCT02008357. cards.headline: Synthesis: target engagement without clinical effect — the A4 null closes the prevention case for solanezumab
cards.summary: Synthesis: target engagement without clinical effect — the A4 null closes the prevention case for solanezumab
cards.people: One randomised phase 3 trial of 1,169 amyloid-positive, cognitively unimpaired adults treated for 240 weeks (A4). No second randomised trial of solanezumab in preclinical Alzheimer's disease exists to card.
cards.result: Cognition (PACC change at 240 weeks): −1.43 solanezumab versus −1.13 placebo (difference −0.30; 95% CI −0.82 to 0.22; P=0.26). Amyloid accumulation: +11.6 versus +19.3 centiloids — a biomarker separation with no cognitive counterpart. Safety: ARIA-oedema under 1% in both groups; ARIA-microhaemorrhage/haemosiderosis 29.2% versus 32.8%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference). Tier C is set: the shelf rests on a single trial.
cards.watchOut: Because this is the only prevention-stage trial, the stamp is POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY despite the trial's size and duration — one trial, one antibody, one stage of disease. The slower amyloid accumulation is printed on the card so the null is not misread as 'the drug did nothing at all': it did something biological that did not help patients.

shelves.title: Shunt valves in normal-pressure hydrocephalus: starting pressure and valve design changed overdrainage complications — 5 versus 29 cases in SVASONA — but not who improved
shelves.question: In idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus, do shunt-valve pressure settings change gait and clinical outcome after ventriculoperitoneal shunting?
shelves.mesh: Data Interpretation, Statistical · Equipment Design · Equipment Failure · Follow-Up Studies · Gait Disorders, Neurologic/etiology/physiopathology · Humans · Hydrocephalus, Normal Pressure/therapy · Nervous System Diseases/epidemiology/etiology · Netherlands · Pressure · Prospective Studies · Subdural Effusion/epidemiology/etiology · Treatment Outcome · Ventriculoperitoneal Shunt/instrumentation
shelves.balance: SPLIT — valve choices move overdrainage complications, not clinical improvement. In the DEPSS trial (58 patients with suspected idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus), an adjustable Strata valve preset at the highest performance level (2.5, lowered stepwise) produced no statistically significant difference in clinical improvement versus a valve preset low (performance level 1.0), but significantly more subdural effusions were observed in the improved patients in the low-preset group — the authors recommend starting high and lowering until improvement or radiological overdrainage appears, accepting slower improvement and more adjustments. The companion valve trial, SVASONA (145 patients), compared gravitational with programmable valves: overdrainage signs at 6 months occurred in 5 patients on gravitational valves versus 29 on standard valves (risk difference −36%, 95% CI −49% to −23%; p<0.001 — about one overdrainage complication avoided for every third patient), while disease-specific outcome scales did not differ between groups. PROPOSED SPLIT: start-high/valve-design strategies cut overdrainage harm; neither trial showed better gait or disease-specific clinical outcome from the valve choice itself.

cards.headline: DEPSS (Delwel 2013): high preset (PL 2.5, lowered stepwise) versus low preset (PL 1.0) — improvement did not differ significantly, subdural effusions clustered in the low-preset improvers
cards.summary: DEPSS (Delwel 2013): high preset (PL 2.5, lowered stepwise) versus low preset (PL 1.0) — improvement did not differ significantly, subdural effusions clustered in the low-preset improvers
cards.people: 58 patients with suspected idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus in a Dutch multicentre prospective randomised trial: 30 assigned to a Strata shunt (Medtronic) with the adjustable valve preset at performance level 1.0 (control), and 28 to the same valve preset at performance level 2.5, with the level allowed to be lowered until clinical improvement or radiological signs of overdrainage occurred.
cards.result: There was no statistically significant difference in improvement between the two groups overall. Significantly more subdural effusions were observed in the improved patients of the low-preset (PL 1.0) group. The authors recommend treating INPH with an adjustable valve preset at the highest opening pressure, lowered until clinical improvement or radiological signs of overdrainage occur, although slower improvement and more shunt adjustments might be the consequence. The record's abstract reports no event counts or effect sizes for the effusion comparison, so none are carded.
cards.watchOut: A 58-patient trial whose abstract gives the effusion result only as 'significantly more' in a subgroup (improved patients) — the least robust form of reporting, with no counts to audit. Enrolment was of patients 'suspected' of INPH, a diagnostically uncertain population in whom shunt response itself varies, so a null on improvement may reflect case mix as much as valve physics.
cards.source: Delwel EJ et al. A randomised trial of high and low pressure level settings on an adjustable ventriculoperitoneal shunt valve for idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus: results of the Dutch evaluation programme Strata shunt (DEPSS) trial. cards.headline: SVASONA (Lemcke 2013): overdrainage at 6 months in 5 patients on gravitational valves versus 29 on programmable valves (risk difference −36%, p<0.001) — disease-specific outcomes did not differ
cards.summary: SVASONA (Lemcke 2013): overdrainage at 6 months in 5 patients on gravitational valves versus 29 on programmable valves (risk difference −36%, p<0.001) — disease-specific outcomes did not differ
cards.type: Randomised pragmatic open-label multicentre trial (Lemcke 2013, SVASONA)
cards.people: 145 patients with idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus eligible for ventriculoperitoneal shunting (mean age 71.9 years, SD 6.9), enrolled in a pragmatic randomised open-label multicentre trial of gravitational valves versus non-gravitational programmable valves; 137 were available for endpoint analysis at 6 months.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — any clinical or radiological sign of overdrainage (headache, nausea, vomiting, subdural effusion or slit ventricle) at 6 months — occurred in 29 patients in the standard-valve group and 5 in the gravitational-valve group (risk difference −36%, 95% CI −49% to −23%; p<0.001), a difference that exceeded predetermined stopping rules and stopped recruitment early; implanting a gravitational valve avoids one additional overdrainage complication in about every third patient shunted. Disease-specific outcome scales (Black and Kiefer) did not differ between groups, although the SF-12 Mental Component Score favoured the gravitational device at 6 and 12 months.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with a partly clinical primary endpoint (headache, nausea) that knowledge of the valve could influence, and stopped early for benefit — early stopping on a large effect tends to overstate it. It answers a valve-design question (gravitational versus programmable), not the DEPSS pressure-setting question; it is carded as the companion evidence that overdrainage, not efficacy, is what valve choices move.
cards.source: Lemcke J et al. Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery, and Psychiatry. 2013. PMID: 23457222. Registry ID: ISRCTN51046698. cards.headline: Synthesis: two 2013 valve trials agree — settings and designs change overdrainage, not who improves
cards.summary: Synthesis: two 2013 valve trials agree — settings and designs change overdrainage, not who improves
cards.people: Two randomised multicentre trials in idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus from 2013: DEPSS (58 patients, high versus low initial pressure setting on an adjustable valve) and SVASONA (145 patients, gravitational versus programmable valve).
cards.result: Clinical improvement / disease-specific outcome: no significant difference in either trial. Overdrainage harm: significantly more subdural effusions among improvers on the low-preset strategy (DEPSS, no counts in the record), and 5 versus 29 patients with overdrainage signs at 6 months favouring gravitational valves (risk difference −36%, 95% CI −49% to −23%; p<0.001; SVASONA). PROPOSED SPLIT, with the complication benefit and the efficacy null both on the face of the shelf. Tier C is set: the complication claim rests on one small trial with uncounted events and one open-label trial stopped early.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial was blinded, samples are small, and the two interventions (initial pressure setting; valve mechanism) are cousins, not twins — the synthesis claims agreement on the pattern (harm moves, efficacy does not), not a pooled estimate. A later generation of valves and the question of shunting itself are different shelves.
cards.source: Synthesis of Delwel EJ et al. Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery, and Psychiatry. 2013 (PMID: 23408069); Lemcke J et al. Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery, and Psychiatry. 2013 (PMID: 23457222).

shelves.title: Lithium augmentation in resistant depression: response odds 2.89 in the 2014 pooling and 2.06 in 2026 — an effect that bias adjustment and trial sequential analysis then erase
shelves.question: In depression unresponsive to antidepressants, does lithium augmentation improve response and remission versus placebo or continued antidepressant alone?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Major Depressive Disorder/drug therapy · Antipsychotic Agents/therapeutic use · Triiodothyronine/therapeutic use · Drug Therapy, Combination · Lithium Compounds/therapeutic use · Antidepressive Agents/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the conventional meta-analyses say yes; the robustness checks say 'not proven'. Pooling nine placebo-controlled trials (237 patients), Nelson 2014 found lithium augmentation more than doubled the odds of response versus placebo (odds ratio 2.89, 95% CI 1.65 to 5.05; p=0.0002), with effects for both tricyclic and second-generation antidepressant backbones and no excess discontinuation for adverse events. The 2026 bias-adjusted reappraisal (56 augmentation trials, 13,616 patients) still found a conventional lithium benefit across 17 trials (OR 2.06, 95% CI 1.30 to 3.27), but trial sequential analysis did not support it — the accrued evidence reached only 8% of the required information size — and the effect became statistically non-significant after publication-bias adjustment (PET-PEESE and selection models). Most lithium trials also predate the modern operational definition of treatment-resistant depression. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): lithium augmentation probably helps some antidepressant non-responders, on an evidence base that is positive but small, old, and fragile to bias adjustment.

cards.headline: Hsu 2026 reappraisal: lithium response OR 2.06 (1.30–3.27) in conventional pooling — but trial sequential analysis unsupported (8% of required information) and bias-adjusted estimates non-significant
cards.summary: Hsu 2026 reappraisal: lithium response OR 2.06 (1.30–3.27) in conventional pooling — but trial sequential analysis unsupported (8% of required information) and bias-adjusted estimates non-significant
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis with bias-adjustment analyses (Hsu 2026)
cards.people: Systematic review of 56 placebo-controlled augmentation RCTs (13,616 adults with major depressive disorder responding inadequately to antidepressants) covering lithium, triiodothyronine and second-generation antipsychotics; the lithium analysis pooled 17 trials. Primary outcome was response (≥50% reduction in depressive symptoms).
cards.result: Second-generation antipsychotic augmentation beat placebo (OR 1.53, 95% CI 1.42 to 1.65; 45 trials) with trial-sequential-analysis support. Lithium showed benefit in conventional meta-analysis (OR 2.06, 95% CI 1.30 to 3.27; 17 trials; I²=11.5%), but the effect was not supported by trial sequential analysis (accrued information size reached 8% of the required information size; TSA-adjusted 95% CI 0.02 to 189.11) and became statistically non-significant in the PET-PEESE-adjusted and selection models. The authors note most lithium trials were conducted before treatment-resistant depression was operationally defined in contemporary research.
cards.watchOut: This is the candidate anchor, and its own conclusion is caution: the same dataset reads 'effective' through a conventional random-effects lens and 'unproven' through sequential and bias-adjusted lenses. The lithium trials are largely tricyclic-era, short, and small — the pooled OR inherits all three limitations, and no large modern lithium augmentation trial exists to settle it.
cards.source: Hsu TW et al. Reappraising lithium, triiodothyronine and second-generation antipsychotic augmentation treatment for major depression: a systematic review and meta-analysis with bias-adjustment analyses. BMJ Mental Health. 2026. PMID: 42532626. cards.headline: Nelson 2014: response odds ratio 2.89 (1.65–5.05) for lithium versus placebo across nine trials and 237 patients, on tricyclic and second-generation backbones alike
cards.summary: Nelson 2014: response odds ratio 2.89 (1.65–5.05) for lithium versus placebo across nine trials and 237 patients, on tricyclic and second-generation backbones alike
cards.people: Nine randomised placebo-controlled trials of lithium augmentation including 237 patients with unipolar major depression, adding lithium to tricyclic antidepressants (seven contrasts) or second-generation antidepressants (three contrasts).
cards.result: The odds ratio for response to lithium versus placebo across all contrasts was 2.89 (95% CI 1.65 to 5.05; z=3.72, p=0.0002), with very low heterogeneity (I²=0%). Adjunctive lithium was effective with tricyclics and with second-generation agents. Discontinuation due to adverse events was infrequent and did not differ between lithium and placebo. The authors note the meta-analysis is limited by the small size and number of trials and limited data for treatment-resistant patients.
cards.watchOut: Nine trials and 237 patients is a thin base for a doubling-of-odds claim: small old trials are exactly where publication bias lives, which is what the 2026 reappraisal's adjusted analyses then detect. Response (≥50% symptom reduction) is also a softer endpoint than remission, which these trials rarely powered.
cards.source: Nelson JC et al. A systematic review and meta-analysis of lithium augmentation of tricyclic and second generation antidepressants in major depression. Journal of Affective Disorders. 2014. PMID: 25069082.
