cards.headline: Synthesis: two meta-analyses, one direction — and a robustness warning printed on the newer one
cards.summary: Synthesis: two meta-analyses, one direction — and a robustness warning printed on the newer one
cards.people: Nelson 2014 (9 placebo-controlled trials, 237 patients) and the lithium arm of Hsu 2026 (17 trials within a 56-trial, 13,616-patient augmentation reappraisal with trial sequential and publication-bias-adjustment analyses).
cards.result: Response odds versus placebo: OR 2.89 (95% CI 1.65 to 5.05) in 2014 pooling; OR 2.06 (95% CI 1.30 to 3.27) in 2026 conventional pooling — shrinking as more trials accrue, and non-significant after bias adjustment, with trial sequential analysis reaching only 8% of the required information size. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit). Tier C is set: the benefit claim rests on small, mostly pre-modern-definition trials whose pooled effect does not survive the 2026 robustness analyses, so the developer reviews this one personally.
cards.watchOut: Nothing here compares lithium augmentation head-to-head with the antipsychotic augmentation strategies the 2026 review found TSA-supported; 'lithium probably works' is not 'lithium first'. Lithium's monitoring burden and narrow therapeutic index are outside these efficacy records and belong to the prescribing decision, not this stamp.

shelves.title: T3 augmentation in resistant depression: 10 of 17 responded versus 3 of 16 on placebo in the one head-to-head trial — but double-blind-only pooling has never been significant
shelves.question: In treatment-resistant depression, does triiodothyronine (T3) augmentation improve response versus lithium augmentation or placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Ambulatory Care · Antidepressive Agents, Tricyclic/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Depressive Disorder/drug therapy/psychology · Desipramine/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Drug Synergism · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Imipramine/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Lithium Carbonate/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Male · Placebos · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Triiodothyronine/pharmacology/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the positive signal lives in the weaker designs. The one head-to-head randomised trial (Joffe 1993, 50 tricyclic non-responders) found response in 10 of 17 patients on triiodothyronine, 9 of 17 on lithium and 3 of 16 on placebo over two weeks — T3 and lithium indistinguishable from each other, both ahead of placebo. But the 1996 meta-analysis of eight studies (292 patients) that pooled a relative response of 2.09 (95% CI 1.31 to 3.32) also reported that among the four randomised double-blind studies alone, the pooled effect was not significant (relative response 1.53, 95% CI 0.70 to 3.35; P=.29). The SSRI-era review (Cooper-Kazaz 2008) found five randomised trials too disparate to pool and called the enhancement evidence inconclusive. The 2026 bias-adjusted reappraisal carded on the companion lithium shelf (#3656) likewise found T3 response no better than control (OR 1.19, 95% CI 0.53 to 2.70; 6 trials) — it is mentioned here, not re-carded. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): T3 augmentation may help a subgroup of tricyclic-era non-responders, but the double-blind-only evidence has never reached significance.

cards.headline: Joffe 1993: response in 10/17 on T3, 9/17 on lithium and 3/16 on placebo at two weeks — the only direct T3-versus-lithium randomised comparison
cards.summary: Joffe 1993: response in 10/17 on T3, 9/17 on lithium and 3/16 on placebo at two weeks — the only direct T3-versus-lithium randomised comparison
cards.people: 50 outpatients with unipolar, nonpsychotic major depression who had failed to respond to desipramine or imipramine, at a Toronto mood-disorders programme, randomised double-blind to liothyronine (triiodothyronine), lithium carbonate, or placebo augmentation for 2 weeks.
cards.result: Both liothyronine and lithium were more effective than placebo in reducing Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression scores, and their augmenting effects did not differ from each other. With response defined as a ≥50% reduction in Hamilton scores plus a final score under 10, 10 of 17 subjects responded to liothyronine, 9 of 17 to lithium, and 3 of 16 to placebo. The authors concluded both compounds may be considered alternatives for augmenting tricyclic response.
cards.watchOut: Fifty patients, three arms, two weeks: the trial can show a short-horizon signal and nothing about durability, and its tricyclic backbone (desipramine/imipramine) is no longer the usual first-line antidepressant. The T3-versus-placebo contrast (10/17 versus 3/16) is the shelf's best single number and it rests on 33 patients.

randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (joffe 1993) 50 outpatients with unipolar, nonpsychotic major depression who had failed to respond to desipramine or imipramine, at a toronto mood-disorders programme, randomised double-blind to liothyronine (triiodothyronine), lithium carbonate, or placebo augmentation for 2 weeks. both liothyronine and lithium were more effective than placebo in reducing hamilton rating scale for depression scores, and their augmenting effects did not differ from each other. with response defined as a ≥50% reduction in hamilton scores plus a final score under 10, 10 of 17 subjects responded to liothyronine, 9 of 17 to lithium, and 3 of 16 to placebo. the authors concluded both compounds may be considered alternatives for augmenting tricyclic response. fifty patients, three arms, two weeks: the trial can show a short-horizon signal and nothing about durability, and its tricyclic backbone (desipramine/imipramine) is no longer the usual first-line antidepressant. the t3-versus-placebo contrast (10/17 versus 3/16) is the shelf's best single number and it rests on 33 patients. joffe rt et al. a placebo-controlled comparison of lithium and triiodothyronine augmentation of tricyclic antidepressants in unipolar refractory depression. archives of general psychiatry. 1993. pmid: 8489327. mesh: adult · ambulatory care · antidepressive agents, tricyclic/pharmacology/therapeutic use · depressive disorder/drug therapy/psychology · desipramine/pharmacology/therapeutic use · double-blind method · drug synergism · drug therapy, combination · female · humans · imipramine/pharmacology/therapeutic use · lithium carbonate/pharmacology/therapeutic use · male · placebos · psychiatric status rating scales · triiodothyronine/pharmacology/therapeutic use

cards.headline: Aronson 1996 meta-analysis: relative response 2.09 across eight studies — but 1.53 and not significant (P=.29) among the four double-blind trials alone
cards.summary: Aronson 1996 meta-analysis: relative response 2.09 across eight studies — but 1.53 and not significant (P=.29) among the four double-blind trials alone
cards.people: Eight controlled studies totalling 292 euthyroid, nonpsychotic patients with depression refractory to tricyclic antidepressants, comparing triiodothyronine augmentation with controls; four of the studies were randomised double-blind trials.
cards.result: Aggregating all eight studies, patients on triiodothyronine augmentation were twice as likely to respond as controls (relative response 2.09; 95% CI 1.31 to 3.32; P=.002), a 23.2% absolute improvement in response rates (95% CI 4.5% to 41.9%; P=.02), with a standardised effect on depression scores of 0.62 (P<.001). However, study quality was uneven and results heterogeneous: among the four randomised double-blind studies, pooled effects were not significant (relative response 1.53; 95% CI 0.70 to 3.35; P=.29), with one negative study accounting for most of the heterogeneity.
cards.watchOut: The headline 2.09 pools controlled studies of uneven quality; the double-blind subset — the subset this library's stamp discipline trusts — is null. Both numbers are printed on this card so the shelf cannot be quoted from the flattering one alone.
cards.source: Aronson R et al. Triiodothyronine augmentation in the treatment of refractory depression. A meta-analysis. Archives of General Psychiatry. 1996. PMID: 8792761. cards.headline: Cooper-Kazaz 2008: in the SSRI era, five randomised trials were too disparate to pool — enhancement evidence inconclusive, augmentation support resting on open studies and one large trial
cards.summary: Cooper-Kazaz 2008: in the SSRI era, five randomised trials were too disparate to pool — enhancement evidence inconclusive, augmentation support resting on open studies and one large trial
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised and open studies (Cooper-Kazaz 2008)
cards.people: Literature review of triiodothyronine supplementation of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors in major depressive disorder: five randomised controlled trials (three enhancement studies giving T3 from the start of treatment, two augmentation studies in non-responders) and three open augmentation studies.
cards.result: The randomised trials were too disparate in methodology for meta-analysis. Of the enhancement studies, one showed strongly positive effects of T3, one showed no effect, and one showed a trend. The open augmentation studies supported an effect of T3 in SSRI non-responsive patients, with some support from a large RCT; a smaller, underpowered RCT did not show efficacy. T3 was well tolerated in most studies. The authors concluded further research is needed before T3's effectiveness as an SSRI supplement can be definitively established.
cards.watchOut: A narrative review carded for its honest verdict, not for numbers — it contributes no pooled estimate, and its 'some support from a large RCT' phrasing cannot be audited from the record's abstract. It marks where the evidence stopped: the SSRI-era question was never answered by an adequately powered trial.
cards.source: Cooper-Kazaz R et al. Efficacy and safety of triiodothyronine supplementation in patients with major depressive disorder treated with specific serotonin reuptake inhibitors. cards.headline: Synthesis: T3's case rests on one small positive trial and open/controlled pooling; every blinded-only synthesis is null
cards.summary: Synthesis: T3's case rests on one small positive trial and open/controlled pooling; every blinded-only synthesis is null
cards.people: The tricyclic-era randomised comparison (Joffe 1993, 50 patients), the 1996 meta-analysis (8 studies, 292 patients, with its double-blind subset reported separately), and the SSRI-era review (Cooper-Kazaz 2008, 5 randomised trials unpoolable). The 2026 reappraisal's T3 estimate (OR 1.19, 95% CI 0.53 to 2.70) is carded on shelf #3656 and mentioned here only.
cards.result: Response: 10/17 on T3 versus 3/16 on placebo in the single head-to-head trial. Pooled relative response: 2.09 (95% CI 1.31 to 3.32) across all controlled studies versus 1.53 (95% CI 0.70 to 3.35; P=.29) in double-blind trials only. SSRI-era randomised evidence: inconclusive. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit). Tier C is set: a benefit claim whose blinded evidence base is a handful of small, old, mutually inconsistent trials.
cards.watchOut: T3 versus lithium has exactly one small trial behind it (Joffe 1993, no difference) — any claim that one augmenter is preferable to the other exceeds the record. Thyroid-function monitoring and the cardiac/bone cautions of thyroid hormone are clinical-practice matters outside these efficacy records.

shelves.title: Pramipexole for treatment-resistant bipolar depression (PAX-BD): primary endpoint missed in 39 patients — late response 46% versus 6%, with hypomania ratings up
shelves.question: In treatment-resistant bipolar depression already on mood stabilisers, does adjunctive pramipexole improve depressive symptoms versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Pramipexole/adverse effects/administration & dosage · Double-Blind Method · Bipolar Disorder/drug therapy · Female · Male · Middle Aged · Adult · Depressive Disorder, Treatment-Resistant/drug therapy · Drug Therapy, Combination · Treatment Outcome · Dopamine Agonists/adverse effects/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Aged · Benzothiazoles/adverse effects/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Antimanic Agents/adverse effects/administration & dosage/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a clinically large signal in a trial too small to confirm it. PAX-BD randomised just 39 patients with treatment-resistant bipolar depression (of a much larger planned sample; recruitment closed early) to pramipexole (maximum 2.5 mg/day) or placebo added to mood stabilisers. At the 12-week primary endpoint, the QIDS-SR reduction was 4.4 points (SD 4.8) on pramipexole versus 2.1 (5.1) on placebo — a medium effect (d=−0.72) that was not statistically significant (95% CI −0.4 to 6.3; p=0.087). Later timepoints tilted pramipexole's way: a significant 6.28-point QIDS-SR advantage at 36 weeks (95% CI 1.85 to 10.71), and at trial exit response in 46% versus 6% (p=0.026) and remission in 31% versus 0% (p=0.030). Against that, hypomania ratings were significantly higher on pramipexole at 12 weeks. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): pramipexole may help treatment-resistant bipolar depression over months, but the only randomised trial enrolled 39 patients, missed its primary endpoint, and raised hypomania ratings — a hypothesis, not an answer.

cards.headline: PAX-BD (McAllister-Williams 2025): 12-week QIDS-SR difference not significant (p=0.087) in 39 patients — exit response 46% versus 6% and remission 31% versus 0%, with higher hypomania ratings
cards.summary: PAX-BD (McAllister-Williams 2025): 12-week QIDS-SR difference not significant (p=0.087) in 39 patients — exit response 46% versus 6% and remission 31% versus 0%, with higher hypomania ratings
cards.people: 39 adults (18 pramipexole, 21 placebo) with treatment-resistant bipolar depression — failure to respond to, tolerate, or a contraindication/refusal of at least two of quetiapine, olanzapine, lamotrigine or lurasidone — randomised 1:1 to pramipexole (maximum 2.5 mg/day, salt weight) or placebo added to ongoing mood stabiliser therapy, with a 12-week primary endpoint (QIDS-SR, self-rated) and follow-up to 48 weeks. The trial closed early with a much smaller sample than planned.
cards.result: At 12 weeks, QIDS-SR fell by 4.4 points (SD 4.8) on pramipexole versus 2.1 (5.1) on placebo — a medium-sized (d=−0.72) but not statistically significant difference (95% CI −0.4 to 6.3; p=0.087). A non-significant approximate 2-point advantage in pleasure (anhedonia) scores appeared at 6 weeks (d=−0.76; 95% CI −0.11 to 4.20). Significant advantages emerged later: QIDS-SR by 6.28 points at 36 weeks (95% CI 1.85 to 10.71), psychosocial function by 5.36 points (95% CI 0.38 to 10.35), and at trial exit (48 weeks, or last available data after 16 weeks for those affected by the early closure) response in 46% versus 6% (p=0.026) and remission in 31% versus 0% (p=0.030). Hypomania ratings were significantly higher on pramipexole at 12 weeks; otherwise pramipexole was well tolerated, with dose titration a practical complication.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-nine patients: every late-trial percentage is a handful of people (46% versus 6% at exit is roughly 8 versus 1 responders), the exit analysis mixes 48-week completers with last-available data after an early closure, and the significant results sit at secondary timepoints after a missed primary. The higher hypomania ratings are the expected dopamine-agonist hazard in bipolar disorder and are the reason this cannot be read as a free win.
cards.source: McAllister-Williams RH et al. A randomised double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of pramipexole in addition to mood stabilisers for patients with treatment-resistant bipolar depression (the PAX-BD study). Journal of Psychopharmacology. 2025. PMID: 39829389. cards.headline: Synthesis: one small trial, a missed primary, a late signal, and a switch-risk warning — MAYBE is the ceiling
cards.summary: Synthesis: one small trial, a missed primary, a late signal, and a switch-risk warning — MAYBE is the ceiling
cards.people: One randomised double-blind trial (PAX-BD, 39 patients) is the entire placebo-controlled evidence base for pramipexole in treatment-resistant bipolar depression beyond the two small short-term trials its authors cite as prior suggestion; no second confirmatory trial exists to card.
cards.result: Primary endpoint (QIDS-SR at 12 weeks): difference favouring pramipexole, 95% CI −0.4 to 6.3, p=0.087 — not significant. Late endpoints: QIDS-SR advantage 6.28 points (95% CI 1.85 to 10.71) at 36 weeks; exit response 46% versus 6% (p=0.026); exit remission 31% versus 0% (p=0.030). Harm signal: hypomania ratings significantly higher at 12 weeks. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit). Tier C is set: a single small trial carrying a benefit claim.
cards.watchOut: The pattern 'primary missed, later timepoints significant' in a 39-patient trial with early closure is one of the most over-read patterns in psychiatry trials; the stamp credits the direction of the evidence without crediting its strength. A larger confirmatory trial — which the authors themselves call for — would move this shelf in either direction.
cards.source: Synthesis of McAllister-Williams RH et al. Journal of Psychopharmacology. 2025 (PMID: 39829389).

shelves.title: Minocycline in treatment-resistant depression: small trials pool positive (SMD −0.59) — the one large trial found nothing on any outcome
shelves.question: In treatment-resistant depression, does adjunctive minocycline improve depressive symptoms versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Antidepressive Agents/therapeutic use · Depression/drug therapy · Depressive Disorder, Treatment-Resistant/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Minocycline/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the meta-analysis of small trials is positive; the one large rigorous trial is null. Pooling five randomised trials (374 patients), Qiu 2023 found minocycline reduced depression severity scores versus control (standardised mean difference −0.59, 95% CI −0.98 to −0.20; P=0.003), including in the treatment-resistant subgroup (SMD −0.36, 95% CI −0.64 to −0.09; P=0.010). But the largest single trial — Hellmann-Regen 2022, 168 patients in the intention-to-treat population, minocycline 200 mg/day added to usual antidepressant treatment for six weeks — found no difference in MADRS change (difference 1.46, 95% CI −1.04 to 3.96; P=.25) and no significant effect on any secondary outcome. Minocycline was well tolerated in the large trial, and the meta-analysis found no excess of adverse events other than dizziness or of discontinuation. PROPOSED SPLIT: small-trial pooling says minocycline helps depression scores; the best-powered test in treatment-resistant depression says it does not — the large trial governs for the resistant population.

cards.headline: Hellmann-Regen 2022: MADRS difference 1.46 (95% CI −1.04 to 3.96; P=.25) — the large multicentre trial of adjunctive minocycline in TRD is null on every outcome
cards.summary: Hellmann-Regen 2022: MADRS difference 1.46 (95% CI −1.04 to 3.96; P=.25) — the large multicentre trial of adjunctive minocycline in TRD is null on every outcome
cards.people: 173 patients randomised (168 in the intention-to-treat population: 81 minocycline, 87 placebo) with major depressive disorder and treatment resistance (Hamilton score ≥16, CGI-S ≥4, inadequate response to initial standard antidepressant), mean age 46.1 years (SD 13.1), mean baseline MADRS 26.5 (5.0), at nine German university hospitals; minocycline 200 mg/day or placebo added to antidepressant treatment as usual for 6 weeks, with 6-month follow-up. Completion was 83.3% on minocycline and 83.1% on placebo.
cards.result: Minocycline did not alter the course of depression severity versus placebo: the difference in MADRS decrease over 6 weeks was 1.46 (95% CI −1.04 to 3.96; P=.25). No secondary outcome — response, remission, or other rating scales — showed a statistically significant effect. Minocycline was well tolerated. The authors concluded minocycline at 200 mg/day for 6 weeks was not superior to placebo in treatment-resistant depression.
cards.watchOut: Six weeks may be short for an anti-inflammatory mechanism, and the trial did not select patients by inflammatory markers — a biomarker-selected subgroup could in principle differ, but that subgroup claim has no randomised support in this record and cannot lift the stamp. Within its design, this is a clean, adequately sized null.
cards.source: Hellmann-Regen J et al. Effect of Minocycline on Depressive Symptoms in Patients With Treatment-Resistant Depression: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Network Open. 2022. PMID: 36103181. Registry ID: EudraCT 2015-001456-29 (from the record's abstract). cards.headline: Qiu 2023 meta-analysis: severity SMD −0.59 (−0.98 to −0.20) across five small trials — and −0.36 in the treatment-resistant subgroup
cards.summary: Qiu 2023 meta-analysis: severity SMD −0.59 (−0.98 to −0.20) across five small trials — and −0.36 in the treatment-resistant subgroup
cards.people: Five randomised controlled trials with 374 patients with depression, with or without treatment resistance, comparing adjunctive minocycline with control, identified from Embase, PubMed and the Cochrane Library to October 2022.
cards.result: The minocycline group showed a significant reduction in depression severity scores (SMD −0.59, 95% CI −0.98 to −0.20; P=0.003) and in Clinical Global Impression scores (SMD −0.28, 95% CI −0.56 to −0.01; P=0.042), but no significant difference in Beck Depression Inventory scores, response, or partial response. The treatment-resistant subgroup also favoured minocycline on severity (SMD −0.36, 95% CI −0.64 to −0.09; P=0.010), and a Hamilton-scale subgroup showed higher response (relative risk 2.51, 95% CI 1.13 to 5.57; P=0.024). No significant differences were found in adverse events other than dizziness, or in all-cause discontinuation.
cards.watchOut: Five trials and 374 patients, with the pooled significance carried by small studies — the classic setup for small-study effects, and the largest trial in the field (carded above, 168 patients) found nothing on any outcome. The meta-analysis's own response and partial-response endpoints were not significant even in its favourable pooling.
cards.source: Qiu Y et al. Efficacy and tolerability of minocycline in depressive patients with or without treatment-resistant: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Frontiers in Psychiatry. 2023. PMID: 37342175. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Synthesis: small trials pool positive, the large trial is null — for treatment-resistant depression the large trial governs
cards.summary: Synthesis: small trials pool positive, the large trial is null — for treatment-resistant depression the large trial governs
cards.people: One large multicentre RCT in treatment-resistant depression (Hellmann-Regen 2022, 168 intention-to-treat) against a five-trial meta-analysis of mixed depression populations (Qiu 2023, 374 patients).
cards.result: Severity scores: SMD −0.59 (95% CI −0.98 to −0.20) favouring minocycline in pooled small trials; SMD −0.36 (95% CI −0.64 to −0.09) in the pooled treatment-resistant subgroup. Largest single trial: MADRS difference 1.46 (95% CI −1.04 to 3.96; P=.25), all secondary outcomes null. Tolerability: no excess adverse events other than dizziness in pooling; well tolerated in the large trial. PROPOSED SPLIT. Tier C is set: the positive claim rests on small-trial pooling contradicted by the best-powered trial, so the developer reviews this one personally.
cards.watchOut: A split stamp is not a compromise — it records that the answer depends on which evidence tier is trusted, and this library's discipline trusts the large preregistered-style trial over small-trial pooling. If a future biomarker-selected trial is positive, it will be a different, narrower shelf.

shelves.title: Extended-release ketamine tablets in resistant depression: 180 mg held MADRS 6.1 points below placebo and halved relapse — in a phase 2 trial of patients pre-selected for responding
shelves.question: In treatment-resistant depression, do extended-release ketamine tablets improve depressive symptoms versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Ketamine/administration & dosage/therapeutic use/adverse effects · Male · Female · Delayed-Action Preparations · Middle Aged · Adult · Depressive Disorder, Treatment-Resistant/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Tablets · Antidepressive Agents/administration & dosage/therapeutic use/adverse effects · Treatment Outcome · Major Depressive Disorder/drug therapy · Aged
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — one phase 2 trial, in a population pre-selected for responding. In Glue 2024, 231 adults with treatment-resistant depression and MADRS scores of at least 20 entered an open-label enrichment phase on extended-release ketamine tablets (R-107, 120 mg/day for 5 days); the 168 who responded by day 8 were randomised to twice-weekly R-107 at 30, 60, 120 or 180 mg, or placebo, for 12 further weeks, mostly dosed at home. The primary objective was met at the top dose: the least-square mean MADRS difference for 180 mg versus placebo at 13 weeks was −6.1 (P=0.019), and relapse during double-blind treatment showed a dose response from 70.6% on placebo to 42.9% on 180 mg. Tolerability was excellent by ketamine standards — no blood-pressure changes, minimal sedation and minimal dissociation; headache, dizziness and anxiety were the commonest adverse events. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): in patients already shown to respond to the tablets, continuing the 180 mg dose held depression scores down better than switching to placebo — an enriched-withdrawal result that says nothing about starting the drug in unselected patients.

cards.headline: Glue 2024 (ENLIGHTEN phase 2): MADRS difference −6.1 at 180 mg versus placebo at 13 weeks (P=0.019); relapse 42.9% versus 70.6% — in patients enriched for initial response
cards.summary: Glue 2024 (ENLIGHTEN phase 2): MADRS difference −6.1 at 180 mg versus placebo at 13 weeks (P=0.019); relapse 42.9% versus 70.6% — in patients enriched for initial response
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 2 trial with open-label enrichment (Glue 2024)
cards.people: 329 adults with treatment-resistant major depression (MADRS ≥20) screened; 231 entered the 5-day open-label enrichment phase on extended-release ketamine tablets (R-107) 120 mg/day, and the 168 responders at day 8 (MADRS ≤12 and ≥50% reduction) were randomised 1:1:1:1:1 to double-blind R-107 30, 60, 120 or 180 mg, or placebo, twice weekly for 12 weeks. Non-responders exited the study. Most dosing during the randomised phase occurred at home.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — least-square mean change in MADRS at 13 weeks, tested by a fixed-sequence step-down procedure starting with the 180 mg dose — was met: the difference for the 180 mg group versus placebo was −6.1 (95% CI printed as 1.0 to 11.16 in absolute terms; P=0.019). Relapse rates during double-blind treatment showed a dose response, from 70.6% on placebo to 42.9% on 180 mg. Tolerability was excellent: no changes in blood pressure, minimal sedation and minimal dissociation; the most common adverse events were headache, dizziness and anxiety.
cards.watchOut: The enrichment design is the whole caveat: only patients who had already responded to the drug were randomised, so the trial measures maintenance in responders, not efficacy in the general treatment-resistant population — and randomised-withdrawal designs flatter the drug by construction. It is also a single phase 2 trial with five arms carved from 168 randomised patients, so each dose group is small; the lower doses did not carry the headline.
cards.source: Glue P et al. Extended-release ketamine tablets for treatment-resistant depression: a randomized placebo-controlled phase 2 trial. Nature Medicine. 2024. PMID: 38914860. shelves.title: Gepirone extended-release for major depression: two positive 8-week trials, remission 28.7% versus 14.9% — and dizziness in 45% on the drug versus 10% on placebo
shelves.question: In major depressive disorder, does gepirone extended-release — a selective 5-HT1A agonist — improve depressive symptoms versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Ambulatory Care · Delayed-Action Preparations · Demography · Major Depressive Disorder/diagnosis/drug therapy/psychology · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pyrimidines/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Serotonin Receptor Agonists/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Severity of Illness Index · Surveys and Questionnaires
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two placebo-controlled trials, both positive on their primary scale, neither printing the size of the score difference in its record. Feiger 2003 randomised 209 outpatients with moderate-to-severe major depression to gepirone extended-release (20–80 mg/day) or placebo for 8 weeks: HAM-D-17 change was significantly greater on gepirone at weeks 3 (p=.013) and 8 (p=.018), with response in 33.7% versus 18.8% at week 3 and remission in 28.7% versus 14.9% at week 8. Bielski 2008, a second 8-week trial in the same population, found significantly greater HAM-D-17 reductions on gepirone-ER from week 4 (p=.004) through week 8 (p=.032), with secondary scales also favouring gepirone. The price is early dizziness and nausea: in Bielski, dizziness occurred in 45% on gepirone versus 10% on placebo and nausea in 36% versus 13%, concentrated during up-titration; in Feiger, 9.8% versus 2.8% discontinued for adverse events. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): gepirone-ER beats placebo on depression scores over 8 weeks in two concordant trials, with a characteristic early dizziness/nausea burden.

cards.headline: Feiger 2003: HAM-D-17 change significantly greater on gepirone-ER at weeks 3 and 8 — response 33.7% versus 18.8%, remission 28.7% versus 14.9%
cards.summary: Feiger 2003: HAM-D-17 change significantly greater on gepirone-ER at weeks 3 and 8 — response 33.7% versus 18.8%, remission 28.7% versus 14.9%
cards.people: 209 patients aged 18 to 70 years with DSM-IV moderate-to-severe major depressive disorder and baseline HAM-D-17 score of at least 20, randomised after a 4- to 7-day placebo washout to gepirone-ER 20–80 mg/day (103 assigned; 101 in the intent-to-treat set) or placebo (106 assigned; 103 intent-to-treat) for 56 days.
cards.result: Mean HAM-D-17 change was significantly greater with gepirone-ER than placebo at weeks 3 (p=.013) and 8 (p=.018). HAM-D-17 responders were significantly more frequent on gepirone at week 3 (33.7% versus 18.8%) and week 4 (38.6% versus 24.8%), and remitters at week 6 (24.8% versus 13.9%) and week 8 (28.7% versus 14.9%). Discontinuation due to adverse events was 9.8% on gepirone versus 2.8% on placebo; common adverse events (dizziness, nausea, insomnia) were mild, with no statistical difference in weight gain or sedation and no serious adverse events in gepirone-treated patients. The record's abstract does not print the mean HAM-D point difference, so none is carded.
cards.watchOut: A 2003 sponsor-era trial reported through p-values and responder proportions: the absolute HAM-D separation — the number that tells a clinician whether the effect is 2 points or 5 — is not in the record's abstract. Responder/remitter gaps of roughly 14 percentage points are real but modest, and 8 weeks says nothing about continuation.
cards.source: Feiger AD et al. Gepirone extended-release: new evidence for efficacy in the treatment of major depressive disorder. The Journal of Clinical Psychiatry. 2003. PMID: 12716264. cards.headline: Bielski 2008: HAM-D-17 reductions significantly greater from week 4 (p=.004) to week 8 (p=.032) — dizziness 45% versus 10%, nausea 36% versus 13%
cards.summary: Bielski 2008: HAM-D-17 reductions significantly greater from week 4 (p=.004) to week 8 (p=.032) — dizziness 45% versus 10%, nausea 36% versus 13%
cards.people: Adult outpatients aged 18 to 64 years with moderate-to-severe major depressive disorder (DSM-IV-TR) and baseline HAM-D-17 total score of at least 20, in an 8-week double-blind trial conducted October 2003 to August 2004; gepirone-ER was titrated from 20 to 80 mg/day (most patients on 60 or 80 mg/day by week 3) versus placebo. The record's abstract does not print the randomised sample size, so none is stated.
cards.result: Significantly greater reductions in HAM-D-17 total scores occurred on gepirone-ER versus placebo by week 4 (p=.004), continuing through week 6 (p=.006) and week 8 (p=.032); secondary outcomes (HAM-D-28, depressed-mood item, Bech scale, MADRS, Clinical Global Impressions) also improved significantly at multiple timepoints including endpoint. The most frequent adverse events on gepirone-ER versus placebo were dizziness (45% versus 10%), nausea (36% versus 13%) and headache (24% versus 16%); dizziness occurred most often during initial dosing and up-titration.
cards.watchOut: As with Feiger, significance is reported without the mean point separation in the abstract, and a 45% dizziness rate is a partial unblinding hazard in a trial whose outcomes are clinician-rated symptom scales. Both gepirone trials are short, industry-era, and in non-resistant outpatients — the stamp does not extend to treatment-resistant depression.
cards.source: Bielski RJ et al. Gepirone extended-release in the treatment of adult outpatients with major depressive disorder: a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled, parallel-group study. cards.result: Primary scale (HAM-D-17 change): significantly greater on gepirone in both trials (week 8 p=.018 and p=.032). Tier C is not set: two concordant randomised trials carry the shelf.
cards.watchOut: POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY because neither record prints the mean HAM-D difference — the library cannot verify the effect's size, only its direction and its responder proportions. Gepirone's later regulatory history and its sexual-function profile are outside these two records.

shelves.title: Esketamine in acute suicidal depression (ASPIRE I & II): MADRS down an extra ~4 points within 24 hours in both trials — suicidal ideation itself no different from placebo
shelves.question: In major depression with active suicidal ideation with intent, does esketamine nasal spray plus standard care reduce depressive symptoms within 24 hours versus placebo nasal spray — and does it change suicidal ideation itself?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intranasal · Adolescent · Adult · Antidepressive Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Major Depressive Disorder/drug therapy/psychology · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Ketamine/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Nasal Sprays · Suicidal Ideation · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT — depressive symptoms fell faster on esketamine; suicidal ideation itself did not separate from placebo. In ASPIRE I (226 hospitalised adults with major depression and active suicidal ideation with intent), esketamine 84 mg nasal spray plus comprehensive standard care beat placebo spray plus standard care on MADRS change at 24 hours (least-squares mean difference −3.8; 95% CI −6.56 to −1.09; P=.006). ASPIRE II (230 randomised) replicated it almost exactly: MADRS −15.7 versus −12.4 points, difference −3.9 (95% CI −6.60 to −1.11; P=.006), with separation already at 4 hours (−4.2; 95% CI −6.38 to −1.94). But in both trials the key secondary endpoint — severity of suicidality on the CGI-SS-r — did not differ significantly between groups (ASPIRE I: median treatment difference 0.0, 95% CI −1.00 to 0.00; P=.107): suicidal ideation fell rapidly in both arms under hospitalisation and optimised antidepressants. Dizziness, dissociation, nausea, headache and somnolence were the commonest esketamine adverse events. PROPOSED SPLIT: a rapid, replicated ~4-point antidepressant advantage at 24 hours, with no demonstrated advantage on suicidal ideation itself — the outcome the admission was for.

cards.headline: ASPIRE I (Fu 2020): MADRS difference −3.8 at 24 hours (P=.006) — suicidality difference 0.0, not significant (P=.107)
cards.summary: ASPIRE I (Fu 2020): MADRS difference −3.8 at 24 hours (P=.006) — suicidality difference 0.0, not significant (P=.107)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind phase 3 trial (Fu 2020, ASPIRE I)
cards.people: 226 adults with DSM-5 major depressive disorder, active suicidal ideation with intent, and need for psychiatric hospitalisation, enrolled June 2017 to December 2018; randomised 1:1 to esketamine 84 mg or placebo nasal spray twice weekly for 4 weeks, each with comprehensive standard care (initial psychiatric hospitalisation and newly initiated or optimised oral antidepressant therapy).
cards.result: The primary endpoint favoured esketamine: change in MADRS total score at 24 hours after the first dose differed by −3.8 points (least-squares mean difference, SE 1.39; 95% CI −6.56 to −1.09; two-sided P=.006), with advantages also at 4 hours and later timepoints over 4 weeks. The key secondary endpoint did not: the between-group difference in Clinical Global Impression of Severity of Suicidality (revised) was not statistically significant (median treatment difference 0.0; 95% CI −1.00 to 0.00; P=.107). The most common adverse events on esketamine were dizziness, dissociation, headache, nausea and somnolence.
cards.watchOut: Both arms received the full inpatient package — hospitalisation plus a new or optimised antidepressant — so the trial isolates the spray's added value, which is exactly the right design, and the added value on suicidality was zero. A −3.8-point MADRS gap at 24 hours in patients whose scores are falling fast on standard care is a speed advantage, not yet a suicide-prevention claim; no suicide-outcome endpoint was powered.
cards.source: Fu DJ et al. Esketamine Nasal Spray for Rapid Reduction of Major Depressive Disorder Symptoms in Patients Who Have Active Suicidal Ideation With Intent: Double-Blind, Randomized Study (ASPIRE I). cards.headline: ASPIRE II (Ionescu 2021): MADRS −15.7 versus −12.4 at 24 hours (difference −3.9, P=.006), separation at 4 hours — suicidality again not significantly different
cards.summary: ASPIRE II (Ionescu 2021): MADRS −15.7 versus −12.4 at 24 hours (difference −3.9, P=.006), separation at 4 hours — suicidality again not significantly different
cards.type: Randomised double-blind phase 3 trial (Ionescu 2021, ASPIRE II)
cards.people: 230 adults aged 18 to 64 years with major depressive disorder and active suicidal ideation with intent, randomised 115 per arm to esketamine 84 mg or placebo nasal spray twice weekly for 4 weeks with comprehensive standard care (hospitalisation of at least 5 days and newly initiated or optimised oral antidepressants); 227 received study drug and 184 (80.0%) completed double-blind treatment.
cards.result: MADRS change at 24 hours was −15.7 (SD 11.56) on esketamine versus −12.4 (10.43) on placebo, each with standard care (least-squares mean difference −3.9, SE 1.39; 95% CI −6.60 to −1.11; P=.006), with a difference already at 4 hours (−4.2; 95% CI −6.38 to −1.94). Both groups improved rapidly on the CGI-Severity of Suicidality (revised), and the between-group difference was not statistically significant. Commonest esketamine adverse events: dizziness, dissociation, nausea, dysgeusia, somnolence, headache and paraesthesia.
cards.watchOut: A near-exact replication of ASPIRE I, including its null: two trials agreeing that depression scores separate and suicidality scores do not is stronger evidence for the split than either trial alone. Dissociation and dizziness partly unblind patients in both trials, which matters most for the subjective scale that did separate.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the fastest replicated antidepressant effect in this population — and a replicated null on the ideation it was meant to treat
cards.summary: Synthesis: the fastest replicated antidepressant effect in this population — and a replicated null on the ideation it was meant to treat
cards.people: Two phase 3 double-blind trials totalling 456 randomised hospitalised patients with major depression and active suicidal ideation with intent (ASPIRE I, 226; ASPIRE II, 230), each testing esketamine 84 mg twice weekly for 4 weeks added to comprehensive standard care.
cards.result: MADRS at 24 hours: −3.8 (95% CI −6.56 to −1.09; P=.006) and −3.9 (95% CI −6.60 to −1.11; P=.006) — consistent, rapid, modest. Suicidality severity (CGI-SS-r): not significantly different in either trial (ASPIRE I P=.107). Adverse events: dizziness, dissociation, nausea, headache, somnolence predominate. PROPOSED SPLIT, with the depression benefit and the suicidality null both on the face of the shelf. Tier C is not set: two concordant randomised trials carry both halves of the split.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial measured suicide attempts or deaths as endpoints, and 4 weeks in hospitalised, closely observed patients is the most favourable possible setting. The esketamine shelves for treatment-resistant depression without acute suicidality (#223, #407) are separate questions and are not re-carded here.
cards.source: Synthesis of Fu DJ et al. The Journal of Clinical Psychiatry. 2020 (PMID: 32412700); Ionescu DF et al. The International Journal of Neuropsychopharmacology. 2021 (PMID: 32861217).

shelves.title: Adjunctive celecoxib for major depression: pooled Hamilton advantage 3.26 points — from four trials totalling just 150 patients, with odds ratios too large to take at face value
shelves.question: In major depressive disorder, does adjunctive celecoxib improve response versus antidepressant alone?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/therapeutic use · Celecoxib · Databases, Bibliographic/statistics & numerical data · Major Depressive Disorder/drug therapy · Humans · Pyrazoles/therapeutic use · Sulfonamides/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — large-looking effects from a very small evidence base. The 2014 meta-analysis (Na) pooled the four randomised trials of adjunctive celecoxib in major depression — 150 patients in total — and found a Hamilton score advantage of 3.26 points (weighted mean difference, 95% CI 1.81 to 4.71), with remission odds of 6.58 (95% CI 2.55 to 17.00) and response odds of 6.49 (95% CI 2.89 to 14.55) versus antidepressant plus placebo. The component trials are pilots: Müller 2006 added celecoxib 400 mg/day to reboxetine in 40 patients for 6 weeks and found significantly greater Hamilton improvement; Akhondzadeh 2009 added celecoxib 400 mg/day to fluoxetine in 40 outpatients for 6 weeks with the same directional result and no significant difference in observed side effects. Odds ratios above 6 from 150 randomised patients are the signature of small-study inflation, and neither component record prints its own effect size. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): adjunctive celecoxib may add a few Hamilton points to an antidepressant over six weeks, on pilot-trial evidence that a larger trial could shrink or erase.

cards.headline: Na 2014 meta-analysis: Hamilton advantage 3.26 points (1.81–4.71), remission OR 6.58 and response OR 6.49 — across four trials totalling 150 patients
cards.summary: Na 2014 meta-analysis: Hamilton advantage 3.26 points (1.81–4.71), remission OR 6.58 and response OR 6.49 — across four trials totalling 150 patients
cards.people: Four randomised controlled trials with 150 patients with depressive episodes (75 on adjunctive celecoxib, 75 on placebo), all using celecoxib as the adjunctive non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug added to antidepressant treatment, identified from Medline, Embase and the Cochrane Central Register to 2014.
cards.result: Patients on adjunctive celecoxib had significantly higher mean Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression change than placebo (weighted mean difference 3.26, 95% CI 1.81 to 4.71), with better remission (odds ratio 6.58, 95% CI 2.55 to 17.00) and response rates (OR 6.49, 95% CI 2.89 to 14.55). The all-cause dropout rate favoured celecoxib but not significantly (OR 0.45, 95% CI 0.18 to 1.13; p=0.09). The authors called for larger samples and longer duration to confirm efficacy and tolerability.
cards.watchOut: One hundred and fifty patients is the entire randomised base, and remission/response odds ratios of ~6.5 in depression adjunct trials are implausibly large — larger than the effects of the antidepressants themselves in most trials — which is what small, selectively published pilot literatures produce. The pooled Hamilton difference (3.26 points) is the more believable number and is itself modest.
cards.source: Na KS et al. Efficacy of adjunctive celecoxib treatment for patients with major depressive disorder: a meta-analysis. Progress in Neuro-Psychopharmacology & Biological Psychiatry. 2014. PMID: 24056287. cards.headline: Müller 2006: celecoxib 400 mg/day added to reboxetine beat reboxetine plus placebo on Hamilton improvement over 6 weeks — in 40 patients
cards.summary: Müller 2006: celecoxib 400 mg/day added to reboxetine beat reboxetine plus placebo on Hamilton improvement over 6 weeks — in 40 patients
cards.people: 40 patients with an acute depressive episode, randomised double-blind after washout to reboxetine 4–10 mg/day plus celecoxib 400 mg/day (20 patients) or reboxetine plus placebo (20 patients) for 6 weeks; groups did not differ in age, sex, illness duration or severity, or reboxetine dose or plasma levels.
cards.result: Both groups improved significantly on the Hamilton Depression Scale over 6 weeks, and the celecoxib group showed significantly greater improvement than the reboxetine-alone group. The record's abstract reports the comparison as significant without printing the point difference or an effect size, so none is carded. No significant between-group tolerability finding is reported in the record.
cards.watchOut: Self-described pilot, 20 patients per arm, on reboxetine — an antidepressant backbone now little used — so both the size and the setting limit transfer. A pilot that cannot print its own effect size in its abstract contributes direction, not magnitude.
cards.source: Müller N et al. The cyclooxygenase-2 inhibitor celecoxib has therapeutic effects in major depression: results of a double-blind, randomized, placebo controlled, add-on pilot study to reboxetine. Molecular Psychiatry. 2006. PMID: 16491133. cards.headline: Akhondzadeh 2009: fluoxetine plus celecoxib 400 mg/day superior to fluoxetine plus placebo on Hamilton scores over 6 weeks — again 40 patients
cards.summary: Akhondzadeh 2009: fluoxetine plus celecoxib 400 mg/day superior to fluoxetine plus placebo on Hamilton scores over 6 weeks — again 40 patients
cards.people: 40 adult outpatients meeting DSM-IV-TR criteria for major depression with a baseline Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression score of at least 18, randomised to fluoxetine 40 mg/day plus celecoxib 400 mg/day (200 mg twice daily; 20 patients) or fluoxetine 40 mg/day plus placebo (20 patients) for 6 weeks, assessed at baseline and weeks 1, 2, 4 and 6.
cards.result: Both protocols significantly decreased Hamilton scores over the trial, and the fluoxetine-plus-celecoxib combination showed significant superiority over fluoxetine alone in treating depressive symptoms. There were no significant differences between the groups in observed side effects. As with the companion pilot, the record's abstract does not print the size of the Hamilton difference, so none is carded.
cards.watchOut: A second 40-patient, single-centre, 6-week pilot with the same reporting pattern. Two concordant pilots justify MAYBE and a call for a real trial; they do not justify importing the meta-analysis's odds ratios of ~6.5 into practice, and celecoxib's cardiovascular and gastrointestinal cautions sit outside these short records.
cards.source: Akhondzadeh S et al. Clinical trial of adjunctive celecoxib treatment in patients with major depression: a double blind and placebo controlled trial. Depression and Anxiety. 2009. PMID: 19496103. cards.headline: Synthesis: direction consistent, magnitude untrustworthy — pilot evidence only
cards.summary: Synthesis: direction consistent, magnitude untrustworthy — pilot evidence only
cards.people: Four randomised trials, 150 patients total (Na 2014 pooling), including the two 40-patient pilots carded in full above (Müller 2006 on reboxetine; Akhondzadeh 2009 on fluoxetine), each 6 weeks of celecoxib 400 mg/day added to an antidepressant.
cards.result: Pooled Hamilton advantage: 3.26 points (95% CI 1.81 to 4.71). Pooled remission OR 6.58 (95% CI 2.55 to 17.00) and response OR 6.49 (95% CI 2.89 to 14.55) — printed here with their provenance (150 patients) attached. Component trials: both significantly favoured celecoxib, neither printing its effect size in its record. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit). Tier C is set: a benefit claim resting on pilot trials whose pooled odds ratios are not credible at face value.
cards.watchOut: The 2026 updated meta-analysis of celecoxib adjuncts exists in the literature but was not carded: this shelf's stamp is deliberately built from the candidate's 2014 anchor and its auditable component trials. Any future larger trial — positive or negative — should replace this shelf's evidence base wholesale rather than be averaged into it.

shelves.title: Deprexis internet CBT for depression (EVIDENT): PHQ-9 effect d=0.39 over usual care in 1,013 patients, holding at 6 months — a small effect with a large reach
shelves.question: In major depression, does a guided internet-delivered CBT programme (Deprexis) reduce symptoms versus waitlist or care as usual?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy/methods · Depression/therapy · Female · Germany · Humans · Internet/statistics & numerical data · Logistic Models · Male · Middle Aged · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Severity of Illness Index · Single-Blind Method · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a large pragmatic trial of the named programme, backed by an individual-participant meta-analysis of the wider class. In EVIDENT, 1,013 adults with mild-to-moderate depressive symptoms (PHQ-9 score 5–14) were randomised to usual care alone or usual care plus the 12-week internet intervention Deprexis: the between-group effect on PHQ-9 at 3 months was d=0.39 (95% CI 0.13 to 0.64), holding at 6 months (d=0.32, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.69), and 35.6% versus 20.2% achieved at least a minimally important PHQ-9 change — a number needed to treat of 7 (95% CI 5 to 10). The individual-participant-data meta-analysis of self-guided internet CBT (13 studies, 3,876 participants) found a smaller average effect (Hedges g=0.27) with a response odds ratio of 1.95 (95% CI 1.52 to 2.50; NNT 8), and adherence predicted better outcomes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): Deprexis added to usual care produces a small-to-moderate, durable symptom reduction in mild-to-moderate depression — an access intervention with a modest per-person effect, not a substitute for therapy in severe illness.

cards.headline: EVIDENT (Klein 2016): Deprexis plus usual care beat usual care alone — PHQ-9 effect d=0.39 at 3 months, d=0.32 at 6 months, NNT 7 for a minimally important change
cards.summary: EVIDENT (Klein 2016): Deprexis plus usual care beat usual care alone — PHQ-9 effect d=0.39 at 3 months, d=0.32 at 6 months, NNT 7 for a minimally important change
cards.people: 1,013 adults with mild-to-moderate depressive symptoms (PHQ-9 score 5–14) recruited from clinical and non-clinical settings in Germany, randomised to care as usual alone or to a 12-week internet intervention (Deprexis) adjunctive to usual care, in an assessor-blinded trial with outcomes at baseline, 3 months (post-assessment) and 6 months (follow-up); the primary outcome was self-rated depression severity (PHQ-9), analysed intention-to-treat with linear mixed models.
cards.result: Changes in PHQ-9 differed significantly between groups (main effect of group p<0.001). The post-assessment between-group effect size favouring the intervention was d=0.39 (95% CI 0.13 to 0.64), stable at follow-up with d=0.32 (95% CI 0.06 to 0.69). The rate of participants achieving at least a minimally clinically important PHQ-9 change at post-assessment was 35.6% in the intervention group versus 20.2% on usual care alone, a number needed to treat of 7 (95% CI 5 to 10).
cards.watchOut: The population is mild-to-moderate symptoms (PHQ-9 5–14), much of it recruited outside clinics — the effect cannot be extrapolated to major depression of clinical severity, and self-rated PHQ-9 in an unblinded-by-design intervention trial is exposed to expectation effects. An effect of d=0.39 also means most individual users notice little; the case for the programme is reach and cost, not potency.
cards.source: Klein JP et al. Effects of a Psychological Internet Intervention in the Treatment of Mild to Moderate Depressive Symptoms: Results of the EVIDENT Study, a Randomized Controlled Trial. Psychotherapy and Psychosomatics. 2016. PMID: 27230863. cards.headline: Karyotaki 2017 IPD meta-analysis: self-guided internet CBT beat controls with Hedges g=0.27 and response OR 1.95 (NNT 8) across 3,876 participants
cards.summary: Karyotaki 2017 IPD meta-analysis: self-guided internet CBT beat controls with Hedges g=0.27 and response OR 1.95 (NNT 8) across 3,876 participants
cards.people: Individual participant data from 13 of 16 eligible randomised trials (3,876 participants with symptoms of depression; mean age 42.0 years, 66.0% female) comparing self-guided internet-based CBT with usual care, waiting list, or attention control; outcomes were standardised depression scores (Beck Depression Inventory, CES-D, PHQ-9) and treatment response.
cards.result: Self-guided iCBT was significantly more effective than controls on depression severity (β=−0.21; Hedges g=0.27) and on treatment response (β=0.53; odds ratio 1.95, 95% CI 1.52 to 2.50; number needed to treat 8). Adherence was associated with lower depressive symptoms (β=−0.19; P=.001) and greater response (β=0.90; P<.001). No examined participant- or study-level variable moderated outcomes. The authors propose self-guided iCBT as an evidence-based first-step approach, with limitations to address before routine dissemination.
cards.watchOut: This card covers the class (self-guided internet CBT, mostly against waitlist or usual-care controls, which flatter effects), not Deprexis specifically — it corroborates direction and approximate size, and its g=0.27 is smaller than EVIDENT's d=0.39, a gap consistent with waitlist-free usual-care comparison and programme differences. Three of 16 eligible trials did not contribute data.
cards.source: Karyotaki E et al. Efficacy of Self-guided Internet-Based Cognitive Behavioral Therapy in the Treatment of Depressive Symptoms: A Meta-analysis of Individual Participant Data. JAMA Psychiatry. 2017. PMID: 28241179. cards.headline: Synthesis: a named programme with a large usual-care-controlled trial, and a class effect a notch smaller — small, real, durable to 6 months
cards.summary: Synthesis: a named programme with a large usual-care-controlled trial, and a class effect a notch smaller — small, real, durable to 6 months
cards.people: EVIDENT (1,013 randomised, Deprexis adjunctive to usual care, mild-to-moderate symptoms) and the individual-participant meta-analysis of self-guided internet CBT (13 trials, 3,876 participants).
cards.result: Deprexis: PHQ-9 effect d=0.39 (95% CI 0.13 to 0.64) at 3 months and d=0.32 (95% CI 0.06 to 0.69) at 6 months; minimally important change 35.6% versus 20.2% (NNT 7). Class effect: Hedges g=0.27; response OR 1.95 (95% CI 1.52 to 2.50; NNT 8); adherence predicts outcome. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit). Tier C is not set: a large randomised trial of the named programme plus a 3,876-participant IPD meta-analysis carry the shelf.
cards.watchOut: Both evidence layers concern mild-to-moderate symptoms; nothing here supports internet CBT as sole treatment for severe, psychotic, or suicidal depression. Effects this size depend on engagement — the adherence gradient in the IPD analysis means real-world rollouts with poor completion should expect less than the trial numbers.

shelves.title: Vortioxetine and cognition in depression (FOCUS): DSST up 5.6 and 5.0 points over placebo in working patients, 9.2 and 9.0 in professionals — an effect that survived adjustment for mood
shelves.question: In working adults with major depression, does vortioxetine improve objective cognitive performance — processing speed and executive function — versus placebo, beyond its antidepressant effect?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Anti-Anxiety Agents/therapeutic use · Cognition Disorders/etiology · Major Depressive Disorder/complications · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Duloxetine Hydrochloride/therapeutic use · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neuropsychological Tests · Piperazines/therapeutic use · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Sulfides/therapeutic use · Surveys and Questionnaires · Treatment Outcome · Vortioxetine · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for objective processing-speed performance, in the one dedicated cognition trial and its working-patient analysis. FOCUS randomised adults with major depression who self-reported cognitive dysfunction to vortioxetine 10–20 mg, duloxetine 60 mg (active reference), or placebo for 8 weeks, with the Digit Symbol Substitution Test (DSST) as the prespecified primary endpoint: vortioxetine was statistically superior to placebo on the DSST (P<0.05), on the subjective Perceived Deficits Questionnaire (P<0.01), and on the performance-based UPSA functional-capacity measure (P<0.001), while duloxetine did not separate from placebo on the DSST or UPSA. In the post hoc working-patient analysis (McIntyre 2017), the DSST effect versus placebo was 5.6 points at 10 mg and 5.0 at 20 mg (P<0.001 for both) — larger than the 4.0-point effect in the total population, and reaching 9.2 and 9.0 points in patients in professional positions — and it remained significant after adjusting for change in depression (MADRS) scores, with path analysis in FOCUS likewise attributing the cognitive benefit primarily to a direct effect rather than to mood improvement. A 2022 meta-analysis of six randomised trials (1,782 patients) confirmed significant DSST, PDQ and MADRS advantages at both 10 and 20 mg, without printing pooled effect sizes in its record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): vortioxetine improves DSST performance more than placebo over 8 weeks, with the largest gains in working patients, and the effect is not fully explained by feeling less depressed.

cards.headline: FOCUS (Mahableshwarkar 2015): vortioxetine beat placebo on the prespecified DSST primary endpoint and on functional capacity (UPSA, P<0.001); duloxetine did not separate on either
cards.summary: FOCUS (Mahableshwarkar 2015): vortioxetine beat placebo on the prespecified DSST primary endpoint and on functional capacity (UPSA, P<0.001); duloxetine did not separate on either
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled active-reference trial (Mahableshwarkar 2015, FOCUS)
cards.people: Adults aged 18 to 65 years with major depressive disorder who self-reported cognitive dysfunction, in a multicentre double-blind trial randomised to flexible-dose vortioxetine 10–20 mg, duloxetine 60 mg (active reference), or placebo for 8 weeks. The prespecified primary endpoint was change in Digit Symbol Substitution Test (DSST) correct symbols at week 8; key secondaries were the Perceived Deficits Questionnaire (PDQ) and Clinical Global Impression, with the UPSA performance-based functional-capacity measure and MADRS as additional endpoints. The record's abstract does not print the randomised sample size, so none is stated.
cards.result: Vortioxetine was statistically superior to placebo on the DSST (P<0.05), PDQ (P<0.01), CGI-I (P<0.001), MADRS (P<0.05) and UPSA (P<0.001). A prespecified path analysis indicated the cognitive benefit was primarily a direct treatment effect rather than due to alleviation of depressive symptoms. Duloxetine was not significantly different from placebo on the DSST or UPSA, though it was superior on PDQ, CGI-I and MADRS. Common adverse events on vortioxetine (incidence at least 5%) were nausea, headache and diarrhoea. The record's abstract reports significance levels without mean point differences, so none are carded from this record.
cards.watchOut: The trial enrolled patients who self-reported cognitive dysfunction — a selected subgroup — and lasted 8 weeks. Its abstract gives p-values rather than the DSST point separation, so the size of the primary-endpoint win must be taken from the companion analysis carded below; a P<0.05 primary with unprinted magnitude is weaker evidence than the same claim with the number on its face.
cards.source: Mahableshwarkar AR et al. A Randomized, Placebo-Controlled, Active-Reference, Double-Blind, Flexible-Dose Study of the Efficacy of Vortioxetine on Cognitive Function in Major Depressive Disorder. Neuropsychopharmacology. 2015. PMID: 25687662. cards.headline: McIntyre 2017 (working-patient analysis of FOCUS): DSST effect versus placebo 5.6 (10 mg) and 5.0 (20 mg) in working patients — 9.2 and 9.0 in professional positions — independent of MADRS change
cards.summary: McIntyre 2017 (working-patient analysis of FOCUS): DSST effect versus placebo 5.6 (10 mg) and 5.0 (20 mg) in working patients — 9.2 and 9.0 in professional positions — independent of MADRS change
cards.type: Post hoc analysis of a randomised trial (McIntyre 2017, FOCUS working-patient analysis)
cards.people: Post hoc analysis of FOCUS (double-blind, placebo-controlled, December 2011 to May 2013; adults with recurrent major depressive disorder) stratified by working status and workplace position at baseline, examining DSST, Trail Making Test A/B, Stroop, and Perceived Deficits Questionnaire changes versus placebo, with MADRS change drawn from FOCUS plus three additional short-term placebo-controlled studies and one relapse-prevention study.
cards.result: In working patients, the DSST effect versus placebo was 5.6 for vortioxetine 10 mg and 5.0 for 20 mg (P<0.001 for both doses), compared with 4.0 (P<0.001 for both doses) in the total study population. In patients in professional positions, the effect was 9.2 for 10 mg (P=.006) and 9.0 for 20 mg (P=.001). The effect remained significant when adjusting for change in MADRS score. A similar pattern was observed for Trail Making A/B, Stroop, PDQ and MADRS; duloxetine's efficacy did not differ in working patients on MADRS. The authors concluded the cognitive benefits are greater in working patients and independent of improvement in depressive symptoms.
cards.watchOut: Post hoc subgroup analysis: 'working' and 'professional' strata were not the randomisation strata, and slicing a positive trial by employment invites both multiplicity and confounding (professionals may simply have more DSST headroom or practice gains). The independence-from-mood claim rests on statistical adjustment and path analysis, not on a design that separates the two. This is the candidate's anchor record; the FOCUS primary report is carded separately above and the two must not be read as two independent trials.
cards.source: McIntyre RS et al. Efficacy of Vortioxetine on Cognitive Functioning in Working Patients With Major Depressive Disorder. The Journal of Clinical Psychiatry. 2017. PMID: 27780334. Registry ID: NCT01422213 (FOCUS; the record lists five registered trials drawn on). cards.headline: Huang 2022 meta-analysis: six randomised trials, 1,782 patients — DSST, PDQ and MADRS all significantly favoured vortioxetine at 10 and 20 mg
cards.summary: Huang 2022 meta-analysis: six randomised trials, 1,782 patients — DSST, PDQ and MADRS all significantly favoured vortioxetine at 10 and 20 mg
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Huang 2022)
cards.people: Six randomised controlled trials with 1,782 patients with major depressive disorder and cognitive dysfunction, comparing vortioxetine with placebo, identified from PubMed, Embase and the Cochrane databases; outcomes were the DSST, PDQ and MADRS.
cards.result: The meta-analysis demonstrated that vortioxetine improved DSST, PDQ and MADRS scores in patients with major depressive disorder; results were consistent at the 10 mg and 20 mg doses, and in the 20 mg group the decrease in MADRS scores was more significant than with placebo. Both doses significantly increased DSST scores and decreased PDQ and MADRS scores. The record's abstract prints no pooled effect sizes, so none are carded; the authors call for longer-follow-up studies of mental function.
cards.watchOut: A confirmatory-direction synthesis without auditable magnitudes in its record: it tells the reader the pooled result is significant on all three measures, not how large it is. Its six trials include FOCUS, so it is corroboration of consistency across the programme, not independent replication of the working-patient claim.
cards.source: Huang IC et al. Effect of Vortioxetine on Cognitive Impairment in Patients With Major Depressive Disorder: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. cards.headline: Synthesis: one dedicated cognition trial, analysed two ways, plus a six-trial pooling — DSST gains are real, largest at work, and not just mood in disguise
cards.summary: Synthesis: one dedicated cognition trial, analysed two ways, plus a six-trial pooling — DSST gains are real, largest at work, and not just mood in disguise
cards.people: FOCUS (the dedicated randomised cognition trial in MDD with self-reported cognitive dysfunction, 8 weeks), its working-patient post hoc analysis, and a six-trial meta-analysis (1,782 patients).
cards.result: DSST versus placebo: significant in FOCUS (P<0.05, magnitude unprinted in the primary record); 5.6 (10 mg) and 5.0 (20 mg) points in working patients, 9.2 and 9.0 in professional positions, 4.0 in the total population (working-patient analysis); significant in six-trial pooling at both doses. Functional capacity (UPSA) also favoured vortioxetine in FOCUS (P<0.001) while the duloxetine reference arm did not separate on DSST or UPSA. Adjustment and path analyses attribute the cognitive effect primarily to a direct drug effect. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit). Tier C is not set: a dedicated randomised trial plus a concordant meta-analysis carry the shelf, though the working-patient magnification is post hoc and is flagged as such on its card.
cards.watchOut: The DSST is a processing-speed test, not a measure of remembered appointments or job performance; the UPSA result is the closest thing to real-world function here and comes from the same single trial. Vortioxetine's antidepressant efficacy per se is live shelf #1432 and is not re-carded; this shelf is only the cognition question.
cards.source: Synthesis of Mahableshwarkar AR et al. Neuropsychopharmacology. 2015 (PMID: 25687662); McIntyre RS et al. The Journal of Clinical Psychiatry. 2017 (PMID: 27780334); Huang IC et al. The International Journal of Neuropsychopharmacology. 2022 (PMID: 35981958).

shelves.title: Catatonia treatment: lorazepam remits 55% and ECT responds at 59–100% across the case-series literature — the lorazepam-first sequence has never been tested head-to-head
shelves.question: In catatonia, how do benzodiazepines (lorazepam) and ECT compare — who responds to lorazepam first, and what does the systematic evidence support when it fails?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Catatonia/drug therapy · Benzodiazepines/therapeutic use/administration & dosage · Lorazepam/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a consistent, large clinical signal with no controlled trials behind it. The 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis (Bot) screened 1,336 articles and included 53 studies, most of them case series of lorazepam at doses from 2 to 60 mg/day (median 8 mg/day), usually for no more than a week: the overall remission rate was 55% and the overall response rate 77%, with a pooled Bush–Francis Catatonia Rating Scale improvement of −11.88 points (Cohen's d=−3.15) and no significant dose–response relationship in meta-regression. The earlier systematic review (Pelzer 2018; 31 articles) found lorazepam and ECT the most investigated treatments, with response percentages of 66% to 100% for lorazepam in Western studies and 59% to 100% for ECT, and no evidence supporting antipsychotics in catatonia without an underlying psychotic disorder. No randomised head-to-head trial of lorazepam versus ECT exists: the sequence the literature supports is lorazepam first, ECT when lorazepam fails — a practice consensus built on case series, not a tested comparison. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): benzodiazepines, usually lorazepam, remit about half of reported catatonia cases and produce some response in about three quarters, with ECT the established fallback — all on uncontrolled evidence.

cards.headline: Bot 2026 meta-analysis: remission 55% and response 77% on benzodiazepines (mostly lorazepam, median 8 mg/day) — BFCRS improvement −11.88 points, no dose–response found
cards.summary: Bot 2026 meta-analysis: remission 55% and response 77% on benzodiazepines (mostly lorazepam, median 8 mg/day) — BFCRS improvement −11.88 points, no dose–response found
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of mostly case series (Bot 2026)
cards.people: 53 studies of benzodiazepine treatment in catatonia (from 1,336 screened articles), most of them case series using lorazepam at dosages from 2 to 60 mg/day (median 8 mg/day), with treatment duration predominantly not exceeding 1 week; a targeted meta-analysis pooled cases and studies with documented Bush–Francis Catatonia Rating Scale (BFCRS) scores before and after treatment and well-defined dosage regimens.
cards.result: The overall remission rate was 55% and the overall response rate 77%. The targeted analysis showed an overall effect of −11.88 points on the BFCRS when a benzodiazepine was used (Cohen's d=−3.15). Meta-regression found no significant dose–response relationship. The authors concluded benzodiazepines are highly effective for catatonia but optimal dosing remains unclear, and called for well-designed controlled studies.
cards.watchOut: There is no control group anywhere in this evidence: catatonia can remit with treatment of the underlying disorder or spontaneously, case series publish successes more readily than failures, and a pre–post Cohen's d of −3.15 is not comparable to a randomised effect size. The 55%/77% figures describe what happened after lorazepam was given, not what lorazepam caused — the stamp is capped at MAYBE for exactly this reason.
cards.source: Bot L et al. The Effect of Benzodiazepines on Catatonia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Acta Psychiatrica Scandinavica. 2026. PMID: 42009596. cards.headline: Pelzer 2018: lorazepam response 66–100% in Western studies, ECT response 59–100% — the two investigated treatments, with no protocol-grade evidence for either
cards.summary: Pelzer 2018: lorazepam response 66–100% in Western studies, ECT response 59–100% — the two investigated treatments, with no protocol-grade evidence for either
cards.people: 31 articles meeting inclusion criteria in a systematic review of catatonia treatment in adults (case series, cohort and randomised studies using valid outcome measures), searching the Cochrane Library, MEDLINE, EMBASE and PsycINFO; lorazepam and ECT were the most investigated interventions.
cards.result: Response percentages in Western studies varied between 66% and 100% for lorazepam (in Asian and Indian studies, between 0% and 100%); for ECT, response percentages were 59% to 100%. There was no evidence for the use of antipsychotics in catatonic patients without an underlying psychotic disorder. The authors concluded lorazepam and ECT are effective treatments supported by the clinical literature, but that the evidence was too limited to develop a treatment protocol and stringent treatment studies are warranted.
cards.watchOut: Response ranges spanning 0% to 100% across regions signal heterogeneous case definitions, doses and reporting rather than a stable treatment effect. The review's candour is the point: as of 2018 the field could not support a protocol, and the 2026 update carded above adds pooling without adding controls.
cards.source: Pelzer AC et al. Systematic review of catatonia treatment. Neuropsychiatric Disease and Treatment. 2018. PMID: 29398916. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Synthesis: lorazepam first, ECT on failure — the universal sequence rests entirely on uncontrolled series
cards.summary: Synthesis: lorazepam first, ECT on failure — the universal sequence rests entirely on uncontrolled series
cards.people: Two systematic reviews eight years apart (Pelzer 2018, 31 articles; Bot 2026, 53 studies) covering the benzodiazepine and ECT literature in catatonia; no randomised controlled trial of either treatment, and no head-to-head comparison, appears in either.
cards.result: Benzodiazepines (mostly lorazepam, median 8 mg/day): remission 55%, response 77%, BFCRS improvement −11.88 points (pre–post, uncontrolled). Lorazepam response ranges 66–100% (Western series); ECT response ranges 59–100%. Dose–response for benzodiazepines: not found. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit). Tier C is set: the shelf rests entirely on observational/case-series evidence.
cards.watchOut: MAYBE (weak evidence) here does not mean clinicians doubt lorazepam works — the bedside signal is strong and the alternative (untreated catatonia) is dangerous. It means this library's stamp grades the evidence design, and by design there is nothing controlled to grade. A lorazepam-challenge randomised trial remains the field's missing study.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bot L et al. Acta Psychiatrica Scandinavica. 2026 (PMID: 42009596); Pelzer AC et al. Neuropsychiatric Disease and Treatment. 2018 (PMID: 29398916).

shelves.title: ECT in acute mania: randomised pooling favours adding ECT to medication — but the pooled SMD of −3.50 is too large to believe, and memory impairment rose
shelves.question: In acute mania, does electroconvulsive therapy improve response versus pharmacotherapy in patients who have not responded to drugs?
shelves.mesh: Double-Blind Method · Electroconvulsive Therapy · Humans · Mania · Memory Disorders · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a meta-analysis of randomised trials whose headline effect is too large to take at face value. Zhang 2021 pooled 12 randomised trials (863 patients) of ECT combined with medication versus medication alone in acute mania: the combination outperformed medication alone on manic-symptom reduction (standardised mean difference −3.50, 95% CI −4.57 to −2.44; p<0.00001), with the difference appearing after 3–5 treatments or one week. An SMD of −3.50 would be among the largest effects in psychiatry and arrives with high heterogeneity across mostly small, unblindable trials — the direction is consistent, the magnitude is not credible. The combination also increased memory impairment (the record prints the statistic as SMD 8.33, 95% CI 2.73 to 25.45; p=0.0002 — an odds-ratio-shaped figure), with no other significant differences in side effects or dropout. The 80-year clinical review (Elias 2021) places ECT where guidelines now do: no longer first-line for mania, reserved largely for pharmacological resistance, with randomised trials 'in limited numbers'. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): adding ECT to medication probably speeds and deepens manic-symptom reduction in acute mania, at a real cost in memory effects, on trial evidence too heterogeneous to quantify honestly.

cards.headline: Zhang 2021 meta-analysis: ECT plus medication beat medication alone on manic symptoms (SMD −3.50, −4.57 to −2.44) across 12 RCTs and 863 patients — with significantly more memory impairment
cards.summary: Zhang 2021 meta-analysis: ECT plus medication beat medication alone on manic symptoms (SMD −3.50, −4.57 to −2.44) across 12 RCTs and 863 patients — with significantly more memory impairment
cards.people: 12 randomised controlled trials including 863 patients with acute mania, comparing electroconvulsive therapy combined with medication against medication alone, identified from Chinese and English databases from inception to February 2020.
cards.result: ECT combined with medication outperformed medication alone in reducing manic symptoms from baseline to endpoint (standardised mean difference −3.50, 95% CI −4.57 to −2.44; p<0.00001), with the significant difference occurring after 3–5 treatments or after 1 week of treatment. The ECT-combination group had significantly increased memory impairment compared with medication alone (printed in the record as SMD 8.33, 95% CI 2.73 to 25.45; p=0.0002 — a statistic whose shape is that of an odds ratio, not a standardised mean difference). No other statistically significant differences in side effects or dropout rates were found. The authors call for larger randomised double-blind studies with standardised regimens, citing the high heterogeneity of the included trials.
cards.watchOut: An SMD of −3.50 is not a plausible drug-effect size — it signals small, unblinded (ECT cannot be blinded), heterogeneous trials, many from a single country's literature, with probable publication bias; the honest reading is 'direction positive, size unknown'. The memory-impairment statistic is also mislabelled in the record itself, which is why this card quotes it with its shape flagged rather than repeating it as an SMD.
