cards.headline: Elias 2021 (80-year review): ECT in mania is now a treatment for pharmacological resistance — randomised trials exist 'in limited numbers', and technique (frequency, electrode placement, pulse width) shapes the balance
cards.summary: Elias 2021 (80-year review): ECT in mania is now a treatment for pharmacological resistance — randomised trials exist 'in limited numbers', and technique (frequency, electrode placement, pulse width) shapes the balance
cards.type: Narrative review of clinical and trial evidence (Elias 2021)
cards.people: Comprehensive narrative review of 80 years of clinical experience and research with ECT in mania, including related syndromes (delirious mania, mixed affective states), covering efficacy, safety, combination with pharmacological agents including lithium, maintenance use, ultrabrief ECT, and technical parameters.
cards.result: The review records that resistance to pharmacological agents is commonly encountered in acute mania; that ECT, once a widely used standalone intervention, is no longer considered first-line in contemporary guidelines; and that stigma, logistics and ethical factors lead to its underutilisation. Randomised controlled trials exist albeit in limited numbers, and the past three decades' work — ultrabrief ECT, combination with pharmacotherapy including lithium, and maintenance strategies — has refined when and how to use it. Technical parameters, particularly treatment frequency, electrode placement and pulse width, are discussed against recent evidence. The record's abstract reports no pooled effect sizes, so none are carded.
cards.watchOut: A review card contributes placement, not proof: it tells the reader where ECT sits in the modern mania algorithm (after drugs, especially on resistance) and that its trial base is thin — it cannot rescue the meta-analysis's implausible effect size, and this shelf does not ask it to.

cards.headline: Synthesis: direction positive across randomised pooling and 80 years of practice; magnitude and memory cost both unquantified by trustworthy numbers
cards.summary: Synthesis: direction positive across randomised pooling and 80 years of practice; magnitude and memory cost both unquantified by trustworthy numbers
cards.people: One meta-analysis of 12 randomised trials (863 patients) of ECT plus medication versus medication alone in acute mania, and one comprehensive 80-year clinical review.
cards.result: Manic-symptom reduction: SMD −3.50 (95% CI −4.57 to −2.44; p<0.00001) favouring the combination, significant after 3–5 treatments — direction credible, magnitude not, given heterogeneity the authors themselves flag. Memory impairment: significantly increased with ECT (statistic printed as 8.33, 95% CI 2.73 to 25.45). Other side effects and dropout: no significant differences. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit). Tier C is set: the benefit claim rests on small heterogeneous unblindable trials with an implausible pooled effect.
cards.watchOut: The candidate question asks about patients who have not responded to drugs; the randomised trials mostly test ECT added early to medication, not ECT as salvage after documented non-response — the resistance setting is supported by the clinical review and practice, not by the trials. That mismatch is stated here rather than smoothed over.

shelves.title: Antipsychotic augmentation in SRI-resistant OCD: aripiprazole −5.4 Y-BOCS points and risperidone −3.3 in network pooling — the two agents that carry the effect
shelves.question: In treatment-resistant obsessive–compulsive disorder, does antipsychotic augmentation of a serotonin reuptake inhibitor improve response versus continuing the SRI alone — and which agents carry the effect?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Ondansetron/therapeutic use · Drug Therapy, Combination · Lamotrigine/therapeutic use · Bayes Theorem · Granisetron/therapeutic use · Memantine/therapeutic use · Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for antipsychotic augmentation, aripiprazole carries the clearest effect and risperidone a smaller one. In the Maiti 2023 Bayesian network meta-analysis (59 trials of SRI augmentation in OCD), the antipsychotics significantly reduced Yale–Brown Obsessive–Compulsive Scale scores versus control: aripiprazole by a mean difference of −5.4 points (95% credible interval −9.1 to −1.6) and risperidone by −3.3 points (−6.4 to −0.20); several non-antipsychotic agents also separated (memantine −6.2, lamotrigine −6.0, ondansetron −5.7, pregabalin −8.1, topiramate −5.3, granisetron −5.6), with augmentation working better in SRI-refractory than non-refractory patients. The Suhas 2023 network meta-analysis, restricted to SRI-resistant OCD (55 RCTs, 2,011 participants), likewise found aripiprazole effective (standardised mean difference −1.36, 95% CI −2.56 to −0.17) and ranked it among the first-line options alongside ondansetron, deep TMS and therapist-administered CBT. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): adding aripiprazole (best supported) or risperidone to an SRI reduces Y-BOCS scores in resistant OCD — network estimates built from many small trials, with wide intervals.

cards.summary: Maiti 2023 network meta-analysis: aripiprazole −5.4 Y-BOCS points (CrI −9.1 to −1.6) and risperidone −3.3 (−6.4 to −0.20) among the agents significantly beating control
cards.people: 59 clinical trials of pharmacological augmentation of serotonin reuptake inhibitors in obsessive-compulsive disorder, pooled in a random-effects Bayesian network meta-analysis of change in Yale–Brown Obsessive–Compulsive Scale (YBOCS) score from baseline to study end, with SUCRA ranking, node-split consistency checks, and meta-regression for SRI-refractoriness and augmentation duration.
cards.result: Agents significantly reducing YBOCS versus control included pregabalin (mean difference −8.1; 95% CrI −16 to −0.43), memantine (−6.2; −9.9 to −2.3), lamotrigine (−6.0; −12 to −0.47), ondansetron (−5.7; −11 to −0.67), granisetron (−5.6; −11 to −0.44), aripiprazole (−5.4; −9.1 to −1.6), topiramate (−5.3; −9.6 to −0.97) and risperidone (−3.3; −6.4 to −0.20). Node-split analysis showed direct and indirect estimates were comparable. Meta-regression found augmentation effects significantly associated with SRI-refractory status (better in refractory patients) but not with augmentation duration. The authors ranked memantine most effective with moderate certainty of evidence, followed by lamotrigine, ondansetron and granisetron.
cards.watchOut: Network estimates lean heavily on indirect comparisons between small single-centre trials; several credible intervals are very wide (pregabalin's spans −16 to −0.43), and the two antipsychotics' intervals include small effects. Rankings (SUCRA) in such networks are unstable — the shelf credits the agents whose intervals exclude zero in both network analyses, not the rank order.

cards.headline: Suhas 2023 network meta-analysis (SRI-resistant OCD only): aripiprazole SMD −1.36 (−2.56 to −0.17), ranked with ondansetron, deep TMS and therapist CBT as first-line options
cards.summary: Suhas 2023 network meta-analysis (SRI-resistant OCD only): aripiprazole SMD −1.36 (−2.56 to −0.17), ranked with ondansetron, deep TMS and therapist CBT as first-line options
cards.people: 55 randomised controlled trials examining 19 treatments or placebo in 2,011 participants with SRI-resistant obsessive-compulsive disorder, including pharmacological, psychological, neuromodulation and neurosurgical interventions, pooled in a frequentist network meta-analysis with change in Y-BOCS score as the primary outcome and design-by-treatment inconsistency modelling.
cards.result: The four best-ranked treatments by SUCRA were ondansetron (standardised mean difference −2.01, 95% CI −3.19 to −0.83; SUCRA 85.4%), deep transcranial magnetic stimulation (−1.95, −3.25 to −0.65; 83.2%), therapist-administered CBT (−1.46, −2.93 to 0.01; 80.3% — narrowly missing statistical significance) and aripiprazole (−1.36, −2.56 to −0.17; 67.9%). In sensitivity analyses deep TMS ranked best. The authors caution that small subject numbers in individual studies, high confidence-interval limits and wide prediction intervals warrant cautious interpretation, and conclude deep TMS, ondansetron, therapist CBT and aripiprazole may be considered first-line interventions for SRI-resistant OCD in adults.
cards.watchOut: Effect sizes of −1.36 to −2.01 standard deviations exceed what the underlying small trials can credibly deliver and reflect the same small-study inflation seen across this literature; the prediction intervals (which the authors flag) are wider than the confidence intervals quoted. Risperidone does not appear among this analysis's top ranks — its support comes from the Maiti network alone.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two 2023 networks agree on aripiprazole; risperidone's support is one network deep — augmentation works, rankings do not deserve trust
cards.summary: Synthesis: two 2023 networks agree on aripiprazole; risperidone's support is one network deep — augmentation works, rankings do not deserve trust
cards.people: Two network meta-analyses from 2023: Maiti (59 augmentation trials, all-comer SRI-treated OCD) and Suhas (55 RCTs, 2,011 participants, SRI-resistant OCD only).
cards.result: Aripiprazole: Y-BOCS mean difference −5.4 (95% CrI −9.1 to −1.6) and SMD −1.36 (95% CI −2.56 to −0.17) — significant in both. Risperidone: −3.3 (95% CrI −6.4 to −0.20) in Maiti; not top-ranked in Suhas. Non-antipsychotic augmenters (memantine, ondansetron) rank at or above the antipsychotics in both networks. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for antipsychotic augmentation, aripiprazole first. Tier C is not set: two concordant network meta-analyses of randomised trials carry the shelf.
cards.watchOut: Neither network can price the harms that decide real antipsychotic use in OCD — weight, metabolic effects, akathisia — because the underlying short trials barely report them; the stamp is an efficacy stamp only. Exposure-and-response-prevention CBT remains the non-drug augmenter on live shelf #701 and is not displaced by anything here.

shelves.title: Memantine augmentation in OCD: remission 89% versus 32% in a 42-patient trial and SMD −1.17 in pooling — numbers that outrun their evidence base
shelves.question: In obsessive–compulsive disorder with inadequate SRI response, does adjunctive memantine improve obsessive–compulsive symptoms versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Analysis of Variance · Antidepressive Agents, Second-Generation/therapeutic use · Antiparkinson Agents/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Drug Synergism · Female · Fluvoxamine/therapeutic use · Humans · Male · Memantine/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder/drug therapy · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Time Factors · Young Adult
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — striking percentages from very small trials. The one double-blind trial carded in full (Ghaleiha 2013) randomised 42 patients with moderate-to-severe OCD to memantine (20 mg/day) or placebo added to fluvoxamine for 8 weeks: by week 8, all patients in the memantine group versus 32% on placebo met partial-or-complete response criteria, and 89% versus 32% achieved remission. The 2025 meta-analysis of seven randomised trials (315 participants) found memantine augmentation superior to placebo on Y-BOCS (standardised mean difference −1.17, 95% CI −2.14 to −0.20; p=0.02), with significant heterogeneity, benefit concentrated at 20 mg/day and at eight weeks (SMD −1.06, 95% CI −1.77 to −0.36), and a significantly increased risk of mild rash (relative risk 7.00, 95% CI 1.31 to 37.47). The 2023 network meta-analysis carded on shelf #3668 also ranked memantine its most effective SRI augmenter (mean difference −6.2 Y-BOCS points) — mentioned here, not re-carded. Effect sizes above one standard deviation from trials of a few dozen patients are the classic small-study pattern. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): memantine 20 mg/day added to an SRI may substantially reduce OCD symptoms over eight weeks, on evidence whose size is exactly what makes it suspect.

cards.headline: Ghaleiha 2013: response in 100% on memantine versus 32% on placebo, remission 89% versus 32% at 8 weeks — in 42 randomised patients
cards.summary: Ghaleiha 2013: response in 100% on memantine versus 32% on placebo, remission 89% versus 32% at 8 weeks — in 42 randomised patients
cards.people: 42 patients with moderate-to-severe obsessive-compulsive disorder (DSM-IV-TR; Yale–Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale score at least 21), randomised double-blind to memantine (10 mg/day for the first week, then 20 mg/day) or placebo, each added to fluvoxamine, for 8 weeks with Y-BOCS assessment every 2 weeks; 38 patients completed the study.
cards.result: Repeated-measures analysis showed a significant time-by-treatment interaction for the Y-BOCS total scale (P=0.006) and the obsession subscale (P=0.002), with a near-significant effect for the compulsion subscale (P=0.065). By week 8, all patients in the memantine group and six (32%) in the placebo group met criteria for partial and complete response (Fisher's exact test P<0.001). At trial end, 17 (89%) memantine patients versus six (32%) on placebo achieved remission (P<0.001). The frequency of side effects was not significantly different between the groups.
cards.watchOut: A 100%-versus-32% response split in 38 completers is the kind of result small single-centre trials produce and large multicentre trials almost never reproduce; four randomised patients did not complete, and the analysis is of completers' trajectories. One fluvoxamine backbone, one centre, eight weeks — the trial generates the hypothesis the meta-analysis then amplifies.
cards.source: Ghaleiha A et al. Memantine add-on in moderate to severe obsessive-compulsive disorder: randomized double-blind placebo-controlled study. Journal of Psychiatric Research. 2013. cards.headline: Zhang 2025 meta-analysis: Y-BOCS SMD −1.17 (−2.14 to −0.20) across seven trials and 315 participants, with significant heterogeneity — and mild rash RR 7.00
cards.summary: Zhang 2025 meta-analysis: Y-BOCS SMD −1.17 (−2.14 to −0.20) across seven trials and 315 participants, with significant heterogeneity — and mild rash RR 7.00
cards.people: Seven randomised controlled trials involving 315 participants with refractory obsessive-compulsive disorder, comparing memantine augmentation with placebo, identified from inception to January 2024, pooled with random-effects models and dose/duration subgroup analyses.
cards.result: Memantine augmentation was significantly superior to placebo (SMD −1.17, 95% CI −2.14 to −0.20; p=0.02), with significant heterogeneity between studies. The compulsion subscale improved significantly (SMD −0.99, 95% CI −1.45 to −0.52; p<0.001). At eight weeks and at a dose of 20 mg/day, the total Y-BOCS improvement was SMD −1.06 (95% CI −1.77 to −0.36; p=0.003). Memantine significantly increased the risk of mild rash (relative risk 7.00, 95% CI 1.31 to 37.47; p=0.02). The authors conclude memantine is safe and effective for OCD augmentation at 20 mg/day for at least eight weeks.
cards.watchOut: Seven trials averaging 45 patients each, significant heterogeneity, and a pooled SMD beyond −1 — pooling does not launder small-study effects when every contributing study is small. The rash relative risk of 7.00 rests on a confidence interval from 1.31 to 37.47, i.e., on very few events; both the benefit and the harm estimates are fragile in the same way.

cards.headline: Synthesis: every synthesis points the same way and every one is built from trials too small to trust the size
cards.summary: Synthesis: every synthesis points the same way and every one is built from trials too small to trust the size
cards.people: One double-blind trial carded in full (Ghaleiha 2013, 42 randomised) within a seven-trial meta-analysis (Zhang 2025, 315 participants); the 2023 network meta-analysis on shelf #3668 independently ranked memantine first among SRI augmenters (mean difference −6.2 Y-BOCS points) and is mentioned, not re-carded.
cards.result: Response/remission in the index trial: 100%/89% on memantine versus 32%/32% on placebo at 8 weeks. Pooled Y-BOCS: SMD −1.17 (95% CI −2.14 to −0.20; p=0.02), significant heterogeneity; 20 mg/day and 8-week subgroups SMD −1.06 (95% CI −1.77 to −0.36). Harm: mild rash relative risk 7.00 (95% CI 1.31 to 37.47). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit). Tier C is set: a benefit claim resting on small single-centre trials with implausibly large effects.
cards.watchOut: If memantine truly produced remission in 89% of SRI-resistant patients it would have transformed OCD care in the decade since Ghaleiha; it has not, which is itself evidence about the likely true effect size. The shelf waits for one adequately powered multicentre trial to move in either direction.

shelves.title: Guanfacine for PTSD in veterans: no effect on symptoms, sleep or mood in either of the two placebo-controlled trials
shelves.question: In veterans with PTSD, does guanfacine reduce PTSD symptoms versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic alpha-Agonists/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Chronic Disease · Comorbidity · Double-Blind Method · Guanfacine/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Humans · Mood Disorders/drug therapy/epidemiology/psychology · Placebos · Sleep/drug effects · Stress Disorders, Post-Traumatic/drug therapy/epidemiology/psychology · Treatment Outcome · Veterans/psychology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — two placebo-controlled trials in veterans, both null on every outcome. Neylan 2006 randomised 63 veterans with chronic PTSD to guanfacine (29) or placebo (34) for 8 weeks: guanfacine had no effect on PTSD symptoms, subjective sleep quality, or general mood disturbances, and was associated with a number of side effects; the authors concluded the results do not support alpha-2 agonists in veterans with chronic PTSD. Davis 2008 randomised veterans with chronic PTSD to 8 weeks of double-blind guanfacine or placebo (with stable antidepressants allowed) and found no significant differences on clinician-administered or self-report measures — CAPS, MADRS, CGI-S, CGI-I and the Davidson Trauma Scale — though the drug was well tolerated in that small, predominantly male combat-veteran sample. The noradrenergic rationale was reasonable; the trials simply did not confirm it. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): guanfacine does not reduce PTSD symptoms in veterans in the two randomised trials that tested it.

cards.headline: Neylan 2006: guanfacine (n=29) versus placebo (n=34) for 8 weeks — no effect on PTSD symptoms, sleep quality, or mood, with side effects attached
cards.summary: Neylan 2006: guanfacine (n=29) versus placebo (n=34) for 8 weeks — no effect on PTSD symptoms, sleep quality, or mood, with side effects attached
cards.people: 63 veterans with chronic PTSD, medication-free or on stable pharmacotherapy, randomly assigned double-blind to guanfacine (29) or placebo (34) for 8 weeks.
cards.result: Guanfacine had no effect on PTSD symptoms, subjective sleep quality, or general mood disturbances. Guanfacine was associated with a number of side effects. The authors concluded that these results do not support the use of alpha-2 agonists in veterans with chronic PTSD. The record's abstract reports the null qualitatively, without effect sizes, so none are carded.
cards.watchOut: Sixty-three patients cannot exclude a small effect — but the burden of proof sits on the drug, and this trial found not even a trend worth printing in its abstract. Chronic, combat-related, predominantly long-standing PTSD in veterans is also the population least likely to respond to any single agent, so the null is strongest exactly where it was tested.

cards.headline: Davis 2008: no significant drug–placebo difference on CAPS, MADRS, CGI or self-report scales in a second veteran trial — well tolerated, ineffective
cards.summary: Davis 2008: no significant drug–placebo difference on CAPS, MADRS, CGI or self-report scales in a second veteran trial — well tolerated, ineffective
cards.people: Veterans with chronic PTSD (a small sample, predominantly male combat veterans; the record's abstract does not print the randomised number, so none is stated), randomised 1:1 to guanfacine or placebo for 8 weeks of double-blind treatment followed by a 2-month open-label extension, maintained on stable doses of allowed antidepressants.
cards.result: There were no significant differences between guanfacine and placebo on any clinician-administered or patient self-report outcome measure: the Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale (CAPS), Montgomery–Åsberg Depression Rating Scale, Clinical Global Impression–Severity and –Improvement, and the Davidson Trauma Scale. cards.watchOut: A pilot-sized sample with a null on five separate instruments is consistent evidence of no large effect, not proof of no effect at all. The open-label extension that followed cannot rescue efficacy — unblinded follow-on phases in null trials measure hope and retention, not drug action.

shelves.title: Topiramate for PTSD: overall effect not significant (p=.082) in five small trials — only hyperarousal symptoms improved significantly
shelves.question: In PTSD, does topiramate — as monotherapy or adjunctive treatment — reduce symptom severity versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Anticonvulsants/therapeutic use · Arousal · Avoidance Learning · Chemotherapy, Adjuvant · Drug Therapy, Combination · Humans · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Stress Disorders, Post-Traumatic/drug therapy/psychology · Topiramate/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the overall effect is a non-significant trend, and only the hyperarousal cluster reached significance. Varma 2018 meta-analysed the randomised placebo-controlled trials of topiramate as monotherapy or adjunctive treatment in adults with PTSD (six trials identified; one excluded from the statistical analysis for a high dropout rate of 16 of 40 participants, leaving five). For overall symptomatology, topiramate showed a medium but not significant effect (standardised mean difference 0.55; p=.082). By symptom cluster, hyperarousal fell by a small, significant amount (SMD 0.35, 95% CI 0.029 to 0.689; p=.033), while re-experiencing (SMD 0.29, 95% CI −0.019 to 0.597; p=.067) and avoidance (SMD 0.20, 95% CI −0.105 to 0.509; p=.198) did not reach significance. Results did not differ significantly between veteran and non-veteran subjects, or between monotherapy and adjunctive use. The authors note prescribers' reluctance given topiramate's commonly reported cognitive impairment, sedation, fatigue and headache. PROPOSED SPLIT: a possible small benefit confined to hyperarousal symptoms, with overall PTSD severity not significantly improved — on five small trials.

cards.headline: Varma 2018 meta-analysis: overall SMD 0.55 but p=.082 (not significant); hyperarousal SMD 0.35 (p=.033) the only significant cluster
cards.summary: Varma 2018 meta-analysis: overall SMD 0.55 but p=.082 (not significant); hyperarousal SMD 0.35 (p=.033) the only significant cluster
cards.people: Randomised controlled trials of topiramate as monotherapy or adjunctive therapy versus placebo in adults with PTSD, identified from PubMed, PsycInfo and Cochrane Central: six studies met criteria, one was excluded from the statistical meta-analysis because of a high dropout rate (16 of 40 participants), leaving five in the pooled analysis; one study also lacked the subscale data for the symptom-cluster analysis.
cards.result: For overall symptomatology, topiramate showed a medium but not significant effect (standardised mean difference 0.55; p=.082). Topiramate significantly reduced hyperarousal symptoms (SMD 0.35, 95% CI 0.029 to 0.689; p=.033), but did not significantly reduce re-experiencing symptoms (SMD 0.29, 95% CI −0.019 to 0.597; p=.067) or avoidance symptoms (SMD 0.20, 95% CI −0.105 to 0.509; p=.198). Results did not differ significantly between veteran and non-veteran subjects, or between topiramate as monotherapy and as adjunctive therapy.
cards.watchOut: Five small trials, one significant subscale out of three (a multiplicity invitation), and a headline overall effect whose p-value (.082) the abstract itself calls not significant. The excluded sixth trial lost 40% of its participants — attrition of that size in a topiramate trial usually tracks tolerability, which is the drug's known weakness (cognitive impairment, sedation, fatigue, headache).
cards.source: Varma A et al. Topiramate as Monotherapy or Adjunctive Treatment for Posttraumatic Stress Disorder: A Meta-Analysis. Journal of Traumatic Stress. 2018. PMID: 29388709. cards.headline: Synthesis: one significant symptom cluster out of three, from five small trials — a split, not a treatment effect
cards.summary: Synthesis: one significant symptom cluster out of three, from five small trials — a split, not a treatment effect
cards.people: The complete randomised literature as of 2018 as pooled by Varma: five analysable trials of topiramate (monotherapy or adjunctive) versus placebo in adult PTSD, spanning veteran and non-veteran populations.
cards.result: Overall PTSD severity: SMD 0.55, p=.082 — not significant. Hyperarousal: SMD 0.35 (95% CI 0.029 to 0.689; p=.033). Re-experiencing: SMD 0.29 (p=.067) — not significant. Avoidance: SMD 0.20 (p=.198) — not significant. No significant moderation by veteran status or by monotherapy versus adjunctive use. PROPOSED SPLIT. Tier C is set: the positive half of the split rests on a single significant subscale within a small-trial meta-analysis whose primary pooling missed significance.
cards.watchOut: A shelf built on one meta-analysis of five small trials is a snapshot, not a settlement: a single adequately powered trial would outweigh this entire evidence base. The hyperarousal signal is biologically plausible for an anticonvulsant, but plausibility plus p=.033 on a subscale is precisely the combination this library stamps cautiously.
cards.source: Synthesis of Varma A et al. Journal of Traumatic Stress. 2018 (PMID: 29388709).

shelves.title: Omega-3 in ultra-high-risk psychosis (NEURAPRO): transition 11.5% versus 11.2% at 12 months — the multicentre trial that failed to replicate the single-centre promise
shelves.question: In young people at ultra-high risk of psychosis, do omega-3 fatty acids prevent transition to psychosis versus placebo when both groups receive cognitive–behavioural case management?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Case Management · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy · Cohort Studies · Combined Modality Therapy · Dietary Supplements/adverse effects · Disease Progression · Double-Blind Method · Early Medical Intervention · Fatty Acids, Omega-3/administration & dosage · Female · Humans · Male · Psychotic Disorders/drug therapy · Risk · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the large multicentre replication of a famous single-centre result found nothing. NEURAPRO randomised 304 young people at ultrahigh risk for psychotic disorders (mean age 19.1 years) to omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids 1.4 g/day (153) or paraffin-oil placebo (151), both with up to 20 sessions of cognitive-behavioural case management over 6 months. Transition to psychosis at 6 months was 6.7% on omega-3 versus 5.1% on placebo, and at 12 months 11.5% versus 11.2% (hazard ratio 1.1, 95% CI 0.55 to 2.23; P=.76) — the point estimate favours placebo. Both groups improved substantially in symptoms and functioning on the psychosocial intervention, which the authors suggest may have created a ceiling effect; they also note the lower-than-expected transition rate may have limited the test. Their stated conclusion is nonetheless plain: omega-3 fatty acids are not effective under conditions where good-quality evidence-based psychosocial treatment is available, and the trial clearly failed to replicate the original single-centre finding. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): added to good psychosocial care, omega-3 does not prevent transition to psychosis in ultrahigh-risk young people.

cards.headline: NEURAPRO (McGorry 2017): transition to psychosis 6.7% on omega-3 versus 5.1% on placebo at 6 months; 11.5% versus 11.2% at 12 months (HR 1.1, P=.76)
cards.summary: NEURAPRO (McGorry 2017): transition to psychosis 6.7% on omega-3 versus 5.1% on placebo at 6 months; 11.5% versus 11.2% at 12 months (HR 1.1, P=.76)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled multicentre trial (McGorry 2017, NEURAPRO)
cards.people: 304 young people at ultrahigh risk for psychotic disorders (mean age 19.1 years, SD 4.6; 45.7% male) at 10 specialised early-psychosis services in Australia, Asia and Europe, randomised double-blind to omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids 1.4 g/day (153) or paraffin-oil placebo (151) for 6 months, both groups receiving 20 or fewer sessions of cognitive-behavioural case management; primary outcome was transition to psychosis at 6 months, analysed intention-to-treat, with follow-up to 12 months.
cards.result: Kaplan–Meier-estimated transition rates at 6 months were 6.7% (95% CI 2.3% to 10.8%) in the omega-3 group and 5.1% (95% CI 1.3% to 8.7%) in the control group; at 12 months, 11.5% (95% CI 5.8% to 16.9%) versus 11.2% (95% CI 5.5% to 16.7%). There was no significant difference between transition rates (hazard ratio 1.1, 95% CI 0.55 to 2.23; P=.76). Both groups showed substantial symptomatic and functional improvement. The authors concluded the trial clearly failed to replicate the original single-centre trial and that omega-3 PUFAs lack efficacy under these conditions.
cards.watchOut: The observed transition rate (about 11% at a year) was lower than the rates the original single-centre trial era produced, shrinking power for a prevention effect — the authors raise this themselves. But a hazard ratio of 1.1 with a point estimate against the supplement is not a near-miss: if omega-3 has any effect on top of good psychosocial care, this trial bounds it as small.
cards.source: McGorry PD et al. Effect of ω-3 Polyunsaturated Fatty Acids in Young People at Ultrahigh Risk for Psychotic Disorders: The NEURAPRO Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Psychiatry. 2017. PMID: 27893018. Registry ID: ACTRN12608000475347 (from the record's abstract). cards.headline: Synthesis: one large multicentre null outweighs the earlier single-centre promise — on top of good psychosocial care, omega-3 adds nothing measurable
cards.summary: Synthesis: one large multicentre null outweighs the earlier single-centre promise — on top of good psychosocial care, omega-3 adds nothing measurable
cards.people: One randomised double-blind multicentre trial (NEURAPRO, 304 ultrahigh-risk young people, 10 services, three continents) is the cardable evidence; the earlier positive single-centre trial it failed to replicate is discussed within the NEURAPRO record itself and is not separately carded.
cards.result: Transition to psychosis: 6.7% versus 5.1% at 6 months and 11.5% versus 11.2% at 12 months, omega-3 versus placebo (HR 1.1, 95% CI 0.55 to 2.23; P=.76). Symptoms and functioning: substantial improvement in both groups under cognitive-behavioural case management, with no significant between-group advantage reported for the supplement. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference). Tier C is set: the shelf rests on a single trial.
cards.watchOut: The null is conditional on the co-intervention: both arms received high-quality psychosocial care, and the shelf does not claim omega-3 is inert where no such care exists — it claims the supplement added nothing where care was good, which is the setting that matters for services deciding whether to fund it. The supplement shelves for omega-3 in other conditions are separate questions.
cards.source: Synthesis of McGorry PD et al. JAMA Psychiatry. 2017 (PMID: 27893018).

shelves.title: Cannabidiol in schizophrenia: positive symptoms down 1.4 PANSS points at 1,000 mg/day in one small trial — cognition null in both trials, 600 mg null throughout
shelves.question: In schizophrenia, does adjunctive cannabidiol improve positive symptoms and cognition versus placebo added to antipsychotic treatment?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antipsychotic Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Cannabidiol/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Male · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Schizophrenia/drug therapy
shelves.balance: SPLIT — a small positive-symptom gain at the higher dose in one exploratory trial; cognition null in both trials, and the lower-dose trial null on symptoms too. McGuire 2018 randomised 88 patients with schizophrenia to cannabidiol 1,000 mg/day (43) or placebo (45) added to existing antipsychotics for 6 weeks: positive symptoms were lower on CBD (PANSS treatment difference −1.4, 95% CI −2.5 to −0.2), clinicians rated more CBD patients improved (CGI-I difference −0.5, 95% CI −0.8 to −0.1), but cognitive performance (BACS difference 1.31, 95% CI −0.10 to 2.72) and functioning (GAF difference 3.0, 95% CI −0.4 to 6.4) fell short of significance. Boggs 2018 randomised 36 stable outpatients to CBD 600 mg/day or placebo for 6 weeks with cognition as the target: there was no drug effect on the MATRICS battery — only the placebo group improved over time — and no significant drug-by-time effect on PANSS total scores (p=0.18); sedation was more prevalent on CBD, with other side effects similar. PROPOSED SPLIT: adjunctive CBD may trim positive symptoms slightly at 1,000 mg/day; at 600 mg/day it did nothing measurable, and no trial shows a cognitive benefit.

cards.headline: McGuire 2018: CBD 1,000 mg/day lowered positive symptoms by 1.4 PANSS points (−2.5 to −0.2) at 6 weeks — cognition and functioning improvements fell short of significance
cards.summary: McGuire 2018: CBD 1,000 mg/day lowered positive symptoms by 1.4 PANSS points (−2.5 to −0.2) at 6 weeks — cognition and functioning improvements fell short of significance
cards.people: 88 patients with schizophrenia in an exploratory double-blind parallel-group multicentre trial, randomised 1:1 to cannabidiol 1,000 mg/day (43) or placebo (45) alongside existing antipsychotic medication for 6 weeks; assessed with the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS), the Brief Assessment of Cognition in Schizophrenia (BACS), the Global Assessment of Functioning (GAF), and Clinical Global Impressions improvement and severity scales.
cards.result: After 6 weeks, the CBD group had lower positive psychotic symptoms than placebo (PANSS treatment difference −1.4, 95% CI −2.5 to −0.2) and was more likely to be rated improved by the treating clinician (CGI-I difference −0.5, 95% CI −0.8 to −0.1) and not severely unwell (CGI-S difference −0.3, 95% CI −0.5 to 0.0). Improvements in cognitive performance (BACS difference 1.31, 95% CI −0.10 to 2.72) and overall functioning (GAF difference 3.0, 95% CI −0.4 to 6.4) fell short of statistical significance. CBD was well tolerated, with adverse-event rates similar to placebo.
cards.watchOut: Self-described exploratory, 88 patients, and the significant symptom effect is 1.4 points on the PANSS positive subscale — a small average shift of uncertain clinical meaning, with the confidence interval reaching −0.2. The trial supports a larger confirmatory study (which its authors imply), not a practice claim; the cognition result the field hoped for was not significant even here.
cards.source: McGuire P et al. Cannabidiol (CBD) as an Adjunctive Therapy in Schizophrenia: A Multicenter Randomized Controlled Trial. The American Journal of Psychiatry. 2018. PMID: 29241357. randomised double-blind multicentre trial (mcguire 2018) 88 patients with schizophrenia in an exploratory double-blind parallel-group multicentre trial, randomised 1:1 to cannabidiol 1,000 mg/day (43) or placebo (45) alongside existing antipsychotic medication for 6 weeks; assessed with the positive and negative syndrome scale (panss), the brief assessment of cognition in schizophrenia (bacs), the global assessment of functioning (gaf), and clinical global impressions improvement and severity scales. after 6 weeks, the cbd group had lower positive psychotic symptoms than placebo (panss treatment difference −1.4, 95% ci −2.5 to −0.2) and was more likely to be rated improved by the treating clinician (cgi-i difference −0.5, 95% ci −0.8 to −0.1) and not severely unwell (cgi-s difference −0.3, 95% ci −0.5 to 0.0). improvements in cognitive performance (bacs difference 1.31, 95% ci −0.10 to 2.72) and overall functioning (gaf difference 3.0, 95% ci −0.4 to 6.4) fell short of statistical significance. cbd was well tolerated, with adverse-event rates similar to placebo. self-described exploratory, 88 patients, and the significant symptom effect is 1.4 points on the panss positive subscale — a small average shift of uncertain clinical meaning, with the confidence interval reaching −0.2. the trial supports a larger confirmatory study (which its authors imply), not a practice claim; the cognition result the field hoped for was not significant even here. mcguire p et al. cannabidiol (cbd) as an adjunctive therapy in schizophrenia: a multicenter randomized controlled trial. the american journal of psychiatry. 2018. pmid: 29241357. mesh: adult · antipsychotic agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · cannabidiol/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · double-blind method · drug therapy, combination · female · humans · male · psychiatric status rating scales · schizophrenia/drug therapy

cards.headline: Boggs 2018: CBD 600 mg/day did not improve cognition (only placebo improved on the MATRICS battery) and did not separate on PANSS total (drug × time p=0.18)
cards.summary: Boggs 2018: CBD 600 mg/day did not improve cognition (only placebo improved on the MATRICS battery) and did not separate on PANSS total (drug × time p=0.18)
cards.people: 36 stable antipsychotic-treated outpatients with chronic schizophrenia in a 6-week randomised placebo-controlled parallel-group fixed-dose trial of oral cannabidiol 600 mg/day versus placebo augmentation, with the MATRICS Consensus Cognitive Battery at baseline and week 6 and PANSS assessed biweekly.
cards.result: There was no main effect of time or drug on the MCCB composite score, but a significant drug-by-time effect (p=0.02) driven by the placebo group: post hoc analysis showed only placebo-treated subjects improved over time (p=0.03). PANSS total scores decreased significantly over time in the trial overall (p<0.0001) with no significant drug-by-time interaction (p=0.18). Side effects were similar between groups except sedation, which was more prevalent on CBD; there was no worsening of mood, suicidality, or movement side effects.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-six patients at a lower dose (600 versus 1,000 mg/day) in stable chronic outpatients — the trial cannot exclude a dose effect, and its placebo group improving on repeat cognitive testing (practice effects) while the CBD group did not is a curious pattern that cuts against, not for, a procognitive claim. It is the only trial designed around cognition, and it is null.
cards.source: Boggs DL et al. The effects of cannabidiol (CBD) on cognition and symptoms in outpatients with chronic schizophrenia a randomized placebo controlled trial. Psychopharmacology. 2018. PMID: 29619533. Registry ID: NCT00588731. cards.headline: Synthesis: dose-split evidence — a small symptom signal at 1,000 mg, nothing at 600 mg, and cognition negative in both
cards.summary: Synthesis: dose-split evidence — a small symptom signal at 1,000 mg, nothing at 600 mg, and cognition negative in both
cards.people: Two randomised double-blind trials of adjunctive cannabidiol in schizophrenia: McGuire 2018 (88 patients, 1,000 mg/day, symptoms primary) and Boggs 2018 (36 stable outpatients, 600 mg/day, cognition primary), each 6 weeks added to antipsychotic treatment.
cards.result: Positive symptoms: −1.4 PANSS points (95% CI −2.5 to −0.2) favouring CBD at 1,000 mg/day; no significant PANSS separation at 600 mg/day (interaction p=0.18). Cognition: not significant at 1,000 mg (BACS 1.31, 95% CI −0.10 to 2.72) and null at 600 mg, where only placebo improved on the MATRICS battery. Tolerability: adverse events similar overall; sedation more prevalent on CBD in Boggs. PROPOSED SPLIT. Tier C is set: the benefit half rests on a single small exploratory trial.
cards.watchOut: This shelf concerns pharmaceutical cannabidiol at defined doses added to antipsychotics — not cannabis, not dispensary CBD products of variable content, and not CBD as a substitute for antipsychotic treatment, none of which these trials test. Cannabidiol for childhood epilepsy syndromes is live shelf #991, a different question.
cards.source: Synthesis of McGuire P et al. The American Journal of Psychiatry. 2018 (PMID: 29241357); Boggs DL et al. Psychopharmacology. 2018 (PMID: 29619533).

shelves.title: AVATAR therapy for distressing voices: severity down 3.82 points at 12 weeks and distress improved at 16 weeks in two trials — gone by 28 weeks in the larger one
shelves.question: In people with psychosis who hear distressing voices, does AVATAR therapy — dialogue with a digital avatar of the persecutory voice — reduce voice severity versus supportive counselling?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Affective Disorders, Psychotic/diagnosis/psychology · Computers · Female · Hallucinations/therapy · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pattern Recognition, Physiological · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Psychological Techniques/instrumentation · Recognition, Psychology · Schizophrenia/diagnosis/therapy · Schizophrenic Psychology · Single-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — voice severity and distress improve by the end of therapy in both trials; the distress benefit was gone by 28 weeks in the larger one. In the first AVATAR trial (Craig 2018), 150 people with persistent auditory verbal hallucinations despite treatment were randomised to AVATAR therapy — facilitated dialogue with a digital avatar of the persecutory voice, voiced by the therapist and conceding power over the sessions — or supportive counselling: at 12 weeks the reduction in hallucination severity (PSYRATS-AH) was significantly greater with AVATAR (mean difference −3.82, 95% CI −6.70 to −0.94; p=0.0093), with no adverse events attributable to either therapy. AVATAR2 (Garety 2024) randomised 345 participants to AVATAR-Brief, AVATAR-Extended, or treatment as usual: voice-related distress improved versus usual care at 16 weeks for both forms (Brief: −1.05 points, Cohen's d=0.38, P=0.035; Extended: −1.60 points, d=0.58, P=0.029) but not at 28 weeks (P=0.316 and P=0.175); voice severity likewise improved at 16 weeks only, while voice frequency was reduced in the Extended form at both timepoints. No related serious adverse events occurred. PROPOSED SPLIT: a real, moderate short-term reduction in voice severity and distress — strongest for the Extended protocol — whose distress benefit did not persist to 28 weeks.

cards.headline: Craig 2018: PSYRATS-AH reduction greater with AVATAR than supportive counselling at 12 weeks (difference −3.82, 95% CI −6.70 to −0.94; p=0.0093)
cards.summary: Craig 2018: PSYRATS-AH reduction greater with AVATAR than supportive counselling at 12 weeks (difference −3.82, 95% CI −6.70 to −0.94; p=0.0093)
cards.people: 150 adults aged 18 to 65 years with a schizophrenia-spectrum (ICD-10 F20–29) or psychotic affective (F30–39) diagnosis and enduring auditory verbal hallucinations over the previous 12 months despite continued treatment, at a single London NHS trust; randomised 1:1 to AVATAR therapy (75) or supportive counselling (75), with masked outcome assessment at baseline, 12 and 24 weeks; 124 (83%) provided the primary outcome. AVATAR therapy consists of dialogue with a digital representation of the presumed persecutor, voiced by the therapist, which becomes less hostile and concedes power over the course of therapy.
cards.result: The reduction in auditory verbal hallucinations at 12 weeks (PSYRATS-AH total score) was significantly greater for AVATAR therapy than for supportive counselling (mean difference −3.82, SE 1.47; 95% CI −6.70 to −0.94; p=0.0093), analysed intention-to-treat with linear mixed models; the authors describe the effect size as large. There was no evidence of adverse events attributable to either therapy. The authors call for multicentre studies to establish effectiveness.
cards.watchOut: Single-centre, single-blind (participants know whether they are confronting their avatar or receiving counselling), against a supportive-counselling control that matches attention but not expectancy of a novel technology. The 24-week assessment exists in the design but the record's abstract reports the 12-week result — durability cannot be audited from this record, which is why the second trial's follow-up matters.
cards.source: Craig TK et al. AVATAR therapy for auditory verbal hallucinations in people with psychosis: a single-blind, randomised controlled trial. The Lancet Psychiatry. 2018. PMID: 29175276. Registry ID: ISRCTN65314790 (from the record's abstract). cards.headline: AVATAR2 (Garety 2024): distress improved at 16 weeks for Brief (−1.05, d=0.38) and Extended (−1.60, d=0.58) forms — not significant at 28 weeks for either
cards.summary: AVATAR2 (Garety 2024): distress improved at 16 weeks for Brief (−1.05, d=0.38) and Extended (−1.60, d=0.58) forms — not significant at 28 weeks for either
cards.people: 345 participants with psychosis and distressing voices in a randomised phase 2/3 trial of AVATAR-Brief (AV-BRF) or AVATAR-Extended (AV-EXT), each combined with treatment as usual, versus treatment as usual alone; data were available for 300 participants (86.9%) at 16 weeks and 298 (86.4%) at 28 weeks. The primary outcome was voice-related distress at both timepoints; voice severity and frequency were key secondaries.
cards.result: Voice-related distress improved versus treatment as usual in both forms at 16 weeks (AV-BRF: −1.05 points, 96.5% CI −2.110 to 0, P=0.035, Cohen's d=0.38; AV-EXT: −1.60 points, 96.5% CI −3.133 to −0.058, P=0.029, d=0.58) but not at 28 weeks (AV-BRF: −0.62, P=0.316; AV-EXT: −1.06, P=0.175). Voice severity improved in both forms at 16 weeks but not at 28 weeks, whereas voice frequency was reduced in AV-EXT, but not AV-BRF, at both timepoints. AV-EXT met the authors' threshold for a clinically significant change. There were no related serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: The control here is treatment as usual rather than an attention-matched therapy, so part of the 16-week advantage may be non-specific; and the primary outcome's loss of significance by 28 weeks is the trial's own result, not a critic's gloss — the distress benefit attenuates. Confidence intervals at the 96.5% level reflect the multi-arm design and several brush zero.
cards.source: Garety PA et al. Digital AVATAR therapy for distressing voices in psychosis: the phase 2/3 AVATAR2 trial. Nature Medicine. 2024. PMID: 39468363. Registry ID: ISRCTN55682735 (from the record's abstract). cards.headline: Synthesis: two positive short-term trials, one honest durability problem — the Extended protocol is the form the evidence supports studying further
cards.summary: Synthesis: two positive short-term trials, one honest durability problem — the Extended protocol is the form the evidence supports studying further
cards.people: Two randomised trials of AVATAR therapy in psychosis with persistent distressing voices: Craig 2018 (150 participants, versus supportive counselling, 12-week primary) and AVATAR2 (345 participants, Brief and Extended forms versus treatment as usual, 16- and 28-week outcomes).
cards.result: Voice severity: −3.82 PSYRATS-AH points versus counselling at 12 weeks (95% CI −6.70 to −0.94; p=0.0093); improved at 16 weeks in AVATAR2, not at 28 weeks. Voice distress: −1.05 (Brief, d=0.38) and −1.60 (Extended, d=0.58) points at 16 weeks, both non-significant at 28 weeks. Voice frequency: reduced at both timepoints for the Extended form only. Safety: no attributable or related serious adverse events in either trial. PROPOSED SPLIT. Tier C is not set: two randomised trials carry both halves of the split.
cards.watchOut: AVATAR is a named non-drug programme, named here as the publications name it, per the library's programme-naming exception. Delivery requires trained therapists and the avatar software, so the trials' effects are effects of the whole package in specialist services — not of an app a patient can download, and not evidence about voices that are not distressing or persecutory in form.
cards.source: Synthesis of Craig TK et al. The Lancet Psychiatry. 2018 (PMID: 29175276); Garety PA et al. Nature Medicine. 2024 (PMID: 39468363).

shelves.title: Roluperidone for negative symptoms: phase 2 positive at both doses (d=0.45 and 0.57) — phase 3 primary missed in the full analysis (P=.064), functioning endpoint hit
shelves.question: In schizophrenia with predominant negative symptoms, does roluperidone improve negative symptoms versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Antipsychotic Agents/adverse effects · Humans · Indoles/adverse effects · Schizophrenia/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the phase 2 trial was cleanly positive; the larger phase 3 missed its primary endpoint in the full analysis set and hit it only in the modified set, while its functioning endpoint succeeded in both. In phase 2 (Davidson 2017), 244 stabilised patients with prominent negative symptoms were randomised to roluperidone (then MIN-101) 32 mg/day, 64 mg/day, or placebo for 12 weeks after antipsychotic washout: the PANSS negative factor score improved significantly more on both doses, with effect sizes of d=0.45 and d=0.57, supported by the Brief Negative Symptom Scale and CGI severity, with no significant difference in positive symptoms and no clinically significant changes in weight, metabolic indices, or movement scores. In phase 3 (Davidson 2022), 513 patients with moderate-to-severe negative symptoms received the same doses or placebo for 12 weeks: at 64 mg the Negative Symptom Factor Score marginally missed significance in the intention-to-treat analysis (P≤.064) and reached nominal significance in the modified intention-to-treat set (P≤.044), while the Personal and Social Performance functioning score was significantly better than placebo in both analyses (P≤.021 and P≤.017). PROPOSED SPLIT: roluperidone probably improves everyday functioning at 64 mg/day, with its negative-symptom score effect confirmed in phase 2 but only borderline in the phase 3 primary analysis.

cards.headline: Davidson 2017 (phase 2, MIN-101): PANSS negative factor effect sizes d=0.45 (32 mg) and d=0.57 (64 mg) versus placebo at 12 weeks, both significant
cards.summary: Davidson 2017 (phase 2, MIN-101): PANSS negative factor effect sizes d=0.45 (32 mg) and d=0.57 (64 mg) versus placebo at 12 weeks, both significant
cards.people: 244 patients with schizophrenia, symptomatically stable for at least 3 months, with a score of at least 20 on the PANSS negative subscale, randomised after at least 5 days' withdrawal from all antipsychotic medication to roluperidone (MIN-101) 32 mg/day, 64 mg/day, or placebo for 12 weeks. The primary outcome was the PANSS negative factor score (pentagonal structure model); secondaries included PANSS total, CGI, the Brief Negative Symptom Scale, cognition (BACS) and depression (Calgary) scales.
cards.result: A statistically significant difference in PANSS negative factor score was observed, with lower scores on roluperidone 32 mg/day and 64 mg/day than on placebo (effect sizes d=0.45 and d=0.57 respectively), supported by similar effects on the PANSS negative symptom, total and activation factor scores, CGI severity, and the Brief Negative Symptom Scale. There were no statistically significant differences in PANSS positive scale scores. No clinically significant changes were observed in vital signs, routine laboratory values, weight, metabolic indices, or Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale scores.
cards.watchOut: Patients were withdrawn from all antipsychotics and treated with roluperidone alone — a monotherapy design in stabilised patients that does not match how the drug would be used in ordinary practice, and one where any destabilisation lands in the placebo arm's favour or disfavour unpredictably. Two hundred and forty-four patients across three arms is a modest base for the d=0.57 headline.
cards.source: Davidson M et al. Efficacy and Safety of MIN-101: A 12-Week Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial of a New Drug in Development for the Treatment of Negative Symptoms in Schizophrenia. The American Journal of Psychiatry. 2017. PMID: 28750582. Registry ID: EudraCT 2014-004878-42. cards.summary: Davidson 2022 (phase 3): Negative Symptom Factor Score at 64 mg missed significance in ITT (P≤.064), hit it in modified ITT (P≤.044); functioning (PSP) significant in both (P≤.021)
cards.people: 513 patients with schizophrenia with moderate-to-severe negative symptoms in a multinational placebo-controlled trial, randomised to roluperidone 32 mg/day, 64 mg/day, or placebo for 12 weeks. The primary endpoint was the PANSS-derived Negative Symptom Factor Score (NSFS); the key secondary endpoint was the Personal and Social Performance (PSP) total score.
cards.result: NSFS scores were lower (improved) on roluperidone 64 mg than placebo, marginally missing statistical significance in the intention-to-treat analysis (P≤.064) but reaching nominal significance in the modified intention-to-treat set (P≤.044). Changes in PSP total score were statistically significantly better on roluperidone 64 mg than placebo in both the ITT (P≤.021) and modified ITT (P≤.017) analyses. The authors conclude the results confirm roluperidone's potential for treating negative symptoms and improving everyday functioning. The record's abstract does not print the score differences for either dose, so none are carded.
cards.watchOut: A primary endpoint that needs the modified analysis set to cross p<.05 is a missed primary endpoint by the discipline this library applies — the ITT result governs. The functioning (PSP) result is genuinely positive in both sets, but it was the key secondary, and secondary endpoints inherit the primary's failure for confirmatory purposes. The 32 mg dose does not feature in the record's reported results.
cards.source: Davidson M et al. Efficacy and Safety of Roluperidone for the Treatment of Negative Symptoms of Schizophrenia. Schizophrenia Bulletin. 2022. PMID: 35211743. cards.headline: Synthesis: phase 2 said yes, phase 3 said 'almost, on symptoms; yes, on functioning' — a split, not a confirmation
cards.summary: Synthesis: phase 2 said yes, phase 3 said 'almost, on symptoms; yes, on functioning' — a split, not a confirmation
cards.people: Two randomised double-blind placebo-controlled 12-week trials of roluperidone 32 and 64 mg/day in schizophrenia with predominant negative symptoms: phase 2 (Davidson 2017, 244 stabilised patients, monotherapy after washout) and phase 3 (Davidson 2022, 513 patients, multinational).
cards.result: Negative-symptom scores: significant at both doses in phase 2 (d=0.45 and d=0.57); at 64 mg in phase 3, P≤.064 (ITT) and P≤.044 (modified ITT) — borderline and analysis-set-dependent. Functioning (PSP, phase 3): significant at 64 mg in both analysis sets (P≤.021, P≤.017). Positive symptoms: no significant effect in phase 2. Tolerability in phase 2: no clinically significant weight, metabolic or movement changes. PROPOSED SPLIT. Tier C is set: the benefit claim's largest trial missed its primary endpoint in the full analysis set, so the developer reviews this one personally.
cards.watchOut: Negative-symptom trials are notoriously vulnerable to pseudospecificity (improvement driven by depression, sedation or positive-symptom change); phase 2's flat positive and depression-scale results argue against that here, but the phase 3 borderline primary means the question 'does it treat negative symptoms' remains open in a way 'does it improve functioning scores' does not.
cards.source: Synthesis of Davidson M et al. The American Journal of Psychiatry. 2017 (PMID: 28750582); Davidson M et al. Schizophrenia Bulletin. 2022 (PMID: 35211743).

shelves.title: Glycine-site agents added to antipsychotics: small-to-medium gains in negative symptoms across two meta-analyses — and nothing added to clozapine, where glycine made positive symptoms worse
shelves.question: In schizophrenia, do glycine-site agents (D-serine, sarcosine, glycine) improve negative symptoms added to antipsychotics versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Antipsychotic Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects/pharmacology · Drug Therapy, Combination · Humans · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Receptors, N-Methyl-D-Aspartate/drug effects/metabolism · Schizophrenia/drug therapy/physiopathology · Severity of Illness Index
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — real but modest, and fenced off from clozapine. Two meta-analyses of double-blind placebo-controlled add-on trials agree: Singh SP et al. (PMID: 21936588), pooling 29 trials and 1,253 patients, found adjunctive NMDA-receptor modulators improved negative symptoms with a standardised mean difference of -0.27 and total symptoms with -0.40, with D-serine (negative-symptom SMD -0.53) and sarcosine (SMD -0.39) among the better agents when added to non-clozapine antipsychotics. Goh KK et al. (PMID: 33406959), pooling 40 trials and 4,937 patients, likewise found glycine, D-serine and sarcosine had the better treatment profiles of the seven glutamatergic agents analysed. The fence is consistent in both: augmentation worked only alongside antipsychotics other than clozapine, and in Singh's analysis glycine added to clozapine worsened positive symptoms (SMD +0.56). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): glycine-site agents give small-to-medium symptom gains as add-ons to non-clozapine antipsychotics; they are not a clozapine add-on.

cards.headline: Goh 2021: 40 double-blind trials, 4,937 patients — NMDA modulators improved symptoms, particularly negative symptoms; glycine, D-serine and sarcosine had the better profiles
cards.summary: Goh 2021: 40 double-blind trials, 4,937 patients — NMDA modulators improved symptoms, particularly negative symptoms; glycine, D-serine and sarcosine had the better profiles
cards.people: 40 double-blinded, randomised, placebo-controlled trials involving 4,937 patients with schizophrenia, testing NMDA-receptor modulator supplements (seven glutamatergic agents) added to antipsychotic treatment.
cards.result: When added to antipsychotic treatments, NMDA-receptor modulators improved multiple schizophrenia symptoms, particularly negative symptoms, with satisfactory side effects and safety profile. Among the seven agents analysed, glycine, D-serine and sarcosine had better treatment profiles than the others, and NMDA-receptor co-agonists as a group reduced symptoms compared with antipsychotics without supplementation. Augmentation was only effective among patients treated with antipsychotics other than clozapine.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports the direction and the subgroup pattern rather than pooled effect sizes, so the size of the gain has to come from the older, smaller meta-analysis (Card 2). Trials were short add-on studies in chronic schizophrenia; functional outcomes were not the endpoint.
cards.source: Goh KK et al. Efficacy of N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor modulator augmentation in schizophrenia: A meta-analysis of randomised, placebo-controlled trials. Journal of Psychopharmacology. 2021. PMID: 33406959. cards.headline: Singh 2011: negative-symptom SMD -0.27 and total-symptom SMD -0.40 for the class; D-serine -0.53 and sarcosine -0.39 for negative symptoms on non-clozapine antipsychotics — glycine on clozapine worsened positive symptoms (+0.56)
cards.summary: Singh 2011: negative-symptom SMD -0.27 and total-symptom SMD -0.40 for the class; D-serine -0.53 and sarcosine -0.39 for negative symptoms on non-clozapine antipsychotics — glycine on clozapine worsened positive symptoms (+0.56)
cards.people: 29 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials with a total sample of 1,253 patients with chronic schizophrenia, testing NMDA-receptor modulators as add-on therapy with standardised rating scales.
cards.result: The overall effect size for NMDA modulators as a group was small for negative symptoms (SMD -0.27) and medium for total symptoms (SMD -0.40). As adjuncts to non-clozapine antipsychotics, D-serine (SMD -0.54), N-acetylcysteine (-0.45) and sarcosine (-0.39) improved negative symptoms, and glycine improved total symptoms (SMD -1.12 in that subgroup). When added to clozapine, none of the drugs showed therapeutic potential, and glycine worsened positive symptoms (SMD +0.56).
cards.watchOut: Subgroup effect sizes rest on few small trials each — the glycine total-symptom SMD of -1.12 in one subgroup is implausibly large next to the class effect of -0.40 and should be read as small-study noise around a real but modest signal. N-acetylcysteine is not a glycine-site agent and is carded on its own shelf elsewhere; it is included here only as part of this meta-analysis's class pool.
cards.source: Singh SP et al. Meta-analysis of the efficacy of adjunctive NMDA receptor modulators in chronic schizophrenia. CNS Drugs. 2011. PMID: 21936588. cards.headline: Synthesis: two meta-analyses, one direction, one hard fence at clozapine
cards.summary: Synthesis: two meta-analyses, one direction, one hard fence at clozapine
cards.people: Two meta-analyses of randomised double-blind placebo-controlled add-on trials in schizophrenia: 29 trials / 1,253 patients (Singh 2011) and 40 trials / 4,937 patients (Goh 2021).
cards.result: Negative symptoms: class SMD -0.27 (Singh); total symptoms: SMD -0.40. Best-supported agents: D-serine, sarcosine and glycine, added to non-clozapine antipsychotics. Added to clozapine: no benefit for any agent, and glycine worsened positive symptoms (SMD +0.56). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), with the clozapine fence on the face of the shelf.
cards.watchOut: Both syntheses pool many small, short trials with heterogeneous doses; publication bias in this literature is plausible and neither abstract reports a functional outcome. The claim is symptom scores, not recovery.
cards.source: Synthesis of Goh KK et al. Journal of Psychopharmacology. 2021 (PMID: 33406959); Singh SP et al. CNS Drugs. 2011 (PMID: 21936588).

shelves.title: Bipolar maintenance: lithium plus valproate beat valproate alone (relapse hazard ratio 0.59) but not lithium alone (0.82, not significant) — and lithium alone beat valproate alone (0.71) in BALANCE
shelves.question: In bipolar disorder, how do lithium, valproate and their combination compare for preventing relapse in maintenance treatment?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Antimanic Agents/therapeutic use · Bipolar Disorder/drug therapy · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Lithium Carbonate/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Proportional Hazards Models · Secondary Prevention · Treatment Outcome · Valproic Acid/therapeutic use · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the combination wins only against the weaker partner. In BALANCE (Geddes JR et al., PMID: 20092882), 330 patients with bipolar I disorder were randomised to lithium, valproate, or both for up to 24 months; a new intervention for an emergent mood episode occurred in 54% on the combination, 59% on lithium, and 69% on valproate. The hazard ratios were 0.59 (95% CI 0.42–0.83) for combination versus valproate, 0.82 (0.58–1.17, not significant) for combination versus lithium, and 0.71 (0.51–1.00) for lithium versus valproate. The Cochrane review of valproate maintenance (Cipriani A et al., PMID: 24132760) points the same way: no difference between valproate and lithium (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.87–1.20), and combination therapy more likely to prevent relapse than valproate alone (RR 0.78, 0.63–0.96). PROPOSED SPLIT: if the choice is between the two single drugs, lithium has the edge; adding valproate to lithium was not shown to help, but adding lithium to valproate was.

cards.headline: BALANCE (Geddes 2010): primary outcome in 54% on lithium plus valproate, 59% on lithium, 69% on valproate — combination vs valproate HR 0.59, combination vs lithium HR 0.82 (not significant), lithium vs valproate HR 0.71
cards.summary: BALANCE (Geddes 2010): primary outcome in 54% on lithium plus valproate, 59% on lithium, 69% on valproate — combination vs valproate HR 0.59, combination vs lithium HR 0.82 (not significant), lithium vs valproate HR 0.71
cards.type: Randomised open-label trial with blinded outcome adjudication (BALANCE)
cards.people: 330 patients aged 16 years and older with bipolar I disorder at 41 sites in the UK, France, USA and Italy, randomised after a 4–8 week run-in on the combination to open-label lithium monotherapy (plasma 0.4–1.0 mmol/L, n=110), valproate monotherapy (750–1250 mg, n=110), or both (n=110), followed for up to 24 months.
cards.result: A primary outcome event (initiation of new intervention for an emergent mood episode) occurred in 59 of 110 (54%) on combination therapy, 65 of 110 (59%) on lithium, and 76 of 110 (69%) on valproate. Hazard ratios: 0.59 (95% CI 0.42–0.83, p=0.0023) for combination versus valproate; 0.82 (0.58–1.17, p=0.27) for combination versus lithium; 0.71 (0.51–1.00, p=0.0472) for lithium versus valproate. Serious adverse events after randomisation occurred in 16 participants: seven on valproate (three deaths), five on lithium (two deaths), four on combination (one death).
cards.watchOut: Open-label treatment (only outcome adjudication was masked) and every participant had already tolerated the combination during run-in — a design that flatters the combination arm and under-recruits people who cannot tolerate one of the drugs. The trial could neither confirm nor refute a combination advantage over lithium, and its own authors say so.
cards.source: Geddes JR et al. Lithium plus valproate combination therapy versus monotherapy for relapse prevention in bipolar I disorder (BALANCE): a randomised open-label trial. The Lancet. 2010. PMID: 20092882. Registry ID: ISRCTN55261332. cards.headline: Cipriani 2013 (Cochrane): valproate versus lithium RR 1.02 for withdrawal due to a mood episode — no difference; lithium plus valproate versus valproate alone RR 0.78
cards.summary: Cipriani 2013 (Cochrane): valproate versus lithium RR 1.02 for withdrawal due to a mood episode — no difference; lithium plus valproate versus valproate alone RR 0.78
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials
cards.people: Six randomised controlled trials (876 participants) of valproate maintenance treatment lasting 6 to 24 months: two trials (312 participants) against placebo, four (618) against lithium, one (23) against olanzapine, and one (220) against the combination of valproate plus lithium.
cards.result: Valproate was more effective than placebo in preventing study withdrawal due to any mood episode (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.93; NNTB 8), but no difference in efficacy was found between valproate and lithium (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.20). Combination therapy with lithium plus valproate was more likely to prevent relapse than monotherapy with valproate (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.63 to 0.96). Valproate was associated with fewer dropouts for any cause than placebo or lithium (RR 0.82 and 0.87 respectively); lithium brought more diarrhoea, polyuria, thirst and enuresis, valproate more sedation and infection.
cards.watchOut: Only six trials and 876 participants carry the whole valproate maintenance literature, most with incompletely reported allocation concealment and blinding — the RR 1.02 'no difference' is as much absence of precision as proven equivalence. The combination estimate rests essentially on BALANCE.
cards.source: Cipriani A et al. Valproic acid, valproate and divalproex in the maintenance treatment of bipolar disorder. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2013. PMID: 24132760. cards.headline: Vieta 2011: across 20 maintenance trials (5,364 patients) every intervention except perphenazine plus a mood stabiliser had a relapse relative risk below 1.0 — with wide variation in significance
cards.summary: Vieta 2011: across 20 maintenance trials (5,364 patients) every intervention except perphenazine plus a mood stabiliser had a relapse relative risk below 1.0 — with wide variation in significance
cards.people: 20 placebo-controlled or active-comparator bipolar maintenance trials of at least 6 months' duration with at least 15 patients per group, totalling 5,364 patients (1993 to July 2010); lithium (eight trials) and quetiapine (five) were the most studied agents.
cards.result: All interventions, with the exception of perphenazine plus a mood stabiliser, showed a relative risk for manic/mixed or depressive relapse below 1.0, although statistical significance versus placebo varied. No monotherapy was associated with a significantly reduced risk for both manic/mixed and depressed relapse. The authors conclude that the efficacy of lithium and divalproex has been confirmed, with several atypical antipsychotics also effective.
cards.watchOut: Most trials enrolled patients who had already responded to the study drug for an acute episode (enrichment), which inflates maintenance effects for every agent and makes cross-drug ranking from this pool unreliable — the head-to-head answer comes from BALANCE, not from here.

meta-analysis of randomised maintenance trials (vieta 2011) 20 placebo-controlled or active-comparator bipolar maintenance trials of at least 6 months' duration with at least 15 patients per group, totalling 5,364 patients (1993 to july 2010); lithium (eight trials) and quetiapine (five) were the most studied agents. all interventions, with the exception of perphenazine plus a mood stabiliser, showed a relative risk for manic/mixed or depressive relapse below 1.0, although statistical significance versus placebo varied. no monotherapy was associated with a significantly reduced risk for both manic/mixed and depressed relapse. the authors conclude that the efficacy of lithium and divalproex has been confirmed, with several atypical antipsychotics also effective. most trials enrolled patients who had already responded to the study drug for an acute episode (enrichment), which inflates maintenance effects for every agent and makes cross-drug ranking from this pool unreliable — the head-to-head answer comes from balance, not from here. vieta e et al. effectiveness of psychotropic medications in the maintenance phase of bipolar disorder: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. international journal of neuropsychopharmacology. 2011. pmid: 21733231. mesh: antimanic agents/therapeutic use · antipsychotic agents/therapeutic use · bipolar disorder/drug therapy · disease progression · drug therapy, combination · female · humans · male · psychotropic drugs/therapeutic use · randomized controlled trials as topic · secondary prevention · time factors · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Synthesis: lithium is the stronger single agent; the combination's proven win is over valproate alone only
cards.summary: Synthesis: lithium is the stronger single agent; the combination's proven win is over valproate alone only
cards.people: One head-to-head randomised trial (BALANCE, 330 patients, up to 24 months), one Cochrane review of valproate maintenance (6 trials, 876 participants), and one meta-analysis of 20 maintenance trials (5,364 patients).
cards.result: Relapse/intervention events in BALANCE: 54% combination, 59% lithium, 69% valproate; HR 0.59 for combination versus valproate, 0.82 (not significant) versus lithium, 0.71 for lithium versus valproate. Cochrane: valproate versus lithium RR 1.02; combination versus valproate RR 0.78. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C because the combination claim rests on the single BALANCE trial.
cards.watchOut: BALANCE was open-label with a combination-tolerant run-in; the wider maintenance literature is enrichment-designed. Nothing here addresses bipolar II disorder or rapid cycling specifically.

shelves.title: Acute mania: 13 drugs beat placebo on response in a 72-trial network meta-analysis — cariprazine among them — but only four beat placebo on staying in the trial
shelves.question: In acute mania in bipolar I disorder, how do antipsychotics including cariprazine compare with placebo for response at three weeks?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antipsychotic Agents/therapeutic use · Aripiprazole · Benzodiazepines/therapeutic use · Bipolar Disorder/drug therapy · Carbamazepine/therapeutic use · Female · Haloperidol/therapeutic use · Humans · Lithium/therapeutic use · Male · Mania · Olanzapine/therapeutic use · Paliperidone Palmitate · Quetiapine Fumarate/therapeutic use · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Risperidone/therapeutic use · Tamoxifen/therapeutic use · Valproic Acid
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for the class, with acceptability splitting the field. Kishi T et al. (PMID: 34642461) pooled 72 double-blind randomised trials of 23 drugs and placebo (n=16,442, mean study duration 3.96 weeks): aripiprazole, asenapine, carbamazepine, cariprazine, haloperidol, lithium, olanzapine, paliperidone, quetiapine, risperidone, tamoxifen, valproate and ziprasidone all outperformed placebo on treatment response (56 trials, n=14,503), but only aripiprazole, olanzapine, quetiapine and risperidone had lower all-cause discontinuation than placebo. The earlier network meta-analysis by Yildiz A et al. (PMID: 25036226) — 14,256 patients, 18 treatments — found the same shape: standardised mean differences against placebo of 0.32 to 0.66 for the 12 effective drugs, with no single drug superior to the rest except risperidone over aripiprazole and valproate. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): antimanic efficacy at about three weeks is established for the class including cariprazine; the choice between agents turns on tolerability and discontinuation, not on a proven efficacy champion.

cards.headline: Kishi 2022: 72 double-blind trials, 16,442 patients — 13 treatments including cariprazine beat placebo on response; only aripiprazole, olanzapine, quetiapine and risperidone beat placebo on all-cause discontinuation
cards.summary: Kishi 2022: 72 double-blind trials, 16,442 patients — 13 treatments including cariprazine beat placebo on response; only aripiprazole, olanzapine, quetiapine and risperidone beat placebo on all-cause discontinuation
cards.type: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of double-blind randomised trials (Kishi 2022)
cards.people: 72 double-blind randomised trials of 23 drugs and placebo in adults with acute bipolar mania (79 eligible trials identified; mean study duration 3.96 ± 2.39 weeks; n=16,442; mean age 39.55 years; 50.93% male); oral monotherapy trials of at least 10 days, excluding trials that allowed rescue antipsychotics.
cards.result: Compared with placebo, aripiprazole, asenapine, carbamazepine, cariprazine, haloperidol, lithium, olanzapine, paliperidone, quetiapine, risperidone, tamoxifen, valproate and ziprasidone outperformed on response to treatment (56 trials, n=14,503) and on improvement of mania symptoms (61 trials, n=15,466). Only aripiprazole, olanzapine, quetiapine and risperidone had lower all-cause discontinuation than placebo; topiramate had higher all-cause discontinuation.
cards.watchOut: A network meta-analysis ranks mostly through indirect comparisons, and the abstract does not print drug-by-drug response rates — the honest reading is 'these agents work, these four are also easiest to stay on', not a league table. Trials averaged under four weeks; maintenance is a different shelf.
cards.source: Kishi T et al. Pharmacological treatment for bipolar mania: a systematic review and network meta-analysis of double-blind randomized controlled trials. Molecular Psychiatry. 2022. PMID: 34642461. cards.headline: Yildiz 2015: 14,256 patients across 18 treatments — effect sizes against placebo of 0.32 to 0.66 for the 12 effective drugs, no superiority of one over another except risperidone over aripiprazole and valproate
cards.summary: Yildiz 2015: 14,256 patients across 18 treatments — effect sizes against placebo of 0.32 to 0.66 for the 12 effective drugs, no superiority of one over another except risperidone over aripiprazole and valproate
cards.type: Bayesian network meta-analysis of randomised blinded trials (Yildiz 2015)
cards.people: Randomised, blinded, short-term monotherapy trials in adults with bipolar I mania: 14,256 manic patients randomised to one of 18 active treatments or placebo, providing 95 direct comparisons on 128 data points (literature to 15 January 2014).
cards.result: For the primary outcome (standardised mean difference, Hedges' g), the 12 effective antimanic drugs had SMDs against placebo ranging from 0.32 to 0.66, without superiority of one over another except for risperidone versus aripiprazole and valproate. Aripiprazole, olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone and valproate had lower all-cause discontinuation rates than placebo. Sensitivity analysis by drug class showed similar efficacy profiles for haloperidol, second-generation antipsychotics and mood stabilisers.
cards.watchOut: Tamoxifen appears in these pools on the strength of very small trials — a reminder that network estimates inherit the frailty of their smallest nodes. Effect sizes of 0.32–0.66 are symptom-scale differences over a few weeks, not remission guarantees.
cards.source: Yildiz A et al. A network meta-analysis on comparative efficacy and all-cause discontinuation of antimanic treatments in acute bipolar mania. Psychological Medicine. 2015. PMID: 25036226. cards.headline: Synthesis: efficacy is a class property; acceptability is the discriminator
cards.summary: Synthesis: efficacy is a class property; acceptability is the discriminator
cards.people: Two network meta-analyses of randomised blinded monotherapy trials in acute bipolar mania: 72 trials / 16,442 patients (Kishi 2022) and 95 direct comparisons / 14,256 patients (Yildiz 2015).
cards.result: Response: 13 treatments beat placebo in Kishi 2022, including cariprazine; 12 effective drugs with SMDs of 0.32 to 0.66 versus placebo in Yildiz 2015. Acceptability: only aripiprazole, olanzapine, quetiapine and risperidone (Kishi) beat placebo on all-cause discontinuation. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for antimanic efficacy of the class at ~3 weeks.
cards.watchOut: Both syntheses are built on short monotherapy trials that exclude the mixed, psychotic-complicated and rescue-medicated presentations common on inpatient units; neither answers combination therapy, which is how severe mania is usually treated.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kishi T et al. Molecular Psychiatry. 2022 (PMID: 34642461); Yildiz A et al. Psychological Medicine. 2015 (PMID: 25036226).
