shelves.title: Allopurinol added to lithium for acute mania: one 180-patient trial with a small effect (d=0.32) and a five-trial meta-analysis at d=0.294 — promising, thin, and unreplicated at scale
shelves.question: In acute mania, does adjunctive allopurinol improve response versus placebo added to mood stabilisers?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Allopurinol/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Antipsychotic Agents/therapeutic use · Bipolar Disorder/diagnosis/drug therapy/rehabilitation · Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders · Dipyridamole/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Therapy, Combination · Enzyme Inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Hospitalization · Humans · Lithium Carbonate/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Phosphodiesterase Inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Severity of Illness Index · Surveys and Questionnaires
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a small effect on a thin base. The anchor trial (Machado-Vieira R et al., PMID: 18681754) randomised 180 inpatients with bipolar I mania to allopurinol 600 mg/day, dipyridamole 200 mg/day, or placebo, each added to lithium for 4 weeks: allopurinol produced greater reductions in Young Mania Rating Scale scores at day 21 (p<0.001) and day 28 (p=0.003), with an effect size of d=0.32 (95% CI 0.07 to 0.57), and remission rates significantly higher than with dipyridamole or placebo (p=0.008). The meta-analysis by Chen AT et al. (PMID: 29017068) found five placebo-controlled trials: four showed efficacy on the primary outcome and one did not, with an overall effect size of d=0.294 across the four positive studies, and no significant difference in side effects. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): adjunctive allopurinol probably trims mania scores modestly on top of a mood stabiliser; Tier C because the whole base is five small trials and one 180-patient anchor.

cards.headline: Machado-Vieira 2008: allopurinol 600 mg on lithium cut YMRS more than placebo at days 21 and 28 (d=0.32); remission significantly higher (p=0.008); dipyridamole did not separate
cards.summary: Machado-Vieira 2008: allopurinol 600 mg on lithium cut YMRS more than placebo at days 21 and 28 (d=0.32); remission significantly higher (p=0.008); dipyridamole did not separate
cards.people: 180 adult inpatients with DSM-IV-TR bipolar I disorder, current episode manic with or without psychotic features (rapid cyclers and mixed episodes excluded; no antipsychotic used), randomised to fixed-dose allopurinol 600 mg/day (n=60), dipyridamole 200 mg/day (n=60), or placebo (n=60), each added to lithium for 4 weeks (September 2003 to September 2006).
cards.result: Allopurinol resulted in greater mean reductions in Young Mania Rating Scale scores from baseline to day 21 (p<0.001) and day 28 (p=0.003) compared with placebo (d=0.32, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.57). Remission rates were significantly higher for allopurinol compared with dipyridamole and placebo (p=0.008). The decrease in plasma uric acid levels showed a significant positive association with antimanic effects in the allopurinol group (p<0.001). Allopurinol was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre-style inpatient trial with no antipsychotics allowed — cleaner pharmacology, less resemblance to real mania care — and the abstract does not print the remission percentages behind the p=0.008, so the absolute gain cannot be stated from this record. The uric-acid association is a mechanism hint, not proof.
cards.source: Machado-Vieira R et al. A double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled 4-week study on the efficacy and safety of the purinergic agents allopurinol and dipyridamole adjunctive to lithium in acute bipolar mania. cards.headline: Chen 2018: five placebo-controlled trials — four positive, one null; pooled effect d=0.294 in the four positive studies; no side-effect difference
cards.summary: Chen 2018: five placebo-controlled trials — four positive, one null; pooled effect d=0.294 in the four positive studies; no side-effect difference
cards.people: Five placebo-controlled, randomised, double-blind trials of allopurinol as an adjunct for acute mania in bipolar disorder (three inpatient, one outpatient, one mixed), all using the Young Mania Rating Scale as the primary outcome measure.
cards.result: Four of the five studies showed efficacy on the primary outcome, with significantly reduced YMRS scores for allopurinol versus placebo; one study showed no significant effect. The overall effect size for the four studies is d=0.294. No significant difference in side effects was found between groups in any of the studies. The authors note adjunctive efficacy may relate to which mood stabiliser is used, and call for larger trials with homogeneous dosing.
cards.watchOut: Pooling the four positive studies and setting the null one aside flatters the estimate — read d=0.294 as an upper bound from small, heterogeneous trials (different background stabilisers and settings), not as a settled effect size.
cards.source: Chen AT et al. Allopurinol augmentation in acute mania: A meta-analysis of placebo-controlled trials. Journal of Affective Disorders. 2018. PMID: 29017068. cards.headline: Synthesis: a real-looking small signal that has never been tested at scale
cards.summary: Synthesis: a real-looking small signal that has never been tested at scale
cards.people: One 180-patient double-blind trial of allopurinol added to lithium (Machado-Vieira 2008) and a meta-analysis of five placebo-controlled adjunctive trials (Chen 2018).
cards.result: YMRS effect: d=0.32 (95% CI 0.07 to 0.57) in the anchor trial; d=0.294 across the four positive trials in the meta-analysis, with one of five trials null. Side effects: no significant difference in any study. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C — five small trials total, none large.
cards.watchOut: Allopurinol's appeal (cheap, familiar, well tolerated) is exactly why a small positive literature should be read cautiously: no large multicentre replication exists, and background-stabiliser differences may drive the heterogeneity.
cards.source: Synthesis of Machado-Vieira R et al. Journal of Clinical Psychiatry. 2008 (PMID: 18681754); Chen AT et al. Journal of Affective Disorders. 2018 (PMID: 29017068).

shelves.title: Nurse-delivered sleep restriction therapy in primary care: insomnia severity 10.9 versus 13.9 at six months in 642 patients — four sessions, and cost-effective at £2,076 per QALY (HABIT)
shelves.question: In primary-care insomnia, does nurse-delivered sleep restriction therapy improve insomnia severity versus sleep hygiene alone?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Male · Female · Young Adult · Middle Aged · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders/therapy · Treatment Outcome · State Medicine · Habits · Primary Health Care · Sleep · Quality of Life
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large, well-run pragmatic trial. In HABIT (Kyle SD et al., PMID: 37573859), 642 adults with insomnia disorder from 35 general practices in England were randomised to four sessions of nurse-delivered sleep restriction therapy plus a sleep hygiene booklet, or the booklet alone: at 6 months the mean Insomnia Severity Index score was 10.9 (SD 5.5) with sleep restriction versus 13.9 (5.2) with sleep hygiene (adjusted mean difference -3.05, 95% CI -3.83 to -2.28; p<0.0001; Cohen's d -0.74). The incremental cost per QALY gained was £2,076, with a 95.3% probability of being cost-effective at a £20,000 threshold. Serious adverse events numbered eight in each group, none judged related to the intervention. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a brief, nurse-delivered single-component therapy delivers a moderate insomnia gain in primary care; Tier C because it is a single (open-label) trial awaiting replication.

cards.headline: HABIT (Kyle 2023): ISI 10.9 versus 13.9 at 6 months (difference -3.05, d -0.74); £2,076 per QALY; eight serious adverse events in each group, none related
cards.summary: HABIT (Kyle 2023): ISI 10.9 versus 13.9 at 6 months (difference -3.05, d -0.74); £2,076 per QALY; eight serious adverse events in each group, none related
cards.people: 642 adults with insomnia disorder recruited from 35 general practices across England (mean age 55.4 years, range 19–88; 489 women [76.2%], 153 men), randomised 1:1 to four sessions of nurse-delivered sleep restriction therapy plus a sleep hygiene booklet (n=321) or a sleep hygiene booklet only (n=321), with no restriction on usual care; 580 participants (90.3%) provided at least one outcome measurement.
cards.result: At 6 months, mean Insomnia Severity Index score was 10.9 (SD 5.5) for sleep restriction therapy and 13.9 (5.2) for sleep hygiene (adjusted mean difference -3.05, 95% CI -3.83 to -2.28; p<0.0001; Cohen's d -0.74). The incremental cost per QALY gained was £2,076, giving a 95.3% probability that treatment was cost-effective at a £20,000-per-QALY threshold. Eight participants in each group had serious adverse events, none judged related to the intervention.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with a self-reported primary endpoint: patients who received four sessions of attention knew it, and expectation can move an ISI score. The comparison is a booklet, not full CBT-I — HABIT shows a deliverable component works, not that it matches the full therapy. Effects at 12 months and on hypnotic use sit in the full HTA report rather than this abstract.

shelves.title: Prolonged-release melatonin 2 mg after 55: responders 26% versus 15% in one trial, better sleep quality and morning alertness in both — a three-week, questionnaire-scale benefit
shelves.question: In insomnia in adults aged 55 and over, does prolonged-release melatonin improve sleep quality and next-day alertness versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Delayed-Action Preparations · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Melatonin/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Placebos · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders/drug therapy/physiopathology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — modest, short-horizon, and specific to the prolonged-release formulation in older patients. Wade AG et al. (PMID: 17875243) randomised 354 primary-care patients aged 55–80 to prolonged-release melatonin 2 mg (the publication names the formulation Circadin) or placebo for 3 weeks: the responder rate (combined improvement in sleep quality and morning alertness) was 26% versus 15% (p=0.014), and sleep latency shortened by -24.3 versus -12.9 minutes (p=0.028). Lemoine P et al. (PMID: 18036082), in 170 outpatients aged 55 and over on the same 2 mg prolonged-release formulation for 3 weeks, found better quality of sleep (-22.5 versus -16.5 mm, p=0.047) and morning alertness (-15.7 versus -6.8 mm, p=0.002), with no rebound or withdrawal on stopping. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): prolonged-release melatonin improves perceived sleep quality and next-morning alertness in insomnia over 55 — over three weeks, on questionnaires, with no objective sleep-architecture claim.

cards.headline: Wade 2007: responders 26% versus 15% (p=0.014); sleep latency -24.3 versus -12.9 minutes (p=0.028); quality of life also improved (p=0.034)
cards.summary: Wade 2007: responders 26% versus 15% (p=0.014); sleep latency -24.3 versus -12.9 minutes (p=0.028); quality of life also improved (p=0.034)
cards.people: 354 men and women aged 55–80 years with insomnia in primary care in the West of Scotland (177 prolonged-release melatonin, 177 placebo), after a 2-week single-blind placebo run-in; treatment was one prolonged-release melatonin 2 mg tablet (named in the publication as Circadin) or placebo daily, 2 hours before bedtime, for 3 weeks; 20 patients did not complete the final visit.
cards.result: Significant differences favoured prolonged-release melatonin on the responder analysis — concomitant clinically relevant improvement in quality of sleep and morning alertness — at 26% versus 15% (p=0.014), and on each parameter separately. Sleep latency shortened by -24.3 versus -12.9 minutes (p=0.028), and quality of life improved significantly (p=0.034).
cards.watchOut: Three weeks, subjective scales (Leeds Sleep Evaluation Questionnaire, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index), and a run-in that removed placebo responders before randomisation — all three inflate the apparent effect versus routine practice. The publication names the formulation (Circadin 2 mg) but the record does not name its manufacturer, so none is stated here.
cards.source: Wade AG et al. Efficacy of prolonged release melatonin in insomnia patients aged 55-80 years: quality of sleep and next-day alertness outcomes. Current Medical Research and Opinion. 2007. PMID: 17875243. cards.headline: Lemoine 2007: quality of sleep -22.5 versus -16.5 mm (p=0.047), morning alertness -15.7 versus -6.8 mm (p=0.002) — and no rebound insomnia or withdrawal after stopping
cards.summary: Lemoine 2007: quality of sleep -22.5 versus -16.5 mm (p=0.047), morning alertness -15.7 versus -6.8 mm (p=0.002) — and no rebound insomnia or withdrawal after stopping
cards.people: 170 primary-insomnia outpatients aged 55 years and older, treated with prolonged-release melatonin 2 mg or placebo for 3 weeks, with quality of sleep and morning alertness measured on the Leeds Sleep Evaluation Questionnaire and discontinuation effects assessed after treatment ended.
cards.result: Prolonged-release melatonin significantly improved quality of sleep (-22.5 versus -16.5 mm, p=0.047), quality of night (0.89 versus 0.46 units, p=0.003) and morning alertness (-15.7 versus -6.8 mm, p=0.002) compared with placebo; improvements in sleep quality and alertness were strongly correlated (R=0.77, p<0.001). There was no evidence of rebound insomnia or withdrawal effects after discontinuation, and adverse events were few and mostly minor.
cards.watchOut: Millimetre differences on visual-analogue-style scales are statistically real but clinically small, and the p=0.047 for the headline sleep-quality outcome is fragile. Same formulation, same 3-week horizon, and a partly overlapping investigator community as Wade — concordant, but not fully independent replication.

shelves.title: Trazodone for insomnia: sleep quality and continuity improve in a 44-trial meta-analysis, subjective total sleep time does not (difference 0.73 minutes) — and patients drop out for adverse effects at twice the placebo rate
shelves.question: In chronic insomnia, does trazodone improve subjective sleep onset and maintenance versus placebo — and how thin is the randomised evidence behind its widespread off-label use?
shelves.mesh: Trazodone/pharmacology/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Humans · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders/drug therapy · Sleep/drug effects · Sleep Wake Disorders/drug therapy
shelves.balance: SPLIT — it improves how sleep feels and some measured sleep, but not the outcome patients name first. Kokkali M et al. (PMID: 39123094) pooled 44 randomised trials with 3,935 participants: trazodone did not significantly change subjective total sleep time (weighted mean difference 0.73 minutes, 95% CI -24.62 to 26.07; p=0.96), but improved sleep quality (SMD -0.58, 95% CI -0.87 to -0.28), reduced nocturnal awakenings (SMD -0.57) and time awake after sleep onset (-13.47 minutes), and lengthened polysomnography-measured total sleep time by 27.98 minutes. The price: dropouts due to adverse effects were more than doubled (RR 2.30, 95% CI 1.45 to 3.64). The Cochrane review of antidepressants for insomnia (Everitt H et al., PMID: 29761479) is the colder read: for trazodone specifically there were too few studies to draw clear conclusions, with a possible small improvement in sleep quality on short-term low-dose use. PROPOSED SPLIT: a real but modest continuity/quality effect on a thin primary-insomnia base, no gain in perceived sleep duration, and a tolerability cost — Tier C so the developer sees how thin the insomnia-specific evidence is.

cards.headline: Kokkali 2024: subjective total sleep time unchanged (0.73 minutes, p=0.96) but sleep quality SMD -0.58, awakenings SMD -0.57, wake after sleep onset -13.47 minutes, objective sleep time +27.98 minutes — adverse-effect dropouts RR 2.30
cards.summary: Kokkali 2024: subjective total sleep time unchanged (0.73 minutes, p=0.96) but sleep quality SMD -0.58, awakenings SMD -0.57, wake after sleep onset -13.47 minutes, objective sleep time +27.98 minutes — adverse-effect dropouts RR 2.30
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Kokkali 2024)
cards.people: 44 randomised controlled trials with 3,935 participants comparing trazodone with placebo and reporting sleep outcomes (minimum treatment 5 days; searches to 1 May 2024); populations spanned sleep disturbances and insomnia across diagnoses, not primary insomnia alone.
cards.result: Trazodone did not significantly impact subjective total sleep time (weighted mean difference 0.73 min, 95% CI -24.62 to 26.07, p=0.96) but improved sleep quality (SMD -0.58, 95% CI -0.87 to -0.28, p<0.01), number of nocturnal awakenings (SMD -0.57, 95% CI -0.85 to -0.30), nocturnal time awake after sleep onset (-13.47 min, 95% CI -23.09 to -3.86), objective total sleep time by polysomnography (27.98 min, 95% CI 4.02 to 51.95, p=0.02), and sleep efficiency (3.32%, p=0.02). Dropouts owing to adverse effects were higher on trazodone (RR 2.30, 95% CI 1.45 to 3.64), as were adverse effects overall (RR 1.18, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.33).
cards.watchOut: Most of the 44 trials were not primary-insomnia trials — many enrolled patients whose sleep was disturbed by other conditions or drugs — so the pooled benefit travels to the insomnia clinic only approximately. Effects on sleep latency and daytime impairment were minor, per the authors.

cards.headline: Everitt 2018 (Cochrane): for trazodone in insomnia itself — too few studies to draw clear conclusions; a possible small sleep-quality improvement with short-term low-dose use
cards.summary: Everitt 2018 (Cochrane): for trazodone in insomnia itself — too few studies to draw clear conclusions; a possible small sleep-quality improvement with short-term low-dose use
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (Everitt 2018)
cards.people: 23 randomised trials (2,806 participants) of antidepressants for insomnia in adults with a primary diagnosis of insomnia, across all drug classes; the trazodone subset was small.
cards.result: The review found that there may be a small improvement in sleep quality with short-term use of low-dose doxepin and trazodone compared with placebo, but that the evidence for trazodone's efficacy and tolerability in primary insomnia is uncertain, with too few studies to draw clear conclusions. There was no evidence for long-term antidepressant use for insomnia, and tolerability reporting was limited throughout.
cards.watchOut: This is the fence on the whole shelf: the world's commonest off-label insomnia prescription rests, for insomnia as the primary diagnosis, on a handful of small short trials. The Cochrane searches incorporated here ran to July 2015 (updated to December 2017 without incorporation).
cards.source: Everitt H et al. Antidepressants for insomnia in adults. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2018. PMID: 29761479. cards.result: Subjective total sleep time: +0.73 minutes (not significant). Sleep quality: SMD -0.58. Wake after sleep onset: -13.47 minutes. Objective total sleep time: +27.98 minutes. shelves.title: Eptinezumab: about one extra migraine day a month beyond placebo in episodic migraine (-4.3 versus -3.2 days) and about two in chronic migraine (-8.2 versus -5.6) in the PROMISE trials
shelves.question: In episodic and chronic migraine, does intravenous eptinezumab prevent attacks versus placebo — the PROMISE programme?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intravenous · Adult · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/administration & dosage/blood · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Migraine Disorders/blood/diagnosis/drug therapy
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two concordant phase 3 trials, with the size of the prize stated plainly. In PROMISE-1 (Ashina M et al., PMID: 32075406; episodic migraine, 888 patients, baseline about 8.6 monthly migraine days), eptinezumab 100 mg and 300 mg reduced monthly migraine days over weeks 1–12 by -3.9 and -4.3 versus -3.2 on placebo (p=0.0182 and p=0.0001); the 30 mg dose (-4.0) did not meet the primary endpoint comparison as reported. In PROMISE-2 (Lipton RB et al., PMID: 32209650; chronic migraine, 1,072 patients, baseline about 16.1 monthly migraine days), the reductions were -7.7 (100 mg) and -8.2 (300 mg) versus -5.6 on placebo (both p<0.0001). Treatment-emergent adverse events ran at placebo-like rates (57.6–63.2% across eptinezumab arms in PROMISE-1 versus 59.5% on placebo), with upper respiratory infection and fatigue the common excess events. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): quarterly intravenous eptinezumab prevents roughly one to two more migraine days a month than placebo over 12 weeks, in line with the rest of the CGRP class.

cards.headline: PROMISE-1 (Ashina 2020): monthly migraine days -3.9 (100 mg) and -4.3 (300 mg) versus -3.2 on placebo over weeks 1–12; adverse events 57.6–63.2% versus 59.5%
cards.summary: PROMISE-1 (Ashina 2020): monthly migraine days -3.9 (100 mg) and -4.3 (300 mg) versus -3.2 on placebo over weeks 1–12; adverse events 57.6–63.2% versus 59.5%
cards.people: 888 adults with episodic migraine treated across 84 study sites (mean baseline monthly migraine days about 8.6), randomised to intravenous eptinezumab 30 mg, 100 mg or 300 mg, or placebo, every 12 weeks for up to four doses; primary endpoint was change in monthly migraine days over weeks 1–12.
cards.result: Eptinezumab 100 mg and 300 mg met the primary endpoint, significantly reducing monthly migraine days across weeks 1–12 compared with placebo (30 mg, -4.0; 100 mg, -3.9, p=0.0182; 300 mg, -4.3; placebo, -3.2, p=0.0001 for the 300 mg comparison). Treatment-emergent adverse events were reported by 58.4% (30 mg), 63.2% (100 mg), 57.6% (300 mg) and 59.5% (placebo) of patients; upper respiratory tract infection (9.9–11.4% on eptinezumab versus 7.2% on placebo) and fatigue (2.3–3.6% versus <1%) were the events exceeding placebo by at least 2%.
cards.watchOut: The placebo group itself lost 3.2 migraine days a month — the drug's added value is the roughly 0.7–1.1 day difference, not the headline -4.3. The 30 mg dose's -4.0 change did not reach significance as reported, a reminder that these between-group gaps are small relative to within-patient variability. Twelve weeks is the measured horizon.
cards.source: Ashina M et al. Eptinezumab in episodic migraine: A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study (PROMISE-1). Cephalalgia. 2020. PMID: 32075406. Registry ID: NCT02559895. cards.headline: PROMISE-2 (Lipton 2020): chronic migraine days -7.7 (100 mg) and -8.2 (300 mg) versus -5.6 on placebo (both p<0.0001); nasopharyngitis 9.4% versus 6.0% the only notable excess event
cards.summary: PROMISE-2 (Lipton 2020): chronic migraine days -7.7 (100 mg) and -8.2 (300 mg) versus -5.6 on placebo (both p<0.0001); nasopharyngitis 9.4% versus 6.0% the only notable excess event
cards.people: 1,072 treated adults with chronic migraine (baseline mean monthly migraine days about 16.1), randomly assigned to intravenous eptinezumab 100 mg, eptinezumab 300 mg, or placebo on day 0 and week 12; primary endpoint was change in mean monthly migraine days over weeks 1 to 12.
cards.result: Eptinezumab 100 mg and 300 mg significantly reduced monthly migraine days across weeks 1 to 12 compared with placebo (placebo -5.6; 100 mg -7.7, p<0.0001; 300 mg -8.2, p<0.0001). Treatment-emergent adverse events were reported by 43.5% (100 mg), 52.0% (300 mg) and 46.7% (placebo) of patients; nasopharyngitis was the only event reported for more than 2% of eptinezumab patients at more than 2% over placebo (300 mg arm: 9.4% versus 6.0%). The trial provides Class I evidence that a single dose of eptinezumab reduces monthly migraine days over 12 weeks.
cards.watchOut: Chronic-migraine placebo responses are large (-5.6 days here), and patients with medication overuse and daily headache phenotypes typical of clinic practice are under-represented in phase 3 pools. No head-to-head against the subcutaneous CGRP antibodies exists; the intravenous route's speed claim rests on pharmacokinetics, not a comparative trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the CGRP class effect, delivered by infusion — about 1 extra day in episodic, about 2 in chronic migraine
cards.summary: Synthesis: the CGRP class effect, delivered by infusion — about 1 extra day in episodic, about 2 in chronic migraine
cards.people: Two randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trials: PROMISE-1 (episodic migraine, 888 patients) and PROMISE-2 (chronic migraine, 1,072 patients), each testing quarterly intravenous eptinezumab 100 mg and 300 mg over 12 weeks.
cards.result: Monthly migraine days versus placebo: episodic, -3.9 and -4.3 versus -3.2; chronic, -7.7 and -8.2 versus -5.6. Adverse-event rates were close to placebo in both trials. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit), Tier C not set: two large concordant phase 3 trials.
cards.watchOut: Both trials were industry phase 3 programmes with 12-week primary endpoints; durability, discontinuation and comparative effectiveness against oral preventives are outside this record. The library's CGRP umbrella shelf covers the class; this shelf is the eptinezumab-specific record.

shelves.title: Zavegepant nasal spray for acute migraine: pain freedom at 2 hours in 24% versus 15% on placebo in phase 3 — a real, modest gain, paid for in bad taste (dysgeusia up to 16.1%)
shelves.question: In acute migraine, does zavegepant nasal spray achieve pain freedom at two hours versus placebo nasal spray?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Analgesics/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Migraine Disorders/diagnosis · Nasal Sprays · Nausea · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — modest absolute gains, twice replicated. In the phase 3 trial (Lipton RB et al., PMID: 36804093), 1,269 patients in the efficacy set treated a single moderate-to-severe attack: pain freedom at 2 hours occurred in 24% on zavegepant 10 mg versus 15% on placebo (risk difference 8.8 percentage points, 95% CI 4.5 to 13.1; p<0.0001), and freedom from the most bothersome symptom in 40% versus 31% (risk difference 8.7 points, 3.4 to 13.9; p=0.0012). The earlier dose-ranging trial (Croop R et al., PMID: 36239038) found the same shape: pain freedom 22.5% (10 mg) and 23.1% (20 mg) versus 15.5% on placebo, with the 5 mg dose not significant. The commonest adverse events were dysgeusia (13.5% to 16.1% versus 3.5%), nausea (2.7% to 4.1% versus 0.5%) and nasal discomfort (1.3% to 5.2% versus 0.2%). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): zavegepant nasal spray gives roughly one extra pain-free response per 11 treated attacks over placebo, as the non-oral gepant option.

cards.headline: Lipton 2023 (phase 3): pain freedom at 2 hours 24% versus 15% (risk difference 8.8 points); most-bothersome-symptom freedom 40% versus 31%
cards.summary: Lipton 2023 (phase 3): pain freedom at 2 hours 24% versus 15% (risk difference 8.8 points); most-bothersome-symptom freedom 40% versus 31%
cards.people: 1,978 adults recruited at 90 US centres; 1,405 eligible participants with 2–8 moderate or severe migraine attacks per month were assigned to zavegepant 10 mg nasal spray (703) or matching placebo (702) to self-treat a single attack of moderate or severe pain; 1,269 (623 zavegepant, 646 placebo) formed the efficacy analysis set.
cards.result: Two hours after the dose, more participants on zavegepant than placebo had pain freedom (147 of 623 [24%] versus 96 of 646 [15%]; risk difference 8.8 percentage points, 95% CI 4.5–13.1; p<0.0001) and freedom from their most bothersome symptom (247 [40%] versus 201 [31%]; risk difference 8.7 points, 3.4–13.9; p=0.0012). Safety was analysed in all who received a dose; the abstract's adverse-event detail is truncated in this record beyond the common events at or above 2%.
cards.watchOut: Single-attack treatment in trial volunteers with 2–8 attacks a month; repeated-attack consistency, and performance in patients with vomiting (the very group the nasal route targets), are not what this design measures. The absolute gain — about 9 points — is the class-typical gepant gain, not a breakthrough.
cards.source: Lipton RB et al. Safety, tolerability, and efficacy of zavegepant 10 mg nasal spray for the acute treatment of migraine in the USA: a phase 3, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled multicentre trial. The Lancet Neurology. 2023. PMID: 36804093. Registry ID: NCT04571060. cards.headline: Croop 2022 (phase 2/3): pain freedom 22.5% (10 mg) and 23.1% (20 mg) versus 15.5% on placebo; 5 mg not significant; dysgeusia 13.5–16.1% versus 3.5%
cards.summary: Croop 2022 (phase 2/3): pain freedom 22.5% (10 mg) and 23.1% (20 mg) versus 15.5% on placebo; 5 mg not significant; dysgeusia 13.5–16.1% versus 3.5%
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled dose-ranging phase 2/3 trial (Croop 2022)
cards.people: 1,673 adults aged 18–79 (mean age 40.8 years, 85.5% female) randomised at US sites; 1,581 analysed for efficacy across zavegepant 5 mg (n=387), 10 mg (n=391), 20 mg (n=402) and placebo (n=401), each treating a single attack of moderate to severe pain.
cards.result: Zavegepant 10 and 20 mg beat placebo on pain freedom at 2 hours (placebo 15.5%; 10 mg 22.5%, p=0.0113; 20 mg 23.1%, p=0.0055) and on freedom from the most bothersome symptom (placebo 33.7%; 10 mg 41.9%, p=0.0155; 20 mg 42.5%, p=0.0094); the 5 mg dose was not significant. The most common treatment-emergent adverse events on 10 and 20 mg versus placebo were dysgeusia (13.5% to 16.1% versus 3.5%), nausea (2.7% to 4.1% versus 0.5%) and nasal discomfort (1.3% to 5.2% versus 0.2%); most were mild or moderate, and there was no signal of hepatotoxicity.
cards.watchOut: Dysgeusia at these rates can partly unblind a nasal-spray trial — patients who taste the drug may guess their allocation — which matters for subjective 2-hour endpoints. The 20 mg dose added nothing over 10 mg on efficacy.
cards.source: Croop R et al. Zavegepant nasal spray for the acute treatment of migraine: A Phase 2/3 double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled, dose-ranging trial. Headache. 2022. PMID: 36239038. Registry ID: NCT03872453. shelves.title: Candesartan for migraine prevention: headache days 13.6 versus 18.5 over 12 weeks in the first crossover trial, and responders 43% versus 23% on placebo in the second — matching propranolol head-to-head
shelves.question: In episodic migraine, does candesartan prevent migraine days versus placebo — and how does it compare with propranolol?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Angiotensin II/antagonists & inhibitors · Angiotensin Receptor Antagonists · Benzimidazoles/therapeutic use · Biphenyl Compounds · Cross-Over Studies · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Middle Aged · Migraine Disorders/prevention & control · Severity of Illness Index · Tetrazoles/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two small crossover trials, both positive, one with an active comparator. Tronvik E et al. (PMID: 12503978) randomised 60 patients with 2–6 attacks a month to candesartan 16 mg and placebo in crossover: over 12 weeks, days with headache averaged 13.6 on candesartan versus 18.5 on placebo (p=0.001), days with migraine 9.0 versus 12.6 (p<0.001), and 40.4% were responders for migraine days. Stovner LJ et al. (PMID: 24335848), in a triple-blind double-crossover study of 72 patients, found migraine days per month of 2.95 on candesartan and 2.91 on propranolol slow-release 160 mg versus 3.53 on placebo (p=0.02 for both comparisons), with responders at 43% on candesartan and 40% on propranolol versus 23% on placebo, and candesartan non-inferior to propranolol. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): candesartan 16 mg prevents migraine about as well as propranolol 160 mg in these small trials — a useful option when beta-blockers are unsuitable, pending a large parallel-group trial.

cards.headline: Tronvik 2003: headache days 13.6 versus 18.5 and migraine days 9.0 versus 12.6 over 12 weeks (both favouring candesartan); migraine-day responders 40.4%
cards.summary: Tronvik 2003: headache days 13.6 versus 18.5 and migraine days 9.0 versus 12.6 over 12 weeks (both favouring candesartan); migraine-day responders 40.4%
cards.people: 60 patients aged 18–65 years with 2–6 migraine attacks per month, recruited mainly from newspaper advertisements at a Norwegian neurological outpatient clinic; after a 4-week placebo run-in, two 12-week treatment periods (candesartan 16 mg daily or placebo) separated by a 4-week placebo washout; intention-to-treat analysis n=57.
cards.result: In 12 weeks, the mean number of days with headache was 13.6 with candesartan versus 18.5 with placebo (p=0.001); hours with headache 95 versus 139 (p<0.001); days with migraine 9.0 versus 12.6 (p<0.001); hours with migraine 59.4 versus 92.2 (p<0.001); days of sick leave 1.4 versus 3.9 (p=0.01). Responders (at least 50% reduction versus placebo) numbered 18 of 57 (31.6%) for days with headache and 23 of 57 (40.4%) for days with migraine. Adverse events were similar in the two periods.
cards.watchOut: A 60-patient crossover from 2001–02 with advertisement-recruited volunteers; crossover designs in migraine can carry period and carryover effects despite washout, and the trial predates trial registration, so outcome selection cannot be audited. The effect has never been retested in a large parallel-group trial.
cards.source: Tronvik E et al. Prophylactic treatment of migraine with an angiotensin II receptor blocker: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2003. PMID: 12503978. randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial (tronvik 2003) 60 patients aged 18–65 years with 2–6 migraine attacks per month, recruited mainly from newspaper advertisements at a norwegian neurological outpatient clinic; after a 4-week placebo run-in, two 12-week treatment periods (candesartan 16 mg daily or placebo) separated by a 4-week placebo washout; intention-to-treat analysis n=57. in 12 weeks, the mean number of days with headache was 13.6 with candesartan versus 18.5 with placebo (p=0.001); hours with headache 95 versus 139 (p<0.001); days with migraine 9.0 versus 12.6 (p<0.001); hours with migraine 59.4 versus 92.2 (p<0.001); days of sick leave 1.4 versus 3.9 (p=0.01). responders (at least 50% reduction versus placebo) numbered 18 of 57 (31.6%) for days with headache and 23 of 57 (40.4%) for days with migraine. adverse events were similar in the two periods. a 60-patient crossover from 2001–02 with advertisement-recruited volunteers; crossover designs in migraine can carry period and carryover effects despite washout, and the trial predates trial registration, so outcome selection cannot be audited. the effect has never been retested in a large parallel-group trial. tronvik e et al. prophylactic treatment of migraine with an angiotensin ii receptor blocker: a randomized controlled trial. jama. 2003. pmid: 12503978. mesh: adult · angiotensin ii/antagonists & inhibitors · angiotensin receptor antagonists · benzimidazoles/therapeutic use · biphenyl compounds · cross-over studies · double-blind method · humans · middle aged · migraine disorders/prevention & control · severity of illness index · tetrazoles/therapeutic use · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Stovner 2014: migraine days per month 2.95 on candesartan, 2.91 on propranolol, 3.53 on placebo; responders 43% and 40% versus 23%; candesartan non-inferior to propranolol
cards.summary: Stovner 2014: migraine days per month 2.95 on candesartan, 2.91 on propranolol, 3.53 on placebo; responders 43% and 40% versus 23%; candesartan non-inferior to propranolol
cards.people: 72 adult patients with episodic or chronic migraine, each passing through three 12-week treatment periods on candesartan 16 mg, propranolol slow-release 160 mg, or placebo, in random order; modified intention-to-treat analysis.
cards.result: Candesartan and propranolol were both superior to placebo on migraine days per month: 2.95 (95% CI 2.35–3.55) and 2.91 (2.36–3.45) versus 3.53 (2.98–4.08) (p=0.02 for both comparisons). Candesartan was non-inferior to propranolol (and vice versa). Responders (over 50% reduction in migraine days) were 43% on candesartan and 40% on propranolol versus 23% on placebo (p=0.025 and p<0.050). Adverse events were more frequent on candesartan (n=133) and propranolol (n=143) than on placebo (n=90), with differing profiles.
cards.watchOut: Seventy-two patients each serving as their own control three times over — efficient, but the non-inferiority claim inherits the precision limits of a small crossover, and chronic-migraine patients were mixed into an episodic-migraine question. Absolute separation from placebo is about 0.6 migraine days a month.
cards.source: Stovner LJ et al. A comparative study of candesartan versus propranolol for migraine prophylaxis: A randomised, triple-blind, placebo-controlled, double cross-over study. Cephalalgia. 2014. PMID: 24335848. Registry ID: NCT00884663. cards.headline: Synthesis: an ARB that matches a beta-blocker, on crossover-trial evidence only
cards.summary: Synthesis: an ARB that matches a beta-blocker, on crossover-trial evidence only
cards.people: Two randomised double-blind crossover trials of candesartan 16 mg daily for migraine prevention: 60 patients versus placebo (Tronvik 2003) and 72 patients versus placebo and propranolol 160 mg (Stovner 2014).
cards.result: Headache days over 12 weeks: 13.6 versus 18.5 (Tronvik). Migraine days per month: 2.95 candesartan, 2.91 propranolol, 3.53 placebo (Stovner); responders 43%, 40% and 23% respectively. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C not set — two concordant randomised trials, both small.
cards.watchOut: Everyone in these trials could, in principle, detect blood-pressure-related side effects; and candesartan for migraine remains off-label in most jurisdictions, dosed here at the full antihypertensive 16 mg — hypotension-prone patients were not the study population.
cards.source: Synthesis of Tronvik E et al. JAMA. 2003 (PMID: 12503978); Stovner LJ et al. Cephalalgia. 2014 (PMID: 24335848).

shelves.title: Melatonin for migraine prevention splits by age: adults gained 2.7 fewer migraine days a month versus 1.1 on placebo — the children's trial found a difference of 0 days and closed early, underpowered
shelves.question: In migraine prevention, does melatonin reduce attack frequency versus placebo — in adults, and in children and adolescents?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Amitriptyline/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Melatonin/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Middle Aged · Migraine Disorders/prevention & control · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT — positive in adults, unproven in children. In adults, Gonçalves AL et al. (PMID: 27165014) randomised 196 patients with 2–8 attacks a month to melatonin 3 mg, amitriptyline 25 mg, or placebo for 3 months: headache frequency fell by 2.7 migraine days on melatonin, 2.2 on amitriptyline, and 1.1 on placebo, with melatonin significantly better than placebo (p=0.009) but not different from amitriptyline (p=0.19), and better tolerated. In children and adolescents, Gelfand AA et al. (PMID: 37466211) randomised just 42 patients aged 10–17 (the trial closed early for slow enrolment, aiming at 210): median migraine days in the final treatment weeks were 2 on melatonin and 2 on placebo, a difference in medians of 0 days (95% CI -9 to 3), with heavy missing diary data — a result the authors say should not be read as proof of inefficacy. PROPOSED SPLIT: melatonin 3 mg probably prevents migraine in adults about as well as low-dose amitriptyline with fewer side effects; in children the question remains open, not answered no.

cards.headline: Gonçalves 2016 (adults): migraine days fell 2.7 on melatonin 3 mg, 2.2 on amitriptyline 25 mg, 1.1 on placebo — melatonin beat placebo (p=0.009), matched amitriptyline (p=0.19), and was better tolerated
cards.summary: Gonçalves 2016 (adults): migraine days fell 2.7 on melatonin 3 mg, 2.2 on amitriptyline 25 mg, 1.1 on placebo — melatonin beat placebo (p=0.009), matched amitriptyline (p=0.19), and was better tolerated
cards.people: 196 men and women aged 18–65 years with migraine with or without aura and 2–8 attacks per month; after a 4-week baseline phase, randomised to placebo, amitriptyline 25 mg, or melatonin 3 mg nightly; 178 took a study medication and were followed for 3 months (12 weeks).
cards.result: Mean headache frequency reduction was 2.7 migraine headache days in the melatonin group, 2.2 for amitriptyline and 1.1 for placebo. Melatonin significantly reduced headache frequency compared with placebo (p=0.009), but not compared with amitriptyline (p=0.19). Melatonin was superior to amitriptyline in the percentage of patients with a greater than 50% reduction in migraine frequency, and was better tolerated; weight fell in the melatonin group and rose significantly in amitriptyline users.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre trial of 196 patients with a 3-month horizon, and the abstract does not print the responder percentages behind the 'superior to amitriptyline' claim, so that comparison is stated as the authors report it, without absolute rates. Melatonin here is a specific 3 mg nightly dose; supplement products vary.
cards.source: Gonçalves AL et al. Randomised clinical trial comparing melatonin 3 mg, amitriptyline 25 mg and placebo for migraine prevention. Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery, and Psychiatry. 2016. PMID: 27165014. cards.headline: Gelfand 2023 (children and adolescents): median migraine days 2 versus 2 — difference 0 days (95% CI -9 to 3); only 42 of a planned 210 randomised before the trial closed
cards.summary: Gelfand 2023 (children and adolescents): median migraine days 2 versus 2 — difference 0 days (95% CI -9 to 3); only 42 of a planned 210 randomised before the trial closed
cards.people: Children and adolescents aged 10–17 years with migraine and 4–28 headache days per 28 days, recruited from a university headache programme, child neurology clinic and social media; after an 8-week single-blind placebo run-in, 42 of 70 enrolled participants were randomised (14 per arm) to placebo, melatonin 3 mg, or melatonin 6 mg nightly for 8 weeks; the study closed early due to slow enrolment, having aimed for 210.
cards.result: Median migraine/migrainous days in weeks 5–8 of double-blind treatment was 2 (IQR 1–7) in the placebo group versus 2 (1–12) in the combined melatonin groups; the difference in medians was 0 days (95% CI -9 to 3). There was no suggestion of superiority of melatonin, and no differences in adverse events; melatonin was generally well tolerated with no serious adverse events. Only 27 of 42 randomised participants had enough diary data (at least 21 of 28 days) for the analysed set.
cards.watchOut: This is an underpowered null, not a negative answer: 42 randomised against a 210 target, 21% of run-in participants failing randomisation criteria, and missing data heavier in the placebo arm. The authors state explicitly that the result should not be interpreted as proof of inefficacy.
cards.source: Gelfand AA et al. Melatonin for migraine prevention in children and adolescents: A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial after single-blind placebo lead-in. Headache. 2023. PMID: 37466211. cards.headline: Synthesis: one adult win, one paediatric shrug — the split is the answer
cards.summary: Synthesis: one adult win, one paediatric shrug — the split is the answer
cards.people: One adult three-arm trial (196 randomised, melatonin 3 mg versus amitriptyline 25 mg versus placebo) and one paediatric trial (42 randomised of 210 planned, melatonin 3 or 6 mg versus placebo).
cards.result: Adults: migraine-day reduction 2.7 on melatonin versus 1.1 on placebo (p=0.009) and 2.2 on amitriptyline. Children: median migraine days 2 versus 2, difference 0 days (95% CI -9 to 3). PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C — the adult claim rests on a single trial and the paediatric trial is inconclusive.
cards.watchOut: Do not let the adult result prescribe for children, and do not let the child result veto the adult one — different populations, and one of the two trials simply did not finish. Dose and product consistency (3 mg) matter for applying the adult finding.
cards.source: Synthesis of Gonçalves AL et al. Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery, and Psychiatry. 2016 (PMID: 27165014); Gelfand AA et al. Headache. 2023 (PMID: 37466211).

shelves.title: Laser ablation versus open resection for mesial temporal lobe epilepsy: pooled data give open surgery the seizure-freedom edge (72.5% versus 57.1% beyond two years), laser the gentler recovery — all of it observational
shelves.question: In mesial temporal lobe epilepsy resistant to drugs, does MRI-guided laser interstitial thermal therapy match open resection on seizure freedom — and at what cost to memory and reoperation?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Epilepsy, Temporal Lobe/surgery · Retrospective Studies · Propensity Score · Treatment Outcome · Laser Therapy/methods · Drug Resistant Epilepsy/surgery · Magnetic Resonance Imaging/methods · Seizures · Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy · Lasers
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the trade-off is the finding, and no randomised trial exists. The meta-analysis by Ekman FR et al. (PMID: 39332763), pooling comparative studies with follow-up beyond 24 months, found seizure freedom in 72.5% after open temporal lobe resection versus 57.1% after MRI-guided laser interstitial thermal therapy (p<0.01), while minor (transient) complications were commoner with open surgery (9.9% versus 4.1%, p=0.04) and major complications did not differ (2.0% versus 2.7%). The propensity-matched cohort by Mo J et al. (PMID: 37800596) found no significant differences in memory preservation (p=0.95) or surgical outcomes (p=0.96) in 26 matched pairs — a much smaller, shorter comparison than the pooled analysis. Visual field deficits were frequent after both (79.4% open versus 49.8% laser in the meta-analysis, p=0.08, not significant). PROPOSED SPLIT: open resection probably buys more seizure freedom; laser ablation probably buys a gentler recovery; Tier C because every number here is observational and confounding by case selection runs in both directions.

cards.headline: Mo 2024: 26 propensity-matched pairs — no significant difference in memory preservation (p=0.95) or surgical outcomes (p=0.96) between laser ablation and open surgery
cards.summary: Mo 2024: 26 propensity-matched pairs — no significant difference in memory preservation (p=0.95) or surgical outcomes (p=0.96) between laser ablation and open surgery
cards.people: 244 patients with drug-resistant mesial temporal lobe epilepsy treated at three centres between 2015 and 2023 (33 MRI-guided laser interstitial thermal therapy, 211 open surgery); the primary propensity-matched analysis compared 26 matched pairs on demographic and non-invasive evaluation data, with a 32-pair sensitivity analysis matching additionally on stereoelectroencephalography implantation.
cards.result: There were no significant differences in memory preservation (p=0.95) or surgical outcomes (p=0.96) between the groups in the primary matched analysis, and the sensitivity analysis showed similar results. Subset analysis of early and late laser cases found no significant differences in memory decline (p=0.42) or seizure control (p=1.00). Patients who underwent stereoelectroencephalography implantation were 96% less likely to achieve seizure freedom after laser therapy (p=0.02).
cards.watchOut: Twenty-six matched pairs cannot exclude a clinically large seizure-freedom difference — 'no significant difference' here is absence of power, not evidence of equivalence. Laser patients were older at seizure onset (median 22.0 versus 12.3 years) before matching, the signature of selection that matching on recorded variables may not fully remove.
cards.source: Mo J et al. Magnetic resonance-guided laser interstitial thermal therapy vs. open surgery for drug-resistant mesial temporal lobe epilepsy: a propensity score matched retrospective cohort study. International Journal of Surgery. 2024. PMID: 37800596. cards.headline: Ekman 2024: seizure freedom beyond 24 months 72.5% with open resection versus 57.1% with laser ablation (p<0.01); minor complications 9.9% versus 4.1% (p=0.04); major complications 2.0% versus 2.7%
cards.summary: Ekman 2024: seizure freedom beyond 24 months 72.5% with open resection versus 57.1% with laser ablation (p<0.01); minor complications 9.9% versus 4.1% (p=0.04); major complications 2.0% versus 2.7%
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of comparative observational studies (Ekman 2024)
cards.people: Comparative studies of temporal lobe resection versus MRI-guided laser interstitial thermal therapy for mesial temporal lobe epilepsy, pooled for seizure outcomes at follow-up exceeding 24 months, visual field deficits by perimetry, and overall, minor (transient, under 6 months) and major (persistent, over 6 months) complication rates.
cards.result: For seizure freedom, open resection was superior: 72.5% (95% CI 65.6–78.5) of patients achieved postoperative seizure freedom compared with 57.1% (51.2–62.7) for laser ablation (p<0.01). Visual field deficits were observed in 79.4% (59.5–91.0) of resection patients and 49.8% (23.6–76.0) of laser patients (p=0.08, not significant). Overall complication rates were 11.4% (7.4–17.2) versus 6.5% (3.3–12.3) (p=0.15); major complications 2.0% (1.1–3.09) versus 2.7% (1.4–5.2) (p=0.54); minor complications were significantly more frequent with resection, 9.9% (6.4–15.0) versus 4.1% (1.9–8.4) (p=0.04). Laser ablation had a more favourable outcome on confrontation naming; the verbal-memory data were insufficient for firm conclusions.
cards.watchOut: Every pooled study is observational: patients offered laser ablation differ systematically (older, dominant-side concerns, comorbidity) from those offered resection, and the 15-point seizure-freedom gap could shrink or grow under randomisation. Follow-up beyond 24 months also selects for centres that report long-term data.
cards.source: Ekman FR et al. Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy versus Open Surgery for Mesial Temporal Lobe Epilepsy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. World Neurosurgery. 2024. cards.headline: Synthesis: choose the operation by which currency matters more — seizure freedom or recovery burden
cards.summary: Synthesis: choose the operation by which currency matters more — seizure freedom or recovery burden
cards.people: One propensity-matched retrospective cohort (244 patients, 26 primary matched pairs; Mo 2024) and one meta-analysis of comparative observational studies with follow-up beyond 24 months (Ekman 2024). No randomised trial of laser ablation versus open resection exists in this record.
cards.result: Seizure freedom: 72.5% open resection versus 57.1% laser ablation in the pooled analysis (p<0.01); no significant difference in the small matched cohort (p=0.96). Minor complications: 9.9% versus 4.1% (p=0.04); major complications: 2.0% versus 2.7% (not significant). Memory: no significant difference in the matched cohort (p=0.95); naming favoured laser ablation in the meta-analysis. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C — observational evidence only.
cards.watchOut: Reoperation and repeat-ablation rates — part of the question — are not reported in either record's abstract, so the shelf cannot price laser ablation's 'second chance' pathway. A randomised trial in dominant-side mesial temporal lobe epilepsy is the study this literature needs.
cards.source: Synthesis of Mo J et al. International Journal of Surgery. 2024 (PMID: 37800596); Ekman FR et al. World Neurosurgery. 2024 (PMID: 39332763).

shelves.title: Modified Atkins diet for drug-resistant epilepsy: at least half of seizures gone in 26.2% versus 2.5% on drugs alone at six months in the randomised trial — and a paediatric network meta-analysis at odds ratio 11.3
shelves.question: In adults with drug-resistant epilepsy, does a modified Atkins diet reduce seizure frequency versus control diet?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Child · Adolescent · Humans · Quality of Life · Diet, High-Protein Low-Carbohydrate · Prospective Studies · Treatment Outcome · Drug Resistant Epilepsy/drug therapy · Seizures · Diet, Ketogenic · Epilepsy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a striking responder gap in one open trial, backed by the paediatric diet-therapy literature. Manral M et al. (PMID: 36599697) randomised 160 adolescents and adults with drug-resistant epilepsy to a modified Atkins diet plus standard drug therapy or standard therapy alone: at 6 months, a greater than 50% seizure reduction occurred in 26.2% on the diet versus 2.5% on drugs alone (95% CI for the difference 13.5 to 33.9; p<0.001), and quality of life improved more (mean difference 9.6 points, 95% CI 4.3 to 14.9). The network meta-analysis by Devi N et al. (PMID: 36716045) — 12 randomised trials, 907 children — found the modified Atkins diet more efficacious than care as usual for at least 50% seizure reduction in the short term (odds ratio 11.3, 95% CI 5.1 to 25.1), with adverse-event discontinuation also raised (odds ratio 6.5, 1.4 to 31.2). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for drug-resistant epilepsy, adding a modified Atkins diet gives roughly one in four patients a halving of seizures within six months, against roughly one in forty without it — in trials that cannot be blinded.

cards.headline: Manral 2023: >50% seizure reduction in 26.2% on modified Atkins plus drugs versus 2.5% on drugs alone (p<0.001); quality of life better by 9.6 points
cards.summary: Manral 2023: >50% seizure reduction in 26.2% on modified Atkins plus drugs versus 2.5% on drugs alone (p<0.001); quality of life better by 9.6 points
cards.people: 160 adolescents and adults (80 adults, 80 adolescents) aged 10–55 years with drug-resistant epilepsy at a tertiary referral centre in India — more than 2 seizures per month despite at least 3 appropriate antiseizure medications at maximum tolerated doses, and no diet therapy in the past year — randomised to standard drug therapy plus modified Atkins diet or standard drug therapy alone for 6 months; intention-to-treat analysis.
cards.result: At 6 months, a greater than 50% reduction in seizure frequency was seen in 26.2% in the intervention group versus 2.5% in the control group (95% CI 13.5–33.9; p<0.001). Quality of life improved more on the diet (52.1 ± 17.6 versus 42.5 ± 16.4; mean difference 9.6; 95% CI 4.3 to 14.9; p<0.001), and behaviour scores improved in the 49 patients assessed. Adverse events were few: one patient had weight loss and two had diarrhoea.
cards.watchOut: A diet trial cannot be blinded, and seizure counts are diary-reported — expectation effects run with the intervention. The journal classifies this as Class III evidence, it is a single-centre trial, and the control arm's 2.5% responder rate is unusually low, which widens the contrast. Adherence beyond 6 months is the known failure mode of dietary therapy and is outside this record.
cards.source: Manral M et al. Safety, Efficacy, and Tolerability of Modified Atkins Diet in Persons With Drug-Resistant Epilepsy: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Neurology. 2023. PMID: 36599697. Registry ID: CTRI/2015/07/006048. cards.headline: Devi 2023: across 12 randomised trials in children, modified Atkins beat care as usual for ≥50% seizure reduction (OR 11.3) and ≥90% reduction (OR 5.1) — with adverse-event discontinuation OR 6.5
cards.summary: Devi 2023: across 12 randomised trials in children, modified Atkins beat care as usual for ≥50% seizure reduction (OR 11.3) and ≥90% reduction (OR 5.1) — with adverse-event discontinuation OR 6.5
cards.type: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised trials (Devi 2023)
cards.people: 12 randomised clinical trials (907 patients) in childhood drug-resistant epilepsy comparing ketogenic diet, modified Atkins diet, and low glycaemic index therapy with each other or with care as usual (literature to April 2022); primary outcomes were short-term (up to 3 months) seizure reductions of at least 50% and at least 90%, and withdrawal due to adverse events.
cards.result: In the short term, all dietary interventions were more efficacious than care as usual for at least 50% seizure reduction (low glycaemic index therapy: odds ratio 24.7 [95% CI 5.3–115.4]; modified Atkins diet: OR 11.3 [95% CI 5.1–25.1]; ketogenic diet: OR 8.6 [3.7–20.0]). For at least 90% reduction, ketogenic diet (OR 6.5 [2.3–18.0]) and modified Atkins diet (OR 5.1 [2.2–12.0]) beat care as usual. Adverse-event-related discontinuation was significantly higher for ketogenic diet (OR 8.6 [1.8–40.6]) and modified Atkins diet (OR 6.5 [1.4–31.2]). Indirectly, no dietary therapy differed significantly from another in efficacy or safety, and the modified Atkins diet had better tolerability than the ketogenic diet.
cards.watchOut: This card is children, short-term (up to 3 months), and odds ratios from small trials — OR 11.3 overstates the risk ratio when control response is not rare, which is why the adult shelf rests on Manral's absolute rates (26.2% versus 2.5%). It corroborates the diet class; it does not independently prove the adult effect.
cards.source: Devi N et al. Efficacy and Safety of Dietary Therapies for Childhood Drug-Resistant Epilepsy: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-analysis. JAMA Pediatrics. 2023. PMID: 36716045. cards.headline: Synthesis: one in four versus one in forty — a large responder gap that blinding cannot explain away entirely, and cannot confirm either
cards.summary: Synthesis: one in four versus one in forty — a large responder gap that blinding cannot explain away entirely, and cannot confirm either
cards.people: One randomised trial in adolescents and adults (160 patients, 6 months; Manral 2023) and one network meta-analysis of 12 randomised trials in children (907 patients; Devi 2023).
cards.result: Greater than 50% seizure reduction: 26.2% with modified Atkins plus drugs versus 2.5% with drugs alone at 6 months. Paediatric short-term odds ratio for the same outcome: 11.3 (95% CI 5.1–25.1) versus care as usual; adverse-event discontinuation odds ratio 6.5 (1.4–31.2). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C not set — randomised evidence in two age groups, honestly fenced for the absence of blinding.
cards.watchOut: Dietary trials recruit motivated families and patients; the effect in an unselected clinic population will be smaller, driven by adherence. Lipids, growth (in adolescents) and kidney-stone risk need monitoring that these short trials barely capture.
cards.source: Synthesis of Manral M et al. Neurology. 2023 (PMID: 36599697); Devi N et al. JAMA Pediatrics. 2023 (PMID: 36716045).

shelves.title: High-intensity treadmill exercise in new Parkinson's: motor scores stood still (change 0.3) while usual care worsened (3.2) over six months in the SPARX phase 2 trial — enough to justify a phase 3, not enough to claim disease modification
shelves.question: In de novo Parkinson's disease with motor symptoms, does high-intensity treadmill exercise slow motor progression versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Exercise Test/methods · Exercise Therapy/methods · Female · High-Intensity Interval Training · Humans · Longitudinal Studies · Male · Middle Aged · Parkinson Disease/physiopathology/therapy · Retrospective Studies · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a phase 2 nonfutility signal, honestly labelled. In SPARX (Schenkman M et al., PMID: 29228079), 128 patients with de novo Parkinson disease (Hoehn and Yahr stages 1–2, not yet on dopaminergic medication) were randomised to high-intensity treadmill exercise (80–85% of maximum heart rate, 4 days a week), moderate-intensity exercise (60–65%), or wait-list usual care for 6 months. The mean change in Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale motor score was 0.3 (95% CI -1.7 to 2.3) in the high-intensity group versus 3.2 (1.4 to 5.1) in the usual-care group (p=0.03); the high-intensity group, but not the moderate-intensity group, met the predefined nonfutility threshold. Patients actually exercised 2.8 days per week at 80.2% of maximum heart rate in the high-intensity arm, and anticipated musculoskeletal adverse events were not severe. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): high-intensity treadmill exercise may slow early motor progression; Tier C because this is a single phase 2 trial designed to justify — not replace — a phase 3 efficacy trial.

cards.headline: SPARX (Schenkman 2018): UPDRS motor change 0.3 on high-intensity treadmill versus 3.2 on usual care (p=0.03); moderate intensity did not reach nonfutility; adherence 2.8 days/week at 80.2% of maximum heart rate
cards.summary: SPARX (Schenkman 2018): UPDRS motor change 0.3 on high-intensity treadmill versus 3.2 on usual care (p=0.03); moderate intensity did not reach nonfutility; adherence 2.8 days/week at 80.2% of maximum heart rate
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised clinical trial with masked assessors (SPARX)
cards.people: 128 patients with idiopathic Parkinson disease (Hoehn and Yahr stages 1–2; mean age 64 years; 57.0% male) within 5 years of diagnosis, not exercising at moderate intensity more than 3 times weekly and not expected to need dopaminergic medication within 6 months, randomised to high-intensity treadmill exercise (n=43; 80–85% maximum heart rate, 4 days/week), moderate-intensity exercise (n=45; 60–65%), or wait-list control (n=40) for 6 months, enrolled 2012–2015.
cards.result: Exercise rates were 2.8 (95% CI 2.4–3.2) days per week at 80.2% (78.8–81.7%) of maximum heart rate in the high-intensity group and 3.2 (2.8–3.6) days per week at 65.9% (64.2–67.7%) in the moderate group. The mean change in Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale motor score was 0.3 (95% CI -1.7 to 2.3) in the high-intensity group compared with 3.2 (1.4 to 5.1) in the usual-care group (p=0.03). The high-intensity group, but not the moderate-intensity group, reached the predefined nonfutility threshold compared with control. Anticipated adverse musculoskeletal events were not severe.
cards.watchOut: Nonfutility is a screening design: it asks 'not obviously useless', not 'proven'. Six months in untreated early disease, a wait-list control (no attention matching), and exercise that cannot be blinded all soften the p=0.03. Whether the effect is disease modification or better fitness expressing itself on a motor scale is exactly what a phase 3 must separate.
cards.source: Schenkman M et al. Effect of High-Intensity Treadmill Exercise on Motor Symptoms in Patients With De Novo Parkinson Disease: A Phase 2 Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Neurology. 2018. PMID: 29228079. Registry ID: NCT01506479. shelves.title: Lixisenatide in early Parkinson's: motor disability scores improved by -0.04 points while placebo worsened by 3.04 over 12 months (difference 3.08) in LIXIPARK — with nausea in 46% and vomiting in 13%
shelves.question: In early Parkinson's disease, does the GLP-1 agonist lixisenatide slow motor disability progression versus placebo over 12 months?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Antiparkinson Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Persons with Disabilities · Double-Blind Method · Motor Disorders/drug therapy · Parkinson Disease/drug therapy · Peptides/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Disease Progression · Neuroprotective Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Injections, Subcutaneous · Glucagon-Like Peptide-2 Receptor
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one positive phase 2 trial, read alongside the class's phase 3 failure elsewhere in this library. In LIXIPARK (Meissner WG et al., PMID: 38598572), 156 patients with Parkinson disease diagnosed less than 3 years earlier, on stable symptomatic medication and without motor complications, received daily subcutaneous lixisenatide or placebo for 12 months: Movement Disorder Society UPDRS part III scores changed by -0.04 points on lixisenatide versus 3.04 points of worsening on placebo (difference 3.08; 95% CI 0.86 to 5.30; p=0.007), assessed in the on-medication state. After a 2-month washout, off-medication motor scores were 17.7 on lixisenatide versus 20.6 on placebo. The cost was gastrointestinal: nausea in 46% and vomiting in 13% of the lixisenatide group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): lixisenatide slowed measured motor progression over one year in early Parkinson disease; Tier C — a single phase 2 trial, and the related exenatide programme's phase 3 was null, so replication is the whole question.

cards.headline: LIXIPARK (Meissner 2024): MDS-UPDRS part III change -0.04 on lixisenatide versus +3.04 on placebo (difference 3.08, p=0.007); after washout, off-state scores 17.7 versus 20.6; nausea 46%, vomiting 13%
cards.summary: LIXIPARK (Meissner 2024): MDS-UPDRS part III change -0.04 on lixisenatide versus +3.04 on placebo (difference 3.08, p=0.007); after washout, off-state scores 17.7 versus 20.6; nausea 46%, vomiting 13%
cards.people: 156 persons with Parkinson disease diagnosed less than 3 years earlier, receiving a stable dose of symptomatic medication and without motor complications, randomised 1:1 (78 per group) to daily subcutaneous lixisenatide or placebo for 12 months, followed by a 2-month washout; baseline MDS-UPDRS part III scores were approximately 15 in both groups; the primary endpoint was change in part III score in the on-medication state at 12 months.
cards.result: At 12 months, MDS-UPDRS part III scores had changed by -0.04 points (improvement) in the lixisenatide group and 3.04 points (worsening) in the placebo group (difference 3.08; 95% CI 0.86 to 5.30; p=0.007). At 14 months, after the 2-month washout, mean off-medication MDS-UPDRS motor scores were 17.7 (95% CI 15.7 to 19.7) with lixisenatide and 20.6 (18.5 to 22.8) with placebo. Other secondary endpoints did not differ substantially between groups. Nausea occurred in 46% of participants receiving lixisenatide and vomiting in 13%.
cards.watchOut: A 3-point difference on a 132-point scale over 12 months, in one phase 2 trial, with nearly half the treatment group nauseated — a side effect that can partly unblind and that itself alters eating, weight and possibly motor performance. The persistence after washout argues against a purely symptomatic effect but does not prove disease modification; the authors themselves call for longer and larger trials.

shelves.title: Tai chi in Parkinson's: balance measures beat both resistance training and stretching in one 195-patient trial, and falls fell versus stretching — but not versus resistance training
shelves.question: In Parkinson's disease, does tai chi improve postural stability and reduce falls versus resistance training or stretching?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Gait · Humans · Male · Muscle Stretching Exercises · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Parkinson Disease/physiopathology/therapy · Postural Balance · Resistance Training · Tai Ji
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one well-conducted trial, with the falls claim fenced to the weaker comparator. Li F et al. (PMID: 22316445) randomised 195 patients with Hoehn and Yahr stage 1–4 Parkinson disease to tai chi, resistance training, or stretching, in 60-minute sessions twice weekly for 24 weeks. On the primary limits-of-stability outcomes, tai chi beat both comparators: maximum excursion improved by 5.55 percentage points more than resistance training (95% CI 1.12 to 9.97) and 11.98 points more than stretching (7.21 to 16.74), with directional control ahead by 10.45 and 11.38 points respectively. Tai chi also beat stretching on all secondary outcomes and beat resistance training on stride length and functional reach. Falls were fewer with tai chi than with stretching, but not significantly fewer than with resistance training; effects persisted 3 months after the intervention ended, and no serious adverse events occurred. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): tai chi improves postural stability in mild-to-moderate Parkinson disease; Tier C because a single trial carries the shelf and the falls result is comparator-dependent.

cards.headline: Li 2012: maximum excursion +5.55 points versus resistance training and +11.98 versus stretching; directional control +10.45 and +11.38; falls lower than stretching, not lower than resistance training
cards.summary: Li 2012: maximum excursion +5.55 points versus resistance training and +11.98 versus stretching; directional control +10.45 and +11.38; falls lower than stretching, not lower than resistance training
cards.people: 195 patients with idiopathic Parkinson disease, Hoehn and Yahr stages 1 to 4, randomly assigned to tai chi, resistance training, or stretching, each delivered as 60-minute sessions twice weekly for 24 weeks; primary outcomes were change in limits-of-stability measures (maximum excursion and directional control, range 0–100%); follow-up included a 3-month post-intervention assessment.
cards.result: The tai chi group performed consistently better than the resistance-training and stretching groups in maximum excursion (between-group difference in change from baseline: 5.55 percentage points, 95% CI 1.12 to 9.97, versus resistance training; 11.98 points, 7.21 to 16.74, versus stretching) and in directional control (10.45 points, 3.89 to 17.00; and 11.38 points, 5.50 to 17.27, respectively). Tai chi beat stretching on all secondary outcomes and beat resistance training on stride length and functional reach. Tai chi lowered the incidence of falls compared with stretching but not compared with resistance training. Effects were maintained 3 months after the intervention; no serious adverse events were observed.
cards.watchOut: Exercise trials cannot blind participants, and the laboratory balance measures (limits of stability) are surrogates — the patient-important outcome, falls, separated tai chi only from the weakest comparator. One trial, one tai chi protocol (a tailored programme), one country's instructors: replication and protocol fidelity are open questions.
cards.source: Li F et al. Tai chi and postural stability in patients with Parkinson's disease. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2012. PMID: 22316445. Registry ID: NCT00611481. shelves.title: LSVT LOUD for Parkinson's dysarthria: voice handicap scores 8.0 points better than no therapy and 9.6 better than standard NHS speech therapy in PD COMM — while standard therapy itself showed no benefit over none
shelves.question: In Parkinson's disease with dysarthria, does Lee Silverman Voice Treatment (LSVT LOUD) improve voice and communication versus NHS speech therapy or no treatment?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Dysarthria/etiology/therapy/rehabilitation · Language Therapy/methods · Parkinson Disease/complications · Speech Therapy/methods · State Medicine · Treatment Outcome · United Kingdom · Voice Training
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large pragmatic trial with an uncomfortable second finding. In PD COMM (Sackley CM et al., PMID: 38986549), 388 people with Parkinson disease and dysarthria were randomised to LSVT LOUD (four 50-minute sessions a week for four weeks, plus home practice), standard NHS speech and language therapy, or no therapy. At 3 months, self-reported Voice Handicap Index scores were lower (better) with LSVT LOUD than with no therapy by -8.0 points (99% CI -13.3 to -2.6; p<0.001) and lower than with NHS therapy by -9.6 points (-14.9 to -4.4; p<0.001) — while NHS therapy showed no evidence of difference from no therapy (1.7 points, -3.8 to 7.1; p=0.43). Adverse events, predominantly vocal strain, numbered 93 in the LSVT LOUD group, 46 in the NHS group and none in the no-therapy group, with no serious adverse events. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the intensive, protocolised LSVT LOUD programme — a named non-drug programme — improves patient-reported voice handicap where usual-dose therapy did not; Tier C as a single unblinded trial with a self-reported endpoint.

cards.headline: PD COMM (Sackley 2024): Voice Handicap Index at 3 months -8.0 points for LSVT LOUD versus no therapy and -9.6 versus NHS therapy; NHS therapy versus none +1.7 (p=0.43); vocal-strain events 93 versus 46 versus 0
cards.summary: PD COMM (Sackley 2024): Voice Handicap Index at 3 months -8.0 points for LSVT LOUD versus no therapy and -9.6 versus NHS therapy; NHS therapy versus none +1.7 (p=0.43); vocal-strain events 93 versus 46 versus 0
cards.type: Pragmatic multicentre three-arm unblinded randomised controlled trial (PD COMM)
cards.people: 388 people with Parkinson disease and dysarthria in the UK, randomly assigned 1:1:1 to LSVT LOUD (130; four face-to-face or remote 50-minute sessions weekly over four weeks, plus daily home practice), NHS speech and language therapy (129; dose set by the local therapist, estimated at about one session weekly over six to eight weeks), or no speech and language therapy (129); interventions delivered in outpatient or home settings, 2016–2020; primary outcome was the self-reported Voice Handicap Index total score at 3 months, analysed by intention to treat.
cards.result: People who received LSVT LOUD reported lower Voice Handicap Index scores at 3 months than those who received no therapy (-8.0 points, 99% CI -13.3 to -2.6; p<0.001) and than those randomised to NHS speech and language therapy (-9.6 points, -14.9 to -4.4; p<0.001). There was no evidence of a difference between NHS therapy and no therapy (1.7 points, -3.8 to 7.1; p=0.43). Ninety-three adverse events (predominantly vocal strain) were reported in the LSVT LOUD group, 46 in the NHS group, and none in the no-therapy group; no serious adverse events were recorded.
cards.watchOut: Unblinded, with a self-reported primary outcome and a fourfold difference in treatment intensity between the two therapy arms — PD COMM cannot separate 'LSVT LOUD the method' from 'LSVT LOUD the dose'. The null for usual NHS therapy may be a dose finding as much as a method finding. LSVT LOUD is a named, certified programme; delivery by uncertified therapists is not the tested intervention.

shelves.title: Ublituximab versus teriflunomide in relapsing multiple sclerosis: relapse rates roughly halved in both ULTIMATE trials (0.08–0.09 versus 0.18–0.19 a year) and MRI lesions nearly abolished — disability worsening not significantly different
shelves.question: In relapsing multiple sclerosis, does ublituximab reduce relapses and MRI lesions versus teriflunomide?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal/therapeutic use · Crotonates · Double-Blind Method · Gadolinium/therapeutic use · Humans · Hydroxybutyrates · Immunosuppressive Agents/therapeutic use · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Multiple Sclerosis/complications/diagnostic imaging/drug therapy/pathology · Multiple Sclerosis, Relapsing-Remitting/complications/diagnostic imaging/drug therapy/pathology · Nitriles · Toluidines
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two identical twin trials, concordant on relapses and lesions, null on disability. In ULTIMATE I (Steinman L et al., PMID: 36001711), the annualised relapse rate was 0.08 on ublituximab versus 0.19 on teriflunomide (rate ratio 0.41, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.62; p<0.001); in ULTIMATE II, 0.09 versus 0.18 (rate ratio 0.51, 0.33 to 0.78; p=0.002). Mean gadolinium-enhancing lesions numbered 0.02 versus 0.49 in ULTIMATE I and 0.01 versus 0.25 in ULTIMATE II. But pooled 12-week confirmed disability worsening was 5.2% on ublituximab versus 5.9% on teriflunomide (hazard ratio 0.84, 0.50 to 1.41; p=0.51) — not significant. Infusion-related reactions occurred in 47.7% of the ublituximab group, and serious infections in 5.0% versus 2.9%. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): ublituximab suppresses relapses and MRI activity more than teriflunomide over 96 weeks; a disability advantage was not shown.

cards.headline: ULTIMATE I: annualised relapse rate 0.08 versus 0.19 (rate ratio 0.41); gadolinium-enhancing lesions 0.02 versus 0.49 (rate ratio 0.03)
cards.summary: ULTIMATE I: annualised relapse rate 0.08 versus 0.19 (rate ratio 0.41); gadolinium-enhancing lesions 0.02 versus 0.49 (rate ratio 0.03)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind double-dummy phase 3 trial (ULTIMATE I)
cards.people: 549 participants with relapsing multiple sclerosis, randomised 1:1 to intravenous ublituximab (150 mg on day 1, 450 mg on day 15 and at weeks 24, 48 and 72) plus oral placebo, or oral teriflunomide 14 mg daily plus intravenous placebo; median follow-up 95 weeks; primary endpoint was the annualised relapse rate, with MRI lesions by 96 weeks and disability worsening as secondary endpoints.
cards.result: The annualised relapse rate was 0.08 with ublituximab and 0.19 with teriflunomide (rate ratio 0.41; 95% CI 0.27 to 0.62; p<0.001). The mean number of gadolinium-enhancing lesions was 0.02 in the ublituximab group and 0.49 in the teriflunomide group (rate ratio 0.03; 95% CI 0.02 to 0.06; p<0.001).
cards.watchOut: Teriflunomide is a mid-efficacy oral comparator, not the high-efficacy infusion standard — beating it on relapses and lesions was the expected result for a B-cell-depleting antibody, and no comparison with ocrelizumab or ofatumumab exists in this record. Ninety-six weeks is short for disability in relapsing multiple sclerosis.
cards.source: Steinman L et al. Ublituximab versus Teriflunomide in Relapsing Multiple Sclerosis. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2022. PMID: 36001711. Registry ID: NCT03277261, NCT03277248. cards.headline: ULTIMATE II: annualised relapse rate 0.09 versus 0.18 (rate ratio 0.51); lesions 0.01 versus 0.25 (rate ratio 0.04); pooled disability worsening 5.2% versus 5.9% (HR 0.84, not significant)
cards.summary: ULTIMATE II: annualised relapse rate 0.09 versus 0.18 (rate ratio 0.51); lesions 0.01 versus 0.25 (rate ratio 0.04); pooled disability worsening 5.2% versus 5.9% (HR 0.84, not significant)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind double-dummy phase 3 trial (ULTIMATE II)
cards.people: 545 participants with relapsing multiple sclerosis, randomised with the identical design to ULTIMATE I (intravenous ublituximab plus oral placebo versus oral teriflunomide 14 mg plus intravenous placebo); median follow-up 95 weeks.
cards.result: The annualised relapse rate was 0.09 with ublituximab and 0.18 with teriflunomide (rate ratio 0.51; 95% CI 0.33 to 0.78; p=0.002). The mean number of gadolinium-enhancing lesions was 0.01 and 0.25 respectively (rate ratio 0.04; 95% CI 0.02 to 0.06; p<0.001). In the pooled analysis of both trials, 5.2% of the ublituximab group and 5.9% of the teriflunomide group had worsening of disability at 12 weeks (hazard ratio 0.84; 95% CI 0.50 to 1.41; p=0.51). Infusion-related reactions occurred in 47.7% of ublituximab participants; serious infections occurred in 5.0% versus 2.9%.
cards.watchOut: The disability null is pooled across both trials and printed here, on the twin trial's card, so it cannot be missed: relapse and lesion suppression did not translate into significantly less confirmed worsening over 96 weeks.
