shelves.title: Clemastine in multiple sclerosis: visual evoked potential latency shortened by 1.7 ms per eye in the 50-patient ReBUILD crossover — the first randomised remyelination signal, on a surrogate, with fatigue as the price
shelves.question: In multiple sclerosis with chronic optic neuropathy, does clemastine fumarate improve visual evoked potential latency — the first remyelination signal in a randomised trial?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Clemastine/therapeutic use · Cross-Over Studies · Double-Blind Method · Evoked Potentials, Visual/drug effects · Female · Humans · Male · Multiple Sclerosis/drug therapy · Remyelination/drug effects · Tomography, Optical Coherence · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a genuine first, at surrogate scale. In ReBUILD (Green AJ et al., PMID: 29029896), 50 patients with relapsing multiple sclerosis and chronic demyelinating optic neuropathy, on stable immunomodulatory therapy, were randomised in a double-blind crossover to clemastine fumarate 5.36 mg twice daily and placebo in sequence over 150 days. The primary endpoint was met: clemastine reduced the P100 visual evoked potential latency delay by 1.7 ms per eye (95% CI 0.5 to 2.9; p=0.0048) in the crossover analysis. Clemastine treatment was associated with fatigue; no serious adverse events were reported. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): clemastine produced the first randomised evidence that a drug can improve a remyelination marker in chronic multiple sclerosis lesions — 1.7 milliseconds on an evoked potential, not a demonstrated gain in vision or function; Tier C for a single small single-centre trial on a surrogate endpoint.

cards.headline: ReBUILD (Green 2017): P100 latency delay shortened by 1.7 ms/eye (95% CI 0.5–2.9; p=0.0048) on clemastine; fatigue the associated adverse effect; no serious adverse events
cards.summary: ReBUILD (Green 2017): P100 latency delay shortened by 1.7 ms/eye (95% CI 0.5–2.9; p=0.0048) on clemastine; fatigue the associated adverse effect; no serious adverse events
cards.people: 50 patients with relapsing multiple sclerosis and chronic demyelinating optic neuropathy, on stable immunomodulatory therapy, with disease duration under 15 years, at a single centre; randomised 1:1 (25 per group) to clemastine fumarate 5.36 mg orally twice daily for 90 days then placebo for 60 days, or placebo for 90 days then clemastine for 60 days, over 150 days; all patients completed the study; the primary outcome was shortening of P100 latency delay on full-field pattern-reversal visual evoked potentials, analysed by intention to treat.
cards.result: The primary efficacy endpoint was met: clemastine fumarate treatment reduced the latency delay by 1.7 ms/eye (95% CI 0.5–2.9; p=0.0048) when the trial was analysed as a crossover. Clemastine treatment was associated with fatigue, but no serious adverse events were reported. The authors describe this as the first randomised controlled trial to document efficacy of a remyelinating drug for chronic demyelinating injury in multiple sclerosis.
cards.watchOut: Latency is a conduction surrogate: 1.7 ms is statistically robust here and biologically suggestive, but ReBUILD does not show that patients saw better, and a 50-patient single-centre crossover cannot carry a clinical claim. Clemastine is a sedating first-generation antihistamine used at 5.36 mg twice daily — well above over-the-counter allergy doses — and fatigue in multiple sclerosis is already a dominant symptom.
cards.source: Green AJ et al. Clemastine fumarate as a remyelinating therapy for multiple sclerosis (ReBUILD): a randomised, controlled, double-blind, crossover trial. The Lancet. 2017. shelves.title: Ozanimod versus weekly interferon beta-1a in relapsing multiple sclerosis: relapse rates 0.18 versus 0.35 a year in SUNBEAM and 0.17 versus 0.28 over two years in RADIANCE at the 1 mg dose
shelves.question: In relapsing multiple sclerosis, does ozanimod reduce relapses versus weekly interferon beta-1a?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Atrioventricular Block/chemically induced · Bradycardia/chemically induced · Brain/pathology · Cognition Disorders/etiology · Disease Progression · Female · Gray Matter/pathology · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Indans/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Interferon beta-1a/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Male · Middle Aged · Multiple Sclerosis, Relapsing-Remitting/drug therapy/pathology/psychology · Neuroimaging · Organ Size · Oxadiazoles/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Quality of Life · Severity of Illness Index · Sphingosine-1-Phosphate Receptors/antagonists & inhibitors
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two phase 3 trials, one result. In SUNBEAM (Comi G et al., PMID: 31492651; 1,346 participants, at least 12 months), the adjusted annualised relapse rate was 0.18 on ozanimod 1.0 mg versus 0.35 on weekly intramuscular interferon beta-1a (rate ratio 0.52, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.66; p<0.0001), and 0.24 on the 0.5 mg dose (rate ratio 0.69, 0.55 to 0.86). In RADIANCE (Cohen JA et al., PMID: 31492652; 1,320 participants, 24 months), the adjusted rates were 0.17 on ozanimod 1.0 mg versus 0.28 on interferon (rate ratio 0.62, 0.51 to 0.77; p<0.0001), and 0.22 on 0.5 mg (rate ratio 0.79, 0.65 to 0.96). No first-dose clinically significant bradycardia or second- or third-degree atrioventricular block was reported in SUNBEAM. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): ozanimod roughly halves the relapse rate of weekly interferon beta-1a — against a comparator the field already regards as modest-efficacy.

cards.headline: SUNBEAM (Comi 2019): annualised relapse rate 0.18 on ozanimod 1.0 mg and 0.24 on 0.5 mg versus 0.35 on interferon beta-1a (rate ratios 0.52 and 0.69); no first-dose significant bradycardia or high-grade AV block
cards.summary: SUNBEAM (Comi 2019): annualised relapse rate 0.18 on ozanimod 1.0 mg and 0.24 on 0.5 mg versus 0.35 on interferon beta-1a (rate ratios 0.52 and 0.69); no first-dose significant bradycardia or high-grade AV block
cards.people: 1,346 participants aged 18–55 years with relapsing multiple sclerosis (EDSS 0.0–5.0, with a relapse in the prior 12 months, or a relapse within 24 months plus a gadolinium-enhancing lesion within 12 months) at 152 centres in 20 countries, randomised 1:1:1 to once-daily oral ozanimod 1.0 mg (n=447), ozanimod 0.5 mg (n=451), or weekly intramuscular interferon beta-1a 30 µg (n=448) for at least 12 months; 91 participants (6.8%) discontinued the study drug.
cards.result: Adjusted annualised relapse rates were 0.35 (95% CI 0.28–0.44) for interferon beta-1a, 0.18 (0.14–0.24) for ozanimod 1.0 mg (rate ratio 0.52 [0.41–0.66] versus interferon; p<0.0001), and 0.24 (0.19–0.31) for ozanimod 0.5 mg (rate ratio 0.69 [0.55–0.86]; p=0.0013). Few participants discontinued because of adverse events (2.9% on ozanimod 1.0 mg, 1.5% on 0.5 mg, 3.6% on interferon). No first-dose, clinically significant bradycardia or second-degree or third-degree atrioventricular block was reported.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is weekly intramuscular interferon beta-1a — among the weakest disease-modifying therapies in current use — so 'half the relapses of interferon' is a lower bar than comparison with high-efficacy agents. Minimum 12-month follow-up cannot speak to disability accumulation or long-term S1P-modulator risks.

cards.headline: RADIANCE (Cohen 2019): over 24 months, annualised relapse rate 0.17 on ozanimod 1.0 mg and 0.22 on 0.5 mg versus 0.28 on interferon beta-1a (rate ratios 0.62 and 0.79)
cards.summary: RADIANCE (Cohen 2019): over 24 months, annualised relapse rate 0.17 on ozanimod 1.0 mg and 0.22 on 0.5 mg versus 0.28 on interferon beta-1a (rate ratios 0.62 and 0.79)
cards.people: 1,320 participants aged 18–55 years with relapsing multiple sclerosis (2010 McDonald criteria, EDSS 0.0–5.0, recent clinical or MRI activity) at 147 centres in 21 countries, randomised 1:1:1 to daily oral ozanimod 1.0 mg (433 treated), ozanimod 0.5 mg (439), or weekly intramuscular interferon beta-1a 30 µg (441) for 24 months; 1,138 participants (86.7%) completed 24 months of treatment.
cards.result: Adjusted annualised relapse rates were 0.17 (95% CI 0.14–0.21) with ozanimod 1.0 mg, 0.22 (0.18–0.26) with ozanimod 0.5 mg, and 0.28 (0.23–0.32) with interferon beta-1a, with rate ratios versus interferon of 0.62 (95% CI 0.51–0.77; p<0.0001) for 1.0 mg and 0.79 (0.65 to 0.96; p=0.0167) for 0.5 mg. The incidence of treatment-emergent adverse events was higher in the interferon beta-1a group (365 of 440 participants [83.0%]) than in the ozanimod groups, per the record's report.
cards.watchOut: A 24-month relapse endpoint in a young, relapsing population; the trial was not powered to settle disability progression, and the marketed dose is the 0.92 mg salt equivalent of the 1.0 mg tested dose — a labelling subtlety prescribers meet in practice. Ozanimod's ulcerative colitis evidence sits on its own shelf elsewhere in the library; this shelf is multiple sclerosis only.

shelves.title: Ponesimod versus teriflunomide in relapsing multiple sclerosis: relapses 0.202 versus 0.290 a year (a 30.5% relative rate reduction) and 56% fewer active MRI lesions in OPTIMUM — confirmed disability accumulation not significantly different
shelves.question: In relapsing multiple sclerosis, does ponesimod reduce relapses versus teriflunomide?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Crotonates/pharmacology · Disease Progression · Female · Humans · Hydroxybutyrates/pharmacology · Immunologic Factors/therapeutic use · Magnetic Resonance Imaging/methods · Male · Middle Aged · Multiple Sclerosis, Relapsing-Remitting/drug therapy · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local/drug therapy · Nitriles/pharmacology · Thiazoles/pharmacology · Toluidines/pharmacology · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large active-comparator trial. In OPTIMUM (Kappos L et al., PMID: 33779698), 1,133 patients with relapsing multiple sclerosis were randomised to ponesimod 20 mg or teriflunomide 14 mg daily for 108 weeks: the annualised relapse rate was 0.202 on ponesimod versus 0.290 on teriflunomide (a 30.5% relative rate reduction; p<0.001), and combined unique active MRI lesions per year numbered 1.405 versus 3.164 (a 56% relative risk reduction; p<0.001). Fatigue symptom scores also favoured ponesimod (mean difference -3.57; p<0.001). But time to 12-week and 24-week confirmed disability accumulation did not differ significantly (10.1% versus 12.4%, p=0.29; and 8.1% versus 9.9%, p=0.37). Treatment-emergent adverse events were near-identical (88.8% versus 88.2%), as were serious events (8.7% versus 8.1%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): ponesimod controls relapses and MRI activity better than teriflunomide; Tier C because a single trial carries the claim and its disability endpoints were null.

cards.people: 1,133 patients aged 18–55 years with relapsing multiple sclerosis (2010 McDonald criteria, relapsing course from onset, EDSS 0–5.5, recent clinical or MRI activity; median age 37.0 years; 735 women [64.9%]), randomised 1:1 to ponesimod 20 mg once daily (567; with a 14-day gradual up-titration from 2 mg) or teriflunomide 14 mg once daily (566), with matching placebos, for 108 weeks.
cards.result: The relative rate reduction for ponesimod versus teriflunomide in the annualised relapse rate was 30.5% (0.202 versus 0.290; p<0.001); the mean difference in the fatigue symptom domain score was -3.57 (p<0.001); the relative risk reduction in combined unique active lesions per year was 56% (1.405 versus 3.164; p<0.001). Reductions in time to 12-week and 24-week confirmed disability accumulation were 17% (10.1% versus 12.4%; p=0.29) and 16% (8.1% versus 9.9%; p=0.37) — neither significant. Brain volume loss at week 108 was lower by 0.34 percentage points (-0.91% versus -1.25%; p<0.001), and the odds ratio for achieving no-evidence-of-disease-activity (NEDA-3) status was 1.70 (25.0% versus 16.4%; p<0.001). Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 88.8% versus 88.2%, and serious events in 8.7% versus 8.1%.
cards.watchOut: A single trial, and the first head-to-head of two oral therapies — its relapse and lesion wins are real, but the disability endpoints patients ultimately care about did not separate over 108 weeks. Teriflunomide is, again, a mid-efficacy comparator; nothing here ranks ponesimod against the S1P class leader or antibody therapies.

shelves.title: Tenecteplase 4.5–24 hours after stroke: disability-free survival 33.0% versus 24.2% where thrombectomy was not available (TRACE-III) — but a null result where most patients went on to thrombectomy (TIMELESS), with symptomatic bleeding 3.0% versus 0.8%
shelves.question: In Chinese patients with perfusion-selected stroke 4.5–24 hours from onset and no thrombectomy access, does tenecteplase improve outcome versus standard care?
shelves.mesh: Tissue Plasminogen Activator/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Time-to-Treatment · Male · China · Fibrinolytic Agents/therapeutic use/adverse effects/administration & dosage · Ischemic Stroke/drug therapy/etiology/surgery · East Asian People · Female · Humans · Tenecteplase/therapeutic use/adverse effects · Aged · Infarction, Middle Cerebral Artery/drug therapy/surgery · Thrombectomy · Intracranial Hemorrhages/etiology · Middle Aged
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the population the question names. In TRACE-III (Xiong Y et al., PMID: 38884324), 516 Chinese patients with large-vessel occlusion, perfusion-imaging salvageable tissue, and no access to endovascular thrombectomy were randomised 4.5–24 hours after last-known-well to tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg or standard medical treatment: absence of disability (modified Rankin scale 0–1) at 90 days occurred in 33.0% on tenecteplase versus 24.2% on standard care (relative rate 1.37, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.81; p=0.03). Mortality was 13.3% versus 13.1%, and symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage within 36 hours was 3.0% versus 0.8%. The boundary, stated without its numbers because that trial is carded on its own shelf in this library: the same drug and window in patients most of whom went on to thrombectomy was null — the late-window drug has its proven case where no thrombectomy follows. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): late-window tenecteplase helps perfusion-selected patients who cannot get thrombectomy; Tier C — a single trial with a stroke-outcome benefit claim and a quadrupled symptomatic-bleed rate.

cards.headline: TRACE-III (Xiong 2024): no disability at 90 days in 33.0% on tenecteplase versus 24.2% on standard care (relative rate 1.37, p=0.03); mortality 13.3% versus 13.1%; symptomatic haemorrhage 3.0% versus 0.8%
cards.summary: TRACE-III (Xiong 2024): no disability at 90 days in 33.0% on tenecteplase versus 24.2% on standard care (relative rate 1.37, p=0.03); mortality 13.3% versus 13.1%; symptomatic haemorrhage 3.0% versus 0.8%
cards.people: 516 patients in China with large-vessel occlusion of the middle cerebral artery or internal carotid artery and salvageable brain tissue on perfusion imaging, who did not have access to endovascular thrombectomy, randomised 4.5 to 24 hours after last-known-well (including wake-up and unwitnessed stroke) to tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg (maximum 25 mg; n=264) or standard medical treatment (n=252); fewer than 2% in either group (4 and 5 patients) underwent rescue thrombectomy; the primary outcome was a modified Rankin scale score of 0 or 1 at day 90.
cards.result: Treatment with tenecteplase resulted in a higher percentage of patients with a modified Rankin scale score of 0 or 1 at 90 days than standard medical treatment (33.0% versus 24.2%; relative rate 1.37; 95% CI 1.04 to 1.81; p=0.03). Mortality at 90 days was 13.3% with tenecteplase and 13.1% with standard treatment, and the incidence of symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage within 36 hours was 3.0% and 0.8% respectively.
cards.watchOut: Open treatment (no placebo infusion) with a disability-scale endpoint, a single country and health system, and perfusion-imaging selection that many no-thrombectomy settings also lack — the trial's patients were selected by exactly the imaging that resource-limited centres may not have. The symptomatic-bleed excess (3.0% versus 0.8%) is the price printed on the same card.
cards.source: Xiong Y et al. Tenecteplase for Ischemic Stroke at 4.5 to 24 Hours without Thrombectomy. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2024. PMID: 38884324. Registry ID: NCT05141305. shelves.title: Mobile stroke units in intracerebral haemorrhage: imaging 17.75 minutes sooner and arrival blood pressure 16.31 mmHg lower in the Berlin B_PROUD cohort — 7-day mortality and functional outcome no different
shelves.question: In intracerebral haemorrhage, does mobile stroke unit dispatch improve early blood-pressure management and outcome versus conventional care?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Female · Male · Aged · Cerebral Hemorrhage/drug therapy/mortality · Middle Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Mobile Health Units · Blood Pressure/drug effects · Stroke/drug therapy/mortality · Prospective Studies · Emergency Medical Services/methods · Time-to-Treatment · Ambulances · Hematoma/diagnostic imaging/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome · Hypertension/drug therapy/complications
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the process wins are real, the outcome wins are absent, in haemorrhage specifically. In the B_PROUD intracerebral haemorrhage cohort (Schwabauer E et al., PMID: 38014623), 95 patients received additional mobile stroke unit dispatch and 78 conventional ambulance care in Berlin: after inverse-probability weighting, dispatch-to-imaging time was 17.75 minutes shorter (95% CI -27.16 to -8.21) and systolic blood pressure at hospital arrival was 16.31 mmHg lower (-30.64 to -6.19) with the mobile unit. But the primary outcome, 7-day mortality, did not differ significantly (adjusted odds ratio 1.43, 0.68 to 3.31), nor did favourable functional outcome (adjusted odds ratio 0.67, 0.27 to 1.67). The same Berlin programme's ischaemic-stroke analysis — carded on its own shelf in this library, and not re-carded here — did find better functional outcomes with dispatch, which makes the haemorrhage null a finding about haemorrhage, not about the vehicle. PROPOSED SPLIT: mobile stroke units deliver faster imaging and earlier blood-pressure control in intracerebral haemorrhage, with no demonstrated outcome benefit in that population; Tier C — non-randomised evidence throughout.

cards.headline: B_PROUD ICH cohort (Schwabauer 2024): dispatch-to-imaging -17.75 minutes and arrival systolic pressure -16.31 mmHg with mobile stroke unit dispatch — 7-day mortality adjusted OR 1.43 (not significant), favourable outcome OR 0.67 (not significant)
cards.summary: B_PROUD ICH cohort (Schwabauer 2024): dispatch-to-imaging -17.75 minutes and arrival systolic pressure -16.31 mmHg with mobile stroke unit dispatch — 7-day mortality adjusted OR 1.43 (not significant), favourable outcome OR 0.67 (not significant)
cards.type: Prospective controlled intervention cohort with inverse-probability weighting (B_PROUD ICH analysis)
cards.people: 173 patients with acute intracerebral haemorrhage in Berlin, February 2017 to May 2019, evaluated as a cohort of the controlled B_PROUD study, in which mobile stroke unit availability alone determined whether a unit was dispatched in addition to a conventional ambulance: 95 patients received mobile stroke unit dispatch (mean age 72 ± 13 years, 45% female) and 78 received conventional ambulance care only (mean age 71 ± 12 years, 44% female); analyses adjusted for confounding by inverse probability of treatment weighting.
cards.result: After adjustment, the mobile stroke unit group had a shorter dispatch-to-imaging time (mean difference -17.75 minutes, 95% CI -27.16 to -8.21) and lower systolic blood pressure at hospital arrival (mean difference -16.31 mmHg, 95% CI -30.64 to -6.19). There was no statistically significant difference in 7-day mortality (adjusted odds ratio 1.43, 95% CI 0.68 to 3.31) or favourable outcome (adjusted odds ratio 0.67, 95% CI 0.27 to 1.67), nor in haematoma volume, anticoagulation reversal, or length of stay.
cards.watchOut: Not randomised: dispatch depended on unit availability, and weighting adjusts only for measured confounders. With 173 patients, the confidence interval for 7-day mortality (0.68 to 3.31) excludes neither meaningful benefit nor meaningful harm — this is an imprecise null, and the point estimate leans the wrong way. Blood pressure at arrival is a process measure; the trial-level question of whether earlier pressure lowering improves haemorrhage outcomes belongs to the blood-pressure shelves.
cards.source: Schwabauer E et al. Effects of Mobile Stroke Unit dispatch on blood pressure management and outcomes in patients with intracerebral haematoma: Results from the Berlin Prehospital Or Usual Care Delivery in acute Stroke (B_PROUD) controlled intervention study. cards.headline: Synthesis: in haemorrhage, the unit speeds everything except the outcome
cards.summary: Synthesis: in haemorrhage, the unit speeds everything except the outcome
cards.people: The intracerebral haemorrhage cohort of the Berlin B_PROUD controlled intervention study (173 patients; Schwabauer 2024): a prospective, non-randomised analysis with dispatch determined by unit availability and confounding handled by inverse-probability weighting. The programme's ischaemic-stroke population is carded on its own shelf in this library.
cards.result: In intracerebral haemorrhage: dispatch-to-imaging -17.75 minutes; arrival systolic pressure -16.31 mmHg; 7-day mortality adjusted OR 1.43 (95% CI 0.68–3.31); favourable outcome OR 0.67 (0.27–1.67) — process improved, outcomes not significantly different. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C — non-randomised evidence, small haemorrhage cohort.
cards.watchOut: Haemorrhage care's active ingredients (pressure lowering, reversal, neurosurgical triage) may need more than a 17-minute head start to move outcomes, or the cohort may simply be too small to see the effect; the record cannot distinguish those explanations. Systems buying mobile units for haemorrhage outcomes are buying beyond this evidence.

shelves.title: Anti-inflammatory add-ons fail in bipolar depression: minocycline and celecoxib, alone or together, no better than placebo in a 266-patient factorial trial
shelves.question: In bipolar depression, do adjunctive minocycline, celecoxib, or their combination improve depressive symptoms versus placebo in a factorial design?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Bipolar Disorder/drug therapy/psychology · Case-Control Studies · Celecoxib/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Major Depressive Disorder/drug therapy/psychology · Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Minocycline/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Pakistan/epidemiology · Placebos/administration & dosage · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in a 266-patient 2×2 factorial trial in Pakistan, HAMD-17 scores fell in all four groups (from 24.5–25.2 to 11.3–12.8 over 12 weeks), but neither minocycline (adjusted difference 1.48, 95% CI −0.41 to 3.36; p=0.123) nor celecoxib (−0.74, −2.61 to 1.14; p=0.443) beat placebo. Serious adverse effects did not differ between groups (31 participants had a manic switch across the trial). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): one large, well-designed factorial trial found no evidence that adjunctive minocycline or celecoxib helps bipolar depression.

cards.headline: Husain 2020: HAMD-17 fell in all groups; minocycline difference 1.48 (p=0.123) and celecoxib −0.74 (p=0.443) versus placebo — neither significant
cards.summary: Husain 2020: HAMD-17 fell in all groups; minocycline difference 1.48 (p=0.123) and celecoxib −0.74 (p=0.443) versus placebo — neither significant
cards.people: 266 adults (18–65 years) with DSM-5 bipolar I or II disorder in a major depressive episode at four outpatient psychiatric clinics in Pakistan, randomised 1:1:1:1 to minocycline plus celecoxib (n=68), minocycline plus placebo (n=66), celecoxib plus placebo (n=66), or double placebo (n=66) for 12 weeks.
cards.result: HAMD-17 scores fell from 24.5–25.2 at baseline to 11.3–12.8 at week 12 in all four groups, with no significant between-group differences. Main effects: minocycline adjusted difference 1.48 (95% CI −0.41 to 3.36; p=0.123); celecoxib −0.74 (−2.61 to 1.14; p=0.443). Serious adverse effect rates did not differ between groups; 31 participants had a manic switch, two self-harmed, and one died in a motor vehicle accident.
cards.watchOut: A single trial, conducted in one country, and the large improvement in every group (including double placebo) shows how much of the apparent effect of add-on anti-inflammatories in earlier small studies may have been background care and natural course.
cards.source: Husain MI et al. Minocycline and celecoxib as adjunctive treatments for bipolar depression: a multicentre, factorial design randomised controlled trial. Lancet Psychiatry. 2020. shelves.title: Internet CBT (Amiria) cuts depression in multiple sclerosis: BDI-II about 6 points better than usual care, effect size near 1.0, in a 279-patient phase 3 trial
shelves.question: In people with multiple sclerosis and depressive symptoms, does internet-delivered CBT reduce depression versus waitlist?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Depression/therapy · Multiple Sclerosis/complications/therapy · Major Depressive Disorder/therapy · Quality of Life · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy · Internet
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in a five-centre phase 3 trial, 279 people with multiple sclerosis and depressive symptoms randomised to stand-alone or therapist-guided internet CBT (the MS-specific programme Amiria) or usual care: at 12 weeks the BDI-II score was 6.32 points better with stand-alone iCBT (95% CI 3.37–9.27; effect size d=0.97) and 5.80 points better with guided iCBT (2.71–8.88; d=0.96) than control, both p<0.0001. Clinically relevant worsening occurred in three control participants, one stand-alone participant and no guided participants; there were no deaths and no suicidality. The limits: one trial, an unblinded waitlist-style control, and 18% dropout by week 12. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a scalable online programme produced a large short-term reduction in MS depressive symptoms in its single confirmatory trial.

cards.headline: Gold 2023 (depINet): BDI-II 6.32 points better with stand-alone iCBT and 5.80 with guided iCBT versus control at 12 weeks (both p<0.0001, d≈0.96–0.97)
cards.summary: Gold 2023 (depINet): BDI-II 6.32 points better with stand-alone iCBT and 5.80 with guided iCBT versus control at 12 weeks (both p<0.0001, d≈0.96–0.97)
cards.people: 279 patients with neurologist-confirmed multiple sclerosis and depressive symptoms at five academic centres in Germany and the USA, randomised to treatment as usual plus stand-alone iCBT (n=101), therapist-guided iCBT (n=85), or treatment as usual with iCBT offered after 6 months (n=93); primary endpoint BDI-II at week 12; dropout 18% at week 12.
cards.result: Between-group BDI-II differences versus control: stand-alone iCBT 6.32 points (95% CI 3.37–9.27), p<0.0001, effect size d=0.97 (0.64–1.30); guided iCBT 5.80 points (2.71–8.88), p<0.0001, d=0.96 (0.62–1.30). Clinically relevant worsening of depressive symptoms: three participants in control, one in stand-alone iCBT, none in guided iCBT. No suicidality and no deaths.
cards.watchOut: Participants could not be masked to a talking-therapy programme and the control was usual care with deferred access, which inflates effect sizes versus an active control; a single trial from the programme's own developers, with the stand-alone and guided versions performing alike.
cards.source: Gold SM et al. shelves.title: Cariprazine maintenance does not prevent bipolar relapse: relapse 16.8–17.9% on drug versus 19.7% on placebo, hazard ratios 0.83–0.89 with confidence intervals crossing 1
shelves.question: In bipolar I disorder, does cariprazine maintenance prevent relapse into mood episodes versus placebo after stabilisation?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Bipolar Disorder/drug therapy · Male · Female · Double-Blind Method · Adult · Middle Aged · Piperazines/administration & dosage/therapeutic use/adverse effects · Young Adult · Secondary Prevention · Treatment Outcome · Antipsychotic Agents/administration & dosage/therapeutic use/adverse effects · Adolescent · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — 896 patients with bipolar I disorder entered open-label cariprazine 3.0 mg/day; the 440 who stabilised were randomised to cariprazine 1.5 mg, 3.0 mg, or placebo for up to 39 weeks. Relapse rates were 16.8% (1.5 mg), 17.9% (3.0 mg) and 19.7% (placebo), and neither dose beat placebo on time to relapse (HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.5–1.4; HR 0.89, 0.5–1.5). The authors note relapse on placebo was unusually low — an enriched, stabilised population in which a maintenance effect is hardest to show. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): in this trial, continuing cariprazine after stabilisation did not prevent relapse better than switching to placebo.

cards.headline: McIntyre 2024: relapse 17.9% (3.0 mg), 16.8% (1.5 mg) versus 19.7% on placebo; HR 0.89 and 0.83, both confidence intervals including 1
cards.summary: McIntyre 2024: relapse 17.9% (3.0 mg), 16.8% (1.5 mg) versus 19.7% on placebo; HR 0.89 and 0.83, both confidence intervals including 1
cards.people: 896 patients with bipolar I disorder with acute manic or depressive episodes treated open-label with cariprazine 3.0 mg/day for 16 weeks; the 440 who met stability criteria were randomised to cariprazine 3.0 mg/day (n=148), 1.5 mg/day (n=147), or placebo (n=145) for up to 39 weeks; primary endpoint time to relapse of any mood episode.
cards.result: Relapse rates: 17.9% on cariprazine 3.0 mg/day, 16.8% on 1.5 mg/day, 19.7% on placebo. Neither dose was more effective than placebo on the primary outcome (3.0 mg: HR 0.89, 95% CI 0.5–1.5; 1.5 mg: HR 0.83, 0.5–1.4). Most frequent double-blind adverse events (≥5% in open label) included akathisia, headache, insomnia and nausea; in the double-blind period, increased weight and insomnia; discontinuation for adverse events 7.5% (open label) and 1.6% (double blind).
cards.watchOut: An enriched withdrawal design: only patients who already tolerated and stabilised on cariprazine were randomised, and the placebo relapse rate (19.7%) was unusually low, leaving little room to show a maintenance effect; a null here does not exclude benefit in unselected patients.
cards.source: McIntyre RS et al. Cariprazine as a maintenance therapy in the prevention of mood episodes in adults with bipolar I disorder. Bipolar Disorders. 2024. PMID: 38609342. shelves.title: PTSD: trauma-focused psychotherapy first — at long-term follow-up it beats medication (SMD −0.83 in network, −0.63 pairwise), though nothing separates the approaches at end of treatment
shelves.question: In PTSD, does trauma-focused psychotherapy outperform pharmacotherapy as first-line treatment — and how do their effects compare head to head in the meta-analytic evidence?
shelves.mesh: Antidepressive Agents/therapeutic use · Combined Modality Therapy · Humans · Piperazines · Psychotherapy/methods · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Sertraline/therapeutic use · Stress Disorders, Post-Traumatic/therapy · Treatment Outcome · Triazoles/therapeutic use · Venlafaxine Hydrochloride/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for psychotherapy as the first-line choice. Lee 2016 found trauma-focused psychotherapies produced larger effects against active controls than medications did against placebo, with more sustained benefit over time, while several drugs (paroxetine, fluoxetine) improved symptoms only slightly and others (bupropion, citalopram, topiramate and more) failed to separate from placebo at all. Merz 2019's network meta-analysis of the 12 head-to-head RCTs (922 participants) found no approach superior at end of treatment, but at last follow-up psychotherapy beat pharmacotherapy (network SMD −0.83, 95% CI −1.59 to −0.07; pairwise SMD −0.63, −1.18 to −0.09), with no difference in dropout acceptability. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the durable advantage sits with trauma-focused psychotherapy; medication is a second-line or adjunct option, not an equal first-line one.

cards.headline: Lee 2016: trauma-focused psychotherapy effects exceeded medication effects, and lasted; sertraline and venlafaxine were the best-performing drugs, several others never beat placebo
cards.summary: Lee 2016: trauma-focused psychotherapy effects exceeded medication effects, and lasted; sertraline and venlafaxine were the best-performing drugs, several others never beat placebo
cards.people: Randomised trials of at least 8 weeks in PTSD using structured-interview outcomes, active-control conditions and intention-to-treat analysis, grouped at 3, 6 and 9 months of follow-up.
cards.result: Effect sizes for trauma-focused psychotherapies versus active control conditions were greater than medications versus placebo and other psychotherapies versus active controls, and trauma-focused psychotherapy benefit was better sustained over time. Sertraline, venlafaxine and nefazodone outperformed other medications; improvement on paroxetine and fluoxetine was small; bupropion, citalopram, divalproex, mirtazapine, tiagabine and topiramate failed to differentiate from placebo, as did aripiprazole, divalproex, guanfacine and olanzapine added to an antidepressant.
cards.watchOut: An indirect comparison across separate literatures (therapy trials versus drug trials with different controls), with high potential for methodological bias in the drug trials the authors themselves flag; it ranks classes, it does not randomise patients between them.
cards.source: Lee DJ et al. Psychotherapy versus pharmacotherapy for posttraumatic stress disorder: systemic review and meta-analyses to determine first-line treatments. Depression and Anxiety. 2016. PMID: 27126398. cards.headline: Merz 2019: no winner at end of treatment in 12 head-to-head trials (922 patients); at last follow-up psychotherapy beat drugs (SMD −0.83 network, −0.63 pairwise)
cards.summary: Merz 2019: no winner at end of treatment in 12 head-to-head trials (922 patients); at last follow-up psychotherapy beat drugs (SMD −0.83 network, −0.63 pairwise)
cards.people: 12 published RCTs comprising 922 adults with PTSD contributing 23 direct comparisons between psychotherapeutic, pharmacological and combined treatments, searched to February 2018.
cards.result: No treatment approach was superior at end of treatment (all 95% CIs included 0). At last follow-up, psychotherapeutic treatments showed greater benefit than pharmacological treatments in network (SMD −0.83, 95% CI −1.59 to −0.07) and pairwise (SMD −0.63, −1.18 to −0.09; 3 RCTs) meta-analyses. Combined treatment beat pharmacotherapy in the network analysis (SMD −0.96, −1.87 to −0.04) but not pairwise (SMD −1.02, −2.77 to 0.72; 2 RCTs). No differential acceptability (dropout) between approaches.
cards.watchOut: Only 12 head-to-head trials and very few long-term follow-ups — the authors state the scarcity of long-term data hampers definite conclusions; the long-term psychotherapy advantage rests on a handful of trials.
cards.source: Merz J et al. Comparative Efficacy and Acceptability of Pharmacological, Psychotherapeutic, and Combination Treatments in Adults With Posttraumatic Stress Disorder: A Network Meta-analysis. JAMA Psychiatry. 2019. PMID: 31188399. cards.headline: Synthesis: equal at the finish line, therapy ahead a year later — two independent meta-analyses point the same way
cards.summary: Synthesis: equal at the finish line, therapy ahead a year later — two independent meta-analyses point the same way
cards.people: Lee 2016 (indirect comparison across the therapy and drug trial literatures) and Merz 2019 (network meta-analysis of 12 direct head-to-head RCTs, 922 participants).
cards.result: End of treatment: no significant difference between psychotherapy and pharmacotherapy. Long-term follow-up: psychotherapy superior (SMD −0.63 to −0.83); trauma-focused therapy effects more sustained than drug effects; dropout acceptability equal. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for psychotherapy-first.

shelves.title: GLP-1 agonists reverse antipsychotic weight gain: 3.71 kg more lost than control in participant-level data, 6.74 kg in a 2026 pooled analysis — nausea the price
shelves.question: In people with schizophrenia and antipsychotic-induced weight gain, do GLP-1 receptor agonists reduce weight versus control?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Antipsychotic Agents/adverse effects · Body Weight/drug effects · Cardiovascular Diseases/chemically induced/prevention & control · Drug Administration Schedule · Exenatide/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Female · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Liraglutide/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Male · Metabolic Diseases/chemically induced/prevention & control · Middle Aged · Obesity/chemically induced/prevention & control · Risk Factors · Schizophrenia/drug therapy · Weight Gain/drug effects · Young Adult · Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — Siskind 2019's individual-participant meta-analysis of three randomised trials (n=164, mean weight 105.8 kg) found GLP-1 agonists (exenatide weekly ×2 trials, liraglutide daily ×1) produced 3.71 kg more weight loss than control over ~16 weeks (95% CI 2.44–4.99; p<0.001), with a number-needed-to-treat of 3.8 for ≥5% weight loss, and larger effects on clozapine/olanzapine (4.70 kg) than other antipsychotics (1.5 kg, CI crossing zero). A 2026 GRADE-assessed meta-analysis of 8 RCTs (664 patients) found a larger pooled difference (−6.74 kg, −10.05 to −3.43), with semaglutide the strongest agent (−11.06 kg). The price is gastrointestinal: nausea in 53.6% versus 27.5% in the participant-level data (number-needed-to-harm 3.8). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): GLP-1 agonists are the best-evidenced pharmacological answer to antipsychotic weight gain, on short trials with small total numbers.

cards.headline: Siskind 2019: 3.71 kg greater weight loss on GLP-1 agonists versus control (n=164); NNT 3.8 for ≥5% loss; nausea 53.6% versus 27.5%
cards.summary: Siskind 2019: 3.71 kg greater weight loss on GLP-1 agonists versus control (n=164); NNT 3.8 for ≥5% loss; nausea 53.6% versus 27.5%
cards.people: 164 participants (mean age 40.0 years, mean body weight 105.8 kg) from three randomised studies of GLP-1 receptor agonists versus control in antipsychotic-treated patients with schizophrenia — exenatide once-weekly in two studies, liraglutide once-daily in one — treated 16.2 ± 4.0 weeks.
cards.result: Body weight loss was 3.71 kg greater for GLP-1 agonists versus control (95% CI 2.44–4.99; p<0.001); number-needed-to-treat for ≥5% body weight loss 3.8 (2.6–7.2). Waist circumference, BMI, HbA1c, fasting glucose and visceral adiposity were each significantly lower. Weight loss was greater in clozapine/olanzapine-treated patients (4.70 kg, 3.13–6.27; n=141) than with other antipsychotics (1.5 kg, −1.47 to 4.47; n=27). Nausea: 53.6% versus 27.5% (p=0.002; number-needed-to-harm 3.8).
cards.watchOut: Only 164 participants and ~16 weeks of treatment in the participant-level data — enough to show the direction, not durability, psychiatric safety over years, or what happens on stopping; the non-clozapine/olanzapine subgroup estimate crosses zero.
cards.source: Siskind D et al. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists for antipsychotic-associated cardio-metabolic risk factors: A systematic review and individual participant data meta-analysis. Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism. 2019. PMID: 30187620. cards.headline: Moubarak 2026: across 8 RCTs (664 patients), weight −6.74 kg and BMI −2.37 versus control; semaglutide subgroup −11.06 kg; gastrointestinal adverse events significantly more frequent
cards.summary: Moubarak 2026: across 8 RCTs (664 patients), weight −6.74 kg and BMI −2.37 versus control; semaglutide subgroup −11.06 kg; gastrointestinal adverse events significantly more frequent
cards.people: 8 randomised controlled trials with 664 patients with schizophrenia-spectrum or bipolar disorders treated with antipsychotics, GLP-1 receptor agonists versus control, searched to May 2026.
cards.result: GLP-1 agonists reduced body weight (mean difference −6.74 kg, 95% CI −10.05 to −3.43), BMI (−2.37 kg/m², −3.52 to −1.23), waist circumference (−4.27 cm, −6.65 to −1.89), HbA1c (−0.61%, −1.06 to −0.17) and fasting glucose (−6.82, −11.89 to −1.76). Semaglutide showed the greatest weight reduction (−11.06 kg). Overall adverse events (p=0.77), serious adverse events (p=0.09) and discontinuation for adverse events (p=0.20) were similar, but gastrointestinal adverse events including nausea, vomiting and constipation were significantly more frequent (all p<0.01).
cards.watchOut: A 2026 synthesis of still-small trials with wide confidence intervals; the semaglutide subgroup drives the largest numbers and between-agent comparisons are indirect. Longer, larger trials are needed, as the authors state.
cards.source: Moubarak ES et al. Adjunctive GLP-1 receptor agonists for cardiometabolic risk in antipsychotic-treated patients: A GRADE-assessed meta-analysis of randomized trials. Journal of Psychopharmacology. 2026. PMID: 42746999. shelves.title: Argentine tango in Parkinson's: motor scores improved 28.7% over 12 months while controls stood still — small, unblinded trials from one research group
shelves.question: In Parkinson's disease, does Argentine tango dance training improve balance, gait and quality of life versus an exercise control?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Dance Therapy/methods · Disease Progression · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Gait/physiology · Humans · Male · Parkinson Disease/physiopathology/psychology/rehabilitation · Postural Balance/physiology · Psychomotor Performance · Residence Characteristics · Severity of Illness Index · Surveys and Questionnaires · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · Upper Extremity/physiopathology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in Duncan and Earhart's 12-month randomised trial, 62 people with Parkinson's disease assigned to twice-weekly community Argentine tango or a no-intervention control: the tango group's MDS-UPDRS-3 motor score fell 28.7% (12.8 points) while controls showed no significant change, with significant group-by-time interactions favouring tango on the MiniBESTest balance test, Freezing of Gait Questionnaire, 6-Minute Walk Test, forward and dual-task walking velocity, and the Nine-Hole Peg Test. A 2-year pilot extension in just 10 participants found the same pattern. The honest limits: the control was no intervention (not the exercise control the question poses), participants cannot be blinded to dancing, and both trials come from one group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a year of tango improved motor severity and balance measures versus doing nothing; superiority over other exercise is untested in this record.

cards.headline: Duncan 2012: tango group's motor score fell 28.7% (12.8 points) over 12 months; controls unchanged; balance, freezing, walking speed and dexterity interactions all favoured tango
cards.summary: Duncan 2012: tango group's motor score fell 28.7% (12.8 points) over 12 months; controls unchanged; balance, freezing, walking speed and dexterity interactions all favoured tango
cards.people: 62 people with Parkinson's disease randomly assigned to a twice-weekly community-based Argentine tango programme or a control group with no intervention for 12 months, assessed off anti-Parkinson medication at baseline, 3, 6 and 12 months; primary outcome MDS-UPDRS-3.
cards.result: Groups did not differ at baseline. The tango group improved while the control group showed little change on most measures: MDS-UPDRS-3 showed no significant change in controls, whereas the tango group had a reduction of 28.7% (12.8 points). Significant group-by-time interactions favoured tango for MDS-UPDRS-3, MiniBESTest, Freezing of Gait Questionnaire, 6-Minute Walk Test, forward and dual-task walking velocities, and Nine-Hole Peg Test.
cards.watchOut: The comparator was no intervention, not exercise — so this shows tango beats inactivity, not that tango beats other exercise; participants and (for most measures) the intervention itself cannot be blinded, and assessments off medication may not reflect everyday on-medication function.
cards.source: Duncan RP et al. Randomized controlled trial of community-based dancing to modify disease progression in Parkinson disease. Neurorehabilitation and Neural Repair. 2012. PMID: 21959675. cards.headline: Duncan 2014: over 2 years in a 10-person pilot, tango participants kept lower motor scores than controls (interaction p<0.0001), with balance and walk-test advantages
cards.summary: Duncan 2014: over 2 years in a 10-person pilot, tango participants kept lower motor scores than controls (interaction p<0.0001), with balance and walk-test advantages
cards.people: 10 individuals with Parkinson's disease randomly assigned to Argentine tango classes (n=5; mean age 69.6 years) or no prescribed exercise (n=5; mean age 66 years), 1 hour twice weekly for 2 years, with blinded assessments at baseline, 12 and 24 months.
cards.result: No baseline differences. A significant group-by-time interaction (F[2,8]=17.59; p<0.0001) for MDS-UPDRS III, with the tango group lower at 12 and 24 months; significant interactions also for MiniBESTest, MDS-UPDRS II and I, and the 6-Minute Walk Test. The control group declined on some measures over 2 years while tango participants improved in motor and nonmotor severity, activities of daily living and balance.
cards.watchOut: Five participants per arm — a pilot that can show feasibility and direction, not a reliable effect size; attrition and expectancy in a 2-year dance commitment are unmeasurable at this scale.
cards.source: Duncan RP et al. Are the effects of community-based dance on Parkinson disease severity, balance, and functional mobility reduced with time? A 2-year prospective pilot study. shelves.title: Coenzyme Q10 for migraine prevention: half of patients responded in the one good small trial (47.6% versus 14.4%), and a meta-analysis finds 1.52 fewer attacks — severity unmoved
shelves.question: In migraine prevention, does coenzyme Q10 reduce attack frequency versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Migraine Disorders/prevention & control · Treatment Outcome · Ubiquinone/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — Sándor 2005 randomised 42 migraine patients to coenzyme Q10 300 mg/day or placebo: by the third month CoQ10 was superior on attack frequency, headache days and days with nausea, with a 50%-responder rate of 47.6% versus 14.4% (number-needed-to-treat 3). Sazali 2021's meta-analysis of six studies (371 participants) found CoQ10 reduced attack frequency (mean difference −1.52, 95% CI −2.40 to −0.65; p<0.001) and attack duration (−0.19, −0.27 to −0.11) versus control, but found no statistically significant reduction in headache severity. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): CoQ10 probably reduces how often migraines come, modestly, on small-trial evidence; it does not demonstrably make attacks milder. The publication names no branded product or company, and current products may differ in content and quality.

cards.headline: Sándor 2005: 50%-responder rate 47.6% on CoQ10 versus 14.4% on placebo (NNT 3) in 42 patients over 3 months
cards.summary: Sándor 2005: 50%-responder rate 47.6% on CoQ10 versus 14.4% on placebo (NNT 3) in 42 patients over 3 months
cards.people: 42 migraine patients randomised to coenzyme Q10 (3 × 100 mg/day) or placebo in a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, with outcomes assessed by treatment month.
cards.result: CoQ10 was superior to placebo for attack frequency, headache days and days with nausea in the third treatment month and was well tolerated. The 50%-responder rate for attack frequency was 47.6% for CoQ10 and 14.4% for placebo (number-needed-to-treat: 3).
cards.watchOut: A single-centre trial of 42 patients reporting p-value-led results for most endpoints — the responder rates are the solid numbers; three months is short for a preventive, and the abstract gives no absolute attack counts.
cards.source: Sándor PS et al. Efficacy of coenzyme Q10 in migraine prophylaxis: a randomized controlled trial. Neurology. 2005. PMID: 15728298. cards.headline: Sazali 2021: six studies, 371 participants — attack frequency −1.52 and duration −0.19 versus control; severity not significantly reduced
cards.summary: Sazali 2021: six studies, 371 participants — attack frequency −1.52 and duration −0.19 versus control; severity not significantly reduced
cards.people: Six randomised trials (371 participants) of coenzyme Q10 versus placebo or as adjunct treatment for migraine prophylaxis in adults, searched to December 2019.
cards.result: CoQ10 reduced the frequency of migraine headache versus control (mean difference −1.52, 95% CI −2.40 to −0.65; random effects; I²=0%; p<0.001) and reduced attack duration (mean difference −0.19, −0.27 to −0.11; p<0.00001). There was no statistically significant reduction in severity of migraine headache with CoQ10 supplementation.
cards.watchOut: Six small trials totalling 371 participants, mixing CoQ10 alone and as an adjunct; a −1.52 attack difference is meaningful only against each trial's baseline frequency, which the pooled abstract does not state. No branded product or company is named in the publications, and current products may differ in safety and effectiveness.

shelves.title: SMILE self-management course for poorly controlled epilepsy: no gain in quality of life, seizure control or distress at 12 months in a 404-patient pragmatic trial
shelves.question: In epilepsy, does a seizure self-management programme reduce seizure frequency and improve quality of life versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Drug Resistant Epilepsy/therapy · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Education as Topic/methods · Quality of Life · Self-Management/methods · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — SMILE (UK) randomised 404 adults with poorly controlled epilepsy (≥2 seizures in the prior year) to a 2-day group self-management course plus usual care or usual care alone. At 12 months, quality of life (QOLIE-31-P) was 67.4 in the course group and 69.5 in controls — no significant difference — and no secondary outcome (seizure frequency or recency, psychological distress, impact or stigma of epilepsy, self-mastery, medication adherence, adverse effects) differed either. The companion HTA report adds that the course was cost-saving and possibly cost-effective despite the lower quality of life, and that interviewed participants said the group increased their confidence. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): a well-run pragmatic trial of the flagship self-management course found no measurable clinical benefit at a year.

cards.type: Health technology assessment report of the same trial (Ridsdale 2018, SMILE UK)
cards.people: The same 404 participants (SMILE n=205, treatment as usual n=199) recruited from eight hospitals in London and south-east England, with cost-effectiveness analysis and a 20-participant process evaluation; 61.5% of the intervention group completed all course sessions.
cards.result: Intention-to-treat analysis showed no change in any measure at 12 months (QOLIE-31-P: SMILE 67.4, SD 13.5; usual care 69.5, SD 14.8). The cost-effectiveness study showed SMILE was possibly cost-effective but was also associated with lower quality of life; the course was cost-saving. At baseline, clinically relevant anxiety symptoms were reported by 53.6% and depression symptoms by 28.0% of participants. No adverse events were related to the intervention. Interviewed participants reported the group course increased confidence and improved self-management behaviours.
cards.watchOut: This is the full report of the same trial as the Epilepsia paper, not independent confirmation — it is carded for its economic and process findings. 'Possibly cost-effective with lower quality of life' is an artefact of cost savings, not a health gain.

shelves.title: Baclofen for alcohol use disorder splits its two big trials: Bacloville hit its consumption target (57% versus 36%) on a contested analysis, ALPADIR missed abstinence entirely (11.9% versus 10.5%) — with more serious adverse events on baclofen
shelves.question: In adults with alcohol use disorder, does baclofen reduce return to heavy drinking versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Alcohol Drinking/drug therapy · Alcohol-Related Disorders/drug therapy · Baclofen/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · GABA-B Receptor Agonists/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Harm Reduction · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Outpatients
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by trial and by endpoint. Bacloville (Rigal 2020; 320 primary-care patients drinking 129 g/day, baclofen titrated to up to 300 mg/day) met its primary endpoint: success (no or low-risk drinking in the final month) in 57% on baclofen versus 36% on placebo, a 21-percentage-point difference (95% CI 8–34; p=0.003) — but when patients who switched to open-label baclofen were not automatically counted as failures, the difference shrank to 62% versus 55% (6 points, CI −7 to 20), and serious adverse events occurred in 85 patients on baclofen (7 deaths) versus 36 on placebo (3 deaths). ALPADIR (Reynaud 2017; 320 alcohol-dependent patients, target 180 mg/day) missed its primary endpoint: 20 weeks of continuous abstinence in 11.9% versus 10.5% (OR 1.20, 0.58–2.50; p=0.618), with consumption differences non-significant (10.9 g/day at month 6, p=0.095) though craving fell (p=0.017). PROPOSED SPLIT: baclofen may reduce consumption in high-risk primary-care drinkers on one contested analysis; it does not maintain abstinence after detoxification, and its high-dose adverse-event burden is real.

cards.headline: Rigal 2020 (Bacloville): primary success 57% versus 36% (difference 21 points, p=0.003) — but 62% versus 55% when switchers were not auto-failed, and serious adverse events in 85 versus 36 patients
cards.summary: Rigal 2020 (Bacloville): primary success 57% versus 36% (difference 21 points, p=0.003) — but 62% versus 55% when switchers were not auto-failed, and serious adverse events in 85 versus 36 patients
cards.people: 320 outpatients with high-risk alcohol consumption (>40 g/day for women, >60 g/day for men; mean consumption 129 g/day in both arms) at 62 French primary-care centres, randomised to titrated baclofen up to 300 mg/day (n=162) or placebo (n=158) for 12 months; switching to open-label baclofen was allowed for perceived inefficacy; discontinuation 30% versus 34%, and last-month diary return rates only 42% versus 34%.
cards.result: Primary success (no or low-risk consumption in the last month, switchers counted as failures): 57% baclofen versus 36% placebo (difference 21 percentage points, 95% CI 8–34; p=0.003). When switchers were not classified as failures unless they failed: 62% versus 55% (difference 6 points, −7 to 20). Over 12 months, daily consumption was 11 g lower and abstinence days 3.3 higher on baclofen. Adverse events (mostly drowsiness, fatigue, insomnia) were more frequent on baclofen; serious adverse events occurred in 85 patients (7 deaths) on baclofen versus 36 (3 deaths) on placebo.
cards.watchOut: The headline result depends on counting open-label switchers as failures and on diaries returned by barely a third of participants — the trial's own sensitivity analysis erases the significance; the serious-adverse-event imbalance (85 vs 36 patients) is part of the result, not a footnote.

cards.summary: Reynaud 2017 (ALPADIR): continuous abstinence 11.9% versus 10.5% (OR 1.20, p=0.618) at 180 mg/day — consumption trend only, craving significantly lower
cards.people: 320 adult alcohol-dependent patients randomised after detoxification (baclofen n=158, placebo n=162) to baclofen titrated over 7 weeks to a target of 180 mg/day, maintained 17 weeks, then tapered over 2 weeks.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — percentage abstinent over 20 consecutive weeks — was 11.9% on baclofen versus 10.5% on placebo (OR 1.20, 95% CI 0.58–2.50; p=0.618). Consumption fell in both groups; the month-6 difference of 10.9 g/day in baclofen's favour was not significant (p=0.095), nor was the high-drinking-risk subgroup difference of 15.6 g/day (p=0.089). Craving (Obsessive-Compulsive Drinking Scale) decreased significantly more on baclofen (p=0.017). No major safety concern was observed.
cards.watchOut: A detoxified, abstinence-goal population is a different question from Bacloville's reduction-goal primary-care drinkers — the split between the trials is partly population and endpoint, not just chance; fixed target dosing (180 mg/day) may also miss the individually titrated dose Bacloville allowed.

shelves.title: Folic acid added to enalapril cut first stroke in hypertensive adults in China: 2.7% versus 3.4% over 4.5 years (a 21% relative reduction) — in a low-folate population with no folic-acid food fortification
shelves.question: In hypertensive adults in China, does folic acid added to enalapril reduce first stroke versus enalapril alone?
shelves.mesh: Antihypertensive Agents/therapeutic use* · China · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Enalapril/therapeutic use* · Folic Acid/blood/therapeutic use* · Humans · Hypertension/drug therapy* · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Methylenetetrahydrofolate Reductase (NADPH2)/genetics · Middle Aged · Polymorphism, Genetic · Primary Prevention · Risk · Stroke/epidemiology/prevention & control* · Vitamin B Complex/therapeutic use*
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the one large trial that asked exactly this question, in exactly this population. In CSPPT (Huo Y et al., PMID: 25771069), 20,702 Chinese adults with hypertension and no history of stroke or myocardial infarction were randomised to a single-pill combination of enalapril 10 mg plus folic acid 0.8 mg daily (n=10,348) or enalapril 10 mg alone (n=10,354). Over a median treatment duration of 4.5 years, first stroke occurred in 2.7% on enalapril–folic acid versus 3.4% on enalapril alone (hazard ratio 0.79, 95% CI 0.68–0.93) — a 21% relative reduction, an absolute difference of 0.7 percentage points. First ischemic stroke (2.2% versus 2.8%; hazard ratio 0.76, 95% CI 0.64–0.91) and the composite of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction and stroke (3.1% versus 3.9%; hazard ratio 0.80, 95% CI 0.69–0.92) also favoured the combination, while hemorrhagic stroke, myocardial infarction and all-cause death did not differ significantly, and adverse-event frequencies did not differ significantly between groups. The supporting meta-analysis (Huo Y et al., PMID: 22607506; 55,764 participants) points the same way only where food is not fortified: across the 10 trials with no or partial folic acid fortification (n=43,426) folic acid supplementation was associated with an 11% relative reduction in stroke risk (relative risk 0.89, 95% CI 0.82–0.97), while in the five trials in fortified populations (n=12,338) it had no effect (relative risk 1.03, 95% CI 0.88–1.21). The population boundary is part of the finding: CSPPT was run in China, which does not fortify food with folic acid, in adults the authors describe as having low baseline folate levels — the result must not be generalised to folate-replete, fortified populations. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): adding folic acid 0.8 mg to enalapril reduced first stroke in hypertensive Chinese adults in one large double-blind trial, with a concordant meta-analysis signal confined to non-fortified populations; a single pivotal trial carries the claim, so the shelf is Tier C for the developer's personal verdict.

cards.headline: Huo 2015 (CSPPT): first stroke 2.7% on enalapril plus folic acid versus 3.4% on enalapril alone (hazard ratio 0.79) — a 21% relative reduction over a median 4.5 years
cards.summary: Huo 2015 (CSPPT): first stroke 2.7% on enalapril plus folic acid versus 3.4% on enalapril alone (hazard ratio 0.79) — a 21% relative reduction over a median 4.5 years
cards.people: 20,702 adults with hypertension and no history of stroke or myocardial infarction, in 32 communities in Jiangsu and Anhui provinces in China (trial conducted May 19, 2008 to August 24, 2013). Participants, stratified by MTHFR C677T genotypes (CC, CT, and TT), were randomly assigned to double-blind daily treatment with a single-pill combination of enalapril 10 mg and folic acid 0.8 mg (n=10,348) or a tablet containing enalapril 10 mg alone (n=10,354). Median treatment duration was 4.5 years.
cards.result: First stroke (the primary outcome) occurred in 2.7% of the enalapril–folic acid group versus 3.4% of the enalapril-alone group (hazard ratio 0.79, 95% CI 0.68–0.93) — a 21% relative reduction, with the absolute rates printed alongside (an absolute difference of 0.7 percentage points). First ischemic stroke: 2.2% versus 2.8% (hazard ratio 0.76, 95% CI 0.64–0.91). Composite of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction and stroke: 3.1% versus 3.9% (hazard ratio 0.80, 95% CI 0.69–0.92). Hemorrhagic stroke (hazard ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.65–1.34), myocardial infarction (hazard ratio 1.04, 95% CI 0.60–1.82) and all-cause death (hazard ratio 0.94, 95% CI 0.81–1.10) did not differ significantly between the groups, and there were no significant differences in the frequencies of adverse events. The authors concluded that, among adults with hypertension in China without a history of stroke or MI, combined enalapril and folic acid significantly reduced the risk of first stroke compared with enalapril alone, consistent with benefits from folate use among adults with hypertension and low baseline folate levels.
cards.watchOut: One trial, one country, one population: China does not fortify food with folic acid and the authors frame the benefit as applying to adults with low baseline folate levels, so the result is a finding about a low-folate, non-fortification population and must not be generalised beyond it. The absolute gain is modest — 0.7 percentage points over a median 4.5 years — and the benefit was confined to ischemic stroke; hemorrhagic stroke, myocardial infarction and all-cause mortality were unmoved. The comparison also tests a fixed single-pill combination (enalapril 10 mg plus folic acid 0.8 mg), not folic acid added to blood-pressure treatment in general.

cards.headline: Huo 2012 meta-analysis: folic acid associated with an 11% relative reduction in stroke in trials without folic-acid fortification (relative risk 0.89) — and no effect where food was fortified (relative risk 1.03)
cards.summary: Huo 2012 meta-analysis: folic acid associated with an 11% relative reduction in stroke in trials without folic-acid fortification (relative risk 0.89) — and no effect where food was fortified (relative risk 1.03)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of published randomised trials of folic acid supplementation for stroke prevention, totalling 55,764 participants: 10 trials conducted in populations with no or partial folic acid fortification (n=43,426) and five trials in populations with folic acid fortification (n=12,338). Effects are reported as relative risks from a fixed-effects model; the record reports no absolute event rates.
cards.result: Overall, folic acid supplementation was associated with an 8% relative reduction in stroke risk (n=55,764; relative risk 0.92, 95% CI 0.86–1.00, p=0.038). In the 10 trials with no or partial folic acid fortification (n=43,426), stroke risk was reduced by 11% in relative terms (relative risk 0.89, 95% CI 0.82–0.97, p=0.010); within these trials, a greater beneficial effect was seen among trials with a lower percent use of statins (≤80% (median); relative risk 0.77, 95% CI 0.64–0.92, p=0.005). In the five trials conducted in populations with folic acid fortification (n=12,338), folic acid supplementation had no effect on stroke risk (relative risk 1.03, 95% CI 0.88–1.21). A daily dose of 0.4–0.8 mg folic acid appeared adequate for stroke prevention in comparison with larger doses. The authors concluded that folic acid supplementation is effective in stroke prevention in populations with no or partial folic acid fortification, underscoring the importance of identifying target populations that can particularly benefit.
cards.watchOut: This meta-analysis predates CSPPT (published 2012; CSPPT reported in 2015), so it is independent supporting evidence rather than a summary that includes the pivotal trial — but its overall effect is borderline (relative risk 0.92, 95% CI 0.86–1.00) and the benefit appears only in the no-or-partial-fortification subgroup, with a flat null in fortified populations. The record reports relative risks only, with no absolute rates, so no absolute benefit can be quoted from it. The statin-use subgroup finding is a between-trial comparison, not a randomised one.
cards.source: Huo Y et al. Efficacy of folic acid supplementation in stroke prevention: new insight from a meta-analysis. International journal of clinical practice. 2012. PMID: 22607506. cards.headline: Synthesis: one large double-blind trial answers this exact question in this exact population — benefit real but bounded by low folate and no fortification, with the re-card declared on the face of the shelf
cards.summary: Synthesis: one large double-blind trial answers this exact question in this exact population — benefit real but bounded by low folate and no fortification, with the re-card declared on the face of the shelf
cards.people: One randomised, double-blind trial of 20,702 hypertensive adults in China without prior stroke or myocardial infarction (CSPPT: enalapril 10 mg plus folic acid 0.8 mg daily versus enalapril 10 mg alone, median 4.5 years), supported by a 2012 meta-analysis of randomised folic acid trials totalling 55,764 participants, split by population fortification status.
cards.result: First stroke: 2.7% on enalapril–folic acid versus 3.4% on enalapril alone (hazard ratio 0.79, 95% CI 0.68–0.93) — a 21% relative reduction, 0.7 percentage points absolute. Meta-analysis: 11% relative reduction in stroke in trials with no or partial fortification (relative risk 0.89, 95% CI 0.82–0.97); no effect in fortified populations (relative risk 1.03, 95% CI 0.88–1.21). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Re-card declaration: CSPPT (Huo Y et al., PMID: 25771069) is also carded as a supporting card on live shelf #203 ("Does lowering homocysteine with B vitamins or folic acid prevent stroke?"), where it serves as the positive trial inside a broad cross-population question whose answer turns on folate status. This shelf asks CSPPT's specific population-and-regimen question — in hypertensive adults in China, does folic acid added to enalapril reduce first stroke versus enalapril alone — a genuinely different question, built under the Nov 15 #3104 (RACING) precedent, as applied at #3325 (STRENGTH), #3489 (CAROLINA) and #3597 (PROPATRIA). Cross-point: for the broader homocysteine-lowering question across populations, see live shelf #203. Population boundary, stated plainly: CSPPT's population had low baseline folate levels and China does not fortify food with folic acid; the meta-analysis found no benefit in fortified populations, so this shelf's benefit must not be generalised to folate-replete, fortified populations. Tier C is set because the shelf is a stroke-benefit claim resting on one pivotal trial, which goes to the developer's personal verdict regardless of the supporting meta-analysis.
cards.source: Synthesis of Huo Y et al. JAMA. 2015 (PMID: 25771069); Huo Y et al. International journal of clinical practice. 2012 (PMID: 22607506).

shelves.title: Neurocysticercosis: albendazole cut seizures with generalisation by 67% relative but not total seizures — and adding praziquantel raised complete cyst resolution from 37% to 64%
shelves.question: In people with viable parenchymal brain cysticercosis and seizures, does antiparasitic treatment (albendazole, with corticosteroids) reduce seizures versus placebo — and does adding praziquantel to albendazole destroy more cysts than albendazole alone?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Albendazole/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Anti-Inflammatory Agents/therapeutic use · Anticestodal Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Anticonvulsants/therapeutic use · Brain/pathology · Brain Diseases/complications/drug therapy/pathology · Dexamethasone/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Granuloma/etiology · Humans · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Male · Middle Aged · Neurocysticercosis/complications/drug therapy/pathology · Seizures/drug therapy/etiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — real but narrower than the headline version. In the double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Garcia HH et al., PMID: 14724304), 120 patients with living brain cysticerci and seizures received albendazole 800 mg/day plus dexamethasone 6 mg/day for 10 days, or double placebo, alongside antiepileptic drugs. Over months 2–30, the total number of seizures fell 46% relative on albendazole — but that reduction was not statistically significant (95% CI −74 to 83), and the proportions having partial seizures were similar (19 of 57 versus 16 of 59); what did fall significantly was seizures with generalisation, down 67% relative (95% CI 20 to 86), with a greater tendency to generalise on placebo (22 of 59 versus 13 of 57; RR 1.63, 0.91–2.92). More cysts resolved on albendazole, and side effects other than abdominal pain did not differ. A decade later, the same group's phase 3 trial (Garcia HH et al., PMID: 24999157) showed how to kill more cysts: complete resolution at 6-month MRI in 25 (64%) of 39 patients on combined albendazole plus praziquantel versus 15 (37%) of 41 on standard albendazole (RR 1.75, 1.10–2.79), with no significant difference in adverse events; higher-dose albendazole alone (53%) did not significantly beat standard dosing. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): antiparasitic therapy clears cysts and reduces generalised seizures, with the combination the most cysticidal regimen tested — Tier C, because the seizure claim rests on the single 2004 trial and its primary count was not significant.

cards.headline: Garcia 2004: total seizures down 46% relative but not significant; seizures with generalisation down 67% relative (95% CI 20–86); more cysts resolved
cards.summary: Garcia 2004: total seizures down 46% relative but not significant; seizures with generalisation down 67% relative (95% CI 20–86); more cysts resolved
cards.people: 120 patients with living cysticerci in the brain and seizures treated with antiepileptic drugs, randomised to albendazole 800 mg/day plus dexamethasone 6 mg/day for 10 days (60 patients) or two placebos (60 patients); followed for 30 months or until seizure-free for 6 months after antiepileptic tapering.
cards.result: During months 2–30 there was a 46% relative reduction in the number of seizures on albendazole (95% CI −74 to 83), which was not statistically significant: a non-significant 41% relative reduction in partial seizures and a significant 67% relative reduction in seizures with generalisation (95% CI 20 to 86). The proportions with partial seizures were similar (19 of 57 albendazole versus 16 of 59 placebo), while placebo patients tended more to generalisation (22 of 59 versus 13 of 57; risk ratio 1.63, 0.91–2.92). More intracranial cystic lesions resolved in the albendazole group; side effects did not differ significantly except abdominal pain.
cards.watchOut: The trial's headline outcome — total seizure count — missed significance, skewed by a few patients with many partial seizures; the defensible claim is about generalised seizures and cyst resolution. Both arms received antiepileptic drugs and the albendazole arm received dexamethasone, so this is a treatment package, not albendazole alone, and it applies to viable parenchymal cysts, not calcified lesions or extraparenchymal disease.
cards.source: Garcia HH et al. A trial of antiparasitic treatment to reduce the rate of seizures due to cerebral cysticercosis. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2004. PMID: 14724304. cards.headline: Garcia 2014 (phase 3): complete cyst resolution at 6 months in 64% on albendazole plus praziquantel versus 37% on albendazole alone (RR 1.75)
cards.summary: Garcia 2014 (phase 3): complete cyst resolution at 6 months in 64% on albendazole plus praziquantel versus 37% on albendazole alone (RR 1.75)
cards.people: 124 patients with viable intraparenchymal neurocysticercosis randomised to 10 days of combined albendazole (15 mg/kg/day) plus praziquantel (50 mg/kg/day), standard albendazole (15 mg/kg/day), or increased-dose albendazole (22.5 mg/kg/day); primary outcome complete cyst resolution on 6-month MRI; enrolment stopped early after an interim analysis showed parasiticidal superiority of one group.
cards.result: Complete resolution of brain cysts occurred in 25 (64%) of 39 patients in the combined group versus 15 (37%) of 41 in the standard albendazole group (rate ratio 1.75, 95% CI 1.10–2.79; p=0.014). Increased-dose albendazole achieved 20 (53%) of 38 versus 37% on standard dose (RR 1.44, 0.87–2.38; p=0.151), not significant. Adverse events did not differ significantly between groups (18 events in the combined group, 11 in standard, 19 in increased-dose).
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is an MRI surrogate — cyst disappearance — and the trial was stopped early for superiority, which tends to inflate effects; whether the extra cyst clearance converts into fewer seizures than standard albendazole is inferred from the 2004 trial's logic, not measured here.
cards.source: Garcia HH et al. Efficacy of combined antiparasitic therapy with praziquantel and albendazole for neurocysticercosis: a double-blind, randomised controlled trial. cards.headline: Synthesis: killing cysts works and the combination kills most — the seizure dividend is proven only for generalised seizures, in one trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: killing cysts works and the combination kills most — the seizure dividend is proven only for generalised seizures, in one trial
cards.people: Two double-blind randomised trials from the Peruvian cysticercosis programme: 120 patients (albendazole plus dexamethasone versus placebo, 30 months) and 124 patients (combination versus standard versus high-dose albendazole, 6-month MRI).
cards.result: Cyst resolution: combination 64%, high-dose albendazole 53%, standard albendazole 37% (combination versus standard RR 1.75). Seizures: total count down 46% relative, not significant; seizures with generalisation down 67% relative (95% CI 20–86) for albendazole-based therapy versus placebo. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C — the clinical-outcome leg is a single trial whose primary count missed significance.
cards.watchOut: Everything here concerns viable parenchymal cysts with steroid cover; antiparasitic treatment of calcified granulomas, subarachnoid or ventricular disease is a different question with different risks, and treatment without corticosteroids courts the inflammatory harm these protocols were built to avoid.
cards.source: Synthesis of Garcia HH et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2004 (PMID: 14724304); Garcia HH et al. The Lancet Infectious Diseases. 2014 (PMID: 24999157).
