shelves.title: Inhaled levodopa for Parkinson's OFF periods: motor scores improve about 4 points more than placebo 30 minutes after a dose — proven in clinic, not yet in daily life
shelves.question: In people with Parkinson's disease who have daily OFF periods on oral levodopa, does self-administered inhaled levodopa powder improve motor function during an OFF period compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antiparkinson Agents/administration & dosage · Antiparkinson Agents/adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Levodopa/administration & dosage · Levodopa/adverse effects · Male · Middle Aged · Motor Activity/drug effects · Parkinson Disease/drug therapy · Powders · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for getting out of an OFF period faster, measured in the clinic. In the phase 3 SPAN-PD trial, inhaled levodopa 84 mg improved the UPDRS motor score from predose to 30 minutes postdose by -9.83 points versus -5.91 on placebo inhaler (between-group difference -3.92 [95% CI -6.84 to -1.00]; p=0.0088). An earlier phase 2 study of a single 50 mg dose in 24 patients found 77% reached a plasma levodopa rise of more than 400 ng/ml within 10 minutes versus 27% after oral carbidopa/levodopa, with significant motor improvement at the earliest assessments. Severe adverse events were uncommon and similar across arms (4% on 84 mg, 6% on 60 mg, 2% on placebo in SPAN-PD); cough at inhalation was the characteristic side effect in the phase 2 work. What is not shown: benefit on OFF time across an ordinary day at home, or any long-term efficacy — the pivotal endpoint was a single in-clinic OFF episode at week 12. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): inhaled levodopa speeds motor recovery from an OFF period by a modest margin over placebo, with the real-world and long-term value still untested in the carded record.

cards.headline: LeWitt 2019 (SPAN-PD): UPDRS motor change at 30 minutes -9.83 on inhaled levodopa 84 mg versus -5.91 on placebo (difference -3.92; p=0.0088)
cards.summary: LeWitt 2019 (SPAN-PD): UPDRS motor change at 30 minutes -9.83 on inhaled levodopa 84 mg versus -5.91 on placebo (difference -3.92; p=0.0088)
cards.people: 351 patients with Parkinson's disease aged 30-85 years on oral levodopa with daily OFF periods of at least 2 hours and at least 25% UPDRS motor improvement from OFF to ON after oral levodopa, at 65 sites in Canada, Poland, Spain and the USA, randomised to inhaled levodopa 60 mg (115), 84 mg (120) or placebo powder (116), self-administered as needed for OFF periods up to five times daily for 12 weeks; 339 received treatment.
cards.result: The least-squares mean change in UPDRS motor score from predose to 30 minutes postdose at week 12 was -9.83 (SE 1.51) on levodopa 84 mg versus -5.91 (SE 1.50) on placebo — a between-group difference of -3.92 (95% CI -6.84 to -1.00; p=0.0088). Severe adverse events occurred in 5 (4%) of 114 patients on 84 mg, 7 (6%) of 113 on 60 mg and 2 (2%) of 112 on placebo; serious adverse events in 11 (3%) of 339 patients overall, with hypotension and atrial fibrillation each assessed as possibly related to study drug in one patient.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint is one supervised in-clinic OFF episode at week 12 — not OFF time accumulated at home, falls, or quality of life. Patients were pre-selected for a robust oral levodopa response, so the result may not extend to poor responders.
cards.source: LeWitt PA et al. Safety and efficacy of CVT-301 (levodopa inhalation powder) on motor function during off periods in patients with Parkinson's disease: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial. The Lancet. Neurology. 2019. PMID: 30663606. Registry ID: NCT02240030. cards.headline: Lipp 2016 (phase 2): a single inhaled 50 mg dose put plasma levodopa up by >400 ng/ml within 10 minutes in 77% versus 27% after oral dosing, with motor gains at 5-15 minutes
cards.summary: Lipp 2016 (phase 2): a single inhaled 50 mg dose put plasma levodopa up by >400 ng/ml within 10 minutes in 77% versus 27% after oral dosing, with motor gains at 5-15 minutes
cards.type: Phase 1/2 translational study with a randomised placebo-controlled patient component (Lipp 2016)
cards.people: Preclinical dog work, 18 healthy volunteers comparing inhaled levodopa with oral carbidopa/levodopa pharmacokinetics, and 24 patients with Parkinson's disease given a single inhaled 50 mg levodopa dose during an OFF episode, compared with oral carbidopa/levodopa 25 mg/100 mg and placebo assessments.
cards.result: In the 24 patients, 77% showed an increase in plasma levodopa of more than 400 ng/ml within 10 minutes of inhalation versus 27% for oral dosing. Improvements in timed finger tapping and overall motor function (UPDRS Part III) were seen 5 and 15 minutes after administration — the earliest assessment points — and were statistically significant compared with placebo for average and best change. The most common adverse event was cough, mild to moderate, at the time of inhalation, resolving rapidly and becoming less frequent after initial dosing.
cards.watchOut: A single-dose pharmacokinetic and short-latency motor study in 24 patients: it establishes speed of absorption, not repeated-dose benefit, durability, or safety over months. The development-phase record also includes animal and healthy-volunteer data, which are described here only as context for the patient component.
cards.source: Lipp MM et al. Preclinical and clinical assessment of inhaled levodopa for OFF episodes in Parkinson's disease. Science translational medicine. 2016. PMID: 27733560. cards.headline: Synthesis: one pivotal trial, one small speed-of-onset study — faster OFF recovery in clinic, daily-life benefit unproven
cards.summary: Synthesis: one pivotal trial, one small speed-of-onset study — faster OFF recovery in clinic, daily-life benefit unproven
cards.people: One randomised double-blind phase 3 trial (SPAN-PD, 351 randomised, 339 treated) and one phase 2 single-dose study (24 patients) of inhaled levodopa powder (CVT-301) for OFF periods in Parkinson's disease on oral levodopa.
cards.result: UPDRS motor score change at 30 minutes: -9.83 on 84 mg versus -5.91 on placebo (difference -3.92; p=0.0088). Plasma levodopa rose >400 ng/ml within 10 minutes in 77% (inhaled, phase 2) versus 27% (oral). Severe adverse events 4% (84 mg) versus 2% (placebo) in the phase 3 trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C because the benefit claim rests on a single phase 3 trial with a surrogate-style in-clinic endpoint.
cards.watchOut: No carded trial measures total daily OFF time, patient-reported benefit at home, or use beyond 12 weeks; a rescue therapy can win the 30-minute clinic test and still add little to a patient's day. Tier C is set for that single-pivotal-trial basis.
cards.source: Synthesis of LeWitt PA et al. The Lancet. Neurology. 2019 (PMID: 30663606); Lipp MM et al. Science translational medicine. 2016 (PMID: 27733560).

shelves.title: IncobotulinumtoxinA for chronic drooling: salivary flow and global impression both beat placebo at 4 weeks in adults (SIAXI) and in children (SIPEXI)
shelves.question: In adults and children with chronic sialorrhea (drooling) from neurological disorders, do incobotulinumtoxinA injections into the salivary glands reduce salivary flow and improve global impression compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Botulinum Toxins, Type A/therapeutic use · Brain Injuries, Traumatic/complications · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Parkinson Disease/complications · Sialorrhea/drug therapy · Sialorrhea/etiology · Stroke/complications · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two placebo-controlled phase 3 trials, one in adults and one in children, agree. In adults (SIAXI), incobotulinumtoxinA 100 U significantly reduced unstimulated salivary flow rate at week 4 versus placebo (p=0.004) and improved patients' Global Impression of Change scores (p=0.002), with an effect lasting to week 16; dry mouth (2.7% at 100 U) and dysphagia (0.0% at 100 U) were the commonest treatment-related adverse events. In children aged 6-17 (SIPEXI), the same drug beat placebo on both coprimary endpoints — mean salivary flow decrease difference -0.06 g/min (p=0.0012) and carers' global impression difference 0.28 points (p=0.032) — with adverse-event rates comparable to placebo. The absolute flow reductions are small; the claim rests on the pairing of an objective flow measure with a global-impression benefit in two independent trials. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): gland injections of incobotulinumtoxinA modestly reduce drooling in adults and children with neurological sialorrhea, with dry mouth and dysphagia as the trade-off to watch.

cards.headline: Jost 2019 (SIAXI): the 100 U dose significantly cut salivary flow (p=0.004) and improved global impression (p=0.002) at week 4, lasting to week 16
cards.summary: Jost 2019 (SIAXI): the 100 U dose significantly cut salivary flow (p=0.004) and improved global impression (p=0.002) at week 4, lasting to week 16
cards.people: 184 adults with chronic sialorrhea due to Parkinson disease (70.7%), atypical parkinsonism (8.7%), stroke (19.0%) or traumatic brain injury (2.7%), randomised 2:2:1 to a single treatment cycle of incobotulinumtoxinA 75 U (n=74), 100 U (n=74) or placebo (n=36) injected into the salivary glands.
cards.result: Both dose groups reduced mean unstimulated salivary flow rate at week 4, significantly so for 100 U versus placebo (p=0.004); patients' Global Impression of Change scores also improved, significantly for 100 U (p=0.002). A lasting effect was observed at week 16. The most frequent treatment-related adverse events were dry mouth (5.4% on 75 U, 2.7% on 100 U) and dysphagia (2.7% on 75 U, 0.0% on 100 U).
cards.watchOut: The record reports p-values for the coprimary endpoints without the absolute flow-rate changes, so the size of the drying effect cannot be quantified from the abstract; the placebo group was small (n=36) by the 2:2:1 design, and only one treatment cycle was studied blinded.
cards.source: Jost WH et al. SIAXI: Placebo-controlled, randomized, double-blind study of incobotulinumtoxinA for sialorrhea. Neurology. 2019. PMID: 30918101. Registry ID: NCT02091739. cards.headline: Berweck 2021 (SIPEXI): in children 6-17, salivary flow fell more on incobotulinumtoxinA (difference -0.06 g/min; p=0.0012) and carers rated greater improvement (0.28 points; p=0.032)
cards.summary: Berweck 2021 (SIPEXI): in children 6-17, salivary flow fell more on incobotulinumtoxinA (difference -0.06 g/min; p=0.0012) and carers rated greater improvement (0.28 points; p=0.032)
cards.people: 220 children and adolescents aged 6-17 years with chronic sialorrhea due to neurologic disorders or intellectual disability, randomised to body-weight-dependent incobotulinumtoxinA 20-75 U (n=148) or placebo (n=72) for one blinded injection cycle, followed by an open-label extension; a separate uncontrolled cohort of 35 children aged 2-5 years received active treatment throughout.
cards.result: At week 4, mean unstimulated salivary flow rate decreased significantly more with incobotulinumtoxinA than placebo (difference -0.06 g/min; p=0.0012) and carers' Global Impression of Change ratings favoured active treatment (difference 0.28 points; p=0.032); secondary endpoints consistently supported the coprimary results and benefit was sustained in the extension. Adverse-event incidences were comparable between incobotulinumtoxinA and placebo and did not increase notably with repeated injections; the most common adverse events were respiratory infections.
cards.watchOut: The absolute flow difference (-0.06 g/min) is small and its day-to-day meaning for clothing, skin and aspiration is inferred from the modest 0.28-point carer-impression gap rather than measured directly; the 2-5-year-old cohort had no placebo control. This record carries no MeSH terms.
cards.source: Berweck S et al. Placebo-Controlled Clinical Trial of IncobotulinumtoxinA for Sialorrhea in Children: SIPEXI. Neurology. 2021. PMID: 34341153. Registry ID: NCT02270736. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Synthesis: two phase 3 trials, two age groups, both coprimary endpoint pairs met — small absolute effects, consistently in the same direction
cards.summary: Synthesis: two phase 3 trials, two age groups, both coprimary endpoint pairs met — small absolute effects, consistently in the same direction
cards.people: Two randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trials of incobotulinumtoxinA for chronic sialorrhea: SIAXI (184 adults, mainly Parkinson disease and stroke) and SIPEXI (220 children aged 6-17 with neurologic disorders or intellectual disability).
cards.result: Adults: significant salivary-flow reduction and global-impression improvement at week 4 for the 100 U dose (p=0.004 and p=0.002), lasting to week 16; treatment-related dry mouth 2.7% and dysphagia 0.0% at 100 U. Children: flow difference -0.06 g/min (p=0.0012), carer impression difference 0.28 points (p=0.032), adverse events comparable to placebo. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Neither trial was powered for aspiration pneumonia, hospitalisation or quality-of-life endpoints; repeat-cycle evidence is open-label. The stamp is POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY because absolute effect sizes are small and partly unreported in the adult record.
cards.source: Synthesis of Jost WH et al. Neurology. 2019 (PMID: 30918101); Berweck S et al. Neurology. 2021 (PMID: 34341153).

shelves.title: Mexiletine for ALS muscle cramps: cramp frequency fell to 16-31% of placebo rates at 300-900 mg in one trial, and from 5.3 to 3.5 cramps a day in a crossover trial
shelves.question: In people with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis troubled by muscle cramps, does mexiletine reduce cramp frequency and severity compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis/drug therapy · Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis/physiopathology · Disease Progression · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Mexiletine/adverse effects · Mexiletine/pharmacokinetics · Mexiletine/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Muscle Cramp/drug therapy · Muscle Cramp/physiopathology · Postural Balance/drug effects · Treatment Outcome · Voltage-Gated Sodium Channel Blockers/adverse effects · Voltage-Gated Sodium Channel Blockers/pharmacokinetics · Voltage-Gated Sodium Channel Blockers/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for cramps specifically, not for the disease. In a 60-patient phase 2 trial, mexiletine cut muscle cramp frequency to 31% of the placebo rate at 300 mg/day (p=0.047) and 16% at 900 mg/day (p=0.002), with cramp intensity at 25% of placebo on the higher dose (p=0.005); rates of decline in ALSFRS-R and slow vital capacity did not differ from placebo. A second, crossover trial in 20 patients found cramps fell from 5.3 per day on placebo to 3.5 on mexiletine 150 mg twice daily, with cramp severity down 15 units on a 100-unit scale (p=0.01). Tolerability splits by dose: 300 mg/day was well tolerated, while 32% of patients on 900 mg/day discontinued study drug versus 5% on placebo (p=0.026). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): mexiletine at about 300 mg/day substantially reduces ALS cramp frequency and severity in two small randomised trials, with no shown effect on disease progression.

cards.headline: Weiss 2016: cramp frequency 31% of placebo at 300 mg/day (p=0.047) and 16% at 900 mg/day (p=0.002) — but 32% stopped the 900 mg dose versus 5% on placebo
cards.summary: Weiss 2016: cramp frequency 31% of placebo at 300 mg/day (p=0.047) and 16% at 900 mg/day (p=0.002) — but 32% stopped the 900 mg dose versus 5% on placebo
cards.people: 60 participants with sporadic ALS at 10 centres, randomised 1:1:1 to placebo, mexiletine 300 mg/day or mexiletine 900 mg/day for 12 weeks; primary endpoints were safety and tolerability, with cramp frequency and severity, ALSFRS-R and slow vital capacity as secondary endpoints.
cards.result: Muscle cramp frequency fell significantly on mexiletine: rates were 31% of placebo at 300 mg/day (p=0.047) and 16% of placebo at 900 mg/day (p=0.002); cramp intensity was 45% of placebo at 300 mg (p=0.08) and 25% at 900 mg (p=0.005) — relative effects as reported in the record. Rates of decline of ALSFRS-R and slow vital capacity did not differ from placebo. The only serious adverse event among active-arm participants was one episode of imbalance; 32% of participants on 900 mg discontinued study drug versus 5% on placebo (p=0.026).

cards.headline: Oskarsson 2018 (crossover): cramps fell from 5.3 a day on placebo to 3.5 on mexiletine, severity down 15 points on a 100-point scale (p=0.01)
cards.summary: Oskarsson 2018 (crossover): cramps fell from 5.3 a day on placebo to 3.5 on mexiletine, severity down 15 points on a 100-point scale (p=0.01)
cards.people: 20 patients with ALS requesting treatment for symptomatic muscle cramps, in a multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial of mexiletine 150 mg twice daily.
cards.result: Muscle cramp frequency was reduced in 18 of 20 patients, with 13 reductions attributed to treatment (P<0.05); the average reduction was 1.8 cramps per day, from 5.3 with placebo to 3.5 with mexiletine. Estimated cramp severity fell by 15 units on a 100-unit scale (p=0.01) from a baseline average of 46. No effect on fasciculations was noted. One patient discontinued because of dizziness and one to start open-label mexiletine; no serious adverse event occurred.
cards.watchOut: Only 20 patients in a crossover design, so carry-over and period effects are hard to exclude and the estimate is fragile; the record carries no MeSH terms and no registry ID.
cards.source: Oskarsson B et al. Mexiletine for muscle cramps in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis: A randomized, double-blind crossover trial. Muscle & nerve. 2018. PMID: 29510461. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Synthesis: two small trials, one symptom, large relative reductions — and a clear dose ceiling set by tolerability
cards.summary: Synthesis: two small trials, one symptom, large relative reductions — and a clear dose ceiling set by tolerability
cards.people: Two randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials of mexiletine for muscle cramps in ALS: a 60-patient parallel-group dose trial (300 and 900 mg/day, 12 weeks) and a 20-patient crossover trial (150 mg twice daily).
cards.result: Cramp frequency: 31% of placebo at 300 mg/day and 16% at 900 mg/day (parallel trial); 5.3 to 3.5 cramps/day (crossover). Cramp severity: down to 25% of placebo at 900 mg; -15/100 units in crossover. Disease progression (ALSFRS-R, vital capacity): no difference detected. Discontinuation: 32% at 900 mg/day versus 5% on placebo. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for cramp relief at tolerated doses.
cards.watchOut: Total randomised experience is 80 patients with short follow-up; neither trial addresses survival, function or cramps beyond 12 weeks. The benefit claim is symptom-only and should not be read as disease modification.
cards.source: Synthesis of Weiss MD et al. Neurology. 2016 (PMID: 26911633); Oskarsson B et al. Muscle & nerve. 2018 (PMID: 29510461).

shelves.title: Rotigotine patch for restless legs syndrome: severity scores fell about 5 points more than placebo at the 2-3 mg doses in two 6-month trials — skin reactions in up to 43%
shelves.question: In adults with moderate-to-severe idiopathic restless legs syndrome, does the once-daily rotigotine transdermal patch reduce symptom severity compared with placebo over 6 months?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Cutaneous · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Analysis of Variance · Dopamine Agonists/therapeutic use · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Restless Legs Syndrome/drug therapy · Retrospective Studies · Severity of Illness Index · Tetrahydronaphthalenes/therapeutic use · Thiophenes/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two 6-month placebo-controlled trials of the dopamine-agonist patch agree. In the European-led trial (458 patients), IRLS severity scores fell by -16.2 (2 mg/24 h) and -16.8 (3 mg/24 h) versus -8.6 on placebo (p<0.0001 for each dose versus placebo), with parallel gains in clinical global impression. In the US trial (505 patients), adjusted IRLS differences versus placebo were -4.5 (95% CI -6.9 to -2.2) at 2 mg/24 h and -5.2 (-7.5 to -2.9) at 3 mg/24 h (both p<0.001 on the coprimary measures). The price is the patch itself: skin reactions in 145 (43%) of 341 rotigotine patients versus 2 (2%) of 117 on placebo in the first trial, and in 27% in the second, alongside nausea (18.1%) and headache (11.6%). No augmentation was noted within the 6-month trial period — but augmentation is a longer-horizon harm these trials cannot exclude. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): rotigotine 2-3 mg/24 h relieves restless legs symptoms over 6 months, with application-site reactions as its signature cost.

cards.headline: Trenkwalder 2008: IRLS fell -16.2 (2 mg) and -16.8 (3 mg) versus -8.6 on placebo (p<0.0001) — skin reactions 43% versus 2%
cards.summary: Trenkwalder 2008: IRLS fell -16.2 (2 mg) and -16.8 (3 mg) versus -8.6 on placebo (p<0.0001) — skin reactions 43% versus 2%
cards.people: 458 patients with moderate-to-severe idiopathic restless legs syndrome (mean baseline IRLS sum score 28.1), randomised to rotigotine 1 mg/24 h (n=115), 2 mg/24 h (n=112), 3 mg/24 h (n=114) or placebo (n=117) by once-daily patch for 6 months; efficacy analysed in 447 patients.
cards.result: Mean IRLS change at end of maintenance was -13.7 (1 mg), -16.2 (2 mg), -16.8 (3 mg) and -8.6 (placebo), with p<0.0001 for the treatment difference versus placebo at each dose; clinical global impression item 1 changed by -2.09, -2.41, -2.55 and -1.34 respectively (p<0.0001 each dose versus placebo). Skin reactions, mostly mild or moderate, occurred in 145 (43%) of 341 rotigotine patients versus 2 (2%) of 117 on placebo; ten patients had serious adverse events deemed related to rotigotine, six of them application-site reactions. No signs of augmentation were noted.
cards.watchOut: Six months is short for a chronic nightly therapy, and augmentation — the paradoxical worsening dopamine agonists can cause — typically declares itself later; the trial's 'no augmentation' is an absence within a short window, not a clearance. The placebo response was large (-8.6 IRLS points), so the drug-attributable gain is the roughly 5-8 point difference, not the full fall.
cards.source: Trenkwalder C et al. Efficacy of rotigotine for treatment of moderate-to-severe restless legs syndrome: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. The Lancet. Neurology. 2008. PMID: 18515185. Registry ID: NCT00136045. cards.headline: Hening 2010 (US trial): adjusted IRLS differences versus placebo -4.5 at 2 mg/24 h and -5.2 at 3 mg/24 h over 6 months
cards.summary: Hening 2010 (US trial): adjusted IRLS differences versus placebo -4.5 at 2 mg/24 h and -5.2 at 3 mg/24 h over 6 months
cards.people: 505 participants in the United States with moderate-to-severe restless legs syndrome (IRLS sum score at least 15), randomised to placebo or fixed-dose rotigotine 0.5, 1, 2 or 3 mg/24 h by once-daily patch over a 6-month maintenance period.
cards.result: On both coprimary measures (IRLS sum score and clinical global impressions item 1), rotigotine 2 and 3 mg/24 h was superior to placebo (P<0.001). Adjusted IRLS treatment differences versus placebo were -4.5 (95% CI -6.9 to -2.2) for 2 mg/24 h and -5.2 (95% CI -7.5 to -2.9) for 3 mg/24 h; CGI item 1 differences were -0.65 and -0.9 respectively. Skin reactions occurred in 27% of rotigotine subjects, with nausea in 18.1% and headache in 11.6%, mostly mild or moderate.
cards.watchOut: The lower doses (0.5 and 1 mg/24 h) did not win on the coprimary endpoints — the effective range is the top two doses, which also carry the most skin reactions. As with the companion trial, follow-up ends at 6 months.

shelves.title: Ravulizumab for generalised myasthenia gravis: MG-ADL improved -3.1 versus -1.4 on placebo at 26 weeks in a single phase 3 trial (CHAMPION MG)
shelves.question: In adults with anti-acetylcholine-receptor antibody-positive generalised myasthenia gravis, does the long-acting C5 complement inhibitor ravulizumab improve daily-function and clinician-rated weakness scores compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Myasthenia Gravis/drug therapy · Myasthenia Gravis/immunology · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/adverse effects · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/administration & dosage · Male · Female · Double-Blind Method · Middle Aged · Adult · Aged · Complement Inactivating Agents/therapeutic use · Complement Inactivating Agents/administration & dosage · Complement Inactivating Agents/adverse effects · Complement Inactivating Agents/pharmacology · Activities of Daily Living · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one well-conducted phase 3 trial. In CHAMPION MG, 175 adults with anti-AChR antibody-positive generalised myasthenia gravis were randomised to intravenous ravulizumab (loading dose, then maintenance every 8 weeks) or placebo for 26 weeks. The patient-reported MG-ADL score improved by -3.1 on ravulizumab versus -1.4 on placebo (P<0.001), and the clinician-reported QMG score by -2.8 versus -0.8 (P<0.001); improvements appeared within 1 week and were sustained to week 26, and a QMG improvement of at least 5 points occurred in 30.0% versus 11.3% (P=0.005). No notable differences in adverse events were observed between groups in the trial window. What is missing: a second trial, any comparison with the other complement and FcRn therapies now used in this disease, and outcomes beyond 26 weeks of blinded treatment. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): ravulizumab improves MG-ADL and QMG scores over 26 weeks in AChR-positive generalised myasthenia gravis, on the strength of a single trial.

cards.headline: Vu 2022 (CHAMPION MG): MG-ADL -3.1 versus -1.4 and QMG -2.8 versus -0.8 at week 26 (both P<0.001); QMG ≥5-point responders 30.0% versus 11.3%
cards.summary: Vu 2022 (CHAMPION MG): MG-ADL -3.1 versus -1.4 and QMG -2.8 versus -0.8 at week 26 (both P<0.001); QMG ≥5-point responders 30.0% versus 11.3%
cards.people: 175 patients with anti-acetylcholine-receptor antibody-positive generalised myasthenia gravis, randomised 1:1 in a multinational double-blind trial to intravenous ravulizumab (loading dose day 1, maintenance from day 15 every 8 weeks) or placebo for 26 weeks.
cards.result: Mean change from baseline to week 26 favoured ravulizumab on both the primary endpoint, MG-ADL (-3.1 versus -1.4; P<0.001), and the first secondary endpoint, QMG (-2.8 versus -0.8; P<0.001). Improvements in both measures occurred within 1 week and were sustained through week 26. A QMG improvement of 5 points or more occurred in 30.0% of ravulizumab patients versus 11.3% on placebo (P=0.005). No notable differences in adverse events were observed.
cards.watchOut: A single 26-week trial in AChR-antibody-positive disease only: it says nothing about MuSK-positive or seronegative myasthenia, about myasthenic crisis or hospitalisation endpoints, or about how ravulizumab compares with eculizumab, efgartigimod or rozanolixizumab. Complement blockade's infection precautions (meningococcal risk management) are a programme requirement that a 175-patient trial cannot size.
cards.source: Vu T et al. Terminal Complement Inhibitor Ravulizumab in Generalized Myasthenia Gravis. NEJM evidence. 2022. PMID: 38319212. Registry ID: NCT03920293. shelves.title: Optic neuritis steroids (ONTT): intravenous methylprednisolone speeds visual recovery but does not improve final acuity — and oral prednisone alone raises recurrence (relative risk 1.79)
shelves.question: In adults with acute optic neuritis, does corticosteroid treatment — intravenous methylprednisolone followed by oral prednisone, or oral prednisone alone — improve visual recovery compared with placebo, and does either change the risk of new episodes?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Administration, Oral · Adolescent · Adult · Color Perception · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Injections, Intravenous · Male · Methylprednisolone/administration & dosage · Methylprednisolone/adverse effects · Methylprednisolone/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Multiple Sclerosis · Optic Neuritis/drug therapy · Optic Neuritis/physiopathology · Patient Compliance · Prednisone/administration & dosage · Prednisone/adverse effects · Prednisone/therapeutic use · Recurrence · Visual Acuity · Visual Fields
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the route decides. In the Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial (457 patients), intravenous methylprednisolone followed by oral prednisone sped recovery of visual function versus placebo — most clearly for visual-field defects (P=0.0001) — and left slightly better visual fields (P=0.054), contrast sensitivity (P=0.026) and colour vision (P=0.033) at 6 months, but not better visual acuity (P=0.66). Oral prednisone alone did not differ from placebo on visual outcomes at all, and it carried a higher rate of new episodes of optic neuritis in either eye (relative risk 1.79; 95% CI 1.08 to 2.95 versus placebo) — a relative effect printed with its confidence interval in the record. So the intravenous regimen buys speed, not a better final result, and the oral-only regimen buys nothing and adds recurrence risk. PROPOSED SPLIT: intravenous methylprednisolone for faster recovery when speed matters; oral prednisone alone should not be used for acute optic neuritis.

cards.headline: Beck 1992 (ONTT): IV methylprednisolone sped recovery (visual fields P=0.0001) with no acuity advantage at 6 months (P=0.66); oral prednisone matched placebo and raised recurrence (relative risk 1.79)
cards.summary: Beck 1992 (ONTT): IV methylprednisolone sped recovery (visual fields P=0.0001) with no acuity advantage at 6 months (P=0.66); oral prednisone matched placebo and raised recurrence (relative risk 1.79)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Beck 1992, Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial)
cards.people: 457 patients with acute optic neuritis at 15 clinical centres, randomised to oral prednisone 1 mg/kg/day for 14 days, intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g/day for 3 days followed by oral prednisone 1 mg/kg/day for 11 days, or oral placebo for 14 days; visual function followed for 6 months.
cards.result: Visual function recovered faster with intravenous methylprednisolone than placebo, particularly for visual-field defects (P=0.0001). At 6 months the intravenous group still had slightly better visual fields (P=0.054), contrast sensitivity (P=0.026) and colour vision (P=0.033), but not visual acuity (P=0.66). The oral-prednisone group's visual outcomes did not differ from placebo. New episodes of optic neuritis in either eye were more frequent on oral prednisone than placebo (relative risk 1.79; 95% CI 1.08 to 2.95); no such increase was seen with intravenous methylprednisolone.
cards.watchOut: One trial from 1992, before modern MS disease-modifying therapy and current MRI-based management: its recurrence finding concerns optic neuritis episodes, and the trial was not designed to test effects on long-term disability or conversion management as practised now. The recurrence result is a relative risk; the record does not print the absolute episode rates in the abstract.
cards.source: Beck RW et al. A randomized, controlled trial of corticosteroids in the treatment of acute optic neuritis. The Optic Neuritis Study Group. The New England journal of medicine. 1992. shelves.title: Ataluren in nonsense-mutation Duchenne dystrophy: the phase 3 trial missed its walking endpoint (13.0 m difference, p=0.213) — the only significant signal sits in one prespecified middle subgroup
shelves.question: In ambulant boys with Duchenne muscular dystrophy, does ataluren improve walking distance compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Child · Codon, Nonsense/genetics · Double-Blind Method · Dystrophin/deficiency/genetics · Global Health · Humans · Male · Muscular Dystrophy, Duchenne/drug therapy/genetics · Oxadiazoles/administration & dosage · Treatment Outcome · Walking
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on the trials' own primary endpoints. In the phase 3 ACT DMD trial (McDonald CM et al., PMID: 28728956), change in 6-minute walk distance at week 48 was −47.7 m on ataluren versus −60.7 m on placebo, a difference of 13.0 m (95% CI −7.4 to 33.4; p=0.213) — not significant. The earlier phase 2b trial (Bushby K et al., PMID: 25042182) likewise only favoured its low dose in a post hoc analysis (difference 31.3 m, post hoc p=0.056). The one nominally significant result in either trial is a prespecified ACT DMD subgroup — boys with a baseline walk distance of 300 m to less than 400 m, difference 42.9 m (95% CI 11.8–74.0; p=0.007) — while the subgroups below 300 m (−7.7 m; p=0.749) and at 400 m or more (−9.5 m; p=0.580) showed nothing. Ataluren was generally well tolerated in both trials; in ACT DMD, serious adverse events occurred in 8 patients (3%), 4 per group. Two randomised blinded trials that both miss their primary endpoint cannot carry a benefit stamp; the middle-subgroup signal is hypothesis-generating only. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): ataluren has not been shown to improve walking distance overall in nonsense-mutation Duchenne dystrophy; a possible effect confined to boys in the transitional 300–400 m walk range rests on a single subgroup analysis.

cards.headline: McDonald 2017 (ACT DMD): walk distance fell 47.7 m on ataluren versus 60.7 m on placebo — difference 13.0 m, p=0.213; only the 300–400 m subgroup differed (42.9 m, p=0.007)
cards.summary: McDonald 2017 (ACT DMD): walk distance fell 47.7 m on ataluren versus 60.7 m on placebo — difference 13.0 m, p=0.213; only the 300–400 m subgroup differed (42.9 m, p=0.007)
cards.people: 230 boys aged 7–16 years with nonsense-mutation Duchenne muscular dystrophy and a baseline 6-minute walk distance of at least 150 m and no more than 80% of predicted, at 54 sites in 18 countries, randomised to ataluren 40 mg/kg per day orally in three divided doses (n=115) or placebo (n=115) for 48 weeks; 228 formed the intention-to-treat population.
cards.result: Least-squares mean change in 6-minute walk distance from baseline to week 48 was −47.7 m (SE 9.3) on ataluren and −60.7 m (SE 9.3) on placebo — difference 13.0 m (SE 10.4; 95% CI −7.4 to 33.4; p=0.213), not significant. In prespecified subgroups the difference was −7.7 m (95% CI −54.9 to 39.5; p=0.749) for baseline walk under 300 m, 42.9 m (95% CI 11.8–74.0; p=0.007) for 300 m to less than 400 m, and −9.5 m (95% CI −43.2 to 24.2; p=0.580) for 400 m or more. Serious adverse events occurred in 8 patients (3%), 4 in each group, and were deemed unrelated to treatment except one placebo-group event.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint was missed, so the 300–400 m subgroup result — although prespecified — is a subgroup of a negative trial and was not adjusted into a confirmatory claim; the two flanking subgroups point the other way. Walk distance is a functional measure, not a survival or loss-of-ambulation outcome.
cards.source: McDonald CM et al. Ataluren in patients with nonsense mutation Duchenne muscular dystrophy (ACT DMD): a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial. cards.headline: Bushby 2014 (phase 2b): low-dose ataluren favoured on walk distance by 31.3 m — but only in a post hoc analysis (p=0.056); the higher dose showed no such signal
cards.summary: Bushby 2014 (phase 2b): low-dose ataluren favoured on walk distance by 31.3 m — but only in a post hoc analysis (p=0.056); the higher dose showed no such signal
cards.people: 174 males aged at least 5 years with nonsense-mutation dystrophinopathy, randomised to ataluren 10, 10, 20 mg/kg (n=57), ataluren 20, 20, 40 mg/kg (n=60), or placebo (n=57), given orally three times daily for 48 weeks.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — change in 6-minute walk distance at week 48 — favoured the lower ataluren dose over placebo by 31.3 m, but this was a post hoc analysis with p=0.056, short of conventional significance; the record reports no significant primary result for the higher dose. Timed function tests, as secondary endpoints, showed differences the authors describe as meaningful for the low dose versus placebo. Ataluren was generally well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: A post hoc p=0.056 in the lower of two dose arms, with the higher dose null, is the classic shape of a chance finding; this trial is supportive context for ACT DMD, not independent confirmation — and ACT DMD, testing the higher total daily dose, then missed outright.
cards.source: Bushby K et al. Ataluren treatment of patients with nonsense mutation dystrophinopathy. Muscle & Nerve. 2014. PMID: 25042182. cards.summary: Synthesis: two blinded trials, two missed primary endpoints, one subgroup — the honest grade is weak evidence of no demonstrated overall benefit
cards.people: Two randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials of oral ataluren in nonsense-mutation Duchenne dystrophy totalling 404 boys and males (phase 2b, n=174, 48 weeks; phase 3 ACT DMD, n=230, 48 weeks), both using change in 6-minute walk distance as the primary endpoint.

shelves.title: Satralizumab in NMOSD: relapses cut in two phase 3 trials — 20% versus 43% added to immunosuppressants (HR 0.38) and 30% versus 50% alone (HR 0.45) — with the effect concentrated in aquaporin-4-positive patients
shelves.question: In patients with neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, does satralizumab reduce relapse risk compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Aquaporin 4/immunology · Autoantibodies/blood · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Immunoglobulin G/blood · Immunosuppressive Agents/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Neuromyelitis Optica/drug therapy/immunology · Receptors, Interleukin-6/antagonists & inhibitors/immunology · Recurrence · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two phase 3 trials, one answer. Added to stable immunosuppressant treatment (SAkuraSky, Yamamura T et al., PMID: 31774956), satralizumab 120 mg subcutaneously every 4 weeks produced a first protocol-defined relapse in 8 of 41 patients (20%) versus 18 of 42 (43%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.38; 95% CI 0.16–0.88) — a 62% relative reduction in relapse hazard. As monotherapy (SAkuraStar, Traboulsee A et al., PMID: 32333898), relapses occurred in 19 of 63 patients (30%) versus 16 of 32 (50%) (hazard ratio 0.45; 95% CI 0.23–0.89; p=0.018) — a 55% relative reduction. The benefit concentrates in aquaporin-4-IgG-seropositive patients: in SAkuraSky their hazard ratio was 0.21 (95% CI 0.06–0.75), against 0.66 (95% CI 0.20–2.24) in seronegative patients. Neither trial showed an effect on pain or fatigue scores, and rates of serious adverse events and infections did not differ between groups in SAkuraSky. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): satralizumab roughly halves relapse risk in NMOSD, as add-on therapy and alone, with the clearest effect in aquaporin-4-positive disease; the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE in this band.

cards.headline: Yamamura 2019 (SAkuraSky): relapse in 20% on satralizumab added to immunosuppressants versus 43% on placebo (HR 0.38); in aquaporin-4-positive patients, 11% versus 43% (HR 0.21)
cards.summary: Yamamura 2019 (SAkuraSky): relapse in 20% on satralizumab added to immunosuppressants versus 43% on placebo (HR 0.38); in aquaporin-4-positive patients, 11% versus 43% (HR 0.21)
cards.people: 83 patients with NMOSD, seropositive or seronegative for aquaporin-4-IgG, randomised 1:1 to satralizumab 120 mg (n=41) or placebo (n=42) subcutaneously at weeks 0, 2 and 4 and every 4 weeks thereafter, each added to stable immunosuppressant treatment; median double-blind treatment duration with satralizumab was 107.4 weeks.
cards.result: First protocol-defined relapse occurred in 8 patients (20%) on satralizumab and 18 (43%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.38; 95% CI 0.16–0.88), a 62% relative reduction in relapse hazard, with absolute rates of 20% versus 43%. Among 55 aquaporin-4-IgG-seropositive patients, relapse occurred in 11% on satralizumab versus 43% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.21; 95% CI 0.06–0.75); among 28 seronegative patients, 36% versus 43% (hazard ratio 0.66; 95% CI 0.20–2.24). Pain (VAS difference 4.08; 95% CI −8.44 to 16.61) and fatigue (FACIT-F difference −3.10; 95% CI −8.38 to 2.18) did not differ, and rates of serious adverse events and infections did not differ between groups.
cards.watchOut: Only 83 patients and 26 relapses drive the headline hazard ratio, so the confidence interval is wide (0.16–0.88); the seronegative subgroup — a third of the trial — shows no clear effect, and the trial cannot separate satralizumab's contribution from the background immunosuppressants every patient was taking.
cards.source: Yamamura T et al. Trial of Satralizumab in Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2019. PMID: 31774956. Registry ID: NCT02028884. cards.headline: Traboulsee 2020 (SAkuraStar): satralizumab alone cut protocol-defined relapses to 30% versus 50% on placebo (HR 0.45, p=0.018), with similar serious adverse event rates
cards.summary: Traboulsee 2020 (SAkuraStar): satralizumab alone cut protocol-defined relapses to 30% versus 50% on placebo (HR 0.45, p=0.018), with similar serious adverse event rates
cards.people: 95 adults aged 18–74 years with aquaporin-4-seropositive or seronegative NMOSD and at least one documented attack in the previous 12 months, at 44 sites in 13 countries, randomised 2:1 to satralizumab 120 mg (n=63) or placebo (n=32) subcutaneously at weeks 0, 2 and 4 and every 4 weeks thereafter, with concomitant immunosuppressants prohibited.
cards.result: Protocol-defined relapses occurred in 19 patients (30%) receiving satralizumab and 16 (50%) receiving placebo (hazard ratio 0.45; 95% CI 0.23–0.89; p=0.018), a 55% relative reduction in relapse hazard with absolute rates of 30% versus 50%. Adverse events occurred at 473.9 per 100 patient-years on satralizumab and 495.2 per 100 patient-years on placebo; the incidence of serious adverse events and of adverse events leading to withdrawal was similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: The placebo group is only 32 patients, follow-up ends at the first relapse or the close of the double-blind phase, and — as in SAkuraSky — disability accumulation, the outcome relapses are meant to prevent, is not itself a reported endpoint here; relapse prevention is the proven claim.
cards.source: Traboulsee A et al. Safety and efficacy of satralizumab monotherapy in neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder: a randomised, double-blind, multicentre, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial. cards.headline: Synthesis: two small phase 3 trials agree — relapse hazard roughly halved, seropositive patients gaining most, pain and fatigue unmoved
cards.summary: Synthesis: two small phase 3 trials agree — relapse hazard roughly halved, seropositive patients gaining most, pain and fatigue unmoved
cards.people: Two randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trials totalling 178 patients with NMOSD: SAkuraSky (n=83, satralizumab added to immunosuppressants) and SAkuraStar (n=95, satralizumab monotherapy).
cards.result: Relapse: 20% versus 43% (HR 0.38; 95% CI 0.16–0.88) as add-on therapy; 30% versus 50% (HR 0.45; 95% CI 0.23–0.89) as monotherapy. Aquaporin-4-positive subgroup (SAkuraSky): HR 0.21; seronegative: HR 0.66 with a confidence interval crossing 1. Pain and fatigue scores: no difference. Serious adverse events and infections: no excess shown. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), the band cap for this relaxed tier.
cards.watchOut: Both trials are small, event counts are low (26 and 35 relapses), and neither measures disability directly. Tier C is set for every shelf in this band. shelves.title: THALES: ticagrelor plus aspirin cut 30-day stroke or death to 5.5% versus 6.6% on aspirin alone after minor stroke or TIA — a 1.1-point absolute gain bought with five times the severe bleeding (0.5% versus 0.1%)
shelves.question: In adults after TIA or minor ischaemic stroke, does ticagrelor plus aspirin reduce subsequent stroke compared with aspirin alone?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Aspirin/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Disability Evaluation · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Hemorrhage/chemically induced · Humans · Ischemic Attack, Transient/complications/drug therapy · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Purinergic P2Y Receptor Antagonists/therapeutic use · Secondary Prevention · Stroke/complications/drug therapy/mortality/prevention & control · Ticagrelor/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — from a single large trial, flagged single-trial. In THALES (Johnston SC et al., PMID: 32668111), 11,016 patients with mild-to-moderate acute noncardioembolic ischaemic stroke (NIHSS score 5 or less) or TIA, randomised within 24 hours and not receiving thrombolysis or thrombectomy, took 30 days of ticagrelor plus aspirin or aspirin alone. The composite of stroke or death within 30 days occurred in 303 patients (5.5%) on ticagrelor–aspirin versus 362 (6.6%) on aspirin alone (hazard ratio 0.83; 95% CI 0.71–0.96; p=0.02) — a 17% relative reduction, and 1.1 percentage points absolute. Ischaemic stroke occurred in 276 patients (5.0%) versus 345 (6.3%) (hazard ratio 0.79; 95% CI 0.68–0.93; p=0.004). Disability at 30 days did not differ significantly. The price was bleeding: severe bleeding in 28 patients (0.5%) versus 7 (0.1%) (p=0.001). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): 30 days of ticagrelor plus aspirin modestly reduces early stroke or death after minor stroke or TIA, at a real severe-bleeding cost — one trial only, so the developer decides whether a single-trial shelf stands.

cards.headline: Johnston 2020 (THALES): stroke or death at 30 days in 5.5% on ticagrelor–aspirin versus 6.6% on aspirin alone (HR 0.83); severe bleeding 0.5% versus 0.1%
cards.summary: Johnston 2020 (THALES): stroke or death at 30 days in 5.5% on ticagrelor–aspirin versus 6.6% on aspirin alone (HR 0.83); severe bleeding 0.5% versus 0.1%
cards.people: 11,016 patients with mild-to-moderate acute noncardioembolic ischaemic stroke (National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale score of 5 or less) or TIA, not undergoing thrombolysis or thrombectomy, randomised within 24 hours of symptom onset to ticagrelor (180 mg loading dose, then 90 mg twice daily) plus aspirin (300–325 mg on day 1, then 75–100 mg daily) (n=5,523) or matching placebo plus aspirin (n=5,493), for 30 days.
cards.result: A primary-outcome event (composite of stroke or death within 30 days) occurred in 303 patients (5.5%) in the ticagrelor–aspirin group and 362 (6.6%) in the aspirin group (hazard ratio 0.83; 95% CI 0.71–0.96; p=0.02) — a 17% relative reduction with absolute rates of 5.5% versus 6.6%. Ischaemic stroke occurred in 276 patients (5.0%) versus 345 (6.3%) (hazard ratio 0.79; 95% CI 0.68–0.93; p=0.004), a 21% relative reduction. The incidence of disability did not differ significantly between groups. Severe bleeding occurred in 28 patients (0.5%) versus 7 (0.1%) (p=0.001).
cards.watchOut: Single-trial shelf under the relaxed intake tier: no second randomised trial of ticagrelor plus aspirin versus aspirin alone after stroke or TIA exists in this record set, so the result is unreplicated. The benefit is a 1.1-percentage-point absolute reduction over 30 days, disability was unchanged, and severe bleeding was five times as frequent — the net gain is narrow and confined to patients treated within 24 hours who were not thrombolysed.
cards.source: Johnston SC et al. Ticagrelor and Aspirin or Aspirin Alone in Acute Ischemic Stroke or TIA. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2020. PMID: 32668111. Registry ID: NCT03354429. shelves.title: Lofexidine eases opioid withdrawal and keeps more people in treatment: completion 41.5% and 39.6% versus 27.8% on placebo in the larger trial, with symptom scores lower in both trials
shelves.question: In patients with opioid withdrawal, does lofexidine reduce withdrawal severity and improve treatment completion compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Analgesics, Opioid/adverse effects · Animals · Clonidine/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Inpatients · Male · Middle Aged · Narcotic Antagonists/therapeutic use · Opioid-Related Disorders/drug therapy · Substance Withdrawal Syndrome/drug therapy · United Kingdom
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two concordant double-blind placebo-controlled trials. Gorodetzky 2017 (PMID: 28527421, n=264) found lower Day 3 withdrawal scores on lofexidine than placebo (SOWS-Gossop 6.32 versus 8.67, p=0.0212) and fewer early terminators (59 versus 80). Fishman 2019 (PMID: 30531234, n=603) found significantly lower overall SOWS-Gossop scores at both doses (differences −0.21 and −0.26 on log-transformed scores; P=0.02 and P=0.003) and higher 7-day completion: 41.5% on 2.16 mg/day and 39.6% on 2.88 mg/day versus 27.8% on placebo — absolute gains of about 14 and 12 percentage points (relative increases of 85% and 71% as printed in the record). The price is cardiovascular: orthostatic hypotension, hypotension and bradycardia were the common adverse events, though they rarely stopped treatment. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): lofexidine modestly reduces withdrawal symptoms and meaningfully improves completion of a withdrawal episode.

cards.headline: Gorodetzky 2017: Day 3 withdrawal score 6.32 on lofexidine versus 8.67 on placebo (p=0.0212), with fewer early terminators (59 versus 80)
cards.summary: Gorodetzky 2017: Day 3 withdrawal score 6.32 on lofexidine versus 8.67 on placebo (p=0.0212), with fewer early terminators (59 versus 80)
cards.people: 264 inpatients dependent on short-acting opioids undergoing opioid withdrawal, randomised to lofexidine hydrochloride or placebo in an 8-day parallel-group registration trial; primary measures were SOWS-Gossop score on Day 3 and time to dropout.
cards.result: Mean Day 3 SOWS-Gossop scores were 6.32 on lofexidine versus 8.67 on placebo (p=0.0212). Fewer lofexidine patients were early terminators (59 versus 80), and non-completers on lofexidine stayed in the study longer than those on placebo (p=0.0034). Secondary endpoints consistently favoured lofexidine, and the record reports lofexidine was well tolerated in this trial.
cards.watchOut: A symptom-score difference of about 2.3 points on Day 3 is real but modest, and even on lofexidine most patients did not complete — this is help through withdrawal, not a cure for dependence. The record's abstract does not print the lofexidine dose used.
cards.source: Gorodetzky CW et al. A phase III, randomized, multi-center, double blind, placebo controlled study of safety and efficacy of lofexidine for relief of symptoms in individuals undergoing inpatient opioid withdrawal. Drug and Alcohol Dependence. 2017. PMID: 28527421. cards.headline: Fishman 2019: completion 41.5% (2.16 mg) and 39.6% (2.88 mg) versus 27.8% on placebo, with symptom scores significantly lower at both doses
cards.summary: Fishman 2019: completion 41.5% (2.16 mg) and 39.6% (2.88 mg) versus 27.8% on placebo, with symptom scores significantly lower at both doses
cards.people: 603 adults (mean age 35 years, 71% male) dependent on short-acting opioids and seeking withdrawal treatment at 18 US centres, randomised 3:3:2 to lofexidine 2.88 mg/day (n=222), lofexidine 2.16 mg/day (n=230) or placebo (n=151) for 7 days; primary outcome was SOWS-Gossop scores over days 1–7.
cards.result: Overall SOWS-Gossop scores (log-transformed least squares means) differed significantly from placebo for lofexidine 2.16 mg (difference −0.21, 95% CI −0.37 to −0.04; P=0.02) and 2.88 mg (−0.26, 95% CI −0.44 to −0.09; P=0.003). Completion rates were 41.5% on 2.16 mg (odds ratio 1.85; P=0.007) and 39.6% on 2.88 mg (odds ratio 1.71; P=0.02) versus 27.8% on placebo — absolute gains of about 14 and 12 percentage points, printed in the record as relative increases of 85% and 71%. Overall adverse event rates were similar across groups; common lofexidine events were orthostatic hypotension, hypotension and bradycardia, with few discontinuations.
cards.watchOut: Fewer than half of participants in every group completed even a 7-day withdrawal — the absolute completion gain (about one extra completer in eight) is the honest size of the benefit. The primary symptom outcome is a log-transformed score difference, which cannot be read as points on the scale patients feel.
cards.source: Fishman M et al. Safety and Efficacy of Lofexidine for Medically Managed Opioid Withdrawal: A Randomized Controlled Clinical Trial. Journal of Addiction Medicine. 2019. PMID: 30531234. cards.headline: Synthesis: two trials, same direction on symptoms and retention — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: two trials, same direction on symptoms and retention — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.people: Two randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials totalling 867 patients withdrawing from short-acting opioids (Gorodetzky 2017, inpatient, n=264; Fishman 2019, 18 US centres, n=603).
cards.result: Withdrawal scores: 6.32 versus 8.67 on Day 3 (Gorodetzky); significant overall reductions at both doses (Fishman). Completion: 41.5% and 39.6% versus 27.8% (Fishman); early terminators 59 versus 80 (Gorodetzky). Harms: orthostatic hypotension, hypotension, bradycardia. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for withdrawal severity and completion of the withdrawal episode — no evidence here about relapse or long-term abstinence.
cards.watchOut: Both trials measure a 7–8 day withdrawal episode, not what happens after it; a shelf about withdrawal relief must not be read as a shelf about recovery from opioid use disorder. Tier C: held for the developer's personal verdict under the relaxed 4,000–5,000 intake tier.
cards.source: Synthesis of Gorodetzky CW et al. Drug and Alcohol Dependence. 2017 (PMID: 28527421); Fishman M et al. Journal of Addiction Medicine. 2019 (PMID: 30531234).

shelves.title: Greater occipital nerve blocks for chronic migraine: headache days fell from 18.1 to 8.8 on bupivacaine versus 16.9 to 13.2 on saline at one month in the larger of two small placebo trials
shelves.question: In adults with migraine or cluster headache, do greater occipital nerve blocks reduce attack frequency or pain compared with sham or placebo injection?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anesthetics, Local/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Bupivacaine/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Migraine Disorders/drug therapy · Nerve Block/methods
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for chronic migraine only; no placebo trial for cluster headache was verified for this shelf. Inan LE et al. (PMID: 25765043) randomised 84 patients with chronic migraine to four weekly greater occipital nerve blocks with bupivacaine or saline: after 1 month headache days had fallen from 18.1 to 8.8 on bupivacaine versus 16.9 to 13.2 on saline (between-group P=0.004), and pain scores fell from 8.4 to 5.3 versus 8.1 to 6.7 (P=0.004), while headache duration did not differ between groups (P=0.767). Gul HL et al. (PMID: 27910088), in 44 patients with chronic migraine given the same four-weekly regimen, found significant decreases in headache frequency and pain scores on bupivacaine at the first, second and third months of follow-up, whereas the placebo group's improvement was significant only at the first month; no severe adverse effects occurred in either trial. Two small short trials from similar settings agree, but neither exceeds 84 patients or a few months of blinded follow-up. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): weekly bupivacaine occipital blocks reduce headache days in chronic migraine for at least a month beyond placebo, on small-trial evidence.

cards.headline: Inan 2015: headache days 18.1→8.8 on bupivacaine versus 16.9→13.2 on saline at 1 month (P=0.004); pain 8.4→5.3 versus 8.1→6.7 (P=0.004); headache duration not different (P=0.767)
cards.summary: Inan 2015: headache days 18.1→8.8 on bupivacaine versus 16.9→13.2 on saline at 1 month (P=0.004); pain 8.4→5.3 versus 8.1→6.7 (P=0.004); headache duration not different (P=0.767)
cards.people: 84 patients with chronic migraine randomised to four weekly greater occipital nerve blocks with bupivacaine (group B) or saline (group A); 72 patients completed the blinded month, after which blinding was removed and both groups received bupivacaine monthly for 2 further months.
cards.result: After 1 month, headache days decreased from 18.1 ± 5.3 to 8.8 ± 4.8 on bupivacaine and from 16.9 ± 5.7 to 13.2 ± 6.7 on saline (P=0.004 between groups). Visual analogue pain scores decreased from 8.4 ± 1.5 to 5.3 ± 2.1 versus 8.1 ± 0.9 to 6.7 ± 1.6 (P=0.004 between groups). Headache duration decreased within the bupivacaine group but did not differ between groups (P=0.767).
cards.watchOut: Only the first month is blinded and placebo-controlled; everything after unblinding is an open comparison, and 12 of 84 randomised patients did not complete the study. A saline injection at the same site is itself an active-feeling intervention, which makes the between-group gap more credible but the absolute falls less so.
cards.source: Inan LE et al. Greater occipital nerve blockade for the treatment of chronic migraine: a randomized, multicenter, double-blind, and placebo-controlled study. Acta neurologica Scandinavica. 2015. PMID: 25765043. cards.headline: Gul 2017: bupivacaine gains held at months 1–3 of follow-up while the placebo group's gains were significant only at month 1 — 44 patients, no severe adverse effects
cards.summary: Gul 2017: bupivacaine gains held at months 1–3 of follow-up while the placebo group's gains were significant only at month 1 — 44 patients, no severe adverse effects
cards.people: 44 patients with chronic migraine randomised to four weekly greater occipital nerve blocks with bupivacaine or saline (placebo), then followed monthly for 3 months with headache frequency and visual analogue pain scores compared against pretreatment values; all 44 completed the study.
cards.result: The bupivacaine group showed a significant decrease in headache frequency and visual analogue scores at the first, second and third months of follow-up. The placebo group also improved significantly at the first month, but the second and third months showed no significant difference from pretreatment. No severe adverse effects occurred. (The record reports significance patterns rather than the monthly means, so no absolute day counts are quoted here.)
cards.watchOut: Forty-four patients and within-group significance testing: 'significant in one arm, not in the other' is weaker evidence than a direct between-group contrast, which this record does not report for the later months.
cards.source: Gul HL et al. The efficacy of greater occipital nerve blockade in chronic migraine: A placebo-controlled study. Acta neurologica Scandinavica. 2017. PMID: 27910088. cards.headline: Synthesis: two small placebo trials in chronic migraine agree for a month and diverge thereafter — nothing verified for cluster headache
cards.summary: Synthesis: two small placebo trials in chronic migraine agree for a month and diverge thereafter — nothing verified for cluster headache
cards.people: Two randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials totalling 128 patients with chronic migraine (Inan 2015, n=84; Gul 2017, n=44), each testing four weekly greater occipital nerve blocks with bupivacaine against saline.
cards.result: Headache days at 1 month: 18.1→8.8 versus 16.9→13.2 (Inan, P=0.004 between groups). Durability: bupivacaine gains significant to month 3, placebo gains only to month 1 (Gul). No severe adverse effects in either trial. No placebo-controlled trial in cluster headache was verified for this shelf, so the cluster half of the candidate question is unanswered here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for chronic migraine.
cards.watchOut: Both trials are small, short and from similar practice settings; publication bias in a two-trial literature is a real risk, and the unblinded extension phases should not be quoted as controlled evidence.
cards.source: Synthesis of Inan LE et al. Acta neurologica Scandinavica. 2015 (PMID: 25765043); Gul HL et al. Acta neurologica Scandinavica. 2017 (PMID: 27910088).

shelves.title: Essential tremor: propranolol and primidone each beat placebo on accelerometer-measured tremor in tiny 1980s–90s crossover trials — primidone's first dose made about a quarter of patients acutely ill
shelves.question: In patients with essential tremor, does propranolol or primidone reduce tremor amplitude compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Clinical Trials as Topic · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Primidone/therapeutic use · Propranolol/therapeutic use · Random Allocation · Tremor/drug therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the two first-line drugs each beat placebo, in trials too small and old to carry more. In a double-blind randomised crossover trial of 14 patients, both propranolol and primidone significantly improved accelerometer-measured tremor versus placebo (p<0.01 for each; Gorman WP et al., PMID: 3514797), with no significant difference between the two drugs. A double-blind placebo-controlled trial of primidone in 22 patients found it significantly superior to placebo for hand tremor, comparable to propranolol, with tremor reduced to non-symptomatic levels in two patients — but an acute toxic reaction to an initial 62.5 mg dose occurred in six of 22 patients (Findley LJ et al., PMID: 3900296). A third randomised double-blind crossover trial in 16 patients found propranolol 40 mg three times daily significantly reduced tremor on all measures at day 15, comparably to gabapentin (Gironell A et al., PMID: 10199338). No trial measured disability, quality of life or long-term outcomes, and none enrolled more than 22 patients. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): propranolol and primidone reduce measured tremor amplitude short-term; the evidence is three small crossover trials from 1985–1999, and primidone carries a notable first-dose intolerance.

cards.headline: Gorman 1986: both propranolol and primidone beat placebo on accelerometer tremor (p<0.01 each) in 14 patients — no difference between the drugs
cards.summary: Gorman 1986: both propranolol and primidone beat placebo on accelerometer tremor (p<0.01 each) in 14 patients — no difference between the drugs
cards.people: 14 patients with essential tremor studied in a double-blind randomised crossover comparison of placebo, propranolol and primidone, with objective tremor measurement by accelerometer and spectral analysis.
cards.result: Both propranolol (p<0.01) and primidone (p<0.01) gave significant improvement in tremor versus placebo, with no significant difference in improvement between the two drugs. Patients with higher dominant tremor frequencies tended to respond to both drugs; those with lower frequencies improved on one or the other.
cards.watchOut: Fourteen patients, a laboratory accelerometer endpoint, and no disability or quality-of-life outcome — this shows the drugs move a tracing, in a handful of patients, over a short crossover period.
cards.source: Gorman WP et al. A comparison of primidone, propranolol, and placebo in essential tremor, using quantitative analysis. Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery, and Psychiatry. 1986. PMID: 3514797. cards.headline: Findley 1985: primidone significantly beat placebo for hand tremor (not head tremor) — acute toxic reaction to the first 62.5 mg dose in 6 of 22 patients
cards.summary: Findley 1985: primidone significantly beat placebo for hand tremor (not head tremor) — acute toxic reaction to the first 62.5 mg dose in 6 of 22 patients
cards.people: 22 patients with essential tremor of the hands and head in a double-blind placebo-controlled trial of primidone, assessed by clinical and objective methods.
cards.result: Primidone was significantly superior to placebo in reducing the magnitude of hand tremor, its efficacy comparable to that of propranolol; in two patients tremor was reduced to non-symptomatic levels. No consistent attenuation of head tremor was found, and there was no correlation between serum primidone or derived phenobarbitone concentrations and hand-tremor reduction. An acute toxic reaction to an initial small dose (62.5 mg) of primidone was seen in six of 22 patients.
cards.watchOut: The first-dose reaction — ataxia, nausea and vomiting in the record's adverse-effect indexing — affected more than a quarter of patients at a deliberately small starting dose, which is the practical limit on primidone use; head tremor, often the most socially disabling form, did not consistently respond.
cards.source: Findley LJ et al. Primidone in essential tremor of the hands and head: a double blind controlled clinical study. Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery, and Psychiatry. 1985. PMID: 3900296. cards.headline: Gironell 1999: propranolol 40 mg three times daily significantly reduced tremor on all measures at day 15 in 16 patients, comparably to gabapentin
cards.summary: Gironell 1999: propranolol 40 mg three times daily significantly reduced tremor on all measures at day 15 in 16 patients, comparably to gabapentin
cards.people: 16 patients with essential tremor (6 new onset, 10 after a 2-week washout of previous propranolol) receiving gabapentin 400 mg three times daily, propranolol hydrochloride 40 mg three times daily, and placebo, each for 15 days with a 1-week washout between treatments; outcomes were a Tremor Clinical Rating Scale, accelerometric recordings and a self-reported disability scale.
cards.result: At day 15, both gabapentin and propranolol demonstrated significant and comparable efficacy in reducing tremor from baseline in all tremor measures. On initial (day 1) accelerometry, placebo produced no significant change, while gabapentin and propranolol significantly reduced tremor power.
cards.watchOut: Fifteen days per treatment in 16 patients, ten of whom were already known propranolol users after washout — a design that can favour the familiar drug; the trial was designed around gabapentin, with propranolol as the active comparator.
cards.source: Gironell A et al. A randomized placebo-controlled comparative trial of gabapentin and propranolol in essential tremor. Archives of Neurology. 1999. PMID: 10199338. cards.headline: Synthesis: three small crossover trials agree the drugs reduce measured tremor — none shows patients function better, and primidone's first dose is its main hazard
cards.summary: Synthesis: three small crossover trials agree the drugs reduce measured tremor — none shows patients function better, and primidone's first dose is its main hazard
cards.people: Three double-blind randomised crossover/placebo-controlled trials totalling 52 patients with essential tremor (Gorman 1986, n=14; Findley 1985, n=22; Gironell 1999, n=16), testing propranolol and/or primidone against placebo over days to weeks.
cards.result: Propranolol beat placebo in both trials that tested it (p<0.01, Gorman; significant on all measures at day 15, Gironell) and primidone beat placebo in both trials that tested it (p<0.01, Gorman; significantly superior for hand tremor, Findley), with no significant difference between the two drugs head-to-head. Harm: acute toxic reaction to a first 62.5 mg primidone dose in 6 of 22 patients (Findley). Head tremor did not consistently respond. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: consistent short-term tremor-amplitude benefit from very small, old trials with surrogate endpoints.
cards.watchOut: Every trial predates modern essential-tremor rating standards, enrolled at most 22 patients, and measured tremor amplitude rather than disability; long-term tolerance, falls, and bradycardia or bronchospasm risks of propranolol in older patients are outside this record. Tier C is set: small single-centre crossover evidence only.

shelves.title: SSRIs for generalised social anxiety: paroxetine and sertraline each roughly doubled the response rate versus placebo in large 12-week trials — 55% versus 24%, and 47% versus 26%
shelves.question: In patients with social anxiety disorder, does sertraline or paroxetine improve symptoms compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Antidepressive Agents, Second-Generation/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Logistic Models · Male · Middle Aged · Multicenter Studies as Topic · Paroxetine/therapeutic use · Personality Tests · Phobic Disorders/drug therapy · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two large double-blind placebo-controlled trials, one per drug, agree that an SSRI roughly doubles the response rate in generalised social anxiety disorder over about 12 weeks. Paroxetine made 55.0% of patients much or very much improved versus 23.9% on placebo (odds ratio 3.88), with Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale scores falling 30.5 points versus 14.5 (Stein MB et al., PMID: 9728642). Sertraline, in patients with severe generalised disease, cut LSAS scores by 31.0 points versus 21.7 on placebo (p=.001), with intent-to-treat responder rates of 46.8% versus 25.5% (Liebowitz MR et al., PMID: 12934979). The benefit is symptomatic and short-term as tested — neither trial shows what happens beyond 12 weeks, whether gains persist after stopping, or how the drugs compare with the cognitive-behavioural therapy shelved separately. Tolerability was acceptable in both, though sertraline patients stopped for adverse events more often than placebo patients (7.6% versus 2.9%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): SSRIs are a proven short-term treatment for generalised social anxiety, at the stamp this band allows.

cards.headline: Stein 1998: paroxetine — 55.0% much or very much improved versus 23.9% on placebo (odds ratio 3.88) in generalised social phobia
cards.summary: Stein 1998: paroxetine — 55.0% much or very much improved versus 23.9% on placebo (odds ratio 3.88) in generalised social phobia
cards.people: 187 adults meeting DSM-IV criteria for generalised social phobia randomised at 13 US centres and 1 Canadian centre (183 assessed for efficacy; 91 paroxetine, 92 placebo), treated for 11 weeks after a 1-week placebo run-in with paroxetine 20 mg/day flexibly increased to a maximum of 50 mg/day or matching placebo. The primary outcome was the proportion much or very much improved on the Clinical Global Impression Global Improvement item; the Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale was the main symptom measure.
cards.result: Responders: 50 of 91 (55.0%) on paroxetine versus 22 of 92 (23.9%) on placebo (odds ratio 3.88, 95% CI 2.81–5.36). cards.headline: Liebowitz 2003: sertraline in severe generalised social anxiety — LSAS down 31.0 versus 21.7 points, responders 46.8% versus 25.5% (intent-to-treat)
cards.summary: Liebowitz 2003: sertraline in severe generalised social anxiety — LSAS down 31.0 versus 21.7 points, responders 46.8% versus 25.5% (intent-to-treat)
cards.people: 415 adults with DSM-IV generalised social phobia and severe disease randomised after a 1-week single-blind placebo lead-in to 12 weeks of flexible-dose sertraline 50–200 mg/day (211 assigned; intent-to-treat 205) or placebo (204 assigned; intent-to-treat 196), in data collected in 2000–2001. Primary outcomes were change in Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale total score and the Clinical Global Impressions-Improvement responder rate (score of 2 or better).
cards.result: At week 12, LSAS total score fell by 31.0 points on sertraline versus 21.7 on placebo (last observation carried forward; p=.001). Responder rates were 55.6% versus 29% among week-12 completers and 46.8% versus 25.5% in the intent-to-treat sample (p<.001 for both). Sertraline was well tolerated overall, but 7.6% discontinued for adverse events versus 2.9% on placebo.
cards.watchOut: A severe, generalised population with a placebo lead-in — the population least likely to improve spontaneously, which flatters the drug–placebo gap relative to ordinary clinic caseloads. Last-observation-carried-forward analysis and a 12-week horizon leave long-term benefit and discontinuation effects untested.

shelves.title: Long-acting injectable versus the same antipsychotic taken orally: randomised trials show at most a small relapse edge (pooled risk ratio 0.88) — the large benefits live in mirror-image studies, and the biggest pragmatic trial was null
shelves.question: In adults with chronic schizophrenia, does a long-acting injectable antipsychotic reduce relapse and hospitalisation compared with the same antipsychotic taken orally?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Antipsychotic Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Delayed-Action Preparations · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Hospitalization · Hospitals, Veterans · Humans · Injections, Intramuscular · Intention to Treat Analysis · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Compliance · Proportional Hazards Models · Quality of Life · Risperidone/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Schizophrenia/drug therapy
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by study design: in randomised trials the advantage of a long-acting injectable (LAI) over oral treatment is small or absent, while in pre-post (mirror-image) studies it looks large. The largest pragmatic randomised trial (Rosenheck RA et al., PMID: 21366475) found hospitalisation in 39% on long-acting risperidone versus 45% on a psychiatrist's choice of oral antipsychotic (hazard ratio 0.87, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.20 — not significant). The one double-blind same-drug trial (Fleischhacker WW et al., PMID: 24925984) showed non-inferiority, not superiority: estimated impending relapse at week 26 was 7.12% on aripiprazole once-monthly 400 mg versus 7.76% on oral aripiprazole. The comparative meta-analysis (Kishimoto T et al., PMID: 33862018) pooled a risk ratio for hospitalisation or relapse of 0.88 (95% CI 0.79 to 0.99) across randomised trials, 0.92 (0.88 to 0.98) across cohort studies, and 0.44 (0.39 to 0.51) across pre-post studies — the design most prone to bias gives by far the biggest number. This shelf is distinct from shelf #994 (depot versus placebo in stabilised schizophrenia) and pack #2419 (LAI versus usual-care oral treatment in early-phase schizophrenia): it asks the chronic-schizophrenia, formulation-only question. PROPOSED SPLIT: randomised evidence supports at most a modest relapse/hospitalisation advantage for LAIs over oral antipsychotics; claims of large benefit rest on pre-post designs.

cards.headline: Rosenheck 2011 (VA Cooperative): hospitalisation 39% on long-acting risperidone versus 45% on oral antipsychotics — hazard ratio 0.87 (0.63 to 1.20), not significant, with more injection-site and extrapyramidal effects
cards.summary: Rosenheck 2011 (VA Cooperative): hospitalisation 39% on long-acting risperidone versus 45% on oral antipsychotics — hazard ratio 0.87 (0.63 to 1.20), not significant, with more injection-site and extrapyramidal effects
cards.type: Randomised pragmatic trial (Rosenheck 2011, VA Cooperative Studies Program)
cards.people: 369 patients in the US Veterans Affairs system with schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder who had been hospitalised within the previous 2 years or were at imminent risk of hospitalisation (40% hospitalised at randomisation), assigned to long-acting injectable risperidone 25 to 50 mg every two weeks or a psychiatrist's choice of oral antipsychotic, followed for up to 2 years.
cards.result: The rate of hospitalisation after randomisation was not significantly lower with long-acting risperidone: 39% after 10.8 months versus 45% after 11.3 months on oral treatment (hazard ratio 0.87, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.20). Psychiatric symptoms, quality of life, global functioning and neurologic side effects were not significantly improved; patients on the injectable reported more injection-site adverse events and more extrapyramidal symptoms.
cards.watchOut: The oral comparator was psychiatrist's choice, not risperidone itself, so this is a formulation-strategy trial rather than a strict same-molecule test; it was also open-label. Its population — unstable, recently hospitalised veterans — is exactly the group in whom an adherence advantage should be easiest to show, which makes the null result hard to dismiss.
cards.source: Rosenheck RA et al. Long-acting risperidone and oral antipsychotics in unstable schizophrenia. The New England journal of medicine. 2011. PMID: 21366475. Registry ID: NCT00132314. cards.headline: Fleischhacker 2014: aripiprazole once-monthly was non-inferior to oral aripiprazole — impending relapse 7.12% versus 7.76% at week 26 — a same-drug trial that shows equivalence, not superiority
cards.summary: Fleischhacker 2014: aripiprazole once-monthly was non-inferior to oral aripiprazole — impending relapse 7.12% versus 7.76% at week 26 — a same-drug trial that shows equivalence, not superiority
cards.people: 662 patients with schizophrenia who had responded to oral aripiprazole, randomised (2:2:1) to aripiprazole once-monthly 400 mg, oral aripiprazole 10–30 mg/day, or aripiprazole once-monthly 50 mg (a sub-therapeutic dose included for assay sensitivity), for 38 weeks.
cards.result: Kaplan–Meier estimated impending relapse rates at week 26 were 7.12% for aripiprazole once-monthly 400 mg and 7.76% for oral aripiprazole — a difference of −0.64% (95% CI −5.26 to 3.99), which excluded the predefined non-inferiority margin of 11.5%. Both active treatments were superior to the 50 mg once-monthly dose (21.80%, P ≤ 0.001).
cards.watchOut: An enriched design: only patients who had already responded to and tolerated oral aripiprazole were randomised, and the trial was powered for non-inferiority — it can show the injection is not worse than the tablet in stabilised responders, and says nothing about superiority in unselected or unstable patients.
cards.source: Fleischhacker WW et al. Aripiprazole once-monthly for treatment of schizophrenia: double-blind, randomised, non-inferiority study. The British journal of psychiatry : the journal of mental science. 2014. PMID: 24925984. Registry ID: NCT00706654.
