cards.headline: Kishimoto 2021: pooled hospitalisation/relapse risk ratio 0.88 in randomised trials, 0.92 in cohort studies, 0.44 in pre-post studies — the weaker the design, the bigger the LAI advantage
cards.summary: Kishimoto 2021: pooled hospitalisation/relapse risk ratio 0.88 in randomised trials, 0.92 in cohort studies, 0.44 in pre-post studies — the weaker the design, the bigger the LAI advantage
cards.type: Systematic review and comparative meta-analysis of randomised, cohort and pre-post studies (Kishimoto 2021)
cards.people: 137 studies (397,319 patients) comparing long-acting injectable with oral antipsychotics for maintenance treatment of schizophrenia in studies lasting at least 6 months: 32 randomised trials (8,577 patients), 65 cohort studies (377,447 patients) and 40 pre-post studies (11,295 patients).
cards.result: Long-acting injectables were associated with a lower risk of hospitalisation or relapse than oral antipsychotics in each design, but the size differed sharply: randomised trials (29 studies, 7,833 patients) risk ratio 0.88 (95% CI 0.79 to 0.99, p=0.033); cohort studies (44 studies, 106,136 patients) 0.92 (0.88 to 0.98); pre-post studies (28 studies, 17,876 patients) 0.44 (0.39 to 0.51). Across all other outcomes, LAIs were more beneficial in 60 of 328 comparisons (18.3%), not different in 252 (76.8%), and less beneficial in 16 (4.9%). Publication bias was apparent in the cohort and pre-post studies.
cards.watchOut: The pre-post (mirror-image) design compares patients with their own pre-LAI period — a period usually selected because it went badly — so regression to the mean inflates the apparent benefit; the randomised estimate of 0.88 is the conservative anchor, and even it pools trials with differing comparators and enrichment strategies.
cards.source: Kishimoto T et al. Long-acting injectable versus oral antipsychotics for the maintenance treatment of schizophrenia: a systematic review and comparative meta-analysis of randomised, cohort, and pre-post studies. The lancet. Psychiatry. 2021. PMID: 33862018. cards.headline: Synthesis: the injection guarantees delivery, not superiority — a small randomised edge, a null largest trial, and equivalence in the one same-drug blinded trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: the injection guarantees delivery, not superiority — a small randomised edge, a null largest trial, and equivalence in the one same-drug blinded trial
cards.people: One large pragmatic randomised trial (369 unstable VA patients), one double-blind same-drug non-inferiority trial (662 stabilised responders), and one comparative meta-analysis spanning 137 studies and 397,319 patients.
cards.result: Hospitalisation on long-acting risperidone 39% versus 45% on oral treatment (hazard ratio 0.87, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.20); impending relapse on aripiprazole once-monthly 7.12% versus 7.76% on oral aripiprazole; pooled hospitalisation/relapse risk ratio 0.88 (0.79 to 0.99) in randomised trials versus 0.44 (0.39 to 0.51) in pre-post studies. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C: the formulation question splits by design — randomised evidence supports at most a modest advantage, and the dramatic benefits quoted from mirror-image data should not be presented as trial findings.
cards.watchOut: None of these designs captures the patient for whom the injection is the only realistic way any antipsychotic is taken at all; the trials enrol people willing to be randomised between formulations, which already selects for some adherence. Single-trial flag not applicable; the split is a design split, declared on the face of the shelf.

shelves.title: Methadone started in prison: treatment entry 68.6% vs 7.8% and opioid-positive urines 27.6% vs 62.9% at one month in the US trial — and in the Australian cohort, nobody died while retained on methadone, against 17 deaths off it
shelves.question: In prisoners with opioid use disorder, does methadone maintenance started in prison reduce post-release overdose and reincarceration compared with no treatment or forced withdrawal?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Baltimore · Counseling/methods · Follow-Up Studies · Heroin Dependence/rehabilitation · Humans · Male · Methadone/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Narcotics/therapeutic use · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Patient Acceptance of Health Care/statistics & numerical data · Prisoners/statistics & numerical data · Substance Abuse Treatment Centers
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — starting methadone before release changes what happens after it. In the Baltimore randomised trial (211 heroin-dependent pre-release inmates), methadone plus counselling in prison, continued in the community, beat counselling with passive referral on every early measure: community treatment entry at one month 68.6% versus 7.8% (Kinlock TW et al., PMID: 17628351), opioid-positive urine 27.6% versus 62.9%, and at six months the methadone group was still significantly more likely to be retained in treatment (P=0.0001) and less likely to test opioid-positive (P=0.002), with fewer self-reported days of heroin use and criminal activity (Gordon MS et al., PMID: 18855822). The Australian randomised trial (382 prisoners; Dolan KA et al., PMID: 14563543) found significantly lower heroin use, injecting and syringe sharing on methadone versus a wait-list at five months, with no difference in HIV or hepatitis C incidence over that window. Its four-year follow-up carries the mortality and reincarceration answer (Dolan KA et al., PMID: 15918812): no deaths occurred while subjects were enrolled in methadone treatment, against 17 deaths off treatment (untreated mortality 2.0 per 100 person-years, 95% CI 1.2 to 3.2), and reincarceration risk was lowest during methadone episodes of eight months or longer (adjusted hazard ratio 0.3, 0.2 to 0.5). No trial randomised overdose death itself — the overdose claim rests on retention, heroin-use and all-cause-mortality data. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): prison-initiated methadone with community continuation is one of the few prison health interventions with randomised evidence behind both its drug-use and its survival-relevant outcomes.

cards.headline: Kinlock 2007 (1 month): treatment entry 68.6% on prison-started methadone vs 50.0% transfer-only vs 7.8% counselling only; opioid-positive urine 27.6% vs 41.0% vs 62.9%
cards.summary: Kinlock 2007 (1 month): treatment entry 68.6% on prison-started methadone vs 50.0% transfer-only vs 7.8% counselling only; opioid-positive urine 27.6% vs 41.0% vs 62.9%
cards.people: 211 adult pre-release inmates in Baltimore (heroin-dependent in the year before incarceration), randomised to counselling only with passive referral (n=70), counselling plus transfer to community methadone on release (n=70), or methadone maintenance and counselling begun in prison and continued in the community (n=71); 200 located for the one-month follow-up.
cards.result: Entered community-based treatment: 68.6% (counselling + methadone), 50.0% (counselling + transfer), 7.8% (counselling only) — all pairwise comparisons significant (all p<.05). Opioid-positive urine at one month: 27.6%, 41.0% and 62.9% respectively, with counselling only significantly more likely to test positive than counselling + methadone.
cards.watchOut: Open-label by necessity — methadone cannot be blinded — and one month is the honeymoon window; the comparison that matters for policy (starting inside vs merely referring out) already shows a gap at this point, which is the trial's most useful finding.
cards.source: Kinlock TW et al. A randomized clinical trial of methadone maintenance for prisoners: results at 1-month post-release. Drug and Alcohol Dependence. 2007. PMID: 17628351. cards.headline: Gordon 2008 (6 months): prison-started methadone still ahead — retained in treatment (P=0.0001), fewer opioid-positive urines (P=0.002), fewer heroin-use and crime days
cards.summary: Gordon 2008 (6 months): prison-started methadone still ahead — retained in treatment (P=0.0001), fewer opioid-positive urines (P=0.002), fewer heroin-use and crime days
cards.people: The same 211 Baltimore pre-release inmates (2003–2005), assessed six months post-release with the Addiction Severity Index, treatment-record review and urine testing for opioids, cocaine and other illicit drugs.
cards.result: Counselling + methadone participants were significantly more likely than both other groups to be retained in drug abuse treatment (P=0.0001) and significantly less likely than counselling-only participants to have an opioid-positive urine specimen (P=0.002). They also reported significantly fewer days of heroin use and of criminal activity than counselling-only participants. The record reports P values for these six-month outcomes without printing the percentages.
cards.watchOut: Same trial as the one-month report — it is one randomised trial with two reports, not two trials; the independent replication is the Australian trial below. Six months still says nothing directly about overdose deaths.

cards.headline: Dolan 2003 (Australia): heroin use, injecting and syringe sharing all significantly lower on prison methadone versus wait-list at five months; HIV/hepatitis C incidence unchanged
cards.summary: Dolan 2003 (Australia): heroin use, injecting and syringe sharing all significantly lower on prison methadone versus wait-list at five months; HIV/hepatitis C incidence unchanged
cards.people: 382 prisoners in the New South Wales prison system (of 593 eligible prisoners seeking drug treatment, 1997–1998) randomised to methadone maintenance treatment (n=191) or a wait-list control (n=191); 129 treated and 124 control participants followed up at five months, with hair analysis, self-report and serology.
cards.result: Heroin use was significantly lower among treated than control subjects at follow-up, and treated subjects reported lower levels of drug injection and syringe sharing. There was no difference in HIV or hepatitis C incidence over the follow-up window. The record reports significance without printing the group percentages.
cards.watchOut: A wait-list control in a system where methadone was otherwise unavailable is close to a no-treatment comparison; attrition (about a third not followed up) and the short window limit the infection outcomes, which need years, not months.
cards.source: Dolan KA et al. A randomised controlled trial of methadone maintenance treatment versus wait list control in an Australian prison system. Drug and Alcohol Dependence. 2003. cards.headline: Dolan 2005 (4-year follow-up): zero deaths while on methadone vs 17 deaths off it (2.0 per 100 person-years); reincarceration hazard 0.3 during methadone episodes of 8+ months
cards.summary: Dolan 2005 (4-year follow-up): zero deaths while on methadone vs 17 deaths off it (2.0 per 100 person-years); reincarceration hazard 0.3 during methadone episodes of 8+ months
cards.type: Cohort follow-up of a randomised trial population (Dolan 2005)
cards.people: The 382 imprisoned male heroin users from the New South Wales randomised trial, followed between 1998 and 2002 in the community and in prison for all-cause mortality, re-incarceration, hepatitis C/HIV serostatus and methadone retention, analysed by time actually spent in treatment.
cards.result: No deaths were recorded while subjects were enrolled in methadone treatment; 17 subjects died while out of treatment, an untreated mortality rate of 2.0 per 100 person-years (95% CI 1.2 to 3.2). Re-incarceration risk was lowest during methadone episodes of eight months or longer (adjusted hazard ratio 0.3, 95% CI 0.2 to 0.5; P<0.001), while episodes of two months or less carried the greatest risk. Hepatitis C seroconversion risk rose with methadone episodes under five months (adjusted HR 4.2, 1.4 to 12.6) and sentences under two months (adjusted HR 20, 5 to 76). HIV incidence was 0.3 per 100 person-years.
cards.watchOut: This is an observational analysis by time-on-treatment within the trial cohort — people who stay on methadone differ from people who drop out, so the mortality contrast is supportive, not randomised, evidence; its size (zero deaths in treatment) is nonetheless the strongest survival signal this literature offers.
cards.source: Dolan KA et al. Four-year follow-up of imprisoned male heroin users and methadone treatment: mortality, re-incarceration and hepatitis C infection. Addiction. 2005. PMID: 15918812. cards.headline: Synthesis: start inside, continue outside — randomised gains in entry, retention and heroin use; survival and reincarceration gains track time retained
cards.summary: Synthesis: start inside, continue outside — randomised gains in entry, retention and heroin use; survival and reincarceration gains track time retained
cards.people: Two randomised trials (211 US pre-release inmates; 382 Australian prisoners) plus a four-year cohort follow-up of the Australian trial population.
cards.result: Treatment entry at one month 68.6% vs 7.8%; opioid-positive urine 27.6% vs 62.9%; six-month retention and urine advantages significant; heroin use, injecting and sharing significantly lower in the second trial. Mortality: 0 deaths on methadone vs 2.0 per 100 person-years off it; reincarceration adjusted HR 0.3 with retention of eight months or longer. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Overdose-specific mortality was never a randomised endpoint, both trials predate the fentanyl era and buprenorphine-first pathways, and benefit depends on community continuation actually existing on release. Tier C: mortality-adjacent benefit claim, developer reviews personally.

shelves.title: Stopping nail biting: habit reversal training beat wait-list and a rival behavioural method in a 91-child trial — N-acetylcysteine beat placebo at one month in a 42-child pilot, then lost its edge by month two
shelves.question: How do I stop biting my nails? In children, adolescents and adults with chronic nail biting (onychophagia), do habit reversal training, object manipulation, or the supplement N-acetylcysteine (NAC) help nails grow and biting stop?
shelves.mesh: Acetylcysteine/administration & dosage · Acetylcysteine/adverse effects · Acetylcysteine/therapeutic use · Adolescent · Child · Chronic Disease · Comorbidity · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Nail Biting/therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) for habit reversal training (HRT); MAYBE (weak evidence) for N-acetylcysteine. HRT — awareness training plus a competing response — is the best-tested treatment for nail biting: in a 91-child randomised trial, HRT and object manipulation training both increased nail length versus wait-list at 1 month (P<0.001 each), and by 3 months HRT was ahead of object manipulation (P<0.021), with complete stopping in 8 of 30 children on HRT and 7 of 30 on object manipulation, versus 0 on wait-list during its month of waiting. NAC 800 mg/day beat placebo on nail growth at 1 month in a 42-child double-blind pilot (5.21 mm versus 1.18 mm) but not at 2 months, and dropout was high. An uncontrolled retrospective series of 93 children given NAC for mixed habit disorders (nail biting among them) rated 49 of 93 (53%) significantly better or completely clear — without a control group that cannot separate a drug effect from time, expectation and staying on treatment. No trial in this area is large, and none follows patients beyond 3 months.

cards.headline: Ghanizadeh 2013 (91 children and adolescents): habit reversal and object manipulation both beat wait-list at 1 month; by 3 months habit reversal was ahead — complete stopping in 8 of 30 versus 7 of 30
cards.summary: Ghanizadeh 2013 (91 children and adolescents): habit reversal and object manipulation both beat wait-list at 1 month; by 3 months habit reversal was ahead — complete stopping in 8 of 30 versus 7 of 30
cards.type: Three-group randomised controlled trial of behavioural treatments (Ghanizadeh 2013)
cards.people: 91 children and adolescents with chronic nail biting in Iran, randomly allocated to habit reversal training (n=30), object manipulation training (n=30) or a wait-list control group (n=31), with outcomes evaluated up to 3 months after randomisation; mean nail length was the main outcome.
cards.result: After 1 month, mean nail length had increased in both the habit reversal and object manipulation groups compared with the wait-list group (P<0.001 for each). In the long term both treatments increased mean nail length (P<0.01), but habit reversal was more effective than object manipulation (P<0.021); parent-reported frequency of nail biting showed similar results. The number of children who completely stopped nail biting during 3 months was 8 in the habit reversal group and 7 in the object manipulation group; during its 1 month, the wait-list group had 0.
cards.watchOut: Children and adolescents only, and the wait-list comparison lasted only 1 month — being promised treatment later is not a placebo, and families knew which group they were in. Nail length is a proxy outcome: it shows nails grew, which usually means less biting, but biting frequency itself was parent-reported.
cards.source: Ghanizadeh A, Bazrafshan A, Firoozabadi A, Dehbozorgi G. Habit Reversal versus Object Manipulation Training for Treating Nail Biting: A Randomized Controlled Clinical Trial. cards.headline: Ghanizadeh 2013 (42 children, double-blind): NAC 800 mg/day grew nails faster than placebo at 1 month (5.21 mm versus 1.18 mm) — no difference at 2 months, and 2 children stopped NAC for adverse events
cards.summary: Ghanizadeh 2013 (42 children, double-blind): NAC 800 mg/day grew nails faster than placebo at 1 month (5.21 mm versus 1.18 mm) — no difference at 2 months, and 2 children stopped NAC for adverse events
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot trial of N-acetylcysteine (Ghanizadeh 2013)
cards.people: 42 children and adolescents with chronic nail biting, given N-acetylcysteine (NAC) 800 mg/day or placebo for 2 months; the duration of nail biting averaged 3.63 years (SD 2.45) in the NAC group and 5.09 years (SD 3.74) in the placebo group (P=0.14). Nail length was the objective outcome, measured before treatment and at 1 and 2 months.
cards.result: Nail length increased in both groups. After the first month the increase was significantly greater on NAC: 5.21 mm (SD 5.75) versus 1.18 mm (SD 3.02) on placebo. After two months there was no difference between the groups. Two patients in the NAC group discontinued medication due to adverse events: one experienced headache, agitation and social withdrawal, and another expressed severe aggression after taking the medication and was withdrawn.
cards.watchOut: A pilot trial whose authors warn of a high dropout rate, and the one positive time point is the early one — a pattern that can arise by chance when several time points are tested. Even taken at face value, the advantage did not persist to 2 months although treatment continued.
cards.source: Ghanizadeh A, Derakhshan N, Berk M. N-acetylcysteine versus placebo for treating nail biting, a double blind randomized placebo controlled clinical trial. Anti-Inflammatory & Anti-Allergy Agents in Medicinal Chemistry. 2013. PMID: 23651231. Registry ID: IRCT201103023930N3 (Iranian Registry of Clinical Trials). cards.headline: Zarowin 2025 (retrospective series, 93 children on NAC for habit disorders including nail biting): 8% completely clear, 45% significantly better, 27% no effect — with no control group
cards.summary: Zarowin 2025 (retrospective series, 93 children on NAC for habit disorders including nail biting): 8% completely clear, 45% significantly better, 27% no effect — with no control group
cards.people: 93 children at the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia with outcome data, treated with oral NAC for habit-driven skin, hair and nail abnormalities — 16 behavioural issues in all, including nail biting, skin picking and hair pulling. NAC doses ranged from 400 to 3000 mg/day in divided doses; the most commonly recommended dose was 600 mg twice daily.
cards.result: On a 6-point clinician-rated scale: 7 patients (8%) were completely clear of their habit-driven activities, 42 (45%) were significantly better, 19 (20%) were somewhat better and 26 (27%) experienced no effect; none had somewhat worse or worse outcomes. No significant adverse effects were observed; adherence problems included medication taste (7 patients, 8%), pill size (5 patients, 5%), cost (1 patient) and mild gastrointestinal upset (1 patient).
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and uncontrolled: patients with a significantly better or clear outcome had stayed on NAC much longer (mean 34.8 months, SD 31.9) than those with neutral or somewhat better outcomes (15.3 months, SD 20.5; P<0.001), which may mean the drug works — or that families stop a drug that is not working. Nail biting was only one of 16 pooled conditions, outcome data were missing for about half of the children prescribed NAC, and the odds of a good outcome were not significantly associated with any condition (all P>0.05).
cards.source: Zarowin DH, Stein AB, Sheppard SE, Treat JR. A Retrospective Review of Oral N-Acetylcysteine for Habit-Driven Cutaneous Disorders. Pediatric Dermatology. 2025. PMID: 39821896. Registry ID: none in the record (retrospective chart review). retrospective case series (zarowin 2025) 93 children at the children's hospital of philadelphia with outcome data, treated with oral nac for habit-driven skin, hair and nail abnormalities — 16 behavioural issues in all, including nail biting, skin picking and hair pulling. nac doses ranged from 400 to 3000 mg/day in divided doses; the most commonly recommended dose was 600 mg twice daily. on a 6-point clinician-rated scale: 7 patients (8%) were completely clear of their habit-driven activities, 42 (45%) were significantly better, 19 (20%) were somewhat better and 26 (27%) experienced no effect; none had somewhat worse or worse outcomes. no significant adverse effects were observed; adherence problems included medication taste (7 patients, 8%), pill size (5 patients, 5%), cost (1 patient) and mild gastrointestinal upset (1 patient). retrospective and uncontrolled: patients with a significantly better or clear outcome had stayed on nac much longer (mean 34.8 months, sd 31.9) than those with neutral or somewhat better outcomes (15.3 months, sd 20.5; p<0.001), which may mean the drug works — or that families stop a drug that is not working. nail biting was only one of 16 pooled conditions, outcome data were missing for about half of the children prescribed nac, and the odds of a good outcome were not significantly associated with any condition (all p>0.05). zarowin dh, stein ab, sheppard se, treat jr. a retrospective review of oral n-acetylcysteine for habit-driven cutaneous disorders. pediatric dermatology. 2025. pmid: 39821896. registry id: none in the record (retrospective chart review). mesh: acetylcysteine/administration & dosage · acetylcysteine/adverse effects · acetylcysteine/therapeutic use · administration, oral · adolescent · child · child, preschool · female · habits · humans · infant · male · retrospective studies · skin diseases/drug therapy · skin diseases/etiology · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Synthesis: habit reversal is the best-supported route; NAC has one fleeting pilot result and one uncontrolled series
cards.summary: Synthesis: habit reversal is the best-supported route; NAC has one fleeting pilot result and one uncontrolled series
cards.people: Children and adolescents with chronic nail biting (the trial evidence is almost entirely paediatric; adults asking this question are extrapolating).
cards.result: The behavioural evidence is the strongest available: habit reversal training beat wait-list at 1 month and beat object manipulation training by 3 months in the only three-group trial (91 children), with about 1 in 4 children stopping completely. For NAC, the only placebo-controlled trial (42 children) found faster nail growth at 1 month (5.21 mm versus 1.18 mm) and no difference at 2 months; a 93-child uncontrolled series is consistent with benefit but cannot prove it. Nothing here has been tested in a large trial or beyond 3 months.
cards.watchOut: All three sources are small and short, two come from a single research group, and the adult evidence base is thinner still — the well-known adult habit-reversal trial (Twohig 2003) could not be verified against its PubMed record for this build and is not carded. Stamps stay at POSSIBLE for that reason.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ghanizadeh A et al. Iranian Journal of Psychiatry. 2013 (PMID: 24130603); Ghanizadeh A et al. Anti-Inflammatory & Anti-Allergy Agents in Medicinal Chemistry. 2013 (PMID: 23651231); Zarowin DH et al. Pediatric Dermatology. 2025 (PMID: 39821896).

shelves.title: Do antidepressants work — and which is best? All 21 drugs beat placebo across 522 trials (response odds ratios 1.37–2.13, relative measures), but the average drug–placebo difference is 1.75 Hamilton points, and only about 15% of patients get a substantial drug-specific benefit
shelves.question: Do antidepressants work — and which is best? In adults with major depressive disorder, how much do antidepressants beat placebo, how big is the benefit in absolute terms, how does it change with severity, and which drugs rank best for efficacy and for staying on treatment?
shelves.mesh: Antidepressive Agents/adverse effects · Antidepressive Agents/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Evidence-Based Medicine/methods · Humans · Major Depressive Disorder/drug therapy · Patient Dropouts/statistics & numerical data · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic/methods · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit), modest average size, growing with severity. The anchor is Cipriani 2018: 522 double-blind trials, 116,477 participants, and all 21 antidepressants beat placebo on response (odds ratios — relative measures — from 2.13 for amitriptyline down to 1.37 for reboxetine); between drugs the differences were smaller (ORs 1.15–1.55 across all trials), and only agomelatine and fluoxetine had fewer dropouts than placebo. Absolute framing comes from Stone 2022's individual-participant analysis of 232 FDA-submitted trials (73,388 participants): the mean drug–placebo difference was 1.75 Hamilton points, responses were trimodal, and a large response occurred in 24.5% on drug versus 9.6% on placebo — the authors' estimate that about 15% of participants obtain a substantial antidepressant effect beyond placebo. Fournier 2010's patient-level analysis adds the severity gradient: below a Hamilton score of 23 the drug–placebo effect size was under 0.20, crossing the NICE clinical-significance threshold only at a score of 25. So: the drugs work on average, 'which is best' has only small separations (escitalopram, mirtazapine, paroxetine, venlafaxine, vortioxetine and agomelatine ranked higher for efficacy; agomelatine, citalopram, escitalopram, fluoxetine, sertraline and vortioxetine for acceptability), and the expected benefit is least in mild depression. Certainty in the network analysis was moderate to very low.

cards.headline: Cipriani 2018 (network meta-analysis, 522 trials, 116,477 participants): all 21 antidepressants beat placebo — response ORs from 2.13 (amitriptyline) to 1.37 (reboxetine); only agomelatine and fluoxetine had fewer dropouts than placebo
cards.summary: Cipriani 2018 (network meta-analysis, 522 trials, 116,477 participants): all 21 antidepressants beat placebo — response ORs from 2.13 (amitriptyline) to 1.37 (reboxetine); only agomelatine and fluoxetine had fewer dropouts than placebo
cards.people: Adults (18 years and older) with major depressive disorder diagnosed by standard criteria, in 522 double-blind randomised trials of 21 antidepressants — placebo-controlled and head-to-head — for acute treatment; 116,477 participants in total.
cards.result: Efficacy (response rate): all antidepressants were more effective than placebo, with odds ratios (relative measures) ranging from 2.13 (95% credible interval 1.89–2.41) for amitriptyline to 1.37 (1.16–1.63) for reboxetine. Acceptability (all-cause discontinuation): only agomelatine (OR 0.84, 0.72–0.97) and fluoxetine (0.88, 0.80–0.96) were associated with fewer dropouts than placebo, whereas clomipramine was worse than placebo (1.30, 1.01–1.68). Considering all trials, drug-versus-drug odds ratios ranged from 1.15 to 1.55 for efficacy and 0.64 to 0.83 for acceptability, with wide credible intervals on most comparisons. In head-to-head studies, agomelatine, amitriptyline, escitalopram, mirtazapine, paroxetine, venlafaxine and vortioxetine were more effective than other antidepressants (ORs 1.19–1.96), while fluoxetine, fluvoxamine, reboxetine and trazodone were least efficacious (0.51–0.84); the most tolerable were agomelatine, citalopram, escitalopram, fluoxetine, sertraline and vortioxetine (0.43–0.77), and the highest dropout rates were with amitriptyline, clomipramine, duloxetine, fluvoxamine, reboxetine, trazodone and venlafaxine (1.30–2.32). Risk of bias: 46 trials (9%) high, 380 (73%) moderate, 96 (18%) low; certainty of evidence moderate to very low.
cards.watchOut: Odds ratios are relative measures and the abstract prints no absolute response rates, so this card alone cannot say how many extra patients respond per 100 treated — that framing is on the Stone card. Rankings between drugs rest heavily on indirect comparisons with wide credible intervals, and the authors rate the certainty moderate to very low; 'best' here means 'ranked first on average', not 'clearly superior for the next patient'.
cards.source: Cipriani A, Furukawa TA, Salanti G, Chaimani A, Atkinson LZ, Ogawa Y, Leucht S, Ruhe HG, Turner EH, Higgins JPT, Egger M, Takeshima N, Hayasaka Y, Imai H, Shinohara K, Tajika A, Ioannidis JPA, Geddes JR. Comparative efficacy and acceptability of 21 antidepressant drugs for the acute treatment of adults with major depressive disorder: a systematic review and network meta-analysis. The Lancet. 2018. PMID: 29477251. Registry ID: PROSPERO CRD42012002291. cards.headline: Stone 2022 (individual participant data, 232 FDA trials, 73,388 participants): mean advantage 1.75 Hamilton points — but responses are trimodal: a large response in 24.5% on drug versus 9.6% on placebo, so about 15% get a substantial drug-specific benefit
cards.summary: Stone 2022 (individual participant data, 232 FDA trials, 73,388 participants): mean advantage 1.75 Hamilton points — but responses are trimodal: a large response in 24.5% on drug versus 9.6% on placebo, so about 15% get a substantial drug-specific benefit
cards.type: Individual participant data analysis of FDA-submitted trials (Stone 2022)
cards.people: 73,388 adult and child participants in 232 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled monotherapy trials for major depressive disorder submitted to the US Food and Drug Administration between 1979 and 2016.
cards.result: The mean difference between drug and placebo favoured drug by 1.75 Hamilton (HAMD17) points (95% CI 1.63–1.86), and the difference increased significantly with greater baseline severity (P<0.001). Response distributions were best fitted by three groups with mean improvements of 16.0 points (Large response), 8.9 points (Non-specific response) and 1.7 points (Minimal response). Participants treated with a drug were more likely to have a Large response (24.5% versus 9.6% on placebo) and less likely to have a Minimal response (12.2% versus 21.5%). The authors conclude that about 15% of participants have a substantial antidepressant effect beyond a placebo effect.
cards.watchOut: These are acute monotherapy trials submitted for drug approval — industry-run, typically 6–8 weeks, in patients selected for trials; the trimodal split is a statistical model of the response distribution, not three kinds of patient identified in advance. The 24.5% versus 9.6% contrast is the cleanest absolute framing available, and it still means most of the average improvement on drug also occurs on placebo (the 8.9-point non-specific response).
cards.source: Stone MB, Yaseen ZS, Miller BJ, Richardville K, Kalaria SN, Kirsch I. Response to acute monotherapy for major depressive disorder in randomized, placebo controlled trials submitted to the US Food and Drug Administration: individual participant data analysis. BMJ. 2022. PMID: 35918097. Registry ID: none in the record (individual participant data analysis). cards.headline: Fournier 2010 (patient-level meta-analysis, 6 trials, 718 patients): below a Hamilton score of 23 the drug–placebo effect size was under 0.20 — the NICE clinical-significance threshold was crossed only at a score of 25
cards.summary: Fournier 2010 (patient-level meta-analysis, 6 trials, 718 patients): below a Hamilton score of 23 the drug–placebo effect size was under 0.20 — the NICE clinical-significance threshold was crossed only at a score of 25
cards.people: 718 adult outpatients with major or minor depressive disorder in 6 randomised placebo-controlled trials (at least 6 weeks, Hamilton Depression Rating Scale outcomes) whose authors provided individual patient data; the drugs studied were paroxetine and imipramine.
cards.result: Medication-versus-placebo differences varied substantially with baseline severity. Among patients with Hamilton scores below 23, Cohen d effect sizes for the drug–placebo difference were estimated at less than 0.20 (a standard definition of a small effect). The estimated superiority of medication over placebo increased with baseline severity and crossed the threshold defined by the National Institute for Clinical Excellence for a clinically significant difference at a baseline Hamilton score of 25. The authors conclude the benefit over placebo may be minimal or nonexistent, on average, in patients with mild or moderate symptoms, and is substantial in very severe depression.
cards.watchOut: Only 6 trials and 2 drugs, and inclusion required trialists to share their raw data — a selected subset of the literature. The severity gradient itself is corroborated by the much larger Stone 2022 analysis (difference increased with baseline severity, P<0.001), but the exact cut-points (23, 25) come from this small dataset and should not be treated as sharp clinical boundaries.
cards.source: Fournier JC, DeRubeis RJ, Hollon SD, Dimidjian S, Amsterdam JD, Shelton RC, Fawcett J. Antidepressant drug effects and depression severity: a patient-level meta-analysis. JAMA. 2010. PMID: 20051569. Registry ID: none in the record (patient-level meta-analysis). cards.headline: Synthesis: yes, they work on average — a small mean advantage concentrated in a minority with large responses, largest in severe depression; drug rankings differ by less than the headlines suggest
cards.summary: Synthesis: yes, they work on average — a small mean advantage concentrated in a minority with large responses, largest in severe depression; drug rankings differ by less than the headlines suggest
cards.people: Adults with major depressive disorder considering or choosing an antidepressant, and clinicians advising them.
cards.result: Three complementary analyses converge: the class beats placebo in every one of 522 trials' pooled comparisons (Cipriani 2018), the average symptom advantage is 1.75 Hamilton points with a large response in 24.5% on drug versus 9.6% on placebo — about 15% of patients gaining a substantial drug-specific benefit (Stone 2022) — and the drug–placebo gap widens with severity, from possibly negligible in mild symptoms to substantial in very severe depression (Fournier 2010; Stone 2022). For 'which is best': escitalopram, mirtazapine, paroxetine, venlafaxine, vortioxetine, agomelatine and amitriptyline ranked highest for efficacy in head-to-head data, while agomelatine, citalopram, escitalopram, fluoxetine, sertraline and vortioxetine ranked best for staying on treatment — with small separations and moderate-to-very-low certainty.
cards.watchOut: All of this is acute-phase (roughly 6–8 week) trial evidence in major depressive disorder; it does not cover long-term relapse prevention, treatment-resistant depression, or combinations with psychotherapy, and individual adverse-effect profiles — often what actually decides between two drugs — are only crudely captured by dropout rates.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cipriani A et al. The Lancet. 2018 (PMID: 29477251); Stone MB et al. BMJ. 2022 (PMID: 35918097); Fournier JC et al. JAMA. 2010 (PMID: 20051569).

shelves.title: Anxiety in pregnancy: individual CBT-based sessions halved-and-more postnatal illness in a large trial and internet CBT helped anxiety — brief group CBT did not beat a booklet, and the SSRI malformation signal fades against the right comparison
shelves.question: How is anxiety treated in pregnancy — in pregnant women with anxiety, do psychological therapies (CBT-based programmes, internet CBT, group CBT) reduce anxiety, and what does the safety evidence say about SSRI use in pregnancy?
shelves.mesh: Anxiety/prevention & control · Anxiety Disorders/prevention & control · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy · Depression · Depression, Postpartum/diagnosis · Depression, Postpartum/prevention & control · Female · Humans · Major Depressive Disorder/therapy · Pregnancy · Single-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the two halves of this question have very different evidence. For psychological treatment of anxiety in pregnancy, the largest trial is strongly positive: the HMHB trial (Surkan 2024, PMID: 38365951; NCT03880032), a CBT-based intervention delivered by non-specialists to pregnant women with at least mild anxiety and no clinical depression, cut major depressive episodes at 6 weeks postpartum to 12% versus 41% with enhanced usual care, with adjusted odds (relative measures) of 0.19 for depression-or-anxiety combined, 0.19 for depressive episode and 0.26 for moderate-to-severe anxiety. Unguided internet CBT also beat treatment as usual on anxiety in a small trial (Loughnan 2019, PMID: 30266030; 87 women; GAD-7 effect size g = 0.76). But brief group CBT in an earlier trial did not beat an information booklet (Austin 2008, PMID: 17490753; anxiety diagnoses fell similarly in both groups) — so format and intensity matter. For SSRI safety, the records allow only pregnancy-wide data, not anxiety-specific cohorts: a meta-analysis of 29 cohort studies and 9,085,954 births (Gao 2018, PMID: 30415641) found small relative increases in major congenital anomalies (RR 1.11, 95% CI 1.03–1.19) and heart defects (RR 1.24, 1.11–1.37) with first-trimester exposure — which disappeared when the analysis was restricted to women with a psychiatric diagnosis (RR 1.04 and 1.06, both non-significant), the signature of confounding by indication. PROPOSED SPLIT: structured CBT-based help for antenatal anxiety is supported (one large trial, one small positive, one null); SSRI malformation risk, if real, is small in relative terms and not separable from the underlying illness in these data. Boundary declared: postpartum depression treatment (brexanolone, zuranolone, sertraline recurrence prevention) and postpartum prevention programmes are homed on other shelves (#229, #836, #2743, #3773) and are not re-carded here.

cards.headline: HMHB 2024 (phase 3 RCT, 755 women assessed postpartum): CBT-based sessions in pregnancy cut postnatal major depressive episodes to 12% versus 41% — adjusted odds 0.19 for depression-or-anxiety, 0.26 for moderate-to-severe anxiety (relative measures)
cards.summary: HMHB 2024 (phase 3 RCT, 755 women assessed postpartum): CBT-based sessions in pregnancy cut postnatal major depressive episodes to 12% versus 41% — adjusted odds 0.19 for depression-or-anxiety, 0.26 for moderate-to-severe anxiety (relative measures)
cards.type: Phase 3 single-blind randomised trial of a CBT-based antenatal intervention (HMHB, Surkan 2024)
cards.people: Pregnant women in Pakistan at 22 weeks' gestation or less with at least mild anxiety and no clinical depression, randomised to six 1-to-1 CBT-based sessions (the Happy Mother, Healthy Baby intervention) delivered by non-specialists, or to enhanced usual care; postnatal outcome assessments were completed by 755 women (380 intervention, 375 control).
cards.result: At 6 weeks postpartum, 12% of the intervention group and 41% of the control group had a major depressive episode. The intervention group had lower adjusted odds (relative measures) of experiencing a major depressive episode or moderate-to-severe anxiety combined (adjusted odds ratio 0.19, 95% CI 0.14–0.28), a major depressive episode alone (aOR 0.19, 95% CI 0.13–0.28) and moderate-to-severe anxiety alone (aOR 0.26, 95% CI 0.17–0.40) — that is, 81% lower odds of the combined outcome and 74% lower odds of moderate-to-severe anxiety, in relative terms, against absolute postnatal depression rates of 12% versus 41%. A companion birth-outcomes analysis found no significant intention-to-treat effect on low birthweight, preterm birth or small-for-gestational-age.
cards.watchOut: The intervention treated anxiety during pregnancy, but the headline outcomes were measured after birth — this is as much a prevention-of-postnatal-illness trial as an antenatal-anxiety treatment trial, and the control event rate (41% postnatal depressive episodes) reflects a high-risk, low-resource population, so the absolute benefit will not transfer to lower-risk settings even if the relative effect does. The trial's registration reports a larger randomised total than the 755 who completed postnatal assessment; this card uses the abstract's assessed numbers.

cards.headline: MUMentum 2019 (RCT, 87 women): unguided internet CBT beat treatment as usual on anxiety (effect size g = 0.76) and distress (g = 0.88); depression effects were small and non-significant
cards.summary: MUMentum 2019 (RCT, 87 women): unguided internet CBT beat treatment as usual on anxiety (effect size g = 0.76) and distress (g = 0.88); depression effects were small and non-significant
cards.type: Randomised trial of unguided internet CBT in pregnancy (MUMentum, Loughnan 2019)
cards.people: 87 pregnant women (43 allocated to internet CBT, 44 to treatment as usual) meeting clinical thresholds for generalised anxiety disorder and/or depression, given unguided access to a 3-lesson internet CBT programme (MUMentum Pregnancy) designed for antenatal anxiety and depression.
cards.result: Compared with treatment as usual, internet CBT produced significantly larger reductions in anxiety symptoms (GAD-7, Hedges' g = 0.76) and psychological distress (K10, g = 0.88); treatment effects for depression outcomes were small and non-significant (g < 0.35). Of the 43 women allocated, 36 started the programme and 26 completed all lessons. The authors concluded the programme was effective for anxiety and distress symptoms in pregnancy, with further research needed on its effects on depression.
cards.watchOut: Eighty-seven women, self-reported outcomes, and a mixed anxiety-and-depression sample — the anxiety result is genuine but the trial cannot say whether guided delivery, or women with anxiety alone, would do better or worse. A quarter of starters never finished the three lessons, which is the standing problem of unguided digital therapy.
cards.source: Loughnan SA, et al. A randomised controlled trial of 'MUMentum Pregnancy': internet-delivered cognitive behavioral therapy for antenatal anxiety and depression. Journal of Affective Disorders. 2019. PMID: 30266030. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Austin 2008 (RCT, 277 women randomised): brief group CBT did not beat an information booklet — anxiety diagnoses fell from 28% to 16% in the CBT group, with similar reductions in controls (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Austin 2008 (RCT, 277 women randomised): brief group CBT did not beat an information booklet — anxiety diagnoses fell from 28% to 16% in the CBT group, with similar reductions in controls (the treatment made no difference)
cards.type: Randomised trial of brief group CBT versus information booklet (Austin 2008)
cards.people: 277 women in mid-pregnancy accepted as suitable and randomised — 191 to a brief CBT group programme and 86 to a control condition receiving an information booklet — with 52% overall dropout; outcomes included depression scores (EPDS) and anxiety diagnoses on the MINI interview in late pregnancy and at 2 and 4 months postpartum.
cards.result: On intention-to-treat analysis there was no reduction in depression scores over time in either group. The proportion of women in the CBT group meeting MINI criteria for an anxiety diagnosis fell from 28% in late pregnancy to 16% at 4 months postpartum — but similar reductions occurred in the control group, so there was no between-group treatment effect on anxiety or depression outcomes. The authors noted the very high dropout (52%) as a limitation.
cards.watchOut: With 52% dropout and a booklet control that itself informed and reassured, this trial may show that brief low-intensity group CBT adds nothing to good written information — or simply that a trial losing half its participants cannot detect what the intervention does. Either way it is the necessary counterweight to the two positive cards: 'CBT in pregnancy' is not one thing, and the brief group format is the version with a null result.
cards.source: Austin MP, Frilingos M, Lumley J, et al. Brief antenatal cognitive behaviour therapy group intervention for the prevention of postnatal depression and anxiety: a randomised controlled trial. Journal of Affective Disorders. 2008. cards.headline: Gao 2018 (meta-analysis, 29 cohort studies, 9,085,954 births): first-trimester SSRI exposure carried small relative increases in major anomalies (RR 1.11) and heart defects (RR 1.24) — both gone when restricted to women with a psychiatric diagnosis (RR 1.04 and 1.06, non-significant)
cards.summary: Gao 2018 (meta-analysis, 29 cohort studies, 9,085,954 births): first-trimester SSRI exposure carried small relative increases in major anomalies (RR 1.11) and heart defects (RR 1.24) — both gone when restricted to women with a psychiatric diagnosis (RR 1.04 and 1.06, non-significant)
cards.type: Meta-analysis of cohort studies, SSRI exposure in pregnancy (Gao 2018)
cards.people: 29 published cohort studies covering 9,085,954 births, comparing congenital malformation rates in infants exposed to selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors in the first trimester with unexposed infants; subgroup analyses restricted the comparison to women with a psychiatric diagnosis, the group relevant to anxiety treatment.
cards.result: Overall, first-trimester SSRI exposure was associated with a higher relative risk of major congenital anomalies (RR 1.11, 95% CI 1.03–1.19) and congenital heart defects (RR 1.24, 95% CI 1.11–1.37) — relative measures, corresponding to small absolute differences against low baseline rates. When the analysis was restricted to women with a psychiatric diagnosis, neither association remained significant: major anomalies RR 1.04 (95% CI 0.95–1.13) and heart defects RR 1.06 (95% CI 0.90–1.26). The authors concluded the small overall risk might be attributable to the underlying maternal disease rather than the medication.
cards.watchOut: Scope limit, stated plainly: these cohorts are SSRI use in pregnancy generally — mostly depression populations — because anxiety-specific malformation cohorts were not found in the records fetched; the psychiatric-diagnosis-restricted analysis is the closest anxiety-relevant cut and it is null. Observational throughout: women who take SSRIs in pregnancy differ from women who do not in illness severity, smoking, and other exposures, and no pooling removes that. Relative risks of 1.11–1.24 on outcomes with low baseline rates are small absolute risks even if causal.
cards.source: Gao SY, Wu QJ, Zhang TN, et al. Fluoxetine and other SSRIs: a meta-analysis of the association between first trimester exposure to SSRIs and risk of congenital malformations. BMC Medicine. 2018. PMID: 30415641. Registry ID: PROSPERO CRD42018088358 (review registration, as printed in the record). cards.headline: Synthesis: CBT-based help for anxiety in pregnancy works in its structured forms (one large trial, one small positive internet trial, one null brief-group trial); SSRI malformation signals are small, relative, and vanish against the fair comparison group
cards.summary: Synthesis: CBT-based help for anxiety in pregnancy works in its structured forms (one large trial, one small positive internet trial, one null brief-group trial); SSRI malformation signals are small, relative, and vanish against the fair comparison group
cards.people: Surkan 2024 (phase 3 RCT, 755 assessed), Loughnan 2019 (RCT, 87 women), Austin 2008 (RCT, 277 randomised), Gao 2018 (meta-analysis, 29 cohorts, 9,085,954 births).
cards.result: Psychological treatment: postnatal depressive episodes 12% versus 41% and moderate-to-severe anxiety adjusted odds 0.26 (relative) after six individual CBT-based sessions (Surkan); anxiety effect size g = 0.76 for unguided internet CBT versus usual care (Loughnan); no between-group effect for brief group CBT versus a booklet (Austin). Medication safety: overall relative risks 1.11 (major anomalies) and 1.24 (heart defects) with first-trimester SSRI exposure, attenuating to 1.04 and 1.06 — non-significant — within women who had a psychiatric diagnosis (Gao). PROPOSED SPLIT — treatment benefit is real but format-dependent, and the medication-safety question cannot be answered anxiety-specifically from the published cohorts; untreated antenatal anxiety is itself the exposure the HMHB trial shows can be modified.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. Boundary: postpartum depression pharmacotherapy and prevention are homed elsewhere (brexanolone Shelf #229, zuranolone #836, interpersonal-therapy prevention #2743, sertraline recurrence prevention #3773) and are not re-carded; this shelf is antenatal anxiety treatment plus the SSRI-safety context a prescriber needs, with the anxiety-specificity limit of the safety data declared on its card.
cards.source: Synthesis of Surkan PJ et al. Nature Medicine. 2024 (PMID: 38365951; NCT03880032); Loughnan SA et al. Journal of Affective Disorders. 2019 (PMID: 30266030); Austin MP et al. Journal of Affective Disorders. 2008 (PMID: 17490753); Gao SY et al. BMC Medicine. 2018 (PMID: 30415641).

shelves.title: Psychotherapy for dissociative disorders: an adjunctive online programme beat a waitlist in one interim RCT (n=291), while a stabilising group programme added nothing immediate in the other RCT (n=59)
shelves.question: In people with dissociative disorders (including dissociative identity disorder), does psychotherapy — phase-oriented treatment or structured add-on programmes — improve symptoms and functioning compared with waiting list or with individual therapy alone?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Dissociative Disorders/psychology · Dissociative Disorders/therapy · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Psychotherapy/methods · Stress Disorders, Post-Traumatic/therapy · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the two randomised trials test different add-ons and point in different directions. In the interim report of an ongoing RCT (Brand BL et al., PMID: 40014495; 291 outpatients with dissociative identity disorder, dissociative PTSD, other specified dissociative disorders, complex PTSD or unspecified dissociative disorder, all continuing their own outpatient psychotherapy), immediate access to the online Finding Solid Ground (FSG) psychoeducational programme produced significantly greater improvement than a 6-month waitlist in emotion regulation, PTSD symptoms, self-compassion and adaptive capacities at 6 months; by 12 months the immediate group showed large within-group effect sizes versus entry (|g| = 0.95–1.32), and the waitlist group improved comparably after it too received FSG. The abstract prints no between-group effect sizes, and this is an interim report of an ongoing trial. In the only other RCT (Bækkelund H et al., PMID: 35578194; 59 patients with complex dissociative disorders), adding 20 sessions of manualised stabilising group treatment to individual therapy produced no immediate advantage over individual therapy alone on functioning or any secondary outcome, although both groups improved significantly over 6 months of follow-up. A 2025 systematic review of phase-oriented treatment (Griffiths TA et al., PMID: 40891466) screened 6,088 articles and found only 19 pre–post studies, nearly all uncontrolled: every treatment type was associated with improvement, and the reviewers state plainly that high-powered controlled trials are needed. PROPOSED SPLIT: one specific adjunctive programme (FSG) has a positive waitlist-controlled interim result; structured group stabilisation as an add-on does not; and the core phase-oriented therapy itself has never been randomised.

cards.headline: Brand 2025 (FSG RCT, interim report): immediate access to the online Finding Solid Ground programme beat a 6-month waitlist on emotion regulation, PTSD symptoms, self-compassion and adaptive capacities; 12-month within-group effects were large (|g| = 0.95–1.32)
cards.summary: Brand 2025 (FSG RCT, interim report): immediate access to the online Finding Solid Ground programme beat a 6-month waitlist on emotion regulation, PTSD symptoms, self-compassion and adaptive capacities; 12-month within-group effects were large (|g| = 0.95–1.32)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial — interim report of an ongoing trial (Brand 2025)
cards.people: 291 outpatients internationally with dissociative identity disorder, dissociative PTSD, other specified dissociative disorders, complex PTSD, or dissociative disorder unspecified (ICD-10), all continuing psychotherapy with their own outpatient therapists, randomly assigned to immediate access to the adjunctive online Finding Solid Ground (FSG) psychoeducational programme or to a 6-month waitlist before accessing it. Suicidality, non-suicidal self-injury, recent hospitalisation and substance abuse were not exclusions.
cards.result: Groups were initially comparable. At 6 months the Immediate FSG group showed significant improvement in emotion regulation, PTSD symptoms, self-compassion and adaptive capacities compared with the Waitlist group. At 12 months the Immediate group showed large effect-size changes in these areas compared with study entry (|g| = 0.95–1.32), and the Waitlist group showed comparable improvements after accessing FSG for 6 months. The abstract does not print the between-group effect sizes or confidence intervals for the 6-month comparison, so the size of the advantage over waitlist cannot be stated from the record.
cards.watchOut: An interim report of an ongoing trial, against a waitlist — the weakest control in psychotherapy research, since waitlisted patients know they are waiting and expectancy alone can widen a gap. The headline 12-month figures (|g| 0.95–1.32) are within-group changes from entry, not advantages over any comparator, and the population mixes dissociative disorders with complex PTSD and dissociative-subtype PTSD, so the result is not a pure dissociative-disorders estimate. Final trial results may differ.

cards.headline: Bækkelund 2022 (the first RCT in complex dissociative disorders): 20 sessions of stabilising group treatment added to individual therapy gave no immediate advantage on any outcome; both groups improved by 6-month follow-up
cards.summary: Bækkelund 2022 (the first RCT in complex dissociative disorders): 20 sessions of stabilising group treatment added to individual therapy gave no immediate advantage on any outcome; both groups improved by 6-month follow-up
cards.people: 59 patients with complex dissociative disorders (dissociative identity disorder or other specified dissociative disorder) at a Norwegian outpatient clinic, randomised to 20 sessions of structured stabilising group treatment based on the manual Coping with Trauma-Related Dissociation, conjoint with individual therapy, or to individual therapy alone in a delayed-treatment design. Primary outcome: Global Assessment of Functioning; secondary outcomes: PTSD and dissociative symptoms, general psychopathology, interpersonal difficulties.
cards.result: Mixed-effect models showed no condition × time interaction during the delayed-treatment period — no immediate differences between conditions on the primary outcome, and similar results for the secondary outcomes. Within-group effects were non-significant in both conditions from baseline to end of treatment, but significant improvements in psychosocial function, PTSD symptoms and general psychopathology were observed over the 6-month follow-up period. The authors conclude that stabilising group treatment did not produce immediate superior outcomes, while psychological treatment overall was associated with later improvement.
cards.watchOut: Fifty-nine patients is small for a psychotherapy trial, the delayed-treatment design means the control group also receives the group programme (so later comparisons are not controlled), and the individual therapy running underneath in both arms was uncontrolled and variable. A null here rules out a large immediate add-on effect of this 20-session group format; it does not test phase-oriented individual therapy itself.
cards.source: Bækkelund H, Ulvenes P, Boon-Langelaan S, Arnevik EA. Group treatment for complex dissociative disorders: a randomized clinical trial. BMC Psychiatry. 2022. PMID: 35578194. Registry ID: NCT02450617. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Griffiths 2025 (systematic review of phase-oriented treatment): 19 studies from 6,088 screened — every treatment type improved, but the studies were pre–post and essentially uncontrolled; 'high-powered controlled trials are needed'
cards.summary: Griffiths 2025 (systematic review of phase-oriented treatment): 19 studies from 6,088 screened — every treatment type improved, but the studies were pre–post and essentially uncontrolled; 'high-powered controlled trials are needed'
cards.people: Systematic review of studies from 1980–2025 in people with a primary diagnosis of dissociative identity disorder or other specified dissociative disorder examining phase-oriented treatment (the ISSTD-recommended approach) and/or other treatments, with at least one pre- and post-treatment outcome measure; study quality assessed with the EPHPP tool.
cards.result: Of 6,088 articles screened, 19 met the inclusion criteria. All treatment types were associated with improvements in dissociation symptoms, general mental health symptoms, psychopathology and general functioning; when compared with one another, each treatment type had strengths depending on the outcome of interest. The reviewers' conclusion: the review demonstrates an emerging evidence base for psychological interventions in dissociative disorders, and high-powered controlled trials are needed to build on these results.
cards.watchOut: Pre–post improvement in uncontrolled series is what this whole field mostly consists of: people in long-term therapy for severe disorders improve on average for many reasons (regression to the mean, concurrent care, selection of who stays in treatment) that a pre–post design cannot separate from the treatment. The review is carded as the honest map of the evidence base — 19 studies, two RCTs in the entire literature (the two cards above) — not as proof that phase-oriented treatment works.
cards.source: Griffiths TA, Dimitrova LI, Linington M, Terhune DB, Reinders AATS. Effectiveness of phase-oriented treatment for trauma-related dissociative disorders: a systematic review. European Journal of Psychotraumatology. 2025. PMID: 40891466. Registry ID: none in the record (systematic review). cards.headline: Synthesis: two RCTs, two different add-ons, two different answers — and the core therapy has never been randomised
cards.summary: Synthesis: two RCTs, two different add-ons, two different answers — and the core therapy has never been randomised
cards.people: Two randomised trials (Brand 2025, n=291, interim report; Bækkelund 2022, n=59) and one systematic review of 19 mostly uncontrolled studies (Griffiths 2025).
cards.result: Finding Solid Ground added to ongoing psychotherapy: significant advantage over waitlist at 6 months on emotion regulation, PTSD symptoms, self-compassion and adaptive capacities (between-group sizes not printed); large within-group gains by 12 months (|g| 0.95–1.32). Stabilising group treatment added to individual therapy: no immediate advantage on functioning or symptoms; both arms improved by 6-month follow-up. Phase-oriented treatment overall: associated with improvement across 19 pre–post studies, with no controlled estimate. PROPOSED SPLIT — the stamp follows the intervention tested, not the diagnosis.
cards.watchOut: Nothing on this shelf tests phase-oriented individual psychotherapy — the treatment most guidelines actually recommend — against any control; that trial does not exist. Drug treatment of dissociative disorders is likewise untested in RCTs and is not covered here. Tier C: two small-to-moderate RCTs of add-on programmes and an uncontrolled literature.
cards.source: Synthesis of Brand BL et al. Psychological Trauma. 2025 (PMID: 40014495); Bækkelund H et al. BMC Psychiatry. 2022 (PMID: 35578194); Griffiths TA et al. European Journal of Psychotraumatology. 2025 (PMID: 40891466).

shelves.title: Gender dysphoria and incongruence: hormone therapy outcomes are observational only — youth cohorts report better mental-health scores on treatment, register data show no time-on-hormones association, long-term risks stay above the general population, and estrogen carries a clotting signal
shelves.question: I have gender dysphoria (gender incongruence) — if I start gender-affirming hormone treatment, what does the evidence say happens to mental health and to physical health such as blood clots?
shelves.mesh: Depression · Gender Dysphoria/drug therapy · Gender Dysphoria/epidemiology · Gender Dysphoria/psychology · Gender Dysphoria/therapy · Gender-Affirming Procedures/psychology · Gonadal Steroid Hormones/adverse effects · Mental Health · Suicidal Ideation · Transgender Persons/psychology · Transgender Persons/statistics & numerical data · Venous Thromboembolism/epidemiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — every study on this shelf is observational; there are no randomised trials of gender-affirming hormone therapy, so all findings are associations and the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE. The fetched record, stated plainly in both directions: (1) In a prospective US clinic cohort of 104 youths aged 13–20, those who had started puberty blockers and/or hormones had lower adjusted odds of depression (aOR 0.40, 95% CI 0.17–0.95 — 60% lower odds, a relative measure) and of suicidality (aOR 0.27, 0.11–0.65 — 73% lower odds, relative) over 12 months than those who had not, with no association for anxiety (aOR 1.01) (Tordoff 2022, PMID: 35212746). (2) In a prospective cohort of 315 transgender and nonbinary youth aged 12–20 followed through 2 years of hormones, appearance congruence, positive affect and life satisfaction increased and depression and anxiety symptoms decreased; suicidal ideation occurred in 11 participants (3.5%) and 2 died by suicide; there was no comparison group (Chen 2023, PMID: 36652355). (3) In Swedish national register data (2,679 people with a gender incongruence diagnosis), years since starting hormones were not associated with mental-health treatment (aOR 1.01, 0.98–1.03 per year); the paper's original analysis linked time since last gender-affirming surgery to reduced treatment (aOR 0.92, 0.87–0.98), but a published correction stated the design supported no such conclusion and a reanalysis showed no advantage of surgery on those outcomes (Bränström & Pachankis 2020, PMID: 31581798). (4) In long-term Swedish follow-up of 324 people after sex-reassignment surgery (1973–2003) versus matched general-population controls, overall mortality (adjusted HR 2.8, 1.8–4.3) and death by suicide (aHR 19.1, 5.8–62.9) remained higher than in the general population (Dhejne 2011, PMID: 21364939). (5) In a US health-system cohort (2,842 transfeminine and 2,118 transmasculine people), transfeminine participants had more venous thromboembolism than cisgender comparators — risk differences of 4.1 per 1,000 at 2 years and 16.7 per 1,000 at 8 years versus cisgender men — with differences more pronounced among those who initiated hormones during follow-up; overall stroke and myocardial infarction incidence was similar across groups (Getahun 2018, PMID: 29987313). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: short-term youth cohorts associate treatment with better mental-health scores; register and long-term data show persistently elevated risks relative to the general population and no demonstrated association between time on hormones and mental-health treatment; a venous thromboembolism signal accompanies transfeminine estrogen therapy.

cards.headline: Tordoff 2022: youths who started blockers/hormones had 60% lower adjusted odds of depression and 73% lower odds of suicidality over 12 months (relative measures); anxiety unchanged
cards.summary: Tordoff 2022: youths who started blockers/hormones had 60% lower adjusted odds of depression and 73% lower odds of suicidality over 12 months (relative measures); anxiety unchanged
cards.people: 104 transgender and nonbinary youths aged 13–20 years (mean 15.8) at a US multidisciplinary gender clinic, followed prospectively for 12 months; 69 (66.3%) received puberty blockers, gender-affirming hormones, or both, and 35 received neither. At baseline, 59 (56.7%) had moderate-to-severe depression, 52 (50.0%) moderate-to-severe anxiety, and 45 (43.3%) reported self-harm or suicidal thoughts.
cards.result: After adjustment for temporal trends and confounders, youths who had initiated blockers or hormones had lower odds of moderate-to-severe depression (adjusted odds ratio 0.40, 95% CI 0.17–0.95 — i.e. 60% lower odds, a relative measure) and of self-harm/suicidal thoughts (aOR 0.27, 0.11–0.65 — 73% lower odds, relative) than youths who had not initiated treatment. There was no association with anxiety (aOR 1.01, 0.41–2.51). The authors concluded the interventions were associated with lower odds of depression and suicidality over 12 months.
cards.watchOut: Not randomised: youths who started treatment differed from those who did not (including time in care and clinical readiness), and adjustment cannot remove that. Odds ratios are relative measures — the paper's own absolute rates are the baseline figures quoted in the people field; 12 months is a short horizon, and the comparison group shrank as participants started treatment during follow-up.
cards.source: Tordoff DM, Wanta JW, Collin A, Stepney C, Inwards-Breland DJ, Ahrens K. Mental Health Outcomes in Transgender and Nonbinary Youths Receiving Gender-Affirming Care. JAMA Network Open. 2022. PMID: 35212746. Registry ID: none in the record (prospective observational cohort). cards.headline: Chen 2023 (NEJM): over 2 years of hormones, life satisfaction and appearance congruence rose and depression/anxiety symptoms fell in 315 youths — with no comparison group; 2 participants died by suicide
cards.summary: Chen 2023 (NEJM): over 2 years of hormones, life satisfaction and appearance congruence rose and depression/anxiety symptoms fell in 315 youths — with no comparison group; 2 participants died by suicide
cards.people: 315 transgender and nonbinary youth aged 12–20 years (mean 16 ± 1.9; 190 transmasculine, 60.3%; 25 [7.9%] had previously received pubertal suppression) at 4 US sites, followed prospectively through 2 years of gender-affirming hormone therapy.
cards.result: Over the 2 years, appearance congruence, positive affect and life satisfaction increased, and depression and anxiety symptoms decreased on the study's standardised measures. Suicidal ideation was reported in 11 participants (3.5%), and 2 participants died by suicide during follow-up. The authors reported the psychosocial functioning measures improved over the treatment period.
cards.watchOut: There is no untreated or wait-list comparison group, so the improvements cannot be separated from time, concurrent mental-health care, expectancy, or regression to the mean — the study describes what happened during treatment, not what treatment caused. The two deaths by suicide (2 of 315) are reported on the face of this card because they are part of the record; the cohort is too small to estimate a suicide rate or its direction of change.
cards.source: Chen D, Berona J, Chen YM, et al. Psychosocial Functioning in Transgender Youth after 2 Years of Hormones. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2023. PMID: 36652355. Registry ID: none in the record (prospective observational cohort). MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Bränström & Pachankis 2020: years since starting hormones were NOT associated with mental-health treatment (aOR 1.01); the paper's surgery finding was withdrawn in a published correction after reanalysis showed no advantage
cards.summary: Bränström & Pachankis 2020: years since starting hormones were NOT associated with mental-health treatment (aOR 1.01); the paper's surgery finding was withdrawn in a published correction after reanalysis showed no advantage
cards.type: National register study, with published correction (Bränström & Pachankis 2020)
cards.people: Swedish total-population register study: 2,679 people with a diagnosis of gender incongruence (2005–2015) identified within a population of 9,747,324, with mental-health treatment (care visits, prescriptions, hospitalisation after suicide attempt) tracked in national registers.
cards.result: Compared with the general population, people with a gender incongruence diagnosis had about 6 times the likelihood of a mood or anxiety care visit, more than 3 times the likelihood of antidepressant or anxiolytic prescriptions, and more than 6 times the likelihood of hospitalisation after a suicide attempt. Years since initiation of hormone treatment were not related to subsequent mental-health treatment (adjusted odds ratio 1.01 per year, 95% CI 0.98–1.03). The original analysis reported that time since last gender-affirming surgery was associated with reduced mental-health treatment (aOR 0.92, 0.87–0.98); a subsequent published correction stated that the study design was neither a prospective cohort nor a randomised trial, that the original conclusion was too strong, and that reanalysis showed no advantage of surgery over no surgery on these outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Both halves of this card must travel together: the uncorrected surgery figure (aOR 0.92) is still widely quoted, but the authors and journal corrected it, and the corrected reading is no demonstrated advantage. Register outcomes measure treatment utilisation (visits, prescriptions, hospitalisations), not symptoms or wellbeing directly — less treatment can mean better health or less contact with services, and the design cannot distinguish these.
cards.source: Bränström R, Pachankis JE. Reduction in Mental Health Treatment Utilization Among Transgender Individuals After Gender-Affirming Surgeries: A Total Population Study. American Journal of Psychiatry. 2020. PMID: 31581798. Registry ID: none in the record (national register study). cards.headline: Dhejne 2011: decades after sex-reassignment surgery, mortality (aHR 2.8) and suicide death (aHR 19.1) remained higher than in matched general-population controls
cards.summary: Dhejne 2011: decades after sex-reassignment surgery, mortality (aHR 2.8) and suicide death (aHR 19.1) remained higher than in matched general-population controls
cards.people: All 324 sex-reassigned persons in Sweden from 1973–2003 (191 male-to-female, 133 female-to-male), in a population-based matched cohort study with random population controls matched 10:1 by birth year and birth sex or reassigned sex; hazard ratios adjusted for immigrant status and psychiatric morbidity before sex reassignment.
cards.result: Overall mortality during follow-up was higher than in birth-sex-matched controls (adjusted hazard ratio 2.8, 95% CI 1.8–4.3), particularly death from suicide (aHR 19.1, 5.8–62.9). Risks were also increased for suicide attempts (aHR 4.9, 2.9–8.5) and psychiatric inpatient care (aHR 2.8, 2.0–3.9); comparisons against controls matched on reassigned sex were similar. Female-to-male persons, but not male-to-female, had a higher risk of criminal convictions than birth-sex controls. The authors concluded that after sex reassignment, risks of mortality, suicidal behaviour and psychiatric morbidity remain considerably higher than in the general population, and that reassignment alone may not suffice as treatment, suggesting improved psychiatric and somatic follow-up.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is the general population, not untreated people with gender dysphoria — so this study measures how this group fares against the population average, and cannot show whether surgery or hormones raised, lowered or left unchanged the risks relative to no treatment. The cohort was treated in 1973–2003 under older diagnostic criteria, older hormone regimens and a different social era; absolute event counts behind the suicide hazard ratio are small, hence the wide interval (5.8–62.9).
cards.source: Dhejne C, Lichtenstein P, Boman M, Johansson ALV, Långström N, Landén M. Long-term follow-up of transsexual persons undergoing sex reassignment surgery: cohort study in Sweden. PLoS ONE. 2011. PMID: 21364939. Registry ID: none in the record (population-based matched cohort study). MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Getahun 2018: transfeminine people had more venous thromboembolism than cisgender comparators (risk difference 16.7 per 1,000 by 8 years vs cisgender men); stroke and heart attack rates were overall similar
cards.summary: Getahun 2018: transfeminine people had more venous thromboembolism than cisgender comparators (risk difference 16.7 per 1,000 by 8 years vs cisgender men); stroke and heart attack rates were overall similar
cards.people: Electronic-record cohort from integrated US health systems: 2,842 transfeminine and 2,118 transmasculine members (mean follow-up 4.0 and 3.6 years), each matched to 10 cisgender men and 10 cisgender women (48,686 cisgender men and 48,775 cisgender women in total), with venous thromboembolism (VTE), ischaemic stroke and myocardial infarction ascertained from diagnostic codes through 2016.
cards.result: Transfeminine participants had a higher incidence of VTE, with risk differences versus cisgender men of 4.1 per 1,000 persons (95% CI 1.6–6.7) at 2 years and 16.7 per 1,000 (6.4–27.5) at 8 years, and versus cisgender women of 3.4 (1.1–5.6) and 13.7 (4.1–22.7) per 1,000. Overall analyses for ischaemic stroke and myocardial infarction showed similar incidence across groups. Differences for VTE and ischaemic stroke were more pronounced among transfeminine participants who initiated hormone therapy during follow-up. The evidence was insufficient to draw conclusions for transmasculine participants.
cards.watchOut: Hormone exposure was incompletely captured — the authors note they could not determine which members received hormones elsewhere — so the transfeminine-versus-cisgender comparison mixes treated and untreated people, and the hormone-initiator subgroup analysis carries that uncertainty. Event counts in the transmasculine group were too few for conclusions, which the card states rather than fills in.

cards.headline: Synthesis: observational data associate treatment with better short-term youth mental-health scores, show no time-on-hormones association in registers, persistently elevated risk versus the general population, and a clotting signal with estrogen
cards.summary: Synthesis: observational data associate treatment with better short-term youth mental-health scores, show no time-on-hormones association in registers, persistently elevated risk versus the general population, and a clotting signal with estrogen
cards.people: Five observational sources: two prospective youth clinic cohorts (104 and 315 participants; Tordoff 2022, Chen 2023), a Swedish total-population register study (2,679 diagnosed individuals; Bränström & Pachankis 2020, as corrected), a Swedish matched cohort after surgery (324 people, 1973–2003; Dhejne 2011), and a US health-system cohort (4,960 transgender members; Getahun 2018).
cards.result: Mental health, short term: initiation of blockers/hormones was associated with lower adjusted odds of depression (aOR 0.40) and suicidality (aOR 0.27) over 12 months in one youth cohort; a second youth cohort improved on functioning measures over 2 years of hormones without a comparison group (2 deaths by suicide among 315). Mental health, register/long term: years since hormone initiation showed no association with mental-health treatment (aOR 1.01/year); the one positive surgery analysis was corrected to no advantage; and a post-surgical cohort retained higher mortality (aHR 2.8) and suicide mortality (aHR 19.1) than general-population controls. Physical health: transfeminine status/hormone initiation was associated with excess venous thromboembolism (up to 16.7 extra cases per 1,000 by 8 years versus cisgender men), with stroke and myocardial infarction rates overall similar. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — associations in both directions, all observational, none of it randomised.
cards.watchOut: No card on this shelf can support a causal claim in either direction: the youth cohorts lack randomisation (and one lacks any control group), the register studies compare against the general population or measure service use rather than symptoms, and the surgical cohort predates modern practice. This shelf reports the fetched numbers as they stand, including the published correction, and takes no position beyond the stamp the evidence grade permits. Tier C: developer's personal verdict.
