shelves.title: Tension-type headache: paracetamol and ibuprofen beat placebo modestly for acute attacks (NNT 22 and 14 for pain-free at 2 hours); tricyclics prevent about 5 headaches a month; acupuncture beats usual care clearly but sham only slightly
shelves.question: For my tension-type headaches, what actually works — a painkiller for an attack, a daily preventive such as amitriptyline, or acupuncture?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: SPLIT — acute and preventive treatment are different questions with different answers, and this shelf keeps them apart (migraine trials are a different question again and are not carded here). Acute: two Cochrane reviews find modest, real benefits over placebo for a single attack of frequent episodic tension-type headache — paracetamol 1000 mg made 24 of 100 people pain-free at 2 hours versus 19 of 100 on placebo (Stephens 2016, PMID: 27306653; 23 studies, 8,079 participants; NNT 22), and ibuprofen 400 mg made 23 of 100 versus 16 of 100 (Derry 2015, PMID: 26230487; 12 studies, 3,094 participants; NNT 14); neither drug separated from placebo at 1 hour, and adverse events matched placebo for both. Prevention: tricyclic antidepressants reduced headache frequency by a weighted mean of 4.8 headaches a month versus placebo (from roughly 21 to roughly 16 a month) across 22 RCTs, 8 of them placebo-controlled, and beat SSRIs, while tetracyclics did not beat placebo (Jackson 2017; DOI 10.1007/s11606-017-4121-z; PMID not captured this session). Acupuncture roughly doubled-to-tripled the ≥50%-responder rate versus routine care (48% vs 19%, RR 2.5) but exceeded sham acupuncture only slightly (51% vs 43%, RR 1.3) across 12 trials and 2,349 participants (Linde 2016, PMID: 27092807) — the signature of a mostly contextual effect. PROPOSED SPLIT: small genuine drug benefits for attacks; a moderate preventive benefit for tricyclics; acupuncture's advantage over sham is small.

cards.headline: Stephens 2016 (Cochrane, paracetamol): pain-free at 2 hours in 24 of 100 on paracetamol 1000 mg versus 19 of 100 on placebo — NNT 22
cards.summary: Stephens 2016 (Cochrane, paracetamol): pain-free at 2 hours in 24 of 100 on paracetamol 1000 mg versus 19 of 100 on placebo — NNT 22
cards.people: 23 studies, 8,079 participants with frequent episodic tension-type headache, comparing paracetamol (acetaminophen) with placebo or other treatments for a single headache attack.
cards.result: For paracetamol 1000 mg versus placebo, 24 of 100 people were pain-free at 2 hours versus 19 of 100 on placebo (high-quality evidence; 8 studies, 5,890 participants; number needed to treat 22, 95% CI 15 to 40). For the softer outcome of pain-free or mild pain at 2 hours, the figures were 59 versus 49 per 100 (NNT 10, 95% CI 7.9 to 14). There was no difference between paracetamol and placebo at 1 hour. Fewer people on paracetamol needed rescue medication (NNT to prevent one rescue use 7.8). Adverse events were no more common than with placebo (relative risk 1.1, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.3). Paracetamol 500–650 mg was not shown superior to placebo, on limited data.
cards.watchOut: The benefit is real but small in absolute terms — five extra people pain-free at 2 hours per 100 treated — and it belongs to the 1000 mg dose in frequent episodic tension-type headache. It should not be read across to chronic daily headache, where regular analgesic use itself becomes part of the problem; medication-overuse headache is a different question.

cards.headline: Derry 2015 (Cochrane, ibuprofen): pain-free at 2 hours in 23 of 100 on ibuprofen 400 mg versus 16 of 100 on placebo — NNT 14
cards.summary: Derry 2015 (Cochrane, ibuprofen): pain-free at 2 hours in 23 of 100 on ibuprofen 400 mg versus 16 of 100 on placebo — NNT 14
cards.people: 12 studies, 3,094 participants with frequent episodic tension-type headache, comparing ibuprofen with placebo or active comparators for a single headache attack.
cards.result: For ibuprofen 400 mg versus placebo, 23 of 100 people were pain-free at 2 hours versus 16 of 100 on placebo (4 studies, moderate-quality evidence; NNT 14, 95% CI 8.4 to 47); there was no difference at 1 hour. A global evaluation of 'very good' or 'excellent' gave an NNT of 5.9 (95% CI 4.2 to 9.5). Adverse events occurred in about 4 of 100 people, the same as with placebo (relative risk 1.1, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.7).
cards.watchOut: Moderate-quality evidence with a wide NNT interval (8.4 to 47) — the true advantage may be smaller than the point estimate. This shelf cannot rank ibuprofen against paracetamol: the two Cochrane reviews share placebo, not each other, as the comparator, and indirect NNT comparisons across reviews are unreliable.

cards.headline: Jackson 2017 (tricyclic meta-analysis): about 4.8 fewer headaches a month on a tricyclic versus placebo — from roughly 21 to roughly 16 a month
cards.summary: Jackson 2017 (tricyclic meta-analysis): about 4.8 fewer headaches a month on a tricyclic versus placebo — from roughly 21 to roughly 16 a month
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs (Jackson 2017)
cards.people: 22 randomised controlled trials of tricyclic or tetracyclic antidepressants for the prevention of frequent episodic or chronic tension-type headache in adults; 8 trials included a placebo comparison and 19 compared at least two active treatments.
cards.result: High-quality evidence showed tricyclics were superior to placebo in reducing headache frequency (weighted mean difference −4.8 headaches/month, 95% CI −6.63 to −2.95; the review's capsule summary expresses this as a fall from about 21 to about 16 headaches a month) and reduced analgesic consumption (WMD −21.0 doses/month, 95% CI −38.2 to −3.8). Tricyclics were more effective than SSRIs and superior to buspirone. Tetracyclics were no better than placebo for chronic tension-type headache.
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials are mostly old, small and short, and this record quantifies benefit, not tolerability — the tricyclics' side-effect burden (dry mouth, sedation, weight gain) is the usual reason patients stop them. The −4.8/month is a mean across largely chronic tension-type headache populations starting near 21 headaches a month; someone with 6 headaches a month should not expect the same absolute gain.
cards.source: Jackson JL, Mancuso JM, Nickoloff S, Bernstein R, Kay C. cards.headline: Linde 2016 (Cochrane, acupuncture): half of patients halved their headache frequency versus 19% with routine care — but 51% versus 43% against sham
cards.summary: Linde 2016 (Cochrane, acupuncture): half of patients halved their headache frequency versus 19% with routine care — but 51% versus 43% against sham
cards.people: 12 trials, 2,349 participants with episodic or chronic tension-type headache, comparing a course of acupuncture with routine care alone, sham acupuncture, or other interventions, for prevention.
cards.result: Versus routine care alone (2 large trials), at least a 50% reduction in headache frequency was achieved by 48% (302/629) with acupuncture versus 19% (121/636) with routine care (relative risk 2.5, 95% CI 2.1 to 3.0), and in the second comparison 45% (60/132) versus 4% (3/75) (RR 11, 95% CI 3.7 to 35). Versus sham acupuncture (4 trials, moderate-quality evidence), 51% (205/391) versus 43% (133/312) achieved a ≥50% reduction (RR 1.3, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.5), with a similar small advantage at 6 months. Adverse effects were reported by 17% (29/174) with acupuncture versus 12% (12/103) with sham (odds ratio 1.3, 95% CI 0.60 to 2.7); 1 of 420 acupuncture patients dropped out because of adverse effects versus 0 of 343 on sham.
cards.watchOut: The pattern — a large effect against routine care and a small effect against sham needling — is the classic signature of a treatment whose benefit is mostly contextual (attention, ritual, expectation). That does not make the relief unreal for the patient, but it does mean the specific needling points and technique are not what the evidence supports paying a premium for.
cards.source: Linde et al. Acupuncture for the prevention of tension-type headache. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2016. PMID: 27092807. Registry ID: none in the record (systematic review). MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.summary: Synthesis: small real drug effects for attacks, a moderate preventive effect for tricyclics, and an acupuncture effect that mostly survives only against no treatment

shelves.title: Hoarding disorder: CBT beats waitlist and self-help books in small trials (about a quarter to a third off symptom scores); no drug has ever passed a placebo-controlled test — venlafaxine's 32–36% improvements are open-label only
shelves.question: For hoarding disorder, does cognitive behavioural therapy work — and is there any medication with real evidence behind it?
shelves.mesh: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy/methods · Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder/diagnosis · Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder/psychology · Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder/therapy · Severity of Illness Index · Surveys and Questionnaires · Waiting Lists
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) for CBT; pharmacotherapy unproven. The CBT record is three small controlled trials pointing the same way. Steketee 2010 (PMID: 20336804) randomised 46 patients to manualised multicomponent CBT or waitlist: CBT was superior at 12 weeks on hoarding severity and mood, and by session 26, 71% were rated improved by therapists, 81% rated themselves improved, and 41% of completers were clinically significantly improved. Tolin 2019 (PMID: 31008633; NCT01956344) randomised 87 adults to 16-session group CBT or waitlist and found CBT efficacious, with 83% of CBT patients classified as responders. Muroff 2012 (DOI 10.1002/da.21923; PMID not captured this session) randomised 38 patients and found group CBT cut Saving Inventory–Revised scores by 23.3–29.9% while bibliotherapy alone managed 9% and did not significantly improve — the shelf's most practically useful negative, since unguided self-help is what most people with hoarding actually get. Against this, every control is a waitlist or a book: no trial compares CBT with an active psychological placebo, so expectancy effects are unmeasured and the stamp stays at POSSIBLE. For drugs there is nothing controlled at all: venlafaxine extended-release improved scores by 32–36% over 12 weeks in an open-label study of 24 patients (Saxena & Sumner 2014, PMID: 24722633), and the only other drug data (open-label paroxetine, mean decrease 31%, Saxena 2007, PMID: 16790250) are of the same uncontrolled kind; a 2019 review confirms no placebo-controlled drug trial for hoarding disorder exists. PROPOSED: POSSIBLE (benefit) for CBT; no stamp available for any medication.

cards.headline: Steketee 2010: manualised CBT beat waitlist at 12 weeks; by session 26, 71% were rated improved by therapists and 41% of completers were clinically significantly improved
cards.summary: Steketee 2010: manualised CBT beat waitlist at 12 weeks; by session 26, 71% were rated improved by therapists and 41% of completers were clinically significantly improved
cards.type: Waitlist-controlled randomised trial of individual multicomponent CBT (Steketee 2010)
cards.people: 46 patients with hoarding randomised to multicomponent CBT (manualised in Steketee & Frost 2007) or waitlist control; 40 completed the 12-week assessment and 36 completed 26 sessions.
cards.result: At 12 weeks, CBT was superior to waitlist on hoarding severity and on mood, with moderate effect sizes. At session 26, 71% of patients were rated improved on therapist Clinical Global Impression, 81% rated themselves improved, and 41% of completers were clinically significantly improved.
cards.watchOut: Waitlist is the weakest control in psychotherapy research — patients know they are untreated, so expectancy and disappointment inflate the contrast. The 41% clinically-significant-improvement figure is among completers of a 26-session treatment, not among all who started, and 'improved' is not 'recovered': most treated patients still have clinically significant clutter.

cards.headline: Tolin 2019: 16-session group CBT beat waitlist, with 83% of CBT patients classified as responders
cards.summary: Tolin 2019: 16-session group CBT beat waitlist, with 83% of CBT patients classified as responders
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial of group CBT versus waitlist (Tolin 2019)
cards.people: 87 adults with a primary diagnosis of hoarding disorder, randomised to immediate group CBT (16 weekly 90-minute sessions) or waitlist control (NCT01956344).
cards.result: Group CBT was efficacious for hoarding symptoms compared with waitlist; 83% of CBT patients were classified as improved/responders. Reductions in maladaptive saving cognitions partially mediated the treatment outcome. (The abstract reports no group mean Saving Inventory–Revised point values, so none are claimed here.)
cards.watchOut: Again a waitlist control, and responder classifications in CBT trials are generous — response is not remission. The practical point of this trial is delivery: 16 group sessions are far cheaper than 26 individual ones, with the same direction of effect, which is what makes CBT for hoarding deliverable at scale at all.

cards.headline: Muroff 2012 (pilot RCT): group CBT cut SI-R scores by 23–30%; the self-help book alone managed 9% and did not significantly improve
cards.summary: Muroff 2012 (pilot RCT): group CBT cut SI-R scores by 23–30%; the self-help book alone managed 9% and did not significantly improve
cards.type: Pilot randomised trial, group CBT versus bibliotherapy (Muroff 2012)
cards.people: 38 patients with hoarding randomised to group CBT with nonclinician home assistants (n=11), group CBT without home assistants (n=14), or bibliotherapy (n=13) — the 'Buried in Treasures' self-help programme worked through over 20 weeks; the group CBT arms ran 20 weekly sessions with therapist home visits.
cards.result: Saving Inventory–Revised reductions were 29.9% for group CBT with home assistants and 23.3% for group CBT alone (26.5% and 25.4% respectively on the second reported measure), versus 9% for bibliotherapy. The group CBT arms improved significantly on hoarding and depression symptoms, whereas bibliotherapy did not. Adding nonclinician home assistants made no significant difference in this small sample.
cards.watchOut: Arms of 11–14 patients make this a pilot, and its percentages swing widely with a few patients either way. Its durable contribution is the negative one: unguided self-help — the intervention most people with hoarding actually receive — did not significantly move symptoms, so 'give them the book' is not a treatment plan.
cards.source: Muroff J, Steketee G, Bratiotis C, Ross A. Group Cognitive and Behavioral Therapy and Bibliotherapy for Hoarding: A Pilot Trial. Depression and Anxiety. 2012. PMID: not captured from the record this session (DOI 10.1002/da.21923). Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Saxena 2014: venlafaxine improved hoarding scores by 32–36% over 12 weeks — in an open-label study with no control group
cards.summary: Saxena 2014: venlafaxine improved hoarding scores by 32–36% over 12 weeks — in an open-label study with no control group
cards.people: 24 patients meeting DSM-5 criteria for hoarding disorder, treated with venlafaxine extended-release for 12 weeks; 23 completed.
cards.result: Mean symptom scores fell by 36% on the UCLA Hoarding Severity Scale and by 32% on the Saving Inventory–Revised; 16 of 23 completers (70%) were classified as responders. There was no placebo group and no comparison treatment.
cards.watchOut: Open-label improvements of 30% or more are what expectancy, regression to the mean and clinician enthusiasm routinely produce in this field — compare the waitlist and bibliotherapy arms elsewhere on this shelf. The only other drug data are of the same kind (paroxetine, open-label, mean symptom decrease 31%, Saxena 2007, PMID: 16790250, and poorly tolerated), and a 2019 review confirms that no placebo-controlled drug trial for hoarding disorder exists. Medication for hoarding itself is unproven; medication for comorbid depression or OCD is a different question with its own evidence.
cards.source: Saxena S, Sumner J. [Venlafaxine extended-release treatment of hoarding disorder — article title not captured verbatim this session]. International Clinical Psychopharmacology. 2014. cards.headline: Synthesis: CBT helps a meaningful minority-to-majority of patients by trial measures, self-help alone does not, and no drug has ever faced a placebo
cards.summary: Synthesis: CBT helps a meaningful minority-to-majority of patients by trial measures, self-help alone does not, and no drug has ever faced a placebo
cards.people: Four sources: two waitlist-controlled CBT trials (Steketee 2010, n=46; Tolin 2019, n=87, NCT01956344), one pilot RCT against bibliotherapy (Muroff 2012, n=38), and one open-label drug study (Saxena & Sumner 2014, n=24).
cards.result: CBT versus waitlist: superior on hoarding severity and mood at 12 weeks with moderate effect sizes (Steketee 2010); 83% classified responders after 16 group sessions (Tolin 2019); 41% of completers clinically significantly improved after 26 individual sessions (Steketee 2010). CBT versus self-help: SI-R reductions of 23.3–29.9% versus 9%, with bibliotherapy not significantly improving (Muroff 2012). Drugs: venlafaxine −36% (UHSS) and −32% (SI-R) open-label; no placebo-controlled drug trial exists. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for CBT — consistent direction across three small trials, capped by waitlist/bibliotherapy controls and the absence of any active-comparison trial; pharmacotherapy carries no stamp.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. A large PCORI-funded trial (323 adults) reported peer-led workbook groups noninferior to therapist-led group CBT (mean difference 1.82 SI-R points; overall SI-R 65.6 → 46.8, a 26.7% reduction, with 66% responders) — a potentially important delivery finding, but its record was captured from a Bookshelf report (NBK595719), not from PubMed this session, so it is flagged here rather than carded. Hoarding with imminent safety hazards (fire, sanitation, eviction) needs case management alongside any therapy; no card here measures those outcomes.
cards.source: Synthesis of Steketee et al. Depression and Anxiety. 2010 (PMID: 20336804); Tolin et al. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology. 2019 (PMID: 31008633); Muroff J et al. Depression and Anxiety. 2012 (PMID not captured this session; DOI 10.1002/da.21923); Saxena S, Sumner J. International Clinical Psychopharmacology. 2014 (PMID: 24722633).

shelves.title: Personality disorders beyond borderline: outpatient therapy beat usual care or waitlist across 54 trials (g = 0.78), Cluster A trials total only 468 people (g 0.60–0.91, exploratory), and for antisocial personality disorder no treatment has compelling evidence
shelves.question: For personality disorders other than borderline personality disorder (which has its own shelf), what does treatment — psychotherapy or medication — achieve: for personality disorder in general, for Cluster A disorders, and for antisocial personality disorder?
shelves.mesh: Anxiety / therapy · Humans · Outpatients* · Personality · Personality Disorders · Psychotherapy*
shelves.balance: SPLIT. Borderline personality disorder has its own shelf (#708) and is not re-carded here; this shelf covers the generic and other-disorder question, where the evidence splits sharply by diagnosis. Katakis 2023 (PMID: 36681805) pooled 54 outpatient RCTs (n=3,716) in personality disorder/complex emotional needs: psychosocial treatment beat usual care or waitlist with g = 0.78 for personality-disorder symptoms — but that outcome is borderline-weighted. For Cluster A disorders, Cheli 2025 (PMID: 40111791) found only 468 participants in 19 studies, with exploratory pooled effects of g 0.60 to 0.91 and large heterogeneity. For antisocial personality disorder, Gibbon 2020 (PMID: 32880104) found 19 trials and no intervention with compelling evidence of changing antisocial behaviour. Proposed stamp: SPLIT (general outpatient therapy: benefit shown on a borderline-weighted base · Cluster A: POSSIBLE on tiny samples · antisocial: no proven treatment).

cards.headline: Katakis 2023: outpatient psychosocial treatment beat usual care or waitlist across 54 trials (n=3,716) — but the symptom outcome is borderline-weighted
cards.summary: Katakis 2023: outpatient psychosocial treatment beat usual care or waitlist across 54 trials (n=3,716) — but the symptom outcome is borderline-weighted
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs (Katakis 2023)
cards.people: 3,716 participants in 54 randomised trials of psychological and psychosocial interventions delivered in community or outpatient settings for 'personality disorder' / complex emotional needs.
cards.result: Effect on 'borderline personality disorder' symptoms versus treatment as usual or waitlist: g = 0.78 (95% CI 0.56 to 1.01; p < 0.0001), maintained at follow-up (g = 1.01, 95% CI 0.37 to 1.65; p = 0.002). Anxiety symptoms g = 0.58 (95% CI 0.21 to 0.95), depressive symptoms g = 0.57 (95% CI 0.32 to 0.83) and global psychiatric symptoms g = 0.50 (95% CI 0.35 to 0.66). Intervention types were equally effective; treatment duration and intensity did not moderate effects. These are standardised effect sizes; absolute response rates are not printed in the record.
cards.watchOut: The primary symptom outcome is explicitly BPD symptoms and the trial base is dominated by borderline samples — this card supports 'structured outpatient therapy helps personality-disorder patients' in general, but it is not clean evidence for the non-borderline disorders this shelf is about; borderline personality disorder itself is homed on Shelf #708.
cards.source: Katakis P, Schlief M, Barnett P, Sheridan Rains L, Rowe S, Pilling S, Johnson S. Effectiveness of outpatient and community treatments for people with a diagnosis of 'personality disorder': systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Psychiatry. 2023. PMID: 36681805. cards.headline: Cheli 2025: Cluster A disorders (paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal) — 19 studies, only 468 participants; pooled effects g 0.60 to 0.91 with large heterogeneity
cards.summary: Cheli 2025: Cluster A disorders (paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal) — 19 studies, only 468 participants; pooled effects g 0.60 to 0.91 with large heterogeneity
cards.people: 468 participants with paranoid, schizoid or schizotypal personality disorder in 19 studies; the two meta-analyses pooled 291 participants (5 studies, distinctive clinical features) and 213 participants (5 studies, general functioning).
cards.result: Both meta-analyses showed medium-to-large effect sizes (g = 0.60 to 0.91) for psychosocial and pharmacological treatments, with a low overall attrition rate (0.23) in the pooled studies — but the authors state the analyses were limited by small sample sizes and large heterogeneity. Their conclusion: treatments for Cluster A disorders may be feasible and effective.
cards.watchOut: The authors themselves label the meta-analyses exploratory: five small studies per pool, mixed drug and psychosocial treatments combined, and large heterogeneity — the effect sizes are a reason to offer and study treatment, not a reliable estimate of how much it helps.
cards.source: Cheli S, Wisepape CN, Witten CDY, Floridi M, Cavalletti V, Hasson-Ohayon I, Brüne M, Ottaviani C. Psychosocial and pharmacological interventions for cluster a personality disorders: A systematic review and two exploratory meta-analyses. Personal Disord. 2025. PMID: 40111791. cards.headline: Gibbon 2020: antisocial personality disorder — 19 trials, and no intervention showed compelling evidence of changing antisocial behaviour
cards.summary: Gibbon 2020: antisocial personality disorder — 19 trials, and no intervention showed compelling evidence of changing antisocial behaviour
cards.people: Adults with antisocial personality disorder in 19 randomised trials; data were available from only 10 studies involving 605 participants; most participants (75%) were male, mean age 35.5 years.
cards.result: Cognitive behaviour therapy plus treatment as usual versus usual care: no evidence of a difference in physical aggression (odds ratio 0.92, 95% CI 0.28 to 3.07; 52 participants; low-certainty). Impulsive lifestyle counselling: no difference in trait aggression (mean difference 0.07, 95% CI -0.35 to 0.49; 118 participants; very low-certainty). Only three of the eight interventions reporting primary outcomes (contingency management plus standard maintenance, schema therapy, dialectical behaviour therapy) showed any evidence of being more effective than control, and no intervention reported compelling evidence of change in antisocial behaviour. Overall certainty: low or very low.
cards.watchOut: Most trials recruited antisocial subgroups inside substance-misuse or offender programmes rather than pure antisocial personality disorder samples, and few measured aggression or reconviction at all — absence of evidence here is partly absence of proper trials.
cards.source: Gibbon S, Khalifa NR, Cheung NH-Y, Völlm BA, McCarthy L. Psychological interventions for antisocial personality disorder. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2020. PMID: 32880104. cards.headline: Synthesis: 'personality disorder' is not one evidence base — therapy helps in the (borderline-weighted) outpatient pool, Cluster A evidence is embryonic, antisocial evidence is negative-to-absent
cards.summary: Synthesis: 'personality disorder' is not one evidence base — therapy helps in the (borderline-weighted) outpatient pool, Cluster A evidence is embryonic, antisocial evidence is negative-to-absent
cards.people: Three reviews: Katakis 2023 (54 RCTs, n=3,716, general personality disorder/complex emotional needs), Cheli 2025 (19 studies, n=468, Cluster A), Gibbon 2020 (19 RCTs, antisocial personality disorder). Borderline personality disorder treatment itself is homed on Shelf #708 and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: Outpatient psychosocial interventions versus usual care/waitlist: g = 0.78 for personality-disorder symptoms (Katakis 2023). Cluster A: pooled g 0.60 to 0.91 from five-study meta-analyses the authors call exploratory (Cheli 2025). Antisocial: no intervention with compelling evidence; CBT plus usual care odds ratio 0.92 for physical aggression (Gibbon 2020). Proposed stamp: SPLIT.
cards.watchOut: No carded review isolates narcissistic, avoidant, obsessive-compulsive or other specific non-borderline, non-Cluster-A, non-antisocial disorders — for those, the honest position is extrapolation from the general pool, not direct evidence.

shelves.title: Poor social engagement tracks with dementia: a poor social network carried a relative risk of 1.59 and poor support 1.28 across 2,370,452 participants, and loneliness carried a relative risk of 1.23 for dementia and 1.72 for Alzheimer's disease in a second meta-analysis — observational evidence only
shelves.question: In older adults, are low social engagement and loneliness associated with incident dementia?
shelves.mesh: Alzheimer Disease/*psychology; Dementia/*psychology; Humans; Loneliness/*psychology; Risk Assessment; Social Isolation/*psychology; Social Support
shelves.balance: Observational evidence only, so this shelf caps at POSSIBLE. Penninkilampi 2018 (33 studies, 2,370,452 participants) found poor social network relative risk 1.59 (95% CI 1.31 to 1.96) and poor social support 1.28 (95% CI 1.01 to 1.62) for dementia, while its loneliness estimate was non-significant (RR 1.38, 95% CI 0.98 to 1.94) (PMID: 30452410). A 2022 loneliness-specific meta-analysis (16 cohorts, 62,345 people, 4,625 dementia cases) did find loneliness associated with dementia (RR 1.23, 95% CI 1.16 to 1.31) and Alzheimer's disease (RR 1.72, 95% CI 1.32 to 2.23), but not mild cognitive impairment or vascular dementia (PMID: 36530204). A third synthesis put prolonged loneliness/isolation at HR 1.49 (95% CI 1.37 to 1.61) (PMID: 34369248). The structural question (which relationship features predict onset) is homed separately on #5477. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only.

cards.headline: Penninkilampi 2018: across 33 studies and 2,370,452 participants, a poor social network carried a relative risk of 1.59 (95% CI 1.31–1.96) for dementia and poor social support 1.28 (95% CI 1.01–1.62), while loneliness alone was non-significant (RR 1.38, 95% CI 0.98–1.94)
cards.summary: Penninkilampi 2018: across 33 studies and 2,370,452 participants, a poor social network carried a relative risk of 1.59 (95% CI 1.31–1.96) for dementia and poor social support 1.28 (95% CI 1.01–1.62), while loneliness alone was non-significant (RR 1.38, 95% CI 0.98–1.94)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (Penninkilampi 2018)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 31 cohort and 2 case-control studies (search January 2012 to May 2017, plus extraction from previous reviews) comprising 2,370,452 participants, examining social engagement or loneliness and dementia risk (PROSPERO CRD42017067074).
cards.result: Poor social engagement indices were associated with increased dementia risk: poor social network RR 1.59 (95% CI 1.31 to 1.96; I² = 0.00%) and poor social support RR 1.28 (95% CI 1.01 to 1.62; I² = 55.51%) — both relative measures. In long-term studies (≥10 years) good social engagement was modestly protective (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.80 to 0.96). Loneliness was non-significantly associated with increased risk (RR 1.38, 95% CI 0.98 to 1.94; I² = 45.32).
cards.watchOut: Observational only, and the loneliness estimate in this synthesis did not reach significance — the shelf's loneliness claim rests on the companion meta-analyses below. Preclinical dementia itself reduces social engagement, so reverse causation is a standing alternative explanation.
cards.source: Penninkilampi R, Casey AN, Singh MF, Brodaty H. Journal of Alzheimer's Disease. 2018. PMID: 30452410. Registry ID: CRD42017067074 (PROSPERO registration printed in the record). cards.headline: Loneliness-and-dementia meta-analysis 2022: across 16 cohort studies (62,345 people, 4,625 dementia cases) loneliness carried a relative risk of 1.23 (95% CI 1.16–1.31) for dementia and 1.72 (95% CI 1.32–2.23) for Alzheimer's disease, with no significant association for mild cognitive impairment or vascular dementia
cards.summary: Loneliness-and-dementia meta-analysis 2022: across 16 cohort studies (62,345 people, 4,625 dementia cases) loneliness carried a relative risk of 1.23 (95% CI 1.16–1.31) for dementia and 1.72 (95% CI 1.32–2.23) for Alzheimer's disease, with no significant association for mild cognitive impairment or vascular dementia
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 16 cohort studies (15 articles) with 62,345 individuals and 4,625 dementia cases, searched to 17 February 2022.
cards.result: Loneliness was associated with an increased risk of Alzheimer's disease (RR 1.72, 95% CI 1.32 to 2.23; P < 0.001) and of dementia overall (RR 1.23, 95% CI 1.16 to 1.31; P < 0.00001) — relative measures. No significant association was found for mild cognitive impairment (RR 1.34, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.87; P = 0.080) or vascular dementia (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.51 to 1.99; P = 0.973).
cards.watchOut: Observational cohorts with varying loneliness measures; the null findings for mild cognitive impairment and vascular dementia argue against a uniform effect across cognitive outcomes.

cards.headline: Lazzari & Rabottini 2022: across 10 studies (average 8,239 people each, mean follow-up 6.41 years) prolonged loneliness and social isolation in older people carried a hazard ratio of 1.49 (95% CI 1.37–1.61) for developing dementia
cards.summary: Lazzari & Rabottini 2022: across 10 studies (average 8,239 people each, mean follow-up 6.41 years) prolonged loneliness and social isolation in older people carried a hazard ratio of 1.49 (95% CI 1.37–1.61) for developing dementia
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (Lazzari & Rabottini 2022)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 10 studies of community-dwelling older people aged 50 and over without dementia at enrolment, with cohorts averaging 8,239 people followed for a mean of 6.41 years; framed around social isolation and loneliness including the COVID-19 lockdown period.
cards.result: The pooled risk of developing dementia with prolonged loneliness and social isolation was about 49–60% relatively higher than in people who were not lonely or socially isolated (HR 1.49, 95% CI 1.37 to 1.61). The authors argued for integrated social programmes to reduce risk in older people.
cards.watchOut: Only 10 studies, an opportunistic community sample, and a COVID-era framing; the pooled hazard ratio mixes loneliness and isolation exposures rather than isolating either one.

cards.headline: Synthesis: three observational meta-analyses converge on a 20–60% relative higher dementia risk with poor engagement, poor networks or loneliness — with one non-significant loneliness estimate and reverse causation unresolved
cards.summary: Synthesis: three observational meta-analyses converge on a 20–60% relative higher dementia risk with poor engagement, poor networks or loneliness — with one non-significant loneliness estimate and reverse causation unresolved

cards.result: Poor social network RR 1.59 and poor support RR 1.28 (PMID: 30452410); loneliness RR 1.23 for dementia and 1.72 for Alzheimer's disease (PMID: 36530204); prolonged loneliness/isolation HR 1.49 (PMID: 34369248). The one discordant note is internal: loneliness was non-significant (RR 1.38, CI crossing 1) in the largest synthesis. Which specific relationship features predict onset is homed on #5477, and the loneliness-versus-isolation contrast on #5478 — not re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational evidence only.
cards.watchOut: All relative measures from observational data; none of these syntheses can separate loneliness causing dementia from early dementia causing withdrawal.

shelves.title: The relationship features that predict dementia are participation, contact and loneliness — low participation relative risk 1.41, infrequent contact 1.57, loneliness 1.58 across 19 cohorts — while network size was inconsistent and network satisfaction showed no significant association (RR 1.25, CI crossing 1)
shelves.question: Across longitudinal cohorts, which aspects of social relationships (network size, contact, support) predict dementia onset?
shelves.mesh: Aging/*psychology; Dementia/epidemiology/psychology; Humans; Interpersonal Relations; Longitudinal Studies; Risk Assessment; Risk Factors; Social Environment; Social Participation/*psychology; Social Support
shelves.balance: Observational evidence only, so this shelf caps at POSSIBLE. Kuiper 2015 pooled 19 longitudinal cohorts and separated the relationship features: low social participation RR 1.41 (95% CI 1.13 to 1.75), less frequent social contact RR 1.57 (95% CI 1.32 to 1.85) and more loneliness RR 1.58 (95% CI 1.19 to 2.09) predicted incident dementia, while network-size results were inconsistent and low network satisfaction was not significant (RR 1.25, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.62) (PMID: 25956016). Marital status — the crudest structural measure — shows the same pattern in 15 studies (812,047 participants): widowed RR 1.20 and lifelong single RR 1.42 versus married, divorced not significant (PMID: 29183957). The 20-year Paquid cohort (2,854 people) found engagement in social, physical or intellectual pursuits related to lower dementia risk at population level, though social measures did not explain its cognitive-trajectory subgroups (PMID: 26499254). The engagement/loneliness pooling is homed on #5476. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only.

cards.headline: Kuiper 2015: across 19 longitudinal cohorts, low social participation (RR 1.41, 95% CI 1.13–1.75), less frequent social contact (RR 1.57, 95% CI 1.32–1.85) and more loneliness (RR 1.58, 95% CI 1.19–2.09) each predicted incident dementia — network satisfaction did not (RR 1.25, 95% CI 0.96–1.62)
cards.summary: Kuiper 2015: across 19 longitudinal cohorts, low social participation (RR 1.41, 95% CI 1.13–1.75), less frequent social contact (RR 1.57, 95% CI 1.32–1.85) and more loneliness (RR 1.58, 95% CI 1.19–2.09) each predicted incident dementia — network satisfaction did not (RR 1.25, 95% CI 0.96–1.62)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of longitudinal cohort studies (Kuiper 2015)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 19 longitudinal cohort studies in the general population examining social relationship factors and incident dementia, pooled with random-effects models.
cards.result: Low social participation (RR 1.41, 95% CI 1.13 to 1.75), less frequent social contact (RR 1.57, 95% CI 1.32 to 1.85) and more loneliness (RR 1.58, 95% CI 1.19 to 2.09) were significantly associated with incident dementia — all relative measures. Results for social network size were inconsistent, and no significant association was found for low satisfaction with the social network (RR 1.25, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.62). The authors judged the significant associations comparable in strength to low education, physical inactivity and late-life depression.
cards.watchOut: Observational only: the feature-by-feature contrast is the value of this card — quantity of contact and participation predict onset, while how satisfied people feel with their network does not, and network size alone is unreliable.

cards.headline: Sommerlad 2018: across 15 studies and 812,047 participants, lifelong single people (RR 1.42, 95% CI 1.07–1.90) and widowed people (RR 1.20, 95% CI 1.02–1.41) had higher dementia risk than married people; divorced people did not
cards.summary: Sommerlad 2018: across 15 studies and 812,047 participants, lifelong single people (RR 1.42, 95% CI 1.07–1.90) and widowed people (RR 1.20, 95% CI 1.02–1.41) had higher dementia risk than married people; divorced people did not
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (Sommerlad 2018)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 15 observational studies with 812,047 participants, reporting age- and sex-adjusted associations between marital status and dementia.
cards.result: Compared with married people, lifelong single people had a relative risk of 1.42 (95% CI 1.07 to 1.90) and widowed people 1.20 (95% CI 1.02 to 1.41) for dementia; no association was found for divorced people. Less education partly confounded the widowhood risk and worse physical health the lifelong-single risk, and studies that clinically examined all participants found higher risks for the unmarried than register-based studies.
cards.watchOut: Marital status is a proxy, not a mechanism: it bundles contact, support, income, education and health selection into marriage itself. The widowed estimate (1.20) is modest and partly confounded by education.

cards.headline: Paquid cohort (Marioni 2015): in 2,854 people (mean age 77) followed 20 years, greater engagement in social, physical or intellectual pursuits was associated with higher cognitive ability and lower incident dementia risk — but social measures did not explain the cohort's fast/medium/no-decline trajectory subgroups
cards.summary: Paquid cohort (Marioni 2015): in 2,854 people (mean age 77) followed 20 years, greater engagement in social, physical or intellectual pursuits was associated with higher cognitive ability and lower incident dementia risk — but social measures did not explain the cohort's fast/medium/no-decline trajectory subgroups
cards.people: 2,854 participants in the French Paquid cohort (mean baseline age 77 years) with social, physical and intellectual engagement, social network size, feeling understood and relationship satisfaction assessed at baseline and related to incident dementia and cognitive change over 20 years.
cards.result: In the whole population, increased engagement in social, physical or intellectual pursuits was associated with increased cognitive ability (but not with rate of decline) and decreased risk of incident dementia, and feeling understood was associated with slower cognitive decline. Three trajectory sub-populations (fast, medium and no cognitive decline) were identified, but baseline social-environment measures did not explain the heterogeneity of decline or dementia risk between them. No single pooled effect size is printed in the record.
cards.watchOut: Social, physical and intellectual engagement are bundled in the headline association, so the social share cannot be separated; the subgroup null is a genuine caution against over-reading the population-level association.

cards.headline: Synthesis: participation, contact frequency and loneliness predict dementia onset (RR 1.41–1.58); marital-structure proxies agree (widowed 1.20, lifelong single 1.42); network size and satisfaction do not reliably predict — observational throughout
cards.summary: Synthesis: participation, contact frequency and loneliness predict dementia onset (RR 1.41–1.58); marital-structure proxies agree (widowed 1.20, lifelong single 1.42); network size and satisfaction do not reliably predict — observational throughout
cards.people: The carded evidence: one 19-cohort feature-by-feature meta-analysis, one 15-study marital-status meta-analysis (812,047 participants), and one 20-year cohort of 2,854 people.
cards.result: Feature contrast (PMID: 25956016): participation RR 1.41, contact RR 1.57, loneliness RR 1.58 — significant; satisfaction RR 1.25 — not significant; network size — inconsistent. Marital status (PMID: 29183957): widowed RR 1.20, lifelong single RR 1.42, divorced no association. shelves.title: Loneliness and isolation are not interchangeable: in Amsterdam, feelings of loneliness predicted dementia (OR 1.64, 95% CI 1.05–2.56) while objective isolation did not; in Chicago both predicted decline and Alzheimer's, and isolated-but-not-lonely elders declined fastest
shelves.question: Do loneliness (subjective) and social isolation (objective) carry different risks for cognitive decline and Alzheimer's disease?
shelves.mesh: Humans; Female; Male; Aged; Chicago/epidemiology; Alzheimer Disease/epidemiology/psychology; Social Isolation/psychology; Cognitive Dysfunction/epidemiology/psychology; Prospective Studies; Loneliness/psychology
shelves.balance: Observational evidence only, so this shelf caps at POSSIBLE — and the honest answer to its question is 'partly different'. In the Amsterdam AMSTEL cohort (2,173 people, 3 years), feelings of loneliness predicted dementia onset (OR 1.64, 95% CI 1.05 to 2.56) while objective social isolation (living alone, unmarried, no support) did not survive adjustment (PMID: 23232034). In the Chicago CHAP cohort (7,760 people, mean follow-up 7.9 years) both predicted decline and Alzheimer's — isolation OR 1.183 per index point and loneliness OR 2.117 for incident Alzheimer's — and the isolated-but-not-lonely group showed accelerated decline without significantly raised Alzheimer's odds (PMID: 40015756). In the Rush cohort (823 people, up to 4 years) loneliness more than doubled Alzheimer's risk at the 90th versus 10th percentile, independent of isolation indicators, yet was unrelated to Alzheimer's pathology at autopsy in 90 brains (PMID: 17283291). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only.

cards.headline: Chicago CHAP cohort 2025 (Ng): in 7,760 older adults followed a mean of 7.9 years, each point of social isolation raised Alzheimer's odds (OR 1.183, 95% CI 1.016–1.379) and loneliness more than doubled them (OR 2.117, 95% CI 1.227–3.655); isolated-but-not-lonely elders showed accelerated cognitive decline without significantly raised Alzheimer's odds
cards.summary: Chicago CHAP cohort 2025 (Ng): in 7,760 older adults followed a mean of 7.9 years, each point of social isolation raised Alzheimer's odds (OR 1.183, 95% CI 1.016–1.379) and loneliness more than doubled them (OR 2.117, 95% CI 1.227–3.655); isolated-but-not-lonely elders showed accelerated cognitive decline without significantly raised Alzheimer's odds
cards.people: 7,760 biracial community-dwelling older adults in the Chicago Health and Aging Project (mean age 72.3 years; 64% Black, 63% women), mean follow-up 7.9 years; social isolation indexed 0–5 and loneliness scored 0–1, analysed with linear mixed and logistic regression models.
cards.result: Both isolation and loneliness were significantly associated with cognitive decline (per-point beta −0.002, SE 0.001, p = 0.022 for isolation; −0.012, SE 0.003, p < 0.001 for loneliness — similar effect sizes given the different scale ranges). For incident Alzheimer's disease: isolation OR 1.183 (95% CI 1.016 to 1.379, p = 0.029) and loneliness OR 2.117 (95% CI 1.227 to 3.655, p = 0.006). Stratified by loneliness, socially isolated but not lonely participants showed accelerated decline (−0.003, SE 0.001, p = 0.004 versus neither isolated nor lonely) with no significantly increased Alzheimer's odds.
cards.watchOut: A single cohort analysis: the loneliness odds ratio (2.117) is per full 0–1 scale, so it is not directly comparable with the per-point isolation odds ratio (1.183) — the authors themselves judged the decline effect sizes similar.
cards.source: Ng TKS, Beck T, Dennis KR, Desai P, Krueger K, Dhana K, Wilson RS, Evans DA, Rajan KB. Journal of Prevention of Alzheimer's Disease. 2025. PMID: 40015756. cards.headline: Wilson 2007 (Rush cohort): in 823 dementia-free older people followed up to 4 years, Alzheimer's risk was more than doubled in the loneliest (90th percentile) versus least lonely (10th percentile) — yet in 90 autopsied brains loneliness was unrelated to Alzheimer's pathology or cerebral infarction
cards.summary: Wilson 2007 (Rush cohort): in 823 dementia-free older people followed up to 4 years, Alzheimer's risk was more than doubled in the loneliest (90th percentile) versus least lonely (10th percentile) — yet in 90 autopsied brains loneliness was unrelated to Alzheimer's pathology or cerebral infarction
cards.people: 823 older persons free of dementia at enrolment, recruited from senior facilities in and around Chicago, with annual in-home follow-up for up to 4 years; loneliness measured on a 5-item scale (mean 2.3, SD 0.6); 76 developed clinical Alzheimer's disease; uniform postmortem brain examination in 90 decedents.
cards.result: Risk of Alzheimer's disease was more than doubled in lonely persons (score 3.2, 90th percentile) compared with persons who were not lonely (score 1.4, 10th percentile), and controlling for social-isolation indicators did not change the finding. Loneliness was associated with lower baseline cognition and more rapid decline. In the 90 autopsied participants, loneliness was unrelated to summary measures of Alzheimer's pathology or to cerebral infarction — loneliness predicted the clinical syndrome, not its leading pathological causes.
cards.watchOut: Only 76 incident cases and 90 autopsies; the pathology null may reflect power, but as printed it breaks any simple 'loneliness causes plaques' story — the association may run through resilience, mood or ascertainment rather than pathology.
cards.source: Wilson RS, Krueger KR, Arnold SE, Schneider JA, Kelly JF, Barnes LL, Tang Y, Bennett DA. Archives of General Psychiatry. 2007. PMID: 17283291. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Amsterdam AMSTEL cohort (Holwerda 2014): in 2,173 non-demented older people followed 3 years, feelings of loneliness predicted dementia onset (OR 1.64, 95% CI 1.05–2.56) while objective social isolation — living alone, unmarried, without social support — was not associated with higher dementia risk after adjustment
cards.summary: Amsterdam AMSTEL cohort (Holwerda 2014): in 2,173 non-demented older people followed 3 years, feelings of loneliness predicted dementia onset (OR 1.64, 95% CI 1.05–2.56) while objective social isolation — living alone, unmarried, without social support — was not associated with higher dementia risk after adjustment
cards.people: 2,173 non-demented community-living older persons in the Amsterdam Study of the Elderly, followed 3 years to a dementia diagnosis assessed with the Geriatric Mental State AGECAT; models controlled for sociodemographic factors, medical conditions, depression, cognitive functioning and functional status.
cards.result: After adjustment, older persons with feelings of loneliness were more likely to develop dementia (OR 1.64, 95% CI 1.05 to 2.56) than people without such feelings. Social isolation, defined objectively (living alone, unmarried, without social support), was not associated with a higher dementia risk in multivariate analysis. The authors concluded that feeling lonely rather than being alone is the risk state deserving clinical attention.
cards.watchOut: Three years is short follow-up for dementia, and the isolation null contradicts the Chicago cohort's isolation finding — the honest summary is that the two constructs overlap but do not behave identically across cohorts.
cards.source: Holwerda TJ, Deeg DJH, Beekman ATF, van Tilburg TG, Stek ML, Jonker C, Schoevers RA. Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery & Psychiatry. 2014. PMID: 23232034. cards.headline: Synthesis: loneliness predicts dementia/Alzheimer's in all three cohorts; objective isolation predicts it in Chicago but not Amsterdam; and loneliness tracks the clinical syndrome without tracking Alzheimer's pathology at autopsy
cards.summary: Synthesis: loneliness predicts dementia/Alzheimer's in all three cohorts; objective isolation predicts it in Chicago but not Amsterdam; and loneliness tracks the clinical syndrome without tracking Alzheimer's pathology at autopsy
cards.people: The carded evidence: three prospective cohorts — 7,760 (Chicago CHAP), 823 with 90 autopsies (Rush), and 2,173 (Amsterdam AMSTEL) older adults.
cards.result: Loneliness: Alzheimer's OR 2.117 in CHAP (PMID: 40015756), risk more than doubled at the loneliness extremes in Rush (PMID: 17283291), dementia OR 1.64 in AMSTEL (PMID: 23232034). Isolation: Alzheimer's OR 1.183 per point in CHAP, no adjusted association in AMSTEL. Pathology: no relation between loneliness and Alzheimer's pathology or infarction at autopsy (PMID: 17283291). The broader dementia-risk pooling is homed on #5476/#5477. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational evidence only.
cards.watchOut: Scales differ across cohorts (isolation index 0–5, loneliness 0–1, 5-item loneliness scale), so cross-cohort size comparisons are approximate; all three cohorts are observational.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ng TKS et al. Journal of Prevention of Alzheimer's Disease. 2025 (PMID: 40015756); Wilson RS et al. Archives of General Psychiatry. 2007 (PMID: 17283291); Holwerda TJ et al. Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery & Psychiatry. 2014 (PMID: 23232034).

shelves.title: Loneliness interventions work modestly, and changing thinking beats adding contact: psychological interventions reduced loneliness with a small-to-medium effect (g = 0.43) across 28 randomised trials (3,039 people), and the strategies that addressed maladaptive social cognition were the most successful in randomised comparisons
shelves.question: Across randomised studies, do interventions reduce loneliness, and do interventions targeting maladaptive social cognition outperform those that only increase social contact?
shelves.mesh: COVID-19/psychology; Humans; Loneliness/*psychology; Psychosocial Intervention/methods; Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Two concordant syntheses plus a youth synthesis support a real but modest effect, capped at POSSIBLE because effects are small-to-medium and heterogeneous. Masi 2011 compared the four strategy families (social skills, social support, social contact, maladaptive social cognition) and found that among randomised comparison studies the cognition-targeting interventions were the most successful, while single-group and non-randomised designs inflated effects (PMID: 20716644). Hickin 2021 pooled 28 randomised trials (3,039 people; 31 studies, 3,959 people in the review) and found psychological interventions significantly reduced loneliness versus control with effect size g = 0.43, cognitive behavioural therapy being the most common type (PMID: 34339939). In young people (≤25 years), a 39-study meta-analysis (25 randomised trials) likewise found interventions reduced loneliness, though trials rarely targeted young people who actually reported loneliness (PMID: 32406165). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Masi 2011: across the loneliness-intervention literature, randomised comparison studies showed smaller effects than pre-post or non-randomised studies — and among randomised studies, interventions addressing maladaptive social cognition were the most successful of the four strategy families
cards.summary: Masi 2011: across the loneliness-intervention literature, randomised comparison studies showed smaller effects than pre-post or non-randomised studies — and among randomised studies, interventions addressing maladaptive social cognition were the most successful of the four strategy families
cards.people: Integrative meta-analysis of loneliness-reduction interventions in adults, classifying studies into four strategies: (a) improving social skills, (b) enhancing social support, (c) increasing opportunities for social contact, and (d) addressing maladaptive social cognition. Pooled N not documented as a single figure in the record.
cards.result: Single-group pre-post and non-randomised comparison studies yielded larger mean effect sizes than randomised comparison studies — a design-inflation warning. Among randomised comparison studies, the most successful interventions addressed maladaptive social cognition (the negative thoughts and expectations lonely people bring to social encounters), consistent with current theory on the aetiology of loneliness. The record prints the strategy ranking qualitatively rather than as a single pooled effect size.
cards.watchOut: The headline ranking rests on the randomised subset only; the same paper shows weaker designs overstate benefit, so any large effect quoted from a pre-post loneliness study should be discounted.
cards.source: Masi CM, Chen HY, Hawkley LC, Cacioppo JT. Personality and Social Psychology Review. 2011. PMID: 20716644. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hickin 2021: across 28 randomised trials (3,039 people), psychological interventions significantly reduced loneliness versus control with a small-to-medium effect (g = 0.43); 31 studies (3,959 people) met review criteria, cognitive behavioural therapy the most common intervention
cards.summary: Hickin 2021: across 28 randomised trials (3,039 people), psychological interventions significantly reduced loneliness versus control with a small-to-medium effect (g = 0.43); 31 studies (3,959 people) met review criteria, cognitive behavioural therapy the most common intervention
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Hickin 2021)
cards.people: Systematic review of 31 randomised trials of psychological interventions for loneliness across the lifespan (N = 3,959; diverse cultures, ages and populations; mostly face-to-face, group-based, weekly), with 28 trials (N = 3,039) in the meta-analysis; quality assessed with the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool and interventions described as mixed quality.
cards.result: Psychological interventions significantly reduced loneliness compared with control groups, yielding a small-to-medium effect size (g = 0.43). Intervention type was approaching significance as a moderator in subgroup analysis and meta-regression. There was considerable heterogeneity in effectiveness, which the authors say argues for studying what works for whom and personalising treatment.
cards.watchOut: g = 0.43 is a standardised mean difference on loneliness scales, not a remission rate; heterogeneity was considerable and included-study quality mixed, which is why this shelf does not claim more than POSSIBLE.
cards.source: Hickin N, Kall A, Shafran R, Sutcliffe S, Manzotti G, Langan D. Clinical Psychology Review. 2021. PMID: 34339939. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: COVID-19/psychology; Humans; Loneliness/*psychology; Psychosocial Intervention/methods; Treatment Outcome

cards.headline: Loades/Eccles & Qualter 2021 (young people): across 39 studies (25 randomised trials) in people aged 25 and under, interventions reduced loneliness — but trials usually targeted at-risk groups rather than young people who reported being lonely
cards.summary: Loades/Eccles & Qualter 2021 (young people): across 39 studies (25 randomised trials) in people aged 25 and under, interventions reduced loneliness — but trials usually targeted at-risk groups rather than young people who reported being lonely
cards.type: Meta-analysis of intervention studies in youth (Eccles & Qualter 2021)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 39 studies (14 single-group and 25 randomised trials) published 1980–2019 measuring loneliness as an outcome in youth aged 25 years or younger, with moderator analyses of sample demographics, intervention characteristics and study quality.
cards.result: Interventions were shown to reduce loneliness among young people in both single-group and randomised-trial meta-analyses (the record prints the conclusion without a single pooled effect size). Interventions often targeted youth viewed as at risk — for example those with health concerns — and rarely targeted youth who reported loneliness, and there was no indication whether participants had chronic loneliness.
cards.watchOut: A youth population (≤25 years) carded to show the lifespan reach of the intervention evidence — its targeting gap (treating at-risk rather than actually lonely young people) mirrors the adult literature's weakness.

cards.headline: Synthesis: randomised evidence says loneliness is reducible — psychological treatment g = 0.43 — and the strategy evidence favours changing maladaptive social cognition over simply adding social contact
cards.summary: Synthesis: randomised evidence says loneliness is reducible — psychological treatment g = 0.43 — and the strategy evidence favours changing maladaptive social cognition over simply adding social contact
cards.people: The carded evidence: three meta-analyses — the four-strategy adult synthesis, a 28-trial randomised pooling (3,039 people), and a 39-study youth synthesis (25 randomised trials).
cards.result: Psychological interventions versus control: g = 0.43 (PMID: 34339939). Strategy ranking in randomised comparisons: maladaptive-social-cognition interventions most successful; weaker designs inflate effects (PMID: 20716644). Youth interventions also reduced loneliness, with a targeting gap (PMID: 32406165). Older-adult-specific intervention evidence is homed on #5483 and not re-carded here. shelves.title: Treating isolation in mental illness: across 30 randomised trials only a minority significantly reduced isolation — supported socialisation and cognitive approaches are leads, not proven treatments
shelves.question: In people with mental-health conditions, do interventions reduce subjective and objective social isolation?
shelves.mesh: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy/methods · Female · Humans · Loneliness/psychology · Male · Mental Disorders/psychology/therapy · Mental Health Services · Persons with Psychiatric Disorders/psychology · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Social Isolation/psychology · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence). Three syntheses agree the trial base is thin and mixed. Ma/Mann 2020 (PMID: 31741017) found 30 randomised trials in people with mental-health problems, with significant isolation reductions in only a minority; cognitive modification (for subjective isolation) and supported socialisation within mixed strategies (for objective isolation) were the preliminary signals. Webber 2017 (PMID: 28286914) found only 6 of 19 social-participation interventions had been randomised, with the strongest network gains for supported community engagement. Toh 2022 (PMID: 35549899) found digital approaches supported only by feasibility studies and small trials. No intervention category has two adequate trials behind it, so no benefit stamp above MAYBE is honest. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).

cards.headline: Mann/Ma 2020: across 30 randomised trials in people with mental-health problems, only a minority significantly reduced isolation — cognitive modification for subjective isolation and supported socialisation for objective isolation looked most promising
cards.summary: Mann/Ma 2020: across 30 randomised trials in people with mental-health problems, only a minority significantly reduced isolation — cognitive modification for subjective isolation and supported socialisation for objective isolation looked most promising
cards.people: 30 randomised controlled trials of interventions for people with mental health problems reporting subjective isolation (loneliness, perceived support; 15 trials), objective isolation (11 trials), or both (4 trials). Total participant N not documented in the record.
cards.result: Significant results were reported in only a minority of trials, with considerable variability in interventions and participants, and small samples limiting many conclusions. The reviewers judged the evidence not yet strong enough for specific practice recommendations; preliminary signals favoured cognitive modification approaches for subjective isolation, and mixed-strategy interventions with supported socialisation for objective isolation.
cards.watchOut: A review of trials, not one trial: heterogeneity and small, underpowered studies mean the promising categories are hypotheses for better trials, not established treatments.

cards.headline: Webber 2017: of 19 social-participation interventions for people with mental-health problems, only 6 were randomised trials — network gains looked strongest for supported community engagement, but the evidence was limited
cards.summary: Webber 2017: of 19 social-participation interventions for people with mental-health problems, only 6 were randomised trials — network gains looked strongest for supported community engagement, but the evidence was limited
cards.people: 19 interventions from 14 countries for people with mental health problems, grouped as individual social skills training, group skills training, supported community engagement, group-based community activities, employment interventions, and peer support; 6 were evaluated in randomised controlled trials.
cards.result: Social network gains appeared strongest for supported community engagement interventions, but overall evidence was limited: the studies were few, heterogeneous, and not quality-appraised in this review. The authors call for experimental designs with sufficient samples and follow-up beyond 12 months before firm recommendations can be made.
cards.watchOut: Not quality-appraised and largely non-randomised: this card maps what is being tried and where signals sit; it cannot estimate an effect size.

cards.headline: Toh 2022: 32 studies of digital interventions for isolation in mental-health conditions — mostly feasibility work, with no large randomised trials, so clinical effectiveness cannot be judged
cards.summary: Toh 2022: 32 studies of digital interventions for isolation in mental-health conditions — mostly feasibility work, with no large randomised trials, so clinical effectiveness cannot be judged
cards.people: 32 studies (16 feasibility, 7 single-group, 9 effectiveness trials) of digital interventions — web-based and phone-based programmes, blended interventions, socially assistive robots and virtual reality — in people with mental health conditions, published 2000–2020.
cards.result: Feasibility outcomes were generally satisfactory, indicating potential for future trials, but studies varied widely and many were not fully powered to detect an effect. The reviewers concluded that clear conclusions about clinical effectiveness cannot be reached and that large-scale randomised trials with rigorous methods are needed.
cards.watchOut: A scoping review counts and describes studies rather than pooling effects; satisfactory feasibility is not evidence that loneliness or isolation actually falls.

cards.headline: Synthesis: isolation in mental illness is treatable in principle, but after 30 randomised trials no specific intervention has earned a firm recommendation — supported socialisation and cognitive approaches are the leads to test properly
cards.summary: Synthesis: isolation in mental illness is treatable in principle, but after 30 randomised trials no specific intervention has earned a firm recommendation — supported socialisation and cognitive approaches are the leads to test properly
cards.people: The carded evidence: one systematic review of 30 RCTs, one review of 19 participation interventions (6 randomised), and one scoping review of 32 digital-intervention studies, all in people with mental-health problems.
cards.result: Only a minority of the 30 RCTs in Ma/Mann 2020 reported significant reductions in subjective or objective isolation; Webber 2017 found the same pattern for social-participation programmes, with supported community engagement ahead; Toh 2022 found digital interventions feasible but untested at scale. The consistent message across three independent syntheses is an underpowered, heterogeneous evidence base — promising directions, no proven programme. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: General-population loneliness interventions are homed on neighbouring shelves (#5482, #5483); this shelf is only about people with mental-health problems, where baseline isolation is higher and trial quality is the binding constraint.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ma R, Mann F, Wang J et al. Social Psychiatry and Psychiatric Epidemiology. 2020 (PMID: 31741017); Webber M, Fendt-Newlin M. Social Psychiatry and Psychiatric Epidemiology. 2017 (PMID: 28286914); Toh G, Pearce E, Vines J et al. BMC Psychiatry. 2022 (PMID: 35549899).

shelves.title: Befriending: pooled randomised trials show a modest cut in depressive symptoms (SMD −0.27 short term) — but whether visiting actually reduces loneliness is still very uncertain
shelves.question: Does befriending (a trained volunteer forming a social relationship with an isolated person) reduce depressive symptoms and distress?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Community Mental Health Services/economics/methods · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Depression/therapy · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Social Support · Stress, Psychological/therapy · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) for depressive symptoms and distress; unproven for loneliness itself. Mead 2010 (PMID: 20118451) pooled randomised trials and found a modest significant reduction in depressive symptoms (SMD −0.27 short term; −0.18 long term). But the loneliness-specific evidence is very low certainty: Laermans 2023 (PMID: 38034902) found only 470 older adults across 13 small studies of friendly visiting and could not judge effectiveness. Fakoya 2021 (PMID: 34499682) identifies plausible mechanisms (reciprocity, empathy, autonomy, privacy). The largest single trial here, Charlesworth 2008 (PMID: 18505757; 236 dementia carers), found offering a befriending scheme made no difference to mood or quality of life. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), scoped to depressive symptoms.

cards.headline: Mead 2010: befriending modestly reduced depressive symptoms across randomised trials — standardised mean difference −0.27 short term and −0.18 long term
cards.summary: Mead 2010: befriending modestly reduced depressive symptoms across randomised trials — standardised mean difference −0.27 short term and −0.18 long term
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Mead 2010)
cards.people: Randomised trials of befriending (emotional support from a trained volunteer) versus usual care or no treatment in community populations with emotional distress or depressive symptoms; nine studies contributed short-term and five long-term estimates. Total participant N not documented in the record.
cards.result: Compared with usual care or no treatment, befriending had a modest but significant effect on depressive symptoms in the short term (standardised mean difference −0.27, 95% CI −0.48 to −0.06, nine studies) and the long term (SMD −0.18, 95% CI −0.32 to −0.05, five studies). The reviewers called for work on active ingredients, target populations and delivery methods.
cards.watchOut: The pooled effect is on depressive symptoms and distress, not on loneliness itself, and it is modest — about a quarter of a standard deviation — in varied patient groups.
cards.source: Mead N, Lester H, Chew-Graham C, Gask L, Bower P. Effects of befriending on depressive symptoms and distress: systematic review and meta-analysis. The British Journal of Psychiatry. 2010. PMID: 20118451. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Fakoya 2021: in five Northern Ireland befriending programmes, reciprocity, empathy, autonomy and privacy were the mechanisms that relieved loneliness — each triggered only in the right context
cards.summary: Fakoya 2021: in five Northern Ireland befriending programmes, reciprocity, empathy, autonomy and privacy were the mechanisms that relieved loneliness — each triggered only in the right context
cards.people: Five case-study befriending programmes for older people in Northern Ireland, varying in service-user and provider characteristics; data from service documentation and semi-structured interviews with 46 stakeholders (recipients and deliverers).
cards.result: A realist evaluation tested eight initial programme theories and identified four mechanisms: reciprocity (triggered where befriender and user shared characteristics, the befriender was a volunteer, and befriending was physical companionship), empathy (shared experiences), autonomy (long-term relationships not fixed on predefined priorities), and privacy (one-to-one delivery where users had cognitive or sensory impairment). Services should be tailored to mobility, impairments and delivery characteristics.
cards.watchOut: Qualitative mechanism evidence from five programmes in one region: it explains how befriending may work and for whom, but measures no effect size.
cards.source: Fakoya OA, McCorry NK, Donnelly M. How do befriending interventions alleviate loneliness and social isolation among older people? A realist evaluation study. PLoS One. 2021. PMID: 34499682. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Laermans 2023 (Campbell review): face-to-face friendly visiting by volunteers — 9 randomised trials and 4 non-randomised studies, 470 older adults in total — the evidence for reducing loneliness or isolation is very uncertain
cards.summary: Laermans 2023 (Campbell review): face-to-face friendly visiting by volunteers — 9 randomised trials and 4 non-randomised studies, 470 older adults in total — the evidence for reducing loneliness or isolation is very uncertain
cards.people: Nine randomised trials and four non-randomised studies, mostly from the United States, totalling 470 older adults (mean or median ages 72–83 years); individual studies enrolled only 20–88 participants. Programmes lasted 6–12 weeks, mostly weekly visits (often by undergraduate students) to community-dwelling older adults.
cards.result: All studies had major shortcomings in design and execution. The evidence on face-to-face friendly visiting for loneliness was very uncertain in the short term (one RCT in 88 and one non-RCT in 35 participants) and intermediate term (one RCT in 86 participants), and likewise for social isolation and wellbeing outcomes (all very low-certainty). The reviewers could not say whether friendly visiting works and called for larger, better-designed studies.
cards.watchOut: This is the loneliness-specific verdict and it is weaker than the depression-symptom verdict on the Mead card: tiny trials (20–88 people) cannot settle whether visiting reduces loneliness.
cards.source: Laermans J, Scheers H, Vandekerckhove P, De Buck E. Friendly visiting by a volunteer for reducing loneliness or social isolation in older adults: A systematic review. cards.headline: Charlesworth 2008: in 236 carers of people with dementia, access to a befriending scheme made no difference to carers' mood or quality of life at 15 months
cards.summary: Charlesworth 2008: in 236 carers of people with dementia, access to a befriending scheme made no difference to carers' mood or quality of life at 15 months
cards.people: 236 family carers of people with primary progressive dementia in community settings in East Anglia and London, randomised to contact with a befriender facilitator plus an offer of matching with a trained lay volunteer befriender, or to no facilitator contact; all continued usual care. Outcomes at 15 months: carers' mood (Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale depression subscale) and health-related quality of life (EuroQol).
cards.result: The intention-to-treat analysis showed no benefit for access to a befriender facilitator on the primary outcome or on any secondary outcome — the treatment made no difference. The authors note befriending schemes are not taken up by all carers, so the trial tests offering access, not befriending received.
cards.watchOut: A null trial of offering a scheme, with incomplete uptake: it refutes easy claims for befriending-as-offered in dementia carers, not necessarily befriending actually received over a sustained period.
cards.source: Charlesworth G, Shepstone L, Wilson E, Reynolds S, Mugford M, Price D. Befriending carers of people with dementia: randomised controlled trial. BMJ. 2008. PMID: 18505757. cards.headline: Synthesis: befriending probably eases depressive symptoms a little, but whether it reduces loneliness — its stated purpose — remains unproven, and simply offering a scheme to dementia carers did nothing
cards.summary: Synthesis: befriending probably eases depressive symptoms a little, but whether it reduces loneliness — its stated purpose — remains unproven, and simply offering a scheme to dementia carers did nothing
cards.people: The carded evidence: one meta-analysis of randomised befriending trials, one Campbell systematic review of friendly visiting (13 studies, 470 older adults), one realist evaluation (5 programmes, 46 interviews), and one randomised trial in 236 dementia carers.
cards.result: Depressive symptoms fell modestly with befriending in pooled trials (SMD −0.27 short term, −0.18 long term; Mead 2010). For loneliness and isolation outcomes the friendly-visiting evidence is very low certainty (Laermans 2023). Mechanisms that plausibly carry any benefit — reciprocity, empathy, autonomy, privacy — depend on matching and sustained one-to-one contact (Fakoya 2021). Offering access alone, without assured uptake, made no difference in carers (Charlesworth 2008). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for depressive symptoms; loneliness benefit unproven.
cards.watchOut: Read the stamp narrowly: it covers depressive symptoms and distress in mixed community populations. It does not certify befriending as a loneliness treatment, and programme design (matching, duration, one-to-one delivery) appears to decide whether the active mechanisms fire at all.

shelves.title: Music therapy for depression: added to usual care it cut symptoms substantially in the short term — Cochrane clinician-rated SMD −0.98 across 9 studies and 421 participants
shelves.question: In depression, does music therapy added to usual care improve depressive symptoms?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anxiety/therapy · Combined Modality Therapy · Depression/therapy · Humans · Music Therapy/methods · Patient Reported Outcome Measures · Psychotherapy · Quality of Life · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) for short-term depressive symptoms when added to usual care. The Cochrane review (Aalbers 2017; PMID: 29144545) found large effects on moderate-quality evidence: clinician-rated SMD −0.98 and patient-reported SMD −0.85 for music therapy plus usual care versus usual care alone (9 studies, 421 participants). An independent meta-analysis of 55 randomised trials (Tang 2020; PMID: 33206656) found a smaller but concordant effect for music therapy proper (SMD −0.66). The best single trial (Erkkilä 2011; PMID: 21474494; ISRCTN84185937; n = 79) found a 4.65-point greater depression improvement and a response odds ratio of 2.96 at 3 months. Limits: effects are short-term, trials are small, quality of life did not significantly improve in the Cochrane analysis, and comparison with psychological therapy is untested. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit), short-term and adjunctive only.

cards.headline: Aalbers 2017 (Cochrane): music therapy added to usual care produced large short-term reductions in depressive symptoms — clinician-rated SMD −0.98 and patient-reported SMD −0.85 — on moderate-quality evidence from 9 studies and 421 participants
cards.summary: Aalbers 2017 (Cochrane): music therapy added to usual care produced large short-term reductions in depressive symptoms — clinician-rated SMD −0.98 and patient-reported SMD −0.85 — on moderate-quality evidence from 9 studies and 421 participants
cards.people: Nine studies totalling 421 participants with depression (411 in the meta-analysis of short-term effects): randomised and controlled clinical trials of music therapy versus treatment as usual, psychological, pharmacological or other therapies, in people of any age with a diagnosis of depression.
cards.result: Music therapy plus treatment as usual beat usual care alone on clinician-rated depressive symptoms (SMD −0.98, 95% CI −1.69 to −0.27; 3 RCTs and 1 controlled clinical trial, n = 219) and patient-reported symptoms (SMD −0.85, 95% CI −1.37 to −0.34; n = 142), both moderate-quality evidence, with no difference in adverse events or in leaving the study early. Music therapy plus usual care was also superior for anxiety and functioning, but not for quality of life (SMD 0.32, 95% CI −0.17 to 0.80; n = 67, low-quality). Against psychological therapies the evidence was uncertain (clinician-rated SMD −0.78, 95% CI −2.36 to 0.81; one RCT, n = 11, very low quality).
cards.watchOut: Effects are short-term and the pooled trials are small (the clinician-rated estimate rests on 219 people); nothing here shows durability, and the comparison against psychological therapy is essentially untested (n = 11).
cards.source: Aalbers S, Fusar-Poli L, Freeman RE et al. Music therapy for depression. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2017. PMID: 29144545. Registry ID: none in the record.
