cards.headline: Erkkilä 2011: individual music therapy plus standard care beat standard care alone in 79 working-age adults with depression — depression scores improved by 4.65 points more at 3 months, and the response rate was nearly threefold (odds ratio 2.96)
cards.summary: Erkkilä 2011: individual music therapy plus standard care beat standard care alone in 79 working-age adults with depression — depression scores improved by 4.65 points more at 3 months, and the response rate was nearly threefold (odds ratio 2.96)
cards.people: 79 participants with an ICD-10 diagnosis of depression, randomised to individual music therapy plus standard care (20 twice-weekly sessions) or standard care only, in Finland; outcomes at baseline, 3 months (after intervention) and 6 months, including depression, anxiety, general functioning, quality of life and alexithymia.
cards.result: At 3 months the music-therapy group showed greater improvement in depression symptoms (mean difference 4.65, 95% CI 0.59 to 8.70), anxiety symptoms (1.82, 95% CI 0.09 to 3.55) and general functioning (−4.58, 95% CI −8.93 to −0.24). The response rate was significantly higher with music therapy plus standard care (odds ratio 2.96, 95% CI 1.01 to 9.02).
cards.watchOut: One trial, 79 people, one country, an improvisational individual model: it anchors the Cochrane signal but cannot carry generalisation to group formats, other models, or longer-term outcomes by itself.
cards.source: Erkkilä J, Punkanen M, Fachner J et al. Individual music therapy for depression: randomised controlled trial. The British Journal of Psychiatry. 2011. PMID: 21474494. cards.headline: Tang 2020: across 55 randomised trials, music therapy reduced depressive symptoms (SMD −0.66) and music medicine — listening without a therapist — reduced them more (SMD −1.33), with effects varying by method
cards.summary: Tang 2020: across 55 randomised trials, music therapy reduced depressive symptoms (SMD −0.66) and music medicine — listening without a therapist — reduced them more (SMD −1.33), with effects varying by method
cards.people: 55 randomised controlled trials of music-based interventions for depression identified from PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Central Register and other databases to May 2020, comparing music therapy (delivered by a music therapist) and music medicine (music listening without a therapist) against control conditions. Total participant N not documented in the record.
cards.result: Music therapy significantly reduced depressive symptoms versus control (SMD −0.66, 95% CI −0.86 to −0.46; P < 0.001); music medicine showed a larger pooled effect (SMD −1.33, 95% CI −1.96 to −0.70; P < 0.001). Effects differed by method — recreative music therapy SMD −1.41, guided imagery and music −1.08, music-assisted relaxation −0.81, improvisational music therapy −0.27 — and both approaches showed stronger effects at short and medium intervention lengths than at long ones.
cards.watchOut: Pooling 55 heterogeneous small trials invites publication-bias and quality concerns the abstract does not resolve; the music-medicine estimate (−1.33) is implausibly large for a passive intervention and should be read as a warning about the underlying trial quality, not as a dose of confidence.
cards.source: Tang Q, Huang Z, Zhou H, Ye P. Effects of music therapy on depression: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. PLoS One. 2020. PMID: 33206656. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: music therapy added to usual care likely reduces depressive symptoms in the short term — two independent syntheses and the field's best single trial agree — but durability, quality-of-life benefit and standing against psychological therapy are unproven
cards.summary: Synthesis: music therapy added to usual care likely reduces depressive symptoms in the short term — two independent syntheses and the field's best single trial agree — but durability, quality-of-life benefit and standing against psychological therapy are unproven
cards.people: The carded evidence: one Cochrane review (9 studies, 421 participants), one randomised trial (79 participants), and one meta-analysis of 55 randomised trials, all in diagnosed depression.
cards.result: Effect estimates for music therapy versus control range from SMD −0.66 (Tang 2020, music therapy only) to −0.98 clinician-rated (Aalbers 2017, versus usual care). Erkkilä 2011 supplies the concrete trial behind the syntheses: 4.65 points greater improvement and response odds ratio 2.96 at 3 months. Anxiety and functioning also improved in the Cochrane analysis; quality of life did not. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — short-term, as an addition to usual care.
cards.watchOut: Do not extend this stamp to music listening alone ('music medicine'), to children and adolescents (the Cochrane authors call for adequate trials), or to long-term relapse prevention — none of those is established by the carded evidence.
cards.source: Synthesis of Aalbers S et al. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2017 (PMID: 29144545); Erkkilä J et al. The British Journal of Psychiatry. 2011 (PMID: 21474494; ISRCTN84185937); Tang Q et al. PLoS One. 2020 (PMID: 33206656).

shelves.title: Dance movement therapy for depression: a wider review of 351 people found benefit in every study, but the randomised-trials-only Cochrane review found no reliable effect (SMD -0.67, 95% CI -1.40 to 0.05)
shelves.question: In adults with depression, does dance movement therapy improve symptoms versus control?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Antidepressive Agents · Dance Therapy · Depression · Empathy · Female · Humans · Male · Movement · Psychotherapy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Sensation
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the two syntheses disagree and the only primary trial carded is small and in adolescents. The Cochrane review (Meekums 2015, PMID: 25695871) found only 3 trials with 147 participants and no reliable effect of dance movement therapy on depression (SMD -0.67, 95% CI -1.40 to 0.05; very low quality evidence). Karkou 2019 (PMID: 31130889), widening beyond randomised designs to 8 studies with 351 people, concluded dance movement therapy plus usual care was effective, with the largest effect in lower-bias studies of adults up to 65. Jeong 2005 (PMID: 16287635) randomised 40 adolescents with mild depression and found psychological distress scores fell after 12 weeks of dance movement therapy. Tier C: small, mixed-design evidence. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit).

cards.headline: Karkou 2019: across 8 studies with 351 people, depression scores fell in favour of dance movement therapy groups in every study, and the authors concluded it is effective added to usual care
cards.summary: Karkou 2019: across 8 studies with 351 people, depression scores fell in favour of dance movement therapy groups in every study, and the authors concluded it is effective added to usual care
cards.type: Systematic review with meta-analyses, mixed designs (Karkou 2019)
cards.people: 351 people with mild to severe depression across 8 studies meeting inclusion criteria (192 attended dance movement therapy groups while receiving treatment as usual, 159 received treatment as usual only); designs ranged beyond randomised trials, and a sensitivity analysis excluding high-risk-of-bias randomised trials left studies of adults up to age 65.
cards.result: Qualitative findings showed a decrease in depression scores in favour of dance movement therapy groups in all studies. Subgroup analysis of scores before and 3 months after completion also favoured dance movement therapy. In the sensitivity analysis restricted to lower-bias randomised trials in adults up to 65, the highest effect size favoured dance movement therapy plus treatment as usual over treatment as usual only. The authors concluded, on studies of moderate to high quality, that dance movement therapy is an effective intervention for adults with depression, while noting a paucity of high-quality studies.
cards.watchOut: This review deliberately included non-randomised designs because randomised trials in this field are rare; its positive conclusion is therefore weaker than a randomised-trials-only synthesis — and the Cochrane review below, restricted to randomised trials, reached the opposite conclusion.
cards.source: Karkou V et al. Effectiveness of Dance Movement Therapy in the Treatment of Adults With Depression: A Systematic Review With Meta-Analyses. Frontiers in psychology. 2019. PMID: 31130889. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Cochrane 2015: only 3 randomised trials with 147 participants existed, and there was no reliable effect of dance movement therapy on depression (SMD -0.67, 95% CI -1.40 to 0.05; very low quality evidence)
cards.summary: Cochrane 2015: only 3 randomised trials with 147 participants existed, and there was no reliable effect of dance movement therapy on depression (SMD -0.67, 95% CI -1.40 to 0.05; very low quality evidence)
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (Meekums 2015)
cards.people: 147 participants in 3 randomised trials (107 adults and 40 adolescents; 74 received dance movement therapy, 73 were controls): two adult studies (outpatients, and inpatients at an urban hospital) and one study of female adolescents in a middle-school setting.
cards.result: There was no reliable effect of dance movement therapy on depression (SMD -0.67, 95% CI -1.40 to 0.05; very low quality evidence), with statistical heterogeneity between the three studies. A subgroup analysis in adults (2 studies, 107 participants) showed a positive effect that failed to meet clinical significance. Drop-out did not differ significantly in the one adult study reporting it (odds ratio 1.82, 95% CI 0.35 to 9.45). The reviewers concluded the low-quality evidence from three small trials does not allow firm conclusions and that larger, high-quality trials are needed.
cards.watchOut: The adult subgroup figure printed in the record (SMD -7.33) is on a raw-score scale and is not comparable with the pooled SMD; this card does not rely on it. The headline is the pooled result: no reliable effect.
cards.source: Meekums B et al. Dance movement therapy for depression. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2015. PMID: 25695871. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Jeong 2005: in 40 adolescents with mild depression, 12 weeks of dance movement therapy reduced psychological distress scores and raised plasma serotonin while lowering dopamine
cards.summary: Jeong 2005: in 40 adolescents with mild depression, 12 weeks of dance movement therapy reduced psychological distress scores and raised plasma serotonin while lowering dopamine
cards.people: 40 middle-school seniors (mean age 16 years) with mild depression, randomly assigned to a dance movement group (n = 20) or control group (n = 20) for 12 weeks.
cards.result: All subscale scores of psychological distress and global scores decreased significantly after the 12 weeks in the dance movement therapy group. Plasma serotonin concentration increased and dopamine concentration decreased in the dance movement therapy group, which the authors interpreted as stabilising the sympathetic nervous system.
cards.watchOut: A small, single trial in adolescents with mild depression — not the adult population of this shelf's question; it is carded as the only primary randomised evidence fetched this session and cannot carry an adult claim on its own.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a randomised-trials-only review found no reliable effect, a wider review found benefit, and the one primary trial is small and adolescent — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.summary: Synthesis: a randomised-trials-only review found no reliable effect, a wider review found benefit, and the one primary trial is small and adolescent — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.people: The carded evidence: one mixed-design systematic review (8 studies, 351 people), one Cochrane review of randomised trials (3 trials, 147 participants), and one small randomised trial in adolescents (40 participants).
cards.result: Restricted to randomised trials, the evidence does not show a reliable effect (Cochrane 2015: SMD -0.67, 95% CI -1.40 to 0.05, very low quality). Widening to other designs, every included study favoured dance movement therapy (Karkou 2019), and a 12-week randomised trial in adolescents found reduced distress (Jeong 2005). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a possible effect that the randomised evidence has not yet confirmed.
cards.watchOut: Karkou 2019 and the Cochrane review overlap in the trials they cover; they are not independent bodies of evidence, and their disagreement is mainly about which designs count.

shelves.title: Yoga for depression: 12 randomised trials (619 people) showed a short-term effect versus usual care (SMD -0.69), but the largest adjunctive trial found no difference at 10 weeks
shelves.question: In major depression, does yoga improve symptoms versus control in randomised trials?
shelves.mesh: Depression · Depressive Disorder · Humans · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Treatment Outcome · Yoga
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), short-term and as an adjunct — not established as monotherapy. Cramer 2013 (PMID: 23922209) meta-analysed 12 randomised trials with 619 participants and found moderate evidence for short-term effects on depression severity versus usual care (SMD -0.69, 95% CI -0.99 to -0.39). The two primary trials carded point both ways on timing: Prathikanti 2017 (PMID: 28301561; NCT01210651; 38 adults) found a significantly greater 8-week fall in Beck Depression Inventory scores with hatha yoga as monotherapy for mild-to-moderate major depression (P = 0.034), while Uebelacker 2017 (PMID: 28382883; 122 adults on antidepressants) found no significant difference at the 10-week primary endpoint (P = 0.36) but lower depression over the full follow-up and more responders at 6 months (51% vs 31%). This shelf is distinct from live #455, which homes exercise for depression generally. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Cramer 2013: 12 randomised trials with 619 participants — moderate evidence for a short-term effect of yoga on depression severity versus usual care (SMD -0.69, 95% CI -0.99 to -0.39; P < .001)
cards.summary: Cramer 2013: 12 randomised trials with 619 participants — moderate evidence for a short-term effect of yoga on depression severity versus usual care (SMD -0.69, 95% CI -0.99 to -0.39; P < .001)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Cramer 2013)
cards.people: 619 participants in 12 randomised trials of yoga for patients with depressive disorders and individuals with elevated levels of depression; only 3 trials had low risk of bias, and no trial reported safety data.
cards.result: For severity of depression there was moderate evidence for short-term effects of yoga compared with usual care (SMD -0.69, 95% CI -0.99 to -0.39; P < .001), and limited evidence compared with relaxation (SMD -0.62, 95% CI -1.03 to -0.22; P = .003) and aerobic exercise (SMD -0.59, 95% CI -0.99 to -0.18; P = .004). Subgroup analyses found effects both in patients with depressive disorders and in individuals with elevated depression levels. No meta-analysis of long-term effects was possible. The authors concluded yoga could be considered an ancillary treatment option.
cards.watchOut: Most included trials carried methodological drawbacks and none reported safety data; the evidence is explicitly short-term, and 'moderate evidence' here rests on only 3 low-risk-of-bias trials.

cards.headline: Prathikanti 2017: 8 weeks of hatha yoga as sole treatment beat attention-control education on depression scores in 38 adults with mild-to-moderate major depression (P = 0.034; effect size d = -0.96)
cards.summary: Prathikanti 2017: 8 weeks of hatha yoga as sole treatment beat attention-control education on depression scores in 38 adults with mild-to-moderate major depression (P = 0.034; effect size d = -0.96)
cards.people: 38 adults in San Francisco with mild-to-moderate major depression (Beck Depression Inventory-II scores 14-28; mean 22.4; 68% female; mean age 43.4 years), randomised to 90-minute hatha yoga groups twice weekly for 8 weeks (n = 20) or 90-minute attention-control education groups (n = 18); people in psychotherapy, on antidepressants, or using other mood therapies were excluded.
cards.result: In intent-to-treat analysis, yoga participants showed a significantly greater 8-week decline in Beck Depression Inventory scores than controls (P = 0.034), with a large effect size (Cohen's d = -0.96, 95% CI -1.81 to -0.12). Among participants completing final measures, yoga participants were more likely to achieve remission, defined as a final score of 9 or below (P = 0.018). Self-efficacy and self-esteem change scores did not differ between groups.
cards.watchOut: A pilot trial of 38 people at one centre, testing yoga as monotherapy in mild-to-moderate depression only; the remission analysis was restricted to completers, and the confidence interval around the effect is very wide.
cards.source: Prathikanti S et al. Treating major depression with yoga: A prospective, randomized, controlled pilot trial. PloS one. 2017. PMID: 28301561. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01210651. cards.headline: Uebelacker 2017: adjunctive yoga did not beat health education at the 10-week primary endpoint (P = 0.36), but depression was lower across follow-up and 51% vs 31% had responded by 6 months
cards.summary: Uebelacker 2017: adjunctive yoga did not beat health education at the 10-week primary endpoint (P = 0.36), but depression was lower across follow-up and 51% vs 31% had responded by 6 months
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial of adjunctive yoga (Uebelacker 2017)
cards.people: 122 adults with persistent major depression despite antidepressant medication (elevated symptoms and current antidepressant use), randomised to weekly hatha yoga classes (n = 63) or health education classes (Healthy Living Workshop, an attention control; n = 59) for 10 weeks, with follow-up 3 and 6 months afterwards.
cards.result: At 10 weeks there was no statistically significant difference between groups in depression symptoms (b = -0.82, s.e. = 0.88, P = 0.36) — at the primary endpoint the treatment made no difference. Over the entire intervention and follow-up period, controlling for baseline, yoga participants showed lower depression than health-education participants (b = -1.38, s.e. = 0.57, P = 0.02). At 6-month follow-up, 51% of yoga participants versus 31% of health-education participants had responded (at least a 50% reduction in symptoms; odds ratio 2.31 relative, P = 0.04), and yoga participants showed better social and role functioning and general health perceptions over time.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint was negative; the positive findings come from the whole-period analysis and a later follow-up, so this trial supports a possible delayed or accumulating benefit, not an end-of-treatment effect.
cards.source: Uebelacker LA et al. Adjunctive yoga v. health education for persistent major depression: a randomized controlled trial. Psychological medicine. 2017. PMID: 28382883. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adult · Antidepressive Agents · Combined Modality Therapy · Major Depressive Disorder · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Health Education · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Yoga

shelves.title: Reminiscence and life review for late-life depression: meta-analyses found a large effect on depressive symptoms (d = 0.84), rising to 1.23 in older people with elevated symptoms
shelves.question: In older adults, do reminiscence/life-review interventions reduce depressive symptoms?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Depressive Disorder · Humans · Mental Recall
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — consistent meta-analytic effects from controlled studies, but the base is older and not all randomised. Bohlmeijer 2003 (PMID: 14677140) found an overall effect size of 0.84 (95% CI 0.31 to 1.37) on depressive symptoms across 20 controlled studies, larger (d = 1.23) in people with elevated symptoms. Pinquart & Forstmeier 2012 (PMID: 22304736), across 128 controlled studies, found a moderate depression effect (g = 0.57), rising to g = 1.09 in depressed individuals and g = 1.28 for life-review therapy specifically. Pinquart 2007 (PMID: 18074252), in clinically depressed older adults, likewise rated reminiscence among the interventions with large effects. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Bohlmeijer 2003: across 20 controlled studies, reminiscence and life review had a large effect on late-life depressive symptoms (d = 0.84, 95% CI 0.31 to 1.37), and d = 1.23 in people with elevated symptoms
cards.summary: Bohlmeijer 2003: across 20 controlled studies, reminiscence and life review had a large effect on late-life depressive symptoms (d = 0.84, 95% CI 0.31 to 1.37), and d = 1.23 in people with elevated symptoms
cards.people: Older adults in 20 controlled outcome studies of reminiscence and life review retrieved from Psychlit, Medline and Dissertation Abstracts; the record does not state a total participant count, so the total N is not documented on this card.
cards.result: A random-effects meta-analysis found an overall effect size of 0.84 (95% CI 0.31 to 1.37) — a statistically and clinically significant effect on depressive symptomatology in elderly people, comparable to effects commonly found for pharmacotherapy and psychological treatments. The effect was larger in subjects with elevated depressive symptomatology (d = 1.23) than in other subjects (d = 0.37). The authors called for randomised trials with sufficient statistical power to confirm the results.
cards.watchOut: Controlled studies, not all randomised, and a 2003 search; the authors themselves said adequately powered randomised trials were still needed.
cards.source: Bohlmeijer E et al. Effects of reminiscence and life review on late-life depression: a meta-analysis. International journal of geriatric psychiatry. 2003. PMID: 14677140. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Depressive Disorder · Humans · Mental Recall

cards.headline: Pinquart 2012: across 128 controlled studies, reminiscence improved depression moderately overall (g = 0.57), with larger effects in depressed individuals (g = 1.09) and for life-review therapy (g = 1.28)
cards.summary: Pinquart 2012: across 128 controlled studies, reminiscence improved depression moderately overall (g = 0.57), with larger effects in depressed individuals (g = 1.09) and for life-review therapy (g = 1.28)
cards.people: Participants in 128 controlled trials of reminiscence interventions aggregated across 9 outcome variables; the record does not state a total participant count, so the total N is not documented on this card.
cards.result: Compared with control-group change, moderate improvements were observed at post-test for ego-integrity (g = 0.64) and depression (g = 0.57 standard deviation units), with small effects on purpose in life, mastery, mental health symptoms, positive well-being, social integration and cognitive performance. Most effects were maintained at follow-up. Improvements in depressive symptoms were larger in depressed individuals (g = 1.09) and in people with chronic physical disease (g = 0.94) than in others, and larger with life-review therapy (g = 1.28) than with life review or simple reminiscence.
cards.watchOut: This meta-analysis covers reminiscence for all psychosocial outcomes, not depression alone, and mixes therapeutic and preventive samples; the depression-specific figures are the subgroup values carded here.
cards.source: Pinquart M et al. Effects of reminiscence interventions on psychosocial outcomes: a meta-analysis. Aging & mental health. 2012. PMID: 22304736. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Pinquart 2007: in clinically depressed older adults, a meta-analysis of 57 controlled studies found large average improvements (self-rated d = 0.84; clinician-rated d = 0.93), with reminiscence among the large-effect interventions
cards.summary: Pinquart 2007: in clinically depressed older adults, a meta-analysis of 57 controlled studies found large average improvements (self-rated d = 0.84; clinician-rated d = 0.93), with reminiscence among the large-effect interventions
cards.type: Meta-analysis of behavioural interventions in depressed older adults (Pinquart 2007)
cards.people: Clinically depressed older patients in 57 controlled intervention studies of psychotherapy and other behavioural interventions; 18.9% of participants on average did not complete the intervention, with higher dropout in group and longer interventions.
cards.result: On average, self-rated depression improved by d = 0.84 standard deviation units and clinician-rated depression by d = 0.93. Effect sizes were large for cognitive and behavioural therapy and for reminiscence, and medium for psychodynamic therapy, psychoeducation, physical exercise and supportive interventions. Weaker effects were found with active control groups and in physically ill or cognitively impaired patients. The authors concluded that cognitive-behavioural therapy and reminiscence are particularly well-established and acceptable forms of depression treatment in older adults.
cards.watchOut: This is a meta-analysis of all behavioural treatments, not of reminiscence alone; it is carded because it independently ranks reminiscence among the large-effect options in the clinically depressed population this shelf is about.
cards.source: Pinquart M et al. Effects of psychotherapy and other behavioral interventions on clinically depressed older adults: a meta-analysis. Aging & mental health. 2007. PMID: 18074252. cards.people: The carded evidence: three meta-analyses of controlled studies (20, 128 and 57 studies) in older adults.
cards.result: Effects on depressive symptoms were d = 0.84 overall and 1.23 in elevated-symptom samples (Bohlmeijer 2003); g = 0.57 overall, 1.09 in depressed individuals and 1.28 for life-review therapy (Pinquart 2012); and reminiscence ranked among the large-effect interventions in clinically depressed older adults (Pinquart 2007). shelves.title: Assertive community treatment in homeless people with severe mental illness: randomised trials showed a 37% greater reduction in homelessness than standard case management (relative comparison)
shelves.question: In homeless populations with severe mental illness, does assertive community treatment improve housing and clinical outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Case Management · Community Mental Health Services · Female · Ill-Housed Persons · Humans · Male · Mental Disorders · Middle Aged · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) for housing and symptom outcomes in homeless populations specifically. Coldwell & Bender 2007 (PMID: 17329462) meta-analysed 10 studies with 5,775 homeless subjects: in randomised trials, assertive community treatment produced a 37% greater reduction in homelessness (relative comparison, 95% CI 18% to 55%) and a 26% greater improvement in psychiatric symptom severity (relative comparison, 95% CI 7% to 44%) than standard case management, with no significant difference in hospitalisation. Aubry 2015 (PMID: 26720504) reports the At Home/Chez Soi randomised project (1,158 Housing First vs 990 standard care), in which assertive community treatment or intensive case management supported rapid, stable housing with superior housing outcomes. Burns & Santos 1995 (PMID: 7552556) reviewed the randomised assertive community treatment trials of 1990-1994, including homeless populations. Assertive community treatment for severe mental illness generally (hospital use) is homed at live #3273 and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Coldwell 2007: in randomised trials of homeless people with severe mental illness, assertive community treatment gave a 37% greater reduction in homelessness and 26% greater improvement in symptom severity than standard case management (relative comparisons)
cards.summary: Coldwell 2007: in randomised trials of homeless people with severe mental illness, assertive community treatment gave a 37% greater reduction in homelessness and 26% greater improvement in symptom severity than standard case management (relative comparisons)
cards.people: 5,775 homeless subjects with severe mental illness across 10 studies meeting inclusion criteria (6 randomised trials and 4 observational studies) of assertive community treatment-based rehabilitation versus standard case management or pretreatment comparison.
cards.result: In randomised trials, assertive community treatment subjects demonstrated a 37% (95% CI 18% to 55%) greater reduction in homelessness and a 26% (95% CI 7% to 44%) greater improvement in psychiatric symptom severity compared with standard case management; these are relative comparisons and the record does not report the absolute rates. Hospitalisation outcomes were not significantly different between the groups. In observational studies the further reductions were larger (104% for homelessness, 95% CI 67% to 141%; 62% for symptom severity, 95% CI 0% to 124%).
cards.watchOut: The headline percentages are relative comparisons against standard case management, not absolute reductions in homelessness; the observational-study estimates are much larger and much less secure than the randomised-trial estimates.

cards.headline: Aubry 2015 (At Home/Chez Soi): Housing First delivered with assertive community treatment or intensive case management achieved superior housing outcomes in a 5-city randomised project (1,158 vs 990 people)
cards.summary: Aubry 2015 (At Home/Chez Soi): Housing First delivered with assertive community treatment or intensive case management achieved superior housing outcomes in a 5-city randomised project (1,158 vs 990 people)
cards.type: Review including the At Home/Chez Soi randomised project (Aubry 2015)
cards.people: 2,148 people with severe mental illness who were homeless in the At Home/Chez Soi demonstration project, a randomised controlled trial in 5 Canadian cities between 2009 and 2013: 1,158 received Housing First (regular housing supported through assertive community treatment or intensive case management) and 990 received standard care.
cards.result: People receiving Housing First achieved superior housing outcomes and showed more rapid improvements in community functioning and quality of life than those receiving treatment as usual. The review reports that Housing First was successfully adapted to different contexts and populations without losing fidelity, and that earlier United States research likewise showed superior outcomes in rapidly exiting homelessness and establishing stable housing.
cards.watchOut: Housing First bundles the housing itself (with rent support) together with assertive community treatment or intensive case management, so its housing advantage cannot be credited to the clinical team model alone; this card supports the combined programme in homeless populations.

cards.headline: Synthesis: homeless-specific randomised evidence favours assertive community treatment for staying housed and for symptoms, not for hospitalisation — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: homeless-specific randomised evidence favours assertive community treatment for staying housed and for symptoms, not for hospitalisation — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.people: The carded evidence: one homeless-specific meta-analysis (10 studies, 5,775 subjects), one 5-city randomised Housing First project (2,148 people) using assertive community treatment or intensive case management, and one review of the 1990-1994 randomised trials.
cards.result: In randomised trials, assertive community treatment reduced homelessness more than standard case management (37% greater reduction, relative) and improved symptom severity more (26% greater improvement, relative), with hospitalisation not significantly different (Coldwell 2007). shelves.title: Social skills training in schizophrenia: meta-analysis found moderate gains in community functioning (d = 0.52) and negative symptoms (d = 0.40), on evidence Cochrane rated very low quality
shelves.question: In schizophrenia, does social skills training improve social functioning and negative symptoms?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Schizophrenia · Social Behavior · Socialization · Teaching
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two syntheses agree on improved skills and functioning, but the Cochrane evidence is rated very low quality and the effect disappears against an active discussion-group control. Kurtz & Mueser 2008 (PMID: 18540742) meta-analysed 22 controlled studies with 1,521 clients: large effects on content mastery (d = 1.20), moderate effects on performance-based skills and community functioning (both d = 0.52) and negative symptoms (d = 0.40). Almerie 2015 (PMID: 26059249), the Cochrane review of 13 randomised trials with 975 participants, found social functioning, relapse (relative risk 0.52, 95% CI 0.34 to 0.79; 2 trials, 263 participants) and rehospitalisation favoured social skills programmes versus standard care, all on very low quality evidence, with no significant differences versus a discussion group. Kurtz 2015 (PMID: 25640526) shows the training used as a platform alongside other rehabilitation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Kurtz 2008: across 22 controlled studies with 1,521 clients, social skills training had moderate effects on community functioning (d = 0.52) and negative symptoms (d = 0.40), and a large effect on skills content mastery (d = 1.20)
cards.summary: Kurtz 2008: across 22 controlled studies with 1,521 clients, social skills training had moderate effects on community functioning (d = 0.52) and negative symptoms (d = 0.40), and a large effect on skills content mastery (d = 1.20)
cards.people: 1,521 clients with schizophrenia in 22 randomised, controlled studies of social skills training, with outcomes ordered from most proximal (content-mastery tests, performance-based skill measures) to most distal (community functioning, negative symptoms, general symptoms, relapse).
cards.result: Weighted mean effect sizes were large for content-mastery exams (d = 1.20), moderate for performance-based measures of social and daily living skills (d = 0.52), moderate for community functioning (d = 0.52) and negative symptoms (d = 0.40), and small for other symptoms (d = 0.15) and relapse (d = 0.23). The authors concluded the results support the efficacy of social skills training for improving psychosocial functioning in schizophrenia.
cards.watchOut: Effects shrink steadily as outcomes move from what was directly taught (content mastery) toward distal outcomes such as relapse, so the large proximal numbers should not be read as equally large real-world gains.
cards.source: Kurtz MM et al. A meta-analysis of controlled research on social skills training for schizophrenia. Journal of consulting and clinical psychology. 2008. PMID: 18540742. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Humans · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Schizophrenia · Social Behavior · Socialization · Teaching

cards.headline: Cochrane 2015: 13 randomised trials with 975 participants favoured social skills programmes over standard care on social functioning, relapse (relative risk 0.52) and rehospitalisation — all very low quality evidence, and no difference versus a discussion group
cards.summary: Cochrane 2015: 13 randomised trials with 975 participants favoured social skills programmes over standard care on social functioning, relapse (relative risk 0.52) and rehospitalisation — all very low quality evidence, and no difference versus a discussion group
cards.people: 975 participants with schizophrenia in 13 randomised trials comparing social skills programmes with standard care or a discussion group.
cards.result: Evidence favoured social skills programmes compared with standard care on all measures of social functioning. Relapse rates were lower (2 randomised trials, n = 263, relative risk 0.52, 95% CI 0.34 to 0.79, very low quality evidence), as were rehospitalisation rates (1 trial, n = 143, relative risk 0.53, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.93, very low quality evidence); mental state and quality of life also favoured social skills programmes in single trials. Against a discussion-group control, however, there were no significant differences in social functioning, relapse, mental state or quality of life. The reviewers concluded social skills training may improve social skills and reduce relapse, but the evidence is very limited and rated very low quality.
cards.watchOut: Every favourable estimate rests on very low quality evidence from one or two small trials, and the null result against an attention-matched discussion group raises the possibility that group contact itself, not the skills curriculum, drives part of the effect.
cards.source: Almerie MQ et al. Social skills programmes for schizophrenia. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2015. PMID: 26059249. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Kurtz 2015: when social skills training was given to everyone, adding computer-assisted cognitive remediation improved attention, working memory and empathy more than computer-skills training — but not other functioning measures
cards.summary: Kurtz 2015: when social skills training was given to everyone, adding computer-assisted cognitive remediation improved attention, working memory and empathy more than computer-skills training — but not other functioning measures
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial with social skills training in both arms (Kurtz 2015)
cards.people: 64 individuals with schizophrenia at two treatment sites, randomly assigned for 6 months to standardised social skills training plus computer-assisted cognitive remediation, or the same social skills training plus a computer-skills training active control; outcomes were rated by blinded raters.
cards.result: The cognitive remediation group improved significantly more in attention, working memory and empathy than the computer-skills group, but there were no differences between groups on other measures of psychosocial functioning or skills. The authors suggested cognitive remediation used in the context of other evidence-based psychosocial interventions such as social skills training improves working memory, an effect that may generalise to improved empathy.
cards.watchOut: This trial does not compare social skills training with no training — both arms received it — so it cannot add proof of the training's own effect; it is carded, as the slate specified, as evidence about how the training performs as a rehabilitation platform.
cards.source: Kurtz MM et al. Social skills training and computer-assisted cognitive remediation in schizophrenia. Schizophrenia research. 2015. PMID: 25640526. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Family-to-Family, the peer-taught family education programme: a randomised study of 318 family members improved coping and empowerment, though subjective burden did not differ
shelves.question: For families of people with mental illness, does the peer-taught Family-to-Family education programme improve family outcomes in a randomised study?
shelves.mesh: Adaptation, Psychological · Adult · Aged · Caregivers · Consumer Organizations · Cost of Illness · Emotions · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Maryland · Mental Disorders · Middle Aged · Peer Group · Power, Psychological · Problem Solving · Social Support · Surveys and Questionnaires
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single randomised programme, consistently positive on coping and empowerment, not on subjective burden. Dixon 2011 (PMID: 21632725) randomised 318 family members: Family-to-Family participants improved significantly more in problem-focused coping (empowerment and illness knowledge), with exploratory gains in acceptance, distress and problem solving, but subjective illness burden did not differ. The earlier waitlist-controlled study (Dixon 2004, PMID: 14984393; 95 family members) found reduced subjective burden and increased empowerment, sustained at 6 months; the randomised programme's benefits were still present at 9 months (Lucksted 2013, PMID: 22804103), and a pre-post study in Mexico City (Domínguez-Martinez 2017, PMID: 27842466; 230 relatives) found reduced negative emotional attitudes and improved understanding. This is the peer-taught Family-to-Family programme, distinct from clinician family intervention in schizophrenia, homed at live #2685. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Dixon 2011: in a randomised study of 318 family members, the peer-taught Family-to-Family course improved problem-focused coping (empowerment and illness knowledge) versus waiting, but subjective illness burden did not differ
cards.summary: Dixon 2011: in a randomised study of 318 family members, the peer-taught Family-to-Family course improved problem-focused coping (empowerment and illness knowledge) versus waiting, but subjective illness burden did not differ
cards.type: Randomised study of the Family-to-Family programme (Dixon 2011)
cards.people: 318 consenting family members of adults with mental illness in five Maryland counties, randomly assigned to take the 12-week National Alliance on Mental Illness Family-to-Family course immediately or to wait at least 3 months (with free use of any other supports), interviewed at enrolment and at 3 months.
cards.result: Family-to-Family participants had significantly greater improvements in problem-focused coping, as measured by empowerment and illness knowledge. Exploratory analyses showed significantly enhanced emotion-focused coping (increased acceptance of the family member's illness), reduced distress and improved problem solving. Subjective illness burden did not differ between groups. The authors concluded Family-to-Family is effective for enhancing coping and empowerment, although not for reducing subjective burden.
cards.watchOut: The control was a waitlist, not an active programme, and several positive outcomes (acceptance, distress, problem solving) come from exploratory analyses the authors said require replication.
cards.source: Dixon LB et al. Outcomes of a randomized study of a peer-taught Family-to-Family Education Program for mental illness. Psychiatric services (Washington, D.C.). 2011. PMID: 21632725. cards.people: 95 consenting family members of adults with serious mental illness who were on a waiting list of 3 months or more for the Family-to-Family Education Program, interviewed at waitlist, pre-course, post-course and 6 months post-course on burden, empowerment and depression.
cards.result: The programme was associated with reduced subjective burden (P < 0.01) and increased empowerment (P < 0.01), without changes in objective burden. shelves.title: Peer-supported self-management after a mental-health crisis: readmission within a year was 29% versus 38% in the CORE randomised trial (441 people)
shelves.question: In people discharged from mental-health crisis care, does peer-supported self-management improve outcomes and cost-effectiveness?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Crisis Intervention · Female · Humans · Male · Mental Disorders · Patient Discharge · Peer Group · Recurrence · Self-Management · Social Support
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) for the specific crisis-discharge programme; the wider peer-support trial literature is weak. Lloyd-Evans 2014 (PMID: 24528545) meta-analysed 18 randomised trials with 5,597 participants and found little or no evidence that peer support improved hospitalisation, overall symptoms or satisfaction, with some inconsistent evidence for hope, recovery and empowerment. The CORE randomised trial (Johnson 2018, PMID: 30102174; ISRCTN01027104; 441 people discharged from crisis teams) then found readmission to acute care within 1 year in 29% of the peer-supported self-management group versus 38% of controls (odds ratio 0.66 relative, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.99; P = 0.0438). Its cost-effectiveness analysis (Le Novere 2023, PMID: 37333912) put the probability of cost-effectiveness at a £20,000-per-QALY threshold between 57% and 96% depending on method. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Johnson 2018 (CORE trial): peer-supported self-management after crisis-team discharge cut 1-year readmission to acute care to 29% versus 38% with a workbook alone (odds ratio 0.66 relative, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.99; P = 0.0438)
cards.summary: Johnson 2018 (CORE trial): peer-supported self-management after crisis-team discharge cut 1-year readmission to acute care to 29% versus 38% with a workbook alone (odds ratio 0.66 relative, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.99; P = 0.0438)
cards.people: 441 people discharged from six crisis resolution teams in England who had been on the caseload at least a week: 221 assigned to up to ten sessions with a peer support worker helping them complete a personal recovery workbook (recovery goals and crisis plans), and 220 to receive the workbook by post plus usual care; primary-outcome data were obtained for 218 and 216 respectively.
cards.result: Within 1 year, 64 of 218 participants (29%) in the intervention group versus 83 of 216 (38%) in the control group were readmitted to acute care (odds ratio 0.66 relative, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.99; P = 0.0438) — a 9-percentage-point absolute difference. Seventy-one serious adverse events were identified (29 in the treatment group, 42 in the control group). The authors noted admission rates were lower than anticipated and confidence intervals relatively wide.
cards.watchOut: A single trial, and the intervention bundles peer support with a structured self-management workbook and crisis planning, so the peer element alone cannot be isolated; the confidence interval reaches 0.99, close to no effect.
cards.source: Johnson S et al. Peer-supported self-management for people discharged from a mental health crisis team: a randomised controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2018. PMID: 30102174. Registry ID: ISRCTN01027104, stated in the record. cards.headline: Le Novere 2023: the CORE programme's probability of being cost-effective at £20,000 per QALY ranged from 57% to 96% depending on the analysis method — a minimum 57% chance
cards.summary: Le Novere 2023: the CORE programme's probability of being cost-effective at £20,000 per QALY ranged from 57% to 96% depending on the analysis method — a minimum 57% chance
cards.type: Cost-effectiveness analysis of the CORE trial (Le Novere 2023)
cards.people: The 441 CORE trial participants (221 peer-supported self-management, 220 usual care plus workbook), recruited from six crisis resolution teams in England between March 2014 and July 2015, with resource use from patient records and quality-adjusted life-years from EQ-5D-3L over 12 months.
cards.result: The probability that the peer support worker intervention was cost-effective compared with workbook plus usual care at 12 months varied with the method used, ranging from 57% to 96% at a cost-effectiveness threshold of £20,000 per QALY gained; there was a minimum 57% chance under the primary complete-case analysis. The probability varied by 40% when methods accounting for the relationship between costs and QALYs restricted the sample to participants with complete cost and utility data. The authors cautioned that methods chosen to increase precision may introduce bias when missing data are unbalanced.
cards.watchOut: This is an economic analysis of the same single CORE trial as the Johnson 2018 card, not independent evidence; the wide 57%-96% range is itself the finding — the cost-effectiveness verdict is method-sensitive.
cards.source: Le Novere M et al. Cost-effectiveness of peer-supported self-management for people discharged from a mental health crisis team: methodological challenges and recommendations. Frontiers in psychiatry. 2023. PMID: 37333912. Registry ID: ISRCTN01027104, stated in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Lloyd-Evans 2014: across 18 randomised trials with 5,597 participants, there was little or no evidence peer support improved hospitalisation, symptoms or satisfaction in severe mental illness, with some inconsistent evidence for hope, recovery and empowerment
cards.summary: Lloyd-Evans 2014: across 18 randomised trials with 5,597 participants, there was little or no evidence peer support improved hospitalisation, symptoms or satisfaction in severe mental illness, with some inconsistent evidence for hope, recovery and empowerment
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Lloyd-Evans 2014)
cards.people: 5,597 participants in 18 randomised trials of non-residential peer support for people with severe mental illness: 4 trials of mutual support programmes, 11 of peer support services, and 3 of peer-delivered services, searched to July 2013.
cards.result: There was little or no evidence that peer support was associated with positive effects on hospitalisation, overall symptoms or satisfaction with services. There was some evidence of positive effects on measures of hope, recovery and empowerment at and beyond the end of the intervention, although this was not consistent within or across types of peer support. Outcomes were incompletely reported and there was high risk of bias. The authors concluded current evidence does not support policy requirements for services to provide peer support programmes, and that further programmes should be implemented within high-quality research.
cards.watchOut: This review predates the CORE trial and pools very different peer models; its null headline is about peer support as a class, which is exactly why this shelf's stamp is tied to the specific crisis-discharge programme rather than to peer support generally.
cards.source: Lloyd-Evans B et al. A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials of peer support for people with severe mental illness. BMC psychiatry. 2014. PMID: 24528545. cards.summary: Synthesis: peer support as a class has little trial support, but the one crisis-discharge programme trial reduced readmissions (29% vs 38%) — POSSIBLE (benefit), programme-specific
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised trial of peer-supported self-management after crisis discharge (441 participants) with its cost-effectiveness analysis, and one meta-analysis of 18 randomised trials of peer support in severe mental illness (5,597 participants).

shelves.title: Telephone peer support to prevent postnatal depression: in 701 high-risk women, probable depression at 12 weeks was 14% with peer support versus 25% with usual care
shelves.question: In high-risk women, does telephone-based peer support from experienced mothers prevent postnatal depression?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anxiety · Depression, Postpartum · Female · Humans · Interpersonal Relations · Loneliness · Mothers · Ontario · Patient Satisfaction · Peer Group · Prognosis · Regression Analysis · Risk Factors · Social Support · Telephone · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large randomised trial plus supportive meta-analysis. Dennis 2009 (PMID: 19147637; ISRCTN68337727) randomised 701 high-risk women: at 12 weeks, 14% of the telephone peer-support group versus 25% of controls scored above 12 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (number needed to treat 8.8, 95% CI 5.9 to 19.6); groups did not differ at 24 weeks, after women identified with clinical depression at 12 weeks had been referred for treatment. Huang 2020 (PMID: 32738663) meta-analysed 10 randomised trials of peer support for perinatal depression: reduced depressive scores (standardised mean difference -0.37, 95% CI -0.66 to -0.08) and reduced risk of depression (relative risk 0.69, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.96). The Cochrane prevention review (Dennis 2013, PMID: 23450532) singled out lay (peer)-based telephone support among promising interventions (relative risk 0.54, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.77) — an estimate resting on the Dennis trial itself. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Dennis 2009: telephone peer support from experienced mothers cut probable postnatal depression at 12 weeks to 14% versus 25% in high-risk women (number needed to treat 8.8)
cards.summary: Dennis 2009: telephone peer support from experienced mothers cut probable postnatal depression at 12 weeks to 14% versus 25% in high-risk women (number needed to treat 8.8)
cards.people: 701 women in the first two weeks postpartum, identified as high risk for postnatal depression on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, across seven health regions in Ontario, Canada, randomised to proactive individualised telephone peer support (from a community volunteer who had herself recovered from postnatal depression and had 4 hours of training, starting within 48-72 hours) or usual care; over 85% were followed up, including 613 women at 12 weeks and 600 at 24 weeks.
cards.result: At 12 weeks, 14% (40/297) of women in the intervention group and 25% (78/315) in the control group had an Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale score above 12 (P < 0.001; number needed to treat 8.8, 95% CI 5.9 to 19.6; the record reports a relative risk reduction of 0.46, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.62) — an 11-percentage-point absolute difference. There was a positive trend for maternal anxiety but not for loneliness or health-service use. At 24 weeks the groups did not differ, after women identified with clinical depression at 12 weeks had been referred for treatment. Over 80% of the 221 women who received and evaluated peer support were satisfied and would recommend it to a friend.
cards.watchOut: The benefit is at 12 weeks only; the 24-week comparison was ethically contaminated by referral of depressed women for treatment, so durability is unknown rather than disproven. Screening identified 701 eligible women from 21,470 women approached.

cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Huang 2020)
cards.people: Women in the prenatal and postpartum populations in 10 randomised controlled trials of peer support interventions targeting perinatal depression, identified from five English and three Chinese databases to April 2019; the record does not state a total participant count, so the total N is not documented on this card.
cards.result: Peer support intervention reduced standardised mean depressive scores (-0.37, 95% CI -0.66 to -0.08) and reduced the relative risk of depression (0.69, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.96). Clinical heterogeneity was observed among the included studies, suggesting potential mediators such as the intensity, frequency or type of peer support. The authors concluded peer support may effectively prevent perinatal depression or reduce its harm, and called for larger, better-designed studies.
cards.watchOut: Perinatal, not purely postnatal: the pooled trials mix prevention and treatment and different peer models, and the review itself flags heterogeneity; the relative risk is a relative measure and the record gives no pooled absolute rates.

cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of prevention interventions (Dennis & Dowswell 2013)
cards.people: Almost 17,000 women in 28 trials of psychosocial or psychological interventions to prevent postnatal depression (20 trials with 14,727 women in the main analysis); the peer-based telephone support estimate comes from 1 trial with 612 women.
cards.result: Women who received a psychosocial or psychological intervention were significantly less likely to develop postnatal depression than those receiving standard care (average relative risk 0.78, 95% CI 0.66 to 0.93; 20 trials, 14,727 women). Promising interventions included intensive individualised postpartum home visits by nurses or midwives (relative risk 0.56), lay (peer)-based telephone support (relative risk 0.54, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.77; 1 trial, 612 women), and interpersonal psychotherapy. Interventions were more effective in women identified as at risk (relative risk 0.66, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.88; 8 trials, 1,853 women).
cards.watchOut: The peer-support estimate in this review rests on a single trial — the Dennis 2009 trial carded above (612 women analysed at 12 weeks) — so this card corroborates the framing, it is not independent confirmation of the peer effect.

shelves.title: Safety planning after a suicidal crisis: suicidal behaviour was 3.03% with safety planning plus follow-up calls versus 5.29% with usual care over 6 months — from a non-randomised cohort comparison, with no randomised trial of the standalone intervention
shelves.question: In suicidal patients seen in emergency departments, does safety planning with follow-up reduce suicidal behaviour versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: Promising but non-randomised throughout — this shelf's face says so. The standalone Safety Planning Intervention evidence rests on one large cohort comparison, Stanley 2018 (PMID: 29998307; 1,640 veterans in 9 Veterans Health Administration emergency departments): suicidal behaviour over 6 months was 3.03% with safety planning plus follow-up telephone contact versus 5.29% with usual care (odds ratio 0.56, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.95), and outpatient mental-health attendance more than doubled in relative terms (odds ratio 2.06). A meta-analysis of safety planning-type interventions, Nuij 2021 (PMID: 35048835; 6 studies, 3,536 participants), pooled a relative risk of suicidal behaviour of 0.570 (95% CI 0.408 to 0.795) with no significant effect on suicidal ideation, and a systematic review, Ferguson 2022 (PMID: 33913799; 26 studies), found supportive but heterogeneous evidence, half of it for safety planning combined with other interventions. No randomised trial of the standalone intervention is carded here. The ED-SAFE 2 system package, which includes safety planning as one component of a multicomponent programme, is homed at live shelf #1169 and is cross-pointed, not re-carded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational and pooled non-randomised evidence only.

cards.headline: Stanley 2018: in 1,640 suicidal veterans treated in emergency departments, safety planning plus follow-up calls was followed by less suicidal behaviour over 6 months — 3.03% versus 5.29% (odds ratio 0.56) — and more than double the relative odds of attending outpatient mental-health care
cards.summary: Stanley 2018: in 1,640 suicidal veterans treated in emergency departments, safety planning plus follow-up calls was followed by less suicidal behaviour over 6 months — 3.03% versus 5.29% (odds ratio 0.56) — and more than double the relative odds of attending outpatient mental-health care
cards.people: 1,640 patients (1,186 in the intervention group and 454 in the comparison group) aged 18 years or older with an emergency department visit for a suicide-related concern at 9 Veterans Health Administration hospital emergency departments (5 intervention sites, 4 control sites), where inpatient hospitalisation was not clinically indicated; intervention-group patients had a mean age of 47.15 years and 88.5% were men, comparison-group patients a mean age of 49.38 years and 88.1% were men. Data were collected between 2010 and 2015.
cards.result: Patients in the safety planning plus follow-up group were less likely to engage in suicidal behavior during the 6-month follow-up (36 of 1,186; 3.03%) than those receiving usual care (24 of 454; 5.29%): 45% fewer suicidal behaviors in relative terms, approximately halving the odds of suicidal behavior (odds ratio 0.56; 95% CI 0.33 to 0.95; P = .03). The absolute rates were 3.03% versus 5.29%. Intervention patients had more than double the odds of attending at least 1 outpatient mental health visit (odds ratio 2.06; 95% CI 1.57 to 2.71; P < .001).
cards.watchOut: Not randomised: intervention and comparison patients came from different emergency departments, so site differences and case-mix may explain part of the gap, and the intervention bundles the safety plan with at least two follow-up telephone contacts — the plan alone cannot be separated from the calls. The population was overwhelmingly male veterans.
cards.source: Stanley B, Brown GK, Brenner LA, Galfalvy HC, Currier GW, Knox KL, et al. Comparison of the Safety Planning Intervention With Follow-up vs Usual Care of Suicidal Patients Treated in the Emergency Department. JAMA Psychiatry. 2018. PMID: 29998307. cards.headline: Nuij 2021 meta-analysis: across 6 studies with 3,536 participants, safety planning-type interventions were associated with a relative risk of suicidal behaviour of 0.570 (95% CI 0.408 to 0.795) — and no significant effect on suicidal ideation
cards.summary: Nuij 2021 meta-analysis: across 6 studies with 3,536 participants, safety planning-type interventions were associated with a relative risk of suicidal behaviour of 0.570 (95% CI 0.408 to 0.795) — and no significant effect on suicidal ideation
cards.people: 6 studies with 3,536 participants comparing a safety planning-type intervention with a control condition, with suicidal behaviour or ideation as outcomes; the review was registered at PROSPERO (registration number CRD42020129185, as reported in the record).
cards.result: The relative risk of suicidal behaviour among patients who received a safety planning-type intervention compared with control was 0.570 (95% CI 0.408 to 0.795; P = 0.001), a relative measure corresponding to a 43% relative risk reduction, with a number needed to treat of 16 as reported by the authors. No significant effect was found for suicidal ideation.
cards.watchOut: Only 6 studies, and 'safety planning-type' is broader than the standalone Stanley intervention — several included studies bundle safety planning with follow-up contact or other care, and the underlying studies are largely non-randomised, so the pooled relative risk inherits their biases.

cards.headline: Ferguson 2022 systematic review: 26 studies of the Safety Planning Intervention supported improvements in suicidality, depression, hospitalisations and treatment engagement — but heterogeneity made the intervention's specific impact difficult to determine
cards.summary: Ferguson 2022 systematic review: 26 studies of the Safety Planning Intervention supported improvements in suicidality, depression, hospitalisations and treatment engagement — but heterogeneity made the intervention's specific impact difficult to determine
cards.people: 26 studies meeting the inclusion criteria, primarily quantitative (n = 20), largely with general adult or veteran samples; half included the Safety Planning Intervention as a standalone intervention and half examined it in combination with other interventions; most interventions were delivered in person with a hard-copy safety plan.
cards.result: The evidence supports improvements in suicidality (ideation, behavior and deaths; 10 studies), suicide-related outcomes such as depression and hopelessness (5 studies) and treatment outcomes such as hospitalizations and treatment engagement (7 studies), with complementary findings suggesting the intervention is feasible and acceptable. The reviewers state that these positive findings are limited by the heterogeneity of interventions and study designs, making the specific impact of the Safety Planning Intervention difficult to both determine and generalize.
cards.watchOut: A narrative synthesis without a pooled effect: 'supports improvements' across mixed designs is weaker than it sounds, and studies of safety planning combined with other interventions cannot be credited to the plan alone.
cards.source: Ferguson M, Rhodes K, Loughhead M, McIntyre H, et al. The Effectiveness of the Safety Planning Intervention for Adults Experiencing Suicide-Related Distress: A Systematic Review. shelves.title: Caring letters after a suicidal crisis: suicide rates were lower in all five contact years in the 843-patient Motto trial (significant for the first two years, P = .04) — an effect that faded after the letters stopped
shelves.question: In patients hospitalised after depression/suicidal crisis who declined follow-up, do regular caring letters reduce suicide deaths?
shelves.mesh: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: One landmark randomised trial, one supportive but imprecise synthesis, and one small pilot. Motto & Bostrom 2001 (PMID: 11376235) randomised 843 patients who had been hospitalised for a depressive or suicidal state and refused ongoing care: those sent caring letters at least four times a year for five years had a lower suicide rate in all five years, significantly so for the first two years (P = .04), with the difference gradually diminishing and gone by year 14. The updated systematic review and meta-analysis, Skopp 2023 (PMID: 35420858; 6 randomised trials, 6,218 participants), found summary risk ratios ranging from 0.57 to 1.29 across outcomes and time points, a protective effect for suicide attempts at 1 year, and 1-year interval estimates for suicide deaths consistent with either an increase or a decrease in risk. The military Caring Letters pilot, Luxton 2012 (PMID: 21940244; 110 inpatients), established feasibility only. A single trial carries the deaths outcome, so the stamp is capped. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Motto & Bostrom 2001: among 843 hospitalised patients who refused follow-up care, regular caring letters for five years were followed by a lower suicide rate in all five years — significantly lower for the first two years (P = .04), with no difference left by year 14
cards.summary: Motto & Bostrom 2001: among 843 hospitalised patients who refused follow-up care, regular caring letters for five years were followed by a lower suicide rate in all five years — significantly lower for the first two years (P = .04), with no difference left by year 14
cards.people: 843 patients, drawn from 3,005 persons hospitalised because of a depressive or suicidal state who were contacted 30 days after discharge about follow-up treatment and refused ongoing care, randomly divided into a contact group sent a letter at least four times a year for five years and a control group receiving no further contact; deaths were identified during the five-year contact period and the subsequent ten years.
cards.result: Patients in the contact group had a lower suicide rate in all five years of the study. Formal survival analyses revealed a significantly lower rate in the contact group (P = .04) for the first two years; differences in the rates gradually diminished, and by year 14 no differences between groups were observed. The authors conclude that a systematic program of contact appears to exert a significant preventive influence for at least two years, and that diminution and discontinuation of contact reduce and eventually eliminate this influence. The record does not print the group suicide counts or rates numerically in its abstract.

cards.headline: Skopp 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis: across 6 randomised trials with 6,218 participants, caring contacts showed a protective effect for suicide attempts at 1 year, while the 1-year estimates for suicide deaths were imprecise — consistent with either an increase or a decrease in risk
cards.summary: Skopp 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis: across 6 randomised trials with 6,218 participants, caring contacts showed a protective effect for suicide attempts at 1 year, while the 1-year estimates for suicide deaths were imprecise — consistent with either an increase or a decrease in risk
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Skopp 2023)
cards.people: 13 publications comprising 6 randomised controlled trials, encompassing 6,218 participants across four countries and military, veteran and civilian health care systems; the primary outcome was suicide mortality and secondary outcomes were suicide attempts and emergency department presentations or hospitalizations.
cards.result: Summary risk ratio estimates ranged from 0.57 to 1.29 across outcomes and time points; most estimates indicated a protective effect. For suicide deaths and emergency department presentations/hospitalization, interval estimates at 1-year postrandomization were consistent with either an increase or a decrease in risk. A protective effect was observed for suicide attempts at 1-year postrandomization. These risk ratios are relative measures.
cards.watchOut: Pooling six heterogeneous trials does not firm up the deaths outcome: the review is honest that at 1 year the data cannot distinguish benefit from harm for suicide deaths, even though attempts favour the intervention.
cards.source: Skopp NA, Smolenski DJ, Bush NE, Beech EH, et al. Caring contacts for suicide prevention: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Psychological Services. 2023. PMID: 35420858. cards.people: 110 psychiatric inpatients at a military treatment facility who consented and were interviewed, then received personalized handwritten letters or e-mails at regular intervals following discharge; most participants indicated a preference for e-mail versus postal mail.
cards.result: A total of 436 letters and e-mails were sent. Fifteen participants were readmitted for treatment compared to 20 patients in usual care. cards.watchOut: A feasibility pilot with a small, non-randomised readmission comparison (15 versus 20 patients): it shows the intervention can be delivered and is welcomed, and contributes no reliable evidence on suicide deaths or attempts.

cards.headline: Synthesis: caring letters reduced suicide rates for at least two years in the one large randomised trial of patients who refused care, and pooled trial evidence favours fewer suicide attempts — but the pooled evidence on suicide deaths remains imprecise
cards.summary: Synthesis: caring letters reduced suicide rates for at least two years in the one large randomised trial of patients who refused care, and pooled trial evidence favours fewer suicide attempts — but the pooled evidence on suicide deaths remains imprecise
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised trial (843 patients who refused follow-up care), one systematic review and meta-analysis (6 randomised trials, 6,218 participants) and one feasibility pilot (110 inpatients).
cards.result: Motto & Bostrom 2001 found a lower suicide rate in the letter group in all five contact years, significant for the first two years (P = .04) and gone by year 14 (PMID: 11376235). Skopp 2023 pooled risk ratios of 0.57 to 1.29 across outcomes, with a protective effect for suicide attempts at 1 year and 1-year death estimates consistent with either an increase or a decrease in risk (PMID: 35420858). Luxton 2012 showed delivery is feasible in a military inpatient setting (PMID: 21940244). The culturally adapted caring-contacts trial in American Indian and Alaska Native communities was assigned its own number in this wave and is not carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single randomised trial carries the deaths outcome.
cards.watchOut: The intervention is cheap and harmless, which lowers the bar for using it — but the honest evidence statement is a time-limited effect in one trial plus an imprecise pooled estimate for deaths, not a proven mortality reduction.

shelves.title: Postcards after self-poisoning: repeat episodes fell in Australia (risk ratio 0.55) and attempts fell in Iran (42% relative risk reduction), but the share of patients repeating was not significantly reduced and a New Zealand trial found no difference
shelves.question: After hospital-treated self-poisoning, do repeated postcards reduce repeat episodes?
shelves.mesh: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: Three randomised trials, genuinely discordant. Carter 2005 (PMID: 16183654; 772 patients after deliberate self-poisoning in Australia) found no significant difference in the proportion of patients who repeated (15.1% versus 17.3%) but fewer repeat episodes per person (incidence risk ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.87). Hassanian-Moghaddam 2011 (PMID: 21343332; 2,300 patients in Iran) found significant relative reductions in suicidal ideation and suicide attempts at 12 months. Beautrais 2010 (PMID: 20592434; New Zealand, after self-harm of any method) found no significant differences at all — the treatment made no difference in that trial. Effects may depend on population (self-poisoning versus all self-harm) and setting; no trial was powered for suicide deaths. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Carter 2005 (Postcards from the EDge): in 772 patients after deliberate self-poisoning, eight postcards over 12 months did not significantly reduce the proportion who repeated (15.1% vs 17.3%) but did reduce the number of repeat episodes per person (incidence risk ratio 0.55)
cards.summary: Carter 2005 (Postcards from the EDge): in 772 patients after deliberate self-poisoning, eight postcards over 12 months did not significantly reduce the proportion who repeated (15.1% vs 17.3%) but did reduce the number of repeat episodes per person (incidence risk ratio 0.55)
cards.people: 772 patients aged over 16 years with deliberate self poisoning treated at a regional referral service in Newcastle, Australia; the intervention was eight postcards over 12 months plus standard treatment, compared with standard treatment alone (378 intervention and 394 control patients in the repetition analysis).
cards.result: The proportion of patients with one or more repeat episodes did not differ significantly between groups (57/378, 15.1%, 95% CI 11.5% to 18.7%, versus 68/394, 17.3%, 95% CI 13.5% to 21.0%: difference −2%, 95% CI −7% to 3%). In unadjusted analysis the number of repetitions was significantly reduced (incidence risk ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.87), a relative measure set against the absolute repetition rates of 15.1% versus 17.3% above.
cards.watchOut: The headline depends on which outcome is read: the proportion of people repeating — arguably the more important outcome — was not significantly reduced; only the count of episodes per person fell, and that in unadjusted analysis.
cards.source: Carter GL, Clover K, Whyte IM, Dawson AH, D'Este C. Postcards from the EDge project: randomised controlled trial of an intervention using postcards to reduce repetition of hospital treated deliberate self poisoning. BMJ. 2005. PMID: 16183654. cards.headline: Hassanian-Moghaddam 2011 (Postcards in Persia): in 2,300 patients after self-poisoning in Iran, nine postcards over 12 months reduced suicidal ideation (31% relative risk reduction) and suicide attempts (42% relative risk reduction)
cards.summary: Hassanian-Moghaddam 2011 (Postcards in Persia): in 2,300 patients after self-poisoning in Iran, nine postcards over 12 months reduced suicidal ideation (31% relative risk reduction) and suicide attempts (42% relative risk reduction)
cards.people: 2,300 individuals who self-poisoned and were hospital-treated in Iran, randomised to nine postcards sent over 12 months versus usual treatment; outcomes were assessed at 12 months in 2,113 participants.
cards.result: There was a significant reduction in any suicidal ideation (relative risk reduction = 0.31, 95% CI 0.22 to 0.38 — that is, a 31% relative risk reduction), any suicide attempt (relative risk reduction = 0.42, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.63 — a 42% relative risk reduction) and number of attempts (incidence rate ratio 0.64, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.97). There was no significant reduction in any self-cutting (relative risk reduction = 0.14, 95% CI −0.29 to 0.42) or self-cutting events (incidence rate ratio 1.03, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.39). The record reports these as relative measures without printing the underlying absolute group rates in its abstract.
cards.watchOut: The largest and most positive postcard trial, but its outcomes are self-reported ideation and attempts at 12 months in one country's self-poisoning population, reported as relative reductions; the same intervention family produced a null result in New Zealand (Beautrais 2010, carded on this shelf).

cards.headline: Beautrais 2010: in a New Zealand randomised trial after emergency-department self-harm, six postcards over 12 months made no difference — no significant reduction in the proportion re-presenting with self-harm or in the number of re-presentations
cards.summary: Beautrais 2010: in a New Zealand randomised trial after emergency-department self-harm, six postcards over 12 months made no difference — no significant reduction in the proportion re-presenting with self-harm or in the number of re-presentations
cards.people: Patients presenting to the emergency department in Christchurch, New Zealand, with self-harm; the intervention consisted of six postcards mailed during the 12 months following the index attendance. N not documented in the record.
cards.result: After adjustment for prior self-harm, there were no significant differences between the control and intervention groups in the proportion of participants re-presenting with self-harm or in the total number of re-presentations for self-harm in the 12 months following the initial presentation — the treatment made no difference in this trial. The authors conclude that, together with previous results, the postcard intervention may be effective only for selected subgroups.
cards.watchOut: The population was all self-harm presentations, not only self-poisoning, and the outcome was hospital re-presentation rather than self-reported attempts — either difference could explain why this trial is null where the self-poisoning trials found episode reductions.

cards.headline: Synthesis: postcards after self-poisoning reduced repeat episodes in the Australian trial and ideation and attempts in the large Iranian trial, but did not reduce the proportion of repeaters in Australia and made no difference at all in New Zealand
cards.summary: Synthesis: postcards after self-poisoning reduced repeat episodes in the Australian trial and ideation and attempts in the large Iranian trial, but did not reduce the proportion of repeaters in Australia and made no difference at all in New Zealand
cards.people: The carded evidence: three randomised trials — 772 patients after self-poisoning (Australia), 2,300 after self-poisoning (Iran), and an emergency-department self-harm population in New Zealand (N not documented in the record).
cards.result: Carter 2005: repeaters 15.1% versus 17.3% (not significant), repeat episodes incidence risk ratio 0.55 (PMID: 16183654). Hassanian-Moghaddam 2011: 31% relative risk reduction in ideation and 42% relative risk reduction in attempts (PMID: 21343332). Beautrais 2010: no significant differences on either outcome — the treatment made no difference (PMID: 20592434). No carded trial measured suicide deaths. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — two positive trials on episode/attempt outcomes against one null trial, with the patient-level repetition outcome unproven.
cards.watchOut: Setting and case-mix track the results — self-poisoning cohorts in Australia and Iran versus all-method self-harm in New Zealand — so a service should not assume the Iranian result transfers to its own population.
