shelves.title: Brief intervention and contact after a suicide attempt: suicide deaths were 0.2% versus 2.2% at 18 months in a 1,867-patient five-country trial — while a 200-patient trial of the same model found no difference in repeat presentations
shelves.question: After a suicide attempt, does brief intervention plus scheduled follow-up contact reduce repeat attempts and deaths?
shelves.mesh: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: One strongly positive multisite trial on deaths, one null trial on repeat presentations, and a strategy review. Fleischmann 2008 (PMID: 18797646; 1,867 suicide attempters in five low- and middle-income countries) found suicide deaths at 18 months of 0.2% with brief intervention and contact versus 2.2% with treatment as usual (P < 0.001). Amadéo 2015 (PMID: 26605034; 200 randomised patients in French Polynesia, the WHO START study) found no significant differences in repeat hospital presentations for suicidal behaviour — the treatment made no difference on that outcome in that setting. Zalsman 2016 (PMID: 27289303), a 10-year systematic review of suicide-prevention strategies, found the strongest evidence for restricting access to lethal means and for school-based awareness programmes, placing brief contact interventions in a wider, mixed evidence base. Discordant trials cap the stamp. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Fleischmann 2008 (WHO SUPRE-MISS): in 1,867 suicide attempters across five countries, brief intervention and contact was followed by far fewer suicide deaths at 18 months — 0.2% versus 2.2% with treatment as usual (P < 0.001)
cards.summary: Fleischmann 2008 (WHO SUPRE-MISS): in 1,867 suicide attempters across five countries, brief intervention and contact was followed by far fewer suicide deaths at 18 months — 0.2% versus 2.2% with treatment as usual (P < 0.001)
cards.people: 1,867 suicide attempters identified by medical staff in the emergency units of eight collaborating hospitals in five sites (Campinas, Brazil; Chennai, India; Colombo, Sri Lanka; Karaj, Iran; and Yuncheng, China), randomised to treatment as usual or treatment as usual plus brief intervention and contact (patient education and follow-up), from January 2002 to October 2005; 91% completed the study.
cards.result: Significantly fewer deaths from suicide occurred in the brief intervention and contact group than in the treatment-as-usual group at 18-month follow-up (0.2% versus 2.2%, respectively; chi-square = 13.83, P < 0.001). These are the absolute rates as reported in the record; the corresponding relative reduction is about 91% in relative terms. The authors conclude this low-cost brief intervention may be an important part of suicide prevention programmes for underresourced low- and middle-income countries.

cards.summary: Amadéo 2015 (WHO START, French Polynesia): in 200 randomised patients after suicidal behaviour, brief intervention plus nine phone contacts over 18 months made no difference to repeat hospital presentations for suicidal behaviour
cards.people: 200 participants randomised (100 to treatment as usual and 100 to treatment as usual plus brief intervention and contact), drawn from 515 patients admitted to the emergency department of the Centre Hospitalier de Polynésie Française for suicidal behavior over 2008–2010 and hospitalised in the Psychiatry Emergency Unit; the intervention was a psycho-education session plus 9 phone contacts over an 18-month period.
cards.result: At the end of follow-up there were no significant differences between the two groups in terms of number of presentations to the hospital for repeated suicidal behaviors — the treatment made no difference on this outcome. The authors note the study nonetheless raised public attention and awareness of the need for suicide prevention in French Polynesia, and that the model seemed to suit the geographical and health care context.
cards.watchOut: Much smaller than the five-country trial (200 versus 1,867 participants) and its outcome was repeat presentations rather than deaths, so it does not directly refute the mortality finding — but it is the same intervention model returning a null result, and it prevents any stronger stamp.

cards.headline: Zalsman 2016: a 10-year systematic review of suicide-prevention strategies found the strongest evidence for restricting access to lethal means (analgesic control associated with a 43% decrease; jumping hot-spots with an 86% reduction) and for school-based awareness programmes (attempts odds ratio 0.45)
cards.summary: Zalsman 2016: a 10-year systematic review of suicide-prevention strategies found the strongest evidence for restricting access to lethal means (analgesic control associated with a 43% decrease; jumping hot-spots with an 86% reduction) and for school-based awareness programmes (attempts odds ratio 0.45)
cards.people: 1,797 studies identified for 2005–2014, including 23 systematic reviews, 12 meta-analyses, 40 randomised controlled trials, 67 cohort trials and 22 ecological or population-based investigations, covering public and physician education, media strategies, screening, restricting access to suicide means, treatments, and internet or hotline support; 18 suicide prevention experts from 13 European countries rated the strength of evidence.
cards.result: Evidence for restricting access to lethal means strengthened since 2005, especially control of analgesics (overall decrease of 43% since 2005) and hot-spots for suicide by jumping (reduction of 86% since 2005, 95% CI 79% to 91%). School-based awareness programmes reduced suicide attempts (odds ratio 0.45, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.85; P = .014) and suicidal ideation (odds ratio 0.5, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.92; P = .025) — relative measures as reported in the record. The anti-suicidal effects of clozapine and lithium were substantiated. Heterogeneity did not permit formal meta-analysis, so the review is a narrative analysis.
cards.watchOut: This card is context, not a test of brief intervention and contact itself: the review's strongest verdicts concern means restriction (homed on its own shelf in this wave) and school programmes, and brief contact interventions sit in a broader, more mixed part of its evidence base.
cards.source: Zalsman G, Hawton K, Wasserman D, van Heeringen K, Arensman E, Sarchiapone M, et al. Suicide prevention strategies revisited: 10-year systematic review. The Lancet Psychiatry. 2016. cards.headline: Synthesis: brief intervention and contact after a suicide attempt was followed by markedly fewer suicide deaths in one large five-country trial (0.2% vs 2.2%), but a smaller trial of the same model found no difference in repeat presentations
cards.summary: Synthesis: brief intervention and contact after a suicide attempt was followed by markedly fewer suicide deaths in one large five-country trial (0.2% vs 2.2%), but a smaller trial of the same model found no difference in repeat presentations
cards.people: The carded evidence: two randomised trials of the brief intervention and contact model (1,867 and 200 participants) and one 10-year strategy systematic review (1,797 studies identified).
cards.result: Fleischmann 2008 found suicide deaths of 0.2% versus 2.2% at 18 months (P < 0.001) across five low- and middle-income countries (PMID: 18797646). Amadéo 2015 found no significant differences in repeat hospital presentations in French Polynesia — the treatment made no difference on that outcome (PMID: 26605034). Zalsman 2016 places contact interventions within a strategy evidence base whose strongest elements are means restriction and school-based programmes (PMID: 27289303). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — one positive mortality trial, unreplicated, against one null trial.
cards.watchOut: Deaths and repeat presentations are different outcomes: the evidence is compatible with contact reducing deaths without measurably reducing presentations, but it is equally compatible with the five-country mortality result being a small-numbers finding — only replication can separate those readings.
cards.source: Synthesis of Fleischmann A et al. Bulletin of the World Health Organization. 2008 (PMID: 18797646); Amadéo S et al. Mental Illness. 2015 (PMID: 26605034); Zalsman G et al. The Lancet Psychiatry. 2016 (PMID: 27289303).

shelves.title: Means restriction: locking away barbecue charcoal in one Taiwanese city was followed by a 30% fall in charcoal-burning suicide with no rise in other methods — and two systematic reviews conclude restricting lethal means reduces suicide rates
shelves.question: Does restricting access to lethal means (firearms, pesticides, charcoal, bridges, pack sizes) reduce method-specific and overall suicide rates?
shelves.mesh: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: Policy and natural-experiment evidence only — no randomised trials of means restriction exist, and this shelf's face says so, which caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Two expert systematic reviews converge: Mann 2005 (PMID: 16249421; 10 systematic reviews/meta-analyses, 18 randomised trials, 24 cohort and 41 ecological studies) concluded that restricting access to lethal methods reduces suicide rates, and Yip 2012 (PMID: 22726520) reviewed the empirical studies and concluded that means restriction is effective, with substitution, where it occurs, usually to less lethal methods. The one carded natural experiment with hard numbers, Chen 2015 (PMID: 26305374), found that moving barbecue charcoal to locked storage in New Taipei City was followed by a 30% reduction in charcoal-burning suicide after accounting for secular trends (95% CI 14% to 44%), no compensatory rise in other methods, and an estimated 91 lives saved over 20 months. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational/policy evidence only.

cards.headline: Yip 2012 (Lancet review): across the empirical literature, restricting access to lethal means reduces suicide — and where people substitute another method, the means chosen are typically less lethal and associated with fewer deaths
cards.summary: Yip 2012 (Lancet review): across the empirical literature, restricting access to lethal means reduces suicide — and where people substitute another method, the means chosen are typically less lethal and associated with fewer deaths
cards.people: A narrative review of the empirical studies of means restriction for suicide prevention, covering firearms, pesticides, charcoal, bridges and other methods and the role of media spread of method information; no single study population — N not documented for the review as a whole.
cards.result: Many empirical studies have shown that means restriction is effective. Although some individuals might seek other methods, many do not; when they do, the means chosen are less lethal and are associated with fewer deaths than when more dangerous ones are available. The review also discusses how the spread of information about suicide methods through formal and informal media potentially affects method choice, and the challenges of implementation.
cards.watchOut: A narrative review without a pooled effect size: its conclusion rests on before-after and ecological studies of individual restrictions, each vulnerable to secular trends in suicide rates, which is why the shelf also cards a controlled natural experiment.
cards.source: Yip PS, Caine E, Yousuf S, Chang SS, Wu KC, Chen YY. Means restriction for suicide prevention. Lancet. 2012. PMID: 22726520. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Humans; Mass Media; Public Health; Risk Reduction Behavior; Suicide; Suicide Prevention

cards.headline: Mann 2005 (JAMA systematic review): of all suicide-prevention strategies reviewed, physician education in depression recognition and treatment and restricting access to lethal methods were the two found to reduce suicide rates
cards.summary: Mann 2005 (JAMA systematic review): of all suicide-prevention strategies reviewed, physician education in depression recognition and treatment and restricting access to lethal methods were the two found to reduce suicide rates
cards.people: A systematic review including 10 systematic reviews and meta-analyses, 18 randomised controlled trials, 24 cohort studies and 41 ecological or population-based studies published between 1966 and June 2005, covering education and awareness, screening, treatment of psychiatric disorders, restricting access to lethal means and responsible media reporting; experts from 15 countries reviewed the studies.
cards.result: Education of physicians and restricting access to lethal means were found to prevent suicide. Other methods, including public education, screening programs and media education, need more testing. The authors conclude that physician education in depression recognition and treatment and restricting access to lethal methods reduce suicide rates, and that ascertaining which components of suicide prevention programs are effective is essential to optimise use of limited resources. Heterogeneity did not permit formal meta-analysis; a narrative synthesis is presented.
cards.watchOut: A 2005 verdict on a pre-2005 literature, and a narrative synthesis: it establishes that expert reviewers found means restriction among the very few strategies with supporting evidence, not a quantified effect size.
cards.source: Mann JJ, Apter A, Bertolote J, Beautrais A, Currier D, Haas A, et al. Suicide prevention strategies: a systematic review. JAMA. 2005. PMID: 16249421. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Chen 2015 (Taiwan natural experiment): moving barbecue charcoal to locked storage in New Taipei City was followed by a 30% reduction in charcoal-burning suicide after accounting for secular trends, no compensatory rise in other methods, and an estimated 91 lives saved in 20 months
cards.summary: Chen 2015 (Taiwan natural experiment): moving barbecue charcoal to locked storage in New Taipei City was followed by a 30% reduction in charcoal-burning suicide after accounting for secular trends, no compensatory rise in other methods, and an estimated 91 lives saved in 20 months
cards.type: Quasi-experimental community intervention study — natural experiment (Chen 2015)
cards.people: A quasi-experimental comparison of suicide rates in New Taipei City (intervention site, population 3.9 million), where from 1 May 2012 major retail stores removed barbecue charcoal from open shelves to locked storage, against Taipei City and Kaohsiung City (control sites, each 2.7 million residents) with no such measure; the pre-intervention period was 1 January 2009 to 30 April 2012 and the post-intervention period 1 May 2012 to 31 December 2013.
cards.result: Compared with the pre-intervention period, the estimated rate reduction of charcoal-burning suicide in New Taipei City was 37% (95% CI 17% to 50%) after the intervention; taking secular trends into account, the reduction was 30% (95% CI 14% to 44%). No compensatory rise in non-charcoal-burning suicide was observed in New Taipei City, and no significant reduction in charcoal-burning suicide was observed in the two control sites. A simulation estimated that 91 lives (95% CI 55 to 128) in New Taipei City were saved during the 20 months of the intervention, and the authors report the programme reduced method-specific and overall suicides.
cards.watchOut: One method, one city, one policy: charcoal burning was a common, highly lethal and heavily publicised method in Taiwan at the time, and the '91 lives saved' figure is a simulation estimate, not a count — the design cannot exclude every concurrent change in the intervention city.
cards.source: Chen YY, Chen F, Chang SS, Wong J, Yip PS. Assessing the Efficacy of Restricting Access to Barbecue Charcoal for Suicide Prevention in Taiwan: A Community-Based Intervention Trial. PLoS One. 2015. PMID: 26305374. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: two expert systematic reviews conclude that restricting access to lethal means reduces suicide rates, and a controlled natural experiment found a 30% fall in method-specific suicide with no compensatory rise — all of it policy and natural-experiment evidence, with no randomised trials
cards.summary: Synthesis: two expert systematic reviews conclude that restricting access to lethal means reduces suicide rates, and a controlled natural experiment found a 30% fall in method-specific suicide with no compensatory rise — all of it policy and natural-experiment evidence, with no randomised trials
cards.people: The carded evidence: two systematic/narrative reviews of the means-restriction literature and one quasi-experimental city-level intervention study (population 3.9 million, with two control cities).
cards.result: Mann 2005 found means restriction one of only two strategies with evidence of reducing suicide rates (PMID: 16249421). Yip 2012 concluded many empirical studies show means restriction is effective and that substitution, when it occurs, is usually to less lethal methods (PMID: 22726520). Chen 2015 found a 30% reduction in charcoal-burning suicide after secular-trend adjustment (95% CI 14% to 44%), no compensatory rise in other methods, and an estimated 91 lives saved over 20 months (PMID: 26305374). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational/policy evidence only; no randomised trials of means restriction exist, and the face of this shelf says so.
cards.watchOut: Effects are method- and place-specific: a restriction works where the method is common and lethal, and each new restriction needs its own local evaluation for substitution — the reviews support the strategy, not any single untried measure.
cards.source: Synthesis of Yip PS et al. Lancet. 2012 (PMID: 22726520); Mann JJ et al. JAMA. 2005 (PMID: 16249421); Chen YY et al. PLoS One. 2015 (PMID: 26305374).

shelves.title: Targeted grief therapy beats standard therapy in randomised trials: response 51% versus 28% for complicated-grief treatment over interpersonal therapy, CBT beat supportive counselling, and adding exposure cut still-meeting-criteria rates to 14.8% versus 37.9%
shelves.question: In complicated/prolonged grief disorder, does targeted grief therapy (complicated-grief treatment or CBT) beat supportive/interpersonal therapy?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: Adaptation, Psychological · Adjustment Disorders · Adult · Affective Symptoms · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy · Major Depressive Disorder · Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders · Female · Grief · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Mood Disorders · Prospective Studies · Psychotherapy, Brief · Stress Disorders, Post-Traumatic
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit). Three independent randomised trials point the same way. Shear 2005 (PMID: 15928281; 95 people with complicated grief) found response in 51% on complicated-grief treatment versus 28% on interpersonal psychotherapy (P = .02; number needed to treat 4.3). Boelen 2007 (PMID: 17469885; 54 mourners) found cognitive-behavioural therapy (cognitive restructuring plus exposure, in either order) produced more improvement in complicated grief and general psychopathology than supportive counselling, with exposure the stronger component. Bryant 2014 (PMID: 25338187; ACTRN12609000229279; 80 patients with prolonged grief disorder) found group CBT plus individual exposure sessions beat the same group CBT plus supportive counselling at 6 months, with fewer completers still meeting prolonged-grief criteria (14.8% vs 37.9%). The trials are small and use active comparators rather than no treatment, so the stamp is for targeted therapy over supportive/interpersonal therapy, not over nothing. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).

cards.headline: Shear 2005: complicated-grief treatment beat interpersonal psychotherapy — response 51% versus 28% (P = .02), number needed to treat 4.3
cards.summary: Shear 2005: complicated-grief treatment beat interpersonal psychotherapy — response 51% versus 28% (P = .02), number needed to treat 4.3
cards.people: 95 people (83 women, 12 men; aged 18 to 85 years) meeting criteria for complicated grief, randomised to complicated grief treatment (n = 49) or interpersonal psychotherapy (n = 46); both given in 16 sessions over an average of 19 weeks.
cards.result: Both treatments improved complicated-grief symptoms, but the response rate was greater for complicated grief treatment (51%) than for interpersonal psychotherapy (28%; P = .02), time to response was faster (P = .02), and the number needed to treat was 4.3. Response was defined as an independent evaluator Clinical Global Improvement score of 1 or 2, or a 20-point or better improvement on the Inventory of Complicated Grief.
cards.watchOut: The comparator was an active, credible psychotherapy, not no treatment — so this shows the targeted treatment is better than a standard therapy, not how much either beats natural recovery; the sample was mostly women recruited through referral and media announcements.
cards.source: Shear K et al. Treatment of complicated grief: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2005. PMID: 15928281. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Boelen 2007: CBT (cognitive restructuring plus exposure) improved complicated grief more than supportive counselling, and exposure was the stronger component
cards.summary: Boelen 2007: CBT (cognitive restructuring plus exposure) improved complicated grief more than supportive counselling, and exposure was the stronger component
cards.people: 54 mourners with clinically significant complicated grief, allocated by minimisation to cognitive restructuring then exposure (6 sessions each), exposure then cognitive restructuring, or 12 sessions of supportive counselling.
cards.result: The two cognitive-behavioural conditions produced more improvement in complicated grief and general psychopathology than supportive counselling, in both completer and intention-to-treat groups. 'Pure' exposure was more effective than 'pure' cognitive restructuring; adding exposure to restructuring brought more additional improvement than the reverse order, and exposure-then-restructuring was the most efficacious sequence. The fetched record reports no numeric effect sizes, so none are printed here.
cards.watchOut: Small (54 people across three arms) and allocated by minimisation rather than simple randomisation; with no numeric results in the fetched record, this card supports direction, not size, of effect.
cards.source: Boelen PA et al. Treatment of complicated grief: a comparison between cognitive-behavioral therapy and supportive counseling. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology. 2007. cards.headline: Bryant 2014: adding exposure sessions to group CBT for prolonged grief gave greater symptom reductions at 6 months, and fewer completers still met criteria (14.8% versus 37.9%)
cards.summary: Bryant 2014: adding exposure sessions to group CBT for prolonged grief gave greater symptom reductions at 6 months, and fewer completers still met criteria (14.8% versus 37.9%)
cards.people: 80 patients with prolonged grief disorder at a university traumatic-stress clinic; all received 10 weekly 2-hour group CBT sessions, plus 4 individual sessions randomised to exposure therapy for memories of the death or supportive counselling.
cards.result: At 6-month follow-up, CBT/exposure led to greater reductions in prolonged grief than CBT alone (quadratic time-by-condition interaction B [SE] 0.49 [0.16]; P = .003), and to greater reductions in depression (P = .005), negative appraisals (P = .009) and functional impairment (P = .003). Among completers, 14.8% in the CBT/exposure condition still met prolonged-grief criteria versus 37.9% with CBT alone (odds ratio 3.51; 95% CI 0.96 to 12.89; P = .04).
cards.watchOut: This is a component trial — everyone received group CBT — so it shows exposure adds to CBT, not that CBT alone beats no treatment; the still-meeting-criteria contrast is in completers, and its confidence interval (0.96 to 12.89) is wide.
cards.source: Bryant RA et al. Treating prolonged grief disorder: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA Psychiatry. 2014. PMID: 25338187. Registry ID: ACTRN12609000229279. cards.headline: Synthesis: targeted, grief-focused therapy — especially with an exposure component — beats supportive or interpersonal therapy across three small randomised trials
cards.summary: Synthesis: targeted, grief-focused therapy — especially with an exposure component — beats supportive or interpersonal therapy across three small randomised trials
cards.people: The carded evidence: three randomised trials, 95, 54 and 80 participants (229 in total), all in complicated/prolonged grief, all against active comparators.
cards.result: Complicated-grief treatment beat interpersonal psychotherapy on response (51% vs 28%; Shear 2005); CBT beat supportive counselling on grief and general psychopathology, with exposure the stronger ingredient (Boelen 2007); and CBT plus exposure beat CBT plus supportive counselling at 6 months, including fewer completers still meeting criteria (14.8% vs 37.9%; Bryant 2014). No carded trial compares targeted therapy with no treatment or a waiting list. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — two-trial gate met against active therapy, with a consistent exposure signal.
cards.watchOut: These trials treat diagnosed complicated/prolonged grief, not ordinary bereavement — nothing here supports routine therapy for normal grief, and all three samples are small by modern trial standards.
cards.source: Synthesis of Shear K et al. JAMA. 2005 (PMID: 15928281); Boelen PA et al. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology. 2007 (PMID: 17469885); Bryant RA et al. JAMA Psychiatry. 2014 (PMID: 25338187; ACTRN12609000229279).

shelves.title: START coping programme for dementia family carers: anxiety/depression scores 1.8 points lower at 8 months and 2.58 points lower at 2 years than usual care in its one randomised trial, with case-level depression odds cut (odds ratio 0.24)
shelves.question: In family carers of people with dementia, does the manual-based START coping programme improve carer mental health cost-effectively?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: Adaptation, Psychological · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anxiety · Caregivers · Dementia · Depression · Elder Abuse · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Manuals as Topic · Middle Aged · Psychological Tests · Psychotherapy · Quality of Life · Single-Blind Method · Social Support · Surveys and Questionnaires
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), single-trial programme cap. All three cards are reports of the same pragmatic randomised trial of START (STrAtegies for RelaTives), an 8-session manual-based coping programme delivered by supervised psychology graduates — the main clinical-effectiveness report pinned at this build gate is Livingston 2013 (PMID: 24162942). In 260 carers, affective symptoms (Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale total) were lower with START than treatment as usual over 8 months (adjusted difference −1.80 points; 95% CI −3.29 to −0.31; P = 0.02), case-level depression was less likely (odds ratio 0.24; 95% CI 0.07 to 0.76), and carer quality of life was higher. The nested economic report (PMID: 24162943) found a greater than 99% chance of cost-effectiveness at a £30,000-per-QALY threshold, and the 2-year report (PMID: 26361313) found the mood benefit persisted (difference −2.58 points; P = 0.003). REACH II and the Mittelman NYU intervention are NOT re-carded here — they are homed at live shelf #795; this shelf homes START only. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Livingston 2013 (START main clinical report, pinned at build gate): carers' anxiety/depression scores were 1.80 points lower than usual care over 8 months, and case-level depression odds were cut to 0.24
cards.summary: Livingston 2013 (START main clinical report, pinned at build gate): carers' anxiety/depression scores were 1.80 points lower than usual care over 8 months, and case-level depression odds were cut to 0.24
cards.type: Pragmatic randomised controlled trial — main clinical-effectiveness report (Livingston 2013)
cards.people: 260 family carers of people with dementia in London and Essex, UK, randomised to the 8-session manual-based START coping programme delivered by supervised psychology graduates (n = 173) or treatment as usual (n = 87).
cards.result: Mean Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale total scores were lower in the START group over the 8-month period (adjusted difference in means −1.80 points; 95% CI −3.29 to −0.31; P = 0.02). Carers in the START group were less likely to have case-level depression (odds ratio 0.24; 95% CI 0.07 to 0.76), with a non-significant trend to less case-level anxiety (odds ratio 0.30; 95% CI 0.08 to 1.05). Carer quality of life was higher (difference 4.09; 95% CI 0.34 to 7.83); the care recipient's quality of life did not differ, and less abusive behaviour by carers was reported but not significant (odds ratio 0.47; 95% CI 0.18 to 1.23).
cards.watchOut: One trial, one country, one delivery model (supervised psychology graduates): the effect is on carer symptoms and carer quality of life, not on the person with dementia, whose quality of life did not change.
cards.source: Livingston G et al. Clinical effectiveness of a manual based coping strategy programme (START, STrAtegies for RelaTives) in promoting the mental health of carers of family members with dementia: pragmatic randomised controlled trial. BMJ. 2013. PMID: 24162942. Registry ID: ISCTRN70017938 (as printed in the record). cards.headline: Knapp 2013 (START economic report): no significant cost difference, a 0.03 QALY gain, and a greater than 99% chance of being cost-effective at £30,000 per QALY
cards.summary: Knapp 2013 (START economic report): no significant cost difference, a 0.03 QALY gain, and a greater than 99% chance of being cost-effective at £30,000 per QALY
cards.type: Cost-effectiveness analysis nested in the START randomised trial (Knapp 2013)
cards.people: The same 260 START trial participants (173 START, 87 usual treatment); costs and outcomes analysed over 8 months from a health and social care perspective.
cards.result: Mean affective-symptom scores were lower with START (mean difference −1.79; 95% CI −3.32 to −0.33) and quality-adjusted life years slightly higher (0.03; 95% CI −0.01 to 0.08). Costs did not differ between groups (£252 higher for START; 95% CI −28 to 565). The calculations suggested START had a greater than 99% chance of being cost-effective compared with usual treatment at a willingness-to-pay threshold of £30,000 per QALY gained.
cards.watchOut: An economic analysis of the same single trial, not independent evidence of effect: the QALY gain's confidence interval crosses zero, and the >99% figure is a probability from the trial's own cost-effectiveness modelling at a UK threshold.
cards.source: Knapp M et al. Cost effectiveness of a manual based coping strategy programme in promoting the mental health of family carers of people with dementia (the START (STrAtegies for RelaTives) study): a pragmatic randomised controlled trial. BMJ. 2013. PMID: 24162943. Registry ID: ISCTRN 70017938 (as printed in the record's abstract). cards.headline: Livingston 2014 (START 2-year report): the mood benefit persisted at 24 months (difference −2.58 points; P = 0.003), and control carers were seven times more likely to have clinically significant depression
cards.summary: Livingston 2014 (START 2-year report): the mood benefit persisted at 24 months (difference −2.58 points; P = 0.003), and control carers were seven times more likely to have clinically significant depression
cards.people: 260 carers recruited to the START trial; 209 (80%) were included in the long-term clinical efficacy analysis (140 START, 69 treatment as usual), with masked outcome assessment at 12 and 24 months.
cards.result: At 24 months the START group was significantly better on affective symptoms (Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale total mean difference −2.58 points; 95% CI −4.26 to −0.90; P = 0.003). Carers in the control group were seven times more likely to have clinically significant depression than those receiving START. Over 24 months the intervention was cost-effective for carer and patient outcomes, with a 67% probability of cost-effectiveness at a £20,000-per-QALY threshold and 70% at £30,000 per QALY.
cards.watchOut: Still the same single trial: 20% of recruits were excluded from the efficacy analysis for missing data at both follow-ups, and a 2-year effect from 8 sessions is unusually durable — replication outside this programme has not been carded on this shelf.
cards.source: Livingston G et al. Long-term clinical and cost-effectiveness of psychological intervention for family carers of people with dementia: a single-blind, randomised, controlled trial. cards.headline: Synthesis: START improved dementia carers' mood in its one randomised trial, the benefit was still present at 2 years, and the programme was probably cost-effective — a single-trial programme, so the stamp is capped
cards.summary: Synthesis: START improved dementia carers' mood in its one randomised trial, the benefit was still present at 2 years, and the programme was probably cost-effective — a single-trial programme, so the stamp is capped
cards.people: The carded evidence: one pragmatic randomised trial (260 carers) reported three ways — 8-month clinical outcomes, 8-month cost-effectiveness, and 24-month clinical and cost outcomes — plus no independent replication carded here.
cards.result: START lowered carer affective symptoms at 8 months (−1.80 points; case-level depression odds ratio 0.24; Livingston 2013), cost no significantly more than usual care with a >99% modelled chance of cost-effectiveness at £30,000 per QALY (Knapp 2013), and remained effective at 24 months (−2.58 points; P = 0.003; Livingston 2014). A 2026 cultural-adaptation and feasibility study of START in India (PMID: 42001414; 22 caregivers recruited, 18 completing all sessions) shows the programme can be adapted and delivered virtually, but reports no comparative effectiveness outcome and is therefore noted here, not carded. REACH II and the Mittelman NYU intervention are homed at live shelf #795 and are not re-carded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-trial cap.
cards.watchOut: Three cards, one trial: do not read this shelf as three independent confirmations. The named programme is START (STrAtegies for RelaTives), named for clarification as a manualised programme, not a drug.
cards.source: Synthesis of Livingston G et al. BMJ. 2013 (PMID: 24162942); Knapp M et al. BMJ. 2013 (PMID: 24162943); Livingston G et al. The Lancet Psychiatry. 2014 (PMID: 26361313).

shelves.title: Telephone ACT for dementia caregivers: depressive symptoms were significantly lower after 8 weekly telephone sessions in the one telephone randomised trial (81 caregivers), with most effects gone by 6 months
shelves.question: In caregivers of people with dementia, does telephone-delivered ACT improve caregiver outcomes in a randomised trial?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: Humans · Caregivers · Female · Male · Dementia · Aged · Adaptation, Psychological · Acceptance and Commitment Therapy · Telephone · Quality of Life · Middle Aged · Depression · Social Support · Anxiety · Aged, 80 and over · Grief
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), single-trial cap for the telephone question. The only randomised trial of telephone-delivered acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT) for family caregivers of people with dementia is Risch 2024 (PMID: 39169671; DRKS00006355; 81 caregivers): after 8 weekly telephone sessions, depressive symptoms were significantly lower than in an untreated control group, with several secondary benefits, but most effects were not maintained at 6 months and the authors call the results preliminary because of the small sample. Two neighbouring ACT records support the approach without answering the telephone question directly: a 19-person pilot randomised trial of videoconferencing ACT (PMID: 36591636; NCT04847986) and a 135-caregiver face-to-face trial in which ACT matched CBT against control on depression and beat it on anxiety at post-treatment (PMID: 26075381). This shelf is distinct from live shelf #795 (REACH II / Mittelman NYU) and from shelf #5515 (START), neither of which is re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Risch 2024: 8 weekly telephone ACT sessions lowered dementia caregivers' depressive symptoms versus untreated control — but most effects were not maintained at 6 months
cards.summary: Risch 2024: 8 weekly telephone ACT sessions lowered dementia caregivers' depressive symptoms versus untreated control — but most effects were not maintained at 6 months
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial of telephone-delivered ACT (Risch 2024)
cards.people: 81 family caregivers of persons with dementia, randomised to telephone-based ACT (n = 41) or an untreated control group (n = 40); the intervention was 8 weekly telephone sessions, with post-assessment and a 6-month follow-up. Registry DRKS00006355.
cards.result: Compared with controls, the telephone-ACT group had significantly lower depressive symptoms at post-assessment, fewer physical symptoms (rheumatic pain), better physical health, more resource utilisation (coping with daily hassles, social support), better coping with the care situation and better emotional well-being. At 6-month follow-up the ACT group showed less pre-death grief, fewer physical symptoms and more use of daily-hassle coping resources — but most post-treatment effects were not maintained, leading the authors to suggest booster sessions. The fetched record gives significance, not numeric effect sizes, so none are printed here.

cards.headline: Han 2023: in a 19-caregiver pilot randomised trial, videoconferencing ACT reduced grief more than psychoeducation alone at post-treatment (medium effect)
cards.summary: Han 2023: in a 19-caregiver pilot randomised trial, videoconferencing ACT reduced grief more than psychoeducation alone at post-treatment (medium effect)
cards.type: Pilot randomised controlled trial of videoconferencing ACT (Han 2023)
cards.people: 19 distressed family caregivers of people living with dementia in the USA, randomly assigned to an 8-week videoconferencing ACT programme supplemented with psychoeducation materials, or to psychoeducation materials only; assessed at pretest, posttest and 1-month follow-up. Registry NCT04847986. N = 19 is printed on the face of this card.
cards.result: Compared with the control group, the ACT group showed a significantly larger reduction in grief at posttest, with a medium effect size. Small effects favouring ACT were found for anxiety, psychological quality of life and engagement in meaningful activities at posttest, and for grief, engagement in meaningful activities and psychological flexibility at follow-up. The authors state these findings warrant a full-scale randomised trial with adequate power.
cards.watchOut: A pilot with only 19 participants (N printed on the face): it tests feasibility and gives preliminary effects only, and it is videoconferencing, not telephone delivery — it supports the ACT approach, not the telephone claim directly.

cards.headline: Losada 2015: face-to-face ACT matched CBT against control for depressed dementia caregivers (depression effect size 1.17; number needed to treat 3.53), and beat CBT on anxiety at post-treatment
cards.summary: Losada 2015: face-to-face ACT matched CBT against control for depressed dementia caregivers (depression effect size 1.17; number needed to treat 3.53), and beat CBT on anxiety at post-treatment
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial of face-to-face ACT versus CBT (Losada 2015)
cards.people: 135 dementia family caregivers with high depressive symptomatology, randomly allocated to ACT, CBT or a control group, with pre-, post-intervention and follow-up measurements.
cards.result: For depression, both ACT (P < .001; effect size d = 1.17; number needed to treat 3.53) and CBT (P < .001; d = 0.98; NNT 3.61) beat control at post-intervention, but the effect was maintained at follow-up only for CBT. Clinically significant change was seen in 24.2% on ACT, 26.7% on CBT and 0% on control. For anxiety at post-intervention, ACT participants scored lower than both CBT (P < .05; d = 0.50) and control (P < .01; d = 0.79; NNT 3.86), with no anxiety effects at follow-up. Changes in experiential avoidance occurred only with ACT.
cards.watchOut: Face-to-face delivery in caregivers selected for high depressive symptoms: it establishes that ACT can work in this population, not that telephone delivery preserves the effect — and ACT's own depression effect was not maintained at follow-up in this trial either.
cards.source: Losada A et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: ACT helps dementia caregivers in the short term across delivery modes, but the telephone-specific evidence is one small trial whose effects mostly faded by 6 months
cards.summary: Synthesis: ACT helps dementia caregivers in the short term across delivery modes, but the telephone-specific evidence is one small trial whose effects mostly faded by 6 months
cards.people: The carded evidence: one telephone randomised trial (81 caregivers), one videoconferencing pilot randomised trial (19 caregivers), and one face-to-face randomised trial (135 caregivers).
cards.result: Telephone ACT lowered depressive symptoms and several secondary outcomes at post-treatment, with most effects gone by 6 months (Risch 2024). Videoconferencing ACT showed a medium grief effect in a 19-person pilot (Han 2023). Face-to-face ACT matched CBT against control on depression and beat it on anxiety at post-treatment, again without maintained ACT effects at follow-up (Losada 2015). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single small telephone trial, short-term effects, booster sessions untested.
cards.watchOut: Nothing carded here tests telephone ACT against an active attention control, and no carded trial tests the booster sessions the telephone trial's authors suggest — durability is the open question on this shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Risch AK et al. Clinical Gerontologist. 2025 (PMID: 39169671; DRKS00006355); Han A et al. Journal of Health Psychology. 2023 (PMID: 36591636; NCT04847986); Losada A et al. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology. 2015 (PMID: 26075381).

shelves.title: AI therapy chatbots: two small, short randomised trials in students found less depression with Woebot (P = .01) and with Tess than with an information-only control — and no randomised evidence for AI 'companions' as a loneliness treatment was found
shelves.question: Do AI chatbots improve depression/anxiety symptoms — and what is actually randomised?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), with the honest-evidence limits printed on the face. What is actually randomised: Woebot, a fully automated CBT conversational agent, in 70 students over 2 weeks (PMID: 28588005) — depression symptoms fell significantly in the Woebot group and not in the information-only control (P = .01); and Tess, an integrative psychological AI, in 74 students over 2 to 4 weeks (PMID: 30545815; ISRCTN61214172) — depression and anxiety reductions versus the same kind of information-only control. What is only observational: Wysa (PMID: 30470676), where self-selected high users improved more than low users (mean 5.84 vs 3.52 points; P = .03) — a comparison that cannot separate the app from the motivation to use it. No randomised evidence for AI 'companions' as a loneliness treatment was found this session: the randomised agents are symptom-therapy chatbots tested in students for 2 to 4 weeks, and that absence is part of this shelf, not a gap to paper over. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Fitzpatrick 2017 (Woebot): in the one randomised trial of a named therapy chatbot, students' depression symptoms fell significantly over 2 weeks while the information-only control group's did not (P = .01)
cards.summary: Fitzpatrick 2017 (Woebot): in the one randomised trial of a named therapy chatbot, students' depression symptoms fell significantly over 2 weeks while the information-only control group's did not (P = .01)
cards.people: 70 individuals aged 18 to 28 years recruited online from a university community, randomised to 2 weeks (up to 20 sessions) of CBT-derived self-help content delivered by the text-based conversational agent Woebot (n = 34) or to the National Institute of Mental Health ebook 'Depression in College Students' as an information-only control (n = 36); 83% provided follow-up data at 2 to 3 weeks.
cards.result: Intent-to-treat analysis showed a significant group difference on depression: the Woebot group significantly reduced symptoms on the 9-item Patient Health Questionnaire (F = 6.47; P = .01) while the control group did not. In completers, both groups significantly reduced anxiety on the 7-item Generalized Anxiety Disorder scale (F1,54 = 9.24; P = .004). Woebot users engaged with the agent an average of 12.14 times over the study period.
cards.watchOut: Small, unblinded, 2 weeks long, in self-selected students with self-identified symptoms, against an ebook rather than any human or active therapy — this is preliminary efficacy for a therapy chatbot, not evidence about AI companionship or loneliness.
cards.source: Fitzpatrick KK et al. Delivering Cognitive Behavior Therapy to Young Adults With Symptoms of Depression and Anxiety Using a Fully Automated Conversational Agent (Woebot): A Randomized Controlled Trial. JMIR Mental Health. 2017. PMID: 28588005. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Fulmer 2018 (Tess): a second small randomised trial of a psychological AI found depression and anxiety reductions versus an information-only control over 2 to 4 weeks
cards.summary: Fulmer 2018 (Tess): a second small randomised trial of a psychological AI found depression and anxiety reductions versus an information-only control over 2 to 4 weeks
cards.people: 75 students recruited from 15 US universities (74 completed), randomised to unlimited access to the integrative psychological AI Tess with daily check-ins for 2 weeks (n = 24), Tess with biweekly check-ins for 4 weeks (n = 26), or an information-only control given a National Institute of Mental Health ebook link (n = 24). Registry ISRCTN61214172, as printed in the record.
cards.result: The 2-week Tess group reported a significant reduction in depression symptoms on the Patient Health Questionnaire versus control (P = .03), while the control group did not improve. Both Tess groups reported significant anxiety reductions on the Generalized Anxiety Disorder scale versus control (2-week group P = .045; 4-week group P = .02). A significant difference on the Positive and Negative Affect Scale was also found for the 2-week group versus control (P = .03).
cards.watchOut: Again small, short and student-only, with an information-only comparator and several outcomes tested at an alpha of .05 — two concordant pilot-scale trials are a signal, not a settled effect, and neither trial enrolled people for loneliness.
cards.source: Fulmer R et al. Using Psychological Artificial Intelligence (Tess) to Relieve Symptoms of Depression and Anxiety: Randomized Controlled Trial. JMIR Mental Health. 2018. PMID: 30545815. Registry ID: ISRCTN61214172 (as printed in the record). MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Inkster 2018 (Wysa): observational only — self-selected high users improved more than low users (mean 5.84 versus 3.52 points; P = .03), which cannot show the app caused the improvement
cards.summary: Inkster 2018 (Wysa): observational only — self-selected high users improved more than low users (mean 5.84 versus 3.52 points; P = .03), which cannot show the app caused the improvement
cards.type: Observational real-world data evaluation, no randomisation (Inkster 2018)
cards.people: Anonymous global users who voluntarily installed the Wysa empathy-driven conversational AI app and self-reported depression symptoms on the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 at two consecutive screening points, divided by usage into high users (n = 108) and low users (n = 21). No randomisation and no control group.
cards.result: Average improvement in self-reported depression scores was significantly higher in high users (mean 5.84 [SD 6.66]) than in low users (mean 3.52 [SD 6.15]; Mann-Whitney P = .03), with a moderate effect size of 0.63. In user feedback responses, 67.7% found the app experience helpful and encouraging. The authors state that further work in larger samples over longer periods is required to validate these findings.
cards.watchOut: Observational only, and printed as such: people who use an app more may differ from low users in motivation, severity and natural recovery, so the high-versus-low contrast is compatible with the app doing nothing. This card must not be read as trial evidence.
cards.source: Inkster B et al. An Empathy-Driven, Conversational Artificial Intelligence Agent (Wysa) for Digital Mental Well-Being: Real-World Data Evaluation Mixed-Methods Study. JMIR mHealth and uHealth. 2018. PMID: 30470676. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: therapy chatbots have two small positive randomised trials in students; companion-style AI for loneliness has no randomised evidence at all — that absence is part of this shelf
cards.summary: Synthesis: therapy chatbots have two small positive randomised trials in students; companion-style AI for loneliness has no randomised evidence at all — that absence is part of this shelf
cards.people: The carded evidence: two randomised trials (70 and 74 students, 2 to 4 weeks, information-only controls) and one observational app study (108 high users, 21 low users).
cards.result: Woebot reduced depression symptoms versus an ebook control (P = .01; Fitzpatrick 2017) and Tess reduced depression and anxiety versus an ebook control (Fulmer 2018). Wysa's evidence is observational only and cannot establish causation (Inkster 2018). No randomised evidence for AI 'companions' as a loneliness treatment was found this session — the randomised record covers short CBT-style symptom programmes in young students, nothing about companionship, older adults, or loneliness as an outcome. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for short chatbot-delivered CBT content on student depression/anxiety symptoms only.
cards.watchOut: Named products (Woebot, Tess, Wysa) are named for clarification as the specific tested programmes, not as recommendations; versions tested in 2017–2018 may differ from versions offered now.

shelves.title: Animal-assisted therapy: a Cochrane review of 9 randomised trials (305 people with dementia) found people may be slightly less depressed (mean difference −2.87) but no quality-of-life improvement, on low-to-moderate certainty evidence
shelves.question: Does animal-assisted therapy improve outcomes in randomised trials, including agitation/depression in dementia?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: Animal Assisted Therapy · Animals · Cats · Dogs · Female · Guinea Pigs · Humans · Male · Mental Disorders · Rabbits · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), for depressive symptoms only and with the certainty limits on the face. The Cochrane review for dementia (PMID: 31763689; 9 randomised trials, 305 participants) found animal-assisted therapy may leave people slightly less depressed (mean difference −2.87; 95% CI −5.24 to −0.50; 2 studies, 83 participants; low-certainty evidence), with no quality-of-life improvement and no clear differences in social functioning, problematic behaviour, agitation or daily activities. The matched dementia trial (PMID: 23831177) found symptoms stayed constant with therapy while they worsened in controls — a delay-of-progression pattern, not an improvement. The broader systematic review of randomised trials across conditions (PMID: 24731910; 11 trials) judged the trials relatively low quality and could not meta-analyse them. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Kamioka 2014: across 11 randomised trials, animal-assisted therapy may help mental and behavioural disorders — but the trials were of relatively low quality and too heterogeneous to meta-analyse
cards.summary: Kamioka 2014: across 11 randomised trials, animal-assisted therapy may help mental and behavioural disorders — but the trials were of relatively low quality and too heterogeneous to meta-analyse
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised controlled trials (Kamioka 2014)
cards.people: 11 randomised controlled trials of animal-assisted therapy published from 1990 to October 2012, using dogs, cats, dolphins, birds, cows, rabbits, ferrets and guinea pigs; seven studies concerned mental and behavioural disorders.
cards.result: The review could not perform a meta-analysis because of heterogeneity. Its conclusion is that, in study environments limited to people who like animals, animal-assisted therapy may be an effective treatment for mental and behavioural disorders such as depression, schizophrenia and alcohol/drug addictions. The authors call for proper randomised methodology, reporting of reasons for non-participation, intervention dose, adverse effects and withdrawals, and costs in future research.
cards.watchOut: A qualitative 'may be effective' from low-quality, unpoolable trials in animal-liking volunteers is the weakest form of systematic-review conclusion — it justifies a POSSIBLE stamp at most, and only alongside the Cochrane card.
cards.source: Kamioka H et al. Effectiveness of animal-assisted therapy: A systematic review of randomized controlled trials. Complementary Therapies in Medicine. 2014. PMID: 24731910. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Animal Assisted Therapy · Animals · Cats · Dogs · Female · Guinea Pigs · Humans · Male · Mental Disorders · Rabbits · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic

cards.headline: Majić 2013: in nursing-home residents with dementia, agitation and depression stayed constant with animal-assisted therapy while they significantly worsened in controls over 10 weeks
cards.summary: Majić 2013: in nursing-home residents with dementia, agitation and depression stayed constant with animal-assisted therapy while they significantly worsened in controls over 10 weeks
cards.people: 65 nursing-home residents with dementia (mean age 81.8 years; mean Mini-Mental State Examination score 7.1), of whom 27 matched pairs (N = 54) were randomly assigned to treatment as usual or treatment as usual plus animal-assisted therapy over 10 weekly sessions; blinded raters assessed agitation/aggression (Cohen-Mansfield Agitation Inventory) and depression (Dementia Mood Assessment Scale).
cards.result: In the control group, symptoms of agitation/aggression and depression significantly increased over 10 weeks; in the intervention group, frequency and severity stayed constant (agitation/aggression F1,48 = 6.43; P < 0.05; depression F1,48 = 26.54; P < 0.001). Symptom amelioration did not occur in either group. The authors interpret this as animal-assisted therapy possibly delaying progression of neuropsychiatric symptoms in demented nursing-home residents.
cards.watchOut: Read the result exactly: nobody improved — the treated group held steady while controls worsened, in residents with very severe cognitive impairment (mean MMSE 7.1). A 10-week holding pattern in 54 analysed residents is not evidence of lasting benefit.
cards.source: Majić T et al. Animal-assisted therapy and agitation and depression in nursing home residents with dementia: a matched case-control trial. The American Journal of Geriatric Psychiatry. 2013. PMID: 23831177. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Animals · Case-Control Studies · Dementia · Depression · Dogs · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neuropsychological Tests · Nursing Homes · Pets · Psychomotor Agitation

cards.headline: Lai 2019 (Cochrane): animal-assisted therapy for dementia may slightly reduce depression (mean difference −2.87; low certainty) but did not improve quality of life, agitation or behaviour across 9 trials and 305 participants
cards.summary: Lai 2019 (Cochrane): animal-assisted therapy for dementia may slightly reduce depression (mean difference −2.87; low certainty) but did not improve quality of life, agitation or behaviour across 9 trials and 305 participants
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (Lai 2019)
cards.people: Nine randomised trials (10 reports, 305 participants with dementia) conducted in Europe and the US, mostly using dogs (one study used horses), with interventions from 6 weeks to 6 months; all studies were at high risk of performance bias and unclear risk of selection bias, and certainty was rated very low to moderate.
cards.result: Versus no animal-assisted therapy, participants who received it may be slightly less depressed after the intervention (mean difference −2.87; 95% CI −5.24 to −0.50; 2 studies, 83 participants; low-certainty evidence), but did not appear to have improved quality of life (mean difference 0.45; 95% CI −1.28 to 2.18; 3 studies, 164 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). There were no clear differences in social functioning, problematic behaviour (standardised mean difference −0.34; 95% CI −0.98 to 0.30; very-low certainty), agitation (−0.39; −0.89 to 0.10; very-low certainty), activities of daily living or self-care. No data on adverse events were reported.
cards.watchOut: The headline depression figure rests on only 2 of the 9 trials and 83 participants at low certainty, and the review's comparisons against robotic animals and soft toys are not summarised here — the honest summary is a possible small depression effect and nothing established beyond it.
cards.source: Lai NM et al. Animal-assisted therapy for dementia. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2019. PMID: 31763689. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Activities of Daily Living · Animal Assisted Therapy · Animals · Cognition · Dementia · Depression · Dogs · Horses · Humans · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic

cards.headline: Synthesis: animal-assisted therapy may slightly ease depressive symptoms in dementia, but agitation, behaviour and quality of life show no clear benefit, and the whole randomised base is small and low quality
cards.summary: Synthesis: animal-assisted therapy may slightly ease depressive symptoms in dementia, but agitation, behaviour and quality of life show no clear benefit, and the whole randomised base is small and low quality
cards.people: The carded evidence: a systematic review of 11 randomised trials across conditions, one matched randomised dementia trial (54 analysed residents), and a Cochrane review of 9 randomised trials (305 participants with dementia).
cards.result: Depression is the only outcome with a pooled positive signal, and it is small and low-certainty (mean difference −2.87; Cochrane 2019). In the one dementia trial carded individually, therapy held symptoms constant while controls worsened (Majić 2013). Quality of life, agitation, behaviour and daily activities show no clear differences (Cochrane 2019), and the wider trial literature is relatively low quality and unpoolable (Kamioka 2014). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — depressive symptoms only.
cards.watchOut: Trials recruit people willing to work with animals, often people who like animals — effects in unselected residents, and any infection, allergy or bite risks, are not established by the carded records, which reported no adverse-event data.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kamioka H et al. Complementary Therapies in Medicine. 2014 (PMID: 24731910); Majić T et al. The American Journal of Geriatric Psychiatry. 2013 (PMID: 23831177); Lai NM et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2019 (PMID: 31763689).

shelves.title: Sleepio for insomnia — daytime outcomes: one large trial (1,711 adults) found better sleep-related quality of life (−18.72 points), functional health and well-being than sleep-hygiene education at 24 weeks, with depressive-symptom and older-adult benefits in secondary analyses
shelves.question: In insomnia disorder, does digital CBT-I (Sleepio) improve sleep, daytime functioning and quality of life versus sleep-hygiene education or waitlist?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy/methods · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Quality of Life · Self Report · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders/psychology/therapy · Therapy, Computer-Assisted/methods · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large randomised trial of the named programme, Sleepio, plus secondary analyses of the Sleepio trial programme. In 1,711 adults with insomnia symptoms, digital CBT-I (Sleepio) beat sleep-hygiene education on all three primary outcomes at 24 weeks: functional health by an adjusted 1.76 points, psychological well-being by 2.95 points, and sleep-related quality of life by −18.72 points on a 1–100 impairment scale, with a large improvement in insomnia mediating the gains (Espie 2019, PMID: 30264137). Secondary analyses point the same way for the outcomes patients feel: in 3,352 participants with probable insomnia and significant depressive symptoms, Sleepio improved depressive symptoms (g = 0.48) and nearly tripled the odds of clinically significant improvement (OR 2.9) (Henry 2021, PMID: 32810921); and in 315 participants aged 65 and over pooled from three Sleepio trials, post-treatment insomnia remission was 60% versus 16% on control (Tarnai 2025, PMID: 40176550). The broader question of app- and web-delivered CBT-I for sleep itself is homed at live shelf #437 (which cards the OASIS trial and the 2012 Sleepio trial) and is cross-pointed, not re-carded here; this shelf stands on Sleepio's functioning and quality-of-life outcomes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for digital CBT-I (Sleepio) on sleep-related quality of life, daytime functioning and well-being versus sleep-hygiene education.

cards.headline: Espie 2019: in 1,711 adults, Sleepio beat sleep-hygiene education on functional health, well-being and sleep-related quality of life at 24 weeks — a large gain in sleep-related quality of life (−18.72 points), small gains in general health and well-being
cards.summary: Espie 2019: in 1,711 adults, Sleepio beat sleep-hygiene education on functional health, well-being and sleep-related quality of life at 24 weeks — a large gain in sleep-related quality of life (−18.72 points), small gains in general health and well-being
cards.people: 1,711 participants with self-reported symptoms of insomnia (77.7% female; mean age 48.0 years), recruited online between December 2015 and December 2016, randomised to digital cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (Sleepio, delivered by web and/or mobile plus treatment as usual) or sleep hygiene education (a website and downloadable booklet plus treatment as usual); primary outcomes were functional health (PROMIS Global Health Scale, range 10–50), psychological well-being (Warwick-Edinburgh scale, range 14–70) and sleep-related quality of life (Glasgow Sleep Impact Index, range 1–100, higher = greater impairment), assessed at 0, 4, 8 and 24 weeks.
cards.result: Digital CBT-I was associated with a small improvement in functional health compared with sleep-hygiene education (adjusted difference at week 24: 1.76; 95% CI 1.22 to 2.30) and in psychological well-being (week 24: 2.95; 95% CI 2.13 to 3.76), and with a large improvement in sleep-related quality of life (week 24: −18.72; 95% CI −22.04 to −15.41) (all P < .01). A large improvement in insomnia, measured with the Sleep Condition Indicator, mediated these outcomes. The trial's first author reports being a cofounder, chief medical officer and shareholder of Big Health Ltd, the developer of Sleepio, as printed in the record's conflict-of-interest statement.
cards.watchOut: Self-reported insomnia symptoms rather than a clinician-made diagnosis, all outcomes self-reported, and the programme's developer is a trial author and shareholder — the large effect is on the sleep-specific quality-of-life scale, while the general health and well-being gains are small in absolute points.
cards.source: Espie CA et al. Effect of Digital Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia on Health, Psychological Well-being, and Sleep-Related Quality of Life: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Psychiatry. 2019. PMID: 30264137. Registry ID: ISRCTN60530898. MeSH: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy/methods · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Quality of Life · Self Report · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders/psychology/therapy · Therapy, Computer-Assisted/methods · Treatment Outcome

cards.headline: Henry 2021: in 3,352 Sleepio trial participants with insomnia and significant depressive symptoms, digital CBT-I improved depressive symptoms (g = 0.48) and nearly tripled the odds of clinically significant improvement (OR 2.9)
cards.summary: Henry 2021: in 3,352 Sleepio trial participants with insomnia and significant depressive symptoms, digital CBT-I improved depressive symptoms (g = 0.48) and nearly tripled the odds of clinically significant improvement (OR 2.9)
cards.type: Sub-analysis of two randomised controlled trials (Henry 2021)
cards.people: Sub-analysis of participant data from two large randomised controlled trials of digital CBT-I (Sleepio): all participants met criteria for probable insomnia disorder and had clinically significant depressive symptomatology (PHQ-9 of 10 or more); n = 3,352; outcomes at post-intervention (weeks 8–10). The two source trials are the programme's large trials; their primary reports are homed elsewhere (live shelf #437) and are not re-carded here.
cards.result: Digital CBT-I significantly improved insomnia (p < .001; g = 0.76) and depressive symptoms (p < .001; g = 0.48) at post-intervention, and increased the odds of clinically significant improvement in depressive symptoms (PHQ-9 below 10) (OR = 2.9; 95% CI 2.34 to 3.65). Improvements in insomnia symptoms at mid-intervention mediated 87% of the effect on depressive symptoms at post-intervention, and no variables moderated the effects. The authors conclude insomnia is an important therapeutic target in managing depressive symptoms.
cards.watchOut: A sub-analysis, not a new trial: it re-uses participants from the programme's two large trials (one of which is carded above), selected for depressive symptoms — it extends the outcome picture to mood but adds no independent randomised evidence.
cards.source: Henry AL et al. Insomnia as a mediating therapeutic target for depressive symptoms: A sub-analysis of participant data from two large randomized controlled trials of a digital sleep intervention. Journal of Sleep Research. 2021. PMID: 32810921. Registry ID: ISRCTN61272251; ISRCTN60530898. MeSH: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy/methods · Depression/complications · Female · Humans · Male · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders/psychology · Treatment Outcome

cards.headline: Tarnai 2025: in 315 adults aged 65 and over pooled from three Sleepio trials, insomnia remission was 60% on digital CBT-I versus 16% on control, with large insomnia effects (g up to −1.88) sustained at 24 weeks
cards.summary: Tarnai 2025: in 315 adults aged 65 and over pooled from three Sleepio trials, insomnia remission was 60% on digital CBT-I versus 16% on control, with large insomnia effects (g up to −1.88) sustained at 24 weeks
cards.type: Secondary individual-participant-data analysis of three randomised trials (Tarnai 2025)
cards.people: Secondary analysis using individual participant data from three published randomised controlled trials of digital CBT for insomnia (Sleepio) versus controls, restricted to participants aged 65 years and older with insomnia disorder (N = 315); insomnia, anxiety and depression scores were standardised as z-scores; outcomes at post-treatment (8–10 weeks) and follow-up (24 weeks).
cards.result: Compared with controls, digital CBT-I generated significantly greater improvements at post-treatment and follow-up in insomnia (g ≤ −1.88; p < 0.001) and depression (g ≤ −0.44; p ≤ 0.001), and in anxiety at post-treatment (g = −0.33; p < 0.001). Post-treatment insomnia remission rates were higher on digital CBT-I (60% versus 16%; p < 0.001). The authors conclude digital CBT-I can effectively improve insomnia, anxiety and depression symptoms in adults aged 65 and over and may avoid adverse effects of common pharmacological treatments.
cards.watchOut: A secondary analysis of three existing trials in an age subgroup (N = 315) — the striking 60% versus 16% remission contrast comes from pooled trial data already published in primary form, not from a dedicated older-adult trial.
cards.source: Tarnai KA et al. Efficacy of digital cognitive behavioral therapy for treating insomnia in adults aged 65 and older: a secondary analysis using individual participant data from three randomized controlled trials. Aging & Mental Health. 2025. PMID: 40176550. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: Sleepio improves sleep-related quality of life substantially and general functioning modestly versus sleep-hygiene education, with mood benefits in secondary analyses — one large trial programme, capped at POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: Sleepio improves sleep-related quality of life substantially and general functioning modestly versus sleep-hygiene education, with mood benefits in secondary analyses — one large trial programme, capped at POSSIBLE
cards.people: The carded evidence: one large randomised trial of Sleepio versus sleep-hygiene education (1,711 participants) reporting functioning and quality-of-life outcomes, plus two secondary analyses of the Sleepio trial programme (3,352 participants with depressive symptoms; 315 participants aged 65 and over). The OASIS trial and the 2012 Sleepio trial are homed at live shelf #437 and cross-pointed, not re-carded.
cards.result: Sleepio improved sleep-related quality of life by −18.72 points at 24 weeks, with small improvements in functional health (1.76 points) and psychological well-being (2.95 points), mediated by improved insomnia (Espie 2019). Secondary analyses found improved depressive symptoms (g = 0.48; OR 2.9 for clinically significant improvement; Henry 2021) and, in older adults, 60% versus 16% insomnia remission (Tarnai 2025). With a single distinct large trial for the primary outcomes, the stamp caps at POSSIBLE. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for digital CBT-I (Sleepio) on sleep-related quality of life, daytime functioning and well-being versus sleep-hygiene education.
cards.watchOut: Two of the three evidence cards are secondary analyses of the same trial programme as the first, so the shelf's independence is limited; participants were self-selected online volunteers with self-reported symptoms, and the developer's authorship interest is printed on the primary card.
cards.source: Synthesis of Espie CA et al. JAMA Psychiatry. 2019 (PMID: 30264137); Henry AL et al. Journal of Sleep Research. 2021 (PMID: 32810921); Tarnai KA et al. Aging & Mental Health. 2025 (PMID: 40176550).

shelves.title: Mirtazapine after stroke: reasonable for post-stroke depression on single-trial and network evidence — but its sleep advantage is a 10-patient uncontrolled observation with a sleep-apnoea caution attached
shelves.question: Should mirtazapine be used for post-stroke depression in patients with poor sleep?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antidepressive Agents, Tricyclic · Depressive Disorder · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Mianserin · Middle Aged · Mirtazapine · Neurologic Examination · Prognosis · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Stroke · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single small open trial programme for the depression outcome, and almost nothing for sleep itself. Niedermaier 2004 randomised 70 acute-stroke patients openly to mirtazapine 30 mg from day 1 or no antidepressant: post-stroke depression developed in 5.7% (2/35) versus 40% (14/35), and 15 of the 16 patients who did develop depression remitted once mirtazapine was started (an uncontrolled treatment phase). A network meta-analysis of 51 randomised trials ranked mirtazapine highest for response at endpoint and among the best at 8 weeks for post-stroke depression (Li 2020). But the poor-sleep half of the question rests on one 10-patient open study in non-depressed stroke patients with sleep apnoea (Brunner 2008): sleep efficiency rose from 63.1% to 75.7%, yet the respiratory disturbance index initially worsened and mirtazapine was stopped in four patients — a standing caution in a population where sleep apnoea is common. No trial has enrolled post-stroke depression patients selected for poor sleep or measured their sleep as an outcome. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for the depression, with the sleep benefit itself unproven and an apnoea caution on the face.

cards.headline: Niedermaier 2004: mirtazapine 30 mg from day 1 after stroke — depression developed in 5.7% (2/35) versus 40% (14/35) without prophylaxis, in an open randomised study of 70 patients
cards.summary: Niedermaier 2004: mirtazapine 30 mg from day 1 after stroke — depression developed in 5.7% (2/35) versus 40% (14/35) without prophylaxis, in an open randomised study of 70 patients
cards.people: 70 patients with acute ischaemic stroke enrolled between August 2001 and December 2002, randomised openly to mirtazapine 30 mg daily from day 1 after the stroke or to no antidepressant medication, and re-examined on days 7, 44, 90, 180, 270 and 360 with neurological, functional and depression rating scales; patients in the no-treatment group who developed depression (DSM-IV) were then given mirtazapine.
cards.result: Post-stroke depression developed in 40% (14/35) of untreated patients versus 5.7% (2/35) of mirtazapine-treated patients — absolute rates as printed in the record; the authors report mirtazapine significantly reduced the rate of post-stroke depression. Altogether 16 patients developed depression, and 15 of them remitted after mirtazapine treatment was initiated (an uncontrolled phase, since every depressed patient received the drug). The study was a prevention trial: it did not enrol patients who already had post-stroke depression, and it measured no sleep outcome.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, 70 patients, one centre, and a prevention design whose 'treatment' result (15 of 16 remitted) has no control group — expectancy and spontaneous post-stroke recovery can both inflate it. It supports mirtazapine against post-stroke depression occurring, not a sleep claim.
cards.source: Niedermaier N et al. Prevention and treatment of poststroke depression with mirtazapine in patients with acute stroke. Journal of Clinical Psychiatry. 2004. PMID: 15641866. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Li 2020 (network meta-analysis, 51 RCTs): mirtazapine ranked among the best antidepressants for post-stroke depression — highest response rate at endpoint, top-ranked at 8 weeks alongside the leaders
cards.summary: Li 2020 (network meta-analysis, 51 RCTs): mirtazapine ranked among the best antidepressants for post-stroke depression — highest response rate at endpoint, top-ranked at 8 weeks alongside the leaders
cards.people: Network meta-analysis of 51 randomised controlled trials of nine antidepressants (citalopram, escitalopram, venlafaxine, paroxetine, duloxetine, amitriptyline, doxepin, sertraline and mirtazapine) for post-stroke depression, with Hamilton Depression Scale outcomes at 2, 4 and 8 weeks and response at endpoint; the total participant number across the 51 trials is not documented in the record.
cards.result: At 2 weeks, escitalopram, mirtazapine, sertraline, citalopram, venlafaxine and paroxetine all reduced Hamilton scores more than placebo, with escitalopram ranked best. At 8 weeks, all nine antidepressants beat placebo on Hamilton change, and mirtazapine ranked higher than citalopram and escitalopram. At endpoint, mirtazapine was related to the highest response rate, followed by venlafaxine and escitalopram. The authors conclude escitalopram relieves depression more quickly, but mirtazapine was probably the best option for 8-week efficacy; amitriptyline and doxepin were nearly the worst choices at every duration. No sleep outcome is reported in the record for any drug.
cards.watchOut: Rankings from a network meta-analysis of trials conducted in Chinese patients, with no dose restriction and indirect comparisons doing much of the work: 'ranked highest' is a fragile summary, and none of the 51 trials was selected for, or reported on, poor sleep.
cards.source: Li X et al. Comparative efficacy of nine antidepressants in treating Chinese patients with post-stroke depression: A network meta-analysis. Journal of Affective Disorders. 2020. PMID: 32056924. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Brunner 2008: in 10 non-depressed stroke patients with sleep apnoea, mirtazapine consolidated sleep (efficiency 63.1% to 75.7%) but breathing worsened at first and the drug was stopped in four patients
cards.summary: Brunner 2008: in 10 non-depressed stroke patients with sleep apnoea, mirtazapine consolidated sleep (efficiency 63.1% to 75.7%) but breathing worsened at first and the drug was stopped in four patients
cards.type: Preliminary open trial, no control group (Brunner 2008)
cards.people: 10 inpatients (nine male, one female; mean age 68.7 years) with stroke (basal ganglia bleeding 3, middle cerebral artery ischaemia 4, basal ganglia ischaemia 1, cerebellar bleeding 2) and sleep apnoea who had refused CPAP, offered mirtazapine as alternative treatment in a preliminary open trial with overnight polysomnography; mean illness duration before the first sleep study was 52.6 days. Single-study N = 10, printed here.
cards.result: Mirtazapine consolidated sleep in all patients: sleep efficiency increased significantly from 63.1 ± 4.8% to 75.7 ± 5.0%. But the respiratory disturbance index rose moderately during initial administration (to 137.4 ± 15.3% of baseline, at a mean intake duration of 15.8 days); by a mean of 51.9 days it had fallen in 'responders' (to 51.9% of baseline, responder defined arbitrarily as a reduction of at least 25% at any time point) and risen in 'non-responders' (154.4% of baseline), and mirtazapine was stopped in the four patients whose breathing worsened. The author cautions that mirtazapine may worsen central and mixed sleep apnoea and that patients given it after stroke — including for post-stroke depression with sleep disturbances — should be monitored for changes in breathing during sleep.
cards.watchOut: Ten patients, no control group, non-depressed patients treated for apnoea rather than depression — this card is on the shelf because it is the only carded record measuring sleep after mirtazapine in stroke patients at all, and its clearest signal is a safety caution, not a benefit.
cards.source: Brunner H et al. Success and failure of mirtazapine as alternative treatment in elderly stroke patients with sleep apnea-a preliminary open trial. Sleep and Breathing. 2008. PMID: 18369672. Registry ID: none in the record.
