cards.headline: Synthesis: mirtazapine has real but single-trial support against post-stroke depression and a top network ranking — while its sleep benefit in this population is a 10-patient uncontrolled observation carrying an apnoea warning
cards.summary: Synthesis: mirtazapine has real but single-trial support against post-stroke depression and a top network ranking — while its sleep benefit in this population is a 10-patient uncontrolled observation carrying an apnoea warning
cards.people: The carded evidence: one open randomised prevention trial (70 acute-stroke patients), one network meta-analysis of 51 randomised trials (total participant N not documented in the record), and one open 10-patient sleep study. Summing the countable studies gives 80 patients plus the meta-analysis's uncounted total — over the small-N threshold overall, but the sleep-specific evidence is exactly 10 patients and is labelled as such on its card and in the stamp.
cards.result: Depression: development of post-stroke depression 5.7% vs 40% with prophylactic mirtazapine (Niedermaier 2004), and the highest endpoint response ranking among nine antidepressants (Li 2020). Sleep: efficiency 63.1% to 75.7% in 10 apnoea patients, with initial worsening of the respiratory disturbance index and four discontinuations (Brunner 2008). No trial has tested mirtazapine in post-stroke depression patients chosen for poor sleep. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for post-stroke depression; the poor-sleep advantage is unproven, with a sleep-apnoea caution.
cards.watchOut: The clinical intuition behind this shelf — a sedating antidepressant for a depressed stroke patient who sleeps badly — is exactly the part the trials did not test: depression trials measured no sleep, and the one sleep study enrolled non-depressed patients and flagged breathing harm.
cards.source: Synthesis of Niedermaier N et al. Journal of Clinical Psychiatry. 2004 (PMID: 15641866); Li X et al. Journal of Affective Disorders. 2020 (PMID: 32056924); Brunner H et al. Sleep and Breathing. 2008 (PMID: 18369672).

shelves.title: Dual antiplatelet therapy after minor stroke with carotid stenosis: embolic signals fell by about 40% in relative terms in two small trials, but a reduction in clinical stroke itself has never been demonstrated in this group
shelves.question: Does dual antiplatelet therapy reduce stroke after minor stroke with carotid stenosis?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aspirin/administration & dosage · Carotid Stenosis/complications/drug therapy · Clopidogrel · Drug Monitoring/methods · Drug Therapy, Combination · Embolism/complications/diagnostic imaging/prevention & control · Female · Humans · Ischemic Attack, Transient/etiology/prevention & control · Male · Middle Aged · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Stroke/etiology/prevention & control · Ticlopidine/administration & dosage/analogs & derivatives · Ultrasonography, Doppler, Transcranial
shelves.balance: The direct evidence is two small randomised trials that measured a surrogate — microembolic signals on transcranial Doppler — rather than stroke. In CARESS (PMID: 15851601), patients with recently symptomatic carotid stenosis of 50% or more who had embolic signals were randomised (107 patients) to clopidogrel plus aspirin or aspirin alone: by day 7, 43.8% of dual-therapy patients remained signal-positive versus 72.7% on monotherapy (relative risk reduction 39.8%), and the treatment-emergent clinical events ran the same way (no strokes and 4 TIAs on dual therapy versus 4 strokes and 7 TIAs on aspirin alone) in numbers far too small to settle the clinical question. CLAIR (PMID: 20335070) found the same surrogate effect (day-2 signal-positive 14 of 45 versus 27 of 50; relative risk reduction 42.4%) but its population was predominantly intracranial stenosis — 93 of 100 patients — so its carotid read-across is indirect and is printed as such on its card. The only analysis inside a large clinical-outcome trial, the CHANCE-2 post hoc (PMID: 39773886), included just 197 patients with symptomatic carotid stenosis and compared two dual regimens (aspirin–ticagrelor 12.15% stroke recurrence versus aspirin–clopidogrel 12.22%; adjusted HR 1.04), so it says nothing about dual versus single therapy. The large minor-stroke dual-therapy trials were not carotid-specific, and guideline practice for symptomatic carotid stenosis remains revascularisation plus single antiplatelet therapy. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): the embolisation biology responds to dual therapy; whether that converts into fewer strokes after minor stroke with carotid stenosis is unproven.

cards.headline: CARESS 2005: in symptomatic carotid stenosis with embolic signals, adding clopidogrel to aspirin cut day-7 signal positivity from 72.7% to 43.8% (relative risk reduction 39.8%) — a surrogate endpoint in 107 randomised patients
cards.summary: CARESS 2005: in symptomatic carotid stenosis with embolic signals, adding clopidogrel to aspirin cut day-7 signal positivity from 72.7% to 43.8% (relative risk reduction 39.8%) — a surrogate endpoint in 107 randomised patients
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind trial with surrogate primary endpoint (CARESS, 2005)
cards.people: Patients with recently symptomatic carotid stenosis of 50% or more, screened with transcranial Doppler: microembolic signals were detected in 110 of 230 screened patients, of whom 107 were randomised to clopidogrel plus aspirin or aspirin alone in a randomised, double-blind study, with repeat Doppler recordings on days 2 and 7. Randomised N = 107, printed here because the trial is small.
cards.result: On intention-to-treat analysis, 43.8% of dual-therapy patients were microembolic-signal positive on day 7 versus 72.7% of monotherapy patients (relative risk reduction 39.8%, 95% CI 13.8 to 58.0; P = 0.0046). Signal frequency per hour fell by 61.4% from baseline at day 7 and 61.6% at day 2 in the dual-therapy group. Treatment-emergent ipsilateral clinical events were 0 strokes and 4 TIAs on dual therapy versus 4 strokes and 7 TIAs on monotherapy — directionally favourable but far too few events to establish a clinical-stroke benefit.
cards.watchOut: Microembolic signals are a validated risk marker, not the outcome patients feel: CARESS was designed and powered to show a Doppler difference over 7 days, and its handful of clinical events cannot carry a claim that dual therapy prevents stroke.
cards.source: Markus HS et al. Dual antiplatelet therapy with clopidogrel and aspirin in symptomatic carotid stenosis evaluated using doppler embolic signal detection: the Clopidogrel and Aspirin for Reduction of Emboli in Symptomatic Carotid Stenosis (CARESS) trial. Circulation. 2005. PMID: 15851601. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: CLAIR 2010: clopidogrel plus aspirin also reduced embolic signals (relative risk reduction 42.4% at day 2) — but 93 of its 100 patients had intracranial, not carotid, stenosis
cards.summary: CLAIR 2010: clopidogrel plus aspirin also reduced embolic signals (relative risk reduction 42.4% at day 2) — but 93 of its 100 patients had intracranial, not carotid, stenosis
cards.type: Randomised, open-label, blinded-endpoint trial with surrogate primary endpoint (CLAIR, 2010)
cards.people: 100 patients with acute ischaemic stroke or transient ischaemic attack within 7 days of symptom onset, symptomatic large artery stenosis in the cerebral or carotid arteries, and microembolic signals on transcranial Doppler, randomised to clopidogrel (300 mg day 1, then 75 mg daily) plus aspirin (75–160 mg daily) or aspirin alone for 7 days (dual n = 47; aspirin n = 53). 93 of the 100 patients had symptomatic intracranial stenosis (intracranial internal carotid or middle cerebral artery); only a small minority had extracranial carotid stenosis — printed on the face because it limits what this card can say about the carotid question.
cards.result: At day 2, 14 of 45 dual-therapy patients versus 27 of 50 monotherapy patients with available data had at least one microembolic signal (relative risk reduction 42.4%, 95% CI 4.6 to 65.2; p = 0.025). Adverse events were similar; no patient had intracranial or severe systemic haemorrhage, and two dual-therapy patients had minor haemorrhages. The authors' own conclusion is that clinical trials are now warranted to test whether the combination also reduces stroke incidence — that trial, in carotid stenosis, still has not been reported.
cards.watchOut: Carded as corroboration of the anti-embolic effect in large-artery stenosis, not as carotid evidence: a reader who needs carotid-specific proof has CARESS alone, with 107 patients and a Doppler endpoint.
cards.source: Wong KS et al. Clopidogrel plus aspirin versus aspirin alone for reducing embolisation in patients with acute symptomatic cerebral or carotid artery stenosis (CLAIR study): a randomised, open-label, blinded-endpoint trial. The Lancet. Neurology. 2010. PMID: 20335070. Registry ID: CUHK_CCT00164 (Centre for Clinical Trials, Chinese University of Hong Kong, from the record). cards.headline: Xie 2025 (CHANCE-2 post hoc): among 197 patients with symptomatic carotid stenosis, stroke recurrence was 12.15% on aspirin–ticagrelor versus 12.22% on aspirin–clopidogrel (adjusted HR 1.04) — a comparison of two dual regimens, not of dual versus single therapy
cards.summary: Xie 2025 (CHANCE-2 post hoc): among 197 patients with symptomatic carotid stenosis, stroke recurrence was 12.15% on aspirin–ticagrelor versus 12.22% on aspirin–clopidogrel (adjusted HR 1.04) — a comparison of two dual regimens, not of dual versus single therapy
cards.type: Post hoc subgroup analysis of a randomised trial (CHANCE-2, 2025)
cards.people: Post hoc analysis of the CHANCE-2 trial (carriers of CYP2C19 loss-of-function alleles with transient ischaemic attack or minor stroke): 5,920 of 6,412 patients analysed, of whom 197 (3.3%) had symptomatic internal carotid artery stenosis and 5,723 did not. Primary endpoint was new stroke within 90 days. The carotid subgroup N = 197 is printed on the face.
cards.result: In patients with symptomatic carotid stenosis, stroke recurrence occurred in 13 patients (12.15%) on aspirin–ticagrelor and 11 (12.22%) on aspirin–clopidogrel (adjusted HR 1.04, 95% CI 0.46 to 2.36; p = 0.930) — the two dual regimens made no difference to each other in this subgroup. In patients without carotid stenosis, recurrence was 5.52% versus 7.76% (HR 0.70, 0.57 to 0.86). The treatment-by-stenosis interaction was not significant (p = 0.405), so the record does not establish that carotid patients truly differ — only that the subgroup is small and its event rate high.
cards.watchOut: Every patient in CHANCE-2 received dual therapy, so this card cannot answer dual versus single; and with 24 strokes in the carotid subgroup, its confidence interval (0.46 to 2.36) spans large benefit and large harm for the ticagrelor comparison.
cards.source: Xie X et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: dual therapy suppresses embolisation from symptomatic large-artery stenosis by roughly 40% in relative terms, but the step from quieter Doppler signals to fewer clinical strokes after carotid minor stroke remains untested
cards.summary: Synthesis: dual therapy suppresses embolisation from symptomatic large-artery stenosis by roughly 40% in relative terms, but the step from quieter Doppler signals to fewer clinical strokes after carotid minor stroke remains untested
cards.people: The carded evidence: CARESS (107 randomised, carotid stenosis, Doppler endpoint), CLAIR (100 randomised, predominantly intracranial stenosis, Doppler endpoint), and the CHANCE-2 carotid post hoc subgroup (197 patients, clinical endpoint, dual-versus-dual comparison). No carded study randomised carotid-stenosis patients to dual versus single antiplatelet therapy with stroke as its endpoint, so no small-N total is claimed beyond the individual Ns printed on each card.
cards.result: Day-7 signal positivity 43.8% versus 72.7% (CARESS) and day-2 signal positivity 14/45 versus 27/50 (CLAIR) show a consistent, sizeable relative reduction in embolisation. Clinical events in CARESS ran in dual therapy's favour (0 versus 4 strokes) without the numbers to prove it, and the CHANCE-2 carotid subgroup shows a high 90-day recurrence rate (~12%) on either dual regimen. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) for the clinical-stroke question as asked.
cards.watchOut: The honest gap: for the patient whose carotid stenosis will not be operated on, dual therapy is biologically attractive and widely used, but this shelf's evidence for fewer strokes is a surrogate signal plus a handful of events — not a demonstrated outcome.
cards.source: Synthesis of Markus HS et al. Circulation. 2005 (PMID: 15851601); Wong KS et al. The Lancet. Neurology. 2010 (PMID: 20335070); Xie X et al. Stroke and vascular neurology. 2025 (PMID: 39773886).

shelves.title: Starting anticoagulation at day 4 versus day 14 after a moderate AF stroke: the earliest start was favoured in the one trial that randomised the exact days, and pooled data show fewer early recurrences with starts within 4 days — with no extra intracranial bleeding
shelves.question: Should a patient with atrial fibrillation start anticoagulation 4 days versus 14 days after a moderate ischemic stroke?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Atrial Fibrillation/complications/drug therapy · Female · Male · Aged · Ischemic Stroke/drug therapy/etiology/prevention & control · Anticoagulants/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Aged, 80 and over · Time-to-Treatment · Middle Aged · Time Factors · Secondary Prevention/methods · Stroke/etiology
shelves.balance: This shelf is the narrow, day-specific cut of the general early-versus-late timing question, whose home is shelf #1612 (the ELAN, TIMING and OPTIMAS trials are carded there and are not re-carded here). What is carded here is the evidence that speaks to the exact days in the question. The START trial (Warach 2025, PMID: 40163159) randomised 200 patients with mild-to-moderate atrial-fibrillation stroke (median NIHSS 6.5) to start a direct oral anticoagulant on day 3–4, day 6, day 10 or day 14: ischaemic events numbered 0, 3, 2 and 2 across those groups and haemorrhagic events 1, 1, 1 and 0, and the response-adaptive design gave the day 3–4 start the highest posterior probability (0.41) of being optimal and the day-14 start the lowest (0.15) — suggestive, not decisive, at this size. The CATALYST individual-participant meta-analysis (Dehbi 2025, PMID: 40570866) pooled the four randomised timing trials (5,441 participants, including START) on exactly this shelf's cut — start within 4 days versus day 5 or later — and found the 30-day composite of recurrent ischaemic stroke, symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage or unclassified stroke in 2.1% of early starters versus 3.0% of later starters (OR 0.70, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.98), driven by fewer recurrent ischaemic strokes (1.7% versus 2.6%; OR 0.66) with symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage identical at 0.4% in both groups. Real-world practice is less tidy: in the Berlin Atrial Fibrillation Registry (Olma 2024, PMID: 39299734), severity-rule-based timing was followed in only 39.2% of patients and adherence to the rule was not associated with the 3-month composite outcome (the treatment made no difference in that observational comparison). FLAG for the developer: this pack is built under the wave 7–8 precedent for a genuinely narrower question on free reports, with #1612 cross-pointed rather than re-carded; CATALYST pools the #1612 trials, so if the developer prefers, this shelf can be folded into #1612 as an update instead of standing alone. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for a moderate AF stroke, starting by day 4 rather than waiting to day 14 is the better-supported choice on the carded evidence.

cards.headline: START 2025 (Warach): randomising the exact days — start on day 3–4, 6, 10 or 14 — the earliest start had the highest probability of being optimal (0.41) and day 14 the lowest (0.15), in 200 patients with mild-to-moderate stroke
cards.summary: START 2025 (Warach): randomising the exact days — start on day 3–4, 6, 10 or 14 — the earliest start had the highest probability of being optimal (0.41) and day 14 the lowest (0.15), in 200 patients with mild-to-moderate stroke
cards.people: Phase 2, pragmatic, response-adaptive randomised trial at acute care hospitals in Texas (2017–2023): 200 patients with mild-to-moderate ischaemic stroke (minimum lesion diameter 1.5 cm; median NIHSS 6.5, IQR 4–14) and atrial fibrillation, prescribed a direct oral anticoagulant within 2 weeks, randomised within 3–4 days of onset to a start-date group: day 3–4, day 6, day 10, or day 14. Trial N = 200, printed on the face because it is small.
cards.result: Ischaemic events (stroke or systemic embolism) within 30 days numbered 0 in the day 3–4 group, 3 in the day-6 group, 2 in the day-10 group and 2 in the day-14 group; haemorrhagic events numbered 1, 1, 1 and 0 respectively. Posterior probabilities of being the optimal start were 0.41 (day 3–4), 0.26 (day 6), 0.17 (day 10) and 0.15 (day 14). The authors conclude that a clearly superior day was not identified, but the evidence suggests starting earlier is better than later within the first 2 weeks. The record reports event counts by group rather than a single day-4-versus-day-14 effect size.
cards.watchOut: Ten total outcome events across four arms cannot rank four start days with confidence — the adaptive probabilities are a graded suggestion, and the trial's lesion-size entry criterion (at least 1.5 cm) means its 'mild-to-moderate' population is not every moderate stroke.
cards.source: Warach SJ et al. Optimal Delay Time to Initiate Anticoagulation After Ischemic Stroke in Atrial Fibrillation: A Pragmatic, Response-Adaptive Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA neurology. 2025. PMID: 40163159. Registry ID: NCT03021928. cards.headline: CATALYST 2025: pooling all four randomised timing trials (5,441 patients), starting a DOAC within 4 days beat starting at day 5 or later — composite 2.1% versus 3.0% (OR 0.70), recurrent ischaemic stroke 1.7% versus 2.6%, symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage 0.4% in both groups
cards.summary: CATALYST 2025: pooling all four randomised timing trials (5,441 patients), starting a DOAC within 4 days beat starting at day 5 or later — composite 2.1% versus 3.0% (OR 0.70), recurrent ischaemic stroke 1.7% versus 2.6%, symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage 0.4% in both groups
cards.type: Individual participant data meta-analysis of randomised trials (CATALYST, 2025)
cards.people: Prospective individual participant data meta-analysis of the four pre-registered randomised trials of early versus later direct oral anticoagulant initiation after acute ischaemic stroke with atrial fibrillation (the TIMING, ELAN, OPTIMAS and START trials; those trials' general early-versus-late question is homed on shelf #1612 and they are not re-carded here): 5,441 participants analysed (mean age 77.7 years; 45.4% women; median NIHSS 5), of whom primary-outcome data were available for 5,429.
cards.result: The primary composite (recurrent ischaemic stroke, symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage, or unclassified stroke within 30 days) occurred in 57 of 2,683 early starters (2.1%) versus 83 of 2,746 later starters (3.0%): OR 0.70 (95% CI 0.50 to 0.98; p = 0.039) — a relative reduction with an absolute difference of 0.9 percentage points. Recurrent ischaemic stroke occurred in 1.7% versus 2.6% (OR 0.66, 0.45 to 0.96). Symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage was identical: 10 of 2,683 (0.4%) versus 10 of 2,746 (0.4%) (OR 1.02, 0.43 to 2.46).
cards.watchOut: The pooled contrast is 'within 4 days' versus 'day 5 or later' — the later group mixes day 5–7 starts with day 12–14 starts, so CATALYST supports starting by day 4 without directly measuring the day-14 arm of this shelf's question; it also re-uses patients from the trials homed on #1612, including the START patients carded above.
cards.source: Dehbi HM et al. Lancet (London, England). 2025. PMID: 40570866. Registry ID: PROSPERO CRD42024522634 (from the record). cards.headline: Berlin AF Registry 2024: in routine practice only 39.2% of restarts followed the severity-based timing rule, and following it made no difference to the 3-month composite outcome (the treatment made no difference in this observational comparison)
cards.summary: Berlin AF Registry 2024: in routine practice only 39.2% of restarts followed the severity-based timing rule, and following it made no difference to the 3-month composite outcome (the treatment made no difference in this observational comparison)
cards.type: Retrospective registry cohort study (Berlin Atrial Fibrillation Registry, 2024)
cards.people: Retrospective multicentre registry analysis of 708 patients with known atrial fibrillation before stroke, hospitalised within 72 hours of acute ischaemic stroke (432 were already anticoagulated at stroke onset); 661 patients who (re)started oral anticoagulation were assessed for adherence to the '1-3-6-12 days rule', which assigns the restart day by stroke severity, and followed for the 3-month composite of recurrent stroke, systemic embolism, myocardial infarction, major bleeding or death.
cards.result: Oral anticoagulation was (re)started according to the 1-3-6-12 days rule in 255 patients (39.2%). Non-adherence to the rule was not associated with the composite endpoint within 3 months (log-rank p = 0.74), and results were similar in the 521 patients restarted on a non-vitamin-K oral anticoagulant. The record reports no effect size for the adherence comparison beyond the log-rank result — the finding is a null, printed as such.
cards.watchOut: Observational and confounded by indication — clinicians delay restarts in exactly the patients (large infarcts, haemorrhagic transformation) most likely to do badly — so this null cannot overturn the randomised signal; it shows only that rule-adherent timing, as practised, did not separate outcomes.
cards.source: Olma MC et al. Timing of oral anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation patients after acute ischaemic stroke and outcome after 3 months: results of the multicentre Berlin Atrial Fibrillation Registry. Open heart. 2024. PMID: 39299734. Registry ID: NCT02306824. cards.headline: Synthesis: for the day-4-versus-day-14 choice after a moderate AF stroke, the randomised evidence leans early — fewest events and the top optimality ranking at day 3–4, a pooled 30-day advantage to starting within 4 days, and no bleeding penalty
cards.summary: Synthesis: for the day-4-versus-day-14 choice after a moderate AF stroke, the randomised evidence leans early — fewest events and the top optimality ranking at day 3–4, a pooled 30-day advantage to starting within 4 days, and no bleeding penalty
cards.people: The carded evidence: START (200 randomised patients assigned to exact start days 3–4, 6, 10 or 14), CATALYST (5,441 randomised patients pooled across the four timing trials, overlapping START's patients), and the Berlin registry (708 observed patients, 661 analysed for restart timing). The general timing trials themselves remain homed on shelf #1612; this shelf answers only the narrower day-specific question.
cards.result: START's earliest arm had no ischaemic events and the highest posterior probability of optimality (0.41 versus 0.15 for day 14). CATALYST found the 30-day composite in 2.1% of within-4-day starters versus 3.0% of later starters (OR 0.70), with symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage at 0.4% in both. The registry's null for rule-adherent timing is the one discordant note and is observational. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for starting by day 4 rather than day 14.
cards.watchOut: No study randomised moderate strokes specifically to day 4 versus day 14 with adequate power: the answer is assembled from a small exact-days trial, a pooled analysis whose 'later' arm is mostly earlier than day 14, and clinical judgement about infarct size and haemorrhagic transformation that no card here replaces.

shelves.title: Carotid endarterectomy within 14 days of symptoms: yes for stable patients — the pooled trials give a number needed to treat of 5 when surgery follows within 2 weeks, versus 125 when it waits beyond 12 weeks
shelves.question: Should carotid endarterectomy be done within 14 days of a symptomatic carotid stenosis stroke?
shelves.mesh: Age Factors · Aged · Carotid Stenosis/classification/diagnostic imaging/surgery · Cerebral Angiography · Endarterectomy/methods · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Selection · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Severity of Illness Index · Sex Factors · Stroke/prevention & control · Survival Analysis · Time Factors
shelves.balance: The benefit of endarterectomy for symptomatic stenosis decays with delay, and the decay is steep. The pooled analysis of the two founding randomised trials (Rothwell 2004, PMID: 15043958; 5,893 patients from the European Carotid Surgery Trial and the North American Symptomatic Carotid Endarterectomy Trial, 33,000 patient-years) found that time from the last symptomatic event to randomisation modified the effectiveness of surgery (p = 0.009): for stenosis of 50% or more, the number needed to treat to prevent one ipsilateral stroke in 5 years was 5 for patients randomised within 2 weeks, versus 125 for those randomised after more than 12 weeks — most of the operation's value is spent by waiting. The safety half of the question is answered by the timing-and-risk systematic review (Rerkasem 2009, PMID: 19661467): across 47 operative series, neurologically stable patients with recent transient ischaemic attack or nondisabling stroke faced no significant difference in operative stroke and death between surgery within 1 week versus later (OR 1.2, 0.9 to 1.7) or within 2 weeks versus later (OR 1.2, 0.9 to 1.6) — while genuinely unstable presentations were dangerous whenever operated (stroke-in-evolution 20.2%, crescendo transient ischaemic attack 11.4%). The pooled individual-patient analysis of the four endarterectomy-versus-stenting trials (Rantner 2017, PMID: 28455318; 4,138 patients) adds that within the first week the endarterectomy arm's 30-day stroke-or-death risk was 1.3% — low in absolute terms, and far below early stenting (8.3%). Two independent pooled analyses of randomised data plus a concordant risk review support LIKELY. The carve-outs are on the cards: unstable neurology, and the pooled trials' era (medical therapy has improved since, which shrinks absolute benefit at every delay without changing the direction of the timing effect). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): do the endarterectomy within 14 days in a neurologically stable patient with symptomatic stenosis.

cards.headline: Rothwell 2004: pooling ECST and NASCET (5,893 patients), surgical benefit was greatest within 2 weeks of the last event — number needed to treat 5 — and collapsed to 125 beyond 12 weeks
cards.summary: Rothwell 2004: pooling ECST and NASCET (5,893 patients), surgical benefit was greatest within 2 weeks of the last event — number needed to treat 5 — and collapsed to 125 beyond 12 weeks
cards.type: Pooled analysis of two randomised trials (ECST and NASCET, 2004)
cards.people: Pooled individual analysis of the European Carotid Surgery Trial and the North American Symptomatic Carotid Endarterectomy Trial: 5,893 patients with recently symptomatic carotid stenosis and 33,000 patient-years of follow-up, analysed for how the risk of ipsilateral ischaemic stroke on medical treatment, the perioperative risk of stroke and death, and the overall benefit of surgery varied with clinical subgroups and with time from the last symptomatic event to randomisation.
cards.result: Sex (p = 0.003), age (p = 0.03) and time from the last symptomatic event to randomisation (p = 0.009) modified the effectiveness of surgery. Benefit was greatest in men, in patients aged 75 years or older, and in those randomised within 2 weeks of their last ischaemic event, and fell rapidly with increasing delay. For stenosis of 50% or higher, the number needed to treat to prevent one ipsilateral stroke in 5 years was 9 for men versus 36 for women, 5 for age 75 or older versus 18 for under 65, and 5 for randomisation within 2 weeks versus 125 for randomisation after more than 12 weeks. Results were consistent across the two trials. The authors conclude the procedure should ideally be done within 2 weeks of the patient's last symptoms.
cards.watchOut: These trials randomised in an era before modern statin and antiplatelet therapy, so today's absolute benefits are smaller at every time point; the timing gradient — early good, late nearly futile — is the durable finding, and it is driven substantially by the high early recurrence risk on medical therapy.

cards.headline: Rerkasem 2009: in neurologically stable patients, operating within 1–2 weeks carried no higher operative risk than waiting (OR 1.2, not significant) — but stroke-in-evolution carried a 20.2% operative risk
cards.summary: Rerkasem 2009: in neurologically stable patients, operating within 1–2 weeks carried no higher operative risk than waiting (OR 1.2, not significant) — but stroke-in-evolution carried a 20.2% operative risk
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of operative series (Rerkasem 2009)
cards.people: Systematic review of all studies published 1980–2008 reporting the risk of stroke and death from carotid endarterectomy in relation to time since the presenting symptom: of 494 published operative series, 47 stratified risk by timing and were pooled by Mantel-Haenszel meta-analysis.
cards.result: Pooled absolute risks of stroke and death after urgent endarterectomy were high in stroke-in-evolution (20.2%, 95% CI 12.0 to 28.4) and crescendo transient ischaemic attack (11.4%, 6.1 to 16.7), with no trend to lower risks in more recent studies. In neurologically stable patients with recent transient ischaemic attack or nondisabling stroke there was no significant difference between early and later surgery: under 1 week versus 1 week or more, OR 1.2 (0.9 to 1.7; P = 0.17); under 2 weeks versus 2 weeks or more, OR 1.2 (0.9 to 1.6; P = 0.13). Odds ratios are relative measures; the review's message is the absence of an early-surgery penalty in stable patients, set against the very high risk of operating on unstable ones.
cards.watchOut: Operative series are observational and selected — surgeons choose which early patients to operate on — so the 'no extra risk' finding applies to patients judged stable enough for early surgery, not to every patient presenting within 14 days.
cards.source: Rerkasem K et al. Systematic review of the operative risks of carotid endarterectomy for recently symptomatic stenosis in relation to the timing of surgery. Stroke. 2009. cards.headline: Rantner 2017: in the four randomised endarterectomy-versus-stenting trials (4,138 patients), endarterectomy done within 7 days carried a 1.3% 30-day stroke-or-death risk — far below early stenting at 8.3%
cards.summary: Rantner 2017: in the four randomised endarterectomy-versus-stenting trials (4,138 patients), endarterectomy done within 7 days carried a 1.3% 30-day stroke-or-death risk — far below early stenting at 8.3%
cards.type: Pooled individual patient data analysis of four randomised trials (Carotid Stenosis Trialists' Collaboration, 2017)
cards.people: Pooled individual patient data analysis by the Carotid Stenosis Trialists' Collaboration of four randomised trials comparing carotid artery stenting with endarterectomy for symptomatic internal carotid artery stenosis: 4,138 patients analysed per protocol by timing of treatment (0–7 days versus more than 7 days after the qualifying event); 11% of endarterectomy patients and 14% of stenting patients were treated within 7 days.
cards.result: Among patients treated within 1 week of symptoms, 30-day stroke or death occurred in 1.3% after endarterectomy versus 8.3% after stenting (risk ratio 6.7 for stenting versus endarterectomy, 95% CI 2.1 to 21.9, adjusted for age, sex and qualifying event type). For interventions after 1 week the risks were 3.6% (endarterectomy) versus 7.1% (stenting) (adjusted risk ratio 2.0, 1.5 to 2.7). The endarterectomy figure that matters for this shelf is the absolute one: early surgery's own procedural risk in the trials was low (1.3% within a week), so the timing benefit documented by Rothwell is not bought with a procedural penalty.
cards.watchOut: This card compares early endarterectomy with early stenting, not early with delayed endarterectomy; it is carded for the absolute early-operative-risk figure (1.3%), which complements — and does not replace — the timing-of-benefit analysis on the Rothwell card.

cards.headline: Synthesis: operate within 14 days — benefit is front-loaded (number needed to treat 5 inside 2 weeks), and in stable patients the operation is no riskier early than late
cards.summary: Synthesis: operate within 14 days — benefit is front-loaded (number needed to treat 5 inside 2 weeks), and in stable patients the operation is no riskier early than late
cards.people: The carded evidence: the pooled ECST/NASCET analysis (5,893 randomised patients), a systematic review of 47 timing-stratified operative series, and the pooled individual-patient analysis of four randomised stenting-versus-surgery trials (4,138 patients). Populations overlap between the pooled analyses and the underlying trials, so no single summed N is claimed.
cards.result: Benefit from endarterectomy was greatest when patients were randomised within 2 weeks of their last event (number needed to treat 5 for stenosis of 50% or more, versus 125 beyond 12 weeks). Operative risk in stable patients did not differ significantly between surgery inside and outside 1–2 weeks (OR 1.2 in both comparisons), and the trials' own early endarterectomy risk was 1.3% at 30 days. The exception is unstable neurology: stroke-in-evolution carried a 20.2% operative risk. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for endarterectomy within 14 days in neurologically stable symptomatic stenosis.
cards.watchOut: The 14-day window is a benefit gradient, not a cliff: a patient randomised at day 15 has lost some, not all, of the operation's value — and a patient with stroke-in-evolution sits outside this shelf's answer entirely.
cards.source: Synthesis of Rothwell PM et al. Lancet (London, England). 2004 (PMID: 15043958); Rerkasem K et al. Stroke. 2009 (PMID: 19661467); Rantner B et al. Stroke. 2017 (PMID: 28455318).

shelves.title: Intensive blood pressure lowering after stroke (target below 120 versus below 140): the dedicated trial pointed the right way without proving it (HR 0.73, CI crossing 1) — the pooled trials show a 22% relative reduction in recurrent stroke
shelves.question: Does intensive blood pressure lowering to below 120 mm Hg systolic reduce recurrent stroke compared with a target below 140?
shelves.mesh: Antihypertensive Agents/pharmacology · Blood Pressure/physiology · Cerebral Infarction/chemically induced/drug therapy · Hemorrhagic Stroke · Humans · Hypertension/chemically induced/complications/drug therapy · Ischemic Stroke · Stroke/chemically induced · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Only one randomised trial has tested the exact targets in the question in patients with prior stroke. RESPECT (Kitagawa 2019, PMID: 31355878) randomised 1,280 Japanese patients with stroke in the previous 3 years to below 120/80 or below 140/90 mm Hg; the trial was stopped early, achieved mean systolic pressures were 126.7 versus 133.2 mm Hg (a separation of only about 6.5 mm Hg — the intensive arm never averaged below 120), and recurrent stroke gave HR 0.73 (95% CI 0.49 to 1.11; P = .15) — directionally favourable, not significant. The same paper's updated meta-analysis, pooling RESPECT with three previous relevant trials, found intensive control did reduce recurrent stroke: relative risk 0.78 (0.64 to 0.96), absolute risk difference −1.5 percentage points, number needed to treat 67. RESPECT's post hoc analysis in patients whose index event was ischaemic stroke (Kitagawa 2022, PMID: 35241817) localises the benefit: annual recurrence was 1.74% versus 2.17% overall (P = 0.351), ischaemic recurrence was identical (1.74% versus 1.75%), and haemorrhagic recurrence fell to 0.00% versus 0.39% per year (P = 0.005) — the gain, where it appeared, was in preventing brain haemorrhage, not ischaemic recurrence. The achievability caveat is carded directly: PAST-BP (Mant 2016, PMID: 26919870) showed that even a milder intensive target (below 130 versus below 140) produced only a 2.9 mm Hg extra systolic reduction in primary care. The related lacunar-stroke blood-pressure trial (SPS3, targets below 130 versus 130–149) asks a different target question and is homed on shelf #2842; it is cross-pointed here, not re-carded. One underpowered stopped-early trial plus its own supportive meta-analysis caps this shelf at POSSIBLE. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): aiming below 120 probably reduces recurrent stroke modestly, chiefly haemorrhagic recurrence, but the exact-target trial has not proven it on its own.

cards.headline: RESPECT 2019 (Kitagawa): intensive control (target below 120/80) versus standard (below 140/90) after stroke — recurrent stroke HR 0.73 (95% CI 0.49 to 1.11), not significant in the stopped-early trial; significant when pooled with three earlier trials (relative risk 0.78)
cards.summary: RESPECT 2019 (Kitagawa): intensive control (target below 120/80) versus standard (below 140/90) after stroke — recurrent stroke HR 0.73 (95% CI 0.49 to 1.11), not significant in the stopped-early trial; significant when pooled with three earlier trials (relative risk 0.78)
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial with updated meta-analysis (RESPECT, 2019)
cards.people: Multicentre randomised trial in 140 hospitals in Japan: 1,280 patients with a history of stroke within the previous 3 years randomised 1:1 to blood pressure control below 140/90 mm Hg (standard, n = 640) or below 120/80 mm Hg (intensive, n = 640); 1,263 were analysed (630 standard, 633 intensive; mean age 67.2 years; 69.4% male), with mean follow-up 3.9 years. The trial was stopped early. The same publication reports an updated meta-analysis pooling this trial with three previous relevant randomised trials.
cards.result: Mean blood pressure through follow-up was 133.2/77.7 mm Hg on standard treatment and 126.7/77.4 mm Hg on intensive treatment — the intensive group did not, on average, reach its below-120 systolic target. Ninety-one first recurrent strokes occurred. Recurrent stroke was non-significantly lower with intensive treatment (HR 0.73, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.11; P = .15). In the updated meta-analysis, the relative risk favoured intensive control (0.78, 0.64 to 0.96; P = .02), with an absolute risk difference of −1.5% (95% CI −2.6% to −0.4%) and a number needed to treat of 67 (39 to 250). The authors conclude the meta-analysis supports a target below 130/80 mm Hg in secondary stroke prevention — a softer target than the below-120 arm actually tested.
cards.watchOut: A stopped-early trial whose confidence interval spans a 51% relative reduction and an 11% relative increase cannot carry the claim alone; and because achieved systolic pressure averaged 126.7 mm Hg, this is evidence about aiming below 120, not about being below 120.
cards.source: Kitagawa K et al. Effect of Standard vs Intensive Blood Pressure Control on the Risk of Recurrent Stroke: A Randomized Clinical Trial and Meta-analysis. JAMA neurology. 2019. PMID: 31355878. Registry ID: NCT01198496. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: RESPECT post hoc 2022: in patients whose index stroke was ischaemic, intensive control left ischaemic recurrence unchanged (1.74% versus 1.75% per year) but abolished haemorrhagic recurrence (0.00% versus 0.39% per year, P = 0.005)
cards.summary: RESPECT post hoc 2022: in patients whose index stroke was ischaemic, intensive control left ischaemic recurrence unchanged (1.74% versus 1.75% per year) but abolished haemorrhagic recurrence (0.00% versus 0.39% per year, P = 0.005)
cards.type: Post hoc subgroup analysis of a randomised trial (RESPECT, 2022)
cards.people: Post hoc analysis of the RESPECT randomised trial restricted to the 1,074 participants with a history of cerebral infarction (the trial also enrolled intracerebral haemorrhage survivors): baseline mean blood pressure 140.7/81.4 mm Hg; follow-up mean 133.4/77.5 mm Hg (standard) versus 126.7/74.1 mm Hg (intensive); mean follow-up 3.9 years, during which 78 first recurrent strokes occurred in this subgroup.
cards.result: Intensive treatment tended to reduce overall annual stroke recurrence (1.74% intensive versus 2.17% standard; P = 0.351 by log-rank) and did not change ischaemic stroke recurrence (1.74% versus 1.75%; P = 0.999) — for ischaemic recurrence, the treatment made no difference — but markedly reduced haemorrhagic stroke (0.00% versus 0.39% per year; P = 0.005). The authors frame the benefit of intensive control as concentrated in patients at high risk of haemorrhagic stroke.
cards.watchOut: Post hoc and subgroup: the haemorrhagic result rests on a small number of events (a zero in one arm), so its precision is illusory even though its direction matches blood-pressure biology; it explains where benefit may live, it does not add an independent trial.

cards.headline: PAST-BP 2016 (Mant): even a below-130 (versus below-140) systolic target in primary care produced only 2.9 mm Hg of extra lowering — the achievability problem behind the intensive-target trials
cards.summary: PAST-BP 2016 (Mant): even a below-130 (versus below-140) systolic target in primary care produced only 2.9 mm Hg of extra lowering — the achievability problem behind the intensive-target trials
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial of blood-pressure targets, pressure outcome only (PAST-BP, 2016)
cards.people: Open-label randomised trial in 99 general practices in England: 529 people (mean age 72) with a history of stroke or transient ischaemic attack and systolic blood pressure of 125 mm Hg or above, randomised to an intensive systolic target (below 130 mm Hg, or a 10 mm Hg reduction if baseline was below 140) or a standard target (below 140 mm Hg), both arms actively managed by the primary care team; 379 patients contributed to the primary analysis and 84 withdrew during follow-up.
cards.result: At 12 months, mean systolic pressure had fallen 16.1 mm Hg to 127.4 mm Hg in the intensive arm and 12.8 mm Hg to 129.4 mm Hg in the standard arm — a between-group difference of 2.9 mm Hg (95% CI 0.2 to 5.7; P = 0.03). The trial measured achieved blood pressure, not recurrent stroke: it is carded to show that target separation in real practice is a few mm Hg, which is why the outcome trials above compare strategies ('aim low') more than achieved levels.
cards.watchOut: PAST-BP tested a below-130 target, not below 120, and reports no stroke outcomes; its role on this shelf is strictly to calibrate how much separation an intensive-target strategy actually buys.
cards.source: Mant J et al. randomised controlled trial of blood-pressure targets, pressure outcome only (past-bp, 2016) open-label randomised trial in 99 general practices in england: 529 people (mean age 72) with a history of stroke or transient ischaemic attack and systolic blood pressure of 125 mm hg or above, randomised to an intensive systolic target (below 130 mm hg, or a 10 mm hg reduction if baseline was below 140) or a standard target (below 140 mm hg), both arms actively managed by the primary care team; 379 patients contributed to the primary analysis and 84 withdrew during follow-up. at 12 months, mean systolic pressure had fallen 16.1 mm hg to 127.4 mm hg in the intensive arm and 12.8 mm hg to 129.4 mm hg in the standard arm — a between-group difference of 2.9 mm hg (95% ci 0.2 to 5.7; p = 0.03). the trial measured achieved blood pressure, not recurrent stroke: it is carded to show that target separation in real practice is a few mm hg, which is why the outcome trials above compare strategies ('aim low') more than achieved levels. past-bp tested a below-130 target, not below 120, and reports no stroke outcomes; its role on this shelf is strictly to calibrate how much separation an intensive-target strategy actually buys. mant j et al. different systolic blood pressure targets for people with history of stroke or transient ischaemic attack: past-bp (prevention after stroke--blood pressure) randomised controlled trial. bmj (clinical research ed.). 2016. pmid: 26919870. registry id: isrctn29062286. mesh: aged · antihypertensive agents/therapeutic use · blood pressure/physiology · female · general practice · humans · hypertension/drug therapy/physiopathology · ischemic attack, transient/physiopathology · male · middle aged · stroke/physiopathology · systole/physiology

cards.headline: Synthesis: aiming below 120 after stroke probably prevents some recurrent strokes — the pooled relative risk is 0.78 — but the only exact-target trial was inconclusive alone, and the visible benefit is in haemorrhagic, not ischaemic, recurrence
cards.summary: Synthesis: aiming below 120 after stroke probably prevents some recurrent strokes — the pooled relative risk is 0.78 — but the only exact-target trial was inconclusive alone, and the visible benefit is in haemorrhagic, not ischaemic, recurrence
cards.people: The carded evidence: RESPECT (1,263 analysed patients; the only randomised trial of below-120/80 versus below-140/90 targets after stroke, stopped early), its ischaemic-index post hoc analysis (1,074 of the same patients — the same cohort, not additional patients), its embedded meta-analysis with three earlier trials, and PAST-BP (529 patients, achieved-pressure outcome). Unique randomised participants across the outcome evidence are RESPECT's 1,263 plus the three pooled earlier trials reported within the RESPECT paper.
cards.result: RESPECT alone: recurrent stroke HR 0.73 (0.49 to 1.11). Pooled: relative risk 0.78 (0.64 to 0.96), absolute difference −1.5 percentage points, number needed to treat 67. In the ischaemic-index subgroup, ischaemic recurrence was unchanged (1.74% versus 1.75% per year) while haemorrhagic recurrence fell from 0.39% to 0.00% per year. Achieved systolic separation was about 6.5 mm Hg in RESPECT and 2.9 mm Hg in PAST-BP's milder comparison. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Do not read the pooled relative risk as proof of the below-120 target specifically: the meta-analysis mixes target definitions, the intensive arms rarely averaged below 120, and no card here addresses the harms side (falls, syncope, kidney injury) of pushing systolic pressure that low in older stroke survivors.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kitagawa K et al. JAMA neurology. 2019 (PMID: 31355878); Kitagawa K et al. Hypertension research. 2022 (PMID: 35241817); Mant J et al. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2016 (PMID: 26919870). The SPS3 blood-pressure comparison (different targets) is homed on shelf #2842.

shelves.title: rTMS for post-stroke aphasia: small randomised trials consistently favour stimulation — naming most reliably — but protocols vary and no large multicentre trial exists
shelves.question: Does repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation improve post-stroke aphasia recovery?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation/methods · Aphasia/etiology/therapy · Stroke/therapy · Stroke Rehabilitation · Treatment Outcome · Prefrontal Cortex
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). The direction of the randomised evidence is consistently favourable: a 47-trial meta-analysis (2,190 patients) reports improvement in repetition, naming and spontaneous language (no pooled effect sizes in its record, printed plainly), a 4-trial meta-analysis finds a naming benefit (standardised mean difference 0.51) with no significant difference for repetition or comprehension, and one small sham-controlled trial of personalised theta-burst stimulation shows aphasia-quotient gains of about 13–15 points over sham. The stamp is capped at POSSIBLE because the individual trials are small, protocols and targets vary widely, and no large multicentre sham-controlled trial anchors the field. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): rTMS improves some language outcomes after stroke, most consistently naming, as an adjunct to speech-language therapy.

cards.headline: Cheng 2024: a meta-analysis of 47 randomised trials (2,190 patients) found rTMS improved repetition, naming and spontaneous language in post-stroke non-fluent aphasia — but the record reports no pooled effect sizes, printed plainly here
cards.summary: Cheng 2024: a meta-analysis of 47 randomised trials (2,190 patients) found rTMS improved repetition, naming and spontaneous language in post-stroke non-fluent aphasia — but the record reports no pooled effect sizes, printed plainly here
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Cheng 2024)
cards.people: Patients with non-fluent aphasia after stroke in 47 randomised controlled trials of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) versus no therapy or other therapy, encompassing 2,190 patients overall, as reported in the record.
cards.result: The record reports that the indexes indicated rTMS has the potential to decrease the severity of non-fluent aphasia, including improvement of repetition, naming and spontaneous language, and that serum brain-derived neurotrophic factor was also increased; rTMS also reduced the likelihood of depression in stroke patients. No pooled effect size, confidence interval or P value for the language outcomes is reported in the record — that absence is printed plainly rather than filled in.
cards.watchOut: The largest synthesis reports direction without pooled numbers in its record, and its 47 trials are mostly small, single-centre and heterogeneous in stimulation site, frequency and timing after stroke — the size and durability of the benefit cannot be read off this record.
cards.source: Cheng J et al. Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation for post-stroke non-fluent aphasia: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Frontiers in Neurology. 2024. PMID: 38751884. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Ren 2023: in a randomised sham-controlled trial (44 patients treated), imaging-guided theta-burst stimulation over the superior frontal gyrus improved the aphasia quotient by about 14 points more than sham at 3 weeks
cards.summary: Ren 2023: in a randomised sham-controlled trial (44 patients treated), imaging-guided theta-burst stimulation over the superior frontal gyrus improved the aphasia quotient by about 14 points more than sham at 3 weeks
cards.people: Patients with aphasia from a first left-hemisphere stroke at least one month earlier; 97 screened, 45 randomised and 44 received intervention (15 intermittent theta-burst stimulation to the ipsilesional superior frontal gyrus, 15 continuous theta-burst stimulation to the contralesional superior frontal gyrus, 14 sham), each coupled with 3 weeks of speech-language therapy. Treated N = 44, printed on the face.
cards.result: Both active groups showed significantly greater improvement than sham in Western Aphasia Battery-Revised aphasia quotient after the 3-week intervention (estimated difference 14.75 for intermittent theta-burst, P < 0.001; 13.43 for continuous theta-burst, P < 0.001) and immediately after one week of treatment (P < 0.001 for both). Adverse events were similar across groups; one seizure was recorded three days after the end of treatment in the intermittent theta-burst group.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre trial of 44 treated patients testing a novel personalised target; the effect is large for its size, one seizure occurred after treatment, and independent replication at other centres does not yet exist in the records fetched.
cards.source: Ren J et al. Personalized functional imaging-guided rTMS on the superior frontal gyrus for post-stroke aphasia: A randomized sham-controlled trial. Brain Stimulation. 2023. PMID: 37652135. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Li 2015: a meta-analysis of 4 randomised trials found low-frequency rTMS improved naming (standardised mean difference 0.51) but made no significant difference to repetition or comprehension
cards.summary: Li 2015: a meta-analysis of 4 randomised trials found low-frequency rTMS improved naming (standardised mean difference 0.51) but made no significant difference to repetition or comprehension
cards.people: Patients with post-stroke aphasia in the 4 randomised controlled trials of low-frequency rTMS included in the final analysis (879 articles identified; total participant N not documented in the record).
cards.result: Low-frequency rTMS was beneficial for naming (standardised mean difference 0.51, 95% CI 0.16 to 0.86). Changes in repetition (standardised mean difference 0.31, 95% CI -0.04 to 0.65) and comprehension (standardised mean difference 0.31, 95% CI -0.14 to 0.75) were not significant — for those two outcomes the treatment made no difference that the data could distinguish. No adverse effects were reported in the included trials, which the record rates as high methodological quality.
cards.watchOut: Only 4 trials, and the benefit is confined to naming: repetition and comprehension did not significantly improve, so this card supports a narrow language-domain benefit, not global aphasia recovery.
cards.source: Li Y et al. Low-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation for patients with aphasia after stoke: A meta-analysis. Journal of Rehabilitation Medicine. 2015. PMID: 26181486. cards.headline: Synthesis: rTMS probably helps some language domains after stroke — naming most consistently — but the trials are small, protocols vary widely, and the biggest meta-analysis reports no pooled effect size in its record
cards.summary: Synthesis: rTMS probably helps some language domains after stroke — naming most consistently — but the trials are small, protocols vary widely, and the biggest meta-analysis reports no pooled effect size in its record
cards.people: The carded evidence: one meta-analysis of 47 randomised trials (2,190 patients, no pooled effect sizes in the record), one randomised sham-controlled trial (44 treated patients) of personalised theta-burst stimulation, and one meta-analysis of 4 randomised trials of low-frequency rTMS. Total carded participants exceed 2,200, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the limitation is trial size and heterogeneity, not the total.
cards.result: Naming improved in both meta-analytic reads (standardised mean difference 0.51, 95% CI 0.16 to 0.86, in Li 2015; direction favourable in Cheng 2024), repetition and spontaneous language improved in the 47-trial synthesis while repetition did not reach significance in the 4-trial low-frequency analysis, and the single sham-controlled trial showed aphasia-quotient gains of about 13–15 points over sham at 3 weeks (Ren 2023). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Heterogeneity is the honest caveat: stimulation site (right inferior frontal gyrus versus superior frontal gyrus), frequency, dose and time since stroke all differ across trials, so no single protocol can be recommended from this evidence.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cheng J et al. Frontiers in Neurology. 2024 (PMID: 38751884); Ren J et al. Brain Stimulation. 2023 (PMID: 37652135); Li Y et al. Journal of Rehabilitation Medicine. 2015 (PMID: 26181486).

shelves.title: Rivastigmine patch vs capsules: about two-thirds less nausea (7.2% vs 23.1%) and vomiting (6.2% vs 17.0%) at equal efficacy in the 1,195-patient IDEAL trial
shelves.question: Does rivastigmine patch cause fewer gastrointestinal side effects than oral rivastigmine in Alzheimer's disease?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Cutaneous · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Alzheimer Disease/*drug therapy · Area Under Curve · Cholinesterase Inhibitors/*administration & dosage/adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Drug Delivery Systems/methods/statistics & numerical data · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · International Cooperation · Male · Mental Status Schedule · Middle Aged · Neuropsychological Tests · Phenylcarbamates/*administration & dosage/adverse effects · Placebos · Rivastigmine · Statistics, Nonparametric · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit — fewer gastrointestinal side effects). One definitive large randomised trial answers this question directly: in IDEAL (N = 1,195), the 9.5 mg/24 h patch matched the efficacy of 6 mg twice-daily capsules while nausea fell from 23.1% to 7.2% and vomiting from 17.0% to 6.2%, rates statistically indistinguishable from placebo. A post hoc analysis of the same programme confirms no loss of functional benefit, and the pharmacologic rationale (lower peak plasma levels with transdermal delivery) is coherent. The stamp is LIKELY rather than higher because the evidence is a single trial programme and the advantage belongs to the 9.5 mg/24 h dose — the 17.4 mg/24 h patch tolerates like capsules. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): the rivastigmine patch causes substantially fewer gastrointestinal side effects than oral rivastigmine at the standard dose.

cards.headline: IDEAL 2007: in the 1,195-patient randomised trial, the 9.5 mg/24 h rivastigmine patch caused about two-thirds less nausea (7.2% vs 23.1%) and vomiting (6.2% vs 17.0%) than 6 mg twice-daily capsules, with similar efficacy
cards.summary: IDEAL 2007: in the 1,195-patient randomised trial, the 9.5 mg/24 h rivastigmine patch caused about two-thirds less nausea (7.2% vs 23.1%) and vomiting (6.2% vs 17.0%) than 6 mg twice-daily capsules, with similar efficacy
cards.people: 1,195 patients with Alzheimer's disease in a 24-week, double-blind, double-dummy, placebo- and active-controlled trial, randomised to placebo, 10-cm2 rivastigmine patch (9.5 mg/24 hours), 20-cm2 patch (17.4 mg/24 hours), or rivastigmine capsules 6 mg twice daily.
cards.result: All rivastigmine groups improved significantly relative to placebo on the primary efficacy measures. The 10-cm2 patch showed similar efficacy to capsules, with approximately two-thirds fewer reports of nausea (7.2% vs 23.1%) and vomiting (6.2% vs 17.0%); those incidences were statistically not significantly different from placebo (5.0% nausea and 3.3% vomiting). The 20-cm2 patch showed numerically superior cognitive scores with tolerability similar to capsules. Local skin tolerability was good.
cards.watchOut: The comparison is against the maximum capsule dose (6 mg twice daily); the patch advantage is a tolerability advantage at matched efficacy, not an efficacy advantage, and application-site skin reactions are the patch's own trade-off.
cards.source: Winblad B et al. IDEAL: a 6-month, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of the first skin patch for Alzheimer disease. Neurology. 2007. PMID: 17646619. cards.headline: Grossberg 2011: in a post hoc analysis of the same trial programme (n = 892), patch and capsules both beat placebo on total activities of daily living, confirming the patch loses no functional efficacy
cards.summary: Grossberg 2011: in a post hoc analysis of the same trial programme (n = 892), patch and capsules both beat placebo on total activities of daily living, confirming the patch loses no functional efficacy
cards.type: Post hoc analysis of a randomised controlled trial (Grossberg 2011)
cards.people: Patients (n = 892) with probable Alzheimer's disease in the 24-week randomised, double-blind, placebo- and active-controlled trial, receiving rivastigmine patch 9.5 mg/24 hours, capsules 6 mg twice daily, or placebo; activities of daily living were assessed on basic, high-level function and autonomy subscales. This analysis overlaps the IDEAL population and is not an independent trial.
cards.result: At week 24 both rivastigmine groups performed significantly better than placebo on the total activities-of-daily-living score (patch P = .013; capsules P = .039). For basic activities, capsules performed significantly better than placebo (P = .012); for high-level function the patch performed better than placebo (P = .056); for autonomy the patch performed significantly better than placebo (P = .017). The record's framing states that patches provide similar efficacy to capsules with a lower incidence of gastrointestinal side effects.
cards.watchOut: Post hoc and drawn from the same trial as the IDEAL card — it corroborates preserved efficacy, it does not independently replicate the gastrointestinal finding.
cards.source: Grossberg G et al. Impact of rivastigmine patch and capsules on activities of daily living in Alzheimer's disease. American Journal of Alzheimer's Disease and Other Dementias. 2011. PMID: 21282280. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Sadowsky 2014: a clinical review of the registration programme concludes transdermal delivery improves tolerability by lowering peak plasma levels, letting more patients reach high therapeutic doses
cards.summary: Sadowsky 2014: a clinical review of the registration programme concludes transdermal delivery improves tolerability by lowering peak plasma levels, letting more patients reach high therapeutic doses
cards.type: Clinical review of the registration programme (Sadowsky 2014)
cards.people: Review of the pivotal rivastigmine capsule and patch studies and the US prescribing information, covering Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease dementia; no new participants.
cards.result: The review reports that gastrointestinal adverse events limit access to optimal oral doses, that strategies lowering maximum plasma concentration and prolonging time to peak — transdermal delivery — improve tolerability, and that registration studies demonstrated improved tolerability of the 9.5-mg/24-h patch versus 6-mg twice-daily capsules in mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease. No new effect sizes are reported in the record.
cards.watchOut: A narrative review, carded for the pharmacologic rationale and programme summary only — the quantitative claim on this shelf rests on the IDEAL trial card.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the patch causes substantially fewer gastrointestinal side effects than oral rivastigmine at equal efficacy — nausea 7.2% vs 23.1% and vomiting 6.2% vs 17.0% in the one large head-to-head trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: the patch causes substantially fewer gastrointestinal side effects than oral rivastigmine at equal efficacy — nausea 7.2% vs 23.1% and vomiting 6.2% vs 17.0% in the one large head-to-head trial
cards.people: The carded evidence: one definitive 24-week randomised, double-blind, double-dummy trial (N = 1,195) with a direct patch-versus-capsule comparison, a post hoc functional-outcome analysis of the same programme (n = 892, overlapping population), and a narrative review. Unique participants = 1,195, so no small-N labelling applies.
cards.result: In IDEAL, the 9.5 mg/24 h patch matched capsule efficacy against placebo while cutting nausea from 23.1% to 7.2% and vomiting from 17.0% to 6.2% — rates not significantly different from placebo itself — and activities of daily living were preserved (Grossberg 2011). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit — fewer gastrointestinal side effects), on the strength of one definitive large randomised trial with a direct head-to-head comparison.
cards.watchOut: The evidence is one trial programme: there is no second independent head-to-head trial, and the higher-dose 17.4 mg/24 h patch loses the gastrointestinal advantage, with tolerability similar to capsules.
cards.source: Synthesis of Winblad B et al. Neurology. 2007 (PMID: 17646619); Grossberg G et al. American Journal of Alzheimer's Disease and Other Dementias. 2011 (PMID: 21282280); Sadowsky CH et al. Primary Care Companion for CNS Disorders. 2014 (PMID: 25667813).

shelves.title: Lecanemab and ApoE4: brain swelling (ARIA-E) in 34.5% of ε4 homozygotes vs 16.8% of carriers overall in trial safety data — risk rises steeply with ε4 copies
shelves.question: What is the risk of brain swelling or bleeding with lecanemab in patients who carry ApoE4?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Alzheimer Disease/drug therapy · Male · Double-Blind Method · Female · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/therapeutic use/adverse effects · Middle Aged · Amyloid beta-Peptides/metabolism · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (risk, graded by ApoE ε4 copy number) — evidence types labelled on the face: randomised-trial safety data plus real-world observational cohorts. In the Clarity AD safety update, ARIA-E (brain swelling) occurred in 34.5% of ApoE ε4 homozygotes and 16.8% of ε4 carriers overall, with ARIA-E in 13.6% and ARIA-H microhaemorrhages in 16.0% of all lecanemab-treated participants; a US real-world cohort found any ARIA in 44% of homozygotes (4 of 9, small denominator) versus 17% of heterozygotes. Most ARIA is asymptomatic and MRI-detected, but fatal intracerebral haemorrhage has occurred, including alongside thrombolysis and anticoagulation. The Clarity AD primary efficacy record is homed on live shelf #333 (anti-amyloid benefit and risk); this shelf answers the narrower ApoE4-stratified risk question from the programme's safety report and two independent cohorts, and does not re-card the homed record. PROPOSED LIKELY (risk): carrying two ApoE ε4 copies roughly triples the ARIA-E risk seen in carriers overall, and about one in three homozygotes develops brain swelling on lecanemab.

cards.headline: Honig 2024 (Clarity AD safety update, trial data): ARIA-E occurred in 34.5% of ApoE ε4 homozygotes and 16.8% of ε4 carriers overall on lecanemab; ARIA-H microhaemorrhages in 16.0% and ARIA-E in 13.6% of all lecanemab-treated participants (Core + open-label extension)
cards.summary: Honig 2024 (Clarity AD safety update, trial data): ARIA-E occurred in 34.5% of ApoE ε4 homozygotes and 16.8% of ε4 carriers overall on lecanemab; ARIA-H microhaemorrhages in 16.0% and ARIA-E in 13.6% of all lecanemab-treated participants (Core + open-label extension)
cards.type: Phase 3 trial safety report — Clarity AD Core + open-label extension (Honig 2024)
cards.people: Participants with early Alzheimer's disease in the 18-month double-blind Clarity AD core study (1,795 participants) and its open-label extension (1,612 participants received at least one lecanemab dose across Core + extension), treated with lecanemab 10 mg/kg biweekly or placebo. Evidence type: randomised-trial safety data, labelled on the face.
cards.result: In Core + extension, the most common adverse events on lecanemab were infusion-related reactions (24.5%), ARIA with haemosiderin deposits (ARIA-H) microhaemorrhages (16.0%) and ARIA with oedema (ARIA-E, 13.6%). ARIA-E generally occurred within 3–6 months of treatment, was more common in ApoE ε4 carriers (16.8%) and most common in ApoE ε4 homozygous participants (34.5%). Three deaths in Core + extension were due to intracerebral haemorrhage (1 on placebo in the Core; 2 on lecanemab in the extension, one with tissue plasminogen activator and one on anticoagulant therapy). No deaths were related to lecanemab in the Core study; 4 of 9 extension deaths were deemed possibly related to treatment.
cards.watchOut: This is a safety report of the same Clarity AD programme whose primary efficacy record is homed on live shelf #333; it is carded here because this shelf asks the narrower ApoE4-stratified risk question, and the homed primary record is cross-pointed, not re-carded. Extension-phase rates lack a placebo comparator.
cards.source: Honig LS et al. Updated safety results from phase 3 lecanemab study in early Alzheimer's disease. Alzheimer's Research & Therapy. 2024. PMID: 38730496. Registry ID: NCT03887455. cards.headline: Shields 2024 (real-world cohort, observational): of 71 patients treated at a regional centre, ARIA appeared in 44% of ApoE4 homozygotes (4 of 9) and 17% of heterozygotes (6 of 36) who had monitoring MRIs — small denominators, printed on the face
cards.summary: Shields 2024 (real-world cohort, observational): of 71 patients treated at a regional centre, ARIA appeared in 44% of ApoE4 homozygotes (4 of 9) and 17% of heterozygotes (6 of 36) who had monitoring MRIs — small denominators, printed on the face
cards.people: The first 71 patients treated with lecanemab at a regional US memory centre (mean age 72 years); 36 (51%) were heterozygous and 9 (13%) homozygous for ApoE4. Fifty patients completed one or more safety-monitoring MRIs after infusion. Evidence type: retrospective observational cohort, labelled on the face. Subgroup denominators are small (9 homozygotes) and are printed here.
cards.result: Of the 50 patients with monitoring MRIs, 12 (24%) had ARIA detected: solitary ARIA-H (haemorrhage) in 5, solitary ARIA-E (oedema) in 3, and both in 4; 9 of the 12 were asymptomatic. Of the 9 ApoE4 homozygotes, 4 (44%) had ARIA; of the 36 heterozygotes, 6 (17%) had ARIA. Twenty-six patients (37%) had infusion reactions after the first infusion. One patient died of a myocardial infarction shortly after the first infusion; whether it was related to treatment is uncertain in the record.
cards.watchOut: Only 50 of 71 patients had monitoring MRIs, so the 24% figure is a rate among the scanned, and the homozygote estimate rests on 9 patients — it corroborates the trial gradient, it cannot refine it.
cards.source: Shields LBE et al. Initial Experience with Lecanemab and Lessons Learned in 71 Patients in a Regional Medical Center. Journal of Prevention of Alzheimer's Disease. 2024. PMID: 39559868. cards.headline: Shang 2025 (real-world cohort, observational): in 76 early-stage patients in eastern China, ARIA occurred in 11 patients (7 ARIA-H alone, 4 ARIA-E with or without microhaemorrhage), all asymptomatic; 64.5% were ApoE ε4 carriers
cards.summary: Shang 2025 (real-world cohort, observational): in 76 early-stage patients in eastern China, ARIA occurred in 11 patients (7 ARIA-H alone, 4 ARIA-E with or without microhaemorrhage), all asymptomatic; 64.5% were ApoE ε4 carriers
cards.people: 76 participants with early-stage Alzheimer's disease treated with lecanemab at a single centre in eastern China (mean age 66 years; 67.1% female); 49 (64.5%) were ApoE ε4 carriers, including 34 (44.7%) heterozygotes and 15 (19.7%) homozygotes. Evidence type: prospective observational cohort, labelled on the face.
cards.result: ARIA was observed in 11 participants: solitary ARIA-H in 7 and ARIA-E with or without cerebral microhaemorrhage in 4; all 11 were asymptomatic. Infusion-related side effects occurred in 14 participants (18.4%), primarily after the first infusion. The record does not report ARIA rates stratified by ε4 copy number, so no homozygote-specific rate can be taken from this card — that absence is printed plainly. The authors note ARIA-E events were less common than in Clarity AD.
cards.watchOut: Single-centre, short and uneven follow-up (58 patients beyond 3 months, only 12 beyond 12 months), so late ARIA is under-counted and the unstratified ARIA count cannot answer the ApoE4 question by itself.
cards.source: Shang J et al. Real-world application of lecanemab in early-stage alzheimer's disease: a single-center prospective cohort analysis. Alzheimer's Research & Therapy. 2025. PMID: 41250246. cards.people: The carded evidence: one phase 3 trial safety report (1,795 core participants; 1,612 lecanemab-exposed across core + extension) and two real-world observational cohorts (71 and 76 patients). Evidence types are labelled on each card's face, as this is a risk-quantification shelf. The Clarity AD primary efficacy record is homed on live shelf #333 and is cross-pointed here, not re-carded.
cards.result: ARIA-E: 34.5% in ApoE ε4 homozygotes and 16.8% in ε4 carriers overall in the trial safety data (Honig 2024), with any ARIA in 44% of homozygotes (4 of 9) versus 17% of heterozygotes (6 of 36) in the US real-world cohort (Shields 2024) and 11 of 76 patients affected, all asymptomatic, in the Chinese cohort (Shang 2025). Most ARIA is radiographic and asymptomatic, but intracerebral haemorrhage deaths occurred in the extension, including with thrombolysis and anticoagulation. PROPOSED LIKELY (risk, graded by ApoE ε4 copy number).
cards.watchOut: Genotype is the dominant modifier but not the only one: baseline microhaemorrhages, cerebral amyloid angiopathy and antithrombotic or thrombolytic treatment add risk, and real-world cohorts are small with incomplete MRI follow-up.

shelves.title: Agonist vs levodopa in early Parkinson's: fewer dyskinesias (odds ratio 0.51) but NOT equal motor efficacy — levodopa relieves symptoms better and agonists cause more dropouts
shelves.question: Is a dopamine agonist as effective as levodopa for motor symptoms in early Parkinson's disease with fewer dyskinesias?
shelves.mesh: Antiparkinson Agents/*therapeutic use · Dopamine Agonists/*therapeutic use · Dyskinesia, Drug-Induced · Humans · Levodopa/therapeutic use · Parkinson Disease/*drug therapy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: SPLIT (fewer dyskinesias: benefit; symptom control and tolerability: harm). The dyskinesia half of the question is answered yes: pooled across 29 trials, agonists halve the odds of dyskinesia versus levodopa (odds ratio 0.51), and a 5-year trial shows absolute dyskinesia rates of 9.5% versus 21.2%. The efficacy half is answered no: in both long head-to-head trials, levodopa gave significantly greater motor improvement, and the meta-analysis concludes symptom control is poorer with agonists, alongside more oedema, somnolence, hallucinations and a more-than-doubled odds of stopping for adverse events (odds ratio 2.49). PROPOSED SPLIT: an agonist-first strategy trades better long-term motor-complication rates for weaker symptom control and worse non-motor tolerability.

cards.headline: Stowe 2008 (Cochrane meta-analysis, 29 trials, 5,247 participants): dopamine agonists halved the odds of dyskinesia versus levodopa (odds ratio 0.51) — but symptom control was poorer and non-motor side effects and dropouts were higher
cards.summary: Stowe 2008 (Cochrane meta-analysis, 29 trials, 5,247 participants): dopamine agonists halved the odds of dyskinesia versus levodopa (odds ratio 0.51) — but symptom control was poorer and non-motor side effects and dropouts were higher
cards.people: 5,247 participants with early Parkinson's disease in 29 randomised trials of an oral dopamine agonist (with or without levodopa) versus placebo or levodopa.
cards.result: Compared with levodopa, agonist-treated participants were less likely to develop dyskinesia (odds ratio 0.51, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.59), dystonia (odds ratio 0.64, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.81) and motor fluctuations (odds ratio 0.75, 95% CI 0.63 to 0.90) — relative measures from the record; the record gives no absolute dyskinesia rates for this pooled comparison. But oedema (odds ratio 3.68), somnolence (1.49), constipation (1.59), dizziness (1.45), hallucinations (1.69) and nausea (1.32) were all increased, discontinuation for adverse events was more than doubled (odds ratio 2.49, 95% CI 2.08 to 2.98), and symptomatic control was better with levodopa (reported too inconsistently to meta-analyse).
cards.watchOut: Many included trials allowed levodopa rescue in the agonist arms, so part of the dyskinesia advantage reflects lower total levodopa exposure rather than an intrinsic agonist property; the pooled symptom-control data could not be meta-analysed.
cards.source: Stowe RL et al. Dopamine agonist therapy in early Parkinson's disease. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2008. PMID: 18425954. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Oertel 2006 (PELMOPET, strict monotherapy RCT, N = 294): pergolide delayed dyskinesia and lessened motor-complication severity over 3 years, but levodopa gave significantly greater symptomatic relief and fewer patients stopped levodopa for adverse events (9.6% vs 17.6%)
cards.summary: Oertel 2006 (PELMOPET, strict monotherapy RCT, N = 294): pergolide delayed dyskinesia and lessened motor-complication severity over 3 years, but levodopa gave significantly greater symptomatic relief and fewer patients stopped levodopa for adverse events (9.6% vs 17.6%)
cards.people: 294 dopamine-naive patients with early Parkinson's disease (Hoehn and Yahr stage 1–2.5) in a multicentre, double-blind, randomised 3-year trial of strict pergolide monotherapy (n = 148, mean 3.23 mg/day) versus levodopa monotherapy (n = 146, mean 504 mg/day), with no levodopa rescue.
cards.result: Severity of motor complications was significantly lower and time to onset of dyskinesia was significantly delayed with pergolide, although time to onset of motor complications overall was not longer after 3 years. Symptomatic relief (Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale total, parts II and III, and global impression scores) was significantly greater with levodopa. Adverse events led to discontinuation in 17.6% of pergolide patients and 9.6% of levodopa patients. The record reports no absolute dyskinesia percentages for this trial — printed plainly.
cards.watchOut: Pergolide is an ergot agonist no longer representative of first-line agonist choice, and strict monotherapy without rescue is not how agonists are usually used — the trial isolates the class trade-off rather than modelling practice.
cards.source: Oertel WH et al. Pergolide versus levodopa monotherapy in early Parkinson's disease patients: The PELMOPET study. Movement Disorders. 2006. PMID: 16211594. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Bracco 2004 (5-year RCT, N = 419): starting on cabergoline instead of levodopa cut dyskinesia from 21.2% to 9.5% and motor complications from 33.7% to 22.3% — at the cost of significantly less motor improvement and more peripheral oedema (16.1% vs 3.4%)
cards.summary: Bracco 2004 (5-year RCT, N = 419): starting on cabergoline instead of levodopa cut dyskinesia from 21.2% to 9.5% and motor complications from 33.7% to 22.3% — at the cost of significantly less motor improvement and more peripheral oedema (16.1% vs 3.4%)
cards.people: 419 levodopa-, agonist- and selegiline-naive patients with newly diagnosed Parkinson's disease randomised to cabergoline (n = 211) or levodopa (n = 209) as initial therapy for up to 5 years; supplemental levodopa was allowed, and the cabergoline group received under half the levodopa dose of the levodopa group (mean 322–431 mg vs 784 mg daily).
cards.result: Motor complications were delayed (P = 0.0175) and less frequent on cabergoline (22.3% vs 33.7%); the relative risk of developing them was 0.46 (P < 0.001) — a relative measure, with the absolute rates beside it here. Dyskinesia occurred in 9.5% on cabergoline versus 21.2% on levodopa (P < 0.001). However, levodopa produced a significantly greater improvement in motor disability over time (P < 0.001), and peripheral oedema was significantly more frequent on cabergoline (16.1% vs 3.4%, P < 0.0001).
cards.watchOut: Most cabergoline patients eventually took supplemental levodopa, so this is an agonist-first strategy trial, not pure monotherapy; cabergoline is also an ergot agonist, and class tolerability differs among modern non-ergot agonists.
cards.source: Bracco F et al. The long-acting dopamine receptor agonist cabergoline in early Parkinson's disease: final results of a 5-year, double-blind, levodopa-controlled study. CNS Drugs. 2004. PMID: 15330687. Registry ID: none in the record.
