cards.headline: Synthesis: the trade is real on both sides — agonist-first treatment roughly halves dyskinesia (odds ratio 0.51 pooled; 9.5% vs 21.2% at 5 years in one trial) but is NOT as effective as levodopa for motor symptoms and carries more non-motor side effects and dropouts
cards.summary: Synthesis: the trade is real on both sides — agonist-first treatment roughly halves dyskinesia (odds ratio 0.51 pooled; 9.5% vs 21.2% at 5 years in one trial) but is NOT as effective as levodopa for motor symptoms and carries more non-motor side effects and dropouts
cards.people: The carded evidence: a Cochrane meta-analysis of 29 trials (5,247 participants), a 3-year strict-monotherapy trial (N = 294) and a 5-year initial-therapy trial (N = 419). Total carded participants exceed 5,900 (the two trials sit inside the meta-analysis's era and may overlap its count), so no small-N labelling applies.
cards.result: Dyskinesia and motor fluctuations are consistently fewer with agonists (pooled odds ratios 0.51 and 0.75; Stowe 2008), while motor symptom relief is consistently better with levodopa (both individual trials, significantly) and agonists bring more oedema, somnolence, hallucinations and treatment discontinuation (odds ratio 2.49 for discontinuation). PROPOSED SPLIT (fewer dyskinesias: benefit; symptom control and tolerability: harm).
cards.watchOut: The answer to the question as asked is no on efficacy and yes on dyskinesias: an agonist is not as effective as levodopa for motor symptoms, and the dyskinesia sparing is partly bought with lower levodopa exposure and worse tolerability.
cards.source: Synthesis of Stowe RL et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2008 (PMID: 18425954); Oertel WH et al. Movement Disorders. 2006 (PMID: 16211594); Bracco F et al. CNS Drugs. 2004 (PMID: 15330687).

shelves.title: Extended-release levodopa cuts off time by ~1.2 extra hours/day vs immediate-release (23.8% vs 29.8% of waking hours) in phase 3 trials
shelves.question: Does extended-release levodopa reduce off time compared with immediate-release levodopa in advanced Parkinson's disease?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Carbidopa/*administration & dosage · Chemistry, Pharmaceutical · Delayed-Action Preparations/administration & dosage · Double-Blind Method · Drug Combinations · Female · Humans · Levodopa/*administration & dosage · Male · Middle Aged · Motor Skills Disorders/*drug therapy/*epidemiology · Parkinson Disease/*drug therapy/*epidemiology · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit). Two concordant phase 3 randomised trials of the extended-release carbidopa-levodopa formulation show less off time than immediate-release treatment: in the direct head-to-head trial, off time was 23.82% versus 29.79% of waking hours, an extra 1.17 hours/day removed (Hauser 2013, N = 393), and against immediate-release plus entacapone the figures were 3.8 versus 5.2 hours/day (Stocchi 2014, N = 91), without increased troublesome dyskinesia. The honest caveat, printed on the cards, is that conversion raised the total levodopa dose, so the benefit belongs to the formulation as dosed in its trials. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): extended-release levodopa reduces off time compared with immediate-release levodopa in advanced Parkinson's disease.

cards.headline: Hauser 2013 (phase 3 RCT, N = 393 randomised): extended-release carbidopa-levodopa cut off time to 23.8% of waking hours vs 29.8% on immediate-release — an extra 1.17 hours of off time removed per day
cards.summary: Hauser 2013 (phase 3 RCT, N = 393 randomised): extended-release carbidopa-levodopa cut off time to 23.8% of waking hours vs 29.8% on immediate-release — an extra 1.17 hours of off time removed per day
cards.people: Patients with Parkinson's disease and at least 2.5 hours/day of off time at 68 centres in North America and Europe; 471 enrolled, 393 randomised (201 extended-release, 192 immediate-release) to 13 weeks of double-blind treatment after open-label dose adjustment and conversion. Extended-release was taken a mean of 3.6 times/day versus 5.0 times/day for immediate-release.
cards.result: Covariate-adjusted end-of-study off time was 23.82% of waking hours on extended-release versus 29.79% on immediate-release (mean difference -5.97 percentage points, 95% CI -9.05 to -2.89; P < 0.0001). Extended-release reduced daily off time by an extra -1.17 hours (95% CI -1.69 to -0.66; P < 0.0001) compared with immediate-release. In the double-blind period the most common adverse events were insomnia (3% vs 1%), nausea (3% vs 2%) and falls (3% vs 2%).
cards.watchOut: The extended-release arm received a higher total levodopa dose after conversion, so part of the gain may be dose rather than formulation; the trial's own conversion design makes the two inseparable.
cards.source: Hauser RA et al. Extended-release carbidopa-levodopa (IPX066) compared with immediate-release carbidopa-levodopa in patients with Parkinson's disease and motor fluctuations: a phase 3 randomised, double-blind trial. Lancet Neurology. 2013. PMID: 23485610. Registry ID: NCT00974974. cards.headline: Stocchi 2014 (phase 3 crossover RCT, N = 91): extended-release also beat immediate-release PLUS entacapone — off time 24.0% vs 32.5% of the day (3.8 vs 5.2 hours/day)
cards.summary: Stocchi 2014 (phase 3 crossover RCT, N = 91): extended-release also beat immediate-release PLUS entacapone — off time 24.0% vs 32.5% of the day (3.8 vs 5.2 hours/day)
cards.people: 91 randomised patients with advanced Parkinson's disease and motor fluctuations on a stable regimen of immediate-release carbidopa-levodopa plus entacapone (84 completed); after 6-week conversion, two 2-week double-blind crossover periods compared extended-release against immediate-release plus entacapone. Median daily levodopa dose was 1,495 mg from extended-release versus 600 mg from the comparator, an approximately 22% higher levodopa exposure after bioavailability correction.
cards.result: Compared with immediate-release plus entacapone, extended-release gave lower percent off time (24.0% vs 32.5%; P < 0.0001), lower off time (3.8 vs 5.2 hours/day; P < 0.0001) and higher on time without troublesome dyskinesia (11.4 vs 10.0 hours/day; P < 0.0001). Adverse events in double-blind treatment were reported by 20.2% on extended-release and 13.6% on the comparator.
cards.watchOut: The comparator here is immediate-release levodopa combined with entacapone, not immediate-release alone, and levodopa exposure was about 22% higher on extended-release — the comparison favours the formulation-plus-dose package, not the formulation alone.
cards.source: Stocchi F et al. Comparison of IPX066 with carbidopa-levodopa plus entacapone in advanced PD patients. Parkinsonism & Related Disorders. 2014. PMID: 25306200. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: LeWitt 2018 (post hoc analysis of both phase 3 trials, N = 393 + 91): the off-time advantage held alongside dopamine agonists and MAO-B inhibitors, with about an extra hour of good on time; the amantadine subgroup did not reach significance
cards.summary: LeWitt 2018 (post hoc analysis of both phase 3 trials, N = 393 + 91): the off-time advantage held alongside dopamine agonists and MAO-B inhibitors, with about an extra hour of good on time; the amantadine subgroup did not reach significance
cards.type: Post hoc analysis of two phase 3 randomised trials (LeWitt 2018)
cards.people: Post hoc subgroups of the two phase 3 trials (ADVANCE-PD n = 393, extended-release vs immediate-release; ASCEND-PD n = 91, extended-release vs immediate-release plus entacapone), split by concomitant dopamine agonist, rasagiline or selegiline, or amantadine use. These populations overlap the two trial cards above and are not independent patients.
cards.result: Concomitant dopamine agonist or MAO-B inhibitor use did not diminish the efficacy of extended-release versus its comparators on off time and on time without troublesome dyskinesia, whereas the improvement with concomitant amantadine failed to reach significance. Safety and tolerability were similar among subgroups, extended-release did not increase troublesome dyskinesia, and the record summarises the gain as approximately an additional hour of 'good' on time for patients switching from an immediate-release to an extended-release formulation while on an agonist and/or MAO-B inhibitor.
cards.watchOut: Post hoc subgroup analysis: the amantadine subgroup's non-significance may reflect subgroup size rather than a true interaction, and no new patients are added by this card.
cards.source: LeWitt PA et al. Effect of Concomitant Medications on the Safety and Efficacy of Extended-Release Carbidopa-Levodopa (IPX066) in Patients With Advanced Parkinson Disease: A Post Hoc Analysis. Clinical Neuropharmacology. 2018. PMID: 29432286. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: extended-release levodopa reduces off time versus immediate-release by about 1.2 hours/day (23.8% vs 29.8% of waking hours) in the definitive head-to-head trial, with a concordant win against immediate-release plus entacapone
cards.summary: Synthesis: extended-release levodopa reduces off time versus immediate-release by about 1.2 hours/day (23.8% vs 29.8% of waking hours) in the definitive head-to-head trial, with a concordant win against immediate-release plus entacapone
cards.people: The carded evidence: two phase 3 randomised trials (393 + 91 randomised patients) of the same extended-release formulation and a post hoc analysis of both. Unique randomised participants = 484, so no small-N labelling applies.
cards.result: Off time fell further on extended-release in both trials (extra -1.17 hours/day, 95% CI -1.69 to -0.66, Hauser 2013; 3.8 vs 5.2 hours/day against the entacapone combination, Stocchi 2014), on time without troublesome dyskinesia rose, and troublesome dyskinesia did not increase. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit), on two concordant phase 3 randomised trials of one formulation.
cards.watchOut: Both trials converted patients to a higher levodopa dose on the extended-release formulation, so the shelf answers 'the extended-release product as dosed in its trials' — a dose-matched formulation-only effect has not been isolated.
cards.source: Synthesis of Hauser RA et al. Lancet Neurology. 2013 (PMID: 23485610); Stocchi F et al. Parkinsonism & Related Disorders. 2014 (PMID: 25306200); LeWitt PA et al. Clinical Neuropharmacology. 2018 (PMID: 29432286).

shelves.title: Brand-to-generic antiseizure switch: associated with more breakthrough seizures in observational data (odds ratio 1.85) — no randomised evidence, pharmacokinetics unchanged on average
shelves.question: Does switching from brand to generic antiseizure medication increase breakthrough seizures?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Age Factors · Aged · Anticonvulsants/*therapeutic use · Cohort Studies · Drug Substitution · Drugs, Generic/therapeutic use · Epilepsy/*drug therapy/*epidemiology · Female · Germany/epidemiology · Humans · Logistic Models · Male · Middle Aged · Prescription Drugs/therapeutic use · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only, printed on the face. No randomised trial answers this question. The largest dataset (3,530 German patients) associates a manufacturer switch with breakthrough seizures (brand-to-generic odds ratio 1.85, a relative measure, with switch rates of 5.5% versus 2.4%), a solicited case series documents 50 breakthrough events after switching with lower drug levels in 21 of 26 paired cases, and a 67-study systematic review finds average pharmacokinetics unchanged but clinical reports inconsistent in both directions. The stamp is capped at POSSIBLE by the evidence type, and the prudent clinical reading — avoid manufacturer switches in seizure-free patients — is the cohort authors' own conclusion. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only.

cards.headline: Lang 2018 (nationwide observational cohort, N = 3,530): patients whose manufacturer was switched had more breakthrough seizures — brand-to-generic switch odds ratio 1.85, generic-to-generic 1.45 (relative measures; switch rates 5.5% vs 2.4% and 14.7% vs 7.1%)
cards.summary: Lang 2018 (nationwide observational cohort, N = 3,530): patients whose manufacturer was switched had more breakthrough seizures — brand-to-generic switch odds ratio 1.85, generic-to-generic 1.45 (relative measures; switch rates 5.5% vs 2.4% and 14.7% vs 7.1%)
cards.people: 3,530 people with epilepsy in German neurologist practice prescription data (2011–2016), matched 1:1 as a seizure group (n = 1,765) and seizure-free controls (n = 1,765) on age, gender, insurance status and treating physician. Evidence type: retrospective observational (case-control within a prescription cohort), labelled on the face.
cards.result: Patients with seizures had switched the drug manufacturer more often than controls (26.8% vs 14.2%; odds ratio 1.35, 95% CI 1.08 to 1.69; P = 0.009) — an odds ratio is a relative measure; the absolute switch-rate differences beside it are 12.6 percentage points overall, 3.1 points for brand-to-generic (5.5% vs 2.4%; odds ratio 1.85, 95% CI 1.30 to 2.64) and 7.6 points for generic-to-generic (14.7% vs 7.1%; odds ratio 1.45, 95% CI 1.13 to 1.87). The authors conclude it would be prudent to avoid switching the manufacturer of anticonvulsants in seizure-free patients, while noting the retrospective design cannot exclude other simultaneous changes in care.
cards.watchOut: Association is not causation: a manufacturer switch may coincide with pharmacy, adherence or care changes that themselves provoke seizures, and prescription data record dispensing, not ingestion or blood levels.
cards.source: Lang JD et al. Switching the manufacturer of antiepileptic drugs is associated with higher risk of seizures: A nationwide study of prescription data in Germany. Annals of Neurology. 2018. PMID: 30298621. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Berg 2008 (case series, N = 50): fifty patients well controlled on a brand antiseizure drug had a breakthrough seizure or more seizures after switching to a generic with no other provoking factor; 21 of 26 with paired levels had lower drug levels on the generic
cards.summary: Berg 2008 (case series, N = 50): fifty patients well controlled on a brand antiseizure drug had a breakthrough seizure or more seizures after switching to a generic with no other provoking factor; 21 of 26 with paired levels had lower drug levels on the generic
cards.people: 50 patients reported by 69 physicians in a survey-based case review, each well controlled on a brand antiseizure drug and subsequently experiencing a breakthrough seizure or increased seizure frequency after switching to a generic without other provoking factors. Drugs: phenytoin (15 cases), valproic acid (14), carbamazepine (7), gabapentin (8), zonisamide (8). Case-series N = 50, printed on the face. Evidence type: observational case evidence, labelled on the face.
cards.result: In 26 cases serum drug levels were known before and after substitution; 21 had lower levels at the time of the breakthrough seizure on the generic. Loss of seizure control cost 30 patients their driving privileges and 9 missed school or work days. The authors conclude that changing from a brand to a generic antiseizure drug may result in seizures in some patients and question whether standard therapeutic-equivalence testing is adequate for these drugs.
cards.watchOut: Cases were solicited because harm was suspected — there is no denominator of uneventful switches, so this card can show that breakthrough after switching happens, never how often.
cards.source: Berg MJ et al. Generic substitution in the treatment of epilepsy: case evidence of breakthrough seizures. Neurology. 2008. PMID: 18695164. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Weitzel 2020 (systematic review, 67 studies): pharmacokinetic measures barely moved on switching, but clinical reports were inconsistent — some found more seizures and adverse events after exchange, others none; the two small randomised lamotrigine switch trials are the best data available
cards.summary: Weitzel 2020 (systematic review, 67 studies): pharmacokinetic measures barely moved on switching, but clinical reports were inconsistent — some found more seizures and adverse events after exchange, others none; the two small randomised lamotrigine switch trials are the best data available
cards.people: 67 studies of generic exchange of solid oral dosage forms in neurological disorders (searches to October 2018), with epilepsy the leading indication; designs ranged from two small randomised lamotrigine switch trials to cohorts, case-control studies and case reports. Evidence type: systematic review of mostly observational studies, labelled on the face.
cards.result: Analysis found no significant differences in pharmacokinetic parameters (area under the curve, peak concentration) when switching to generic drugs. The clinical picture was heterogeneous: some studies found increased seizure frequencies and adverse-drug events after exchange, others showed no complications, and adherence and patient satisfaction seemed impaired. The authors conclude that generic exchange in epilepsy should be a carefully balanced decision; most included reports were of poor quality, and lamotrigine had the best available data.
cards.watchOut: Bioequivalence on average does not exclude individual-level excursions in narrow-therapeutic-index drugs, and the review's clinical studies point both ways — the inconsistency is itself the finding.
cards.source: Weitzel J et al. Effects of generic exchange of solid oral dosage forms in neurological disorders: a systematic review. International Journal of Clinical Pharmacy. 2020. PMID: 32274633. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: switching manufacturer is associated with more breakthrough seizures in the largest observational dataset (odds ratio 1.85 for brand-to-generic), case evidence shows it happens with lower drug levels, but pharmacokinetic studies and some clinical series find no difference — observational evidence only, no randomised verdict
cards.summary: Synthesis: switching manufacturer is associated with more breakthrough seizures in the largest observational dataset (odds ratio 1.85 for brand-to-generic), case evidence shows it happens with lower drug levels, but pharmacokinetic studies and some clinical series find no difference — observational evidence only, no randomised verdict
cards.people: The carded evidence: one nationwide observational study (N = 3,530), one solicited case series (N = 50) and one systematic review of 67 mostly observational studies. All evidence on this shelf is observational or case-based, labelled on each card's face; total N is far above the small-N threshold, and the cap here comes from evidence type, not size.
cards.result: The association is consistent in direction in the cohort data (Lang 2018) and mechanistically supported by lower measured levels in 21 of 26 paired cases (Berg 2008), yet average pharmacokinetics do not differ and clinical studies conflict (Weitzel 2020). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only: switching from brand to generic antiseizure medication is associated with increased breakthrough seizures in seizure-free patients, and avoiding manufacturer switches in well-controlled patients is the prudent reading.
cards.watchOut: No randomised trial has tested brand-to-generic switching against breakthrough seizures as an outcome; regulatory bioequivalence and the observational signal answer different questions, and both are reported here without merging them.
cards.source: Synthesis of Lang JD et al. Annals of Neurology. 2018 (PMID: 30298621); Berg MJ et al. Neurology. 2008 (PMID: 18695164); Weitzel J et al. International Journal of Clinical Pharmacy. 2020 (PMID: 32274633).

shelves.title: Early high-efficacy vs escalation in MS: observational cohorts consistently favour starting high (0.6–0.9 fewer EDSS points at 5–10 years) — randomised proof still pending
shelves.question: Does early high-efficacy disease-modifying therapy improve long-term disability in relapsing multiple sclerosis compared with escalation therapy?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Adolescent · Adult · Alemtuzumab/therapeutic use · Cohort Studies · Crotonates/therapeutic use · Dimethyl Fumarate/therapeutic use · Disease Progression · Early Medical Intervention/methods · Female · Fingolimod Hydrochloride/therapeutic use · Glatiramer Acetate/therapeutic use · Humans · Hydroxybutyrates · Immunologic Factors/*therapeutic use · Immunosuppressive Agents/therapeutic use · Interferons/therapeutic use · Male · Multiple Sclerosis, Relapsing-Remitting/*drug therapy/physiopathology · Natalizumab/therapeutic use · Nitriles · Retrospective Studies · Toluidines/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face. Three large observational comparisons agree: a population-based cohort found a 5-year EDSS rise of 0.3 with early intensive treatment versus 1.2 with escalation (adjusted difference -0.85), and two propensity-matched Italian registry analyses found the disability gap widening over a decade (0.30 EDSS points at 5 years, 0.63–0.67 at 10 years, with escalation carrying a hazard ratio of 1.36 for confirmed disability accrual, a relative measure). The stamp is capped at POSSIBLE because no randomised strategy trial has reported; confounding by indication is the standing caveat, and it conventionally biases against the early-intensive group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: early high-efficacy therapy is associated with less long-term disability than escalation.

cards.headline: Harding 2019 (population-based observational cohort, N = 592): starting with high-efficacy therapy instead of escalating later gave a smaller 5-year disability rise (EDSS change 0.3 vs 1.2; adjusted difference -0.85)
cards.summary: Harding 2019 (population-based observational cohort, N = 592): starting with high-efficacy therapy instead of escalating later gave a smaller 5-year disability rise (EDSS change 0.3 vs 1.2; adjusted difference -0.85)
cards.people: 592 patients with multiple sclerosis from a population-based cohort (of 720 prescribed a disease-modifying therapy, 1998–2016), classified by first-line strategy: high-efficacy early intensive treatment or moderate-efficacy therapy with later escalation. Evidence type: observational cohort, labelled on the face.
cards.result: Mean 5-year change in Expanded Disability Status Scale score was lower with early intensive treatment than escalation (0.3 vs 1.2), remaining significant after adjustment (beta -0.85, 95% CI -1.38 to -0.32; P = .002). Median time to sustained accumulation of disability was 6.0 years for early intensive versus 3.14 years for escalation (P = .05), although after adjustment there was no difference in the hazard of sustained accumulation; notably, 60% of patients who later escalated developed sustained disability while still on their initial moderate-efficacy treatment, before escalation.
cards.watchOut: Treatment was chosen, not randomised: patients given high-efficacy therapy first usually had worse prognostic features, which biases against the early-intensive group, yet residual confounding by indication cannot be excluded in either direction.
cards.source: Harding K et al. Clinical Outcomes of Escalation vs Early Intensive Disease-Modifying Therapy in Patients With Multiple Sclerosis. JAMA Neurology. 2019. PMID: 30776055. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Iaffaldano 2021 (registry observational study, 363 matched pairs): disability trajectories diverged year by year — the EDSS gap between early-intensive and escalation strategies grew from 0.1 at 1 year to 0.30 at 5 years and 0.67 at 10 years
cards.summary: Iaffaldano 2021 (registry observational study, 363 matched pairs): disability trajectories diverged year by year — the EDSS gap between early-intensive and escalation strategies grew from 0.1 at 1 year to 0.30 at 5 years and 0.67 at 10 years
cards.people: 2,702 patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis from the Italian MS Registry with at least 5 years of follow-up; propensity matching produced 363 pairs (early intensive: first therapy fingolimod, natalizumab, mitoxantrone, alemtuzumab, ocrelizumab or cladribine; escalation: a high-efficacy therapy only after at least a year of a moderate-efficacy therapy), followed a median of 8.5 years. Evidence type: observational registry study, labelled on the face.
cards.result: Mean annual EDSS change from baseline was significantly higher in the escalation group at every time point (all P < 0.02). The between-group difference in EDSS change grew from 0.1 (95% CI 0.01 to 0.19; P = 0.03) at 1 year to 0.30 (0.07 to 0.53; P = 0.009) at 5 years and 0.67 (0.31 to 1.03; P = 0.0003) at 10 years. The authors conclude the early intensive strategy is more effective than escalation in controlling disability progression over time.
cards.watchOut: Propensity matching balances measured features only; registry EDSS scoring is unblinded, and patients matched at first treatment may still differ in ways the registry does not capture.
cards.source: Iaffaldano P et al. Long-term disability trajectories in relapsing multiple sclerosis patients treated with early intensive or escalation treatment strategies. Therapeutic Advances in Neurological Disorders. 2021. PMID: 34104220. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Iaffaldano 2025 (registry observational study, 908 matched pairs): at 10 years the early-intensive group had accumulated 0.63 fewer EDSS points, and escalation carried higher risks of confirmed disability accrual (hazard ratio 1.36) and progression independent of relapses (1.22) — relative measures
cards.summary: Iaffaldano 2025 (registry observational study, 908 matched pairs): at 10 years the early-intensive group had accumulated 0.63 fewer EDSS points, and escalation carried higher risks of confirmed disability accrual (hazard ratio 1.36) and progression independent of relapses (1.22) — relative measures
cards.people: 4,878 patients with relapsing multiple sclerosis from the Italian MS and Related Disorders Register who started a first disease-modifying therapy within 3 years of onset with at least 5 years of follow-up; propensity matching produced 908 pairs of early intensive versus escalation patients. Evidence type: observational registry study, labelled on the face.
cards.result: At 10 years the difference in EDSS change between groups was -0.63 points favouring early intensive treatment (95% CI -0.83 to -0.43; P < 0.0001). Escalation was associated with higher risks of confirmed disability accrual (hazard ratio 1.36, 95% CI 1.20 to 1.54), progression independent of relapse activity (hazard ratio 1.22, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.40) and relapse-associated worsening (hazard ratio 1.55, 95% CI 1.17 to 2.05) — hazard ratios are relative measures; the record gives no absolute event rates for these outcomes, printed plainly.
cards.watchOut: Same registry family as the 2021 card, so the two Italian analyses are corroborating reads of overlapping data, not fully independent replications; no randomised strategy trial has reported.
cards.source: Iaffaldano P et al. Early Intensive Versus Escalation Approach: Ten-Year Impact on Disability in Relapsing Multiple Sclerosis. Annals of Clinical and Translational Neurology. 2025. PMID: 40619726. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.people: The carded evidence: three observational comparisons (592 population-based patients; 363 and 908 propensity-matched pairs from the Italian registry), totalling several thousand patients, so no small-N labelling applies. No completed randomised trial of treatment strategy is carded, because none has reported in the records fetched; the stamp is capped by evidence type.
cards.result: Five-year EDSS change was 0.3 versus 1.2 favouring early intensive treatment (Harding 2019), and the Italian trajectories diverged progressively to 0.67 EDSS points at 10 years (Iaffaldano 2021) and -0.63 points with higher accrual hazards on escalation (Iaffaldano 2025). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only.
cards.watchOut: Confounding by indication runs through every card: clinicians reserve early high-efficacy treatment for worse-looking disease, which should bias against it — the consistency of the direction despite that bias is reassuring, but only a randomised strategy trial settles causation.

shelves.title: Vitamin D for MS relapses: pooled trials show no reduction in relapse rate (rate difference -0.05, CI spans zero) — supplementation does not prevent relapses
shelves.question: Should vitamin D supplementation reduce relapse rate in multiple sclerosis?
shelves.mesh: Cholecalciferol/*therapeutic use · Ergocalciferols/*therapeutic use · Fatigue/drug therapy · Humans · Multiple Sclerosis/*drug therapy · Quality of Life · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Vitamins/*therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (no benefit shown) — the treatment made no difference in the randomised evidence. The Cochrane review of 12 trials (933 participants) finds no effect on the annualised relapse rate at 52 weeks (rate difference -0.05, 95% CI -0.17 to 0.07, very low-quality evidence); a dose-ranging trial after clinically isolated syndrome found no delay in conversion at 1,000, 5,000 or 10,000 IU daily; and in a SOLAR substudy a verified rise in blood vitamin D to 281 nmol/L (about 112 ng/mL) left the nerve-injury marker neurofilament light chain unchanged. The SOLAR primary report is homed on pack #2364, which covers vitamin D in clinically isolated syndrome and early relapsing disease; this shelf answers the relapse-rate question in established multiple sclerosis from the pooled review and the free reports, cross-pointing #2364 rather than re-carding it. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (no benefit shown): vitamin D supplementation should not be expected to reduce the relapse rate in multiple sclerosis.

cards.headline: Jagannath 2018 (Cochrane review, 12 RCTs, 933 participants): vitamin D made no difference to the annualised relapse rate at 52 weeks (rate difference -0.05, 95% CI -0.17 to 0.07; very low-quality evidence)
cards.summary: Jagannath 2018 (Cochrane review, 12 RCTs, 933 participants): vitamin D made no difference to the annualised relapse rate at 52 weeks (rate difference -0.05, 95% CI -0.17 to 0.07; very low-quality evidence)
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (Jagannath 2018)
cards.people: 933 people with multiple sclerosis in 12 randomised or quasi-randomised trials of vitamin D versus placebo, routine care or low-dose vitamin D (464 vitamin D, 469 comparator); 11 trials tested vitamin D3 and one vitamin D2, given alone or with calcium, with background therapies used equally across arms.
cards.result: Vitamin D3 had no effect on the annualised relapse rate at 52 weeks (rate difference -0.05, 95% CI -0.17 to 0.07; 5 trials, 417 participants; very low-quality evidence by GRADE) — the treatment made no difference the data could distinguish. The effect on the Expanded Disability Status Scale at 52 weeks was likewise a null point estimate (mean difference -0.25, 95% CI -0.61 to 0.10; 5 trials, 221 participants).
cards.watchOut: 'Very low-quality' is the review's own GRADE rating: the trials are small and short, so the pooled null excludes a large relapse effect but cannot exclude a modest one.
cards.source: Jagannath VA et al. Vitamin D for the management of multiple sclerosis. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2018. PMID: 30246874. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Butzkueven 2024 (dose-ranging RCT, N = 199 analysed): after a high-risk clinically isolated syndrome, vitamin D3 at 1,000, 5,000 or 10,000 IU daily did not delay conversion to definite multiple sclerosis at any dose (hazard ratios 0.87, 1.37 and 1.28 vs placebo — relative measures, all non-significant)
cards.summary: Butzkueven 2024 (dose-ranging RCT, N = 199 analysed): after a high-risk clinically isolated syndrome, vitamin D3 at 1,000, 5,000 or 10,000 IU daily did not delay conversion to definite multiple sclerosis at any dose (hazard ratios 0.87, 1.37 and 1.28 vs placebo — relative measures, all non-significant)
cards.people: 204 participants with high-risk clinically isolated syndrome (abnormal MRI with at least three T2 lesions) in Australia and New Zealand, randomised to placebo or 1,000, 5,000 or 10,000 IU of oral vitamin D3 daily for up to 48 weeks; 199 were included in the intention-to-treat analysis, of whom 116 (58%) converted to clinically definite multiple sclerosis, defined by a clinical relapse or a new MRI T2 lesion.
cards.result: Compared with placebo, the hazard ratios for conversion were 0.87 (95% CI 0.50 to 1.50) at 1,000 IU, 1.37 (0.82 to 2.29) at 5,000 IU and 1.28 (0.76 to 2.14) at 10,000 IU — hazard ratios are relative measures, and none showed a reduction; adjusted hazard ratios were 0.80, 1.36 and 1.07 respectively. Vitamin D3 was safe and well tolerated. The authors conclude supplementation did not reduce multiple sclerosis disease activity after a high-risk clinically isolated syndrome.
cards.watchOut: This trial answers the earliest-disease version of the question (conversion after clinically isolated syndrome, an outcome mixing relapses with MRI lesions), not relapse rate in established relapsing multiple sclerosis — it corroborates the null, it does not replace the Cochrane read.
cards.source: Butzkueven H et al. Vitamin D did not reduce multiple sclerosis disease activity after a clinically isolated syndrome. Brain. 2024. PMID: 38085047. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Smolders 2020 (SOLAR biomarker substudy, N = 40): 14,000 IU/day of vitamin D3 raised blood levels to 281 vs 72 nmol/L (about 112 vs 29 ng/mL) yet neurofilament light chain — a marker of nerve injury — was identical at 48 weeks (25.4 vs 25.3 pg/mL, P = .74; the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Smolders 2020 (SOLAR biomarker substudy, N = 40): 14,000 IU/day of vitamin D3 raised blood levels to 281 vs 72 nmol/L (about 112 vs 29 ng/mL) yet neurofilament light chain — a marker of nerve injury — was identical at 48 weeks (25.4 vs 25.3 pg/mL, P = .74; the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: 40 Dutch interferon beta-treated participants with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis from the SOLAR trial with plasma samples at baseline and 48 weeks: 24 supplemented with 14,000 IU/day of vitamin D3 and 16 with placebo. Substudy N = 40, printed on the face.
cards.result: Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D3 at 48 weeks was far higher on supplementation (median 281 nmol/L, about 112 ng/mL, vs 72 nmol/L, about 29 ng/mL; P < .01), confirming the dose was absorbed. Neurofilament light chain at 48 weeks did not differ between groups (median 25.4 vs 25.3 pg/mL; P = .74). The authors conclude high-dose vitamin D3 was not associated with lower neurofilament levels and the study does not support an effect on this biomarker of neuro-axonal injury. The SOLAR trial's primary clinical report is homed on pack #2364 and is cross-pointed, not re-carded, on this shelf.
cards.watchOut: A 40-patient biomarker substudy cannot rule on relapses; its value is showing that a large, verified rise in vitamin D levels did not move a sensitive injury marker in the parent trial's population.
cards.source: Smolders J et al. Vitamin D(3) supplementation and neurofilament light chain in multiple sclerosis. Acta Neurologica Scandinavica. 2020. PMID: 31657006. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: pooled randomised trials show no reduction in relapse rate from vitamin D (rate difference -0.05, CI spanning zero), a dose-ranging trial in early disease was null at every dose, and a verified large rise in blood levels moved no injury biomarker — supplementation should not be expected to reduce relapses
cards.summary: Synthesis: pooled randomised trials show no reduction in relapse rate from vitamin D (rate difference -0.05, CI spanning zero), a dose-ranging trial in early disease was null at every dose, and a verified large rise in blood levels moved no injury biomarker — supplementation should not be expected to reduce relapses
cards.people: The carded evidence: a Cochrane review of 12 randomised trials (933 participants), a 4-arm dose-ranging randomised trial (199 analysed) and a randomised biomarker substudy (N = 40). Total carded participants exceed 1,100 (the substudy sits inside the SOLAR programme counted within the review's era), so no small-N labelling applies. The SOLAR primary report is homed on pack #2364 (vitamin D in clinically isolated syndrome / early relapsing multiple sclerosis) and is cross-pointed here; this shelf asks the relapse-rate question in established multiple sclerosis.
cards.result: Annualised relapse rate at 52 weeks: rate difference -0.05 (95% CI -0.17 to 0.07) — no effect (Jagannath 2018). Conversion after clinically isolated syndrome: hazard ratios 0.87, 1.37 and 1.28 across a ten-fold dose range — no effect at any dose (Butzkueven 2024). Neurofilament light chain after 48 weeks of 14,000 IU/day: 25.4 vs 25.3 pg/mL — no effect (Smolders 2020). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (no benefit shown): on current randomised evidence, vitamin D supplementation does not reduce the relapse rate in multiple sclerosis (the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: Correcting a documented vitamin D deficiency remains good general care; what the trials refute is a relapse-preventing effect of supplementation in people with multiple sclerosis, and the pooled evidence is graded very low quality, so a small effect is not excluded.
cards.source: Synthesis of Jagannath VA et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2018 (PMID: 30246874); Butzkueven H et al. Brain. 2024 (PMID: 38085047); Smolders J et al. Acta Neurologica Scandinavica. 2020 (PMID: 31657006).

shelves.title: Exercise for MS fatigue: yes — pooled randomised evidence shows a clear reduction (standardised mean difference -0.53), with combined and resistance programmes best
shelves.question: Does a structured exercise program reduce fatigue in multiple sclerosis?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Exercise Therapy/*methods · Fatigue/etiology/*therapy · Humans · Multiple Sclerosis/*complications/*rehabilitation · Physical Conditioning, Human/*methods · Physical Endurance · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Resistance Training · Yoga
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit). Two independent syntheses of randomised trials agree: the Cochrane review (45 trials, 2,250 participants) finds fatigue reduced versus no exercise (standardised mean difference -0.53, 95% CI -0.73 to -0.33), and a 58-study network meta-analysis ranks combined exercise and resistance training highest. A randomised trial enrolling only fatigued patients confirms a clinically relevant effect size (about 10 fatigue-scale points over 12 weeks of resistance training). The standing caveat is that fatigue is self-reported and exercise cannot be blinded. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): a structured exercise programme reduces fatigue in multiple sclerosis.

cards.headline: Heine 2015 (Cochrane review, 45 trials, 2,250 participants): exercise therapy reduced fatigue versus no exercise (standardised mean difference -0.53, 95% CI -0.73 to -0.33), with moderate-quality evidence and substantial heterogeneity
cards.summary: Heine 2015 (Cochrane review, 45 trials, 2,250 participants): exercise therapy reduced fatigue versus no exercise (standardised mean difference -0.53, 95% CI -0.73 to -0.33), with moderate-quality evidence and substantial heterogeneity
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (Heine 2015)
cards.people: 2,250 people with multiple sclerosis (mostly relapsing-remitting, Expanded Disability Status Scale under 6.0) in 45 randomised trials of 69 exercise interventions — endurance (23), muscle power (9), task-oriented (5), mixed (15) and other including yoga (17); 36 trials with 1,603 participants contributed fatigue data to the meta-analysis.
cards.result: Across 26 trials using a non-exercise control, exercise significantly reduced fatigue (standardised mean difference -0.53, 95% CI -0.73 to -0.33; P < 0.01), with significant heterogeneity (I2 over 58%). By type, endurance training (standardised mean difference -0.43), mixed training (-0.73) and 'other' training (-0.54) each significantly favoured exercise over no exercise. The record rates the methodological quality and the combined body of evidence as moderate.
cards.watchOut: Fatigue is self-reported and exercise cannot be blinded, so expectation effects are built into every included trial; heterogeneity across programmes is high, and effects are averages across very different interventions.
cards.source: Heine M et al. Exercise therapy for fatigue in multiple sclerosis. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2015. PMID: 26358158. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Torres-Costoso 2022 (network meta-analysis, 58 randomised studies): combined exercise was the most effective type for physical fatigue (effect -1.51 vs control) and resistance training the most effective for total fatigue (-1.15)
cards.summary: Torres-Costoso 2022 (network meta-analysis, 58 randomised studies): combined exercise was the most effective type for physical fatigue (effect -1.51 vs control) and resistance training the most effective for total fatigue (-1.15)
cards.people: People with multiple sclerosis in 58 randomised controlled trials of exercise interventions, network-meta-analysed across 7–8 intervention types for physical and total fatigue scores; total participant N not documented in the record.
cards.result: The highest pairwise effects were for combined exercise and resistance training versus control (ranging from -0.74 to -1.24). In the network analysis, combined exercise achieved the largest effect for physical fatigue (-1.51, 95% CI -2.01 to -1.01) and resistance training the largest for total fatigue (-1.15, 95% CI -1.81 to -0.49), each versus control. The authors conclude exercise should be considered an effective fatigue management strategy, with combined exercise the most effective modality for both physical and total fatigue.
cards.watchOut: Network rankings rest partly on indirect comparisons between trials that never met head-to-head, and effect metrics are standardised score differences, not hours of fatigue or absolute response rates.
cards.source: Torres-Costoso A et al. Effect of Exercise on Fatigue in Multiple Sclerosis: A Network Meta-analysis Comparing Different Types of Exercise. cards.headline: Englund 2022 (RCT in fatigued patients, 71 randomised): 12 weeks of high-intensity resistance training cut fatigue scores by about 10 points versus a matched non-intervention control (difference -10.3, 95% CI -12.9 to -7.7; P < 0.001); once-weekly worked as well as twice-weekly
cards.summary: Englund 2022 (RCT in fatigued patients, 71 randomised): 12 weeks of high-intensity resistance training cut fatigue scores by about 10 points versus a matched non-intervention control (difference -10.3, 95% CI -12.9 to -7.7; P < 0.001); once-weekly worked as well as twice-weekly
cards.people: 71 people with multiple sclerosis scoring at least 53 on the Fatigue Scale for Motor and Cognitive Functions, randomised 1:1 to supervised high-intensity resistance training twice weekly (group A) or once weekly (group B) for 12 weeks, plus a non-randomised score-matched non-intervention control group (n = 69). Randomised N = 71, printed on the face.
cards.result: Fatigue scores fell by a mean of -10.9 points (95% CI -14.8 to -6.9) in group A and -9.8 (-13.2 to -6.3) in group B, with no significant difference between the two training frequencies. Against the non-intervention control, the combined training groups differed by -10.3 points (95% CI -12.9 to -7.7) while controls changed by +1.5 (-0.6 to 3.6), P < 0.001. The authors describe the reductions as clinically relevant and recommend high-intensity resistance training for fatigued patients.
cards.watchOut: The control group was matched but not randomised, so the -10.3-point contrast is not a pure randomised comparison; the randomised contrast (once vs twice weekly) showed no difference, meaning dose-response is unproven.
cards.source: Englund S et al. High-intensity resistance training in people with multiple sclerosis experiencing fatigue: A randomised controlled trial. cards.headline: Synthesis: structured exercise reduces multiple sclerosis fatigue across dozens of randomised trials (pooled standardised mean difference -0.53), with combined and resistance programmes performing best — the evidence supports prescribing it for fatigue
cards.summary: Synthesis: structured exercise reduces multiple sclerosis fatigue across dozens of randomised trials (pooled standardised mean difference -0.53), with combined and resistance programmes performing best — the evidence supports prescribing it for fatigue
cards.people: The carded evidence: a Cochrane review of 45 trials (2,250 participants), a network meta-analysis of 58 randomised studies and one randomised trial in specifically fatigued patients (71 randomised, plus 69 matched controls). Total carded participants exceed 2,300, so no small-N labelling applies.
cards.result: Fatigue fell with exercise versus no exercise in the Cochrane pooling (standardised mean difference -0.53, 95% CI -0.73 to -0.33; Heine 2015); combined exercise and resistance training ranked highest in the network analysis (Torres-Costoso 2022); and a targeted trial in fatigued patients showed a roughly 10-point fatigue-score reduction over 12 weeks (Englund 2022). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit), on two concordant syntheses of randomised trials plus a confirmatory trial in the symptomatic population.
cards.watchOut: All fatigue outcomes are self-reported in unblindable trials, so some of the average effect may be expectation and attention; the consistency across 100+ trial comparisons and the size of the targeted-trial effect argue the benefit is not only that.
cards.source: Synthesis of Heine M et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2015 (PMID: 26358158); Torres-Costoso A et al. Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation. 2022 (PMID: 34509464); Englund S et al. Multiple Sclerosis and Related Disorders. 2022 (PMID: 36037752).

shelves.title: Plasma exchange for steroid-refractory MS relapses: yes, it helps — 42.1% vs 5.9% on sham in the randomised trial, best when given early
shelves.question: Does plasma exchange help severe relapses in multiple sclerosis that do not respond to steroids?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Demyelinating Autoimmune Diseases, CNS/physiopathology/*therapy · Disability Evaluation · Double-Blind Method · Female · Gait · Humans · Male · Multiple Sclerosis/therapy · Plasma Exchange/adverse effects · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). The one randomised test is positive and large in relative terms: in severe demyelinating attacks that had failed intravenous steroids, moderate-or-better improvement occurred in 42.1% of plasma-exchange courses versus 5.9% on sham (Weinshenker 1999). Two observational cohorts in steroid-refractory disease point the same way (59% of 153 patients improving moderately to markedly; 78.8% of 118 multiple sclerosis patients improving markedly or mildly, with earlier treatment responding better). The stamp is capped at POSSIBLE because the randomised trial is single, small, counts courses rather than patients, and mixes multiple sclerosis with related demyelinating diseases. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): plasma exchange helps severe multiple sclerosis relapses that do not respond to steroids.

cards.headline: Weinshenker 1999 (randomised sham-controlled trial): plasma exchange produced moderate-or-better improvement in 42.1% of treatment courses versus 5.9% on sham, in severe demyelinating attacks that had failed intravenous steroids
cards.summary: Weinshenker 1999 (randomised sham-controlled trial): plasma exchange produced moderate-or-better improvement in 42.1% of treatment courses versus 5.9% on sham, in severe demyelinating attacks that had failed intravenous steroids
cards.people: Patients with recently acquired, severe neurological deficits from attacks of inflammatory demyelinating disease (multiple sclerosis and related conditions) who had failed to recover after intravenous corticosteroids; the record reports outcomes by treatment course (19 active, 17 sham) with crossover to the opposite treatment for non-responders, and does not state the total patient count in the record — printed plainly.
cards.result: Moderate or greater improvement in neurological disability occurred during 8 of 19 (42.1%) courses of active plasma exchange compared with 1 of 17 (5.9%) courses of sham treatment; the primary analysis was positive. Improvement occurred early and was sustained on follow-up, although 4 responders had new attacks within 6 months, and only 2 of 13 patients who failed the treatment phase improved during follow-up.
cards.watchOut: The trial mixes multiple sclerosis with other inflammatory demyelinating diseases and counts courses, not patients; it is small, single, and now decades old — it establishes that plasma exchange can rescue steroid-refractory attacks, not a precise response rate for multiple sclerosis alone.
cards.source: Weinshenker BG et al. A randomized trial of plasma exchange in acute central nervous system inflammatory demyelinating disease. Annals of Neurology. 1999. PMID: 10589540. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Magana 2011 (Mayo Clinic observational cohort, N = 153): 59% of patients treated with plasma exchange for a steroid-refractory demyelinating attack had moderate-to-marked functional improvement within 6 months
cards.summary: Magana 2011 (Mayo Clinic observational cohort, N = 153): 59% of patients treated with plasma exchange for a steroid-refractory demyelinating attack had moderate-to-marked functional improvement within 6 months
cards.people: All 153 Mayo Clinic patients treated with plasma exchange between 1999 and 2007 for a steroid-refractory central nervous system inflammatory demyelinating attack (multiple sclerosis and related conditions). Evidence type: historical observational cohort, labelled on the face.
cards.result: 90 of 153 patients (59%) exhibited moderate to marked functional neurological improvement within 6 months following plasma exchange. Features associated with a beneficial response included shorter disease duration (P = .02), preserved deep tendon reflexes (P = .001), a diagnosis of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (P = .008), ring-enhancing lesions (odds ratio 4.00, a relative measure; P = .03) and mass effect on imaging (odds ratio 3.00; P = .02). Plasma exchange was less effective in patients who later developed a progressive course (P = .046).
cards.watchOut: No untreated comparison group: some steroid-refractory attacks recover spontaneously over 6 months, so the 59% figure is an upper bound on the treatment's own contribution.
cards.source: Magana SM et al. Beneficial plasma exchange response in central nervous system inflammatory demyelination. Archives of Neurology. 2011. PMID: 21403003. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Blechinger 2021 (two-centre observational study, N = 118, multiple sclerosis only): 78.8% of patients with glucocorticosteroid-refractory relapses improved markedly or mildly after plasma exchange, and earlier treatment predicted a better response
cards.summary: Blechinger 2021 (two-centre observational study, N = 118, multiple sclerosis only): 78.8% of patients with glucocorticosteroid-refractory relapses improved markedly or mildly after plasma exchange, and earlier treatment predicted a better response
cards.people: 118 patients with multiple sclerosis treated with therapeutic plasma exchange for glucocorticosteroid-refractory relapses at two tertiary multiple sclerosis centres; response was graded marked, mild or none, with change in disability score as a secondary outcome. Evidence type: retrospective observational study, labelled on the face.
cards.result: Marked or mild improvement was observed in 78.8% of patients. Response was predicted by a relapsing multiple sclerosis diagnosis (odds ratio 3.1, a relative measure), gadolinium enhancement on MRI (odds ratio 3.2), younger age (odds ratio 0.5 per 5 years older) and shorter time from relapse onset to plasma exchange (odds ratio 0.7 per 7 days longer). Improvement correlated inversely with time from relapse to treatment start (P = 0.001). No sustained effects were observed during follow-up, and patients with longer disease duration and higher disability were more likely to progress or relapse within 6 months.
cards.watchOut: 'Marked or mild' is a softer bar than the trial's 'moderate or greater', which is why this response rate (78.8%) runs higher than the randomised figure (42.1%); without a control arm the natural-history share is unknown.
cards.source: Blechinger S et al. Therapeutic plasma exchange in steroid-refractory multiple sclerosis relapses. A retrospective two-center study. Therapeutic Advances in Neurological Disorders. 2021. PMID: 33552236. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: plasma exchange helps a substantial share of severe steroid-refractory relapses — 42.1% vs 5.9% on sham in the one randomised trial, with 59–79% improving in uncontrolled multiple sclerosis cohorts, and earlier treatment responding better
cards.summary: Synthesis: plasma exchange helps a substantial share of severe steroid-refractory relapses — 42.1% vs 5.9% on sham in the one randomised trial, with 59–79% improving in uncontrolled multiple sclerosis cohorts, and earlier treatment responding better
cards.people: The carded evidence: one small randomised sham-controlled trial (36 treatment courses; total patient count not stated in its record), one 153-patient observational cohort and one 118-patient multiple-sclerosis-only observational cohort. Total carded patients exceed 270, so no small-N labelling applies; the cap comes from having a single small randomised trial, which included related demyelinating diseases as well as multiple sclerosis.
cards.result: Active plasma exchange beat sham by 42.1% to 5.9% for moderate-or-better improvement (Weinshenker 1999); 59% of 153 steroid-refractory patients improved moderately to markedly within 6 months (Magana 2011); and 78.8% of 118 multiple sclerosis patients improved markedly or mildly, with response falling as time from relapse onset grew (Blechinger 2021). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): plasma exchange helps severe multiple sclerosis relapses that do not respond to steroids, and should not be delayed once steroids have failed.
cards.watchOut: Response is not recovery for everyone: responders in the trial still had new attacks within months, and patients with progressive disease, long disease duration or delayed treatment respond least — plasma exchange is a rescue, not a disease-modifying therapy.
cards.source: Synthesis of Weinshenker BG et al. Annals of Neurology. 1999 (PMID: 10589540); Magana SM et al. Archives of Neurology. 2011 (PMID: 21403003); Blechinger S et al. Therapeutic Advances in Neurological Disorders. 2021 (PMID: 33552236).

shelves.title: IV immunoglobulin for multifocal motor neuropathy: improves strength — 78% versus 4% improved in the pooled crossover trials, with consistent results in both small placebo-controlled trials
shelves.question: Does IV immunoglobulin improve strength in multifocal motor neuropathy?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Immunoglobulins, Intravenous · Male · Middle Aged · Nervous System Diseases · Neural Conduction
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit). Two small double-blind, placebo-controlled trials agree that intravenous immunoglobulin improves strength and function in multifocal motor neuropathy: in a 16-patient crossover trial the neurologic disability score improved by 6.7 points on IVIg while falling 2.1 points on placebo, and grip strength rose 6.4 kg on the weaker side versus a 1.0 kg fall on placebo; in a 19-patient trial, seven of nine patients given IVIg first were responders at month 4 versus two of nine given placebo first (P = 0.03). The 2022 Cochrane review of six crossover randomised trials (90 participants in total) found strength improved in 21 of 27 (78%) IVIg-naive participants on IVIg versus 1 of 27 (4%) on placebo (relative risk 11.00, 95% CI 2.86 to 42.25; low-certainty evidence), while the disability result was weaker (39% versus 11%; relative risk 3.00, 95% CI 0.89 to 10.12). The trials are individually tiny and mostly crossover, so the size of the effect is imprecise even though its direction is consistent. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): IV immunoglobulin improves strength in multifocal motor neuropathy.

cards.headline: Federico 2000: in 16 patients, IVIg improved the disability score by 6.7 points while placebo worsened it by 2.1, and grip strength rose 6.4 kg on the weaker side versus a 1.0 kg fall on placebo (N = 16 on the face)
cards.summary: Federico 2000: in 16 patients, IVIg improved the disability score by 6.7 points while placebo worsened it by 2.1, and grip strength rose 6.4 kg on the weaker side versus a 1.0 kg fall on placebo (N = 16 on the face)
cards.people: 16 patients with multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block, each given both treatments — IVIg 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 consecutive days and placebo (dextrose or saline) — in a randomised, double-blind crossover design, evaluated about 28 days after each treatment. Trial N = 16.
cards.result: Subjective functional improvement on IVIg was rated dramatic or very good in nine patients, moderate in one, mild in one and absent in five, and was absent after placebo. The neurologic disability score improved by 6.7 ± 3.3 points with IVIg and decreased by 2.1 ± 3.0 with placebo (P = 0.038). Grip strength on the weaker side increased by 6.4 ± 1.9 kg with IVIg and decreased by 1.0 ± 0.8 kg with placebo (P = 0.0021). Conduction block improved by 12.68% with IVIg and worsened by 12.98% with placebo (P = 0.037), and was reversed in five patients on IVIg but not on placebo.
cards.watchOut: Sixteen patients is a very small trial, and a crossover design in a fluctuating disease can flatter a treatment whose effect carries over; the result supports direction, not a precise effect size.
cards.source: Federico P et al. Multifocal motor neuropathy improved by IVIg: randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study. Neurology. 2000. PMID: 11087764. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Léger 2001: seven of nine patients given IVIg first were responders at month 4 versus two of nine given placebo first (P = 0.03), in 19 enrolled patients (N on the face)
cards.summary: Léger 2001: seven of nine patients given IVIg first were responders at month 4 versus two of nine given placebo first (P = 0.03), in 19 enrolled patients (N on the face)
cards.people: 19 patients with multifocal motor neuropathy with persistent conduction block: 10 never previously treated with IVIg and nine with recurrent symptoms after previously successful IVIg. Patients were randomised to IVIg or placebo 500 mg/kg/day for 5 consecutive days, once a month for 3 months; responders stayed on the same treatment and non-responders switched at month 4. 18 patients completed the study.
cards.result: Considering the 18 completers together, seven of the nine patients who received IVIg first were responders at month 4, compared with two of the nine who received placebo first (P = 0.03). There was no significant difference in MRC score at month 4, but a significant difference in the self-evaluation score favouring IVIg. Electrophysiological motor parameters did not differ significantly at month 4. Of five patients with significantly high anti-GM1 titres at baseline, four responded to IVIg.
cards.watchOut: Half the participants were previous IVIg responders, a group selected for being likely to respond again, and the objective MRC strength score itself did not differ significantly — the responder and self-evaluation outcomes carry this card.
cards.source: Léger JM et al. Intravenous immunoglobulin therapy in multifocal motor neuropathy: a double-blind, placebo-controlled study. Brain. 2001. PMID: 11133794. randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (léger 2001) 19 patients with multifocal motor neuropathy with persistent conduction block: 10 never previously treated with ivig and nine with recurrent symptoms after previously successful ivig. patients were randomised to ivig or placebo 500 mg/kg/day for 5 consecutive days, once a month for 3 months; responders stayed on the same treatment and non-responders switched at month 4. 18 patients completed the study. considering the 18 completers together, seven of the nine patients who received ivig first were responders at month 4, compared with two of the nine who received placebo first (p = 0.03). there was no significant difference in mrc score at month 4, but a significant difference in the self-evaluation score favouring ivig. electrophysiological motor parameters did not differ significantly at month 4. of five patients with significantly high anti-gm1 titres at baseline, four responded to ivig. half the participants were previous ivig responders, a group selected for being likely to respond again, and the objective mrc strength score itself did not differ significantly — the responder and self-evaluation outcomes carry this card. léger jm et al. intravenous immunoglobulin therapy in multifocal motor neuropathy: a double-blind, placebo-controlled study. brain. 2001. pmid: 11133794. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adult · aged · autoantibodies · double-blind method · electromyography · female · g(m1) ganglioside · humans · immunoglobulin m · immunoglobulins, intravenous · male · middle aged · motor neuron disease · motor skills · neural conduction · polyradiculoneuropathy · prospective studies · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Cochrane 2022: across six crossover trials (90 participants), strength improved in 78% on IVIg versus 4% on placebo (relative risk 11.00) — but the disability result was imprecise and certainty was low
cards.summary: Cochrane 2022: across six crossover trials (90 participants), strength improved in 78% on IVIg versus 4% on placebo (relative risk 11.00) — but the disability result was imprecise and certainty was low
cards.people: Cochrane review of six crossover randomised trials including a total of 90 participants with definite or probable multifocal motor neuropathy; five trials compared IVIg with placebo and one compared IVIg with subcutaneous immunoglobulin. Four of the IVIg-versus-placebo trials enrolled IVIg-naive participants (induction treatment).
cards.result: In IVIg-naive participants, strength improved in 21 of 27 (78%) treated with IVIg versus 1 of 27 (4%) on placebo (relative risk 11.00, 95% CI 2.86 to 42.25; 3 trials, 27 participants; low-certainty evidence). Disability improved in 7 of 18 (39%) after IVIg versus 2 of 18 (11%) after placebo (relative risk 3.00, 95% CI 0.89 to 10.12; low-certainty evidence) — an interval consistent with anything from almost no effect to a large one. Resolution of at least one conduction block gave a relative risk of 7.00 (95% CI 0.95 to 51.70), also consistent with no effect. In the one maintenance trial, disability increased in 17 of 42 (40%) people switched to placebo versus 7 of 42 (17%) remaining on IVIg (relative risk 2.43, 95% CI 1.13 to 5.24; moderate-certainty evidence).
cards.watchOut: The whole randomised evidence base is 90 people in crossover trials, three of the six at high risk of bias in at least one domain; the headline relative risk of 11 rests on 27 participants and must not be read as a precise estimate.
cards.source: Keddie S et al. Immunoglobulin for multifocal motor neuropathy. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2022. PMID: 35015296. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Humans · Immunoglobulins, Intravenous · Plasma Exchange · Polyneuropathies · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic

cards.summary: Synthesis: two small placebo-controlled trials and their Cochrane synthesis all point the same way — IVIg improves strength in MMN, with wide uncertainty about how much
cards.people: The carded evidence: Federico 2000 (16 patients, crossover), Léger 2001 (19 enrolled, 18 completed) and the Cochrane 2022 synthesis of six crossover trials totalling 90 unique participants (which includes the two trials above, so participants are not additive). Total unique evidence base is about 90 people, above the small-N stamp threshold, though every individual trial is small and each card prints its N on its face.
cards.result: Disability score +6.7 points on IVIg versus −2.1 on placebo and grip strength +6.4 kg versus −1.0 kg (Federico 2000); responders 7/9 on IVIg first versus 2/9 on placebo first (Léger 2001); pooled strength improvement 78% versus 4%, relative risk 11.00 (95% CI 2.86 to 42.25), low certainty (Cochrane 2022). cards.watchOut: LIKELY reflects consistent direction across independent small trials, not precision: no trial here can say how long benefit lasts, which patients respond, or how IVIg compares with subcutaneous immunoglobulin (one small trial in the review).

shelves.title: Erenumab in chronic migraine after preventive failure: about 2.5–4.3 fewer migraine days than placebo in the failed-treatment subgroups of the one chronic-migraine trial
shelves.question: Does erenumab reduce monthly migraine days in chronic migraine after failure of other preventives?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Antibodies, Monoclonal · Chronic Disease · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Injections, Subcutaneous · Male · Middle Aged · Migraine Disorders · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Receptors, Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single trial programme, capped at POSSIBLE. All three cards report one randomised trial (NCT02066415; 667 patients with chronic migraine): erenumab 70 mg and 140 mg each reduced monthly migraine days by 6.6 days versus 4.2 days on placebo (difference −2.5 days, 95% CI −3.5 to −1.4). The card that answers this shelf's question directly is the prespecified-style subgroup analysis of patients who had previously failed preventives: among those with at least one prior failed medication category, the advantage over placebo at month 3 was −2.5 days (70 mg) and −3.3 days (140 mg), and among those with at least two failed categories it was −2.7 and −4.3 days — if anything larger than in patients who had never failed (−2.2 and −0.5 days). Patient-reported outcomes (headache impact, disability, quality of life) improved in parallel. There is no second, independent trial in prior-failure chronic migraine in the records fetched, so the programme cap applies. The episodic-migraine erenumab trial (Goadsby 2017) is homed on its own live shelf and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): erenumab reduces monthly migraine days in chronic migraine, including after failure of other preventives.

cards.headline: Tepper 2017: erenumab cut monthly migraine days by 6.6 days versus 4.2 on placebo (difference −2.5 days) in 667 patients with chronic migraine
cards.summary: Tepper 2017: erenumab cut monthly migraine days by 6.6 days versus 4.2 on placebo (difference −2.5 days) in 667 patients with chronic migraine
cards.people: 667 adults aged 18–65 with chronic migraine (15 or more headache days per month, at least 8 of them migraine days), randomised 3:2:2 at 69 centres in North America and Europe to subcutaneous placebo (n = 286), erenumab 70 mg (n = 191) or erenumab 140 mg (n = 190) every 4 weeks for 12 weeks.
cards.result: Both erenumab doses reduced monthly migraine days versus placebo in weeks 9–12: −6.6 days on each erenumab dose versus −4.2 days on placebo (difference −2.5, 95% CI −3.5 to −1.4, P < 0.0001). Adverse events were reported in 39% (placebo), 44% (70 mg) and 47% (140 mg); the most frequent were injection-site pain, upper respiratory tract infection and nausea. Serious adverse events occurred in 2%, 3% and 1% respectively, and 637 of 667 patients completed treatment.
cards.watchOut: This is the parent trial for the whole shelf: the subgroup and patient-reported-outcome cards below are the same 667 patients, not independent confirmation, and 12 weeks says nothing about longer-term benefit or safety.
cards.source: Tepper S et al. Safety and efficacy of erenumab for preventive treatment of chronic migraine: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial. Lancet Neurol. 2017. PMID: 28460892. Registry ID: NCT02066415. cards.headline: Ashina 2018: in patients who had already failed preventives, erenumab's advantage over placebo was −2.5 to −3.3 days (≥1 failed category) and −2.7 to −4.3 days (≥2 failed categories) at month 3
cards.summary: Ashina 2018: in patients who had already failed preventives, erenumab's advantage over placebo was −2.5 to −3.3 days (≥1 failed category) and −2.7 to −4.3 days (≥2 failed categories) at month 3
cards.type: Subgroup analysis of a randomised controlled trial (Ashina 2018)
cards.people: Subgroup analysis of the same randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled chronic migraine trial (667 patients), dividing participants into those who had never failed a preventive, those with at least one prior failed medication category, and those with at least two prior failed medication categories; outcomes at month 3.
cards.result: Change in monthly migraine days, treatment difference versus placebo (95% CI): never failed, −2.2 (−4.1 to −0.3) for 70 mg and −0.5 (−2.4 to 1.5) for 140 mg; at least one prior failed category, −2.5 (−3.8 to −1.2) for 70 mg and −3.3 (−4.6 to −2.1) for 140 mg; at least two prior failed categories, −2.7 (−4.2 to −1.2) for 70 mg and −4.3 (−5.8 to −2.8) for 140 mg. Similar patterns were seen for monthly acute migraine-specific medication days and for achieving at least 50% and at least 75% reductions in monthly migraine days. No new or unexpected safety issues were reported in any subgroup. The record reports no effect size for the responder endpoints in its abstract, and none is printed here.
cards.watchOut: Subgroups of a single trial are hypothesis-supporting, not proof: the prior-failure groups were not separately randomised, their sizes are not stated in the record, and the never-failed 140 mg estimate (−0.5 days, interval crossing zero) shows how noisy subgroup splits can be.
cards.source: Ashina M et al. Efficacy and safety of erenumab (AMG334) in chronic migraine patients with prior preventive treatment failure: A subgroup analysis of a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study. Cephalalgia. 2018. PMID: 29984601. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Lipton 2019: the same trial's patient-reported outcomes improved — HIT-6 fell 5.6 points on erenumab versus 3.1 on placebo, and MIDAS disability improved by about 19–20 days versus 7.5
cards.summary: Lipton 2019: the same trial's patient-reported outcomes improved — HIT-6 fell 5.6 points on erenumab versus 3.1 on placebo, and MIDAS disability improved by about 19–20 days versus 7.5
cards.type: Patient-reported outcomes report of a randomised double-blind trial (Lipton 2019)
cards.people: The same 667 adults with chronic migraine randomised to placebo or erenumab 70 mg or 140 mg monthly; exploratory endpoints were migraine-specific quality of life (MSQ), headache impact (HIT-6), migraine disability (MIDAS) and pain interference (PROMIS), assessed to month 3.
cards.result: Improvements were observed for all endpoints in both erenumab groups at month 3, with greater changes than placebo already at month 1 for many outcomes. HIT-6 scores changed by −5.6 for both erenumab doses versus −3.1 for placebo. MIDAS scores improved by −19.4 days (70 mg) and −19.8 days (140 mg) versus −7.5 days (placebo). Treatment differences exceeded established minimally important differences for the MSQ role function-restrictive (≥3.2) and emotional functioning (≥7.5) domains at both doses, and for role function-preventive (≥4.5) at 140 mg. The record gives no confidence intervals for these exploratory endpoints, and none are printed here.
cards.watchOut: Exploratory endpoints in the same single trial: they show the day-count benefit is felt by patients, but they add no independent randomised evidence and were not the trial's primary basis.
cards.source: Lipton RB et al. Erenumab in chronic migraine: Patient-reported outcomes in a randomized double-blind study. Neurology. 2019. PMID: 30996060. Registry ID: NCT02066415. shelves.title: Continuing a CGRP antibody after a <30% response at 3 months: one in five early non-responders respond by month 6, and no validated stopping rule exists (observational only)
shelves.question: Should a CGRP monoclonal antibody be continued after 3 months if migraine days fall by less than 30 percent?
shelves.mesh: Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide Receptor Antagonists · Humans · Migraine Disorders · Receptors, Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit of continuing) — observational only, printed on the face. No randomised trial in the records fetched tests a 30%-at-3-months stopping rule. The one directly relevant dataset is a real-life erenumab study of 100 highly refractory patients with daily diaries over 6 months: 20% of patients who had NOT reached a 30% average reduction in monthly migraine days over the first 3 months went on to reach at least 30% in the last 3 months, and almost 90% of early responders sustained their response; its authors propose continuing treatment for at least 6 months before judging response. The two guideline records carded — the American Headache Society consensus statement (2021) and the European Headache Federation guideline update (2022) — recommend these antibodies and address long-term management, but neither abstract prints a numeric 30% stopping threshold, and the EHF states that for several clinical questions the evidence was insufficient and guidance rested on expert opinion. A hard stop at 3 months for a <30% response would therefore abandon roughly one in five patients who would have responded by month 6, on the basis of a threshold no carded trial has validated. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: continue to about 6 months before deciding, rather than stopping at 3 months solely for a <30% reduction.

cards.headline: de Vries Lentsch 2021: 20% of erenumab patients without a 30% response in the first 3 months had a delayed response (≥30%) in months 4–6 — the authors propose continuing at least 6 months (N = 100 on the face)
cards.summary: de Vries Lentsch 2021: 20% of erenumab patients without a 30% response in the first 3 months had a delayed response (≥30%) in months 4–6 — the authors propose continuing at least 6 months (N = 100 on the face)
cards.people: All 100 erenumab-treated patients at a Dutch headache centre, described as highly refractory to previous prophylactics, episodic and chronic migraine, followed for 6 months with a time-locked daily electronic diary; response was the reduction in monthly migraine days (MMD) versus baseline. Study N = 100.
cards.result: MMD and acute medication days fell in all months versus baseline (P < 0.001), and well-being and coping with pain improved. 36% of patients had an MMD reduction of at least 50% in at least 3 of 6 months, and 6% in all 6 months; for at least 30% reduction the figures were 60% and 24%. Almost 90% of patients with an average MMD reduction of at least 30% over the first 3 months had a sustained response in the last 3 months. Crucially for this shelf, 20% of patients without an initial response (average <30% over the first 3 months) had a delayed response (average ≥30%) in the last 3 months. The authors propose, as a practical guideline, that treatment be continued for at least 6 months and that patients with a ≥30% MMD reduction in at least half of the treatment period be considered responders.
cards.watchOut: One centre, 100 patients, no control group: some 'delayed responses' may be natural fluctuation or regression to the mean rather than late drug effect, and the study tested erenumab only — other CGRP antibodies are extrapolated, not measured.
cards.source: de Vries Lentsch S et al. Treatment with the monoclonal calcitonin gene-related peptide receptor antibody erenumab: A real-life study. Eur J Neurol. 2021. PMID: 34424593. Registry ID: none in the record. real-life observational study (de vries lentsch 2021) all 100 erenumab-treated patients at a dutch headache centre, described as highly refractory to previous prophylactics, episodic and chronic migraine, followed for 6 months with a time-locked daily electronic diary; response was the reduction in monthly migraine days (mmd) versus baseline. study n = 100. mmd and acute medication days fell in all months versus baseline (p < 0.001), and well-being and coping with pain improved. 36% of patients had an mmd reduction of at least 50% in at least 3 of 6 months, and 6% in all 6 months; for at least 30% reduction the figures were 60% and 24%. almost 90% of patients with an average mmd reduction of at least 30% over the first 3 months had a sustained response in the last 3 months. crucially for this shelf, 20% of patients without an initial response (average <30% over the first 3 months) had a delayed response (average ≥30%) in the last 3 months. the authors propose, as a practical guideline, that treatment be continued for at least 6 months and that patients with a ≥30% mmd reduction in at least half of the treatment period be considered responders. one centre, 100 patients, no control group: some 'delayed responses' may be natural fluctuation or regression to the mean rather than late drug effect, and the study tested erenumab only — other cgrp antibodies are extrapolated, not measured. de vries lentsch s et al. treatment with the monoclonal calcitonin gene-related peptide receptor antibody erenumab: a real-life study. eur j neurol. 2021. pmid: 34424593. registry id: none in the record. mesh: antibodies, monoclonal, humanized · calcitonin gene-related peptide receptor antagonists · humans · migraine disorders · receptors, calcitonin gene-related peptide

cards.people: American Headache Society consensus update on integrating new acute and preventive migraine treatments into clinical practice, built from the expanded evidence base, emerging expert consensus and patient perspectives, reviewed by the Society's Board and patient advocates.
cards.result: The statement covers the new preventive options, including the anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies, and states that integration of new treatments should be informed by potential benefit relative to established therapies and by individual patient characteristics and preferences. Its record reports no trial of continuation versus stopping at any response threshold, and prints no effect size for any stopping rule — none is invented here. The absence of a validated numeric cut-off in this consensus record is itself part of this shelf's answer.
cards.watchOut: A consensus statement is expert guidance, not evidence: it can legitimise either continuing or stopping, and this shelf does not present it as data for either.
