cards.headline: Synthesis: no validated 30% stopping rule exists in the carded records; the only direct data show one in five early non-responders responding by month 6 — observational only
cards.summary: Synthesis: no validated 30% stopping rule exists in the carded records; the only direct data show one in five early non-responders responding by month 6 — observational only
cards.people: The carded evidence: one real-life observational study (100 patients, 6 months of daily diaries) and two guideline/consensus records that print no numeric stopping threshold. Total carded participants with outcome data: 100, above the small-N stamp threshold but a single uncontrolled cohort, so the observational-only cap applies.
cards.result: 20% of initial <30% responders gained a ≥30% response in months 4–6; almost 90% of early responders sustained response (de Vries Lentsch 2021). Neither guideline record validates a 3-month, 30% cut-off. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit of continuing) — observational only.
cards.watchOut: The honest uncertainty: continuing everyone to 6 months also means 4 in 5 early non-responders in that cohort still did not reach 30% — cost and injection burden during those months are real, and no carded study weighs them.

shelves.title: Switching after SSRI nonresponse works for a minority: a second SSRI remitted 23.5% of nonresponders in pooled trials — nearly as many as switching class (28%) — and switching early beat switching later by no significant margin
shelves.question: Does switching to a different SSRI work after nonresponse to a first SSRI in major depression?
shelves.mesh: Bupropion · Cyclohexanols · Major Depressive Disorder · Drug Resistance · Humans · Mianserin · Mirtazapine · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors · Venlafaxine Hydrochloride
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). Switching after a first SSRI fails does help a minority: in the pooled randomised evidence (Papakostas 2008, PMID: 17919460; four trials, n = 1,496), 23.5% of patients switched to a second SSRI remitted, so a within-class switch is a real treatment and not a placebo manoeuvre. Switching out of class did modestly better (28% remission; relative risk 1.29, an absolute gain of about 4.5 percentage points, NNT about 22), and response rates did not differ. The EMC trial (Tadic 2016, PMID: 26899588) adds a caution about timing: an early-switch strategy at 2 weeks (24% remission) did not significantly beat guideline-based continuation with later switch (16%; p = 0.2056 — the treatment made no difference on the primary outcome). The only uncontrolled card (Kaplan 2002, PMID: 12182262) reports implausibly high open-label rates and is carded only to be discounted. The STAR*D switch trial itself (Rush 2006, PMID: 16554525) is homed on live shelf #230 and is not re-carded here; this shelf is built on the free comparative reports above, per the one-home rule — flagged for the developer. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a second SSRI remits roughly 1 in 4 SSRI nonresponders; switching class remits slightly more, and no fetched evidence shows that switching early beats switching after an adequate trial.

cards.headline: Papakostas 2008: in pooled switch trials, a second SSRI remitted 23.5% of SSRI-resistant patients — switching class remitted 28% (relative risk 1.29), a modest absolute gain of about 4.5 points
cards.summary: Papakostas 2008: in pooled switch trials, a second SSRI remitted 23.5% of SSRI-resistant patients — switching class remitted 28% (relative risk 1.29), a modest absolute gain of about 4.5 points
cards.people: Meta-analysis of four randomised clinical trials (n = 1,496) in patients with major depression who had failed to respond to an SSRI, comparing a switch to a second SSRI (within class) with a switch to a non-SSRI antidepressant (bupropion, mirtazapine or venlafaxine; across class).
cards.result: Patients switched to a non-SSRI were more likely to remit than patients switched to a second SSRI (relative risk = 1.29, p = .007); pooled remission rates were 28% (non-SSRI) and 23.5% (second SSRI), an absolute difference of about 4.5 percentage points (NNT nearly 22 for one additional remitter). There was no difference in response rates between the strategies, and a nonsignificant trend (p = .1) toward more discontinuation for intolerance with the across-class switch (relative risk = 1.23).
cards.watchOut: The pooled advantage of switching class is statistically real but small — an NNT of about 22 falls below the NNT = 10 benchmark the authors cite — so the practical message is that a second SSRI works nearly as well, not that it fails.
cards.source: Papakostas GI et al. Treatment of SSRI-resistant depression: a meta-analysis comparing within- versus across-class switches. Biological psychiatry. 2008. PMID: 17919460. cards.headline: Tadic 2016 (EMC trial): switching early, at 2 weeks of non-improvement, did not beat guideline care — remission 24% versus 16%, p = 0.2056 (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Tadic 2016 (EMC trial): switching early, at 2 weeks of non-improvement, did not beat guideline care — remission 24% versus 16%, p = 0.2056 (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: 889 patients with major depressive disorder were enrolled and 879 received the SSRI escitalopram; the 192 patients with no improvement after 14 days (under 20% reduction on the Hamilton scale) were randomised to an early medication change strategy (n = 97; venlafaxine XR, with lithium augmentation if still unimproved at day 28) or treatment as usual (n = 95; escitalopram continuation, with nonresponders switched to venlafaxine XR at day 28).
cards.result: Remission (Hamilton score 7 or less) at 8 weeks was 24% with early medication change and 16% with treatment as usual, which was not significantly different (p = 0.2056). Sensitivity analyses favoured the early-change strategy on secondary endpoints, but the primary comparison was null: the early-switch strategy made no difference to remission.
cards.watchOut: This trial tests when to switch (early, in initial non-improvers on escitalopram) rather than whether switching ever works, and its early-change arm switched out of class to venlafaxine — it does not directly test a second SSRI.
cards.source: Tadic A et al. Randomized controlled study of early medication change for non-improvers to antidepressant therapy in major depression--The EMC trial. cards.headline: Kaplan 2002: an open-label, uncontrolled switch series reported 94% response after switching to venlafaxine — carded to be discounted, because without a control group such rates cannot be credited
cards.summary: Kaplan 2002: an open-label, uncontrolled switch series reported 94% response after switching to venlafaxine — carded to be discounted, because without a control group such rates cannot be credited
cards.people: 73 outpatients with major depressive disorder who had not responded, or had not sustained a response, to at least 6 weeks of an SSRI (fluoxetine, sertraline or paroxetine) were switched openly to venlafaxine immediate- or extended-release for at least 6 weeks; 69 were analysed after 4 discontinued for drug-related adverse events and were excluded.
cards.result: After 6 to 8 weeks, 94.2% (65/69) were classed as responders and 87% (60/69) as remitters on the Hamilton-based criterion — rates far above the 23.5–28% remission seen in the randomised switch trials carded here. The authors themselves conclude that randomised, controlled trials are needed before any conclusions can be drawn.
cards.watchOut: Uncontrolled, unblinded ratings by a single unblinded psychiatrist, with non-completers excluded: expectancy, natural course and rating bias can manufacture most of this apparent effect. It is evidence about why control groups matter, not about how well switching works.
cards.source: Kaplan EM et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: switching after SSRI nonresponse remits about 1 in 4 patients — a second SSRI (23.5%) nearly matched switching class (28%), and switching early did not beat switching later
cards.summary: Synthesis: switching after SSRI nonresponse remits about 1 in 4 patients — a second SSRI (23.5%) nearly matched switching class (28%), and switching early did not beat switching later
cards.people: The carded evidence: one meta-analysis of four randomised switch trials (n = 1,496), one randomised early-switch strategy trial (192 randomised non-improvers from 889 enrolled), and one small open-label uncontrolled series (n = 73) carded to be discounted. The STAR*D switch trial is homed on live shelf #230 and is not re-carded. Total carded participants exceed 1,700 (the meta-analysis overlaps the trial literature), so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: A second SSRI remitted 23.5% of SSRI-resistant patients and a non-SSRI switch 28% (relative risk 1.29; NNT about 22) in pooled randomised trials (Papakostas 2008). An early-switch strategy did not significantly improve remission over guideline care (24% versus 16%, p = 0.2056; Tadic 2016). Open-label switch rates of 94% (Kaplan 2002) are not credible against the controlled data. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: No carded trial isolates the exact manoeuvre in the question — a switch from one named SSRI to a different named SSRI with a placebo or continuation control — so the answer rests on pooled within-class switch arms and one strategy trial, which is why the stamp is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY.
cards.source: Synthesis of Papakostas GI et al. Biological psychiatry. 2008 (PMID: 17919460); Tadic A et al. European neuropsychopharmacology. 2016 (PMID: 26899588); Kaplan EM et al. Clinical therapeutics. 2002 (PMID: 12182262).

shelves.title: Valproate in women of childbearing potential (observational only): spina bifida odds ratio 12.7, malformation risk rising with dose, and age-6 IQ 97 versus 105–108 after alternatives — avoid in bipolar disorder whenever an effective alternative exists
shelves.question: Should valproate be avoided in women of childbearing potential with bipolar disorder?
shelves.mesh: Abnormalities, Drug-Induced · Anticonvulsants · Case-Control Studies · Cohort Studies · Female · Humans · Infant, Newborn · Male · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Complications · Pregnancy Trimester, First · Prenatal Exposure Delayed Effects · Prevalence · Risk Factors · Valproic Acid
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only, printed on the face: there are no randomised trials of valproate in pregnancy, and there never will be, so the stamp is capped by design type even though the observational evidence is large, concordant and dose-dependent. Four independent data systems point the same way: a case-control analysis of 3.8 million births found six specific malformations significantly more common after first-trimester valproate monotherapy, with an adjusted odds ratio of 12.7 for spina bifida (Jentink 2010, PMID: 20558369); the EURAP registry found malformation risk rose with dose for every drug studied and was significantly higher for valproate than for low-dose lamotrigine at all doses (Tomson 2011, PMID: 21652013); the prospective NEAD study found age-6 IQ of 97 after valproate exposure versus 105–108 after the comparator drugs, again dose-dependent (Meador 2013, PMID: 23352199); and a 3.18-million-child UK–Swedish cohort found more autism, intellectual disability and ADHD diagnoses after valproate exposure, with little evidence of such associations for lamotrigine (Madley-Dowd 2024, PMID: 39548057). All carded cohorts enrolled women treated mainly for epilepsy, because that is where pregnancy exposure data exist; the exposure — valproate at comparable doses in women of the same age — is the same in bipolar disorder, and no fetched record suggests the fetal risk differs by indication. The comparative malformation analysis homed on live shelf #2676 (EURAP 2018 and the North American registry) is cross-pointed, not re-carded. None of the carded records measures the maternal relapse risk of stopping valproate in bipolar disorder, which is the other side of the decision and must be weighed separately. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only: yes, valproate should be avoided in women of childbearing potential with bipolar disorder whenever an effective alternative exists, and where it is used, the lowest effective dose with folate and specialist review is the risk-minimising course the evidence supports.

cards.headline: Jentink 2010: first-trimester valproate monotherapy was associated with six specific malformations — spina bifida adjusted odds ratio 12.7, cleft palate 5.2, hypospadias 4.8, craniosynostosis 6.8
cards.summary: Jentink 2010: first-trimester valproate monotherapy was associated with six specific malformations — spina bifida adjusted odds ratio 12.7, cleft palate 5.2, hypospadias 4.8, craniosynostosis 6.8
cards.type: Cohort synthesis and population case-control study (Jentink 2010)
cards.people: Two linked analyses: a combined analysis of eight published cohort studies (1,565 valproate-exposed pregnancies, 118 major malformations) that identified 14 candidate malformations, then a case-control study in the EUROCAT congenital-anomaly database — 98,075 malformation registrations among 3.8 million births in 14 European countries (1995–2005), with 180 registrations exposed to valproate monotherapy. Women were treated with antiepileptic drugs, predominantly for epilepsy.
cards.result: Compared with no antiepileptic drug use in the first trimester, valproate monotherapy was associated with significantly increased risks for 6 of the 14 malformations: spina bifida, adjusted odds ratio 12.7 (95% CI 7.7 to 20.7); atrial septal defect, 2.5 (1.4 to 4.4); cleft palate, 5.2 (2.8 to 9.9); hypospadias, 4.8 (2.9 to 8.1); polydactyly, 2.2 (1.0 to 4.5); and craniosynostosis, 6.8 (1.8 to 18.8). Results were similar when valproate was compared with other antiepileptic drugs.
cards.watchOut: Odds ratios for rare outcomes are relative measures: even a 12.7-fold relative increase in spina bifida acts on a low background rate, and these are epilepsy-treatment cohorts — the indication differs from bipolar disorder even though the fetal exposure is the same drug.
cards.source: Jentink J et al. Valproic acid monotherapy in pregnancy and major congenital malformations. The New England journal of medicine. 2010. PMID: 20558369. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Tomson 2011 (EURAP): malformation risk rose with dose for every drug — and valproate's risk was significantly higher than low-dose lamotrigine at every dose studied
cards.summary: Tomson 2011 (EURAP): malformation risk rose with dose for every drug — and valproate's risk was significantly higher than low-dose lamotrigine at every dose studied
cards.people: Prospective EURAP epilepsy and pregnancy registry analysis (42 countries) of monotherapy pregnancies: 1,402 carbamazepine, 1,280 lamotrigine, 1,010 valproic acid and 217 phenobarbital exposures, with major congenital malformations assessed up to 12 months after birth by dose at conception.
cards.result: Malformation rates increased with increasing dose at conception for all four drugs. The lowest rates were with lamotrigine under 300 mg/day (2.0%) and carbamazepine under 400 mg/day (3.4%); compared with that low-dose lamotrigine group, risks were significantly higher with valproic acid and phenobarbital at all investigated doses, and with carbamazepine above 400 mg/day. The record does not print valproate's dose-band malformation rates in its abstract — the dose gradient and the significant excess over low-dose lamotrigine at every dose are what it reports. Parental history of major congenital malformations also raised risk (odds ratio 4.4).
cards.watchOut: Registry enrolment is voluntary and observational: dose is confounded by illness severity, and the abstract withholds the valproate dose-band rates, so no 'safe valproate dose' can be read off this record — only that risk climbs with dose and exceeds the safest comparator at every dose.
cards.source: Tomson T et al. Dose-dependent risk of malformations with antiepileptic drugs: an analysis of data from the EURAP epilepsy and pregnancy registry. The Lancet. Neurology. 2011. PMID: 21652013. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Meador 2013 (NEAD): children exposed to valproate in utero had age-6 IQ of 97 versus 105–108 after the other drugs — a dose-dependent gap, with periconceptional folate associated with higher IQ
cards.summary: Meador 2013 (NEAD): children exposed to valproate in utero had age-6 IQ of 97 versus 105–108 after the other drugs — a dose-dependent gap, with periconceptional folate associated with higher IQ
cards.people: Prospective, assessor-masked observational NEAD study at 25 epilepsy centres in the UK and USA: 305 mothers on antiepileptic monotherapy (carbamazepine, lamotrigine, phenytoin or valproate) and 311 children, 224 of whom completed follow-up to age 6 years; analysis adjusted for maternal IQ, drug, standardised dose, gestational age and periconceptional folate.
cards.result: Age-6 IQ was lower after valproate exposure (mean 97, 95% CI 94–101) than after carbamazepine (105; p = 0.0015), lamotrigine (108; p = 0.0003) or phenytoin (108; p = 0.0006), and valproate-exposed children did worse on verbal and memory measures. Higher valproate dose was negatively associated with IQ (r = −0.56, p < 0.0001) and with verbal, non-verbal, memory and executive scores; no such dose association was seen for the other drugs. Mean IQ was higher in children exposed to periconceptional folate (108) than in unexposed children (101; p = 0.0009).
cards.watchOut: Observational and epilepsy-based: mothers who need valproate may differ from those who do not, and adjustment cannot remove all confounding — but the within-valproate dose gradient is harder to explain away and points the same way as the malformation data.
cards.source: Meador KJ et al. Fetal antiepileptic drug exposure and cognitive outcomes at age 6 years (NEAD study): a prospective observational study. The Lancet. Neurology. 2013. PMID: 23352199. Registry ID: NCT00021866. cards.headline: Madley-Dowd 2024: in 3.18 million children, prenatal valproate exposure was followed by more autism, intellectual disability and ADHD diagnoses; lamotrigine showed little such evidence
cards.summary: Madley-Dowd 2024: in 3.18 million children, prenatal valproate exposure was followed by more autism, intellectual disability and ADHD diagnoses; lamotrigine showed little such evidence
cards.people: Cohort built from UK primary-care data and nationwide Swedish registries: 3,182,773 children, of whom 17,495 were exposed to antiseizure medications in pregnancy, followed for neurodevelopmental diagnoses.
cards.result: Children exposed to valproate were more likely to receive a diagnosis of autism, intellectual disability and ADHD than children not exposed to antiseizure medications; the record reports this direction for valproate without printing its effect sizes in the abstract. For scale on other drugs, topiramate exposure carried 2.5 times the likelihood of intellectual disability (95% CI 1.23–4.98) and carbamazepine 1.25 times the likelihood of autism (1.05–1.48), while there was little evidence that lamotrigine exposure was associated with neurodevelopmental diagnoses.
cards.watchOut: Registry diagnoses are not standardised testing, and the abstract gives no valproate effect sizes — this card corroborates the NEAD IQ findings at population scale rather than quantifying the valproate risk itself.
cards.source: Madley-Dowd P et al. Antiseizure medication use during pregnancy and children's neurodevelopmental outcomes. Nature communications. 2024. PMID: 39548057. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: four independent data systems agree — valproate in pregnancy raises specific malformation risk (spina bifida odds ratio 12.7), climbs with dose, and lowers child IQ by about 8–11 points versus alternatives
cards.summary: Synthesis: four independent data systems agree — valproate in pregnancy raises specific malformation risk (spina bifida odds ratio 12.7), climbs with dose, and lowers child IQ by about 8–11 points versus alternatives
cards.people: The carded evidence: a case-control/cohort synthesis covering 3.8 million births (Jentink 2010), a 3,909-pregnancy prospective registry analysis including 1,010 valproate exposures (Tomson 2011), a 311-child prospective IQ cohort (Meador 2013), and a 3,182,773-child population cohort (Madley-Dowd 2024). All are observational; total participants run into the millions, so no small-N labelling applies. The comparative registry analysis on live shelf #2676 is cross-pointed, not re-carded.
cards.result: First-trimester valproate monotherapy was associated with six specific malformations, most strikingly spina bifida (adjusted odds ratio 12.7). Malformation risk increased with dose for all drugs and was significantly higher for valproate than for low-dose lamotrigine at every dose. Age-6 IQ averaged 97 after valproate versus 105–108 after carbamazepine, lamotrigine or phenytoin, dose-dependently. Population data add higher rates of autism, intellectual disability and ADHD diagnoses after valproate, with little such evidence for lamotrigine. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only.
cards.watchOut: Every carded cohort treated women mainly for epilepsy, not bipolar disorder, and none measures what happens to the mother if valproate is stopped — the avoidance recommendation transfers the fetal-risk evidence to bipolar care while leaving the relapse side of the trade-off to clinical judgement and other shelves.
cards.source: Synthesis of Jentink J et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2010 (PMID: 20558369); Tomson T et al. The Lancet. Neurology. 2011 (PMID: 21652013); Meador KJ et al. The Lancet. Neurology. 2013 (PMID: 23352199); Madley-Dowd P et al. Nature communications. 2024 (PMID: 39548057).

shelves.title: Buspirone add-on for generalised anxiety disorder after SSRI nonresponse is untested: it works as GAD monotherapy (NNT 4.4) and matched bupropion as an add-on in depression — but no trial has studied the asked use
shelves.question: Is buspirone effective as add-on therapy for generalized anxiety disorder after SSRI nonresponse?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Anxiety Agents · Antidepressive Agents · Anxiety Disorders · Benzodiazepines · Buspirone · Humans · Psychotherapy · Pyrimidines · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence). No fetched record reports a trial of buspirone added to an SSRI in generalised anxiety disorder (GAD) after SSRI nonresponse — the exact use in the question is untested in the carded evidence, and the shelf says so on its face. What exists is indirect: as monotherapy, azapirones including buspirone beat placebo in GAD across 36 trials and 5,908 participants, with a number needed to treat of 4.4 on global impression (Chessick 2006, PMID: 16856115), and the 89-trial network meta-analysis also found buspirone efficacious versus placebo while warning its estimate rests on small samples (Slee 2019, PMID: 30712879). The only randomised add-on evidence for buspirone after SSRI failure is in a different illness — depression — where buspirone augmentation of citalopram remitted 30.1% of nonremitters in STAR*D, the same as bupropion augmentation (Trivedi 2006, PMID: 16554526). Extrapolating a depression augmentation result to anxiety after SSRI failure is a guess the evidence does not make. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): buspirone is a proven GAD monotherapy and a plausible add-on, but its effectiveness as add-on therapy for GAD after SSRI nonresponse has not been tested in any trial carded here.

cards.headline: Chessick 2006 (Cochrane): buspirone-class drugs beat placebo as GAD monotherapy — NNT 4.4 on global impression across 36 trials — but these were not add-on trials after SSRI failure
cards.summary: Chessick 2006 (Cochrane): buspirone-class drugs beat placebo as GAD monotherapy — NNT 4.4 on global impression across 36 trials — but these were not add-on trials after SSRI failure
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised monotherapy trials (Chessick 2006, Cochrane)
cards.people: Cochrane review of 36 randomised trials with 5,908 participants with generalised anxiety disorder, comparing azapirones (including buspirone) with placebo, benzodiazepines, antidepressants, psychotherapy or kava; study length was 4 to 9 weeks, with one study lasting 14 weeks. Evidence type: systematic review of monotherapy trials.
cards.result: Azapirones, including buspirone, were superior to placebo for GAD; the number needed to treat on the Clinical Global Impression scale was 4.4 (95% CI 2.16 to 15.4). Azapirones may be less effective than benzodiazepines, and the reviewers could not conclude whether azapirones were superior to antidepressants, kava or psychotherapy. Azapirones appeared well tolerated, though more participants stopped azapirones than benzodiazepines.
cards.watchOut: Monotherapy in largely benzodiazepine-naive trial populations is not add-on therapy in SSRI nonresponders: patients who have already failed one serotonergic drug are a harder-to-treat group, and none of these 36 trials enrolled them as such.
cards.source: Chessick CA et al. Azapirones for generalized anxiety disorder. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2006. PMID: 16856115. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Slee 2019: in an 89-trial network meta-analysis buspirone was among the drugs efficacious versus placebo in GAD — with the explicit caveat that its finding rests on small sample sizes
cards.summary: Slee 2019: in an 89-trial network meta-analysis buspirone was among the drugs efficacious versus placebo in GAD — with the explicit caveat that its finding rests on small sample sizes
cards.people: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of 89 randomised trials including 25,441 adult outpatients with generalised anxiety disorder, comparing 22 active drugs and placebo on Hamilton Anxiety Scale change and acceptability. Evidence type: network meta-analysis of monotherapy trials.
cards.result: Duloxetine (mean difference −3.13), pregabalin (−2.79), venlafaxine (−2.69) and escitalopram (−2.45) were more efficacious than placebo with relatively good acceptability; mirtazapine, sertraline, fluoxetine, buspirone and agomelatine were also found efficacious and well tolerated, but these findings were limited by small sample sizes. The record does not print a buspirone-specific effect size in its abstract. Quetiapine had the largest effect (−3.60) but was poorly tolerated.
cards.watchOut: A network estimate built on small buspirone trials, again as monotherapy: it supports buspirone having real anxiolytic effect, and says nothing about adding it after an SSRI has failed.
cards.source: Slee A et al. Pharmacological treatments for generalised anxiety disorder: a systematic review and network meta-analysis. Lancet (London, England). 2019. PMID: 30712879. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Trivedi 2006 (STAR*D): the only randomised buspirone add-on trial after SSRI failure is in depression, not anxiety — buspirone augmentation remitted 30.1%, the same as bupropion augmentation (the comparison made no difference)
cards.summary: Trivedi 2006 (STAR*D): the only randomised buspirone add-on trial after SSRI failure is in depression, not anxiety — buspirone augmentation remitted 30.1%, the same as bupropion augmentation (the comparison made no difference)
cards.type: Randomised augmentation trial in depression — indirect evidence (Trivedi 2006, STAR*D)
cards.people: 565 adult outpatients with nonpsychotic major depressive disorder who had not remitted after a mean of 11.9 weeks of citalopram were randomised to augmentation with sustained-release bupropion (up to 400 mg/day) and 286 to augmentation with buspirone (up to 60 mg/day). Evidence type: randomised augmentation trial in major depression — a different diagnosis from the one in this shelf's question, carded and labelled as indirect evidence.
cards.result: Remission on the Hamilton scale was 29.7% with bupropion augmentation and 30.1% with buspirone augmentation — the two augmentation strategies made no difference to remission. Bupropion augmentation produced a greater reduction in self-reported symptoms (25.3% versus 17.1%, P < 0.04) and fewer dropouts for intolerance (12.5% versus 20.6%, P < 0.009) than buspirone augmentation. There was no placebo-augmentation arm, so neither rate can be separated from the effect of simply continuing treatment longer.
cards.watchOut: Depression is not generalised anxiety disorder, citalopram nonremission is not GAD SSRI nonresponse, and without a placebo arm the 30.1% remission cannot be attributed to buspirone itself. This card bounds what is known; it does not answer the shelf's question.

randomised augmentation trial in depression — indirect evidence (trivedi 2006, star*d) 565 adult outpatients with nonpsychotic major depressive disorder who had not remitted after a mean of 11.9 weeks of citalopram were randomised to augmentation with sustained-release bupropion (up to 400 mg/day) and 286 to augmentation with buspirone (up to 60 mg/day). evidence type: randomised augmentation trial in major depression — a different diagnosis from the one in this shelf's question, carded and labelled as indirect evidence. remission on the hamilton scale was 29.7% with bupropion augmentation and 30.1% with buspirone augmentation — the two augmentation strategies made no difference to remission. bupropion augmentation produced a greater reduction in self-reported symptoms (25.3% versus 17.1%, p < 0.04) and fewer dropouts for intolerance (12.5% versus 20.6%, p < 0.009) than buspirone augmentation. there was no placebo-augmentation arm, so neither rate can be separated from the effect of simply continuing treatment longer. depression is not generalised anxiety disorder, citalopram nonremission is not gad ssri nonresponse, and without a placebo arm the 30.1% remission cannot be attributed to buspirone itself. this card bounds what is known; it does not answer the shelf's question. trivedi mh et al. medication augmentation after the failure of ssris for depression. the new england journal of medicine. 2006. pmid: 16554526. registry id: nct00021528. mesh: adult · bupropion · buspirone · citalopram · delayed-action preparations · major depressive disorder · dopamine uptake inhibitors · drug administration schedule · drug therapy, combination · female · humans · logistic models · male · remission induction · serotonin receptor agonists · selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors · treatment failure

cards.headline: Synthesis: buspirone works as GAD monotherapy and as a depression add-on, but no trial has tested it as an add-on for GAD after SSRI nonresponse — the asked use is untested
cards.summary: Synthesis: buspirone works as GAD monotherapy and as a depression add-on, but no trial has tested it as an add-on for GAD after SSRI nonresponse — the asked use is untested
cards.people: The carded evidence: a Cochrane review of 36 GAD monotherapy trials (5,908 participants), a network meta-analysis of 89 GAD trials (25,441 patients), and one randomised augmentation trial in major depression (851 patients). No carded study enrolled patients with generalised anxiety disorder who had failed an SSRI and then added buspirone. Total carded participants exceed 30,000 across the reviews and trial, so no small-N labelling applies; the limitation is indirectness, not size.
cards.result: Azapirones beat placebo in GAD (NNT 4.4 on global impression; Chessick 2006) and buspirone was efficacious in the GAD network meta-analysis, on small samples (Slee 2019). In depression, buspirone augmentation after citalopram failure remitted 30.1%, equal to bupropion augmentation and without a placebo control (Trivedi 2006). For GAD after SSRI nonresponse specifically, there is no direct trial evidence in the records fetched. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Clinicians do use buspirone this way, and the monotherapy data make the practice plausible — but plausibility is all the carded evidence offers for the add-on-after-SSRI-failure use, and the stamp says so.
cards.source: Synthesis of Chessick CA et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2006 (PMID: 16856115); Slee A et al. Lancet (London, England). 2019 (PMID: 30712879); Trivedi MH et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2006 (PMID: 16554526).

shelves.title: Depression in pregnancy (SPLIT): psychotherapy works and is the evidence-backed first step for moderate illness — antidepressant safety divides between a large adjusted null on cardiac defects and drug-specific signals in a depressed-women cohort
shelves.question: Should antidepressants be used in pregnancy for moderate depression, or does psychotherapy work as well?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Antidepressive Agents · Antidepressive Agents, Tricyclic · Cohort Studies · Confounding Factors, Epidemiologic · Depressive Disorder · Female · Heart Defects, Congenital · Humans · Infant, Newborn · Logistic Models · Male · Middle Aged · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Complications · Pregnancy Trimester, First · Propensity Score · Risk · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the evidence divides by question, and the stamp names the split. On whether psychotherapy works: two meta-analyses of randomised trials agree it does — a pooled effect of g = 0.67 with an NNT of 4.39 across 43 studies and 6,270 participants (Cuijpers 2023, PMID: 37310303), and CBT and interpersonal therapy each beating treatment as usual by about 1.7 Edinburgh scale points across 44 trials (Couch 2025, PMID: 41183344). On whether antidepressants are safe enough to use when therapy is insufficient or declined: the largest cohort (949,504 pregnancies) found the apparent cardiac-defect excess disappeared with full adjustment for depression and confounders (fully adjusted relative risk 1.06, 95% CI 0.93–1.22; Huybrechts 2014, PMID: 24941178), while a cohort restricted to depressed women found drug-specific signals — citalopram for major malformations overall and paroxetine for cardiac defects (Bérard 2017, PMID: 28082367). No head-to-head randomised trial of an antidepressant versus psychotherapy in pregnancy is carded, so 'works as well' cannot be answered directly; what the evidence supports is psychotherapy first for moderate depression in pregnancy, with antidepressants a reasonable option — not a proven-safe one — when therapy fails, is unavailable, or the illness is more severe. PROPOSED SPLIT (psychotherapy benefit consistent; antidepressant safety signals divide between cohorts).

cards.headline: Huybrechts 2014: in 949,504 pregnancies, the cardiac-defect excess with first-trimester antidepressants vanished after full adjustment — relative risk 1.06 (0.93–1.22) in women with depression
cards.summary: Huybrechts 2014: in 949,504 pregnancies, the cardiac-defect excess with first-trimester antidepressants vanished after full adjustment — relative risk 1.06 (0.93–1.22) in women with depression
cards.people: Cohort nested in the US Medicaid Analytic eXtract, 2000–2007: 949,504 pregnant women and their liveborn infants; 64,389 women (6.8%) used antidepressants during the first trimester. Evidence type: population cohort with propensity adjustment restricted to women with depression.
cards.result: Cardiac defects occurred in 90.1 per 10,000 antidepressant-exposed infants versus 72.3 per 10,000 unexposed. The relative risk for SSRIs was 1.25 (95% CI 1.13 to 1.38) unadjusted, 1.12 (1.00 to 1.26) when restricted to women with depression, and 1.06 (0.93 to 1.22) in the fully adjusted depressed-cohort analysis — no significant association. The specific feared pairings were also null: paroxetine and right ventricular outflow tract obstruction, relative risk 1.07 (0.59 to 1.93); sertraline and ventricular septal defects, 1.04 (0.76 to 1.41).
cards.watchOut: Adjustment can hide a real effect as well as remove a spurious one, and Medicaid pregnancies are not all pregnancies — but the stepwise attenuation toward 1.0 as depression severity is controlled is the classic signature of confounding by indication, which is why this study reassures on cardiac defects specifically, not on every outcome.
cards.source: Huybrechts KF et al. Antidepressant use in pregnancy and the risk of cardiac defects. The New England journal of medicine. 2014. PMID: 24941178. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Bérard 2017: in a cohort of depressed women, citalopram was associated with major malformations overall (adjusted odds ratio 1.36) and paroxetine with cardiac defects (1.45) — signals the larger cohort did not find
cards.summary: Bérard 2017: in a cohort of depressed women, citalopram was associated with major malformations overall (adjusted odds ratio 1.36) and paroxetine with cardiac defects (1.45) — signals the larger cohort did not find
cards.type: Population cohort study in depressed women (Bérard 2017)
cards.people: Quebec Pregnancy Cohort analysis of 18,487 pregnancies in women with a diagnosis of depression or anxiety, or antidepressant exposure in the year before pregnancy, ending in a live-born singleton; first-trimester exposure to specific antidepressants was compared with non-exposure in depressed women. Evidence type: population cohort restricted to depressed/anxious women.
cards.result: Only citalopram increased the overall risk of major congenital malformations (adjusted odds ratio 1.36, 95% CI 1.08 to 1.73; 88 exposed cases). Organ-specific associations included paroxetine with cardiac defects (adjusted odds ratio 1.45, 1.12 to 1.88) and septal defects (1.39, 1.00 to 1.93), citalopram with musculoskeletal defects (1.92) and craniosynostosis (3.95), tricyclics with eye/ear/face/neck (2.45) and digestive (2.55) defects, and venlafaxine with respiratory defects (2.17). The authors conclude that serotonin-reuptake-active antidepressants increased the risk of some organ-specific malformations in this depressed cohort.
cards.watchOut: Many drug–organ combinations were tested, so some signals are expected by chance, and several rest on small exposed-case counts; this cohort's positive findings and the larger cohort's adjusted null (carded beside it) are the split this shelf is named for.
cards.source: Berard A et al. Antidepressant use during pregnancy and the risk of major congenital malformations in a cohort of depressed pregnant women: an updated analysis of the Quebec Pregnancy Cohort. BMJ open. 2017. PMID: 28082367. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cuijpers 2023: psychological treatment of perinatal depression works — pooled effect g = 0.67, NNT 4.39, across 43 randomised studies and 6,270 participants, lasting 6–12 months
cards.summary: Cuijpers 2023: psychological treatment of perinatal depression works — pooled effect g = 0.67, NNT 4.39, across 43 randomised studies and 6,270 participants, lasting 6–12 months
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 43 randomised studies (49 comparisons, 6,270 participants) of psychological interventions for depression during pregnancy and after birth, drawn from a database of randomised trials of psychotherapies for adult depression. Evidence type: meta-analysis of randomised trials.
cards.result: The overall effect size versus control was g = 0.67 (95% CI 0.45 to 0.89), corresponding to a number needed to treat of 4.39, with high heterogeneity (I² = 80%). The effect remained significant in sensitivity analyses and at 6–12 months of follow-up, and significant effects were also found for social support, anxiety, functional limitations, parental stress and marital stress, though on fewer studies. Some publication bias was detected.
cards.watchOut: Perinatal mixes pregnant and postpartum women, and controls were often waitlist or usual care rather than an active drug — so this proves psychotherapy beats not treating, not that it equals an antidepressant head-to-head.
cards.source: Cuijpers P et al. Psychological treatment of perinatal depression: a meta-analysis. Psychological medicine. 2023. PMID: 37310303. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Couch 2025: CBT and interpersonal therapy each beat usual care by about 1.7 Edinburgh scale points in perinatal depression (moderate-strength evidence); recovery relative risk 1.7 for CBT
cards.summary: Couch 2025: CBT and interpersonal therapy each beat usual care by about 1.7 Edinburgh scale points in perinatal depression (moderate-strength evidence); recovery relative risk 1.7 for CBT
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Couch 2025, Annals of Internal Medicine)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis for the US Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality: 44 randomised trials of psychological therapies for depression during pregnancy and up to 1 year postpartum, including CBT (25 trials, n = 2,962) and interpersonal therapy (9 trials, n = 1,003). Evidence type: systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials.
cards.result: CBT was probably more effective than treatment as usual, reducing symptoms by an equivalent 1.7 points on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (95% CI −2.0 to −1.3; moderate strength of evidence), and may give greater recovery rates (relative risk 1.7, 95% CI 1.3 to 2.3; low strength). Behavioural activation may also help (−1.5 points; low strength). Interpersonal therapy was probably more effective than usual care (−1.7 points, −2.9 to −0.5; moderate strength), with recovery relative risk 1.2 (0.97 to 1.5; low strength). The reviewers note the differences may not be clinically important and participants could not be blinded.
cards.watchOut: A 1.7-point average gain on a 30-point scale is modest, and 'treatment as usual' in pregnancy often means little treatment — the trials support offering therapy first for moderate depression, not that therapy suffices for every patient.
cards.source: Couch E et al. Effectiveness of Psychological Therapies for Depression During the Perinatal Period : A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Annals of internal medicine. 2025. PMID: 41183344. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: psychotherapy is the evidence-backed first step for moderate depression in pregnancy; antidepressant safety evidence splits between a large adjusted null and a depressed-cohort signal study
cards.summary: Synthesis: psychotherapy is the evidence-backed first step for moderate depression in pregnancy; antidepressant safety evidence splits between a large adjusted null and a depressed-cohort signal study
cards.people: The carded evidence: two population cohorts (949,504 and 18,487 pregnancies) on first-trimester antidepressant safety, and two meta-analyses (43 and 44 randomised trials; 6,270 participants in the one reporting a pooled N) on psychological treatment. No carded study randomises pregnant women to an antidepressant versus psychotherapy. Totals run to hundreds of thousands, so no small-N labelling applies.
cards.result: Fully adjusted, the largest cohort found no substantial cardiac-malformation increase (relative risk 1.06, CI including 1; Huybrechts 2014); the depressed-women cohort found citalopram and paroxetine signals (Bérard 2017). Psychotherapy beat control conditions consistently (g = 0.67, NNT 4.39, Cuijpers 2023; CBT and interpersonal therapy −1.7 scale points versus usual care, Couch 2025). PROPOSED SPLIT (psychotherapy benefit consistent; antidepressant safety signals divide).
cards.watchOut: 'Does psychotherapy work as well?' has no direct trial answer in pregnancy — the honest position is therapy first for moderate illness on its own positive evidence, with medication reserved and chosen knowing the safety literature is observational and divided.
cards.source: Synthesis of Huybrechts KF et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2014 (PMID: 24941178); Berard A et al. BMJ open. 2017 (PMID: 28082367); Cuijpers P et al. Psychological medicine. 2023 (PMID: 37310303); Couch E et al. Annals of internal medicine. 2025 (PMID: 41183344).

shelves.title: Sertraline in breastfeeding (exposure evidence): infant levels usually undetectable in pooled data and a calculated infant dose of 0.54% of the mother's — among the preferred antidepressants while nursing
shelves.question: Is sertraline the preferred antidepressant during breastfeeding?
shelves.mesh: Antidepressive Agents · Breast Feeding · Depression, Postpartum · Depressive Disorder · Female · Humans · Infant · Infant, Newborn · Lactation · Maternal Exposure · Milk, Human
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on exposure data, with evidence types labelled on every card as this shelf's brief requires. There are no randomised outcome trials of antidepressants in breastfeeding; the preference for sertraline rests on pharmacokinetic evidence of three labelled types, all pointing the same way. A pooled analysis of infant-level studies found sertraline (with nortriptyline and paroxetine) usually produces undetectable infant plasma levels, while fluoxetine left 22% of infants with levels above 10% of the maternal level (Weissman 2004, PMID: 15169695 — pooled analysis). A review and meta-analysis of sertraline levels found 87.4% of 167 infant sertraline levels below the limit of detection and no significant correlation between maternal and infant sertraline concentrations (Pinheiro 2015, PMID: 25589155 — meta-analysis of serum-level studies). A pharmacokinetic study of 26 nursing women put the infant's calculated sertraline dose at 0.54% of the maternal daily dose, with no adverse events in any infant (Stowe 2003, PMID: 12590627 — pharmacokinetic study). 'Preferred' therefore means lowest demonstrated infant exposure with no signal of harm in the level literature — paroxetine shares the undetectable-level property, so sertraline is a preferred choice rather than the only one, and infant clinical-outcome data beyond case reports do not exist in the carded records. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): yes — on concordant exposure evidence, sertraline is among the preferred antidepressants during breastfeeding.

cards.headline: Weissman 2004 [evidence type: pooled analysis of infant drug-level studies]: sertraline, paroxetine and nortriptyline usually produce undetectable infant levels — fluoxetine left 22% of infants above 10% of the maternal level
cards.summary: Weissman 2004 [evidence type: pooled analysis of infant drug-level studies]: sertraline, paroxetine and nortriptyline usually produce undetectable infant levels — fluoxetine left 22% of infants above 10% of the maternal level
cards.people: Pooled analysis of 57 studies of maternal plasma, breast milk and/or infant plasma antidepressant levels in nursing mother–infant pairs, identified from 67 relevant studies (two unpublished), with infant levels standardised against the average maternal level for each drug.
cards.result: Nortriptyline, paroxetine and sertraline usually produce undetectable infant levels. Fluoxetine produced the highest proportion of elevated infant levels — 22% of infants above 10% of the average maternal level — and citalopram data (on smaller numbers) indicated elevated levels in 17% of infants. The authors conclude that nortriptyline, paroxetine and sertraline may be preferred choices in breastfeeding women, and that current data do not support monitoring breast-milk levels in individual patients.
cards.watchOut: These are drug levels, not clinical outcomes: undetectable infant plasma is a strong proxy for low exposure, but the pooled studies were small level studies and case material, and symptomatic infants in case reports were analysed separately.
cards.source: Weissman AM et al. Pooled analysis of antidepressant levels in lactating mothers, breast milk, and nursing infants. The American journal of psychiatry. 2004. PMID: 15169695. cards.search: weissman 2004 [evidence type: pooled analysis of infant drug-level studies]: sertraline, paroxetine and nortriptyline usually produce undetectable infant levels — fluoxetine left 22% of infants above 10% of the maternal level weissman 2004 [evidence type: pooled analysis of infant drug-level studies]: sertraline, paroxetine and nortriptyline usually produce undetectable infant levels — fluoxetine left 22% of infants above 10% of the maternal level is sertraline the preferred antidepressant during breastfeeding? pooled analysis of infant-level studies (weissman 2004) pooled analysis of 57 studies of maternal plasma, breast milk and/or infant plasma antidepressant levels in nursing mother–infant pairs, identified from 67 relevant studies (two unpublished), with infant levels standardised against the average maternal level for each drug. nortriptyline, paroxetine and sertraline usually produce undetectable infant levels. fluoxetine produced the highest proportion of elevated infant levels — 22% of infants above 10% of the average maternal level — and citalopram data (on smaller numbers) indicated elevated levels in 17% of infants. the authors conclude that nortriptyline, paroxetine and sertraline may be preferred choices in breastfeeding women, and that current data do not support monitoring breast-milk levels in individual patients. these are drug levels, not clinical outcomes: undetectable infant plasma is a strong proxy for low exposure, but the pooled studies were small level studies and case material, and symptomatic infants in case reports were analysed separately. weissman am et al. pooled analysis of antidepressant levels in lactating mothers, breast milk, and nursing infants. the american journal of psychiatry. 2004. pmid: 15169695. registry id: none in the record. mesh: antidepressive agents · breast feeding · depression, postpartum · depressive disorder · female · humans · infant · infant, newborn · lactation · maternal exposure · milk, human

cards.headline: Pinheiro 2015 [evidence type: systematic review and meta-analysis of serum-level studies]: 87.4% of 167 infant sertraline levels were below detection, with no significant maternal–infant level correlation
cards.summary: Pinheiro 2015 [evidence type: systematic review and meta-analysis of serum-level studies]: 87.4% of 167 infant sertraline levels were below detection, with no significant maternal–infant level correlation
cards.people: Review of the PubMed and LactMed literature on sertraline in breastfeeding plus previously unpublished data, with a correlation-based meta-analysis of sertraline serum levels in mother–infant pairs: 167 infant sertraline levels and 150 infant desmethylsertraline levels.
cards.result: Of 167 infant sertraline levels, 146 (87.4%) were below the limit of detection, and the meta-analysis found no significant relationship between maternal and infant sertraline concentrations. Of 150 infant desmethylsertraline levels, 105 (70.0%) were below detection; infant metabolite levels did correlate with maternal levels, but the metabolite has only a fraction of sertraline's activity. The authors call sertraline a first-line drug for breastfeeding women on documented low infant exposure and very few adverse events in case reports, with routine paediatric care as appropriate monitoring.
cards.watchOut: A level meta-analysis cannot exclude rare or long-term infant effects, and 'very few adverse events in case reports' is passive surveillance — reassurance about exposure, not proof of zero clinical risk.
cards.source: Pinheiro E et al. Sertraline and breastfeeding: review and meta-analysis. Archives of women's mental health. 2015. PMID: 25589155. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Stowe 2003 [evidence type: pharmacokinetic study, N = 26 on the face]: the calculated infant sertraline dose was 0.54% of the maternal daily dose, and no infant had an adverse event
cards.summary: Stowe 2003 [evidence type: pharmacokinetic study, N = 26 on the face]: the calculated infant sertraline dose was 0.54% of the maternal daily dose, and no infant had an adverse event
cards.people: 26 nursing women with major depressive disorder taking sertraline monotherapy (25–200 mg/day, mean 123.9 mg/day); 15 women submitted 182 breast-milk samples for gradient and time-course analysis, and 22 mother–infant serum pairs were obtained. Study N = 26.
cards.result: The mean maximum calculated nursing infant dose of sertraline was 0.67 mg/day, representing 0.54% of the maternal daily dose (metabolite 1.44 mg/day). Sertraline was detectable in 4 of 22 infants (18%) and desmethylsertraline in 11 (50%), at low levels; milk concentrations peaked in hindmilk 8–9 hours after the maternal dose, and modelling suggested discarding milk at 9 hours would cut the infant dose by a mean of 17.1%. No adverse events were reported or documented in any infant.
cards.watchOut: A 26-woman pharmacokinetic study measures exposure precisely but cannot detect uncommon infant harms; its no-adverse-events finding is supportive detail, not a safety trial.
cards.source: Stowe ZN et al. The pharmacokinetics of sertraline excretion into human breast milk: determinants of infant serum concentrations. The Journal of clinical psychiatry. 2003. PMID: 12590627. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: three labelled evidence types agree — sertraline gives among the lowest measurable infant exposures of any antidepressant, which is the entire basis for calling it preferred in breastfeeding
cards.summary: Synthesis: three labelled evidence types agree — sertraline gives among the lowest measurable infant exposures of any antidepressant, which is the entire basis for calling it preferred in breastfeeding
cards.people: The carded evidence, types labelled: one pooled analysis of 57 infant-level studies (Weissman 2004), one meta-analysis of 167 infant sertraline levels (Pinheiro 2015), and one 26-woman pharmacokinetic study (Stowe 2003). The pooled and meta-analytic evidence bases each exceed 30 infants, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the single pharmacokinetic study's N = 26 is printed on its card face.
cards.result: Sertraline usually produces undetectable infant levels, in the same preferred group as paroxetine and nortriptyline, unlike fluoxetine (22% of infants above 10% of maternal level). In sertraline-specific data, 87.4% of infant levels were undetectable and the calculated infant dose was 0.54% of the maternal dose, with no adverse events reported in the pharmacokinetic study. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — on exposure data.
cards.watchOut: 'Preferred' is a ranking of infant drug exposure, not of antidepressant efficacy or of proven infant outcomes — a mother already stable on another agent is a different question from choosing a first agent while breastfeeding, and the carded evidence addresses the choice, not a switch.
cards.source: Synthesis of Weissman AM et al. The American journal of psychiatry. 2004 (PMID: 15169695); Pinheiro E et al. Archives of women's mental health. 2015 (PMID: 25589155); Stowe ZN et al. The Journal of clinical psychiatry. 2003 (PMID: 12590627).

shelves.title: Combined hormonal contraception and menstrual migraine (SPLIT): attacks concentrate in the hormone-free interval on standard pills, a step-down pill improved them in a small pilot — and with aura, observational stroke evidence says avoid estrogen
shelves.question: Does combined hormonal contraception worsen menstrual migraine, and should it be avoided with aura?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Contraceptives, Oral, Combined · Female · Humans · Menstruation · Middle Aged · Migraine Disorders · Pilot Projects · Substance Withdrawal Syndrome · Tryptamines
shelves.balance: SPLIT — observational only for the vascular risk. On worsening: combined hormonal contraception predictably manufactures a monthly estrogen-withdrawal window, and in users with menstrual migraine the attacks land there — a mean of 2.2 migraine days in the hormone-free interval, almost half lasting over 24 hours despite rescue medication (Merki-Feld 2017). Yet 'worsens menstrual migraine' is not universal: a small uncontrolled pilot of a step-down estradiol valerate/dienogest pill found fewer, shorter, less severe attacks (Nappi 2013; 32 women), so formulation and regimen decide the direction. On aura: the evidence is observational throughout and consistent — migraine with aura carried a relative ischaemic-stroke risk of 2.27 (relative), rising to 8.72 (relative) in oral-contraceptive users in the older meta-analysis (Etminan 2005), and all four low-dose case-control studies reported increased odds with combined exposure, apparently driven by aura (Ornello 2020). No carded record prints absolute stroke rates. PROPOSED SPLIT: standard combined contraception worsens the withdrawal-week pattern of menstrual migraine for many users while a step-down formulation improved it in one small pilot; and estrogen-containing contraception should be avoided in migraine with aura on consistent observational stroke evidence — a risk-based rule, not a trial finding.

cards.headline: Merki-Feld 2017: in combined-hormonal-contraceptive users, menstrual migraine concentrates in the hormone-free interval — a mean of 2.2 migraine days there, with almost half of attacks lasting over 24 hours despite rescue medication
cards.summary: Merki-Feld 2017: in combined-hormonal-contraceptive users, menstrual migraine concentrates in the hormone-free interval — a mean of 2.2 migraine days there, with almost half of attacks lasting over 24 hours despite rescue medication
cards.people: Observational diary-based pilot study: 40 women using combined hormonal contraceptives who had menstrually related migraine in at least 2 of 3 cycles, attending a clinic between 2009 and 2015; 103 cycles of daily headache diaries were analysed, tracking migraine onset against hormone withdrawal and bleeding onset.
cards.result: The mean number of migraine days in the hormone-free interval was 2.2 ± 1.6. Migraine typically started on days 1–5 of the hormone-free interval and bleeding on days 3–5; relative to the first bleeding day, migraines started on days −1 to 4. Almost half of the migraine attacks lasted longer than 24 hours despite rescue medication. The authors suggest starting short-term prevention on the last day of pill use or the first hormone-free day and continuing for 5 days. The study had no non-contraceptive comparison group, so it documents the withdrawal pattern rather than comparing contraception with none — printed plainly.
cards.watchOut: Forty selected clinic patients who already had menstrual migraine on contraceptives: this shows where attacks land in the cycle, not whether starting contraception worsens migraine overall — women whose migraine worsened may already have stopped and left the sampling frame.
cards.source: Merki-Feld GS et al. Temporal relations in hormone-withdrawal migraines and impact on prevention- a diary-based pilot study in combined hormonal contraceptive users. The journal of headache and pain. 2017. PMID: 28842849. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Nappi 2013: in a small uncontrolled pilot (32 women, printed on the face), a step-down estradiol valerate/dienogest pill reduced the number, duration and severity of menstrual migraine attacks by the third cycle
cards.summary: Nappi 2013: in a small uncontrolled pilot (32 women, printed on the face), a step-down estradiol valerate/dienogest pill reduced the number, duration and severity of menstrual migraine attacks by the third cycle
cards.people: Prospective diary-based pilot study: 32 women over 35 years old with menstrually related migraine (18 who had never used combined oral contraceptives and 14 previous users), observed over a 3-cycle run-in and then treated for 6 cycles with a combined pill containing estradiol valerate and dienogest using an estrogen step-down and progestogen step-up regimen.
cards.result: The number of migraine attacks was significantly reduced at the third (P < .001) and sixth cycles (P < .001) compared with the run-in period, as were attack duration and head-pain severity (both P < .001 at the third and sixth cycles), and analgesic use fell further by the sixth cycle. The record reports P values without printing the underlying attack counts, which is stated here plainly rather than reconstructed. Duration and severity of head pain correlated with days of dysmenorrhoea in women without complete remission of menstrual cramps.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-two women, no control group, and a formulation designed to soften estrogen withdrawal: regression to the mean and expectancy can mimic this result, and it cannot be generalised to standard ethinylestradiol pills taken with a 7-day break — the regimen most associated with withdrawal attacks.
cards.source: Nappi RE et al. Effect of a contraceptive pill containing estradiol valerate and dienogest (E2V/DNG) in women with menstrually-related migraine (MRM). Contraception. 2013. PMID: 23453784. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Etminan 2005: migraine itself carried a relative risk of ischaemic stroke of 2.16 (relative), 2.27 with aura — and 8.72 in those taking oral contraceptives (all relative, observational)
cards.summary: Etminan 2005: migraine itself carried a relative risk of ischaemic stroke of 2.16 (relative), 2.27 with aura — and 8.72 in those taking oral contraceptives (all relative, observational)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (Etminan 2005)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (1966 to June 2004) of migraine and ischaemic stroke: 14 studies (11 case-control and 3 cohort).
cards.result: The risk of ischaemic stroke was increased in people with migraine (relative risk 2.16 [95% CI 1.89 to 2.48], a relative measure), consistently in migraine with aura (relative risk 2.27 [95% CI 1.61 to 3.19]) and migraine without aura (relative risk 1.83 [95% CI 1.06 to 3.15]), and in those taking oral contraceptives (relative risk 8.72 [95% CI 5.05 to 15.05]). The authors conclude migraine may be a risk factor for ischaemic stroke and that the risk among oral contraceptive users needed further investigation. All estimates are relative; the record gives no absolute stroke rates, printed here plainly.
cards.watchOut: Observational, and the contraceptive-era data largely predate modern low-dose pills: the 8.72 figure pools older formulations and cannot separate the pill's contribution from aura status, smoking and hypertension in the source studies.
cards.source: Etminan M et al. Risk of ischaemic stroke in people with migraine: systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2005. PMID: 15596418. cards.headline: Ornello 2020: all four case-control studies of low-dose combined contraceptives (12,256 women) reported increased ischaemic-stroke odds in women with migraine using them — and the association appears driven by migraine with aura
cards.summary: Ornello 2020: all four case-control studies of low-dose combined contraceptives (12,256 women) reported increased ischaemic-stroke odds in women with migraine using them — and the association appears driven by migraine with aura
cards.people: Systematic review of observational studies (to May 2019) reporting ischaemic-stroke effect sizes in women with migraine using low-dose combined hormonal contraceptives (under 50 µg ethinylestradiol) compared with women without migraine not using them: 4 case-control studies including 12,256 women in total. Heterogeneity was significant, so no meta-analysis was performed.
cards.result: All four included studies reported increased odds of ischaemic stroke in women with migraine and low-dose combined-contraceptive use compared with women with neither exposure — the record reports the direction consistently across studies without a pooled effect size, printed here plainly. The authors' expert conclusion is that the association with ischaemic stroke is driven by migraine with aura, that strong data on the joint effect are lacking (especially on aura and headache frequency), and that more robust data are needed on whether these contraceptives remain viable in migraine without aura or could extend to some women with aura.
cards.watchOut: Four case-control studies with significant heterogeneity and a comparison group of women with neither migraine nor contraceptive use: this design can show the combined-exposure group is at higher risk without cleanly separating how much the contraceptive adds to aura alone.
cards.source: Ornello R et al. Migraine, low-dose combined hormonal contraceptives, and ischemic stroke in young women: a systematic review and suggestions for future research. cards.headline: Synthesis: the headache answer divides by regimen — withdrawal-interval attacks are the predictable harm pattern, one small pilot of a step-down pill improved — while the aura answer rests on consistent observational stroke evidence: combined exposure carries the highest relative risk in every study
cards.summary: Synthesis: the headache answer divides by regimen — withdrawal-interval attacks are the predictable harm pattern, one small pilot of a step-down pill improved — while the aura answer rests on consistent observational stroke evidence: combined exposure carries the highest relative risk in every study
cards.people: The carded evidence: two small diary studies in contraceptive users (40 women, 103 cycles; and a 32-woman uncontrolled pilot — Ns printed on their faces), one meta-analysis of 14 observational stroke studies, and one systematic review of 4 case-control studies (12,256 women). There are no randomised trials of contraception and stroke, and none will be done; the vascular half of this shelf is observational by necessity and is labelled as such.
cards.result: Menstrual migraine in contraceptive users concentrates in the hormone-free interval (mean 2.2 migraine days; Merki-Feld 2017), yet a step-down estradiol valerate pill reduced attack number, duration and severity in a small pilot (Nappi 2013). For stroke, migraine with aura carried a relative risk of 2.27 (relative) and oral-contraceptive use in migraine a relative risk of 8.72 (relative) in the older meta-analysis (Etminan 2005), and all four low-dose case-control studies reported increased odds with combined exposure, apparently driven by aura (Ornello 2020). PROPOSED SPLIT — observational only for the vascular risk, as detailed in the stamp.
cards.watchOut: Relative risks of 2–9 sound alarming without absolute rates, which none of the carded records prints: ischaemic stroke in young women is uncommon, and the clinical rule to avoid estrogen contraception with aura rests on consistent observational relative risks applied to a serious outcome, not on measured absolute harm in a trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Merki-Feld GS et al. The journal of headache and pain. 2017 (PMID: 28842849); Nappi RE et al. Contraception. 2013 (PMID: 23453784); Etminan M et al. synthesis the carded evidence: two small diary studies in contraceptive users (40 women, 103 cycles; and a 32-woman uncontrolled pilot — ns printed on their faces), one meta-analysis of 14 observational stroke studies, and one systematic review of 4 case-control studies (12,256 women). there are no randomised trials of contraception and stroke, and none will be done; the vascular half of this shelf is observational by necessity and is labelled as such. menstrual migraine in contraceptive users concentrates in the hormone-free interval (mean 2.2 migraine days; merki-feld 2017), yet a step-down estradiol valerate pill reduced attack number, duration and severity in a small pilot (nappi 2013). for stroke, migraine with aura carried a relative risk of 2.27 (relative) and oral-contraceptive use in migraine a relative risk of 8.72 (relative) in the older meta-analysis (etminan 2005), and all four low-dose case-control studies reported increased odds with combined exposure, apparently driven by aura (ornello 2020). proposed split — observational only for the vascular risk, as detailed in the stamp. relative risks of 2–9 sound alarming without absolute rates, which none of the carded records prints: ischaemic stroke in young women is uncommon, and the clinical rule to avoid estrogen contraception with aura rests on consistent observational relative risks applied to a serious outcome, not on measured absolute harm in a trial. synthesis of merki-feld gs et al. the journal of headache and pain. 2017 (pmid: 28842849); nappi re et al. contraception. 2013 (pmid: 23453784); etminan m et al. bmj (clinical research ed.). 2005 (pmid: 15596418); ornello r et al. expert review of neurotherapeutics. 2020 (pmid: 32056462).

shelves.title: Sertraline for postnatal depression during breastfeeding — split: efficacy is divided (no difference from placebo on the primary outcome; CBT beat it in a small trial), but infant exposure through milk is consistently very low (about 0.54% of the maternal dose) with no infant adverse events reported
shelves.question: In women with postnatal depression, is sertraline effective and safe during breastfeeding?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Breast Feeding · Combined Modality Therapy · Depression, Postpartum · Female · Humans · Iowa · Male · Person-Centered Psychotherapy · Postpartum Period · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Rhode Island · Sertraline · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT — efficacy and breastfeeding safety point in different directions and are graded separately on the face. Efficacy is divided: the one placebo-controlled trial (O'Hara 2019, 162 women, breastfeeding and non-breastfeeding) found no significant effect of sertraline on its primary outcome, the HamD-17 (the treatment made no difference on that measure), although sertraline scored better on a secondary self-report depression scale; and in a small three-arm trial (Milgrom 2015, 45 women) all groups improved but cognitive behavioural therapy alone was superior to sertraline alone at 12 weeks. Breastfeeding safety, by contrast, is consistent across the pharmacokinetic evidence: in Stowe 2003 the calculated infant dose was 0.54% of the maternal dose, sertraline itself was detectable in only 4 of 22 infants, and no adverse events were reported in any infant; a pooled analysis of 57 studies (Weissman 2004) likewise found sertraline usually produces undetectable infant levels and named it among the preferred antidepressants in breastfeeding women. That safety evidence is observational — drug-level studies, not randomised infant-outcome trials. PROPOSED SPLIT (efficacy: divided — null on the primary outcome of the one placebo-controlled trial and inferior to CBT in a small trial; breastfeeding safety: consistently very low infant exposure in observational pharmacokinetic data, with no infant adverse events reported).

cards.headline: O'Hara 2019: in the placebo-controlled trial, sertraline made no difference on the primary outcome (HamD-17) over 12 weeks, though it scored better on a secondary self-report depression scale
cards.summary: O'Hara 2019: in the placebo-controlled trial, sertraline made no difference on the primary outcome (HamD-17) over 12 weeks, though it scored better on a secondary self-report depression scale
cards.people: 162 breastfeeding and non-breastfeeding women with a major depressive episode in the first year postpartum, at two sites (Iowa and Rhode Island), randomly assigned to interpersonal psychotherapy (IPT), sertraline with clinical management (CM), or pill placebo with CM over 12 weeks. Clinical management included infant-focused psychoeducation. Depression and social adjustment were measured at baseline and at 4, 8 and 12 weeks.
cards.result: There was no significant effect for treatment condition on the primary outcome measure, the HamD-17 (the treatment made no difference on that measure). There was a significant effect for sertraline-CM relative to the IPT and placebo conditions on the General Depression scale of the Inventory of Depression and Anxiety Symptoms. Across all three conditions, women improved significantly over the 12 weeks. The record reports no sertraline dose and no breastfeeding-specific subgroup result, and no effect size for the secondary scale.
cards.watchOut: The trial mixed breastfeeding and non-breastfeeding women and the record does not report the breastfeeding subgroup separately, so it answers efficacy in postnatal depression generally, not efficacy specifically in breastfeeding women. The authors note significant non-engagement with the assigned condition and differential IPT effects across the two sites.
cards.source: O'Hara MW et al. A placebo controlled treatment trial of sertraline and interpersonal psychotherapy for postpartum depression. Journal of affective disorders. 2019. PMID: 30447565. Registry ID: NCT00602355. cards.headline: Milgrom 2015: all three treatments improved symptoms, but CBT alone was superior to sertraline alone — and to the combination — at 12 weeks, in 45 women (small N on the face)
cards.summary: Milgrom 2015: all three treatments improved symptoms, but CBT alone was superior to sertraline alone — and to the combination — at 12 weeks, in 45 women (small N on the face)
cards.people: 45 postpartum women with a DSM-IV diagnosis of depression, randomised to cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), sertraline, or a combination of both, with psychometric measures collected weekly for 12 weeks and follow-up at 24 weeks. N = 45.
cards.result: Symptoms of depression and anxiety were reduced to a significant degree following all three treatments. CBT mono-therapy was superior to both sertraline mono-therapy and combination therapy after 12 weeks, and the CBT group showed the most rapid initial gains. There was no detectable advantage of combining pharmacological and psychological treatments in the short term. The record reports no effect sizes, no sertraline dose, and no breastfeeding-specific data.
cards.watchOut: No placebo arm and only 45 women: the trial can rank the three active treatments against each other but cannot show that sertraline beats no treatment, and its ranking rests on a small sample from a specialised CBT programme.
cards.source: Milgrom J et al. Treatment of postnatal depression with cognitive behavioural therapy, sertraline and combination therapy: a randomised controlled trial. cards.headline: Stowe 2003: breastfed infants received about 0.54% of the maternal sertraline dose; sertraline was detectable in 4 of 22 infants and no adverse events were reported in any infant (26 mothers)
cards.summary: Stowe 2003: breastfed infants received about 0.54% of the maternal sertraline dose; sertraline was detectable in 4 of 22 infants and no adverse events were reported in any infant (26 mothers)
cards.type: Pharmacokinetic study in breastfeeding mother–infant pairs (Stowe 2003)
cards.people: 26 nursing women with DSM-IV major depressive disorder treated with sertraline monotherapy 25–200 mg/day (mean 123.9 mg/day); 15 women submitted 182 breast milk samples, and 22 mother–infant serum pairs were obtained.
cards.result: The maximum calculated nursing infant dose of sertraline was 0.67 mg/day, representing 0.54% of the maternal daily dose (the metabolite desmethylsertraline represented a further calculated dose of 1.44 mg/day). Sertraline was detectable in 4 infants (18% of the sample) and desmethylsertraline in 11 infants (50%). Milk concentrations peaked in hindmilk 8 to 9 hours after the maternal dose; modelling suggested discarding milk 9 hours after the dose would cut the infant's daily sertraline dose by a mean of 17.1%. No adverse events were reported or documented in any infant.
cards.watchOut: A drug-level study of 26 mothers, not an infant-outcome trial: 'no adverse events reported' in 22 sampled infants cannot exclude uncommon or longer-term effects, and detectability used a 2 ng/mL assay limit.
cards.source: Stowe ZN et al. The pharmacokinetics of sertraline excretion into human breast milk: determinants of infant serum concentrations. The Journal of clinical psychiatry. 2003. PMID: 12590627. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Weissman 2004: pooled analysis of 57 studies — sertraline, like nortriptyline and paroxetine, usually produces undetectable infant levels and is a preferred choice in breastfeeding women
cards.summary: Weissman 2004: pooled analysis of 57 studies — sertraline, like nortriptyline and paroxetine, usually produces undetectable infant levels and is a preferred choice in breastfeeding women
cards.type: Pooled analysis of lactation pharmacokinetic studies (Weissman 2004)
cards.people: Pooled analysis of 57 studies of maternal plasma, breast milk and/or infant plasma antidepressant levels in nursing mother–infant pairs, drawn from 67 relevant studies identified in the literature to July 2002.
cards.result: Nortriptyline, paroxetine and sertraline usually produce undetectable infant levels. By contrast, fluoxetine produced the highest proportion (22%) of infant levels elevated above 10% of the average maternal level, and citalopram produced elevated levels in 17% of infants on smaller numbers. The authors conclude that nortriptyline, paroxetine and sertraline may be preferred choices in breastfeeding women, and that current data do not support monitoring breast milk levels in individual patients. The record reports no sertraline-specific pooled percentage.
cards.watchOut: The underlying studies are small observational level-measurements assembled by consensus selection, and symptomatic infants reported as case reports were analysed separately — the reassurance applies to typical reported exposures, not to every dose or every infant.
cards.source: Weissman AM et al. Pooled analysis of antidepressant levels in lactating mothers, breast milk, and nursing infants. The American journal of psychiatry. 2004. PMID: 15169695. Registry ID: none in the record.
