cards.headline: Synthesis: sertraline's efficacy in postnatal depression is unproven against placebo on the primary outcome of the one controlled trial, while its breastfeeding exposure profile is consistently among the lowest of any antidepressant
cards.summary: Synthesis: sertraline's efficacy in postnatal depression is unproven against placebo on the primary outcome of the one controlled trial, while its breastfeeding exposure profile is consistently among the lowest of any antidepressant
cards.people: The carded evidence: two randomised treatment trials (162 and 45 women), one pharmacokinetic study (26 nursing mothers, 22 infant serum pairs), and one pooled analysis of 57 lactation studies. Efficacy and safety rest on different evidence types and are not summed into a single N.
cards.result: Against placebo, sertraline made no difference on the HamD-17 primary outcome in O'Hara 2019, with a favourable signal only on a secondary self-report scale; against active treatment in Milgrom 2015, sertraline alone was inferior to CBT alone at 12 weeks, though all groups improved. For the breastfed infant, the calculated sertraline dose was 0.54% of the maternal dose (Stowe 2003), infant levels were usually undetectable across 57 pooled studies (Weissman 2004), and no infant adverse events were reported in the carded pharmacokinetic study. PROPOSED SPLIT (efficacy: divided — null on the primary outcome of the one placebo-controlled trial and inferior to CBT in a small trial; breastfeeding safety: consistently very low infant exposure in observational pharmacokinetic data, with no infant adverse events reported).
cards.watchOut: 'Safe during breastfeeding' on this shelf means low measured infant exposure and no reported adverse events in small observational studies — it is not the result of a randomised infant-safety trial, and the efficacy trials do not report breastfeeding subgroups.
cards.source: Synthesis of O'Hara MW et al. Journal of affective disorders. 2019 (PMID: 30447565); Milgrom J et al. The Australian and New Zealand journal of psychiatry. 2015 (PMID: 25586754); Stowe ZN et al. The Journal of clinical psychiatry. 2003 (PMID: 12590627); Weissman AM et al. shelves.title: Vitamin D on enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs: deficiency in 54% (vs 37% on non-inducing drugs), supplementation prevents the fall — monitor and supplement when low; fracture benefit untested
shelves.question: Should vitamin D be monitored and supplemented in people taking enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anticonvulsants · Bone Density · Epilepsy · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Retrospective Studies · Risk Factors · Vitamin D · Vitamin D Deficiency · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). Deficiency is common and measurably worse on enzyme-inducing drugs: in 596 adults with epilepsy, vitamin D deficiency (under 20 ng/mL) was present in 54% of the enzyme-inducing group versus 37% of the non-enzyme-inducing group (Teagarden 2014). The one randomised supplementation trial carded (Viraraghavan 2019, 83 children newly started on antiepileptic drugs) shows the fall is preventable: without supplementation mean 25(OH)D fell significantly over 6 months (18 to 13 ng/mL), while monthly vitamin D3 maintained levels (25 to 26 ng/mL; between-group P = 0.005). A 2024 Epilepsia narrative review (Sourbron 2024) concludes regular vitamin D measurement is a cost-effective, practical monitoring method in people with epilepsy, with densitometry added in high-risk patients, but states there is not enough evidence to advocate continuous supplementation in everyone. No carded trial tests fractures or other clinical endpoints, so the case rests on deficiency prevalence plus a biochemical prevention trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): monitor vitamin D in people on enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs and supplement when low — deficiency is frequent and drug-related, and supplementation prevents the measured fall, but clinical-outcome benefit is untested.

cards.headline: Teagarden 2014: vitamin D deficiency in 45% of 596 adults with epilepsy — 54% on enzyme-inducing drugs versus 37% on non-enzyme-inducing drugs
cards.summary: Teagarden 2014: vitamin D deficiency in 45% of 596 adults with epilepsy — 54% on enzyme-inducing drugs versus 37% on non-enzyme-inducing drugs
cards.people: 596 consecutive adult patients with epilepsy treated at the Emory University Epilepsy Center, 2008–2011 (mean age 41 years, 56% women); vitamin D 25-OH levels categorised as low (under 20 ng/mL), borderline (20–29 ng/mL) or normal (30 ng/mL or above), and antiepileptic drugs categorised by enzyme-inducing properties. Observational study.
cards.result: Mean vitamin D level was 22.5 ng/mL (SD 11.9) and 45% had a level under 20 ng/mL. Mean levels and deficiency frequencies differed across drug groups (P = .002): deficiency was present in 54% of the enzyme-inducing group and 37% of the non-enzyme-inducing group. The authors conclude vitamin D deficiency is common in epilepsy and monitoring should be considered part of routine management.
cards.watchOut: Cross-sectional levels cannot prove the drugs caused the deficiency — diet, sunlight, disability and seizure burden all differ between groups — but the enzyme-inducing gradient is the pattern the drug mechanism predicts.
cards.source: Teagarden DL et al. Low vitamin D levels are common in patients with epilepsy. Epilepsy Research. 2014. PMID: 25060996. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Viraraghavan 2019: in the carded randomised trial, monthly vitamin D3 prevented the fall in 25(OH)D seen without supplementation in 83 children newly started on antiepileptic drugs
cards.summary: Viraraghavan 2019: in the carded randomised trial, monthly vitamin D3 prevented the fall in 25(OH)D seen without supplementation in 83 children newly started on antiepileptic drugs
cards.people: 83 children aged 5–10 years newly started on antiepileptic drugs at a tertiary children's hospital in New Delhi, randomised to oral vitamin D3 60,000 IU/month under direct supervision plus antiepileptic drugs for 6 months (group A) or antiepileptic drugs without vitamin D3 (group B). The record does not restrict enrolment to enzyme-inducing drugs — printed plainly here.
cards.result: In group A, mean 25(OH)D was maintained at 6 months (26 ng/mL, 95% CI 20–34) versus baseline (25 ng/mL; P = 0.83). In group B it fell significantly, from 18 ng/mL (95% CI 13–24) at baseline to 13 ng/mL (95% CI 9–17) at 6 months (P = 0.01). At 6 months mean 25(OH)D was significantly higher in group A than group B (P = 0.005). The authors conclude monthly 60,000 IU vitamin D3 is sufficient to maintain levels and prevent deficiency over 6 months in children newly started on antiepileptic drugs.
cards.watchOut: A 6-month biochemical endpoint in 83 children on mixed antiepileptic drugs: it proves supplementation holds the blood level, not that it prevents fractures, and it does not isolate enzyme-inducing drugs.
cards.source: Viraraghavan VR et al. Effect of high dose vitamin d supplementation on vitamin d nutrition status of pre-pubertal children on anti-epileptic drugs - A randomized controlled trial. Clinical Nutrition ESPEN. 2019. PMID: 30661698. Registry ID: CTRI/2017/08/009234. cards.headline: Sourbron 2024: narrative review — enzyme-inducing antiseizure medication is an important risk factor for vitamin D deficiency; regular measurement is cost-effective and practical, but evidence does not support supplementing everyone continuously
cards.summary: Sourbron 2024: narrative review — enzyme-inducing antiseizure medication is an important risk factor for vitamin D deficiency; regular measurement is cost-effective and practical, but evidence does not support supplementing everyone continuously
cards.people: Narrative review in Epilepsia of the evidence in people with epilepsy on risk factors for vitamin D deficiency, higher-risk groups, and how to monitor bone health. Higher-risk groups identified: intellectual or physical disability, institutionalised patients, puberty, early-onset epilepsy and developmental epileptic encephalopathies, postmenopausal women, and users of multiple antiseizure medications or concomitant drugs such as corticosteroids.
cards.result: The review reports that antiseizure medication use — especially enzyme-inducing medication and valproate — is an important risk factor for impaired bone health (osteoporosis, fractures and/or vitamin D deficiency); that regular vitamin D measurement in people with epilepsy is a cost-effective and practical method for monitoring deficiency, with vitamin D measurement plus bone densitometry recommended in high-risk patients; and that there is not enough evidence to advocate continuous vitamin D supplementation in all people with epilepsy, though children should receive the recommended daily intake for age with added monitoring and supplementation if at higher risk. No pooled effect size is reported in the record.
cards.watchOut: A narrative review, not a systematic review with pooled numbers: its monitoring scheme is expert synthesis of the same observational literature carded above, not independent trial evidence.
cards.source: Sourbron J et al. Vitamin D prophylaxis in persons with epilepsy? Epilepsia. 2024. PMID: 39494692. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Humans · Epilepsy · Vitamin D Deficiency · Vitamin D · Anticonvulsants · Osteoporosis · Risk Factors · Bone Density · Female

cards.headline: Synthesis: deficiency is frequent and drug-graded (54% on enzyme-inducing drugs), supplementation prevents the measured fall, and the field's own review endorses monitoring — but no trial has tested fractures or other clinical outcomes
cards.summary: Synthesis: deficiency is frequent and drug-graded (54% on enzyme-inducing drugs), supplementation prevents the measured fall, and the field's own review endorses monitoring — but no trial has tested fractures or other clinical outcomes
cards.people: The carded evidence: one observational prevalence study (N = 596 adults), one small randomised supplementation trial (N = 83 children, 6 months, biochemical endpoint), and one narrative review (no participant N). Total carded participants exceed 600, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the limitation is endpoint type, not size.
cards.result: Deficiency (under 20 ng/mL) affected 45% of adults with epilepsy overall and 54% of those on enzyme-inducing drugs versus 37% on non-enzyme-inducing drugs (Teagarden 2014). Without supplementation, children's 25(OH)D fell from 18 to 13 ng/mL over 6 months on antiepileptic drugs; monthly vitamin D3 held it at 26 ng/mL (Viraraghavan 2019). The 2024 review endorses regular measurement, densitometry for high-risk patients, and targeted — not universal continuous — supplementation (Sourbron 2024). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Everything favourable is about blood levels: whether monitoring-and-supplementing prevents fractures in this population has never been tested in a completed trial carded here.
cards.source: Synthesis of Teagarden DL et al. Epilepsy Research. 2014 (PMID: 25060996); Viraraghavan VR et al. Clinical Nutrition ESPEN. 2019 (PMID: 30661698); Sourbron J et al. Epilepsia. 2024 (PMID: 39494692).

shelves.title: Antidepressants while breastfeeding (observational exposure evidence only): sertraline and paroxetine were undetectable in infant serum in the comparative study, citalopram was low, and fluoxetine carries the one growth signal — exposure data, not infant-outcome trials
shelves.question: Which antidepressants are safest to use while breastfeeding?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aryl Hydrocarbon Hydroxylases · Breast Feeding · Cytochrome P-450 CYP2C19 · Cytochrome P-450 CYP2D6 · Cytochrome P-450 Enzyme System · Depression, Postpartum · Female · Genotype · Humans · Infant · Infant, Newborn · Lactation · Male · Maternal Exposure · Milk, Human · Mixed Function Oxygenases · Paroxetine · Pharmacogenetics · Phenotype · Pregnancy · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors · Sertraline · Triglycerides
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (safest-exposure ranking) — observational only, printed on the face. This shelf answers the comparative class question; the sertraline-specific evidence is homed on shelf #5734 (sertraline as the preferred antidepressant during breastfeeding) and shelf #5770 (sertraline for postnatal depression during breastfeeding), whose carded reports (PMIDs 15169695, 12590627, 25589155) are cross-pointed here and deliberately not re-carded. On the free comparative evidence carded here, the ranking is consistent: in the head-to-head exposure study, sertraline and paroxetine were undetectable in infant serum while venlafaxine was measurable in all exposed infants and citalopram was undetectable or low (Berle 2004); SSRI milk transfer overall was low (median relative infant dose 1.5%) with differences among drugs (Pogliani 2019); paroxetine-exposed infants grew normally to 12 months (Merlob 2004). The caution end is fluoxetine, the one agent with an adverse signal — a 392 g average growth deficit in exposed infants (Chambers 1999) — compounded by its long half-life, which the exposure literature consistently flags. All of this is small observational and pharmacokinetic evidence, not infant-outcome trials. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (safest-exposure ranking) — observational only: sertraline and paroxetine are the safest-supported choices while breastfeeding; fluoxetine is the one to avoid where an alternative exists.

cards.headline: Berle 2004: in the head-to-head exposure study, sertraline and paroxetine were not detected in any infant's serum, citalopram was undetectable or low, and all venlafaxine-exposed infants had measurable levels — 25 mothers, 26 infants
cards.summary: Berle 2004: in the head-to-head exposure study, sertraline and paroxetine were not detected in any infant's serum, citalopram was undetectable or low, and all venlafaxine-exposed infants had measurable levels — 25 mothers, 26 infants
cards.people: 25 lactating women treated with citalopram (n = 9), sertraline (n = 6), paroxetine (n = 6), fluoxetine (n = 1) or venlafaxine (n = 3) and their 26 breastfed infants; drug concentrations were measured in maternal and infant serum and milk, with a control group of 68 medication-free breastfeeding mothers for the adverse-event questionnaire. Subgroup Ns are printed here because they are small.
cards.result: Sertraline and paroxetine were not detected in any of the drug-exposed infants. Infant serum citalopram was either undetectable (n = 4) or low (n = 6). All venlafaxine-exposed infants had measurable drug concentrations. There was no evidence of adverse events in the drug-exposed infants. The authors conclude the data add to evidence that breastfeeding should not be generally discouraged in women using serotonin reuptake inhibitor antidepressants. The record reports detection and levels, not a formal effect size for infant outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Per-drug subgroups are tiny (fluoxetine n = 1), so 'not detected' for sertraline and paroxetine rests on six infants each; this is exposure evidence — undetectable serum levels are reassuring but are not proof of no developmental effect.
cards.source: Berle JØ et al. Breastfeeding during maternal antidepressant treatment with serotonin reuptake inhibitors: infant exposure, clinical symptoms, and cytochrome p450 genotypes. The Journal of clinical psychiatry. 2004. PMID: 15367050. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Pogliani 2019: SSRIs passed into milk at a median relative infant dose of 1.5%, with differences among the individual drugs, and no milk-related side effects were found in 19 newborns — small N on the face
cards.summary: Pogliani 2019: SSRIs passed into milk at a median relative infant dose of 1.5%, with differences among the individual drugs, and no milk-related side effects were found in 19 newborns — small N on the face
cards.people: 19 women treated with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors during the third trimester of pregnancy and lactation; milk-to-plasma ratios and relative infant dose (RID) were measured by HPLC–mass spectrometry in the first days after delivery, with follow-up at 1 week. N = 19 mother–infant pairs, printed on the face.
cards.result: Human milk-to-plasma ratios ranged from 51.1% to 703.4% across the SSRIs studied. The median RID was 1.5%, with differences among the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (the record does not print a per-drug RID table in its abstract). No side effects due to passage of SSRIs into human milk were found. The authors advise that breastfeeding not be precluded a priori but recommended with careful follow-up.
cards.watchOut: Nineteen women across several different SSRIs means only a few per drug, follow-up was one week, and exposure continued from pregnancy — this study ranks transfer in principle, not the safety of any single named drug.
cards.source: Pogliani L et al. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors' passage into human milk of lactating women. The journal of maternal-fetal & neonatal medicine : the official journal of the European Association of Perinatal Medicine, the Federation of Asia and Oceania Perinatal Societies, the International Society of Perinatal Obstetricians. 2019. cards.headline: Chambers 1999: infants breastfed by mothers taking fluoxetine gained 392 g less between 2 weeks and 6 months than infants of mothers taking no psychotherapeutic medication — the one adverse growth signal in this shelf's evidence
cards.summary: Chambers 1999: infants breastfed by mothers taking fluoxetine gained 392 g less between 2 weeks and 6 months than infants of mothers taking no psychotherapeutic medication — the one adverse growth signal in this shelf's evidence
cards.people: Retrospective cohort from a teratogen information service pregnancy outcome study: 64 women who had taken fluoxetine during pregnancy were interviewed; 26 breastfed while continuing fluoxetine and 38 breastfed without taking it postnatally. Postnatal weight gain came from pediatric records.
cards.result: Infants breastfed by mothers taking fluoxetine had a growth curve significantly below that of infants breastfed by mothers not taking the drug; the average deficit in measurements between 2 weeks and 6 months of age was 392 g (95% CI −5 to −780 g, as printed in the record). In a repeated-measures analysis the difference was approximately 1.2 standard deviations (P = .005). No mother reported unusual symptoms she attributed to the medication, and the record notes there was no excess of infants below a growth threshold in the data presented (abstract truncated in the record).
cards.watchOut: Exposure began in pregnancy, so the growth difference cannot be attributed to milk alone; the study is small, retrospective, and unblinded — it is a caution signal for fluoxetine specifically, not proof of harm, and it is why fluoxetine sits at the cautious end of this shelf's ranking.
cards.source: Chambers CD et al. Weight gain in infants breastfed by mothers who take fluoxetine. Pediatrics. 1999. PMID: 10545587. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Merlob 2004: paroxetine during breastfeeding did not affect infant weight gain at 6 and 12 months in a prospective cohort of 27 exposed mothers, with one report of irritability
cards.summary: Merlob 2004: paroxetine during breastfeeding did not affect infant weight gain at 6 and 12 months in a prospective cohort of 27 exposed mothers, with one report of irritability
cards.people: Prospective cohort: 27 mothers who took paroxetine for at least 2 weeks while breastfeeding, 19 mothers who did not take paroxetine and did not breastfeed, and 27 mothers who breastfed without taking any drugs; infant weight and developmental milestones were recorded at 3, 6 and 12 months.
cards.result: There were no statistically significant differences between the paroxetine group and control groups in mean infant weight at ages 6 and 12 months, and the usual developmental milestones were reached in all groups. No adverse effects of paroxetine during lactation were reported except irritability in one infant. The authors conclude paroxetine may be acceptable in lactating women under the restrictions they studied (lowest dose, close infant follow-up). The record reports no effect size beyond the absence of significant differences.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-seven exposed infants cannot exclude uncommon or long-term effects, and the reassurance is tied to the study's own conditions (paroxetine 20 mg/day, single bedtime dose, no drug combinations, close follow-up).
cards.source: Merlob P et al. Paroxetine during breast-feeding: infant weight gain and maternal adherence to counsel. European journal of pediatrics. 2004. PMID: 14745552. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: on measured infant exposure, sertraline and paroxetine sit at the safest end (undetectable infant serum; normal growth on paroxetine), citalopram exposure is low, and fluoxetine is the cautious choice (measurable exposure class-wide concern plus a 392 g growth deficit signal) — all from small observational studies
cards.summary: Synthesis: on measured infant exposure, sertraline and paroxetine sit at the safest end (undetectable infant serum; normal growth on paroxetine), citalopram exposure is low, and fluoxetine is the cautious choice (measurable exposure class-wide concern plus a 392 g growth deficit signal) — all from small observational studies
cards.people: The carded evidence: one comparative exposure study (25 mothers, 26 infants, 68 controls), one milk-transfer study (19 women), one retrospective fluoxetine cohort (64 women; 26 exposed-breastfed) and one prospective paroxetine cohort (73 mothers across groups). Summed unique participants exceed 30, so no small-N stamp label applies, but every per-drug subgroup is small and that is printed on the cards. The sertraline-specific pooled analyses are homed on shelves #5734 and #5770 and are cross-pointed in the balance, not re-carded here.
cards.result: Sertraline and paroxetine were undetectable in infant serum (Berle 2004); paroxetine-exposed infants gained weight normally to 12 months (Merlob 2004). SSRI transfer into milk overall was a median relative infant dose of 1.5% with differences among drugs and no milk-related side effects (Pogliani 2019). The outlier is fluoxetine: its exposed infants gained on average 392 g less by 6 months (Chambers 1999). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (safest-exposure ranking) — observational only: sertraline and paroxetine have the lowest measured infant exposure; fluoxetine is the agent to avoid where an alternative exists.
cards.watchOut: No carded study randomised mothers to different antidepressants or followed infants for long-term neurodevelopment by drug: 'safest' here means lowest measured exposure plus absence of a signal in small cohorts — a pharmacokinetic ranking, not a proven outcome ranking.
cards.source: Synthesis of Berle JØ et al. The Journal of clinical psychiatry. 2004 (PMID: 15367050); Pogliani L et al. shelves.title: Andexanet alfa in factor Xa inhibitor major bleeding: anti-Xa activity falls by over 90% and 80–82% achieve good or excellent haemostasis in the single-arm ANNEXA-4 programme, with lower in-hospital mortality than 4-factor PCC in observational comparison (odds ratio 0.50) — but no randomised trial covers major bleeding generally
shelves.question: Does andexanet alfa improve outcomes in major bleeding associated with a direct oral anticoagulant (factor Xa inhibitor)?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Atrial Fibrillation · Coagulants · Factor Xa · Factor Xa Inhibitors · Female · Gastrointestinal Hemorrhage · Hemorrhage · Humans · Intracranial Hemorrhages · Male · ROC Curve · Recombinant Proteins
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion: live shelf #849 covers factor Xa inhibitor intracerebral haemorrhage (the randomised ANNEXA-I slice); this shelf covers the uncovered slice — DOAC-related major bleeding generally, across bleeding sites. In the single-arm ANNEXA-4 programme, andexanet reduced anti-factor Xa activity by 92% and 82% of evaluable patients achieved excellent or good haemostasis at 12 hours, while 14% died and 10% had a thrombotic event within 30 days (Connolly 2019); the final programme report (479 patients, 69% intracranial and 23% gastrointestinal bleeding) found the same pattern — 80% good or excellent haemostasis, 10% thrombotic events (Milling 2023) — and the small edoxaban subgroup behaved similarly (Benz 2022; n = 36, printed on its card). The only comparative outcome evidence is observational: in 4,395 hospitalised patients, in-hospital mortality odds were 50% lower with andexanet than with 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate, consistently for intracranial and gastrointestinal bleeds (Dobesh 2023). There is no randomised comparison for major bleeding overall — the randomised evidence is confined to the intracranial slice homed on #849. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — haemostatic efficacy is consistent within a single-arm programme and the comparative signal is observational only, both printed on the face.

cards.headline: Connolly 2019 (ANNEXA-4): in 352 patients with acute major bleeding on a factor Xa inhibitor, andexanet cut anti-Xa activity by 92% and 82% achieved excellent or good haemostasis at 12 hours — with 14% dead and 10% thrombosed by 30 days, and no control group
cards.summary: Connolly 2019 (ANNEXA-4): in 352 patients with acute major bleeding on a factor Xa inhibitor, andexanet cut anti-Xa activity by 92% and 82% achieved excellent or good haemostasis at 12 hours — with 14% dead and 10% thrombosed by 30 days, and no control group
cards.people: 352 patients with acute major bleeding within 18 hours of taking a factor Xa inhibitor (mean age 77 years, most with substantial cardiovascular disease), treated with an andexanet bolus followed by a 2-hour infusion; bleeding was intracranial in 227 (64%) and gastrointestinal in 90 (26%); haemostatic efficacy was assessed in the subgroup with confirmed major bleeding and baseline anti-Xa activity ≥75 ng/mL.
cards.result: Median anti-factor Xa activity fell by 92% after the bolus in both apixaban patients (149.7 to 11.1 ng/mL; 95% CI for reduction 91–93) and rivaroxaban patients (211.8 to 14.2 ng/mL; 88–94). Excellent or good haemostasis occurred in 204 of 249 evaluable patients (82%). Within 30 days, death occurred in 49 patients (14%) and a thrombotic event in 34 (10%). Reduction in anti-Xa activity was not predictive of haemostatic efficacy overall, but was modestly predictive in intracranial haemorrhage.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm with no comparator: 82% haemostasis cannot be compared with what supportive care or PCC would have achieved in the same patients, and the 14% mortality and 10% thrombosis rates have no control rates beside them.
cards.source: Connolly SJ et al. Full Study Report of Andexanet Alfa for Bleeding Associated with Factor Xa Inhibitors. New England Journal of Medicine. 2019. PMID: 30730782. cards.headline: Milling 2023 (ANNEXA-4 final report): in the completed programme of 479 patients (69% intracranial, 23% gastrointestinal bleeding), excellent or good haemostasis was 80% and thrombotic events 10% — confirming the interim pattern at full enrolment
cards.summary: Milling 2023 (ANNEXA-4 final report): in the completed programme of 479 patients (69% intracranial, 23% gastrointestinal bleeding), excellent or good haemostasis was 80% and thrombotic events 10% — confirming the interim pattern at full enrolment
cards.type: Single-arm prospective cohort, final report (Milling 2023, ANNEXA-4)
cards.people: 479 patients with acute major bleeding within 18 hours of a factor Xa inhibitor (mean age 78 years, 54% men, 81% anticoagulated for atrial fibrillation; apixaban 51%, rivaroxaban 37%, edoxaban 8%, enoxaparin 5%; median 11.4 hours since last dose), in a multicentre prospective phase 3b/4 single-group cohort; 342 patients were evaluable for haemostatic efficacy.
cards.result: Median anti-Xa activity fell by 93% in apixaban patients, 94% in rivaroxaban, 71% in edoxaban and 75% in enoxaparin patients. Excellent or good haemostasis occurred in 274 of 342 evaluable patients (80%, 95% CI 75–84). In the safety population, thrombotic events occurred in 50 patients (10%); no thrombotic episodes occurred after oral anticoagulation was restarted. Anti-Xa reduction predicted haemostatic efficacy in intracranial haemorrhage (area under the curve 0.62) and correlated with lower mortality in patients under 75.
cards.watchOut: The same single-arm programme as the Connolly card at full enrolment — the two cards are one evidence base at two time points, not two independent confirmations.
cards.source: Milling TJ Jr et al. Final Study Report of Andexanet Alfa for Major Bleeding With Factor Xa Inhibitors. Circulation. 2023. PMID: 36802876. Registry ID: NCT02329327. cards.headline: Benz 2022: in the edoxaban subgroup of ANNEXA-4 (36 patients — small N on the face), andexanet reduced anti-Xa activity by 68.9% and 78.6% of evaluable patients achieved excellent or good haemostasis, with 11.1% thrombotic events and 11.1% deaths at 30 days
cards.summary: Benz 2022: in the edoxaban subgroup of ANNEXA-4 (36 patients — small N on the face), andexanet reduced anti-Xa activity by 68.9% and 78.6% of evaluable patients achieved excellent or good haemostasis, with 11.1% thrombotic events and 11.1% deaths at 30 days
cards.people: 36 patients (mean age 82 years, 61.1% men, 91.7% with atrial fibrillation) with acute major bleeding within 18 hours of edoxaban intake, prospectively enrolled and treated with an andexanet bolus and 2-hour infusion; bleeding was intracranial in 29 (80.6%); the efficacy population was 28 patients with confirmed major bleeding and baseline anti-Xa activity ≥40 ng/mL. Subgroup N = 36 printed here on the face.
cards.result: Median anti-factor Xa activity decreased from 121.1 ng/mL at baseline to 24.0 ng/mL at the end of the bolus (median decrease 68.9%, 95% CI 56.1–77.7). Excellent or good haemostasis at 12 hours was achieved in 78.6% (95% CI 59.0–91.7) of evaluable patients. Within 30 days, four patients (11.1%) had a thrombotic event and four (11.1%) died.
cards.watchOut: A 36-patient subgroup, mostly intracranial bleeding: it shows the edoxaban case behaves like the apixaban/rivaroxaban majority, but its confidence intervals are wide and it is not independent of the parent programme.
cards.source: Benz AP et al. Andexanet Alfa for Specific Anticoagulation Reversal in Patients with Acute Bleeding during Treatment with Edoxaban. Thrombosis and Haemostasis. 2022. PMID: 34996121. cards.headline: Dobesh 2023: in 4,395 hospitalised patients with rivaroxaban- or apixaban-related major bleeding, in-hospital mortality odds were 50% lower with andexanet than with 4-factor PCC (odds ratio 0.50) — consistently for intracranial (0.55) and gastrointestinal (0.49) bleeds; observational only
cards.summary: Dobesh 2023: in 4,395 hospitalised patients with rivaroxaban- or apixaban-related major bleeding, in-hospital mortality odds were 50% lower with andexanet than with 4-factor PCC (odds ratio 0.50) — consistently for intracranial (0.55) and gastrointestinal (0.49) bleeds; observational only
cards.people: 4,395 patients hospitalised with major bleeding on rivaroxaban or apixaban across 354 US hospitals (May 2018 to September 2022), treated with andexanet alfa (n = 2,122) or 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (n = 2,273); bleeding was intracranial in 1,328, gastrointestinal in 2,567, and critical-compartment or other in 500.
cards.result: In multivariable analysis, the odds of in-hospital mortality were 50% lower with andexanet than with 4F-PCC (odds ratio 0.50, 95% CI 0.39–0.65, P < .01), consistent for intracranial haemorrhage (odds ratio 0.55, 0.39–0.76) and gastrointestinal bleeds (odds ratio 0.49, 0.29–0.81); propensity score-weighted analyses gave similar results. Odds ratios are relative measures, as printed in the record; the record does not print the absolute mortality rates beside them.
cards.watchOut: Observational comparison from electronic health records: hospitals and clinicians choosing andexanet differ from those choosing PCC, and adjustment cannot exclude confounding by bleed severity, timing, or centre — this is a signal, not a randomised result.
cards.source: Dobesh PP et al. Lower mortality with andexanet alfa vs 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate for factor Xa inhibitor-related major bleeding in a U.S. hospital-based observational study. Research and Practice in Thrombosis and Haemostasis. 2023. PMID: 37753225. Registry ID: NCT05548777. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: andexanet reliably reverses anti-Xa activity (>90%) and achieves good or excellent haemostasis in about 80% of major bleeds in a single-arm programme, and the only comparative outcome data — observational — favour it over 4F-PCC for in-hospital mortality (odds ratio 0.50); no randomised trial covers major bleeding generally
cards.summary: Synthesis: andexanet reliably reverses anti-Xa activity (>90%) and achieves good or excellent haemostasis in about 80% of major bleeds in a single-arm programme, and the only comparative outcome data — observational — favour it over 4F-PCC for in-hospital mortality (odds ratio 0.50); no randomised trial covers major bleeding generally
cards.people: The carded evidence: the ANNEXA-4 single-arm programme at interim (352 patients) and final (479 patients) enrolment — one evidence base, counted once — its edoxaban subgroup (36 patients, N on its card), and one observational comparison against 4F-PCC (4,395 patients). Unique patients exceed 4,800, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the limits are design (single-arm, observational), printed here.
cards.result: Haemostasis excellent or good: 82% (interim) and 80% (final) in ANNEXA-4; 78.6% in the edoxaban subgroup. Thirty-day death 14% and thrombotic events 10% in the interim report, with no comparator. Versus 4F-PCC observationally: in-hospital mortality odds ratio 0.50 (95% CI 0.39–0.65). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — consistent haemostatic efficacy in a single-arm programme plus an observational mortality signal; the randomised intracerebral-haemorrhage slice is homed on live shelf #849.
cards.watchOut: Nothing carded here randomises andexanet against PCC or usual care in major bleeding overall; thrombotic events in about 1 in 10 treated patients are part of the outcome picture, not a footnote.
cards.source: Synthesis of Connolly SJ et al. New England Journal of Medicine. 2019 (PMID: 30730782); Milling TJ Jr et al. Circulation. 2023 (PMID: 36802876); Benz AP et al. shelves.title: Idarucizumab in dabigatran-related bleeding: reversal is near-universal (100% median within 4 hours) and bleeding stopped within 24 hours in 68.7% of gastrointestinal bleeds (median 2.4 hours), with >91% normal haemostasis when it enabled urgent surgery — all from a single-arm cohort, so clinical benefit is inferred, not randomised
shelves.question: Does idarucizumab reversal improve clinical outcomes in dabigatran-related bleeding?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Anticoagulants · Dabigatran · Drug Substitution · Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Gastrointestinal Hemorrhage · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Risk Assessment · United States · Venous Thromboembolism · Vitamin K
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion: live shelf #849 covers idarucizumab reversal (the reversal-effect question, including the RE-VERSE AD full-cohort report, which is homed there and not re-carded here); this shelf covers the uncovered slice — clinical bleeding outcomes after reversal: whether bleeding stops, how fast, and what happens to patients. The free reports are the programme's outcome-focused analyses. In gastrointestinal bleeding (137 patients), reversal was complete in 97.5% by diluted thrombin time, bleeding cessation within 24 hours was reported in 68.7% after a median 2.4 hours, and by 90 days 4.4% had a thromboembolic event and 14.6% had died (Van der Wall 2019). In patients needing urgent surgery (202 patients), normal haemostasis was achieved in over 91%, surgery began within 2 hours in most groups, 30-day thromboembolic events were 5% and mortality 12.6% (Levy 2021). Across the full cohort split by renal function, median reversal was 100% within 4 hours regardless of kidney function, bleeding cessation and procedural haemostasis were similar across renal strata, dabigatran levels re-rose by 12–24 hours in over half of severely impaired patients, and mortality was higher with severe renal impairment (Eikelboom 2019). No report includes a control group, so none of these outcome rates can be credited to idarucizumab against a counterfactual. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — reversal is certain and the ensuing clinical course is consistently favourable in a single-arm programme; outcome improvement itself remains unrandomised.

cards.headline: Van der Wall 2019: in 137 RE-VERSE AD patients with major gastrointestinal bleeding, idarucizumab completely reversed dabigatran in 97.5% (by diluted thrombin time), bleeding stopped within 24 hours in 68.7% (median 2.4 hours), and by 90 days 4.4% had thromboembolism and 14.6% had died
cards.summary: Van der Wall 2019: in 137 RE-VERSE AD patients with major gastrointestinal bleeding, idarucizumab completely reversed dabigatran in 97.5% (by diluted thrombin time), bleeding stopped within 24 hours in 68.7% (median 2.4 hours), and by 90 days 4.4% had thromboembolism and 14.6% had died
cards.type: Prospective cohort, gastrointestinal bleeding (Van der Wall 2019, RE-VERSE AD)
cards.people: 137 patients with uncontrollable gastrointestinal bleeding requiring reversal, enrolled in the prospective multicentre open-label RE-VERSE AD study (June 2014 to July 2016) and followed for 90 days; 84% of bleeds were adjudicated major or life-threatening, 35.0% upper gastrointestinal, 31.4% lower, and 33.6% both or unknown; all received 5 g intravenous idarucizumab as two 2.5 g bolus infusions.
cards.result: Complete reversal of dabigatran was observed in 118 of 121 patients (97.5%) with an elevated diluted thrombin time and 95 of 131 (72.5%) with an elevated ecarin clotting time, similarly for upper and lower gastrointestinal bleeding. Bleeding cessation within 24 hours was reported in 92 of 134 evaluable patients (68.7%) after a median duration of 2.4 hours (interquartile range 2.0–3.9). During 90-day follow-up, 6 patients (4.4%) had a postreversal thromboembolic event and 20 (14.6%) died.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm: bleeding cessation and mortality have no untreated comparison, and gastrointestinal bleeding often stops with supportive care alone — the card shows the clinical course after reversal, not the drug's added effect.
cards.source: Van der Wall SJ et al. Idarucizumab for Dabigatran Reversal in the Management of Patients With Gastrointestinal Bleeding. Circulation. 2019. PMID: 30586692. Registry ID: NCT02104947. cards.headline: Levy 2021: in 202 RE-VERSE AD patients needing urgent surgery or procedures, idarucizumab gave normal haemostasis in over 91%, surgery started within 2 hours in most groups, and 30-day outcomes were 5% thromboembolic events and 12.6% mortality
cards.summary: Levy 2021: in 202 RE-VERSE AD patients needing urgent surgery or procedures, idarucizumab gave normal haemostasis in over 91%, surgery started within 2 hours in most groups, and 30-day outcomes were 5% thromboembolic events and 12.6% mortality
cards.type: Prospective cohort, urgent surgery (Levy 2021, RE-VERSE AD)
cards.people: 202 dabigatran-treated patients in RE-VERSE AD who received 5 g idarucizumab before urgent surgery or procedural intervention — 49 abdominal, 45 orthopaedic, 34 vascular, 8 neurologic and 4 genitourinary operations, plus 29 catheter-based cases, 20 drainage procedures and 8 diagnostic procedures; 5 patients did not undergo their intended intervention.
cards.result: Complete reversal occurred within minutes in almost all patients, with normal haemostasis in more than 91%. The median time from the first vial of idarucizumab to surgery or procedure was less than 2 hours in all groups except neurosurgery (3.3 hours). Fresh frozen plasma and packed red cells were the most frequently transfused products. Postreversal thromboembolic events occurred in 10 patients (5%) at 30 days — 5 of whom had restarted anticoagulation before the event — and overall 30-day mortality was 12.6%, with no serious adverse safety signals attributed to idarucizumab.
cards.watchOut: A surgical subanalysis of the same single-arm cohort: 'normal haemostasis in >91%' is surgeon-assessed without a control group, and the 12.6% mortality reflects how ill patients needing emergency surgery on anticoagulation are, in both directions of interpretation.
cards.source: Levy JH et al. Dabigatran Reversal With Idarucizumab in Patients Requiring Urgent Surgery: A Subanalysis of the RE-VERSE AD Study. Annals of Surgery. 2021. PMID: 31599808. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Eikelboom 2019: across all 503 RE-VERSE AD patients, median dabigatran reversal was 100% within 4 hours whatever the renal function, and bleeding cessation and procedural haemostasis were similar across renal strata — but dabigatran levels re-rose by 12–24 hours in 56% of severely impaired patients, whose mortality was higher
cards.summary: Eikelboom 2019: across all 503 RE-VERSE AD patients, median dabigatran reversal was 100% within 4 hours whatever the renal function, and bleeding cessation and procedural haemostasis were similar across renal strata — but dabigatran levels re-rose by 12–24 hours in 56% of severely impaired patients, whose mortality was higher
cards.type: Prospective cohort, by renal function (Eikelboom 2019, RE-VERSE AD)
cards.people: All 503 nondialysis patients in RE-VERSE AD receiving idarucizumab, compared by baseline creatinine clearance: normal ≥80, mild 50 to <80, moderate 30 to <50, and severe <30 mL/min; patients with worse renal function were older, more often women, with more comorbidity, higher CHADS2 scores and higher dabigatran levels despite more frequent low-dose dabigatran.
cards.result: Regardless of renal function, median reversal by dilute thrombin time was 100% within 4 hours, and over 98% of patients achieved reversal with undetectable unbound dabigatran. By 12 or 24 hours, dabigatran levels above 20 ng/mL had recurred in 56% of patients with severe, 29.1% with moderate and 9.2% with mild renal impairment, versus 8.3% with normal function. Time to cessation of bleeding and the proportion with normal procedural haemostasis were similar regardless of renal function, but patients with severe renal impairment had higher 30- and 90-day mortality rates (the record states this without printing the rates).
cards.watchOut: The renal analysis re-cuts the same 503-patient cohort carded in part on the other two cards — one evidence base, not three — and its mortality gradient by renal function is a prognosis finding, not a treatment effect.
cards.source: Eikelboom JW et al. Dabigatran Reversal With Idarucizumab in Patients With Renal Impairment. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2019. PMID: 31582135. Registry ID: NCT02104947. cards.headline: Synthesis: after idarucizumab, dabigatran reversal is complete in >98% of patients, gastrointestinal bleeding stops within 24 hours in about two-thirds (median 2.4 hours), urgent surgery proceeds with normal haemostasis in >91% — a consistently favourable clinical course in one single-arm programme of 503 patients, with no controlled outcome comparison
cards.summary: Synthesis: after idarucizumab, dabigatran reversal is complete in >98% of patients, gastrointestinal bleeding stops within 24 hours in about two-thirds (median 2.4 hours), urgent surgery proceeds with normal haemostasis in >91% — a consistently favourable clinical course in one single-arm programme of 503 patients, with no controlled outcome comparison
cards.people: The carded evidence is one prospective single-arm programme (RE-VERSE AD, 503 patients) read three ways: gastrointestinal bleeding (137 patients), urgent surgery/procedures (202 patients), and the full cohort by renal function (503 patients). Unique patients total 503, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the limitation is the absence of any comparator, printed here.
cards.result: Reversal: 100% median maximum reversal within 4 hours; complete reversal in 97.5% of gastrointestinal bleeders by diluted thrombin time. Clinical course: bleeding cessation within 24 hours in 68.7% (median 2.4 hours); normal procedural haemostasis in >91%; thromboembolic events 4.4–5%; mortality 12.6% at 30 days (surgical group) and 14.6% at 90 days (gastrointestinal group). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — the reversal effect is certain and outcomes after it are consistently favourable, but improved clinical outcomes versus no reversal are unproven by any controlled comparison; the full-cohort reversal report is homed on live shelf #849.
cards.watchOut: Every carded number comes from the same uncontrolled cohort: this shelf must never be quoted as showing idarucizumab reduces mortality or rebleeding, only that reversal is rapid and complete and the observed clinical course follows the pattern on the cards.
cards.source: Synthesis of Van der Wall SJ et al. Circulation. 2019 (PMID: 30586692); Levy JH et al. Annals of Surgery. 2021 (PMID: 31599808); Eikelboom JW et al. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2019 (PMID: 31582135).

shelves.title: Amitriptyline vs topiramate for migraine prevention in poor sleepers — untested as asked: the adult head-to-head trial (in episodic migraine) found no difference in migraine frequency, only in sedation and weight, and chronic migraine has no amitriptyline trial at all
shelves.question: Is amitriptyline better than topiramate for chronic migraine prevention in patients with poor sleep?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Amitriptyline · Body Weight · Central Nervous System Agents · Disability Evaluation · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fructose · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Migraine Disorders · Patient Satisfaction · Quality of Life · Severity of Illness Index · Surveys and Questionnaires · Time Factors · Topiramate · Treatment Outcome · United States
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #873, which covers amitriptyline and topiramate versus placebo in children and adolescents (the CHAMP trial) — this pack covers the slice #873 does not: adults, head-to-head, with poor sleep in view. The honest headline is a gap: no randomised trial has enrolled adults with chronic migraine selected for poor sleep, and none has compared these two drugs on sleep outcomes. The nearest evidence is a 26-week adult head-to-head noninferiority trial in episodic migraine (Dodick 2009, PMID: 19393844; 331 patients), in which monthly migraine episodes fell by 2.6 on topiramate and 2.7 on amitriptyline — the treatment made no difference on the primary outcome (95% CI -0.6 to 0.7) — while the side-effect profiles diverged in ways that matter for sleep: somnolence in 17.8% on amitriptyline versus 11.9% on topiramate, dry mouth 35.5% on amitriptyline, paresthesia 29.9% on topiramate, and mean weight change +2.4 kg on amitriptyline versus -2.4 kg on topiramate. A network meta-analysis of episodic migraine prophylaxis (Jackson 2015, PMID: 26172390) ranked amitriptyline above topiramate but called the evidence for that superiority weak. For chronic migraine specifically, a 2024 NIHR health technology assessment (Mistry 2024, PMID: 39365169) found topiramate trials to include but no amitriptyline trial meeting its criteria at all. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): in unselected adults the two drugs look equivalent for migraine prevention, amitriptyline is the more sedating of the two, and the asked question — chronic migraine in poor sleepers — is untested.

cards.headline: Dodick 2009: in 331 adults with episodic migraine, topiramate and amitriptyline reduced monthly migraine episodes by 2.6 and 2.7 — the treatment made no difference on the primary outcome; amitriptyline was more sedating (somnolence 17.8% vs 11.9%) and added weight (+2.4 kg vs -2.4 kg)
cards.summary: Dodick 2009: in 331 adults with episodic migraine, topiramate and amitriptyline reduced monthly migraine episodes by 2.6 and 2.7 — the treatment made no difference on the primary outcome; amitriptyline was more sedating (somnolence 17.8% vs 11.9%) and added weight (+2.4 kg vs -2.4 kg)
cards.people: Adults with 3 to 12 migraines per month (episodic migraine — not chronic migraine, and not selected for poor sleep) randomised 1:1 to topiramate or amitriptyline, each titrated from 25 mg/day to a maximum of 100 mg/day over 26 weeks in a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, double-dummy noninferiority trial. The intent-to-treat population was 331 subjects (172 topiramate, 159 amitriptyline; 84.9% female; mean age 38.8 years).
cards.result: The least squares mean change from baseline in mean monthly migraine episodes was -2.6 on topiramate and -2.7 on amitriptyline (95% CI for the difference -0.6 to 0.7) — no significant difference, and no significant differences on any prespecified secondary outcome. Topiramate improved functional disability during attacks more (P = 0.040) and several quality-of-life domains. Mean weight change was -2.4 kg on topiramate versus +2.4 kg on amitriptyline, with weight satisfaction improving on topiramate and deteriorating on amitriptyline (P < 0.001). Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 66.7% (topiramate) and 66.3% (amitriptyline); common events on topiramate were paresthesia 29.9%, fatigue 16.9%, somnolence 11.9%; on amitriptyline dry mouth 35.5%, fatigue 24.3%, somnolence 17.8%, weight increase 13.6%, dizziness 10.7%. No sleep outcome was measured.
cards.watchOut: This is the wrong population for the shelf's question twice over — episodic rather than chronic migraine, and unselected for sleep — and it is carded as the nearest adult head-to-head evidence with that mismatch printed on its face, not as a trial of poor sleepers. Noninferiority on migraine frequency also cannot speak to which drug helps a poor sleeper sleep.
cards.source: Dodick DW et al. Topiramate versus amitriptyline in migraine prevention: a 26-week, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, double-dummy, parallel-group noninferiority trial in adult migraineurs. Clinical Therapeutics. 2009. PMID: 19393844. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Jackson 2015: in a network meta-analysis of episodic migraine prophylaxis, amitriptyline (SMD -1.2 vs placebo) ranked better than topiramate (-1.1 headaches/month) and several other drugs — but the authors call the evidence for amitriptyline's superiority weak
cards.summary: Jackson 2015: in a network meta-analysis of episodic migraine prophylaxis, amitriptyline (SMD -1.2 vs placebo) ranked better than topiramate (-1.1 headaches/month) and several other drugs — but the authors call the evidence for amitriptyline's superiority weak
cards.people: Network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials of adults with migraine headaches of at least 4 weeks' duration (trials to 18 May 2014), including 11 tricyclic antidepressant trials, 32 anticonvulsant trials and 53 head-to-head drug-comparison trials across drug classes; populations were episodic migraine, not selected for chronic migraine or poor sleep. Total participant N is not documented as a single figure in the record.
cards.result: Drugs more effective than placebo for episodic migraine included amitriptyline (SMD -1.2, 95% CI -1.7 to -0.82) and topiramate (-1.1 headaches/month, 95% CI -1.9 to -0.73). The network meta-analysis found amitriptyline to be better than several other medications including candesartan, fluoxetine, propranolol, topiramate and valproate, and no different from atenolol, flunarizine, clomipramine or metoprolol. The authors' own summary: there is good evidence supporting the efficacy of several drugs, and weak evidence supporting amitriptyline's superiority over some drugs; selection should be tailored to patient preferences, characteristics and side-effect profiles. No sleep outcome is reported in the record.
cards.watchOut: Network rankings lean on indirect comparisons across trials from different eras and doses; a rank above topiramate built largely on indirect evidence, self-described as weak, is not a head-to-head win — and again, none of these trials enrolled patients for poor sleep.
cards.source: Jackson JL et al. A Comparative Effectiveness Meta-Analysis of Drugs for the Prophylaxis of Migraine Headache. PLoS One. 2015. PMID: 26172390. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Clinical Trials as Topic · Humans · Migraine Disorders · Treatment Outcome

cards.headline: Mistry 2024 (NIHR HTA): for chronic migraine itself, the assessors found 11 trials of 6 drugs in 7,352 adults — topiramate among them (about 1.1–1.5 fewer headache/migraine days per month) — and no trial of amitriptyline that met their criteria at all
cards.summary: Mistry 2024 (NIHR HTA): for chronic migraine itself, the assessors found 11 trials of 6 drugs in 7,352 adults — topiramate among them (about 1.1–1.5 fewer headache/migraine days per month) — and no trial of amitriptyline that met their criteria at all
cards.type: Systematic review and network meta-analysis with economic modelling (Mistry 2024)
cards.people: UK NIHR Health Technology Assessment systematic reviews and network meta-analysis of randomised trials in adults with chronic migraine, requiring more than 100 participants per arm for efficacy (adverse-event review: trials in episodic or chronic migraine). Eleven randomised trials testing six drugs (topiramate, onabotulinumtoxinA, eptinezumab, erenumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab) versus placebo in 7,352 adults with chronic migraine were included; the adverse-events review covered 40 randomised trials with 25,891 participants and three additional drugs including amitriptyline.
cards.result: Calcitonin gene-related peptide monoclonal antibodies reduced headache/migraine days by 2.0–2.5 per month, onabotulinumtoxinA by just under two, and topiramate by less than 1.5 (1.1–1.5 in the plain-language summary). The assessors state plainly: 'We found no trials of the commonly used drugs, such as propranolol or amitriptyline, to include in the analysis' for chronic migraine efficacy, and topiramate was the only oral drug with includable data. Serious adverse events were very few and none linked to the medications; people using topiramate or amitriptyline commonly had nervous-system or gastrointestinal adverse events. No sleep-selected population and no sleep outcome appears in the record.
cards.watchOut: 'No includable amitriptyline trial' reflects this review's size and quality thresholds for chronic migraine, not proof amitriptyline does nothing in chronic migraine — but it does mean the chronic-migraine half of this shelf's question has no cardable amitriptyline trial behind it.
cards.source: Mistry H et al. Preventive drug treatments for adults with chronic migraine: a systematic review with economic modelling. Health Technology Assessment. 2024. PMID: 39365169. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: no trial answers the question as asked — in unselected adults the two drugs tie on migraine prevention, amitriptyline is more sedating and weight-adding, and chronic migraine in poor sleepers remains untested for either drug
cards.summary: Synthesis: no trial answers the question as asked — in unselected adults the two drugs tie on migraine prevention, amitriptyline is more sedating and weight-adding, and chronic migraine in poor sleepers remains untested for either drug
cards.people: The carded evidence: one adult head-to-head randomised trial (331 patients, episodic migraine, 26 weeks), one network meta-analysis of episodic migraine prophylaxis, and one chronic-migraine health technology assessment (11 trials, 7,352 adults, none of amitriptyline). No carded study enrolled patients with chronic migraine selected for poor sleep, and none measured a sleep outcome; total head-to-head participants = 331.
cards.result: Monthly migraine episodes fell by 2.6 (topiramate) and 2.7 (amitriptyline) in the head-to-head trial — the treatment made no difference on the primary outcome — while somnolence (17.8% vs 11.9%), dry mouth (35.5%, amitriptyline) and weight (+2.4 kg amitriptyline vs -2.4 kg topiramate) separated the drugs (Dodick 2009). A network meta-analysis ranked amitriptyline above topiramate on weak evidence (Jackson 2015). For chronic migraine, topiramate has placebo-controlled data (about 1.1–1.5 fewer days per month) and amitriptyline has no includable trial (Mistry 2024). Whether amitriptyline's sedation translates into better sleep — or topiramate's alerting profile into worse sleep — in chronic migraine patients with poor sleep is inference from side-effect lists, not trial evidence. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Home shelf #873 is the paediatric placebo-controlled question (CHAMP); this shelf must not borrow CHAMP's null verdict for adults, nor present Dodick's episodic-migraine equivalence as a chronic-migraine result. The poor-sleep selection in the question is, as of this build, an evidence gap printed on the face of the shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Dodick DW et al. Clinical Therapeutics. 2009 (PMID: 19393844); Jackson JL et al. PLoS One. 2015 (PMID: 26172390); Mistry H et al. Health Technology Assessment. 2024 (PMID: 39365169).

synthesis the carded evidence: one adult head-to-head randomised trial (331 patients, episodic migraine, 26 weeks), one network meta-analysis of episodic migraine prophylaxis, and one chronic-migraine health technology assessment (11 trials, 7,352 adults, none of amitriptyline). no carded study enrolled patients with chronic migraine selected for poor sleep, and none measured a sleep outcome; total head-to-head participants = 331. monthly migraine episodes fell by 2.6 (topiramate) and 2.7 (amitriptyline) in the head-to-head trial — the treatment made no difference on the primary outcome — while somnolence (17.8% vs 11.9%), dry mouth (35.5%, amitriptyline) and weight (+2.4 kg amitriptyline vs -2.4 kg topiramate) separated the drugs (dodick 2009). a network meta-analysis ranked amitriptyline above topiramate on weak evidence (jackson 2015). for chronic migraine, topiramate has placebo-controlled data (about 1.1–1.5 fewer days per month) and amitriptyline has no includable trial (mistry 2024). whether amitriptyline's sedation translates into better sleep — or topiramate's alerting profile into worse sleep — in chronic migraine patients with poor sleep is inference from side-effect lists, not trial evidence. proposed maybe (weak evidence). home shelf #873 is the paediatric placebo-controlled question (champ); this shelf must not borrow champ's null verdict for adults, nor present dodick's episodic-migraine equivalence as a chronic-migraine result. the poor-sleep selection in the question is, as of this build, an evidence gap printed on the face of the shelf. synthesis of dodick dw et al. clinical therapeutics. 2009 (pmid: 19393844); jackson jl et al. plos one. 2015 (pmid: 26172390); mistry h et al. health technology assessment. 2024 (pmid: 39365169).

shelves.title: Carotid stenting in symptomatic patients over 70: not as safe as endarterectomy — early stroke or death 12.0% vs 5.9% (relative risk 2.04) in the pooled symptomatic trials, and later durability is equal, so the early harm is never repaid
shelves.question: Is carotid stenting as safe as endarterectomy in symptomatic carotid stenosis over 70?
shelves.mesh: Age Factors · Aged · Aging · Angioplasty · Carotid Stenosis · Endarterectomy, Carotid · Evidence-Based Medicine · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Odds Ratio · Patient Selection · Prospective Studies · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Regression Analysis · Risk Assessment · Risk Factors · Severity of Illness Index · Stents · Stroke · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #335, which compares carotid stenting and endarterectomy overall — by age, symptoms and era, including the four-trial age analysis (Howard 2016) in its full population. This pack isolates the slice #335 does not present on its own: symptomatic patients aged 70 and over. FLAG FOR THE DEVELOPER (precedent-b build): the four-trial age anchor is already carded on home #335 and is NOT re-carded here; this pack is built on three free reports that address the symptomatic older-patient cut directly. In the pooled individual-patient analysis of the three European symptomatic trials (Bonati 2011, PMID: 21269847; 3,433 patients), age was the only variable that significantly modified the treatment effect (interaction P = 0.0053): under 70, 120-day stroke or death was 5.8% with stenting versus 5.7% with endarterectomy (relative risk 1.00); at 70 or over it was 12.0% versus 5.9% — a relative risk of 2.04 (95% CI 1.48 to 2.82), an absolute excess of about 6 extra strokes or deaths per 100 patients treated with stenting. The four-trial pooled long-term analysis (Brott 2019, PMID: 30738706) shows the excess is periprocedural: beyond 120 days, annual ipsilateral stroke rates were nearly identical (0.64% stenting vs 0.60% endarterectomy per person-year), yet combined risks still favoured endarterectomy by 2.8–4.1 percentage points out to 9 years. ICSS long-term follow-up (Bonati 2015, PMID: 25453443) agrees: fatal or disabling stroke did not differ (the treatment made no difference: 5-year risk 6.4% vs 6.5%), but any stroke was more frequent after stenting (5-year risk 15.2% vs 9.4%; HR 1.71). PROPOSED LIKELY (harm): in symptomatic patients over 70, stenting is not as safe as endarterectomy — its early stroke/death risk is about double, and later durability does not repay it.

cards.headline: Bonati 2011: in symptomatic patients aged 70 or over, 120-day stroke or death was 12.0% with stenting versus 5.9% with endarterectomy (relative risk 2.04) — while under 70 the two were identical (5.8% vs 5.7%, relative risk 1.00)
cards.summary: Bonati 2011: in symptomatic patients aged 70 or over, 120-day stroke or death was 12.0% with stenting versus 5.9% with endarterectomy (relative risk 2.04) — while under 70 the two were identical (5.8% vs 5.7%, relative risk 1.00)
cards.type: Pooled individual-patient-data analysis of randomised trials (Bonati 2011)
cards.people: Pooled individual-patient data from all 3,433 patients randomised in the three European trials of stenting versus endarterectomy for symptomatic carotid stenosis — EVA-3S, SPACE and ICSS — analysed with fixed-effect models adjusted for source trial; the primary outcome was any stroke or death within 120 days of randomisation (intention-to-treat). Age 70 was the median and the prespecified cut examined here.
cards.result: In the first 120 days, the primary outcome occurred in 153/1725 patients in the stenting group (8.9%) versus 99/1708 in the endarterectomy group (5.8%; relative risk 1.53, 95% CI 1.20 to 1.95, P = 0.0006; absolute risk difference 3.2, 95% CI 1.4 to 4.9). Age was the only subgroup variable that significantly modified the treatment effect: in patients under 70 years, 120-day stroke or death risk was 5.8% with stenting and 5.7% with endarterectomy (relative risk 1.00, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.47); in patients 70 years or older there was an estimated two-fold increase in risk with stenting over endarterectomy (12.0% vs 5.9%, relative risk 2.04, 95% CI 1.48 to 2.82; interaction P = 0.0053). The authors conclude endarterectomy was safer in the short term because of the increased stroke risk of stenting in patients over 70, and that stenting should be avoided in older patients but may be as safe as endarterectomy in younger patients.
cards.watchOut: These are 2000s-era trials: stent design, embolic protection and operator experience have moved on, and the analysis pools the trials' own era against itself. The age interaction is nonetheless the most replicated finding in this literature, and no newer symptomatic-trial data in the records fetched overturns it.
cards.source: Bonati LH et al. Age modifies the relative risk of stenting versus endarterectomy for symptomatic carotid stenosis--a pooled analysis of EVA-3S, SPACE and ICSS. European Journal of Vascular and Endovascular Surgery. 2011. PMID: 21269847. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Brott 2019: pooling all four symptomatic trials (4,754 patients followed up to 12.4 years), the harm of stenting was front-loaded — after the periprocedural period, ipsilateral stroke rates were 0.64% vs 0.60% per year, yet combined risk still favoured endarterectomy by 2.8–4.1 points at 1–9 years
cards.summary: Brott 2019: pooling all four symptomatic trials (4,754 patients followed up to 12.4 years), the harm of stenting was front-loaded — after the periprocedural period, ipsilateral stroke rates were 0.64% vs 0.60% per year, yet combined risk still favoured endarterectomy by 2.8–4.1 points at 1–9 years
cards.type: Pooled individual-patient-data analysis of randomised trials, long-term (Brott 2019)
cards.people: Preplanned pooled analysis of individual patient-level data from the four largest randomised trials of carotid artery stenting versus endarterectomy for symptomatic carotid stenosis (EVA-3S, SPACE, ICSS and CREST); 4,775 patients were randomly assigned, 4,754 (99.6%) followed for a maximum of 12.4 years (median follow-up 2.0 to 6.9 years across trials), analysed intention-to-treat.
cards.result: Periprocedural outcome events numbered 206 in patients allocated stenting versus 129 in patients allocated endarterectomy, with 57 versus 55 postprocedural events. After the periprocedural period, annual rates of ipsilateral stroke per person-year were similar for the two treatments: 0.64% (95% CI 0.49 to 0.83) for stenting and 0.60% (95% CI 0.46 to 0.79) for endarterectomy. The periprocedural and postprocedural risks combined favoured endarterectomy, with treatment differences at 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9 years all ranging between 2.8% (95% CI 1.1 to 4.4) and 4.1% (95% CI 2.0 to 6.3). The authors conclude that the similarity of postprocedural rates suggests both procedures are durable, and that improving the periprocedural safety of stenting could equalise outcomes in future.
cards.watchOut: This analysis pools all ages: it establishes that the stenting penalty is periprocedural and never repaid, which is the mechanism behind the over-70 result on the card above — but the record reports no over-70 subgroup figures of its own, and none are claimed here.
cards.source: Brott TG et al. Long-term outcomes of stenting and endarterectomy for symptomatic carotid stenosis: a preplanned pooled analysis of individual patient data. The Lancet Neurology. 2019. PMID: 30738706. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Bonati 2015 (ICSS long-term): fatal or disabling stroke did not differ between stenting and endarterectomy at 5 years (6.4% vs 6.5%; HR 1.06 — the treatment made no difference), but any stroke was more frequent after stenting (15.2% vs 9.4%; HR 1.71), mainly non-disabling strokes
cards.summary: Bonati 2015 (ICSS long-term): fatal or disabling stroke did not differ between stenting and endarterectomy at 5 years (6.4% vs 6.5%; HR 1.06 — the treatment made no difference), but any stroke was more frequent after stenting (15.2% vs 9.4%; HR 1.71), mainly non-disabling strokes
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, long-term follow-up (Bonati 2015, ICSS)
cards.people: Patients with symptomatic carotid stenosis randomised 1:1 to stenting (n = 855) or endarterectomy (n = 858) at 50 centres worldwide in the International Carotid Stenting Study (ICSS); 1,713 assigned, 1,710 in the intention-to-treat population, followed for a median of 4.2 years (maximum 10.0). The primary endpoint was fatal or disabling stroke in any territory.
cards.result: The number of fatal or disabling strokes (52 vs 49) and the cumulative 5-year risk did not differ significantly between stenting and endarterectomy (6.4% vs 6.5%; hazard ratio 1.06, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.57, P = 0.77 — the treatment made no difference on the primary endpoint). Any stroke was more frequent in the stenting group (119 vs 72 events; 5-year cumulative risk 15.2% vs 9.4%; hazard ratio 1.71, 95% CI 1.28 to 2.30, P < 0.001), but these were mainly non-disabling strokes. The distribution of modified Rankin scale scores at 1 year, 5 years or final follow-up did not differ significantly between groups.
cards.watchOut: ICSS enrolled symptomatic patients of all adult ages, so this card supports the pooled picture rather than the over-70 cut directly; its 'any stroke' excess after stenting includes the periprocedural events that the age analysis shows are concentrated in older patients.
cards.source: Bonati LH et al. Long-term outcomes after stenting versus endarterectomy for treatment of symptomatic carotid stenosis: the International Carotid Stenting Study (ICSS) randomised trial. The Lancet. 2015. PMID: 25453443. Registry ID: ISRCTN25337470. cards.headline: Synthesis: for symptomatic patients over 70 the answer is no — stenting carries about double the early stroke-or-death risk of endarterectomy, and equal long-term durability never closes that early gap
cards.summary: Synthesis: for symptomatic patients over 70 the answer is no — stenting carries about double the early stroke-or-death risk of endarterectomy, and equal long-term durability never closes that early gap
cards.people: The carded evidence: a pooled individual-patient analysis of the three European symptomatic trials (3,433 patients) reporting the age-70 cut directly; a four-trial pooled long-term analysis (4,754 patients followed); and ICSS long-term follow-up (1,710 patients). The pooled analyses share the same underlying trial patients by design, so participants are not summed across cards; the directly relevant population is the 3,433-patient symptomatic pool, of whom roughly half were 70 or older.
cards.result: At 70 or over, 120-day stroke or death was 12.0% with stenting versus 5.9% with endarterectomy (relative risk 2.04, 95% CI 1.48 to 2.82), while under 70 the procedures were identical (relative risk 1.00) and age was the only significant effect modifier (interaction P = 0.0053) (Bonati 2011). Long-term, postprocedural ipsilateral stroke rates converge (0.64% vs 0.60% per person-year) but the combined risk still favours endarterectomy by 2.8–4.1 percentage points out to 9 years (Brott 2019), and ICSS found no difference in fatal or disabling stroke (HR 1.06) alongside an excess of any stroke after stenting (5-year risk 15.2% vs 9.4%; HR 1.71) (Bonati 2015). PROPOSED LIKELY (harm) for stenting in symptomatic patients aged 70 and over.
cards.watchOut: Home shelf #335 holds the four-trial age analysis (Howard 2016) and the overall comparison; this shelf isolates the symptomatic over-70 cut from three further reports and must not be read as superseding #335's wider account, including its note that a 2026 trial re-asks the question against modern medical therapy — these pooled data come from 2000s-era procedures.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bonati LH et al. European Journal of Vascular and Endovascular Surgery. 2011 (PMID: 21269847); Brott TG et al. The Lancet Neurology. 2019 (PMID: 30738706); Bonati LH et al. The Lancet. 2015 (PMID: 25453443).

shelves.title: Tai chi versus usual activity in Parkinson's disease (partial completion of #3693, which uses active comparators): falls roughly halved in the one no-intervention trial — POSSIBLE benefit
shelves.question: Does tai chi reduce falls in Parkinson's disease compared with usual activity?
shelves.mesh: Accidental Falls · Exercise Test · Humans · Parkinson Disease · Postural Balance · Stroke · Tai Ji
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #3693, which compares tai chi with resistance training and stretching in Parkinson's disease (Li 2012, carded there and not re-carded here; on that shelf falls were lower only against stretching). The uncovered slice is tai chi against usual activity — no intervention. On that comparison there is one direct randomised trial: Gao 2014 (PMID: 24519923) randomised 76 patients who had already fallen to 12 weeks of tai chi or no intervention, and over 6 months 21.6% of the tai chi group fell versus 48.7% of controls, with fewer falls per person. Two meta-analyses point the same way: Winser 2018 (PMID: 29737198) pooled a relative falls odds ratio of 0.47 in Parkinson's disease across tai chi trials with active or no-treatment controls, and Ni 2014 (PMID: 24927169) found falls reduction greater after tai chi (mostly added to medication) than in control groups, while printing no pooled falls effect size. The direct usual-activity evidence is therefore a single small trial in prior fallers, supported by concordant pooling that mixes comparators. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — tai chi probably reduces falls in Parkinson's disease versus usual activity, on one small direct trial plus supportive meta-analyses.

cards.headline: Gao 2014: tai chi versus no intervention — 21.6% of the tai chi group fell over 6 months versus 48.7% of controls, with fewer falls per person (0.30 versus 0.64)
cards.summary: Gao 2014: tai chi versus no intervention — 21.6% of the tai chi group fell over 6 months versus 48.7% of controls, with fewer falls per person (0.30 versus 0.64)
cards.people: 76 patients over 40 with idiopathic Parkinson's disease who could walk independently and had fallen at least once in the past 12 months, in a single-blind randomised controlled trial with 6 months' follow-up: the tai chi group (n = 37) received 24-form Yang style tai chi for 60 minutes three times a week for 12 weeks; the control group (n = 39) received no intervention (usual activity).
cards.result: During the 6-month follow-up, 8 of 37 patients (21.6%) in the tai chi group experienced falls compared with 19 of 39 (48.7%) in the control group (p < 0.05), and the average number of falls was 0.30 ± 0.62 in the tai chi group compared with 0.64 ± 0.74 in the control group (p < 0.05). The tai chi group also improved more on the Berg Balance Scale (p < 0.05), but there was no difference on UPDRS III scores or the Timed Up and Go test (p > 0.05).
cards.watchOut: One small single-centre trial (76 patients) in people who had already fallen — the group most likely to benefit; participants could not be blinded to exercise, and the fall counts rest on follow-up reporting.
cards.source: Gao Q et al. Effects of Tai Chi on balance and fall prevention in Parkinson's disease: a randomized controlled trial. Clinical rehabilitation. 2014. PMID: 24519923. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Winser 2018: tai chi reduced falls incidence in Parkinson's disease (relative odds ratio 0.47) across trials against active or no-treatment controls
cards.summary: Winser 2018: tai chi reduced falls incidence in Parkinson's disease (relative odds ratio 0.47) across trials against active or no-treatment controls
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials of tai chi compared with active or no-treatment control in neurological disorders, measuring balance and number of falls: 10 studies involving 720 participants were reviewed, seven in Parkinson's disease and three in stroke; seven studies were of high methodological quality and three low.
cards.result: Tai chi significantly reduced falls incidence in Parkinson's disease (odds ratio 0.47, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.77; P = 0.003 — a relative measure; the record does not print the absolute fall rates behind it). Balance measured by the Timed Up and Go test in Parkinson's disease improved versus no treatment (weighted mean difference −2.13, 95% CI −3.26 to −1.00; P < 0.001) but not versus active treatment (weighted mean difference −0.19, 95% CI −1.74 to 1.35; P = 0.81).
cards.watchOut: The pooled falls estimate mixes trials whose controls were active treatments with trials whose controls were no treatment, so it supports — but does not by itself isolate — the usual-activity comparison this shelf asks about.
