shelves.title: Levetiracetam versus carbamazepine in newly diagnosed focal epilepsy (partial completion of #337, first-line comparisons broadly): equal seizure control, better tolerated and better retained — in trials of patients over 60
shelves.question: Is levetiracetam as effective as carbamazepine for newly diagnosed focal epilepsy with fewer side effects?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anticonvulsants · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Epilepsies, Partial · Europe · Female · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Logistic Models · Longitudinal Studies · Male · Middle Aged · Retrospective Studies · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #337, which covers first-line antiseizure comparisons broadly — its SANAD II focal arm pits levetiracetam against lamotrigine (carded there and not re-carded here) but never against carbamazepine head-to-head. On that uncovered pairing, the direct randomised evidence sits in patients aged 60 and over, and it answers the question in two parts. For effectiveness, levetiracetam and controlled-release carbamazepine did not differ: seizure freedom rates were not different in the double-blind elderly trial (Werhahn 2015, PMID: 25684224), and time to first seizure was similar in the KOMET elderly subgroup (Pohlmann-Eden 2016, PMID: 27552848; hazard ratio 1.02). For tolerability, levetiracetam clearly won on staying on treatment: 58-week retention 61.5% versus 45.8%, with discontinuation for adverse events or death roughly half (17.2% versus 32.2%); in KOMET, 12-month withdrawal was 25.0% versus 46.6% and adverse-event discontinuation 11.3% versus 35.0%. The Cochrane individual-participant network meta-analysis (Nevitt 2022, PMID: 35363878) is concordant at network level: lamotrigine and levetiracetam did not differ on treatment failure (HR 1.01) and both performed better than carbamazepine (lamotrigine versus carbamazepine HR 1.26). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit — tolerability and retention, not seizure superiority): levetiracetam appears as effective as carbamazepine for newly diagnosed focal epilepsy with fewer treatment-limiting side effects, on direct evidence confined to older adults.

cards.headline: Werhahn 2015: in newly diagnosed focal epilepsy over 60, levetiracetam retention at 58 weeks was 61.5% versus 45.8% for controlled-release carbamazepine — with seizure freedom not different and half the adverse-event discontinuations
cards.summary: Werhahn 2015: in newly diagnosed focal epilepsy over 60, levetiracetam retention at 58 weeks was 61.5% versus 45.8% for controlled-release carbamazepine — with seizure freedom not different and half the adverse-event discontinuations
cards.people: 361 patients aged 60 or over with new-onset focal epilepsy randomised 1:1:1 at 47 sites in Germany, Austria and Switzerland to controlled-release carbamazepine (n = 121), lamotrigine (n = 117) or levetiracetam (n = 122); 359 were included in the modified intent-to-treat population (mean age 71.4 years). Doses were up-titrated over 6 weeks and could be adjusted over a further 52 weeks; the primary outcome was retention on treatment at week 58.
cards.result: At week 58, the retention rate for levetiracetam was significantly higher than for controlled-release carbamazepine (61.5% vs. 45.8%, p = 0.02) and similar to lamotrigine (55.6%). Seizure freedom rates at weeks 30 and 58 were not different across the groups. Twice as many patients receiving carbamazepine discontinued due to adverse events or death compared with the levetiracetam group (32.2% vs. 17.2%; odds ratio 2.28, 95% CI 1.25 to 4.19, p = 0.007 — a relative measure), whereas discontinuation was intermediate for lamotrigine (26.3%). Median daily doses of completers were carbamazepine 380 mg/day and levetiracetam 950 mg/day.
cards.watchOut: This is the only fully double-blind head-to-head trial carded, and it enrolled only patients aged 60 and over with slow dose titration — retention and tolerability advantages may not transfer unchanged to younger adults or faster titration.
cards.source: Werhahn KJ et al. A randomized, double-blind comparison of antiepileptic drug treatment in the elderly with new-onset focal epilepsy. Epilepsia. 2015. PMID: 25684224. cards.headline: Pohlmann-Eden 2016 (KOMET elderly subgroup): 12-month withdrawal was 25.0% on levetiracetam versus 46.6% on controlled-release carbamazepine, adverse-event discontinuation 11.3% versus 35.0%, time to first seizure similar
cards.summary: Pohlmann-Eden 2016 (KOMET elderly subgroup): 12-month withdrawal was 25.0% on levetiracetam versus 46.6% on controlled-release carbamazepine, adverse-event discontinuation 11.3% versus 35.0%, time to first seizure similar
cards.type: Post-hoc subgroup analysis of a randomised trial (Pohlmann-Eden 2016)
cards.people: Post-hoc subgroup analysis of the unblinded, randomised, 52-week KOMET study in patients aged 60 or over with newly diagnosed epilepsy (n = 308): in the carbamazepine stratum, patients were randomised to levetiracetam (n = 104) or controlled-release carbamazepine (n = 103); a parallel stratum compared levetiracetam with extended-release valproate. Mean age was 69.6 years. The analysis was exploratory, as KOMET was not powered for an age subgroup.
cards.result: Time to treatment withdrawal favoured levetiracetam over controlled-release carbamazepine (hazard ratio 0.45, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.72 — a relative measure), with 12-month withdrawal rates of 25.0% versus 46.6%. Time to first seizure was similar between levetiracetam and carbamazepine (hazard ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.63). Adverse events were reported by 76.2% of levetiracetam patients and 82.5% of carbamazepine patients, but discontinuation rates due to adverse events were 11.3% versus 35.0%. The authors note the withdrawal advantage was likely due to the more favourable tolerability profile of levetiracetam.
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc and unblinded: physicians chose the standard-drug stratum before randomisation, and the subgroup was not powered in advance, so this card corroborates Werhahn 2015 rather than standing alone.

cards.headline: Nevitt 2022 (Cochrane network meta-analysis of individual participant data): levetiracetam and lamotrigine did not differ on treatment failure in focal seizures (HR 1.01), and both performed better than carbamazepine (lamotrigine versus carbamazepine HR 1.26)
cards.summary: Nevitt 2022 (Cochrane network meta-analysis of individual participant data): levetiracetam and lamotrigine did not differ on treatment failure in focal seizures (HR 1.01), and both performed better than carbamazepine (lamotrigine versus carbamazepine HR 1.26)
cards.type: Cochrane network meta-analysis of individual participant data (Nevitt 2022)
cards.people: Cochrane individual participant data network meta-analysis of randomised monotherapy trials in children and adults with focal onset or generalised tonic-clonic seizures, comparing 12 antiseizure medicines: 22,049 eligible participants, with individual participant data provided for 14,789 participants (67%) from 39 of 89 eligible trials. The primary outcome was time to treatment failure; the focal-seizure evidence for this outcome was rated high certainty.
cards.result: For individuals with focal seizures, network meta-analysis showed lamotrigine performed better than most other treatments on treatment failure, including carbamazepine: hazard ratios for treatment failure for any reason for lamotrigine versus levetiracetam 1.01 (95% CI 0.88 to 1.20), versus carbamazepine 1.26 (95% CI 1.10 to 1.44) and versus topiramate 1.50 (95% CI 1.23 to 1.81) — all relative measures. No significant difference between lamotrigine and levetiracetam was shown for any treatment failure outcome, and both seemed to perform better than all other antiseizure medicines. The record does not print a single direct levetiracetam-versus-carbamazepine hazard ratio; the comparison is read through the network estimates above.
cards.watchOut: Network estimates combine direct and indirect evidence across trials of different eras and doses, and individual data were available for only 43% of eligible trials; the head-to-head claim on this shelf rests on the two elderly trials above.

shelves.title: Triptan overuse headache (partial completion of #2381, withdrawal strategies generally): triptan overusers improve most after stopping, and the supported strategy is stop-plus-preventive — POSSIBLE, triptan-specific evidence observational only
shelves.question: Should triptans be stopped and preventive therapy started in medication-overuse headache?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Analgesics · Chronic Disease · Denmark · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Headache Disorders, Secondary · Humans · Incidence · Male · Middle Aged · Migraine Disorders · Risk Assessment · Treatment Outcome · Withholding Treatment
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #2381, which compares withdrawal and preventive strategies in medication-overuse headache generally (the Carlsen 2020 three-strategy trial is carded there and is not re-carded here). The uncovered slice is triptan overuse specifically, and no randomised trial restricted to triptan overusers was found in the records fetched — the triptan-specific evidence is a subgroup of a prospective withdrawal cohort. In that cohort (Zeeberg 2006, PMID: 16707727), triptan/ergot overusers improved the most after a 2-month drug-free period (p < 0.0001), within an overall picture in which 45% of patients who stayed drug-free improved. The strategy evidence is drug-class-general: the one randomised strategy trial (Hagen 2009, PMID: 18823363; 56 patients) found no significant difference in headache days between prophylaxis-from-the-start, withdrawal alone and no specific treatment, though the prophylaxis group reduced total headache suffering more; and a systematic review (Chiang 2016, PMID: 26122645) concluded that adding preventive medication to early discontinuation led to a better outcome than discontinuation alone, while the evidence for discontinuation alone is low because controlled studies are absent. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — for triptan overuse, stop the triptan and start a preventive together: triptan overusers are the subgroup that responds best to withdrawal, and the combined strategy is the review-supported default, but the triptan-specific leg is observational only.

cards.headline: Zeeberg 2006: after a 2-month drug-free period, triptan/ergot overusers improved the most of any overuse group (p < 0.0001) — 45% of all patients who stayed drug-free improved
cards.summary: Zeeberg 2006: after a 2-month drug-free period, triptan/ergot overusers improved the most of any overuse group (p < 0.0001) — 45% of all patients who stayed drug-free improved
cards.people: Prospective cohort from the Danish Headache Center: among 1,326 patients treated and discharged in 2002 and 2003, 337 had probable medication-overuse headache, and 216 who stayed medication-free for 2 months were eligible for the analysis of headache frequency before and after withdrawal, recorded in prospective daily headache diaries. Median age was 48 years and the male/female ratio was 1:2.7.
cards.result: Overall, 45% of the patients improved, 48% had no change, and 7% had more headaches after the drug-free period. The relative reduction in headache frequency varied by diagnosis (median reduction 67% in migraine, 0% in tension-type headache, 37% in patients with both), and triptan/ergot overusers improved the most (p < 0.0001); the difference between the migraine-plus-tension-type group and tension-type headache alone remained significant when triptan/ergot overuse was controlled (p < 0.05). The authors conclude the data demonstrate the benefit of withdrawal in already established medication overuse.
cards.watchOut: Observational and self-selected: only patients who managed to stay drug-free for 2 months were analysed, there was no control group continuing triptans, and the triptan finding is a subgroup comparison — it shows triptan overusers do well after withdrawal, not that withdrawal caused the whole difference.
cards.source: Zeeberg P et al. Probable medication-overuse headache: the effect of a 2-month drug-free period. Neurology. 2006. PMID: 16707727. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hagen 2009: prophylaxis from the start without detox did not differ from withdrawal alone on headache days (the treatment made no difference on the primary outcome) — but reduced total headache suffering more at months 3 and 12
cards.summary: Hagen 2009: prophylaxis from the start without detox did not differ from withdrawal alone on headache days (the treatment made no difference on the primary outcome) — but reduced total headache suffering more at months 3 and 12
cards.people: 56 patients with medication-overuse headache in a 1-year randomised, multicentre, open-label trial, assigned to prophylactic treatment from the start without detoxification, a standard outpatient detoxification programme without prophylactic treatment from the start, or no specific treatment (5-month follow-up); intention-to-treat analyses were performed.
cards.result: The primary outcome measure, change in headache days per month, did not differ significantly between groups. However, the prophylaxis group had the greatest decrease in headache days compared with baseline, and a significantly more pronounced reduction in total headache index (headache days per month × headache intensity × headache hours) at months 3 (P = 0.003) and 12 (P = 0.017) compared with the withdrawal group. At month 12, 53% of patients in the prophylaxis group had a reduction of 50% or more in monthly headache days compared with 25% in the withdrawal group (P = 0.081). The authors conclude early preventive treatment without a previous detoxification programme reduced total headache suffering more effectively than abrupt withdrawal.
cards.watchOut: Small (56 patients), open-label, and not triptan-specific — the overused drugs were mixed; it tests the sequencing question (preventive now versus withdrawal first), not whether triptans in particular should be stopped.
cards.source: Hagen K et al. Management of medication overuse headache: 1-year randomized multicentre open-label trial. Cephalalgia : an international journal of headache. 2009. PMID: 18823363. Registry ID: NCT00159588. cards.headline: Chiang 2016: adding preventive medication to early discontinuation led to a better outcome than discontinuation alone — while the evidence for discontinuation alone is low for lack of controlled studies
cards.summary: Chiang 2016: adding preventive medication to early discontinuation led to a better outcome than discontinuation alone — while the evidence for discontinuation alone is low for lack of controlled studies
cards.people: Systematic review of treatment strategies for medication-overuse headache, searching PubMed for articles published between 2004 and August 2014: the initial search resulted in 1,313 articles, of which 68 met the inclusion criteria and were discussed, with levels of evidence determined according to the American Academy of Neurology clinical practice guideline manual.
cards.result: The level of evidence to support early discontinuation/withdrawal of overused medications alone is low due to the absence of controlled studies. Adding preventive medication to early discontinuation led to a better outcome than early discontinuation alone. For patients with chronic migraine and medication overuse, large randomised trials support onabotulinumtoxinA and topiramate without early discontinuation, though that evidence comes from post hoc analyses. Considering the available evidence and the systemic toxicity of overusing acute headache medication, the authors suggest discontinuation of the overused medication with the addition of preventive medication, and call for appropriately sized randomised trials of preventive plus early discontinuation versus preventive alone versus discontinuation alone.
cards.watchOut: A narrative systematic review without pooled effect sizes in the record, covering all overused drug classes together — it supports the combined stop-plus-preventive strategy in general, and is not triptan-specific evidence.
cards.source: Chiang CC et al. Treatment of medication-overuse headache: A systematic review. Cephalalgia : an international journal of headache. 2016. PMID: 26122645. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Headache Disorders, Secondary · Humans

cards.headline: Synthesis: for triptan overuse, the pieces point the same way — triptan overusers respond best to a drug-free period, and pairing discontinuation with a preventive beats discontinuation alone — but no triptan-only randomised trial exists
cards.summary: Synthesis: for triptan overuse, the pieces point the same way — triptan overusers respond best to a drug-free period, and pairing discontinuation with a preventive beats discontinuation alone — but no triptan-only randomised trial exists
cards.people: The carded evidence: one prospective withdrawal cohort with a triptan-overuser subgroup (216 patients analysed of 337 with probable medication-overuse headache; Zeeberg 2006), one small randomised strategy trial in mixed-drug overuse (56 patients; Hagen 2009) and one systematic review of 68 articles (Chiang 2016). Participant totals exceed the small-N threshold, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the triptan-specific leg is observational only, printed on the stamp.
cards.result: Triptan/ergot overusers improved the most after a 2-month drug-free period (p < 0.0001), in a cohort where 45% improved overall (Zeeberg 2006). Prophylaxis from the start did not beat withdrawal on headache days but reduced total headache suffering more (Hagen 2009). Adding a preventive to early discontinuation led to better outcomes than discontinuation alone, whose evidence base is low (Chiang 2016). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only for the triptan-specific claim.
cards.watchOut: Home shelf #2381 holds the general strategy comparison (Carlsen 2020); this shelf's triptan slice is assembled from a cohort subgroup and class-general strategy evidence, and should be re-cut if a triptan-specific randomised trial appears.
cards.source: Synthesis of Zeeberg P et al. Neurology. 2006 (PMID: 16707727); Hagen K et al. Cephalalgia. 2009 (PMID: 18823363); Chiang CC et al. Cephalalgia. 2016 (PMID: 26122645).

shelves.title: Topiramate in medication-overuse headache (partial completion of #2381, withdrawal strategies generally): SPLIT — one small strongly positive trial against a 2023 verdict of insufficient population-specific evidence
shelves.question: Does topiramate reduce headache days in medication-overuse headache after withdrawal?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Analgesics · Chi-Square Distribution · Chronic Disease · Confidence Intervals · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fructose · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Migraine Disorders · Multivariate Analysis · Odds Ratio · Topiramate
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #2381, which covers withdrawal and preventive strategies in medication-overuse headache generally (Carlsen 2020 is carded there and is not re-carded here). The uncovered slice is topiramate's own effect on headache days in patients with medication overuse — and the evidence genuinely divides. A small double-blind trial in chronic migraine with analgesic overuse (Silvestrini 2003, PMID: 14510929) found a large effect at only 50 mg/day (8.1 versus 20.6 headache days per 28 days in the last maintenance month). A review of the two large chronic-migraine trials (Diener 2009, PMID: 19735529) reports topiramate was effective in patients both with and without medication overuse, but prints no effect sizes, and one of those underlying trials is already carded elsewhere in the library, so it is not re-carded here. Against that, a 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis restricted to randomised trials in chronic migraine with medication overuse (Giri 2023, PMID: 36856015) concluded there is currently insufficient evidence to determine the impact of topiramate in this population. The only post-withdrawal data carded (Valguarnera 2010, PMID: 20464616) combine topiramate with amitriptyline and inpatient withdrawal, so topiramate's isolated contribution cannot be separated. PROPOSED SPLIT (small positive trial and positive subgroup reviews versus a 2023 meta-analysis finding the randomised evidence in medication overuse insufficient) — topiramate may reduce headache days in medication-overuse headache, but its isolated effect, especially after withdrawal, is not established.

cards.headline: Silvestrini 2003: topiramate 50 mg/day cut headache days from about 21 to 8.1 per 28 days versus 20.6 on placebo in chronic migraine with analgesic overuse (P < 0.0007) — participant N not documented in the record
cards.summary: Silvestrini 2003: topiramate 50 mg/day cut headache days from about 21 to 8.1 per 28 days versus 20.6 on placebo in chronic migraine with analgesic overuse (P < 0.0007) — participant N not documented in the record
cards.people: Patients suffering from chronic migraine with analgesic overuse in a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled, parallel-group study: after an 8-week baseline phase, patients were randomly assigned 1:1 to topiramate or placebo, titrated in 25-mg increments over one week to 50 mg daily, followed by an 8-week maintenance phase. The total participant N is not documented in the record — that absence is printed here plainly.
cards.result: At baseline there was no difference in days with headache between the topiramate and placebo groups (mean ± SD: 20.9 ± 3.2 and 20.8 ± 3.2 days per 28-day period). During the last 4 weeks of maintenance, topiramate-treated patients had a significantly lower 28-day headache frequency than placebo (mean number of days with headache ± SD: 8.1 ± 8.1 vs. 20.6 ± 3.4, P < 0.0007). The authors conclude topiramate at low doses proved effective in reducing headache frequency in patients with chronic migraine and analgesic overuse.
cards.watchOut: A strikingly large effect in a record that does not even state how many patients were studied, at a low 50 mg/day dose, in analgesic (not specifically triptan) overuse, with no withdrawal phase — exactly the kind of result the later meta-analysis below could not confirm from the randomised literature.
cards.source: Silvestrini M et al. Topiramate in the treatment of chronic migraine. Cephalalgia : an international journal of headache. 2003. PMID: 14510929. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Diener 2009: two large randomised trials showed topiramate effective in chronic migraine both with and without medication overuse — the review prints no effect sizes, and its authors suggest detoxification before prophylaxis may not be required in all patients
cards.summary: Diener 2009: two large randomised trials showed topiramate effective in chronic migraine both with and without medication overuse — the review prints no effect sizes, and its authors suggest detoxification before prophylaxis may not be required in all patients
cards.people: Narrative review summarising two similarly designed, randomised, placebo-controlled, multicentre studies of topiramate for chronic migraine conducted in the USA and the European Union, examining efficacy and safety in patient populations both with and without acute medication overuse.
cards.result: Both studies demonstrate the efficacy and safety of topiramate for the treatment of chronic migraine in patient populations both with and without medication overuse, as summarised by the reviewers. The record reports this conclusion without printing headache-day reductions, response rates or any other effect size for the medication-overuse subgroups — that absence is printed here plainly. The reviewers suggest the findings may imply that detoxification prior to initiating prophylactic therapy may not be required in all patients if medication overuse is present.
cards.watchOut: This is a review article reporting other trials' conclusions without numbers, and the medication-overuse analyses of those trials were post hoc; one of the two underlying trials is already carded elsewhere in the library and is deliberately not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Giri 2023: restricted to randomised trials in chronic migraine with medication overuse, the meta-analysis found insufficient evidence to determine topiramate's impact — while botulinum toxin A and CGRP monoclonal antibodies were positive
cards.summary: Giri 2023: restricted to randomised trials in chronic migraine with medication overuse, the meta-analysis found insufficient evidence to determine topiramate's impact — while botulinum toxin A and CGRP monoclonal antibodies were positive
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials of topiramate, botulinum toxin type A and monoclonal antibodies targeting CGRP in patients with chronic migraine and medication overuse headache, searching to May 2022: 10 studies met the inclusion criteria and seven studies with sufficient data were included in the meta-analysis.
cards.result: There is currently insufficient evidence to determine the impact of topiramate in chronic migraine patients with medication overuse headache. By contrast, studies assessing botulinum toxin type A included 1,139 patients and showed a mean reduction in headache frequency of 1.92 days per month compared with placebo (−1.92; 95% CI −2.68 to −1.16), and studies of human monoclonal antibodies included 1,982 patients and showed significant positive effects for all measured outcomes, with an overall odds ratio for the 50% response rate of 2.90 (95% CI 2.23 to 3.78 — a relative measure).
cards.watchOut: 'Insufficient evidence' reflects how few randomised trials report the medication-overuse population separately and with response rates — it is a verdict on the analysable record, and it directly contradicts reading the small positive trial above as settled.
cards.source: Giri S et al. cards.headline: Valguarnera 2010: after inpatient withdrawal on amitriptyline plus topiramate prophylaxis, 89% were free of overuse at 1 month, falling to 45% at 6 months — a combination protocol that cannot isolate topiramate
cards.summary: Valguarnera 2010: after inpatient withdrawal on amitriptyline plus topiramate prophylaxis, 89% were free of overuse at 1 month, falling to 45% at 6 months — a combination protocol that cannot isolate topiramate
cards.people: 105 patients with chronic daily headache and medication overuse admitted over 4 years; the protocol was applied in 52 patients (age 29 to 65 years): one week of inpatient withdrawal therapy with intravenous dexamethasone and diazepam, plus prophylaxis with amitriptyline (10 to 20 mg/day) plus topiramate (50 to 100 mg/day) continued for at least 6 months. The overused drugs were combinations in 38%, analgesics in 29% and triptans in 29%.
cards.result: At 1 month, 89% of the patients had not fallen back into medication overuse; at 3 months 64% remained free of overuse; and at 6 months 45% remained free from overuse. The authors suggest patients with chronic daily headache and medication overuse benefit from withdrawal therapy performed during hospitalisation plus prophylaxis with amitriptyline plus topiramate, and that the combination seems a good pharmacological solution to reduce the risk of relapse. Headache-day counts are not reported in the record.
cards.watchOut: No control group, two prophylactic drugs plus inpatient withdrawal and steroids given together, and the outcome is relapse into overuse rather than headache days — nothing in this card can be attributed to topiramate alone.
cards.source: Valguarnera F et al. The efficacy of withdrawal therapy in subjects with chronic daily headache and medication overuse following prophylaxis with topiramate and amitriptyline. Neurological sciences : official journal of the Italian Neurological Society and of the Italian Society of Clinical Neurophysiology. 2010. PMID: 20464616. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT — a small trial and the chronic-migraine subgroup reviews say topiramate works in medication overuse; the 2023 randomised-evidence meta-analysis for this exact population says the impact cannot be determined
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT — a small trial and the chronic-migraine subgroup reviews say topiramate works in medication overuse; the 2023 randomised-evidence meta-analysis for this exact population says the impact cannot be determined
cards.people: The carded evidence: one small double-blind trial in chronic migraine with analgesic overuse (participant N not documented in its record; Silvestrini 2003), one narrative review of two large chronic-migraine trials' overuse subgroups (Diener 2009), one meta-analysis of randomised trials in chronic migraine with medication overuse (10 studies; Giri 2023) and one uncontrolled combination-protocol series (52 treated patients; Valguarnera 2010).
cards.result: Headache days fell to 8.1 versus 20.6 per 28 days on topiramate 50 mg/day in the small trial (Silvestrini 2003). The two-trial review reports efficacy with and without overuse but no numbers (Diener 2009). The population-specific meta-analysis found insufficient evidence for topiramate while finding botulinum toxin A and CGRP monoclonal antibodies positive (Giri 2023). Post-withdrawal relapse data exist only for a topiramate-plus-amitriptyline combination (Valguarnera 2010). PROPOSED SPLIT (positive small trial and subgroup reviews versus insufficient population-specific randomised evidence).
cards.watchOut: Home shelf #2381 answers the strategy question for medication-overuse headache generally; this shelf isolates topiramate, and on that narrower question the honest verdict is a split, not the general impression left by the chronic-migraine trials.
cards.source: Synthesis of Silvestrini M et al. Cephalalgia. 2003 (PMID: 14510929); Diener HC et al. Cephalalgia. 2009 (PMID: 19735529); Giri S et al. Cephalalgia. 2023 (PMID: 36856015); Valguarnera F et al. Neurological sciences. 2010 (PMID: 20464616).

shelves.title: Rimegepant — one gepant, both jobs (partial completion of #689, acute treatment only): three concordant trials support every-other-day prevention, 0.8–1.6 fewer migraine days a month — LIKELY
shelves.question: Is rimegepant effective for both acute treatment and prevention of migraine?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide Receptor Antagonists · Double-Blind Method · Drug Evaluation · Female · Humans · Male · Migraine Disorders · Piperidines · Pyridines · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #689, which covers the gepants for acute treatment only (the ACHIEVE II ubrogepant trial and the Croop 2019 acute rimegepant trial are carded there and are not re-carded here). The uncovered slice is prevention — and with it the dual-indication question, since rimegepant is the one gepant tested in both roles. Three placebo-controlled prevention trials of rimegepant 75 mg every other day are now carded here, and they agree: the phase 2/3 trial (Croop 2021, PMID: 33338437; 747 randomised) reduced monthly migraine days by 4.3 versus 3.5 on placebo (difference −0.8 days); the Japanese phase 3 trial (Kitamura 2025, PMID: 40542538; 484 in the efficacy analysis) found a difference of −1.1 days; and a phase 4 trial in patients who had already failed 2 to 4 categories of oral preventives (Pozo-Rosich 2025, PMID: 41255098; 652 treated) found −2.1 versus −0.5 days (difference −1.6) with a 20.1-percentage-point advantage in 50% responders. Tolerability resembled placebo in all three. Combined with the acute efficacy homed on #689, the dual claim holds. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — rimegepant is effective for prevention of migraine (about 0.8 to 1.6 fewer migraine days per month than placebo across three concordant trials), and, with its acute benefit on #689, it is effective for both acute treatment and prevention.

cards.headline: Croop 2021: rimegepant 75 mg every other day cut monthly migraine days by 4.3 versus 3.5 on placebo (difference −0.8 days, p = 0.0099) in the phase 2/3 prevention trial
cards.summary: Croop 2021: rimegepant 75 mg every other day cut monthly migraine days by 4.3 versus 3.5 on placebo (difference −0.8 days, p = 0.0099) in the phase 2/3 prevention trial
cards.people: Adults with at least a 1-year history of migraine at 92 sites in the USA: after a 4-week observation period, 747 participants were randomly allocated to oral rimegepant 75 mg (n = 373) or matching placebo (n = 374) every other day for 12 weeks; 695 participants were included in the efficacy analysis and 741 in the safety analysis. The primary endpoint was change in mean monthly migraine days in the last 4 weeks of treatment (weeks 9 to 12).
cards.result: The change in mean monthly migraine days during weeks 9 to 12 was −4.3 days (95% CI −4.8 to −3.9) with rimegepant and −3.5 days (−4.0 to −3.0) with placebo (least squares mean difference −0.8 days, 95% CI −1.46 to −0.20; p = 0.0099). Adverse events were reported by 133 (36%) of 370 patients on rimegepant and 133 (36%) of 371 on placebo; seven (2%) on rimegepant and four (1%) on placebo discontinued due to an adverse event, and no patients died.
cards.watchOut: The placebo-subtracted gain is under one migraine day a month in this first trial — statistically solid but modest — and the double-blind phase lasted only 12 weeks, so long-term prevention rests on open-label follow-up rather than this card.
cards.source: Croop R et al. Oral rimegepant for preventive treatment of migraine: a phase 2/3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2021. PMID: 33338437. Registry ID: NCT03732638. cards.headline: Kitamura 2025: in Japan, rimegepant every other day beat placebo by 1.1 monthly migraine days (p = 0.002) — the second placebo-controlled prevention trial, in a second population
cards.summary: Kitamura 2025: in Japan, rimegepant every other day beat placebo by 1.1 monthly migraine days (p = 0.002) — the second placebo-controlled prevention trial, in a second population
cards.people: Adults in Japan with a history of 4 to 18 migraine attacks per month of moderate or severe intensity, in a phase 3, double-blind, randomised, multicentre trial (August 2022 to January 2024): after a 28-day observation phase (mean monthly migraine days 9.3 on rimegepant and 9.0 on placebo), participants took rimegepant 75 mg or placebo every other day for 12 weeks; 484 participants were evaluable for efficacy and 496 for safety.
cards.result: The trial met its primary endpoint: the mean change in monthly migraine days in the last 4 weeks of treatment differed between rimegepant and placebo by −1.1 days (95% CI −1.73 to −0.38, p = 0.002). Adverse events were reported by 54.7% of the rimegepant group and 41.0% of the placebo group, and serious adverse events by 0.8% and 0.4% respectively; no signal of drug-induced liver injury was identified.
cards.watchOut: Adverse events were numerically more frequent on rimegepant than placebo in this trial (54.7% versus 41.0%), unlike the near-identical rates in Croop 2021 — the record does not break down which events drove the difference.
cards.source: Kitamura S et al. Efficacy and safety of rimegepant for the preventive treatment of migraine in Japan: A double-blind, randomized controlled trial. Headache. 2025. PMID: 40542538. cards.headline: Pozo-Rosich 2025: in patients who had already failed 2 to 4 oral preventive categories, rimegepant beat placebo by 1.6 monthly migraine days (p < 0.0001), with a 20.1-point advantage in 50% responders
cards.summary: Pozo-Rosich 2025: in patients who had already failed 2 to 4 oral preventive categories, rimegepant beat placebo by 1.6 monthly migraine days (p < 0.0001), with a 20.1-point advantage in 50% responders
cards.people: Adults with episodic migraine (4 to 14 monthly migraine days) and a documented history of inadequate response to 2 to 4 categories of traditional oral preventive medication — most commonly anticonvulsants (61%), beta-blockers (56%) and amitriptyline (51%) — in a multinational phase 4 trial: 328 participants received rimegepant 75 mg orally disintegrating tablet and 324 received placebo, every other day for 12 weeks after a 28-day observation phase (mean monthly migraine days 8.4 and 8.3).
cards.result: Across the 12-week treatment phase, monthly migraine days changed by −2.1 days on rimegepant versus −0.5 days on placebo (difference −1.6 days, 95% CI −2.1 to −1.2; p < 0.0001). All key secondary endpoints favoured rimegepant, including the proportion with a reduction of 50% or more in monthly migraine days of moderate or severe intensity (difference 20.1 percentage points, 95% CI 13.7 to 26.5; p < 0.0001) and migraine-specific quality of life (difference 6.6 points, 95% CI 3.6 to 9.5). Rimegepant was well tolerated, with a safety profile not notably different from placebo.
cards.watchOut: This trial enrolled only episodic migraine in preventive-experienced patients, so its larger placebo-subtracted effect (−1.6 days, against a low placebo response of −0.5) should not be read as the expected effect in preventive-naive or chronic migraine populations.
cards.source: Pozo-Rosich P et al. A phase 4, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial evaluating the efficacy and tolerability of rimegepant for the prevention of episodic migraine in adults with a history of inadequate response to traditional oral preventive medications. Cephalalgia : an international journal of headache. 2025. PMID: 41255098. Registry ID: NCT05518123. cards.headline: Synthesis: three concordant placebo-controlled trials establish rimegepant for prevention — and with the acute benefit homed on #689, the dual-indication claim holds
cards.summary: Synthesis: three concordant placebo-controlled trials establish rimegepant for prevention — and with the acute benefit homed on #689, the dual-indication claim holds
cards.people: The carded evidence: three randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled prevention trials of rimegepant 75 mg every other day — 747 randomised (Croop 2021), 484 in the efficacy analysis (Kitamura 2025) and 652 treated (Pozo-Rosich 2025) — in US, Japanese and multinational populations, the last in patients who had failed multiple oral preventives. Totals far exceed the small-N threshold, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Placebo-subtracted reductions in monthly migraine days were −0.8 days (p = 0.0099), −1.1 days (p = 0.002) and −1.6 days (p < 0.0001) across the three trials, with tolerability resembling placebo in each. The acute-treatment half of the dual claim is homed on live shelf #689 (ubrogepant and rimegepant versus placebo for pain freedom at 2 hours) and is cross-pointed, not re-carded. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — effective for both acute treatment and prevention.
cards.watchOut: Prevention trials ran 12 weeks of double-blind treatment; the dual claim joins two separate evidence bases (acute single-attack trials on #689, prevention trials here) rather than one trial testing both uses in the same patients.
cards.source: Synthesis of Croop R et al. Lancet (London, England). 2021 (PMID: 33338437); Kitamura S et al. Headache. 2025 (PMID: 40542538); Pozo-Rosich P et al. Cephalalgia. 2025 (PMID: 41255098).

shelves.title: Ubrogepant in triptan non-responders (partial completion of #689, gepants versus placebo generally): efficacy consistent across triptan-response subgroups — POSSIBLE benefit, post-hoc evidence only
shelves.question: Does ubrogepant work for acute migraine in patients who do not respond to triptans?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide Receptor Antagonists · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Migraine Disorders · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Pyridines · Pyrroles · Serotonin 5-HT1 Receptor Agonists
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #689, which covers the gepants versus placebo for acute migraine generally (the ACHIEVE II primary report and the acute rimegepant trial are carded there and are not re-carded here). The uncovered slice is patients who do not respond to triptans — and for ubrogepant that evidence is entirely post hoc. A pooled post-hoc analysis of ACHIEVE I and II (Blumenfeld 2021, PMID: 33749826) classified 451 of 1,799 participants as triptan-insufficient responders and found ubrogepant's efficacy did not differ by historical triptan experience (interaction p = 0.290 for pain freedom), though the record does not print the subgroup's own pain-freedom rates. A companion post-hoc analysis (Lipton 2022, PMID: 35468729) found functional benefits in that subgroup: normal function at 2 hours in 38% on ubrogepant versus 29% on placebo, and satisfaction at 24 hours in 58% versus 28%. A network meta-analysis restricted to triptan-insufficient responders (Laohapiboolrattana 2024, PMID: 39516789; 5 trials, 3,004 patients) found lasmiditan, rimegepant and ubrogepant all significantly superior to placebo for 2-hour pain freedom, without printing ubrogepant-specific estimates separately. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — ubrogepant probably works in triptan non-responders about as well as in responders, but no trial has prospectively enrolled non-responders to test it, so the claim rests on subgroup analyses of trials homed on #689 — flagged here for the developer: these are secondary reports of those same trials, carded because the subgroup is the question, with distinct PMIDs not used on the home shelf.

cards.headline: Blumenfeld 2021: in ACHIEVE I and II, ubrogepant's efficacy did not differ by historical triptan response (interaction p = 0.290 for pain freedom) — 451 of 1,799 participants were triptan-insufficient responders; the record prints no subgroup pain-freedom rates
cards.summary: Blumenfeld 2021: in ACHIEVE I and II, ubrogepant's efficacy did not differ by historical triptan response (interaction p = 0.290 for pain freedom) — 451 of 1,799 participants were triptan-insufficient responders; the record prints no subgroup pain-freedom rates
cards.type: Post-hoc analysis of two randomised trials (Blumenfeld 2021)
cards.people: Post-hoc analysis of pooled data from the identically designed ACHIEVE I and II phase 3, randomised, double-blind, single-attack trials of ubrogepant for acute migraine: in the pooled analysis population of 1,799 participants, 682 were triptan responders (placebo 350, ubrogepant 50 mg 332), 451 were triptan-insufficient responders (placebo 223, ubrogepant 228) and 666 were triptan-naïve (placebo 339, ubrogepant 327), classified by historical experience with triptans. Co-primary endpoints were pain freedom and absence of the most bothersome symptom 2 hours after the initial dose.
cards.result: Response rates on the co-primary efficacy endpoints were higher for ubrogepant versus placebo across all groups. Treatment-by-subgroup interaction p values based on odds ratios for pain freedom (p = 0.290) and absence of the most bothersome symptom (p = 0.705) indicated no significant impact of historical triptan experience on ubrogepant efficacy, and adverse-event incidence did not differ appreciably across subgroups. The record does not print the pain-freedom or symptom-freedom rates within the triptan-insufficient responder subgroup itself — that absence is printed here plainly, so this card establishes consistency across subgroups rather than a subgroup effect size.
cards.watchOut: Post hoc and self-reported: triptan response was classified from participants' historical experience, not from a prospective triptan challenge, and a non-significant interaction test is weaker evidence than a positive result within the subgroup itself.
cards.source: Blumenfeld AM et al. Efficacy of ubrogepant based on prior exposure and response to triptans: A post hoc analysis. Headache. 2021. PMID: 33749826. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.summary: Lipton 2022: in triptan insufficient responders, ubrogepant beat placebo on normal function at 2 hours (38% versus 29%), satisfaction at 24 hours (58% versus 28%) and global impression of improvement (30% versus 18%)
cards.type: Post-hoc analysis of two randomised trials (Lipton 2022)
cards.people: Post-hoc analysis of the pooled ACHIEVE I and ACHIEVE II randomised trials examining patient-reported outcomes in participants who were self-reported triptan insufficient responders — defined as unable to take triptans due to contraindications, tolerability issues or insufficient efficacy: 451 (25%) of the pooled population of 1,799 were triptan insufficient responders, most (80%) reporting insufficient efficacy with triptan use. Outcomes were the Functional Disability Scale, satisfaction with medication and the Patient Global Impression of Change for pooled ubrogepant 50 mg versus placebo.
cards.result: A significantly higher proportion of triptan insufficient responders treated with ubrogepant versus placebo reported being able to function normally from 2 to 8 hours post dose (P < 0.05), including at the 2-hour primary assessment point (38% for ubrogepant vs 29% for placebo, P = 0.048). More responders in the ubrogepant arm were satisfied with treatment at 2 hours (33% vs 21%, P = 0.006) and 24 hours (58% vs 28%, P < 0.001) and indicated their migraine improved at 2 hours (30% vs 18%, P = 0.006). Results were generally similar in the insufficient-efficacy subpopulation, and ubrogepant was safe and well tolerated with no new safety signals.
cards.watchOut: These are secondary, patient-reported outcomes in a post-hoc subgroup — function, satisfaction and global impression, not the pain-freedom endpoint — and the 2-hour function difference (38% versus 29%) only just reaches significance (P = 0.048).
cards.source: Lipton RB et al. Functionality, satisfaction, and global impression of change with ubrogepant for the acute treatment of migraine in triptan insufficient responders: a post hoc analysis of the ACHIEVE I and ACHIEVE II randomized trials. The journal of headache and pain. 2022. PMID: 35468729. Registry ID: NCT02828020, NCT02867709. cards.headline: Laohapiboolrattana 2024: across 5 trials in triptan insufficient responders (3,004 patients), lasmiditan, rimegepant and ubrogepant were all superior to placebo for 2-hour pain freedom (relative risk 1.93) — ubrogepant-specific estimates not printed separately
cards.summary: Laohapiboolrattana 2024: across 5 trials in triptan insufficient responders (3,004 patients), lasmiditan, rimegepant and ubrogepant were all superior to placebo for 2-hour pain freedom (relative risk 1.93) — ubrogepant-specific estimates not printed separately
cards.people: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials comparing lasmiditan, rimegepant and ubrogepant in migraine patients who self-reported insufficient response to triptans, searching to May 2024: five phase 3 randomised trials involving 3,004 patients were included.
cards.result: All three agents were significantly superior to placebo for two-hour pain freedom (relative risk 1.93, 95% CI 1.52 to 2.46), freedom from the most bothersome symptoms at two hours (relative risk 1.55, 95% CI 1.37 to 1.75) and pain relief at two hours (relative risk 1.46, 95% CI 1.35 to 1.58) — relative measures as printed for the agents in this population; the record does not print ubrogepant's own separate estimate or the absolute rates. No statistically significant differences in efficacy outcomes were observed among the three agents.
cards.watchOut: The pooled relative risks are printed for the three-agent class in this population, not for ubrogepant alone, and the underlying trials again defined insufficient response by self-report rather than prospective testing.
cards.source: Laohapiboolrattana W et al. Efficacy of lasmiditan, rimegepant and ubrogepant for acute treatment of migraine in triptan insufficient responders: systematic review and network meta-analysis. The journal of headache and pain. 2024. PMID: 39516789. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: ubrogepant probably works in triptan non-responders — its effect did not vary by triptan history, functional outcomes favoured it within the subgroup, and the class pooling in non-responders is positive — but every strand is post hoc
cards.summary: Synthesis: ubrogepant probably works in triptan non-responders — its effect did not vary by triptan history, functional outcomes favoured it within the subgroup, and the class pooling in non-responders is positive — but every strand is post hoc
cards.people: The carded evidence: two post-hoc analyses of the pooled ACHIEVE I and II trials (1,799 participants, of whom 451 were triptan-insufficient responders; Blumenfeld 2021 and Lipton 2022) and one network meta-analysis restricted to triptan-insufficient responders (5 trials, 3,004 patients; Laohapiboolrattana 2024). Participant totals exceed the small-N threshold, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Ubrogepant's efficacy showed no significant interaction with historical triptan experience (p = 0.290 for pain freedom; Blumenfeld 2021). Within the insufficient-responder subgroup, normal function at 2 hours was 38% versus 29% and satisfaction at 24 hours 58% versus 28% (Lipton 2022). The non-responder-restricted network meta-analysis found all three novel agents, ubrogepant included, superior to placebo for 2-hour pain freedom (relative risk 1.93; Laohapiboolrattana 2024). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Home shelf #689 holds the primary ACHIEVE evidence for ubrogepant versus placebo generally; this shelf's non-responder claim is built from secondary reports of those same trials plus a class-level pooling, and a prospectively designed trial in confirmed triptan non-responders remains the missing evidence.
cards.source: Synthesis of Blumenfeld AM et al. Headache. 2021 (PMID: 33749826); Lipton RB et al. The journal of headache and pain. 2022 (PMID: 35468729); Laohapiboolrattana W et al. The journal of headache and pain. 2024 (PMID: 39516789).

shelves.title: Atogepant after oral preventives have failed (PARTIAL completion of #1448): in ELEVATE, atogepant cut monthly migraine days by 2.4 days more than placebo in episodic migraine failed by 2–4 preventive classes — one trial programme
shelves.question: Does atogepant prevent episodic migraine in patients who failed two oral preventives?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Humans · Male · Antibodies, Monoclonal/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Europe · European People · Migraine Disorders/drug therapy/prevention & control · North America · North American People · Piperidines · Pyridines · Pyrroles · Spiro Compounds · Treatment Outcome · Adolescent · Young Adult · Middle Aged · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · White People
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1448, which covers atogepant in episodic migraine generally (the ADVANCE trial) and in chronic migraine (PROGRESS); this shelf covers only the slice #1448 does not: patients whose episodic migraine had already been failed by two to four classes of conventional oral preventive treatments. In that dedicated population, the single phase 3b ELEVATE trial (Tassorelli 2024, PMID: 38364831) found monthly migraine days fell by 4.2 days on atogepant 60 mg daily versus 1.9 days on placebo over 12 weeks (difference −2.4 days, 95% CI −3.2 to −1.5). A post hoc pooled subgroup of high-frequency episodic migraine patients who had failed at least two preventive classes (Ashina 2026, PMID: 43036972) found a consistent −2.65-day difference, and a pooled patient-reported-outcomes analysis of three phase 3 trials (Gottschalk 2024, PMID: 39648617) found the largest quality-of-life and headache-impact gains of any of its trial populations in the ELEVATE population. Constipation was the commonest adverse event (10% versus 3%); serious adverse events occurred in 3% on atogepant versus none on placebo. All three cards come from one trial programme anchored on a single randomised trial, so the stamp is capped. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): atogepant 60 mg daily reduced monthly migraine days by about 2.4 days more than placebo over 12 weeks in episodic migraine patients who had failed two to four classes of oral preventives — a single-trial-programme result.

cards.headline: ELEVATE (Tassorelli 2024): in episodic migraine failed by 2–4 classes of oral preventives, atogepant cut monthly migraine days by 4.2 versus 1.9 on placebo (difference −2.4 days) over 12 weeks — 315 patients randomised
cards.summary: ELEVATE (Tassorelli 2024): in episodic migraine failed by 2–4 classes of oral preventives, atogepant cut monthly migraine days by 4.2 versus 1.9 on placebo (difference −2.4 days) over 12 weeks — 315 patients randomised
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3b trial (ELEVATE; Tassorelli 2024)
cards.people: Adults aged 18–80 years with episodic migraine who had previously been failed by two to four classes of conventional oral treatments for migraine prevention, at 73 sites in 13 countries; 540 were screened, 315 randomly assigned and 313 received at least one dose (89% female, 96% White). Randomised to oral atogepant 60 mg once daily or placebo for 12 weeks.
cards.result: Least squares mean change in monthly migraine days across the 12-week period was −4.2 days (SE 0.4) with atogepant versus −1.9 (SE 0.4) with placebo: least squares mean difference −2.4 days (95% CI −3.2 to −1.5; adjusted P < 0.0001). The most common treatment-emergent adverse event with atogepant was constipation, in 16 (10%) of 156 participants versus 4 (3%) of 157 on placebo. Serious adverse events occurred in 4 (3%) of 156 on atogepant versus none on placebo, and adverse events led to discontinuation in 3 (2%) versus 2 (1%).
cards.watchOut: One trial, 12 weeks, in a population that was 96% White; the trial tested failure of two to four preventive classes, so it does not separately report the narrower subgroup who failed exactly two oral preventives named in this shelf's question.
cards.source: Tassorelli C et al. Safety and efficacy of atogepant for the preventive treatment of episodic migraine in adults for whom conventional oral preventive treatments have failed (ELEVATE): a randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 3b trial.. The Lancet. Neurology. 2024. PMID: 38364831. Registry ID: NCT04740827. cards.headline: Ashina 2026: in the pooled high-frequency episodic migraine subgroup that had failed ≥2 preventive classes, atogepant beat placebo by 2.65 migraine days a month — a post hoc, exploratory analysis (n = 269)
cards.summary: Ashina 2026: in the pooled high-frequency episodic migraine subgroup that had failed ≥2 preventive classes, atogepant beat placebo by 2.65 migraine days a month — a post hoc, exploratory analysis (n = 269)
cards.type: Post hoc subgroup analysis of two randomised trials (Ashina 2026)
cards.people: Post hoc subgroup analysis of two 12-week phase 3 randomised trials (ADVANCE and ELEVATE). The pooled HFEM TF2+ subgroup comprised 269 participants with high-frequency episodic migraine (8–14 monthly migraine days at baseline) who had had an inadequate response to at least two classes of conventional oral non-migraine-specific preventive treatments.
cards.result: Atogepant 60 mg once daily versus placebo: least squares mean difference in monthly migraine days −2.65 (95% CI −3.60 to −1.71; nominal P < 0.001) and in monthly acute medication use days −2.80 (95% CI −3.61 to −2.00; nominal P < 0.001). Migraine-Specific Quality of Life Role Function-Restrictive scores also favoured atogepant (difference 16.94, 95% CI 11.93 to 21.96). All P values are nominal, from a post hoc exploratory analysis.
cards.watchOut: Post hoc and exploratory: the subgroup was not the primary population of either parent trial, its P values are unadjusted, and it pools ADVANCE patients (not selected for treatment failure) with ELEVATE patients — it supports, but cannot independently confirm, the ELEVATE result.
cards.source: Ashina H et al. Atogepant for the preventive treatment of high-frequency episodic migraine: Subgroup analysis from the ADVANCE and ELEVATE trials.. Headache. 2026. PMID: 43036972. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Gottschalk 2024: across three phase 3 trials, the ELEVATE (prior-failure) population showed the largest patient-reported gains on atogepant — quality-of-life difference 17.7 points and headache-impact difference −6.5 versus placebo
cards.summary: Gottschalk 2024: across three phase 3 trials, the ELEVATE (prior-failure) population showed the largest patient-reported gains on atogepant — quality-of-life difference 17.7 points and headache-impact difference −6.5 versus placebo
cards.type: Pooled patient-reported-outcomes analysis of three randomised trials (Gottschalk 2024)
cards.people: Patient-reported-outcome analyses of three 12-week randomised, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials of atogepant 60 mg once daily: ADVANCE (episodic migraine), PROGRESS (chronic migraine) and ELEVATE (episodic migraine in patients previously failed by two to four classes of oral preventive treatments). Participant totals per trial are not stated in this record.
cards.result: In ELEVATE, least squares mean differences (atogepant versus placebo) at week 12 were 17.7 points (95% CI 13.1 to 22.3) on the Migraine-Specific Quality of Life questionnaire Role Function-Restrictive domain and −6.5 (95% CI −8.3 to −4.7) on the Headache Impact Test-6; the Activity Impairment in Migraine-Diary Performance of Daily Activities difference across 12 weeks was −4.7 (95% CI −6.4 to −3.1). Each of these ELEVATE differences was larger than the corresponding differences in ADVANCE and PROGRESS as reported in the record (all P < 0.05).
cards.watchOut: These are secondary, patient-reported outcomes from the same trial programme as the primary card — they show the migraine-day benefit was felt by patients, but they are not independent evidence and add no new randomised comparison.
cards.source: Gottschalk C et al. Effect of preventive treatment with atogepant on quality of life, daily functioning, and headache impact across the spectrum of migraine: Findings from three double-blind, randomized, phase 3 trials.. Cephalalgia : an international journal of headache. 2024. PMID: 39648617. Registry ID: NCT04740827 (ELEVATE), NCT03777059 (ADVANCE), NCT03855137 (PROGRESS). cards.headline: Synthesis: one dedicated trial in prior-failure episodic migraine shows a 2.4-day advantage over placebo, with consistent subgroup and quality-of-life findings — a single trial programme, so POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: one dedicated trial in prior-failure episodic migraine shows a 2.4-day advantage over placebo, with consistent subgroup and quality-of-life findings — a single trial programme, so POSSIBLE
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised phase 3b trial in the target population (ELEVATE, 315 randomised), one post hoc pooled subgroup analysis including 269 prior-failure high-frequency patients, and one pooled patient-reported-outcomes analysis spanning that programme. Unique randomised participants in the target population number about 315, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the limitation is that there is only one trial, not that it is tiny.
cards.result: Monthly migraine days: −4.2 on atogepant versus −1.9 on placebo (difference −2.4 days, 95% CI −3.2 to −1.5) in ELEVATE; −2.65 days (95% CI −3.60 to −1.71) in the pooled prior-failure high-frequency subgroup. Quality of life and headache impact favoured atogepant most strongly in the ELEVATE population. Constipation 10% versus 3%; serious adverse events 3% versus 0%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme (ELEVATE).
cards.watchOut: Everything on this shelf descends from ELEVATE and its parent programme; a second trial in prior-failure patients, or longer than 12 weeks, would be needed to lift the stamp.

shelves.title: Trigeminal neuralgia first-line ranking (PARTIAL completion of #5032): carbamazepine remains first — the guideline's only Level A drug, unbeaten head-to-head, on an old and poor-quality comparative base
shelves.question: Is carbamazepine still the most effective first treatment for trigeminal neuralgia?
shelves.mesh: Europe · Evidence-Based Medicine · Humans · Neurology/standards · Quality of Health Care · Societies, Medical/standards · Trigeminal Neuralgia/diagnosis/therapy · United States
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of pack #5032, which covers only carbamazepine versus placebo in the old crossover trials; this shelf covers the slice #5032 does not: how carbamazepine ranks against the alternatives as first treatment. The AAN–EFNS evidence-based practice parameter (Gronseth 2008, PMID: 18716236) graded carbamazepine Level A (established effective) — the only drug at that level — with oxcarbazepine Level B and baclofen and lamotrigine Level C. The one comparative meta-analysis found (Wang 2011, PMID: 21936587) pooled six small, poor-quality Chinese trials of topiramate versus carbamazepine (354 patients): no difference at 1 month, and a relative advantage for topiramate at 2 months (relative risk 1.20) that the authors themselves say is limited by trial quality. An evidence-based pharmacology review (Di Stefano 2018, PMID: 30178160) likewise keeps carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine as first choice, with lamotrigine or baclofen as add-ons. So no alternative has beaten carbamazepine in adequate head-to-head trials — but the comparative base is old, small and poor quality, which caps the stamp. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: carbamazepine remains the most effective first treatment for trigeminal neuralgia on current evidence — the guideline's only Level A drug, with no alternative shown superior in adequate trials.

cards.headline: Gronseth 2008 (AAN–EFNS practice parameter): carbamazepine is the only Level A (established effective) drug for trigeminal neuralgia pain control; oxcarbazepine is Level B, baclofen and lamotrigine Level C
cards.summary: Gronseth 2008 (AAN–EFNS practice parameter): carbamazepine is the only Level A (established effective) drug for trigeminal neuralgia pain control; oxcarbazepine is Level B, baclofen and lamotrigine Level C
cards.type: Practice guideline / evidence-based systematic review (AAN–EFNS; Gronseth 2008)
cards.people: Evidence-based review by a panel of the American Academy of Neurology and the European Federation of Neurological Societies, systematically reviewing the literature on diagnosis and treatment of classic and symptomatic trigeminal neuralgia. Participant numbers are those of the underlying trials reviewed and are not totalled in this record.
cards.result: For pain control in classic trigeminal neuralgia, the panel concluded carbamazepine (Level A) or oxcarbazepine (Level B) should be offered, while baclofen and lamotrigine (Level C) may be considered useful. Level A is the guideline's strongest grade ('established as effective'). No other drug received a Level A or B rating for pain control.
cards.watchOut: A 2008 guideline grading rests on the same old, small trials carded on pack #5032; Level A here certifies the strength of the placebo-controlled evidence for carbamazepine, not the result of modern head-to-head trials against newer drugs, which largely do not exist.

cards.headline: Wang 2011: topiramate versus carbamazepine meta-analysis — no difference at 1 month; a relative advantage at 2 months (relative risk 1.20) from six poor-quality trials, 354 patients
cards.summary: Wang 2011: topiramate versus carbamazepine meta-analysis — no difference at 1 month; a relative advantage at 2 months (relative risk 1.20) from six poor-quality trials, 354 patients
cards.people: Meta-analysis of six randomised controlled trials, all conducted in China and all rated poor methodological quality, including altogether 354 patients with classical trigeminal neuralgia treated with topiramate or carbamazepine.
cards.result: Topiramate was more effective than carbamazepine after 2 months of treatment (relative risk [RR] = 1.20, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.39, P = 0.01 — a relative measure; the record gives no absolute response rates beside it). There was no difference in effectiveness at 1 month (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.14), in remission at 1 month (RR 1.06) or 2 months (RR 1.31, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.80), or in adverse events. The authors conclude the overall effectiveness and tolerability of topiramate did not seem to differ from carbamazepine and call for large, international, well-conducted trials.
cards.watchOut: Six small trials from one country, all poor quality by the reviewers' own rating: the single positive 2-month result is exactly the kind of finding such a base cannot carry, and the review's own conclusion is equivalence, not superiority.
cards.source: Wang QP et al. Topiramate versus carbamazepine for the treatment of classical trigeminal neuralgia: a meta-analysis.. CNS drugs. 2011. PMID: 21936587. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Di Stefano 2018: evidence-based pharmacology review keeps carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine as first choice for paroxysmal pain, effective in 'virtually the totality of patients' but with withdrawals from side effects in an important percentage
cards.summary: Di Stefano 2018: evidence-based pharmacology review keeps carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine as first choice for paroxysmal pain, effective in 'virtually the totality of patients' but with withdrawals from side effects in an important percentage
cards.people: Evidence-based review of pharmacological treatment of typical and atypical trigeminal neuralgia, searching PubMed, EMBASE, the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews and ClinicalTrials.gov to February 2018, with two authors independently selecting studies and assessing bias. No participant total is given in the record.
cards.result: The review concludes that carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine are the first-choice drugs for paroxysmal pain; when sodium channel blockers cannot reach full dosage because of side effects, add-on lamotrigine or baclofen should be considered; in atypical trigeminal neuralgia, gabapentin and antidepressants are expected to be efficacious as add-ons. It notes that although carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine are effective in virtually the totality of patients, side effects cause withdrawal from treatment in an important percentage of cases, and that a better-tolerated sodium channel blocker (vixotrigine) was under development.
cards.watchOut: A narrative review, not a new comparison: its first-choice ranking restates the guideline position and the old trial base rather than adding head-to-head data, and its 'virtually the totality' efficacy phrasing is the authors' summary, not a pooled response rate.
cards.source: Di Stefano G et al. Current and Innovative Pharmacological Options to Treat Typical and Atypical Trigeminal Neuralgia.. Drugs. 2018. PMID: 30178160. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: carbamazepine keeps the strongest evidence grade and no alternative has beaten it head-to-head — but the comparative trial base is old, small and poor quality, so POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: carbamazepine keeps the strongest evidence grade and no alternative has beaten it head-to-head — but the comparative trial base is old, small and poor quality, so POSSIBLE
cards.people: The carded evidence: one international evidence-based guideline (2008), one meta-analysis of six poor-quality head-to-head trials (354 patients), and one evidence-based pharmacology review (2018). Total carded participants exceed 30, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the limitation is trial quality and age, printed here.
cards.result: Carbamazepine: Level A, the guideline's only top grade (oxcarbazepine Level B; baclofen and lamotrigine Level C). Topiramate, the only alternative with a head-to-head meta-analysis, did not differ overall from carbamazepine (relative risk 1.20 at 2 months in poor-quality trials only). The 2018 review keeps carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine first choice. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: carbamazepine remains the most effective first treatment on current evidence.
cards.watchOut: 'Still most effective' here means 'never beaten and best graded', not 'proven better than every alternative in modern trials' — for oxcarbazepine in particular, the practical first-line choice often turns on tolerability and interactions, which this evidence base barely tests.
cards.source: Synthesis of Gronseth G et al. Neurology. 2008 (PMID: 18716236); Wang QP et al. CNS drugs. 2011 (PMID: 21936587); Di Stefano G et al. Drugs. 2018 (PMID: 30178160).

shelves.title: Antidepressants after a second depressive episode (PARTIAL completion of #705): continue at least 12 months — PREVENT and the imipramine programme agree at 1, 2, 3 and 5 years
shelves.question: Should antidepressants be continued for at least 12 months after a second depressive episode to prevent relapse?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Ambulatory Care · Clinical Protocols · Combined Modality Therapy · Depressive Disorder/drug therapy/prevention & control/psychology · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Imipramine/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Dropouts · Placebos · Probability · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Psychotherapy · Recurrence · Survival Analysis
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #705, which covers continuation versus tapering in primary-care patients already well on antidepressants (ANTLER) and the older maintenance base in general; this shelf covers the slice #705 does not isolate: patients with recurrent depression — the second-episode-and-beyond population — and durations of at least 12 months. Every dedicated trial in that population favours continuation, at every duration tested. In the Pittsburgh recurrent-depression programme (Frank 1990, PMID: 2244793), full-dose imipramine maintained over 3 years had a highly significant prophylactic effect against recurrence; its extension (Kupfer 1992, PMID: 1417428) found the protection persisted beyond 3 years and concluded patients whose episodes come less than 2½ years apart merit at least 5 years. In PREVENT, 12 months of maintenance venlafaxine ER halved recurrence versus placebo (23.1% versus 42.0%; Kocsis 2007, PMID: 17685736), a second maintenance year again favoured continuation (8.0% versus 44.8%; Keller 2007, PMID: 17854250), and the combined 24-month recurrence probability was 28.5% versus 47.3%. Two independent programmes, concordant, with large absolute differences — the stamp can be strong. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): continuing antidepressants for at least 12 months after a second (recurrent) depressive episode prevents relapse, and the trial evidence supports continuing well beyond 12 months in frequently recurring illness.

cards.headline: Frank 1990: in recurrent depression, full-dose imipramine maintained for 3 years had a highly significant prophylactic effect against recurrence — 128 patients; the record reports no recurrence percentages, printed plainly
cards.summary: Frank 1990: in recurrent depression, full-dose imipramine maintained for 3 years had a highly significant prophylactic effect against recurrence — 128 patients; the record reports no recurrence percentages, printed plainly
cards.people: 128 patients with recurrent depression who had responded to combined short-term and continuation treatment with imipramine and interpersonal psychotherapy, randomised in a five-cell design to 3 years of maintenance imipramine (at the acute-episode dose, averaging 200 mg), maintenance interpersonal psychotherapy, both, or placebo-based cells.
cards.result: Survival analysis demonstrated a highly significant prophylactic effect for active imipramine maintained at an average dose of 200 mg, and a modest prophylactic effect for monthly interpersonal psychotherapy (which lengthened time between episodes in patients not receiving active medication). The record reports the significance and direction of these effects but no recurrence percentages or hazard ratios, and none are invented here. The authors conclude full-dose maintenance imipramine is an effective means of preventing recurrence over 3 years.
cards.watchOut: An enriched design: only patients who had already responded to imipramine entered maintenance, and the drug is a tricyclic at full acute dose — the result supports continuation of an effective antidepressant, not any antidepressant at any dose, and its record gives no absolute recurrence rates.
cards.source: Frank E et al. Three-year outcomes for maintenance therapies in recurrent depression.. Archives of general psychiatry. 1990. PMID: 2244793. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Kupfer 1992: the prophylactic effect of maintenance imipramine persisted beyond 3 years — patients with episodes less than 2½ years apart 'merit continued prophylaxis for at least 5 years'
cards.summary: Kupfer 1992: the prophylactic effect of maintenance imipramine persisted beyond 3 years — patients with episodes less than 2½ years apart 'merit continued prophylaxis for at least 5 years'
cards.people: Survivors of the Frank 1990 3-year maintenance trial who had remained well on active medication (with or without psychotherapy) and agreed to a further 2-year randomised trial of continued active imipramine versus switch to placebo. The record does not state how many patients entered this extension.
cards.result: Survival analysis demonstrated a highly significant continued prophylactic effect for active imipramine maintained at an average dose of 200 mg beyond 3 years, compared with discontinuation after 3 years of effective maintenance. As with the parent trial record, no recurrence percentages are reported in the record. The authors conclude that patients with previous episodes less than 2½ years apart merit continued prophylaxis for at least 5 years.
cards.watchOut: A survivor cohort twice over — patients who responded to imipramine and then stayed well on it for 3 years — so it answers 'should a long-term responder stop at year 3?' (no), not 'what happens if an unselected patient continues?'.

cards.headline: Kocsis 2007 (PREVENT, 1-year maintenance): recurrence 23.1% on venlafaxine ER versus 42.0% on placebo over 12 months (P = .005) in recurrent depression
cards.summary: Kocsis 2007 (PREVENT, 1-year maintenance): recurrence 23.1% on venlafaxine ER versus 42.0% on placebo over 12 months (P = .005) in recurrent depression
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled maintenance trial (PREVENT year 1; Kocsis 2007)
cards.people: Patients with recurrent unipolar depression who had responded to acute (10 weeks) and continuation (6 months) venlafaxine ER and entered a 12-month maintenance phase; the efficacy-evaluable sample was 129 patients per group, on a mean venlafaxine ER dose of 224.7 mg/day versus placebo.
cards.result: The cumulative probability of recurrence through 12 months was 23.1% (95% CI 15.3 to 30.9) on venlafaxine ER versus 42.0% (95% CI 31.8 to 52.2) on placebo (P = .005, log-rank test) — an absolute difference of about 19 percentage points. Recurrence was defined as a 17-item Hamilton score above 12 with less than 50% reduction from acute-phase baseline.
cards.watchOut: Also an enriched responder design (only venlafaxine responders were randomised to continue or switch), and 'recurrence' is a scale-based definition; the absolute rates apply to patients who had already done well on the drug for about 9 months.
cards.source: Kocsis JH et al. Prevention of recurrent episodes of depression with venlafaxine ER in a 1-year maintenance phase from the PREVENT Study.. The Journal of clinical psychiatry. 2007. cards.headline: Keller 2007 (PREVENT, 2-year outcomes): a second maintenance year again favoured continuation (recurrence 8.0% versus 44.8%), and combined 24-month recurrence was 28.5% versus 47.3%
cards.summary: Keller 2007 (PREVENT, 2-year outcomes): a second maintenance year again favoured continuation (recurrence 8.0% versus 44.8%), and combined 24-month recurrence was 28.5% versus 47.3%
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind maintenance trial (PREVENT year 2 and combined phases; Keller 2007)
cards.people: PREVENT participants who remained responders through the first 12-month maintenance phase and were re-randomised for a second 12 months (venlafaxine ER n = 43, placebo n = 40); the combined-phase analysis covers the 129 patients per group first randomised at maintenance entry. The parent study enrolled 1,096 outpatients with recurrent unipolar depression.
cards.result: Second-year cumulative recurrence probability was 8.0% (95% CI 0.0 to 16.8) on venlafaxine ER versus 44.8% (95% CI 27.6 to 62.0) on placebo (P < .001). Over the combined 24 months, cumulative recurrence was 28.5% (95% CI 18.3 to 38.7) on venlafaxine ER versus 47.3% (95% CI 36.4 to 58.2) on placebo (P = .005). Overall discontinuation was 28% versus 63%; adverse events were the primary reason for discontinuation in 2% versus 10%.
cards.watchOut: The second-year comparison rests on only 83 re-randomised long-term responders, so its dramatic percentages have wide intervals; the combined 24-month analysis (258 patients) is the sturdier number on this card.
cards.source: Keller MB et al. The Prevention of Recurrent Episodes of Depression with Venlafaxine for Two Years (PREVENT) Study: Outcomes from the 2-year and combined maintenance phases.. The Journal of clinical psychiatry. 2007. PMID: 17854250. Registry ID: NCT00046020. cards.headline: Synthesis: two independent recurrent-depression programmes agree at 1, 2, 3 and 5 years — continuation prevents recurrence, with absolute differences of roughly 19 points at 12 months
cards.summary: Synthesis: two independent recurrent-depression programmes agree at 1, 2, 3 and 5 years — continuation prevents recurrence, with absolute differences of roughly 19 points at 12 months
cards.people: The carded evidence: the Pittsburgh imipramine programme (128 patients randomised for 3 years, plus its 2-year extension) and PREVENT (258 patients in the combined maintenance analysis, 83 in the second-year re-randomisation). Total carded participants exceed 30, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: PREVENT: 12-month recurrence 23.1% versus 42.0%; 24-month 28.5% versus 47.3%; second year 8.0% versus 44.8% — all favouring continuation. Pittsburgh: highly significant prophylaxis from full-dose imipramine at 3 years and beyond, with the authors recommending at least 5 years when episodes recur within 2½ years. No carded trial in recurrent depression favoured stopping at or before 12 months. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): continue for at least 12 months after a second episode — and the evidence supports longer in frequently recurring illness.
cards.watchOut: All four cards are enriched responder designs in recurrent (not single-episode) depression, using imipramine or venlafaxine ER: they answer this shelf's recurrent-episode question directly, but say nothing about first-episode patients or about antidepressants never tested in maintenance trials.
cards.source: Synthesis of Frank E et al. Archives of general psychiatry. 1990 (PMID: 2244793); Kupfer DJ et al. Archives of general psychiatry. 1992 (PMID: 1417428); Kocsis JH et al.
