shelves.title: Esketamine versus quetiapine augmentation (PARTIAL completion of #407): ESCAPE-TRD remission 27.1% versus 17.6% at week 8 — one open-label head-to-head trial
shelves.question: Is esketamine nasal spray effective for treatment-resistant depression compared with augmentation with quetiapine?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Antidepressive Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Delayed-Action Preparations · Depression/drug therapy · Drug Therapy, Combination · Nasal Sprays · Quetiapine Fumarate/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Recurrence · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Serotonin and Noradrenaline Reuptake Inhibitors/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Single-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome · Ketamine/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Depressive Disorder, Treatment-Resistant/drug therapy
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #407, which covers esketamine as an add-on to a newly started oral antidepressant versus that antidepressant alone; this shelf covers the slice #407 does not: the head-to-head comparison against an active augmentation strategy, quetiapine extended-release, in ESCAPE-TRD. In that single open-label, rater-blinded trial (Reif 2023, PMID: 37792613), remission at week 8 was 27.1% on esketamine versus 17.6% on quetiapine XR (P = 0.003), and 21.7% versus 14.1% were relapse-free through week 32 after remitting at week 8. The trial's safety reports (McIntyre 2024, PMID: 38954874; Mattingly 2024, PMID: 43010384) show adverse events were more frequent on esketamine (91.9% versus 78.0%) but usually resolved the same day (92.0% versus 12.1% of events), and fewer esketamine patients discontinued for adverse events (4.2% versus 11.0%). Absolute remission remained low on both arms, the trial was open-label, and patients who discontinued were counted as failures — a convention that interacts with the differing discontinuation rates. One trial programme only, so the stamp is capped. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): esketamine nasal spray beat quetiapine XR augmentation on remission at week 8 and on sustained remission to week 32 in the single head-to-head trial.

cards.headline: ESCAPE-TRD (Reif 2023): remission at week 8 in 27.1% on esketamine versus 17.6% on quetiapine XR (P = 0.003); relapse-free through week 32 in 21.7% versus 14.1% — 676 patients
cards.summary: ESCAPE-TRD (Reif 2023): remission at week 8 in 27.1% on esketamine versus 17.6% on quetiapine XR (P = 0.003); relapse-free through week 32 in 21.7% versus 14.1% — 676 patients
cards.type: Randomised, open-label, rater-blinded, active-controlled phase 3b trial (ESCAPE-TRD; Reif 2023)
cards.people: Patients with treatment-resistant depression (lack of response to two or more consecutive treatments in the current episode), randomised 1:1 to flexible-dose esketamine nasal spray (n = 336) or extended-release quetiapine (n = 340), each combined with an ongoing SSRI or SNRI, in an open-label, single-blind (blinded raters), multicentre phase 3b trial.
cards.result: Remission at week 8 (Montgomery–Åsberg Depression Rating Scale score ≤ 10) occurred in 91 of 336 patients (27.1%) on esketamine versus 60 of 340 (17.6%) on quetiapine XR (P = 0.003) — an absolute difference of about 9.5 percentage points. No relapse through week 32 after remission at week 8: 73 of 336 (21.7%) versus 48 of 340 (14.1%). Remission and response percentages and change in MADRS score over 32 weeks all favoured esketamine. Patients who discontinued trial treatment were counted as having had an unfavourable outcome in all analyses.
cards.watchOut: Open-label: patients and treating clinicians knew the allocation (only raters were blinded), and counting discontinuers as failures penalises the arm with more discontinuations — quetiapine's higher adverse-event discontinuation (see safety card) is built into this efficacy result, not separate from it. Absolute remission was low on both arms.
cards.source: Reif A et al. Esketamine Nasal Spray versus Quetiapine for Treatment-Resistant Depression.. The New England journal of medicine. 2023. PMID: 37792613. Registry ID: NCT04338321. cards.headline: McIntyre 2024 (ESCAPE-TRD safety): adverse events were commoner on esketamine (91.9% versus 78.0%) but 92.0% resolved the same day versus 12.1% — and fewer esketamine patients stopped treatment for adverse events (4.2% versus 11.0%)
cards.summary: McIntyre 2024 (ESCAPE-TRD safety): adverse events were commoner on esketamine (91.9% versus 78.0%) but 92.0% resolved the same day versus 12.1% — and fewer esketamine patients stopped treatment for adverse events (4.2% versus 11.0%)
cards.type: Secondary safety analysis of a randomised trial (ESCAPE-TRD; McIntyre 2024)
cards.people: Safety population of ESCAPE-TRD: 334 patients who received at least one dose of esketamine nasal spray and 336 who received at least one dose of quetiapine XR, each with an ongoing SSRI or SNRI. P values in this secondary publication were not adjusted for multiple testing.
cards.result: Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 91.9% on esketamine versus 78.0% on quetiapine XR (P < 0.001) but were typically mild or moderate and transient: 92.0% of esketamine events resolved the same day versus 12.1% of quetiapine events, and the median proportion of days spent with adverse events was 11.9% versus 21.3% (P < 0.001). Adverse events led to discontinuation in 4.2% on esketamine versus 11.0% on quetiapine XR (P < 0.001). No new safety signals were identified.
cards.watchOut: A secondary, sponsor-programme publication of the same single trial — it characterises the primary trial's harms, it is not independent confirmation of anything, and its unadjusted P values across many comparisons invite selective reading.
cards.source: McIntyre RS et al. Safety and tolerability of esketamine nasal spray versus quetiapine extended release in patients with treatment resistant depression.. European neuropsychopharmacology : the journal of the European College of Neuropsychopharmacology. 2024. PMID: 38954874. Registry ID: NCT04338321. cards.headline: Mattingly 2024 (ESCAPE-TRD, US-label-dosing subgroup): dizziness 47.1% on esketamine versus 7.9% on quetiapine XR; nausea 29.9% versus 3.2%; somnolence the reverse, 15.0% versus 23.4% — 636 patients
cards.summary: Mattingly 2024 (ESCAPE-TRD, US-label-dosing subgroup): dizziness 47.1% on esketamine versus 7.9% on quetiapine XR; nausea 29.9% versus 3.2%; somnolence the reverse, 15.0% versus 23.4% — 636 patients
cards.type: Subgroup safety analysis of a randomised trial (ESCAPE-TRD; Mattingly 2024)
cards.people: Subgroup of ESCAPE-TRD participants aged 18–64 years dosed according to US prescribing information (esketamine 56 or 84 mg; quetiapine XR 150–300 mg): 316 assigned to esketamine and 320 to quetiapine XR, of whom 314 and 316 received at least one dose. Results are summarised descriptively in the record.
cards.result: Across the acute and maintenance phases, adverse events occurred in 92.0% on esketamine versus 78.5% on quetiapine XR. The commonest esketamine events were dizziness (47.1% versus 7.9%), nausea (29.9% versus 3.2%) and headache (25.5% versus 13.0%); somnolence was commoner on quetiapine (23.4% versus 15.0%). Of adverse events occurring in more than 5% of either arm, 91.8% resolved within 1 day on esketamine versus 11.6% on quetiapine; dissociation resolved the same day in 99.6% of events and usually within 2 hours of dosing. Discontinuation for adverse events: 4.4% versus 10.6%.
cards.watchOut: A dosing-defined subgroup of the same single trial, reported descriptively without comparative testing: it refines the harm picture (brief, dosing-day effects versus quetiapine's lingering somnolence) but adds no new randomised evidence.
cards.source: Mattingly G et al. Adverse Event Duration with Esketamine Versus Quetiapine XR in Adults With Treatment-Resistant Depression: A Subgroup Analysis of ESCAPE-TRD.. CNS spectrums. 2024. PMID: 43010384. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #574, which covers rTMS versus sham; this shelf covers the slice #574 does not: rTMS against the active standard, ECT, in nonpsychotic major depression. The evidence splits by population. In the one trial restricted to nonpsychotic depression (Grunhaus 2003, PMID: 12586451; 40 patients referred for ECT), response was 12 of 20 on ECT versus 11 of 20 on rTMS — no significant difference. In a larger multicentre trial of severe depression in ECT-referred patients (Eranti 2007, PMID: 17202547), ECT was clearly superior at the end of treatment (remission 59.1% versus 16.7%), though Hamilton scores no longer differed at 6 months. The meta-analysis (Ren 2014, PMID: 24556538; 9 trials, 425 patients) found ECT superior overall for response (64.4% versus 48.7%; relative risk 1.41) and remission (52.9% versus 33.6%; relative risk 1.38), but its subgroup analysis found the superiority concentrated in psychotic depression, with high-frequency rTMS as effective as ECT in nonpsychotic depression; specific cognitive domains (visual memory, verbal fluency) were more impaired after ECT in the few studies reporting them. PROPOSED SPLIT: rTMS matched ECT in the nonpsychotic-restricted trial and in the meta-analysis's nonpsychotic subgroup, but ECT was superior in severe, ECT-referred populations and overall — 'as effective' holds only for the nonpsychotic, less severe end of the spectrum, on small trials.

cards.headline: Grunhaus 2003: in nonpsychotic major depression, response was 12 of 20 on ECT versus 11 of 20 on rTMS — no significant difference (the treatment made no difference between groups)
cards.summary: Grunhaus 2003: in nonpsychotic major depression, response was 12 of 20 on ECT versus 11 of 20 on rTMS — no significant difference (the treatment made no difference between groups)
cards.people: 40 patients with severe and resistant nonpsychotic major depression referred for ECT, randomised to ECT by established protocols or to rTMS over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (20 sessions of 10-Hz stimulation, 1,200 pulses per day at 90% motor threshold, over 4 weeks). Response required at least a 50% fall in Hamilton score with a final score of 10 or less and a Global Assessment of Functioning rating of at least 60.
cards.result: The overall response rate was 58% (23 of 40). In the ECT group 12 patients responded and 8 did not; in the rTMS group 11 responded and 9 did not (chi-square = 0.10, not significant — the treatment made no difference to response in this trial). The authors conclude patients with nonpsychotic major depression responded as well to either treatment, while noting their earlier report found ECT superior in psychotic major depression.
cards.watchOut: Forty patients, single centre, no sham arm and a strict composite response definition: 'no significant difference' in a trial this size is compatible with a real advantage to either treatment — it is the only card restricted to this shelf's exact (nonpsychotic) population, and it cannot carry an equivalence claim alone.

cards.headline: Eranti 2007: in severe depression referred for ECT, remission at end of treatment was 59.1% on ECT versus 16.7% on rTMS — but Hamilton scores did not differ at 6 months (46 patients)
cards.summary: Eranti 2007: in severe depression referred for ECT, remission at end of treatment was 59.1% on ECT versus 16.7% on rTMS — but Hamilton scores did not differ at 6 months (46 patients)
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial with 6-month follow-up (Eranti 2007)
cards.people: 46 patients with major depression referred for ECT at multiple centres, randomised to a 15-day course of rTMS of the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (n = 24) or a standard course of ECT (n = 22), with 6-month follow-up. The population was severe depression referred for ECT and was not restricted to nonpsychotic depression.
cards.result: End-of-treatment Hamilton scores were significantly lower for ECT, with remission (Hamilton ≤ 8) in 13 of 22 patients (59.1%) on ECT versus 4 of 24 (16.7%) on rTMS. At 6 months, Hamilton scores did not differ between groups (the treatment made no difference at 6 months), although Beck, visual analogue mood and Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale scores remained lower for ECT at both time points. Self- and observer-rated cognitive measures were similar in the two groups. The authors conclude rTMS was not as effective as ECT for short-term treatment.
cards.watchOut: This trial's population — severe, ECT-referred, not restricted to nonpsychotic illness — is sicker than this shelf's question specifies; it shows where the equivalence claim breaks (severe illness, short term), and its 6-month convergence rests on few patients still followed.

cards.headline: Ren 2014 meta-analysis: ECT superior overall (response 64.4% versus 48.7%; remission 52.9% versus 33.6%) — but in nonpsychotic depression, high-frequency rTMS was as effective as ECT (9 trials, 425 patients)
cards.summary: Ren 2014 meta-analysis: ECT superior overall (response 64.4% versus 48.7%; remission 52.9% versus 33.6%) — but in nonpsychotic depression, high-frequency rTMS was as effective as ECT (9 trials, 425 patients)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Ren 2014)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of all randomised trials directly comparing rTMS with ECT for major depression in English- and Chinese-language databases: 10 articles reporting 9 trials, 425 patients in total.
cards.result: ECT was superior to high-frequency rTMS for response (64.4% versus 48.7%; relative risk 1.41, P = 0.03) and remission (52.9% versus 33.6%; relative risk 1.38, P = 0.006); discontinuation did not differ (8.3% versus 9.4%). In subgroup analysis, ECT's superiority was more apparent in psychotic depression, while high-frequency rTMS was as effective as ECT in nonpsychotic depression; the same pattern held against low-frequency rTMS. ECT's advantage on Hamilton score change was not significant (P = 0.11). Data on medium- and long-term efficacy were insufficient; results from 3 studies suggested visual memory and verbal fluency were more impaired after ECT.
cards.watchOut: The nonpsychotic subgroup finding — the result this shelf's question turns on — is a subgroup of small, heterogeneous trials, and the review itself flags the lack of good-quality long-term and cognitive comparisons; subgroup equivalence here is a signal, not a settled result.
cards.source: Ren J et al. Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation versus electroconvulsive therapy for major depression: a systematic review and meta-analysis.. cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT by population — comparable in nonpsychotic depression in the restricted trial and the meta-analysis subgroup; ECT superior in severe ECT-referred illness and overall
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT by population — comparable in nonpsychotic depression in the restricted trial and the meta-analysis subgroup; ECT superior in severe ECT-referred illness and overall
cards.people: The carded evidence: two randomised head-to-head trials (40 patients restricted to nonpsychotic depression; 46 patients with severe ECT-referred depression) and one meta-analysis of 9 trials (425 patients, overlapping the trial literature). Total carded participants exceed 30, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the trials are nonetheless small, which the stamp reflects.
cards.result: Nonpsychotic-restricted trial: response 12/20 versus 11/20 (the treatment made no difference). Severe ECT-referred trial: remission 59.1% versus 16.7% for ECT at end of treatment, converging by 6 months. Meta-analysis: ECT superior overall (relative risk 1.41 for response, 1.38 for remission) with rTMS as effective as ECT in the nonpsychotic subgroup. PROPOSED SPLIT (nonpsychotic, less severe: as effective on small-trial evidence; severe/psychotic-spectrum: ECT superior).
cards.watchOut: No carded trial was powered as an equivalence or non-inferiority trial in nonpsychotic depression: 'as effective' on this shelf means 'no difference detected in small trials and a subgroup analysis', which is weaker than proven equivalence.

shelves.title: Lamotrigine's polarity (PARTIAL completion of #1436, flagged): its maintenance benefit is preventing bipolar depression (hazard ratio 0.59), not mania (hazard ratio 0.91; worse than lithium for mania)
shelves.question: Is lamotrigine effective for prevention of bipolar depression rather than mania?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anticonvulsants/therapeutic use · Bipolar Disorder/drug therapy · Humans · Lamotrigine/adverse effects · Quality of Life · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1436, which covers lamotrigine maintenance against any mood episode (the Calabrese and Bowden 18-month trials) — and which already reports, on its cards, that lamotrigine's advantage in those trials was against depressive episodes. This shelf was nonetheless built under the one-home precedent for a genuinely different outcome cut, on three free reports that address the polarity question directly and are NOT carded on #1436; it is flagged prominently in the part summary for the developer's ruling. The pooled analysis of the two home trials (Goodwin 2004, PMID: 15096085) found lamotrigine superior to placebo for time to intervention for depression, with 'more robust activity against depression' than mania. A meta-analysis restricted to women of childbearing age across four maintenance trials (Vieta 2024, PMID: 37775363) found lamotrigine delayed intervention for depressive episodes (hazard ratio 0.59, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.90) with no difference for manic episodes (hazard ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.52 to 1.58 — the treatment made no difference for mania). The Cochrane review (Hashimoto 2021, PMID: 34523118) found the mirror image against lithium: manic recurrence at one year was higher on lamotrigine than lithium (relative risk 2.13, 95% CI 1.32 to 3.44), while its abstract reports no depression-specific pooled estimate. All underlying trials used enriched designs (randomising only patients stabilised on open-label lamotrigine), as disclosed on #1436. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit, for depression prevention specifically): lamotrigine maintenance prevents bipolar depressive episodes rather than manic ones — the polarity is consistent across the pooled analysis, the four-trial subgroup meta-analysis and the Cochrane comparison with lithium.

cards.headline: Goodwin 2004 (pooled analysis of the two 18-month trials): lamotrigine was superior to placebo for time to intervention for depression, with 'more robust activity against depression' than against mania — 638 randomised
cards.summary: Goodwin 2004 (pooled analysis of the two 18-month trials): lamotrigine was superior to placebo for time to intervention for depression, with 'more robust activity against depression' than against mania — 638 randomised
cards.type: Pooled analysis of two randomised maintenance trials (Goodwin 2004)
cards.people: Pooled analysis of two prospectively designed, placebo-controlled 18-month trials in bipolar I disorder (recently depressed or recently manic patients): 1,315 patients entered the open-label lamotrigine stabilisation phase and 638 stabilised patients were randomised to lamotrigine (n = 280), lithium (n = 167) or placebo (n = 191). These are the same two trials carded individually on live shelf #1436 — this card is their pooled re-analysis, a distinct publication, and is flagged as derivative in the part summary.
cards.result: Median time to intervention for any mood episode: 197 days on lamotrigine and 184 days on lithium versus 86 days on placebo. Lamotrigine was superior to placebo for time to intervention for depression (median survival not calculable for lamotrigine versus 270 days for placebo); both lithium and lamotrigine were superior to placebo for intervention for mania in the unadjusted analysis, but after adjustment for index mood only lithium remained superior for mania. The authors conclude lamotrigine was effective against depression and mania, with more robust activity against depression, while lithium was effective against mania. Diarrhoea (19% versus 7%) and tremor (15% versus 4%) were commoner on lithium than lamotrigine.
cards.watchOut: Derivative by construction: this is the #1436 trial pair re-analysed together, in an enriched design that randomised only patients who had already stabilised on open-label lamotrigine — it sharpens the polarity reading of the home trials but is not independent evidence for it.
cards.source: Goodwin GM et al. A pooled analysis of 2 placebo-controlled 18-month trials of lamotrigine and lithium maintenance in bipolar I disorder.. The Journal of clinical psychiatry. 2004. cards.headline: Vieta 2024: across four maintenance trials in women of childbearing age, lamotrigine delayed intervention for depressive episodes (hazard ratio 0.59) with no difference for manic episodes (hazard ratio 0.91) — 287 randomised
cards.summary: Vieta 2024: across four maintenance trials in women of childbearing age, lamotrigine delayed intervention for depressive episodes (hazard ratio 0.59) with no difference for manic episodes (hazard ratio 0.91) — 287 randomised
cards.type: Meta-analysis of four randomised maintenance trials, women subgroup (Vieta 2024)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of four randomised, placebo-controlled lamotrigine maintenance trials (up to 76 weeks, after up to 16 weeks of open-label lamotrigine), restricted to women aged 18–45 years with bipolar I disorder: 717 women entered the open-label phase and 287 responders were randomised (lamotrigine n = 153, placebo n = 134); the randomised group had averaged 2.0 manic and 2.5 depressive episodes in the 3 years before screening.
cards.result: Median time to intervention for any mood episode was 323 days on lamotrigine versus 127 days on placebo (hazard ratio 0.69, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.96; P = 0.030). Lamotrigine delayed time to intervention for a depressive episode (hazard ratio 0.59, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.90; P = 0.014), with no treatment difference for manic episodes (hazard ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.52 to 1.58; P = 0.732 — the treatment made no difference for mania). Serious rash-related adverse events occurred in 2 of 717 women (under 1%) during the open-label phase; adverse-event and withdrawal rates were similar between randomised groups.
cards.watchOut: A sex- and age-restricted subgroup pooling that includes the two #1436 trials plus two further maintenance studies, all enriched for lamotrigine responders: it is the cleanest depression-versus-mania contrast on this shelf, but its population (women 18–45) is narrower than the shelf's question.
cards.source: Vieta E et al. Lamotrigine efficacy, safety, and tolerability for women of childbearing age with bipolar I disorder: Meta-analysis from four randomized, placebo-controlled maintenance studies.. cards.headline: Hashimoto 2021 (Cochrane): lamotrigine beat placebo on recurrence outcomes, but manic recurrence at one year was higher on lamotrigine than on lithium (relative risk 2.13) — the polarity seen from the other side; no depression-specific pooled estimate in the record
cards.summary: Hashimoto 2021 (Cochrane): lamotrigine beat placebo on recurrence outcomes, but manic recurrence at one year was higher on lamotrigine than on lithium (relative risk 2.13) — the polarity seen from the other side; no depression-specific pooled estimate in the record
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (Cochrane; Hashimoto 2021)
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of lamotrigine maintenance treatment in bipolar disorder: 11 randomised studies with 2,314 participants (1,146 lamotrigine, 869 placebo, 299 lithium). All studies had at least one domain at unclear risk of bias, and five were at high risk of detection bias.
cards.result: Against placebo, the relative risk of recurrence of manic symptoms at one year was 0.67 (95% CI 0.51 to 0.87; 3 studies, 663 participants; low-certainty evidence) and of clinical worsening needing additional psychotropic treatment 0.82 (95% CI 0.70 to 0.98; 4 studies, 756 participants; moderate-certainty). The record's abstract reports no depression-specific pooled relative risk, and none is printed here. Against lithium, efficacy was similar overall except manic recurrence at one year, which was higher on lamotrigine (relative risk 2.13, 95% CI 1.32 to 3.44; 3 studies, 602 participants; moderate-certainty); adverse effects at 6–12 months were less frequent on lamotrigine than lithium (relative risk 0.70, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.96).
cards.watchOut: The review's headline placebo comparisons are for manic symptoms and overall worsening, not depression — its contribution to this shelf is the lithium contrast (lamotrigine clearly weaker against mania) and its bias warnings, which apply to every card here.
cards.source: Hashimoto Y et al. Lamotrigine in the maintenance treatment of bipolar disorder.. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2021. PMID: 34523118. systematic review of randomised trials (cochrane; hashimoto 2021) cochrane systematic review of lamotrigine maintenance treatment in bipolar disorder: 11 randomised studies with 2,314 participants (1,146 lamotrigine, 869 placebo, 299 lithium). all studies had at least one domain at unclear risk of bias, and five were at high risk of detection bias. against placebo, the relative risk of recurrence of manic symptoms at one year was 0.67 (95% ci 0.51 to 0.87; 3 studies, 663 participants; low-certainty evidence) and of clinical worsening needing additional psychotropic treatment 0.82 (95% ci 0.70 to 0.98; 4 studies, 756 participants; moderate-certainty). the record's abstract reports no depression-specific pooled relative risk, and none is printed here. against lithium, efficacy was similar overall except manic recurrence at one year, which was higher on lamotrigine (relative risk 2.13, 95% ci 1.32 to 3.44; 3 studies, 602 participants; moderate-certainty); adverse effects at 6–12 months were less frequent on lamotrigine than lithium (relative risk 0.70, 95% ci 0.51 to 0.96). the review's headline placebo comparisons are for manic symptoms and overall worsening, not depression — its contribution to this shelf is the lithium contrast (lamotrigine clearly weaker against mania) and its bias warnings, which apply to every card here. hashimoto y et al. lamotrigine in the maintenance treatment of bipolar disorder.. the cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2021. pmid: 34523118. registry id: nct00274677, nct00056277, nct00550407, nct00226135, nct01588457 (registry ids listed in the record). mesh: adult · anticonvulsants/therapeutic use · bipolar disorder/drug therapy · humans · lamotrigine/adverse effects · quality of life · randomized controlled trials as topic

cards.result: Depression: hazard ratio 0.59 (95% CI 0.39 to 0.90) for intervention for a depressive episode (Vieta 2024); lamotrigine superior to placebo for time to intervention for depression in the pooled analysis (Goodwin 2004). Mania: hazard ratio 0.91 (95% CI 0.52 to 1.58, the treatment made no difference) in Vieta 2024; manic recurrence higher on lamotrigine than lithium, relative risk 2.13 (95% CI 1.32 to 3.44), in the Cochrane review. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit, for bipolar depression prevention rather than mania prevention).
cards.watchOut: Every route back leads to the same enriched trials — patients randomised only after stabilising on open-label lamotrigine — so the polarity finding is consistent but not independently replicated in unenriched populations, and live shelf #1436 already carries the underlying trials with this same polarity reading.

shelves.title: Trauma-focused CBT vs EMDR for PTSD (PARTIAL, split): no consistent winner head-to-head — EMDR modestly ahead immediately in one meta-analysis, no difference in two others, exposure ahead in the one direct trial, and nothing between them at follow-up
shelves.question: Does trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy work better than EMDR for posttraumatic stress disorder?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Behavior Therapy/methods · Chronic Disease · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy/methods · Humans · Psychotherapy/methods · Psychotherapy, Group · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Stress Disorders, Post-Traumatic/psychology · Stress Disorders, Post-Traumatic/therapy
shelves.balance: SPLIT — PARTIAL completion of live shelf #2408. That shelf compares EMDR with an antidepressant (fluoxetine) and asks whether EMDR's gains persist; it does not card the psychotherapy head-to-head. This shelf covers the uncovered slice: trauma-focused CBT against EMDR in adults. The direct evidence genuinely divides. The adult Cochrane review found no statistically significant difference between individual trauma-focused CBT and EMDR immediately after treatment (both clearly better than waitlist/usual care), and graded that comparison very low quality (Bisson 2013). One direct meta-analysis of randomised trials found EMDR modestly better for post-traumatic symptoms immediately after treatment (standardised mean difference −0.43, 11 trials, n = 547) but not at 3-month follow-up (Khan 2018); a second found no difference for PTSD symptoms at treatment end or at 3- and 6-month follow-up (Hudays 2022). The one carded three-way randomised trial (N = 60) found exposure therapy — a trauma-focused CBT — produced larger reductions in avoidance and re-experiencing than EMDR, with EMDR no better than relaxation (Taylor 2003). No carded analysis shows either treatment ahead at follow-up. PROPOSED SPLIT (EMDR modestly ahead immediately in one meta-analysis; no difference in the Cochrane and second meta-analysis; exposure ahead on some symptoms in the single direct trial — and no difference at follow-up in any).

cards.headline: Bisson 2013 (Cochrane): no statistically significant difference between individual trauma-focused CBT and EMDR immediately after treatment in adults with chronic PTSD — both beat waitlist/usual care
cards.summary: Bisson 2013 (Cochrane): no statistically significant difference between individual trauma-focused CBT and EMDR immediately after treatment in adults with chronic PTSD — both beat waitlist/usual care
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (Bisson 2013)
cards.people: 70 randomised studies involving 4,761 participants with chronic post-traumatic stress disorder in adults, comparing individual trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy (TFCBT), EMDR, non-trauma-focused CBT, other therapies and group formats against one another or waitlist/usual care; the primary outcome was clinician-rated PTSD symptom severity.
cards.result: Individual TFCBT and EMDR were each more effective than waitlist/usual care (standardised mean difference −1.62; 95% CI −2.03 to −1.21; 28 studies, n = 1,256 for TFCBT, and SMD −1.17; 95% CI −2.04 to −0.30; 6 studies, n = 183 for EMDR — relative standardised effects, not absolute rates). There was no statistically significant difference between individual TFCBT, EMDR and stress management immediately post-treatment, although there was some evidence that individual TFCBT and EMDR were superior to non-trauma-focused CBT at follow-up. The reviewers assessed the quality of evidence for each comparison as very low, with many studies at high or unclear risk of bias and considerable unexplained heterogeneity.
cards.watchOut: The head-to-head TFCBT-versus-EMDR comparison inside this review rests on few, small trials, and the reviewers themselves graded every comparison very low quality — 'no significant difference' here is not proof the two treatments are equal.

cards.headline: Khan 2018: across 11 randomised trials (n = 547), EMDR reduced post-traumatic symptoms more than CBT immediately after treatment (standardised mean difference −0.43) — but the difference was gone at 3-month follow-up
cards.summary: Khan 2018: across 11 randomised trials (n = 547), EMDR reduced post-traumatic symptoms more than CBT immediately after treatment (standardised mean difference −0.43) — but the difference was gone at 3-month follow-up
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised clinical trials (Khan 2018)
cards.people: 14 randomised clinical trials comparing CBT with EMDR in patients with post-traumatic stress disorder (children, adolescents and adults in the eligible literature; 11 studies with 547 participants in the post-traumatic-symptom meta-analysis, and 4 studies with 186 participants at 3-month follow-up).
cards.result: EMDR was better than CBT in reducing post-traumatic symptoms immediately after treatment (standardised mean difference −0.43; 95% CI −0.73 to −0.12; P = 0.006; 11 studies, n = 547 — a relative standardised effect; the record prints no absolute symptom rates). At 3-month follow-up there was no statistically significant difference (SMD −0.21; 95% CI −0.50 to 0.08; P = 0.15; 4 studies, n = 186). EMDR was also better for anxiety (SMD −0.71; 95% CI −1.21 to −0.21; P = 0.005), with no difference for depression (SMD −0.21; 95% CI −0.44 to 0.02; P = 0.08). The authors recommend large randomised trials with longer follow-up.
cards.watchOut: This review's CBT comparator is broader than trauma-focused CBT alone, and its eligible trials span children and adults, so its immediate-treatment edge for EMDR cannot be read as an adult trauma-focused-CBT verdict; its own follow-up analysis finds no difference.

cards.headline: Hudays 2022: in 8 studies published 2010–2020, EMDR and CBT did not differ for PTSD symptoms (standardised mean difference −0.14, P = 0.44) — and did not differ at 3- or 6-month follow-up either
cards.summary: Hudays 2022: in 8 studies published 2010–2020, EMDR and CBT did not differ for PTSD symptoms (standardised mean difference −0.14, P = 0.44) — and did not differ at 3- or 6-month follow-up either
cards.people: 8 studies comparing EMDR with cognitive behavior therapy for post-traumatic stress disorder, anxiety and depression, drawn from a search of articles published between 2010 and 2020; the included studies covered children, adolescents and adults. The record does not print a pooled total participant number.
cards.result: For reducing PTSD symptoms, EMDR and CBT showed no statistically significant difference (standardised mean difference −0.14; 95% CI −0.48 to 0.21; P = 0.44 — a relative standardised effect). EMDR reduced depression symptoms more than CBT in three studies (SMD −2.43; 95% CI −3.93 to −0.94; P = 0.001) and anxiety more in three studies in children and adolescents (SMD −3.99; 95% CI −5.47 to −2.52; P < 0.001). At 3-month and 6-month follow-up there was no statistically significant difference for depression (P = 0.31), anxiety (P = 0.59) or PTSD (P = 0.55). The authors recommend randomised trials with larger samples and longer follow-up.
cards.watchOut: The depression and anxiety advantages come from three studies each and the anxiety result is in children and adolescents, not the adults this shelf asks about; the very large standardised effects (−2.43, −3.99) come from few studies and should not be quoted as adult effect sizes.

cards.headline: Taylor 2003: in the one carded three-way randomised trial (N = 60), exposure therapy — a trauma-focused CBT — beat EMDR on avoidance and re-experiencing symptoms; EMDR and relaxation did not differ
cards.summary: Taylor 2003: in the one carded three-way randomised trial (N = 60), exposure therapy — a trauma-focused CBT — beat EMDR on avoidance and re-experiencing symptoms; EMDR and relaxation did not differ
cards.people: 60 patients with posttraumatic stress disorder randomised to prolonged exposure (exposure therapy), EMDR, or relaxation training; efficacy, speed of response and incidence of symptom worsening were compared. N = 60 printed on the face.
cards.result: The treatments did not differ in attrition, in the incidence of symptom worsening, or in their effects on numbing and hyperarousal symptoms. Compared with EMDR and relaxation training, exposure therapy produced significantly larger reductions in avoidance and re-experiencing symptoms, tended to be faster at reducing avoidance, and tended to yield a greater proportion of participants who no longer met criteria for PTSD after treatment. EMDR and relaxation did not differ from one another in speed or efficacy. The record prints no effect sizes or percentages for these comparisons.
cards.watchOut: One small, single trial (N = 60) from 2003, and its trauma-focused arm is prolonged exposure specifically — it cannot by itself settle EMDR against the whole trauma-focused CBT family, and it points the opposite way from Khan 2018's pooled immediate-treatment result.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the head-to-head evidence divides — one meta-analysis gives EMDR a modest immediate edge, two find no difference, and the one three-way trial favours exposure therapy on some symptoms; at follow-up, nothing separates them
cards.summary: Synthesis: the head-to-head evidence divides — one meta-analysis gives EMDR a modest immediate edge, two find no difference, and the one three-way trial favours exposure therapy on some symptoms; at follow-up, nothing separates them
cards.people: The carded evidence: one Cochrane review of 70 studies (4,761 participants) in adults with chronic PTSD, two direct EMDR-versus-CBT meta-analyses (11 trials, n = 547; and 8 studies, pooled N not documented in the record), and one three-way randomised trial (N = 60). Total carded participants exceed 5,000 across the reviews and the trial, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the direct head-to-head subsets are much smaller than the review totals, which is printed on the cards.
cards.result: Cochrane found no statistically significant difference between individual trauma-focused CBT and EMDR immediately post-treatment, with both clearly better than waitlist/usual care, and graded the comparison very low quality (Bisson 2013). Khan 2018 found EMDR modestly better for post-traumatic symptoms immediately (standardised mean difference −0.43) but not at 3 months; Hudays 2022 found no difference for PTSD symptoms at treatment end or at 3- and 6-month follow-up. The single three-way trial found exposure therapy superior to EMDR for avoidance and re-experiencing, with EMDR no better than relaxation (Taylor 2003). PROPOSED SPLIT — the direct comparisons disagree, and no analysis shows either treatment ahead at follow-up.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote any single card as the answer: the split is the finding. The two meta-analyses that disagree (Khan 2018, Hudays 2022) both include children and broader CBT comparators, while the adult-specific Cochrane comparison and the one direct trial point to equivalence or an exposure edge.

shelves.title: Buprenorphine vs methadone for illicit opioid use (PARTIAL, split): no advantage in the randomised trials — positive-urine rates did not differ; only completer and non-randomised analyses favour buprenorphine
shelves.question: Does buprenorphine maintenance reduce illicit opioid use better than methadone?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Buprenorphine/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Male · Methadone/therapeutic use · Narcotic Antagonists/therapeutic use · Opioid-Related Disorders/rehabilitation · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — PARTIAL completion of live shelf #402. That shelf homes the two drugs' mortality comparison and cards the Cochrane review (Mattick 2014), whose retained-patient analysis already notes that suppression of illicit opioid use did not differ between the drugs; the review itself is NOT re-carded here. This shelf covers the uncovered slice — illicit opioid use as the primary question — from the free individual reports. In the largest randomised double-blind trial (405 patients, 13 weeks) there were no significant differences in morphine-positive urines or self-reported heroin use (Mattick 2003), and among completers of a second double-blind trial the drugs produced very similar outcomes on opioid-positive urines (Strain 1996). The reports tilting toward buprenorphine are weaker cuts: completers of a small open trial (N = 60) had lower illicit opiate consumption on buprenorphine (P = 0.04; Fischer 1999), and a non-randomised comparison (N = 154) found fewer illicit-opioid users on buprenorphine at week 12 (25.6% vs 32.1%; Gerra 2004). Retention favoured methadone where reported. FLAG for the developer: the anchor review is homed on #402, so this pack is built on the free individual trials under the standing precedent for genuinely different slices, with the home cross-pointed here and the review's PMID kept out of the card source lines. PROPOSED SPLIT (randomised trials: the treatment made no difference to illicit opioid use; completer and observational analyses tilt to buprenorphine).

cards.headline: Mattick 2003: in 405 patients, buprenorphine did not differ from methadone on morphine-positive urines or self-reported heroin use over 13 weeks — methadone retained patients longer
cards.summary: Mattick 2003: in 405 patients, buprenorphine did not differ from methadone on morphine-positive urines or self-reported heroin use over 13 weeks — methadone retained patients longer
cards.people: 405 opioid-dependent patients seeking treatment at three methadone clinics in Australia, randomised to buprenorphine or methadone with flexible dosing in a double-blind, double-dummy trial over 13 weeks; from weeks 7–13 buprenorphine patients received double their week-6 dose on alternate days. Illicit opioid use was determined by urinalysis, with self-reported drug use a secondary outcome.
cards.result: Intention-to-treat analyses revealed no significant difference in completion rates at 13 weeks, although methadone was superior to buprenorphine in time to termination over the 13-week period (Wald chi-square = 4.371, df = 1, P = 0.037). There were no significant between-group differences in morphine-positive urines, or in self-reported heroin or other illicit drug use (the treatment made no difference to illicit opioid use in this trial). The majority (85%) of buprenorphine patients transferred to alternate-day dosing were maintained on it. The record prints no percentages of positive urines by group.
cards.watchOut: This is the largest carded head-to-head trial and it is a null on the illicit-use outcome — but 13 weeks is short for maintenance treatment, and the authors suggest the poorer buprenorphine retention may reflect too-slow induction rather than the maintenance drug itself.

cards.headline: Strain 1996: among 86 patients who completed 16 weeks, buprenorphine and methadone produced very similar outcomes on opioid-positive urines and self-reported illicit opioid use
cards.summary: Strain 1996: among 86 patients who completed 16 weeks, buprenorphine and methadone produced very similar outcomes on opioid-positive urines and self-reported illicit opioid use
cards.people: Patients who completed the 16-week maintenance phase of a double-blind trial comparing buprenorphine (N = 43 completers; average dose 9.0 mg/day sublingually) with methadone (N = 43 completers; average dose 54 mg/day orally) in outpatient treatment of opioid dependence, with individual counselling, weekly group therapy and on-site medical services. Completer N = 86 printed on the face.
cards.result: Patients in both medication groups showed significant and substantial improvements over time in psychosocial functioning (Addiction Severity Index), rates of urinalysis tests positive for opioids, and self-reports of opioid withdrawal symptoms, illicit opioid use and cocaine use. Buprenorphine and methadone produced very similar outcomes on the wide array of outcome measures assessed, and improvements for both groups were large and occurred rapidly after treatment entry. A trend toward continued improvement in opioid-positive urines over time was noted for the buprenorphine but not the methadone group. The record prints no group percentages of positive urines.
cards.watchOut: A completer analysis: patients who dropped out — where the drugs may differ most — are excluded by design, so 'very similar outcomes' describes only the 86 patients who stayed 16 weeks.
cards.source: Strain EC et al. Buprenorphine versus methadone in the treatment of opioid dependence: self-reports, urinalysis, and addiction severity index. cards.headline: Fischer 1999: in 60 patients over 24 weeks, methadone retained significantly better — but patients completing on buprenorphine had significantly lower rates of illicit opiate consumption (P = 0.04)
cards.summary: Fischer 1999: in 60 patients over 24 weeks, methadone retained significantly better — but patients completing on buprenorphine had significantly lower rates of illicit opiate consumption (P = 0.04)
cards.people: 60 subjects (19 women and 41 men) meeting DSM-IV criteria for opioid dependence, randomised in an open comparative study at a Vienna drug addiction outpatient clinic to sublingual buprenorphine (2-mg or 8-mg tablets; maximum daily dose 8 mg) or oral methadone (maximum daily dose 80 mg) over 24 weeks, with a stable dose after a 6-day induction. Retention and illicit substance use (opiates, cocaine, benzodiazepines) were assessed by urinalysis. N = 60 printed on the face.
cards.result: The retention rate was significantly better in the methadone-maintained group (P < 0.05), but subjects completing the study in the buprenorphine group had significantly lower rates of illicit opiate consumption (P = 0.04). The authors conclude the results support the superiority of methadone for retention, while confirming buprenorphine as an alternative in maintenance therapy, suggesting a specific subgroup may benefit from buprenorphine. The record prints no percentages of positive urines by group.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, small (N = 60), and the illicit-use advantage is in completers only — the group from which methadone's retention advantage had already removed more buprenorphine patients; the buprenorphine dose ceiling (8 mg/day) is also below modern maintenance doses.
cards.source: Fischer G et al. Buprenorphine versus methadone maintenance for the treatment of opioid dependence. Addiction (Abingdon, England). 1999. PMID: 10615719. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Gerra 2004 (non-randomised, N = 154): at week 12, methadone patients were more likely to be using illicit opioids than buprenorphine patients (32.1% vs 25.6%, P < 0.05) — while overall positive-urine risk was similar
cards.summary: Gerra 2004 (non-randomised, N = 154): at week 12, methadone patients were more likely to be using illicit opioids than buprenorphine patients (32.1% vs 25.6%, P < 0.05) — while overall positive-urine risk was similar
cards.type: Non-randomised clinical comparison (Gerra 2004) — observational, printed on the face
cards.people: 154 applicants with severe long-lasting heroin addiction to a 12-week treatment programme, assigned in a clinical non-experimental setting to methadone (78; mean dose 81.5 ± 36.4 mg) or buprenorphine (76; mean dose 9.2 ± 3.4 mg); retention, abstinence from illicit drugs by urinalysis and mood changes were evaluated.
cards.result: Methadone patients showed a higher retention rate at week 4 (78.2% vs 65.8%; P < 0.05), but the treatments were equally effective for retention and compliance at week 12 (61.5% vs 59.2%). The risk of positive urine testing was similar between methadone and buprenorphine overall; at week 12, patients treated with methadone showed more risk of illicit opioid use than those treated with buprenorphine (32.1% vs 25.6%; P < 0.05 — absolute percentages as printed). Negative urines were associated with higher doses in both groups. The authors caution that the data need interpretation with care because of the observational, non-random procedure.
cards.watchOut: Not randomised: clinicians and patients chose the drug in routine care, so the week-12 difference may reflect who was given which drug rather than the drugs; it is carded as the only carded report giving absolute positive-urine percentages, labelled observational on its face.
cards.source: Gerra G et al. Buprenorphine versus methadone for opioid dependence: predictor variables for treatment outcome. Drug and alcohol dependence. 2004. PMID: 15225887. cards.headline: Synthesis: buprenorphine does not reduce illicit opioid use better than methadone in the randomised trials — the two double-blind trials found no difference; only completer and non-randomised analyses tilt toward buprenorphine
cards.summary: Synthesis: buprenorphine does not reduce illicit opioid use better than methadone in the randomised trials — the two double-blind trials found no difference; only completer and non-randomised analyses tilt toward buprenorphine
cards.people: The carded evidence: two randomised double-blind trials (405 patients over 13 weeks; 86 completers over 16 weeks), one small randomised open trial (60 patients over 24 weeks), and one non-randomised clinical comparison (154 patients over 12 weeks). Unique participants total 705 across the four reports, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: In the largest trial there were no significant between-group differences in morphine-positive urines or self-reported heroin use (Mattick 2003), and among completers of the second double-blind trial the two drugs produced very similar outcomes on opioid-positive urines (Strain 1996). The tilts toward buprenorphine come from weaker cuts of the data: completers of a small open trial had lower illicit opiate consumption on buprenorphine (P = 0.04; Fischer 1999), and a non-randomised comparison found fewer illicit-opioid users on buprenorphine at week 12 (25.6% vs 32.1%; Gerra 2004). Retention, where reported, favoured methadone. PROPOSED SPLIT (randomised trials: the treatment made no difference to illicit opioid use; completer and observational analyses: fewer positive urines on buprenorphine).
cards.watchOut: The pattern to notice: the cleaner the design, the smaller the buprenorphine advantage — randomised intention-to-treat analyses are null, and the favourable results appear only after dropouts (who differ by drug) are removed or when treatment was chosen clinically.
cards.source: Synthesis of Mattick RP et al. Addiction (Abingdon, England). 2003 (PMID: 12653814); Strain EC et al. Journal of clinical psychopharmacology. 1996 (PMID: 8834420); Fischer G et al. Addiction (Abingdon, England). 1999 (PMID: 10615719); Gerra G et al. Drug and alcohol dependence. 2004 (PMID: 15225887).

shelves.title: Magnesium for menstrual migraine (partial completion of #2442): one small 1991 trial of magnesium pyrrolidone carboxylic acid favours benefit — weak, unreplicated evidence, named preparations on the face
shelves.question: Does magnesium supplementation reduce migraine frequency in women with menstrual migraine?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Magnesium · Menstrual Cycle · Migraine Disorders · Surveys and Questionnaires
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #2442, which covers magnesium (the Peikert trial) for migraine prevention in people with migraine generally; this shelf asks the menstrual-migraine slice in women, which #2442 does not separate out. The direct evidence is a single small trial. Facchinetti 1991 randomised 20 women with menstrual migraine to magnesium pyrrolidone carboxylic acid — the exact tested preparation named in the record — 360 mg/day from day 15 of the cycle until the next menses, or placebo: headache days fell only on active treatment and the pain index was lowest on magnesium. The supporting cards are adjacent, and are labelled as such: ionised magnesium deficiency was found in 45% of women during menstrual attacks (Mauskop 2002, observational — a mechanism signal, not a treatment result), and the same preparation improved premenstrual symptoms in a 32-woman randomised trial (Facchinetti 1991, Obstetrics and Gynecology), as did a named modified-release product, Sincromag 250 mg, in a 41-woman open pilot (Quaranta 2007) — neither of those two trials measured migraine frequency. Supplement rule applied: the tested preparations are named exactly as the publications give them (magnesium pyrrolidone carboxylic acid; Sincromag modified-release magnesium 250 mg tablet); no other carded record names a brand or formulation beyond its salt, and current shop products may differ from these preparations. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): one 20-woman double-blind trial favours cycle-timed magnesium for menstrual migraine, and everything else carded is mechanism or premenstrual-symptom evidence — the slice is real but thin, and no larger or modern trial was found in PubMed this session.

cards.headline: Facchinetti 1991: in the only direct trial found — 20 women with menstrual migraine (N printed on the face) — magnesium pyrrolidone carboxylic acid 360 mg/day from cycle day 15 to menses cut headache days, while placebo did not
cards.summary: Facchinetti 1991: in the only direct trial found — 20 women with menstrual migraine (N printed on the face) — magnesium pyrrolidone carboxylic acid 360 mg/day from cycle day 15 to menses cut headache days, while placebo did not
cards.people: 20 patients with menstrual migraine in a double-blind, placebo-controlled study. After a two-cycle run-in, treatment with magnesium pyrrolidone carboxylic acid (the preparation named in the record) 360 mg/day or placebo started on the 15th day of the cycle and continued until the next menses, for two months; oral magnesium was then supplemented in an open design for the next two months. Randomised N = 20.
cards.result: At the second month, the Pain Total Index decreased on both placebo and magnesium, with patients on active drug showing the lowest values (P < 0.03). The number of days with headache was reduced only in the patients on active drug. Magnesium treatment also improved premenstrual complaints (significant reduction in Menstrual Distress Questionnaire scores), and the reductions were also observed at the fourth month, when magnesium was supplemented in all patients. Intracellular magnesium was lower in menstrual-migraine patients than controls and rose in lymphocytes and polymorphonuclear cells during oral treatment; no exact headache-day counts or effect size are reported in the record.
cards.watchOut: Twenty women, two blinded cycles, 1991: this single small trial is the entire direct evidence base for the question, the pain index also fell on placebo, and no effect size is printed in the record — the stamp is capped at MAYBE (weak evidence) for exactly these reasons.
cards.source: Facchinetti F et al. Magnesium prophylaxis of menstrual migraine: effects on intracellular magnesium. Headache. 1991. PMID: 1860787. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Mauskop 2002: ionised magnesium deficiency in 45% of women during menstrual attacks versus 14–15% at other times — an observational mechanism signal, not a treatment trial (61 women with menstrual migraine measured)
cards.summary: Mauskop 2002: ionised magnesium deficiency in 45% of women during menstrual attacks versus 14–15% at other times — an observational mechanism signal, not a treatment trial (61 women with menstrual migraine measured)
cards.people: Prospective observational study: 270 women seen at a headache clinic were evaluated, and in 61 women with menstrual migraine ionised magnesium, total magnesium and ionised calcium levels were measured to calculate the ionised calcium/ionised magnesium ratio, during menstrual attacks, non-menstrual attacks, menstruation without migraine, and between menstruations and attacks.
cards.result: The incidences of ionised magnesium deficiency were 45% during menstrual attacks, 15% during non-menstrual attacks, 14% during menstruation without a migraine, and 15% between menstruations and between migraine attacks. Serum ionised calcium levels were within the reference range, but the ionised calcium/ionised magnesium ratio was elevated (P < .01) in menstrual migraine. The authors conclude the findings support a possible role for magnesium deficiency in the development of menstrual migraine. No supplementation was given and no migraine-frequency outcome was measured.
cards.watchOut: Low measured magnesium during attacks may be a correlate or a consequence of the attack rather than its cause; this card explains why the question is asked and must never be cited as evidence that supplementation works.
cards.source: Mauskop A et al. Serum ionized magnesium levels and serum ionized calcium/ionized magnesium ratios in women with menstrual migraine. Headache. 2002. PMID: 12010379. cards.headline: Facchinetti 1991 (premenstrual syndrome): the same preparation — magnesium pyrrolidone carboxylic acid, 360 mg three times a day as printed in the record — beat placebo on total premenstrual symptom and negative-affect scores in 32 women; migraine frequency was not measured
cards.summary: Facchinetti 1991 (premenstrual syndrome): the same preparation — magnesium pyrrolidone carboxylic acid, 360 mg three times a day as printed in the record — beat placebo on total premenstrual symptom and negative-affect scores in 32 women; migraine frequency was not measured
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, premenstrual symptoms (Facchinetti 1991)
cards.people: 32 women aged 24–39 years with premenstrual syndrome confirmed by the Moos Menstrual Distress Questionnaire, in a double-blind randomised design: after two months of baseline recording, participants were randomly assigned to placebo or magnesium for two cycles, and in the next two cycles both groups received magnesium. Magnesium pyrrolidone carboxylic acid (360 mg magnesium, as printed in the record) or placebo was administered three times a day from the 15th day of the menstrual cycle to the onset of menstrual flow.
cards.result: The Menstrual Distress Questionnaire 'pain' cluster score fell significantly during the second month in both groups, whereas magnesium treatment significantly affected both the total Menstrual Distress Questionnaire score and the 'negative affect' cluster. In the second month, women on treatment showed a significant increase in magnesium in lymphocytes and polymorphonuclear cells, with no changes in plasma or erythrocytes. The authors conclude magnesium supplementation could represent an effective treatment of premenstrual symptoms related to mood changes. Migraine frequency was not an outcome of this trial.

cards.headline: Quaranta 2007: a named product — Sincromag, a patented modified-release magnesium 250 mg tablet — lowered total premenstrual symptom scores by about a third in a 41-woman open-label pilot; no control group, no migraine outcome
cards.summary: Quaranta 2007: a named product — Sincromag, a patented modified-release magnesium 250 mg tablet — lowered total premenstrual symptom scores by about a third in a 41-woman open-label pilot; no control group, no migraine outcome
cards.people: Open-label pilot study of 41 women aged 18–45 years with regular menstrual cycles (25–35 days) and premenstrual syndrome (score above 25 on a premenstrual syndrome questionnaire). After a three-month observational period, participants took the modified-release magnesium 250 mg tablet (Sincromag, the product named in the record) over three menstrual cycles, beginning 20 days after the start of the last menstrual period and continuing until the start of the next menstrual period.
cards.result: After three months, the mean total premenstrual syndrome score (investigator-assessed, Moos' Modified Menstrual Distress Questionnaire) was significantly lower than before therapy (P < .0001), as were patient-diary scores (P < .0001 for all subscales). The relative decreases in total scores were 35.1% (investigator) and 33.5% (patient) — relative changes from baseline in an uncontrolled study, printed as such. The tablet was well tolerated, with vertigo the only treatment-related adverse event (one patient). The authors call the study preliminary. Migraine frequency was not measured.
cards.watchOut: Uncontrolled and open-label: symptom scores commonly fall by a third on attention alone in premenstrual studies, and this product-specific result cannot be transferred to other magnesium salts or doses, which may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Quaranta S et al. Pilot study of the efficacy and safety of a modified-release magnesium 250 mg tablet (Sincromag) for the treatment of premenstrual syndrome. cards.headline: Synthesis: one 20-woman double-blind trial favours cycle-timed magnesium pyrrolidone carboxylic acid for menstrual migraine; the rest of the carded record is a deficiency signal and premenstrual-symptom trials — the slice is real, and thin
cards.summary: Synthesis: one 20-woman double-blind trial favours cycle-timed magnesium pyrrolidone carboxylic acid for menstrual migraine; the rest of the carded record is a deficiency signal and premenstrual-symptom trials — the slice is real, and thin
cards.people: The carded evidence: one direct randomised trial in menstrual migraine (N = 20), one observational magnesium-level study (61 women with menstrual migraine measured, of 270 evaluated), and two adjacent premenstrual-syndrome studies of named preparations (N = 32 randomised; N = 41 open-label). Total documented participants exceed 30, so no small-N stamp labelling applies to the shelf as a whole; the direct trial's N = 20 is printed on its face, and it alone caps the stamp.
cards.result: Headache days fell only on active magnesium in the direct trial, with the lowest pain index on magnesium (Facchinetti 1991, Headache); ionised magnesium deficiency clustered in menstrual attacks (45% versus 14–15%; Mauskop 2002); and the same or named preparations improved premenstrual symptom scores (Facchinetti 1991, Obstetrics and Gynecology; Quaranta 2007). General migraine prevention with magnesium stays on live shelf #2442. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — a single small direct trial, unreplicated in PubMed as of this session.
cards.watchOut: A reader who needs a number for migraine frequency will not find one here: the direct trial reports direction and a P value, not counts — and two of the four cards answer a neighbouring question (premenstrual symptoms), which is printed on their faces rather than smoothed over.

shelves.title: Hearing aids, quality of life and cognition in older adults (PARTIAL completion of live #350): quality of life improves; a cognitive benefit is unproven in trials
shelves.question: Do hearing aids improve quality of life and cognition in older adults with hearing loss?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Analysis of Variance · Communication · Comorbidity · Hearing Aids · Hearing Loss · Hearing Loss, Conductive · Hearing Loss, Sensorineural · Humans · Male · Patient Compliance · Patient Dropouts · Quality of Life · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the two halves of the question have different answers. Quality of life: hearing aids consistently improve hearing-specific quality of life (Cochrane pooling: Hearing Handicap Inventory difference −26.47 points) and general quality of life by a smaller amount, in trials and reviews spanning 1990–2017. Cognition: the only randomised cognitive-function signal is a small subscale improvement inside the 1990 Mulrow trial; the large pooled association (19% lower hazard of cognitive decline in hearing-aid users) comes from observational studies, labelled observational here, and the one large randomised cognition trial — ACHIEVE — is homed on live shelf #350, where its primary result was null, and is not re-carded on this shelf. This pack is a PARTIAL completion of #350: it answers the quality-of-life question that shelf does not ask, and gathers the non-ACHIEVE cognition evidence without duplicating the homed trial.

cards.headline: Mulrow 1990 randomised trial: hearing aids improved social/emotional function (+34.0), communication (+24.2), a cognitive-function score (+0.28, P = 0.008) and depression at 4 months in 194 elderly veterans
cards.summary: Mulrow 1990 randomised trial: hearing aids improved social/emotional function (+34.0), communication (+24.2), a cognitive-function score (+0.28, P = 0.008) and depression at 4 months in 194 elderly veterans
cards.people: 194 elderly veterans identified as hearing-impaired from a screening survey of 771 consecutive primary-care clinic patients, randomised to receive a hearing aid (n = 95) or join a waiting list (n = 99); 188 (97%) completed the trial, with disease-specific and generic quality-of-life measures at baseline, 6 weeks and 4 months. Average self-reported daily aid use was 8 hours.
cards.result: Compared with the waiting list, the hearing-aid group showed significant score improvements in social and emotional function (34.0; 95% CI 27.3–40.8; P < 0.0001), communication function (24.2; 95% CI 17.2–31.2; P < 0.0001), cognitive function (0.28; 95% CI 0.08–0.48; P = 0.008) and depression (0.80; 95% CI 0.09–1.51; P = 0.03). At baseline, 82% of subjects had reported adverse effects of hearing impairment on quality of life and 24% were depressed; the authors concluded those effects are reversible with hearing aids.
cards.watchOut: An unblinded waiting-list comparison in male veterans with 1990-era aids: expectation and attention effects can inflate self-reported gains, and the 'cognitive function' result is one self-rated subscale over 4 months — not a dementia or objective-cognition outcome.
cards.source: Mulrow CD et al. Quality-of-life changes and hearing impairment. A randomized trial. Annals of internal medicine. 1990. PMID: 2197909. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cochrane 2017 (Ferguson): hearing aids produced a large benefit on hearing-specific quality of life (HHIE −26.47 points) and a small benefit on general quality of life (SMD −0.38) across 5 RCTs
cards.summary: Cochrane 2017 (Ferguson): hearing aids produced a large benefit on hearing-specific quality of life (HHIE −26.47 points) and a small benefit on general quality of life (SMD −0.38) across 5 RCTs
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials, Cochrane (Ferguson 2017)
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of randomised controlled trials of hearing aids versus passive or active control in adults with mild to moderate hearing loss: 5 RCTs, 825 participants, conducted in the USA and Europe (1987–2017), average ages 69–83, follow-up six weeks to six months.
cards.result: Hearing aids had a large beneficial effect on hearing-specific health-related quality of life (participation in daily life, Hearing Handicap Inventory for the Elderly, scale 1–100) versus the unaided/placebo condition (mean difference −26.47, 95% CI −42.16 to −10.77; 722 participants, 3 studies; moderate-quality evidence), a small beneficial effect on general health-related quality of life (standardised mean difference −0.38, 95% CI −0.55 to −0.21; 568 participants, 2 studies; moderate-quality evidence), and a large beneficial effect on listening ability (standardised mean difference −1.88, 95% CI −3.24 to −0.52; 534 participants, 2 studies). Adverse effects were measured in only one study (48 participants) and none were reported.
cards.watchOut: Blinding was inadequate or absent in most included trials (high risk of performance and detection bias), follow-up was at most six months, and the population is mild-to-moderate loss in people who sought help — not the severely impaired or the screening-detected.
cards.source: Ferguson MA et al. Hearing aids for mild to moderate hearing loss in adults. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2017. PMID: 28944461. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Chisolm 2007 (American Academy of Audiology task force review): hearing aids had medium-to-large effects on disease-specific quality of life and small effects on generic measures across 16 studies
cards.summary: Chisolm 2007 (American Academy of Audiology task force review): hearing aids had medium-to-large effects on disease-specific quality of life and small effects on generic measures across 16 studies
cards.people: Systematic review with meta-analysis of 16 studies (randomised, quasi-experimental and pre-post designs) of hearing aids for health-related quality of life in adults with sensorineural hearing loss.
cards.result: Disease-specific instruments showed small-to-medium effects in within-subject designs and medium-to-large effects in between-subject designs, while generic measures showed at least a small effect in between-subject studies but no demonstrated benefit in within-subject designs. The task force concluded that hearing aids improve adults' health-related quality of life by reducing the psychological, social and emotional effects of sensorineural hearing loss, and called for future studies with control groups using randomised designs.
cards.watchOut: Much of the underlying evidence is pre-post without a control group, so part of the measured gain may reflect fitting attention and expectation; the generic quality-of-life signal is inconsistent across designs, which is why this shelf claims the hearing-specific benefit most strongly.
cards.source: Chisolm TH et al. cards.headline: Yeo 2023 meta-analysis: hearing-aid use was associated with a 19% lower hazard of cognitive decline (HR 0.81) — observational evidence, labelled as such
cards.summary: Yeo 2023 meta-analysis: hearing-aid use was associated with a 19% lower hazard of cognitive decline (HR 0.81) — observational evidence, labelled as such
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, predominantly observational (Yeo 2023)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of hearing restorative devices (hearing aids and cochlear implants) and cognition: 31 studies (25 observational, 6 trials) with 137,484 participants; the long-term cognitive-decline pooling covered 8 studies with 126,903 participants followed 2–25 years, and the short-term cognitive-test pooling covered 11 studies with 568 participants.
cards.result: Hearing-aid users had significantly lower hazards of any cognitive decline than participants with uncorrected hearing loss (hazard ratio 0.81, 95% CI 0.76–0.87; I² = 0%) — a 19% relative reduction in hazard, from predominantly observational data in which people who obtain and wear aids differ from those who do not. Short-term cognitive test scores improved by 3% after hearing restoration (ratio of means 1.03, 95% CI 1.02–1.04). The authors state a cognitive benefit should be further investigated in randomized trials; the largest such trial is homed on live shelf #350 and is not carded here.
cards.watchOut: Observational: hearing-aid users are wealthier, healthier and more engaged than non-users with the same audiogram, and no adjustment removes that confounding by indication; the pooled devices also mix hearing aids with cochlear implants. This card must not be quoted as trial proof that aids prevent dementia.
cards.source: Yeo BSY et al. Association of Hearing Aids and Cochlear Implants With Cognitive Decline and Dementia: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. JAMA neurology. 2023. PMID: 36469314. cards.headline: Synthesis: quality of life — yes, consistently; cognition — unproven in randomised trials: SPLIT
cards.summary: Synthesis: quality of life — yes, consistently; cognition — unproven in randomised trials: SPLIT
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised trial (Mulrow 1990, n = 194), two systematic reviews of quality of life (Ferguson 2017, 5 RCTs, 825 participants; Chisolm 2007, 16 studies), and one predominantly observational cognition meta-analysis (Yeo 2023, 137,484 participants). Total carded participants exceed 30, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Quality-of-life outcomes favour hearing aids in every carded source (HHIE −26.47 points pooled; social/emotional +34.0 and communication +24.2 in the randomised trial; medium-to-large disease-specific effects in the task-force review). Cognitive outcomes rest on a small self-rated subscale gain in one 1990 trial and an observational hazard ratio of 0.81; the dedicated randomised cognition trial is homed on live shelf #350 (primary result null) and is deliberately not re-carded here. PROPOSED SPLIT: quality-of-life benefit supported; cognitive benefit not established by randomised evidence.
cards.watchOut: Do not merge the halves: 'hearing aids help people live better with hearing loss' is trial-supported; 'hearing aids prevent cognitive decline' is, on current carded evidence, an observational association awaiting randomised confirmation.

shelves.title: Adjunctive corticosteroid in herpes simplex encephalitis: DexEnceph published null — verbal memory 71 versus 69 — with a null pooled estimate and a null 3,933-patient cohort
shelves.question: In adults with herpes simplex encephalitis, does adjunctive corticosteroid improve outcomes versus acyclovir alone?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Dexamethasone · Male · Female · Encephalitis, Herpes Simplex · Adult · Middle Aged · Acyclovir · Antiviral Agents · United Kingdom · Single-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Treatment Outcome · Aged · Young Adult · Anti-Inflammatory Agents
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — adjunctive corticosteroid made no difference to the outcomes measured, in the one completed phase 3 trial and in the pooled and nationwide evidence around it. Publication status was verified this session before carding: the DexEnceph randomised trial has now published its results (Lancet Neurology, 2026). DexEnceph randomised 94 adults with herpes simplex virus encephalitis in 53 UK hospitals to dexamethasone plus acyclovir or acyclovir alone; the primary outcome, verbal memory score at 26 weeks, was 71 versus 69 (adjusted difference 1.77, 95% CI −9.57 to 13.12; P = 0.76) — the treatment made no difference — with similar adverse-event rates and no treatment-related deaths. The 2026 meta-analysis of all comparative studies (four studies, 209 patients) found the randomised pooled estimates likewise centred on no effect: unfavourable outcome relative risk 1.00 (95% CI 0.68–1.47) and mortality relative risk 0.92 (95% CI 0.35–2.40), while the retrospective estimates conflicted and were seriously confounded. The largest single dataset, a Japanese nationwide retrospective cohort of 3,933 patients, found adjusted in-hospital mortality of 4.2% with early corticosteroid versus 3.2% without (difference 1.0%, 95% CI −0.6% to 2.1%), no difference in consciousness or functional independence at discharge, and a longer hospital stay in the steroid group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: routine adjunctive corticosteroid is not supported — the trial was small and dexamethasone began a median 7 days after admission, so an earlier-treatment benefit is not excluded, only undemonstrated.

cards.headline: DexEnceph 2026: dexamethasone plus acyclovir made no difference to verbal memory at 26 weeks — scores 71 versus 69 (adjusted difference 1.77, P = 0.76)
cards.summary: DexEnceph 2026: dexamethasone plus acyclovir made no difference to verbal memory at 26 weeks — scores 71 versus 69 (adjusted difference 1.77, P = 0.76)
cards.people: 94 adults (aged 16 years or older) with herpes simplex virus encephalitis — positive HSV type 1 or 2 PCR in cerebrospinal fluid — admitted to 53 hospitals in the UK, randomised to intravenous dexamethasone four times daily for 4 days plus intravenous acyclovir for at least 14 days (47 patients) or intravenous acyclovir alone (47 patients); 81 patients (39 dexamethasone, 42 control) were in the modified intention-to-treat analysis after withdrawals and losses to follow-up. Dexamethasone was started a median 7 days (IQR 4–8) after hospital admission.
cards.result: The primary outcome, verbal memory score at 26 weeks on the Wechsler Memory Scale-IV auditory memory index, did not differ significantly between groups: 71 (SD 26) in the dexamethasone group versus 69 (SD 25) in the control group (adjusted difference 1.77, 95% CI −9.57 to 13.12; P = 0.76) — the treatment made no difference. Adverse events involved 18 participants (40%) in the dexamethasone group and 18 (38%) in the control group; there were no treatment-related deaths. The authors conclude dexamethasone had a satisfactory safety profile but did not improve verbal memory compared with acyclovir alone.
cards.watchOut: A rare-disease trial of 94 patients: the confidence interval (−9.57 to 13.12 points) cannot exclude a clinically meaningful benefit or harm, and dexamethasone began a median 7 days after admission — this tests late adjunctive steroid, not steroid given at first suspicion of encephalitis.
cards.source: Solomon T et al. cards.headline: Zhang 2026 meta-analysis: across all four comparative studies (209 patients), the randomised pooled estimates centred on no effect — unfavourable outcome relative risk 1.00, mortality relative risk 0.92
cards.summary: Zhang 2026 meta-analysis: across all four comparative studies (209 patients), the randomised pooled estimates centred on no effect — unfavourable outcome relative risk 1.00, mortality relative risk 0.92
cards.type: Meta-analysis of randomised and observational studies (Zhang 2026)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of randomised trials and comparative observational studies of systemic corticosteroids added to antiviral therapy (acyclovir in all studies that specified the regimen) versus the same antiviral therapy alone in herpes simplex virus encephalitis; four comparative studies with 209 patients in total (two randomised trials and two retrospective studies), searched to July 2026.
cards.result: Across the randomised trials, pooled estimates showed no difference in unfavourable global outcome (relative risk 1.00, 95% CI 0.68–1.47), mortality (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.35–2.40), serious adverse events (RR 1.14, 95% CI 0.54–2.44), or seizures during follow-up (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.33–1.62); Barthel Index results were likewise inconclusive and cognitive findings were not consistently favourable. The retrospective estimates conflicted and were seriously compromised by confounding. In DexEnceph, HSV DNA remained detectable at about day 14 in 4 of 36 dexamethasone recipients versus 9 of 43 controls, and five relapses were reported with dexamethasone versus none with control — too few events for a causal conclusion.
cards.watchOut: The meta-analysis overlaps the DexEnceph card — it pools that trial with one other small randomised trial and two retrospective studies — so it is a consistency check on the whole literature, not independent evidence added to DexEnceph's 94 patients.
cards.source: Zhang D et al. Adjunctive corticosteroids in herpes simplex virus encephalitis: a meta-analysis of randomized and observational studies. Journal of neurology. 2026. PMID: 42704513. Registry ID: none in the record.
