cards.headline: Shinmoto 2026 nationwide cohort: in 3,933 patients, early corticosteroid was not associated with lower mortality (adjusted 4.2% versus 3.2%) or better function — and stay was 5.9 days longer
cards.summary: Shinmoto 2026 nationwide cohort: in 3,933 patients, early corticosteroid was not associated with lower mortality (adjusted 4.2% versus 3.2%) or better function — and stay was 5.9 days longer
cards.people: Retrospective cohort from the Japanese national inpatient database: 3,933 patients hospitalised with herpes simplex encephalitis who received intravenous acyclovir within 2 days of admission (mean age 58.9 years; 58.1% male); 1,385 received intravenous corticosteroids at a prednisolone-equivalent dose of at least 30 mg/day within 2 days of admission and 2,548 received acyclovir alone. Outcomes were compared with multivariable adjustment.
cards.result: Adjusted in-hospital mortality was 4.2% in the corticosteroid group versus 3.2% in the acyclovir-alone group (difference 1.0%, 95% CI −0.6% to 2.1%); discharge with full consciousness was 75.3% versus 75.0% (difference 0.3%, 95% CI −2.6% to 2.6%) and discharge with functional independence 62.7% versus 61.9% (difference 0.8%, 95% CI −1.8% to 3.7%) — no significant differences. Adjusted hospital stay was longer with corticosteroid (35.5 versus 29.6 days; difference 5.9 days, 95% CI 3.8–8.0) and costs were higher. The authors conclude early adjunctive corticosteroid was not associated with lower mortality or better functional outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Observational and exposed to confounding by indication — steroids are likelier to be given to patients who look worse — but the adjusted estimates still show no hint of the benefit the treatment is given for, in by far the largest population studied.
cards.source: Shinmoto K et al. In-Hospital Outcomes of Acyclovir With or Without Corticosteroid for Herpes Simplex Encephalitis: A Nationwide Retrospective Cohort Study. Neurology. Clinical practice. 2026. PMID: 42913452. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: adjunctive corticosteroid in herpes simplex encephalitis — a null phase 3 trial, a null pooled estimate, and a null 3,933-patient cohort
cards.summary: Synthesis: adjunctive corticosteroid in herpes simplex encephalitis — a null phase 3 trial, a null pooled estimate, and a null 3,933-patient cohort
cards.people: The carded evidence: the DexEnceph randomised phase 3 trial (94 patients), a meta-analysis of all four comparative studies (209 patients, overlapping DexEnceph), and a Japanese nationwide retrospective cohort (3,933 patients).
cards.result: Verbal memory at 26 weeks did not differ in the trial (71 versus 69; adjusted difference 1.77, 95% CI −9.57 to 13.12 — the treatment made no difference); the randomised pooled relative risk for unfavourable outcome was 1.00 (95% CI 0.68–1.47); and adjusted mortality in the nationwide cohort was 4.2% with steroid versus 3.2% without (difference 1.0%, 95% CI −0.6% to 2.1%), with no functional advantage and a longer stay. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: adjunctive corticosteroid added to acyclovir has not been shown to improve outcomes in herpes simplex encephalitis, and routine use is not supported by the evidence now available.
cards.watchOut: The honest boundary: DexEnceph started dexamethasone a median 7 days after admission and enrolled only 94 patients, so a benefit from steroid given immediately, or in a selected subgroup, remains untested rather than disproven.

shelves.title: Fremanezumab for episodic and chronic migraine (drug-specific slice; HALO primaries homed on live #336): sustained migraine-day reductions over 52 weeks and pooled disability benefit versus placebo, built on free long-term and pooled reports
shelves.question: Does fremanezumab reduce monthly migraine days in episodic and chronic migraine versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Antibodies, Monoclonal/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Migraine Disorders/drug therapy,prevention & control · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: FLAG — PRECEDENT (b), documented prominently: the two primary HALO trials (HALO EM, Dodick 2018; HALO CM, Silberstein 2017) are already carded with their figures on live shelf #336, the CGRP-class shelf, so under the one-home rule their PMIDs are NOT re-carded here and do not appear in any card source line on this shelf. This fremanezumab-specific shelf is built instead on three or more free, distinct reports of the same programme, as the genuinely different drug-specific slice. On those reports: over 52 weeks in a randomised long-term study of 1,890 patients, fremanezumab reduced monthly migraine days from baseline by 7.2 days (chronic, quarterly) and 8.0 days (chronic, monthly) and by 5.2 and 5.1 days in episodic migraine, with injection-site reactions the commonest adverse events (induration 33%, pain 31%, erythema 26%) — a within-treatment long-term study, not a placebo comparison (Goadsby 2020). The placebo-controlled benefit is carried by the pooled phase 3 analyses: clinically meaningful disability improvement (≥5-point HIT-6 reduction) in 53% (quarterly) and 55% (monthly) versus 39% on placebo, with MIDAS responder proportions also significantly higher (McAllister 2022, pooling HALO EM, HALO CM and FOCUS, 2,842 patients in the companion safety pooling); overall adverse events occurred in 58–65% and serious adverse events in under 1–2% across fremanezumab and placebo groups, with cardio- and cerebrovascular events infrequent at 2–6% regardless of vascular history (Diener 2022). Among patients who responded in the HALO trials, ≥50% reductions in monthly migraine days were achieved by 59.8–63.7% of episodic responders and 52.8–59.0% of chronic responders (Silberstein 2021, post hoc). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single drug programme whose primary trials are homed on the class shelf — the drug-specific evidence is consistent and placebo-controlled in its pooled form, but this shelf's own cards are a long-term study, pooled analyses and a post hoc responder analysis, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE rather than upgraded on the homed primaries.

cards.headline: Goadsby 2020: over 52 weeks in 1,890 patients, fremanezumab reduced monthly migraine days by 7.2–8.0 days in chronic migraine and 5.1–5.2 days in episodic migraine; injection-site reactions were the commonest adverse events
cards.summary: Goadsby 2020: over 52 weeks in 1,890 patients, fremanezumab reduced monthly migraine days by 7.2–8.0 days in chronic migraine and 5.1–5.2 days in episodic migraine; injection-site reactions were the commonest adverse events
cards.people: 1,890 adults with chronic migraine (551 quarterly, 559 monthly) or episodic migraine (394 quarterly, 386 monthly) in a 52-week multicentre randomised double-blind parallel-group long-term study of fremanezumab monthly or quarterly; safety, tolerability and exploratory efficacy were assessed.
cards.result: Fremanezumab reduced monthly migraine days from baseline to 12 months: chronic migraine −7.2 days (quarterly) and −8.0 days (monthly); episodic migraine −5.2 days (quarterly) and −5.1 days (monthly). Headache days of at least moderate severity fell by 6.4–6.8 days (chronic) and 4.2–4.4 days (episodic), and reductions in acute headache medication use and headache-related disability were maintained over 12 months. The most commonly reported adverse events were injection-site reactions (induration 33%, pain 31%, erythema 26%). The authors classed this as Class IV evidence that long-term fremanezumab is safe, well tolerated and sustains reductions in migraine and headache days.
cards.watchOut: FLAG: this long-term study had no placebo arm — its day-count reductions are changes from baseline within treated patients and cannot by themselves separate drug effect from regression and expectation; the placebo-controlled leg of this shelf is the pooled analyses below. The primary HALO trials are homed on live shelf #336 and are not re-carded here.
cards.source: Goadsby PJ et al. Long-term safety, tolerability, and efficacy of fremanezumab in migraine: A randomized study. Neurology. 2020. PMID: 32913018. Registry ID: NCT02638103. cards.headline: McAllister 2022: pooling three phase 3 trials, clinically meaningful disability improvement (≥5-point HIT-6 reduction) occurred in 53–55% on fremanezumab versus 39% on placebo
cards.summary: McAllister 2022: pooling three phase 3 trials, clinically meaningful disability improvement (≥5-point HIT-6 reduction) occurred in 53–55% on fremanezumab versus 39% on placebo
cards.type: Pooled analysis of three phase 3 trials (McAllister 2022)
cards.people: Pooled analysis of three double-blind phase 3 trials (HALO EM, HALO CM and FOCUS) in which patients with episodic or chronic migraine were randomised 1:1:1 to quarterly fremanezumab, monthly fremanezumab or matched placebo for 12 weeks; disability was assessed by HIT-6 and MIDAS questionnaires.
cards.result: Proportions achieving a ≥5-point HIT-6 reduction were 53% (quarterly) and 55% (monthly) on fremanezumab versus 39% on placebo (both P < 0.0001). In patients with baseline MIDAS scores of 11–20 (n = 234), ≥5-point MIDAS reductions occurred in 71% (quarterly) and 70% (monthly) versus 49% on placebo (both P ≤ 0.01); in those with baseline MIDAS >20 (n = 1,266), ≥30% MIDAS reductions occurred in 69% and 79% versus 58% on placebo (both P < 0.001). Shifts of 1–3 grades down in MIDAS or HIT-6 disability severity were significantly greater on fremanezumab than placebo (all P < 0.0001).
cards.watchOut: FLAG: this pooling draws on the HALO trials whose primary reports are homed on live shelf #336 — this card reports only this pooled report's own disability figures, and the homed PMIDs are kept out of this shelf's source lines under precedent (b). Disability is a patient-reported secondary outcome, not the monthly-migraine-days primary.
cards.source: McAllister P et al. Impact of fremanezumab on disability outcomes in patients with episodic and chronic migraine: a pooled analysis of phase 3 studies. The journal of headache and pain. 2022. PMID: 36038833. Registry ID: NCT02621931 (HALO CM), NCT02629861 (HALO EM), NCT03308968 (FOCUS) — as named in the record. cards.headline: Diener 2022: in 2,842 pooled phase 3 patients, overall adverse events occurred in 58–65% and serious adverse events in under 1–2% across fremanezumab and placebo groups, with no cardio- or cerebrovascular signal
cards.summary: Diener 2022: in 2,842 pooled phase 3 patients, overall adverse events occurred in 58–65% and serious adverse events in under 1–2% across fremanezumab and placebo groups, with no cardio- or cerebrovascular signal
cards.type: Pooled safety analysis of three phase 3 trials (Diener 2022)
cards.people: Pooled safety analysis of three randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trials (12 weeks) in 2,842 patients with episodic or chronic migraine receiving quarterly fremanezumab, monthly fremanezumab or placebo, with cardio- and cerebrovascular adverse events analysed by vascular history, risk factors and medication use.
cards.result: Overall adverse events occurred in 58–65% and serious adverse events in <1–2% in similar proportions across fremanezumab and placebo groups. Cardio- and cerebrovascular adverse events were infrequent (2–6%) regardless of cardio- and cerebrovascular medical history, occurred in low, similar proportions in patients with cardiovascular risk factors and in those using cardio- and cerebrovascular medications or triptans, and no cardio- or cerebrovascular signals were identified.
cards.watchOut: Twelve-week pooled trial safety cannot exclude rare or long-latency vascular harm; the reassurance here is the absence of a signal in 2,842 patients over 12 weeks, read alongside the 52-week study's injection-site burden on the first card.
cards.source: Diener HC et al. Safety and tolerability of fremanezumab in patients with episodic and chronic migraine: a pooled analysis of phase 3 studies. cards.headline: Silberstein 2021: among HALO responders, ≥50% reductions in monthly migraine days were achieved by 59.8–63.7% (episodic) and 52.8–59.0% (chronic) — a post hoc view of benefit in those who respond
cards.summary: Silberstein 2021: among HALO responders, ≥50% reductions in monthly migraine days were achieved by 59.8–63.7% (episodic) and 52.8–59.0% (chronic) — a post hoc view of benefit in those who respond
cards.type: Post hoc responder analysis of two placebo-controlled trials (Silberstein 2021)
cards.people: Post hoc responder analysis of the two placebo-controlled HALO trials: 857 participants identified as responders (episodic migraine 429, 73.8%; chronic migraine 428, 56.7%), where response was defined as a reduction of ≥2 monthly migraine days (episodic) or ≥4 (chronic) on quarterly or monthly fremanezumab over 12 weeks.
cards.result: Reductions in monthly migraine days among responders were 5.4 days (quarterly) and 5.5 days (monthly) in episodic migraine and 8.7 and 9.1 days in chronic migraine. The proportion achieving ≥50% reduction in monthly migraine days was 59.8% (quarterly) and 63.7% (monthly) in episodic responders and 52.8% and 59.0% in chronic responders, with greater reductions in acute headache medication use, disability scores and quality-of-life improvements among responders than in the overall populations.
cards.watchOut: Responder analyses describe the subgroup already selected for doing well — they answer 'how much do responders gain?', never 'how likely is response?'; the placebo-controlled average effects live in the pooled cards above and, for the primary trials, on live shelf #336.

shelves.title: Diroximel versus dimethyl fumarate in relapsing-remitting MS: fewer gastrointestinal events in the head-to-head trial (34.8% vs 49.0%), with equal efficacy inferred from bioequivalent active-metabolite exposure — not from a relapse trial
shelves.question: Is diroximel fumarate as effective as dimethyl fumarate in relapsing-remitting MS with fewer gastrointestinal adverse events?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Dimethyl Fumarate/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fumarates/therapeutic use · Gastrointestinal Diseases/drug therapy · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents/therapeutic use · Male · Multiple Sclerosis, Relapsing-Remitting/drug therapy · Recurrence
shelves.balance: The dimethyl fumarate home, pack #2359, answers dimethyl fumarate versus placebo (DEFINE/CONFIRM) and does not answer this head-to-head question — verified against that pack. The two fumarates deliver the same active metabolite: diroximel fumarate 462 mg and dimethyl fumarate 240 mg produce bioequivalent exposure of monomethyl fumarate and are therefore expected to have similar efficacy (Naismith 2020, EVOLVE-MS-2 record). That expectation is the efficacy leg — there is no head-to-head relapse trial — and it is supported only indirectly by diroximel's own open-label programme: in EVOLVE-MS-1, 1,057 patients treated for up to 96 weeks had an adjusted annualized relapse rate of 0.13 (95% CI 0.11–0.15) and a 72.7% reduction in gadolinium-enhancing lesions from baseline, exploratory endpoints without a comparator (Singer 2023). The tolerability leg is directly randomised: in the 5-week head-to-head EVOLVE-MS-2 trial, diroximel patients had a 46% relative reduction in days with a gastrointestinal symptom intensity score ≥2 (rate ratio 0.54, 95% CI 0.39–0.75), gastrointestinal adverse events in 34.8% versus 49.0%, and gastrointestinal discontinuations in 0.8% versus 4.8% (Naismith 2020); the companion quality-of-life analysis found gastrointestinal symptoms interfered 'quite a bit' or 'extremely' with daily activities in 9.5% on diroximel versus 28.9% on dimethyl fumarate (Wundes 2021). Early open-label data had already shown gastrointestinal events in 30.9% of 696 patients, under 1% discontinuing for them (Palte 2019, described in the synthesis). PROPOSED SPLIT (evidence type): fewer gastrointestinal adverse events than dimethyl fumarate is randomised-trial proven; equal effectiveness is inferred from bioequivalent active-metabolite exposure plus uncontrolled relapse data, not from a head-to-head efficacy trial.

cards.headline: EVOLVE-MS-2 (Naismith 2020): diroximel beat dimethyl fumarate on gastrointestinal tolerability — 46% relative fewer days with symptom score ≥2, GI adverse events 34.8% vs 49.0%, GI discontinuations 0.8% vs 4.8%
cards.summary: EVOLVE-MS-2 (Naismith 2020): diroximel beat dimethyl fumarate on gastrointestinal tolerability — 46% relative fewer days with symptom score ≥2, GI adverse events 34.8% vs 49.0%, GI discontinuations 0.8% vs 4.8%
cards.people: Patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis in EVOLVE-MS-2, a phase 3 randomised double-blind head-to-head 5-week study of diroximel fumarate 462 mg versus dimethyl fumarate 240 mg, both twice daily (504 patients received study drug — 253 diroximel, 251 dimethyl fumarate — per the companion report of the same trial), using the self-administered IGISIS and GGISIS gastrointestinal symptom scales.
cards.result: Diroximel-treated patients had a statistically significant 46% relative reduction in the number of days with an IGISIS symptom intensity score ≥2 compared with dimethyl fumarate (rate ratio 0.54, 95% CI 0.39–0.75; p = 0.0003). Gastrointestinal adverse events (including diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain) occurred in 34.8% on diroximel versus 49.0% on dimethyl fumarate. Discontinuations because of adverse events were 1.6% versus 5.6%, and because of gastrointestinal adverse events 0.8% versus 4.8%. The record states the two doses produce bioequivalent monomethyl fumarate exposure and are therefore expected to have similar efficacy/safety profiles.
cards.watchOut: Five weeks is the early-titration window when fumarate gastrointestinal events peak — the trial proves an early tolerability advantage, not a lifetime one, and it was not designed or powered to compare relapse efficacy between the two drugs.
cards.source: Naismith RT et al. cards.headline: EVOLVE-MS-1 final (Singer 2023): in 1,057 patients on diroximel for up to 96 weeks, adjusted annualized relapse rate was 0.13 and gadolinium-enhancing lesions fell 72.7% from baseline — exploratory, with no comparator
cards.summary: EVOLVE-MS-1 final (Singer 2023): in 1,057 patients on diroximel for up to 96 weeks, adjusted annualized relapse rate was 0.13 and gadolinium-enhancing lesions fell 72.7% from baseline — exploratory, with no comparator
cards.type: Open-label single-arm phase 3 study, final results (EVOLVE-MS-1)
cards.people: 1,057 patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis in EVOLVE-MS-1, an open-label 96-week phase 3 study of diroximel fumarate; 75.7% (800/1,057) completed the study, median exposure 1.8 years. Primary endpoint was safety and tolerability; efficacy endpoints were exploratory.
cards.result: Adverse events occurred in 938 patients (88.7%), mostly mild (28.9%) or moderate (50.3%); diroximel was discontinued for adverse events in 85 patients (8.0%), with under 2% discontinuing for gastrointestinal or flushing/flushing-related events. At week 96 the mean number of gadolinium-enhancing lesions was significantly reduced from baseline (72.7%; p < 0.0001) and the adjusted annualized relapse rate was 0.13 (95% CI 0.11–0.15).
cards.watchOut: Observational in effect — a single-arm open-label study cannot show diroximel equals dimethyl fumarate on relapses; its 0.13 relapse rate is consistent with the fumarate class effect homed on pack #2359, and is labelled here as uncontrolled programme data, not comparative evidence.
cards.source: Singer BA et al. Diroximel fumarate in patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis: Final safety and efficacy results from the phase 3 EVOLVE-MS-1 study. Multiple sclerosis (Houndmills, Basingstoke, England). 2023. PMID: 37905526. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Wundes 2021: in EVOLVE-MS-2, gastrointestinal symptoms interfered 'quite a bit' or 'extremely' with daily activities in 9.5% on diroximel versus 28.9% on dimethyl fumarate
cards.summary: Wundes 2021: in EVOLVE-MS-2, gastrointestinal symptoms interfered 'quite a bit' or 'extremely' with daily activities in 9.5% on diroximel versus 28.9% on dimethyl fumarate
cards.type: Post hoc quality-of-life analysis of a randomised head-to-head trial (EVOLVE-MS-2)
cards.people: Post hoc quality-of-life analysis of EVOLVE-MS-2: 504 patients received study drug (diroximel n = 253; dimethyl fumarate n = 251) and 502 completed at least one post-baseline gastrointestinal questionnaire (IGISIS/GGISIS eDiary).
cards.result: Gastrointestinal symptoms were less likely to interfere 'quite a bit' or 'extremely' with regular daily activities on diroximel (9.5%, 24/253) than on dimethyl fumarate (28.9%, 72/249), and with work productivity (6.1%, 10/165, versus 11.3%, 18/159). Diroximel patients had fewer days with ≥1 hour of missed work (43 days, n = 20, versus 88 days, n = 26). Gastrointestinal tolerability adverse events were 34.8% (88/253) versus 48.2% (121/251), symptomatic-medication use among those with events 19.3% versus 30.6%, and gastrointestinal discontinuations 0.8% versus 4.8%.
cards.watchOut: A post hoc analysis of the same 5-week trial as the first card — it deepens the tolerability finding (daily-life and work impact) but is not an independent trial, and it inherits the 5-week window.
cards.source: Wundes A et al. Improved gastrointestinal profile with diroximel fumarate is associated with a positive impact on quality of life compared with dimethyl fumarate: results from the randomized, double-blind, phase III EVOLVE-MS-2 study. Therapeutic advances in neurological disorders. 2021. PMID: 33796143. Registry ID: NCT03093324. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: gastrointestinal advantage is randomised and real; equal efficacy is an inference from bioequivalence, not a head-to-head result — SPLIT (evidence type)
cards.summary: Synthesis: gastrointestinal advantage is randomised and real; equal efficacy is an inference from bioequivalence, not a head-to-head result — SPLIT (evidence type)
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised head-to-head tolerability trial (EVOLVE-MS-2, 504 patients, 5 weeks) reported twice (primary report and quality-of-life post hoc), and one open-label single-arm programme study (EVOLVE-MS-1, 1,057 patients, 96 weeks; its early interim report, Palte 2019, PMID: 31538304, found gastrointestinal events in 30.9% of 696 patients with under 1% discontinuing for them — described here in prose, not carded, as an interim report of the same study).
cards.result: Gastrointestinal: days with symptom score ≥2 reduced 46% relative (rate ratio 0.54); GI adverse events 34.8% vs 49.0%; GI discontinuations 0.8% vs 4.8%; daily-life interference 9.5% vs 28.9%. Efficacy: no head-to-head relapse comparison exists in the carded record — equivalence rests on bioequivalent monomethyl fumarate exposure stated in the EVOLVE-MS-2 record, plus EVOLVE-MS-1's uncontrolled adjusted annualized relapse rate of 0.13. PROPOSED SPLIT (evidence type).
cards.watchOut: Answering 'as effective?' with the tolerability trial alone would overstate the record: clinicians choosing diroximel for a stomach that failed dimethyl fumarate are relying on shared-metabolite bioequivalence for efficacy, and this shelf prints that reliance on its face.

shelves.title: Natalizumab every 6 weeks versus every 4 weeks in stable relapsing MS (PARTIAL slice of #2360): clinical outcomes maintained in NOVA with a numerical MRI excess, and lower PML risk only in observational TOUCH data
shelves.question: In relapsing MS stable on natalizumab, does extended-interval dosing (every 6 weeks) preserve efficacy versus standard every-4-week dosing, and does it lower PML risk?
shelves.mesh: Double-Blind Method · Humans · Leukoencephalopathy, Progressive Multifocal/chemically induced,etiology · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Multiple Sclerosis, Relapsing-Remitting/drug therapy · Natalizumab/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Retrospective Studies · Risk Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of pack #2360 (natalizumab versus placebo, AFFIRM/SENTINEL): that home answers whether natalizumab works at all; this shelf answers only the uncovered slice — the dosing-interval strategy and PML risk by interval — and re-cards no PMID from #2360. The two sub-questions rest on different evidence types and are stamped separately, so the randomised leg cannot upgrade the observational leg. Efficacy (randomised): in NOVA, 499 patients stable on every-4-week natalizumab for at least 12 months were randomised to switch to every 6 weeks or continue every 4 weeks; at week 72 the adjusted mean numbers of new or newly enlarging T2 lesions were 0.20 versus 0.05 (mean lesion ratio 4.24, 95% CI 0.86–20.85; p = 0.076 on the primary estimand; ratio 4.93, p = 0.044 on the secondary estimand), with most excess lesions contributed by two patients with ≥25 lesions — a numerical difference in a trial where control-arm activity was lower than expected, not a clean preservation proof (Foley 2022). Exploratory clinical and patient-reported outcomes showed no significant differences between intervals (EDSS improvement 11.7% vs 10.8%; Ryerson 2023). PML risk (observational): in the TOUCH programme's 35,521 anti-JC-virus-antibody-positive patients, extended-interval dosing was associated with hazard ratios for PML of 0.06 (primary analysis) and 0.12 (secondary) versus standard dosing — relative risk reductions of 94% and 88% — in retrospective analyses, Class III evidence (Ryerson 2019). NOVA itself was not powered for PML and recorded one asymptomatic PML case in the 6-week arm. PROPOSED SPLIT (evidence type): clinical outcomes were maintained in the randomised trial with a small numerical MRI excess on extended dosing, while the lower PML risk rests on observational data only and is labelled observational.

cards.headline: NOVA (Foley 2022): switching stable patients to every-6-week natalizumab gave numerically more new T2 lesions at week 72 than staying every 4 weeks (adjusted means 0.20 vs 0.05) — not significant on the primary estimand, significant on the secondary
cards.summary: NOVA (Foley 2022): switching stable patients to every-6-week natalizumab gave numerically more new T2 lesions at week 72 than staying every 4 weeks (adjusted means 0.20 vs 0.05) — not significant on the primary estimand, significant on the secondary
cards.people: 499 patients aged 18–60 with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, treated with intravenous natalizumab 300 mg every 4 weeks with no relapses for at least 12 months and no missed doses in the previous 3 months, randomised at 89 centres to switch to every 6 weeks (n = 251) or continue every 4 weeks (n = 248) in a randomised controlled open-label phase 3b trial with masked MRI reading and neurology assessment; primary endpoint was new or newly enlarging T2 lesions at week 72.
cards.result: After prespecified adjustments, mean new or newly enlarging T2 lesions at week 72 were 0.20 (95% CI 0.07–0.63) on every-6-week dosing versus 0.05 (0.01–0.22) on every-4-week dosing (mean lesion ratio 4.24, 95% CI 0.86–20.85; p = 0.076, primary estimand) and 0.31 versus 0.06 (ratio 4.93, 95% CI 1.05–23.20; p = 0.044, secondary estimand). Two participants in the 6-week group with extreme lesion numbers (≥25) contributed most of the excess. Adverse events occurred in 78% versus 77% and serious adverse events in 7% versus 7%; no deaths were reported. One case of asymptomatic progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy occurred in the 6-week group and none in the 4-week group; the trial was not powered to assess PML risk differences.
cards.watchOut: NOVA enrolled only patients already stable and relapse-free for a year on standard dosing — its result does not licence extended intervals from treatment start, and the authors themselves warn that lower-than-expected activity in the 4-week arm limits interpretation of the lesion difference in both directions.

cards.headline: Ryerson 2023 (NOVA exploratory): no significant differences between every-6-week and every-4-week dosing in disability, walking, hand function, cognition or patient-reported outcomes at week 72
cards.summary: Ryerson 2023 (NOVA exploratory): no significant differences between every-6-week and every-4-week dosing in disability, walking, hand function, cognition or patient-reported outcomes at week 72
cards.type: Exploratory outcomes report of a randomised controlled trial (NOVA)
cards.people: Exploratory analysis of NOVA in patients who received at least one dose and had at least one post-baseline efficacy assessment (every 6 weeks n = 247; every 4 weeks n = 242), assessing EDSS, Timed 25-Foot Walk, 9-Hole Peg Test, Symbol Digit Modalities Test and patient-reported outcomes including MSIS-29, fatigue and treatment satisfaction.
cards.result: Estimated proportions with confirmed EDSS improvement at week 72 were 11.7% (19/163) on every-6-week versus 10.8% (17/158) on every-4-week dosing (hazard ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.53–1.98; p = 0.9501). There were no significant differences in least-squares mean change for Timed 25-Foot Walk (difference 0.00, p = 0.975), 9-Hole Peg Test (dominant 0.22, p = 0.533; nondominant 0.09, p = 0.862) or Symbol Digit Modalities Test (−1.03, p = 0.194), nor for any patient-reported outcome; a higher proportion of 6-week patients met the worsening threshold on the EQ-5D-5L index (p = 0.0475).
cards.watchOut: Exploratory endpoints in a trial whose primary MRI endpoint was numerically worse on extended dosing: 'no significant difference' on underpowered clinical measures is absence of a detected difference, not proof of equivalence.

cards.headline: Ryerson 2019 (TOUCH, observational): extended-interval natalizumab was associated with 94% and 88% relative lower PML risk than standard dosing in 35,521 JC-virus-antibody-positive patients — retrospective, Class III evidence
cards.summary: Ryerson 2019 (TOUCH, observational): extended-interval natalizumab was associated with 94% and 88% relative lower PML risk than standard dosing in 35,521 JC-virus-antibody-positive patients — retrospective, Class III evidence
cards.people: Retrospective cohort study of 35,521 anti-JC virus antibody-positive patients in the TOUCH (Tysabri Outreach: Unified Commitment to Health) programme database as of June 1, 2017, comparing extended-interval dosing (mean average intervals 35.0–43.0 days) with standard-interval dosing (29.8–30.5 days) across three planned analyses (primary: 1,988 extended vs 13,132 standard; secondary: 3,331 vs 15,424; tertiary: 815 vs 23,168), adjusted for age, sex, prior immunosuppressants, time since initiation and cumulative infusions.
cards.result: Hazard ratios for progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy with extended versus standard interval dosing were 0.06 (95% CI 0.01–0.22; p < 0.001) in the primary analysis and 0.12 (0.05–0.29; p < 0.001) in the secondary analysis — relative risk reductions of 94% and 88%. The tertiary analysis included no cases of PML with extended-interval dosing. The authors graded this Class III evidence that extended-interval dosing is associated with a lower PML risk.
cards.watchOut: Observational and labelled as such: patients were not randomised to intervals, so channeling (clinicians extending intervals in patients they judged lower-risk, and differences in cumulative exposure) can manufacture part of an association this large; the relative reductions are printed with their observational status, and no absolute PML rates are given in the record for these analyses.
cards.source: Ryerson LZ et al. Risk of natalizumab-associated PML in patients with MS is reduced with extended interval dosing. Neurology. 2019. PMID: 31515290. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: extended dosing maintained clinical outcomes in the randomised trial with a small numerical MRI excess, and was associated with much lower PML risk only in observational data — SPLIT (evidence type)
cards.summary: Synthesis: extended dosing maintained clinical outcomes in the randomised trial with a small numerical MRI excess, and was associated with much lower PML risk only in observational data — SPLIT (evidence type)
cards.people: The carded evidence for this PARTIAL slice of pack #2360: one randomised interval trial (NOVA, 499 stable patients) reported twice (primary MRI/safety report and exploratory clinical report), and one retrospective TOUCH cohort (35,521 JC-virus-antibody-positive patients). No PMID from #2360 (AFFIRM/SENTINEL) is re-carded.
cards.result: Efficacy leg (randomised): new T2 lesions 0.20 vs 0.05 adjusted means at week 72 (ratio 4.24, p = 0.076 primary estimand), no significant clinical or patient-reported differences. PML leg (observational): hazard ratios 0.06 and 0.12 for extended versus standard dosing (94% and 88% relative reductions). One asymptomatic PML case occurred on extended dosing in NOVA itself. PROPOSED SPLIT (evidence type) — the randomised leg must not upgrade the observational leg.
cards.watchOut: The clinical decision trades a proven-interval's certainty against an observational risk association: this shelf presents both legs at their own evidence grades and does not merge them into a single 'extended dosing is better' claim.

shelves.title: Simvastatin 80 mg in secondary progressive MS: the phase 2 brain-atrophy signal (43% relative reduction) failed in phase 3 — MS-STAT2 showed no difference in disability progression (40% vs 36%)
shelves.question: Does simvastatin 80 mg slow disability progression in secondary progressive MS versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Simvastatin/therapeutic use,administration & dosage · Double-Blind Method · Disease Progression · Multiple Sclerosis, Chronic Progressive/drug therapy · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Disability Evaluation
shelves.balance: The phase 2 signal did not survive phase 3, and this shelf's stamp follows the full evidence, not the phase 2 result. In MS-STAT (phase 2, 140 patients), simvastatin 80 mg reduced the annualised rate of whole-brain atrophy by 43% relative versus placebo (0.288% vs 0.584% per year; adjusted difference −0.254% per year, 95% CI −0.422 to −0.087; p = 0.003) — a surrogate imaging endpoint (Chataway 2014). Its cognitive secondary analysis found a 1.2-point better frontal assessment battery score and a 2.5-point better physical quality-of-life component at 24 months, with no effect on other cognitive, neuropsychiatric or quality-of-life measures (Chan 2017). In MS-STAT2 (phase 3, 964 patients, up to 4.5 years), the primary outcome went the other way numerically: 6-month confirmed disability progression occurred in 40% (192/482) on simvastatin versus 36% (173/482) on placebo (adjusted hazard ratio 1.13, 95% CI 0.91–1.39; p = 0.26) — the treatment made no difference, and the authors concluded simvastatin in MS should be confined to existing vascular indications (Chataway 2025). No emergent safety issues were seen in phase 3 apart from one serious adverse reaction of rhabdomyolysis in the simvastatin group. PROPOSED stamp: no benefit on disability progression — the large phase 3 trial is the answer to the question as asked, and the brain-atrophy finding is presented as the unconfirmed surrogate signal that prompted it.

cards.headline: MS-STAT2 2025 (phase 3): simvastatin 80 mg made no difference to disability progression in 964 patients with secondary progressive MS — progression in 40% vs 36% (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: MS-STAT2 2025 (phase 3): simvastatin 80 mg made no difference to disability progression in 964 patients with secondary progressive MS — progression in 40% vs 36% (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: 964 participants aged 18–65 with secondary progressive multiple sclerosis and EDSS 4.0–6.5, randomised 1:1 at 31 UK neuroscience centres and district general hospitals to oral simvastatin 80 mg (n = 482) or matched placebo (n = 482) for up to 4.5 years; mean age 54 years, 73% female. Primary outcome was time to 6-month EDSS confirmed disability progression, analysed intention-to-treat.
cards.result: Confirmed disability progression occurred in 192 of 482 participants (40%) in the simvastatin group and 173 of 482 (36%) in the placebo group (adjusted hazard ratio 1.13, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.39; p = 0.26) — the treatment made no difference. No emergent safety issues were seen; there was one serious adverse reaction (rhabdomyolysis) in the simvastatin group, and cardiovascular serious adverse events occurred in 5 participants (1%) on simvastatin versus 12 (2%) on placebo. The authors concluded the trial did not show a treatment effect and that simvastatin use in MS should be confined to existing vascular indications.
cards.watchOut: This is the definitive test of the question as asked — disability progression, not brain volume — and its point estimate favours placebo numerically; quoting the phase 2 atrophy result without this trial would misstate the evidence.
cards.source: Chataway J et al. Effect of repurposed simvastatin on disability progression in secondary progressive multiple sclerosis (MS-STAT2): a phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2025. PMID: 41045938. Registry ID: NCT03387670; ISRCTN82598726. cards.headline: MS-STAT 2014 (phase 2): simvastatin 80 mg reduced the annualised brain atrophy rate by 43% relative versus placebo (0.288% vs 0.584% per year) in 140 patients — a surrogate endpoint
cards.summary: MS-STAT 2014 (phase 2): simvastatin 80 mg reduced the annualised brain atrophy rate by 43% relative versus placebo (0.288% vs 0.584% per year) in 140 patients — a surrogate endpoint
cards.people: 140 patients aged 18–65 with secondary progressive multiple sclerosis randomised 1:1 at three UK neuroscience centres to simvastatin 80 mg (n = 70) or placebo (n = 70); primary outcome was the annualised rate of whole-brain atrophy on serial volumetric MRI, analysed intention-to-treat and per protocol.
cards.result: The mean annualised atrophy rate was 0.288% per year (SD 0.521) on simvastatin versus 0.584% per year (0.498) on placebo; the adjusted difference was −0.254% per year (95% CI −0.422 to −0.087; p = 0.003), a 43% relative reduction. Simvastatin was well tolerated, with serious adverse events in 9 participants (13%) on simvastatin versus 14 (20%) on placebo. The authors stated these results supported advancement to phase 3 testing.
cards.watchOut: Brain atrophy is a surrogate: a slower shrinkage rate over 2 years in 140 patients did not predict the disability outcome when 964 patients were followed for up to 4.5 years in MS-STAT2 — this card is the hypothesis the phase 3 trial tested and did not confirm.
cards.source: Chataway J et al. Effect of high-dose simvastatin on brain atrophy and disability in secondary progressive multiple sclerosis (MS-STAT): a randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 2 trial. cards.headline: Chan 2017 (MS-STAT secondary analysis): frontal-function score 1.2 points higher and physical quality-of-life component 2.5 points better on simvastatin at 24 months; no effect on other cognitive or neuropsychiatric measures
cards.summary: Chan 2017 (MS-STAT secondary analysis): frontal-function score 1.2 points higher and physical quality-of-life component 2.5 points better on simvastatin at 24 months; no effect on other cognitive or neuropsychiatric measures
cards.type: Secondary analysis of a randomised phase 2 trial (MS-STAT cognitive substudy)
cards.people: Secondary analysis of the MS-STAT trial (140 patients with secondary progressive MS randomised to simvastatin 80 mg or placebo for 24 months; cognitive assessments in 130–133 patients), covering frontal assessment battery, memory batteries, Hamilton Depression Rating Scale, Neuropsychiatric Inventory Questionnaire and SF-36 quality of life.
cards.result: At 24 months the frontal assessment battery score was 1.2 points higher in the simvastatin group than placebo (95% CI 0.2–2.3), and the mean SF-36 physical component score was 2.5 points better (95% CI 0.3–4.8; p = 0.028). No treatment effect was noted for any other cognitive, neuropsychiatric or quality-of-life outcome, and verbal and non-verbal memory scores worsened significantly over the trial in the cohort overall (declines of 5.7 and 6.8 T-score points).
cards.watchOut: Two positive measures among many tested, in the same 140-patient phase 2 trial whose disability hypothesis later failed in phase 3 — these are hypothesis-generating secondary findings, not a reason to prescribe simvastatin for cognition in secondary progressive MS.
cards.source: Chan D et al. cards.summary: Synthesis: a 43% relative brain-atrophy signal in phase 2, then no difference in disability progression in the 964-patient phase 3 — the treatment made no difference
cards.people: The carded evidence: MS-STAT2 phase 3 (964 patients, up to 4.5 years, disability primary), MS-STAT phase 2 (140 patients, brain-atrophy primary), and the MS-STAT cognitive secondary analysis (same 140-patient trial). Total distinct randomised participants: 1,104.
cards.result: Disability progression (the question asked): 40% on simvastatin versus 36% on placebo, adjusted hazard ratio 1.13 (95% CI 0.91–1.39; p = 0.26) — the treatment made no difference. Brain atrophy (surrogate, phase 2): 43% relative reduction. Cognition/quality of life (secondary, phase 2): isolated frontal and physical-component gains, no other effects. The stamp follows the phase 3 disability result.
cards.watchOut: MS-STAT2's readout status was verified from the fetched 2025 Lancet record this session: the phase 3 has reported, it is negative on its primary outcome, and any shelf built on the phase 2 signal alone would now be wrong.

shelves.title: Foslevodopa–foscarbidopa infusion in advanced Parkinson's: 1.75 extra hours of ON time without troublesome dyskinesia versus oral levodopa–carbidopa in the phase 3 trial (active-controlled, not placebo-infusion — premise corrected; BouNDless is a different product)
shelves.question: In advanced Parkinson's disease, does continuous subcutaneous foslevodopa–foscarbidopa infusion increase ON time without troublesome dyskinesia versus placebo infusion?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Carbidopa/adverse effects · Levodopa/adverse effects · Antiparkinson Agents/adverse effects · Parkinson Disease/drug therapy · Infusions, Subcutaneous · Dyskinesias/drug therapy
shelves.balance: PREMISE CORRECTION, verified from the fetched records: the foslevodopa–foscarbidopa phase 3 trial was NOT a placebo-infusion trial. It was a double-blind, double-dummy, active-controlled trial in which the control group received oral immediate-release levodopa–carbidopa plus a continuous subcutaneous placebo-solution infusion, and the treatment group received foslevodopa–foscarbidopa infusion plus oral placebo (Soileau 2022). So the question's 'versus placebo infusion' is answered in the only form the evidence allows: infusion versus oral therapy, with placebo infusion present in the control arm. (The placebo-infusion phase 3 named BouNDless tests a different product, ND0612 levodopa–carbidopa infusion, and is not carded here — a different intervention.) On the corrected comparison: foslevodopa–foscarbidopa increased ON time without troublesome dyskinesia by 2.72 hours versus 0.97 hours on oral levodopa–carbidopa at 12 weeks (difference 1.75 hours, 95% CI 0.46–3.05; p = 0.0083) and reduced OFF time more (−2.75 vs −0.96 hours; difference −1.79 hours; p = 0.0054), at the cost of infusion-site adverse events (erythema 27%, pain 26%, cellulitis 19%) and a 22% versus 1% premature discontinuation rate for adverse events (Soileau 2022). A separate 52-week single-arm open-label study of 244 patients found ON time without troublesome dyskinesia improved by 3.8 hours and OFF time by −3.5 hours from baseline, with 107 of 244 discontinuing (Aldred 2023 — uncontrolled, labelled as such). A phase 1 study in 28 patients showed the infusion holds levodopa exposure steady with minimal fluctuation over 72 hours (Rosebraugh 2021). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one randomised active-controlled trial — a single programme caps at POSSIBLE — showing about 1.75 extra hours of good ON time versus oral levodopa–carbidopa, with a substantial infusion-site burden.

cards.headline: Soileau 2022 (phase 3, active-controlled): foslevodopa–foscarbidopa increased ON time without troublesome dyskinesia by 2.72 hours vs 0.97 hours on oral levodopa–carbidopa (difference 1.75 hours; p = 0.0083) at 12 weeks
cards.summary: Soileau 2022 (phase 3, active-controlled): foslevodopa–foscarbidopa increased ON time without troublesome dyskinesia by 2.72 hours vs 0.97 hours on oral levodopa–carbidopa (difference 1.75 hours; p = 0.0083) at 12 weeks
cards.type: Randomised double-blind double-dummy active-controlled phase 3 trial
cards.people: 141 patients with levodopa-responsive advanced Parkinson's disease inadequately controlled on current therapy (at least 2.5 hours average daily OFF time), randomised at 65 US and Australian centres to continuous subcutaneous foslevodopa–foscarbidopa plus oral placebo (n = 74) or oral immediate-release levodopa–carbidopa plus continuous subcutaneous placebo-solution infusion (n = 67) for 12 weeks, double-blind and double-dummy. Primary endpoint: change in ON time without troublesome dyskinesia; first key secondary: OFF time.
cards.result: ON time without troublesome dyskinesia increased by a model-based mean 2.72 hours (SE 0.52) on foslevodopa–foscarbidopa versus 0.97 hours (0.50) on oral levodopa–carbidopa (difference 1.75 hours, 95% CI 0.46 to 3.05; p = 0.0083). OFF time fell by −2.75 hours (0.50) versus −0.96 hours (0.49) (difference −1.79 hours, 95% CI −3.03 to −0.54; p = 0.0054). Adverse events occurred in 85% (63/74) versus 63% (42/67); serious adverse events were similar (8% vs 6%). The commonest foslevodopa–foscarbidopa events were infusion-site erythema (27%), pain (26%), cellulitis (19%) and oedema (12%), and adverse events led to premature discontinuation in 22% (16/74) versus 1% (1/67).
cards.watchOut: PREMISE: the comparator was oral levodopa–carbidopa (with placebo infusion in that arm), not placebo infusion alone — this trial cannot say what infusion adds over no treatment, and its 22% adverse-event discontinuation rate is part of the answer, not a footnote.

Safety and efficacy of continuous subcutaneous foslevodopa-foscarbidopa in patients with advanced Parkinson's disease: a randomised, double-blind, active-controlled, phase 3 trial. The Lancet. cards.headline: Aldred 2023 (52-week open-label, uncontrolled): ON time without troublesome dyskinesia improved 3.8 hours and OFF time fell 3.5 hours from baseline; 107 of 244 patients discontinued
cards.summary: Aldred 2023 (52-week open-label, uncontrolled): ON time without troublesome dyskinesia improved 3.8 hours and OFF time fell 3.5 hours from baseline; 107 of 244 patients discontinued
cards.people: 244 patients with levodopa-responsive advanced Parkinson's disease and at least 2.5 hours of OFF time per day in a separate 52-week single-arm open-label phase 3 study of 24-hour/day foslevodopa–foscarbidopa continuous subcutaneous infusion at individually optimised doses (approximately 700–4,250 mg levodopa per 24 hours); primary endpoint was safety/tolerability. 137 patients completed treatment.
cards.result: At week 52, normalised ON time without troublesome dyskinesia had improved by a mean 3.8 hours (SD 3.3) and normalised OFF time by −3.5 hours (3.1) from baseline. Morning akinesia fell from 77.7% of patients at baseline to 27.8% at week 52, and sleep quality (PDSS-2) and quality of life (PDQ-39, EQ-5D-5L) improved. Infusion-site events were the most common adverse events; adverse events were mostly non-serious, with 25.8% of patients reporting serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Uncontrolled and labelled as such: with no comparator, baseline-to-week-52 gains mix drug effect, dose optimisation, expectation and survivor bias — 107 of 244 patients discontinued, so week-52 averages describe those who stayed on therapy.
cards.source: Aldred J et al. Continuous Subcutaneous Foslevodopa/Foscarbidopa in Parkinson's Disease: Safety and Efficacy Results From a 12-Month, Single-Arm, Open-Label, Phase 3 Study. Neurology and therapy. 2023. PMID: 37632656. Registry ID: NCT03781167. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Rosebraugh 2021 (phase 1, n = 28): subcutaneous foslevodopa–foscarbidopa held levodopa exposure steady with minimal fluctuation over 72 hours across four infusion rates
cards.summary: Rosebraugh 2021 (phase 1, n = 28): subcutaneous foslevodopa–foscarbidopa held levodopa exposure steady with minimal fluctuation over 72 hours across four infusion rates
cards.people: 28 adults with Parkinson's disease at seven US sites in a phase 1 single-ascending-dose single-blind study, stratified into four groups receiving fixed foslevodopa–foscarbidopa abdominal subcutaneous infusion rates based on their oral daily levodopa intake, infused over 72 hours with serial plasma pharmacokinetic sampling. N = 28.
cards.result: Levodopa exposure quickly reached steady state and remained stable with minimal fluctuations; average steady-state levodopa exposure ranged from 747 to 4,660 ng/mL across the different infusion-rate groups. Foslevodopa–foscarbidopa provided stable levodopa and carbidopa exposures over 72 hours with very low fluctuation across a wide range of clinically relevant exposures, and had a favourable safety profile in this short study.
cards.watchOut: A 72-hour pharmacokinetic study in 28 patients: it establishes the mechanism the phase 3 result depends on (steady levodopa levels), and says nothing by itself about ON time, dyskinesia or longer-term skin tolerability.
cards.source: Rosebraugh M et al. Foslevodopa/Foscarbidopa Is Well Tolerated and Maintains Stable Levodopa and Carbidopa Exposure Following Subcutaneous Infusion. Journal of Parkinson's disease. 2021. PMID: 34366380. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Probiotics for constipation in Parkinson's disease: bowel frequency improved in three small placebo-controlled trials (+1.3 to +2.97 movements per week) — differing multi-strain products, strains named only where the publication names them
shelves.question: In Parkinson's disease with chronic constipation, do probiotics improve bowel-movement frequency and constipation scores versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Constipation/etiology,physiopathology,therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Parkinson Disease/complications,physiopathology · Probiotics/therapeutic use · Quality of Life
shelves.balance: Four small randomised trials and their meta-analysis point the same way on bowel frequency, over 4–8 weeks, with different multi-strain products — so the benefit is a class-of-products signal in small trials, not proof for any one formulation. The largest trial (Tan 2021, 72 patients, 4 weeks) used a multistrain probiotic capsule — the fetched record does not name the strains or a brand/company, and this shelf says so plainly rather than guessing — and found spontaneous bowel movements increased by 1.0 per week on probiotics versus a decrease of 0.3 on placebo (mean difference 1.3, 95% CI 0.8–1.8; p < 0.001), with stool consistency and constipation-related quality of life also improved and satisfaction 65.6% versus 21.6%. A 2025 trial (Zareie, 72 patients, 6 weeks) names its product's strains exactly — Lactobacillus acidophilus, Lactobacillus casei, Lactobacillus rhamnosus, Bifidobacterium lactis, Bifidobacterium longum and Bifidobacterium breve, 1 × 10⁹ CFU each, total 12 × 10⁹ CFU/day — and found a larger difference (spontaneous bowel movements +3.41 vs +0.44; between-group difference 2.97, 95% CI 2.46–3.53; p < 0.001) with constipation quality of life improved. A third small trial (Ghalandari 2023, 27 analysed patients, 8 weeks, multi-strain product whose strains are not named in the fetched record) found bowel-movement frequency 4 versus 2 per week favouring probiotics (p = 0.02). Pooling the three randomised trials available in 2023 gave a standardised mean difference of 0.92 (95% CI 0.65–1.19) for bowel-movement frequency (Ghalandari meta-analysis 2023). No trial showed a motor benefit. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): consistent direction across several small short trials of differing products, capped at POSSIBLE by size, duration and product heterogeneity.

cards.headline: Tan 2021: multistrain probiotics increased spontaneous bowel movements by 1.0 per week versus a 0.3 fall on placebo in 72 patients with Parkinson's constipation (mean difference 1.3; p < 0.001)
cards.summary: Tan 2021: multistrain probiotics increased spontaneous bowel movements by 1.0 per week versus a 0.3 fall on placebo in 72 patients with Parkinson's constipation (mean difference 1.3; p < 0.001)
cards.people: 72 eligible patients with Parkinson's disease and constipation (280 screened) in a double-blind randomised placebo-controlled single-centre trial, block-randomised 1:1 to multistrain probiotics capsules (n = 34) or identical-appearing placebo (n = 38) for 4 weeks; primary endpoint was change in average spontaneous bowel movements per week in the last 2 weeks of treatment versus the 2-week pre-intervention phase, by daily stool diary. PRODUCT NAMING: the fetched record describes the intervention only as 'multistrain probiotics capsules' — it does not name the strains, brand or company, and this shelf does not guess them.
cards.result: Spontaneous bowel movements increased by 1.0 ± 1.2 per week on probiotics and decreased by 0.3 ± 1.0 per week on placebo (mean difference 1.3, 95% CI 0.8–1.8; p < 0.001). Stool consistency (p = 0.009) and quality of life related to constipation (p = 0.001) also improved significantly after correction for multiple comparisons. Satisfaction with the intervention was reported by 65.6% on probiotics versus 21.6% on placebo (p < 0.001). One patient (2.9%) in the treatment group withdrew for a non-serious adverse event; faecal calprotectin did not change significantly. The authors classed this as Class I evidence.
cards.watchOut: Four weeks, one centre, 72 patients, and a product whose strains the record does not name: the result supports trying a multistrain probiotic for Parkinson's constipation, but it cannot be read as evidence for whichever product is on a given pharmacy shelf, whose strains and doses may differ.
cards.source: Tan AH et al. Probiotics for Constipation in Parkinson Disease: A Randomized Placebo-Controlled Study. Neurology. 2021. PMID: 33046607. Registry ID: NCT03377322. cards.headline: Zareie 2025: a named six-strain probiotic increased spontaneous bowel movements by 3.41 per week versus 0.44 on placebo in 72 patients (difference 2.97; p < 0.001) over 6 weeks
cards.summary: Zareie 2025: a named six-strain probiotic increased spontaneous bowel movements by 3.41 per week versus 0.44 on placebo in 72 patients (difference 2.97; p < 0.001) over 6 weeks
cards.people: 72 patients with Parkinson's disease aged 50–80 years with functional constipation (Rome IV criteria), randomised 1:1 to probiotics or placebo for 6 weeks in a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial. PRODUCT NAMING, exactly as published: the probiotic capsule contained Lactobacillus acidophilus, Lactobacillus casei, Lactobacillus rhamnosus, Bifidobacterium lactis, Bifidobacterium longum, and Bifidobacterium breve, 1 × 10⁹ colony-forming units (CFU) each, total 12 × 10⁹ CFU/day; no brand or company is named in the fetched record.
cards.result: The probiotic group showed a mean spontaneous bowel movement increase of 3.41 versus 0.44 in the placebo group (between-group difference 2.97, 95% CI 2.46–3.53; p < 0.001). Constipation-related quality of life (PAC-QOL) improved significantly (adjusted mean difference −15.22, 95% CI −22.32 to −8.11; p < 0.001). No significant change was observed in UPDRS Part III motor scores. The authors called for larger multicentre trials to confirm efficacy.
cards.watchOut: The largest effect on this shelf comes from one of its smallest, shortest trials — an unusually clean 2.97-movement difference in 72 patients over 6 weeks should be read as promising, not settled, until a larger multicentre trial repeats it with this named formulation.

cards.summary: Ghalandari 2023 (trial): multi-strain probiotics raised bowel-movement frequency to 4 versus 2 per week against placebo in 27 analysed patients over 8 weeks (p = 0.02)
cards.people: 30 patients with Parkinson's disease and constipation by Rome IV criteria (15 per group; 27 completed — 13 women, 17 men at entry) in a blinded randomised controlled trial of multi-strain probiotics versus placebo for 8 weeks, with lifestyle-modification education in both groups; primary outcome was frequency of defecation. PRODUCT NAMING: the fetched record describes the intervention only as multi-strain probiotics — it does not name the strains, brand or company, and this shelf does not guess them.
cards.result: Between-group analysis showed frequency of bowel movements significantly increased in the probiotic group (median 4, range 3–5) compared with placebo (median 2, range 2–3) (p = 0.02). Stool consistency also improved in the probiotic group (p = 0.04). There were no significant between-group differences in laxative use, sense of complete evacuation or UPDRS motor scale, and no significant effect on motor function in 8 weeks.
cards.watchOut: Only 27 analysed patients — the smallest trial on this shelf; its medians are compatible with the larger trials' direction but add little precision, and its product is unnamed in the record, so it cannot guide product choice.

cards.headline: Ghalandari 2023 (meta-analysis): pooling 3 randomised trials, probiotics improved bowel-movement frequency in Parkinson's constipation (standardised mean difference 0.92, 95% CI 0.65–1.19)
cards.summary: Ghalandari 2023 (meta-analysis): pooling 3 randomised trials, probiotics improved bowel-movement frequency in Parkinson's constipation (standardised mean difference 0.92, 95% CI 0.65–1.19)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 3 randomised trials
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised clinical trials of probiotics for constipation in Parkinson's disease: 944 studies screened, 3 randomised trials ultimately included; bowel-movement frequency per week was the only outcome that could be summarised across the records.
cards.result: The pooled standardised mean difference for bowel-movement frequency was 0.92 (95% CI 0.65 to 1.19; I² = 57.0%; p < 0.001) in favour of probiotics. The authors concluded probiotic intake has beneficial effects on constipation in Parkinson's patients and called for multicentre research on long-term efficacy and safety.
cards.watchOut: A meta-analysis of only three small trials with moderate heterogeneity (I² = 57%) pools different multi-strain products as if they were one intervention — the pooled number summarises a direction of effect across products, not the effect of any single named formulation.

cards.headline: Synthesis: bowel frequency improves across several small short trials of differing multi-strain products — POSSIBLE, product-specific proof lacking
cards.summary: Synthesis: bowel frequency improves across several small short trials of differing multi-strain products — POSSIBLE, product-specific proof lacking
cards.people: The carded evidence: three randomised placebo-controlled trials (Tan 2021, n = 72, 4 weeks; Zareie 2025, n = 72, 6 weeks; Ghalandari 2023, n = 27 analysed, 8 weeks) and one meta-analysis of 3 trials. Total distinct randomised participants across the three trials: 171. Only the Zareie record names its strains; the other two records do not name strains, brand or company.
cards.result: Spontaneous bowel movements versus placebo: mean difference +1.3 per week (Tan); between-group difference +2.97 per week (Zareie); median frequency 4 vs 2 per week (Ghalandari); pooled standardised mean difference 0.92. Constipation quality-of-life scores improved in both trials that measured them; no motor benefit was shown anywhere. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Current products on sale may differ in strains, dose and quality from the tested preparations — where a record named its strains this shelf prints them, and where it did not, this shelf says so; do not transfer the pooled result to an arbitrary probiotic product.

shelves.title: Depression in Parkinson's disease: pramipexole beat placebo in one large trial (80% of effect direct), paroxetine beat placebo in a smaller trial, but the pooled SSRI estimate was null — a drug-by-drug split
shelves.question: In Parkinson's disease with depression, does pramipexole improve depressive symptoms versus placebo, and how do SSRIs compare?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antidepressive Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Depressive Disorder/complications,drug therapy · Dopamine Agonists/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Parkinson Disease/complications,drug therapy · Pramipexole · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Sertraline/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Pramipexole has the single largest placebo-controlled trial in this question, and its benefit was mostly a direct antidepressant effect rather than a by-product of motor improvement. In Barone 2010 (287 patients analysed, 12 weeks), Beck Depression Inventory scores fell by an adjusted mean 5.9 points on pramipexole versus 4.0 on placebo (difference 1.9, 95% CI 0.5–3.4; p = 0.01), and a prespecified path analysis attributed 80% of the total treatment effect to a direct effect on depressive symptoms. In the earlier head-to-head trial, recovery (Hamilton Depression Rating Scale ≤8) occurred in 60.6% on pramipexole versus 27.3% on sertraline 50 mg in 67 patients without motor fluctuations (p = 0.006) — an open-label comparison, so it cannot carry the same weight (Barone 2006). For SSRIs proper, the best single trial is Richard 2012: paroxetine improved Hamilton scores by 6.2 points more than placebo (97.5% CI 2.2–10.3; p = 0.0007) and the SNRI venlafaxine XR by 4.2 points more (97.5% CI 0.1–8.4; p = 0.02) in 115 patients, with no effect on motor function. But the pooled SSRI record is weaker than that one trial: a 2010 meta-analysis of six SSRI-versus-placebo randomised trials found a combined risk ratio of 1.08 (95% CI 0.77–1.55; p = 0.67) — insufficient evidence to reject no difference — and warned a false negative could not be excluded given small samples (Skapinakis 2010). PROPOSED SPLIT (drug): pramipexole improves depressive symptoms versus placebo in one large trial (POSSIBLE, single-trial cap); SSRI evidence is mixed — one positive paroxetine trial against a null pooled SSRI estimate — so the SSRI leg is MAYBE (weak evidence) at class level.

cards.headline: Barone 2010: pramipexole reduced Beck Depression Inventory scores by 5.9 points versus 4.0 on placebo in 287 patients with Parkinson's depression (difference 1.9; p = 0.01), with 80% of the effect direct, not via motor improvement
cards.summary: Barone 2010: pramipexole reduced Beck Depression Inventory scores by 5.9 points versus 4.0 on placebo in 287 patients with Parkinson's depression (difference 1.9; p = 0.01), with 80% of the effect direct, not via motor improvement
cards.people: Patients with mild-to-moderate Parkinson's disease on stable antiparkinsonian therapy without motor fluctuations, with depressive symptoms (15-item Geriatric Depression Scale ≥5 and UPDRS part 1 depression item ≥2), at 76 centres in 12 European countries and South Africa: 323 enrolled, 296 randomised, 287 in the primary analysis (pramipexole 139, placebo 148), treated 12 weeks with pramipexole 0.125–1.0 mg three times daily or placebo. Primary endpoint: change in Beck Depression Inventory score.
cards.result: Beck Depression Inventory scores decreased by an adjusted mean 5.9 points (SE 0.5) on pramipexole versus 4.0 points (0.5) on placebo (difference 1.9, 95% CI 0.5–3.4; p = 0.01). UPDRS motor scores also improved more on pramipexole (decrease 4.4 vs 2.2 points; difference 2.2, 95% CI 0.7–3.7; p = 0.003), but prespecified path analysis showed the direct effect of pramipexole on depressive symptoms accounted for 80% of the total treatment effect (p = 0.04). Adverse events were reported in 105 of 144 pramipexole patients and 101 of 152 placebo patients, consistent with the drug's known safety profile.
cards.watchOut: The placebo group also improved by 4.0 points — the drug's added benefit is the 1.9-point difference, a modest average gain; and the trial enrolled patients without motor fluctuations, so it does not directly cover depressed patients whose mood tracks their OFF periods.
cards.source: Barone P et al. Pramipexole for the treatment of depressive symptoms in patients with Parkinson's disease: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. The Lancet. Neurology. 2010. PMID: 20452823. Registry ID: NCT00297778; EudraCT 2005-003788-22. cards.headline: Barone 2006: recovery from major depression in 60.6% on pramipexole versus 27.3% on sertraline in 67 patients — an open-label head-to-head, not placebo-controlled
cards.summary: Barone 2006: recovery from major depression in 60.6% on pramipexole versus 27.3% on sertraline in 67 patients — an open-label head-to-head, not placebo-controlled
cards.type: Randomised open-label head-to-head trial versus sertraline (Barone 2006)
cards.people: 67 Parkinson's outpatients with major depression but no history of motor fluctuations or dyskinesia at seven Italian centres, randomised to open-label pramipexole 1.5–4.5 mg/day or sertraline 50 mg/day for 14 weeks (Hamilton Depression Rating Scale followed over 12 weeks of treatment); recovery was defined as a final Hamilton score ≤8.
cards.result: Hamilton scores decreased throughout treatment in both groups, but the proportion who recovered was significantly higher on pramipexole (60.6%) than on sertraline (27.3%) (p = 0.006). Patients' self-ratings improved in both groups. All adverse events were mild or moderate, but five patients (14.7%) withdrew from the sertraline group. Pramipexole recipients also improved on the UPDRS motor subscore despite the absence of motor complications at entry.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with a single fixed low sertraline dose (50 mg) and only 67 patients: expectation effects and an under-dosed comparator can each manufacture a gap this size, so this card supports — but cannot establish — pramipexole's edge over an SSRI.
cards.source: Barone P et al. Pramipexole versus sertraline in the treatment of depression in Parkinson's disease: a national multicenter parallel-group randomized study. Journal of neurology. 2006. cards.headline: Richard 2012: paroxetine improved Hamilton depression scores by 6.2 points more than placebo and venlafaxine XR by 4.2 points more, in 115 patients with Parkinson's depression, with no motor worsening
cards.summary: Richard 2012: paroxetine improved Hamilton depression scores by 6.2 points more than placebo and venlafaxine XR by 4.2 points more, in 115 patients with Parkinson's depression, with no motor worsening
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial of an SSRI and an SNRI (Richard 2012)
cards.people: 115 subjects with Parkinson's disease at 20 sites, meeting DSM-IV criteria for a depressive disorder or operationally defined subsyndromal depression with a Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression (17-item) score >12, randomised to paroxetine (n = 42, maximum 40 mg/day), venlafaxine extended release (n = 34, maximum 225 mg/day) or placebo (n = 39) for 12 weeks.
cards.result: Treatment effects relative to placebo, expressed as mean 12-week reductions in Hamilton score, were 6.2 points for paroxetine (97.5% CI 2.2 to 10.3; p = 0.0007) and 4.2 points for venlafaxine XR (97.5% CI 0.1 to 8.4; p = 0.02). No treatment effects were seen on motor function. Both medications were generally safe and well tolerated and did not worsen motor function; the authors classed this as Class I evidence for paroxetine and venlafaxine XR in Parkinson's depression.
cards.watchOut: Venlafaxine is an SNRI, not an SSRI — this card's SSRI leg is the paroxetine arm alone (42 patients); a single small arm should not be read as settling the SSRI class question, which the pooled card below leaves open.
cards.source: Richard IH et al. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of antidepressants in Parkinson disease. Neurology. 2012. PMID: 22496199. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Skapinakis 2010 (meta-analysis): across six SSRI-versus-placebo randomised trials in Parkinson's depression, the combined risk ratio was 1.08 (95% CI 0.77–1.55) — insufficient evidence of an SSRI effect
cards.summary: Skapinakis 2010 (meta-analysis): across six SSRI-versus-placebo randomised trials in Parkinson's depression, the combined risk ratio was 1.08 (95% CI 0.77–1.55) — insufficient evidence of an SSRI effect
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (SSRI class)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors for depression in Parkinson's disease: 10 studies included in total, with six studies in the SSRI-versus-placebo comparison and three in the SSRI-versus-tricyclic comparison.
cards.result: In the SSRI-versus-placebo comparison the combined risk ratio (random effects) was 1.08 (95% CI 0.77–1.55; p = 0.67) — the treatment made no demonstrated difference in the pooled estimate. Against tricyclic antidepressants the combined risk ratio was 0.75 (0.39–1.42; p = 0.37). Acceptability analysis showed SSRIs were generally well tolerated. The authors concluded there is insufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis of no difference between SSRIs and placebo, while noting small samples mean a type II error (false negative) cannot be excluded.
cards.watchOut: This pooling predates the Richard 2012 paroxetine trial, so the class picture is 'one later positive trial against an earlier null pool' — genuinely unresolved, which is why this shelf stamps the SSRI leg MAYBE (weak evidence) rather than averaging the two into a false certainty.
cards.source: Skapinakis P et al. Efficacy and acceptability of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors for the treatment of depression in Parkinson's disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. BMC neurology. 2010. PMID: 20565960. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: pramipexole beats placebo in one large trial; SSRIs are one positive paroxetine trial against a null pooled estimate — SPLIT (drug)
cards.summary: Synthesis: pramipexole beats placebo in one large trial; SSRIs are one positive paroxetine trial against a null pooled estimate — SPLIT (drug)
cards.people: The carded evidence: pramipexole versus placebo (Barone 2010, 287 analysed), pramipexole versus sertraline open-label (Barone 2006, 67), paroxetine and venlafaxine XR versus placebo (Richard 2012, 115), and an SSRI-class meta-analysis (Skapinakis 2010, six placebo-controlled trials pooled).
cards.result: Pramipexole: Beck score difference 1.9 points versus placebo (p = 0.01), 80% of effect direct; recovery 60.6% vs 27.3% against open-label sertraline. Paroxetine: 6.2 points better than placebo (p = 0.0007). SSRI class pooled (pre-2012): risk ratio 1.08, no demonstrated difference. PROPOSED SPLIT (drug): pramipexole POSSIBLE (single large trial); SSRIs MAYBE (weak evidence) as a class.
cards.watchOut: Depression scales, populations (major depression vs depressive symptoms; fluctuating vs non-fluctuating) and comparators differ across these reports — the split stamp is the honest summary, and no card here licenses stopping an effective antidepressant to switch to pramipexole.

shelves.title: Memantine for migraine prevention: one small positive placebo-controlled trial (n = 60) and two uncontrolled reports — a thin base that stays at MAYBE (weak evidence)
shelves.question: Does memantine prevent episodic migraine versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Double-Blind Method · Excitatory Amino Acid Antagonists/therapeutic use · Female · Humans · Male · Memantine/therapeutic use · Migraine Disorders/prevention & control · Migraine without Aura/prevention & control · Retrospective Studies · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: THIN BASE, confirmed at build: the ≥3-report gate is met only by counting one small placebo-controlled trial plus two uncontrolled reports — there is exactly one randomised placebo-controlled trial of memantine for migraine prevention in the fetched record. In that trial (Noruzzadeh 2016, 60 patients with migraine without aura, 12 weeks), memantine 10 mg/day reduced monthly attack frequency by a mean 3.4 attacks versus 1.0 on placebo (mean difference 2.3, 95% CI 1.1–3.5; p < 0.001), with migraine days also reduced more on memantine. The supporting reports have no placebo arm: in Bigal 2008, 28 patients with refractory migraine (episodic with 8–14 headache days per month or transformed migraine, having failed at least two preventives) fell from 21.8 to 16.1 headache days per month over 3 months on memantine 10–20 mg/day (p < 0.01, within-group); in Charles 2007, 36 of 54 patients treated for at least 2 months in a retrospective clinic series of 60 reported a significant reduction in estimated headache frequency. A 2014 review of the primary-headache literature reached the same shape of conclusion — data from several retrospective reports and two prospective trials suggested memantine may be useful, mostly in refractory chronic migraine (Huang 2014, described in the synthesis, not carded as a fourth evidence card to avoid double-counting the same reports). Because uncontrolled before–after falls in migraine frequency are exactly what placebo arms and regression also produce, the uncontrolled reports cannot corroborate the trial. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): one small positive trial, no replication, supporting evidence uncontrolled.

cards.headline: Noruzzadeh 2016: the only placebo-controlled trial — memantine 10 mg/day reduced monthly attack frequency by 3.4 versus 1.0 on placebo in 60 patients with migraine without aura (mean difference 2.3; p < 0.001)
cards.summary: Noruzzadeh 2016: the only placebo-controlled trial — memantine 10 mg/day reduced monthly attack frequency by 3.4 versus 1.0 on placebo in 60 patients with migraine without aura (mean difference 2.3; p < 0.001)
cards.people: 60 patients with migraine without aura in a 12-week randomised double-blind placebo-controlled parallel-group study, randomised to memantine 10 mg/day or placebo; 25 patients in the memantine group and 27 in the placebo group completed the study. Primary outcome: difference in change from baseline in monthly attack frequency at week 12, by migraine diary.
cards.result: Patients on memantine showed a significantly greater reduction in monthly attack frequency (mean change 3.4, 95% CI 2.3–4.4) than placebo (mean change 1.0, 95% CI 0.3–1.7) (mean difference 2.3, 95% CI 1.1–3.5; p < 0.001). Migraine days were also reduced more on memantine in both complete-case (mean difference 4.9 days, 95% CI 2.6–7.2) and intention-to-treat analyses (mean difference 5.2, 95% CI 2.0–8.5) (both p < 0.01), as were work-absence days, severity and disability scores. Quality of life, sleep, depression and anxiety did not differ between groups. Three memantine patients reported sedation, mild vertigo/nausea or drowsiness; one placebo patient reported nausea and another discontinued after 2 weeks for vertigo.
cards.watchOut: One trial, 60 randomised and 52 completing, from a single programme, never replicated in the fetched record: a mean difference this size in a trial this small is fragile, and the question's stamp is capped by that single-trial base.
cards.source: Noruzzadeh R et al. Memantine for Prophylactic Treatment of Migraine Without Aura: A Randomized Double-Blind Placebo-Controlled Study. Headache. 2016. PMID: 26638119. Registry ID: IRCT2013120115616N1 (Iranian Registry of Clinical Trials). cards.headline: Bigal 2008: in 28 patients with refractory migraine, headache days fell from 21.8 to 16.1 per month over 3 months on memantine — an uncontrolled pilot with no placebo arm
cards.summary: Bigal 2008: in 28 patients with refractory migraine, headache days fell from 21.8 to 16.1 per month over 3 months on memantine — an uncontrolled pilot with no placebo arm
cards.people: 28 patients (intention-to-treat population) with refractory migraine — episodic migraine with 8–14 headache days per month or transformed migraine — who had previously failed at least two adequate preventive trials, treated openly with memantine 10–20 mg/day for 3 months; other preventives were allowed at stable doses. Primary endpoint: days with headache at month 3.
cards.result: Monthly headache frequency fell from 21.8 days at baseline to 16.1 at 3 months (p < 0.01, within-group). Days with severe pain fell from 7.8 to 3.2 (p < 0.01) and mean disability scores from 54.9 to 36.6 (p < 0.01); trail-making test times also improved. Side effects were present in 37.5% of patients and 5.5% dropped out for poor tolerability; most adverse events were mild. The authors called this preliminary evidence and stated double-blind studies were required.
cards.watchOut: No control group: in refractory migraine, enrolment at a bad patch followed by regression, expectation and stable co-preventives can each produce a fall of this size — this report is carded as context for the trial, labelled uncontrolled, and contributes nothing to the placebo comparison.
cards.source: Bigal M et al. Memantine in the preventive treatment of refractory migraine. Headache. 2008. PMID: 19031499. Registry ID: none in the record.
