cards.headline: Charles 2007: in a retrospective clinic series, 36 of 54 patients treated at least 2 months reported a significant reduction in estimated headache frequency on memantine
cards.summary: Charles 2007: in a retrospective clinic series, 36 of 54 patients treated at least 2 months reported a significant reduction in estimated headache frequency on memantine
cards.people: Retrospective study of 60 cases: all patients in a university headache clinic who received memantine as preventive therapy for frequent migraine over a 15-month period were mailed surveys and consent forms for record review; memantine was started at 5 mg/day and increased by 5 mg/week as needed up to 10 mg twice daily. 54 patients were treated for at least 2 months and form the analysed group.
cards.result: The majority of patients (36 out of 54) treated with memantine for at least 2 months reported a significant reduction in estimated headache frequency and improved function. Side effects were uncommon and generally mild. The authors concluded this limited retrospective case review suggests memantine may be an effective preventive for frequent migraine and that a prospective trial is warranted.
cards.watchOut: Observational, survey-based and retrospective, with outcomes as patients' estimated headache frequency: the weakest design on this shelf, labelled as such — it shows the drug was tried and tolerated in a refractory clinic population, not that it works.
cards.source: Charles A et al. Memantine for prevention of migraine: a retrospective study of 60 cases. The journal of headache and pain. 2007. PMID: 17901918. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: one small positive placebo-controlled trial (n = 60) plus two uncontrolled reports (n = 28 and 54 analysed) — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.summary: Synthesis: one small positive placebo-controlled trial (n = 60) plus two uncontrolled reports (n = 28 and 54 analysed) — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.people: The carded evidence: Noruzzadeh 2016 (randomised, 60 patients), Bigal 2008 (open pilot, 28 patients), Charles 2007 (retrospective series, 60 cases, 54 analysed). Total carded participants: 148. A 2014 narrative review of memantine for primary headache disorders (Huang L et al., The Annals of pharmacotherapy, PMID: 25159002) is described in the balance prose, not carded, because it summarises these same reports.
cards.result: Placebo-controlled: monthly attack frequency reduction 3.4 versus 1.0 (mean difference 2.3, 95% CI 1.1–3.5; p < 0.001) in the single trial. Uncontrolled: headache days 21.8 to 16.1 per month (Bigal); 36 of 54 reporting significant frequency reduction (Charles). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — the ≥3-report gate is met, but only one report is a placebo-controlled trial and it is small and unreplicated.
cards.watchOut: Migraine frequency falls on placebo and with time in almost every preventive study ever run; until a second, larger placebo-controlled trial exists, memantine's migraine claim stays at MAYBE (weak evidence) however clean the single trial's p-value looks.

shelves.title: Lisinopril for migraine prevention: 21% relative fewer migraine days versus placebo in one small 2001 crossover trial — no replication, class pooling inconclusive, MAYBE (weak evidence)
shelves.question: Does lisinopril prevent migraine attacks versus placebo in frequent episodic migraine?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Blood Pressure · Cross-Over Studies · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Lisinopril/therapeutic use · Migraine Disorders/physiopathology,prevention & control,drug therapy
shelves.balance: THIN BASE, confirmed at build: lisinopril itself rests on exactly one placebo-controlled trial — the ≥3-report gate for this shelf is met by that trial plus two pooled analyses of the wider blood-pressure-drug class, and the stamp does not pretend otherwise. The candesartan home, pack #3686, is a different drug and does not answer this question — verified against that pack's question. In Schrader 2001, a double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial in 60 patients with two to six migraine episodes a month, lisinopril 20 mg daily (after one week at 10 mg) reduced hours with headache by 20% (95% CI 5% to 36%), days with headache by 17% (5% to 30%), days with migraine by 21% (9% to 34%) and headache severity index by 20% (3% to 37%) versus placebo in the 47 participants with complete data, with intention-to-treat analysis of 55 patients supporting the differences; days with migraine fell by at least 50% in 14 participants on active treatment versus placebo. The class-level pooling is broader but shallower for lisinopril specifically: a 2023 meta-analysis of 50 blood-pressure-medication trials found ACE inhibitors as a class reduced monthly headache days by a standardised estimate of −1.3 (95% CI −2.9 to 0.2) versus placebo — a class estimate whose confidence interval crosses zero, with the separately significant specific drugs listed not including lisinopril (Carcel 2023). A 2019 systematic review of ACE inhibitors and ARBs in migraine found 18 reports, noted the lisinopril evidence was open-label in the reports it counted at 5 mg, and concluded these drugs are not recommended as first-line prophylactics on the limited trials and small samples, though they may be useful where hypertension coexists (Dorosch 2019). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): one small crossover trial from 2001, never followed by a second lisinopril trial in the fetched record.

cards.headline: Schrader 2001: lisinopril reduced days with migraine by 21% and hours with headache by 20% versus placebo in a 60-patient double-blind crossover trial — the only lisinopril trial
cards.summary: Schrader 2001: lisinopril reduced days with migraine by 21% and hours with headache by 20% versus placebo in a 60-patient double-blind crossover trial — the only lisinopril trial
cards.people: 60 patients aged 19–59 years with migraine with two to six episodes a month at a neurological outpatient clinic, in a double-blind placebo-controlled crossover study: 12 weeks of lisinopril (one 10 mg tablet daily for one week, then two 10 mg tablets daily for 11 weeks) and 12 weeks of matched placebo, separated by a 2-week washout, with 30 participants in each sequence order. Primary endpoints: hours with headache, days with headache, days with migraine. Complete data were available for 47 participants; intention-to-treat analysis covered 55.
cards.result: In the 47 participants with complete data, hours with headache, days with headache, days with migraine and headache severity index were significantly reduced on lisinopril versus placebo by 20% (95% CI 5% to 36%), 17% (5% to 30%), 21% (9% to 34%) and 20% (3% to 37%) respectively — all relative reductions, printed as the record gives them, without absolute day counts. Days with migraine were reduced by at least 50% in 14 participants for active treatment versus placebo. Intention-to-treat analysis of 55 patients supported the differences in favour of lisinopril for the primary endpoints.
cards.watchOut: A single 2001 crossover trial — 60 randomised, 47 with complete data — is the entire direct evidence for lisinopril in migraine; crossover designs in migraine are vulnerable to period and carryover effects, and no second trial has tested the finding in the fetched record.
cards.source: Schrader H et al. Prophylactic treatment of migraine with angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor (lisinopril): randomised, placebo controlled, crossover study. cards.headline: Carcel 2023 (meta-analysis of 50 trials): ACE inhibitors as a class reduced monthly headache days versus placebo by −1.3 (95% CI −2.9 to 0.2) — an interval crossing zero, and lisinopril was not among the separately significant drugs
cards.summary: Carcel 2023 (meta-analysis of 50 trials): ACE inhibitors as a class reduced monthly headache days versus placebo by −1.3 (95% CI −2.9 to 0.2) — an interval crossing zero, and lisinopril was not among the separately significant drugs
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 50 randomised trials (class-level)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials of blood-pressure-lowering medications versus placebo in episodic migraine: 50 trials (70% crossover) comprising 60 comparisons; mean age 39 years, 79% female. Outcomes were monthly headache or migraine days and attacks, pooled as standardised mean differences.
cards.result: Monthly headache days were fewer on all drug classes than placebo, statistically significant for all but one class: ACE inhibitors −1.3 (95% CI −2.9 to 0.2), angiotensin II receptor blockers −0.9 (−1.6 to −0.1), beta-blockers −0.4 (−0.8 to −0.0), calcium channel blockers −1.8 (−3.4 to −0.2) and alpha-blockers −0.7 (−1.2 to −0.1). Specific drugs separately significant included candesartan, atenolol, bisoprolol, metoprolol, propranolol, timolol, nicardipine, verapamil and clonidine — lisinopril is not in that list. The authors concluded a broader range of blood-pressure medications reduces headache frequency than guidelines currently include.
cards.watchOut: Class-level pooling cannot rescue a drug-specific claim: the ACE-inhibitor estimate mixes drugs and its interval crosses zero, so this card is context for plausibility, not corroboration of Schrader's lisinopril result.

cards.headline: Dorosch 2019 (systematic review): 18 ACE-inhibitor/ARB migraine reports, small samples throughout — 'not recommended as first-line' but possibly useful with coexisting hypertension
cards.summary: Dorosch 2019 (systematic review): 18 ACE-inhibitor/ARB migraine reports, small samples throughout — 'not recommended as first-line' but possibly useful with coexisting hypertension
cards.type: Systematic review of ACE-inhibitor/ARB migraine reports (Dorosch 2019)
cards.people: Systematic review of ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers for prophylactic treatment of migraine in adults aged 18–70, searching PubMed, MEDLINE, Embase and the Cochrane Library from 1990 to 2017: 2,461 articles retrieved, 18 reports (randomised trials, meta-analyses, systematic reviews or guidelines) included.
cards.result: Three randomised trials (telmisartan 80 mg, candesartan 16 mg, enalapril 10 mg) and two open-label trials (lisinopril 5 mg and ramipril 5 mg) found high numbers of responders with greater than 50% reduction in migraine attack frequency versus a 4-week baseline period; candesartan was superior to placebo while telmisartan and enalapril were not. The authors concluded lipophilic ACE inhibitors and ARBs can be effective prophylactic agents, but based on the limited number of published trials and small sample size they are not recommended as first-line prophylactics, though in populations with comorbidities such as hypertension they may be useful as first- or second-line prophylactics.
cards.watchOut: Note the tension this review creates, printed rather than smoothed over: the lisinopril reports it counted were open-label at 5 mg, while the placebo-controlled lisinopril evidence on this shelf is Schrader's 20 mg crossover trial — the review's responder counts are versus baseline, not versus placebo, and cannot be quoted as controlled effects.
cards.source: Dorosch T et al. Efficacy of Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors and Angiotensin Receptor Blockers in the Preventative Treatment of Episodic Migraine in Adults. cards.headline: Synthesis: one small crossover trial of lisinopril itself (60 patients), supported only by class-level pooling whose ACE estimate crosses zero — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.summary: Synthesis: one small crossover trial of lisinopril itself (60 patients), supported only by class-level pooling whose ACE estimate crosses zero — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.people: The carded evidence: Schrader 2001 (randomised crossover, 60 patients, 47 with complete data), Carcel 2023 (meta-analysis of 50 blood-pressure-drug trials, class-level), Dorosch 2019 (systematic review, 18 ACE-inhibitor/ARB reports). The direct lisinopril evidence base is the single Schrader trial.
cards.result: Lisinopril versus placebo: days with migraine −21% relative (95% CI 9% to 34%), hours with headache −20% relative, ≥50% migraine-day reduction in 14 participants on active treatment versus placebo. ACE-inhibitor class pooled: −1.3 (95% CI −2.9 to 0.2) monthly headache days — not significant. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: The plausible real-world use — a migraine patient who also needs an ACE inhibitor for blood pressure — is a comorbidity argument, not stronger migraine evidence; this shelf's stamp stays at MAYBE (weak evidence) until a second lisinopril trial exists.

shelves.title: Acupuncture for migraine prevention: a small real advantage over sham (response 50% vs 41%), and short-term effects at least matching prophylactic drugs
shelves.question: Does acupuncture reduce migraine frequency versus sham acupuncture and versus prophylactic drug treatment?
shelves.mesh: Acupuncture Therapy/adverse effects · Female · Humans · Male · Migraine Disorders/drug therapy/prevention & control · Migraine with Aura/prevention & control · Migraine without Aura/prevention & control · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: Acupuncture reduced migraine frequency a small amount more than sham acupuncture and at least as much as prophylactic drug treatment in the short term. The updated Cochrane review (Linde 2016; 22 trials, 4,985 participants) found a small but significant advantage over sham after treatment (standardised mean difference -0.18; response — headache frequency at least halved — in 50% on true acupuncture vs 41% on sham, relative risk 1.23) and a larger short-term advantage over prophylactic drugs (SMD -0.25 after treatment; response 57% vs 46%, relative risk 1.24) that was not maintained at follow-up, with fewer adverse-effect dropouts than drugs. Two later randomised trials point the same way against sham: Zhao 2017 (true acupuncture cut attack frequency by 3.2 vs 2.1 attacks on sham at week 16) and Xu 2020 (manual acupuncture cut migraine days more than non-penetrating sham at weeks 17–20). No single named acupuncture programme was tested across these studies: the records describe session-based manual acupuncture at true points (20 sessions in both Zhao and Xu), with point selection varying between trials, and no branded or single named protocol is given in the publications carded. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit, small over sham): a real but small advantage over sham, and short-term effects at least similar to prophylactic drugs, on moderate-quality evidence.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2016 (Linde): across 22 trials (4,985 people), acupuncture beat sham by a small margin (response 50% vs 41%) and beat prophylactic drugs short-term (response 57% vs 46%), with fewer adverse-effect dropouts than drugs
cards.summary: Cochrane 2016 (Linde): across 22 trials (4,985 people), acupuncture beat sham by a small margin (response 50% vs 41%) and beat prophylactic drugs short-term (response 57% vs 46%), with fewer adverse-effect dropouts than drugs
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 22 randomised trials (Cochrane, Linde 2016)
cards.people: 22 randomised trials including 4,985 adults with episodic migraine in total (median 71 participants per trial); 15 trials used a sham-acupuncture control and 5 used a prophylactic-drug comparator. Interventions were session-based acupuncture as delivered in the individual trials; no single named programme or point protocol was common to the trials.
cards.result: Versus sham: after treatment, headache frequency fell slightly more with true acupuncture (SMD -0.18, 95% CI -0.28 to -0.08; 12 trials, 1,646 participants), and frequency at least halved in 50% on true acupuncture vs 41% on sham (pooled relative risk 1.23, 95% CI 1.11 to 1.36; 14 trials, 1,825 participants), a number needed to treat of 11. Versus prophylactic drugs: acupuncture reduced frequency more after treatment (SMD -0.25, 95% CI -0.39 to -0.10; 3 trials, 739 participants; response 57% vs 46%, relative risk 1.24), but the advantage was not maintained at follow-up (SMD -0.13, 95% CI -0.28 to 0.01). Participants on acupuncture were less likely than those on drugs to drop out because of adverse effects (OR 0.27) or to report adverse effects (OR 0.25). The review graded the evidence moderate quality.
cards.watchOut: The pooled advantage over sham is small (about 9 extra responders per 100 treated); the drug comparison rests on only 3–5 trials, could not be blinded, and its advantage faded at follow-up.
cards.source: Linde K et al. Acupuncture for the prevention of episodic migraine. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2016. PMID: 27351677. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Zhao 2017: true acupuncture cut migraine attacks by 3.2 vs 2.1 on sham at week 16 (difference 1.1 attacks) in migraine without aura
cards.summary: Zhao 2017: true acupuncture cut migraine attacks by 3.2 vs 2.1 on sham at week 16 (difference 1.1 attacks) in migraine without aura
cards.people: 249 participants aged 18 to 65 with migraine without aura (2 to 8 attacks per month) at 3 clinical sites in China, randomised to true acupuncture, sham acupuncture, or a waiting-list control; 245 were included in the intention-to-treat analyses. The true and sham groups received 20 sessions over 4 weeks (5 days per week), followed by 20 weeks of follow-up.
cards.result: At week 16 the mean reduction in migraine attack frequency was 3.2 (SD 2.1) attacks on true acupuncture, 2.1 (2.5) on sham, and 1.4 (2.5) on waiting list. True acupuncture beat sham by 1.1 attacks (95% CI 0.4 to 1.9; P = .002) and waiting list by 1.8 attacks (95% CI 1.1 to 2.5; P < .001); sham did not differ significantly from waiting list (difference 0.7 attacks; P = .07).
cards.watchOut: One trial in migraine without aura only, with an intensive 20-session, 4-week schedule that may not match acupuncture as usually delivered; the sham group also improved substantially, so most of the total improvement was not specific to true points.
cards.source: Zhao L et al. The Long-term Effect of Acupuncture for Migraine Prophylaxis: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA internal medicine. 2017. PMID: 28241154. cards.headline: Xu 2020 (BMJ): 20 sessions of manual acupuncture cut migraine days more than non-penetrating sham at weeks 17–20 (adjusted difference -2.1 days per 4 weeks)
cards.summary: Xu 2020 (BMJ): 20 sessions of manual acupuncture cut migraine days more than non-penetrating sham at weeks 17–20 (adjusted difference -2.1 days per 4 weeks)
cards.people: 150 acupuncture-naive patients with episodic migraine without aura at 7 hospitals in China, randomised to 20 sessions of manual acupuncture at true acupuncture points plus usual care, 20 sessions of non-penetrating sham acupuncture at heterosegmental non-acupuncture points plus usual care, or usual care alone over 8 weeks; 147 were included in the full analysis set.
cards.result: Compared with sham, manual acupuncture produced a significantly greater reduction in migraine days at weeks 13 to 20 and in migraine attacks at weeks 17 to 20. The reduction in mean migraine days was 3.9 (SD 3.0) on manual acupuncture vs 2.2 (3.2) on sham at weeks 17 to 20 (adjusted difference -2.1, 95% CI -2.9 to -1.2; P < .001), and the reduction in attacks was 2.3 (1.7) vs 1.6 (2.5) (adjusted difference -1.0, 95% CI -1.5 to -0.5; P < .001). No severe adverse events were reported, and blinding held (needle penetration perceived by 79% vs 75%; P = 0.891).
cards.watchOut: The record's MeSH tags this trial 'Migraine with Aura' although its title, population and abstract all specify migraine without aura — the card follows the abstract. Participants were acupuncture-naive and treated in China; effects in chronic migraine or in people with aura were not tested here.

cards.headline: Synthesis: acupuncture beats sham by a small, consistent margin and matches prophylactic drugs short-term — LIKELY (benefit, small over sham)
cards.summary: Synthesis: acupuncture beats sham by a small, consistent margin and matches prophylactic drugs short-term — LIKELY (benefit, small over sham)
cards.people: The carded evidence: one Cochrane review of 22 trials (4,985 participants), and two sham-controlled randomised trials (249 and 150 participants). Total carded participants exceed 5,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: All three reports favour true over sham acupuncture: Cochrane response 50% vs 41% (relative risk 1.23), Zhao a 1.1-attack greater reduction at week 16, and Xu a 2.1-day greater reduction in migraine days per 4 weeks at weeks 17–20. Against prophylactic drugs, the Cochrane review found acupuncture at least as effective after treatment (response 57% vs 46%) with fewer adverse effects, the advantage not maintained at follow-up. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit, small over sham): the benefit over sham is real but small; the comparison with drugs is short-term and unblinded.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote the total improvement on acupuncture (roughly halving of frequency in half of patients) as the specific effect: sham treatment produced most of it. The specific gain over sham is the 9-percentage-point response difference and the 1–2 fewer attacks or days per month on the trial cards.

shelves.title: Vestibular migraine prevention: the only placebo-controlled trial (metoprolol) was null, and the positive evidence is small trials without placebo controls
shelves.question: In vestibular migraine, do preventive treatments used for migraine (e.g., beta-blockers, tricyclics, triptan-based strategies) reduce vertigo attack frequency versus placebo?

shelves.balance: The vestibular-migraine prevention evidence is thin and mostly not placebo-controlled. The only placebo-controlled trial carded, PROVEMIG, randomised 130 patients to metoprolol or placebo, was stopped early for poor accrual (266 planned), and found no difference in vertiginous attacks (incidence rate ratio 0.983, 95% CI 0.902 to 1.071) — the treatment made no difference. Small active-comparator trials report large within-group falls in attacks on propranolol and on venlafaxine (Salviz 2016, 64 patients, no placebo group) and a vertigo-frequency advantage for adding flunarizine to betahistine-based episodic treatment (Lepcha 2014, 48 patients). A 2023 network meta-analysis of the whole randomised base — 5 trials, 334 patients — found valproate superior to placebo or abortive treatment alone for vertigo frequency (mean difference -4.12 attacks) and handicap gains for flunarizine, valproate and venlafaxine, while grading the certainty low and metoprolol worst for efficacy. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): some migraine preventives may reduce vertigo attacks in vestibular migraine, but the one adequately blinded placebo test was null and the positive signals come from small trials without placebo controls.

cards.headline: PROVEMIG 2019: metoprolol did not reduce vertiginous attacks versus placebo (incidence rate ratio 0.983) — the trial stopped early at 130 of 266 planned patients (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: PROVEMIG 2019: metoprolol did not reduce vertiginous attacks versus placebo (incidence rate ratio 0.983) — the trial stopped early at 130 of 266 planned patients (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: 130 adults with probable or definitive vestibular migraine (Neuhauser criteria) randomised at German university hospitals to metoprolol succinate (maintenance 95 mg daily) or placebo for 6 months, in a phase III double-blind trial planned for 266 patients and discontinued for poor accrual.
cards.result: For the full analysis set, the incidence rate ratio for vertiginous attacks in months 4 to 6 was 0.983 (95% CI 0.902 to 1.071) for metoprolol versus placebo — no evidence of a difference (the treatment made no difference). Monthly vertigo attacks fell over time in both groups (factor 0.830, 95% CI 0.776 to 0.887), results were consistent across secondary measures, and treatment was well tolerated with no unexpected safety findings.
cards.watchOut: PROVEMIG stopped at about half its planned size, so a modest metoprolol effect cannot be excluded; but it is the only placebo-controlled card here, and its point estimate is almost exactly 1.0. It tests metoprolol only — it does not settle propranolol, venlafaxine or valproate.
cards.source: Bayer O et al. Results and lessons learnt from a randomized controlled trial: prophylactic treatment of vestibular migraine with metoprolol (PROVEMIG). Trials. 2019. PMID: 31888723. Registry ID: EudraCT 2009-013701-34, from the record's abstract text; the record's databank fields carry no registry ID. cards.headline: Salviz 2016: vertiginous attacks fell from about 12 to about 2 per period on both propranolol and venlafaxine over 4 months — with no placebo group to separate drug effect from natural course
cards.summary: Salviz 2016: vertiginous attacks fell from about 12 to about 2 per period on both propranolol and venlafaxine over 4 months — with no placebo group to separate drug effect from natural course
cards.people: 64 subjects with definite vestibular migraine, randomised prospectively to propranolol (group P, n = 33) or venlafaxine (group V, n = 31) for prophylaxis, with outcomes recorded before and 4 months after treatment.
cards.result: The mean number of vertiginous attacks fell from 12.6 to 1.9 on propranolol and from 12.2 to 2.6 on venlafaxine (both P < .001 within group); Dizziness Handicap Inventory total scores fell from 55.8 to 31.3 and from 50.9 to 19.9 respectively, and Vertigo Severity Scores fell similarly. Treatment effects did not differ between the groups (P > .05). Depression scores improved only on venlafaxine.
cards.watchOut: Without a placebo or untreated arm, the dramatic within-group falls cannot be credited to the drugs: PROVEMIG's placebo group also improved markedly over time. This card shows propranolol and venlafaxine performed alike, not that either beat no treatment.
cards.source: Salviz M et al. Propranolol and venlafaxine for vestibular migraine prophylaxis: A randomized controlled trial. The Laryngoscope. 2016. PMID: 26228645. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Lepcha 2014: adding flunarizine 10 mg to betahistine-based episodic treatment improved vertigo frequency (P = 0.010) and severity (P = 0.046), but not headache, over 12 weeks
cards.summary: Lepcha 2014: adding flunarizine 10 mg to betahistine-based episodic treatment improved vertigo frequency (P = 0.010) and severity (P = 0.046), but not headache, over 12 weeks
cards.people: 48 patients with definitive migrainous vertigo who completed a 12-week randomised trial at a tertiary referral centre. Arm A received flunarizine 10 mg daily along with betahistine 16 mg and paracetamol 1 g during episodes; arm B received betahistine and paracetamol during episodes only.
cards.result: Analysis of the frequency of vertiginous episodes showed a significant difference favouring the flunarizine arm (P = 0.010), as did improvement in severity of vertigo (P = 0.046). Headache frequency and severity did not improve significantly in the flunarizine arm compared with control. The main side effects were weight gain and somnolence, not significantly different between groups. The record reports P values without the underlying attack counts for this comparison.
cards.watchOut: The comparison is flunarizine added to betahistine-based care versus that care alone — not flunarizine versus placebo — in 48 patients diagnosed under the older 'migrainous vertigo' label, and the abstract gives significance levels without attack counts, so the size of the advantage cannot be stated.
cards.source: Lepcha A et al. Flunarizine in the prophylaxis of migrainous vertigo: a randomized controlled trial. European archives of oto-rhino-laryngology. 2014. PMID: 24166742. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Chu 2023 network meta-analysis: across all 5 randomised trials (334 patients), valproate beat placebo/abortive care on vertigo frequency (mean difference -4.12), but certainty was low and metoprolol ranked worst
cards.summary: Chu 2023 network meta-analysis: across all 5 randomised trials (334 patients), valproate beat placebo/abortive care on vertigo frequency (mean difference -4.12), but certainty was low and metoprolol ranked worst
cards.type: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of 5 randomised trials (Chu 2023)
cards.people: Five randomised trials comprising 334 patients with vestibular migraine, comparing beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, antiseizure medicines and antidepressants (tricyclics and serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors), with efficacy measured as vertigo frequency per month and Dizziness Handicap Inventory improvement after 3–6 months.
cards.result: Valproate was superior to placebo or abortive treatment alone in reducing vertigo frequency (mean difference -4.12, 95% CI -8.09 to -0.15). Flunarizine (MD 20.00, 95% CI 10.90 to 29.10), valproate (MD 18.88, 95% CI 10.42 to 27.34) and venlafaxine (MD 11.48, 95% CI 9.84 to 13.12) improved Dizziness Handicap Inventory more than placebo or abortive treatment. Valproate ranked best for vertigo frequency but third-to-last for tolerability; flunarizine ranked best for handicap but worst for tolerability; metoprolol ranked worst for efficacy and best for tolerability. The authors state the certainty is low, the sample limited, and head-to-head trials are warranted.
cards.watchOut: A network built on 5 small trials (334 patients in total, overlapping with the trials carded above) — its rankings rest heavily on indirect comparisons and on the same few studies, so it corroborates the thinness of the base rather than adding an independent large body of evidence.
cards.source: Chu H et al. Prophylactic treatments for vestibular migraine: a systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials. Frontiers in pharmacology. 2023. PMID: 38186654. Registry ID: PROSPERO CRD42023422258, from the record's abstract text. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: one null placebo-controlled trial, small positive active-comparator trials, and a low-certainty network — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.summary: Synthesis: one null placebo-controlled trial, small positive active-comparator trials, and a low-certainty network — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.people: The carded evidence: one placebo-controlled trial (PROVEMIG, 130 patients), two small randomised active-comparator trials (64 and 48 patients), and one network meta-analysis of 5 trials (334 patients, overlapping with the trials above).
cards.result: Against placebo, the only direct test — metoprolol in PROVEMIG — made no difference (incidence rate ratio 0.983). Against active or episodic-treatment comparators, propranolol, venlafaxine and flunarizine arms all improved, and the network meta-analysis found valproate, flunarizine and venlafaxine ahead of placebo or abortive care on some outcomes at low certainty. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): preventive migraine drugs may reduce vertigo attacks in vestibular migraine, but no agent has beaten placebo in an adequately sized direct trial carded here.
cards.watchOut: The gap between the within-group improvements in the uncontrolled comparisons and PROVEMIG's null result is the central caution of this shelf: vestibular migraine attacks fluctuate and trial participants improve on placebo, so pre–post falls of the Salviz size cannot be read as drug effects.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bayer O et al. Trials. 2019 (PMID: 31888723); Salviz M et al. The Laryngoscope. 2016 (PMID: 26228645); Lepcha A et al. European archives of oto-rhino-laryngology. 2014 (PMID: 24166742); Chu H et al. Frontiers in pharmacology. 2023 (PMID: 38186654).

shelves.title: Soticlestat for Dravet and Lennox–Gastaut syndromes: phase 2 Dravet signal, phase 3 primary missed in Dravet and flatly null in Lennox–Gastaut (SKYLINE/SKYWAY, published 2026)
shelves.question: In Dravet syndrome and Lennox–Gastaut syndrome, does soticlestat reduce convulsive/drop seizure frequency versus placebo as adjunctive therapy?
shelves.mesh: Anticonvulsants/adverse effects · Child · Double-Blind Method · Epilepsies, Myoclonic/chemically induced/drug therapy · Epileptic Syndromes · Humans · Lennox Gastaut Syndrome/drug therapy · Piperidines · Pyridines · Seizures/drug therapy · Spasms, Infantile/chemically induced/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: FLAG — phase 3 publication status verified from the fetched records this session: SKYLINE (Dravet) and SKYWAY (Lennox–Gastaut) have both now published in Epilepsia (2026), so the cardable base is three randomised reports, not ELEKTRA alone. The phase 2 ELEKTRA trial (141 children) met its combined primary endpoint (placebo-adjusted median seizure-frequency reduction 30.21%, P = .0008), driven by Dravet convulsive seizures (50.00%, P = .0002); its Lennox–Gastaut drop-seizure result was not significant (17.08%, P = .1160). The phase 3 trials did not confirm those signals on their primaries: SKYLINE (144 participants with Dravet) narrowly missed (median convulsive-seizure change -22.16% on soticlestat vs -8.64% on placebo; difference -15.64%, P = .061), although 27.4% vs 9.9% achieved a 50% response (nominal P = .008); SKYWAY (270 participants with Lennox–Gastaut) was flatly null on major motor drop seizures (difference -1.17%, P = .785 — the treatment made no difference). PROPOSED SPLIT (syndrome and phase): a phase 2 Dravet signal that phase 3 did not confirm on its primary endpoint, and no demonstrated benefit in Lennox–Gastaut syndrome in either phase.

cards.headline: ELEKTRA 2022 (phase 2): combined placebo-adjusted median seizure reduction 30.21% (P = .0008) — 50.00% for Dravet convulsive seizures (P = .0002) but 17.08% and not significant for Lennox–Gastaut drop seizures
cards.summary: ELEKTRA 2022 (phase 2): combined placebo-adjusted median seizure reduction 30.21% (P = .0008) — 50.00% for Dravet convulsive seizures (P = .0002) but 17.08% and not significant for Lennox–Gastaut drop seizures
cards.people: 141 children aged 2–17 years enrolled (139 in the modified intention-to-treat population: 51 with Dravet syndrome with 3 or more convulsive seizures per month, and 88 with Lennox–Gastaut syndrome with 4 or more drop seizures per month), randomised to adjunctive soticlestat (up to 300 mg twice daily, weight-adjusted) or placebo over 20 weeks (8-week dose optimisation, 12-week maintenance).
cards.result: ELEKTRA met its combined primary endpoint: a placebo-adjusted median reduction in seizure frequency of 30.21% during maintenance (P = .0008). By syndrome, the placebo-adjusted median reduction was 50.00% for convulsive seizures in Dravet syndrome (P = .0002) and 17.08% for drop seizures in Lennox–Gastaut syndrome (P = .1160, not significant). Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 80.3% on soticlestat vs 74.3% on placebo, serious events in 15.5% vs 18.6%; lethargy and constipation were more common on soticlestat, and there were no deaths.
cards.watchOut: The headline combined endpoint pools two syndromes with opposite significance: the Dravet subgroup was only 51 children, and the Lennox–Gastaut result inside this same trial was already null — read the syndrome split, not the pooled 30.21%.
cards.source: Hahn CD et al. A phase 2, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study to evaluate the efficacy and safety of soticlestat as adjunctive therapy in pediatric patients with Dravet syndrome or Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (ELEKTRA). Epilepsia. 2022. PMID: 35841234. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03650452. cards.headline: SKYLINE 2026 (phase 3, Dravet): primary endpoint narrowly missed — median convulsive-seizure change -22.16% vs -8.64% on placebo (difference -15.64%, P = .061); 50% responders 27.4% vs 9.9% (nominal P = .008)
cards.summary: SKYLINE 2026 (phase 3, Dravet): primary endpoint narrowly missed — median convulsive-seizure change -22.16% vs -8.64% on placebo (difference -15.64%, P = .061); 50% responders 27.4% vs 9.9% (nominal P = .008)
cards.people: 144 children and young adults aged 2–21 years with Dravet syndrome and uncontrolled convulsive seizures (4 or more per month despite treatment), randomised to oral soticlestat 300 mg (weight-adjusted) twice daily (n = 73) or matching placebo (n = 71) for 16 weeks (4-week titration, 12-week maintenance); 81.3% were receiving 3 or more antiseizure medications.
cards.result: The primary endpoint was not met: median change in convulsive seizure frequency over the full treatment period was -22.16% on soticlestat vs -8.64% on placebo, a difference of -15.64% (P = .061); in the maintenance period the difference was -14.29% (P = .089). The proportion with a 50% or greater reduction was 27.4% on soticlestat vs 9.9% on placebo (nominal P = .008), and caregiver and clinical global-impression scales favoured soticlestat (nominal P values .004 or lower). The commonest drug-related adverse events were somnolence, change in seizure presentation, decreased appetite and insomnia; no new safety concerns emerged.
cards.watchOut: Responder and global-impression advantages are reported with nominal P values after the primary endpoint missed — they are supportive signals, not a confirmed primary benefit, and this card does not upgrade them into one.
cards.source: Sullivan J et al. Soticlestat as an adjunctive therapy in children and young adults with Dravet syndrome. Epilepsia. 2026. PMID: 41784472. cards.headline: SKYWAY 2026 (phase 3, Lennox–Gastaut): no difference in major motor drop seizures (difference -1.17%, P = .785) — the treatment made no difference
cards.summary: SKYWAY 2026 (phase 3, Lennox–Gastaut): no difference in major motor drop seizures (difference -1.17%, P = .785) — the treatment made no difference
cards.people: 270 participants aged 2–55 years with Lennox–Gastaut syndrome (adjudicated by the Epilepsy Study Consortium), randomised 1:1 to adjunctive soticlestat (up to 300 mg twice daily, weight-adjusted; n = 134) or placebo (n = 136) on stable background medication over 16 weeks (4-week titration, 12-week maintenance); 95% were receiving 2 or more antiseizure medications.
cards.result: The difference in median change from baseline in major motor drop seizure frequency for soticlestat versus placebo was -1.17% (P = .785) over the full treatment period and +2.43% (P = .778) during maintenance — the treatment made no difference. No meaningful difference was observed on most key secondary endpoints. Treatment-related adverse events were reported in 74.6% on soticlestat vs 68.4% on placebo (somnolence most frequent on soticlestat); serious treatment-related events occurred in 3 participants on soticlestat and 1 on placebo. The authors conclude that targeting cholesterol 24-hydroxylase is not a suitable strategy for Lennox–Gastaut syndrome.
cards.watchOut: SKYWAY is the largest soticlestat trial carded and it is unambiguously null on its primary endpoint; together with ELEKTRA's non-significant Lennox–Gastaut subgroup, there is no randomised support for soticlestat in Lennox–Gastaut syndrome.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a phase 2 Dravet signal not confirmed on phase 3 primaries, and no Lennox–Gastaut benefit in either phase — SPLIT (syndrome and phase)
cards.summary: Synthesis: a phase 2 Dravet signal not confirmed on phase 3 primaries, and no Lennox–Gastaut benefit in either phase — SPLIT (syndrome and phase)
cards.people: The carded evidence: one phase 2 trial pooling both syndromes (141 children), one phase 3 Dravet trial (144 participants), and one phase 3 Lennox–Gastaut trial (270 participants) — all from the single soticlestat development programme.
cards.result: In Dravet syndrome, ELEKTRA's convulsive-seizure reduction (placebo-adjusted 50.00%, P = .0002) was followed by SKYLINE's narrower, non-significant primary result (difference -15.64%, P = .061) with a nominally significant responder advantage (27.4% vs 9.9%). In Lennox–Gastaut syndrome, both tests were null: ELEKTRA's drop-seizure subgroup (17.08%, P = .1160) and SKYWAY's primary endpoint (-1.17%, P = .785). PROPOSED SPLIT (syndrome and phase): possible benefit in Dravet syndrome rests on a phase 2 result and phase 3 secondary measures; for Lennox–Gastaut syndrome the randomised answer is no demonstrated benefit.
cards.watchOut: All three trials come from one sponsor programme for one drug; there is no independent replication. Quoting ELEKTRA's pooled 30.21% without the syndrome and phase split would misstate what the phase 3 programme found.
cards.source: Synthesis of Hahn CD et al. Epilepsia. 2022 (PMID: 35841234); Sullivan J et al. Epilepsia. 2026 (PMID: 41784472); Guerrini R et al. Epilepsia. 2026 (PMID: 41891667).

shelves.title: Plasma p-tau217 for Alzheimer's pathology in people with cognitive symptoms: about 90% accuracy at predefined cutoffs — with each figure tied to its named assay and setting
shelves.question: How accurately does a plasma phosphorylated-tau (p-tau217) blood test identify Alzheimer's disease pathology in people presenting with cognitive symptoms?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Alzheimer Disease/blood/diagnosis · Amyloid beta-Peptides · Area Under Curve · Biomarkers/blood · Cross-Sectional Studies · Female · Humans · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Male · Middle Aged · Mutation · Neurodegenerative Diseases/blood/diagnosis · Plaque, Amyloid/blood · Positron-Emission Tomography · Presenilin-1/genetics · tau Proteins/blood
shelves.balance: In people with cognitive symptoms, plasma p-tau217 identified Alzheimer's disease pathology with high accuracy in every carded cohort — but the numbers are assay- and setting-dependent, and each card names the assay or method its figures belong to. Palmqvist 2020 (1,402 participants across an Arizona neuropathology cohort, BioFINDER-2, and a Colombian autosomal-dominant kindred) found an area under the curve of 0.96 for clinical Alzheimer's dementia versus other neurodegenerative diseases and 0.93 for abnormal tau-PET. Palmqvist 2024 tested a mass-spectrometry method (percentage p-tau217, alone and combined with the amyloid-beta 42/40 ratio as the APS2 score) prospectively in 1,213 Swedish patients with cognitive symptoms: diagnostic accuracy was 88–92% in primary and secondary care at predefined cutoffs, against 61% for primary care physicians and 73% for dementia specialists using clinical workup alone. Ashton 2024 validated the commercially available ALZpath pTau217 immunoassay in 786 participants (TRIAD, WRAP and SPIN cohorts): AUC 0.92–0.96 for amyloid pathology and 0.93–0.97 for tau pathology. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (test-accuracy, cohort evidence): accuracy around 90% at predefined cutoffs in symptomatic populations is consistently reported, but cutoffs and performance do not transfer automatically between assays, platforms or care settings.

cards.headline: Palmqvist 2020 (JAMA): plasma P-tau217 separated Alzheimer's dementia from other neurodegenerative diseases with AUC 0.96, and abnormal from normal tau-PET with AUC 0.93, across 1,402 participants in 3 cohorts
cards.summary: Palmqvist 2020 (JAMA): plasma P-tau217 separated Alzheimer's dementia from other neurodegenerative diseases with AUC 0.96, and abnormal from normal tau-PET with AUC 0.93, across 1,402 participants in 3 cohorts
cards.people: 1,402 participants in three cross-sectional cohorts: an Arizona neuropathology cohort (34 with Alzheimer's disease and 47 without), the Swedish BioFINDER-2 cohort (301 cognitively unimpaired, 178 with mild cognitive impairment, 121 with Alzheimer's dementia, 99 with other neurodegenerative diseases), and a Colombian autosomal-dominant Alzheimer's kindred (365 PSEN1 E280A carriers and 257 noncarriers). The reference standards were neuropathology, clinical diagnosis, and tau- and amyloid-PET.
cards.result: Antemortem plasma P-tau217 differentiated neuropathologically defined Alzheimer's disease from non-Alzheimer's disease with AUC 0.89 (95% CI 0.81 to 0.97), significantly more accurately than plasma P-tau181 or neurofilament light (AUC range 0.50–0.72). In BioFINDER-2, accuracy for clinical Alzheimer's dementia versus other neurodegenerative diseases was AUC 0.96 (95% CI 0.93 to 0.98), not significantly different from cerebrospinal fluid P-tau217, P-tau181 or tau-PET (AUC range 0.90–0.99); for discriminating abnormal from normal tau-PET scans the AUC was 0.93 (95% CI 0.91 to 0.96). In the Colombian kindred, plasma P-tau217 was already significantly higher in mutation carriers from about age 25, some 20 years before estimated mild cognitive impairment onset.
cards.watchOut: These were selected research cohorts — including a neuropathology series and a young autosomal-dominant kindred (mean age 35.8 years) — not unselected clinic attenders; the record does not name a commercial assay platform, and the authors state the assay still needed optimisation and validation in unselected, diverse populations.
cards.source: Palmqvist S et al. Discriminative Accuracy of Plasma Phospho-tau217 for Alzheimer Disease vs Other Neurodegenerative Disorders. JAMA. 2020. PMID: 32722745. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Palmqvist 2024 (JAMA): a mass-spectrometry percentage p-tau217 test (APS2) reached 88–92% diagnostic accuracy in 1,213 patients with cognitive symptoms in primary and secondary care — versus 61% and 73% for clinicians' own workup
cards.summary: Palmqvist 2024 (JAMA): a mass-spectrometry percentage p-tau217 test (APS2) reached 88–92% diagnostic accuracy in 1,213 patients with cognitive symptoms in primary and secondary care — versus 61% and 73% for clinicians' own workup
cards.type: Prospective diagnostic-accuracy cohort study, primary and secondary care (Palmqvist 2024)
cards.people: 1,213 patients undergoing clinical evaluation for cognitive symptoms in Sweden (23% subjective cognitive decline, 44% mild cognitive impairment, 33% dementia; 50% had Alzheimer's pathology), assessed in primary care and secondary care cohorts, in single-batch analyses and in a prospective biweekly analysis, using predefined biomarker cutoff values established in an independent cohort. The test used mass spectrometry to measure the ratio of plasma phosphorylated tau 217 to non-phosphorylated tau 217 (percentage p-tau217), alone and combined with the plasma amyloid-beta 42/40 ratio as the amyloid probability score 2 (APS2); the reference standard was abnormal cerebrospinal fluid amyloid-beta 42/40 and p-tau217.
cards.result: With APS2, AUC was 0.96–0.97 in both settings and both analysis modes; positive predictive values were 88–91% and negative predictive values 87–92%, and diagnostic accuracy ranged from 88% to 92% across the four cohorts. Overall diagnostic accuracy with APS2 was 90% (95% CI 88% to 92%), not different from percentage p-tau217 alone (90%, 95% CI 88% to 91%). Primary care physicians identified clinical Alzheimer's disease with 61% accuracy (95% CI 53% to 69%) after examination, cognitive testing and CT, versus 91% using APS2; dementia specialists achieved 73% (95% CI 68% to 79%) versus 91% with APS2.
cards.watchOut: Predictive values were measured where half the patients had Alzheimer's pathology; in a lower-prevalence setting the same test would yield more false positives. The figures belong to this mass-spectrometry percentage p-tau217 method and its predefined cutoffs — they are not a property of every p-tau217 assay.
cards.source: Palmqvist S et al. Blood Biomarkers to Detect Alzheimer Disease in Primary Care and Secondary Care. JAMA. 2024. PMID: 39068545. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ashton 2024: the commercially available ALZpath pTau217 immunoassay identified amyloid pathology with AUC 0.92–0.96 and tau pathology with AUC 0.93–0.97 across 786 participants in 3 cohorts
cards.summary: Ashton 2024: the commercially available ALZpath pTau217 immunoassay identified amyloid pathology with AUC 0.92–0.96 and tau pathology with AUC 0.93–0.97 across 786 participants in 3 cohorts
cards.type: Diagnostic-accuracy cohort study, 3 cohorts (Ashton 2024, ALZpath assay)
cards.people: 786 participants (mean age 66.3 years; 64.1% women) with and without cognitive impairment from three single-centre observational cohorts — TRIAD (Canada), the Wisconsin Registry for Alzheimer's Prevention (WRAP), and SPIN (Spain) — grouped by amyloid and tau status using PET or cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers. The tested product is named as published: the ALZpath pTau217 assay, a commercially available plasma p-tau217 immunoassay.
cards.result: Plasma p-tau217 on the ALZpath assay showed high accuracy for elevated amyloid-beta (AUC 0.92–0.96, 95% CI 0.89–0.99) and for tau pathology (AUC 0.93–0.97, 95% CI 0.84–0.99) across all cohorts, comparable with cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers for determining abnormal PET signal. A 3-range reference for abnormal amyloid pathology gave reproducible results and reduced confirmatory testing by approximately 80%. Longitudinally, plasma p-tau217 rose annually only in amyloid-positive individuals, most in those also tau-positive.
cards.watchOut: WRAP is a prevention registry enriched for Alzheimer's risk and many participants were cognitively unimpaired, so these AUCs describe detecting pathology across a wide spectrum — accuracy for the narrower question 'does this symptomatic patient's presentation reflect Alzheimer's pathology' comes mainly from the Palmqvist 2024 card. AUC ranges span cohorts; no single cutoff performed identically everywhere.
cards.source: Ashton NJ et al. Diagnostic Accuracy of a Plasma Phosphorylated Tau 217 Immunoassay for Alzheimer Disease Pathology. JAMA neurology. 2024. PMID: 38252443. cards.headline: Synthesis: accuracy is consistently high in symptomatic cohorts — around 90% at predefined cutoffs — and is a property of a named assay in a named setting, not of 'p-tau217' in general
cards.summary: Synthesis: accuracy is consistently high in symptomatic cohorts — around 90% at predefined cutoffs — and is a property of a named assay in a named setting, not of 'p-tau217' in general
cards.people: The carded evidence: three diagnostic-accuracy reports covering more than 3,300 participants — a 3-cohort discrimination study (1,402), a prospective primary/secondary care study (1,213 patients with cognitive symptoms), and a 3-cohort validation of the ALZpath immunoassay (786).
cards.result: Reported accuracy clusters tightly despite different methods: AUC 0.96 for Alzheimer's dementia versus other neurodegenerative disease (research assay, BioFINDER-2), 88–92% diagnostic accuracy at predefined cutoffs in primary and secondary care (mass-spectrometry percentage p-tau217/APS2), and AUC 0.92–0.97 for amyloid and tau pathology (ALZpath immunoassay). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (test-accuracy, cohort evidence): plasma p-tau217 identifies Alzheimer's pathology accurately in people with cognitive symptoms, with the caveat that each figure belongs to its assay, cutoff and population.
cards.watchOut: Accuracy is not clinical utility: none of these cards shows that testing changed management or outcomes, and predictive values will fall where Alzheimer's pathology is less prevalent than the 50% seen in the 2024 care cohorts. Do not carry one assay's cutoff or accuracy figure onto another platform.

shelves.title: Post-stroke dysphagia: thickened fluids and chin-down posture are unproven for preventing pneumonia or death in stroke — and protocolised free water showed no pneumonia penalty in selected patients
shelves.question: After stroke with dysphagia, do thickened fluids and chin-down posture prevent aspiration pneumonia and death versus thin fluids with free-water access?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Critical Care Nursing/methods · Critical Illness/nursing/therapy · Deglutition Disorders/prevention & control · Drinking · Female · Guidelines as Topic · Humans · Logistic Models · Male · Middle Aged · Multivariate Analysis · Patient Care Team/organization & administration · Patient Safety · Reference Values · Single-Blind Method · Stroke/diagnosis/nursing/therapy · Treatment Outcome · Wounds and Injuries/diagnosis/nursing/therapy
shelves.balance: No stroke trial carded here shows that thickened fluids or chin-down posture prevent aspiration pneumonia or death. The direct head-to-head trial of chin-down posture versus nectar- and honey-thick liquids enrolled people with dementia or Parkinson disease, not stroke, so it is not carded on this shelf and no figures are taken from it. In stroke specifically, the randomised evidence tests the other side of the question — whether allowing thin water is harmful — and in carefully selected patients it did not show harm: a free-water trial in acute stroke and trauma patients (104 participants) found no significant outcome differences and too few pneumonias to compare, and a post-stroke water-protocol trial found no pneumonia in either group (with only 14 participants analysed). A systematic review of free-water protocols (8 studies, 245 patients with dysphagia, mostly in rehabilitation) found low-quality evidence of no increased lung complications. The Cochrane review of all swallowing therapy after stroke (41 trials, 2,660 participants) found no effect on death or dependency (OR 1.05) or case fatality (OR 1.00) — the treatment made no difference — although chest infection or pneumonia may have been reduced across a heterogeneous mix of interventions (OR 0.36, very low-quality evidence) that was not a test of thickened fluids or chin-down posture specifically. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): the preventive claim for thickened fluids and chin-down posture is unproven in stroke, and free-water access for selected patients has not been shown to increase pneumonia.

cards.headline: Kenedi 2019: in 104 acute stroke and trauma patients, a free water protocol produced no significant differences in positive outcomes, and pneumonia and other negative indicators were too infrequent to compare
cards.summary: Kenedi 2019: in 104 acute stroke and trauma patients, a free water protocol produced no significant differences in positive outcomes, and pneumonia and other negative indicators were too infrequent to compare
cards.people: 104 eligible acute stroke and trauma patients treated over 3 years at one hospital system, randomly assigned to a free water protocol group with access to water and ice under specific guidelines, or a control group without such access; outcomes were recorded by trained staff and analysed blinded, with a small subgroup (n = 15) followed into rehabilitation.
cards.result: No significant group differences in positive outcomes (diet upgrade, days to diet upgrade, days in the study) were found (all P values > .40). Negative clinical indicators — pneumonia, intubation, diet downgrade — were too infrequent to allow statistical comparison of the two groups. No negative clinical indicators occurred in the 15 patients followed into rehabilitation. The authors conclude larger-scale studies are needed for decisive conclusions.
cards.watchOut: The population mixes stroke with trauma patients and the record does not report how many of the 104 had stroke; with pneumonia too rare to analyse, this trial can show an absence of an obvious signal, not safety proven to a narrow margin.
cards.source: Kenedi H et al. Implementation and Analysis of a Free Water Protocol in Acute Trauma and Stroke Patients. Critical care nurse. 2019. PMID: 31154338. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Murray 2016: in post-stroke thin-liquid aspiration, a water protocol versus thickened liquids only — no pneumonia in either group, identical beverage volumes (1,103 mL/day in both), more urinary tract infections on thickened liquids only
cards.summary: Murray 2016: in post-stroke thin-liquid aspiration, a water protocol versus thickened liquids only — no pneumonia in either group, identical beverage volumes (1,103 mL/day in both), more urinary tract infections on thickened liquids only
cards.people: Patients in rehabilitation facilities with known thin-liquid aspiration after stroke, randomised to thickened liquids only or to a water protocol; 14 participants' data proceeded to analysis — the analysed N is printed here because it is very small.
cards.result: Total beverage consumption did not differ between groups (mean 1,103 mL per day in both; SD 215 and 247). Water-protocol participants drank on average 299 mL (SD 274) of water but offset this by drinking less thickened liquid. No participants in either group were diagnosed with pneumonia. Urinary tract infection was diagnosed significantly more often in the thickened-liquids-only group (P = 0.024); diagnoses of dehydration (21% of the total sample) and constipation did not differ between groups, and hydration differences over time were not significant.
cards.watchOut: Only 14 participants were analysed, so the absence of pneumonia carries almost no statistical weight; the trial's contribution is showing that selected rehabilitation patients drank water without an obvious penalty and that thickened-only management came with more urinary tract infections in this small sample.
cards.source: Murray J et al. Does a Water Protocol Improve the Hydration and Health Status of Individuals with Thin Liquid Aspiration Following Stroke? A Randomized Controlled Trial. Dysphagia. 2016. PMID: 26886370. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Gillman 2017 systematic review: across 8 free-water studies (245 patients with dysphagia), low-quality evidence that the protocol did not increase lung complications, with fluid intake possibly increased
cards.summary: Gillman 2017 systematic review: across 8 free-water studies (245 patients with dysphagia), low-quality evidence that the protocol did not increase lung complications, with fluid intake possibly increased
cards.people: 8 studies (5 randomised trials, 2 matched cohort studies, 1 pre–post study) covering 215 rehabilitation inpatients and 30 acute patients with oropharyngeal dysphagia who required thickened fluids or were nil by mouth by bedside assessment and/or videofluoroscopy or endoscopic evaluation. Populations were mixed-aetiology dysphagia in rehabilitation and acute settings, including stroke, rather than stroke-only.
cards.result: Meta-analyses of the rehabilitation studies found low-quality evidence that implementing the free water protocol did not result in increased odds of lung complications, and low-quality evidence that fluid intake may increase; patients' perceptions of swallow-related quality of life appeared to improve. The authors conclude the protocol can be offered to carefully selected rehabilitation inpatients under strict exclusion criteria (including cognition and mobility assessment), and that further research is required outside inpatient rehabilitation.
cards.watchOut: 'Carefully selected' is doing heavy work in this conclusion: patients were screened, supervised and subject to oral-care and between-meals rules, and most evidence comes from rehabilitation rather than acute stroke units. The review does not license unrestricted thin fluids for all post-stroke aspirators.
cards.source: Gillman A et al. Implementing the Free Water Protocol does not Result in Aspiration Pneumonia in Carefully Selected Patients with Dysphagia: A Systematic Review. Dysphagia. 2017. PMID: 27878598. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Bath 2018 (Cochrane): swallowing therapy after stroke overall made no difference to death or dependency (OR 1.05) or case fatality (OR 1.00) across 41 trials, though chest infection or pneumonia may have fallen (OR 0.36, very low-quality evidence)
cards.summary: Bath 2018 (Cochrane): swallowing therapy after stroke overall made no difference to death or dependency (OR 1.05) or case fatality (OR 1.00) across 41 trials, though chest infection or pneumonia may have fallen (OR 0.36, very low-quality evidence)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 41 randomised trials (Cochrane, Bath 2018)
cards.people: 41 randomised trials with 2,660 participants with dysphagia within 6 months of stroke, testing swallowing therapy of many kinds: acupuncture (11 studies), behavioural interventions (9), drug therapy (3), neuromuscular or pharyngeal electrical stimulation (10), physical stimulation (3), and transcranial stimulation (11). Behavioural interventions in this literature include compensatory strategies such as posture and fluid modification, but the review does not report a separate pooled result for thickened fluids or chin-down posture.
cards.result: Swallowing therapy had no effect on death or dependency/disability at the end of the trial (OR 1.05, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.75; 306 participants, 2 studies; moderate-quality evidence) — the treatment made no difference — and no effect on case fatality (OR 1.00, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.52; 766 participants, 14 studies). It may have reduced the proportion with dysphagia at trial end (OR 0.42, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.55) and may have reduced chest infection or pneumonia (OR 0.36, 95% CI 0.16 to 0.78; 618 participants, 9 studies; very low-quality evidence), and probably shortened inpatient stay by about 2.9 days.
cards.watchOut: The pneumonia signal pools unlike interventions (stimulation, acupuncture, drugs and behavioural therapy together); attributing it to thickened fluids or chin-down posture specifically would go beyond what this review reports. For the named strategies, this shelf's direct stroke evidence is the two small free-water trials above.
cards.source: Bath PM et al. Swallowing therapy for dysphagia in acute and subacute stroke. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2018. PMID: 30376602. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: thickened fluids and chin-down posture have no demonstrated pneumonia or death benefit in stroke; free water in selected patients showed no pneumonia penalty in small studies — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.summary: Synthesis: thickened fluids and chin-down posture have no demonstrated pneumonia or death benefit in stroke; free water in selected patients showed no pneumonia penalty in small studies — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.people: The carded evidence: two small randomised free-water trials in stroke or mixed acute populations (104 randomised; 14 analysed), one systematic review of free-water protocols (245 patients, mixed aetiologies), and one Cochrane review of all post-stroke swallowing therapy (41 trials, 2,660 participants).
cards.result: No carded stroke study randomised patients to thickened fluids or chin-down posture and showed fewer pneumonias or deaths; the Cochrane review found swallowing therapy overall made no difference to death, dependency or fatality. The free-water studies consistently found no increase in lung complications when thin water was allowed under protocol in selected patients. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): routine thickening and chin-down posture after stroke rest on aspiration seen on imaging, not on demonstrated prevention of pneumonia or death, and protocolised free water appears a reasonable alternative for carefully selected patients — pending a properly powered trial.
cards.watchOut: Absence of demonstrated benefit is not demonstrated absence of benefit: pneumonia events were rare and samples small in every direct study here, so a modest protective effect of thickening in unselected aspirators remains untested rather than disproved.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kenedi H et al. Critical care nurse. 2019 (PMID: 31154338); Murray J et al. Dysphagia. 2016 (PMID: 26886370); Gillman A et al. Dysphagia. 2017 (PMID: 27878598); Bath PM et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2018 (PMID: 30376602).

shelves.title: Vagus nerve stimulation for treatment-resistant depression: primary outcomes null versus sham in both blinded trials — secondary measures and a 5-year registry favour it
shelves.question: In treatment-resistant depression, does adjunctive vagus nerve stimulation improve response and remission versus sham or treatment as usual over 12 months?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Vagus Nerve Stimulation/methods/adverse effects · Male · Female · Depressive Disorder, Treatment-Resistant/therapy · Middle Aged · Double-Blind Method · Adult · Treatment Outcome · Aged · Major Depressive Disorder/therapy
shelves.balance: The sham-controlled evidence splits by outcome measure. RECOVER (493 adults with marked treatment-resistant depression, 12 months of active versus no-stimulation sham vagus nerve stimulation, both plus treatment as usual) missed its primary outcome — percent time in Montgomery–Åsberg response did not distinguish the groups — while clinician global impression, self-report and clinician-rated secondary measures showed significantly more time in response and partial response on active stimulation, and a companion report found quality-of-life and function advantages. The earlier acute sham trial (Rush 2005, D-02; 235 patients, 10 weeks) likewise missed its primary outcome (Hamilton response 15.2% vs 10.0%, P = .251 — the treatment made no difference on that measure) with one secondary self-report measure favouring active treatment. The long-term support comes from a non-randomised registry (Aaronson 2017; 795 patients, 5 years): cumulative response 67.6% with adjunctive vagus nerve stimulation plus usual care versus 40.9% on usual care alone, and first-time remission 43.3% versus 25.7% — observational evidence, with the vagus group more severely depressed at baseline. PROPOSED SPLIT (outcome measure and design): blinded primaries are null in both sham trials; secondary blinded measures and unblinded long-term observational data favour vagus nerve stimulation.

cards.headline: RECOVER 2025: over 12 months in 493 patients with marked treatment-resistant depression, active vagus nerve stimulation missed its primary outcome (percent time in MADRS response) but won on clinician- and patient-rated secondary measures
cards.summary: RECOVER 2025: over 12 months in 493 patients with marked treatment-resistant depression, active vagus nerve stimulation missed its primary outcome (percent time in MADRS response) but won on clinician- and patient-rated secondary measures
cards.people: 493 adults with marked treatment-resistant major depression (4 or more adequate but unsuccessful antidepressant trials in the current episode) in a multicentre double-blind trial, randomised to active vagus nerve stimulation (n = 249) or no-stimulation sham (n = 244), both adjunctive to treatment as usual, over 12 months; 88.4% completed the trial. The primary outcome was percent time in response across months 3–12, response defined as a 50% or greater improvement on the Montgomery–Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS).
cards.result: Percent time in MADRS response did not distinguish active from sham vagus nerve stimulation — the primary outcome was not met (the treatment made no difference on that measure). Secondary measures favoured active stimulation: significantly more percent time in response on the Clinical Global Impression–Improvement (P = 0.004) and the self-report Quick Inventory of Depressive Symptomatology (P = 0.049), and significantly more percent time in partial response (30% or greater improvement) on the CGI-I (P < 0.001) and the clinician-rated QIDS (P = 0.006). Dyspnoea was more frequent on active stimulation (P = 0.035); no new adverse events were identified. The record reports these secondary results as P values without the underlying percentages.
cards.watchOut: A missed primary with positive secondaries is a weaker form of evidence than a met primary: the MADRS was the prespecified yardstick, it was rated by masked offsite raters in part to resist unblinding, and stimulation side effects such as dyspnoea and voice effects can reveal allocation. Read this trial as 'benefit on some measures', not as a clean win.
cards.source: Conway CR et al. Vagus nerve stimulation in treatment-resistant depression: A one-year, randomized, sham-controlled trial. Brain stimulation. 2025. PMID: 39706521. cards.headline: Rush 2005 (D-02): at 10 weeks, Hamilton response was 15.2% on active versus 10.0% on sham vagus nerve stimulation (P = .251, not significant) in 235 patients with treatment-resistant depression
cards.summary: Rush 2005 (D-02): at 10 weeks, Hamilton response was 15.2% on active versus 10.0% on sham vagus nerve stimulation (P = .251, not significant) in 235 patients with treatment-resistant depression
cards.people: 235 outpatients with nonpsychotic major depressive disorder (n = 210) or depressed-phase bipolar disorder (n = 25) who had not responded adequately to between 2 and 6 research-qualified medication trials in the current episode, implanted and then randomised after a 2-week no-stimulation recovery period to 10 weeks of masked active or sham adjunctive vagus nerve stimulation with medications kept stable; 222 were evaluable for the primary outcome.
cards.result: Response (50% or greater reduction on the 24-item Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression) at 10 weeks was 15.2% on active stimulation (n = 112) and 10.0% on sham (n = 110) (P = .251, last observation carried forward) — not significant; the treatment made no difference on the primary outcome. A secondary self-report measure (Inventory of Depressive Symptomatology response) favoured active treatment, 17.0% vs 7.3% (P = .032). Vagus nerve stimulation was well tolerated; 1% (3 of 235) left the study because of adverse events. The authors concluded the study did not yield definitive evidence of short-term efficacy.
cards.watchOut: Ten weeks may be too short for a therapy whose proponents claim benefits accrue over a year — the reason this shelf also cards the 12-month RECOVER trial and the 5-year registry. But duration does not rescue the primary-outcome pattern: the 12-month trial's primary was also null.
cards.source: Rush AJ et al. Vagus nerve stimulation for treatment-resistant depression: a randomized, controlled acute phase trial. Biological psychiatry. 2005. PMID: 16139580. Registry ID: none in the record. the treatment made no difference on the primary outcome. a secondary self-report measure (inventory of depressive symptomatology response) favoured active treatment, 17.0% vs 7.3% (p = .032). vagus nerve stimulation was well tolerated; 1% (3 of 235) left the study because of adverse events. the authors concluded the study did not yield definitive evidence of short-term efficacy. ten weeks may be too short for a therapy whose proponents claim benefits accrue over a year — the reason this shelf also cards the 12-month recover trial and the 5-year registry. but duration does not rescue the primary-outcome pattern: the 12-month trial's primary was also null. rush aj et al. vagus nerve stimulation for treatment-resistant depression: a randomized, controlled acute phase trial. biological psychiatry. 2005. pmid: 16139580. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adult · aged · analysis of variance · antidepressive agents/therapeutic use · bipolar disorder/therapy · case-control studies · major depressive disorder/therapy · drug resistance · electric stimulation therapy · female · humans · male · middle aged · mood disorders/therapy · psychiatric status rating scales · reference values · treatment outcome · vagus nerve/physiology/radiation effects

cards.headline: Aaronson 2017 registry (observational): over 5 years, cumulative response was 67.6% with adjunctive vagus nerve stimulation plus usual care versus 40.9% on usual care alone, and remission 43.3% versus 25.7%
cards.summary: Aaronson 2017 registry (observational): over 5 years, cumulative response was 67.6% with adjunctive vagus nerve stimulation plus usual care versus 40.9% on usual care alone, and remission 43.3% versus 25.7%
cards.type: Prospective observational registry, 5 years (Aaronson 2017) — observational evidence
cards.people: 795 patients at 61 US sites in a prospective, open-label, non-randomised observational registry, experiencing a major depressive episode (unipolar or bipolar) of at least 2 years' duration or with 3 or more episodes, having failed 4 or more depression treatments including electroconvulsive therapy options; the adjunctive vagus nerve stimulation group was more severely depressed at baseline (mean MADRS 33.1, SD 7.0) than the treatment-as-usual group (29.3, SD 6.9).
cards.result: The adjunctive vagus nerve stimulation group had a significantly higher 5-year cumulative response rate (response: 50% or greater MADRS reduction at any post-baseline visit) than treatment as usual alone, 67.6% compared with 40.9%, and a significantly higher cumulative first-time remission rate, 43.3% compared with 25.7%. The response advantage appeared both in patients with a history of response to electroconvulsive therapy (71.3% vs 56.9%) and in electroconvulsive-therapy nonresponders (59.6% vs 34.1%).
cards.watchOut: This is observational evidence and is labelled as such: patients were not randomised, the groups differed at baseline, 'response at any visit over 5 years' is a generous cumulative definition, and people who receive an implanted device differ from those who do not in ways adjustment cannot fully remove. It cannot override the null blinded primaries on the other cards.
cards.source: Aaronson ST et al. A 5-Year Observational Study of Patients With Treatment-Resistant Depression Treated With Vagus Nerve Stimulation or Treatment as Usual: Comparison of Response, Remission, and Suicidality. cards.headline: Synthesis: blinded primaries null at 10 weeks and at 12 months; secondary blinded measures and 5-year observational data favour vagus nerve stimulation — SPLIT (outcome measure and design)
cards.summary: Synthesis: blinded primaries null at 10 weeks and at 12 months; secondary blinded measures and 5-year observational data favour vagus nerve stimulation — SPLIT (outcome measure and design)
cards.people: The carded evidence: two randomised sham-controlled trials (235 patients over 10 weeks; 493 patients over 12 months) and one non-randomised 5-year registry (795 patients).
cards.result: On prespecified primary symptom outcomes, adjunctive vagus nerve stimulation made no difference versus sham in either trial (Hamilton response P = .251 at 10 weeks; percent time in MADRS response not distinguishing groups at 12 months). On secondary clinician- and patient-rated measures in RECOVER, and on cumulative response and remission in the observational registry (67.6% vs 40.9%; 43.3% vs 25.7%), it favoured active treatment. PROPOSED SPLIT (outcome measure and design): whether vagus nerve stimulation 'works' in treatment-resistant depression currently depends on which outcome and which design you read — the strongest designs give the weakest answers.
cards.watchOut: Do not average these into a single verdict: the registry's large percentages and the trials' null primaries answer the same clinical question with different protection against bias, and the honest shelf-level statement is the split itself.
cards.source: Synthesis of Conway CR et al. Brain stimulation. 2025 (PMID: 39706521); Rush AJ et al. Biological psychiatry. 2005 (PMID: 16139580); Aaronson ST et al. The American journal of psychiatry. 2017 (PMID: 28359201).

shelves.title: Desvenlafaxine 50 mg vs 100 mg for major depression: both doses beat placebo in the pooled programme — and 100 mg has never been shown to beat 50 mg
shelves.question: Does desvenlafaxine (50 mg vs 100 mg) improve major depression versus placebo, and is the higher dose more effective?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antidepressive Agents, Second-Generation/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Cyclohexanols/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Major Depressive Disorder/drug therapy/psychology · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Venlafaxine Hydrochloride
shelves.balance: Both desvenlafaxine 50 mg and 100 mg beat placebo on the primary depression scale in the pooled phase 3 programme, but individual trials were inconsistent and no report carded here shows 100 mg outperforming 50 mg. Boyer 2008 (483 patients) found both doses effective (Hamilton change -13.2 on 50 mg and -13.7 on 100 mg vs -10.7 on placebo). Liebowitz 2008 (447 patients) found 50 mg significant (-11.5 vs -9.5, P = 0.018) while 100 mg missed on the primary scale (-11.0, P = 0.065) though it won on several secondary measures. Tourian 2009 (615 patients in the trial) failed its primary global test; pairwise, 100 mg was significant unadjusted (P = 0.028) and 50 mg was not — but that trial's own post hoc pooling with the two earlier 50/100 mg trials (1,388 patients) found both doses effective (-11.5 and -11.8 vs -9.6, both P < 0.001). A symptom-level pooling of 9 studies (Kornstein 2009) states symptom relief was similar at all doses examined, including 50 mg. All carded reports come from the single sponsor phase 3 programme, which caps the stamp. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit versus placebo; single programme): desvenlafaxine improves major depression versus placebo at both doses, with no demonstrated advantage for 100 mg over 50 mg.

cards.headline: Boyer 2008: both desvenlafaxine doses beat placebo — Hamilton change -13.2 (50 mg) and -13.7 (100 mg) versus -10.7 (placebo) in 483 outpatients
cards.summary: Boyer 2008: both desvenlafaxine doses beat placebo — Hamilton change -13.2 (50 mg) and -13.7 (100 mg) versus -10.7 (placebo) in 483 outpatients
cards.people: 483 outpatients with major depressive disorder in Europe and South Africa, randomised in a multicentre double-blind trial to fixed-dose desvenlafaxine 50 mg/day (n = 164), 100 mg/day (n = 158), or placebo (n = 161) for 8 weeks; the primary variable was the 17-item Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression total score.
cards.result: Adjusted mean change from baseline on the Hamilton scale was significantly greater for desvenlafaxine 50 mg (-13.2; P = 0.002) and 100 mg (-13.7; P < 0.001) than placebo (-10.7), and Clinical Global Impressions–Improvement scores also significantly favoured both doses (P = 0.002 and P < 0.001). The two doses differed from each other by half a Hamilton point. The most common treatment-emergent adverse events were nausea, dizziness, insomnia, constipation, fatigue, anxiety and decreased appetite; both doses were generally well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: This is the cleanest of the three 50/100 mg trials; the other two missed at least one dose on their primary analyses. A half-point Hamilton difference between doses is far below any clinically meaningful threshold.
cards.source: Boyer P et al. Efficacy, safety, and tolerability of fixed-dose desvenlafaxine 50 and 100 mg/day for major depressive disorder in a placebo-controlled trial. International clinical psychopharmacology. 2008. PMID: 18703933. Registry ID: none in the record.
