cards.headline: Liebowitz 2008: desvenlafaxine 50 mg beat placebo on the primary scale (-11.5 vs -9.5, P = 0.018) but 100 mg did not (-11.0, P = 0.065), in 447 outpatients
cards.summary: Liebowitz 2008: desvenlafaxine 50 mg beat placebo on the primary scale (-11.5 vs -9.5, P = 0.018) but 100 mg did not (-11.0, P = 0.065), in 447 outpatients
cards.people: 447 patients with major depressive disorder (17-item Hamilton score 20 or more), randomised to fixed-dose desvenlafaxine 50 mg/day, 100 mg/day, or placebo for 8 weeks in a multicentre double-blind trial; the primary efficacy measure was change on the 17-item Hamilton scale at the final on-therapy evaluation.
cards.result: Desvenlafaxine 50 mg produced a significantly greater adjusted mean Hamilton change than placebo (-11.5 vs -9.5; P = 0.018); the 100 mg group (-11.0) did not reach significance on the primary measure (P = 0.065) — on that measure, the higher dose made no demonstrated difference — although it did improve significantly versus placebo on several secondary measures, including the 6-item Hamilton scale (P = 0.038) and the Visual Analog Scale–Pain Intensity total score (P = 0.041). Adverse events at 10% or more and twice the placebo rate in either dose group were dry mouth, constipation, insomnia, decreased appetite, hyperhidrosis and dizziness.
cards.watchOut: If 100 mg were genuinely more effective than 50 mg, this trial should not have produced a smaller, non-significant primary effect at the higher dose. Single-trial dose orderings bounce around; the dose answer comes from the pooled cards, not from any one trial.
cards.source: Liebowitz MR et al. Efficacy, safety, and tolerability of desvenlafaxine 50 mg/day and 100 mg/day in outpatients with major depressive disorder. Current medical research and opinion. 2008. PMID: 18507895. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00277823. cards.headline: Tourian 2009: the trial itself failed its primary global test (pairwise: 100 mg -10.5, P = 0.028 unadjusted; 50 mg not significant), but its post hoc pooling of all three 50/100 mg trials (1,388 patients) found both doses effective (-11.5 and -11.8 vs -9.6, both P < 0.001)
cards.summary: Tourian 2009: the trial itself failed its primary global test (pairwise: 100 mg -10.5, P = 0.028 unadjusted; 50 mg not significant), but its post hoc pooling of all three 50/100 mg trials (1,388 patients) found both doses effective (-11.5 and -11.8 vs -9.6, both P < 0.001)
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled trial with post hoc pooled analysis (Tourian 2009)
cards.people: 615 patients in the intention-to-treat population of an 8-week phase III trial at 21 US centres (outpatients 18 or older with major depressive disorder, Hamilton score 20 or more), randomised to fixed-dose desvenlafaxine 50 or 100 mg/day, duloxetine 60 mg/day (included for assay sensitivity, not powered for comparison), or placebo. The post hoc pooled analysis combined this trial with the two earlier similarly designed 50/100 mg trials (total intention-to-treat 1,388 patients).
cards.result: The primary endpoint did not reach significance on the prespecified global F test controlling multiplicity across the desvenlafaxine doses. On pairwise comparison, Hamilton change was -10.5 on desvenlafaxine 100 mg (P = 0.028, unadjusted) and -10.3 on duloxetine versus -8.7 on placebo; no significant difference was observed between desvenlafaxine 50 mg and placebo on any scale in this trial. In the pooled analysis of all three trials, both desvenlafaxine 50 mg (-11.5; P < 0.001) and 100 mg (-11.8; P < 0.001) beat placebo (-9.6) on the Hamilton scale and on the CGI-I, MADRS and 6-item Hamilton scales. Discontinuation due to adverse events was 5% (50 mg), 7% (100 mg), 13% (duloxetine) and 6% (placebo).
cards.watchOut: The pooled rescue is post hoc and pools this trial with the two positive trials carded above — it is the same evidence re-averaged, not new evidence. The trial-level fact stands: in this study the prespecified primary analysis failed, and 50 mg separated from placebo on nothing.
cards.source: Tourian KA et al. Desvenlafaxine 50 and 100 mg/d in the treatment of major depressive disorder: an 8-week, phase III, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group trial and a post hoc pooled analysis of three studies. Clinical therapeutics. 2009. PMID: 19698901. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00384033. cards.headline: Kornstein 2009 (pooled, 9 studies): desvenlafaxine beat placebo across depression symptom items, and 'symptom relief was similar with all desvenlafaxine doses examined, including 50 mg/d'
cards.summary: Kornstein 2009 (pooled, 9 studies): desvenlafaxine beat placebo across depression symptom items, and 'symptom relief was similar with all desvenlafaxine doses examined, including 50 mg/d'
cards.people: Pooled data from 9 double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled 8-week studies in adult outpatients with major depressive disorder: fixed doses of 50, 100, 200 or 400 mg/day (n = 1,342), flexible doses of 100 to 400 mg/day (n = 463), or placebo (n = 1,108). Final scores on individual items of the 17-item Hamilton scale and the Montgomery–Åsberg scale were compared.
cards.result: Desvenlafaxine (all doses pooled) was significantly better than placebo on 10 of 17 Hamilton items (including depressed mood, guilt, suicide item, work and activities, and psychic anxiety; item differences -0.1 to -0.4, all P .003 or lower) and on all Montgomery–Åsberg items except reduced appetite (range -0.1 to -0.5; all P .019 or lower). Examining efficacy by dose in the fixed-dose subset, the authors report that symptom relief was similar with all desvenlafaxine doses examined, including 50 mg/day — no dose gradient was found across 50 to 400 mg/day.
cards.watchOut: A symptom-item pooling is a secondary lens on the same sponsor programme, and 'similar relief across doses' is an absence-of-gradient finding within trials designed to test doses against placebo, not against each other. Higher doses in the wider programme carried more blood-pressure elevation and discontinuations in other pooled reports, which are not carded here.
cards.source: Kornstein SG et al. Analysis of depressive symptoms in patients with major depressive disorder treated with desvenlafaxine or placebo. Psychopharmacology bulletin. 2009. PMID: 19752839. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: both 50 mg and 100 mg beat placebo in the pooled programme; no report shows 100 mg beating 50 mg — POSSIBLE (benefit versus placebo; single programme)
cards.summary: Synthesis: both 50 mg and 100 mg beat placebo in the pooled programme; no report shows 100 mg beating 50 mg — POSSIBLE (benefit versus placebo; single programme)
cards.people: The carded evidence: three randomised 50/100 mg trials (483, 447 and 615 intention-to-treat patients) and two pooled analyses of the same programme (1,388 patients across the three trials; 2,913 patients across 9 studies).
cards.result: Versus placebo, the pooled Hamilton advantage is about 2 points at both doses (-11.5 on 50 mg and -11.8 on 100 mg vs -9.6 on placebo in the 3-trial pooling), and the 9-study pooling found no dose gradient from 50 to 400 mg/day. Individual trials disagreed about which dose was significant, which is what sampling variation around a flat dose–response looks like. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit versus placebo; single programme): desvenlafaxine improves major depression versus placebo at 50 mg and at 100 mg, and the higher dose has not been shown to be more effective.
cards.watchOut: Every card derives from one manufacturer's phase 3 programme with 8-week trials in outpatients without major comorbidity; there is no independent replication, which is why the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE despite the pooled significance.

shelves.title: Chronic PTSD: venlafaxine extended-release beat placebo in two large trials — CAPS and remission both favoured the drug
shelves.question: In chronic PTSD, does venlafaxine extended-release improve core PTSD symptoms versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Antidepressive Agents, Second-Generation · Cyclohexanols · Delayed-Action Preparations · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Sertraline · Stress Disorders, Post-Traumatic · Venlafaxine Hydrochloride
shelves.balance: Two large placebo-controlled trials agree. In the 12-week trial (538 outpatients), venlafaxine extended-release (ER) lowered the Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale (CAPS-SX17) score by 41.8 points versus 33.9 on placebo, with remission in 30.2% versus 19.6%. In the 24-week trial (329 outpatients), the CAPS fall was 51.7 versus 43.9 points (P=.006), with remission in 50.9% versus 37.5%. A 2015 systematic review and meta-analysis of PTSD pharmacotherapy (51 studies) likewise found venlafaxine among the few individual agents with statistically significant efficacy over placebo in two or more trials, while noting effect sizes across the drug literature were small. The SSRI trials for this condition are homed separately on shelf-2410 and are not re-carded here; the 12-week trial's sertraline arm, which did not separate significantly from placebo on the primary score in that study, sits inside the venlafaxine trial report itself. PROPOSED LIKELY: venlafaxine ER improves core PTSD symptoms versus placebo over 12–24 weeks, with absolute remission gains of roughly 11–13 percentage points.

cards.headline: Davidson 2006 (12-week trial): in 538 outpatients with chronic PTSD, venlafaxine ER beat placebo on the CAPS-SX17 total score (−41.8 vs −33.9) and on remission (30.2% vs 19.6%)
cards.summary: Davidson 2006 (12-week trial): in 538 outpatients with chronic PTSD, venlafaxine ER beat placebo on the CAPS-SX17 total score (−41.8 vs −33.9) and on remission (30.2% vs 19.6%)
cards.people: 538 adult outpatients with a primary DSM-IV diagnosis of PTSD, symptoms for 6 months or more and a CAPS-SX17 score of 60 or more, randomised double-blind to flexible-dose venlafaxine ER (37.5–300 mg/day), sertraline (25–200 mg/day), or placebo for 12 weeks.
cards.result: Mean CAPS-SX17 change was −41.8 for venlafaxine ER (P < 0.05 vs placebo), −39.4 for sertraline, and −33.9 for placebo. Venlafaxine ER also beat placebo on the avoidance/numbing and hyperarousal cluster scores and on Davidson Trauma Scale scores. Week-12 remission (CAPS-SX17 ≤20) was 30.2% on venlafaxine ER (P < 0.05 vs placebo), 24.3% on sertraline, and 19.6% on placebo. Mean maximum daily doses were 225 mg venlafaxine ER and 151 mg sertraline; both treatments were generally well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: This trial's sertraline arm did not separate significantly from placebo on the primary total score, which is a within-trial result and does not overturn the sertraline evidence homed on shelf-2410; the shelf question here is venlafaxine ER versus placebo.
cards.source: Davidson J et al. Venlafaxine extended release in posttraumatic stress disorder: a sertraline- and placebo-controlled study. The Journal of clinical psychopharmacology. 2006. cards.headline: Davidson 2006 (24-week trial): in 329 outpatients, venlafaxine ER beat placebo over 6 months — CAPS fall −51.7 vs −43.9 (P=.006), remission 50.9% vs 37.5%
cards.summary: Davidson 2006 (24-week trial): in 329 outpatients, venlafaxine ER beat placebo over 6 months — CAPS fall −51.7 vs −43.9 (P=.006), remission 50.9% vs 37.5%
cards.people: 329 adult outpatients at 56 international sites with a primary DSM-IV diagnosis of PTSD, symptoms for 6 months or longer and a CAPS score of 60 or higher, randomised double-blind to flexible-dose venlafaxine ER (37.5–300 mg/day) or placebo for 24 weeks.
cards.result: Mean change in CAPS total score at endpoint was −51.7 on venlafaxine ER versus −43.9 on placebo (P=.006). Improvement was significantly greater for reexperiencing (P=.008) and avoidance/numbing (P=.006) clusters, but not for hyperarousal. Remission (CAPS ≤20) was 50.9% versus 37.5% (P=.01). Mean maximum daily dose was 221.5 mg/day. Withdrawal rates were similar between groups, with no significant difference in dropouts attributable to adverse events; dizziness, headache and nausea appear in the record's MeSH adverse-event terms.
cards.watchOut: A 24-week placebo arm in chronic PTSD selects for patients who stay in a long trial; the remission percentages are higher in both arms than in the 12-week trial, so the between-group difference — not the absolute remission rate — is the transportable figure.
cards.source: Davidson J et al. Treatment of posttraumatic stress disorder with venlafaxine extended release: a 6-month randomized controlled trial. Archives of general psychiatry. 2006. cards.headline: Hoskins 2015 meta-analysis: across 51 PTSD drug trials, venlafaxine was one of the few individual agents with significant efficacy over placebo in two or more trials — with small effect sizes across the field
cards.summary: Hoskins 2015 meta-analysis: across 51 PTSD drug trials, venlafaxine was one of the few individual agents with significant efficacy over placebo in two or more trials — with small effect sizes across the field
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 51 randomised trials (Hoskins 2015)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 51 randomised controlled trials of pharmacotherapy as monotherapy for PTSD, pooling symptom change versus placebo across drug classes and individual agents.
cards.result: SSRIs as a class were statistically superior to placebo with a small effect (standardised mean difference −0.23, 95% CI −0.33 to −0.12). For individual agents tested in two or more trials, the review found small statistically significant evidence of efficacy for fluoxetine, paroxetine and venlafaxine. The authors conclude some drugs have a small positive impact on PTSD symptoms and are acceptable, and that for most drugs the evidence is inadequate.
cards.watchOut: The meta-analysis pools venlafaxine with the wider drug literature and reports standardised effects, not venlafaxine-specific absolute remission rates; the two trial cards above carry the absolute numbers for this shelf's question.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two large trials and a 51-trial meta-analysis point the same way — venlafaxine ER gives a modest, real improvement in core PTSD symptoms over placebo
cards.summary: Synthesis: two large trials and a 51-trial meta-analysis point the same way — venlafaxine ER gives a modest, real improvement in core PTSD symptoms over placebo
cards.people: The carded evidence: two double-blind placebo-controlled trials of venlafaxine ER in chronic PTSD (538 patients over 12 weeks; 329 over 24 weeks) and one systematic review/meta-analysis of 51 PTSD pharmacotherapy trials. Total carded trial participants: 867, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: CAPS-SX17 falls favoured venlafaxine ER in both trials (−41.8 vs −33.9 at 12 weeks; −51.7 vs −43.9 at 24 weeks, P=.006), and remission favoured it in both (30.2% vs 19.6%; 50.9% vs 37.5%). The meta-analysis independently lists venlafaxine among the few agents with significant efficacy in two or more trials, while characterising drug effects in PTSD as small. PROPOSED LIKELY: venlafaxine ER improves core PTSD symptoms versus placebo, with absolute remission gains of about 11–13 percentage points.
cards.watchOut: Both pivotal trials were flexible-dose, industry-era studies in chronic, mostly non-combat outpatient PTSD; the shelf does not answer venlafaxine ER versus trauma-focused psychotherapy, which is a different question.
cards.source: Synthesis of Davidson J et al. The Journal of clinical psychopharmacology. 2006 (PMID: 16702890); Davidson J et al. Archives of general psychiatry. 2006 (PMID: 17015818); Hoskins M et al. The British journal of psychiatry : the journal of mental science. 2015 (PMID: 25644881).

shelves.title: Bipolar I depression: the olanzapine–fluoxetine combination beat olanzapine alone and placebo — remission 48.8% vs 32.8% vs 24.5%, at a metabolic cost
shelves.question: In bipolar I depression, does the olanzapine–fluoxetine combination improve depressive symptoms versus olanzapine alone and versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antidepressive Agents, Second-Generation · Antipsychotic Agents · Benzodiazepines · Bipolar Disorder · Depression · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Fluoxetine · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Olanzapine · Pirenzepine · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: The pivotal 8-week trial (833 patients with bipolar I depression) found the olanzapine–fluoxetine combination (OFC) lowered MADRS scores by 18.5 points, against 15.0 on olanzapine alone and 11.9 on placebo; remission was 48.8% on OFC, 32.8% on olanzapine and 24.5% on placebo, with no excess of treatment-emergent mania (6.4% vs 5.7% vs 6.7%). A 2013 systematic review and meta-analysis of four randomised trials (1,330 patients) found OFC improved response versus olanzapine (relative risk 1.58) and versus placebo (relative risk 1.99) — relative measures; the record reports no absolute rates for those pooled comparisons, and the trial card above carries the absolute figures. Against lamotrigine, a separate 410-patient trial found OFC modestly more effective on depression scores but with more somnolence, weight gain and cholesterol elevation. The cost side is metabolic: weight gain and lipid rises are the combination's recurring price. PROPOSED LIKELY: OFC improves bipolar I depressive symptoms more than olanzapine alone and more than placebo over 8 weeks, at a metabolic tolerability cost.

cards.headline: Tohen 2003: in 833 patients with bipolar I depression, the combination beat both olanzapine alone and placebo — MADRS falls of 18.5 vs 15.0 vs 11.9 points; remission 48.8% vs 32.8% vs 24.5%
cards.summary: Tohen 2003: in 833 patients with bipolar I depression, the combination beat both olanzapine alone and placebo — MADRS falls of 18.5 vs 15.0 vs 11.9 points; remission 48.8% vs 32.8% vs 24.5%
cards.people: 833 randomised adults with bipolar I depression (MADRS score at least 20) at 84 sites in 13 countries, assigned double-blind for 8 weeks to placebo (n=377), olanzapine 5–20 mg/day (n=370), or olanzapine–fluoxetine combination (6/25, 6/50, or 12/50 mg/day; n=86).
cards.result: Both active groups improved significantly more than placebo at every week (P<.001). At week 8, MADRS total scores had fallen by 11.9 points on placebo, 15.0 on olanzapine, and 18.5 on the combination; the combination was also significantly better than olanzapine alone at weeks 4–8. Remission was met by 24.5% (87/355) on placebo, 32.8% (115/351) on olanzapine, and 48.8% (40/82) on the combination. Treatment-emergent mania did not differ among groups (placebo 6.7%, olanzapine 5.7%, combination 6.4%). Adverse events for the combination were similar to olanzapine's, with some higher rates noted in the full report.
cards.watchOut: The combination arm was much smaller than the other arms (86 randomised, 82 in the remission denominator), so its 48.8% remission figure carries wider uncertainty than the placebo and olanzapine figures beside it.
cards.source: Tohen M et al. Efficacy of olanzapine and olanzapine-fluoxetine combination in the treatment of bipolar I depression. Archives of general psychiatry. 2003. PMID: 14609883. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Brown 2006: against lamotrigine, the combination improved depression scores modestly more (effect size 0.24) and faster — but with more weight gain and higher cholesterol and triglycerides
cards.summary: Brown 2006: against lamotrigine, the combination improved depression scores modestly more (effect size 0.24) and faster — but with more weight gain and higher cholesterol and triglycerides
cards.people: 410 patients with DSM-IV bipolar I disorder, depressed, randomised double-blind for 7 weeks to olanzapine–fluoxetine combination (6/25, 6/50, 12/25, or 12/50 mg/day; n=205) or lamotrigine titrated to 200 mg/day (n=205), November 2003 to August 2004.
cards.result: The combination produced significantly greater improvement than lamotrigine on the Clinical Global Impressions–Severity scale (primary outcome; p=.002, effect size 0.26), MADRS (p=.002, effect size 0.24) and Young Mania Rating Scale scores (p=.001). Response rates (≥50% MADRS reduction) did not differ significantly (68.8% vs 59.7%; p=.073), but time to response was shorter on the combination (median 17 vs 23 days; p=.010). Somnolence, increased appetite, dry mouth, sedation, weight gain and tremor were more frequent on the combination, and weight, total cholesterol and triglyceride levels were significantly higher (all p≤.001). Suicidal and self-injurious behaviour adverse events were less frequent on the combination (0.5% vs 3.4%; p=.037).
cards.watchOut: This trial has no placebo or olanzapine-alone arm, so it cannot answer this shelf's primary comparison; it is carded because it prices the combination against the main non-antipsychotic alternative and documents the metabolic cost in a head-to-head design. Its 25-week continuation was reported separately (PMID: 19079815) and is not double-carded.
cards.source: Brown EB et al. A 7-week, randomized, double-blind trial of olanzapine/fluoxetine combination versus lamotrigine in the treatment of bipolar I depression. The Journal of clinical psychiatry. 2006. PMID: 16889444. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Silva 2013 meta-analysis: pooling four randomised trials (1,330 patients), the combination improved response versus olanzapine (relative risk 1.58) and versus placebo (relative risk 1.99)
cards.summary: Silva 2013 meta-analysis: pooling four randomised trials (1,330 patients), the combination improved response versus olanzapine (relative risk 1.58) and versus placebo (relative risk 1.99)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 4 randomised trials (Silva 2013)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials of olanzapine plus fluoxetine in bipolar depression; four trials with 1,330 patients met inclusion from 627 unique records.
cards.result: The combination improved response compared with olanzapine (relative risk 1.58, 95% CI 1.27–1.97) and compared with placebo (relative risk 1.99, 95% CI 1.49–2.65), but not compared with lamotrigine (low-quality evidence); similar patterns held for remission and relapse. These are relative measures — the record reports no absolute response rates for the pooled comparisons; the Tohen 2003 card above carries absolute MADRS and remission figures. No differences were found for incidence of mania (moderate-quality evidence). Adverse effects were more common on the combination than on lamotrigine (relative risk 1.13, 95% CI 1.04–1.23), with no difference versus olanzapine (low-quality evidence). The authors flag attrition and reporting bias as concerns and note how few trials exist.
cards.watchOut: Four trials is a thin pool and two of them share the lamotrigine comparison; the pooled relative risks lean heavily on the single large placebo-controlled trial carded above.
cards.source: Silva MT et al. Olanzapine plus fluoxetine for bipolar disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of affective disorders. 2013. PMID: 23218251. cards.headline: Synthesis: the combination beats placebo and beats olanzapine alone on depression scores and remission — the trade is weight and lipids
cards.summary: Synthesis: the combination beats placebo and beats olanzapine alone on depression scores and remission — the trade is weight and lipids
cards.people: The carded evidence: one large 8-week placebo- and olanzapine-controlled trial (833 patients), one 7-week head-to-head trial against lamotrigine (410 patients), and one meta-analysis of four trials (1,330 patients). Total carded trial participants exceed 1,200 in distinct trials, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: In Tohen 2003, MADRS fell 18.5 points on the combination versus 15.0 on olanzapine and 11.9 on placebo, with remission 48.8% versus 32.8% versus 24.5% and no excess switch into mania. The meta-analysis' relative response advantages (relative risk 1.58 vs olanzapine; 1.99 vs placebo) point the same way. Against lamotrigine the combination was modestly more effective and faster, with significantly more weight gain and higher cholesterol and triglycerides. PROPOSED LIKELY: the olanzapine–fluoxetine combination improves bipolar I depressive symptoms versus olanzapine alone and versus placebo, at a metabolic tolerability cost.
cards.watchOut: Almost all controlled evidence is 7–8 weeks long; the shelf answers acute symptom improvement, not long-term relapse prevention or long-term metabolic outcomes.

shelves.title: Generalised anxiety disorder: quetiapine XR beat placebo in three trials (evidence question, not a recommendation) — SSRI comparison rests on one paroxetine arm
shelves.question: In generalised anxiety disorder, does quetiapine extended-release reduce anxiety symptoms versus placebo, and how does it compare with SSRIs?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Antipsychotic Agents · Anxiety Disorders · Dibenzothiazepines · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Delivery Systems · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Quetiapine Fumarate · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: This is an evidence question, not a recommendation: quetiapine extended-release (XR) is not a guideline-endorsed first-line treatment for generalised anxiety disorder (GAD), and this shelf presents the trial evidence plainly. Three placebo-controlled trials agree that it works over 8–9 weeks. Bandelow 2010 (873 patients, with a paroxetine active-control arm) found both quetiapine XR doses and paroxetine beat placebo on the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAM-A), with quetiapine separating from placebo by day 4 and remission at 42.6% for the 150 mg dose versus 27.2% on placebo and 38.8% on paroxetine — the trial was not powered as a formal head-to-head against the SSRI, so 'compares with SSRIs' rests on this single active-control arm showing effects in the same range. Khan 2011 (951 patients) found the 50 mg and 150 mg doses beat placebo (−13.31 and −13.54 vs −11.10 HAM-A points) but the 300 mg dose did not (−11.87; P=0.240). In older patients (Mezhebovsky 2013, 450 patients aged 66+), flexible-dose quetiapine XR beat placebo clearly (−14.97 vs −7.21; P<0.001). The recurring adverse events are somnolence, dry mouth, sedation, dizziness and fatigue. PROPOSED LIKELY (versus placebo): quetiapine XR reduces GAD symptoms over 8–9 weeks at 50–150 mg/day, with effects in the same range as the one SSRI comparator tested, and a sedative adverse-event profile.

cards.headline: Bandelow 2010: in 873 patients with GAD, quetiapine XR 50 mg and 150 mg and paroxetine all beat placebo on HAM-A — remission 42.6% (150 mg) vs 38.8% (paroxetine) vs 27.2% (placebo)
cards.summary: Bandelow 2010: in 873 patients with GAD, quetiapine XR 50 mg and 150 mg and paroxetine all beat placebo on HAM-A — remission 42.6% (150 mg) vs 38.8% (paroxetine) vs 27.2% (placebo)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Bandelow 2010, placebo- and paroxetine-controlled)
cards.people: 873 patients with generalised anxiety disorder randomised double-blind in a multicentre phase III trial to quetiapine XR 50 mg/day, quetiapine XR 150 mg/day, paroxetine 20 mg/day, or placebo, over 8 weeks of active treatment (study NCT00322595).
cards.result: At week 8, all active agents produced significant improvements versus placebo in HAM-A total and psychic subscale scores; the somatic subscale improved significantly only on 150 mg quetiapine XR. Separation from placebo in HAM-A total score was significant at day 4 for quetiapine XR 50 mg (−4.43 vs −2.90 for placebo; p<0.001) and 150 mg (−3.86; p<0.05), but not for paroxetine (−2.69). Remission (HAM-A ≤7) at week 8 was 42.6% on quetiapine XR 150 mg (p<0.01 vs placebo), 38.8% on paroxetine (p<0.05) and 27.2% on placebo. The most common adverse events on quetiapine XR were dry mouth, somnolence, fatigue, dizziness and headache; sexual dysfunction was reported less often on quetiapine XR (0.9–1.8%) than on paroxetine (7.4%).
cards.watchOut: Paroxetine was an active control for assay sensitivity, not a powered head-to-head comparator; similar week-8 outcomes for quetiapine XR and paroxetine in this trial do not establish equivalence or superiority against SSRIs as a class.
cards.source: Bandelow B et al. Extended-release quetiapine fumarate (quetiapine XR): a once-daily monotherapy effective in generalized anxiety disorder. Data from a randomized, double-blind, placebo- and active-controlled study. The international journal of neuropsychopharmacology. 2010. PMID: 19691907. Registry ID: NCT00322595. cards.headline: Khan 2011: in 951 patients, quetiapine XR 50 mg and 150 mg beat placebo on HAM-A (−13.31 and −13.54 vs −11.10) — but the 300 mg dose did not (−11.87; P=0.240)
cards.summary: Khan 2011: in 951 patients, quetiapine XR 50 mg and 150 mg beat placebo on HAM-A (−13.31 and −13.54 vs −11.10) — but the 300 mg dose did not (−11.87; P=0.240)
cards.people: 951 patients with generalised anxiety disorder randomised double-blind to quetiapine XR 50 mg/day (n=234), 150 mg/day (n=241), 300 mg/day (n=241), or placebo (n=235) for 8 weeks of active treatment (study D1448C00009; NCT00329264).
cards.result: At week 8, HAM-A total score improved significantly versus placebo (−11.10) on quetiapine XR 50 mg/day (−13.31; P<0.001) and 150 mg/day (−13.54; P<0.001), but not on 300 mg/day (−11.87; P=0.240). All three doses separated from placebo at week 1. The 50 mg and 150 mg doses also improved HAM-A psychic and somatic cluster scores, response rates and Clinical Global Impression–Improvement versus placebo; sleep quality (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index) improved on all three doses. Adverse events in at least 10% on quetiapine XR were dry mouth, somnolence, sedation, dizziness, headache and fatigue.
cards.watchOut: The flat-to-inverse dose pattern — 300 mg no better than placebo while 50 mg worked — is unexplained in the report and is part of the evidence picture: more quetiapine XR was not more anxiolytic in this programme.

cards.headline: Mezhebovsky 2013: in 450 patients aged 66 and over, flexible-dose quetiapine XR beat placebo clearly on HAM-A (−14.97 vs −7.21; P<0.001)
cards.summary: Mezhebovsky 2013: in 450 patients aged 66 and over, flexible-dose quetiapine XR beat placebo clearly on HAM-A (−14.97 vs −7.21; P<0.001)
cards.people: 450 patients aged 66 years or older with DSM-IV generalised anxiety disorder (HAM-A ≥20, CGI-S ≥4, MADRS ≤16) randomised double-blind at 47 sites to flexibly dosed quetiapine XR (50–300 mg/day; n=223) or placebo (n=227) for 9 weeks (study D1448C00015; NCT00389064).
cards.result: At week 9, quetiapine XR significantly reduced HAM-A total score versus placebo (least-squares mean −14.97 vs −7.21; P<0.001), with significant separation already at week 1. Quetiapine XR also beat placebo on HAM-A response and remission, psychic and somatic clusters, MADRS, CGI-S, sleep quality, pain and quality-of-life scores (all P<0.001). Adverse events above 5% in either group included somnolence, dry mouth, dizziness, headache and nausea.
cards.watchOut: The placebo group's HAM-A fall (−7.21) was much smaller than in the younger-adult trials, which inflates the between-group gap; and a 9-week trial in older adults cannot speak to falls, metabolic or cognitive effects of longer use in this age group.

cards.headline: Synthesis: three trials, one direction versus placebo — quetiapine XR 50–150 mg reduces GAD symptoms over 8–9 weeks; the SSRI comparison rests on a single paroxetine control arm
cards.summary: Synthesis: three trials, one direction versus placebo — quetiapine XR 50–150 mg reduces GAD symptoms over 8–9 weeks; the SSRI comparison rests on a single paroxetine control arm
cards.people: The carded evidence: three double-blind placebo-controlled trials of quetiapine XR monotherapy in generalised anxiety disorder (873, 951 and 450 patients; the first with a paroxetine active-control arm). Total carded participants: 2,274, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Quetiapine XR beat placebo on HAM-A in all three trials — by about 2.2–2.4 points over placebo at 50–150 mg/day in younger adults (Khan 2011) and by 7.8 points in older adults (Mezhebovsky 2013) — with remission 42.6% vs 27.2% on placebo in Bandelow 2010, where paroxetine's remission was 38.8%. The 300 mg dose failed to separate from placebo in Khan 2011. Somnolence, dry mouth, sedation and dizziness recur across the programme. PROPOSED LIKELY (versus placebo): quetiapine XR reduces anxiety symptoms in GAD over 8–9 weeks; evidence for how it compares with SSRIs is limited to one active-control arm showing effects in the same range as paroxetine 20 mg.
cards.watchOut: This shelf is an evidence record, not a recommendation: quetiapine XR is not guideline-endorsed first-line treatment for GAD, all carded trials are 8–9 weeks, and none tests quetiapine XR against an SSRI as a powered primary comparison.

shelves.title: OCD: clomipramine beats placebo clearly, but its claimed edge over SSRIs dissolves head-to-head — and tolerability favours the SSRIs
shelves.question: In obsessive-compulsive disorder, is clomipramine more effective than SSRIs, and at what tolerability cost?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Ambulatory Care · Clomipramine · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Hospitalization · Humans · Male · Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder · Placebos · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Severity of Illness Index
shelves.balance: The answer divides by method. Clomipramine itself clearly works: the 1991 Clomipramine Collaborative Study (520 patients, two studies) found Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS) scores fell 38% and 44% on clomipramine versus 3% and 5% on placebo over 10 weeks. Whether it beats SSRIs is where the split sits. Older meta-analyses that compared effect sizes across separate placebo-controlled trials favoured clomipramine — but Pigott 1999's review notes 5 of 6 direct head-to-head comparisons against fluoxetine or fluvoxamine found similar efficacy with fewer side effects on the SSRI, and a multicentre paroxetine-versus-clomipramine trial found paroxetine as effective with significantly fewer adverse-effect dropouts. The 2016 Lancet Psychiatry network meta-analysis (54 trials, 6,652 participants) settled the direct-plus-indirect comparison: clomipramine's effect versus placebo (−4.72 Y-BOCS points) was numerically larger than the SSRI class effect (−3.49), but clomipramine was not better than SSRIs (difference −1.23, 95% credible interval −3.41 to 0.94 — the interval crosses no difference). The tolerability cost is the tricyclic profile: anticholinergic effects dominate, with seizures and raised aminotransferases as the uncommon serious risks named in the 1991 report. PROPOSED SPLIT (by method): indirect cross-trial comparisons favoured clomipramine; head-to-head trials and the network meta-analysis find no confirmed advantage over SSRIs, with worse tolerability.

cards.headline: Clomipramine Collaborative Study 1991: in 520 patients, clomipramine cut Y-BOCS scores by 38% and 44% versus 3% and 5% on placebo — with a tricyclic adverse-effect profile
cards.summary: Clomipramine Collaborative Study 1991: in 520 patients, clomipramine cut Y-BOCS scores by 38% and 44% versus 3% and 5% on placebo — with a tricyclic adverse-effect profile
cards.type: Randomised controlled trials (Clomipramine Collaborative Study 1991, two studies)
cards.people: 520 patients with obsessive-compulsive disorder in two double-blind studies at 21 centres (239 patients ill for at least 2 years in study 1; 281 ill for at least 1 year in study 2), treated with clomipramine hydrochloride up to 300 mg/day or matching placebo for 10 weeks.
cards.result: Clomipramine was significantly more effective than placebo on both principal measures (Y-BOCS and the NIMH Global Obsessive Compulsive Scale) in both studies. Mean Y-BOCS reduction at 10 weeks was 38% (study 1) and 44% (study 2) on clomipramine versus 3% and 5% on placebo. The most frequently observed adverse effects were those typically associated with tricyclic antidepressants; seizures and elevated aminotransferase values were uncommon but potentially serious side effects. The authors judged clomipramine generally well tolerated and effective in reducing obsessive and compulsive symptoms.

cards.headline: Skapinakis 2016 network meta-analysis: clomipramine was NOT better than SSRIs (difference −1.23 Y-BOCS points, 95% credible interval −3.41 to 0.94) across 54 trials and 6,652 participants
cards.summary: Skapinakis 2016 network meta-analysis: clomipramine was NOT better than SSRIs (difference −1.23 Y-BOCS points, 95% credible interval −3.41 to 0.94) across 54 trials and 6,652 participants
cards.people: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of 54 randomised trials (6,652 participants) of pharmacological and psychotherapeutic interventions for obsessive-compulsive disorder in adults, comparing all treatments directly and indirectly against placebo on Y-BOCS symptom severity (PROSPERO CRD42012002441).
cards.result: Clomipramine (13 trials, 831 patients) reduced Y-BOCS scores versus placebo by a mean difference of −4.72 points (95% credible interval −6.85 to −2.60); the SSRI class effect (37 trials, 3,158 patients) was −3.49 points (−5.12 to −1.81). The direct network comparison found clomipramine was not better than SSRIs (mean difference −1.23, 95% credible interval −3.41 to 0.94). Behavioural and cognitive therapies showed larger effects than medications, though most psychotherapy trials allowed stable antidepressant doses. The authors stress considerable uncertainty about relative efficacy across the field.
cards.watchOut: The credible interval for clomipramine versus SSRIs is wide — it excludes neither a modest clomipramine advantage nor a small SSRI advantage; 'not shown to be better' is the accurate reading, not 'proven equal'.

cards.headline: Pigott 1999 review: two meta-analyses favoured clomipramine, but 5 of 6 head-to-head trials found SSRI efficacy similar — with fewer side effects, and fewer adverse-effect dropouts on paroxetine than clomipramine
cards.summary: Pigott 1999 review: two meta-analyses favoured clomipramine, but 5 of 6 head-to-head trials found SSRI efficacy similar — with fewer side effects, and fewer adverse-effect dropouts on paroxetine than clomipramine
cards.type: Narrative review of trials and meta-analyses (Pigott 1999)
cards.people: Review of the placebo-controlled and head-to-head trial literature for clomipramine and the SSRIs (fluoxetine, sertraline, fluvoxamine, paroxetine) in obsessive-compulsive disorder, including two contemporary meta-analyses and six direct comparisons.
cards.result: The review records that clomipramine, though efficacious, is often associated with substantial adverse events, particularly anticholinergic side effects. While two recent meta-analyses supported superior efficacy of clomipramine over SSRIs, 5 of 6 head-to-head comparisons of fluoxetine or fluvoxamine versus clomipramine found similar efficacy but a lower incidence of side effects with the SSRI. A multicentre 12-week double-blind trial of paroxetine versus clomipramine versus placebo found paroxetine as effective as clomipramine, with significantly fewer dropouts due to adverse effects on paroxetine — superior tolerability. The review's conclusion is that SSRIs possess efficacy similar to clomipramine with a better tolerability profile.
cards.watchOut: This is a narrative review, not a pooled analysis; its head-to-head summary is carded because it is the tolerability half of this shelf's question, and its efficacy reading is superseded in method by the 2016 network meta-analysis carded above.
cards.source: Pigott TA et al. A review of the efficacy of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors in obsessive-compulsive disorder. The Journal of clinical psychiatry. 1999. PMID: 10084636. cards.headline: Synthesis: clomipramine works against placebo, but the claimed superiority over SSRIs dissolves in head-to-head data — and it costs more side effects
cards.summary: Synthesis: clomipramine works against placebo, but the claimed superiority over SSRIs dissolves in head-to-head data — and it costs more side effects
cards.people: The carded evidence: the two 1991 collaborative placebo-controlled studies (520 patients), a 2016 network meta-analysis of 54 trials (6,652 participants), and a 1999 review of the head-to-head and meta-analytic literature. Total carded participants exceed 7,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Versus placebo, clomipramine's efficacy is large and consistent (Y-BOCS falls of 38–44% vs 3–5%; network estimate −4.72 points). Versus SSRIs, the network meta-analysis found no significant advantage (−1.23 points, credible interval crossing zero), and head-to-head trials summarised by Pigott 1999 mostly found similar efficacy with fewer side effects — and significantly fewer adverse-effect dropouts — on the SSRI. PROPOSED SPLIT (by method): cross-trial meta-analytic comparisons favoured clomipramine; direct comparisons do not confirm an advantage, and tolerability favours SSRIs.
cards.watchOut: None of the carded evidence addresses sequencing — whether clomipramine helps after an SSRI has failed — which is the common clinical use and a different question from first-line comparative efficacy.
cards.source: Synthesis of Clomipramine Collaborative Study Group et al. Archives of general psychiatry. 1991 (PMID: 1883256); Skapinakis P et al. The lancet. Psychiatry. 2016 (PMID: 27318812); Pigott TA et al. The Journal of clinical psychiatry. 1999 (PMID: 10084636).

shelves.title: Intravenous scopolamine for major depression: rapid effects in small single-centre crossover trials (N=19–52) — replicated internally, not yet at scale
shelves.question: Does intravenous scopolamine produce rapid antidepressant effects in major depression versus placebo infusion?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antidepressive Agents · Bipolar Disorder · Depressive Disorder · Major Depressive Disorder · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Male · Muscarinic Antagonists · Pilot Projects · Placebos · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Research Design · Scopolamine · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: FLAG — small, single-centre evidence base: every carded trial comes from one research group (the US National Institute of Mental Health intramural programme), samples are tiny (N=19, N=23 and N=52 across the three reports, and the N=52 report may overlap the earlier cohorts), and no large independent replication exists. Within those limits the results are striking and internally replicated: in the first crossover trial (19 randomised, 18 completing; recurrent major depressive or bipolar depression), three intravenous scopolamine infusions (4 µg/kg) reduced depression and anxiety scores versus placebo blocks (P<.001), with effects evident within days. The independent-sample replication restricted to major depressive disorder (23 patients, 22 analysed) found a 32% MADRS reduction after scopolamine versus 6.5% under placebo in the first block (P=.009 for the contrast), significant at the first post-infusion evaluation. The group's 2013 review reports placebo-adjusted remission rates of 56% and 45% for the initial and replication studies, with improvement persisting more than 2 weeks after the final infusion. A 2023 systematic review of all randomised scopolamine trials (PMID: 37893010, described here in prose, not carded) is more cautious: four trials, routes and combinations varied, and not all confirmed a significant reduction versus placebo. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: intravenous scopolamine produces rapid antidepressant effects versus placebo infusion in small crossover trials from a single centre; the finding awaits large independent confirmation.

cards.headline: Furey & Drevets 2006: in a crossover trial (19 randomised, 18 completed), intravenous scopolamine cut depression scores versus placebo (P<.001) within days
cards.summary: Furey & Drevets 2006: in a crossover trial (19 randomised, 18 completed), intravenous scopolamine cut depression scores versus placebo (P<.001) within days
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled crossover trial (Furey 2006; N=19 randomised)
cards.people: 19 randomised outpatients aged 18–50 (18 completed) with recurrent major depressive disorder or bipolar disorder, currently depressed, in a double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial at the National Institute of Mental Health: blocks of three intravenous infusions of scopolamine hydrobromide (4 µg/kg) or placebo, sessions 3–5 days apart, in placebo/scopolamine or scopolamine/placebo sequence. N=19 is printed here because the sample is small.
cards.result: The placebo/scopolamine group showed no significant change during placebo infusion versus baseline, then significant reductions in depression (Montgomery–Åsberg Depression Rating Scale) and anxiety (Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale) scores after scopolamine versus placebo (P<.001 for both). The scopolamine/placebo group likewise showed reductions after scopolamine (P<.001). A preceding dose-finding pilot in the same report had first flagged the effect (P=.002 versus placebo).
cards.watchOut: The sample mixes major depressive disorder with bipolar depression, so it does not answer the major-depression question in a pure population — the next card's replication is the major-depression-only test. Crossover carryover is also a live concern: improvement persisted into the placebo block in the scopolamine-first group.
cards.source: Furey ML et al. Antidepressant efficacy of the antimuscarinic drug scopolamine: a randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trial. Archives of general psychiatry. 2006. PMID: 17015814. cards.headline: Drevets 2010 replication: in major depressive disorder only (N=23; 22 analysed), scopolamine cut MADRS by 32% versus 6.5% under placebo in the first block
cards.summary: Drevets 2010 replication: in major depressive disorder only (N=23; 22 analysed), scopolamine cut MADRS by 32% versus 6.5% under placebo in the first block
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled crossover replication trial (Drevets 2010; N=23)
cards.people: 23 outpatients with major depressive disorder (22 included in analyses) in a double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial (NCT00369915): blocks of three intravenous scopolamine sessions (4.0 µg/kg) or three placebo sessions, 3–5 days apart, in placebo-first or scopolamine-first sequence. N=23 is printed here because the sample is small.
cards.result: Following the initial block, the scopolamine-first group showed a 32% reduction in MADRS scores (P<.001), exceeding the 6.5% change under placebo in the placebo-first group (P=.009), confirming the a priori hypothesis. Improvement was significant at the first evaluation after scopolamine (P=.011). In block 2, the placebo-first group showed a 53% MADRS reduction after crossing to scopolamine, while the scopolamine-first group's gains persisted through its placebo block. Scopolamine caused drowsiness, blurred vision, dry mouth, light-headedness and reduced blood pressure; no subject dropped out because of side effects.
cards.watchOut: Scopolamine's perceptible side effects (dry mouth, blurred vision, drowsiness) risk unblinding against an inert saline placebo — the authors of a later protocol (described in prose in this shelf's build record) chose an active placebo for exactly this reason; effect sizes from inert-placebo crossovers should be read with that discount.

cards.headline: Furey 2010: in a larger crossover cohort (N=52), the rapid antidepressant effect held in both sexes — and was larger in women
cards.summary: Furey 2010: in a larger crossover cohort (N=52), the rapid antidepressant effect held in both sexes — and was larger in women
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled crossover trial, sex-difference analysis (Furey 2010; N=52)
cards.people: 52 male and female outpatients with recurrent major depressive or bipolar disorder in a double-blind randomised placebo-controlled crossover trial of seven intravenous infusions (single-blind placebo lead-in, then blocks of three placebo and three scopolamine 4 µg/kg sessions). N=52 is printed here because the sample is small.
cards.result: A treatment-by-block interaction was significant for MADRS scores (F=21.0, P<0.001), with significant reduction by the evaluation following the first scopolamine administration (F=8.4, P=0.006). The interaction was significant in men (F=3.8, P=0.043) and women (F=35.6, P<0.001) separately, and a block-by-sex interaction (F=7.4, P=0.009) indicated a larger response magnitude in women. The antianxiety (HAM-A) interaction was significant overall (F=12.0, P<0.001) and in women but not in men (F=1.3, P=0.30).
cards.watchOut: This report comes from the same centre and programme as the other two cards and its cohort may overlap theirs; it is carded as a distinct report of the effect in a larger combined sample, not as an independent replication — there is no independent-centre replication in the carded evidence.

cards.headline: Synthesis: rapid, large effects in three small crossover reports from one centre — promising, internally replicated, and not yet independently confirmed at scale
cards.summary: Synthesis: rapid, large effects in three small crossover reports from one centre — promising, internally replicated, and not yet independently confirmed at scale
cards.people: The carded evidence: three double-blind placebo-controlled crossover reports of intravenous scopolamine (4 µg/kg, three-infusion blocks) — N=19 randomised (mixed major depressive and bipolar depression), N=23 (major depressive disorder only) and N=52 (mixed). Summed enrolment across reports is 94, but cohorts come from one programme and may overlap, so the distinct-participant total is smaller and not documented as a single figure in the records.
cards.result: Effects were rapid (significant at the first post-infusion rating) and large for the design: 32% versus 6.5% MADRS reduction in the major-depression replication's first block, with the originating group's review reporting placebo-adjusted remission of 56% and 45% in the initial and replication studies and persistence beyond 2 weeks. Against this, a 2023 systematic review of the whole randomised literature (four trials, varied routes) found not all studies confirmed significant benefit. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: intravenous scopolamine produces rapid antidepressant effects versus placebo infusion, on small single-centre crossover evidence.
cards.watchOut: Every carded number traces to one research group; until an independent centre replicates the effect in a larger parallel-group trial with an active placebo, the stamp stays at POSSIBLE however large the within-trial effects look.

synthesis the carded evidence: three double-blind placebo-controlled crossover reports of intravenous scopolamine (4 µg/kg, three-infusion blocks) — n=19 randomised (mixed major depressive and bipolar depression), n=23 (major depressive disorder only) and n=52 (mixed). summed enrolment across reports is 94, but cohorts come from one programme and may overlap, so the distinct-participant total is smaller and not documented as a single figure in the records. effects were rapid (significant at the first post-infusion rating) and large for the design: 32% versus 6.5% madrs reduction in the major-depression replication's first block, with the originating group's review reporting placebo-adjusted remission of 56% and 45% in the initial and replication studies and persistence beyond 2 weeks. against this, a 2023 systematic review of the whole randomised literature (four trials, varied routes) found not all studies confirmed significant benefit. proposed possible: intravenous scopolamine produces rapid antidepressant effects versus placebo infusion, on small single-centre crossover evidence. every carded number traces to one research group; until an independent centre replicates the effect in a larger parallel-group trial with an active placebo, the stamp stays at possible however large the within-trial effects look. synthesis of furey ml et al. archives of general psychiatry. 2006 (pmid: 17015814); drevets wc et al. biological psychiatry. 2010 (pmid: 20074703); furey ml et al. neuropsychopharmacology : official publication of the american college of neuropsychopharmacology. 2010 (pmid: 20736989).

shelves.title: Wake therapy alone (PARTIAL of combined-chronotherapy shelf-2426): a next-day response in about half of patients, gone after recovery sleep
shelves.question: Does wake therapy (therapeutic sleep deprivation) alone, without combined light/phase-shift chronotherapy, speed antidepressant response in major depression?
shelves.mesh: Antidepressive Agents · Depression · Humans · Phototherapy · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Psychological Techniques · Sleep Deprivation · Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion: shelf-2426 homes the combined chronotherapy package (wake therapy plus bright light plus sleep-phase stabilisation, added to duloxetine); this shelf asks only about wake therapy on its own, and no card here re-uses that trial. Alone, one night of total or partial sleep deprivation produces a response in roughly half of patients by the next day — the 2017 meta-analysis of 66 studies (which excluded studies that seamlessly combined sleep deprivation with other therapies) found response rates of 45% among studies with a randomised control group and 50% among those without. The effect is fast but fragile: in the tryptophan-depletion experiment, 22 of 30 drug-free inpatients responded to one night of total sleep deprivation, and the field's central problem is relapse after the next night of recovery sleep. A randomised crossover comparison (39 inpatients) found total sleep deprivation slightly more effective than late partial sleep deprivation, with day-after response rates of 0–53% depending on the rating scale used — a warning that the headline response rate is measurement-sensitive. Almost none of this literature is placebo-controlled in the drug-trial sense, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: wake therapy alone speeds antidepressant response within 24 hours in about half of patients, with relapse after recovery sleep the rule unless something sustains the gain.

cards.headline: Boland 2017 meta-analysis: across 66 studies of sleep deprivation used on its own, 45–50% of depressed patients responded — 45% in studies with a randomised control group
cards.summary: Boland 2017 meta-analysis: across 66 studies of sleep deprivation used on its own, 45–50% of depressed patients responded — 45% in studies with a randomised control group
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 66 independent studies (1974–2016) of experimental total or partial sleep deprivation in depression that reported the percentage of responders against an a priori response definition, excluding studies that seamlessly combined sleep deprivation with other therapies such as chronotherapeutics or repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation.
cards.result: The overall response rate to sleep deprivation was 45% among studies that used a randomised control group and 50% among studies that did not. Response was not significantly affected by the type of sleep deprivation (total vs partial), the nature of the clinical sample (unipolar vs bipolar), medication status, the definition of response used, or patients' age and sex. The authors conclude the findings support a significant antidepressant effect of sleep deprivation and call for work on who responds and how to sustain it.
cards.watchOut: Most included studies had no control condition at all — the 50% figure from uncontrolled studies and the 45% from controlled ones are response rates after one night, not drug-trial-style separations from a placebo arm; expectation and the inpatient setting are unmeasured contributors.
cards.source: Boland EM et al. Meta-Analysis of the Antidepressant Effects of Acute Sleep Deprivation. The Journal of clinical psychiatry. 2017. PMID: 28937707. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Giedke 2003 crossover: in 39 inpatients, total sleep deprivation beat late partial sleep deprivation slightly — but day-after response ranged from 0% to 53% depending on the scale
cards.summary: Giedke 2003 crossover: in 39 inpatients, total sleep deprivation beat late partial sleep deprivation slightly — but day-after response ranged from 0% to 53% depending on the scale
cards.people: 39 inpatients with major depression (mainly unipolar) in a randomised balanced crossover study comparing one night of total sleep deprivation with late partial sleep deprivation (sleep in the early night, then kept awake) within a 1-week interval, rated non-blindly.
cards.result: Response was defined as at least a 30% reduction on the 6-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale and/or one of two self-rating scales. Overall day-after response rates were low and scale-dependent (0–53% across the ratings used). Total sleep deprivation proved slightly, and in about half the comparisons significantly, more effective than late partial sleep deprivation. First treatments worked better than second treatments; 10–20% of responses persisted to the second day; and in up to 10% of treatments patients worsened after sleep deprivation. The authors infer a possible dose-response relation between hours of sleep lost and effect within one night.
cards.watchOut: Ratings were non-blind and naps/microsleep were not recorded — both biases run in favour of the intervention; the honest takeaway is the ordering (total > partial) and the scale-dependence of response, not a precise response rate.
cards.source: Giedke H et al. Direct comparison of total sleep deprivation and late partial sleep deprivation in the treatment of major depression. Journal of affective disorders. 2003. PMID: 12943937. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Neumeister 1998: 22 of 30 drug-free inpatients responded to one night of total sleep deprivation — and the experiment's premise was the relapse that follows recovery sleep
cards.summary: Neumeister 1998: 22 of 30 drug-free inpatients responded to one night of total sleep deprivation — and the experiment's premise was the relapse that follows recovery sleep
cards.type: Randomised mechanistic study in sleep-deprivation responders (Neumeister 1998; N=30)
cards.people: 30 drug-free depressed inpatients who underwent one night of total sleep deprivation (day 1 to day 2); the 22 responders were then randomised to tryptophan depletion or sham depletion on the morning after sleep deprivation, to probe mechanism and the relapse after the recovery night.
cards.result: Twenty-two of 30 patients (73%) showed a favourable outcome after total sleep deprivation in this selected inpatient sample. Tryptophan depletion did not reverse the antidepressant effect during the day after sleep deprivation, but — unexpectedly — it prevented the depressive relapse after the recovery night in most patients, whereas sham-depletion patients relapsed as usual. The authors conclude sleep deprivation does not act through a single monoamine mechanism.
cards.watchOut: The 73% response figure comes from a small, drug-free inpatient sample in a mechanism study, not an efficacy trial; it sits above the meta-analytic 45–50% and should not be quoted as the expected response rate.
cards.source: Neumeister A et al. Effects of tryptophan depletion in drug-free depressed patients who responded to total sleep deprivation. Archives of general psychiatry. 1998. PMID: 9477931. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: wake therapy alone works within a day for roughly half of patients — and wears off with the next night's sleep
cards.summary: Synthesis: wake therapy alone works within a day for roughly half of patients — and wears off with the next night's sleep
cards.people: The carded evidence: a 66-study meta-analysis restricted to sleep deprivation not combined with other chronotherapies, one randomised crossover comparison of total versus partial deprivation (N=39), and one randomised mechanistic study of responders (N=30). The combined wake-plus-light-plus-phase package is homed on shelf-2426 and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: Response by the day after one night of total or partial sleep deprivation was 45% in controlled studies and 50% in uncontrolled studies (Boland 2017); total deprivation was slightly superior to late partial deprivation head-to-head; and relapse after recovery sleep is the consistent finding the mechanistic literature is built around. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: wake therapy alone speeds antidepressant response within 24 hours in about half of patients, transiently. The evidence is largely uncontrolled, which caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.
cards.watchOut: Speed is the whole claim: nothing carded here shows wake therapy alone changing outcomes at 4–8 weeks, and the sustaining strategies (light, phase advance, lithium, antidepressants) belong to the combined-chronotherapy shelf-2426, not this one.
cards.source: Synthesis of Boland EM et al. The Journal of clinical psychiatry. 2017 (PMID: 28937707); Giedke H et al. Journal of affective disorders. 2003 (PMID: 12943937); Neumeister A et al. Archives of general psychiatry. 1998 (PMID: 9477931).

shelves.title: Memantine in Lewy body dementias: a small global-impression benefit concentrated in dementia with Lewy bodies — cognition scores, behaviour scores and daily function did not improve
shelves.question: In dementia with Lewy bodies and Parkinson's disease dementia, does memantine improve cognition and global function versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Brain/drug effects,metabolism,physiopathology · Cognition/drug effects,physiology · Cognition Disorders/drug therapy,metabolism,physiopathology · Double-Blind Method · Excitatory Amino Acid Antagonists/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Female · Glutamic Acid/metabolism · Humans · Lewy Body Disease/drug therapy,metabolism,physiopathology · Male · Memantine/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Neuropsychological Tests · Outcome Assessment, Health Care/methods · Parkinson Disease/drug therapy,metabolism,physiopathology · Patient Selection · Placebo Effect · Placebos · Psychomotor Performance/drug effects,physiology · Reaction Time/drug effects,physiology · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT (population and outcome) — the two randomised trials and their meta-analysis agree on a narrow pattern. On global clinical impression, memantine looked better: Aarsland 2009 (72 patients with Parkinson's disease dementia [PDD] or dementia with Lewy bodies [DLB]) found a 0.7-point better clinical global impression of change score at 24 weeks (p = 0.03), and the pooled meta-analysis (Matsunaga 2015) found the same outcome significant across both trials (standardised mean difference −0.26). But the larger trial (Emre 2010, 199 patients) found no significant global benefit in its total population (p = 0.120) — the significant result sat in the DLB subgroup (−0.6, p = 0.023), with PDD null (−0.1, p = 0.576) — and on everything else the evidence is flat: no significant differences in cognition test scores (including the Mini-Mental State Exam in the meta-analysis), neuropsychiatric inventory scores overall, activities of daily living, motor function, or caregiver burden. Memantine 20 mg/day was well tolerated in both trials, with adverse-event withdrawals similar to placebo. The neighbouring Lewy-body shelves home the cholinesterase inhibitors — donepezil on #3650 and rivastigmine on #2850 — and neither cards these memantine trials. PROPOSED SPLIT (population and outcome): a modest global-impression signal in DLB that does not extend to measured cognition or function, and no shown benefit in PDD.

cards.headline: Aarsland 2009: memantine 20 mg/day improved global impression of change at 24 weeks (mean difference 0.7; p = 0.03) in 72 patients with PDD or DLB — secondary measures were null except attention speed
cards.summary: Aarsland 2009: memantine 20 mg/day improved global impression of change at 24 weeks (mean difference 0.7; p = 0.03) in 72 patients with PDD or DLB — secondary measures were null except attention speed
cards.people: 72 patients with Parkinson's disease dementia (UK Parkinson's Disease Society Brain Bank criteria plus DSM-IV dementia at least 1 year after motor onset) or dementia with Lewy bodies (revised consensus criteria), at clinics in Norway, Sweden and the UK, randomly assigned to memantine 20 mg/day (34) or placebo (38) for 24 weeks; 56 (78%) completed, with withdrawals all due to adverse events but in similar proportions in both groups. Primary outcome was clinical global impression of change (CGIC, 1–7; lower is better).
cards.result: At week 24 the memantine group had better CGIC scores than placebo (mean difference 0.7, 95% CI 0.04–1.39; p = 0.03). With the exception of improved speed on an attentional task (quick test of cognition form difference 12.4, 95% CI 6.0–30.9; p = 0.004), there were no significant differences between groups on secondary outcome measures. Memantine was well tolerated; the authors call the findings preliminary and ask for large-scale confirmation.
cards.watchOut: Seventy-two patients pooled across two diagnoses, a confidence interval for the primary outcome that only just excludes zero (0.04–1.39), and a 22% dropout rate driven by adverse events in both arms — a fragile base for the global-impression claim, which is why the larger trial's subgroup pattern matters.
cards.source: Aarsland D et al. Memantine in patients with Parkinson's disease dementia or dementia with Lewy bodies: a double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre trial. The Lancet. Neurology. 2009. PMID: 19520613. Registry ID: ISRCTN89624516. cards.headline: Emre 2010: in 199 patients, memantine showed no significant global benefit overall (p = 0.120) — the benefit sat in the DLB subgroup (−0.6; p = 0.023), with PDD null and cognition scores unchanged
cards.summary: Emre 2010: in 199 patients, memantine showed no significant global benefit overall (p = 0.120) — the benefit sat in the DLB subgroup (−0.6; p = 0.023), with PDD null and cognition scores unchanged
cards.people: 199 patients aged 50 or older with mild-to-moderate Parkinson's disease dementia or dementia with Lewy bodies at 30 specialist centres in eight countries, randomly assigned to memantine 20 mg/day (34 DLB and 62 PDD) or placebo (41 DLB and 58 PDD) for 24 weeks; 159 (80%) completed, and 93 memantine and 97 placebo patients entered the efficacy analysis. No primary endpoint was prespecified; global status was measured by the ADCS clinical global impression of change.
cards.result: At week 24, DLB patients on memantine improved more on global impression than those on placebo (mean change 3.3 vs 3.9; difference −0.6, 95% CI −1.2 to −0.1; p = 0.023), and DLB neuropsychiatric inventory scores also improved more (−4.3 vs 1.7; difference −5.9, 95% CI −11.6 to −0.2; p = 0.041). In PDD, neither outcome differed significantly (global −0.1, p = 0.576; NPI −1.4, p = 0.522), and in the total population neither did (global −0.3, p = 0.120; NPI −2.9, p = 0.092). Most cognitive test scores, activities of daily living and caregiver burden scores showed no significant differences in any population. Adverse events and discontinuations were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: The DLB-versus-PDD contrast is a subgroup reading of a trial whose total-population result was null and which prespecified no primary endpoint; subgroup effects of this kind are hypothesis-strengthening, not proof, and the DLB subgroup numbered only 75 patients.
cards.source: Emre M et al. Memantine for patients with Parkinson's disease dementia or dementia with Lewy bodies: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. The Lancet. Neurology. 2010. PMID: 20729148. Registry ID: NCT00855686. cards.headline: Matsunaga 2015 meta-analysis: pooling the Lewy-body memantine trials, only global impression favoured memantine (standardised mean difference −0.26) — cognition, behaviour, daily function and motor scores did not
cards.summary: Matsunaga 2015 meta-analysis: pooling the Lewy-body memantine trials, only global impression favoured memantine (standardised mean difference −0.26) — cognition, behaviour, daily function and motor scores did not
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials of memantine versus placebo in Lewy body disorders (dementia with Lewy bodies and Parkinson's disease dementia), evaluating global impression, Mini-Mental State Exam, Neuropsychiatric Inventory, activities of daily living, motor function, discontinuation and side effects.
cards.result: Memantine was superior to placebo on Alzheimer's Disease Cooperative Study–Clinical Global Impression of Change scores (standardised mean difference −0.26, 95% CI −0.51 to −0.02; p = 0.04; two studies; N = 258). No significant effects were found on motor function scores, Mini-Mental State Exam scores, Neuropsychiatric Inventory scores, or activities of daily living scores. Dropout for all causes, inefficacy or adverse events, and rates of serious adverse events, somnolence/tiredness, stroke, dizziness/vertigo and confusion, were similar between groups. The authors conclude memantine did not benefit cognition or motor function but may be superior for overall impression, and was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: The pooled global-impression effect is small (standardised mean difference −0.26) and rests on the same two trials carded above; a clinician-rated global scale can register change that no objective cognition, behaviour or function measure on this shelf corroborates.
cards.source: Matsunaga S et al. Memantine for Lewy body disorders: systematic review and meta-analysis. The American journal of geriatric psychiatry : official journal of the American Association for Geriatric Psychiatry. 2015. PMID: 24406251. Registry ID: none in the record. systematic review and meta-analysis (matsunaga 2015) systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials of memantine versus placebo in lewy body disorders (dementia with lewy bodies and parkinson's disease dementia), evaluating global impression, mini-mental state exam, neuropsychiatric inventory, activities of daily living, motor function, discontinuation and side effects. memantine was superior to placebo on alzheimer's disease cooperative study–clinical global impression of change scores (standardised mean difference −0.26, 95% ci −0.51 to −0.02; p = 0.04; two studies; n = 258). no significant effects were found on motor function scores, mini-mental state exam scores, neuropsychiatric inventory scores, or activities of daily living scores. dropout for all causes, inefficacy or adverse events, and rates of serious adverse events, somnolence/tiredness, stroke, dizziness/vertigo and confusion, were similar between groups. the authors conclude memantine did not benefit cognition or motor function but may be superior for overall impression, and was well tolerated. the pooled global-impression effect is small (standardised mean difference −0.26) and rests on the same two trials carded above; a clinician-rated global scale can register change that no objective cognition, behaviour or function measure on this shelf corroborates. matsunaga s et al. memantine for lewy body disorders: systematic review and meta-analysis. the american journal of geriatric psychiatry : official journal of the american association for geriatric psychiatry. 2015. pmid: 24406251. registry id: none in the record. mesh: excitatory amino acid antagonists/adverse effects,therapeutic use · humans · lewy body disease/drug therapy · memantine/adverse effects,therapeutic use · patient dropouts/statistics & numerical data

cards.headline: Synthesis: global impression improves a little, driven by DLB; measured cognition and function do not — a split verdict by population and by outcome
cards.summary: Synthesis: global impression improves a little, driven by DLB; measured cognition and function do not — a split verdict by population and by outcome
cards.people: The carded evidence: two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled 24-week trials of memantine 20 mg/day (72 and 199 patients with PDD or DLB) and their meta-analysis (global-impression N = 258).
cards.result: Global impression favoured memantine in the smaller trial (difference 0.7, p = 0.03) and in the pooled analysis (standardised mean difference −0.26, p = 0.04), but in the larger trial the total-population result was null (p = 0.120) and significance was confined to the DLB subgroup. Cognition scores, neuropsychiatric scores overall, daily function, motor function and caregiver burden showed no significant benefit in any report. PROPOSED SPLIT (population and outcome): POSSIBLE (benefit) for global clinical impression in dementia with Lewy bodies; no demonstrated benefit for cognition or function, and none shown in Parkinson's disease dementia.
cards.watchOut: Do not summarise this shelf as 'memantine works in Lewy body dementia': the affirmative half is one clinician-rated global scale, concentrated in one diagnosis, while every objective measure carded here is null — and the cholinesterase-inhibitor evidence for these diagnoses lives on shelves #3650 and #2850, not here.

shelves.title: Memantine in frontotemporal dementia: no benefit on behaviour or global impression in either randomised trial (81 and 49 patients) — a well-conducted negative evidence base
shelves.question: In frontotemporal dementia, does memantine improve behaviour or cognition versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Chi-Square Distribution · Double-Blind Method · Excitatory Amino Acid Antagonists/therapeutic use · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Frontotemporal Lobar Degeneration/drug therapy · Humans · Male · Memantine/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Neuropsychological Tests · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Retrospective Studies · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — this shelf is the clean negative the trials support. Memantine was widely used off-label in frontotemporal dementia (FTD) after an open-label study suggested transient benefit; the two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials then tested it properly and both were negative. Boxer 2013 (81 patients with behavioural-variant FTD or semantic dementia, memantine 20 mg/day for 26 weeks) found no effect on the neuropsychiatric inventory (mean difference 2.2, 95% CI −3.9 to 8.3; p = 0.47) or on clinical global impression of change (mean difference 0.0; p = 0.90), and patients on memantine had more frequent cognitive adverse events (6 patients versus 1). Vercelletto 2011 (49 patients with behavioural-variant FTD, 10 mg twice daily for a full year) found no significant difference on the primary global endpoint (p = 0.4458) or on MMSE, dementia rating, neuropsychiatric, disability or caregiver-burden scores; the single positive secondary result (frontal behavioural inventory, p = 0.0417) sits among many null comparisons. Pooling both trials (130 patients), the Kishi 2015 meta-analysis found no significant differences on Mini-Mental State Exam, neuropsychiatric inventory, caregiver burden or discontinuation, with only a marginal, non-significant trend on global impression (standardised mean difference −0.34; p = 0.06). PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): the data do not support memantine use in FTD, in the words of the largest trial itself.

cards.headline: Boxer 2013: memantine had no effect on neuropsychiatric symptoms (difference 2.2; p = 0.47) or global impression (difference 0.0; p = 0.90) in 81 patients with FTD — and caused more cognitive adverse events
cards.summary: Boxer 2013: memantine had no effect on neuropsychiatric symptoms (difference 2.2; p = 0.47) or global impression (difference 0.0; p = 0.90) in 81 patients with FTD — and caused more cognitive adverse events
cards.people: 81 patients meeting Neary criteria for behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia or semantic dementia, with characteristic brain atrophy, randomly assigned to oral memantine 20 mg daily (39) or matched placebo (42) for 26 weeks in a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial; acetylcholinesterase inhibitors were prohibited; 76 patients completed. Primary endpoints were change in total neuropsychiatric inventory (NPI) score and clinical global impression of change (CGIC) after 26 weeks.
cards.result: Memantine treatment had no effect on either the NPI (mean difference 2.2, 95% CI −3.9 to 8.3; p = 0.47) or the CGIC (mean difference 0.0, 95% CI −0.4 to 0.4; p = 0.90) after 26 weeks — the treatment made no difference. Memantine was generally well tolerated, but patients in the memantine group had more frequent cognitive adverse events (six patients) than those in the placebo group (one). The authors conclude the data do not support memantine use in FTD.
cards.watchOut: Enrolment (81) fell short of plan because many patients preferred open-label memantine to trial participation — a recruitment caveat the authors report; even so, the global-impression confidence interval (−0.4 to 0.4) is narrow enough to exclude a meaningful average benefit on that endpoint.
cards.source: Boxer AL et al. Memantine in patients with frontotemporal lobar degeneration: a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. The Lancet. Neurology. 2013. PMID: 23290598. Registry ID: NCT00545974.
