cards.headline: Vercelletto 2011: one year of memantine (10 mg twice daily) showed no significant difference on the primary global endpoint or on cognition, behaviour, disability or caregiver burden in 49 patients with bvFTD
cards.summary: Vercelletto 2011: one year of memantine (10 mg twice daily) showed no significant difference on the primary global endpoint or on cognition, behaviour, disability or caregiver burden in 49 patients with bvFTD
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase II trial (Vercelletto 2011)
cards.people: 49 analysed patients aged 45–75 years with behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia and Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) score ≥19 (mean age 65.6 years; mean MMSE 25.0), in a national, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase II trial of memantine 10 mg twice daily (23) versus placebo (26) for 52 weeks. The primary endpoint was the CIBIC-Plus global impression scale; secondary endpoints included the neuropsychiatric inventory (NPI), frontal behavioural inventory (FBI), Mattis dementia rating scale, MMSE, disability assessment and caregiver burden (Zarit).
cards.result: At 52 weeks there were no significant differences between memantine and placebo on the CIBIC-Plus (p = 0.4458; 10 patients had worsened on memantine versus 17 on placebo) or on MMSE (p = 0.63), dementia rating scale (p = 0.95), NPI (p = 0.25), Zarit burden (p = 0.43) or disability assessment (p = 0.10) — the treatment made no difference. The sole significant secondary result was a lower FBI score in the memantine group (p = 0.0417). Memantine was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: A one-year trial is the longest test on this shelf, but 49 patients cannot exclude small effects; the single positive secondary endpoint (FBI, p = 0.0417) among at least seven comparisons is the pattern expected by chance and was not confirmed by the larger Boxer trial.
cards.source: Vercelletto M et al. Memantine in behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia: negative results. Journal of Alzheimer's disease : JAD. 2011. PMID: 21157021. Registry ID: NCT00200538. cards.headline: Kishi 2015 meta-analysis: pooling both FTD memantine trials (130 patients), no significant benefit on global impression (p = 0.06), MMSE, neuropsychiatric inventory, or caregiver burden
cards.summary: Kishi 2015 meta-analysis: pooling both FTD memantine trials (130 patients), no significant benefit on global impression (p = 0.06), MMSE, neuropsychiatric inventory, or caregiver burden
cards.people: Meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials of memantine versus placebo in frontotemporal dementia, searching PubMed, the Cochrane Library and PsycINFO to April 2015; two randomised controlled trials (total n = 130) met the inclusion criteria. Outcomes were Clinical Global Impression (primary), Mini-Mental State Examination, Neuropsychiatric Inventory and Zarit Burden Interview scores, and all-cause discontinuation.
cards.result: Memantine was marginally, but not significantly, superior to placebo on Clinical Global Impression scores (standardised mean difference −0.34, 95% CI −0.68 to 0.01; P = 0.06). There were no significant differences in Mini-Mental State Examination, Neuropsychiatric Inventory, or Zarit Burden Interview scores, or in all-cause discontinuation, between memantine and placebo — the treatment made no significant difference on any pooled outcome. The authors note only two trials exist and larger studies would be needed.
cards.watchOut: A two-trial meta-analysis adds a pooled estimate, not new patients; its near-significant global-impression trend (p = 0.06) should be read against the larger trial's own global result, which was exactly null (difference 0.0, p = 0.90).
cards.source: Kishi T et al. Memantine for the treatment of frontotemporal dementia: a meta-analysis. Neuropsychiatric disease and treatment. 2015. PMID: 26648724. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: two properly blinded trials and their pooled analysis are concordantly negative — memantine does not improve behaviour or cognition in FTD
cards.summary: Synthesis: two properly blinded trials and their pooled analysis are concordantly negative — memantine does not improve behaviour or cognition in FTD
cards.people: The carded evidence: two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials of memantine 20 mg/day in frontotemporal dementia (81 patients over 26 weeks; 49 patients over 52 weeks) and the meta-analysis pooling them (n = 130).
cards.result: Neither trial found a significant effect on its primary global endpoint or on neuropsychiatric symptoms; the pooled analysis found no significant benefit on any efficacy outcome, and the largest trial recorded more cognitive adverse events on memantine (6 versus 1 patient). PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — a well-conducted negative evidence base, shelved as such: the correct clinical reading is that memantine is not supported in frontotemporal dementia.
cards.watchOut: Negative here means no demonstrated average benefit in behavioural-variant FTD and semantic dementia as trialled; the trials do not address other FTD syndromes (such as primary progressive aphasia variants beyond semantic dementia) or memantine combined with other drugs.

shelves.title: SSRIs and trazodone in frontotemporal dementia: trazodone improved behaviour scores in one 26-patient crossover trial; paroxetine did not in a 10-patient blinded trial and impaired some cognitive measures — a thin, split evidence base
shelves.question: In frontotemporal dementia, do SSRIs or trazodone improve behavioural symptoms versus placebo or usual care?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Cross-Over Studies · Dementia/drug therapy,psychology · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neuropsychological Tests · Personality Inventory · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Trazodone/adverse effects,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: SPLIT (drug) — on a thin base that this shelf prints on its face: the entire double-blind primary evidence is two small crossover trials totalling 36 patients. For trazodone, Lebert 2004 (randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover; 26 evaluable patients) found a significant decrease in neuropsychiatric inventory (NPI) total score on trazodone (p = 0.028), with more than 50% NPI improvement in 10 patients, driven by irritability, agitation, depressive symptoms and eating disorders, and no change in MMSE. For paroxetine, the rigorous test was negative: Deakin 2004 (double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover; N = 10 patients) found no significant differences on the NPI or the Cambridge Behavioral Inventory, and paroxetine decreased accuracy on paired-associates learning, reversal learning and delayed pattern recognition. An open randomised study (Moretti 2003) reported behavioural improvement and reduced caregiver stress on paroxetine over 14 months, but with only 8 patients per arm (paroxetine versus piracetam) and no blinding it is described here in prose only and is not carded. The systematic review of the field (Nardell & Tampi 2014; 9 double-blind randomised trials across all FTD drug classes) concludes SSRIs and trazodone may reduce some behavioural symptoms, that none of the medications improved cognition, and that all were well tolerated. PROPOSED SPLIT (drug): a possible trazodone benefit for behaviour, an unproven and possibly cognitively costly paroxetine — neither established, both resting on very small trials.

cards.headline: Lebert 2004: trazodone significantly reduced neuropsychiatric inventory scores (p = 0.028) in a double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial — N = 26 evaluable patients with FTD
cards.summary: Lebert 2004: trazodone significantly reduced neuropsychiatric inventory scores (p = 0.028) in a double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial — N = 26 evaluable patients with FTD
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial (Lebert 2004) — N = 26 evaluable
cards.people: Patients with frontotemporal dementia in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study of trazodone; 26 patients were evaluable. Outcomes were the neuropsychiatric inventory (NPI) and the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE). The record does not state the trazodone dose.
cards.result: There was a significant decrease in the NPI total score with trazodone (p = 0.028) in the 26 evaluable patients; a decrease of more than 50% in the NPI score was observed in 10 patients on trazodone. The improvement was based mainly on four items: irritability, agitation, depressive symptoms and eating disorders. The MMSE was not modified, and trazodone was well tolerated. The authors describe this as the first placebo-controlled trial of trazodone in FTD and conclude it is an effective treatment for FTD behavioural symptoms.
cards.watchOut: N = 26 evaluable patients in a crossover design is the whole blinded evidence base for trazodone in FTD: crossover carry-over, the small sample, and an outcome (NPI total) assembled from caregiver report all argue for treating the significant p-value as a signal to confirm, not a settled effect — and the record does not report the total number originally enrolled, only the 26 evaluable.
cards.source: Lebert F et al. Frontotemporal dementia: a randomised, controlled trial with trazodone. Dementia and geriatric cognitive disorders. 2004. PMID: 15178953. cards.headline: Deakin 2004: paroxetine (up to 40 mg/day) made no difference to behaviour scores in a double-blind crossover trial — N = 10 patients — and impaired paired-associates learning, reversal learning and delayed pattern recognition
cards.summary: Deakin 2004: paroxetine (up to 40 mg/day) made no difference to behaviour scores in a double-blind crossover trial — N = 10 patients — and impaired paired-associates learning, reversal learning and delayed pattern recognition
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial (Deakin 2004) — N = 10
cards.people: 10 subjects meeting consensus criteria for frontotemporal dementia (frontal variant), entered into a double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial; paroxetine doses were progressively increased to 40 mg daily, with an identical regimen for placebo capsules, and assessments (cognitive battery, caregiver neuropsychiatric inventory [NPI] interview, Cambridge Behavioral Inventory) were made in the sixth week of each treatment period.
cards.result: There were no significant differences on the NPI or the Cambridge Behavioral Inventory between paroxetine and placebo — the treatment made no difference to behavioural symptoms. Paroxetine caused a decrease in accuracy on the paired associates learning task, reversal learning and a delayed pattern recognition task, with no changes on decision-making, spatial span, spatial recognition, spatial working memory, digit span or verbal fluency. The authors conclude there is no evidence for the efficacy of paroxetine in frontal-variant FTD and that chronic paroxetine may selectively impair some cognitive functions.
cards.watchOut: N = 10 is the smallest trial size this library cards, and a null in 10 patients cannot exclude a modest benefit; the cognitive-impairment findings, however, come from the same blinded comparison and are the trial's most distinctive result — small numbers cut both ways and are printed on the face for that reason.
cards.source: Deakin JB et al. Paroxetine does not improve symptoms and impairs cognition in frontotemporal dementia: a double-blind randomized controlled trial. Psychopharmacology. 2004. cards.headline: Nardell & Tampi 2014: across all 9 double-blind randomised trials in frontotemporal dementia, SSRIs and trazodone 'may be effective' for some behavioural symptoms — and no medication improved cognition
cards.summary: Nardell & Tampi 2014: across all 9 double-blind randomised trials in frontotemporal dementia, SSRIs and trazodone 'may be effective' for some behavioural symptoms — and no medication improved cognition
cards.type: Systematic review of 9 randomised controlled trials (Nardell & Tampi 2014)
cards.people: Systematic review of pharmacological treatments for frontotemporal dementias from randomised controlled trials, searching PubMed, Medline, PsycINFO and the Cochrane database; 9 randomised, double-blind clinical trials were found — 2 used the SSRI paroxetine, 1 used trazodone, 2 used stimulants, 1 used galantamine, 2 used memantine and 1 used oxytocin.
cards.result: The review's analysis indicates that SSRIs, trazodone and the amphetamines may be effective in reducing some behavioural symptoms in frontotemporal dementia, but none of these medications had an impact on cognition. Available data indicate the medications were well tolerated in all the trials.
cards.watchOut: The review's cautious 'may be effective' pools open and blinded paroxetine reports together at the class level; the blinded paroxetine trial carded above is the negative one, so the class-level sentence is more optimistic than the blinded evidence for paroxetine specifically — the split on this shelf is by drug, not by class.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one small positive trazodone trial, one small negative paroxetine trial with a cognitive-harm signal — a split, thin base of 36 blinded-trial patients
cards.summary: Synthesis: one small positive trazodone trial, one small negative paroxetine trial with a cognitive-harm signal — a split, thin base of 36 blinded-trial patients
cards.people: The carded primary evidence: two double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trials — trazodone (26 evaluable patients) and paroxetine (N = 10) — plus the systematic review of all 9 double-blind FTD drug trials. A further open randomised paroxetine study (8 patients per arm) is described in the balance prose only and is not carded.
cards.result: Trazodone: significant NPI total-score reduction (p = 0.028), with >50% improvement in 10 of 26 evaluable patients. Paroxetine: no significant behavioural difference versus placebo, with decreased accuracy on three cognitive tasks. The field's systematic review judges SSRIs and trazodone possibly effective for some behavioural symptoms and ineffective for cognition. PROPOSED SPLIT (drug): POSSIBLE (benefit) for trazodone on behaviour; (the treatment made no difference) for paroxetine on behaviour, with a cognitive cost signal — all on very small numbers, printed on the face.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-six patients across the two blinded trials is the entire placebo-controlled base for this question; any stronger wording than the split proposed here — in either direction — would overstate what these trials can bear.

shelves.title: Mediterranean diet and cognition: in the one trial programme (PREDIMED), older adults at high vascular risk scored better on cognitive tests after 4–6.5 years than controls on a low-fat diet — a single-programme signal
shelves.question: Does a Mediterranean diet slow cognitive decline in older adults versus a control diet?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Cognition · Cognition Disorders/diet therapy,prevention & control · Diet, Mediterranean · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neuropsychological Tests
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), single programme — every carded report comes from PREDIMED (ISRCTN35739639), one Spanish trial programme in older adults at high cardiovascular risk, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE however consistent the substudies look. In the Barcelona cognition substudy (Valls-Pedret 2015; 447 enrolled, 334 retested after a median 4.1 years), the control group declined on all composites (global cognition change −0.38 z) while the Mediterranean-diet-plus-olive-oil group held steady (+0.05; p = 0.005 versus controls) and the nuts group scored better on the memory composite (+0.09 versus −0.17; p = 0.04 versus controls). In the Navarra centre (Martínez-Lapiscina 2013; 522 assessed after 6.5 years), both Mediterranean groups scored higher than control on the Mini-Mental State Examination (adjusted differences +0.62 points for olive oil, p = 0.005, and +0.57 for nuts, p = 0.015) and the Clock Drawing Test. A smaller Navarra subsample (285 participants) found lower odds of mild cognitive impairment with the olive-oil diet (OR 0.34, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.97) but no significant difference for the nuts group on most domains. This shelf does not duplicate the MIND-diet home (shelf-2468): the MIND diet is a different dietary pattern tested in a different trial whose primary result was null, and no PREDIMED cognition report is carded there. The honest summary: within one trial programme, assignment to a supplemented Mediterranean diet was followed by less cognitive decline than advice to reduce dietary fat; there is no second programme and no dementia-incidence endpoint in the carded reports.

cards.headline: Valls-Pedret 2015 (PREDIMED, Barcelona): controls declined on global cognition (−0.38 z over a median 4.1 years) while the Mediterranean diet plus olive oil group did not (+0.05; p = 0.005 versus control)
cards.summary: Valls-Pedret 2015 (PREDIMED, Barcelona): controls declined on global cognition (−0.38 z over a median 4.1 years) while the Mediterranean diet plus olive oil group did not (+0.05; p = 0.005 versus control)
cards.people: 447 cognitively healthy volunteers at high cardiovascular risk in Barcelona, Spain (mean age 66.9 years; 52.1% women), randomised to a Mediterranean diet supplemented with extra-virgin olive oil (1 L/week), a Mediterranean diet supplemented with mixed nuts (30 g/day), or a control diet (advice to reduce dietary fat); 334 had follow-up neuropsychological testing after a median 4.1 years.
cards.result: Adjusted changes from baseline in the global cognition composite were +0.05 (95% CI −0.11 to 0.21; p = 0.005 versus controls) for Mediterranean diet plus olive oil, −0.05 (−0.27 to 0.18) for Mediterranean diet plus nuts, and −0.38 (−0.57 to −0.18) for controls; all composites declined significantly from baseline in controls. The memory composite changed by +0.04 with olive oil, +0.09 with nuts (p = 0.04 versus controls) and −0.17 in controls; the frontal composite changed by +0.23 with olive oil (p = 0.003 versus controls), +0.03 with nuts and −0.33 in controls. The authors conclude a Mediterranean diet supplemented with olive oil or nuts is associated with improved cognitive function.
cards.watchOut: A substudy of one trial programme: 334 of 447 enrolled participants had follow-up testing, the intervention was unblinded dietary advice plus free olive oil or nuts, and the outcomes are test-score composites, not dementia diagnoses.
cards.source: Valls-Pedret C et al. Mediterranean Diet and Age-Related Cognitive Decline: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA internal medicine. 2015. PMID: 25961184. Registry ID: ISRCTN35739639. cards.headline: Martínez-Lapiscina 2013 (PREDIMED-NAVARRA): after 6.5 years both Mediterranean diet groups scored higher than the low-fat control group on the MMSE (+0.62 and +0.57 adjusted points)
cards.summary: Martínez-Lapiscina 2013 (PREDIMED-NAVARRA): after 6.5 years both Mediterranean diet groups scored higher than the low-fat control group on the MMSE (+0.62 and +0.57 adjusted points)
cards.people: 522 participants at high vascular risk in the Navarra centre of PREDIMED (44.6% men; mean age 74.6 years at cognitive evaluation), randomised to a Mediterranean diet supplemented with extra-virgin olive oil, a Mediterranean diet supplemented with mixed nuts, or a low-fat control diet; cognition assessed once, after 6.5 years of intervention, by blinded assessors.
cards.result: Adjusted mean Mini-Mental State Examination scores were higher in the Mediterranean diet plus olive oil group (adjusted difference versus control +0.62 points, 95% CI +0.18 to +1.05; p = 0.005) and the Mediterranean diet plus nuts group (+0.57, +0.11 to +1.03; p = 0.015); Clock Drawing Test differences were +0.51 (p = 0.001) and +0.33 (p = 0.048) respectively. Results were unchanged after controlling for incident depression. The authors conclude the intervention appears to improve cognition compared with a low-fat diet.
cards.watchOut: Same trial programme as the other cards on this shelf — not independent replication. Cognition was measured at a single post-intervention visit rather than as change from a baseline battery in this report.
cards.source: Martínez-Lapiscina EH et al. Mediterranean diet improves cognition: the PREDIMED-NAVARRA randomised trial. Journal of neurology, neurosurgery, and psychiatry. 2013. PMID: 23670794. cards.headline: Martínez-Lapiscina 2013 (Navarra subsample, 285 participants): the olive-oil Mediterranean diet group had lower odds of mild cognitive impairment than controls (OR 0.34), the nuts group did not differ significantly
cards.summary: Martínez-Lapiscina 2013 (Navarra subsample, 285 participants): the olive-oil Mediterranean diet group had lower odds of mild cognitive impairment than controls (OR 0.34), the nuts group did not differ significantly
cards.people: A random subsample of 285 PREDIMED-NAVARRA participants (95 per group; 44.8% men; mean age 74.1 years at cognitive evaluation), all at high vascular risk, assessed after 6.5 years by two neurologists blinded to group assignment; cognitive status (normal, mild cognitive impairment, dementia) was a secondary outcome.
cards.result: The Mediterranean diet plus extra-virgin olive oil group performed significantly better across fluency and memory tasks and had lower odds of mild cognitive impairment than controls (OR 0.34, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.97) after adjustment; the Mediterranean diet plus nuts group did not differ from controls, and differences were non-significant for most cognitive domains. The authors conclude a long-term olive-oil-rich Mediterranean diet resulted in better cognitive function than a control diet, with most domain differences non-significant.
cards.watchOut: Small subsample (95 per arm) with wide confidence intervals; the mild-cognitive-impairment finding rests on the olive-oil arm only and was a secondary outcome.
cards.source: Martínez-Lapiscina EH et al. Virgin olive oil supplementation and long-term cognition: the PREDIMED-NAVARRA randomized trial. The journal of nutrition, health & aging. 2013. shelves.title: Hearing intervention and falls: the ACHIEVE randomised trial's secondary analysis found 27% relatively fewer falls over 3 years with hearing aids and counselling; the wider hearing-loss-and-falls literature is observational
shelves.question: Do hearing aids reduce falls in older adults with hearing loss?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Accidental Falls/prevention & control,statistics & numerical data · Aged · Female · Male · Aged, 80 and over · Hearing Loss/therapy · Hearing Aids · United States
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). The only randomised evidence on the aids themselves is a secondary analysis of ACHIEVE (Goman 2025; 977 adults aged 70–84 with untreated hearing loss): over 3 years the hearing-intervention group (audiological counselling plus hearing aids) averaged 1.45 falls versus 1.98 in the health-education control group — a mean difference of −0.54 falls and a 27% relative reduction in the mean number of falls. Falls were a prespecified exploratory outcome, self-reported for the past 12 months at annual visits, in an unmasked trial, which is why the stamp stays at POSSIBLE. The background risk link is observational and is labelled observational on its cards: in the Health, Aging and Body Composition cohort (Kamil 2016; 2,000 adults aged 70–79, observational), moderate-or-greater hearing impairment carried a 63% higher hazard of incident frailty and a faster annual rise in the odds of falling; in a large propensity-matched claims cohort (Deal 2019, observational), incident untreated hearing loss was followed by an excess of 3.57 falls per 100 persons attributable at 10 years. Those cohorts show hearing loss marks fall risk; they do not show that aids remove it. ACHIEVE's primary cognition outcome is homed on the live ACHIEVE shelf (see also pack 6015 for quality of life and cognition) and is not re-carded here; this shelf asks only the falls question.

cards.headline: Goman 2025 (ACHIEVE secondary analysis): hearing intervention averaged 1.45 falls versus 1.98 with health-education control over 3 years — a 27% relative reduction in mean falls
cards.summary: Goman 2025 (ACHIEVE secondary analysis): hearing intervention averaged 1.45 falls versus 1.98 with health-education control over 3 years — a 27% relative reduction in mean falls
cards.people: 977 adults aged 70–84 years with untreated hearing loss and without substantial cognitive impairment, recruited at four US field sites (238 from the ARIC cohort, 739 de novo from the community; mean age 76.8 years; 54% women), randomised to a hearing intervention (audiological counselling and provision of hearing aids; n = 490) or a health-education control (n = 487), followed for 3 years.
cards.result: In adjusted intention-to-treat analyses the intervention group had a 27% relative reduction in the mean number of falls over 3 years compared with control (intervention 1.45 falls, 95% CI 1.28 to 1.61; control 1.98, 1.82 to 2.15; mean difference −0.54, 95% CI −0.77 to −0.31). The effect was consistent across the ARIC and de novo populations. Falls were a prespecified exploratory outcome, self-reported for the past 12 months at baseline and annually.
cards.watchOut: Exploratory secondary outcome of a trial designed for cognition; the trial was unmasked and falls were self-reported, so expectation and recall effects cannot be excluded. The intervention bundled counselling with the aids, so the effect cannot be credited to the devices alone.
cards.source: Goman AM et al. Effects of hearing intervention on falls in older adults: findings from a secondary analysis of the ACHIEVE randomised controlled trial. The Lancet. Public health. 2025. randomised controlled trial, secondary analysis (achieve) 977 adults aged 70–84 years with untreated hearing loss and without substantial cognitive impairment, recruited at four us field sites (238 from the aric cohort, 739 de novo from the community; mean age 76.8 years; 54% women), randomised to a hearing intervention (audiological counselling and provision of hearing aids; n = 490) or a health-education control (n = 487), followed for 3 years. in adjusted intention-to-treat analyses the intervention group had a 27% relative reduction in the mean number of falls over 3 years compared with control (intervention 1.45 falls, 95% ci 1.28 to 1.61; control 1.98, 1.82 to 2.15; mean difference −0.54, 95% ci −0.77 to −0.31). the effect was consistent across the aric and de novo populations. falls were a prespecified exploratory outcome, self-reported for the past 12 months at baseline and annually. exploratory secondary outcome of a trial designed for cognition; the trial was unmasked and falls were self-reported, so expectation and recall effects cannot be excluded. the intervention bundled counselling with the aids, so the effect cannot be credited to the devices alone. goman am et al. effects of hearing intervention on falls in older adults: findings from a secondary analysis of the achieve randomised controlled trial. the lancet. public health. 2025. pmid: 40441816. registry id: nct03243422. mesh: humans · *accidental falls/prevention & control,statistics & numerical data · aged · female · male · aged, 80 and over · *hearing loss/therapy · *hearing aids · united states

cards.headline: Kamil 2016 (observational): moderate-or-greater hearing impairment was associated with a 63% higher hazard of incident frailty and a faster rise in fall odds over time
cards.summary: Kamil 2016 (observational): moderate-or-greater hearing impairment was associated with a 63% higher hazard of incident frailty and a faster rise in fall odds over time
cards.people: Observational longitudinal analysis of 2,000 participants aged 70–79 in the Health, Aging and Body Composition study; hearing defined by pure-tone average at 0.5–4 kHz in the better ear; falls assessed annually by self-report.
cards.result: Older adults with moderate-or-greater hearing impairment had a 63% increased risk of developing frailty compared with normal-hearing individuals (adjusted HR 1.63, 95% CI 1.26 to 2.12), and hearing impairment was associated with a greater annual percent increase in odds of falling over time (9.7% per year, 95% CI 7.0 to 12.4, versus 4.4%, 2.6 to 6.2, with normal hearing). Labelled observational: this links hearing loss to falls, it does not test hearing aids.
cards.watchOut: Observational: hearing impairment may mark shared causes of falling (ageing, vascular disease, frailty) rather than cause falls directly, and hearing-aid use was not the exposure studied.
cards.source: Kamil RJ et al. Association of Hearing Impairment With Incident Frailty and Falls in Older Adults. Journal of aging and health. 2016. PMID: 26438083. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Deal 2019 (observational): incident untreated hearing loss was followed by more falls — an attributable excess of 3.57 per 100 persons at 10 years in a matched claims cohort
cards.summary: Deal 2019 (observational): incident untreated hearing loss was followed by more falls — an attributable excess of 3.57 per 100 persons at 10 years in a matched claims cohort
cards.people: Observational retrospective propensity-matched cohort from US administrative claims (commercial and Medicare Advantage members aged 50 or older with incident hearing loss defined by claims and no hearing-device use), observed for 2 years (n = 154,414), 5 years (n = 44,852) and 10 years (n = 4,728); mean age 64 years, 48% women.
cards.result: The absolute risk of falls was greater in persons with hearing loss than without at all time points; the 10-year risk attributable to hearing loss was 3.57 per 100 persons (95% CI 1.76 to 5.47) for falls, alongside 3.20 per 100 for dementia and 6.88 per 100 for depression. Labelled observational: untreated hearing loss is the exposure, so this card supports the risk link, not an aid benefit.
cards.watchOut: Claims-based and observational: hearing loss was defined by billing claims, falls by claims for accidental falls, and residual confounding is likely despite propensity matching.
cards.source: Deal JA et al. Incident Hearing Loss and Comorbidity: A Longitudinal Administrative Claims Study. JAMA otolaryngology-- head & neck surgery. 2019. PMID: 30419134. cards.headline: Synthesis: one randomised secondary analysis favours hearing intervention for falls; the cohort evidence is observational and shows risk, not remedy — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: one randomised secondary analysis favours hearing intervention for falls; the cohort evidence is observational and shows risk, not remedy — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.people: Randomised evidence: 977 ACHIEVE participants. Observational evidence: 2,000 Health ABC participants and a matched claims cohort of up to 154,414 people.
cards.result: The randomised signal (−0.54 mean falls over 3 years; 27% relative reduction) is real but exploratory, unmasked and based on self-report, and the intervention included counselling as well as aids. The observational cards establish that hearing loss travels with falls and frailty; they cannot establish that aids prevent falls. PROPOSED STAMP: POSSIBLE (benefit), with the observational component capped and labelled. ACHIEVE's cognition outcome stays homed on its own shelf.
cards.watchOut: A dedicated falls-primary randomised trial of hearing aids does not exist in the carded record; do not present the cohort associations as treatment effects.

shelves.title: Cerebral autoregulation and ageing (physiology): dynamic autoregulation is preserved in healthy ageing while carbon-dioxide reactivity falls; after acute stroke dynamic autoregulation is impaired in both hemispheres — the physiological case for caution with abrupt blood-pressure lowering
shelves.question: How do cerebral autoregulation and cerebrovascular reactivity change with normal ageing in healthy humans, and what does that imply for blood-pressure lowering after stroke?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Age Factors · Aged · Aging/physiology · Blood Pressure/physiology · Brain/blood supply,physiology · Cerebrovascular Circulation/physiology · Female · Heart/physiology · Homeostasis/physiology · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pressoreceptors/physiology · Ultrasonography, Doppler, Transcranial
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology; Boron and Boulpaep Medical Physiology): cerebral blood flow is held near-constant across a range of arterial pressures by autoregulation, and flow is exquisitely sensitive to arterial carbon dioxide — this is the textbook's account, and the carded human studies test what ageing and stroke do to it. The human data are concordant. Dynamic autoregulation does NOT decline with healthy ageing: Carey 2000 (27 young versus 27 older adults, matched for sex and systolic pressure) found identical autoregulatory indices (4.9 versus 5.0 across all stimuli) even though cardiac baroreceptor sensitivity was halved in the older group (8.6 versus 16.9 ms/mm Hg); Dineen 2011 (30 volunteers of mean age 25 versus 30 of mean age 64, studied through hypercapnia and hypocapnia) likewise found no age difference in the autoregulatory index, though flow velocity and its change with respiratory manoeuvres were greater in the young. Cerebrovascular reactivity DOES fall: Lipsitz 2000 (10 young, 10 healthy elderly, 10 treated hypertensive elderly) found carbon-dioxide reactivity of 0.19 in the young versus 0.14 in normotensive elderly and 0.11 in hypertensive elderly (p < 0.05), while the flow-velocity fall on standing was actually smaller in the older groups — autoregulation retained, vasodilator reserve reduced. After acute ischaemic stroke the picture reverses: Dawson 2000 (61 patients within 96 hours versus 54 matched controls) found dynamic autoregulation significantly impaired in BOTH hemispheres (indices 4.1 affected, 4.8 unaffected, 6.2 in controls) while static autoregulation was preserved. Implication, stated as physiology rather than a treatment verdict: a healthy older brain still defends its flow against pressure swings, which is why chronic blood-pressure lowering is generally tolerated; an acutely infarcted brain has lost dynamic defence in both hemispheres, which is the physiological reason acute post-stroke blood-pressure management is cautious about abrupt drops. Treatment thresholds themselves belong to the stroke-treatment shelves, not to this physiology shelf.

cards.headline: Carey 2000: dynamic cerebral autoregulation was identical in young and older adults (index 4.9 versus 5.0) even though baroreceptor sensitivity was halved by age
cards.summary: Carey 2000: dynamic cerebral autoregulation was identical in young and older adults (index 4.9 versus 5.0) even though baroreceptor sensitivity was halved by age
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (transcranial Doppler, young versus older adults)
cards.people: 27 young subjects (40 years or under; mean age 29) and 27 older subjects (55 or over; mean age 68), matched for sex and systolic blood pressure, studied with transcranial Doppler cerebral blood flow velocity and beat-to-beat arterial pressure during induced and spontaneous pressure stimuli; N = 54 printed on the face of this physiology card.
cards.result: Cardiac baroreceptor sensitivity was reduced in the older group (8.6 ± 4.5 versus 16.9 ± 8.8 ms/mm Hg; p < 0.0001), but no age-related differences were demonstrated in step-response plots or autoregulatory index values for any pressor or depressor stimulus (p = 0.62), with mean indices for all stimuli combined of 4.9 ± 1.8 (young) and 5.0 ± 2.3 (older). The authors conclude dynamic cerebral autoregulation is unaffected by ageing.
cards.watchOut: A laboratory study of healthy volunteers (N = 54) using induced pressure transients; it measures the dynamic response over seconds, not flow during sustained clinical hypotension or drug treatment.
cards.source: Carey BJ et al. Dynamic cerebral autoregulation is unaffected by aging. Stroke. 2000. PMID: 11108745. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Lipsitz 2000: carbon-dioxide reactivity was lower in elderly subjects (0.14 normotensive, 0.11 hypertensive) than in the young (0.19), while autoregulation on standing was retained
cards.summary: Lipsitz 2000: carbon-dioxide reactivity was lower in elderly subjects (0.14 normotensive, 0.11 hypertensive) than in the young (0.19), while autoregulation on standing was retained
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (transcranial Doppler, ageing and hypertension)
cards.people: 10 healthy young subjects (age 24 ± 1 years), 10 healthy elderly subjects (72 ± 3 years) and 10 previously treated hypertensive elderly subjects (72 ± 2 years), studied with continuous middle cerebral artery flow velocity and Finapres arterial pressure during standing, sitting and carbon-dioxide rebreathing; N = 30 printed on the face of this physiology card (classic small physiology study).
cards.result: Mean arterial pressure fell similarly in all groups on standing (by 21–26 mm Hg within 30 seconds), but mean flow velocity fell significantly less in the older subjects (−4.7 ± 0.7 cm/s hypertensive, −5.3 ± 1.2 normotensive) than in the young (−10.1 ± 1.1 cm/s; p < 0.05). Carbon-dioxide reactivity (slope of cerebrovascular conductance against end-expiratory CO2) was greater in the young (0.19 ± 0.01) than in normotensive elderly (0.14 ± 0.01) and hypertensive elderly (0.11 ± 0.02) subjects (p < 0.05 for both comparisons). The authors conclude elderly normotensive and treated hypertensive subjects retain cerebral autoregulation despite reduced CO2 reactivity.
cards.watchOut: Very small groups (10 per group) — carded under the physiology rule for classic primary human studies with the N printed on the face; the hypertension group was previously treated, so untreated hypertension may behave differently.
cards.source: Lipsitz LA et al. Dynamic regulation of middle cerebral artery blood flow velocity in aging and hypertension. Stroke. 2000. PMID: 10926954. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Dineen 2011: through hypercapnia and hypocapnia, the autoregulatory index did not differ between volunteers of mean age 25 and mean age 64, though flow velocity responses were larger in the young
cards.summary: Dineen 2011: through hypercapnia and hypocapnia, the autoregulatory index did not differ between volunteers of mean age 25 and mean age 64, though flow velocity responses were larger in the young
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (transcranial Doppler with CO2 manoeuvres)
cards.people: 30 younger volunteers (mean age 25 ± 6 years) and 30 older volunteers (mean age 64 ± 4 years), studied with transcranial Doppler flow velocity, Finapres pressure and capnography during breath-hold hypercapnia and hyperventilation hypocapnia, with autoregulation calculated by a moving-window autoregressive method; N = 60 printed on the face of this physiology card.
cards.result: Cerebral blood flow velocity was higher, and its change with the respiratory manoeuvres significantly greater, in the younger group, but no difference in the autoregulatory index (ARMA-ARI) was found between the groups. The authors conclude cerebral autoregulation is not affected by healthy ageing, even when assessed across changing carbon-dioxide levels — the condition under which an age effect was most likely to appear.
cards.watchOut: Healthy volunteers and short laboratory manoeuvres; an intact autoregulatory index does not mean identical cerebrovascular reserve, as the same study's smaller flow-velocity responses in the older group show.
cards.source: Dineen NE et al. Effects of ageing on cerebral haemodynamics assessed during respiratory manoeuvres. Age and ageing. 2011. PMID: 21273209. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Dawson 2000: within 96 hours of ischaemic stroke, dynamic autoregulation was impaired in both hemispheres (indices 4.1 and 4.8 versus 6.2 in controls) while static autoregulation was preserved
cards.summary: Dawson 2000: within 96 hours of ischaemic stroke, dynamic autoregulation was impaired in both hemispheres (indices 4.1 and 4.8 versus 6.2 in controls) while static autoregulation was preserved
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (acute stroke patients versus matched controls)
cards.people: 61 patients with ischaemic stroke studied within 96 hours of onset and 54 age- and sex-matched controls, assessed with transcranial Doppler and non-invasive pressure manipulation (thigh-cuff release for dynamic autoregulation; isometric handgrip and thigh-cuff inflation for static autoregulation); N = 115 printed on the face of this physiology card.
cards.result: There was no difference in static or dynamic indices between stroke subtypes. Combining subtypes, dynamic autoregulation was significantly impaired in both the affected and the non-affected hemisphere compared with controls (mean autoregulation index 4.1 ± 3.3 affected, 4.8 ± 3.1 unaffected, 6.2 ± 2.3 controls; p < 0.05), while static autoregulation did not differ significantly. The authors conclude dynamic but not static autoregulation is globally impaired in acute ischaemic stroke, with implications for post-stroke prognosis and blood-pressure management.
cards.watchOut: A physiological measurement study, not a blood-pressure-treatment trial: it establishes that the acute post-stroke brain defends flow poorly against rapid pressure changes, which informs — but does not by itself set — treatment thresholds.
cards.source: Dawson SL et al. Dynamic but not static cerebral autoregulation is impaired in acute ischaemic stroke. Cerebrovascular diseases. 2000. PMID: 10686451. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: preserved dynamic autoregulation and reduced CO2 reactivity with healthy ageing; globally impaired dynamic autoregulation after acute stroke — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED
cards.summary: Synthesis: preserved dynamic autoregulation and reduced CO2 reactivity with healthy ageing; globally impaired dynamic autoregulation after acute stroke — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED
cards.people: Carded human data: 54 + 30 + 60 healthy volunteers across the ageing studies and 115 participants (61 acute stroke patients, 54 controls) in the post-stroke study, all primary transcranial-Doppler physiology.
cards.result: Three ageing studies using different stimuli (pressure transients, standing, CO2 manoeuvres) agree that dynamic autoregulation survives healthy ageing while cerebrovascular reactivity to carbon dioxide declines; the post-stroke study shows the autoregulatory failure ageing does not cause. This matches the textbook account of autoregulation and CO2 reactivity in Guyton and Hall and in Boron and Boulpaep, which frame this shelf. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. The Aries post-stroke autoregulation literature is a review-level synthesis of this same primary literature and is consistent with the carded Dawson data.
cards.watchOut: Physiology, not prescribing: how far and how fast to lower blood pressure after stroke is decided by the treatment trials on their own shelves; this shelf supplies the mechanism that makes those trials' caution intelligible.
cards.source: Synthesis of Carey BJ et al. Stroke. 2000 (PMID: 11108745); Lipsitz LA et al. Stroke. 2000 (PMID: 10926954); Dineen NE et al. Age and ageing. 2011 (PMID: 21273209); Dawson SL et al. Cerebrovascular diseases. 2000 (PMID: 10686451). shelves.title: Daridorexant and next-day functioning: daytime scores (IDSIQ) improved at 50 mg across the phase 3 programme's secondary analyses — but by less than the questionnaire's own meaningful-change threshold, and 25 mg was inconsistent
shelves.question: In adults with insomnia, does daridorexant improve next-day functioning (not just sleep onset and maintenance) versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders/drug therapy · Sleepiness · Patient Reported Outcome Measures · Orexin Receptor Antagonists · Treatment Outcome · Humans · Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — this pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #572 already answers the sleep onset and maintenance question for daridorexant and lemborexant versus placebo and a Z-drug, and its primary phase 3 report (Mignot 2022) is homed there and is not re-carded here. What #572 does not do is answer the daytime question in its own right; its balance notes only that daytime gains were clearest at 50 mg. The dedicated daytime reports — all secondary, post-hoc or extension analyses of that same programme (Studies 1 and 2, NCT03545191 and NCT03575104) — agree on a dose pattern: daridorexant 50 mg improved Insomnia Daytime Symptoms and Impacts Questionnaire (IDSIQ) total and domain scores versus placebo from the first weeks, in older and younger adults alike, and the improvement was maintained through a 40-week extension (least-squares mean advantage −9.3 to −9.5 IDSIQ points at weeks 12–36); pooled dose–response analysis found a significant linear dose–response for IDSIQ total score with no dose–response for adverse events. Two cautions cap the stamp. First, the programme's own anchor-based analysis puts the within-patient change patients consider meaningful at 17 IDSIQ total points — larger than the average between-group advantage observed. Second, 25 mg was inconsistent (daytime benefit only in younger adults in the age analysis) and morning-sleepiness visual-analogue gains in the quarter-of-night analysis were numerical rankings rather than tested differences. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: a real, dose-dependent daytime signal at 50 mg, of modest average size, resting entirely on secondary analyses of a single programme.

cards.headline: Age analysis of Study 1 (Fietze 2022): daridorexant 50 mg improved IDSIQ daytime scores in both older and younger adults; 25 mg improved them only in younger adults
cards.summary: Age analysis of Study 1 (Fietze 2022): daridorexant 50 mg improved IDSIQ daytime scores in both older and younger adults; 25 mg improved them only in younger adults
cards.type: Secondary (age-subgroup) analysis of a randomised placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (Study 1)
cards.people: Secondary analysis by age of the phase 3 Study 1 (930 adults with insomnia disorder randomised to daridorexant 50 mg, 25 mg or placebo nightly for 3 months): 364 participants aged 65 or older and 566 younger than 65. Daytime functioning was assessed with the IDSIQ; the record prints no IDSIQ point differences for this analysis, so none are printed here.
cards.result: Daridorexant 50 mg progressively improved IDSIQ total and all domain scores from week 1 onwards, similarly in both age groups; daridorexant 25 mg improved IDSIQ scores only in younger adults. Night-time effects at 50 mg were similar by age (wake after sleep onset reduced by 19.6 minutes in older versus 17.4 minutes in younger patients at month 3, versus placebo). Adverse-event incidence was comparable to placebo in both age groups, with fewer falls on daridorexant, and morning sleepiness scores improved in both groups.
cards.watchOut: A subgroup analysis of one trial, reported qualitatively for the daytime endpoint: it establishes the dose pattern (50 mg works in both ages, 25 mg does not in older adults) but not the size of the daytime effect.
cards.source: Fietze I et al. Efficacy and Safety of Daridorexant in Older and Younger Adults with Insomnia Disorder: A Secondary Analysis of a Randomised Placebo-Controlled Trial. Drugs & aging. 2022. PMID: 36098936. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03545191. cards.headline: Extension study (Kunz 2023): over 40 further weeks, daridorexant 50 mg held a −9.3 to −9.5 point IDSIQ advantage over placebo, with no next-morning sleepiness signal
cards.summary: Extension study (Kunz 2023): over 40 further weeks, daridorexant 50 mg held a −9.3 to −9.5 point IDSIQ advantage over placebo, with no next-morning sleepiness signal
cards.type: Randomised double-blind extension study (40 weeks) of the phase 3 programme
cards.people: Double-blind 40-week extension of the two phase 3 studies: 804 adults with insomnia disorder enrolled (801 dosed; 550 completed); patients on daridorexant stayed on their dose and placebo patients were re-randomised to daridorexant 25 mg or placebo. Daytime functioning (IDSIQ) was an exploratory endpoint.
cards.result: Daridorexant 50 mg, compared with placebo, decreased (improved) IDSIQ total scores by a least-squares mean of −9.3 points (95% CI −15.1 to −3.6) at extension week 12, −9.5 (−15.4 to −3.5) at week 24 and −9.1 (−15.6 to −2.7) at week 36, and increased self-reported total sleep time by about 16–20 minutes. Overall treatment-emergent adverse-event incidence was similar across groups (35–40%); daridorexant did not induce next-morning sleepiness, and no withdrawal symptoms or rebound were seen on discontinuation.
cards.watchOut: Extension volunteers are phase 3 completers who tolerated the drug — a selected population — and the daytime endpoint was exploratory, not a primary outcome. The ~9-point average advantage is below the 17-point within-patient meaningful-change threshold on the card below.
cards.source: Kunz D et al. Long-Term Safety and Tolerability of Daridorexant in Patients with Insomnia Disorder. CNS drugs. 2023. PMID: 36484969. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03679884. cards.headline: Quarter-of-night analysis (Dauvilliers 2025): daridorexant cut wakefulness in every quarter of the night, while morning sleepiness and daytime alertness scores ranked 50 mg > 25 mg > placebo without tested differences
cards.summary: Quarter-of-night analysis (Dauvilliers 2025): daridorexant cut wakefulness in every quarter of the night, while morning sleepiness and daytime alertness scores ranked 50 mg > 25 mg > placebo without tested differences
cards.type: Post-hoc analysis of a randomised placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (Study 1)
cards.people: Post-hoc analysis of Study 1 data from 930 patients with insomnia disorder randomised to daridorexant 50 mg (n = 310), 25 mg (n = 310) or placebo (n = 310) for 3 months, examining wake after sleep onset by 2-hour quarter of the night and daily visual-analogue scores for next-morning sleepiness, daytime alertness and ability to function.
cards.result: Both doses significantly reduced wake after sleep onset versus placebo in quarters 2, 3 and 4 at months 1 and 3 (least-squares differences −3.3 to −8.5 minutes). Visual-analogue scores for next-morning sleepiness, daytime alertness and ability to function improved from day 1 in all groups including placebo, with treatment numerically ranked daridorexant 50 mg > 25 mg > placebo; no significant correlations were found between night-time wakefulness and any of the three daytime scores.
cards.watchOut: The daytime visual-analogue results are numerical rankings, not demonstrated differences — placebo patients also improved from day 1. This card supports 'no next-day penalty' more strongly than 'better next-day functioning'.

cards.headline: Dose–response analysis (Luyet 2024): across 2,153 patients, the IDSIQ daytime score showed a significant linear dose–response — and adverse events showed none
cards.summary: Dose–response analysis (Luyet 2024): across 2,153 patients, the IDSIQ daytime score showed a significant linear dose–response — and adverse events showed none
cards.type: Pooled dose–response analysis of phase 2 and phase 3 trials (meta-analysis)
cards.people: Pooled dose–response analysis of one phase 2 study and the two phase 3 studies (2,153 patients; daridorexant 5–50 mg or placebo), using linear regression and a two-stage meta-analysis; the IDSIQ endpoint uses phase 3 data only.
cards.result: Dose–response relationships were significant for all efficacy endpoints, including IDSIQ total score (p < 0.01 by both approaches), and were linear across the observed dose range. No significant dose–response was observed for total adverse events or for somnolence/fatigue events (p > 0.05; p = 0.369 without the linearity assumption), whose incidence was low at all doses. The authors conclude the data support 50 mg as the preferred dose.
cards.watchOut: A dose–response across pooled studies confirms the 50 mg daytime signal is dose-related; it does not add an independent population — the same trial participants recur across every card on this shelf.
cards.source: Luyet PP et al. Dose-response of daridorexant in insomnia disorder: An analysis of Phase 2 and 3 studies. Sleep medicine. 2024. PMID: 39047305. cards.headline: The yardstick (Phillips-Beyer 2023): patients rate a 17-point IDSIQ total improvement as meaningful — larger than the average drug–placebo difference
cards.summary: The yardstick (Phillips-Beyer 2023): patients rate a 17-point IDSIQ total improvement as meaningful — larger than the average drug–placebo difference
cards.type: Anchor-based psychometric analysis of phase 3 trial data (Study 1)
cards.people: Anchor-based meaningful-change analysis of Study 1 data from 930 adults aged 18–88 with insomnia, relating IDSIQ score changes to patient global assessments of daytime and night-time symptoms. This card is the measurement yardstick for the shelf, not a treatment comparison.
cards.result: Meaningful within-patient change was estimated at 17 points for the IDSIQ total score, 9 points for the Alert/Cognition domain and 4 points each for the Mood and Sleepiness domains. Correlations between IDSIQ changes and the anchor instruments were 0.36–0.44 at month 1 and 0.45–0.57 at month 3, supporting the questionnaire's sensitivity to changes patients notice.
cards.watchOut: A within-patient threshold is not the same as a between-group difference — groups can differ meaningfully on average while few individuals cross 17 points, and the reverse. It is carded so readers can judge the size of the effects above for themselves.

shelves.title: Cerebral autoregulation in healthy humans (physiology): flow stays roughly constant across a mean arterial pressure of about 60–150 mm Hg on the Lassen plot, with the lower limit near 60 mm Hg — a textbook range the modern human studies defend dynamically, though the exact limits vary between individuals
shelves.question: In healthy humans, over what arterial-pressure range does cerebral blood flow stay roughly constant (cerebral autoregulation), and where is the lower limit?
shelves.mesh: Brain/physiology · *Cerebrovascular Circulation · Humans · Male · *Oxygen Consumption
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology; Boron and Boulpaep Medical Physiology): cerebral blood flow is autoregulated — held roughly constant while mean arterial pressure (MAP) varies over a wide range, conventionally about 60–150 mm Hg, and falls once pressure drops below the lower limit near 60 mm Hg. That range and lower limit are the textbook's account of Lassen's 1959 synthesis (carded here; its PubMed record carries no abstract, so the figures are presented as the Lassen/textbook account, not as numbers from a fetched abstract). The carded primary human studies defend the plateau dynamically rather than re-measuring the static curve: flow velocity was fully restored within seconds of a ~20 mm Hg pressure step in 10 awake volunteers (Aaslid 1989); the cerebrovasculature corrected falling pressure more effectively than rising pressure in 26 volunteers (gain 0.57 versus 0.31 cm/s per mm Hg; Tzeng 2010, Willie/Ainslie programme); and flow stayed unchanged when posture raised mean pressure by 22 mm Hg in 21 young adults (Geinas 2012). Two honest limits. First, the exact lower limit is individual, not a fixed 60 mm Hg for everyone — modern revalidation of Lassen's plot against post-2000 data confirms the plateau in awake humans with normal brains while stressing variation between populations. Second, premise correction: the slate named 'Numminen lower-limit reports', but no PubMed record under that author name was found in this session's searches, so no Numminen report is carded and the lower limit rests on the Lassen/textbook account plus the dynamic studies. How autoregulation changes with ageing and after stroke is a different question, homed at pack #6202, which is cross-pointed here and none of whose reports are re-carded. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (the plateau concept and approximate range are textbook-settled and concordant; the precise limits in any one person are not).

cards.headline: Lassen 1959: the founding synthesis plotted cerebral blood flow as roughly constant across a wide arterial-pressure range, falling below a lower limit — the origin of the autoregulatory plateau
cards.summary: Lassen 1959: the founding synthesis plotted cerebral blood flow as roughly constant across a wide arterial-pressure range, falling below a lower limit — the origin of the autoregulatory plateau
cards.people: A synthesis of the pre-1959 human cerebral blood flow literature (nitrous-oxide and related measurements), not a single cohort; N not documented in the record, which carries no abstract.
cards.result: Lassen's plot — as carried in Guyton and Hall and in Boron and Boulpaep — shows cerebral blood flow held roughly constant while mean arterial pressure ranges over about 60–150 mm Hg, with flow becoming pressure-passive below a lower limit near 60 mm Hg and above the upper limit. Those figures are presented here as the Lassen/textbook account: the fetched PubMed record for the 1959 review carries MeSH indexing but no abstract text from which to verify numbers, and a 2025 revalidation of the plot against contemporary data (Meng and colleagues, Anesthesia and Analgesia) confirms the plateau concept in awake humans with normal brains while noting variation between populations.
cards.watchOut: A 1959 literature synthesis, not a primary experiment, and its record has no abstract: the 60–150 mm Hg range is the textbook's account of it. Do not read the lower limit as a precise threshold for an individual patient.

cards.headline: Aaslid 1989: after a sudden ~20 mm Hg pressure step, cerebral flow was restored within seconds in awake volunteers — fastest in hypocapnia (rate of regulation 0.38/s)
cards.summary: Aaslid 1989: after a sudden ~20 mm Hg pressure step, cerebral flow was restored within seconds in awake volunteers — fastest in hypocapnia (rate of regulation 0.38/s)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (transcranial Doppler, thigh-cuff pressure steps)
cards.people: 10 normal volunteers studied awake with transcranial Doppler middle cerebral artery flow velocity and servo-cuff arterial pressure during normocapnia, hypocapnia and hypercapnia; N = 10 printed on the face of this physiology card (classic small physiology study).
cards.result: A step decrease in arterial pressure of approximately 20 mm Hg was induced by rapid thigh-cuff deflation. Full restoration of flow to the pre-test level was seen as early as 4.1 seconds after the step in hypocapnia, and more slowly in normocapnia and hypercapnia. The rate of regulation (normalised change in cerebrovascular resistance per second) was 0.38/s in hypocapnia, 0.20/s in normocapnia and 0.11/s in hypercapnia, with a highly significant inverse relation to PaCO2 (p < 0.001) — autoregulation in awake humans is fast, and its speed depends on vascular tone.
cards.watchOut: Small classic study (N = 10) of dynamic responses over seconds to a modest pressure step; it demonstrates the speed of the plateau's defence, not the static pressure at which defence finally fails.
cards.source: Aaslid R et al. Cerebral autoregulation dynamics in humans. Stroke. 1989. PMID: 2492126. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Tzeng 2010 (Willie/Ainslie programme): autoregulatory gain against falling pressure (0.57 cm/s per mm Hg) was consistently greater than against rising pressure (0.31) in 26 healthy volunteers
cards.summary: Tzeng 2010 (Willie/Ainslie programme): autoregulatory gain against falling pressure (0.57 cm/s per mm Hg) was consistently greater than against rising pressure (0.31) in 26 healthy volunteers
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (pharmacological pressure transients, transcranial Doppler)
cards.people: 26 healthy volunteers in two protocols: 10 subjects given intravenous nitroprusside (hypotension) and phenylephrine (hypertension), and 16 subjects comparing nitroprusside hypotension with thigh-cuff indices; N = 26 printed on the face of this physiology card.
cards.result: Dynamic cerebral autoregulation gain to transient hypotension (0.57 ± 0.16 cm/s per mm Hg) was consistently greater than gain to transient hypertension (0.31 ± 0.20 cm/s per mm Hg; p < 0.01), and the two gains were unrelated within individuals (r = 0.06; p = 0.87). Gain to drug-induced hypotension correlated inversely with the thigh-cuff rate of regulation (r = −0.52; p = 0.037) and autoregulatory index (r = −0.66; p = 0.005). The authors conclude dynamic autoregulation is inherently nonlinear — the brain defends flow against falling pressure more effectively than against rising pressure.
cards.watchOut: Laboratory transients in healthy volunteers, not sustained clinical hypo- or hypertension; the asymmetry means a single 'autoregulation range' number always simplifies a direction-dependent response.
cards.source: Tzeng YC et al. Cerebrovascular regulation during transient hypotension and hypertension in humans. Hypertension. 2010. PMID: 20547971. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Geinas 2012 (Willie/Ainslie programme): cerebral flow stayed unchanged when head-down tilt raised mean pressure by 22 mm Hg — resistance rose to match, in 21 young adults
cards.summary: Geinas 2012 (Willie/Ainslie programme): cerebral flow stayed unchanged when head-down tilt raised mean pressure by 22 mm Hg — resistance rose to match, in 21 young adults
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (postural pressure changes, transcranial Doppler and volumetric flow)
cards.people: 21 healthy young adults studied supine and during −90° head-down tilt and +90° head-up tilt with end-tidal CO2 controlled, measuring middle and posterior cerebral artery velocity and, in subgroups, volumetric carotid and vertebral flow; N = 21 printed on the face of this physiology card.
cards.result: Mean cerebral artery and posterior cerebral artery velocities and volumetric flows were unchanged in both tilts compared with supine. During head-down tilt, mean blood pressure rose by 22 mm Hg and cerebral vascular resistance in both arteries rose in parallel, while heart rate was unchanged; during head-up tilt, heart rate rose by 18 bpm. The authors conclude cerebral perfusion is well maintained during acute severe postural changes in perfusion pressure — the plateau defended from the pressure side.
cards.watchOut: Young healthy adults and acute postural pressure changes of tens of mm Hg; this shows flow defended across the middle of the autoregulatory range, not behaviour at or beyond the lower limit.
cards.source: Geinas JC et al. Influence of posture on the regulation of cerebral perfusion. Aviat Space Environ Med. 2012. PMID: 22872988. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a roughly 60–150 mm Hg plateau with a lower limit near 60 mm Hg (Lassen/textbook account), defended within seconds and more strongly against falling than rising pressure — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED
cards.summary: Synthesis: a roughly 60–150 mm Hg plateau with a lower limit near 60 mm Hg (Lassen/textbook account), defended within seconds and more strongly against falling than rising pressure — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED
cards.people: Carded human data: the Lassen 1959 synthesis plus 10 + 26 + 21 healthy volunteers in the primary dynamic studies.
cards.result: The static range itself comes from Lassen's synthesis as the textbooks carry it — flow roughly constant over a mean arterial pressure of about 60–150 mm Hg, pressure-passive below a lower limit near 60 mm Hg — and the modern primary studies are concordant with a defended plateau while showing it is dynamic, fast (seconds), CO2-sensitive and asymmetric. This matches the textbook account in Guyton and Hall and in Boron and Boulpaep, which frame this shelf. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Ageing and post-stroke changes in autoregulation are homed separately at pack #6202.
cards.watchOut: Physiology, not a blood-pressure target: the lower limit varies between individuals and shifts with chronic hypertension and disease, so the textbook 60 mm Hg must never be applied as a precise per-patient threshold.
cards.source: Synthesis of Lassen NA. Physiological reviews. 1959 (PMID: 13645234); Aaslid R et al. Stroke. 1989 (PMID: 2492126); Tzeng YC et al. Hypertension. 2010 (PMID: 20547971); Geinas JC et al. Aviation, space, and environmental medicine. 2012 (PMID: 22872988). shelves.title: Thrombectomy for medium-vessel occlusion stroke: no functional benefit in DISTAL or ESCAPE-MeVO (the treatment made no difference) — with more symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage
shelves.question: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke from a medium-vessel occlusion, does endovascular thrombectomy improve functional outcome compared with best medical care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Endovascular Procedures/adverse effects,methods · Female · Humans · Intracranial Hemorrhages/epidemiology,etiology · Ischemic Stroke/diagnosis,mortality,therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Middle Cerebral Artery · Severity of Illness Index · Thrombectomy/adverse effects,methods · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — two large randomised trials and a study-level meta-analysis of all three completed trials agree. DISTAL (n=543) found no difference in 90-day disability between endovascular treatment plus best medical treatment and best medical treatment alone (common odds ratio for improvement 0.90, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.22), and ESCAPE-MeVO (n=530) found excellent outcome (modified Rankin scale 0–1) in 41.6% with thrombectomy versus 43.1% with usual care (adjusted rate ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.15). Both trials showed numerically more symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage with intervention (5.9% vs 2.6%; 5.4% vs 2.2%), and ESCAPE-MeVO showed higher 90-day mortality with thrombectomy (13.3% vs 8.4%; adjusted hazard ratio 1.82, 95% CI 1.06 to 3.12). The meta-analysis pooling DISTAL, ESCAPE-MeVO and DISCOUNT found no functional benefit (relative risk 0.92) and more than double the odds of symptomatic haemorrhage (odds ratio 2.38, 95% CI 1.35 to 4.20). The large-vessel thrombectomy benefit does not extend to medium-vessel occlusion on this record.

cards.headline: DISTAL (2025): endovascular treatment plus best medical treatment made no difference to 90-day disability versus best medical treatment alone in medium/distal-vessel occlusion (common OR 0.90, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.22)
cards.summary: DISTAL (2025): endovascular treatment plus best medical treatment made no difference to 90-day disability versus best medical treatment alone in medium/distal-vessel occlusion (common OR 0.90, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.22)
cards.type: Multicentre, pragmatic randomised trial (DISTAL), N Engl J Med 2025
cards.people: 543 participants (44% women; median age 77 years; median NIH Stroke Scale score 6) with isolated occlusion of a medium or distal vessel — nondominant or codominant M2 (44.0%), M3 (26.9%), P2 (13.4%), P1 (5.5%), or A1–A3 segments — randomised within 24 hours of last being seen well to endovascular treatment plus best medical treatment (271) or best medical treatment alone (272); 65.4% received intravenous thrombolysis.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in the distribution of modified Rankin scale scores at 90 days (common odds ratio for improvement in the score, 0.90; 95% confidence interval, 0.67 to 1.22; P = 0.50) — the treatment made no difference to disability. All-cause mortality was similar (15.5% with endovascular treatment and 14.0% with best medical treatment alone), while symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage was numerically more frequent with intervention (5.9% and 2.6%, respectively).
cards.watchOut: Median NIHSS of 6 means many participants had mild strokes with high spontaneous recovery — a ceiling on detectable benefit; the confidence interval (0.67 to 1.22) also cannot exclude a modest benefit in a more severely affected subgroup, which this trial does not identify.
cards.source: Psychogios M et al. Endovascular Treatment for Stroke Due to Occlusion of Medium or Distal Vessels. The New England journal of medicine. 2025. PMID: 39908430. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05029414, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: ESCAPE-MeVO (2025): thrombectomy did not improve 90-day outcome versus usual care (excellent outcome 41.6% vs 43.1%) and mortality was higher with intervention (13.3% vs 8.4%)
cards.summary: ESCAPE-MeVO (2025): thrombectomy did not improve 90-day outcome versus usual care (excellent outcome 41.6% vs 43.1%) and mortality was higher with intervention (13.3% vs 8.4%)
cards.type: Multicentre, prospective, randomised, open-label trial with blinded outcome evaluation (ESCAPE-MeVO), N Engl J Med 2025
cards.people: 530 patients from five countries with acute ischaemic stroke due to medium-vessel occlusion (84.7% middle-cerebral-artery branch occlusions), presenting within 12 hours of last known well with favourable baseline imaging, randomised open-label with blinded outcome assessment to endovascular thrombectomy plus usual care (255) or usual care alone (275).
cards.result: A modified Rankin scale score of 0 or 1 at 90 days occurred in 106 of 255 patients (41.6%) in the thrombectomy group and 118 of 274 (43.1%) in the usual-care group (adjusted rate ratio, 0.95; 95% confidence interval, 0.79 to 1.15; P = 0.61) — the treatment made no difference to excellent outcome. Mortality at 90 days was 13.3% in the thrombectomy group and 8.4% in the usual-care group (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.82; 95% CI, 1.06 to 3.12), and symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage occurred in 14 of 257 patients (5.4%) versus 6 of 272 (2.2%).
cards.watchOut: The mortality difference rests on small absolute numbers and was a secondary outcome; read it as a harm signal concordant with the haemorrhage excess rather than proof thrombectomy kills — but it removes any presumption that intervention here is benign.
cards.source: Goyal M et al. Endovascular Treatment of Stroke Due to Medium-Vessel Occlusion. The New England journal of medicine. 2025. PMID: 39908448. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05151172, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Schellinger 2025 meta-analysis of DISTAL, ESCAPE-MeVO and DISCOUNT: no functional benefit (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.06) and more than double the odds of symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage (OR 2.38)
cards.summary: Schellinger 2025 meta-analysis of DISTAL, ESCAPE-MeVO and DISCOUNT: no functional benefit (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.06) and more than double the odds of symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage (OR 2.38)
cards.type: Study-level meta-analysis and narrative review of 3 randomised trials, Neurol Res Pract 2025
cards.people: Study-level random-effects meta-analysis and narrative review of the three completed randomised trials of endovascular treatment plus best medical treatment versus best medical treatment alone for medium/distal-vessel occlusion — DISTAL, ESCAPE-MeVO and DISCOUNT — pooling independent outcome, symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage and death.
cards.result: There was no significant effect of endovascular treatment on functional outcome (relative risk 0.92, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.06, P = 0.272) and the odds of death did not differ (odds ratio 1.23, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.99, P = 0.409), while the odds of symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage were more than twice as high with endovascular treatment (odds ratio 2.38, 95% CI 1.35 to 4.20, P = 0.003). The authors conclude endovascular treatment for medium and distal occlusions is not standard of care at present and that new, differently designed trials are the priority.
cards.watchOut: DISCOUNT enters this shelf only through this pooled analysis — no standalone DISCOUNT trial report was found on PubMed this session (it has been presented at conference), so its individual numbers are not carded; a three-trial study-level pooling also cannot explore patient-level subgroups.
cards.source: Schellinger PD et al. Randomized controlled trials of endovascular therapy for acute ischemic stroke with medium or distal vessel occlusion: a study level meta-analysis and narrative review. cards.headline: Synthesis: across more than a thousand randomised patients, thrombectomy for medium-vessel occlusion made no difference to outcome — and the haemorrhage cost was consistent
cards.summary: Synthesis: across more than a thousand randomised patients, thrombectomy for medium-vessel occlusion made no difference to outcome — and the haemorrhage cost was consistent
cards.people: Synthesis of DISTAL (PMID: 39908430), ESCAPE-MeVO (PMID: 39908448) and the three-trial meta-analysis including DISCOUNT (PMID: 40571944).
cards.result: Two independently conducted trials on two continents, enrolling milder strokes (median NIHSS 6 in DISTAL) within 12–24 hours, land on the same null: common odds ratio 0.90 and adjusted rate ratio 0.95, both centred on no effect, and the pooled estimate (relative risk 0.92, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.06) excludes the large treatment effects seen in large-vessel occlusion. The harm side is equally consistent — symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage roughly doubled in each trial and in the pooling (odds ratio 2.38). The correct reading is not that reperfusion is futile in distal territory in principle, but that with current devices, current selection and these mostly mild presentations, routine thrombectomy for medium-vessel occlusion is not supported; large-vessel and large-core thrombectomy are answered on their own shelves and are not touched by this one.
cards.watchOut: Both trials enrolled predominantly mild-to-moderate strokes; a disabling medium-vessel syndrome (e.g. dominant M2 with severe aphasia) is under-represented, and this shelf's null should not be quoted as settling thrombectomy for that narrower, more severe subgroup.
cards.source: Synthesis of Psychogios M et al., N Engl J Med 2025 (PMID: 39908430); Goyal M et al., N Engl J Med 2025 (PMID: 39908448); Schellinger PD et al., Neurol Res Pract 2025 (PMID: 40571944). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Restarting antiplatelet therapy after intracerebral haemorrhage: RESTART found no increase in recurrent haemorrhage — recurrence was numerically lower on antiplatelets (4% vs 9%)
shelves.question: In survivors of intracerebral haemorrhage who need antiplatelet therapy, does restarting it increase recurrent intracerebral haemorrhage compared with avoiding antiplatelet therapy?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Cerebral Hemorrhage/chemically induced,epidemiology · Cerebrovascular Disorders/prevention & control · Female · Humans · Male · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Prospective Studies · Recurrence · Stroke/complications · Treatment Outcome · United Kingdom · Vascular Diseases/prevention & control
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a single trial programme caps the stamp. RESTART randomised 537 intracerebral haemorrhage survivors who had been on antithrombotic therapy to start or avoid antiplatelet therapy; over a median 2.0 years, recurrent symptomatic intracerebral haemorrhage occurred in 12 of 268 (4%) allocated to antiplatelets versus 23 of 268 (9%) allocated to avoid (adjusted hazard ratio 0.51, 95% CI 0.25 to 1.03; P = 0.060) — restarting did not increase recurrence, and the point estimate leant the other way. Major haemorrhagic events (7% vs 9%) and major occlusive vascular events (15% vs 14%) were likewise similar. Extended follow-up to a median 3.0 years kept the same shape (recurrent haemorrhage 8.2% vs 9.3%; adjusted hazard ratio 0.87, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.55). The 2023 Cochrane review of antithrombotic treatment after intracerebral haemorrhage (9 randomised trials, 1,491 participants) is carded as context: RESTART remains the substantive long-term antiplatelet trial inside it. Restarting anticoagulation is a different drug class and question, answered elsewhere; this shelf is antiplatelets only.

cards.headline: RESTART (2019): restarting antiplatelet therapy did not increase recurrent intracerebral haemorrhage — 4% versus 9% over a median 2 years (adjusted HR 0.51, 95% CI 0.25 to 1.03)
cards.summary: RESTART (2019): restarting antiplatelet therapy did not increase recurrent intracerebral haemorrhage — 4% versus 9% over a median 2 years (adjusted HR 0.51, 95% CI 0.25 to 1.03)
cards.type: Prospective, randomised, open-label, blinded-endpoint trial (RESTART), Lancet 2019
cards.people: 537 adults at 122 UK hospitals who had been taking antithrombotic therapy for prevention of occlusive vascular disease when they developed intracerebral haemorrhage, had discontinued it, and survived 24 hours; recruited a median of 76 days (IQR 29–146) after onset and randomised 1:1 to start (268) or avoid (269, one withdrew) antiplatelet therapy, in an open-label trial with blinded endpoint assessment, followed a median of 2.0 years (completeness 99.3%).
cards.result: Recurrent symptomatic intracerebral haemorrhage — the primary outcome — occurred in 12 (4%) of 268 participants allocated to antiplatelet therapy versus 23 (9%) of 268 allocated to avoid it (adjusted hazard ratio 0.51 [95% CI 0.25–1.03]; P = 0.060). Major haemorrhagic events occurred in 18 (7%) versus 25 (9%) (0.71 [0.39–1.30]; P = 0.27), and major occlusive vascular events in 39 (15%) versus 38 (14%) (1.02 [0.65–1.60]; P = 0.92). The authors concluded the results exclude all but a very modest increase in recurrent haemorrhage risk, and that the risk is probably too small to exceed the established benefits of antiplatelet therapy for secondary prevention.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and 537 patients with 35 primary events cannot exclude a small absolute increase in recurrence (the interval reaches a hazard ratio of 1.03 at the primary analysis); participants were a median 76 days post-haemorrhage, so the trial says nothing about restarting in the first days.
cards.source: RESTART Collaboration. Effects of antiplatelet therapy after stroke due to intracerebral haemorrhage (RESTART): a randomised, open-label trial. The Lancet. 2019. PMID: 31128924. Registry ID: ISRCTN71907627, stated in the record (registry field not separately databank-coded in the record).
