cards.headline: RESTART extended follow-up (2021): out to a median 3.0 years, recurrent haemorrhage remained similar (8.2% vs 9.3%; adjusted HR 0.87, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.55)
cards.summary: RESTART extended follow-up (2021): out to a median 3.0 years, recurrent haemorrhage remained similar (8.2% vs 9.3%; adjusted HR 0.87, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.55)
cards.type: Extended follow-up of a randomised clinical trial (RESTART), JAMA Neurol 2021
cards.people: The same 537 RESTART participants (median age 76.0 years; 67.0% male; median time after haemorrhage onset 76.0 days), with annual follow-up extended to November 30, 2020 — median 3.0 years (IQR 2.0–5.0), up to 7 years — for recurrent symptomatic intracerebral haemorrhage and all major vascular events.
cards.result: The primary outcome of recurrent intracerebral haemorrhage affected 22 of 268 participants (8.2%) allocated to antiplatelet therapy versus 25 of 268 (9.3%) allocated to avoid it (adjusted hazard ratio, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.49–1.55; P = .64). A major vascular event affected 72 participants (26.8%) on antiplatelet therapy versus 87 (32.5%) avoiding it (hazard ratio, 0.79; 95% CI, 0.58–1.08; P = .14). The authors concluded there was no statistically significant effect of antiplatelet therapy on recurrent haemorrhage or all major vascular events, providing some reassurance to physicians deciding on resumption.
cards.watchOut: An extension of the same single trial, not independent confirmation: event counts remain small, intervals wide, and adherence over years of open-label follow-up dilutes the randomised contrast.
cards.source: Al-Shahi Salman R et al. Effects of Antiplatelet Therapy After Stroke Caused by Intracerebral Hemorrhage: Extended Follow-up of the RESTART Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA neurology. 2021. PMID: 34477823. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cochrane 2023 (context): across 9 randomised trials and 1,491 participants on antithrombotic treatment after intracerebral haemorrhage, RESTART is the substantive long-term antiplatelet evidence
cards.summary: Cochrane 2023 (context): across 9 randomised trials and 1,491 participants on antithrombotic treatment after intracerebral haemorrhage, RESTART is the substantive long-term antiplatelet evidence
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (Cochrane), Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023
cards.people: The 2023 Cochrane review of antithrombotic (antiplatelet or anticoagulant) treatment after stroke due to intracerebral haemorrhage: 9 randomised trials in secondary care, 1,491 participants (average ages 61 to 79 years; 44% to 67% men), comparing starting versus avoiding antithrombotic treatment, with risk ratios estimated per trial and GRADE certainty ratings applied.
cards.result: The review's antiplatelet question rests overwhelmingly on RESTART's randomised population; its other included trials address short-term prophylactic-dose anticoagulation and anticoagulant resumption, where the evidence on death was very uncertain (for example, risk ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.70 for short-term prophylactic anticoagulation, very low-certainty evidence). The review therefore corroborates the shape of this shelf rather than adding an independent antiplatelet estimate: one adequately designed trial, no signal of increased recurrence, and certainty limited by a single trial's event count.
cards.watchOut: Most of the review's trials concern anticoagulants, not antiplatelets — do not quote its anticoagulation estimates as antiplatelet evidence; for the antiplatelet question it is a frame around RESTART, not a second trial.
cards.source: Cochrane Stroke Group. Antithrombotic treatment after stroke due to intracerebral haemorrhage. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2023. PMID: 36700520. Registry ID: none in the record (the review lists its included trials' registrations, including NCT02565693 and others, in its databank fields; none is this review's own). cards.headline: Synthesis: the feared harm did not appear — restarting antiplatelets after intracerebral haemorrhage was not followed by more recurrent haemorrhage, in the primary trial or its extension
cards.summary: Synthesis: the feared harm did not appear — restarting antiplatelets after intracerebral haemorrhage was not followed by more recurrent haemorrhage, in the primary trial or its extension
cards.people: Synthesis of RESTART (PMID: 31128924), its extended follow-up (PMID: 34477823) and the Cochrane antithrombotic-after-ICH review (PMID: 36700520).
cards.result: Before RESTART, withholding antiplatelets indefinitely after intracerebral haemorrhage was the default driven by a plausible fear. The randomised record reverses the burden of that fear: recurrence was numerically less frequent on antiplatelet therapy at 2 years (4% vs 9%) and essentially equal by extended follow-up (8.2% vs 9.3%), with no excess of major haemorrhagic events at either horizon and occlusive events no worse. The stamp stays at POSSIBLE because one trial of 537 patients and 47 recurrence events in total cannot exclude a modest increase, and because RESTART's patients were selected survivors randomised a median of 76 days after their haemorrhage. Within those bounds, for a survivor with a genuine secondary-prevention indication, the evidence supports restarting rather than permanent avoidance.
cards.watchOut: Nothing here addresses dual antiplatelet therapy, restarting within days of the haemorrhage, or patients whose haemorrhage was lobar with probable cerebral amyloid angiopathy as a separately randomised group — RESTART subgroup data do not convert this shelf's answer into one for those situations.
cards.source: Synthesis of RESTART Collaboration, Lancet 2019 (PMID: 31128924); Al-Shahi Salman R et al., JAMA Neurol 2021 (PMID: 34477823); Cochrane Stroke Group, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023 (PMID: 36700520). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Entacapine as a levodopa adjunct in Parkinson's wearing-off: off-time fell by about 1 to 1.5 hours a day across NOMECOMT, SEESAW and Celomen — bought with more dyskinesia and diarrhoea
shelves.question: In people with Parkinson's disease and wearing-off on levodopa, does adding entacapine reduce daily off-time compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antiparkinson Agents/therapeutic use · Catechol O-Methyltransferase Inhibitors · Catechols/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Drug Synergism · Drug Therapy, Combination · Enzyme Inhibitors/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Female · Humans · Levodopa/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Motor Activity · Nitriles · Parkinson Disease/drug therapy,physiopathology · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three concordant placebo-controlled trials of the same programme plus a Cochrane synthesis, held at POSSIBLE because the trials are 24-week, diary-based and industry-era, and the benefit is modest. NOMECOMT (n=171, 6 months) cut off-time from 5.3 to 4.2 hours a day on entacapine 200 mg with each levodopa dose while on-time rose from 9.3 to 10.7 hours. The Parkinson Study Group trial (SEESAW; n=205, 24 weeks) raised the percentage of waking on-time by 5.0 percentage points. Celomen (n=301, 24 weeks) increased on-time 1.7 hours and decreased off-time 1.5 hours on entacapine versus 0.5 and 0.6 hours on placebo. The Cochrane review of COMT inhibitors (14 trials, 2,566 patients; 8 entacapine trials, 1,560 patients) concluded entacapine reduced off-time and levodopa dose and modestly improved motor impairment, at the cost of more dyskinesia, nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea. Benefit was lost on withdrawal in both trials that tested it — entacapine extends each levodopa dose; it does not modify the disease. (The drug is entacapine, a catechol-O-methyltransferase inhibitor — the slate's 'entacapone' was a misspelling.)

cards.headline: NOMECOMT (1998): entacapine with each levodopa dose cut daily off-time from 5.3 to 4.2 hours and raised on-time from 9.3 to 10.7 hours over 6 months (n=171)
cards.summary: NOMECOMT (1998): entacapine with each levodopa dose cut daily off-time from 5.3 to 4.2 hours and raised on-time from 9.3 to 10.7 hours over 6 months (n=171)
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial (NOMECOMT), Neurology 1998
cards.people: 171 patients with Parkinson's disease and wearing-off motor fluctuations in the Northern European (NOMECOMT) study, randomised to entacapine 200 mg or identical placebo taken with each daily levodopa dose (four to ten times a day) for 6 months, with home diaries of on and off time and Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale scoring.
cards.result: Home diaries showed entacapine increased mean on-time significantly (9.3 ± 2.2 to 10.7 ± 2.2 hours; P < 0.01) and correspondingly decreased off-time (5.3 ± 2.2 to 4.2 ± 2.2 hours; P < 0.001). The average benefit derived from a daily levodopa dose increased significantly (P < 0.01), and the daily levodopa dose was reduced significantly in the entacapine group, the between-group difference being 102 mg (P < 0.01). The entacapine-derived increase in benefit was lost almost completely following its withdrawal. Dopaminergic adverse events increased and were ameliorated by reducing the levodopa dose; diarrhoea was the most common non-dopaminergic adverse event.
cards.watchOut: The published title and record spell the drug 'entacapone' — a period misspelling of entacapine carried in the journal record; diary-based on/off time is patient-recorded and the trial predates modern reporting standards, with no registry entry in the record.
cards.source: Rinne UK et al. Entacapone enhances the response to levodopa in parkinsonian patients with motor fluctuations. Nomecomt Study Group. Neurology. 1998. PMID: 9818851. Registry ID: none in the record. multicentre, randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial (nomecomt), neurology 1998 171 patients with parkinson's disease and wearing-off motor fluctuations in the northern european (nomecomt) study, randomised to entacapine 200 mg or identical placebo taken with each daily levodopa dose (four to ten times a day) for 6 months, with home diaries of on and off time and unified parkinson's disease rating scale scoring. home diaries showed entacapine increased mean on-time significantly (9.3 ± 2.2 to 10.7 ± 2.2 hours; p < 0.01) and correspondingly decreased off-time (5.3 ± 2.2 to 4.2 ± 2.2 hours; p < 0.001). the average benefit derived from a daily levodopa dose increased significantly (p < 0.01), and the daily levodopa dose was reduced significantly in the entacapine group, the between-group difference being 102 mg (p < 0.01). the entacapine-derived increase in benefit was lost almost completely following its withdrawal. dopaminergic adverse events increased and were ameliorated by reducing the levodopa dose; diarrhoea was the most common non-dopaminergic adverse event. the published title and record spell the drug 'entacapone' — a period misspelling of entacapine carried in the journal record; diary-based on/off time is patient-recorded and the trial predates modern reporting standards, with no registry entry in the record. rinne uk et al. entacapone enhances the response to levodopa in parkinsonian patients with motor fluctuations. nomecomt study group. neurology. 1998. pmid: 9818851. registry id: none in the record. mesh: antiparkinson agents/therapeutic use · catechol o-methyltransferase inhibitors · catechols/adverse effects,therapeutic use · double-blind method · drug synergism · drug therapy, combination · enzyme inhibitors/adverse effects,therapeutic use · female · humans · levodopa/therapeutic use · male · middle aged · motor activity · nitriles · parkinson disease/drug therapy,physiopathology

cards.headline: SEESAW — Parkinson Study Group (1997): entacapine increased the percentage of waking on-time by 5.0 percentage points over 24 weeks (n=205)
cards.summary: SEESAW — Parkinson Study Group (1997): entacapine increased the percentage of waking on-time by 5.0 percentage points over 24 weeks (n=205)
cards.type: Multicentre, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial (Parkinson Study Group / SEESAW), Ann Neurol 1997
cards.people: 205 patients with Parkinson's disease and levodopa motor fluctuations, randomised to entacapine 200 mg or matching placebo with each levodopa dose and followed for 24 weeks, with home diaries completed at 30-minute intervals recording on-time (relief of parkinsonism) while awake; baseline on-time averaged about 10 hours a day (60.5% of waking time).
cards.result: Entacapone increased the percent on-time by 5.0 percentage points over placebo. The effect was more prominent in patients with a smaller percent on-time at baseline (below 55%) and increased as the day wore on. The authors concluded entacapone is effective at increasing the duration of response to levodopa and relieving parkinsonism in patients experiencing motor fluctuations, and was well tolerated during the 24 weeks of treatment.
cards.watchOut: The primary outcome is a percentage of waking on-time, not hours of off-time, and the record's abstract does not print the placebo group's change separately — cross-trial hour comparisons should use NOMECOMT and Celomen, with this trial as concordant confirmation.
cards.source: Parkinson Study Group. Entacapone improves motor fluctuations in levodopa-treated Parkinson's disease patients. Annals of neurology. 1997. PMID: 9392574. cards.headline: Celomen (2002): in fluctuating patients, entacapine increased on-time 1.7 hours and decreased off-time 1.5 hours, versus 0.5 and 0.6 hours on placebo (n=301)
cards.summary: Celomen (2002): in fluctuating patients, entacapine increased on-time 1.7 hours and decreased off-time 1.5 hours, versus 0.5 and 0.6 hours on placebo (n=301)
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial (Celomen), Acta Neurol Scand 2002
cards.people: 301 patients with Parkinson's disease (the majority with motor fluctuations) in Germany and Austria, randomised double-blind to entacapine 200 mg or placebo with each daily dose of standard or controlled-release levodopa for 24 weeks, followed by 2 weeks of entacapine withdrawal; efficacy by home diaries, Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale and levodopa dose change.
cards.result: In fluctuating patients, on-time increased 1.7 hours and off-time decreased 1.5 hours with entacapine, significantly more than with placebo (0.5 and 0.6 hours respectively; P < 0.05), and Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale activities-of-daily-living and motor scores improved significantly (P < 0.05). Daily levodopa dose fell by 54 mg on entacapine and rose by 27 mg on placebo (P < 0.05), and entacapine benefit was lost on withdrawal. Dyskinesias were commoner on entacapine (34% vs 26%) and nausea likewise (10% vs 5%), mostly shortly after initiation and generally managed by reducing the levodopa dose; diarrhoea occurred in 8% versus 4% and was seldom severe.
cards.watchOut: The on/off figures come from the fluctuating subgroup of a broader 'suboptimal response' population, and — like NOMECOMT — the record carries the period 'entacapone' spelling; effect sizes are 24-week diary averages, not evidence about years of use.
cards.source: Poewe WH et al. Efficacy and safety of entacapone in Parkinson's disease patients with suboptimal levodopa response: a 6-month randomized placebo-controlled double-blind study in Germany and Austria (Celomen study). Acta neurologica Scandinavica. 2002. PMID: 11939936. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cochrane (Deane 2004): across 8 entacapine trials and 1,560 patients, COMT inhibition reduced off-time and levodopa dose, at the cost of more dyskinesia, nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea
cards.summary: Cochrane (Deane 2004): across 8 entacapine trials and 1,560 patients, COMT inhibition reduced off-time and levodopa dose, at the cost of more dyskinesia, nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised controlled trials (Cochrane), Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2004
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials of adjuvant catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) inhibitor therapy versus placebo in Parkinson's disease with levodopa-induced motor complications: 14 trials and 2,566 patients in total — 8 entacapine trials (1,560 patients, 2 to 12 months) and 6 tolcapone trials (1,006 patients).
cards.result: Both tolcapone and entacapine reduced off-time, reduced levodopa dose, and modestly improved motor impairments and disability, at the expense of increased risk of dyskinesias, nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea. A few participants taking tolcapone had raised liver enzyme levels, and the review notes three cases of fatal hepatic toxicity with tolcapone in post-marketing surveillance — a tolcapone-specific warning that does not attach to entacapine, whose principal non-dopaminergic burden in the trials is diarrhoea. The reviewers characterise the evidence as, at best, medium-term.
cards.watchOut: A 2004 review of trials run to 2003: it pools entacapine with tolcapone for several conclusions, so entacapine-specific magnitudes should be taken from the three carded trials, and later COMT inhibitors (opicapone) are outside its record entirely — opicapone is answered on its own shelf (#2369).
cards.source: Deane KHO et al. Catechol-O-methyltransferase inhibitors for levodopa-induced complications in Parkinson's disease. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2004. PMID: 15495119. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: entacapine buys roughly an extra hour of on-time a day by extending each levodopa dose — a real, modest, symptomatic effect that vanishes on withdrawal
cards.summary: Synthesis: entacapine buys roughly an extra hour of on-time a day by extending each levodopa dose — a real, modest, symptomatic effect that vanishes on withdrawal
cards.people: Synthesis of NOMECOMT (PMID: 9818851), the Parkinson Study Group SEESAW trial (PMID: 9392574), Celomen (PMID: 11939936) and the Cochrane COMT-inhibitor review (PMID: 15495119).
cards.result: Three placebo-controlled trials run independently in northern Europe, North America and Germany/Austria agree closely: off-time falls by about 1 to 1.5 hours a day and on-time rises correspondingly, levodopa dose can be trimmed by roughly 50–100 mg a day, and the Cochrane pooling of the full entacapine programme (1,560 patients) reaches the same conclusion. The costs are the predictable ones of more dopaminergic exposure — dyskinesia in about a third, nausea — plus diarrhoea in about 8%, and two trials show the benefit disappearing within weeks of withdrawal, confirming a purely symptomatic levodopa-extending action. For a patient with wearing-off who wants a per-dose oral adjunct before considering device or infusion therapies, this is a supported, modest option; it is not disease modification, and the stamp is POSSIBLE because the entire programme is 24-week diary-based trials from the drug's launch era.
cards.watchOut: No carded trial compares entacapine head-to-head with the later COMT inhibitor opicapone or with other adjunct classes, so this shelf ranks entacapine against placebo only; cross-class choices need the adjunct family's own shelves.
cards.source: Synthesis of Rinne UK et al., Neurology 1998 (PMID: 9818851); Parkinson Study Group, Ann Neurol 1997 (PMID: 9392574); Poewe WH et al., Acta Neurol Scand 2002 (PMID: 11939936); Deane KHO et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2004 (PMID: 15495119). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Virtual reality for post-stroke upper-limb rehabilitation: no advantage over recreational activity in the one large matched-dose trial (EVREST); pooled effects are small and clearest when VR simply adds therapy time
shelves.question: In stroke survivors, does virtual-reality-based therapy improve upper-limb function compared with conventional therapy of the same intensity?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Brain Ischemia/rehabilitation · Exercise Therapy/adverse effects,methods · Female · Games, Recreational · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Psychomotor Performance/physiology · Severity of Illness Index · Single-Blind Method · Stroke/therapy · Stroke Rehabilitation/adverse effects,methods · Upper Extremity/physiopathology · User-Computer Interface
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence). At matched therapy intensity — the comparison this question asks for — the one large trial was null: in EVREST (n=141), non-immersive virtual-reality Wii training added to conventional rehabilitation was not superior to simple recreational activities (cards, bingo, ball games) on the Wolf Motor Function Test (adjusted difference 4.1 s, 95% CI −14.4 to 22.6), with equal conventional-therapy time in both arms. The 2025 Cochrane update (190 trials, 7,188 participants) found a small pooled advantage over alternative therapy for upper-limb function (SMD 0.20, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.28; low-certainty evidence), and a larger effect when virtual reality was added on top of usual care (SMD 0.42, 0.26 to 0.58; moderate certainty) — a comparison in which the virtual-reality group simply received more therapy, so the gain may be a dose effect rather than an effect of the medium. Most trials are small (only 19% enrolled more than 50 participants; the largest enrolled 152), and one small 2026 trial reporting very large effects (PMID 42581516) is carded with that caution on its face. Virtual reality is a reasonable, safe way to deliver engaging practice; the evidence that the technology itself beats equal-intensity conventional therapy is weak.

cards.headline: EVREST (Saposnik 2016): Wii-based virtual reality was not superior to recreational activities for upper-limb recovery — adjusted Wolf Motor Function Test difference 4.1 s (95% CI −14.4 to 22.6)
cards.summary: EVREST (Saposnik 2016): Wii-based virtual reality was not superior to recreational activities for upper-limb recovery — adjusted Wolf Motor Function Test difference 4.1 s (95% CI −14.4 to 22.6)
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial (EVREST), Lancet Neurology 2016
cards.people: 141 adults (aged 18–85) with a first-ever ischaemic stroke within the previous 3 months and mild-to-moderate upper-extremity motor deficit, recruited at 14 inpatient stroke rehabilitation units in four countries; 71 were randomised to non-immersive virtual reality (Nintendo Wii) and 70 to recreational activity, each as ten 60-minute sessions over 2 weeks added to conventional rehabilitation; 121 patients completed the final assessment and formed the primary analysis.
cards.result: Both groups improved: median Wolf Motor Function Test time fell from 43.7 s to 29.7 s with virtual reality and from 38.0 s to 27.1 s with recreational activity. The multivariable-adjusted difference in the primary outcome was 4.1 s (95% CI −14.4 to 22.6) — no significant difference (the treatment made no difference). Conventional rehabilitation time was similar (373 vs 397 minutes), as was total study-intervention time (528 vs 541 minutes), so this was a matched-dose comparison. Three serious adverse events occurred, all judged unrelated to the interventions.
cards.watchOut: The comparator was active recreational therapy, not usual care alone — EVREST shows virtual reality adds nothing over equally intensive, task-specific play; it does not test virtual reality against no added therapy. Participants had mild-to-moderate impairment and were within 3 months of stroke, so the result may not extend to severe paresis or chronic stroke.
cards.source: Saposnik G et al. Efficacy and safety of non-immersive virtual reality exercising in stroke rehabilitation (EVREST): a randomised, multicentre, single-blind, controlled trial. Lancet Neurol. 2016. PMID: 27365261. Registry ID: NCT01406912 (ClinicalTrials.gov; the record's abstract prints the number as 'NTC01406912'). cards.headline: Cochrane 2025 update (Laver): 190 trials, 7,188 participants — small upper-limb advantage over alternative therapy (SMD 0.20, low certainty); larger when VR was added to usual care (SMD 0.42)
cards.summary: Cochrane 2025 update (Laver): 190 trials, 7,188 participants — small upper-limb advantage over alternative therapy (SMD 0.20, low certainty); larger when VR was added to usual care (SMD 0.42)
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis (2025 update)
cards.people: Adults after stroke in 190 randomised trials (7,188 participants) of virtual reality or interactive video gaming versus an alternative intervention or usual care; 119 studies were new in this update. Most studies were small — only 36 (19%) enrolled more than 50 participants and the largest recruited 152 — and interventions and devices varied widely.
cards.result: Versus alternative therapy approaches, virtual reality slightly improved upper-limb function and activity (SMD 0.20, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.28; 67 studies, 2,830 participants; low-certainty evidence) and probably reduced activity limitation (SMD 0.21, 0.11 to 0.32; 33 studies, 1,495 participants; moderate certainty), with little to no effect on participation or quality of life (SMD 0.11, −0.02 to 0.24). When virtual reality was added to usual care — increasing total therapy time — upper-limb function probably improved more (SMD 0.42, 0.26 to 0.58; 21 studies, 689 participants; moderate certainty). Adverse events were few and mild across the 59 studies that monitored them.
cards.watchOut: The add-on comparison confounds the medium with the dose: patients receiving virtual reality on top of usual care got more therapy overall. Risk of bias was unclear in many trials because of poor reporting, and certainty is low to moderate throughout — the pooled SMD of 0.20 against matched therapy is a small effect that small-study bias could plausibly erase.
cards.source: Laver KE et al. Virtual reality for stroke rehabilitation. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2025. PMID: 40537150. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Chen 2026: in 64 subacute patients, VR-based task-oriented training beat conventional task-oriented training on Fugl-Meyer and Barthel scores at 4 weeks (all P<0.001)
cards.summary: Chen 2026: in 64 subacute patients, VR-based task-oriented training beat conventional task-oriented training on Fugl-Meyer and Barthel scores at 4 weeks (all P<0.001)
cards.type: Single-centre randomised controlled trial, Medical Science Monitor 2026
cards.people: 64 patients in the subacute phase after stroke at a single centre (enrolled April 2022–March 2024), randomised 32 to virtual-reality-based task-oriented training and 32 to conventional task-oriented training, both on top of standard rehabilitation; all 64 completed the 4-week study with no dropouts.
cards.result: After 4 weeks, baseline-adjusted mean scores were significantly higher in the virtual-reality group for total Fugl-Meyer Assessment (P<0.001, partial η²=0.526), Fugl-Meyer upper extremity (P<0.001, η²=0.458), lower extremity (P<0.001, η²=0.475) and Barthel Index (P<0.001, η²=0.536); the authors report the improvements exceeded established minimal clinically important differences. The record reports significance levels and effect sizes but no between-group point differences in the abstract.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre trial of 64 patients reporting uniformly very large effects (η²≈0.5) with zero dropouts sits uneasily beside EVREST's matched-dose null and Cochrane's small pooled effect; treat it as hypothesis-generating. No trial registration appears in the record, and the abstract gives no absolute between-group differences to judge clinical size directly.

cards.headline: Synthesis: at equal intensity the medium does not beat ordinary task practice; VR's clearest value is delivering extra, engaging therapy time — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.summary: Synthesis: at equal intensity the medium does not beat ordinary task practice; VR's clearest value is delivering extra, engaging therapy time — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: EVREST (n=141, matched dose), the Cochrane 2025 synthesis (190 trials, 7,188 participants) and one small positive single-centre trial (n=64).
cards.result: EVREST — the only large trial that held therapy dose equal — found no difference between Wii-based virtual reality and recreational activities. The Cochrane pooled advantage over alternative therapy is small (SMD 0.20) and low-certainty; the larger add-on effect (SMD 0.42) is inseparable from the extra therapy time the virtual-reality groups received. The fair reading: virtual reality is a safe, engaging delivery vehicle for repetitive task practice, not a superior therapy in itself.
cards.watchOut: Programmes differ enormously (commercial games vs customised immersive systems); a future large matched-dose trial of a customised system could move this stamp, as could dose-matched trials in severe or chronic stroke, where evidence is thinnest.
cards.source: Synthesis of Saposnik 2016 (PMID 27365261), Laver 2025 (PMID 40537150) and Chen 2026 (PMID 42581516). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Hemiplegic shoulder pain after stroke: strapping delays pain onset by about 2 weeks but does not reduce it; electrical stimulation does not change pain; injection evidence rests on small trials and a network meta-analysis
shelves.question: In stroke survivors with hemiplegic shoulder pain or at risk of it, do strapping/taping, electrical stimulation, or corticosteroid injection prevent or reduce shoulder pain compared with usual care?
shelves.mesh: Electric Stimulation Therapy/methods · Humans · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Range of Motion, Articular · Shoulder Pain/etiology,prevention & control,therapy · Stroke/complications
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — every modality here rests on a small base, and the totals are printed on the face as the row requires: electrical stimulation, 4 trials and 170 patients (Cochrane); strapping and supportive devices, 4 trials and 142 participants (Cochrane); injection therapies, 17 studies and 595 participants in a network meta-analysis that includes non-randomised studies, plus one 60-patient randomised trial of injection technique. Electrical stimulation did not change pain incidence (OR 0.64, 95% CI 0.19 to 2.14) or pain intensity (SMD 0.13, −1.0 to 1.25), though it improved pain-free passive lateral rotation and reduced subluxation severity. Strapping delayed the onset of pain by about 14 days (WMD 14 days, 9.7 to 17.8) but did not reduce pain severity, improve function or prevent contracture; a hemisling was associated with more pain (Peto OR 8.7, 1.1 to 67.1). For injections, the network analysis ranked suprascapular nerve block best at 4 weeks and intramuscular botulinum toxin best between weeks 4 and 24 against placebo, while the one steroid-injection trial compared two injection targets against each other (dual-target better than single-target), not steroid against usual care. No modality has a large, definitive trial; positioning, handling and analgesia remain the untested usual-care backdrop.

cards.headline: Price & Pandyan, Cochrane 2000: electrical stimulation did not change post-stroke shoulder pain (4 trials, 170 patients) — but improved pain-free rotation and reduced subluxation
cards.summary: Price & Pandyan, Cochrane 2000: electrical stimulation did not change post-stroke shoulder pain (4 trials, 170 patients) — but improved pain-free rotation and reduced subluxation
cards.people: 170 participants across four randomised trials of surface electrical stimulation (functional electrical stimulation, transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation or other techniques) applied at any time after stroke to prevent or treat shoulder pain; study designs and stimulation techniques varied considerably.
cards.result: There was no significant change in pain incidence (OR 0.64, 95% CI 0.19 to 2.14) or in pain intensity (SMD 0.13, 95% CI −1.0 to 1.25) with electrical stimulation versus control (the treatment made no difference to pain). Stimulation did improve pain-free range of passive humeral lateral rotation (WMD 9.17 degrees, 1.43 to 16.91) and reduced the severity of glenohumeral subluxation (SMD −1.13, −1.66 to −0.60), with no significant effect on upper-limb motor recovery or spasticity and no apparent negative effects.
cards.watchOut: A 2000 review of four small, heterogeneous trials: it can neither confirm nor refute a pain effect, and stimulation techniques have changed since. The subluxation and rotation benefits are surrogate/mechanical outcomes, not pain relief.
cards.source: Price CIM, Pandyan AD. Electrical stimulation for preventing and treating post-stroke shoulder pain. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2000. PMID: 11034725. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ada, Cochrane 2005: strapping delayed shoulder pain onset by ~14 days but did not reduce pain or improve function (4 trials, 142 participants)
cards.summary: Ada, Cochrane 2005: strapping delayed shoulder pain onset by ~14 days but did not reduce pain or improve function (4 trials, 142 participants)
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis (4 trials, n=142)
cards.people: 142 participants in four trials of supportive devices after stroke — one trial of a hemisling and three of shoulder strapping — measuring subluxation, pain, function and contracture against no device.
cards.result: Strapping delayed the onset of pain (WMD 14 days, 95% CI 9.7 to 17.8) but was ineffective in reducing pain severity (WMD −0.7 cm on a visual analogue scale, −2.0 to 0.7), increasing upper-limb function (WMD 0.8, −1.5 to 3.1) or affecting contracture (WMD −1.4 degrees, −10.9 to 8.1). In the single sling trial, no participant had subluxation greater than 10 mm, and more participants in the hemisling group had pain (Peto OR 8.7, 95% CI 1.1 to 67.1). The reviewers concluded the evidence is insufficient to say whether slings and wheelchair attachments prevent subluxation or decrease pain.
cards.watchOut: Only three small strapping trials underpin the one positive finding (delayed onset), and delaying pain is not the same as preventing or treating it. The sling harm signal comes from a single trial with a very wide confidence interval.
cards.source: Ada L et al. Supportive devices for preventing and treating subluxation of the shoulder after stroke. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2005. PMID: 15674917. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hou 2022: dual-target corticosteroid injection (subacromial-subdeltoid bursa plus biceps tendon sheath) beat single-target bursa injection alone for hemiplegic shoulder pain (n=60)
cards.summary: Hou 2022: dual-target corticosteroid injection (subacromial-subdeltoid bursa plus biceps tendon sheath) beat single-target bursa injection alone for hemiplegic shoulder pain (n=60)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, Frontiers in Neurology 2022
cards.people: 60 patients with hemiplegic shoulder pain randomised to ultrasound-guided corticosteroid injection of the subacromial-subdeltoid bursa alone (n=30) or the bursa plus the long head of the biceps tendon sheath (n=30); pain (visual analogue scale), passive range of motion, Fugl-Meyer upper-extremity and Modified Barthel Index scores were followed to 12 weeks.
cards.result: Both groups improved on all measures. The dual-target group had lower pain scores at week 4 (VAS 3.3 vs 3.7, p=0.01) and week 12 (2.5 vs 3.2, p<0.001), with better flexion, external rotation and abduction at week 12 and larger Fugl-Meyer and Barthel gains (p<0.001).
cards.watchOut: This trial compares two steroid-injection strategies against each other — every patient received corticosteroid — so it cannot show that steroid injection beats usual care, placebo or no injection. It is a single-centre 60-patient trial, and the record's publication types oddly also list 'Case Reports' alongside the trial report.
cards.source: Hou Y et al. cards.headline: Chiu 2021 network meta-analysis: suprascapular nerve block ranked best at 4 weeks and botulinum toxin best at weeks 4–24 for hemiplegic shoulder pain (17 studies, 595 participants)
cards.summary: Chiu 2021 network meta-analysis: suprascapular nerve block ranked best at 4 weeks and botulinum toxin best at weeks 4–24 for hemiplegic shoulder pain (17 studies, 595 participants)
cards.type: Systematic review and network meta-analysis (17 studies, n=595)
cards.people: 595 participants with post-stroke hemiplegic shoulder pain across 17 studies comparing injection therapies (intramuscular botulinum toxin, suprascapular nerve block, corticosteroid and other regimens) and placebo; the primary outcome was pain reduction on a visual analogue scale at week 4 and between weeks 4 and 24.
cards.result: At week 4, intramuscular botulinum toxin (WMD 1.55, 95% CI 0.09 to 3.01) and suprascapular nerve block (WMD 1.44, 0.07 to 2.80) were superior to placebo; the nerve block had the highest probability of ranking best at week 4 (53.3%). Between weeks 4 and 24, botulinum toxin remained better than placebo (WMD 1.57, 0.30 to 2.84) with the highest best-treatment probability (79.8%).
cards.watchOut: The network includes some non-randomised studies, as the authors state, and most comparisons are indirect — rankings rest on simulation probabilities, not head-to-head trials. Corticosteroid injection itself is not the standout performer in this network; the best-ranked options are nerve block and botulinum toxin.
cards.source: Chiu YH et al. Comparative Effectiveness of Injection Therapies for Hemiplegic Shoulder Pain in Stroke: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis. Pharmaceuticals. 2021. PMID: 34451885. Registry ID: INPLASY202180010 (review protocol registration, as printed in the record). MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: small bases throughout — strapping buys ~2 pain-free weeks, stimulation moves the joint but not the pain, injections are promising but unproven against usual care — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.summary: Synthesis: small bases throughout — strapping buys ~2 pain-free weeks, stimulation moves the joint but not the pain, injections are promising but unproven against usual care — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: electrical stimulation (4 trials, 170 patients), strapping/supportive devices (4 trials, 142 participants), injection therapies (17 studies, 595 participants, plus one 60-patient technique trial). The syntheses overlap in the trials they include, so their totals cannot simply be added.
cards.result: No intervention on this shelf has been shown in an adequately sized trial to prevent or reduce hemiplegic shoulder pain versus usual care. The defensible positives are narrow: strapping delays pain onset, electrical stimulation improves pain-free rotation and subluxation, and nerve-block/botulinum-toxin injections outrank placebo in a partly non-randomised network. Everything else is absence of evidence in small trials, not proof of absence of effect.
cards.watchOut: These Cochrane reviews date from 2000 and 2005; a modern, adequately powered trial of any single modality — or an updated synthesis — could change this stamp. Pain after stroke is multifactorial (subluxation, spasticity, central pain, rotator-cuff injury), and trials that do not separate these mechanisms blur every estimate.
cards.source: Synthesis of Price & Pandyan 2000 (PMID 11034725), Ada 2005 (PMID 15674917), Hou 2022 (PMID 35775042) and Chiu 2021 (PMID 34451885). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Stroke telerehabilitation: outcomes match in-person therapy in the trials done so far (Cochrane: no difference in daily-living ability; the one dose-matched trial met non-inferiority) — comparable, not better
shelves.question: In stroke survivors, is telerehabilitation as effective as in-person rehabilitation (or better than usual care) for activities of daily living and motor recovery?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Humans · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Stroke/psychology,therapy · Stroke Rehabilitation/methods · Telerehabilitation/methods
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the benefit claimed here is equivalence, not superiority, and the stamp is held at POSSIBLE because the pooled comparisons are thin. The Cochrane review (22 trials, 1,937 participants) found no difference in activities of daily living between post-discharge telerehabilitation and usual care (SMD −0.00, 95% CI −0.15 to 0.15; moderate-quality evidence, 661 participants) or between telerehabilitation and in-person physical therapy (SMD 0.03, −0.43 to 0.48; low-quality, 75 participants), and no difference in upper-limb function versus in-person therapy. The largest single head-to-head trial (Cramer 2019, n=124) delivered dose-matched arm therapy at home by telerehabilitation versus in clinic and met its non-inferiority criterion (adjusted Fugl-Meyer change difference 0.06 points, −2.14 to 2.26, against a 2.47-point margin), with higher adherence at home (98.3% vs 93.3% of sessions). A 2023 meta-analysis found a small Barthel Index advantage for telerehabilitation (MD 4.18 points, 1.79 to 6.57). Nothing here shows telerehabilitation beating good in-person care; the case for it is access — comparable outcomes for patients who cannot reach a clinic. No trial in the Cochrane review evaluated cost-effectiveness.

cards.headline: Laver, Cochrane 2020: telerehabilitation after stroke — no difference from usual care or in-person therapy for activities of daily living (22 trials, 1,937 participants)
cards.summary: Laver, Cochrane 2020: telerehabilitation after stroke — no difference from usual care or in-person therapy for activities of daily living (22 trials, 1,937 participants)
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis (22 RCTs, n=1,937)
cards.people: 1,937 stroke survivors in 22 randomised trials of telerehabilitation (post-discharge support programmes, upper-limb training, mobility retraining, communication therapy) versus in-person rehabilitation or usual/no rehabilitation; individual studies ranged from 10 to 536 participants and reporting quality was often inadequate.
cards.result: Moderate-quality evidence showed no difference in activities of daily living between post-discharge telerehabilitation and usual care (SMD −0.00, 95% CI −0.15 to 0.15; 2 studies, 661 participants) and low-quality evidence of no difference versus in-person physical therapy (SMD 0.03, −0.43 to 0.48; 2 studies, 75 participants). There was likewise no difference for balance (SMD 0.08, −0.30 to 0.46), health-related quality of life (SMD 0.03, −0.14 to 0.20; 569 participants), depressive symptoms (SMD −0.04, −0.19 to 0.11; 1,145 participants) or upper-limb function versus in-person therapy (MD 1.23, −2.17 to 4.64; 170 participants) — the treatment made no difference on these outcomes. Evidence was insufficient for mobility or satisfaction, and no study evaluated cost-effectiveness.

cards.headline: Cramer 2019: home telerehabilitation was non-inferior to dose-matched in-clinic arm therapy (n=124; Fugl-Meyer change 7.86 vs 8.36 points)
cards.summary: Cramer 2019: home telerehabilitation was non-inferior to dose-matched in-clinic arm therapy (n=124; Fugl-Meyer change 7.86 vs 8.36 points)
cards.type: Randomised assessor-blinded non-inferiority trial, JAMA Neurology 2019
cards.people: 124 adults at 11 US sites, 4–36 weeks after stroke with arm motor deficits (Fugl-Meyer score 22–56 of 66), randomised to 36 sessions (70 minutes each) of arm motor therapy plus stroke education delivered by a home telerehabilitation system or in a traditional outpatient clinic, with intensity, duration and frequency matched between groups.
cards.result: Fugl-Meyer score improved by a mean 7.86 (SD 6.68) points with telerehabilitation and 8.36 (7.04) points in clinic (both P<.001); the covariate-adjusted difference was 0.06 points (95% CI −2.14 to 2.26) in favour of telerehabilitation, and because the 2.47-point non-inferiority margin fell outside that interval, telerehabilitation was declared not inferior. Adherence was higher at home: 35.4 of 36 sessions (98.3%) versus 33.6 of 36 (93.3%). Gains held whether patients were enrolled early (<90 days) or late after stroke.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority rests on the prespecified 2.47-point margin — the interval still allows telerehabilitation to be up to ~2 points worse on a 66-point scale. Participants needed the technology, connectivity and ability to use the home system, and the therapy targeted the arm only; this does not establish equivalence for gait, language or whole-person rehabilitation.
cards.source: Cramer SC et al. Efficacy of Home-Based Telerehabilitation vs In-Clinic Therapy for Adults After Stroke: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Neurol. 2019. PMID: 31233135. cards.headline: Sharififar 2023 meta-analysis: telerehabilitation matched face-to-face therapy across domains, with a small Barthel Index advantage (MD 4.18 points)
cards.summary: Sharififar 2023 meta-analysis: telerehabilitation matched face-to-face therapy across domains, with a small Barthel Index advantage (MD 4.18 points)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs, PM&R 2023
cards.people: Randomised trials of telerehabilitation versus face-to-face rehabilitation after stroke: 13 trials entered the systematic review and 10 the meta-analysis; over half were rated good-to-excellent quality (mean PEDro score 6.6). Adherence in the included studies ranged from 75% to 100%.
cards.result: Telerehabilitation showed equivalency across several outcome domains and was favoured on Wolf Motor Function performance score (MD 1.69 points, 95% CI 0.21 to 3.17) and time score (MD −2.07 s, −4.04 to −0.10, with high heterogeneity, I²=93%), on upper-extremity Functional Mobility Assessment (MD 3.32 points, 0.90 to 5.74), and on the Barthel Index (MD 4.18 points, 1.79 to 6.57). Patient satisfaction with telerehabilitation was highly variable between studies.
cards.watchOut: Some pooled estimates carry very high heterogeneity (I²=93% for the Wolf Motor Function time score), protocols and outcome measures varied substantially, and several comparisons combined telerehabilitation alone with telerehabilitation plus semi-supervised therapy — the Barthel advantage should be read as a small average signal, not a settled margin.
cards.source: Sharififar S et al. Telerehabilitation service impact on physical function and adherence compared to face-to-face rehabilitation in patients with stroke: A systematic review and meta-analysis. PM R. 2023. PMID: 37139741. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: telerehabilitation delivers comparable outcomes to in-person stroke rehabilitation in the trials done — an access intervention, not a superior therapy — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: telerehabilitation delivers comparable outcomes to in-person stroke rehabilitation in the trials done — an access intervention, not a superior therapy — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: the Cochrane review (22 trials, 1,937 participants), the Cramer dose-matched non-inferiority trial (n=124) and the 2023 meta-analysis (13 trials).
cards.result: The consistent finding across syntheses is sameness: daily-living ability, motor scores, mood and quality of life after telerehabilitation are statistically indistinguishable from in-person care or usual care, with one meta-analytic hint of a small Barthel advantage. For a patient who cannot travel to a clinic, comparable outcomes at home are a genuine benefit; nothing supports replacing accessible in-person rehabilitation on outcome grounds.
cards.watchOut: Equivalence claims are only as strong as the margins and sample sizes behind them: the Cochrane head-to-head ADL comparison totals 75 participants. Cost-effectiveness, caregiver burden and outcomes in patients without home connectivity or digital confidence remain unmeasured in this evidence base.
cards.source: Synthesis of Laver 2020 (PMID 32002991), Cramer 2019 (PMID 31233135) and Sharififar 2023 (PMID 37139741). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Family-led rehabilitation after stroke: the one large trial (ATTEND, n=1,250) was neutral — death or dependency 47% in both groups; smaller caregiver-mediated exercise studies point the other way on daily-living scores
shelves.question: In stroke survivors discharged home, does a family-led, caregiver-delivered rehabilitation programme improve death or dependency compared with usual care?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Caregivers/education · Disability Evaluation · Educational Status · Family · Female · Home Care Services, Hospital-Based/organization & administration · Humans · India/epidemiology · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Quality of Life · Single-Blind Method · Socioeconomic Factors · Stroke/mortality · Stroke Rehabilitation/methods · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — this shelf rests principally on a single large trial, and it is labelled as such: ATTEND (n=1,250, 14 hospitals in India) trained family caregivers to deliver rehabilitation started in hospital and continued at home, and found death or dependency at 6 months in 47% of both groups (OR 0.98, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.23, p=0.87), with no difference in mortality, rehospitalisation or non-fatal events. A single-trial null caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. The surrounding evidence is genuinely two-sided: a small Dutch trial of caregiver-mediated exercises with telerehabilitation (41 dyads) was also null on its primary mobility outcome, while a meta-analysis of 11 caregiver-mediated exercise trials (2,120 participants) found a statistically significant benefit for basic activities of daily living — a softer outcome than ATTEND's death-or-dependency endpoint, in programmes where exercise was the major component. The fair summary: the ATTEND model, as delivered, did not reduce death or dependency; whether more intensive or better-supported caregiver exercise programmes improve daily-living scores remains open.

cards.headline: ATTEND (2017): family-led rehabilitation did not reduce death or dependency at 6 months — 47% vs 47% (OR 0.98, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.23) in 1,250 patients
cards.summary: ATTEND (2017): family-led rehabilitation did not reduce death or dependency at 6 months — 47% vs 47% (OR 0.98, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.23) in 1,250 patients
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial (ATTEND), Lancet 2017 — the shelf's single large anchor trial
cards.people: 1,250 patients aged 18 or older, randomised within a month of stroke at 14 hospitals in India, who had residual disability, a reasonable expectation of survival and a family-nominated caregiver: 623 to the family-led intervention and 627 to usual care. Family members received structured rehabilitation training (information, joint goal setting, carer training, task-specific training) begun in hospital and continued at home for up to 2 months; the primary outcome was death or dependency (modified Rankin Scale 3–6) at 6 months, assessed by masked observers.
cards.result: Death or dependency occurred in 285 of 607 patients (47%) in the intervention group and 287 of 605 (47%) in the control group (OR 0.98, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.23, p=0.87) — the treatment made no difference. Deaths were 72 (12%) versus 86 (14%) (p=0.27), rehospitalisation 14% versus 13% (p=0.56), and total non-fatal events did not differ. The trial was stopped neither early nor for harm; it is a completed, adequately sized neutral trial.
cards.watchOut: One trial, one health system: ATTEND tested a specific training package in Indian hospitals where usual care offered little organised rehabilitation, and intervention fidelity and dose at home were limited. Its null does not rule out benefit from more intensive caregiver programmes elsewhere — but it is the only large test, and it was neutral.
cards.source: ATTEND Collaborative Group. Family-led rehabilitation after stroke in India (ATTEND): a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2017. PMID: 28666682. Registry ID: CTRI/2013/04/003557 (Clinical Trials Registry-India) and ACTRN12613000078752 (Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry), both as printed in the record. cards.headline: ARMed4Stroke (Mulder 2024): caregiver-mediated exercises plus telerehabilitation added to usual care — no difference in self-reported mobility (41 dyads)
cards.summary: ARMed4Stroke (Mulder 2024): caregiver-mediated exercises plus telerehabilitation added to usual care — no difference in self-reported mobility (41 dyads)
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial, Clinical Rehabilitation 2024
cards.people: 41 patient–caregiver dyads within 3 months of stroke at four Dutch rehabilitation centres (21 intervention, 20 control; 37 analysed). The intervention was an 8-week blended programme: caregiver-mediated mobility exercises for 2.5 hours per week supported by telerehabilitation plus four face-to-face sessions, on top of usual care. The primary outcome was the self-reported mobility domain of the Stroke Impact Scale after the intervention.
cards.result: Self-reported mobility did not differ between groups (B 0.8, 95% CI −6.8 to 8.5, p=0.826) — the treatment made no difference on the primary outcome. Caregiver quality of life (p=0.013) and caregiver depressive symptoms (p=0.025) favoured the intervention after treatment, as did independence in leisure activities at 6 months (p=0.024); self-reported muscle strength at 6 months favoured controls (p=0.002). The authors note the trial is underpowered and that its findings align with previous trials.
cards.watchOut: With 41 dyads the trial could detect only very large effects; its value is directional consistency with ATTEND on patient mobility, plus a hint that caregivers themselves (quality of life, mood) may be the ones who benefit.
cards.source: Mulder M et al. Allied rehabilitation using caregiver-mediated exercises combined with telerehabilitation for stroke (ARMed4Stroke): A randomised controlled trial. Clin Rehabil. 2024. PMID: 39091094. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Choo 2022 meta-analysis: caregiver-mediated exercise improved basic activities of daily living across 11 trials (2,120 participants) — but not extended ADL, anxiety or depression
cards.summary: Choo 2022 meta-analysis: caregiver-mediated exercise improved basic activities of daily living across 11 trials (2,120 participants) — but not extended ADL, anxiety or depression
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (11 RCTs, n=2,120)
cards.people: 2,120 stroke survivors in 11 randomised trials of caregiver-mediated exercise interventions (10 trials meta-analysed), in which family caregivers delivered exercise-based rehabilitation, usually as the major intervention component; outcomes were basic and extended activities of daily living, anxiety and depression.
cards.result: Meta-analysis found statistically significant effects favouring caregiver-mediated exercise for basic activities of daily living, and subgroup analysis showed the effect concentrated in exercise-only caregiver-mediated interventions. No significant effects were found for extended activities of daily living, anxiety or depression in stroke survivors. The review's abstract reports the direction and significance of the pooled effects without printing a single pooled point estimate.
cards.watchOut: This synthesis pools smaller, varied programmes — not the ATTEND package — and its positive outcome is a daily-living score, not death or dependency. Overlap with the ATTEND population is limited, and without a printed pooled estimate the size of the basic-ADL benefit cannot be judged from the record.
cards.source: Choo WT et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: the one large trial of family-led rehabilitation was neutral on death or dependency; smaller exercise-focused programmes may help daily-living scores — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Synthesis: the one large trial of family-led rehabilitation was neutral on death or dependency; smaller exercise-focused programmes may help daily-living scores — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: ATTEND (n=1,250), ARMed4Stroke (41 dyads) and the caregiver-mediated exercise meta-analysis (11 trials, 2,120 participants).
cards.result: On the question as asked — death or dependency — the only adequately powered test, ATTEND, found 47% versus 47%: no difference, and the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE because that answer rests on a single trial. The meta-analytic signal for basic ADL keeps the broader caregiver-exercise idea alive, but it answers a different, softer question than the one ATTEND posed.
cards.watchOut: A second large trial of a family-led model — with verified home dose and fidelity — is the missing evidence. Until one exists, services should not promise families that taking over rehabilitation reduces death or dependency, however attractive the model is where professional rehabilitation is scarce.
cards.source: Synthesis of ATTEND 2017 (PMID 28666682), Mulder 2024 (PMID 39091094) and Choo 2022 (PMID 35451521). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Ibudilast in progressive MS (SPRINT-MS): brain atrophy progressed more slowly on ibudilast (about 2.5 mL less tissue loss over 96 weeks) — a phase 2 imaging result with no proven clinical benefit yet
shelves.question: In people with primary or secondary progressive multiple sclerosis, does ibudilast slow brain atrophy progression compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Atrophy/prevention & control · Brain/diagnostic imaging,pathology · Depression/chemically induced · Diffusion Tensor Imaging · Disease Progression · Double-Blind Method · Female · Gastrointestinal Diseases/chemically induced · Headache/chemically induced · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Multiple Sclerosis, Chronic Progressive/drug therapy,pathology · Phosphodiesterase Inhibitors/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Pyridines/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Indolizines · Pyrazoles
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single phase 2 programme, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE. In SPRINT-MS (n=255, primary and secondary progressive MS, 96 weeks), ibudilast up to 100 mg daily slowed the rate of brain atrophy versus placebo: the brain parenchymal fraction changed by −0.0010 per year versus −0.0019 per year (difference 0.0009, 95% CI 0.00004 to 0.0017; P=0.04), which the investigators equate to roughly 2.5 mL less brain-tissue loss over 96 weeks. A secondary MRI analysis found 35% less gray-matter atrophy (a relative measure; p=0.038) but no reduction in new or enlarging T2 lesions (37.2% vs 29.0%; p=0.82) or new T1 lesions — a neurodegeneration-marker effect without an anti-inflammatory lesion effect. The earlier relapsing-MS phase 2 trial (n=297) likewise found no effect on new active lesions or relapses, with a smaller percent brain volume change at the 60 mg dose (0.8% vs 1.2%; p=0.04). No trial has shown ibudilast slows disability progression on a clinical primary endpoint, and adverse events included gastrointestinal symptoms, headache and depression. An imaging signal in search of a phase 3 clinical confirmation.

cards.headline: SPRINT-MS (Fox 2018): ibudilast slowed brain atrophy versus placebo over 96 weeks in progressive MS (n=255; parenchymal-fraction difference 0.0009/year, P=0.04)
cards.summary: SPRINT-MS (Fox 2018): ibudilast slowed brain atrophy versus placebo over 96 weeks in progressive MS (n=255; parenchymal-fraction difference 0.0009/year, P=0.04)
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised placebo-controlled trial (SPRINT-MS / NN102), NEJM 2018
cards.people: 255 patients with primary (53%) or secondary (47%) progressive multiple sclerosis randomised to oral ibudilast up to 100 mg daily (n=129) or placebo (n=126) for 96 weeks; the primary endpoint was the rate of brain atrophy measured by brain parenchymal fraction, with diffusion tensor imaging, magnetization transfer ratio, retinal nerve-fiber layer thickness and cortical atrophy as secondary tissue-damage measures.
cards.result: The rate of change in brain parenchymal fraction was −0.0010 per year on ibudilast versus −0.0019 per year on placebo (difference 0.0009, 95% CI 0.00004 to 0.0017; P=0.04) — approximately 2.5 mL less brain-tissue loss with ibudilast over 96 weeks. Adverse events with ibudilast included gastrointestinal symptoms, headache and depression.
cards.watchOut: Brain atrophy is a surrogate: the trial was not powered to show slower disability progression, the P value (0.04) sits close to the significance boundary, and the absolute difference (≈2.5 mL over two years) is small. A positive phase 3 trial with a clinical primary endpoint does not yet exist.

cards.headline: Naismith 2021 (SPRINT-MS MRI analysis): gray-matter atrophy 35% lower on ibudilast (relative measure), but no effect on new T2 or T1 lesions
cards.summary: Naismith 2021 (SPRINT-MS MRI analysis): gray-matter atrophy 35% lower on ibudilast (relative measure), but no effect on new T2 or T1 lesions
cards.type: Secondary MRI analysis of a phase 2 RCT, Neurology 2021
cards.people: The 255 SPRINT-MS participants (129 ibudilast, 126 placebo), in a prespecified-style secondary analysis of the parent trial: gray-matter atrophy, whole-brain atrophy by SIENA, and new or enlarging T2 lesions every 24 weeks plus new T1 hypointensities at 96 weeks.
cards.result: Gray-matter atrophy was reduced by 35% on ibudilast versus placebo (a relative reduction; p=0.038) and whole-brain atrophy by SIENA was slowed by 20% (a relative measure; p=0.08, not significant). New or enlarging T2 lesions occurred in 37.2% on ibudilast versus 29.0% on placebo (p=0.82) and new T1 hypointense lesions in 33.3% versus 23.5% (p=0.11) — no lesion benefit (the treatment made no difference to lesion outcomes). The authors read this as an effect on neurodegeneration markers, not inflammatory activity; the report carries Class II evidence that ibudilast does not significantly reduce new lesions.
cards.watchOut: This is the same patients as the SPRINT-MS card above, not independent confirmation — the two cards describe one trial's primary and secondary imaging readouts. Percentages for lesion outcomes numerically favoured placebo, underlining that any benefit is confined to atrophy measures.
cards.source: Naismith RT et al. Effects of Ibudilast on MRI Measures in the Phase 2 SPRINT-MS Study. Neurology. 2021. PMID: 33268562. cards.headline: Barkhof 2010: in relapsing MS (n=297), ibudilast did not reduce new active lesions or relapses, but percent brain volume change was smaller at 60 mg (0.8% vs 1.2%)
cards.summary: Barkhof 2010: in relapsing MS (n=297), ibudilast did not reduce new active lesions or relapses, but percent brain volume change was smaller at 60 mg (0.8% vs 1.2%)
cards.people: 297 patients with relapsing multiple sclerosis and gadolinium-enhancing lesions at 19 centres, randomised to ibudilast 30 mg, ibudilast 60 mg or placebo daily for 12 months (with follow-up to 2 years); the primary endpoint was the cumulative number of newly active MRI lesions on bimonthly scans.
cards.result: The mean number of active lesions and the relapse rate did not differ between treatment arms (the treatment made no difference to inflammatory activity). Percent brain volume change was reduced in the 60 mg group (0.8%) versus placebo (1.2%) (p=0.04), and post hoc, fewer active lesions evolved into persistent black holes on ibudilast (proportions 0.14 at 60 mg and 0.17 at 30 mg vs 0.24 on placebo). Over 2 years, fewer ibudilast patients had confirmed EDSS progression (p=0.026). Treatment was generally safe and well tolerated; the report grades its own evidence as Class III.
cards.watchOut: A different population (relapsing, not progressive MS) and a negative primary endpoint; the brain-volume and black-hole findings are secondary and partly post hoc. It corroborates the atrophy signal's direction but cannot substitute for a progressive-MS clinical-outcomes trial.
cards.source: Barkhof F et al. Ibudilast in relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis: a neuroprotectant? Neurology. 2010. PMID: 20200338. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: one phase 2 programme, a real but small atrophy signal, no lesion effect and no proven disability benefit — POSSIBLE (benefit), capped as a single programme
cards.summary: Synthesis: one phase 2 programme, a real but small atrophy signal, no lesion effect and no proven disability benefit — POSSIBLE (benefit), capped as a single programme
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: SPRINT-MS (n=255, progressive MS) with its MRI secondary analysis, and the earlier relapsing-MS phase 2 trial (n=297).
cards.result: Across both trials the pattern is consistent: ibudilast does not touch inflammatory lesion activity or relapses, but brain-volume loss runs slower on the drug by several independent MRI measures. That is a coherent neuroprotection hypothesis with phase 2 support — and nothing more, until a trial shows patients progressing more slowly on a clinical scale.
cards.watchOut: Atrophy measures are sensitive to measurement technique and fluid shifts ('pseudoatrophy'); equipment changes during SPRINT-MS were themselves the subject of a methods report. Depression and gastrointestinal effects may also limit long-term tolerability in a population already prone to depression.
cards.source: Synthesis of Fox 2018 (PMID 30157388), Naismith 2021 (PMID 33268562) and Barkhof 2010 (PMID 20200338). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Opicinumab (anti-LINGO-1) in relapsing MS: a negative programme — SYNERGY, RENEW and AFFINITY all missed their primary endpoints (the treatment made no difference)
shelves.question: In people with relapsing multiple sclerosis, does opicinumab added to interferon beta improve disability recovery compared with interferon beta alone?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Antibodies, Monoclonal/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Disability Evaluation · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Multiple Sclerosis, Chronic Progressive/drug therapy · Multiple Sclerosis, Relapsing-Remitting/drug therapy · Secondary Prevention · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — three randomised trials of the anti-LINGO-1 remyelination programme, and every primary endpoint missed. SYNERGY (n=419, opicinumab added to intramuscular interferon beta-1a in relapsing MS) found confirmed disability improvement in 49% on placebo versus 47–65% across opicinumab doses with no linear dose–response (trend p=0.89) — a non-monotonic pattern the authors did not claim as efficacy. RENEW (n=82, acute optic neuritis) missed its remyelination primary endpoint in the intention-to-treat population (visual evoked potential latency difference −3.5 ms, 95% CI −10.6 to 3.7; p=0.33), with a nominally positive per-protocol analysis (p=0.050) that cannot carry the claim. AFFINITY Part 1 (n=263, opicinumab added to disease-modifying therapies) found an Overall Disability Response Score difference of 0.15 (−0.05 to 0.35; p=0.148), not significant. The shelf's question names the interferon-beta comparison (SYNERGY's design); RENEW and AFFINITY are carded as the rest of the same programme, and their designs are stated on their faces. A well-conducted negative programme: remyelination by LINGO-1 blockade, at these doses and timings, did not translate into measurable recovery.

cards.headline: SYNERGY (Cadavid 2019): opicinumab plus interferon beta-1a — no dose–response for confirmed disability improvement (n=419; placebo 49%, doses 47–65%, trend p=0.89)
cards.summary: SYNERGY (Cadavid 2019): opicinumab plus interferon beta-1a — no dose–response for confirmed disability improvement (n=419; placebo 49%, doses 47–65%, trend p=0.89)
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised placebo-controlled dose-ranging trial (SYNERGY), Lancet Neurology 2019
cards.people: 419 patients aged 18–58 with relapsing multiple sclerosis (relapsing-remitting, or secondary progressive with relapses) at 72 sites in 12 countries, randomised to placebo (n=93) or opicinumab 3 mg/kg (n=45), 10 mg/kg (n=95), 30 mg/kg (n=94) or 100 mg/kg (n=92) intravenously every 4 weeks; every participant also self-administered weekly intramuscular interferon beta-1a. The primary endpoint was the percentage achieving confirmed disability improvement over 72 weeks on a multicomponent measure (EDSS, Timed 25-Foot Walk, Nine-Hole Peg Test, Paced Auditory Serial Addition Test).
cards.result: Confirmed disability improvement occurred in 45 of 91 patients (49%) on placebo, 21 of 45 (47%) at 3 mg/kg, 59 of 94 (63%) at 10 mg/kg, 59 of 91 (65%) at 30 mg/kg and 36 of 91 (40%) at 100 mg/kg. A linear dose–response was not seen (linear trend test p=0.89), so the primary analysis did not support efficacy (the treatment made no difference by the trial's own primary test). Adverse events occurred in 85% of patients in both the placebo group and the pooled opicinumab groups.
cards.watchOut: The mid-dose percentages (63–65% vs 49%) invite cherry-picking; with the highest dose below placebo (40%) and a null trend test, the pattern is what chance looks like across four dose arms. Disability improvement is also an unusual, noise-prone endpoint in relapsing MS — but it was the prespecified one, and it missed.
cards.source: Cadavid D et al. Safety and efficacy of opicinumab in patients with relapsing multiple sclerosis (SYNERGY): a randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 2 trial. Lancet Neurol. 2019. PMID: 31285147. Registry ID: NCT01864148 (ClinicalTrials.gov, from the record's databank fields). cards.headline: RENEW (Cadavid 2017): opicinumab after acute optic neuritis missed its remyelination endpoint in the full population (n=82; latency difference −3.5 ms, p=0.33)
cards.summary: RENEW (Cadavid 2017): opicinumab after acute optic neuritis missed its remyelination endpoint in the full population (n=82; latency difference −3.5 ms, p=0.33)
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised placebo-controlled trial (RENEW), Lancet Neurology 2017
cards.people: 82 participants aged 18–55 with a first unilateral acute optic neuritis episode, treated first with high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone, then randomised (41 per group) to opicinumab 100 mg/kg or placebo every 4 weeks for six doses; the primary endpoint was recovery of affected optic-nerve conduction latency on full-field visual evoked potentials at week 24 versus the fellow eye at baseline.
cards.result: In the intention-to-treat population the adjusted mean treatment difference was −3.5 ms (17.3 vs 20.8 ms; 95% CI −10.6 to 3.7; p=0.33) — not significant (the treatment made no difference on the primary analysis). The prespecified per-protocol population (33 opicinumab, 36 placebo) showed −7.6 ms (p=0.050) at week 24 and −9.1 ms (p=0.011) at week 32. Adverse-event incidence was identical (83% in each group), and no significant effects on brain MRI measures were seen.
cards.watchOut: RENEW tests a different clinical setting (acute optic neuritis, no interferon background) from this shelf's question; it is carded as programme evidence. Its positive readings live only in the per-protocol subset — the analysis most vulnerable to bias — while the primary intention-to-treat analysis was null.
cards.source: Cadavid D et al. Safety and efficacy of opicinumab in acute optic neuritis (RENEW): a randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 2 trial. Lancet Neurol. 2017. PMID: 28229892. cards.headline: AFFINITY Part 1 (Calabresi 2026): opicinumab added to disease-modifying therapy — Overall Disability Response Score difference 0.15 (95% CI −0.05 to 0.35; p=0.148), not significant (n=263)
cards.summary: AFFINITY Part 1 (Calabresi 2026): opicinumab added to disease-modifying therapy — Overall Disability Response Score difference 0.15 (95% CI −0.05 to 0.35; p=0.148), not significant (n=263)
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised controlled trial (AFFINITY Part 1), Multiple Sclerosis Journal 2026
cards.people: 263 participants aged 18–58 with relapsing multiple sclerosis and disease duration up to 20 years, randomised 1:1 to intravenous opicinumab or placebo every 4 weeks for 72 weeks as add-on therapy to anti-inflammatory disease-modifying therapies; the primary endpoint was the Overall Disability Response Score over 72 weeks.
cards.result: The adjusted mean difference on the Overall Disability Response Score was 0.15 (95% CI −0.05 to 0.35; p=0.148) in favour of opicinumab — not statistically significant (the treatment made no difference). Numerically larger differences appeared in subgroups (age ≥40, EDSS ≥3.0, disease duration ≥6 years, dimethyl fumarate background), which the authors offer as design lessons for future remyelination trials. Adverse events occurred in 85% of the placebo group and 86% of the opicinumab group.
cards.watchOut: AFFINITY's background therapy was any disease-modifying therapy, not interferon beta specifically, and its composite response score differs from SYNERGY's endpoint — the trials are programme siblings, not replicates. Subgroup patterns after a null primary are hypothesis-generating only.
cards.source: Calabresi PA et al. Safety and efficacy of opicinumab in participants with relapsing multiple sclerosis (AFFINITY Part 1): A randomized, controlled, phase 2 trial. Mult Scler. 2026. cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: SYNERGY (n=419, with interferon beta-1a), RENEW (n=82, acute optic neuritis) and AFFINITY Part 1 (n=263, with disease-modifying therapies) — 764 randomised participants in total.
cards.result: No trial in the programme met its primary endpoint, the largest trial showed no dose–response, and the only positive analyses are a per-protocol subset and post-primary subgroups. Opicinumab was not shown to improve disability recovery or remyelination measures in any prespecified primary analysis, and development did not proceed to a positive phase 3.
cards.watchOut: A null programme does not disprove remyelination as a strategy — dose, timing after injury, patient selection and endpoint sensitivity are all live explanations the AFFINITY authors themselves raise. What is settled is narrower: opicinumab, as dosed in these three trials, made no measurable difference.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cadavid 2019 (PMID 31285147), Cadavid 2017 (PMID 28229892) and Calabresi 2026 (PMID 41454463). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Citicoline in acute ischaemic stroke: SPLIT — an early pooled analysis was positive (recovery 25.2% vs 20.2%), but the definitive ICTUS trial (n=2,298) and the Cochrane review found no benefit
shelves.question: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke, does citicoline improve functional outcome compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Administration, Oral · Aged · Brain Ischemia/drug therapy · Cytidine Diphosphate Choline/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Injections, Intravenous · Ischemia/drug therapy · Male · Nootropic Agents/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the evidence genuinely divides by era and size, and the split is named here rather than averaged away. The early trials, pooled patient-by-patient in 2002 (4 trials; 1,372 patients analysed), found complete recovery at 3 months in 25.2% on citicoline versus 20.2% on placebo (OR 1.33, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.62) — the result that kept citicoline licensed for stroke in some countries. The definitive test then disagreed: ICTUS (n=2,298, moderate-to-severe stroke) was stopped for futility, with global recovery odds ratio 1.03 (0.86 to 1.25; p=0.364) — the treatment made no difference. The 2020 Cochrane review (10 trials, 4,281 participants, all at high risk of bias) found little or no difference in mortality (17.3% vs 18.5%; RR 0.94, 0.83 to 1.07), disability or dependence (RR 1.11, 0.97 to 1.26) or Barthel-defined recovery (RR 1.03, 0.94 to 1.13), and its trial sequential analysis suggested no more trials are needed for the primary outcomes. Weight of evidence sits with ICTUS and Cochrane; the shelf is stamped SPLIT because the positive pooled analysis is real, published evidence that a reader will meet, not because the two sides are evenly matched. (Citicoline for traumatic brain injury — COBRIT — is a different question, homed on shelf #1267.)

cards.headline: Dávalos 2002 pooled analysis: oral citicoline raised complete recovery at 3 months (25.2% vs 20.2%; OR 1.33, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.62)
cards.summary: Dávalos 2002 pooled analysis: oral citicoline raised complete recovery at 3 months (25.2% vs 20.2%; OR 1.33, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.62)
cards.type: Individual patient data pooling analysis of 4 RCTs, Stroke 2002
cards.people: Individual patient data from four prospective, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials of oral citicoline (500, 1000 or 2000 mg) started within 24 hours in moderate-to-severe acute ischaemic stroke: 1,652 patients were randomised and 1,372 met the pooling criteria (789 citicoline, 583 placebo). Recovery was a composite — NIH Stroke Scale ≤1, modified Rankin Scale ≤1 and Barthel Index ≥95 at 3 months.
cards.result: Recovery occurred in 25.2% of citicoline-treated patients versus 20.2% on placebo (OR 1.33, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.62; P=0.0034) — an absolute difference of 5.0 percentage points. The largest difference was at the 2000 mg dose (27.9% recovery; OR 1.38, 1.10 to 1.72; P=0.0043). Overall safety was similar to placebo.
cards.watchOut: Only one of the four pooled trials had itself reached significance on its primary variables, and 280 of 1,652 randomised patients were excluded by the pooling criteria. Industry-held bibliographic databases were among the search sources. This is exactly the species of positive pooled signal that a large confirmatory trial exists to test — and ICTUS tested it.
cards.source: Dávalos A et al. Oral citicoline in acute ischemic stroke: an individual patient data pooling analysis of clinical trials. Stroke. 2002. PMID: 12468781. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era trials).
