cards.headline: ICTUS (Dávalos 2012): citicoline did not improve global recovery — OR 1.03 (95% CI 0.86 to 1.25); the trial was stopped for futility (n=2,298)
cards.summary: ICTUS (Dávalos 2012): citicoline did not improve global recovery — OR 1.03 (95% CI 0.86 to 1.25); the trial was stopped for futility (n=2,298)
cards.people: 2,298 patients with moderate-to-severe acute ischaemic stroke at 59 university hospitals in Spain, Portugal and Germany, randomised within 24 hours of onset to citicoline (1,148) or placebo (1,150): 1000 mg intravenously every 12 hours for 3 days, then oral citicoline for a total of 6 weeks. The primary outcome was global recovery at 90 days, combining NIH Stroke Scale ≤1, modified Rankin score ≤1 and Barthel Index ≥95.
cards.result: Global recovery was similar in both groups (OR 1.03, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.25; p=0.364) — the treatment made no difference. The trial was stopped for futility at the third interim analysis, on complete data from 2,078 patients. No significant differences appeared in safety variables, symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage, neurological deterioration, mortality or overall adverse events.
cards.watchOut: ICTUS enrolled in the thrombolysis era and used the same global-recovery construct as the pooled analysis, so the disagreement cannot be explained away by endpoints. The trial was funded by the drug's manufacturer (Ferrer Grupo, declared in the record) — which makes its futility-stopped null more, not less, credible.
cards.source: Dávalos A et al. Citicoline in the treatment of acute ischaemic stroke: an international, randomised, multicentre, placebo-controlled study (ICTUS trial). Lancet. 2012. PMID: 22691567. Registry ID: NCT00331890 (ClinicalTrials.gov, from the record's databank fields). cards.headline: Cochrane 2020: across 10 trials (4,281 participants) citicoline showed little or no difference in mortality, disability or functional recovery
cards.summary: Cochrane 2020: across 10 trials (4,281 participants) citicoline showed little or no difference in mortality, disability or functional recovery
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis (10 RCTs, n=4,281)
cards.people: 4,281 participants with acute ischaemic stroke in 10 randomised trials of citicoline (oral, intravenous or both; 500–2000 mg/day) versus placebo or standard care. All included trials were assessed as at high risk of bias, and drug companies sponsored six of them.
cards.result: Pooled mortality was 17.3% on citicoline versus 18.5% on placebo (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.07; 8 trials; low-quality evidence). Disability or dependence on the Rankin scale did not differ (21.72% vs 19.23%; RR 1.11, 0.97 to 1.26; 4 trials), nor did Barthel Index ≥95 recovery (32.78% vs 30.70%; RR 1.03, 0.94 to 1.13) or NIH Stroke Scale ≤1 (24.31% vs 22.44%; RR 1.08, 0.96 to 1.21). Serious cardiovascular adverse events were similar (RR 1.04, 0.84 to 1.29). A pre-planned trial sequential analysis suggested no more trials may be needed for the primary outcomes; no trial reported quality of life.
cards.watchOut: The review's certainty is low throughout because every trial carried high risk of bias and harms were poorly reported — so its verdict is 'little or no difference' rather than proof of exact equivalence. It nonetheless includes ICTUS, and its pooled null is dominated by that trial's weight.
cards.source: Martí-Carvajal AJ et al. Citicoline for treating people with acute ischemic stroke. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2020. PMID: 32860632. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT — the early pooled signal was positive, the definitive trial and the Cochrane synthesis are null; the weight of evidence is against benefit
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT — the early pooled signal was positive, the definitive trial and the Cochrane synthesis are null; the weight of evidence is against benefit
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: the 2002 individual-patient pooled analysis (1,372 patients analysed), ICTUS (n=2,298) and the Cochrane review (10 trials, 4,281 participants).
cards.result: This is the classic neuroprotection arc: small early trials pool to a promising 5-point absolute recovery gain, and the one trial large enough to settle the question finds an odds ratio of 1.03. The shelf records both, because clinicians will encounter citicoline prescribed on the strength of the earlier literature — but a reader weighing where the evidence now sits should land on ICTUS and Cochrane.
cards.watchOut: Citicoline remains approved for stroke in some countries, so exposure continues despite the trial record. No prespecified subgroup in ICTUS rescued the result; claims for benefit in older patients or specific severities rest on post hoc analyses of the early trials.
cards.source: Synthesis of Dávalos 2002 (PMID 12468781), Dávalos 2012 ICTUS (PMID 22691567) and Martí-Carvajal 2020 (PMID 32860632). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Prehospital magnesium in acute stroke (FAST-MAG): treatment started a median 45 minutes after onset still did not improve 90-day disability — mean Rankin score 2.7 in both groups (the treatment made no difference)
shelves.question: In patients with suspected acute stroke, does intravenous magnesium sulphate started by paramedics in the field improve 90-day functional outcome compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Aged · Brain Ischemia/complications · Double-Blind Method · Emergency Medical Services · Female · Hemorrhage/etiology · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Intracranial Hemorrhages/complications · Magnesium Sulfate/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Neuroprotective Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Stroke/drug therapy,etiology,mortality · Time-to-Treatment
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference). FAST-MAG removed the usual excuse for neuroprotection failures — delay: paramedics started intravenous magnesium a median of 45 minutes after symptom onset, within 2 hours in all 1,700 enrolled patients with suspected stroke, yet 90-day disability was identical (mean modified Rankin score 2.7 in both groups, P=1.00; shift analysis P=0.28) and mortality was 15.4% versus 15.5%. The earlier in-hospital trial agreed: IMAGES (n=2,589, treatment within 12 hours) found a primary-outcome odds ratio of 0.95 (95% CI 0.80 to 1.13, p=0.59), with mortality if anything higher on magnesium (hazard ratio 1.18, 0.97 to 1.42). A 2019 meta-analysis of seven trials (4,347 patients) found no improvement in global outcome (SMD −0.01, −0.12 to 0.10), functional outcome or mortality (OR 1.10, 0.94 to 1.29); its one positive subgroup signal (ischaemic stroke only) is flagged by its own authors as needing extreme caution. Prehospital magnesium is feasible and safe — and ineffective for stroke outcome.

cards.headline: FAST-MAG (Saver 2015): paramedic-started magnesium within 2 hours did not improve 90-day disability (n=1,700; mean Rankin 2.7 vs 2.7, P=1.00)
cards.summary: FAST-MAG (Saver 2015): paramedic-started magnesium within 2 hours did not improve 90-day disability (n=1,700; mean Rankin 2.7 vs 2.7, P=1.00)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised placebo-controlled prehospital trial (FAST-MAG), NEJM 2015
cards.people: 1,700 patients with suspected acute stroke (857 magnesium, 843 placebo), mean age 69, enrolled by paramedics in the field: an intravenous magnesium loading dose started before hospital arrival within 2 hours of symptom onset, followed by a 24-hour maintenance infusion in hospital. The final diagnosis was cerebral ischaemia in 73.3%, intracranial haemorrhage in 22.8% and a stroke mimic in 3.9%. Median time from last-known-well to infusion start was 45 minutes, and 74.3% were treated within the first hour.
cards.result: There was no significant shift in the distribution of 90-day disability on the modified Rankin scale (P=0.28), and mean 90-day scores were identical (2.7 in each group, P=1.00) — the treatment made no difference. Mortality was 15.4% on magnesium versus 15.5% on placebo (P=0.95), with no significant difference in all serious adverse events. Prehospital initiation was safe and achieved start times no in-hospital trial could match.
cards.watchOut: About a quarter of enrollees turned out to have haemorrhage or a mimic, diluting any ischaemia-specific effect — but the trial's question was deliberately the real-world prehospital one, where the diagnosis is not yet known. The result closes the 'we just gave it too late' argument for magnesium: 45 minutes was not too late to matter; the drug simply did not work.
cards.source: Saver JL et al. Prehospital use of magnesium sulfate as neuroprotection in acute stroke. N Engl J Med. 2015. PMID: 25651247. Registry ID: NCT00059332 (ClinicalTrials.gov, from the record's databank fields). cards.headline: IMAGES (Muir 2004): intravenous magnesium within 12 hours of stroke did not reduce death or disability (n=2,589; OR 0.95, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.13)
cards.summary: IMAGES (Muir 2004): intravenous magnesium within 12 hours of stroke did not reduce death or disability (n=2,589; OR 0.95, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.13)
cards.people: 2,589 patients randomised within 12 hours of acute stroke to intravenous magnesium sulphate (16 mmol over 15 minutes, then 65 mmol over 24 hours) or matching placebo; the efficacy dataset included 2,386 patients. The primary outcome was a global endpoint expressed as the common odds ratio for death or disability at day 90, with prespecified subgroups by time to treatment (<6 vs ≥6 hours), ischaemic versus non-ischaemic stroke and cortical versus non-cortical syndromes.
cards.result: The primary outcome was not improved by magnesium (OR 0.95, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.13, p=0.59) — the treatment made no difference. Mortality was slightly higher in the magnesium group (hazard ratio 1.18, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.42, p=0.098), and no secondary outcome (Barthel <95, Barthel <60, modified Rankin >1) showed a treatment effect. A planned subgroup analysis unexpectedly favoured magnesium in non-cortical (lacunar-type) strokes (p=0.011), opposite to the cortical benefit the investigators had expected.
cards.watchOut: The lacunar subgroup signal was one of several prespecified cuts and ran against the trial's own mechanistic expectation; FAST-MAG's much earlier treatment did not reproduce any benefit. The mortality point estimate above 1.0 is not significant but leaves no room to claim a hidden survival advantage.
cards.source: Muir KW et al. Magnesium for acute stroke (Intravenous Magnesium Efficacy in Stroke trial): randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2004. PMID: 14962524. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.summary: Avgerinos 2019 meta-analysis: seven trials, 4,347 patients — intravenous magnesium did not improve global outcome, functional outcome or mortality at 90 days
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (7 RCTs, n=4,347), Stroke 2019
cards.people: 4,347 patients with acute stroke (ischaemic and non-ischaemic) in seven randomised trials of intravenous magnesium sulphate versus placebo, synthesising 90-day global outcome (modified Rankin Scale), functional outcome (Barthel Index) and mortality with random-effects models.
cards.result: Treatment did not improve functional outcome (Barthel Index >60: OR 1.05, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.19; >95: OR 0.95, 0.76 to 1.20) or global outcome (modified Rankin standardised mean difference −0.01, −0.12 to 0.10), and mortality was unaltered (OR 1.10, 0.94 to 1.29) — the treatment made no difference on any pooled outcome. A subgroup meta-analysis confined to ischaemic stroke showed a lower Rankin score (weighted mean difference −0.96, −1.34 to −0.58), which the authors state should be viewed with extreme caution given the limited number of patients included.
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials are dominated by IMAGES and FAST-MAG, so this is corroboration of the two large trials rather than independent evidence. The ischaemic-only subgroup rests on few patients and contradicts FAST-MAG's design lesson; it should not drive practice.
cards.source: Avgerinos KI et al. Intravenous Magnesium Sulfate in Acute Stroke. Stroke. 2019. PMID: 30852968. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: given within the hour by paramedics or within 12 hours in hospital, magnesium did not change stroke outcome in over 4,000 randomised patients — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Synthesis: given within the hour by paramedics or within 12 hours in hospital, magnesium did not change stroke outcome in over 4,000 randomised patients — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: FAST-MAG (n=1,700, prehospital), IMAGES (n=2,589, in-hospital) and the 2019 meta-analysis (7 trials, 4,347 patients).
cards.result: Magnesium is the cleanest negative in stroke neuroprotection: biologically plausible, safe, deliverable earlier than any competing agent — and null on disability and mortality in every large test. The prehospital delivery model FAST-MAG pioneered remains valuable for testing other agents; magnesium itself should not be given to improve stroke outcome.
cards.watchOut: This shelf concerns magnesium for the stroke itself. Magnesium for other indications in the same patients — eclampsia prevention, fetal neuroprotection before preterm birth — is settled on other shelves and is unaffected by this null.

shelves.title: Subdural drain after burr-hole evacuation of chronic subdural haematoma: recurrence fell from 24% to 9.3% in the Santarius trial, and two syntheses agree — drains roughly halve recurrence
shelves.question: In patients undergoing burr-hole evacuation of chronic subdural haematoma, does leaving a subdural drain reduce recurrence compared with no drain?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Craniotomy · Drainage · Female · Hematoma, Subdural, Chronic/complications,diagnosis,mortality,surgery · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Survival Rate · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit). The anchor trial was stopped early because the benefit was already clear: in Santarius 2009 (215 patients randomised after burr-hole evacuation), recurrence needing re-drainage occurred in 9.3% with a subdural drain versus 24% without (p=0.003) — an absolute reduction of about 15 percentage points — and 6-month mortality was also lower (8.6% vs 18.1%, p=0.042), with similar complication rates. Both syntheses agree on recurrence: the Cochrane review (9 trials, 968 participants) found a relative risk of recurrence of 0.45 (95% CI 0.32 to 0.61) with external drains — a 55% relative risk reduction, labelled relative — with no strong evidence of more complications (RR 1.15, 0.77 to 1.72) and an uncertain mortality effect (RR 0.78, 0.45 to 1.33); the 2023 meta-analysis (10 studies, 1,961 patients) found recurrence odds ratio 0.39 (0.28 to 0.55) and mortality odds ratio 0.65 (0.43 to 0.97). Recurrence is the outcome every source agrees on; the mortality benefit rests mainly on the single stopped-early trial and one meta-analysis, so it is stated more cautiously than the recurrence claim. (Dexamethasone for chronic subdural haematoma is a different, medical question, homed on shelf #2391; middle meningeal artery embolisation is homed on live shelf #339.)

cards.headline: Santarius 2009: a subdural drain after burr-hole evacuation cut recurrence from 24% to 9.3% (p=0.003) — the trial was stopped early for benefit (n=215 randomised)
cards.summary: Santarius 2009: a subdural drain after burr-hole evacuation cut recurrence from 24% to 9.3% (p=0.003) — the trial was stopped early for benefit (n=215 randomised)
cards.people: 269 patients aged 18 or older with chronic subdural haematoma at one UK centre were assessed; 215 were randomised after burr-hole evacuation — 108 to a drain inserted into the subdural space and 107 to no drain. The primary endpoint was recurrence needing re-drainage, analysed by intention to treat; the trial was stopped early because of the significant reduction in recurrence.
cards.result: Recurrence occurred in 10 of 108 patients (9.3%) with a drain versus 26 of 107 (24%) without (p=0.003) — an absolute reduction of about 15 percentage points. At 6 months, mortality was 9 of 105 (8.6%) with a drain versus 19 of 105 (18.1%) without (p=0.042). Medical and surgical complications were much the same between the groups.
cards.watchOut: Trials stopped early for benefit tend to overestimate effect size, and this was a single centre; the mortality difference (a secondary outcome) is the figure most likely to shrink on replication. The recurrence direction, however, is confirmed by both syntheses carded below.
cards.source: Santarius T et al. Use of drains versus no drains after burr-hole evacuation of chronic subdural haematoma: a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2009. PMID: 19782872. Registry ID: ISRCTN97314294 (from the record's databank fields). cards.headline: Cochrane 2016 (Peng & Liu): external drains after burr-hole evacuation — recurrence relative risk 0.45 (95% CI 0.32 to 0.61) across 9 trials (968 participants)
cards.summary: Cochrane 2016 (Peng & Liu): external drains after burr-hole evacuation — recurrence relative risk 0.45 (95% CI 0.32 to 0.61) across 9 trials (968 participants)
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis (9 RCTs, n=968)
cards.people: 968 adults with chronic subdural haematoma in nine randomised trials comparing external subdural drains with no drains after burr-hole evacuation; only one trial (the large single-centre Santarius trial) reported adequate allocation concealment.
cards.result: All included trials reported reduced recurrence with drains; the pooled relative risk of recurrence was 0.45 (95% CI 0.32 to 0.61; I²=38%; moderate-quality evidence) — a 55% relative risk reduction, labelled relative. There was no strong evidence of increased complications (RR 1.15, 0.77 to 1.72; 7 studies, 710 participants; low-quality evidence), and effects on mortality (RR 0.78, 0.45 to 1.33; 5 studies, 539 participants) and poor functional outcome (RR 0.68, 0.44 to 1.05) were uncertain.
cards.watchOut: The pooled estimate leans heavily on Santarius — most other trials were small and at unclear risk of bias — so the Cochrane and Santarius cards are not fully independent. The reviewers themselves caution that further research may change the estimate, particularly for mortality and function.
cards.source: Peng D et al.. External drains versus no drains after burr-hole evacuation for the treatment of chronic subdural haematoma in adults. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2016. PMID: 27578263. cards.headline: Aljabali 2023 meta-analysis: drainage reduced recurrence (OR 0.39), mortality (OR 0.65) and gross focal neurological deficit (OR 0.58) across 1,961 patients
cards.summary: Aljabali 2023 meta-analysis: drainage reduced recurrence (OR 0.39), mortality (OR 0.65) and gross focal neurological deficit (OR 0.58) across 1,961 patients
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (10 studies, n=1,961), Neurosurgical Review 2023
cards.people: 1,961 patients with chronic subdural haematoma in 10 studies (searched to June 2022) comparing drainage versus no drainage after burr-hole evacuation, pooled as odds ratios for recurrence, mortality, gross focal neurological deficit and Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15.
cards.result: Drainage was significantly more effective than no drainage for recurrence (OR 0.39, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.55; P<0.00001), mortality (OR 0.65, 0.43 to 0.97; P=0.04) and gross focal neurological deficit (OR 0.58, 0.37 to 0.89; P=0.01). There was no significant difference in achieving a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15 (OR 1.21, 0.84 to 1.76; P=0.30).
cards.watchOut: Odds ratios exaggerate the apparent size of effects when events are common (recurrence ~24% in controls), so the OR of 0.39 should not be read as a 61% relative risk reduction. The study set overlaps the Cochrane set and includes the Santarius trial; concordance is reassuring but the sources are not independent.
cards.source: Aljabali A et al. Drainage versus no drainage after burr-hole evacuation of chronic subdural hematoma: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 1961 patients. Neurosurg Rev. 2023. cards.headline: Synthesis: leave the drain — recurrence is roughly halved in the trial and both syntheses, with no complication penalty shown — LIKELY (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: leave the drain — recurrence is roughly halved in the trial and both syntheses, with no complication penalty shown — LIKELY (benefit)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Santarius 2009 (215 randomised), the Cochrane review (9 trials, 968 participants) and the 2023 meta-analysis (10 studies, 1,961 patients).
cards.result: A subdural drain after burr-hole evacuation is one of the simpler wins in neurosurgery: recurrence needing reoperation fell from about one in four patients to about one in eleven in the anchor trial, both meta-analyses point the same way, and no source shows a complication cost. The mortality claim is softer than the recurrence claim and is flagged as such on the cards.
cards.watchOut: Open details the evidence does not settle: drain duration, subdural versus subperiosteal/subgaleal position, and whether drains help equally in patients also receiving middle meningeal artery embolisation (live shelf #339) — those are separate questions with their own, thinner literatures.
cards.source: Synthesis of Santarius 2009 (PMID 19782872), Peng 2016 (PMID 27578263) and Aljabali 2023 (PMID 37726502). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: NITE-AD sleep programme in Alzheimer's dementia: fewer night awakenings at 2 months in two small trials — POSSIBLE
shelves.question: In people with Alzheimer's dementia and sleep disturbance, does the NITE-AD multicomponent programme (sleep hygiene, daily walking, light exposure) improve sleep compared with education control?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Alzheimer Disease/complications,therapy · Caregivers/education · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders/etiology,psychology,therapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). The NITE-AD programme — caregiver-delivered sleep-hygiene education, daily walking and increased light exposure — was tested in two randomised trials from one research programme. In the first (McCurry 2005, n=36 — N printed on the face per the build flag), patients on NITE-AD showed significantly greater posttest reductions in number of nighttime awakenings, total time awake at night and depression, and more weekly exercise days, than education controls, with gains maintained at 6 months. In the larger four-arm trial (McCurry 2011, n=132), walking, light and the combination each improved actigraphic total wake time versus contact control at posttest (effect sizes 0.51–0.63), but no group differences remained at 6 months and caregiver-rated sleep quality did not significantly improve. A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of non-pharmacological sleep interventions in Alzheimer's disease (14 randomised trials, 937 participants) found a modest improvement in subjective sleep quality (PSQI standardised mean difference −0.46, 95% CI −0.70 to −0.21), noted that caregiver-delivered programmes such as NITE-AD modestly reduced nocturnal awakenings, and found no significant effects on objective actigraphic outcomes. One programme, small first trial, fading durability: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: McCurry 2005 (NITE-AD, n=36): fewer nighttime awakenings, less time awake at night and less depression than education control at 2 months, gains maintained at 6 months
cards.summary: McCurry 2005 (NITE-AD, n=36): fewer nighttime awakenings, less time awake at night and less depression than education control at 2 months, gains maintained at 6 months
cards.people: 36 community-dwelling patients with Alzheimer's disease and their family caregivers in a randomised controlled trial; active treatment n=17, control n=19. Sleep measured by 1 week of wrist actigraphy (Actillume) at baseline, posttest (2 months) and 6-month follow-up.
cards.result: All participants received written sleep-hygiene materials. Caregivers in the active arm received specific training to implement a sleep hygiene programme and behaviour-management skills; patients were instructed to walk daily and increase daytime light exposure with a light box. Controls received general dementia education and caregiver support. NITE-AD patients showed significantly greater (P<.05) posttest reductions in number of nighttime awakenings, total time awake at night, and depression, and increases in weekly exercise days than controls. At 6-month follow-up, treatment gains were maintained and additional significant improvements in duration of night awakenings emerged; with cognitive level controlled, NITE-AD patients had lower longitudinal ratings of daytime sleepiness.
cards.watchOut: Very small first trial (n=36) from the programme's own developers; actigraphy-based outcomes over 1-week windows; the control arm received education and support, not no treatment.
cards.source: McCurry SM et al. Nighttime insomnia treatment and education for Alzheimer's disease: a randomized, controlled trial. J Am Geriatr Soc. 2005. PMID: 15877554. cards.headline: McCurry 2011 (n=132): walking, light and the combination each improved actigraphic total wake time versus control at posttest (effect sizes 0.51–0.63) — but no group differences at 6 months
cards.summary: McCurry 2011 (n=132): walking, light and the combination each improved actigraphic total wake time versus control at posttest (effect sizes 0.51–0.63) — but no group differences at 6 months
cards.people: 132 community-dwelling people with Alzheimer's disease and their in-home caregivers in a randomised controlled trial with blinded assessors, assigned to walking, light exposure, combination treatment (walking, light and sleep education) or contact control, with three or six in-home visits.
cards.result: Primary outcomes were actigraphic total wake time and caregiver ratings on the Sleep Disorders Inventory (SDI). At posttest, walking (P=.05), light (P=.04) and combination treatment (P=.01) each produced significantly greater improvements in total wake time than control, with effect sizes 0.51–0.63, and moderate effect-size improvements in actigraphic sleep percentage; there was no significant improvement on the SDI and no significant differences between the active arms. At 6 months there were no group differences for any sleep outcome. Participants with better adherence (4 days/week) to walking and light recommendations had significantly less total wake time (P=.006) and better sleep efficiency (P=.005) at posttest than those with poorer adherence.
cards.watchOut: Benefits were actigraphic, not caregiver-rated, and had faded by 6 months; effects depended on adherence, which dementia itself undermines.
cards.source: McCurry SM et al. Increasing walking and bright light exposure to improve sleep in community-dwelling persons with Alzheimer's disease: results of a randomized, controlled trial. cards.headline: Zhang 2026 (meta-analysis, 14 RCTs, 937 participants): non-pharmacological interventions modestly improved subjective sleep quality (SMD −0.46); no significant objective actigraphic effects; NITE-AD-type programmes modestly reduced nocturnal awakenings
cards.summary: Zhang 2026 (meta-analysis, 14 RCTs, 937 participants): non-pharmacological interventions modestly improved subjective sleep quality (SMD −0.46); no significant objective actigraphic effects; NITE-AD-type programmes modestly reduced nocturnal awakenings
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis (PRISMA) of randomised controlled trials of non-pharmacological interventions for sleep in Alzheimer's disease, searched through June 6, 2025; 14 trials, 937 participants. Primary outcome Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI); secondary outcomes actigraphic.
cards.result: Non-pharmacological interventions significantly reduced PSQI scores (standardised mean difference −0.46, 95% CI −0.70 to −0.21). Neuromodulation-based interventions showed potentially favourable PSQI effects, and caregiver-delivered programmes such as NITE-AD modestly reduced nocturnal awakenings. No significant effects were observed for sleep efficiency, total sleep time, wake after sleep onset, or time in bed. The authors conclude subjective sleep quality may improve modestly while objective benefits remain limited, and call for larger multicentre trials.
cards.watchOut: The pool mixes many different interventions (including neuromodulation), so it supports the class, not NITE-AD alone; the objective-outcome null tempers the two programme trials' actigraphic wins.
cards.source: Zhang Q et al. Non-pharmacological interventions for sleep improvement in Alzheimer's disease: A systematic review and meta-analysis. J Alzheimers Dis. 2026. PMID: 42678693. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: one programme, two positive posttests, fading durability — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: one programme, two positive posttests, fading durability — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: McCurry 2005 (n=36), McCurry 2011 (n=132) — total programme N=168 — and Zhang 2026 (meta-analysis, 14 RCTs, 937 participants).
cards.result: NITE-AD and its component arms improved actigraphic sleep at posttest in both trials, and the class-level meta-analysis agrees on subjective sleep quality while finding no objective pooled effect; the larger trial's benefits were gone at 6 months. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single programme with a small first trial caps at POSSIBLE.
cards.watchOut: Do not upgrade on the meta-analysis: it pools other interventions too, and its objective outcomes were null.

shelves.title: tDCS after stroke: the Cochrane pool and the largest trial find no arm-function benefit; two smaller trials are positive — SPLIT
shelves.question: In stroke survivors, does transcranial direct-current stimulation added to rehabilitation improve upper-limb motor recovery compared with sham stimulation?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Adult · Aged · Bias · Cognition Disorders/rehabilitation · Confidence Intervals · Female · Humans · Lower Extremity/physiology · Male · Middle Aged · Motor Activity/physiology · Muscle Strength · Patient Dropouts/statistics & numerical data · Perceptual Disorders/rehabilitation · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Recovery of Function · Stroke Rehabilitation · Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation · Upper Extremity/physiology
shelves.balance: SPLIT. The biggest and most rigorous evidence is null for the arm itself: the Cochrane review (Elsner 2020; 67 studies, 1,729 participants in total) found no effect of tDCS on upper-extremity function at the end of intervention (34 trials, 985 participants; absolute-value analysis standardised mean difference 0.17, 95% CI −0.05 to 0.38) or at follow-up, and no effect on muscle strength or leg function; a small activities-of-daily-living signal (SMD 0.28) did not persist in the sensitivity analysis restricted to trials with proper allocation concealment. The largest single multicentre trial carded here (Hesse 2011, n=96, tDCS plus bilateral robot-assisted arm training in severe subacute paresis) found no between-group difference at 6 weeks or 3 months. Against that, two smaller trials were positive: Khedr 2013 (n=40; combined anodal/cathodal tDCS beat sham on functional scales at 3 months) and Garrido 2023 (n=70; bihemispheric tDCS with modified constraint-induced movement therapy beat sham on Fugl-Meyer and Wolf Motor Function Test, between-group Fugl-Meyer difference 4.9 points). Many small trials, heterogeneous montages and doses, and a null synthesis: the split is named on the stamp.

cards.headline: Elsner 2020 (Cochrane, 67 studies, 1,729 participants): no effect of tDCS on upper-extremity function (34 trials, 985 participants; SMD 0.17, 95% CI −0.05 to 0.38) or muscle strength; the small ADL signal vanished in the allocation-concealment sensitivity analysis
cards.summary: Elsner 2020 (Cochrane, 67 studies, 1,729 participants): no effect of tDCS on upper-extremity function (34 trials, 985 participants; SMD 0.17, 95% CI −0.05 to 0.38) or muscle strength; the small ADL signal vanished in the allocation-concealment sensitivity analysis
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials of tDCS versus sham or control after stroke (search to January 2019): 67 studies, 1,729 participants, mostly ischaemic stroke, mean ages 43–75, acute to chronic phases; 116 further studies ongoing.
cards.result: For activities of daily living at end of intervention, 19 studies (686 participants) showed an effect (SMD 0.28, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.44; moderate-quality evidence), but the results did not persist in a sensitivity analysis including only trials with proper allocation concealment. For upper-extremity function, 24 studies (792 participants, absolute values) found no effect (SMD 0.17, 95% CI −0.05 to 0.38; moderate-quality evidence) and 10 studies (193 participants, change values) also found no effect (SMD 0.33, 95% CI −0.12 to 0.79; low-quality evidence); at follow-up, five studies (211 participants) showed no effect. Twelve studies (258 participants) on lower-extremity function and 18 studies (553 participants) on muscle strength found no effect (high-quality evidence for the end-of-intervention analyses). Dropouts and adverse events did not differ (47 studies, 1,330 participants; risk ratio 1.25, 95% CI 0.74 to 2.13 — relative measure). The authors call for further large parallel-group randomised trials.
cards.watchOut: Included trials differed widely in stimulation type, site, dose and stroke phase; the ADL result is fragile to trial quality, and the arm-function result — this shelf's question — is null.
cards.source: Elsner B et al. Transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) for improving activities of daily living, and physical and cognitive functioning, in people after stroke. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2020. PMID: 33175411. Registry ID: NCT00542256. cards.headline: Hesse 2011 (n=96, multicentre): neither anodal nor cathodal tDCS added anything to bilateral robot-assisted arm training in severe subacute paresis — Fugl-Meyer gains identical across arms
cards.summary: Hesse 2011 (n=96, multicentre): neither anodal nor cathodal tDCS added anything to bilateral robot-assisted arm training in severe subacute paresis — Fugl-Meyer gains identical across arms
cards.people: 96 patients with ischaemic supratentorial stroke 3–8 weeks earlier and severe upper-limb impairment (Fugl-Meyer upper-limb score <18), randomised double-blind at multiple centres to anodal tDCS of the lesioned hemisphere, cathodal tDCS of the nonlesioned side (both 20 minutes at 2.0 mA), or sham, for 6 weeks alongside 400 repetitions of two bilateral movements on a robotic assistive device.
cards.result: Fugl-Meyer scores improved in all groups at 6 weeks (P<.001) with no between-group differences: initial versus finish scores 7.8 ± 3.8 versus 19.1 ± 14.4 (anodal), 7.9 ± 3.4 versus 18.8 ± 10.5 (cathodal), and 8.2 ± 4.4 versus 19.2 ± 15.0 (sham). No significant between-group differences were present at 3 months. The authors conclude neither polarity enhanced bilateral arm training in patients with cortical involvement and severe weakness.
cards.watchOut: Exploratory trial in the most severely impaired subgroup, paired with robotic bilateral training rather than conventional therapy — a null here does not exclude effects in milder paresis, but it is the largest and most rigorous single trial carded.
cards.source: Hesse S et al. Combined transcranial direct current stimulation and robot-assisted arm training in subacute stroke patients: an exploratory, randomized multicenter trial. Neurorehabil Neural Repair. 2011. PMID: 21825004. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Khedr 2013 (n=40, pilot): anodal and cathodal tDCS each beat sham on functional scales at 3 months when combined and compared with sham (P=.002 for each scale)
cards.summary: Khedr 2013 (n=40, pilot): anodal and cathodal tDCS each beat sham on functional scales at 3 months when combined and compared with sham (P=.002 for each scale)
cards.people: 40 patients with ischaemic stroke undergoing rehabilitation, randomised to anodal tDCS (over the affected hemisphere), cathodal tDCS (over the unaffected hemisphere) or sham — 2 mA for 25 minutes daily for 6 consecutive days over the motor-cortex hand area; assessed with NIH Stroke Scale, Orgogozo MCA scale, Barthel Index and MRC strength scale to 3 months.
cards.result: All groups improved on all scales by 3 months. Improvement was equal in the anodal and cathodal groups; when the two treated groups were combined and compared with sham, significant interactions were seen for the Orgogozo MCA scale and Barthel Index (P=.002 for each). Cortical excitability of the affected hemisphere increased in all groups, more with real than sham stimulation; muscle-strength improvements were borderline significant. The authors conclude a brief course of either polarity is superior to sham in enhancing rehabilitation training.
cards.watchOut: Pilot-sized (n=40), single-centre, only 6 stimulation sessions, and the headline comparison pools the two active arms post hoc — hypothesis-generating against the Cochrane null.
cards.source: Khedr EM et al. Effect of anodal versus cathodal transcranial direct current stimulation on stroke rehabilitation: a pilot randomized controlled trial. Neurorehabil Neural Repair. 2013. PMID: 23609526. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Garrido 2023 (n=70, multicentre): bihemispheric tDCS with modified constraint-induced movement therapy beat sham on motor and functional upper-limb recovery (Fugl-Meyer between-group difference 4.9 points) and on ADL independence at 90 days
cards.summary: Garrido 2023 (n=70, multicentre): bihemispheric tDCS with modified constraint-induced movement therapy beat sham on motor and functional upper-limb recovery (Fugl-Meyer between-group difference 4.9 points) and on ADL independence at 90 days
cards.people: 70 hospitalised patients with acute or subacute stroke in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled multicentre trial (2018–2021): 7 consecutive days of 20-minute active or sham bihemispheric tDCS (anodal ipsilesional, cathodal contralesional) combined with a modified constraint-induced movement therapy protocol; outcomes on days 0, 5, 7, 10 and 90.
cards.result: The active group showed a statistically significant advantage over sham across the trend of Fugl-Meyer Assessment (motor function and joint pain) and Wolf Motor Function Test scores (P<0.05), reaching the minimal clinically important difference: Fugl-Meyer between-group difference 4.9 points (95% CI 0.007 to 9.799) and Wolf Motor Function Test difference 6.54 points (95% CI 1.10 to 14.15). Activities-of-daily-living independence (Functional Independence Measure difference 8.63, 95% CI 1.37 to 18.64) and perceived quality-of-life recovery at 90 days (P=0.0176) also favoured active stimulation.
cards.watchOut: The co-intervention (modified constraint-induced movement therapy) is itself an active treatment, the confidence interval for the Fugl-Meyer difference nearly touches zero, and 7 days of treatment is a very short course.
cards.source: Garrido MM et al. Early transcranial direct current stimulation with modified constraint-induced movement therapy for motor and functional upper limb recovery in hospitalized patients with acute and subacute stroke. Brain Stimul. 2023. PMID: 36584748. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: null where the evidence is largest, positive where it is smallest — SPLIT
cards.summary: Synthesis: null where the evidence is largest, positive where it is smallest — SPLIT
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Elsner 2020 Cochrane review (67 studies, 1,729 participants; 985 for upper-extremity function), Hesse 2011 (n=96), Khedr 2013 (n=40), Garrido 2023 (n=70).
cards.result: For upper-limb motor recovery — this shelf's question — the Cochrane pool and the largest multicentre trial are null, while two smaller trials combining tDCS with intensive task practice are positive. PROPOSED SPLIT, with the split named: benefit unproven at synthesis level; small-trial positives may reflect co-therapy, montage or chance.
cards.watchOut: Do not average the split away: the ADL signal in the Cochrane review does not survive its own quality sensitivity analysis.

shelves.title: Brexpiprazole + sertraline for PTSD: two flexible-dose trials positive, the fixed-dose trial negative — SPLIT
shelves.question: In adults with PTSD, does brexpiprazole combined with sertraline reduce PTSD symptom severity compared with sertraline plus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Sertraline/administration & dosage,adverse effects,pharmacology,therapeutic use · Female · Male · Double-Blind Method · Thiophenes/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use,pharmacology · Adult · Middle Aged · Stress Disorders, Post-Traumatic/drug therapy · Drug Therapy, Combination · Quinolones/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Treatment Outcome · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the programme genuinely divides by trial design. The full-factorial trial (Hobart 2025, n=321, flexible dose) found brexpiprazole + sertraline beat sertraline + placebo on CAPS-5 change at week 10 (−5.08 points, P=.011), while neither drug alone differed from placebo. Trial 071 (Davis 2025, JAMA Psychiatry, n=416, flexible-dose brexpiprazole 2–3 mg + sertraline 150 mg) was likewise positive: CAPS-5 least-squares mean difference −5.59 (95% CI −8.79 to −2.38; P<.001), with all key secondary endpoints met. Trial 072 (Davis 2025, J Clin Psychopharmacol, n=553, fixed-dose brexpiprazole 2 or 3 mg + sertraline) was negative at both doses (differences +1.03, P=0.52, and −0.71, P=0.66). A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of the programme (4 randomised trials) found a significant pooled CAPS-5 advantage (mean difference −3.77, 95% CI −6.79 to −0.75) but no significant difference on CGI-S, with more weight gain (mean difference 1.47 kg) and somnolence (risk ratio 2.39, relative) on the combination. Two positives, one adequately sized negative, and a split meta-analysis: SPLIT.

cards.headline: Hobart 2025 (full-factorial, n=321): the combination beat sertraline + placebo on CAPS-5 (−5.08 points, P=.011) — neither brexpiprazole alone nor sertraline alone differed from placebo
cards.summary: Hobart 2025 (full-factorial, n=321): the combination beat sertraline + placebo on CAPS-5 (−5.08 points, P=.011) — neither brexpiprazole alone nor sertraline alone differed from placebo
cards.people: 321 adult outpatients with PTSD (DSM-5) at 48 US sites, randomised 1:1:1:1 after a 1-week placebo run-in to brexpiprazole + sertraline, brexpiprazole + placebo, sertraline + placebo, or placebo + placebo for 11 weeks; flexible doses (brexpiprazole 1–3 mg/day; sertraline 100–200 mg/day). Primary endpoint CAPS-5 change from week 1 to week 10.
cards.result: Completion rates were 58/82 (70.7%) combination, 50/75 (66.7%) brexpiprazole alone, 59/81 (72.8%) sertraline alone and 64/83 (77.1%) placebo. At week 10 the combination improved CAPS-5 by a least-squares mean −16.4 versus −11.4 on sertraline + placebo (difference −5.08, 95% CI −8.96 to −1.20; P=.011), and also beat brexpiprazole + placebo and placebo + placebo; brexpiprazole + placebo and sertraline + placebo did not differ from placebo + placebo. cards.headline: Davis 2025 — Trial 071 (n=416, flexible dose): CAPS-5 improved −5.59 points more on brexpiprazole + sertraline than sertraline + placebo (P<.001); all key secondary endpoints met
cards.summary: Davis 2025 — Trial 071 (n=416, flexible dose): CAPS-5 improved −5.59 points more on brexpiprazole + sertraline than sertraline + placebo (P<.001); all key secondary endpoints met
cards.people: 416 adult outpatients with PTSD at 86 US sites (2019–2023), randomised after a 1-week placebo run-in to brexpiprazole 2–3 mg/day (flexible) + sertraline 150 mg/day or sertraline 150 mg/day + placebo for 11 weeks; 74.5% women, mean age 37.4 years. Primary endpoint CAPS-5 change from week 1 to week 10.
cards.result: CAPS-5 least-squares mean change was −19.2 on the combination (n=148 analysed) versus −13.6 on sertraline + placebo (n=134): difference −5.59 (95% CI −8.79 to −2.38; P<.001). Completion was 137/214 (64.0%) versus 113/202 (55.9%). Treatment-emergent adverse events ≥5% on the combination (versus control) were nausea (12.2% vs 11.7%), fatigue (6.8% vs 4.1%), weight increase (5.9% vs 1.5%) and somnolence (5.4% vs 2.6%); discontinuation for adverse events was 3.9% on the combination.
cards.watchOut: High attrition in both arms (only ~56–64% completed) and a placebo run-in design; the analysed efficacy population (282) is much smaller than the randomised population (416).

cards.headline: Davis 2025 — Trial 072 (n=553, fixed dose): primary endpoint NOT met at either dose — CAPS-5 differences +1.03 (P=0.52) and −0.71 (P=0.66) versus sertraline + placebo (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Davis 2025 — Trial 072 (n=553, fixed dose): primary endpoint NOT met at either dose — CAPS-5 differences +1.03 (P=0.52) and −0.71 (P=0.66) versus sertraline + placebo (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: 553 adult outpatients with PTSD at 95 US sites (2019–2023), randomised 1:1:1 after a 1-week placebo run-in to brexpiprazole 2 mg/day + sertraline 150 mg/day (n=191), brexpiprazole 3 mg/day + sertraline (n=185), or sertraline + placebo (n=177) for 11 weeks. Primary endpoint CAPS-5 change from week 1 to week 10.
cards.result: CAPS-5 least-squares mean changes were −16.5 (2 mg combination), −18.3 (3 mg combination) and −17.6 (sertraline + placebo); differences versus control were +1.03 (95% CI −2.09 to 4.16; P=0.52) and −0.71 (95% CI −3.88 to 2.46; P=0.66) — the primary endpoint was not met at either dose (the treatment made no difference). Adverse events ≥5% were headache, nausea and diarrhoea at similar rates across arms. The authors note this differs from the two prior trials of the combination and report no new safety signals.
cards.watchOut: The largest trial of the three and the only fixed-dose one; its control arm improved more (−17.6) than the control arm of Trial 071 (−13.6), which may have erased the drug–placebo gap.

cards.headline: Kotochinsky 2026 (meta-analysis, 4 RCTs): pooled CAPS-5 favoured the combination (mean difference −3.77) but CGI-S did not; weight gain +1.47 kg and somnolence risk ratio 2.39 (relative)
cards.summary: Kotochinsky 2026 (meta-analysis, 4 RCTs): pooled CAPS-5 favoured the combination (mean difference −3.77) but CGI-S did not; weight gain +1.47 kg and somnolence risk ratio 2.39 (relative)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials of brexpiprazole + SSRI versus SSRI ± placebo in PTSD; 4 randomised trials with 981 patients in the analysed populations (51.3% receiving brexpiprazole), follow-up 8–12 weeks.
cards.result: CAPS-5 improved significantly more with brexpiprazole + SSRI (mean difference −3.77, 95% CI −6.79 to −0.75; P=0.01), but pooled CGI-S showed no significant difference (mean difference −0.15, 95% CI −0.33 to 0.04; P=0.12). Brexpiprazole increased body weight (mean difference 1.47 kg, 95% CI 0.84 to 2.09) and somnolence (risk ratio 2.39, 95% CI 1.03 to 5.57 — relative measure); overall treatment-emergent adverse-event incidence and metabolic laboratory parameters did not differ. The authors call for larger, longer-term trials.
cards.watchOut: The pool is dominated by the same three trials carded above (plus one further small trial), so it summarises rather than independently confirms them; its two efficacy scales disagree with each other.
cards.source: Kotochinsky M et al. Efficacy and tolerability of brexpiprazole augmentation of SSRI therapy in PTSD: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. J Psychiatr Res. 2026. PMID: 41172929. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Hobart 2025 (n=321), Davis 2025 Trial 071 (n=416), Davis 2025 Trial 072 (n=553), Kotochinsky 2026 (meta-analysis, 4 RCTs).
cards.result: Whether brexpiprazole + sertraline beats sertraline alone depends on which trial you read: the two flexible-dose trials are positive by ~5 CAPS-5 points, the largest fixed-dose trial is null, and the meta-analysis splits by outcome scale. PROPOSED SPLIT, with weight gain and somnolence as the consistent price.
cards.watchOut: Do not present the programme as positive on the strength of the two flexible-dose trials alone — Trial 072 is the largest trial and it is negative.

shelves.title: Cariprazine for predominant negative symptoms: one large head-to-head trial beat risperidone by 1.46 PANSS-FSNS points — POSSIBLE
shelves.question: In adults with schizophrenia and predominant negative symptoms, does cariprazine improve negative symptoms compared with risperidone?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antipsychotic Agents/therapeutic use · Behavioral Symptoms/drug therapy,etiology,psychology · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Piperazines/therapeutic use · Risperidone/therapeutic use · Schizophrenia/complications,drug therapy · Schizophrenic Psychology · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). This shelf is the dedicated negative-symptom slice: shelf #1430 cards cariprazine for acute exacerbation of schizophrenia (Durgam 2015, Kane 2015) and is cross-pointed, not re-carded — its PMIDs do not appear in this shelf's card source lines. In the dedicated trial (Németh 2017; 461 randomised adults with long-term stable schizophrenia and predominant negative symptoms, 26 weeks), cariprazine (target 4.5 mg/day) improved the PANSS factor score for negative symptoms more than risperidone (target 4 mg/day): least-squares mean change −8.90 versus −7.44 points, difference −1.46 (95% CI −2.39 to −0.53; P=0.0022; effect size 0.31). A post-hoc trajectory analysis of the same trial (Leucht 2023) found a single trajectory best described response — rapid, steady improvement rather than distinct responder subgroups. The systematic review of antipsychotics for predominant or prominent negative symptoms (Krause 2018; 21 trials, 3,451 participants) likewise records cariprazine outperforming risperidone in that one large, well-controlled trial (standardised mean difference −0.29, 95% CI −0.48 to −0.11), while noting it was manufacturer-sponsored and that amisulpride is the only agent to have beaten placebo in this population. One trial, modest margin over an active comparator: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Németh 2017 (n=461, 26 weeks): cariprazine beat risperidone on negative symptoms — PANSS-FSNS change −8.90 vs −7.44 points (difference −1.46, P=0.0022; effect size 0.31)
cards.summary: Németh 2017 (n=461, 26 weeks): cariprazine beat risperidone on negative symptoms — PANSS-FSNS change −8.90 vs −7.44 points (difference −1.46, P=0.0022; effect size 0.31)
cards.people: 461 adults aged 18–65 with long-term (>2 years), stable schizophrenia and predominant negative symptoms (>6 months) at 66 centres in 11 European countries, randomised 1:1 to 26 weeks of monotherapy with cariprazine (3, 4.5 [target] or 6 mg/day; n=230) or risperidone (3, 4 [target] or 6 mg/day; n=231); mean daily doses 4.2 mg and 3.8 mg. Primary outcome: change in PANSS factor score for negative symptoms (PANSS-FSNS) in the modified intention-to-treat population (227 cariprazine, 229 risperidone); 77% in each group completed 26 weeks.
cards.result: Cariprazine produced a greater least-squares mean PANSS-FSNS improvement than risperidone: −8.90 versus −7.44 points; least-squares mean difference −1.46 (95% CI −2.39 to −0.53; P=0.0022; effect size 0.31). Treatment-emergent adverse events (including insomnia, akathisia, worsening of schizophrenia, headache and anxiety) occurred in 123 (54%) on cariprazine and 131 (57%) on risperidone. One patient in the risperidone group died of a cause regarded as unrelated to treatment. The trial was funded by Gedeon Richter Plc, cariprazine's manufacturer.
cards.watchOut: No placebo arm — the margin is over risperidone, an active comparator that itself treats negative symptoms somewhat; the absolute advantage (1.46 points, effect size 0.31) is modest, and the trial was manufacturer-funded.
cards.source: Németh G et al. Cariprazine versus risperidone monotherapy for treatment of predominant negative symptoms in patients with schizophrenia: a randomised, double-blind trial. Lancet. 2017. PMID: 28185672. Registry ID: EudraCT 2012-005485-36 (as stated in the record). cards.headline: Leucht 2023 (post-hoc of the Németh trial): a single response trajectory — patients with predominant negative symptoms improved rapidly and steadily on either drug, with no distinct responder subgroups
cards.summary: Leucht 2023 (post-hoc of the Németh trial): a single response trajectory — patients with predominant negative symptoms improved rapidly and steadily on either drug, with no distinct responder subgroups
cards.type: Post-hoc trajectory analysis of a randomized trial
cards.people: Post-hoc group-based trajectory-modelling analysis of the 26-week Németh 2017 trial population (cariprazine or risperidone), examining heterogeneity of response on the PANSS-FSNS and Clinical Global Impression severity and improvement scales.
cards.result: A single trajectory best described treatment response for predominant negative symptoms, in preference to competing multi-group models: patients with over ten years of schizophrenia responded rapidly to adequate treatment and followed a course of steady improvement, rather than separating into responder and non-responder classes.
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc and descriptive — it characterises the parent trial's response pattern and adds no independent comparative evidence; the parent trial is carded above and this analysis must not be double-counted as a second trial.
cards.source: Leucht S et al. Single trajectory treatment response for predominant negative symptoms: Post-hoc analysis of a clinical trial with cariprazine and risperidone. Schizophr Res. 2023. cards.people: Systematic review and pairwise meta-analyses of randomised, blinded antipsychotic trials in schizophrenia with predominant or prominent negative symptoms (search to December 12, 2017): 21 randomised trials, 3,451 participants, with separate analyses by population and checks for confounding by depressive, positive and extrapyramidal symptoms.
cards.result: In predominant negative symptoms: amisulpride was superior to placebo (4 trials, n=590; standardised mean difference 0.47, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.71, though with a parallel reduction in depression), olanzapine was superior to haloperidol in one small trial (n=35), and cariprazine outperformed risperidone (1 trial, n=456; standardised mean difference −0.29, 95% CI −0.48 to −0.11). In prominent negative symptoms, single trials favoured olanzapine and quetiapine over risperidone, but those studies were potentially more confounded by improvement in secondary negative symptoms. The authors note the cariprazine trial was well controlled for secondary negative symptoms but sponsored by its manufacturer.
cards.watchOut: The review's cariprazine estimate is the same single Németh trial carded above — corroboration of interpretation, not independent replication; no placebo-controlled cariprazine trial exists in this population.
cards.source: Krause M et al. Antipsychotic drugs for patients with schizophrenia and predominant or prominent negative symptoms: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Eur Arch Psychiatry Clin Neurosci. 2018. PMID: 29368205. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Antipsychotic Agents/pharmacology · Humans · Schizophrenia/drug therapy,physiopathology

shelves.title: Galcanezumab for migraine prevention: EVOLVE-2, REGAIN and CONQUER all positive — POSSIBLE on this shelf, with EVOLVE-1 homed on live #336
shelves.question: In adults with episodic or chronic migraine, does galcanezumab reduce monthly migraine days compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antibodies, Monoclonal/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide/blood,immunology · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Injections, Subcutaneous/adverse effects · Male · Middle Aged · Migraine Disorders/blood,drug therapy,physiopathology,prevention & control · Quality of Life · Surveys and Questionnaires · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), with the #6155 precedent flag on the face: EVOLVE-1 (Stauffer 2018) is already carded with its figures on live shelf #336, the CGRP-class shelf (62.3% versus 38.6% achieving ≥50% response), so under the one-home rule its PMID does not appear in any card source line on this shelf; fremanezumab received the analogous drug-specific slice as pack #6155 under the same discipline. On the free reports carded here, galcanezumab is consistently positive: EVOLVE-2 (915 patients with episodic migraine) reduced monthly migraine headache days by 4.3 (120 mg) and 4.2 (240 mg) versus 2.3 on placebo (differences −2.0 and −1.9 days); REGAIN (1,113 patients with chronic migraine) reduced them by 4.8 and 4.6 versus 2.7 on placebo; CONQUER (462 patients who had failed preventive medications from two to four categories) reduced them by 4.1 versus 1.0 days (difference −3.1, effect size 0.72); and a 12-month open-label study (270 patients) sustained reductions of 5.6–6.5 days with injection-site pain the commonest adverse event. Injection-site reactions are the consistent harm across the programme.

cards.headline: Skljarevski 2018 — EVOLVE-2 (915 patients, episodic migraine): monthly migraine days fell 4.3 (120 mg) and 4.2 (240 mg) versus 2.3 on placebo — differences of −2.0 and −1.9 days
cards.summary: Skljarevski 2018 — EVOLVE-2 (915 patients, episodic migraine): monthly migraine days fell 4.3 (120 mg) and 4.2 (240 mg) versus 2.3 on placebo — differences of −2.0 and −1.9 days
cards.people: 915 intent-to-treat patients with episodic migraine in a global double-blind 6-month trial, randomised to monthly subcutaneous galcanezumab 120 mg (n=231), 240 mg (n=223) or placebo (n=461). Primary endpoint: overall mean change from baseline in monthly migraine headache days; key secondaries included ≥50%, ≥75% and 100% response rates.
cards.result: Monthly migraine headache days fell by 4.3 days (120 mg) and 4.2 days (240 mg) versus 2.3 days on placebo; group differences were −2.0 (95% CI −2.6 to −1.5) and −1.9 (95% CI −2.4 to −1.4) days. Both doses were superior to placebo on all key secondary endpoints. Injection-site pain was the most common treatment-emergent adverse event at similar rates in all groups; injection-site reactions and pruritus were significantly more frequent on galcanezumab, and erythema significantly more frequent at 240 mg.
cards.watchOut: The 240 mg dose added nothing over 120 mg; EVOLVE-1, the companion episodic-migraine trial, is homed on live #336 and is deliberately not re-carded here.
cards.source: Skljarevski V et al. Efficacy and safety of galcanezumab for the prevention of episodic migraine: Results of the EVOLVE-2 Phase 3 randomized controlled clinical trial. Cephalalgia. 2018. PMID: 29848108. Registry ID: NCT02614196. cards.headline: Detke 2018 — REGAIN (1,113 patients, chronic migraine): monthly migraine headache days fell 4.8 (120 mg) and 4.6 (240 mg) versus 2.7 on placebo (both P<0.001)
cards.summary: Detke 2018 — REGAIN (1,113 patients, chronic migraine): monthly migraine headache days fell 4.8 (120 mg) and 4.6 (240 mg) versus 2.7 on placebo (both P<0.001)
cards.people: 1,113 patients aged 18–65 with chronic migraine (baseline mean 19.4 monthly migraine headache days) randomised 2:1:1 to monthly subcutaneous placebo (n=558), galcanezumab 120 mg with a 240 mg loading dose (n=278), or galcanezumab 240 mg (n=277), in a 3-month double-blind phase followed by a 9-month open-label extension.
cards.result: Both galcanezumab doses produced greater overall mean reductions in monthly migraine headache days than placebo (placebo −2.7; 120 mg −4.8; 240 mg −4.6; P<0.001 for each dose versus placebo). No clinically meaningful safety or tolerability differences emerged except higher incidences of treatment-emergent injection-site reaction (P<0.01), injection-site erythema (P<0.001), injection-site pruritus (P<0.01) and sinusitis (P<0.05) in the 240 mg group. The paper classifies this as Class I evidence of superiority over placebo.
cards.watchOut: The blinded phase lasted only 3 months in a chronic-migraine population with ~19 migraine days a month; the 9-month extension was open-label.
cards.source: Detke HC et al. Galcanezumab in chronic migraine: The randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled REGAIN study. Neurology. 2018. PMID: 30446596. Registry ID: NCT02614261. cards.headline: Mulleners 2020 — CONQUER (462 patients who had failed 2–4 preventive categories): migraine days fell 4.1 versus 1.0 on placebo (difference −3.1; effect size 0.72)
cards.summary: Mulleners 2020 — CONQUER (462 patients who had failed 2–4 preventive categories): migraine days fell 4.1 versus 1.0 on placebo (difference −3.1; effect size 0.72)
cards.people: 462 patients aged 18–75 with episodic (58%) or chronic (42%) migraine and documented failure of preventive medications from two to four categories in the past 10 years (lack of efficacy or tolerability), randomised 1:1 at 64 sites in 12 countries to galcanezumab 120 mg monthly (240 mg loading dose; n=232) or placebo (n=230) for 3 months.
cards.result: Galcanezumab produced a significantly greater reduction in monthly migraine headache days across months 1–3: −4.1 days from a baseline of 13.4 versus −1.0 from 13.0 on placebo (between-group difference −3.1, 95% CI −3.9 to −2.3; P<0.0001; effect size 0.72). Treatment-emergent adverse events were reported in 119 (51%) on galcanezumab and 122 (53%) on placebo, with two serious adverse events (1%) in each group. Funded by Eli Lilly.
cards.watchOut: A treatment-resistant population and a 3-month horizon; the larger effect size here partly reflects the low placebo response (−1.0 day) in patients who had already failed several preventives.
cards.source: Mulleners WM et al. Safety and efficacy of galcanezumab in patients for whom previous migraine preventive medication from two to four categories had failed (CONQUER): a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3b trial. Lancet Neurol. 2020. PMID: 32949542. Registry ID: NCT03559257. cards.headline: Camporeale 2018 (12-month open-label, 270 patients): migraine days fell 5.6 (120 mg) and 6.5 (240 mg) days over a year; injection-site pain the commonest adverse event; 3.7% had a serious adverse event
cards.summary: Camporeale 2018 (12-month open-label, 270 patients): migraine days fell 5.6 (120 mg) and 6.5 (240 mg) days over a year; injection-site pain the commonest adverse event; 3.7% had a serious adverse event
cards.people: 270 patients aged 18–65 with episodic or chronic migraine (mean 10.6 migraine headache days per month at baseline; >80% women), galcanezumab-naive, randomised to open-label galcanezumab 120 mg or 240 mg monthly for 12 months (135 per group); 77.8% completed the treatment phase. Safety was the primary focus; effectiveness was assessed secondarily.
cards.result: Treatment-emergent adverse events in ≥10% of either group were injection-site pain, nasopharyngitis, upper respiratory tract infection, injection-site reaction, back pain and sinusitis; 3.7% of patients experienced a serious adverse event and 4.8% discontinued because of adverse events, with no clinically meaningful laboratory, vital-sign or ECG differences between doses. Overall mean reductions in monthly migraine headache days over 12 months were 5.6 days (120 mg) and 6.5 days (240 mg), with improved functioning and reduced headache-related disability in both groups.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with no placebo arm — the within-group reductions cannot be separated from natural history and expectation; its value is the 12-month safety picture.
cards.source: Camporeale A et al. A phase 3, long-term, open-label safety study of Galcanezumab in patients with migraine. BMC Neurol. 2018. PMID: 30413151. Registry ID: NCT02614287. shelves.title: Parkinson's psychosis: clozapine beat placebo in both its trials; quetiapine failed in all three of its trials — SPLIT
shelves.question: In people with Parkinson's disease psychosis, do low-dose clozapine or quetiapine improve psychosis without worsening motor function compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antiparkinson Agents/adverse effects · Antipsychotic Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Clozapine/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Parkinson Disease/drug therapy · Psychoses, Substance-Induced/drug therapy,etiology · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the two drugs have opposite trial records, and shelf #1112 (pimavanserin, cross-pointed here) does not cover either. Clozapine: the Parkinson Study Group trial (1999, n=60, mean dose 24.7 mg/day) improved all three psychosis measures versus placebo (Clinical Global Impression +1.6 versus +0.5 points, P<0.001; Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale +9.3 versus +2.6, P=0.002) with no deleterious effect on parkinsonism — tremor actually improved — at the price of weekly blood monitoring and one discontinuation for leukopenia. The French trial (Pollak 2004, n=60, mean dose 35.8 mg/day) replicated it (CGI +1.8 versus +0.6, P=0.001), and 19 of the patients who recovered relapsed within a month of stopping. Quetiapine: three double-blind trials (Ondo 2005, n=31; Rabey 2007, n=58; Shotbolt 2009, n=24) all failed to show significant benefit over placebo on any psychosis measure, though none showed motor worsening either. Total carded N=233, all pre-registration-era trials with no registry ID in their records. Clozapine works in trials but carries the blood-monitoring burden; quetiapine's trial record is negative despite its wide clinical use.

cards.headline: Parkinson Study Group 1999 (n=60): low-dose clozapine (mean 24.7 mg/day) beat placebo on all three psychosis scales (CGI +1.6 vs +0.5, P<0.001) without worsening parkinsonism — one leukopenia discontinuation
cards.summary: Parkinson Study Group 1999 (n=60): low-dose clozapine (mean 24.7 mg/day) beat placebo on all three psychosis scales (CGI +1.6 vs +0.5, P<0.001) without worsening parkinsonism — one leukopenia discontinuation
cards.people: 60 patients (mean age 72 years) with idiopathic Parkinson's disease and drug-induced psychosis of at least 4 weeks' duration at six sites, randomised double-blind to clozapine 6.25–50 mg/day or placebo for 4 weeks, on fixed antiparkinsonian doses, with weekly blood-count monitoring.
cards.result: Clozapine improved psychosis significantly more than placebo on all three measures: Clinical Global Impression Scale +1.6 ± 0.3 versus +0.5 ± 0.2 points (P<0.001); Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale +9.3 ± 1.5 versus +2.6 ± 1.3 (P=0.002); Scale for the Assessment of Positive Symptoms +11.8 ± 2.0 versus +3.8 ± 1.9 (P=0.01). Seven clozapine patients improved by at least 3 CGI points versus one on placebo. Clozapine improved tremor and had no deleterious effect on parkinsonism severity; in one patient it was discontinued because of leukopenia.
cards.watchOut: Only 4 weeks long and small (n=60); the agranulocytosis risk that mandates weekly blood counts is the reason this effective drug is a last resort in practice.

randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial 60 patients (mean age 72 years) with idiopathic parkinson's disease and drug-induced psychosis of at least 4 weeks' duration at six sites, randomised double-blind to clozapine 6.25–50 mg/day or placebo for 4 weeks, on fixed antiparkinsonian doses, with weekly blood-count monitoring. clozapine improved psychosis significantly more than placebo on all three measures: clinical global impression scale +1.6 ± 0.3 versus +0.5 ± 0.2 points (p<0.001); brief psychiatric rating scale +9.3 ± 1.5 versus +2.6 ± 1.3 (p=0.002); scale for the assessment of positive symptoms +11.8 ± 2.0 versus +3.8 ± 1.9 (p=0.01). seven clozapine patients improved by at least 3 cgi points versus one on placebo. clozapine improved tremor and had no deleterious effect on parkinsonism severity; in one patient it was discontinued because of leukopenia. only 4 weeks long and small (n=60); the agranulocytosis risk that mandates weekly blood counts is the reason this effective drug is a last resort in practice. parkinson study group. low-dose clozapine for the treatment of drug-induced psychosis in parkinson's disease. n engl j med. 1999. pmid: 10072410. registry id: none in the record. mesh: aged · antiparkinson agents/adverse effects · antipsychotic agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects · clozapine/administration & dosage,adverse effects · double-blind method · female · humans · male · parkinson disease/drug therapy · psychoses, substance-induced/drug therapy,etiology · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Pollak 2004 (n=60): clozapine replicated — CGI +1.8 vs +0.6 (P=0.001), PANSS positive +5.6 vs +0.8 (P<0.0001), no motor worsening; 19 patients relapsed within a month of stopping
cards.summary: Pollak 2004 (n=60): clozapine replicated — CGI +1.8 vs +0.6 (P=0.001), PANSS positive +5.6 vs +0.8 (P<0.0001), no motor worsening; 19 patients relapsed within a month of stopping
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial with open follow-up
cards.people: 60 patients with Parkinson's disease and drug-induced psychosis in a 4-week randomised double-blind parallel comparison of clozapine (mean end-of-blind dose 35.8 mg/day) versus placebo, followed by a 12-week open clozapine period and a 1-month post-discontinuation period; outcomes included CGI, PANSS positive subscore, UPDRS and MMSE.
cards.result: CGI improved by a mean 1.8 (SD 1.5) on clozapine versus 0.6 (1.1) on placebo (P=0.001); PANSS positive subscore improved 5.6 (3.9) versus 0.8 (2.8) (P<0.0001). UPDRS motor and MMSE scores did not change significantly in either group. At the end of the open period, 25 patients had completely recovered from delusions and hallucinations, and 19 experienced a relapse within one month after clozapine washout. Somnolence was more frequent with clozapine.
cards.watchOut: Same small size and short blinded phase as the 1999 trial; the relapse-after-stopping data come from the unblinded follow-up period.

cards.headline: Ondo 2005 (n=31): quetiapine up to 200 mg/day did NOT improve hallucinations versus placebo on any measure (the treatment made no difference) — but did not worsen motor scores
cards.summary: Ondo 2005 (n=31): quetiapine up to 200 mg/day did NOT improve hallucinations versus placebo on any measure (the treatment made no difference) — but did not worsen motor scores
cards.people: 31 patients with Parkinson's disease, prominent visual hallucinations and Mini-Mental State Examination >21 at a single site, randomised 2:1 double-blind to quetiapine (up to 200 mg/day; n=21) or placebo (n=10) for 12 weeks; outcomes included UPDRS, the Baylor PD Hallucination Questionnaire, Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale and neuropsychological tests.
cards.result: There were no significant changes versus placebo in the hallucination questionnaire, the Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale, or its hallucination item, and no significant changes on any neuropsychological measure; UPDRS activities-of-daily-living and motor scores also did not significantly change. Sedation occurred in 9 patients on quetiapine, with no drug-related discontinuations and no serious drug-related events. The authors conclude quetiapine was well tolerated and did not worsen UPDRS scores, but showed no significant improvement in psychosis ratings, and suggest larger doses and sample sizes for future studies.
cards.watchOut: Very small (n=31, only 10 on placebo) — a null here is weak evidence of no effect, but it is the first of three concordant quetiapine nulls.
cards.source: Ondo WG et al. Double-blind, placebo-controlled, unforced titration parallel trial of quetiapine for dopaminergic-induced hallucinations in Parkinson's disease. Mov Disord. 2005. PMID: 15800937. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Rabey 2007 (n=58): quetiapine (mean 119 mg/day) showed no benefit over placebo on any scale over 3 months (the treatment made no difference); only 55% completed
cards.summary: Rabey 2007 (n=58): quetiapine (mean 119 mg/day) showed no benefit over placebo on any scale over 3 months (the treatment made no difference); only 55% completed
cards.people: 58 consecutive psychotic Parkinson's disease patients (mean age 75 years; 29 with dementia) randomised double-blind to quetiapine (mean dose 119.2 mg/day; n=30) or placebo (n=28) for 3 months; outcomes included UPDRS motor, Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale, MMSE, Hamilton Depression Scale, Epworth Sleepiness Score and Clinical Global Impression.
cards.result: No significant difference was found between the groups in any parameter. Only 32 patients (55%) completed the 3-month study (15 quetiapine, 17 placebo); treatment was interrupted in 15 quetiapine and 11 placebo patients. The authors conclude the study did not show a beneficial effect of quetiapine for drug-induced psychosis in Parkinson's disease, that the high withdrawal rate probably influenced the results, and that larger double-blind studies are required.
cards.watchOut: A 45% dropout rate undermines the comparison in both directions; doses (mean ~119 mg/day) were in the range used clinically, so under-dosing is not an obvious explanation.
cards.source: Rabey JM et al. Effect of quetiapine in psychotic Parkinson's disease patients: a double-blind labeled study of 3 months' duration. Mov Disord. 2007. PMID: 17034006. cards.headline: Shotbolt 2009 (n=24): quetiapine up to 150 mg/day again failed — dropout for lack of improvement came earlier on quetiapine than placebo (P=0.68, not significant) and no secondary outcome moved
cards.summary: Shotbolt 2009 (n=24): quetiapine up to 150 mg/day again failed — dropout for lack of improvement came earlier on quetiapine than placebo (P=0.68, not significant) and no secondary outcome moved
cards.people: 24 consenting patients with Parkinson's disease psychosis in a 12-week double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial of quetiapine (up to 150 mg/day); primary outcome was time to dropout due to lack of improvement of psychosis, with standard Parkinson's and psychiatric rating scales as secondaries.
cards.result: Patients on quetiapine dropped out earlier than those on placebo, but the difference was not significant (P=0.68), and no significant changes were found for any secondary outcome measure in either group. Quetiapine did not appear to worsen motor functioning, but its use was limited by faster dropout than placebo. The authors state the small sample size allows no conclusive interpretation and note recruitment difficulty and natural symptom fluctuation as impediments.
cards.watchOut: The smallest of the three quetiapine trials (n=24); individually inconclusive, it completes a three-for-three negative pattern.
cards.source: Shotbolt P et al. A randomized controlled trial of quetiapine for psychosis in Parkinson's disease. Neuropsychiatr Dis Treat. 2009. PMID: 19557142. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: clozapine positive twice, quetiapine negative three times — SPLIT by drug
cards.summary: Synthesis: clozapine positive twice, quetiapine negative three times — SPLIT by drug
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: clozapine — Parkinson Study Group 1999 (n=60) and Pollak 2004 (n=60); quetiapine — Ondo 2005 (n=31), Rabey 2007 (n=58) and Shotbolt 2009 (n=24). Total N=233. Pimavanserin is homed on #1112.
cards.result: The split is between the drugs, not within them: low-dose clozapine reproducibly improves Parkinson's psychosis without motor worsening (with blood monitoring and somnolence as its costs), while quetiapine has never beaten placebo in a randomised trial for this indication. PROPOSED SPLIT, named as such.
cards.watchOut: All five trials are small and old; the clozapine verdict rests on 120 randomised patients in total, and quetiapine's nulls are individually underpowered even though they agree.
