shelves.title: Shunting itself for iNPH: gait improved versus a closed valve in PENS and versus postponed surgery in SINPHONI-2 — POSSIBLE
shelves.question: In patients with idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus, does shunt surgery improve gait compared with conservative management or a placebo (closed-valve) shunt setting?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Female · Humans · Male · Cerebrospinal Fluid Shunts/adverse effects,instrumentation,methods · Cognition/physiology · Double-Blind Method · Gait/physiology · Gait Disorders, Neurologic/diagnosis,etiology,physiopathology,therapy · Hydrocephalus, Normal Pressure/surgery,complications,physiopathology · Postural Balance/physiology · Urinary Bladder, Overactive/diagnosis,etiology,physiopathology,therapy · Urinary Incontinence/diagnosis,etiology,physiopathology,therapy · Treatment Outcome · Hematoma, Subdural/epidemiology,etiology · Headache/epidemiology,etiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). Shelf #3655 cards which valve settings and designs to use once shunting is decided; this shelf asks the prior question — whether shunting itself beats no effective shunt — and #3655's PMIDs are not re-carded here. PENS (Luciano 2025, NEJM; n=99) is the first double-blind test: all participants received a shunt and were randomised to an open valve setting or a placebo (effectively closed, >400 mm water) setting; at 3 months gait velocity had risen 0.23 m/s on the open setting versus 0.03 m/s on placebo (treatment difference 0.21 m/s, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.31; P<0.001), with better Tinetti scores but no significant cognitive or bladder advantage, and more subdural bleeding (12% versus 2%) and positional headaches (59% versus 28%) on the open setting, against more falls on placebo (46% versus 24%). SINPHONI-2 (Kazui 2015; n=93, open-label) found favourable outcome (≥1-point modified Rankin improvement) at 3 months in 65% with immediate lumboperitoneal shunting versus 5% with surgery postponed 3 months (difference 61%). The SINPHONI-1 prospective cohort (Hashimoto 2010; n=100, observational) found 69% favourable outcome at 1 year after ventriculoperitoneal shunting. Both trials have real limits — PENS enrolled only patients who had already responded to temporary CSF drainage, and SINPHONI-2 was unblinded — hence POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY.

cards.headline: Luciano 2025 — PENS (n=99, double-blind): an open shunt valve beat a placebo (closed) valve setting on gait velocity at 3 months (+0.21 m/s difference, P<0.001) — with more subdural bleeding (12% vs 2%)
cards.summary: Luciano 2025 — PENS (n=99, double-blind): an open shunt valve beat a placebo (closed) valve setting on gait velocity at 3 months (+0.21 m/s difference, P<0.001) — with more subdural bleeding (12% vs 2%)
cards.people: 99 participants with idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus, selected for shunt surgery on the basis of gait-velocity improvement with temporary CSF drainage, all implanted with a noninvasively adjustable shunt and randomised double-blind to an open valve setting (opening pressure 110 mm water) or a placebo setting (>400 mm water). Primary outcome: change in gait velocity at 3 months; secondaries included Tinetti scale, Montreal Cognitive Assessment and Overactive Bladder Questionnaire scores.
cards.result: Gait velocity increased by a mean 0.23 ± 0.23 m/s in the open-shunt group (49 assessed) and was essentially unchanged on placebo (0.03 ± 0.23 m/s; 49 assessed): treatment difference 0.21 m/s (95% CI 0.12 to 0.31; P<0.001). Tinetti scores improved significantly more on the open setting (mean change 2.9 versus 0.5 points; P=0.003), but MoCA (1.3 versus 0.3 points) and bladder scores (−3.3 versus −1.5) did not differ significantly. Adverse events were mixed: more falls on placebo (46% versus 24%), equal cerebral bleeding (2% both groups), but more subdural bleeding (12% versus 2%) and positional headaches (59% versus 28%) on the open setting.
cards.watchOut: Everyone was operated on and everyone had already responded to temporary CSF drainage — the trial proves the open valve, not the decision to operate, and only in pre-selected responders; subdural bleeding is the open valve's real price.
cards.source: Luciano MG et al. A Randomized Trial of Shunting for Idiopathic Normal-Pressure Hydrocephalus. N Engl J Med. 2025. PMID: 40960253. Registry ID: NCT05081128. cards.headline: Kazui 2015 — SINPHONI-2 (n=93, open-label): immediate lumboperitoneal shunting gave favourable outcome in 65% versus 5% with surgery postponed 3 months (difference 61%, P<0.0001)
cards.summary: Kazui 2015 — SINPHONI-2 (n=93, open-label): immediate lumboperitoneal shunting gave favourable outcome in 65% versus 5% with surgery postponed 3 months (difference 61%, P<0.0001)
cards.people: 93 patients aged 60–85 with idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus, ventriculomegaly and tight high-convexity/medial subarachnoid spaces on MRI, at 20 Japanese centres, randomised 1:1 to lumboperitoneal shunt surgery within 1 month (n=49) or surgery postponed for 3 months (n=44); patients and assessors were not masked. Primary endpoint: favourable outcome (≥1-point improvement on the modified Rankin scale) at 3 months, intention-to-treat.
cards.result: Favourable outcome at 3 months occurred in 32 (65%) of 49 immediate-surgery patients versus 2 (5%) of 44 postponed patients (difference 61%, 95% CI 42 to 68; P<0.0001). At 12 months after surgery the proportions were similar between groups (30 [67%] of 45 immediate versus 22 [58%] of 38 postponed; difference 9%, 95% CI −14 to 31; P=0.496) — as expected once the postponed group had also been shunted. Serious adverse-event proportions did not differ significantly between groups.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with a subjective component in the Rankin assessment and a postponed-treatment (not sham) control — expectation effects cannot be excluded, which is why PENS's blinded design matters.
cards.source: Kazui H et al. Lumboperitoneal shunt surgery for idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (SINPHONI-2): an open-label randomised trial. Lancet Neurol. 2015. PMID: 25934242. Registry ID: UMIN000002730 (as stated in the record). open-label randomized trial (sinphoni-2) 93 patients aged 60–85 with idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus, ventriculomegaly and tight high-convexity/medial subarachnoid spaces on mri, at 20 japanese centres, randomised 1:1 to lumboperitoneal shunt surgery within 1 month (n=49) or surgery postponed for 3 months (n=44); patients and assessors were not masked. primary endpoint: favourable outcome (≥1-point improvement on the modified rankin scale) at 3 months, intention-to-treat. favourable outcome at 3 months occurred in 32 (65%) of 49 immediate-surgery patients versus 2 (5%) of 44 postponed patients (difference 61%, 95% ci 42 to 68; p<0.0001). at 12 months after surgery the proportions were similar between groups (30 [67%] of 45 immediate versus 22 [58%] of 38 postponed; difference 9%, 95% ci −14 to 31; p=0.496) — as expected once the postponed group had also been shunted. serious adverse-event proportions did not differ significantly between groups. open-label with a subjective component in the rankin assessment and a postponed-treatment (not sham) control — expectation effects cannot be excluded, which is why pens's blinded design matters. kazui h et al. lumboperitoneal shunt surgery for idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (sinphoni-2): an open-label randomised trial. lancet neurol. 2015. pmid: 25934242. registry id: umin000002730 (as stated in the record). mesh: aged · aged, 80 and over · cerebrospinal fluid shunts/adverse effects,methods · female · follow-up studies · humans · hydrocephalus, normal pressure/surgery · japan · lumbosacral region/surgery · male · peritoneum/surgery · subarachnoid space/surgery · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Hashimoto 2010 — SINPHONI-1 (n=100, prospective cohort, observational): 69% achieved a favourable outcome 1 year after ventriculoperitoneal shunting; 80% were shunt responders
cards.summary: Hashimoto 2010 — SINPHONI-1 (n=100, prospective cohort, observational): 69% achieved a favourable outcome 1 year after ventriculoperitoneal shunting; 80% were shunt responders
cards.people: Prospective multicentre cohort (26 Japanese centres) of 100 patients aged 60–85 with idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus diagnosed by the MRI-based scheme (ventriculomegaly with tight high-convexity and medial subarachnoid spaces), all receiving ventriculoperitoneal shunts with a programmable valve; primary endpoint favourable outcome (≥1-level modified Rankin improvement) at 1 year. Observational — no control group.
cards.result: A favourable outcome was achieved by 69.0% at 1 year and 80.0% were shunt responders (improvement at any evaluation point within the year); improvement of ≥1 point on the iNPH grading scale occurred in 77.0% at 1 year, with response at any point in 89.0%. Serious adverse events were recorded in 15 patients, three related to surgery or the shunt; subdural effusion and orthostatic headache were non-serious shunt-related events controlled by pressure readjustment.
cards.watchOut: Observational and uncontrolled: spontaneous fluctuation, regression to the mean and selection (MRI-defined responders) all inflate the apparent benefit; carded as supporting context for the two randomised trials, labelled observational.

cards.headline: Yamada 2017 (post-hoc cohort analysis, n=83): severe preoperative disability predicted poor outcome — patients with severe preoperative Rankin scores had 4.7 times the relative risk of severe scores at 12 months
cards.summary: Yamada 2017 (post-hoc cohort analysis, n=83): severe preoperative disability predicted poor outcome — patients with severe preoperative Rankin scores had 4.7 times the relative risk of severe scores at 12 months
cards.people: Post-hoc analysis of 83 patients (mean age 76.4 years) who underwent lumboperitoneal shunt surgery in the SINPHONI programme, followed to 12 months, examining whether presurgical symptom severity, disease duration and tap-test response predicted outcome; age-adjusted and multivariate relative risks by Cox regression. Observational analysis.
cards.result: At 3 months, 45 (54%) had improved by 1 modified Rankin point and 6 (7%) by ≥2 points; at 12 months, 39 (47%) and 13 (16%) respectively, while 5 (6%) had worse Rankin scores at 12 months. Patients with severe preoperative Rankin scores had a 4.7-times higher multivariate relative risk of severe scores at 12 months, and those with severe preoperative gait disturbance a 46.5-times greater relative risk of severe gait disturbance at 12 months (relative measures). Patients without gait improvement on the tap test had multivariate relative risks of unimproved gait of 7.54 (3 months) and 11.2 (12 months). Disease duration was not significantly associated with outcome.
cards.watchOut: Observational and post-hoc: it identifies who benefits least (the most severely affected) rather than testing shunting; the very large relative risks rest on small subgroups.
cards.source: Yamada S et al. Disability risk or unimproved symptoms following shunt surgery in patients with idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus: post hoc analysis of SINPHONI and SINPHONI-2. J Neurosurg. 2017. PMID: 27419822. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Winter SAD itself: light and CBT-SAD are equal acutely; CBT-SAD halves second-winter recurrence (27.3% vs 45.6%) — SPLIT by time horizon
shelves.question: In adults with winter seasonal affective disorder, does bright light therapy or CBT-SAD reduce depressive symptoms acutely, and which better prevents recurrence the following winter?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy · Major Depressive Disorder/therapy · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Phototherapy/methods · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Seasonal Affective Disorder/therapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT by time horizon. Shelf #497 cards bright light for conditions other than seasonal depression (its Golden 2005 card addresses nonseasonal depression); the seasonal disorder itself — this shelf's question — was uncovered there, and the Rohan trials below are not carded on #497. Acutely, the large head-to-head trial (Rohan 2015; 177 adults with recurrent seasonal major depression; 6 weeks of group CBT-SAD versus 10,000-lux morning light) found the treatments indistinguishable: depression scores improved significantly and comparably, with remission 47.6% versus 47.2% on the SIGH-SAD and 56.0% versus 63.6% on the BDI-II. The earlier four-arm trial (Rohan 2007; n=61) found CBT, light and their combination each beat a wait-list control, with the combination's remission rate (73%) significantly above control (20%). The treatments separate only with time: in the follow-up of the 177-patient cohort (Rohan 2016), the first winter did not differ, but at the second winter recurrence was 27.3% after CBT-SAD versus 45.6% after light therapy, with remission (BDI-II ≤8) in 68.3% versus 44.5% — a durability advantage for the psychological treatment once the light box is put away.

cards.headline: Rohan 2015 (n=177, acute): CBT-SAD and bright light were indistinguishable over 6 weeks — remission 47.6% vs 47.2% (SIGH-SAD) and 56.0% vs 63.6% (BDI-II)
cards.summary: Rohan 2015 (n=177, acute): CBT-SAD and bright light were indistinguishable over 6 weeks — remission 47.6% vs 47.2% (SIGH-SAD) and 56.0% vs 63.6% (BDI-II)
cards.people: 177 adults with a current episode of major depression recurrent with a seasonal pattern, randomised to 6 weeks of CBT-SAD (n=88; 12 group sessions of the SAD-tailored protocol, two 90-minute sessions weekly, delivered by PhD psychologists) or light therapy (n=89; 10,000-lux cool-white fluorescent light, starting at 30 minutes each morning and adjusted by a response/side-effect algorithm). Outcomes: SIGH-SAD weekly, BDI-II before/at week 3/after treatment, and post-treatment remission by cut-points.
cards.result: Depression severity on both the SIGH-SAD and BDI-II improved significantly and comparably with CBT-SAD and light therapy, and the treatments did not differ in remission rates on the SIGH-SAD (47.6% and 47.2%, respectively) or the BDI-II (56.0% and 63.6%). A baseline comorbid diagnosis was associated with higher depression scores across all time points in both treatments.
cards.watchOut: No placebo or wait-list arm — 'comparably effective' rests on both arms improving, benchmarked against the earlier controlled trial (card below); blinding is impossible for either treatment.
cards.source: Rohan KJ et al. Randomized Trial of Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy Versus Light Therapy for Seasonal Affective Disorder: Acute Outcomes. Am J Psychiatry. 2015. PMID: 25859764. Registry ID: NCT01714050. cards.headline: Rohan 2016 (follow-up of the same 177): no difference at the first winter — but at the second winter recurrence was 27.3% after CBT-SAD vs 45.6% after light, and remission 68.3% vs 44.5%
cards.summary: Rohan 2016 (follow-up of the same 177): no difference at the first winter — but at the second winter recurrence was 27.3% after CBT-SAD vs 45.6% after light, and remission 68.3% vs 44.5%
cards.type: Randomized trial follow-up (one and two winters)
cards.people: Prospective one- and two-winter follow-up of the 177 participants randomised in Rohan 2015 (CBT-SAD n=88; light therapy n=89), assessed in January/February each winter with the SIGH-SAD, plus BDI-II, remission status, and telephone tracking of major-depression status in October and December of the first year. Primary outcome: winter depression recurrence on the SIGH-SAD.
cards.result: The treatments did not differ on any outcome during the first follow-up winter. At the second winter, CBT-SAD was associated with a smaller proportion of SIGH-SAD recurrences (27.3% compared with 45.6%), less severe symptoms on both measures, and a larger proportion of remissions defined as BDI-II ≤8 (68.3% compared with 44.5%) than light therapy. Non-recurrence at the first winter was more strongly associated with non-recurrence at the second winter among CBT-SAD participants (relative risk 5.12) than light-therapy participants (relative risk 1.92) — relative measures. The authors conclude CBT-SAD shows greater durability two winters after acute treatment.
cards.watchOut: A follow-up of the acute trial, not a new randomisation — differential attrition and any further treatment obtained during the two winters are uncontrolled, and the separation appears only at winter two.
cards.source: Rohan KJ et al. Outcomes One and Two Winters Following Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy or Light Therapy for Seasonal Affective Disorder. Am J Psychiatry. 2016. PMID: 26539881. Registry ID: NCT01714050. cards.headline: Rohan 2007 (n=61, four arms): CBT, light and their combination each beat wait-list; combined treatment's remission rate was 73% vs 20% on control
cards.summary: Rohan 2007 (n=61, four arms): CBT, light and their combination each beat wait-list; combined treatment's remission rate was 73% vs 20% on control
cards.people: 61 adults with major depression, recurrent with seasonal pattern, randomised to one of four 6-week conditions: CBT (1.5-hour twice-weekly group therapy), light therapy (10,000 lux for 90 minutes/day, timing individually adjusted), combined CBT + light, or a minimal-contact/delayed-light control (light after 6 weeks of monitoring). The first controlled psychotherapy trial for seasonal affective disorder.
cards.result: CBT, light therapy and the combination significantly and comparably improved depression severity relative to the wait-list control in intent-to-treat and completer samples. The combination (73%) had a significantly higher remission rate than control (20%); using summer mood status to estimate the functional population, the combination also produced significantly more clinically significant change than control. The light-therapy arm's outcomes virtually replicated prior light trials.
cards.watchOut: Small (n=61 across four arms) and wait-list rather than placebo controlled — it establishes that both treatments beat monitoring, not the size of any specific effect.
cards.source: Rohan KJ et al. A randomized controlled trial of cognitive-behavioral therapy, light therapy, and their combination for seasonal affective disorder. J Consult Clin Psychol. 2007. PMID: 17563165. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Factor XIa inhibition after non-cardioembolic stroke: asundexian's phase 3 trial cut recurrent ischaemic stroke by 26% relative (6.2% vs 8.4%) with no excess major bleeding — after both phase 2 programmes had been neutral
shelves.question: In patients with acute non-cardioembolic ischaemic stroke or high-risk TIA, does adding a factor XIa inhibitor to antiplatelet therapy reduce recurrent ischaemic stroke without increasing major bleeding, compared with antiplatelet therapy alone?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Benzamides/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Cardiovascular Diseases/mortality · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination/adverse effects,methods · Factor XIa/antagonists & inhibitors · Hemorrhage/chemically induced,epidemiology · Hydrocarbons, Fluorinated/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Incidence · Ischemic Attack, Transient/drug therapy · Ischemic Stroke/drug therapy,epidemiology,mortality,prevention & control · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Myocardial Infarction/epidemiology,mortality · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Recurrence · Secondary Prevention/methods · Triazoles/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT, by development stage. The phase 3 OCEANIC-STROKE trial (n=12,327) found adding asundexian 50 mg daily to antiplatelet therapy lowered recurrent ischaemic stroke from 8.4% to 6.2% — a 26% relative reduction (hazard ratio 0.74) and a 2.2-percentage-point absolute reduction — with major bleeding essentially unchanged (1.9% vs 1.7%). Both earlier phase 2 dose-finding trials were neutral on their primary composites, which combined symptomatic stroke with MRI-detected covert infarcts: PACIFIC-Stroke (asundexian, n=1,808) showed no dose response, and AXIOMATIC-SSP (milvexian, n=2,366) likewise, neither with a meaningful major-bleeding signal. The split is therefore not drug-versus-drug contradiction so much as endpoint and power: the covert-infarct composites did not move, while the large symptomatic-event trial did. This shelf is the post-stroke antiplatelet add-on question; asundexian versus apixaban in atrial fibrillation (OCEANIC-AF) is a different population and comparator, homed on shelf #3108. Note: the slate for this row asserted a 2026 regulatory approval for asundexian; no fetched record in this session states any approval, so this pack makes no approval claim.

cards.headline: OCEANIC-STROKE 2026: in 12,327 patients, asundexian added to antiplatelet therapy cut ischaemic stroke to 6.2% vs 8.4% (HR 0.74 — a 26% relative reduction; 2.2 percentage points absolute), with major bleeding 1.9% vs 1.7%
cards.summary: OCEANIC-STROKE 2026: in 12,327 patients, asundexian added to antiplatelet therapy cut ischaemic stroke to 6.2% vs 8.4% (HR 0.74 — a 26% relative reduction; 2.2 percentage points absolute), with major bleeding 1.9% vs 1.7%
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 trial (OCEANIC-STROKE), New England Journal of Medicine 2026
cards.people: 12,327 patients randomised double-blind (6,162 asundexian, 6,165 placebo) within 72 hours of a noncardioembolic ischaemic stroke or high-risk TIA, all with a nonlacunar infarct on imaging, a history of atherosclerosis, or atherosclerotic plaque on cerebrovascular imaging, and all receiving planned dual or single antiplatelet therapy; asundexian dose 50 mg once daily.
cards.result: Ischaemic stroke occurred in 6.2% on asundexian versus 8.4% on placebo (cause-specific hazard ratio 0.74; 95% CI 0.65 to 0.84; P<0.001) — a 26% relative reduction, 2.2 percentage points absolute. The composite of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction or stroke was also lower on asundexian. Major bleeding was 1.9% versus 1.7% (hazard ratio 1.10; 95% CI 0.85 to 1.44). Overall adverse events (69.3% vs 70.1%) and serious adverse events (19.2% vs 19.5%) were similar.
cards.watchOut: A single phase 3 trial, however large: the class claim rests on this one programme, and the same drug at the same 50 mg dose failed outright against apixaban in atrial fibrillation (#3108) — dose adequacy is population-specific. The record gives no follow-up duration in the abstract, so event percentages should not be annualised.
cards.source: Sharma M et al. Asundexian for Secondary Stroke Prevention. The New England journal of medicine. 2026. PMID: 41985132. Registry ID: NCT05686070 (as printed in the record). cards.headline: PACIFIC-Stroke 2022: phase 2b asundexian showed no dose response — covert infarct or recurrent stroke in 19% on placebo vs 19%, 22% and 20% across the 10, 20 and 50 mg doses (the treatment made no difference to the primary outcome)
cards.summary: PACIFIC-Stroke 2022: phase 2b asundexian showed no dose response — covert infarct or recurrent stroke in 19% on placebo vs 19%, 22% and 20% across the 10, 20 and 50 mg doses (the treatment made no difference to the primary outcome)
cards.people: 1,808 patients (mean age 67 years, 34% women) randomised within 48 hours of acute non-cardioembolic ischaemic stroke at 196 hospitals in 23 countries to asundexian 10, 20 or 50 mg once daily or placebo, each added to usual antiplatelet therapy (43% received dual therapy), followed 26–52 weeks with MRI at entry and 26 weeks.
cards.result: The primary composite (incident MRI-detected covert brain infarct or recurrent symptomatic ischaemic stroke by 26 weeks) occurred in 87/456 (19%) on placebo versus 86/455 (19%), 99/450 (22%) and 90/447 (20%) on ascending asundexian doses (dose-response t statistic −0.68; p=0.80) — the treatment made no difference. Major or clinically relevant non-major bleeding occurred in 11/452 (2%) on placebo versus 19, 14 and 19 patients across doses (pooled hazard ratio 1.57; 90% CI 0.91 to 2.71) — numerically higher, not statistically established.
cards.watchOut: The primary outcome was dominated by covert MRI infarcts, a surrogate the phase 3 trial did not use; a neutral phase 2 on this composite does not contradict a positive phase 3 on symptomatic stroke — but it does mean the covert-infarct burden was never shown to fall.
cards.source: Shoamanesh A et al. Factor XIa inhibition with asundexian after acute non-cardioembolic ischaemic stroke (PACIFIC-Stroke): an international, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 2b trial. Lancet (London, England). 2022. PMID: 36063821. Registry ID: NCT04304508 (as printed in the record). cards.headline: AXIOMATIC-SSP 2024: milvexian added to dual antiplatelet therapy showed no dose response — symptomatic stroke or covert infarct in an estimated 16.8% on placebo vs 15.3–16.7% across five doses (the treatment made no difference); major bleeding ~1% in every arm
cards.summary: AXIOMATIC-SSP 2024: milvexian added to dual antiplatelet therapy showed no dose response — symptomatic stroke or covert infarct in an estimated 16.8% on placebo vs 15.3–16.7% across five doses (the treatment made no difference); major bleeding ~1% in every arm
cards.type: Randomised phase 2 dose-finding trial (AXIOMATIC-SSP), Lancet Neurology 2024
cards.people: 2,366 participants (median age 71 years, 36% women) at 367 hospitals in 27 countries, randomised within 48 hours of acute ischaemic stroke or high-risk TIA to milvexian (25 mg once daily, or 25, 50, 100 or 200 mg twice daily) or placebo for 90 days; everyone received clopidogrel 75 mg daily for 21 days and aspirin 100 mg daily for 90 days.
cards.result: Estimated primary-outcome rates (symptomatic ischaemic stroke or incident covert brain infarct on MRI at 90 days) were 16.8% on placebo and 16.7%, 16.6%, 15.6%, 15.4% and 15.3% across ascending milvexian doses, with model-based relative risks of 0.99, 0.99, 0.93, 0.92 and 0.91 versus placebo and no significant dose-response — the treatment made no difference to the composite. Major bleeding showed no dose-response either (1% on placebo; 1–2% across doses). Five treatment-emergent deaths occurred, four judged unrelated to study drug.
cards.watchOut: Ninety days of treatment and an MRI-heavy composite limit what this trial can say about long-term symptomatic prevention; its role was dose selection for a phase 3 trial. Its bleeding neutrality at ~1% is reassuring but underpowered for rare major haemorrhage.
cards.source: Sharma M et al. Safety and efficacy of factor XIa inhibition with milvexian for secondary stroke prevention (AXIOMATIC-SSP): a phase 2, international, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, dose-finding trial. The Lancet. Neurology. 2024. PMID: 38101902. Registry ID: NCT03766581 (as printed in the record; EU Clinical Trials Register 2017-005029-19 also printed). cards.headline: Synthesis: the phase 3 symptomatic-event trial is positive and bleeding-neutral; both phase 2 covert-infarct programmes were neutral — SPLIT by endpoint and stage
cards.summary: Synthesis: the phase 3 symptomatic-event trial is positive and bleeding-neutral; both phase 2 covert-infarct programmes were neutral — SPLIT by endpoint and stage
cards.people: Synthesis of the three cards above.
cards.result: Read together: factor XIa inhibition added to antiplatelet therapy after non-cardioembolic stroke has one large positive phase 3 result (asundexian: 26% relative, 2.2-point absolute reduction in recurrent ischaemic stroke; major bleeding 1.9% vs 1.7%) and two neutral phase 2 dose-finding trials whose composites leaned on covert MRI infarcts. The fair stamp is SPLIT: a prescriber can cite a genuine phase 3 win for asundexian, but the class has no second positive trial yet, and milvexian's phase 3 readout is not in this evidence set. The atrial-fibrillation comparison lives on shelf #3108 and must not be merged with this one.

shelves.title: MONEAD: children exposed in utero to newer antiseizure medications scored the same on verbal ability at ages 3 and 6 as unexposed children — but higher drug concentrations tracked with worse scores on some secondary measures
shelves.question: In children exposed in utero to antiseizure medications, how do neurodevelopmental outcomes at ages 3 and 6 compare across medications (and with unexposed children), and how do maternal seizure control and breastfeeding on medication factor in?
shelves.mesh: Child, Preschool · Child · Humans · Female · Pregnancy · Anticonvulsants/adverse effects · Cohort Studies · Prospective Studies · Epilepsy/drug therapy · Cognition · Prenatal Exposure Delayed Effects/chemically induced,drug therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE, observational by design and labelled as such. MONEAD is a prospective multicentre cohort, not a trial: 456 pregnant women (351 with epilepsy, 105 without) enrolled at 20 US specialty centres and their children followed with blinded testing. Its primary comparisons are reassuring nulls — Verbal Index scores at age 3 (102.7 vs 102.3) and age 6 (difference −0.6; 95% CI −3.2 to 1.9) did not differ between children of women with epilepsy, mostly taking lamotrigine or levetiracetam, and children of healthy women (the exposures made no difference to the primary outcome). The caution lives in the secondary analyses: exposure-dependent effects appeared on several measures and varied by medication, including executive-function scores tracking third-trimester concentrations at age 4.5 years — the cohort's own reading is to dose high enough to protect mother and fetus from seizures but no higher. Early-pregnancy folate was positively associated with cognition and behaviour with no high-dose risk signal, and breastfeeding on contemporary regimens for at least 6 months was associated with better adaptive behaviour, not harm. Structural malformations after exposure are a separate question, homed on shelf #2676; periconception folic acid is homed on #5727/#6025.

cards.headline: MONEAD age 3 (2023): Verbal Index 102.7 in exposed children vs 102.3 in unexposed — no difference; maximum third-trimester drug concentration also showed no primary effect (−2.9; 95% CI −6.7 to 1.0)
cards.summary: MONEAD age 3 (2023): Verbal Index 102.7 in exposed children vs 102.3 in unexposed — no difference; maximum third-trimester drug concentration also showed no primary effect (−2.9; 95% CI −6.7 to 1.0)
cards.people: Prospective observational cohort at 20 US specialty epilepsy centres: 456 pregnant women enrolled at ≤20 weeks (351 with epilepsy, 105 without); 345 children born to women with epilepsy and 106 to women without. At age 3, Verbal Index was assessed blind in 284 exposed and 87 unexposed children; the concentration analysis included 258 exposed children.
cards.result: Verbal Index scores did not differ between children of women with and without epilepsy (adjusted least-square mean 102.7, 95% CI 101.4 to 103.9, vs 102.3, 99.8 to 104.7) — the exposures made no difference to the primary outcome. Maximum third-trimester antiseizure blood concentrations likewise showed no significant association (−2.9; 95% CI −6.7 to 1.0). Significant predictors of lower scores were maternal IQ, maternal education, post-birth anxiety, gestational age at enrolment, child sex and ethnicity. In secondary analyses, exposure-dependent effects were present on multiple cognitive measures and varied by medication.
cards.watchOut: Observational: women were not randomised to medications, so drug comparisons are confounded by indication, dose and seizure type; the cohort is dominated by newer agents and cannot speak for valproate-era exposures. The null is on the primary verbal outcome — secondary exposure-dependent signals are part of this card, not a contradiction of it.
cards.source: Meador KJ et al. Cognitive outcomes at age 3 years in children with fetal exposure to antiseizure medications (MONEAD study) in the USA: a prospective, observational cohort study. The Lancet. Neurology. 2023. PMID: 37479375. Registry ID: NCT01730170 — the registry number as printed in the companion MONEAD records; this record's abstract prints it truncated as 'NCT0730170'. cards.headline: MONEAD age 6 (2025): verbal ability still did not differ (−0.6; 95% CI −3.2 to 1.9; P=.64); 78% of exposures were lamotrigine or levetiracetam; early folate tracked with better cognition, with no high-dose risk signal
cards.summary: MONEAD age 6 (2025): verbal ability still did not differ (−0.6; 95% CI −3.2 to 1.9; P=.64); 78% of exposures were lamotrigine or levetiracetam; early folate tracked with better cognition, with no high-dose risk signal
cards.type: Prospective non-randomised cohort study (MONEAD), JAMA Neurology 2025
cards.people: The same MONEAD cohort followed to age 6 (assessed 2019–2022): 298 children of women with epilepsy and 89 children of healthy women in the primary analysis; 232 of the 298 exposed children (78%) were exposed to lamotrigine or levetiracetam alone or in combination.
cards.result: Verbal Index scores did not differ between exposed and unexposed children (parameter estimate −0.6; 95% CI −3.2 to 1.9; P=.64) — again, the exposures made no difference to the primary outcome. Exposure-dependent outcomes differed across medications in secondary analyses, though assessment of other medications was limited by the lamotrigine/levetiracetam predominance. Folate supplementation during the first 12 weeks of pregnancy had positive associations with cognition and behaviour, with no signal of risk at higher folate doses.
cards.watchOut: Attrition from 456 enrolled pregnancies to 387 children in the age-6 primary analysis, and a specialty-centre population, limit generalisability; the folate findings are associations within an observational cohort, not randomised evidence, and are homed in more depth on the folate shelves.
cards.source: Meador KJ et al. Neuropsychological Outcomes in 6-Year-Old Children of Women With Epilepsy: A Prospective Nonrandomized Clinical Trial. JAMA neurology. 2025. PMID: 39585668. Registry ID: NCT01730170 (as printed in the record). cards.headline: MONEAD age 4.5 (2024): creativity and executive function did not differ overall (−3.2; 95% CI −9.0 to 2.7), but executive-function scores worsened with higher third-trimester exposure (7.0 points per ratio unit; levetiracetam 12.9)
cards.summary: MONEAD age 4.5 (2024): creativity and executive function did not differ overall (−3.2; 95% CI −9.0 to 2.7), but executive-function scores worsened with higher third-trimester exposure (7.0 points per ratio unit; levetiracetam 12.9)
cards.people: MONEAD children assessed blind at 4.5 years: 251 children of women with epilepsy and 73 children of healthy women in the primary analysis of figural creativity (Torrance Test) and executive function (BRIEF-Preschool Global Executive Composite), with exposure quantified as ratios of maximum observed third-trimester concentrations and of defined daily dose.
cards.result: No differences in creativity or executive function were found between children of women with epilepsy and healthy women (creativity −3.2; 95% CI −9.0 to 2.7; p=0.286), and no exposure-dependent effects on creativity (−2.6; 95% CI −11.0 to 5.7; p=0.530). Secondary analyses did show exposure-dependent effects on executive function for both concentration ratio and dose ratio (7.0; 95% CI 2.9 to 11.2; p=0.001), most marked for levetiracetam (12.9; 95% CI 4.2 to 21.6; p=0.004) — higher exposure tracking with worse executive-function ratings.
cards.watchOut: The executive-function signal is a secondary, exposure-response association in an observational cohort — sicker mothers may both need higher doses and differ in other ways. It argues for lowest-effective-dose care, not for avoiding levetiracetam, whose primary-outcome record in this same cohort is null.

cards.headline: MONEAD breastfeeding (2026): breastfeeding on contemporary antiseizure regimens was not associated with harm at age 6 — and ≥6 months of breastfeeding tracked with better adaptive behaviour (+4.68 points)
cards.summary: MONEAD breastfeeding (2026): breastfeeding on contemporary antiseizure regimens was not associated with harm at age 6 — and ≥6 months of breastfeeding tracked with better adaptive behaviour (+4.68 points)
cards.type: Prospective multicentre cohort analysis (MONEAD), JAMA Network Open 2026
cards.people: MONEAD children followed to age 6: 273 children of women with epilepsy and 84 children of healthy women; exposures primarily levetiracetam and lamotrigine. Breastfeeding duration was grouped as none, under 6 months, or 6 months or longer; outcomes were Verbal Index and the Adaptive Behavior Assessment System General Adaptive Composite.
cards.result: Adjusted verbal language (difference 0.75; 95% CI −2.40 to 3.89; P=.64) and adaptive behaviour (difference 0.78; 95% CI −2.52 to 4.07; P=.64) did not differ between children of women with epilepsy and healthy women. Within the epilepsy cohort, breastfeeding for ≥6 months was associated with higher adaptive behaviour scores than no breastfeeding (estimate 4.68; 95% CI 1.34 to 8.03; P=.01), driven by practical and conceptual subdomains; under 6 months did not differ. Outcomes were comparable within each regimen — levetiracetam, lamotrigine, other monotherapy, polytherapy — regardless of breastfeeding duration.
cards.watchOut: Breastfeeding duration is self-selected and confounded (maternal health, seizure control, socioeconomic factors); the adaptive-behaviour association is not proof that breastfeeding caused the gain. The defensible claim is the negative one: no neurodevelopmental harm signal from breastfeeding on these regimens.
cards.source: Li Y et al. Breastfeeding and Neurodevelopmental Outcomes in Children of Women Taking Antiseizure Medications. JAMA network open. 2026. PMID: 42814461. Registry ID: none in the record (MONEAD cohort; registry number as on the companion records is NCT01730170). cards.headline: Synthesis: primary outcomes null at 3, 4.5 and 6 years for contemporary regimens; dose-dependent secondary signals argue for lowest effective dose — POSSIBLE (observational)
cards.summary: Synthesis: primary outcomes null at 3, 4.5 and 6 years for contemporary regimens; dose-dependent secondary signals argue for lowest effective dose — POSSIBLE (observational)
cards.people: Synthesis of the four MONEAD cards above.
cards.result: One cohort, four reports, one pattern: children exposed in utero to contemporary antiseizure medications — overwhelmingly lamotrigine and levetiracetam — tested the same as unexposed children on the pre-specified primary outcomes at every age examined, and breastfeeding on medication showed no harm signal. Against that reassurance, secondary exposure-response analyses repeatedly found higher third-trimester concentrations tracking with worse scores on some measures. The stamp is capped at POSSIBLE because the evidence is observational throughout: it can support 'no large primary-outcome harm detected for these drugs at these doses', never a randomised-grade safety claim, and it cannot be extrapolated to valproate or to high-dose polytherapy, which this cohort barely contains.
cards.watchOut: MONEAD is a single cohort reported in slices — the four cards are not four independent studies. Seizure control in pregnancy itself (the other half of the clinical balance) is addressed by the cohort's maternal-outcome reports, not by these child-outcome cards.
cards.source: Synthesis of Meador KJ et al. Lancet Neurol. 2023 (PMID: 37479375); Meador KJ et al. JAMA Neurol. 2025 (PMID: 39585668); Meador KJ et al. Neurology. 2024 (PMID: 38810172); Li Y et al. shelves.title: SUDEP and the night: nocturnal supervision was associated with lower SUDEP risk in case-control studies (odds ratios 0.4 and below), but the Cochrane review grades the evidence very low certainty — and no study has tested whether seizure-detection devices prevent SUDEP
shelves.question: In people with epilepsy at risk of sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP), are nocturnal supervision or listening/seizure-detection devices associated with lower SUDEP risk?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Anticonvulsants/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Caregivers/statistics & numerical data · Case-Control Studies · Comorbidity · Death, Sudden/epidemiology,prevention & control · Epilepsy, Tonic-Clonic/drug therapy,mortality · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Risk Factors · United Kingdom/epidemiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE, and observational throughout — there are no randomised trials of SUDEP prevention and there cannot readily be, given an incidence of roughly 1–2 per 1,000 patient-years. The strongest signal is for human supervision at night: in the UK case-control study (154 autopsy-confirmed SUDEP cases, 616 matched controls), sharing a bedroom or using special precautions such as a listening device was associated with lower odds of SUDEP (odds ratio 0.4 for supervision; 0.1 for the listening-device/special-precautions subgroup), while recent generalised tonic-clonic seizures carried an odds ratio of 13.8. A second analysis of the same case series found SUDEP was mainly sleep-related (58%) and unwitnessed (86%), and that nocturnal seizures independently raised risk — the mechanistic opening supervision is meant to close. The Cochrane review, however, found only one cohort and three case-control studies, all at serious to critical risk of bias, with results too heterogeneous to pool, and graded the supervision evidence 'limited, very low-certainty'. For seizure-detection devices specifically, no study has measured a SUDEP outcome at all — the device studies Cochrane found measured detection sensitivity only. Supervision is a reasonable, low-harm precaution to discuss; it is not a proven preventive.

cards.headline: Langan 2005: in 154 SUDEP cases vs 616 controls, nocturnal supervision was protective (OR 0.4) and special precautions such as a listening device more so (OR 0.1); recent tonic-clonic seizures raised risk 14-fold (OR 13.8)
cards.summary: Langan 2005: in 154 SUDEP cases vs 616 controls, nocturnal supervision was protective (OR 0.4) and special precautions such as a listening device more so (OR 0.1); recent tonic-clonic seizures raised risk 14-fold (OR 13.8)
cards.people: Case-control study in the UK: 154 people with epilepsy whose sudden death was confirmed as SUDEP at postmortem examination, each matched to four living community controls with epilepsy by age and geographic location (616 controls). Risk and protective factors were estimated by backward stepwise conditional logistic regression.
cards.result: A history of generalised tonic-clonic seizures in the previous 3 months was the dominant risk factor (odds ratio 13.8; 95% CI 6.6 to 29.1). Supervision at night was protective (OR 0.4; 95% CI 0.2 to 0.8) — defined as a supervising person sharing the same bedroom — and when special precautions such as a listening device were employed the association was stronger (OR 0.1; 95% CI 0.0 to 0.3). The authors concluded SUDEP is a seizure-related phenomenon, that controlling tonic-clonic seizures matters most, and that nocturnal supervision seems to protect.
cards.watchOut: Case-control associations are not intervention effects: families who supervise at night differ in many ways from those who do not, and the listening-device subgroup estimate (OR 0.1 with a confidence interval reaching 0.0) rests on small numbers. Odds ratios from this design also overstate relative risk reductions if read as such; they are reported here as odds ratios, as in the record.
cards.source: Langan Y et al. Case-control study of SUDEP. Neurology. 2005. PMID: 15824334. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Lamberts 2012: SUDEP was mainly a sleep-related (58%), unwitnessed (86%) event, and a history of nocturnal seizures independently raised risk (adjusted OR 2.6)
cards.summary: Lamberts 2012: SUDEP was mainly a sleep-related (58%), unwitnessed (86%) event, and a history of nocturnal seizures independently raised risk (adjusted OR 2.6)
cards.people: The same UK SUDEP series analysed by seizure pattern: 154 autopsy-confirmed SUDEP cases and 616 living controls with epilepsy, classified as having exclusively diurnal or nocturnal seizures; SUDEP events were classified sleep-related or not from eyewitness accounts and circumstances of death.
cards.result: SUDEP was primarily sleep-related (58%) and unwitnessed (86%); if sleep-related, it was more likely to be unwitnessed (OR 4.4; 95% CI 1.6 to 12). People with sleep-related SUDEP were more likely to have a history of nocturnal seizures than those with non-sleep-related SUDEP (OR 3.6; 95% CI 1.4 to 9.4). Those who died were more likely to have nocturnal seizures than living controls (OR 3.9; 95% CI 2.5 to 6.0), and nocturnal seizures remained a significant risk factor after correction for previously established SUDEP risk factors (OR 2.6; 95% CI 1.3 to 5.0).
cards.watchOut: This card establishes who is at risk and when deaths happen — it does not itself test supervision or any device. Its value to this shelf is the rationale: if deaths cluster at night, unwitnessed, in people with nocturnal seizures, then night-time presence or monitoring is the intervention the case-control signal (previous card) attaches to.
cards.source: Lamberts RJ et al. Sudden unexpected death in epilepsy: people with nocturnal seizures may be at highest risk. Epilepsia. 2012. PMID: 22192074. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cochrane 2020: only four eligible studies of SUDEP prevention, all at serious to critical risk of bias; two case-control studies favoured supervision (unadjusted ORs 0.34 and 0.08) but could not be pooled — 'limited, very low-certainty evidence'
cards.summary: Cochrane 2020: only four eligible studies of SUDEP prevention, all at serious to critical risk of bias; two case-control studies favoured supervision (unadjusted ORs 0.34 and 0.08) but could not be pooled — 'limited, very low-certainty evidence'
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review (CD011792, 2020 update) of randomised trials, cohort and case-control studies of interventions to prevent SUDEP — supervision, seizure-monitoring devices, safety pillows, education, early surgical evaluation, SSRIs and others. From 1,277 records it included one cohort study and three case-control studies.
cards.result: The 6-month prospective cohort (SUDEP-information provision) found no significant effect on compliance, quality of life, anxiety or depression, and no deaths occurred in either group. Two case-control studies reported a protective effect of nocturnal supervision (unadjusted OR 0.34; 95% CI 0.22 to 0.53; and OR 0.08; 95% CI 0.02 to 0.27) but significant heterogeneity prevented meta-analysis; the supervision effect in the larger study was independent of seizure control. A third case-control study, in residential care where night checks already occurred, found no added effect of more intensive supervision, though the centre with the lowest supervision level had the highest SUDEP incidence. Five device studies were excluded because they measured detection sensitivity, not SUDEP. The authors concluded there is limited, very low-certainty evidence that night supervision reduces SUDEP, and that the effectiveness of devices and all other interventions is unknown.
cards.watchOut: The unadjusted odds ratios quoted by the review are not adjusted effect estimates and the two positive studies overlap in era and design with the Langan card — this is one thin evidence base described three ways, not three independent bases. 'Very low certainty' is the operative phrase for any clinical conversation.
cards.source: Maguire MJ et al. Treatments for the prevention of Sudden Unexpected Death in Epilepsy (SUDEP). The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2020. PMID: 32239759. cards.headline: Synthesis: supervision at night is associated with less SUDEP in every observational dataset that looked — but the base is four biased studies, and devices are untested for the outcome that matters — POSSIBLE (observational)
cards.summary: Synthesis: supervision at night is associated with less SUDEP in every observational dataset that looked — but the base is four biased studies, and devices are untested for the outcome that matters — POSSIBLE (observational)
cards.people: Synthesis of the three cards above.
cards.result: The direction of evidence is consistent: tonic-clonic and nocturnal seizures mark the risk, deaths cluster at night unwitnessed, and being supervised — a person in the room, or precautions such as a listening device — is associated with substantially lower odds of SUDEP in case-control data. The certainty is not consistent with the size of those associations: Cochrane grades the whole prevention literature very low certainty, no randomised or prospective intervention data exist, and seizure-detection devices have never been evaluated against SUDEP itself. The stamp is therefore POSSIBLE with the observational label on its face: supervision is a defensible precaution to offer high-risk patients (frequent nocturnal tonic-clonic seizures), presented as association, not promise.
cards.watchOut: Never present the odds ratios as a proven percentage reduction in any individual's risk, and never extend the supervision association to commercial seizure-detection devices — for devices, the fetched record shows detection-sensitivity studies only.
cards.source: Synthesis of Langan Y et al. Neurology. 2005 (PMID: 15824334); Lamberts RJ et al. Epilepsia. 2012 (PMID: 22192074); Maguire MJ et al. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2020 (PMID: 32239759). Registry IDs: none in the records. MeSH: as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Anti-NMDAR encephalitis: when first-line immunotherapy fails, second-line rituximab or cyclophosphamide was associated with better outcomes (OR 2.69 for good outcome) — in observational cohorts only; no randomised trial exists
shelves.question: In patients with anti-NMDAR autoimmune encephalitis who do not respond to first-line immunotherapy (steroids, IVIG, plasma exchange), does second-line therapy (rituximab and/or cyclophosphamide) improve functional outcome?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Age Factors · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Analysis of Variance · Anti-N-Methyl-D-Aspartate Receptor Encephalitis/blood,cerebrospinal fluid,diagnosis,therapy · Autoantibodies/blood,cerebrospinal fluid · Child · Child, Preschool · Cohort Studies · Female · Humans · Immunoglobulins, Intravenous · Immunotherapy/methods · Infant · Logistic Models · Male · Middle Aged · Observation · Receptors, N-Methyl-D-Aspartate/immunology · Retrospective Studies · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE, observational throughout and labelled as such. The defining dataset is the 577-patient international cohort (Titulaer 2013): 94% received first-line immunotherapy (steroids, intravenous immunoglobulin, plasma exchange) or tumour removal, and 53% of those improved within 4 weeks. Among the 221 who did not improve, the 125 who went on to second-line therapy (rituximab and/or cyclophosphamide) reached a good outcome (modified Rankin Scale 0–2) more often than those who did not (odds ratio 2.69; 95% CI 1.24 to 5.80) — an association from non-randomised treatment choices, open to confounding in both directions (sicker patients may be escalated, or may be deemed too sick to escalate). Later observational work points the same way for relapse prevention: rituximab exposure was associated with a 71% relative lower hazard of first relapse in a US cohort (hazard ratio 0.29; Class IV evidence), and in an Italian paediatric cohort, receiving three or more different immune therapies at the first event was associated with a lower relapse hazard (HR 0.208). Recovery is slow — outcomes kept improving for up to 18 months — so 'failure' of first-line therapy should not be declared in days. No completed randomised trial of second-line therapy was found in the fetched records; treatment remains cohort-guided.

cards.headline: Titulaer 2013: of 221 patients who failed first-line therapy, those given second-line immunotherapy reached good outcome more often (OR 2.69; 95% CI 1.24 to 5.80); overall 79% reached mRS 0–2 by 24 months and 30 of 501 died
cards.summary: Titulaer 2013: of 221 patients who failed first-line therapy, those given second-line immunotherapy reached good outcome more often (OR 2.69; 95% CI 1.24 to 5.80); overall 79% reached mRS 0–2 by 24 months and 30 of 501 died
cards.people: Multi-institutional observational cohort of 577 patients with antibody-confirmed anti-NMDAR encephalitis (median age 21 years, range 8 months to 85 years; 211 children), enrolled 2007–2012; treatment and outcome were assessable in 501 patients with median follow-up of 24 months. First-line therapy was steroids, intravenous immunoglobulin and/or plasma exchange, plus tumour removal where applicable; second-line therapy was rituximab and/or cyclophosphamide.
cards.result: 472 of 501 patients (94%) received first-line immunotherapy or tumour removal, and 251 (53%) improved within 4 weeks. Of the 221 who did not improve, 125 (57%) received second-line immunotherapy and had better outcomes (good outcome, mRS 0–2) than those who did not (odds ratio 2.69; CI 1.24 to 5.80; p=0.012). Overall, 394 of 501 (79%) achieved a good outcome during the first 24 months (median time 6 months), 30 died, and at 24 months 203 of 252 assessed (81%) had a good outcome. Predictors of good outcome were early treatment and no intensive-care admission. Relapses occurred in 45 patients (12% risk within 2 years) and were usually milder than the first episode. In the 177 children with assessable data, predictors and the magnitude of the second-line effect were similar.
cards.watchOut: Treatment was chosen by clinicians, not randomised: the OR 2.69 compares patients selected for escalation with those not selected, and confounding by severity, tumour status and era cannot be removed from this design. It is the best evidence available and the reason the stamp is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY.
cards.source: Titulaer MJ et al. Treatment and prognostic factors for long-term outcome in patients with anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis: an observational cohort study. The Lancet. Neurology. 2013. cards.headline: Yang 2023: rituximab was associated with a 71% relative lower hazard of first relapse (HR 0.29; 95% CI 0.09 to 0.85) in a US autoimmune-encephalitis cohort — Class IV evidence
cards.summary: Yang 2023: rituximab was associated with a 71% relative lower hazard of first relapse (HR 0.29; 95% CI 0.09 to 0.85) in a US autoimmune-encephalitis cohort — Class IV evidence
cards.type: Retrospective cohort study with survival analysis, Neurology 2023
cards.people: Retrospective cohort at UC San Diego and Rady Children's Hospital, 2007–2021: 584 patients screened, 105 included (30 paediatric, 75 adult) with clinical autoimmune encephalitis; anti-NMDAR was the commonest antibody subtype (76% of paediatric, 34% of adult cases). Rituximab exposure was modelled as a time-dependent variable in Cox regression.
cards.result: Relapses occurred in 31% of paediatric antibody-positive, 40% of adult antibody-positive and 20% of adult antibody-negative patients; mean time to first relapse was 10.6, 13.1 and 6.9 months respectively. Rituximab — the commonest second-line agent — was associated with a 71% relative lower hazard of time to first relapse (HR 0.29; 95% CI 0.09 to 0.85) in the pooled analysis; age- and subtype-stratified estimates (children HR 0.30; adults HR 0.29; anti-NMDAR HR 0.42) all pointed the same way with wide intervals. The authors graded this Class IV evidence that rituximab is associated with lower relapse hazard.
cards.watchOut: This card answers the relapse half of the second-line question, not acute functional recovery, and mixes antibody subtypes — only a third of the adult cohort had anti-NMDAR encephalitis. Retrospective, single-system, and rituximab use again reflects clinician choice.
cards.source: Yang JH et al. Survival Analysis of Immunotherapy Effects on Relapse Rate in Pediatric and Adult Autoimmune Encephalitis. Neurology. 2023. PMID: 37827848. cards.headline: Nosadini 2019: in 62 children, 21% relapsed; receiving three or more different immune therapies at the first event was associated with a lower relapse hazard (HR 0.208; 95% CI 0.046 to 0.941)
cards.summary: Nosadini 2019: in 62 children, 21% relapsed; receiving three or more different immune therapies at the first event was associated with a lower relapse hazard (HR 0.208; 95% CI 0.046 to 0.941)
cards.type: Retrospective paediatric cohort study, Developmental Medicine & Child Neurology 2019
cards.people: Retrospective Italian cohort of 62 children with anti-NMDAR encephalitis onset at ≤18 years (39 girls; median onset age 9 years 10 months; onset 2005–2018), followed for a median of 84 months in relapsing and 32 months in monophasic patients.
cards.result: Thirteen children (21%) relapsed, with a median of two total events and median time to first relapse of 31.5 months; relapses were milder than onset episodes (median mRS 3 vs 5; no intensive-care admissions at relapse in the assessed subgroup vs 3 of 10 at onset). In survival analysis, the risk of relapse was significantly lower in patients who received three or more different immune therapies at the first disease event (HR 0.208; 95% CI 0.046 to 0.941; p=0.042). Neurological outcome at follow-up did not differ significantly between relapsing and monophasic patients (mRS 0–1 in 39/49 vs 12/13; p=0.431).
cards.watchOut: Small, retrospective and paediatric-only; 'three or more immune therapies' is a proxy for treatment intensity that bundles first- and second-line agents, so it supports escalation in general rather than any single drug. The wide confidence interval (0.046 to 0.941) barely excludes no effect.
cards.source: Nosadini M et al. Relapse risk factors in anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor encephalitis. Developmental medicine and child neurology. 2019. PMID: 31175679. cards.headline: Synthesis: second-line immunotherapy after first-line failure is associated with better recovery and fewer relapses in every cohort that examined it — POSSIBLE (observational), pending any randomised trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: second-line immunotherapy after first-line failure is associated with better recovery and fewer relapses in every cohort that examined it — POSSIBLE (observational), pending any randomised trial
cards.people: Synthesis of the three cards above.
cards.result: The Titulaer cohort supplies the acute-outcome association (OR 2.69 for good outcome when second-line therapy followed first-line failure); two later cohorts supply a concordant relapse association for rituximab and for more intensive early immunotherapy. All of it is observational, all treatment allocation was clinician-chosen, and no fetched record reports a completed randomised trial — so the stamp is POSSIBLE with the observational label, and the clinical posture it supports is 'escalate rather than persist with a failing first-line regimen, while expecting recovery to take months', not a proven treatment effect of a stated size.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote OR 2.69 or HR 0.29 to families as the expected benefit of treatment for an individual patient; they are cohort associations under confounding, presented here because they are the best evidence that exists.
cards.source: Synthesis of Titulaer MJ et al. Lancet Neurol. 2013 (PMID: 23290630); Yang JH et al. Neurology. 2023 (PMID: 37827848); Nosadini M et al. Dev Med Child Neurol. 2019 (PMID: 31175679). Registry IDs: none in the records. MeSH: as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: CSF production in adult humans: about 500–650 mL per day, swinging two- to three-fold across the day with a peak near 02:00 — the whole ~150 mL volume turning over roughly three to four times daily
shelves.question: At what rate is cerebrospinal fluid produced in adult humans, what fraction comes from the choroid plexus, and how many times per day does the CSF volume turn over?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Calibration · Cerebrospinal Fluid/metabolism · Circadian Rhythm · Female · Humans · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Male · Regression Analysis
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the production rate and its circadian swing; the choroid-plexus fraction is presented as the textbook's account, because no fetched human record quantifies it. Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall; Ganong's Review; Boron & Boulpaep — named here as framing, not as evidence cards): CSF is formed at roughly 500 mL/day, the total CSF volume is about 150 mL, so the volume turns over about three to four times a day, and the choroid plexuses are credited with the majority of production, the remainder arising from extrachoroidal sources. The primary human records fetched this session confirm the rate's order and refine it: MRI aqueduct-flow measurement put 24-hour production near 650 mL with a strong circadian rhythm (from ~12 mL/h in the early evening to ~42 mL/h near 02:00 — i.e. roughly 0.2 to 0.7 mL/min across the day, averaging ~0.4 mL/min), and the nocturnal peak was blunted by a beta-1 blocker, pointing to sympathetic/choroid-plexus regulation. The 2018 mechanistic work states the adult human rate as 500 mL/day and identifies the choroid-plexus cotransporter NKCC1 as contributing approximately half of production — demonstrated in mice in vivo and ex vivo plexus preparations, so the 'half' is a mechanism finding, not a human fraction measurement. One further human datum: production was significantly lower in healthy elderly volunteers than in young ones (May 1990; the record reports the direction, not numeric rates). Two classic anchors were refused this session and are not carded: Cutler 1968 (formation and absorption in man) has an empty abstract in the fetched record, and the Ekstedt 1978 hydrodynamic record's abstract reports no numeric formation rate — neither could carry a verified number.

cards.headline: Nilsson 1992: MRI-measured CSF production in 6 volunteers swung from 12 ± 7 mL/h in the early evening to 42 ± 2 mL/h near 02:00, totalling about 650 mL over 24 hours
cards.summary: Nilsson 1992: MRI-measured CSF production in 6 volunteers swung from 12 ± 7 mL/h in the early evening to 42 ± 2 mL/h near 02:00, totalling about 650 mL over 24 hours
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (phase-contrast MRI aqueduct flow), American Journal of Physiology 1992
cards.people: Six normal adult volunteers; net cerebrospinal fluid flow through the cerebral aqueduct was quantified by magnetic resonance imaging at different times across a 24-hour period and used as the measure of CSF production.
cards.result: Production varied greatly within and between individuals but showed a clear circadian pattern: a minimum of 30% of maximum values (12 ± 7 mL/h) at approximately 18:00 and a nightly peak of 42 ± 2 mL/h at approximately 02:00. Total production over the whole 24 hours, averaged across all measurements, was 650 mL for the group, and 630 mL for the repeated measurements in the one volunteer studied at every time interval.
cards.watchOut: Aqueduct net flow is an indirect measure of production — it assumes aqueduct flow equals formation minus absorption upstream — and six volunteers with wide individual variation cannot fix a precise population rate. The robust findings are the ~650 mL/day total and the two- to three-fold circadian swing, not any single hourly figure.
cards.source: Nilsson C et al. Circadian variation in human cerebrospinal fluid production measured by magnetic resonance imaging. The American journal of physiology. 1992. PMID: 1733335. cards.headline: Nilsson 1994: the nocturnal production rise (0.34 ± 0.06 to 0.61 ± 0.05 mL/min) was abolished or reversed by atenolol in most volunteers — implicating beta-1 (sympathetic) control of choroid-plexus secretion
cards.summary: Nilsson 1994: the nocturnal production rise (0.34 ± 0.06 to 0.61 ± 0.05 mL/min) was abolished or reversed by atenolol in most volunteers — implicating beta-1 (sympathetic) control of choroid-plexus secretion
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (MRI measurement with pharmacological probe), American Journal of Physiology 1994
cards.people: Fourteen healthy adult volunteers of both sexes. CSF production was measured by MRI phase imaging in the afternoon interval (15:00–18:00) and again at night (23:00–02:00): nine volunteers without drug, and ten (five of them repeats, plus five new) one week later after 100 mg oral atenolol given at 18:00.
cards.result: Without drug, all nine volunteers showed a significant increase in production at night, from 0.34 ± 0.06 mL/min in the afternoon to 0.61 ± 0.05 mL/min (P <0.005), confirming circadian variation. After atenolol, five volunteers decreased production at night, two were unchanged and three increased; average night production was 32% lower than afternoon (0.27 ± 0.10 vs 0.40 ± 0.07 mL/min; P =0.37, not significant) — the normal nocturnal peak was lost as a group phenomenon.
cards.watchOut: Small numbers and a non-significant post-drug group comparison: the atenolol result is a pattern across individuals, not a proven inhibitory effect size. Daytime values (~0.34–0.40 mL/min, roughly 490–580 mL/day if sustained) sit between the two Nilsson studies' extremes, as a circadian quantity should.
cards.source: Nilsson C et al. The nocturnal increase in human cerebrospinal fluid production is inhibited by a beta 1-receptor antagonist. The American journal of physiology. 1994. PMID: 7810751. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Steffensen 2018: the adult human production rate is stated as 500 mL/day, and the choroid-plexus cotransporter NKCC1 accounts for approximately half of production — shown in mouse in-vivo and ex vivo plexus experiments
cards.summary: Steffensen 2018: the adult human production rate is stated as 500 mL/day, and the choroid-plexus cotransporter NKCC1 accounts for approximately half of production — shown in mouse in-vivo and ex vivo plexus experiments
cards.type: Mechanistic physiology study (mouse in vivo + ex vivo choroid plexus; human tissue expression), Nature Communications 2018
cards.people: Mechanistic study combining ex vivo choroid plexus live imaging and isotope flux with in vivo CSF production determination in mice, plus expression work in human choroid plexus tissue; the human production figure (500 mL/day) is the paper's stated adult human rate, framing the mechanism experiments.
cards.result: The Na+/K+/2Cl− cotransporter NKCC1, expressed in the luminal (CSF-facing) membrane of choroid plexus epithelium, contributes approximately half of CSF production, acting in an unusual outward direction and directly coupling water transport to ion translocation — a route by which fluid can be secreted even where conventional osmotic gradients do not suffice. The authors present cotransporter-mediated water transport as a missing link in the model of CSF formation and a pharmacological target for disorders of brain fluid dynamics.
cards.watchOut: Species discipline: the 'approximately half' fraction was demonstrated in mice and isolated plexus, not measured in living humans, and this card must not be quoted as a human choroid-plexus fraction. What it establishes for humans is the stated 500 mL/day rate and a plausible molecular mechanism resident in human plexus tissue.
cards.source: Steffensen AB et al. Cotransporter-mediated water transport underlying cerebrospinal fluid formation. Nature communications. 2018. PMID: 29867199. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: May 1990: CSF production was significantly lower in 7 healthy elderly volunteers (67–84 years) than in 7 young volunteers (21–36 years) — N = 7 per group, printed on the face
cards.summary: May 1990: CSF production was significantly lower in 7 healthy elderly volunteers (67–84 years) than in 7 young volunteers (21–36 years) — N = 7 per group, printed on the face
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (small, N = 7 per group), Neurology 1990
cards.people: Seven young healthy volunteers (age 21–36 years) and seven elderly healthy volunteers (age 67–84 years); CSF production rate measured by a modified Masserman technique, with serial-fraction CSF protein gradients assessed in parallel. Small classic study — N = 7 per group, stated plainly per the small-N labelling rule.
cards.result: The mean rate of CSF production was significantly less in the elderly than in the young subjects (the fetched record reports the direction and significance, not the numeric rates, so none are claimed here). Mean CSF total protein was higher in the elderly, with significant rostrocaudal protein gradients of similar slope in both groups, and no correlation between production rate and protein concentration or gradient slope. The authors reason that reduced production plus age-related ventricular dilatation should reduce CSF turnover and thereby influence lumbar CSF constituent concentrations.
cards.watchOut: Fourteen volunteers in total and a record that withholds its own numbers: this card supports 'production falls with healthy ageing' and nothing more quantitative. It should never be cited for a rate.
cards.source: May C et al. Cerebrospinal fluid production is reduced in healthy aging. Neurology. 1990. PMID: 2314595. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Synthesis: ~500–650 mL/day, ~0.3–0.4 mL/min on average, two- to three-fold circadian swing, turnover ~3–4 times daily — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED; the choroid-plexus fraction remains the textbook's account
cards.summary: Synthesis: ~500–650 mL/day, ~0.3–0.4 mL/min on average, two- to three-fold circadian swing, turnover ~3–4 times daily — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED; the choroid-plexus fraction remains the textbook's account
cards.people: Synthesis of the four cards above, framed by Guyton & Hall, Ganong's Review and Boron & Boulpaep as named in the balance.
cards.result: The human measurements converge: production of roughly 500 mL/day (Steffensen's stated human rate) to roughly 650 mL/day (Nilsson's MRI-integrated 24-hour total), i.e. about 0.3–0.4 mL/min averaged over the day, with a reproducible circadian rhythm peaking near 02:00 at about twice the daytime rate and sensitive to beta-1 blockade, and a significant fall with healthy ageing. Against the textbook total volume of ~150 mL, 500–650 mL/day gives a turnover of roughly three to four times daily — the standard teaching figure, consistent with the fetched records. What the fetched human records do not contain is a measured fraction of production attributable to the choroid plexus in living humans: the plexus-majority share is the textbook account (Guyton & Hall; Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep), and the NKCC1 'approximately half' figure is a mouse/ex vivo mechanism result. Both are labelled as such wherever this shelf states them.
cards.watchOut: Refused anchors, reported plainly: Cutler 1968 (Brain) was not carded because its fetched record has an empty abstract, and Ekstedt 1978 was not carded for numbers because its abstract reports none. Any future version of this shelf that wants a human choroid-plexus fraction needs a fetched record that actually measures one.

shelves.title: Placebo analgesia is opioid physiology: naloxone reverses it (in placebo responders only), placebo expectation activates μ-opioid neurotransmission on PET, and naloxone abolishes the brainstem coupling that carries the effect
shelves.question: Is placebo analgesia in humans mediated by endogenous opioid release — specifically, is it reversed by naloxone and accompanied by μ-opioid system activation in descending pain-control circuits?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Analgesia · Anesthesia, Dental · Clinical Trials as Topic · Drug Evaluation · Drug Therapy, Combination · Endorphins/physiology · Female · Humans · Male · Molar/surgery · Morphine/therapeutic use · Naloxone/therapeutic use · Postoperative Pain/prevention & control · Placebos/therapeutic use · Research Design · Time Factors · Tooth Extraction · Tooth, Impacted/surgery
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Three independent human experimental approaches, three decades apart, converge on the same mechanism. Levine, Gordon & Fields (1978) showed pharmacological reversibility: after dental surgery, naloxone increased reported pain only in patients who had responded to a placebo — the naloxone effect was entirely accounted for by the placebo responders, exactly what an endogenous-opioid mechanism predicts. Zubieta (2005) showed the molecular event directly: during sustained pain, a placebo presented as an analgesic activated μ-opioid receptor-mediated neurotransmission in rostral anterior cingulate, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, insula and nucleus accumbens, in parallel with lower pain ratings. Eippert (2009) closed the circuit: with fMRI, naloxone reduced behavioural and neural placebo effects and abolished the placebo-induced coupling between rostral anterior cingulate cortex and periaqueductal gray that predicted the analgesia — the descending pain-control system is opioidergically gated. Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall; Ganong's Review; Boron & Boulpaep — framing, not evidence cards): the descending analgesia system, periaqueductal gray and endogenous opioid peptides are the standard account into which these experiments fit. Honest limits: these are small laboratory studies (the fetched records do not print their sample sizes, so none are claimed), in experimental or postoperative pain, in selected volunteers — and 'mediated by endogenous opioids' applies to the expectation-driven placebo paradigm studied, not to every placebo response in every condition.

cards.headline: Levine 1978: naloxone increased postoperative dental pain only in placebo responders — in non-responders it added nothing, so the whole naloxone effect was accounted for by reversing placebo analgesia
cards.summary: Levine 1978: naloxone increased postoperative dental pain only in placebo responders — in non-responders it added nothing, so the whole naloxone effect was accounted for by reversing placebo analgesia
cards.type: Primary human experimental study (randomised, double-blind naloxone challenge), Lancet 1978
cards.people: Patients undergoing extraction of impacted mandibular third molars under diazepam, nitrous oxide and local mepivacaine block; 3 and 4 hours after surgery they received naloxone or placebo under randomised, double-blind conditions, with pain rated on a visual analogue scale. The fetched record does not print the sample size — N not documented in the record.
cards.result: Patients given naloxone reported significantly greater pain than those given placebo. Patients whose first drug was placebo separated into responders (pain reduced or unchanged) and non-responders (pain increased). Naloxone given as the second drug produced no additional increase in pain in non-responders, but did increase pain in placebo responders — and non-responders' final mean pain rating was identical to that of responders who received naloxone second. The enhancement of pain by naloxone was thus entirely accounted for by its effect on placebo responders, consistent with endorphin release mediating placebo analgesia for dental postoperative pain.
cards.watchOut: The founding experiment, with the limits of its era: a single postoperative pain model, responder classification made post hoc from the placebo response itself, and no sample size in the fetched record. Its inference — naloxone reverses the placebo component specifically — is the part later studies confirmed, not any effect magnitude.
cards.source: Levine JD et al. The mechanism of placebo analgesia. Lancet (London, England). 1978. PMID: 80579. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Zubieta 2005: a placebo presented as analgesic activated μ-opioid neurotransmission (PET) in rostral anterior cingulate, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, insula and nucleus accumbens, in parallel with lower pain intensity and affect ratings
cards.summary: Zubieta 2005: a placebo presented as analgesic activated μ-opioid neurotransmission (PET) in rostral anterior cingulate, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, insula and nucleus accumbens, in parallel with lower pain intensity and affect ratings
cards.type: Primary human experimental study (μ-opioid PET imaging), Journal of Neuroscience 2005
cards.people: Healthy human volunteers undergoing a sustained pain challenge with and without administration of a placebo described as having analgesic properties; endogenous opioid activity at μ-opioid receptors was imaged directly with positron-emission tomography. The fetched record does not print the sample size — N not documented in the record.
cards.result: Significant placebo-induced activation of μ-opioid receptor-mediated neurotransmission was observed in higher-order and subcortical regions: pregenual and subgenual rostral anterior cingulate, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, insular cortex and nucleus accumbens. The regional activations were paralleled by lower ratings of pain intensity, reductions in its sensory and affective qualities, and improvement in the volunteers' negative emotional state — direct molecular evidence that expectation of relief engages the endogenous opioid system regionally, not globally.
cards.watchOut: PET displacement measures are an indirect index of endogenous opioid release, and the design links activation to ratings correlationally within subjects. The study shows activation accompanies placebo analgesia; the causal antagonist test is supplied by the Levine and Eippert cards.
cards.source: Zubieta JK et al. Placebo effects mediated by endogenous opioid activity on mu-opioid receptors. The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience. 2005. PMID: 16120776. Registry ID: none in the record.
