cards.headline: Eippert 2009: naloxone reduced behavioural and neural placebo effects and abolished placebo-induced rostral-cingulate–periaqueductal coupling — the opioidergic link in the descending pain-control system
cards.summary: Eippert 2009: naloxone reduced behavioural and neural placebo effects and abolished placebo-induced rostral-cingulate–periaqueductal coupling — the opioidergic link in the descending pain-control system
cards.type: Primary human experimental study (fMRI with naloxone challenge), Neuron 2009
cards.people: Healthy human volunteers in a placebo-analgesia paradigm studied with functional MRI, with and without administration of the opioid antagonist naloxone (double-blind); brainstem-specific analysis covered the hypothalamus, periaqueductal gray (PAG) and rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM). The fetched record does not print the sample size — N not documented in the record.
cards.result: Naloxone reduced both behavioural and neural placebo effects, and reduced placebo-induced responses in pain-modulatory cortical structures including the rostral anterior cingulate cortex (rACC). In the descending pain-control system, naloxone similarly modulated placebo-induced responses in hypothalamus, PAG and RVM. Most importantly, naloxone abolished the placebo-induced coupling between rACC and PAG — coupling which itself predicted both the neural and behavioural placebo effects and the activation of the RVM. The authors concluded opioidergic signalling in pain-modulating areas and their projections to the descending system's effectors is crucial for placebo analgesia.
cards.watchOut: An experimental heat-pain paradigm in healthy volunteers, not clinical pain; abolition of coupling under naloxone shows opioid signalling is necessary for this circuit expression of placebo analgesia, not that opioids are the only system involved in every placebo phenomenon.
cards.source: Eippert F et al. Activation of the opioidergic descending pain control system underlies placebo analgesia. Neuron. 2009. PMID: 19709634. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: reversal (1978), molecular activation (2005) and circuit abolition (2009) triangulate one mechanism — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED
cards.summary: Synthesis: reversal (1978), molecular activation (2005) and circuit abolition (2009) triangulate one mechanism — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED
cards.people: Synthesis of the three cards above, framed by Guyton & Hall, Ganong's Review and Boron & Boulpaep as named in the balance.
cards.result: Each design covers the others' weakness: the antagonist experiment gives causality but no anatomy; the PET study gives the molecular event and its regions but is correlational; the fMRI-antagonist study gives causality at circuit level, localising the necessary opioid step to signalling between rostral anterior cingulate cortex and the periaqueductal gray within the descending pain-control system. Together they establish that expectation-driven placebo analgesia in humans is, in substantial part, endogenous-opioid physiology — reversed by naloxone, accompanied by μ-opioid activation, and dependent on opioidergic descending coupling. The claim is bounded to the paradigms studied: experimental and postoperative pain in small volunteer samples whose sizes the fetched records do not document.
cards.watchOut: Do not generalise to 'the placebo effect is opioids': placebo responses in other systems (e.g. dopaminergic placebo effects in Parkinson's disease) run through other transmitters and are outside this shelf's fetched evidence.
cards.source: Synthesis of Levine JD et al. Lancet. 1978 (PMID: 80579); Zubieta JK et al. J Neurosci. 2005 (PMID: 16120776); Eippert F et al. Neuron. 2009 (PMID: 19709634). Registry IDs: none in the records. MeSH: as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Vestibulo-ocular reflex gain and adaptation (physiology): dark gain is ~0.7–0.75 and vision brings it to ~1.0; magnifying spectacles drive gain up within minutes (7–46% in 15 min), reversing prisms reshape it over days with retention for weeks, and two context-specific gains can coexist
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what is the gain of the vestibulo-ocular reflex, and how does it adapt when vision is magnified, minified or reversed?
shelves.mesh: Adaptation, Physiological · Adult · Eyeglasses · Eye Movements · Female · Humans · Male · Neuronal Plasticity · Reflex, Vestibulo-Ocular · Rotation · Vision, Ocular
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology): the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) rotates the eyes opposite the head to hold the image still, ideally at a gain (eye velocity ÷ head velocity) of 1.0, and retinal image slip is its teaching signal. The human measurements refine the textbook number: in darkness the reflex alone runs at ~0.74 ± 0.10 (Demer 1987, N = 7) and ~0.7 at 0.1 Hz (Demer 1989); ordinary vision tops it up to 1.07. Adaptation is fast, specific and storable: 15 minutes in ×2.2–×6 telescopic spectacles raised dark gain 7–46% in about half to two-thirds of subjects and improved dynamic visual acuity 30–100% (Demer 1987, 1989); up to 27 days in reversing dove prisms reshaped the response across frequencies, with a retained gain attenuation lasting 2–3 weeks after removal (Melvill Jones & Gonshor 1982); and two gains can be held simultaneously and selected by gaze context (Shelhamer 1992, N = 3). The minifying-spectacle limb (gain driven down) rests on the same slip mechanism and is presented as the textbook's account; the carded records test magnification, reversal and context directly.

cards.headline: Demer 1987: baseline VOR gain in darkness was 0.74 — with unmagnified vision 1.07, with ×2.2 telescopic spectacles 1.37 — and after 15 minutes of rotation in the spectacles, dark gain rose to 0.83 and magnified gain to 1.54
cards.summary: Demer 1987: baseline VOR gain in darkness was 0.74 — with unmagnified vision 1.07, with ×2.2 telescopic spectacles 1.37 — and after 15 minutes of rotation in the spectacles, dark gain rose to 0.83 and magnified gain to 1.54
cards.type: Human physiological study (VOR gain and telescopic-spectacle adaptation), Aviat Space Environ Med 1987
cards.people: 7 volunteers; VOR gain (slow-phase eye velocity / head velocity) measured in darkness and in light during passive sinusoidal rotation, before and after 15 min of rotation while wearing ×2.2 telescopic spectacles; dynamic visual acuity (vision during head rotation) also measured. N = 7 printed on the face of this physiology card (classic small physiology study).
cards.result: Initial gain in darkness was 0.74 ± 0.10; with unmagnified vision 1.07 ± 0.04; with magnified vision 1.37 ± 0.53. cards.headline: Demer 1989: 15 minutes of rotation through ×2, ×4 or ×6 telescopes raised dark VOR gain by 7–46% in about half to two-thirds of subjects — telescope power mattered little, and an unobstructed unmagnified periphery abolished most of the effect
cards.summary: Demer 1989: 15 minutes of rotation through ×2, ×4 or ×6 telescopes raised dark VOR gain by 7–46% in about half to two-thirds of subjects — telescope power mattered little, and an unobstructed unmagnified periphery abolished most of the effect
cards.type: Human physiological study (VOR plasticity to telescopic spectacles), Invest Ophthalmol Vis Sci 1989
cards.people: Normal subjects (number not documented in the record) rotated sinusoidally at 0.1 Hz (60°/s amplitude) for 15 min while viewing a remote display through ×2, ×4 or ×6 binocular telescopic spectacles, with the unmagnified peripheral field either occluded or open; VOR gain measured in darkness before and after. N not documented in the record.
cards.result: Baseline vertical-axis VOR gain was about 0.7. After adaptation with the periphery occluded, 47–70% of subjects showed significant gain increases of 7–46%; telescope power had little effect on the size of the change, all powers beat no-telescope adaptation, and the change generalised across head-rotation frequencies. With the unmagnified peripheral field unobstructed, gains rose significantly less — no more than adaptation without telescopes — showing the adapting signal is the magnified retinal slip, which a conflicting normal periphery can veto. Adaptation also relieved the oscillopsia and motion discomfort ~20% of subjects felt on first wearing the telescopes.
cards.watchOut: Inter-individual variability is the headline caveat — a substantial minority did not adapt measurably in 15 minutes; subject number is not printed in the record, and vertical-axis rotation at one frequency was the adapting stimulus.
cards.source: Demer JL et al. Adaptation to telescopic spectacles: vestibulo-ocular reflex plasticity. Investigative ophthalmology & visual science. 1989. PMID: 2912909. cards.headline: Melvill Jones & Gonshor 1982: after up to 27 days in vision-reversing (dove prism) goggles, the ocular response to head oscillation was adaptively reshaped — and a simple gain attenuation was still retained 2–3 weeks after the goggles came off
cards.summary: Melvill Jones & Gonshor 1982: after up to 27 days in vision-reversing (dove prism) goggles, the ocular response to head oscillation was adaptively reshaped — and a simple gain attenuation was still retained 2–3 weeks after the goggles came off
cards.type: Human physiological study (long-term reversing-prism VOR adaptation), Exp Brain Res 1982
cards.people: Human volunteers (number not documented in the record) wearing dove-prism goggles that reversed horizontal (not vertical) vision for up to 27 days; eye movements by electro-oculography and head movements by search coil during active head oscillation at 0.5–5.0 Hz, with visual tracking and saccades also tested. N not documented in the record.
cards.result: Visual tracking and saccade dynamics stayed normal throughout — the adaptation was specific to the vestibulo-ocular response. In the fully adapted state, smooth eye movements were of reversed phase at 0.5–1.0 Hz but normal phase from ~2 Hz up. After the goggles were permanently removed, that complex pattern was shed within 36 hours, leaving a simpler retained attenuation of gain (eye velocity / head velocity) that persisted 2–3 weeks and was monotonically related to frequency. Adaptation in the horizontal plane never produced blur in the unreversed sagittal plane — the plasticity is geometrically specific.
cards.watchOut: The classic reversing-spectacle experiment: small, intensively studied volunteers (number not printed in the record), active (self-generated) head oscillation rather than passive chair rotation, and a two-component (simple + complex) interpretation that is the authors' model of their data.
cards.source: Melvill Jones G et al. Oculomotor response to rapid head oscillation (0.5-5.0 Hz) after prolonged adaptation to vision-reversal. "Simple" and "complex" effects. Experimental brain research. 1982. PMID: 7056337. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Shelhamer 1992: humans can hold two VOR gains at once — after context-paired training, gain was ~8% higher looking up and ~6% lower looking down, selected by gaze direction alone
cards.summary: Shelhamer 1992: humans can hold two VOR gains at once — after context-paired training, gain was ~8% higher looking up and ~6% lower looking down, selected by gaze direction alone
cards.type: Human physiological study (context-specific dual VOR gains), J Vestib Res 1992
cards.people: 3 subjects rotated sinusoidally (0.2 Hz, 30°/s peak) in a chair inside an optokinetic drum for 2 h in alternating 10-minute blocks: drum counter-rotation driving gain toward 1.7 while looking up 20°, drum coupled driving gain toward zero while looking down 20°; gains then measured with step rotations while looking up or down. N = 3 printed on the face of this physiology card (classic small physiology study).
cards.result: After training, VOR gain was consistently context-dependent: on average ~8% higher when looking up and ~6% lower when looking down, with the nonvisual context cue (gaze direction) alone selecting which gain the reflex used. The authors conclude humans can maintain and switch between two VOR gains by situational context — the laboratory version of what bifocal and glasses on/off adaptation requires daily.
cards.watchOut: N = 3 — a proof-of-principle study; the dual-gain separation (~14 percentage points between contexts) is modest next to the ×2 demand of telescopic spectacles, and durability beyond the session was not the question asked.
cards.source: Shelhamer M et al. Context-specific adaptation of the gain of the vestibulo-ocular reflex in humans. Journal of vestibular research. 1992. PMID: 1342386. cards.headline: Synthesis: resting VOR gain in darkness is ~0.7–0.75 (vision restores it to ~1.0), and retinal slip recalibrates it within minutes toward magnified demands, over days toward reversed demands — with a retained gain change lasting weeks
cards.summary: Synthesis: resting VOR gain in darkness is ~0.7–0.75 (vision restores it to ~1.0), and retinal slip recalibrates it within minutes toward magnified demands, over days toward reversed demands — with a retained gain change lasting weeks
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded human studies above (Demer 1987; Demer 1989; Melvill Jones & Gonshor 1982; Shelhamer 1992), framed by Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology account of the vestibulo-ocular reflex as textbook framing.
cards.result: The numbers form one story. The unaided reflex under-compensates: gain ~0.74 in darkness (Demer 1987) and ~0.7 at 0.1 Hz (Demer 1989), with vision normally topping it up to ~1.07 — which is why the textbook's 'gain of 1' is a vision-assisted value, not the reflex alone. Magnification exposes the gap (gain 1.37 through ×2.2 telescopes against a requirement of ~2.2) and retinal slip closes part of it fast: +7–46% in 15 minutes in about half to two-thirds of people, vetoed by a conflicting unmagnified periphery. Reversal is the extreme case: over up to 27 days the response is reshaped frequency-by-frequency, and a simple gain attenuation survives 2–3 weeks after normal vision returns (Melvill Jones & Gonshor) — adaptation is stored, not momentary. And the storage is addressable: two gains can coexist and be selected by gaze context (Shelhamer). Minifying spectacles demand the mirror-image change (gain down); the carded records here test magnification and reversal directly, so the minification limb is presented as the textbook's account of the same slip-driven mechanism.
cards.watchOut: All carded studies are small (N = 3–7 where printed) laboratory studies in healthy volunteers; clinical VOR testing in patients, and adaptation over months of spectacle wear, are different literatures.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards on this shelf (PMIDs 3675487, 2912909, 7056337, 1342386), framed by Ganong Review of Medical Physiology. No additional source.

shelves.title: Tirofiban in acute ischaemic stroke without thrombectomy-eligible occlusion (RESCUE BT2, n=1,177): excellent outcome 29.1% vs 22.2% on aspirin — symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage 1.0% vs 0%
shelves.question: In adults with acute ischaemic stroke who are not eligible for (or are beyond) thrombolysis/thrombectomy, does intravenous tirofiban improve 90-day functional outcome versus aspirin/standard antiplatelet care?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Aspirin/adverse effects · Brain Ischemia/drug therapy/etiology · Fibrinolytic Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Intracranial Hemorrhages/chemically induced · Ischemic Stroke/diagnosis/drug therapy/etiology · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Tirofiban/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Cerebral Arterial Diseases/drug therapy/etiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large trial carries the claim, and its harm sits beside its benefit. In RESCUE BT2 (Zi 2023; 1,177 patients in China with stroke and no large or medium-sized vessel occlusion), an excellent 90-day outcome (modified Rankin scale 0–1) occurred in 29.1% on intravenous tirofiban versus 22.2% on aspirin (adjusted risk ratio 1.26, 95% CI 1.04–1.53 — a relative measure; the absolute gain is 6.9 percentage points), while symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage occurred in 1.0% versus 0% and mortality was similar. The TREND trial (Zhao 2024; n=425) supports the mechanism on an earlier endpoint — early neurological deterioration in 4.2% versus 13.2% (adjusted relative risk 0.32, 95% CI 0.16–0.65), with no symptomatic haemorrhage — but did not show a significant 90-day functional difference. A 2026 meta-analysis of nine studies (3,225 patients) pools an odds ratio of 1.66 for excellent outcome in relative terms, driven by these same trials. All the randomised evidence is from China and the populations are heterogeneous (four different presentations in RESCUE BT2), so a single-programme cap applies: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: RESCUE BT2 — Zi 2023 (n=1,177): excellent outcome (mRS 0–1) 29.1% on tirofiban vs 22.2% on aspirin; symptomatic ICH 1.0% vs 0%
cards.summary: RESCUE BT2 — Zi 2023 (n=1,177): excellent outcome (mRS 0–1) 29.1% on tirofiban vs 22.2% on aspirin; symptomatic ICH 1.0% vs 0%
cards.people: 1,177 patients in China with acute ischaemic stroke, no occlusion of large or medium-sized vessels, NIH Stroke Scale score ≥5 with at least one moderately to severely weak limb, across four presentations (thrombolysis/thrombectomy-ineligible within 24 hours; progression at 24–96 hours; early deterioration after thrombolysis; or no improvement 4–24 hours after thrombolysis), randomised to intravenous tirofiban plus oral placebo (n=606) or oral aspirin 100 mg daily plus intravenous placebo (n=571) for 2 days, then oral aspirin to day 90. Most had small, presumed atherosclerotic infarctions.
cards.result: An excellent outcome (modified Rankin scale 0–1) at 90 days occurred in 29.1% on tirofiban versus 22.2% on aspirin (adjusted risk ratio 1.26, 95% CI 1.04–1.53; P=0.02) — a relative measure; the absolute difference is 6.9 percentage points. Secondary endpoints were generally not consistent with the primary result. Mortality was similar, and symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage occurred in 1.0% on tirofiban versus 0% on aspirin.
cards.watchOut: A heterogeneous, single-country trial whose secondary endpoints did not line up behind the primary one, with a real (if small) symptomatic haemorrhage cost: roughly 1 extra symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage per 100 treated, against roughly 7 extra excellent outcomes per 100.

cards.headline: TREND — Zhao 2024 (n=425): early neurological deterioration 4.2% on tirofiban vs 13.2% on aspirin (adjusted RR 0.32); no symptomatic ICH; 90-day function not significantly different
cards.summary: TREND — Zhao 2024 (n=425): early neurological deterioration 4.2% on tirofiban vs 13.2% on aspirin (adjusted RR 0.32); no symptomatic ICH; 90-day function not significantly different
cards.people: 425 patients aged 18–80 with acute noncardioembolic stroke within 24 hours of onset and NIH Stroke Scale scores of 4–20, at ten comprehensive stroke centres in China, randomised to intravenous tirofiban (n=213) or oral aspirin (n=212) for 72 hours, then oral aspirin; the trial is the TREND study (NCT04491695, whose published protocol carries the same registry number and design).
cards.result: Early neurological deterioration (NIHSS increase ≥4 points within 72 hours) occurred in 4.2% (9/213) on tirofiban versus 13.2% (28/212) on aspirin (adjusted relative risk 0.32, 95% CI 0.16–0.65; P=0.002) — a relative measure; the absolute difference is 9.0 percentage points. No patient on tirofiban had symptomatic intracerebral haemorrhage. At 90 days, deaths were 1.3% versus 1.5% and median modified Rankin scores were identical (1.0 in both groups; adjusted OR 1.28, 95% CI 0.90–1.83; P=0.17).
cards.watchOut: Open-label treatment (blinded endpoint assessment), an early surrogate-style primary endpoint, and no significant 90-day functional benefit — TREND supports tirofiban's early anti-deterioration effect, not the 90-day claim on its own.

cards.headline: Jiao 2026 meta-analysis (9 studies, 3,225 patients): excellent outcome OR 1.66 in relative terms; peripheral bleeding OR 1.87; sICH not significantly increased
cards.summary: Jiao 2026 meta-analysis (9 studies, 3,225 patients): excellent outcome OR 1.66 in relative terms; peripheral bleeding OR 1.87; sICH not significantly increased
cards.people: Nine studies with 3,225 patients with acute ischaemic stroke without large- or medium-vessel occlusion, comparing tirofiban with conventional antiplatelet therapy, searched to December 2025; subgroup analyses separated randomised from non-randomised designs and patients with and without prior intravenous thrombolysis.
cards.result: Tirofiban was associated with higher odds of excellent 90-day outcome (mRS 0–1: OR 1.66, 95% CI 1.34–2.06; P<0.001) and favourable outcome (mRS 0–2: OR 1.79, 95% CI 1.30–2.47) — odds ratios, which are relative measures. Symptomatic intracerebral haemorrhage was not significantly increased (OR 4.02, 95% CI 0.91–17.70; P=0.07) and 90-day mortality did not differ (OR 1.06, 95% CI 0.53–2.12), but peripheral bleeding was more frequent (OR 1.87, 95% CI 1.32–2.66; P<0.001). Benefit appeared confined to patients without prior thrombolysis; the randomised-trial subgroup was homogeneous (I²=0% for mRS 0–1).
cards.watchOut: The pool mixes randomised and observational studies and is dominated by RESCUE BT2 and TREND — it summarises the same evidence rather than replicating it, and the symptomatic-haemorrhage confidence interval (0.91–17.70) is too wide to declare safety settled.
cards.source: Jiao J et al. Efficacy and safety of tirofiban for acute ischemic stroke without large and medium vessel occlusion: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Frontiers in Neurology. 2026. PMID: 42158008. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: one large positive trial, one supportive early-endpoint trial, and a bleeding price that must stay on the face
cards.summary: Synthesis: one large positive trial, one supportive early-endpoint trial, and a bleeding price that must stay on the face
cards.people: RESCUE BT2 (n=1,177), TREND (n=425) and a nine-study meta-analysis (3,225 patients) — all randomised evidence from China, in stroke without thrombectomy-eligible occlusion.
cards.result: Excellent 90-day outcome 29.1% vs 22.2% (absolute gain 6.9 points; adjusted RR 1.26 in relative terms) against symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage 1.0% vs 0% in the pivotal trial; early deterioration roughly a third as frequent on tirofiban in TREND (adjusted RR 0.32, relative) without a proven 90-day gain there. Benefit and harm are both real and both belong in any use decision — POSSIBLE (benefit), pending replication outside China and in better-defined subgroups.
cards.watchOut: This shelf does not cover tirofiban as an adjunct to thrombectomy or thrombolysis rescue, where the evidence and the bleeding balance differ; RESCUE BT2's post-thrombolysis subgroups were only part of its mixed population.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards above. No new data.

shelves.title: Intra-arterial alteplase after successful thrombectomy: excellent outcome rises in three randomised trials — but 90-day mortality rose in the largest one (CHOICE-2)
shelves.question: In adults with large-vessel-occlusion stroke and successful endovascular reperfusion, does adjunctive intra-arterial alteplase improve 90-day functional outcome versus thrombectomy alone?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Brain Ischemia · Combined Modality Therapy · Fibrinolytic Agents · Infusions, Intra-Arterial · Intracranial Hemorrhages · Ischemic Stroke · Thrombectomy · Thrombolytic Therapy · Tissue Plasminogen Activator · Treatment Outcome · Adult · Aged, 80 and over
shelves.balance: Three randomised trials of the same manoeuvre — a single intra-arterial alteplase dose (0.225 mg/kg) given after successful thrombectomy — point the same way on function and split on survival. CHOICE (Spain, n=121, stopped early) found excellent outcome (mRS 0–1 at 90 days) in 59.0% vs 40.4%. PEARL (China, n=324) found 44.8% vs 30.2%. CHOICE-2 (Spain, n=440), the largest and most recent, found 57.5% vs 42.5% (adjusted risk difference 15.0%) — and, in the same trial, 90-day mortality of 12.1% on alteplase vs 6.4% without it (adjusted risk difference 5.9%, P=.03), a signal PEARL echoed non-significantly (17.1% vs 11.3%) while the small CHOICE trial ran the other way (8% vs 15%). Symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage was not significantly increased in any trial. A treatment that frees more patients from disability while possibly killing more of them cannot be stamped above POSSIBLE until the mortality signal is explained or refuted.

cards.headline: CHOICE (Renú 2022): excellent outcome 59.0% vs 40.4% — a small phase 2b trial stopped early, so the result is preliminary by its authors' own wording
cards.summary: CHOICE (Renú 2022): excellent outcome 59.0% vs 40.4% — a small phase 2b trial stopped early, so the result is preliminary by its authors' own wording
cards.type: Phase 2b randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (CHOICE), JAMA 2022
cards.people: 121 patients with large-vessel-occlusion stroke treated with thrombectomy within 24 hours and an expanded TICI score of 2b50–3, at 7 stroke centres in Catalonia, Spain (mean age 70.6 years; 47% women); 113 were treated as randomised: intra-arterial alteplase 0.225 mg/kg (maximum 22.5 mg) over 15–30 minutes (n=61) or placebo (n=52).
cards.result: Excellent outcome (mRS 0–1 at 90 days) occurred in 59.0% (36/61) on alteplase vs 40.4% (21/52) on placebo (adjusted risk difference 18.4%; 95% CI 0.3% to 36.4%; P=.047). Symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage within 24 hours was 0% vs 3.8%, and 90-day mortality was 8% vs 15% (risk difference −7.2%; 95% CI −19.2% to 4.8%).
cards.watchOut: The trial was terminated early because placebo supply and enrolment could not be maintained during the COVID-19 pandemic, and the confidence interval for the benefit nearly touches zero (0.3% to 36.4%). The authors themselves call the findings preliminary and requiring replication — which is why CHOICE-2 and PEARL, carded next, carry the weight on this shelf.

cards.headline: CHOICE-2 (Renú 2026): excellent outcome 57.5% vs 42.5% — but 90-day mortality was higher on alteplase, 12.1% vs 6.4% (P=.03)
cards.summary: CHOICE-2 (Renú 2026): excellent outcome 57.5% vs 42.5% — but 90-day mortality was higher on alteplase, 12.1% vs 6.4% (P=.03)
cards.type: Randomised, open-label trial with blinded outcome assessment, phase 3 (CHOICE-2), JAMA 2026
cards.people: 440 patients with large-vessel-occlusion stroke treated with thrombectomy within 24 hours and an expanded TICI score of 2b50–3, at 14 stroke centres in Spain; 433 treated as randomised (median age 76 years; 51% female): thrombectomy plus intra-arterial alteplase 0.225 mg/kg (maximum 20 mg) over 15 minutes (n=221 randomised) or thrombectomy alone (n=219).
cards.result: Excellent outcome at 90 days: 57.5% (123/214) with alteplase vs 42.5% (93/219) without (adjusted risk difference 15.0%; 95% CI 5.7% to 24.3%; P=.002). Residual hypoperfusion on follow-up CT perfusion was less frequent with alteplase (28.6% vs 50.5%). Symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage was 1.4% vs 0.5% (not significant). Mortality at 90 days was 12.1% (26/214) with alteplase vs 6.4% (14/219) without (adjusted risk difference 5.9%; 95% CI 0.5% to 11.3%; P=.03).
cards.watchOut: The mortality excess is the single most important number on this shelf: it was statistically significant in the largest trial, its cause is not established in the report, and four of six secondary outcomes showed no significant difference. Open-label treatment (with blinded outcome assessment) is a further reason not to upgrade the stamp.
cards.source: Renú A et al. Adjunctive Intra-Arterial Alteplase After Successful Thrombectomy for Acute Ischemic Stroke: The CHOICE-2 Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2026. PMID 42096239 · NCT05797792. DOI 10.1001/jama.2026.5164

cards.headline: PEARL (2025): excellent outcome 44.8% vs 30.2% in China — mortality again numerically higher on alteplase (17.1% vs 11.3%, not significant)
cards.summary: PEARL (2025): excellent outcome 44.8% vs 30.2% in China — mortality again numerically higher on alteplase (17.1% vs 11.3%, not significant)
cards.people: 324 patients with anterior-circulation large-vessel-occlusion stroke within 24 hours of onset who achieved successful reperfusion (expanded TICI ≥2b50) after thrombectomy, at 28 hospitals in China (median age 68 years; 30.6% women); guideline-based intravenous thrombolysis was allowed. Intra-arterial alteplase 0.225 mg/kg (maximum 20 mg; n=164) vs standard treatment (n=160).
cards.result: Excellent outcome (mRS 0–1 at 90 days): 44.8% (73/163) with alteplase vs 30.2% (48/159) with standard treatment (adjusted risk ratio 1.45; 95% CI 1.08–1.96; P=.01) — a 45% relative increase, printed beside the absolute rates. Symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage within 36 hours: 4.3% vs 5.0%. Any intracranial haemorrhage: 32.9% vs 26.9%. All-cause 90-day mortality: 17.1% vs 11.3% (adjusted hazard ratio 1.60; 95% CI 0.88–2.89; P=.12).
cards.watchOut: PEARL was open-label and single-country (China), and its mortality and any-haemorrhage point estimates both ran against alteplase without reaching significance. Read with CHOICE-2, the pattern is consistent functional benefit alongside an unresolved mortality question — not a clean win.
cards.source: Yang X et al. Intra-Arterial Alteplase After Successful Endovascular Reperfusion in Acute Stroke: The PEARL Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2025. PMID 42262770 · NCT05856851. DOI 10.1001/jama.2025.16876

cards.headline: Synthesis: consistent functional benefit across three trials, an unresolved mortality signal — POSSIBLE, not LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: consistent functional benefit across three trials, an unresolved mortality signal — POSSIBLE, not LIKELY
cards.people: Synthesis population: 885 randomised patients across CHOICE, PEARL and CHOICE-2 (Spain and China), all with successful reperfusion after thrombectomy for large-vessel-occlusion stroke.
cards.result: All three trials found more excellent 90-day outcomes with adjunctive intra-arterial alteplase (absolute gains of about 15–19 percentage points), and none found a significant increase in symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage. Against that, 90-day mortality was significantly higher on alteplase in CHOICE-2 (12.1% vs 6.4%) and numerically higher in PEARL (17.1% vs 11.3%), while the smallest, earliest-stopped trial (CHOICE) ran the other way. The functional benefit is real enough to card; the survival cost is real enough to cap the stamp.
cards.watchOut: Until a trial or pooled analysis explains the CHOICE-2 mortality excess, quoting only the excellent-outcome percentages from this shelf would mislead. The neighbouring shelf on bridging intravenous thrombolysis before thrombectomy asks a different, earlier-timing question.
cards.source: Synthesis of the carded records above (PMIDs 35143603, 42096239, 42262770). No new data.

shelves.title: Intravenous prourokinase vs alteplase within 4.5 hours: non-inferior for excellent outcome in two Chinese phase 3 trials, with less systemic bleeding — a single-country (China) programme
shelves.question: In adults with acute ischaemic stroke within 4.5 hours who are ineligible for or refuse thrombectomy, is intravenous recombinant human prourokinase non-inferior to alteplase for excellent functional outcome, and with what bleeding cost?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Administration, Intravenous · Fibrinolytic Agents · Infusions, Intravenous · Ischemic Stroke · Recombinant Proteins · Thrombolytic Therapy · Tissue Plasminogen Activator · Treatment Outcome · Urokinase-Type Plasminogen Activator
shelves.balance: Every trial in this programme was run in China — that is printed here, not in fine print. In PROST-2 (n=1,552), intravenous recombinant human prourokinase (15 mg bolus + 20 mg infusion) was non-inferior to alteplase for excellent outcome at 90 days (mRS 0–1: 72.0% vs 68.7%), with less symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage (0.3% vs 1.3%) and less major bleeding. The earlier phase 3 trial (Song 2023, n=663 in the modified intention-to-treat population) found the same non-inferiority (65.2% vs 64.3%) with similar symptomatic haemorrhage and less systemic bleeding (25.8% vs 42.2%). A small phase 2a dose study in the later 4.5–6-hour window (n=80, no alteplase comparator) is carded for completeness and carries no comparative weight. Non-inferiority in one country's programme supports prourokinase as an alternative thrombolytic where alteplase supply is short — the use the PROST-2 authors themselves propose — and caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: PROST-2 (Li 2025): prourokinase non-inferior to alteplase — excellent outcome 72.0% vs 68.7%, symptomatic haemorrhage 0.3% vs 1.3%
cards.summary: PROST-2 (Li 2025): prourokinase non-inferior to alteplase — excellent outcome 72.0% vs 68.7%, symptomatic haemorrhage 0.3% vs 1.3%
cards.type: Phase 3, open-label, non-inferiority randomised controlled trial (PROST-2), Lancet Neurology 2025
cards.people: 1,552 patients older than 18 years with acute ischaemic stroke within 4.5 hours of onset who were ineligible for or refused endovascular thrombectomy, at 61 hospitals in China: intravenous recombinant human prourokinase (15 mg bolus followed by 20 mg infused within 30 minutes; n=775) or intravenous alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (n=777). Open-label with masked outcome assessment.
cards.result: Excellent outcome (mRS 0–1 at 90 days): 72.0% (558/775) on prourokinase vs 68.7% (534/777) on alteplase (risk ratio 1.04; 95% CI 0.98–1.10; p<0.0001 for non-inferiority against a risk-ratio margin of 0.93). Symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage within 36 hours: 0.3% (2/770) vs 1.3% (10/775). Major bleeding at 7 days: 0.5% vs 2.1%. All-cause mortality within 7 days: 0.6% vs 1.7% (not significant).
cards.watchOut: Single-country (China) and open-label: both limits are on the face of this shelf. Non-inferiority means 'not unacceptably worse than alteplase', not 'better'; the lower bleeding rates are secondary findings in a trial powered for the functional non-inferiority question. Funded in part by the manufacturer (Tasly Biopharmaceuticals) alongside Chinese national funders, per the record.
cards.source: Li S et al. Safety and efficacy of intravenous recombinant human prourokinase for acute ischaemic stroke within 4.5 h after stroke onset (PROST-2): a phase 3, open-label, non-inferiority, randomised controlled trial. cards.summary: Song 2023 phase 3: the earlier alteplase-controlled trial found the same non-inferiority (65.2% vs 64.3%) with less systemic bleeding
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised, alteplase-controlled, open-label trial, JAMA Network Open 2023
cards.people: 663 patients in the modified intention-to-treat population (mean age 61.0 years; 24.3% women; median baseline NIHSS 6) with acute ischaemic stroke treated within 4.5 hours of onset, at 35 medical centres in China: intravenous recombinant human prourokinase (n=330) or alteplase (n=333). Open-label, alteplase-controlled.
cards.result: Excellent outcome (mRS 0–1 at 90 days): 65.2% (215/330) on prourokinase vs 64.3% (214/333) on alteplase (risk difference 0.89 percentage points; 95.4% CI −6.52 to 8.29), meeting the prespecified non-inferiority margin of less than 10%. Symptomatic intracerebral haemorrhage: 1.5% vs 1.8%. Systemic bleeding within 90 days: 25.8% vs 42.2% (P<.001). Thrombolysis-related deaths by 90 days: 1.5% in each group.
cards.watchOut: A second single-country (China) non-inferiority result strengthens consistency but does not widen generalisability: both phase 3 trials enrolled Chinese populations with relatively low median NIHSS scores, and neither was blinded. The systemic-bleeding difference is large and worth noting, but systemic bleeding is a softer endpoint than symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage, which did not differ here.
cards.source: Song H et al. Efficacy and Safety of Recombinant Human Prourokinase in the Treatment of Acute Ischemic Stroke Within 4.5 Hours of Stroke Onset: A Phase 3 Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Netw Open. 2023. PMID 37490291 · NCT03541668. DOI 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2023.25415

cards.headline: Phase 2a late-window study (Song 2024): prourokinase at 4.5–6 hours — 80 patients, two doses, no comparator, so no efficacy conclusion is drawn
cards.summary: Phase 2a late-window study (Song 2024): prourokinase at 4.5–6 hours — 80 patients, two doses, no comparator, so no efficacy conclusion is drawn
cards.type: Phase 2a randomised, open-label, multicentre dose study, CNS Drugs 2024
cards.people: 80 patients with acute ischaemic stroke treated between 4.5 and 6 hours after onset, at 17 medical centres in China, randomised to intravenous recombinant human prourokinase 50 mg (n=39) or 35 mg (n=39 analysed). Open-label dose comparison with no alteplase or placebo arm.
cards.result: Functional independence at 90 days was 61.54% on 50 mg and 69.23% on 35 mg (P=0.475). No symptomatic intracerebral haemorrhage occurred in either group; one death occurred in the 50 mg group. NIHSS scores fell from baseline at both doses, with no significant between-dose differences in mortality or serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: With no control arm, the 61–69% independence rates cannot be attributed to the drug — spontaneous recovery sits in the same range in mild stroke. This card exists so the late-window question is answered honestly: it is untested against any comparator, and this study does not extend the 4.5-hour evidence.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a credible alteplase alternative from one country's programme — POSSIBLE, with the single-country limit on the face
cards.summary: Synthesis: a credible alteplase alternative from one country's programme — POSSIBLE, with the single-country limit on the face
cards.people: Synthesis population: 2,215 patients in the two alteplase-controlled phase 3 trials (PROST-2 and Song 2023), plus 80 patients in an uncontrolled late-window dose study — all enrolled in China.
cards.result: Two phase 3 trials agree that intravenous prourokinase is non-inferior to alteplase for excellent 90-day outcome within 4.5 hours, with symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage rates that were lower (PROST-2) or similar (Song 2023) and consistently less systemic bleeding. That is a coherent alternative-thrombolytic claim, not a superiority claim, and it rests entirely on Chinese trial populations and open-label designs — hence POSSIBLE, and hence the country is named in this shelf's title and balance.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote this shelf as showing prourokinase is safer overall: the symptomatic-haemorrhage advantage appeared in one of two trials, and neither trial enrolled thrombectomy-eligible patients as its target population (PROST-2 enrolled patients ineligible for or refusing thrombectomy).
cards.source: Synthesis of the carded records above (PMIDs 39617030, 37490291, 38030867). No new data.

shelves.title: Argatroban or eptifibatide added to intravenous thrombolysis: no functional benefit in either phase 3 programme — MOST was stopped for futility with higher mortality, and ARAIS was neutral (the treatment made no difference)
shelves.question: In adults receiving intravenous thrombolysis for acute ischaemic stroke, does adding argatroban or eptifibatide improve functional outcome versus thrombolysis alone?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Arginine · Drug Therapy, Combination · Eptifibatide · Fibrinolytic Agents · Infusions, Intravenous · Intracranial Hemorrhages · Ischemic Stroke · Peptides · Pipecolic Acids · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors · Single-Blind Method · Sulfonamides · Thrombolytic Therapy · Combined Modality Therapy · Thrombectomy · Treatment Outcome · Anticoagulants · Adult
shelves.balance: This shelf corrects a common misreading of the record. The two phase 3 programmes do not split positive-versus-negative on functional outcome: both are negative. MOST (United States, n=514), an adaptive three-arm trial of argatroban or eptifibatide added to intravenous thrombolysis, was stopped for futility — utility-weighted 90-day Rankin scores were lower on both adjuncts than on placebo, and 90-day mortality was higher (argatroban 24%, eptifibatide 12%, placebo 8%). ARAIS (China, n=817), testing argatroban added to alteplase, was neutral on its primary endpoint: excellent outcome 63.8% vs 64.9% (P=.78) — the treatment made no difference — with similar bleeding. The only positive signal in the programme's history is a 65-patient open-label pilot (2012) in which the combination looked safe and recanalisation was frequent; recanalisation is a surrogate, and the pilot had no control arm. Post-hoc ARAIS subgroup analyses do not overturn a neutral primary endpoint. On the phase 3 record, adding either drug to thrombolysis should not be expected to help, and in MOST it was associated with harm.

cards.headline: MOST (Adeoye 2024): both adjuncts stopped for futility — disability scores worse than placebo and mortality higher (argatroban 24%, eptifibatide 12%, placebo 8%)
cards.summary: MOST (Adeoye 2024): both adjuncts stopped for futility — disability scores worse than placebo and mortality higher (argatroban 24%, eptifibatide 12%, placebo 8%)
cards.type: Phase 3, three-group, adaptive, single-blind randomised controlled trial (MOST), New England Journal of Medicine 2024
cards.people: 514 patients with acute ischaemic stroke who received intravenous thrombolysis within 3 hours of onset (70% alteplase, 30% tenecteplase; 44% also underwent thrombectomy), at 57 sites in the United States, randomised within 75 minutes of thrombolysis to intravenous argatroban (n=59), eptifibatide (n=227) or placebo (n=228). Phase 3, three-group, adaptive, single-blind design.
cards.result: Mean utility-weighted 90-day modified Rankin scores (0–10, higher is better) were 5.2 with argatroban, 6.3 with eptifibatide and 6.8 with placebo; the posterior probability that either adjunct was better than placebo was 0.002 (argatroban) and 0.041 (eptifibatide). Symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage was similar (4%, 3% and 2%). Mortality at 90 days was higher with argatroban (24%) and eptifibatide (12%) than with placebo (8%). The trial was stopped for futility.
cards.watchOut: The argatroban arm is small (n=59) because the adaptive design cut it early — so its 24% mortality estimate is imprecise — but the direction was consistent across both adjuncts and the trial's own conclusion is that neither reduced disability and both were associated with increased mortality. Funded by the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke.
cards.source: Adeoye O et al. Adjunctive Intravenous Argatroban or Eptifibatide for Ischemic Stroke. N Engl J Med. 2024. PMID 39231343 · NCT03735979. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2314779

cards.headline: ARAIS (Chen 2023): argatroban plus alteplase vs alteplase alone — excellent outcome 63.8% vs 64.9% (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: ARAIS (Chen 2023): argatroban plus alteplase vs alteplase alone — excellent outcome 63.8% vs 64.9% (the treatment made no difference)
cards.type: Multicentre, open-label, blinded-endpoint randomised clinical trial (ARAIS), JAMA 2023
cards.people: 817 patients with acute ischaemic stroke randomised within 4.5 hours of onset at 50 hospitals in China (median age 65 years; 29.1% women; median NIHSS 9): argatroban (100 µg/kg bolus, then 1.0 µg/kg per minute for 48 hours) started within 1 hour after alteplase (n=402) or alteplase alone (n=415). Open-label with blinded endpoint assessment; 760 patients completed the trial.
cards.result: Excellent functional outcome (mRS 0–1 at 90 days): 63.8% (210/329) with argatroban plus alteplase vs 64.9% (238/367) with alteplase alone (risk difference −1.0%; 95% CI −8.1% to 6.1%; risk ratio 0.98; P=.78). Symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage was 2.1% vs 1.8%, parenchymal haematoma type 2 was 2.3% vs 2.5%, and major systemic bleeding was 0.3% vs 0.5% — no significant safety penalty and no efficacy gain.
cards.watchOut: ARAIS is sometimes described as the 'positive' counterpart to MOST. On its prespecified primary endpoint it was not positive: the point estimate slightly favoured alteplase alone. Later post-hoc and subgroup analyses of ARAIS explore whether particular territories or severities differ; they are hypothesis-generating and do not change the primary result carded here.
cards.source: Chen HS et al. Effect of Argatroban Plus Intravenous Alteplase vs Intravenous Alteplase Alone on Neurologic Function in Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke: The ARAIS Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2023. PMID 36757755 · NCT03740958. DOI 10.1001/jama.2023.0550

cards.headline: Pilot safety study (Barreto 2012): the early promise — 65 patients, no control arm, frequent recanalisation, significant haemorrhage in 6.2%
cards.summary: Pilot safety study (Barreto 2012): the early promise — 65 patients, no control arm, frequent recanalisation, significant haemorrhage in 6.2%
cards.people: 65 patients with ischaemic stroke due to proximal intracranial occlusion (45% men; mean age 63 years; median NIHSS 13) treated at a single programme with standard-dose intravenous tPA plus argatroban (100 µg/kg bolus, then a 48-hour infusion titrated to a partial thromboplastin time 1.75× baseline). Open-label pilot with no comparator group.
cards.result: Significant intracerebral haemorrhage occurred in 4 patients (6.2%; 95% CI 1.7–15.0), of whom 3 (4.6%) were symptomatic; 7 patients (10%) died within 7 days. Among 47 patients monitored by transcranial Doppler, recanalisation within 2 hours occurred in 29 (61%) — complete in 19 (40%) and partial in 10 (21%). The authors concluded the combination was potentially safe and warranted continued evaluation.
cards.watchOut: This is the record the phase 3 trials were built on, and it shows why pilots mislead when read as efficacy: a 61% recanalisation rate with no control arm cannot separate drug effect from what tPA alone achieves, and recanalisation is a surrogate for — not a guarantee of — better functional outcome. ARAIS and MOST tested the functional question directly and answered it negatively.
cards.source: Barreto AD et al. The Argatroban and Tissue-Type Plasminogen Activator Stroke Study: Final Results of a Pilot Safety Study. Stroke. 2012. PMID 22223235 · NCT00268762. DOI 10.1161/STROKEAHA.111.625574

cards.headline: Synthesis: two negative phase 3 programmes outweigh a positive-surrogate pilot — do not add these drugs expecting functional benefit
cards.summary: Synthesis: two negative phase 3 programmes outweigh a positive-surrogate pilot — do not add these drugs expecting functional benefit
cards.people: Synthesis population: 514 patients in MOST (United States) and 817 randomised patients in ARAIS (China), preceded by a 65-patient uncontrolled pilot.
cards.result: On functional outcome — the endpoint patients feel — argatroban added to thrombolysis made no difference in ARAIS (63.8% vs 64.9% excellent outcome) and both argatroban and eptifibatide performed worse than placebo in MOST, which was stopped for futility with higher 90-day mortality on both adjuncts (24% and 12% vs 8%). Bleeding rates were not significantly increased in either phase 3 trial. The honest summary is not a split verdict: it is a negative programme with a harm signal in its largest adjunct comparison.
cards.watchOut: This shelf's verdict applies to adding argatroban or eptifibatide to intravenous thrombolysis in acute ischaemic stroke. It says nothing about argatroban's separate, established use in heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, which is shelved elsewhere in the library.
cards.source: Synthesis of the carded records above (PMIDs 39231343, 36757755, 22223235). No new data.

shelves.title: Edaravone dexborneol in acute ischaemic stroke: better than edaravone alone in TASTE, borderline against placebo before thrombectomy in TASTE-2 — a single-country (China) programme, and TASTE has no placebo arm
shelves.question: In adults with acute ischaemic stroke, does edaravone dexborneol improve 90-day functional outcome versus edaravone alone (TASTE) or versus placebo given before thrombectomy (TASTE-2)?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Edaravone · Male · Female · Middle Aged · Ischemic Stroke · Double-Blind Method · Aged · Thrombectomy · Adult · Treatment Outcome · Endovascular Procedures · Aged, 80 and over · China · Free Radical Scavengers
shelves.balance: The whole programme is single-country (China) — stated here on the face. Two design facts decide how this shelf may be quoted. First, TASTE (n=1,165) had no placebo arm: edaravone dexborneol beat edaravone alone on excellent outcome (67.2% vs 59.0%), which shows the dexborneol component adds something over edaravone, but cannot show either drug beats no treatment. Second, the placebo-controlled test, TASTE-2 (n=1,360 analysed), given before thrombectomy, landed exactly on the borderline: functional independence 55.0% vs 49.6% (risk ratio 1.11; 95% CI 1.00–1.23; P=0.05), with the effect concentrated in a prespecified mismatch subgroup, and a small phase 2 placebo-controlled trial after successful reperfusion (n=200) found no significant difference (58.7% vs 52.1%; P=0.29). Serious adverse events were similar to placebo in TASTE-2. That is a POSSIBLE: a real but fragile signal, untested outside China.

cards.headline: TASTE (Xu 2021): edaravone dexborneol beat edaravone alone — excellent outcome 67.18% vs 58.97% — in a trial with no placebo arm
cards.summary: TASTE (Xu 2021): edaravone dexborneol beat edaravone alone — excellent outcome 67.18% vs 58.97% — in a trial with no placebo arm
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, double-blind, active-comparator trial (TASTE), Stroke 2021
cards.people: 1,165 patients with acute ischaemic stroke (ages 35–80; NIHSS 4–24; treated within 48 hours of onset) at 48 hospitals in China, randomised to a 14-day infusion of edaravone dexborneol (n=585) or edaravone alone (n=580). Multicentre, randomised, double-blind, active-comparator phase 3 design.
cards.result: Good functional outcome (mRS ≤1 at 90 days): 67.18% on edaravone dexborneol vs 58.97% on edaravone alone (odds ratio 1.42; 95% CI 1.12–1.81; P=0.004). A prespecified subgroup analysis suggested greater benefit in women than in men (odds ratio 2.26 vs 1.14).
cards.watchOut: There is no placebo arm — the comparison isolates the added dexborneol component against edaravone, a drug whose own benefit in this setting is not established by this trial. Quoting TASTE as 'edaravone dexborneol works' skips that step. The sex-subgroup difference is a subgroup finding, not a basis for sex-specific use.
cards.source: Xu J et al. Edaravone Dexborneol Versus Edaravone Alone for the Treatment of Acute Ischemic Stroke: A Phase III, Randomized, Double-Blind, Comparative Study. Stroke. 2021. PMID 33588596 · NCT02430350. DOI 10.1161/STROKEAHA.120.031197

cards.headline: TASTE-2 (Wang 2026): against placebo before thrombectomy — functional independence 55.0% vs 49.6%, risk ratio 1.11 with a confidence interval touching 1.00 (P=0.05)
cards.summary: TASTE-2 (Wang 2026): against placebo before thrombectomy — functional independence 55.0% vs 49.6%, risk ratio 1.11 with a confidence interval touching 1.00 (P=0.05)
cards.type: Multicentre, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial (TASTE-2), BMJ 2026
cards.people: 1,362 patients with acute ischaemic stroke within 24 hours of onset (ages 18–80; NIHSS 6–25; ASPECTS 6–10; confirmed anterior-circulation large-vessel occlusion) planned for endovascular thrombectomy, at 106 hospitals in China: edaravone dexborneol 37.5 mg (n=690) or placebo (n=672) started before thrombectomy and continued twice daily for 10–14 days; 1,360 patients were analysed.
cards.result: Functional independence (mRS 0–2 at 90 days): 55.0% (379/689) on edaravone dexborneol vs 49.6% (333/671) on placebo (risk ratio 1.11; 95% CI 1.00–1.23; P=0.05; risk difference 5.4%; 95% CI 0.1% to 10.7%) — an 11% relative increase, printed beside the absolute rates. In the prespecified mismatch subgroup the difference was larger (55.5% vs 42.9%; P for interaction=0.003). Serious adverse events: 27.2% vs 25.7% (not significant).
cards.watchOut: A P value of exactly 0.05 with a confidence interval whose lower bound is 1.00 is a borderline result: small changes in analysis or a few outcomes would move it across the line. The overall effect also appears driven by the mismatch subgroup, which the authors themselves say needs dedicated trials. Single-country (China) conduct applies to this trial as to the whole programme.
cards.source: Wang C et al. Edaravone dexborneol versus placebo on functional outcomes in patients with acute ischaemic stroke undergoing endovascular thrombectomy (TASTE-2). BMJ. 2026. PMID 41500725 · NCT05249920. DOI 10.1136/bmj-2025-086850

cards.headline: Phase 2 after successful reperfusion (Chen 2025): no significant difference vs placebo — favourable outcome 58.7% vs 52.1% (P=0.29) in 200 patients
cards.summary: Phase 2 after successful reperfusion (Chen 2025): no significant difference vs placebo — favourable outcome 58.7% vs 52.1% (P=0.29) in 200 patients
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, Nature Communications 2025
cards.people: 200 patients with anterior-circulation stroke and successful endovascular reperfusion, randomised to intravenous edaravone dexborneol 37.5 mg twice daily for 12 days (n=97) or placebo (n=103). Randomised, double-blind, multicentre phase 2 design.
cards.result: Favourable functional outcome (mRS 0–2 at 90 days) in the analysed population: 58.7% (54/92) on edaravone dexborneol vs 52.1% (49/94) on placebo (unadjusted odds ratio 1.37; 95% CI 0.76–2.44; P=0.29). The authors conclude the treatment was safe but did not statistically improve 90-day functional outcomes in this post-reperfusion population.
cards.watchOut: Timing may matter — TASTE-2 gave the drug before thrombectomy, this trial after successful reperfusion — but with 200 patients this null is also compatible with a modest true effect. It is carded so the shelf is not built only from the programme's two headline trials.

cards.headline: Synthesis: an added-component win, a borderline placebo win, and a small null — POSSIBLE, single-country throughout
cards.summary: Synthesis: an added-component win, a borderline placebo win, and a small null — POSSIBLE, single-country throughout
cards.people: Synthesis population: 1,165 patients in TASTE (active comparator), 1,360 analysed in TASTE-2 (placebo, pre-thrombectomy) and 200 in the phase 2 post-reperfusion trial — all in China.
cards.result: Edaravone dexborneol outperformed edaravone alone (TASTE), just reached significance against placebo when started before thrombectomy (TASTE-2: 55.0% vs 49.6%, P=0.05), and did not significantly beat placebo after successful reperfusion in a small phase 2 trial. Harms look unremarkable against placebo (serious adverse events 27.2% vs 25.7% in TASTE-2). The balance is a genuine but fragile POSSIBLE, resting on one country's programme and one borderline primary result.
cards.watchOut: Never cite TASTE without its comparator: it compared two active infusions, not drug versus nothing. Edaravone's separate shelf in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is a different drug use and population and lends this shelf no support.
cards.source: Synthesis of the carded records above (PMIDs 33588596, 41500725, 40064868). No new data.

shelves.title: Aducanumab in early Alzheimer's disease: two identical phase 3 trials disagreed — EMERGE met its endpoint at high dose, ENGAGE did not — and the programme was terminated and the drug withdrawn
shelves.question: In patients with early Alzheimer's disease, did aducanumab slow clinical decline versus placebo — and why did its two identical phase 3 trials disagree?
shelves.mesh: Alzheimer Disease · Amyloid beta-Peptides · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Biomarkers · Humans
shelves.balance: This shelf cards only the aducanumab slice. The neighbouring live shelf #333 covers lecanemab and donanemab and mentions aducanumab only as a cautionary arc; the EMERGE and ENGAGE results themselves are carded here, from their joint report, and none of #333's references is carded on this shelf. The record is genuinely split. EMERGE (n=1,638) met its primary endpoint at the high dose: CDR-SB difference −0.39 versus placebo (95% CI −0.69 to −0.09; P=.012), described in the report as a 22% relative slowing. ENGAGE (n=1,647), an identically designed twin trial, did not: difference +0.03 (95% CI −0.26 to 0.33; P=.833). Both trials were halted early on a futility analysis of pooled data from roughly the first half of participants, then analysed on the larger dataset accumulated by the halt — the procedural fact at the centre of every later dispute about this programme. Both trials showed dose-dependent amyloid and biomarker reduction, and the commonest adverse event was amyloid-related imaging abnormality with oedema (ARIA-E). Aducanumab received accelerated US approval in 2021 on the amyloid surrogate, and the programme was subsequently terminated with the drug withdrawn in 2024, as the #333 shelf records. A split phase 3 pair, stopped early, followed by withdrawal is not a basis for expecting clinical benefit: the stamp is SPLIT because the trials themselves split.

cards.headline: EMERGE (Budd Haeberlein 2022): the primary endpoint was met at high dose — CDR-SB difference −0.39 vs placebo (P=.012)
cards.summary: EMERGE (Budd Haeberlein 2022): the primary endpoint was met at high dose — CDR-SB difference −0.39 vs placebo (P=.012)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (EMERGE), reported jointly with ENGAGE in the Journal of Prevention of Alzheimer's Disease 2022
cards.people: EMERGE randomised 1,638 patients aged 50–85 with early Alzheimer's disease (mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer's disease or mild Alzheimer's dementia) and confirmed amyloid pathology, at 348 sites in 20 countries across the two-trial programme. Participants were assigned 1:1:1 to low-dose aducanumab (3 or 6 mg/kg target), high-dose aducanumab (10 mg/kg target) or placebo, by intravenous infusion every 4 weeks over 76 weeks; the primary outcome was change in CDR-SB at week 78.
cards.result: In EMERGE the primary endpoint was met for high-dose aducanumab: CDR-SB difference −0.39 versus placebo (95% CI −0.69 to −0.09; P=.012), reported as a 22% relative decrease in decline. The report states that EMERGE showed statistically significant change across all four primary and secondary clinical endpoints, and biomarker substudies confirmed target engagement with dose-dependent reduction in markers of Alzheimer's pathophysiology. The most common adverse event in the programme was amyloid-related imaging abnormalities with oedema (ARIA-E).
cards.watchOut: EMERGE cannot be quoted without its twin: the same report's ENGAGE trial, carded next, missed the same endpoint outright. Both trials were halted on a futility analysis and analysed on data beyond that analysis set, and across the two trials only 55.2% of participants completed the study — attrition and the early halt shadow any single-trial reading.
cards.source: Budd Haeberlein S et al. Two Randomized Phase 3 Studies of Aducanumab in Early Alzheimer's Disease. J Prev Alzheimers Dis. 2022. PMID 35542991. DOI 10.14283/jpad.2022.30 (No registry ID printed in the fetched record.)

cards.headline: ENGAGE (Budd Haeberlein 2022): the identical twin trial missed its primary endpoint — CDR-SB difference +0.03 vs placebo (P=.833) (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: ENGAGE (Budd Haeberlein 2022): the identical twin trial missed its primary endpoint — CDR-SB difference +0.03 vs placebo (P=.833) (the treatment made no difference)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (ENGAGE), reported jointly with EMERGE in the Journal of Prevention of Alzheimer's Disease 2022
cards.people: ENGAGE randomised 1,647 patients with the same eligibility criteria, doses, schedule and primary outcome as EMERGE (early Alzheimer's disease with confirmed amyloid pathology, ages 50–85; low-dose, high-dose or placebo aducanumab every 4 weeks over 76 weeks; CDR-SB change at week 78).
cards.result: In ENGAGE the primary endpoint was not met: CDR-SB difference for high-dose aducanumab versus placebo was +0.03 (95% CI −0.26 to 0.33; P=.833), reported as a 2% relative increase in decline — the treatment made no difference. ENGAGE did not meet its primary or secondary endpoints, although, as in EMERGE, a dose- and time-dependent reduction in pathophysiological markers of Alzheimer's disease was observed.
cards.watchOut: Two identically designed trials of the same drug in the same population giving opposite primary results is the definition of an unresolved programme. Explanations offered after the fact (dose exposure differences between the trials) are post-hoc readings of a split record, not a third trial — and no confirmatory trial rescued the programme before its termination.
cards.source: Budd Haeberlein S et al. Two Randomized Phase 3 Studies of Aducanumab in Early Alzheimer's Disease. J Prev Alzheimers Dis. 2022. PMID 35542991. DOI 10.14283/jpad.2022.30 (No registry ID printed in the fetched record.)

cards.headline: PRIME phase 1b (Sevigny 2016): amyloid plaques fell dose-dependently and decline appeared to slow — the early signal the phase 3 pair then split on
cards.summary: PRIME phase 1b (Sevigny 2016): amyloid plaques fell dose-dependently and decline appeared to slow — the early signal the phase 3 pair then split on
cards.people: Patients with prodromal or mild Alzheimer's disease received monthly intravenous aducanumab infusions for one year in this phase 1b randomised study (the fetched abstract record does not print the participant number).
cards.result: One year of monthly aducanumab reduced brain amyloid-beta in a dose- and time-dependent manner, accompanied in the report by slowing of clinical decline on the CDR-SB and MMSE. The main safety and tolerability findings were amyloid-related imaging abnormalities. The authors state the results justified the phase 3 programme and that confirmation of the clinical slowing in phase 3 would support the amyloid hypothesis.
cards.watchOut: A small early-phase study with exploratory clinical measures is a hypothesis generator, not evidence of benefit — PRIME's own framing. Its amyloid result was real and was replicated at phase 3 scale; its clinical signal is exactly what EMERGE and ENGAGE then disagreed about. Participant number is not printed in the fetched abstract record and is therefore not stated on this card.
cards.source: Sevigny J et al. The antibody aducanumab reduces Aβ plaques in Alzheimer's disease. Nature. 2016. PMID 27582220. DOI 10.1038/nature19323 (No registry ID printed in the fetched record.)

cards.headline: Synthesis: one positive twin, one negative twin, early termination, approval on a surrogate, then withdrawal — a SPLIT record that ended the programme
cards.summary: Synthesis: one positive twin, one negative twin, early termination, approval on a surrogate, then withdrawal — a SPLIT record that ended the programme
cards.people: Synthesis population: 1,638 patients in EMERGE and 1,647 in ENGAGE (3,285 randomised across the twin phase 3 trials), preceded by the PRIME phase 1b study.
cards.result: Aducanumab lowered amyloid dose-dependently in every study — the biomarker half of the record is consistent. The clinical half split: EMERGE met its CDR-SB endpoint at high dose (−0.39; P=.012) and ENGAGE did not (+0.03; P=.833), after both were halted on a pooled futility analysis. The programme's later history — accelerated approval in 2021 on the amyloid surrogate and termination with withdrawal in 2024 — is recorded on live shelf #333, which this shelf cross-points to for the lecanemab and donanemab evidence; this shelf's own verdict is SPLIT, because the two trials that were supposed to confirm each other did not.
cards.watchOut: Do not average EMERGE and ENGAGE into a single 'small positive' number: the disagreement, the early halt, and the withdrawal are the finding. Any future citation of aducanumab as proof that amyloid lowering produces clinical benefit must answer ENGAGE first.
cards.source: Synthesis of the carded records above (PMID 35542991, PMID 27582220). No new data. Home shelf cross-point: live #333 (lecanemab/donanemab) — its references are not carded here.

shelves.title: Gantenerumab in early Alzheimer's disease: GRADUATE I and II both missed their primary endpoint (the treatment made no difference) despite lowering amyloid — a well-conducted negative programme
shelves.question: In patients with early Alzheimer's disease, does gantenerumab slow clinical decline versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Alzheimer Disease · Amyloid beta-Peptides · Antibodies, Monoclonal · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Positron-Emission Tomography · Middle Aged · Aged · Aged, 80 and over
shelves.balance: This is a clean negative programme, and the shelf's job is to hold that answer plainly. In GRADUATE I (n=985) the CDR-SB difference at week 116 was −0.31 (95% CI −0.66 to 0.05; P=0.10); in GRADUATE II (n=980) it was −0.19 (95% CI −0.55 to 0.17; P=0.30) — neither significant, both small. The drug did what it was designed to do biologically: amyloid on PET fell by about 56–66 centiloids more than on placebo, and roughly 27–28% of treated participants reached amyloid-negative status. It also carried the class harm: ARIA-E in 24.9% of treated participants, symptomatic in 5.0%. The earlier SCarlet RoAD trial in prodromal disease (n=797, lower monthly doses) had already been halted for futility with no clinical differences, and its exploratory dose signal is what justified GRADUATE's higher, more frequent dosing — which then also failed on the clinical endpoint. Amyloid lowering without clinical slowing, twice at phase 3 scale, is the answer. The neighbouring live shelf #333 covers the two antibodies in this class that did slow decline (lecanemab, donanemab); gantenerumab is not among them.

cards.headline: GRADUATE I (Bateman 2023): CDR-SB difference −0.31 at week 116 (P=0.10) — the primary endpoint was missed (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: GRADUATE I (Bateman 2023): CDR-SB difference −0.31 at week 116 (P=0.10) — the primary endpoint was missed (the treatment made no difference)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (GRADUATE I), New England Journal of Medicine 2023
cards.people: 985 participants aged 50–90 with mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia due to Alzheimer's disease and amyloid confirmed on PET or in cerebrospinal fluid, randomised to subcutaneous gantenerumab or placebo every 2 weeks; baseline CDR-SB 3.7. Primary outcome: change in CDR-SB at week 116.
cards.result: CDR-SB change at week 116 was 3.35 on gantenerumab vs 3.65 on placebo (difference −0.31; 95% CI −0.66 to 0.05; P=0.10) — not significant. Amyloid on PET fell 66.44 centiloids more on gantenerumab than placebo, and 28.0% of treated participants reached amyloid-negative status. Across both GRADUATE trials, ARIA-E occurred in 24.9% of gantenerumab participants and was symptomatic in 5.0%.
cards.watchOut: A −0.31 point difference whose interval includes zero, in a trial of nearly a thousand patients, is a negative result — not a 'trend' to be quoted as near-benefit. The amyloid clearance in the same patients is what makes the null informative: the biomarker moved and the clinical course did not.
cards.source: Bateman RJ et al. Two Phase 3 Trials of Gantenerumab in Early Alzheimer's Disease. N Engl J Med. 2023. PMID 37966285 · NCT03444870 (GRADUATE I). DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2304430

cards.headline: GRADUATE II (Bateman 2023): CDR-SB difference −0.19 at week 116 (P=0.30) — the twin trial confirmed the null
cards.summary: GRADUATE II (Bateman 2023): CDR-SB difference −0.19 at week 116 (P=0.30) — the twin trial confirmed the null
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (GRADUATE II), New England Journal of Medicine 2023
cards.people: 980 participants with the same eligibility criteria as GRADUATE I (early Alzheimer's disease, ages 50–90, amyloid confirmed on PET or CSF), randomised to subcutaneous gantenerumab or placebo every 2 weeks; baseline CDR-SB 3.6. Primary outcome: change in CDR-SB at week 116.
cards.result: CDR-SB change at week 116 was 2.82 on gantenerumab vs 3.01 on placebo (difference −0.19; 95% CI −0.55 to 0.17; P=0.30) — not significant. Amyloid on PET fell 56.46 centiloids more on gantenerumab than placebo, and 26.8% of treated participants reached amyloid-negative status. CSF phosphorylated tau 181 was lower and Aβ42 higher on gantenerumab, while aggregated tau accumulation on PET was similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: Two concordant nulls close the question the programme asked: at this dose, schedule and disease stage, gantenerumab did not slow decline. That distinguishes it from the discordant aducanumab pair carded on the neighbouring shelf — here there is no positive twin to argue over.

cards.headline: SCarlet RoAD (Ostrowitzki 2017): the earlier prodromal trial was halted for futility — no clinical differences at lower monthly doses
cards.summary: SCarlet RoAD (Ostrowitzki 2017): the earlier prodromal trial was halted for futility — no clinical differences at lower monthly doses
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (SCarlet RoAD), Alzheimer's Research & Therapy 2017
cards.people: 797 patients with prodromal Alzheimer's disease randomised (of 3,089 screened) to subcutaneous gantenerumab 105 mg or 225 mg or placebo every 4 weeks for 2 years; primary endpoint CDR-SB change at week 104. A futility analysis was prespecified once 50% of patients completed 2 years.
cards.result: The study was halted early for futility, dosing was discontinued and the study unblinded. CDR-SB change was 1.60 on placebo, 1.69 on gantenerumab 105 mg and 1.73 on 225 mg — no differences on the primary or secondary clinical endpoints (the treatment made no difference). Amyloid-related imaging abnormalities increased in a dose- and APOE ε4-dependent manner. Exploratory analyses suggested dose-dependent effects, which the authors took as grounds to test higher dosing.
cards.watchOut: SCarlet RoAD used lower doses given monthly, in an earlier disease stage, so its null alone would not settle the GRADUATE question — it is carded as the programme's first futility stop, and because its exploratory dose signal is the stated reason GRADUATE dosed higher and more often. That escalation was tested and also failed on the clinical endpoint.

cards.headline: Synthesis: amyloid fell, decline did not — a concordant negative programme, UNLIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: amyloid fell, decline did not — a concordant negative programme, UNLIKELY
cards.people: Synthesis population: 1,965 participants across GRADUATE I and II, plus 797 in the earlier prodromal SCarlet RoAD trial.
cards.result: Across three phase 3 trials, gantenerumab lowered brain amyloid substantially and produced ARIA-E in about a quarter of treated participants (symptomatic in 5.0% in GRADUATE), while the clinical endpoint — CDR-SB change — showed no significant slowing in any trial (differences −0.31 and −0.19 in GRADUATE; none in SCarlet RoAD). A well-conducted negative programme is a complete answer: gantenerumab should not be expected to slow early Alzheimer's decline, and its record is a standing caution against treating amyloid clearance alone as clinical benefit.
cards.watchOut: Contrast with live shelf #333 is instructive and must stay precise: lecanemab and donanemab did slow CDR-SB decline statistically (by amounts below the meaningful-difference yardstick carded there), while gantenerumab did not separate from placebo at all. 'Anti-amyloid antibody' is not a single verdict.
cards.source: Synthesis of the carded records above (PMIDs 37966285, 29221491). No new data.

shelves.title: Evobrutinib in relapsing multiple sclerosis: not superior to teriflunomide in evolutionRMS1 and 2 (relapse rates identical) — with a liver-enzyme cost (elevations ≥5× the upper limit of normal in 5.0% vs <1%)
shelves.question: In people with relapsing multiple sclerosis, is the BTK inhibitor evobrutinib superior to teriflunomide for relapse rate, and what is its liver cost?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Adult · Double-Blind Method · Female · Male · Multiple Sclerosis, Relapsing-Remitting · Protein Kinase Inhibitors · Agammaglobulinaemia Tyrosine Kinase · Treatment Outcome · Middle Aged · Young Adult
shelves.balance: The phase 3 answer is unusually plain, because the trialists state it themselves: the efficacy of evobrutinib was not superior to that of teriflunomide, and together the efficacy and liver findings do not support its use in relapsing multiple sclerosis. In evolutionRMS1 (n=1,124 in the full analysis set) the annualised relapse rate was 0.15 on evobrutinib vs 0.14 on teriflunomide (adjusted rate ratio 1.02; p=0.55); in evolutionRMS2 (n=1,166) it was 0.11 vs 0.11 (rate ratio 1.00; p=0.51). The liver cost was asymmetric: alanine aminotransferase elevations of at least 5 times the upper limit of normal occurred in 5.0% on evobrutinib vs fewer than 1% on teriflunomide, concentrated in the first 12 weeks, and three evobrutinib patients (vs one on teriflunomide) met the biochemical definition of Hy's law, all resolving after discontinuation. The earlier phase 2 trial (n=267) had shown fewer gadolinium-enhancing MRI lesions at the 75 mg once-daily dose — a real imaging signal that did not convert into fewer relapses than an established oral comparator at phase 3. This shelf's verdict is about evobrutinib versus teriflunomide in relapsing MS; it is not a verdict on the BTK-inhibitor class in other MS phenotypes.

cards.headline: evolutionRMS1 (Montalban 2024): annualised relapse rate 0.15 vs 0.14 on teriflunomide (rate ratio 1.02; p=0.55) — not superior (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: evolutionRMS1 (Montalban 2024): annualised relapse rate 0.15 vs 0.14 on teriflunomide (rate ratio 1.02; p=0.55) — not superior (the treatment made no difference)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised, double-blind, double-dummy, active-controlled trial (evolutionRMS1), Lancet Neurology 2024
cards.people: 1,124 participants in the full analysis set (560 evobrutinib, 564 teriflunomide) — adults aged 18–55 with relapsing multiple sclerosis (EDSS 0.0–5.5), at centres within the 701-site, 52-country evolutionRMS programme; 66.8% female. Evobrutinib 45 mg twice daily or teriflunomide 14 mg once daily, double-blind, double-dummy. Primary endpoint: annualised relapse rate up to 156 weeks.
cards.result: Annualised relapse rate was 0.15 (95% CI 0.12–0.18) on evobrutinib vs 0.14 (0.11–0.18) on teriflunomide (adjusted rate ratio 1.02; 95% CI 0.75–1.39; p=0.55). The report's pooled safety findings for the two trials are carded with evolutionRMS2 below: overall treatment-emergent adverse events were similar between groups, serious events were somewhat more frequent on evobrutinib (7.5% vs 5.6%), and liver-enzyme elevations ≥5× the upper limit of normal were more common on evobrutinib (5.0% vs <1%).
cards.watchOut: This was a superiority comparison against an active drug, not a placebo trial: matching teriflunomide's relapse rate means evobrutinib worked about as well as an established therapy on relapses — but the trial's question was superiority, it was not shown, and the liver profile was worse. 'As good as teriflunomide with more liver monitoring' is not a case for switching.

cards.headline: evolutionRMS2 (Montalban 2024): annualised relapse rate 0.11 vs 0.11 (rate ratio 1.00; p=0.51) — and the programme's liver signal sits in this card
cards.summary: evolutionRMS2 (Montalban 2024): annualised relapse rate 0.11 vs 0.11 (rate ratio 1.00; p=0.51) — and the programme's liver signal sits in this card
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised, double-blind, double-dummy, active-controlled trial (evolutionRMS2), Lancet Neurology 2024
cards.people: 1,166 participants in the full analysis set (583 per group) with relapsing multiple sclerosis (ages 18–55; EDSS 0.0–5.5); 67.2% female. Same interventions as evolutionRMS1: evobrutinib 45 mg twice daily vs teriflunomide 14 mg once daily, double-blind, double-dummy, primary endpoint annualised relapse rate up to 156 weeks.
cards.result: Annualised relapse rate was 0.11 (95% CI 0.09–0.13) in both groups (adjusted rate ratio 1.00; 95% CI 0.74–1.35; p=0.51). Pooled across both trials: any treatment-emergent adverse event in 85.6% on evobrutinib vs 87.2% on teriflunomide; alanine aminotransferase increased in 15.2% vs 17.8% at any grade, but elevations ≥5× the upper limit of normal in 5.0% (55 patients) vs <1% (9 patients), particularly in the first 12 weeks; three evobrutinib patients and one teriflunomide patient met the biochemical definition of Hy's law, all resolving after discontinuation. Two deaths (one per group) were unrelated to treatment. The authors conclude the findings do not support the use of evobrutinib in relapsing multiple sclerosis.
cards.watchOut: Any-grade transaminase increases were actually reported slightly less often on evobrutinib — the liver concern is specifically the severe-elevation tail (≥5× the upper limit of normal) and the Hy's law cases, which is why this card prints the ≥5× figures rather than the any-grade ones. Both trials are recorded as terminated in the registry entry quoted by the report.

cards.headline: Phase 2 (Montalban 2019): the earlier signal — fewer gadolinium-enhancing lesions at 75 mg once daily, no significant relapse or disability effect, liver aminotransferase elevations already visible
cards.summary: Phase 2 (Montalban 2019): the earlier signal — fewer gadolinium-enhancing lesions at 75 mg once daily, no significant relapse or disability effect, liver aminotransferase elevations already visible
cards.type: Phase 2 double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial, New England Journal of Medicine 2019
cards.people: 267 patients with relapsing multiple sclerosis randomised to placebo, evobrutinib 25 mg once daily, 75 mg once daily or 75 mg twice daily, or open-label dimethyl fumarate as reference, over 24 weeks. Primary endpoint: total gadolinium-enhancing lesions on T1-weighted MRI at weeks 12, 16, 20 and 24.
cards.result: Mean total enhancing lesions were 3.85 on placebo, 4.06 on evobrutinib 25 mg, 1.69 on 75 mg once daily and 1.15 on 75 mg twice daily; the baseline-adjusted rate ratio vs placebo was 0.30 (P=0.005) for 75 mg once daily and 0.44 (P=0.06) for 75 mg twice daily. Unadjusted annualised relapse rates at week 24 ranged from 0.08 to 0.57 across groups with no significant effect on relapse rate or EDSS change at any dose. Elevations in liver aminotransferase values were observed with evobrutinib.
cards.watchOut: An MRI lesion endpoint in 267 patients over 24 weeks is a mechanism signal, not a relapse outcome — and the phase 2 doses (75 mg once or twice daily) differ from the phase 3 regimen (45 mg twice daily), so the imaging result cannot be carried across as an expectation of clinical benefit. The liver-enzyme observation, by contrast, did carry across.
