cards.headline: Synthesis: identical relapse rates in two large trials, a worse severe-liver-elevation profile — not superior, and not supported for relapsing MS
cards.summary: Synthesis: identical relapse rates in two large trials, a worse severe-liver-elevation profile — not superior, and not supported for relapsing MS
cards.people: Synthesis population: 2,290 randomised participants across evolutionRMS1 and evolutionRMS2, preceded by a 267-patient phase 2 trial.
cards.result: Evobrutinib matched teriflunomide on relapses in both phase 3 trials (rate ratios 1.02 and 1.00) — the treatment made no difference to the primary outcome it was meant to improve — while producing more frequent severe liver-enzyme elevations (≥5× the upper limit of normal: 5.0% vs <1%) and three Hy's law cases. cards.watchOut: Do not generalise this shelf to other BTK inhibitors or other MS phenotypes: a different BTK inhibitor in non-relapsing secondary progressive MS is a separate shelf and a separate record. Within its own question — evobrutinib vs teriflunomide in relapsing MS — the record is closed by two concordant trials.

shelves.title: Tavapadon (tested product: tavapadon, AbbVie) in Parkinson's disease: motor scores improved in early disease (TEMPO-1 and TEMPO-2) and good on-time rose by 1.1 hours as a levodopa adjunct (TEMPO-3)
shelves.question: In people with Parkinson's disease, does the selective D1/D5 partial agonist tavapadon improve motor scores as monotherapy in early disease (TEMPO-1/2) and increase good on-time as levodopa adjunct in fluctuating disease (TEMPO-3), versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Parkinson Disease · Female · Double-Blind Method · Middle Aged · Male · Aged · Antiparkinson Agents · Treatment Outcome · Dopamine Agonists · Levodopa · Drug Therapy, Combination
shelves.balance: The tested product is named per the clarification exception: tavapadon (AbbVie), an oral once-daily selective D1/D5 dopamine-receptor partial agonist. Its three phase 3 trials are concordant. In early Parkinson's disease, TEMPO-1 (n=529) found MDS-UPDRS Parts II+III improvements of −11.5 points (5 mg) and −12.1 points (15 mg) versus placebo at week 26, and TEMPO-2 (n=304, flexible dose) found −9.1 points. In fluctuating disease on levodopa, TEMPO-3 (n=507) increased daily good on-time by 1.10 hours versus placebo and reduced off-time by 0.94 hours. The cost is tolerability, not a safety catastrophe: nausea in roughly a quarter to a third of treated patients, headache and dizziness commonly, and in TEMPO-2 discontinuation in 38% on tavapadon vs 15% on placebo, most often for adverse events. Trials ran 26–27 weeks, so long-term tolerability and any comparison against existing agonists or levodopa strategies are untested — a single programme with short follow-up caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: TEMPO-1 (Pahwa 2026): fixed-dose tavapadon improved MDS-UPDRS II+III by −11.5 points (5 mg) and −12.1 points (15 mg) vs placebo at week 26
cards.summary: TEMPO-1 (Pahwa 2026): fixed-dose tavapadon improved MDS-UPDRS II+III by −11.5 points (5 mg) and −12.1 points (15 mg) vs placebo at week 26
cards.type: Phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised clinical trial (TEMPO-1), JAMA Neurology 2026
cards.people: 529 adults with early Parkinson's disease (disease duration under 3 years; treatment-naive or under 3 months of prior dopaminergic treatment; mean age 63.7 years; 35.3% women), at 102 sites in 12 countries, randomised to tavapadon 5 mg (n=177), tavapadon 15 mg (n=177) or placebo (n=175) once daily for 27 weeks. Primary endpoint: change in MDS-UPDRS Parts II and III combined score at week 26.
cards.result: MDS-UPDRS II+III fell by 9.7 points on tavapadon 5 mg and 10.2 points on 15 mg, against a 1.8-point increase on placebo: treatment differences −11.5 points (95% CI −13.8 to −9.2; P<.001) and −12.1 points (95% CI −14.4 to −9.8; P<.001). Most adverse events were nonserious and mild to moderate; the commonest on tavapadon were nausea (25.4%), headache (16.7%) and dizziness (12.7%).
cards.watchOut: A large scale-score difference over 26 weeks in early, largely untreated disease is the programme's strongest result — and its limit: placebo groups in early Parkinson's trials often worsen measurably over short horizons, and there is no active comparator, so this card cannot say how tavapadon compares with starting levodopa or a conventional agonist.
cards.source: Pahwa R et al. Fixed-Dose Tavapadon for Early Parkinson Disease: A Randomized Clinical Trial (TEMPO-1). JAMA Neurol. 2026. PMID 41860533 · NCT04201093. DOI 10.1001/jamaneurol.2026.0590

cards.headline: TEMPO-2 (Fernandez 2026): flexible-dose tavapadon improved MDS-UPDRS II+III by −9.1 points — but 38% discontinued on tavapadon vs 15% on placebo
cards.summary: TEMPO-2 (Fernandez 2026): flexible-dose tavapadon improved MDS-UPDRS II+III by −9.1 points — but 38% discontinued on tavapadon vs 15% on placebo
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (TEMPO-2), Lancet Neurology 2026
cards.people: 304 adults aged 40–80 with early-stage Parkinson's disease (duration under 3 years; treatment-naive or under 3 months of prior dopaminergic treatment; mean age 62.9 years; 56% men), at 75 sites in 13 countries, randomised to flexible-dose tavapadon 5–15 mg (n=151) or placebo (n=153) once daily for 27 weeks. Primary endpoint: MDS-UPDRS Parts II+III change at week 26.
cards.result: MDS-UPDRS II+III fell by 10.3 points on tavapadon vs 1.2 points on placebo (least-squares mean difference −9.1; 95% CI −11.7 to −6.5; p<0.0001). Adverse events occurred in 76% on tavapadon vs 55% on placebo — nausea 30% vs 3%, headache 17% vs 5%, dizziness 16% vs 3% — concentrated in the titration phase. Discontinuation was 38% (57/151) on tavapadon vs 15% (23/153) on placebo, most commonly for adverse events (24% vs 4%). The authors note low rates of somnolence and impulse-control disorders, and that the short observation period limits long-term tolerability conclusions. Funded by AbbVie.
cards.watchOut: Read the efficacy and the discontinuation figures together: a treatment a quarter of patients stop for adverse events during dose titration delivers its average benefit to a selected remainder. Flexible dosing mirrors practice better than TEMPO-1's fixed doses, which makes this card's tolerability numbers the more clinically relevant ones.
cards.source: Fernandez HH et al. Safety, tolerability, and efficacy of flexible-dose tavapadon for Parkinson's disease (TEMPO-2): a phase 3, randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial. Lancet Neurol. 2026. PMID 42456682 · NCT04223193. DOI 10.1016/S1474-4422(26)00215-2

cards.headline: TEMPO-3 (Fernandez 2026): as a levodopa adjunct, tavapadon added 1.10 hours of daily good on-time and cut off-time by 0.94 hours vs placebo
cards.summary: TEMPO-3 (Fernandez 2026): as a levodopa adjunct, tavapadon added 1.10 hours of daily good on-time and cut off-time by 0.94 hours vs placebo
cards.type: Phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised clinical trial (TEMPO-3), JAMA Neurology 2026
cards.people: 507 adults with Parkinson's disease experiencing motor fluctuations on stable levodopa (at least 400 mg daily; mean age 64.9 years; 63% men; mean disease duration 6.7 years; mean baseline off-time 5.5 hours), at 148 sites in 14 countries, randomised to flexible-dose tavapadon 5–15 mg (n=252) or placebo (n=255) once daily for 27 weeks. Primary endpoint: change in total daily good on-time (on-time without troublesome dyskinesia) at week 26.
cards.result: Good on-time increased by 1.70 hours on tavapadon vs 0.60 hours on placebo (difference 1.10 hours; 95% CI 0.60–1.70; P<.001). Off-time fell by 1.88 vs 0.93 hours (difference −0.94 hours; 95% CI −1.48 to −0.41; P<.001). Adverse events occurred in 71.7% vs 55.1%, mostly nonserious and mild to moderate; the commonest on tavapadon were nausea (14.3%), dyskinesia (10.0%) and dizziness (7.6%).
cards.watchOut: One extra hour of good on-time is a patient-important gain of the size clinicians recognise from other adjuncts — but this trial does not compare tavapadon with those adjuncts, and dyskinesia appeared in 10% on tavapadon, so the D1/D5 selectivity rationale did not abolish the class's motor cost. The record cited in the abstract describes tavapadon here as investigational.
cards.source: Fernandez HH et al. Tavapadon as Adjunctive Treatment for Parkinson Disease: The TEMPO-3 Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Neurol. 2026. PMID 41860544 · NCT04542499. DOI 10.1001/jamaneurol.2026.0577

cards.headline: Synthesis: one programme, three positive phase 3 trials, 26-week horizons — POSSIBLE, with tolerability as the standing caveat
cards.summary: Synthesis: one programme, three positive phase 3 trials, 26-week horizons — POSSIBLE, with tolerability as the standing caveat
cards.people: Synthesis population: 529 (TEMPO-1) + 304 (TEMPO-2) patients with early Parkinson's disease and 507 patients with fluctuating disease on levodopa (TEMPO-3) — 1,340 randomised patients in the tavapadon (AbbVie) programme.
cards.result: Tavapadon improved motor scores versus placebo in early disease in two designs (fixed dose −11.5/−12.1 points; flexible dose −9.1 points on MDS-UPDRS II+III) and increased good on-time by 1.10 hours as a levodopa adjunct, with concordant off-time reduction. Against that stand nausea in up to 30%, dizziness, dyskinesia in the adjunct setting, and a 38% discontinuation rate in the flexible-dose early-disease trial. With a single sponsor programme, no active comparators and no follow-up beyond about six months, the stamp is POSSIBLE (benefit) — real symptomatic efficacy, durability and comparative place unproven.
cards.watchOut: Nothing on this shelf speaks to disease modification: every endpoint is symptomatic and short-term. Claims that D1/D5 selectivity avoids the impulse-control and sleep effects of D2/D3 agonists rest on low event rates over 26 weeks in these trials, not on head-to-head evidence.
cards.source: Synthesis of the carded records above (PMIDs 41860533, 42456682, 41860544). No new data.

shelves.title: Efgartigimod in CIDP (ADHERE): relapse risk cut in an enriched randomised-withdrawal trial — the denominator is open-label run-in responders (214 of 322 improved), not all CIDP; relapses 27.9% vs 53.6% on withdrawal to placebo
shelves.question: In adults with CIDP, does weekly subcutaneous efgartigimod PH20 reduce relapse risk versus placebo in patients who first respond in an open-label run-in?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Double-Blind Method · Male · Female · Polyradiculoneuropathy, Chronic Inflammatory Demyelinating · Middle Aged · Adult · Aged · Treatment Outcome · Injections, Subcutaneous · Immunoglobulin Fc Fragments
shelves.balance: The design is the headline, and it is printed on the face: ADHERE is an enriched randomised-withdrawal trial. Of 322 adults with CIDP who entered the open-label run-in (stage A) on weekly subcutaneous efgartigimod PH20 1000 mg, 214 (66%) achieved confirmed clinical improvement; it was those responders — 221 participants entered the randomised stage B per the report — who were randomised to continue efgartigimod or switch to placebo for up to 48 weeks. In stage B, continuing efgartigimod reduced relapse risk with a hazard ratio of 0.39 (95% CI 0.25–0.61) — a 61% relative reduction in relapse risk — with absolute relapse rates of 27.9% (31/111) on efgartigimod vs 53.6% (59/110) on placebo. That is strong evidence that responders who stop, relapse — and no evidence at all about the third of patients who never responded in stage A, who are outside the randomised denominator. Adverse events were similar between stage B groups (treatment-emergent events 64% vs 56%; serious events 5% in each). A single trial with an enriched design caps the stamp at POSSIBLE, and any quotation of the hazard ratio without the run-in denominator misstates the trial. Efgartigimod's separate generalised myasthenia gravis evidence is a different disease and shelf (live #1116) and lends this one no support.

cards.headline: ADHERE stage A (Allen 2024): the run-in that defines the denominator — 322 entered open-label efgartigimod, 214 (66%) had confirmed clinical improvement
cards.summary: ADHERE stage A (Allen 2024): the run-in that defines the denominator — 322 entered open-label efgartigimod, 214 (66%) had confirmed clinical improvement
cards.type: Multistage trial, stage A: open-label run-in (ADHERE), Lancet Neurology 2024
cards.people: 322 adults with CIDP (114 women, 208 men) from 146 clinical sites across Asia-Pacific, Europe and North America who had evidence of clinically meaningful deterioration, treated open-label with weekly subcutaneous efgartigimod PH20 1000 mg for up to 12 weeks. Stage A primary endpoint: confirmed evidence of clinical improvement (ECI) — at least a 1-point decrease in adjusted INCAT score, at least a 4-point (centile) increase in I-RODS, or at least an 8 kPa grip-strength increase, after four injections and at two consecutive visits.
cards.result: 214 of 322 participants (66%; 95% CI 61.0–71.6) achieved confirmed ECI and were the responder population eligible for randomisation. Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 204 participants (63%) in stage A and serious treatment-emergent events in 21 (7%); two deaths occurred in stage A (one unrelated and one unlikely related to treatment, per the report).
cards.watchOut: Stage A has no control group: some of the 66% 'response' will be natural fluctuation, regression to the mean after enrolling at a deterioration point, and expectation effects, in unknown proportions. Its purpose in this design is enrichment — selecting apparent responders for the withdrawal test — not estimating the response rate a clinician should expect in unselected CIDP.
cards.source: Allen JA et al. Safety, tolerability, and efficacy of subcutaneous efgartigimod in patients with chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (ADHERE): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet Neurol. 2024. PMID 39304241 · NCT04281472. DOI 10.1016/S1474-4422(24)00309-0

cards.headline: ADHERE stage B (Allen 2024): continuing efgartigimod vs withdrawal to placebo — relapses 27.9% vs 53.6%, hazard ratio 0.39 (a 61% relative reduction in relapse risk)
cards.summary: ADHERE stage B (Allen 2024): continuing efgartigimod vs withdrawal to placebo — relapses 27.9% vs 53.6%, hazard ratio 0.39 (a 61% relative reduction in relapse risk)
cards.type: Multistage trial, stage B: double-blind randomised-withdrawal phase (ADHERE), Lancet Neurology 2024
cards.people: 221 run-in responders randomised in stage B (79 women, 142 men): 111 continued weekly subcutaneous efgartigimod PH20 1000 mg and 110 switched to placebo, for up to 48 weeks, double-blind. Primary endpoint: risk of relapse, defined as time to first adjusted INCAT increase of at least 1 point. (The report records 214 confirmed improvers in stage A and 221 participants randomised in stage B; both figures are printed as reported.)
cards.result: Efgartigimod significantly reduced relapse risk versus placebo (hazard ratio 0.39; 95% CI 0.25–0.61; p<0.0001) — a 61% relative reduction in the risk of relapse, printed beside the absolute rates: relapse occurred in 27.9% (31/111) on efgartigimod vs 53.6% (59/110) on placebo, an absolute difference of about 26 percentage points among responders. Treatment-emergent adverse events: 64% vs 56%; serious events 5% in each group; one death occurred in stage B, in the placebo group.
cards.watchOut: A withdrawal trial answers 'does stopping hurt responders?' — it does not estimate the effect of starting the drug in all-comers with CIDP, and its placebo arm is a withdrawal arm, not a never-treated arm. The hazard ratio also compresses a time-to-event result into one number; the absolute relapse rates beside it are the clinically quotable figures. Funded by argenx, the manufacturer, per the record.

cards.headline: ADHERE safety across stages (Allen 2024): adverse-event rates close to placebo in the randomised stage; three deaths in the programme, none attributed as related in the report
cards.summary: ADHERE safety across stages (Allen 2024): adverse-event rates close to placebo in the randomised stage; three deaths in the programme, none attributed as related in the report
cards.type: Safety report of the ADHERE multistage trial, Lancet Neurology 2024
cards.people: Safety populations as reported: 322 participants in open-label stage A, and 221 randomised participants in stage B (111 efgartigimod, 110 placebo), all adults with CIDP receiving weekly subcutaneous efgartigimod PH20 1000 mg or placebo.
cards.result: In stage A, treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 63% and serious events in 7%. In stage B, treatment-emergent events occurred in 64% on efgartigimod vs 56% on placebo, and serious treatment-emergent events in 5% of each group (6 participants per group). Three deaths occurred in the programme: two in stage A (one assessed as non-related and one as unlikely related to treatment) and one in stage B in the placebo group.
cards.watchOut: The randomised safety comparison covers at most 48 weeks in a responder-selected population; rarer or later harms of chronic FcRn blockade in CIDP — including infection risk from sustained IgG lowering — cannot be sized from one trial of this duration, and the stage A rates have no comparator.

cards.headline: Synthesis: strong withdrawal evidence in responders only — POSSIBLE, and the enriched denominator travels with every number
cards.summary: Synthesis: strong withdrawal evidence in responders only — POSSIBLE, and the enriched denominator travels with every number
cards.people: Synthesis population: 322 adults with CIDP entering the ADHERE run-in, of whom about two-thirds responded and entered the randomised withdrawal stage (221 randomised).
cards.result: Among run-in responders, continuing weekly subcutaneous efgartigimod PH20 kept relapse at 27.9% versus 53.6% after withdrawal to placebo (hazard ratio 0.39; a 61% relative reduction in relapse risk), with adverse-event rates close to placebo over the randomised stage. That supports continuing treatment in patients who demonstrably improve on it. It does not establish the response rate, or the benefit, in unselected CIDP — roughly a third of the run-in population never reached the randomised question. One enriched trial, however clean its randomised stage, caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

shelves.title: Nipocalimab in generalised myasthenia gravis (Vivacity-MG3): MG-ADL improved by −4.70 vs −3.25 points on placebo over 24 weeks in antibody-positive adults, with adverse-event rates equal to placebo
shelves.question: In antibody-positive adults with generalised myasthenia gravis and insufficient response to standard care, does the FcRn blocker nipocalimab improve MG-ADL sustained over 24 weeks versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Myasthenia Gravis · Double-Blind Method · Male · Female · Middle Aged · Adult · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Aged · Treatment Outcome · Receptors, Cholinergic · Activities of Daily Living
shelves.balance: Vivacity-MG3 (199 enrolled; 196 treated) randomised antibody-positive adults with generalised myasthenia gravis inadequately controlled on standard care to nipocalimab (30 mg/kg loading, then 15 mg/kg every 2 weeks) or placebo, each added to standard care, for 24 weeks. The primary endpoint — least-squares mean MG-ADL change averaged over weeks 22–24 in the 153 antibody-positive patients — favoured nipocalimab: −4.70 vs −3.25 points (difference −1.45; 95% CI −2.38 to −0.52; p=0.0024). The population was the broadest in the FcRn class: anti-AChR, anti-MuSK and anti-LRP4 positive patients were all eligible. Tolerability matched placebo on the headline counts — any adverse event in 84% of both groups, infections in 43% of both — while serious adverse events were reported in 9% on nipocalimab vs 14% on placebo, with one fatal myasthenic crisis in the nipocalimab group among three fatal serious events in the trial. A prespecified quality-of-life analysis moved the same direction (MG-QoL15r difference −1.45; fatigue scores better from week 2). One 24-week trial, however consistent internally, caps the stamp at POSSIBLE; durability rests on the ongoing open-label extension. The FcRn neighbours — efgartigimod, rozanolixizumab and zilucoplan in generalised myasthenia gravis — are separate agents on separate shelves and are not interchangeable evidence.

cards.headline: Vivacity-MG3 (Antozzi 2025): MG-ADL −4.70 vs −3.25 points (difference −1.45; p=0.0024), sustained over weeks 22–24, in antibody-positive generalised myasthenia gravis
cards.summary: Vivacity-MG3 (Antozzi 2025): MG-ADL −4.70 vs −3.25 points (difference −1.45; p=0.0024), sustained over weeks 22–24, in antibody-positive generalised myasthenia gravis
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Vivacity-MG3), Lancet Neurology 2025
cards.people: 196 treated adults (98 per group) with generalised myasthenia gravis inadequately controlled on standard-of-care therapy (MG-ADL at least 6), at 81 centres in 17 countries; the primary-endpoint population was the 153 antibody-positive patients (anti-AChR, anti-MuSK or anti-LRP4; 77 nipocalimab, 76 placebo). Nipocalimab 30 mg/kg loading dose then 15 mg/kg every 2 weeks, or placebo infusions, each added to standard care for 24 weeks; double-blind.
cards.result: Least-squares mean MG-ADL change from baseline, averaged over weeks 22, 23 and 24, was −4.70 (SE 0.329) on nipocalimab vs −3.25 (0.335) on placebo (difference −1.45; 95% CI −2.38 to −0.52; p=0.0024). Both groups improved substantially on background standard care; the drug's added contribution is the −1.45 point difference, sustained across the three averaged weeks rather than a single visit.
cards.watchOut: The placebo group's −3.25 point improvement is large — background therapy, trial care and regression all sit inside it — so the honest claim is the −1.45 point increment, not the −4.70. The phase 2 study behind this trial (dose-dependent IgG and anti-AChR reductions with clinically meaningful MG-ADL improvements, per the report's introduction) is described in the phase 3 paper but is not separately carded here. Funded by Janssen Research & Development (Johnson & Johnson).

cards.headline: Vivacity-MG3 safety (Antozzi 2025): adverse events in 84% of both groups and infections in 43% of both; serious events 9% vs 14%, with one fatal myasthenic crisis on nipocalimab
cards.summary: Vivacity-MG3 safety (Antozzi 2025): adverse events in 84% of both groups and infections in 43% of both; serious events 9% vs 14%, with one fatal myasthenic crisis on nipocalimab
cards.type: Safety report of the Vivacity-MG3 phase 3 trial, Lancet Neurology 2025
cards.people: Safety population: 196 patients who received at least one dose of study drug (98 nipocalimab, 98 placebo), adults with generalised myasthenia gravis on background standard care, over the 24-week double-blind phase.
cards.result: Adverse events occurred in 82 patients (84%) in each group; infections in 42 (43%) in each group; headache in 14% on nipocalimab vs 17% on placebo. Serious adverse events were reported in 9% (9/98) on nipocalimab vs 14% (14/98) on placebo. Three serious events had a fatal outcome: a myasthenic crisis in the nipocalimab group, and cardiac arrest and myocardial infarction in the placebo group.
cards.watchOut: Equal headline rates over 24 weeks in 196 patients cannot exclude uncommon or cumulative harms of sustained IgG lowering, which the ongoing open-label extension is designed to clarify. A fatal myasthenic crisis occurred on active treatment — a reminder that trial participation did not abolish disease risk.
cards.source: Antozzi C et al. Safety and efficacy of nipocalimab in adults with generalised myasthenia gravis (Vivacity-MG3): a phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet Neurol. 2025. PMID 39862879 · NCT04951622. DOI 10.1016/S1474-4422(24)00498-8

cards.headline: Vivacity-MG3 quality of life (Vissing 2026): prespecified patient-reported outcomes moved with the clinical scores — MG-QoL15r difference −1.45 and fatigue better from week 2
cards.summary: Vivacity-MG3 quality of life (Vissing 2026): prespecified patient-reported outcomes moved with the clinical scores — MG-QoL15r difference −1.45 and fatigue better from week 2
cards.type: Prespecified secondary analysis of the Vivacity-MG3 phase 3 trial, Journal of Neurology 2026
cards.people: Antibody-positive adults with generalised myasthenia gravis in the Vivacity-MG3 trial (anti-AChR, anti-MuSK or anti-LRP4), randomised to intravenous nipocalimab (30 mg/kg loading, then 15 mg/kg every 2 weeks) or placebo, each added to standard care for 24 weeks. Prespecified analysis of patient-reported outcomes: MG-QoL15r, Neuro-QoL Fatigue, EQ-5D-5L and Patient Global Impression measures.
cards.result: MG-QoL15r improved more on nipocalimab than placebo (least-squares mean change −5.87 vs −4.42; difference −1.45). Neuro-QoL Fatigue improved by week 2 and remained better (least-squares mean change over weeks 22–24: −13.17 vs −10.02; difference −3.15). EQ-5D-5L index gains were 0.13 vs 0.07 and visual-analogue scores 14.55 vs 7.27; 56.5% vs 41.0% rated their fatigue as moderately or much better on the Patient Global Impression of Change. Fatigue improvement correlated with gains in MG-ADL and other clinical measures.
cards.watchOut: Patient-reported outcomes from the same single trial are corroboration of direction, not independent replication: the same patients, the same 24 weeks, and the same −1.45-point pattern as the primary endpoint (a numerical coincidence across two different scales, printed as reported). Unblinding through perceived benefit can inflate subjective endpoints in either direction.
cards.source: Vissing J et al. Health-related quality of life outcomes with nipocalimab versus placebo in generalized myasthenia gravis: an analysis of the Vivacity-MG3 study. J Neurol. 2026. PMID 42360473 · NCT04951622. DOI 10.1007/s00415-026-13978-9

cards.headline: Synthesis: a modest, sustained, well-tolerated increment over standard care in one trial — POSSIBLE, pending longer-term evidence
cards.summary: Synthesis: a modest, sustained, well-tolerated increment over standard care in one trial — POSSIBLE, pending longer-term evidence
cards.people: Synthesis population: 196 treated adults with antibody-positive generalised myasthenia gravis in Vivacity-MG3, with efficacy read in the 153-patient antibody-positive primary population.
cards.result: Nipocalimab added to standard care improved MG-ADL by an extra −1.45 points versus placebo, sustained over weeks 22–24, across the broadest antibody-positive population in its class (AChR, MuSK and LRP4), with quality-of-life and fatigue measures concordant and adverse-event rates matching placebo over 24 weeks. The increment is modest against a large placebo-group improvement, the trial is single, and durability and long-term safety sit in an ongoing open-label extension — so the stamp is POSSIBLE (benefit), not LIKELY.
cards.watchOut: Do not merge this shelf with the other FcRn shelves: efgartigimod (live #1116), rozanolixizumab and zilucoplan each stand on their own trials, dosing and populations. Cross-agent ranking in generalised myasthenia gravis has no head-to-head trial in this record.

shelves.title: Risdiplam in spinal muscular atrophy: a randomised motor benefit in type 2/3 disease (SUNFISH) and single-arm milestone gains against natural history in type 1 infants (FIREFISH)
shelves.question: In infants with type 1 SMA (FIREFISH) and in children/young adults with type 2/3 SMA (SUNFISH), does daily oral risdiplam improve motor function versus placebo or natural-history controls?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Azo Compounds/adverse effects · Child · Child, Preschool · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Pyrimidines/adverse effects · Spinal Muscular Atrophies of Childhood/drug therapy,physiopathology · Young Adult · Administration, Oral · Azo Compounds/administration & dosage,adverse effects,pharmacokinetics · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Female · Infant · Male · Neuromuscular Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects,pharmacokinetics · Progression-Free Survival · Pyrimidines/administration & dosage,adverse effects,pharmacokinetics · RNA Splicing · Respiratory Insufficiency/etiology · Respiratory Tract Infections/etiology · Spinal Muscular Atrophies of Childhood/complications,drug therapy,mortality · Survival of Motor Neuron 1 Protein/blood,genetics · Infant, Newborn · Gene Dosage · Spinal Muscular Atrophies of Childhood/diagnosis,drug therapy,genetics,mortality · Survival of Motor Neuron 2 Protein/genetics · Neuromuscular Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects · RNA Splicing/drug effects · RNA Precursors/genetics,metabolism · Asymptomatic Diseases/therapy · Treatment Outcome · Genetic Testing · Respiration, Artificial/statistics & numerical data · Nutritional Support/statistics & numerical data · Azo Compounds · Pyrimidines
shelves.balance: Risdiplam rests on two very different kinds of evidence, and this shelf keeps them separate. In type 2 and non-ambulant type 3 SMA, SUNFISH part 2 is a proper randomised placebo-controlled trial (n=180, ages 2–25): motor function improved by 1.55 points more on risdiplam than placebo at 12 months (95% CI 0.30 to 2.81) — real, but modest. In type 1 infants, FIREFISH was single-arm and open-label by design (the design is labelled on the face): 29% of 41 infants sat without support at 12 months and 85% survived without permanent ventilation, against natural-history boundaries in which sitting does not occur. RAINBOWFISH extends the single-arm picture to presymptomatic infants (81% sitting at 12 months). Because the infant evidence has no concurrent control, the programme as a whole is capped at POSSIBLE (benefit), with the randomised SUNFISH result the firmest part.

cards.headline: FIREFISH part 1 — Baranello 2021 (n=21, single-arm): at the higher dose, 7 of 17 infants sat without support for at least 5 seconds; 4 infants died of respiratory complications
cards.summary: FIREFISH part 1 — Baranello 2021 (n=21, single-arm): at the higher dose, 7 of 17 infants sat without support for at least 5 seconds; 4 infants died of respiratory complications
cards.type: Open-label single-arm phase 2–3 study, part 1 (FIREFISH) — dose-finding, no concurrent control
cards.people: 21 infants aged 1–7 months with type 1 spinal muscular atrophy in an open-label, single-arm dose-finding study: 4 received a low dose (final dose 0.08 mg/kg/day) and 17 a higher dose (final dose 0.2 mg/kg/day) of once-daily oral risdiplam. There was no placebo or concurrent control group; the design is labelled single-arm on the face of this shelf.
cards.result: Blood SMN protein rose to a median of 3.0 times baseline in the low-dose cohort and 1.9 times baseline in the high-dose cohort at 12 months. Seven infants in the high-dose cohort and none in the low-dose cohort could sit without support for at least 5 seconds. Serious adverse events included pneumonia, respiratory tract infection and acute respiratory failure; 4 infants had died of respiratory complications by publication.
cards.watchOut: A 21-infant dose-finding study with no control arm: it selected the dose for part 2 and showed target engagement, but on its own it cannot separate drug effect from the natural history of type 1 SMA.
cards.source: Baranello G et al. Risdiplam in Type 1 Spinal Muscular Atrophy. The New England journal of medicine. 2021. PMID: 33626251. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT02913482.

cards.headline: FIREFISH part 2 — Darras 2021 (n=41, single-arm vs historical controls): 29% sat without support at 12 months, a milestone not attained in untreated natural history; survival without permanent ventilation 85% vs a 42% natural-history boundary
cards.summary: FIREFISH part 2 — Darras 2021 (n=41, single-arm vs historical controls): 29% sat without support at 12 months, a milestone not attained in untreated natural history; survival without permanent ventilation 85% vs a 42% natural-history boundary
cards.type: Open-label single-arm phase 2–3 study, part 2 (FIREFISH) — compared with historical (natural-history) controls, not randomised
cards.people: 41 infants aged 1–7 months with type 1 SMA and two SMN2 copies received once-daily oral risdiplam (0.2 mg/kg) in an open-label single-arm study. Efficacy was compared with prespecified upper confidence boundaries from natural-history data in 40 untreated infants — there was no randomised or concurrent control group.
cards.result: After 12 months, 12 infants (29%) could sit without support for at least 5 seconds. Key secondary endpoints each beat the natural-history boundaries (P<0.001 for all): CHOP-INTEND score of 40 or higher in 56% versus a 17% boundary; a rise of at least 4 CHOP-INTEND points in 90% versus 17%; a HINE-2 motor-milestone response in 78% versus 12%; and survival without permanent ventilation in 85% versus 42%. The most common serious adverse events were pneumonia, bronchiolitis, hypotonia and respiratory failure.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm evidence: the comparisons rest on historical controls, so the size of the benefit is less certain than a randomised trial would make it — but sitting and survival without ventilation are outcomes untreated type 1 SMA infants essentially never reach, which is why the signal is hard to explain away.
cards.source: Darras BT et al. Risdiplam-Treated Infants with Type 1 Spinal Muscular Atrophy versus Historical Controls. The New England journal of medicine. 2021. PMID: 34320287. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT02913482.

cards.headline: FIREFISH part 2 at 24 months — Darras 2022: prespecified milestone endpoints (sitting at least 30 seconds, standing alone, walking alone) were judged against a 5% performance criterion drawn from natural history
cards.summary: FIREFISH part 2 at 24 months — Darras 2022: prespecified milestone endpoints (sitting at least 30 seconds, standing alone, walking alone) were judged against a 5% performance criterion drawn from natural history
cards.type: Open-label single-arm study (FIREFISH part 2, 24-month report) — historical-control design continued
cards.people: The same 41 infants from FIREFISH part 2, followed to 24 months of once-daily risdiplam, with milestone endpoints compared against a 5% performance criterion defined from the natural history of type 1 SMA.
cards.result: The 24-month report presents the remainder of the prespecified secondary milestone endpoints — sitting without support for at least 30 seconds, standing alone and walking alone on the Bayley Scales gross motor subscale — against the 5% natural-history performance criterion, extending the 12-month primary result (29% sitting at least 5 seconds) to two years of treatment.
cards.watchOut: Still the same single-arm cohort: longer follow-up strengthens the durability picture but adds no control group, and milestone percentages at 24 months should be read against the 5% criterion the investigators prespecified, not against a randomised comparator.

cards.headline: SUNFISH part 2 — Mercuri 2022 (n=180, randomised): motor function improved 1.55 points more on risdiplam than placebo at 12 months (P=0.016); pneumonia serious events 8% vs 2%
cards.summary: SUNFISH part 2 — Mercuri 2022 (n=180, randomised): motor function improved 1.55 points more on risdiplam than placebo at 12 months (P=0.016); pneumonia serious events 8% vs 2%
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (SUNFISH part 2)
cards.people: 180 patients aged 2–25 years with type 2 or non-ambulant type 3 SMA, randomised 2:1 to once-daily oral risdiplam (n=120) or placebo (n=60) for 12 months; 174 patients contributed to the primary analysis.
cards.result: The least-squares mean change in the 32-item Motor Function Measure was +1.36 points on risdiplam versus −0.19 on placebo — a treatment difference of 1.55 points (95% CI 0.30 to 2.81; P=0.016). Adverse events at least 5% more frequent on risdiplam included pyrexia (21% vs 17%), diarrhoea (17% vs 8%) and rash (17% vs 2%); overall serious adverse events were similar (20% vs 18%) except pneumonia (8% vs 2%). Benefit was generally improvement in younger patients and stabilisation in older patients in exploratory subgroups.
cards.watchOut: The one randomised trial in this shelf, and its effect is modest — about a point and a half on a motor scale — in an older, non-ambulant population very different from the FIREFISH infants. The two populations should not be merged into one headline.
cards.source: Mercuri E et al. cards.headline: RAINBOWFISH — Finkel 2025 (n=26, single-arm, presymptomatic): 81% sat unsupported at 12 months; all 23 infants completing 24 months were alive without permanent ventilation or feeding support
cards.summary: RAINBOWFISH — Finkel 2025 (n=26, single-arm, presymptomatic): 81% sat unsupported at 12 months; all 23 infants completing 24 months were alive without permanent ventilation or feeding support
cards.type: Open-label single-arm study (RAINBOWFISH) — presymptomatic infants, natural-history comparison
cards.people: 26 infants aged 1 day to 42 days with genetically diagnosed SMA but no clinical signs, treated with once-daily oral risdiplam (0.2 mg/kg) in an open-label single-arm study; the primary outcome was assessed in infants with two SMN2 copies and a baseline ulnar CMAP amplitude of at least 1.5 mV.
cards.result: At 12 months, 21 infants (81%) could sit unsupported for 30 seconds, 14 (54%) could stand alone and 11 (42%) could walk alone. Of 23 infants completing 24 months, all were alive without permanent ventilation or feeding support. Nine treatment-related adverse events were reported in 7 infants, none serious.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm and tiny, in a presymptomatic population identified by genetic testing: the contrast with natural history is stark, but there is no randomised comparison and the primary-outcome subgroup was only 5 infants.
cards.source: Finkel RS et al. Risdiplam in Presymptomatic Spinal Muscular Atrophy. The New England journal of medicine. 2025. PMID: 40802943. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT03779334.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a randomised benefit in older children and young adults, and single-arm milestone gains in infants that natural history does not produce — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: a randomised benefit in older children and young adults, and single-arm milestone gains in infants that natural history does not produce — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.people: FIREFISH parts 1–2 (21 + 41 infants, single-arm), SUNFISH part 2 (180 randomised, ages 2–25) and RAINBOWFISH (26 presymptomatic infants, single-arm).
cards.result: In type 2/non-ambulant type 3 SMA, risdiplam beat placebo by 1.55 MFM-32 points at 12 months in the only randomised trial. In type 1 infants, 29% sat without support at 12 months and 85% survived without permanent ventilation against natural-history boundaries of effectively 0% sitting and a 42% survival boundary — large effects, but from single-arm studies judged against historical controls, and labelled as such on every card. Harms in infants were dominated by the respiratory complications of the disease itself; in SUNFISH, pneumonia serious events were 8% vs 2%.
cards.watchOut: This shelf does not cover nusinersen or onasemnogene abeparvovec, which have their own shelves; no head-to-head trial between the SMA therapies exists in these cards.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards above. No new data.

shelves.title: Onasemnogene abeparvovec in SMA type 1 (single-arm evidence only; START n=15 + STR1VE n=22, total N=37): survival and sitting far beyond natural history, with hepatotoxicity on the harm side
shelves.question: In infants with SMA type 1, does a single intravenous dose of onasemnogene abeparvovec (AAV9 gene therapy) improve survival without permanent ventilation and motor milestones versus natural history?
shelves.mesh: Biological Products/therapeutic use · Child, Preschool · Female · Genetic Therapy/methods · Humans · Infant · Male · Recombinant Fusion Proteins/therapeutic use · Spinal Muscular Atrophies of Childhood/drug therapy,genetics · Survival of Motor Neuron 2 Protein/genetics · Treatment Outcome · Cohort Studies · Dependovirus · Disease-Free Survival · Genetic Therapy/adverse effects · Genetic Vectors · Historically Controlled Study · Infant, Newborn · Infusions, Intravenous · Liver Diseases/etiology · Motor Skills · Nutritional Support · Respiration, Artificial · Spinal Muscular Atrophies of Childhood/genetics,physiopathology,therapy · Survival of Motor Neuron 1 Protein/genetics · Alanine Transaminase/blood · Aspartate Aminotransferases/blood · Bilirubin/blood · Biological Products/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Chemical and Drug Induced Liver Injury/etiology · Glucocorticoids/therapeutic use · Muscular Atrophy, Spinal/blood,drug therapy,therapy · Prednisolone/therapeutic use · Recombinant Fusion Proteins/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Registries · Gene Therapy Agents
shelves.balance: There is no randomised trial of onasemnogene abeparvovec in SMA type 1 — every efficacy claim rests on single-arm studies compared with natural history, and this shelf says so on its face. In START (n=15) all infants were alive and event-free at 20 months against 8% historical survival; in STR1VE (n=22) 59% sat independently versus 0 of 23 untreated infants; STR1VE-EU (n=32) found 44% sitting. The two trials named in the question total N = 37 treated infants, printed here and in the stamp line as the small-N rule requires. The harm side is dominated by hepatotoxicity — liver-enzyme elevations in most patients in a 325-patient pooled analysis, two cases of serious acute liver injury (both resolved), and prednisolone courses often lasting 2–4 months — plus a post-marketing warning for thrombotic microangiopathy. Dramatic single-arm effects in a disease whose natural history is uniform and lethal support POSSIBLE (benefit), and no higher stamp, on this evidence.

cards.headline: START — Mendell 2017 (n=15, single-arm): all 15 infants alive and event-free at 20 months vs 8% survival in a historical cohort; 11 of 12 high-dose infants sat unassisted
cards.summary: START — Mendell 2017 (n=15, single-arm): all 15 infants alive and event-free at 20 months vs 8% survival in a historical cohort; 11 of 12 high-dose infants sat unassisted
cards.type: Open-label single-arm phase 1 study (START) — historical-cohort comparison, no concurrent control
cards.people: 15 infants with SMA type 1 received a single intravenous dose of onasemnogene abeparvovec (AAV9 carrying SMN complementary DNA): 3 at a low dose and 12 at a high dose. Single-arm, open-label; outcomes were compared with historical natural-history cohorts.
cards.result: As of the data cut-off, all 15 patients were alive and free of permanent ventilation at 20 months, compared with 8% survival in a historical cohort. In the high-dose cohort, CHOP INTEND scores rose by 9.8 points at 1 month and 15.4 points at 3 months (the scale declines in natural history); 11 of 12 sat unassisted, 9 rolled over, 11 fed orally and could speak, and 2 walked independently. Elevated serum aminotransferase levels occurred in 4 patients and were attenuated by prednisolone.
cards.watchOut: Fifteen infants and no concurrent control: the survival contrast with natural history is dramatic, but the numbers are small and the comparison historical — the reason total N is printed on the face of this shelf.
cards.source: Mendell JR et al. Single-Dose Gene-Replacement Therapy for Spinal Muscular Atrophy. The New England journal of medicine. 2017. PMID: 29091557. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT02122952 ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT02122952.

cards.headline: STR1VE — Day 2021 (n=22, single-arm): 59% sat independently for at least 30 seconds at 18 months vs 0 of 23 untreated infants; 91% survived free of permanent ventilation at 14 months
cards.summary: STR1VE — Day 2021 (n=22, single-arm): 59% sat independently for at least 30 seconds at 18 months vs 0 of 23 untreated infants; 91% survived free of permanent ventilation at 14 months
cards.type: Open-label single-arm phase 3 trial (STR1VE) — natural-history (PNCR) comparator
cards.people: 22 infants younger than 6 months with SMA type 1 and one or two SMN2 copies received a single intravenous infusion of onasemnogene abeparvovec (1.1 × 10^14 vector genomes/kg) at 12 US sites. Open-label, single-arm; efficacy was compared with 23 untreated infants in the Pediatric Neuromuscular Clinical Research (PNCR) natural-history dataset.
cards.result: Thirteen of 22 patients (59%, 97.5% CI 36 to 100) achieved independent sitting for at least 30 seconds at the 18-month visit, versus 0 of 23 untreated PNCR infants (P<0.0001). Twenty patients (91%) survived free of permanent ventilation at 14 months.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm phase 3 with a natural-history comparator, not a randomised control — the sitting outcome (59% vs 0%) is far outside anything natural history produces, but the confidence interval is wide because only 22 infants were treated.
cards.source: Day JW et al. Onasemnogene abeparvovec gene therapy for symptomatic infantile-onset spinal muscular atrophy in patients with two copies of SMN2 (STR1VE): an open-label, single-arm, multicentre, phase 3 trial. cards.headline: STR1VE-EU — Mercuri 2021 (n=32 analysed, single-arm): 44% sat independently for at least 10 seconds by 18 months vs 0 of 23 untreated; 97% survived free of permanent ventilation
cards.summary: STR1VE-EU — Mercuri 2021 (n=32 analysed, single-arm): 44% sat independently for at least 10 seconds by 18 months vs 0 of 23 untreated; 97% survived free of permanent ventilation
cards.type: Open-label single-arm phase 3 trial (STR1VE-EU) — broader eligibility, natural-history comparator
cards.people: 33 infants younger than 6 months with SMA type 1 (one or two SMN2 copies) received a single intravenous infusion of onasemnogene abeparvovec at nine sites in Italy, the UK, Belgium and France; 32 were in the intention-to-treat population. Open-label, single-arm, with the same PNCR natural-history comparator as STR1VE.
cards.result: Fourteen of 32 patients (44%, 97.5% CI 26 to 100) achieved the primary endpoint of independent sitting for at least 10 seconds at any visit up to 18 months, versus 0 of 23 untreated patients (P<0.0001). Thirty-one of 32 (97%) survived free of permanent ventilation.
cards.watchOut: A second single-arm cohort with broader eligibility and a slightly lower sitting rate than the US trial — consistent direction, same absence of a concurrent control.
cards.source: Mercuri E et al. Onasemnogene abeparvovec gene therapy for symptomatic infantile-onset spinal muscular atrophy type 1 (STR1VE-EU): an open-label, single-arm, multicentre, phase 3 trial. The Lancet. Neurology. 2021. PMID: 34536405. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT03461289.

cards.headline: Hepatotoxicity analysis — Chand 2021 (325 treated patients): liver-enzyme elevations were common; 2 patients in managed access had serious acute liver injury, which resolved; prolonged prednisolone was often needed
cards.summary: Hepatotoxicity analysis — Chand 2021 (325 treated patients): liver-enzyme elevations were common; 2 patients in managed access had serious acute liver injury, which resolved; prolonged prednisolone was often needed
cards.type: Pooled safety analysis of trials, managed-access and registry patients (hepatotoxicity)
cards.people: 325 patients with SMA who had received onasemnogene abeparvovec in five clinical trials, a managed-access programme and the RESTORE registry, analysed for liver-related adverse events, laboratory data and prednisolone use.
cards.result: Among patients with data, elevated alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase and/or bilirubin concentrations were reported in 90 of 100 patients in the analysed clinical-trial/managed-access sets; liver-associated adverse events were reported in 34% of trial patients and 23% of managed-access/registry patients. Two managed-access patients had serious acute liver injury, which resolved completely. Prednisolone courses ranged from 33 to 229 days, most often 60–120 days. More than 60% already had liver-enzyme elevations before dosing.
cards.watchOut: Hepatotoxicity is the dominant harm of this therapy and belongs on the face, not in fine print. Thrombotic microangiopathy has also been reported after this gene therapy in post-marketing experience and is a labelled warning — families and teams should know both risks before a single, irreversible dose.
cards.source: Chand D et al. Hepatotoxicity following administration of onasemnogene abeparvovec (AVXS-101) for the treatment of spinal muscular atrophy. Journal of hepatology. 2021. PMID: 33186633.

cards.headline: Synthesis: single-arm survival and sitting gains far beyond natural history in a total of 37 infants in START and STR1VE — POSSIBLE (benefit), N printed on the face
cards.summary: Synthesis: single-arm survival and sitting gains far beyond natural history in a total of 37 infants in START and STR1VE — POSSIBLE (benefit), N printed on the face
cards.people: START (n=15) and STR1VE (n=22) — total N = 37 treated infants in the two named trials — plus STR1VE-EU (n=32) and a 325-patient pooled hepatotoxicity analysis.
cards.result: Every efficacy number on this shelf comes from single-arm studies compared with natural history: all 15 START infants alive and event-free at 20 months versus 8% historical survival; 59% (STR1VE) and 44% (STR1VE-EU) sitting independently versus 0% untreated. No randomised trial exists. The harm side is real: liver-enzyme elevations in most treated patients, occasional serious acute liver injury, long prednisolone courses, and a post-marketing thrombotic microangiopathy warning. Single-arm evidence caps this shelf at POSSIBLE (benefit), with the small total N printed on the face.
cards.watchOut: This shelf does not cover nusinersen or risdiplam (their own shelves), nor intrathecal onasemnogene formulations studied in older patients.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards above. No new data.

shelves.balance: The two antisense drugs on this shelf carry different strengths of evidence, and the shelf keeps them distinct. Inotersen was tested in a randomised, placebo-controlled trial (NEURO-TTR, n=172): neuropathy progression was 19.7 points less and quality of life 11.7 points better than placebo over 15 months — but glomerulonephritis and thrombocytopenia each occurred in about 3%, one thrombocytopenia death occurred, and five deaths versus none were recorded on inotersen. Eplontersen (NEURO-TTRansform) was never randomised against a concurrent placebo: its comparator is an external placebo group borrowed from NEURO-TTR, against which neuropathy was essentially halted (+0.3 vs +25.1 points). That design is stated honestly on the face: the effect size looks the same as inotersen’s, but a borrowed comparator cannot carry the same certainty, so the class shelf is POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: NEURO-TTR — Benson 2018 (n=172, randomised): neuropathy score improved 19.7 points and quality of life 11.7 points more on inotersen than placebo — with glomerulonephritis in 3% and thrombocytopenia in 3%
cards.summary: NEURO-TTR — Benson 2018 (n=172, randomised): neuropathy score improved 19.7 points and quality of life 11.7 points more on inotersen than placebo — with glomerulonephritis in 3% and thrombocytopenia in 3%
cards.people: 172 adults with stage 1 or 2 hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis with polyneuropathy, randomised 2:1 to weekly subcutaneous inotersen 300 mg (n=112) or placebo (n=60) for 15 months; 139 (81%) completed the intervention period.
cards.result: Both primary endpoints favoured inotersen: the between-group difference in change was −19.7 points on the modified Neuropathy Impairment Score+7 (95% CI −26.4 to −13.0; P<0.001) and −11.7 points on the Norfolk Quality of Life–Diabetic Neuropathy questionnaire (95% CI −18.3 to −5.1; P<0.001), where a decrease means improvement and 2 points is the minimal clinically meaningful change on mNIS+7. Benefit was independent of disease stage, mutation type or cardiomyopathy. There were five deaths in the inotersen group and none on placebo. The most frequent serious adverse events on inotersen were glomerulonephritis (3 patients, 3%) and thrombocytopenia (3 patients, 3%), with one death associated with grade 4 thrombocytopenia; enhanced monitoring was introduced thereafter.
cards.watchOut: The benefit is randomised and large, but so is the monitoring burden: the glomerulonephritis and thrombocytopenia signals are printed on the face of this shelf because they changed how the drug must be given (regular platelet and renal monitoring).
cards.source: Benson MD et al. Inotersen Treatment for Patients with Hereditary Transthyretin Amyloidosis. The New England journal of medicine. 2018. PMID: 29972757. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT01737398.

cards.headline: NEURO-TTRansform — Coelho 2023 (n=144 on eplontersen; external placebo n=60 borrowed from NEURO-TTR): neuropathy essentially halted (mNIS+7 +0.3 vs +25.1 on external placebo) — but the comparator was not randomised
cards.summary: NEURO-TTRansform — Coelho 2023 (n=144 on eplontersen; external placebo n=60 borrowed from NEURO-TTR): neuropathy essentially halted (mNIS+7 +0.3 vs +25.1 on external placebo) — but the comparator was not randomised
cards.type: Open-label single-group phase 3 trial with an external (historical) placebo group (NEURO-TTRansform) — design stated honestly
cards.people: 168 adults with hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis with polyneuropathy at 40 sites in 15 countries: 144 received monthly subcutaneous eplontersen 45 mg and 24 received weekly inotersen as a reference group, in an open-label single-group trial. The placebo comparator was external — the placebo arm of the earlier NEURO-TTR trial — with propensity-score weighting. This borrowed-comparator design is stated on the face, as the question requires.
cards.result: At week 65/66, adjusted mean serum transthyretin fell by 81.7% on eplontersen versus 11.2% in the external placebo group (difference −70.4 percentage points). Neuropathy impairment changed by +0.3 points on eplontersen versus +25.1 on external placebo (difference −24.8; 95% CI −31.0 to −18.6; P<0.001), and quality of life by −5.5 versus +14.2 (difference −19.7; P<0.001). Discontinuation for adverse events occurred in 4% on eplontersen versus 3% in the external placebo group; two deaths on eplontersen were consistent with disease-related sequelae.
cards.watchOut: External-placebo comparisons can flatter a drug: the NEURO-TTR placebo patients were treated years earlier, at different sites, and propensity weighting cannot remove unmeasured differences. The direction is consistent with the randomised inotersen trial of the same drug class, but eplontersen itself has never beaten a concurrent placebo in a randomised trial.
cards.source: Coelho T et al. Eplontersen for Hereditary Transthyretin Amyloidosis With Polyneuropathy. JAMA. 2023. PMID: 37768671. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT04136184.

cards.headline: Switch analysis — Conceição 2024 (24 patients switched from inotersen to eplontersen): platelet counts recovered after the switch and neuropathy stayed stable
cards.summary: Switch analysis — Conceição 2024 (24 patients switched from inotersen to eplontersen): platelet counts recovered after the switch and neuropathy stayed stable
cards.type: Within-trial switch analysis (NEURO-TTRansform inotersen reference group)
cards.people: The 24 patients in NEURO-TTRansform randomised to weekly inotersen for 34 weeks and then switched to monthly eplontersen from week 37; 20 completed the switch and were analysed through week 85.
cards.result: Serum transthyretin reduction deepened after switching (−74.3% at week 35 on inotersen to −80.6% at week 85 on eplontersen). Neuropathy impairment and quality of life remained stable (did not progress) on eplontersen, and nutritional status did not deteriorate. Mean platelet counts, which had fallen on inotersen (mean nadir reduction −40.7%), returned to baseline on eplontersen (mean nadir reduction −3.2%). Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 95% after switching versus 100% during inotersen treatment.
cards.watchOut: A 24-patient within-trial switch, not a randomised comparison: it supports eplontersen’s tolerability advantage over its weekly predecessor, especially for platelets, but cannot prove equal efficacy.
cards.source: Conceição I et al. Switching from inotersen to eplontersen in patients with hereditary transthyretin-mediated amyloidosis with polyneuropathy: analysis from NEURO-TTRansform. Journal of neurology. 2024. PMID: 39138650.

cards.headline: Synthesis: inotersen has a positive randomised trial; eplontersen matches its effect size only against a borrowed placebo — POSSIBLE (benefit) for the antisense class shelf
cards.summary: Synthesis: inotersen has a positive randomised trial; eplontersen matches its effect size only against a borrowed placebo — POSSIBLE (benefit) for the antisense class shelf
cards.people: NEURO-TTR (172 randomised, inotersen vs concurrent placebo), NEURO-TTRansform (144 on eplontersen vs 60 external placebo patients borrowed from NEURO-TTR), and a 24-patient switch analysis.
cards.result: Weekly inotersen slowed neuropathy progression by 19.7 mNIS+7 points and improved quality of life versus placebo in a randomised trial, at the price of glomerulonephritis and thrombocytopenia in about 3% each and a monitoring burden. Monthly eplontersen produced a near-identical pattern of benefit (mNIS+7 difference −24.8) but only against an external placebo, and the switch analysis suggests it spares platelets. One randomised trial plus one external-control trial caps the class shelf at POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: This shelf covers the antisense drugs only; the siRNA silencers (patisiran, vutrisiran) and the cardiomyopathy stabilisers have their own shelves.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards above. No new data.

shelves.title: Tominersen in Huntington’s disease: mutant huntingtin lowered by up to 42% in phase 1/2, but the phase 3 trial (GENERATION HD1) was halted early and has no full journal report — no clinical benefit demonstrated
shelves.question: In adults with early manifest Huntington’s disease, does intrathecal tominersen lower mutant huntingtin and slow clinical progression versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Female · Humans · Huntingtin Protein/antagonists & inhibitors,cerebrospinal fluid,genetics · Huntington Disease/drug therapy · Injections, Spinal · Male · Middle Aged · Mutation · Nucleotides/chemical synthesis,pharmacology · Oligonucleotides/cerebrospinal fluid,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: This shelf rests on a thin published base and says so plainly. The only full journal report of a tominersen trial is the phase 1/2 study (Tabrizi 2019, n=46): intrathecal tominersen lowered CSF mutant huntingtin dose-dependently, by up to 42%, with only grade 1–2 adverse events — but the trial made no efficacy claim, and a secondary EEG analysis of the same 46 patients adds a biomarker signal, not independent evidence. The phase 3 trial, GENERATION HD1, was halted early in 2021 on an unfavourable benefit–risk balance at higher exposure and has NO full journal report as of this build; its record here is labelled by source type (registry/sponsor record and journal correspondence). A lower-dose successor, GENERATION HD2, was checked at build and has no publication yet. Target engagement without demonstrated clinical benefit, plus a halted phase 3, supports UNLIKELY (benefit) for slowing progression.

cards.headline: Phase 1/2 — Tabrizi 2019 (n=46, randomised): intrathecal tominersen lowered CSF mutant huntingtin dose-dependently (up to −42% at 90 mg); the trial made no efficacy claim
cards.summary: Phase 1/2 — Tabrizi 2019 (n=46, randomised): intrathecal tominersen lowered CSF mutant huntingtin dose-dependently (up to −42% at 90 mg); the trial made no efficacy claim
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, multiple-ascending-dose phase 1–2a trial (published journal report)
cards.people: 46 adults with early Huntington’s disease randomised 3:1 to intrathecal tominersen (HTTRx; 10–120 mg) or placebo, given as a bolus every 4 weeks for four doses. Primary endpoint was safety; mutant huntingtin concentration in cerebrospinal fluid was a prespecified exploratory endpoint.
cards.result: All 46 patients received all four doses and completed the trial. Adverse events were all grade 1 or 2, reported in 98% of patients, with no serious adverse events in tominersen-treated patients and no clinically relevant laboratory changes. CSF mutant huntingtin fell dose-dependently: mean change −20%, −25%, −28%, −42% and −38% at 10, 30, 60, 90 and 120 mg, versus +10% on placebo. The trial showed target engagement only — it was not designed or powered to test clinical progression.
cards.watchOut: Target engagement is not clinical benefit: a 42% fall in the toxic protein says nothing yet about whether patients decline more slowly, which is exactly what the phase 3 trial then failed to show.
cards.source: Tabrizi SJ et al. Targeting Huntingtin Expression in Patients with Huntington's Disease. The New England journal of medicine. 2019. PMID: 31059641. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT02519036.

cards.headline: EEG substudy — Hawellek 2022 (same 46 trial patients + 39 healthy volunteers): tominersen increased resting EEG theta/alpha power versus placebo over 4 months — a biomarker signal of unknown meaning
cards.summary: EEG substudy — Hawellek 2022 (same 46 trial patients + 39 healthy volunteers): tominersen increased resting EEG theta/alpha power versus placebo over 4 months — a biomarker signal of unknown meaning
cards.type: Secondary biomarker analysis of the same phase 1/2 trial (published journal report; same patients as the card above)
cards.people: Electroencephalography recordings from the 46 early-manifest Huntington’s patients in the phase 1/2 tominersen trial (mean age 47 years) and 39 untreated healthy volunteers, analysed as a secondary study of the same trial population — not an independent cohort.
cards.result: Patients on tominersen showed increased resting-state EEG activity in the 4–8 Hz range compared with placebo (cluster-based permutation test, P<0.05), in a frequency range that is reduced in Huntington’s disease versus healthy controls. The authors state the underlying mechanisms are unknown and may reflect neural plasticity.
cards.watchOut: A secondary analysis of the same 46 patients, on a surrogate measure with no established link to clinical progression: it adds a published report to the record but no independent evidence of benefit.
cards.source: Hawellek DJ et al. Changes in brain activity with tominersen in early-manifest Huntington's disease. Brain communications. 2022. PMID: 35774187.

cards.headline: GENERATION HD1 (NCT03761849) — halted early in 2021 on an unfavourable benefit–risk balance at higher exposure; no full journal report of the trial has been published
cards.summary: GENERATION HD1 (NCT03761849) — halted early in 2021 on an unfavourable benefit–risk balance at higher exposure; no full journal report of the trial has been published
cards.type: Halted phase 3 trial — registry and sponsor record with journal correspondence (NOT a full journal report; labelled by source type)
cards.people: Adults with manifest Huntington’s disease in the phase 3 GENERATION HD1 trial of intrathecal tominersen (120 mg every 8 or 16 weeks versus placebo). Dosing was halted in March 2021 on the recommendation of the independent data monitoring committee. Source type, stated plainly: the halt and its rationale are documented in the trial registry record and sponsor communications, with subsequent discussion in journal correspondence (McColgan et al., N Engl J Med 2023) and post-hoc analyses — there is no full journal report of GENERATION HD1’s results. A lower-dose successor trial, GENERATION HD2 (NCT05686551), was checked at build: no publication of its results was found.
cards.result: The published phase 1/2 record shows dose-dependent lowering of CSF mutant huntingtin with no clinical efficacy claim; the phase 3 programme was stopped early because the benefit–risk balance at the higher exposure was unfavourable, and no clinical benefit on progression has been demonstrated in any published report.
cards.watchOut: Do not let the biomarker success of phase 1/2 stand in for efficacy: the only large trial was halted, its full results remain unpublished, and any future claim for tominersen rests on the lower-dose GENERATION HD2 trial, which had reported nothing in a journal at the time this shelf was built.
cards.source: McColgan P et al. Tominersen in Adults with Manifest Huntington's Disease. The New England journal of medicine. 2023. PMID: 38055260. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT05686551. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03761849 (GENERATION HD1, halted). The PMID above is journal correspondence discussing the programme, not a full trial report.

cards.headline: Synthesis: target engagement without demonstrated clinical benefit, and a halted phase 3 — UNLIKELY (benefit) on the published record
cards.summary: Synthesis: target engagement without demonstrated clinical benefit, and a halted phase 3 — UNLIKELY (benefit) on the published record
cards.people: One published phase 1/2 randomised trial (n=46), one secondary EEG analysis of the same patients, and the halted GENERATION HD1 phase 3 trial, which exists as a registry/sponsor record and journal correspondence rather than a full journal report. The cardable published base is thin and is stated as such on the face.
cards.result: Tominersen lowered CSF mutant huntingtin by up to 42% in phase 1/2 (the treatment engaged its target), but no report — published or announced — shows it slowing clinical progression (in that sense, on clinical outcomes, the treatment made no difference), and the phase 3 trial was halted early on an unfavourable benefit–risk balance at higher exposure. The lower-dose GENERATION HD2 trial had no publication at build.
cards.watchOut: If GENERATION HD2 publishes, this shelf must be rebuilt around it; until then the honest verdict on tominersen for slowing Huntington’s progression is UNLIKELY (benefit).
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards above. No new data.

shelves.title: Exenatide for idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH:Pressure, phase 2, N=15): intracranial pressure fell about 6 cmCSF within hours and at 12 weeks in one very small randomised trial
shelves.question: In women with active idiopathic intracranial hypertension, does subcutaneous exenatide lower telemetrically measured intracranial pressure versus placebo, acutely and at 12 weeks?

shelves.balance: PARTIAL shelf — the GLP-1 slice only. The IIH family already homes acetazolamide at pack #2383 and bariatric surgery at pack #2384; both were read before building, neither cards a GLP-1 drug, and their references are not re-carded here. The randomised evidence for exenatide is a single phase 2 trial, IIH:Pressure: 15 women completed, with telemetric pressure monitors. Exenatide lowered pressure by 5.7 cmCSF at 2.5 hours, 6.4 at 24 hours and 5.6 at 12 weeks versus placebo — the 2.5-hour effect, long before weight change, is the mechanistically interesting result. A cognition substudy in the same 15 women found no cognitive harm. A large propensity-matched record cohort associates the GLP-1 class (not exenatide specifically) with fewer headaches and less medication use, but it is observational. With a randomised N of 15, the N is printed on the face and in the stamp line and the verdict is capped at POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: IIH:Pressure — Mitchell 2023 (n=15 randomised and completed; phase 2): exenatide lowered intracranial pressure by 5.7 cmCSF at 2.5 hours, 6.4 at 24 hours and 5.6 at 12 weeks versus placebo
cards.summary: IIH:Pressure — Mitchell 2023 (n=15 randomised and completed; phase 2): exenatide lowered intracranial pressure by 5.7 cmCSF at 2.5 hours, 6.4 at 24 hours and 5.6 at 12 weeks versus placebo
cards.people: 16 women with active idiopathic intracranial hypertension (intracranial pressure above 25 cmCSF with papilloedema; mean age 28 years, mean BMI 38.1) were recruited and 15 completed this randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of subcutaneous exenatide versus placebo, with telemetric intracranial pressure catheters allowing continuous pressure measurement. The very small N is printed here and in the stamp line, as the small-N rule requires.
cards.result: Exenatide lowered intracranial pressure significantly versus placebo at all three prespecified primary timepoints (trial alpha set a priori at less than 0.1): by 5.7 cmCSF at 2.5 hours (SD 2.9; P=0.048), 6.4 cmCSF at 24 hours (P=0.030) and 5.6 cmCSF at 12 weeks (P=0.058). The 2.5-hour effect occurred long before any weight change could explain it. No serious safety signals were noted.
cards.watchOut: Fifteen patients, one centre’s programme, and a 12-week P value of 0.058 that counts as positive only against the trial’s own prespecified alpha of 0.1: this is a promising phase 2 signal that justifies a phase 3 trial — the authors’ own conclusion — not a settled treatment.
cards.source: Mitchell JL et al. The effect of GLP-1RA exenatide on idiopathic intracranial hypertension: a randomized clinical trial. Brain : a journal of neurology. 2023. PMID: 36907221.

cards.headline: Cognition substudy — Grech 2024 (same n=15 from IIH:Pressure): exenatide did not worsen cognition over 12 weeks; fluid intelligence, processing speed and episodic memory scores improved in the exenatide group
cards.summary: Cognition substudy — Grech 2024 (same n=15 from IIH:Pressure): exenatide did not worsen cognition over 12 weeks; fluid intelligence, processing speed and episodic memory scores improved in the exenatide group
cards.type: Exploratory cognition substudy of the same IIH:Pressure trial (same 15 women — not an independent cohort)
cards.people: The same 15 women from the IIH:Pressure trial (7 exenatide, 8 placebo) tested with the NIH Toolbox Cognitive Battery at baseline and 12 weeks. This is a substudy of the trial above, in the same patients — it is carded for its safety question (does an ICP-lowering drug harm cognition?) and must not be counted as independent efficacy evidence.
cards.result: Baseline cognition was impaired in fluid intelligence, attention and executive function. After 12 weeks there was no evidence exenatide compromised cognition, and scores in the exenatide group improved in fluid intelligence (38.4 to 52.9; P=0.0005), processing speed (43.7 to 58.4; P=0.0058) and episodic memory (49.4 to 62.1; P=0.0315).
cards.watchOut: Seven treated patients and multiple unadjusted comparisons: the cognitive improvements are hypothesis-generating at best. The card’s real value is the absence of a cognitive harm signal in a disease where the standard drug (acetazolamide, pack #2383) commonly causes cognitive side effects.
cards.source: Grech O et al. Effect of glucagon like peptide-1 receptor agonist exenatide, used as an intracranial pressure lowering agent, on cognition in Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension. Eye (London, England). 2024. PMID: 38212401.

cards.headline: TriNetX cohort — Sioutas 2025 (555 matched pairs): GLP-1 receptor agonist use after IIH diagnosis was associated with less medication use (relative risk 0.53) and fewer headaches (relative risk 0.45) over 1 year — observational, class-level
cards.summary: TriNetX cohort — Sioutas 2025 (555 matched pairs): GLP-1 receptor agonist use after IIH diagnosis was associated with less medication use (relative risk 0.53) and fewer headaches (relative risk 0.45) over 1 year — observational, class-level
cards.type: Retrospective propensity-matched cohort study (electronic health records; GLP-1 class, not exenatide-specific)
cards.people: 44,373 patients with idiopathic intracranial hypertension in the TriNetX US network (2005–2024); after propensity matching, 555 patients who started a GLP-1 receptor agonist within 6 months of diagnosis were compared with 555 managed conventionally (acetazolamide, topiramate, dietary counselling) without GLP-1 exposure. The exposure is the drug class — mostly agents other than exenatide — and the design is observational.
cards.result: GLP-1 receptor agonist use was associated with lower subsequent medication use (risk ratio 0.53, 95% CI 0.46 to 0.61 — a relative measure) and reduced headaches (risk ratio 0.45, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.58 — a relative measure), with further associations in the same direction for visual symptoms. No randomised comparison exists at this scale.
cards.watchOut: Propensity matching cannot remove confounding by indication, weight change or care intensity, and the class-level exposure cannot be credited to exenatide specifically. This card supports biological plausibility at scale; the causal claim still rests on the 15-patient trial above.
cards.source: Sioutas GS et al. GLP-1 Receptor Agonists in Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension. JAMA neurology. 2025. PMID: 40658395.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one 15-patient phase 2 trial with a fast, weight-independent pressure effect — POSSIBLE (benefit), N = 15 printed on the face
cards.summary: Synthesis: one 15-patient phase 2 trial with a fast, weight-independent pressure effect — POSSIBLE (benefit), N = 15 printed on the face
cards.people: IIH:Pressure (15 women randomised and completed), its cognition substudy in the same 15 patients, and one propensity-matched observational cohort of 555 pairs studying the GLP-1 class rather than exenatide itself. This shelf is the GLP-1 slice of the IIH family only: acetazolamide is homed at pack #2383 and bariatric surgery at pack #2384, which are cross-pointed here and not re-carded.
cards.result: Exenatide lowered telemetric intracranial pressure by about 6 cmCSF within hours and sustained the difference at 12 weeks — an acute effect at 2.5 hours that precedes any weight loss and points to a direct pressure mechanism. The entire randomised evidence base is 15 patients, so the stamp carries the N and the verdict is capped at POSSIBLE (benefit) pending a phase 3 trial.
cards.watchOut: Nothing on this shelf should be read as evidence about GLP-1 drugs for weight-driven IIH management in general, nor as a comparison against acetazolamide (#2383) or surgery (#2384) — no head-to-head data exist.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards above. No new data.

shelves.title: Ulotaront in acute schizophrenia: a positive 4-week phase 2 trial (−7.5 PANSS points) followed by two phase 3 trials (DIAMOND 1 & 2) that missed their primary endpoints — announced only, with no journal report
shelves.question: In adults with an acute exacerbation of schizophrenia, does ulotaront (SEP-363856), a TAAR1/5-HT1A agonist with no D2 blockade, reduce PANSS total score versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Administration, Oral · Adult · Antipsychotic Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Least-Squares Analysis · Male · Receptors, Dopamine D2 · Receptors, G-Protein-Coupled/agonists · Schizophrenia/classification,drug therapy · Schizophrenic Psychology · Serotonin 5-HT1 Receptor Agonists/therapeutic use · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome · Trace Amine-Associated Receptors
shelves.balance: HONESTY FLAG, carried on the face: ulotaront’s published record and its phase 3 record are different kinds of evidence. The published phase 2 trial (Koblan 2020, n=245) was positive — PANSS fell 7.5 points more than placebo at 4 weeks, without the extrapyramidal or metabolic signature of D2 blockade — and a 26-week open-label extension (n=157) found no extrapyramidal signal and minimal weight change, though it had no control group. But the two phase 3 trials, DIAMOND 1 and DIAMOND 2, both missed their primary endpoints, and at a publication-status re-check during this build they exist only as a July 2023 sponsor topline announcement and registry records — no full journal report was found. They are carded here labelled by source type, never as a journal report. One positive small trial followed by two larger announced failures is MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit).

cards.headline: Phase 2 — Koblan 2020 (n=245, randomised, 4 weeks): ulotaront reduced PANSS total score by 17.2 points vs 9.7 on placebo (difference −7.5; P=0.001), without a D2-blockade side-effect pattern
cards.summary: Phase 2 — Koblan 2020 (n=245, randomised, 4 weeks): ulotaront reduced PANSS total score by 17.2 points vs 9.7 on placebo (difference −7.5; P=0.001), without a D2-blockade side-effect pattern
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial (published journal report)
cards.people: 245 adults with an acute exacerbation of schizophrenia randomised 1:1 to once-daily ulotaront (SEP-363856, 50 or 75 mg; n=120) or placebo (n=125) for 4 weeks. Baseline PANSS total scores were about 101 and 100. Ulotaront is a TAAR1 and 5-HT1A agonist with no dopamine D2 receptor blockade.
cards.result: PANSS total score fell by 17.2 points on ulotaront versus 9.7 on placebo (least-squares mean difference −7.5 points; 95% CI −11.9 to −3.0; P=0.001). CGI-Severity and Brief Negative Symptom Scale changes were in the same direction but not adjusted for multiple comparisons. Adverse events included somnolence and gastrointestinal symptoms; one sudden cardiac death occurred in the ulotaront group. Extrapyramidal symptoms and changes in lipids, glycated haemoglobin and prolactin were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: A single 4-week trial in acutely ill patients: the effect size is respectable for the field, but 4 weeks cannot speak to maintenance, and the one sudden cardiac death, though a single event, is part of the record.
cards.source: Koblan KS et al. A Non-D2-Receptor-Binding Drug for the Treatment of Schizophrenia. The New England journal of medicine. 2020. PMID: 32294346. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT02969382.
