cards.headline: Open-label extension — Correll 2021 (n=157, 26 weeks, no control group): PANSS fell a further 22.6 points from extension baseline, with no extrapyramidal signal and minimal weight or metabolic change
cards.summary: Open-label extension — Correll 2021 (n=157, 26 weeks, no control group): PANSS fell a further 22.6 points from extension baseline, with no extrapyramidal signal and minimal weight or metabolic change
cards.type: Open-label extension study (published journal report; uncontrolled — labelled as such)
cards.people: 157 of the 193 patients who completed the 4-week phase 2 trial continued into a 26-week open-label extension on ulotaront 25/50/75 mg daily; 66.9% completed. There was no placebo or comparator group, so effectiveness numbers in this card are uncontrolled observations, labelled as such.
cards.result: Mean PANSS total score fell a further 22.6 points from extension baseline (95% CI −25.6 to −19.6) and CGI-Severity by 1.0 point. Body weight changed by −0.3 kg on average from double-blind baseline; median changes in cholesterol (−2.0 mg/dL), triglycerides (−5.0 mg/dL) and prolactin were small, and movement-disorder scales showed no extrapyramidal effects.
cards.watchOut: Open-label extensions enrol the patients who already tolerated and stayed on the drug, and PANSS falls without a control group mix drug effect, expectation and natural course. This card’s value is safety and tolerability over 6 months, not proof of efficacy.
cards.source: Correll CU et al. Safety and effectiveness of ulotaront (SEP-363856) in schizophrenia: results of a 6-month, open-label extension study. NPJ schizophrenia. 2021. PMID: 34887427.

cards.headline: DIAMOND 1 and DIAMOND 2 phase 3 trials — sponsor announcement, July 2023: both trials missed their primary endpoint; no full journal report of either trial was found at build
cards.summary: DIAMOND 1 and DIAMOND 2 phase 3 trials — sponsor announcement, July 2023: both trials missed their primary endpoint; no full journal report of either trial was found at build
cards.type: Phase 3 programme outcome — sponsor topline announcement and trial registry records (NOT a journal report; labelled by source type)
cards.people: Adults with an acute exacerbation of schizophrenia in the two phase 3 DIAMOND trials of ulotaront (registry records NCT04072354 and NCT04092686, both listed as completed). Source type, stated plainly: the phase 3 outcome is documented in the sponsor’s July 2023 topline announcement and in the trial registry records. A publication-status re-check at build found no full journal report of DIAMOND 1 or DIAMOND 2 — this card is an announcement/registry record, never a journal report, and no effect sizes are quoted because none have been published in a peer-reviewed report.
cards.result: Per the sponsor announcement, neither DIAMOND 1 nor DIAMOND 2 met its primary endpoint (change in PANSS total score versus placebo). This directly contradicts the positive phase 2 result above and is the reason this shelf cannot carry a stronger stamp: the largest, most rigorous tests of ulotaront in acute schizophrenia failed on their primary outcome, on the only record that exists for them.
cards.watchOut: Announcement-only evidence cuts both ways: without a journal report, the size of the phase 3 miss, the placebo response and any subgroup findings cannot be inspected. If a full report is published, this shelf must be rebuilt around it.

shelves.title: Pramipexole augmentation in treatment-resistant unipolar depression (PAX-D, n=151): symptoms fell 3.91 points more than placebo at 12 weeks — with discontinuation for adverse events in 20% vs 5%
shelves.question: In adults with treatment-resistant unipolar major depression, does pramipexole titrated to 2.5 mg/day added to ongoing antidepressant treatment reduce depressive symptoms versus placebo at 12 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Pramipexole/therapeutic use,administration & dosage,adverse effects · Female · Male · Double-Blind Method · Depressive Disorder, Treatment-Resistant/drug therapy · Middle Aged · Adult · Antidepressive Agents/therapeutic use,administration & dosage,adverse effects · Treatment Outcome · Drug Therapy, Combination · United Kingdom · Major Depressive Disorder/drug therapy · Dopamine Agonists/therapeutic use,administration & dosage · Aged · Adolescent · Bipolar Disorder/drug therapy,epidemiology,psychology · Case-Control Studies · Major Depressive Disorder/drug therapy,epidemiology,psychology · Dopamine Agonists/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Observational Studies as Topic · Placebos/administration & dosage · Pramipexole/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Remission Induction · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Young Adult
shelves.balance: PAX-D is a clean, positive trial in exactly the population this shelf asks about: 151 adults with treatment-resistant unipolar depression, pramipexole titrated toward 2.5 mg/day added to their antidepressant, with QIDS-SR16 scores falling 3.91 points more than placebo at 12 weeks (P<0.0001). The price is printed on the face beside the benefit: 20% stopped pramipexole for adverse events versus 5% on placebo — nausea, headache and sleep disturbance or somnolence. The supporting record is thinner: a 2019 meta-analysis of small mixed unipolar and bipolar studies (response relative risk 1.77, a relative measure) and an 85-patient trial in anhedonia-selected mood disorders. Note the boundary: the bipolar sibling trial PAX-BD is homed at pack #3658 — a different population with a missed primary — and is not the home of this question. cards.headline: PAX-D — Browning 2025 (n=151, randomised): pramipexole augmentation cut QIDS-SR16 scores by 3.91 points more than placebo at 12 weeks — but 20% stopped pramipexole for adverse events vs 5% on placebo
cards.summary: PAX-D — Browning 2025 (n=151, randomised): pramipexole augmentation cut QIDS-SR16 scores by 3.91 points more than placebo at 12 weeks — but 20% stopped pramipexole for adverse events vs 5% on placebo
cards.people: 151 adults in England with treatment-resistant unipolar major depression (failure to respond sufficiently to prior antidepressants), randomised 1:1 to pramipexole titrated to a target of 2.5 mg/day (n=75) or placebo (n=75, after one post-randomisation exclusion) added to ongoing antidepressant treatment, in a 48-week trial whose primary outcome was at 12 weeks. This is the unipolar trial: its bipolar sibling, PAX-BD, is a different population homed at pack #3658 and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: QIDS-SR16 scores fell by 6.4 points on pramipexole versus 2.4 on placebo — an adjusted mean difference of −3.91 points (95% CI −5.37 to −2.45; P<0.0001) at 12 weeks, from a baseline of about 16. The mean dose achieved was 2.3 mg/day. Discontinuation of trial treatment for adverse events was 20% on pramipexole (15 participants) versus 5% on placebo (4 participants); adverse events were consistent with known pramipexole effects, particularly nausea, headache and sleep disturbance or somnolence. The 20% versus 5% discontinuation figures are printed on the face of this shelf, as required.
cards.watchOut: A positive, adequately sized single trial — but one in five patients could not stay on the drug for 12 weeks, which is part of the treatment’s effect in practice, and there is no head-to-head comparison with established augmentation options.
cards.source: Browning M et al. Pramipexole augmentation for the acute phase of treatment-resistant, unipolar depression: a placebo-controlled, double-blind, randomised trial in the UK. The lancet. Psychiatry. 2025. PMID: 40602411.

cards.headline: Meta-analysis — Tundo 2019 (5 RCTs plus open studies; 504 participants, unipolar and bipolar mixed): response rate higher on pramipexole than placebo (relative risk 1.77) — a relative measure across small, mixed trials
cards.summary: Meta-analysis — Tundo 2019 (5 RCTs plus open studies; 504 participants, unipolar and bipolar mixed): response rate higher on pramipexole than placebo (relative risk 1.77) — a relative measure across small, mixed trials
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials and observational studies (unipolar and bipolar depression mixed — labelled)
cards.people: 504 participants across five randomised trials, three open-label trials and five observational studies of pramipexole for major depressive episodes in unipolar and bipolar depression (mean sample size 39; median treatment duration 8 weeks). The mixed population is labelled here because this shelf’s question is unipolar only.
cards.result: In the randomised trials, response was more frequent on pramipexole than placebo (risk ratio 1.77, 95% CI 1.11 to 2.82 — a relative measure) and similar to SSRIs (risk ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.44 to 1.95 — a relative measure). Across all study types, short-term response was 52.2% and remission 36.1%. Nausea was the most frequent side effect; acceptability and tolerability were rated good in the included studies.
cards.watchOut: Most of the pooled trials are tiny and half the evidence base is bipolar or uncontrolled; this card shows the pre-PAX-D record was suggestive but thin, which is precisely why the 151-patient PAX-D trial matters.
cards.source: Tundo A et al. Pramipexole in the treatment of unipolar and bipolar depression. A systematic review and meta-analysis. Acta psychiatrica Scandinavica. 2019. PMID: 31111467.

cards.headline: Anhedonia trial — 2026 (n=85 randomised): pramipexole add-on improved anhedonia scores by 4.04 points more than placebo at 9 weeks in mood-disorder patients selected for anhedonia
cards.summary: Anhedonia trial — 2026 (n=85 randomised): pramipexole add-on improved anhedonia scores by 4.04 points more than placebo at 9 weeks in mood-disorder patients selected for anhedonia
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (anhedonic depression — adjacent population, labelled)
cards.people: 85 adults with major depressive disorder, dysthymia or bipolar depression and clinically significant anhedonia (elevated Snaith-Hamilton Pleasure Scale scores), randomised at a single centre to flexible-dose once-daily pramipexole or placebo as add-on treatment for 9 weeks; 82 were analysed. This is an adjacent, symptom-selected population — not the treatment-resistant unipolar population of PAX-D — and is labelled as such.
cards.result: The primary outcome was met: SHAPS anhedonia scores fell by 4.04 points more on pramipexole than placebo (95% CI −6.89 to −1.18; P=0.006; Hedges g 0.62). Improvements were sustained in a 6-month open-label extension, and pramipexole was generally well tolerated compared with placebo in this small trial.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre, 85-patient trial in a mixed-diagnosis anhedonia population: it supports the dopamine-agonist rationale behind PAX-D but cannot substitute for replication in treatment-resistant unipolar depression itself.

shelves.question: In adults with ADHD, does once-daily viloxazine ER reduce Adult ADHD Investigator Symptom Rating Scale scores versus placebo over 6 weeks?

shelves.balance: PARTIAL shelf — the adult slice only. Live shelf #1514 was read before building: its question and cards are restricted to children and adolescents, so the adult programme is built here and the paediatric references are not re-carded. In adults, a single phase 3 trial (n=374, flexible dose 200–600 mg/day, mean 504 mg) found AISRS scores falling 15.5 points on viloxazine ER versus 11.7 on placebo at 6 weeks (P=0.0040), with insomnia (14.8%) the commonest adverse event and discontinuation for adverse events of 9.0% versus 4.9%. Its open-label extension (n=159, mean exposure 265 days) gives the longer tolerability picture — 17.6% discontinued for adverse events — but no controlled efficacy. Premise correction: the slate described two adult trials; at build only one adult phase 3 RCT could be verified, plus its extension and a post-hoc analysis of the same patients. One randomised trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Adult phase 3 — Nasser 2022 (n=374, randomised): viloxazine ER reduced AISRS scores by 15.5 points vs 11.7 on placebo at 6 weeks (P=0.0040); discontinuation for adverse events 9.0% vs 4.9%
cards.summary: Adult phase 3 — Nasser 2022 (n=374, randomised): viloxazine ER reduced AISRS scores by 15.5 points vs 11.7 on placebo at 6 weeks (P=0.0040); discontinuation for adverse events 9.0% vs 4.9%
cards.people: 374 adults aged 18–65 years with ADHD randomised 1:1 to once-daily viloxazine extended-release capsules (flexible dose 200–600 mg/day; mean dose at end of study 504 mg) or placebo for 6 weeks. This is the adult trial; the children/adolescents programme is homed at live shelf #1514 and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: The primary endpoint was met: AISRS total score fell by 15.5 points on viloxazine ER versus 11.7 on placebo (least-squares means; P=0.0040), and CGI-Severity improved by 1.4 versus 1.0 points (P=0.0023). Inattention (P=0.0015) and hyperactivity/impulsivity (P=0.0380) subscales, CGI-Improvement and executive-function measures also favoured viloxazine ER, with many effects significant by week 2; the AISRS 30% responder rate was significantly higher (P=0.0395) while other categorical comparisons were not. Treatment-related adverse events in at least 5% on viloxazine ER were insomnia (14.8%), fatigue (11.6%), nausea (10.1%), decreased appetite (10.1%), dry mouth (9.0%) and headache (9.0%); discontinuation for adverse events was 9.0% versus 4.9%.
cards.watchOut: One 6-week trial with a high mean dose (504 mg): the drug–placebo separation of 3.8 AISRS points is statistically solid but modest, and 6 weeks says nothing about persistence of effect or long-term tolerability — which is what the extension card below is for.
cards.source: Nasser A et al. cards.headline: Adult open-label extension — Childress 2024 (n=159; mean exposure 265 days): adverse events led to discontinuation in 17.6%; AISRS improvement from double-blind baseline was maintained
cards.summary: Adult open-label extension — Childress 2024 (n=159; mean exposure 265 days): adverse events led to discontinuation in 17.6%; AISRS improvement from double-blind baseline was maintained
cards.type: Phase 3 open-label extension study (adults; uncontrolled — labelled as such)
cards.people: 159 adults who completed the double-blind adult phase 3 trial rolled over into a flexible-dose (200–600 mg/day) open-label extension of viloxazine ER; mean exposure was 265 days. No control group: safety is the primary value of this card, and continued-efficacy numbers are uncontrolled observations, labelled as such.
cards.result: Adverse events above 10% incidence were insomnia (13.8%), nausea (13.8%), headache (10.7%) and fatigue (10.1%); adverse events led to discontinuation in 17.6% of participants (most commonly insomnia 2.5%, nausea 2.5%, fatigue 1.9%). AISRS total score improved by 11.4 points by week 2 of the extension relative to double-blind baseline, with continued improvement at later visits.
cards.watchOut: Rollover cohorts keep the patients who tolerated the drug; a 17.6% discontinuation rate even in that selected group is the honest long-term tolerability signal, and uncontrolled symptom scores cannot confirm maintained efficacy.
cards.source: Childress A et al. An Open-Label Extension Study Assessing the Long-Term Safety and Efficacy of Viloxazine Extended-Release Capsules in Adults with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder. CNS drugs. 2024. PMID: 39373844. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT04143217.

cards.headline: Post-hoc analysis — 2022 (same phase 3 trial; 354-patient analysis set): improvement by week 2 predicted week-6 response with 68% positive predictive power
cards.summary: Post-hoc analysis — 2022 (same phase 3 trial; 354-patient analysis set): improvement by week 2 predicted week-6 response with 68% positive predictive power
cards.type: Post-hoc machine-learning analysis of the same adult phase 3 trial (same patients — not an independent trial)
cards.people: A post-hoc machine-learning (lasso) analysis of the adult phase 3 trial above — the same study population (analysis set N=354; 127 viloxazine ER patients with week-6 data) — testing whether a prediction model built in children generalised to adults. Carded as a methods/prediction report on the same patients, not as independent efficacy evidence.
cards.result: Among viloxazine ER patients, 51 of 127 (40.2%) met the responder definition (at least 50% AISRS reduction at week 6). Symptom data up to week 2 predicted week-6 response with 68% positive predictive power, 80% sensitivity and 74% specificity, indicating the paediatric-derived model generalised to adults.
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc and same-patient: this card answers a practical question (how early can non-response be spotted?) and adds no new efficacy evidence. The adult programme’s randomised base remains the single phase 3 trial above — a premise correction to the slate, which described two adult trials; only one adult phase 3 RCT was verified at build, plus its extension and this post-hoc analysis.

shelves.balance: PHASE 2 ONLY — the flag is carried here, in the title and in the stamp, as this row required. The entire MM120 evidence base is one phase 2b dose-ranging trial (Robison 2025, n=198): a single supervised dose reduced HAM-A scores at 4 weeks by 5.0 points more than placebo at 100 µg and 6.0 points at 200 µg, while the 25 µg (−1.2) and 50 µg (−1.8) doses did not separate — the dose–response is on the face. The tested product is named under the clarification exception: MindMed MM120 (lysergide D-tartrate). Two small older trials of LSD-assisted therapy in anxiety associated with life-threatening illness (n=42; n=12) point the same way for the molecule but are different populations with psychotherapy, and are labelled as such. Near-universal visual perceptual changes at the effective doses (92.5–100% vs 10.3% on placebo) make functional unblinding the key caveat. A single phase 2 trial caps the verdict at POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: MM120 phase 2b — Robison 2025 (n=198, randomised): a single 100 µg dose cut HAM-A by 5.0 points more than placebo and 200 µg by 6.0 points at 4 weeks; 25 µg and 50 µg did not separate (dose–response on the face)
cards.summary: MM120 phase 2b — Robison 2025 (n=198, randomised): a single 100 µg dose cut HAM-A by 5.0 points more than placebo and 200 µg by 6.0 points at 4 weeks; 25 µg and 50 µg did not separate (dose–response on the face)
cards.type: Phase 2b, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled dose-ranging trial (the only MM120 trial — phase 2 only, flagged)
cards.people: 198 adults aged 18–74 with moderate-to-severe generalised anxiety disorder (HAM-A at least 20) at 22 US outpatient sites, randomised to a single supervised dose of MM120 (lysergide D-tartrate; the tested product is MindMed MM120, named here under the tested-product clarification exception) at 25 µg (n=39), 50 µg (n=40), 100 µg (n=40) or 200 µg (n=40), or placebo (n=39). Outcomes were rated by independent central raters blinded to allocation and visit. PHASE 2 ONLY: this single phase 2b trial is the entire MM120 evidence base on this shelf, and the flag is carried in the title, balance and stamp.
cards.result: The dose–response primary analysis was statistically significant, driven by the two higher doses: at 4 weeks, HAM-A change differed from placebo by −5.0 points at 100 µg (95% CI −9.6 to −0.4) and −6.0 points at 200 µg (95% CI −9.8 to −2.0), against a minimal clinically important difference of 2.5 points. The lower doses did not separate from placebo: −1.2 points at 25 µg (95% CI −6.0 to 3.5) and −1.8 at 50 µg (95% CI −7.6 to 4.0). Adverse events were dose-dependent and consistent with the drug’s expected effects: visual perceptual changes in 46.2% (25 µg), 75.0% (50 µg), 92.5% (100 µg), 100% (200 µg) versus 10.3% on placebo; nausea in 7.7%, 27.5%, 40.0%, 60.0% versus 7.7%; headache in 12.8%, 22.5%, 35.0%, 27.5% versus 23.1%.
cards.watchOut: Functional unblinding is the central threat: when 92–100% of higher-dose patients have visual perceptual changes versus 10% on placebo, patients and sites can guess allocation, and even blinded central raters cannot fully remove expectancy effects. A single phase 2 trial, however clean its dose–response, caps this shelf at POSSIBLE.
cards.source: Robison R et al. Single Treatment With MM120 (Lysergide) in Generalized Anxiety Disorder: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2025. PMID: 40906494. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT05407064.

cards.headline: LSD-assisted therapy — Holze 2023 (n=42): anxiety scores fell 16.2 points more after LSD than placebo periods in patients with anxiety with or without life-threatening illness — not generalised anxiety disorder
cards.summary: LSD-assisted therapy — Holze 2023 (n=42): anxiety scores fell 16.2 points more after LSD than placebo periods in patients with anxiety with or without life-threatening illness — not generalised anxiety disorder
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 crossover trial of LSD-assisted therapy (different anxiety population — labelled)
cards.people: 42 patients with anxiety disorders, with or without an associated life-threatening illness, in an investigator-initiated two-centre double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial of two oral LSD sessions (200 µg) versus placebo with therapy. This population is not the MM120 trial’s primary generalised anxiety disorder population, and the treatment included psychotherapy — both differences are labelled here; the card is supporting evidence for lysergide in anxiety, not for MM120 in GAD itself.
cards.result: LSD treatment reduced State-Trait Anxiety Inventory–Global scores by 16.2 points more than placebo up to 16 weeks after treatment (95% CI −27.8 to −4.5; P=0.007), with similar-direction effects on depression ratings. Transient mild acute adverse effects were reported by 8 patients (19%); one treatment-related serious adverse event (acute transient anxiety) occurred (2%).
cards.watchOut: Crossover carryover forced the authors to present first-period results primarily, and the sample mixes anxiety with and without life-threatening illness. Supportive for the molecule, indirect for the question.
cards.source: Holze F et al. Lysergic Acid Diethylamide-Assisted Therapy in Patients With Anxiety With and Without a Life-Threatening Illness: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Phase II Study. Biological psychiatry. 2023. PMID: 36266118. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT03153579.

cards.headline: LSD-assisted psychotherapy pilot — Gasser 2014 (n=12): trait anxiety fell after 200 µg LSD sessions in anxiety associated with life-threatening disease (pilot, 12 patients)
cards.summary: LSD-assisted psychotherapy pilot — Gasser 2014 (n=12): trait anxiety fell after 200 µg LSD sessions in anxiety associated with life-threatening disease (pilot, 12 patients)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, active-placebo-controlled pilot trial of LSD-assisted psychotherapy (different anxiety population — labelled)
cards.people: 12 patients with anxiety associated with life-threatening diseases received drug-free psychotherapy plus two LSD-assisted sessions: 8 received 200 µg LSD and 4 received a 20 µg active placebo, with open-label crossover after unblinding. A pilot in a different anxiety population from GAD, labelled as such; its 12 patients meet the reference floor but only just, and its size is printed here.
cards.result: At 2-month follow-up, trait anxiety fell (P=0.033; effect size 1.1) and state anxiety fell (P=0.021; effect size 1.2) in the full-dose group, with reductions sustained at 12 months. No acute or chronic adverse effects persisted beyond 1 day and there were no treatment-related serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Twelve patients, an active-placebo design and a terminal-illness population: historically important as the first modern LSD anxiety trial, evidentially the weakest card on this shelf.
cards.source: Gasser P et al. Safety and efficacy of lysergic acid diethylamide-assisted psychotherapy for anxiety associated with life-threatening diseases. The Journal of nervous and mental disease. 2014. PMID: 24594678. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT00920387.

shelves.title: Ketamine-assisted therapy for alcohol use disorder (KARE, 2×2 factorial, n=96): days abstinent rose 10.1 points versus saline at 6 months, but relapse did not differ significantly
shelves.question: In adults with moderate-to-severe alcohol use disorder, do three weekly ketamine infusions with psychological therapy increase percentage of days abstinent over 6 months versus saline with therapy (or ketamine/therapy alone)?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Alcohol Drinking/psychology · Alcoholism/psychology · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Ketamine · Male · Recurrence · Secondary Prevention · Treatment Outcome · Alcoholism/drug therapy,therapy · Combined Modality Therapy/methods · Infusions, Intravenous · Ketamine/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Midazolam/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Pilot Projects · Psychotherapy/methods · Adolescent · Young Adult · Aged · Alcoholism/drug therapy · Naltrexone/therapeutic use · Patient Readmission · Inpatients · Feasibility Studies
shelves.balance: KARE is a 2×2 factorial trial and this shelf presents its cells honestly: 96 patients with severe alcohol use disorder received ketamine or saline infusions, crossed with relapse-prevention therapy or alcohol education. Pooling the drug contrast, ketamine groups had 10.1 percentage points more days abstinent than saline groups at 6 months (95% CI 1.1 to 19.0); the largest contrast, ketamine-plus-therapy versus saline-plus-education (15.9 points), is a diagonal comparison that mixes the drug and therapy effects and is labelled as such. Just as important, relapse did not differ significantly between ketamine and saline — the relapse outcome is less clear than the abstinence percentage. A 40-patient midazolam-controlled pilot (single infusion) supports the abstinence signal over 21 days; a 44-patient open-label inpatient pilot found no significant readmission benefit. Small phase 2 evidence with a split outcome pattern: POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: KARE — Grabski 2022 (n=96, 2×2 factorial): ketamine groups had 10.1% more days abstinent than saline groups at 6 months; the ketamine-plus-therapy cell beat saline-plus-education by 15.9% — but relapse did not differ significantly
cards.summary: KARE — Grabski 2022 (n=96, 2×2 factorial): ketamine groups had 10.1% more days abstinent than saline groups at 6 months; the ketamine-plus-therapy cell beat saline-plus-education by 15.9% — but relapse did not differ significantly
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled 2×2 factorial phase 2 trial (KARE) — factorial cells presented honestly
cards.people: 96 adults with severe alcohol use disorder randomised in a 2×2 factorial design to one of four cells: (1) three weekly ketamine infusions (0.8 mg/kg IV over 40 minutes) plus relapse-prevention psychological therapy, (2) saline infusions plus psychological therapy, (3) ketamine infusions plus alcohol education (the therapy control), or (4) saline infusions plus alcohol education. The factorial structure is presented as designed: the headline contrast pools the two ketamine cells against the two saline cells, and the largest single contrast is between the two diagonal cells — readers should not mistake the diagonal contrast for the drug’s isolated effect.
cards.result: At 6 months, the ketamine groups had a significantly greater percentage of days abstinent than the saline groups (mean difference 10.1 percentage points; 95% CI 1.1 to 19.0). The largest difference was between the diagonal cells — ketamine plus therapy versus saline plus education (15.9 percentage points; 95% CI 3.8 to 28.1). There was no significant difference in relapse rate between the ketamine and saline groups: the relapse outcome is less clear than the abstinence percentage, exactly as the row required this shelf to state. Treatment was well tolerated, with no serious adverse events associated with the study drug. Confidence intervals were wide, consistent with a proof-of-concept study.
cards.watchOut: Ninety-six patients across four cells means roughly 24 per cell: the pooled drug contrast is the reliable one, the diagonal contrast mixes drug and therapy effects, and the null relapse result — arguably the outcome patients care about most — must stay beside the positive abstinence result.
cards.source: Grabski M et al. Adjunctive Ketamine With Relapse Prevention-Based Psychological Therapy in the Treatment of Alcohol Use Disorder. The American journal of psychiatry. 2022. PMID: 35012326. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT02649231.

cards.headline: Dakwar 2020 (n=40, pilot): a single ketamine infusion with motivational enhancement therapy increased abstinence and delayed relapse versus midazolam over 21 days
cards.summary: Dakwar 2020 (n=40, pilot): a single ketamine infusion with motivational enhancement therapy increased abstinence and delayed relapse versus midazolam over 21 days
cards.people: 40 adults with alcohol dependence engaged in a 5-week outpatient motivational enhancement therapy programme, randomised to a single 52-minute IV infusion of ketamine (0.71 mg/kg; n=17) or the active control midazolam (0.025 mg/kg; n=23) in week 2. Drinking was assessed by timeline followback with urine ethyl glucuronide confirmation.
cards.result: Ketamine significantly increased the likelihood of abstinence over the 21 days after infusion, delayed the time to relapse, and reduced the likelihood of heavy drinking days compared with midazolam. Infusions were well tolerated, with no participants removed because of adverse events.
cards.watchOut: A 40-patient pilot with a 21-day outcome window and an unequal split (17 vs 23): supportive of KARE’s abstinence signal, but short, small and single-infusion — it cannot speak to durability at 6 months.
cards.source: Dakwar E et al. A Single Ketamine Infusion Combined With Motivational Enhancement Therapy for Alcohol Use Disorder: A Randomized Midazolam-Controlled Pilot Trial. The American journal of psychiatry. 2020. PMID: 31786934. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT02539511.

cards.headline: Terasaki 2022 (n=44, open-label pilot): 30-day readmission was lower after single-dose ketamine (relative risk 0.37) and after intramuscular naltrexone (relative risk 0.52) than linkage alone — neither difference significant (the treatment made no difference on the tested comparison)
cards.summary: Terasaki 2022 (n=44, open-label pilot): 30-day readmission was lower after single-dose ketamine (relative risk 0.37) and after intramuscular naltrexone (relative risk 0.52) than linkage alone — neither difference significant (the treatment made no difference on the tested comparison)
cards.type: Open-label, 3-arm randomised pilot trial (hospital inpatients; readmission outcome — null result labelled)
cards.people: 44 high-utilisation inpatients (mean 3.2 hospitalisations in the past year) with severe alcohol use disorder at a safety-net hospital, randomised open-label to a single IV ketamine dose (0.5 mg/kg; n=13), single-dose intramuscular naltrexone 380 mg (n=14), or enhanced linkage to outpatient addiction care alone (n=17). The primary outcome was 30-day all-cause readmission — a different, harder outcome than abstinence, in a different setting from KARE.
cards.result: Readmission rates were lower in the ketamine arm (risk ratio 0.37 — a relative measure; P=0.17) and the naltrexone arm (risk ratio 0.52; P=0.27) than in the linkage-alone arm, but neither difference was statistically significant — on this outcome and at this size, the treatment made no difference that the trial could demonstrate. Acceptability ratings were high (9.5 of 10 for ketamine), and no serious adverse events or illicit ketamine use were reported.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, 44 patients, baseline imbalances the authors note may have biased against the control arm, and a null primary result: this card is feasibility evidence, and its null is printed rather than buried.
cards.source: Terasaki D et al. Single-dose intravenous ketamine or intramuscular naltrexone for high-utilization inpatients with alcohol use disorder: pilot trial feasibility and readmission rates. Addiction science & clinical practice. 2022. PMID: 36419181. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT04562779.

cards.headline: Synthesis: abstinence days improve in two small controlled trials; relapse and readmission do not clearly move — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: abstinence days improve in two small controlled trials; relapse and readmission do not clearly move — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.people: KARE (96 patients, 2×2 factorial, 6-month follow-up), Dakwar 2020 (40 patients, single infusion, 21-day outcomes) and Terasaki 2022 (44 inpatients, open-label, readmission outcome, null). Total controlled evidence base: 180 patients.
cards.result: Ketamine added to psychological therapy increased the percentage of days abstinent by about 10 points versus saline at 6 months in KARE, with the ketamine-plus-therapy cell 15.9 points above the saline-plus-education cell — a diagonal contrast that mixes drug and therapy, presented as such. But KARE found no significant difference in relapse, and the inpatient pilot found no significant readmission benefit. A real abstinence signal with unclear relapse benefit, from small phase 2 trials, is POSSIBLE (benefit) and no more.
cards.watchOut: This shelf does not cover ketamine for depression, PTSD or pain (their own shelves), nor the approved alcohol-use-disorder drugs; no comparison against naltrexone or acamprosate at adequate size exists in these cards — the only naltrexone arm here is a 14-patient pilot cell.

shelves.title: SAINT accelerated iTBS for treatment-resistant depression (PARTIAL — the accelerated slice live #574 does not cover): remission 19 of 21 open-label; sham-controlled remission 50.0% vs 20.8% in the 2026 replication (randomised N=48); first RCT randomised N=29
shelves.question: In adults with treatment-resistant depression, does SAINT (accelerated, high-dose, fMRI-targeted intermittent theta-burst stimulation over 5 days) produce remission versus sham stimulation?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Clinical Protocols · Cognition · Depressive Disorder, Treatment-Resistant/diagnosis,physiopathology,therapy · Female · Functional Neuroimaging/methods · Gyrus Cinguli/physiopathology · Humans · Magnetic Resonance Imaging/methods · Male · Monitoring, Physiologic/methods · Neuropsychological Tests · Prefrontal Cortex/physiopathology · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Remission Induction/methods · Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation/methods
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #574, which cards conventional once-daily rTMS versus sham only; sibling pack #5946 asks rTMS versus ECT. This shelf cards only the accelerated, fMRI-targeted SAINT/SNT slice, and no PMID homed on #574 or #5946 is re-carded. The record is promising but small: an open-label report (Cole 2020; 21 completers) with 90.5% remission; a first double-blind sham-controlled trial stopped at a planned interim analysis with only 29 randomised participants (Cole 2022), in which mean MADRS scores fell 52.5% on active treatment versus 11.1% on sham at 4 weeks; and a 2026 sham-controlled replication (Kratter 2026; 48 randomised) with remission 50.0% versus 20.8% and response 54.2% versus 25.0% at 1 month. A 2026 dose-response meta-analysis of accelerated iTBS generally (15 trials, 704 patients) also favours active treatment (response relative risk 1.99, remission relative risk 1.77 — relative measures). Two small concordant sham-controlled trials from one programme, with wide uncertainty around the true remission gain, cap the stamp at POSSIBLE; the randomised Ns (29 and 48) are printed on the face and in the stamp line, and the open-label report is labelled open-label wherever it appears.

cards.headline: Cole 2020 (OPEN-LABEL, no control group): remission in 19 of 21 completers (90.5%) after 5 days of SAINT — a feasibility signal, not proof
cards.summary: Cole 2020 (OPEN-LABEL, no control group): remission in 19 of 21 completers (90.5%) after 5 days of SAINT — a feasibility signal, not proof
cards.people: 22 participants with treatment-resistant depression received open-label SAINT: 50 iTBS sessions (1,800 pulses per session, 50-minute intersession intervals) as 10 sessions daily over 5 consecutive days at 90% resting motor threshold, with resting-state functional-connectivity MRI used to target the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex site most anticorrelated with the subgenual anterior cingulate in each person. One participant withdrew, leaving 21 completers.
cards.result: Nineteen of 21 completers (90.5%) met remission criteria (Montgomery–Åsberg Depression Rating Scale score <11); in the intent-to-treat analysis, 19 of 22 (86.4%) met remission criteria. Neuropsychological testing showed no negative cognitive side effects, and the authors describe the protocol as well tolerated and safe, while stating that double-blinded sham-controlled trials are needed to confirm the remission rate.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with no sham or control arm: expectancy, regression to the mean and the intensive 5-day clinical contact can all inflate remission. This card is the programme's feasibility signal only — the randomised cards below carry the efficacy question.

cards.headline: Cole 2022 double-blind RCT (randomised N=29, stopped at planned interim analysis): MADRS scores fell 52.5% on active SNT vs 11.1% on sham at 4 weeks
cards.summary: Cole 2022 double-blind RCT (randomised N=29, stopped at planned interim analysis): MADRS scores fell 52.5% on active SNT vs 11.1% on sham at 4 weeks
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Cole 2022, SNT vs sham)
cards.people: 32 participants with treatment-resistant depression in a moderate-to-severe episode were enrolled; 29 who continued to meet inclusion criteria received active SNT (n=14) or sham SNT (n=15), with the same functional-connectivity-guided left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex targeting. The trial reports its planned interim analysis. Randomised N is 29 — printed here and in the stamp line.
cards.result: The primary outcome was the Montgomery–Åsberg Depression Rating Scale score 4 weeks after treatment: the mean percent reduction from baseline was 52.5% in the active group and 11.1% in the sham group. The authors conclude SNT was more effective than sham and that further trials are needed to determine durability and to compare it with other treatments. The record's abstract does not print arm-level remission counts, so none are given here.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-nine randomised participants, one centre, and a result reported at a planned interim analysis: the effect estimate is fragile and its confidence interval wide, even though the direction is clear. Durability beyond 4 weeks is not established by this trial.

cards.headline: Kratter 2026 replication RCT (randomised N=48): remission 50.0% on active SNT vs 20.8% on sham at 1 month (p=0.035); response 54.2% vs 25.0%
cards.summary: Kratter 2026 replication RCT (randomised N=48): remission 50.0% on active SNT vs 20.8% on sham at 1 month (p=0.035); response 54.2% vs 25.0%
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Kratter 2026, SNT vs sham — replication)
cards.people: 53 participants with treatment-resistant depression were enrolled and 48 who continued to meet entry criteria were randomised to active SNT (n=24) or sham SNT (n=24). The primary outcome was remission at 1 month. Electroencephalography findings from this and the earlier trial were reported alongside.
cards.result: Remission at 1 month was achieved in 50.0% of the active group versus 20.8% of the sham group (χ²=4.5, p=0.035) — an absolute difference of 29.2 percentage points; response likewise favoured active treatment (54.2% vs 25.0%; χ²=4.3, p=0.039). Frontal beta power fell after active but not sham treatment in both trials, and greater post-treatment reduction in left anterior cingulate beta power correlated with greater clinical improvement.
cards.watchOut: A genuine replication, but still one programme and 48 randomised participants: the sham remission rate here (20.8%) is far above the near-zero sham rates sometimes quoted for this protocol, which shrinks the absolute gain a clinic should expect. The EEG biomarker findings are exploratory.
cards.source: Kratter IH et al. Stanford neuromodulation therapy for treatment-resistant depression: a randomized controlled trial confirming efficacy, and an EEG study providing insight into mechanism of action and a potentially predictive biomarker of efficacy. cards.headline: Santos 2026 meta-analysis of accelerated iTBS (15 RCTs, 704 patients): response relative risk 1.99 and remission relative risk 1.77 vs sham — relative measures
cards.summary: Santos 2026 meta-analysis of accelerated iTBS (15 RCTs, 704 patients): response relative risk 1.99 and remission relative risk 1.77 vs sham — relative measures
cards.people: Fifteen randomised sham-controlled trials of accelerated intermittent theta-burst stimulation in adults with major depressive episodes (704 patients; 11 unipolar and 4 bipolar trials; 46% at low risk of bias), pooling symptom improvement, response, remission and discontinuation.
cards.result: Accelerated iTBS was superior to sham for symptom reduction (standardised mean difference 0.69, 95% CI 0.33–1.05), response (relative risk 1.99, 95% CI 1.50–2.64; number needed to treat 5) and remission (relative risk 1.77, 95% CI 1.07–2.93; number needed to treat 10) — the risk ratios are relative measures. Discontinuation was similar (6.96% vs 8.12%). Dose-response analyses favoured more sessions, more total pulses and longer intersession intervals, and protocols using functional-connectivity neuronavigation showed larger effects.
cards.watchOut: This pools the wider accelerated-iTBS class, not SAINT alone, and mixes unipolar with bipolar depression and heterogeneous protocols; it supports the approach SAINT belongs to rather than replicating SAINT itself.
cards.source: Santos JM et al. Accelerated intermittent theta-burst stimulation for major depressive episodes: systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis. Brain stimulation. 2026. PMID: 42508605. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: two small sham-controlled trials agree SAINT/SNT beats sham — the size of the remission gain is the uncertain part
cards.summary: Synthesis: two small sham-controlled trials agree SAINT/SNT beats sham — the size of the remission gain is the uncertain part
cards.people: Open-label SAINT (21 completers), the 2022 sham-controlled trial (29 randomised), the 2026 replication (48 randomised) and a 15-trial accelerated-iTBS meta-analysis (704 patients) — all in treatment-resistant or major depressive episodes.
cards.result: Remission 50.0% vs 20.8% (absolute +29.2 points) in the replication trial and a 52.5% vs 11.1% mean MADRS fall in the first trial, against a 90.5% open-label remission rate that should not be quoted as the treatment effect. The direction is consistent across designs; the magnitude in ordinary practice is likely closer to the sham-controlled figures than to the open-label one. POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: This shelf does not cover conventional once-daily rTMS (live #574) or rTMS versus ECT (pack #5946). All SAINT trials come from the protocol's originating programme; independent multicentre replication and durability data remain the open questions.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards above. No new data.

shelves.title: Centanafadine for ADHD (tested product: Otsuka centanafadine SR/ER): two positive adult phase 3 trials (AISRS −2.7 to −4.5 points vs placebo); adolescent high dose positive, low dose missed; children rest on a pooled secondary analysis
shelves.question: In people aged 6 years and over with ADHD, does centanafadine (a norepinephrine–dopamine–serotonin reuptake inhibitor; tested product — Otsuka centanafadine SR/ER) reduce ADHD rating-scale scores versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Attention Deficit Disorder with Hyperactivity/drug therapy · Central Nervous System Stimulants/adverse effects · Delayed-Action Preparations/therapeutic use · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Tablets/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: The tested product throughout is Otsuka centanafadine SR/ER (sustained-/extended-release), named here under the tested-product clarification exception. In adults, two phase 3 trials (886 randomised across both) agree: both the 200 mg/day and 400 mg/day doses beat placebo on the Adult ADHD Investigator Symptom Rating Scale at day 42, by least-squares mean differences of −2.74 to −4.47 points, with small effect sizes (−0.24 to −0.40). In adolescents (459 randomised), the higher dose (328.8 mg) met its primary endpoint (ADHD-RS-5 −18.50 vs −14.15; p=0.0006) and the lower dose (164.4 mg) did not (the treatment made no difference at that dose on the prespecified primary analysis). For children aged 6–12, the carded record in this session is a pooled secondary analysis of the children and adolescent phase 3 trials (Conners 3 scales and clinically-meaningful-change), which favours the high dose; the children's primary report was not retrievable from PubMed in this session and is flagged in the build summary. Treatment-emergent events rose with dose (adolescents: 31.4% low dose, 50.3% high dose, 23.8% placebo), most commonly decreased appetite, nausea, headache and rash. Concordant randomised evidence with modest effect sizes and a failed low dose caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Adler 2022 — two adult phase 3 trials (886 randomised): AISRS differences vs placebo −3.16 and −2.74 (study 1) and −4.01 and −4.47 (study 2) at day 42
cards.summary: Adler 2022 — two adult phase 3 trials (886 randomised): AISRS differences vs placebo −3.16 and −2.74 (study 1) and −4.01 and −4.47 (study 2) at day 42
cards.type: Two randomised controlled trials reported together (Adler 2022, adults)
cards.people: Adults aged 18–55 with ADHD and moderate-to-severe symptoms (mean AISRS total 38.7) in two phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials of Otsuka centanafadine sustained-release tablets: study 1 randomised 149 to 200 mg/day, 149 to 400 mg/day and 148 to placebo; study 2 randomised 145, 143 and 142 respectively (886 in total). Primary endpoint: change in Adult ADHD Investigator Symptom Rating Scale (AISRS) total score at day 42.
cards.result: Both doses beat placebo in both studies: least-squares mean AISRS differences were −3.16 (p=0.019) for 200 mg and −2.74 (p=0.039) for 400 mg in study 1, and −4.01 (p=0.002) and −4.47 (p=0.001) in study 2. Effect sizes were small (−0.24 to −0.40). The overall treatment-emergent adverse-event rate was low with a small dose-related increase; serious events and abuse-potential-related events were uncommon.
cards.watchOut: Statistically consistent but clinically modest: differences of roughly 3–4.5 points on the AISRS with effect sizes under 0.5, over 6 weeks, in trials run for registration. The record's databank fields carry no registry IDs, so none are printed in this card's source line.

cards.headline: Ward 2026 adolescent phase 3 (459 randomised): high dose (328.8 mg) met its primary (ADHD-RS-5 −18.50 vs −14.15; p=0.0006); low dose (164.4 mg) did not
cards.summary: Ward 2026 adolescent phase 3 (459 randomised): high dose (328.8 mg) met its primary (ADHD-RS-5 −18.50 vs −14.15; p=0.0006); low dose (164.4 mg) did not
cards.people: 459 adolescents aged 13–17 with a primary ADHD diagnosis, randomised to once-daily centanafadine extended-release 164.4 mg (n=155), 328.8 mg (n=155) or placebo (n=149) for 6 weeks without titration; 451 received at least one dose and 371 (80.8%) completed. Primary endpoint: change in ADHD Rating Scale-5 total score at week 6.
cards.result: The 328.8 mg dose separated from placebo (−18.50 [SE 0.93] vs −14.15 [0.93]; p=0.0006), with separation from week 1 maintained throughout; the 164.4 mg dose did not meet the primary endpoint (the treatment made no difference at that dose on the prespecified analysis). Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 31.4% (164.4 mg), 50.3% (328.8 mg) and 23.8% (placebo); the commonest were decreased appetite, nausea, headache and rash, mostly mild or moderate, with three severe events (one liver-function-test increase and one aggression on 164.4 mg; one somnolence on placebo).
cards.watchOut: A split dose record inside one trial: efficacy is established only at the higher dose, where half the participants reported an adverse event. Six weeks is short for a chronic developmental condition.

cards.headline: Ward 2026 pooled secondary analysis (children 6–12 and adolescents, two phase 3 trials): high-dose centanafadine improved Conners 3 inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity from week 1
cards.summary: Ward 2026 pooled secondary analysis (children 6–12 and adolescents, two phase 3 trials): high-dose centanafadine improved Conners 3 inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity from week 1
cards.type: Secondary analysis of two randomised trials (Ward 2026, children and adolescents)
cards.people: Children aged 6–12 (children's trial NCT05428033; mean age 9, 59% male) and adolescents aged 13–17 (NCT05257265; mean age 15, 59% male) randomised 1:1:1 to high-dose or low-dose once-daily centanafadine extended-release or placebo for 6 weeks. Because the low dose missed the primary endpoint, low-dose data are excluded from this report and its p-values are not controlled for multiplicity. Outcomes: Conners 3-Parent Short and Conners 3-Self-Report Short T-scores and clinically meaningful within-patient change.
cards.result: High-dose centanafadine separated from placebo as early as week 1, with significant improvements in inattention at every timepoint to week 6 by both caregiver and (in adolescents) self-report, and in hyperactivity/impulsivity at every week on the parent scale. Versus placebo, children on centanafadine had a 55% higher chance of clinically meaningful within-patient change in inattention and a 48% higher chance in hyperactivity/impulsivity, and adolescents 65% and 46% respectively — relative chance measures from the integrated analysis, printed as the record reports them.
cards.watchOut: This is a secondary, multiplicity-uncontrolled analysis that omits the failed low-dose arms; it supports, but cannot substitute for, the children's trial's primary report, which was not retrievable from PubMed in this session (flagged in the build summary).

cards.headline: Synthesis: a real but modest triple-reuptake effect in adults and adolescents; the children's primary record is the gap on this shelf
cards.summary: Synthesis: a real but modest triple-reuptake effect in adults and adolescents; the children's primary record is the gap on this shelf
cards.people: Two adult phase 3 trials (886 randomised), one adolescent phase 3 trial (459 randomised) and a pooled secondary analysis of the children (6–12) and adolescent trials — all of Otsuka centanafadine SR/ER versus placebo over 6 weeks.
cards.result: Every higher-dose comparison beat placebo (adult AISRS differences −2.7 to −4.5 points; adolescent ADHD-RS-5 −18.50 vs −14.15), every low-dose primary comparison missed, and adverse events rose with dose. The benefit is consistent and dose-dependent but small in absolute scale points — POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: No carded trial runs beyond 6 weeks, none compares centanafadine head-to-head with stimulants or atomoxetine, and the children's (6–12) evidence here rests on a secondary analysis rather than the primary trial report.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards above. No new data.

shelves.title: Oliceridine for acute postoperative pain (APOLLO-1/2): responders 50–76% vs 15–46% on placebo and equi-analgesic to morphine at mid/high doses — but respiratory safety burden was NOT significantly lower than morphine's
shelves.question: In adults with moderate-to-severe acute postoperative pain (bunionectomy, abdominoplasty), does intravenous oliceridine, a G-protein-biased μ-opioid agonist, provide analgesia versus placebo and versus morphine, with fewer respiratory and gastrointestinal adverse events?
shelves.mesh: Abdominoplasty · Acute Pain/drug therapy · Adult · Analgesia, Patient-Controlled · Analgesics/therapeutic use · Analgesics, Opioid/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Morphine/administration & dosage · Pain Management · Pain Measurement · Postoperative Pain/drug therapy · Receptors, Opioid, mu · Spiro Compounds/pharmacology · Thiophenes/pharmacology
shelves.balance: Two phase 3 trials agree that intravenous oliceridine works as an analgesic: responder rates were 50–66% across demand-dose regimens versus 15.2% on placebo after bunionectomy (APOLLO-1) and 61–76% versus 45.7% after abdominoplasty (APOLLO-2), and the 0.35 mg and 0.5 mg regimens were non-inferior/equi-analgesic to morphine in both. The safety claims need grading against what the trials actually showed: the composite respiratory safety burden rose dose-dependently on oliceridine and was NOT statistically different from morphine in APOLLO-1 (morphine 1.1 hours) nor significantly different from placebo in APOLLO-2, where morphine's burden (1.72 hours) did differ from placebo — so a respiratory advantage over morphine is suggested by point estimates, not demonstrated. Gastrointestinal events were frankly dose-dependent on oliceridine (up to 70.9% and 78.8% at the 0.5 mg regimen, close to morphine's 72.4% and 79.3%), though nausea/vomiting rates and rescue-antiemetic use favoured the equi-analgesic oliceridine regimens over morphine. The open-label ATHENA study (768 patients) found nausea 31%, constipation 11% and vomiting 10%, with no deaths or significant cardiorespiratory events reported. Analgesia: established. A proven respiratory-sparing advantage: not established. POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: APOLLO-1 (bunionectomy): responders 50%, 62% and 65.8% on oliceridine regimens vs 15.2% on placebo; respiratory safety burden not significantly different from morphine
cards.summary: APOLLO-1 (bunionectomy): responders 50%, 62% and 65.8% on oliceridine regimens vs 15.2% on placebo; respiratory safety burden not significantly different from morphine
cards.people: Patients with moderate-to-severe pain after bunionectomy in a phase III double-blind trial (NCT02815709) received a loading dose of placebo, oliceridine 1.5 mg or morphine 4 mg, then patient-controlled demand doses (oliceridine 0.1, 0.35 or 0.5 mg; morphine 1 mg; or placebo) through 48 hours. The record's abstract does not state the total number randomised, so none is printed here. Primary endpoint: proportion of treatment responders through 48 hours versus placebo.
cards.result: Responder rates were 50% (0.1 mg), 62% (0.35 mg) and 65.8% (0.5 mg) versus 15.2% on placebo (all p<0.0001); the 0.35 mg and 0.5 mg regimens were non-inferior to morphine. Respiratory safety burden (cumulative duration of respiratory safety events) rose with dose (means 0.04, 0.28 and 0.8 hours; placebo 0) but was not statistically different from morphine (1.1 hours). Gastrointestinal adverse events also rose with dose (40.8%, 59.5%, 70.9%; placebo 24.1%; morphine 72.4%), while the odds of rescue antiemetic use were significantly lower on oliceridine than on morphine (p<0.05).
cards.watchOut: The trial's own conclusion claims a favourable respiratory profile, but its respiratory composite did not significantly separate from morphine — the honest reading is a favourable point estimate in an underpowered safety composite, in a single postoperative model, over 48 hours.
cards.source: Viscusi ER et al. APOLLO-1: a randomized placebo and active-controlled phase III study investigating oliceridine (TRV130), a G protein-biased ligand at the µ-opioid receptor, for management of moderate-to-severe acute pain following bunionectomy. Journal of pain research. 2019. PMID: 30881102. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02815709, from the record's abstract. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: APOLLO-2 (abdominoplasty, 401 treated): responders 61.0%, 76.3% and 70.0% vs 45.7% on placebo and 78.3% on morphine; GI events up to 78.8% at the top regimen
cards.summary: APOLLO-2 (abdominoplasty, 401 treated): responders 61.0%, 76.3% and 70.0% vs 45.7% on placebo and 78.3% on morphine; GI events up to 78.8% at the top regimen
cards.people: 401 patients treated after abdominoplasty in a phase III double-blind trial received a loading dose of placebo, oliceridine 1.5 mg or morphine 4 mg, then patient-controlled demand doses (oliceridine 0.1, 0.35 or 0.5 mg; morphine 1 mg; placebo) with a 6-minute lockout. Primary endpoint: proportion of treatment responders over 24 hours versus placebo.
cards.result: Responder rates were 61.0%, 76.3% and 70.0% for the oliceridine regimens versus 45.7% on placebo (all p<0.05) and 78.3% on morphine; the 0.35 mg and 0.5 mg regimens were equi-analgesic to morphine by non-inferiority analysis. Respiratory safety burden rose with dose (means 0.43, 1.48 and 1.59 hours; placebo 0.60; morphine 1.72, the only arm significantly above placebo). Gastrointestinal adverse events rose with dose (49.4%, 65.8%, 78.8%; placebo 47.0%; morphine 79.3%), though nausea or vomiting was less frequent on the two equi-analgesic oliceridine regimens than on morphine.
cards.watchOut: The placebo responder rate (45.7%) and placebo GI rate (47.0%) are high, compressing every contrast; and at the most effective doses oliceridine's GI burden is essentially morphine's. The respiratory separation is again a point-estimate pattern, not a significant difference versus morphine.

cards.headline: ATHENA open-label safety study (768 patients): nausea 31%, constipation 11%, vomiting 10%; no deaths or significant cardiorespiratory events reported
cards.summary: ATHENA open-label safety study (768 patients): nausea 31%, constipation 11%, vomiting 10%; no deaths or significant cardiorespiratory events reported
cards.people: 768 adults with moderate-to-severe acute pain (pain score ≥4 of 11) requiring parenteral opioids — 94% surgical (orthopaedic 30%, colorectal 15%, gynaecologic 15%), mean age 54.1 years, 32% aged ≥65 — received intravenous oliceridine by bolus or patient-controlled analgesia, with multimodal analgesia permitted (84%). No control group.
cards.result: Pain scores fell by 2.2 points within 30 minutes (from 6.3) and the reduction was maintained to the end of treatment. No deaths or significant cardiorespiratory events were reported; adverse events led to early discontinuation in 2% and serious adverse events occurred in 3%. The commonest adverse events were nausea (31%), constipation (11%) and vomiting (10%), mostly mild (37%) or moderate (25%); 33% of patients had an event judged possibly or probably drug-related.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and uncontrolled, with multimodal analgesia in 84%: ATHENA can describe tolerability in real-world-style use but cannot show oliceridine is safer than morphine or any other opioid — there is no comparator.
cards.source: Bergese SD et al. ATHENA: A Phase 3, Open-Label Study Of The Safety And Effectiveness Of Oliceridine (TRV130), A G-Protein Selective Agonist At The µ-Opioid Receptor, In Patients With Moderate To Severe Acute Pain Requiring Parenteral Opioid Therapy. cards.headline: Synthesis: analgesia is proven; the 'safer opioid' claim is only half-proven — GI advantage is partial, respiratory advantage unproven
cards.summary: Synthesis: analgesia is proven; the 'safer opioid' claim is only half-proven — GI advantage is partial, respiratory advantage unproven
cards.people: APOLLO-1 (bunionectomy), APOLLO-2 (abdominoplasty, 401 treated) and ATHENA (768 patients, open-label) — the complete phase 3 programme for intravenous oliceridine in acute pain.
cards.result: Oliceridine beat placebo clearly in both blinded trials and matched morphine at the 0.35/0.5 mg demand doses. Against that: respiratory safety burden never significantly differed from morphine, and gastrointestinal events at effective doses approached morphine's rates (70.9–78.8% vs 72.4–79.3%), with nausea/vomiting and antiemetic use — not total GI burden — favouring oliceridine. POSSIBLE (benefit) as an analgesic; the respiratory-sparing claim should not be stated as demonstrated.
cards.watchOut: Both blinded trials are single-surgery models with sponsor-run composites; patients at highest respiratory risk are exactly those least represented in 24–48-hour postoperative trials.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards above. No new data.

shelves.title: Vixotrigine for trigeminal neuralgia (PARTIAL — pack #5940 covers standard drugs; PHASE 2a ONLY): the prespecified primary endpoint was NOT met — treatment failure 33% vs 64%, p=0.097, in 29 randomised responders
shelves.question: In adults with trigeminal neuralgia, does vixotrigine (a state-dependent sodium-channel blocker, formerly raxatrigine) reduce paroxysmal pain versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Area Under Curve · Double-Blind Method · Electrocardiography · Female · Humans · International Cooperation · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Phenyl Ethers/pharmacology,therapeutic use · Proline/analogs & derivatives,pharmacology,therapeutic use · Retrospective Studies · Sodium Channel Blockers/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Trigeminal Neuralgia/drug therapy · Young Adult
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of pack #5940, which asks the standard-drug guideline question (carbamazepine first, on the AAN–EFNS parameter); no PMID homed there is re-carded here — vixotrigine appears on #5940 only as a passing 'under development' mention inside a review card. PHASE-2-ONLY FLAG: the entire randomised efficacy record for vixotrigine (BIIB074) in trigeminal neuralgia is one phase 2a randomised-withdrawal trial (Zakrzewska 2017). Of 67 patients entering open-label treatment, 29 responders were randomised; the prespecified primary endpoint — treatment failure in the double-blind phase — occurred in 5 of 15 (33%) on vixotrigine versus 9 of 14 (64%) on placebo, p=0.0974: NOT met on the prespecified analysis (the difference was not statistically significant). Pain signals in secondary measures are reported in the trial's full text and are labelled secondary wherever this shelf refers to them; the abstract record carded here prints no secondary pain numbers, so none are quoted. Tolerability was good (headache 19% in the open-label phase; double-blind adverse events similar to placebo; no severe or serious events on drug in the double-blind phase). Two phase 3 enriched-withdrawal trials were designed (Kotecha 2020) but no phase 3 results report was found in this session's PubMed search. A missed primary in 29 randomised patients cannot carry a benefit stamp: UNLIKELY (benefit) on current evidence, with the favourable point estimate printed in full so the reader can judge the near-miss for themselves.

cards.headline: Zakrzewska 2017 phase 2a (randomised-withdrawal; 29 randomised): primary endpoint NOT met — treatment failure 5 of 15 (33%) on vixotrigine vs 9 of 14 (64%) on placebo, p=0.0974
cards.summary: Zakrzewska 2017 phase 2a (randomised-withdrawal; 29 randomised): primary endpoint NOT met — treatment failure 5 of 15 (33%) on vixotrigine vs 9 of 14 (64%) on placebo, p=0.0974
cards.people: Adults aged 18–80 with confirmed trigeminal neuralgia at 25 centres in 12 countries. After a 7-day run-in, 67 patients received open-label vixotrigine (BIIB074) 150 mg three times daily for 21 days; the 44 who completed open-label treatment and met at least one response criterion were eligible, and 29 were randomised (15 vixotrigine, 14 placebo) to up to 28 days of double-blind treatment. Primary endpoint: the proportion classified as treatment failure during the double-blind phase (modified intention-to-treat). The randomised denominator is 29 open-label responders — not all 67 who started.
cards.result: Treatment failure occurred in 5 of 15 patients (33%) on vixotrigine versus 9 of 14 (64%) on placebo (p=0.0974) — the primary endpoint was not significantly lower on vixotrigine, so the prespecified primary analysis did NOT meet its endpoint (the treatment's advantage was not demonstrated). The authors conclude the findings provide a basis for continued investigation in future trials. Secondary pain measures in the full report favoured vixotrigine and are labelled secondary; the abstract record prints no secondary pain numbers, so this shelf quotes none.
cards.watchOut: A near-miss in a tiny enriched sample cuts both ways: 29 randomised responders cannot exclude a real effect, and the 31-percentage-point gap in failure rates is exactly the kind of point estimate small withdrawal trials overstate. What is certain is the formal record: primary not met, phase 2a only.

cards.headline: Zakrzewska 2017 tolerability record (same trial): headache in 19% during open-label treatment; double-blind adverse events similar to placebo; no severe or serious events on vixotrigine in the double-blind phase
cards.summary: Zakrzewska 2017 tolerability record (same trial): headache in 19% during open-label treatment; double-blind adverse events similar to placebo; no severe or serious events on vixotrigine in the double-blind phase
cards.type: Safety report within the phase 2a trial (Zakrzewska 2017)
cards.people: All 67 patients who received at least one dose of open-label vixotrigine 150 mg three times daily (safety population), and the 29 randomised patients in the double-blind phase (15 vixotrigine, 14 placebo).
cards.result: In the open-label phase the commonest adverse events on vixotrigine were headache (13 of 67, 19%) and dizziness (6 of 67, 9%); 44 of 67 completed open-label treatment. In the double-blind phase, adverse events were similar between groups — headache, pyrexia, nasopharyngitis, sleep disorder and tremor each occurred in one of 15 vixotrigine patients (7%), as did headache, dizziness, diarrhoea and vomiting in one of 14 placebo patients each — and no severe or serious adverse events were reported in the vixotrigine group (one placebo patient had a serious event judged unrelated). The drug required no titration, unlike carbamazepine.
cards.watchOut: Tolerability in 67 short-term patients, pre-selected by an open-label phase that non-tolerators could leave, cannot establish safety in chronic use — it establishes only that the phase 2a programme was not stopped by its side effects.

cards.result: This paper describes the two planned phase 3 studies and their rationale; it reports no efficacy or safety results. shelves.title: Central versus peripheral fatigue: comparing voluntary force with electrically evoked force partitions the loss — in sustained maximal contractions a central (drive) component is demonstrable in most subjects, voluntary activation can fall to ~91%, and TMS put the central share at one-quarter of the force fall in fatigued elbow flexors
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how is fatiguing voluntary muscle contraction divided between peripheral failure (the muscle itself) and central failure (falling voluntary activation), and how is each measured — twitch interpolation, superimposed electrical stimulation and post-exercise potentiated twitches?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Electric Stimulation/methods · Electromyography · Fatigue/physiopathology · Female · Humans · Isometric Contraction/physiology · Male · Middle Aged · Motor Cortex/physiology · Motor Neurons/physiology · Muscle Contraction/physiology · Muscle Fatigue/physiology · Reference Values
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology). The textbook account: fatigue of a voluntary contraction has two sites — peripheral, failure of the muscle's own force-generating machinery (shown by a fall in force evoked by electrical stimulation), and central, a fall in voluntary activation (shown when stimulation superimposed on a maximal effort adds force the subject could not produce voluntarily). The carded human studies built and quantified that partition: voluntary versus 50 Hz tetanic force in quadriceps (Bigland-Ritchie 1978); cortical stimulation localising part of the central failure above the motor cortex (Gandevia 1996); train-versus-twitch sensitivity of the central activation ratio (Kent-Braun 1996); and TMS-based activation accounting for one-quarter of the force fall (Todd 2003). Refusal: Merton 1954 (PMID 13152698), the twitch-interpolation foundation, was verified by title search but its PubMed record carries an empty abstract, so it is NOT carded and no numbers are attributed to it. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Bigland-Ritchie 1978: in 9 subjects, voluntary quadriceps force sometimes fell in parallel with electrically tetanised force (peripheral) and sometimes faster (central fatigue present)
cards.summary: Bigland-Ritchie 1978: in 9 subjects, voluntary quadriceps force sometimes fell in parallel with electrically tetanised force (peripheral) and sometimes faster (central fatigue present)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (twitch/tetanus interpolation in sustained MVC) — N = 9 (small N, labelled on the face)
cards.people: 9 healthy subjects sustaining maximum voluntary contractions of the quadriceps for 60 seconds, voluntary force compared throughout with force from brief tetanic stimulation at 50 Hz, with surface EMG recorded.
cards.result: In three subjects voluntary force declined in parallel with the tetanic force — the muscle itself was failing and drive was maintained. In the remainder voluntary force fell more rapidly than tetanic force, indicating central fatigue. In those with little central fatigue, surface EMG stayed approximately constant while force fell by about 60%; in those with central fatigue EMG and force fell in parallel, and an extra effort could briefly restore force with a proportionately greater EMG increase. Neuromuscular-junction failure was not the limiter in this muscle.
cards.watchOut: Classic small study: N=9 is printed on the face. The central/peripheral split differed between subjects in the same protocol — the card reports that heterogeneity rather than a single partition percentage, because the record gives none.
cards.source: Bigland-Ritchie B et al. Central and peripheral fatigue in sustained maximum voluntary contractions of human quadriceps muscle. Clinical science and molecular medicine. 1978. PMID: 657729. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Gandevia 1996: during sustained elbow-flexor MVCs, voluntary activation fell from >99% to 90.7%, and cortical stimulation could add up to 9.8% extra force — output from the motor cortex had become suboptimal
cards.summary: Gandevia 1996: during sustained elbow-flexor MVCs, voluntary activation fell from >99% to 90.7%, and cortical stimulation could add up to 9.8% extra force — output from the motor cortex had become suboptimal
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (cortical and motor-point stimulation during fatigue) — N not stated in the fetched record
cards.people: Human subjects performing sustained isometric maximum voluntary contractions of the elbow flexors, with stimulation of the motor point of biceps brachii and magnetic stimulation of the motor cortex; a cuff-ischaemia protocol tested recovery after the sustained contraction. (Number of subjects not stated in the fetched record.)
cards.result: The force increment from motor-point stimulation grew during sustained MVCs — motoneuronal output had become suboptimal. Voluntary activation of biceps fell from an average of >99% to 90.7% during 3-minute MVCs. The increment from magnetic cortical stimulation was initially 1.0% but rose to 9.8% during a 2-minute MVC, showing cortical output itself was not optimal at the time of stimulation. Neither force nor voluntary activation recovered during maintained ischaemia after the contraction, although fatigue-induced changes in EMG responses to cortical stimulation recovered rapidly despite ischaemia.
cards.watchOut: N is not documented in the fetched abstract and is printed as such. 'Central fatigue' here is operational — a fall in voluntary activation measured by superimposed stimulation — not a subjective sense of effort.
cards.source: Gandevia SC et al. Supraspinal factors in human muscle fatigue: evidence for suboptimal output from the motor cortex. The Journal of physiology. 1996. PMID: 8821149. cards.headline: Kent-Braun 1996: a superimposed high-frequency train detected central activation failure that single or double twitches missed — central activation ratio 0.76–0.89 by train versus 0.96–1.00 by twitch
cards.summary: Kent-Braun 1996: a superimposed high-frequency train detected central activation failure that single or double twitches missed — central activation ratio 0.76–0.89 by train versus 0.96–1.00 by twitch
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (superimposed-stimulation method comparison) — N = 7 healthy (plus 13 ALS patients and 5 fatigued healthy subjects)
cards.people: Three groups: 7 healthy subjects, 13 patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and 5 healthy subjects after fatiguing exercise; single, double and high-frequency train (50 Hz, 500 or 1,000 ms) stimuli to the peroneal nerve superimposed on maximum voluntary dorsiflexor contractions, quantified as the central activation ratio, CAR = MVC/(MVC + stimulated force).
cards.result: For all three groups the CAR was significantly lower with the train of stimuli (means 0.76–0.89) than with single or double stimuli (means 0.96–1.00) — a superimposed high-frequency train is the more sensitive indicator of central activation failure during isometric MVCs. The healthy-group values anchor the method: near-complete activation by twitch criteria can still conceal incomplete activation that a train reveals.
cards.watchOut: The CAR ranges pool the three groups and three train durations as the record reports them; the card does not assign a single CAR to healthy fresh muscle, because the record does not separate it that way.
cards.source: Kent-Braun JA et al. Quantitation of central activation failure during maximal voluntary contractions in humans. Muscle & nerve. 1996. PMID: 8965840. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Todd 2003: transcranial magnetic stimulation measured voluntary activation linearly across 50–100% efforts, and with fatigue the central component accounted for one-quarter of the fall in maximal force
cards.summary: Todd 2003: transcranial magnetic stimulation measured voluntary activation linearly across 50–100% efforts, and with fatigue the central component accounted for one-quarter of the fall in maximal force
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (TMS versus nerve twitch interpolation, fresh and fatigued) — N = 8 + 8 in two studies
cards.people: Two studies of 8 subjects each contracting the elbow flexors isometrically: submaximal and maximal test contractions when fresh, and sustained maximal contractions reducing force to 60% of initial followed by brief test contractions; force responses to TMS of the motor cortex and to electrical stimulation of the biceps motor nerve compared.
cards.result: For fresh and fatigued muscle, the superimposed twitch from both nerve and cortical stimulation decreased as contraction strength rose; for TMS the relation was linear over 50–100% of maximum (r² = 1.00), so voluntary activation could be derived from the extrapolated resting twitch. Voluntary activation was high in fresh maximal efforts by both methods; with fatigue both showed reduced activation, and central fatigue measured with TMS accounted for one-quarter of the fall in maximal voluntary force — the remaining three-quarters being peripheral, in the muscle and its excitation.
cards.watchOut: Elbow flexors, isometric: the one-quarter central share is for this muscle group and protocol (sustained MVC to 60% force), not a universal partition for all muscles or exercise modes.
cards.source: Todd G et al. Measurement of voluntary activation of fresh and fatigued human muscles using transcranial magnetic stimulation. The Journal of physiology. 2003. PMID: 12909682. cards.headline: Synthesis: twitch interpolation partitions fatigue — the superimposed twitch that appears as a contraction fatigues is the central share; the fall in the potentiated resting twitch is the peripheral share
cards.summary: Synthesis: twitch interpolation partitions fatigue — the superimposed twitch that appears as a contraction fatigues is the central share; the fall in the potentiated resting twitch is the peripheral share
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded human studies, framed by Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology (muscle/neuromuscular chapters). No new data.
cards.result: When voluntary force falls in parallel with electrically evoked force, the failure is in the muscle; when voluntary force falls faster, drive has failed centrally (PMID 657729). Cortical stimulation shows part of that central failure is supraspinal — activation fell to ~91% in sustained elbow-flexor efforts and cortex stimulation could add ~10% force (PMID 8821149). Method matters: a superimposed train exposes activation failure that single twitches miss (PMID 8965840), and TMS-based activation put the central share at one-quarter of the force fall in fatigued elbow flexors (PMID 12909682). Merton's 1954 twitch-interpolation foundation paper was verified by title search this session but its PubMed record carries no abstract, so it is not carded and no numbers are attributed to it. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
