synthesis synthesis of the carded human studies, framed by ganong's review of medical physiology and boron & boulpaep medical physiology (muscle/neuromuscular chapters). no new data. when voluntary force falls in parallel with electrically evoked force, the failure is in the muscle; when voluntary force falls faster, drive has failed centrally (pmid 657729). cortical stimulation shows part of that central failure is supraspinal — activation fell to ~91% in sustained elbow-flexor efforts and cortex stimulation could add ~10% force (pmid 8821149). method matters: a superimposed train exposes activation failure that single twitches miss (pmid 8965840), and tms-based activation put the central share at one-quarter of the force fall in fatigued elbow flexors (pmid 12909682). merton's 1954 twitch-interpolation foundation paper was verified by title search this session but its pubmed record carries no abstract, so it is not carded and no numbers are attributed to it. proposed stamp: physiology — established. scope: whole-limb voluntary fatigue partitioning in healthy humans. motor-unit loss with ageing is pack #6206 and diaphragm fatigue specifically is pack #6355 — neighbours, not homes for this question. synthesis of the cards on this shelf (pmids 657729, 8821149, 8965840, 12909682), framed by ganong's review of medical physiology and boron & boulpaep medical physiology. no additional source.

shelves.title: Prasinezumab in early Parkinson's disease (PASADENA and PADOVA)
shelves.question: In adults with early-stage Parkinson's disease, does the anti-α-synuclein antibody prasinezumab, compared with placebo, slow clinical progression on the MDS-UPDRS?
shelves.balance: Two randomised programmes, two missed primary endpoints — the shelf leads with that. PASADENA (phase 2, n = 316, largely treatment-naive or MAO-B-inhibitor patients) missed its primary endpoint (change in MDS-UPDRS parts I+II+III at week 52) at both doses. PADOVA (phase 2b, n = 586, patients on stable symptomatic medication) missed its primary endpoint too (time to confirmed motor progression: HR 0.84; p = 0.066). PREMISE CORRECTION to the slate: PADOVA existed only as sponsor/congress material at mining time, but at build it is a full journal report in The Lancet (PMID 42208564, verified from the fetched record) and is therefore carded as published evidence, not fenced as congress-reported — the developer may wish to note the change. What remains positive is exploratory: smaller Part III motor-score increases during PASADENA's double-blind year, and an open-label extension analysis against an external observational comparator (PMI/PPMI cohort) suggesting sustained separation — a non-randomised comparison that cannot confirm efficacy. Infusion reactions were common in PASADENA (19% and 34% by dose). Class lesson: prasinezumab's sister anti-α-synuclein antibody cinpanemab also missed definitively in its phase 2 programme (SPARK) — that shelf is being built this wave as #6729 and is cross-pointed here in prose; two antibodies against the same target have now missed their primaries, which is the honest state of the anti-synuclein antibody hypothesis in early Parkinson's disease. A phase 3 trial (PARAISO) is ongoing per the PADOVA report.

cards.headline: PASADENA 2022 (primary report): prasinezumab had no meaningful effect on MDS-UPDRS progression at week 52 — the primary endpoint was missed at both doses, n = 316
cards.summary: PASADENA 2022 (primary report): prasinezumab had no meaningful effect on MDS-UPDRS progression at week 52 — the primary endpoint was missed at both doses, n = 316
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (PASADENA), N Engl J Med 2022
cards.people: 316 participants with early-stage Parkinson's disease randomised 1:1:1 to intravenous placebo (105), prasinezumab 1500 mg (105) or prasinezumab 4500 mg (106) every 4 weeks for 52 weeks. Primary endpoint: change from baseline to week 52 in the sum of MDS-UPDRS parts I, II and III scores (range 0–236; higher = greater impairment). Funded by F. Hoffmann-La Roche and Prothena Biosciences.
cards.result: Mean (±SE) change in MDS-UPDRS total score was 9.4 ± 1.2 on placebo, 7.4 ± 1.2 on 1500 mg (difference vs placebo −2.0; 80% CI −4.2 to 0.2; P = 0.24) and 8.8 ± 1.2 on 4500 mg (difference −0.6; 80% CI −2.8 to 1.6; P = 0.72) — neither dose separated significantly from placebo. There was no substantial difference in dopamine transporter levels on SPECT, and most clinical secondary endpoints were similar between groups. Serious adverse events occurred in 6.7% (1500 mg) and 7.5% (4500 mg); infusion reactions occurred in 19.0% and 34.0% respectively.
cards.watchOut: Missed primary endpoint, printed on the face as required. The confidence intervals reported are 80% intervals (the trial's prespecified convention) — do not read them as 95% intervals.
cards.source: PASADENA — Pagano G, Taylor KI, Anzures-Cabrera J, et al. Trial of Prasinezumab in Early-Stage Parkinson's Disease. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2022. PMID: 35921451. Registry ID: NCT03100149. cards.headline: PASADENA open-label extension 2024: motor scores separated from an EXTERNAL observational comparator over 4 years — exploratory, non-randomised, and not confirmatory
cards.summary: PASADENA open-label extension 2024: motor scores separated from an EXTERNAL observational comparator over 4 years — exploratory, non-randomised, and not confirmatory
cards.type: Open-label extension with external comparator (PASADENA OLE), Nat Med 2024
cards.people: PASADENA participants who entered the open-label extension (delayed-start n = 94; early-start n = 177), compared not with the trial's own placebo group (no longer on placebo) but with an external comparator arm drawn from the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative observational study (n = 303). Outcomes: change in MDS-UPDRS Part III (OFF and ON states) and Part II over 4 years from trial start.
cards.result: The delayed-start and early-start groups showed smaller increases (slower decline) in MDS-UPDRS Part III OFF-state scores (−51% and −65% relative differences vs the external comparator), ON-state scores (−94% and −118%) and Part II scores (−48% and −40%) than the external comparator. The authors label this an exploratory analysis requiring confirmation in future studies.
cards.watchOut: External-comparator, open-label, exploratory: differences of −51% to −118% are relative differences against a non-randomised cohort and are exactly the kind of signal that the randomised PADOVA trial was designed to test — and PADOVA missed its primary endpoint (next card).
cards.source: PASADENA open-label extension — Pagano G, Monnet A, Reyes A, et al. Sustained effect of prasinezumab on Parkinson's disease motor progression in the open-label extension of the PASADENA trial. Nature Medicine. 2024. PMID: 39379705. Registry ID: NCT03100149. cards.headline: PADOVA (phase 2b, published in full at build): time to confirmed motor progression HR 0.84 (95% CI 0.69 to 1.01; p = 0.066) — the primary endpoint was NOT met, n = 586
cards.summary: PADOVA (phase 2b, published in full at build): time to confirmed motor progression HR 0.84 (95% CI 0.69 to 1.01; p = 0.066) — the primary endpoint was NOT met, n = 586
cards.type: Phase 2b randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (PADOVA), Lancet 2026
cards.people: 586 participants with early-stage Parkinson's disease (age 50–85, 3 months to 3 years from diagnosis, Hoehn and Yahr stage 1–2) on stable symptomatic medication, randomised 1:1 (293 per group) to intravenous prasinezumab 1500 mg or placebo every 4 weeks for at least 76 weeks, at 110 centres in nine countries in Europe and North America. Primary endpoint: time to a confirmed motor progression event (≥5-point increase in MDS-UPDRS Part III off-medication score). Funded by F. Hoffmann-La Roche.
cards.result: The primary endpoint was not met: hazard ratio 0.84 (95% CI 0.69 to 1.01; p = 0.066) — a relative measure whose interval includes 1. Median time to confirmed motor progression was 61.1 weeks (95% CI 52.3 to 71.9) on prasinezumab vs 49.7 weeks (40.1 to 58.1) on placebo. Serious adverse events were similar (34 [12%] of 292 vs 34 [12%] of 290) and three deaths were recorded as unrelated to study drug. The authors note prespecified exploratory evidence of clinical activity and an ongoing phase 3 trial (PARAISO, NCT07174310).
cards.watchOut: PREMISE CORRECTION: at slate-mining time PADOVA existed only as sponsor/congress material and the row instructed congress-only mention; at build it is verified as a full Lancet journal report and is carded as such. Its result is a missed primary endpoint — the HR 0.84 must always travel with p = 0.066 and its confidence interval.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two programmes, two missed primaries — prasinezumab has not been shown to slow Parkinson's progression (PMIDs 35921451, 39379705, 42208564)
cards.summary: Synthesis: two programmes, two missed primaries — prasinezumab has not been shown to slow Parkinson's progression (PMIDs 35921451, 39379705, 42208564)
cards.people: Adults with early-stage Parkinson's disease; randomised base 902 patients (PASADENA 316 + PADOVA 586), plus a 271-patient open-label extension compared with 303 external observational controls.
cards.result: Neither randomised trial met its primary endpoint (the treatment made no difference at the prespecified standard in either programme). The remaining case rests on exploratory motor-subscore signals and a non-randomised external-comparator extension analysis; a phase 3 trial is ongoing. The class lesson — a second anti-α-synuclein antibody, cinpanemab, also failed its phase 2 programme — is homed in the companion shelf #6729 (built this wave), cross-pointed here in prose. Synthesis rests on PMIDs 35921451, 39379705 and 42208564.
cards.watchOut: Stamp records a null: do not upgrade on the extension analysis or on PADOVA's exploratory subgroups. PADOVA's publication status changed between slate and build and is flagged in the balance and the part summary.

shelves.title: SPARK: cinpanemab made no difference in early Parkinson's disease — every dose matched placebo on the MDS-UPDRS and DaT-SPECT, and development was discontinued
shelves.question: In adults with early Parkinson's disease, does the anti-alpha-synuclein antibody cinpanemab, versus placebo, slow progression on the MDS-UPDRS or DaT-SPECT?
shelves.balance: SPARK (Lang et al., PMID 35921450) randomised 357 people with early Parkinson's disease to placebo or cinpanemab 250/1250/3500 mg every 4 weeks: MDS-UPDRS total score worsened 10.8 points on placebo vs 10.5, 11.3 and 10.9 points on the three doses at week 52 (all differences non-significant), DaT-SPECT showed no separation, and the trial was stopped after the week-72 interim analysis for lack of efficacy, after which development was discontinued. The biomarker companion report (PMID 38315945) found no treatment effect on any CSF, plasma or imaging measure. A phase 1 CSF analysis (PMID 39892989) shows the antibody did engage alpha-synuclein in the central compartment, dose-dependently — so this is target engagement without clinical benefit, the same pattern as the second anti-alpha-synuclein antibody programme, prasinezumab, homed on Shelf #6728 (built this wave): two antibodies, two missed programmes, and a mechanism-concordant meta-analysis of both (PMID 42992461; n=673) pooling to a mean difference of -0.047 (95% CI -0.202 to 0.108). PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: SPARK 2022: MDS-UPDRS worsened 10.8 points on placebo vs 10.5 / 11.3 / 10.9 on cinpanemab — no dose differed from placebo, and DaT-SPECT showed no separation
cards.summary: SPARK 2022: MDS-UPDRS worsened 10.8 points on placebo vs 10.5 / 11.3 / 10.9 on cinpanemab — no dose differed from placebo, and DaT-SPECT showed no separation
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial (SPARK, Lang 2022)
cards.people: 357 participants with early Parkinson's disease randomised 2:1:2:2 to intravenous placebo (n=100) or cinpanemab 250 mg (n=55), 1250 mg (n=102) or 3500 mg (n=100) every 4 weeks for 52 weeks, followed by a dose-blinded active-treatment extension; the trial was stopped after the week-72 interim analysis for lack of efficacy.
cards.result: Change in MDS-UPDRS total score at week 52: 10.8 points on placebo vs 10.5 (250 mg), 11.3 (1250 mg) and 10.9 (3500 mg) — adjusted differences vs placebo -0.3 (95% CI -4.9 to 4.3; P=0.90), 0.5 (-3.3 to 4.3; P=0.80) and 0.1 (-3.8 to 4.0; P=0.97). Week-72 comparisons were likewise null, secondary endpoints matched the primary, and DaT-SPECT at week 52 showed no difference between any cinpanemab group and placebo. The most common adverse events were headache, nasopharyngitis and falls.
cards.watchOut: A definitively negative phase 2 trial: every dose, every clinical scale and the imaging endpoint agree. This is a settled negative at phase 2 scale, not a maybe — and development of cinpanemab was discontinued after it.
cards.source: SPARK (Lang AE et al.) Trial of Cinpanemab in Early Parkinson's Disease. N Engl J Med. 2022. PMID: 35921450. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03318523. cards.headline: SPARK biomarker report 2024: no cinpanemab effect on any biomarker — alpha-synuclein seeding stayed positive in 99% of participants through week 52
cards.summary: SPARK biomarker report 2024: no cinpanemab effect on any biomarker — alpha-synuclein seeding stayed positive in 99% of participants through week 52
cards.type: Biomarker companion report of a randomised phase 2 trial (SPARK, Hutchison 2024)
cards.people: The same 357 SPARK participants (diagnosed within 3 years, aged 40-80, modified Hoehn and Yahr <=2.5, with striatal dopaminergic deficit on imaging); DaT-SPECT and MRI quantified the nigrostriatal pathway and regional atrophy, and CSF/plasma assays measured total alpha-synuclein, alpha-synuclein seeding and neurofilament light chain. Labelled as a second, distinct report of the SPARK trial (PMID 35921450 is the primary report, carded above).
cards.result: At baseline, 93% (110/118) of the CSF subgroup were alpha-synuclein seed-positive and 99% of them remained positive at week 52. Clinical progression occurred but did not differ between cinpanemab and placebo groups, and no statistically significant between-group changes were seen across any biomarker measure; about 3.8% (15/398) of SPECT-imaged participants had no dopaminergic deficit and were screen-failed.
cards.watchOut: The biomarker null matters: the drug did not merely miss a clinical scale — it moved nothing measurable in CSF, plasma or imaging either, so a dosing or duration rescue of this programme has no biomarker foothold.

cards.headline: Phase 1 CSF analysis 2025: cinpanemab DID bind alpha-synuclein in human cerebrospinal fluid, dose-dependently — target engagement without clinical benefit
cards.summary: Phase 1 CSF analysis 2025: cinpanemab DID bind alpha-synuclein in human cerebrospinal fluid, dose-dependently — target engagement without clinical benefit
cards.people: Cerebrospinal fluid samples from a phase 1 single-ascending-dose study of cinpanemab (BIIB054): 46 healthy volunteers and 18 people with Parkinson's disease. A zero-length crosslinking assay was developed because the drug-target complexes dissociate too fast for conventional measurement.
cards.result: Dose- and time-dependent cinpanemab-alpha-synuclein complexes were measurable in CSF at doses >=15 mg/kg, and complex formation correlated directly with drug concentration (Spearman rank correlation 0.8295 in healthy volunteers and 0.8032 in Parkinson's disease; P<0.0001 for both) — the first demonstration of alpha-synuclein binding by an antibody in human central nervous system samples.
cards.watchOut: Engagement is not efficacy: this small laboratory analysis (64 sample sets) shows the antibody reached and bound its target in CSF, which makes the SPARK clinical null harder to explain away as a delivery failure.

cards.headline: Meta-analysis 2026: pooling the two anti-alpha-synuclein antibody trials (cinpanemab + prasinezumab, n=673) gives a mean difference of -0.047 — no benefit
cards.summary: Meta-analysis 2026: pooling the two anti-alpha-synuclein antibody trials (cinpanemab + prasinezumab, n=673) gives a mean difference of -0.047 — no benefit
cards.people: Systematic review of Parkinson's disease immunotherapy trials published 2010 to February 2026; four phase 2 randomised trials (n=960) contributed quantitative efficacy data, and the prespecified mechanism-concordant analysis pooled the two passive anti-alpha-synuclein antibody programmes (SPARK and PASADENA).
cards.result: Anti-alpha-synuclein antibodies showed no benefit: mean difference -0.047 (95% CI -0.202 to 0.108; I-squared=13%). An extended cross-mechanism synthesis adding azathioprine and venglustat was also null (standardised mean difference 0.038, 95% CI -0.123 to 0.198). The authors conclude randomised evidence does not currently support disease modification by immune-based therapy in Parkinson's disease.
cards.watchOut: A class-level synthesis, carded as context: it pools this shelf's trial with the prasinezumab programme homed on Shelf #6728 and must not be read as a second cinpanemab trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: engagement without benefit — SPARK was null on every clinical, imaging and biomarker measure, and the pooled antibody evidence is null
cards.summary: Synthesis: engagement without benefit — SPARK was null on every clinical, imaging and biomarker measure, and the pooled antibody evidence is null
cards.people: One phase 2 RCT (357 participants), its biomarker companion report, a phase 1 CSF target-engagement analysis (46 healthy volunteers, 18 patients), and a meta-analysis pooling 673 antibody-trial participants.
cards.result: MDS-UPDRS change at week 52: 10.8 on placebo vs 10.5-11.3 across cinpanemab doses (all P>=0.80); DaT-SPECT and all biomarkers null; pooled anti-alpha-synuclein antibody effect -0.047 (95% CI -0.202 to 0.108). PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: Phase-2-only evidence, and the answer is negative rather than uncertain: two anti-alpha-synuclein antibody programmes (cinpanemab here; prasinezumab on Shelf #6728) have now missed in the same way.

shelves.title: evoke and evoke+: oral semaglutide made no difference in early Alzheimer's disease — both phase 3 trials negative in 3,808 participants
shelves.question: In adults with early symptomatic Alzheimer's disease, does oral semaglutide 14 mg daily, versus placebo, slow decline on the CDR-SB over about 2 years?
shelves.balance: The evoke and evoke+ phase 3 trials (Cummings et al., PMID 41865758 — the PMID re-verified against its PubMed record at build time) randomised 3,808 people with amyloid-confirmed early Alzheimer's disease to oral semaglutide 14 mg daily or placebo: CDR-SB difference at week 104 was -0.08 (p=0.57) in evoke and +0.10 (p=0.46) in evoke+, and both trials were discontinued for the negative outcome. Adverse events were more frequent on semaglutide (91.2% vs 84.8%), gastrointestinal events dominate the older-adult safety profile (PMID 40337158), and weight loss — a liability in this population — was consistent. A 2026 meta-analysis of all seven GLP-1-agonist RCTs in Alzheimer's disease and MCI (PMID 42890838; 4,132 participants) is concordant: no cognitive or CDR-SB benefit. The shelf's value is closing the GLP-1-in-Alzheimer's question at phase 3 scale. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: evoke/evoke+ 2026: CDR-SB difference -0.08 (p=0.57) in evoke and +0.10 (p=0.46) in evoke+ — oral semaglutide did not slow early Alzheimer's disease in 3,808 participants
cards.summary: evoke/evoke+ 2026: CDR-SB difference -0.08 (p=0.57) in evoke and +0.10 (p=0.46) in evoke+ — oral semaglutide did not slow early Alzheimer's disease in 3,808 participants
cards.type: Two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials reported in one paper (evoke and evoke+, Cummings 2026)
cards.people: 3,808 participants aged 55-85 with amyloid-confirmed early Alzheimer's disease (mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia) across 566 sites in 40 countries, randomised 1:1 to oral semaglutide up to 14 mg daily or placebo: 1,855 in evoke (928 semaglutide, 927 placebo) and 1,953 in evoke+ (976 semaglutide, 977 placebo; evoke+ also admitted significant small-vessel pathology, present in 54 participants, 2.8%). Mean age 72.2 years; mean baseline CDR-SB 3.7. The cited PMID for this report was re-verified against the PubMed record at build time and matches this paper.
cards.result: Mean CDR-SB change to week 104: 2.3 on semaglutide vs 2.3 on placebo in evoke (estimated difference -0.08, 95% CI -0.35 to 0.20; p=0.57) and 2.2 vs 2.1 in evoke+ (difference 0.10, 95% CI -0.17 to 0.38; p=0.46). Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 91.2% (1,729/1,896) on semaglutide vs 84.8% (1,613/1,902) on placebo; five fatalities were considered treatment-related by investigators (one on semaglutide, four on placebo). Both trials were discontinued because of the negative clinical outcome.
cards.watchOut: Two large, concordant phase 3 nulls at the same dose and duration — this closes the oral-semaglutide-in-Alzheimer's question at phase 3 scale rather than leaving it open. The result is for oral semaglutide 14 mg in amyloid-confirmed early disease; it does not test injectable semaglutide or prevention in people without symptoms.
cards.source: evoke and evoke+ (Cummings JL et al.) Efficacy and safety of oral semaglutide 14 mg (flexible dose) in early-stage symptomatic Alzheimer's disease (evoke and evoke+): two phase 3, randomised, placebo-controlled trials. Lancet. 2026. PMID: 41865758. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04777396, ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04777409. cards.headline: Pooled safety analysis 2025 (3,529 participants aged >=65, from diabetes/obesity programmes): gastrointestinal events dominate; discontinuation for adverse events 9.3-12.4% in older adults
cards.summary: Pooled safety analysis 2025 (3,529 participants aged >=65, from diabetes/obesity programmes): gastrointestinal events dominate; discontinuation for adverse events 9.3-12.4% in older adults
cards.type: Post hoc pooled safety analysis of three phase 3a programmes (Sabbagh 2025)
cards.people: Post hoc pooled analysis of adverse-event data from three semaglutide phase 3a programmes (type 2 diabetes and/or overweight/obesity) in 3,529 participants aged >=65 years (mean age 69.3-70.2 years), written specifically to inform the safety interpretation of the evoke programme in older adults with Alzheimer's disease.
cards.result: Adverse events on semaglutide occurred in 73.6-92.4% of participants aged >=65 (vs 73.2-90.8% in the overall populations); events leading to permanent discontinuation were more frequent at >=65 (9.3-12.4% vs 5.7-8.7% overall). Gastrointestinal disorders were the commonest events in older adults (44.6-73.8%). In a subset, estimated weight change at week 52 was -3.8% on semaglutide vs 0.1% on placebo (a percentage weight change, not a relative risk).
cards.watchOut: Not an Alzheimer's trial: these are diabetes/obesity populations, carded for the safety profile an older Alzheimer's population would face — notably weight loss of about 3.8% of body weight, which carries a different meaning in frail people with dementia than in obesity trials.
cards.source: Pooled semaglutide safety analysis in adults aged 65 years and over (Sabbagh M et al.) Safety considerations of semaglutide in the potential treatment of Alzheimer's disease: A pooled analysis of semaglutide in adults aged ≥ 65 years. Alzheimers Dement (N Y). 2025. PMID: 40337158. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Meta-analysis 2026 (7 RCTs, 4,132 participants): GLP-1 agonists did not improve cognition (SMD -0.05) or CDR-SB (mean difference 0.09) in Alzheimer's disease or MCI
cards.summary: Meta-analysis 2026 (7 RCTs, 4,132 participants): GLP-1 agonists did not improve cognition (SMD -0.05) or CDR-SB (mean difference 0.09) in Alzheimer's disease or MCI
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Siqueira 2026)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials of GLP-1 receptor agonists versus placebo, standard care or non-intervention across the Alzheimer's continuum, searched to 22 April 2026; seven studies, 4,132 participants, mean age 72.1 years.
cards.result: No significant benefit on cognition (ADAS-Cog standardised mean difference -0.05, 95% CI -0.12 to 0.02; p=0.19) or disease progression (CDR-SB mean difference 0.09, 95% CI -0.10 to 0.28; p=0.36). Adverse events were more frequent on GLP-1 agonists (risk ratio 1.07 relative, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.10) and weight loss much more frequent (risk ratio 5.01 relative, 95% CI 3.99 to 6.27). Biomarker and imaging findings were inconsistent and did not translate into clinical benefit.
cards.watchOut: A class-level synthesis that includes the evoke programme among its seven studies — it corroborates the null rather than adding an independent semaglutide trial, and it pools different GLP-1 drugs and populations.
cards.source: Meta-analysis of GLP-1 receptor agonists in Alzheimer's disease and MCI (Siqueira RGP et al.) GLP-1 receptor agonists in Alzheimer's disease and MCI: a meta-analysis. Alzheimers Dement (N Y). 2026. PMID: 42890838. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

shelves.title: ELAD: liraglutide did not preserve cerebral glucose metabolism in Alzheimer's disease — the phase 2b primary outcome was negative, with only exploratory secondary signals
shelves.question: In adults with mild Alzheimer's disease, does liraglutide, versus placebo, preserve cerebral glucose metabolism, cognition or brain volume over 52 weeks?
shelves.balance: ELAD (Edison et al., PMID 41326666; the slate's 'Femminella' attribution is corrected by the PubMed record) randomised 204 people with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease without diabetes to daily liraglutide or placebo for 52 weeks and missed its primary outcome: cerebral glucose metabolic rate difference -0.17 (95% CI -0.39 to 0.06; p=0.14). The ADAS-Exec secondary favoured liraglutide (0.15; unadjusted p=0.01) but was unadjusted for multiplicity, and ADCS-ADL and CDR-Sum of Boxes were null. The earlier supporting trial (Gejl et al., PMIDs 27252647 and 29235507 — two reports of one 38-patient trial) found placebo-group metabolic decline that liraglutide appeared to prevent, and a rise in blood-brain glucose transfer capacity, but no cognitive change and no amyloid effect. Phase-2-only evidence; the small-trial surrogate story has not been confirmed at ELAD's scale. PROPOSED SPLIT, leaning negative on the primary outcome.

cards.headline: ELAD 2026: the primary FDG-PET outcome was negative (difference -0.17, p=0.14) — liraglutide did not preserve cerebral glucose metabolism in 204 participants
cards.summary: ELAD 2026: the primary FDG-PET outcome was negative (difference -0.17, p=0.14) — liraglutide did not preserve cerebral glucose metabolism in 204 participants
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2b trial (ELAD, Edison 2026)
cards.people: 204 participants with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease syndrome without diabetes, in a multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 2b trial of daily liraglutide injections or placebo for 52 weeks, with FDG-PET, MRI and detailed neuropsychometric testing. (The slate named this report as Femminella et al.; the PubMed record gives Edison P et al. as first author — the record governs.)
cards.result: Primary outcome (change in cerebral glucose metabolic rate): no significant difference (difference -0.17, 95% CI -0.39 to 0.06; P=0.14). The secondary ADAS-Exec score favoured liraglutide (0.15, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.28; unadjusted P=0.01), but ADCS-ADL (-0.58, 95% CI -3.13 to 1.97; unadjusted P=0.65) and CDR-Sum of Boxes (-0.06, 95% CI -0.57 to 0.44; unadjusted P=0.81) did not differ. Liraglutide was generally safe and well tolerated in these non-diabetic patients.
cards.watchOut: Phase-2-only evidence with a missed primary: the ADAS-Exec signal is a secondary outcome, unadjusted for multiplicity, sitting alongside two null functional/global secondaries — it must not outrun the primary on this shelf's face.
cards.source: ELAD (Edison P et al.) Liraglutide in mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease: a phase 2b clinical trial. Nat Med. 2026. PMID: 41326666. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01843075. cards.headline: Gejl 2016 (n=38): placebo patients' brain glucose metabolism declined significantly over 26 weeks while liraglutide patients' did not — but cognition did not change and amyloid load rose in both groups
cards.summary: Gejl 2016 (n=38): placebo patients' brain glucose metabolism declined significantly over 26 weeks while liraglutide patients' did not — but cognition did not change and amyloid load rose in both groups
cards.people: 38 patients with Alzheimer's disease randomised to liraglutide (n=18) or placebo (n=20) for 26 weeks, with amyloid imaging ([11C]PIB), FDG-PET cerebral glucose metabolism (CMRglc) and WMS-IV cognition.
cards.result: CMRglc declined significantly in the placebo group in precuneus, parietal, temporal and occipital regions and cerebellum, while the liraglutide group showed a numerical, non-significant increase; amyloid (PIB) binding increased significantly in both groups, with no between-group difference (P>=0.38). Cognitive scores did not change. The authors state the study was underpowered for amyloid and cognition conclusions.
cards.watchOut: A 38-patient imaging study: the 'prevented decline' framing rests on within-group significance patterns rather than a powered between-group difference, and the same trial shows amyloid still accumulating on treatment.
cards.source: Liraglutide FDG-PET trial (Gejl 2016) (Gejl M et al.) In Alzheimer's Disease, 6-Month Treatment with GLP-1 Analog Prevents Decline of Brain Glucose Metabolism: Randomized, Placebo-Controlled, Double-Blind Clinical Trial. Front Aging Neurosci. 2016. cards.headline: Gejl 2017: in the same 38-patient trial, liraglutide raised blood-brain glucose transfer capacity (Tmax) from 0.72 to 1.1 umol/g/min — a mechanism report, not a clinical outcome
cards.summary: Gejl 2017: in the same 38-patient trial, liraglutide raised blood-brain glucose transfer capacity (Tmax) from 0.72 to 1.1 umol/g/min — a mechanism report, not a clinical outcome
cards.type: Randomised trial mechanism report (Gejl 2017) — second report of the Gejl 2016 trial
cards.people: Second report of the same 38-patient randomised trial carded above (liraglutide n=18, placebo n=20, 6 months), analysing blood-brain glucose transfer capacity (Tmax), with a healthy age-matched comparison group of 6. Labelled as a second report of one trial — it is not an independent study.
cards.result: Baseline Tmax correlated inversely with Alzheimer's disease duration; liraglutide, compared with placebo, raised cortical Tmax estimates from 0.72 to 1.1 umol/g/min, equal to estimates in the healthy volunteers. The authors interpret this as restoration of glucose transport at the blood-brain barrier.
cards.watchOut: A transport-capacity surrogate in 38 patients (and 6 healthy comparators): even if the mechanism is real, ELAD's larger FDG-PET primary — the downstream metabolic readout — was negative, so the mechanism has not been shown to buy patients anything clinical.
cards.source: Blood-brain glucose transfer report (Gejl 2017) (Gejl M et al.) Blood-Brain Glucose Transfer in Alzheimer's disease: Effect of GLP-1 Analog Treatment. Sci Rep. 2017. PMID: 29235507. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: SNIFF: intranasal insulin made no difference in MCI and Alzheimer's dementia over 12 months — and the 5-trial meta-analysis agrees
shelves.question: In adults with amnestic MCI or Alzheimer's dementia, does daily intranasal insulin, versus placebo, improve cognition or function over 12 months?
shelves.balance: SNIFF (Craft et al., PMID 32568367) randomised 289 adults with amnestic MCI or Alzheimer's dementia to intranasal insulin 40 IU daily (Humulin R U-100, Lilly, as named in the record) or placebo for 12 months and found an ADAS-Cog12 difference of 0.03 points (p=0.98) in its primary cohort, with all clinical and CSF secondaries null. The delivery device is part of the intervention: the first device proved unreliable in the first 49 participants and was replaced; neither SNIFF device is named in the record, while the earlier positive pilot (PMID 21911655; n=104) used a device named in its record as Kurve Technology (Bothell, Washington). A secondary white-matter imaging analysis (PMID 34101779) and the pilot's memory signal were not borne out clinically, and a 2026 meta-analysis of five RCTs (PMID 41436338; 540 participants) found no benefit on any cognitive, functional or biomarker outcome. Presented as a settled negative at trial scale. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: SNIFF 2020: ADAS-Cog12 difference 0.03 points (p=0.98) — intranasal insulin made no difference over 12 months; the first delivery device proved unreliable and was replaced mid-trial
cards.summary: SNIFF 2020: ADAS-Cog12 difference 0.03 points (p=0.98) — intranasal insulin made no difference over 12 months; the first delivery device proved unreliable and was replaced mid-trial
cards.people: 289 adults aged 55-85 with amnestic mild cognitive impairment or Alzheimer's dementia randomised at 27 US sites to intranasal insulin 40 IU daily (insulin named in the record as Humulin R U-100, Lilly) or placebo for 12 months, plus a 6-month open-label extension. The first 49 participants used a first device with inconsistent reliability; the remaining 240, treated with a second device, form the primary intention-to-treat cohort. The record does not name either SNIFF delivery device.
cards.result: Primary outcome (ADAS-Cog12 change to month 12) in the device-2 cohort: difference 0.0258 points (95% CI -1.771 to 1.822; P=0.98). No differences on other clinical or cerebrospinal fluid outcomes in the primary analysis, and no clinically important adverse events were associated with treatment. 260 participants completed the blinded phase.
cards.watchOut: The device failure is part of the intervention's story: the primary cohort is the 240 participants treated after the device swap, and even in that cleaner cohort the effect estimate is almost exactly zero.
cards.source: SNIFF (Craft S et al.) Safety, Efficacy, and Feasibility of Intranasal Insulin for the Treatment of Mild Cognitive Impairment and Alzheimer Disease Dementia: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Neurol. 2020. PMID: 32568367. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01767909. cards.headline: Pilot 2012 (n=104): 20 IU intranasal insulin improved delayed memory (P<0.05) and both doses preserved caregiver-rated function over 4 months — the signal SNIFF was built to test
cards.summary: Pilot 2012 (n=104): 20 IU intranasal insulin improved delayed memory (P<0.05) and both doses preserved caregiver-rated function over 4 months — the signal SNIFF was built to test
cards.people: 104 adults with amnestic mild cognitive impairment (n=64) or mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease (n=40) at a Veterans Affairs clinical research unit, randomised to placebo (n=30), insulin 20 IU (n=36) or 40 IU (n=38) daily for 4 months, delivered with a nasal drug delivery device named in the record as Kurve Technology (Bothell, Washington).
cards.result: Delayed story recall improved with 20 IU (P<0.05); both insulin doses preserved caregiver-rated functional ability (P<0.01) and, in subgroups, general cognition (ADAS-Cog) and activities of daily living. CSF biomarkers did not change overall; placebo participants lost FDG uptake in parietotemporal, frontal, precuneus and cuneus regions while insulin minimised progression. No treatment-related severe adverse events occurred.
cards.watchOut: A 104-patient, 4-month pilot with several outcomes and subgroup findings — exactly the profile that needs a large confirmatory trial, and the confirmatory trial (SNIFF, carded above) found nothing.
cards.source: Intranasal insulin pilot trial (Craft 2012) (Craft S et al.) Intranasal insulin therapy for Alzheimer disease and amnestic mild cognitive impairment: a pilot clinical trial. cards.headline: SNIFF secondary analysis 2021: intranasal insulin reduced white-matter hyperintensity progression in a 49-participant analysis — a secondary imaging signal inside a negative trial
cards.summary: SNIFF secondary analysis 2021: intranasal insulin reduced white-matter hyperintensity progression in a 49-participant analysis — a secondary imaging signal inside a negative trial
cards.type: Secondary analysis of a randomised phase 2 trial (Kellar 2021)
cards.people: Secondary analyses of the SNIFF trial (same registry number, NCT01767909): 49 participants (32 men) enrolled in this analysis cohort, receiving intranasal insulin 20 IU twice daily or placebo for 12 months, with MRI white-matter hyperintensity (WMH) volumes related to CSF biomarkers and clinical scales. Labelled as a secondary analysis of the trial carded above, not an independent trial.
cards.result: The insulin group showed significantly reduced WMH volume change in deep and frontal regions after 12 months, with a similar trend for global volume; WMH progression correlated with worsening CSF biomarker profile and cognition, with correlation patterns differing by treatment group.
cards.watchOut: Secondary, multiplicity-prone and imaging-only: a WMH signal in 49 participants cannot overturn the same programme's null primary outcome in 240, and no clinical benefit accompanied it.
cards.source: SNIFF secondary analysis — white matter hyperintensities (Kellar 2021) (Kellar D et al.) Intranasal Insulin Reduces White Matter Hyperintensity Progression in Association with Improvements in Cognition and CSF Biomarker Profiles in Mild Cognitive Impairment and Alzheimer's Disease. cards.headline: Meta-analysis 2026 (5 RCTs, 540 participants): no significant benefit on any cognitive, functional or CSF biomarker outcome
cards.summary: Meta-analysis 2026 (5 RCTs, 540 participants): no significant benefit on any cognitive, functional or CSF biomarker outcome
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Silva 2026)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials of intranasal insulin versus placebo in mild cognitive impairment or mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease, searched to April 2025; five RCTs, 540 participants, Cochrane RoB 2 assessment.
cards.result: Pooled effects were non-significant for ADAS-Cog13 (mean difference -1.09, 95% CI -4.89 to 2.71), ADCS-ADL (0.06, 95% CI -0.33 to 0.45), CDR-SB, dementia severity rating and delayed recall, and for CSF Abeta42, total tau and p-tau181. Gastrointestinal adverse events were more frequent on insulin (risk ratio 1.57 relative, 95% CI 1.15 to 2.14); discontinuation rates were comparable. The authors conclude current evidence does not support routine clinical use.
cards.watchOut: The pooled estimate includes the positive pilot — and is still null — which is why this shelf reads as a settled negative at trial scale rather than an open question.
cards.source: Meta-analysis of intranasal insulin RCTs in MCI and Alzheimer's disease (Silva AMP et al.) Intranasal insulin for mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's disease: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Rev Neurol (Paris). 2026. PMID: 41436338. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a positive pilot, a null 289-participant trial, and a null 5-trial meta-analysis — a settled negative
cards.summary: Synthesis: a positive pilot, a null 289-participant trial, and a null 5-trial meta-analysis — a settled negative
cards.people: One phase 2/3 RCT (289 randomised; 240 in the primary cohort), one pilot RCT (104), a 49-participant secondary imaging analysis of the same large trial, and a meta-analysis of 5 RCTs (540 participants).
cards.result: SNIFF primary difference 0.03 ADAS-Cog12 points (p=0.98); pooled meta-analysis non-significant on every cognitive, functional and biomarker outcome. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: Delivery-device reliability is part of this intervention's evidence: the pilot's named device (Kurve Technology) and SNIFF's two unnamed devices are not interchangeable, and results should not be transferred to other intranasal devices or insulin formulations.

shelves.title: GEMINI 1 & 2: tolebrutinib was no better than teriflunomide for relapses in relapsing MS — a disability signal outside the testing hierarchy, and a liver-injury risk that needs weekly monitoring
shelves.question: In adults with relapsing MS, is the BTK inhibitor tolebrutinib superior to teriflunomide on relapses or disability worsening?
shelves.balance: Premise verified at build: Shelf #2849 holds tolebrutinib only for non-relapsing secondary progressive MS (HERCULES), and its trial (PMID 40202696) is not carded here. In relapsing MS, GEMINI 1 and GEMINI 2 (Oh et al., PMID 40202623; 1,873 participants) compared tolebrutinib 60 mg daily with teriflunomide 14 mg daily and missed their primary endpoint in both trials: annualised relapse rate ratios 1.06 and 1.00. The pooled 6-month confirmed disability worsening result (8.3% vs 11.3%; hazard ratio 0.71 relative) was a secondary outcome that received no formal hypothesis testing because the hierarchy stopped at the failed primary — a genuine signal, honestly labelled, not a demonstrated benefit. Phase 2b MRI data (PMID 34418400) show real anti-inflammatory activity that did not convert into relapse superiority. The safety price is hepatic: across 2,958 exposed participants programme-wide (PMID 42546561), ALT rose >3x ULN in 4.7%, six participants met Hy's-law criteria, and one died after liver transplantation; weekly liver testing for the first 12 weeks mitigates but does not remove the risk. PROPOSED SPLIT.

cards.headline: GEMINI 1 & 2 2025: tolebrutinib was NOT superior to teriflunomide for relapses (rate ratios 1.06 and 1.00) — the honest headline is 'no better than teriflunomide for relapses'
cards.summary: GEMINI 1 & 2 2025: tolebrutinib was NOT superior to teriflunomide for relapses (rate ratios 1.06 and 1.00) — the honest headline is 'no better than teriflunomide for relapses'
cards.type: Two randomised, double-blind, active-comparator phase 3 trials reported in one paper (GEMINI 1 and GEMINI 2, Oh 2025)
cards.people: 1,873 participants with relapsing multiple sclerosis in two phase 3 double-blind, double-dummy, event-driven trials — GEMINI 1 (n=974) and GEMINI 2 (n=899) — randomised 1:1 to tolebrutinib 60 mg once daily or teriflunomide 14 mg once daily, each with matching placebo; median follow-up 139 weeks.
cards.result: Annualised relapse rate: 0.13 vs 0.12 in GEMINI 1 (rate ratio 1.06, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.39; P=0.67) and 0.11 vs 0.11 in GEMINI 2 (rate ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.75 to 1.32; P=0.98) — the primary endpoint was not met in either trial. The pooled proportion with 6-month confirmed disability worsening was 8.3% on tolebrutinib vs 11.3% on teriflunomide (hazard ratio 0.71 relative, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.95), but no formal hypothesis testing was conducted because the prespecified hierarchical testing plan stopped at the failed primary, and the interval is unadjusted for multiple testing. Overall adverse-event rates were similar; minor bleeding was more frequent on tolebrutinib (petechiae 4.5% vs 0.3%; heavy menses 2.6% vs 1.0%).
cards.watchOut: The disability-worsening figure is a secondary outcome outside the formal testing hierarchy after a failed primary — it is a signal to test, not a demonstrated benefit, and it must never be quoted without that label. The comparator is teriflunomide, an approved oral therapy, not placebo.
cards.source: GEMINI 1 and GEMINI 2 (Oh J et al.) Tolebrutinib versus Teriflunomide in Relapsing Multiple Sclerosis. N Engl J Med. 2025. PMID: 40202623. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04410978, ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04410991. cards.headline: Phase 2b 2021 (n=130): dose-dependent reduction in new gadolinium-enhancing lesions, greatest at 60 mg (0.13 vs 1.03 lesions on placebo) — the MRI result that set the phase 3 dose
cards.summary: Phase 2b 2021 (n=130): dose-dependent reduction in new gadolinium-enhancing lesions, greatest at 60 mg (0.13 vs 1.03 lesions on placebo) — the MRI result that set the phase 3 dose
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2b crossover trial (Reich 2021)
cards.people: 130 adults aged 18-55 with relapsing multiple sclerosis at 40 centres in Europe and North America, in a 16-week randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover dose-finding trial of tolebrutinib 5, 15, 30 or 60 mg daily (126 in the primary analysis).
cards.result: New gadolinium-enhancing lesions after 12 weeks of treatment fell dose-dependently: mean lesions per patient 1.39 (5 mg), 0.77 (15 mg), 0.76 (30 mg) and 0.13 (60 mg) vs 1.03 on placebo (p=0.03 for the dose-response). One serious adverse event occurred (hospital admission for an MS relapse, 60 mg group); headache was the commonest non-serious event.
cards.watchOut: An MRI-lesion dose-finding study over 12 treatment weeks: it shows biological activity on focal inflammation, yet in phase 3 that activity did not translate into fewer relapses than teriflunomide — the MRI-to-clinical gap is the central caution of this programme.
cards.source: Tolebrutinib phase 2b dose-finding trial (Reich 2021) (Reich DS et al.) cards.headline: Phase 2b extension 2025 (n=125, uncontrolled): over 2 years on tolebrutinib, annualised relapse rate was 0.17 and EDSS was stable — class IV evidence with no comparator
cards.summary: Phase 2b extension 2025 (n=125, uncontrolled): over 2 years on tolebrutinib, annualised relapse rate was 0.17 and EDSS was stable — class IV evidence with no comparator
cards.type: Open-label long-term extension of a phase 2b trial (Oh 2025)
cards.people: 125 of the 129 phase 2b completers entered the long-term safety extension (mean age 37.8 years at core-study baseline; 69% women), continuing their core dose double-blind (Part A) before all switched to open-label tolebrutinib 60 mg daily with food (Part B); 114 remained on study at the February 2022 cut-off.
cards.result: The commonest treatment-emergent adverse events were COVID-19 (26/125, 21%) and headache (17/125, 14%). At week 96, 79% of the continuous-60 mg group had no new gadolinium-enhancing lesions since the previous scan; annualised relapse rate on 60 mg for at least 8 weeks was 0.17 (95% CI 0.12 to 0.25) and median EDSS was stable. The authors grade this class IV evidence: an uncontrolled study without a comparator group.
cards.watchOut: Uncontrolled extension data describe people who stayed on drug; relapse rates and stability in such cohorts cannot be compared with the randomised GEMINI results and are carded for durability and safety context only.

cards.headline: Liver-safety overview 2026 (2,958 exposed across the programme): ALT >3x the upper limit of normal in 4.7%, Hy's-law cases in 0.20%, and one death after liver transplant — all cases began within 90 days
cards.summary: Liver-safety overview 2026 (2,958 exposed across the programme): ALT >3x the upper limit of normal in 4.7%, Hy's-law cases in 0.20%, and one death after liver transplant — all cases began within 90 days
cards.type: Programme-wide safety review of pooled trial data (Maxwell 2026)
cards.people: Programme-wide safety overview of all 2,958 participants exposed to tolebrutinib across four phase 3 trials and the open-label extension, spanning relapsing MS (GEMINI 1 & 2), non-relapsing secondary progressive MS (HERCULES) and primary progressive MS (PERSEUS).
cards.result: Drug-induced liver injury emerged as an important identified risk: 139/2,958 (4.7%) had ALT elevations >3x ULN, including 49 (1.66%) >8x ULN and 17 (0.57%) >20x ULN; six (0.20%) met Hy's-law criteria for serious liver injury. All cases occurred within the first 90 days; all resolved without sequelae except one participant who required a liver transplant and died of postoperative complications. After enhanced monitoring was introduced, only one Hy's-law case occurred among 920 exposed (0.11%), and weekly liver testing for 12 weeks detected elevations earlier (40 vs 60 days) with faster recovery (44 vs 57 days). Liver-spheroid studies showed no direct hepatocellular toxicity, supporting an idiosyncratic mechanism.
cards.watchOut: Pooled across MS phenotypes — including the HERCULES population whose efficacy question is homed on Shelf #2849 and whose trial (PMID 40202696) is deliberately NOT carded here. The monitoring burden (weekly liver tests for the first 12 weeks) is part of this drug's real cost and belongs beside any efficacy claim.
cards.source: Tolebrutinib liver-safety overview (Maxwell 2026) (Maxwell CR et al.) Tolebrutinib liver safety: A detailed overview. Mult Scler Relat Disord. 2026. PMID: 42546561. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04411641, ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04458051, ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04410991, ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06372145, ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04410978. shelves.title: MINT: inebilizumab improved MG-ADL by 1.9 points more than placebo at week 26 in generalised myasthenia gravis, on a protocolised steroid taper
shelves.question: In adults with generalised MG (AChR- or MuSK-positive), does inebilizumab, versus placebo, improve MG-ADL with protocolised steroid taper?
shelves.balance: Premise verified at build: inebilizumab's existing homes are NMOSD (live Shelf #1118, N-MOmentum) and IgG4-related disease (live Shelf #1818, MITIGATE) — neither touches myasthenia gravis, and MINT is a distinct trial answering a distinct question. MINT (Nowak et al., PMID 40202593) randomised 238 adults with AChR- or MuSK-positive generalised MG to inebilizumab or placebo with a protocolised glucocorticoid taper in both arms: MG-ADL change at week 26 was -4.2 vs -2.2 (difference -1.9; p<0.001) and QMG -4.8 vs -2.3 (difference -2.5). A prespecified analysis (PMID 42573995) found fewer exacerbations on inebilizumab (hazard ratio 0.41 relative at week 26), with the MuSK-positive subgroup small (48 participants) and its estimate imprecise. Serious adverse events were not more frequent on inebilizumab. An indirect network meta-analysis (PMID 42495790) ranks another class member first on most endpoints, so MINT establishes that inebilizumab works in generalised MG, not that it leads the class. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single trial caps the stamp.

cards.headline: MINT 2025: MG-ADL improved -4.2 on inebilizumab vs -2.2 on placebo (difference -1.9, p<0.001) at week 26, with a protocolised steroid taper in both groups
cards.summary: MINT 2025: MG-ADL improved -4.2 on inebilizumab vs -2.2 on placebo (difference -1.9, p<0.001) at week 26, with a protocolised steroid taper in both groups
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (MINT, Nowak 2025)
cards.people: 238 adults with generalised myasthenia gravis positive for anti-acetylcholine-receptor (190 participants) or anti-muscle-specific-kinase (48 participants) antibodies, randomised 1:1 (119 per group) to intravenous inebilizumab 300 mg (days 1 and 15 for all; an additional day-183 dose for AChR-positive participants) or placebo, over 52 weeks (AChR-positive) or 26 weeks (MuSK-positive). Glucocorticoids were tapered from week 4 to a target of 5 mg/day by week 24 in both groups.
cards.result: Primary endpoint (MG-ADL change at week 26, combined population): least-squares mean -4.2 on inebilizumab vs -2.2 on placebo (adjusted difference -1.9, 95% CI -2.9 to -1.0; P<0.001). QMG change: -4.8 vs -2.3 (difference -2.5, 95% CI -3.8 to -1.2; P<0.001). The commonest adverse events on inebilizumab were headache, cough, nasopharyngitis, infusion-related reactions and urinary tract infections; inebilizumab was not associated with a higher incidence of serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: A single trial caps this shelf at POSSIBLE. The MuSK-positive subgroup is small (48 of 238), so the combined-population result is carried mainly by AChR-positive patients; the steroid taper applied to both arms, so the benefit is on top of — not instead of — a taper protocol.
cards.source: MINT (Nowak RJ et al.) A Phase 3 Trial of Inebilizumab in Generalized Myasthenia Gravis. N Engl J Med. 2025. PMID: 40202593. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04524273. randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (mint, nowak 2025) 238 adults with generalised myasthenia gravis positive for anti-acetylcholine-receptor (190 participants) or anti-muscle-specific-kinase (48 participants) antibodies, randomised 1:1 (119 per group) to intravenous inebilizumab 300 mg (days 1 and 15 for all; an additional day-183 dose for achr-positive participants) or placebo, over 52 weeks (achr-positive) or 26 weeks (musk-positive). glucocorticoids were tapered from week 4 to a target of 5 mg/day by week 24 in both groups. primary endpoint (mg-adl change at week 26, combined population): least-squares mean -4.2 on inebilizumab vs -2.2 on placebo (adjusted difference -1.9, 95% ci -2.9 to -1.0; p<0.001). qmg change: -4.8 vs -2.3 (difference -2.5, 95% ci -3.8 to -1.2; p<0.001). the commonest adverse events on inebilizumab were headache, cough, nasopharyngitis, infusion-related reactions and urinary tract infections; inebilizumab was not associated with a higher incidence of serious adverse events. a single trial caps this shelf at possible. the musk-positive subgroup is small (48 of 238), so the combined-population result is carried mainly by achr-positive patients; the steroid taper applied to both arms, so the benefit is on top of — not instead of — a taper protocol. mint (nowak rj et al.) a phase 3 trial of inebilizumab in generalized myasthenia gravis. n engl j med. 2025. pmid: 40202593. registry id: clinicaltrials.gov nct04524273. mesh: adult · female · humans · male · middle aged · activities of daily living · antibodies, monoclonal, humanized/administration & dosage/adverse effects* · autoantibodies/blood · double-blind method · glucocorticoids/therapeutic use · myasthenia gravis/blood/diagnosis/drug therapy/immunology* · receptor protein-tyrosine kinases/immunology · receptors, cholinergic/immunology · treatment outcome · severity of illness index

cards.headline: MINT prespecified analysis 2026: inebilizumab reduced exacerbation risk (hazard ratio 0.41 relative at week 26), including in the small MuSK-positive subgroup (0.21 relative)
cards.summary: MINT prespecified analysis 2026: inebilizumab reduced exacerbation risk (hazard ratio 0.41 relative at week 26), including in the small MuSK-positive subgroup (0.21 relative)
cards.type: Prespecified secondary analysis of a randomised phase 3 trial (MINT, Nowak 2026)
cards.people: Prespecified analysis of the same MINT trial (238 participants at 81 sites in 18 countries; mean age 47.5 years, 61% women, mean baseline MG-ADL 9.1), examining exacerbations — defined as myasthenic crisis, worsening of individual MG-ADL items, or rescue-therapy use (intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange) — during the protocol-specified corticosteroid taper. Labelled as a second report of MINT (PMID 40202593 is the primary report, carded above), not an independent trial.
cards.result: Inebilizumab reduced exacerbation risk versus placebo in the combined population by week 26 (hazard ratio 0.41 relative, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.70), in the AChR-positive subpopulation by week 52 (0.39 relative, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.68), and in the MuSK-positive subpopulation by week 26 (0.21 relative, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.79).
cards.watchOut: Hazard ratios are relative measures; the abstract does not print absolute exacerbation rates, so none are quoted here. The MuSK-positive interval (0.06 to 0.79) is wide because the subgroup is 48 people — directionally supportive, not precise.

cards.headline: Network meta-analysis 2026: most biologics beat placebo on MG-ADL and QMG, but indirect rankings put efgartigimod IV first on nearly all endpoints — MINT does not establish inebilizumab as the best in class
cards.summary: Network meta-analysis 2026: most biologics beat placebo on MG-ADL and QMG, but indirect rankings put efgartigimod IV first on nearly all endpoints — MINT does not establish inebilizumab as the best in class
cards.people: De novo network meta-analysis of phase 3 placebo-controlled trials of six biologics in acetylcholine-receptor-antibody-positive generalised myasthenia gravis (efgartigimod IV, inebilizumab, nipocalimab, ravulizumab, rozanolixizumab, zilucoplan), with numbers-needed-to-treat and a US cost-per-improved-outcome analysis using 2026 prices.
cards.result: Most therapies showed significantly greater efficacy than placebo across MG-ADL and QMG outcomes. Efgartigimod IV ranked highest on nearly all endpoints (QMG numbers needed to treat 2.18 for a >=3-point and 1.88 for a >=5-point improvement; MG-ADL 2.77 and 1.94) and had the lowest cost per improved outcome. The abstract reports no inebilizumab-specific estimate, so none is quoted on this card.
cards.watchOut: Indirect comparisons across trials with different designs, populations and endpoint timing — hypothesis-level context for class positioning, not head-to-head evidence. It is carded to prevent the single-trial MINT result being read as class leadership.

shelves.title: Batoclimab in generalised myasthenia gravis: the China phase 3 trial — published in full in JAMA Neurology in 2024 — found sustained MG-ADL response in 58.2% vs 31.3% on placebo
shelves.question: In adults with generalised MG, does the FcRn antagonist batoclimab, versus placebo, produce sustained MG-ADL improvement?
shelves.balance: Publication status first, because this row carried a possibly-unpublished flag: at build time the flag does not survive re-checking. The phase 3 trial (27 centres in China, NCT05039190) has a full journal report — Yan et al., JAMA Neurology 2024 (PMID 38436998) — and every number on this shelf comes from fetched journal records; the October 2026 sponsor/regulatory material concerned approval, not first publication, and no release numbers are carded. In that trial, sustained MG-ADL response was 58.2% on batoclimab vs 31.3% on placebo (odds ratio 3.45 relative, absolute rates beside it), with treatment-related adverse events in 70.1% vs 36.9%. Two small Chinese/US phase 2 studies (PMIDs 35412216, n=30; 38062618, n=17) point the same way on scores and IgG reduction, and a post hoc analysis (PMID 42867600) ties IgG fall to improvement. A separate global phase 3 trial (NCT05403541) remains design-paper-only and is not carded. Single-country phase 3 evidence: PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Phase 3 2024: sustained MG-ADL response 58.2% on batoclimab vs 31.3% on placebo (odds ratio 3.45 relative; p=0.001) — a full journal report of the China phase 3 trial
cards.summary: Phase 3 2024: sustained MG-ADL response 58.2% on batoclimab vs 31.3% on placebo (odds ratio 3.45 relative; p=0.001) — a full journal report of the China phase 3 trial
cards.type: Multicentre randomised clinical trial, phase 3 (Yan 2024, JAMA Neurology)
cards.people: 132 adults with generalised myasthenia gravis at 27 centres in China (mean age 43.8 years; 67.2% women; 131 antibody-positive), randomised to subcutaneous batoclimab 680 mg weekly or matching placebo, each treatment cycle being 6 weekly injections followed by 4 weeks of observation, on top of standard care; a second cycle was given where continuing treatment was required. The primary outcome was sustained improvement — a >=3-point MG-ADL reduction from baseline for at least 4 consecutive weeks in the first cycle — in AChR- or MuSK-antibody-positive patients.
cards.result: Sustained MG-ADL improvement in cycle 1: 58.2% (39/67) on batoclimab vs 31.3% (20/64) on placebo (odds ratio 3.45 relative, 95% CI 1.62 to 7.35; P=0.001 — absolute rates printed beside the relative measure). Scores diverged as early as week 2; the maximum mean MG-ADL difference was -1.9 points (95% CI -2.8 to -1.0) one week after the last dose. Treatment-related adverse events: 70.1% (47/67) on batoclimab vs 36.9% (24/65) on placebo; severe treatment-emergent events 3.0% (2/67) vs 7.7% (5/65).
cards.watchOut: Single-country (China) phase 3 with a cyclic dosing design, not continuous maintenance: the 58.2% figure is a sustained-response rate within the first 6-week cycle plus observation, and the trial was not sized to characterise uncommon harms (the authors themselves call for larger safety studies).
cards.source: Batoclimab phase 3 trial in generalised MG (Yan 2024) (Yan C et al.) Batoclimab vs Placebo for Generalized Myasthenia Gravis: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Neurol. 2024. PMID: 38436998. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05039190. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Phase 2 2022 (n=30): MG-ADL change at day 43 was -4.7 (340 mg) and -4.4 (680 mg) vs -2.2 on placebo
cards.summary: Phase 2 2022 (n=30): MG-ADL change at day 43 was -4.7 (340 mg) and -4.4 (680 mg) vs -2.2 on placebo
cards.people: 30 Chinese patients with generalised myasthenia gravis randomised to batoclimab 680 mg (n=11), batoclimab 340 mg (n=10) or placebo (n=9), dosed on days 1, 8, 15, 22, 29 and 36, followed by an open-label period (batoclimab 340 mg on days 50, 64 and 78) and follow-up to day 120.
cards.result: MG-ADL change from baseline to day 43: -2.2 (placebo), -4.7 (340 mg) and -4.4 (680 mg); QMG, MGC and MG-QoL15 scores moved similarly, and the proportion with clinically significant improvement at day 43 was higher on batoclimab. By day 120 — after the placebo group had crossed to open-label batoclimab — the placebo group's scales had improved more, with total serum IgG reaching a plateau. No death or adverse event led to discontinuation.
cards.watchOut: Thirty patients and a crossover into open-label treatment: the day-120 reversal is an artefact of the design (everyone was on drug by then), not evidence the effect wears off — and the day-43 differences rest on groups of 9-11 patients.
cards.source: Batoclimab phase 2 trial in Chinese patients with generalised MG (Yan 2022) (Yan C et al.) cards.headline: Phase 2a 2024 (n=17): batoclimab cut total IgG and anti-AChR antibodies significantly vs placebo at 6 weeks; clinical measures moved favourably but the study was not powered for efficacy
cards.summary: Phase 2a 2024 (n=17): batoclimab cut total IgG and anti-AChR antibodies significantly vs placebo at 6 weeks; clinical measures moved favourably but the study was not powered for efficacy
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2a proof-of-concept trial (Nowak 2024)
cards.people: 17 patients with generalised myasthenia gravis and anti-acetylcholine-receptor antibodies randomised 1:1:1 to once-weekly subcutaneous batoclimab 340 mg (n=5), 680 mg (n=6) or placebo (n=6) for 6 weeks, after which all could enter an open-label extension (batoclimab 340 mg every 2 weeks for 6 weeks). Primary endpoints were safety, tolerability and change in total IgG, IgG subclasses and anti-AChR antibodies.
cards.result: Batoclimab produced significantly greater reductions in total IgG and anti-AChR antibodies than placebo at 6 weeks, with IgG-subclass reductions generally consistent with total IgG. Clinical measures (MG-ADL, QMG, MGC, MG-QoL15r) improved directionally over time. No safety issues were identified.
cards.watchOut: Seventeen patients: a pharmacodynamic proof-of-concept, carded as programme support. Its job is to show the FcRn mechanism engages in this disease; the efficacy case rests on the phase 3 card above.

cards.headline: Post hoc analysis 2026: in the phase 3 trial's AChR-positive batoclimab patients (n=65), faster IgG reduction tracked clinical improvement (r=0.37 for MG-ADL, r=0.49 for QMG)
cards.summary: Post hoc analysis 2026: in the phase 3 trial's AChR-positive batoclimab patients (n=65), faster IgG reduction tracked clinical improvement (r=0.37 for MG-ADL, r=0.49 for QMG)
cards.type: Post hoc biomarker analysis of a phase 3 randomised trial (Li 2026)
cards.people: Post hoc analysis of the phase 3 trial carded above (NCT05039190), restricted to 65 AChR-antibody-positive patients treated with batoclimab at 27 centres in China, relating serum IgG and AChR-antibody changes to MG-ADL and QMG changes using correlation, mixed-effects and multivariate models. Labelled as a post hoc analysis of the phase 3 trial, not an independent study.
cards.result: Within-patient correlations: IgG reduction vs MG-ADL change r=0.372 (p<0.001) and vs QMG change r=0.492 (p<0.001). Modelling estimated that an 80% IgG reduction corresponded to a 59% probability of a >=3-point MG-ADL improvement and a 77% probability of a >=3-point QMG improvement. Higher baseline body mass index independently predicted slower IgG decline.
cards.watchOut: Post hoc and correlational, in the treated arm only: IgG reduction tracking improvement is consistent with the mechanism but cannot separate drug effect from natural history, and the modelled probabilities are not response rates from a randomised comparison.

cards.summary: Synthesis: one published phase 3 trial (n=132) with two small supporting phase 2 studies — POSSIBLE, single-country
cards.people: One phase 3 RCT (132 randomised), one phase 2 RCT (30), one phase 2a proof-of-concept trial (17), and a post hoc analysis of the phase 3 treated arm (65).
cards.result: Sustained MG-ADL response 58.2% vs 31.3% (odds ratio 3.45 relative) in the phase 3 trial; phase 2 day-43 MG-ADL changes -4.4 to -4.7 vs -2.2; treatment-related adverse events 70.1% vs 36.9% in phase 3. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

shelves.title: EPIDYS: givinostat (Duvyzat, Italfarmaco) slowed four-stair-climb decline in Duchenne muscular dystrophy — a slowing, not an improvement
shelves.question: In ambulant boys >=6 years with Duchenne MD on stable corticosteroids, does the HDAC inhibitor givinostat, versus placebo, slow functional decline on the four-stair climb?
shelves.balance: Product naming, per the clarification exception: the tested drug is givinostat, marketed as Duvyzat (Italfarmaco); the publications use the generic name. EPIDYS (Mercuri et al., PMID 38508835) randomised 179 ambulant boys with Duchenne muscular dystrophy on stable corticosteroids to givinostat or placebo for 72 weeks: in the primary population (group A, n=120), four-stair climb worsened in both groups but significantly less on givinostat (geometric least-squares ratio 1.27 vs 1.48; ratio 0.86; p=0.035). The effect is a slowing of decline, not an improvement, and the commonest costs were diarrhoea (36% vs 18%) and vomiting (29% vs 13%), with a mid-trial dose reduction after an interim safety analysis. Supporting evidence is uncontrolled: a 20-boy phase 2 biopsy study (PMID 27566866) showed histological improvement without functional gain, and an open-label extension (PMID 40830818) offers post hoc natural-history comparisons only. FDA approval followed in March 2024. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: EPIDYS 2024: four-stair climb worsened less on givinostat (geometric least-squares ratio 1.27 vs 1.48; ratio 0.86, p=0.035) — a slowing of decline, not an improvement
cards.summary: EPIDYS 2024: four-stair climb worsened less on givinostat (geometric least-squares ratio 1.27 vs 1.48; ratio 0.86, p=0.035) — a slowing of decline, not an improvement
cards.type: Multicentre randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (EPIDYS, Mercuri 2024)
cards.people: 179 ambulant boys aged >=6 years with genetically confirmed Duchenne muscular dystrophy on systemic corticosteroids for at least 6 months, at 41 sites in 11 countries, randomised 2:1 to oral givinostat (n=118) or placebo (n=61) twice daily for 72 weeks, dose weight-based and reducible if not tolerated. The primary analysis population (group A, n=120) was defined by baseline vastus lateralis fat fraction >5% and <=30%.
cards.result: In group A, the four-stair climb result at 72 weeks vs baseline gave a geometric least-squares mean ratio of 1.27 on givinostat vs 1.48 on placebo (ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.745 to 0.989; p=0.035) — both groups worsened; the decline was significantly smaller on givinostat. Commonest adverse events: diarrhoea 36% (43/118) vs 18% (11/61) and vomiting 29% (34/118) vs 13% (8/61). No treatment-related deaths occurred. The givinostat starting dose was reduced after an interim safety analysis, following a masked futility assessment at 12 months in the first 50 group A boys.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint is a ratio of worsening on one timed test, in a fat-fraction-defined subgroup (group A, 120 of 179 randomised), with a mid-trial dose reduction — a real but modest and narrowly framed effect. The trial record does not report the thrombocytopenia or triglyceride numbers sometimes quoted for this drug, so none are printed here.
cards.source: EPIDYS (Mercuri E et al.) Safety and efficacy of givinostat in boys with Duchenne muscular dystrophy (EPIDYS): a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial. Lancet Neurol. 2024. PMID: 38508835. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02851797. cards.headline: Phase 2 2016 (n=20, single-arm): after >=12 months of givinostat, biopsies showed more muscle tissue and less fibrosis, necrosis and fatty replacement — with no functional improvement observed
cards.summary: Phase 2 2016 (n=20, single-arm): after >=12 months of givinostat, biopsies showed more muscle tissue and less fibrosis, necrosis and fatty replacement — with no functional improvement observed
cards.people: 20 ambulant boys with Duchenne muscular dystrophy aged 7 to <11 years on stable corticosteroid treatment, all treated with givinostat for at least 12 months, with muscle biopsy at start and end; histological change was the primary objective. There was no placebo or comparator group.
cards.result: Givinostat significantly increased the fraction of muscle tissue in biopsies and reduced fibrotic tissue, tissue necrosis and fatty replacement. The drug was safe and tolerated overall. Improvement in functional tests was not observed, though the sample size was insufficient for definitive functional conclusions.
cards.watchOut: Uncontrolled histology in 20 boys: biopsy improvement without a comparator cannot separate drug effect from biopsy-site and natural-history variation, and function — the outcome families feel — did not improve in this study.
cards.source: Givinostat phase 2 histology study (Bettica 2016) (Bettica P et al.) Histological effects of givinostat in boys with Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Neuromuscul Disord. 2016. cards.headline: Long-term extension 2025 (n=194, open-label): post hoc comparisons against natural-history cohorts suggest milestones delayed by medians of 2.0-3.3 years
cards.summary: Long-term extension 2025 (n=194, open-label): post hoc comparisons against natural-history cohorts suggest milestones delayed by medians of 2.0-3.3 years
cards.type: Open-label long-term extension study with post hoc natural-history comparisons (McDonald 2025)
cards.people: 194 patients with Duchenne muscular dystrophy who had completed the phase 2 study or EPIDYS (or were screened but not randomised into EPIDYS), all receiving open-label givinostat oral suspension at a flexible weight-based dose plus systemic corticosteroids, with visits every 4 months; mean givinostat exposure in the extension was 559.6 days, and maximum total exposure including prior studies exceeded 8 years.
cards.result: At least one adverse event was reported by 169/194 (87.1%), mostly mild or moderate, consistent with prior studies. Post hoc propensity-matched comparisons with natural-history datasets (ImagingDMD and CINRG) suggested givinostat plus corticosteroids significantly delayed loss of the ability to rise from the floor, loss of the ability to complete the four-stair climb, and loss of ambulation, by medians of 2.0-3.3 years (all nominal p<0.05).
cards.watchOut: Non-randomised external comparisons, analysed post hoc with nominal p-values: useful for durability and safety, but matched natural-history cohorts cannot carry an efficacy claim the way EPIDYS's randomised comparison can.
cards.source: Givinostat long-term extension with natural-history comparisons (McDonald 2025) (McDonald CM et al.) shelves.title: SAPPHIRE: apitegromab (Scholar Rock) added +1.8 HFMSE points over placebo on top of SMN therapy in SMA — a pooled-dose result, with the 20 mg/kg arm alone not significant
shelves.question: In non-ambulatory children and young adults (2-21 years) with SMA type 2/3 already on nusinersen or risdiplam, does apitegromab (anti-myostatin), versus placebo, improve motor function on the HFMSE?
shelves.balance: Product naming: apitegromab (Scholar Rock), an anti-myostatin antibody given as add-on therapy — every participant in every carded study was already on nusinersen or risdiplam. SAPPHIRE (Crawford et al., PMID 40818473) randomised 188 nonambulatory participants aged 2-21 with type 2/3 SMA: in the primary population (aged 2-12), combined apitegromab doses beat placebo on HFMSE change at 12 months by +1.8 points (p=0.019), but the dose split must be read honestly — the 20 mg/kg arm alone was not significant (+1.4; p=0.11), and the record's abstract does not report a standalone 10 mg/kg estimate, so the slate's '+2.2 for 10 mg/kg' figure is not carried onto this shelf. Adverse events matched placebo and nobody discontinued for them. The phase 2 TOPAZ programme (PMIDs 38330285, 39105058) is uncontrolled and supportive only. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: SAPPHIRE 2025: pooled-dose HFMSE difference +1.8 points (p=0.019) in 2-12-year-olds — but the 20 mg/kg arm alone was not significant (+1.4, p=0.11)
cards.summary: SAPPHIRE 2025: pooled-dose HFMSE difference +1.8 points (p=0.019) in 2-12-year-olds — but the 20 mg/kg arm alone was not significant (+1.4, p=0.11)
cards.type: Phase 3, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial (SAPPHIRE, Crawford 2025)
cards.people: 188 participants aged 2-21 years with genetically documented nonambulatory type 2 or type 3 spinal muscular atrophy (HFMSE 10-45) at 48 hospitals in nine countries, all already on nusinersen (>=10 months) or risdiplam (>=6 months): 156 aged 2-12 years (randomised 1:1:1 to apitegromab 20 mg/kg, 10 mg/kg, or placebo every 4 weeks) and 32 aged 13-21 years (randomised 2:1 to apitegromab 20 mg/kg or placebo); 128 received apitegromab and 60 placebo overall. The primary endpoint — HFMSE change at 12 months — was assessed in the 2-12-year population.
cards.result: In participants aged 2-12, the least-squares mean HFMSE difference for combined apitegromab doses vs placebo was +1.8 points (95% CI 0.30 to 3.32; p=0.019; least-squares means 0.6 vs -1.2), while apitegromab 20 mg/kg alone vs placebo gave +1.4 (95% CI -0.34 to 3.13; p=0.11) — not significant. The 10 mg/kg arm's standalone estimate is not reported in the record's abstract and is not quoted here. Adverse-event incidence and severity were similar between groups (pyrexia 26% vs 28%; nasopharyngitis 25% vs 23%; cough 23% vs 20%; vomiting 23% vs 17%; upper respiratory infection 22% vs 30%; headache 21% vs 20%), and no participant discontinued because of adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Read the dose split honestly: the significant headline is the pooled-dose comparison in 2-12-year-olds; the higher dose alone missed significance, which is the reverse of a tidy dose-response, and the older (13-21) stratum was not the primary population. This is add-on benefit on top of SMN-targeted therapy, not instead of it.
cards.source: SAPPHIRE (Crawford TO et al.) Safety and efficacy of apitegromab in nonambulatory type 2 or type 3 spinal muscular atrophy (SAPPHIRE): a phase 3, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet Neurol. 2025. PMID: 40818473. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05156320. cards.headline: TOPAZ phase 2 2024 (n=58, no placebo group): within-group HFMSE changes at 12 months ranged from -0.3 to +7.1 points across three cohorts
cards.summary: TOPAZ phase 2 2024 (n=58, no placebo group): within-group HFMSE changes at 12 months ranged from -0.3 to +7.1 points across three cohorts
cards.type: Phase 2 trial with open-label and blinded-dose cohorts (TOPAZ, Crawford 2024)
cards.people: 58 participants aged 2-21 years with later-onset type 2 or type 3 SMA at 16 US and European sites, previously treated with nusinersen for a mean of 25.9 months, in three cohorts: ambulatory participants aged 5-21 on apitegromab 20 mg/kg alone or with nusinersen (cohort 1, n=23); nonambulatory participants aged 5-21 on apitegromab 20 mg/kg with nusinersen (cohort 2, n=15); and younger participants >=2 years randomised blinded to apitegromab 2 or 20 mg/kg with nusinersen (cohort 3, n=20). (A second record, PMID 38830133, is a published erratum to this report and is not carded.)
cards.result: Mean HFMSE change at month 12: -0.3 points (95% CI -2.1 to 1.4) in cohort 1; +0.6 (-1.4 to 2.7) in cohort 2; and in cohort 3, +5.3 (-1.5 to 12.2) on 2 mg/kg (n=8) and +7.1 (1.8 to 12.5) on 20 mg/kg (n=9). The five commonest treatment-emergent events were headache (24.1%), pyrexia (22.4%), upper respiratory tract infection (22.4%), cough (22.4%) and nasopharyngitis (20.7%); no deaths or serious adverse reactions were reported. The study provides Class III evidence.
cards.watchOut: Mostly uncontrolled within-group changes in small cohorts: children on background nusinersen can gain points for reasons other than the study drug, which is precisely why the placebo-controlled SAPPHIRE result (carded above) is the one that carries the claim.
cards.source: TOPAZ phase 2 study (Crawford 2024) (Crawford TO et al.) Safety and Efficacy of Apitegromab in Patients With Spinal Muscular Atrophy Types 2 and 3: The Phase 2 TOPAZ Study. cards.summary: TOPAZ 36-month report 2024: in the nonambulatory group (n=35), mean HFMSE change was +4.0 points at 36 months on continued apitegromab — open-label, no comparator
cards.type: Open-label extension report of a phase 2 study (TOPAZ 36-month, Crawford 2024)
cards.people: 35 nonambulatory patients from TOPAZ (mean age 7.3 years) who continued into the open-label extension on apitegromab 20 mg/kg every 4 weeks, assessed with HFMSE, the Revised Upper Limb Module, WHO motor milestones and caregiver-reported outcomes (PEDI-CAT, PROMIS Fatigue).
cards.result: Mean change from baseline at 36 months: HFMSE +4.0 points (SD 7.54) and RULM +2.4 (SD 3.24; excluding 7 patients after scoliosis surgery). Caregiver-reported daily-activity, mobility and fatigue outcomes improved from baseline, and 28 of 32 assessed patients improved or maintained their WHO motor milestones. Commonest treatment-emergent events: pyrexia 48.6%, nasopharyngitis 45.7%, COVID-19 40.0%, vomiting 40.0% and upper respiratory tract infection 31.4%. No new safety findings.
cards.watchOut: Three years without a control group in a disease whose treated natural history is still being written: durability is encouraging and consistent with SAPPHIRE, but extension gains cannot be attributed to apitegromab alone.
