shelves.title: Masitinib in ALS (AB10015): a 3.4-point ALSFRS-R advantage only in the 'normal progressor' population, a post-hoc enriched survival cohort (69 vs 44 months) — and no regulatory approval; the confirmatory trial has never reported
shelves.question: In adults with ALS, does masitinib added to riluzole, versus riluzole alone, slow ALSFRS-R decline or prolong survival?
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence), and the contest is the story of this shelf. AB10015 (394 patients, masitinib plus riluzole versus riluzole alone) met its primary endpoint only inside its prospectively declared 'Normal Progressor' primary population (progression from onset to baseline under 1.1 ALSFRS-R points/month): a 3.4-point advantage at 48 weeks on the 4.5 mg/kg/day dose, a 27% relative slowing of decline. In the broader 'Normal and Fast Progressor' population the same dose showed no significant effect, and the 3.0 mg/kg/day dose showed none anywhere. The survival headline — median 69 versus 44 months, hazard ratio 0.53 — comes from a long-term follow-up analysis in an enriched cohort defined after the fact (107 of the trial's patients), built to resemble the population of the planned confirmatory trial; it is a post-hoc subgroup result, not a trial-level survival finding. Against the benefit: adverse events were more frequent on masitinib (88% versus 79% on placebo at 4.5 mg/kg/day; serious adverse events 31% versus 18%), and a safety meta-analysis across the masitinib neurodegenerative programme found adverse events, severe events and discontinuations all significantly more common on the drug. Regulators in Europe and the US have refused approval on this evidence base. Confirmatory status at build (November 2026, checked against sponsor and registry reporting): the original confirmatory trial AB19001 was suspended in 2021 after a potential ischaemic heart disease signal and has never reported results; a replacement confirmatory study (AB23005) has been authorised but has published nothing. Until a confirmatory trial reports, masitinib in ALS is an unproven, subgroup-dependent claim — presented here in full because patients ask about it, not because the evidence is settled.

cards.headline: AB10015 (Mora 2020): masitinib 4.5 mg/kg/day beat placebo by 3.4 ALSFRS-R points at 48 weeks in the 'Normal Progressor' primary population (p=0.016) — but not in the broader population, and not at 3.0 mg/kg/day
cards.summary: AB10015 (Mora 2020): masitinib 4.5 mg/kg/day beat placebo by 3.4 ALSFRS-R points at 48 weeks in the 'Normal Progressor' primary population (p=0.016) — but not in the broader population, and not at 3.0 mg/kg/day
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2/3 trial (AB10015; Mora 2020)
cards.people: 394 patients with ALS, randomly assigned 1:1:1 to riluzole 100 mg/day plus placebo, or plus masitinib 4.5 or 3.0 mg/kg/day. A prospectively defined two-tiered design made patients with an ALSFRS-R progression rate from disease onset to baseline (ΔFS) under 1.1 points/month ('Normal Progressors') the primary efficacy population, with the broader population assessed secondarily. Primary endpoint: decline in ALSFRS-R at week 48, with last-observation-carried-forward imputation and sensitivity analyses.
cards.result: In the primary efficacy population, masitinib 4.5 mg/kg/day (n=99) showed a between-group difference in ALSFRS-R decline of 3.4 points versus placebo (n=102) (95% CI 0.65 to 6.13; p=0.016), corresponding to a 27% relative slowing of functional decline; sensitivity analyses including multiple imputation were convergent (difference 3.4; p=0.020), and secondary endpoints (ALSAQ-40, forced vital capacity, time-to-event) were also significant. Conversely, no significant treatment effect was seen in the broader 'Normal and Fast Progressor' 4.5 mg/kg/day cohort or in either 3.0 mg/kg/day cohort. Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 88% on masitinib 4.5 mg/kg/day, 85% on 3.0 mg/kg/day and 79% on placebo; serious adverse events in 31%, 23% and 18% respectively; no deaths were related to masitinib.
cards.watchOut: The positive claim lives and dies with the progression-rate restriction: the trial's own broader-population analysis was null, and an editorial published alongside the trial (van Eijk & van den Berg, 'In pursuit of the normal progressor') questioned whether the subgroup definition is a sound basis for a treatment claim. Last-observation-carried-forward imputation in a relentlessly progressive disease also flatters the active arm when dropout differs. This is one sponsor-run trial, never independently replicated.

cards.headline: AB10015 long-term survival analysis (Mora 2021): median survival 69 vs 44 months (HR 0.53) — in a post-hoc enriched cohort of 107 patients, not in the trial population as randomised
cards.summary: AB10015 long-term survival analysis (Mora 2021): median survival 69 vs 44 months (HR 0.53) — in a post-hoc enriched cohort of 107 patients, not in the trial population as randomised
cards.type: Long-term survival follow-up analysis of a randomised trial (AB10015; Mora 2021) — enriched-cohort analysis
cards.people: All participants originally randomised in AB10015, with survival status collected from investigational sites (average follow-up 75 months from diagnosis). The headline analysis is restricted to an enriched cohort defined by baseline ALSFRS-R progression rate under 1.1 points/month AND a score of at least 2 on every individual ALSFRS-R component (no complete loss of any function): 45 patients on masitinib 4.5 mg/kg/day and 62 on placebo — the population the confirmatory study AB19001 was designed to enrol.
cards.result: In the enriched cohort, masitinib 4.5 mg/kg/day was associated with a 25-month survival benefit (p=0.037) and a 47% relative reduction in the risk of death (hazard ratio 0.53; 95% CI 0.31 to 0.92; p=0.025), with median overall survival of 69 months versus 44 months on placebo. The authors conclude masitinib could prolong survival by over 2 years provided treatment starts before severe impairment of functionality.
cards.watchOut: This is the most-quoted masitinib number and the least protected: the enriched cohort was defined after the trial read out, it holds barely a quarter of the randomised patients, and small post-hoc cohorts in ALS have a long record of not replicating. The survival claim should be read as the hypothesis the confirmatory trial was built to test — a test that, as of this shelf's build, has still not reported.

cards.headline: Safety meta-analysis (Hamad 2024): across five masitinib RCTs in neurodegenerative disease, adverse events were significantly commoner on masitinib (RR 1.12), as were severe events and discontinuations
cards.summary: Safety meta-analysis (Hamad 2024): across five masitinib RCTs in neurodegenerative disease, adverse events were significantly commoner on masitinib (RR 1.12), as were severe events and discontinuations
cards.people: Five randomised controlled trials of masitinib versus placebo across multiple sclerosis, Alzheimer's disease and ALS, pooled for safety outcomes by masitinib dose (3 and 4.5 mg/kg/day).
cards.result: The incidence of adverse events was significantly higher on masitinib than control regardless of grade or dose (risk ratio 1.12; 95% CI 1.07 to 1.17; P<0.01), as were adverse events categorised as severe, non-fatal serious, leading to dose reduction and leading to permanent discontinuation (P≤0.01). At 4.5 mg/kg/day the adverse-event risk ratio was 1.11 (P<0.01); at 3.0 mg/kg/day it was 1.13 (P=0.01), though severe and non-fatal serious events did not differ significantly from placebo at the lower dose. The authors conclude masitinib use in neurodegenerative diseases presents safety concerns that may affect quality of life.
cards.watchOut: A safety pool across three different diseases and populations — it cannot price the harm for an individual ALS patient, and it contains no efficacy information. Its role on this shelf is narrower: it confirms the AB10015 pattern (more adverse and serious events on drug) is a programme-wide property of masitinib, not a single-trial quirk.
cards.source: Hamad AA et al. Safety of masitinib in patients with neurodegenerative diseases: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Neurological Sciences. 2024. PMID: 38627298. cards.headline: Synthesis: one trial, one restricted population, one post-hoc survival cohort — masitinib's ALS claim is unconfirmed and regulator-rejected
cards.summary: Synthesis: one trial, one restricted population, one post-hoc survival cohort — masitinib's ALS claim is unconfirmed and regulator-rejected
cards.people: Synthesis of the three reports carded on this shelf: the AB10015 phase 2/3 trial (394 randomised), its long-term survival follow-up (enriched cohort n=107), and a five-trial safety meta-analysis spanning the masitinib neurodegenerative programme.
cards.result: The functional benefit (3.4 ALSFRS-R points, 27% relative slowing) exists only inside the slower-progressor population and only at 4.5 mg/kg/day; the survival benefit (69 vs 44 months) exists only inside a post-hoc enriched cohort; harms are consistently higher on drug across the programme. No second trial has tested the claim, regulators have refused approval on it, and the confirmatory trial designed to settle it (AB19001) was suspended in 2021 and never reported, with a successor study (AB23005) authorised but unpublished at build.
cards.watchOut: MAYBE (weak evidence) is the ceiling for a single sponsor trial whose positive analyses are population-restricted and post-hoc. If AB23005 or another confirmatory trial reports, this shelf's stamp should be re-ruled on that result, in either direction.

shelves.title: CNM-Au8 in ALS (HEALEY Platform, Regimen C): no benefit on the clinical primary endpoint (disease rate ratio 0.97) — the case for the drug rests on exploratory survival and biomarker signals from a 45-patient phase 2 trial
shelves.question: In adults with ALS, does CNM-Au8 (gold nanocrystal suspension), versus placebo, slow disease progression over 24 weeks?
mesh: United States Food and Drug Administration
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence). CNM-Au8 is a suspension of catalytically active gold nanocrystals made by Clene Nanomedicine — an unapproved, single-source product, named here under the library's clarification exception because its identity and maker are the point. The randomised clinical evidence is negative where it was designed to be read: in the HEALEY ALS Platform Trial's Regimen C (161 participants), the primary endpoint — a Bayesian model of function and survival — gave a disease rate ratio of 0.97 (95% credible interval 0.783 to 1.175), and all three secondary endpoints likewise suggested no benefit or harm. In the smaller RESCUE-ALS phase 2 trial (45 participants), the primary neurophysiological endpoint (motor unit number index) and forced vital capacity did not differ significantly at 36 weeks. What keeps the programme alive is exploratory: in RESCUE-ALS's long-term follow-up, originally active-treated patients had lower all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 0.408, with a confidence interval reaching 1.001) and slower progression-event accrual in the open-label extension — analyses the trialists themselves label exploratory and hypothesis-supporting rather than confirmatory. Tolerability was acceptable in both trials (diarrhoea and nausea the commonest excess events in HEALEY). The honest summary: a well-tolerated, biologically interesting product with two negative randomised primaries and an unconfirmed survival signal that only a further adequately powered trial can settle.

cards.summary: HEALEY Regimen C (Berry 2025): CNM-Au8 showed no benefit on the primary endpoint at 24 weeks — disease rate ratio 0.97 (95% credible interval 0.783–1.175); all three secondary endpoints likewise neutral
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind phase 2/3 platform-trial regimen report (HEALEY ALS Platform Trial, Regimen C; Berry 2025)
cards.people: 161 participants with ALS at 54 US sites (July 2020 to March 2022), randomised within Regimen C in a 3:3:2 ratio to CNM-Au8 60 mg daily (n=61), CNM-Au8 30 mg daily (n=59) or matching placebo (n=41) for 24 weeks; the primary analysis combined the two CNM-Au8 dose groups against the regimen placebo group plus 123 concurrently randomised placebo participants from other platform regimens. Mean age 58.4 years; 37.9% female; 90% completed the trial. Primary endpoint: change through week 24 in a Bayesian shared-parameter model of ALSFRS-R function and survival, expressed as a disease rate ratio (under 1 = benefit).
cards.result: The primary endpoint showed no benefit: disease rate ratio 0.97 (95% credible interval 0.783 to 1.175; posterior probability of benefit 0.65) for combined CNM-Au8 versus combined placebo. The three secondary endpoints — combined assessment of function and survival, rate of decline in slow vital capacity, and survival free of permanent assisted ventilation — likewise suggested no benefit or harm. In the active (n=120) versus placebo (n=163) groups, the commonest adverse events were diarrhoea (19% vs 7%), nausea (14.2% vs 8.6%), fatigue (10.8% vs 18.4%) and muscular weakness (20% vs 27.6%). The authors' conclusion: no benefit of CNM-Au8 on ALS disease progression was observed at 24 weeks.
cards.watchOut: A platform-trial regimen is a phase 2/3 screening design, not a registrational trial: 24 weeks is short in ALS, the shared-placebo construction borrows patients randomised against other drugs, and the credible interval (0.783 to 1.175) cannot exclude a modest benefit — or modest harm. What it does exclude is the large, fast effect the programme hoped for. Biomarker arguments made for CNM-Au8 since this report are not part of this trial's clinical endpoints and are not carded as efficacy here.
cards.source: Berry JD et al. CNM-Au8 in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis: The HEALEY ALS Platform Trial. JAMA. 2025. PMID: 40067821. Registry ID: NCT04297683, NCT04414345. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: RESCUE-ALS double-blind phase (Vucic 2023, report 1 of 2 from this publication): primary MUNIX endpoint not met at 36 weeks (difference 7.7%, p=0.43); forced vital capacity also not significant
cards.summary: RESCUE-ALS double-blind phase (Vucic 2023, report 1 of 2 from this publication): primary MUNIX endpoint not met at 36 weeks (difference 7.7%, p=0.43); forced vital capacity also not significant
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial — double-blind report (RESCUE-ALS; Vucic 2023)
cards.people: 45 participants with early symptomatic ALS at two multidisciplinary ALS clinics in Sydney, Australia, randomised 1:1 to CNM-Au8 30 mg daily or matching placebo for 36 weeks, in addition to background riluzole. Primary outcome: mean percent change in summed motor unit number index (MUNIX), a neurophysiological biomarker of lower motor neuron function; secondary outcomes included total MUNIX change and forced vital capacity change.
cards.result: There was no significant difference between CNM-Au8 and placebo in summated MUNIX percent change (least-squares mean difference 7.7%; 95% CI −11.9 to 27.3; p=0.43), total MUNIX score change (18.8; 95% CI −56.4 to 94.0), or forced vital capacity change (least-squares mean difference 3.6; 95% CI −12.4 to 19.7). ALSFRS-R change, quality of life and disease-progression events were exploratory outcomes. CNM-Au8 was well tolerated with no safety signals identified.
cards.watchOut: Forty-five patients and a biomarker primary endpoint: this trial could only ever generate hypotheses about clinical benefit, and on its own prespecified terms it generated a negative one. It is carded in two explicitly labelled reports because the same publication carries the long-term extension data on the next card — the two must not be read as two independent trials.

cards.headline: RESCUE-ALS extension and survival follow-up (Vucic 2023, report 2 of 2 from this publication): all-cause mortality lower in the originally CNM-Au8-treated group (HR 0.408; 95% CI 0.166–1.001) — an exploratory analysis of 45 randomised patients
cards.summary: RESCUE-ALS extension and survival follow-up (Vucic 2023, report 2 of 2 from this publication): all-cause mortality lower in the originally CNM-Au8-treated group (HR 0.408; 95% CI 0.166–1.001) — an exploratory analysis of 45 randomised patients
cards.type: Open-label extension and long-term survival analysis of a phase 2 trial — exploratory report (RESCUE-ALS; Vucic 2023)
cards.people: The same 45 RESCUE-ALS participants, followed for vital status through at least 12 months after the double-blind period ended; 36 participants entered the open-label extension (all receiving CNM-Au8 30 mg daily). Outcomes: all-cause mortality by original randomisation, and time to disease-progression events (death, tracheostomy, non-invasive ventilation or gastrostomy) in the extension.
cards.result: Survival analysis showed a lower all-cause mortality hazard in the group originally randomised to CNM-Au8 (hazard ratio 0.408; 95% Wald CI 0.166 to 1.001; log-rank p=0.0429) — described by the authors as a 60% relative reduction in all-cause mortality. Participants originally on CNM-Au8 who entered the extension also showed a slower rate of disease-progression events than those originally on placebo. The authors characterise these as clinically meaningful exploratory results that support further investigation of CNM-Au8 in ALS.
cards.watchOut: Exploratory in every dimension: 45 patients, few deaths, a confidence interval whose upper bound is 1.001, an open-label extension in which everyone receives the drug (so later differences partly encode who chose to continue), and no multiplicity protection. This is the single most favourable CNM-Au8 result in print and it is exactly the kind of signal that evaporates in confirmatory trials — it earns the programme another trial, not a benefit claim.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two randomised trials, two missed primaries, one exploratory survival signal — CNM-Au8 has not demonstrated clinical benefit in ALS
cards.summary: Synthesis: two randomised trials, two missed primaries, one exploratory survival signal — CNM-Au8 has not demonstrated clinical benefit in ALS
cards.people: Synthesis of the reports carded on this shelf: HEALEY ALS Platform Trial Regimen C (161 participants in-regimen) and RESCUE-ALS (45 participants), the latter carded as two explicitly labelled reports of one publication (double-blind phase; extension/survival follow-up).
cards.result: On prespecified clinical and biomarker primary endpoints, CNM-Au8 did not separate from placebo in either trial (HEALEY disease rate ratio 0.97; RESCUE-ALS MUNIX difference 7.7%, p=0.43). The only favourable efficacy signal anywhere in the programme is the exploratory survival analysis from the 45-patient trial's follow-up (HR 0.408, interval reaching 1.001). Tolerability was good in both trials.
cards.watchOut: MAYBE (weak evidence): the shelf's claim is deliberately narrow — no demonstrated benefit, one hypothesis-grade survival signal, a confirmatory trial still owed. Any future approval argument built on biomarker surrogates rather than clinical endpoints should be read against this card set, which is what the randomised clinical evidence actually shows.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards on this shelf (PMIDs 40067821, 37396808). No additional source.

shelves.title: Ultra-high-dose methylcobalamin in early ALS (JETALS): ALSFRS-R decline slowed by 1.97 points over 16 weeks (a ~43% relative slowing) in selected early, moderate-progressor patients — a single-country (Japan) programme
shelves.question: In adults within 1 year of ALS onset with moderate progression rate, does methylcobalamin 50 mg intramuscularly twice weekly, versus placebo, slow ALSFRS-R decline?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), tightly fenced. JETALS is a properly positive phase 3 trial: in 130 Japanese patients within a year of ALS onset who were still progressing at a moderate rate after a 12-week observation run-in, methylcobalamin 50 mg intramuscularly twice weekly slowed ALSFRS-R decline over 16 weeks by 1.97 points versus placebo — a ~43% relative slowing of decline over that short window. The earlier, larger phase 2/3 programme (373 patients, all disease durations up to 36 months) missed both its primary endpoints outright; its supportive early-treatment signal is post-hoc, in patients entered within 12 months of onset — the observation JETALS was then designed to test prospectively, which is the right order of operations and raises the signal above pure data-dredging. The fences: every randomised patient in this programme is Japanese; JETALS's randomised period is only 16 weeks, so nothing here speaks to survival or to benefit beyond four months; the population is selected twice over (early disease, moderate progression, preserved respiratory function, ambulatory); and the very first study in the line (1998, n=24) measured a nerve-electrophysiology surrogate, not function. Methylcobalamin at this dose is approved for ALS in Japan and is not licensed for ALS in the US or Europe. Adverse events in JETALS were similar between groups (the trial reports no excess on drug).

cards.headline: JETALS (Oki 2022): methylcobalamin slowed ALSFRS-R decline by 1.97 points over 16 weeks (−2.66 vs −4.63; p=0.012) in early-stage ALS — adverse events similar to placebo
cards.summary: JETALS (Oki 2022): methylcobalamin slowed ALSFRS-R decline by 1.97 points over 16 weeks (−2.66 vs −4.63; p=0.012) in early-stage ALS — adverse events similar to placebo
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (JETALS; Oki 2022)
cards.people: 130 patients (129 in the full analysis set) with ALS diagnosed within 1 year of onset by updated Awaji criteria, recruited at 25 neurology centres in Japan; after a 12-week observation period, only patients with a 1- or 2-point ALSFRS-R decline during observation, forced vital capacity over 60%, no respiratory support and ambulatory status were randomised — 65 to methylcobalamin 50 mg intramuscularly twice weekly and 65 to placebo, for a 16-week randomised period. Mean age 61.0 years; 56.9% men; 126 completed the double-blind stage and 124 entered the open-label extension.
cards.result: Change in ALSFRS-R total score at week 16 was −2.66 on methylcobalamin versus −4.63 on placebo — a least-squares mean difference of 1.97 points (95% CI 0.44 to 3.50; P=0.01), i.e. about a 43% relative slowing of decline over 16 weeks. The incidence of adverse events was similar between the two groups, and the authors conclude ultrahigh-dose methylcobalamin was efficacious in slowing functional decline in early-stage ALS with moderate progression rate, and safe over the 16-week treatment period.
cards.watchOut: Sixteen weeks is a very short lens on a disease measured in years: this trial cannot speak to survival, ventilation or durability, and its twice-selected population (within a year of onset AND declining at exactly the moderate rate the run-in was built to find) is a minority of clinic ALS. The 43% figure is a relative slowing of a 16-week decline — in absolute terms it is 1.97 points on a 48-point scale.
cards.source: Oki R et al. Efficacy and Safety of Ultrahigh-Dose Methylcobalamin in Early-Stage Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Neurology. 2022. PMID: 35532908. Registry ID: NCT03548311. cards.headline: Phase 2/3 programme (Kaji 2019): in 373 patients the primary endpoints were NOT met (minimum p=0.087) — the early-entry benefit (entered ≤12 months from onset) is a post-hoc analysis
cards.summary: Phase 2/3 programme (Kaji 2019): in 373 patients the primary endpoints were NOT met (minimum p=0.087) — the early-entry benefit (entered ≤12 months from onset) is a post-hoc analysis
cards.people: 373 patients with ALS (El Escorial definite, probable or laboratory-supported probable; disease duration up to 36 months), randomly assigned to placebo or methylcobalamin 25 mg or 50 mg intramuscularly. Primary endpoints: time to a primary event (death or full ventilation support) and change in ALSFRS-R from baseline to week 182. Post-hoc analyses examined patients diagnosed and entered early, within 12 months of symptom onset.
cards.result: No significant differences were detected in either primary endpoint in the whole cohort (minimal p value 0.087). In post-hoc analyses, methylcobalamin-treated patients entered within 12 months of onset showed a longer time to the primary event (p<0.025) and smaller decreases in ALSFRS-R score (p<0.025) than placebo. The incidence of treatment-related adverse events was similar and low in all groups. The authors conclude ultra-high-dose methylcobalamin did not show significant efficacy in the whole cohort but may prolong survival and retard progression if started early.
cards.watchOut: Read this card before the JETALS card and the programme's logic is clear: a negative all-comers trial, a post-hoc early-disease signal, then a confirmatory trial (JETALS) built on exactly that signal. That sequence is legitimate — but it means the entire clinical claim rests on JETALS's 130 selected patients, and the 182-week survival question the phase 2/3 trial posed was never answered positively in a prespecified analysis.
cards.source: Kaji R et al. Ultra-high-dose methylcobalamin in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis: a long-term phase II/III randomised controlled study. Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery, and Psychiatry. 2019. PMID: 30636701. Registry ID: NCT00444613. cards.headline: First dose study (Kaji 1998): ultrahigh-dose methylcobalamin increased compound muscle action potential amplitude at 4 weeks — a surrogate endpoint in 24 patients
cards.summary: First dose study (Kaji 1998): ultrahigh-dose methylcobalamin increased compound muscle action potential amplitude at 4 weeks — a surrogate endpoint in 24 patients
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind controlled study (Kaji 1998) — surrogate endpoint
cards.people: 24 patients with ALS, 12 assigned to ultrahigh-dose methylcobalamin (25 mg/day intramuscularly for 14 days) and 12 to low-dose (0.5 mg/day). Outcome: averaged compound muscle action potential (CMAP) amplitude at 2 and 4 weeks — an electrophysiological measure of functioning motor units, not a clinical or functional outcome.
cards.result: No significant CMAP changes occurred in the low-dose group at 2 or 4 weeks; the ultrahigh-dose group showed a significant increase in CMAP amplitude at 4 weeks. The authors propose the method may provide a clinically useful measure to improve or retard muscle wasting if a larger extended trial fulfils its promise.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-four patients, fourteen days of treatment, and a surrogate that has never been validated against survival or function in ALS. This card is the programme's origin story — the dose rationale for everything after it — and is evidence of biological activity at most, not of patient benefit.
cards.source: Kaji R et al. Effect of ultrahigh-dose methylcobalamin on compound muscle action potentials in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis: a double-blind controlled study. Muscle & Nerve. 1998. PMID: 9843082. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a real phase 3 positive, in a narrow slice of ALS, over 16 weeks — POSSIBLE, Japan-only, durability unknown
cards.summary: Synthesis: a real phase 3 positive, in a narrow slice of ALS, over 16 weeks — POSSIBLE, Japan-only, durability unknown
cards.people: Synthesis of the three reports carded on this shelf: JETALS phase 3 (130 randomised), the earlier phase 2/3 trial (373 randomised) and the 1998 dose/surrogate study (24 patients) — all from the same Japanese research programme.
cards.result: The prespecified evidence arc is: negative all-comers phase 2/3 (primary endpoints missed), post-hoc early-entry signal, then a positive phase 3 restricted to that early, moderate-progressor population (1.97 ALSFRS-R points over 16 weeks, ~43% relative slowing, adverse events similar to placebo). No trial in the programme has shown a survival benefit in a prespecified analysis, and no non-Japanese population has been randomised.
cards.watchOut: POSSIBLE (benefit) is the programme ceiling for a single-country, single-programme result with a 16-week randomised horizon. Generalising JETALS to all-stage ALS, or to a survival claim, goes beyond anything carded here.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards on this shelf (PMIDs 35532908, 30636701, 9843082). No additional source.

shelves.title: Azetukalner (XEN1101) in focal epilepsy: median seizure-frequency reduction 53.2% at 25 mg vs 10.4% on placebo in phase 3 (X-TOLE2), replicating phase 2b — an unapproved Kv7 opener from a single development programme
shelves.question: In adults with focal-onset seizures on stable antiseizure medication, does the Kv7 potassium-channel opener XEN1101 (azetukalner), versus placebo, reduce monthly seizure frequency?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). The drug developed as XEN1101 is now named azetukalner (Xenon Pharmaceuticals) — both names are carried on this shelf, as the publications themselves use both. The randomised evidence is unusually consistent for an epilepsy programme: in phase 2b (X-TOLE, 325 patients) median monthly focal-seizure frequency fell 52.8% on 25 mg versus 18.2% on placebo, with a clean dose-response (46.4% at 20 mg, 33.2% at 10 mg); in phase 3 (X-TOLE2, 374 patients with highly drug-resistant epilepsy — a median of five previously failed antiseizure medications) the 25 mg dose again gave a 53.2% median reduction versus 10.4% on placebo, and the 15 mg dose 34.5%. The open-label extension suggests the effect is sustained over two years in patients who stay on the drug, though extension data have no comparator and shed non-responders. The limits are structural: this is one company's programme with no independent replication; the randomised periods are 8–12 weeks; the commonest adverse events are dizziness and somnolence (with memory impairment reported in 10.9% in the extension); and the Kv7-opener class carries a cautionary history — the earlier Kv7 opener retigabine was withdrawn from the market — so long-term, large-population safety is not yet characterised. Azetukalner was not an approved drug at the time this shelf was built; a US new drug application was submitted in 2026 (sponsor-reported).

cards.headline: X-TOLE phase 2b (French 2023): dose-dependent seizure reduction — median 52.8% at 25 mg, 46.4% at 20 mg, 33.2% at 10 mg vs 18.2% on placebo over 8 weeks
cards.summary: X-TOLE phase 2b (French 2023): dose-dependent seizure reduction — median 52.8% at 25 mg, 46.4% at 20 mg, 33.2% at 10 mg vs 18.2% on placebo over 8 weeks
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2b dose-ranging trial (X-TOLE; French 2023)
cards.people: 325 adults with focal-onset seizures (4 or more monthly) on stable treatment with 1–3 antiseizure medications, at 97 sites in North America and Europe, randomised 2:1:1:2 to XEN1101 (azetukalner) 25, 20 or 10 mg or placebo, taken once daily with food for 8 weeks without titration; 285 completed the double-blind phase. Mean age 40.8 years; 51.7% female. Primary endpoint: median percent change from baseline in monthly focal-seizure frequency.
cards.result: Median percent reduction in monthly focal-seizure frequency was 52.8% on 25 mg (P<0.001 vs placebo), 46.4% on 20 mg (P<0.001) and 33.2% on 10 mg (P=0.04), versus 18.2% on placebo — a robust dose-response. XEN1101 was generally well tolerated, treatment-emergent adverse events were similar to those of commonly prescribed antiseizure medications, and no treatment-emergent adverse event led to death.
cards.watchOut: Eight weeks of double-blind treatment in a lifelong disease, and a median-percent-change endpoint that flatters responders: the interquartile ranges are wide (at 25 mg, −80.4% to −16.9%), meaning a substantial minority gained little. Phase 2b populations in epilepsy programmes are also typically less treatment-resistant than the phase 3 population turned out to be — which makes the phase 3 replication on the next card the more important result.
cards.source: French JA et al. Efficacy and Safety of XEN1101, a Novel Potassium Channel Opener, in Adults With Focal Epilepsy: A Phase 2b Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Neurology. 2023. PMID: 37812429. Registry ID: NCT03796962. cards.headline: X-TOLE2 phase 3 (French 2026): azetukalner 25 mg cut median monthly seizure frequency by 53.2% vs 10.4% on placebo (p<0.001) in patients who had already failed a median of five antiseizure medications
cards.summary: X-TOLE2 phase 3 (French 2026): azetukalner 25 mg cut median monthly seizure frequency by 53.2% vs 10.4% on placebo (p<0.001) in patients who had already failed a median of five antiseizure medications
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (X-TOLE2; French 2026)
cards.people: 374 adults with focal epilepsy experiencing 4 or more focal seizures per month despite stable treatment with 1–3 antiseizure medications, at 138 sites across North America, South America, Europe and Asia-Pacific, randomised 1:1:1 to azetukalner 25 mg (n=124), 15 mg (n=125) or placebo (n=125) once daily with the evening meal for 12 weeks, no titration. Mean age 40.0 years; 50.8% female; baseline median seizure frequency 12.75 per month; participants had previously tried and stopped a median of 5 antiseizure medications, and 89.8% were receiving 2–3 concomitant antiseizure medications.
cards.result: Median change from baseline in monthly focal-seizure frequency was −53.2% on azetukalner 25 mg (P<0.001 vs placebo) and −34.5% on 15 mg (P<0.001), versus −10.4% on placebo. Azetukalner was generally well tolerated, and treatment-emergent adverse events were comparable to those observed in the phase 2b X-TOLE trial. The authors describe the 25 mg result as one of the largest median percentage reductions versus placebo reported in drug-resistant epilepsy.
cards.watchOut: A sponsor-run phase 3 reported in the programme's own terms: the headline is a median, in a population whose placebo response (10.4%) was low, over 12 weeks. Seizure-freedom rates and responder proportions — the outcomes patients feel — are not in this report's abstracted results, and no active comparator exists anywhere in the programme: azetukalner has never been tested head-to-head against another antiseizure medication.
cards.source: French JA et al. Azetukalner in Adults With Focal Seizures: The X-TOLE2 Phase 3 Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Neurology. 2026. PMID: 43002431. Registry ID: NCT05614063. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: X-TOLE open-label extension interim (French 2025): at 24 months, median seizure reduction 83.2% from double-blind baseline among those remaining on azetukalner; dizziness 21.8%, somnolence 12.7%, memory impairment 10.9%
cards.summary: X-TOLE open-label extension interim (French 2025): at 24 months, median seizure reduction 83.2% from double-blind baseline among those remaining on azetukalner; dizziness 21.8%, somnolence 12.7%, memory impairment 10.9%
cards.type: Open-label extension interim analysis (X-TOLE extension; French 2025) — uncontrolled
cards.people: Of 285 participants who completed the X-TOLE double-blind phase, 275 (96.5%) entered the 7-year open-label extension at azetukalner 20 mg once daily with food. At the 24-month interim analysis (September 2023), 182 participants had been treated for at least 12 months and 165 for at least 24 months; 152 (55.3%) remained in the study; median treatment duration 26.3 months.
cards.result: Median percent reduction in monthly focal-seizure frequency was 83.2% at 24 months versus the double-blind baseline. Across all extension entrants, 56.4% achieved a 50% or greater seizure reduction, 19.6% achieved a 90% or greater reduction, and 14.9% were seizure-free for a consecutive 12-month period or longer (23.6% among those treated at least 24 months). Most treatment-emergent adverse events were mild or moderate; the commonest were dizziness (21.8%), headache (15.3%), coronavirus infection (15.3%), somnolence (12.7%), falls (12.7%) and memory impairment (10.9%); serious adverse events occurred in 12.7%.
cards.watchOut: Extension numbers describe survivors, not starters: by 24 months nearly half the entrants had left, and patients who do not benefit or do not tolerate a drug leave first, so the 83.2% figure cannot be compared with the randomised results. The card's real value is safety exposure and the absence of new safety signals over two years — plus the memory-impairment rate, which deserves watching for a centrally acting drug taken for decades.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a consistent, dose-dependent ~50% median seizure reduction across phase 2b and phase 3 — POSSIBLE pending approval, independent replication and long-term safety
cards.summary: Synthesis: a consistent, dose-dependent ~50% median seizure reduction across phase 2b and phase 3 — POSSIBLE pending approval, independent replication and long-term safety
cards.people: Synthesis of the three reports carded on this shelf: X-TOLE phase 2b (325 treated), X-TOLE2 phase 3 (374 randomised) and the X-TOLE open-label extension interim analysis (275 entrants) — one development programme (Xenon Pharmaceuticals).
cards.result: Two randomised, placebo-controlled trials agree closely at the top dose (median reductions 52.8% and 53.2% at 25 mg versus 18.2% and 10.4% on placebo), with a dose-response in phase 2b and a second effective dose (15 mg) in phase 3. Extension data suggest durability in continuers and no new safety signals over two years, with dizziness, somnolence and memory impairment the events to watch.
cards.watchOut: POSSIBLE is the single-programme ceiling: no independent group has randomised azetukalner, no head-to-head trial exists, randomised exposure totals 12 weeks, and the Kv7 class history (retigabine's withdrawal) means rare or late harms are simply not yet observable. The stamp should be revisited at approval and after post-marketing exposure accrues.

shelves.title: Intravenous glibenclamide in large hemispheric infarction (CHARM): no improvement in 90-day functional outcome (common OR 1.17; p=0.42) in a phase 3 trial stopped early by its sponsor — benefit not shown, and not definitively excluded
shelves.question: In adults 18–70 with large hemispheric infarction, does intravenous glibenclamide (glyburide), versus placebo, improve 90-day functional outcome by limiting cerebral oedema?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — with the underpowered caveat printed, not buried. The phase 3 CHARM trial (431 patients in its primary analysis population) found no favourable shift in 90-day modified Rankin Scale scores with intravenous glibenclamide (the drug called glyburide in the US) versus placebo (common odds ratio 1.17; 95% CI 0.80 to 1.71; p=0.42), and mortality was numerically higher on drug (32% vs 29%). But CHARM was stopped early by its sponsor for strategic and operational reasons — slow COVID-era enrolment — before unblinding, so it is underpowered for the modest effect it sought: the honest answer is 'not shown to work', not 'disproven'. The phase 2 GAMES-RP trial was likewise neutral on its composite primary outcome (41% vs 39%), though it and its exploratory follow-ups showed less midline shift and lower MMP-9 on drug, and an exploratory survival advantage in patients aged 70 or under — the signal that shaped CHARM's design. A post-hoc CHARM analysis restricted to infarct cores under 125 mL found a favourable shift (adjusted common OR 2.11), strongest in thrombectomy-treated patients; that is a hypothesis for a future trial, not a result to act on. Hypoglycaemia is the drug's predictable harm (6% vs 2% in CHARM). This shelf is the companion answer to the oedema question in large hemispheric infarction: a biologically coherent idea, tested at phase 3 scale, that has not demonstrated a functional benefit.

cards.headline: CHARM (Sheth 2024): IV glibenclamide did not improve 90-day functional outcome (mRS shift common OR 1.17, 0.80–1.71; p=0.42); mortality 32% vs 29%; hypoglycaemia 6% vs 2% — trial stopped early by the sponsor
cards.summary: CHARM (Sheth 2024): IV glibenclamide did not improve 90-day functional outcome (mRS shift common OR 1.17, 0.80–1.71; p=0.42); mortality 32% vs 29%; hypoglycaemia 6% vs 2% — trial stopped early by the sponsor
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (CHARM; Sheth 2024)
cards.people: 535 patients aged 18–85 with large hemispheric infarction (ASPECTS 1–5, or ischaemic core 80–300 mL on CT perfusion or diffusion MRI) at 143 centres in 21 countries, randomised to intravenous glibenclamide (8.6 mg over 72 hours, started within 10 hours of onset) or placebo; 518 received a dose. The primary efficacy population was the 431 patients aged 18–70 (217 glibenclamide, 214 placebo); mean age about 58 years, median NIHSS 19. Primary outcome: shift in the distribution of modified Rankin Scale scores at day 90.
cards.result: Intravenous glibenclamide was not associated with a favourable shift in the modified Rankin Scale at 90 days (common odds ratio 1.17; 95% CI 0.80 to 1.71; p=0.42). Mortality at 90 days was 32% (70 of 217) on glibenclamide versus 29% (61 of 214) on placebo (hazard ratio 1.20; 95% CI 0.85 to 1.70; p=0.30). Hypoglycaemia occurred in 15 of 259 (6%) on glibenclamide versus 4 of 259 (2%) on placebo, leading to dose interruption or reduction in 7 patients (3%) versus 1. The trial was stopped early by the sponsor (Biogen) for strategic and operational reasons — slow enrolment because of COVID-19 — before any unblinding, and the authors state it was underpowered to make definitive conclusions.
cards.watchOut: A negative primary in an underpowered trial cuts both ways: it neither establishes benefit nor proves futility, and the confidence interval (0.80 to 1.71) is wide enough to contain a clinically meaningful effect in either direction. What CHARM does settle is that no large treatment effect exists in unselected large hemispheric infarction — any real benefit, if present, is modest or confined to a subgroup.

cards.summary: GAMES-RP (Sheth 2016): phase 2 primary outcome neutral — mRS 0–4 without decompressive craniectomy in 41% on IV glyburide vs 39% on placebo (adjusted OR 0.87; p=0.77); enrolment stopped for funding
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial (GAMES-RP; Sheth 2016)
cards.people: 86 patients aged 18–80 with large anterior-circulation hemispheric infarction (diffusion-weighted MRI lesion volume 82–300 cm³) presenting within 10 hours, at 18 US hospitals, randomised to intravenous glyburide (RP-1127; glibenclamide — 0.13 mg bolus, then 0.16 mg/h for 6 hours, then 0.11 mg/h for 66 hours) or placebo. Per-protocol population: 41 on glyburide, 36 on placebo. Primary efficacy outcome: modified Rankin Scale score 0–4 at 90 days without decompressive craniectomy.
cards.result: The primary outcome was achieved by 17 of 41 patients (41%) on intravenous glyburide and 14 of 36 (39%) on placebo (adjusted odds ratio 0.87; 95% CI 0.32 to 2.32; p=0.77). Cardiac events occurred in 10 of 44 (23%) on glyburide and 10 of 39 (26%) on placebo, with one cardiac death in each group. The drug was well tolerated. Enrolment was stopped because of funding reasons, and the authors conclude further study was warranted to assess the potential clinical benefit of the reduction in swelling seen with glyburide.
cards.watchOut: Eighty-six randomised patients and a per-protocol primary analysis: GAMES-RP was a safety-and-signal trial, and its composite endpoint (function plus avoiding craniectomy) mixes a drug effect with surgical decision-making. Its neutral primary is part of the record — the programme's encouraging findings have always lived in secondary and exploratory analyses, which is precisely the pattern CHARM was built to test and did not confirm.
cards.source: Sheth KN et al. Safety and efficacy of intravenous glyburide on brain swelling after large hemispheric infarction (GAMES-RP): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial. The Lancet Neurology. 2016. PMID: 27567243. Registry ID: NCT01794182. cards.headline: GAMES-RP long-term exploratory analysis (Sheth 2018): in patients aged ≤70, mortality was lower on IV glyburide (HR 0.34; p=0.04), with less midline shift (4.7 vs 9 mm) and lower MMP-9 — exploratory, and the origin of CHARM's age restriction
cards.summary: GAMES-RP long-term exploratory analysis (Sheth 2018): in patients aged ≤70, mortality was lower on IV glyburide (HR 0.34; p=0.04), with less midline shift (4.7 vs 9 mm) and lower MMP-9 — exploratory, and the origin of CHARM's age restriction
cards.type: Exploratory long-term analysis of a phase 2 trial (GAMES-RP; Sheth 2018)
cards.people: Participants in GAMES-RP aged 70 years or under who met per-protocol criteria: 35 treated with intravenous glyburide and 30 with placebo. Outcomes: mortality at 90 days and 12 months, functional outcome (modified Rankin Scale, Barthel Index), quality of life (EQ-5D), and oedema measures (plasma MMP-9 and brain midline shift).
cards.result: Participants aged 70 or under treated with intravenous glyburide had lower mortality at all time points (hazard ratio for survival 0.34; log-rank P=0.04). Functional outcome showed a trend toward benefit at 90 days after age adjustment (odds ratio 2.31; P=0.07), with significant treatment effects on the Barthel Index (P=0.03) and EQ-5D (P=0.05) in repeated-measures analysis across 90 days, 6 and 12 months. Glyburide-treated participants had lower plasma MMP-9 (189 vs 376 ng/mL; P<0.001) and less midline shift (4.7 vs 9 mm; P<0.001) than placebo.
cards.watchOut: Exploratory, age-restricted, per-protocol and small (65 patients): every classic inflation factor in one analysis. It is carded because it is the documented reason CHARM restricted its primary population to patients 70 and under — and CHARM then tested that exact population and found no significant benefit, which is how the reader should weigh it.
cards.source: Sheth KN et al. Long-Term Outcomes in Patients Aged ≤70 Years With Intravenous Glyburide From the Phase II GAMES-RP Study of Large Hemispheric Infarction: An Exploratory Analysis. Stroke. 2018. PMID: 29789393. Registry ID: NCT01794182. cards.headline: CHARM post-hoc subgroup analysis (Kimberly 2025): in infarct cores under 125 mL, IV glyburide showed a favourable mRS shift (adjusted common OR 2.11) — hypothesis-generating only, from the trial whose primary analysis was negative
cards.summary: CHARM post-hoc subgroup analysis (Kimberly 2025): in infarct cores under 125 mL, IV glyburide showed a favourable mRS shift (adjusted common OR 2.11) — hypothesis-generating only, from the trial whose primary analysis was negative
cards.type: Post-hoc subgroup analysis of a phase 3 trial (CHARM; Kimberly 2025) — explicitly labelled second report of CHARM
cards.people: 147 CHARM participants aged 70 or under with a baseline ischaemic core volume under 125 mL on CT perfusion or diffusion MRI (mean age 58 years; 37% women; median core volume 92 mL; baseline NIHSS 18), analysed post-hoc by treatment arm, including the subgroup who underwent endovascular thrombectomy. Primary endpoint: shift analysis of the 90-day modified Rankin Scale.
cards.result: Within this smaller-core subgroup, intravenous glyburide was associated with a favourable shift in 90-day outcome versus placebo (adjusted common odds ratio 2.11; 95% CI 1.10 to 4.01; p=0.02). Among thrombectomy-treated patients the adjusted common odds ratio was 8.19 (95% CI 1.60 to 42.0; p=0.01), with fewer decompressive craniectomies (0% vs 25%; p=0.02), less midline shift (4.2 vs 7.6 mm; p=0.02) and lower 90-day mortality (5.6% vs 31%; p=0.05). The authors state these results are hypothesis-generating and require confirmation in a prospective randomised trial.
cards.watchOut: This is a post-hoc volume cut inside a negative trial, and the thrombectomy numbers rest on very small cell counts (a confidence interval from 1.60 to 42.0 is a warning label, not an estimate). It must not be quoted without its parent result: in the whole CHARM primary population the same drug, dose and endpoint gave a common odds ratio of 1.17 with p=0.42.

cards.headline: Synthesis: phase 2 neutral, phase 3 negative-but-underpowered, subgroups favourable — IV glibenclamide has not demonstrated a functional benefit in large hemispheric infarction
cards.summary: Synthesis: phase 2 neutral, phase 3 negative-but-underpowered, subgroups favourable — IV glibenclamide has not demonstrated a functional benefit in large hemispheric infarction
cards.people: Synthesis of the four reports carded on this shelf: CHARM phase 3 (431 in the primary population), GAMES-RP phase 2 (86 randomised), its exploratory long-term analysis (65 patients aged ≤70), and the post-hoc CHARM smaller-core subgroup analysis (147 patients).
cards.result: Every prespecified primary analysis in the programme is neutral: GAMES-RP 41% vs 39% (p=0.77); CHARM common odds ratio 1.17 (p=0.42) with mortality 32% vs 29%. Every favourable finding — less midline shift, lower MMP-9, the under-70 survival signal, the under-125 mL subgroup — is secondary, exploratory or post-hoc. The drug's mechanism (less oedema) is supported by the imaging and biomarker data; a patient-level functional benefit is not.
cards.watchOut: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) carries CHARM's own caveat: the trial stopped early and was underpowered, so a modest benefit is not excluded. A future trial restricted to smaller-core or thrombectomy-treated patients would be testing the post-hoc hypothesis on the last card — until one reports, the demonstrated answer is no benefit shown.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards on this shelf (PMIDs 39577921, 27567243, 29789393, 40476628). No additional source.

shelves.title: Colchicine started acutely after stroke or TIA (CHANCE-3): new stroke in 6.3% vs 6.5% over 90 days (HR 0.98) — no benefit from starting colchicine within 24 hours in hs-CRP-selected patients
shelves.question: In adults with acute minor ischaemic stroke or high-risk TIA and hs-CRP ≥2 mg/L, does colchicine 0.5 mg started within 24 hours for 90 days, versus placebo, prevent new stroke?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference). This shelf answers the acute question — start colchicine within 24 hours of a minor stroke or high-risk TIA, in patients selected for inflammation (hs-CRP at least 2 mg/L), and treat for 90 days — and the answer from CHANCE-3 (8,343 patients, 244 hospitals in China) is no: new stroke occurred in 6.3% on colchicine versus 6.5% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.98), with serious adverse events balanced (2.2% vs 2.1%). Unlike many negative trials, this one was large enough for its null to mean something. Two further cautions sit on the face. First, the trial's prespecified intracranial-stenosis analysis found the point estimate reversed in patients with symptomatic intracranial atherosclerotic stenosis (10.5% vs 8.5% recurrent stroke on colchicine; adjusted HR 1.30), with a significant treatment-by-subgroup interaction — hypothesis-grade, but a harm signal, not a benefit signal. Second, a 2026 meta-analysis of five randomised trials (18,336 participants, including the long-term trials) found no significant reduction in recurrent stroke (relative risk 0.86; 95% CI 0.65 to 1.12). This is the companion shelf to live shelf #1613, which holds the separate long-term colchicine question (CONVINCE); the acute-initiation slice is not carded there, and CONVINCE's own card stays in its home — it appears here only as one pooled component of the meta-analysis card. Flags: CHANCE-3 is a single-country (China) trial in a biomarker-selected population; its result does not answer colchicine questions in other populations or at other timings.

cards.headline: CHANCE-3 (Li 2024): colchicine started within 24 hours did not prevent new stroke at 90 days — 6.3% vs 6.5% (HR 0.98, 0.83–1.16; p=0.79); serious adverse events 2.2% vs 2.1%
cards.summary: CHANCE-3 (Li 2024): colchicine started within 24 hours did not prevent new stroke at 90 days — 6.3% vs 6.5% (HR 0.98, 0.83–1.16; p=0.79); serious adverse events 2.2% vs 2.1%
cards.people: 8,343 patients aged 40 or older with minor-to-moderate non-cardioembolic ischaemic stroke or transient ischaemic attack and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein at least 2 mg/L, at 244 hospitals in China, randomised 1:1 within 24 hours of symptom onset to colchicine (0.5 mg twice daily on days 1–3, then 0.5 mg daily; n=4,176) or placebo (n=4,167) for 90 days. Primary efficacy outcome: any new stroke within 90 days; primary safety outcome: any serious adverse event. All analyses by intention to treat.
cards.result: Stroke occurred within 90 days in 264 patients (6.3%) on colchicine and 270 (6.5%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.98; 95% CI 0.83 to 1.16; P=0.79). Any serious adverse event was observed in 91 patients (2.2%) on colchicine and 88 (2.1%) on placebo (P=0.83). The authors conclude the study did not provide evidence that low-dose colchicine reduces the risk of subsequent stroke within 90 days in this population.
cards.watchOut: A single-country (China) trial in a biomarker-selected population: hs-CRP at least 2 mg/L was an entry requirement, so the null applies to inflammation-selected patients — the group in whom an anti-inflammatory drug had its best theoretical shot, which strengthens rather than weakens the negative reading. The 90-day horizon and minor-to-moderate severity range bound the claim: CHANCE-3 does not address major stroke, cardioembolic stroke, or treatment beyond three months.
cards.source: Li J et al. Colchicine in patients with acute ischaemic stroke or transient ischaemic attack (CHANCE-3): multicentre, double blind, randomised, placebo controlled trial. BMJ. 2024. PMID: 38925803. Registry ID: NCT05439356. cards.headline: CHANCE-3 prespecified stenosis analysis (Li 2025): in patients WITH symptomatic intracranial stenosis, recurrent stroke was commoner on colchicine (10.5% vs 8.5%; adjusted HR 1.30) — interaction p=0.01
cards.summary: CHANCE-3 prespecified stenosis analysis (Li 2025): in patients WITH symptomatic intracranial stenosis, recurrent stroke was commoner on colchicine (10.5% vs 8.5%; adjusted HR 1.30) — interaction p=0.01
cards.type: Prespecified subgroup analysis of a randomised trial (CHANCE-3; Li 2025) — explicitly labelled second report of CHANCE-3
cards.people: 7,567 CHANCE-3 participants with baseline assessment of the intracranial arteries, divided by the presence or absence of symptomatic intracranial artery stenosis (sICAS). Primary efficacy outcome: new stroke at 90 days; secondary: combined vascular events (ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke, TIA, myocardial infarction, vascular death); safety: any serious adverse event, with diarrhoea reported by subgroup.
cards.result: In patients with sICAS, recurrent stroke occurred in 141 (10.5%) on colchicine versus 115 (8.5%) on placebo (adjusted hazard ratio 1.30; 95% CI 1.01 to 1.69; p=0.04); in patients without sICAS the rates were 4.2% versus 5.2% (adjusted hazard ratio 0.80; 95% CI 0.62 to 1.05; p=0.10), with a significant interaction (adjusted p=0.01), also present for combined vascular events (interaction p=0.02) and stronger in older patients (interaction p<0.001): in elderly patients with sICAS the adjusted hazard ratio was 1.58 (95% CI 1.13 to 2.20). There was no interaction for serious adverse events (p=0.54). Diarrhoea was commoner on colchicine in both subgroups (with sICAS 1.8% vs 0.5%, p=0.002; without 1.8% vs 0.8%, p=0.004). The authors state the effect of colchicine may differ by sICAS status and that prospective confirmation is needed.
cards.watchOut: Prespecified is not the same as proven: this is one subgroup split of a null trial, the harm estimate in sICAS barely excludes 1.0, and subgroup interactions in stroke trials have a poor replication record. Its correct use on this shelf is directional discipline — it removes any temptation to hunt for a hidden benefit population inside CHANCE-3, because the only significant interaction in the trial points the other way.

cards.headline: Meta-analysis of colchicine trials (Barboza 2026): across five RCTs and 18,336 participants, recurrent stroke was not significantly reduced (relative risk 0.86, 0.65–1.12); the stroke/TIA-only sensitivity analysis stayed near the null
cards.summary: Meta-analysis of colchicine trials (Barboza 2026): across five RCTs and 18,336 participants, recurrent stroke was not significantly reduced (relative risk 0.86, 0.65–1.12); the stroke/TIA-only sensitivity analysis stayed near the null
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Barboza 2026)
cards.people: Five randomised controlled trials (18,336 participants) of colchicine in patients with non-cardioembolic ischaemic stroke or high-risk TIA, plus atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease cohorts reporting cerebrovascular outcomes; searches to 20 October 2025. The stroke/TIA-dedicated trials in the prespecified sensitivity analysis were CHANCE-3, CONVINCE and COPS. Primary outcome: recurrent stroke; certainty rated with GRADE.
cards.result: Colchicine did not significantly reduce recurrent stroke versus control (relative risk 0.86; 95% CI 0.65 to 1.12), nor vascular events (relative risk 0.70; 95% CI 0.40 to 1.23, with substantial heterogeneity), nor did it significantly increase serious adverse events (relative risk 1.14; 95% CI 0.43 to 2.97). Restricted to the stroke/TIA-dedicated trials, the point estimate for recurrent stroke remained close to the null. Gastrointestinal adverse events and study-drug discontinuation were commoner on colchicine. GRADE certainty was moderate for recurrent stroke and low for vascular events and serious adverse events. The authors conclude current evidence does not support routine colchicine use for secondary stroke prevention.
cards.watchOut: This pool mixes timings and populations — acute initiation (CHANCE-3), long-term prevention (CONVINCE, whose own card is homed on live shelf #1613 and is not re-carded here) and coronary cohorts — so it corroborates the acute null rather than re-testing it. Its weight on this shelf is that no pooling of the randomised record rescues an acute-start benefit.

cards.headline: Synthesis: starting colchicine within 24 hours of a minor stroke or high-risk TIA does not prevent the next stroke — a large acute null, a harm-pointing subgroup, and a null pooled record
cards.summary: Synthesis: starting colchicine within 24 hours of a minor stroke or high-risk TIA does not prevent the next stroke — a large acute null, a harm-pointing subgroup, and a null pooled record
cards.people: Synthesis of the three reports carded on this shelf: CHANCE-3 (8,343 randomised), its prespecified intracranial-stenosis analysis (7,567 with artery imaging), and a five-trial meta-analysis (18,336 participants).
cards.result: The acute-initiation question has a direct, adequately powered answer: hazard ratio 0.98 for new stroke at 90 days, with balanced serious adverse events. The only significant subgroup interaction points toward harm in symptomatic intracranial stenosis (adjusted HR 1.30), and the pooled randomised record across timings is also null for recurrent stroke (relative risk 0.86, interval crossing 1).
cards.watchOut: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) is scoped to acute initiation for 90 days in hs-CRP-selected minor stroke/TIA. The separate long-term prevention question lives on live shelf #1613 (CONVINCE) and is not re-ruled here; coronary colchicine trials answer a different population's question and are not imported.

shelves.title: Butylphthalide as an adjunct to reperfusion in acute ischaemic stroke (BAST): favourable 90-day outcome in 56.7% vs 44.0% (OR 1.70) — a positive trial from a single-country (China) programme; the drug is not licensed in the US or Europe
shelves.question: In adults with acute ischaemic stroke receiving intravenous thrombolysis and/or endovascular treatment, does dl-3-n-butylphthalide for 90 days, versus placebo, improve 90-day functional outcome?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), with the geography on the face: every randomised patient in this evidence base was treated in China, where dl-3-n-butylphthalide (NBP; Shijiazhuang Pharmaceutical Group) is an approved stroke drug; it is not licensed in the United States or Europe, and the product is named here under the library's clarification exception because preparations and regulatory status differ by market. The pivotal result is genuinely positive: in BAST (1,216 patients, 59 Chinese centres, all receiving intravenous thrombolysis and/or endovascular treatment), a favourable 90-day outcome occurred in 56.7% on butylphthalide versus 44.0% on placebo (odds ratio 1.70; 95% CI 1.35 to 2.14), with serious adverse events no higher on drug (10.1% vs 12.0%). Two qualifications define the claim. First, BAST's primary outcome used a baseline-severity-stratified definition of 'favourable' — modified Rankin Scale thresholds of 0 to 2 points depending on baseline NIHSS — rather than a single cut-off, so the 56.7% figure is not interchangeable with a plain mRS 0–2 rate. Second, the supporting evidence is thinner than the headline: a post-hoc BAST analysis tying benefit to favourable immune-inflammation trajectories is exploratory, and the one other placebo-controlled trial on this shelf (EBCAS, 99 patients) measured cerebral autoregulation, a physiological surrogate, not clinical outcome. A 2026 Chinese timing trial (204 patients, all receiving butylphthalide; early start within 3 hours versus 3–6 hours) found no significant difference on its primary outcome (relative risk 1.16; 95% CI 0.94 to 1.44; PMID: 43021208) — it had no placebo arm and does not test efficacy. Independent replication outside China is the missing piece.

cards.headline: BAST (Wang 2023): favourable 90-day outcome in 56.7% on butylphthalide vs 44.0% on placebo (OR 1.70, 1.35–2.14; p<0.001) in 1,216 reperfusion-treated patients; serious adverse events 10.1% vs 12.0%
cards.summary: BAST (Wang 2023): favourable 90-day outcome in 56.7% on butylphthalide vs 44.0% on placebo (OR 1.70, 1.35–2.14; p<0.001) in 1,216 reperfusion-treated patients; serious adverse events 10.1% vs 12.0%
cards.people: 1,216 patients aged 18 or older with acute ischaemic stroke (NIHSS 4–25) who received intravenous thrombolysis and/or endovascular treatment, at 59 centres in China, randomised 1:1 within 6 hours of symptom onset to dl-3-n-butylphthalide (607) or placebo (609) for 90 days; 68.0% men, median age 66 years. Primary outcome: the proportion with a favourable outcome at 90 days, defined by modified Rankin Scale thresholds of 0 to 2 points depending on baseline stroke severity (a baseline-NIHSS-stratified definition).
cards.result: A favourable functional outcome at 90 days occurred in 344 patients (56.7%) in the butylphthalide group and 268 (44.0%) in the placebo group (odds ratio 1.70; 95% CI 1.35 to 2.14; P<0.001). Serious adverse events within 90 days occurred in 61 patients (10.1%) on butylphthalide and 73 (12.0%) on placebo. The authors conclude that among patients with acute ischaemic stroke receiving intravenous thrombolysis and/or endovascular treatment, butylphthalide was associated with a higher proportion achieving a favourable functional outcome at 90 days than placebo.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint's stratified definition matters: 'favourable' meant different mRS ceilings for different baseline severities, so this trial's 56.7% cannot be lined up against other trials' mRS 0–2 rates, and a stratified endpoint chosen by the investigators deserves more scepticism than a standard one. Add the structural limits: one trial, one country, one sponsor ecosystem, in a drug class (stroke neuroprotection) with a decades-long record of single-region positives that did not travel.
cards.source: Wang A et al. Efficacy and Safety of Butylphthalide in Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Neurology. 2023. PMID: 37358859. Registry ID: NCT03539445. cards.headline: BAST post-hoc inflammation analysis (Zhou 2026): patients whose systemic immune-inflammation index stayed favourable and who received butylphthalide had the best outcomes (favourable mRS OR 3.60) — exploratory, not a treatment-effect estimate
cards.summary: BAST post-hoc inflammation analysis (Zhou 2026): patients whose systemic immune-inflammation index stayed favourable and who received butylphthalide had the best outcomes (favourable mRS OR 3.60) — exploratory, not a treatment-effect estimate
cards.type: Post-hoc secondary analysis of a randomised trial (BAST; Zhou 2026) — explicitly labelled second report of BAST
cards.people: 837 BAST participants with systemic immune-inflammation index (SII, from routine blood counts) measured at baseline and day 14, classified into four SII change patterns (persistent favourable, unfavourable-to-favourable, favourable-to-unfavourable, persistent unfavourable). Outcomes: favourable modified Rankin Scale score and mRS 0–2 at day 90, and recurrent stroke, vascular events and death within 90 days, examined by SII pattern and treatment assignment.
cards.result: Compared with the persistent-unfavourable group, the unfavourable-to-favourable and persistent-favourable SII groups had higher odds of a favourable mRS score (odds ratio 2.79; 95% CI 1.64 to 4.73; and 2.60; 1.66 to 4.06) and of mRS 0–2 at day 90, and lower risks of recurrent stroke, vascular events and death. Patients with persistently favourable SII who received butylphthalide showed the most favourable profile, including the highest proportion with a favourable mRS score at day 90 (odds ratio 3.60; 95% CI 1.97 to 6.58) and mRS 0–2 (odds ratio 4.38; 95% CI 2.23 to 8.62). The authors present these as exploratory associations possibly involving neuroinflammation and vascular pathways.
cards.watchOut: SII trajectory is itself an outcome of how the stroke evolves, so these comparisons largely re-describe prognosis: patients whose inflammation settles do better, with or without the drug. Nothing in this analysis can separate 'butylphthalide improves inflammation' from 'recovering patients have quieter blood counts'. It is carded to show what the programme's secondary literature does and does not add — it does not add an efficacy estimate.
cards.source: Zhou Q et al. Favorable Systemic Immune-Inflammation Status Enhances the Neuroprotective Effects of Butylphthalide in Ischemic Stroke: A Post Hoc Analysis of BAST Trial. cards.headline: EBCAS (Guo 2023): butylphthalide improved cerebral autoregulation versus placebo over 90 days in 99 patients with large-artery atherosclerosis stroke — a physiological endpoint, with no clinical-outcome claim
cards.summary: EBCAS (Guo 2023): butylphthalide improved cerebral autoregulation versus placebo over 90 days in 99 patients with large-artery atherosclerosis stroke — a physiological endpoint, with no clinical-outcome claim
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled multicentre trial — physiological endpoint (EBCAS; Guo 2023)
cards.people: 99 patients with acute ischaemic stroke due to large-artery atherosclerosis, randomised 2:1 to butylphthalide (intravenous infusion for 14 days, then oral capsules for a further 76 days) or matching placebo (saline infusion and simulated capsules); 80 patients completed follow-up (52 butylphthalide, 28 placebo). Primary outcomes: cerebral autoregulation (transfer-function phase difference and gain) on the affected side at day 14 and day 90.
cards.result: Phase difference on the affected side at day 14 (or discharge) and at day 90 was higher in the butylphthalide group than the placebo group, indicating better cerebral autoregulation; differences in safety outcomes were not significant. The authors conclude butylphthalide treatment for 90 days can significantly improve cerebral autoregulation in patients with acute ischaemic stroke.
cards.watchOut: A surrogate-mechanism trial: better autoregulation numbers are not fewer disabled survivors, the analysed sample is the 80 completers rather than the 99 randomised, and the population (large-artery atherosclerosis, not reperfusion-treated) differs from BAST's. Its role here is mechanistic coherence for the BAST result — nothing more.
cards.source: Guo ZN et al. Effectiveness of butylphthalide on cerebral autoregulation in ischemic stroke patients with large artery atherosclerosis (EBCAS study): A randomized, controlled, multicenter trial. Journal of Cerebral Blood Flow and Metabolism. 2023. PMID: 37021629. Registry ID: NCT03413202. cards.headline: Synthesis: one positive pivotal trial, one exploratory post-hoc, one surrogate-endpoint trial — POSSIBLE (benefit), wholly within a single-country programme
cards.summary: Synthesis: one positive pivotal trial, one exploratory post-hoc, one surrogate-endpoint trial — POSSIBLE (benefit), wholly within a single-country programme
cards.people: Synthesis of the three reports carded on this shelf: BAST (1,216 randomised), its post-hoc inflammation analysis (837 with biomarker data), and EBCAS (99 randomised) — all conducted in China.
cards.result: BAST provides a genuine randomised positive on a functional outcome (odds ratio 1.70 for its stratified favourable-outcome definition; serious adverse events 10.1% vs 12.0%). Neither supporting card adds independent clinical-outcome evidence: one re-analyses BAST by biomarker trajectory, the other shows a physiological effect in a different population. No trial outside China has randomised butylphthalide for stroke.
cards.watchOut: POSSIBLE (benefit) is capped by single-country, single-programme evidence and by BAST's non-standard primary-outcome definition. The result should not be extrapolated to health systems where the drug is unlicensed and untested, and a non-Chinese confirmatory trial would be the event that re-opens this stamp.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards on this shelf (PMIDs 37358859, 42329209, 37021629). No additional source.

shelves.title: Lumateperone as adjunctive therapy in major depression: MADRS advantage of −4.5 and −4.9 points at 6 weeks in two phase 3 trials, with a small independent Iranian replication — benefit with a discontinuation cost (adverse-event dropouts up to 12.4% vs 0.8%)
shelves.question: In adults with major depressive disorder and inadequate response to 1–2 antidepressants, does adjunctive lumateperone 42 mg, versus adjunctive placebo, improve MADRS at 6 weeks?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). This is lumateperone's third indication home in the library — schizophrenia is live shelf #1433 and bipolar depression is pack #2404; the adjunctive major-depression question is answered here on its own trials, and those trials' cards are not duplicated in the other homes. Two phase 3 trials from the development programme (Studies 501 and 502; pooled n=964) agree: adjunctive lumateperone 42 mg beat adjunctive placebo on MADRS change at day 43 by −4.5 points (American Journal of Psychiatry report) and −4.9 points (Journal of Clinical Psychiatry report, NCT04985942), with matching advantages on clinician severity and self-reported symptoms. A small independent Iranian trial (n=58, added to sertraline, HDRS outcome) points the same way, though its response rates (100% vs 82.1% at week 8) are implausibly high and it found no remission advantage. The cost side is consistent and should not be softened: treatment-emergent adverse events in the pooled programme occurred in 68.1% on lumateperone versus 45.1% on placebo, and discontinuation because of adverse events was 8.7% versus 0.8% pooled — 12.4% versus 0.8% in the American Journal of Psychiatry trial — driven by dizziness, somnolence, dry mouth, nausea, fatigue, diarrhoea and tremor. In the drug's favour, weight gain and cardiometabolic changes were minimal and similar to placebo, and extrapyramidal effects were uncommon. Record note: the two primary reports do not map onto their registry numbers the way secondary sources describe — the Journal of Clinical Psychiatry report carries NCT04985942 in its own record, while the American Journal of Psychiatry report carries no registry ID in its record; the pooled analysis identifies the pair as NCT04985942 and NCT05061706, and the cards follow each record exactly. The US FDA approved the adjunctive-MDD indication in 2025.

cards.headline: Phase 3 trial, American Journal of Psychiatry report (Durgam 2025): adjunctive lumateperone improved MADRS by −4.5 points vs placebo at day 43 — but 12.4% vs 0.8% stopped treatment because of adverse events
cards.summary: Phase 3 trial, American Journal of Psychiatry report (Durgam 2025): adjunctive lumateperone improved MADRS by −4.5 points vs placebo at day 43 — but 12.4% vs 0.8% stopped treatment because of adverse events
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (Durgam 2025, Am J Psychiatry)
cards.people: 480 adults aged 18–65 with DSM-5 major depressive disorder and inadequate response to one to two antidepressants in the current episode (MADRS total score at least 24), randomised 1:1 to 6 weeks of oral lumateperone 42 mg plus their antidepressant (n=242) or placebo plus antidepressant (n=238), taken once daily in the evening; the continued antidepressant was the latest drug to which they had responded inadequately (under 50% improvement). Primary and key secondary outcomes: change to day 43 in MADRS total score and CGI-Severity score.
cards.result: Lumateperone plus antidepressant met the primary and key secondary endpoints: MADRS difference versus placebo −4.5 points (least-squares mean difference; effect size −0.56) and CGI-S difference −0.5 (effect size −0.51) at day 43, with patient-reported depression also improved (QIDS-SR-16 difference −2.2; effect size −0.45). The treatment was generally well tolerated, but 12.4% of the lumateperone group versus 0.8% of the placebo group discontinued because of treatment-emergent adverse events; the commonest events (at least 5% and twice the placebo rate) were dizziness, somnolence, dry mouth, nausea, diarrhoea and fatigue. Extrapyramidal symptom risk was minimal, cardiometabolic abnormalities and weight gain were similar to placebo, and emergence of suicidal ideation was low.
cards.watchOut: A one-in-eight adverse-event dropout rate against a −4.5-point average advantage on a subjective rating scale is the real clinical equation of this drug class, and six weeks says nothing about maintenance. Note also what the record does not contain: this report's PubMed record carries no registry ID, so none is printed — the trial is one of the pair (NCT04985942 / NCT05061706) identified in the pooled analysis carded below.
cards.source: Durgam S et al. Adjunctive Lumateperone in Patients With Major Depressive Disorder: Results From a Randomized, Double-Blind, Phase 3 Trial. The American Journal of Psychiatry. 2025. the continued antidepressant was the latest drug to which they had responded inadequately (under 50% improvement). primary and key secondary outcomes: change to day 43 in madrs total score and cgi-severity score. lumateperone plus antidepressant met the primary and key secondary endpoints: madrs difference versus placebo −4.5 points (least-squares mean difference; effect size −0.56) and cgi-s difference −0.5 (effect size −0.51) at day 43, with patient-reported depression also improved (qids-sr-16 difference −2.2; effect size −0.45). the treatment was generally well tolerated, but 12.4% of the lumateperone group versus 0.8% of the placebo group discontinued because of treatment-emergent adverse events; cards.headline: Phase 3 trial, Journal of Clinical Psychiatry report (Durgam 2025): MADRS difference −4.9 points (p<0.0001) and CGI-S −0.7 at day 43; dry mouth 10.8%, fatigue 9.5%, tremor 5.0%
cards.summary: Phase 3 trial, Journal of Clinical Psychiatry report (Durgam 2025): MADRS difference −4.9 points (p<0.0001) and CGI-S −0.7 at day 43; dry mouth 10.8%, fatigue 9.5%, tremor 5.0%
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (Durgam 2025, J Clin Psychiatry; NCT04985942)
cards.people: 485 adult outpatients aged 18–65 with DSM-5 major depressive disorder and inadequate response to 1 or 2 antidepressants in the current episode (MADRS at least 24, CGI-S at least 4, QIDS-SR-16 at least 14), enrolled July 2021 to February 2024, randomised to 6 weeks of oral adjunctive lumateperone 42 mg (n=242) or adjunctive placebo (n=243). Primary and key secondary endpoints: change to day 43 in MADRS total and CGI-S scores.
cards.result: Adjunctive lumateperone met the primary and key secondary endpoints: MADRS least-squares mean difference versus placebo −4.9 points (effect size −0.61; P<0.0001), CGI-S difference −0.7 (effect size −0.67; P<0.0001), and patient-reported QIDS-SR-16 difference −2.4 (effect size −0.50; P<0.0001). Treatment-emergent adverse events at least 5% and twice the placebo rate were dry mouth (10.8% vs 2.1%), fatigue (9.5% vs 2.1%) and tremor (5.0% vs 0.4%). Weight gain and cardiometabolic risk were minimal, and emergence of suicidal ideation was low (1.4% lumateperone vs 3.5% placebo).
cards.watchOut: A near-replica of its sister trial — same sponsor, same design, same population, same 6-week horizon — so the two phase 3 reports are concordant but not independent in the way a second research group's trial would be. The effect size (−4.9 MADRS points) is at the favourable end for adjunctive antipsychotics in depression and should be expected to shrink in ordinary practice, where blinding is absent and discontinuation is easier.

cards.headline: Independent Iranian RCT (Hosseinnia 2026): lumateperone added to sertraline improved HDRS more than sertraline alone over 8 weeks (time-by-treatment p=0.027) — n=58, with no remission advantage
cards.summary: Independent Iranian RCT (Hosseinnia 2026): lumateperone added to sertraline improved HDRS more than sertraline alone over 8 weeks (time-by-treatment p=0.027) — n=58, with no remission advantage
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial — independent, single-region (Hosseinnia 2026)
cards.people: 58 analysed patients with major depressive disorder (mean age 36.9 years; 69.0% male), randomised to sertraline 100 mg/day plus lumateperone 42 mg/day or sertraline plus placebo for 8 weeks; depression measured with the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale. Trial registered in the Iranian Registry of Clinical Trials (IRCT20090117001556N141, as stated in the report).
cards.result: There was a significant time-by-treatment interaction on HDRS (P=0.027), favouring the lumateperone combination. The proportion achieving at least a 50% HDRS reduction was higher on lumateperone at week 4 (90.0% vs 60.7%; P=0.014) and week 8 (100% vs 82.1%; P=0.021), but the remission rate did not differ between groups. No serious adverse events were reported. The authors conclude lumateperone can be considered an effective and safe adjuvant treatment for major depression, while calling for larger trials with longer follow-up.
cards.watchOut: Fifty-eight patients, response rates (100% at week 8) that no antidepressant trial reproduces at scale, a different rating scale (HDRS) and background drug (fixed-dose sertraline for everyone) from the phase 3 programme, and no remission benefit: this is directional corroboration from an independent group — valuable precisely because it is independent, and weak in every other respect.
