cards.headline: Pooled safety analysis of Studies 501 and 502 (Earley 2026): adverse events in 68.1% vs 45.1%, discontinuation for adverse events 8.7% vs 0.8% — with weight gain (≥7%: 0.4% vs 1.3%) and cardiometabolic changes no worse than placebo
cards.summary: Pooled safety analysis of Studies 501 and 502 (Earley 2026): adverse events in 68.1% vs 45.1%, discontinuation for adverse events 8.7% vs 0.8% — with weight gain (≥7%: 0.4% vs 1.3%) and cardiometabolic changes no worse than placebo
cards.type: Pooled safety analysis of two randomised phase 3 trials (Earley 2026) — explicitly labelled pooled report of the two trials above
cards.people: Pooled population of the two phase 3 adjunctive-lumateperone trials in major depression (Studies 501 and 502; registered as NCT04985942 and NCT05061706): 964 patients randomised to 6 weeks of lumateperone 42 mg plus antidepressant (n=483) or placebo plus antidepressant (n=481). Safety measures: adverse events, body morphology, cardiometabolic parameters, prolactin, extrapyramidal symptom scales and suicidality.
cards.result: Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 68.1% on lumateperone versus 45.1% on placebo, and discontinuation because of an adverse event in 8.7% versus 0.8%; 96.3% of events on lumateperone were mild or moderate. The commonest events (at least 5% and more than twice placebo) were dizziness, dry mouth, somnolence, nausea, fatigue and diarrhoea. Potentially significant weight increase (at least 7%) occurred in 0.4% on lumateperone versus 1.3% on placebo; cardiometabolic parameters and prolactin changed minimally and similarly to placebo. Extrapyramidal-symptom adverse events occurred in 5.8% versus 1.7% (tremor 3.9% vs 0.2%, mean duration 11.9 days). Emergence of suicidal ideation was infrequent (1.6% vs 2.5%).
cards.watchOut: A pooled safety report adds precision, not new patients — it is the same 964 people as the two efficacy cards, and it is carded for the harm profile only. Six weeks of exposure also cannot price the long-term risks of a dopamine-serotonin modulator taken for years; the open-label extension literature, not this analysis, is where those data will come from.

cards.headline: Synthesis: adjunctive lumateperone improves depression scores by about 5 MADRS points at 6 weeks — a real, class-typical benefit with an unusually visible tolerability cost
cards.summary: Synthesis: adjunctive lumateperone improves depression scores by about 5 MADRS points at 6 weeks — a real, class-typical benefit with an unusually visible tolerability cost
cards.people: Synthesis of the four reports carded on this shelf: the two sponsor phase 3 trials (480 and 485 randomised), their pooled safety analysis (964 patients), and one independent 58-patient Iranian trial — the MDD-adjunct evidence only; schizophrenia (#1433) and bipolar depression (#2404) are separate homes.
cards.result: Efficacy is consistent across the programme: MADRS advantages of −4.5 and −4.9 points at day 43, concordant clinician-severity and self-report results, and a small independent trial in the same direction. Harm is equally consistent: adverse events in about two-thirds of patients, adverse-event discontinuation of 8.7–12.4% versus 0.8% on placebo, offset by a metabolically quiet profile (no excess weight gain or cardiometabolic change over 6 weeks).
cards.watchOut: POSSIBLE (benefit): two of the three efficacy reports share one sponsor and one design, the independent replication is 58 patients, and nothing carded here extends beyond 8 weeks. The stamp covers short-term adjunctive efficacy in antidepressant inadequate responders — not maintenance, not first-line use, and not a comparison against other adjunctive antipsychotics, which has never been tested head-to-head.

shelves.title: Deep TMS (H-coil) for OCD: Y-BOCS fell 6.0 vs 3.3 points vs sham in the pivotal trial, with response 38.1% vs 11.1% — one programme, one pivotal trial
shelves.question: In adults with OCD inadequately responsive to pharmacotherapy/psychotherapy, does high-frequency deep TMS over medial prefrontal/anterior cingulate cortex after symptom provocation, versus sham, reduce Y-BOCS?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). The intervention as tested is high-frequency (20 Hz) deep transcranial magnetic stimulation over the medial prefrontal cortex and anterior cingulate cortex, delivered daily for 6 weeks immediately after individualised symptom provocation; the fetched records do not name the device manufacturer or coil model, so none is printed here. In the pivotal multicentre sham-controlled trial (n=99), Y-BOCS fell 6.0 points on active treatment versus 3.3 on sham, with response (≥30% reduction) in 38.1% versus 11.1%, widening slightly at 1-month follow-up (45.2% versus 17.8%). An earlier small randomised feasibility trial from the same group pointed the same way, and a secondary analysis of the pivotal trial reports benefit even in patients who had failed multiple medications and CBT — though its abstract prints no subgroup figures, and the card says so. Deep TMS appears as a card inside other OCD shelves in this library; this is its question home. The sham response (3.3 Y-BOCS points, 11.1% response) is a reminder that provocation plus daily clinic ritual is itself an intervention.

cards.headline: Pivotal multicentre trial (Carmi 2019): Y-BOCS reduction 6.0 vs 3.3 points vs sham; response 38.1% vs 11.1%, and 45.2% vs 17.8% at 1-month follow-up
cards.summary: Pivotal multicentre trial (Carmi 2019): Y-BOCS reduction 6.0 vs 3.3 points vs sham; response 38.1% vs 11.1%, and 45.2% vs 17.8% at 1-month follow-up
cards.people: 99 adults with OCD at 11 centres, randomly allocated to high-frequency (20 Hz) deep TMS or sham deep TMS, given daily for 6 weeks after individualised symptom provocation; the primary endpoint was change in Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS) score from baseline to post-treatment. 89% of the active group and 96% of the sham group completed the study. Registered as NCT02229903.
cards.result: Y-BOCS reduction was significantly greater with active deep TMS than sham (reductions of 6.0 points and 3.3 points respectively). Response rates (≥30% Y-BOCS reduction) were 38.1% on active treatment versus 11.1% on sham post-treatment, and 45.2% versus 17.8% at the 1-month follow-up, with significant between-group differences maintained at follow-up.
cards.watchOut: The average advantage over sham is 2.7 Y-BOCS points — real, but modest against a 6-point fall that includes a large sham/provocation effect. The fetched abstract does not report adverse-event rates, so no harm figures are printed on this card; durability beyond 1 month after treatment is untested in this report.

cards.headline: Feasibility randomised trial (Carmi 2018): high-frequency deep TMS response rate was significantly higher than sham for at least 1 month — small groups (HF n=18, sham n=15 at completion)
cards.summary: Feasibility randomised trial (Carmi 2018): high-frequency deep TMS response rate was significantly higher than sham for at least 1 month — small groups (HF n=18, sham n=15 at completion)
cards.people: Treatment-resistant OCD participants treated double-blind with high-frequency (20 Hz), low-frequency (1 Hz) or sham deep TMS over the medial prefrontal and anterior cingulate cortices for 5 weeks, all after symptom provocation, with EEG during a Stroop task; the low-frequency arm (n=8) was terminated after an interim analysis showed no improvement. Registered as NCT01343732.
cards.result: At interim analysis, Y-BOCS scores improved significantly after high-frequency stimulation (n=7 at that point) but not low-frequency (n=8) versus sham (n=8). On completion, the response rate in the high-frequency group (n=18) was significantly higher than in the sham group (n=15) for at least 1 month after treatment ended; clinical response in the high-frequency group correlated with increased error-related negativity on the Stroop task. The report's abstract gives no response percentages, so none are printed.
cards.watchOut: Very small groups, an arm stopped at interim analysis, and no percentages in the abstract: this trial's job in the programme was to choose the frequency (20 Hz) and target carried into the pivotal trial, not to estimate the effect. It is corroboration of direction from the same research group, not independent replication.

shelves.title: PHYSIOLOGY — Cortical spreading depolarisation: the human physiology of migraine aura, and of secondary injury after stroke, subarachnoid haemorrhage and traumatic brain injury
shelves.question: In humans, does a slowly propagating wave of cortical depolarisation (≈2–9 mm/min) account for the migraine aura, and do the same events, recorded directly from injured human cortex, worsen outcome after stroke, subarachnoid haemorrhage and traumatic brain injury?
shelves.balance: Framing (textbook account, named as such): Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep's Medical Physiology present cortical spreading depolarisation (spreading depression) as a slowly propagating wave (≈2–9 mm/min, the range in this entry's question) of near-complete neuronal and glial depolarisation with silencing of electrical activity, followed by recovery in healthy tissue. What human studies directly show, carded here: during spontaneous migraine visual aura, fMRI BOLD changes propagate across occipital cortex at 3.5 ± 1.1 mm/min, retinotopically matched to the patient's percept, with at least eight features of spreading depolarisation (Hadjikhani, n=3 — printed on the card; the claim rests on convergence, not that n alone); direct electrocorticography in neurocritical-care patients records spreading depolarisations abundantly after subarachnoid haemorrhage, stroke and traumatic brain injury, with clusters time-locked to delayed ischaemic deficits (Dreier 2006: 298 events in 13 of 18 patients) and an independent association with unfavourable outcome after TBI (Hartings 2011: 1,328 events in 56% of 103 analysed patients; isoelectric spreading depolarisation common odds ratio 7.58 for unfavourable outcome). Direct electrophysiological evidence that spreading-depolarisation-induced spreading depression is the aura's correlate is reviewed by Major/Dreier 2020. The ESTABLISHED/EMERGING split, explained: that spreading depolarisation IS the aura mechanism and DOES occur in injured human brain is established by convergent human imaging plus direct recordings. That these events CAUSE lesion growth in injured brain — rather than marking severely injured tissue — is supported by their timing, their association with delayed infarcts in the recording area, and animal experiments (animal mechanism appears in this entry only as this labelled sentence), but no human trial of suppressing them has proven an outcome benefit; that causal clause is therefore graded EMERGING within the entry.

cards.headline: Hadjikhani 2001 (N = 3): fMRI BOLD changes during spontaneous visual aura propagated at 3.5 ± 1.1 mm/min, retinotopically congruent with the percept
cards.summary: Hadjikhani 2001 (N = 3): fMRI BOLD changes during spontaneous visual aura propagated at 3.5 ± 1.1 mm/min, retinotopically congruent with the percept
cards.type: Primary human functional-imaging physiology study, PNAS 2001
cards.people: 3 subjects (N = 3, printed on the face) studied with high-field functional MRI with near-continuous recording during spontaneous migraine visual aura, with the BOLD signal compared against the retinotopy of each subject's perceived visual disturbance.
cards.result: An initial focal BOLD increase in extrastriate cortex (area V3A) progressed contiguously and slowly (3.5 ± 1.1 mm/min) over occipital cortex, congruent with the retinotopy of the visual percept, followed by BOLD diminution and a reduced BOLD response to visual activation along the same progression; during scintillations without visual stimulation, BOLD still followed the percept's retinotopic march. The changes showed at least eight characteristics of cortical spreading depression, time-locked to the aura.
cards.watchOut: N = 3, printed on the face — a classic small study carded under the physiology rule with its N labelled. It is imaging of a haemodynamic signature, not a direct electrical recording of aura in healthy cortex (which cannot ethically be obtained); the ESTABLISHED grade rests on its convergence with the direct recordings carded below.
cards.source: Hadjikhani N et al. Mechanisms of migraine aura revealed by functional MRI in human visual cortex. Proc Natl Acad Sci USA. 2001. PMID 11287655. cards.headline: Dreier 2006 (COSBID): 298 spreading depolarisations recorded in 13 of 18 SAH patients; delayed ischaemic deficits were time-locked to clusters in every case
cards.summary: Dreier 2006 (COSBID): 298 spreading depolarisations recorded in 13 of 18 SAH patients; delayed ischaemic deficits were time-locked to clusters in every case
cards.people: 18 patients with major subarachnoid haemorrhage requiring aneurysm surgery, monitored prospectively in a multicentre study with a subdural electrocorticography strip on cerebral cortex for up to 10 days (2,110 hours of recording analysed); clinical state monitored every 6 hours and delayed infarcts verified by serial CT/MRI.
cards.result: Electrocorticography revealed 298 spreading depolarisations in 13 of 18 patients (72%). A delayed ischaemic neurological deficit (DIND) occurred in 7 patients at a mean 7.8 days after SAH and was time-locked to a sequence of recurrent spreading depolarisations in every single case (positive and negative predictive values 86% and 100%). In 4 patients, delayed infarcts developed in the recording area, each preceded by progressive prolongation of the depression periods associated with spreading depolarisations to >60 minutes.
cards.watchOut: Direct human recordings — the strongest design available for this question — but observational and small (18 patients): time-locking and prediction are shown; that suppressing the events would prevent the infarcts is not, which is why the causal clause in this entry is graded EMERGING.
cards.source: Dreier JP et al. Delayed ischaemic neurological deficits after subarachnoid haemorrhage are associated with clusters of spreading depolarizations. Brain. 2006. PMID 17067993. cards.headline: Hartings 2011: spreading depolarisations in 56% of TBI patients independently predicted unfavourable outcome (isoelectric SD common OR 7.58)
cards.summary: Hartings 2011: spreading depolarisations in 56% of TBI patients independently predicted unfavourable outcome (isoelectric SD common OR 7.58)
cards.type: Primary human prospective observational electrocorticography study, Lancet Neurology 2011
cards.people: 109 adults who needed neurosurgery for acute traumatic brain injury, enrolled prospectively at seven centres; spreading depolarisations monitored by electrocorticography during intensive care and classified as cortical spreading depression (in spontaneously active cortex) or isoelectric spreading depolarisation (in isoelectric cortex); treating and outcome-assessing investigators were masked to the recordings. 103 patients were analysed for outcome.
cards.result: 1,328 spreading depolarisations arose in 58 patients (56%): 38 had only cortical spreading depression and 20 had at least one isoelectric spreading depolarisation. In multivariate ordinal regression, both the conventional prognostic score (p=0.0009) and spreading-depolarisation category (p=0.0008) predicted 6-month extended Glasgow Outcome Scale scores; common odds ratios for unfavourable outcome were 1.56 (95% CI 0.72–3.37) for spreading depression only and 7.58 (2.64–21.8) for isoelectric spreading depolarisation. Adding depolarisation category raised explained outcome variance from 9% to 22%.
cards.watchOut: Observational: an independent statistical association with outcome, in patients sick enough to need neurosurgery and monitoring. Isoelectric events occur in the most severely injured cortex, so confounding by injury severity is the standing alternative explanation — the reason the causal claim stays EMERGING.
cards.source: Hartings JA et al. Spreading depolarisations and outcome after traumatic brain injury: a prospective observational study. Lancet Neurol. 2011. PMID 22056157. cards.headline: Major & Dreier 2020 (review with direct electrophysiological evidence): spreading-depolarisation-induced spreading depression is the aura's pathophysiological correlate
cards.summary: Major & Dreier 2020 (review with direct electrophysiological evidence): spreading-depolarisation-induced spreading depression is the aura's pathophysiological correlate
cards.type: Review with primary direct-recording evidence, GeroScience 2020
cards.people: A review of the spreading-depolarisation continuum, presenting direct electrophysiological evidence — recorded in patients — that spreading depolarisation induces the spreading depression of activity whose march produces the aura's spreading neurological symptoms, and setting out the continuum from reversible events in well-supplied tissue to injury-amplifying events in ischaemic tissue.
cards.result: The paper documents spreading depolarisation as a large negative DC-potential shift with neuronal swelling, dendritic beading and massive ion translocation causing cytotoxic oedema and glutamate release; whether the accompanying depression of activity spreads (as in migraine aura or migraine stroke) or does not spread (as in TIA or typical stroke) determines the clinical deficit pattern, while the depolarisation itself — the neuronal injury potential — occurs across these conditions. Clinical cases (aneurysmal SAH, cerebral amyloid angiopathy) illustrate how neuroimaging and neuromonitoring bridge the basic science and the clinic.
cards.watchOut: Carded as a labelled review/evidence synthesis, not as a fourth primary study: the pack's primary human evidence is the three cards above. Its role is to state the direct electrophysiological link for the aura that imaging alone (Hadjikhani) could only suggest.
cards.source: Major S et al. cards.summary: Synthesis: ESTABLISHED that spreading depolarisation is the aura mechanism and occurs in injured human brain; EMERGING that it causally grows lesions

shelves.title: Semorinemab in early Alzheimer's disease: no slowing of functional or global decline in two phase 2 trials — one cognitive coprimary met in Lauriet, everything else null
shelves.question: In adults with prodromal-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease, does the anti-tau antibody semorinemab, versus placebo, slow decline on the CDR-SB or ADAS-Cog?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Alzheimer Disease · Amyloid beta-Peptides · Antibodies, Monoclonal · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Phase-2-only, split record — presented exactly that way. Tauriel (prodromal-to-mild, n=422 analysed) was flatly negative: CDR-SB worsening 2.19 on placebo vs 2.36–2.41 across three semorinemab doses over 73 weeks. Lauriet (mild-to-moderate, n=238 analysed) split its coprimaries: ADAS-Cog11 met (42.2% relative slowing, −2.89 points, p=0.0008 — relative measure labelled) while ADCS-ADL missed (−0.83 points, p=0.52) and MMSE and CDR-SB were also null, making the trial negative on its prespecified endpoints and Class I evidence against a functional benefit. The joint biomarker report shows pathway engagement (plasma pTau181 and CSF YKL-40 rose; GFAP stabilised in Lauriet only) without clinical benefit. Cross-point: the other anti-tau antibodies, gosuranemab and tilavonemab, are homed at pack #5405 in progressive supranuclear palsy — a different disease and question. PROPOSED SPLIT.

cards.headline: Tauriel 2022: semorinemab (the treatment made no difference) — CDR-SB worsening was 2.19 points on placebo vs 2.36–2.41 across all three semorinemab doses over 73 weeks, N = 422 (modified intention-to-treat)
cards.summary: Tauriel 2022: semorinemab (the treatment made no difference) — CDR-SB worsening was 2.19 points on placebo vs 2.36–2.41 across all three semorinemab doses over 73 weeks, N = 422 (modified intention-to-treat)
cards.people: 422 adults aged 50–80 with prodromal to mild Alzheimer's disease (MMSE 20–30, amyloid-confirmed) at 97 sites, randomised to intravenous placebo or semorinemab 1,500 mg, 4,500 mg or 8,100 mg (every 2 weeks for the first three infusions, then every 4 weeks) for 73 weeks; safety cohort 441. Primary outcome: change on the Clinical Dementia Rating–Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB).
cards.result: CDR-SB increased by 2.19 points (95% CI 1.74–2.63) on placebo and by 2.36, 2.36 and 2.41 points in the 1,500 mg, 4,500 mg and 8,100 mg semorinemab arms respectively — no dose slowed progression. Adverse-event proportions were similar across arms (about 89–95%). The authors conclude semorinemab did not slow clinical progression but was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: Unambiguously negative at every dose in prodromal-to-mild disease — this is the larger and earlier-stage of the two trials, and it found not even a trend (semorinemab arms numerically worse).

cards.headline: Lauriet 2023: split coprimaries — ADAS-Cog11 met (42.2% relative slowing, −2.89 points, p=0.0008) but ADCS-ADL not met (−0.83 points, p=0.52), so the trial was negative on its prespecified endpoints, N = 272 randomised / 238 analysed
cards.summary: Lauriet 2023: split coprimaries — ADAS-Cog11 met (42.2% relative slowing, −2.89 points, p=0.0008) but ADCS-ADL not met (−0.83 points, p=0.52), so the trial was negative on its prespecified endpoints, N = 272 randomised / 238 analysed
cards.people: 272 adults with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease randomised to intravenous semorinemab 4,500 mg or placebo every 4 weeks for 48 or 60 weeks (238 in the modified intention-to-treat population), with coprimary endpoints of change on ADAS-Cog11 and the ADCS activities-of-daily-living scale at week 49 or 61, and an optional open-label extension.
cards.result: On ADAS-Cog11, semorinemab showed a 42.2% reduction in decline relative to placebo (−2.89 points, 95% CI −4.56 to −1.21, p=0.0008) — the 42.2% is a relative measure. On the ADCS-ADL coprimary there was no treatment effect (−0.83 points, 95% CI −3.39 to 1.72, p=0.52), and none on the secondary MMSE or CDR-SB either. Because the prespecified coprimaries were not both met, the study was negative; it provides Class I evidence that semorinemab does not slow functional decline in mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease. Semorinemab was safe and well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: The ADAS-Cog11 signal, without any functional or global correlate (ADL, MMSE and CDR-SB all null), is the classic profile of a chance or measurement artefact among multiple endpoints — the shelf presents it as a met coprimary inside a negative trial, never as evidence the drug works.

cards.headline: Schauer 2024: across both phase 2 trials semorinemab engaged its pathway — plasma pTau181 and CSF YKL-40 rose on treatment and plasma GFAP stabilised in Lauriet only — biomarker movement without clinical benefit
cards.summary: Schauer 2024: across both phase 2 trials semorinemab engaged its pathway — plasma pTau181 and CSF YKL-40 rose on treatment and plasma GFAP stabilised in Lauriet only — biomarker movement without clinical benefit
cards.type: Biomarker/pharmacodynamic report of the two phase 2 trials (Schauer 2024)
cards.people: Biomarker analysis of participant samples from both carded phase 2 trials (Tauriel in prodromal-to-mild disease and Lauriet in mild-to-moderate disease), measuring tau, amyloid, glial, neuroinflammation, synaptic and neurodegeneration biomarkers in plasma and cerebrospinal fluid with qualified assays.
cards.result: Plasma phosphorylated tau 181 and CSF chitinase-3-like protein 1 (YKL-40) increased after semorinemab treatment in both studies; in Lauriet, rising plasma glial fibrillary acidic protein stabilised on semorinemab, which was not seen in Tauriel. Other biomarkers showed no consistent response. The authors interpret the YKL-40 rise as possible microglial activation in the presence of Alzheimer's tau pathology — a mechanistic signal that accompanied, and did not rescue, the negative clinical results.
cards.watchOut: A pharmacodynamic report of the same two trials, not a third trial: it shows the antibody did something measurable to tau-related markers while doing nothing measurable for patients — target engagement is not efficacy.
cards.source: Schauer SP et al. Pharmacodynamic effects of semorinemab on plasma and CSF biomarkers of Alzheimer's disease pathophysiology. Alzheimer's & Dementia. 2024. PMID: 39513754. cards.headline: Synthesis: two phase 2 trials, one flatly negative and one negative on its prespecified coprimaries despite a single cognitive-scale signal — semorinemab does not slow functional or global decline at either disease stage tested
cards.summary: Synthesis: two phase 2 trials, one flatly negative and one negative on its prespecified coprimaries despite a single cognitive-scale signal — semorinemab does not slow functional or global decline at either disease stage tested
cards.people: Carded evidence: the complete randomised record of semorinemab in Alzheimer's disease — Tauriel (prodromal-to-mild, 422 analysed) and Lauriet (mild-to-moderate, 238 analysed) — plus their joint biomarker report. Phase-2-only evidence; no phase 3 trial exists. The other anti-tau antibodies (gosuranemab, tilavonemab) are homed in progressive supranuclear palsy at pack #5405, a different disease, cross-pointed here in prose.
cards.result: Tauriel found no effect at any dose on CDR-SB over 73 weeks. Lauriet met one coprimary (ADAS-Cog11, 42.2% relative slowing) and missed the other (ADCS-ADL) plus both global/functional secondaries, and is negative by its prespecified rule. Biomarkers moved (pTau181, YKL-40 up; GFAP stabilised in one trial) without clinical benefit. PROPOSED SPLIT, naming the split: negative overall, with the single Lauriet cognitive coprimary as the discordant limb.
cards.watchOut: GAP-E framing: a completeness shelf for a failed programme. Semorinemab is not approved for Alzheimer's disease, and the Lauriet ADAS-Cog11 result should not be quoted without its failed coprimary beside it.
cards.source: Synthesis of Teng E et al. 2022 (PMID: 35696185); Monteiro C et al. 2023 (PMID: 37643887); Schauer SP et al. 2024 (PMID: 39513754).

shelves.title: Hydromethylthionine (LMTM) in Alzheimer's disease: negative randomised primaries, positive only in revised and delayed-start analyses
shelves.question: In adults with MCI or mild-to-moderate dementia due to Alzheimer's disease, does oral hydromethylthionine mesylate, versus low-dose methylthioninium control, slow cognitive and functional decline?
shelves.balance: The randomised record is negative and the positive record is not randomised — that asymmetry is the whole story of this shelf. Two prespecified phase 3 primary analyses (Gauthier 2016, n = 891, mild-to-moderate disease; LUCIDITY's 52-week co-primaries, n = 598) found no separation from control. The programme's explanation — that the low-dose methylthioninium 'control', included to mask urine discolouration, is itself symptomatically active — is stated on the face of the LUCIDITY report, and it cuts both ways: it may have masked a real effect, and it also means no trial in the programme ever tested the drug against a truly inert placebo on a clinical endpoint. The supportive evidence is a pre-unblinding-revised, non-randomised monotherapy cohort analysis of the mild-Alzheimer's phase 3 (Wilcock 2018; monotherapy subgroups of only 79 and 76 patients) and LUCIDITY's delayed-start MCI findings at 78–104 weeks with biomarker support (neurofilament light chain, grey-matter atrophy). Those are reasons to run a clean trial, not evidence that the drug works. Harms are modest (headache, diarrhoea, gastrointestinal/urinary effects, haemoglobin reductions at high doses). The tau-antibody shelves elsewhere in this library ask a different question about a different mechanism and are not evidence for or against this small molecule.

cards.headline: LUCIDITY phase 3: co-primary endpoints not separable at 52 weeks because the low-dose control itself was active — MCI delayed-start differences emerged only at 78–104 weeks (N = 598)
cards.summary: LUCIDITY phase 3: co-primary endpoints not separable at 52 weeks because the low-dose control itself was active — MCI delayed-start differences emerged only at 78–104 weeks (N = 598)
cards.people: 598 amyloid-PET-positive participants (263 with MCI due to Alzheimer's disease, 335 with mild-to-moderate dementia due to Alzheimer's disease) at 82 centres, randomised to hydromethylthionine mesylate 16 mg/day or 8 mg/day versus methylthioninium chloride 4 mg twice weekly (intended as an inactive urinary colourant control), with all participants receiving hydromethylthionine 16 mg/day to 104 weeks in a modified delayed-start phase.
cards.result: It was not possible to demonstrate significant differences on the co-primary clinical endpoints (ADAS-Cog11 and ADCS-ADL23) at 52 weeks due to symptomatic activity in the control arm (the treatment made no difference on the prespecified co-primaries). In participants with MCI, differences in cognitive decline (ADAS-Cog13) between early- and delayed-start hydromethylthionine 16 mg/day emerged at 78 weeks (p = 0.0291) and 104 weeks (p = 0.0308) in analyses specified prior to the 24-month database lock. Biomarker outcomes included a significant reduction in progression of neurodegeneration by neurofilament light chain change (p = 0.0291) at 52 weeks in the whole population. Headache (1.5%) and diarrhoea (1.2%) were the most frequent adverse effects.
cards.watchOut: The control was not a true placebo: the low-dose methylthioninium colourant arm itself showed symptomatic activity, so the trial could not separate drug from control on its co-primaries. The positive MCI findings come from the delayed-start phase and a different scale (ADAS-Cog13), not from the missed 52-week co-primary endpoints.

cards.headline: First phase 3 (mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's): prespecified primary analysis negative at both high doses (N = 891)
cards.summary: First phase 3 (mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's): prespecified primary analysis negative at both high doses (N = 891)
cards.people: 891 participants younger than 90 years with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease at 115 centres in 16 countries, randomised (3:3:4) to leuco-methylthioninium bis(hydromethanesulfonate) 75 mg twice daily, 125 mg twice daily, or control (4 mg twice daily, to maintain blinding for urine/faecal discolouration), for 15 months; concomitant Alzheimer's medicines were permitted.
cards.result: The prespecified primary analyses showed no treatment benefit at either dose on the coprimary outcomes at week 65: change in ADAS-Cog versus control was −0.02 points (95% CI −1.60 to 1.56, p = 0.9834) for 75 mg twice daily and −0.43 (95% CI −2.06 to 1.20, p = 0.9323) for 125 mg twice daily, with similarly null ADCS-ADL differences (the treatment made no difference). Gastrointestinal and urinary effects were the most common adverse events and causes of discontinuation; dose-dependent, non-clinically significant reductions in haemoglobin were the most common laboratory abnormality, and amyloid-related imaging abnormalities occurred in under 1% (8/885).
cards.watchOut: This was an add-on trial (standard Alzheimer's medicines allowed), and its control was again a low dose of the same moiety rather than an inert placebo — the design feature the programme later blamed for its null results. As randomised and prespecified, the answer is negative.
cards.source: Gauthier S, Feldman HH, Schneider LS, et al. Lancet (London, England). 2016. PMID: 27863809. Registry ID: NCT01689246. cards.headline: Second phase 3 (mild Alzheimer's, N = 800): the randomised comparison was reframed before unblinding into non-randomised monotherapy cohort analyses, which were significant
cards.summary: Second phase 3 (mild Alzheimer's, N = 800): the randomised comparison was reframed before unblinding into non-randomised monotherapy cohort analyses, which were significant
cards.type: Phase 3 trial — non-randomised cohort analysis as modified primary outcome — N = 800 randomised; monotherapy subgroups n = 79 and n = 76
cards.people: 800 patients with mild Alzheimer's disease randomised to leuco-methylthioninium 100 mg twice daily or 4 mg twice daily for 18 months; before unblinding, the statistical analysis plan was revised to compare the 100 mg twice-daily monotherapy subgroup (n = 79) against the 4 mg twice-daily group as randomised (n = 396), and 4 mg twice-daily monotherapy (n = 76) against 4 mg twice-daily add-on therapy (n = 297).
cards.result: The revised, non-randomised cohort analyses were statistically significant at the required threshold (p < 0.025) in both comparisons for change in ADAS-Cog, ADCS-ADL, MRI atrophy and glucose uptake, and the brain atrophy rate in monotherapy patients declined after 9 months to rates reported for normal elderly controls. The authors report that baseline severity or diagnosis differences did not account for the findings.
cards.watchOut: This is not a randomised result: the comparisons were redefined before unblinding and contrast small self-selected monotherapy subgroups (n = 79 and n = 76) with larger groups. It is hypothesis-generating for the low-dose monotherapy claim, not confirmatory evidence, and it does not overturn the two negative prespecified randomised analyses on the other cards.
cards.source: Wilcock GK, Gauthier S, Frisoni GB, et al. Journal of Alzheimer's disease : JAD. 2018. PMID: 29154277. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: every prespecified randomised primary analysis missed; the positive claims rest on an active control problem, a revised cohort analysis, and delayed-start subgroup findings
cards.summary: Synthesis: every prespecified randomised primary analysis missed; the positive claims rest on an active control problem, a revised cohort analysis, and delayed-start subgroup findings
cards.people: Synthesis of the three phase 3 reports above (LUCIDITY, N = 598; mild-to-moderate trial, N = 891; mild Alzheimer's trial, N = 800).
cards.result: As randomised, hydromethylthionine / leuco-methylthioninium made no difference on its prespecified co-primary cognitive and functional endpoints in any phase 3 trial. The programme's counter-claim is coherent but unproven: the low-dose control was pharmacologically active, and benefit is said to appear with low-dose monotherapy (non-randomised cohort analysis, Wilcock 2018) and in the MCI subgroup of LUCIDITY's delayed-start phase at 78–104 weeks, alongside biomarker (neurofilament light chain, atrophy) signals. Safety was generally benign (headache, diarrhoea, gastrointestinal and urinary effects; dose-dependent haemoglobin reductions at high doses). No fetched record shows a positive prespecified randomised clinical endpoint.
cards.watchOut: Delayed-start and monotherapy-subgroup analyses cannot substitute for a positive placebo-controlled primary endpoint, and the 'active control' explanation is the sponsor-investigators' interpretation of their own null trials. Regulatory status is not established by any carded record.

cards.search: synthesis: every prespecified randomised primary analysis missed; the positive claims rest on an active control problem, a revised cohort analysis, and delayed-start subgroup findings synthesis: every prespecified randomised primary analysis missed; the positive claims rest on an active control problem, a revised cohort analysis, and delayed-start subgroup findings in adults with mci or mild-to-moderate dementia due to alzheimer's disease, does oral hydromethylthionine mesylate, versus low-dose methylthioninium control, slow cognitive and functional decline? synthesis synthesis of the three phase 3 reports above (lucidity, n = 598; mild-to-moderate trial, n = 891; mild alzheimer's trial, n = 800). as randomised, hydromethylthionine / leuco-methylthioninium made no difference on its prespecified co-primary cognitive and functional endpoints in any phase 3 trial. the programme's counter-claim is coherent but unproven: the low-dose control was pharmacologically active, and benefit is said to appear with low-dose monotherapy (non-randomised cohort analysis, wilcock 2018) and in the mci subgroup of lucidity's delayed-start phase at 78–104 weeks, alongside biomarker (neurofilament light chain, atrophy) signals. safety was generally benign (headache, diarrhoea, gastrointestinal and urinary effects; dose-dependent haemoglobin reductions at high doses). no fetched record shows a positive prespecified randomised clinical endpoint. delayed-start and monotherapy-subgroup analyses cannot substitute for a positive placebo-controlled primary endpoint, and the 'active control' explanation is the sponsor-investigators' interpretation of their own null trials. regulatory status is not established by any carded record. synthesis of wischik cm et al. the journal of prevention of alzheimer's disease. 2026 (pmid: 41570392); gauthier s et al. lancet (london, england). 2016 (pmid: 27863809); wilcock gk et al. journal of alzheimer's disease : jad. 2018 (pmid: 29154277).

shelves.title: Sodium oligomannate (GV-971) in Alzheimer's disease: one positive Chinese phase 3, a negative phase 2 primary, no confirmation elsewhere
shelves.question: In adults with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease, does sodium oligomannate 900 mg daily, versus placebo, improve cognition over 36 weeks?
shelves.balance: One positive pivotal trial, one negative phase 2 primary, and nothing confirmatory outside China. The phase 3 result (−2.15 ADAS-Cog12 points at 36 weeks, n = 818) is a real randomised finding and is printed in full; so is the phase 2 trial's failure on the same scale at the same dose, and the small third trial's scattered significant time points. The product — sodium oligomannate (Shanghai Green Valley Pharmaceuticals), named under the clarification exception — was conditionally approved in China in 2019 and its development outside China was halted after the international phase 3 was terminated without results (slate desk-check). Its gut-microbiota mechanism rests principally on animal work, which this shelf does not card as evidence. A clinician reading this shelf should take away: possible cognitive benefit in the population and setting tested, unproven anywhere else, with a placebo-like adverse-event profile in the trials.

cards.headline: Phase 3 (China, N = 818): ADAS-Cog12 difference −2.15 points at 36 weeks favouring sodium oligomannate 900 mg
cards.summary: Phase 3 (China, N = 818): ADAS-Cog12 difference −2.15 points at 36 weeks favouring sodium oligomannate 900 mg
cards.people: 818 participants with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's dementia in China, randomised to sodium oligomannate (GV-971) 900 mg daily (n = 408) or placebo (n = 410) for 36 weeks. The tested product is sodium oligomannate (Shanghai Green Valley Pharmaceuticals), named here under the clarification exception because it is not FDA-approved and is poorly regulated outside China.
cards.result: The drug–placebo difference in change from baseline on ADAS-Cog12 was −2.15 points (95% CI −3.07 to −1.23, p < 0.0001; effect size 0.531) after 36 weeks, with a significant difference present at each measurement point from week 4. Treatment-emergent adverse event incidence was comparable (73.9% on GV-971, 75.4% on placebo); two deaths in the GV-971 group were judged unrelated to the drug.
cards.watchOut: Single-country (China) evidence with no completed confirmatory trial elsewhere: the international phase 3 was terminated without results, per the slate desk-check. Secondary global/function outcomes are not reported as positive in the abstract record, and the mechanism and data have been contested in the literature — the card prints the cognitive result exactly as the record gives it, no more.

cards.headline: Phase 2 (China, N = 242): primary ADAS-Cog12 endpoint negative at both doses; a global-impression responder outcome favoured 900 mg
cards.summary: Phase 2 (China, N = 242): primary ADAS-Cog12 endpoint negative at both doses; a global-impression responder outcome favoured 900 mg
cards.people: 242 patients with Alzheimer's dementia in China randomised 1:1:1 to sodium oligomannate 900 mg (n = 83), 600 mg (n = 76) or placebo (n = 83) for 24 weeks, with a fluorodeoxyglucose-PET cerebral glucose metabolism subgroup.
cards.result: On the primary outcome, ADAS-Cog12 change versus placebo (change −1.45) was −1.39 for 600 mg (p = 0.89) and −2.58 for 900 mg (p = 0.30) — not significant at either dose (the treatment made no difference on the primary endpoint). CIBIC-Plus treatment responders were significantly higher on 900 mg than placebo (92.77% vs 79.52%, p < 0.05), and the 900 mg subgroup showed less decline in cerebral glucose metabolism in several regions at uncorrected p = 0.05. Treatment-related adverse event rates were 5.9% (900 mg), 14.3% (600 mg) and 3.5% (placebo).
cards.watchOut: The phase 2 primary endpoint was negative; the positive global-impression responder rate and the uncorrected PET subgroup findings are secondary. The 900 mg dose carried into phase 3 was selected from this trial despite the null primary.

cards.headline: Small 48-week randomised comparison (N = 72): GV-971 scored better than control on some scales at some time points, and similar to donepezil
cards.summary: Small 48-week randomised comparison (N = 72): GV-971 scored better than control on some scales at some time points, and similar to donepezil
cards.people: 72 patients with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease randomised into three groups (GV-971, donepezil and control, per the record) and assessed on ADAS-Cog, ADL, CIBIC-Plus, NPI and CSDD at 0, 12, 24, 36 and 48 weeks.
cards.result: The CIBIC-Plus score differed significantly for GV-971 versus control at week 12 (p = 0.007) and week 24 (p = 0.005), and ADAS-Cog at week 24 (p = 0.01); versus donepezil, CIBIC-Plus differed at week 24 (p = 0.01) and week 48 (p = 0.04) and CSDD at week 48 (p = 0.02). Adverse reactions were increased stool frequency in 2 GV-971 patients (5.67%) and nausea in 2 donepezil patients (8.33%). The authors conclude GV-971 is as effective as donepezil, and may be better.
cards.watchOut: A small, single report with many scales at many time points and no correction for multiplicity described in the abstract; group sizes and the control condition are not fully specified in the record. It is supportive colour only — the shelf's weight rests on the phase 3 and phase 2 cards.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one positive single-country phase 3 against a negative phase 2 primary — possible benefit, unconfirmed outside China
cards.summary: Synthesis: one positive single-country phase 3 against a negative phase 2 primary — possible benefit, unconfirmed outside China
cards.people: Synthesis of the three randomised reports above (phase 3, N = 818; phase 2, N = 242; 48-week comparison, N = 72; total randomised N = 1,132, all in China).
cards.result: Sodium oligomannate 900 mg daily improved ADAS-Cog12 by −2.15 points versus placebo at 36 weeks in the one completed phase 3 trial, with adverse-event rates similar to placebo. Against that stand the phase 2 trial's negative primary endpoint at the same dose and the absence of any completed confirmatory trial outside China. The honest summary is a single positive pivotal trial from a single country for a product (sodium oligomannate, Shanghai Green Valley Pharmaceuticals) that is conditionally approved in China, not FDA-approved, and whose proposed gut-microbiota mechanism remains contested.
cards.watchOut: All carded evidence comes from China and substantially from the sponsor's own programme; the preclinical gut-microbiota mechanism paper behind the product was not carded as evidence (it is principally animal work). Consumer or imported 'GV-971' products may differ from the tested pharmaceutical product in content and effect.

shelves.title: Delandistrogene moxeparvovec (EMBARK) in Duchenne muscular dystrophy: missed randomised primary, favourable external-control follow-up
shelves.question: In ambulant boys aged 4 to <8 years with Duchenne muscular dystrophy, does one intravenous dose of delandistrogene moxeparvovec, versus placebo or external controls, improve motor function (NSAA) over 1–3 years?
shelves.balance: EMBARK is two different kinds of evidence wearing one name. Year 1 is a proper randomised trial and it missed: NSAA difference 0.65 points, p = 0.2441, despite clear micro-dystrophin expression (34.29%) and an exploratory MRI substudy showing slower fat-fraction progression. Years 2–3, after crossover destroyed the internal control, compare treated boys with propensity-matched external controls and look progressively better (+4.39 NSAA points at 3 years, nominal p values). Both halves are printed here at full strength, with the design of each stated in its headline, because quoting either half alone misleads. Safety in-trial was manageable (11.1% treatment-related serious adverse events in year 1; no treatment-related deaths to year 3), but hepatic risk is a labelled concern for this product (Elevidys, Sarepta Therapeutics — named under the clarification exception) and is not quantified in the carded abstracts. Cross-point: the exon-skipping phosphorodiamidate morpholino shelf in this library covers the other dystrophin-raising drug class in Duchenne muscular dystrophy, with a similarly surrogate-led record.

cards.headline: EMBARK phase 3 at 1 year: primary NSAA endpoint missed (difference 0.65 points, p = 0.2441) despite micro-dystrophin expression of 34.29% (N = 125)
cards.summary: EMBARK phase 3 at 1 year: primary NSAA endpoint missed (difference 0.65 points, p = 0.2441) despite micro-dystrophin expression of 34.29% (N = 125)
cards.people: 125 ambulant boys aged 4 to under 8 years with Duchenne muscular dystrophy, randomised to a single intravenous dose of delandistrogene moxeparvovec (Elevidys, Sarepta Therapeutics — named under the clarification exception as the specific tested gene-therapy product) 1.33 × 10^14 vector genomes/kg (n = 63) or placebo (n = 62).
cards.result: At week 52 the primary endpoint, change in North Star Ambulatory Assessment (NSAA) score, was not met: least-squares mean change 2.57 (treatment) versus 1.92 (placebo) points, between-group difference 0.65 (95% CI −0.45 to 1.74, p = 0.2441) (the treatment made no difference on the primary endpoint). Mean micro-dystrophin expression at week 12 was 34.29% on treatment versus 0.00% on placebo. Some timed-function secondary endpoints numerically favoured treatment, with no statistical significance claimable. There were 674 adverse events on treatment versus 514 on placebo, no deaths or discontinuations, and 7 patients (11.1%) experienced 10 treatment-related serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: The randomised, placebo-controlled year of EMBARK is the only unbiased functional comparison in this programme, and it missed its primary endpoint. Everything longer-term on this shelf is measured against external controls, not against the trial's own placebo arm, because of the crossover design.
cards.source: Mendell JR, Muntoni F, McDonald CM, et al. Nature medicine. 2025. PMID: 39385046. Registry ID: NCT05096221. cards.headline: EMBARK at 2 years: functional outcomes favoured treatment versus a propensity-matched external control (non-randomised comparison)
cards.summary: EMBARK at 2 years: functional outcomes favoured treatment versus a propensity-matched external control (non-randomised comparison)
cards.type: Phase 3 trial 2-year follow-up versus external control — N = 125 treated in part 1
cards.people: Boys who received delandistrogene moxeparvovec in EMBARK part 1 (N = 125 randomised in the trial), whose 2-year functional outcomes were compared, by prespecified analysis, with a matched propensity score-weighted external control cohort after the crossover design ended the placebo comparison.
cards.result: At 2 years, EMBARK patients showed statistically significant benefit versus the external control cohort in functional outcomes prognostic for delaying loss of ambulation (NSAA, Time to Rise, 10-m Walk/Run), described by the authors as sustained stabilisation or slowing of disease progression. Micro-dystrophin expression and sarcolemmal localisation were maintained over 64 weeks. No new safety signals appeared between weeks 52 and 104; there were no treatment-related deaths, discontinuations due to adverse events, or clinically significant complement-mediated adverse events.
cards.watchOut: External-control comparisons cannot exclude confounding by differences in care, era, steroid use or outcome measurement, however careful the matching. The abstract record does not print the 2-year effect sizes, so none are printed here.

cards.headline: EMBARK at 3 years: NSAA difference +4.39 points versus matched external controls (nominal p = 0.0002), all p values nominal
cards.summary: EMBARK at 3 years: NSAA difference +4.39 points versus matched external controls (nominal p = 0.0002), all p values nominal
cards.type: Phase 3 trial 3-year follow-up versus external control — n = 64 treated, n = 143 external controls
cards.people: 64 patients treated with delandistrogene moxeparvovec in EMBARK part 1 (single intravenous dose 1.33 × 10^14 vg/kg), compared at 3 years with a matched propensity score-weighted external control cohort (n = 143) drawn from placebo arms of other trials and natural-history datasets; treated patients were aged 7–10 years at the 3-year point.
cards.result: At 3 years, the between-cohort least-squares mean difference in change from baseline favoured treatment on NSAA total score (+4.39 points, p = 0.0002), Time to Rise (−6.05 s, p < 0.0001) and 10-m Walk/Run (−2.70 s, p = 0.0039), which the authors describe as durable slowing of disease progression; all p values are nominal. No new safety signals were identified through year 3, left ventricular ejection fraction remained above 55%, and there were no treatment-related deaths or discontinuations due to adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Nominal p values from a non-randomised external-control comparison, in the 64 of 125 part-1 patients followed to 3 years. This is the programme's strongest-looking functional evidence and its least protected against bias — both facts belong together.

cards.headline: EMBARK muscle MRI substudy (n = 39): less fat-fraction progression on treatment at 52 weeks (exploratory endpoint)
cards.summary: EMBARK muscle MRI substudy (n = 39): less fat-fraction progression on treatment at 52 weeks (exploratory endpoint)
cards.type: Randomised trial exploratory imaging substudy — n = 39
cards.people: 39 boys from EMBARK who underwent quantitative muscle MRI (19 on delandistrogene moxeparvovec, 20 on placebo; mean age 6.10 years), with proton MR spectroscopy and Dixon imaging measuring muscle fat fraction and spin-echo MRI measuring T2 in leg muscles important for ambulation.
cards.result: Treated patients showed less disease progression than placebo on MR measures at week 52: across muscles and modalities, magnitudes of fat-fraction change favoured delandistrogene moxeparvovec. Change in muscle MR was a prespecified exploratory endpoint of the randomised trial.
cards.watchOut: An exploratory imaging substudy in under a third of the trial: it supports a biological effect on muscle, but imaging fat fraction is a surrogate and does not rescue the missed clinical primary endpoint.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a missed randomised primary, then increasingly favourable — and increasingly confounded — external-control follow-up
cards.summary: Synthesis: a missed randomised primary, then increasingly favourable — and increasingly confounded — external-control follow-up
cards.people: Synthesis of the four EMBARK reports above (randomised N = 125; 3-year treated n = 64 versus 143 external controls).
cards.result: Delandistrogene moxeparvovec (Elevidys, Sarepta Therapeutics) produces micro-dystrophin (34.29% at week 12) and slows muscle fat-fraction progression, but in the only randomised functional comparison it made no difference on the primary NSAA endpoint at 1 year. At 2 and 3 years, treated boys did better than propensity-matched external controls on NSAA and timed function, with a manageable safety profile in-trial (treatment-related serious adverse events in 11.1% at year 1; no treatment-related deaths through year 3). Whether the long-term differences are the drug or the comparison is exactly what an external-control design cannot settle.
cards.watchOut: Liver injury is a recognised serious risk of this product class and of this product's labelling history; no carded abstract quantifies hepatic events, so no rate is printed — check the current label before any clinical use. The 1-year randomised result, not the external-control follow-up, is the unbiased anchor.

shelves.title: Exon-skipping PMOs in Duchenne muscular dystrophy: dystrophin up, functional benefit unproven in randomised trials
shelves.question: In boys with DMD amenable to exon 51, 53 or 45 skipping, do the PMO antisense drugs (eteplirsen, golodirsen, casimersen, viltolarsen), versus placebo or natural history, improve motor function — or only dystrophin production?
shelves.balance: This shelf's value is stating plainly what the published record does and does not show. All four phosphorodiamidate morpholinos (eteplirsen, golodirsen, casimersen, viltolarsen — generic names; these are regulated pharmaceutical products, so no clarification-exception naming applies) hold FDA accelerated approval on increased dystrophin production, a surrogate. The carded journal reports demonstrate that surrogate — dystrophin rising to roughly 1% of normal with golodirsen and roughly 6% with viltolarsen — in cohorts of 12 to 79 boys, and show generally mild tolerability. What they do not contain is a randomised placebo-controlled functional benefit; functional claims are open-label or external-control comparisons. The confirmatory randomised trials that were meant to settle function (ESSENCE for golodirsen/casimersen, RACER53 for viltolarsen) were recorded at slate stage as having missed their primary functional endpoints, but no journal publications of them were found in this session's PubMed search, so they are fenced in prose on the synthesis card rather than carded. Cross-point: the delandistrogene moxeparvovec (EMBARK) shelf in this library covers the gene-therapy approach to the same dystrophin problem, with its own missed randomised primary.

cards.headline: Eteplirsen PROMOVI (open-label, N = 79 treated): dystrophin rose 7-fold; walk-test decline was smaller than in external natural-history controls, not than in a randomised control
cards.summary: Eteplirsen PROMOVI (open-label, N = 79 treated): dystrophin rose 7-fold; walk-test decline was smaller than in external natural-history controls, not than in a randomised control
cards.type: Open-label phase 3 study with external-control comparisons — N = 79 treated
cards.people: 79 ambulatory patients aged 7–16 years with Duchenne muscular dystrophy amenable to exon 51 skipping, treated open-label with eteplirsen 30 mg/kg weekly intravenously for 96 weeks (78 completed); an untreated cohort with mutations not amenable to exon 51 skipping (n = 30 enrolled) was judged an inappropriate control because of genotype-driven differences in trajectory.
cards.result: At week 96, eteplirsen-treated patients showed an 18.7-fold increase in exon skipping and a 7-fold increase in dystrophin protein versus baseline. Post-hoc comparisons with external natural-history controls suggested attenuation of 6-minute walk decline (PROMOVI −68.9 m versus external controls −133.8 m over 96 weeks) and of percent-predicted forced vital capacity decline (−3.3% versus −6.0% per year, p < 0.001). Adverse events were generally mild to moderate and unrelated; the most frequent treatment-related events were headache and vomiting, and none led to discontinuation.
cards.watchOut: No randomised functional comparison exists in this report: the functional claims are post-hoc and external-controlled, and the trial's own untreated cohort was discarded as a comparator by the investigators. Eteplirsen's FDA approval was accelerated, on dystrophin production as a surrogate.

cards.headline: Golodirsen 4053-101 (N = 25): dystrophin rose ~16-fold to a mean of 1.019% of normal at week 48 — a biomarker result, with no functional endpoint
cards.summary: Golodirsen 4053-101 (N = 25): dystrophin rose ~16-fold to a mean of 1.019% of normal at week 48 — a biomarker result, with no functional endpoint
cards.type: Phase 1/2 randomised dose-titration plus open-label study — N = 25 (12 randomised in part 1)
cards.people: 25 boys with Duchenne muscular dystrophy amenable to exon 53 skipping: 12 randomised in part 1 (8 to golodirsen dose titration, 4 to placebo, for 12 weeks), with all 12 plus 13 additional patients receiving golodirsen 30 mg/kg weekly in open-label part 2, with muscle biopsies at baseline and week 48.
cards.result: Golodirsen produced a significant increase in exon 53 skipping associated with an approximately 16-fold increase over baseline in dystrophin protein at week 48, to a mean of 1.019% of normal (range 0.09%–4.30%), with significantly increased dystrophin-positive fibres and correct sarcolemmal localisation. Safety findings were consistent with previous experience in paediatric Duchenne patients, and most drug was excreted within 4 hours of infusion. No functional (motor) outcome result is reported in this record.
cards.watchOut: The randomised limb lasted 12 weeks and randomised 12 boys; the dystrophin result is open-label and biopsy-based. A mean dystrophin level of about 1% of normal is the entire efficacy basis carded here — whether that amount changes function is not answered by this study.

cards.headline: Viltolarsen phase 2 (N = 16): dystrophin reached a mean of 5.7%–5.9% of normal after 20–24 weeks; functional comparisons were against natural history, not placebo
cards.summary: Viltolarsen phase 2 (N = 16): dystrophin reached a mean of 5.7%–5.9% of normal after 20–24 weeks; functional comparisons were against natural history, not placebo
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised clinical trial (dose comparison) — N = 16
cards.people: 16 boys aged 4–9 years with Duchenne muscular dystrophy amenable to exon 53 skipping, randomised to viltolarsen 40 mg/kg (low dose) or 80 mg/kg (high dose) weekly intravenously, in a 4-week randomised safety phase followed by 20 weeks of open-label treatment, at US and Canadian sites.
cards.result: After 20–24 weeks, drug-induced dystrophin production was a mean of 5.7% of normal (range 3.2–10.3) at 40 mg/kg and 5.9% (range 1.1–14.4) at 80 mg/kg. Viltolarsen was well tolerated: no treatment-emergent adverse event required dose reduction, interruption or discontinuation, and no serious adverse events or deaths occurred. Functional comparisons in the record are against 65 age-matched natural-history controls, not against a concurrent placebo group.
cards.watchOut: N = 16, printed plainly: this is a dose-comparison and biomarker trial, not a placebo-controlled test of function. The larger randomised confirmatory trial of viltolarsen (RACER53) was reported by the slate desk-check as negative on its functional endpoint; no journal report of it was found in this session's PubMed search, so it is fenced here rather than carded.

cards.headline: Casimersen phase 1/2 (N = 12): a safety and pharmacokinetic trial — well tolerated over a mean 139.6 weeks, with no efficacy endpoint tested
cards.summary: Casimersen phase 1/2 (N = 12): a safety and pharmacokinetic trial — well tolerated over a mean 139.6 weeks, with no efficacy endpoint tested
cards.people: 12 participants aged 7–21 years with Duchenne muscular dystrophy amenable to exon 45 skipping and limited ambulation or non-ambulatory, randomised 2:1 to weekly casimersen at escalating doses (4, 10, 20, 30 mg/kg) or placebo in a 12-week double-blind dose titration, followed by open-label casimersen for up to 132 weeks.
cards.result: Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in all participants in both groups and were mostly mild (over 91.4%) and unrelated to casimersen or its dose; there were no deaths, dose reductions, laboratory or vital-sign abnormalities, or casimersen-related serious adverse events. Plasma concentrations rose with dose with no suggestion of accumulation. The study's objectives were safety, tolerability and pharmacokinetics; it reports no dystrophin or functional efficacy result.
cards.watchOut: N = 12, at the reference floor, and a safety study: casimersen's accelerated approval, like the others on this shelf, rests on dystrophin production shown in other reports, not on a functional benefit demonstrated in a randomised trial carded here.

cards.headline: Synthesis: four accelerated approvals, all on dystrophin — no carded randomised trial shows a functional benefit
cards.summary: Synthesis: four accelerated approvals, all on dystrophin — no carded randomised trial shows a functional benefit
cards.people: Synthesis of the four drug programmes above (eteplirsen N = 79 treated open-label; golodirsen N = 25; viltolarsen N = 16; casimersen N = 12).
cards.result: Each phosphorodiamidate morpholino raises dystrophin — eteplirsen 7-fold from baseline, golodirsen to a mean 1.019% of normal, viltolarsen to a mean 5.7%–5.9% of normal — and each is generally well tolerated in these small studies. None of the carded reports is a randomised, placebo-controlled demonstration of better motor function: the functional claims are open-label, post-hoc or natural-history comparisons. The slate desk-check records that the randomised confirmatory trials ESSENCE (golodirsen/casimersen) and RACER53 (viltolarsen) did not meet their primary functional endpoints; neither was found as a journal publication in this session's PubMed search, so those results are flagged here in prose and not carded — the confirmatory record, as published, remains outstanding or negative, and the approvals remain surrogate-based.
cards.watchOut: Per-drug Ns are small (12–79) and are printed on each card. This shelf deliberately does not import effect claims from sponsor releases or congress reports for ESSENCE or RACER53; if their journal reports appear, they belong on this shelf as cards.

shelves.title: Remibrutinib in relapsing multiple sclerosis (REMODEL-1/2): fewer relapses than teriflunomide in two concordant phase 3 trials
shelves.question: In adults with relapsing MS, does the oral BTK inhibitor remibrutinib 100 mg twice daily, versus teriflunomide, reduce relapses and MRI lesion activity?
shelves.balance: Two large, identical, double-blind phase 3 trials, both positive on the same primary endpoint against an active comparator — that is a better randomised record than most new multiple-sclerosis drugs arrive with, and it is printed here at full strength: rate ratios 0.648 and 0.688 for annualised relapse rate, labelled relative with the small absolute differences (about 0.04 relapses per patient-year) beside them. The limits are equally plain: a single sponsor programme reported in a single publication (hence the POSSIBLE cap), teriflunomide rather than a high-efficacy monoclonal as comparator, follow-up to 30 months, and no MRI or disability-progression numbers in the carded abstract record — so this shelf claims relapse reduction only. On safety, the absence of a liver signal is the class-relevant finding, contrasting with the hepatic problems of the tolebrutinib programme covered elsewhere in this library; remibrutinib's other library home is its chronic spontaneous urticaria shelf, a separate question.

cards.headline: REMODEL-1: annualised relapse rate 0.073 on remibrutinib versus 0.112 on teriflunomide (rate ratio 0.648 — a 35.2% relative reduction; N = 1,000)
cards.summary: REMODEL-1: annualised relapse rate 0.073 on remibrutinib versus 0.112 on teriflunomide (rate ratio 0.648 — a 35.2% relative reduction; N = 1,000)
cards.people: 1,000 adults aged 18–55 with relapsing multiple sclerosis (EDSS 0–5.5, recent disease activity) randomised 1:1 to oral remibrutinib 100 mg twice daily (n = 502) or teriflunomide 14 mg once daily (n = 498), in a double-blind, double-dummy, event-driven phase 3 trial with up to 30 months of follow-up; mean age 38.2 years, 66.6% female.
cards.result: The primary endpoint, annualised relapse rate, was significantly lower with remibrutinib than teriflunomide: 0.073 versus 0.112 confirmed relapses per patient-year, rate ratio 0.648 (95% CI 0.453–0.927, p = 0.018) — a 35.2% relative reduction, an absolute difference of 0.039 relapses per patient-year.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is teriflunomide, an active drug — superiority here does not by itself rank remibrutinib against the high-efficacy monoclonal therapies. The PubMed abstract record carded here reports the relapse primary endpoint and safety; MRI lesion and confirmed-disability-progression results are not in that abstract and no numbers for them are printed on this shelf.
cards.source: Wiendl H, Bermel R, Airas L, et al. Lancet (London, England). 2026. PMID: 42915009. Registry ID: NCT05147220 and NCT05156281. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: REMODEL-2: annualised relapse rate 0.080 versus 0.116 (rate ratio 0.688 — a 31.2% relative reduction; N = 1,007) — the twin trial replicates REMODEL-1
cards.summary: REMODEL-2: annualised relapse rate 0.080 versus 0.116 (rate ratio 0.688 — a 31.2% relative reduction; N = 1,007) — the twin trial replicates REMODEL-1
cards.people: 1,007 adults aged 18–55 with relapsing multiple sclerosis randomised 1:1 to remibrutinib 100 mg twice daily (n = 504) or teriflunomide 14 mg once daily (n = 503), in a phase 3 trial identical in design to REMODEL-1; the two trials together randomised 2,007 patients at 407 centres in 46 countries; mean age 39.0 years, 67.0% female.
cards.result: Annualised relapse rate was 0.080 on remibrutinib versus 0.116 on teriflunomide, rate ratio 0.688 (95% CI 0.487–0.972, p = 0.034) — a 31.2% relative reduction, an absolute difference of 0.036 relapses per patient-year. Together with REMODEL-1, this is two concordant positive phase 3 trials on the same primary endpoint from a single development programme, reported in one publication.
cards.watchOut: One publication reports both trials (a single programme), which is why this shelf's stamp caps at POSSIBLE despite the concordance. Both trials remain ongoing per the record, and longer-term disability outcomes are not in the carded abstract.

cards.headline: REMODEL-1/2 pooled safety: fewer discontinuations on remibrutinib than teriflunomide (3.1% vs 5.8%), and no liver safety concerns reported
cards.summary: REMODEL-1/2 pooled safety: fewer discontinuations on remibrutinib than teriflunomide (3.1% vs 5.8%), and no liver safety concerns reported
cards.type: Phase 3 pooled safety report (REMODEL-1 and REMODEL-2) — N = 2,007
cards.people: The pooled safety populations of REMODEL-1 and REMODEL-2: 1,006 patients on remibrutinib 100 mg twice daily and 1,001 on teriflunomide 14 mg once daily.
cards.result: The most common adverse events were upper respiratory tract infection (13.1% on remibrutinib vs 13.7% on teriflunomide), nasopharyngitis (9.1% vs 12.3%), diarrhoea (8.3% vs 10.9%) and alopecia (5.8% vs 13.5%). Adverse events leading to treatment discontinuation were less frequent with remibrutinib (31 patients, 3.1%) than teriflunomide (58, 5.8%). The authors report the safety profile was consistent with other remibrutinib indications, including no liver safety concerns.
cards.watchOut: 'No liver safety concerns' is the trial report's own summary and is notable because liver injury has been the class problem for other BTK inhibitors in multiple sclerosis (the tolebrutinib programme, covered elsewhere in this library); follow-up here is up to 30 months and rare or late hepatic events cannot be excluded by these data. Remibrutinib's established home in this library is its chronic spontaneous urticaria shelf — a different disease and question.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two concordant phase 3 wins on relapses against teriflunomide, from one programme and one publication
cards.summary: Synthesis: two concordant phase 3 wins on relapses against teriflunomide, from one programme and one publication
cards.people: Synthesis of REMODEL-1 (N = 1,000) and REMODEL-2 (N = 1,007), reported together in The Lancet in 2026.
cards.result: Remibrutinib 100 mg twice daily beat teriflunomide on annualised relapse rate in both trials (rate ratios 0.648 and 0.688; 35.2% and 31.2% relative reductions; absolute differences of about 0.04 relapses per patient-year), with fewer treatment discontinuations and no liver safety signal reported. The evidence is strong in design — two large, identical, double-blind phase 3 trials — but it is a single sponsor programme in a single publication, the comparator is a moderate-efficacy oral drug, and the carded record does not include MRI or disability-progression numbers, so this shelf makes no disability claim.
cards.watchOut: No phase 2 multiple-sclerosis report of remibrutinib was found in this session's PubMed search, and no preclinical work is carded as evidence. If MRI, disability or long-term extension reports from REMODEL are published, they belong on this shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Wiendl H et al. Lancet (London, England). 2026 (PMID: 42915009), reporting REMODEL-1 (NCT05147220) and REMODEL-2 (NCT05156281).

shelves.title: Venous sinus stenting in refractory idiopathic intracranial hypertension: consistent observational improvement, no randomised trial
shelves.question: In adults with IIH and a transverse-sinus stenosis with a significant pressure gradient who have failed or not tolerated medical therapy, does venous sinus stenting improve papilloedema, headache and visual outcomes?
shelves.balance: There is no randomised trial of venous sinus stenting in idiopathic intracranial hypertension — everything on this shelf is observational, and it is labelled that way on every card. What the observational record shows consistently is that carefully selected patients (transverse-sinus stenosis, usually a measured pressure gradient, failure or intolerance of medical therapy) usually improve after stenting: papilloedema improvement around 89%–94% and headache improvement around 79% in the pooled series, against treatment failure around 8%, symptom recurrence around 10%, major complications around 2%–5%, later shunting in 6.2% of one large series, and a re-stenting burden for restenosis. Two cautions are built into the cards: the two meta-analyses pool overlapping series, so they are one evidence base, not two; and the low-gradient series suggests the manometry thresholds used to select patients may not predict who improves. Dual antiplatelet therapy after stenting is a real cost. The competing strategies — weight-loss surgery and acetazolamide-class medical therapy — have their own shelves in this library.

cards.headline: 113-patient stenting series: 82.3% complete symptom relief at 3 months; 6.2% later shunted, 1.8% re-stented for restenosis (observational)
cards.summary: 113-patient stenting series: 82.3% complete symptom relief at 3 months; 6.2% later shunted, 1.8% re-stented for restenosis (observational)
cards.people: 113 patients (all female, mean age 30 ± 8 years, mean BMI 30 ± 3.1) with idiopathic intracranial hypertension and venous sinus stenosis who underwent venous sinus stenting at a single tertiary centre, from a prospectively collected database reviewed retrospectively (2021–2023).
cards.result: Stenting was technically successful in all patients; post-stenting angioplasty was needed in 3 cases (2.6%). Complications occurred in 1 case (0.9%) — a rim of subdural haematoma without clinical sequelae. At 3 months, 93 patients (82.3%) had complete relief of symptoms, 11 (9.7%) still had headache without papilloedema, and 9 (8%) had papilloedema. Seven patients (6.2%) went on to ventriculoperitoneal shunting and 2 (1.8%) had restenosis treated with another stent.
cards.watchOut: Observational evidence only: no control group, short (3-month) outcome horizon, and a selected population (stenosis on imaging, refractory cases). Symptom relief after a procedure in an uncontrolled series cannot separate the stent's effect from natural history, co-treatment and placebo effects.
cards.source: Abdelkhalek H, El Malky I, Elkordy A, Ahmed HS. World neurosurgery. 2025. PMID: 40582504. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Low-gradient series (N = 53): patients with pressure gradients ≤4 mmHg improved as much as those with gradients >8 mmHg (observational)
cards.summary: Low-gradient series (N = 53): patients with pressure gradients ≤4 mmHg improved as much as those with gradients >8 mmHg (observational)
cards.people: 53 patients with medically refractory idiopathic intracranial hypertension undergoing venous sinus stenting at a single centre, grouped by trans-stenotic pressure gradient: ≤4, 5–8, and >8 mmHg.
cards.result: Mean change in lumbar puncture opening pressure at 6 months was similar across gradient groups (13.4, 12.9 and 12.4 cmH2O, p = 0.47), papilloedema improved in 100%, 93% and 86% of the groups respectively (p = 0.7), and all clinical symptoms improved across groups, with no significant between-group differences in retinal nerve fibre layer change or visual-field mean deviation. The authors conclude low-gradient patients seem to benefit equally and call for prospective confirmatory studies.
cards.watchOut: This card matters because manometry gradient thresholds are the field's main selection rule, and this series undermines them — but it is a small, retrospective, uncontrolled comparison in which 'benefit' is within-group change. It is a reason to question the threshold, not proof that stenting works at any gradient.
cards.source: Inam ME, Martinez-Gutierrez JC, Kole MJ, et al. Neurosurgery. 2022. PMID: 35960743. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Updated meta-analysis (36 studies, 1,066 patients): papilloedema improved in 89%, headache in 79%, tinnitus in 95% — with 8.35% treatment failure and 5.35% complications (observational studies pooled)
cards.summary: Updated meta-analysis (36 studies, 1,066 patients): papilloedema improved in 89%, headache in 79%, tinnitus in 95% — with 8.35% treatment failure and 5.35% complications (observational studies pooled)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies — 36 studies, N = 1,066
cards.people: 1,066 patients who underwent venous sinus stenting for idiopathic intracranial hypertension across 36 studies included in a PRISMA systematic review and meta-analysis.
cards.result: After stenting, trans-stenotic gradient pressure and cerebrospinal fluid opening pressure fell significantly. Clinical outcomes showed improvement in tinnitus (95%), papilloedema (89%), visual disturbances (88%) and headache (79%). However, 13.7% of patients experienced treatment failure or complications: the treatment failure rate was 8.35% (worsening or recurrent symptoms) and the complications rate 5.35%, including subdural haemorrhage, urinary tract infection and stent thrombus formation. The authors call for further investigation of long-term outcomes and safety.
cards.watchOut: Pooling uncontrolled series pools their biases: publication bias favours successful series, and 'improvement' rates are within-patient changes without any comparator. The failure and complication rates on this card are the most decision-relevant numbers in the pool.

cards.headline: Earlier meta-analysis (20 articles, 474 patients): papilloedema improved in 93.7%, headache in 79.6%, symptom recurrence 9.8%, major complications 1.9% (observational studies pooled)
cards.summary: Earlier meta-analysis (20 articles, 474 patients): papilloedema improved in 93.7%, headache in 79.6%, symptom recurrence 9.8%, major complications 1.9% (observational studies pooled)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies — 20 articles, N = 474
cards.people: 474 patients (418 female, 88%; mean age 35, mean BMI 35 kg/m2) from 20 articles at 18 centres, with median follow-up of 18 months, in a random-effects meta-analysis of venous sinus stenting for idiopathic intracranial hypertension refractory to medical therapy.
cards.result: Improvement in papilloedema was 93.7% (95% CI 90.5% to 96.9%), improvement or resolution of headache 79.6% (95% CI 73.3% to 85.9%), and resolution of pulsatile tinnitus 90.3% (95% CI 83.8% to 96.7%). Recurrence of IIH symptoms after stenting was 9.8% (95% CI 6.7% to 13%), and the rate of major complications was 1.9% (95% CI 0.07% to 3.1%).
cards.watchOut: This pool overlaps substantially with the 2024 update on the previous card — the two meta-analyses are not independent evidence. Both rest on the same uncontrolled case-series literature, and neither can estimate what stenting adds over medical therapy, weight loss or shunting.
cards.source: Nicholson P, Brinjikji W, Radovanovic I, Hilditch CA. Journal of neurointerventional surgery. 2019. PMID: 30166333. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: consistent, large within-patient improvements in uncontrolled series — and no randomised trial to say how much is the stent
cards.summary: Synthesis: consistent, large within-patient improvements in uncontrolled series — and no randomised trial to say how much is the stent
cards.people: Synthesis of the observational evidence above (series of 113 and 53 patients; meta-analyses pooling 474 and 1,066 patients, with overlapping primary studies).
cards.result: Across every published series, most stented patients report better headache, resolved pulsatile tinnitus and improved papilloedema, with major complications around 2%–5%, treatment failure around 8%, symptom recurrence around 10%, and a minority needing shunting (6.2% in the 113-patient series) or re-stenting for restenosis. None of this is randomised: there is no trial of venous sinus stenting versus medical therapy, weight-loss treatment or shunting, so the causal contribution of the stent itself is unknown. Patient selection by pressure gradient — the field's gatekeeping rule — is itself questioned by the low-gradient series carded here. Stenting also commits patients to dual antiplatelet therapy, a cost of the procedure that belongs in any decision.
cards.watchOut: Observational evidence, labelled as such on every card: this shelf supports 'patients selected for stenting usually improve afterwards', not 'stenting causes the improvement'. The IIH weight-loss surgery and acetazolamide-class shelves in this library cover the alternative strategies this question competes with.
