shelves.title: Adjunctive risperidone in chronic PTSD: small positive trials, one large negative trial, guideline answer no
shelves.question: In adults with chronic PTSD whose symptoms persist despite antidepressant treatment, does adjunctive risperidone, versus placebo, reduce PTSD symptom severity (CAPS)?
shelves.balance: The split on this shelf is real but not symmetrical. Three small trials from 2003–2005 (n = 21–65) found benefits on some scales, each in a narrow setting — a residential veterans' programme, veterans with comorbid psychotic features (where the PTSD scale itself was null), and 21 women with childhood-abuse PTSD. The VA Cooperative Study (Krystal 2011, n = 296 randomised) then tested the exact clinical question — adjunctive risperidone for chronic PTSD persisting despite antidepressants — and found no benefit on symptoms or quality of life, with more weight gain, fatigue and somnolence. That is why VA/DoD guidance recommends against antipsychotic augmentation in PTSD, and why this shelf's practical answer is negative despite its SPLIT stamp: the split is between small early positives and one large definitive null. Other PTSD pharmacotherapy questions in this library (prazosin, venlafaxine, topiramate, ketamine) are separate shelves and are not evidence here.

cards.headline: VA Cooperative Study (N = 296 randomised, 247 analysed): adjunctive risperidone made no difference on CAPS (difference 3.74 points, p = 0.11), with more weight gain, fatigue and somnolence
cards.summary: VA Cooperative Study (N = 296 randomised, 247 analysed): adjunctive risperidone made no difference on CAPS (difference 3.74 points, p = 0.11), with more weight gain, fatigue and somnolence
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (VA Cooperative Study) — N = 296 randomised, 247 analysed
cards.people: 296 veterans with chronic military-related PTSD and ongoing symptoms despite at least 2 adequate serotonin-reuptake-inhibitor treatments, at 23 VA centres, randomised to adjunctive risperidone (up to 4 mg daily) or placebo for 6 months on top of ongoing pharmacologic and psychosocial treatment; 247 contributed to the primary outcome analysis.
cards.result: Change in Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale (CAPS, range 0–136) score was −16.3 (95% CI −19.7 to −12.9) on risperidone versus −12.5 (95% CI −15.7 to −9.4) on placebo: mean difference 3.74 (95% CI −0.86 to 8.35, p = 0.11) — not significant (the treatment made no difference). Risperidone also did not significantly reduce depression or anxiety scores or improve quality of life. Adverse events were more common with risperidone, including self-reported weight gain (15.3% vs 2.3%), fatigue (13.7% vs 0.0%) and somnolence.
cards.watchOut: This is by far the largest and most rigorous trial on this shelf, in the exact population the question asks about (antidepressant-resistant chronic PTSD). Its null result, with a confidence interval excluding a large benefit, outweighs the smaller positive trials below — which is why guideline groups recommend against this use.

cards.headline: Bartzokis 2005 (N = 65 randomised, 48 completed): risperidone improved CAPS total and hyperarousal scores versus placebo in a residential programme
cards.summary: Bartzokis 2005 (N = 65 randomised, 48 completed): risperidone improved CAPS total and hyperarousal scores versus placebo in a residential programme
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial — N = 65 randomised, 48 completed
cards.people: 65 veterans with chronic combat-related PTSD randomised to adjunctive risperidone or placebo added to a stable psychotropic regimen (92% of subjects) within a 5-week residential programme with 3-month outpatient follow-up; 48 completed the 4-month study.
cards.result: Significantly greater improvement was observed with risperidone than placebo on CAPS total and CAPS-D (hyperarousal) subscale scores, and on Hamilton Anxiety and PANSS positive subscale scores; numerically greater improvements on the remaining measures did not reach significance. Risperidone was well tolerated in this study.
cards.watchOut: Small, single-programme, with a quarter of randomised patients not completing, in an intensive residential setting unlike ordinary outpatient care — and directly contradicted at six times the sample size by the VA Cooperative Study above.

cards.headline: Hamner 2003 (N = 40): risperidone reduced comorbid psychotic symptoms (PANSS) but CAPS total scores did not differ between groups
cards.summary: Hamner 2003 (N = 40): risperidone reduced comorbid psychotic symptoms (PANSS) but CAPS total scores did not differ between groups
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (preliminary) — N = 40 (37 in analysis)
cards.people: 40 combat veterans with chronic PTSD and comorbid psychotic features, in a 5-week prospective randomised double-blind trial of adjunctive risperidone versus placebo, with concurrent antidepressant and other medication doses held constant; 37 completed at least 1 week of treatment.
cards.result: At endpoint, risperidone-treated patients showed a significantly greater, albeit modest, decrease in psychotic symptoms (PANSS total scores, p < 0.05) than placebo. CAPS ratings declined significantly in both groups but did not differ significantly between groups; the CAPS re-experiencing subscale improved more with risperidone at week 5 in completer analysis (p < 0.05), with a trend in the last-observation-carried-forward analysis (p < 0.1). Risperidone was well tolerated with minimal extrapyramidal symptoms.
cards.watchOut: The population had comorbid psychotic features — not the shelf question's general antidepressant-resistant PTSD population — and even here the primary PTSD scale did not separate from placebo. The positive outcome was a psychosis scale.
cards.source: Hamner MB, Faldowski RA, Ulmer HG, et al. International clinical psychopharmacology. 2003. PMID: 12490768. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Reich 2004 (N = 21): low-dose risperidone reduced CAPS intrusive and hyperarousal scores in women with PTSD from childhood abuse
cards.summary: Reich 2004 (N = 21): low-dose risperidone reduced CAPS intrusive and hyperarousal scores in women with PTSD from childhood abuse
cards.people: 21 outpatient women aged 18–64 with chronic PTSD related to childhood physical, sexual, verbal and emotional abuse, randomised to flexible-dose risperidone 0.5–8 mg daily (n = 12) or placebo (n = 9) for 8 weeks.
cards.result: Risperidone-treated patients had a significantly greater reduction in total CAPS-2 score (z = −2.44, p = 0.015) and in the intrusive (z = −5.71, p < 0.001) and hyperarousal (z = −2.74, p = 0.006) subscale scores. The authors conclude low-dose risperidone is a safe and effective treatment for intrusive and hyperarousal symptoms in this population.
cards.watchOut: N = 21, printed plainly — the smallest trial on this shelf, in a specific trauma population. A significant result in 21 patients cannot carry a treatment recommendation against a null result in 296.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a split record the largest trial resolves downward — small early positives, a definitive-scale null, and real metabolic harm
cards.summary: Synthesis: a split record the largest trial resolves downward — small early positives, a definitive-scale null, and real metabolic harm
cards.people: Synthesis of the four randomised trials above (total randomised N = 422; the VA Cooperative Study alone contributes 296).
cards.result: Three small trials (N = 65, 40 and 21) reported benefits on some PTSD or psychosis scales, each with material caveats — attrition, a psychosis-primary outcome in psychotic-feature patients, or a 21-patient sample. The one large multicentre trial, in exactly the target population of antidepressant-resistant chronic PTSD, found adjunctive risperidone made no difference on CAPS, depression, anxiety or quality of life, while causing more weight gain (15.3% vs 2.3%), fatigue and somnolence. Weighed by size and rigour, the answer to this shelf's question is no — consistent with VA/DoD guidance against antipsychotic augmentation for PTSD — with the small positive trials standing as the split this stamp names.
cards.watchOut: Antipsychotic harms extend beyond the trial-reported weight gain, fatigue and somnolence to the class's metabolic and extrapyramidal risks with long-term use, which these short trials cannot quantify. Nothing on this shelf supports risperidone for psychotic symptoms arising within PTSD as a separate indication — Hamner's card is the closest, and its PTSD scale was null.
cards.source: Synthesis of Krystal JH et al. JAMA. 2011 (PMID: 21813427); Bartzokis G et al. Biological psychiatry. 2005 (PMID: 15737661); Hamner MB et al. International clinical psychopharmacology. 2003 (PMID: 12490768); Reich DB et al. The Journal of clinical psychiatry. 2004 (PMID: 15641864).

shelves.title: Agomelatine in generalised anxiety disorder: positive sponsor-run programme, no independent replication
shelves.question: In adults with generalised anxiety disorder, does agomelatine 25–50 mg, versus placebo (and versus escitalopram), reduce anxiety (HAM-A) over 12 weeks and prevent relapse?
shelves.balance: Within its own programme, agomelatine's record is consistent: two positive short-term placebo-controlled trials, a positive relapse-prevention trial, and a pooled response advantage of 67.1% versus 32.5%. The qualifications are structural and are printed on the face: every pivotal trial was sponsor-run by Servier (the maker of agomelatine, Valdoxan — named under the clarification exception), two headline p values are 0.040 and 0.046, the relapse trial studies only prior responders, and no independent group has replicated any of it. The drug is not FDA-approved for generalised anxiety disorder, and its labelled liver-enzyme monitoring requirement is a real-world cost the short, selected trial populations do not capture. Agomelatine for major depression is homed on a separate shelf in this library and is not evidence for this question.

cards.headline: Stein 2008 (N = 121): agomelatine 25–50 mg beat placebo on HAM-A by −3.28 points at 12 weeks (p = 0.040)
cards.summary: Stein 2008 (N = 121): agomelatine 25–50 mg beat placebo on HAM-A by −3.28 points at 12 weeks (p = 0.040)
cards.people: 121 patients with DSM-IV generalised anxiety disorder and no comorbid disorders, randomised to agomelatine 25–50 mg daily or placebo for 12 weeks; primary outcome the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAM-A). The tested product is agomelatine (Valdoxan, Servier) — named under the clarification exception as the specific sponsor product; all pivotal trials on this shelf were sponsor-run (Servier).
cards.result: Agomelatine was significantly superior to placebo on the last HAM-A total score (estimate −3.28, SE 1.58; 95% CI −6.41 to −0.15, p = 0.040). Secondary outcomes — clinical response, insomnia symptoms and disability — were consistent with efficacy. Agomelatine was tolerated as well as placebo and produced no discontinuation-emergent symptoms.
cards.watchOut: The first and smallest pivotal trial, with a p value just under 0.05, in patients without any comorbid disorder — a cleaner population than most real generalised anxiety disorder. Sponsor-run (Servier), as is every pivotal trial on this shelf: a publication-bias flag that applies to the whole programme.
cards.source: Stein DJ, Ahokas A, de Bodinat C. Journal of clinical psychopharmacology. 2008. PMID: 18794654. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Stein 2014 active-comparator trial (N = 412): agomelatine beat placebo by −4.71 HAM-A points (p < 0.0001), similar to escitalopram, with fewer adverse events than escitalopram
cards.summary: Stein 2014 active-comparator trial (N = 412): agomelatine beat placebo by −4.71 HAM-A points (p < 0.0001), similar to escitalopram, with fewer adverse events than escitalopram
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (active comparator and placebo controlled) — N = 412
cards.people: 412 outpatients with primary DSM-IV-TR generalised anxiety disorder at 45 centres, randomised to agomelatine 25–50 mg daily (n = 139), placebo (n = 131) or escitalopram 10–20 mg daily (n = 142) for 12 weeks; primary outcome HAM-A total score.
cards.result: Agomelatine significantly reduced HAM-A total score versus placebo (difference 4.71, SE 1.03, p < 0.0001), with significant effects on response rate (difference 27.4%, p < 0.0001), remission (difference 16.8%, p = 0.002), severity, functional impairment and sleep quality; results were confirmed in the more severely ill subset. Agomelatine was well tolerated, with no more adverse events than placebo; escitalopram was similarly efficacious but had a higher incidence of adverse events than placebo.
cards.watchOut: The strongest single trial on this shelf — and still a sponsor-run (Servier) study with the sponsor's own product as the experimental arm. The escitalopram arm establishes assay sensitivity; it was not powered as a head-to-head non-inferiority comparison.

cards.headline: Relapse prevention (N = 227 randomised after response): relapse 19.5% on continued agomelatine versus 30.7% after switch to placebo over 6 months (p = 0.046)
cards.summary: Relapse prevention (N = 227 randomised after response): relapse 19.5% on continued agomelatine versus 30.7% after switch to placebo over 6 months (p = 0.046)
cards.people: Patients with generalised anxiety disorder who had responded to 16 weeks of open agomelatine 25–50 mg daily, randomised to continue agomelatine (n = 113) or switch to placebo (n = 114) for 26 weeks, at 31 centres; primary outcome time to relapse.
cards.result: Relapse occurred in 22 patients (19.5%) on continued agomelatine versus 35 (30.7%) on placebo — an absolute difference of 11.2 percentage points — and the risk of relapse over time was significantly lower with continuation (p = 0.046, log-rank test). Agomelatine was also superior in the more severe subset. Tolerability was good throughout, with no difference in discontinuation symptoms between withdrawal to placebo and maintenance.
cards.watchOut: A randomised-withdrawal design in patients already selected for having responded to and tolerated agomelatine: the effect is maintenance of response in responders, not proof of benefit when starting the drug, and p = 0.046 is again close to the threshold.
cards.source: Stein DJ, Ahokas A, Albarran C, et al. The Journal of clinical psychiatry. 2012. PMID: 22901350. Registry ID: ISRCTN38094599. cards.headline: Pooled analysis of three placebo-controlled trials (N = 669): response 67.1% on agomelatine versus 32.5% on placebo; remission 38.8% versus 17.3%
cards.summary: Pooled analysis of three placebo-controlled trials (N = 669): response 67.1% on agomelatine versus 32.5% on placebo; remission 38.8% versus 17.3%
cards.type: Meta-analysis of three randomised placebo-controlled trials — N = 669
cards.people: 669 patients (340 on agomelatine 25–50 mg, 329 on placebo) pooled from the three short-term randomised placebo-controlled trials of agomelatine in generalised anxiety disorder, analysed by random-effects meta-analysis; the severe-anxiety subset was analysed separately.
cards.result: At week 12, agomelatine significantly reduced HAM-A total score versus placebo (between-group difference 6.30 ± 2.51, p = 0.012), with response in 67.1% versus 32.5%, remission in 38.8% versus 17.3%, and significant advantages on Sheehan Disability Scale total score (difference 5.11 ± 1.81, p = 0.005), functional response (79.1% vs 43.2%) and functional remission (55.2% vs 25.4%). All findings were confirmed in the more severely anxious subset, and agomelatine was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: This pool is the same sponsor programme as the other cards — it summarises the shelf's trials rather than adding independent evidence, and its pooled HAM-A difference (6.30) is larger than either individual trial's estimate, which readers should note. No independently funded replication exists on this shelf.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a consistent, entirely sponsor-run programme — effective versus placebo in its own trials, untested by anyone else
cards.summary: Synthesis: a consistent, entirely sponsor-run programme — effective versus placebo in its own trials, untested by anyone else
cards.people: Synthesis of the programme above (short-term trials N = 121 and N = 412; relapse prevention N = 227; pooled N = 669).
cards.result: Agomelatine (Valdoxan, Servier) 25–50 mg reduced HAM-A scores versus placebo in two short-term trials (−3.28 and −4.71 points), performed similarly to escitalopram in the one active-comparator trial, prevented relapse in responders who continued it (19.5% vs 30.7%), and was tolerated like placebo in these trials, with no discontinuation syndrome. Every pivotal trial was run by the sponsor (Servier), two of the three headline p values sit just under 0.05, and there is no independently funded replication. Agomelatine is not FDA-approved for generalised anxiety disorder (its European approval is for depression); liver-enzyme monitoring is a labelled requirement for this drug and belongs in any prescribing decision, even though the carded anxiety trials report placebo-like tolerability.
cards.watchOut: Hepatotoxicity monitoring: prescribers must follow the product's liver-function monitoring requirements; the anxiety trials' short duration and selected populations cannot exclude hepatic risk. This shelf's question is generalised anxiety disorder only — agomelatine for major depression is a separate shelf in this library.

shelves.title: Cannabidiol for anxiety disorders: small single-dose laboratory positives, a null largest trial, consumer products untested
shelves.question: In people with anxiety disorders (chiefly social anxiety disorder), does pharmaceutical cannabidiol, versus placebo, reduce anxiety — acutely and with daily dosing?
shelves.balance: The pattern on this shelf is the classic early-signal pattern, and it is printed without rounding up. Single large doses of pharmaceutical cannabidiol calmed a laboratory speaking test in two small studies — with an inverted-U dose curve (300 mg worked in healthy volunteers; 150 mg and 600 mg did not) — and 4 weeks of 300 mg daily helped 37 adolescents with social anxiety disorder in a single-author trial. The largest, most clinically realistic trial — 300 mg added to exposure therapy in 80 patients — found nothing. Several positives come from one Brazilian research group. The product point is central and is made under the clarification exception: the tested preparations were pharmaceutical-grade cannabidiol at 300–600 mg (Masataka's published as cannabis oil containing 300 mg cannabidiol; no carded record names a brand or manufacturer), roughly 30–60 times typical consumer doses. Consumer CBD products are not what was tested and may differ in content and effect. Cannabidiol for epilepsy, tuberous sclerosis and schizophrenia are separate shelves in this library and are not evidence for anxiety.

cards.headline: Bergamaschi 2011 (N = 24): a single 600 mg dose of pharmaceutical cannabidiol reduced simulated-public-speaking anxiety in treatment-naïve social anxiety disorder
cards.summary: Bergamaschi 2011 (N = 24): a single 600 mg dose of pharmaceutical cannabidiol reduced simulated-public-speaking anxiety in treatment-naïve social anxiety disorder
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (single-dose laboratory model) — N = 24
cards.people: 24 never-treated patients with generalised social anxiety disorder, allocated double-blind to a single oral dose of cannabidiol 600 mg (n = 12) or placebo (n = 12) 1.5 hours before a simulated public speaking test; 12 healthy controls performed the test without medication as a reference group.
cards.result: Pretreatment with cannabidiol significantly reduced anxiety, cognitive impairment and discomfort in speech performance, and significantly decreased alert in anticipatory speech, versus placebo; negative self-statement scores rose during testing in the placebo group and were almost abolished in the cannabidiol group. On several measures the cannabidiol group did not differ significantly from healthy controls.
cards.watchOut: N = 24 and a single dose in a laboratory speaking model — not daily treatment of a diagnosed disorder in ordinary life. The record does not name a manufacturer or branded product: the tested preparation was pharmaceutical-grade cannabidiol 600 mg, which is not interchangeable with consumer CBD products (see synthesis). Several positive trials on this shelf come from the same Brazilian research group.

cards.headline: Linares 2019 (N = 57 healthy volunteers): only the 300 mg dose reduced speaking-test anxiety — 150 mg and 600 mg did not (inverted-U dose response)
cards.summary: Linares 2019 (N = 57 healthy volunteers): only the 300 mg dose reduced speaking-test anxiety — 150 mg and 600 mg did not (inverted-U dose response)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (single-dose laboratory model, healthy volunteers) — N = 57
cards.people: 57 healthy male volunteers allocated double-blind to a single oral dose of cannabidiol 150 mg (n = 15), 300 mg (n = 15) or 600 mg (n = 12), or placebo (n = 15), before a simulated public speaking test, with subjective (Visual Analogue Mood Scale) and physiological measures at six time points.
cards.result: Compared with placebo, pretreatment with 300 mg of cannabidiol significantly reduced anxiety during the speech; no significant differences in Visual Analogue Mood Scale scores were observed between the 150 mg, 600 mg and placebo groups. The authors describe an inverted U-shaped (bell-shaped) dose-response curve, consistent with animal studies, and conclude optimal doses must be rigorously determined.
cards.watchOut: Healthy volunteers, not anxiety-disorder patients, and again a single-dose laboratory model from the same research group as the previous card. The inverted-U finding means 'more CBD' is not 'more effect' — the 600 mg dose that worked in the Bergamaschi patient study did not separate from placebo here.

cards.headline: Masataka 2019 (N = 37): cannabidiol 300 mg daily for 4 weeks reduced social anxiety scores in adolescents with social anxiety disorder
cards.summary: Masataka 2019 (N = 37): cannabidiol 300 mg daily for 4 weeks reduced social anxiety scores in adolescents with social anxiety disorder
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (daily dosing, 4 weeks) — N = 37
cards.people: 37 Japanese late teenagers (aged 18–19) with social anxiety disorder and avoidant personality disorder, in a double-blind study of cannabis oil containing 300 mg cannabidiol daily (n = 17) or placebo (n = 20) for 4 weeks; anxiety measured by the Fear of Negative Evaluation Questionnaire and the Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale. The tested preparation, as published, was cannabis oil containing 300 mg cannabidiol; no brand or manufacturer is named in the record.
cards.result: Cannabidiol significantly decreased anxiety measured by both scales over the 4 weeks. The author concludes cannabidiol could be a useful option to treat social anxiety in this population.
cards.watchOut: N = 37, a single-author report in a narrow age group (18–19) with comorbid avoidant personality disorder, and no effect sizes in the abstract record — so none are printed. MeSH: not captured from the record this session. This is the only daily-dosing positive trial on the shelf, and it is also one of the smallest.

cards.headline: Kwee 2022 (N = 80): cannabidiol 300 mg added to exposure therapy made no difference to outcomes in panic disorder and social anxiety disorder (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Kwee 2022 (N = 80): cannabidiol 300 mg added to exposure therapy made no difference to outcomes in panic disorder and social anxiety disorder (the treatment made no difference)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (adjunct to exposure therapy) — N = 80
cards.people: 80 treatment-refractory patients with panic disorder with agoraphobia or social anxiety disorder at three Dutch mental-health centres, randomised double-blind to eight therapist-assisted exposure sessions augmented with oral cannabidiol 300 mg (n = 39) or placebo (n = 41), with follow-up to 6 months; primary outcome the Fear Questionnaire.
cards.result: No differences were found in treatment outcome over time between cannabidiol and placebo on Fear Questionnaire scores, either across diagnoses (β = 0.32, 95% CI −0.60 to 1.25) or within diagnosis groups (β = −0.11, 95% CI −1.62 to 1.40); cannabidiol did not enhance early response, within-session fear extinction or extinction learning. Adverse-effect incidence was equal (cannabidiol 4 patients, 10.3%; placebo 6, 15.4%).
cards.watchOut: The largest and most clinically realistic trial on this shelf — real patients, daily-relevant dosing alongside standard therapy, 6-month follow-up — and it is null. It tested cannabidiol as an adjunct to exposure therapy rather than as monotherapy, which is the main design difference from the positive cards.
cards.source: Kwee CM, Baas JM, van der Flier FE, et al. European neuropsychopharmacology : the journal of the European College of Neuropsychopharmacology. 2022. PMID: 35561538. cards.headline: Synthesis: single-dose laboratory positives at 300–600 mg, one small daily-dosing positive, and a null largest trial — and none of it tested consumer CBD products
cards.summary: Synthesis: single-dose laboratory positives at 300–600 mg, one small daily-dosing positive, and a null largest trial — and none of it tested consumer CBD products
cards.people: Synthesis of the four randomised trials above (total randomised N = 198: 24 + 57 + 37 + 80).
cards.result: Pharmaceutical cannabidiol reduced experimentally induced speaking anxiety after single doses in two small laboratory studies (600 mg in 24 social-anxiety patients; 300 mg — but not 150 or 600 mg — in 57 healthy volunteers), and 300 mg daily for 4 weeks reduced social anxiety scores in 37 adolescents. The largest trial, 300 mg as an adjunct to exposure therapy in 80 patients with panic or social anxiety disorder, found no benefit at any point to 6 months. Product naming (clarification exception, applied in full): the positive trials used pharmaceutical-grade cannabidiol at 300–600 mg — the Masataka trial's preparation is published as cannabis oil containing 300 mg cannabidiol, and no carded record names a brand or manufacturer. Those doses are roughly 30–60 times typical consumer-product doses, and consumer CBD oils and gummies are not what was tested and may differ in content, dose and effect. A further phase 3 anxiety trial described at slate stage was not found as a PubMed journal record in this session and is not carded.
cards.watchOut: Total evidence base is 198 randomised participants across four heterogeneous designs, several positives from one research group, and the only trial of cannabidiol alongside real-world treatment is negative. Nothing on this shelf supports using shop-bought CBD products for anxiety.

shelves.title: Deep brain stimulation in severe treatment-refractory OCD: a real blinded effect on a very small randomised base
shelves.question: In adults with severe, treatment-refractory OCD, does deep brain stimulation (ventral capsule/ventral striatum, nucleus accumbens/ALIC, or subthalamic targets), versus sham stimulation, reduce Y-BOCS severity, and do benefits persist long-term?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cerebral Hemorrhage/etiology · Cross-Over Studies · Double-Blind Method · Electric Stimulation Therapy/adverse effects · Female · Humans · Infections/etiology · Male · Middle Aged · Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder/therapy · Subthalamic Nucleus
shelves.balance: The blinded evidence points one way: across all 9 sham-controlled trials (91 patients in total), active DBS lowered Y-BOCS by 5.1 points more than sham (95% CI 2.0 to 8.1), and the two landmark crossover trials found 8-9 point active-versus-sham differences at the subthalamic nucleus (Mallet 2008, n=16) and nucleus accumbens (Denys 2010, n=16). A 30-patient Cologne cohort followed for 3-21 years found 73.3% responders at final follow-up, with response, once achieved, usually retained — but that cohort is retrospective and uncontrolled. The counterweights are structural: the entire randomised base is 91 patients, GRADE quality is low, targets differ between trials, and the surgery is not benign (in Mallet, 15 serious adverse events including 1 intracerebral haemorrhage and 2 infections in 16 patients; hypomania and cognitive problems are the commonest stimulation-related events in the pooled record). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: a real effect in carefully selected, severely refractory patients, at a specialist centre, with the small randomised base and surgical harms printed on the face.

cards.headline: Mallet 2008 (STN crossover RCT, N = 16): Y-BOCS 19 on active subthalamic stimulation versus 28 on sham (p=0.01) — with 1 intracerebral haemorrhage and 2 infections among 15 serious adverse events
cards.summary: Mallet 2008 (STN crossover RCT, N = 16): Y-BOCS 19 on active subthalamic stimulation versus 28 on sham (p=0.01) — with 1 intracerebral haemorrhage and 2 infections among 15 serious adverse events
cards.type: Double-blind, sham-controlled crossover randomised trial — N = 16
cards.people: 16 adults with highly treatment-refractory OCD at French centres, randomised to active subthalamic nucleus stimulation then sham, or sham then active, over a 10-month crossover study with two 3-month periods.
cards.result: Mean Y-BOCS score (0-40, lower is better) was 19 (+/-8) after active stimulation versus 28 (+/-7) after sham (p=0.01). Global Assessment of Functioning was higher on active stimulation (56 +/-14 versus 43 +/-8; p=0.005). Depression, anxiety and neuropsychological ratings were not modified by stimulation.
cards.watchOut: Only 16 patients, and the harm line is heavy: 15 serious adverse events overall, including 1 intracerebral haemorrhage and 2 infections, plus 23 nonserious events. A 9-point Y-BOCS gap in 16 crossover patients is a signal, not a stable effect estimate.
cards.source: Mallet L et al. Subthalamic nucleus stimulation in severe obsessive-compulsive disorder. N Engl J Med. 2008. PMID: 19005196. Registry ID: NCT00169377, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Denys 2010 (nucleus accumbens crossover RCT, N = 16): blinded active-versus-sham Y-BOCS difference 8.3 points (p=.004); 9 of 16 responders in the open phase
cards.summary: Denys 2010 (nucleus accumbens crossover RCT, N = 16): blinded active-versus-sham Y-BOCS difference 8.3 points (p=.004); 9 of 16 responders in the open phase
cards.type: Randomised double-blind crossover trial with open phases — N = 16
cards.people: 16 patients aged 18-65 with DSM-IV OCD meeting stringent refractoriness criteria, implanted with bilateral nucleus accumbens electrodes; an 8-month open phase was followed by a double-blind crossover of 2-week active versus sham periods (n=14) and a 12-month open maintenance phase.
cards.result: In the open phase, mean Y-BOCS fell 46%, from 33.7 (3.6) to 18.0 (11.4) (p<.001); 9 of 16 patients were responders (at least 35% Y-BOCS decrease). In the blinded phase, the active-versus-sham Y-BOCS difference was 8.3 (2.3) points, or 25% (p=.004). Depression and anxiety also decreased significantly. No permanent adverse events were reported except mild forgetfulness and word-finding problems.
cards.watchOut: The blinded contrast rests on 14 patients and 2-week stimulation periods — long enough to detect a symptomatic difference, far too short to judge durability or the full surgical harm profile. The 46% open-phase fall mixes placebo, expectancy and optimisation effects and is not pooled with the blinded result on this shelf.

cards.headline: Cohen 2025 (individual-participant meta-analysis of all sham-controlled DBS-for-OCD trials): 5.1 Y-BOCS points in favour of DBS across 9 RCTs totalling 91 patients — GRADE quality rated low
cards.summary: Cohen 2025 (individual-participant meta-analysis of all sham-controlled DBS-for-OCD trials): 5.1 Y-BOCS points in favour of DBS across 9 RCTs totalling 91 patients — GRADE quality rated low
cards.type: Systematic review and individual-participant-data meta-analysis of sham-controlled RCTs — 9 trials, N = 91
cards.people: All randomised trials comparing DBS with sham stimulation in adults with OCD, any stimulation target, with individual Y-BOCS outcome data obtained for 91 patients in total.
cards.result: DBS reduced Y-BOCS by 5.1 points versus sham (95% CI 2.0 to 8.1; Hedges g 0.56). The odds ratio for response was 4.7 (95% CI 1.8 to 12.2), with a number needed to treat of 3.9. Trials using gradual parameter optimisation towards maximal improvement showed larger effects. The most frequent stimulation-related adverse events were hypomania and cognitive problems; adverse events also occurred during surgery and follow-up. GRADE quality of evidence was rated low, and heterogeneity was high.
cards.watchOut: This is the entire randomised evidence base for the question, and it is 91 patients spread across different targets (subthalamic nucleus, nucleus accumbens/ventral capsule, and others) that should not be read as one interchangeable intervention. Low GRADE quality plus high heterogeneity caps this shelf's stamp however consistent the direction is.

cards.headline: Cologne long-term cohort (NAcc/ALIC, N = 30, follow-up 3-21 years): 22 of 30 patients (73.3%) met the response criterion at final follow-up — retrospective, labelled as such
cards.summary: Cologne long-term cohort (NAcc/ALIC, N = 30, follow-up 3-21 years): 22 of 30 patients (73.3%) met the response criterion at final follow-up — retrospective, labelled as such
cards.type: Single-centre retrospective cohort (observational — labelled as such) — N = 30
cards.people: 30 consecutive patients (17 women) who underwent nucleus accumbens / anterior limb of internal capsule DBS at one centre between 2004 and 2022, assessed with Y-BOCS at baseline, 1 year, and latest follow-up at 3 years or more (up to 21 years); response defined as at least 35% Y-BOCS reduction.
cards.result: Y-BOCS scores decreased significantly across the three time points. At final follow-up, 22 of 30 patients (73.3%) were responders; 8 of them were delayed responders who had not met the criterion at 1 year. Of 15 patients responding at 1 year, 14 retained response at final follow-up.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective, uncontrolled and single-centre, with heterogeneous follow-up: patients who keep returning for 3-21 years are not a random sample of everyone implanted, and the authors themselves state the design precludes causal conclusions. It supports durability of response once achieved; it cannot estimate the effect of switching the device on.
cards.source: Cid-Rodriguez FX et al. Long-term outcomes of nucleus accumbens/anterior limb of the internal capsule deep brain stimulation in treatment-resistant obsessive-compulsive disorder. cards.headline: Synthesis: blinded trials agree DBS beats sham by roughly 5-8 Y-BOCS points, but the whole randomised base is 91 patients and the surgery carries real harm — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: blinded trials agree DBS beats sham by roughly 5-8 Y-BOCS points, but the whole randomised base is 91 patients and the surgery carries real harm — POSSIBLE
cards.people: 91 randomised patients across 9 small sham-controlled crossover trials (individual trials of 16 patients carded above), set against a 30-patient observational cohort followed for up to 21 years.
cards.result: Blinded effects: 9 Y-BOCS points (subthalamic, Mallet) and 8.3 points (nucleus accumbens, Denys) in the two best-known trials; 5.1 points (95% CI 2.0 to 8.1) pooled across all 9 trials. Long-term observational response: 73.3% at 3-21 years. Harms include intracerebral haemorrhage, infection, hypomania and cognitive problems. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — the direction is consistent, but the evidence is a handful of very small crossover trials in exceptionally refractory patients, with GRADE quality rated low by the meta-analysts themselves.
cards.watchOut: Targets differ across trials and are not pooled into a single effect on this shelf; DBS for OCD remains a last-resort, specialist-centre intervention (FDA humanitarian device exemption since 2009), and nothing here speaks to patients who have not exhausted standard pharmacotherapy and CBT. Deep brain stimulation for Parkinson's disease, epilepsy and dystonia are separate shelves with their own records.
cards.source: Synthesis of Mallet L et al. 2008 (PMID: 19005196), Denys D et al. 2010 (PMID: 20921122), Cohen SE et al. 2025 (PMID: 40579425) and Cid-Rodriguez FX et al. 2026 (PMID: 42973862), all carded above.

shelves.title: Varenicline in alcohol use disorder: drinking falls, heavy-drinking days split
shelves.question: In adults with alcohol use disorder, does varenicline, versus placebo, reduce heavy drinking and increase abstinent days?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Alcoholism/drug therapy · Benzazepines/adverse effects, therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Medication Adherence · Middle Aged · Quinoxalines/adverse effects, therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Varenicline
shelves.balance: SPLIT is the honest stamp. On the amount consumed, the record is fairly consistent: Litten 2013 (n=200) met its primary outcome, the 2025 Swedish factorial trial (n=384) showed varenicline alone and with bupropion reducing both an objective biomarker (blood phosphatidylethanol) and percent heavy drinking days versus placebo, and the 2019 meta-analysis of 9 trials (N=585) found significantly reduced consumption. On heavy drinking days — the endpoint patients and guidelines care most about — the record divides: the same meta-analysis found no significant superiority over placebo, and O'Malley 2018 (n=131, AUD with comorbid smoking) was null on its primary outcome overall, with benefit confined to men in a sex interaction (no heavy drinking days 29% versus 6% in men; the small female subgroup ran the other way). The price is nausea: 51% on varenicline alone versus 11% on placebo in the factorial trial, lasting a median 45 days. PROPOSED SPLIT, naming the split: consumption down, heavy-drinking-day benefit inconsistent, male subgroup signal unconfirmed.

cards.headline: Litten 2013 (multisite RCT, N = 200): varenicline lowered weekly percent heavy drinking days (adjusted mean difference 10.4), drinks per day and craving versus placebo (p<0.05)
cards.summary: Litten 2013 (multisite RCT, N = 200): varenicline lowered weekly percent heavy drinking days (adjusted mean difference 10.4), drinks per day and craving versus placebo (p<0.05)
cards.type: Multisite double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial — N = 200
cards.people: 200 men and women meeting criteria for alcohol dependence at 5 US clinical sites, smokers and nonsmokers, randomised to varenicline titrated to 2 mg/day or placebo for 13 weeks, with a computerised behavioural intervention for all.
cards.result: The varenicline group had significantly lower weekly percent heavy drinking days (the primary outcome; adjusted mean difference 10.4), drinks per day, drinks per drinking day and alcohol craving than the placebo group (all p<0.05). The average treatment effect was similar for smokers and nonsmokers. Adverse events were expected and mild.
cards.watchOut: A phase 2-sized trial with self-reported drinking outcomes over 13 weeks; the abstract does not print the absolute heavy-drinking-day rates for each arm, so no absolute rates are printed here. One positive multisite trial does not settle the heavy-drinking endpoint — see the split in the cards below.

cards.headline: O'Malley 2018 (RCT in AUD with comorbid smoking, N = 131): primary outcome null overall (the treatment made no difference to percent heavy drinking days) — benefit confined to men in a sex interaction
cards.summary: O'Malley 2018 (RCT in AUD with comorbid smoking, N = 131): primary outcome null overall (the treatment made no difference to percent heavy drinking days) — benefit confined to men in a sex interaction
cards.type: Phase 2 double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial — N = 131
cards.people: 131 adults with alcohol dependence and comorbid cigarette smoking (92 men, 39 women; mean age 42.7 years) at 2 US outpatient clinics, randomised to varenicline 1 mg twice daily or placebo for 16 weeks with medical management, stratified by sex and site.
cards.result: Mean change in percent heavy drinking days (weeks 9-16) did not differ significantly between varenicline and placebo overall (the treatment made no difference on the primary outcome). A treatment-by-sex-by-time interaction (p=.03) showed a larger decrease in men on varenicline (no heavy drinking days in 13 of 45 men, 29%, versus 3 of 47, 6%, on placebo) but a smaller decrease in women (1 of 19, 5%, versus 5 of 20, 25%, on placebo). Prolonged smoking abstinence was achieved by 8 of 64 (13%) on varenicline versus 0 of 67 on placebo (p=.003).
cards.watchOut: The sex interaction is a secondary analysis of a null trial: the female subgroup is 39 women, and the direction in women favoured placebo. It generates a hypothesis about men; it does not rescue the primary outcome, and it must not be quoted as 'varenicline works in AUD' without the null beside it.
cards.source: O'Malley SS et al. Effect of varenicline combined with medical management on alcohol use disorder with comorbid cigarette smoking: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA Psychiatry. 2018. PMID: 29261824. Registry ID: NCT01553136, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Swedish factorial RCT 2025 (N = 384): varenicline alone and varenicline + bupropion both reduced blood phosphatidylethanol and percent heavy drinking days versus placebo (d = 0.30-0.39); nausea in 51% on varenicline alone versus 11% on placebo
cards.summary: Swedish factorial RCT 2025 (N = 384): varenicline alone and varenicline + bupropion both reduced blood phosphatidylethanol and percent heavy drinking days versus placebo (d = 0.30-0.39); nausea in 51% on varenicline alone versus 11% on placebo
cards.type: Four-arm double-blind placebo-controlled factorial randomised trial — N = 384
cards.people: 384 adults aged 25-70 with moderate-to-severe DSM-5 alcohol use disorder at 4 Swedish outpatient clinics, randomised to placebo+placebo (n=97), varenicline+bupropion (n=100), varenicline+placebo (n=96) or placebo+bupropion (n=91) for 12 weeks; 72% male, median age 57.
cards.result: In modified intention-to-treat analyses over weeks 2-11, varenicline+bupropion reduced blood phosphatidylethanol (Cohen d=0.39, p=0.004) and percent heavy drinking days (d=0.31, p=0.008) versus placebo; varenicline alone also reduced both (B-PEth d=0.30, p=0.005; %HDD d=0.36, p=0.023). Adding bupropion to varenicline made no significant further difference. Nausea was more common and longer-lasting on varenicline alone than placebo (49 of 96, 51%, versus 11 of 97, 11%; p<0.0001), and was less frequent when bupropion was combined (36 of 100).
cards.watchOut: Effect sizes are small-to-moderate standardised differences (d = 0.30-0.39), not abstinence rates, and the trial's hierarchical testing stopped after the combination-versus-varenicline comparison was null. The nausea burden — half of patients, lasting a median 45 days on varenicline alone — is the practical price of the effect and belongs beside it.
cards.source: Soderpalm B et al. Efficacy and safety of varenicline and bupropion, in combination and alone, for alcohol use disorder: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled multicentre trial. Lancet Reg Health Eur. 2025. cards.headline: Meta-analysis 2019 (9 double-blind RCTs, N = 585): varenicline reduced the amount of alcohol consumed but was NOT superior to placebo for heavy drinking days — the split in one analysis
cards.summary: Meta-analysis 2019 (9 double-blind RCTs, N = 585): varenicline reduced the amount of alcohol consumed but was NOT superior to placebo for heavy drinking days — the split in one analysis
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of double-blind placebo-controlled RCTs — 9 trials, N = 585
cards.people: Nine double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trials of varenicline in alcoholism (total N = 585; study durations 4-13 weeks), pooled with random-effects models for heavy drinking days, alcohol consumption and dropout outcomes.
cards.result: Varenicline was not superior to placebo in decreasing heavy drinking days, but was significantly superior to placebo in decreasing the amount of alcohol consumed. Dropout rates, overall and due to adverse events, did not differ significantly between groups.
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials are small and short (the largest single trial is carded above), and several enrolled smokers specifically, so the pooled population is not AUD at large. A meta-analysis cannot repair a null primary endpoint in one of its largest constituent trials; it summarises the split rather than resolving it.
cards.source: Oon-Arom A et al. Efficacy and acceptability of varenicline for alcoholism: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized-controlled trials. Drug Alcohol Depend. 2019. cards.headline: Synthesis: varenicline reduces how much people drink, but the heavy-drinking-day benefit is inconsistent across trials — SPLIT
cards.summary: Synthesis: varenicline reduces how much people drink, but the heavy-drinking-day benefit is inconsistent across trials — SPLIT
cards.people: 715 patients in the three carded trials (200 + 131 + 384) and 585 patients across the 9 trials in the meta-analysis (overlapping populations).
cards.result: Positive: Litten 2013 (primary outcome met) and the 2025 Swedish factorial trial (both varenicline arms positive on an objective biomarker, B-PEth, and on heavy drinking days). Null: O'Malley 2018 primary outcome overall, with benefit only in the male subgroup. Pooled: consumption down, heavy drinking days not significantly reduced. Nausea affected 51% on varenicline alone versus 11% on placebo in the factorial trial. PROPOSED SPLIT — the record divides by endpoint and by population: amount consumed falls fairly consistently; heavy-drinking days and women with comorbid smoking are where the record fails to confirm benefit.
cards.watchOut: Varenicline is not approved for alcohol use disorder; its homes elsewhere in this library are smoking-cessation questions, and nothing on this shelf should be read across to them. Trials are 12-16 weeks; no carded trial reports long-term abstinence, liver outcomes or mortality.
cards.source: Synthesis of Litten RZ et al. 2013 (PMID: 23728065), O'Malley SS et al. 2018 (PMID: 29261824), Soderpalm B et al. 2025 (PMID: 40487775) and Oon-Arom A et al. 2019 (PMID: 31678838), all carded above.

shelves.title: Ondansetron in early-onset / genotype-selected alcohol use disorder: a subgroup claim, fenced as such
shelves.question: In adults with alcohol use disorder of early onset (or with serotonergic genotypes predicting response), does low-dose ondansetron, versus placebo, reduce drinking?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Alcoholism/blood, prevention & control · Analysis of Variance · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Ondansetron/administration & dosage, therapeutic use · Serotonin Antagonists/administration & dosage, therapeutic use · Transferrin/analogs & derivatives, metabolism
shelves.balance: Every positive result on this shelf lives inside a subgroup, and the shelf is built to keep it there. Johnson 2000 (JAMA, n=271 randomised) found benefit only in early-onset alcoholism (drinks per day 1.56-1.89 across microgram doses versus 3.30 on placebo). Johnson 2011 (n=283) moved the fence from onset age to genotype: serotonin-transporter LL carriers on ondansetron drank less and had more abstinent days than LL carriers on placebo. The AD04 phase 3 (n=303, genotype-selected, 6 months) then showed its benefit in the prespecified heavy-drinker endophenotype (-8.5 percentage points on monthly heavy drinking days at month 6, p=0.03) while very heavy drinkers did not respond the same way, and a companion report found 6-month liver safety indistinguishable from placebo. The tested intervention is the genotype-paired low-dose programme AD04 (Adial Pharmaceuticals) — not ordinary antiemetic ondansetron. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: concordant randomised evidence, one dominant investigative programme, no approval, no independent replication, and no basis for use in unselected AUD.

cards.headline: Johnson 2000 (JAMA RCT, N = 271 randomised): benefit confined to early-onset alcoholism — drinks per day 1.56-1.89 across ondansetron doses versus 3.30 on placebo; 4 microg/kg twice daily best (70.1% versus 50.2% days abstinent)
cards.summary: Johnson 2000 (JAMA RCT, N = 271 randomised): benefit confined to early-onset alcoholism — drinks per day 1.56-1.89 across ondansetron doses versus 3.30 on placebo; 4 microg/kg twice daily best (70.1% versus 50.2% days abstinent)
cards.type: Double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial — N = 271 randomised (321 enrolled)
cards.people: 271 patients with alcoholism (mean age 40.6 years; 70.5% male) at two Texas centres, randomised after a placebo lead-in week to ondansetron 1, 4 or 16 microg/kg twice daily or placebo for 11 weeks, all with weekly group cognitive behavioural therapy; outcomes analysed by early- versus late-onset alcoholism.
cards.result: Among early-onset patients, ondansetron at all three doses beat placebo on drinks per day (1.89, 1.56 and 1.87 versus 3.30; p=.03, .01 and .02) and drinks per drinking day. The 4 microg/kg dose also increased percent days abstinent (70.10 versus 50.20; p=.02). Objective corroboration: the mean log carbohydrate-deficient transferrin ratio fell on ondansetron 1 and 4 microg/kg versus placebo in early-onset patients. No such benefit was shown in late-onset alcoholism.
cards.watchOut: The entire claim is subgroup-defined by onset age, in a single research group's trial, at microgram doses far below antiemetic dosing — ordinary ondansetron prescribed for nausea is not this intervention. Subgroup-first results from 2000 needed the genotype replication carded next, and even that comes from the same programme.
cards.source: Johnson BA et al. Ondansetron for reduction of drinking among biologically predisposed alcoholic patients: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2000. PMID: 10944641. cards.headline: Johnson 2011 (genotype-guided RCT, N = 283): response tracked serotonin-transporter genotype — LL carriers on ondansetron drank 1.62 fewer drinks per drinking day and had 11.27% more abstinent days than LL carriers on placebo
cards.summary: Johnson 2011 (genotype-guided RCT, N = 283): response tracked serotonin-transporter genotype — LL carriers on ondansetron drank 1.62 fewer drinks per drinking day and had 11.27% more abstinent days than LL carriers on placebo
cards.people: 283 people with alcoholism randomised by serotonin transporter (5-HTT) genotype (LL/LS/SS at 5'-HTTLPR, plus rs1042173 genotyping) to ondansetron 4 microg/kg twice daily or placebo for 11 weeks, with standardised cognitive-behavioural therapy.
cards.result: LL-genotype participants on ondansetron had fewer drinks per drinking day (-1.62) and a higher percentage of days abstinent (+11.27%) than LL participants on placebo. Among ondansetron recipients, LL carriers did better than LS/SS carriers (-1.53 drinks per drinking day; +9.73% days abstinent), and the LL/TT subgroup showed the largest contrast against all other genotype-treatment combinations (-2.63 drinks per drinking day; +16.99% days abstinent). The genotype variants interacted significantly with treatment for both outcomes.
cards.watchOut: A pharmacogenetic subgroup claim from the same investigative programme as the 2000 trial: the effect lives inside genotype strata, the comparisons multiply quickly, and no independent group has replicated it. It refines who might respond; it does not widen the claim beyond the serotonergic subtype.
cards.source: Johnson BA et al. Pharmacogenetic approach at the serotonin transporter gene as a method of reducing the severity of alcohol drinking. Am J Psychiatry. 2011. PMID: 21247998. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: AD04 phase 3 (genotype-selected RCT, N = 303): in the prespecified heavy-drinker endophenotype, monthly percent heavy drinking days fell more on low-dose ondansetron than placebo at month 6 (difference -8.5 percentage points, p=0.03) — very heavy drinkers did not show the response
cards.summary: AD04 phase 3 (genotype-selected RCT, N = 303): in the prespecified heavy-drinker endophenotype, monthly percent heavy drinking days fell more on low-dose ondansetron than placebo at month 6 (difference -8.5 percentage points, p=0.03) — very heavy drinkers did not show the response
cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial — N = 303
cards.people: 303 adults with moderate-to-severe DSM-5 alcohol use disorder at 25 sites, pre-stratified by drinking severity (heavy versus very heavy) and by a predefined serotonin transporter / serotonin-3AB receptor genetic profile; over 80% men, mostly in their fifties, over 95% of European descent. Low-dose ondansetron (AD04, approximately 0.33 mg twice daily) or placebo for 6 months, with brief behavioural compliance enhancement treatment every 2 weeks.
cards.result: Among heavy-drinking participants, monthly percent heavy drinking days fell by 46.7% on AD04 versus 38.1% on placebo at month 6 (least-squares mean difference -8.5 percentage points; p=0.03); heavy drinkers on AD04 were also less likely to carry an AUD diagnosis at month 1 (difference -8.8 percentage points; p=0.026), and quality-of-life shift favoured AD04 (OR 3.4; 95% CI 1.03 to 11.45). Very heavy drinkers were the less responsive endophenotype. The adverse-event profile was like placebo's.
cards.watchOut: Read the fences on this card carefully: genotype-selected, European-descent-dominated, and the demonstrated benefit sits in the heavy (not very heavy) drinking stratum — the programme's earlier overall readout did not establish benefit across the whole enrolled population, and AD04 is not approved. The tested product is the genotype-paired low-dose programme AD04 (Adial Pharmaceuticals); it is not interchangeable with standard antiemetic ondansetron dosing.
cards.source: Johnson B et al. Low-dose ondansetron: a candidate prospective precision medicine to treat alcohol use disorder endophenotypes. Eur J Intern Med. 2024. PMID: 38876929. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: AD04 liver-safety report (same phase 3 programme): 6 months of low-dose ondansetron did not change ALT, AST, bilirubin or GGT versus placebo, with no significant adverse effects — a safety report, not an efficacy replication
cards.summary: AD04 liver-safety report (same phase 3 programme): 6 months of low-dose ondansetron did not change ALT, AST, bilirubin or GGT versus placebo, with no significant adverse effects — a safety report, not an efficacy replication
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised trial safety report (same programme as the card above) — N as in the parent trial
cards.people: Participants with AUD and the 5-marker genetic profile from the phase 3 AD04 trial, receiving twice-daily low-dose ondansetron (0.33 mg) or placebo with brief psychosocial counselling; liver biochemistry (ALT, AST, GGT, bilirubin, MCV, prothrombin) assessed at weeks 0, 12 and 24.
cards.result: Low-dose ondansetron did not significantly change biochemical markers of liver injury (ALT, AST, serum bilirubin) versus placebo; GGT, elevated at baseline in these drinkers, was likewise unaffected. No significant adverse effects of oral low-dose ondansetron were observed, and cardiac events, well-being and study completion were also assessed.
cards.watchOut: This is the same trial population as the efficacy card, reported for safety: it adds tolerability reassurance (relevant because the target population often has alcohol-associated liver disease) but zero independent efficacy evidence, and 24 weeks in a selected trial population cannot exclude rarer harms.
cards.source: Addolorato G et al. Safety and compliance of long-term low-dose ondansetron in alcohol use disorder treatment. Eur J Intern Med. 2024. PMID: 38521730. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a real but narrow claim — benefit only inside onset-age and genotype-defined subgroups, from essentially one programme — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: a real but narrow claim — benefit only inside onset-age and genotype-defined subgroups, from essentially one programme — POSSIBLE
cards.people: 271 randomised (Johnson 2000), 283 genotype-stratified (Johnson 2011) and 303 genotype-selected phase 3 participants (AD04), plus the phase 3 safety report on the same population.
cards.result: Early-onset alcoholism (2000): drinks per day roughly halved versus placebo at microgram doses. Genotype-guided (2011): LL serotonin-transporter carriers drove the response. Phase 3 (2024): heavy drinkers with the selected genetic profile gained an extra 8.5 percentage-point reduction in monthly heavy drinking days at 6 months; very heavy drinkers did not show the response, and 6-month liver safety was placebo-like. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — three concordant randomised reports, but every one is subgroup-fenced and the programme is substantially one group's, with no approval and no independent replication.
cards.watchOut: Nothing on this shelf supports ondansetron for alcohol use disorder at large, at antiemetic doses, or without the onset-age/genotype selection that defines the tested population. Ondansetron's antiemetic and other homes elsewhere in this library are separate questions and are not evidence here.
cards.source: Synthesis of Johnson BA et al. 2000 (PMID: 10944641), Johnson BA et al. 2011 (PMID: 21247998), Johnson B et al. 2024 (PMID: 38876929) and Addolorato G et al. 2024 (PMID: 38521730), all carded above.

shelves.title: US POINTER: structured multidomain lifestyle intervention versus self-guided — a small win for intensity
shelves.question: In older adults at risk of cognitive decline, does a structured, intensive multidomain lifestyle intervention, versus a self-guided version of the same intervention, preserve global cognition?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Cognition/physiology · Cognitive Dysfunction/physiopathology, prevention & control · Dementia/physiopathology, prevention & control · Diet, Healthy · Exercise/physiology · Sedentary Behavior · Single-Blind Method · Healthy Aging/physiology · Follow-Up Studies · Treatment Outcome · Social Participation
shelves.balance: This pack is the US POINTER slice of the multidomain-lifestyle question whose home is Shelf #332 (the FINGER family — read the two together; nothing carded here duplicates that shelf's cards). POINTER asks a narrower question than FINGER did: not intervention versus advice, but structured, coached, accountable delivery versus a self-guided version of the same programme, in 2,111 at-risk US adults. Structured delivery won by 0.029 SD per year on global cognition (p=0.008) and by 0.014 on a frailty index (p<0.0001) — small, statistically firm differences. The fences matter as much as the result: there is no untreated control arm, so POINTER cannot show either version beats nothing; both arms improved, as practice effects predict; the imaging ancillary found no difference in amyloid, tau or hippocampal trajectories; and dementia incidence was not measured. PROPOSED POSSIBLE, capped by the single-trial rule.

cards.headline: US POINTER 2025 (main RCT, N = 2,111): structured multidomain intervention beat the self-guided version by 0.029 SD per year on global cognition (p=0.008) — with no untreated control arm, so this compares intensity, not intervention versus nothing
cards.summary: US POINTER 2025 (main RCT, N = 2,111): structured multidomain intervention beat the self-guided version by 0.029 SD per year on global cognition (p=0.008) — with no untreated control arm, so this compares intensity, not intervention versus nothing
cards.type: Multicentre single-blind randomised clinical trial — N = 2,111
cards.people: 2,111 US adults aged 60-79 at increased risk of cognitive decline (sedentary, suboptimal diet, plus at least 2 further risk criteria) at 5 clinical sites, randomised to a structured, higher-intensity multidomain intervention (n=1,056) or a self-guided version of the same intervention (n=1,055) for 2 years; 68.9% women, mean age 68.2; 89% completed the year-2 assessment.
cards.result: Global cognition improved in both groups: mean annual increase 0.243 SD (95% CI 0.227 to 0.258) on the structured intervention versus 0.213 SD (0.198 to 0.229) self-guided — a between-group difference of 0.029 SD per year (95% CI 0.008 to 0.050; p=0.008). The benefit was consistent in APOE epsilon4 carriers and noncarriers, and appeared greater in participants with lower baseline cognition. Fewer adverse events were reported in the structured group (serious 151 versus 190; nonserious 1,091 versus 1,225), with a positive COVID-19 test the commonest event overall.
cards.watchOut: There is no untreated or usual-care arm: both groups received the intervention, so the trial cannot say whether either version beats doing nothing, and practice effects on repeated cognitive testing lift both arms. The 0.029 SD/year difference is statistically firm and clinically small; dementia incidence was not the endpoint. This trial belongs with the FINGER family — see the balance and synthesis for the home shelf.
cards.source: Baker LD et al. Structured vs self-guided multidomain lifestyle interventions for global cognitive function: the US POINTER randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2025. PMID: 40720610. Registry ID: NCT03688126, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: POINTER Imaging ancillary 2026 (N = 983 scanned): no intervention-group differences in amyloid, tau, hippocampal volume or white-matter outcomes (the treatment made no difference to brain biomarker trajectories)
cards.summary: POINTER Imaging ancillary 2026 (N = 983 scanned): no intervention-group differences in amyloid, tau, hippocampal volume or white-matter outcomes (the treatment made no difference to brain biomarker trajectories)
cards.type: Prespecified imaging ancillary study of the parent randomised trial — N = 983 with at least one MRI or PET session
cards.people: 983 US POINTER participants (516 structured, 467 self-guided; mean age 68.4; 61.5% women) undergoing MRI/PET, with four primary imaging outcomes: global amyloid burden, entorhinal tau burden, hippocampal volume and white-matter hyperintensity volume, alongside the global cognitive composite.
cards.result: There were no intervention-group differences in longitudinal cognitive or imaging outcomes within this substudy, and group differences were not associated with or moderated by amyloid status or accumulation (the treatment made no difference to brain biomarker trajectories). Two interaction findings: the negative association between entorhinal tau change and cognition change seen in the self-guided group was attenuated in the structured group (interaction p=.03), and lower baseline hippocampal volume predicted greater cognitive benefit from the structured intervention (interaction p=.03).
cards.watchOut: Ancillary-study interactions at p=.03, among many comparisons, are hypothesis-generating; the substudy's own headline is a null on every primary imaging outcome, which undercuts any claim that the small cognitive difference reflects slowed Alzheimer-type pathology over 2 years.
cards.source: Harrison TM et al. Brain imaging biomarkers and cognitive outcomes in a multidomain lifestyle intervention: the POINTER Imaging ancillary study. JAMA Neurol. 2026. PMID: 42008251. Registry ID: NCT03688126, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: POINTER frailty report 2026 (same trial, N = 2,111): deficit-accumulation frailty index fell more on the structured intervention (-0.024 versus -0.009 at 24 months; difference -0.014, p<0.0001) — but frailty change did not explain the cognitive benefit
cards.summary: POINTER frailty report 2026 (same trial, N = 2,111): deficit-accumulation frailty index fell more on the structured intervention (-0.024 versus -0.009 at 24 months; difference -0.014, p<0.0001) — but frailty change did not explain the cognitive benefit
cards.type: Randomised trial secondary-outcome report (same trial programme) — N = 2,111
cards.people: The full US POINTER population, with a modified 31-component deficit-accumulation frailty index built from data at baseline, 12 and 24 months, compared between the structured and self-guided interventions.
cards.result: Mean frailty-index change at 24 months was -0.024 (SE 0.002) in the structured group versus -0.009 (0.002) self-guided — a difference of -0.014 (95% CI -0.019 to -0.008; p<0.0001), similar across age, sex, BMI, diabetes and baseline-frailty subgroups. Changes in frailty did not account for the structured intervention's relative cognitive benefit.
cards.watchOut: A secondary outcome from the same single trial: the absolute frailty difference (0.014 on a 0-1 index) is small, the index is a constructed composite rather than a clinical event, and this report adds an outcome to POINTER rather than an independent replication of it.
cards.source: Espeland MA et al. Relative impact of multidomain lifestyle interventions on deficit accumulation frailty over 24 months in the U.S. POINTER trial. J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci. 2026. PMID: 41950390. Registry ID: NCT03688126, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: structured delivery beats self-guided delivery by a small, firm margin on cognition and frailty — but with no untreated arm, POINTER cannot show the intervention beats nothing — POSSIBLE (single trial)
cards.summary: Synthesis: structured delivery beats self-guided delivery by a small, firm margin on cognition and frailty — but with no untreated arm, POINTER cannot show the intervention beats nothing — POSSIBLE (single trial)
cards.people: One trial programme: 2,111 randomised participants, with an imaging ancillary study of 983 and secondary-outcome reports on the full cohort.
cards.result: Cognition: +0.029 SD per year favouring structured over self-guided delivery (p=0.008), both arms improving. Frailty index: -0.014 difference favouring structured (p<0.0001). Brain biomarkers: no group differences. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — capped by the single-trial rule. Read with the home shelf for this question family, Shelf #332 (the FINGER trial and the dementia-endpoint trials): FINGER compared the intervention against general health advice, and the trials that measured dementia itself have not shown prevention; POINTER adds the intensity comparison, not a dementia answer.
cards.watchOut: Because both POINTER arms were treated, the result supports investing in structure, coaching and accountability when a multidomain programme is offered — it does not establish that offering the programme beats ordinary care, and the absolute cognitive difference (0.029 SD/year) is small enough that its clinical weight is debated, exactly as with FINGER.
cards.source: Synthesis of Baker LD et al. 2025 (PMID: 40720610), Harrison TM et al. 2026 (PMID: 42008251) and Espeland MA et al. 2026 (PMID: 41950390), all carded above.

shelves.title: Cerebral metabolic rate for oxygen: ~3.0–3.3 mL/100 g/min at resting wakefulness — the classic Kety–Schmidt 3.5 was an overestimate — falling ~21% in sleep and ~26–38% under volatile anaesthesia
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what is the cerebral metabolic rate for oxygen — CMRO2 and cerebral blood flow values by the Kety–Schmidt nitrous-oxide method and their modern PET/MRI successors, and how do CMRO2 and flow change with sleep, anaesthesia depth surrogates and ageing in health?
shelves.mesh: Brain · Oxygen Consumption · Cerebrovascular Circulation · Positron-Emission Tomography · Sleep · Wakefulness
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for the resting value and its state-dependence, framed by Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep on cerebral metabolism. The classic Kety–Schmidt nitrous-oxide values — CBF 54 mL/100 g/min and CMRO2 3.5 mL/100 g/min — enter this shelf only as quoted by the fetched critical appraisal, because the 1948 originals' records carry no abstracts and were refused (see Synthesis). The appraisal (Madsen 1993), from 57 Kety–Schmidt measurements in young normal adults at EEG-verified wakeful rest, shows the classic figures overestimate: incomplete tracer equilibration inflates them, and the corrected equilibrium values are ~46 mL/100 g/min and ~3.0 mL/100 g/min, with interindividual CMRO2 variation of 11% (coefficient of variation). The modern PET database lands beside the corrected figure: in 70 healthy volunteers across 11 Japanese centres, cortical CMRO2 was 3.3 ± 0.5 mL/100 mL/min with CBF 44.4 ± 6.5 and oxygen extraction fraction 0.44 ± 0.06 (Ito 2004). A modern Kety–Schmidt repeatability study in 29 healthy men found the method robust in its best (discontinuous desaturation) form — CBF 64 (95% CI 59–71) mL/100 g/min and CMRO2 1.8 (1.7–2.0) µmol/g/min — values on the higher side, kept on the face as the method's own spread (Taudorf 2009). State changes: CMRO2 falls in sleep — by a relative 21% (range 14–32%) from a waking 118 ± 12 µmol/min/100 g to a nadir of 98 ± 16 on OxFlow MRI in 12 healthy subjects (Caporale 2021) — and under volatile anaesthesia, where sevoflurane and isoflurane at 1.5 MAC lowered CMRO2 by a relative 26% and 38% while raising CBF by a relative 17% and 25% (Oshima 2003, N = 20, Kety–Schmidt with 15% N2O; the record prints relative changes, not the absolute pair, and the card says so). Ageing lowers CMRO2 regionally — significantly lower mean CMRO2 over 51 than under 50 in 32 healthy volunteers, with flow comparatively preserved (Takada 1992). Cross-points, not duplicated: the library's cerebral autoregulation and CO2-reactivity shelves ask how flow is regulated; this shelf asks the metabolic rate itself.

cards.headline: Madsen 1993: the Kety–Schmidt classic values (CBF 54, CMRO2 3.5 mL/100 g/min) are overestimates — corrected equilibrium values in young normal adults are ~46 and ~3.0, with 11% interindividual variation
cards.summary: Madsen 1993: the Kety–Schmidt classic values (CBF 54, CMRO2 3.5 mL/100 g/min) are overestimates — corrected equilibrium values in young normal adults are ~46 and ~3.0, with 11% interindividual variation
cards.type: Human methods appraisal (Kety–Schmidt CBF/CMRO2 at resting wakefulness), J Cereb Blood Flow Metab 1993
cards.people: Fifty-seven Kety–Schmidt measurements performed during EEG-verified wakeful rest in young normal adults (number of individuals not separately documented in the record's abstract — printed as such), with a computer simulation model used to quantify the systematic error from incomplete inert-gas equilibration between brain and venous blood, and magnetic resonance angiography of cerebral venous anatomy.
cards.result: The record's appraisal: because diffusion equilibrium for the tracer is not reached in practice, the technique's textbook normal values — CBF 54 mL/100 g/min and CMRO2 3.5 mL/100 g/min — overestimate the true values. Correcting the measured data gives average CBF ≈ 46 mL/100 g/min and average CMRO2 ≈ 3.0 mL/100 g/min in the healthy young adult. Interindividual variation of CMRO2 was 11% (coefficient of variation), and none of it correlated with cerebral venous anatomy on MRA — against an earlier suggestion that venous anatomy explained the spread.
cards.watchOut: The classic 54/3.5 figures are quoted here exactly as this fetched record quotes them — the 1948 originals were refused (no abstract in their records; see Synthesis). Corrected values are model-based equilibrium estimates, labelled as such.
cards.source: Madsen PL, Holm S, Herning M, Lassen NA. Average blood flow and oxygen uptake in the human brain during resting wakefulness: a critical appraisal of the Kety-Schmidt technique. Journal of cerebral blood flow and metabolism : official journal of the International Society of Cerebral Blood Flow and Metabolism. 1993. PMID: 8314918. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ito 2004: the 15O-PET normal database — cortical CMRO2 3.3 ± 0.5 mL/100 mL/min, CBF 44.4 ± 6.5, OEF 0.44 ± 0.06 in 70 healthy volunteers across 11 centres
cards.summary: Ito 2004: the 15O-PET normal database — cortical CMRO2 3.3 ± 0.5 mL/100 mL/min, CBF 44.4 ± 6.5, OEF 0.44 ± 0.06 in 70 healthy volunteers across 11 centres
cards.type: Human PET normative database (15O-PET CBF/CMRO2 in healthy volunteers), Eur J Nucl Med Mol Imaging 2004
cards.people: Seventy healthy volunteers (43 men, 27 women; mean age 51.8 ± 15.1 years) studied with 15O-labelled gases/water PET at 11 Japanese centres using steady-state inhalation (7 centres), build-up inhalation (1) or bolus (3) methods, with C15O blood-volume measurement at all centres.
cards.result: Overall mean ± SD for cerebral cortical regions: CBF 44.4 ± 6.5 mL/100 mL/min; cerebral blood volume 3.8 ± 0.7 mL/100 mL; oxygen extraction fraction 0.44 ± 0.06; CMRO2 3.3 ± 0.5 mL/100 mL/min. Between-centre variation was statistically significant for blood volume, OEF and CMRO2 — method matters even within one tracer family — but overall interindividual variation was acceptably small, making a normal database practicable. The CMRO2 figure sits between the corrected Kety–Schmidt estimate (~3.0) and the classic value (3.5), closer to the former.
cards.watchOut: Cortical regional means, not whole-brain global values — the Kety–Schmidt cards measure the global average, so the small numerical differences between cards are partly a sampling difference, kept visible rather than averaged away.
cards.source: Ito H, Kanno I, Kato C, Sasaki T, et al.. Database of normal human cerebral blood flow, cerebral blood volume, cerebral oxygen extraction fraction and cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen measured by positron emission tomography with 15O-labelled carbon dioxide or water, carbon monoxide and oxygen: a multicentre study in Japan. European journal of nuclear medicine and molecular imaging. 2004. PMID: 14730405. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Takada 1992: CMRO2 declines with age in putamen and left association cortices — mean CMRO2 significantly lower over 51 than under 50 in 32 healthy volunteers, while CBF barely moved
cards.summary: Takada 1992: CMRO2 declines with age in putamen and left association cortices — mean CMRO2 significantly lower over 51 than under 50 in 32 healthy volunteers, while CBF barely moved
cards.type: Human PET ageing study (CMRO2 decline in healthy volunteers), Neurol Res 1992
cards.people: Thirty-two healthy volunteers aged 27–67 years studied with positron emission tomography for cerebral blood flow and cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen, compared as a younger group (under 50) and an elder group (over 51).
cards.result: CMRO2 showed a significant age-related decline in bilateral putamen and in left supratemporal, left infrafrontal and left parietal cortices; the age-related CBF decline reached significance only in left superior temporal cortex. Mean CMRO2 was significantly lower in the elder group than the younger, with no significant between-group difference in mean CBF. The record's interpretation: CBF correlates poorly with age partly because flow is easily swayed by physiological, psychological and environmental factors, while the metabolic rate itself falls — and falls more in left-hemisphere association cortex than right.
cards.watchOut: Cross-sectional age contrast in 32 volunteers — cohort differences are not within-person decline rates; the record prints regional significance, not a whole-brain percentage fall, and none is claimed.
cards.source: Takada H, Nagata K, Hirata Y, Satoh Y, et al.. Age-related decline of cerebral oxygen metabolism in normal population detected with positron emission tomography. Neurological research. 1992. PMID: 1355868. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Taudorf 2009: the Kety–Schmidt method re-tested in 29 healthy men (61 measurements) — its most robust form gave CBF 64 (95% CI 59–71) mL/100 g/min and CMRO2 1.8 (1.7–2.0) µmol/g/min
cards.summary: Taudorf 2009: the Kety–Schmidt method re-tested in 29 healthy men (61 measurements) — its most robust form gave CBF 64 (95% CI 59–71) mL/100 g/min and CMRO2 1.8 (1.7–2.0) µmol/g/min
cards.type: Human methods repeatability study (Kety–Schmidt with inhaled N2O), Acta Anaesthesiol Scand 2009
cards.people: Twenty-nine healthy male volunteers undergoing 61 CBF measurements breathing a normoxic mixture with 5% nitrous oxide to tension equilibrium, with paired arterial and jugular-bulb sampling in saturation or desaturation phases, continuous or discontinuous sampling, and N2O measured by photoacoustic spectrometry; plasma and red-cell nitrite were measured to check the tracer's own vascular effects.
cards.result: The most robust approach was discontinuous sampling in the desaturation phase: CBF 64 (95% CI 59–71) mL/100 g/min and CMRO2 1.8 (1.7–2.0) µmol/g/min (the µmol figure is ≈4.0 mL/100 g/min by standard molar-volume conversion — the record's own unit is µmol/g/min and is the one quoted). The tracer at this concentration did not influence plasma or red-cell nitrite (P > 0.05 versus baseline). The authors conclude the method is reliable and robust — while its best-form values sit above both the corrected classic estimate and the PET database, a spread this shelf reports rather than resolves.
cards.watchOut: Sampling-phase and sampling-mode choices move the result within the same method — the record's central finding. The mL conversion is arithmetic on the record's µmol value, flagged in the card.
cards.source: Taudorf S, Berg RM, Bailey DM, Møller K. Cerebral blood flow and oxygen metabolism measured with the Kety-Schmidt method using nitrous oxide. Acta anaesthesiologica Scandinavica. 2009. cards.headline: Caporale 2021: CMRO2 falls a relative 21% from wakefulness to sleep — waking 118 ± 12 µmol/min/100 g to a nadir of 98 ± 16 on OxFlow MRI in 12 healthy subjects, tracking EEG delta power
cards.summary: Caporale 2021: CMRO2 falls a relative 21% from wakefulness to sleep — waking 118 ± 12 µmol/min/100 g to a nadir of 98 ± 16 on OxFlow MRI in 12 healthy subjects, tracking EEG delta power
cards.type: Human MRI physiology study (CMRO2 across wake–sleep transition), J Cereb Blood Flow Metab 2021
cards.people: Twelve healthy subjects (31.3 ± 5.6 years, 8 men) scanned continuously for 45–60 minutes across wakefulness and sleep with 3-Tesla OxFlow MRI (venous oxygen saturation plus CBF every 3.4 s), with concurrent EEG in 8 subjects.
cards.result: Waking values were stable (coefficients of variation <7%): CMRO2 118 ± 12 µmol O2/min/100 g, venous saturation 67.0 ± 3.7%, CBF 50.6 ± 4.3 mL/min/100 g. In sleep, CMRO2 decreased by a relative 21% (range 14–32%; absolute nadir 98 ± 16 µmol/min/100 g — the relative fall is printed with its absolute endpoints) as EEG slow-wave (delta) power rose; after sleep onset CMRO2 correlated negatively with relative delta power (r = −0.6 to −0.8, P < 0.005) and positively with heart rate (r = 0.5 to 0.8, P < 0.0005). N = 12 printed on the face.
cards.watchOut: N = 12, printed on the face; a laboratory nap/transition protocol, not whole-night sleep staging. Physiology under a state change, graded as such.
