cards.headline: Oshima 2003: at 1.5 MAC, sevoflurane and isoflurane raised CBF (relative +17% and +25%) while lowering CMRO2 (relative −26% and −38%) by Kety–Schmidt in 20 patients without neurological disorders
cards.summary: Oshima 2003: at 1.5 MAC, sevoflurane and isoflurane raised CBF (relative +17% and +25%) while lowering CMRO2 (relative −26% and −38%) by Kety–Schmidt in 20 patients without neurological disorders
cards.type: Human anaesthesia physiology study (Kety–Schmidt CBF/CMRO2 under volatile agents), Eur J Anaesthesiol 2003
cards.people: Twenty ASA I patients undergoing knee-joint endoscopic surgery, anaesthetised with midazolam and fentanyl plus epidural anaesthesia to avoid noxious stimuli, with global CBF and cerebral arteriovenous oxygen difference measured by the Kety–Schmidt method with 15% nitrous oxide before and after 60 minutes of either sevoflurane or isoflurane at 1.5 minimum alveolar concentration.
cards.result: Both agents increased cerebral blood flow (sevoflurane relative +17%, isoflurane relative +25%; P < 0.05) and decreased CMRO2 (relative −26%, P < 0.01; relative −38%, P < 0.01) — flow and metabolism uncoupled in opposite directions, with no significant difference between the two agents on either measure. These are relative (percentage) changes exactly as the record prints them; the record does not print the absolute before/after pair in its abstract, and this card does not invent one. Physiology measured under anaesthesia, graded as such.
cards.watchOut: Background midazolam/fentanyl/epidural in both arms — the contrast is the volatile agent on that background, in surgical patients without neurological disorders, not in resting volunteers.
cards.source: Oshima T, Karasawa F, Okazaki Y, Wada H, et al.. Effects of sevoflurane on cerebral blood flow and cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen in human beings: a comparison with isoflurane. cards.headline: Synthesis: resting CMRO2 is ~3.0–3.3 mL/100 g/min by corrected Kety–Schmidt and PET alike; it falls in sleep (~21% relative) and under volatile anaesthesia (~26–38% relative), and declines regionally with age
cards.summary: Synthesis: resting CMRO2 is ~3.0–3.3 mL/100 g/min by corrected Kety–Schmidt and PET alike; it falls in sleep (~21% relative) and under volatile anaesthesia (~26–38% relative), and declines regionally with age
cards.people: Synthesis of the six carded human studies above (Madsen 1993; Ito 2004; Takada 1992; Taudorf 2009; Caporale 2021; Oshima 2003), framed by the Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep account of cerebral metabolism as textbook framing, not as an evidence card.
cards.result: The resting number, triangulated: the classic Kety–Schmidt 3.5 mL/100 g/min was an equilibration artefact — corrected, the same method gives ~3.0; the 11-centre PET database gives 3.3 ± 0.5 (cortical); a modern best-form Kety–Schmidt runs higher (1.8 µmol/g/min), and that spread is reported, not hidden. The state-dependence is the physiology: sleep lowers CMRO2 by about a fifth in step with delta power; volatile anaesthetics lower it by a quarter to a third while raising flow — metabolism and flow are separately controlled, which is why this shelf (the rate) is distinct from the library's autoregulation and CO2-reactivity shelves (the regulation), cross-pointed here and not duplicated. Ageing lowers the rate regionally, association cortex first, with flow relatively spared. REFUSALS, stated plainly: Kety & Schmidt's two 1948 Journal of Clinical Investigation papers — the nitrous-oxide method paper and the brain blood-flow/oxygen-consumption paper — were NOT carded: both PubMed records carry no abstract, so the classic values on this shelf (54 and 3.5) appear only as quoted and corrected by the fetched 1993 appraisal. No animal cerebral-metabolism data are carded.
cards.watchOut: Global (Kety–Schmidt), cortical-regional (PET) and MRI global estimates are related but not identical quantities; each card names its sampling. Relative state changes are always printed with their absolute endpoints where the record gives them.
cards.source: Synthesis of the carded records above (PMIDs 8314918, 14730405, 1355868, 19076112, 32538283, 12884987), with textbook framing as cited. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

shelves.title: Arimoclomol in Niemann-Pick disease type C: slowed progression in one 50-patient randomised trial, strongest with miglustat
shelves.question: In patients with Niemann-Pick disease type C, does arimoclomol (with or without miglustat), versus placebo, slow progression on the NPC clinical severity scale?
shelves.mesh: Niemann-Pick Disease, Type C · Disease Progression · Severity of Illness Index · Hydroxylamines · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: One small randomised trial is the whole controlled base: NPC-002 randomised 50 patients aged 2–18 years (34 arimoclomol, 16 placebo) for 12 months and found slower progression on the 5-domain NPC Clinical Severity Scale (mean change 0.76 vs 2.15; treatment difference −1.40, 95% CI −2.76 to −0.03; P=.046) — a borderline-significant result in 50 patients, with the effect larger in the prespecified miglustat stratum (difference −2.06; P=.006), where arimoclomol essentially stabilised scores. Most patients received miglustat as routine care, so this is substantially an add-on question — and the US approval (September 2024) is explicitly in combination with miglustat. The rescored 4-domain analysis is a post-hoc re-scoring of the same trial (difference −1.70; P=.0155), supportive but not independent. The 48-month open-label extension (41 entered, 29 completed) has no control group: switchers from placebo slowed after starting arimoclomol, consistent with — not proof of — a sustained effect. Tolerability was good (serious adverse events 14.7% on arimoclomol vs 31.3% on placebo in the trial; two treatment-related serious events, urticaria and angioedema). Product naming (clarification exception, as directed for this shelf): arimoclomol (Miplyffa, Zevra Therapeutics) — the tested product as published. The stamp carries the small base: N = 50 randomised patients underpin every efficacy claim.

cards.headline: NPC-002 randomised trial: arimoclomol slowed 12-month progression by 1.40 points on the 5-domain severity scale vs placebo in 50 children (P=.046)
cards.summary: NPC-002 randomised trial: arimoclomol slowed 12-month progression by 1.40 points on the 5-domain severity scale vs placebo in 50 children (P=.046)
cards.type: Phase 2/3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (NPC-002), J Inherit Metab Dis 2021
cards.people: 50 patients aged 2–18 years with Niemann-Pick disease type C randomised 2:1 to oral arimoclomol three times daily (n=34) or placebo (n=16) for 12 months, stratified by miglustat use, with routine clinical care maintained; 42 completed the double-blind phase. Phase 2/3, double-blind, placebo-controlled.
cards.result: Mean progression on the 5-domain NPC Clinical Severity Scale at month 12 was 0.76 points with arimoclomol vs 2.15 with placebo — a treatment difference of −1.40 (95% CI −2.76 to −0.03; P=.046), corresponding to a 65% relative reduction in annual disease progression (a relative measure, printed as such). In the prespecified miglustat subgroup, arimoclomol stabilised disease severity, with a treatment difference of −2.06 (P=.006). Adverse events occurred in 88.2% on arimoclomol vs 75.0% on placebo; serious adverse events were fewer on arimoclomol (14.7% vs 31.3%), with two treatment-related serious events (urticaria and angioedema).
cards.watchOut: N=50 with a P value of .046 and a confidence interval ending at −0.03: the result is statistically fragile — a small number of patients changing course would erase significance — and the trial population was children and adolescents aged 2–18, not adults.
cards.source: Mengel E, Patterson MC, Da Riol RM, et al. Efficacy and safety of arimoclomol in Niemann-Pick disease type C: Results from a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled, multinational phase 2/3 trial of a novel treatment. Journal of Inherited Metabolic Disease. 2021. PMID: 34418116. Registry ID: NCT02612129. cards.headline: Rescored 4-domain analysis (post-hoc, same trial): treatment difference −1.70 points favouring arimoclomol (P=.0155), larger with miglustat (−2.21)
cards.summary: Rescored 4-domain analysis (post-hoc, same trial): treatment difference −1.70 points favouring arimoclomol (P=.0155), larger with miglustat (−2.21)
cards.type: Post-hoc re-analysis of a randomised trial (NPC-002), Mol Genet Metab Rep 2025
cards.people: The same 50 NPC-002 patients (arimoclomol n=34, placebo n=16), re-analysed post-hoc on a rescored 4-domain NPC Clinical Severity Scale (R4DNPCCSS) — cognition domain removed and the swallow domain rescored for linearity, with the rescoring validated against global-impression, NPC database, ataxia, peg-test and swallowing measures; the miglustat subgroup comprised 22 arimoclomol and 12 placebo patients.
cards.result: Mean (SE) change on the rescored scale was 0.35 (0.40) with arimoclomol vs 2.05 (0.54) with placebo — a treatment effect of −1.70 (P=.0155). In the miglustat subgroup, change was −0.23 (1.02) vs 1.92 (3.37), a treatment effect of −2.21 (P=.0077). Construct and convergent validity analyses supported the rescored scale, and the authors conclude it shows consistent outcomes with the prespecified 5-domain endpoint.
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc by design: the endpoint was rescored after the trial read out, in the same 50 patients — it strengthens confidence in the direction of the primary result but is not independent confirmation, and post-hoc endpoints carry an inherent optimism bias.
cards.source: Mengel E, Patterson MC, Da Riol RM, et al. Efficacy results from a 12-month double-blind randomized trial of arimoclomol for treatment of Niemann-Pick disease type C (NPC): Presenting a rescored 4-domain NPC Clinical Severity Scale. cards.headline: 48-month open-label extension: patients switching from placebo slowed after starting arimoclomol (annual 5-domain change 2.0 → 0.1 in year one) — uncontrolled
cards.summary: 48-month open-label extension: patients switching from placebo slowed after starting arimoclomol (annual 5-domain change 2.0 → 0.1 in year one) — uncontrolled
cards.type: Open-label extension (NPC-002, uncontrolled), Mol Genet Metab 2025
cards.people: 41 of the 50 NPC-002 patients entered the open-label extension, in which all received arimoclomol plus routine clinical care; 29 completed 48 months. The miglustat-treated subset numbered 33. No control group.
cards.result: Over 48 months, mean (SD) scores rose by 3.2 (4.8) points on the 5-domain scale and 2.7 (4.2) on the rescored 4-domain scale — progression continued, more slowly than the placebo year. Among patients switching from placebo to arimoclomol, mean annual 5-domain change fell from 2.0 (on placebo) to 0.1 in the first arimoclomol year, and rescored-scale change from 1.9 to 0.2; annual scores remained numerically smaller than during the double-blind phase throughout. The 17-domain scale and NPC clinical database scores supported the pattern. Arimoclomol was well tolerated over 48 months with no new safety concerns.
cards.watchOut: Uncontrolled extension with attrition (41 of 50 entered; 29 of 50 completed): slower progression after switching is what a real effect would look like, but it is also what survivor selection and natural-history variability look like — only the 12-month randomised phase carries comparative weight.
cards.source: Mengel E, Da Riol RM, Del Toro M, et al. Long-term efficacy and safety of arimoclomol in Niemann-Pick disease type C: Final results of the phase 2/3 NPC-002 48-month open-label extension trial. Molecular Genetics and Metabolism. 2025. PMID: 40663813. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: one 50-patient randomised trial shows slowed NPC progression, strongest on background miglustat — POSSIBLE, on a small base
cards.summary: Synthesis: one 50-patient randomised trial shows slowed NPC progression, strongest on background miglustat — POSSIBLE, on a small base
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded reports above — all from the single NPC-002 programme (randomised phase n=50; post-hoc rescoring of the same patients; 48-month open-label extension, 41 entrants).
cards.result: Arimoclomol slowed progression of Niemann-Pick disease type C over 12 months in the only randomised test (5-domain scale difference −1.40, P=.046; rescored 4-domain difference −1.70), with the clearest effect — stabilisation — in patients also receiving miglustat (difference −2.06 to −2.21), which matches its US approval in combination with miglustat. The open-label extension is consistent with a sustained effect over 48 months but cannot prove one. Tolerability was good. Because every efficacy claim traces to 50 randomised children and adolescents, and the primary P value is borderline, the stamp is POSSIBLE and carries the N on its face. A note on completeness: the programme's infant substudy (ages 6–<24 months) enrolled only 5 patients — below this library's 10-human evidence floor — and is therefore not carded; no efficacy conclusion for infants under 2 years can be drawn from this shelf.
cards.watchOut: One trial, 50 patients, three reports: the re-analysis and the extension describe the same children as the randomised phase — the evidence base is N=50 however it is counted.

shelves.title: Levacetylleucine in Niemann-Pick disease type C: a 1.28-point SARA advantage over placebo in a 60-patient crossover trial
shelves.question: In patients with Niemann-Pick disease type C, does levacetylleucine (N-acetyl-L-leucine), versus placebo in a crossover design, improve ataxia and neurological function on the SARA and related scales?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Leucine/analogs & derivatives,therapeutic use · Niemann-Pick Disease, Type C/drug therapy · Cross-Over Studies · Double-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: one small randomised programme from a single sponsor. The phase 3 crossover trial (60 patients) found a least-squares mean SARA difference of -1.28 points favouring levacetylleucine over 12 weeks (95% CI -1.91 to -0.65; P<0.001), and the earlier open-label rater-blinded phase 2 (33 patients) met its blinded-rater primary endpoint, with the effect lost after washout — the pattern of a symptomatic treatment. The 2025 open-label extension compares 53 patients against a historical natural-history trajectory and its authors frame the result as disease-modifying and neuroprotective; that framing is the investigators' interpretation of a Class IV, historically controlled comparison, not a randomised finding, and is labelled as such here. A separate phase 3 trial in ataxia-telangiectasia asks a different disease question and is cross-pointed in prose only, not carded here. Product naming (clarification exception): levacetylleucine (Aqneursa, IntraBio), the funder of the phase 3 programme.

cards.headline: Phase 3 crossover (2024): SARA improved by -1.97 points on levacetylleucine versus -0.60 on placebo over 12 weeks (difference -1.28; P<0.001)
cards.summary: Phase 3 crossover (2024): SARA improved by -1.97 points on levacetylleucine versus -0.60 on placebo over 12 weeks (difference -1.28; P<0.001)
cards.people: 60 patients aged 5 to 67 years with genetically confirmed Niemann-Pick disease type C, randomised 1:1 to levacetylleucine then placebo or placebo then levacetylleucine, each period 12 weeks; dosing 2-4 g/day by weight at ages 4-12 and 4 g/day at 13 years and older.
cards.result: Mean change in SARA total score was -1.97 (±2.43) points after 12 weeks on levacetylleucine versus -0.60 (±2.39) on placebo (least-squares mean difference -1.28 points; 95% CI -1.91 to -0.65; P<0.001). Secondary endpoints (Clinical Global Impression of Improvement, Spinocerebellar Ataxia Functional Index, Modified Disability Rating Scale) were generally supportive but not adjusted for multiple comparisons. Adverse-event incidence was similar on drug and placebo, with no treatment-related serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: A 12-week symptomatic endpoint in 60 patients with a rare disease: the trial cannot speak to long-term progression, and the crossover design assumes no carry-over between periods.
cards.source: Bremova-Ertl T et al. Trial of N-Acetyl-l-Leucine in Niemann-Pick Disease Type C. The New England journal of medicine. 2024. PMID: 38294974. Registry ID: NCT05163288 (ClinicalTrials.gov); EudraCT 2021-005356-10. cards.headline: Phase 2 (2022): blinded raters scored improvement on treatment, and the effect was lost after the 6-week washout
cards.summary: Phase 2 (2022): blinded raters scored improvement on treatment, and the effect was lost after the 6-week washout
cards.type: Open-label, rater-blinded phase 2 study with washout period
cards.people: 33 subjects aged 7 to 64 years with confirmed Niemann-Pick disease type C (32 in the primary modified intention-to-treat analysis), treated openly for 6 weeks with N-acetyl-L-leucine 4 g/day (weight-tiered at ages 6-12), then observed through a 6-week washout.
cards.result: The primary Clinical Impression of Change in Severity endpoint, scored by blinded centralised raters comparing randomised video pairs, was met (mean difference 0.86, SD 2.52, 90% CI 0.25 to 1.75; p=0.029), and secondary cerebellar, global-impression and quality-of-life endpoints moved the same way. The clinical effect was lost after the 6-week washout. No treatment-related serious adverse events occurred.
cards.watchOut: Open-label treatment with blinded rating only: patients and clinicians knew treatment status, and a 33-patient single-arm study cannot separate drug effect from expectation and natural fluctuation — its washout reversal is the most informative feature.
cards.source: Bremova-Ertl T et al. Efficacy and safety of N-acetyl-L-leucine in Niemann-Pick disease type C. Journal of neurology. 2022. PMID: 34387740. cards.headline: Open-label extension (2025): progression on the 5-domain NPC-CSS was slower than a historical natural-history cohort — the authors' 'disease-modifying' claim, labelled as their interpretation
cards.summary: Open-label extension (2025): progression on the 5-domain NPC-CSS was slower than a historical natural-history cohort — the authors' 'disease-modifying' claim, labelled as their interpretation
cards.type: Open-label extension with historical-cohort comparison (Class IV evidence)
cards.people: 53 patients aged 5 to 67 years (45.3% female) who had completed the placebo-controlled crossover trial and continued on open-label levacetylleucine, compared with the expected annual trajectory from natural-history studies.
cards.result: At 12 months the mean change on the modified 5-domain NPC Clinical Severity Scale was -0.27 (±2.42) on levacetylleucine versus +1.5 (±3.16) in the historical cohort (95% CI -3.05 to -0.48; p=0.009), reported by the authors as a 118% relative reduction in annual disease progression; at 18 months the change was +0.05 (±2.95) versus +2.25 (±4.74) (p=0.023). SARA improvements from the parent trial were sustained. No treatment-related adverse events or serious reactions occurred.
cards.watchOut: Historical controls, no concurrent comparator, and a relative measure (118%) built on small absolute score differences: this is hypothesis-supporting Class IV evidence, and the 'disease-modifying, neuroprotective' wording is the investigators' interpretation, not a randomised result.
cards.source: Patterson MC et al. Disease-Modifying, Neuroprotective Effect of N-Acetyl-l-Leucine in Adult and Pediatric Patients With Niemann-Pick Disease Type C. Neurology. 2025. PMID: 40513057. Registry ID: NCT05163288 (ClinicalTrials.gov). cards.headline: Synthesis: a real short-term symptomatic benefit in one small programme; disease modification unproven — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: a real short-term symptomatic benefit in one small programme; disease modification unproven — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: the phase 3 crossover trial (60 patients), the phase 2 rater-blinded study (33 patients) and its open-label extension (53 patients, overlapping cohort) — one programme, substantially the same patients.
cards.result: The randomised evidence supports a modest symptomatic gain over 12 weeks (SARA difference -1.28 points) with a benign short-term safety profile, and the phase 2 washout reversal fits a symptomatic rather than a curative action. The long-term claim rests on a historical comparison and is presented here as the investigators' interpretation. One programme, small numbers and sponsor funding (IntraBio) cap the stamp at POSSIBLE.
cards.watchOut: Do not merge the separate ataxia-telangiectasia phase 3 programme into this question — different disease, cross-point only. Families should not be told the drug is proven to slow the disease itself.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bremova-Ertl T et al. N Engl J Med. 2024. PMID: 38294974; Bremova-Ertl T et al. J Neurol. 2022. PMID: 34387740; Patterson MC et al. Neurology. 2025. PMID: 40513057. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Selumetinib in NF1 plexiform neurofibromas (SPRINT): confirmed partial responses in 70% of 50 children, single-arm against natural history
shelves.question: In children with neurofibromatosis type 1 and symptomatic, inoperable plexiform neurofibromas, does selumetinib, versus natural history with no concurrent control, shrink tumour volume and improve pain and function?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Benzimidazoles/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Child · Child, Preschool · Female · Humans · Male · Mitogen-Activated Protein Kinase Kinases/antagonists & inhibitors · Neurofibroma, Plexiform/complications,drug therapy,pathology · Neurofibromatosis 1/complications,drug therapy,pathology · Pain/etiology · Patient Reported Outcome Measures · Progression-Free Survival · Protein Kinase Inhibitors/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Tumor Burden/drug effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: single-arm evidence throughout, framed as such. In the SPRINT phase 2 study, 35 of 50 children (70%) had a confirmed partial response (≥20% volumetric shrinkage), most durable ≥1 year, with a mean 2-point fall in child-reported tumour pain at 1 year; the preceding phase 1 study saw confirmed partial responses in 17 of 24 children (71%). There is no randomised or concurrent control — the comparison is with the known natural history of plexiform neurofibromas, which rarely shrink spontaneously, which is why volumetric response carries weight despite the design; the stamp still caps at POSSIBLE for a single programme without a control arm. Harms are dominated by gastrointestinal effects, acneiform rash, paronychia and asymptomatic creatine kinase rises; 5 of 50 children stopped for possibly related toxicity, and ocular and cardiac monitoring is part of the treatment burden. A different MEK inhibitor programme in a broader (adult-inclusive) population asks a separate question and is cross-pointed in prose only. Product naming (clarification exception): selumetinib (Koselugo, AstraZeneca) as published.

cards.headline: SPRINT phase 2 (2020): 35 of 50 children (70%) had a confirmed partial response, 28 of them durable for at least a year
cards.summary: SPRINT phase 2 (2020): 35 of 50 children (70%) had a confirmed partial response, 28 of them durable for at least a year
cards.people: 50 children (median age 10.2 years, range 3.5-17.4) with neurofibromatosis type 1 and symptomatic inoperable plexiform neurofibromas, given oral selumetinib 25 mg/m² twice daily in continuous 28-day cycles; commonest symptoms were disfigurement (44), motor dysfunction (33) and pain (26).
cards.result: Confirmed partial response (≥20% tumour-volume decrease on volumetric MRI) occurred in 35 patients (70%), and 28 of these responses were durable (lasting ≥1 year). After 1 year, mean child-reported tumour pain intensity fell by 2 points, a clinically meaningful improvement, with meaningful gains also in pain interference (38% child-reported, 50% parent-reported), health-related quality of life, strength (56%) and range of motion (38%). Six patients had disease progression and 5 discontinued for toxic effects possibly related to selumetinib; the most frequent toxic effects were nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea, asymptomatic creatine phosphokinase increase, acneiform rash and paronychia.
cards.watchOut: No concurrent control group: response is judged against natural history, and the pain and function outcomes are unblinded patient/parent reports, which expectation can move.
cards.source: Gross AM et al. Selumetinib in Children with Inoperable Plexiform Neurofibromas. The New England journal of medicine. 2020. PMID: 32187457. Registry ID: NCT01362803 (ClinicalTrials.gov). cards.headline: Phase 1 (2016): partial responses in 17 of 24 children (71%) at a maximum tolerated dose of 25 mg/m² twice daily
cards.summary: Phase 1 (2016): partial responses in 17 of 24 children (71%) at a maximum tolerated dose of 25 mg/m² twice daily
cards.people: 24 children (median age 10.9 years, range 3.0-18.5) with neurofibromatosis type 1 and inoperable plexiform neurofibromas (median tumour volume 1205 mL), treated with selumetinib 20-30 mg/m² twice daily on a continuous schedule; median 30 cycles received (range 6-56).
cards.result: The maximum tolerated dose was 25 mg/m² twice daily (about 60% of the recommended adult dose). Confirmed partial responses occurred in 17 of 24 children (71%), and no disease progression (≥20% volume increase) had been observed at reporting. Common toxic effects were acneiform rash, gastrointestinal effects and asymptomatic creatine kinase elevation; anecdotal decreases in tumour-related pain, disfigurement and functional impairment were noted.
cards.watchOut: A dose-finding study of 24 children: its response rate is encouraging but imprecise, and it was designed for tolerability and pharmacokinetics, not efficacy.
cards.source: Dombi E et al. Activity of Selumetinib in Neurofibromatosis Type 1-Related Plexiform Neurofibromas. The New England journal of medicine. 2016. PMID: 28029918. cards.headline: Long-term follow-up (2026): over a median 5.1 years in 98 SPRINT participants, over 90% of blood counts stayed in the normal range
cards.summary: Long-term follow-up (2026): over a median 5.1 years in 98 SPRINT participants, over 90% of blood counts stayed in the normal range
cards.type: Long-term safety follow-up of the SPRINT phase 1/2 programme
cards.people: 98 paediatric participants from the SPRINT phase 1/2 programme with a median follow-up of 5.1 years (range 0.2-11 years).
cards.result: Across timepoints, over 90% of values for white cell count, platelet count, absolute neutrophil count and absolute lymphocyte count remained within normal limits. There was a statistically significant but, in the authors' judgement, unlikely clinically significant decrease in absolute lymphocyte count and increase in mean corpuscular volume. The authors conclude selumetinib was not associated with apparent clinically significant haematologic changes.
cards.watchOut: A haematology-only safety slice of the same single programme — it adds long-term tolerability reassurance, not independent efficacy evidence, and the cohort overlaps the two efficacy cards above.
cards.source: Siegel AH et al. Long-Term Hematologic Effects of Selumetinib Treatment in Children With Neurofibromatosis Type 1-Associated Plexiform Neurofibromas. Pediatric blood & cancer. 2026. cards.headline: Synthesis: consistent ~70% volumetric responses in a single-arm programme — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: consistent ~70% volumetric responses in a single-arm programme — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: SPRINT phase 2 (50 children), the phase 1 study (24 children) and the pooled long-term haematology follow-up (98 participants, overlapping cohorts) — one programme, one registry number.
cards.result: Two dose cohorts independently show confirmed partial responses in about 70% of children, with durability beyond a year in most responders and clinically meaningful pain improvement at 1 year — a pattern spontaneous shrinkage does not explain. But every number comes from uncontrolled treatment of a selected trial population, so the honest stamp is POSSIBLE, with ocular and cardiac monitoring and mostly low-grade but chronic gastrointestinal and skin toxicity as the standing cost.
cards.watchOut: Do not read the 70% response rate as a randomised effect size, and do not merge the separate adult-inclusive MEK-inhibitor programme (a different molecule and population) into this shelf — it is cross-pointed in prose only.

shelves.title: Vestibulo-ocular reflex testing in health: vHIT gain ~1.02-1.06, catch-up saccades in up to half of healthy ears, little change with age until after 70 — and every number belongs to its device
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what are normal vestibulo-ocular reflex measures — video head impulse test gain by canal and device, refixation-saccade prevalence, and caloric response magnitudes — and how do they change with age?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Age Factors · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Child · Eye Movements/physiology · Female · Head Impulse Test · Head Movements/physiology · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Reference Values · Reflex, Vestibulo-Ocular/physiology · Saccades/physiology · Semicircular Canals/physiology · Vestibule, Labyrinth/physiology · Young Adult · Video Recording · Aging/physiology · Algorithms · Case-Control Studies · Head Impulse Test/instrumentation · Reflex, Vestibulo-Ocular · Vestibular Diseases/physiopathology · Head Impulse Test/methods · Healthy Volunteers · Acceleration · Caloric Tests · Electromyography · Electronystagmography · Evoked Potentials/physiology · Neck Muscles/innervation · Nerve Degeneration/physiopathology · Pitch Discrimination/physiology · Rotation · Sound Spectrography · Vestibular Function Tests/methods · Vestibular Nerve/physiopathology
shelves.balance: Textbook framing (Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology; Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology): the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) holds gaze steady by rotating the eyes at the same speed as the head, so its gain (eye velocity / head velocity) should be 1.0 — the companion physiology shelf on VOR gain and adaptation (pack #6449) covers the reflex in darkness and its recalibration by magnifying or reversing spectacles. This shelf covers the CLINICAL normative measurements: the video head impulse test (vHIT), which impulses the head in each semicircular canal's plane, and the caloric test. The fetched healthy-subject data converge on gain at or just above 1.0 for the lateral canal — 1.06 (SD 0.07) in 212 healthy subjects (Matiño-Soler 2015) and 1.02 (SD 0.07) in 50 subjects tested decade by decade (Yang 2016) — with gain falling as head-impulse velocity rises, and refixation (catch-up) saccades appearing in a substantial minority of entirely healthy people: 52 of 212 subjects in one series, and in 49% of ears (22.6% of trials) in the other, so a saccade alone is not disease. Age effects are small and late: gain held steady until about age 70 for fast impulses and 90 for slow ones (Matiño-Soler), was largely unaffected by age into the 80s across all six canals (McGarvie 2015), and showed no effect up to age 78 on any of three devices (Janky 2017). The caloric/rotational battery (Maes 2010, N = 80) found only subtle age change — caloric slow-component velocity actually increased with age, rotational gains were essentially flat — with the large age trends confined to vestibular-evoked myogenic potentials. The one systematic distortion is the instrument: gains differ significantly between commercial devices and between gain-calculation methods (Janky 2017; Lee 2018), so each device needs its own normal values — devices are named on the cards as published. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Lateral-canal vHIT in 212 healthy people: mean gain 1.06 (SD 0.07), no sex difference — and refixation saccades in 52 healthy subjects (Matiño-Soler 2015)
cards.summary: Lateral-canal vHIT in 212 healthy people: mean gain 1.06 (SD 0.07), no sex difference — and refixation saccades in 52 healthy subjects (Matiño-Soler 2015)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (normative vHIT, lateral canal)
cards.people: 212 healthy subjects with no history of vestibular or neurologic impairment; video head impulse testing in the lateral (yaw) semicircular canal plane; 9,654 impulses analysed (4,947 rightward, 4,707 leftward).
cards.result: Mean VOR gain was 1.06 (SD 0.07), with no differences between sexes. Gain decreased as head impulse velocity increased. Evaluated by age and velocity, gain was steady until age 70 years for higher-velocity impulses and until age 90 years for lower-velocity impulses; thereafter it dropped progressively. Refixation saccades were detected in 52 subjects, occurring after impulses to both sides in 22 of them; the number of subjects with saccades was significantly higher after age 71 years, and saccade velocity correlated with head impulse velocity, not age.
cards.watchOut: Lateral canal only, one device/protocol: vertical-canal gains and other devices' values differ (see the device-comparison cards) — and a quarter of healthy subjects showing refixation saccades sets the false-positive floor for reading saccades as pathology.
cards.source: Matiño-Soler E et al. Otology & neurotology : official publication of the American Otological Society, American Neurotology Society [and] European Academy of Otology and Neurotology. 2015. PMID: 25473958. cards.headline: Decade-by-decade vHIT (N = 50): gain 1.02 (SD 0.07) and asymmetry 2.4% at every age from the 20s to the 60s — catch-up saccades in 49% of healthy ears (Yang 2016)
cards.summary: Decade-by-decade vHIT (N = 50): gain 1.02 (SD 0.07) and asymmetry 2.4% at every age from the 20s to the 60s — catch-up saccades in 49% of healthy ears (Yang 2016)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (normative vHIT gains and catch-up saccades by age)
cards.people: 50 healthy subjects with no vestibular impairment history, 10 in each decade from their 20s to their 60s; video head impulse testing in the lateral semicircular canal plane, with covert and overt catch-up saccades characterised.
cards.result: Mean vHIT gain was 1.02 (SD 0.07) and mean gain asymmetry 2.39% (SD 1.96%), with no significant differences among age groups. Catch-up saccades were observed in 22.6% of trials and in 49% of ears; their incidence was not associated with age. Mean saccade velocity was 55.5 degrees/s (SD 16.9) with a mean interaural difference of 11.8 degrees/s (SD 10.7). The authors suggest abnormal criteria of 0.8 for gain, 8% for gain asymmetry, 100 degrees/s for saccade amplitude and 40 degrees/s for interaural saccade difference can be used regardless of age.
cards.watchOut: Ages stop at the 60s and the sample is 10 per decade: the 'regardless of age' criteria are the authors' proposal from this cohort, to be read alongside the larger series showing gain decline after 70-90 years.
cards.source: Yang CJ et al. Clinical otolaryngology : official journal of ENT-UK ; official journal of Netherlands Society for Oto-Rhino-Laryngology & Cervico-Facial Surgery. 2016. PMID: 26453356. cards.headline: All six canals, every decade from 10-19 to 80-89: VOR gain falls at high head velocities but is largely unaffected by age into the ninth decade (McGarvie 2015)
cards.summary: All six canals, every decade from 10-19 to 80-89: VOR gain falls at high head velocities but is largely unaffected by age into the ninth decade (McGarvie 2015)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (age-dependent normative vHIT values, all canals)
cards.people: At least 10 healthy subjects in each decade age band (10-19 through 80-89 years); vestibulo-ocular reflex gain measured for all six semicircular canals across a range of head velocities with the ICS impulse prototype system, every impulse delivered by the same operator, right eye measured.
cards.result: VOR gain decreased at high head velocities, but was largely unaffected by age into the 80- to 89-year age group. Small but systematic differences between the two directions of head rotation appeared largely attributable to measuring only the right eye. The authors conclude these normative values allow a patient's result to be compared with healthy people in their own age range, for example to detect bilateral vestibular loss.
cards.watchOut: The fetched record carries no MeSH terms and no numeric gain table in its abstract — the canal-by-canal numbers live in the full text; this card claims only what the record states (velocity effect, age stability, directional asymmetry), with numeric lateral-canal values supplied by the two series above.

cards.headline: Same subjects, three commercial devices: vHIT gain differs significantly by device and gain algorithm — yet normal/abnormal classification mostly agrees, and age has no effect to 78 years (Janky 2017)
cards.summary: Same subjects, three commercial devices: vHIT gain differs significantly by device and gain algorithm — yet normal/abnormal classification mostly agrees, and age has no effect to 78 years (Janky 2017)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (device/algorithm comparison in healthy controls and patients)
cards.people: 61 normal control adults (ages 20-78) and 11 adults with unilateral or bilateral vestibular loss (32-79), each tested the same day on three devices in randomised order: Impulse (Otometrics; monocular right-eye recording; area-under-the-curve gain), EyeSeeCam (Interacoustics; monocular left-eye; instantaneous gain) and VisualEyes (MicroMedical; binocular; position gain). Devices named as published.
cards.result: There was a significant mean difference in vHIT gain among devices/algorithms in both the normal and vestibular-loss groups, and gain was significantly larger in the ipsilateral direction of the eye used to measure it. Despite those differences, classification of gain as normal versus abnormal was consistent across devices/algorithms, with the exception of instantaneous gain at 40 ms. There was no effect of age on vHIT gain up to 78 years on any device/algorithm. The authors conclude care is needed when comparing absolute gain values between devices/algorithms.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports significance, not the per-device mean gains — the shelf therefore claims device-dependence qualitatively from this record and takes its absolute gain values from the single-device normative series; do not carry a cut-off from one device to another.
cards.source: Janky KL et al. Journal of the American Academy of Audiology. 2017. PMID: 28972467. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Two devices worn simultaneously, five ways to compute gain (N = 25): the device and the maths both move the number — area-under-the-curve gain is lowest and least variable (Lee 2018)
cards.summary: Two devices worn simultaneously, five ways to compute gain (N = 25): the device and the maths both move the number — area-under-the-curve gain is lowest and least variable (Lee 2018)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (device and gain-method comparison in healthy subjects)
cards.people: 25 healthy subjects undergoing video head impulse testing with two commercially available devices simultaneously; gains compared between instruments and across five methods of computing position and velocity gains over different head-movement intervals.
cards.result: The two devices produced different vHIT gain results with the same method of analysis, and gains differed significantly across the five analytical methods. The method comparing the areas under the velocity curves (AUC) of head and eye movements gave lower gains than a peak-velocity comparison, and produced the smallest standard deviation of the five procedures. The authors conclude each device should have its own normal values.
cards.watchOut: Small healthy sample (N = 25) and a methods study: it establishes that 'vHIT gain' is not a single number across systems — any normative value must travel with its device and algorithm attached.

cards.headline: The older test battery across 18-80 years (N = 80): caloric slow-phase velocity rises slightly with age, rotational gains are essentially flat, and only VEMP shows large age trends (Maes 2010)
cards.summary: The older test battery across 18-80 years (N = 80): caloric slow-phase velocity rises slightly with age, rotational gains are essentially flat, and only VEMP shows large age trends (Maes 2010)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (age effects across caloric, rotational and VEMP tests)
cards.people: 80 healthy subjects (38 men, 42 women) aged 18-80 years given an extensive vestibular battery: sinusoidal harmonic acceleration, pseudorandom rotation and velocity step tests, caloric testing, and vestibular-evoked myogenic potentials (VEMP).
cards.result: No significant age trends were found for the sinusoidal harmonic acceleration or velocity step response parameters, in contrast to subtle decreasing gain values with advancing age on the pseudorandom rotation test. Caloric slow-component velocity values increased with age, while the caloric frequency parameter showed no relevant age change. The largest age trends were in VEMP — decreasing amplitudes, increasing thresholds and decreasing N1 latencies. All asymmetry parameters remained stable across age categories.
cards.watchOut: The abstract gives directions of age effects, not caloric magnitudes in degrees per second — this card therefore anchors the age question for calorics (no clinically large decline; if anything a rise in slow-phase velocity) rather than a numeric caloric norm, which the fetched records do not state.

cards.headline: Synthesis: healthy vHIT gain is ~1.0-1.06 for the lateral canal, refixation saccades occur in up to half of healthy ears, age costs little until after 70 — and the number belongs to its device
cards.summary: Synthesis: healthy vHIT gain is ~1.0-1.06 for the lateral canal, refixation saccades occur in up to half of healthy ears, age costs little until after 70 — and the number belongs to its device
cards.people: Synthesis of the six primary human studies above.
cards.result: The clinical normative picture, framed by the textbooks (Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep) and distinct from the adaptation physiology on pack #6449: lateral-canal vHIT gain averages 1.06 (SD 0.07; N = 212) and 1.02 (SD 0.07; N = 50) in the two normative series, falls as impulse velocity rises, and is largely age-stable — steady to ~70 years for fast impulses and ~90 for slow (Matiño-Soler 2015), and unaffected into the 80s across all six canals (McGarvie 2015). Refixation/catch-up saccades are normal findings at low frequency: 52 of 212 healthy subjects, 22.6% of trials and 49% of ears — presence alone does not diagnose loss; size and consistency do (proposed abnormal saccade velocity 100 degrees/s; Yang 2016). Caloric and rotational testing show the same late, small age signature (Maes 2010). Over everything sits the device caveat, proven twice (Janky 2017; Lee 2018): gain is device- and algorithm-specific, so normal values and cut-offs (gain ~0.8, asymmetry ~8%) must be applied within the system that generated them. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Normative series are lateral-canal heavy and device-bound; vertical-canal norms rest chiefly on the McGarvie dataset, whose numeric tables are in its full text, not its abstract.

shelves.title: Normal nerve conduction: velocity and amplitude fall with age (motor velocity correlations r −0.37 to −0.46), sensory amplitudes fall earliest, and height — not temperature within the studied range — drives late-response latencies
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what are normal nerve conduction velocities and amplitudes (median, ulnar, sural) by age, height and skin temperature — how much does conduction slow per decade and per degree of cooling?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Age Factors · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Body Height · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neural Conduction · Sex Factors · Skin Temperature
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology (nerve conduction and its temperature dependence; textbook framing, not evidence). Three primary healthy-subject studies are carded: a four-limb study of 68 healthy Chinese adults correlating conduction with age, sex, height and skin temperature; a prospectively standardised upper-limb study of 155 carefully screened healthy elderly people with temperature controlled; and a 150-person study stratified into three age bands (18–30, 31–45, 46–60) for median and common peroneal conduction and late responses. They agree: ageing brings longer latencies, smaller amplitudes and slower velocities, with sensory amplitudes and late responses changing most; height lengthens late-response latencies (longer axons); and within the warm, controlled ranges actually studied, skin temperature showed no significant correlation — the familiar per-degree slowing is the textbook's account of the wider temperature range, stated as such on the Synthesis card, not as a carded measurement. No carded study reports a per-decade m/s slope, so none is printed as data.

cards.headline: Lin 1993: in 68 healthy adults, age correlated negatively with motor conduction velocity (r −0.37 to −0.46) and with muscle and sensory amplitudes, but not with sensory conduction velocity; height drove H-reflex and F-wave latencies
cards.summary: Lin 1993: in 68 healthy adults, age correlated negatively with motor conduction velocity (r −0.37 to −0.46) and with muscle and sensory amplitudes, but not with sensory conduction velocity; height drove H-reflex and F-wave latencies
cards.people: 68 consecutively collected healthy subjects (50 men, 18 women; mean age 50.8 ± 17.9 years, range 15–88; mean height 162.7 cm) undergoing electrophysiological examination of four limbs; mean skin temperature 32.75°C at the wrist and 30.9°C at the lower leg.
cards.result: Mean values with standard deviations were reported for distal latency, conduction velocity, amplitude, duration and area of compound muscle and sensory action potentials, and minimal H-reflex and F-response latencies, with side-to-side differences. Age was negatively correlated with motor nerve conduction velocity (P<0.05, r=−0.37 to −0.46), compound muscle action potential amplitude (r=−0.32 to −0.43) and sensory action potential amplitude (r=−0.33 to −0.65), but not with sensory nerve conduction velocity. Height correlated with minimal H-reflex and F-response latencies (r=0.45 to 0.76). Gender and skin temperature (within the studied range) correlated with no parameter.
cards.watchOut: A single-ethnicity sample of 68 with only 18 women, studied over a narrow, warm skin-temperature range — the null temperature finding applies within that range and does not contradict the textbook temperature effect over wider ranges.

Zhonghua Yi Xue Za Zhi (Taipei). 1993. PMID: 8299024. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era physiology). cards.headline: Falco 1992: standardised upper-limb values in 155 healthy elderly (ages 60–95) — age had a significant but weak effect on ulnar velocities/latencies and on distal sensory amplitudes of all three nerves; sex had the larger effect
cards.summary: Falco 1992: standardised upper-limb values in 155 healthy elderly (ages 60–95) — age had a significant but weak effect on ulnar velocities/latencies and on distal sensory amplitudes of all three nerves; sex had the larger effect
cards.people: 155 carefully screened healthy elderly individuals aged 60–95 years, studied prospectively in one upper limb with constant measured distances and upper-limb temperature controlled; median, ulnar and radial nerves examined with standard techniques.
cards.result: A normative electrodiagnostic database for the healthy elderly was established; mean parameters compared favourably with published younger-population values. Age had a statistically significant but low-strength effect on all ulnar nerve conduction velocities and distal latencies and on the distal sensory amplitudes of all three nerves. Gender had a greater effect than age on those parameters and on median sensory distal latency. Other median motor and sensory parameters and radial sensory distal latency were not significantly related to age or gender on two-way analysis of variance. The practical lesson: elderly reference values must come from elderly subjects, and sex must be accounted for alongside age.
cards.watchOut: Upper limb only, one side, in screened healthy elderly — values describe the healthy end of the elderly spectrum and should not be applied to unselected clinic populations or to lower-limb nerves.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study (prospective standardised normative study) | Falco FJ, Hennessey WJ, Braddom RL, Goldberg G. Standardized nerve conduction studies in the upper limb of the healthy elderly. Am J Phys Med Rehabil. 1992. PMID: 1388972. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era physiology). cards.headline: Palve 2018: across three age bands (N=150), older subjects had longer latencies, smaller amplitudes and slower velocities — the age change was greatest in sensory conduction and late responses
cards.summary: Palve 2018: across three age bands (N=150), older subjects had longer latencies, smaller amplitudes and slower velocities — the age change was greatest in sensory conduction and late responses
cards.people: 150 healthy individuals in three age groups — Group I ages 18–30 (n=80), Group II ages 31–45 (n=43), Group III ages 46–60 (n=27); 93 men and 57 women. Median and common peroneal conduction (motor and sensory) plus F-wave and H-reflex late responses were measured; the report also tabulates ulnar and tibial latencies, amplitudes and velocities.
cards.result: Patients in the older groups had longer latencies, smaller amplitudes and slower conduction velocities than the younger group, and the change with age was greater in sensory nerve conduction and in late responses than in motor conduction, across the peripheral nerves studied. The authors conclude ageing has a definite correlation with conduction velocity and late responses and that reference values need to be age-related. The record reports the direction and relative pattern of the age effect rather than a single pooled per-decade slope, so this shelf prints the pattern, not an invented slope.
cards.watchOut: The oldest band stops at age 60 and is the smallest (n=27), and the fetched record carries no MeSH this session — pair this study with the elderly-specific Falco standards for ages above 60.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study | Palve SS, Palve SB. Impact of Aging on Nerve Conduction Velocities and Late Responses in Healthy Individuals. J Neurosci Rural Pract. 2018. PMID: 29456354. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: conduction slows and amplitudes shrink with age — sensory fibres and late responses first — while height lengthens late responses; the per-degree temperature coefficient is textbook physiology, not a carded number
cards.summary: Synthesis: conduction slows and amplitudes shrink with age — sensory fibres and late responses first — while height lengthens late responses; the per-degree temperature coefficient is textbook physiology, not a carded number
cards.people: Synthesis of Lin 1993 (N=68), Falco 1992 (N=155) and Palve 2018 (N=150), framed by Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology (textbook framing, not an evidence card).
cards.result: The carded human data settle the pattern. Age is negatively correlated with motor conduction velocity (r=−0.37 to −0.46) and more strongly with sensory amplitudes (r down to −0.65) in the four-limb correlational study; the age-stratified study finds the largest age changes in sensory conduction and late responses; and the elderly-specific standardised study shows that even within ages 60–95, age retains a significant (if weak) effect on ulnar velocities and latencies and on distal sensory amplitudes of the median, ulnar and radial nerves, with sex exerting the larger effect on several parameters. Height, not age, is the main driver of H-reflex and F-wave minimal latencies (r=0.45 to 0.76), as longer axons take longer. On temperature: the carded studies either controlled limb temperature or sampled a narrow warm range and found no within-range correlation. The often-quoted rule that conduction velocity falls by roughly 2 m/s for each 1°C of cooling is presented here as the textbook's account (Boron & Boulpaep) of the wider temperature range — no carded record on this shelf measured that coefficient, so it is not printed as data. No carded study reports a single per-decade m/s slope; the honest summary is the correlation pattern above, applied with age- and sex-matched reference values.
cards.watchOut: Synthesis: the three studies span different nerves, limbs and eras and none quantifies a per-decade slope or a temperature coefficient — the shelf's stamp covers the settled direction and pattern of the age, height and sex effects, not a universal numeric table.
cards.source: Synthesis of Lin KP et al. Zhonghua Yi Xue Za Zhi. 1993 (PMID: 8299024); Falco FJ et al. Am J Phys Med Rehabil. 1992 (PMID: 1388972); Palve SS, Palve SB. J Neurosci Rural Pract. 2018 (PMID: 29456354). Registry IDs: none in the records.

shelves.title: Ecopipam for Tourette syndrome
shelves.question: In children, adolescents and adults with Tourette syndrome, does the selective dopamine D1-receptor antagonist ecopipam, versus placebo, reduce tic severity (YGTSS) without the metabolic and movement harms of D2-blocking antipsychotics?
shelves.mesh: Tourette Syndrome/drug therapy · Benzazepines/therapeutic use · Dopamine Antagonists/therapeutic use · Receptors, Dopamine D1/antagonists & inhibitors · Tics/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three randomised trials from one development programme point the same way, but samples are small-to-moderate and the acute effect is modest (about 3 points on the Yale Global Tic Severity Scale total tic score), which keeps the stamp at POSSIBLE. The acute claim rests on the phase 2b trial (153 children and adolescents; least-squares mean difference −3.44 versus placebo at 12 weeks) and the small crossover trial (40 children; difference −3.2 at 30 days). The phase 3 trial is a randomised-withdrawal study in prior responders — it shows maintenance (relapse risk roughly halved in paediatric participants, hazard ratio 0.47, a relative measure) and must not be read as an acute-effect estimate; its adult stratum was tiny (14 randomised) and not significant. The shelf's clinical point is the harm contrast with D2-blocking antipsychotics: across the programme there was no clinically meaningful weight or metabolic signal and no drug-induced movement disorders were observed — but that is absence of signal in small, short samples, not proof of long-term safety. The commonest adverse events were central (somnolence, anxiety, headache, insomnia, fatigue). The 12-month open-label extension (121 patients, a follow-on from the phase 2b trial) supports tolerability over a year; being open-label it cannot re-prove efficacy.

cards.headline: Phase 3 randomised-withdrawal trial (Gilbert 2026): continuing ecopipam halved relapse risk versus withdrawal to placebo in paediatric responders (hazard ratio 0.47); the adult stratum (n = 14) was not significant — a maintenance result, not an acute-effect estimate
cards.summary: Phase 3 randomised-withdrawal trial (Gilbert 2026): continuing ecopipam halved relapse risk versus withdrawal to placebo in paediatric responders (hazard ratio 0.47); the adult stratum (n = 14) was not significant — a maintenance result, not an acute-effect estimate
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised-withdrawal trial — double-blind withdrawal in open-label responders (Gilbert 2026)
cards.people: 216 people aged 6 years and over with Tourette syndrome (167 paediatric, 77.3%) entered a 12-week open-label ecopipam period (target dose 1.8 mg/kg/day); responders (at least 25% improvement in Yale Global Tic Severity Scale total tic score at weeks 8 and 12) were randomised to continue ecopipam or taper to placebo for 12 weeks — 43 paediatric and 8 adult participants to ecopipam, 47 paediatric and 6 adult to placebo.
cards.result: In paediatric participants, ecopipam significantly reduced relapse risk versus placebo (hazard ratio 0.47; 95% CI 0.26–0.84; P = .008; n = 90 — a relative measure). In adults the effect was directionally similar (hazard ratio 0.51; 95% CI 0.11–2.30; P = .37; n = 14) but not significant. The most frequent adverse events with ecopipam across both periods were somnolence (11.1%), anxiety (9.7%), headache (9.7%), insomnia (8.8%), tic (7.9%) and fatigue (6.5%). There was no clinically meaningful impact on weight, metabolic parameters or psychiatric scale measures, and no drug-induced movement disorders were observed.
cards.watchOut: Randomised withdrawal enriches for responders and tolerators: only 104 of 216 entrants were randomised, so the maintenance effect applies to people who already improved on and tolerated the drug. Relapse was defined as losing at least half of the open-label improvement — a design that cannot estimate what ecopipam does for a new patient.
cards.source: Gilbert DL et al. Efficacy and Safety of Ecopipam for Tourette Syndrome: A Phase 3 Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA neurology. 2026. PMID: 42189524. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05615220. phase 3 randomised-withdrawal trial — double-blind withdrawal in open-label responders (gilbert 2026) 216 people aged 6 years and over with tourette syndrome (167 paediatric, 77.3%) entered a 12-week open-label ecopipam period (target dose 1.8 mg/kg/day); responders (at least 25% improvement in yale global tic severity scale total tic score at weeks 8 and 12) were randomised to continue ecopipam or taper to placebo for 12 weeks — 43 paediatric and 8 adult participants to ecopipam, 47 paediatric and 6 adult to placebo. in paediatric participants, ecopipam significantly reduced relapse risk versus placebo (hazard ratio 0.47; 95% ci 0.26–0.84; p = .008; n = 90 — a relative measure). in adults the effect was directionally similar (hazard ratio 0.51; 95% ci 0.11–2.30; p = .37; n = 14) but not significant. the most frequent adverse events with ecopipam across both periods were somnolence (11.1%), anxiety (9.7%), headache (9.7%), insomnia (8.8%), tic (7.9%) and fatigue (6.5%). there was no clinically meaningful impact on weight, metabolic parameters or psychiatric scale measures, and no drug-induced movement disorders were observed. randomised withdrawal enriches for responders and tolerators: only 104 of 216 entrants were randomised, so the maintenance effect applies to people who already improved on and tolerated the drug. relapse was defined as losing at least half of the open-label improvement — a design that cannot estimate what ecopipam does for a new patient. gilbert dl et al. efficacy and safety of ecopipam for tourette syndrome: a phase 3 randomized clinical trial. jama neurology. 2026. pmid: 42189524. registry id: clinicaltrials.gov nct05615220. mesh: humans · double-blind method · male · female · tourette syndrome/drug therapy · child · adolescent · benzazepines/therapeutic use,adverse effects,pharmacology · dopamine antagonists/therapeutic use,adverse effects · adult · young adult · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Phase 2b randomised trial (Gilbert 2023): ecopipam reduced total tic score more than placebo over 12 weeks (least-squares mean difference −3.44, P = .01) in 153 children and adolescents, with more weight gain on placebo than on ecopipam
cards.summary: Phase 2b randomised trial (Gilbert 2023): ecopipam reduced total tic score more than placebo over 12 weeks (least-squares mean difference −3.44, P = .01) in 153 children and adolescents, with more weight gain on placebo than on ecopipam
cards.people: 153 children and adolescents aged 6 to under 18 years with moderate-to-severe Tourette syndrome (baseline Yale Global Tic Severity Scale total tic score at least 20), randomised 1:1 to ecopipam (76) or placebo (77) for 12 weeks, in a multicentre double-blind trial.
cards.result: Total tic scores fell significantly more on ecopipam than placebo (least-squares mean difference −3.44; 95% CI −6.09 to −0.79; P = .01), and Clinical Global Impression of Tourette Syndrome Severity also improved more (P = .03). More weight gain was seen in the placebo group; no metabolic or electrocardiogram changes were identified. The most common adverse events on ecopipam were headache (15.8%), insomnia (14.5%), fatigue (7.9%) and somnolence (7.9%).
cards.watchOut: A 3.44-point average advantage on a 0–50 tic scale is real but modest, and tic severity fluctuates naturally — the placebo group's own improvement is inside that contrast. Twelve weeks says nothing about years of treatment in a developmental disorder.
cards.source: Gilbert DL et al. Ecopipam for Tourette Syndrome: A Randomized Trial. Pediatrics. 2023. PMID: 36628546. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Phase 2 crossover trial (Gilbert 2018): ecopipam reduced total tic score versus placebo by 3.7 points at day 16 and 3.2 points at day 30 in 40 children and adolescents; N = 40
cards.summary: Phase 2 crossover trial (Gilbert 2018): ecopipam reduced total tic score versus placebo by 3.7 points at day 16 and 3.2 points at day 30 in 40 children and adolescents; N = 40
cards.people: 40 young people aged 7–17 years with Tourette syndrome and a total tic score of at least 20, randomised to ecopipam (50 mg/day if under 34 kg, 100 mg/day if over) or placebo for 30 days, then crossed to the other treatment after a 2-week washout. Stimulants and tic-suppressing medicines were excluded. N = 40 printed on the face.
cards.result: Reduction in total tic score was greater on ecopipam than placebo at 16 days (mean difference −3.7; 95% CI −6.5 to −0.9; P = .011) and at 30 days (mean difference −3.2; 95% CI −6.1 to −0.3; P = .033). There was no weight gain, no drug-induced dyskinesias, and no changes in laboratory tests, electrocardiograms, vital signs or comorbid symptom scales. The dropout rate was 5% (2 of 40); adverse events were predominantly mild to moderate.
cards.watchOut: Forty patients and 30-day periods: a crossover in a waxing-and-waning condition is efficient but fragile, and carryover after a 2-week washout cannot be excluded. Fixed doses here differ from the weight-based dosing of the later trials.
cards.source: Gilbert DL et al. Ecopipam, a D1 receptor antagonist, for treatment of tourette syndrome in children: A randomized, placebo-controlled crossover study. cards.headline: 12-month open-label extension (Gilbert 2025) — follow-on from the phase 2b trial, same programme: tolerability held over a year in 121 children and adolescents, with no significant change in BMI z-score, glycated haemoglobin or cholesterol
cards.summary: 12-month open-label extension (Gilbert 2025) — follow-on from the phase 2b trial, same programme: tolerability held over a year in 121 children and adolescents, with no significant change in BMI z-score, glycated haemoglobin or cholesterol
cards.type: Open-label extension — no comparator (Mov Disord Clin Pract 2025)
cards.people: 121 patients aged 6–18 years with Tourette syndrome who had completed the phase 2b randomised trial (the trial carded above — this extension is a further report of that programme, not an independent cohort), treated open-label with ecopipam titrated to 1.8 mg/kg/day for 12 months; 80 (66%) completed the study.
cards.result: The most common adverse events were nasopharyngitis (14.0%) and anxiety (9.1%), with no new adverse events detected. At month 12 there were no significant changes in body-mass-index z-score (mean change 0.05; P = .35), glycated haemoglobin (0.03%; P = .60) or total cholesterol (0.2 mmol/L (≈7.7 mg/dL); P = .14), and no notable changes in akathisia, movement-disorder, anxiety or depression scales. Tic scores and quality-of-life scores were significantly improved versus baseline at all time points (P < .001) — an uncontrolled comparison.
cards.watchOut: Open-label follow-up of trial completers, a third of whom did not finish the year: 'improvement versus baseline' in an uncontrolled extension is expected from natural fluctuation and expectation, so this card is evidence about tolerability, not efficacy.
cards.source: Gilbert DL et al. Safety and Effect of 12-Month Ecopipam Treatment in Pediatric Patients with Tourette Syndrome. Movement disorders clinical practice. 2025. PMID: 40353708. cards.headline: Synthesis: ecopipam reduces tics modestly versus placebo and maintains benefit in responders — POSSIBLE (benefit), with no antipsychotic-type metabolic signal seen in small samples
cards.summary: Synthesis: ecopipam reduces tics modestly versus placebo and maintains benefit in responders — POSSIBLE (benefit), with no antipsychotic-type metabolic signal seen in small samples
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded reports: the phase 3 randomised-withdrawal trial (216 entered, 104 randomised), the phase 2b trial (153 randomised), the crossover trial (40 randomised), and the 12-month open-label extension of the phase 2b trial (121 patients, same programme). A 2025 systematic review/meta-analysis of the programme (251 participants across the completed trials) found a pooled mean difference of −3.0 points in total tic score versus placebo, consistent with the individual trials carded here.
cards.result: Two acute placebo-controlled trials agree on a roughly 3-point total-tic-score advantage, and the withdrawal trial shows the benefit is maintained in responders (relapse hazard ratio 0.47 in paediatric participants). The absence of weight, metabolic and movement-disorder signals is consistent across reports but rests on small samples and short exposures, so the stamp is POSSIBLE (benefit) rather than higher.
cards.watchOut: All trials come from one development programme with overlapping investigators; there is no head-to-head trial against an antipsychotic or alpha-agonist, and adult efficacy rests on a 14-patient exploratory stratum.
cards.source: Synthesis of Gilbert DL et al. JAMA neurology. 2026 (PMID: 42189524); Gilbert DL et al. Pediatrics. 2023 (PMID: 36628546); Gilbert DL et al. Movement disorders. 2018 (PMID: 30192018); Gilbert DL et al. Movement disorders clinical practice. 2025 (PMID: 40353708), all carded above.

shelves.title: Glabellar botulinum toxin A injection for major depressive disorder
shelves.question: In adults with major depressive disorder, does a single session of botulinum toxin A injected into the glabellar (frown) musculature, versus placebo injection, reduce depressive symptoms over the following 6–24 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Botulinum Toxins, Type A/therapeutic use,administration & dosage · Major Depressive Disorder/drug therapy · Depression/drug therapy · Facial Muscles/drug effects · Injections, Intramuscular · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the direction is consistent across three small randomised trials, a pooled analysis of them and an updated meta-analysis, but every primary trial is small and the intervention visibly paralyses the frown, so functional unblinding is this shelf's central bias problem: a participant who cannot frown knows they were treated, and mood ratings are subjective. The pooled individual-patient analysis of the three early trials (134 patients) found response in 54.2% on botulinum toxin A versus 10.7% on placebo at 6 weeks; the updated meta-analysis (8 randomised trials, 636 participants) found a standardised mean difference of −0.81 versus control, with a null result in the high-dose pan-facial subgroup — the effect, if real, belongs to the standard glabellar protocol, not to more toxin in more places. Product naming (clarification exception): the early trials tested onabotulinumtoxinA preparations, named on each card as the trials report them (29 units for women and about 39–40 units for men in two of the trials); the meta-analysis reports facial botulinum toxin A across trials without a single tested product. The facial-feedback mechanism — that paralysing frown muscles feeds back to lift mood — is a hypothesis, not an established mechanism, and is labelled as such wherever it appears here. Harms in the meta-analysis were no more frequent overall than in controls, with transient local reactions the typical cost.

cards.headline: Wollmer 2012: a single glabellar onabotulinumtoxinA treatment reduced Hamilton depression scores by 47.1% versus 9.2% on placebo at 6 weeks in 30 patients — the first randomised trial; N = 30
cards.summary: Wollmer 2012: a single glabellar onabotulinumtoxinA treatment reduced Hamilton depression scores by 47.1% versus 9.2% on placebo at 6 weeks in 30 patients — the first randomised trial; N = 30
cards.people: 30 patients with major depression who had not improved sufficiently on previous medication, randomised to a single glabellar injection of onabotulinumtoxinA (15) or saline placebo (15), as adjunctive treatment, with 16 weeks of follow-up. N = 30 printed on the face.
cards.result: Depressive symptoms improved significantly more in the onabotulinumtoxinA group across the 16-week follow-up (P < .001). At 6 weeks, Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (17-item) scores had fallen by an average of 47.1% on onabotulinumtoxinA versus 9.2% on placebo (P = .002; effect size d = 1.28), with an even larger effect size at the end of the study (d = 1.80). Improvement was also reflected in the Beck Depression Inventory and Clinical Global Impressions scale.
cards.watchOut: Thirty patients and a very large effect size (d = 1.28–1.80) — effects that large in samples that small usually shrink on replication. The treatment visibly paralyses the glabella, so participants could tell their allocation: functional unblinding is a live alternative explanation for part of the mood difference.
cards.source: Wollmer MA et al. Facing depression with botulinum toxin: a randomized controlled trial. Journal of psychiatric research. 2012. PMID: 22364892. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Finzi 2014: response rate 52% on onabotulinumtoxinA versus 15% on placebo at 6 weeks (74 analysed of 85 randomised); remission 27% versus 7%
cards.summary: Finzi 2014: response rate 52% on onabotulinumtoxinA versus 15% on placebo at 6 weeks (74 analysed of 85 randomised); remission 27% versus 7%
cards.people: 85 outpatients with DSM-IV major depressive disorder randomised to a single treatment of onabotulinumtoxinA (29 units for women, 40 units for men) or saline, injected into the corrugator and procerus frown muscles; 74 were entered into the analysis. Ratings at screening and at 3 and 6 weeks.
cards.result: The primary outcome — response, at least a 50% fall in Montgomery–Åsberg Depression Rating Scale score at 6 weeks — occurred in 52% on onabotulinumtoxinA versus 15% on placebo (P < .001). Remission (score 10 or less) occurred in 27% versus 7% (P < .02). Mean score reduction was 47% versus 21% (P < .0005).
cards.watchOut: Eleven of 85 randomised patients are missing from the analysis, and the outcome is a clinician-rated mood scale in a trial where the active treatment changes the face the rater is looking at — raters, as well as patients, can be functionally unblinded by a paralysed frown.
cards.source: Finzi E et al. Treatment of depression with onabotulinumtoxinA: a randomized, double-blind, placebo controlled trial. Journal of psychiatric research. 2014. PMID: 24345483. cards.headline: Magid 2014: 24-week crossover trial (30 patients) — Hamilton response 55% in the botulinum-toxin-first group versus 0% in the placebo group during the placebo-controlled phase; benefit persisted after cosmetic effects wore off
cards.summary: Magid 2014: 24-week crossover trial (30 patients) — Hamilton response 55% in the botulinum-toxin-first group versus 0% in the placebo group during the placebo-controlled phase; benefit persisted after cosmetic effects wore off
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial, 24 weeks (Magid 2014)
cards.people: 30 patients with DSM-IV major depressive disorder randomised to botulinum toxin A (onabotulinumtoxinA; 29 units for women, 39 units for men) injected into the forehead/glabellar region, or placebo, with crossover at week 12 and assessments to week 24.
cards.result: Hamilton (21-item) response rates were 55% (6 of 11) in the botulinum-toxin-first group and 24% (4 of 17) in the botulinum-toxin-second group, versus 0% (0 of 19) in the placebo group (P < .0001); remission rates were 18%, 18% and 0% respectively (P = .057). Hamilton scores fell 46% and 35% in the two botulinum-toxin groups versus 2% on placebo (P < .0001). Beck Depression Inventory results were concordant. Improvement continued over 24 weeks in the first-treated group even though the cosmetic effect wore off at 12–16 weeks.
cards.watchOut: The denominators are periods, not people (11, 17 and 19 observations from 30 patients across a crossover), so the percentages are not three independent groups; and persistence of benefit after the cosmetic effect faded cuts both ways — it argues against pure appearance effects, but a crossover cannot cleanly separate carryover from durability.
cards.source: Magid M et al. Treatment of major depressive disorder using botulinum toxin A: a 24-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study. The Journal of clinical psychiatry. 2014. randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial, 24 weeks (magid 2014) 30 patients with dsm-iv major depressive disorder randomised to botulinum toxin a (onabotulinumtoxina; 29 units for women, 39 units for men) injected into the forehead/glabellar region, or placebo, with crossover at week 12 and assessments to week 24. hamilton (21-item) response rates were 55% (6 of 11) in the botulinum-toxin-first group and 24% (4 of 17) in the botulinum-toxin-second group, versus 0% (0 of 19) in the placebo group (p < .0001); remission rates were 18%, 18% and 0% respectively (p = .057). hamilton scores fell 46% and 35% in the two botulinum-toxin groups versus 2% on placebo (p < .0001). beck depression inventory results were concordant. improvement continued over 24 weeks in the first-treated group even though the cosmetic effect wore off at 12–16 weeks. the denominators are periods, not people (11, 17 and 19 observations from 30 patients across a crossover), so the percentages are not three independent groups; and persistence of benefit after the cosmetic effect faded cuts both ways — it argues against pure appearance effects, but a crossover cannot cleanly separate carryover from durability. magid m et al. treatment of major depressive disorder using botulinum toxin a: a 24-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study. the journal of clinical psychiatry. 2014. pmid: 24910934. registry id: clinicaltrials.gov nct01392963. mesh: adolescent · adult · aged · botulinum toxins, type a/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · major depressive disorder/drug therapy · double-blind method · female · humans · injections, intramuscular · male · middle aged · neuromuscular agents/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · psychiatric status rating scales · time factors · treatment outcome · young adult

cards.headline: Pooled individual-patient analysis (Magid 2015) — the three early trials combined, labelled as such: response 54.2% versus 10.7% and remission 30.5% versus 6.7% at 6 weeks (n = 134)
cards.summary: Pooled individual-patient analysis (Magid 2015) — the three early trials combined, labelled as such: response 54.2% versus 10.7% and remission 30.5% versus 6.7% at 6 weeks (n = 134)
cards.type: Pooled individual-patient analysis of the three carded trials — same patients, labelled (Pharmacopsychiatry 2015)
cards.people: Individual patient data from the three randomised trials carded above (Wollmer 2012; Finzi 2014; Magid 2014) pooled and analysed as one study: 134 patients, 59 treated with botulinum toxin A and 75 with placebo. This is a re-analysis of the same patients, not new evidence.
cards.result: Improvement at 6 weeks was 45.7% on botulinum toxin A versus 14.6% on placebo (P < .0001), corresponding to a response rate of 54.2% versus 10.7% and a remission rate of 30.5% versus 6.7%.
cards.watchOut: Pooling the same three small trials does not cure their shared weakness — functional unblinding is present in every one of them, so the pooled precision is precision around a potentially biased estimate. Investigator overlap with the primary trials is also substantial.
cards.source: Magid M et al. Treating depression with botulinum toxin: a pooled analysis of randomized controlled trials. Pharmacopsychiatry. 2015. PMID: 26252721. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Updated systematic review and meta-analysis (Gao 2026): 8 randomised trials, 636 participants — depressive symptoms reduced versus control (standardised mean difference −0.81), but the high-dose pan-facial subgroup was null
cards.summary: Updated systematic review and meta-analysis (Gao 2026): 8 randomised trials, 636 participants — depressive symptoms reduced versus control (standardised mean difference −0.81), but the high-dose pan-facial subgroup was null
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (J Affect Disord 2026)
cards.people: Eight randomised controlled trials of facial botulinum toxin A injection for depression, comprising 636 participants, comparing botulinum toxin A against placebo and against the active antidepressant sertraline, in a systematic review and meta-analysis searching to December 2025. The review reports facial botulinum toxin A across trials; it does not name a single tested product.
cards.result: Facial botulinum toxin A was associated with a significant reduction in depressive symptoms versus control conditions (standardised mean difference −0.81; 95% CI −1.23 to −0.38; P < .001). Against placebo the difference was −1.04; against sertraline it was −0.23 (comparable efficacy). Standard glabellar protocols were effective, while the high-dose pan-facial subgroup showed no statistically significant difference from controls (the treatment made no difference in that subgroup). Anxiety scores did not differ significantly between groups. Overall adverse-event rates were similar to controls (risk ratio 1.04, a relative measure); botulinum toxin A caused transient local reactions and avoided sertraline's systemic side effects.
cards.watchOut: Eight trials and 636 participants is still a small evidence base, and a meta-analysis inherits the functional-unblinding problem of every included trial. The null pan-facial subgroup matters: it argues the claim belongs to the standard glabellar protocol only, and it is also what a dose-unblinding artefact might not predict — the honest read is that the mechanism, facial feedback included, remains a hypothesis.
cards.source: Gao Z et al. Antidepressant effects of facial botulinum toxin a injections: Insights from randomized controlled trials. Journal of affective disorders. 2026. PMID: 42669382. Registry ID: PROSPERO CRD420261277524 (as stated in the record).
