cards.headline: Synthesis: glabellar botulinum toxin A probably reduces depressive symptoms — POSSIBLE (benefit), with functional unblinding the standing alternative explanation
cards.summary: Synthesis: glabellar botulinum toxin A probably reduces depressive symptoms — POSSIBLE (benefit), with functional unblinding the standing alternative explanation
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded reports: three small randomised trials (30, 74 analysed and 30 patients), their pooled individual-patient analysis (134 patients, same trials), and an updated meta-analysis (8 trials, 636 participants).
cards.result: Every synthesis favours a single session of glabellar onabotulinumtoxinA over placebo at 6 weeks (pooled response 54.2% vs 10.7%), and the wider meta-analysis agrees while bounding the claim (null for high-dose pan-facial treatment; anxiety unchanged). Because all primary trials are small and none can be truly blinded against a paralysed frown, the stamp is POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: No large, independently run confirmatory trial exists in this record, and durability beyond a single session's months, repeat-dose effects, and who responds are all unresolved.

shelves.title: Sodium benzoate as adjunctive treatment in schizophrenia
shelves.question: In people with schizophrenia on stable antipsychotics — including clozapine-treated and early-psychosis populations — does adjunctive sodium benzoate, versus placebo, improve positive, negative and overall symptoms?
shelves.mesh: Schizophrenia/drug therapy · Sodium Benzoate/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · D-Amino-Acid Oxidase/antagonists & inhibitors · Clozapine/therapeutic use · Psychotic Disorders/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by population, and averaging the split away would misstate the record. In chronic schizophrenia on stable antipsychotics, a 52-patient Taiwanese trial found a 21% improvement in PANSS total score with large effect sizes; in clozapine-resistant schizophrenia, a 60-patient trial found both 1 g/day and 2 g/day beat placebo on negative symptoms, with the 2 g dose also better on PANSS total and positive scores. Against that, the largest and most rigorous trial — 100 participants with early psychosis in Australia — found no benefit at all (the treatment made no difference: PANSS difference −1.2 points, P = .63, with no differences on any secondary measure), and a 68-patient early-schizophrenia feasibility trial of benzoate (with N-acetylcysteine, factorial) was not powered for effect and found no main effects on most outcomes. The meta-analysis lands between: across four trials, add-on benzoate improved positive symptoms (mean difference −1.87 PANSS points) but made no difference to negative symptoms, total PANSS, cognition, functioning or quality of life, and extrapyramidal symptoms were significantly higher on benzoate. So the honest claim is narrow: possible benefit for positive (and, in the clozapine trial, negative) symptoms in chronic/clozapine-resistant disease, no demonstrated benefit in early psychosis, and no established cognitive or functional benefit. All trials are small and short (6–12 weeks); print the Ns.

cards.headline: Lane 2013: add-on sodium benzoate 1 g/day produced a 21% improvement in PANSS total score over 6 weeks in 52 patients with chronic schizophrenia — large effect sizes in a small trial; N = 52
cards.summary: Lane 2013: add-on sodium benzoate 1 g/day produced a 21% improvement in PANSS total score over 6 weeks in 52 patients with chronic schizophrenia — large effect sizes in a small trial; N = 52
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial — chronic schizophrenia add-on (Lane 2013)
cards.people: 52 patients with chronic schizophrenia, stabilised on antipsychotics for at least 3 months, at two major medical centres in Taiwan, randomised to add-on sodium benzoate 1 g/day or placebo for 6 weeks. N = 52 printed on the face.
cards.result: Benzoate produced a 21% improvement in PANSS total score, with large effect sizes (range 1.16–1.69) across PANSS total and subscales, the Scale for the Assessment of Negative Symptoms, Global Assessment of Functioning, Quality of Life Scale and Clinical Global Impression, plus improvement in neurocognitive subtests (processing speed and visual learning domains). Benzoate was well tolerated without significant adverse effects.
cards.watchOut: Effect sizes above 1.1 on nearly every scale from 52 patients over 6 weeks are implausibly uniform for an adjunctive agent in chronic schizophrenia; single research group, single country. This trial is the positive pole of the split — the early-psychosis trial carded below is its counterweight.
cards.source: Lane HY et al. Add-on treatment of benzoate for schizophrenia: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of D-amino acid oxidase inhibitor. JAMA psychiatry. 2013. PMID: 24089054. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00960219. cards.headline: Lin 2018: added to clozapine, sodium benzoate beat placebo on negative symptoms at both doses, and at 2 g/day on PANSS total and positive scores, in 60 clozapine-resistant inpatients
cards.summary: Lin 2018: added to clozapine, sodium benzoate beat placebo on negative symptoms at both doses, and at 2 g/day on PANSS total and positive scores, in 60 clozapine-resistant inpatients
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial — clozapine augmentation (Lin 2018)
cards.people: 60 inpatients with schizophrenia who had responded poorly to clozapine and were stabilised on it, randomised to add-on sodium benzoate 1 g/day, sodium benzoate 2 g/day, or placebo for 6 weeks. A secondary analysis of this same trial (glutathione levels) is noted on this card, not counted as separate evidence.
cards.result: Both benzoate doses produced better improvement than placebo on the Scale for the Assessment of Negative Symptoms; the 2 g/day dose also produced better improvement in PANSS total score, PANSS positive score and Quality of Life Scale. Benzoate was well tolerated without evident side effects. Changes in catalase (an antioxidant) differed between groups and correlated with symptom improvement in the benzoate group; a later secondary analysis of this trial linked benzoate to increased glutathione levels whose changes correlated with symptom and functional improvement among benzoate recipients.
cards.watchOut: Sixty patients split three ways (about 20 per arm) for 6 weeks, from the same research group as the 2013 trial: the dose-response pattern (2 g better than 1 g) is encouraging but rests on very small arms, and clozapine-resistant inpatients are a narrow population.
cards.source: Lin CH et al. Sodium Benzoate, a D-Amino Acid Oxidase Inhibitor, Added to Clozapine for the Treatment of Schizophrenia: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial. Biological psychiatry. 2018. PMID: 29397899. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Scott 2020: in early psychosis, sodium benzoate made no difference — PANSS total difference −1.2 points versus placebo (P = .63) in the largest trial on this shelf (n = 100)
cards.summary: Scott 2020: in early psychosis, sodium benzoate made no difference — PANSS total difference −1.2 points versus placebo (P = .63) in the largest trial on this shelf (n = 100)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial — early psychosis (Scott 2020)
cards.people: 100 participants aged 15–45 years with early psychosis at five clinical sites in Queensland, Australia, randomised 1:1 to sodium benzoate 500 mg twice daily (50) or placebo (50) for 12 weeks. Mean age 21.4 years; 73% male; mean baseline PANSS 75.3.
cards.result: There was no improvement in PANSS total score with benzoate versus placebo (least-squares mean difference −1.2; P = .63 — the treatment made no difference), and no differences in any PANSS subscale, any secondary measure (Clinical Global Impression, depression, functioning, quality of life), or amino acid concentrations. Benzoate was well tolerated, with no clinically significant differences in treatment-emergent adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Early psychosis is not chronic schizophrenia: shorter illness, different background treatment and possibly different biology — the null may mark a population boundary rather than refuting the chronic-disease trials. But it is the largest, longest and most independently run trial here, and its result is unambiguously null.
cards.source: Scott JG et al. Effect of Sodium Benzoate vs Placebo Among Individuals With Early Psychosis: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA network open. 2020. PMID: 33170261. Registry ID: ANZCTR ACTRN12615000187549. cards.headline: Feasibility trial (Husain 2024): add-on sodium benzoate with N-acetylcysteine in early schizophrenia was feasible and well tolerated in 68 adults, and — as designed — showed no main effects on most clinical outcomes
cards.summary: Feasibility trial (Husain 2024): add-on sodium benzoate with N-acetylcysteine in early schizophrenia was feasible and well tolerated in 68 adults, and — as designed — showed no main effects on most clinical outcomes
cards.type: Randomised double-blind feasibility trial — factorial benzoate/N-acetylcysteine, early schizophrenia (Schizophr Bull Open 2024)
cards.people: 68 adults with early schizophrenia spectrum disorder in a multicentre 2 × 2 factorial randomised trial of sodium benzoate and N-acetylcysteine added to standard treatment for 12 weeks; 78% (53) were retained at 12 weeks. A feasibility trial, not powered to detect clinical effects.
cards.result: Recruitment reached the target sample and retention and assessment completion supported feasibility; the medications were well tolerated with no dropouts due to side effects. As expected for its design, no main effects were found on the majority of clinical outcomes (the treatment made no difference on those outcomes in this underpowered test).
cards.watchOut: A factorial feasibility study cannot isolate a benzoate effect (benzoate was combined with N-acetylcysteine in one factor) and was never powered to find one: its null is weak evidence, counted here for completeness of the early-population record, not as a fourth efficacy trial.
cards.source: Husain MO et al. cards.headline: Meta-analysis (Seetharam 2022): across 4 trials, add-on benzoate improved positive symptoms only (mean difference −1.87 PANSS points) — no benefit on negative symptoms, total PANSS, cognition or functioning, and extrapyramidal symptoms were higher
cards.summary: Meta-analysis (Seetharam 2022): across 4 trials, add-on benzoate improved positive symptoms only (mean difference −1.87 PANSS points) — no benefit on negative symptoms, total PANSS, cognition or functioning, and extrapyramidal symptoms were higher
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Asian J Psychiatr 2022)
cards.people: Four clinical trials of add-on sodium benzoate for schizophrenia, pooled in a systematic review and meta-analysis following PRISMA, with random-effects estimation and risk-of-bias assessment.
cards.result: Add-on benzoate significantly improved positive symptoms (mean difference −1.87; 95% CI −3.25 to −0.48; P = .008) but had no significant favourable effect on negative symptoms (P = .84), general psychopathology (P = .49) or total PANSS score (P = .19), and no significant improvement in functioning (P = .43), Clinical Global Impression (P = .58), cognition (P = .46) or quality of life (P = .73) — the treatment made no difference on those outcomes. Extrapyramidal symptoms were significantly higher on benzoate (mean difference 0.39; 95% CI 0.19–0.60; P = .0002); other adverse events did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: Four trials is a thin pool dominated by the small positive Taiwanese studies, and the pooled picture (positive symptoms only) is more modest than either positive trial's own claims — note also the extrapyramidal-symptom signal, which the individual trials' 'well tolerated' summaries did not highlight.

cards.headline: Synthesis: adjunctive sodium benzoate — SPLIT by population: positive small trials in chronic and clozapine-resistant schizophrenia, a null trial in early psychosis, and a meta-analysis supporting positive symptoms only
cards.summary: Synthesis: adjunctive sodium benzoate — SPLIT by population: positive small trials in chronic and clozapine-resistant schizophrenia, a null trial in early psychosis, and a meta-analysis supporting positive symptoms only
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded reports: Lane 2013 (52 chronic patients), Lin 2018 (60 clozapine-resistant patients, with its glutathione secondary analysis labelled as the same trial), Scott 2020 (100 early-psychosis participants), Husain 2024 (68 early-schizophrenia participants, feasibility), and the 2022 meta-analysis of four trials.
cards.result: The record splits cleanly: chronic and clozapine-treated populations show benefit in two small trials from one research group; early-psychosis populations show none in a larger independent trial; pooling everything leaves a positive-symptom effect only, with more extrapyramidal symptoms. The stamp is SPLIT, naming that population split — benzoate is neither 'effective in schizophrenia' nor 'ineffective' on this record.
cards.watchOut: No trial exceeds 12 weeks or 100 patients, the positive evidence comes overwhelmingly from one group, and dose (1 g versus 2 g) and target population for any future trial remain unsettled.

shelves.title: Home-based, fully remote tDCS for major depressive disorder
shelves.question: In adults with major depressive disorder, does self-administered home-based transcranial direct-current stimulation (prefrontal, typically 2 mA, multi-week courses), versus sham, improve depressive symptoms — and does a longer active course beat a shorter one?
shelves.mesh: Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation/methods,adverse effects · Major Depressive Disorder/therapy · Depressive Disorder/therapy · Treatment Outcome · Follow-Up Studies
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the sham-controlled evidence for the home-based, fully remote delivery model rests mainly on one well-run phase 2 trial (Woodham 2025, 174 participants: Hamilton score improvement 9.41 points on active versus 7.14 on sham at 10 weeks, P = .012; response 58.3% versus 37.8% in the follow-up report), supported by a meta-analysis of five small home-based trials (415 patients) finding modest advantages over sham. That is a single-trial-plus-synthesis base, so the stamp is POSSIBLE. The duration question has a clean answer from the second randomised trial (197 participants): 3 weeks of active stimulation followed by 3 weeks of sham did just as well as 6 weeks of active stimulation (the treatment made no difference between the longer and shorter courses; both groups improved, but with no sham-only arm those within-group improvements are comparative, not causal). Six-month follow-up of the Woodham trial showed high sustained response (76% at 6 months among the UK follow-up attenders), but by then everyone had been offered open-label active treatment, so durability is uncontrolled. Blinding integrity is the standing caveat for home devices: active stimulation tingles, and sham protocols mimic it only briefly. Tested product (clarification exception): the Woodham trial used the Flow Neuroscience headset, named as reported. This shelf is only the home-based, fully remote, self-administered slice: the clinic-based stimulation question (theta-burst/rTMS non-inferiority and clinic tDCS against escitalopram) is homed at live shelf #993, and none of that record is carded here.

cards.headline: Fully remote phase 2 trial (Woodham 2025): 10 weeks of home-based tDCS improved Hamilton scores more than sham (9.41 versus 7.14 points, P = .012) in 174 adults with major depression
cards.summary: Fully remote phase 2 trial (Woodham 2025): 10 weeks of home-based tDCS improved Hamilton scores more than sham (9.41 versus 7.14 points, P = .012) in 174 adults with major depression
cards.type: Fully remote randomised double-blind sham-controlled phase 2 trial (Woodham 2025)
cards.people: 174 adults (120 women, 54 men) with major depressive disorder in a current episode of at least moderate severity (mean Hamilton score 19.07), randomised to active (87) or sham (87) home-based tDCS in a fully remote, multisite, double-blind trial. Treatment was 30-minute sessions, five per week for 3 weeks then three per week for 7 weeks, anode over the left and cathode over the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (active 2 mA; sham 0 mA with brief ramp up/down), using the Flow Neuroscience headset as reported, followed by a 10-week open-label phase.
cards.result: Depressive symptoms improved significantly more on active treatment: Hamilton improvement 9.41 ± 6.25 points (10-week mean 9.58 ± 6.02) versus 7.14 ± 6.10 points on sham (10-week mean 11.66 ± 5.96), a difference whose 95% confidence interval was 0.51–4.01 points (P = .012). There were no differences in discontinuation rates, and the authors report high acceptability and safety.
cards.watchOut: The advantage over sham is about 2.3 Hamilton points on average — statistically solid, clinically modest — and the sham group itself improved by 7.14 points, so most of the average patient's improvement is not the current. Home stimulation tingles: sham mimics the sensation only with brief ramps, so blinding integrity over 36 sessions is a genuine question.
cards.source: Woodham RD et al. Home-based transcranial direct current stimulation treatment for major depressive disorder: a fully remote phase 2 randomized sham-controlled trial. Nature medicine. 2025. PMID: 39433921. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05202119. cards.headline: Six-month follow-up (Woodham 2025) — same trial, labelled: response was 58.3% on active versus 37.8% on sham at the end of the randomised phase, and 76% at 6 months among follow-up attenders after everyone was offered open-label treatment
cards.summary: Six-month follow-up (Woodham 2025) — same trial, labelled: response was 58.3% on active versus 37.8% on sham at the end of the randomised phase, and 76% at 6 months among follow-up attenders after everyone was offered open-label treatment
cards.type: Follow-up report of the Woodham trial — randomised phase plus open-label phase, same programme, labelled (J Psychiatr Res 2025)
cards.people: The Woodham trial cohort carded above (174 randomised), with 111 participants completing the subsequent 10-week open-label active phase; the UK cohort (77) was invited to 3- and 6-month follow-ups, and 42 participants attended at least one follow-up visit (total study period 11 months from randomisation). Device use continued optionally during follow-up (59% using at 3 months, 55% at 6 months).
cards.result: At the end of the 10-week randomised phase, clinical response was 58.3% in the active arm versus 37.8% on sham (P = .017). At follow-up, response rates were 64% at 3 months and 76% at 6 months, and among participants who had responded after the open-label phase, 90% maintained their response at 6 months. The authors summarise long-term follow-up as showing high and sustained response rates regardless of continued device use.
cards.watchOut: After the randomised phase everyone could take active treatment and keep using the device, and only 42 of 77 invited UK participants attended follow-up: the 76% figure describes a self-selected, openly treated subgroup and cannot be compared with the original sham arm.
cards.source: Woodham RD et al. cards.headline: Duration trial (Park 2025): 3 weeks of active home tDCS followed by 3 weeks of sham did as well as 6 weeks of active stimulation in 197 randomised patients — the longer course made no difference
cards.summary: Duration trial (Park 2025): 3 weeks of active home tDCS followed by 3 weeks of sham did as well as 6 weeks of active stimulation in 197 randomised patients — the longer course made no difference
cards.type: Randomised double-blind active-duration comparison — no sham-only arm (Brain Behav 2025)
cards.people: 197 participants with major depressive disorder randomised to 3 weeks of active stimulation followed by 3 weeks of sham (89) or 6 weeks of active stimulation (108), in a double-blind home-based trial with assessments at baseline and weeks 3, 6 and 12 (N confirmed from the full text this session; the record's abstract does not state it). There was no sham-only arm.
cards.result: Both groups improved significantly over time on the Beck Depression Inventory-II (model-derived mean change to week 12, −7.53 points) and the Montgomery–Åsberg scale (−6.61 points), and cognitive test scores improved (+6.62 points), but there was no significant group-by-time interaction for any outcome — the longer active course made no difference versus the shorter one. A total of 76 adverse events were reported, most frequently skin stinging (40) and itching (11), mostly mild and transient; participants taking tianeptine reported significantly more adverse events than other medication groups.
cards.watchOut: With no sham-only group, this trial answers only the duration question (3 weeks appears sufficient); its within-group improvements cannot be credited to stimulation, since natural course, expectation and concurrent medication are all inside them. Dropout was substantial and uneven (by week 6, 57 remained in the shorter-course group and 89 in the longer-course group).
cards.source: Park HY et al. Real-World Effects of Home-Based Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation in Depression: A Randomized Controlled Trial of 3-Week Versus 6-Week Protocols. cards.headline: Meta-analysis of home-based tDCS (Moshfeghinia 2025): five randomised trials, 415 patients — active treatment beat sham on depression scores by about 2–3 points, with skin effects the typical harm
cards.summary: Meta-analysis of home-based tDCS (Moshfeghinia 2025): five randomised trials, 415 patients — active treatment beat sham on depression scores by about 2–3 points, with skin effects the typical harm
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Sci Rep 2025)
cards.people: Five randomised controlled trials of home-based transcranial direct current stimulation in depressive disorders, comprising 415 patients, pooled in a systematic review and meta-analysis (searches to November 2024), with Cochrane risk-of-bias assessment.
cards.result: Active home-based tDCS reduced depression scores significantly more than sham: weighted mean difference −2.74 points on the Montgomery–Åsberg scale (four studies, 269 patients; I² = 0%) and −2.24 points on the Hamilton scale (four studies, 438 patients as reported; I² = 46.63%), with anxiety scores also lower (−1.97 on the Hamilton Anxiety scale; two studies, 211 participants). Reported adverse effects included skin lesions, pain, burning sensations, increased sensitivity, redness and mild headaches.
cards.watchOut: Five small trials, one of which (the Woodham trial carded above) dominates the patient count, so the meta-analysis largely restates that trial rather than independently confirming it; its Hamilton analysis reports 438 patients across four studies, more than the 415 total it reports overall — an internal inconsistency in the record that is printed here as reported.
cards.source: Moshfeghinia R et al. Efficacy and safety of home-based transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) on patients with depressive disorders: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials. Scientific reports. 2025. PMID: 41398008. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: home-based, fully remote tDCS probably improves depression modestly versus sham — POSSIBLE (benefit); a 3-week active course appears to do as much as 6 weeks
cards.summary: Synthesis: home-based, fully remote tDCS probably improves depression modestly versus sham — POSSIBLE (benefit); a 3-week active course appears to do as much as 6 weeks
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded reports: the Woodham fully remote sham-controlled trial (174 randomised) and its 6-month follow-up (same programme), the Park duration trial (197 randomised), and the meta-analysis of five home-based trials (415 patients, overlapping the Woodham trial).
cards.result: Against sham, home-based tDCS shows a consistent small advantage (about 2–3 scale points; response 58.3% vs 37.8% in the one large remote trial). On duration, the only direct randomised comparison found no advantage for 6 active weeks over 3. Because the sham-controlled case rests mainly on a single trial and small pooled studies, the stamp is POSSIBLE (benefit). The clinic-based stimulation question is a different shelf (live #993) and is not evidence here.
cards.watchOut: Long-term benefit beyond the open-label follow-up, optimal session frequency, and performance in treatment-resistant depression specifically are not established by the carded home-based record; adherence outside a trial's remote-supervision structure is also untested here.
cards.source: Synthesis of Woodham RD et al. Nature medicine. 2025 (PMID: 39433921); Woodham RD et al. Journal of psychiatric research. 2025 (PMID: 40209536); Park HY et al. Brain and behavior. 2025 (PMID: 41376187); Moshfeghinia R et al. Scientific reports. 2025 (PMID: 41398008), all carded above.

shelves.title: CSF opening pressure at lumbar puncture: 95% interval 10–25 cm CSF, falling with age, higher in men and with higher BMI — upper limit unsettled
shelves.question: In adults having lumbar puncture in the lateral decubitus position, what is the cerebrospinal fluid opening pressure — its reference interval, the 90th/95th percentiles, and how much do body-mass index, age and position move it?
shelves.mesh: Cerebrospinal Fluid Pressure/physiology · Spinal Puncture/standards · Reference Values · Body Mass Index · Age Factors
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — framed by Guyton & Hall ch. 62 (cerebrospinal fluid system) and Boron & Boulpaep on CSF formation and pressure, and resting on three human lumbar-puncture datasets that agree on the shape but not on the upper limit — which is the point. The prospective reference-interval study (242 adults) gives a 95% reference interval of 10–25 cm CSF; the 339-patient outpatient study gives a mean of 17.5 cm H2O (range 4.0–30.0) and proposes higher, factor-adjusted cut-offs (men <30 cm H2O, <25 if over 70; women <25, 27.5 if BMI over 30); and the 12,118-patient Mayo record review shows pressure in mmHg falling steadily after age 50 (mean 11.5 ± 2.8 mmHg at 20–49 years, 8.4 ± 2.4 mmHg at 90–95). Age (lower), male sex (higher) and BMI (higher) move pressure in every dataset. The 'upper limit of normal' — 20 versus 25 versus factor-adjusted 30 cm H2O — is genuinely unsettled, so the stamp is EMERGING, not a settled interval.

cards.headline: Whiteley 2006: the 95% reference interval for lumbar CSF opening pressure in 242 prospectively measured adults was 10–25 cm CSF — BMI had only a small, clinically insignificant influence
cards.summary: Whiteley 2006: the 95% reference interval for lumbar CSF opening pressure in 242 prospectively measured adults was 10–25 cm CSF — BMI had only a small, clinically insignificant influence
cards.people: 242 adults who had a lumbar puncture with concomitant measurement of weight and height, with CSF opening pressure recorded prospectively.
cards.result: The 95% reference interval for lumbar CSF opening pressure was 10 to 25 cm CSF. Body mass index had a small but clinically insignificant influence on opening pressure — the record's abstract reports the interval and that judgement in full, and no further numerical breakdown is printed here because the record does not give it.
cards.watchOut: A short record: it fixes a 95% interval but says little about age, sex or position within it — the other two cards supply those determinants, and they complicate the tidy 10–25 picture.

cards.headline: Bø 2020: in 339 outpatients, mean CSF opening pressure was 17.5 cm H2O (range 4.0–30.0) — male sex, younger age and higher BMI each raised it, and the authors propose factor-adjusted cut-offs up to 30 cm H2O
cards.summary: Bø 2020: in 339 outpatients, mean CSF opening pressure was 17.5 cm H2O (range 4.0–30.0) — male sex, younger age and higher BMI each raised it, and the authors propose factor-adjusted cut-offs up to 30 cm H2O
cards.type: Human prospective outpatient study, J Neurol 2020
cards.people: 339 patients with a normal distribution of age and BMI included consecutively from an ordinary neurological outpatient sample, with CSF opening pressure collected at lumbar puncture by a standardised procedure (60% female); age, sex and BMI registered and analysed by descriptive statistics and linear regression.
cards.result: Mean CSF opening pressure was 17.5 cm H2O (range 4.0–30.0). In multivariable regression, age, sex and BMI all independently affected pressure: male sex (β = 1.5, P = 0.002), lower age (β = −0.095 per year, P < 0.001) and higher BMI (β = 0.42 per BMI unit, P < 0.001) were all associated with higher pressure. Using two standard deviations, the authors suggest as a rule of thumb cut-offs of <30 cm H2O for men (<25 if over age 70) and <25 cm H2O for women (27.5 if BMI over 30), and argue a diagnosis of intracranial hypertension should not be given without such considerations.
cards.watchOut: An outpatient sample having lumbar puncture for clinical reasons — not healthy volunteers — so its mean and range describe people referred for investigation, and its cut-offs are the authors' proposal from two standard deviations, not a consensus threshold; note they sit above the Whiteley interval.
cards.source: Bø SH et al. Cerebrospinal fluid opening pressure in clinical practice - a prospective study. Journal of Neurology. 2020. PMID: 32681283. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Fleischman 2012: in 12,118 Mayo Clinic patients, CSF pressure (in mmHg) fell steadily after age 50 — mean 11.5 ± 2.8 mmHg at 20–49 years, 8.4 ± 2.4 mmHg at 90–95 — and women ran lower, BMI higher, at every age
cards.summary: Fleischman 2012: in 12,118 Mayo Clinic patients, CSF pressure (in mmHg) fell steadily after age 50 — mean 11.5 ± 2.8 mmHg at 20–49 years, 8.4 ± 2.4 mmHg at 90–95 — and women ran lower, BMI higher, at every age
cards.type: Human retrospective record review (Mayo Clinic lumbar punctures), PLoS One 2012
cards.people: Electronic medical records of 33,922 patients who had a lumbar puncture at Mayo Clinic in 1996–2009, of whom 12,118 met all entry criteria after excluding medications or diagnoses known to affect CSF pressure, neurosurgical procedures and repeat punctures; age, sex, race, BMI, intraocular pressure and opening pressure were extracted, in a retrospective study.
cards.result: Relative to the mean CSF pressure at age 20–49 years (11.5 ± 2.8 mmHg), mean pressure declined steadily after age 50, with a 2.5% relative reduction for the 50–54 group (mean 11.2 ± 2.7 mmHg) rising to a 26.9% relative reduction for the 90–95 group (mean 8.4 ± 2.4 mmHg) — both reductions relative to the 20–49 mean, with the absolute means printed beside them. Females had lower pressure than males throughout all age groups, and BMI was positively and independently associated with pressure within all age groups.
cards.watchOut: Pressure here is in mmHg, not cm H2O (11.5 mmHg ≈ 15.6 cm H2O), so compare across cards only after converting units; and the cohort had lumbar puncture for clinical reasons — the study's purpose was the glaucoma hypothesis, and its age trend is the quantity this shelf uses.
cards.source: Fleischman D et al. Cerebrospinal fluid pressure decreases with older age. PLoS One. 2012. PMID: 23300737. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: opening pressure centres at roughly 10–25 cm CSF, falls with age, rises with male sex and BMI — but the upper limit is unsettled (20 vs 25 vs factor-adjusted 30 cm H2O)
cards.summary: Synthesis: opening pressure centres at roughly 10–25 cm CSF, falls with age, rises with male sex and BMI — but the upper limit is unsettled (20 vs 25 vs factor-adjusted 30 cm H2O)
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded human records (the 242-adult prospective reference interval; the 339-patient outpatient study; the 12,118-patient Mayo record review), framed by Guyton & Hall ch. 62 and Boron & Boulpaep on CSF formation and pressure.
cards.result: The distribution is settled in shape: opening pressure at lumbar puncture in the lateral decubitus position centres in the mid-teens cm H2O, with a 95% interval of 10–25 cm CSF in the prospective study and a mean of 17.5 cm H2O (range 4.0–30.0) in the outpatient study. Three determinants are concordant: pressure falls with older age (in the Mayo data by 26.9% relative between the 20–49 and 90–95 groups), is higher in men, and rises with BMI. The upper limit is not settled: the conventional 20-versus-25 cm H2O disagreement is the subject, and the 2020 study proposes factor-adjusted cut-offs reaching 30 cm H2O for younger men — so a single 'normal up to' number is not printed as a fact on this shelf. Position, body habitus and age must be named beside any value before it is called normal or high.
cards.watchOut: No carded record here isolates the lateral-decubitus versus sitting position effect on opening pressure in the same people — position is a stated determinant in the question and the textbooks' account, but no positional contrast is quantified from a fetched record here, so none is printed as data.
cards.source: Synthesis of Whiteley W et al. Neurology. 2006 (PMID: 17101909); Bø SH et al. Journal of Neurology. 2020 (PMID: 32681283); Fleischman D et al. shelves.title: Adjunctive cariprazine in major depression: SPLIT — two of four RCTs positive at one dose each (in opposite directions), two negative; no dose has won twice
shelves.question: In adults with major depressive disorder and inadequate response to antidepressant monotherapy, does adjunctive cariprazine (1.5–4.5 mg/day), versus adjunctive placebo, improve depressive symptoms (MADRS), response and remission — and at which dose? (PARTIAL scope: cariprazine's schizophrenia, bipolar and negative-symptom questions are homed at live #1430 and packs #2403, #3678, #3705 and #6381.)
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Major Depressive Disorder · Treatment Outcome · Antipsychotic Agents · Antidepressive Agents · Double-Blind Method · Piperazines
shelves.balance: SPLIT, on four distinct randomised trials (PARTIAL scope: cariprazine in schizophrenia is homed at live #1430, in bipolar I depression at pack #2403, in mania at pack #3678, in bipolar maintenance at pack #3705 and for negative symptoms at pack #6381 — none is re-carded here). The four adjunctive-MDD trials disagree, and they disagree by dose in opposite directions: Durgam 2016 (n=819) found the higher flexible dose (2–4.5 mg/day) effective (MADRS least-squares mean difference −2.2 vs placebo) but not 1–2 mg/day; Sachs 2023 (mITT n=751) found 1.5 mg/day effective (−14.1 vs −11.5 MADRS change) but not 3.0 mg/day; Riesenberg 2023 (mITT n=750), a near-identical phase 3 design, found NEITHER 1.5 nor 3 mg/day significantly different from placebo; and Fava 2018 (n=231, phase 2, low doses 0.1–2.0 mg/day) found no significant effect at either dose. No dose has separated from placebo in more than one trial. The 2024 meta-analysis of these four trials pools a small average benefit (standardised mean difference −1.79 as printed in its abstract, with a variable magnitude of effects; response relative risk 1.21, relative; remission relative risk 0.99 — no difference). Added harms over antidepressant alone are consistent across trials: akathisia (up to 22.3% at 2–4.5 mg/day), restlessness, insomnia and nausea.

cards.headline: Phase 2/3 flexible-dose RCT (Durgam 2016): adjunctive cariprazine 2–4.5 mg/day beat placebo on MADRS (difference −2.2 points); 1–2 mg/day did not
cards.summary: Phase 2/3 flexible-dose RCT (Durgam 2016): adjunctive cariprazine 2–4.5 mg/day beat placebo on MADRS (difference −2.2 points); 1–2 mg/day did not
cards.type: Multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled flexible-dose trial, adjunctive cariprazine vs placebo in MDD
cards.people: 819 adults with major depressive disorder and inadequate response to standard antidepressant therapy were randomised to 8 weeks of adjunctive placebo (n=269), cariprazine 1–2 mg/day (n=274) or cariprazine 2–4.5 mg/day (n=276), in a multicentre double-blind trial run 2011–2013.
cards.result: At week 8, MADRS total-score reduction was significantly greater with cariprazine 2–4.5 mg/day than placebo (least-squares mean difference −2.2; adjusted P=.0114) but not with 1–2 mg/day (difference −0.9; adjusted P=.2404). The higher-dose group separated at weeks 2, 4 and 6 as well. Treatment-emergent adverse events in ≥10% of the 2–4.5 mg/day group were akathisia (22.3%), insomnia (13.6%) and nausea (12.8%). Mean metabolic, vital-sign and ECG changes were generally similar between groups, and no suicide-related adverse events were reported.
cards.watchOut: Flexible dosing means the 'dose groups' are dose ranges, and the positive result sits in the higher range only — the same higher range that carries the 22.3% akathisia rate.
cards.source: Durgam S et al. Efficacy and safety of adjunctive cariprazine in inadequate responders to antidepressants: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study in adult patients with major depressive disorder. cards.headline: Phase 2 low-dose RCT (Fava 2018): adjunctive cariprazine 0.1–0.3 and 1.0–2.0 mg/day — NEITHER dose differed significantly from placebo on any predefined endpoint (n=231)
cards.summary: Phase 2 low-dose RCT (Fava 2018): adjunctive cariprazine 0.1–0.3 and 1.0–2.0 mg/day — NEITHER dose differed significantly from placebo on any predefined endpoint (n=231)
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, adjunctive low-dose cariprazine vs placebo in treatment-resistant MDD
cards.people: 231 adults with treatment-resistant major depressive disorder were randomised in a 19-week double-blind phase 2 study of adjunctive cariprazine 0.1–0.3 mg/day or 1.0–2.0 mg/day versus placebo, on top of antidepressant treatment.
cards.result: None of the predefined parameters reached significance for either cariprazine dose. The 1.0–2.0 mg/day group showed numerically greater mean changes in MADRS and Clinical Global Impression scores and numerically higher response and remission rates than placebo, but no measure separated the 0.1–0.3 mg/day group from placebo. Common treatment-emergent adverse events (≥5% and twice the placebo rate) in the cariprazine groups included headache, arthralgia, restlessness, fatigue, increased appetite, insomnia, dry mouth and constipation.
cards.watchOut: The smallest of the four trials (n=231) and the only one testing doses below 1.5 mg/day — a negative result at low doses does not answer the licensed-dose question, but it is part of the programme's dose pattern.

cards.summary: Phase 3 RCT, Study 301 (Sachs 2023): adjunctive cariprazine 1.5 mg/day beat placebo on week-6 MADRS (−14.1 vs −11.5); 3.0 mg/day did not
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Study 301), adjunctive cariprazine 1.5 or 3.0 mg/day vs placebo in MDD
cards.people: 751 patients in the modified intention-to-treat population (placebo n=249; cariprazine 1.5 mg/day n=250; cariprazine 3.0 mg/day n=252) — adults with major depressive disorder and nonresponse to at least one antidepressant monotherapy, randomised 1:1:1 for 6 weeks.
cards.result: At week 6, MADRS reduction was significantly greater with cariprazine 1.5 mg/day than placebo (−14.1 vs −11.5), with significant differences also at weeks 2 and 4; cariprazine 3.0 mg/day (−13.1) did NOT differ significantly from placebo. MADRS response was more likely on 1.5 mg/day than placebo (44.0% vs 34.9% — absolute rates); remission rates did not differ significantly among groups. Common treatment-emergent adverse events (≥5% in either cariprazine group and twice the placebo rate) were akathisia and nausea.
cards.watchOut: The dose pattern is inverted relative to Durgam 2016: here the LOWER fixed dose worked and the higher did not. A conference-abstract version of this same trial (PMID 43010275, Study 301) exists in the literature and is not carded separately — it is the same trial, not a fifth report.

cards.headline: Phase 3 RCT (Riesenberg 2023): adjunctive cariprazine 1.5 and 3 mg/day — NEITHER dose differed significantly from placebo on the primary or secondary outcomes (mITT n=750)
cards.summary: Phase 3 RCT (Riesenberg 2023): adjunctive cariprazine 1.5 and 3 mg/day — NEITHER dose differed significantly from placebo on the primary or secondary outcomes (mITT n=750)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, adjunctive cariprazine 1.5 or 3 mg/day vs placebo in MDD
cards.people: 750 patients in the modified intention-to-treat population (placebo n=249; cariprazine 1.5 mg/day n=250; cariprazine 3 mg/day n=251) — adults with major depressive disorder per DSM-5 and inadequate response to ongoing antidepressant therapy, randomised 1:1:1 in a study run 2018–2021, near-identical in design to the Sachs 2023 trial above.
cards.result: At week 6, least-squares mean MADRS change was −13.8 (cariprazine 1.5 mg/day), −14.8 (cariprazine 3 mg/day) and −13.4 (placebo); the differences versus placebo were NOT statistically significant for either dose, and the secondary CGI-S outcome was also not significant (a trend for 3 mg/day, P=.0573, not adjusted for multiplicity). Common treatment-emergent adverse events (≥5% in either cariprazine group and twice the placebo rate) were akathisia and insomnia. No new safety concerns were detected.
cards.watchOut: This is the programme's replication failure and the reason the shelf is SPLIT rather than positive: the same doses, the same endpoint and the same population as Sachs 2023 produced a null result, with a notably large placebo response (−13.4 MADRS points).

cards.headline: Meta-analysis of the four RCTs (Gill 2024): pooled response favoured cariprazine (relative risk 1.21, relative) but remission did not (relative risk 0.99), with a variable magnitude of effects across trials
cards.summary: Meta-analysis of the four RCTs (Gill 2024): pooled response favoured cariprazine (relative risk 1.21, relative) but remission did not (relative risk 0.99), with a variable magnitude of effects across trials
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of the four adjunctive cariprazine RCTs carded above
cards.people: The four randomised controlled trials carded above were the trials included in this systematic review's meta-analysis (five studies were included in its qualitative review) — a synthesis of the same programme, not independent evidence.
cards.result: The random-effects model found a moderate pooled antidepressant effect on MADRS (standardised mean difference −1.79, 95% CI −2.89 to −0.69, as printed in the record). The pooled response relative risk was 1.21 (95% CI 1.05 to 1.39; P=0.008 — a relative measure) and the pooled remission relative risk was 0.99 (95% CI 0.84 to 1.17; P=0.91 — no difference). Two of the four trials found a statistically significant treatment response and one observed a remission advantage. The authors note the variable magnitude of effects and that further results are needed to clarify the relation.
cards.watchOut: A pooled average over two positive-by-dose and two negative trials describes the programme's centre, not a consistent effect: no single dose of adjunctive cariprazine has beaten placebo in more than one trial.
cards.source: Gill H et al. Adjunctive cariprazine for major depressive disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis. CNS spectrums. 2024. PMID: 38555956. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: four distinct randomised trials split — two found a benefit at one dose each (in opposite dose directions), two found none; the honest summary is a small, dose-inconsistent average benefit bought with akathisia
cards.summary: Synthesis: four distinct randomised trials split — two found a benefit at one dose each (in opposite dose directions), two found none; the honest summary is a small, dose-inconsistent average benefit bought with akathisia
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf (four distinct RCTs plus their meta-analysis).
cards.result: Adjunctive cariprazine in antidepressant-inadequate major depression: Durgam 2016 (n=819) was positive only at 2–4.5 mg/day (MADRS difference −2.2); Sachs 2023 (mITT n=751) was positive only at 1.5 mg/day (−14.1 vs −11.5) and not at 3 mg/day; Riesenberg 2023 (mITT n=750), the near-replicate phase 3, was negative at both doses; Fava 2018 (n=231) was negative at low doses. The meta-analysis pools to a response relative risk of 1.21 (relative) with no remission advantage (relative risk 0.99). Post-hoc reports of the Sachs trial (anhedonia, anxiety) were not counted toward the trial floor, and the conference abstract of that trial was not carded as a separate report. Akathisia, restlessness, insomnia and nausea are the consistent added harms. Cariprazine's other indications are homed separately (schizophrenia live #1430; bipolar I depression pack #2403; mania pack #3678; bipolar maintenance pack #3705; negative symptoms pack #6381) and are not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Intrathecal ziconotide for severe refractory pain: all three (old, short) RCTs positive on pain scores — 53.1% vs 18.1% fast-titrated, 14.7% vs 7.2% slow-titrated — with CNS harms scaling with dose speed
shelves.question: In adults with severe chronic pain (malignant and non-malignant) refractory to conventional therapy including intrathecal opioids, does intrathecal ziconotide, versus placebo infusion, reduce pain intensity, and at what neuropsychiatric cost — and how does titration speed change both?
shelves.mesh: Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Analgesics · Calcium Channel Blockers · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Injections, Spinal · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasms · Pain · Pain Measurement · Intractable Pain · omega-Conotoxins
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) for short-term pain reduction, at a substantial neuropsychiatric price — and the entire randomised base is three small, old, short trials (enrolment era 1996–2004), with no modern trial in existence. All three placebo-controlled trials found significantly greater pain-intensity (VASPI) reduction on intrathecal ziconotide: Staats 2004 (cancer/AIDS pain, fast titration) 53.1% vs 18.1% mean improvement; Wallace 2006 (nonmalignant pain, fast titration later dose-reduced for adverse events) 31.2% vs 6.0%; Rauck 2006 (slow titration to a low maximum dose) 14.7% vs 7.2% — the smallest effect, and the best tolerated. Titration speed is the shelf's central fact: the fast-titration trials bought larger pain reductions with heavy burdens of dizziness, confusion, ataxia, abnormal gait, memory impairment, nausea, urinary retention and other CNS effects, while slow titration shrank both benefit and harm. Treatment courses in these trials were days to three weeks — nothing in the randomised base speaks to long-term efficacy or safety.

cards.headline: Fast-titration RCT (Staats 2004): intrathecal ziconotide in cancer/AIDS refractory pain — mean VASPI improvement 53.1% vs 18.1% on placebo; moderate-to-complete relief in 52.9% vs 17.5%
cards.summary: Fast-titration RCT (Staats 2004): intrathecal ziconotide in cancer/AIDS refractory pain — mean VASPI improvement 53.1% vs 18.1% on placebo; moderate-to-complete relief in 52.9% vs 17.5%
cards.type: Multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (fast titration, with crossover of nonresponders), intrathecal ziconotide vs placebo
cards.people: 111 patients aged 24–85 with cancer or AIDS and refractory pain (mean Visual Analog Scale of Pain Intensity ≥50 mm), randomised 2:1 to intrathecal ziconotide or placebo at 32 centres in the USA, Australia and the Netherlands (1996–1998). Almost all were taking opioids at baseline (98.5% of the ziconotide group, 95% of placebo; median morphine-equivalent 300 vs 600 mg/day) and 36 had used intrathecal morphine.
cards.result: Mean VASPI scores improved 53.1% (95% CI 44.0% to 62.2%) on ziconotide versus 18.1% (95% CI 4.8% to 31.4%) on placebo (P<.001) over the 5–6-day titration, with no loss of efficacy in the 5-day maintenance phase for responders. Pain relief was moderate to complete in 52.9% versus 17.5% (P<.001); five ziconotide patients achieved complete relief; 50.0% versus 17.5% responded to therapy (P=.001). Nonresponders crossed over to the opposite treatment after the initial period.
cards.watchOut: A 1996–1998 trial with a roughly two-week randomised horizon in a very refractory, heavily opioid-treated population — it establishes short-term analgesia only. The fast titration used here is the regimen the later slow-titration trial was designed to soften.
cards.source: Staats PS et al. Intrathecal ziconotide in the treatment of refractory pain in patients with cancer or AIDS: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2004. PMID: 14709577. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Slow-titration RCT (Rauck 2006): intrathecal ziconotide titrated slowly over 3 weeks — VASPI improvement 14.7% vs 7.2% on placebo, significant but modest, and better tolerated than the fast-titration trials
cards.summary: Slow-titration RCT (Rauck 2006): intrathecal ziconotide titrated slowly over 3 weeks — VASPI improvement 14.7% vs 7.2% on placebo, significant but modest, and better tolerated than the fast-titration trials
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (slow titration over 3 weeks), intrathecal ziconotide vs placebo
cards.people: 220 adults with severe chronic pain randomised to intrathecal ziconotide (n=112) or placebo (n=108). Ziconotide started at 0.1 µg/hour (2.4 µg/day) and rose in 0.05–0.1 µg/hour increments over 3 weeks to a mean dose at termination of 0.29 µg/hour (6.96 µg/day). Baseline VASPI was 80.7 (SD 15).
cards.result: Mean percentage VASPI improvement from baseline to week 3 was 14.7% on ziconotide versus 7.2% on placebo (P=0.036), with significance on many secondary efficacy measures. Significant adverse events in the ziconotide group were dizziness, confusion, ataxia, abnormal gait and memory impairment; discontinuation rates for adverse events and serious adverse events were comparable between groups. The authors conclude slow titration to a low maximum dose improved pain significantly and was better tolerated than in the two previous controlled trials that used faster titration to a higher mean dose.
cards.watchOut: The tolerable regimen is also the weakest: a 7.5-percentage-point average advantage in pain improvement over placebo. Three weeks is the longest randomised exposure on this shelf.
cards.source: Rauck RL et al. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of intrathecal ziconotide in adults with severe chronic pain. Journal of pain and symptom management. 2006. cards.headline: Fast-titration RCT (Wallace 2006): intrathecal ziconotide in chronic nonmalignant pain — mean VASPI reduction 31.2% vs 6.0% on placebo over 6 days, with a considerable adverse-event incidence that forced mid-trial dose reductions
cards.summary: Fast-titration RCT (Wallace 2006): intrathecal ziconotide in chronic nonmalignant pain — mean VASPI reduction 31.2% vs 6.0% on placebo over 6 days, with a considerable adverse-event incidence that forced mid-trial dose reductions
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (fast titration, dose-reduced mid-trial), intrathecal ziconotide vs placebo in nonmalignant pain
cards.people: 255 patients with severe chronic nonmalignant pain unresponsive to conventional therapy and VASPI ≥50 mm (169 ziconotide, 86 placebo), treated over 6 days as inpatients. The starting dose (0.4 µg/hour) and maximum dose (7.0 µg/hour) were reduced mid-trial to 0.1 and 2.4 µg/hour respectively because of adverse events.
cards.result: Mean percent reduction in VASPI from baseline was 31.2% on ziconotide versus 6.0% on placebo (P≤0.001). During initial titration a significantly greater percentage of ziconotide patients reported adverse events, including abnormal gait, amblyopia, dizziness, nausea, nystagmus, pain, urinary retention and vomiting. The authors conclude ziconotide provided significant analgesia in patients for whom conventional therapy failed, but with a considerable incidence of adverse events due to the rapid titration and high doses administered.
cards.watchOut: The mid-trial dose reduction means two different regimens sit inside one trial's result. The record carries no MeSH terms (printed as 'none in the record' on this card) and the journal record is a 2006 article indexed under a later-assigned PMID — the trial itself is of the same early-2000s era as the other two.

cards.headline: Synthesis: three small old trials, all positive on short-term pain scores, with benefit and neuropsychiatric harm both scaling with titration speed — and no randomised evidence beyond three weeks
cards.summary: Synthesis: three small old trials, all positive on short-term pain scores, with benefit and neuropsychiatric harm both scaling with titration speed — and no randomised evidence beyond three weeks
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf (the entire randomised base for intrathecal ziconotide).
cards.result: Staats 2004 (n=111, cancer/AIDS, fast titration): VASPI improvement 53.1% vs 18.1%. Wallace 2006 (n=255, nonmalignant, fast titration): VASPI reduction 31.2% vs 6.0%, with the starting and maximum doses cut mid-trial for adverse events. Rauck 2006 (n=220, slow titration): VASPI improvement 14.7% vs 7.2%, better tolerated. The consistent direction across three independent trials supports real short-term analgesia in truly refractory pain; the consistent CNS harm list (dizziness, confusion, ataxia, abnormal gait, memory impairment) and the absence of any trial longer than 3 weeks bound how far the claim extends. Ziconotide remains a licensed intrathecal option whose entire randomised base is these three trials — there is no modern trial to card.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Zonisamide adjunctive in Parkinson's wearing-off: 'off' time −0.72 vs −0.01 hours at 50 mg (n=389), no extra dyskinesia — modest benefit, Japanese trial base; retracted meta-analysis excluded
shelves.question: In patients with Parkinson's disease on levodopa with insufficient response or wearing-off, does adjunctive zonisamide (25–50 mg daily), versus placebo, improve motor scores (UPDRS Part III) and reduce daily 'off' time, without increasing dyskinesia?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anticonvulsants · Dopamine Agents · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Isoxazoles · Japan · Male · Middle Aged · Parkinson Disease · Treatment Outcome · Zonisamide
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) of modest size. Three randomised placebo-controlled trials support adjunctive zonisamide in Parkinson's disease on levodopa: a Japanese dose-ranging trial (2007; the PubMed record does not state the total randomised N — printed as N not documented in the record) found significant UPDRS Part III improvement at 25 mg and 50 mg and reduced 'off' time at 50 mg and 100 mg, with adverse-event incidence higher at 100 mg; a Japanese confirmatory wearing-off trial (2015, n=389 randomised) found 'off' time reduced by 0.719 hours with zonisamide 50 mg versus 0.011 hours with placebo (P=.005) — an absolute benefit of about 0.7 hours a day; and a 2024 randomised crossover trial (n=69 assessed at 1 month) found MDS-UPDRS III 'on' scores significantly improved with zonisamide 25 mg versus placebo (P=.009). Dyskinesia was NOT increased in any trial. Somnolence was the recurring excess harm (6.3% at 50 mg vs 2.3% on placebo in the 2015 trial). The two large trials are Japanese, and zonisamide is approved for Parkinson's disease in Japan, not for this indication by the FDA or EMA — that single-region weight is stated on the face. A 2022 zonisamide-in-Parkinson's meta-analysis (PMID 36132085) is a RETRACTED publication and is deliberately NOT carded anywhere on this shelf. Cross-points (prose only): opicapone (pack #2369), istradefylline (pack #2370), safinamide (live #1445), and zonisamide in epilepsy (pack #2825) answer different questions.

cards.headline: Dose-ranging RCT (Murata 2007, Japan): adjunctive zonisamide improved UPDRS Part III at 25 mg and 50 mg and reduced 'off' time at 50 mg and 100 mg, without increasing dyskinesia; adverse events were more frequent at 100 mg
cards.summary: Dose-ranging RCT (Murata 2007, Japan): adjunctive zonisamide improved UPDRS Part III at 25 mg and 50 mg and reduced 'off' time at 50 mg and 100 mg, without increasing dyskinesia; adverse events were more frequent at 100 mg
cards.type: Multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled dose-ranging trial, zonisamide 25/50/100 mg/day adjunctive to levodopa (Japan)
cards.people: Patients in Japan with Parkinson's disease showing insufficient response to levodopa, randomised to placebo or zonisamide 25, 50 or 100 mg/day added to levodopa for 12 weeks (after a 2-week placebo run-in), in a multicentre double-blind parallel-group trial. The total randomised N is not stated in the PubMed record (N not documented in the record).
cards.result: The primary endpoint — change in UPDRS Part III total score — improved significantly in the 25-mg and 50-mg groups versus placebo. Total daily 'off' time was significantly reduced in the 50-mg and 100-mg groups versus placebo. Dyskinesia was not increased in the zonisamide groups. The incidence of adverse effects was similar between the 25-mg, 50-mg and placebo groups but higher in the 100-mg group. The authors concluded zonisamide 25 to 100 mg/day is safe, effective and well tolerated as adjunctive treatment.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports significance without effect sizes or the total randomised N (N not documented in the record), so this card supports direction, not magnitude; the dose pattern (motor score best at 25–50 mg, 'off' time at 50–100 mg, harms up at 100 mg) is why later trials settled on 25–50 mg.
cards.source: Murata M et al. Zonisamide improves motor function in Parkinson disease: a randomized, double-blind study. Neurology. 2007. PMID: 17200492. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Wearing-off confirmatory RCT (Murata 2015, Japan; n=389): zonisamide 50 mg reduced daily 'off' time by 0.719 hours versus 0.011 hours on placebo (P=.005); dyskinesia and hallucination rates were comparable to placebo
cards.summary: Wearing-off confirmatory RCT (Murata 2015, Japan; n=389): zonisamide 50 mg reduced daily 'off' time by 0.719 hours versus 0.011 hours on placebo (P=.005); dyskinesia and hallucination rates were comparable to placebo
cards.type: Multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled confirmatory trial, zonisamide 25/50 mg/day adjunctive therapy in wearing-off (Japan)
cards.people: 389 patients with Parkinson's disease and wearing-off on existing therapy, randomised in Japan (131 placebo, 130 zonisamide 25 mg, 128 zonisamide 50 mg) to 12 weeks of adjunctive treatment after a 4-week placebo run-in; 354 completed the study.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — change in daily 'off' time from patient diaries — was a reduction of 0.719 ± 0.179 hours with zonisamide 50 mg versus 0.011 ± 0.173 hours with placebo (P=.005), an absolute difference of about 0.7 hours per day. Somnolence occurred in 6.3% on zonisamide 50 mg and 3.1% on 25 mg versus 2.3% on placebo; the incidences of other adverse events, including dyskinesia and hallucination, were comparable between zonisamide and placebo.
cards.watchOut: The headline effect is real but modest in absolute terms (~0.7 hours of 'off' time per day at 50 mg); the 25-mg dose did not carry the primary endpoint in this trial, and the population is Japanese — zonisamide's Parkinson's approval is Japan-only.

cards.headline: Advanced-disease crossover RCT (Essam 2024; n=69): zonisamide 25 mg significantly improved MDS-UPDRS III 'on' scores versus placebo (P=.009), with no dyskinesia worsening and no non-motor or quality-of-life change
cards.summary: Advanced-disease crossover RCT (Essam 2024; n=69): zonisamide 25 mg significantly improved MDS-UPDRS III 'on' scores versus placebo (P=.009), with no dyskinesia worsening and no non-motor or quality-of-life change
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial, zonisamide 25/50 mg adjunctive therapy in advanced Parkinson's disease
cards.people: Patients with advanced Parkinson's disease (Hoehn and Yahr stage ≥2 in the 'on' state, at least 2 hours of daily 'off' time) randomised in a double-blind placebo-controlled crossover study to zonisamide 25 mg, zonisamide 50 mg or placebo sequences as adjunctive therapy; 69 patients were assessed at the 1-month follow-up and 58 at 3 months.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — change in total MDS-UPDRS III 'on' score — improved significantly in the zonisamide 25 mg group compared with placebo (P=.009). At final assessment the 25 mg group also showed significant improvement in total and Part IV MDS-UPDRS, bradykinesia, tremor and the functional impact of fluctuations versus placebo. There was no change in dyskinesia, non-motor symptoms or quality of life, and no side-effect difference except sedation.
cards.watchOut: A small crossover trial (69 assessed at 1 month, 58 at 3 months) — it corroborates the motor direction of the two larger Japanese trials but cannot carry an effect-size claim, and its null non-motor and quality-of-life reads are part of its result.
cards.source: Essam M et al. Role of zonisamide in advanced Parkinson's disease: a randomized placebo-controlled study. Neurological sciences : official journal of the Italian Neurological Society and of the Italian Society of Clinical Neurophysiology. 2024. PMID: 38376645. Registry ID: NCT04182399. shelves.title: Glatiramer acetate in relapsing-remitting MS: relapses cut by about a third in relative terms across three placebo-controlled trials (annualised rate 0.331 vs 0.505 in GALA), with injection reactions the main harm
shelves.question: In patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, does glatiramer acetate 20 mg daily (or 40 mg three times weekly) reduce relapse rates and MRI lesion activity versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Disability Evaluation · Double-Blind Method · Drugs, Investigational · Female · Glatiramer Acetate · Humans · Male · Multiple Sclerosis · Peptides · Recurrence
shelves.balance: LIKELY benefit, modest in size. Three placebo-controlled trials in relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis agree: glatiramer acetate reduced relapses by about a third in relative terms — pivotal 20 mg daily trial (mean relapses over 2 years 1.19 vs 1.68, a 29% relative reduction), European/Canadian MRI trial (relapses reduced 33% relative; total enhancing lesions −10.8 vs placebo) and GALA (40 mg three times weekly; annualised relapse rate 0.331 vs 0.505, a 34% relative reduction). Harms are modest: injection-site reactions (35.5% vs 5.0% in GALA) and a transient systemic post-injection reaction (15.2% vs 3.2% in the pivotal trial). No long-term disability effect is claimed from these trials.

cards.headline: Pivotal phase 3 trial (Johnson 1995): glatiramer acetate (copolymer 1) 20 mg daily reduced relapses in relapsing-remitting MS — mean relapses over 2 years 1.19 versus 1.68 on placebo, a 29% relative reduction (P=.007); transient systemic post-injection reaction 15.2% vs 3.2%
cards.summary: Pivotal phase 3 trial (Johnson 1995): glatiramer acetate (copolymer 1) 20 mg daily reduced relapses in relapsing-remitting MS — mean relapses over 2 years 1.19 versus 1.68 on placebo, a 29% relative reduction (P=.007); transient systemic post-injection reaction 15.2% vs 3.2%
cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial, glatiramer acetate 20 mg daily vs placebo, relapsing-remitting MS
cards.people: 251 patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis randomised to copolymer 1 (glatiramer acetate) 20 mg by daily subcutaneous injection (125) or placebo (126) for 2 years, in an 11-centre double-blind trial; the primary endpoint was the difference in relapse rate.
cards.result: The final 2-year relapse rate was 1.19 ± 0.13 on copolymer 1 versus 1.68 ± 0.13 on placebo — a 29% relative reduction (P=.007); annualised rates were 0.59 versus 0.84. Trends in the proportion of relapse-free patients and median time to first relapse favoured copolymer 1. On the Expanded Disability Status Scale analysis, significantly more copolymer-1 patients improved and more placebo patients worsened by ≥1 step (P=.037). Withdrawals were 19 (15.2%) on copolymer 1 and 17 (13.5%) on placebo. The most common adverse experience was an injection-site reaction; a transient self-limited systemic reaction followed injection in 15.2% of copolymer-1 patients versus 3.2% on placebo.
cards.watchOut: Do not substitute PMID 11902590 for this report: it is a 2001 reprint of this same trial, not a second report, and it is not carded. The disability finding is a categorical EDSS analysis, not a confirmed-progression endpoint of the modern kind.
cards.source: Johnson KP et al. Copolymer 1 reduces relapse rate and improves disability in relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis: results of a phase III multicenter, double-blind placebo-controlled trial. The Copolymer 1 Multiple Sclerosis Study Group. Neurology. 1995. PMID: 7617181. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: European/Canadian MRI trial (Comi 2001): glatiramer acetate reduced MRI lesion activity — total enhancing lesions reduced by 10.8 lesions versus placebo over 9 months (P=.003) — and the relapse rate by 33% relative
cards.summary: European/Canadian MRI trial (Comi 2001): glatiramer acetate reduced MRI lesion activity — total enhancing lesions reduced by 10.8 lesions versus placebo over 9 months (P=.003) — and the relapse rate by 33% relative
cards.type: Multicentre double-blind randomised placebo-controlled MRI trial, glatiramer acetate 20 mg daily vs placebo, relapsing-remitting MS
cards.people: 239 patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (119 glatiramer acetate 20 mg daily, 120 placebo), with at least one relapse in the previous 2 years and at least one enhancing lesion on screening MRI, undergoing monthly MRI scans and clinical assessments over 9 months; the primary outcome was the total number of enhancing lesions on T1-weighted images.
cards.result: Glatiramer acetate significantly reduced the total number of enhancing lesions compared with placebo (−10.8 lesions, 95% CI −18.0 to −3.7; P=.003). Almost all secondary MRI endpoints favoured treatment: number of new enhancing lesions (P<.003), monthly change in enhancing-lesion volume (P=.01), and change in volume (P=.006) and number of new T2 lesions (P<.003). The relapse rate was also significantly reduced, by 33% relative, on glatiramer acetate (P=.012). All effects increased over time.
cards.watchOut: A 9-month MRI-primary trial: it establishes biological activity on lesion measures and supports the relapse result, but MRI lesion counts are a surrogate and the trial was not powered for disability.
cards.source: Comi G et al. European/Canadian multicenter, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled study of the effects of glatiramer acetate on magnetic resonance imaging--measured disease activity and burden in patients with relapsing multiple sclerosis. cards.summary: GALA (Khan 2013): glatiramer acetate 40 mg three times weekly reduced the annualised relapse rate versus placebo (0.331 vs 0.505 — a 34% relative reduction, P<.0001); injection-site reactions 35.5% vs 5.0%
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind trial (GALA), glatiramer acetate 40 mg three times weekly vs placebo, relapsing-remitting MS
cards.people: 1,404 patients with relapsing-remitting MS (943 glatiramer acetate 40 mg subcutaneously three times weekly, 461 placebo) with at least one documented relapse in the 12 months before screening (or two in 24 months) and EDSS ≤5.5, randomised 2:1 for 12 months at 142 sites in 17 countries; 93% (placebo) and 91% (glatiramer) completed the study.
cards.result: Glatiramer acetate 40 mg three times weekly was associated with a 34.0% relative reduction in the risk of confirmed relapses (mean annualised relapse rate 0.331 vs 0.505; P<.0001). The cumulative number of gadolinium-enhancing T1 lesions was reduced by 44.8% relative and new or newly enlarging T2 lesions by 34.7% relative at months 6 and 12 (both P<.0001). The treatment was safe and well tolerated; the most common adverse events were injection-site reactions (35.5% on glatiramer vs 5.0% on placebo).
cards.watchOut: A 12-month trial of the less frequent regimen: it confirms the relapse effect at 40 mg three times weekly but, like the earlier trials, its weight is on relapses and MRI, not long-term disability.
cards.source: Khan O et al. Three times weekly glatiramer acetate in relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis. Annals of neurology. 2013. PMID: 23686821. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: three placebo-controlled trials consistently show glatiramer acetate reducing relapses in relapsing-remitting MS by roughly a third in relative terms — the pivotal 20 mg daily trial (mean 2-year relapses 1.19 vs 1.68, a 29% relative reduction), the European/Canadian MRI trial (relapses reduced 33% relative; enhancing lesions −10.8 vs placebo) and GALA at 40 mg three times weekly (annualised relapse rate 0.331 vs 0.505, a 34% relative reduction) — with injection-site reactions and a transient systemic post-injection reaction as the modest pricing harms

shelves.title: Interferon beta in relapsing-remitting MS: beta-1b cut annual exacerbations (0.84 vs 1.27) with no discernible disability effect; PRISMS beta-1a cut relapses by 27–33% relative and delayed disability progression
shelves.question: In patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, does interferon beta (beta-1b every other day; beta-1a three times weekly) reduce exacerbation rates and MRI activity versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Double-Blind Method · Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay · Female · Humans · Interferon-beta · Lymphopenia · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Male · Middle Aged · Multiple Sclerosis · Neurologic Examination · Recurrence · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY benefit for relapses, modest for disability. Interferon beta-1b every other day (pivotal trial, 372 randomised) reduced the annual exacerbation rate versus placebo (0.84 on 8 MIU vs 1.27; the 1.6 MIU dose gave 1.17 — a dose effect), with an MRI companion showing less disease activity, but NO discernible disability effect. Interferon beta-1a three times weekly (PRISMS, 560 randomised) reduced mean 2-year relapses versus placebo (1.73 on 44 µg and 1.82 on 22 µg vs 2.56 — relative reductions of 33% and 27%) and delayed disability progression during the study, with all MRI measures favouring treatment, dose-related. Two products, labelled slices, never pooled.

cards.headline: IFNB-1b pivotal trial — clinical report (IFNB Multiple Sclerosis Study Group 1993): interferon beta-1b 8 MIU every other day reduced the annual exacerbation rate versus placebo (0.84 vs 1.27 at 2 years, P=.0001), with a dose effect — and NO discernible disability effect
cards.summary: IFNB-1b pivotal trial — clinical report (IFNB Multiple Sclerosis Study Group 1993): interferon beta-1b 8 MIU every other day reduced the annual exacerbation rate versus placebo (0.84 vs 1.27 at 2 years, P=.0001), with a dose effect — and NO discernible disability effect
cards.type: Multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (interferon beta-1b pivotal), clinical report, relapsing-remitting MS
cards.people: 372 ambulatory patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (EDSS 0 to 5.5; at least two exacerbations in the previous 2 years) randomised in thirds to placebo, interferon beta-1b 1.6 MIU, or 8 MIU, self-administered subcutaneously every other day; primary endpoints were exacerbation rates and the proportion remaining exacerbation-free.
cards.result: The annual exacerbation rate was 1.27 on placebo, 1.17 on 1.6 MIU and 0.84 on 8 MIU after 2 years — significantly lower in both treatment groups (8 MIU vs placebo P=.0001; 1.6 MIU vs placebo P=.0101; 8 MIU vs 1.6 MIU P=.0086), indicating a dosage effect; the 8 MIU rate is a reduction of about a third relative to placebo, printed beside the absolute rates. The reduction in exacerbation severity in the 8 MIU group reflected a twofold reduction in moderate and severe attacks. More 8 MIU patients (36) than placebo patients (18) were exacerbation-free at 2 years (P=.007). EDSS scores changed little in all arms: a significant change in disability could NOT be discerned in this trial, and that null is printed here rather than dropped.
cards.watchOut: The beta-1b slice of this shelf. The abstract in the record is truncated at 250 words; every number carded is from the fetched record. The disability null belongs on the face: this trial showed relapse reduction without a discernible disability effect.

cards.headline: IFNB-1b pivotal trial — MRI companion report (Paty 1993): interferon beta-1b reduced MRI disease activity (median 80% relative reduction in active scans, P=.0082) and burden of disease (mean group difference 23%, P=.001) — a labelled companion of the same trial
cards.summary: IFNB-1b pivotal trial — MRI companion report (Paty 1993): interferon beta-1b reduced MRI disease activity (median 80% relative reduction in active scans, P=.0082) and burden of disease (mean group difference 23%, P=.001) — a labelled companion of the same trial
cards.type: Labelled companion: MRI analysis report of the interferon beta-1b pivotal randomised trial (same trial as the card above — not an independent trial)
cards.people: Yearly MRI analyses in 327 of the 372 patients in the interferon beta-1b pivotal trial (clinical results in the card above); 52 patients at one centre formed a cohort for frequent MRI (every 6 weeks) to assess disease activity. Baseline MRI characteristics were the same in all treatment groups.
cards.result: MRI results supported the clinical results: a significant reduction in disease activity as measured by numbers of active scans (median 80% relative reduction, P=.0082) and appearance of new lesions, and a significant reduction in MRI-detected burden of disease in the treatment compared with placebo groups (mean group difference of 23%, P=.001).
cards.watchOut: A companion report of the same trial, carded and labelled as such: MRI activity is a surrogate, and this report adds no independent clinical evidence.

cards.headline: PRISMS (PRISMS Study Group 1998): interferon beta-1a three times weekly reduced relapses versus placebo over 2 years (mean relapses per patient 1.82 on 22 µg and 1.73 on 44 µg vs 2.56 — relative reductions of 27% and 33%), delayed disability progression, and improved all MRI measures, dose-related
cards.summary: PRISMS (PRISMS Study Group 1998): interferon beta-1a three times weekly reduced relapses versus placebo over 2 years (mean relapses per patient 1.82 on 22 µg and 1.73 on 44 µg vs 2.56 — relative reductions of 27% and 33%), delayed disability progression, and improved all MRI measures, dose-related
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (PRISMS), interferon beta-1a 22 µg or 44 µg three times weekly vs placebo, relapsing/remitting MS
cards.people: 560 patients with relapsing/remitting multiple sclerosis (EDSS 0–5.0) at 22 centres in nine countries, randomised to subcutaneous interferon beta-1a 22 µg (189), 44 µg (184) or placebo (187) three times weekly for 2 years; clinical data on 533 patients (95%) were available at 2 years, analysed by intention to treat.
cards.result: The relapse rate was significantly lower at 1 and 2 years on both doses than on placebo (mean relapses per patient 1.82 for 22 µg and 1.73 for 44 µg versus 2.56 for placebo: relative risk reductions of 27% [95% CI 14 to 39] and 33% [21 to 44]). Time to first relapse was prolonged by 3 months (22 µg) and 5 months (44 µg), and the proportion of relapse-free patients was significantly increased (P<.05). Interferon beta-1a delayed progression in disability and decreased accumulated disability during the study, and the accumulation of burden of disease and number of active MRI lesions were lower on both doses — effects in a dose-related manner. The treatment was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: The beta-1a slice of this shelf — a different product and regimen from beta-1b, labelled as such and never pooled with it. The disability claim is kept as modest as PRISMS printed it: delayed progression during the 2-year study, not prevention.

cards.headline: PRISMS long-term follow-up (Kappos 2006): patients originally randomised to interferon beta-1a 44 µg three times weekly showed lower EDSS progression, relapse rate and T2 burden up to 8 years than patients whose treatment was delayed — a labelled follow-up companion
cards.summary: PRISMS long-term follow-up (Kappos 2006): patients originally randomised to interferon beta-1a 44 µg three times weekly showed lower EDSS progression, relapse rate and T2 burden up to 8 years than patients whose treatment was delayed — a labelled follow-up companion
cards.type: Labelled companion: long-term follow-up (up to 8 years) of the PRISMS randomised cohort (same programme as the card above — not an independent trial)
cards.people: The original PRISMS cohort of 560 patients; after the 2-year placebo-controlled phase, placebo patients were re-randomised to active treatment and the blinded study continued 4 more years. The long-term follow-up visit, 7–8 years after baseline, was attended by 382 patients (68.2% of the original cohort), of whom 275 (72.0%) were still receiving interferon beta-1a three times weekly.
cards.result: Patients originally randomised to interferon beta-1a 44 µg three times weekly showed lower EDSS progression, relapse rate and T2 burden of disease up to 8 years compared with the late-treatment group; brain parenchymal volume did not differ by treatment group. Overall, 19.7% of patients (75 of 381) progressed to secondary progressive MS between baseline and long-term follow-up. No new safety concerns were identified and treatment was generally well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: A follow-up of the same cohort with the limitations the authors state — only 68.2% attended, and returning and non-returning patients may differ — so the early-versus-delayed comparison is supportive, not definitive.
