shelves.title: Divalproex for migraine prophylaxis: three placebo-controlled trials show a real but modest reduction (about 0.6–2.2 fewer attacks per 4 weeks); teratogenicity is the dominant harm frame
shelves.question: In patients with frequent migraine, does divalproex sodium (immediate- or extended-release) reduce migraine frequency versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Migraine Disorders · Placebos · Valproic Acid
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE benefit — real but modest, on small short trials, with a heavy harm frame. Three placebo-controlled trials agree that divalproex sodium reduces migraine frequency: mean frequency 3.5 vs 5.7 attacks per 4 weeks (Mathew 1995, 107 randomised); mean reductions of 1.7–2.0 vs 0.5 attacks per 4 weeks across 500–1500 mg with no gain at the top dose (Klapper 1997, 176 randomised); and a reduction of 1.2 vs 0.6 attacks for the extended-release form (Freitag 2002; N not documented in its record). Absolute effects, not responder percentages alone, are printed. Teratogenicity is the dominant harm frame for valproate in a largely female, reproductive-age population, with weight gain and tremor; nausea and dizziness were also more frequent at higher doses.

cards.headline: Mathew 1995: divalproex reduced migraine frequency versus placebo (mean attacks per 4 weeks 3.5 vs 5.7 during treatment, P≤.001; ≥50% reduction in 48% vs 14%); discontinuation for intolerance 13% vs 5% (not significant)
cards.summary: Mathew 1995: divalproex reduced migraine frequency versus placebo (mean attacks per 4 weeks 3.5 vs 5.7 during treatment, P≤.001; ≥50% reduction in 48% vs 14%); discontinuation for intolerance 13% vs 5% (not significant)
cards.type: Multicentre double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial, divalproex sodium vs placebo, migraine prophylaxis
cards.people: 107 patients randomised (70 divalproex sodium, 37 placebo, in a 2:1 ratio) at eight US headache/neurology clinics, in a double-blind trial with a 4-week single-blind placebo baseline and a 12-week treatment phase; doses were titrated to trough valproate concentrations of about 70 to 120 mg/L. NOTE: the fetched record for this report is in Archives of neurology (1995), as printed in the source line.
cards.result: During treatment, mean migraine headache frequency per 4 weeks was 3.5 on divalproex versus 5.7 on placebo (P≤.001), from baselines of 6.0 and 6.4 respectively — an absolute difference of about 2.2 attacks per 4 weeks, printed beside the responder figures. Forty-eight percent of divalproex patients versus 14% on placebo achieved a ≥50% reduction in migraine frequency (P<.001). Divalproex patients reported significantly less functional restriction and used significantly less symptomatic medication per episode; no significant differences were seen in peak severity or duration of individual attacks. Treatment was stopped for intolerance in 13% versus 5% (not significant).
cards.watchOut: A small, short (12-week) trial from 1995 with a 2:1 randomisation and a small placebo arm (37 patients): the effect is consistent with the later trials, but no single card on this shelf should be read alone.

cards.headline: Klapper 1997 dose-controlled trial: divalproex 500, 1000 and 1500 mg each reduced migraine attacks versus placebo (mean reductions 1.7, 2.0 and 1.7 attacks per 4 weeks vs 0.5; ≥50% responders 44–45% vs 21%) — with nausea, dizziness and tremor significantly more frequent at 1500 mg
cards.summary: Klapper 1997 dose-controlled trial: divalproex 500, 1000 and 1500 mg each reduced migraine attacks versus placebo (mean reductions 1.7, 2.0 and 1.7 attacks per 4 weeks vs 0.5; ≥50% responders 44–45% vs 21%) — with nausea, dizziness and tremor significantly more frequent at 1500 mg
cards.type: Multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled dose-controlled randomised trial, divalproex sodium 500/1000/1500 mg vs placebo, migraine prophylaxis
cards.people: 176 patients randomised (44 placebo, 132 divalproex across the 500, 1000 and 1500 mg daily-dose groups) who were previously untreated or had failed no more than two adequate prophylactic trials; 171 provided efficacy data and 137 completed the 12-week experimental phase (4 weeks dose escalation, 8 weeks maintenance) after a 4-week placebo baseline. The primary variable was 4-week migraine attack frequency.
cards.result: After adjustment for baseline frequency, mean reductions were 1.7 (500 mg), 2.0 (1000 mg) and 1.7 (1500 mg) migraine attacks per 4 weeks versus 0.5 on placebo (P≤.05 versus placebo for each dose) — absolute reductions, showing no gain from the highest dose. Forty-four to 45% of divalproex patients versus 21% on placebo achieved a ≥50% reduction in attack frequency (P≤.05). Adverse events were similar to placebo except nausea, dizziness and tremor, whose incidence was significantly higher at 1500 mg (nausea was also higher at 500 mg). The author concluded the recommended initial dose is 500 mg per day.
cards.watchOut: The flat dose–response (1500 mg no better than 500 mg, with more adverse effects) is part of the answer: more divalproex is not more prophylaxis.
cards.source: Klapper J et al. Divalproex sodium in migraine prophylaxis: a dose-controlled study. Cephalalgia : an international journal of headache. 1997. PMID: 9137847. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adult · Aged · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Migraine Disorders · Valproic Acid

cards.headline: Freitag 2002 extended-release trial: once-daily divalproex sodium extended-release reduced the 4-week migraine rate more than placebo (mean reduction 1.2 vs 0.6 attacks, P=.006); discontinuation for adverse events 8% vs 9% — the randomised number is not documented in the fetched record
cards.summary: Freitag 2002 extended-release trial: once-daily divalproex sodium extended-release reduced the 4-week migraine rate more than placebo (mean reduction 1.2 vs 0.6 attacks, P=.006); discontinuation for adverse events 8% vs 9% — the randomised number is not documented in the fetched record
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, divalproex sodium extended-release vs placebo, migraine prophylaxis
cards.people: Patients with more than two migraine attacks during a 4-week baseline, randomised 1:1 to extended-release divalproex sodium once daily (500 mg for 1 week, then 1000 mg, with an option to reduce to 500 mg for intolerance) or matching placebo for 12 weeks. The total randomised number is NOT documented in the abstract record fetched this session and is therefore not printed — see the watch-out.
cards.result: The mean reduction in 4-week migraine headache rate was 1.2 (from a baseline mean of 4.4) on extended-release divalproex versus 0.6 (from a baseline mean of 4.2) on placebo (P=.006) — an absolute between-group difference of 0.6 attacks per 4 weeks, the smallest effect on this shelf, printed as such. Reductions were significantly greater on divalproex in all three 4-week treatment segments. No significant differences were detected in the overall incidence or any specific treatment-emergent adverse event; 8% on divalproex and 9% on placebo discontinued for adverse events.
cards.watchOut: N not documented in the fetched record: the abstract gives rates and percentages but no randomised total, so this card prints no N rather than importing one from outside the record. The between-group effect (0.6 attacks per 4 weeks) is modest and should be quoted in absolute terms.
cards.source: Freitag FG et al. A randomized trial of divalproex sodium extended-release tablets in migraine prophylaxis. Neurology. 2002. PMID: 12058094. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: three placebo-controlled trials from 1995–2002 consistently show divalproex sodium reducing migraine frequency — by about 2.2 attacks per 4 weeks versus placebo in the Mathew trial (3.5 vs 5.7), by 1.7–2.0 versus 0.5 attacks in the dose-controlled Klapper trial (with no benefit above 500–1000 mg and more nausea, dizziness and tremor at 1500 mg), and by a smaller 0.6 attacks per 4 weeks for the extended-release form — a real but modest effect, in a drug whose dominant harm frame is valproate's teratogenicity in a largely female, reproductive-age population, alongside weight gain and tremor

cards.result: Responder proportions tell the same story in relative dress (≥50% reduction in 48% vs 14%; 44–45% vs 21%), which is why this shelf leads with the absolute attack-frequency numbers, as the commissioning row directs. The trials are small (107 and 176 randomised; the extended-release trial's N is not documented in its record) and short (12 weeks each), so the stamp is POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY despite three concordant positive trials. Teratogenicity is stated qualitatively on this card as the governing harm frame for valproate in women who could become pregnant; no teratogenicity rate is printed, because none appears in the records carded here.

shelves.title: TCD normal velocities: MCA 58 ± 15.6 cm/s by conventional TCD (106 volunteers, falling with age); women-only MCA ≈68 cm/s falling to ≈60 after 50; angle-corrected duplex MCA range 37.7–112.5 cm/s
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what are the normal transcranial Doppler (TCD) blood-flow velocities — mean velocities in the middle cerebral, anterior and posterior cerebral, carotid siphon and basilar arteries — by age and sex, and how much do insonation-angle correction (transcranial colour-coded duplex) and age move them?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Blood Flow Velocity/physiology · Brain/anatomy & histology,blood supply · Cephalometry · Cerebral Arteries/anatomy & histology,diagnostic imaging,physiology · Child · Echoencephalography · Humans · Middle Aged · Reference Values · Skull/anatomy & histology,diagnostic imaging · Vertebral Artery/anatomy & histology,diagnostic imaging,physiology
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Boron & Boulpaep / Guyton & Hall, cerebral circulation sections — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary normative ultrasound literature, and says so. Three independent adult datasets, carded PER METHOD because conventional transcranial Doppler (uncorrected insonation angle) and transcranial colour-coded duplex (angle-corrected) velocities are not interchangeable: the 1990 conventional-TCD dataset of 106 normal volunteers (middle cerebral artery M1 mean 58 ± 15.6 cm/s, posterior cerebral 39 ± 9.9, carotid siphon 47 ± 13.8, basilar trunk 41 ± 10, with a marked decrease with age and low side-to-side differences); a women-only dataset of 100 healthy Italian women (middle cerebral mean ≈67–68 cm/s overall, falling from ≈81–83 cm/s under 20 years to ≈59–61 cm/s over 50 — labelled women-only on its card); and a 2020 colour-coded-duplex dataset (195 enrolled, 162 analysed) whose angle-corrected 2.5th–97.5th percentile ranges (middle cerebral 37.7–112.5 cm/s; anterior cerebral 25.6–71.2; posterior cerebral 29.2–80.8) differ widely from its own 0° values. The paediatric dataset and the normative-ranges book chapter named at mining are NOT carded — a secondary source and a different population, respectively. The stamp is graded down because the total base is three datasets, one is women-only, one predates colour-coded duplex, and the method split means there is no single method-free normal velocity. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING.

cards.headline: First normative dataset, conventional TCD (Ringelstein 1990, 106 normal volunteers): mean flow velocities — MCA M1 segment 58 ± 15.6 cm/s, posterior cerebral 39 ± 9.9, carotid siphon 47 ± 13.8, basilar trunk 41 ± 10 — with a marked decrease with age and low side-to-side differences
cards.summary: First normative dataset, conventional TCD (Ringelstein 1990, 106 normal volunteers): mean flow velocities — MCA M1 segment 58 ± 15.6 cm/s, posterior cerebral 39 ± 9.9, carotid siphon 47 ± 13.8, basilar trunk 41 ± 10 — with a marked decrease with age and low side-to-side differences
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset (conventional transcranial Doppler normative velocities and insonation landmarks, 106 normal volunteers)
cards.people: 106 normal volunteers examined by transcranial Doppler sonography, within a study that also elaborated anatomical landmarks from 64 carotid and 42 vertebral angiograms, 40 contrast-enhanced CT scans, 122 normal sagittal MRI scans, 40 cadaver skulls and 38 fresh cadavers, plus 59 patients with subclavian steal mechanisms. Insonation depths are part of the normative data: inner internal carotid bifurcation 60.4 ± 7 mm, M1 segment 40 ± 8 to 60.4 ± 7 mm, carotid siphon C3 segment 62 ± 4 mm, vertebral artery junction 84 ± 8 mm, top of the basilar artery 108 ± 8 mm.
cards.result: Normal mean flow velocities were 58 ± 15.6 cm/s in the M1 segment of the middle cerebral artery, 39 ± 9.9 cm/s in the posterior cerebral artery, 47 ± 13.8 cm/s in the carotid siphon and 41 ± 10 cm/s in the basilar trunk, and revealed a marked decrease with age. Intraindividual side-to-side differences were low. Vertebrobasilar data from neuroradiological material closely matched the in-vivo findings in normals and patients, and the paper provides criteria for identifying the various vessel segments.
cards.watchOut: Conventional (blind, angle-uncorrected) TCD from 1990: these means are the reference for that technique only. The colour-coded card below shows how far angle correction moves the numbers, so a 1990 mean must never be applied as a cut-off to an angle-corrected duplex measurement.
cards.source: Ringelstein EB et al. Transcranial Doppler sonography: anatomical landmarks and normal velocity values. Ultrasound in medicine & biology. 1990. PMID: 2095006. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Women-only normative dataset (Liboni 2006, 100 healthy Italian women): MCA mean velocity 68.06 ± 9.22 cm/s (left) and 66.71 ± 8.79 (right) overall, falling with age from 82.55 ± 6.85 (left, under 20 years) to 60.67 ± 6.85 (over 50 years) — labelled women-only
cards.summary: Women-only normative dataset (Liboni 2006, 100 healthy Italian women): MCA mean velocity 68.06 ± 9.22 cm/s (left) and 66.71 ± 8.79 (right) overall, falling with age from 82.55 ± 6.85 (left, under 20 years) to 60.67 ± 6.85 (over 50 years) — labelled women-only
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset (transcranial Doppler MCA normative ranges across the lifespan, women only)
cards.people: 100 healthy women (mean age 38 ± 15.14 years, range 12–78) in Italy, examined by transcranial Doppler of the middle cerebral artery and subdivided into four age groups: under 20 years, 20–34, 35–50, and over 50 years. A women-only dataset, labelled as such; it includes adolescents at the youngest end, and the adult age bands are the carded content.
cards.result: There was no statistically significant difference between mean blood-flow velocity in the left and right middle cerebral arteries (left 68.06 ± 9.22 cm/s; right 66.71 ± 8.79 cm/s). Velocities decreased significantly with increasing age: left/right MCA 82.55 ± 6.85 / 80.27 ± 4.13 cm/s in the youngest group; 72.15 ± 6.37 / 70.68 ± 6.79 cm/s at 20–34 years; 63.85 ± 7.08 / 63.06 ± 7.29 cm/s at 35–50 years; and 60.67 ± 6.85 / 59.10 ± 5.36 cm/s over 50 years. The study defines a normal age-related range of MCA velocities for comparison with pathological female subjects.
cards.watchOut: Women only, one vessel (the middle cerebral artery), and one national population: it cannot supply male norms or norms for the anterior/posterior cerebral, siphon or basilar arteries. Its overall MCA mean (≈67–68 cm/s) sits above the 1990 mixed-sex M1 mean (58 cm/s) — a sex-, era- and technique-bound difference, not a contradiction to be averaged away.
cards.source: Liboni W et al. Transcranial Doppler for monitoring the cerebral blood flow dynamics: normal ranges in the Italian female population. Panminerva medica. 2006. PMID: 17122755. cards.headline: Angle-corrected colour-coded duplex norms (Barrientos-Guerra 2020, 195 healthy adults enrolled, 162 analysed): after insonation-angle correction, 2.5th–97.5th percentile velocity ranges were MCA 37.7–112.5 cm/s, ACA 25.6–71.2 and PCA 29.2–80.8 — with wide discrepancies from the uncorrected 0° values
cards.summary: Angle-corrected colour-coded duplex norms (Barrientos-Guerra 2020, 195 healthy adults enrolled, 162 analysed): after insonation-angle correction, 2.5th–97.5th percentile velocity ranges were MCA 37.7–112.5 cm/s, ACA 25.6–71.2 and PCA 29.2–80.8 — with wide discrepancies from the uncorrected 0° values
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset (transcranial colour-coded duplex normative values with insonation-angle correction, three age groups)
cards.people: 195 healthy adults equally allocated to three age groups (18–40, 41–60, ≥61 years), studied by conventional pulsed transcranial Doppler and transcranial colour-coded sonography (TCCS) through the temporal window; 33 were excluded (inadequate acoustic window 10.3%, carotid disease 2.1%, embryonic variants 4.6%), leaving 162 for the final analysis (50% female, median age 48 years). Peak systolic, end-diastolic and mean velocities and pulsatility/resistance indices were registered at 0° and after angle correction.
cards.result: The 2.5th–97.5th percentiles of the corrected insonation angle were 0°–60° for the middle cerebral artery, 0°–44° for the anterior cerebral artery and 30°–60° for the posterior cerebral artery. After angle correction, the 2.5th–97.5th percentile flow-velocity ranges were 37.7–112.5 cm/s (MCA), 25.6–71.2 cm/s (ACA) and 29.2–80.8 cm/s (PCA). There were wide discrepancies between haemodynamic values obtained at 0° and after angle correction; no differences were found between methods at exactly 0° or between hemispheres, but values differed by age and sex. The authors conclude that specific normative tables should be used in TCCS whenever the corrected angle is greater than 0°.
cards.watchOut: The method lesson is the content: angle correction is not a refinement of the same number but a different number — the corrected MCA range (up to 112.5 cm/s) would read as abnormal against uncorrected norms. One in ten healthy adults (10.3%) had an inadequate temporal acoustic window and contributes no values at all.

cards.headline: Synthesis: normal TCD velocities are method-bound — conventional TCD centres the MCA near 58 cm/s with a clear age decline, women-only MCA data run higher and fall from ≈82 to ≈60 cm/s across adult life, and angle-corrected duplex ranges are far wider and higher
cards.summary: Synthesis: normal TCD velocities are method-bound — conventional TCD centres the MCA near 58 cm/s with a clear age decline, women-only MCA data run higher and fall from ≈82 to ≈60 cm/s across adult life, and angle-corrected duplex ranges are far wider and higher
cards.people: Synthesis of the three primary datasets carded above.
cards.result: Framed by Boron & Boulpaep / Guyton & Hall (cerebral circulation; framing brief — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary normative ultrasound literature). All three datasets agree on the qualitative physiology: velocities fall with age, and side-to-side differences within a person are small. They do not yield one universal number: Ringelstein 1990 (conventional TCD, 106 volunteers) gives MCA M1 58 ± 15.6, PCA 39 ± 9.9, siphon 47 ± 13.8 and basilar 41 ± 10 cm/s; Liboni 2006 (women only, 100) gives an overall MCA mean of ≈67–68 cm/s declining by age band; Barrientos-Guerra 2020 (colour-coded duplex, 162 analysed) shows angle correction widening and raising the ranges (MCA 37.7–112.5 cm/s). PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: the adult normative base is three datasets, one women-only and one from the pre-duplex era, and every value is bound to its insonation method, as printed on each card.
cards.watchOut: Never apply an uncorrected-TCD reference range to an angle-corrected duplex study or vice versa, and never use the women-only MCA ranges as male norms.

shelves.title: Adjunctive levetiracetam in refractory partial seizures: responder rates roughly tripled versus placebo with a dose gradient, in three randomised trials
shelves.question: In patients with refractory partial seizures, does adjunctive levetiracetam (1,000–3,000 mg/day) reduce seizure frequency versus placebo, and can responders convert to levetiracetam monotherapy?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Anticonvulsants · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Electroencephalography · Epilepsies, Partial · Female · Humans · Levetiracetam · Male · Middle Aged · Piracetam · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit). Three randomised placebo-controlled trials of adjunctive levetiracetam in refractory partial seizures agree, with a dose gradient: ≥50% responder rates 22.8% (1,000 mg/day, European trial) and 33.0% (1,000 mg/day, Cereghino) rising to 31.6% (2,000 mg/day) and 39.8% (3,000 mg/day), versus 10.4–10.8% on placebo (absolute rates). In Cereghino, 11 levetiracetam patients became seizure-free and no placebo patient did. Harms are modest: asthenia, somnolence and dizziness, with overall adverse-event incidence no different from placebo in the European trial (73.2%). The third report (Ben-Menachem) is a labelled responder-selected design: its monotherapy conversion figures (59.2% responder rate, 18.4% seizure-free) describe only patients who had already responded to add-on levetiracetam, never unselected patients.

cards.headline: Cereghino 2000 RCT: adjunctive levetiracetam cut refractory partial seizures — ≥50% responder rates 33.0% at 1,000 mg/day and 39.8% at 3,000 mg/day versus 10.8% on placebo (absolute rates); 11 levetiracetam patients became seizure-free, none on placebo
cards.summary: Cereghino 2000 RCT: adjunctive levetiracetam cut refractory partial seizures — ≥50% responder rates 33.0% at 1,000 mg/day and 39.8% at 3,000 mg/day versus 10.8% on placebo (absolute rates); 11 levetiracetam patients became seizure-free, none on placebo
cards.type: Double-blind randomised placebo-controlled parallel-group multicentre trial, adjunctive levetiracetam 1,000 or 3,000 mg/day in refractory partial seizures
cards.people: 294 patients with uncontrolled partial seizures (at least 12 per 12 weeks), with or without secondary generalisation, randomised after a 12-week baseline to adjunctive placebo (n=95), levetiracetam 1,000 mg/day (n=98) or levetiracetam 3,000 mg/day (n=101), with 4 weeks of upward titration, 14 weeks of fixed-dose treatment and an 8-week withdrawal or follow-up period; 268 completed the study.
cards.result: Partial seizure frequency over the whole evaluation period was significantly lower with levetiracetam than placebo (P≤0.001 for both doses). More patients responded (at least a 50% reduction in partial seizure frequency) on levetiracetam than placebo: 33.0% at 1,000 mg/day and 39.8% at 3,000 mg/day versus 10.8% on placebo (P<0.001) — absolute responder rates, a difference of roughly 22–29 percentage points. Of 199 patients receiving levetiracetam, 11 became seizure-free; no placebo patient did. Treatment-emergent adverse events at ≥10% incidence and more frequent than on placebo — mostly mild to moderate — were asthenia, dizziness, flu syndrome, headache, infection, rhinitis and somnolence.
cards.watchOut: Short fixed-dose evaluation (14 weeks) in highly refractory patients already failing other drugs — responder rates here are add-on effects on top of existing therapy, not what levetiracetam achieves as first treatment. No registry ID is in the PubMed record (pre-registration era).
cards.source: Cereghino et al. Levetiracetam for partial seizures: results of a double-blind, randomized clinical trial. Neurology. 2000. PMID: 10908898. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: European Levetiracetam Study Group RCT (Shorvon 2000): adjunctive levetiracetam responder rates 22.8% at 1,000 mg/day and 31.6% at 2,000 mg/day versus 10.4% on placebo — with adverse-event incidence no different from placebo (73.2%)
cards.summary: European Levetiracetam Study Group RCT (Shorvon 2000): adjunctive levetiracetam responder rates 22.8% at 1,000 mg/day and 31.6% at 2,000 mg/day versus 10.4% on placebo — with adverse-event incidence no different from placebo (73.2%)
cards.type: Multicentre double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial (European Levetiracetam Study Group), adjunctive levetiracetam 1,000 or 2,000 mg/day in refractory partial seizures
cards.people: 324 patients with uncontrolled simple or complex partial seizures, with or without secondary generalisation, in a European multicentre double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial of levetiracetam 500 or 1,000 mg twice daily versus placebo as add-on therapy, after an 8- or 12-week baseline, with 4 weeks of titration and a 12-week evaluation period.
cards.result: Levetiracetam significantly decreased partial seizure frequency versus placebo. A reduction in seizure frequency of ≥50% occurred in 22.8% of patients in the 1,000-mg/day group and 31.6% in the 2,000-mg/day group, compared with 10.4% on placebo (absolute rates). Levetiracetam did not affect plasma concentrations of concomitant antiepileptic drugs or alter vital signs or laboratory parameters. There was no significant difference in adverse-event incidence between the levetiracetam groups (70.8% at 1,000 mg/day, 75.5% at 2,000 mg/day) and placebo (73.2%); the commonest adverse effects on levetiracetam were asthenia, headache and somnolence.
cards.watchOut: A 12-week evaluation period — durability beyond three months is not tested here. The absence of an adverse-event excess over placebo in this trial should be read alongside the Cereghino card, where several events did exceed placebo. No registry ID is in the PubMed record.

cards.headline: Ben-Menachem 2000 — RESPONDER-SELECTED design, labelled: patients who responded to add-on levetiracetam 3,000 mg/day (responder rate 42.1% vs 16.7% on placebo) could convert to levetiracetam monotherapy, where 59.2% responded and 18.4% remained seizure-free
cards.summary: Ben-Menachem 2000 — RESPONDER-SELECTED design, labelled: patients who responded to add-on levetiracetam 3,000 mg/day (responder rate 42.1% vs 16.7% on placebo) could convert to levetiracetam monotherapy, where 59.2% responded and 18.4% remained seizure-free
cards.type: Multicentre double-blind responder-selected study (European Levetiracetam Study Group): add-on levetiracetam 3,000 mg/day, with responders converting to levetiracetam monotherapy — labelled responder-selected design
cards.people: 286 patients with refractory partial seizures entered a double-blind add-on phase, randomised 2:1 to oral levetiracetam 1,500 mg twice daily (n=181) or placebo (n=105) for 12 weeks. Only treatment responders (≥50% reduction in partial seizure frequency) entered the monotherapy phase — 86 patients (69 levetiracetam, 17 placebo) — with up to 12 weeks of down-titration of other drugs and 12 weeks of monotherapy at 3,000 mg/day.
cards.result: During the add-on phase the responder rate was significantly higher on levetiracetam than placebo (42.1% vs 16.7%; P<0.001 — absolute rates). Thirty-six of 181 levetiracetam patients (19.9%) completed the entire study versus 10 of 105 (9.5%) on placebo (P=0.029); the odds of completing on levetiracetam were 2.36 times those on placebo (95% CI 1.08 to 5.57 — a relative measure). In the levetiracetam monotherapy group the median reduction in partial seizure frequency versus baseline was 73.8% (P=0.037), with a responder rate of 59.2%, and nine patients (18.4%) remained seizure-free on monotherapy.
cards.watchOut: The monotherapy figures describe only the pre-selected minority who had already responded to levetiracetam as add-on therapy — 69 of 181 levetiracetam patients reached that phase. They must never be read as monotherapy results in unselected patients. No registry ID is in the PubMed record.

shelves.title: Adjunctive lamotrigine in refractory partial seizures: modest benefit, significant only at 500 mg/day in the one parallel-group trial, with two small labelled crossovers
shelves.question: In patients with partial seizures refractory to established antiseizure drugs, does adjunctive lamotrigine reduce seizure frequency versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Anticonvulsants · Double-Blind Method · Epilepsies, Partial · Female · Humans · Lamotrigine · Male · Middle Aged · Triazines
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). One parallel-group randomised trial carries the weight (Matsuo, n=216): adjunctive lamotrigine reduced median seizure frequency by 36% at 500 mg/day versus 8% on placebo, with one-third of the 500-mg group achieving ≥50% reduction — but the 300-mg dose was not significant. Two labelled crossover companions point the same way: Smith (n=81) found a 29.7% relative reduction in total seizures yet only 11 patients halved their seizures, and Schapel (n=41 — small, labelled) found 22% versus 0% achieving ≥50% reduction. Harms in the trials were mostly minor, with 9% withdrawing for adverse experiences in Matsuo; none of the carded records quantifies lamotrigine's serious-rash titration risk, which is a label matter outside this evidence base.

cards.headline: U.S. Lamotrigine Protocol 0.5 RCT (Matsuo 1993): adjunctive lamotrigine reduced median seizure frequency by 20% at 300 mg/day and 36% at 500 mg/day versus 8% on placebo — significant only at 500 mg; one-third of the 500-mg group achieved ≥50% reduction
cards.summary: U.S. Lamotrigine Protocol 0.5 RCT (Matsuo 1993): adjunctive lamotrigine reduced median seizure frequency by 20% at 300 mg/day and 36% at 500 mg/day versus 8% on placebo — significant only at 500 mg; one-third of the 500-mg group achieved ≥50% reduction
cards.type: Multicentre randomised double-blind parallel-group placebo-controlled trial (U.S. Lamotrigine Protocol 0.5), adjunctive lamotrigine 300 or 500 mg/day in refractory partial seizures — the shelf's load-bearing trial
cards.people: 216 patients with refractory partial seizures in a multicentre randomised double-blind parallel-group placebo-controlled study of add-on lamotrigine 300 or 500 mg/day over 6 months of treatment.
cards.result: Median seizure frequency decreased by 8% with placebo, 20% with lamotrigine 300 mg/day and 36% with 500 mg/day (percentage reductions in median frequency, as published). Seizure frequency fell by ≥50% in one-third of the 500-mg group and one-fifth of the 300-mg group. Reductions in seizure frequency and seizure days were statistically significant versus placebo for the 500-mg group but not the 300-mg group. Most adverse events were minor and resolved over time; 9% of patients on lamotrigine withdrew because of adverse experiences. Lamotrigine plasma concentrations were a linear function of dose, and the drug did not affect plasma concentrations of concomitant antiepileptic drugs.
cards.watchOut: The significant effect is at 500 mg/day only — the 300-mg dose did not separate significantly from placebo, so the dose matters to the conclusion. This 1993 record does not quantify rash; the serious-rash titration risk of lamotrigine is a regulatory-label matter and is not measured in any abstract carded here. No registry ID is in the PubMed record (pre-registration era).

cards.headline: Smith 1993 crossover RCT: adjunctive lamotrigine reduced seizure frequency relative to placebo by 29.7% for total seizures and 33.4% for complex partial seizures (relative measures) — but only 11 of 81 patients achieved a ≥50% reduction, the report's own caution
cards.summary: Smith 1993 crossover RCT: adjunctive lamotrigine reduced seizure frequency relative to placebo by 29.7% for total seizures and 33.4% for complex partial seizures (relative measures) — but only 11 of 81 patients achieved a ≥50% reduction, the report's own caution
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial, adjunctive lamotrigine in refractory partial epilepsy, with quality-of-life outcomes — labelled crossover companion
cards.people: 81 patients with refractory partial seizures in a randomised placebo-controlled double-blind crossover study of add-on lamotrigine, which also tested a health-related quality-of-life model with seizure-severity, happiness and mastery scales as secondary measures.
cards.result: The reduction in seizure frequency with lamotrigine, relative to placebo, was 29.7% (95% CI 17.8% to 39.9%) for total seizure count, 33.4% (14.8% to 47.9%) for complex partial seizures and 20.3% (0.3% to 36.2%) for secondarily generalised tonic-clonic seizures — all relative measures, as published. However, although 41 patients elected to continue lamotrigine, only 11 experienced at least a 50% reduction in total seizures. Seizure-severity scores (ictal subscale P=0.017; caregiver subscale P=0.035) and happiness (P=0.003) and mastery (P=0.003) scores also favoured lamotrigine, and the authors' analyses indicated these effects were independent of the seizure-frequency effect.
cards.watchOut: A crossover design in 81 patients: period effects and carryover cannot be excluded from the record, and the headline percentage reductions are relative to placebo-period counts, not responder rates — only 11 patients halved their seizures. No registry ID is in the PubMed record.
cards.source: Smith et al. Outcomes of add-on treatment with lamotrigine in partial epilepsy. Epilepsia. 1993. PMID: 8453943. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Schapel 1993 crossover RCT — SMALL, n=41, labelled: total seizure counts were significantly lower on adjunctive lamotrigine than placebo (P<0.001), and 22% achieved ≥50% reduction versus none on placebo
cards.summary: Schapel 1993 crossover RCT — SMALL, n=41, labelled: total seizure counts were significantly lower on adjunctive lamotrigine than placebo (P<0.001), and 22% achieved ≥50% reduction versus none on placebo
cards.type: Multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial, adjunctive lamotrigine in treatment-resistant partial seizures — SMALL (n=41), labelled companion
cards.people: 41 patients with partial seizures poorly controlled by established antiepileptic drugs, entered at four centres into a multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial: two 12-week treatment periods, each followed by a 4-week washout. Lamotrigine dose was 150 or 300 mg daily depending on concomitant drugs, targeting concentrations of 1–3 mg/L. All 41 patients completed the study. SMALL TRIAL (n=41) — labelled on the face and never load-bearing.
cards.result: There was a highly significant (P<0.001) decrease in total seizure counts on lamotrigine compared with placebo. Overall, 22% of patients experienced at least a 50% reduction in the total number of all seizure types on lamotrigine, compared with none on placebo (absolute rates). Total numbers of partial seizures (simple and complex) were also significantly reduced (P<0.05); the trend for secondarily generalised seizures did not reach significance (0.05<P<0.1). Concomitant antiepileptic drug plasma concentrations were virtually unchanged.
cards.watchOut: n=41 is a small crossover: the 22%-versus-none responder contrast rests on about nine patients, and the study cannot price harms. It is carded as a labelled companion to the n=216 Matsuo trial, which carries the shelf's weight. No registry ID is in the PubMed record.

shelves.title: Sumatriptan for acute migraine: subcutaneous relief at 1 hour and oral relief at 2 hours, with no gain above 100 mg orally
shelves.question: In adults treating an acute migraine attack, does sumatriptan — 6 mg subcutaneously or 100 mg orally — relieve headache and associated symptoms versus placebo, and what does the dose–response look like?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Administration, Oral · Humans · Indoles · Migraine Disorders · Pyrrolidines · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Recurrence · Serotonin Receptor Agonists · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome · Triazoles · Tryptamines
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit), by both routes, carded as labelled limbs. Subcutaneous 6 mg (two trials, 1,104 randomised): at 1 hour, headache reduced to mild/none in 70% versus 22% and complete relief in 49% versus 9% (absolute rates), with tingling, dizziness, warm/hot sensations and injection-site reactions, and no statistical evidence that a second injection adds benefit. Oral (1,130 patients): 2-hour response 67% at 100 mg, 73% at 200 mg and 67% at 300 mg versus 27% on placebo, while adverse events rose with dose (36%, 47%, 53% vs 17%) — no efficacy gain above 100 mg. The labelled Ferrari meta-analysis (53 triptan trials, 24,089 patients) gives class context: sumatriptan 100 mg response 59%, pain-free 29%, sustained pain-free 20%, with placebo-subtracted chest adverse events of 1.9%.

cards.headline: SUBCUTANEOUS limb — Cady 1991 (two parallel trials, 1,104 randomised): sumatriptan 6 mg subcutaneously reduced headache to mild/none at 1 hour in 70% versus 22% on placebo and gave complete relief in 49% versus 9% (absolute rates); a second injection showed no statistical evidence of added benefit
cards.summary: SUBCUTANEOUS limb — Cady 1991 (two parallel trials, 1,104 randomised): sumatriptan 6 mg subcutaneously reduced headache to mild/none at 1 hour in 70% versus 22% on placebo and gave complete relief in 49% versus 9% (absolute rates); a second injection showed no statistical evidence of added benefit
cards.type: Two parallel-group randomised double-blind trials, subcutaneous sumatriptan 6 mg for acute migraine — subcutaneous limb
cards.people: Adult migraine patients in two parallel-group trials conducted in the United States, randomised to 6 mg sumatriptan succinate subcutaneously (n=734) or placebo (n=370) for an acute attack. Patients with residual migraine received another injection: those who had received sumatriptan received either a second active injection (n=187) or placebo (n=178); those who had received placebo received a second placebo injection (n=335).
cards.result: At 1 hour, sumatriptan was significantly more effective than placebo in reducing moderate or severe headache pain to mild or no pain (70% vs 22%), in completely relieving headache (49% vs 9%) and in improving clinical disability (76% vs 34%) — all absolute rates. Sumatriptan also reduced nausea and photophobia significantly better than placebo. Statistical evidence for benefit of a second sumatriptan injection was absent. Adverse events associated with sumatriptan were tingling, dizziness, warm/hot sensations and injection-site reactions.
cards.watchOut: Two trials reported together in one paper, with a 1-hour endpoint specific to the injectable route — the speed advantage over oral treatment is a route property, and these rates must not be compared directly with the oral card's 2-hour rates. No registry ID is in the PubMed record (pre-registration era).

cards.headline: ORAL limb — Oral Sumatriptan Dose-Defining Study Group 1991: 2-hour headache response was 67% at 100 mg, 73% at 200 mg and 67% at 300 mg versus 27% on placebo, while adverse events rose with dose (36%, 47%, 53% vs 17%) — no efficacy gain above 100 mg
cards.summary: ORAL limb — Oral Sumatriptan Dose-Defining Study Group 1991: 2-hour headache response was 67% at 100 mg, 73% at 200 mg and 67% at 300 mg versus 27% on placebo, while adverse events rose with dose (36%, 47%, 53% vs 17%) — no efficacy gain above 100 mg
cards.type: Double-blind placebo-controlled parallel-group dose-defining study (Oral Sumatriptan Dose-Defining Study Group), oral sumatriptan 100–300 mg for acute migraine — oral limb
cards.people: 1,130 patients from 51 centres in eight countries treating up to three migraine attacks at home over 3 months, in a double-blind placebo-controlled parallel-group study of oral sumatriptan 100, 200 or 300 mg as dispersible tablets, with results recorded on diary cards and monthly clinic safety follow-ups.
cards.result: All doses of sumatriptan were significantly (P<0.001) more effective than placebo at relieving headache within 2 hours. Response rates were: placebo 27%; sumatriptan 100 mg 67%; 200 mg 73%; 300 mg 67% (absolute rates). The proportion requiring rescue medication within 2 hours was significantly lower in all active groups than placebo. Response was the same irrespective of migraine type (with or without aura) or duration of symptoms before treatment. Sumatriptan also gave significant relief from nausea and photophobia versus placebo. Most adverse events were mild to moderate and transient, but their incidence at the first treated attack was dose-related: 36%, 47% and 53% for 100, 200 and 300 mg respectively, versus 17% on placebo (P<0.001 for each dose versus placebo).
cards.watchOut: Patients treated up to three attacks, so attack-level and patient-level results are intertwined in this 1991 record. The flat efficacy curve with rising adverse events is the prescribing point: nothing in this trial supports doses above 100 mg. No registry ID is in the PubMed record.

double-blind placebo-controlled parallel-group dose-defining study (oral sumatriptan dose-defining study group), oral sumatriptan 100–300 mg for acute migraine — oral limb 1,130 patients from 51 centres in eight countries treating up to three migraine attacks at home over 3 months, in a double-blind placebo-controlled parallel-group study of oral sumatriptan 100, 200 or 300 mg as dispersible tablets, with results recorded on diary cards and monthly clinic safety follow-ups. all doses of sumatriptan were significantly (p<0.001) more effective than placebo at relieving headache within 2 hours. response rates were: placebo 27%; sumatriptan 100 mg 67%; 200 mg 73%; 300 mg 67% (absolute rates). the proportion requiring rescue medication within 2 hours was significantly lower in all active groups than placebo. response was the same irrespective of migraine type (with or without aura) or duration of symptoms before treatment. sumatriptan also gave significant relief from nausea and photophobia versus placebo. most adverse events were mild to moderate and transient, but their incidence at the first treated attack was dose-related: 36%, 47% and 53% for 100, 200 and 300 mg respectively, versus 17% on placebo (p<0.001 for each dose versus placebo). patients treated up to three attacks, so attack-level and patient-level results are intertwined in this 1991 record. the flat efficacy curve with rising adverse events is the prescribing point: nothing in this trial supports doses above 100 mg. no registry id is in the pubmed record. oral sumatriptan dose-defining study group. sumatriptan--an oral dose-defining study. the oral sumatriptan dose-defining study group. european neurology. 1991. pmid: 1653137. registry id: none in the record. mesh: administration, oral · adult · consumer behavior · double-blind method · female · humans · indoles · male · migraine disorders · nausea · sulfonamides · sumatriptan · vasoconstrictor agents · vomiting

cards.headline: COMPANION meta-analysis, labelled (Ferrari 2001): across 53 triptan trials (24,089 patients), sumatriptan 100 mg orally gave 2-hour headache response 59%, pain-free 29% and sustained pain-free 20% (absolute summary rates), with placebo-subtracted chest adverse events of 1.9%
cards.summary: COMPANION meta-analysis, labelled (Ferrari 2001): across 53 triptan trials (24,089 patients), sumatriptan 100 mg orally gave 2-hour headache response 59%, pain-free 29% and sustained pain-free 20% (absolute summary rates), with placebo-subtracted chest adverse events of 1.9%
cards.type: Meta-analysis of 53 oral triptan trials (Ferrari et al.) — labelled meta-analytic companion, class context only
cards.people: 53 double-blind randomised controlled trials of oral triptans in migraine (12 unpublished), involving 24,089 patients, in a meta-analysis built from raw patient data obtained from pharmaceutical companies and principal investigators. This card is a labelled meta-analytic companion giving class context for the two primary sumatriptan reports above — it is not a third sumatriptan trial.
cards.result: Mean results for sumatriptan 100 mg were 59% (95% CI 57 to 60) for 2-hour headache response, 29% (27 to 30) for 2-hour pain-free, 20% (18 to 21) for sustained pain-free (pain-free by 2 hours with no recurrence or rescue medication at 2–24 hours) and 67% (63 to 70) for consistency (response in at least two of three treated attacks) — absolute summary rates. Placebo-subtracted proportions for patients with at least one adverse event were 13% (8 to 18), for at least one central nervous system adverse event 6% (3 to 9), and for at least one chest adverse event 1.9% (1.0 to 2.7). Across the class, all oral triptans at marketed doses were effective and well tolerated; 10 mg rizatriptan showed better efficacy and consistency than sumatriptan 100 mg, and 80 mg eletriptan better efficacy with lower tolerability.
cards.watchOut: A class meta-analysis, not sumatriptan-only evidence: 41 of its 53 trials tested other triptans, and 12 trials were unpublished data supplied by manufacturers. Its sumatriptan 100 mg summary rates (59% response) sit below the dose-defining trial's 67% because they pool many trials — the two figures describe different evidence sets and are not a contradiction. No registry ID is in the PubMed record.

shelves.title: Alteplase in acute ischaemic stroke: benefit within 3 hours and at 3–4.5 hours, an unproven primary endpoint up to 6 hours (IST-3) — windows never pooled
shelves.question: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke, does intravenous alteplase (0.9 mg/kg where the record states it) improve functional outcome versus placebo/control — within 3 hours (NINDS), at 3–4.5 hours (ECASS III), and in a wider population up to 6 hours (IST-3) — and at what intracranial-haemorrhage cost?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Aged · Brain Ischemia/drug therapy · Cerebral Hemorrhage/chemically induced · Cerebrovascular Disorders/complications,drug therapy,mortality · Disability Evaluation · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Male · Middle Aged · Tissue Plasminogen Activator/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by time window, with the windows and doses never pooled. Within 3 hours (NINDS, 624 patients in a labelled two-part design: Part 1 n=291, Part 2 n=333), alteplase made patients at least 30% more likely to have minimal or no disability at 3 months (global odds ratio 1.7, relative), with symptomatic intracerebral haemorrhage in 6.4% vs 0.6%. At 3–4.5 hours (ECASS III, 821), favourable outcome was 52.4% vs 45.2% (odds ratio 1.34, relative) with symptomatic haemorrhage 2.4% vs 0.2%. Up to 6 hours in a wider, older population (IST-3, 3,035; 53% over 80), the primary endpoint was NOT significant (alive and independent 37% vs 35%; adjusted odds ratio 1.13, P=0.181), although an ordinal shift favoured rt-PA (common odds ratio 1.27, relative), with symptomatic haemorrhage 7% vs 1% and more deaths in the first 7 days, offset thereafter. The dose throughout is 0.9 mg/kg where the record states it. The ~6–7% symptomatic-haemorrhage rate in the widest windows is the pricing harm.

cards.headline: NINDS 1995 — TWO-PART design, labelled (Part 1 n=291, Part 2 n=333; 624 in total, treated within 3 hours): Part 1's 24-hour primary was NOT significant, but at 3 months t-PA patients were at least 30% more likely to have minimal or no disability (global odds ratio 1.7, relative); symptomatic intracerebral haemorrhage 6.4% vs 0.6%
cards.summary: NINDS 1995 — TWO-PART design, labelled (Part 1 n=291, Part 2 n=333; 624 in total, treated within 3 hours): Part 1's 24-hour primary was NOT significant, but at 3 months t-PA patients were at least 30% more likely to have minimal or no disability (global odds ratio 1.7, relative); symptomatic intracerebral haemorrhage 6.4% vs 0.6%
cards.type: Randomised double-blind trial in TWO parts (labelled), alteplase vs placebo within 3 hours (NINDS)
cards.people: 624 patients with acute ischaemic stroke treated within 3 hours of onset, in a randomised double-blind trial of intravenous recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (t-PA, alteplase) versus placebo, conducted in two parts: Part 1 (291 patients) tested clinical activity — improvement of ≥4 points on the NIH stroke scale or resolution of the deficit within 24 hours; Part 2 (333 patients) used a global test statistic for outcome at 3 months across the Barthel index, modified Rankin scale, Glasgow outcome scale and NIH stroke scale.
cards.result: In Part 1 there was no significant difference between t-PA and placebo in the percentage with neurologic improvement at 24 hours, although a benefit for t-PA was observed at 3 months on all four outcome measures. In Part 2 the predicted long-term benefit was confirmed: global odds ratio for a favourable outcome 1.7 (95% CI 1.2 to 2.6 — a relative measure); compared with placebo, t-PA patients were at least 30% more likely to have minimal or no disability at 3 months on the assessment scales. Symptomatic intracerebral haemorrhage within 36 hours occurred in 6.4% on t-PA versus 0.6% on placebo (P<0.001). Mortality at 3 months was 17% versus 21% (P=0.30 — no significant difference).
cards.watchOut: The two-part design is labelled, not merged silently: Part 1's own primary endpoint (24-hour improvement) was null, and the 3-month benefit rests on Part 2's global statistic. Pre-registration-era trial (1995). The ~6% symptomatic haemorrhage rate is the pricing harm of this window.
cards.source: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke rt-PA Stroke Study Group. Tissue plasminogen activator for acute ischemic stroke. The New England journal of medicine. 1995. PMID: 7477192. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: ECASS III (Hacke 2008, 821 randomised at 3–4.5 hours): favourable outcome (modified Rankin 0–1) in 52.4% on alteplase vs 45.2% on placebo (odds ratio 1.34, relative); symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage 2.4% vs 0.2%
cards.summary: ECASS III (Hacke 2008, 821 randomised at 3–4.5 hours): favourable outcome (modified Rankin 0–1) in 52.4% on alteplase vs 45.2% on placebo (odds ratio 1.34, relative); symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage 2.4% vs 0.2%
cards.type: Randomised double-blind trial (ECASS III), alteplase 0.9 mg/kg vs placebo at 3–4.5 hours
cards.people: 821 patients with acute ischaemic stroke (418 alteplase, 403 placebo), after exclusion of brain haemorrhage or major infarction on CT, randomised double-blind to intravenous alteplase 0.9 mg/kg or placebo between 3 and 4.5 hours after symptom onset; median administration time was 3 hours 59 minutes. The primary endpoint was disability at 90 days, dichotomised as favourable (modified Rankin score 0–1) versus unfavourable (2–6).
cards.result: More patients had a favourable outcome with alteplase than placebo: 52.4% versus 45.2% (odds ratio 1.34, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.76; P=0.04 — a relative measure, with the absolute rates beside it: an absolute difference of 7.2 percentage points). The global outcome analysis also favoured alteplase (odds ratio 1.28, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.65). Intracranial haemorrhage was more frequent on alteplase — any intracranial haemorrhage 27.0% versus 17.6% (P=0.001) and symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage 2.4% versus 0.2% (P=0.008). Mortality did not differ significantly (7.7% vs 8.4%; P=0.68), nor did other serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: A selected population (major infarction and haemorrhage excluded on CT) and a smaller absolute gain than the under-3-hour window — this is the 3–4.5-hour slice only and is never pooled with the other windows on this shelf.
cards.source: Hacke W et al. Thrombolysis with alteplase 3 to 4.5 hours after acute ischemic stroke. The New England journal of medicine. 2008. PMID: 18815396. Registry ID: NCT00153036. cards.headline: IST-3 (Sandercock 2012, 3,035 randomised up to 6 hours, 53% aged over 80): the PRIMARY endpoint was NOT significant — alive and independent at 6 months 37% vs 35% (adjusted odds ratio 1.13, P=0.181) — with a significant ordinal shift (common odds ratio 1.27, relative); symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage 7% vs 1% and more deaths within 7 days on rt-PA (11% vs 7%)
cards.summary: IST-3 (Sandercock 2012, 3,035 randomised up to 6 hours, 53% aged over 80): the PRIMARY endpoint was NOT significant — alive and independent at 6 months 37% vs 35% (adjusted odds ratio 1.13, P=0.181) — with a significant ordinal shift (common odds ratio 1.27, relative); symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage 7% vs 1% and more deaths within 7 days on rt-PA (11% vs 7%)
cards.type: International multicentre randomised open-treatment trial (IST-3), alteplase vs control up to 6 hours
cards.people: 3,035 patients with acute ischaemic stroke at 156 hospitals in 12 countries, randomised in an open-treatment trial to 0.9 mg/kg intravenous recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (1,515) or control (1,520) within 6 hours of onset; 1,617 (53%) were older than 80 years. The primary outcome was the proportion alive and independent (Oxford Handicap Score 0–2) at 6 months.
cards.result: At 6 months, 554 (37%) on rt-PA versus 534 (35%) on control were alive and independent — an adjusted odds ratio of 1.13 (95% CI 0.95 to 1.35; P=0.181), a NON-significant absolute increase of 14 per 1,000. An ordinal analysis showed a significant shift in Oxford Handicap scores (common odds ratio 1.27, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.47; P=0.001 — a relative measure). Fatal or non-fatal symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage within 7 days occurred in 104 (7%) versus 16 (1%) — an absolute excess of 58 per 1,000. More deaths occurred within 7 days on rt-PA (163 [11%] vs 107 [7%]; absolute increase 37 per 1,000), offset by fewer deaths thereafter, so total deaths by 6 months were similar (408 [27%] vs 407 [27%]). Benefit did not seem diminished in elderly patients.
cards.watchOut: Open-treatment (not placebo-blinded) and a much wider, older population than NINDS or ECASS III. The primary endpoint is printed as the null it was — the ordinal shift is a secondary analysis and must not be upgraded into a primary-endpoint win.
cards.source: Sandercock P et al. cards.summary: Synthesis: a window gradient, never pooled — clear benefit within 3 hours (NINDS), a smaller benefit at 3–4.5 hours (ECASS III), and an unproven primary endpoint (with an ordinal-shift signal) in IST-3's wider, older population treated up to 6 hours; symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage prices every window
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: three trials in three labelled windows — NINDS (624, within 3 hours, two-part design labelled), ECASS III (821, 3–4.5 hours) and IST-3 (3,035, up to 6 hours, 53% over 80). Windows and populations are never pooled into one number.
cards.result: Within 3 hours, alteplase made patients at least 30% more likely to have minimal or no disability at 3 months (global odds ratio 1.7, relative), at a symptomatic haemorrhage cost of 6.4% vs 0.6%. At 3–4.5 hours the favourable-outcome rates were 52.4% vs 45.2% (odds ratio 1.34, relative), with symptomatic haemorrhage 2.4% vs 0.2%. Up to 6 hours in IST-3's wider population, the primary endpoint (alive and independent, 37% vs 35%) was not significant, the ordinal shift was significant (common odds ratio 1.27, relative), symptomatic haemorrhage was 7% vs 1% and early deaths were higher, offset later. Context: live #153 (tenecteplase versus alteplase) and pack #1605 (unknown-onset WAKE-UP/EXTEND slice) both presuppose this founding benefit and are not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Each window is a separate slice with its own population and selection rules; the shelf must not be read as 'alteplase works up to 6 hours' — IST-3's primary analysis does not say that. See the individual cards; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: Topiramate in episodic migraine: about two fewer attacks a month versus one on placebo, responder rates roughly doubled, 100 mg/day matched propranolol — 200 mg adds nothing but tolerability cost
shelves.question: In patients with episodic migraine (3–12 attacks per month), does topiramate 100–200 mg/day reduce monthly migraine frequency versus placebo, and how does it compare with propranolol?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Anticonvulsants/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Child · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fructose/adverse effects,analogs & derivatives,therapeutic use · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Migraine Disorders/prevention & control · Topiramate · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — modest in absolute terms. Two large 26-week placebo-controlled trials (487 and 483 randomised) agree: topiramate 100–200 mg/day reduced monthly migraine frequency by about −2.1 to −2.4 attacks versus −1.1 on placebo, with 50%-responder rates of roughly 47–54% versus roughly 23%. A third trial (575 randomised) found topiramate 100 mg/day similar to propranolol 160 mg/day on every efficacy measure. Across all three, 200 mg/day added no efficacy over 100 mg/day and was less well tolerated — the flat dose gradient is the prescribing point. Paraesthesia, fatigue and nausea are the pricing harms.

cards.headline: MIGR-001 (Silberstein 2004): topiramate 100 and 200 mg/day cut monthly migraine frequency from about 5.5 to 3.3 attacks versus 5.6 to 4.6 on placebo; responder rates 54.0% and 52.3% versus 22.6%
cards.summary: MIGR-001 (Silberstein 2004): topiramate 100 and 200 mg/day cut monthly migraine frequency from about 5.5 to 3.3 attacks versus 5.6 to 4.6 on placebo; responder rates 54.0% and 52.3% versus 22.6%
cards.people: 487 patients aged 12 to 65 years with a 6-month history of migraine and 3 to 12 migraines per month (no more than 15 headache days per month at baseline), randomised to placebo or topiramate 50, 100 or 200 mg/day in a 26-week double-blind trial at 49 US centres; 469 formed the intention-to-treat population.
cards.result: Mean monthly migraine frequency fell significantly at 100 mg/day (from 5.4 to 3.3) and 200 mg/day (from 5.6 to 3.3) versus placebo (from 5.6 to 4.6), with improvement within the first month — absolute frequencies as published. The proportion with a 50% or greater reduction in monthly migraine frequency was 35.9% at 50 mg/day, 54.0% at 100 mg/day and 52.3% at 200 mg/day versus 22.6% on placebo. Adverse events included paraesthesia, fatigue, nausea, anorexia and taste perversion.
cards.watchOut: The gain from 100 to 200 mg/day is flat on frequency (both end at 3.3 per month) — the dose comparison, not just the placebo contrast, is the prescribing point. The trial enrolled adolescents from age 12 as well as adults.
cards.source: Silberstein SD et al. Topiramate in migraine prevention: results of a large controlled trial. Archives of neurology. 2004. PMID: 15096395. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: MIGR-002 (Brandes 2004): topiramate reduced monthly migraine frequency by −2.1 (100 mg/day) and −2.4 (200 mg/day) versus −1.1 on placebo, significant within the first month
cards.summary: MIGR-002 (Brandes 2004): topiramate reduced monthly migraine frequency by −2.1 (100 mg/day) and −2.4 (200 mg/day) versus −1.1 on placebo, significant within the first month
cards.people: 483 patients aged 12 to 65 years with a 6-month history of migraine and 3 to 12 migraines per month (no more than 15 headache days per month at baseline), randomised to topiramate 50, 100 or 200 mg/day or placebo in a 26-week double-blind trial at 52 North American centres; 468 provided post-baseline efficacy data.
cards.result: Mean monthly migraine frequency fell by −2.1 at 100 mg/day (P=.008) and −2.4 at 200 mg/day (P<.001) versus −1.1 on placebo — absolute changes as published. Responder rates (50% or greater reduction) were 39% at 50 mg/day, 49% at 100 mg/day and 47% at 200 mg/day versus 23% on placebo. Reductions in migraine days and rescue-medication use were also significant at 100 and 200 mg/day. Adverse events leading to discontinuation in the topiramate groups included paraesthesia, fatigue and nausea.
cards.watchOut: A replicate-design companion to MIGR-001 with the same dose range and the same flat 100-to-200 mg gradient; the two trials agree, which is why the shelf can be firmer than a single-trial shelf — but neither tests doses between 50 and 100 mg/day as a target.
cards.source: Brandes JL et al. Topiramate for migraine prevention: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2004. PMID: 14982912. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Diener 2004: topiramate 100 mg/day was superior to placebo and similar to propranolol 160 mg/day on every efficacy measure; 200 mg/day was less well tolerated than 100 mg/day
cards.summary: Diener 2004: topiramate 100 mg/day was superior to placebo and similar to propranolol 160 mg/day on every efficacy measure; 200 mg/day was less well tolerated than 100 mg/day
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial with propranolol as active control
cards.people: 575 subjects with episodic migraine with and without aura, randomised at 61 centres in 13 countries to topiramate 100 mg/day, topiramate 200 mg/day, propranolol 160 mg/day (active control) or placebo, in a randomised double-blind trial.
cards.result: Topiramate 100 mg/day was superior to placebo on reduction in monthly migraine frequency, overall 50% responder rate, reduction in monthly migraine days and reduction in daily rescue-medication use. The topiramate 100 mg/day and propranolol groups were similar on reductions in migraine frequency, responder rate, migraine days and daily rescue-medication use. Topiramate 100 mg/day was better tolerated than 200 mg/day and generally comparable to propranolol; no unusual or unexpected safety risks emerged. The fetched record prints no numeric effect sizes for these contrasts, so none are claimed here.
cards.watchOut: Similarity to propranolol is a descriptive finding in a trial designed against placebo, not a formal non-inferiority result; and with no numeric effects in the fetched record, this card supports direction and tolerability only.

shelves.title: CSF protein and glucose reference values: 5 protein + 3 glucose datasets — protein rises with age (upper limits to 93.4 mg/dL, not 45), and the glucose ratio falls as serum glucose rises; most datasets are indirect derivations
shelves.question: In adults, what are the reference intervals for cerebrospinal fluid total protein and for cerebrospinal fluid glucose (and the CSF:serum glucose ratio) — how steeply does total protein rise with age, how much higher is it in men, how far do modern age-partitioned upper limits sit above the traditional 45 mg/dL, and how must the normal glucose ratio be adjusted for the serum glucose?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Cerebrospinal Fluid · Cerebrospinal Fluid Proteins · Humans · Japan · Middle Aged · Reference Values · Retrospective Studies · Volunteers · Adolescent · Adult · Aged, 80 and over · Blood Glucose · Erythrocyte Count · Female · Leukocyte Count · Male · Medical Records · Sex Characteristics · Young Adult · Spinal Stenosis · Lipopolysaccharides · Spinal Puncture · Aging · Cross-Sectional Studies · Sex Factors · Age Factors · Child · China · Child, Preschool · Glucose · Infant · Infant, Newborn · Lactic Acid · Practice Patterns, Physicians' · Cell Count · Hyperglycemia · Nervous System Diseases · Nonlinear Dynamics · Cerebral Ventricles · Spinal Cord
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, cerebrospinal fluid sections, and Boron & Boulpaep — brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference-interval literature, and says so. Datasets: 5 for total protein and 3 for glucose / the CSF:serum ratio. Protein rises markedly with age and is higher in men in every dataset; modern age-partitioned upper limits sit far above the traditional ~45 mg/dL (Mayo 95% interval to 93.4 mg/dL; Huashan upper limit 900 mg/L (90 mg/dL) above 76 years). The glucose limb is a ratio limb — median CSF glucose ~60% of serum, with lower limits that fall as serum glucose rises. METHOD HONESTY IS THE SPINE: only 2 of the 8 datasets sampled people not undergoing diagnostic work-up; the rest are indirect derivations from screened patient / reference-like populations, the field's standard method, stated on every card. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the age / sex protein pattern and the serum-adjusted ratio; the exact limits remain method- and population-bound.

cards.headline: Protein — direct healthy-volunteer dataset (69 Japanese volunteers aged 55–73): mean CSF total protein 41.7 ± 12.3 mg/dL, 2.5th–97.5th percentiles 22.5–73.2 mg/dL, against a then-current Japanese laboratory range of 10–40 mg/dL
cards.summary: Protein — direct healthy-volunteer dataset (69 Japanese volunteers aged 55–73): mean CSF total protein 41.7 ± 12.3 mg/dL, 2.5th–97.5th percentiles 22.5–73.2 mg/dL, against a then-current Japanese laboratory range of 10–40 mg/dL
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset (direct healthy-volunteer CSF protein, 69 older Japanese volunteers)
cards.people: 69 healthy Japanese volunteers aged 55–73 years whose cerebrospinal fluid was collected by lumbar puncture and retrospectively analysed; the older subgroup (≥65 years) was compared with the younger (55–64 years). One of only two datasets on this shelf sampled from people not undergoing diagnostic work-up — and it covers older adults only.
cards.result: Mean (SD) CSF total protein was 41.7 (12.3) mg/dL (417 ± 123 mg/L), higher in the ≥65-year group than in the 55–64-year group. The 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles were 22.5 and 73.2 mg/dL (225 and 732 mg/L) — above the current reference range in Japan of 10–40 mg/dL (100–400 mg/L). The authors conclude the reference interval in the older population should be reconsidered.
cards.watchOut: Direct sampling, but narrow: older Japanese adults only (55–73 years), so its interval cannot be generalised to younger adults or other populations — the large indirect datasets on the next cards supply the age span.

cards.headline: Protein — indirect derivation from 20 years of patient data (6,068 included samples): marked age dependence, higher values in men at every age, and small (~0.04 g/L) platform differences
cards.summary: Protein — indirect derivation from 20 years of patient data (6,068 included samples): marked age dependence, higher values in men at every age, and small (~0.04 g/L) platform differences
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset (indirect, screened patient-data derivation, 6,068 samples, 20 years)
cards.people: Twenty years of hospital database CSF total protein results (initial dataset 19,591 samples), reduced to 6,068 included samples (63% from women) after exclusions for incomplete data, white cells >5 × 10⁶/L, red cells >50 × 10⁶/L and glucose <2.5 mmol/L (approx. <45 mg/dL), plus detailed chart review excluding 60 conditions expected to raise CSF protein; results came from 3 analytical platforms (Siemens Vista 1500, Beckman Lx20, Roche Hitachi 917).
cards.result: Continuous reference intervals were determined by quantile regression, with age- and sex-partitioned intervals in 5-year age bins. CSF total protein showed a marked age dependence, and men had significantly higher values than women across all ages. Results from the 3 instruments differed by small (approximately 0.04 g/L, i.e. 4 mg/dL) but statistically significant amounts. CSF protein correlated weakly with white and red cell counts and was independent of serum total protein and creatinine. The authors conclude age-partitioned intervals will be more accurate than a single cut-off, particularly with advancing age. The fetched abstract prints the method and gradients, not a single numeric interval, and this card claims no single interval from it.

cards.headline: Protein — population-based cohort (Mayo Clinic Study of Aging, 633 community participants aged 32–95): mean 52.2 ± 18.4 mg/dL, 95% reference interval 24.0–93.4 mg/dL, with a repeatability coefficient of 26.1 mg/dL on serial puncture
cards.summary: Protein — population-based cohort (Mayo Clinic Study of Aging, 633 community participants aged 32–95): mean 52.2 ± 18.4 mg/dL, 95% reference interval 24.0–93.4 mg/dL, with a repeatability coefficient of 26.1 mg/dL on serial puncture
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset (population-based community cohort CSF protein, 633 participants)
cards.people: 633 community participants (58.1% men; 99.1% White; mean age 70.9 ± 11.6 years, range 32–95) in the population-based Mayo Clinic Study of Aging, Olmsted County, Minnesota, who underwent lumbar puncture between 2007 and 2017; 66 participants had repeated punctures within 2.5 years.
cards.result: Mean ± SD CSF protein was 52.2 ± 18.4 mg/dL (522 ± 184 mg/L), with a 95% reference interval of 24.0 to 93.4 mg/dL (240 to 934 mg/L) and an observed range of 14.0–148.0 mg/dL. Increasing age, male sex and diabetes were independently associated with higher levels (all P < 0.001); spinal stenosis and arterial hypertension were associated on univariable analysis. In the 66 participants with repeated punctures the coefficient of repeatability was 26.1 mg/dL (261 mg/L), and 11 (16.7%) differed by 20 mg/dL or more between serial punctures. The authors note the levels are higher than listed in many laboratories.
cards.watchOut: A community cohort, not a screened-patient derivation — the second of the two non-diagnostic-work-up datasets — but 99.1% White and older-skewing, and its own serial data show one person's value can move by ~26 mg/dL between punctures, so the wide interval is partly within-person variability, not just between-person spread.

cards.headline: Protein — dry-chemistry intervals from 6,173 'apparently healthy' samples (Huashan Hospital): median 462 mg/L, intervals rising from 170–580 mg/L at 18–25 years to 250–900 mg/L above 76 years, higher in men
cards.summary: Protein — dry-chemistry intervals from 6,173 'apparently healthy' samples (Huashan Hospital): median 462 mg/L, intervals rising from 170–580 mg/L at 18–25 years to 250–900 mg/L above 76 years, higher in men
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset (indirect, 'apparently healthy' screened samples, dry chemistry, 6,173 samples)
cards.people: 40,198 CSF test records from Huashan Hospital, Fudan University (2018–2024), reduced after exclusions for conditions known to elevate CSF total protein to 6,173 'apparently healthy' samples in a Han Chinese population; age- and sex-specific reference intervals (P2.5–P97.5) were established by quantile regression using a dry-chemistry method. (The paper's neurological-disease subgroup comparisons are not reference data and are not carded.)
cards.result: CSF total protein increased with age (Spearman r = 0.369; P < 0.001). Overall median was 462 mg/L (46.2 mg/dL), with men 481 mg/L (48.1 mg/dL) higher than women 424 mg/L (42.4 mg/dL). Established intervals rose progressively with age, from 170–580 mg/L (17–58 mg/dL) at 18–25 years to 220–810 mg/L (22–81 mg/dL) at 61–65 years and 250–900 mg/L (25–90 mg/dL) above 76 years; within the same age strata the upper limit was consistently higher in men than women, except above 76 years, where it was slightly higher in women.
cards.watchOut: INDIRECT derivation from hospital records labelled 'apparently healthy' after exclusions — stated on the face; a single-centre Han Chinese population on one dry-chemistry method, so its age-banded limits are method- and population-bound like every dataset here.

cards.headline: Protein — 19-year retrospective reference-like subset (251 cases): overall interval 18.13–73.33 mg/dL; 17.15–55.37 mg/dL at 18–48 years vs 21.85–80.51 mg/dL at 49–85 years
cards.summary: Protein — 19-year retrospective reference-like subset (251 cases): overall interval 18.13–73.33 mg/dL; 17.15–55.37 mg/dL at 18–48 years vs 21.85–80.51 mg/dL at 49–85 years
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset (indirect, reference-like subset of diagnostic punctures, 251 cases, 19 years)
cards.people: 29,519 CSF total protein test records from adults undergoing diagnostic lumbar puncture at Zhongshan City People's Hospital (2006–2025), reduced to 4,217 records meeting basic age and laboratory criteria, then to 253 candidate cases after structured chart review, and 251 included cases after 2 statistical outliers were removed; intervals (P2.5–P97.5) estimated nonparametrically with bootstrap 90% confidence intervals.
cards.result: The overall reference interval was 18.13 to 73.33 mg/dL (181 to 733 mg/L). By age, the interval was 17.15 to 55.37 mg/dL (172 to 554 mg/L) at 18–48 years and 21.85 to 80.51 mg/dL (219 to 805 mg/dL) at 49–85 years; median protein was 34.3 mg/dL in the younger group and 40.9 mg/dL in the older (19.2% higher), and men's median (38.7 mg/dL) exceeded women's (34.2 mg/dL) (P < 0.001). Age correlated positively with protein (Spearman ρ = 0.35; P < 0.001). The authors state these intervals require direct-method validation.
cards.watchOut: The most heavily filtered dataset here — 251 cases surviving from 29,519 records — and explicitly a 'reference-like subset' of people undergoing diagnostic puncture, not healthy volunteers; its authors' call for direct-method validation prints with its interval.
cards.source: Tian Y et al. Age-stratified reference intervals for cerebrospinal fluid total protein in adults undergoing lumbar puncture: A 19-year retrospective study. Medicine. 2026. PMID: 42994902. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Glucose / ratio — Nijmegen observational CSF study (8,871 samples for CSF glucose; 4,516 for the ratio): age-specific 5th–95th percentile ranges for glucose, ratio and lactate, all age- but not sex-dependent
cards.summary: Glucose / ratio — Nijmegen observational CSF study (8,871 samples for CSF glucose; 4,516 for the ratio): age-specific 5th–95th percentile ranges for glucose, ratio and lactate, all age- but not sex-dependent
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset (observational CSF database, indirect derivation, 8,871 / 4,516 samples)
cards.people: All CSF samples analysed at the Nijmegen laboratory 1993–2008 in the Nijmegen Observational CSF Study; after exclusion of samples with unknown or elevated erythrocyte or leucocyte counts or elevated bilirubin, free haemoglobin or total protein, 9,036 samples were studied — CSF glucose in 8,871, CSF/plasma glucose ratio in 4,516 and CSF lactate in 7,614. (The study spans all ages including neonates; the adult-relevant finding is the age dependence itself.)
cards.result: CSF glucose, the CSF/plasma glucose ratio and CSF lactate were age- but not sex-dependent, with reference ranges defined as 5th–95th percentile ranges. CSF glucose 5th percentile values ranged from 1.8 to 2.9 mmol/L (approx. 32 to 52 mg/dL) and 95th percentile values from 3.8 to 5.6 mmol/L (approx. 68 to 101 mg/dL) across age groups; ratio 5th percentile values ranged 0.41 to 0.53 and 95th percentile values 0.82 to 1.19. Ranges were widest in neonates and narrowest in toddlers, with lower and upper limits increasing with age. Hypoglycaemia was associated with an increased CSF/plasma ratio, whereas hyperglycaemia did not affect the ratio in this study.
cards.watchOut: INDIRECT derivation from a clinical laboratory database — stated on the face; and this is a ratio limb: no standalone 'normal CSF glucose' may be read off it without the paired plasma value, as the row's framing requires.
cards.source: Leen WG et al. Cerebrospinal fluid glucose and lactate: age-specific reference values and implications for clinical practice. PloS one. 2012. PMID: 22880096. cards.headline: Glucose ratio — serum-glucose-adjusted cut-offs from 1,036 paired samples: median CSF glucose ~60% of serum; 5th-percentile cut-offs 0.5, 0.4 and 0.3 across rising serum-glucose bands
cards.summary: Glucose ratio — serum-glucose-adjusted cut-offs from 1,036 paired samples: median CSF glucose ~60% of serum; 5th-percentile cut-offs 0.5, 0.4 and 0.3 across rising serum-glucose bands
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset (paired CSF/serum samples with normal protein and cell counts, 1,036 pairs)
cards.people: 1,036 paired lumbar CSF and serum samples with cell count <15/3, erythrocyte count <1500/3 and normal CSF total protein, processed within 1 h of withdrawal, screened from a clinical database; glucose in CSF and serum measured by enzymatic spectrophotometry.
cards.result: Median glucose concentration in CSF was approximately 60% of that in serum. The CSF/serum glucose ratio correlated negatively with serum glucose (R = −0.586; P < 0.001), in a non-linear manner. Cut-off values for a normal ratio, defined as the 5th percentile, were 0.5 for serum glucose <100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L), 0.4 for 100–149 mg/dL (5.6–8.3 mmol/L) and 0.3 for serum glucose ≥150 mg/dL (8.3 mmol/L). The authors conclude cut-offs for a normal ratio must be adjusted to serum glucose, probably explaining the varying cut-offs previously reported.
cards.watchOut: A screened clinical sample (normal protein and cell counts required), not healthy volunteers — stated on the face; processing within 1 h is part of the method, because CSF glucose falls with delay, so these cut-offs assume prompt processing.
cards.source: Hegen H et al. Serum glucose adjusted cut-off values for normal cerebrospinal fluid/serum glucose ratio: implications for clinical practice. Clinical chemistry and laboratory medicine. 2014. PMID: 24731954. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Glucose ratio — ventricular vs lumbar compartments (1,808 sample pairs): the ratio is similar in the two compartments after adjustment, with serum-glucose-banded lower limits of 0.51, 0.45 and 0.36 for ventricular CSF
cards.summary: Glucose ratio — ventricular vs lumbar compartments (1,808 sample pairs): the ratio is similar in the two compartments after adjustment, with serum-glucose-banded lower limits of 0.51, 0.45 and 0.36 for ventricular CSF
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset (paired ventricular and lumbar CSF/serum samples, 1,808 pairs)
cards.people: 1,808 paired CSF and serum samples collected by lumbar puncture or ventricular drainage, with red cell count <500/µL, normal white cell count and age-related normal total protein, a simultaneously withdrawn serum sample and time to laboratory processing ≤2 h; glucose measured by enzymatic spectrophotometry.
cards.result: After adjustment for age, sex, time between withdrawal and processing, CSF white and red cell counts, CSF total protein and serum glucose in a multiple linear regression model, the CSF:serum glucose ratio was similar in the ventricular and lumbar compartments. Lower limits for the ventricular ratio (5th percentile) were 0.51 for serum glucose <100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L), 0.45 for ≥100 and <150 mg/dL (5.6–8.3 mmol/L) and 0.36 for ≥150 mg/dL (8.3 mmol/L). The ratio depended mainly on time to laboratory processing and absolute serum glucose; the authors conclude previously established lumbar lower limits can also be applied to ventricular CSF.
cards.watchOut: Ventricular samples come from patients with drains in place — a clinical, screened population, not healthy volunteers — stated on the face; the ≤2 h processing condition is part of the result, not a detail.
cards.source: Hegen H et al. Cerebrospinal fluid:serum glucose ratio in the ventricular and lumbar compartments: implications for clinical practice. European journal of neurology. 2018.
