cards.result: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, cerebrospinal fluid sections, and Boron & Boulpaep, CSF formation chapter — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference-interval literature, and says so. THE INDIRECT-DERIVATION FRAMING GAP, stated on the face as commissioned: only the Japanese dataset (69 volunteers aged 55–73) and the Mayo community cohort (633 participants; 95% interval 24.0–93.4 mg/dL) sampled people not undergoing diagnostic work-up; the large protein datasets (6,068 screened samples over 20 years; 6,173 'apparently healthy' Huashan samples with upper limits rising from 580 mg/L (58 mg/dL) at 18–25 years to 900 mg/L (90 mg/dL) above 76 years; and a 251-case reference-like subset, overall 18.13–73.33 mg/dL) and all three glucose datasets are indirect derivations from screened patient / reference-like populations — which is how CSF intervals are necessarily built, because healthy-volunteer lumbar puncture is rare. Protein rises with age and is higher in men in every dataset. For glucose, the ratio is the quantity: median CSF glucose ~60% of serum, with 5th-percentile lower limits falling as serum glucose rises (0.5 / 0.4 / 0.3 by serum band in lumbar CSF; 0.51 / 0.45 / 0.36 ventricular), and similar in ventricular and lumbar compartments. Cross-points only: CSF opening pressure (pack #7174), CSF production rate (pack #6394) and CSF hypocretin-1 (pack #6598) are different measurements; no dataset is shared.
cards.watchOut: Protein values print in mg/dL with mg/L equivalents, per the standing US-units rule; the traditional upper limit (~45 mg/dL) and the modern age-partitioned upper limits are different claims and both print — neither may be substituted for the other.

shelves.title: Serum NfL reference values: 4 datasets — levels rise 2.9% per year, so 'normal' exists only age-banded (upper limit 9.7 ng/L at 18–40 years, 53.8 ng/L over 65) or as Z scores
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what are the reference intervals for serum neurofilament light chain (NfL) — how steeply do levels rise with age (and body-mass index), what do age-banded upper limits look like on single-molecule-array (Simoa) measurement, and how are individual values expressed as age-corrected percentiles and Z scores against a large reference database?
shelves.mesh: Biomarkers · Disease Progression · Humans · Intermediate Filaments · Multiple Sclerosis · Multiple Sclerosis, Chronic Progressive · Neurofilament Proteins · Retrospective Studies · Adolescent · Adult · Age Factors · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Female · Healthy Volunteers · Male · Middle Aged · Nerve Tissue · Reference Values · Scandinavian and Nordic Countries · Glial Fibrillary Acidic Protein · Young Adult · Cross-Sectional Studies
shelves.balance: Guyton & Hall and Boron & Boulpaep have no NfL reference chapter — this shelf rests on the primary reference literature alone, with the textbooks framing axonal-injury biology only, and says so. Four datasets (one of them a pooled four-cohort reference database, labelled as such and counted as one): Benkert's 5,390-control database (exponential age rise, steeper after ~50, BMI-modulated, expressed as percentiles and Z scores); Scandinavian Simoa intervals in 342 subjects (+2.9% per year; upper limits 9.7 ng/L at 18–40 years rising to 53.8 ng/L over 65); a Thai range in 223 adults (median 5.8 pg/mL; 97.5th percentiles 8.7 pg/mL in the 20s to 18.2 in the 60s); and age-split values in 116 adults (<10 pg/mL below 45, <15 above; GFAP limb secondary, single-dataset). NfL is meaningless without age — no unbanded range is printed. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the age-banded structure across 4 datasets.

cards.headline: Pooled reference database (Benkert 2022) — LABELLED as pooled: 5,390 people without CNS disease across four European and North American cohorts, 10,133 samples, giving age- and BMI-modelled percentiles and Z scores; levels rise exponentially with age, steeper after ~50
cards.summary: Pooled reference database (Benkert 2022) — LABELLED as pooled: 5,390 people without CNS disease across four European and North American cohorts, 10,133 samples, giving age- and BMI-modelled percentiles and Z scores; levels rise exponentially with age, steeper after ~50
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset (POOLED four-cohort reference database, 5,390 controls, 10,133 samples) — labelled as pooled
cards.people: A control group of 5,390 people with no evidence of CNS disease taking part in four cohort studies in Europe and North America, contributing 10,133 blood samples (median 1 sample per person); percentiles and Z scores were derived with a generalised additive model for location, scale and shape, modelling age-related increase and BMI-dependent modulation. Counted as ONE dataset, with its pooled composition on the face, as commissioned. (The paper's multiple-sclerosis prognostication cohorts are the database's application, not reference data.)
cards.result: In the control group, serum neurofilament light chain concentrations rose exponentially with age, at a steeper rate after approximately 50 years of age, and were modulated by body-mass index — which is why the database expresses individual values as age- and BMI-corrected percentiles and Z scores rather than a single range. In the application cohorts, a Z score above 1.5 was associated with increased risk of future clinical or MRI disease activity (odds ratio 3.15, 95% CI 2.35 to 4.23 — an odds ratio), and Z scores outperformed absolute raw cut-off values for diagnostic accuracy.
cards.watchOut: A pooled database, not a single population: it is counted as one of this shelf's four datasets with its four-cohort composition stated, and its Z-score scale is only as portable as the assay and model behind it.
cards.source: Benkert P et al. Serum neurofilament light chain for individual prognostication of disease activity in people with multiple sclerosis: a retrospective modelling and validation study. The Lancet. Neurology. 2022. PMID: 35182510. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Scandinavian reference interval (342 reference subjects aged 18–87, Simoa): NfL rises 2.9% per year; age-partitioned intervals 2.8–9.7 ng/L (18–40 years), 4.6–21.4 ng/L (41–65) and 7.5–53.8 ng/L (over 65)
cards.summary: Scandinavian reference interval (342 reference subjects aged 18–87, Simoa): NfL rises 2.9% per year; age-partitioned intervals 2.8–9.7 ng/L (18–40 years), 4.6–21.4 ng/L (41–65) and 7.5–53.8 ng/L (over 65)
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset (age-partitioned Simoa reference interval, 342 Scandinavian subjects)
cards.people: 342 Scandinavian reference subjects aged 18–87 years; serum neurofilament light chain measured by single-molecule array (Simoa) under internal and external quality control established for routine clinical use; the age-partitioned reference interval was established to Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute guidelines, with estimated upper limits per 10-year age group and preanalytical properties examined.
cards.result: Serum NfL increased 2.9% per year. Non-parametric reference intervals were 2.8–9.7 ng/L for ages 18–40 years, 4.6–21.4 ng/L for 41–65 years and 7.5–53.8 ng/L for over 65 years; estimated upper limits per 10-year interval corresponded well with the 90% confidence limits of the non-parametric interval. Recovery after seven days at room temperature was 93% (95% CI 89 to 97%) and after three freeze-thaw cycles 92% (95% CI 83 to 102%); serum levels were only slightly higher than plasma levels.
cards.watchOut: Simoa-measured, Scandinavian-population intervals: the >65 upper limit (53.8 ng/L) is more than five times the 18–40 upper limit (9.7 ng/L) — the clearest single demonstration on this shelf that an unbanded 'normal range' for NfL is meaningless.
cards.source: Hviid CVB et al. Reference interval and preanalytical properties of serum neurofilament light chain in Scandinavian adults. Scandinavian journal of clinical and laboratory investigation. 2020. PMID: 32077769. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Thai reference range (223 healthy adults aged 18–70): median 5.8 pg/mL, crude interval 2.3–15.9 pg/mL, age-group 97.5th percentiles rising from 8.7 pg/mL in the 20s to 18.2 pg/mL in the 60s (this fetched record carries no MeSH terms)
cards.summary: Thai reference range (223 healthy adults aged 18–70): median 5.8 pg/mL, crude interval 2.3–15.9 pg/mL, age-group 97.5th percentiles rising from 8.7 pg/mL in the 20s to 18.2 pg/mL in the 60s (this fetched record carries no MeSH terms)
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset (age-banded reference range, 223 healthy Thai adults)
cards.people: 223 healthy Thai adults (96 men, 127 women) aged 18–70 years without a history of neurological disease, screened at Siriraj Hospital; the crude reference interval was calculated as the 2.5th–97.5th percentiles and an age-normative percentile curve derived with a generalised additive model for location, scale and shape. This record carries no MeSH terms (see source line).
cards.result: Median serum NfL was 5.8 pg/mL (95% CI 5.4 to 6.2), ranging from 1.0 to 18.4 pg/mL, with a crude reference interval of 2.3–15.9 pg/mL. Age-group 2.5th–97.5th percentile intervals were 1.7–8.7 pg/mL (20–29 years, n = 57), 2.5–10.6 (30–39, n = 58), 3.5–14.3 (40–49, n = 59), 4.7–15.8 (50–59, n = 37) and 4.2–18.2 pg/mL (60–69, n = 12). Male sex (P = 0.008) and older age (P < 0.001) were significantly associated with higher levels. The age-normative curve predicted 97.5th percentiles of 8.2, 9.9, 11.7, 14.6 and 19.9 pg/mL at ages 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60.
cards.watchOut: The oldest band rests on only 12 people (60–69 years), so its 18.2 pg/mL upper percentile is the least firm number on this card; pg/mL and ng/L are the same scale, and values print as published per dataset.
cards.source: Sukhonpanich N et al. Reference range for serum neurofilament light chain: findings from healthy Thai adults. Brain communications. 2025. PMID: 40351384. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Age-split normal values (116 healthy adults aged 18–69, Simoa): NfL <10 pg/mL below age 45 and <15 pg/mL above it — with the paired GFAP limb (<140 / <280 pg/mL by age 55) carded as a secondary analyte only
cards.summary: Age-split normal values (116 healthy adults aged 18–69, Simoa): NfL <10 pg/mL below age 45 and <15 pg/mL above it — with the paired GFAP limb (<140 / <280 pg/mL by age 55) carded as a secondary analyte only
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset (age-split normal values for NfL, with a secondary GFAP limb, 116 healthy adults)
cards.people: 116 healthy controls aged 18–69 years (67.5% women, n = 79) in a cross-sectional study; serum neurofilament light chain and serum glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) measured using single-molecule arrays, with demographic differences examined.
cards.result: Age and body-mass index affected NfL values, with age the most important factor. Normal NfL values were established as <10 pg/mL for individuals younger than 45 years and <15 pg/mL for older individuals; a Z score of 1.5 was relevant for all controls. GFAP — the SECONDARY analyte on this card, resting on this one dataset only — was affected only by age, with the highest normality limit 140 pg/mL for controls under 55 years and 280 pg/mL for older controls.
cards.watchOut: The simplest, coarsest banding on this shelf (two age bands) from the smallest dataset (N = 116): usable as a rough rule, not a substitute for the age-partitioned intervals above; and the GFAP limb rests on this single dataset and is a secondary-analyte card only, never a standalone interval claim.

Four datasets, smallest N = 116, all above the ~10-human floor: the Benkert pooled reference database (labelled as pooled — 5,390 controls across four cohorts, 10,133 samples; exponential age rise, steeper after ~50, BMI-modulated, expressed as percentiles and Z scores); the Scandinavian Simoa interval (342 subjects; +2.9% per year; 2.8–9.7 ng/L at 18–40 years, 4.6–21.4 at 41–65, 7.5–53.8 over 65); the Thai range (223 adults; median 5.8 pg/mL, crude 2.3–15.9 pg/mL, 97.5th percentiles 8.7 pg/mL in the 20s to 18.2 in the 60s); and the 116-adult age-split values (<10 pg/mL below 45 years, <15 above, with a single-dataset secondary GFAP limb). ng/L and pg/mL are the same scale and print as published per dataset.
cards.watchOut: No card on this shelf prints an unbanded 'normal range' for NfL, because every dataset shows the value is meaningless without age; Z scores and percentiles are assay- and model-bound like the intervals themselves.

synthesis all reports carded on this shelf. guyton & hall and boron & boulpaep have no nfl reference chapter: this shelf rests on the primary reference literature alone, with the textbooks framing axonal-injury biology only, and says so. four datasets, smallest n = 116, all above the ~10-human floor: the benkert pooled reference database (labelled as pooled — 5,390 controls across four cohorts, 10,133 samples; exponential age rise, steeper after ~50, bmi-modulated, expressed as percentiles and z scores); the scandinavian simoa interval (342 subjects; +2.9% per year; 2.8–9.7 ng/l at 18–40 years, 4.6–21.4 at 41–65, 7.5–53.8 over 65); the thai range (223 adults; median 5.8 pg/ml, crude 2.3–15.9 pg/ml, 97.5th percentiles 8.7 pg/ml in the 20s to 18.2 in the 60s); and the 116-adult age-split values (<10 pg/ml below 45 years, <15 above, with a single-dataset secondary gfap limb). ng/l and pg/ml are the same scale and print as published per dataset. no card on this shelf prints an unbanded 'normal range' for nfl, because every dataset shows the value is meaningless without age; z scores and percentiles are assay- and model-bound like the intervals themselves. synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Founding thrombectomy trials: all five 2015 trials favoured thrombectomy in anterior-circulation LVO stroke (HERMES pool NNT 2.6); MR CLEAN independence 32.6% vs 19.1%
shelves.question: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke caused by a proximal intracranial occlusion of the anterior circulation, does endovascular (intra-arterial) thrombectomy plus usual care improve 90-day functional outcome versus usual care alone?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Brain Ischemia · Catheterization · Combined Modality Therapy · Female · Fibrinolytic Agents · Humans · Logistic Models · Male · Mechanical Thrombolysis · Middle Aged · Odds Ratio · Single-Blind Method · Stroke · Tissue Plasminogen Activator · Urokinase-Type Plasminogen Activator
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — the founding 2015 programme: five randomised trials of endovascular thrombectomy for proximal anterior-circulation occlusion, every one favouring thrombectomy on 90-day functional outcome, pooled by the HERMES individual-patient meta-analysis (1,287 patients; adjusted common odds ratio 2.49 for reduced disability — a relative measure — with a number needed to treat of 2.6 for one patient to improve by at least one Rankin level; mortality and symptomatic haemorrhage did not differ in the pool). The trials are labelled limbs, never a single pooled trial: MR CLEAN (n=500) is the generalisability anchor — broad eligibility, treatment within 6 hours, 89% pre-treated with intravenous alteplase, functional independence 32.6% vs 19.1%; ESCAPE (n=316), EXTEND-IA (n=70), REVASCAT (n=206) and SWIFT PRIME (n=196) used progressively tighter imaging selection (small infarct core, moderate-to-good collaterals, salvageable tissue) and several stopped early — ESCAPE, EXTEND-IA and SWIFT PRIME for efficacy, REVASCAT for loss of equipoise — which belongs on the face. This shelf cards the founding early-window question only; the library's later, different thrombectomy questions (large-core, basilar, post-thrombectomy blood pressure, nerinetide) are separate homes and are not folded in.

cards.headline: MR CLEAN (Berkhemer 2015): intra-arterial treatment within 6 hours improved 90-day functional outcome — adjusted common odds ratio 1.67 (relative) for a lower Rankin score; functional independence 32.6% vs 19.1% (absolute difference 13.5 points); no significant mortality or symptomatic haemorrhage difference
cards.summary: MR CLEAN (Berkhemer 2015): intra-arterial treatment within 6 hours improved 90-day functional outcome — adjusted common odds ratio 1.67 (relative) for a lower Rankin score; functional independence 32.6% vs 19.1% (absolute difference 13.5 points); no significant mortality or symptomatic haemorrhage difference
cards.type: Multicentre randomised trial (MR CLEAN), intra-arterial treatment + usual care vs usual care alone, Netherlands
cards.people: 500 patients with acute ischaemic stroke from a proximal anterior-circulation occlusion confirmed on vessel imaging, treatable intra-arterially within 6 hours, at 16 centres in the Netherlands (233 intra-arterial treatment plus usual care, 267 usual care alone; mean age 65 years). Intravenous alteplase had been given to 445 patients (89.0%) before randomisation; retrievable stents were used in 190 of 233 intervention patients (81.5%). Primary outcome modified Rankin scale score at 90 days.
cards.result: The adjusted common odds ratio for a lower (better) Rankin score was 1.67 (95% CI 1.21 to 2.30) — a relative measure from the shift analysis. Functional independence (Rankin 0–2) was 32.6% with intra-arterial treatment versus 19.1% with usual care (absolute difference 13.5 percentage points, 95% CI 5.9 to 21.2). There were no significant differences in mortality or symptomatic intracerebral haemorrhage.
cards.watchOut: The broadest eligibility of the five trials — its independence rates (32.6% vs 19.1%) are lower than the imaging-selected trials' precisely because it selected least. 'Intra-arterial treatment' here was predominantly stent-retriever thrombectomy (81.5%) but not exclusively.
cards.source: Berkhemer OA et al. A randomized trial of intraarterial treatment for acute ischemic stroke. The New England journal of medicine. 2015. PMID: 25517348. Registry ID: ISRCTN10888758. cards.headline: ESCAPE (Goyal 2015): rapid endovascular treatment in imaging-selected patients (small core, moderate-to-good collaterals, up to 12 hours) — functional independence 53.0% vs 29.3% (P<0.001) and mortality 10.4% vs 19.0% (P=0.04); stopped early for efficacy
cards.summary: ESCAPE (Goyal 2015): rapid endovascular treatment in imaging-selected patients (small core, moderate-to-good collaterals, up to 12 hours) — functional independence 53.0% vs 29.3% (P<0.001) and mortality 10.4% vs 19.0% (P=0.04); stopped early for efficacy
cards.type: Multicentre randomised trial (ESCAPE), endovascular thrombectomy + standard care vs standard care, imaging-selected, stopped early for efficacy
cards.people: 316 participants with a proximal intracranial anterior-circulation occlusion, a small infarct core and moderate-to-good collateral circulation on CT/CT angiography (large core or poor collaterals excluded), included up to 12 hours after onset at 22 centres worldwide, randomised to standard care plus endovascular thrombectomy or standard care alone; 238 received intravenous alteplase. Median time from study CT to first reperfusion in the intervention group was 84 minutes.
cards.result: Functional independence (90-day Rankin 0–2) was 53.0% with intervention versus 29.3% with control (P<0.001); the primary shift outcome favoured intervention (common odds ratio 2.6, 95% CI 1.7 to 3.8; P<0.001 — a relative measure). Mortality was 10.4% versus 19.0% (P=0.04). Symptomatic intracerebral haemorrhage occurred in 3.6% versus 2.7% (P=0.75). The trial was stopped early because of efficacy.
cards.watchOut: Imaging selection (small core, good collaterals) and early stopping both flatter the estimate relative to unselected practice — ESCAPE's 53.0% independence rate is not transportable to patients with large cores or poor collaterals.
cards.source: Goyal M et al. Randomized assessment of rapid endovascular treatment of ischemic stroke. The New England journal of medicine. 2015. PMID: 25671798. Registry ID: NCT01778335. cards.headline: EXTEND-IA (Campbell 2015): perfusion-imaging-selected thrombectomy with the Solitaire FR stent retriever — reperfusion at 24 hours 100% vs 37% (medians), functional independence 71% vs 40% (P=0.01); stopped early for efficacy at n=70
cards.summary: EXTEND-IA (Campbell 2015): perfusion-imaging-selected thrombectomy with the Solitaire FR stent retriever — reperfusion at 24 hours 100% vs 37% (medians), functional independence 71% vs 40% (P=0.01); stopped early for efficacy at n=70
cards.type: Randomised trial (EXTEND-IA), thrombectomy with Solitaire FR + alteplase vs alteplase alone, perfusion-imaging-selected, stopped early for efficacy
cards.people: 70 patients (35 per group) receiving intravenous alteplase within 4.5 hours of ischaemic stroke onset, with internal carotid or middle cerebral artery occlusion and salvageable brain tissue with an ischaemic core under 70 mL on CT perfusion imaging, randomised to endovascular thrombectomy with the Solitaire FR stent retriever or alteplase alone; endovascular therapy began at a median 210 minutes after onset.
cards.result: The percentage of ischaemic territory reperfused at 24 hours was greater with thrombectomy (median 100% vs 37%; P<0.001). Early neurological improvement at 3 days occurred in 80% versus 37% (P=0.002), and functional independence (Rankin 0–2) at 90 days in 71% versus 40% (P=0.01). There were no significant differences in death or symptomatic intracerebral haemorrhage. The trial was stopped early because of efficacy.
cards.watchOut: The smallest founding trial (n=70), stopped early, in the most tightly perfusion-selected population — its 71% independence rate is the programme's ceiling, not its expectation.
cards.source: Campbell BC et al. Endovascular therapy for ischemic stroke with perfusion-imaging selection. The New England journal of medicine. 2015. PMID: 25671797. Registry ID: NCT01492725. cards.headline: REVASCAT (Jovin 2015): Solitaire stent-retriever thrombectomy within 8 hours — functional independence 43.7% vs 28.2% (adjusted odds ratio 2.1, relative); symptomatic haemorrhage 1.9% in both groups; enrolment halted early for loss of equipoise at n=206 of a planned 690
cards.summary: REVASCAT (Jovin 2015): Solitaire stent-retriever thrombectomy within 8 hours — functional independence 43.7% vs 28.2% (adjusted odds ratio 2.1, relative); symptomatic haemorrhage 1.9% in both groups; enrolment halted early for loss of equipoise at n=206 of a planned 690
cards.type: Randomised trial (REVASCAT), Solitaire thrombectomy + medical therapy vs medical therapy alone, registry-embedded (Catalonia)
cards.people: 206 patients at four centres in Catalonia, Spain, treatable within 8 hours of anterior-circulation stroke onset with confirmed proximal occlusion and no large infarct on neuroimaging, in whom alteplase had either not achieved revascularisation or was contraindicated, randomised to medical therapy (including alteplase when eligible) plus Solitaire thrombectomy or medical therapy alone, within a population-based stroke registry.
cards.result: Thrombectomy reduced disability across the Rankin range (adjusted odds ratio for a 1-point improvement 1.7, 95% CI 1.05 to 2.8 — a relative measure) and raised functional independence to 43.7% versus 28.2% (adjusted odds ratio 2.1, 1.1 to 4.0). Symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage was 1.9% in both groups (P=1.00) and death 18.4% versus 15.5% (P=0.60). Enrolment was halted early because positive results from the other trials destroyed equipoise.
cards.watchOut: Stopped at 206 of a planned 690 patients, so its estimates are imprecise; uniquely, its patients were alteplase non-responders or alteplase-ineligible, a different entry limb from the alteplase-first trials.
cards.source: Jovin TG et al. Thrombectomy within 8 hours after symptom onset in ischemic stroke. The New England journal of medicine. 2015. PMID: 25882510. Registry ID: NCT01692379. cards.headline: SWIFT PRIME (Saver 2015): stent-retriever thrombectomy after intravenous t-PA — functional independence 60% vs 35% (P<0.001), with disability reduced across the whole Rankin range; stopped early for efficacy at n=196
cards.summary: SWIFT PRIME (Saver 2015): stent-retriever thrombectomy after intravenous t-PA — functional independence 60% vs 35% (P<0.001), with disability reduced across the whole Rankin range; stopped early for efficacy at n=196
cards.type: Multicentre randomised trial (SWIFT PRIME), stent-retriever thrombectomy + intravenous t-PA vs t-PA alone, stopped early for efficacy
cards.people: 196 patients (98 per group) at 39 centres who were receiving or had received intravenous t-PA for stroke from a confirmed proximal anterior intracranial occlusion without a large ischaemic-core lesion, randomised to continue t-PA alone or to undergo stent-retriever thrombectomy within 6 hours; median time from qualifying imaging to groin puncture was 57 minutes and substantial reperfusion was achieved in 88% of the intervention group.
cards.result: Thrombectomy reduced disability at 90 days across the entire Rankin range (P<0.001) and raised functional independence (Rankin 0–2) to 60% versus 35% (P<0.001). There were no significant differences in 90-day mortality (9% vs 12%; P=0.50) or symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage (0% vs 3%; P=0.12). The study was stopped early because of efficacy.
cards.watchOut: All patients were t-PA-treated and core-selected, and the trial stopped early — its 60% independence rate sits between ESCAPE's and EXTEND-IA's selected-population readings, well above MR CLEAN's broader-population 32.6%.
cards.source: Saver JL et al. Stent-retriever thrombectomy after intravenous t-PA vs. t-PA alone in stroke. The New England journal of medicine. 2015. PMID: 25882376. Registry ID: NCT01657461. cards.headline: HERMES individual-patient meta-analysis (Goyal 2016): pooling all five 2015 trials (1,287 patients) — thrombectomy reduced disability at 90 days (adjusted common odds ratio 2.49, relative; number needed to treat 2.6 for a one-level Rankin improvement), with no mortality or haemorrhage difference and no subgroup heterogeneity
cards.summary: HERMES individual-patient meta-analysis (Goyal 2016): pooling all five 2015 trials (1,287 patients) — thrombectomy reduced disability at 90 days (adjusted common odds ratio 2.49, relative; number needed to treat 2.6 for a one-level Rankin improvement), with no mortality or haemorrhage difference and no subgroup heterogeneity
cards.type: Individual-patient-data meta-analysis (HERMES) of the five randomised trials carded above — a synthesis of the same programme, not an independent trial
cards.people: Individual patient data for 1,287 patients (634 thrombectomy, 653 control) pooled by the HERMES collaboration from the five trials carded above — MR CLEAN, ESCAPE, REVASCAT, SWIFT PRIME and EXTEND IA (conducted December 2010 to December 2014) — a pooled synthesis of the same programme of trials, labelled as such, not a sixth trial.
cards.result: Endovascular thrombectomy significantly reduced disability at 90 days versus control (adjusted common odds ratio 2.49, 95% CI 1.76 to 3.53; P<0.0001 — a relative measure), with a number needed to treat of 2.6 to reduce disability by at least one Rankin level for one patient. No heterogeneity of treatment effect was found across prespecified subgroups (P for interaction 0.43); effects favoured thrombectomy in patients aged 80 or older (cOR 3.68), those randomised more than 300 minutes after onset (cOR 1.76) and those ineligible for intravenous alteplase (cOR 2.43). Mortality at 90 days and the risks of parenchymal haematoma and symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage did not differ between groups.
cards.watchOut: HERMES pools exactly the five trials on this shelf — it must never be counted as a sixth trial or as independent confirmation. Its pooled estimate inherits the early stopping and imaging selection of its component trials.
cards.source: Goyal M et al. Endovascular thrombectomy after large-vessel ischaemic stroke: a meta-analysis of individual patient data from five randomised trials. Lancet (London, England). 2016. PMID: 26898852. Registry ID: none in the record. individual-patient-data meta-analysis (hermes) of the five randomised trials carded above — a synthesis of the same programme, not an independent trial individual patient data for 1,287 patients (634 thrombectomy, 653 control) pooled by the hermes collaboration from the five trials carded above — mr clean, escape, revascat, swift prime and extend ia (conducted december 2010 to december 2014) — a pooled synthesis of the same programme of trials, labelled as such, not a sixth trial. endovascular thrombectomy significantly reduced disability at 90 days versus control (adjusted common odds ratio 2.49, 95% ci 1.76 to 3.53; p<0.0001 — a relative measure), with a number needed to treat of 2.6 to reduce disability by at least one rankin level for one patient. no heterogeneity of treatment effect was found across prespecified subgroups (p for interaction 0.43); effects favoured thrombectomy in patients aged 80 or older (cor 3.68), those randomised more than 300 minutes after onset (cor 1.76) and those ineligible for intravenous alteplase (cor 2.43). mortality at 90 days and the risks of parenchymal haematoma and symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage did not differ between groups. hermes pools exactly the five trials on this shelf — it must never be counted as a sixth trial or as independent confirmation. its pooled estimate inherits the early stopping and imaging selection of its component trials. goyal m et al. endovascular thrombectomy after large-vessel ischaemic stroke: a meta-analysis of individual patient data from five randomised trials. lancet (london, england). 2016. pmid: 26898852. registry id: none in the record. mesh: aged · aged, 80 and over · brain ischemia · endovascular procedures · female · fibrinolytic agents · humans · intracranial hemorrhages · male · middle aged · odds ratio · randomized controlled trials as topic · stroke · thrombectomy · tissue plasminogen activator · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Synthesis: the founding programme is unanimous — five 2015 trials (500 + 316 + 70 + 206 + 196 patients) all favoured thrombectomy on 90-day functional outcome, and HERMES (1,287 patients) put the pooled number needed to treat at 2.6, with no excess mortality or symptomatic haemorrhage
cards.summary: Synthesis: the founding programme is unanimous — five 2015 trials (500 + 316 + 70 + 206 + 196 patients) all favoured thrombectomy on 90-day functional outcome, and HERMES (1,287 patients) put the pooled number needed to treat at 2.6, with no excess mortality or symptomatic haemorrhage
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Functional independence (Rankin 0–2) rose with thrombectomy in every trial: 32.6% vs 19.1% (MR CLEAN, broadest eligibility), 53.0% vs 29.3% (ESCAPE), 71% vs 40% (EXTEND-IA), 43.7% vs 28.2% (REVASCAT) and 60% vs 35% (SWIFT PRIME) — the gradient tracks imaging selection, not disagreement. Only ESCAPE showed a mortality difference (10.4% vs 19.0%); the HERMES pool showed none. This shelf answers the founding early-window anterior-circulation question only; large-core, basilar-artery, blood-pressure-after-thrombectomy and nerinetide questions are different, later questions with their own homes.
cards.watchOut: Two PMIDs carried in the commissioning row for the remaining primaries (25843965, 25850704) were refused on fetch this session — they resolve to unrelated papers (lake geochemistry; a corneal case report) — and were replaced by the verified REVASCAT (PMID 25882510) and SWIFT PRIME (PMID 25882376) records. See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: Pramipexole in early Parkinson's disease: starting the agonist instead of levodopa halved dyskinesias (relative HR 0.37) but gave no long-term disability advantage at 6 years; extended-release matched immediate-release against placebo in early and advanced disease
shelves.question: In early Parkinson's disease, does starting pramipexole rather than levodopa change the development of dopaminergic motor complications and long-term disability (CALM-PD)? And in early and advanced disease, does once-daily extended-release pramipexole improve UPDRS scores and off-time versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Benzothiazoles · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Levodopa · Male · Middle Aged · Parkinson Disease · Pramipexole · Proportional Hazards Models · Quality of Life · Severity of Illness Index · Thiazoles
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the CALM-PD trade-off is the face. Initial pramipexole reduced dyskinesias (24.5% vs 54%; relative hazard ratio 0.37) and wearing off (47% vs 62.7%; relative hazard ratio 0.68) vs initial levodopa, but initial levodopa reduced freezing, gave greater UPDRS improvement, and caused less somnolence and oedema — and at a mean of 6 years self-reported disability was similar (79.9 vs 82.5, P=.19), so the complication advantage did not convert into a disability advantage. Separately, labelled limbs: extended-release pramipexole beat placebo and matched immediate-release over 18 weeks in advanced disease (n=507) and early disease (n=259). Limbs are labelled per report and never pooled.

cards.headline: CALM-PD 4-year RCT (Holloway 2004): initial pramipexole vs initial levodopa — dyskinesias 24.5% vs 54% (relative hazard ratio 0.37) and wearing off 47% vs 62.7% (relative hazard ratio 0.68), but freezing was LESS common on initial levodopa, UPDRS improvement was greater on levodopa, and somnolence (36% vs 21%) and oedema (42% vs 15%) were more common on pramipexole
cards.summary: CALM-PD 4-year RCT (Holloway 2004): initial pramipexole vs initial levodopa — dyskinesias 24.5% vs 54% (relative hazard ratio 0.37) and wearing off 47% vs 62.7% (relative hazard ratio 0.68), but freezing was LESS common on initial levodopa, UPDRS improvement was greater on levodopa, and somnolence (36% vs 21%) and oedema (42% vs 15%) were more common on pramipexole
cards.type: Multicentre double-blind randomised strategy trial (CALM-PD, 4-year report), initial pramipexole vs initial levodopa in early Parkinson's disease
cards.people: 301 patients with early Parkinson's disease requiring dopaminergic therapy, randomised to initial pramipexole 0.5 mg three times daily (n=151) or carbidopa/levodopa 25/100 mg three times daily (n=150), with dose escalation and open-label levodopa supplementation permitted, at 22 US and Canadian sites, followed to 48 months. Limb: initial-therapy strategy in early disease.
cards.result: Initial pramipexole significantly reduced dyskinesias (24.5% vs 54%; hazard ratio 0.37, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.56, P<.001 — a relative measure) and wearing off (47% vs 62.7%; hazard ratio 0.68, P=.02 — a relative measure). Initial levodopa significantly reduced freezing (25.3% vs 37.1% with initial pramipexole; hazard ratio 1.7, 95% CI 1.11 to 2.59, P=.01 — a relative measure). Disabling dyskinesias by 48 months were uncommon and did not differ significantly. Mean total UPDRS improvement from baseline to 48 months was greater on initial levodopa (+2 vs −3.2 points, P=.003). Somnolence (36% vs 21%, P=.005) and oedema (42% vs 15%, P<.001) were more common on pramipexole. Quality-of-life changes did not differ.
cards.watchOut: A strategy trial, not a pure drug comparison: open-label levodopa could be added in both arms, so the contrast is 'start with the agonist' vs 'start with levodopa'. The trade-off is whole — fewer dyskinesias bought with more freezing, somnolence and oedema and less UPDRS improvement.
cards.source: Holloway RG et al. Pramipexole vs levodopa as initial treatment for Parkinson disease: a 4-year randomized controlled trial. Archives of neurology. 2004. PMID: 15262734. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: CALM-PD long-term follow-up (Parkinson Study Group CALM Cohort Investigators 2009): at a mean of 6.0 years, self-reported disability was SIMILAR (Schwab & England 79.9 vs 82.5, P=.19) — the early motor-complication advantage did not convert into a long-term disability advantage; sleepiness scores remained higher on initial pramipexole
cards.summary: CALM-PD long-term follow-up (Parkinson Study Group CALM Cohort Investigators 2009): at a mean of 6.0 years, self-reported disability was SIMILAR (Schwab & England 79.9 vs 82.5, P=.19) — the early motor-complication advantage did not convert into a long-term disability advantage; sleepiness scores remained higher on initial pramipexole
cards.type: Long-term extended follow-up report OF the CALM-PD randomised trial — same trial as the card above, not an independent trial
cards.people: 222 of the original 301 CALM-PD patients who consented to extended open follow-up, assessed at a mean (SD) of 6.0 (0.2) years after randomisation to initial pramipexole (n=151 originally) or initial levodopa (n=150). Limb: long-term follow-up of the initial-therapy strategy above — a second report of the same trial, labelled as such.
cards.result: Self-reported weighted Schwab & England disability scores were similar: 79.9 (16.2) on initial pramipexole vs 82.5 (14.6) on initial levodopa (P=.19, not significant). Dopaminergic motor complications (wearing off, on-off effects or dyskinesias) remained more common in the initial-levodopa group (68.4% vs 50.0%, P=.002), though disabling dyskinesias were uncommon in both. Mean Epworth Sleepiness Scale score was significantly higher on initial pramipexole (11.3 vs 8.6, P<.001). Total UPDRS change did not differ significantly (P=.11).
cards.watchOut: Only 222 of 301 patients consented to extended follow-up, and treatment after the trial phase was open — attrition and open treatment soften the long-term contrast. The headline stands: no long-term disability difference.
cards.source: Parkinson Study Group CALM Cohort Investigators et al. Long-term effect of initiating pramipexole vs levodopa in early Parkinson disease. Archives of neurology. 2009. PMID: 19433655. Registry ID: NCT00804479. cards.headline: Extended-release in advanced PD RCT (Schapira 2011): 507 patients with motor fluctuations on levodopa — UPDRS II+III fell by −11.0 (ER) and −12.8 (IR) vs −6.1 on placebo at 18 weeks; off-time fell by −2.1 and −2.5 vs −1.4 hours/day. Limb: advanced disease, ER vs placebo
cards.summary: Extended-release in advanced PD RCT (Schapira 2011): 507 patients with motor fluctuations on levodopa — UPDRS II+III fell by −11.0 (ER) and −12.8 (IR) vs −6.1 on placebo at 18 weeks; off-time fell by −2.1 and −2.5 vs −1.4 hours/day. Limb: advanced disease, ER vs placebo
cards.type: Multicentre randomised double-blind trial, pramipexole ER and IR vs placebo as adjunct to levodopa in advanced Parkinson's disease
cards.people: 507 patients with advanced Parkinson's disease experiencing motor fluctuations while taking levodopa, randomised to once-daily extended-release pramipexole, immediate-release pramipexole three times daily, or placebo (flexible titration, then maintenance at 0.375–4.5 mg/day), with 18-week primary analyses and a 33-week subset. Limb: advanced disease.
cards.result: UPDRS part II+III scores decreased by an adjusted mean of −11.0 (ER, P=0.0001 vs placebo) and −12.8 (IR, P<0.0001) vs −6.1 on placebo. Off-time decreased by −2.1 (ER, P=0.0199) and −2.5 (IR, P<0.0001) vs −1.4 hours/day on placebo. Early-morning off symptoms also improved significantly, findings were largely maintained at 33 weeks in the subset, and both formulations were well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: This trial establishes that the once-daily ER formulation works like the IR formulation against placebo — formulation equivalence in advanced disease, not a new efficacy claim and not evidence about initial therapy.
cards.source: Schapira AH et al. Extended-release pramipexole in advanced Parkinson disease: a randomized controlled trial. Neurology. 2011. PMID: 21832216. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Extended-release in early PD RCT (Hauser 2010): 259 patients — UPDRS II+III change −8.1 (ER) and −8.4 (IR) vs −5.1 on placebo at week 18; levodopa rescue required by 14% on placebo vs 2.9% (ER) and 1.0% (IR); somnolence, nausea, constipation and fatigue more common on pramipexole. Limb: early disease, ER vs placebo
cards.summary: Extended-release in early PD RCT (Hauser 2010): 259 patients — UPDRS II+III change −8.1 (ER) and −8.4 (IR) vs −5.1 on placebo at week 18; levodopa rescue required by 14% on placebo vs 2.9% (ER) and 1.0% (IR); somnolence, nausea, constipation and fatigue more common on pramipexole. Limb: early disease, ER vs placebo
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo- and active-comparator-controlled trial, pramipexole ER vs IR vs placebo in early Parkinson's disease
cards.people: 259 subjects with early Parkinson's disease, randomised 2:2:1 to pramipexole ER once daily, pramipexole IR three times daily, or placebo, with the primary efficacy and safety evaluation at week 18. Limb: early disease — a different limb from both the CALM-PD strategy trial and the advanced-disease trial above.
cards.result: Adjusted mean change in UPDRS II (activities of daily living) + III (motor) scores, including post-rescue evaluations, was −8.1 (ER, P=0.0282 vs placebo) and −8.4 (IR, P=0.0153) vs −5.1 on placebo; censoring post-rescue data, −7.4 and −7.5 vs −2.7 (P=0.0010 and P=0.0006). Levodopa rescue was required by 7 placebo subjects (14%) vs 3 on ER (2.9%, P=0.0160) and 1 on IR (1.0%, P=0.0017). Adverse events more common on ER than placebo included somnolence, nausea, constipation and fatigue.
cards.watchOut: An 18-week formulation trial: it shows ER matches IR against placebo in early disease. It says nothing about the long-term strategy question CALM-PD asked, and the limbs must not be pooled.
cards.source: Hauser RA et al. Randomized, double-blind, multicenter evaluation of pramipexole extended release once daily in early Parkinson's disease. Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society. 2010. PMID: 20669317. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: one strategy trial with two reports (CALM-PD: fewer dyskinesias and wearing-off on agonist-first, at the cost of more freezing, somnolence and oedema, with NO long-term disability difference at 6 years) plus two formulation trials (ER vs placebo in advanced disease, n=507, and in early disease, n=259 — both showing ER ≈ IR > placebo over 18 weeks); limbs labelled per report and never pooled
cards.summary: Synthesis: one strategy trial with two reports (CALM-PD: fewer dyskinesias and wearing-off on agonist-first, at the cost of more freezing, somnolence and oedema, with NO long-term disability difference at 6 years) plus two formulation trials (ER vs placebo in advanced disease, n=507, and in early disease, n=259 — both showing ER ≈ IR > placebo over 18 weeks); limbs labelled per report and never pooled
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: CALM-PD 4-year report (n=301), CALM-PD long-term follow-up (222 of the same cohort), ER advanced trial (n=507) and ER early trial (n=259).
cards.result: Print the CALM-PD dissociation plainly: a relative hazard ratio of 0.37 for dyskinesias on the agonist-first strategy, no disability advantage at 6 years, and the agonist class harms (somnolence; oedema) on the face. The ER trials establish formulation equivalence, not a new efficacy claim.

shelves.title: Ropinirole prolonged release (and patch) as adjunct in advanced Parkinson's disease: off-time fell a net ~1.8 hours/day vs placebo in the pivotal trial, the dose-response study points to 8 mg as the likely lowest maximally effective dose, and the patch was non-inferior to the tablet
shelves.question: In patients with advanced Parkinson's disease and motor fluctuations on levodopa, does adjunctive ropinirole 24-hour prolonged release reduce daily off-time versus placebo — and is a once-daily ropinirole patch superior to placebo and non-inferior to the prolonged-release tablet?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antiparkinson Agents · Double-Blind Method · Drug Delivery Systems · Female · Humans · Indoles · International Cooperation · Male · Middle Aged · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Parkinson Disease · Severity of Illness Index · Time Factors
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — as an adjunct for motor fluctuations. Three distinct randomised trials: the 393-patient pivotal trial found ropinirole 24-hour prolonged release reduced daily off-time by 2.1 hours vs 0.3 hours on placebo (net ~1.8 hours/day) with levodopa dose reduction; the fixed-dose study significantly reduced awake off-time at 16 mg and reads 8 mg as the likely lowest maximally effective dose (against the pivotal trial's 18.8 mg mean dose); the patch trial showed superiority over placebo and non-inferiority to the prolonged-release tablet on UPDRS Part III. The price is dyskinesia and the dopamine-agonist class harms (nausea, dizziness, somnolence, hallucinations, orthostatic hypotension).

cards.headline: Ropinirole 24-hour prolonged-release pivotal RCT (Pahwa 2007): 393 patients — daily off-time fell by 2.1 hours vs 0.3 hours on placebo over 24 weeks (a net 1.8 hours/day), at a mean dose of 18.8 mg/day with a mean levodopa reduction of 278 mg; withdrawals for adverse events 5% in both arms
cards.summary: Ropinirole 24-hour prolonged-release pivotal RCT (Pahwa 2007): 393 patients — daily off-time fell by 2.1 hours vs 0.3 hours on placebo over 24 weeks (a net 1.8 hours/day), at a mean dose of 18.8 mg/day with a mean levodopa reduction of 278 mg; withdrawals for adverse events 5% in both arms
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, ropinirole 24-hour prolonged release as adjunct to levodopa in advanced Parkinson's disease
cards.people: 393 patients with Parkinson's disease and motor fluctuations not optimally controlled on levodopa, randomised to ropinirole 24-hour prolonged release (n=202) or placebo (n=191) as adjunct to levodopa for 24 weeks, in a double-blind placebo-controlled study.
cards.result: At week 24, mean daily off-time fell by 2.1 hours on ropinirole 24-hour vs 0.3 hours on placebo. Secondary measures — on-time and on-time without troublesome dyskinesia, UPDRS motor and activities-of-daily-living subscales, PDQ-39 subscales and the PD Sleep Scale — significantly favoured ropinirole. The most common adverse events were dyskinesia, nausea, dizziness, somnolence, hallucinations and orthostatic hypotension; adverse events led to withdrawal in 5% of both arms.
cards.watchOut: The pivotal trial's mean dose (18.8 mg/day) is high — read it beside the dose-response study below, whose own reading is that 8 mg is the likely lowest maximally effective dose. The benefit is bought with dyskinesia and the dopamine-agonist class harms listed on this card.

cards.headline: Fixed-dose dose-response RCT (Zesiewicz 2017): ropinirole PR significantly reduced awake off-time at 16 mg (P=.027), increased on-time without troublesome dyskinesia at 8 mg (P=.036) and improved UPDRS motor scores at all doses (P=.005–.016) — the report's own reading is that 8 mg is the likely lowest maximally effective dose
cards.summary: Fixed-dose dose-response RCT (Zesiewicz 2017): ropinirole PR significantly reduced awake off-time at 16 mg (P=.027), increased on-time without troublesome dyskinesia at 8 mg (P=.036) and improved UPDRS motor scores at all doses (P=.005–.016) — the report's own reading is that 8 mg is the likely lowest maximally effective dose
cards.type: Phase 4 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled fixed-dose dose-response study, ropinirole prolonged release in advanced Parkinson's disease
cards.people: Subjects with advanced Parkinson's disease receiving concomitant levodopa, randomised in a phase 4 double-blind parallel-group study to once-daily fixed doses of ropinirole prolonged release (4, 8, 12, 16 or 24 mg) or placebo, up-titrated over 13 weeks and maintained for 4 weeks. The abstract does not state the total randomised number, and none is claimed here.
cards.result: At maintenance week 4, ropinirole PR significantly reduced total awake off-time at 16 mg (P=.027); increased absolute awake on-time without troublesome dyskinesia at 8 mg (P=.036); and improved UPDRS motor scores vs placebo at all doses (P=.005–.016). Adverse-event incidence was similar between groups with no dose-related trends. The authors concluded 16 mg reduced off-time, 8 mg is the likely lowest maximally effective dose, and the safety profile was consistent with previous studies.
cards.watchOut: Significant cells are scattered across doses and endpoints (off-time at 16 mg only; on-time at 8 mg only) — a multiplicity-exposed pattern, printed as reported. The 8 mg reading tempers the pivotal trial's 18.8 mg mean dose and belongs beside it.

cards.headline: Ropinirole patch RCT (Hattori 2020): UPDRS Part III change −9.8 on patch vs −4.3 on placebo (difference −5.4, 95% CI −7.3 to −3.6 — superiority shown) and −10.1 on prolonged-release tablet (patch–tablet difference 0.3, CI within the 2.5-point non-inferiority margin — non-inferiority shown)
cards.summary: Ropinirole patch RCT (Hattori 2020): UPDRS Part III change −9.8 on patch vs −4.3 on placebo (difference −5.4, 95% CI −7.3 to −3.6 — superiority shown) and −10.1 on prolonged-release tablet (patch–tablet difference 0.3, CI within the 2.5-point non-inferiority margin — non-inferiority shown)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind double-dummy trial, ropinirole patch vs placebo and vs ropinirole extended-release tablet in advanced Parkinson's disease
cards.people: Patients with advanced Parkinson's disease using levodopa, randomised in a double-blind double-dummy trial to ropinirole hydrochloride patch (up to 64 mg/day), ropinirole extended-release tablet (up to 16 mg/day), or placebo, once daily, with the primary endpoint at week 16. The abstract does not state the total randomised number, and none is claimed here.
cards.result: Least-squares mean change in UPDRS Part III (on state) was −9.8 (95% CI −10.8 to −8.7) on patch, −4.3 (−5.8 to −2.8) on placebo and −10.1 (−11.2 to −9.1) on tablet. The patch–placebo difference of −5.4 (−7.3 to −3.6) demonstrated superiority; the patch–tablet difference of 0.3 (−1.2 to 1.8) had an upper confidence limit below the 2.5-point non-inferiority margin, demonstrating non-inferiority to the tablet. Most adverse events in all groups were mild or moderate, with no serious safety concerns reported.
cards.watchOut: The patch's primary endpoint is a UPDRS motor score, not off-time — a different endpoint from the pivotal tablet trial, so the limbs are labelled and not pooled. Non-inferiority is to the tablet formulation, whose own placebo-controlled base is the first two cards.

shelves.title: Adjunctive pramipexole in advanced Parkinson's disease: UPDRS parts II and III improved 26.7% and 34% vs 4.8% and 5.7% on placebo in the founding 247-patient trial, and the Cochrane synthesis of 4 trials (669 patients) found off-time cut by a weighted mean 1.8 hours — at the cost of more dyskinesia
shelves.question: In patients with advanced Parkinson's disease and levodopa-induced motor complications, does adjunctive pramipexole (immediate-release, and extended-release as its modern form) improve motor scores and reduce off-time versus placebo?

shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — as an adjunct in advanced disease, on short- and medium-term trials only (up to 24 weeks' maintenance). The founding 247-patient trial (Guttman 1997) found UPDRS part II improved 26.7% on pramipexole (P = 0.0002) and part III 34% (P = 0.0006) against 4.8% and 5.7% on placebo, with more dyskinesia and nausea on active treatment. The Cochrane synthesis (Clarke 2000) pooled 4 randomised trials in 669 patients: off-time fell by a weighted mean difference of 1.8 hours (95% CI 1.2 to 2.3) versus placebo, levodopa dose fell by a weighted mean 115 mg, UPDRS ADL scores improved in all studies — and dyskinesia as an adverse event was reported more frequently with pramipexole, with significantly more hallucinations. A second founding trial (Lieberman 1997) reports the same direction qualitatively; its abstract prints no sample size and no numeric effects, so it is never load-bearing. The extended-release versus placebo trial in advanced disease (507 patients) is the modern form of this same contrast and lives on shelf #7711 as a cross-point — it is not double-carded here (one-home rule). Nothing here speaks to long-term disability: that strategy question is CALM-PD, on shelf #7711.

cards.headline: Founding advanced-disease RCT (Guttman 1997): 247 patients with wearing off — UPDRS part II improved 26.7% on pramipexole vs 4.8% on placebo (P = 0.0002) and part III 34% vs 5.7% (P = 0.0006); bromocriptine arm improved 14% and 23.8%
cards.summary: Founding advanced-disease RCT (Guttman 1997): 247 patients with wearing off — UPDRS part II improved 26.7% on pramipexole vs 4.8% on placebo (P = 0.0002) and part III 34% vs 5.7% (P = 0.0006); bromocriptine arm improved 14% and 23.8%
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, adjunctive pramipexole and bromocriptine vs placebo in advanced Parkinson's disease (International Pramipexole-Bromocriptine Study Group)
cards.people: 247 patients with advanced Parkinson's disease and motor fluctuations ('wearing off'), Hoehn and Yahr stages II to IV during 'on' times, randomised double-blind to pramipexole (up to 4.5 mg/day), bromocriptine (up to 30 mg/day) or placebo, with dose escalation, 6 months' maintenance and dose reduction; the study was not powered to compare the two active treatments against each other.
cards.result: Primary end points were UPDRS parts II and III. UPDRS part II improved by 26.7% for pramipexole (P = 0.0002) and 14% for bromocriptine (P = 0.02) versus 4.8% for placebo. UPDRS part III improved by 34% for pramipexole (P = 0.0006) and 23.8% for bromocriptine (P = 0.01) versus 5.7% for placebo. There were no major differences in safety data, but the active treatment groups reported more dyskinesia and nausea than placebo. The Global Clinical Assessment of Efficacy comparison between active groups showed a trend favouring pramipexole (P = 0.056). Percent improvements are as published, with the placebo-arm changes beside them.
cards.watchOut: A 1997 pre-registration-era trial: percent UPDRS improvements are relative to each arm's own baseline, not absolute point changes, and the bromocriptine arm exists for context — the trial was not powered for the pramipexole-versus-bromocriptine comparison.
cards.source: Guttman M et al. Double-blind comparison of pramipexole and bromocriptine treatment with placebo in advanced Parkinson's disease. International Pramipexole-Bromocriptine Study Group. Neurology. 1997. PMID: 9339690. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Second founding trial (Lieberman 1997): pramipexole improved 'on' and 'off' motor function and cut 'off' time versus placebo — reported qualitatively only; the abstract prints no sample size and no numeric effects (N not documented in the record)
cards.summary: Second founding trial (Lieberman 1997): pramipexole improved 'on' and 'off' motor function and cut 'off' time versus placebo — reported qualitatively only; the abstract prints no sample size and no numeric effects (N not documented in the record)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, adjunctive pramipexole vs placebo in advanced Parkinson's disease (qualitative report)
cards.people: Patients with advanced Parkinson's disease with motor fluctuations on levodopa treatment, in a double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group study. The fetched abstract states no sample size — N not documented in the record — and gives no numeric effect sizes.
cards.result: As published, qualitatively: pramipexole improved motor function during 'on' and 'off' periods, decreased the time spent in 'off' periods, reduced the severity of 'off' periods, decreased disability and Parkinson's severity during 'on' and 'off' periods as assessed by the UPDRS, and permitted a reduction in levodopa dosage. Central-nervous-system adverse effects were similar to those reported with other dopamine agonists, and gastrointestinal and cardiovascular tolerability was satisfactory.
cards.watchOut: This card is supporting only and never load-bearing: its abstract reports no N and no numbers, so no figure from it may be quoted. The quantitative case rests on the Guttman trial and the Cochrane synthesis.
cards.source: Lieberman A et al. Clinical evaluation of pramipexole in advanced Parkinson's disease: results of a double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group study. Neurology. 1997. cards.headline: Cochrane synthesis (Clarke 2000): 4 randomised trials, 669 patients — off-time cut by a weighted mean 1.8 hours (95% CI 1.2 to 2.3) and levodopa dose by 115 mg vs placebo; dyskinesia adverse events and hallucinations more frequent on pramipexole
cards.summary: Cochrane synthesis (Clarke 2000): 4 randomised trials, 669 patients — off-time cut by a weighted mean 1.8 hours (95% CI 1.2 to 2.3) and levodopa dose by 115 mg vs placebo; dyskinesia adverse events and hallucinations more frequent on pramipexole
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials, adjunctive pramipexole vs placebo for levodopa-induced complications (4 trials, 669 patients)
cards.people: Systematic review of randomised controlled trials of adjuvant pramipexole versus inactive placebo in patients with idiopathic Parkinson's disease already established on levodopa with long-term complications of levodopa therapy: 4 trials, 669 patients — 2 phase III studies with 24 weeks' maintenance and 2 phase II studies with 4 weeks' maintenance. The pooled trials are the founding programme's trials, including the era of the two trials carded above — this is a synthesis of the same programme, not independent evidence.
cards.result: The reduction in off time was significantly greater with pramipexole than placebo (weighted mean difference 1.8 hours; 95% CI 1.2 to 2.3). No significant change was noted in a dyskinesia rating scale in any of the 4 studies, but dyskinesia as an adverse event was reported more frequently with pramipexole. UPDRS complication (part IV) scores improved significantly in 2 studies; UPDRS ADL scores improved significantly in all studies; UPDRS motor scores in the on state improved significantly in 3 of 4. Levodopa dose reduction (allowed in 3 studies) favoured pramipexole (weighted mean difference 115 mg; 95% CI 87 to 143). Trends to more dopaminergic adverse events reached significance only for hallucinations, and withdrawals were significantly fewer on pramipexole. The reviewers' own limit: conclusions rest on short- and medium-term trials (up to 24 weeks).
cards.watchOut: The 669 pooled patients include the founding trials carded above — never add the Ns. A dyskinesia rating scale did not worsen even though dyskinesia adverse-event reports rose; both halves of that finding print together.
cards.source: Clarke CE et al. Pramipexole for levodopa-induced complications in Parkinson's disease. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2000. PMID: 10908540. cards.headline: Synthesis: adjunctive pramipexole in advanced Parkinson's disease beats placebo on UPDRS scores and off-time over up to 24 weeks (founding trial: part II +26.7% and part III +34% vs +4.8% and +5.7%; Cochrane: off-time −1.8 hours, levodopa −115 mg) — bought with more dyskinesia adverse events and hallucinations; the ER form of the contrast is cross-pointed to shelf #7711, not re-carded
cards.summary: Synthesis: adjunctive pramipexole in advanced Parkinson's disease beats placebo on UPDRS scores and off-time over up to 24 weeks (founding trial: part II +26.7% and part III +34% vs +4.8% and +5.7%; Cochrane: off-time −1.8 hours, levodopa −115 mg) — bought with more dyskinesia adverse events and hallucinations; the ER form of the contrast is cross-pointed to shelf #7711, not re-carded
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: the 247-patient founding trial (Guttman 1997), a second founding trial whose abstract documents no N (Lieberman 1997), and the Cochrane synthesis of 4 trials totalling 669 patients (Clarke 2000) — the synthesis pools the founding programme, so the Ns overlap and are never summed.
cards.result: Direction is consistent across the programme: better UPDRS ADL and motor scores, about 1.8 hours less off-time, and a lower levodopa dose on pramipexole than placebo, over 4–24 weeks. The price is dopaminergic: dyskinesia reported more often as an adverse event and significantly more hallucinations. Verification-contract note: this shelf's two slate anchors (PMIDs 9339690 and 10908540) were both fetched and verified with non-empty abstracts before building, per the row's binding contract, so the row stands as rowed rather than contracting into shelf #7711. The 507-patient extended-release versus placebo trial in advanced disease is carded on shelf #7711 and is a cross-point only here.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: 3D-CAM delirium interview: sensitivity 95% and specificity 94% at derivation in 201 inpatients aged ≥75 (96% / 86% in dementia), 94% / 97% for the Chinese version on general units — and 84.6–87.2% / 96.7–97.4% in surgical ICU, at a median 3 minutes
shelves.question: In hospitalised older adults on general wards and in surgical intensive care, how accurately does the 3D-CAM (the 3-minute diagnostic interview operationalising the Confusion Assessment Method) diagnose delirium against an expert / DSM reference standard — what sensitivity and specificity does it deliver in its derivation population, in patients with dementia, and in translated-version validations, and how long does it take at the bedside?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Algorithms · Confusion · Cross-Sectional Studies · Delirium/diagnosis · Female · Hospitalization · Humans · Interviews as Topic · Male · Neuropsychological Tests · Reproducibility of Results · Sensitivity and Specificity · China · Intensive Care Units · Prospective Studies · Cross-Cultural Comparison · Postoperative Cognitive Complications/diagnosis
shelves.balance: DIAGNOSTIC ACCURACY — high, with a setting gradient and a translation caveat. At derivation (Marcantonio 2014; the instrument originators' own report, labelled as such), the 3D-CAM reached sensitivity 95% and specificity 94% against an expert-panel reference standard in 201 inpatients aged ≥75, and held up in dementia (96% / 86%). The Chinese version on general units matched it (Ji 2021: 94% / 97% in 204 patients). In surgical ICU the same translated instrument lost sensitivity (Mu 2020: 87.2% and 84.6% for two interviewers; specificity 96.7% and 97.4%; kappa 0.82) — roughly one in seven delirious patients missed. Median administration was about 3 minutes in both ward studies. Two of the three reports validate the Chinese version: independent cohorts and centres, but the derivation figures may not be presented as replicated in the original-language form outside the derivation centre. A diagnostic-accuracy shelf only — nothing here tests whether finding delirium with the 3D-CAM changes treatment or outcomes. Distinct instruments: CAM-ICU (for patients who cannot speak) and 4AT are separate shelves with no shared anchor.

cards.headline: Derivation and validation (Marcantonio 2014 — the instrument originators' own report): 201 inpatients aged ≥75, 21% delirium — sensitivity 95% (95% CI 84% to 99%), specificity 94% (90% to 97%), median administration 3 minutes; in dementia, 96% / 86%
cards.summary: Derivation and validation (Marcantonio 2014 — the instrument originators' own report): 201 inpatients aged ≥75, 21% delirium — sensitivity 95% (95% CI 84% to 99%), specificity 94% (90% to 97%), median administration 3 minutes; in dementia, 96% / 86%
cards.type: Derivation and prospective validation of the 3D-CAM (originators' report; 201 inpatients aged ≥75)
cards.people: 201 inpatients aged 75 years or older (mean age 84; 28% with dementia) on 4 general medicine units at one academic medical centre; the 20 items best operationalising the 4 CAM features formed the 3D-CAM, administered prospectively by trained research assistants and compared with an expert-panel reference standard built from clinician assessments, patient and family interviews and record review. Programme-labelled: this is the instrument originators' own derivation / validation report.
cards.result: The expert panel identified 21% with delirium, 88% of whom had hypoactive or normal psychomotor features. Median 3D-CAM administration time was 3 minutes (interquartile range 2 to 5). Sensitivity was 95% (95% CI, 84% to 99%) and specificity 94% (CI, 90% to 97%). In patients with dementia, sensitivity was 96% (CI, 82% to 100%) and specificity 86% (CI, 67% to 96%); without dementia, 93% (CI, 66% to 100%) and 96% (CI, 91% to 99%). The authors note the limits: single-centre, cross-sectional, medical patients only.
cards.watchOut: Single-centre derivation by the instrument's own developers, in medical inpatients only — the 95% / 94% pair is a derivation-centre figure until replicated in the original language elsewhere; the dementia specificity interval is wide (67% to 96%).
cards.source: Marcantonio ER et al. 3D-CAM: derivation and validation of a 3-minute diagnostic interview for CAM-defined delirium: a cross-sectional diagnostic test study. Annals of internal medicine. 2014. PMID: 25329203. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.summary: Chinese version, general units (Ji 2021): 204 hospitalised older adults, 54 with delirium — sensitivity 94%, specificity 97%, median assessment about 3 minutes
cards.type: Prospective validation of the Chinese 3D-CAM in general units (204 hospitalised older adults)
cards.people: 204 hospitalised older adults at a geriatric hospital, assessed prospectively with the Chinese version of the 3D-CAM by nurse researchers; 54 were identified as positive for delirium by the reference process described in the report.
cards.result: The sensitivity and specificity of the 3D-CAM Chinese version were 94% and 97%, respectively. The median duration of assessment was about 3 minutes. The authors conclude the Chinese version had highly acceptable sensitivity and specificity when used by nurse researchers among Chinese older adults on general units.
cards.watchOut: A translation validation: it supports the instrument's performance in Chinese-speaking general-unit patients assessed by nurse researchers, and does not by itself replicate the English-language derivation. The abstract reports no confidence intervals for the 94% / 97% pair.

cards.headline: Chinese version, surgical ICU (Mu 2020): 245 patients, 647 paired assessments against a DSM-5 psychiatrist panel — sensitivity 87.2% and 84.6%, specificity 96.7% and 97.4% for two interviewers, kappa 0.82
cards.summary: Chinese version, surgical ICU (Mu 2020): 245 patients, 647 paired assessments against a DSM-5 psychiatrist panel — sensitivity 87.2% and 84.6%, specificity 96.7% and 97.4% for two interviewers, kappa 0.82
cards.type: Cross-cultural validation of the Chinese 3D-CAM in surgical ICU (245 patients, 647 paired assessments)
cards.people: 245 adult surgical-ICU patients assessed on postoperative days 1–3 with the culturally adapted Chinese 3D-CAM (3D-CAM-CN) by two independent interviewers, yielding 647 paired assessments; the reference standard was delirium diagnosis by a psychiatrist panel applying DSM-5 criteria.
cards.result: Against the reference standard, sensitivity and specificity were 87.2% and 96.7% for interviewer A and 84.6% and 97.4% for interviewer B, with good interrater reliability (kappa coefficient = 0.82, P < 0.001). In patients with mild cognitive impairment, sensitivity ranged from 85.7% to 100% and specificity from 95.7% to 96.4%. The authors conclude the 3D-CAM-CN can be used as a reliable and accurate instrument for delirium assessment in surgical patients.
cards.watchOut: Sensitivity fell 8–10 points from the ward validations — in an ICU population that is sicker and harder to interview. The 647 figure is paired assessments in 245 patients; the patient N is the evidence size.
cards.source: Mu DL et al. Cross-cultural adaptation and validation of the 3D-CAM Chinese version in surgical ICU patients. BMC psychiatry. 2020. PMID: 32204700. Registry ID: ChiCTR-OOC-17011887. shelves.title: Rituximab in generalised myasthenia gravis — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 trials, total N = 99, directly split: RINOMAX positive in new-onset disease (minimal manifestations 71% vs 29%) and BeatMG futility in established steroid-dependent disease (steroid-sparing primary 60% vs 56%)
shelves.question: In generalised myasthenia gravis, does add-on rituximab improve disease control versus placebo — and does the answer depend on whether the disease is new-onset or long-established and steroid-dependent?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Female · Aged · Middle Aged · Adolescent · Male · Rituximab/adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Activities of Daily Living · Quality of Life · Treatment Outcome · Myasthenia Gravis/drug therapy · Thymus Neoplasms
shelves.balance: FLOOR-RISK, stated exactly: the complete placebo-controlled base is exactly 2 trials totalling 99 randomised patients, and the two trials are directly split — the count and the split are printed on the face and carried in the stamp line. RINOMAX (47 randomised; new-onset generalised myasthenia gravis, onset ≤12 months, single 500 mg rituximab infusion): minimal disease manifestations at 16 weeks in 71% (17 of 24) vs 29% (6 of 21), P = .007, probability ratio 2.48 (95% CI 1.20–5.11 — a relative measure). BeatMG (52 randomised; established acetylcholine-receptor-antibody-positive disease on prednisone ≥15 mg/day, two-cycle regimen): the steroid-sparing primary was achieved in 60% vs 56%, and the study reached its prespecified futility endpoint (P = 0.03) — the predefined clinically meaningful improvement was unlikely in a larger trial. The populations must never be merged: new-onset, single-dose, QMG-based in one trial; established, steroid-dependent, steroid-sparing, futility-designed in the other. No replacement anchor exists — the rest of the rituximab–myasthenia literature is observational — so this shelf rests on these 99 patients alone, and no pooled verdict is offered.

cards.headline: RINOMAX (Piehl 2022): minimal disease manifestations at 16 weeks in 71% (17 of 24) on a single 500 mg rituximab infusion vs 29% (6 of 21) on placebo (P = .007; probability ratio 2.48 [95% CI 1.20–5.11] — a relative measure), in new-onset generalised myasthenia gravis
cards.summary: RINOMAX (Piehl 2022): minimal disease manifestations at 16 weeks in 71% (17 of 24) on a single 500 mg rituximab infusion vs 29% (6 of 21) on placebo (P = .007; probability ratio 2.48 [95% CI 1.20–5.11] — a relative measure), in new-onset generalised myasthenia gravis
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (RINOMAX), single-dose rituximab in new-onset generalised myasthenia gravis — 1 of exactly 2 trials on this shelf
cards.people: 47 patients with new-onset generalised myasthenia gravis (onset of generalised symptoms ≤12 months, Quantitative Myasthenia Gravis [QMG] score ≥6) at 7 regional clinics in Sweden, randomised 1:1 to a single intravenous infusion of rituximab 500 mg (n = 25) or matching placebo (n = 22), as add-on to standard of care, over 48 weeks. The primary-endpoint analysis set was 24 on rituximab and 21 on placebo, as printed. Minimal disease manifestations were defined as QMG ≤4, prednisolone ≤10 mg/day, and no rescue treatment.
cards.result: A greater proportion on rituximab met the primary endpoint: 71% (17 of 24) vs 29% (6 of 21) (Fisher exact test P = .007; probability ratio 2.48 [95% CI 1.20–5.11] — a relative measure). Rescue treatments were more frequent in the placebo arm (rituximab: 1 [4%]; placebo: 8 [36%]). One patient in the placebo arm had a myocardial infarction with cardiac arrest, and one patient in the active arm experienced a fatal cardiac event.
cards.watchOut: A single small trial (47 randomised, 45 in the primary analysis) in new-onset disease only, with a single 500 mg dose — its result does not transfer to established or refractory disease, which is exactly what the second trial on this shelf tests.
cards.source: Piehl F et al. Efficacy and Safety of Rituximab for New-Onset Generalized Myasthenia Gravis: The RINOMAX Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA neurology. 2022. PMID: 36121672. Registry ID: NCT02950155. cards.headline: RINOMAX secondary readings (Piehl 2022, second outcome card from the SAME report — not a separate trial): secondary endpoints did not differ between groups in the per-protocol analysis with censoring for rescue treatment, but favoured rituximab in a post hoc worst-rank analysis that counted rescue treatment
cards.summary: RINOMAX secondary readings (Piehl 2022, second outcome card from the SAME report — not a separate trial): secondary endpoints did not differ between groups in the per-protocol analysis with censoring for rescue treatment, but favoured rituximab in a post hoc worst-rank analysis that counted rescue treatment
cards.type: Secondary-outcome card from the RINOMAX report — same trial, same publication as the primary card above; never counted as an additional report
cards.people: The same 47 RINOMAX patients and the same publication as the card above — carded separately only to keep the primary and secondary readings distinct; this is one trial and one report, counted once in the shelf's base of exactly 2 trials, N = 99.
cards.result: Secondary endpoints — changes in Myasthenia Gravis Activities of Daily Living and Myasthenia Gravis Quality of Life at 16 weeks, with QMG at 24 weeks — did not differ between groups with censoring for rescue treatment (per-protocol analysis), but were in favour of active treatment when rescue treatment was taken into account by worst-rank imputation (post hoc analysis). The authors conclude a single 500 mg dose of rituximab was associated with a greater probability of minimal manifestations and reduced need for rescue medication, and that further studies are needed on long-term benefit–risk.
cards.watchOut: The positive secondary reading depends on a post hoc imputation choice; the prespecified per-protocol secondary analysis was null. Never quote the post hoc reading without that pairing.

cards.headline: BeatMG (Nowak 2022): the steroid-sparing primary was achieved in 60% on rituximab vs 56% on placebo, and the study REACHED ITS FUTILITY ENDPOINT (P = 0.03) — the predefined clinically meaningful improvement was unlikely in a larger trial — in established AChR-antibody-positive disease on prednisone
cards.summary: BeatMG (Nowak 2022): the steroid-sparing primary was achieved in 60% on rituximab vs 56% on placebo, and the study REACHED ITS FUTILITY ENDPOINT (P = 0.03) — the predefined clinically meaningful improvement was unlikely in a larger trial — in established AChR-antibody-positive disease on prednisone
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 2 futility trial (BeatMG), rituximab in established steroid-dependent AChR-positive generalised myasthenia gravis — 1 of exactly 2 trials on this shelf; MeSH: none in the record (see source line)
cards.people: 52 patients with acetylcholine-receptor-antibody-positive generalised myasthenia gravis (MG Foundation of America class II–IV) receiving prednisone ≥15 mg/day, randomised 1:1 to a two-cycle rituximab or placebo regimen, with follow-up through 52 weeks, in a phase 2 futility-design trial. Mean baseline prednisone dose was 22.1 (±9.7) mg/day; 59.6% were MGFA class II.
cards.result: The primary steroid-sparing outcome (≥75% reduction in mean daily prednisone dose in the 4 weeks before week 52, with clinical improvement or no significant worsening) was achieved in 60% of those on rituximab vs 56% on placebo. The study reached its futility endpoint (p = 0.03), suggesting the predefined clinically meaningful improvement of 30% due to rituximab over placebo was unlikely to be achieved in a subsequent larger trial. No safety issues were identified; rituximab was safe and well tolerated. The report classifies this as Class I evidence that rituximab is safe but unlikely to reduce steroid use by an absolute difference of at least 30% at 1 year in mild-to-moderately symptomatic AChR-antibody-positive disease.
cards.watchOut: A futility design answers a narrower question than 'does it work at all': it rules out the predefined large (30%) steroid-sparing effect in this population, not every possible smaller effect. Its population (established, mild-to-moderate, steroid-dependent) is the opposite limb from RINOMAX's new-onset patients — never merge them. This record carries no MeSH terms, and its source line says so.

RINOMAX (n = 47 randomised, new-onset disease, single 500 mg dose) was positive on minimal disease manifestations at 16 weeks (71% vs 29%; relative probability ratio 2.48); BeatMG (n = 52, established AChR-positive steroid-dependent disease, two cycles) reached futility on its steroid-sparing primary (60% vs 56%)

RINOMAX (n = 47 randomised, new-onset disease, single 500 mg dose) was positive on minimal disease manifestations at 16 weeks (71% vs 29%; relative probability ratio 2.48); BeatMG (n = 52, established AChR-positive steroid-dependent disease, two cycles) reached futility on its steroid-sparing primary (60% vs 56%)

cards.result: No pooled verdict is offered and none is legitimate on this base: the split tracks the populations (new-onset vs established steroid-dependent), the regimens (single dose vs two cycles) and the endpoints (QMG-based manifestations vs steroid sparing). The rest of the rituximab–myasthenia literature is observational and is not carded; if either anchor had failed verification, this shelf would have been withdrawn, as the row directs.
cards.watchOut: Exactly 2 trials, N = 99 — that count is the shelf's central fact and is carried in the title, the balance, every card's type line and the stamp. Never cite either trial as settling rituximab in the other trial's population.
