shelves.title: Atidarsagene autotemcel for early-onset metachromatic leukodystrophy: one programme, three reports, no concurrent control — survival free from severe motor impairment 100% vs 0% at age 6 (pre-symptomatic late-infantile) against natural-history cohorts
shelves.question: In children with early-onset metachromatic leukodystrophy, does atidarsagene autotemcel (arsa-cel; autologous lentiviral haematopoietic stem-cell gene therapy), compared with untreated natural-history controls, preserve motor function and survival?
shelves.mesh: Age of Onset · Cerebroside-Sulfatase/genetics · Child · Child, Preschool · Female · Genetic Therapy · Genetic Vectors · Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation · Humans · Italy · Lentivirus/genetics · Leukodystrophy, Metachromatic/genetics,therapy · Male · Prospective Studies · Treatment Outcome · Adolescent · Adult · Infant · Young Adult · Cerebroside-Sulfatase/genetics,therapeutic use · Follow-Up Studies · Genetic Therapy/adverse effects,methods · Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation/adverse effects,methods · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Leukodystrophy, Metachromatic/therapy,mortality,genetics · Transplantation, Autologous/adverse effects,methods · Genetic Therapy/methods · Gene Therapy Agents/methods · Peripheral Nerves/physiopathology · Leukodystrophy, Metachromatic/enzymology,genetics,pathology,therapy · Neural Conduction · Biopsy · Peripheral Nervous System Diseases/enzymology,genetics,pathology,therapy · Skin/pathology · Cerebroside-Sulfatase/genetics,metabolism
shelves.balance: One programme, three reports — and no randomised or concurrent control exists anywhere in the base; the flag leads. Atidarsagene autotemcel (arsa-cel; autologous lentiviral haematopoietic stem-cell gene therapy) was given to 39 children with early-onset metachromatic leukodystrophy across two open-label studies and expanded access (the 2022 report's 29 are inside that 39), compared throughout with non-concurrent untreated natural-history cohorts. Survival free from severe motor impairment was 100% vs 0% at age 6 in pre-symptomatic late-infantile disease, and 87.5% / 80.0% vs 11.2% at age 10 in early-juvenile disease — dramatic differences that carry the full bias risk of historical comparison in a disease whose ascertainment has changed, with very wide early-juvenile confidence intervals (38.7 to 98.1). Benefit is concentrated in children treated pre-symptomatically. Treatment requires busulfan conditioning, with febrile neutropenia the commonest severe adverse event; no insertional oncogenesis was observed. The product is named as the publications give it — clarification, not promotion.

cards.headline: Phase 1/2 + expanded-access report (Fumagalli 2022, NCT01560182): 29 treated children vs 31 untreated natural-history controls — at analysis 26 treated patients were alive (median follow-up 3.16 years); gross motor function at 2 years differed significantly from matched controls (late-infantile mean difference 66%, 95% CI 48.9 to 82.3; early-juvenile 42%, 95% CI 12.3 to 71.8), and PBMC arylsulfatase A activity rose 18.7-fold (late-infantile) and 5.7-fold (early-juvenile) above baseline
cards.summary: Phase 1/2 + expanded-access report (Fumagalli 2022, NCT01560182): 29 treated children vs 31 untreated natural-history controls — at analysis 26 treated patients were alive (median follow-up 3.16 years); gross motor function at 2 years differed significantly from matched controls (late-infantile mean difference 66%, 95% CI 48.9 to 82.3; early-juvenile 42%, 95% CI 12.3 to 71.8), and PBMC arylsulfatase A activity rose 18.7-fold (late-infantile) and 5.7-fold (early-juvenile) above baseline
cards.type: Prospective non-randomised open-label phase 1/2 study and expanded access — one programme, first report, atidarsagene autotemcel in early-onset metachromatic leukodystrophy (NCT01560182)
cards.people: 29 paediatric patients with pre-symptomatic or early-symptomatic early-onset metachromatic leukodystrophy (biochemical and molecular confirmation), treated with atidarsagene autotemcel (arsa-cel) in a prospective non-randomised open-label phase 1/2 study and expanded access at a single centre (Milan), compared with 31 untreated natural-history controls matched by age and disease subtype.
cards.result: Two treated patients died of disease progression and one of a sudden event judged unlikely related to treatment. After busulfan conditioning, all treated patients showed sustained multilineage engraftment; PBMC ARSA activity at 2 years rose a mean 18.7-fold (95% CI 8.3 to 42.2; p < 0.0001) in late-infantile and 5.7-fold (2.6 to 12.4; p < 0.0001) in early-juvenile patients. Most treated patients acquired motor skills within the predicted healthy range or stabilised (maintaining walking), with normal cognitive development in most and benefits particularly apparent in patients treated before symptom onset. All patients had at least one grade ≥3 adverse event, most related to conditioning or background disease; the only arsa-cel-related event was transient anti-ARSA antibodies in four patients. No abnormal clonal proliferation or replication-competent lentivirus was seen.
cards.watchOut: No randomised or concurrent control exists anywhere in this base: every contrast is against a non-concurrent natural-history cohort, carrying the full bias risk of historical comparison. This report's 29 treated patients are a subset of the programme's later 39 (next card) — the two Ns are never added.
cards.source: Fumagalli et al. Lentiviral haematopoietic stem-cell gene therapy for early-onset metachromatic leukodystrophy: long-term results from a non-randomised, open-label, phase 1/2 trial and expanded access. Lancet (London, England). 2022. PMID: 35065785. Registry ID: NCT01560182. cards.headline: Long-term report (Fumagalli 2025 — a long-term report of the SAME programme, labelled as such; NCT01560182 and NCT03392987): 39 treated vs 49 untreated patients, median follow-up 6.76 years — survival free from severe motor impairment at age 6 was 100% (95% CI 100 to 100) in treated pre-symptomatic late-infantile patients vs 0% untreated; at age 10 it was 87.5% (95% CI 38.7 to 98.1, pre-symptomatic early-juvenile) and 80.0% (95% CI 40.9 to 94.6, early-symptomatic early-juvenile) vs 11.2% (95% CI 0.9 to 36.4) untreated
cards.summary: Long-term report (Fumagalli 2025 — a long-term report of the SAME programme, labelled as such; NCT01560182 and NCT03392987): 39 treated vs 49 untreated patients, median follow-up 6.76 years — survival free from severe motor impairment at age 6 was 100% (95% CI 100 to 100) in treated pre-symptomatic late-infantile patients vs 0% untreated; at age 10 it was 87.5% (95% CI 38.7 to 98.1, pre-symptomatic early-juvenile) and 80.0% (95% CI 40.9 to 94.6, early-symptomatic early-juvenile) vs 11.2% (95% CI 0.9 to 36.4) untreated
cards.type: Long-term report of the same programme (labelled) — two open-label studies plus expanded access, atidarsagene autotemcel in metachromatic leukodystrophy (NCT01560182; NCT03392987)
cards.people: 39 patients with metachromatic leukodystrophy treated with atidarsagene autotemcel in two prospective open-label studies and expanded-access programmes (the same programme as the 2022 report, with longer follow-up and more patients), compared with 49 untreated patients in a natural-history cohort; primary endpoint survival free from severe motor impairment (loss of locomotion and sitting without support, or death).
cards.result: The risk of severe motor impairment or death was significantly lower with treatment in all three subgroups (pre-symptomatic late-infantile P < 0.001; pre-symptomatic early-juvenile P = 0.04; early-symptomatic early-juvenile P < 0.001). No evidence of insertional oncogenesis was found. The most common grade ≥3 adverse event was febrile neutropenia; transient anti-ARSA antibodies occurred in 6 of 39 (15%); three deaths occurred, all judged unrelated to arsa-cel.
cards.watchOut: The early-juvenile confidence intervals are very wide (87.5% with 95% CI 38.7 to 98.1) — the point estimates look exact and are not. Benefit is concentrated in children treated pre-symptomatically; nothing here extends it to later treatment. Historical-cohort comparison, as on every card of this shelf.
cards.source: Fumagalli et al. Long-Term Effects of Atidarsagene Autotemcel for Metachromatic Leukodystrophy. The New England journal of medicine. 2025. PMID: 40267426. cards.headline: Peripheral-nerve post-hoc report (Zambon 2025 — a post-hoc analysis of the SAME programme, labelled as such): 15 treated pre-symptomatic late-infantile patients vs 16 untreated controls — at 36 months of age, treated patients showed higher estimated conduction velocities in all nerves, about 15 m/s higher in motor nerves, than age-matched controls
cards.summary: Peripheral-nerve post-hoc report (Zambon 2025 — a post-hoc analysis of the SAME programme, labelled as such): 15 treated pre-symptomatic late-infantile patients vs 16 untreated controls — at 36 months of age, treated patients showed higher estimated conduction velocities in all nerves, about 15 m/s higher in motor nerves, than age-matched controls
cards.type: Post-hoc analysis of the same programme (labelled) — peripheral nerve conduction outcomes, atidarsagene autotemcel in late-infantile metachromatic leukodystrophy
cards.people: 15 pre-symptomatic late-infantile patients treated with atidarsagene autotemcel within the programme's prospective open-label single-arm trials and expanded access (median age at treatment 13 months), vs 16 untreated natural-history patients studied with the same standardised nerve-conduction protocol. This report's own record carries no registry ID.
cards.result: Peripheral neuropathy was already present in most treated patients before treatment. At 36 months, estimated nerve conduction velocities were higher in treated patients in all nerves (~15 m/s difference in motor nerves); pre-treatment neuropathy severity did not affect 2-year conduction values, younger age at treatment was associated with higher motor ulnar and sensory medial velocities at 2 years, and post-treatment ARSA levels in CD15+ cells correlated with deep peroneal conduction and with slower subsequent decline.
cards.watchOut: A post-hoc, surrogate-endpoint (nerve conduction velocity) analysis of a 15-patient subset of the same programme — supporting detail for the programme's peripheral effects, never an independent report and never a clinical-outcome finding.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one programme, three reports, no randomised or concurrent control anywhere — the programme basis leads. Atidarsagene autotemcel-treated children (39 in the long-term report, which includes the earlier 29) had dramatically higher survival free from severe motor impairment than untreated natural-history cohorts (100% vs 0% at age 6 in pre-symptomatic late-infantile disease), with benefit concentrated in pre-symptomatic treatment — a historical-comparison result of unusual size, carrying the full bias risk of that design
cards.summary: Synthesis: one programme, three reports, no randomised or concurrent control anywhere — the programme basis leads. Atidarsagene autotemcel-treated children (39 in the long-term report, which includes the earlier 29) had dramatically higher survival free from severe motor impairment than untreated natural-history cohorts (100% vs 0% at age 6 in pre-symptomatic late-infantile disease), with benefit concentrated in pre-symptomatic treatment — a historical-comparison result of unusual size, carrying the full bias risk of that design
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf are one programme: the phase 1/2 + expanded-access report (29 treated vs 31 untreated), its long-term report (39 treated vs 49 untreated — the same programme, patients overlapping, counted once) and a post-hoc peripheral-nerve analysis of a 15-patient subset. Total treated N for the programme is 39, never the sum of the reports.
cards.result: Treatment requires busulfan conditioning and autologous stem-cell collection/infusion; all patients in the first report had at least one grade ≥3 adverse event (mostly conditioning- or disease-related) and febrile neutropenia was the commonest grade ≥3 event in the long-term report. No insertional oncogenesis was observed in either report. The tested product is named as the publications give it (atidarsagene autotemcel, arsa-cel) — clarification, not promotion.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data. Single-programme GAP-T basis: the stamp states the programme basis on its face, per standing discipline.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Elivaldogene autotemcel (eli-cel) for early cerebral adrenoleukodystrophy: most boys remained free of major functional disability at 6 years in a single-group programme — and 7 of 67 developed haematologic cancer
shelves.question: In boys with early cerebral adrenoleukodystrophy, does elivaldogene autotemcel (eli-cel; autologous lentiviral haematopoietic stem-cell gene therapy), compared with the untreated course of disease, preserve neurologic function and survival — and at what haematologic-malignancy risk? (GAP-T: one programme, three reports — the ALD-102 interim and full reports are the same study, labelled; no randomised or concurrent control exists in this base; haematologic cancer in 7 of 67 treated patients is load-bearing on the face.)

shelves.balance: GAP-T — one programme, three reports, labelled: this shelf rests on one programme's reports (the ALD-102 interim report, the ALD-102 full report — the same study, never counted as two studies — and a haematologic-cancer safety report across ALD-102 and ALD-104). NO randomised or concurrent control exists anywhere in this base; every efficacy contrast is against the untreated course of disease, so the survival-without-disability figures carry the full bias risk of non-concurrent comparison. The harm report is load-bearing: haematologic cancer developed in 7 of 67 treated patients (myelodysplastic syndrome in 6, acute myeloid leukaemia in 1), with lentiviral vector insertions at MECOM-EVI1 in 5 of the 6 patients with data. The 2017 interim report's 'no treatment-related death' must never be quoted without the 2024 cancer report beside it. Per the standing product-naming rule the tested product is named for clarification, not promotion: elivaldogene autotemcel (eli-cel; autologous CD34+ cells transduced with the Lenti-D lentiviral vector). ALD-104 contributes patients to the safety denominator only; its efficacy is not separately reported and none is claimed.

cards.headline: Report 1 of 3 — ALD-102 interim report (2017, N = 17 boys): 15 of 17 (88%) were alive and free of major functional disability at a median follow-up of 29.4 months, with no treatment-related death or graft-versus-host disease reported at that point — a single-group interim reading, superseded on safety by the 2024 cancer report carded below
cards.summary: Report 1 of 3 — ALD-102 interim report (2017, N = 17 boys): 15 of 17 (88%) were alive and free of major functional disability at a median follow-up of 29.4 months, with no treatment-related death or graft-versus-host disease reported at that point — a single-group interim reading, superseded on safety by the 2024 cancer report carded below
cards.type: Primary report — ALD-102 interim analysis, single-group open-label phase 2-3 (one programme)
cards.people: 17 boys with early-stage cerebral adrenoleukodystrophy and gadolinium enhancement on MRI, in a single-group, open-label phase 2-3 study; the primary end point was being alive with no major functional disability at 24 months after infusion of autologous CD34+ cells transduced with the elivaldogene tavalentivec (Lenti-D) lentiviral vector.
cards.result: All patients had gene-marked cells after engraftment and measurable ALD protein was observed in all. 15 of 17 (88%) were alive and free of major functional disability with minimal clinical symptoms. One patient with rapid neurologic deterioration died from disease progression; another withdrew to undergo allogeneic stem-cell transplantation and later died from transplantation-related complications. No treatment-related death or graft-versus-host disease had been reported at this interim point.
cards.watchOut: Interim, single-group and uncontrolled: there is no concurrent comparator, and the reassuring early safety wording is superseded by the 2024 haematologic-cancer report (card 3) — never quote this card's safety line without it.

cards.headline: Report 2 of 3 — ALD-102 full report (2024, N = 32 patients — the full report of the same ALD-102 study as card 1, labelled as such): at month 24 none of the 29 completers had a major functional disability and overall survival was 94%; at a median follow-up of 6 years, 26 of 32 (81%) had no major functional disabilities and the neurologic function score was stable in 30 of 32 (94%)
cards.summary: Report 2 of 3 — ALD-102 full report (2024, N = 32 patients — the full report of the same ALD-102 study as card 1, labelled as such): at month 24 none of the 29 completers had a major functional disability and overall survival was 94%; at a median follow-up of 6 years, 26 of 32 (81%) had no major functional disabilities and the neurologic function score was stable in 30 of 32 (94%)
cards.type: Primary report — ALD-102 full report, single-group phase 2-3 (one programme; same study as card 1)
cards.people: 32 boys with early-stage cerebral adrenoleukodystrophy and evidence of active inflammation on MRI received eli-cel in the phase 2-3 ALD-102 study; 29 (91%) completed the 24-month study and are monitored in long-term follow-up. The primary efficacy end point was survival without any of six major functional disabilities at month 24.
cards.result: At month 24, none of the 29 completers had major functional disabilities; overall survival was 94%. At the most recent assessment (median follow-up 6 years) the neurologic function score was stable versus baseline in 30 of 32 (94%) and 26 (81%) had no major functional disabilities. Four patients had adverse events directly related to eli-cel. Myelodysplastic syndrome with excess blasts developed in 1 patient at month 92, treated with allogeneic transplantation, after which the patient did not have MDS at the most recent follow-up.
cards.watchOut: This is the full report of the study whose interim analysis is card 1 — one study, two reports, never two independent confirmations. Still no concurrent control: benefit is concentrated in boys treated at an early stage with active MRI inflammation, and no wording may extend it to later treatment.

cards.headline: Report 3 of 3 — haematologic-cancer safety report across ALD-102 and ALD-104 (2024, load-bearing harm): haematologic cancer developed in 7 of 67 patients after eli-cel (1 of 32 in ALD-102; 6 of 35 in ALD-104) — myelodysplastic syndrome in 6 (at 14, 26, 28, 36, 42 and 92 months) and acute myeloid leukaemia in 1 (at 57 months)
cards.summary: Report 3 of 3 — haematologic-cancer safety report across ALD-102 and ALD-104 (2024, load-bearing harm): haematologic cancer developed in 7 of 67 patients after eli-cel (1 of 32 in ALD-102; 6 of 35 in ALD-104) — myelodysplastic syndrome in 6 (at 14, 26, 28, 36, 42 and 92 months) and acute myeloid leukaemia in 1 (at 57 months)
cards.type: Safety report — haematologic cancer across both programme studies and follow-up (one programme; load-bearing harm)
cards.people: 67 patients who received eli-cel in the two completed phase 2-3 studies (ALD-102, 32 patients; ALD-104, 35 patients) and their follow-up study, with integration-site analysis, genetic, flow-cytometry and morphologic studies in peripheral-blood and bone-marrow samples.
cards.result: In the 6 patients with available data, predominant clones contained lentiviral vector insertions at multiple loci, including MECOM-EVI1 in 5 patients and PRDM16 in 1; 6 of 7 also had somatic mutations, and 1 had monosomy 7. Of 5 patients with MDS who underwent allogeneic transplantation, 4 remain free of MDS without recurrence of cerebral adrenoleukodystrophy symptoms and 1 died from presumed graft-versus-host disease 20 months after transplantation; the patient with AML is alive with full donor chimerism after transplantation, and the most recent MDS patient is alive awaiting transplantation.
cards.watchOut: Insertional oncogenesis is not a theoretical risk in this base: about 1 in 10 treated boys developed MDS or AML, several requiring allogeneic transplantation. Any presentation of the 94% survival / 81% disability-free figures without this 7-of-67 count on its face misrepresents the programme.

shelves.question: In adults and children with neurofibromatosis type 1 and symptomatic, inoperable plexiform neurofibromas, does the MEK1/2 inhibitor mirdametinib shrink target tumours on volumetric MRI — and at what dermatologic and gastrointestinal cost? (FLOOR-RISK: exactly 2 reports, both single-arm — the count IS the question's headline.)

shelves.balance: FLOOR-RISK — the exact base prints here and in the stamp: exactly 2 single-arm reports, total N = 133 (ReNeu N = 114 + NF106 N = 19), no randomised trial and no control arm in either. ReNeu (58 adults, 56 children aged 2–17) found blinded-central-review confirmed objective response in 41% of adults and 52% of children, median best volumetric change −41% / −42%, with early, sustained pain and quality-of-life improvement; NF106 (19 patients aged ≥16) found partial response in 42% and stable disease in 53%. The commonest treatment-related events were dermatitis acneiform, diarrhoea and nausea (adults) and dermatitis acneiform, diarrhoea and paronychia (children). A volumetric response rate from an uncontrolled series is never a comparative effect, and this shelf presents it as nothing more. Cross-point only: selumetinib, the sibling MEK inhibitor, is homed at pack #7038 — the two drugs' rates are never merged into a class claim.

cards.headline: ReNeu (Moertel 2025, pivotal phase 2b, single-arm, N = 114 — 58 adults and 56 children aged 2–17): blinded-central-review confirmed objective response (≥20% target-volume reduction on consecutive scans) in 41% of adults (24 of 58) and 52% of children (29 of 56) during the 24-cycle phase, with three further confirmed responses in long-term follow-up; median best volumetric change −41% (adults) and −42% (children)
cards.summary: ReNeu (Moertel 2025, pivotal phase 2b, single-arm, N = 114 — 58 adults and 56 children aged 2–17): blinded-central-review confirmed objective response (≥20% target-volume reduction on consecutive scans) in 41% of adults (24 of 58) and 52% of children (29 of 56) during the 24-cycle phase, with three further confirmed responses in long-term follow-up; median best volumetric change −41% (adults) and −42% (children)
cards.type: Single-arm pivotal phase 2b trial — ReNeu (report 1 of exactly 2 on this FLOOR-RISK shelf)
cards.people: 114 patients (58 adults ≥18 years; 56 children aged 2–17) with neurofibromatosis type 1 and symptomatic, inoperable plexiform neurofibromas causing significant morbidity, treated open-label with mirdametinib 2 mg/m² twice daily (maximum 4 mg twice daily), 3 weeks on / 1 week off in 28-day cycles; primary endpoint confirmed objective response rate by blinded independent central review of volumetric MRI. No control arm.
cards.result: Confirmed objective responses occurred in 24 of 58 adults (41%) and 29 of 56 children (52%) during the 24-cycle treatment phase, with two further adults and one child responding in long-term follow-up. Median best target-tumour volumetric change was −41% (range −90 to 13) in adults and −42% (−91 to 48) in children. Patient- or parent-proxy-reported worst tumour pain severity, pain interference and health-related quality of life improved early and were sustained. The commonest treatment-related adverse events were dermatitis acneiform, diarrhoea and nausea in adults, and dermatitis acneiform, diarrhoea and paronychia in children. The record states no pharmacotherapy was FDA-approved for adults at the time.
cards.watchOut: FLOOR-RISK: this is one of exactly 2 reports on this shelf, both single-arm and uncontrolled. A volumetric response rate is not a comparative effect — there is no control arm, and no card on this shelf may present 41% / 52% as a benefit measured against anything.

cards.headline: NF106 (Weiss 2021, phase 2, single-arm, N = 19): partial response in 42% (8 of 19) by course 12, stable disease in 53% (10 of 19) and progression in 1 patient (5%), at a median baseline tumour volume of 363.8 mL; pain ratings fell significantly and durably
cards.summary: NF106 (Weiss 2021, phase 2, single-arm, N = 19): partial response in 42% (8 of 19) by course 12, stable disease in 53% (10 of 19) and progression in 1 patient (5%), at a median baseline tumour volume of 363.8 mL; pain ratings fell significantly and durably
cards.type: Single-arm phase 2 trial — NF106 (report 2 of exactly 2 on this FLOOR-RISK shelf)
cards.people: 19 patients aged ≥16 years (median 24, range 16–39) with neurofibromatosis type 1 and progressive or morbid inoperable plexiform neurofibromas, treated with mirdametinib 2 mg/m²/dose (maximum 4 mg) twice daily, 3 weeks on / 1 week off, up to 24 courses, in the Neurofibromatosis Clinical Trials Consortium; median baseline tumour volume 363.8 mL (range 3.9–5,161 mL). No control arm.
cards.result: Eight of 19 patients (42%) achieved a partial response of the target plexiform neurofibroma by course 12, 10 (53%) had stable disease and 1 (5%) developed progressive disease at course 8. Significant and durable decreases were observed in pain ratings. The authors describe this as the first published response study for MEK inhibitors in adults with NF1 and plexiform neurofibromas.
cards.watchOut: FLOOR-RISK: N = 19 — the smallest report on this shelf, printed on the face. Single-arm: the 42% partial-response rate has no comparator, and stable disease in a slow-growing tumour cannot be credited to the drug from this design.

cards.headline: Cross-report card (not an additional report): the entire mirdametinib base is exactly 2 single-arm reports, total N = 133 (114 + 19), on the same dose and schedule (2 mg/m² twice daily, maximum 4 mg, 3 weeks on / 1 week off) — response 41% (adults) and 52% (children) in ReNeu and 42% partial response in NF106, with dermatologic and gastrointestinal events the commonest harms and no randomised trial in existence
cards.summary: Cross-report card (not an additional report): the entire mirdametinib base is exactly 2 single-arm reports, total N = 133 (114 + 19), on the same dose and schedule (2 mg/m² twice daily, maximum 4 mg, 3 weeks on / 1 week off) — response 41% (adults) and 52% (children) in ReNeu and 42% partial response in NF106, with dermatologic and gastrointestinal events the commonest harms and no randomised trial in existence
cards.type: Cross-report summary of the two carded reports — not an additional report (source line repeats the ReNeu report for reference)
cards.people: The two carded reports only: ReNeu (N = 114; 58 adults, 56 children) and NF106 (N = 19; aged ≥16). Cross-point in prose only: the sibling selumetinib question in NF1 plexiform neurofibromas is homed at pack #7038 (SPRINT, paediatric, likewise single-arm) — cross-pointed in both directions, never carded here.
cards.result: The two response readings (41–52% in ReNeu by age group; 42% in NF106) are concordant in size and were obtained on the same dose/schedule, but concordance between two uncontrolled series is not comparative evidence: spontaneous volumetric change, selection and measurement variation are unmeasured in both. No head-to-head or comparative data exist between mirdametinib and selumetinib, and the two drugs' response rates are never merged into a class claim. Mirdametinib was FDA-approved in February 2025 for adults and children, as the slate records; the remainder of its literature is reviews, a First Approval note and an erratum to ReNeu — none is a third report.

shelves.title: Gugging Swallowing Screen (GUSS) in acute stroke: sensitivity 96.5–100% at the 14-point cut-off but specificity only 50–69% — collapsing to 20% in severe stroke, with nasogastric feeding overestimated; GUSS-ICU adaptation AUC 0.923 after extubation (N = 45)
shelves.question: In acute stroke (and, in its ICU adaptation, in recently extubated patients), how accurately does the Gugging Swallowing Screen (GUSS — a graded bedside screen scoring saliva, semisolid, liquid and solid swallowing in sequence, 0–20 points, with diet recommendations by score band) detect aspiration and dysphagia against fiberoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing (FEES) — what sensitivity and specificity did its derivation study and its independent revalidation deliver at the 14-point cut-off, how do they collapse in severe stroke, and what pooled accuracy does the systematic review find?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Aged · Deglutition · Deglutition Disorders/diagnosis/etiology/physiopathology · Esophagoscopy · Esophagus/physiopathology · Female · Geriatric Assessment · Humans · Male · Mass Screening/methods · Neurologic Examination/methods · Observer Variation · Pharynx/physiopathology · Pneumonia, Aspiration/prevention & control · Point-of-Care Systems/standards · Predictive Value of Tests · Prospective Studies · Reproducibility of Results · Sensitivity and Specificity · Stroke/complications/physiopathology
shelves.balance: A screening-accuracy shelf, not a treatment shelf: no card implies GUSS-guided diet pathways improve pneumonia or mortality. The GUSS (graded saliva/semisolid/liquid/solid sequence, 0–20 points) was derived by its originators in 50 acute-stroke patients (samples of 20 and 30 — Ns on the face) with sensitivity 100% and specificity 50–69% at the 14-point cut-off against FEES, and independently revalidated in 100 patients at sensitivity 96.5% / specificity 55.8% — splitting by severity to 71.4% / 88.8% in NIHSS <5 and 100% / 20% in NIHSS ≥15, with diet recommendations more conservative than FEES and nasogastric feeding overestimated. The systematic review (8 studies, a synthesis overlapping the primaries) pools sensitivity at 0.97 and specificity at 0.67. The GUSS-ICU adaptation (45 post-extubation patients, a modified instrument, never pooled with the stroke figures) gave AUC 0.923. Specificity is the weak limb throughout, and its false-positive cost — over-restricted diets and excess tube feeding — prints beside the sensitivity headline.

cards.headline: GUSS derivation (Trapl 2007, 50 acute-stroke patients against FEES — the originators' own report, programme-labelled): at the 14-point cut-off, sensitivity 100% and specificity 50% in the 20-patient therapist sample and 100% / 69% in the 30-patient nurse-tested sample, AUC 0.77 and 0.933 respectively; inter-rater kappa 0.835
cards.summary: GUSS derivation (Trapl 2007, 50 acute-stroke patients against FEES — the originators' own report, programme-labelled): at the 14-point cut-off, sensitivity 100% and specificity 50% in the 20-patient therapist sample and 100% / 69% in the 30-patient nurse-tested sample, AUC 0.77 and 0.933 respectively; inter-rater kappa 0.835
cards.type: Derivation / validation study against FEES — originators' own report (programme-labelled)
cards.people: 50 acute-stroke patients assessed prospectively against fiberoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing (FEES): 20 patients rated independently by 2 therapists for inter-rater reliability, and a separate group of 30 patients tested by stroke nurses for external validity. The Gugging Swallowing Screen (GUSS) scores saliva, semisolid, liquid and solid swallowing in sequence (0–20 points) with diet recommendations by score band. Originators' centre (Gugging, Austria).
cards.result: Inter-rater reliability was excellent (kappa = 0.835, P < 0.001). GUSS predicted aspiration risk with AUC 0.77 (95% CI 0.53–1.02) in the 20-patient sample and 0.933 (0.833–1.033) in the 30-patient sample; at the 14-point cut-off, sensitivity was 100% in both samples, specificity 50% and 69% respectively, and negative predictive value 100% in both. Aspiration risk was significantly higher with liquids than with semisolid textures (P = 0.001), confirming the subtest sequence.
cards.watchOut: Programme-labelled: the originators' own report, in small derivation samples (20 + 30 patients — their Ns print here). Sensitivity of 100% in samples this size is fragile, and specificity — the weak limb — was only 50–69% from the start: a positive GUSS over-restricts diet in a substantial minority.

cards.headline: GUSS independent revalidation (Warnecke 2017, 100 consecutive acute-stroke patients, double-blind against FEES): at cut-off 14, sensitivity 96.5% and specificity 55.8% overall (AUC 0.76) — but sensitivity 71.4% / specificity 88.8% in NIHSS <5 against sensitivity 100% / specificity 20% in NIHSS ≥15, with GUSS diet recommendations more conservative than FEES and nasogastric feeding overestimated
cards.summary: GUSS independent revalidation (Warnecke 2017, 100 consecutive acute-stroke patients, double-blind against FEES): at cut-off 14, sensitivity 96.5% and specificity 55.8% overall (AUC 0.76) — but sensitivity 71.4% / specificity 88.8% in NIHSS <5 against sensitivity 100% / specificity 20% in NIHSS ≥15, with GUSS diet recommendations more conservative than FEES and nasogastric feeding overestimated
cards.people: 100 consecutive acute-stroke patients at an independent centre, evaluated a mean 1.7 ± 2.2 days after stroke, in a prospective double-blind design against the FEES scale, with diagnostic properties calculated separately by NIHSS severity subgroup.
cards.result: At the 14-point cut-off the GUSS screened aspiration risk with sensitivity 96.5% and specificity 55.8% (AUC 0.76, 95% CI 0.67–0.84), corresponding well with the original publication overall. Performance split sharply by severity: in NIHSS <5, sensitivity 71.4% and specificity 88.8%; in NIHSS ≥15, sensitivity 100% and specificity 20%, with a high failure rate in completing the first part of the GUSS in the severe group related to the low specificity. Diet recommendations after GUSS were more conservative than after FEES, and the GUSS overestimated the need for nasogastric tube feeding.
cards.watchOut: The severity split is the content: in severe stroke the screen at this cut-off labels almost everyone at risk (specificity 20%), so its diet and tube-feeding recommendations over-restrict — the false-positive cost prints beside the sensitivity headline wherever this shelf is summarised.
cards.source: Warnecke T et al. Aspiration and dysphagia screening in acute stroke - the Gugging Swallowing Screen revisited. European journal of neurology. 2017. PMID: 28322006. cards.headline: GUSS systematic review (Park 2020, 8 studies): pooled sensitivity 0.97 (95% CI 0.93–0.99), pooled specificity 0.67 (0.59–0.74) and AUC 0.9381 against reference standards
cards.summary: GUSS systematic review (Park 2020, 8 studies): pooled sensitivity 0.97 (95% CI 0.93–0.99), pooled specificity 0.67 (0.59–0.74) and AUC 0.9381 against reference standards
cards.type: Systematic review (synthesis — primary studies overlap the other cards; not an independent cohort)
cards.people: Systematic review of studies of the Gugging Swallowing Screen in patients with stroke, searching Ovid MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Cochrane Library and Korean databases to November 2018; of 297 records, 8 articles were included. A synthesis — its primary studies overlap the derivation and revalidation programmes carded on this shelf and it is not an independent cohort.
cards.result: Pooled sensitivity was 0.97 (95% CI 0.93–0.99), pooled specificity 0.67 (0.59–0.74) and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.9381. On benefit, early systematic nurse-performed GUSS screening reduced screening time and pneumonia rate versus a control group (P = 0.004) and X-ray-verified pneumonia was lower than with clinical screening (P < 0.01), but pneumonia incidence did not differ significantly from that predicted using the 10 mL water swallowing test.
cards.watchOut: A synthesis, counted as a synthesis: its pooled figures summarise substantially the same small primary literature carded above and must not be cited as a fourth, independent confirmation. The pneumonia readings come from individual included studies, not from the pooled accuracy analysis.

cards.headline: GUSS-ICU adaptation (Troll 2023, 45 patients intubated ≥24 h, tested after extubation against FEES): 80% had dysphagia on FEES; AUC 0.923 for both rater pairs, sensitivity 91.7–94.4%, specificity 66.7–88.9% and inter-rater kappa 0.84
cards.summary: GUSS-ICU adaptation (Troll 2023, 45 patients intubated ≥24 h, tested after extubation against FEES): 80% had dysphagia on FEES; AUC 0.923 for both rater pairs, sensitivity 91.7–94.4%, specificity 66.7–88.9% and inter-rater kappa 0.84
cards.type: Validation of a modified instrument (GUSS-ICU) in post-extubation ICU patients against FEES
cards.people: 45 consecutive ICU patients intubated for at least 24 hours, recruited at the earliest 24 hours after extubation; the modified GUSS-ICU was performed twice by two speech and language therapists independently, with FEES by an otorhinolaryngologist as the reference standard, all within a 3-hour period and blinded. A modified instrument in a different population (post-extubation), never pooled with the stroke figures.
cards.result: By FEES, 36 of 45 participants (80%) had dysphagia (13 severe, 12 moderate, 11 mild). The GUSS-ICU predicted dysphagia with AUC 0.923 for both rater pairs; sensitivity was 91.7% and 94.4%, specificity 88.9% and 66.7%, positive predictive values 97.1% and 91.9% and negative predictive values 72.7% and 75% for the first and second rater pairs respectively. Dysphagia severity classification correlated strongly with FEES (Spearman's rho 0.61 and 0.60), and inter-rater reliability was good (Cohen's kappa 0.84).
cards.watchOut: N = 45, printed on the face, and a modified instrument: these figures describe the ICU adaptation after extubation, not the stroke GUSS, and the wide specificity interval for one rater pair (66.7%, 95% CI 29.9–92.5%) shows how thin the non-dysphagic denominator (9 patients) is.
cards.source: Troll C et al. A bedside swallowing screen for the identification of post-extubation dysphagia on the intensive care unit - validation of the Gugging Swallowing Screen (GUSS)-ICU. cards.headline: Synthesis: the GUSS detects aspiration risk after stroke with high sensitivity (96.5–100% at the 14-point cut-off; pooled 0.97) and weak specificity (50–69% at derivation, 55.8% on revalidation, pooled 0.67) that collapses to 20% in severe stroke — and its ICU adaptation shows the same shape (AUC 0.923, N = 45) in post-extubation patients
cards.summary: Synthesis: the GUSS detects aspiration risk after stroke with high sensitivity (96.5–100% at the 14-point cut-off; pooled 0.97) and weak specificity (50–69% at derivation, 55.8% on revalidation, pooled 0.67) that collapses to 20% in severe stroke — and its ICU adaptation shows the same shape (AUC 0.923, N = 45) in post-extubation patients
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: derivation (50 patients in two samples), independent revalidation (100 patients), a systematic review of 8 studies (a synthesis, overlapping the primaries) and the GUSS-ICU adaptation (45 patients). Cross-point: the Yale Swallow Protocol (shelf #7786) is a different instrument — a pass/fail 3-ounce water challenge — with no shared anchor.
cards.result: Sensitivity is the established limb and specificity the weak limb throughout, in every population tested. No card on this shelf implies that GUSS-guided diet pathways improve pneumonia or mortality outcomes: this is a screening-accuracy shelf, and the one pneumonia signal inside the review is an individual-study reading, printed as such on its card.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Yale Swallow Protocol (3-ounce water swallow challenge): 907 passers ate and drank without overt signs at 12–24 h in the 1,000-patient originators' series (no instrumental comparator), nurses administer it with 98.01% agreement with pathologists, and against videofluoroscopy in TBI (N = 50) sensitivity was 96.8% / specificity 78.9%
shelves.question: In hospitalised adults at risk of dysphagia, how well does the Yale Swallow Protocol (a brief cognitive screen and oral-mechanism examination followed by an uninterrupted 3-ounce / 90 cc water swallow challenge; pass = drink the full volume without coughing or wet voice) identify patients who can safely start an oral diet — what happened in the 1,000-patient implementation series, how accurately do trained nurses administer it against speech-language pathologists, and what is its diagnostic accuracy against videofluoroscopy in acute moderate-to-severe traumatic brain injury?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Deglutition/physiology · Deglutition Disorders/diagnosis/etiology · Diet · Drinking · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Water
shelves.balance: A screening/implementation shelf, not a treatment shelf — and its three reports answer three different questions, never merged. The implementation series (1,000 consecutively referred patients at the originators' own centre, programme-labelled) found all 907 included passers eating and drinking thin liquids without overt signs of dysphagia 12–24 h later (median next-meal liquid volume 340 cc; diet recommendations followed with 100% accuracy) — but the design has no instrumental reference standard, so it cannot support an aspiration-accuracy claim, and that limitation prints on the face. Trained nurses administered the protocol with 98.01% agreement with speech-language pathologists (101 inpatients) — an agreement result, not accuracy against swallowing physiology. Accuracy rests on the TBI study alone (50 patients against videofluoroscopy: sensitivity 96.8%, specificity 78.9%, PPV 88.2%, NPV 93.8%), whose N prints wherever its figures do. Examiner training is part of the intervention in every report, and no figure extends to postoperative patients.

cards.headline: Yale Swallow Protocol implementation series (Leder 2012 — prospective single-group series, 1,000 consecutively referred hospitalised patients at the protocol originators' own centre, programme-labelled): of 907 passers with stable conditions assessed 12–24 h later, all were eating and drinking thin liquids successfully without overt signs of dysphagia, median liquid volume at the next meal 340 cc, and diet recommendations were followed with 100% accuracy
cards.summary: Yale Swallow Protocol implementation series (Leder 2012 — prospective single-group series, 1,000 consecutively referred hospitalised patients at the protocol originators' own centre, programme-labelled): of 907 passers with stable conditions assessed 12–24 h later, all were eating and drinking thin liquids successfully without overt signs of dysphagia, median liquid volume at the next meal 340 cc, and diet recommendations were followed with 100% accuracy
cards.type: Prospective implementation case series — originators' own centre (programme-labelled; no instrumental reference standard)
cards.people: 1,000 consecutively referred hospitalised patients at a large urban tertiary teaching hospital (Yale — the protocol originators' centre), given the 3-ounce (90 cc) water swallow challenge protocol (brief cognitive screen and oral-mechanism examination, then an uninterrupted 3-ounce water swallow; pass = drink the full volume without coughing or wet voice); 907 met the inclusion criteria of stable medical, surgical or neurological conditions 12–24 h after passing. Care providers were blinded to the study's purpose. There is NO instrumental reference standard in this design — 'success' is absence of overt clinical signs, and that limitation prints on the face.
cards.result: All 907 included passers were both eating and drinking thin liquids successfully and without overt signs of dysphagia 12–24 hours after passing. Median volume of liquid ingested at the next day's meal was 340 cc (interquartile range 240–460). Specific diet recommendations were followed with 100% accuracy. The authors conclude the protocol successfully identified patients who can be safely advanced to an oral diet without subsequent identification of overt signs of aspiration within 12–24 hours, when administered by a trained provider.
cards.watchOut: The largest report on this shelf (N = 1,000) cannot support an aspiration-accuracy claim: without videofluoroscopy or endoscopy, silent aspiration is invisible to this design by construction. It supports an implementation statement — passers ate and drank without overt signs the next day — and nothing stronger.

cards.headline: Nurse administration of the Yale Swallow Protocol (Warner 2014 — prospective blinded study, 101 inpatients, 52 registered nurses trained by web module): nurse-vs-speech-pathologist protocol agreement 98.01%, with the pathologists' own intra- and inter-rater agreement 100%
cards.summary: Nurse administration of the Yale Swallow Protocol (Warner 2014 — prospective blinded study, 101 inpatients, 52 registered nurses trained by web module): nurse-vs-speech-pathologist protocol agreement 98.01%, with the pathologists' own intra- and inter-rater agreement 100%
cards.type: Prospective blinded administration-agreement study (nurses vs speech-language pathologists)
cards.people: 101 inpatients and 52 registered nurses; each patient was first administered the 3-ounce water swallow challenge protocol (with basic cognitive screen and oral-mechanism evaluation) by a speech-language pathologist, then within one hour by a nurse trained via a web-based teaching module, independently and blinded, with a pathologist simultaneously re-rating out of view. This study measures agreement with pathologists administering the same protocol — not accuracy against swallowing physiology — and prints as such.
cards.result: Intra- and inter-rater protocol agreements for the two speech-language pathologists were 100%. Inter-rater protocol agreement between registered nurses and speech-language pathologists was 98.01%. The authors conclude the nurse-administered protocol is reliable and accurate as an administration matter, citing previously reported sensitivity of 96.5%, negative predictive value of 97.9% and a false-negative rate under 2% from the protocol's earlier literature (figures from that literature, not measured in this study).

cards.headline: Yale Swallow Protocol against videofluoroscopy in traumatic brain injury (Weppner 2024 — prospective blinded study, 50 consecutive adults with acute moderate-to-severe TBI at a level-1 trauma centre): against VFSS, sensitivity 96.8%, specificity 78.9%, positive predictive value 88.2% and negative predictive value 93.8% for aspiration
cards.summary: Yale Swallow Protocol against videofluoroscopy in traumatic brain injury (Weppner 2024 — prospective blinded study, 50 consecutive adults with acute moderate-to-severe TBI at a level-1 trauma centre): against VFSS, sensitivity 96.8%, specificity 78.9%, positive predictive value 88.2% and negative predictive value 93.8% for aspiration
cards.type: Prospective blinded diagnostic-accuracy study against VFSS in acute moderate-to-severe TBI
cards.people: 50 consecutive adults with acute moderate-to-severe traumatic brain injury at a level-1 academic trauma centre (July 2020–June 2021); each participant underwent the Yale Swallow Protocol followed within 5–10 minutes by a videofluoroscopic swallow study (VFSS), with excellent inter-rater agreement for identifying aspiration on both (100% agreement between the speech-language pathologists and the radiologist, and between the two pathologists). N = 50 prints on the face — this small study carries the shelf's accuracy claim.
cards.result: Of the 50 participants, 16 passed the protocol and 34 failed; among those who failed, 30 were confirmed to have aspirated on VFSS (true positives) and 4 did not show aspiration (false positives). The protocol demonstrated sensitivity 96.8%, specificity 78.9%, positive predictive value 88.2% and negative predictive value 93.8% for identifying aspiration in this cohort. The authors conclude the protocol is an effective screening tool for prediction of aspiration in acute care patients with moderate-to-severe TBI, due to its high sensitivity and negative predictive value.
cards.watchOut: One population (acute moderate-to-severe TBI), one centre, N = 50: these accuracy figures must not be extended to general hospital patients, to stroke, or — as the row's flag states — to postoperative patients, whose water-swallow slice remains separately unverified. Specificity of 78.9% rests on 19 non-aspirating patients (15 of 19 correctly passed).
cards.source: Weppner J et al. Diagnostic Accuracy of the Yale Swallow Protocol in Moderate-to-Severe Traumatic Brain Injury: A Prospective Blinded Videofluoroscopic Investigation. The Journal of head trauma rehabilitation. 2024. PMID: 38453631. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the Yale Swallow Protocol's implementation record is large and clean (907 passers eating and drinking without overt signs at 12–24 h, in a series with no instrumental comparator), trained nurses administer it as pathologists do (98.01% agreement), and its only instrumental accuracy test — in acute moderate-to-severe TBI, N = 50 — gives sensitivity 96.8% and specificity 78.9% against videofluoroscopy
cards.summary: Synthesis: the Yale Swallow Protocol's implementation record is large and clean (907 passers eating and drinking without overt signs at 12–24 h, in a series with no instrumental comparator), trained nurses administer it as pathologists do (98.01% agreement), and its only instrumental accuracy test — in acute moderate-to-severe TBI, N = 50 — gives sensitivity 96.8% and specificity 78.9% against videofluoroscopy
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: the 1,000-patient implementation series (907 passers analysed), the nurse-administration agreement study (101 inpatients, 52 nurses) and the TBI videofluoroscopic accuracy study (50 patients). Cross-point: the Gugging Swallowing Screen (shelf #7780) is a different instrument — a graded texture sequence vs this pass/fail liquid challenge — with no shared anchor.
cards.result: The three reports answer three different questions — can passers eat safely the next day (implementation), can nurses administer it (agreement), and does it detect aspiration (accuracy, one small TBI study) — and no summary may borrow the large N of the first to strengthen the accuracy claim of the third. Examiner training is part of the intervention in every report; no card presents the challenge as an untrained bedside test. This is a screening/implementation shelf, not a treatment shelf.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Dichlorphenamide for prevention of attacks in primary periodic paralysis — the only randomised evidence in the disease: Class I evidence in hypokalemic paralysis, an underpowered non-significant trial in hyperkalemic paralysis
shelves.question: In patients with primary (hereditary) periodic paralysis, does the carbonic-anhydrase inhibitor dichlorphenamide reduce the frequency and severity of paralytic attacks versus placebo — in hypokalemic periodic paralysis, in hyperkalemic / potassium-sensitive periodic paralysis, and over one year of continued treatment?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Child · Dichlorphenamide/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Paralysis/drug therapy, physiopathology · Prognosis · Time Factors · Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Follow-Up Studies · Paralyses, Familial Periodic/diagnosis, drug therapy · Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors/adverse effects, therapeutic use · Dichlorphenamide/adverse effects, therapeutic use · Paralyses, Familial Periodic/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: The hypokalemic limb is the load-bearing evidence — two randomised programmes, concordant. In the 2000 Working Group crossovers (hypokalemic N = 42; potassium-sensitive N = 31), 11 of the 13 hypokalemic patients who showed an endpoint preference preferred dichlorphenamide, and dichlorphenamide significantly reduced attack rates in the potassium-sensitive trial and in the hypokalemic subjects. In the 2016 parallel trials (hypokalemic N = 44; hyperkalemic N = 21), the median attack rate in hypokalemic patients was 0.3 vs 2.4 attacks/week on placebo (P = 0.02), with a better SF-36 Physical Component Summary change (treatment effect 7.29 points, 95% CI 2.26–12.32, P = 0.006). The hyperkalemic limb must never be averaged into a class claim: the 2016 median attack rate was 0.9 vs 4.8 but NOT significant (P = 0.10), and the paper's own classification — Class I evidence for the hypokalemic limb, insufficient precision for the hyperkalemic limb — is carried exactly. The one-year open-label extension (63 completers of the double-blind phase; 47 completed 61 weeks) showed sustained median attack-rate falls (−1.00 continuous, P < 0.0001; −0.63 after switching from placebo, P = 0.01). The adolescent analysis rests on 7 adolescents and is supportive only. Attack frequency is a patient-counted outcome in all trials. Harms: paresthesia (47% vs 14%) and confusion (19% vs 7%); in the extension, paresthesia and cognition-related events typically appeared in the first month and dose reductions frequently resolved them. Dichlorphenamide is FDA-approved for primary periodic paralysis (2015, on the 2016 programme); the 2000 trials are of the older Daranide formulation era — doses as published. Acetazolamide has no randomised report in this base and is not a limb of this shelf.

cards.headline: 2000 Working Group crossover trials: 11 of 13 hypokalemic patients with an endpoint preference preferred dichlorphenamide; attack rates significantly reduced in the potassium-sensitive trial and in hypokalemic subjects
cards.summary: 2000 Working Group crossover trials: 11 of 13 hypokalemic patients with an endpoint preference preferred dichlorphenamide; attack rates significantly reduced in the potassium-sensitive trial and in hypokalemic subjects
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trials (2000 programme)
cards.people: Two multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trials: 42 subjects with hypokalemic periodic paralysis and 31 with potassium-sensitive periodic paralysis; two 8-week treatment periods separated by an active washout of at least 9 weeks.
cards.result: In the hypokalemic trial (primary outcome: occurrence of an intolerable increase in attack severity or frequency), 13 subjects exhibited a preference for either treatment and 11 of the 13 preferred dichlorphenamide. In the potassium-sensitive trial (primary outcome: attacks per week), dichlorphenamide significantly reduced attack rates relative to placebo; dichlorphenamide also significantly reduced attack rates in the hypokalemic subjects. The authors conclude dichlorphenamide is effective in preventing episodic weakness in both forms.
cards.watchOut: Older Daranide formulation era — doses as published. The hypokalemic primary outcome is a preference endpoint (13 of 42 patients showed a preference); print it as such, not as an attack-rate effect.
cards.source: Tawil R et al. Randomized trials of dichlorphenamide in the periodic paralyses. Working Group on Periodic Paralysis. Annals of neurology. 2000. PMID: 10632100. cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled parallel trials (2016 programme)
cards.people: Two multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled 9-week trials: 44 participants with hypokalemic and 21 with hyperkalemic periodic paralysis; primary outcome the average number of attacks per week over the final 8 weeks.
cards.result: Hypokalemic: median attack rate 0.3 on dichlorphenamide vs 2.4 on placebo (P = 0.02), and the 9-week mean change in SF-36 Physical Component Summary was better on dichlorphenamide (treatment effect 7.29 points, 95% CI 2.26–12.32, P = 0.006). Commonest adverse events (both trials combined): paresthesia 47% on dichlorphenamide vs 14% on placebo, and confusion 19% vs 7%.
cards.watchOut: The hypokalemic/hyperkalemic asymmetry is the content of this shelf: never average the limbs into a class claim. The hyperkalemic trial enrolled only 21 patients.

cards.headline: One-year extension of the 2016 trials: median weekly attack-rate change to week 61 was −1.00 on continuous dichlorphenamide (P < 0.0001) and −0.63 after switching from placebo (P = 0.01)
cards.summary: One-year extension of the 2016 trials: median weekly attack-rate change to week 61 was −1.00 on continuous dichlorphenamide (P < 0.0001) and −0.63 after switching from placebo (P = 0.01)
cards.type: Open-label extension / post hoc analysis of the 2016 randomised programme (not an independent trial)
cards.people: Post hoc analysis of the 2016 programme's 52-week open-label phase: 63 adults completed the 9-week double-blind phase and 47 (74.6%) completed 61 weeks; hyperkalemic and hypokalemic substudies pooled for this analysis.
cards.result: Median decreases in weekly attack rate from baseline to week 61 were −1.00 (continuous dichlorphenamide, n = 25, P < 0.0001) and −0.63 (placebo→dichlorphenamide, n = 20, P = 0.01); severity-weighted attack-rate falls were −2.25 and −1.69 respectively. Common adverse events were paresthesia and cognition-related events, typically first occurring within 1 month of blinded treatment initiation and rarely leading to discontinuation; dose reductions were frequently associated with resolution.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and post hoc, with the two disease limbs pooled — supportive only; it cannot repair the hyperkalemic limb's non-significant randomised result.
cards.source: Sansone VA et al. Long-term efficacy and safety of dichlorphenamide for treatment of primary periodic paralysis. Muscle & nerve. 2021. PMID: 34129236. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.type: Age-subgroup analysis of a crossover programme — supportive only (adolescent N = 7, sub-floor, never load-bearing)
cards.people: Subgroup analysis of a double-blind controlled crossover study in primary periodic paralysis: 7 adolescents (10 to ≤17 years; 5 evaluable for efficacy, 6 for safety) and 66 adults. Adolescent total daily dosing was 50 mg (n = 1) or 100 mg (n = 5).
cards.result: In adolescents, the median decrease from baseline in weekly attacks was −0.96 on dichlorphenamide vs −0.57 on placebo, similar in direction to adults (−0.83 vs −0.24); severity-weighted attack frequency was likewise reduced more on dichlorphenamide in both age groups. The commonest adverse event in adolescents was skin rash (2 of 6, 33%); in adults, numbness (26 of 54, 48%), with rash in 10 of 54 (19%).
cards.watchOut: Adolescent N = 7 is below the ~10-human floor: labelled here, supportive only, never load-bearing. Do not print an adolescent efficacy claim from this report.

cards.headline: Synthesis: dichlorphenamide prevents attacks in hypokalemic periodic paralysis on two concordant randomised programmes; the hyperkalemic evidence is one significant crossover against one underpowered non-significant trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: dichlorphenamide prevents attacks in hypokalemic periodic paralysis on two concordant randomised programmes; the hyperkalemic evidence is one significant crossover against one underpowered non-significant trial
cards.people: Four reports, two randomised programmes (2000 crossovers, N = 42 + 31; 2016 parallel trials, N = 44 + 21, with their one-year extension) plus one age-subgroup analysis (adolescents N = 7, sub-floor, supportive only).
cards.result: Hypokalemic limb: attack rates significantly reduced in both programmes (2016: 0.3 vs 2.4 attacks/week, P = 0.02, with a quality-of-life gain). Hyperkalemic limb: significant in 2000, not significant in 2016 (P = 0.10) — printed as split, never averaged. Harms are dominated by paresthesia and cognitive effects. This is the only randomised evidence base in primary periodic paralysis.
cards.watchOut: Attack frequency is patient-counted in every trial. The 2000 trials predate the modern formulation; doses print as published.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Mexiletine for nondystrophic myotonia, lamotrigine as the alternative sodium-channel blocker, and their head-to-head trial — both drugs beat placebo in small crossovers; lamotrigine's non-inferiority to mexiletine was NOT concluded
shelves.question: In patients with genetically confirmed nondystrophic myotonia (myotonia congenita, paramyotonia congenita; CLCN1/SCN4A), do the sodium-channel blockers mexiletine and lamotrigine reduce myotonia stiffness versus placebo — and is lamotrigine non-inferior to mexiletine head-to-head?

shelves.balance: Mexiletine's placebo-controlled base is three reports totalling 114 patients: the 2012 JAMA crossover (59 patients; stiffness improved, reported by period because of a treatment-by-period interaction), the 2018 aggregated N-of-1 series (30 enrolled, 27 completed; clinically meaningful effect in 24 of 27 completers, 100% posterior probability of a meaningful group effect), and MYOMEX (25 patients; stiffness VAS 71.0 → 16.0 on mexiletine vs 81.0 → 78.0 on placebo, P < 0.001). Lamotrigine's own crossover (26 included, 22 completed) improved the Myotonic Behaviour Scale by 1.3 points vs 0.2 on placebo (estimated effect 1.0, 95% CI 0.5–1.5; number needed to treat 2.6), with one withdrawal for allergic reaction — lamotrigine requires slow titration, printed here. The 2024 head-to-head phase 3 crossover (60 randomised, 53 in the primary analysis) found mean IVR stiffness 2.54 on mexiletine vs 2.77 on lamotrigine (difference −0.23, −0.63 to 0.17) and the trialists were UNABLE to conclude non-inferiority — printed exactly as they stated it; the shelf's balance is 'both drugs beat placebo in small crossovers; they have never been shown equivalent.' Mexiletine is a class IB antiarrhythmic: the cardiac caution (and the diabetic-neuropathy row's 'no heart disease' restriction) carries over onto this face, even though the myotonia trials report no serious cardiac signal at these Ns and durations — gastrointestinal effects were the commonest harm (9 vs 1 in 2012; 70% vs 3% in the N-of-1 series, with one serious allergic skin reaction). Cross-points to packs #4247 (ALS cramps), #5382 (long-QT) and #7725 (painful diabetic neuropathy) are prose only — different questions, no shared anchors.

cards.headline: Mexiletine crossover RCT (JAMA 2012): patient-reported stiffness improved significantly — reported by period because of a treatment-by-period interaction (period 1: 2.53 on mexiletine vs 4.21 on placebo; period 2: 1.60 vs 5.27)
cards.summary: Mexiletine crossover RCT (JAMA 2012): patient-reported stiffness improved significantly — reported by period because of a treatment-by-period interaction (period 1: 2.53 on mexiletine vs 4.21 on placebo; period 2: 1.60 vs 5.27)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial — mexiletine
cards.people: 59 patients with nondystrophic myotonia in a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled 2-period crossover at 7 neuromuscular centres in 4 countries; oral mexiletine 200 mg three times daily or placebo for 4 weeks per period, 1-week washout. Primary outcome: patient-reported stiffness severity on an interactive-voice-response diary (1 = minimal to 9 = worst).
cards.result: Mexiletine significantly improved IVR stiffness; because of a significant treatment-by-period interaction the primary endpoint is presented by period — period 1 means 2.53 (mexiletine) vs 4.21 (placebo), difference −1.68 (95% CI −2.66 to −0.706, P < 0.001); period 2 means 1.60 vs 5.27, difference −3.68 (95% CI −3.85 to −0.139, P = 0.04). Quality of life (INQOL) improved (difference −2.69, P < 0.001) and handgrip myotonia on examination fell (−0.330 seconds, P < 0.001). The commonest adverse effect was gastrointestinal (9 on mexiletine, 1 on placebo); two participants had transient cardiac effects not requiring stopping (one in each group); one serious adverse event was judged unrelated.
cards.watchOut: The period interaction means no single pooled stiffness difference may be printed — period figures only, as the trialists reported them. The authors note some concern about maintenance of blinding. Mexiletine is a class IB antiarrhythmic: cardiac caution applies.
cards.source: Statland JM et al. Mexiletine for symptoms and signs of myotonia in nondystrophic myotonia: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2012. PMID: 23032552. Registry ID: NCT00832000. cards.headline: Mexiletine aggregated N-of-1 trials (JAMA 2018): a clinically meaningful effect in 24 of 27 completers, with 100% posterior probability of a clinically meaningful stiffness reduction for the group overall
cards.summary: Mexiletine aggregated N-of-1 trials (JAMA 2018): a clinically meaningful effect in 24 of 27 completers, with 100% posterior probability of a clinically meaningful stiffness reduction for the group overall
cards.type: Aggregated N-of-1 randomised trials — mexiletine (innovative design, single centre)
cards.people: Series of double-blind randomised placebo-controlled N-of-1 trials at a single academic centre: 30 Dutch adults with genetically confirmed nondystrophic myotonia enrolled (19 CLCN1, 11 SCN4A), 27 completed; mexiletine 600 mg daily vs placebo over multiple 4-week periods.
cards.result: In 24 of 27 completers a clinically meaningful treatment effect (>0.75-point stiffness difference) was found. The Bayesian hierarchical model gave 100% posterior probability of a clinically meaningful reduction for the group overall and the CLCN1 subgroup, and 93% for SCN4A. Median stiffness was 2.50 (95% credible interval 1.77–3.24) on mexiletine vs 5.56 (4.73–6.39) on placebo (difference 3.06, 1.96–4.15); a frequentist reanalysis (mean reduction 3.12, 95% CI 2.46–3.78) was consistent with the earlier RCT. Gastrointestinal discomfort was the commonest event (70% on mexiletine, 3% on placebo); one serious adverse event (allergic skin reaction) occurred on mexiletine.
cards.watchOut: An N-of-1 series, not a conventional parallel RCT — the design prints on the face. Single centre; 3 of 30 dropped out.
cards.source: Stunnenberg BC et al. Effect of Mexiletine on Muscle Stiffness in Patients With Nondystrophic Myotonia Evaluated Using Aggregated N-of-1 Trials. JAMA. 2018. PMID: 30535218. Registry ID: NCT02045667. cards.headline: MYOMEX (2021): stiffness VAS fell from 71.0 to 16.0 on mexiletine and was unchanged on placebo (81.0 to 78.0), P < 0.001, with quality-of-life improvement and no clinically significant adverse events reported
cards.summary: MYOMEX (2021): stiffness VAS fell from 71.0 to 16.0 on mexiletine and was unchanged on placebo (81.0 to 78.0), P < 0.001, with quality-of-life improvement and no clinically significant adverse events reported
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial (MYOMEX) — mexiletine
cards.people: Multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover: 25 patients in the modified intention-to-treat population (13 myotonia congenita, 12 paramyotonia congenita; mean age 43.0 years); mexiletine up-titrated from 200 mg/day to a maximum 600 mg/day over 18 days per crossover period. Primary endpoint: self-reported stiffness severity on a 100 mm VAS.
cards.result: Median VAS stiffness fell from 71.0 at baseline to 16.0 at the end of mexiletine treatment, while on placebo it did not change (81.0 to 78.0); the mixed-effects analysis of ranked absolute changes showed a significant treatment effect (P < 0.001). The overall INQoL quality-of-life score also improved significantly (P < 0.001). No clinically significant adverse events were reported.
cards.watchOut: Small (N = 25) and short (18 days per period): 'no clinically significant adverse events reported' at this N and duration is not a safety statement for chronic use of a class IB antiarrhythmic.
cards.source: Vicart S et al. Efficacy and safety of mexiletine in non-dystrophic myotonias: A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, cross-over study. Neuromuscular disorders : NMD. 2021. PMID: 34702654. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Lamotrigine crossover RCT (Brain 2017): Myotonic Behaviour Scale improved by 1.3 points on lamotrigine vs 0.2 on placebo (estimated effect 1.0, 95% CI 0.5–1.5, P < 0.001); number needed to treat 2.6; one withdrawal for allergic reaction
cards.summary: Lamotrigine crossover RCT (Brain 2017): Myotonic Behaviour Scale improved by 1.3 points on lamotrigine vs 0.2 on placebo (estimated effect 1.0, 95% CI 0.5–1.5, P < 0.001); number needed to treat 2.6; one withdrawal for allergic reaction
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial — lamotrigine
cards.people: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled 2-period crossover in Denmark: 26 patients with genetically confirmed myotonia congenita or paramyotonia congenita included, 22 completed; lamotrigine titrated from 25 mg to 300 mg daily over 8-week periods.
cards.result: Myotonic Behaviour Scale (1 = asymptomatic to 6 = invalidating) changed by 1.3 ± 0.2 points on lamotrigine (P < 0.001) vs 0.2 ± 0.1 on placebo (P = 0.4); estimated effect size 1.0 (95% CI 0.5–1.5, P < 0.001). Number needed to treat was 2.6 (P = 0.006) and number needed to harm 5.2 (P = 0.11, not significant). One patient withdrew because of an allergic reaction to lamotrigine; three withdrew for unrelated reasons. The authors suggested lamotrigine as first-line in treatment-naive patients on availability and cost grounds — their suggestion, printed as such.
cards.watchOut: Lamotrigine requires slow titration (the trial escalated over weeks) and carries the allergic-reaction withdrawal in its own small trial — both print. Small N (22 completers).
cards.source: Andersen G et al. The antimyotonic effect of lamotrigine in non-dystrophic myotonias: a double-blind randomized study. Brain : a journal of neurology. 2017. PMID: 29050397. cards.headline: Head-to-head (Lancet Neurology 2024): lamotrigine's non-inferiority to mexiletine was NOT concluded — mean IVR stiffness 2.54 on mexiletine vs 2.77 on lamotrigine (difference −0.23, 95% CI −0.63 to 0.17, against a 0.5 margin) — although improvements from baseline were similar on both drugs
cards.summary: Head-to-head (Lancet Neurology 2024): lamotrigine's non-inferiority to mexiletine was NOT concluded — mean IVR stiffness 2.54 on mexiletine vs 2.77 on lamotrigine (difference −0.23, 95% CI −0.63 to 0.17, against a 0.5 margin) — although improvements from baseline were similar on both drugs
cards.type: Randomised double-blind crossover non-inferiority phase 3 trial — mexiletine vs lamotrigine head-to-head
cards.people: Randomised double-blind crossover non-inferiority phase 3 trial at a single London centre: 60 participants with genetically confirmed symptomatic nondystrophic myotonia randomised to mexiletine-then-lamotrigine or the reverse (8 weeks each, 7-day washout); 53 contributed to the primary analysis (mean IVR stiffness over the final 2 weeks of each period, 0–9 scale).
cards.result: Mean IVR stiffness was 2.54 (95% CI 1.98–3.10) on mexiletine vs 2.77 (2.21–3.32) on lamotrigine; mean difference −0.23 (95% CI −0.63 to 0.17). The investigators were unable to conclude that lamotrigine is non-inferior to mexiletine, while noting improvements in all outcome measures from baseline were similar between the drugs. The commonest adverse event on both was indigestion/reflux (8 participants on mexiletine, 7 on lamotrigine); no serious adverse events were reported.
cards.watchOut: BINDING: the failed non-inferiority conclusion prints exactly as the trialists stated it. Never summarise this trial as showing the drugs equivalent.
cards.source: Vivekanandam V et al. Mexiletine versus lamotrigine in non-dystrophic myotonias: a randomised, double-blind, head-to-head, crossover, non-inferiority, phase 3 trial. The Lancet. cards.headline: Synthesis: both sodium-channel blockers beat placebo in small crossovers; they have never been shown equivalent — the head-to-head's non-inferiority conclusion failed
cards.summary: Synthesis: both sodium-channel blockers beat placebo in small crossovers; they have never been shown equivalent — the head-to-head's non-inferiority conclusion failed
cards.people: Five reports, five distinct trials: mexiletine placebo-controlled N = 114 (59 + 30 + 25) plus lamotrigine's crossover (26) and the head-to-head (60 randomised, 53 analysed) — overlapping populations across the head-to-head and the placebo trials are different reports of different questions, counted as trials, not summed into one N.
cards.result: Mexiletine reduced stiffness in all three placebo-controlled designs (conventional crossover, aggregated N-of-1, MYOMEX); lamotrigine reduced it in its own crossover (effect 1.0 points, NNT 2.6, one allergic withdrawal). Head-to-head, non-inferiority of lamotrigine was not concluded (difference −0.23, CI crossing the 0.5 margin) despite similar improvements from baseline. Gastrointestinal effects dominate mexiletine's harm profile in these trials; the class IB antiarrhythmic cardiac caution stands on the face regardless.

shelves.title: NIH Stroke Scale reliability between raters: a respectable total-score ICC of 0.85 beside a clinically material spread — total scores varied by four or more points in 64% of certification vignettes, and the ataxia item's kappa was 0.15
shelves.question: At the bedside, how reliable is the NIH Stroke Scale (NIHSS — 15 items: consciousness, gaze, visual fields, facial palsy, arm and leg motor, ataxia, sensory, language, dysarthria, extinction/inattention) between raters — what inter-rater agreement did its first reliability study find item by item, how wide is the spread of total scores when thousands of clinicians rate the same standardised patients for certification, and which items drive the disagreement?

shelves.balance: This is a measurement-reliability shelf, not a prognostic or treatment shelf: no card may convert reliability data into claims about thrombolysis or thrombectomy thresholds. The content is the split. On one side, the total score looks respectable: in the DVD certification validation among general users (8,214 raters), the intraclass correlation coefficient for the total score was 0.85 (95% CI 0.72–0.90), with 11 of 15 items showing moderate agreement and 2 excellent. On the other side, the spread is clinically material: in the large videotape certification analysis (7,405 unique raters, 38,148 item responses), total scores for 7 of 11 patients (64%) had a 5th-to-95th percentile spread of four or more points; the aphasia (kappa 0.60) and facial palsy (0.65) items contributed most to the variance; and taking the examination repeatedly did not improve agreement. Item-level weakness is specific: kappas ranged from 0.15 (ataxia — poor) to 0.81 (level-of-consciousness commands). The first reliability study (1989; 20 stroke patients, each rated by a pair of four clinical stroke fellows — its N prints on the face) found moderate-to-substantial agreement for 9 of 13 items; its abstract reports agreement qualitatively by item, and no pooled kappa may be printed from it. Two of the three anchors measure scoring of videotaped/DVD standardised patients, not live bedside examinations, and print as such — live-examination reliability could differ in either direction and is not what these numbers measure.

cards.type: Certification-examination reliability analysis — videotaped standardised patients (not live bedside examinations)
cards.people: Analysis of the standard videotaped certification examination (1998–2004): 7,405 unique raters (clinicians of several professions) contributing 38,148 individual item responses across standardised videotaped patients whose median scores ranged from 0 to 31.
cards.result: Total NIHSS scores varied widely between raters: scoring for 7 of the 11 patients (64%) showed a difference of four or more points between the 5th and 95th percentiles. The aphasia and facial palsy items contributed most to the variance in total score. Nurses agreed with the most common response more frequently than physicians (P < 0.0001). Taking the certification examination multiple times did not improve agreement. The authors conclude overall scoring was inconsistent and could impact clinical trial results.
cards.watchOut: These are ratings of videotapes, not live patients — printed as such. A ≥4-point total-score spread is clinically material at treatment-threshold scores, but this shelf makes no treatment-threshold claim; it reports the measurement property.

cards.headline: DVD certification validation among general users (2009): item kappas ranged from 0.15 (ataxia) to 0.81 (level-of-consciousness commands), 11 of 15 items moderate and 2 excellent — and the intraclass correlation coefficient for the total score was 0.85 (95% CI 0.72–0.90)
cards.summary: DVD certification validation among general users (2009): item kappas ranged from 0.15 (ataxia) to 0.81 (level-of-consciousness commands), 11 of 15 items moderate and 2 excellent — and the intraclass correlation coefficient for the total score was 0.85 (95% CI 0.72–0.90)
cards.type: Certification validation — DVD standardised patients rated by general users (not live bedside examinations)
cards.people: Validation of the standard NIHSS training/certification DVD (18 patients spanning all scores on 15 items) among general (non-expert) users: 8,214 raters overall (7,419 via the internet, 795 via other venues); 51% previously NIHSS-certified; nurses, emergency physicians and neurologists all represented.
cards.result: Unweighted item kappas ranged from 0.15 (ataxia) to 0.81 (Item 1c, level-of-consciousness commands); of 15 items, 2 showed poor, 11 moderate and 2 excellent agreement. The intraclass correlation coefficient for the total score was 0.85 (95% CI 0.72 to 0.90). Agreement was slightly lower than among expert users for several items (level-of-consciousness, best gaze, visual fields, facial weakness, motor arms, sensory loss); scores were similar across specialties and venues, tending lower for neurologists and higher among raters not previously certified.
cards.watchOut: BINDING: the ICC of 0.85 may never be printed without the spread evidence (card 2) and the weak items (ataxia κ 0.15). DVD vignettes, not live examinations.
