shelves.title: FOUR score versus Glasgow Coma Scale in impaired consciousness: excellent inter-rater reliability for both (weighted kappa 0.88 vs 0.86) and pooled prognostic parity in traumatic brain injury (AUC 0.91 vs 0.92 for mortality) — FOUR's advantage is content the GCS cannot express, not superior accuracy
shelves.question: In patients with impaired consciousness, how well does the FOUR score (Full Outline of UnResponsiveness — eye, motor, brainstem reflexes and respiration, each 0–4, replacing the Glasgow Coma Scale's verbal component) perform against the Glasgow Coma Scale — what inter-rater reliability did its emergency-department validation by non-neurology staff show, how does it behave in spontaneous subarachnoid haemorrhage, and what pooled accuracy do the two scores deliver for predicting death and unfavourable outcome after traumatic brain injury?

shelves.balance: This is a measurement/prognostic-accuracy shelf, not a treatment shelf. The pooled evidence shows parity, and no card may print a FOUR-superiority claim: in the traumatic-brain-injury meta-analysis (20 articles, 2,083 patients), AUC for in-hospital mortality was 0.91 (95% CI 0.88–0.93) for FOUR and 0.92 for GCS, and for unfavourable outcome 0.93 (0.91–0.95) vs 0.95 (0.93–0.97), with diagnostic odds ratios labelled as such in the source (45.16 vs 44.51 for mortality). One figure binds the build: the meta-analysis abstract prints the GCS mortality AUC confidence interval as 0.80–0.91, which does not contain its own point estimate (0.92) — that interval is omitted on this shelf, never printed as fetched. The broader systematic review (37 studies) found FOUR prognosticated in-hospital mortality well to excellently in most studies (AUC >0.80) and poor functional outcome at AUC 0.80–0.90, with some evidence its motor and eye components out-prognosticate its brainstem components. The primary validations are small and their Ns print: the emergency-department validation (69 patients, rated by ED physicians, residents and nurses) found excellent inter-rater reliability for both scores (weighted kappa 0.88 FOUR, 0.86 GCS) with both predicting outcome; the subarachnoid-haemorrhage study (72 ICU patients) reports significant correlations with Hunt–Hess and Fisher stage and 1-month recovery prediction, with reliability reported qualitatively in its abstract — no numeric kappa may be printed from it. FOUR's claimed advantage is content the GCS cannot express — brainstem reflexes, respiratory pattern, usability in intubated patients — not superior pooled accuracy, and the shelf is written that way. Distinct from the GCS-reliability shelf (pack #7784): that shelf asks how reliably the GCS itself is scored; here the GCS is the comparator and no anchor is shared.

cards.headline: Emergency-department validation by non-neurology staff (2009, N = 69): inter-rater reliability was excellent for both scores (weighted kappa 0.88 for FOUR, 0.86 for GCS), and both predicted functional outcome and survival
cards.summary: Emergency-department validation by non-neurology staff (2009, N = 69): inter-rater reliability was excellent for both scores (weighted kappa 0.88 for FOUR, 0.86 for GCS), and both predicted functional outcome and survival
cards.type: Prospective validation — FOUR vs GCS reliability and outcome prediction (emergency department)
cards.people: Prospective study of 69 patients with initial neurological symptoms presenting to an emergency department, each rated with the FOUR score and the GCS by three examiner types (ED physician, ED resident, ED nurse); functional outcome at discharge measured by modified Rankin Score. Small primary validation — its N prints.
cards.result: Inter-rater reliability was excellent for both scores (weighted kappa 0.88 for FOUR and 0.86 for GCS). Both the FOUR score and the GCS predicted functional outcome and overall survival, with and without adjustment for age, sex and alertness group. The authors conclude the FOUR score can be reliably used in the ED by non-neurology staff, and that the neurological detail it incorporates makes it more useful for management and triage — their judgement, printed as such, not an accuracy finding.
cards.watchOut: N = 69, single ED. 'More useful detail' is a content claim by the authors; the measured performance was equal, and this shelf prints parity, not superiority.
cards.source: Stead LG et al. Validation of a new coma scale, the FOUR score, in the emergency department. Neurocritical care. 2009. PMID: 18807215. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis — FOUR vs GCS prognostic accuracy (traumatic brain injury)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 20 articles comprising 2,083 patients with traumatic brain injury comparing GCS and FOUR for prediction of in-hospital mortality and unfavourable outcome (mortality plus disability); diagnostic odds ratios reported and labelled as such in the source.
cards.result: AUC for in-hospital mortality was 0.91 (95% CI 0.88–0.93) for FOUR and 0.92 for GCS; diagnostic odds ratios (labelled as such) were 45.16 (95% CI 24.25–84.09) for FOUR and 44.51 (23.58–84.03) for GCS. For unfavourable outcome, AUCs were 0.93 (0.91–0.95) for FOUR and 0.95 (0.93–0.97) for GCS, with DORs 45.39 (23.09–89.23) and 66.31 (35.05–125.45) respectively. The authors rate the evidence moderate and conclude the two scores' predictive value is comparable, leaving the choice to the clinical situation.
cards.watchOut: BINDING: the source abstract prints the GCS mortality AUC confidence interval as 0.80–0.91, which does not contain its own point estimate (0.92); that interval is omitted here and is never printed as fetched. Parity is the finding — no FOUR-superiority claim may be drawn from this report.
cards.source: Ahmadi S et al. Comparison of Glasgow Coma Scale and Full Outline of UnResponsiveness score for prediction of in-hospital mortality in traumatic brain injury patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis. European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society. 2023. PMID: 36152069. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Systematic review of FOUR and outcome (2019): FOUR prognosticated in-hospital mortality well to excellently in most studies (AUC >0.80) and poor functional outcome at AUC 0.80–0.90, with some evidence its motor and eye components out-prognosticate its brainstem components
cards.summary: Systematic review of FOUR and outcome (2019): FOUR prognosticated in-hospital mortality well to excellently in most studies (AUC >0.80) and poor functional outcome at AUC 0.80–0.90, with some evidence its motor and eye components out-prognosticate its brainstem components
cards.type: Systematic review — FOUR score prognostic performance across impaired-consciousness populations
cards.people: Systematic review of 37 studies (40 records) of adults with impaired consciousness in which FOUR was assessed against mortality or validated functional outcomes; risk of bias low in 2 studies, moderate in 25 and high in 13, with significant heterogeneity in patient characteristics.
cards.result: The FOUR score showed good-to-excellent prognostication of in-hospital mortality in most studies (AUC >0.80) and good prediction of poor functional outcome (AUC 0.80–0.90). There was some evidence that the motor and eye components — the components FOUR shares with the GCS — had better prognostic ability than the brainstem components that distinguish it. The authors call for standardised studies in defined patient groups and direct comparison with the GCS and GCS-Pupils.
cards.watchOut: Mostly moderate/high risk of bias with heterogeneous populations — the AUC ranges print as ranges across studies, not as pooled estimates. The component finding (shared components prognosticate best) qualifies any 'brainstem content adds accuracy' claim.

cards.headline: Synthesis: FOUR is as reliable and as prognostic as the GCS wherever both were measured — its case rests on the content it adds (brainstem reflexes, respiration, use without a verbal response), not on better numbers
cards.summary: Synthesis: FOUR is as reliable and as prognostic as the GCS wherever both were measured — its case rests on the content it adds (brainstem reflexes, respiration, use without a verbal response), not on better numbers
cards.people: Four reports: two small primary validations (ED, N = 69; aneurysmal SAH, N = 72 — Ns printed), one TBI meta-analysis (20 articles, 2,083 patients) and one systematic review (37 studies).
cards.result: Reliability: weighted kappa 0.88 (FOUR) vs 0.86 (GCS) in the ED; excellent agreement reported qualitatively in SAH. Prognosis: TBI AUCs 0.91 vs 0.92 (mortality) and 0.93 vs 0.95 (unfavourable outcome) — parity; across impaired-consciousness studies FOUR's mortality AUCs exceeded 0.80 in most. The GCS mortality interval misprinted in the meta-analysis abstract (0.80–0.91 around 0.92) is omitted, as bound.
cards.watchOut: No superiority claim. The intubated-patient and brainstem-content rationale is a content argument, printed as such wherever it appears.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: MoCA and MMSE at the bedside: MoCA's conventional cut-off of 26 buys sensitivity of 0.94 or more at specificity of 0.60 or less for dementia, MCI accuracy maximises at cut-offs 23–25, and a single MMSE does not identify which patients with MCI will convert to dementia
shelves.question: In older adults, how accurately do the two standard bedside cognitive screens — the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA, 30 points) and the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE, 30 points) — detect mild cognitive impairment and dementia against clinical diagnostic criteria: what pooled sensitivity and specificity does MoCA deliver for MCI at cut-offs below the conventional 26, what did the Cochrane review find for MoCA in dementia at that threshold, what pooled accuracy does MMSE achieve for dementia in community settings at cut-offs 24 and 25, and how poorly does a single MMSE predict which patients with MCI will convert to dementia?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Cognitive Dysfunction/diagnosis, psychology · Mental Status and Dementia Tests · Sensitivity and Specificity · Neurologic Examination · Neuropsychological Tests · Aged · Alzheimer Disease/diagnosis, epidemiology · Cognitive Dysfunction/diagnosis · Cross-Sectional Studies · Dementia/diagnosis, epidemiology · Executive Function · Memory, Short-Term · Orientation · Reference Standards · Alzheimer Disease/diagnosis · Community Health Services · Dementia/diagnosis · Dementia, Vascular/diagnosis · Lewy Body Disease/diagnosis · Mental Status Schedule · Neuropsychological Tests/standards · Primary Health Care · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Cognitive Dysfunction/complications · Dementia/diagnosis, etiology · Dementia, Vascular/diagnosis, etiology · Disease Progression · Early Diagnosis · Frontotemporal Dementia/diagnosis, etiology · Lewy Body Disease/diagnosis, etiology
shelves.balance: This shelf rests on 4 syntheses whose primary-study sets overlap — the count prints as 4 syntheses, not 4 independent cohorts. It is a diagnostic-accuracy shelf, not a treatment shelf: no card may imply screen-triggered pathways improve outcomes. The cut-off dependence is the content. For MCI, the 2023 meta-analysis (13 studies, 2,158 participants, 44% with MCI) found accuracy maximised below the conventional 26: at cut-off <25 sensitivity was 83.8% (95% CI 75.6–89.6) and specificity 70.8% (62.1–78.3); at <24, 79.5% / 83.7%; at <23, 73.5% / 91.3% — with risk of bias high or unclear in most domains, printed. For dementia, the Cochrane MoCA review (7 studies, 9,422 participants) could not meta-analyse because of methodological variation; in the four studies using the recommended threshold of 26, sensitivity was 0.94 or more but specificity 0.60 or less, and the reviewers judged the evidence insufficient to recommend on clinical utility. For dementia in community settings, the Cochrane MMSE review pooled sensitivity 0.85 (95% CI 0.74–0.92) / specificity 0.90 (0.82–0.95) at cut-off 24 and 0.87 (0.78–0.93) / 0.82 (0.65–0.92) at cut-off 25 — and education adjustment moved the estimates materially (in seven adjusted studies, sensitivity 0.97 / specificity 0.70), which prints where figures are given. For prognosis, the Cochrane conversion review (11 studies, 1,569 patients with MCI) found baseline MMSE accuracy for conversion ranging across studies from sensitivity 23% to 76% and specificity 40% to 94%, with no evidence supporting MMSE as a stand-alone single-administration test for identifying who will convert. No single sensitivity/specificity pair may be printed without its cut-off, target condition (MCI vs dementia) and setting attached. Distinct from the Mini-Cog postoperative-delirium shelf and the delirium-instrument shelves (CAM-ICU, 4AT, 3D-CAM, Nu-DESC), which detect an acute confusional state, not chronic cognitive impairment.

cards.summary: MoCA for MCI — meta-analysis (2023): at cut-off <25 sensitivity was 83.8% (95% CI 75.6–89.6) and specificity 70.8% (62.1–78.3); at <24, 79.5% / 83.7%; at <23, 73.5% / 91.3% — accuracy maximised at cut-offs 23–25, below the conventional 26
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis — MoCA diagnostic accuracy for MCI (synthesis; primary-study sets overlap with the other syntheses on this shelf)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 studies, 2,158 participants (948, 44%, with MCI), comparing MoCA with validated diagnostic criteria in general practice (10 studies used Petersen criteria); bivariate meta-analysis. Risk of bias was high or unclear in all domains except the reference standard — printed here as the reviewers state it.
cards.result: Pooled sensitivity/specificity by cut-off: <23 — 73.5% (95% CI 56.7–85.5) / 91.3% (84.6–95.3); <24 — 79.5% (67.1–88.0) / 83.7% (75.4–89.6); <25 — 83.8% (75.6–89.6) / 70.8% (62.1–78.3). The reviewers conclude cut-offs <23 to <25 maximised the sum of sensitivity and specificity for detecting MCI, and that the risk of bias of the included studies limits confidence in these findings.
cards.watchOut: Every pair prints with its cut-off: quoting 'MoCA sensitivity 84%' without '<25, for MCI' misstates this report. High/unclear risk of bias throughout.

cards.headline: MoCA for dementia — Cochrane review (2021): methodological variation precluded meta-analysis; in the four studies using the recommended threshold of 26, sensitivity was 0.94 or more but specificity 0.60 or less, and the reviewers judged the evidence insufficient to recommend on clinical utility
cards.summary: MoCA for dementia — Cochrane review (2021): methodological variation precluded meta-analysis; in the four studies using the recommended threshold of 26, sensitivity was 0.94 or more but specificity 0.60 or less, and the reviewers judged the evidence insufficient to recommend on clinical utility
cards.type: Cochrane diagnostic-accuracy review — MoCA for dementia (synthesis; no pooled estimate exists in this report)
cards.people: Cochrane diagnostic-accuracy review of 7 studies, 9,422 participants (three memory-clinic, two hospital-clinic, two population-derived, none in primary care), cross-sectional designs with case-control studies excluded; dementia prevalence 22–54% in clinic studies and 5–10% in population samples.
cards.result: Most studies recruited only small samples (only one had more than 350 participants). In the four studies using the recommended threshold score of 26 (26 or over indicating normal cognition), MoCA sensitivity was 0.94 or more but specificity 0.60 or less. The reviewers conclude the overall quality and quantity of information is insufficient to make recommendations on the clinical utility of MoCA for detecting dementia in different settings, and that thresholds lower than 26 are likely to be more useful — requiring confirmation in further studies.
cards.watchOut: No pooled MoCA-for-dementia sensitivity/specificity exists in this review — the threshold-26 figures are the range across four studies and print as such. Clinic prevalences (22–54%) are far above community prevalence; predictive values do not transport.
cards.source: Davis DH et al. Montreal Cognitive Assessment for the detection of dementia. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2021. PMID: 34255351. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.summary: MMSE for dementia — Cochrane review (2016): in community settings at cut-off 24, pooled sensitivity was 0.85 (95% CI 0.74–0.92) and specificity 0.90 (0.82–0.95); at cut-off 25, 0.87 (0.78–0.93) and 0.82 (0.65–0.92) — and education adjustment moved the estimates materially (0.97 / 0.70 in adjusted studies)
cards.type: Cochrane diagnostic-accuracy review — MMSE for dementia in community/primary care (synthesis; overlapping primary studies)
cards.people: Cochrane review of the 11-item (30-point) MMSE for dementia in people aged 65 and over in community and primary-care settings without prior testing: 48 studies in the synthesis, with meta-analysis possible on 28 community studies (participant totals per cut-off analysis ranging from 37 to 2,727, median 314). Insufficient data prevented summary estimates for primary care.
cards.result: In the community, pooled accuracy at cut point 24 (15 studies) was sensitivity 0.85 (95% CI 0.74–0.92) and specificity 0.90 (0.82–0.95); at cut point 25 (10 studies), sensitivity 0.87 (0.78–0.93) and specificity 0.82 (0.65–0.92). In the seven studies that adjusted accuracy estimates for level of education, sensitivity was 0.97 (0.83–1.00) and specificity 0.70 (0.50–0.85). The reviewers conclude the MMSE contributes to a diagnosis of dementia in low-prevalence settings but should not be used in isolation to confirm or exclude disease.
cards.watchOut: Community-setting figures; the review could not produce primary-care summary estimates. The education-adjusted pair (0.97/0.70) shows why an unadjusted pair printed without its population misleads.

cards.headline: MMSE for conversion from MCI to dementia — Cochrane review (2021): baseline MMSE accuracy ranged across studies from sensitivity 23% to 76% and specificity 40% to 94%, and the reviewers found NO evidence supporting MMSE as a stand-alone single-administration test for identifying who will convert
cards.summary: MMSE for conversion from MCI to dementia — Cochrane review (2021): baseline MMSE accuracy ranged across studies from sensitivity 23% to 76% and specificity 40% to 94%, and the reviewers found NO evidence supporting MMSE as a stand-alone single-administration test for identifying who will convert
cards.type: Cochrane review — MMSE as a prognostic test for MCI conversion (synthesis; a NOT ESTABLISHED reading)
cards.people: Cochrane review of 11 heterogeneous longitudinal studies, 1,569 patients with MCI followed for conversion to dementia (four studies for all-cause dementia, eight for Alzheimer's dementia, one for vascular dementia); heterogeneity and scarcity precluded the planned subgroup analyses, so estimates are ranges across studies.
cards.result: For conversion to all-cause dementia, baseline MMSE sensitivity ranged from 23% to 76% and specificity from 40% to 94%; for conversion to Alzheimer's dementia, sensitivity 27–89% and specificity 32–90%; the single vascular-dementia study reported sensitivity 36% and specificity 80% (incidence 6.2%). The reviewers conclude there is no evidence supporting a substantial role for the MMSE as a stand-alone single-administration test in identifying MCI patients who will develop dementia, and suggest MMSE change over time or test combinations as the questions for future work.
cards.watchOut: A prognostic question, not a diagnostic one — never merge these ranges with the diagnostic pairs on the other cards. The correct summary is the negative one: not established as a stand-alone predictor.

shelves.title: HINTS examination for acute vestibular syndrome: 94.0% sensitive and 86.9% specific in the Cochrane pooling — but examiner-dependent, with specificity of 44% in the mixed emergency-physician cohort; the near-perfect figures come from neurologists and neuro-otology specialists
shelves.question: In emergency-department patients with acute vestibular syndrome (continuous vertigo with nystagmus, nausea and gait unsteadiness), how accurately does the HINTS examination (head impulse test, nystagmus direction, test of skew — with the hearing limb in HINTS-plus) identify a central cause, principally posterior-circulation stroke, against MRI-based diagnosis — what sensitivity and specificity does the Cochrane review pool for the clinical examination, how much worse is accuracy when the examination is performed by emergency physicians rather than neurologists in the earlier meta-analysis, and how did HINTS compare with the ABCD2 score and with early MRI in the specialist-examined derivation cohort?

shelves.balance: Examiner dependence is the headline of this shelf, not a caveat. The Cochrane review (16 studies, 2,024 participants) pooled the clinical HINTS examination at 94.0% sensitivity (95% CI 82.0–98.2) and 86.9% specificity (75.3–93.6) for a central cause, and HINTS-plus at 95.3% sensitive and 72.9% specific — all on LOW-certainty evidence, which prints. The examiner split comes from the 2020 meta-analysis (5 studies, 617 participants): performed by neurologists, HINTS sensitivity was 96.7% (95% CI 93.1–98.5) and specificity 94.8% (91–97.1%); in the mixed emergency-physician/neurologist cohort, sensitivity was 83% and specificity 44% — and the authors conclude HINTS used in isolation by emergency physicians has not been shown accurate enough to rule out stroke. The derivation cohort (190 high-risk acute-vestibular-syndrome patients examined by neuro-otology specialists, MRI in 97.4% — programme-labelled in effect: the derivation group's own centre and specialist examiners) found HINTS sensitivity for stroke 96.5% and specificity 84.4% (positive likelihood ratio 6.19, negative 0.04, labelled as such), far ahead of ABCD2 ≥4 (61.1% / 62.3%), and initial MRI was falsely negative in 14.3% of infarctions — specialist figures, printed with their examiners attached, never as frontline performance. HINTS applies only to acute vestibular syndrome with nystagmus; no card may extend its figures to undifferentiated dizziness. This is a diagnostic-accuracy shelf, not a treatment shelf. Distinct from pack #7071 (physiology normative video-head-impulse gain values in healthy people — a different question; no anchor shared).

cards.result: The clinical HINTS examination (12 studies, 1,890 participants) was 94.0% sensitive (95% CI 82.0–98.2) and 86.9% specific (75.3–93.6) for a central cause (low-certainty evidence). The reviewers conclude HINTS and HINTS-plus had good sensitivity and reasonable specificity in the emergency department when performed by trained clinicians, on overall low-certainty evidence, with limited data for video assistance and specific subgroups.

cards.result: When performed by neurologists, the HINTS examination had sensitivity 96.7% (95% CI 93.1–98.5, I² = 0%) and specificity 94.8% (91–97.1, I² = 0%). When performed by the mixed emergency-physician/neurologist cohort, sensitivity was 83% (63–95) and specificity 44% (36–51). The authors conclude that the HINTS examination, when used in isolation by emergency physicians, has not been shown to be sufficiently accurate to rule out a stroke in patients presenting with acute vestibular syndrome.

cards.type: Cross-sectional derivation-cohort study — HINTS vs ABCD2 vs early MRI (neuro-otology specialist examiners)
cards.people: Cross-sectional study of 190 high-risk acute-vestibular-syndrome patients (1999–2012) at a single academic centre, all examined by neuro-otology specialists, with neuroimaging in all (97.4% MRI) and follow-up; final diagnoses were vestibular neuritis 34.7%, posterior fossa stroke 59.5% and other central causes 5.8% — an enriched, high-risk spectrum.
cards.result: HINTS sensitivity for stroke was 96.5% and specificity 84.4% (LR+ 6.19, LR− 0.04, labelled as likelihood ratios); for any central lesion, sensitivity was 96.8% and specificity 98.5%, and HINTS-plus reached sensitivity 99.2% / specificity 97.0% for central lesions. ABCD2 ≥4 performed far worse for stroke (sensitivity 61.1%, specificity 62.3%, LR+ 1.62, LR− 0.62), with sensitivity of only 28.9% in patients under 60. Initial MRI was falsely negative in 15 of 105 infarctions (14.3%), all but one obtained within 48 hours of onset. The authors conclude HINTS substantially outperforms ABCD2 and early MRI in this setting.
cards.watchOut: BINDING: specialist examiners at the derivation group's own centre, in a cohort with 59.5% stroke prevalence — these figures describe expert performance in an enriched spectrum, never frontline accuracy. The early-MRI false-negative rate (14.3%) is a within-48-hours figure and prints with that timing.

shelves.title: DN4 for neuropathic pain: strong discrimination in diabetic polyneuropathy (AUC 0.94) against specificity ≤0.65 in a 729-patient referral cohort — accuracy is population-dependent
shelves.question: In patients with chronic pain, how accurately does the DN4 questionnaire (seven interview items and three bedside sensory-examination items; positive at ≥4 of 10) identify neuropathic pain against expert clinical diagnosis — what did its derivation study establish, what accuracy did it achieve in painful diabetic polyneuropathy, and how did it and its questionnaire competitors perform in a 729-patient polyneuropathy-referral cohort judged against NeuPSIG criteria?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Female · Humans · Logistic Models · Male · Middle Aged · Neuralgia/diagnosis,epidemiology · Pain/diagnosis,epidemiology · Pain Measurement/methods,statistics & numerical data · Peripheral Nervous System Diseases/diagnosis,epidemiology · Sensitivity and Specificity · Somatoform Disorders/diagnosis,epidemiology · Syndrome
shelves.balance: The population gradient is the content of this shelf. In an enriched painful-diabetic-polyneuropathy validation the DN4 discriminated strongly (AUC 0.94; at cut-off 4, sensitivity 80%, specificity 92%); in a 729-patient unselected polyneuropathy-referral cohort judged against NeuPSIG criteria it had the highest sensitivity of three tools (0.87) but specificity ≤0.65 for all three, and none could be confidently used. The derivation study (160 patients, originators' report) constructed the 10-item score but its abstract reports no pooled sensitivity or specificity for the finished score, and none is printed from it. Reference standards differ across reports (expert diagnosis, electrophysiological work-up, NeuPSIG grading) and print with their figures. This is a screening-accuracy shelf, not a treatment shelf.

cards.type: Validation study in painful diabetic polyneuropathy
cards.people: 158 patients with diabetes; diabetic polyneuropathy and neuropathic pain assessed by symptom/sign scoring, quantitative sensory testing, nerve conduction studies, pain history and questionnaires; painful diabetic polyneuropathy defined as polyneuropathy plus chronic neuropathic pain in the same area. cards.result: The DN4 score related significantly to all neurological and electrophysiological measurements. Areas under the ROC curve were 0.94 (full DN4) and 0.93 (DN4-interview). At cut-off 4: sensitivity 80%, specificity 92%, PPV 82%, NPV 91%, positive likelihood ratio 9.6 (labelled as such). At cut-off 3, DN4-interview showed sensitivity and specificity 84%, PPV 71%, NPV 92%, positive likelihood ratio 5.3.

cards.headline: DN4 in a polyneuropathy-referral cohort (Dunker 2023, Pain — 729 patients with bilateral distal leg pain at five Norwegian university hospitals, NeuPSIG criteria as reference): DN4 had the highest sensitivity of the three tools (0.87) but all three — DN4, painDETECT and S-LANSS — had specificity ≤0.65, and the probability of a correct classification was three quarters at best
cards.summary: DN4 in a polyneuropathy-referral cohort (Dunker 2023, Pain — 729 patients with bilateral distal leg pain at five Norwegian university hospitals, NeuPSIG criteria as reference): DN4 had the highest sensitivity of the three tools (0.87) but all three — DN4, painDETECT and S-LANSS — had specificity ≤0.65, and the probability of a correct classification was three quarters at best
cards.type: Multicentre diagnostic accuracy study against NeuPSIG criteria
cards.people: 729 patients with bilateral distal lower-extremity pain referred for polyneuropathy assessment; 63% had neuropathic pain by the NeuPSIG reference standard. All underwent clinical examination and nerve conduction measurements.
cards.result: Only DN4 demonstrated high sensitivity (0.87), whereas all three tools had low specificity (≤0.65). Predictive ability was unsatisfactory: the probability of a correct test result was three quarters at best and at worst no better than two fifths. The authors conclude none of DN4, painDETECT or S-LANSS can be confidently used to assess neuropathic pain in this population.
cards.watchOut: Same instrument, different population and reference standard, opposite register: sensitivity holds (0.87) but specificity fails. Population and reference standard print with every figure on this shelf.

cards.headline: Synthesis: DN4 discrimination is population-dependent — AUC 0.94 in enriched diabetic polyneuropathy against specificity ≤0.65 in an unselected 729-patient referral cohort; the derivation report contributes the instrument, not a pooled accuracy figure

cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: Bouhassira 2005 derivation (N = 160, originators), Spallone 2012 diabetic validation (N = 158) and Dunker 2023 referral cohort (N = 729).
cards.result: No single DN4 accuracy figure exists on this shelf: the score performs as a strong discriminator where neuropathic pain is enriched and electrophysiologically confirmed, and as a sensitive but non-specific screen where it is not. No card implies DN4-guided treatment improves outcomes.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: TOR-BSST in acute stroke — FLOOR-RISK, one cohort (N = 311) reported twice plus a Cochrane summary: sensitivity 91.3% at derivation, and the water item needs all ten teaspoons
shelves.question: In acute stroke inpatients, how accurately does the Toronto Bedside Swallowing Screening Test (TOR-BSST — voice quality, tongue movement, pharyngeal sensation and a graded water swallow of ten teaspoons plus a sip, administered by trained screeners in under ten minutes) identify dysphagia against videofluoroscopy — what sensitivity and negative predictive value did its derivation study achieve in acute and rehabilitation settings, how much water does the water item actually require to reach that sensitivity, and where does the test sit in the Cochrane review of 37 bedside screening tests? (FLOOR-RISK base: 1 independent cohort, N = 311, reported twice, plus 1 Cochrane summary resting on that same study.)
shelves.mesh: Aged · Algorithms · Data Interpretation, Statistical · Deglutition/physiology · Deglutition Disorders/diagnosis,etiology,physiopathology · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Point-of-Care Systems · Predictive Value of Tests · Reproducibility of Results · Stroke/diagnosis,physiopathology · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: FLOOR-RISK — this shelf rests on exactly one independent primary cohort (N = 311, with the videofluoroscopic validity subset only ~20% of it) reported twice by its originators, plus a Cochrane summary whose TOR-BSST verdict itself rests on that same study; that exact basis prints here and on every card. No independent-centre revalidation was carried through verification, and no card presents the derivation sensitivity as externally validated performance. Screener training is part of the test as validated (trained nurses, under 10 minutes) and prints. This is a screening-accuracy shelf, not a treatment shelf. Cross-point: GUSS and Yale shelves card the same Cochrane-summary territory for different instruments — this shelf cards it for its TOR-BSST verdict only.

cards.headline: FLOOR-RISK primary report — TOR-BSST derivation and validation (Martino 2009, Stroke — 311 consecutively admitted stroke inpatients: 103 acute, 208 rehabilitation, across four facilities, screened by trained nurses): test-retest ICC was 0.92; against videofluoroscopy in the randomly allocated 20% subset, sensitivity was 91.3% (95% CI 71.9% to 98.7%) with negative predictive values of 93.3% in acute and 89.5% in rehabilitation settings
cards.summary: FLOOR-RISK primary report — TOR-BSST derivation and validation (Martino 2009, Stroke — 311 consecutively admitted stroke inpatients: 103 acute, 208 rehabilitation, across four facilities, screened by trained nurses): test-retest ICC was 0.92; against videofluoroscopy in the randomly allocated 20% subset, sensitivity was 91.3% (95% CI 71.9% to 98.7%) with negative predictive values of 93.3% in acute and 89.5% in rehabilitation settings
cards.type: Derivation and validation study (originators' report; the one independent cohort on this FLOOR-RISK shelf)
cards.people: 311 consecutively admitted stroke inpatients (103 acute, 208 rehabilitation) at 2 acute and 2 rehabilitation facilities; trained nurses administered the TOR-BSST in under 10 minutes; 20% were randomly allocated to videofluoroscopic assessment rated by 4 blinded experts; blinded repeat screenings within 24 hours in the first 50 administrations. Programme-labelled: the originators' own report. The single independent cohort on this FLOOR-RISK shelf.
cards.result: Screening was positive in 59.2% of acute and 38.5% of rehabilitation patients. Test-retest reliability ICC 0.92 (95% CI 0.85 to 0.96). The pharyngeal sensation item did not meet inclusion criteria and was eliminated, leaving voice quality, tongue movement and the graded water swallow. Validity: sensitivity 91.3% (71.9 to 98.7), negative predictive value 93.3% (acute) and 89.5% (rehabilitation) — against the pre-set bar of sensitivity ≥90% and NPV ≥90%, which the rehabilitation NPV did not reach.
cards.watchOut: FLOOR-RISK: this derivation sensitivity (91.3%, CI spanning 71.9–98.7%) rests on the ~20% videofluoroscopy subset of one originator cohort — never present it as externally validated performance.
cards.source: Martino R et al. The Toronto Bedside Swallowing Screening Test (TOR-BSST): development and validation of a dysphagia screening tool for patients with stroke. Stroke. 2009. PMID: 19074483. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: FLOOR-RISK same-cohort secondary analysis — NOT a second cohort (Martino 2014, TOR-BSST water item, same 311-patient cohort reported a second time): the water item alone identified dysphagia in 42.7% of acute and 29.0% of rehabilitation patients, and its sensitivity rose with volume — 79% (95% CI 70% to 86%) at five teaspoons, 92% (85% to 96%) at eight and 96% (90% to 99%) at the full ten teaspoons
cards.summary: FLOOR-RISK same-cohort secondary analysis — NOT a second cohort (Martino 2014, TOR-BSST water item, same 311-patient cohort reported a second time): the water item alone identified dysphagia in 42.7% of acute and 29.0% of rehabilitation patients, and its sensitivity rose with volume — 79% (95% CI 70% to 86%) at five teaspoons, 92% (85% to 96%) at eight and 96% (90% to 99%) at the full ten teaspoons
cards.type: Pre-specified secondary analysis of the same 311-patient cohort (double-reporting stated on the face)
cards.people: The same 311 eligible stroke inpatients as the derivation report (pre-specified secondary analysis of that cohort), administered by trained nurses from acute and rehabilitation facilities. This is the one independent cohort reported twice — counted as one cohort, never as two.
cards.result: Of the four TOR-BSST items, the water swallow contributed to identification of dysphagia in 42.7% (acute) and 29.0% (rehabilitation) of patients. Sensitivity of the water item rose with volume administered: 79% at five teaspoons, 92% at eight, 96% at the full ten teaspoons plus a sip (the standard). The authors conclude the water item alone does not identify all patients with dysphagia and that the full ten teaspoons are critical to its accuracy.
cards.watchOut: Journal note: the slate row named Dysphagia; the PubMed record fetched this session gives International journal of speech-language pathology — the record governs the source line. Shortening the water item to five teaspoons drops its sensitivity from 96% to 79% — volume is part of the test as validated.

cards.headline: FLOOR-RISK Cochrane summary (Kiekens 2022 — summary with commentary of the Cochrane review of bedside swallow screening in acute stroke: 25 studies, 3,953 participants, 37 tests): no single study achieved 100% sensitivity and specificity at low risk of bias, and the best-performing tools — the combined bedside aspiration test, GUSS and TOR-BSST — each rested on single studies with small samples
cards.summary: FLOOR-RISK Cochrane summary (Kiekens 2022 — summary with commentary of the Cochrane review of bedside swallow screening in acute stroke: 25 studies, 3,953 participants, 37 tests): no single study achieved 100% sensitivity and specificity at low risk of bias, and the best-performing tools — the combined bedside aspiration test, GUSS and TOR-BSST — each rested on single studies with small samples
cards.type: Cochrane Review summary with commentary (its TOR-BSST verdict rests on the same single study — not independent evidence)
cards.people: People with acute stroke in the Cochrane review by Boaden et al. (2021) as summarised with commentary: 25 studies, 3,953 participants, 37 screening tests for aspiration risk associated with dysphagia. This summary's TOR-BSST verdict itself rests on the same single derivation study carded above — it is not independent confirmation.
cards.result: No single study demonstrated 100% sensitivity and specificity with low risk of bias for all domains. The best-performing tools were the Bedside Aspiration test (combined water swallow and instrumental tool), the Gugging Swallowing Screen (GUSS) and the TOR-BSST (water only), but these were based on single studies with small sample sizes, and heterogeneity could not be explored. The summary authors conclude no single tool with high accuracy and good-quality evidence could be identified.
cards.watchOut: Journal note: the slate row named Dysphagia; the PubMed record fetched this session gives NeuroRehabilitation — the record governs the source line. FLOOR-RISK: counting this summary as a third independent source would triple-count one cohort.

shelves.title: Single-fibre EMG jitter reference values in healthy volunteers (PHYS, 3 small datasets, N = 57/32/19): suggested limits are muscle- and method-specific — 32/49 µs volitional orbicularis oculi, 26/34 µs stimulated tibialis anterior, 21/30 µs stimulated masseter
shelves.question: What are the reference values for single-fibre electromyography jitter (mean consecutive difference, MCD — the variability of neuromuscular transmission timing between muscle fibres of one motor unit) in healthy volunteers — what upper limits do the concentric-needle orbicularis oculi and frontalis datasets suggest, what mean jitter and suggested limits does stimulated single-fibre EMG give in the tibialis anterior, and what limits were derived for the stimulated masseter? (PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: every limit prints with its muscle and method; all datasets are small and their Ns print.)

shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — no intervention stamp applies. Reference limits are muscle- and method-specific by construction (volitional concentric-needle vs stimulated technique give different mean-consecutive-difference distributions) — no limit is printed without its muscle and method attached. All three datasets are small (N = 57, 32 and 19; total 108) and their Ns print on the face. Volitional concentric-needle jitter in orbicularis oculi (57 Sudanese volunteers) averaged 26.9 ± 3.3 µs with suggested upper limits of 32 µs (mean) and 49 µs (individual pairs), frontalis 31 / 49 µs. Stimulated single-fibre EMG in tibialis anterior (32 subjects) gave mean MCD 19.79 ± 2.72 µs with suggested limits of 26 / 34 µs. Stimulated masseter jitter (19 volunteers, 426 endplates) gave a pooled mean MCD of 16.0 µs with suggested limits of 21 µs (study mean) and 30 µs (individual fibre). The suggested limits are the authors' proposed cut-offs from single samples, not CLSI-derived intervals, and print as 'suggested'. Framing: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING.

cards.headline: Dataset 1 of 3 (Musa 2020, Scientific Reports — 57 healthy Sudanese volunteers, concentric-needle jitter with voluntary activation): mean jitter in orbicularis oculi was 26.9 ± 3.3 µs, with suggested upper limits of 32 µs for the mean and 49 µs for individual fibre pairs (frontalis 31 / 49 µs) — N = 57 prints on the face
cards.summary: Dataset 1 of 3 (Musa 2020, Scientific Reports — 57 healthy Sudanese volunteers, concentric-needle jitter with voluntary activation): mean jitter in orbicularis oculi was 26.9 ± 3.3 µs, with suggested upper limits of 32 µs for the mean and 49 µs for individual fibre pairs (frontalis 31 / 49 µs) — N = 57 prints on the face
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset — concentric-needle jitter, orbicularis oculi and frontalis, volitional (dataset 1 of 3; N = 57)
cards.people: 57 healthy volunteers (20 men, 37 women; mean age 43.6 ± 14.2 years, range 18–70) in Sudan, with voluntarily activated orbicularis oculi and frontalis both tested in the same individual using a concentric needle electrode; jitter expressed as the mean consecutive difference (MCD) of 30 potential pairs. Small dataset — its N prints on the face, per the row.
cards.result: For orbicularis oculi, mean jitter was 26.9 ± 3.3 µs (upper 95% confidence limit 31.97), mean individual fibre-pair jitter 26.1 ± 8.9 µs (upper limit 41.8) and mean outlier jitter 38.5 ± 5.7 µs (upper limit 49.0). For frontalis, the corresponding values were 27.1 ± 3.0 µs (31.32), 26.4 ± 9.4 µs (42.9) and 39.9 ± 5 µs (49.2). The suggested practical upper limits for mean jitter and outliers were 32 and 49 µs for orbicularis oculi, and 31 and 49 µs for frontalis.
cards.watchOut: Suggested limits from a single sample of 57 — the authors' proposed cut-offs, printed as 'suggested', not CLSI-derived intervals. Volitional concentric-needle technique: its limits do not transfer to stimulated technique or to other muscles.
cards.source: Musa AMM et al. Reference Jitter Values for Concentric Needle Electrode of Orbicularis Oculi and Frontalis Muscles Using Voluntary Activation Method in Sudanese Population. Scientific reports. 2020. PMID: 31974444. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.summary: Dataset 2 of 3 (Kouyoumdjian 2022, Frontiers in Neurology — 32 healthy subjects, stimulated single-fibre EMG of tibialis anterior with a concentric needle): mean MCD was 19.79 ± 2.72 µs, with suggested upper limits of 26 µs for the mean and 34 µs for individual pairs — N = 32 prints on the face
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset — stimulated concentric-needle jitter, tibialis anterior (dataset 2 of 3; N = 32)
cards.people: 32 healthy subjects with jitter measured in tibialis anterior by the intramuscular microaxonal stimulation technique using a disposable concentric needle. Small dataset — its N prints on the face. This record carries no MeSH in PubMed; its source line says so, and the shelf's top-level MeSH is taken from the other two datasets.
cards.result: The mean MCD and the mean MCD of the 27th value from the 32 subjects were normally distributed, at 19.79 ± 2.72 µs and 26.88 ± 3.56 µs respectively. The suggested limit for the mean MCD is ≥26 µs (i.e. values at or above are outside the suggested normal limit, as published) and for individual values >34 µs.
cards.watchOut: Stimulated technique in a limb muscle: neither its mean (19.79 µs) nor its limits (26 / 34 µs) may be set beside the volitional facial-muscle values as if one scale — muscle and method attach to every limit on this shelf.

cards.headline: Dataset 3 of 3 (Rousseff 2007, Muscle & Nerve — 19 healthy volunteers, stimulated jitter in masseter): pooled mean MCD was 16.0 µs (mean of individual study means 13.6 µs), with suggested upper limits of 21 µs for a study mean and 30 µs for an individual fibre — small N = 19 prints on the face
cards.summary: Dataset 3 of 3 (Rousseff 2007, Muscle & Nerve — 19 healthy volunteers, stimulated jitter in masseter): pooled mean MCD was 16.0 µs (mean of individual study means 13.6 µs), with suggested upper limits of 21 µs for a study mean and 30 µs for an individual fibre — small N = 19 prints on the face
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset — stimulated jitter, masseter (dataset 3 of 3; N = 19)
cards.people: 19 healthy volunteers (median age 25, range 18–51) with stimulated jitter measured in the masseter: axonal microstimulation via a monopolar needle electrode, recording with a single-fibre EMG electrode; 426 endplates studied. The smallest dataset on this shelf — N = 19 prints on the face and the dataset is never load-bearing alone for a general jitter claim.
cards.result: MCD values for the 426 endplates were skewed, with minimum 4.3 µs, maximum 44.7 µs and the distribution's maximum at 11 µs. Mean pooled MCD was 16.0 µs and the mean of mean MCD per study was 13.6 µs. The 95th upper percentile for an individual fibre was 29.3 µs. The authors suggest an upper normal limit for mean MCD per study of 21 µs and for individual fibres of 30 µs, and describe the stimulated masseter study as easy and reliable — their assessment, printed as such.
cards.watchOut: N = 19 volunteers (426 endplates — endplates are not volunteers, and the two denominators are never interchanged). Suggested limits from a single small sample, printed as 'suggested'.
cards.source: Rousseff RT et al. Stimulated jitter in the masseter muscle: normative values. Muscle & nerve. 2007. PMID: 16955469. Registry ID: none in the record.
